messages.content:
Read this:

Gurpreet had been stuck on the error for forty minutes, and the lab senior, Divyansh, was packing up to leave. Instead of saying “It's not working, help,” Gurpreet took a breath and walked over with the laptop. “I've got an error on line 40, the value comes back empty. I checked the file path, I printed the variable and I tried a smaller input. The variable is fine until the function call. Could you look at just that call for ten minutes?” Divyansh put the bag down and sat. Within five minutes they found a missing argument. “That's how to ask,” Divyansh said, smiling. “I could see where you'd already been.” Gurpreet felt lighter, and a little taller.

On which line was the error?
The error was on line 40, where the value came back empty.
What was Gurpreet feeling before walking over to Divyansh?
Gurpreet felt nervous but determined: a breath before asking, with the file path checked, the variable printed and a smaller input tried already.
What made Gurpreet's request easy for Divyansh to answer?
Gurpreet said what had been tried, where exactly the problem was and what help was needed: ten minutes on one function call.
How does Divyansh feel about the way Gurpreet asked?
Divyansh seems pleased and respected, putting the bag down and smiling, since Gurpreet's clear request showed where Gurpreet had already been.

Read this:

I'm Ira. The year my brother Sachin had his Class 10 boards, the whole house revolved around him. Quiet in the evenings. His favourite food every night. Papa sitting up with him until late.
Nobody asked about my science fair model. I felt invisible, and once I even broke a glass on purpose, just so someone would look at me.
Then one night I sat next to Papa. "It feels like you love Sachin more."
Papa put his arm around me. "He needs more help right now because of his exams. It's not more love."
"Can we do something together? Just us?"
We started walking to the market together every Sunday.

Which exams was Sachin taking?
His Class 10 boards.
Why did Ira break a glass on purpose?
Ira felt invisible and jealous, wanting someone in the family to notice.
What did Ira do that helped more than breaking things?
Ira told Papa honestly how it felt and asked for time together, which led to Sunday walks.
How might Papa see the extra attention Sachin gets?
Papa sees it as meeting Sachin's needs during exams, not as loving him more.
A sign in the shop says no article of clothing can be returned after a week. Why is it called an article? Is it a newspaper piece?

Article also means a single item or thing, often one of a group such as clothing. It is a noun here. The newspaper meaning is the one you know.
Example: She packed every article of clothing neatly so the suitcase would close.

Read this:

When the ordering system in the Lisbon office went dark at ten past two, the chat filled with people typing at once. Beatriz wrote, 'I'll be incident commander. Olga, you investigate. Mateus, you talk to customers and management.' Then she asked everyone else to stay quiet in the main thread unless called on. Olga opened the logs and posted findings every ten minutes. Mateus sent a short note to the support desk and another to the director, and promised the next one at three. Beatriz kept a running list of what had been tried. Nobody dug through the same log twice, and nobody talked over anyone. At ten to four the fix went in and the system came back. Beatriz thanked each role by name and set a review for the next morning.

Who did Beatriz tell to investigate?
Beatriz told Olga, 'you investigate'.
What did Beatriz want when she asked everyone else to stay quiet in the main thread?
Beatriz wanted calm and focus, so that the investigator and the person sending updates could work without being talked over.
What could the team add if an outage ran for many hours?
The team could rotate the roles after some hours so people stay rested, using the running list to hand over.
How might the director have felt about Mateus's updates?
The director would probably feel informed and calmer, since the notes came when promised.
Now you try: which width do you copy in step 3 - the arc radius, or the distance between the two cutting points?
The answer is the distance between the two cutting points.

Read this:

I've worked at the bank branch for three years, next to Ritu at the counters.
Ritu isn't the fastest cashier. That's Vikram, who can count notes like a machine and loves to show it. But Vikram takes sudden days off, and some weeks he's sharp and some weeks he's somewhere else.
Ritu comes at 9:15 every day. Her cash tallies at closing every day. When the manager asks her for the monthly report, it's on his desk the day before it's due. She never announces it.
I noticed who customers asked for. The old uncles waited in Ritu's line even when Vikram's was empty. When the manager went on leave, he left the keys with Ritu, not the senior cashier.
I asked Ritu once if it bothered her that Vikram got the compliments. She shrugged. "Compliments are nice. Keys are better."
I've started coming at 9:15 too.
— Sarita

What time does Ritu come to work every day?
Ritu comes at 9:15 every day.
How does Sarita seem to feel about Ritu by the end?
Sarita seems to admire and trust Ritu, enough to start copying the 9:15 arrival.
What small habit shows how Sarita is learning from Ritu?
Sarita has started coming at 9:15 too, choosing steady reliability over flashy speed.
How might Vikram feel when the keys went to Ritu?
Vikram might feel surprised and a bit put out, since his speed got compliments but not the manager's trust.

metadata.subtype: Colleague who is reliable rather than brilliant [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Diary, Saturday night

Two months in the hostel in Pune. I, Irfan, am doing well. I cook my own instant noodles, I do my own laundry, I even fixed the fan in our room. My roommate Abhinav calls me "the engineer".
Today I felt proud all day. Then at dinner, the mess served dal that tasted nothing like Ammi's. Suddenly I missed everything: her voice calling me for chai, my sister's teasing, the smell of our old house.
I cried a bit in the bathroom. Felt stupid.
Abhinav noticed my eyes. He said, "I miss my mum's food too, yaar. Every day."
It helped. Maybe missing home isn't weakness. Maybe it just means I still belong there.

What did Irfan fix in the room?
Irfan fixed the fan.
How did Irfan feel at dinner when the dal tasted wrong?
Irfan felt a sudden homesick ache for Ammi's voice and food, after feeling proud all day.
What helped Irfan feel less stupid about crying?
Abhinav sharing that he misses his mum's food every day too.
How does Abhinav seem to feel about being away from home?
Abhinav seems homesick too, missing his mother's food daily.

Read this:

After the summer holidays, Parul came back to Class 5 with a new pencil box and a story about the mountains. But on Monday, Rafiq and the others at her table turned their heads away when she spoke. On Tuesday they passed a note right over her desk, as if she were air. Nobody said why. Nobody teased her; that might have been easier. Parul went over the last week of the holidays again and again. Had she forgotten a birthday? Said something wrong in the group call? At lunch she ate her paratha very slowly. That evening Mummy found her on the stairs, still in uniform. "They're not angry," Parul whispered. "They're just not seeing me." Mummy sat down beside her and listened until it was all out.

What did Parul bring back after the summer holidays?
A new pencil box and a story about the mountains.
How did Parul feel when her friends passed the note over her desk?
She felt invisible, anxious and confused, replaying the holidays to work out what she might have done.
What could Mummy and Parul do next?
They could talk it through calmly and, if it goes on, tell the class teacher, who can gently find out what has gone wrong without blaming Parul.
What would change if Rafiq told Parul what was wrong?
Parul could understand and perhaps fix it, instead of being stuck in a silent confusion that hurts more than teasing.

Read this:

It was 11 p.m. and the client deadline was at nine the next morning. Salma was checking the last slides when Anjali, her junior of four months, rolled her chair over again.
"Salma di, should the chart be blue or green? You'll know what's best."
It was the sixth time that evening. Anjali had started dressing like her, using her phrases in meetings, saying "Salma di says" before every opinion. Part of Salma liked it. Part of her felt a prickle of discomfort.
She pushed the laptop back. "Anju, I once lost a client because I chose a chart colour nobody could read on their projector. So don't trust me blindly. What do you think works, and why?"
Anjali hesitated. "Green. The logo's green."
"Good reason. Do it."
At midnight, packing up, Salma sent her a message: "Lead the chart review tomorrow. Your call on it. 🙂"

What time was the client deadline?
At nine the next morning.
How did Salma feel about Anjali copying her, and how can you tell?
Salma felt flattered but uncomfortable; part of her liked it and part of her felt a prickle of discomfort.
How did Salma encourage Anjali to think for herself?
She shared a past mistake, asked Anjali for her own reasoning, and then asked her to lead the chart review the next day.
What might Anjali be feeling when she hesitates before saying "Green"?
Anjali may feel nervous and unsure, used to deferring to Salma, and then encouraged when her own reason is accepted.

Read this:

You want the secret, Yamini? It's not a secret. It's a sentence.

I'm Kiran. Last year I was sleeping at one, two, sometimes later. I'd tell myself I'd stop scrolling "soon", and soon never came. My mum finally said, "You need a rule, not a wish."

So I made one: if the clock says ten, then the phone goes on the shelf in the hallway. Not in my room. Not under my pillow. The hallway.

Then after that, the same small things every night. Hot water on my face. Change into old pyjamas. Read one chapter of whatever novel. Lights off.

For the first few nights my brain was annoyed. It kept thinking of messages I might be missing. But after about ten days, just splashing my face made me yawn. My body had learned the order.

Now I'm usually asleep by eleven. That's all it took: one if and one then.

Where does Kiran's phone go at ten?
On the shelf in the hallway.
How did Kiran feel during the first few nights of the rule?
Kiran felt annoyed and restless, worried about missing messages.
What else could Kiran add if the routine stops working during exams?
Kiran could add a short notepad step to write down worries before bed, so an anxious mind has somewhere to put them.
How might Kiran's mum see the change?
Kiran's mum likely feels relieved and a bit proud, since her advice about a rule instead of a wish actually worked.

metadata.subtype: Approach: wind-down routine with if-then rules [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Friday night

Didn't sign up for the inter-school fest in Mumbai. Zeenat is going. Everyone is going. I told Ma I had a stomach ache.

The truth: I can't stop watching those videos. Trains packed with people hanging out the doors. A car flipping on the expressway. A bus in the rain. My feed is full of them, maybe twenty a day. Every time I open my phone there's another one.

So in my head, travelling to Mumbai = accident.

Zeenat laughed at me. She said, "Kamal, my Chacha has taken that train every day for eleven years. Nothing happened." I said he was lucky.

But now writing this I'm thinking. Twenty videos a day. From the whole country. Maybe from the whole world. And my feed keeps showing them because I keep watching them.

Maybe the trains aren't more dangerous. Maybe my phone just is.

How many accident videos a day does Kamal say the feed shows?
Maybe twenty a day.
Why does Kamal feel that travelling to Mumbai means an accident?
Kamal feels anxious because the feed keeps showing crash videos, so the danger seems everywhere even though the clips come from the whole country.
What could Kamal try to get a truer picture of the risk?
Kamal could stop watching the clips for a while and ask an adult or look up how many people travel that route safely every day.
How might Zeenat see Kamal's decision to skip the fest?
Zeenat probably finds it surprising and a bit sad, since her Chacha has taken that train for eleven years without trouble.

What are these lines in plain modern prose?

Thus in fair words with virtue fraught
The pious glorious saint besought.
But the good speech with poignant sting
Pierced ear and bosom of the king,
Who, stabbed with pangs too sharp to bear,
Fell prostrate and lay fainting there.

That was how the pious and glorious saint pleaded, in fair words full of goodness. But the good speech stung painfully and pierced the ear and heart of the king. Stabbed by pain too sharp to bear, he fell flat on the ground and lay there fainting.

Read this:

Tariq won the spelling bee at his primary school in Manchester. His name went up on the board in gold letters. He grinned all the way through lunch.
By afternoon, though, Mina and her friends were whispering, "Tariq the genius. Tariq the show-off." When he got 20 out of 20 in the spelling test on Friday, someone groaned loudly, "Of course he did."
The next week Tariq made two mistakes on purpose. When his teacher asked why, he shrugged.
At home, his mum asked about the trophy. "Can we not put it on the shelf?" he said. "I don't want anyone to see it."
He went up to his room and closed the door.

What did Tariq win at his school?
Tariq won the spelling bee.
Why did Tariq make two mistakes on purpose?
He felt hurt and embarrassed by being called a show-off, and wanted to seem ordinary so the others would stop teasing.
How could Tariq's teacher support him?
The teacher could talk to Tariq privately about the teasing and help the class learn to celebrate each other instead of mocking.
How might Mina see the change in Tariq?
Mina might not notice at all, or might feel pleased he seems less of a show-off, without realising he is hiding his ability.
Our colony's water tank is cleaned only once a year and some neighbours want it done more often.
That's a reasonable thing to raise. Do you know who looks after it?
The secretary. He says it costs a lot.

You could ask him politely how the cost is shared and whether the neighbours can discuss a schedule together. Something like every six months might be an easy middle point. Raise it at the next meeting, calmly, with the others who agree.
Should I put it in writing?
A short written note is useful, because it can be added to the meeting list. Keep it polite and simple, and mention the reason, which is clean water for everyone.
Orange squash is mixed with water in the ratio 1 : 4. How much squash and how much water are needed to make 1.5 L of drink?

Answer: 300 mL of squash and 1.2 L (1,200 mL) of water.

The drink is 1 + 4 = 5 parts. Change 1.5 L to 1500 mL to avoid decimals. One part = 1500 / 5 = 300 mL. Squash: 1 part = 300 mL. Water: 4 parts = 1200 mL = 1.2 L. Check: 300 + 1200 = 1500 mL. Note that the squash is 1/5 of the drink, not 1/4: the ratio 1 : 4 is squash to water, not squash to drink.

Read this:

"Mahima, when I was your age, I saw an ad in a comic: 'Magic cream, become fair in seven days!' I saved my pocket money for weeks and bought it. Nothing happened, of course. My mother laughed, but I cried. Now I'm a librarian, and do you know what I tell children? Before you believe anything, ask: who made this? Are they selling something? Is there another place that says the same? When you search online, look for the tiny word 'Ad' or 'Sponsored' at the top." Sarita Maasi tapped the screen. "Now, what does this first result want from you?"

What did the ad in the comic promise?
It promised a magic cream to become fair in seven days.
What might Sarita have felt when the cream did nothing?
She likely felt disappointed and foolish, since she cried after saving for weeks.
What questions does Sarita teach Mahima to ask?
Who made this, are they selling something, and does another place say the same?
How might Mahima see online ads after this story?
Mahima may be more careful and look for "Ad" or "Sponsored" before believing a claim.

metadata.subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness

messages.content:
Read this:

Saturday. For her fifth birthday, Neelam masi took Binita to the huge toy shop in the mall. Aisles and aisles. Binita walked up and down, touching everything, then stood in the middle and burst into tears. Masi carried her out with nothing.
Wednesday. Binita kept asking about the shop, but hid behind Masi's leg when she said they could go back.
The next Sunday. Masi put three toys on the bed at home: a skipping rope, a doll and a puzzle. "One is yours." Binita looked for a minute, chose the puzzle, and hugged it all evening.

Which three toys did Masi put on the bed?
A skipping rope, a doll and a puzzle.
Why did Binita burst into tears in the huge toy shop?
Binita felt overwhelmed by aisles and aisles of toys, so choosing just one felt impossible.
What did Masi do differently the next Sunday, and why did it work?
She offered only three toys at home, a small choice that Binita could manage and feel happy with.
How might Neelam masi have felt carrying Binita out with nothing?
Masi probably felt disappointed and puzzled, having planned a happy birthday trip, which led her to try a smaller choice.

Read this:

Shankar moved into the engineering hostel in October, two months late, because of a delay with his scholarship papers. By then the groups were already made.

He noticed Akash's group first: five of them, always at the corner table in the mess, always walking to class in a line, always in Akash's room at night with music playing.

Then the water supply failed for three days during midterms, and everyone had to queue at the one tap near the gate. Standing behind them, Shankar heard one of the five, Faizan, mention that he'd been invited to a study group with the second-years.

"You're going?" Akash asked lightly.

Faizan glanced at the others. "Nah. Just saying."

Shankar watched Faizan's face fall a little as he said it. Nobody had told him not to go. Nobody needed to.

Why did Shankar move into the hostel two months late?
Because of a delay with his scholarship papers.
What does Shankar seem to feel watching the group from the tap queue?
He seems curious and a bit lonely as the latecomer, and uneasy when he notices Faizan's face fall.
How could Faizan's friends make room for him to try other groups?
One of them could say, "Go, tell us how it is," so going to the study group would not feel like leaving them.
What is it like for Faizan when Akash asks "You're going?" lightly?
He feels a quiet pressure and disappointment, sensing that going would look disloyal even though no one forbade it.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Zeenat, you asked how I got so fussy about facts. Sit, I'll tell you.
I was twenty-five, a junior at a small city paper, writing a Sunday piece on the old clock tower. Everybody in the city knew it was built by the British in 1890. My editor said it. The tour guides said it. It was even painted on a sign near the market.
I had the line typed. Then, late at night, something nagged me. I asked myself, "Have I actually seen this anywhere official, or have I just heard it a hundred times?"
Next morning I went to the municipal records room. Dusty ledgers, one fan. The tower was paid for by three local cloth merchants, and finished in 1921.
I went to my editor feeling foolish, admitting I'd nearly printed a thing only because it sounded familiar. He printed the ledger photo.
I'm Raghav, and that sign is still wrong, by the way.

Where did Raghav go to check the clock tower's history?
To the municipal records room.
What was Raghav feeling when something nagged him late at night?
Raghav felt uneasy and doubtful, sensing that hearing the claim a hundred times was not the same as having checked it.
What choice was the turning point in Raghav's story, and why did it matter?
Going to the municipal records room was the turning point, because one primary source showed the familiar story was wrong before it was printed.
How might the editor have seen the young Raghav after the ledger?
The editor seems to have respected Raghav's care, since he printed the ledger photo instead of the familiar version.

A new book sold 15 copies at the bookstore on Wednesday. On Thursday the book sold three times that many copies. On Friday the book sold one-fifth the number of copies it did on Thursday. How many copies of the book did the bookstore sell by Friday?

On Thursday 15*3=45 books were sold.
On Friday 45/5=9 books were sold
Adding up all three days 15+45+9=69 books were sold by Friday
The answer is 69.

Read this:

When I started writing stories at twenty-five, I already knew good writing. I'd read hundreds of books. That was the problem: every sentence I wrote sounded like a school essay next to them, and I wanted to delete everything.
Joseph, who runs our Thursday writing circle, told me not to. "Put it all in a folder called Bad Drafts, Divyansh. Don't open it for a year."
It felt silly, but I did it. I kept writing one story a month and kept dropping the early versions into that folder.
Last week, a year and a bit later, I opened it. Story one had nine adjectives in the first line. I read it out to myself and laughed. Then I read my latest. It isn't great, but it breathes.
I couldn't feel that change while it was happening. The folder could. I'm keeping it.

What was the folder called?
Bad Drafts.
How did Divyansh feel about writing at the start?
Divyansh felt embarrassed and discouraged, since every sentence sounded like a school essay next to the books already read.
Which choice helped Divyansh get past the awkward stage?
Keeping every early draft in a folder instead of deleting it, then comparing a year later, which showed real progress.
What might Joseph have known that Divyansh didn't at the start?
Joseph probably knew from experience that beginners can't see their own progress, so a saved record would reassure Divyansh later.

metadata.subtype: Stage 2: The gap between taste and ability [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

At sixteen, Ankita had a chemistry project due in two weeks. She lit her desk lamp each evening, looked at the blank page, and then decided to tidy her drawers instead. If she tried and the model looked poor, her teacher Pranav might see she was not as capable as her marks suggested. Keeping the page blank felt safer. She handed in a hurried project and told nobody how worried she had been.

At twenty-five, at her desk before a client proposal, Ankita felt the same dread creeping back. This time she said to herself, "Just five minutes." Yesterday evening she had laid out her notes and opened the document to the first heading, so it was waiting. She wrote a clumsy paragraph and kept going. When she thought of all the delays in the past, she added, "That was me being scared. It's okay. I'm here now."

Her colleague Tushar looked at her steady typing and asked, "You seem calm today." Ankita smiled. "Small start, kind voice."

How long did Ankita commit to when she began the client proposal?
Ankita committed to just five minutes.
What changed in how Ankita handles a task she is afraid of between sixteen and twenty-five?

At sixteen she avoids starting to protect her self-image, and the project suffers; at twenty-five she lays out her notes the night before, commits to five minutes and forgives her past delays, which breaks the dread.
What was Ankita feeling as she tidied her drawers at sixteen?
Ankita was afraid that a poor model would show she was not as capable as her marks suggested.
Why does forgiving past delays help Ankita begin?
Speaking kindly to herself takes away the shame of earlier delays, making it easier to face the next task instead of avoiding it.
Each wall of a 3 sided shower has 8 tiles running the width of the wall and 20 tiles running the height of the wall.  How many tiles are in the shower?

There are 8 tiles along the width and 20 tiles along the height for a total of 8*20 = 160 tiles
Each wall has 160 tiles and there are 3 walls so there are 160*3 = 480 tiles in the shower
The answer is 480.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Class 11
Suraj, a scholarship student, came in today. He topped the physics test. He said that since then, classmates keep saying, "Wow, you're surprisingly smart," and one boy, Uday, said, "You're so sharp for someone from your area."
Suraj said, "They think it's praise. But why 'surprisingly'?"
He said it's never one big insult. It's the small sentences, every few days. He's started sitting at the back so nobody notices his marks.
I told him his feelings made sense. With his permission, I'll speak to the class teacher about a session on how compliments can carry assumptions. I'll also check in with him next week.

Which test did Suraj top?
He topped the physics test.
Why has Suraj started sitting at the back?
He feels singled out and uncomfortable, tired of hearing that his success is surprising.
How could the counsellor's plan help?
A class session could help students see how such compliments carry assumptions, and the check-in shows Suraj he is supported.
How might Uday see his own comment?
Uday probably thought it was a compliment, not realising it suggested Suraj's area makes him less likely to be smart.

Read this:

Monday, 9:15 pm
Today was a mess. I pressed snooze till 6:50, ran for the bus and skipped breakfast again. By third period my head felt stuffed with cotton. I read the same history paragraph four times and couldn't remember a word. When Anjali asked to borrow my eraser, I snapped at her for no reason. She looked hurt.
At break she held out half her poha. "You're always grumpy before lunch," she said. "You're just hungry." I ate it, a bit embarrassed. Twenty minutes later my brain came back online.
So here's the plan, written down so I stick to it: bread and a banana on the counter the night before, and an alarm with no snooze. Not a big deal, just something.
Also: say sorry to Anjali.
Ganga

What did Anjali share at break?
Anjali held out half her poha.
How did Ganga feel after snapping at Anjali?
Ganga felt embarrassed and a little guilty, and planned to say sorry.
What simple plan did Ganga make?
Bread and a banana on the counter the night before, and an alarm with no snooze.
What might Anjali have felt when Ganga snapped?
Anjali looked hurt, but still cared enough to share her poha and point out the hunger.

metadata.subtype: Skipping breakfast and crashing by noon [Actor]

messages.content:
Please write this as flowing modern prose, not verse.

While there the high-souled hero spent
His tranquil hours in sweet content,
The glowing autumn passed, and then
Came winter so beloved of men.
While the noble hero spent his quiet hours there in sweet content, the glowing autumn passed, and then came winter, which people love so much.

Read this:

"Mumma, can I have another toffee?"
"You had one after lunch, Nandini. That's it for today."
"Just one small one!"
"No, sweetheart. The jar is closed now."
Nandini's chin wobbled. Her feet began to stamp on the floor, harder and harder.
"No! No! It's not fair!"
"I know you really wanted it."
"I hate you! I hate you, Mumma!"
Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge and knelt down. "You're very cross."
"Go away!" Nandini shouted, stamping again, her cheeks wet and hot.

Where did Sunaina put the jar?
Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge.
Why did Nandini shout "I hate you" at her mother?
She wanted the toffee badly and the no felt unfair; the anger hit her body first, so her feet stamped and the hurtful words burst out before calmer ones could.
What turning point is open to Sunaina in this moment?
She can keep the jar closed, stay close and name the anger calmly, which shows Nandini that the feeling is allowed but shouting will not change the answer.
How might Sunaina feel hearing "Go away!" right after she knelt down?
She may feel pushed away and a little hurt, yet understand that Nandini is overwhelmed, so she might wait nearby rather than leave.
A car uses 20 gallons of gas to travel 400 miles. Mr. Montero's car has 8 gallons in it. How many more gallons of gas does he need to travel 600 miles, back and forth?

Mr. Montero is traveling a total distance of 600 miles + 600 miles = 1200 miles.
There are 1200 miles / 400 miles = 3 sets of 400 miles in 1200 miles.
So Mr. Montero needs 20 gallons/set x 3 sets = 60 gallons in all.
Since his car has 8 gallons already, then he needs to add 60 gallons - 8 gallons = 52 gallons more.
The answer is 52.

Why do some things cost more than others? Can you fix the grammar in "He asked how much does it cost."? A bag holds 6 apples. How many apples are in 9 bags? How can I avoid losing things in a big, busy market?

1. They take more work or material. Because making them needs more time, skill or better tools.
2. Fixed: He asked how much it costs. Why: In an indirect question, use normal order and "costs".
3. 54 apples. Because 6 x 9 = 54.
4. Keep your bag closed and in front, and stay close to your family. Agree on a meeting place in case you get separated.

Read this:

I'm Sudha, and I was nine when Chithi said it at the family lunch. "Why are you not more like Leela? She is first in class and she sits so nicely." Leela is my cousin, and she was sitting right there.
Everyone kept eating. I looked at my rice. My ears went hot, and it felt like something heavy in my chest. I did not say a word. That night I told my doll, "I'm not good like Leela."
Even now I remember the sentence better than the lunch. Leela told me later that she hated being compared too. That helped a little.

How old was Sudha when Chithi made the remark at lunch?
Sudha was nine.
What was Sudha feeling when Chithi compared Sudha with Leela?
Sudha felt hurt and inadequate. The hot ears, the heavy chest and telling the doll "I'm not good like Leela" show it.
What could a grown-up at the lunch have done to help Sudha?
A grown-up could have said something kind and specific about Sudha, or gently changed the subject. That would show that Sudha does not have to be like Leela.
What might it have been like for Leela to sit there while the comparison was made?
Leela probably felt uncomfortable and awkward, and later said that being compared hurt too. Being praised at Sudha's cost is not easy either.

Read this:

In the government school at Kudur village, Sangeeta arrived on Monday with a new school bag: bright blue, with a zip pocket and a picture of a kite. Lakshmi's own bag was her brother's old cloth one, the strap tied in a knot.
All morning Lakshmi kept glancing at the blue bag. At lunch under the neem tree, she told the other girls loudly, "Sangeeta is only showing off. She's jealous of everyone, that's why she wants us all to look."
Sangeeta, who had only put her bag on the bench, looked down at her rice.
Walking home along the canal, Lakshmi kicked a stone the whole way and didn't say why.

What picture was on Sangeeta's new bag?
A picture of a kite.
Why does Lakshmi call Sangeeta jealous?
Lakshmi longs for a bag like that, but calling Sangeeta the jealous one lets her avoid seeing the envy in herself.
What could Lakshmi try the next time she wants what someone else has?
Noticing the pang and saying it honestly, even just to herself or a friend, like 'I wish I had a bag like that', instead of blaming Sangeeta.

Wednesday
Day three of the school relief drive. Sachin wanted to take the bus to the flooded villages himself with a bag of biscuits. I almost went with him. Then Mrs Kulkarni said the roads there are still unsafe and the district team decides where things go, so we can do more good here.
So here's what I did today, 2 to 6 pm, in the school hall with Mrs Kulkarni watching over us: sorted three cartons of clothes by size, checked every food packet for its expiry date, and typed up the list of what came in, so the district team knows exactly what's on the truck. 146 items today.
Boring? A bit. But at 5:30 the truck left with everything labelled, and the driver said the camp can hand things out in minutes because of the lists.
Sachin did the lists with me in the end. He said it felt less heroic, but more useful.
– Vinita

How many items went on today's list?
146 items today.
How did Vinita feel about the day's work?
Vinita found it a bit boring, but satisfied and proud when the driver said the lists would help the camp.
Why is working through the school drive better than travelling alone to the villages?
The roads are unsafe and the district team knows where help is needed, so organised sorting reaches people faster and more safely.
How does Sachin feel about ending up on the lists?
Sachin felt it was less heroic than he'd hoped, but more useful.

An auto-rickshaw charges ₹50 plus ₹12 per km. Meena has at most ₹200. What is the greatest whole number of km she can travel?

Answer: 50 + 12k <= 200 gives k <= 12.5, so at most 12 km.

Let k be the number of km. "At most ₹200" means the cost is less than or equal to 200: 50 + 12k <= 200 12k <= 150 k <= 12.5 k must be a whole number (the meter counts whole km), so the greatest value is 12. Check: 50 + 12 x 12 = ₹194 <= ₹200, and 13 km would cost 50 + 156 = ₹206, too much. Do not round 12.5 UP to 13: that breaks the inequality.

Kunal, you say the cricketers on TV skipped studies and did fine, so you can too? Let your Wasim uncle tell you about my own sixteenth year. Our town had one boy, Irshad, who had played for the state team. Everyone talked about him. He had left school after Class 9. So I decided the same path would work for me. I skipped exams to practise at the maidan every day. What I didn't see were the thirty other boys at that maidan who had made the same choice over the years. They weren't on TV. They were driving autos, working in shops, some still bitter. I only found out when our coach, old Hameed sir, sat me down and named them one by one. That evening I went to my teacher and asked for the missed papers.

After which class did Irshad leave school?
After Class 9.
Why did young Wasim believe skipping exams would work?
He felt hopeful and inspired by Irshad, the only one everyone talked about, and never saw the boys for whom it didn't work.
What turning point changed Wasim's path?
Hameed sir naming the thirty other boys one by one, after which Wasim asked his teacher for the missed papers.
Why might Hameed sir have named the boys one by one?
He probably cared about Wasim and knew that real, familiar faces would make the missing failures impossible to ignore.

He strayed down a walk edged with box, with apple trees, pear trees, and cherry trees on one side, and a border on the other full of all sorts of old-fashioned flowers, stocks, sweet-williams, primroses, pansies, mingled with southernwood, sweet-briar, and various fragrant herbs. They were fresh now as a succession of April showers and gleams, followed by a lovely spring morning, could make them: the sun was just entering the dappled east, and his light illumined the wreathed and dewy orchard trees and shone down the quiet walks under them.

Question: What grows in the walk the person strays down?

Apple, pear and cherry trees grow on one side. A border on the other side is full of old-fashioned flowers such as stocks, sweet-williams, primroses and pansies, mixed with southernwood, sweet-briar and fragrant herbs.

Every morning, Carla puts 79 apples in her backpack to eat for lunch. Unfortunately, Buffy stole some of Carla's apples on the school bus, and 26 apples fell out of a hole on the bottom. So at lunchtime, Carla only had 8 apples remaining. How many apples did Buffy steal from Carla?

Let B be the number of apples that Buffy stole. Then 79 - B - 26 = 8.
Combining constants produces 53 - B = 8.
Adding B to both sides produces 52 = B + 8
Thus the number of apples stolen by Buffy is B = 53 - 8 = 45.
The answer is 45.

A church has 100 members who've volunteered to bake cookies for the homeless in their local town. If each member baked 10 sheets of cookies, and each sheet has 16 cookies, calculate the total number of cookies the church members baked?

A sheet has 16 cookies, so if each church member baked 10 sheets, they each baked 10 sheets/person * 16 cookies/sheet = 160 cookies/person
The total number of church members who decided to volunteer is 100, so in total, they baked 160 cookies/person * 100 people = 16000 cookies
The answer is 16000.

There are 20 cars lined up at a race. Each of the cars have 2 passengers and a driver, then when the cars go past the race's halfway point, each car gains another passenger. The cars then continue racing, and the race finishes once every single car has passed the finish line. People who get into the cars have to stay inside of them until the race is finished. How many people are in the cars by the end of the race?

There are 2 passengers and a driver in each car, which means that in each car there are 2 passengers + 1 driver = 3 people.
This means there are a total of 20 cars * 3 people per car = 60 people in the car at the start of the race.
At the halfway point, there is an additional 20 cars * 1 additional passenger = 20 more people.
So be the end of the race, there are 60 people at the start of the race + 20 additional people = 80 people in the cars.
The answer is 80.
Find the smallest number by which 1,008 must be MULTIPLIED to give a perfect square, and the smallest number by which it must be DIVIDED. Find the square roots obtained.

Answer: 1,008 = 2^4 x 3^2 x 7. Multiply by 7: 7,056 = 84^2. Divide by 7: 144 = 12^2.

Factorise: 1,008 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 7. Pair up: (2 x 2)(2 x 2)(3 x 3) and 7 is left alone. To MULTIPLY to a square, give 7 a partner: 1,008 x 7 = 7,056 = (2^2 x 3 x 7)^2, so sqrt7,056 = 4 x 3 x 7 = 84. To DIVIDE to a square, remove the lonely 7: 1,008 / 7 = 144 = 12^2. If several primes are unpaired, multiply (or divide) by ALL of them: 2,352 = 2^4 x 3 x 7^2, so the smallest multiplier is 3 (giving 7,056 = 84^2).

Counsellor's note, 14 August. Seema Varghese, school counsellor.
Jomon (Class 10) came to see me in July, worried about maths. He said, "I always mean to study after dinner, but I pick up my phone first and then it's eleven." We talked about planning a trigger instead of relying on willpower. He wrote his own rule on a card: "If I've finished dinner, then the maths book comes out before I touch my phone." He stuck it on his cupboard. Today he showed me his tracker: on twenty-three of the last thirty evenings, he opened the book first. He said the hardest part is the first two minutes, and after that he usually keeps going. His last unit test went from 18 to 29 out of 40. What I did next: I asked if he'd like to add a second rule for Sunday mornings. He's thinking about it.

What rule did Jomon write on the card?
"If I've finished dinner, then the maths book comes out before I touch my phone."
What does Jomon find hardest, and what does that suggest?
The first two minutes are hardest, which suggests Jomon feels reluctant at the start, but once the cue gets him going, carrying on feels much easier.
Why might this if-then rule work better than 'I always mean to study after dinner'?
It ties a clear action to a clear cue, so after dinner he doesn't have to decide; he just follows the rule.
How might Seema see Jomon's twenty-three evenings?
Seema likely sees real progress built on his own rule, which is why Seema offers a second one rather than taking over.

In art class at the Chennai school, Karthik rolled his clay ball into a long snake. Pankaj pointed. "Now you have way more clay than me!" Karthik looked at his snake, then at Pankaj's round ball. "No, I don't. I didn't add anything. I just made it long." "But it's longer." "Watch." Karthik rolled the snake back into a ball, the same size as Pankaj's. "Same." Pankaj squinted. "Then do it again." Karthik laughed and rolled it out. "It's still the same, whatever shape."

What did Karthik roll his clay ball into?
A long snake.
How did Pankaj feel when he saw the snake?
He felt surprised and a bit envious, believing Karthik had more clay.
How did Karthik show the amount of clay was the same?
He rolled the snake back into a ball the same size as Pankaj's.
What would change if Karthik had only argued without rolling it back?
Pankaj might stay unconvinced, since seeing the ball return to its size made the point clear.

Kindergarten note, Thursday. At block play, Ira (5) pulled a truck from Tashi, then shouted, "Tashi is mean! Tashi is angry at me!" Tashi just sat there, surprised. Ira's own face was red, her hands clenched on the truck. I knelt and said, "I see a very angry face. Whose anger is it?" "Tashi's!" I didn't argue. "When I grab things, my tummy feels hot and angry. Is yours hot?" A tiny nod. We took three slow breaths, and she gave the truck back. I'll tell her mother at pickup today. — Pema

What did Ira pull away from Tashi?
A truck.
Why did Ira shout that Tashi was angry when Tashi just sat there?
Ira was the angry one after grabbing the truck, and admitting it felt too bad, so she saw the anger in Tashi instead.
Which of Pema's steps helped Ira own the feeling?
Not arguing, describing Pema's own hot, angry tummy, asking Ira gently, then breathing together.
How might Tashi have felt being shouted at across the room?
Tashi looked surprised and was probably confused and a little upset, having done nothing wrong.

The American swallow can lift into the air and carry a maximum of 5 pounds of weight, while the European swallow can lift and carry twice the weight as the American swallow.  If there was a flock of 90 swallows, containing twice as many American as European swallows, what is the maximum combined weight the flock can carry?

If "x" is the number of European swallows, then, for every one European swallow, there would be 2x American swallows.
Thus, the total number of swallows would be 2x+x=90 swallows
Thus, the number of European swallows x=30.
And the number of American swallows is 90-30=60.
A European swallow can carry twice what an American swallow can carry, or 2*5=10 pounds.
30 European swallows can carry a maximum of 30*10=300 pounds.
60 American swallows can carry a maximum of 60*5=300 pounds.
Thus, a flock of 90 birds, with 30 European and 60 American swallows, can carry 300+300=600 pounds
The answer is 600.

Back in the colony after the weekend at the lake, Pema stretched her arms as wide as they could go. "The fish was THIS big!"

Kashish laughed. "That's bigger than you!"

"Almost," Pema said. She let her arms come in a tiny bit. "Papa caught it. And we caught more." She held up three fingers, then looked at them, frowned and folded one down. "Two. One jumped back in."

"Was the first one really that big?"

Pema grinned and spread her arms wide again. "Bigger!"

How many fingers did Pema hold up at first?
Three fingers.
What was Pema feeling when she spread her arms wide again and said "Bigger!"?
She was most likely excited and proud about the fishing trip, and her wide arms showed that excitement more than the fish's real size. She may also have enjoyed teasing Kashish a little.
How could an adult respond to Pema's big fish gesture?
They could enjoy the excitement with her, and maybe ask something playful, like whether it was bigger than the table, without insisting on exact size.
How does Kashish see Pema's story?
Kashish finds it funny and doubts the size, laughing that it is bigger than Pema, but still wants to hear more.

I'm Devika, Wasim's older sister. Wasim is nine and very good at the number puzzles in the newspaper, the easy ones on Monday. He does them in pen, fast. On Saturdays the paper has a harder puzzle, with a star next to it. Abbu always leaves it for him. Wasim never touches it. Last Saturday Abbu asked him why. He said, "I don't like that one," but he'd gone red, and he left the room. Later I saw him through the door, staring at the Saturday puzzle. He wrote one number, very lightly in pencil, then rubbed it out so hard the paper tore. I don't know what he was thinking. He went back to Monday's puzzle, which he'd already finished.

What did Wasim do after writing one number in pencil on the Saturday puzzle?
He rubbed it out so hard the paper tore.
What might Wasim's going red suggest when he said 'I don't like that one'?

What could Abbu or Devika do to help Wasim try the Saturday puzzle?
They could sit and solve it with him in pencil, making mistakes out loud, so being wrong feels ordinary.
How does Devika see Wasim's torn paper?
Devika notices how much the hard puzzle matters to him and suspects fear rather than dislike, though she can't know for sure.
Austin bought his seven friends each a robot. Each robot costs $8.75.  He was charged $7.22 total for tax. He left with $11.53 in change. How much did Austin start with?

First we need to find the total amount for the robots. 7 robots * $8.75 per robot = $61.25 in total.
Now we need to add in the tax $61.25 for the robots + $7.22 for tax = $68.47 total spent in store.
Now to find what was the beginning amount we take the $68.47 total spent in-store + $11.53 in change = $80 to start.
The answer is 80.

Frank is practicing a new dance move.  It starts with him take 5 steps back, and then 10 steps forward, and then 2 steps back, and then double that amount forward.  How many steps forward is Frank from his original starting point?

Frank stars by taking 10 steps forward from a position 5 steps behind where he started, so he's 10-5= 5 steps forward in total
Frank then takes 2 steps back, meaning he's now 5-2=3 steps forward in total from where he began
He then takes double the previous amount of 2 steps forward, so he takes 2*2= 4 steps forward
Since Frank was 3 steps forward before that, that means Frank finishes 3+4=7 steps forward
The answer is 7.

I'm Bhupen, and I share a flat with my older sister Pooja. For most of the month she's the one who organises everyone. But for a few days each month something changes. She calls in sick, stays under the blanket, snaps at me for breathing loudly and then apologises in tears. Her fiancé has started asking me if he's done something wrong. I can't see inside her head. Last month, though, she told me the low felt so heavy it frightened her. I sat down next to her right then and stayed. Before she went to sleep that night, we rang her doctor's clinic together, and they gave her an appointment for the next morning. The doctor took it seriously and made a plan with her. Pooja says the worst part was believing she just had to put up with it.

Pooja's fiancé.
What does Pooja's crying apology suggest she was feeling?
She felt overwhelmed and ashamed, unable to control the snapping and sorry for it.
Which of Bhupen's steps was most important, and why?
Staying with her as soon as she said the low frightened her and calling the doctor's clinic together that same night, because distress that heavy needs care at once.
How does Bhupen see what happens to Pooja each month?
Bhupen sees a big change that cannot be fully understood from outside, and realises it is too much for her to simply put up with.
Here are some cards: 5, S, 0, O, 1, l, 2, Z, 8, B. Which ones are numbers and which ones are letters?

Answer: Numbers: 5, 0, 1, 2, 8. Letters: S, O, l, Z, B.

Numerals and letters are both symbols, but numerals tell "how many" and letters make words. Some look alike. Numeral 0 is a little thinner than letter O; 5 has a flat hat, S does not. Sort numeral and letter cards into two boxes.

At the municipal ward office in Kolkata, Kashish, twenty-four, stood at the counter with a single typed page. For a year, the broken drain outside her lane had flooded every monsoon. Complaints went nowhere.
"I'd like to file an RTI application," she said. "About the drain repair sanctioned last year: how much was sanctioned, which contractor, and why the work hasn't started."
The clerk frowned. "Why so formal, madam?"
"Because I'd like an answer in writing."
Her neighbour Maria, a retired teacher, had helped her draft it and stood beside her. Kashish paid the small fee, got a receipt, and photographed it.
Thirty days later, the reply came. The contractor had been paid; the work had never been done. Kashish forwarded it, calmly, to the ward councillor and a local newspaper.
Within a month, workers were digging.

What was the problem outside Kashish's lane?
The broken drain outside her lane had flooded every monsoon.
What might Kashish have been feeling when the clerk asked "Why so formal"?
Kashish probably felt calm and determined, having decided that only a written answer would work.
What in Kashish's approach made the system move?
She filed an RTI calmly, kept a receipt and a photo, and forwarded the reply to the councillor and newspaper, insisting on the process.
How might Maria feel seeing workers digging?
Maria would likely feel pleased and proud, having helped draft the application.

He slumped over his desk, yawned through dictation and snapped at his bench-mate over a pencil. I nearly sent him out for not paying attention. Instead, at break, I asked him quietly how he was sleeping. He told me his family had moved into one room beside the railway line, and the night trains shook the walls. I spoke to his mother, who found him a corner away from the tracks, and I stopped marking him down for slow mornings. By spring his laugh was back.

What shook the walls at Manoj's new home?
The night trains.
What was Shalini feeling when Manoj snapped over the pencil?
She felt irritated enough to nearly send him out, but also puzzled, because he had always been so cheerful.
What was the turning point in how Shalini handled Manoj, and why did it matter?
Choosing to ask him quietly about sleep at break instead of punishing him; it uncovered the noisy trains, which a punishment would have hidden.
What might that winter have been like for Manoj?
He was probably worn out and cross from broken sleep, and being punished for it would have felt unfair.

messages.content: There were students from three different schools taking part in a debate organized by the town's mayor on a stage. The first school had twice as many students as the second school, and the second school had 40 more students than the third school. If the third school had 200 students, and after the debate was over, every student shook the mayor's hand, calculate the total number of students who shook the mayor's hand on the stage.

If the third school had 200 students, and the second school had 40 more students than the third school, the second school had 200+40 = 240 students.
The third and second schools had 240+200 = 440 students on stage taking part in the debate.
Since the first school had twice as many students as the second school, and the second school had 240 students, the first school had 240*2= 480 students on stage taking part in the debate.
If after the debate was over, every student at the stage shook the mayor's hand, the number of students who shook the mayor's hand is 480+440 = 920 students
The answer is 920.
I want to learn swimming but I'm twenty and I feel embarrassed.
Lots of adults learn to swim, so you would not be the only one. Many pools have adult beginner classes. Have you looked for one near you?
There's a pool near my office. They have classes at seven in the morning.
Early classes are usually quieter, which may help you feel less shy. Instructors who teach adults are used to nervous beginners.
What should I take on the first day?
A swimsuit, a towel, a cap and goggles are the basics. Take a change of clothes and a small bag for wet things. Reach a few minutes early so you can ask the instructor any questions.
Jack and Jill shared the cost of renting a cottage that costs $5 an hour. If they rented it for eight hours, how much did each friend pay?

The total cost of renting the cottage for 8 hours is $5 x 8 = $40.
So, each friend pay $40/2 = $20 each.
The answer is 20.
Are mangoes cheaper at the roadside stall than in the big shop today?
I can't check today's prices, so I don't know which is cheaper. A short walk past both would show you.
Why does a fan make us feel cooler even though it does not cool the air?
A fan helps us feel cooler by helping sweat dry. Because moving air carries away the moisture on our skin and the drying takes heat from the body, we feel cooler even though the air is no colder.

Summarize Holmes's reasoning here as three bullet points.

"The name, you see, is in perfectly black ink, which has dried itself. The rest is of the greyish colour, which shows that blotting-paper has been used. If it had been written straight off, and then blotted, none would be of a deep black shade. This man has written the name, and there has then been a pause before he wrote the address, which can only mean that he was not familiar with it. It is, of course, a trifle, but there is nothing so important as trifles. Let us now see the letter. Ha! there has been an enclosure here!"

- The name is in deep black ink, while the rest of the writing looks greyish because it was blotted.
- This shows the writer paused before the address, so he probably did not know it well.
- Holmes says small details matter most, and then notices that something was once enclosed with the letter.

Zanele had been in the online group for six weeks. At first it was just a place to post drawings. Now her phone lit up from the moment she woke in her Johannesburg bedroom.
'Z, your sketch of the rain is incredible.' 'Z, we saved you a seat in the voice chat.' Last Friday, the older member who ran it had given her a title: welcomer for new members. She had a badge next to her name.
At school she found herself only half-listening to Omar. He was talking about the science fair, and it felt small and far away.
That night one of the older members wrote, 'Best to keep our chats just between us. Your parents wouldn't get it.' Zanele read it twice. She felt a flicker of unease, and then, straight after, warmth: they trusted her.
She typed 'of course', and felt, for the first time in years, like she was exactly where she belonged.

What title did Zanele get last Friday?
She was made welcomer for new members, with a badge next to her name.
What was Zanele feeling when she read the message about keeping chats secret?
She felt a flicker of unease, quickly covered by warmth and pride at being trusted, because belonging meant so much to her.
What would be the wise response to the request to keep the chats from her parents?
A request for secrecy from an online contact is a warning sign; the wise step is to stop the contact and tell a parent or another trusted adult.
How is Omar affected by Zanele's new focus?
Omar is losing his friend's attention, as she only half-listens to him and his science fair plans now feel small to her.

Monday. On her second week as a maintenance trainee at a Shimla hotel, Ira was sent with the senior electrician, Aadhya ma'am, to fix a flickering corridor light. "Don't switch off the main," Aadhya ma'am said. "Guests will complain. Just be careful." Ira's stomach tightened. The training manual said the opposite. But Aadhya ma'am had twenty years here. Ira said nothing and held the ladder.
Wednesday. Another job, same instruction. This time a small spark jumped when Ira handed over the screwdriver. Aadhya ma'am laughed it off. Ira laughed too, hands shaking.
Friday. Ira sat on her hostel bed with the training manual open at the safety page. She typed a message to the maintenance head, deleted it, typed it again. "Who am I to question her?" she said to her roommate. She still hadn't pressed send when the lights went out.

What did the training manual say about switching off the main?
The training manual said the opposite of Aadhya ma'am's instruction.
Why did Ira stay silent even though her stomach tightened?
She respected Aadhya ma'am's twenty years at the hotel, and questioning such a senior felt disrespectful, so fear of seeming rude outweighed her worry about safety.
What would you advise Ira to do about the message she keeps deleting?
Send it to the maintenance head, since a spark has already jumped; raising a safety concern politely is part of doing the job, not disrespect.
How might Aadhya ma'am see the situation if she knew how scared Ira was?
Aadhya ma'am might realise her habit was putting a trainee at risk, and that her seniority was making it impossible for Ira to speak up.
Does my best friend talk about me behind my back?
I can't tell what other people say when you're not there. If you feel unsure, talk to your friend honestly.

After-school care note, Tuesday.
Thomas arrived at 4:30 after a full school day, football practice and a spelling test. At snack time I offered him apple or banana. He stared at the bowl and said, "I don't know." When I asked again, he pushed the bowl away and cried. Later he could not choose between two colouring sheets and threw both on the floor. By six, he had refused every choice offered.
His mother, Sangeeta, told me at pickup that evenings at home are the same.
We agreed a plan: after 4:30, adults offer fewer choices, or simply decide small things for him. Important choices, like which club to join, will be discussed on weekend mornings. I'll try it for two weeks and note the change.

What did Thomas do with the two colouring sheets?
He threw both on the floor.
Why did Thomas cry when offered apple or banana?
He was tired and overwhelmed after a full day, so even a small choice felt too much.
What plan did the carer and Sangeeta agree on, and why is it sensible?
Offering fewer choices after 4:30 and deciding small things for him, keeping big choices for weekend mornings when he is fresh.
How might Sangeeta feel hearing about Thomas's afternoon?
Sangeeta might feel relieved that someone else noticed the pattern she sees at home, and hopeful about the plan.

You want to know what it was like, being the one who chased? I'm Nirmala, and I was that girl at twenty-one.
Manoj would come home from his shift, and before he'd even put his bag down, I'd be at the door. "What's wrong with us? Why are you so distant?" I'd already sent him five messages that afternoon. "Can we talk tonight?" "Please answer." "Are you angry?"
I truly believed if we just talked enough, the closeness would come back. Like it was waiting just past the next talk.
But the more I pushed, the more he went quiet, and the more quiet he went, the harder I pushed.

How many messages did Nirmala send Manoj that afternoon?
Five messages.
What was Nirmala feeling when she met Manoj at the door?
She felt anxious and desperate for closeness, believing that more talking was the only way to reach him.
What turning point was available to Nirmala at this stage?
She could have given Manoj a few minutes to settle after his shift and then asked calmly for one set time to talk, rather than pressing at the door.
What was Manoj likely experiencing when he walked in?
He probably felt overwhelmed and cornered, facing questions before putting his bag down, which made him go quieter.

I'm Nazia. I love silly stories. Last year I told the class I'd been chased to school by a tiger wearing sunglasses. Everyone laughed, because they know me. But Afreen was new, and she went pale. At break she asked, very seriously, whether the tiger was still near the bus stop, because her little sister walks there. My stomach dropped. For me it was obviously a joke. For her it wasn't. I told her straight away: “No tiger. I made it up for fun. Sunglasses, remember?” She laughed, a bit shakily. Now, when there's someone new, I make the story extra ridiculous, or I wink at the end, so everyone's in on it.

What was the tiger in Nazia's story wearing?
The tiger was wearing sunglasses.
What was Afreen feeling when she asked about the bus stop?
Afreen felt worried and scared for her little sister, because she believed the tiger story.
What did Nazia do to keep tall tales from becoming lies?
Nazia told Afreen the truth straight away and now makes stories extra silly or winks, so everyone knows it's a joke.
How did the rest of the class hear the tiger story?
They laughed, because they know Nazia's silly stories and understood it was a joke.

On the terrace of her Kolkata building, Tanuja sat with the statistics marksheet and a cup of cooling tea. Failed, by four marks. "I'm just bad with numbers," she whispered, and then stopped.
Her classmate Yogesh had already announced on the group chat that the paper was unfair. Neither story felt quite right. She turned the sheet over and drew two columns. Evidence for "bad with numbers": this paper. Evidence against: an A in accounts last semester, and the probability questions she'd got fully right.
So what else? She had skipped every doubt-clearing session to take extra shifts at her aunt's shop. The hypothesis-testing section, taught in those weeks, was where she lost almost everything. One change, she wrote: Thursday doubt sessions, no shift swaps.

Where did Tanuja sit with the marksheet?
On the terrace of her Kolkata building.
Why did Tanuja stop after whispering "I'm just bad with numbers"?
She felt doubtful about the harsh verdict; part of her sensed it didn't fit the facts and wanted to check it.
What does Tanuja's two-column list do well?
It tests the harsh story against real evidence, uncovers the missed sessions, and ends with one specific change.
How does Yogesh's reaction to the exam differ from Tanuja's?
Yogesh blames the paper as unfair, while Tanuja looks for evidence and a fix within her control.
How does Mina help the vampire hunters?
She types out all the diaries, letters and newspaper cuttings and puts them in order. Reading them together, the men can follow the Count's movements.

Dear Diary,
Today my team lead asked me to write fifty fake five-star reviews for our client's restaurant. "Just use different names. It's marketing."
I need this job. Rent is due. But I kept thinking of people choosing that restaurant because of reviews I made up.
I talked to Aadhya at lunch. She said, "You could say no and suggest real ways, like asking actual customers for reviews."
So I did. I said to my lead, "I'm not comfortable writing fake reviews. But I can set up a real feedback campaign with the restaurant."
He was irritated. But he said, "Fine. Show me a plan by Friday."
I'm nervous about my job. But I feel clean.
— Uday

How many fake reviews did the team lead ask for?
Fifty.
What was Uday feeling after refusing?
Uday felt nervous about the job but at peace, feeling clean.
What did Uday do that balanced ethics and career risk?
Uday refused the fake reviews but offered an honest alternative plan.
How might the team lead see Uday's suggestion?
The team lead is irritated but willing to see a plan, so may come to accept it.
Xavier is twice as old as Yasmin is. Xavier will 30 years old in six years. What is the total of their ages now?

If in six years Xavier will be 30 years old, he is 30-6 = 24 years old now.
If Xavier is twice as old as Yasmin, Yasmin is 24/2 = 12 years old.
The total of their ages now is 12+24 = 36 years
The answer is 36.
A tiny story of about 50 words about a girl who is afraid to speak in class and finds her voice.

A girl sat at the back and never spoke in class. Her heart pounded whenever the teacher looked at her. One day, the teacher asked a question that she knew well. Slowly, she raised her hand and answered. Her voice shook, but it came out clear. The class clapped, and she smiled.

Three weeks after the flood, Rehana had a contractor's quote for everything: new wiring, a new kitchen counter, fresh paint, tiles for the whole floor. One lakh forty thousand. She had signed nothing yet, which turned out lucky.
The insurance surveyor's letter came on Tuesday: the first payment would be sixty thousand, the rest 'after review'. Her savings covered maybe thirty more.
She sat with her neighbour Elizabeth on the damp steps and crossed things out. 'Wiring first, because the kids can't live without safe power. The kitchen counter, because we have to cook. Paint and tiles wait.'
Elizabeth nodded. 'And if the rest of the claim comes?'
'Then tiles. If it doesn't, the walls stay ugly till next Eid.' She rang the contractor that evening and asked him to split the job in two.

How much would the first insurance payment be?
Sixty thousand, with the rest after review.
What was Rehana probably feeling when the surveyor's letter came?
She was likely worried and disappointed, since the quote was far higher than the first payment and her savings together.
Which other approach could help Rehana if the rest of the claim is delayed?
She could ask the insurer's helpline what the review needs, and keep her list of repairs in order of priority to update as money arrives.
How might Rehana's children experience the staged repairs?
They get safe power and a working kitchen first, so daily life settles, even if the walls stay stained for a while.
The school canteen is adding a new snack menu from Monday. Write a short notice, about 35 words, for the board. Sign it Canteen Management.

NOTICE
From Monday, the school canteen will offer a new snack menu. Students are welcome to try the new items during the break. We hope you enjoy them, so do give them a try!
Canteen Management
Put this sentence into the passive voice: They counted attendance from the register, marked the short maths test, and asked each child for one line on what they liked and disliked.
Attendance was counted from the register, the short maths test was marked, and each child was asked for one line on what they liked and disliked.

Make a two-sentence summary out of this paragraph.

While I still hung over her in the agony of despair, I happened to look up. The windows of the room had before been darkened, and I felt a kind of panic on seeing the pale yellow light of the moon illuminate the chamber. The shutters had been thrown back, and with a sensation of horror not to be described, I saw at the open window a figure the most hideous and abhorred. A grin was on the face of the monster; he seemed to jeer, as with his fiendish finger he pointed towards the corpse of my wife. I rushed towards the window, and drawing a pistol from my bosom, fired; but he eluded me, leaped from his station, and running with the swiftness of lightning, plunged into the lake.

While grieving over the body of the narrator's wife, the narrator sees a hideous monster grinning at the open window. The monster points at the body, the narrator fires a pistol, and it leaps away and runs into the lake.
Cory bought a patio table and 4 chairs for $135. The patio table cost $55. If each chair cost the same amount, how much did each chair cost?

The 4 chairs cost Cory $135 - $55 = $80.
Each chair costs $80 / 4 = $20.
The answer is 20.
Now you try: for one die, are "even", "<= 3" and "prime" mutually independent?
The answer is No: even and prime already fail, P(2) = 1/6 != 1/4.
Tell a six-word story about a missing sandal.
One sandal waited by the door.

Caleb picked a handful of dandelion puffs. He gave 3 to his mom, another 3 to his sister, 5 to his grandmother, and 2 to his dog. Then, he divided the remaining dandelion puffs equally among his 3 friends. How many dandelion puffs did each friend receive if he originally picked 40 dandelion puffs?

Caleb was left with 40 - 3 - 3 - 5 - 2 = 27 dandelion puffs to give to his friends.
They each received 27/3 = 9 dandelion puffs
The answer is 9.

In their Pune housing society, Mridul was known as the boy who always topped. So when his Class 11 chemistry result came back as a fail, he put the report card in his school bag's inner pocket and told his parents the results were "delayed".

His best friend Madhav, from the next building, found out when they were walking to tuition. "You have to tell them."

"I'll just clear the re-exam first. Then I'll tell them it went fine."

For three weeks Mridul barely slept. He jumped every time the landline rang. He couldn't ask his teacher about re-exam forms without a parent signature, so he didn't ask.

Then his mother met his class teacher at the society Ganpati function. The teacher mentioned the re-exam deadline, and that Mridul's form was missing.

At home, his mother held out her hand for the report card. Her voice was quiet. "Three weeks, Mridul. You lied to us for three weeks."

What excuse did Mridul give his parents about the results?
He told them the results were "delayed".
How did Mridul feel during the three weeks of hiding the result?
He felt anxious and on edge, barely sleeping and jumping every time the landline rang.
What could Mridul have done differently on the day the result came?
He could have told his parents with a plan for the re-exam, so they could sign the form in time and help rather than find out from the teacher.
How might Mridul's mother have felt hearing about the missing form from the teacher?
She likely felt shocked, embarrassed and hurt, more by three weeks of lying than by the failed exam.

Rain hammered the tarpaulin over the colony's festival ground and everyone squeezed under it to sing. Mohit, eight, ducked in among the other children, dripping. A man holding a steel ladle stepped in front of him. "Not you. Your family isn't one of ours." The singing carried on behind the man's back. Mohit's ears burned and water ran down his neck. He did not understand what he had done. He stood at the edge in the rain until his Masi Sudha arrived with an umbrella and saw his face. He told her in a rush. She put her arm around him. "That was not because of anything you did. Come, I'm going to speak to the organisers."

What was the man in front of Mohit holding?
He was holding a steel ladle.
What was Mohit feeling and thinking as he stood at the edge in the rain?
He was hurt and confused: his ears burned and he did not understand what he had done.
Who could Mohit tell, and what does that do for him?
He can tell a trusted adult like Masi Sudha, who reassures him it was not because of anything he did and goes to speak up for him 🤍.
How might Masi Sudha see what happened?
As unfair to a child: she put her arm around him and went to speak to the organisers.

After her promotion in Seoul, Soo-ah noticed the bags. Every woman in the new team carried one of three famous designer handbags. Hers was canvas, from a street market in her university days.

At dinner, she said to Wei, "I think I should buy one. It's like a uniform."

Wei, cutting kimchi pancake, asked, "Did anyone say anything?"

"No. But I feel them looking."

"Or you feel yourself looking."

She was quiet. It was true that no one had mentioned it.

That weekend she walked through the department store and stood in front of the bags for a long time. The price was more than her raise for three months. She thought about the trip to visit her grandmother in Busan that she kept postponing.

She walked out without one, a little sad and a little proud. On Monday, she carried the canvas bag. At lunch, a senior colleague asked where she had got it. "My university market," she said. "Ten years ago."

What kind of bag did Soo-ah carry?
Her bag was canvas, from a street market in her university days.
How did Soo-ah feel walking out of the department store?
Soo-ah felt a little sad and a little proud, having chosen what she valued over fitting in.
What helped Soo-ah decide against the bag?
Checking whether anyone had actually commented and comparing the price with the trip to visit her grandmother helped her separate image from needs.
How does Wei see Soo-ah's worry about the bags?
Wei gently suggests the pressure may come from her own feelings more than from colleagues, helping her see it clearly.

At the boarding school in Mussoorie, news travelled fast. By dinner on Tuesday, half the dorm was humming the choir song at Tenzin, and he knew Uday had told them about his crush. Uday was the only one he had told. Tenzin's face burned. He wanted to walk over to Uday's table and say something cruel enough to get even. Instead he went to the study hall after dinner, took out a sheet and wrote two headings. What hurt: not the teasing. That it was Uday. What I want: he stared at the second heading a long time. To make Uday feel bad? For a minute, yes. Then, underneath: for Uday to understand. To be able to trust him again. He folded the page into his pocket and decided to sleep on it before saying anything.

What was the dorm humming at Tenzin?
The choir song.
What was Tenzin feeling at dinner?
He felt humiliated and betrayed, his face burning, and angry enough to want to get even.
What could Tenzin say to Uday the next day, given what he wrote?
Talk privately, say it hurt most because it was Uday, and ask why it happened, since the goal is to be understood and trusted again, not to win.
How might Uday feel when Tenzin doesn't confront him at dinner?
Uday may feel uneasy or guilty, sensing something is wrong, and perhaps relieved there was no scene.

What was America in 1492 but a Loose-Fish, in which Columbus struck the Spanish standard by way of waifing it for his royal master and mistress? What was Poland to the Czar? What Greece to the Turk? What India to England? What at last will Mexico be to the United States? All Loose-Fish.

What examples of Loose-Fish does the narrator give?

America in 1492, when Columbus claimed it for his royal master and mistress, then Poland to the Czar, Greece to the Turk and India to England; the narrator also wonders what Mexico will be to the United States.

Mridul, you're struggling with your final-year project, so let me tell you about your cousin Jomon. I was his uncle, and I let him use my workshop when he was twenty, studying electrical engineering. His radio project kept buzzing. For three nights he changed everything at once, and by the third he was near tears, tired and fed up. I made him tea and said, "Can you make it buzz whenever you want?" He could: only when the volume was high. "Good. Now find where." He tested each section, one at a time, and wrote results on the wall with chalk. By midnight the chalk showed it: a loose earth wire. One change. No more buzz. He left the chalk marks there for years.

What did Jomon find was causing the buzz?
A loose earth wire.
How was Jomon feeling on the third night?
He was near tears, tired and fed up after changing everything at once.
Which choice in the story led to the fix?
Making the buzz happen on purpose, testing one section at a time and writing results in chalk on the wall.
How might the uncle have seen Jomon's first three nights?
The uncle saw circular guessing driven by tiredness, and offered tea and a simple question instead of criticism.

Before: In September, Gautam and his friend Raghav both joined the Saturday sketching club at their school. Gautam's first portrait came out lopsided. He laughed it off.
During: In October, the teacher pinned all the portraits on the corridor board for the parents' day. A group of juniors stopped at Gautam's and giggled. That evening he told his mother, "I'm not a creative person. I'm a maths person. Some people just have it." He didn't go to the club the next Saturday, or the one after.
After: In February, Gautam walked past the corridor board again. Raghav's new portrait hung there, a shaded face with real eyes. Raghav had also been bad in September. Gautam stopped for a second, then walked on quickly. "He's just talented," he muttered. "I'm not."

What did the juniors do at Gautam's portrait?
They stopped and giggled.
Why does Gautam walk away quickly from Raghav's portrait?
He feels uncomfortable and a bit envious, and telling himself Raghav is just talented protects him from seeing that practice made the difference.
What could help Gautam rethink his belief?
Comparing Raghav's September sketch with the February one could show him that skill grew with practice, and he could try one Saturday session again.
How might Raghav see Gautam's claim that he is "just talented"?
Raghav might feel frustrated or unseen, since he knows he was also bad in September and improved through months of practice.

Imran: of course. what's going on?
Farida: I think the donations for the flood appeal are going to a company owned by the director's brother
Imran: that's serious. are you sure?

Farida: my father's retiring, my sister's fees are due. if I lose this job

What does Farida think is happening to the flood appeal donations?
Going to a company owned by the director's brother.
What is Farida feeling before acting?
Farida feels scared and burdened, worried about the family's needs if the job is lost.

He treats preparation as strength: factual notes, telling the family first, and confidential legal advice make a later report stronger.
How does Imran seem to see Farida's fear?
He sees it as understandable and not cowardly, and responds calmly and practically.

Uma arrived at the village school in March with a camera and a volunteer T-shirt. The first week she photographed everything: children at the handpump, the broken toilet block, herself holding a sapling. Her posts got hundreds of likes back in the city. By the third week, the real work began. The toilet block needed clearing out, and parents needed to be visited, one by one, in the heat. Uma started arriving late. Then not at all. Leela, the school's teacher, found her at the tea stall. "The children ask where you are." "I'm just... tired. It's not what I thought." "It's exactly what it is," Leela said. "The photos were never the help." Uma looked at her phone, then at the school. She didn't answer.

What did Uma bring when she arrived at the village school?
A camera and a volunteer T-shirt.
What does Uma's silence at the end suggest about how she feels?
It suggests Uma feels ashamed and uncomfortable, confronted with the gap between her posts and the hard work she avoided.
What could Uma do if she wants her help to be real?
She could return to do the unglamorous tasks, like clearing the toilet block and visiting parents, and listen to Leela about what's needed.
How might the children see Uma's disappearance?
The children ask where she is, so they may feel let down or confused that she stopped coming.

On the hill-top above me sat the rising moon; pale yet as a cloud, but brightening momentarily, she looked over Hay, which, half lost in trees, sent up a blue smoke from its few chimneys: it was yet a mile distant, but in the absolute hush I could hear plainly its thin murmurs of life. My ear, too, felt the flow of currents; in what dales and depths I could not tell: but there were many hills beyond Hay, and doubtless many becks threading their passes. That evening calm betrayed alike the tinkle of the nearest streams, the sough of the most remote.

What can the narrator hear in the evening calm?
The faint sounds of life from the village of Hay a mile away, and the flow of streams both near and far.
