On the night of the village jatra, Yamini climbed the old water tank with her friend Farida instead of watching the drama. Below them the fair glowed; above them the sky was thick with stars she never saw in the town where she studied.
"Do you ever think we're just dust that learned to think?" Yamini said.
Farida laughed. "Only you would say that at a jatra."
"I mean it. Then why does anything matter? Why does Amma pray every morning? Why do I want to be a teacher?"
Farida thought for a while. "Maybe it matters because we're here together for a bit."
Yamini lay back on the cold concrete. She didn't have an answer. But she felt, for a second, very small and very connected, both at once.

Where did Yamini and Farida climb?
The old water tank.
What was Yamini feeling as she lay on the concrete?
She felt small and connected at the same time, full of wonder without an answer.
How could a trusted adult respond if Yamini brought these questions home?
They could listen and share their own view, like why Amma prays, without insisting she agree.
How does Farida see Yamini's big question?
Farida is amused at first but then takes it seriously and offers her own gentle answer.

You asked how we got Baba to accept digital payments at the shop, Tanuja. I'm Omkar, and honestly, I did it wrong first.

Our family kirana store in Kolhapur has been cash-only for twenty-five years. Customers kept asking to pay by phone. I set up a payment code and stuck it on the counter one morning. Baba tore it off by lunch. "What if the money doesn't come? What if the phone lies?" My uncle agreed.

I was annoyed. I thought he was being stubborn. But then I saw him counting the cash drawer that night, three times, the way he always does. He trusts what he can hold.

So I asked him for a deal. One week, only for customers who ask. Every evening, I'd show him the bank messages next to the cash total, so he could see it all matched.

On day four, he asked me, "Why don't we put the code back on the counter?"

How long has the kirana store been cash-only?
Twenty-five years.
What did Omkar feel before and after watching Baba count the cash drawer?
Omkar felt annoyed at first, then understanding, seeing that Baba felt safe with money he could hold and feared losing it.
What made Omkar's second approach work?
Omkar offered a one-week trial only for customers who asked, and showed Baba the bank messages each evening, respecting his fear and letting him see proof.
How might Baba have felt by day four?
Baba probably felt reassured and more confident, which is why he suggested putting the code back himself.

Sunday night. Mridul lay on his hostel bed and pictured Tuesday's presentation on water harvesting. He walks in. Slides flow. The professor nods. Classmates clap at the end. He replayed it three times and fell asleep smiling.
His roommate Yusuf asked on Monday, "Did you practise?"
"In my head. I'm ready."
"What if the projector acts up? It did in my class last week."
"It won't," Mridul said.
Tuesday. The projector showed a blue screen. The technician took ten minutes. Mridul stood at the front with no printout and no notes, trying to remember what was on slide four. He skipped half his points, lost the order, and finished early. The professor wrote something in her notebook without looking up.
That evening he told Yusuf, "I imagined everything except the part that went wrong."

How long did the technician take?
The technician took ten minutes.
How did Mridul feel standing at the front without slides?
He felt panicked and lost, trying to remember slide four and skipping half his points.
What would you change first in how Mridul prepared?
Rehearse aloud at least once, and imagine the projector failing, then carry a printout or notes as a backup.
How might Yusuf see what happened on Tuesday?
Yusuf may feel sorry for Mridul but not surprised, since Yusuf had warned Mridul about the projector.

"Asif, are you crying? Over a football match?" Anirban laughed. "Boys don't cry, yaar."
Asif wiped his face fast. "I'm not crying. It's sweat."
"Sweat from your eyes?"
"We lost the final by one goal! I missed the penalty!"
"So? My dad says crying is for girls."
Asif sat down on the bench. "Why, though? Who made that rule?"
Anirban opened his mouth, then shut it. "I don't know. Everyone says it."
"My Abbu cried when my baby sister was born. He's not weak."
Anirban scuffed the ground. "Okay. I cried when my dog died. Don't tell anyone."
"I won't." Asif laughed wetly. "Next year we'll win and cry about that too."
"Deal," Anirban said, and sat down beside him.

By how much did they lose the final?
By one goal.
Why did Asif say it was just sweat?
He felt embarrassed about crying after Anirban laughed at him.
What did Asif do that challenged the rule?
He asked who made the rule and pointed out that his Abbu cried and is not weak.
How did Anirban's view change during the talk?
He realised he did not know why the rule existed, admitted he had cried too, and sat beside Asif.

In the kitchen of their flat in Buenos Aires, Camila and her mum stuck a sheet of paper on the fridge.
"Plans shared by Thursday for the weekend. Home by ten, or text by nine thirty. Location on when out late."
Underneath, her mum had added in her own handwriting: "If Camila asks honestly, Mum will try to say yes more often."
"And we look at this again at the end of the month," her mum said.
Camila read it twice. "So if I ask to sleep over at Mei's on Saturday?"
"Did you tell me by Thursday?"
"It's Wednesday."
Her mum smiled. "Then yes."

What day did Camila ask about sleeping over at Mei's?
On Wednesday.
What was Camila feeling when she read the sheet twice?
She seemed hopeful and a little unsure, testing whether the new rules would really lead to yes.
Why does this approach help rebuild trust?
The rules are small, specific and visible on the fridge, with a review date, and the mum commits to saying yes more when Camila is honest.
What might Camila's mum be experiencing when she smiles and says yes?
She probably feels pleased and relieved that Camila followed the new rule, and glad to keep her side of the deal.

Now you try: 3/10 of ₹500.
The answer is ₹150.

I'm Yusuf, and last month I nearly let down a friend the easy way.
I had promised Shalini I'd design all the menu cards for her bakery's opening by Friday. On Monday night, my father was admitted to hospital, and I knew I couldn't finish the whole set.
The easy way was to go quiet, then send a vague "something came up" on Thursday. I'd done that before, to other people.
Instead, on Tuesday morning, I called her. "Shalini, I can't do all twelve cards by Friday. My father is in hospital. I know this puts you in a spot three days before opening." She was quiet. Then I said, "I can finish the main menu by Thursday. And my friend Rakesh can do the other cards if you want."
She said, "Thank you for telling me now." The bakery opened on time, with my menu at the counter.

How many cards had Yusuf promised to design?
He had promised to do all twelve cards by Friday.
How might Shalini have felt when Yusuf called on Tuesday?
Shalini probably felt worried at first about the opening, and then grateful that Yusuf told her early.
What made Yusuf's approach work?
He told Shalini early, named the impact on her opening, and offered what he truly could do, the main menu plus a friend's help.
What would have changed if Yusuf had sent a vague excuse on Thursday?
Shalini would have had no time to find help, and her trust in Yusuf would have been badly damaged.
How does hearing "I understand" make people feel better?
They feel less alone. Because being understood makes a person feel heard, the problem seems lighter.

Monday: At the park, Aditi's friend tripped and scraped her knee. Aditi laughed. Reena, her mother, knelt down. "Look at her face. How do you think her knee feels?" Aditi stopped laughing. "Ouchy."
Wednesday: At home, Reena and Aditi played doctor with a teddy. Reena said, "Teddy fell. I think Teddy feels sore and scared. What can we say?" Aditi patted the teddy. "Are you okay?"
Saturday: A boy on the slide bumped his head. Aditi ran up to him first. "Does it hurt?"

What did Aditi's friend scrape at the park?
Her knee.
Why did Reena ask Aditi to look at her friend's face?
Reena felt concerned that Aditi had laughed, and wanted to help her notice the friend's pain by reading her face.
What helped Aditi most between Monday and Saturday?
Pretend play with the teddy, where Reena modelled saying how someone else feels, gave Aditi practice she then used at the slide.
How might the boy on the slide feel when Aditi runs up to him?
He probably feels cared for and less alone after bumping his head.
Mail mein bolna hai "Maaf kijiye, attachment lagana bhool gaya tha." English?
Write: "Sorry, I forgot to add the attachment." You can then add: "Here it is."

I've worked next to Jyoti at the design studio for a year, and at first I thought she was a bit unfriendly. She never came to the loud Friday lunches. She wore big headphones that didn't seem to play anything.
Then I noticed the pattern. She books the small meeting room with the dimmer lights for her afternoon sketching. She eats alone on Mondays and Thursdays, and joins us on the quieter Wednesdays. Before big client presentations, she disappears for twenty minutes and comes back calm.
Once I asked her about the headphones. She said, "The light's hum gets into my head, Rehana. These just make things quieter." She didn't explain more, and I didn't push.
I don't know everything going on for her. But her work is the sharpest on the team, and now I save her a seat on Wednesdays.

On which days does Jyoti eat alone?
Mondays and Thursdays.
Why might Jyoti wear headphones that don't seem to play anything?

A factory decides to stop making cars and start making motorcycles instead. When it made cars, per month, it cost $100 for materials, they could make 4 cars, and they sold each car for $50. Now that they make motorcycles it costs $250 for materials, but they sell 8 of them for $50 each. How much more profit do they make per month selling motorcycles instead of cars?

They sold $200 worth of cars each month because 4 x 50 = 200
They made $100 a month off cars because 200 - 100 = 100
They sold $400 worth of motorcycles each month because 8 x 50 = 400
They make $150 a month off motorcycles because 400 - 250 = 150
They make $50 more a month off motorcycles than cars because 150 - 100 = 50
The answer is 50.

Julio has four bottles of orange soda and seven bottles of grape soda in his fridge. His friend Mateo has a bottle of orange soda and 3 bottles of grape soda in his fridge. If the amount of beverage in each bottle is 2 liters, how many more liters of soda does Julio have?

Julio has 4 * 2 = 8 liters of orange soda
Julio also has 7 * 2 = 14 liters of grape soda.
Julio therefore has a total of 8 + 14 = 22 liters of soda
The amount of orange soda that Mateo has is 1 * 2 = 2 liters of orange soda
In addition, Mateo has 3 * 2 = 6 liters of grape soda.
In total, Mateo has 2 + 6 = 8 liters of soda.
This means that Julio has 22 - 8 = 14 liters more of soda
The answer is 14.
Now you try: strings of length n with no two consecutive 0s AND no two consecutive 1s.
The answer is only 2 for every n >= 1: they must alternate.

Two straight roads meet at a crossing C at an angle of 70 degrees. A lamp post must be the same distance from both roads, inside the 70 degrees angle. Where can it go?

Answer: On the bisector of the 70 degrees angle, the line from C that makes 35 degrees with each road.

The distance from a point to a road is measured along the PERPENDICULAR. Points equally far from two crossing lines lie on the ANGLE BISECTORS. Construction: with centre C draw an arc cutting both roads, at X and Y. With centres X and Y and the same radius draw two arcs crossing at Z. Rule CZ: it splits the angle into 35 degrees + 35 degrees. Why: CX = CY, XZ = YZ and CZ is shared, so the triangles CXZ and CYZ are congruent (SSS), and angle XCZ = angle YCZ. The full locus for the two whole roads is TWO lines at right angles: the bisector of the 70 degrees angle and the bisector of the 110 degrees angle next to it (35 degrees + 55 degrees = 90 degrees).

messages.content: A money plant has 3 leaves. Each week the number of leaves doubles. How many leaves after 1, 2, 3 and 4 weeks? Then count back by halving.

Double 3 is 6, double 6 is 12, double 12 is 24 (20 + 4), double 24 is 48 (40 + 8). To go back, halve: half of 48 is 24, half of 24 is 12, and so on. Write the chain with arrows both ways. Can the child start with 5? (10, 20, 40, 80.)

She said she'd had an idea about the pricing slide on Tuesday, and someone else said something similar ten minutes later, and it went into the plan. 'So maybe it wasn't special. Maybe I'm just not adding much.'
She laughed when she said it, but she didn't look up.
Next session: we'll talk about how everyone's outside looks, compared with her own inside. And one small point to say aloud next week.

What did Pooja have an idea about on Tuesday?
She had an idea about the pricing slide.
What does Pooja believe about her place in the team, and what shows it?
She feels discouraged and unsure she adds much, which shows when she says, 'Maybe I'm just not adding much,' without looking up.
What small step could Pooja try to break the pattern of silence?
She could say one point aloud early in a meeting, even before she is fully sure, so her ideas are heard and credited.
How might Rohit and Sheetal look from their side of the table, compared with how Pooja sees them?
They may have their own doubts too; Pooja only sees their confident outside, not whatever uncertainty they feel inside.

In Kraków, Olga's class was writing about summer holidays. Olga wrote about the week at the Baltic Sea: the cold waves, the ice cream, and the moment she found a crab under a rock and it pinched her finger. She drew the crab carefully. At home, her brother Daniel read it and frowned. "I found the crab. It pinched me. You were building a sandcastle." Olga's cheeks went hot. "No, it was me. I remember the pinch!" Their mother brought out the holiday photos. There was Daniel, holding up his finger with a tiny red mark, and Olga in the background, patting a sandcastle. Olga stared. She had heard Daniel tell the crab story so many times that it had become hers.

What was Olga doing in the background of the photo?
Patting a sandcastle.
Why did Olga's cheeks go hot when Daniel said he found the crab?
Olga felt embarrassed and defensive, sure she remembered the pinch, because Daniel's story had become part of her memory.
What helped sort out whose memory it was, and what could Olga do in future?
The holiday photos showed Daniel with the pinched finger; Olga could check photos or ask family when a memory might be shared.
How might Daniel feel seeing his crab story in Olga's writing?
Daniel might feel annoyed that his adventure was taken, then amused once the photos showed the truth.

What did one classmate hide until Vandana answered?
One classmate hid Vandana's geometry box until Vandana answered.

Vandana thinks the secret is Madhuri's to tell, but wonders whether hiding it bothers Madhuri, since Madhuri flinches when a poem is read aloud.

Which vegetable did Hafsa refuse?
Hafsa refused karela.
How did Hafsa feel when Dadi threatened no sweet?
Hafsa felt upset and pushed; her lip shook and she shoved the plate away.
Why did Reena's approach work better than Dadi's?
Reena offered a tiny piece calmly each day without pressure, so Hafsa could come to it herself instead of fighting.

During the heated months before the national vote, Mei muted and unfollowed everyone in Melbourne who didn't share her views, including her old debate partner, Layla. The relief was instant: no more arguments at midnight, no more tightness in her chest. Her feed felt like a warm room full of people nodding. Three weeks later, in a university seminar, the lecturer asked the class to explain the strongest case for the other side. Mei opened her mouth and realised she couldn't. She had only ever heard it mocked. On the tram home, she felt a strange loneliness, surrounded by agreement. That night she scrolled back to Layla's profile. Layla had never been cruel, only different. Mei kept blocked the two accounts that had sent her abusive messages. She re-followed Layla and sent her a note: 'I miss arguing with you. Coffee? I need to hear the other side from someone who won't sneer.' Layla replied with a coffee cup.

What did the lecturer ask the class to explain?
The lecturer asked them to explain the strongest case for the other side.
What did Mei feel on the tram home?
Mei felt a strange loneliness, surrounded by agreement.
What boundary did Mei keep, and what did she change?
She kept the two abusive accounts blocked but re-followed Layla, keeping respectful dissent in her life.
How does Layla respond to Mei's message?
Layla replies warmly with a coffee cup, open to meeting again.

Sarika scrolled past her cousin Anjali's photos: home-cooked purees in tiny bowls, a spotless nursery, a baby asleep by seven. She looked at Arohi, sticky and wide awake at nine, and thought she was never enough. Then she remembered her paediatrician saying loving and steady mattered more than perfect. She put the phone down and sang the same bedtime song as every night. At the park Arohi wobbled toward the slide and Sarika's heart clamped; she wanted to scoop her up and never let her fall. She stayed one step away with open arms and let Arohi climb a rung by herself. The love felt huge and frightening together. That afternoon Arohi tipped a whole bowl of rice onto the floor for the third time, and Sarika snapped, "Enough! Why can't you just eat?" Arohi's lip trembled. Sarika breathed, knelt down and said, "I raised my voice, and I'm sorry. I was tired. Let's clean it up together." Arohi patted the rice with a small hand, and Sarika laughed, wiping her own eyes.

What did Arohi tip onto the floor?
Arohi tipped a whole bowl of rice onto the floor.
How did Sarika's reaction at the park differ from her reaction over the spilled rice, and what did both show about her love?

At the park Sarika's heart clamped and she wanted to scoop Arohi up, but she stayed one step away and let Arohi climb a rung; over the rice she snapped, then knelt down and apologised, so both moments show huge love and fear that she learns to guide and repair rather than control.
What was Sarika feeling as she scrolled through Anjali's photos?
She felt inadequate and anxious, comparing herself and thinking she was never enough.
What could Sarika keep doing when she compares herself with others online?
She could keep her simple routines, trust her paediatrician, and remember that a steady, loving, imperfect parent is what a child needs. 🙂

Tuesday, 9 p.m.
Something weird happened today. I, Aadhya, sat down with the guitar at six to practise the F to C change that Omkar sir gave me. My fingers have been refusing it for a week.
The first ten minutes were annoying. I kept buzzing the strings. But it was close, not impossible. So I slowed down, then sped up a little, then a little more.
Next thing I knew, Mummy was knocking for dinner. It was eight. My phone was on the bed where I'd thrown it, with fourteen messages I hadn't even heard.
The change isn't perfect, but it's there. And I feel strangely calm. Not excited, just clear, like my head had been swept.
I want to feel this again. Maybe the trick is picking something hard, but not too hard.

What chord change was Aadhya practising?
Aadhya was practising the F to C change.
How does Aadhya feel after practice?
Aadhya feels strangely calm and clear, "like my head had been swept", rather than excited.
What does Aadhya's idea about "hard, but not too hard" suggest for future practice?
Aadhya can choose the next piece just a little beyond current skill, so it holds attention without becoming frustrating.
How might Omkar sir feel hearing that the change is finally coming?
Omkar sir would likely feel pleased that the exercise was pitched right and that Aadhya stuck with it.
Ella has 4 bags with 20 apples in each bag and six bags with 25 apples in each bag. If Ella sells 200 apples, how many apples does Ella has left?

4 bags have 4 x 20 = 80 apples.
And, six bags have 6 x 25 = 150 apples.
Thus, Ella has 80 + 150 = 230 apples in all.
Therefore, Ella has 230 - 200 = 30 apple left.
The answer is 30.

On Christmas Eve in Madrid, Sofia, four, stood on the bottom step of the stairs to the neighbour's door. Her mother Vera held out a hand. Sofia shook her head. "No hand!" She jumped down with both feet together. She wobbled, but stayed up. Her mouth fell open. "Mamá! I jumped!" She climbed back up and jumped again. Then again. Then from the second step. Vera held her breath, then smiled. "Again, Mamá, watch!" By the time the neighbours opened the door, Sofia had jumped fifteen times and her cheeks were pink with pride.

How many times had Sofia jumped by the time the neighbours opened the door?
Sofia had jumped fifteen times.
How did Sofia feel after her first jump?
Sofia felt amazed and proud, her mouth falling open as she shouted to Mamá.
What did Vera do that helped Sofia's new skill grow?
She let Sofia jump without her hand and watched each time, so Sofia could feel able and keep trying.

Vera felt nervous, holding her breath, then relieved and proud when Sofia landed.

Wendy is a fruit vendor, and she sells an apple at $1.50 each and one orange at $1.  In the morning, she was able to sell an average of 40 apples and 30 oranges. In the afternoon, she was able to sell 50 apples and 40 oranges. How much are her total sales for the day?

There were an average of 40 + 50 = 90 apples.
And, there were 30 + 40 = 70 oranges.
Thus, Wendy gained 90 x $1.50 = $135 for selling apples.
And, she gained an additional 70 x $1 = $70 for selling oranges.
Therefore, her total sales for the day is $135 + 70 = $205.
The answer is 205.

Turn his radio down.
How did Chetan feel when Rafiq started gasping?
Chetan felt frightened that something terrible was happening, with shaking hands.
What did Chetan do that helped?
Stayed close, spoke slowly, calmed the surroundings, planned to call an ambulance if it looked serious, and urged Rafiq to tell the parents and see a doctor.
How might Rafiq feel reading this letter?
Rafiq may feel embarrassed at first, then relieved and less alone, knowing Chetan isn't judging.
In civics class we learned that the lower chamber of parliament passed the bill. Is a chamber just a room?

In this sense a chamber is one of the main groups of lawmakers in a parliament, or the hall where they meet. It is a noun. The everyday meaning is a large room.
Example: The upper chamber studied the bill for two weeks before it voted.

In Leila's classroom in Toronto, dividing fractions had a song. "Keep, change, flip!" Leila sang it under her breath through every worksheet, and every answer came back with a check mark. At lunch Dalia asked how she got 3/2 for 1/2 divided by 1/3. "Keep, change, flip," Leila said. "Why does it work?" Leila bit her sandwich. "It just does." Then came the quiz. Question 4: 'A ribbon is 2/3 of a metre long. How many 1/6-metre pieces can you cut?' No division sign, no fractions lined up to flip. Leila read it three times, wrote '2/3 × 1/6?', crossed it out, and moved on, leaving an empty space.

What song did Leila use for dividing fractions?
'Keep, change, flip!'
What was Leila feeling as she crossed out her answer to Question 4?
She felt confused and stuck, since the song didn't tell her the ribbon problem was a division.
What else could Leila try so she understands, not only remembers?
Draw the ribbon and count how many sixths fit into two-thirds; seeing why it works would help her spot division in new shapes.
How might Dalia see Leila's 'It just does'?
Dalia was curious why it works, so the answer may leave Dalia unconvinced that Leila really understands it.

Last winter, my friend Gargi's grandmother died. At school the next week, Gargi looked so lost that I went to hug her in the corridor, arms already open.
She stepped back. “Not now. Please.”
I'm Zeenat. For a second I felt hurt. I only wanted to help. Then I remembered what our counsellor said in the consent session: a no is a full answer, even from a friend, even when you mean well.
So I dropped my arms. “Okay. I'm here if you want anything.”
She nodded. At lunch, she came and sat next to me, silently, and leaned her head on my shoulder for a minute.
That was her choice. It meant more because it was.

What did Gargi say when Zeenat went to hug her?
“Not now. Please.”
How did Zeenat feel when Gargi stepped back?
Zeenat felt hurt for a second, having only wanted to help.
What did Zeenat do that showed respect for Gargi's boundary?
Zeenat dropped the hug, offered to be there, and let Gargi choose when to come close.
How might Gargi feel about Zeenat respecting her no?
She likely felt safe and cared for, which is why she chose to lean on Zeenat later.
I wish I can sleep earlier, but my neighbours are noisy. What is wrong?

I wish I could sleep earlier, but my neighbours are noisy.
Why: "I wish" about now needs a past form (could).

After the movie, Indu's friends spilled out of the Pune multiplex, buzzing. "Best film of the year!" said Vijay. "That ending!" everyone agreed. Indu, fifteen, had found it slow and confusing; she'd checked the time twice. She opened her mouth to say so, then closed it. Six faces, all glowing. Maybe she'd missed something. On the auto home they replayed scenes, and Indu laughed at the right moments. By the time she got home, she was telling her mother it was "really deep." Lying in bed, she tried to remember what she'd actually thought during the film. She couldn't quite find it anymore. Had she changed her mind, or had she just gone quiet so long that her own opinion had faded?

How many times had Indu checked the time during the film?
She'd checked the time twice.
What was Indu feeling lying in bed?
Indu felt confused and unsure, unable to tell whether she had truly changed her mind or just gone quiet.
What could Indu try next time she disagrees with friends?
She could say something small and honest, like "I found it slow, but the ending was good," so her own view doesn't fade.
How might Vijay react if Indu said she found the film slow?
Vijay might be surprised but could accept it, and might even admit a slow part himself.
Why can we not make a circle with ice-cream sticks?

Answer: A circle has no straight sides. Its edge is one curved line.

Give the child a piece of string or a bangle. A circle and an oval are made of a curved line, so they have 0 sides and 0 corners. Run a finger round a bangle: it never turns a corner.

Dr. Seema Rao had fifteen minutes between her 2 o'clock and 3 o'clock classes, and Manjula had run through the rain from the hostel to catch them. Her dissertation chapter was due tomorrow, and the professor's last comment had been one line in red: "Your argument hides behind other people's quotes."
For a week Manjula had avoided her corridor. It felt easier to rewrite blindly than to ask.
Now she stood at the door, dripping. "Ma'am, I have two questions. I'll be quick."
Dr. Rao glanced at the clock. "Go."
"When you said my argument hides, do you mean fewer quotes, or my own claim first?"
"Your own claim first. Then the quotes serve it."
"And the second section, is it off-topic?"
"Yes. Cut it."
Manjula didn't argue. She wrote both answers down and was gone by 2:52. That night she rewrote the opening in her own words. The next comment, a week later, was also in red: "Better. Now push further."

How long did Dr. Rao have between classes?
Fifteen minutes.
Why had Manjula avoided Dr. Rao's corridor for a week?
She felt afraid and intimidated by the red comment, and rewriting blindly seemed easier than asking.
What did Manjula do that respected the professor's time?
She came with exactly two clear questions, accepted the correction without arguing, wrote it down, and left by 2:52.
How might Dr. Rao see Manjula's visit?
As serious and efficient; the later comment "Better. Now push further." shows she values the effort.
Who laid the first brick of our school building?
I wouldn't know that name, since it's a local record. The school's old files or a founder's day booklet may say.

Note, Class 6 science charts. Group C's chart on the water cycle is neat, but during work time Kishore sat sharpening one pencil for a long stretch while three others cut, pasted and labelled. When I asked, Kishore said, "They are doing it fine, and the chart gets one mark for all of us anyway." The other three did not object; one glared. How many labels had Kishore written by the end of the period?
Kishore had written eleven labels by the end of the period.

Kishore believed that shared credit made doing less safe, and felt that effort would go unnoticed; the pencil-sharpening shows avoidance rather than refusal.

Vijay Sir noted each child's part on a tick sheet and gave Kishore a named task, labels, so individual effort could be seen without punishment.

Hana sold 4/7 of her stamp collection for $28. How much would she have earned from selling the entire collection?

Hana sold 4/7 of her collection for $28, so 1/7 of her collection represents: 28/4 = $7.
And as a result, the entire collection represents: 7 * 7 = $49.
The answer is 49.

What is Pablo feeling as he studies the two papers?
He is torn: the town holds his grandmother's voice and the smell of the press, while the firm is the first place that asked for his ideas.

He signed the contract but offered his uncle harvest help every autumn and a look at the press's wiring, so he gave something to each place.

After she failed the first programming test at the polytechnic in Hassan, Chandrika stopped opening the lab computer unless she had to. "Coding isn't for people like me," she told Pranav at the tea stall by the bus stand.
Pranav didn't argue. He tore a page from his notebook. "One tiny problem a day. Ten minutes. Reverse a word, add two numbers, anything. Write it here when it works."
On the first day she printed her name backwards and felt silly writing it down. On the second, a program that sorted even numbers from odd. By the third week the page had nineteen lines, and she had moved it to the inside cover of her lab file.
On the day of the retest, waiting outside the lab, she ran her finger down the list. Twenty-six things that worked. She went in.

What was Chandrika's first tiny problem?
She printed her name backwards.
What did Chandrika feel as she ran her finger down the list?
She felt steadier and more confident; twenty-six working programs were evidence against "coding isn't for people like me".
Why did Pranav's plan work?
Ten-minute problems were small enough to finish every day, and writing each win down built a visible record of skill that pushed her to the next step.
How might Pranav feel watching Chandrika walk into the retest?
Pranav would likely feel glad and relieved that his quiet suggestion helped her find her confidence again. 🙂
Why do we sort dark and light clothes before washing?
Dye can run from dark clothes. Because dark clothes can let out some dye in the water, the dye could stain light clothes if they are washed together.

March. At his appraisal, Tushar heard "meets expectations" for the second year running. He nodded, went back to his desk, and felt stuck. He had assumed good work would get noticed on its own.
April. He booked thirty minutes with his manager, Arohi, and asked the question he had been avoiding: "What would I need to show to be considered for team lead next year?" Arohi was blunt. "Your analysis is strong. But nobody outside our team knows you exist. And you never present your own work." It stung. He wrote it all down.
October. Tushar had presented at three cross-team reviews, shakily at first. He had asked Arohi to mention his name when leads were discussed, and she had. The head of product now stopped by his desk with questions. At the mid-year check-in, Arohi said, "I can make the case now."

What rating did Tushar get for the second year running?
Meets expectations.
What was Tushar feeling when Arohi said nobody outside the team knew he existed?
Tushar felt stung and a bit embarrassed, but wrote it down, choosing to learn from it.
Which steps turned feedback into a promotion plan?
Asking exactly what team lead would need, presenting his work at cross-team reviews, and asking Arohi to speak for him when leads were discussed.
How might Arohi see Tushar by October?
Arohi sees him as visible and ready, and feels confident enough to make the case for his promotion.

Three children spotted the jar of sweets on the top shelf.

Vijay went straight to the kitchen door. "Papa, can you get the jar down?" he said, pointing. His father lifted it down, gave each child one, and put it back.

Deepak rose onto his toes, arms straight up, and stretched. He stretched again and pulled at the air. "If I try hard, my arms will get long," Deepak said. The jar stayed where it was.

Tushar had a different plan. He hauled a chair over to the cupboard and climbed on it. Still too short. He fetched a stool and put it on the chair. Halfway up, the whole stack began to wobble. Tushar's tummy dropped. He climbed down at once and shouted, "Mama! Come, please!" Mama came running, steadied the chair, and took the jar down herself.

What did Tushar put on the chair?
Tushar put a stool on the chair.
How did Vijay's way of reaching the jar differ from Tushar's, and which was safer?
Vijay asked his father, which was quick and safe, while Tushar stacked a stool on a chair and it wobbled until he climbed down and called for help.
What was Tushar feeling when the stack wobbled?
Fear, since his tummy dropped and he climbed down at once.
What could Deepak try instead of stretching?
Deepak could look at how far the jar is and ask a grown-up to get it.

Nikita, beta, your Tanuja masi will tell you something she's never told anyone. When I was twenty-five, two years married, your uncle and I stopped holding hands. Not after a fight. It just stopped.
He came home, ate, watched the news. I came home, cooked, read. He didn't ask about my school, the children I taught, the head who shouted at me. I didn't ask about his shop. We slept in the same bed like two passengers on a night bus.
I have never been so lonely, beta. Not before marriage, not after your grandmother died. Lonely with a man sitting one metre away.
And I said nothing for almost a year. I was afraid that if I opened my mouth, a big, ugly talk would come out, and I didn't have the strength for it.
So when you say "everything's fine" in that small voice, I hear myself.

How long did Tanuja say nothing?
Tanuja said nothing for almost a year.
Why did Tanuja stay silent despite feeling so lonely?
Tanuja was afraid a big, ugly talk would come out and didn't feel strong enough for it.
What might Tanuja's story help Nikita do?
It might help Nikita notice the same quiet distance and speak up sooner, instead of saying 'everything's fine' in a small voice.
How might Tanuja's husband have seen those years?
He may have thought their life was calm and normal, not realising his wife felt lonely beside him every night.
Present perfect, please: Meena finished her homework.
Meena has finished her homework.
I get angry very fast, and then I say things I regret.
Many people struggle with that. Does it usually happen at home, at school, or everywhere?
Mostly at home, with my brother.
A pause can help. When you feel the anger rise, take a slow breath and count to ten before you speak. If you need to, step out of the room for a minute.
What if I'm too angry to stop?
Then walk away and say, 'I need a break.' That's not running away, it's protecting the conversation. Come back when you've calmed down.
And if I've already said something mean?
Apologise briefly and honestly, like, 'I'm sorry I said that. I was angry.' Then try the pause next time. If it keeps happening, a trusted adult or school counsellor can help.

In their Mumbai flat, Vasudha had been waiting for placement results for two weeks. She refreshed her email constantly, even at meals. She sighed loudly at every notification. Her younger sister Aditi, in first year, was fine at first. Then Aditi noticed she was refreshing her own email too, though she wasn't waiting for anything. Her heart jumped at every ping. She started biting her nails. One evening she said, "Didi, I think your worry is getting into me." Vasudha looked up, startled, then laughed shakily. "Mine's getting into me too." They talked for a long time on the balcony. Vasudha admitted she was terrified. Aditi admitted she didn't even know what she was scared of. They agreed on a small routine: phones in the basket during dinner, and a walk together after. The next week, Aditi stopped refreshing her email.

Two weeks.

What helped both sisters?
Talking honestly on the balcony and agreeing on a simple routine, phones away at dinner and a walk after, eased the tension.

At bedtime my head got busy. What if I failed the maths test? What if Mummy's scooter slipped in the rain on the way home from work? I listened for her key in the door and my stomach felt like a tight fist.

Disha didi said worries try to help, but they ring too many bells. So we made a plan. Mummy would text Disha didi when she left the office. We'd read one chapter, the same time every night. Then I'd say three things I liked about the day.

Some nights I still worried, but hearing "She's on her way" and then the key in the door made the fist let go.

What was it like for Disha didi to help with the night worries?
Disha didi probably felt protective and caring, and relieved when the plan helped the fist let go.

Johan has a ten-bedroom house with 8 walls in each room. He paints 3/5 of the rooms in the house green and paints the rest of the rooms with purple color. How many walls in the house did he paint purple?

Since Cristian's house has ten rooms, he painted 3/5*10 = 6 rooms with green color.
The number of rooms he painted with purple is 10-6 = 4 rooms.
Since each room in the house has eight walls, the number of walls painted purple is 8*4= 32.
The answer is 32.
An opera house has 150 rows; each row has ten seats. The ticket costs $10 per show. How much did the opera house earn from one of the shows if 20% of the seats were not taken?

The opera house has 150 x 10 = 1500 seats.
There are 1500 x 20/100 = 300 seats that were not taken.
The total number of seats taken was 1500 - 300 = 1200.
Therefore, the opera house earned $10 x 1200 = $12000 from one of the shows.
The answer is 12000.

In a survey, 72 students chose their favourite sport: cricket 30, football 18, kabaddi 12, badminton 9, chess 3. Find the pie chart angles, and write each sport as a fraction and a percentage of the whole.

Answer: cricket 150 degrees, football 90 degrees, kabaddi 60 degrees, badminton 45 degrees, chess 15 degrees.

One student gets 360 degrees / 72 = 5 degrees. Cricket 30 x 5 degrees = 150 degrees, football 18 x 5 degrees = 90 degrees, kabaddi 12 x 5 degrees = 60 degrees, badminton 9 x 5 degrees = 45 degrees, chess 3 x 5 degrees = 15 degrees. Check: 150 + 90 + 60 + 45 + 15 = 360. Each sector is a FRACTION of 360 degrees: football 90 degrees is 90/360 = 1/4 of the circle, so 25% of students; badminton 45/360 = 1/8 = 12.5%; cricket 150/360 = 5/12, about 41.7%. So a pie chart is a picture of fractions. Common mistake: using 100 instead of 360 (that gives percentages, not angles).

When she finally shut the book, she went straight to the kitchen and ate three of the nimki Ma had kept for guests. Then Bidisha, her little sister, asked to borrow the red crayon, and Nirmala shouted, "No! Get your own!" and slammed the bedroom door.
Ma found her on the bed ten minutes later, face in the pillow. "Tired?"
"My head's full," Nirmala mumbled.
Ma sat down. "Long sums make everyone a bit short-tempered. Next time, a break halfway, and a snack that's allowed." Nirmala peeked out and nodded.

How many sums did Nirmala do in the hour?
Twenty.
Why did Nirmala snap at Bidisha over a crayon?
After an hour of hard sums Nirmala felt worn out and irritable, her "head full", so small things felt like too much and her patience was gone.
What could help Nirmala next time?
As Ma says, a break halfway and an allowed snack; spacing out hard work may help her stay patient, whatever the exact reason tiredness makes it harder.
How might Bidisha feel when the door slams?

Going only by the text, how does Biddy help the narrator try to become uncommon?

That evening Biddy begins their special agreement by passing on information from her catalogue of Prices, under moist sugar. She also lends a large old English D, copied from a newspaper heading, which the narrator took for a buckle design.

Why do people stand in a line to enter a bus?
How can I pack for a short trip?
Please define "befallen".
What is wrong with this sentence? "I could of come earlier."
What is the price of a plane ticket to Goa next week?

1. Queuing lets people board one at a time. Because nobody has to push, boarding is fair and safer.
2. Make a list, and take only what you need for each day. Put important things like tickets in an easy-to-reach pocket.
3. It is the past participle of "befall", a verb meaning to happen to someone, usually something bad.
4. Fixed: I could have come earlier. Why: say "could have"; "of" only sounds like "'ve".
5. I don't know that. Fares change often and I can't see them. Look at the airline's official website for today's fare.

Thursday: Raghav notices her picking up single grains with her thumb and first finger, one at a time, and dropping them into a steel bowl.

Diwali night: she carries the bowl to the rangoli, carefully places three grains in the middle, and looks up at Raghav, beaming.

The career counselling room at the community centre had one fan and a whiteboard covered in someone else's arrows. Joseph, twenty-five, sat across from Reena, the volunteer counsellor, and listed his regrets fast, as if he had rehearsed them: not doing hotel management, two years in a job he disliked, losing touch with his cricket team. Reena handed him the marker. 'Two boxes. Fixable. Not fixable.' He hesitated over hotel management, then wrote it under Fixable; there were evening diplomas. The two years already gone went under Not fixable. The cricket team: Fixable, one phone call. 'Now,' Reena said, 'forget what an uncle at a wedding would want. What should your ordinary Tuesday look like?' Joseph took a long time. 'Cooking for people. Being outside part of the day. Friends.' He looked at the board. 'That's not that far away.'

Which regret did Joseph put under Not fixable?
The two years already gone at the job.
What does Joseph's fast, rehearsed list suggest about how he felt coming in?
It suggests he had been replaying his regrets often and felt weighed down by a vague dread he had not yet sorted.
How does Reena's question about an ordinary Tuesday help Joseph?
It moves him away from what others expect and towards what he values (cooking, being outside, friends), which gives him a direction.
What might Reena notice as Joseph sorts the board?
Reena likely sees him slow down and grow more hopeful as the fixable regrets pile up, a sign the exercise is working 🙂
Rohan says, "20 is odd, because it is a big number." Is he right?

Answer: No. 20 is even: 10 pairs, none left over; its last digit is 0.

Even and odd have nothing to do with big or small. 1 is odd and small; 20 is even and big. Always check by pairing or by the last digit.

Every evening after Mats fell asleep, Sofia opened a small green notebook at the kitchen table in their Copenhagen flat. She wrote the date and only facts.
14 May: M said I never asked him to fetch Mum from the station. I asked at breakfast and texted at 11.
16 May: M said I screamed. I said "please stop" twice, not loud.
The notebook lived in her work bag, not at home.
On Saturdays she walked along the harbour with her old friend Ulla. Today she read out three entries and asked, "Am I being unfair?"
Ulla listened to all of it. "No. This matches what you've told me each week, and what I saw at your birthday." She squeezed Sofia's arm. "Would you talk to someone at the counselling centre too? I'll look up the number with you."
Sofia nodded. For the first time in months, her memory felt like solid ground.

Where did Sofia keep the notebook?
The notebook lived in her work bag, not at home.
How did Sofia feel after Ulla's reply?
She felt steadier and relieved; for the first time in months, her memory felt like solid ground.
Which of Sofia's choices protected her sense of reality?
Writing only dated facts in private, checking them with Ulla, and agreeing to contact the counselling centre gave her anchors outside Mats's version of events.
How does Ulla see the notebook entries?
Ulla sees them as matching what Sofia has said each week and what she saw herself, so she trusts Sofia's account and offers practical help.

That evening I made myself be honest: I was jealous, plain and simple. So I wrote down what Gopika actually did. She organised the inter-house quiz from scratch. She learnt the names of every Class 6 kid. I hadn't done either.

This term I'm running the sports day sign-ups. It's not a badge. It's practice.

I'm Asif. In my final year of the law diploma, I nearly did something I'd have regretted for years.

Our course had a strict rule: essays must be our own, and any AI use must be declared. I had a moot-court essay due, a family wedding, and no time. The AI produced a clean essay in minutes. I read it and thought, this is better than anything I'd write.

My friend Manoj found me staring at the submit button. "Can you explain paragraph three?"

I couldn't. Not really.

"Then in the moot court, when the judge asks you about it, what'll you say?"

That hit hard. I asked for a two-day extension, explaining the wedding. I wrote the essay myself, using the AI only to check grammar, and declared that.

My grade was lower than the AI's essay would have got. But at the moot court I answered every question on it. I'd have been exposed in a minute otherwise.

A two-day extension.

I'm Shreya, and I share a desk with Nazia in the school admissions office. This March her nephew applied for Class 1 here. The waiting list was long, and her sister called her every evening. Once, from across the room, I heard Nazia say on the phone, "Apa, I will fill his form with you, I will pay the fee, I will pick him up every day if he gets in. But I will not move his name up the list." Her voice was gentle and very firm. Her sister must have said something sharp, because Nazia was quiet for a while and then said, "There are forty other families waiting. They trust this list." I don't know how hard it was for her. She went home early that day. But every Saturday she sat with her nephew practising his letters, and when his name came up fairly in May, she brought laddoos for the whole office.

How many other families were waiting on the list, according to Nazia?
Forty other families were waiting.

Priya grouped the heights of her classmates into classes 140 to 145, 145 to 150, 150 to 155 cm. Her friend asked, "Where does a height of exactly 145 cm go?" How should the classes be written?

Answer: As 140 <= h < 145, 145 <= h < 150, 150 <= h < 155. Then 145 cm goes in the class 145 <= h < 150.

Height is CONTINUOUS: it can be 145.3 cm or 149.99 cm, so there must be no gaps between classes, and every height must belong to exactly ONE class. "140 to 145" and "145 to 150" OVERLAP at 145. Using inequalities fixes it: 140 <= h < 145 means "at least 140 but less than 145". The class width is 145 - 140 = 5 cm for every class and the midpoint of the first class is (140 + 145) / 2 = 142.5 cm. For discrete data such as marks, classes like 10 to 19 and 20 to 29 are fine because no mark lies between 19 and 20. Common mistake: classes like 140 to 144, 145 to 149 for heights, which leave out 144.5.
Now you try: two phone towers A and B each cover 20 km. Which region is covered by both?

Leah earned $28 working odd jobs around the neighborhood. She spent a seventh of it on a milkshake and put half of the rest in her savings account. She left the remaining money in her wallet. Her dog got ahold of her wallet and shredded all the money inside but $1. How many dollars did Leah lose?

Leah spent 28 / 7 = $4 on a milkshake.
She had 28 - 4 = $24 left.
She put half in her savings account and half in her wallet, so she had 24 / 2 = $12 in her wallet.
Her dog shredded all the money in her wallet but $1, so Leah lost 12 - 1 = $11.
The answer is 11.

At the bus stop in Accra every morning, the same young woman waited with paint on her fingers and a sketchbook under her arm. She never looked up.
"I've worked her out," Nkechi told Nour. "She's a shy painter who teaches art at a primary school and sells her work at the Saturday market."

messages.content: A plumber is trying to decide which of three different jobs he should take to make the most money.  The first job involves fixing three toilets and three sinks at an apartment complex.  The second involves two toilets and five sinks at a different apartment complex.  The third involves fixing one toilet, two showers and three sinks at a third apartment complex.  If the plumber charges $30 to fix a sink, $40 to fix a shower and $50 to fix a toilet, what is the most money the plumber can earn if he can only choose one of these three jobs?

If the plumber chooses the first job, he would earn 3*50 + 3*30 = $240.
If he chooses the second, he'd earn 2*50 + 5*30 = $250.
If he chooses the third, he'd earn 50 + 2*40 + 3*30 = $220.
Therefore, the most money he can earn from one of these jobs is $250.
The answer is 250.
Why do aluminium foil sheets crinkle and hold their shape?

"What if your daughter's school calls again?"

"I've told my wife to call twice if it's urgent. That comes through."

He wrote without stopping till the timer rang. Then ten minutes: he answered all his messages in one go, called the school back, and made tea. Then another fifty-minute block.

At 4:15 he sent the report. Karthik, still halfway through his own, sighed. "How?"

"Fewer switches," Pradeep said. "That's all."

How long was each of Pradeep's work blocks?
Fifty minutes.
How does Pradeep seem to feel while working in blocks?
He seems calm and in control, trusting that urgent calls will still reach him, so he can focus fully.
What in Pradeep's approach could Karthik copy?
Karthik could silence notifications, work in timed single-task blocks and answer messages together during short breaks.
How might Karthik feel when Pradeep finishes early?
Karthik probably feels a bit envious and curious, wondering how to work the same way.

Nazia, come here. Your Nani Ishita has something to tell you before your board exams. In my Class 12, my whole hostel room crammed all night. I kept three things: bed at a fixed hour, a walk to the mango tree after dinner, and a proper meal. My friends laughed at me, and I felt silly for a day, but I kept my three. On the morning of the physics paper, half of them stared at the questions with blank faces. I remembered the derivation as if it were written on the wall. I am not saying study less. I am saying the hour you save by not sleeping is often the hour you lose in the exam hall. Take your walk, beta.

Nani Ishita tells Nazia that in Class 12, while her roommates crammed all night, she kept a fixed bedtime, an evening walk and a proper meal. In the physics exam many roommates went blank while she remembered the derivation, so she tells Nazia to keep her walk.

In the Kolkata flat, Minakshi, two, was sobbing on the floor because her dupatta-doll's hair was 'wrong'. Her friend Elizabeth, three, patted her head, puzzled. Then Minakshi cried because Elizabeth patted her. Mumma checked the time: past lunch. She brought two bowls of dal-rice. Minakshi ate fast, hiccuping. Her dupatta-doll's hair being 'wrong'.

Minakshi was hungry, which made her upset and cranky over small things.

That it was past lunch, and feeding Minakshi changed her mood quickly.

Last term I was learning a sitar piece that I thought I was playing perfectly. I'm Aparna. My brother Jatin said something sounded "wobbly", but he couldn't say where. So one evening I borrowed Amma's phone, propped it on the pillow and recorded myself. Listening back was awful and useful at the same time. Every time I moved from Sa up to Ga, I slowed down, like a cycle going uphill. I hadn't heard it while playing because I was busy with my fingers. After that I practised only those two notes for three days, back and forth, counting aloud. Then I recorded again. The uphill bit had become flat road.

Where did Aparna prop the phone?
On the pillow.
How did listening back feel to Aparna?
Awful and useful at once: uncomfortable to hear, but a relief to find exactly where the problem was.
What else could Aparna try with the recordings?
Keep the old and new recordings to compare, or play along with a steady clap to keep the beat.
How might Jatin feel about his 'wobbly' comment now?
Jatin's vague comment led to the fix, so Jatin might feel useful and pleased.

The school bus had been stuck in the rain for forty minutes, wipers thumping, thirty children squashed together. Bhupen, eleven, stood up in the aisle. "Okay, okay, what did the toilet say to the toilet paper?"
"We've heard it," said Nirmala from the next seat, without looking up.
"You haven't heard THIS version." He told it, with a burp at the end.
Half the bus groaned. Nirmala said, "Bhupen. Third time today."
He sat down, a bit red. Then he leaned over. "What if I did it quieter, only for the back row? They haven't heard it yet."
"That could work," said Nirmala, and she smiled for the first time since they'd stopped.
He told it in a low voice to the back row, and they laughed.

How long had the school bus been stuck in the rain?
It had been stuck for forty minutes.
What was Bhupen feeling when the half of the bus groaned and Nirmala said it was the third time?
Bhupen felt embarrassed and a little deflated, going red. He wanted the laugh he expected.
What did Bhupen do that turned the groans into useful feedback?
Bhupen adjusted his joke to a smaller audience, telling it quietly to the back row who had not heard it. He listened to the groans and changed.
How might Nirmala have felt about hearing the same joke again on a long, wet ride?
Nirmala was probably tired and fed up, as her reply shows, but she smiled when Bhupen listened and found a fix.

With the design submission two days away and Mehul home with fever, the four of them were already short of hands. At 10 p.m. Binita looked around the studio: Ananya cutting foam board, Kiran fixing the model's roof, and Pankaj on the sofa, laptop open to the same slide he'd opened at six. "Almost done with the render," he said. He'd said that yesterday too.
Nobody answered. Pankaj had been their friend since first year; he'd sat with Kiran through a whole night at the hospital once. Calling him out felt like kicking someone who had helped you.
Binita watched Ananya slice the board harder than needed. Kiran didn't look up. At midnight Ananya muttered, "Some of us are doing a four-person job," to no one in particular. Pankaj laughed as if it were a joke. Kiran's jaw tightened. The model would get finished, Binita thought, but something in the group was starting to crack.

Who was home with fever?
Mehul was home with fever.
How does Binita feel watching the silent studio?
Binita feels uneasy and torn: Pankaj is a loyal old friend, but the unfairness is clearly straining the others.
How could the group raise it without attacking the friendship?
One of them, perhaps Binita, could talk to Pankaj privately, say what is missing and ask what is going on before resentment grows.
What is the night like for Ananya?
Ananya is frustrated and resentful, slicing the board hard and finally muttering about a four-person job.

"Ammi, up! Up!" Irfan tugged at Afreen's dupatta, whining.
"Beta, I'm cooking. Go play with your truck."
"No truck!" He flopped against her legs, cheeks flushed.
Abbu came in from the heat. "He's been cranky since the bazaar. Sleepy too."
"It's this weather," Afreen said. Then she stopped. "When did he last drink?"
Abbu filled the little steel cup. Irfan gulped it down and held it out. "More!"
"If he stays droopy, we'll ring the doctor," Abbu said.

Where had Irfan been before he got cranky?
The bazaar.
What was Irfan feeling when he tugged at Afreen's dupatta?
He felt uncomfortable and needy but could not say he was thirsty, so he whined and clung.
What simple step helped, and what could the family do on the next hot day?
Giving him water; on hot, busy days they could offer his cup regularly instead of waiting for the fussing.
How did Afreen explain the whining at first?
She put it down to the weather, until she stopped and wondered when he had last had a drink.

Milly and Floretta are having a water balloon fight in their garden. They use 3 packs of their own water balloons and also use 2 packs of a neighbor's water balloons. Each pack of water balloons contains 6 balloons. Milly and Floretta fill all of the balloons then split them evenly, but Milly takes an extra 7 balloons when Floretta isn't looking. How many water balloons is Floretta left with?

Milly and Floretta have a total of 3 packs of their own water balloons + 2 packs of the neighbor's water balloons = 5 packs of water balloons.
So there is a total of 5 packs of water balloons * 6 balloons per pack of water balloons = 30 water balloons available.
As they split them evenly, they each have 30 water balloons / 2 = 15 water balloons.
After Milly steals some balloons, Floretta is left with 15 - 7 = 8 water balloons.
The answer is 8.

For the data in D5, find the residuals (observed y - predicted y) and the sum of squared residuals for the least-squares line y = 44.3 + 3.45x and for a line drawn by eye, y = 45 + 3x. Which fits better?

Answer: Least squares: residuals 0.8, -1.1, 1, -1.9, 1.2; sum of squares = 7.9. By eye: residuals 1, 0, 3, 1, 5; sum of squares = 36. The least-squares line fits better.

A RESIDUAL is the vertical gap between a point and the line: positive if the point is above the line, negative if below. For x = 2 the least-squares line predicts 51.2, the actual mark is 52, so the residual is 0.8. The least-squares residuals always add up to 0 (the line goes through the mean point), and their squares have the smallest possible total: 7.9 here, against 36 for the eye line. We square the residuals for the same reason as in the variance: positive and negative gaps would otherwise cancel. A pattern in the residuals (for example all positive at both ends and negative in the middle) warns that a curve would fit better than a line.

Outside the tea shop in the kasba, Jeevan picked up a crumpled twenty-rupee note. "Finders keepers!" said Rashmi, and two other kids joined in. "Chips! Chips!" Jeevan's fingers closed around the note. He wanted them to like him, and he also knew it was somebody's. "Let's ask the tea shop uncle if anyone lost it," he said, his voice a little shaky. A groan went up and someone rolled their eyes, but Rashmi shrugged. "Fine, ask." Later, when the others had run ahead, Rashmi said quietly, "I didn't feel right about it either."

What kind of note did Jeevan pick up?
He picked up a crumpled twenty-rupee note.
Why was Jeevan's voice shaky when he suggested asking the tea shop uncle?
He was torn between wanting the group to like him and knowing the note belonged to somebody, and he may have feared their reaction.
What small step let Jeevan say no without a fight?
He offered a simple alternative, asking the tea shop uncle whether anyone had lost it, instead of lecturing his friends.
How might Rashmi have seen that moment?
Rashmi joined the cheer at first, but later admitted not feeling right about it either, so was probably quietly relieved that someone said it.
I have a small budget and I want to buy a birthday gift for a classmate.
A gift does not have to cost much. What does your classmate like?
They like drawing and cricket.
Then a nice sketchbook or a set of coloured pencils would suit the first interest. For cricket, a small poster or a sports magazine could work.
Which is better?
If you are unsure, take the drawing gift. Art supplies are useful whether or not they follow cricket, and people use them for a long time. A handwritten card makes it more personal.
Do I need to wrap it?
It is not necessary, but wrapping makes a gift feel special. Plain paper with a drawing on it costs almost nothing. Add a short message on the card to finish.

The overnight train to Kochi was packed and noisy, and Thomas, twenty-six, had his five-year-old son Chinmay tucked beside him on the lower berth. When the ticket checker smiled and asked, 'What's your name, little one?' Thomas answered, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.' Chinmay pressed into his father's side. Across the aisle, three children were playing snap. 'Want to play?' a girl called. 'He doesn't like joining in,' Thomas said. Then his office phone rang, and it was his boss, and the connection kept dropping. He went to the door end of the coach to hear. It took twenty minutes. When he came back, Chinmay was sitting cross-legged in the middle of the other berth, slapping cards down. 'I'm Chinmay! I won two!' Thomas stood in the aisle holding his phone, suddenly unsure which of them had been shy.

What did Thomas tell the ticket checker?
Thomas said, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.'
What was Thomas feeling when he came back and saw Chinmay playing?
He felt surprised and unsure, starting to wonder whether the 'shy one' label was really about Chinmay or about his own belief.
What could Thomas try the next time someone asks Chinmay a question?
He could wait and let Chinmay answer for himself, and let him decide whether to join games, instead of saying no for him.
How might the girl who invited Chinmay see him now?
She probably sees him as a fun, chatty player who likes winning at snap, not a shy child at all.

Sunday night

Signed the offer today! I'm moving to Bengaluru next month to join the start-up. I'm so excited I can barely sleep.

But I'm also doing the boring stuff. Ankita laughed at me today because I made a list.

1. Keep some savings aside, untouched, for emergencies. Asked Abbu's CA friend how to think about it.
2. Ask the start-up to put the offer terms in writing.
3. Keep in touch with two other companies that interviewed me, just in case.
4. Give myself three extra weeks to settle in before expecting to love it.

Ankita said, "Aren't you optimistic?" I am! I really believe it will be great.

But if something goes wrong, I want it to be a bump in the plan, not a crash in me.

Hope, but ready. That's the plan.

Nazia

Where is Nazia moving next month?
I'm moving to Bengaluru next month to join the start-up.
How does Nazia feel about the new job?
Nazia feels very excited and hopeful, while also calm because of the backup list.
Why is Nazia's list a wise addition to optimism?
The list adds savings, written terms, backup contacts and extra time, so a setback would be a bump in the plan rather than a crash.
How might Ankita see Nazia's list?
Ankita seems amused at first, perhaps thinking lists mean worry, but may come to see it as smart preparation.

Teacher's note, Eid week, playground duty
Rehana (Class 6) and her younger sister Rukhsar (Class 3) arrived not speaking, after a fight over a hair clip that morning. At lunch, a bigger boy from Class 7 grabbed Rukhsar's tiffin and held it over her head. Rehana came across the playground at a run, stood between them and said, "Give it back. Now." Her voice was shaking, but she did not move. The boy handed it back. Rehana then walked off without a word to her sister, still sulking. I spoke to the Class 7 boy and informed his class teacher and our counsellor the same afternoon. I also told Rehana privately that she was brave, and that next time she can call a teacher too.
Farah, playground duty

What did the two sisters fight over that morning?
A hair clip.
How did Rehana feel as she stood between the boy and Rukhsar?
She felt scared, her voice shaking, but fiercely protective of her sister despite still being angry about the morning.
What did Farah do next, and why was it right?
Farah spoke to the Class 7 boy and told his class teacher and the counsellor the same afternoon, and reminded Rehana she can call a teacher too, so she need not face bullies alone.
How might Rukhsar feel after Rehana rescued her tiffin?
Rukhsar might feel grateful and safe, and a little confused, since her sister protected her but still walked off sulking.

In the Accra school corridor, Paulo held out his phone to Kwame. "Look. I wasn't going to show you, but you should know."
The screen showed a new group chat called "no Kwame". Someone from his class had shared screenshots of Kwame's messages from the class chat, with jokes underneath. Kwame read a line about his football boots and felt his ears go hot. Names he knew, people he had sat with at lunch.
"Thank you for telling me," Kwame said, voice low. He did not go into the class chat. At lunch he went straight to Mr Boateng, the form teacher, and said, "Something happened. Can I show you?"

What was the new group chat called?
The new group chat was called "no Kwame".
What was Kwame feeling as he read the screenshots and the jokes underneath?
Kwame felt hurt and embarrassed. The hot ears and low voice show how it stung to see people laughing behind his back.
What did Kwame choose to do instead of answering in the class chat?
Kwame thanked Paulo and went to his form teacher, Mr Boateng, and asked to show what had happened. Telling a trusted adult kept things from getting worse.
What might it have been like for Paulo to show Kwame the phone?
Paulo was probably nervous but caring, since Paulo said "you should know". Showing something painful took courage and trust in Kwame.

At the municipal engineering office in Nagpur, Darshan's calendar had a new block every morning: 9:00 to 11:00, "Drainage report. No meetings." He had noticed his best thinking came before lunch; by four he was reading the same line three times.
Arnab leaned over the partition at 9:15. "Chai and gossip?"
"At eleven," Darshan said, not looking up. "This is my good-brain time."
"Your what?"
"For months I did emails in the morning and the report at night, then called myself lazy when it didn't get done. It wasn't laziness. I was doing the hardest thing when I was emptiest."
He had done the same with evenings: on Sundays he cooked three dinners and laid out his gym clothes, so after work there was nothing to decide.
At eleven the report section was done. He went for chai with Arnab and let himself enjoy it.

What was blocked on Darshan's calendar from 9:00 to 11:00?
"Drainage report. No meetings."
How does Darshan now feel about his past unfinished reports?
Darshan seems relieved of the old self-blame; he no longer sees himself as lazy, understanding he was doing the hardest work when he was emptiest.
Which two changes help Darshan most, and why?
Putting the hardest task in his best morning hours, and cooking and laying out gym clothes on Sunday so evenings need no decisions; both respect his energy limits instead of blaming his character.
How might Arnab react to "good-brain time"?
Arnab seems amused and puzzled at first, but still gets his chai at eleven with a friend who is actually relaxed. 😄

"You're going for a walk? Now? The test is Friday," Yusuf said, looking up from his desk in the room they shared at their uncle's house.

Anirban tied his shoes. "Thirty minutes. Every day at six. It's in the calendar now."

"Since when do you schedule walks?"

"Since last week, when I fell asleep on the chemistry book and woke up with ink on my face." Anirban showed him his phone calendar. Blocks of study, coaching, meals. And in green: "Walk, 6:00 to 6:30." And on Sunday: "Free, 2 pm to 7 pm. No books."

"That's five hours of nothing."

"It's not nothing. That's when my brain stops buzzing." Anirban shrugged. "Before, I only rested when I'd 'earned' it, and I never earned it. So I was never rested."

Yusuf looked at his own screen, crowded with red. "Can you send me that?"

What time is Anirban's daily walk?
From 6:00 to 6:30, every day.
How did Anirban seem to feel before he started scheduling rest?
Anirban felt exhausted and worn out, falling asleep on the chemistry book and never feeling rested.
What else could Anirban add to the schedule?
He could add a fixed bedtime next to the walk, since steady sleep also supports the rest he is protecting.
How does the idea look to Yusuf by the end?
Yusuf moves from doubting it to wanting a copy, as his own crowded red calendar makes Anirban's plan appealing.

Karthik, you asked how I handled the swap-crazy kids in my Class 4. Let me tell you about Bilal. It was Christmas fair week, and the children were making paper stars to sell. Bilal would give glue only for glitter, glitter only for scissors, every deal exact. Then little Asha, whose father was in hospital, came with nothing. Bilal said, 'Pay me a sticker and you can use my glue.' She had no stickers. I didn't scold him. Children like fairness; it's a good start. I just crouched beside him and asked, 'Bilal, how would you feel if nobody shared with you, right when your papa was sick?' He looked at Asha for a long moment. Then he pushed the glue across. 'Harsha Ma'am, is that allowed?' I told him it was the kindest thing on that table all week.

What did Bilal ask Asha to pay for using his glue?
A sticker.
What might Bilal have felt looking at Asha for a long moment?
Bilal probably felt a pang of sympathy, imagining how lonely it would be if nobody shared while his papa was sick.
Harsha chose to crouch beside Bilal and ask a question instead of scolding. Why was that a good turning point?
It respected Bilal's instinct for fairness while turning his attention to Asha's feelings, so he chose to share on his own.
How might Asha have felt when the glue was pushed across to her?
Asha, already worried about her father, probably felt relieved and cared for, included without having to pay.

Sunday night. Today Jaya and I went to the lake for our one-year anniversary. I spent the first hour setting up photos: the right light, the boat, the matching coffee cups. I made her redo a 'candid' laugh four times. Then I posted it and kept refreshing to see who liked it. At some point I looked up and Jaya was just sitting on the bench, watching the ducks, a bit quiet. I asked if she was okay. She said, 'I miss you. You've been here all day but not really.' That hit hard. I'd been performing us instead of being with her. I scrolled back through my posts and saw that every single one was from a moment I don't really remember. I put the phone in my bag. We fed the ducks, talked about her new job, shared some terrible samosas. No photos. It was the best part of the day.
- Ishita

How many times did Ishita make Jaya redo the 'candid' laugh?
Four times.
What did Ishita feel when Jaya said 'I miss you'?
Ishita felt a hard jolt of guilt, realising the day had gone on performing instead of being together.
What did Ishita do to change the rest of the day?
Put the phone away and simply fed the ducks, talked and shared samosas with Jaya, with no photos 🙂
How was the day for Jaya before the phone went away?
Lonely, with Ishita there all day but not really present.

Last spring, Kamal and I nearly fell out over a client call. I was certain the client had agreed to a Friday deadline. Kamal was just as certain they had said Monday.
The old me would have said, "You weren't listening." Instead I said, "I remember Friday, but let me check." We had both taken notes. Mine said "Fri?" with a question mark. Kamal's said "Mon, confirm by mail." The email, when we found it, said Monday.
What surprised me was how sure I had felt. That feeling had misled me, not Kamal.
Now I start with, "This is how I remember it," and after big calls I send a short summary email the same day. Kamal teases me that I'm the team's recorder. I'm Arohi, and I'm fine with that.

What did Arohi's note from the call say?
Arohi's note said "Fri?" with a question mark.
How did Arohi feel about being so sure, once the email was found?
Arohi was surprised and a little humbled to find that the strong feeling of certainty had been wrong, not Kamal, and that feeling sure is not the same as being right.
What habits did Arohi build after this?
Arohi now starts with "This is how I remember it" and sends a short summary email the same day after big calls.
How might Kamal have felt when Arohi said "let me check" instead of "you weren't listening"?
Kamal probably felt respected rather than accused, which kept the working relationship friendly enough for teasing later. 🙂
What does Renfield eat in the asylum?
He catches flies, feeds them to spiders, and feeds the spiders to sparrows. He then eats the creatures himself, believing he can take in their lives.

In the flat in Singapore, Chen and Yuki both stood at the study table with their homework. "It's mine, I need it at four," said Chen. "No, I need it at four too," said Yuki. Then Yuki stopped. "Wait. Why do you want four?"

"The window makes it bright in the afternoon, and my drawing needs light."

"Oh. I don't need light. I need quiet, and four o'clock is noisy because of the school bus."

Chen thought about it. "After dinner it's quiet. You could have it then."

"And you take the afternoon until dinner?"

They wrote it on a sticky note: Chen 4 to 6, Yuki 7 to 9. Mama stuck it on the table with a smile.

What times did they write on the sticky note?
They wrote Chen 4 to 6 and Yuki 7 to 9.
How did Yuki feel after learning why Chen wanted the afternoon?
Yuki felt relieved and understanding, since the two needs turned out to be different.
What could they do if Chen needs more than two hours for drawing?
They could talk again and find another bright spot for part of the drawing, or trade a weekend afternoon, using what each of them needs.
How might Mama see the sticky note?
Mama may feel pleased and relieved that the two settled it themselves.

Last Friday in PT, Hemant and Ritu were captains for kho-kho. They picked and picked, and I was the very last one standing by the wall. I went red all the way to my ears. At home I told Amma, 'Nobody ever picks me. Never, ever. And I never win anything either.' Amma said, 'Devika, never? What about the drawing prize in March?' I said that didn't count. I said I'd be picked last my whole life, even in college. Then Amma asked who picked me first for the quiz on Monday. It was Hemant. I had forgotten. It had only been one Friday, but it felt like forever.

What game were Hemant and Ritu captains for?
They were captains for kho-kho in PT.
Why did one Friday feel like forever to Devika?
Devika felt embarrassed and hurt at being picked last, and that strong feeling stretched one bad moment into a rule about always and never.
What did Amma's questions help Devika notice?
They brought up counter-examples, the drawing prize and being picked first for the quiz, which showed that 'never' wasn't true.
How might Hemant see the kho-kho picking?
Hemant probably thought little of it, since Hemant had picked Devika first for the quiz on Monday.

"Bhaiya, why does Nani need help to get up now?" Aditi whispered on the verandah.
Nitin looked over. Nani was gripping the chair arm, trying to stand. "Her knees are old and tired. Like when you've run all day, but always."
"And she asked my name twice today."
"Sometimes she forgets. It's part of getting old for her. It doesn't mean she loves you less."
Aditi chewed her lip. "Will she forget me?"
"I don't know. But she remembers how to shell peas better than anyone."
They went over. "Nani, can we help with the peas?" Nitin asked.
Nani's face lit up. "Come, come. Aditi, you split the pods like this."
Aditi sat close. When Nani's hands shook, Aditi held the bowl steady.

What did the children help Nani with?
They helped Nani with the peas, splitting the pods.
What was Aditi afraid of?
She was afraid that Nani would forget her one day.
How did Nitin help Aditi understand Nani?
He gave her simple, honest explanations about Nani's tired knees and forgetting, then found something they could all do together.
How might Nani feel when the children ask to help with the peas?
Nani likely feels happy and useful, as her face lights up and she shows Aditi how to split the pods.

Monday: Jagdish, six, watches Lokesh, four, trip over his loose laces again. "I'll teach you," Jagdish says, just like Papa did with him.
Wednesday: On the front step, Jagdish kneels. "Make bunny ears. Cross them. Pull!" Lokesh's loops flop. Jagdish shows him again, slower.

He tells him to "Make bunny ears."

Monthly money check done. Took twenty minutes with chai. One sheet: savings, the small fund Dad helped me start, what I still owe on the laptop, salary in, spending out. Net: up a little from February. That tiny arrow going up is my favourite thing all month.
Ojas called while I was doing it and asked why I bother, since I 'keep the bonus separate anyway'. I told him I used to. The bonus felt like play money, and I'd spend it in a week while counting every rupee on groceries. Now it all goes on the same sheet. I still label one chunk 'Ladakh trip' so I can see it growing, but it's the same money, just with a name.
Next month the laptop will be fully paid off. Circled it.
Yash

What does Yash still owe money on?
Yash still owes money on the laptop.
What does Yash feel when the net number goes up?
Yash feels quietly pleased and satisfied; the tiny arrow going up is the favourite thing all month.
How does Yash use the 'Ladakh trip' label differently from the old 'play money' bonus?
It's a name for part of the same pool, so the trip can be seen growing, rather than a separate pot spent carelessly.
Why might Ojas question the monthly check?
Ojas still thinks of the bonus as separate, so a single sheet may seem like extra effort.

Shalini lived on the floor above Deepika Aunty in their Chennai apartment block. One evening Aunty knocked with her phone. "Your uncle's cousin sent a voice message, and I can't find where to hear it. My son says it's easy, but he's in Singapore."
Shalini felt the urge to take the phone. Instead she sat on the sofa beside her. "Aunty, you press. See the little triangle next to the message?"
"This one?"
"Yes. Now touch it."
The cousin's voice filled the room. Aunty laughed, then tried to reply. She held the microphone, then let go too soon. "Oh, it stopped!"
"It happens to everyone. Hold it the whole time you speak."
The second try worked. Aunty sat back, pleased. "Don't tell my son it took two tries."
"Two tries is normal," Shalini said. "It took me three the first time."

Where does Deepika Aunty's son live?
He is in Singapore.
What does Aunty's request "Don't tell my son it took two tries" suggest about her feelings?
It suggests she felt proud of managing it herself but also a bit self-conscious about needing help.
What small choice made Shalini's help respectful?
She sat beside Aunty and let her press the buttons, and treated the mistake as normal instead of taking the phone.
What would change if Shalini had simply done it herself?
The message would be heard faster, but Aunty might feel helpless and still not know how to reply next time.
