Jatin, you took twenty minutes with that menu today, and then sulked about your pizza. Let your Ramesh Dadu tell you something.
When I was nine, my uncle took me to a big sweet shop in the old city. "Choose any one sweet," he said. There were rows and rows: jalebi, rasgulla, barfi, sohan halwa, fifty kinds. I walked up and down so long the shopkeeper started laughing.
At last I pointed at the pink barfi. The moment I bit it, I saw my cousin's hot jalebi and thought, why didn't I pick that? I don't even remember the taste of the barfi, only the jalebi I didn't have.
In our village shop there were four sweets, and I was always happy.

Which sweet did young Ramesh pick in the end?
He pointed at the pink barfi.
Why did the barfi lose its charm for young Ramesh as soon as he bit it?
After weighing fifty kinds, he felt unsure, so seeing his cousin's hot jalebi made him feel he had picked wrong.
What could Jatin try the next time a menu is long?
Jatin could pick three things that sound good and choose among only those, like the four-sweet village shop.
How might Jatin feel hearing Dadu's story?
Jatin may feel less embarrassed about sulking, knowing Dadu felt the same as a boy, and may laugh at the barfi and jalebi.

In 5 years, Frank will be three times as old as Ty is now. Ty is currently 4 years more than two times as old as Carla is now. Carla is currently 2 years older than Karen is now. If Karen is currently 2 years old, how old will Frank be in 5 years?

Carla is currently 2 + 2 = 4 years old
Ty is currently (2 * 4) + 4 = 12 years old
In 5 years, Frank will be 12 * 3 = 36 years old
The answer is 36.

Monday. Darshan, fifteen, had watched French videos all weekend: greetings, café phrases, a funny one about verbs. In class he corrected Urmila ma'am's pronunciation of "croissant" and said, "Honestly, the videos teach it better." A few classmates giggled. Urmila ma'am just said, "Wonderful. Then you can help me on Thursday."
Thursday. She gave him a short paragraph to read aloud and translate: a letter from a French student about her village. Darshan got through "Bonjour" and stopped. Past tense verbs. Words he'd never seen. He tried twice and his ears went hot. "I didn't know it had all this," he mumbled.
The next Monday. He stayed after class. "Ma'am, I think the videos gave me the easy parts. I didn't even know what I didn't know." Urmila ma'am smiled. "That's the first real step. Want the grammar sheet?" He took two.

Which word's pronunciation did Darshan correct?
He corrected Urmila ma'am's pronunciation of "croissant."
Why did Darshan feel he knew French better than his teacher on Monday?
Darshan felt proud and confident, because a weekend of videos gave him easy phrases that felt like a lot. He didn't yet know enough to see how much grammar and vocabulary he was missing.

Trying to read the paragraph on Thursday showed him the gaps. The next Monday he stayed after class, admitted it and took two grammar sheets.
How might Urmila ma'am have felt when Darshan corrected her in front of the class?
She may have felt a flicker of annoyance, but she stayed calm and found a way to let him discover the gaps himself.

The monsoon had been pouring for a week in Kochi. On Monday Joseph lent Anjali his big black umbrella because hers had snapped, and he walked home under a plastic bag, soaked to the socks. On Wednesday, with only ten minutes of lunch break left, Joseph's tiffin slipped off the wet bench and his idlis landed in a puddle. He looked straight at Anjali, who had a full box of lemon rice. She was busy copying homework and didn't look up. Joseph's stomach growled. He waited. Nothing. The bell rang. On the way back to class he muttered, 'I gave you my umbrella. I got wet for you. Never again.' Anjali blinked. 'What? I didn't even see.' Joseph didn't answer. He was too hungry to explain.

What happened to Joseph's idlis?
His tiffin slipped off the wet bench and his idlis landed in a puddle.
What was Joseph feeling when Anjali didn't look up?
Joseph felt hurt and cheated, since he had got soaked lending the umbrella and expected help in return.
What could Joseph try instead of muttering 'never again'?
He could simply ask Anjali to share, since she hadn't even seen what happened; asking clearly gives her the chance to help.
How might Anjali feel on hearing 'Never again'?
Anjali is likely confused and a little hurt, since she didn't notice the fallen tiffin and didn't know she had let Joseph down.

messages.content: Which is bigger: 1/3 of a pizza or 1/4 of the same pizza?

Answer: 1/3 is bigger.

Cut one paper circle into 3 equal parts and another the same size into 4 equal parts. Put one third on top of one quarter: the third is bigger. When the whole is cut into MORE parts, each part is SMALLER. So 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4.

While Mavra Kuzminichna was running to her room the officer walked about the yard gazing at his worn-out boots with lowered head and a faint smile on his lips. "What a pity I've missed Uncle! What a nice old woman! Where has she run off to? And how am I to find the nearest way to overtake my regiment, which must by now be getting near the Rogozhski gate?" thought he. Just then Mavra Kuzminichna appeared from behind the corner of the house with a frightened yet resolute look, carrying a rolled-up check kerchief in her hand. While still a few steps from the officer she unfolded the kerchief and took out of it a white twenty-five-ruble assignat and hastily handed it to him.

What does Mavra Kuzminichna do while the officer waits in the yard?
She hurries away, then comes back looking frightened but determined. She unfolds a kerchief and quickly hands him a white twenty-five-ruble note.

Vinita had trained with Vikas sir at the Nagpur badminton academy for two years. His word was law. If he said jump, she jumped higher. A nod from him lit up her whole week.
Before the state trials, she twisted her ankle in practice. It swelled up fast.
"Tape it and play," Vikas sir said. "And don't tell your parents. They'll make a fuss and you'll lose your chance."
Vinita nodded automatically. Then, on the bus home, it bothered her. Why keep it secret? The ankle throbbed.
She thought: he's a brilliant coach. And this was wrong.
At home, she showed her mother the ankle and told her exactly what sir had said. Her mother's face tightened. "You were right to tell me. No coach should ask you to hide an injury." She took Vinita to the doctor that evening and phoned the academy director before dinner.

What did Vinita twist in practice?
Her ankle.
How did Vinita feel on the bus home?
She felt uneasy and conflicted, torn between her admiration for Vikas sir and the sense that hiding the injury was wrong.
Which choice protected Vinita, and why did it matter?
She used her own judgement and told her mother, which got her ankle checked and brought in the academy director.
How does Vinita's mother see Vikas sir's instruction?
She sees it as a coach crossing a line by asking a child to hide an injury, and acts the same evening.

Tuesday. The bus stop was twenty minutes from Bhaskar's home, and he left at 7:40 for the 8:00 bus. Outside the temple, his classmate Mahima called him over to see a beetle. When he looked up, it was 7:52. He ran, and the doors were already closing. The conductor waved him in, and Bhaskar sat down, out of breath.

Wednesday. At breakfast his mother Kavitha noticed him staring at the wall clock. "I'll leave at half past seven," he said. "Ten extra minutes. If Mahima calls me again I can say hello and still walk."

Friday. Bhaskar left at 7:30, stopped by the temple to look at a new beetle for a few minutes, and reached the bus stop at 7:55 with time to spare.

What did Mahima call Bhaskar over to see?
Mahima called Bhaskar over to see a beetle.
How was Bhaskar feeling as he ran for the bus?
Bhaskar was worried and out of breath, afraid the bus would leave without him.

Bhaskar could say he will look another time, or look quickly and check the clock first.
How might Kavitha feel watching Bhaskar plan this himself?
Kavitha may feel proud and relieved that Bhaskar worked out the fix without being told.

March: Gurpreet decided to apply for a design internship in Bengaluru. He opened the portfolio file, changed the font eleven times and closed it. "It has to be perfect, or they'll laugh," he told his sister, Gurleen.
April: The deadline passed. Gurpreet told everyone the internship wasn't worth it anyway. Secretly, he redid the cover page again.
May: Gurleen found a new deadline at a smaller studio and sat with him at the kitchen table. "Send the one you have. Not perfect. Just sent." His hands sweated over the button. He didn't press it that night. The next morning he did, and then felt sick for an hour.

How many times did Gurpreet change the font?
Eleven times.
Why did Gurpreet say the internship wasn't worth it?
He felt ashamed of missing the deadline and used the excuse to hide his fear of an imperfect portfolio.
What helped Gurpreet finally send an application?
Gurleen sitting with him and urging him to send what he had rather than wait for perfect.
How might Gurleen feel watching him hesitate over the button?
Gurleen likely feels patient but worried, wanting him to stop missing chances.

The physics exam was at nine, and at half past midnight Madhav was still scrolling under the blanket, eyes burning, thumb moving on its own. He had said "one more video" about forty times. By morning his head ached, and he snapped at his little sister for asking him to pass the salt.
At school Shankar looked at him. "You look like you haven't slept, and you bit my head off yesterday too." Madhav admitted he couldn't stop at night.
They made a plan: the phone charges in the hall, an old clock for the alarm, a paperback by the bed. If it still didn't work, they would tell Madhav's father or the school counsellor together.
That night the hall charger blinked in the dark, and Madhav opened the book.

Where does the phone charge under the plan Madhav and Shankar made?
It charges in the hall.
What might Madhav be feeling when his thumb keeps moving on its own?
He seems unable to stop, tired and frustrated, since his eyes burn and he snaps at people the next day.
What else could Madhav do if the plan doesn't work?
He could tell his father or the school counsellor, as Shankar suggests, because asking for help is wise if he feels unable to change.

She may have felt confused or hurt, since she only asked for salt; the snap likely came from his tiredness, not from her.
why do people recycle paper? how can I remember new words better? Any idea what "presiding" means? What does "dead end" mean in "a dead end job"?

1. It saves trees. Because old paper can be made into new paper, so fewer trees need to be cut.
2. Use each new word in a sentence of your own on the same day. Review a short list every few days instead of a long list once.
3. It is the -ing form of "preside", a verb meaning to be in charge of a meeting or an event.
4. It means a job with no chance to move up or improve. For example: he left the dead end job to learn a new skill.

Martha is knitting winter clothes for her 3 grandchildren, who are all the same size (identical triplets.) Each set of clothes consists of a woolen hat, a scarf, a sweater, a pair of mittens, and a pair of wooly socks. She can knit a hat in 2 hours. A scarf takes her 3 hours. Each mitten takes her about an hour to knit. A sock takes an hour and a half. Each sweater takes her 6 hours. How long will it take her to knit all the outfits?

A pair of mittens takes 1 hour per mitten * 2 mittens = 2 hours.
A pair of socks takes 1.5 hours per sock * 2 socks = 3 hours.
So a complete outfit for each child takes 2 hours per hat + 3 hours per scarf + 2 hours per pair of mittens + 3 hours per pair of socks + 6 hours per sweater = 16 hours per outfit.
So to knit winter outfits for all three of her grandchildren, Martha will take 3 outfits * 16 hours per outfit = 48 hours.
The answer is 48.

I'm Afreen. Two summers ago, my cousin Chandrika and I had to share one bicycle at Nani's house in Ranchi. For the first three days we fought every hour. She'd grab it after breakfast; I'd grab it after lunch; Nani had to hide it in the cowshed. On the fourth day, I said, “What if you have it every morning and I have it every evening, when it's cooler?” Chandrika said, “But evenings are better.” “Then we swap after one week.” We wrote the deal on the back of a calendar and stuck it by the door. When I forgot once and took it in the morning, Chandrika just pointed at the calendar. I gave it back. We didn't fight once after that.

It was written on the back of a calendar stuck by the door.

Chandrika felt the first plan was unfair and was worried about getting the worse time.

It swapped after a week so both got the better time, and writing it down helped them remember and keep the deal.
How did Nani deal with the fighting before the deal?

She started explaining: the interview had gone well, the manager had smiled, she had prepared for weeks. Shalini didn't give advice. He's been telling everyone." I don't know what was going on inside her, but that was the part she hadn't said before. They talked for an hour after that, mostly about her father. Whose name wasn't on the internship list?
Sudha's name wasn't on it.
What was Sudha feeling underneath her first explanation?
Sudha was disappointed and also worried about letting her father down, which came out only after Shalini named the feeling.

Shalini reflected the emotion instead of giving advice, which showed she was listening for feelings and let Sudha share the harder part about her father.

He had been telling everyone she would get it, so she probably felt pressure and dreaded disappointing him.

The Christmas service at the church in Aizawl would start in ten minutes, and the whole family was waiting at the door. Lalremsiami, five, sat on the floor with one shoe untied.
Her uncle Harish knelt to help. She pushed his hand away. "No! I can do it!"
"Mawii, we'll be late."
"I DO IT." She crossed the laces, missed, tried again. Her face went red.
Harish looked at his watch, then sat down on the step beside her. "Okay. Show me."
It took four tries. The bow was loose and crooked. Lalremsiami stood up, chin high. "I did it myself."
They ran to church and slipped in during the first carol.

How many tries did it take Lalremsiami to tie the bow?
It took four tries.
What was Lalremsiami feeling when she stood up with her chin high?
She felt proud of herself for tying her shoe alone, even though the bow was loose and crooked.

A year after joining the farm advisory office in Barabanki, Indu still didn't know every seed variety by name, and she no longer pretended to. When a farmer asked about a new pest on his okra, she said, "I'm not sure. Let me check with the district lab and come to your field on Thursday," and she did. On Monday a new trainee, Vijay, arrived: pressed shirt, anxious eyes, nodding at every term. At lunch under the neem tree, Indu shared her tiffin and said, "In my first month I thought 'soil health card' was some kind of ID. Nobody knows everything here. Ask me anything." Vijay laughed, surprised, and asked three questions in a row. Walking back, Indu realised she had answered two of them easily. She felt, quietly, that she belonged.

What did Indu tell the farmer about the new pest?
That she wasn't sure and would check with the district lab and come to his field on Thursday.
How did Indu feel walking back after lunch?
She felt quietly settled, a sense that she belonged, after answering two of Vijay's questions easily.
Why does Indu's openness about not knowing help Vijay?
Sharing her own early mistake makes not knowing feel normal, so Vijay can ask questions instead of nodding.
What is lunch under the neem tree like for Vijay?
Vijay arrives anxious but laughs in surprise and feels safe enough to ask three questions.
A dog runs through a field and is joined by a group of 4 cats. 2 rabbits join each cat and 3 hares join each rabbit. How many animals are running through the field?

A pair of rabbits join each cat so there must be 4 cats * 2 rabbits/cat = 8 rabbits.
As 3 hares join each rabbit, there must be 8 rabbits * 3 hares/rabbit = 24 hares.
Counting all the animals shows there are 1 dog + 4 cats + 8 rabbits + 24 hares = 37 animals running through the field.
The answer is 37.

A person's demeanour is their way of behaving, which shows their mood or character. It is a noun; "demeanor" is the American spelling.
Example: The nurse's calm demeanour put the children at ease.

Santosh's grandmother had died on Tuesday. On Friday he sat at the tea stall by the bus stand, hands wrapped round a glass he wasn't drinking. Jomon, who ran the next stall, patted his shoulder. "Think positive, yaar. She lived a full life. Be strong, don't cry, she's in a better place."
Santosh nodded. The tea went cold. He wanted to say he had never learned to make her tea the way she liked it. He wanted to talk about the smell of her shawl. But each time he opened his mouth, Jomon said, "Stay strong!" again.
He left a coin on the counter and walked home the long way. The house was full of relatives. He had never felt so alone in a crowd.

On which day had Santosh's grandmother died?
Santosh's grandmother had died on Tuesday.
What was Santosh feeling as Jomon kept telling him to stay strong?
Santosh felt lonely and unheard in his grief, wanting to talk about his grandmother but finding no space to.
What could Jomon do differently the next time Santosh sits at the stall?
Jomon could ask about the grandmother and let Santosh talk, without telling him to be strong or think positive.
What might Jomon have been feeling when he told Santosh to think positive?
Jomon probably felt awkward and wanted to help, so Jomon reached for a familiar phrase without knowing what else to say.

Tonight Ganga asked me to sit in while she spoke to him. She was calm and specific: 'When the pallets are left in bay two, I lose twenty minutes moving them, and I feel my work is invisible.' For three weeks Minakshi had been crying in the office washroom. At home she stared at the ceiling until four. She forgot her niece's birthday. She stopped answering the family group.

On Saturday her brother Vaibhav dropped by with mangoes. She opened the door and couldn't speak.

"Minu?"

"I'm not managing," she said. Her voice shook. "I thought I could push through. I can't. I need proper help."

Vaibhav set the mangoes down and sat with her on the sofa. She told him everything: the new role, the sleepless nights, the heaviness in the mornings. He listened without trying to fix it.

"What do you want to do?" he asked.

"I found a counsellor near the office. I want to book it. And I want Amma and Appa to know, not find out later."

That afternoon they called their parents together. Then she booked the appointment for Tuesday, while he sat next to her.

Where had Minakshi been crying for three weeks?
In the office washroom.
How was Minakshi feeling when she told Vaibhav she wasn't managing?
Minakshi felt overwhelmed and shaky, but also clear that pushing through wasn't working and she needed proper help.
What steps did Minakshi take, and why were they wise?
Minakshi told her brother, called her parents and booked a counsellor; asking for help showed good judgement rather than weakness.
How might Vaibhav have felt when Minakshi opened the door and couldn't speak?
Vaibhav was probably shocked and worried, but chose to stay calm, sit with her and listen.

She had read it eleven times. She wasn't going to answer. If she said what was wrong, that he'd laughed along when the others mocked her accent at dinner, he would probably say, "Relax, you're overreacting." Silence felt safer. Silence felt like the one thing she could control. Ramesh sir walked between the desks, checking that phones were away. Jomon, you asked why I don't like groups with one boss. Let me tell you. This is your Rashmi aunty, and this is from Class 9.
Our group had a leader, Sheela. Every Monday, she decided who was “in”. If she liked your bag, you were in. If you talked to the wrong girl, you were out, and nobody would sit with you till she said so.
I watched it happen to my friend Mini. For a whole week, Sheela ignored her, and so did everyone. Even me. I was scared I'd be next.
We all behaved perfectly for Sheela. We laughed at her jokes. We gave her our best pens. We were so busy watching her face, we forgot to be friends with each other.
I never stood up to her. That's what I remember most.

Sean needs to replace 2 light bulbs in his bedroom, 1 in both the bathroom and the kitchen and 4 in the basement.  He also needs to replace 1/2 of that amount in the garage.  The bulbs come 2 per pack.  How many packs will he need?

He needs to replace lights in the bedroom, bathroom, kitchen and basement so 2+1+1+4 = 8 lightbulbs
In the garage, he needs to replace half that amount so he needs 8/2 = 4 lightbulbs
All total, he needs 8+4 = 12 light bulbs
They come 2 per pack and he needs 12 lightbulbs so he needs 12/2 = 6 packs of lightbulbs
The answer is 6.

There is very little car traffic on Happy Street. During the week, most cars pass it on Tuesday - 25. On Monday, 20% less than on Tuesday, and on Wednesday, 2 more cars than on Monday. On Thursday and Friday, it is about 10 cars each day. On the weekend, traffic drops to 5 cars per day. How many cars travel down Happy Street from Monday through Sunday?

On Monday there are 20/100 * 25 = 5 cars passing the street less than on Tuesday.
So on Monday, there are 25 - 5 = 20 cars on Happy Street.
On Wednesday, there are 20 + 2 = 22 cars on this street.
On Thursday and Friday, there is a total of 10 * 2 = 20 cars passing.
On the weekend 5 * 2 = 10 cars are passing.
So from Monday through Sunday, there are 20 + 25 + 22 + 20 + 10 = 97 cars traveling down the street.
The answer is 97.

The novelty shop on the Starship Conundrum sells magazines and chocolates.  The cost of four chocolate bars is equal to the cost of 8 magazines.  If one magazine costs $1, how much does a dozen chocolate bars cost, in dollars?

If one magazine costs $1, then 8 magazines cost 8*$1=$8.
Let's define "x" as the cost of one chocolate bar.
The cost of four chocolate bars is equal to the cost of 8 magazines and 4*x=$8.
Dividing each side by 4, we get the cost of one chocolate bar x=$2.
Therefore, a dozen chocolate bars would cost 12*$2=$24.
The answer is 24.

Tarun felt justified, even smug, and no longer bad about it, believing the freshers were lazy and deserved it.
What could the hostel change to prevent this kind of role drift?
Keep the role limited to noting arrivals, with the warden checking regularly, and give freshers a way to complain.
How might Asif feel waiting in the rain?
Asif likely felt humiliated and resentful, punished for coming back from the library.

"You never say you love me," Sahil said, sitting on the steps outside the library.
Ira looked up from his notes, which she'd been highlighting for him. "What?"
"You text 'ok' and 'reached'. That's it."
"Sahil, I just spent two hours making your revision notes. Yesterday I fixed your cycle. Last week I sat with your Nani at the hospital."
"I know. I noticed. But I need to hear it sometimes."
Ira was quiet. "At home, nobody says it. We just do things."
"At mine, Mummy says it ten times a day."
"So what feels caring to you? Tell me."
He thought. "A message in the day. Just one line. And sometimes, you know, the words."
"And what feels caring to you?" he asked.
"Honestly? When you show up. Like with the cycle."
She handed him the notes. "Okay. One line a day. Even if it feels strange."

What did Ira fix for Sahil yesterday?
His cycle.
What was Sahil feeling when he said Ira never says she loves him?
He felt a little hurt and unsure, needing to hear the words even though he noticed all she did.
What did Ira and Sahil do that helped?
They asked each other what feels caring instead of assuming, and agreed on a small change, one line a day.
How does Ira see love?
For Ira, love is shown through actions like revision notes, fixing the cycle and sitting with Nani, as in her home where nobody says it.

metadata.subtype: Loving and admiring in adult relationships [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

That spring Hana started eating lunch with the girls on the school roof in Osaka, and everything about them seemed easy: their jokes, their shared snacks, their hair clips. In April, with cherry blossoms still falling, one of them spotted Hana's calligraphy case. "Wait, you do brush writing? Like a grandma?" The others laughed. Amara, the loudest, said, "That's so uncool."
Hana laughed too. The next week she told the calligraphy teacher she was too busy with homework and stopped going. Her brushes went into the back of the cupboard.
It was November before she took them out, looking for something else. She unrolled the last piece she had made, a single character for "river", and sat on the floor with it for a long time. Her hand still remembered the stroke.

What did Amara say about brush writing?
"That's so uncool."
Why did Hana laugh along and quit?
Hana badly wanted to belong to the easy, confident rooftop group, and the fear of being laughed at felt stronger than her love of calligraphy.
What could Hana have done instead of quitting?
She could have kept calligraphy as her own thing while still sitting with the group, or found even one friend who respected it; belonging shouldn't cost something she loves.
What would change if Amara had asked to see Hana's writing instead of laughing?
Hana might have felt safe keeping her hobby, and the group might even have found it interesting; one mocking word helped push her out of something she loved.

messages.content:
Read this:

Rain had trapped all the children indoors at the housewarming, and the power had just gone out. By candlelight, Naveen and his cousins guarded their pile of building blocks. "You can't play, Lokesh. You're too little." Lokesh clenched his fist and raised it. Nani caught his hand gently. "You're hurt. Can you say it?" "They won't let me," he said, tears spilling. "That feels bad," Nani said. With the lights out there wasn't much else to do, so she picked up a torch. "Shall we make shadow animals? Anyone can come." Two small children joined. Soon Lokesh's shadow dog was barking on the wall.

What did Nani pick up after the lights went out?
Nani picked up a torch.
What was Lokesh feeling when he clenched his fist?
Lokesh felt hurt and angry at being called too little and shut out of the blocks.
How did Nani help Lokesh instead of letting him hit?
Nani held his hand gently, asked him to say the hurt in words, named it, and started a new game anyone could join.
How might Naveen see Lokesh raising his fist?
Naveen might feel startled and defensive, and could hold on to the blocks even more tightly.

Read this:

You keep saying "fine" about your in-laws, Trisha, and your face says something else. So let your Vinita maasi tell you what "fine" cost me.

When I married, your uncle's family lived two floors down. My mother-in-law came up every evening, opened my pots, and said, "Kamla's daughter-in-law makes softer rotis." I said nothing. For eleven years, nothing. But I stopped laughing when she laughed. I found reasons to be busy when they came. Your uncle thought I simply disliked his family.

One night he asked why I had gone so cold. I nearly shouted, but I didn't blame his mother. I told him, "I feel inspected in my own kitchen." He was shocked. Together we asked that visits be on Sundays. It helped. But eleven years of silence had already put ice between us that took long to melt. Don't wait eleven years.

What did Vinita's mother-in-law compare her with?
She compared her with Kamla's daughter-in-law, who made softer rotis.
How did young Vinita feel during those silent years?
She felt resentful and inspected in her own kitchen, and it came out as coldness rather than words.
What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
When her husband asked why she had gone cold, she described her own feeling without blaming his mother, and they agreed on Sunday visits together.
How did Vinita's husband see her coldness before she spoke?
He simply thought she disliked his family, because her silence gave him no other explanation.
There are two mistake in this paragraph. Please fix.

There are two mistakes in this paragraph.
Why: a plural after "two" needs -s.

Read this:

In the village near Hassan, Mohit's mother kept his little daughter Gopika indoors most of the day. "Snakes," she'd say. "In the grass." She had heard of one child, years ago, bitten in the next taluka.
But in the evenings, when the women sat talking by the courtyard well, Gopika toddled right up to its low stone rim, and nobody noticed. The well had no cover.
Mohit saw it on his second evening home from Bengaluru, and his heart jumped.
He didn't argue about snakes. He sat by his mother and said, "Amma, you're right to watch the grass. You've kept her so safe. Can we also put a lid on the well? Then you can relax while you talk."
His mother looked at the well, then at Gopika leaning over the rim. She went quiet.
The next morning Mohit and the neighbour's son fixed a heavy wooden cover with a latch. Amma still watched the grass. But now she let Gopika play in the courtyard in the afternoons.

What did Mohit and the neighbour's son fix on the well?
They fixed a heavy wooden cover with a latch.
What did Mohit feel when he saw Gopika at the well?
Mohit felt a jolt of fear, his heart jumping, seeing the uncovered well while everyone watched only for snakes.
How did Mohit raise the well kindly with his mother?
Mohit praised her care about the grass first, then suggested a lid so she could relax, rather than arguing about snakes.
How might Amma have felt seeing Gopika at the rim?
Amma likely felt shocked and quiet, suddenly seeing a danger she had missed while watching for snakes.
Our new neighbours play loud music late at night, and I have an exam soon.
That's frustrating when you need good sleep before an exam. Has anyone in your family spoken to them yet?
No. My dad says it's awkward to complain.

It doesn't have to sound like a complaint. Someone could knock in the daytime and say, "Welcome to the building. We have exams at home this month. Could you keep the music lower after ten?" Most people respond well to a friendly, specific request.

Read this:

Gurleen first noticed it at the dinner table in their Lajpat Nagar flat. Her cousin Tenzin, who had lived with them since starting college, called his old friends "sleepers" and the group's founder "the Guide." When Gurleen asked what that meant, he smiled as if she were a child. By October he had stopped going to his evening classes. His phone was always face down, and he left the room for calls. One night she heard him on the balcony saying, "I know, I shouldn't have asked. I'll accept the correction." His best friend from school rang the landline looking for him; Tenzin told Gurleen to say he was out. The next morning she saw a printed list on his desk titled "People who hold you back." Her own name was on it. Gurleen sat on her bed for a long time, then went to find her mother.

What did Tenzin call the group's founder?
He called the group's founder the Guide.
How does Gurleen feel when she sees her own name on the list?
Gurleen feels hurt and frightened, because she can see Tenzin is being pushed to cut off the people who care about him.
What turning point can the family use at this stage?
Gurleen and her mother can talk calmly together about the signs, keep warm contact with Tenzin without mocking the group, and look for advice from a counsellor who knows about high-control groups.
What might Tenzin be experiencing when he says he will accept the correction?
He may feel ashamed and afraid for having asked a question, because the group seems to punish doubt.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Class 10B, Friday.

Nandini came in after lunch, bag still on her shoulder. Two weeks ago she told the exam cell that a group had been passing answers during the science term test. The school dealt with it. Since then, her old lunch group moves tables when she arrives, and someone wrote "snitch" on her desk in pencil.

She said, "I'd do it again, but I didn't know it would feel like this." Her voice held until she mentioned the desk.

We talked about how doing the right thing can cost you a place in a group, and that the cost is real, not a sign she was wrong. I asked who still treats her kindly. She named Hemant, who has been saving her a seat in the lab. I suggested she spend her free period with him and the quiz club. I have asked the class teacher to get the desk cleaned and watch the lunch tables.

What was written on Nandini's desk?
Someone wrote "snitch" on her desk in pencil.
What was Nandini feeling when she said she would do it again?
She felt hurt and lonely about losing her lunch group, yet still steady about her choice, since her voice held until she mentioned the desk.
What small step did the counsellor suggest to help Nandini?
The counsellor suggested spending her free period with Hemant and the quiz club, people who were still kind to her.
How might Hemant see the way the class is treating Nandini?
Hemant seems to think she does not deserve to be shut out, which is why he keeps saving her a seat in the lab even when others move away.

Read this:

College career advisor's note, final year

Pema, 21, commerce student, came in today about a place on a six-month wildlife photography course in the forests of Arunachal. It pays nothing and has no guaranteed job after.
Her family expects her to join her uncle's accounting firm. Her brother Arnab came with her and said their parents are "very upset". Pema said, "I love them. I don't want to hurt them. But I've felt most alive in the forest with a camera, and I want to find out if I'm any good."
She knows the risks and has a plan to freelance. I gave her information on portfolio reviews and suggested she invite her parents to her photography exhibition next month.

What course is Pema interested in?
A six-month wildlife photography course in the forests of Arunachal.
How does Pema feel about going against her family's plan?
She is torn: she loves them and doesn't want to hurt them, but feels most alive with a camera and is curious to test herself.
What sensible steps did the note-writer suggest?
Looking at portfolio reviews and inviting her parents to her photography exhibition, so she can build her path while keeping her family close.
How might Arnab see his sister's choice?
Arnab reports that their parents are very upset, yet he came with her, which suggests he supports her in some way.

messages.content: Sally, Sam, and Steve went to play with their marbles. In the beginning, Sam has twice as many marbles as Steve while Sally has 5 less than Sam. After Sam has given Sally and Steve 3 marbles each, Sam has 8 marbles left. How many marbles does Steve have now?

Sam has 8 marbles left after giving 3 marbles/person x 2 people = 6 marbles to Sally and Steve.
Hence, Sam had 8 marbles + 6 marbles = 14 marbles in the beginning.
Sam had twice as many marbles as Steve, therefore Steve has 14 marbles / 2 = 7 marbles in the beginning.
So now, Steve has a total of 7 marbles + 3 marbles = 10 marbles after Sam gave him 3 marbles.
The answer is 10.
When do I use 'who' and when 'whom'?
Use 'who' for the person doing the action, like 'Who called?' Use 'whom' for the person receiving it, like 'Whom did you call?'
Is there a quick test?
Yes. Answer the question with 'he' or 'him'. If 'him' fits, use 'whom'. If 'he' fits, use 'who'. Many people use 'who' in casual speech, but 'whom' is expected in formal writing.

'Kavitha, how long have you been working on this "Water for Every Village" thing?'
'Eight months, Chandrika. The website's almost done. And the brand book.'
'Brand book?'
'Colours, fonts. We need to look serious when we go to big donors.'
'How many villages have water because of it?'
'...It's not launched yet. It's a national plan, it can't start small.'
'Why not?'
'Because one village doesn't change anything.'
'It changes things for that village. Paati's village has had a broken handpump since March. The panchayat just needs someone to follow up, and one mechanic.'
Kavitha looked at her laptop, at the logo glowing on the screen. 'That's not what the vision is.'
'Then the vision will stay on the screen,' Chandrika said gently.

Since when has the handpump in Paati's village been broken?
Since March.
How might Kavitha feel looking at the logo on the screen?
Kavitha seems torn and defensive, attached to the big vision and uneasy that nothing has actually started.
What small first step could Kavitha take?
Kavitha could help Paati's village get the handpump fixed by following up with the panchayat and finding one mechanic.
How does the plan look to Chandrika?
Chandrika sees eight months of branding with no real help given, and gently worries the vision will never leave the screen.

At the Dharamshala nursery during Losar week, Tenzin, four, threw a crayon across the table and turned his back. The teacher, Sabina, sat beside him. 'Your face looks cross, Tenzin. Are you upset?' He didn't answer. 'Maybe cross because Pema took the red crayon?' Tenzin nodded, still turned away. 'You're cross. That's okay. Let's ask Pema for a turn.' Tenzin turned round. 'Cross,' he said, trying the word, then went to ask.

What did Tenzin throw across the table?
A crayon.
What might Sabina have felt when Tenzin turned his back?
Sabina probably felt calm and caring, wanting to help rather than scold.
What did Sabina do that helped Tenzin?
She named his cross face, guessed the reason, said the feeling was okay and offered a next step.
How might Tenzin feel trying the word 'cross'?
Tenzin seems a little proud and calmer, having a word for his feeling.

messages.content:
Read this:

Hi Mitali di,
Exams are done, finally. Weird week though. You remember Vidya from my building? In class, the boys at the back have started calling her "Siren" because her voice goes high when she answers. Every time she speaks, someone makes a siren noise. Yesterday she stopped answering at all, even when Ma'am asked her directly.
Honestly, she needs to toughen up. Everyone gets called something. If she just laughed along, they'd get bored. I told her that at the bus stop, and she looked at me like I'd slapped her. Then she walked the long way home alone.
When Ma'am asked me after class whether something was going on with Vidya, I said I didn't know.
It's easier when people don't make such a big deal, right? Anyway, I'm fine. Write back about college.
Sonali

What do the boys at the back call Vidya?
"Siren".
Why might it feel easier for Sonali to say Vidya should toughen up?
Sonali seems uncomfortable watching the teasing; making Vidya responsible spares Sonali the awkward, scary job of standing up to the boys, and "I'm fine" hints at unease underneath.
What could Sonali do instead?
Sonali could tell Vidya the teasing isn't her fault, refuse to laugh along, and tell Ma'am honestly what has been happening, today rather than later.
How did Sonali's advice land for Vidya?
Vidya looked as if she had been slapped and walked home alone, so it probably felt like a friend taking the bullies' side.

I am Avni, Jomon's big sister. In the toy shop our mother said no to the robot he wanted. Jomon's face went red and he stamped his foot. He crossed his arms and would not look at her. I could not tell what he felt exactly, but his chin shook like he was about to cry. Then he took a breath and said, "Can I have it on my birthday?" Mother smiled. "We can think about it then." He nodded and held her hand.

What did Jomon ask his mother for at the end?
He asked, "Can I have it on my birthday?"
What might Jomon have been feeling when he crossed his arms and would not look at his mother?
He seems furious and maybe hurt, as if his mother did not love him right now. Avni admits she cannot be sure.
Why was asking "Can I have it on my birthday?" a wise move?
It replaced screaming with a request, and it gave his mother something to say yes to. It also kept things calm between them.
How might the shop scene look from Jomon's mother's side?
She probably felt she had to hold the no, and was relieved and pleased when he chose to ask instead of scream.
How would you describe Holi? One sentence, exactly fourteen words.
On Holi, friends joyfully throw coloured powder at each other and welcome the spring.

Put this passage in simple words for a child, three sentences.

At Waterloo we were fortunate in catching a train for Leatherhead, where we hired a trap at the station inn and drove for four or five miles through the lovely Surrey lanes. It was a perfect day, with a bright sun and a few fleecy clouds in the heavens. The trees and wayside hedges were just throwing out their first green shoots, and the air was full of the pleasant smell of the moist earth. To me at least there was a strange contrast between the sweet promise of the spring and this sinister quest upon which we were engaged. My companion sat in the front of the trap, his arms folded, his hat pulled down over his eyes, and his chin sunk upon his breast, buried in the deepest thought. Suddenly, however, he started, tapped me on the shoulder, and pointed over the meadows.

The narrator and a companion take a train from Waterloo to Leatherhead and drive through the Surrey lanes in a hired carriage. It is a bright spring day with fresh green shoots, which seems strange to the narrator when their errand is a dark one. The companion sits deep in thought until he suddenly taps the narrator's shoulder and points across the meadows.

Harish, come sit by your grandmother. You're not talking to your friend? I'll tell you something about me, Lalremsiami, when I was fifteen in Aizawl.
My friend forgot my birthday. I didn't say a word. I just stopped talking to her.
Day one, I felt powerful. She kept coming to my desk, asking, and I liked that she wanted me back.
Day four, I was lonely. I ate lunch alone and pretended to read.
Day seven, I wanted to talk to her so badly. But how could I? After a whole week of silence, just saying "hi" felt ridiculous. My silence was saying: you ought to work out your own mistake. But she didn't.
It took me a month. A whole month, for a birthday.

What did Lalremsiami's friend forget?
Her birthday.
What was young Lalremsiami feeling by day seven?
She felt lonely and wanted to talk, but embarrassed, because after a week of silence even saying "hi" felt ridiculous.
In the story, when was the easiest moment for young Lalremsiami to break the silence?
On day one, when her friend kept coming to her desk to ask, she could have told her about the birthday; each day after made it harder.
What was the friend likely experiencing during the silence?
She probably felt confused and anxious, not knowing what she had done, since she kept asking.

Honestly, Jagdish, the group chat post was the worst idea I had all year. My best friend Minal had promised to sit with me at the quiz and then sat with the debate girls. I was furious. So I typed, "Some people say they're your friend and then disappear." No name. Just that, in the class chat. For about ten minutes it was lovely: hearts, "who is it??", someone writing "been there." Then Minal read it. Everyone knew who, because of the quiz. She left the chat and did not pick up my call. Now when I want to say sorry and explain, I can't even begin, because she thinks the whole class was laughing at her. I wanted one person to hear me, and I told forty. I'm Sharmila, and I would delete that post if I could.

Where did Sharmila post the vague complaint?
Sharmila posted it in the class chat.
What was Sharmila feeling when typing the post, and what set it off?
Sharmila was hurt and furious because Minal promised to sit at the quiz and then sat with the debate girls.
What could Sharmila do instead to be heard by Minal, and why?
Sharmila could ask Minal for a private one-to-one talk and say how the quiz felt, because an honest talk needs to feel safe rather than public.
How does the post look to Minal?
Minal, named by everyone's guess, likely feels embarrassed and rejected, which is why Minal left the chat and ignored the call.

I'm Ganga's younger brother, Divyansh, and I was visiting her flat last Sunday. That evening she video-called our elder sister to vent about her husband's text. Something like "what is your problem?"
I was on the sofa with my phone. I heard Ganga say, "Maybe he's just tired too." And Didi said, "No, Ganga. He always does this. You're too soft."
I watched Ganga's shoulders go up. By the end of the call she was saying, "You're right. He always does this." She'd started the call half-sure. She ended it certain.
Looking back, I wish I'd said something. Didi meant well. But she had only heard one side, and her verdict became Ganga's.

Who did Ganga video-call to vent?
Their elder sister.
What was Divyansh feeling as he watched Ganga's shoulders go up?
He felt uneasy and later regretful, seeing the call turn Ganga's doubt into certainty without his speaking up.
What could Divyansh have said that might have helped?
That none of them had heard her husband's side yet, and she could ask him before deciding.
How did the call change Ganga's feelings?
Ganga started half-sure, even thinking he might be tired, and ended certain and angry.

Arnab, you asked why I stopped coming to family dinners. I'm Lalremsiami, your sister, and I'm going to try to say it without crying.
It wasn't one big thing. It was small things. He didn't like my friends, so I saw them less. He wanted to know where I was, so I started sending him my location. He said my laugh was embarrassing in public, so I laughed less. Now, before I buy vegetables, I think about what he'll say.
He's never hurt me. There's never been a mark. So I kept telling myself it wasn't abuse. It was just him being particular.
But last month I went to a support group at the women's centre, and a woman there described her week, and it was my week. Exactly.
My world is so small now, Arnab. I'm not asking you to do anything big. Just keep calling me. Please don't stop calling.

Where did Lalremsiami go last month?
To a support group at the women's centre.
How does Lalremsiami feel talking to Arnab?
Lalremsiami feels close to tears, ashamed and frightened, recognising how small and controlled her world has become.
What has Lalremsiami already done, and what does she ask of Arnab?
She has joined a support group, and she asks Arnab to keep calling her, not to do anything big.
How might Arnab feel hearing this?
Arnab would likely feel worried and sad, and perhaps want to act, though his sister asks only that he keep calling.

messages.content:
Read this:

I sat behind Tushar in the cafeteria when two boys from our own hostel block spilt trays and shouted at the staff. Tushar shrugged and said, "They just had a bad day." A week later two boys from the other block did the same thing, and Tushar said loudly, "Typical. Those people always behave like this." Ojas, at our table, raised an eyebrow. "You said bad day last week," said Ojas. Tushar blinked. "That was different." I could tell Tushar believed it. I do not think Tushar has noticed the double standard yet.

What did Tushar say when two boys from Tushar's own hostel block spilt trays?
Tushar said, "They just had a bad day."
What does Tushar's "That was different" suggest about what Tushar believes?
It suggests Tushar honestly believes the two cases differ and has not noticed the double standard; the blink shows surprise rather than deceit.
What could Ojas do next time to help Tushar see it without an argument?
Ojas could ask a gentle question, such as "What was different?", and let Tushar answer, instead of only pointing out the contradiction.
How might Ojas be feeling when raising an eyebrow and repeating "You said bad day last week"?
Ojas is probably a little puzzled or irritated by the unfairness, and speaks up while keeping the tone light enough to leave Tushar room to think.

Read this:

Leila found her sketchbook on the living-room floor of their Toronto apartment. Her little brother Ivan had drawn purple robots all over the fox she'd spent a week on.
"IVAN! That's MINE!" she shouted. Ivan's eyes went wide. For a second she wanted to grab his toy truck and snap it.
She didn't. She stomped to her room and counted to twenty.
Then she came back. "Ivan, that fox took me a week. You can't use my sketchbook without asking."
Ivan's lip wobbled. "I wanted to draw like you."
That evening Leila asked Mom for a rule: nobody touches her sketchbook. Mom agreed and gave Leila a drawer with a small lock. Leila gave Ivan some plain paper.

What had Ivan drawn over Leila's fox?
Purple robots.
What was Leila feeling when she saw the fox?
She was furious, wanting to shout and even break Ivan's toy truck.
What did Leila do instead of breaking Ivan's truck?
She calmed down, explained to Ivan what he did wrong, asked Mom for a rule and got a locked drawer for her sketchbook.
How might Ivan have felt when Leila shouted?
Ivan was startled and upset, since he had only wanted to draw like his sister.

Read this:

Thursday night

I can't sleep. Today, reconciling accounts at the NGO, I found six invoices from a "vendor" whose address is our director's cousin's house. The amounts are large. The work was never done. I checked three times.

I'm Saurabh, I'm twenty-two, it's my first job, and I am terrified. If I say something and I'm wrong, I lose everything. If I'm right, maybe I lose everything anyway.

Part of me wants to post it all online tonight and watch them burn. I won't. That's anger talking, and it might wreck the case.

So, plan:
1. Copies of the invoices on a pen drive, kept at home, not on the office laptop.
2. Read the whistleblower policy in the employee handbook.
3. Call Nirmala di on Saturday. She works in a legal firm. Ask her about protections and the safest channel, maybe the board or the funder.

Then sleep.

Saurabh found six invoices.
What is Saurabh feeling after finding the invoices?
Saurabh is terrified of losing everything, and also angry enough to want to post it all online.
Why is Saurabh's plan wiser than posting online tonight?
Keeping safe copies, reading the whistleblower policy and seeking advice from someone in law protects Saurabh and the case, while an angry leak could wreck both.

All week the girls at the bus stop in Kuttanad talked about the toddy shop behind the paddy fields: who had sneaked a sip at the harvest festival, who had gone red and giggly. Gopika laughed along, but at night she kept wondering what it tasted like, and what it felt like to be one of the ones with a story. She explained that alcohol hits a brain that is still growing harder, affecting memory and judgement, and that starting young makes it easier to keep going. Gopika turned a chilli over slowly. 'I think I mostly want to be part of the bus-stop talk,' she admitted. 'Then you already know what you're choosing,' Ankita said. Gopika decided she didn't need the sip.

The toddy shop behind the paddy fields, and who had sneaked a sip at the harvest festival.
What does Gopika's admission on the terrace suggest she was feeling?
She felt curious and a little left out, wanting to belong to the bus-stop talk more than wanting the drink itself.
What helped Gopika make her choice?
Asking Ankita honestly and hearing real effects on a growing brain let her choose with facts instead of image.
How does Ankita see Gopika's question?
She sees it as honest curiosity to answer calmly, not something to scold, so she explains and lets Gopika decide.
Tell me what a hot bowl of soup tastes like on a cold evening, in 45 words, as a short description.

The soup is thick and golden, and the steam warms my face before I take a sip. It tastes of garlic and gentle pepper, and each spoonful slides down like a small hug. My fingers curl around the warm bowl. The cold evening outside feels far away.

The first invitation was a free Saturday workshop on confidence, and Mahima left feeling lighter. Two weeks later came a small donation for the "growth fund," then a bigger one, then talk of leaving college to work for the group full time. Each step felt like a natural follow-on from the one before.

Then the comments started to add up. Shankar, who led the sessions, told members that calls home were a distraction. The fees kept rising. Anyone who asked questions was called weak. Mahima wrote the three things in a notebook and stared at the list.

That week Mahima read accounts by people who had left similar groups and booked a talk with the college counsellor, who listened and said that feeling foolish afterwards was common and no sign of failing. The pattern began to look like something the group did, not something wrong with Mahima.

Mahima told a trusted friend, Ayesha, everything. Together they made a plan: no more one-to-one meetings with Shankar, no more sessions, a call to Mahima's parents every evening, and the parents would collect the last of the belongings. If anyone made threats, the police would be told.

What was the first thing Mahima was invited to?
A free Saturday workshop on confidence.
How did the early steps into the group differ from what Mahima did after noticing the pattern?

The workshop, donations and talk of leaving college each seemed small and pulled Mahima deeper, while noticing the warning signs, getting outside advice and planning an exit with Ayesha and family led out.
What was Mahima probably feeling when the counsellor said that feeling foolish afterwards was common?
Relief and less self-blame, because it showed the pattern was the group's doing and not a personal failing.
What could Mahima do if someone from the group kept sending threatening messages?
Mahima could keep the messages, tell Ayesha and the parents, and pass them to the police, as the plan says.
Ivan had $10 and spent 1/5 of it on cupcakes. He then spent some money on a milkshake and had only $3 left. How much is the milkshake?

Ivan spent a total of $10 - $3 = $7 on cupcakes and a milkshake.
The cost of the cupcake is $10 x 1/5 = $2.
So, $7 - $2 = $5 was spent on the milkshake.
The answer is 5.

Counselling note, session two. Client: Amandeep, 25, software engineer, recently moved from Amritsar to Bengaluru.

Amandeep said her family calls her every evening. Her mother cries on the phone; her uncle has told relatives she "abandoned her parents for money". Last week her father refused to speak to her on his birthday. She described feeling guilty all day and angry all night. "I send money, I call every day, and I'm still the villain."

Her cousin Vandana, who also moved away for work, has told her this is how it was for her too, for a year.

We discussed ways she can show love that fit her real life: a fixed video call three evenings a week, rather than daily; one visit home every two months; a family photo album she is making for her mother. We also discussed that she does not have to justify her job again in every call.

She left saying, "I can be their daughter and still live here." Next session in two weeks.

She moved from Amritsar to Bengaluru.

Amandeep feels guilty all day and angry all night, as though she is the villain.

A fixed video call three evenings a week, a visit every two months, and a photo album for her mother, while no longer justifying her job in every call.

She stopped to buy bangles.

Maybe I'll find Afreen tomorrow.

No seconds before 8:30.

Freya sank down in her seat, face burning. Yosef, two rows ahead, put his hood up.
When they stopped for hot chocolate, Freya went up to her friends. "Please stop. It's not fun for me. It's embarrassing for both of us."
Her best friend Ingrid looked surprised. "Sorry. We thought it was a joke."

Two pieces of ribbon are 2 3/5 m and 1 4/5 m long. What is their total length?

Answer: 4 2/5 m. 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 = 3 7/5 = 4 2/5.

Wholes: 2 + 1 = 3. Fractions: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5, which is more than 1. 7/5 = 1 2/5, so carry the 1 whole to the wholes, just as we carry a ten in column addition: 3 + 1 = 4 and 2/5 is left. The answer is 4 2/5 m. A common mistake is to write 3 7/5 and stop; a mixed number must have a proper fraction part.

messages.content: The weekly pocket money of 9 friends (in ₹) is 50, 60, 60, 70, 80, 80, 90, 100, 500. Find the range and the IQR. Which describes the spread better?

Answer: Range = 500 - 50 = 450. Q1 = 60, Q3 = 95, IQR = 35. The IQR describes the spread of most of the friends much better.

The data are already in order; n = 9, median = 5th value = 80. Lower half: 50, 60, 60, 70, so Q1 = (60 + 60) / 2 = 60. Upper half: 80, 90, 100, 500, so Q3 = (90 + 100) / 2 = 95. IQR = 95 - 60 = 35. The range 450 is huge only because ONE friend gets ₹500. The IQR ignores the top and bottom quarters, so a single extreme value hardly changes it: if the ₹500 became ₹5,000, the range would jump to 4,950 but the IQR would stay 35. That is why the median and IQR go together, just as the mean goes with the range.

messages.content: Karen is constantly trying to stop the raccoons from getting in her trash. The first lock she tries stalls them for 5 minutes. The next lock stalls them for 3 minutes less than three times as long as the first lock. When Karen tries both locks at once, it stalled the raccoons for five times as long as the second lock alone. How long is that?

First find how long the second lock stalls them: 5 minutes * 3 - 3 minutes = 12 minutes
Then multiply that amount by 5 to find the total time the third lock stall the raccoon: 12 minutes * 5 = 60 minutes
The answer is 60.

'Then what does the bulb use?'

Lokesh felt like an expert after three videos but could not answer a basic question. Urmila felt expert after a workshop until a real project dropped her confidence before her skill grew, and Uma, truly skilled, assumed her fixes were easy and doubted herself.
What was Lokesh feeling as his ears went hot?
Embarrassed, as he realised he did not know as much as he had claimed.

messages.content: a) A bag contains 5 red, 8 white and 4 green balls. One ball is taken out at random. Find P(red), P(white) and P(not green). b) Another bag contains 12 balls of which x are black. If 6 more black balls are put in, the probability of drawing a black ball doubles. Find x.

Answer: a) Total 17: P(red) = 5/17, P(white) = 8/17, P(not green) = 13/17. b) x = 3.

a) n(S) = 5 + 8 + 4 = 17. P(not green) = 1 - 4/17 = 13/17 (or count red + white = 13). b) At first P(black) = x/12. After adding 6 black balls there are x + 6 black out of 18: P = (x + 6)/18. "Doubles" gives the equation: (x + 6) / 18 = 2 x (x / 12) (x + 6) / 18 = x / 6 x + 6 = 3x, so 2x = 6 and x = 3 Check: 3/12 = 1/4 and 9/18 = 1/2, which is double. Common mistake: forgetting that the TOTAL also increases (writing (x + 6)/12).

Keaton climbed a 30 feet ladder twenty times while working at the construction site. Reece, also working at the same site, climbed a ladder 4 feet shorter than Keaton's ladder 15 times. What's the total length of the ladders that both workers climbed in inches?

If Keaton climbed his ladder twenty times, he covered a length of 30*20 = 600 feet.
Reece's ladder, 4 feet shorter than Keaton's ladder, was 30-4 = 26 feet long.
If Reece climbed the ladder 15 times, he covered a length of 15*26 = 390 feet.
Keaton and Reece's total length covered while climbing the ladders is 390+600 = 990 feet.
Since one foot is equal to 12 inches, the total length they climbed the ladders in inches is 12*990 = 11880 inches.
The answer is 11880.

What does "all ears" mean?
Also, why do clothes smell fresh after drying in the sun? Please define "influence". Oh, and how can I use my free evenings well? And one more: help me correct this: They has finished their homework.

You can buy 4 apples or 1 watermelon for the same price. You bought 36 fruits evenly split between oranges, apples and watermelons, and the price of 1 orange is $0.50. How much does 1 apple cost if your total bill was $66?

If 36 fruits were evenly split between 3 types of fruits, then I bought 36/3 = 12 units of each fruit
If 1 orange costs $0.50 then 12 oranges will cost $0.50 * 12 = $6
If my total bill was $66 and I spent $6 on oranges then I spent $66 - $6 = $60 on the other 2 fruit types.
Assuming the price of watermelon is W, and knowing that you can buy 4 apples for the same price and that the price of one apple is A, then 1W=4A
If we know we bought 12 watermelons and 12 apples for $60, then we know that $60 = 12W + 12A
Knowing that 1W=4A, then we can convert the above to $60 = 12(4A) + 12A
$60 = 48A + 12A
$60 = 60A
Then we know the price of one apple (A) is $60/60= $1
The answer is 1.

Watching the whole signing space instead of just the fingers, as Seema retold it slowly.
How did Seema respond when Noor didn't follow?
Seema retold the story slowly, which suggests patience and a wish to help Noor learn.

After the burning of Smolensk a war began which did not follow any previous traditions of war. The burning of towns and villages, the retreats after battles, the blow dealt at Borodino and the renewed retreat, the burning of Moscow, the capture of marauders, the seizure of transports, and the guerrilla war were all departures from the rules.

Which events does the writer list as departures from the rules of war?
The burning of towns and villages, retreats after battles, the blow at Borodino, the burning of Moscow, the capture of marauders, the seizure of transports and the guerrilla war.

Robe's car broke and he used $10 from his savings to pay for the repair. Before the repair, he bought 2 kinds of spare parts. A corner light that costs twice the price of the repair fee, and two brake disks; each disk cost thrice the price of the corner light. After that, he had $480 savings left. How much money did Robe have saved before his car broke?

The corner light cost $10 x 2 = $20.
Each brake disk costs $20 x 3 = $60.
So, the total price of the brake disks is $60x 2 = $120.
He spent $10 + $20 + $120 = $150 for the repair.
Therefore, Robe has saved $480 + 150 = $630 before his car broke.
The answer is 630.

"Tushar, my boy, you've been quiet since I told you about the nursing school. Don't carry it for me.
I was sixteen, and the nurses at the district hospital said I had good hands and could train. My father said a girl from our house does not go and live in a hostel. I didn't say one word back. I married at eighteen, and I've been happy enough, beta. But when your cousin qualified last year, I cried in the kitchen.
Now you're twenty-one, thinking of saying no to the Pune fellowship because your mother will worry. I'm not telling you to go. I'm telling you to ask one question: at my age, which choice will let you sit in peace?
You're nodding the way your grandfather did when he had made up his mind. Good. Go and phone them. Your Ganga Dadi will be right here."

What did the nurses at the district hospital tell Dadi when she was sixteen?
That she had good hands and could train.
Why does Dadi tell Tushar not to carry it for her?
She sees he has gone quiet and heavy with her regret, and she wants it to guide him, not burden him.
What question does Dadi give Tushar for his choice about the Pune fellowship?
At her age, which choice will let him sit in peace, rather than simply avoiding his mother's worry.
Why might Dadi have cried in the kitchen when the cousin qualified?
Seeing the cousin qualify reminded her of the training she never spoke up for, stirring old regret alongside her pride.
Now you try: which numbers does a range with start 10, stop 0 and step -3 give?
The answer is 10, 7, 4, 1.
Now you try: mean and SD of the number of sixes in 180 throws of a die.
The answer is 30; sqrt25 = 5.
A driver travels 30 miles per hour for 3 hours and 25 miles per hour for 4 hours to deliver goods to a town every day from Monday to Saturday. How many miles does the driver travel in a week?

The driver travels (3 hours * 30 mph) + (25 mph * 4 hours) = 190 miles per day
From Monday to Saturday he travels in total 190 miles/day * 6 days = 1,140 miles in a week
The answer is 1140.
Is "an one-day trip" right? We took an one-day trip to the beach.

We took a one-day trip to the beach.
Why: "one" starts with a "w" sound, so "a".

"Sahil, why is your umbrella upside down?" giggled Rehana as the monsoon rain drummed on the verandah roof.
"It's a boat! For the frog."
"Frogs don't need boats. They swim!"
"This frog is lazy." Sahil puffed out his cheeks. "Ribbit-ribbit-plop!"
Rehana snorted. "Say it faster!"
"Ribbitribbitplop!"
"Your face looks like a squashed tomato!"
"Then you're a banana in gumboots!"
Rehana laughed so hard she slid off the step. Their Ammi called from inside, "What's so funny?"
"Banana in gumboots!" they both shouted.

What did Sahil say his upside-down umbrella was?
He said it was a boat for the frog.
Why did Rehana laugh so hard she slid off the step?
She was delighted and amused by the silly picture of a banana in gumboots. 😄
How could Ammi join in their fun?
She could ask them to invent another silly animal in rain boots, or add a silly rhyme of her own.
What might Ammi think when she hears "Banana in gumboots!"?
Ammi might be puzzled at first, then amused, glad the children are enjoying each other on a rainy day.

I sit two desks from Chinmay at the bank's analytics hub, so I saw only the outside of it.
In spring, after his review, he spent an afternoon drawing boxes on the whiteboard. I read one: "Promotion committee: 5 people. Who knows me?" Under it, only one name, his own manager's.
The next week he asked to join the fraud-detection working group, which is run by Mrs. D'Souza from risk. I heard him on a call with her: "I'd value your mentoring, and I'd like you to see my work directly."
After that he stayed back on Thursdays to present to her team. I don't know what he was thinking all those evenings. He looked tired but oddly focused.
At the next cycle, I'm told, Mrs. D'Souza spoke for him in the committee. He got the role. I still have the photo of that whiteboard. — Nandini

What did Chinmay write on the whiteboard?
"Promotion committee: 5 people. Who knows me?"
What might Chinmay have been worried about when he wrote that note on the whiteboard?
He seems worried and uneasy that only his own manager in the committee knew him, so nobody else in that room could vouch for his work.
Which other approach could Chinmay combine with finding a sponsor?
He could also ask his own manager exactly what the committee looks for, so the work Mrs. D'Souza sees matches the criteria.
How might Mrs. D'Souza see Chinmay's request?
She gets a capable helper on her working group and sees his work every week, so when he comes up for promotion she has real evidence to speak for him.

Read this:

Wednesday, late.
Grant results tomorrow. The office felt like two different weather systems today.
Sanjeev kept saying, "Chill, we're definitely getting it, the universe owes us." When I asked what happens to the girls' evening classes if we don't, he laughed: "Vandana, you think too much."
Bhavna is just as hopeful, maybe more; she believes our proposal is strong. But she has also sent a smaller request to two other funders and listed which classes we keep going if we get less. She said, "I want it badly. That's why I've planned for a no."
Honestly, Sanjeev's cheer made me more nervous and Bhavna's list made me calmer. Strange. Whatever happens tomorrow, I know whose plan I'm following.

How many other funders did Bhavna send a smaller request to?
Two other funders.
How did Vandana feel around each colleague?
Vandana felt more nervous around Sanjeev's cheer and calmer around Bhavna's list, because only one of them had faced the risk.
How could Sanjeev keep his optimism and still be responsible?
Keep hoping, but take Vandana's question seriously and help plan for the evening classes if the grant falls through.
How does Bhavna see hope and planning?
For Bhavna they go together: wanting the grant badly is exactly why she planned for a no.

Sunday night. Eight weeks in Bengaluru and this is the first place that feels like home. Lakshmi hugged me at the door again and said, "We were waiting for you." Everyone here knows my name. Tonight the leader said people who keep "checking" are scared of being happy. I had a question about the retreat payment and I swallowed it. Maybe the doubt is my own problem, my old habit of not trusting good things. I signed up for the retreat and paid from my rent money. My school friend Meena called twice this week and I let it ring. I'll explain later. Right now it's easier to stay where I'm wanted.

Shalini

What question did Shalini swallow tonight?
Shalini swallowed a question about the retreat payment.
What might Shalini be feeling when swallowing the question about the retreat payment?
Shalini feels lonely and guilty, wanting so much to belong that the doubt is pushed down as a personal failing.
What could Shalini do instead of staying quiet, and why?
Shalini could ask the question aloud and keep in touch with people outside the group, because someone who welcomes questions is a safer sign than someone who calls them fear.
How might Meena see Shalini's silence?
Meena might feel worried and left out, calling twice and hearing nothing back from someone who used to answer.

A cake recipe needs 1/2 cup of sugar and 3/8 cup of honey. How many cups is that altogether?

Now you try: 2/3 + 1/9.
The answer is 6/9 + 1/9 = 7/9.

Teacher's note, Anjali Ma'am, UKG
Today Lalremsiami wrote her full name on her worksheet without looking at the name card. It is a long name! She held up the page and stood tall, cheeks pink, and walked around showing it to everyone. 😊 Later she offered to help a friend with her letters. I have pinned the page on the wall.

What did Lalremsiami write without looking at the name card?
She wrote her full name on her worksheet.
How can you tell Lalremsiami felt proud?
She stood tall with pink cheeks and walked around showing her page to everyone.
Why was pinning the page on the wall a good choice?
It honours her effort and keeps the achievement visible, which can encourage her to keep trying.
How might the friend she helped see Lalremsiami after this?
The friend may look up to her and feel encouraged to learn her own letters.

Nursery note, Tuesday. Written by Neelam, class teacher.
At water time Swati, four, saw Dev push Mahi off the bench. She ran to me first. "Dev did pushing! Now you will be angry?" I asked why pushing is wrong. She thought hard. "Because teacher gets angry. And no star." When I asked what if I hadn't seen, she looked puzzled, as if a rule simply is, like rain.
Later she checked my face before taking her turn on the slide.
Next step: at circle time I'll ask the children how Mahi felt, and read the story about the hurt rabbit. I mentioned it to her mother at pickup; this is very usual at four.

What did Swati say would happen because of the pushing?
She said the teacher gets angry and there would be no star.
What does Swati's puzzled look suggest about how she sees rules?
It suggests she feels a rule simply is, like rain, and hasn't thought that pushing could be wrong even if no teacher saw it.
How could Neelam support Swati at circle time?
By asking how Mahi felt and reading the hurt-rabbit story, Neelam can help Swati link pushing to someone getting hurt, not only to an angry teacher.
How might Mahi feel if everyone only talked about the teacher being angry?
Mahi might feel the fall itself was forgotten, since all the attention went to the rule and not to the one who got pushed. 🥺
When should I use brackets like ( ) in a sentence?

Round brackets, also called parentheses, hold extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence.
Example: My cousin (who lives in Pune) is visiting us this week.
Diego baked 12 cakes for his sister's birthday. Donald also baked 4 cakes, but ate 1 while waiting for the party to start. How many cakes are left?

The total number of cakes baked is 12 + 4 = 16 cakes.
But since Diego ate 1 cake, there are 16 - 1 = 15 cakes left.
The answer is 15.
My school is nearer to my house than yours is. Is this right?

That sentence is correct.
Why: "nearer" with "than" and "near to" are both right.
On the cake box it says "Candles: twelve". How many candles are in the box?

Answer: 12 candles.

t-w-e-l-v-e. Point out that "twelve" starts with "tw", like "two" and "twenty". Many "two" words start with tw: two, twelve, twenty, twins!

Monday: Sachin, nine, heard Mummy and Papa arguing in the kitchen, low and sharp, the same night his maths test came home with 12 out of 20. He lay in bed thinking: It's because of me. If I'd got 20, they wouldn't fight.

Wednesday: He made his bed without being asked, did his homework twice, and didn't laugh at cartoons in case the noise made things worse. When Papa sighed at the electricity bill, Sachin froze and quickly tidied the shoes.

Saturday: Mummy found him re-copying his test corrections at eleven at night. "Sachin, why are you still awake?"

"So you and Papa don't fight."

Tanuja sat on his bed. "Beta, listen. Papa and I argue about money and his long hours. Grown-up things. Never about you. It's not your job to fix it."

He wasn't sure he believed her. But he put the pencil down.

What did Sachin's maths test come home with?
12 out of 20.
Why did Sachin freeze when Papa sighed at the electricity bill?
Sachin believed the tension at home was his fault, so any sign of upset made him try harder to be perfect. He was scared his own behaviour could make things worse.
What was the turning point, and what could his parents keep doing?
When Mummy found him up late and told him the arguments were about money and work, never about him. His parents could keep reassuring him, and try to keep arguments away from his hearing.
How might Tanuja have felt learning why Sachin was awake at eleven?
Tanuja probably felt sad and a bit guilty that Sachin had been carrying their arguments. It likely made her want to protect him from that burden.
Why do we get goosebumps when we are cold?
Tiny muscles pull the hairs upright. Because the body is trying to trap a layer of warm air against the skin, and that reaction is left over from when our ancestors had thicker hair.

Vidya, beta, you ask how your Nani opened the tailoring shop? Everyone in the mohalla called it Sarita's shop for thirty-one years, but at the start I was twenty-five, same as you. Your grandfather thought I'd lose everything, and he said so every night.
I sat with a slate and asked myself three things. What's the worst that can happen? I lose my gold bangles, which I had pawned to rent the room. Can I live through that? Yes, I still had my hands and the sewing work at home. What might I gain? A shop with my name, and enough to put your mother in a proper school.
So I didn't jump blind. I kept my old customers at home for the first year, just in case. I took the risk, but I kept a ladder behind me.
The shop lasted. Not because I was brave. Because I counted both sides.

What had Sarita pawned to rent the room?
Her gold bangles.
What did Sarita believe made the shop last?
She believed it lasted not because she was brave but because she counted both sides before acting.
What choice kept Sarita's risk from being reckless?
She kept her old customers at home for the first year, a ladder behind her in case the shop failed.
How might hearing this story help Vidya with a risky choice now?
Vidya might see that a big step can be taken carefully, by asking about the worst case and keeping a back-up, rather than being reckless or frozen.

Why can the speaker not catch the horse's bridle?

I should have been afraid to touch a horse when alone, but when told to do it, I was disposed to obey. I put down my muff on the stile, and went up to the tall steed; I endeavoured to catch the bridle, but it was a spirited thing, and would not let me come near its head; I made effort on effort, though in vain: meantime, I was mortally afraid of its trampling fore-feet. The traveller waited and watched for some time, and at last he laughed.
The horse is spirited and will not let anyone near its head. The speaker is also afraid of its trampling forefeet.

ABCD is a parallelogram. Find all four angles.
m) angle B = 2angle A - 30 degrees
n) angle A + angle C = 140 degrees
o) angle B + angle D = 250 degrees
p) angle A = (3x + 10) degrees, angle B = (5x - 30) degrees
q) angle A = 2x degrees, angle C = (x + 40) degrees
r) angle B = (4x - 20) degrees, angle D = (2x + 60) degrees

m) angle A = angle C = 70 degrees, angle B = angle D = 110 degrees
n) angle A = angle C = 70 degrees, angle B = angle D = 110 degrees
o) angle A = angle C = 55 degrees, angle B = angle D = 125 degrees
p) angle A = angle C = 85 degrees, angle B = angle D = 95 degrees
q) angle A = angle C = 80 degrees, angle B = angle D = 100 degrees
r) angle A = angle C = 40 degrees, angle B = angle D = 140 degrees
Simplify 3x^2y - 5xy^2 + x^2y + 2xy^2 - 4 + 7.

Answer: 4x^2y - 3xy^2 + 3.

Underline like terms in the same way (x^2y terms, xy^2 terms, constants) and bring them together, keeping each sign with its term: (3x^2y + x^2y) + (-5xy^2 + 2xy^2) + (-4 + 7). Add the coefficients only: 3 + 1 = 4, so 4x^2y; -5 + 2 = -3, so -3xy^2; -4 + 7 = 3. The letters and powers do NOT change when we add: 3x^2y + x^2y is 4x^2y, not 4x^4y^2. Unlike terms stay separate, so the answer has 3 terms. Check with x = 1, y = 2: the start gives 6 - 20 + 2 + 8 - 4 + 7 = -1 and the answer gives 8 - 12 + 3 = -1.

So you asked how we handled Indu in our final-year group? Right. I'm Chinmay.
Indu stopped doing her part in October. The others wanted to go straight to Professor Rao. I said, let me talk to her first. You never know. Last year a friend of mine was quietly ill and nobody knew.
I bought her coffee and asked, “What's going on? Anything I should know?”
She looked at her phone and said, “Nothing, just busy.” I asked if the task was confusing. She said, “Not really. I just don't feel like it.”
Honestly, that was clarifying. I told her kindly that we'd give her until Friday, and after that we'd talk to Professor Rao. She didn't do it, so we did. At least I knew I'd been fair.

Who did the others want to go to?
They wanted to go straight to Professor Rao.
How did Chinmay feel after Indu's honest answer?
Chinmay felt clear and settled, even relieved, knowing it was plain avoidance and that the group had been fair.
Why was it fair to talk to Indu before escalating?
It gave her a chance to share a hidden reason like illness or confusion, and a clear deadline before going to the professor.
How might Indu have felt when Chinmay asked what was going on?
She may have felt a little awkward or guilty, looking at her phone, but also given a fair chance.
