Wed, 11:30 p.m.
Keerthana came to my desk at 6 today, bag already on her shoulder. “The spindle sensors that failed calibration, just release them. I'll take responsibility.”
I said okay. I actually said okay. Then I sat there after she left and felt the word sit in my stomach.
Because it's my login on the release screen. It's my name the auditors will see. She can take responsibility for telling me. She can't take it for my click.
So at 8 I emailed her: “I understand the instruction. I can't release lot 7B without logging the failed calibration. I'm copying the quality lead so we decide properly.”
The quality lead replied at 9:40: “Thanks for flagging. Lot on hold. Let's all meet at 10 tomorrow.”
Keerthana hasn't replied. I'm nervous about tomorrow. But I'd rather be nervous than be the person who clicked. — Ritu

What did Keerthana ask Ritu to release?
She asked Ritu to release the spindle sensors that failed calibration, lot 7B.
Why did the word “okay” sit badly with Ritu after Keerthana left?
Ritu felt uneasy because the login and the name on the release screen were Ritu's own, so Keerthana's promise to take responsibility couldn't really cover Ritu's click.
What made Ritu's email a good countermeasure?
It acknowledged the instruction, stated clearly what Ritu would not do, and copied the quality lead, moving the decision into the proper channel.
How might Keerthana feel when she reads the email?
She may feel embarrassed or annoyed at being overruled, but could also be relieved the decision is now shared with the quality lead.
Please write an email to a supplier asking for a quotation for 20 folding chairs for a community event on 12 December, with delivery by 10 December. About 55 words. I'm Mr. Nambiar.

Subject: Quotation for 20 Folding Chairs

Dear Sir or Madam,
We are organising a community event on 12 December and need 20 folding chairs. Could you please send us a quotation for them? We need the chairs delivered by 10 December. Kindly mention the delivery details in your reply. Thank you.
Yours faithfully,
Mr. Nambiar

I'm Santosh, and for the school craft fair I had to make a model house.
My cousin Nilesh wanted to start with the fun parts: a balcony, curtains, a garden. But I was worried. What if it didn't stand up?
So on Monday I made only a plain box from an old shoe carton, with a folded roof. I showed Sir. He said the walls were fine but the roof was too heavy.
Tuesday, a lighter roof. Wednesday, windows. Thursday, Nilesh helped me paint it yellow and add a moss garden.
At the fair, my roof stayed on all day. A girl's model next to mine had a beautiful balcony, but its roof fell in by lunch.
I felt a bit sorry for her. And quite proud of my boring box.

What did Santosh make the box from?
From an old shoe carton.
How did Santosh feel at the end of the fair?
Santosh felt quite proud of the simple start and a bit sorry for the girl whose roof fell in.
What else could Santosh do in the next project?
Santosh could again show a simple first version early, so any big problem is found before the decorating starts.
How might Nilesh see the plan to start with a plain box?
Nilesh wanted to begin with the fun parts, so may have found it boring at first, but still got to help with the garden later.

"I need pink for the flower," said Irawati.
Pema hugged the pink crayon. "I need it for my princess."
"But you've had it for ages."
"It's the only pink. And it's my favourite."
Mama called from the kitchen, "What's the fight, girls?"
"No fight," Pema called back. She looked at the crayon, then at Irawati's empty flower. "You can do your flower. Then give it back, okay?"
"Okay. I'll be quick."
"Not too quick. Colour it nicely." Pema handed it over and started on her princess's hair in yellow instead.

What colour did Pema use for her princess's hair instead?
She used yellow.
What does Pema hugging the crayon suggest she felt about sharing it?
She hugged it, said it was her favourite and the only pink, and made Irawati promise to give it back.
What could Mama say if she walks in now?
She might notice aloud that Pema gave up her favourite crayon while she still wanted it, without making a big fuss.
How might Irawati feel when Pema tells her to colour it nicely?
She may feel trusted and relieved, and more willing to share with Pema next time. 😊

Jane is trying to decide whether to buy a house or a trailer. A house costs $480,000 and a trailer costs $120,000. Each loan will be paid in monthly installments over 20 years. How much more is the monthly payment on the house compared to the trailer?

First find how many months the loans last: 20 years * 12 months/year = 240 months
Then divide the cost of the house by the number of payments to find the monthly payment before interest: $480,000 / 240 months = $2000/month
Then do the same thing to find the monthly payment before interest on the trailer: $120,000 / 240 months = $500/month
Then subtract the cost of the trailer payment from the cost of the house payment to find the difference: $2000/month - $500/month = $1500/month
The answer is 1500.

The officers, as usual, lived in twos and threes in the roofless, half-ruined houses. The seniors tried to collect straw and potatoes and, in general, food for the men. The younger ones occupied themselves as before, some playing cards (there was plenty of money, though there was no food), some with more innocent games, such as quoits and skittles. The general trend of the campaign was rarely spoken of, partly because nothing certain was known about it, partly because there was a vague feeling that in the main it was going badly.

Question: How do the officers pass their time, and what is rarely discussed?

They live in twos and threes in ruined houses. The seniors gather straw, potatoes and food, while younger ones play cards, quoits and skittles. The campaign is rarely spoken of because nothing is certain.

Rain was coming through the roof of the municipal school in Dharavi, and Nikita, twenty, was trying to save forty donated books from a bucket-shaped puddle. She and Aditi had spent three months collecting them for a tiny reading corner, alongside Nikita's evening prep for her management entrance exam. The inauguration was supposed to be today; the headmistress was stuck in traffic and the electricity had gone. Aditi wiped her glasses. "We could cancel. Nobody would know." Nikita shook her head. She stacked the books on two desks away from the leak and taped the handmade sign above them: READ ANYTHING. A girl in a torn uniform picked up a picture book and sat right there on the floor. Nikita watched her, heart full. She'd be gone to some B-school next year. The corner would still be here.

How many donated books were Nikita and Aditi trying to save?
They were trying to save forty donated books.
What was Nikita feeling as she watched the girl read?
Nikita felt deeply moved and fulfilled, knowing the corner would outlast her time there.
Why was going ahead despite the rain and power cut a good choice?
It kept the project focused on the children, not on a ceremony, so the corner started working at once.
How might Aditi see Nikita's decision not to cancel?
Aditi may have been tired and ready to give up, but likely admired Nikita's commitment when the girl started reading.

At Abuela Jana's eightieth birthday lunch in Valparaíso, Priscila, sixteen, sat between her two grandmothers. Abuela Jana had outlived a husband and a failed bakery, and she spent the meal asking the youngest cousins about their football. When they toasted her, she said, "I got plenty wrong, and I'd still do it all again."
Across the table, Abuela Carmen pushed her plate away. "Enjoy it while you're young, Priscila. It all turns to nothing." She had spent the morning listing what her children had failed to do for her.
On the bus home Priscila stared at the harbour lights. Both women were old; both had lost things. How did one end up grateful and the other so sour? Was it something that happened to you, or something you did? She had no answer. She kept the paper napkin with Jana's toast written on it.

What did Abuela Jana say when they toasted her?
She said, 'I got plenty wrong, and I'd still do it all again.'
What does Priscila keeping the napkin suggest?
It suggests Jana's contentment impressed her and planted a question she wants to hold on to.
What question might Priscila ask Abuela Jana next time to explore her puzzle?
She could ask how Jana stayed grateful after the bakery failed, to learn whether contentment comes from choices and not just luck.
What might be going on for Abuela Carmen when she says it all turns to nothing?
She may feel disappointed and unseen by her children, and that bitterness colours how she sees her whole life.

In their shared flat in São Paulo, Priscila had a poster of the city councillor Lucas Prado above her desk. She had volunteered for his campaign, and after he once shook her hand at a rally, she felt they had a real connection. When news came out that his office had quietly cancelled funding for a children's library, her roommate Jamal read it aloud. 'That's not him,' Priscila said instantly. 'It's his staff.' 'He signed it,' Jamal said, showing her the document. Priscila's cheeks burned; it felt like Jamal was attacking her. She went to her room and wrote Prado a long message. An automatic reply thanked her for her support. She read it twice. For the first time, she noticed he didn't even know her name.

What did Prado's office cancel funding for?
A children's library.
Why did Priscila's cheeks burn when Jamal showed the document?
She felt attacked and defensive, as if criticism of Prado were criticism of her.
What could Priscila do to keep her values and her judgement?
Keep supporting ideas she believes in while looking at facts like the signed document, instead of defending Prado automatically.
How might Jamal feel after Priscila leaves the room?
Probably uncomfortable and worried, since Jamal only showed a document and she took it personally.

The ward sister, Ishita, pinned the new rota to the board during handover. "Payal, you're on Saturday nights now; we're short. That's fine, right?"

Every nurse in the station turned. Payal smiled, nodded and said, "Yes, sister, of course."

Ishita moved on, relieved.

But Payal's pen was pressing hard enough to tear the chart she was holding. That Saturday she had promised to take her grandmother to a family function; she'd said so weeks ago.

At the end of the shift she found Ishita alone in the medicine room. "Sister, can I say something about this morning? I smiled because I didn't want to argue in front of everyone. Actually, Saturday is hard for me."

Ishita put the tray down. "I took your smile as a yes. I'm glad you told me." They looked at the rota together and Payal swapped to Sunday.

Where did Payal find Ishita at the end of the shift?
She found Ishita alone in the medicine room.
What was Payal feeling when she smiled and said yes, and what might the smile have looked like to others?
Payal was upset and stuck, shown by her pen pressing hard enough to tear the chart; to the others her smile looked like willing agreement, and part of it was respect for the ward sister in public.
What did Payal do that helped, and why did it work?
She waited for a private moment and gently explained that her smile had been politeness, which let Ishita change the rota without anyone losing face.
If you were Ishita, what would you want Payal to do next time?
Ishita would probably want Payal to raise a clash quietly, as she did here, rather than agree with a smile and carry the upset alone.

"He's safe?" Hansa's voice cracked into the phone. "You're sure? Okay. Okay."
She put the phone down on the table and made a sound Karthik had never heard from her, a huge, ragged sob. Then another. She folded over her knees.
"Hansa..." Karthik half rose, then stopped. "Is it Mohan?"
She nodded, gasping. "They found him. At the relief camp. Four days, Karthik. Four days I thought..."
"I know." He sat down beside her. "Cry. It's all right. Nobody's here but me."
"I can't stop."
"You don't have to yet."
She cried until her breath came in hiccups. Karthik fetched a glass of water and put it in her hands. "Small sips. Now breathe out slowly with me. Longer. Again."
Her shoulders began to drop. "I held it in for four days," she whispered. "At work, on the bus."
"That's why it all came at once. Want to call your mother now, together?"
"Yes."

Where was Mohan found?
At the relief camp.
Why did Hansa cry so hard after the call?
She was overwhelmed with relief after four days of fear she had held in at work and on the bus, so it all came out at once.
How did Karthik help Hansa's body settle?
He let her cry without hurrying her, then gave her water in small sips, breathed out slowly with her, and suggested calling her mother together.
What might it have been like for Karthik to hear that sob?
Karthik was probably startled and worried at first, having never heard that sound from her, then steady once he understood it was relief.

After five months clean, Asif used again on a Saturday night after a friend's wedding. On Sunday morning in their Lucknow flat, he sat on the bed, head in his hands.
Shalini came in with tea.
"I used last night," he said, before he could stop himself. "I'm sorry. I've ruined everything."
Shalini set the tea down carefully. Her face tightened; she was hurt. But she sat beside him. "You haven't ruined everything. You told me. That matters."
"I'm so ashamed."
"I know. Let's call your counsellor now, together."
Asif nodded. His shoulders were still shaking, but he picked up the phone.

How long had Asif been clean before the lapse?
Five months.
What was Asif feeling when he said "I've ruined everything"?
He felt deeply ashamed and afraid, as if the lapse had destroyed all his progress.
Why was Shalini's response protective for Asif's recovery?
She stayed kind and non-punishing, valued his honesty, and helped him contact his counsellor right away.
What is Shalini experiencing as she sits beside him?
Shalini is hurt, but chooses to support him rather than punish him.

Read this:

Dear Vandana Masi,
I'm sorry about Sunday lunch. When you asked how school was and I said "Ugh," I saw your face go stiff, and Mumma told me later you thought I was being rude to you. I wasn't. "Ugh" is kind of my whole vocabulary this term. Sometimes it means I'm tired, sometimes the bus was awful, and sometimes it's a joke, like when my friends and I say it about exams. On Sunday it meant we'd had three tests that week and I hadn't slept properly. None of it was about you. I love it when you ask. I'm practising tacking a few words onto the ugh, like "Ugh, long week, three tests," so people don't have to guess. Can I tell you about the tests properly next Sunday? One of them was actually funny.
Love,
Gurleen

How many tests did Gurleen have that week?
Three.
What was Gurleen feeling while writing to Masi?
Gurleen felt sorry and a little embarrassed that the 'ugh' had hurt Masi, and wanted her to know it wasn't about her.
What is Gurleen's plan to avoid confusion?
Adding a few words after the 'ugh', like 'long week, three tests', so people don't have to guess.
How did Vandana Masi take the "Ugh" at lunch?
Masi's face went stiff, and she thought Gurleen was being rude to her.

When the results went up on the department board, Jaya read her roll number twice. She had failed one paper. The others in her row crowded round, cheering; Salma, who barely seemed to open a book, had passed everything. A bitter knot rose in Jaya's throat. She walked out with one thought pounding: I am a failure. Karthik found her on the steps. He did not lecture or ask what went wrong. He said, "Come, let's eat," and bought two plates of idli. Jaya almost told him she did not deserve it, almost waved him off, but she sat. Halfway through the second idli her shoulders unclenched. When Salma walked past, Jaya said, "Congratulations, that's great," and meant about half of it. Then she asked, "How did you prepare for the practical?" Salma pulled out a colour-coded timetable. That night Jaya wrote down one thing: sign up for the supplementary exam and book a slot with the lab instructor. She had failed a paper. That was not the same as being a failure.

What did Karthik say when he found Jaya on the steps?
He said, "Come, let's eat," and bought two plates of idli.
How did Jaya's reaction to Salma's result change after Karthik's kindness?
At first she felt a bitter knot, but after eating with Karthik her shoulders unclenched, and she congratulated Salma and asked how to prepare for the practical.
What did Jaya feel when she saw that Salma had passed everything?
She felt a bitter, jealous knot in her throat.
What one next action did Jaya choose, and how does it help?
She chose to sign up for the supplementary exam and book a slot with the lab instructor; a concrete step separates the failed paper from being a failure and restores momentum.

Ujjwal, you won't step on the cracks before your cricket match? Let your Saurabh dadu tell you something.

When I was ten, I had a lucky marble. Green, with a white swirl. I kept it in my pocket for every exam and every match.

One day before the school race, I lost it. I cried and said, "Now I'll lose."

My mother said, "Did the marble run the race, or did you?"

I ran anyway. I came second. Without the marble.

I still kept looking for it for weeks. I knew it didn't really help. But having it made me feel less scared. That's okay, Ujjwal. Just don't forget who does the running.

What colour was Saurabh's lucky marble?
Green, with a white swirl.
Why did young Saurabh keep looking for the marble even after coming second?
He knew it didn't really help, but having it made him feel less scared and more comforted.
What turning point in the story helped Saurabh see the marble differently?
His mother asked whether the marble or he ran the race, and then he ran without it and came second.
How might Saurabh's mother have felt when he cried about the marble?
His mother probably felt sympathetic but wanted to help him see his own strength.

Looking back, it started at the cinema with my friend Rehana. Halfway through the film I whispered, "Did you notice the maid is always the one who trips and gets laughed at?" Rehana grinned. "And the villain always has the same beard." We began counting on the walk home. In the next three films: a cook who was a joke, a driver who was a joke, a bad guy in a cap. The hero was nearly always from one kind of family. We started asking, "Who's missing? Who gets to be the main person?" I felt relieved to have words for something I'd felt but couldn't say. It didn't ruin films; it just made me watch with both eyes. Minakshi

What did Minakshi and Rehana start doing on the walk home?
They began counting the maids, cooks, drivers and villains from the films.
How did Minakshi feel once there were words for the pattern?
Relieved, because the words named something felt but never said.
What question could a viewer ask next?
Who is missing, and who gets to be the main person?
How did Rehana take Minakshi's first whisper?
Rehana grinned and added a point about the villain, showing the pattern had been noticed too.

Every Thursday Pradeep sang in the bhajan circle at the community centre, then helped stack the mats. Tonight Chaitanya pulled him aside by the water cooler. "There's a retreat next weekend with a new teacher. Everyone gives a month's salary to be 'accepted', and doubting is a sin." Pradeep kept his voice mild. "I love the singing and the seva. But I'd want to see where the money goes, and I don't think a good teacher is afraid of questions." He asked Chaitanya to come to the usual circle instead. Chaitanya shrugged, unsure. Pradeep stacked the last mat and went out humming, his faith untouched and his questions still in his pocket.

What does Pradeep do at the community centre every Thursday?
He sings in the bhajan circle and helps stack the mats.
What is Pradeep thinking about the retreat, and what shows it?
He is wary of a group that demands a month's salary and calls doubt a sin. His mild voice and his wish to see where the money goes show that he questions without dropping his faith.
What could Pradeep do if Chaitanya still decides to go to the retreat?
Stay friendly, keep the invitation to the circle open and, if Chaitanya is pressed for money or told to cut off family, encourage talking to a trusted elder. 🙏
How might Chaitanya be feeling as Pradeep answers?
Chaitanya seems unsure, perhaps wanting to be accepted somewhere but a little shaken by the questions, as the shrug suggests.

Class 9B, Thursday, second period.
When I set the group project on water use, Karthik leaned back and said, "Why do we even do these? Does anyone actually read them?" Two boys laughed. His tone was sharp, and my first urge was to explain the marking scheme.
I noticed a few things instead. Karthik's folder had last term's project in it, still with no comments on it; I had returned it late and unmarked because of the exams. He was not looking at me while he spoke, but at the folder.
So I did not defend the project. After class I asked him, "Did it feel like nobody read your last one?" He shrugged and said, "Kind of. I worked on it for a month."
I apologised, gave him written feedback on it by Friday, and he chose the hardest topic this time.
Minakshi Rao, class teacher

What did Karthik have in his folder?
Karthik's folder had last term's project in it, still with no comments on it.
What does Karthik's gaze at the folder suggest about his mood behind the sarcastic question?
It suggests he felt hurt and let down that his month of work seemed unread, not just bored or rude. His sarcasm could also have been partly showing off for the boys who laughed.
What could a teacher learn from how Minakshi handled the remark?
Instead of defending the task in front of the class, a teacher could ask privately about the feeling behind a sarcastic question and fix any real cause, as Minakshi did with the late feedback.
If you were one of the boys who laughed, how might you have read Karthik's question?
You might have heard it as a funny, cheeky jab at homework, with no idea that it came from a project he cared about and felt ignored on.
Elise is buying more dog food. She buys a 15kg bag then another 10kg bag, and she now has 40kg of dog food. How many kilograms of dog food did Elise already have?

Elise has bought a total of 15 kg + 10 kg = 25kg of dog food.
This means she already had 40 kg - 25 kg = 15kg of dog food.
The answer is 15.

On the bus home in Nairobi, Wanjiru bounced on her seat. “Tomas, listen! Wiggle-waggle-woggle-wee! Nobody stinks as much as me!” She collapsed with giggles. Her big brother Tomas groaned. “That doesn't make sense.” “It rhymes!” she said. “Now you!” He sighed. “Jiggle-jaggle-jungle-jee…” “Nobody sings as loud as me!” she finished, and shrieked. A lady in front turned and smiled. By their stop, Tomas was laughing too, and they had a whole song about stinky socks.

What did Wanjiru and Tomas have a song about by their stop?
Stinky socks.
What was Wanjiru feeling when she collapsed with giggles?
She felt joyful and silly, delighted by the sound of her nonsense rhyme.
What would you advise an older sibling when a little one tells silly rhymes?
Play along, as Tomas did in the end, because the fun is in the sound and pattern, not in making sense.
How did Tomas's view of the rhymes change on the bus?
At first he found them silly and senseless, but he ended up laughing and joining in.

Sunday night.

Said no to the big company today. They offered more money than I've ever seen, a nice office, free lunches. Dhruv thinks I've gone mad.

Instead I'm starting the apprenticeship with old Masterji at his instrument workshop. Half the pay. Sawdust everywhere. Two, maybe three years before I'm good enough to make a sitar on my own.

Why? Because when I watched him carve that neck last month, I knew I wanted to do that for the rest of my life. And he's seventy. If I don't learn now, the chance is gone.

Mummy's worried. I'm worried. I'll have to take the bus instead of an auto and forget about new phones for a while.

But in five years, I want my own workshop. This is the price.

Kunal

What will Kunal learn to make at Masterji's workshop?
A sitar.
Why is Kunal willing to accept half the pay?
Kunal is worried about money but determined to master the craft, knowing this chance with Masterji won't last.
What would you advise Kunal to help stick with this choice?
Keep the five-year goal visible and plan a simple budget, so the short-term sacrifices feel manageable.
Why might Dhruv react differently to Kunal's choice?
Dhruv may value the security and comfort of the big company, not seeing the long-term meaning Kunal sees.
Why is it dangerous to touch an electric switch with wet hands?
It can give you a shock. Because water carries electricity well, so wet skin lets current pass through your body more easily.

Monday: Kishore saw a transfer on the joint account: Rekha had sent money to her parents for her father's treatment. He hadn't known. He snapped, "You could have told me." Rekha snapped back, "You send money to your brother every month."
Wednesday: Neither spoke much. Kishore felt hurt; Rekha felt judged. They both slept badly.
Saturday: Rekha suggested they sit down properly. They wrote out what each sent to family and why, and discovered they both felt the same duty and hadn't said it aloud. They agreed on three things: talk before any big transfer, keep some money each could use without asking, and review together every month.
Rekha said, "I wasn't hiding it. I was scared you'd say no."
Kishore said, "I wasn't angry about the money. I was angry at not knowing."
They went for dinner afterwards, the first time that week.

What was Rekha's transfer for?
Her father's treatment.
Why did Kishore feel hurt about the transfer?
Kishore felt hurt and left out, because he wasn't angry about the money but about not being told.
What made their Saturday conversation productive?
They wrote out each person's family support, said their real feelings aloud, and agreed simple rules together.
How did Rekha experience Kishore's reaction on Monday?
Rekha felt judged and scared he would refuse, which is partly why she hadn't told him.

Dear Coach Francis,
I'm writing because I can't say this properly at practice. Since you found out about my condition, you've benched me every time I look tired, and you ask me in front of everyone if I've taken my tablets. I know you mean well. But it makes me feel like a patient, not a player. Last month I even stopped mentioning when I felt dizzy, because I didn't want to be benched. That was stupid, I know.
Here's what I'd like instead. I take my tablets every morning. If I feel unwell, I'll tell you quietly and sit out. You don't need to ask in front of the team. My doctor says I can play.
Can we try it for a month?
Tushar

When does Tushar take the tablets?
Every morning.
How does Tushar feel when asked about tablets in front of everyone?
Tushar feels embarrassed and treated like a patient, not a player.
What plan does Tushar propose?
Tushar will take the tablets every morning and quietly tell the coach and sit out when unwell, without public questions.
How might Coach Francis feel reading this letter?
Coach Francis may feel surprised and a little hurt, but also relieved that Tushar wants to be honest about feeling unwell.

I'm Harish, and I sat next to Rajni in the Class 11 common room when a video went round the group: "Breaking: Voting date changed, go vote tomorrow instead!"
Rajni's grandmother was going to vote. Rajni frowned and didn't forward it. She opened the Election Commission website on her phone, scrolled, and said, "The date is the same. This is fake."
Then she typed in the group: "Checked the official site. Date hasn't changed. Please don't forward."
A few people reacted with thumbs up. One person said she was being preachy.
I don't know if she was angry or just worried about her Nani. But she stayed calm and posted the link.

Which website did Rajni check?
The Election Commission website.
What might Rajni have been feeling when she frowned at the video?
Rajni was probably worried and suspicious, thinking of her grandmother who planned to vote.
What did Rajni do that others could learn from?
She didn't forward the video, checked the official source, and shared the correct link calmly.
How does Harish see Rajni's reaction?
Harish can't tell exactly how Rajni feels but sees her stay calm and use facts.

The school hall in Nagpur buzzed as Principal Mr. Deshmukh announced the drawing prize. Irawati's name was read out, and she skipped to the stage. Sarika sat in the third row with her hands clenched in her lap. She had worked on her own peacock for two weeks. Her stomach twisted. Then she pressed her lips together, stood up and clapped hard, and when Irawati came back down she said, “Well done, it's beautiful.” Irawati beamed. At lunch, Sarika sat quietly. She whispered to a friend, “I wanted it too. But I am happy for her.” Her friend squeezed her hand.

How long had Sarika worked on her peacock?
Two weeks.
What was Sarika feeling as she clapped for Irawati, and how can you tell?
She was disappointed and a little envious, since her hands were clenched and her stomach twisted, yet she chose to celebrate.
What did Sarika do that helped her handle the mixed feelings?
She congratulated Irawati and then named her feeling privately to a friend, so she did not pretend it was not there.
How might Irawati have felt hearing Sarika's congratulation?
She probably felt warm and pleased, since she beamed, and she may not have guessed Sarika was also disappointed.
I put "current" in my cake recipe and my sister laughed. Why?

For a dried berry in cakes, the word is "currant". "Current" means happening now, or a flow of water or electricity.
Examples: Add a handful of currants to the dough. The current news is about the match. The river has a strong current.

The scholarship results were out at six, the hostel corridor was full of drilling for the new water pipes, and Keerthana's phone read 11:11 again.
That made three times today. The bus that morning had been number 111. Her canteen token had said 11. She'd been born on the 11th.
"It's a message," she told Rukmini over the noise. "Things are lining up. I'm getting it."
Rukmini put down her book. "What did it mean when you saw 11:11 last month, before the debate?"
Keerthana paused. She'd lost the debate. "That was different."
"And the times you saw 11 and nothing happened?"
"I don't notice those."
"Exactly," Rukmini said, gently.
Keerthana looked at her phone. 11:12. Her stomach dropped. She'd felt so clever for noticing. Now it only felt like noticing.

What number was the bus that morning?
How did Keerthana feel when the clock changed to 11:12?
Her stomach dropped; she felt deflated and a little foolish, since the sense of a special message had gone.
How could Keerthana test her 11 idea?
She could note down every time she sees 11 and what happens afterwards, including the times nothing happens, and compare it with other numbers.
How does Rukmini see the 11:11 signs?
Rukmini sees them as coincidences that Keerthana notices only when they fit, and she asks questions to help her see it.

Sunday, late. Today I told Hansa I hate my ears and the way my voice cracks. She said, "You look fine, honestly," and I nearly rolled my eyes. Then she told me she hides her forehead under her fringe every single day and hates how loudly she laughs. I'd never noticed either thing.
I realised I'd been carrying my worries around like they were only mine. We ended up laughing about our "flaws club" until Amma knocked to say lights out.
I'm still not sure my ears are fine, but I believe Hansa cares. Tomorrow I'll ask her about the science project instead of our faces.
Santosh

What does Hansa hide under her fringe?
She hides her forehead.
How did Santosh feel after Hansa shared her own insecurities?
Santosh felt less alone, having realised the worries weren't only theirs to carry. 🙂
How can Santosh support Hansa back without attaching worth to looks?
Santosh can listen, share honestly and turn to shared interests like the science project instead of ranking faces.
Why might Hansa have shared her own insecurities?
Hansa may have wanted Santosh to know they weren't alone, which made "you look fine" feel honest instead of just polite.

I'm Damini. Last term, I was so angry with Arohi.

She didn't come to my birthday. She didn't reply to my messages for four days. When she came back to school, she was quiet and didn't even say sorry. I told everyone she was selfish. I thought, that's just who she is.

A week later, our class teacher mentioned that Arohi's family had been moving house suddenly. Her father's job had changed cities. They'd packed in three days. She'd been sleeping on boxes.

I felt awful. I had decided she was selfish without even wondering if something was wrong.

I went to find her at lunch. I said sorry. She said, "I wanted to tell you, but everything was so messy."

Now when someone goes quiet, I try to remember Arohi's boxes. There's usually a reason I can't see.

How many days did Arohi not reply to Damini's messages?
She didn't reply to my messages for four days.
How did Damini feel after learning about Arohi's move?
Damini felt awful and ashamed for deciding Arohi was selfish without wondering if something was wrong.
What does Damini now try to remember, and why is it useful?
Damini remembers Arohi's boxes, a reminder that there's usually a hidden reason when someone goes quiet.
How might Arohi have felt when classmates called her selfish?
Arohi probably felt hurt and alone, already stressed by the sudden move.

I'm Nilesh, Vishal's big brother. Vishal was trying to tie his shoelaces on the step. He tried, got a knot, tried again, then kicked the shoe across the hall and yelled, “I hate laces!” Papa didn't tell him off. He sat next to him. “You've been trying a long time. That's frustrating.” Then he showed him just one step: “Make a bunny ear.” Vishal did. “Now another.” He did. I don't know if he'll remember tomorrow, but he tied one bow.

What did Papa tell Vishal to make first?
A bunny ear.
What was Vishal feeling when he kicked the shoe?
He was frustrated after trying and failing many times, and angry at the laces.
What did Papa do that kept frustration from becoming quitting?
He praised Vishal's effort and taught one small step at a time.
How does Nilesh see Vishal's success?
Nilesh isn't sure Vishal will remember tomorrow, but notices that he managed one bow.
In a shop, there is a sale of clothes. Every shirt costs $5, every hat $4, and a pair of jeans $10. How much do you need to pay for three shirts, two pairs of jeans, and four hats?

Three shirts cost 3 * 5 = $15.
Two pairs of jeans would cost 2 * 10 = $20.
Four hats would in total cost 4 * 4 = $16.
So for three shirts, two pairs of jeans, and four hats, you would need to pay 15 + 20 + 16 = $51.
The answer is 51.

Money is shared between Rahul and Sohan in the ratio 7 : 3. Rahul gets ₹120 more than Sohan. How much does each get? Rahul | 30 | 30 | 30 | 30 | 30 | 30 | 30 | Sohan | 30 | 30 | 30 |<-4 parts = ₹120 ->|

Answer: Rahul ₹210, Sohan ₹90.

Rahul has 7 parts and Sohan 3 parts, so Rahul has 7 - 3 = 4 parts MORE. Those 4 parts are the extra ₹120, so 1 part = 120 / 4 = ₹30. Rahul: 7 x 30 = ₹210; Sohan: 3 x 30 = ₹90. Check: 210 - 90 = 120 and 210 : 90 = 7 : 3. The bar model shows it clearly: the extra boxes on Rahul's bar are the difference.
Why is it rude to interrupt someone who is speaking?
Interrupting treats the speaker's words as unimportant. Because the speaker loses their train of thought and may not get to finish, the talk becomes frustrating for them.

So my dad asks me to wash the steel plates and I go, "Uuuugh," the longest groan in the history of the world. And I'm still walking to the sink. You asked what my groans mean, Harsha? Honestly, they mean I'd rather be doing anything else, but I'm going to do it anyway. Dad just says, "Nice performance, plates are waiting," and hands me the scrubber. If he lectured me, I'd sulk for an hour. But once, when I groaned on the stairs and held my chest, he stopped everything. I'm Uday, by the way. He can tell the difference.

What chore does Uday's dad ask Uday to do?
Dad asks Uday to wash the steel plates.
What is Uday feeling when groaning at the plates?
Uday is bored and reluctant, but is going to do it anyway. Uday says the groans mean wanting to be doing anything else.
What does Uday's dad do well or badly in handling the groan?
He answers lightly and keeps the expectation clear, which avoids a sulk. He also stops when a groan is real pain.
How might Harsha see Uday's groans?
Harsha, hearing the story, sees the groans as harmless venting. The father can tell when a groan is real.

If the sum of two numbers is 33, and if the second number is twice the first number, what is the second number?

The first number is 33/3=11.
The second number is 11*2=22.
The answer is 22.

“Honestly, nobody believes me when I say I didn't argue.” I'm Sabina, and last month a students' march was planned over leaked exam papers. My father, Wasim, said no at once: board prep, crowds, all of it. Instead of shouting, I asked him to tell me every single thing he was scared of. He listed three: getting hurt, losing revision time, being filmed. Then I told him why it mattered, that my cousin lost a whole year because of the leak. Ammi sat down and listened as well. In the end we made a deal. I wouldn't go to the march itself. I'd make posters with the school group at home on Saturday and join the small signature table outside our colony gate. Abbu even carried the posters out. Part of me still wanted to be there, but it felt fair.

What three things was Wasim scared of?
Getting hurt, losing revision time and being filmed.
What might Sabina have been feeling about the deal at the end?
Mixed feelings: part of Sabina still wanted to be at the march, but the outcome felt fair because both sides had been heard.
What could Sabina try if the parents had refused any kind of taking part, and why?
Sabina could write a letter or speak at a school forum from home, since it voices the concern while keeping the family's trust.
How does the deal look to Wasim?
His worries about safety and revision were listened to and answered, so he could accept a smaller way of taking part and even help carry the posters.

metadata.subtype: Approach: talking with parents and weighing their concerns [Action]

messages.content: What did my aunt study in college?
I can't tell you that, because I know nothing about your aunt's life. Ask her, since many people enjoy sharing their student days.

Rain drummed on the window. Monsoon had kept everyone indoors.

"Asif? Asif, bath time," said Kiran from the doorway.

Asif, not yet three, was pushing a wooden train round and round its track.

"Asif!"

Choo, choo. He didn't turn.

Kiran sat on the floor. "Train going to the bath?"

Asif looked up, blinking. "Train!"

"Train comes too."

He picked it up and trotted to the bathroom.

What was Asif pushing around the track?
A wooden train.
What does Asif's blinking suggest when he finally looked up?
It suggests he was deeply absorbed and pleasantly surprised, as if he hadn't noticed Kiran at all.
Why was sitting on the floor a good choice for Kiran?
Coming close and joining the train game caught Asif's attention without a fight.
How might Kiran have felt when Asif didn't turn around?
Kiran might have felt a little impatient at first, then understanding once Asif looked up.

Diwali cleaning day, Saturday
Today Mummy gave me SO many jobs at once. "Jahnavi, fold the clothes, put the diyas on the balcony, water the tulsi, bring the brass lamp from Dadi's room, find the rangoli colours and phone Harish Uncle about lunch."
I said OK and ran. Then I stood in the hall and could only remember the diyas. I put them out and came back.
Mummy sighed. "And the rest?" I felt so stupid 😔
Then Harish Uncle turned up anyway. "Too many at once, na? Let's do three." He wrote 1, 2, 3 on my palm with a pen: clothes, tulsi, lamp. I did all three! Then three more.
Tomorrow I'm making my own list.

What did Harish Uncle write on Jahnavi's palm?
He wrote 1, 2, 3 on the palm: clothes, tulsi, lamp.
How did Jahnavi feel when Mummy asked "And the rest?"
Jahnavi felt stupid and sad, because only the diyas had stayed in memory out of the whole long list 😔
What could Mummy try the next time she has lots of jobs for Jahnavi?
She could give two or three jobs at a time, or write them down the way Harish Uncle did, so they fit in Jahnavi's head.
What might Mummy have been thinking when she sighed?
Mummy was probably tired and rushed on cleaning day, and may not have noticed how many jobs she had given at once.

Read this:

Early July, rain every day: Two-year-old Sudha still wore nappies. Vidya put a small potty in the bathroom and let Sudha sit on it, just to try.
Late July: Sudha said “su-su” once, after the puddle on the floor. Vidya said, “Next time, tell before.”
Mid-August, still monsoon: Sudha stopped playing, said “Su-su, Amma!” and ran to the potty in time. Vidya hugged her. Sudha clapped for herself.

What did Vidya put in the bathroom?
She put a small potty in the bathroom.
How did Sudha feel when she got to the potty in time?
She was proud and happy, clapping for herself.
What in Vidya's approach helped Sudha?
She let Sudha try without pressure and gently reminded her to tell before, so Sudha learned step by step.
How might Vidya feel after Sudha's success in mid-August?
She likely feels relieved and proud after weeks of patient practice.

Read this:

I kept waiting for the right moment to tell my parents about the job in Toronto, and the right moment never came. On every Sunday call I opened my mouth and asked about the neighbours instead. Then, three weeks before my visa interview, my aunt phoned Amma. "Ganga is going abroad, didn't she tell you?" Amma called me that night and her voice was quiet. "Why did I hear it from Bua?" I tried to say I had been protecting them. It sounded thin. It was not the moving that hurt; it was the finding out. It took Papa two days to speak to me. I think if I had told them in March, they would have cried and then helped me pack. Instead I had to earn back something I had not known I could lose. - Ganga

Who told Amma about the job abroad?
Ganga's aunt, Bua, phoned Amma and told her.
What was Amma feeling when she asked "Why did I hear it from Bua?"
Amma felt hurt and shut out, and her voice was quiet.
What could Ganga do now to repair things?
Ganga could apologise sincerely for not telling them, share the plans and a visiting schedule, and listen to their worries.
How might Papa have felt during the two days before he spoke?
Papa may have felt hurt and disappointed, taking time to gather himself before talking.

Read this:

Monday: At the design studio, Nitin clicked between six tabs, none of them his poster brief: shopping sites, a quiz, a blog about bikes. He felt restless and guilty and blamed the dull project. Hafsa, at the next desk, noticed he'd yawned eleven times before lunch.
Wednesday: "When did you last sleep properly?" Hafsa asked. Nitin counted back. His cousin's wedding, two late nights, a long Sunday drive. "Maybe the poster isn't boring," she said. "Maybe you're just empty."
Saturday: Nitin slept till nine, went for a slow walk and didn't open his laptop.
The next Monday he opened the poster brief first thing. It was the same brief. But it held him for two hours, and he didn't open a single other tab.

How many times had Nitin yawned before lunch on Monday?
Eleven times.
Why did Nitin blame the poster project for his restlessness?
Restlessness felt like boredom, and the brief was the obvious target; he didn't notice that his tiredness after the wedding was the real cause.
What was the turning point, and what did Nitin choose after it?
Hafsa's question about sleep; Nitin chose a restful Saturday instead of forcing himself, and on Monday the same brief held his attention.
How does Hafsa see Nitin's week differently from how he sees it?
Where Nitin sees a dull project, Hafsa sees an exhausted colleague, noticing the yawns and guessing he needs rest rather than excitement.

metadata.subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Wanjiru held her phone up in the school yard in Nairobi. "Everyone in Form Two is trying this, Vera. The creator says a bottle of this energy powder makes you unstoppable." She lowered her voice. "But don't tell your mum, or the teachers. That's the rule of the group." Vera liked the idea of belonging, and she liked Wanjiru. Still, something in her stomach twisted at the word 'secret'. She glanced at the video again; nobody said what was in it. "Let me think," she said, smiling so Wanjiru wouldn't feel rejected. That evening she told her mother about the powder and the secret rule. Her mother did not laugh. "Thank you for telling me. Let's read what it says together tomorrow."

Where did Wanjiru show Vera the video?
She showed it in the school yard in Nairobi.
Why did Vera feel uneasy even though she wanted to belong?
The word 'secret' made her uncomfortable, and nobody in the video said what was in the powder. She also wanted to keep Wanjiru's friendship, so her feelings were mixed.
What step would help Vera most from here?
Telling a trusted adult, as she did, and checking the facts about the powder together before deciding anything.
How might Wanjiru see Vera's answer of 'let me think'?
She may feel a bit hurt or worried about being left out, or she may just accept it as a normal pause.

Read this:

At the school gate in Toronto, Maria watched Simran's aunt lean in with open arms. “Come here, give Aunty a big hug!” Simran's shoulders rose. She took a small step back, then held out her hand. “Hello, Aunty,” she said. The aunt paused, then laughed and shook the hand warmly. Later, when Simran's cousin Ravi ran up, Simran gave him a high-five and a huge grin. Maria noticed she chose differently each time. She wondered whether Simran had felt uneasy with the hug, or was only shy that morning. When Simran waved goodbye to the aunt, the aunt waved back, smiling.

What did Simran do when her aunt opened her arms?
She stepped back and held out her hand to shake.
What might Simran have felt when her aunt offered a hug, and what else could explain her choice?
She may have felt uneasy or not in the mood for a hug, though Maria admits she might just have been shy that morning.
What made the moment go well for both of them?
Simran offered another greeting and her aunt accepted it warmly, so nobody was pushed.
How might Simran's aunt have felt when the hug was declined?
She may have felt surprised for a moment, and her laugh and warm handshake suggest she accepted it kindly.

Clara is climbing to the top of a historical tower with stone stairs. Each level has eight huge steps in the stairs. Every step is made up of three massive blocks of stone. By the time she reaches the top, she has climbed past 96 blocks of stone. How many levels are there in the tower?

Clara climbed past 96 / 3 = 32 steps made up of 3 blocks of stone each.
At 8 steps per level, there are 32 / 8 = 4 levels in the tower.
The answer is 4.

Read this:

At the community centre library, five-year-old Jomon came up to the desk holding his father's hand. "C-c-c-can I have the b-b-b-book with the..." His lips pressed together and nothing came for a moment. Simran, the librarian, stayed kneeling at his height. She didn't guess. She didn't say "take your time." She just kept looking at him kindly and waited. "...the r-r-red tractor." "The red tractor book! We have two. One with flaps, one without. Which do you want?" "F-flaps!" "Flaps it is." She stamped his card and handed it to him, not to his father. Jomon hugged the book to his chest.

Which book did Jomon want?
The red tractor book, the one with flaps.
What does Jomon hugging the book suggest he felt?
It suggests he felt proud and happy that he asked for it himself and got what he wanted.
Which of Simran's choices showed respect for Jomon's pace?
She waited without guessing or saying take your time, then gave him a real choice and handed the book to him directly.
What would change for Jomon if Simran had guessed the book for him?
He might feel his words didn't matter, and his father might end up speaking for him.

Read this:

Parul's first months in Mumbai were lonely. Her paying-guest roommates worked night shifts, and her college friends were back in Indore. In the evenings she rewatched Lantern Street, an old animated series, and one night she found its fan group. Two thousand members drew fan art, wrote stories and shared tiny drawings of the lamp-lighter cat. Parul posted a sketch, shyly. Sarita, a fan from Thane, commented, 'This is SO good, you have to join the Sunday draw-along!' The group had one pinned rule: love what you love, don't trash what others love. Now, on Sundays, Parul sketched with twenty people on a video call, laughing about the cat. When Sarita suggested meeting at a comic fair with a few others, Parul checked who else was going, told her aunt, and went.

What was the fan group's pinned rule?
Love what you love, don't trash what others love.
How did Parul feel when Sarita praised her sketch?
Surprised and happy, less lonely, welcomed after months of isolation.
What did Parul do to keep meeting fans safe?
She checked who else was going to the public comic fair and told her aunt before going.
What might the Sunday draw-alongs mean to Sarita?
Sarita seems to enjoy bringing new people in and sharing the fun, so welcoming Parul likely felt good too.
What does it mean when someone writes "Cc'd" in an email, and when do I use Bcc?

"Cc" means "carbon copy": the people in Cc receive a copy that everyone can see. "Bcc" means "blind carbon copy", where the recipient's name is hidden from others. Use Bcc when you do not want to share addresses.
Example: I have copied the principal on this email.

Read this:

Nikita, you think I was always good at chess? When I was eleven, I lost every match in the district junior tournament. Seven games, seven losses. I cried behind the hall. My uncle said, "Yusuf, write down every mistake." So I did, in a school notebook. Every evening for a year I replayed my lost games and set up the pieces the way I should have moved. I lost many more times in between. The next year I won four games. Not the trophy, only four. But I remember that feeling better than any trophy since. Keep your notebook, beta.

How many games did young Yusuf lose in that first tournament?
Seven games, seven losses.
What was young Yusuf feeling while crying behind the hall?
Yusuf was crushed and disappointed after losing every match.
Why did writing down every mistake help Yusuf?
It turned the losses into lessons Yusuf could practise, so the effort had a clear direction over the year.
Why might Yusuf tell Nikita this story now?
Nikita may be facing a setback too, and Yusuf wants Nikita to see that steady effort after losing matters.

School coaches bought sports equipment. Coach A bought ten new basketballs for $29 each, while coach B bought 14 new baseballs for $2.50 each and a baseball bat for $18. How much more did coach A spend than coach B?

Coach A spent $29x 10=$290 for the 10 basketballs.
Coach B spent $2.50x14=$35 for the 14 baseballs.
So, Coach B spent a total of $35+$18=$53 for the baseballs and a bat.
Thus, Coach A spent $290-$53=$237 more than coach B
The answer is 237.

Read this:

Hi Himani,
So, the summer research fellowship results are out. I didn't get it. Which is honestly fine, because now that I think about it, I never wanted it. Two months of lab work in the heat, and everyone says the professor is impossible. I'd much rather rest.
Anyway, how's the new job?
Okay, actually, I just reread that first bit, and it sounds like the fox and the grapes. I did want it. I stayed up three nights on that proposal. I'm going to write and ask them what was weak.
Also I cried a bit. Just saying.
Sarita

What did Sarita stay up three nights working on?
The proposal.
Why did Sarita first write that the fellowship was never wanted?
Deciding it was never wanted softened the disappointment, so the rejection hurt a little less in the moment.
What turning point came when Sarita reread the first bit?
Sarita admitted wanting the fellowship and decided to ask what was weak in the proposal, so the attempt could teach something.
How might Himani feel reading an email that changes its mind halfway?
Himani might smile at the honesty and feel trusted, watching Sarita catch the excuse in real time 🙂

(1) Quick one: why do we write a shopping list?
(2) what should I say when I meet a friend's parents for the first time
(3) Tell me the meaning of "encounter".

1. It helps us remember what to buy. Because once an item is written down, we do not have to keep it in our heads.
2. Greet them politely and say it is nice to meet them. Thank them if they offer you something.
3. Encounter is a verb that means to meet, often without planning to.

Caroline has 40 pairs of socks. She loses 4 pairs of socks at the laundromat. Of the remaining pairs of socks, she donates two-thirds to the thrift store. Then she purchases 10 new pairs of socks, and she receives 3 new pairs of socks as a gift from her dad. How many pairs of socks does Caroline have in total?

After losing some socks, Caroline has 40 - 4 = 36 pairs of socks
Caroline donates 36 * (2/3) = 24 pairs of socks to the thrift store
After donating some socks, Caroline has 36 - 24 = 12 pairs of socks remaining
After getting new socks, Caroline has 12 + 10 + 3 = 25 pairs of socks
The answer is 25.

Read this:

Last month, a man I didn't know started waiting near the gate of my tuition class. First he gave me a chocolate, then a keychain. On Thursday he held out a toy car for my little brother Mohit and said, 'This is our secret, Seema. Don't tell your parents.' My stomach went cold. A present with a secret felt wrong, like a trap. I took Mohit's hand and walked straight home without the toy. I told Mummy everything, even about the chocolate I had already eaten. I thought she would be cross. She hugged me and said, 'You did nothing wrong. Telling me was exactly right.' That evening Papa and Mummy went with me to the tuition teacher and then to the police station near our colony. Now Papa picks us up every day.

Where did the man start waiting?
Near the gate of Seema's tuition class.
What does Seema's cold stomach suggest about how the secret felt?
Seema felt scared and uneasy; a present tied to a secret felt wrong, like a trap.
Which choices kept Seema and Mohit safe?
Refusing the toy, walking straight home and telling Mummy everything the same day; the parents then told the tuition teacher and the police that evening.
How might Mummy have felt when Seema told her?
Worried, but relieved and proud that Seema spoke up; she hugged Seema and said telling was exactly right.

In the courtyard of their Pune housing colony, Ojas and Salma, both five, had one goal: a sand tower tall enough to reach the bottom of the slide. "You bring water, I pat," Salma said. Ojas ran back and forth with a cup. When one side slumped, they both stopped. "More water," Ojas said. "No, too much," said Salma. "Less!" They patted together, carefully. The tower touched the slide, and they jumped up and down, shouting.

What was the tower supposed to reach?
The bottom of the slide.
What were Ojas and Salma feeling when the tower touched the slide?
They were thrilled and proud of reaching their goal together.
What helped them work as a team?
Splitting the jobs, water and patting, and talking about what went wrong when one side slumped.
How might Salma see Ojas as a partner?
As someone who followed the plan and stayed to fix the problem, which made the tower possible.
Ask me a question a child might ask about the moon. Just the question, under twelve words.
Why does the moon seem to follow our car?

Senior associate's note, for my own reflection.
Aadhya is on track for promotion faster than any of us. Honestly, I felt a pang of envy when the partners praised her again on Monday.
But I've watched the cost. She sends emails at 3 a.m. She skipped her best friend's engagement for a client deck. On Wednesday she looked grey and was holding her head during the review. She laughed it off: "Sleep is for after promotion."
I noticed I wanted to say, "Is it even worth it?" I didn't. That's her decision, and it would have sounded like judgment.
What I did next: I asked her to lunch outside the office, just the two of us. I said, "I'm not questioning your goals. I've just noticed you look worn out, and I'm worried. Would it help if I took the Friday client call?" She was quiet, then said yes.
Harish

Whose engagement did Aadhya skip?
Her best friend's engagement.
What mixed feelings did Harish have about Aadhya?
Harish felt a pang of envy at her fast promotion track, but also real worry after seeing how worn out she looked.
Why was Harish's approach at lunch a wise way to help?
Harish showed genuine concern without questioning her goals, and offered a practical break by taking the Friday call.
How might Aadhya have felt when Harish offered to take the call?
She may have been surprised and relieved, since her quiet pause before saying yes suggests she needed the break but hadn't asked.

Read this:

The monsoon rain was stopping, and the gutter stream outside the Kochi house would soon dry up. Kavitha and Suraj had only a few minutes.

"Quick! You fold, I'll write names," Kavitha said.

Suraj folded paper boats as fast as he could. Kavitha wrote a name on each one. They raced out together and launched six boats in a line.

The last boat sailed just as the stream slowed. They jumped and hugged.

How many boats did they launch?
They launched six boats in a line.
How did Kavitha and Suraj feel when the last boat sailed?
They were excited and happy, jumping and hugging.
What helped them finish the boats in time?
Dividing the jobs, one folding and one writing names, helped them work quickly toward the same goal.
How might Suraj feel folding boats so fast?
Suraj might feel rushed but determined to finish before the rain stopped.

Read this:

In the glass meeting room of a Bengaluru start-up, Jyoti, the manager, tapped the slide. "We go with the cheaper vendor. Final call by tomorrow."
Sumit, the youngest on the team, raised a hand. "I read it another way, and here's my worry. Their delivery times slipped twice in the pilot. If it happens at launch, we lose two weeks. I ran the numbers: the dearer vendor costs about six percent more but shows no slips. I'd suggest we pilot both for a month."
Jyoti scrolled through the numbers. "Thank you, that's a fair risk. But the budget is fixed. We take the cheaper one."
"Understood," Sumit said. "I'll set up weekly checks, so if it slips, we know early."
Jyoti smiled. "Good."

How many times did the cheaper vendor's delivery times slip in the pilot?
Their delivery times slipped twice in the pilot.
What was Sumit feeling when raising a hand to say "I read it another way"?
Sumit felt concerned about the launch risk. Raising the point with numbers and a suggestion shows conviction and care, not defiance.
What did Sumit do after the decision went the other way?
Sumit said "Understood" and offered to set up weekly checks so any slip would show early. That accepted the call and still protected the launch.
What might Jyoti have felt hearing the disagreement?
Jyoti probably appreciated the data and the offer of checks, even though the answer stayed the same. Trust grows when disagreement is followed by commitment.
Why do train wheels have a flange on the inside edge?
The flange keeps the wheel on the rail. Because it presses against the side of the track when the train begins to drift, the wheel is guided back into place.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 5, Monday.

Ramesh understands a lot about others now. In story time, he can explain why a character feels jealous or scared. But today, when his friend Bhupen chose to sit with a new boy at lunch, Ramesh said loudly, "He doesn't like me anymore."

I asked him, "Is there another reason Bhupen might sit there?"

Ramesh thought. "Maybe to be kind to the new boy." Then he added, "But he should sit with me."

He can see others' views when he's calm, but it's harder when he feels hurt. I'll keep asking these questions gently, and I've paired him with Bhupen for the project this week.

Who did Bhupen sit with at lunch?
A new boy.
Why did Ramesh say "He doesn't like me anymore"?
He felt hurt and jealous, and those strong feelings made it hard to see Bhupen's reason.
What did the teacher do to help Ramesh?
The teacher asked if Bhupen might have another reason and paired them for the project.
How might Bhupen feel if he heard Ramesh's comment?
Bhupen might feel sad or confused, since he was only being kind to the new boy.

Read this:

Note from Vidya's teacher, for home.
At circle time, Vidya told Sabina, "I have a real dinosaur at home. He sleeps under my bed and eats bananas." Sabina's eyes went round. Vidya looked very sure, even a little worried he might be hungry. I said, "What a fun story! Is it real or pretend?" Vidya thought hard. "Pretend... but a little bit real." Then the whole circle drew banana-eating dinosaurs. 🦕 You may hear more about him at dinner!

What did Vidya say her dinosaur eats?
She said he eats bananas.
What does Vidya's worry about the dinosaur being hungry suggest?
She half believed her own story; she felt playful and a little unsure where pretend ended and real began.
Why was asking "real or pretend?" a wise choice?
It enjoyed her imagination while gently helping her tell story from fact, without calling it a lie.
How might Sabina see Vidya's dinosaur story?
Sabina seems amazed and excited, with round eyes, and enjoys the story.

Read this:

Since Lakshmi started night shifts at the hospital laundry, she had forty minutes between getting home and dropping Sangeeta at the anganwadi. And for a week now, Sangeeta, four, who had been dressing herself since summer, lay on the floor every morning saying, "Baby can't do buttons," in a tiny voice.
Lakshmi's back ached, and the bus was at 8:10. She knelt anyway. "Baby can't do buttons? Then Amma will help this once." She did two buttons, cuddled her, and let Sangeeta do the last one. "Clever baby."
Breakfast was the same idli on the same steel plate, and the same song on the way to the bus stop. She didn't laugh, and she didn't skip the routine. By Friday, Sangeeta announced, "I'm big today," and buttoned everything herself, crookedly.

What did Sangeeta say in a tiny voice every morning?
"Baby can't do buttons."
Why might Sangeeta be acting like a baby since Lakshmi started night shifts?
She may be missing her mother and want to feel looked after, so being small is her way of asking for closeness.
What choice did Lakshmi make despite the 8:10 bus, and why did it work?
She knelt, helped with two buttons, cuddled her and kept breakfast and the song the same, so Sangeeta felt both cared for and safe, and was 'big' again by Friday.
What would change if Lakshmi had said, 'Stop acting like a baby, we're late'?
Sangeeta would probably feel more anxious and cling harder, and the baby behaviour might last longer.

Read this:

At the Mumbai playschool, Ishita and Gargi both yanked the play dough cutters. "Ma'am!" Ishita called. The teacher came over, holding a tiny sand timer. "Each of you has one timer. When the sand runs out, give the cutters over." Ishita watched the sand trickle. When the last bit fell, she held out the cutters to Gargi. "Your turn."

What was the teacher holding?
A tiny sand timer.
What was Ishita feeling as she watched the sand?
She was probably eager and patient, knowing her turn had a clear end.
What else could Ishita try if there were no timer?
She could count to a number, like fifty, and swap.
How does the timer look to Gargi?
Gargi finds it fair and knows her turn is coming.

Read this:

Salma checked the shared sheet for the third time that week. The vendor onboarding was Kishore's job, and Kishore's date had been “Monday”, then “Wednesday”, then “definitely Friday”. Each promise sounded cheerful, and each time Salma had booked the training room and told the finance team to expect the vendor's account. Each time she had rebooked. This Friday the room was booked again, and again the message came at 5 pm: “Some paperwork pending, sorry!” Salma read it twice, closed the laptop and sat silently for a moment. Then she wrote in the sheet next to Kishore's name a line she would never have added before: “Ask for a real date and what could go wrong.”

What dates did Kishore give for the vendor onboarding?
Kishore said “Monday”, then “Wednesday”, then “definitely Friday”.
What does Salma feel as she reads the message twice and sits quietly?
Salma feels frustrated and let down, and her trust in Kishore's dates is wearing thin.
What could Kishore do so the next date is believable?
Look at how long onboarding really took before, give a longer honest date, and say early if any paperwork could delay it.
How might the finance team feel about waiting for the account?
The finance team may be confused and irritated after being told to expect the vendor account three times, which would cost them trust in the plan.

Read this:

Sit, Pooja. You asked how you know if someone is controlling. Let me tell you about Sunita. We were twenty, in the same college in Nagpur, and she started seeing Mahesh from the hostel. First month, all sweetness. Then he began taking her phone at the canteen and scrolling through it. "I just worry about you," he'd say. He decided she shouldn't come to our study group because "those boys look at you". If she laughed with me, he went cold all evening. Everyone said, he's so caring. I thought so too, at first. What changed my mind was small: Sunita started asking him before ordering her own tea. So I asked her, alone, on the library steps, "Do you feel free with him?" She didn't answer. She just cried. We went to the college counsellor together that week. You know me as Lokesh mama, but back then I was only a worried friend, and that question is still the best one I know.

What did Mahesh say when he took Sunita's phone?
He said, “I just worry about you.”
What was Lokesh feeling when Sunita started asking permission for her own tea?
Lokesh felt worried and uneasy, because the small sign showed the so-called caring was taking away Sunita's freedom.
Which choice in the story made a difference?
Asking Sunita alone whether she felt free with Mahesh, then going with her to the college counsellor, gave her a safe way to face what was happening.
How might Sunita have experienced Mahesh's attention at the start?
At first it probably felt like love and care, which is why the control was hard to see until Lokesh's question made her cry.

Read this:

Thomas,
I'm writing this from bed at 3 pm on a Monday. The quarterly deck was due at ten. I set four alarms. I heard every one of them, and I could not make my body get up. Not lazy-couldn't. Couldn't, like my arms were filled with sand.
At eleven I finally messaged my manager: "Unwell, can't make it today." Then I cried for an hour, because I have never, ever done that.
It feels like I've failed at the one thing I'm known for. You know me, the 2 am edits person.
But lying here I keep thinking how I've been saying "I'll rest after this project" since March. Maybe my body just stopped waiting for me to agree.
I'm scared of what I'll say to my manager tomorrow.
Can you call me tonight?
Noor

How many alarms did Noor set?
Noor set four alarms.
Why does Noor feel like a failure after missing the deadline?
Noor is upset because Noor is known for 2 am edits and has never missed work like this, so staying in bed feels like failing at the one thing Noor is known for.
What could Noor do before facing the manager tomorrow?
Noor could rest today, talk it through with Thomas tonight and plan to be honest about months of overwork; if the heavy tiredness keeps going, a doctor visit would help.
What might Thomas feel when this letter arrives?
Thomas may be worried to hear that a friend who never misses deadlines couldn't get out of bed, and glad to be the one Noor reached out to.

Team lead's note, quarterly planning meeting, 9 May. Written by Lakshmi.
Something small happened today that I want to remember.
During the logistics section, the deputy manager presented the new route plan that cut delivery time in the east zone. It was Pallavi's work; I had seen her drafts for weeks. Her name was not on the slide.
Yogesh, who sits beside Pallavi, raised his hand when the slide came up. He said, calmly, "Just so the room knows, Pallavi designed this route plan. She'd be the best person to take questions." He didn't sound angry. He just said it like a fact.
Pallavi answered three questions. The deputy manager nodded and added, "Yes, Pallavi's analysis."
Next steps: I have added a "Prepared by" line to our slide template, and I thanked Yogesh privately. I also told Pallavi to keep sending me her drafts with dates.

What line did Lakshmi add to the slide template?
Lakshmi added a "Prepared by" line.
What does Yogesh's calm tone suggest about what he wanted?
It suggests Yogesh wanted fairness for Pallavi rather than a fight, so he stated the facts plainly instead of accusing anyone.
How did Lakshmi build on Yogesh's action?
Lakshmi made credit part of the system by adding a "Prepared by" line, thanked Yogesh, and asked Pallavi to keep dated drafts.
How might the deputy manager have felt when Yogesh spoke?
The deputy manager was probably caught off guard, but Yogesh's calm fact left room to agree, which is why they added "Yes, Pallavi's analysis".

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Thursday, by Samir Khan.
Ishita (Class 5) came in during break, eyes red. Two weeks ago her grandmother moved in with the family after an illness. Ishita told me that on the first day she refused to hug her because 'the room smelled of medicine', and said, 'I wish you'd gone to Masi's house instead.' Now her grandmother is back in hospital. 'What if she thinks I hate her?' Ishita sobbed. I told her that feeling guilty shows how much she cares, and that it does not have to stay forever. Together we made a card. She wrote: 'Dadi, I'm sorry for what I said. I love you. Please get well.' I phoned her father, who agreed to take her to the hospital that evening.

What did Ishita say the room smelled of?
Medicine.
What was Ishita worried about?
She felt guilty and frightened that Dadi might think she hated her after her unkind words.
What steps did the counsellor take?
Explained that guilt shows care and need not last forever, helped Ishita make a card, and phoned her father so she could visit that evening.
How might Dadi feel reading Ishita's card?
Touched and comforted; the apology and 'I love you' would show her Ishita's real feelings.
Why do owls hunt at night while sparrows sleep?
Owls are built for hunting in the dark. Because their big eyes gather dim light and their hearing is very sharp, they can find mice and insects at night when most other birds are asleep.

Day 1. The brown envelope arrived on a Tuesday. Manjula saw the tax department's stamp, felt her heart thump, and slid it into the drawer under the spare keys. "Probably a mistake," she told herself.
Day 40. The date on the letter passed. Manjula did not open the drawer.
Day 75. A second letter came, and this time it mentioned an extra charge on top of the original amount. Manjula's brother Anand found both envelopes when he came for the keys. He read the first one aloud.
"It was just one figure that didn't match," Anand said quietly. "It would have been a five-minute reply."
They took both letters to a qualified tax practitioner the next morning.

Where did Manjula put the first envelope?
Manjula put it in the drawer under the spare keys.
What was Manjula feeling when she put the envelope in the drawer?
Manjula was frightened, feeling her heart thump, and hoped it was a mistake.
What could Manjula do differently the next time a notice arrives?
Manjula could open it the same day, note the date for a reply and ask a qualified person if it is unclear.
How might Anand have felt reading the first letter aloud?
Anand was probably worried and sorry, speaking quietly, since a small mismatch had become bigger only through waiting.

Yes, roses need water. Because roses are flowers and every flower needs water, the rule that covers all flowers covers roses too.

Nicki spent the last year running a lot. For the first half of the year, she ran a total of 20 miles per week. For the second half of the year, she increased the mileage to 30 miles per week. How many miles total did she run for the year?

Each half of the year consists of 52 / 2 = 26 weeks.
For the first half of the year, Nicki ran a total of 20 * 26 = 520 miles.
For the second half of the year, Nicki ran a total of 30 * 26 = 780 miles.
For the entire year, Nicki ran a total of 520 + 780 = 1,300 miles.
The answer is 1300.

'Seven eights are fifty-six!' Divyansh shouted before Hansa Ma'am had finished the question.
'Right, Divyansh. Next time, hand up first. Can you try?'
'Sorry, Ma'am. It just jumps out.'
Ten minutes later he was standing by the window. 'Ma'am, can I sharpen my pencil?'
'You've sharpened it twice already.' She smiled. 'Tell you what. Be my messenger. Take this note to the office and back. Then sit and finish four sums.'
'Really?' He was already at the door.
When he came back, he finished all four sums, fast.
At home time Hansa Ma'am said, 'Divyansh, I'd like to talk to your Papa tomorrow. Nothing bad. Just how to help you learn best, maybe with advice from someone trained in this.'
'Am I in trouble?'
'No. You're clever. I want to help.'

What answer did Divyansh shout out?
Seven eights are fifty-six.
How does Hansa Ma'am feel about Divyansh's blurting and restlessness?
She feels patient and caring rather than annoyed; she smiles, makes him her messenger and wants to help him learn best.
What choice did Hansa Ma'am make when Divyansh was out of his seat again?
She made him her messenger to the office, giving him a movement break, and afterwards he finished four sums fast.
How might Divyansh feel when Hansa Ma'am says 'You're clever. I want to help'?
He may feel relieved and trusted, since he was afraid he was in trouble.
Write a tiny story for children, about 100 words, about a lost baby elephant who finds his way home by following a song.

Bholu, a baby elephant, wandered away from his herd while chasing a butterfly. Soon he was lost deep in the forest, and the trees all looked the same. He felt scared and began to cry. Then he heard a soft song, far away. It was his mother, humming the tune she sang each night. Bholu followed the sound through the bushes and across the stream. At last he saw the herd and ran into his mother's trunk. "Never wander off again," she said, smiling. Bholu promised, and fell asleep to the song.

"Lalremsiami, look." Ramesh held up his spelling test. "I spelled 'because' wrong."
"And the rest?"
"The rest doesn't matter. It's ruined. The whole test is a disaster."
Lalremsiami took it. "Nineteen out of twenty."
"But it's not twenty. I'm so stupid."
"You got nineteen right."
"One wrong means I'm bad at spelling."
"Ramesh, I got fifteen. Am I stupid?"
"No! Fifteen is good."
"So nineteen is terrible but fifteen is good?"
Ramesh opened his mouth. Closed it. "That's different."
"How?"
He looked at the paper. At the nineteen red ticks. At the one cross.
"Maybe it's not a disaster," he said slowly. "Maybe it's a nineteen."
"It's a very good nineteen."

What word did Ramesh spell wrong?
"Because."
Why did Ramesh call the whole test a disaster?
He felt upset and ashamed about the one mistake, and to him anything short of perfect felt like total failure.
What did Lalremsiami do that helped Ramesh see differently?
She compared her fifteen with his nineteen, showing him he judged himself far more harshly than he judged her.
How might Lalremsiami feel when Ramesh calls himself stupid over nineteen?
Lalremsiami might feel surprised and a bit concerned, knowing her own fifteen was good.

Tuesday. Week three. Things I've worked out without asking: the boss, Kiran, eats at the window table every day with the same four people. After-work chai on Thursdays is for them, and the invitation comes as a glance. On Monday Bhavna from accounts, who sits by the printer and has been here longest, ate alone and nobody minded.

I caught myself planning how to get a window seat. I stopped. Instead I asked Bhavna to explain the invoicing system over lunch, and it turns out she's brilliant and funny. I don't need the window table this month. I need to know how things work.

Maybe I'll be invited someday. We'll see.
— Santosh

Where does Kiran eat every day?
Kiran eats at the window table every day with the same four people.
Why did Santosh stop while planning how to get a window seat?
Santosh saw that chasing the table would drain energy and preferred to learn how things work.
What choice did Santosh make instead of planning for the window seat?
Santosh asked Bhavna to explain the invoicing system over lunch.
What might it be like for Bhavna, eating alone until someone sat down?
Bhavna may feel overlooked at times, and probably feels pleased and respected that a newcomer asked for advice.

Between the physics and chemistry classes at the coaching centre there was a seven-minute gap. Nazia's hand was on her phone before the teacher had finished saying "break". She didn't open anything in particular: a cat video, a meme, somebody's new haircut, next, next. When Bidisha asked what she'd been watching, Nazia honestly couldn't say. It happened again in the lunch queue, waiting for the lift, and during the few seconds while the projector warmed up. On Friday the teacher collected every phone in a basket before a test. In the first empty minute Nazia's hand went to her pocket, found nothing, and she laughed out loud. "My hand went looking on its own," she whispered to Bidisha.

How long was the gap between the physics and chemistry classes?
Seven minutes.
Why did Nazia laugh when her hand found an empty pocket?
She was surprised to see her habit so clearly; she had not decided to reach for the phone, and catching her hand doing it alone felt funny and a little unsettling.
What could Nazia try the next time a pause comes?
Treat the empty moment as the cue and keep a different small action ready, like stretching or talking to Bidisha, with the phone zipped in her bag between classes.
How does Bidisha experience Nazia's scrolling?
Bidisha asks what Nazia watched and gets no answer, so Bidisha sees a friend who is busy but not really present in the gaps they share.
