1/3 of the townspeople have received the full COVID vaccine. 1/3 are immune because they already recovered from COVID. If 1/6 of the townspeople are both vaccinated and already had COVID, what percent of the town is immune in some way?

First add the fractions of vaccinated and recovered townspeople: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3
Then you need to subtract the fraction that are both vaccinated and recovered, since they were double-counted. To do this, start by converting 2/3 to the same denominator as 1/6: 2/3 * 2/2 = 4/6
Then subtract 1/6 from 4/6: 4/6 - 1/6 = 3/6
Then divide the numerator by the denominator and multiply by 100% to express the answer as a percentage: 3/6 * 100% = 50%
The answer is 50.

Madhu stood behind the door, his face red. Sharmila closed her eyes. "Minakshi, enough." Minakshi's smile faded. She had expected Amma to say, good girl for telling. Madhu glared at her and went to the back of the house. He didn't call her for their usual game of stones that night.

What did Minakshi say Madhu broke?
She said he broke the pot at the well.
What did Minakshi expect when she told Amma?
She hoped Amma would praise her as a good girl for telling, so she felt let down when Amma said 'enough' and her smile faded.
What went wrong, and what could fix it?
Mocking and reporting Madhu only tired Amma and hurt Madhu; Minakshi could say sorry to Madhu, and Amma could later talk to each child calmly and separately.
How does Madhu feel after being mocked in front of Amma?
He feels humiliated and angry, so he glares at his sister and skips their usual game of stones.

Read this:

At five, Rashmi knocked the milk glass off the table, saw the white pool spread and crawled behind the sofa. "I'm bad," came a small voice. Aparna, Rashmi's mother, knelt at the sofa's edge. "That was a slip, sweetheart. It doesn't make you bad. Come and help me with the cloth." Rashmi crept out and held one corner of the cloth.

At fifteen, Rashmi snapped at Sangeeta in the canteen, "Just leave me alone, you're so annoying," and Sangeeta went quiet. For four days Rashmi replayed the words at night, ate lunch on the stairs to avoid the canteen, and told herself it proved what kind of person she was. Nothing in that review helped Sangeeta, only kept the shame going.

At twenty-one, Rashmi looked back at a year lost to sleeping late and dropped courses. Every job listing felt like a reminder. One evening Rashmi wrote in the diary: the person who made those choices was doing the best she knew then. That night Rashmi began an application, one small paragraph at a time.

Where did Rashmi crawl after knocking over the milk glass?
Rashmi crawled behind the sofa.
How does Rashmi's way of judging her own mistakes change across five, fifteen and twenty-one?

At five Rashmi treats the spilled milk as identity, saying "I'm bad," until Aparna says the spill was a slip that does not make Rashmi bad. At fifteen Rashmi replays the harsh words for days and avoids the canteen, calling it accountability. At twenty-one Rashmi writes that the earlier self did the best it knew, and starts moving forward.
What was Rashmi feeling while eating lunch on the stairs after snapping at Sangeeta?
Rashmi felt ashamed and wanted to avoid Sangeeta, using harsh self-review as if it were making up for the remark.
What could Rashmi do at fifteen instead of replaying the words for days?
Rashmi could apologise to Sangeeta simply, without a long speech, and then let the matter rest, so that shame does not replace repair.

"Swati, you've counted that money four times," Ramesh said from the doorway. "Just buy the phone."

"Papa, I'm not buying anything yet." Swati spread the notes on the table. Three months of weekend work at the flower stall. "I want to plan it."

"Plan it how?"

"Three parts. Some for home, because you've been doing extra shifts. Some for a laptop for college next year. And a little for me. Movies, a new bag, something."

Ramesh sat down slowly. "You don't have to give anything for home."

"I want to." She opened a notebook with three columns drawn in pen. "And I'm writing everything down, in and out. Every week."

He looked at the columns for a long moment. "When I was your age, I spent my first pay in two days."

Swati grinned. "Then you can check my notebook on Sundays."

Where did Swati work on weekends?
At the flower stall, for three months.
What does Swati counting the money four times suggest about how she feels?
It suggests she feels careful and protective of money she worked hard for, wanting to plan rather than spend on impulse.
What could Swati do if she is unsure about any part of the plan?
She could go through the notebook with Ramesh on Sundays, as she suggested, and ask him before any big spending.
How might Ramesh see his daughter's notebook?
Ramesh likely feels proud and a bit humbled, remembering spending his own first pay in two days.

Read this:

I'm Nakul, and I was on the sofa while my cousin Mridul played online in our flat. He kept grinning at the screen. "An older player gave me a rare skin for free. He says I'm the best he's met, and I should add him on a private chat."
Then Mridul hesitated. "He also said not to tell my parents, because they'd make me stop." His grin dropped a little.
I asked, "Why would a grown-up give free stuff to a kid and want it kept secret?" He shrugged and said the skin was cool, but he didn't look sure.
Later I saw him remove the friend request. At dinner he told his mother. She put down her spoon, thanked him for telling her and said it wasn't his fault. They blocked and reported the account together that evening. I don't know whether he was scared or just tired of it.

What did the older player give Mridul for free?
He gave Mridul a rare skin.
What did Mridul seem to be feeling when he hesitated?
His grin dropped a little and he didn't look sure, so he seemed uneasy about the gift and the secrecy, though Nakul can't know for certain.
What could Mridul do when someone offers gifts that come with secrecy?
He can refuse gifts that come with secrecy, remove the contact and tell his parents or another trusted adult, as he did at dinner.
How did Mridul's mother react when he told her at dinner?
She stayed calm, thanked him for telling her and said it wasn't his fault, then blocked and reported the account with him that same evening.
Lohri pe bonfire hota hai. Ek chhota description English mein chahiye school diary ke liye.
"Lohri is celebrated in January, mostly in Punjab. In the evening, families light a bonfire, sing songs and throw peanuts, popcorn and sweets into the fire. It marks the end of winter."
Rewrite in easy words: The baker prepared a delicious loaf of bread.
The baker made a tasty loaf of bread.

Over the last year I watched my cousin Parul pour more and more into her friend's cloud kitchen. First her bonus, then her savings, then a loan from her father. Every time the numbers came back worse, she defended it harder. 'It's a slow start. Every business loses money the first year. If I pull out now, everything before was for nothing.' When I asked a gentle question at Eid, she snapped that I'd never believed in her. I realised she wasn't defending the kitchen anymore; she was defending herself from feeling foolish. So last month I tried a different door. I said, 'You made the best choice you could with what you knew then. You know more now. Would you sit with a proper financial adviser, just once? I'll come with you.' She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'Noor, can you book it for a Saturday?'

What did Parul put into the cloud kitchen first?
Parul put in her bonus first.
What did Noor realise about Parul's fierce defence, and how did Noor feel?
Noor, worried and a little hurt after the snap at Eid, realised Parul was protecting herself from feeling foolish, not really defending the kitchen.
Why did Noor's new approach give Parul a way to change course without humiliation?
It said her earlier choice made sense with what she knew then, framed change as new information, and offered company to a qualified adviser.
Why did Parul defend the kitchen harder after each loss?
With each loss, admitting the mistake would feel more humiliating, so defending it felt like protecting her own judgement.

You asked about the conference, Nikita? Okay. I'm Bhupen, and I did something I was terrified to do.

The keynote speaker was a famous professor. I'd read all his books. During his talk, he said that remote teams "always" perform worse than office teams.

My own research showed the opposite for software teams. I'd spent two years on it.

At question time, my hands were sweating. I stood up and said, "Professor, thank you. I've admired your work for years. Could you tell us how you reached that conclusion? My study of 300 software teams found remote teams did slightly better."

The room went quiet. He paused. Then he said, "That's interesting. My data was mostly from manufacturing firms. It might not apply to software."

After the talk, he asked for my paper.

I think the trick was separating respect for him from agreeing with him.

How many software teams did Bhupen's study cover?
My study of 300 software teams.
How was Bhupen feeling at question time?
Bhupen felt terrified and nervous, with sweating hands, but determined to ask.
What made Bhupen's challenge respectful and effective?
Bhupen expressed admiration, asked how the conclusion was reached and offered specific evidence, separating respect from agreement.
How did the professor respond?
The professor seemed interested, admitted his data came from manufacturing, and asked for Bhupen's paper.

Christmas in Lalremsiami's village near Champhai meant church, pork stew, and every aunty in the valley asking the same things. 'Siami, you're twenty-one. When is the wedding?' 'Government job yet?' Her college friend Ayesha, visiting from Guwahati, watched her friend's smile tighten with each round. At the fourth house an uncle asked what she earned at her part-time cafe job, and Siami's ears went red. On the walk back past the terraced fields, she kicked a stone. 'They make me feel like I'm late for a train I never bought a ticket for.' Ayesha laughed. 'So tell them your train leaves later.' At the fifth house, when the question came, Siami smiled. 'I want to finish my social work degree first, Pu. Your oranges are the sweetest in the village.' The uncle beamed and gave her three more.

What did the uncle ask at the fourth house?
What she earned at her part-time cafe job.
How did Siami feel as she kicked a stone?
Siami felt frustrated, judged and rushed, like being late for a train she never bought a ticket for.
What worked about Siami's answer at the fifth house?
She stated her own plan kindly and turned to a warm compliment, keeping respect without taking on their timetable.
How does Ayesha see the relatives' questions?
Ayesha finds them a bit funny and helps Siami see she can simply run on her own, later train.

Read this:

"Tushar, you've been staring at that phone since dinner."
"It's nothing, Aai."
Ganga sat beside him on the diwan. "Nothing doesn't make you skip rice."
He sighed. "I made an error in the client sheet last week. I need to email my team lead and tell her."
"When did you find it?"
"Saturday."
"It's Wednesday, beta."
"I know!" He rubbed his eyes. "Every time I type it, I imagine her reply. Or no reply. Or a meeting invite with no title."
"How long is the email?"
"Three lines."
Ganga held out her hand. "Read it to me."
He read it. His voice shook on "my mistake".
"That's a good email," she said. "Clear. Honest."
"She'll be angry."
"Maybe. And then it'll be over. Right now it's been going on since Saturday."

When did Tushar find the error?
On Saturday.
What does Tushar's shaking voice on "my mistake" suggest?
He is frightened of how his team lead will react; saying the admission aloud makes that fear feel real, even in a three-line email.
What choice does Ganga help Tushar make, and why does it help?
She has him read the email aloud and tells him it is clear and honest, turning a dreaded message into a finished one he can send.
How does Ganga see her son's evening?
She notices he skipped rice and has been staring at his phone, and sees that waiting since Saturday is hurting him more than any reply might.

Class teacher's note, Holi week, Class 9B. Sabina
Vijay has changed a lot since June. In term one he sat with the cricket boys and talked only scores. By August he was with the art-club group, nails painted black. Last month he was loudly arguing politics with the debate crowd; this week he sits alone at lunch. Today, at the Holi celebration, he refused colour, then later joined in, then snapped at a friend who asked which group he's with now.
He stayed back and said, "Ma'am, I don't know who I'm supposed to be." He looked genuinely unsettled.
I told him that trying things on is normal at his age and that he does not have to choose today. I will mention to his parents that he seems unsettled, and I have booked him a chat with the school counsellor next week, only to talk.

Which group was Vijay with by August?
The art-club group, nails painted black.
What is Vijay feeling when he says "I don't know who I'm supposed to be"?
He feels unsettled and confused, which also shows in snapping at a friend and sitting alone at lunch.
What did the teacher do next, and why does it help?
The teacher told him trying things on is normal, took away the pressure to choose, and arranged a counsellor chat and a word with his parents, so he has support while exploring.
How might Vijay's friend feel when snapped at?
The friend was likely hurt and puzzled, asking a simple question and getting an angry answer.

Beta, I am Madhav, and I once swore that the compiler in our college lab was broken. My program would not run. I told everyone. For two hours I typed the same lines and grew angrier. My lab partner Parul finally pushed back her chair and asked, "Which file is it actually opening?" I snapped that it was obvious. She said, "Humour me." We checked. I had saved my file in a different folder, and the compiler was faithfully running an old copy. Two hours, and the machine had done nothing wrong. I have wondered ever since what else I stopped checking because I felt so sure.

What did Madhav swear about the compiler?
Madhav swore that the compiler in the college lab was broken.
What was Madhav feeling during the two hours before Parul asked her question?
Madhav grew angrier and stubbornly certain that the machine was at fault, which is why Madhav told everyone.
What was the turning point in the story?
Parul asked which file the compiler was actually opening, and checking showed the file was saved in a different folder while an old copy ran.
Why might Parul have said "Humour me" when Madhav snapped?
Parul probably saw that Madhav was too irritated to think and wanted a small check that would test the assumption behind the anger.

Read this:

"I keep hearing it, Aparna-didi. Nani said, 'Come when your exams finish, no hurry.' And I said, 'Next month, promise.'"
Aparna set down the steel tumblers. "Rukmini, that's the fourth time this week you've told me about that call."
"Because if I'd taken the Friday bus instead of waiting for results, I'd have seen her. I'd have noticed she was breathless. I'd have—"
"You'd have what? Stopped her heart from doing what it did?"
Rukmini twisted her dupatta around her fingers. "At least then it would properly be my fault. Now it's just... nothing I can hold."
Aparna sat beside her on the divan. "Amma says the same about not calling the doctor that Sunday. Three months, and you two keep taking turns blaming yourselves."
"So what do I do with it?"
"Say it to me instead of to the ceiling at two in the morning. And maybe you try the counselling centre at your college. I'll come with you the first time."

What did Rukmini promise Nani on their last phone call?
Rukmini said, 'Next month, promise,' after Nani told her to come when her exams finished.
Why might Rukmini wish the death were 'properly' her fault?
Blaming herself gives her something to hold on to; guilt feels easier than accepting that Nani's death was never in her hands.
What turning point is open to Rukmini at this stage?
She can say the what-ifs out loud to Aparna instead of looping alone at night, and take up the offer to visit the college counselling centre together.
How is Aparna affected as she listens to her sister?
Aparna is grieving Nani too, and she is watching both Amma and Rukmini blame themselves, so she is trying to steady the family while carrying her own loss.

Thursday in the college lab, Samir's juniors crowded around his laptop again. "Your code never breaks," one said. Samir laughed and scrolled to the version that had crashed three times last week. "Look at this mess. I just don't show it." Across the room his classmate Shalini, who had barely spoken to him all term, turned her chair away when he greeted her. He went over recent weeks in his head once: no quarrel, no favour left unreturned. He shrugged and stopped waving at her. That evening he posted the club's result on a public page, and by midnight strangers were mocking his photo and the team. He did not answer a single one. He saved the worst comments in a folder, blocked the accounts, and phoned his roommate, who told him to come and eat. Harish, who sat beside him in class and had beaten him in every test, passed over a marked paper with a higher score. Samir felt his jaw tighten, then asked how Harish had solved the last question. He copied the method into his notebook, and next week he lent Harish his spare charger when the lab socket failed.

What did Samir save in a folder?
He saved the worst comments in a folder.
How did Samir's response to the strangers online differ from his response to Shalini turning her chair away?

With the strangers he did not answer, saved the comments, blocked the accounts and leaned on his roommate; with Shalini he thought once about whether he had done wrong and then stopped waving at her, so in neither case did he keep chasing approval.
How was Samir feeling when Harish passed him the paper with the higher score?
His jaw tightened, so he felt stung and a little envious, but he turned that into curiosity about Harish's method.
What could Samir keep doing so his juniors' praise does not inflate him?
He can keep showing them his crashed versions and admitting his flaws, as he did when he scrolled to the messy code. 🙂

Class 4 teacher's note, Friday
For three weeks Shreya has been on the rota to wipe the board and water the class plants. Each morning she agrees brightly, "Yes, Nazia Ma'am!", and each afternoon the board is still full and the plants are dry. When I remind her, she says, "Oh no, I totally forgot!" with a big smile.
Today I asked her quietly, "Is there a job on the rota you'd rather not do?" After a pause she said, "The chalk dust makes me sneeze, and the boys at the back laugh when I sneeze."
We've swapped her to handing out notebooks. I also told her she can always tell me no, or ask to swap, and I won't be cross.

Which two jobs was Shreya on the rota for?
Wiping the board and watering the class plants.
Why might Shreya say 'I totally forgot!' with a big smile?
She didn't want the board job because of the sneezing and the laughter, but felt she couldn't say no, so a cheerful 'forgot' was easier.
Which choice of the teacher's worked, and why?
Asking quietly whether there was a job Shreya would rather not do, and promising she could say no or swap, which made a direct refusal safe.
What would change for Shreya now that Nazia Ma'am has said 'I won't be cross'?
She may feel safe to say no openly next time, so she won't need to 'forget' to show she doesn't want a job.

I noticed it first in the way Parul said "great job" after my client presentation, with a smile that stopped just short of the eyes. I had been promoted to lead a workstream a year earlier than Parul expected, and everyone could feel the comparison.

I decided not to shrink myself, and not to gloat either. When Parul got stuck on a pivot table, I showed the shortcut I had taken months to learn. I never mentioned the promotion, and I never joked about it in front of others.

Then a shared folder of mine lost half its files, twice. The second time the edit log showed Parul's account. That was no longer envy about progress. I wrote down the dates and asked my manager for a short meeting, because a boundary needed someone else in the room.

I still nod to Parul each morning. 🙂

— Vasudha

What did Vasudha show Parul when Parul got stuck?
Vasudha showed Parul a shortcut for the pivot table that had taken months to learn.
What was Vasudha thinking when the shared folder lost files a second time?
Vasudha realised the problem had moved from envy to something that needed a boundary, because the edit log pointed to Parul's account.
Why was it wise to involve the manager?
Once files were being lost, keeping notes of dates and asking the manager to join set a fair limit without publicly accusing or humiliating Parul.
How might Parul see Vasudha's generosity?
Parul may feel both helped and compared, since the shortcut was kind but also a reminder that Vasudha is ahead.

Hemant: Omkar, I am at the hardware shop and the owner only speaks Bengali. I need a hinge for the cupboard
Omkar: Show him the broken one
Hemant: I did. Then I drew a little door with my finger, opening and closing 😅
Omkar: And?
Hemant: He gave me a lock. Wrong thing
Omkar: Take a photo of the hinge and show it, then say "this one" and point
Hemant: Good idea. Also he nodded in a way I could not read. Yes or no?
Omkar: Ask again with the photo
Hemant: Done. He is smiling and opening a drawer. Fingers crossed 🤞

What did Hemant need from the hardware shop?
He needed a hinge for the cupboard.
Why was Hemant unsure about the owner's nod, and what did he feel?
He could not read whether the nod meant yes or no, and he was uneasy after being handed the wrong item. The nod might have been polite or confirming, so he wanted to check.
What did Omkar suggest to avoid another mistake?
He suggested showing a photo of the hinge and saying "this one" while pointing, so the request is confirmed with an image.
How might the shop owner have felt when Hemant mimed a door?
He may have felt willing to help but uncertain what Hemant wanted, which is why he offered a lock instead.

Read this:

Darshan, don't look at me like that. I'm Urmila, and I'm a sensible person who does not watch shows till 2 a.m. Except last night. The season finale ended with Meher's car going off the bridge. Off the bridge! And then "to be continued." I actually shouted at my phone, and my mother knocked on the door. I tried to sleep. I kept replaying the bridge, working out whether the brakes were cut. So I started the next season "just to check she's alive." That episode ended with a letter nobody opened. I was so angry at the writers, and I still clicked next. It's like my brain refuses to leave a door open.

How did the season finale end?
With Meher's car going off the bridge and then "to be continued."
What was Urmila feeling toward the writers, and why did the watching go on anyway?
Urmila was angry at them for leaving the story hanging, yet the unanswered questions about the bridge and the letter kept nagging, so clicking next felt easier than stopping. 😠
At what point could Urmila have made a different choice, and what might it be?
After shouting at the phone, Urmila could have written down a guess about the brakes and put the phone away, parking the question instead of starting the next season.
What might Urmila's mother think on knocking at the door at night?
Urmila's mother may be worried or annoyed at hearing shouting so late, and wonder why Urmila is still awake.

In January I was in four coaching batches, and I was drowning. I'm Saurabh, and I knew complaining wouldn't work with my parents. They'd paid the fees. They thought more classes meant more marks.

So my friend Arnab helped me prepare like it was a case. I printed my weekly timetable, 64 hours with travel. I brought my last four maths mock scores from the weekend batch: they hadn't moved. And my physics ones, from the batch I liked: rising.

At dinner, I laid it out. "I don't want to stop. I want to drop the weekend maths batch for two months. Use that time to solve problems. If I'm not above 70 in maths by March, I'll go back."

My father went quiet. My mother asked, "And who checks?"

"We all do. March mock, together."

They agreed. By March I had 74.

What were Saurabh's weekly hours with travel?
64 hours with travel.
How did Saurabh feel before the dinner conversation?
Saurabh felt overwhelmed, like drowning, and doubtful that complaining would convince the parents.
What else could Saurabh have included to strengthen the case?
Saurabh could have shown a sample weekly plan for the freed hours, so the parents could see exactly how the time would be used.
How might Saurabh's mother see the agreement?
Saurabh's mother seems cautious but willing; asking who checks shows a wish for a clear way to review the decision.

Weeks one to four. Yash tried everything: app limits, the phone on the hall shelf, if-then cards. Each plan worked for a few days. Then he was scrolling till two in the morning again. His marks slid from seventy-two to fifty-eight. He felt ashamed and told nobody.
Week five. After a bad exam he said to his mother, “I've tried and I can't stop.” She didn't scold. The next morning they both went to see Trisha ma'am, the school counsellor.
Two weeks later. Trisha ma'am had set up a structured routine with Yash, with fixed wind-down time and a weekly check-in. “If it keeps going or worries you, we can look at more support together,” she said. That night Yash was asleep by eleven.

Who did Yash speak to, with his parent?
Trisha ma'am, the school counsellor.
How did Yash feel after several failed plans?
Ashamed and frustrated: he told nobody and only spoke after a bad exam.
What else could Yash do if the routine is not enough, and why?
Tell the counsellor and his parents so they can look at more support, since needing more help is a sign to ask, not a failure.
How does the situation look to Trisha ma'am?
Trisha ma'am sees a student who kept trying and then asked for help, and can offer a routine and follow-up with his parents without blame.

In the kitchen of their village house near the church, Joseph, two, reached for the steel tumbler on the stove. "Joseph, no. Hot," said his mother Bhavna, just once, firmly. His hand stopped in the air. He looked at her, pulled it back and said, "Hot." Then he toddled to his grandfather's chair, climbed up, and laid his head on the old man's arm while Appachan stroked his hair.

What did Joseph reach for on the stove?
The steel tumbler.
What does Joseph pulling his hand back and saying "Hot" suggest?
He trusted his mother's warning and felt it mattered, so he accepted it without a fight.
How could Bhavna build on Joseph listening to her?
Praise him for stopping and keep her warnings short and calm, saving a firm "no" for real dangers.
What might the moment on the chair mean to Appachan?
It probably feels warm and touching to have his grandson come to him for comfort.

Chinmay, you look like you want to break your phone. Sit with me.
When I was fifteen, in our Nashik school, a girl in my class spread a story that I'd been thrown out of my old school for cheating. Not one word of it was true. Within two days, girls stopped sitting near me. I heard whispers on the stairs.
I wanted to scream. I also wanted to spread something worse about her. I knew things.
That night I told my mother. She didn't shout. The next day she came with me to the headmistress, and together we showed my old school's leaving certificate with the conduct remark: "Excellent." That was the turning point.
The headmistress spoke to the class. I said only one thing: "I was never thrown out. Here is my certificate." I didn't say a word about the other girl.
My two real friends stayed close. The rumour died in a week. Your Sangeeta Aaji learned: facts, calm, and good friends.

What did the rumour claim about young Sangeeta?
That she had been thrown out of her old school for cheating.
How did young Sangeeta feel when the whispers started?
She felt frightened and furious, wanting to scream and even to spread something worse about the other girl.
What was the turning point, and why did it work?
Going to the headmistress with her mother and the leaving certificate let her correct the rumour once with facts, without starting a counter-rumour.
How might the girl who spread the rumour have felt when the headmistress spoke?
She probably felt exposed and uncomfortable, especially since Sangeeta didn't attack her back.
Help me fix this line. He borrowed me five hundred rupees last week.

He lent me five hundred rupees last week.
Why: "lend" means give; "borrow" means take; past is "lent".

After a news channel showed a leopard attack in a district two hundred kilometres away, Dhanori changed overnight. Preeti watched it happen from the door of her anganwadi near the temple. Parents stopped letting children walk the field path to school, even at noon. Vijay, the sarpanch's son, organised men with sticks to guard the path and had an announcement made on the loudspeaker twice a day. Nobody in Dhanori had seen a leopard in living memory. Meanwhile, every evening, sugarcane tractor-trolleys roared down the main road with no back lights, and boys still rode on top of the loads, waving. Preeti mentioned the trolleys at the panchayat meeting. Vijay nodded politely and went back to the leopard.

Who organised men with sticks to guard the path?
Vijay, the sarpanch's son, organised them.
What might Preeti be worried about when she raises the trolleys at the meeting?
She seems worried that the everyday danger of unlit, overloaded trolleys is being ignored while everyone fears a leopard no one has seen.
How could Preeti make her point about the trolleys land better?
She could describe a concrete near-miss on the main road and suggest one simple step, like back lights, instead of arguing against the leopard fear.
Why might Vijay keep returning to the leopard rather than the trolleys?
The vivid TV story feels urgent and gives him a visible way to protect people, while the trolleys are familiar and feel normal.

Giselle is in charge of the relay run on track and field day. Last year, the race was 300 meters. This year, it will be 4 times as long. Giselle needs to set up 6 tables for the relay run. The distance between the tables must be the same and the last table will be at the finish line. What is the distance between table 1 and table 3 in meters?

The relay run is 4 times the length of last year's race, so 300 meters x 4 = 1200 meters.
With 6 tables along the route, the distance between tables is 1200 meters / 6 tables = 200 meters.
The distance between tables 1 and 3 is 200 meters x 2 = 400 meters.
The answer is 400.
My friend is going through a tough time at home and doesn't want to talk about it.
It's thoughtful of you to care. Sometimes the best help is to simply be there. How is she at school?
Quieter than usual.
Sit with her at lunch, include her in small things, and tell her you're around if she wishes to talk. Don't push her to share.
What if she doesn't want to talk at all?
That's fine. Being a steady friend still matters. You might share something light, like a funny story, to give her a break from worries.
Should I tell the teacher?
If you're really worried about her, a quiet word with a trusted adult such as a teacher or counsellor can help. Say that you are worried, and let them decide how to help.
My deskmate spreads her things all over our shared desk, and I end up with no space.
That's annoying when you need room to write. A friendly word at the start usually works best. You could say, 'Can we each keep to our own half of the desk?'
What if she forgets after a day?
Then a small marker helps. Place a ruler or pencil box along the middle as a gentle line, and point to it with a smile when things drift across.

The two blocks of the Hebbal apartment complex had never got along: Block A said Block B's kids were rough, Block B said A's were spoilt. Vishal, twenty-six and the new father of a toddler, caught himself nodding along at an A-block meeting. Then one evening at the park his daughter tripped, and it was Usha from Block B who scooped her up and dusted her knees before he could get there. Usha's son had the same scab on the same knee. They both laughed. Sitting on the bench, Vishal realised they were just two tired parents in the same park. At the next A-block meeting, when someone said, "B people never pay maintenance on time," Vishal said, "Let's check the records before we say that." He suggested a joint parents' group for the play area. Some grumbled. Twelve families joined.

Who scooped up Vishal's daughter when she tripped?
Usha from Block B.
What did Vishal realise on the bench with Usha?
That they were just two tired parents in the same park, not rivals from different blocks.
What choices did Vishal make at the next A-block meeting?
He asked to check the records before blaming B people, and suggested a joint parents' group for the play area.
How might Usha see Block A after this?
Usha may feel the divide soften, having been treated as a fellow parent rather than as one of the 'B people'.

At the edge of the village, Kunal's Dadi kept a steel tin of laddoos under the bed just for him. "Skip the cow-shed today, beta, sit and eat," she said. Kunal loved it. His younger brother Samir watched, chewing slowly. When Mummy came in from the fields, Kunal swallowed and said, "Dadi gave me sweets, and I will feed the calf now, before dinner." He did not say Dadi had told him to skip it. Samir raised his eyebrows. Later Kunal whispered, "Dadi's love is sweet. Mummy's is a schedule. I need both." Samir laughed and asked for a laddoo.

Where did Dadi keep the tin of laddoos?
She kept a steel tin of laddoos under the bed.
What was Kunal feeling as he ate the sweets, and what did he do when Mummy came in?
He felt happy and loved by Dadi, yet he still owned up to his chore and said he would feed the calf.
What did Kunal do well in balancing Dadi's treats and Mummy's rules?
He enjoyed his grandmother's sweets without using her as an excuse against his mother. 😊
How might Samir have seen the situation?
Samir probably saw his brother getting a treat and wondered whether he would use it as an excuse, and was amused when Kunal did not.

Wallace's water heater is twice the size of Catherine's water heater. If the capacity of Wallace's water heater is 40 gallons and it's 3/4 full, calculate the total number of gallons of water they both have if Catherine's water heater is also full with water to 3/4 of its capacity.

When 3/4 full of water, Wallace's water heater has 3/4*40 = 30 gallons of water.
Catherine's water heater capacity is 40/2 = 20 gallons
When 3/4 full, Catherine's water heater has 3/4*20 = 15 gallons of water.
Together, when 3/4 full with water, Wallace's and Catherine's water heaters hold 15+30 = 45 gallons of water.
The answer is 45.

Dear Ujjwal sir,

Thank you for meeting me last week. I have been thinking about what you said.

You told me my code is solid but that I say yes to every task, so nobody knows what I'm actually good at. I didn't enjoy hearing that, if I'm honest. But you're right.

I'd like to aim for a tech lead role in about eighteen months. To get there, I'm going to focus on backend performance, since you said it's where the team is weakest. I'll say no to some smaller tasks and explain why.

Would you be willing to meet every two months and tell me honestly if I'm on track? I'd also be grateful if you'd suggest my name when the next performance project comes up.

Thank you for being straight with me.

Tanvir

What role does Tanvir hope to reach in about eighteen months?
Tanvir hopes to become a tech lead.
How did Tanvir feel about Ujjwal's feedback at first?
Tanvir didn't enjoy hearing it, but came to accept it was true.
What makes Tanvir's plan strong?
Tanvir picks a clear focus, plans to say no to some tasks, asks for regular honest check-ins and asks Ujjwal to suggest Tanvir's name.
How might Ujjwal feel reading this email?
Ujjwal might feel that being honest was worth it, and pleased to support someone taking feedback so seriously. 🙂

At two in the morning Rajni drafted a resignation letter. Then she opened a travel site and checked one-way tickets to Bengaluru, and hovered over a message that would end things with her boyfriend. None of it was decided; it was simply the urge for something to change tonight. On a call, her sister Preeti told her, "Don't send any of it tonight."

Instead she took a notebook and split a page in two. Left side: what she could still fix, such as learning to code in the evenings, asking for another team, mending an old friendship. Right side: what was gone, like the year after college and the course she had never done. Then she wrote what she truly valued: making things with her hands, working with people she liked, and the city she loved. It was a direction, not a dread.

So she tried small things. She took a weekend design course, started a side project redesigning the neighbourhood library's posters, and had coffee with Nikita, who worked in design. "It's slow at first, and the pay was worse," Nikita said. "I'd do it again." Rajni learned more from those three things than from six months of dreading.

What did Rajni draft at two in the morning?
She drafted a resignation letter.
How did sorting her regrets and values turn the drastic thoughts into small experiments?

The urge to resign, move and end things was a signal, but Rajni split what she could fix from what was gone and wrote what she valued, which pointed toward design. A weekend course, a poster project and coffee with Nikita then tested it cheaply without burning bridges.
What was Rajni feeling while drafting the letter?
She felt restless and dissatisfied, wanting something to change overnight.
What could Rajni do if the course goes well?
She could keep the experiments small, ask Nikita for feedback, and make bigger changes only after real feedback.
Should I call a teacher "Sir" when I write to him?

In India, "Sir" and "Madam" are polite ways to speak to teachers. In writing, begin with "Dear Sir" for a formal letter, or "Dear Mr. Verma" if you know the name.
Example: Dear Sir, I request leave for two days.

Avni, you asked why I disappeared all Diwali week, so listen. I'm Preeti, sixteen, and in our house Diwali starts ten days early with cleaning. Every cupboard. Every fan. I was supposed to go to the movie with you all on Thursday, remember? Mummy said, "Movie? Who'll clean the kitchen shelves?" I sulked. I scrubbed those shelves like they'd insulted me. Then Friday we made chaklis with Nani, and she told stories about Diwali in her village, and I laughed so much I forgot I was angry. That's the confusing part. I hated the work and I loved being in it. So on Saturday I tried something new. I said, "Mummy, I'll do all the diyas and the rangoli, but can I have Sunday evening with my friends?" She looked surprised, then said yes. So Sunday, I'm yours, Avni.

What did Preeti offer to do in exchange for Sunday evening?
All the diyas and the rangoli.
How did Preeti feel during Diwali week?
Preeti felt resentful and grumpy about the cleaning, but also happy and close to family while making chaklis with Nani.
What worked about Preeti's request on Saturday?
She offered to share some festival duty and calmly asked for specific personal time, which made it easy for Mummy to say yes.
How might Avni have felt when Preeti disappeared all week?
Avni was probably a bit disappointed and confused about the missed movie, and pleased to hear Preeti had kept Sunday for friends.
Priya says: "2,114 is divisible by 4, because it is even." Is she right?

Answer: No. The last two digits make 14, and 14 is not divisible by 4 (14 / 4 is 3 remainder 2). 2,114 / 4 is 528 remainder 2.

Every number divisible by 4 is even, but not every even number is divisible by 4. The 4 table is 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 ... every OTHER even number. So being even is only the first step. Look at the last two digits: 14 is between 12 and 16, not in the 4 table. Another mistake to watch: using the digit sum for 4 (that only works for 3 and 9).

Snow still lay along the fence on Ingrid's street in Bergen when her kick sent the football straight through Mr Olsen's garage window. Rafael, her friend from next door, gasped. "He's going to be so mad." Ingrid crossed her arms. "It's one window. Remember when the teenagers spray-painted the whole bus shelter? And they smashed the lamp at the park. This is nothing next to that." Rafael looked at the jagged hole. "But we did this one." Ingrid didn't answer. She kept her hands in her jacket pockets, and when the garage door creaked open, she took a small step back behind Rafael.

What had the teenagers done that Ingrid brought up?
They spray-painted the whole bus shelter and smashed the lamp at the park.
What does Ingrid's step back behind Rafael suggest about how she really feels?
Even while calling it nothing, she seems nervous and a bit guilty, which hints she knows the window still matters 😰.
What choice could Ingrid make when the garage door opens?
She could step forward, tell Mr Olsen the kick was hers, apologise, and offer to help sort out the window.
How does Rafael see the window differently from Ingrid?
Rafael doesn't compare it with the teenagers at all; Rafael looks at the hole and sees that they did this one.

Team lead's note, design review, Monday.
The whole team was ready to approve the new school-bus route map. Preeti, our junior planner, asked to speak before the vote. She said she'd walked the route on Sunday and found that one stop was on a blind curve with no footpath. She showed photos on her phone, and said, "I might have missed a reason it's placed there. Could we check?" Two senior planners looked annoyed. But the photos were clear. I asked Shalini from road safety to review the stop. She confirmed the danger. We've moved the stop fifty metres to a safer spot. Preeti stayed calm and didn't gloat when she was proved right. I've asked her to present her walking-check method at next week's meeting.

How far was the stop moved?
The stop was moved fifty metres to a safer spot.
What might Preeti have been feeling as the two senior planners looked annoyed?
Preeti was probably nervous, but she stayed calm and steady, trusting the photos she had taken.
Which parts of Preeti's approach are worth copying?
She checked the route herself, gave clear photo evidence, asked politely whether she had missed something, and didn't gloat when proved right.
How might the children using the bus be affected by Preeti speaking up?
The children would be safer, no longer waiting at a stop on a blind curve.

I'm Deepika, and in my second year I worked at the college library desk. I took the rules very seriously.
One day Sarita, a classmate, came with a book four weeks late. Her mother had been in hospital in her village; she'd had to go suddenly.
The rule said: fine, no exceptions. I told her, "I'm sorry, but what if everyone broke the rules? The whole system would fall apart."
She paid. Her hands were shaking. She had borrowed the money.
I felt proud that evening. I'd been fair. I'd kept order.
It was only later, when my own grandfather fell ill and I missed a deadline, that I understood what I'd done. The rule wasn't wrong. But I'd treated a rare case like a normal one.

How late was Sarita's book?
Four weeks late.
How did Deepika feel that evening after charging the fine?
Deepika felt proud of keeping order and being fair, not yet seeing how hard it had been on Sarita.
What could Deepika have done differently with Sarita?
Deepika could have asked a senior librarian whether an exception or waiver was possible for a family emergency, keeping the rule while respecting a rare case.
How might Sarita have felt paying the fine?
She probably felt upset and humiliated, having to borrow money after her mother's illness.

In Class 9, someone in our class chat posted a photo of me from sports day, edited so I had a pig's snout. Then another with my face on a buffalo. I'm Ganga, and I'll never forget the laughing emojis under them. Vikas had made the first one. Others added more.

I felt sick. Hot and exposed, like everyone was staring even when I was alone in my room. My first thought was to make one of Vikas, worse.

I didn't. My cousin had told me what to do once, and I did it: screenshots of everything, with names and times. Then I blocked Vikas and reported the posts on the app. The next morning I went straight to Mrs Joseph, our class teacher, and showed her.

She didn't say "ignore it." She said, "This is not your fault, Ganga. This is bullying." She took the screenshots to the principal that day, and Vikas's parents were called in.

It still stings sometimes. But I didn't become like them.

What was edited onto Ganga's face in the first photo?
A pig's snout was edited onto the photo.
What was Ganga feeling when the edited photos were posted?
Ganga felt sick, hurt and exposed, as if everyone was staring.
What steps did Ganga take instead of retaliating?
Ganga saved screenshots with names and times, blocked Vikas, reported the posts and told Mrs Joseph the next morning.
How did Mrs Joseph respond, and why did it matter?
Mrs Joseph said it was not Ganga's fault, named it as bullying and took it to the principal that day, so Ganga was believed and protected.

"Irawati, your slides were too long. Nobody reads eleven bullet points."
Irawati blinked. "Wow. Okay, Sonali."
"It's true. The birds part was good, though. The part about the barbet nest."
Irawati laughed despite herself. "You're the only one who noticed the birds."
"I've logged forty-three species on campus. I walk at six every morning, same route." Sonali pulled out a worn notebook. "Here. Barbet, coppersmith, the paradise flycatcher by the library."
"Can I come tomorrow?"
"Six sharp. We don't talk near the pond."
"Fine. Six sharp."
Next morning Irawati was at the gate at five-fifty-five.

How many species has Sonali logged on campus?
Sonali has logged forty-three species on campus.
How did Irawati feel when Sonali criticised her slides?
She was a bit stung and surprised at first, then amused and curious once Sonali praised the birds part.
What made the friendship start well despite the blunt comment?
Irawati looked past the direct words and joined Sonali's passion, accepting her routine of six sharp and silence near the pond.
How might Sonali see Irawati turning up at five-fifty-five?
Sonali would likely feel pleased and respected, since Irawati honoured the six-sharp routine and shared the love of birds.

Siddharth, you've stopped opening the college portal since your attendance dropped, haven't you? Let your Gautam mama tell you something. At twenty, in Hyderabad, I had a small loan for my hostel fees. One month I paid late, and the bank sent a letter. I didn't open it. Then another came. I put them in my suitcase, under my sweaters, and felt lighter every time I zipped it shut. Six months later, the warden called me in: the late fees had grown, and the bank had written to my father. My father came on the overnight bus, sat with me, and we opened every envelope together. The first letter asked for a small amount. The last one was frightening. The problem was never the first letter, beta. It was the suitcase.

Where did young Gautam keep the unopened bank letters?
In Gautam's suitcase, under the sweaters.
Why did young Gautam feel lighter each time he zipped the suitcase shut?
Gautam felt a quick relief from not facing the bad news, even though the problem was quietly growing inside the suitcase.
What was the turning point in Mama's story, and what does it suggest for Siddharth?
Gautam's father sitting with him to open every envelope; for Siddharth, it suggests opening the attendance record now, ideally with someone calm, and talking to the college early.
How might Gautam's father have felt on the overnight bus?
Gautam's father was probably worried and upset, yet came to sit beside his son and face it together.
At the stationery shop 4 pens cost ₹5 each and 3 erasers cost ₹6 each. Write one calculation for the total and work it out.

Answer: ₹38. 4 x 5 + 3 x 6 = 20 + 18 = 38.

Each group of things is a multiplication, and then the two amounts are added. Because x comes before +, we do NOT need brackets: 4 x 5 + 3 x 6. Step 1: both multiplications, 20 and 18. Step 2: add, 38. Underline 4 x 5 and 3 x 6 before starting.

Dear Lakshmi,

I hope you don't mind me writing this. I've been meaning to say something since last week's team meeting.

When Pasang came in late on Tuesday, you said to the group that he "doesn't take the job seriously". On Friday, you were late yourself because of the rain and the metro delays. You mentioned the metro, and that made sense.

I think you're a really fair manager, which is why I'm raising it. It seemed like when you're late, it's the circumstances, but when Pasang is, it's his attitude.

I asked him about Tuesday. His landlord had locked him out after a water leak, and he'd spent two hours finding a key.

Maybe next time, we could ask first? I'd want someone to ask me.

Thank you for reading this.

Dolma

Why was Lakshmi late on Friday?
You were late yourself because of the rain and the metro delays.
What does Dolma seem to feel about raising this with Lakshmi?
Dolma seems nervous but respectful, wanting to be fair to Pasang while not offending Lakshmi.
Why is Dolma's letter a helpful way to raise the double standard?
Dolma is respectful, gives facts about both lateness cases and Pasang's reason, and suggests asking first, making feedback more curious.
How might Pasang have felt being called someone who "doesn't take the job seriously"?
Pasang probably felt hurt and misjudged, having spent two hours locked out.

The power had gone out in Hrithik's building an hour before his chemistry test, and his phone was at nine percent. He should have been revising by candlelight. Instead he opened a link from the class group: "Your Hidden Personality in 10 Questions." The result loaded slowly: "You are a natural leader who is often misunderstood. People underestimate you, but you have big plans." Hrithik sat up. That was it, exactly. His father always said he lacked direction. He spent a chunk of his last battery forwarding it to Pankaj with "THIS. Show this to anyone who says I'm lazy." Pankaj replied, "mine said the same lol." The phone died before Hrithik could answer. He stared at the black screen, still sure it meant him.

How much charge did Hrithik's phone have when the power went out?
His phone was at nine percent.
What did Hrithik want the quiz result to prove?
He wanted proof that he isn't lazy or aimless, since his father said he lacked direction. Being called a misunderstood leader felt like finally being seen. 🥺
What choice could Hrithik make after Pankaj said the result was the same?
He could take that as a clue that the words are general and fit many people, then close the quiz and use the candlelight for the chemistry test.
How might Pankaj see the quiz differently from Hrithik?
Pankaj got the same result and treats it lightly with "lol", so to Pankaj it looks like a fun, general quiz rather than a verdict on anyone's character.

Monday. Nani set down a plate of mango slices for Nikita and her cousin Tanuja. Nikita grabbed five at once, before Tanuja could. Tanuja grabbed the rest. Nani came back to an empty plate and two sticky, cross girls. Wednesday. Same plate. Nikita's hand shot out, then stopped. But Tanuja was already reaching, so both grabbed, and a slice fell on the floor. Friday. Nani put the plate down and said, "One each, then wait." Nikita took one. Tanuja took one. Back and forth they went, counting. One slice was left. They looked at each other. "Halves?" said Tanuja.

How many mango slices did Nikita grab on Monday?
Five at once.
Why did Nikita's hand stop and then grab anyway on Wednesday?
She seemed to remember Monday, but when she saw Tanuja reaching she worried she'd miss out and grabbed anyway.
What choice did Nani make on Friday, and why did it work?
Nani set a rule of one each, then wait, so neither girl had to rush to get her share.
What might Tanuja be feeling when she offers 'Halves?'
Tanuja seems relaxed and fair now, trusting that sharing the last slice will not leave her short.

Urmila, stop sighing at the ceiling and listen. I am Anand, and when I was a boy of nine the lights went out across our lane for a whole evening. I sat on the sofa with my arms folded and said "I am bored" every few minutes. Nothing more. My sister was drawing by candle light, my cousin was drumming a rhythm on an upturned bucket, and Nani was telling stories, and I sat there like a stone, waiting for the fan to turn again. Three hours, Urmila, and I did none of it. When the lights came on I was more tired than if I had run around. And nobody had stopped me joining in.

What did Anand say every few minutes during the power cut?
Anand said "I am bored".
How was Anand feeling while sitting on the sofa with folded arms?
Bored and cross, since Anand complained again and again and waited for the fan to turn.
What could Anand have tried instead of waiting, and why?
Anand could have joined the drawing or the drumming on the bucket, because the family activities were right there.
How might Anand's sister and cousin have seen Anand sitting there?
They may have wondered why Anand did not join, since they were busy having fun and nobody had stopped Anand.

It was raining so hard that the whole school was kept indoors for lunch. Sangeeta and Pallavi sat in a corner of the hall.

"Guess what," Sangeeta whispered. "I saw Megha's father come to school today. He was talking to Ma'am for a long time."

Pallavi shrugged. "So?"

Sangeeta wanted her to be excited. So she added, "He looked really angry. Megha must have done something bad. Maybe she stole something."

She had not seen an angry face. The father had looked tired, if anything.

Pallavi's eyes widened. "Stole? What?"

"I don't know. Something big, probably."

By the end of lunch, Sangeeta had half convinced herself it was true. It sounded so real when she said it.

After the bell, Megha walked past, head down. Sangeeta suddenly didn't feel excited at all.

Why was the whole school kept indoors for lunch?
It was raining so hard.
How does Sangeeta feel when Megha walks past after the bell?
She no longer feels excited; she feels uneasy and guilty about the story she made bigger.
What could Sangeeta do now?
Tell Pallavi that she made up the stealing part, so the guess doesn't keep spreading as if it were true.
What might Megha be feeling as she walks past with her head down?
She may be sad or worried about whatever brought her father to school, unaware of the rumour.

I am Vaibhav, and I was in the shop when I saw two toddlers by the toy shelf. Indu, about two, grabbed a red car out of another child's hands. He wailed. Her father knelt and said gently, "Say sorry, Indu." She muttered, "Sorry," and pushed the car back into the boy's hand, then patted his arm. I doubt she knew she had done wrong, but her hand was gentle.

What did Indu take from the other child?
She grabbed a red car.
What does Indu's gentle pat after returning the car suggest, and what else could explain it?
It suggests she wanted to make things better after her father's prompt. She may only have been copying, without understanding that she had upset the boy.
What could Indu's father do next to help her learn?
He can keep showing simple repair, like giving the toy back and offering a hug, and say the boy felt sad without heavy blame.
How might the boy feel when Indu pats him?
He may feel comforted to have his car back, but he might still feel upset for a while.
Put an apple on one side of a balance and a grape on the other. What happens? Which is heavier?

Answer: The apple side goes DOWN. The apple is heavier; the grape is lighter.

On a balance, the heavier side goes down. If both sides stay level, they weigh the same.
Cindy was 5 years old.  Her sister Jan was 2 years older than Cindy.  Their oldest sister Marcia was twice as old as Jan.  Greg was two years older than Marcia.  How old was Greg?

Jan was 2 years older than Cindy who was 5 so 2+5 = 7 years old
Marica was twice as old as Jan so 2*7 = 14 years old
Greg was 2 years older than Marcia who was 14 so 2+14 = 16 years old
The answer is 16.

Sunday night
Ishita messaged again today. That's six messages I haven't opened. "Are you okay?" "Did I do something?" "Bhavna??"
I haven't replied because I don't know how to say it. Ever since the trip, I feel like we don't fit anymore. She talks about the same things; I'm into different stuff now. I want some distance. That's all. But writing that feels so mean.
So I've been hiding. Leaving class fast. Pretending my phone is broken. And every time her name pops up, my stomach goes hollow with guilt.
I realised tonight that I'm hoping she'll just give up. That's worse than saying it. She's lying awake wondering what she did.
I wrote it out and sent it: "Ishita, I'm sorry for going quiet. I've been needing a bit of space. It's not anything you did. I just didn't know how to say it."
It took two minutes. I wasted two weeks.

How many of Ishita's messages had Bhavna not opened?
Six messages.
How does Bhavna feel each time Ishita's name pops up?
Bhavna feels a hollow guilt, knowing the silence is hurting Ishita.
What did Bhavna realise, and what did Bhavna do about it?
Hoping Ishita would give up was worse than being honest, so Bhavna sent a short, kind message explaining the need for space.
What have the two weeks of silence been like for Ishita?
Ishita has felt confused and anxious, sending messages and probably lying awake wondering what she did wrong.

Kashish, you think I was always this calm? Let your Lokesh Chacha tell you about the year I turned twenty.

My Bauji had run the cloth shop in Rohtak for thirty years and wanted me at the counter. I wanted to study food technology in Hisar.

First I sulked. Then one night I shouted, and he threw the ledger on the floor. We didn't speak for a week.

Your Dadi told me, "Shouting makes him deaf. Speak so he can hear."

So one morning I opened the shop with him, swept the floor, made his tea, and said, "Bauji, I respect everything you built. I see my path a little differently. Let me try two years. If it fails, the counter is mine."

He didn't answer that day. The next morning the admission form was on my pillow, signed.

Where did Lokesh want to study?
Lokesh wanted to study food technology in Hisar.
Why did Lokesh first sulk and then shout at twenty?
He felt frustrated and trapped between his own wish and Bauji's plan, and didn't yet know how to say it calmly.
Which choice turned things around for Lokesh?
Following Dadi's advice: working beside Bauji, honouring what he had built, and calmly asking for two years with a fair fallback.
How might Bauji have felt when he signed the form?
Bauji likely felt respected rather than defied, which let him agree quietly by leaving the signed form on the pillow.

Keerthana: Deepa got the team lead role. announced 10 mins ago
Sahil: oh. you wanted that
Keerthana: I'm so annoyed I can't even look at my screen 😠
Sahil: fair. want to rant?
Keerthana: I did rant. to my notebook. then I made myself write 3 lists

Keerthana: I still want to lead a team. just not while stewing about Deepa
Sahil: proud of you 🙂 coffee after work?
Keerthana: yes. and I'll congratulate her properly first

What was Keerthana two years ago?
An intern making tea for everyone.
How did Keerthana feel when Deepa's promotion was announced?
Keerthana was so annoyed that even looking at the screen felt impossible.
What did Keerthana choose to do with the anger, and why did it help?
Keerthana wrote three lists, of what Keerthana has, what Keerthana controls and where Keerthana was two years ago, which kept the ambition while letting the envy cool.
How might Deepa feel when Keerthana congratulates her properly?
Deepa may feel supported and relieved, since a colleague who wanted the role is choosing warmth over resentment.

At the government school in Indore, the weekly spelling test came back on Friday. Gautam, nine, had six out of twenty. He shoved the paper into his desk. "Nikita Ma'am gives me the hardest words," he told his bench-mate. "She reads fast when it's my row." Nikita Ma'am, walking past, heard. She crouched beside him. "Gautam, which words did you practise this week?" He shrugged. "None. It doesn't matter. Some weeks I'm lucky, some weeks not." "Last month you practised with your sister and got fourteen, remember?" Gautam frowned. "That was a good day." He picked at the edge of the desk. It had not occurred to him that the good day and the practice might be the same thing.

What did Gautam score on the spelling test?
Six out of twenty.
Why does Gautam call the fourteen 'a good day'?
Gautam feels discouraged and sure results come from luck or Ma'am's speed, so even his best score seems like chance rather than something his practice caused.
What could Nikita Ma'am do next to help Gautam link practice and marks?
Start a simple weekly chart of words practised and marks, so Gautam can see the practice and the fourteen side by side.

Nandini hasn't eaten her tiffin all week.

At the wedding in their village near Jodhpur, the courtyard was full of relatives Preeti had never met. Her mother led her from elder to elder. Preeti bent and touched each pair of feet, quick and neat, and got pats on the head. Then a tall man with a big moustache, Lokesh-ji, a distant uncle, laughed and grabbed her wrist. “Come, come, touch properly, and give me a hug too.” Preeti's body went stiff, and she pulled back. Her mother stepped between them at once. “She has greeted you with respect, Lokesh-ji. A namaste is enough.” She kept Preeti beside her all evening and later told her, “You were right to pull back.”

What did Lokesh-ji ask Preeti to give him besides touching his feet?
He asked her to give him a hug too.
What was Preeti feeling when her body went stiff?
She felt uncomfortable and uneasy at being grabbed and asked for a hug by a man she didn't know.
How did Preeti's mother protect her?
She stepped between them at once, said a namaste was enough, kept Preeti beside her and told her she was right to pull back.
How might the relatives nearby see her mother's words?
Some might think she was being strict, but others would see a mother making sure respect never means unwanted touch.

The Pongal fair was closing in an hour when Manoj won the school quiz prize: a crisp envelope with two thousand rupees. "Prize money!" he shouted to his sister Nandini. "Let's go wild."
In forty minutes he had bought ride tickets for both of them, a giant cotton candy, a toy drone that stopped working by the gate, and snacks for three friends.
On the bus home Nandini asked, "Can I borrow fifty from your tuition money? For my notebook."
Manoj clutched his bag. "No way. I earned that teaching the Class 5 kids every Saturday for two months. That's serious."
"But you just spent two thousand in forty minutes."
"That was prize money," he said, as if that explained everything. The broken drone rattled in his lap.

What did Manoj win at the school quiz?
A crisp envelope with two thousand rupees.
Why does Manoj refuse to lend from his tuition money after spending the prize so fast?
The prize feels like playful fun money, but the tuition money cost him two months of Saturdays, so he feels protective of it even though every rupee is the same.
What could Manoj ask himself the next time a prize comes?
Whether he would spend the same amount of tuition money on the same things; if not, he could pause and choose calmly, or talk it over with a parent.
How might Nandini feel on the bus?
Nandini may feel puzzled and a bit hurt, since she asked for fifty rupees for a notebook right after he spent two thousand in forty minutes.

In the village kitchen, Ama told Tenzin off for tipping over the tsampa flour. He stood frozen, then marched over and smacked his baby sister Dolma's arm. Dolma howled. Their cousin, sweeping the floor, dropped the broom. "Tenzin! She didn't do anything!" Ama picked up Dolma, then crouched to Tenzin. "You're angry with Ama. Hit this cushion, not Dolma." Tenzin hit the cushion twice, then leaned on Ama's knee, crying.

What did Tenzin tip over?
The tsampa flour.
Why did Tenzin smack Dolma?
He was angry and upset after Ama told him off, and the anger went to his baby sister, the smallest and safest target.
How did Ama redirect the anger?
She named that he was angry with Ama and gave him a cushion to hit instead of Dolma.
What is it like for the cousin who saw it?
The cousin is shocked and protective, dropping the broom and pointing out that Dolma did nothing.

Maria pressed her thumb on the calendar in the hall. The science fair was on the twenty-fourth, exactly three weeks away. "Last week is for the display board," she muttered, and drew a box round the final seven days. "Middle week is the experiment. So the first week is..." She counted backwards with her pencil, stopped at a Monday and tapped it. "Start here. Not later." Her friend Shreya leaned over from the sofa. "You haven't even picked what to grow yet." "That's the Monday job," Maria said, and wrote CHOOSE PLANT in the first box. Her shoulders felt a little lighter.

How many weeks were there until the science fair?
There were three weeks until the science fair.
What was Maria feeling as she wrote CHOOSE PLANT in the first box?
A little relieved, because the plan gave her a clear place to begin; the passage says her shoulders felt lighter.

Kalyani called from the fields in a high, sing-song voice, “Ri-tu, come, come!” and Ritu, two, looked up from her clay pots with a wide smile and toddled towards her. Then, at the edge of the irrigation channel, Kalyani said in a low, flat voice, “Ritu. Stop.” Ritu froze mid-step and looked at her face. Kalyani smiled and knelt. That night, as Ritu whimpered, Kalyani spoke softly and slowly, and Ritu's shoulders dropped as she fell asleep.

Where did Kalyani say “Ritu. Stop.”?
At the edge of the irrigation channel.
What does Ritu's response to the two voices suggest she understands?
She seems to read the high sing-song voice as warm and inviting and the low flat one as serious, even without knowing all the words. She may also be reacting to Kalyani's face.
What could Kalyani do to keep both messages clear?
Kalyani could keep a warm voice for calling and use a calm, firm voice only for real dangers.
How might Ritu feel when Kalyani's voice turns flat?
She may feel a little startled, but seeing Kalyani's face soften helps her feel safe again.

Monday: in the school's cyber-safety talk, the speaker wrote three lines on the board: "Real banks don't ask for secrecy. Real officers don't want gift cards. Real deadlines don't expire in ten minutes." Eshaan copied them into the back of his maths notebook, mostly because Siddharth dared him to.
Thursday: at 4 pm, Eshaan's phone buzzed. "Your school fee account will be BLOCKED. Pay the pending amount by gift card within 30 minutes. Do not tell anyone, as this is confidential." His heart jumped. Papa had paid the fees late once before. Then he remembered the back of his notebook, and he didn't reply.
Saturday: Eshaan and his mother called the school office on the number printed in the diary. No pending fees, the clerk said. Eshaan showed Siddharth the message on Monday, and they reported it together to the class teacher.

How many minutes did the message give to pay by gift card?
It gave 30 minutes.
What was Eshaan feeling when the message arrived?
Eshaan felt a jolt of panic, worried the fees really were late, before the notebook lines helped him slow down.
What rule did Eshaan use, and why does it work against most scams?
He paused and checked through an official number instead of acting, which beats the rush and secrecy most scams depend on.
How might Siddharth see the notebook lines now?
Siddharth may feel surprised and a bit proud that his dare turned into something useful, and more alert to messages like this himself.

Gina can paint six cups an hour with roses and 7 cups an hour with lilies. Her Etsy store gets an order for 6 rose cups and 14 lily cups. If Gina gets paid $90 total for the order, how much does she make per hour?

First find the total time to paint the rose cups: 6 cups / 6 cups/hour = 1 hour
Then find the total time to paint the lily cups: 14 cups / 7 cups/hour = 2 hours
Then add the painting time for each type of cup to find the total painting time: 1 hour + 2 hours = 3 hours
Then divide Gina's total earnings by the number of hours she works to find her hourly wage: $90 / 3 hours = $30/hour
The answer is 30.

"Two minutes to the call," Santosh said. "You look like you're bracing for the dentist."
"I'm tired. The server mess last night." Lalit rolled his shoulders. "But Mr. Rao's team is nervous about the new timeline, so I want to start warm."
"Fake smile?"
"Not fake. I do like these people. I'm just choosing to show that part first." He unclenched his jaw. "Slower voice, and I'll actually look at the camera."
"And the tiredness?"
"Tell you after, over chai."
Twenty-five minutes later Lalit closed the laptop and slumped.
"How was it?" Santosh asked.
"They relaxed by the third minute. Now I need ten minutes with no face on at all."
"Take them. I'll bring the chai."

Which team is nervous about the new timeline?
Mr. Rao's team is nervous about the new timeline.
What does Lalit want from his warm start, and how does he feel underneath?

He wants the nervous team to settle, while he is tired from the server mess last night. He says he likes these people, so the warmth looks like a choice rather than a cover, though he may also be a little anxious about the timeline.
What keeps Lalit's deliberate warmth from turning into constant suppression?
He is honest with Santosh about being tired, saves his real state for after the call, and takes ten minutes with no face on. That way the display is a skill for the meeting, not all-day hiding. 🙂
How might Mr. Rao's team feel in the first minutes of the call?
They probably feel reassured by the slower voice and steady eye contact. They don't know Lalit is tired, and a tense face might have made them more worried about the timeline.

Monday. Mohit bought two energy drinks on the way home and studied till three. His heart was drumming, and when he finally lay down, his legs wouldn't keep still.
Wednesday. After two nights like that, he walked into the physics test shaking. He read the first question three times. His classmate Farida noticed his hand trembling and asked if he was okay. "Too much caffeine, no sleep," he muttered. He left half the paper blank.
The following Monday. No cans. He was asleep by eleven, ate his mother's poha, and took a short walk between chapters. Before the maths test Farida asked again. "Tired," Mohit said, "but not buzzing." He finished the paper.

How many energy drinks did Mohit buy on Monday?
Mohit bought two energy drinks.
How did Mohit feel walking into the physics test?
Mohit felt shaky and anxious, rereading the first question and unable to focus.
What changed before the maths test, and why did it help?
No cans, sleep by eleven, breakfast and short walks between chapters, so Mohit was tired but not buzzing.
What did Farida notice?
Farida noticed Mohit's hand trembling and cared enough to ask if he was okay.

The first time Ankita's manager asked her to backdate a loan document at the branch, she said no quietly, and he let it go. The second time, a week later, he said it in front of the cashier: 'Just do it. You're not the auditor.' The third time, on Friday, he left the file on her chair with a sticky note: 'By Monday.'
That weekend Ankita decided that private refusals weren't working. On Saturday she wrote to the bank's ethics helpline email. She kept it plain: three dates, the exact words of each request, the file number, and that she had refused each time. No adjectives, no guesses about why.
On Monday at ten, Sangeeta from regional HR called her. 'We've received your report. Thank you for writing it so clearly. The file has been moved to another officer, and we're reviewing it. You won't face any consequence for raising this. If anything changes in how you're treated, call me directly.'
Ankita put the sticky note in an envelope, in case they needed it.

What did the sticky note say?
'By Monday.'
What was Ankita feeling when she found the file on her chair?
Pressured and frustrated, seeing that private refusals were not stopping the requests.
Why did it help to keep the report plain and factual?
Dates, exact words and the file number made it easy for HR to act, without it becoming a matter of opinion.
How does Sangeeta respond, and what might she be thinking?
Sangeeta acts quickly and reassures Ankita, probably glad the clear report lets HR protect both the record and the employee.

Zainab, you young people think only old uncles fall for these calls. Listen. When I was branch manager in Kochi, a college boy, Anand, came in shaking. Someone had called "from the bank" saying his account would be frozen, and asked for the OTP to "verify". Anand was sharp, top of his engineering class. He gave it. Why? Because the caller knew his name, his birthday, even his last transaction. People forget how much they have scattered about themselves online. We blocked the card in time, luckily. But Anand's real lesson came after. He went home and removed his birthday, phone number and hometown from every public profile. He told me, "I handed them the key years ago, bit by bit." So, Zainab, before you fill in that online quiz asking your first pet's name, think of Anand. Your Karthik Uncle has seen what happens next.

What did the caller ask Anand for?
The OTP, to verify.
What was Anand feeling when he came into the branch?
Anand was shaking, frightened and probably ashamed that a clever student like him had been tricked.
What was Anand's turning point after the call, and why was it wise?
Removing his birthday, number and hometown from public profiles, because scammers build trust from such scattered details.
How might Karthik, as branch manager, have felt seeing Anand shaking?
Karthik likely felt concerned and protective, acting quickly to block the card, and wanted Anand to see it wasn't about intelligence.

Yara smiled too, but Beatriz noticed that her voice when she said "Great news" was tight and high, and her hands were gripping her coffee cup. Beatriz couldn't tell what was underneath. How are you feeling about it?" Yara let out a breath. "Happy. And terrified. It means four months of fieldwork in Manaus, and my father's been unwell. I don't know how to tell my mother." Beatriz nodded. "That's a lot at once. Do you want to talk it through, or just sit for a bit?" "Talk. Please." They skipped lunch.

How long will Yara's fieldwork in Manaus last?
Four months.
What was Yara feeling about the grant?
Yara felt happy and terrified at once, worried about leaving for fieldwork while her father was unwell.

She waited for a private moment, described the tense cue while admitting she might be wrong, asked how Yara felt, then offered talk or quiet.

"I'm going to post it, Didi. Keerthana told everyone about my crush. So I'll tell everyone what she did at Diwali."

Ishita was sitting on her bed with her phone, thumbs already moving.

Roshni didi took the phone gently out of her hand. "What did she do at Diwali?"

"Doesn't matter. Something she'd hate people knowing."

"And then what?"

"Then she'll know how it feels."

"And everyone will know two secrets instead of one. And tomorrow people will be talking about what you did, not what she did."

Ishita pulled her knees up. "So I just let her get away with it?"

"No. You wait one day. Tomorrow you decide: talk to her, or stop being friends. Either is fine. Just not tonight, when you're this angry."

Ishita stared at the ceiling. "I hate that you're right."

"I'll give your phone back at breakfast," said Roshni.

Keerthana told everyone about Ishita's crush.

Posting Keerthana's secret would have made Ishita the one in the wrong; waiting lets her choose calmly whether to talk or end the friendship.

Distil this passage into three sentences.

"There was just such an informality in the terms of the bequest as to give me no hope from law. A man of honour could not have doubted the intention, but Mr. Darcy chose to doubt it--or to treat it as a merely conditional recommendation, and to assert that I had forfeited all claim to it by extravagance, imprudence, in short, anything or nothing. Certain it is that the living became vacant two years ago, exactly as I was of an age to hold it, and that it was given to another man; and no less certain is it, that I cannot accuse myself of having really done anything to deserve to lose it. I have a warm unguarded temper, and I may perhaps have sometimes spoken my opinion of him, and to him, too freely. I can recall nothing worse. But the fact is, that we are very different sort of men, and that he hates me."

A gift in a will was worded loosely, the speaker says, so the law gives no hope, and Mr. Darcy treated it as mere advice. When the position became vacant two years ago, just as the speaker was old enough to hold it, it went to someone else. The speaker admits only a hot temper and some frank remarks, and says Mr. Darcy hates him.

For most of my first year of CA articleship, I told everyone I loved it. I told myself that most of all.
My parents had framed my foundation result. My father introduced me at weddings as “our future CA, Aadhya.” So when my stomach knotted every morning at the office door, I called it acidity. When I spent lunch breaks sketching sets for the college drama club, I called it a hobby.
My friend Vasudha asked me once, at a chai stall, “When did you last sound happy about balance sheets?” I laughed and changed the subject.
It took a whole year before I let myself finish the sentence I had been editing out: I don't want this. I want to design for theatre.
I haven't told my parents yet. But I've stopped calling the dread acidity.

What did Aadhya call the knotted stomach every morning?
Aadhya called it acidity.
Why did Aadhya keep calling the sketching “a hobby”?
Aadhya felt afraid of disappointing proud parents, so it felt calmer to edit out the real wish than to face it.
What small step could help Aadhya now?
Aadhya could talk with Vasudha or a college counsellor about the theatre interest, and then plan how to share it honestly with the family.
How might Vasudha see Aadhya during that first year?
Vasudha seemed to notice that Aadhya never sounded happy about the work, and may have felt concerned watching the friend pretend.
