Mentor's note, NGO fellowship programme

Elizabeth, 24, joined us after two years in her family's hotel business in Kochi, which her parents always said she would run. She told me she realised she'd never chosen it.
She did not quit in anger or blame her parents. Instead, she asked for a one-year leave to try community work, and kept helping with the hotel's accounts on weekends.
In our sessions she says she wants to keep her love of hospitality and hosting, and add work that serves people. She explained this to her father, Ramesh, in a letter that began, "Thank you for everything."
He visited our centre last week. They seemed at ease together.

What does Elizabeth still help with on weekends?
She keeps helping with the hotel's accounts on weekends.
How does Elizabeth seem to feel about her parents' plans for her?
She seems grateful and respectful rather than resentful, wanting to keep what she values while exploring.
Which of Elizabeth's steps show a respectful way out of a foreclosed identity?
Taking a year's leave instead of quitting, keeping hotel accounts, naming what she wants to keep, and writing to her father with thanks.
How might Ramesh feel visiting the centre?
Ramesh probably feels more at ease and understanding, seeing his daughter's work for himself.

Every family function, my uncle Hemant does the same thing: he grabs my face and squeezes my cheeks, hard, and says, "Look how big you've grown!" Everyone laughs. I used to laugh too.
At my cousin's engagement last month, I stepped back and said, "Please don't do that, Hemant Mama. I don't like it."
He laughed louder. "Arre, Hrithik, you're still my little boy!" and did it again.
I felt my face burning, not from the squeezing. I went to find Mummy in the kitchen. I told her exactly what happened.
She put down the tray. She said, "You said no, and he didn't stop. That's not okay." She went straight out and told Hemant Mama, quietly but firmly, not to do it again. He looked embarrassed. At the next function he just said hello and shook my hand.

What did Hemant Mama say when he squeezed Hrithik's cheeks?
He said, "Look how big you've grown!"
What was Hrithik feeling when his uncle did it again after he said no?
Hrithik felt embarrassed and angry, his face burning, because his clear no had been laughed off.
Which of Hrithik's choices worked, and why?
Saying no clearly and, when that was ignored, telling Mummy straight away worked, because she spoke to Hemant Mama that same day and he stopped.
How might Hemant Mama have seen the cheek squeezing before Mummy spoke to him?
He probably saw it as harmless affection for a little nephew, not realising Hrithik was now old enough to find it uncomfortable and had the right to refuse.
Which one is about weather: "climatic" or "climactic"?

"Climatic" is about climate. "Climactic" is about a climax, the most exciting point of a story or event.
Examples: Climatic changes affect farming. The climactic scene of the film was exciting.

A class of 12 students was about to share 108 oranges equally among themselves when it was discovered that 36 of the oranges were bad and had to be thrown away. How many oranges less will each student get now than if no orange had to be thrown away?

If the 12 students had shared the 108 oranges, each student would have gotten 108/12 = 9 oranges
But 36 were removed so there are 108-36 = 72 oranges left
So 12 shared 72 for each to get 72/12 = 6 oranges
This is 9-6 = 3 less than they would each get if they did not have to throw any orange away.
The answer is 3.

Monday: Neelam, two and a half, sat on her little potty for five minutes, then stood up and wet the floor. She cried. Her brother Anand, seven, fetched a cloth. "It's okay, I did that too."
Wednesday: at dinner she pushed Papa's hand away from her plate. "Me do!" Half the dal went on her frock, but she ate with her own spoon.
The next Saturday: "Potty!" she shouted, and ran. It worked. She clapped for herself, and Anand gave her a high five.

What did Anand fetch on Monday?
Anand fetched a cloth.
What was Neelam feeling when she pushed Papa's hand away?
She felt determined and eager to be independent, wanting to feed herself even if it was messy.
How could the family support Neelam's growing independence?
They could let her try things herself, stay calm about spills and accidents, and cheer when she manages, as Anand did.
How does Anand react to Neelam's accident on Monday?

Ralph is a member of the cross-country relay team. There are four other members on the team who run 3 km to complete their part of the race. Ralph runs twice as much as any member on his team to complete his part of the race. How long is the race?

4 team members each run 3 km, so 4 x 3 = 12 km.
Ralph runs twice as much as any team member and since team members each run 3 km, Ralph runs 2 x 3 km = 6 km.
The length of the race is 6 km run by Ralph + 12 km run by the rest of the team = 18 km.
The answer is 18.

Behind the cowshed in the village, Ritu Bua crouched behind a haystack. "Where's Wasim? Where did he go?"

Wasim, hiding behind the water drum, pressed his hands to his mouth. Then Bua popped up right beside him. "Found you!"

Out came a low, rumbly chuckle, "heh-heh-heh", deep in his chest.

Ritu Bua laughed so hard she sat down in the straw. "That's your Dada's laugh! Exactly his!"

Wasim chuckled it again on purpose, shoulders shaking, and ran off to hide once more.

Where was Wasim hiding?
Behind the water drum.
What was Wasim feeling when the low, rumbly chuckle came out?

How could an adult keep this kind of fun going?
By playing along as Ritu Bua does, with more hide-and-find rounds and laughing with him, so the game stays shared and warm.
How does Ritu Bua react to Wasim's chuckle?
She laughs so hard she sits in the straw, delighted to hear Dada's laugh coming from the little boy.

When Joseph's motorbike broke down in the monsoon, three people he'd met there came to help within half an hour. That night he said to Nazia, "I think I live here now."

Which group did Joseph choose to join?
He chose the library volunteers.
What did Joseph mean when he said, 'I think I live here now'?
He meant he finally felt at home and accepted in the town, no longer like a guest.
What helped Joseph build trusted ties in the town?
Showing up regularly to volunteer, which let people get to know him and ask for his help.
How might Nazia have felt seeing Joseph so quiet at first?
She probably worried he was lonely and unhappy, which is why she pushed him to join something.

School counsellor's note, 5 September
Aparna, Class 9, was referred by her class teacher, Ms Elizabeth, who noticed she asks the same question several times every period: "Is this going to be in the test? Are you sure?" Her mother told me on the phone that at home Aparna asks whether the door is locked, whether the gas is off and whether she will pass, up to twenty times an evening.
In our session Aparna said, "When someone says it's fine, I feel better. Then it starts again." She looked embarrassed. She said she hates asking but can't stop, and that she's scared she is "too weak to handle things on her own".
I explained that reassurance calms worry for a moment yet leaves the mind believing it always needs someone else. We agreed on an experiment: she will write the worry in a notebook and wait ten minutes before asking. Her mother will answer once, kindly, and then say, "You've got this."
Review in two weeks.

Jahnavi, beside him, raised an eyebrow. "Rafiq, Manas from your house did the exact same thing in the last race. He stepped into lane three."

If it keeps coming back like this, I'll ask about the counselling service at work. For now: writing, water, sleep.

"Before the pheras," Damini said quietly, "I want us to agree on some things." Yash nodded. "Say it." "I'm keeping my job at the school. It's twelve kilometres; I'll take the bus." "Of course." "And your mother expects me to do the cooking alone." Yash was quiet. "She did it alone for thirty years." "I know. That's why I don't want to." He looked at the kitchen door. "I'll cook mornings, you evenings. And I'll tell Ma myself, not you." Damini let out a breath. "And money?" "Your salary is yours to decide. The house costs we talk about together." Inside, his mother laughed at something on the radio. Damini found she was smiling too.

Twelve kilometres.

Settling work, chores and money early avoids hidden resentment later and shows how each will handle family pressure.

On Thursday Dalia leaned in the doorway. "Tiny favour? My card's being weird again. Could you cover the groceries? I'll pay you back Friday, promise."
Noa was already reaching for her wallet. Then she glanced at the note and noticed that every Friday on it had come and gone. The same week, Dalia had posted photos from a weekend away at the coast.
Noa's stomach tightened. She liked being the one people could count on. "I can't this time," she said, her voice wobbling. "And I'd like us to sit down and go through the list first."

"We are. That's why I'm saying it."

Inside the kitchen cupboard of their shared flat in Lisbon.

She felt anxious and torn: her stomach tightened and her voice wobbled, because she liked being someone people could count on but saw that every promised Friday had passed.
What could Noa do next to protect both her kindness and herself?
She could hold the talk about the list, stay friendly but firm, and if Dalia keeps asking, talk it through with someone she trusts before agreeing to help again.

Dalia is used to Noa saying yes, so a no feels like a change in the friendship; being asked about the list may also embarrass her.

For which k does the system x + ky + 3z = 0, 3x + ky - 2z = 0, 2x + 3y - 4z = 0 have a solution other than x = y = z = 0? Find those solutions.

Answer: k = 33/2; the solutions are (x, y, z) = t(15, -2, 6) for any real t.

A homogeneous system AX = O always has the TRIVIAL solution X = O. If |A| != 0 that is the only one (X = A^-^1O = O), so non-trivial solutions need |A| = 0: |1 k 3; 3 k -2; 2 3 -4| = 1(-4k + 6) - k(-12 + 4) + 3(9 - 2k) = -4k + 6 + 8k + 27 - 6k = 33 - 2k 33 - 2k = 0, k = 33/2 with k = 33/2, subtract equation 1 from equation 2: 2x - 5z = 0, so x = 5z/2 equation 3: 2(5z/2) + 3y - 4z = 0, 3y = -z, y = -z/3 z = 6t: x = 15t, y = -2t, z = 6t Check in equation 1: 15t + (33/2)(-2t) + 3(6t) = 15t - 33t + 18t = 0. A homogeneous system with |A| = 0 has a whole LINE of solutions through the origin (all multiples of one of them). Common mistake: answering "no solution" when |A| = 0; a homogeneous system is never inconsistent.

Melody planted sunflowers from two different seed packets. She found that the sunflowers from Packet A were 20% taller than the sunflowers from Packet B. If the sunflowers from Packet A were 192 inches tall, how tall were the sunflowers from Packet B?

The height of the sunflowers from Packet A is the same as the height of the sunflowers from Packet B + 20%. If Y represents the height of the sunflowers from Packet B, Y + 0.20Y = the height of sunflowers from Packet A.
We know the height of the sunflowers from Packet A is 192 inches = Y + 0.20Y or 1.2Y.
To figure out Y, we would divide both sides of the equation by 1.2, like this: 192 / 1.2 = 1.2Y / 1.2 or 160 = Y.
The answer is 160.

The cost of a slice of cake is three-fourths of the cost of a cup of milk tea. If the milk tea costs $2.40, how much do 2 slices of cake and 1 cup of milk tea cost?

The cost of a slice of cake is $2.40 x 3/4 = $1.80.

Therefore, 2 slices of cake and 1 cup of milk tea cost $3.60 + $2.40 = $6.
The answer is 6.
A dog barks 30 times per minute.  If 2 dogs bark 30 times per minute, how many times will they have barked after 10 minutes?

There are 2 dogs and they each bark 30 times per minute so together they bark 2*30 = 60 times per minute
2 dogs bark a combined total of 60 times per minutes, after 10 minutes they will have barked 60*10 = 600 times
The answer is 600.

Her little cousin pulled his hand back. “You're not the boss of the game.” Vandana looked up from her sewing. “Aadhya, come here a sec.” “What?” “‘Because I said so.’ Where have you heard that?” Aadhya went pink. “You. When I don't want to do homework.” Vandana laughed. “Fair. It doesn't work on you either, does it?” “No.” “So try asking. ‘Do you want to go there? It gets you closer.’” Aadhya went back. “Do you want to move there? It's a shortcut.” Her cousin looked. “Oh. Okay!” They played until dinner.

Where had Aadhya heard “Because I said so”?
Aadhya had heard it from Vandana, when Aadhya didn't want to do homework.
What was Aadhya feeling when Vandana asked where she'd heard it?
Aadhya felt embarrassed, going pink, realising she was copying Vandana's tone.
What did Vandana coach Aadhya to say instead?
She coached her to ask and give a reason, like “Do you want to move there? It's a shortcut,” instead of ordering.
How did the little cousin feel about being ordered?
He felt bossed and pulled his hand back, saying Aadhya wasn't the boss of the game.

Trisha was organising the craft fair for women weavers in Mahuva, a small town near the coast, and she had booked the big community hall, which held two hundred. But last year only forty people had come, and the empty hall had felt sad.
This time, three weeks before, she sat in the panchayat office with her friend Bidisha and wrote a rule. "If fewer than sixty weavers and buyers confirm by Friday at six, we move to the smaller school hall." She told the school headmaster the same day, and he agreed to keep it free.
"Why decide now?" Bidisha asked.
"Because on the day I'll be panicking and want to hope for the best," Trisha said.
On Friday at six, the count was fifty-one. Trisha didn't argue with herself. She called the school and the community hall, and sent a message to all fifty-one: new venue, same time.
The school hall was full and lively.

How many confirmations were there on Friday at six?
The count was fifty-one.
Why did Trisha want to set the rule three weeks early?
She worried she would panic on the day and just hope for the best, so she wanted the decision made calmly in advance.
What else could Trisha set a trigger for, and why?
She could set a rule for bad weather, such as moving stalls indoors if rain is forecast, so another choice isn't made in a rush.
How might the weavers experience the smaller hall?
They may feel more encouraged, since a full, lively hall feels better than the sad, empty one of last year.

Is it "embarasment" or "embarrassment"?
Also, please improve this sentence: If I will see him, I will tell him.
And what does "wind down" mean?
Then I keep seeing "admirable" in my reading. Meaning?
Last one: could you explain what thoughtful means?

1. It is "embarrassment", with a double "r" and a double "s".
2. Corrected: If I see him, I will tell him. Why: after "if" in this kind of condition, we use the simple present, not "will".
3. It means to relax after a busy time. For example: I read for a while at night to wind down.
4. "Admirable" is an adjective. It means deserving respect and praise.
5. "Thoughtful" is an adjective. It means thinking carefully, or showing care for others.

"Why do we have to stand so still for the anthem?" Yogesh asked in the car.
"To show respect," said Swati. "For the country, and for everyone standing with us."
"But I get itchy."
"Everyone does. It's only a minute. What do you notice when you do it?"
Yogesh thought. "My back gets straight. And I feel like we're all one thing."
"That's the point," Swati said. "What about the lamp?"
"I like it. It's warm and quiet."
He paused. "Can I stand beside Raj tomorrow? He always has the wrong words." Swati smiled. "I think he'd like that." 🙂

Where did Yogesh ask his question about standing still?
He asked it in the car.
What was Yogesh feeling when he said his back gets straight and everyone feels like one thing, and what else did he mention feeling?
He felt a sense of belonging and calm through the shared ritual. He also said he gets itchy standing still, so he feels a bit restless as well.
What could Swati do to help Yogesh find meaning in the anthem?
Swati could keep asking what Yogesh notices, as before, and let him describe the ritual in his own words before adding an explanation.
How might Raj feel if Yogesh stands beside him?
Raj may feel supported, because he always has the wrong words and would have a friend nearby.

Kishore was on the phone with Dada, and it had been a very long call already. "And then, Dada, our teacher said, and I forgot to tell you, we have a class pet now..." Dada laughed and listened. Across the room, Mama held up a hand and mouthed, "Dinner." Kishore said, "And one more thing, Dada," three times. Mama came over and whispered, "Try: Okay Dada, time for me to go." Kishore breathed in. "Okay, Dada, time for me to go. Thank you for listening. I love you. Bye!" Dada said, "Love you too, my champion. Call me tomorrow."

What did Kishore forget to tell Dada about?
A class pet that the teacher told them about.
What was Kishore feeling on the call, and what suggests it?
Happy and eager to keep sharing. Kishore added "one more thing" three times even after Mama mouthed "Dinner."
What did Mama suggest that made ending the call possible?
Mama whispered a signal, "Okay Dada, time for me to go," which Kishore followed with thanks, love and goodbye.
How might Dada have felt about the call ending?
Warm and fond. Dada said "Love you too, my champion" and asked Kishore to call the next day.

I'm Ganga, and our river-protection group was the closest thing to family I had in college. We'd sat in the rain together, shared tiffins at dawn. So when Zeenat, our coordinator, suggested posting the home address of the factory manager who'd been dumping waste, 'so people can go and tell him what they think', everyone cheered. I felt sick. His kids lived there. But I said nothing that night; I didn't want to be the one who spoiled things. At home I couldn't sleep. The next morning, before anything was posted, I called Zeenat. 'I love this group. That's why I'm saying it: posting his address could get someone hurt, and it would make us the story instead of the river.' She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'Say it at the meeting. I think others feel it too.' I did. Three people nodded at once. We filed a complaint with the pollution board instead, and held a sit-in at the factory gate.

What did Zeenat suggest posting?
Zeenat suggested posting the home address of the factory manager.
What did Ganga feel when everyone cheered?
Ganga felt sick and uneasy, worried for the manager's children, but afraid to spoil things.
Why was speaking up the next morning an act of loyalty?
Ganga raised it early and kindly, before anything was posted, to protect people and the group's cause.
How does Zeenat respond to Ganga's concern?
Zeenat listens, thinks, and invites Ganga to raise it at the meeting, suspecting others feel the same.

In their London kitchen, eighteen-month-old Jin crawled to the wall and stopped nose to nose with the plug socket. Two little slots for eyes, a round hole for a surprised mouth. Jin squealed and patted the wall beside it. "Oh! Oh!" Her father Chidi knelt, gently moved her hand away from the socket and pointed at the kettle instead. "Look, another face." Jin stared, then giggled and pointed at the toaster too.

What did the socket's round hole look like to Jin?
A surprised mouth.
What do Jin's squeal and giggles show about how she feels?
She is delighted at finding faces in everyday things.
How did Chidi keep Jin safe while keeping the fun going?
He gently moved her hand away from the socket and pointed at the kettle as "another face", so she kept face-hunting somewhere safe.
What might Chidi be thinking as Jin points at the toaster?
Chidi may be amused and relieved to see her happily finding faces on the kettle and toaster instead of near the socket.

In the Bengaluru software office, Sonali, twenty-six, noticed that her new teammate Dolma never looked the manager, Mr Pieter, in the eye during stand-ups. Pieter, who had moved from Amsterdam, liked people to hold his gaze. After a week, he said to Sonali, "Is Dolma unhappy here? She won't look at me." Sonali didn't want to guess or explain for Dolma. At lunch she asked Dolma, casually, "How are you finding Pieter?" Dolma smiled. "He's nice. But he stares so much! In my family, looking straight at a senior feels rude. I look down to be polite." Sonali laughed. "He thinks you're unhappy." Dolma's eyes widened. "Oh no." Sonali suggested she tell Pieter herself. The next day Dolma did, and Pieter laughed too. "I'll stop staring so hard. And you look up now and then?" "Deal," Dolma said. Both adjusted a little.

Where had Mr Pieter moved from?
From Amsterdam.
What was Dolma feeling when she learned Pieter thought she was unhappy?
She was surprised and a little dismayed, her eyes widening, since she had meant to be polite.
What did Sonali do that avoided a stereotype?
Sonali asked Dolma directly instead of guessing or explaining for her, and suggested Dolma tell Pieter herself.
How did Pieter respond once Dolma explained?
He laughed, agreed to stop staring so hard, and asked her to look up now and then.

Four months into the agency, I've noticed something about myself I don't like. In every review, Avni talks first. She says things like, "I'm not sure, but what if the logo had more space?" and everyone leans in. I sit there with three ideas in my notebook and a voice in my head saying they're obvious, or wrong, or both.
I compare my inside, which is all doubt, with everyone else's outside, which looks like confidence. It isn't a fair match, but it doesn't feel unfair while it's happening.
Last week the creative director said, "Binita, you've been quiet," and I said, "I agree with Avni." I didn't, actually.
Now my name isn't on the new campaign. Of course it isn't. Nobody knows what I think. The silence is making me smaller, and the smaller I get, the more I believe I have nothing to add.

What did Binita say when the creative director mentioned the silence?
I agree with Avni.
What does Binita feel when comparing with Avni in reviews?
Binita feels insecure and small, measuring private doubts against how confident everyone else looks from outside.
What could break the cycle for Binita?
Sharing one of the notebook ideas in the next review, even starting with 'I'm not sure', the way Avni does.
How might Avni experience these reviews?
Avni may feel unsure too but speaks anyway, and probably doesn't realise Binita has ideas waiting in a notebook.

Tuesday. It happened again today. I was answering in class and my voice cracked, right in the middle of "photosynthesis". It squeaked high and then dropped low. Two boys grinned. I felt my face heat up and almost stopped talking. But Parveen, who sits behind me, just whispered, "Keep going." So I did. I even laughed, and said, "Sorry, my voice has a mind of its own." A few people laughed with me and it stopped feeling so big. I'd rather laugh than go silent for weeks. Note to self: the crack isn't about how I feel, it's just my voice. Imran

In class my voice cracked in the middle of "photosynthesis", squeaking high and dropping low, and two boys grinned, but Parveen, who sits behind me, whispered "Keep going", so I did, laughed and said my voice had a mind of its own, and a few people laughed with me. I would rather laugh than go silent for weeks, and I have noted that the crack is not about how I feel, it is just my voice.

At the district post office, Darshan stamped letters harder than he needed to. During the tea break, behind the counter, he opened his phone and scrolled to Vaibhav's page. A photo from Pune: his son with paint on his hands, laughing with strangers. Darshan zoomed in on the face, then shut the phone quickly when a clerk passed.
"Your son is in Pune now, na?" the clerk asked.
"Ungrateful boy," Darshan said. "He made his choice."
That evening, as every evening, he went into Vaibhav's old room and straightened the bedsheet nobody slept on. He had not called in eight months. Calling first, he told himself, would mean begging, and a father does not beg. He sat on the bed a long time, waiting for a phone that didn't ring, and called it dignity.

How long had it been since Darshan called?
He had not called in eight months.
Why does Darshan shut his phone quickly when the clerk passes?
He feels ashamed to be seen longing for his son, since his pride insists he is only angry at an ungrateful boy.
What turning point is available to Darshan now?
He could see that his waiting is hurt rather than dignity, and send one small message or ask a relative to carry a soft word.
What might Vaibhav imagine about his father's silence?
Vaibhav may believe his father has truly given up on him, with no idea that the room is kept ready and his photos are read in secret.

Swati shared a grocery list with the whole leadership team.
Why did Swati keep giggling, according to her?

Say something brief like "wrong tab, one sec," fix it and carry on, as Swati's short follow-up email to Rekha ma'am did.

Dhruv, you lost your race today, na? Sit. Let your Swati Nani tell you something.

When I was eleven, the school winter sports day had a 400-metre race. I came last. Last! The whole school saw me.

I cried behind the shed. My father found me. He didn't say "don't cry". He said, "Do you want to run again next year?"

I did. So every morning that winter, before school, I ran round our field. Some mornings I hated it.

Next year, I came third. Not first. But I ran past the shed where I had cried.

So, Dhruv. Cry today. Tomorrow, run.

Where did young Swati cry?
She cried behind the shed.
How did young Swati feel coming last?
Young Swati felt ashamed and upset, crying behind the shed.
What was the turning point in Swati's story?
Her father asking whether she wanted to run again led her to practise every morning that winter.
How might Swati's father have felt finding her crying?
Her father likely felt caring and wanted to encourage her without dismissing her feelings.
Why does water left in a dark bucket in the sun become warm?

The dark bucket soaks up the sun's energy and heats the water. Because sunlight carries energy, and a dark surface soaks up more of it than a pale surface, the bucket heats up and passes the heat to the water.

Monday. Irawati, five, dropped her doll Guddi down the steps. "Naughty Guddi! I said hold the railing!" Sarika, her mother, heard from the kitchen and said nothing.
Wednesday. Guddi fell off the swing. Irawati scolded her, then stopped. She picked Guddi up and hugged her. "Sorry, I shouted." Sarika sat beside her. "Is Guddi okay?" "She's a bit sad."
Friday. Irawati made a new rule for Guddi: "On the steps, we hold hands." She held Guddi's hand all the way down. Sarika walked behind, smiling.

What did Irawati tell Guddi on the steps on Friday?
"On the steps, we hold hands."
What does Irawati's saying sorry to Guddi suggest she is learning?
She seems to be working out that rules can be kept with kindness, and that shouting can hurt someone she loves.
Which choice by Sarika helped the game grow, and why?
Sarika asked "Is Guddi okay?" instead of laughing or correcting, which let Irawati keep practising kindness and rules.
How might Sarika feel walking behind Irawati on Friday?
Sarika probably feels proud and warm, seeing Irawati turn scolding into a caring rule.

"Ammi, look!" Irfan shouted. It was Eid morning, and he was on his cycle without the side wheels.

"Irfan! You're riding alone!" Jyoti said.

He pedalled to the gate and back. "I didn't fall even once!"

"You practised so much."

"I'm big now." He puffed out his chest.

"Very big. Will you ride to Nani's?"

"Tomorrow. Today I'm showing everyone."

What did Irfan ride without?
He rode his cycle without the side wheels.
How did Irfan feel after riding to the gate and back?
Irfan felt proud and grown-up, puffing out his chest.
How did Jyoti support Irfan's pride?
She praised his practice and asked about his next goal, not just the result.
How might Jyoti feel watching Irfan ride alone?
Jyoti was likely delighted and proud of him.
Tom and Tim both brought 4, six-sided dice to school. How many total sides are there?

There are 8 total dice because 4 plus 4 equals 8
There are 48 sides because 8 times six equals 48
The answer is 48.

After overnight snow in Seoul, the kindergarten yard was slippery. Rosa, a new girl from Spain, slid and landed on her bottom with a shriek.
Soo-ah, holding her mitten, froze. She screamed and cried so loudly that the teacher ran out thinking she was the one hurt. Soo-ah could not step forward.
The teacher helped Rosa up. Rosa was fine and already laughing.
Soo-ah was still sobbing. The teacher knelt. "You were scared for Rosa?" Soo-ah nodded hard.
Later, inside, Soo-ah drew a picture of Rosa with a big plaster and gave it to her.

Why did the teacher run out?
Soo-ah was screaming and crying so loudly that the teacher thought she was the one hurt.
What was Soo-ah feeling when Rosa slipped?
She was scared for Rosa and so overwhelmed by her own distress that she froze and could not step forward.
How could the teacher help Soo-ah next time she freezes like this?
The teacher could calm her first, name the fear kindly as she did, and later practise simple steps like calling a grown-up.
How might Rosa feel when she gets Soo-ah's drawing?
Rosa might feel touched and happy, seeing that the new friend cared about her fall.

Uma, can I tell you something? Last night I had the biggest fight with Papa. I'm Abhinav, the calm one, remember? Right. So I shouted. I admit it. But I shouted because I've had boards stress for three weeks, no sleep, two mock tests. Papa shouted because he wants to control everything, like which tuition, what time I'm home. That's how it felt. Then this morning I heard him talking to Ma in the kitchen. He said, "I only raised my voice because I'm worried about his marks and the office is killing me. But that boy just screams at me because he's angry at the world." Uma, he said the exact opposite of me. His shouting was stress, mine was attitude. I stood there holding my toothbrush. We're both saying the same thing about ourselves.

What did Abhinav hear Papa say in the kitchen?
He only raised his voice because he's worried about his marks and the office is killing him.
What was Abhinav feeling standing there holding the toothbrush?
Abhinav felt stunned and uneasy, seeing that Papa excused his own shouting with stress just as Abhinav did, and blamed Abhinav's character.
What could Abhinav try when they talk next?
Abhinav could say what was stressing him and ask about Papa's office pressure, so both see each other's situation, not only temper.
How does Papa see Abhinav's shouting?
Papa sees it as anger at the world and attitude, not the stress of board exams that Abhinav feels.
Has the wrestling bout at the state games ended, and who won?
I don't know, because I can't see results as they happen. The games' official page posts scores soon after each bout.

Leela, you're angry, and I understand. But before you post anything back, let me tell you what I did at your age.
In Class Ten, someone put a photo of me on a social page, sweaty and red-faced after I fell in the relay, with a nasty caption. I was sure it was Deepesh, the boy who sat behind me. So that same night I found a photo of him asleep on the school bus, mouth open, and posted it with something worse.
By morning, everything flipped. The school didn't ask about my photo first; they asked about his. Deepesh's parents complained. My father sat in the principal's office and said, “Jagdish, what have you done?” The principal said my post could itself count as an offence. And whoever posted mine said, “He did worse,” and got off lightly.
I never even found out if it was Deepesh. So, Leela, give me your phone, and let's report it properly, tonight.

Where had the photo of Deepesh been taken?
Asleep on the school bus, mouth open.
What was young Jagdish feeling when he posted the photo of Deepesh?
He was angry and humiliated, sure Deepesh was to blame and wanting to hurt him back.
What choice in the story could have kept Jagdish the one who was wronged?
Reporting his own photo to the school instead of posting back, which would have kept the focus on whoever started it.
How was Deepesh affected by what young Jagdish did?
Deepesh was mocked in public, perhaps without having done anything, and his parents had to complain to the school.

The 6:15 local was cancelled because of flooding at Kurla, and Aadhya and Salma were stuck on a crowded platform bench with one umbrella between them.
Salma scrolled past a photo and froze. "Isn't that Vivek? Engaged?"
Aadhya looked. Eight months ago that would have wrecked her evening. Now she felt only a small, surprised quiet. "Good for him. Really."
"You're not upset?"
"Not really. He was kind to my Nani when she was in hospital. He also never once asked what I wanted to study. Both are true."
Salma, still raw from her own breakup in March, pulled her dupatta tight. "I'm never doing this again. Love is a trap."
Aadhya bumped her shoulder. "I said that too. What helped was noticing what I kept ignoring, like needing someone curious about my life. Not quitting."
The announcement crackled: next train in forty minutes. They shared the umbrella and a packet of peanuts, and waited.

Why was the 6:15 local cancelled?
Because of flooding at Kurla.
What did Aadhya feel on seeing Vivek's engagement photo?
Only a small, surprised quiet instead of hurt, showing she had moved past the pain in eight months.
What would you advise Salma, based on what Aadhya shares?
To notice what she needs from a partner and what she kept ignoring, rather than swearing off love while the hurt is fresh.
How does Salma see love right now?
As a trap to avoid forever; she is still raw from her breakup in March, so Aadhya's calm surprises her.

I'm Sangeeta, and I've coached at the municipal pool for nine years. This term I've been watching Maria. She's fourteen, strong, and she lights up doing butterfly, all splash and shoulders. Whenever I set kick drills with a board, she does two lengths, then "forgets" and drifts back to butterfly near the deep end. Her friends clap. I can't tell whether she finds the drills dull or feels babyish holding a board beside the younger kids; maybe both. What I can see is that her legs give out by the third length and she lifts her head too high to breathe. On Tuesday I didn't scold. I swam a length of butterfly myself, then said, "That kick you keep skipping is the engine. Give me ten minutes of board every session, and in a month your fly will go twice as far." She rolled her eyes, but she picked up the board.

What does Maria do after two lengths of kick drills?
She "forgets" and drifts back to butterfly near the deep end.
How does Sangeeta seem to feel about Maria's shortcuts?
Sangeeta seems concerned about the gaps but patient and fond, choosing to explain gently rather than scold.
Why did Sangeeta's approach on Tuesday have a good chance of working?
It showed rather than lectured, linked the dull kick drill to the butterfly Maria loves, and asked for only ten minutes a session.
How might the kick drills look from Maria's side?
To Maria they may feel dull and a bit embarrassing next to the younger kids, while butterfly earns claps from friends.
It rained so hard yesterday that our street flooded for a few hours.
That sounds stressful. Heavy rain can flood streets quickly, especially where drains are blocked. Did it get into any houses?
No, but the water was knee-high on the road.
Then it was lucky it stayed outside. After water like that, the road may have loose stones or holes under the surface, so walk carefully for a day or two.
Is it worth telling the local office about the drain?
Yes. Reporting a blocked drain helps them fix it before the next heavy rain. Say the street name, where the water gathered, and how long it stayed.

So here's the weird part of getting the fellowship, Mehr. Everyone assumes it's all celebration.
Naveen and I applied together. When I got it and he didn't, he said, "Congrats, Madam Scholar," and every time since, it's been a joke. "Oh, you'll be too busy for us now." "Must be nice."
For a while I started shrinking. I'd say, "It's just a small fellowship, it's luck, honestly." I stopped mentioning the research trip. Then I realised I was making myself small so he'd feel less small, and neither of us felt better.
So last week I told him: "I know this stings. I'd feel the same. I'm not going to pretend it's nothing, but I'm still me, and I still want our Sunday cricket." He didn't say much. But he came on Sunday.
That's me, Trisha, still learning to be proud and kind at once.

What does Naveen call Trisha after the fellowship?
"Madam Scholar".
Why did Trisha start calling the fellowship "just luck"?
She felt guilty and uncomfortable about Naveen's hurt and tried to shrink herself so he would feel less small.
What did Trisha say that was both warm and honest?
She named that it stings, refused to pretend the fellowship was nothing, and invited Naveen to their Sunday cricket.
How does Naveen seem to feel about Trisha's success?
Envious and hurt at missing out, which comes out as sarcasm, though turning up on Sunday shows he still values the friendship.

"Tell me what happened and what you wanted." "He knocked it and I wanted to finish." "Try saying, I was building, please be careful." On the next Monday a boy walked near the tower and Saurabh said, "I was building! Please go round!" and kept stacking.

What did Saurabh say on the next Monday?
"I was building! Please go round!"
What was Saurabh feeling when he yelled "It's your fault!"?
Distress and frustration at his tower being knocked. Blame is a simple way for him to explain it.
How did Sonali help Saurabh?

How might the boy who bumped the blocks feel to be called mean?
Probably hurt or confused if he did not mean it.

By the fifth missed deadline, Chandrika had written Dilnaz off. The second-year student came late, snapped at her project partner, and hadn't submitted a single lab report since August. 'Attitude problem,' another lecturer said in the staffroom. But Chandrika kept seeing small things: Dilnaz's hands shaking when she was called on, the way she sat nearest the door. After class she asked Dilnaz to stay. 'I'm not calling you in to scold. I've noticed things seem hard lately. What's going on?' Dilnaz stared at the desk. Then it spilled out: she opened the portal every night, felt her chest tighten and shut the laptop, over and over, and then hated herself for it. 'I'm not lazy, ma'am. I just freeze.' Chandrika walked her to the student counsellor's office that afternoon and agreed a new timetable for the reports.

At which missed deadline had Chandrika written Dilnaz off?
By the fifth missed deadline.
What did Chandrika feel as she noticed Dilnaz's shaking hands?
Chandrika felt uneasy and concerned, sensing that something other than attitude might be going on.
What made Chandrika's approach work?
She asked kindly what was hard instead of scolding, then took Dilnaz to the counsellor and set a new timetable.
What is it like for Dilnaz to be called lazy?
It adds shame to her fear, since she already hates herself for freezing each night.

Monday night
Failed the statistics mid-term. I'm Ganga. My first thought was: I'm not a numbers person. I should switch courses.
Then I did the thing Trisha makes me do: write the thought, then check it.
Evidence I'm not a numbers person? I got an A in economics, which is full of numbers. I passed the first quiz.
Other explanations? I skipped two lectures for the fest. I didn't do any practice problems. I crammed the night before.
One change: do ten practice problems every Sunday and go to the tutor's office hours.
I still feel bad. That's fine. But "not a numbers person" doesn't fit the facts.

Which course did Ganga get an A in?
Ganga got an A in economics.
How does Ganga feel after failing the mid-term?
Ganga feels bad and discouraged, and at first wants to switch courses.
What change does Ganga choose, and why is it useful?
Doing ten practice problems every Sunday and going to office hours, because it targets the real causes Ganga found.
How might Trisha see Ganga's diary entry?
Trisha would likely feel pleased that Ganga checked the thought against facts instead of believing it.
A bowler bowls 6 overs. How many legal balls is that, with 6 balls in an over?
36. Because 6 x 6 = 36, so there are 36 balls.
Meera wakes up at 6:15 and the school bus comes at 7:00. How many minutes does she have?
45 minutes. Because from 6:15 to 7:00 is 45 minutes.

I was there when Mohit walked out, so I know it wasn't easy. After school on Friday a bunch of us were at the old railway bridge, and Sahil said the plan was to stand on the ledge and film the express going past, close enough to feel the wind. The others were cheering. Mohit said, "Guys, that's actually how people die." They laughed and called him chicken. He said it again. They laughed louder. So he picked up his bag, walked to the road, and I saw him on the phone, pacing. Twenty minutes later his mother's scooter pulled up, and she marched straight to the bridge and sent everyone home. On Monday Mohit went to Uma Ma'am, the counsellor, and by lunch she had spoken to our whole class. I don't know how he felt walking away. He didn't look back.

What did Sahil plan to film?
The express going past, from the ledge, close enough to feel the wind.
What might Mohit have felt as he repeated his warning and was laughed at?
He likely felt angry and anxious, frustrated that they wouldn't listen but worried enough to keep trying.
What made Mohit's response effective?
He didn't argue endlessly; he left, called his mother, who came and sent everyone home, and then told the counsellor so the whole class was spoken to.
How did the narrator see Mohit walking away?
The narrator saw it wasn't easy, watched him pace on the phone, and couldn't tell how he felt, only that he didn't look back.

Monday: Kashish reached for the biscuit tin. "More! More!" Mohit gave her one, and she munched happily.
Wednesday: after she tumbled off the step, she reached toward the tin again. "More!" But her eyes were wet and her lip shook. Mohit picked her up instead. "You want up. A cuddle." She clung to him.
The next Monday: she stood by his leg, raised both arms and said, "Up!"

What did Kashish reach for on Monday?
The biscuit tin.
What did Kashish really want on Wednesday when she said "More!"?
She was upset after tumbling and wanted comfort; her wet eyes and shaking lip showed she needed a cuddle more than a biscuit.
What habit of Mohit's helped Kashish learn to ask for comfort?
He named what she needed, "You want up. A cuddle," which gave her the word she later used.
What would change if Mohit had simply given her a biscuit on Wednesday?
She would have been left without the comfort she needed and might have stayed upset.

Nursery note, Thursday. Rekha, Butterfly Room.
Omkar was pouring water at the tub. Tushar tripped near the shoe rack and cried. Omkar dropped his cup, stared, and cried too, big tears, though nothing had happened to him.
I held Tushar and sat beside Omkar so both could lean on me, singing the boat song. Tushar quietened first; Omkar watched him, hiccuped, stopped.
Next: telling Omkar's mother at pickup. Little ones catch each other's tears. 🙂

What song did Rekha sing?
Rekha sang the boat song.
What does Omkar's crying suggest about how he felt when Tushar tripped?
It suggests Omkar felt upset simply because Tushar was upset; the feeling spread to him even though nothing had happened to him.
Which of Rekha's choices worked well, and why?
Sitting with both boys together and singing the boat song worked, because once Tushar calmed, Omkar could see it and calm down too.
How might Omkar's mother react if she reads this note?
She would probably feel reassured, knowing that if Omkar seems upset for no clear reason, it may be because he caught another child's tears.

Explain this section to me in two sentences.

"Vaisampayana continued, 'Having listened to all these foremost words fraught with reason and acceptable to the heart, Bhima and others were filled with delight and joining their hands, bowed unto that prince of Kuru's race. Indeed, those foremost of men, O king, having heard that speech of the monarch, well adorned with sweet letters and syllables, acceptable to the heart, and divested of dissonant sounds and words, began to applaud Yudhishthira highly. The high-souled son of Dharma, in return, possessed of great energy, praised his convinced auditors; and once more the king addressed the son of the foremost of rivers, possessed of a high soul, for enquiring about duties.'"

Bhima and the others are delighted by Yudhishthira's speech, bow to him with joined hands and praise him highly. Yudhishthira thanks his listeners and again asks the son of the greatest river about duties.

Rewrite this text as a two-sentence summary.

At three o'clock precisely I was at Baker Street, but Holmes had not yet returned. The landlady informed me that he had left the house shortly after eight o'clock in the morning. I sat down beside the fire, however, with the intention of awaiting him, however long he might be. I was already deeply interested in his inquiry, for, though it was surrounded by none of the grim and strange features which were associated with the two crimes which I have already recorded, still, the nature of the case and the exalted station of his client gave it a character of its own. Indeed, apart from the nature of the investigation which my friend had on hand, there was something in his masterly grasp of a situation, and his keen, incisive reasoning, which made it a pleasure to me to study his system of work, and to follow the quick, subtle methods by which he disentangled the most inextricable mysteries. So accustomed was I to his invariable success that the very possibility of his failing had ceased to enter into my head.

The narrator reaches Baker Street at three, finds that Holmes has been out since eight, and settles by the fire to wait. The narrator is interested in the case, partly for the client's high rank, and expects Holmes to succeed as always.

A few things I want to check.
My notebook has these questions.
I came across "canteen" today. Meaning? What does "hard of hearing" mean?

1. Canteen is a noun that means a place in a school or workplace where meals are served.
2. It means unable to hear well.

Osborn is testing a new way to get dressed in the morning on school days so he goes faster and can get up later. He tracks his time for the week and on Monday is takes him 2 minutes. On Tuesday it takes him 4 minutes. On Wednesday it takes him 3 minutes. On Thursday it takes him 4 minutes. Before Friday arrives he looks at his old way of getting dressed and sees that it was taking him 3 minutes on average to get dressed. How fast does he have to get dressed on Friday so his weekly average ties his old method?

If it takes on average 3 minutes to get dressed, then it takes 15 minutes total on the school week because 5 x 3 = 15
Thus far this week it has taken him 13 minutes to get dressed because 2 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 13
To tie his previous method, he needs to take 2 minutes on Friday because 15 - 13 = 2
The answer is 2.

"Why did you send me a crying face, Zubin?" Ritu asked, holding up the tablet at dinner.
"Because I was sad. My tower fell."

Zubin's tower fell.

Zubin felt sad and a bit amused that the tower fell, so Zubin meant both feelings. Ritu saw a laughing-crying face and thought Zubin was laughing.

Ritu feels confused and a little left out of Zubin's feelings, because Ritu cannot tell whether to comfort Zubin or laugh along.

On the tram in Prague, Jana said she would be up at six to revise for tomorrow's test. Camila arched one eyebrow slowly. "You? At six?" Jana burst into laughter. "Okay, okay, seven!" They had done this dozens of times. The eyebrow meant, of course you will. But at the next stop, Nadia, a new girl who had joined their table that week, said she planned to try out for the school choir. Camila raised the same eyebrow, and Nadia went stiff and looked at her shoes. Jana leaned over quickly. "Camila, it is banter, she does not know you yet," and Camila said, "Sorry, Nadia. That was a joke, I think you will get in."

At what time did Jana say she would wake up to revise?
Jana said she would be up at six to revise.
What did Nadia feel when Camila raised an eyebrow at her?
She stiffened and looked at her shoes, so she probably felt unsure or stung, since she did not know Camila's joking style yet. She might also have been simply shy.
What did Camila do to repair the moment?
Camila apologised, said the eyebrow was a joke and told Nadia, "I think you will get in."
How does the same eyebrow look different to Jana than to Nadia?
For Jana it is a known joke from many past laughs, while for Nadia, who is new, it could look like doubt or mockery.

Friday: Nikita arrived from Dubai for the summer. At the door, her Dada Ramesh waited. Nikita didn't know what to do, so she hung her head and stared at the floor. “Is she upset?” Dada whispered to Papa. Sunday: On the veranda, Dada showed her. “Palms together, a small dip of the head, then look up and smile. It says, I respect you. Hanging the head says, I'm sorry, or I'm sad.” Nikita practised on the cat. Tuesday: When the neighbour aunty came with sweets, Nikita pressed her palms together, dipped her head, looked up and smiled. The aunty beamed. Dada winked at her from his chair.

Where did Nikita arrive from?
Nikita arrived from Dubai.
What was Nikita feeling when she hung her head on Friday?
She felt unsure and shy, not knowing the greeting, so her hanging head looked like sadness even though it was confusion.
How did Dada's lesson on Sunday help?
He showed the difference between a small respectful dip with a smile and a hanging head, giving her a clear way to greet elders.
How did Friday's greeting look to Dada Ramesh?
It looked to him as if she might be upset, since a hanging head can mean sadness or shame.

"Mummy, look at my tower!"
"Mm, lovely, beta." Mahima didn't look up; the baby was feeding.
"Mummy! Wook! Pweeti wants milk too!"
"Preeti, why are you talking like a baby?"
Preeti climbed onto the sofa and pressed against her arm. "You don't wike me now."
Mahima closed her eyes for a moment. "Oh, jaan. I'm tired, but I love you just the same. It's not your fault. When baby sleeps, you and I will have ten whole minutes. Just us. You choose."
"Tower game?"
"Tower game."

What did Mahima promise when the baby sleeps?
She promised Preeti ten whole minutes, just the two of them, with Preeti choosing the game.
Why might Preeti talk like a baby and press against her mother?
She feels pushed out and worried that her mother doesn't like her now, so she acts like the baby to get attention.
What did Mahima do that helped Preeti?
She admitted she was tired, said it wasn't Preeti's fault, and promised ten minutes of undivided time.
What is it like for Mahima when Preeti says "You don't wike me now"?
It probably stings and makes her feel guilty, but it also shows her what Preeti needs.

At nine, Lokesh noticed things nobody explained. Tanuja always ate at the far end of the bench. Her mother came to clean at the flat upstairs. A boy in class teased Tanuja's surname in a sing-song voice. One evening Lokesh asked his father, 'Why does everyone laugh at her name?' His father put down the paper. 'They shouldn't. She is a child like you, and teasing a name is unkind. Tomorrow, sit with her if you like.' Lokesh did, and Tanuja's shy smile stayed on his mind all week.

At twenty, in the hostel common room, voices rose over quotas and merit. 'They take our seats!' 'You don't know what it's like!' Lokesh felt his heart race and slogans rise in his throat. Then he remembered the bench. He turned to Avni, a classmate who had come on a scholarship from a village school. 'What was it like for you?' She told him about her first month: teachers who assumed she would not cope, evenings sharing one library book. Later he found the university's own figures on who stayed and who dropped out. He stayed in the room without shouting, and the next week he asked both sides a question before answering.

What did Lokesh's father tell him to do about Tanuja?
He said teasing a name is unkind and suggested that Lokesh sit with her if he liked.
How did Lokesh's way of dealing with social difference change between nine and twenty?

At nine he noticed things nobody explained, and his father's answer led him to sit with Tanuja. At twenty, pulled toward slogans in a heated quota argument, he asked Avni about her experience, looked up the figures and stayed calm.
What was Lokesh feeling in the common room before he spoke to Avni?
Agitated and pulled toward the loud slogans, as his racing heart shows.
What would you advise a student who feels pulled toward slogans?
Listen to lived experience, check real numbers, and ask questions before picking a side.

Tushar: sure
Kiran: you were on your phone most of the time I was explaining the vendor issue. I couldn't tell if you were bored or dealing with something

Sit, Mohit, and let me tell you how your cousin Divyansh uses that chatbot, because I watched him closely last month. I'm your Ravi Mama, remember.
He asked it to explain photosynthesis. Instead of copying the answer, he explained it back to me at dinner in his own words, and stumbled in two places. So he went to his textbook, found that the chatbot had muddled one detail, and fixed it. "It's a helper, Mama," he said. "Not the teacher, and not the answer key."
Then he asked it to check his homework, but he accepted only the corrections he could reason out himself 🙂. I said nothing. I saw a boy who wanted to learn, not just to finish.

What did Divyansh ask the chatbot to explain?
He asked it to explain photosynthesis.
How does Divyansh seem to feel about the chatbot?
Divyansh seems wary of trusting it fully and keen to learn, calling it a helper rather than the teacher and checking its answers against his textbook.
What could Mohit copy from Divyansh's way of using the chatbot?
Mohit could explain the topic back in Mohit's own words, check the textbook for facts, and accept only corrections that make sense after thinking them through. 👍
How does Ravi Mama see Divyansh's approach?
Ravi Mama sees a boy who wanted to learn rather than just finish, and he chose to watch without interfering.
Is it "collegue" or "colleague" for people I work with?

It is "colleague", spelled c-o-l-l-e-a-g-u-e. A trick: "a colleague" has "ague" at the end, like "league".

Project supervisor's note, Class Nine website project, week four
When this group started, Joseph, Vaibhav and Noor were all “doing everything”, which meant three people editing the same homepage and nobody writing content. In week two I asked them to list every task. They came back with a shared sheet: design (Noor), content (Vaibhav), coding (Joseph), each task with a name and a date beside it. They also fixed two ten-minute check-ins, Tuesdays and Fridays at lunch, standing by the lab door.
I have watched three of those check-ins. They are quick: done, stuck, next. On Friday Vaibhav admitted the history page was late; Joseph offered a simpler layout so it could go in as plain text first.
The site is not finished, but for the first time every page has an owner. I will look at their sheet again next Friday before suggesting anything.

When are the group's ten-minute check-ins?
Tuesdays and Fridays at lunch, standing by the lab door.
How might Vaibhav have felt admitting the history page was late?
Vaibhav was probably a little embarrassed, but safe enough to say it, since the check-in is built for "stuck" as well as "done" 😅
What could the group try if a task's owner falls ill before a due date?
Use the Tuesday check-in to hand that task to whoever is ahead and move its date on the sheet, so the plan stays honest.
How does the new split look from Joseph's side?
Joseph can focus on coding without three people fighting over the homepage, and can spot a way to help when content runs late.

messages.content: Work out 3/5 x 2/7 and explain the rule "multiply tops, multiply bottoms".

Answer: 3/5 x 2/7 = (3 x 2)/(5 x 7) = 6/35.

Think of the area model without drawing all of it: a square cut into 5 rows and 7 columns has 5 x 7 = 35 small pieces, so each piece is 1/35. Shading 3 rows and 2 columns gives 3 x 2 = 6 double-shaded pieces, so the answer is 6/35. That is the rule. Unlike adding, we do NOT need a common denominator. 6/35 cannot be simplified (HCF of 6 and 35 is 1). Common mistake: 3/5 x 2/7 = 6/7 (keeping one denominator, as if adding).

The bus from the district town to Karanpura was packed, and Lalit, twenty-four, the village's computer operator, noticed a young woman standing near the door with two suitcases, swaying at every bump. She was reading a paper with the panchayat office's address, frowning at the Hindi. He stood and offered his seat. "New here?" he asked. She nodded. "Ankita. I'm the new schoolteacher. From Kolkata." Her Hindi was slow, careful.
At the stop, he carried one suitcase to the panchayat office and introduced her to the sarpanch, who asked her questions in thick Haryanvi. Lalit translated gently. She needed a residence form for the teacher's quarters; he sat with her at the bench outside and filled it. The chaiwala sent two cups over on the house. Ankita smiled for the first time. "I thought I'd be lost for weeks," she said. Lalit grinned. "Maybe just days."

What job had Ankita come to Karanpura for?
She was the new schoolteacher.
What was Lalit feeling when he noticed Ankita swaying near the door?
He felt concerned and kind, noticing she was struggling with her suitcases and the address.
Which of Lalit's small welcomes mattered most, and why?
Translating for the sarpanch and filling the residence form, because they removed the biggest barriers for a newcomer with little local language.
How might Ankita see Karanpura after her first day?
She probably feels relieved and more at home than she expected, thanks to Lalit's help and the chaiwala's kindness.

Aparna, your cousin is shouting at the TV again, calling the other team cheats for the same tackle his team made. He reminds me of my brother Gopal. At our school in Madurai there were four houses, and Gopal was Green House, heart and soul. On sports day, when a Green runner stepped over the line, Gopal shouted, "Accident! The chalk was faded!" Ten minutes later a Blue boy did the same, and Gopal was on his feet: "Cheating! Disqualify him!" I was in Blue, so we fought all the way home. Amma laughed and said, "Same line, same feet, Gopal." He's seventy now. Last month, on the phone, he admitted Green was probably the worst house for rules. Your Rukmini Paati still remembers that faded chalk.

Which house was Gopal in?
Gopal was Green House, heart and soul.
Why did Gopal call it an accident for Green but cheating for Blue?
He loved Green House so much that belonging bent his fairness; his own side's foul felt excusable and the other side's felt wicked.
What could Aparna say to the cousin who is shouting at the TV?
Aparna could borrow Amma's line and ask, 'Same tackle, same feet?' to help him see he judges the two teams differently.
How did young Rukmini, in Blue House, experience Gopal's shouting?
Rukmini felt her house was treated unfairly, so they fought all the way home, though now it is a fond memory. 🙂

Nikita landed in Pune after six years in Toronto, and her suitcase did not. The airline said tomorrow. Outside, monsoon rain hammered the taxi rank, drivers shouted prices in Marathi that Nikita understood but answered slowly, and the phone was almost dead. Cousin Kalyani finally found Nikita under the shed. "You look lost," Kalyani said, laughing gently. Nikita's eyes stung. The city had rebuilt itself, and the road to the old school now had a metro pillar in the middle. Even Nikita's own jokes sounded odd in this air. "I don't know who I am here," Nikita said in the car. Kalyani answered, "You're the one who ate all the mango pickle, remember? Give it a week. You'll get the auto rates back." Nikita smiled at the windshield.

What did the airline say about the suitcase?
The airline said tomorrow.
What was Nikita feeling in the car, and what shows it?
Lost and out of step; Nikita's eyes stung and Nikita said not knowing who Nikita is here.
What small step could help Nikita fit in again?
Give it a week, relearn the auto rates and let familiar things like the mango pickle return.
How might Kalyani see Nikita?
As a familiar cousin beneath the changes who needs time; Kalyani laughed gently and recalled the mango pickle.

I'm Leela and I'm ten. Last summer at my Nani's village I nearly died of boredom. There was nothing new. Same mango tree, same well, same cows. So I made up games. I tried climbing to the top branch of the mango tree. I tried jumping over the stream at its widest point. My cousin Rehana said I was mad. "Why can't you just sit and play carrom?" "Carrom is boring! I want to feel my heart go boom!" When I fell in the stream, Nani pulled me out and said, "At least tell me before your next adventure." So I did. The next one was riding the bullock cart with the farmer, holding the rope, with Nani waving. Best day of the whole summer.

What does Leela do to cure her boredom, and what does Nani ask of her?

She makes up daring games, like climbing the top mango branch and jumping the stream. After she falls in the stream, Nani asks her to tell her before the next adventure, and the next one is riding the bullock cart.
Four runners ran a combined total of 195 miles last week. Katarina ran 51 miles. Tomas, Tyler, and Harriet all ran the same distance. How many miles did Harriet run?

195 - 51 = 144 = miles the 3 runners ran
144/3 = 48 miles
Harriet ran 48 miles.
The answer is 48.
Marly has ten $20 bills, eight $10 bills, and four $5 bills. If she wants to change her bills to $100 bills, how many pieces of $100 bills will she have?

The ten $20 bills amount to $20 x 10 = $200.
The eight $10 bills amount to $10 x 8 = $80.
The four $5 bills amount to $5 x 4 = $20.
So, Marly has a total of $200 + $80 + $20 = $300.
Therefore, she will have $300/$100 = 3 pieces of $100 bills
The answer is 3.

Sunday. The day after Dadi's funeral, Swati went back to her hostel in Jaipur. Everyone at the ceremony had cried. She hadn't. She ate lunch, did her readings, felt nothing at all, like a glass wall between her and everything.

The following Saturday. Still nothing. She lay awake wondering what was wrong with her. Did she even love Dadi? She told Neelam over chai, whispering, as if confessing a crime. Neelam said, "My cousin felt nothing for a month after her dad. It's like the mind puts a blanket over it. Keep going to class. Keep eating. If it doesn't lift, the counsellor's good."

Three weeks later. In the market Swati smelled roasted peanuts, the kind Dadi bought her every winter, and her knees went weak. She cried right there by the stall, for a long time. It felt terrible. It also felt like Dadi was back.

What smell made Swati cry in the market?
The smell of roasted peanuts, the kind Dadi bought her every winter.
What was Swati worried about during the numb week?
Swati was anxious that something was wrong with her and afraid it meant she didn't love Dadi.
What advice did Neelam give, and why does it help?
Keep going to class, keep eating, and see the counsellor if it doesn't lift, because numbness often protects people for a while.
How does Neelam see Swati's numbness?
Neelam sees it as a common way the mind protects itself after a loss, not as a sign Swati doesn't care.

At the colony's monthly meeting, Dhruv had already decided which way Vidya from the far block would vote. She always objected, he thought. Then he caught himself and asked her outright, “What worries you about the parking plan?” Vidya blinked. “The lane behind B block floods. Nobody has asked us.” It was a fair point he had missed.

Later, three men near the tea table joked about the security guards, mimicking how they speak. Someone laughed. Dhruv put his cup down. “They've watched over our children's cycles for years. Could we not?” One man shrugged, another looked at his shoes, and the laughing stopped.

Dhruv still walked home with his own block friends, chatting as usual. He just no longer needed them to be the only ones who mattered.

What did Vidya say worries her about the parking plan?
Vidya said the lane behind B block floods and nobody has asked the far block.
Why did Dhruv ask Vidya outright about the parking plan?
Dhruv felt uneasy on catching himself assuming Vidya would object, and was curious to hear Vidya's real reasons instead of guessing.
What did Dhruv do when the joking about the guards began, and what happened next?
Dhruv put his cup down and asked them to stop, mentioning the guards' years of watching over the children's cycles, and the laughing stopped.
How might one of the guards feel if they had overheard the meeting that evening?
They might feel relieved and quietly respected that someone in the group spoke up on their behalf, though the mocking would still sting.

"Did you see it, Vikas? The grocery giant's new pickle box. Same jars, same subscription, same regional recipes. Half our price."
"I saw it at six this morning. I've been angry since."
"Kalyani, they're a massive grocery company. They copied our whole idea."

A large decorative globe is a sphere of radius 21 cm. Find its surface area and volume. (pi = 22/7)

Answer: SA = 5544 cm^2; V = 38,808 cm^3.

SA = 4pir^2 = 4 x 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 4 x 22 x 3 x 21 = 5544 cm^2. V = 4/3 x pir^3 = 4/3 x 22/7 x 21 x 21 x 21 = 38,808 cm^3 (cancel: 21 / 7 = 3 and 21 / 3 = 7, then 4 x 22 x 3 x 7 x 21 = 38,808). Archimedes showed the surface of a sphere is exactly 4 times the area of its great circle (pir^2). In terms of pi, a ball of radius 3 has SA = 4 x pi x 9 = 36pi and V = 4/3 x pi x 27 = 36pi - the same number, but different units (cm^2 and cm^3). Common mistake: 4/3 x pir^2 (mixing the formulas).

'Nice man. But double-check everything he signs. Twice.'
'Has he done something wrong?'
'Not big. Small things. A missed dose chart, a late handover. Everyone knows.'
'That's... a lot to know about someone I've never seen.'
'Welcome to the hospital. By next month, people will be saying things about you too.'
'Like what?'
'Like whether you finish your notes before handover. Whether you answer the ward phone.'
Lavanya looked down at her clipboard, at the notes she hadn't finished yet. 'Okay. Then I'd better finish these.'
Sarika laughed. 'See? You're learning faster than Rao.'

Whose night shifts does Sarika tell Lavanya to take?
Sarika tells her to take Dr Menon's night shifts because she actually explains.
What did Lavanya realise when she looked at her unfinished notes?
She realised that people would soon judge her by small things like finishing notes before handover, just as they judged Dr Rao.
What choice did Lavanya make after the conversation, and why does it matter?
She decided to finish her notes, because small, consistent habits like that are what the ward will remember and pass on about her.
How might Dr Rao feel if he knew what interns were told about him?
He might feel upset or unfairly labelled, since his reputation came from small slips and was spread before new interns ever met him.

Read this:

At the government degree college in the district town, Avni noticed the lines being drawn within a month.
The students from the city, who'd come because they missed cut-offs elsewhere, sat together at the canteen. They spoke English, carried the latest phones and talked about weekend trips. The village students, Simran among them, came by bus, spoke Hindi, and went home straight after class.
In group projects, the city students took the leading roles. Teachers smiled more at their questions. At the college fest, the city group ran the stage.
Nobody said anyone was better. Nobody needed to. Avni, who was somewhere in between, watched Simran answer a hard question perfectly in Hindi one morning, while a city boy smirked and looked at his phone.

How did the village students come to college?
They came by bus.
How did Avni seem to feel watching the city boy smirk?
Avni seemed uncomfortable and unsettled, noticing how status markers were quietly sorting people.
What could Avni do to cross the lines she has noticed?
She could sit with Simran's group, pair with village students in projects, and praise good answers in any language.
How might Simran feel when a good answer met a smirk?
Simran might feel hurt and discouraged, having answered well but still being looked down on.

metadata.subtype: Hierarchies by college, city and money [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Ramesh,
You asked why I've gone quiet on our group chat. Honestly, work has eaten the evenings. Nobody ever told me to reply at night. It started with the team lead sending a message at eleven, "no rush", and someone answering in two minutes. Then everyone did. Then the Sunday messages began, always friendly, always "when you get a chance".
Now I sleep with the phone under my pillow. I check it before brushing my teeth. Last Saturday I was at my niece's birthday and answered four messages during the cake.
The strange part is that I used to love this job. I read design blogs for fun. I haven't opened one since June. I feel tired in a way weekends don't fix.
I'm thinking of setting my status to "offline after 8" and seeing who objects. Tell me if that sounds mad.
Kavitha

When did the team lead send the first late message?
At eleven, saying "no rush".
How does Kavitha feel about the job now compared with before?
Kavitha feels worn out and has lost interest, having once loved the job and read design blogs for fun but not opened one since June.
What small step is Kavitha considering, and what might help it work?
Setting a status of "offline after 8"; saying so openly to the team and sticking to it would bring the unspoken rule into the open.
What would change if the team lead said clearly that night messages can wait till morning?
The unspoken pressure to answer in two minutes might ease, and people like Kavitha could rest without the phone under the pillow.

Read this:

Friday

Worst day ever.

Everyone was looking at me and giggling. At lunch Meenu told me: they're saying I copied my science project from the internet.

I did NOT. My Nani helped me cut the pictures, that's all, and I wrote everything myself. But I did look at one website for the volcano picture. So it's half true and half a lie and I don't even know how to explain it.

I felt hot and small. I wanted to hide under the bench, then to shout at all of them.

After school I told Omkar bhaiya, and he took me straight to Mummy. Mummy listened to everything and said, "You are not in trouble. We'll show Ma'am your notebook tomorrow, and I'm calling her tonight."

She did. I feel a tiny bit better.

— Ritu

Who helped Ritu cut the pictures for the project?
Her Nani.
Why is Ritu so confused as well as upset?
The rumour is half true, because Ritu did look at one website for a picture, so she feels ashamed and angry but doesn't know how to explain it.
How did Omkar bhaiya and Mummy respond, and why did it help?
Omkar took Ritu straight to Mummy, who listened, said Ritu was not in trouble, and called the teacher that night, so Ritu wasn't alone.
How might Meenu have felt telling Ritu at lunch?
She may have felt awkward but wanted to warn Ritu about what people were saying.

Read this:

"Sabina, can you do me a favour?" Sunaina held out her phone.
"You're giving me your phone? Are you okay?"
"The history test is Thursday. Every time the game pings, I go 'one quick round' and it's midnight."
"Just don't open it."
"I tried. I tried so hard last week. Sat there with the phone face-down, and I still flipped it every two minutes."
Sabina laughed. "So what's the plan?"
"I've muted all the game stuff. Now you keep it in your bag till we finish chapter six. You're my locker."
"And if you ask for it?"
"Say no. Say it rudely if you want."
"Deal." Sabina zipped the bag. "What are you going to do with your hands now?"
Sunaina opened her notebook. "Write dates. Loads of dates." 🙂

What did Sunaina ask Sabina to do with her phone?
She asked Sabina to keep it in her bag till they finish chapter six.
How did Sunaina feel last week when she tried just not opening the game?
She felt frustrated and defeated, because even with the phone face-down she kept flipping it every two minutes.
What makes Sunaina's new plan stronger than trying harder?
Muting the game and putting the phone in Sabina's bag removes the temptation from reach, instead of relying on willpower each time it pings.
If you were Sabina, what would you want Sunaina to know?
You would want her to know you are happy to help and that asking for the phone back will get a friendly but firm no.

Frank goes to the store to buy some food. He buys 5 chocolate bars and 2 bags of chips. He hands the cashier $20 and gets $4 back as change. If the chocolate bars each cost $2, how much did each bag of chips cost?

His entire purchase cost $20 - $4 = $16.
The chocolate bars cost 5 * $2 = $10.
The bags of chips cost a total of $16 - $10 = $6.
Each bag of chips cost $6 / 2 = $3.
The answer is 3.

Read this:

To the Internal Committee, Department of Physics
I am reporting behaviour by my project guide, Dr. Gautam Sinha, that has made me afraid to attend meetings.
Since August he has commented on my clothes in almost every meeting ("That colour suits you, you should wear it more often for me"). On 12 September and again on 3 October he kept his hand on my back while reading my screen, though I moved away both times. On 3 October I said clearly, "Please don't touch me." He laughed.
I wrote down each date and his words the same day. The notes are attached. My friend Shruti was present on 12 September.
I wondered whether I was overreacting. I'm not. Please act, and assign me a different guide meanwhile.
Kiran Kumari, MSc Physics, second year
Reply, same evening, 6:40 p.m.: Thank you, Kiran. This is not your fault. A committee member will meet you tomorrow at 10 a.m.; you need not attend meetings with Dr. Sinha meanwhile.

On which dates did Dr. Sinha put his hand on Kiran's back?
On 12 September and 3 October.
How has Dr. Sinha's behaviour made Kiran feel?
Afraid to attend meetings, and at times doubting whether she was overreacting.
What made Kiran's report strong?
Notes written the same day with dates and his exact words, a named witness, and a clear request for action and a different guide.
How does the committee respond?
The same evening it says this is not her fault, sets a meeting for the next morning, and spares her any meetings with Dr. Sinha meanwhile.

Kishore wrote his two rules on the inside of his study-table drawer in their Chandigarh flat, where no one else would see them.
If I sit down to study, the phone goes to the shoe rack by the door.
If it's after ten, the phone sleeps on the hall charger.
The first evening he forgot rule one and found himself twenty minutes into a video with his physics book open. He got up, walked the phone to the shoe rack and came back. The second evening he did it without much thought. By the second week he didn't have to decide at all; sitting down meant the phone went.
His friend Baljeet noticed on Saturday. “You've been replying late.”
“It's on the hall charger after ten,” Kishore said. “Rule.”
“Your rule or your parents'?”
“Mine. That's why it works.”
His test marks that month rose only a little. But he was asleep before eleven most nights.

Where does Kishore's phone go when he sits down to study?
To the shoe rack by the door.
How does Kishore seem to feel about the rules by the second week?
He seems relieved and confident, since the rules had become automatic and no longer needed a decision.
What else could Kishore add if the phone still pulls at the study table?
Keep a clock or timer on the desk, so there is no reason to fetch the phone to check the time.
How do the rules look to Baljeet?
Baljeet first notices only the late replies, then learns the rules are Kishore's own, which may make them seem worth copying.
