Friday

Today in PT, Tejas tripped over a cone and everyone laughed, and I shouted, "Tejas the Tortoise!" Then I did the tortoise walk all the way back to class. The whole row was laughing. It was just a joke. Everyone jokes.

At lunch Tejas sat alone. I told Meenu, "He can't even take a joke."

But then Mr D'Souza called me after lunch. He said Tejas had told him he didn't want to come to school on PT days because of the "tortoise" thing. For three weeks. I didn't know it was three weeks. They were just jokes. Weren't they?

Mr D'Souza said, "If only one person isn't laughing, it isn't a joke." He's calling Mummy tonight. I have to say sorry to Tejas on Monday.

I don't feel funny now.

Vasudha

What did Vasudha shout when Tejas tripped?
Vasudha shouted, "Tejas the Tortoise!"
Why did Vasudha keep calling the teasing a joke?
Vasudha felt it was harmless fun, and the word "joke" hid how much it was hurting Tejas and made it feel less like a choice.
What did Mr D'Souza do that same day?
He told Vasudha how Tejas felt, said it isn't a joke if one person isn't laughing, called Mummy, and asked for an apology on Monday.
How has Tejas felt about PT days?
Tejas has felt so hurt and humiliated that he didn't want to come to school on PT days for three weeks.

Read this:

Sit, Bhavna, the iftar can wait five minutes. You say you're "fine" with that course. I said "fine" once too. I was nineteen, and every winter morning I took the same bus to a typing institute above a sweet shop. The machines jammed, the teacher dozed, and I learned almost nothing. My friend Salim told me about a new computer class across town, better taught, same fees. I said I was happy where I was. Happy! The truth is that switching meant a new form, a new bus, new faces, and my blanket was warm. Salim went. Two years later he was teaching others, and I was still fixing jammed ribbons. That is Imran uncle's great lesson, beta, learned the slow way. Now tell me again how "fine" you are.

Where was the typing institute?
Above a sweet shop.
Why did young Imran say he was happy at the typing institute?
Switching meant a new form, a new bus and new faces, so staying felt comfortable and easy; calling it happiness hid how reluctant he was to make the effort.
What choice in the story could young Imran have made differently?
When Salim told him about the better computer class, he could have visited it once and compared, instead of letting the effort of switching decide for him.
How did things turn out for Salim, who switched?
Salim learned well enough to be teaching others two years later, which shows what staying put cost Imran.
Sandi had $600. She spent half of it at a farmer's market. Gillian spent $150 more than three times Sandi's total. What is the total that Gillian spent at the farmer's market?

Sandi spent 600/2 = 300 dollars at the farmer's market.
Gillian spent 300*3+150 = 1050 dollars at the farmer's market.
The answer is 1050.

Read this:

Sachin, sit here, kanna. You asked why I told you to say no to your friend. When your Paati was a girl in our lane in Madurai, my friend Leela and I did everything together. Every week she said, "Ganga, give me your two annas, we are best friends, I'll return it." She never did. I felt cheated, yet I was afraid she would stop playing with me. One day my tin box was empty and I cried behind the well. My Appa found me there, and I told him everything. He did not scold. He said, "A real friend can hear a no." The next time Leela asked, I said, "Not this week, Leela," in my politest voice. She sulked for two days. Then she came back with her hopscotch stone as if nothing had happened.

Where did young Ganga cry when her tin box was empty?
Behind the well.
Why was young Ganga afraid to refuse Leela?
She felt cheated by the unpaid loans but was scared that Leela would stop playing with her.
Which choice in Paati's story changed things, and why did it work?
Telling her Appa and then giving Leela a polite "not this week"; it stopped the lending without a fight.
How might Leela have felt when Ganga said no?
Leela was probably surprised and annoyed, since she sulked for two days, but she came back to play, so the friendship still mattered to her.

Read this:

The notice board at the girls' school in Rampur said the Annual Function would be in six weeks. Himani had been chosen to play the harmonium for the welcome song. Walking home past the mustard fields with her friend Anjali, she thought it through out loud. "The last week is for playing it in front of people. The week before that, too. So it has to be ready by the end of week four." She counted on her fingers. "Three verses and the chorus. Four weeks. One each week." Anjali said, "What if one verse is hard?" Himani thought. "Then I do the hard one first, while there's time." That evening she wrote the weeks inside her notebook cover, with the third verse next to week one.

What did Himani write inside her notebook cover?
The weeks, with the third verse next to week one.
What was Himani thinking on the walk home?
She felt calm and determined, working backward from the function to fix what each week needed.
What else could help Himani in the last two weeks?
Playing for her family or Anjali each evening, so an audience feels normal by the function.
How might Anjali see the plan?
Anjali raised a real worry and saw Himani adjust for it, so Anjali may feel part of the plan.

metadata.subtype: Approach: setting a goal for a school concert [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Amara sat in her car outside the clinic in Nairobi for ten minutes before going in. For weeks she had been waking at four with her mind racing about work, then dragging through the day. Rafael, a colleague, had said gently, "Maybe talk to someone?" She had read symptom pages online, and every page gave a different explanation. She closed the tabs and booked an appointment instead. Inside, the doctor asked questions and listened, named nothing on the first day, and suggested a follow-up with a counsellor. Amara wrote down what was said and booked the second appointment at the desk. On the drive home she felt something like relief: unsure, but not alone. At a red light she texted Rafael: "I went."

Where did Amara wait before going in to the appointment?
She waited in her car outside the clinic in Nairobi.
What was Amara feeling on the drive home?
Amara felt relieved, unsure of what comes next but no longer alone.
What could Amara do if the guidance feels hard to follow?
Amara could tell the doctor or counsellor at the next appointment and ask for changes, rather than guessing or dropping it.
How might Rafael have felt when the text arrived?
Rafael may have felt glad and relieved that the gentle suggestion had been taken up.

Read this:

"Karthik, what if the moon just disappeared?"
"Lavanya, it's eleven at night."
"No, think. What happens?"
Karthik sighed and rolled onto his back. "Okay. No moonlight. Darker nights."
"And the tides! The moon pulls the sea. So no big tides."
"Then the fishermen at Kovalam would have a different schedule."
"And some sea animals that time things by the moon would get confused."
"Would the days get longer?"
Lavanya frowned, twisting her hair. "I think the moon slows the earth's spin a bit. So without it... maybe faster days, over a long time? I'm not sure."
"You've ruined my sleep," Karthik said.
"Admit it, it's interesting."
"Fine. It's interesting."

What time was it when Lavanya asked her question?
Eleven at night.
How did Karthik's feelings about the question change?
He was annoyed and tired at first, then curious and grudgingly interested.
What could they do to check the ideas they weren't sure about?
They could look up the moon's effect on tides and the earth's spin in a science book or ask a teacher.
How might Lavanya feel when Karthik admits it's interesting?
She would likely feel pleased and satisfied to have drawn him into the question.
Why does the hungry jackal stop fearing the loud sound in the forest?
He finds it is only a war-drum that booms when grasses sway against it. He even creeps inside hoping for fat, but finds only wood and skin.
I like to wonder around the old market on Sunday mornings. Which word is wrong?

I like to wander around the old market on Sunday mornings.
Why: "Wander" means walk around; "wonder" means think.
I finished a long novel and now I don't know what to read next.
That gap after a good book is a real feeling. What did you like most about the one you finished?
The adventure, and that the main character was a girl who solved problems herself.

Then look for adventure stories with a clever young heroine. Ask your librarian for one, since librarians enjoy this kind of request. You could also try a short book next, as a gentle break before another long one.

Read this:

"Redo this. Before six, please." Ishita dropped the printed report on Parveen's desk, two tables circled in red, and was already walking to the lift with her laptop bag, phone at her ear. It was 4:10. Parveen stared at the circles. Were the numbers wrong, or only the layout? The single note in the margin said "no". Her chest tightened. Three weeks into the internship, this was the first real task anyone had trusted her with. She opened a chat to Ishita, typed "Sorry, could you tell me what", then deleted it. Maybe Ishita was rushing to a meeting. Maybe she thought the whole thing was hopeless. The office printer jammed twice while Parveen reprinted the old draft, and the clock kept moving. She rebuilt both tables from scratch, guessing at every line.

What time was the report due, and when did Ishita hand it back?
It was due before six, and it was 4:10 when Ishita dropped the report on Parveen's desk.
Why did Parveen delete the message she had started typing?
She felt anxious and afraid to ask, unsure whether Ishita was just busy or thought the work was hopeless, so asking felt risky.
What small step would help Parveen right now?
She could send one short, specific question, such as whether the problem is the numbers or the layout, so she stops guessing.
How might Ishita see this moment?
Ishita may simply be rushing to a call and think the red circles are clear enough, not realising Parveen reads them as harsh criticism.

Read this:

Urmila had sat at the back of the Class 8 maths room in the Pune school for two terms, head down, handing in half-empty worksheets.
Amandeep Sir had noticed something. On the latest algebra sheet, she had got question 3 fully right, and in question 5 she had set up the equation correctly before getting lost.
After class he put the sheet in front of her. “Look at number 5. You wrote x plus 7 equals 19. That's exactly the hard part. Most people get stuck before that.”
Urmila frowned at the page as if it were someone else's.
“Tomorrow,” he said, “I'm giving you three problems like number 5. Not ten. Three. I think you'll get at least two.”
She got two. The next week she moved one bench forward.

Which equation had Urmila set up correctly in question 5?
She had written x plus 7 equals 19.
What might Amandeep Sir have felt when he noticed question 5?
He likely felt hopeful and encouraged, seeing a real step of progress in a student who usually gave up.
What made Amandeep Sir's approach work?
He pointed to the exact part she did well and gave three similar problems, hard but doable, so she could see herself succeed.
How does Urmila's view of herself change, and what shows it?
She begins to see herself as someone who can do maths, and moving one bench forward shows her growing willingness.

Read this:

I'm Chandrika, and I'm not proud that it took me three weeks to see it. Madhuri used to sit with our group at lunch. Then one day she was on the bench by the library, alone, with her tiffin on her knees. In the group chat, people started making plans in a new group I later realised she wasn't in. I kept thinking it wasn't my business. Then I saw her laugh at something on her phone, alone, and stop, like she'd remembered where she was. The next day I sat down on the library bench, not saying why. "Can I share your shade?" She moved her bag. We talked about the library's terrible fans. Now I sit there twice a week. It was such a small thing. I should have done it sooner.

Where did Madhuri start sitting at lunch?
On the bench by the library.
What was Chandrika feeling when Chandrika finally sat down?
Chandrika felt some regret for waiting three weeks, and quiet concern for Madhuri.
What made Chandrika's approach work?
It was small and quiet: sitting down and asking to share the shade without drawing attention to Madhuri's loneliness.
How might Madhuri feel when someone sits on the library bench?
Madhuri may feel relieved and less invisible, glad to be sought out without being pitied.

Read this:

Thursday
Diary, it's Bidisha. Today at recess I asked Ishani's group if I could sit with them, and Ishani said, 'Sorry, table's full,' even though there were two empty spaces. They all went quiet till I walked away. My whole chest hurt. I ate in the library. But Shreya was there too, drawing horses, and she pushed her sketchbook over and said, 'Help me with the legs?' We laughed at my wonky horse. She's joining the choir next week and asked me to come. Tonight I told Ma about the table. She didn't say 'just ignore them.' She hugged me and said she'd talk to my class teacher tomorrow morning. I still feel sad. But I also have a horse-drawing friend now.

Where did Bidisha eat after being turned away?
In the library.
How did Bidisha feel when Ishani said the table was full?
Deeply hurt and rejected; Bidisha's whole chest hurt.
What helped Bidisha after the rejection?
Finding Shreya, a kind classmate, planning to join the choir, and telling Ma, who hugged Bidisha and promised to talk to the class teacher.
How might Shreya see Bidisha turning up in the library?
As welcome company; she shared her sketchbook and invited Bidisha to choir 🙂

Read this:

Raghav, you think you're the first teenager in this family to doubt the fasts? Your Kalyani paati was worse. At fifteen I refused to fast on Ekadashi. I said, 'If God is love, why does love need hunger?' My mother cried, and my grandmother didn't speak to me for two days. I felt awful. I loved them, and I also couldn't pretend. Then my grandmother called me to the kitchen and said, 'Don't fast, then. But sit with me while I cook for the evening, and ask me your questions.' So every Ekadashi I sat there, asking and arguing, while she explained what her mother had told her. I still don't fast. But I know every story, and now I tell them to you.

On which day did young Kalyani refuse to fast?
On Ekadashi.
How did young Kalyani feel when the grandmother stopped speaking for two days?
She felt awful and torn, loving her family but unable to pretend to believe.
What choice in the story helped both sides?
The grandmother inviting Kalyani to sit and ask questions while she cooked, so Kalyani could stay close without pretending.
How might the grandmother have felt when young Kalyani refused?
She was likely hurt and worried at first, then chose to keep her granddaughter close through questions and stories.

Read this:

Dear Aparna didi,

You asked if I've chosen my stream for Class 11. I haven't. Science because I like biology? Commerce because Papa says it's practical? Arts because I love history? I keep waiting to wake up one morning and just know.

It's been since October. Now the form is due in two weeks, and the commerce seats at my school are already full. So I've lost one option by waiting. My stomach hurts every time Mummy asks.

Maybe there isn't a perfect sign. Maybe I just have to pick the one I'd be least sorry about. Can we talk on Sunday? I need to decide.

Lalit

Which option has Lalit already lost by waiting?
The commerce seats at the school are already full.
How does Lalit feel each time Mummy asks about the stream?
Lalit feels anxious, with a stomach ache, because the decision keeps being postponed.
What could help Lalit decide on Sunday?
Talking it through with Aparna didi and choosing the stream Lalit would be least sorry about, instead of waiting for certainty.
How might Aparna didi feel reading this letter?
Aparna didi might feel concerned but glad that Lalit is asking for help before the form is due.

Read this:

Hrithik, you have to hear this, because you'll do the same thing, I know you. So, I'm Asif, right, and on Friday I told everyone I'd finish the whole history syllabus over the long weekend. Three days, fourteen chapters. I had it all planned. Saturday: ancient. Sunday: medieval. Monday: modern plus revision. I even told my father to take the TV remote away. Saturday I did one and a half chapters. The Mauryan dates just would not stay in my head. Sunday there was a family lunch I'd completely forgotten. Monday I woke up at ten. I'd done four chapters. Four! And I was genuinely shocked, like somebody had stolen my time. But here's the thing: before the unit test I also planned five chapters a day, and I also did one. I just forgot.

How many chapters had Asif finished by Monday?
Four chapters.
What was Asif feeling on seeing only four chapters done?
Asif felt genuinely shocked and cheated, "like somebody had stolen my time," because the plan had seemed so realistic.
What could Asif do before planning the next revision weekend?
Look at how many chapters Asif really managed before the unit test and plan from that, leaving room for things like family lunches.
Why might Hrithik react differently to Asif's plan on hearing it on Friday?
Hrithik knows Asif well, so Hrithik might have doubted the fourteen-chapter plan from the start.

Condense this piece into two sentences.

"'"Samvarta said, 'Listen, O son of Avikshit, excellent as it is the bent of thy mind to perform this act, so too, O king, have I in my mind the ability to perform the sacrifice, I tell thee, O king, that thy good things will become imperishable, and that thou shalt lord it over Sakra and the Celestials with Gandharvas. For myself, I have no desire to amass wealth or sacrificial presents, I shall only do what is disagreeable to both Indra and my brother, I shall certainly make thee attain equality with Sakra, and I tell thee truly that I shall do what is agreeable to thee.'"'"

Samvarta tells the king, the son of Avikshit, that Samvarta can perform the sacrifice and will make the king equal to Sakra, who is Indra. Samvarta wants no wealth or gifts, and will do what pleases the king even if it displeases Indra.
Describe a frog in under twelve words and use the word "pond".
A green frog sits on a lily pad in the pond.

Read this:

March. Bhupen told his parents he had extra lab classes on Wednesday evenings. Really, he was rehearsing with a theatre group in town. His parents were proud of him, and he loved them. But the one time he mentioned acting, his father had gone silent for three days.
May. At a family dinner, his mother told relatives, "Bhupen will be an engineer like his father." Bhupen smiled and nodded. Under the table, his hand was shaking. He felt like an actor at home too.
July. He couldn't sleep. He called his Tushar Mama, his mother's brother, who everyone in the family respected. "Mama, I think I'm living a lie for them. I'm scared to lose them."
Tushar Mama listened for an hour. Then he said, "You're not a bad son for wanting a say. Let me come on Sunday. We'll talk to your parents together."

What did Bhupen tell his parents he had on Wednesday evenings?
Extra lab classes.
How did Bhupen feel at the family dinner in May?
Bhupen felt anxious and trapped, his hand shaking while he smiled and nodded to please his family.
Who did Bhupen turn to, and why was that wise?
He called Tushar Mama, a respected elder, who listened and offered to help talk to his parents on Sunday.
How might Bhupen's parents feel if they learned the truth?
They might feel hurt at first, but also sad that their son felt he had to hide from them.

Read this:

Dear Arnab,
Captaincy is AMAZING. You were right to recommend me. I've already changed everything on the basketball team. Practice is now at 6 am, because I'm fastest in the mornings. I've moved Riddhi to the bench; she argues too much. When Neelima said the 6 am slot is hard for players who take the bus from far away, I told her real players adjust. Coach Sharma says I'm very decisive. The juniors run when I blow the whistle. It's a nice feeling, people doing what you say. Some of them are sulking, but that's their problem. Honestly, I don't remember you having this much trouble with the team. Maybe they just like me less? Anyway, come and watch Saturday's match. We'll win.
Tanuja

What time is practice now?
6 am.
How does Tanuja feel about people doing what the captain says?
Tanuja feels proud and pleased, enjoying being obeyed.
What could Tanuja do to lead better?
Listen to complaints like Neelima's about the bus, set practice times that work for the team, and welcome Riddhi's arguments instead of benching her.
How might Neelima feel being told 'real players adjust'?
Neelima probably feels dismissed and frustrated, since her concern for players who take the bus was ignored.

Read this:

In her third week of clinical posting, Deepika's favourite patient on Ward 4, an old man who called her "doctor-ji" however often she corrected him, died in the night. The next afternoon, in the nursing college library, she read his chart notes twice and traced the fall in his oxygen levels against the sepsis chapter in her textbook. She could see where it had turned.
Her clinical instructor, Farida Ma'am, found her there. "Understanding it is good nursing," Farida said. "And the rest?"
Deepika hesitated. "After evening class I'll sit in the prayer room for half an hour. Just to miss him."
That evening she sat there with her notebook closed and cried quietly for the man who used to hum old film songs while she changed his dressings. Afterwards she felt tired, and lighter, and ready for the next shift.

What did the old man on Ward 4 call Deepika?
"Doctor-ji", however often she corrected him.
Why did tracing the oxygen levels against the sepsis chapter feel useful to Deepika?
It showed her where his illness turned, so the death made sense and she could learn from it as a nurse.
Which choice helped Deepika's understanding lead toward her feelings?
Setting aside half an hour in the prayer room with her notebook closed, so she could miss him instead of only studying his chart.
How does Farida Ma'am seem to see Deepika's study in the library?
She values it as good nursing but gently asks about 'the rest', showing she knows understanding a death is not the same as grieving it.

metadata.subtype: Letting thinking and feeling share the table [Response]

messages.content: Why is it sometimes hard to say no to a friend?
Fear of letting a friend down makes saying no hard. Because we value the friendship and worry that a refusal might upset them or spoil the bond, we may agree even when we do not want to.

Read this:

Monday: Jeevan pushed the wooden stool across the floor, grunting, "Hnnh! Hnnh!" Preeti echoed, "Hnnh! Heavy!" He grinned and pushed harder.
Wednesday, after the park: he flopped onto the rug with a long sigh. "Phew," said Preeti softly. "Tired."
Saturday, in the bath: he splashed and babbled, "Ba-da-ba-da." Preeti babbled back. He stopped, stared, then babbled longer, louder.

What did Jeevan push on Monday?
The wooden stool.
What was Jeevan feeling during each of his sounds?
The grunts showed effort, the long sigh showed he was tired after the park, and the bath babble showed he was content and happy.
What habit of Preeti's supports Jeevan's language?
She echoes his sounds warmly and adds a word, like "Heavy!" or "Tired", so he hears language linked to his feelings.
How might Preeti feel when Jeevan babbles back longer and louder?
She would likely feel delighted, sensing a real conversation starting. 😊

Read this:

Rashmi: yash cricket nets tomorrow?
Yash: can't, helping my dad at the shop
Rashmi: you always have something
Yash: it's one saturday
Rashmi: a real friend would just be free
Yash: that's not fair
Rashmi: whatever. my parents are the same. they should know i hate tuition on sundays but nope
Yash: did you tell them?
Rashmi: i shouldn't have to tell them
Yash: ok but how would they know
Rashmi: they're my parents 😠
Yash: rashmi i'm not your parents. i'm just at the shop
Rashmi: fine
Yash: sunday evening? after your tuition?
Rashmi: seen
[Sunday, 7:10 p.m.]
Yash: still on?
Rashmi: ok. sorry for saturday. i was angry at everyone
Yash: noticed 😅 nets at 7:30

Why couldn't Yash come to cricket nets on Saturday?
Yash was helping Yash's dad at the shop.
Why does Rashmi insist "I shouldn't have to tell them"?
Rashmi feels that people who care should understand without being told, so explaining feels like proof they don't care enough. That rule turns small letdowns into resentment.
What went wrong in the chat, and what helped fix it?
Rashmi judged Yash by a rule that friends should always be free, which led to an unfair jab. Yash's calm offer of Sunday evening, and Rashmi's apology, turned it back into a plan.
How might Yash feel being told a real friend would just be free?
Yash probably felt hurt and unfairly judged, since helping at the shop wasn't a choice against Rashmi. Yash still offered another time, which shows patience.
My British aunt said she will go to the "surgery". Is she having an operation?

Not necessarily. In British English "surgery" can also mean the place where a doctor or dentist sees patients. American English says "doctor's office".
Examples: The surgery opens at nine. The doctor's office opens at nine.

Read this:

You asked what finally worked for us. I'm Deepak, and Manoj and I have been together three years now.
The old pattern was: he comes home drained from the hospital, I want to talk, he goes quiet, I push, he goes quieter.
So we made two rules. First, Thursday evening is ours. No phones, we cook together, however busy the week is. I know it's coming, so I don't have to chase.
Second, Manoj can say, "I'm spent. Give me an hour, then I'm yours." And he means it. He lies down, listens to music, and after an hour he comes and finds me.
I stopped feeling ignored. He stopped feeling guilty. That's it. It's simple, but it saved us.

Which evening did Deepak and Manoj set aside?
Thursday evening.
What was Deepak feeling once the new rules were in place?
He stopped feeling ignored and felt secure, because he knew when their time was coming and didn't have to chase.
Why did the "give me an hour" sentence help?
It gave Manoj a clear, honest way to ask for space without guilt and a promise to return, so Deepak didn't read the quiet as rejection.
What is Manoj experiencing now when he comes home drained?
He can rest without feeling guilty, knowing that asking for an hour is accepted and that he will return to Deepak.

metadata.subtype: Stage 6: Scheduled closeness and honest limits [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Avni, twenty, found out on a Sunday morning: her four closest college friends had gone to a birthday dinner in Koregaon Park, and she hadn't been invited. The photos were everywhere. She sat on the edge of her bed and let herself cry. "This hurts," she wrote in her journal. "It doesn't mean I'm broken." That week she messaged Manoj from her NSS unit, who always saved her a seat at the tree-planting drives. "Chai after the drive on Saturday?" He replied with a thumbs-up. They talked for two hours about their villages and bad hostel food. She joined his Sunday reading group too. When one of the old group asked her for notes later, Avni thought about saying no, as they had to her. She sent them anyway.

Where did Avni's friends go for the birthday dinner?
They went to a birthday dinner in Koregaon Park.
How did Avni feel when she found out, and how did she see herself?
She was deeply hurt and cried, but told herself the hurt did not mean she was broken.
What choice did Avni make when her old friend asked for notes, and why does it matter?
She sent the notes anyway instead of excluding them back, which kept her from becoming like the people who hurt her.
How might Manoj see Avni's message about chai?
Manoj would likely be pleased to be asked, since he already saved her a seat, and glad to spend time with her.
In civics we read about individuals and groups. What is an individual?

An individual is one single person, thought of apart from a group. It is a noun, with the plural Individuals. It can also describe a person with a very personal way of doing things.
Example: The club was made up of ten individuals, and each had a different hobby.

Read this:

Week one: Lalremsiami, fifteen, kept a sleep diary for her health project. Weekdays: asleep at 1 a.m., up at 6. Weekends: asleep at 3, up at noon. Joseph, her project partner, laughed. “You're living in two time zones.”
Week three: She tried one change: same wake-up time every day, even Saturday, 7:30. She hated Saturday. She was yawning at the breakfast table and cranky with her brother.
Week six: Her diary showed she was falling asleep by 11:30 most nights without trying. She had stopped needing three alarms. In the project presentation, she showed the chart and said, “I thought I was a night person. Maybe I was just jet-lagged every Monday.”
Joseph got the class to clap.

What did Joseph say about Lalremsiami's sleep?
“You're living in two time zones.”
How did Lalremsiami feel about waking at 7:30 on Saturdays at first?
She hated it and felt cranky and sleepy.
What change helped Lalremsiami's sleep, and why?
Keeping the same wake-up time every day, which let her body clock settle.
How might Joseph feel about the project result?
He probably feels impressed and pleased that the diary showed such a clear change.

Read this:

Hemant,

I'm writing this because when I try to say it at night, we're both too tired.

Yesterday I heard you on the phone with that difficult supplier. You were so patient. You listened to him for forty minutes, you made a joke, you calmed him right down. I remember falling in love with that voice.

Then you came to bed and I asked how your day was, and you said, "Don't start." I know you didn't mean anything. I know you're exhausted.

But I've noticed it's like this most days. You give all your kindness out there, and by the time you get home, there's none left for us.

I'm not angry. I miss you. Could we try something, maybe a short walk before your last calls, or one evening a week with phones off?

Irawati

How long did Hemant listen to the supplier?
Forty minutes.
Why does Irawati say she's not angry but misses Hemant?
Irawati feels lonely rather than angry, seeing that Hemant's kindness is real but spent on work before he gets home.
Why is Irawati's suggestion a good one?
It offers small, practical changes, like a walk or a phones-off evening, that could save some of his energy for home.
How might Hemant feel reading this letter?
Hemant might feel touched and a little guilty, surprised by how much the tiredness shows at home.

metadata.subtype: Warm at work, cold at home [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Keerthana, you're angry. Good, you should be. But before you walk into that office tomorrow, let your Avni chithi tell you about the worst day of my first job.
I was twenty-one, at a trading company in Madurai. I found out a senior colleague was entering fake sales to earn a bonus. I was so angry my hands shook. And instead of taking the ledger to the owner, I stood in the middle of the office and shouted it at him, in front of everyone.
He shouted back. By evening half the office was on his side; they thought I was a young show-off. That night the pages I had marked in the ledger went missing. When the owner finally asked, I had nothing to show but my word.
I left three months later. He stayed two more years.

messages.content: A car moves at 72 km/h. What is this speed in metres per second?

Answer: 72 km/h = 72 x 5/18 m/s = 20 m/s.

1 km = 1,000 m and 1 h = 60 x 60 = 3,600 s. So 1 km/h = 1,000 m in 3,600 s = 1,000/3,600 m/s = 5/18 m/s. To change km/h into m/s, MULTIPLY BY 5/18: 72 x 5/18 = 72 / 18 x 5 = 4 x 5 = 20 m/s. Check the long way: 72 km/h means 72,000 m in 3,600 s, and 72,000 / 3,600 = 20, so 20 m each second. The numbers that divide nicely are multiples of 18: 18 km/h = 5 m/s, 36 km/h = 10 m/s, 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 90 km/h = 25 m/s.

Two gaming chairs cost $83 x 2 = $166
Leon's total orders amount to $234 + $166 = $400.

messages.content: Parker wants to find out what the average percentage of kernels that pop in a bag is. In the first bag he makes, 60 kernels pop and the bag has 75 kernels. In the second bag, 42 kernels pop and there are 50 in the bag. In the final bag, 82 kernels pop and the bag has 100 kernels.

In the first bag the proportion that pops is .8 because 60 / 75 = .8
In the second bag the proportion that pops is .84 because 42 / 50 = .84
In the third bag the proportion that pops is .82 because 82 / 100 = .82
The proportions totals 2.46 because .8 + . 84 + .82 = 2.46
The average proportion is .82 because 2.46 / 3 = .82
The average percentage is 82 because .82 x 100 = 82
The answer is 82.

At the agricultural college in Dharwad, Pranav got his field-work report back from Dr Minakshi. He flipped straight to the last page and saw it in red: "Soil sample labels inconsistent."

He didn't read anything else. All evening in the hostel he kept thinking: my report is bad. She thinks I'm careless. Maybe I'm not cut out for research.

The next morning his roommate picked up the report from the floor and read the margins aloud. "Thorough interviews with farmers." "Excellent photographs." "Very good analysis of rainfall." "One of the best in the batch."

"One of the best in the batch," the roommate repeated. "Did you even see that?"

Pranav hadn't. He had read the red line five times and nothing else. He fixed the labels that afternoon, in twenty minutes.

What did the red comment say?
The red comment said, "Soil sample labels inconsistent."
Why did Pranav think his report was bad?
Pranav felt stung and anxious about the red comment, and it filtered out all the praise, so a success felt like a failure.
What could Pranav do next time he gets feedback?
Read every comment first, perhaps listing the positives, before deciding what the feedback means.
How might Dr Minakshi see Pranav's report?
Dr Minakshi saw it as one of the best in the batch, with one small fix needed.

When Madhav and I started looking for a wedding venue last year, I did what I always do: I looked at everything. Thirty-one halls in three weeks. I'm Rashmi, and I once spent a whole weekend choosing a kettle, so this was dangerous.
By the third week I was exhausted and angry at every hall for not being perfect.
So I stopped and made rules. First, three criteria: room for two hundred guests, near the station for Madhav's grandparents, free in February. Second, a shortlist of three, no more. Third, the first hall that met all three and felt warm would be the one. No "but maybe there's something better".
The second hall on the shortlist had a mango tree in the courtyard. We booked it that afternoon.
It wasn't perfect. The parking was awful. But I loved it, and I never went back to the list.

How many halls did Rashmi look at in three weeks?
Rashmi looked at thirty-one halls in three weeks.
How did Rashmi feel by the third week?
Rashmi felt exhausted and angry at every hall for not being perfect.
What rules did Rashmi set, and why did they work?
Three criteria, a shortlist of three and choosing the first warm hall that met them, which ended the search for perfect.
How might Madhav's grandparents experience the chosen hall?
They would likely find it easy and comfortable, since being near the station was one of the three criteria.

Visiting hours in the hospital garden end at 7 pm. Please keep silence, so that patients can rest. Do not pluck the flowers. Please keep the paths clear for everyone who walks here. Thank you for your cooperation.
Aaron has four times as many cows as does Matthews. Together, they have 30 more cows than Marovich. If Matthews has 60 cows, how many cows do the three have altogether?

If Matthews has 60 cows, Aaron has 4*60 = 240 cows.
Together, Aaron and Matthews have 240+60 = 300 cows.
Since Marovich has 30 fewer cows than the combined number of cows that Aaron and Matthews have, Marovich has 300-30 = 270 cows.
Altogether, the three have 270+300 = 570 cows
The answer is 570.

Vaibhav, you're nervous about the new school, so let your Gurpreet Dadi tell you about a boy I taught, long ago. His name was Ronak. On his first day he came to my desk after the bell, very red in the face, and said, "Ma'am, I don't know where anything is. I got lost looking for the toilet." Most children never say that. They wander around feeling foolish. So I called Iqbal, the friendliest boy in my class, and said, "Ronak is your buddy this week. Show him the canteen, the library and the toilets." By lunch they were eating together. By Friday Ronak was showing another new child where the library was. It began because he asked.

What had Ronak got lost looking for?
He got lost looking for the toilet.
How was Ronak feeling when he came to the teacher's desk?
He was embarrassed and anxious, red in the face, but brave enough to ask.
What was the turning point in Ronak's first week, and what else could he have done?
The turning point was telling the teacher he felt lost; he could also have asked a classmate directly, but asking the teacher got him a buddy for the whole week.
How might Iqbal have seen being made Ronak's buddy?
Iqbal was probably proud to be trusted with the job and happy to have someone new to eat lunch with.

At the block office in Chhindwara district, the notice came by email at noon: the new primary health centre for Lalit's village had finally been approved. Disha watched Lalit read it. His eyes went wide, he let out a long breath, and when he spoke, his voice was tight and strange. "It's approved." Then he went out onto the verandah and stood very still with his back to everyone. Disha couldn't read it. Was he worried about the land it would take? Upset about something she didn't know? She gave him a few minutes, then went out with two cups of tea and stood beside him. "You looked surprised in there. Are you okay?" He took the tea, eyes wet. "Relieved. My mother had to travel forty kilometres for every check-up last year. Now the village won't have to." Disha nodded and said nothing more, letting him have the quiet. After a while he laughed shakily. "Don't tell anyone I cried at a notice."

How far did Lalit's mother have to travel for check-ups?
Forty kilometres.
What was Lalit feeling after reading the notice?
Lalit felt surprised and deeply relieved, even tearful, because his mother and village would no longer travel so far for care.
How did Disha check in well?
She gave him a few minutes, joined him with tea, named what she saw and asked if he was okay, then let him have quiet.
What would have changed if Disha had assumed Lalit was upset about the land?
She might have offered the wrong comfort or asked awkward questions, missing that he was actually relieved.

In their classroom in Porto, the fish tank crashed to the floor during lunch break. Water everywhere, two goldfish flapping.
Mrs Silva rushed in. “What happened?”
Tomás, who had been leaning on the tank, said quickly, “Jamal bumped it.”
“Yeah, Jamal,” said three voices. Jamal stood by the wall, his face red, trying to speak, stuck on the first word as he sometimes was.
Ines had seen everything. She had been laughing with Tomás right beside the tank. She heard herself say, “Jamal,” too, and felt her chest loosen.
Mrs Silva looked at each of them. “Who actually saw Jamal touch it?”
Silence. Ines looked at Jamal's face, then at the floor. “I didn't,” she whispered. “It was Tomás leaning.”

What were the two goldfish doing on the floor?
They were flapping.
How did Ines feel when she said "Jamal" too?
She felt relieved for a moment, her chest loosening, because the blame was going somewhere else.
What did Mrs Silva's question do well?
Asking who actually saw it made the children check facts instead of repeating the group's blame, which let Ines tell the truth.
How might Jamal have felt standing by the wall?
He likely felt frightened and trapped, blamed while struggling to get his first word out.

Asif (19, midfield). The squad has called him 'Silent Asif' since day one, and I've noticed he has started living up to it. He doesn't call for the ball even when he's free. In the huddle he stands at the back. Today, in a small-sided game, he made a pass that split the defence, and when I asked him how he saw it, he explained the whole move clearly, pointing at the cones. That's not a silent player. That's a player nobody has asked. I told the group what I'd seen, and I've asked Asif to lead the warm-up drill tomorrow. He looked alarmed, then nodded. I'll keep the drill short and stand nearby. I'll also ask the squad to drop the nickname.
Karthik

What has the squad called Asif since day one?
The squad has called him 'Silent Asif'.
Why might Asif have stopped calling for the ball?
Asif may have felt self-conscious after hearing 'Silent Asif' again and again, starting to see himself that way, so speaking up on the pitch felt out of character.
Which of Karthik's steps is most likely to shift the label, and why?
Asking Asif to lead the warm-up gives him a real chance to be seen differently, while keeping it short and standing nearby makes the step manageable.
How might Asif's teammates see him after he leads the warm-up?
The teammates may start to notice the clear thinker Karthik saw, and the nickname may feel less true once they hear Asif explain a drill.

The night before Tomas moved to another city, Tuan, nine, couldn't eat his noodles. He pushed them round the bowl in their kitchen in Brisbane.
"Not hungry?" his dad asked.
"I feel weird."
"Weird how? Sick?"
Tuan shook his head. He put his hand flat on his stomach. "Here. Like it's full of stones. And here." He touched his throat. "It's tight."
"Are you sad about Tomas?"
Tuan frowned. "I don't know. Not sad like crying. Just... weird."
"Nervous? Worried?"
"I don't know!" Tuan's voice went high, and he put his head down on the table.
His dad stopped asking. He just rubbed Tuan's back. "It's okay not to know the word yet."

What did Tuan push round the bowl?
He pushed his noodles round the bowl.
Why does Tuan's voice go high when his dad offers more words?
He is frustrated because he really does feel something strong, but none of the words fits and he cannot explain it.
What did Tuan's dad do well once Tuan got upset, and why did it help?
He stopped offering words and rubbed Tuan's back, telling him it is okay not to know the word yet, which took the pressure off.
How might Tomas feel the same night about moving away?
Tomas might also feel a tight, strange mix of sadness and nerves about leaving Tuan, even if Tomas can't name it either.

Chandrika's diary, Thursday, 1 a.m.
Disha asked for the whole brochure in Tamil AND Hindi by Monday. I said "Of course, no problem!" in that bright voice I use when I'm panicking.
She's my biggest client. If she walks, rent is gone.
But I've already promised three other things this week. I haven't eaten dinner. My neck hurts from sitting. Last month I sent her a translation with two mistakes because I was this tired, and she noticed.
I'm scared of her. That's the truth. Not of her exactly, of losing her.
So tomorrow, first thing, I'm calling her. Script:
"I can do Tamil by Monday, done properly. Hindi by Thursday. If you need both Monday, I'd rather tell you now than do it badly."
Also: I'm messaging that school that asked for translations last month. One client shouldn't feel like my whole life.
Going to sleep. Actually going.

What languages did Disha ask for the brochure in?
Tamil and Hindi, by Monday.
What was Chandrika feeling when saying "Of course, no problem!"?
Chandrika was panicking and scared of losing the biggest client, hiding it behind a bright voice.
What is Chandrika's plan to stop overpromising?
Calling Disha with a realistic timeline, Tamil by Monday and Hindi by Thursday, and contacting another potential client to spread the risk.
How might Disha have felt about last month's translation mistakes?
Disha probably felt annoyed and less confident in the work, which is why an honest timeline may rebuild trust.
Where does my classmate Ritu live?
I don't know, because I can't see a private person's address and shouldn't share one. If you need it for an invitation, ask Ritu directly.

In their Kolkata flat, Kashish, nine, blinked hard three times and made a small "hm" sound, then did it again. India were two wickets from winning, and the room was shouting. Anjali, his mother, opened her mouth to say "Stop blinking" and closed it; last month she had said it, and he had blinked all evening, near tears. "It's like an itch in my eyes. It has to come out," he had told her. Later that evening he sat at the table drawing his comic about a flying auto-rickshaw. Anjali watched from the kitchen. For forty minutes, absorbed in his pencil, he hardly blinked at all. She made him tea and said nothing about it.

What was Kashish's comic about?
His comic was about a flying auto-rickshaw.
Why did Anjali close her mouth instead of saying "Stop blinking"?
She felt worried and remembered that her words last month made him upset and near tears, and made the blinking worse.
What did Anjali learn about when Kashish's tics ease?
They ease when he is absorbed in something calm like drawing, and rise with excitement and being told to stop.
How might Kashish feel when his mother says nothing about the blinking?
He may feel relaxed and accepted, able to get on with his comic without shame.

"No walk yesterday, Saurabh bhaiya?" Chetan grinned from the sofa. "Streak broken! Forty-two days gone!"
Saurabh laced his shoes. "It rained like crazy. I'm going today."
"Aren't you doing two rounds to make up?" Maa called from the kitchen.
"No, Maa. One round, same as always."
"So yesterday is just... lost?" Chetan asked.
"Yesterday was rain. It's not proof I'm lazy. The rule is just: never two days in a row."
Papa lowered the newspaper. "When I gave up smoking, I slipped once at a wedding. Told myself I'd failed and bought a packet the next day. It took me another year."
Saurabh paused at the door. "That's exactly what I don't want."
"Go, go," Papa said. "And take the umbrella."
Chetan was already pulling on his chappals. "Wait. I'm coming. One round."

Why did Saurabh miss his walk yesterday?
It rained like crazy.
Why did Saurabh pause at the door after Papa's story?
He recognised how treating one slip as total failure had cost Papa a year, and felt determined not to fall into the same trap.
What rule does Saurabh use, and why does it help?
Never two days in a row: he restarts with one ordinary round the next day, so the slip stays small instead of becoming a reason to quit.
What does Papa's story show about how he sees slips now?
Papa has learned from his own lost year that calling one slip a failure can undo progress, so he backs Saurabh going out today.

Daycare note, Wednesday. Minakshi.
Sharmila (5) drew alone at the low table for almost an hour today: a long wiggly river with ducks, then boats, then a crocodile 'having a nap'. Nobody was watching; the others were outside. She hummed and talked to the crayons.

Then she put the green crayon down, said 'Finished,' and went off to play. I didn't add a sticker. I'll leave the paper and crayons out tomorrow.

What was the crocodile doing in Sharmila's drawing?
It was 'having a nap'.
Why did Sharmila keep drawing when nobody was watching?
Sharmila was happy and absorbed, humming and talking to the crayons; the fun itself was the reason, not praise.
What choice did Minakshi make after Sharmila said 'Finished', and why was it wise?
Minakshi didn't add a sticker and simply left paper and crayons out for tomorrow, protecting the joy of drawing instead of turning it into something done for a reward.
How might Minakshi, writing the note, see Sharmila's hour of drawing?

Imran sat on the steps of the engineering college in Bengaluru with two forms. One for staying in mechanical. One for switching to architecture, the subject he'd drawn in the margins of every notebook.
His mother had said, "Mechanical is safe." His drawing teacher, Ganga ma'am from school, had said, "You come alive when you sketch."
He had spent a month on it: sitting in architecture studio classes, talking to seniors, looking at the fees and the extra year. He was scared. Architecture meant starting again, alone.
He called Ganga ma'am. "What if I regret it?"
"Then you'll learn from it. But what will you regret more?"
Imran signed the architecture form and sat very still, heart pounding.

What had Imran drawn in the margins of every notebook?
Architecture, the subject he had drawn in every notebook.
How did Imran feel after signing the architecture form?
He felt scared but determined, sitting still with his heart pounding.
What did Imran do well before deciding?
He spent a month testing the choice by sitting in studio classes, talking to seniors and checking fees and time.
How might Imran's mother feel about his choice?

Rain drummed on the tin roof all through the July maths period. "Which jar holds more buttons?" Miss asked. "Hands up for the tall jar." Nearly every hand in the room shot up. Zeenat stared at the short, wide jar. It looked fuller to her. "Zeenat?" Gargi nudged her. "Everybody's saying tall. Just say tall." "But the fat one has more, I think." "If you're wrong, the back bench will laugh at you all week." Zeenat's hand crept up slowly. "Tall," she mumbled. Miss tipped both jars onto the desk and counted aloud. The wide jar won by nine buttons. Gargi gave a small, nervous giggle. "You knew," she whispered. "Why didn't you say?" Zeenat pulled her sleeve over her fingers. "Because everybody else said tall."

Which jar did nearly every hand go up for?
Nearly every hand shot up for the tall jar.
What was Zeenat feeling when she mumbled "Tall"?
She felt anxious and small; she believed the wide jar was fuller but was scared the back bench would laugh at her all week if she stood alone and was wrong.
What small step could help Zeenat say what she really sees next time?
She could give her answer with a reason, like "the wide one looks fuller", and remind herself that being wrong in class is normal and quickly forgotten.
How might Gargi feel once the buttons were counted?
Gargi's nervous giggle and "Why didn't you say?" suggest she felt awkward, noticing that her push to follow everyone kept Zeenat from giving the right answer.
I lost my school ID card and we need it to enter the building tomorrow.
That's stressful, but it's usually easy to sort out. When did you last see it?
I think in the bus this afternoon.
You could ask the bus driver or conductor tomorrow morning, in case someone found it. Also check your bag pockets, your blazer and your desk at home one more time.
I checked everywhere at home. It's not there.
Then go to school a little early tomorrow and tell the guard and the office. Most schools have a way to let students in without an ID for a day. Ask how to apply for a new card.
Will I get in trouble?
Probably not much, especially if you report it honestly. Losing things happens to everyone. You might have to pay a small fee for a new card.
Okay. I'll ask my mom to write a note too.
That's a good idea. A note from a parent makes it even easier for the office. Put it in your bag tonight so you don't forget it.

The power went out in Minakshi's building the night before results. She got ready by candlelight, whispering her rules: Always come first. Never cry.

In the dim classroom, fans silent, the teacher read the ranks. "First, Bhavna. Second, Minakshi."

Minakshi's throat went tight. She pressed her nails into her palm. Don't cry. But her eyes filled anyway, and a tear dropped onto her report card.

Now she had broken both rules. She felt hot all over, ashamed of the rank and ashamed of the tear.

Bhavna turned around. "You got full marks in maths. I didn't."

"Second is nothing," Minakshi muttered, wiping her face fast. All day she kept checking whether anyone had seen her cry.

What were Minakshi's two rules?
Always come first. Never cry.
Why did Minakshi feel ashamed of the tear as well as the rank?
She had a rule that she must never cry, so crying felt like another failure on top of coming second. Breaking two rules at once piled up the shame.
How could a parent or teacher help Minakshi with her rules?

They could gently ask where the rules came from and suggest kinder ones, like "I'll try my best" and "It's okay to cry when I'm upset." Hearing that second place and tears are both normal can ease the pressure.
How might Bhavna feel when Minakshi says "Second is nothing"?
Bhavna may feel puzzled or a bit hurt, having tried to be kind about the maths marks. Bhavna might also realise how much pressure Minakshi puts on herself.

Rob planned on spending three hours reading in preparation for his literature exam. If he ends up spending only three-quarters of this time reading, and he reads a page every fifteen minutes, how many pages did he read in this time?

1 hour is 60 minutes so 3 hours is 3*60 = 180 minutes
Three-quarters of 180 minutes is (3/4)*180 = 135 minutes
He spends 15 minutes on 1 page so he will spend 135 minutes on 135/15 = 9 pages
The answer is 9.

The rains were late in their village near Akola, and Tejas stayed in the fields long after dark. His wife Jaya, heavy with their first child, noticed he barely ate and answered in grunts. At the chai stall he laughed with the others when they teased him about becoming a father, then walked home silent. One night on the charpai, Jaya said, "You've disappeared. Where have you gone?" For a while Tejas said nothing. Then it came out: the crop loan, whether the cotton would fail, whether he could be a better father than his own, how he would miss evenings with his friends. "I didn't want to burden you." Jaya took his hand. "I'm scared too. Tell me. Don't vanish." They decided to ask his brother for help at harvest, and Tejas promised to come to the next check-up at the health centre.

Where did Tejas and Jaya talk that night?
On the charpai.
Why did Tejas keep his worries to himself?
He felt pressured and afraid about money and fatherhood, and did not want to burden Jaya, so he tried to seem strong.
What choice helped, and why?
Tejas sharing his worries with Jaya; it let them plan together, with his brother's help at harvest and his promise to come to the check-up, instead of him withdrawing.
How was Jaya affected by Tejas going quiet?
She felt him slipping away and worried, which is why she asked where he had gone.

After the funeral: Nazia, twenty-five, drove back from her cousin Bilal's funeral on a Thursday and couldn't sleep. He had been twenty-eight. At 2 a.m. she opened her work laptop, looked at a spreadsheet of shipping schedules and thought: is this what my one life is for?
Four days later: On an evening walk, she told her friend Vishal. “I'm not in danger or anything. I'm just scared of wasting it.”
Vishal listened, then said, “Scared how? What would not wasting it look like?”
She didn't know. That annoyed her.
Two weeks later: She sat with a notebook and wrote three questions: Who do I want near me? What do I want to have made? What do I want to have fixed? She didn't answer them all. But she emailed the literacy centre near her office and asked about weekend tutoring. Some nights were still hard. Fewer.

How old was Nazia's cousin Bilal?
He had been twenty-eight.
What was Nazia afraid of after the funeral?
She felt scared of wasting her one life, a dread about meaning rather than any danger to herself.
Why was Vishal's question helpful?
Asking what not wasting it would look like turned a vague dread into something Nazia could start to think through.
What would change if Nazia had kept the fear to herself?
She might have stayed stuck in sleepless worry without the push to name what she wanted and take a small step.

Monthly: finish one module of the coaching course; assist in forty children's lessons. Weekly: two lessons observed by Joseph, the head coach, and one theory chapter. Every Friday after the evening batch, Joseph sat with her on the pool steps for ten minutes. "What worked? What didn't? What's next week?" For pool repairs.
What did Anjali expect Joseph to feel when her chart went blank?

What choice did Joseph make when the pool closed, and why did it help?
He shifted the weekly actions to two theory chapters instead of calling the plan off, so Anjali kept moving and finished theory early.
How might Joseph feel when Anjali passes in May?

messages.content: Mary bought 14 apples, 9 oranges, and 6 blueberries. Mary ate 1 of each. How many fruits in total does she have left?

Mary has 14-1 = 13 apples left.
Mary has 9-1 = 8 oranges left.
Mary has 6-1 = 5 blueberries left.
Mary has 13+8+5 = 26 fruits left in total.
The answer is 26.

The monsoon had flooded the lane outside the gym in Kochi for three days. Uday, twenty-four, had a rule: his favourite comedy series only on the treadmill.
With the lane flooded, he stayed home. “I'll watch one episode now and run double when it clears,” he told his flatmate Gautam.
The rain stopped on Friday. By then Uday had watched nine episodes on the sofa. On Saturday, he didn't feel like the gym. What was the point? The series had lost its pull.

Uday sighed. “You're right. I spent the treat on nothing.”

It was annoying. It was also the only way it had ever worked.

How many episodes did Uday watch on the sofa?
He watched nine episodes on the sofa.

He felt unmotivated and a little annoyed with himself, since the series no longer pulled him to the gym.
What did Uday's sticky note set up, and why could it help?
Series only on the treadmill and a home workout without the series on rainy days, keeping the pleasure reserved for exercise.
How does Gautam see Uday's slip?

Dhruv met Manoj at the film club in October, and they hit it off. Over coffee the first week, Dhruv told him he was nervous about his mid-term. Manoj said, "Same, I always freeze in exams." The next week Dhruv mentioned his parents were arguing a lot, and Manoj shared that his own grandfather was ill. Small, matched steps. By December Dhruv felt safe enough to say he sometimes doubted whether he was good enough for the course. Manoj was quiet for a moment, then said, "I think about that too. Thanks for saying it." Dhruv felt lighter, not exposed. He had noticed that Manoj also never rushed him or repeated it to others. He thought about the first friend he'd told everything in one go, who had drifted away, and smiled.

In which month did Dhruv say he doubted whether he was good enough?
He said it in December.
Why did Dhruv feel lighter and not exposed after his December sharing?
Manoj answered with something of his own, never rushed him and kept it private, so Dhruv felt his trust was returned.
What might Dhruv do if Manoj stopped sharing back?
He could slow down and share only small things until he sees whether Manoj comes back with his own, rather than risk more.
How might Manoj have felt when Dhruv told him about his doubts?
Manoj probably felt trusted and understood, since he replied that he thinks the same thing and thanked Dhruv.

"Because he snatched it. Snatching is naughty."
"Why is snatching naughty?"
Shreya frowned. "Because Ma'am gets angry. And you go in the quiet corner."
"What if Ma'am wasn't looking?"

Where does Shreya say you go when you're naughty?
In the quiet corner.
Why does Shreya think snatching is naughty?
She is worried about the teacher getting angry and the quiet corner; to her, a rule is right because breaking it brings punishment.

Gently ask how Shreya felt when someone took her things, linking rules to feelings, not just punishment.

Kaito had led the design team in Osaka for two years, and he prided himself on smooth meetings. Then a client presentation went badly. The feedback was about something small: the colour scheme failed for colour-blind users. Afterwards, Beatriz, a junior designer from Lisbon, stayed behind. "I noticed it in March," she said quietly. "I didn't want to contradict you in front of everyone." Kaito felt his face burn. March. He thought of all the meetings where he had presented first, and everyone had agreed. He had taken the silence as agreement. The next week he changed the format. Each person would share one concern before he spoke. When Beatriz raised a problem with the new layout, he wrote it on the board and said, "Thank you. This is exactly what I need to hear." Two others spoke after her.

When did Beatriz first notice the colour problem?
She noticed it in March.
What was Kaito feeling when Beatriz told him about March?
He felt embarrassed and shaken, his face burning, as he saw that his team's silence had not been agreement.
What did Kaito change, and what was the effect?
He had everyone share a concern before he spoke and thanked Beatriz publicly, and two others spoke up after her.
What had meetings been like for Beatriz before the change?
Beatriz felt unable to contradict her leader in front of everyone, so she kept a real concern to herself for months.
You wear 4 bangles on each hand. How many bangles is that? What kind of sum is this?

Answer: 8 bangles. 4 + 4 = 8. It is a double (the same number twice).

Doubles are easy to remember: 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 2 = 4, 3 + 3 = 6, 4 + 4 = 8, 5 + 5 = 10. Show them on both hands, on egg boxes and on dominoes.

After failing his first programming project at university in Osaka, Hiroshi stopped opening his laptop for anything but videos. "I'm just not a coder," he told Astrid. In November he tried something smaller. Every evening he solved one tiny problem: reverse a word, count the vowels in a sentence, find the biggest number in a list. Each took ten or twenty minutes. He wrote each one in a small green notebook with the date. By January the notebook had fifty-three entries. One night he flipped back and laughed at problem three, which had taken him an hour. Now he'd do it in two minutes. He showed Astrid. "Fifty-three," she read. "So you are a coder." That weekend he started rebuilding the project he had failed.

How many entries did Hiroshi's notebook have by January?
By January the notebook had fifty-three entries.

Hiroshi felt proud and a little amused, since problem three had taken an hour and now would take two minutes, so he could suddenly see how far he'd come.

How might Astrid see Hiroshi differently in January than in November?
In November Astrid heard 'I'm just not a coder'; by January she sees fifty-three solved problems and tells him plainly that he is one.
Add 45 + 38 on the abacus.

Answer: 83.

Set 45. Add the tens first: tens rod 4 + 3. There is no free lower bead, so small friend: +5 -2, and the tens rod shows 7. Now the ones: 5 + 8. 8 does not fit, so big friend: -2 +10. Taking 2 from 5 needs a small friend too (-5 +3), so the ones rod shows 3; then +10 makes the tens rod 8. Read: 83. Check mentally: 45 + 40 = 85, 85 - 2 = 83. Go slowly - this is a challenge question.

The power cut came at ten, in the middle of a heatwave, and the fan slowed to a stop. Jagdish lay sweating, thinking about the news clip from the evening: melting ice, burning forests, a reporter saying the planet was heating up. What if it kept getting hotter? What if there was no water when he grew up?
His chest felt tight. He tiptoed onto the terrace, where Nilesh Chacha was sleeping on a charpai under the stars.
"Chacha, is the world going to end?"
Chacha sat up. "That worry is real, and it's okay to feel it. Many clever people are working on this. And there are things you can do too."
"Like what?"
"Tomorrow we'll make a list. Switching off lights, planting trees, saving water. Small things add up."
Jagdish lay down beside him. The breeze was cooler up there.

When did the power cut come?
At ten, in the middle of a heatwave.
What was Jagdish afraid of as he lay sweating?
He was anxious that it would keep getting hotter and there would be no water when he grew up.
How did Nilesh Chacha help with Jagdish's fear?

How might Nilesh Chacha have felt being woken with that question?

In Sangamner, the results were printed at the college notice board by the bus stand, and Omkar saw his before his friends did: failed in Cost Accounting.

He walked home past the sugarcane carts without seeing them. At the gate his sister Payal was drying chillies on the roof. "Well?" she called.

"Failed one." He climbed up and sat among the chillies. "I'm not going to pretend it's okay, tai. I'm really disappointed. I studied."

"I know you did."

He was quiet for a while. Then he pulled the question paper from his bag. "But look. I lost marks on the long problems. I read the theory again and again, but I never practised timing. I ran out of time on two answers."

Payal raised an eyebrow. "So?"

"So for the re-exam I do problems with a clock. Maybe with Deshmukh sir's evening group."

She tossed him a chilli. "Good. Now help me with these."

Where were the results printed?
The results were printed at the college notice board by the bus stand.
How was Omkar feeling on the walk home?
Omkar felt really disappointed and dazed, walking past the sugarcane carts without seeing them because he had studied and still failed.

I'm Gurleen, and my roommate Mridul lost his father in June. By November I had stopped telling myself it was only grief. Mridul hadn't been to a lecture in weeks, slept through the afternoons and left plates untouched on the desk we shared. What frightened me most was one night when he said, flatly, "Everyone would be better off without me." I sat down on his bed. My heart was hammering, but I asked him straight out whether he was thinking of not living. He said, "Sometimes." I told him I was glad he'd told me and that I wasn't leaving the room. We called the campus crisis line together, and the next morning I walked with him to the counsellor. She said grief and depression can arrive together, and that getting help wasn't a betrayal of his dad. He still misses his father. But he's getting help now, and he's back in class.

When did Mridul's father die?
In June.

Gurleen was frightened; Gurleen's heart was hammering, yet the question was still asked plainly.
What choice did Gurleen make after Mridul said "Sometimes", and why was it right?
Gurleen stayed in the room, called the campus crisis line with Mridul and walked him to the counsellor next morning, so he was not alone and got professional help.
How might Mridul have felt when Gurleen asked him straight out?
He may have felt some relief at being asked plainly, which made it easier for him to admit how bad things were.

"Your composition's good, Eshaan. Your light's terrible."
"Bhupen Sir, I shot it at noon. It's the only time I'm free."
"Then the photo is at noon. Harsh shadows, squinting faces."
"So what do I do?"

Eshaan groaned. "Six?"
"You want to be paid for this or not?"

Where did Bhupen Sir tell Eshaan to meet?
At the lake, at 6 a.m.
What was Eshaan feeling when he stared at the eleventh shot?
He felt amazed and proud, finally capturing the light on the water.
What did Bhupen Sir push Eshaan to learn?
To shoot in golden hour and use manual settings instead of auto.

He seems quietly pleased, but wants Eshaan to repeat it to build the skill.

At lunch in the school hall, Omar carried his tray past the long bench, not sure where to sit. Ivan waved both arms. "Here! I saved you a seat," he said, patting the bench. Then he leaned close. "You are my best friend." Omar felt warm all over and sat down carefully so as not to squash the coat Ivan was guarding. Ivan whispered that he had a wobbly tooth and did not want anyone else to know. Omar nodded and said, "I won't tell." He shared his apple slices.

What did Ivan do to save a seat for Omar?
Ivan patted the bench and guarded it with a coat.
How did Omar feel when Ivan called him best friend?
Omar felt warm all over, special and secure, because Ivan had chosen him and kept a place for him.
What did Omar do to choose Ivan back, and how could he keep the tooth secret kindly?
Omar shared his apple slices and promised not to tell. He can keep it kindly by not teasing Ivan and by not bringing it up in front of others.
What might Ivan have wanted when he told Omar about the wobbly tooth?
Ivan probably trusted Omar and wanted to share something private with a friend. Whispering shows he did not want the others to hear.
Should I write "pamplet" or "pamphlet" for a small printed booklet?

It is "pamphlet", with "ph" in the middle, making the f sound.
Example: A pamphlet about the science fair came with the newspaper.

Winter sports day, Friday

Came last in the 100 metres. LAST. Kashish came first, again. Everyone crowded round her.

I stood by the water cooler and felt like the slowest person in the world. Why is she good at everything? Running, maths, drawing. I'm not good at anything.

Then Kashish came over. "You ran really straight. I always wobble." I don't know if she was just being nice.

Mumma says I'm good at looking after the class plants. That's not a sport. But still.

Alka

Who came first in the 100 metres?
Kashish came first.
How did Alka feel after coming last?
Alka felt inferior and defeated, like the slowest person in the world.
How could Mumma help Alka with this feeling?
Mumma could keep noticing Alka's real strengths and remind her that everyone is good at different things.
How might Kashish feel coming over to Alka?
Kashish may have felt kind and wanted to encourage Alka.

Sunday. After the zoo, Chetan, five, told Bhavna didi, "I saw an elephant, and a monkey ate a banana."
Tuesday. Didi read him a picture book about a lion that roared at a boy. At dinner Chetan told Papa, "At the zoo a lion roared at ME!" There had been no lion; the lion house was closed.
Saturday. Telling Nani on the phone, Chetan said the lion roared, jumped, and winked. He believed every word, eyes shining. Didi smiled and didn't argue, but later showed him the zoo photos: elephant, monkey, banana.

What did Chetan see at the zoo, according to his first telling?
An elephant, and a monkey that ate a banana.
Why did Chetan believe the lion roared at him?
Chetan felt excited and sure, because the lion from the picture book had blended into his zoo memory, so it felt real.
What did didi do that was gentle and helpful?
She didn't argue, but later showed him the zoo photos, letting the pictures remind him what really happened.
How might Nani feel hearing about the winking lion?
Nani would likely feel amused and charmed, enjoying the story.

The laundromat on Paulo's street in Manila smelled of warm cotton. Paulo, twenty-one, folded his shirts badly while Soo-ah, from his engineering class, waited for her dryer.
"My mother sent money again today," Paulo said. "For rent. I'd told her I didn't need it."
"Did you send it back?"
"No." He creased a sleeve twice. "I chose my course, I found this flat, I cook. But she pays half the rent, and I still call her when I get a fever."
Soo-ah laughed. "My mum sends kimchi by courier, and last month I nearly cried with relief. I also signed my own lease in a foreign country. So am I a child or an adult?"
"Both. Neither."
"Everyone in our class is like this, Paulo. We just don't say it."
He folded the next shirt a little more neatly.

What does Soo-ah's mum send by courier?
She sends kimchi by courier.
Why does Paulo crease the sleeve twice while talking about the money?
He seems uneasy and a bit embarrassed at still taking help from his mother while making his own choices.
What does Soo-ah's remark about the whole class change for Paulo?
It shows the in-between feeling is common, not a personal failure, which seems to settle him as he folds the next shirt more neatly.
How might Paulo's mother see sending the rent money?
She may see it as a way of still caring for him, not as a sign that he has failed to grow up.

Chandrika, you've just made manager and you feel restless? Let your Maria Aunty tell you something. When I was twenty-five, I was the youngest head nurse at the hospital in Goa. Everyone congratulated me. I was content. But I felt like I was standing still. So I started teaching first aid to fishermen's wives in the evenings, in the church hall. I was tired. Some nights only three women came. But one monsoon, one of those women saved her husband when he nearly drowned, because of what we'd practised. She came to thank me with a basket of fish. That's when I understood, beta: growing isn't a place you reach. It's something you keep doing, as long as your hands work.

Where did Maria teach first aid?
In the church hall, in the evenings.
How did Maria feel after becoming head nurse?
Maria felt content but restless, as if standing still.
Which turning point inside the story showed Maria her path?
When a woman she taught saved her drowning husband, which showed that teaching gave her work a purpose beyond herself.
How might the fisherman's wife have felt bringing the basket of fish?
She probably felt grateful and proud, having saved her husband with what she learned.

Read this:

Monday. Before opening his tiffin, Tejas folded his hands and whispered thanks for his family and the aloo parathas, as he did every day. Warmth settled in his chest. Wednesday. Hrithik sat beside him with a tiffin holding just two dry rotis and turned away when Tejas glanced over. Tejas made his thank-you shorter that day and kept thinking about that tiffin all afternoon. Friday. Tejas whispered his thanks, then tore a paratha in half and slid it onto the lid of Hrithik's tiffin. "Mummy packs too many anyway," he said. Hrithik grinned, and Tejas felt the same warmth, only bigger.

What was in Tejas's tiffin on Monday?
It held aloo parathas.
What was Tejas thinking about on Wednesday afternoon?
He kept thinking about Hrithik's tiffin with just two dry rotis, which suggests he was uncomfortable about having so much when a friend had little.
What small step did Tejas take on Friday, and why does it fit his thanks?
He tore a paratha in half and shared it with Hrithik, turning his thankfulness into something he could do 🙂.
How might Hrithik have felt about the shared paratha?
Hrithik turned away on Wednesday, perhaps embarrassed, so the easy way Tejas shared, saying his Mummy packs too many, may have made it simple to accept; the grin suggests he was glad.
Arjun has 12 marbles. He gives away none. Then Asha has 12 marbles and gives away all of them. How many does each child have left?

Answer: Arjun has 12 left (12 - 0 = 12). Asha has 0 left (12 - 12 = 0).

Taking away nothing does not change the number. Taking away everything leaves nothing. These two rules work for every number: 7 - 0 = 7, 7 - 7 = 0, 20 - 0 = 20.
Fatima said costume in class today and I didn't catch it. What does it mean?

A costume is a set of clothes worn for a play, a party or a festival, often to look like a character. It is a noun.
Example: Leela wore a tiger costume for the school play.

Tuesday. Seema Masi phoned Leela, her voice cracking. A caller claiming to be from her bank had got her to send money, and now demanded "one more payment to release it". Leela's first thought was I told you about these calls, but what came out was, "Masi, don't send anything more. I'm coming over."

Thursday. At Masi's flat, Leela rang the bank's helpline on the number printed on the card, then sat beside her as she filed a report on the cyber portal. "I'm so stupid," Seema whispered. "They do this to clever people too," Leela said, and passed her the tea.

Sunday. Leela stuck a note on the fridge: Bank never asks for the code. Hang up. Call Leela. They practised a suspicious call together, laughing, and Masi hung up on the practice caller with a proud little nod.

What did the caller demand on Tuesday?
The caller demanded "one more payment to release it".
How did Leela feel when Seema Masi phoned, and what shows it?
Leela was probably frustrated at first, thinking "I told you about these calls", but concern won out and Leela said "Masi, don't send anything more. I'm coming over."
How could Leela help Masi feel safe from now on?
Keep the note on the fridge, practise hanging up on suspicious calls, use the bank's official number, and call Leela when unsure.
How does Seema feel about herself after the scam, and what changes by Sunday?
At first Seema calls herself stupid; by Sunday, after practising with Leela, she hangs up on the practice caller proudly and seems more confident.

At the school football ground, Sunaina Ma'am marked the register: Parveen absent again, the sixth practice in a row. She found Parveen in the library at half past five, head down on her Chemistry book. "You were my best defender. What happened?" "I made a rule," Parveen said. "Football only after all my revision is done. It was supposed to make me study faster." "Has it?" Parveen shook her head. "The revision never finishes. So I never go. And now I read the same page five times and nothing goes in." She rubbed her eyes. "I'm grumpy at home too." Sunaina Ma'am sat down beside her. "Football isn't the prize at the end. It might be what keeps your head working."

How many practices in a row had Parveen missed?
The sixth practice in a row.
How is Parveen feeling in the library?
She feels tired, grumpy and discouraged, reading the same page five times without anything going in.
What would you change first in Parveen's rule?
Give football a fixed slot, such as two evenings a week, instead of making it wait for finished revision, since the exercise may help her focus.
How does Sunaina Ma'am see the rule?
She sees it backfiring and thinks football may be helping Parveen's concentration rather than competing with it.
