Parveen: bhaiya, did you ever finish that book I gave you on your birthday?
Imran: haha. no. BUT I have a new system
Parveen: oh no 😅
Imran: seriously. I stopped trying to read an hour every night. that never happened
Imran: now it's 2 pages with morning chai. that's it
Parveen: 2 pages??
Imran: the book lives on the chai tray now. kettle goes on, book opens. no decision needed
Imran: and my phone charges in the hall so I can't scroll instead
Parveen: and it's working?
Imran: 12 days straight. most days I read 10 pages, because once it's open, why not
Parveen: ok that's actually clever
Imran: also downloaded audiobooks for the bus. 20 min each way
Parveen: proud of you 👍 now finish my book pls
Imran: page 84 🙂

Where does Imran's book live now?
On the chai tray.
What does Imran's 'no decision needed' suggest he thinks went wrong before?
He seems to think relying on willpower each night failed, so he wants reading to happen automatically with the chai rather than depend on feeling motivated.
Which changes to Imran's setup make the habit easier?
Shrinking it to two pages, tying it to morning chai, charging the phone in the hall and using audiobooks on the bus all remove friction.
How does Parveen's view of Imran's plan change during the chat?
Parveen starts off doubtful, joking 'oh no', but ends up calling it clever and feeling proud of him.
We're making kites for Makar Sankranti this year, and my first kite tore.
That's part of learning. Thin paper tears easily if it is handled roughly. Use light tissue paper, and glue the bamboo sticks carefully along the edges.
Which sticks should I use?
Thin, straight, light ones. Two crossed sticks form the frame, and the paper is stretched over it. Keep the tail long enough so the kite stays steady in the air.
It doesn't fly straight, though.
Then check that both sides are equal in weight and shape. A kite that leans to one side usually has a heavier or longer half. Trim or balance it.
My son is turning six on Sunday and we are holding a pirate-themed party at home at 4 pm. Write an invitation for his friends' parents, about 55 words. I'm Sunita.

Dear Parents,
My son is turning six this Sunday, and we are celebrating with a pirate-themed party at our home at 4 pm. Your child is warmly invited to join the fun. Come dressed as a pirate if you like. I look forward to seeing you both.
Sunita
A film is 2 hours 20 minutes long and starts at 7:50 p.m. When does it finish?
It finishes at 10:10 p.m. Because 7:50 plus 2 hours is 9:50, and 20 more minutes makes 10:10.
Tom, Tim, and Paul are collecting photos of cars. Paul has 10 photos more than Tim. Tim has one hundred photos less than the total amount of photos which is 152. How many photos does Tom have?

Tim has 152 photos - 100 photos = 52 photos.
When Tim has 52 photos, then Paul has 52 + 10 photos = 62 photos.
Tim and Paul have together 52 photos + 62 photos = 114 photos.
That leaves Tom with 152 photos - 114 photos = 38 photos.
The answer is 38.

Relocation coordinator's note — Irfan, transfer from Jaipur to the Hyderabad office. Written by Noor.

Most transferees ask me for a list of "good areas" and sign the first lease a broker shows them. Irfan asked for three days' leave instead.
He arrived on a Thursday and did something simple: he travelled to our office from three different areas at peak hour. Gachibowli, Kondapur and Miyapur. He timed each trip on both mornings, eight-thirty and nine. He walked around each area in the evening, looked at the markets, checked where the nearest clinic was.
On Saturday he messaged me: "Kondapur looks fine online, but the morning traffic is forty-five minutes. Miyapur has the metro; it's thirty-five, reliable."
He signed a lease in Miyapur the following week.
What I did next: I've added a line to our relocation guide suggesting a peak-hour visit before signing.

How long did the Kondapur morning trip take?
Forty-five minutes.
How might Irfan have felt after timing the commutes himself?
He likely felt more confident and reassured, trusting his own experience rather than online guesses.
What else could Irfan check before signing the lease?
He could ask colleagues who moved earlier about broker fees and landlord issues in Miyapur.
How does Irfan's approach look to the relocation coordinator?
The coordinator sees it as a model, adding a peak-hour visit to the relocation guide for others.

25 December

Lalremsiami's family invited us for Christmas again. They sing a Mizo carol with a tune that goes all over the place. When I first heard it last week at their prayer meeting, I thought it was weird. Then they sang it at the cake-cutting, at the church programme, and three times tonight after dinner. Now it's stuck in my head and I LIKE it. I even learned the chorus. Lalremsiami laughed and said, 'Told you!' I didn't do anything different. I just kept hearing it. Mummy says that happens with food too. Maybe that's why I love dal now.

Preeti

How many times was the carol sung after dinner?
Three times.
How does Preeti feel about the carol now?
Preeti feels happy and fond of it, enough to learn the chorus, although it seemed weird at first.
What could Preeti try with other new songs or foods?
Preeti could give them a few more tries before deciding, since hearing something often can make it likeable.
How might Lalremsiami feel hearing Preeti sing the chorus?
Lalremsiami probably feels pleased and proud that a friend has come to love the family's carol.

Swati used to tease her flatmate Nitin about his 'boring' life in their Andheri flat. The same poha every morning. Five nearly identical blue shirts. The same 8:10 train. Then she noticed something. Nitin, a junior architect, never answered anything important in the evening. When his firm offered him the Pune project at 7 p.m. on a Friday, he said, "I'll reply Monday at ten." When the landlord pressed him to renew the lease over dinner, he said, "Tomorrow morning." "Why?" she finally asked. Nitin shrugged. "By evening I've decided a hundred small things at work. I'm tired and hungry and I say yes to everything. The poha and the shirts mean I don't waste decisions in the morning. The big ones get my best hours." On Monday at ten, he turned down Pune, calmly, with reasons. Swati started laying out her clothes the night before.

What does Nitin eat every morning?
Nitin eats the same poha every morning.
Why does Nitin refuse to answer important things in the evening?
Nitin knows he feels tired and hungry by evening and says yes to everything, so he feels safer deciding when his mind is fresh.
Which of Nitin's habits did Swati borrow, and why might it help?
Laying out clothes the night before, which keeps small morning choices routine so her best hours are free for bigger ones.
How has Swati's view of Nitin's 'boring' routine changed?
Swati went from teasing it to seeing it as a smart way to save energy, and started copying part of it.

Sports day at the school ground, and Blue House was winning the relay. Yusuf stood on the bench with his whole row, clapping in time: clap-clap, stamp, "BLUE, BLUE, NEVER THROUGH!" His voice was already hoarse and his chest felt huge.
Then Deepak from Yellow House tripped on the last bend and fell flat. A few Blue boys started a new chant: "Yellow jelly, jelly legs!" It caught fast. Deepak got up slowly, his knee bleeding, and did not look at the stands.
Yusuf's clapping stopped. The chant felt different in his mouth now.
He jumped down, cupped his hands and shouted the loudest thing he could: "Come on, Deepak, finish it!" Two boys beside him joined in. Deepak limped over the line, and the P.T. teacher ran to check his knee.

What did the Blue House row chant while clapping?
"BLUE, BLUE, NEVER THROUGH!"
What was Yusuf feeling before and after Deepak fell?
Before the fall Yusuf felt excited and proud, with a hoarse voice and a huge chest; after the mocking chant began, the stopped clapping suggests he felt uneasy, maybe ashamed to be part of it.
What did Yusuf do that other children in a crowd could copy?
He stopped joining the mocking chant and started a cheer for the fallen runner instead, which turned the crowd's energy back to support.
How might Deepak have felt hearing both chants?
The jelly-legs chant probably made him feel humiliated while he was already hurt, and the cheer for him to finish may have helped him keep going.

Thursday. After the whole dishes war, Siddharth and I finally made a rule that I think will actually work. If either of us misses a chore twice in a row, we don't stew about it, we talk the same evening. No waiting for the weekend. No sighing. Just: "Hey, this is the second time, what's up?" We shook on it like idiots. Siddharth added that we're allowed to say "I can't this week" without a reason, and the other covers, once. I said fine. It feels weirdly grown-up. Last month I would have held it in for ten days and then exploded over a spoon. Now there's a plan for the annoyance before it exists. Let's see if it lasts. — Jatin

How soon do Jatin and Siddharth talk after a chore is missed twice?
They talk the same evening.
What is Jatin feeling at the end of the entry?
Jatin feels hopeful and a little amused, calling the rule weirdly grown-up while doubting whether it will last.
What alternative approach could they use if the rule is broken, and why?
They could ask a neutral friend or the warden to help with the agreement, because a third person can steady a talk that keeps stalling.
How does Siddharth seem to see the rule?
Siddharth shook on it, added the 'I can't this week' allowance and agreed to cover once, so Siddharth wants fairness as well as promptness.

messages.content: Help me make this apology sound sincere: Sorry if you got upset about what I said.
I am sorry for what I said. It was unkind, and I understand why it upset you.
Is it wise to say yes to everything a new friend asks?
No, it is better to think first. Because some requests may not suit you or may be unfair, and a good friend will accept a polite no without getting upset.

In Class 6 our teacher asked us to write a paragraph: “Should school start later?” I'm Rafiq, and I thought it would be easy. I wrote, “Yes, because I'm sleepy.” That was it.
Ms Gurleen gave it back with a note: “Why? Give three reasons. Start with your opinion. End by saying it again.”
So I tried again. I wrote my opinion first. Then three reasons: children would be less sleepy, there would be less traffic at seven, and we could eat breakfast properly. Then I finished with my opinion again.
It was the first time a paragraph felt like a building instead of a pile of bricks.

What did Rafiq write the first time?
“Yes, because I'm sleepy.”
How did Rafiq feel when the paragraph finally worked?
Rafiq felt proud and satisfied, as if the paragraph was a building instead of a pile of bricks.
What did Ms Gurleen's note teach Rafiq?
It showed how to organise a paragraph: opinion first, three reasons, then the opinion again.
How might Ms Gurleen feel reading Rafiq's second paragraph?
Ms Gurleen is likely pleased to see the advice used and the argument made clearly.
How much does the bus pass for students cost this year?
I don't know, because transport boards revise pass rates and I can't see the new ones. The transport corporation's pass counter has the current rate.

You looked worried when you saw me dab my eyes at the retirement lunch, Irfan. Sit, I'll tell you something. I'm Manjula, thirty years in this accounts office, and at twenty-five I cried at this very desk. My father's surgery had gone well that morning; the call came at eleven, after a week of night shifts at the hospital. The relief just spilled out. Mr Bhalla from audit walked past, saw my face and marched to our manager to complain that someone had been harsh with me. Only Lakshmi from payroll came over, set down a cup of tea and asked, "Good tears or bad ones? Do you want company, or shall I shut the door?" I said, "Good. Door, please." She closed it and left me alone for ten minutes. Today at the lunch, my tears were gratitude and a little grief at leaving. You couldn't have known that by looking, so thank you for asking me instead of guessing.

What news came at eleven on the day Manjula cried at the desk?
The call said Manjula's father's surgery had gone well that morning.
What was Manjula feeling when the tears came at twenty-five, and how else were they read?
Manjula felt deep relief after a week of fear and tiring night shifts, so they were good tears; Mr Bhalla read the same tears as hurt from a harsh manager.
Which choice in the story helped most, and why?
Lakshmi's question helped most: she asked what kind of tears they were and offered company or a shut door, so Manjula could choose instead of being guessed about.
How might the manager have felt about Mr Bhalla's complaint, and what would have changed if he had asked first?
The manager may have felt accused of something they never did; if Mr Bhalla had asked Manjula first, he would have learned the tears were relief and skipped the complaint.

On the first night of the festival, Sudha left the phone in her room. She sang garba songs while feeding Jahnavi, clapping between bites. Jahnavi clapped too.
Nine days later, when Sudha sat down with the plate, Jahnavi grabbed both her hands and pushed them together. "Clap! Sing!"

Before Navratri Jahnavi ate silently in front of a cartoon on Sudha's phone, but after Sudha left the phone in her room and fed her with garba songs and clapping, Jahnavi began to clap too, and nine days later she pushed Sudha's hands together, begged her to clap and sing, and ate bouncing.

The number after 9 is 10. Show 9 fingers, add 1 more: all 10 fingers. 10 is a special number: two full hands.
Make your own pattern with blocks. Tell me its rule.

Answer: For example: "blue, blue, green, blue, blue, green - two blues then a green".

Making a pattern is harder than continuing one. Ask the child to repeat the core at least 3 times.
Teacher said me to submit the homework tomorrow. Please check.
Correct form: "The teacher told me to submit the homework tomorrow." Why: "told" takes the person directly; "the teacher" needs "the".

I'm Sonali, Ishwar's sister. Last month Ishwar kept saying he was studying, but every time I walked past his door I heard the little ping of his game. Then one evening, before study time, he walked into the kitchen and held the tablet out to Mummy. "Keep it till nine. Put it somewhere I don't know." Mummy looked as surprised as I was. "Why?" "Because when it's near me, I can't stop." Mummy put it in her handbag. At seven-thirty Ishwar came out and asked for it "just to check one thing". Mummy said, "You told me not to give it." He groaned and went back in. His test marks this month were better. I don't know if he likes the rule, but he still hands it over every evening.

Where did Mummy put the tablet?
In her handbag.
What might Ishwar have felt when Mummy refused at seven-thirty?
Frustrated, as his groan shows, but perhaps quietly relieved that the plan was working.
What else could Ishwar add to the plan?
A short break at eight to check messages, so the urge has a set time and doesn't pull at him all evening.
How does Sonali see the rule?
Sonali notices his better marks and that he keeps handing the tablet over, though unsure whether he likes it.

Daycare note, Abhinav, Tuesday.
Dropping-off: Abhinav cried hard and reached for his papa, Sahil, when he left. I held him by the window and he settled after a while.
Morning: he toddled to the sand tray, then looked back at me, then went further to the slide. Each time he checked, I smiled.
Pick-up: when Sahil came in, Abhinav ran to him, sobbing again, then snuggled in and was calm in a minute.

Where did Abhinav go after the sand tray?
He went further to the slide.
How did Abhinav feel when his papa left?
He was upset and cried hard, reaching for Sahil.
Why does the note-writer smile each time Abhinav looks back?
The smile tells him the carer is still there, so he feels safe to explore further.
What is pick-up like for Sahil?
Sahil gets a run and a sob, then a quick snuggle and calm, a sign that Abhinav trusts him to comfort him.

How should I welcome guests who arrive early?
What did my grandmother cook for lunch?

1. Greet them warmly and offer a seat and some water. Tell them kindly what you are still preparing.
2. I don't know, because I can't see your home. Ask your grandmother, who will be happy to tell you.

July. Darshan had his degree, a certificate in a plastic sleeve, and no idea what came next. He woke at noon in his parents' flat in Vadodara, scrolled short videos until evening, and felt nothing much at all.

August, a Wednesday. Hansa ben, who ran the community kitchen in the temple compound, caught him on the stairs. "You have free hands. We are short of people to chop vegetables on Wednesdays." He said yes mostly to escape.

October. He had not missed a Wednesday. He'd learned to cut onions without crying, and an old man named Mohanbhai told him stories about the textile mills while they worked. Last week, Hansa ben asked him to help set up a spreadsheet for donations. He stayed three hours. On the bus home he realised he hadn't opened the video app all day.

He still didn't know what his life was for. But Wednesdays had a point.

Where did Hansa ben run the community kitchen?
In the temple compound.
What was Darshan feeling in July?
Darshan felt empty and aimless, scrolling all day and feeling nothing much at all.
What helped Darshan begin to feel purpose?
Saying yes to chopping vegetables every Wednesday, meeting people and helping with the donations spreadsheet let purpose grow from action.
How might Hansa ben see Darshan by October?
Hansa ben seems to see him as reliable and capable, trusting him with the donations spreadsheet.
What of these two bags is yours? Fix the first word.

Which of these two bags is yours?
Why: "Which" chooses from a small known set.
Ask a classmate for her science notes in a single polite sentence that includes the word "borrow".
Could I borrow your science notes for tonight, please?
Send my cousin good luck for her dance show in exactly two sentences, with "proud" in the second.
Good luck for your dance show tonight. I am so proud of how hard you have practised.

Daycare note, Friday. Teacher: Keerthana.
Leela (twenty months) found the button-light toy on the shelf today. She pressed the big red button: the light flashed and beeped. She jumped, then pressed it again, eleven times, watching the light each time.
Then she tried the green button, which does nothing. She pressed it hard, frowned, and went back to the red one, pleased.
Next step: drum and stacking cups tomorrow, so she can test more ways to make things happen 😊

How many times did Leela press the red button?
She pressed it again and again, eleven times.
How did Leela feel when the green button did nothing?
She was puzzled and a little frustrated, frowning before going back to the red one.
Why is setting out the drum and cups a good next step?
They give Leela more chances to test how her actions make sounds and changes.
What is it like for Keerthana to watch Leela's experiment?
Keerthana is interested and pleased, seeing Leela learn cause and effect by repeating actions.

Day one: in the Halifax classroom, Elizabeth, five, kept her shoulders stiff and her mouth shut while Ms Anjali asked for show-and-tell. Anjali smiled and moved on.
Day three: Elizabeth's shoulders rose again as she stood to speak. Anjali gave her a small nod. Elizabeth breathed out and said one sentence about her shell.
Day six: her shoulders were only slightly tight; she took a slow breath and showed the whole class, adding, "I got it at the beach."

What did Elizabeth show the class on day six?
She showed her shell and told the class, "I got it at the beach."
What does Elizabeth's change in shoulders across the days suggest about her feelings?
They suggest her nervousness eased as she got used to speaking, and Anjali's nod probably helped. She may still feel some nerves, since her shoulders were slightly tight on day six.
What could Anjali keep doing to help Elizabeth?
She can keep the friendly nod and remind Elizabeth to take a slow breath before she speaks, without pushing her.
How might Elizabeth feel on day six after she finishes speaking?
She may feel relieved and pleased that she managed, and more ready to try again.

Before the second-year viva, I tried something new. Last year I had walked in sure the examiners could see "Urdu-medium, first in the family" written on my forehead, and I blanked on questions I'd answered a hundred times. This time, the night before, I wrote three lines in my pocket notebook: A test checks preparation, not my worth. I taught my sister fractions in two languages. I topped the lab practicals twice. I also went to Professor Akash, who once told our class, "A viva is a rehearsal for the job, not a judgement of you." I asked him to grill me for ten minutes. He did, then said, "You know this, Farhan. Now let the room find that out." Walking in, I read my three lines again. My hands still shook. My answers didn't.

For how long did Farhan ask Professor Akash for a grilling?
Ten minutes.
How did Farhan feel walking into last year's viva?
Farhan felt watched and anxious, sure the examiners saw the Urdu-medium, first-in-the-family label, and that fear caused the blank.
Which steps helped Farhan this time, and why?
Writing that a test checks preparation not worth, recalling real successes, and practising with a mentor who believed in Farhan shrank the fear so the knowledge could show.
How might Professor Akash's way of describing a viva help other students?
Calling it a rehearsal for the job rather than a judgement makes it a chance to grow, so fewer students freeze under a label.

Read this:

Dear Anu,

You asked about hostel life. Forget hostel life. There is a boy in my economics tutorial called Hemant, and I think I might be in trouble.

He is the funniest person I've ever met. Yesterday the professor's microphone died and Hemant did the rest of the lecture in a perfect radio-announcer voice until even the professor laughed. He walks into class like he owns it.

We've talked exactly three times. Once about the canteen samosas, once about a film, once about nothing. And I already know what our flat would look like. Books everywhere. A cat. He would make me laugh every morning.

I know. I KNOW. I don't even know his surname. But you should see how he smiles when he's about to say something ridiculous.

Don't tell Amma.

Your didi,
Kavitha

How many times has Kavitha talked with Hemant?
Exactly three times.
How does Kavitha feel about Hemant, and what does the imagined flat show?
She feels excited and infatuated; imagining their flat after three talks shows she is filling in the blanks with a future she wishes for.
What would you advise Kavitha at this stage?
Enjoy the crush, but get to know Hemant slowly beyond his jokes, so she learns who he really is rather than who she imagines.
How might Hemant see those three conversations?
To him they may have been just friendly, pleasant chats, and he may have no idea she is already imagining a shared flat.

In Everlee's family, there are two adults and four children. In a cookie jar, there are a total of 120 cookies. If the adults eat 1/3 of the cookies and then gives the rest to the children to divide equally, how many cookies does each child get?

The adults ate 1/3*120 = 40 cookies.
The remaining number of cookies is 120-40 = 80 cookies.
If the children divided the cookies equally, each child got 80/4 = 20 cookies
The answer is 20.

Read this:

In Lagos, Chidi, twenty-two, a junior nurse on night shifts, had started to feel like a machine. Work, sleep, work. His sister Ada noticed he'd stopped telling jokes at dinner. One Saturday she dragged him to an afrobeat dance class at a community hall. "I can't dance," he protested. "Nobody here can," she said. The instructor had them copying moves that made everyone look silly. Chidi tripped over his feet, bumped into Ada, and burst out laughing for the first time in weeks. By the end, he was sweaty and grinning. On the bus home, he found himself humming the music. "Same time next week?" Ada asked. "Only if you promise to look as bad as me," he said.

Where was the dance class held?
At a community hall.
What might Chidi have been feeling before the class?
He seemed drained and flat, like a machine, from constant work and night shifts.
What small step helped Chidi feel lighter?
Trying a playful, low-pressure activity with his sister where no one had to be good, which let him laugh again.
How might Ada feel seeing her brother laugh again?
She would likely feel relieved and happy, since she had noticed him stop joking and wanted him back. 🙂

I'm Maria, and I almost didn't report it. When my phone was snatched on the bus in Panaji, my first thought was: the police won't bother, they'll just laugh at me. Devika, my flatmate, said, "Try. What have you lost?"

So the next morning we went to the station with the phone's bill, my ID card, and the phone's number written down. I was nervous. The station was crowded and hot, and we waited for an hour. I kept my voice polite even when the constable at the desk sighed.

The officer who finally saw us wrote down everything. I asked, "May I have the complaint copy, stamped?" He gave me one.

The phone never came back. But with that copy I could block the SIM and claim the insurance. And I learned the station isn't as scary as I'd imagined.

What documents did Maria take to the station?
Maria took the phone's bill, an ID card, and the phone's number written down.
What was Maria feeling on the way to the station?
Maria felt nervous and doubtful, expecting the police not to bother.
Which steps made Maria's visit to the station useful?
Bringing documents, staying polite during the wait, and asking for a stamped copy of the complaint made it useful.
How might Devika see Maria's decision to report?
Devika seems to think trying is always worth it, and would likely feel glad Maria went despite the doubt.

I'm Ishita, and in second year I spent three hours convinced that the university's online judge was broken. My code for sorting names worked on my laptop. On the site, it failed every time. I wrote an angry message to the course forum: "The judge is buggy!" My friend Zubin read it and asked, "Did you check what the input looks like?" I hadn't. I'd assumed every name started with a capital letter, because mine did. The test data had names in lowercase. Three hours of fury, and the mistake was one assumption I'd never checked. I deleted the forum post before anyone replied. Now, when I'm sure the tool is wrong, I check my assumptions first.

What did Ishita assume about the names?
Ishita assumed every name started with a capital letter.
How did Ishita feel while writing the forum message?
Ishita felt angry and certain, sure the online judge was broken rather than the code.
What habit did Ishita build from this, and why is it useful?
Checking assumptions first when sure the tool is wrong, because stubborn faults often sit in what was never verified.
How might Zubin see the angry forum post?
Zubin probably saw it with some amusement and patience, guessing the problem was in the input assumptions.

Tuesday, a week before Durga Puja. Akash calls his cousin Uma. Last year's visit to their grandparents in Siliguri ended with Akash and Jethu arguing about the election until Thamma cried. 'This year, a rule,' Akash says. 'If Jethu starts, you change the subject. Ask about his fishing, or my college fest. If that fails, I'll excuse myself calmly and go help in the kitchen.' Uma agrees and adds, 'I'll sit next to you.'
Saturday, the family lunch. Jethu begins: 'Your generation doesn't understand...' Uma jumps in with a question about the pond. Jethu talks about fish for fifteen minutes. An hour later he tries again. Akash says, 'Jethu, that's a long conversation, let's have it another day,' and carries plates to the kitchen. Thamma follows him and squeezes his arm.
Sunday, the train home. Akash messages Uma: 'No fight. Thamma didn't cry.' Uma replies with a photo of Jethu asleep in his chair, smiling.

Where do their grandparents live?
In Siliguri.
How might Akash feel on the train home?
Relieved and quietly proud that the plan worked and the visit ended without a fight.
What else could Akash and Uma add to the plan for next year?
More topics Jethu enjoys, and perhaps a calm one-to-one talk with Jethu at another time if Akash wants to discuss the election.
What was the lunch like for Thamma this year?
Thamma saw no fight and squeezed Akash's arm in the kitchen, likely relieved and grateful.

metadata.subtype: Approach: set a topic boundary before family gatherings [Action]

messages.content: Jake has 3 snakes.  Each of them lays 2 eggs.  Most of the baby snakes sell for $250 but one super rare one costs 4 times as much.  How much did he get from selling the snakes?

He has 3*2=6 baby snakes
So 6-1=5 sell for $250 each
So those snakes sell for 5*$250=$1250
The other snake sells for $250*4=$1000
So in total, the snakes sold for $1250+$1000=$2250
The answer is 2250.

Read this:

Thursday. Aditi's diary. I lost my bus pass today. I searched my bag three times and felt sick. First I asked Yash, and he just said, “Uh-oh, you'll have to walk,” which didn't help at all. Then I thought, who would actually know what to do? Not Yash. Not the bus driver; he's always grumpy. The school office. I made myself walk in and say, “I need help. I've lost my bus pass.” The lady there didn't even look surprised. She phoned the transport teacher, who wrote me a slip for today and said a new pass would come on Monday. Asking the right person took five minutes. Worrying took all morning.

When will the new bus pass come?
The new pass will come on Monday.
What was Aditi feeling after searching the bag three times?
Aditi felt sick with worry about losing the bus pass.
How did Aditi decide who to ask for help?
Aditi thought about who would actually know what to do and chose the school office instead of Yash or the bus driver.
Why was Yash's reply not much help?
Yash only pointed out the problem, saying Aditi would have to walk, without knowing how to fix it.

Monday. In the sprint meeting, Chetan explained the new dashboard to everyone at normal speed, then turned to Saurabh and repeated it loudly and slowly, word by word. A new intern glanced over. Saurabh touched his hearing aid and said nothing. Maybe Chetan didn't even notice he did it.
Wednesday. At the coffee machine, Saurabh kept his voice light. "Can I ask something? In meetings you slow right down when you talk to me. Is there a reason?" Chetan went pink. "I thought it helped, with your hearing aid." "I appreciate you thinking about it. Honestly, normal pace works best for me. Otherwise it feels a bit like being singled out. If I miss something, I'll ask." "Oh. Got it. Sorry, man."
Next Tuesday. Chetan started to slow down mid-sentence, caught himself, and grinned. Saurabh grinned back.

Where did Saurabh raise the issue with Chetan?
At the coffee machine, on Wednesday.
Why did Saurabh say nothing in Monday's meeting?
He felt unsure whether it was deliberate and wondered if Chetan even noticed, so he held back rather than assume the worst.
Why did asking "Is there a reason?" matter?
It allowed for a real misunderstanding; Chetan thought he was helping, so Saurabh could thank him and still explain what works.
What is it like for Chetan to catch himself the next Tuesday?
Chetan seems a little sheepish but comfortable, since the calm talk left no hard feelings, just a habit to unlearn.

Monday. Mr Nair read out Vidya's science answer again and said, "This is how it's done." From the back, Parveen muttered, "Nair's darling," and a few people laughed. Vidya's cheeks burned. She sat up straighter and smirked back at Parveen. It felt good for a moment.
Wednesday. At lunch nobody saved her a seat. She heard someone say, "She thinks she's better than us." Vidya ate alone, feeling hollow. She thought about her smirk.
Friday. Before the test, Parveen was flipping through her notes in a panic. Vidya hesitated, then sat beside her. "The circuits question always comes. Want me to show you the trick?" Parveen looked suspicious, then nodded.
After the test, Parveen said, "Thanks. That actually helped." When Mr Nair praised Vidya again, she just said, "Parveen asked a good question about circuits earlier," and nobody laughed.

What did Parveen mutter from the back of the class?
"Nair's darling."
How did Vidya feel when she ate alone on Wednesday?
She felt hollow and lonely, and a little ashamed as she thought about her smirk.
What small steps did Vidya take on Friday, and why did they work?
She helped Parveen with circuits and shared credit with her, showing humility instead of smugness.
How does Parveen's view of Vidya change by Friday?
Parveen moves from resentment and suspicion to genuine thanks after Vidya helps her.
Whenever it rains, our school playground floods. Why does that happen?
Water collects wherever it cannot drain away. A playground may flood if it is flatter than the ground around it, or if the drains are blocked or too small.
Could the school fix it?
Often yes. They could clean the drains, add new ones, or change the slope of the ground so water runs off. It depends on the school's resources.
Can students help?
They can report it to the teachers and show photos. Students could also suggest small changes, like keeping drain covers clear of leaves.
Is it dangerous to play there?
Wet ground can be slippery, and puddles can hide holes, so students should be careful. The school is the right place to decide when the playground is safe.
Who should I tell?
Start with your class teacher or the principal. A short written note, with the dates of the flooding, makes it easy for them to act.

Monday: after Sachin's gig at the café, Madhav lay awake making a list on his phone. Things I didn't do. One: music college in Chennai, the audition he'd passed at eighteen and never took up, because Appa said engineers eat and musicians starve. Two: Nisha, who'd moved to Mumbai, and whom he'd never told how he felt.
Thursday: at lunch in the office canteen, he added a third: the year after college he'd spent preparing for an exam he didn't even want. He read the list three times, feeling sick.
The next Monday: Sachin called to ask why he'd left the gig early. Madhav admitted, "Watching you play, I kept thinking, that could have been me. And I didn't even choose not to. I just did what I was told, or what felt safe." Sachin was quiet, then said, "You still play, though. Your guitar's in the corner of your room."

What did Appa say about engineers and musicians?
Appa said engineers eat and musicians starve.
Why does the list make Madhav feel sick?
Madhav feels sharp regret and sadness, because the lost chances were shaped by family pressure and fear rather than his own wishes.
What could Madhav try next with the list?
He could look at which items are still open, like playing the guitar in his room again, and talk them through with Sachin instead of only replaying them.
How might Sachin feel hearing Madhav's admission?
Sachin may feel a little guilty that his gig stirred this up, but also caring enough to point out that Madhav still plays.

I'm Gargi, and I share a room with my older sister Neelam, whose board exams are this month. Here's what I see.
In the morning she's careful. She plans the day in a notebook, picks the right pens, even chooses a proper breakfast. But by evening, after eight hours of papers, she's different.
Yesterday Papa asked if she wanted rice or roti, and she said "whatever" without looking up. Then she ate half a packet of cream biscuits from the cupboard for dinner. When her friend messaged about the study group, she sent a thumbs-up and later couldn't remember what she'd agreed to.
I don't know exactly what's in her head. She just looks like someone with nothing left.

What did Neelam eat for dinner yesterday?
She ate half a packet of cream biscuits from the cupboard.
Why might 'whatever' have felt like the easiest answer for Neelam in the evening?
After eight hours of papers and a day of careful planning, she seemed to have no energy left for even small choices, so any answer that ended the question felt best.
How could Neelam plan her evenings during exams?
She could decide dinner and study-group plans in the morning, while she is still careful, and leave evenings for rest.
How does Gargi see the change in Neelam from morning to evening?
Gargi notices the careful morning sister and the worn-out evening one, and seems concerned but unsure what Neelam is thinking.
Explain austere simply, please.

Austere describes a way of living or a style that is very plain and strict, with no comfort or decoration. It is an adjective.
Example: The monk lived in an austere room with only a mat and a lamp.

The job portal closed at midnight, the hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Rukmini still hadn't sent a single application. For three weeks she'd been polishing one cover letter. Every draft had something wrong: a stiff sentence, a word used twice. "If it's not perfect, they'll bin it anyway," she told Nazia, her roommate, who had already sent fourteen. At eleven the Wi-Fi died completely. Rukmini sat on the floor, surrounded by printed drafts, and felt the familiar mix of panic and relief: now she couldn't send it, so she couldn't fail. Nazia offered her phone's data. Rukmini stared at it. "It's not ready," she said. The clock turned midnight. Nothing was sent.

How many applications had Nazia sent?
Fourteen.
What mix of feelings did Rukmini have when the Wi-Fi died?
She felt panic and relief together, relieved that she couldn't send it and so couldn't fail.
What went wrong, and what could help next time?
Waiting for a perfect letter meant nothing was sent; setting a time limit and sending a good-enough draft could help.
What is it like for Nazia to offer her data and see it refused?
Nazia may feel frustrated and worried for Rukmini, watching the deadline pass.

Sudha ma'am took off her glasses when the young founder said he'd start fundraising once the product was ready. "Let me tell you about Kamal. He was twenty-five when he came to me with a water-testing kit for villages. I asked how much he needed. He said, 'As much as possible.' I sent him away.
He came back a week later with one page. Monthly costs, times eighteen months, plus a small cushion: that was his number. Then he had worked backwards. To find five investors, about fifty good meetings. To have fifty meetings by June, start calling in April. For those meetings to go well, three hundred kits sold by May.
Every week after that he asked one question: are we on track for May? He raised the round in July. Not because he was lucky. Because he knew the date before he knew the investors."

How many kits did Kamal need to have sold by May?
Three hundred kits.
How might Kamal have felt when Sudha sent him away?
He was probably embarrassed and a bit stung, but it pushed him to come back with a real plan.
Which choice in Kamal's story mattered most, and why?
Working backwards from the eighteen-month figure to meetings and a May target, because it gave every week a clear check.
How did Sudha see Kamal's one page?
Sudha saw a founder who finally knew his number and his dates, which made the pitch believable.

Before: Ujjwal and Zainab, both twenty-six and newly married, spent most of their salaries every month without thinking. When Zainab's father had a hospital stay, the bills scared them both.

During: A month later, they sat with a qualified financial adviser at the bank on a Saturday morning. They wrote down their goals: a home someday, a child, security for both sets of parents. The adviser explained health cover, long-term savings and why an emergency fund mattered. Zainab took notes. Ujjwal asked lots of questions and admitted he'd been avoiding the subject.

After: Six months later, a fixed amount went into savings automatically each month. Both sets of parents had health cover. Zainab smiled, looking at the plan on the fridge. "It's boring," Ujjwal said. "Boring is good," she answered.

Where did Ujjwal and Zainab meet the financial adviser?
At the bank, on a Saturday morning.
What made Ujjwal and Zainab decide to plan their money?
They were frightened by the hospital bills when Zainab's father fell ill, which showed them how unprepared they were.
Why was meeting a qualified adviser a wise step?
It gave them reliable guidance matched to their goals, instead of guessing or following hearsay.
How might their parents feel about having health cover?
They would likely feel more secure and cared for, knowing their children planned for them.

Sunday: Urmila told Farhan she wouldn't run the weekend chaat stall with him next season; her new job had Saturday shifts. Farhan stared at the tawa. "After I taught you everything. Fine. I'll manage. Somehow." Urmila went home with her stomach in knots and almost texted, "Forget it, I'll do it."
Tuesday: At the bus stop she made two columns in her notes. Did I break a promise? No, they had agreed on one season. Did I hurt him by lying or being careless? No. Is he sad? Yes. Is that the same as me doing wrong? She sat with that until her bus came.
Friday: She met him at the stall before opening. "I'm grateful you taught me, and I'll miss this. My answer is still no. My cousin Irfan wants weekend work; can I send him over?" Farhan was quiet, then nodded. Urmila walked away sad, but not guilty.

What did Urmila's new job have that clashed with the stall?
Her new job had Saturday shifts.
How did Urmila feel after Farhan's reply on Sunday?
Urmila felt guilty, with her stomach in knots, so pressured that she almost texted to take the stall back.
How did Urmila's two columns help her decide?
They separated real wrongs, such as breaking a promise, from Farhan's sadness, so she could keep her decision while still showing care in words.
What might Farhan feel when Urmila offers her cousin Irfan?
Farhan may still feel disappointed, but the thanks and the offer show care, which may ease his hurt and explain his nod.

"It's their fault, bhaiya. All of them. That's why the stall's losing money."
Siddharth kept wiping the counter of their father's juice stall. "All of who?"
"You know who. The ones who opened the shops near the station. They're taking over everything."
"You're saying every single one of them is the problem?"
"Yes!"
"I don't agree with that. Raju from there lent us his mixer when ours burned out." Siddharth put down the cloth. "But I'm listening. What are you really scared of?"
Lokesh kicked the crate. "That the stall shuts. That Papa's sick and I'll have to run it and I can't. That I'll mess it all up."
"That's a lot to carry."
"Yeah."
"Okay. Tomorrow we sit with the accounts together. Not them. Us."
Lokesh went quiet. Then: "Can you show me how you do the stock list?"

Who lent them a mixer?
Raju from there, when ours burned out.
What was Siddharth thinking when he put down the cloth?
Siddharth felt concerned and patient, disagreeing with the blame but wanting to hear the fear behind it.
Which of Siddharth's moves keeps Lokesh talking?
Disagreeing calmly with blaming everyone, then asking what Lokesh is really scared of and offering to go through the accounts together.
What is Lokesh afraid of beneath the anger?
That the stall will shut and that he will fail if he has to run it while Papa is sick.
The teacher told good morning and we all stood up. Is 'told' right?

The teacher said good morning and we all stood up.
Why: greetings take "said"; "told" needs a person.

Creche note, the week after Losar. For weeks Tenzin (2) used to cry at drop-off. His mother always said the same words, "Amala comes after snack and song," and she always came at five. Today he waved at the door and went to the blocks, and at five he looked up at the gate before she even arrived. When she came, he ran to her, then went back to finish his tower. I'll tell her how settled he is. — Arohi

What time did Tenzin's mother always come?
At five.
What does Tenzin going back to finish his tower suggest?
Tenzin felt secure and calm, trusting his mother would be there, so he could keep playing.
What built Tenzin's trust at drop-off?
His mother's same words each time and always coming when promised, which made the pattern predictable.
How might Tenzin's mother feel reading the note?
She would likely feel relieved and proud that her consistency has helped him settle.
Now you try: is 8 x 5 = 5 x 8? Is 40 / 8 = 8 / 40?
The answer is Yes; no.

The inter-house science quiz ended badly: Irawati's team scored 2, Sabina's scored 3, both last. In the auto home, Irawati pressed her face to the window. "I'm just dumb. Science isn't for me." Sabina counted on her fingers. "We lost on the planets round. We never read that chapter."
The rematch was the next morning, and that evening the power went out in their lane. Sabina came over with a torch and the textbook. "Planets only. Forty minutes." Irawati lay on the bed. "What's the point?"
But Sabina read aloud anyway, and after a while Irawati sat up and asked, "Wait, which one has the rings?"

Which round did Sabina say they lost on?
The planets round.
What was Irawati feeling in the auto home?
She felt ashamed and defeated, seeing the loss as proof she was "just dumb" at science.
What made Sabina's plan workable despite the power cut?
Sabina shrank the fix to one chapter and forty minutes and brought a torch, so trying felt small enough to do.
What would change for Irawati if she explained the loss the way Sabina did?
She would see it as one unread chapter she could fix, and would be more likely to keep trying.

Dear Vandana Akka,
You're the only person in the family who works in finance, so I'm writing before I meet the adviser next week.
Here's what I've understood so far, and please tell me if I've got it wrong.
Health insurance: my company gives some cover, but it ends if I leave the job, so I'm looking at a separate policy too.
Term life insurance: it pays out only if I die during the term; it's for people who depend on me. Amma does, partly.
Retirement: starting early matters because money has more time to grow, even small amounts.
What I don't know: how much cover is "enough", and which retirement options fit someone like me.
I've written down my income, rent, what I send Amma, and my savings, so the adviser can see the real picture.
Is there anything else I should ask?
Ira

Why is Ira looking at a separate health policy?
Because the company cover ends if Ira leaves the job.
How does Ira seem to feel about these decisions?
Ira seems careful and a little unsure, wanting to check understanding before meeting the adviser.
What makes Ira's preparation for the adviser meeting wise?
Ira has learned the basics, listed open questions and written down real income and commitments, so the qualified adviser can give fitting guidance.
How might Vandana Akka feel reading the letter?
Vandana Akka would probably feel impressed and happy to help, seeing Ira has already done homework.
After the quiz Ravi said he felt discouraged. What state is that?

Discouraged means having lost confidence or hope, so you feel less like trying. Here it is an adjective.
Example: Mina felt discouraged after her third failed attempt at the high jump, but her coach cheered her up.
Why does a river rush faster in the hills than on the plains?

The land slopes steeply in the hills and gently on the plains. Because gravity pulls the water downhill harder along a steep slope and the water has little to hold it back, it speeds up, while on flat land it slows and spreads out.
Find 1/9, 2/9, 1/11 and 2/11 as decimals. What patterns do you see?

Answer: 1/9 = 0.(1), 2/9 = 0.(2), 1/11 = 0.(09), 2/11 = 0.(18).

For ninths: 10 / 9 = 1 R 1 for ever, so 1/9 = 0.111... = 0.(1). Then 2/9 = 2 x 0.111... = 0.222... = 0.(2), and in the same way 4/9 = 0.(4) and 8/9 = 0.(8): the numerator repeats. For elevenths: 1 / 11 = 0, 10 / 11 = 0 R 10, 100 / 11 = 9 R 1, and then the remainder 1 returns, so 1/11 = 0.090909... = 0.(09). Every eleventh has a 2-digit block that is 9 times the numerator: 2/11 = 0.(18), 3/11 = 0.(27), 5/11 = 0.(45).

"How was the class vote, Sunaina?" Vikas asked, stirring the dal. "Fine, Papa. We're doing a skit on road safety." "I thought you wanted to do the one about the lake birds." Sunaina picked at the tablecloth. "Everyone else wanted road safety." "Did you say what you wanted?" "No. Ma'am likes it when we don't argue. And Pooja would think I'm showing off." Vikas sat down across from her. "Being polite is good. But your idea counts too." "What if they don't like it?" "Then they don't. But they'll know you had one." Sunaina was quiet. "Maybe I can ask Ma'am if the birds can be a poster instead." Vikas smiled. "That's a start."

What skit is Sunaina's class doing?
A skit on road safety.
What is Sunaina worried about when she keeps her idea to herself?
She worries that Ma'am wants no arguing and that Pooja would think she is showing off, so she fears disapproval.
What choice does Sunaina come to by the end, and why is it a good step?
She decides to ask Ma'am if the lake birds can be a poster, a polite way to share her own idea without upsetting anyone.
How does Vikas see his daughter's silence in class?
Vikas values her politeness but worries her own ideas are getting buried, so he encourages her to share them.

At the farm extension office in a village near Dharwad, Santosh had just become the team head. His three field staff were very different.
Nikita had worked there eight years and knew every farmer by name. He told her, “You plan your own visits this month. Just tell me where you'll be.” She smiled.
Raju had joined two weeks ago. Santosh went with him to the first three farms, showed him how to test soil, and checked his forms every evening.
Farzana was good but always late with reports. Santosh told her plainly, kindly, “Your advice to farmers is excellent. Your reports are a week late. What would help?”
By the end of the month, each had asked for something different, and each had got it.

How long had Nikita worked at the office?
Eight years.
How might Raju have felt with Santosh going to the farms with him?
He probably felt supported and less nervous in his first weeks, learning by doing alongside his boss.
Why does Santosh's approach work for all three staff?
He gives freedom to the experienced, guidance to the new and honest feedback to everyone, based on what each needs.
How might Farzana feel after Santosh's feedback?
She might feel respected rather than scolded, since he praised her strength and asked what would help.

Anjali, come, I will tell you about the time Dorje bragged. I was fifteen, and I had started a coding tutorial three times and quit three times. One Sunday, half joking, I typed into our class group: "I will finish the whole coding tutorial in thirty days." Thumbs-ups came back, and one boy wrote, "Let's see." My ears went hot. I did not want to look foolish. So I took a pencil and drew a chart on the door: one hour every evening after dinner, seven to eight. On the lazy days, the chart and the group were both staring at me. I finished on day twenty-nine. I still think about how the promise pushed me on the tired days.

How many days did Dorje promise?
Dorje promised thirty days.
How did Dorje feel when the boy wrote "Let's see"?
Dorje felt embarrassed and did not want to look foolish.
Which choice inside the story helped Dorje keep the promise?
Drawing a chart for one hour every evening, seven to eight, turned the promise into a daily routine.
How might the classmate who wrote "Let's see" have viewed the promise?
The classmate might have doubted it, since it was a big claim, and may have felt impressed when it was finished.

Class note by Samir, KG teacher.
When I ask Trisha about her drawings, she usually shrugs. Today she drew a big purple animal. I asked, “What's this?” Shrug. I tried, “Is it a dog or a horse?” She shook her head and smiled. “Does it live in water or on land?” She pointed up. “Sky?” She nodded, eyes shining: “A flying elephant.” I think her shrug means “I don't know how to start” more than “I don't care.” I'll keep offering choices.

What colour animal did Trisha draw?
Purple.
What does Trisha's shining look when she says “A flying elephant” suggest?
It suggests she felt proud and happy to share her idea once it was easier to start. Her earlier shrug seems to have been shyness or not knowing how to begin, not a lack of interest.
Which prompts worked, and why?
Simple either-or questions like “dog or horse” and “water or land” gave Trisha an easy way in without pressure.
How might Trisha see the teacher's questions?
She might feel her drawing was interesting to the teacher, which encouraged her to talk. 😊

At the colony park in Pune, Vaibhav was throwing high catches to the younger boys before dark. Ten throws each. Chetan ran and dived and held on, again and again. "Dropped two," Vaibhav called, writing in his little notebook. Chetan's shoulders fell. He kicked the grass all the way to the bench and told his mother at the gate that he was bad at catching. Next evening Vaibhav tried it differently. After Chetan's ten, he shouted, "Eight clean catches!" Chetan punched the air and asked for ten more. On the walk home he stopped. "Vaibhav bhaiya, yesterday I also got eight." "I know." Chetan thought about it all the way up the stairs.

How many throws did each boy get?
Ten throws each.
Why did Chetan kick the grass all the way to the bench?
He felt upset and discouraged because "Dropped two" made him believe he was bad at catching.
What did Vaibhav change the second evening, and what could Chetan learn from it?
Vaibhav announced the eight clean catches instead of the two drops; Chetan could learn to ask for both numbers before judging himself.
How might Vaibhav see the difference between the two evenings?
He seems to realise his wording, not Chetan's catching, changed how Chetan felt, since the score was eight both times.

I'm Avni, and I've worked beside Wasim at the hospital lab for a year. Our shifts rotate every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights. Lately Wasim eats biscuits from the drawer instead of meals, yawns through handovers, and last Tuesday he slammed a tray down when a ward boy asked about a delayed report. That's not the Wasim I know. At tea I asked if he was all right. He rubbed his eyes and said he couldn't remember the last time he'd slept properly. I told him about the free check-up at the staff clinic, and that our supervisor once let me stay on one shift pattern for a month when I asked. He did both. I don't know how he feels inside, but he's packing lunch again.

How often do the lab shifts rotate?
Every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights.
What does Wasim slamming the tray suggest about how he felt?
He seemed exhausted and short-tempered; broken sleep from the rotating shifts had worn his patience thin.
Why were Avni's suggestions wise?
A check-up at the staff clinic and asking the supervisor for a steadier shift pattern protect Wasim's health, since predictable hours help sleep, meals and mood.
How might the ward boy have felt when Wasim slammed the tray?
He was probably startled and a bit hurt, since he had only asked about a delayed report.
A bag of chips weighs 20 ounces, and a tin of cookies weighs 9 ounces. If Jasmine buys 6 bags of chips and 4 times as many tins of cookies, how many pounds does she have to carry?

Jasmine's bags of chips weigh 20*6 = 120 ounces.
Jasmine buys 6*4 = 24 tins of cookies.
Jasmine's tins of cookies weigh 9*24 = 216 ounces.
She has to carry 120+216=336 ounces.
She has to carry 336/16=21 pounds.
The answer is 21.
Rewrite as a friendly invitation: Your presence is requested at the school fair on Saturday.
Please come to the school fair on Saturday. We would love to see you there.
Why does a cut flower last longer when it is kept in a vase of water?
Water in the vase keeps the stem supplied, so the flower stays fresh. Because water travels up thin tubes inside the stem to the petals and leaves, the flower does not dry out.

Swati sat in her high chair with an empty katori. She could not say much, but she tapped the bowl on the tray, looked at her mother Usha and said, "Aur." Usha smiled and filled the bowl again with dal-rice, and Swati patted the tray and got busy with her spoon.

In another kitchen, Varun was hungry too. He tugged at the cupboard where the biscuits lived. It stayed shut. He walked to the fridge and pulled the handle. Nothing. He pointed at the counter and said, "Bi." His father followed his finger and brought a banana.

Varun shoved it away and cried, his face scrunched, his hands out for a biscuit. His father said, "Banana, or wait for dinner." Varun cried harder. Then he sniffled, looked at the banana on the tray, picked it up and took a bite. He chewed slowly, and the crying stopped.

What did Swati say while tapping the katori?
Swati said, "Aur."
How did Swati's way of asking for food differ from Varun's first attempts, and what did each get?
Swati handed her mother the empty bowl and got more food at once, while Varun tried the cupboard, the fridge and pointing, and got a banana rather than the biscuit he wanted.
What was Varun feeling when he shoved the banana away?
Disappointed and frustrated, because he wanted a biscuit and not a banana.
How could Varun's father help?
His father could name the choices, say the biscuit is for later, and let Varun pick between the banana and something else.

Ujjwal: the officer wants me to sign a statement. it's in a language I can't read well
Ujjwal: he says just sign, it's routine
Devika: don't sign anything you haven't understood
Ujjwal: he's getting irritated
Devika: stay polite. ask him to read it out to you, or give you a copy
Devika: I'm calling my cousin Rohan, he's a lawyer
Ujjwal: he read it out. it says I "lost" the phone, not that it was stolen
Devika: then ask for it to say stolen. that's what happened
Ujjwal: he said it'll take longer
Devika: that's fine. we'll wait. Rohan says it's your right to have your statement recorded correctly
Ujjwal: ok. he's rewriting it. my hands are shaking lol
Devika: you're doing everything right. not your fault. I'm coming there now
Ujjwal: thank you. getting a copy with the stamp

What did the statement say instead of "stolen"?
It said Ujjwal had "lost" the phone.
What was Ujjwal feeling at the station?
Ujjwal felt nervous and pressured, hands shaking, as the officer grew irritated and pushed for a signature.
What steps did Devika suggest?
Not signing anything unread, asking for it to be read aloud or copied, insisting on the correct word, contacting a lawyer, and getting a stamped copy.
How might Devika be feeling while texting?
Devika seems worried and protective, calling a lawyer and heading to the station so Ujjwal isn't alone.

The email came at 4:10, while Rania was still in her school uniform at the kitchen table in their Sydney flat. Selective school test: not offered a place.
She read it three times. Then she closed the laptop very gently, as if it might break.
Mum had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery all year to pay for the Tuesday tutoring. Dad had stuck the practice timetable on the fridge. Her little cousins in Beirut had been told she was 'the clever one'.
Not clever, she thought. Just the one who costs them money. Every Saturday, for nothing.
Jin messaged: 'did u get yours??' She turned the phone face down.
When Mum came home and asked, Rania said she had a headache and went to her room. She lay there listening to her parents' voices in the kitchen and decided she was simply the stupid one in the family. That was the whole story now.

Who had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery to pay for tutoring?
Rania's Mum had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery all year.
What does Rania's thought 'Just the one who costs them money' show about how she sees herself?
She has turned one failed test into a verdict on her whole self, feeling ashamed and like a burden on her parents.
What turning point is available to Rania at this stage?
She could tell her Mum or a school counsellor what she is really thinking, so someone can help her see that one result does not decide who she is.
How might Rania's Mum feel hearing that her daughter has 'a headache' and seeing her go straight to her room?
Mum may sense something is wrong and feel worried and shut out, not knowing Rania thinks the tutoring money was wasted on her.

In the sandpit at the park in Berlin, Yosef was driving a shiny red digger. Tuan watched it go back and forth.
Then Tuan reached out and pulled it right out of Yosef's hands.
Yosef's mouth opened. He wailed, loud, tears running down.
Tuan stood very still, holding the digger. He looked at Yosef, then at his own hands. He gave a funny little laugh, then stopped.
Yosef's mum came hurrying over. "What happened?"
Tuan put the digger behind his back. "I didn't do it," he said.

Sonali, you think chai-time talk is harmless. Let your Aparna aunty tell you what I learned at twenty-four.

I worked at the post office in Pune. Every afternoon we three clerks sat with chai, and the best currency at that table was other people's troubles. One day I told them that our colleague Hemlata's husband drank, and that she came to work with swollen eyes. She had told me that alone, by the photocopy machine.

The other two leaned in. I felt so included. So close to them.

That evening I saw Hemlata at the bus stop, and she smiled at me. Just smiled. And I felt ashamed right down to my shoes.

That was my turning point. I asked myself: would she want this told? Of course not. From then on, at chai, I talked about my own things: my mother, my silly poems. The table got a bit quieter. But the friendships I made were real ones.

Where did Hemlata tell Aparna about her husband?
She told her by the photocopy machine.
How did young Aparna feel when the other clerks leaned in?
She felt included and close to them in that moment.
What was the turning point in Aparna's story?
Seeing Hemlata smile at the bus stop made her ashamed, and she began asking whether people would want their troubles told and shared her own life instead.
How might Hemlata have felt if she had known what was said at chai?
Hemlata would likely have felt betrayed and humiliated, since she had trusted Aparna alone.

"Climb the water tank ladder. Top rung. I dare you," said Farhan.
Karthik looked up. The ladder was rusty and very high.
"No way. It's dangerous."
"Scared?"
"Yes. And so should you be." Karthik grinned. "Race you to the ground instead. Loser buys the next bat."
Farhan hesitated. "You're boring."
"And alive."
Farhan laughed. "Fine. But I'm winning."
They ran. At home that evening, Karthik told his father about the rusty ladder. His father called the society secretary right away to have it chained.

What was the ladder like?
Rusty and very high.
What was Karthik feeling when he looked up at the ladder?
Karthik felt scared and wary, knowing the climb was dangerous.
How did Karthik say no without losing Farhan as a friend?
He admitted he was scared, joked, and offered a fun race instead, so they could still play together.
How might Farhan feel when Karthik says "And alive"?
Farhan probably feels amused and a bit relieved, since the joke let him drop the dare without losing face.

Sunday.
Yash asked me to check his job application today, and I heard myself say, "Did you even read it before sending it to me? Sloppy." Word for word, Papa's voice. I saw Yash's shoulders drop, the way mine used to. It shook me. Tonight I made two lists. From Papa, keep: showing up early, finishing what you start, checking every detail. From Papa, drop: the sneer, the word "sloppy", making people feel small. I called Yash, apologised, and went through his application properly, line by line. He was quiet at first, then laughed at my notes. I'm keeping the details. I'm leaving the sneer with Papa.
Anand

What word did Anand use about Yash's application?
"Sloppy."
How did Anand feel after hearing Papa's voice in those words?
Shaken, seeing Yash's shoulders drop the way Anand's used to.
What did Anand decide to keep and drop?
Keep showing up early, finishing what you start and checking every detail; drop the sneer and making people feel small.
How did Yash react to the apology and the careful check?
He was quiet at first, then laughed at the notes, probably relieved.

You asked, Jagdish, how I've kept meditating for three years. I'm Alka, and the honest answer is: badly, and then better.
I started at twenty-three, after a panic-filled year at work. I downloaded an app, did ten minutes a day, felt amazing for two weeks, then stopped. I did that cycle four times.
What changed was a Buddhist teacher at a small centre near my flat. She said, "It's not a performance. Sit even when it's boring. Especially when it's boring."
So I made it smaller and fixed. Fifteen minutes, every morning, before my phone. Same cushion, same corner. On Saturdays, a group sit at the centre, which kept me honest.
There were months when nothing seemed to happen. Then one day my manager shouted in a meeting, and I noticed I didn't shout back. I just breathed. That's all the wisdom I have so far.

How long does Alka meditate every morning?
Fifteen minutes.
How did Alka feel during the months when nothing seemed to happen?
Alka felt bored and unsure, sitting through dry spells without obvious results.
What helped Alka keep the practice going long-term?
Making it small and fixed, before the phone in the same spot, plus a weekly group sit and the teacher's advice to sit even when bored.
How might the manager have experienced Alka's calm response?
The manager may have been surprised and calmed down faster because Alka didn't shout back.
Join these using "so": It rained all night. The roads were flooded in the morning.

Jeanne wants to ride the Ferris wheel, the roller coaster, and the bumper cars. The Ferris wheel costs 5 tickets, the roller coaster costs 4 tickets and the bumper cars cost 4 tickets. Jeanne has 5 tickets. How many more tickets should Jeanne buy?

The total number of tickets needed is 5 tickets + 4 tickets + 4 tickets = 13 tickets.
Jeanne needs 13 tickets - 5 tickets = 8 tickets.
The answer is 8.

Wednesday.
Big client call at 11. Before it, I sat in the washroom and did the slow sighs the yoga aunty taught Mummy and me: long breath in, longer sigh out, three times. It worked. My voice didn't shake once during the demo.
Then, at 3, Mohit asked for the third time how to export the report. And I sighed. Loudly. The whole desk heard it. He went red and said, "Never mind, I'll figure it out." I felt terrible. The same thing that saved me at 11 made him feel like a nuisance at 3.
I went over at 4 with two cups of chai and showed him properly. I said, "Sorry about the sigh, that was about my day, not you." He laughed a bit and said he'd write the steps down this time.
Note to self: sighs for me, quietly. Not at people.
— Aditi

At 11.
How did Aditi feel after sighing loudly at Mohit?
Aditi felt terrible and guilty on seeing Mohit go red and hearing him say he'd figure it out alone.
What did Aditi do to repair things with Mohit?
Aditi went over with chai, showed him the export properly, and apologised, explaining the sigh was about the day, not him.
How did Mohit seem to take the loud sigh?
He went red and backed off, which suggests he felt embarrassed and like a nuisance for asking again.

messages.content: Why does a glass of water on a sunny windowsill sometimes throw a tiny rainbow on the wall?
The glass bends and splits sunlight. Because each colour in white light bends by a slightly different amount, the colours spread apart and land in separate stripes on the wall.

Shreya's salary arrived on the last day of the month, and by the fifth it had always vanished. This time she had set up two standing instructions the week before: a fixed amount to her savings account, and a smaller fixed amount into a monthly investment plan, both due to leave within an hour of the salary landing, before she could see the balance and feel generous. The month was tight; her flatmate Urmila's birthday and a phone repair meant less to play with. "You'll run out by the twentieth," Urmila said. Shreya shrugged. "Then I'll spend less. The savings are already gone. I can't argue with them." On the twentieth she had a little left, and the savings account had grown for the first time in a year without a single decision.

What did Shreya set up in the week before her salary arrived?
She set up two standing instructions: a fixed amount to her savings account and a smaller fixed amount into a monthly investment plan.
What does Shreya's shrug and "I can't argue with them" suggest about how she feels?
It suggests Shreya feels calm and settled about the plan, because the savings leave before she can be tempted.
What other approach could Shreya add to this one?
She could give each spending category an amount, or note where the leftover money goes, so the rest of the month is planned too.
How might Urmila see the plan?
Urmila seems doubtful that what is left will last until the end of the month, though the plan does not depend on willpower.

From their balcony in Gurugram, Avni watched the tall yellow crane swing a load of steel across the sky. Her jaw dropped and stayed dropped. She didn't blink.
A visiting aunty laughed. "Close your mouth, Avni, don't gape. Looks so rude."
Himani, her mother, knelt beside her. "She's not rude, she's amazed." She pointed. "Up goes the crane." Avni followed her finger, mouth still open, and whispered, "Up."

What was the crane carrying?
A load of steel.
What does Avni's dropped jaw suggest she was feeling?
It suggests wonder and awe at the huge moving crane; she was fully caught up in watching rather than being rude.
What would you advise the aunty the next time a toddler gapes like this?
Let the child look and join in by naming what they see, rather than calling it rude.
How does Himani see the open mouth compared with the aunty?
Himani sees amazement, while the aunty sees bad manners.

At the Sunday haat in Holi week, Lalit let his little sister Devika help at the tomato stall.
"Easy," he said. "Tomatoes are twenty a kilo, half a kilo is ten, so if they give fifty for a kilo and a half, you give twenty back." His fingers flicked through the coins.
Devika held a note in each hand and stared at the scale. "Which one is the kilo?"
"The kilo! On the scale!" Lalit's voice went sharp. "I just told you."
A customer was waiting. Devika's eyes filled.
Lalit stopped. He remembered Baba, years ago, showing him one coin at a time. It had taken a whole season.
He knelt. "Okay. Forget kilos. One basket, one ten-rupee coin. You give the basket, you take the coin. That's it."
Devika nodded and held out her hand to the customer.

How much are tomatoes a kilo at the stall?
Tomatoes are twenty a kilo.
Why did Lalit's voice go sharp?
Lalit felt impatient and flustered, because the sums were obvious to him and a customer was waiting.
What did Lalit change, and why did it work?
Lalit dropped the kilos and made it one basket for one coin, a single step Devika could manage.
How did the first minutes at the stall feel for Devika?
Devika felt confused and close to tears, holding notes she didn't understand while being told it was easy.

The power had gone in the whole building in Patna, and it was sticky and hot. Everyone else sat on the balcony complaining. Shreya, ten, sat by the window with a new marble-run kit and the last of the daylight.
The ramps kept falling. She rebuilt them. The marble kept flying off the curve. She tilted it, again and again.
Her father, Naveen, called: “Shreya, dinner!” She didn't answer. He called again. Nothing.
When he came to fetch her, the marble was racing down five levels, through a tunnel and into a cup.
Shreya looked up at him, blinking, as if waking from a dream. “Papa, is it dark already?”
“It's been dark for half an hour.”
She hadn't noticed the heat, the dark, or the hunger. She only knew that the marble finally landed in the cup, every time.

How many levels did the marble race down?
It raced down five levels, through a tunnel and into a cup.
How did Shreya seem to feel when she looked up at her father?
She seemed dazed and happy, as if waking from a dream, too absorbed to notice the dark or heat.
What made the marble-run absorbing for Shreya?
It was challenging enough to need adjustments, but solvable with effort, so it held her full attention.
How might Naveen feel seeing the finished marble run?
Naveen probably feels amused and proud, seeing how deeply Shreya was absorbed.

"Nandini, you're sulking at that rejection email as if it's the last ship leaving," said Thomas uncle, laughing. "Let me tell you about 1989. I was twenty-one, trying to get on a merchant ship as a cadet. I went to the shipping offices in Kochi every Monday for eight months. Every Monday, no. Some clerks knew me by name. One gave me tea out of pity.
My friend Jacob said, 'If it's meant to be, it'll come.' He stopped going. He waited for a letter that never came.
I didn't know if I'd ever get a berth. I knew only that if I stopped going, I definitely wouldn't. On the thirty-fourth Monday, a captain needed someone that day. I was standing there.
It wasn't fate, kutty. It was being there on the day, without knowing."

How long did Thomas uncle keep going to the shipping offices?
Every Monday for eight months.
What was young Thomas feeling during those months of Mondays?
He felt uncertain but determined, not knowing if he'd ever get a berth yet refusing to stop.
What was the turning point in Thomas uncle's story, and what made it possible?
The thirty-fourth Monday, when a captain needed someone that day; it happened because he kept showing up without any guarantee.
How is Jacob's hope different from Thomas's?
Jacob waited for fate and stopped going, so his hope had no action, while Thomas kept acting despite uncertainty.

She was wild to be at home--to hear, to see, to be upon the spot to share with Jane in the cares that must now fall wholly upon her, in a family so deranged; a father absent, a mother incapable of exertion, and requiring constant attendance; and though almost persuaded that nothing could be done for Lydia, her uncle's interference seemed of the utmost importance, and till he entered the room the misery of her impatience was severe. Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner had hurried back in alarm, supposing, by the servant's account, that their niece was taken suddenly ill; but satisfying them instantly on that head, she eagerly communicated the cause of their summons, reading the two letters aloud, and dwelling on the postscript of the last with trembling energy. Though Lydia had never been a favourite with them, Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner could not but be deeply affected. Not Lydia only, but all were concerned in it; and after the first exclamations of surprise and horror, Mr. Gardiner readily promised every assistance in his power. Elizabeth, though expecting no less, thanked him with tears of gratitude; and all three being actuated by one spirit, everything relating to their journey was speedily settled. They were to be off as soon as possible. "But what is to be done about Pemberley?" cried Mrs. Gardiner. "John told us Mr. Darcy was here when you sent for us;--was it so?"

Elizabeth is desperate to get home and help Jane after Lydia's elopement. When her aunt and uncle return, she reads them the letters, and Mr. Gardiner promises to help in every way. They plan to leave at once, and Mrs. Gardiner asks whether Darcy had been there.

Disha's diary, because I need to think on paper. Today Neelam turned three, and at her birthday Maa-ji asked, in front of everyone, why my daughter speaks only English. I smiled and said she's learning. Inside I felt caught.

By choosing on purpose what matters most, Bengali at bedtime, Dida's rhymes and cooking together at Poila Boishakh, and dropping the fasts Disha never believed in.

Carla went to the zoo and counted 12 zebras in their enclosure. She then visited the camels and learned that there were only half as many camels as there were zebras. Next, she visited the monkeys and counted 4 times the number of monkeys as camels. Finally, she saw some giraffes and counted only 2 giraffes. How many more monkeys than giraffes did Carla see?

There were 12 zebras / 2 zebras/camel = 6 camels at the zoo.
There were 4 monkeys/camel x 6 camels = 24 monkeys at the zoo.
Therefore, Carla saw 24 monkeys - 2 giraffes = 22 more monkeys than giraffes.
The answer is 22.

At two, Kashish clamped both lips and shook the head from side to side each time Tanuja held out another spoon of dal. There were no words yet, but the message was clear. Tanuja put the spoon down. "No more. Okay." Kashish relaxed.

At two Kashish shook the head from side to side to refuse the spoon; at five Kashish lowered the head, eyes on the floor, after the tower fell, showing shame; at twenty-five Kashish bowed the head with folded hands at the funeral, showing respect and grief. Kim is an office manager. Every morning she spends 5 minutes making coffee, 2 minutes per employee getting a status update, and 3 minutes per employee updating payroll records. If there are 9 employees in the office, how long does Kim's morning routine take?

First find how many minutes Kim spends on each employee: 2 minutes/employee + 3 minutes/employee = 5 minutes/employee
Then multiply that time by the number of employees to find the total time spent on status and payroll updates: 5 minutes/employee * 9 employees = 45 minutes
Finally, add that time to the time spent making coffee to find the total time: 45 minutes + 5 minutes = 50 minutes
The answer is 50.

messages.content: Tell a children's story, about 100 words, about a crow who learns to share a piece of bread with a hungry dog.

Kallu the crow found a big piece of bread and flew to a high branch. Below, a thin brown dog was looking up at him, sniffing. "Please, can I have a little?" the dog asked. "No!" said Kallu. "It is mine." He began to eat, but a crumb fell, and then the whole piece slipped down. Kallu was sad and hungry. Then the dog picked it up, broke it in two, and offered Kallu half. Kallu was ashamed. "Thank you," he whispered. From then on, they shared everything they found.
