Naming what happened, apologising plainly, asking what would help, and changing his behaviour with calendar reminders.

Janice gets paid $10 an hour for the first 40 hours she works each week, and $15 each hour of overtime after that. If Janice works 60 hours one week, how much money does she make?

Janice makes during her first 40 hours of work $10/hour * 40 hours = $400.
Janice works 60 hours - 40 hours = 20 hours during her overtime.
Janice makes from working overtime $15 * 20 = $300.
The total she makes a week is $400 + $300 = $700.
The answer is 700.

This weekend's football game matched the Seattle Seahawks with the Denver Broncos. The final score was 37-23, with the Seattle Seahawks taking the win. The Seattle Seahawks won so their total points would be 37 with 9 of those points accrued through the scoring of field goals, which makes 37-9=28 points left to be scored by touchdowns.
There are 28 points scored by touchdowns and each touchdown is worth 7 points, so this means that 28/7=4 touchdowns were scored by the Seattle Seahawks throughout the game.
The answer is 4.
Why does the moon look bigger near the horizon?

So it's the same size all night?

messages.content: In Desmos type y = mx + 1 and add a slider for m from -3 to 3. Describe what happens to the line as m changes. Which m gives a horizontal line, and which line is steepest?

Answer: Every line passes through (0, 1). For m > 0 the line rises from left to right, for m < 0 it falls, and m = 0 gives the horizontal line y = 1. The steepest lines are m = 3 (rising) and m = -3 (falling).

The number c = 1 is the y-intercept, so all the lines pivot about the point (0, 1) like the hand of a clock. The slope m is "how much y goes up when x goes up by 1": for y = 2x + 1 the points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5) show y rising 2 each time. As m grows from 0 to 3 the line swings upward and gets steeper; negative m makes it fall. Big negative slopes like -3 are just as steep as 3, only downhill. Ask the child to predict each picture, then drag the slider to check. Desmos can also show a table of points: click the line and choose "table".

Adam earns $40 daily in his job. 10% of his money is deducted as taxes. How much money will Adam have earned after taxes after 30 days of work?

The amount of money deducted from Adam's daily pay is $40 / 10 = $4.

The answer is 1,080.

Zainab, you asked on the podcast about the worst planning habit I've seen. Let Afreen tell you about a team I worked on two years ago.
Our lead, a really kind person, padded every estimate. If a task needed two days, she wrote five. If a report needed a week, she wrote three. She said, "Better safe than sorry."
And for a while it felt great. Nobody was stressed. But here's what happened. With five days for a two-day job, people started on day four. Meetings got longer. Emails piled up. Everyone relaxed, because the deadline looked so far away.
Then everything finished on the last possible afternoon anyway, in a rush, with the same late nights as before.
All that extra time never turned into anything saved. It just filled up. By the end of the year, we were slower than the team next door, which padded nothing.

What would you change first in how the lead planned?
Give realistic estimates for each task and keep one shared buffer at the end, used only for real delays, so the time isn't quietly used up.
How might the team next door have seen Afreen's team?
They may have seen a team with lots of time on paper that still rushed at the end, and finished slower overall.

"The eagerness of a listener quickens the tongue of a narrator." I said this rather to myself than to the gipsy, whose strange talk, voice, manner, had by this time wrapped me in a kind of dream. One unexpected sentence came from her lips after another, till I got involved in a web of mystification; and wondered what unseen spirit had been sitting for weeks by my heart watching its workings and taking record of every pulse.
It means the gipsy talks more freely when the listener is keen. The speaker is so caught up that her strange talk feels like a dream, and wonders what unseen spirit has been watching their own heart.

messages.content: Describe a monkey stealing food on a hill station road, for a funny travel blog post. Around 90 words.

We had stopped at a viewpoint for just five minutes. My uncle opened a packet of peanuts and turned to admire the valley. That was his mistake. A large grey monkey dropped from the railing, snatched the packet and sat on the car bonnet, eating calmly as if he had paid for it. My uncle waved his arms and shouted. The monkey stared back, unimpressed, and cracked another peanut. Then three more monkeys arrived. We retreated into the car and watched the feast through the windscreen, laughing helplessly.

Another word for "big" is "large".

Maria had come to the casino boat in Panaji with her flatmate Dolma for one hour, just to see it. Three hours later she was still at the roulette table, and the last ferry back left at midnight. She had bet on black ten times. Red had come up nine. "Black's due," she muttered. "It's been red forever." She doubled her bet. Red. She had now lost her rent money for the month. Dolma grabbed her arm. "Maria, we're going to miss the ferry." "One more. It has to come." Dolma stood between her and the table. "It doesn't have to. The wheel doesn't remember." On the ferry, Maria sat shaking, staring at the black water. At home, Dolma found the number for a gambling helpline and sat beside her while she called.

How many times had red come up out of Maria's ten bets on black?
Red had come up nine.
What was Maria feeling when she said "It has to come"?
She felt desperate and stubborn, sure black was due after so much red, and couldn't stop.
What did Dolma do, and why was it a good response?
She physically stopped Maria, explained the wheel doesn't remember, got her to the ferry, and sat with her while she called a gambling helpline that night.
How might Dolma have felt standing between Maria and the table?
Dolma was probably frightened and determined, worried about her friend and the last ferry.

Dear Amma,
Don't worry, I'm okay now. I want to tell you something that happened.
Last week I was so homesick I couldn't eat. I missed your sambar, our Chennai sea breeze, even our neighbour's loud TV. I didn't tell anyone here in Delhi.
But my flatmate Anjali noticed. She didn't ask questions. She just made me ginger tea every night and sat on my bed while I studied. On Saturday she took me to a South Indian place near the metro, "so you can argue about the chutney."
Amma, I felt safe for the first time since I got here. It's small, but it tells me I'm not alone.
I'll call you Sunday.
Keerthana

She made ginger tea every night.

Thank her, share some home food or stories, and look out for her in small ways when she needs it.

Cynthia has three children whose ages add up to 35. Matthew is two years older than Rebecca and four years younger than Freddy. How many years old is Freddy?

Let A be Matthew's age.
Rebecca is A - 2 years old.
Freddy is A + 4 years old.
Their ages add up to 35, so A + A - 2 + A + 4 = 3A + 2 = 35.
Therefore, 3A = 35 - 2 = 33.
Matthew is A = 33 / 3 = 11 years old.
Thus, Freddy is 11 + 4 = 15 years old.
The answer is 15.

Class 3 note, Thursday.
This morning we found Bubbles, our class fish, floating at the top of the tank. Most of the children were sad for a few minutes, then went back to drawing. Sumit (8) stayed by the tank. He asked me, "Why do things die? Will Bubbles be sad now? Where does a fish go?" Arnab, next to him, said, "Don't be silly, it's just a fish."
I didn't brush it off. I told Sumit that all living things have a life that ends, that Bubbles can't feel sad anymore, and that people believe different things about what happens after. He listened carefully and asked, "Will you die?" I said, "One day, when I'm very old, I hope."
We buried Bubbles in the garden at lunch. I've told his mother at pickup so she can continue the conversation at home.

Bubbles.

It suggests Sumit was curious and troubled, and wanted to understand death rather than move on like the others.

They answered simply and honestly instead of brushing it off, held a small burial, and told his mother so she could continue the talk at home.

I'm Lavanya, Vishal's flatmate. In our first semester, Vishal, nineteen, slept till noon, skipped morning lectures, and started assignments at midnight. There was no bell, no parent, no one to make him. After failing a quiz, he came into the kitchen looking shaken. The next week he'd taped a timetable to the wall: lectures in green, library in blue, cricket in red, sleep at midnight. He set two alarms. Yara shrank back against the cupboard, shoulders up, eyes on her mother's body, not her face.
Noa noticed. She let out a breath, crouched down low and opened her arms. "It's okay. Come." Yara hesitated, then stepped into the hug, red footprints and all.

Morgan goes to the drive-thru and orders his lunch.  He gets a hamburger for $4, onion rings for $2 and a smoothie for $3. If he pays with a $20 bill, how much change does he receive?

Morgan's lunch cost $4 + $2 + $3 = $9.
If he pays with a $20 bill, he will receive change of $20 - $9 = $11.
The answer is 11.

In the village, the doctor's jeep had come twice in one week, and nine-year-old Chaitanya had started lying awake. He heard whispers at night: "hospital," "the town," "we'll see." In the morning everyone smiled too much. One evening, his mother, Rashmi, found him sitting on the cattle-shed wall, very still. "Chaitu, you're worried about Dadaji." He nodded. "Is he going to die?" Rashmi sat beside him. "Dadaji's heart is tired and weak, and the doctor wants him in the big hospital in town so they can watch him closely. We don't know everything yet. When I know more, I'll tell you. I promise." Chaitanya thought. "I thought it was worse. Because everyone was whispering." "No more whispering. You can ask me anything." "Can I go see him?" "Sunday. We'll take the bus together."

How does Rashmi handle Chaitanya's worry?

She explains simply that Dadaji's heart is weak and he needs hospital care, admits she does not know everything and promises to tell him more. She ends the whispering and promises a bus trip to visit on Sunday.

Keerthana's mouth tightened and the marbles went back in the bag. "Fine, you play, then." Harsha felt stung, then a bit puzzled. Later Harsha tried again. "Would you like some ideas about the game?" Keerthana looked up. "Okay, go on." This time the marbles came out again, and the ideas were used.

At twenty, Harsha led a small lab team and gave out tasks for a long experiment. "Hafsa, please start the second dilution at ten, because the first sample has to settle before we can compare them, and I need the readings by two so we can plan tomorrow." Hafsa nodded, and asked one question about the temperature. She finished early and offered to help with the next table, without being asked.

What did Keerthana say after the marbles went back in the bag?
Keerthana said, "Fine, you play, then."

At ten Harsha called out ideas about the marbles unasked, and Keerthana's mouth tightened until Harsha asked if Keerthana would like ideas. At twenty Harsha gave Hafsa clear directions with the reason and the readings needed, and Hafsa cooperated. Asking, or explaining the reason, works better than commanding.

Keerthana was annoyed and felt bossed around, as if the game was no longer Keerthana's own.

To get to work, Ryan bikes one day a week takes the bus three times a week and gets a ride from a friend once a week. It takes him thirty minutes to bike to work. The bus takes ten minutes longer since it stops at every bus stop for other passengers. His friend driving him is the fastest and cuts two-thirds off his biking time. How many minutes does he spend every week commuting to work?

The bus to Ryan's work takes 10 minutes longer than his bike ride, so it takes 10 + 30 = 40 minutes.
Ryan takes the bus 3 times a week, so the bus rides take 40 * 3 = 120 minutes a week.
His friend cuts two-thirds off his biking time, which is 2/3*30 = 20 minutes a week.
This means his friend takes 30-20 = 10 minutes to drive him.
Therefore, Ryan spends 120 + 10 + 30 = 160 minutes every week commuting to work.
The answer is 160.

Monday, 10 a.m.: The list came out. Not even shortlisted. Charu closed her laptop. "It was all rubbish. Four months of rubbish," she told Lavanya at the next desk, and went to stand at the office window for a long time.

Wednesday evening: At home, Charu opened the file again, mostly to delete it. Instead she caught her own words: all rubbish. Was it? She made a grid. Idea: eight out of ten; the rainwater roof was good. Drawings: six. Cost estimate: three, rushed at the end. Written statement: four, too long.

In my first month I asked my colleague Ankita, whenever she got a chance, for a file I needed that afternoon. She took me at my word and sent it three days later. I was quietly furious. Then in a review my team lead said my updates were "too long to find the point". I went home and cried into my curd rice. It took a chat with Ankita, who had moved from Kolkata two years before, to see it. "Here people say what they need, plainly. It's not rude. It's respect for time." So I tried. "I need this by four." It felt harsh in my mouth. Nobody minded. And when Ankita heard I missed Lucknow's long greetings, she started saying "Adaab" every morning, badly.

Three days later.

Nazia felt quietly furious, not yet realising the polite phrase had signalled there was no hurry.

Stating needs plainly, like 'I need this by four', which matched the office's way of respecting time.

Find your offer letter and see what it says about working hours. On Monday we'll work out who you can talk to, your HR or the labour department's helpline.' Make this verse into two sentences of modern prose.

Before his king with reverence due
Dhumraksha bowed him, and withdrew.
Around him at his summons came
Fierce legions led by chiefs of fame.
Well armed with sword and spear and mace,
They hurried to the gathering place,
And rushed to battle, borne at speed
By elephant and car and steed.

Dhumraksha bowed before his king with due reverence and withdrew, and at his summons fierce legions led by famous chiefs came around him. Well armed with sword, spear and mace, they hurried to the gathering place and rushed to battle, carried at speed by elephants, chariots and horses.

Lily got a new puppy for her birthday.  She was responsible for feeding the puppy 1/4 cup of food three times a day for two weeks starting tomorrow.  For the following 2 weeks, Lily will feed him 1/2 cup of food twice a day.  She has fed him 1/2 cup of food today.  Including today, how much food will the puppy eat over the next 4 weeks?

1 week has 7 days so 2 weeks will have 2*7 = 14 days
The puppy will eat 1/4c three times a day so .25*3= .75 cups per day
The puppy will eat .75 cups of food a day for 14 days for a total of .75*14 =10.5 cups
The puppy will then eat `.5 cup of food twice a day so .5*2 = 1 cup per day
The puppy will eat 1 cup of food a day for 14 days for a total of 1*14 = 14 cups per day
She has already fed him .5 cup of food and he will eat 10.5 cups and another 14 cups for a total of .5+10.5+14 = 25 cups of food
The answer is 25.
From the bus stand, a red bus leaves every 12 minutes and a blue bus every 18 minutes. Both leave together at 8:00 a.m. When do they next leave together?

Answer: At 8:36 a.m. LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes.

Red buses leave after 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72 ... minutes (multiples of 12). Blue buses leave after 18, 36, 54, 72 ... minutes (multiples of 18). The common multiples are 36, 72, ...; the lowest is 36. So they meet again 36 minutes later, at 8:36 a.m., and then every 36 minutes. Tip: list the multiples of the BIGGER number and stop at the first one the smaller number divides (18 no, 36 yes).

Thursday
Caught myself doing it again today. Sarika walked in twenty minutes late to the handover, laughing on her phone, and I rolled my eyes so hard my head moved. In my head I called her something I wouldn't say to my worst enemy. That's the third time this week I've felt that sneer rising, a kind of disgust, like she isn't worth taking seriously.
I don't like who I am when I think like that. Rashid Chacha used to say contempt is the fastest way to ruin any team.
So I named it, right there: that's contempt. Then I went out to the car park and walked two rounds before I trusted my face.
After lunch I asked her for five minutes. "When you're late to handover, I miss the updates on the night cases, and it makes my shift harder. Could we agree on 8:45?" She looked surprised, then apologetic. Her bus route had changed. She'll message me if she's running late.
Imran

How late did Sarika arrive to the handover?
Twenty minutes late.
What did Imran notice feeling toward Sarika?
Imran noticed a rising sneer of contempt and disgust, as if she weren't worth taking seriously, and felt uncomfortable about it.
How did Imran handle the contempt?
Imran named the feeling, took a walk to settle, then raised the specific concern about handover timing respectfully and asked for an agreement.
What was going on for Sarika?
Her bus route had changed, making her late; she was surprised and apologetic when Imran raised it.

What does Dhritarashtra believe about destiny and effort?

Dhritarashtra said, "Tell me, O Sanjaya, how that great bowman Drona and the Panchala prince of Prishata's race encounter each other in battle, each striving his best. I regard destiny to be superior, O Sanjaya, to exertion, when Santanu's son Bhishma (even) could not escape Pandu's son in battle. Indeed, Bhishma, when enraged in battle could destroy all mobile and immobile creatures, why, O Sanjaya, could he not then by his prowess, escape the son of Pandu in battle?"
He thinks destiny is stronger than effort. As proof, he asks how Bhishma, who could destroy all creatures when angry, could not escape the son of Pandu in battle.

After Saturday practice at the district football club, Kishore's friends crowded round one scooter in the club car park. Rohit started it, Faizan climbed on behind, and they both looked at Kishore. "Come on, squeeze in. It's two kilometres." Nobody had a helmet. Half the car park rode like this; the watchman didn't even look up. Kishore's hand was already on the seat. Then he pictured the flyover and the trucks. "I'll take the bus," he said. Faizan rolled his eyes. "Seriously? You sound like my mother." Rohit snapped, "We waited for you, yaar." Kishore's face burned, but he stepped back. Coach Elizabeth, locking the kit room, had heard. "Kishore, I'm going your way. Front seat's free." In the car he stared out of the window, still embarrassed. A few minutes later they passed the scooter, wobbling round a pothole with three heads and no helmets.

Who was locking the kit room?
Coach Elizabeth.
How did Kishore feel after saying he'd take the bus?
He was embarrassed, his face burning at the teasing, even though he stood by his choice.
What made Kishore's choice take courage?
Riding three to a scooter without helmets looked normal to everyone, so saying no meant being mocked by friends who were annoyed they had waited.
How did Rohit and Faizan see Kishore's refusal?
They saw it as fussy and a letdown, rolling their eyes and snapping, because the risk felt ordinary to them.

39. Because 32 - 8 = 24, and 24 + 15 = 39, so 39 people are on the bus.

I'm Mahima, and I've watched Ojas say yes for years: the neighbour's shifting, the office collection, everyone's cousin's admission forms. Lately he seems different. On Sunday afternoons he doesn't answer his phone, and he told us why: "That's my nap time." A few weeks ago he handed the building's water-tank rota to three others, saying, "I'll take it one week in four."
When his colleague asked him to cover a Saturday shift, I heard him say, "I can't do this week, but I can do next month." There was no long apology.
I can't tell how it feels for him inside. He looked a bit nervous when he said no. But he also looked rested, and the people who depend on him are still getting his help.

How often did Ojas say he would take the water-tank rota after handing it over?
He said he would take it one week in four.
How might Ojas feel when he says no?
Ojas looked nervous when he refused, but also rested afterwards, so he may feel both uneasy and relieved.
What made Ojas's no to the Saturday shift work well?
He named what he could not do and offered a later date, without a long apology. That kept his kindness dependable.
What is Mahima feeling as she watches Ojas set limits?
Mahima seems curious and quietly admiring, though unsure what Ojas feels inside.

Before. Two days before Diwali, the Sharma family group had 214 unread messages. Swati scrolled: sweet recipes, a baby photo, then a forwarded video about the opposition, then three uncles arguing in capital letters. Her cousin Ojas had left the group once already. She put the phone down, tired to her bones.

During. On Diwali morning, a new forward arrived claiming a minister had banned firecrackers nationwide. Swati checked; it was false. She typed carefully: "Happy Diwali, everyone! 🪔 Small request: can we keep this group for family news and photos, and check before forwarding? Love you all." Then she posted a picture of Dadi's rangoli.

After. A week later, the group was calmer. One uncle still sent forwards now and then; Swati replied with a photo of her dinner and moved on. Ojas messaged her privately: "Rejoined. It's nice again." She grinned and muted only the uncle's late-night videos.

How many unread messages did the family group have two days before Diwali?
214 unread messages.
How did Swati feel as she scrolled the group before Diwali?
She felt exhausted and weary, loving her family but worn out by the arguments and forwards.
Which of Swati's gentle rules worked, and why?
Asking warmly to keep the group for family news and to check before forwarding worked, because it set a limit without shaming anyone.
How might Ojas see the change in the group?
Ojas seems relieved and glad, rejoining because the group felt "nice again".

Today Aditi and I did a coin-toss contest on the balcony. Heads, she gets a biscuit; tails, I get one. It came heads FIVE times in a row! Aditi was jumping.
I said, "Now it HAS to be tails. It's my turn by law." I was so sure I bet her my two biscuits.
Heads again.
Papa laughed and said, "Good boy, but the coin doesn't remember what it did before. It has no brain." I said coins should be fair. He said fair means every toss is half and half, every single time, even after five heads.
I still think tails is coming. I'll try again tomorrow.
Chirag

How many times in a row did the coin come up heads?
It came heads five times in a row.
Why was Chirag so sure the next toss HAD to be tails?
Chirag felt confident that after five heads the coin owed him a tails to even things out, as if chance keeps score.
What could Chirag try tomorrow to test his idea?
He could write down lots of tosses and look at what comes after every run of heads, to see whether tails is really due.
How did the contest feel for Aditi?
Aditi was jumping with joy at five heads, and winning Chirag's two biscuits as well must have made it a lucky day. 😊
Write a paragraph about stars in the sky, 35 words: they are far-away suns, they twinkle, and sailors used them to find their way. Say they are easy to see on clear nights.
Stars are far-away suns. They twinkle in the sky at night. Long ago, sailors used them to find their way across the sea. Stars are easy to see on clear nights, so look up and enjoy them.

Some kids looked at me like I was being annoying, but Miss said, “Yes, that's a careful way to check.” Then she told me exactly which step was right and which one to fix. I liked that she didn't just say “good.” Mama says I ask a lot of questions, but I think asking is how I learn. Tomorrow I will do the same again when I don't understand fractions. Zainab.

Who did the writer ask about subtraction?
Miss Aditi.
How did Zainab feel about checking the steps with Miss Aditi, even when some kids looked annoyed?
Zainab felt confident and pleased, liking that Miss didn't just say "good" and believing that asking is how to learn.
What made Miss Aditi's reply helpful?
She named which step was right and which to fix, rather than just saying good.
How might the classmates who looked annoyed be feeling?

The school bus stopped at the crossing outside their village, and the others were already jumping off. "Come on, Ayesha," Hrithik called. "Everyone's going to the canal. Skip the practice test. Real friends don't ditch the group." Mehwish and Rinku were watching her. The five of them had shared tiffins since Class 5. Ayesha gripped her bag strap. The test mattered; Abbu had taken a day's leave to help her revise. But if she stayed, would they still save her a seat tomorrow? Would the group still be hers? "You're choosing a test over us?" Hrithik said. Her throat went tight. The driver honked. "I'll see you at lunch," she said quietly, and stayed on. The bus pulled away. Through the dusty window she saw Rinku hesitate, then run back and climb in beside her. Neither of them said anything. They didn't need to.

What did Hrithik say real friends don't do?
Real friends don't ditch the group.
What was Ayesha afraid of as she gripped her bag strap?
Ayesha felt torn and anxious, afraid that choosing the test would cost her the seat, the tiffins and the whole group.

A short, calm answer without a fight, then an ally in Rinku, which made the refusal easier to bear.

In March, Karthik had noticed something odd in the Pune office's billing system: one client was being charged twice for the same server hours. It was a small amount. He meant to mention it. Then the release came, then his leave, and he forgot, or let himself forget.

In September the client's finance team emailed: they had found six months of double charges and were threatening to end the contract.

Karthik read the email three times, his chest tight. He could stay quiet. Nobody knew he had seen it.

That evening he went to his team lead, Nilesh. "I saw this in March and didn't flag it. I should have. Here's what I saw and when."

Nilesh leaned back. "That's not great." A long pause. "But thanks for telling me. Send me your notes. We'll show the client the exact dates." Karthik walked out shaky, and lighter.

What was the client being charged twice for?
The client was being charged twice for the same server hours.
What was Karthik feeling after reading the client's email?
Karthik felt guilty and anxious, his chest tight, and was tempted to stay quiet.
Why was speaking up now better than staying silent again?
Admitting the delay and sharing notes let the team give the client exact facts, instead of letting a hidden problem grow.
How does Nilesh see Karthik's late admission?
Nilesh is disappointed about the delay but appreciates the honesty and uses Karthik's notes to fix things.

Akash sat with a blank page headed Manifesto and realised he had only "better school, better future." That meant nothing. So he decided to ask. During recess, with a notebook and one question, "What one thing would you fix?", he went from bench to bench. Canteen queues, said Aadhya; her Class 9 friends waited twenty minutes for one samosa. The football club had two working balls. The library closed at four, before club practice ended. By Friday he had ninety-one answers in tally marks, and three problems came up again and again. Akash crossed out the vague lines and wrote three: a second canteen counter, more balls, library open until five. "Now I can promise something specific," he said, "and people can check it."

How many answers did Akash collect by Friday?
Akash collected ninety-one answers.
What did Akash realise about the first draft of the manifesto, and how did he feel?
Akash realised 'better school, better future' meant nothing, and felt dissatisfied enough to go and ask classmates.
What other approach could Akash use to check the ideas, and why?
Akash could talk to the principal and canteen staff about what is possible, because a promise voters can check needs to be one that can be kept.
How does Aadhya see the campaign question?
Aadhya likely feels listened to, since a real complaint about the canteen queue was asked for and could turn into a promise.

Counsellor's note, college wellbeing centre, Monday.
Anjali, a final-year student, came in today, very tense. Her father has told her that if she does not agree to marry a man the family has chosen by Diwali, she should "never come home again". Her mother has stopped speaking to her. She said, "Maybe he's just upset. Maybe it's normal." I asked whether she feels she has a real choice. She said no, and that she is afraid to go home for the holidays. We talked about the difference between a parent stating a limit and pressure that removes her choice and makes her afraid. I explained that she does not have to decide anything today. With her permission, I contacted the college's women's cell and a legal aid counsellor, and gave her the helpline number. She will stay in the hostel over the holiday. I will see her on Wednesday.
— Rekha

When does Anjali's father want her to agree by?
By Diwali.
What was Anjali feeling during the session?
She was tense and afraid to go home, and unsure whether her father's pressure was normal.
What steps did the counsellor take that were wise?
She explained Anjali didn't have to decide today, connected her with the women's cell and legal aid with her permission, gave the helpline and arranged for her to stay in the hostel.
How does Rekha see the father's ultimatum?
Rekha sees it as pressure that removes Anjali's choice and makes her afraid, not simply a parent stating a limit.

Lenny bought 20 boxes of pens. Each box contained  5 pens. She gave 40% of the pens to her close friends and one-fourth of what's left to her classmates. How many pens were left for Lenny?

Lenny has 20 x 5 = 100 pens.
She gave her close friends 100 x 40% = 40 pens.
So, 100 - 40 = 60 pens were left.
Half of 60 is 60/4= 15 pens.
Thus, Lenny has 60 - 15 = 45 pens left.
The answer is 45.

Estimate 256 + 348 to the nearest hundred and to the nearest ten. Which estimate is closer to the exact answer?

Answer: Nearest hundred: 300 + 300 = 600. Nearest ten: 260 + 350 = 610. Exact: 604, so the nearest-hundred estimate happens to be closer here.

Usually rounding to the smaller place (tens) gives the closer estimate. But sometimes the roundings cancel: 256 went UP by 44 and 348 went DOWN by 48 when we rounded to hundreds, so the errors almost cancelled (600 is only 4 away from 604). To the nearest ten, both numbers went UP (by 4 and 2), so 610 is 6 too big. Estimates are not "right" or "wrong" - they are sensible or not.

Today I was painting the sunset in my new watercolour book, doing the orange going into pink really slowly so it wouldn't go muddy. Then Mummy called, "Baljeet, go help Samir bring the clothes in, it's going to rain!" I shouted "NOOO" and the pink turned into a blob. I stomped out and didn't talk to Samir the whole time.
Later I felt bad. Mummy said she didn't know I was in the middle of the hard part. We made a deal: if it's not an emergency, she'll say "five minutes" first. Rain is sort of an emergency though 😅

The sunset, with orange going into pink.

Unless it's an emergency, Mummy will say "five minutes" first, which gives time to finish a delicate part.

"Let him cry, Ankita. He'll learn."
"Learn what, Mummy? Something's wrong. Listen, that's his scared cry."
Ankita went to the window. A dog was barking loudly in the lane below, and Sahil was pressed against the wall, crying.

Sahil hid his face in her neck and the crying faded.

A dog.

He was scared of the loud dog barking, and his crying was a signal that he needed help.

Going to him promptly and moving him away from the window worked, because it met his real need for safety.

Friday night
I told Madam today I'm leaving the Kathak class. After six years.
It's because of the new group. Riddhi and the others think classical dance is "aunty stuff". Last week Riddhi saw my ghungroo in my bag and laughed, "Are you going to a wedding?" Everyone laughed. I laughed too.
I want to sit with them at lunch. I want to be in the photos. So I quit.
But tonight Vijay was watching an old video of my performance on Ammi's phone, and I heard the tabla and my heart jumped. I miss the feeling of my feet knowing where to go before I do.
I think I traded something I love for a seat at a lunch table.
Maybe I can't have both. Or maybe I could find friends who don't laugh.
Zainab

How many years had Zainab been learning Kathak?
Six years.
Why did Zainab quit a dance form Zainab loves?
Zainab wanted to belong with Riddhi's group, so their laughter felt more powerful than the love of dancing.

Keeping the dancing alive, perhaps going back to class, and looking for friends who don't laugh at what Zainab loves.

Vijay may feel proud of the dancing in the video and puzzled that Zainab quit.

messages.content: At a certain school, 2/3 of the population are females. One-tenth of the males are foreign students. If the school has 300 students, how many students are non-foreign male students?

There are 300 x 2/3 = 200 females in the school.
So, 300 - 200 = 100 are males.
Out of the 100 males, 100 x 1/10 = 10 are male foreign students.
Thus, there are 100 - 10 = 90 non-foreign male students.
The answer is 90.

Today I cleaned my cupboard, and I found my old stuffed rabbit at the very back. His ear was a bit torn, but he looked just the same. I remember carrying him everywhere when I was little. I sat on the floor and hugged him for a long time. I will not give him away. I put him on my bed.

Lokesh did not look down. His hand slid into the front pocket and came back with the geometry box. "How do you always find it so fast?" Pema whispered. "It lives there," Lokesh whispered back. Hi Parul,
I'm writing this instead of saying it at dinner, because I'd rather be clear than awkward.
Since June I've paid the electricity and internet bills, and you've been paying me back when you remember. By my notes, it's 1,850 now across three months. I've been quietly annoyed about it, and that isn't fair to either of us, because you didn't know.

On Saturday morning Kashish folded a sheet of paper and drew a yellow kite with a smiling sun for Elizabeth's birthday. Her heart hopped as she handed it over at the party, and her mouth stretched into a big smile. Elizabeth had a pile of shop-bought presents, but she kept holding the kite and said it was the best one. Then Elizabeth gave Kashish a drawing of two girls holding hands under a rainbow. "This is us." Kashish said, "Thanks, it's so pretty!" and hugged the paper to her chest, warm all over. She wanted to give something back, so on Sunday she made a card with a crooked red heart for her Papa, Saurabh, and gave it to him while he chopped tomatoes. He wiped his hands, read the wobbly letters aloud and fixed the card to the fridge with a magnet, right in the middle. "Here, where everyone can see," he said. Kashish stood looking at the fridge for a long time.

What did Kashish draw on the card for Elizabeth?
Kashish drew a yellow kite with a smiling sun.
How did Kashish's giving to Elizabeth differ from her receiving Elizabeth's drawing, and how did it lead to the card for Papa?

She gave a kite she made herself with a big smile and Elizabeth loved it; when she received a drawing she hugged it and felt warm and loved, which made her want to give something back, so she made a card for Papa.
What was Kashish feeling as she hugged Elizabeth's drawing?
She felt loved and warm all over.

When the news came that Rajesh from their class had died of dengue during the monsoon holidays, the small school in Mandya felt different. The headmaster held a two-minute silence under the neem tree. Some girls cried openly; a few boys kicked stones and joked about the bus being late. Farhan didn't cry or joke. He sat on the steps where he and Rajesh used to share groundnuts and didn't move till the bell. His friend Karthik, who couldn't sit still, got the class to collect notebooks for Rajesh's little sister. That evening, the class teacher found Farhan still on the steps and sat down beside him without saying anything. After a while, Farhan said, 'He owed me two rupees.' Then his face crumpled.

What did Karthik get the class to collect?
Notebooks for Rajesh's little sister.

Farhan had been holding his grief in silence, and a small, ordinary memory finally let the sadness break through.

The teacher sat beside him quietly without pushing him to talk, giving him room to grieve in his own way.

Keeping busy and doing something useful may be Karthik's way of grieving, since he couldn't sit still.

Saurabh felt torn and uneasy, stomach twisted, because the promise to Swati was pulling against wanting to go to the party.

Bill has played 200 games of poker and won 63% of them. If he plays 100 more games and loses 43 of them, what is his new win percentage?

First find the total number of games Bill has won: 200 games * 63% = 126 games
Then find how many of the next 100 games he wins by subtracting the number he loses from the total: 100 games - 43 games = 57 games
Then add his new wins to his old wins to find his total wins: 57 games + 126 games = 183 games
Then add the old total number of games to the new total number of games to find the overall total number of games: 200 games + 100 games = 300 games
Then divide the total number of games Bill won by the overall total number of games and multiply by 100% to find the percentage of games he won: 183 games / 300 games * 100% = 61%
The answer is 61.
Lucca has 100 balls and 10 percent of his balls are basketballs. Lucien has 200 balls and 20 percent of them are basketballs. In total how many basketballs do Lucca and Lucien have?

Lucca has 100 basketballs x (10 / 100) = 10 basketballs.
Lucien has 200 basketballs x (20 / 100) = 40 basketballs
Together they have 10 basketballs + 40 basketballs = 50 basketballs.
The answer is 50.

A fixer uses 30% of the nails in a container to repair the kitchen. He also used 70% of the remaining nails in the container to repair the fence. If there were 400 nails in the container, how many nails are remaining?

The fixer used 30/100*400 = 120 nails to fix the kitchen.
The number of nails remaining in the container after he fixes the kitchen is 400-120 = 280
He also uses 70/100*280 = 196 of the nails remaining in the container to fix the fence.
The total number of nails which the fixer hasn't used is 280-196 = 84
The answer is 84.

A hall is 4.5 m long and 3.6 m wide. It is to be covered with square tiles, all the same size, without cutting any. What is the largest tile that can be used, and how many are needed?

Answer: Tiles of side 90 cm; 5 x 4 = 20 tiles. HCF(450, 360) = 90.

Change to centimetres so the numbers are whole: 450 cm and 360 cm. The side of the tile must divide both lengths exactly, and we want the LARGEST, so we need the HCF. 450 = 2 x 3^2 x 5^2, 360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5; HCF = 2 x 3^2 x 5 = 90 cm. (Euclid: 450 = 1 x 360 + 90, 360 = 4 x 90 + 0.) Along the length 450 / 90 = 5 tiles, along the width 360 / 90 = 4 tiles, so 20 tiles. Draw the 5 by 4 grid to see it.

A store sells pencils and erasers. It has a rule that for every pencil you buy, you must buy 2 erasers which cost 1/2 the price of the pencils. If they sold 20 pencils and earned $80, how much do erasers cost?

They sold 40 erasers because 20 x 2 = 40
Therefore 20(Pencil Price) + (1/2)(40 x Pencil Price) = 80
Therefore 40(Pencil Price) = 80
Therefore (Pencil Price) equals 2 because 80 / 40 = 2
An eraser costs $1 because 2 / 2 = 1
The answer is 1.

Spot the mistakes. a) "r = -0.9, so there is almost no correlation." b) "r = 0.95 between hours of sleep and marks, so more sleep causes higher marks." c) "The line y = 20 + 4x fits data for x = 1 to 10, so at x = 100 the value is 420." d) "I got r = 1.12." e) "b = -2, so r = 0.7." f) "r = 0, so x and y are unrelated."

Answer: a) -0.9 is a STRONG negative correlation. b) Correlation does not prove causation. c) Extrapolation far outside the data; unreliable. d) Impossible: -1 <= r <= 1, so there is an arithmetic error. e) b and r always have the same sign. f) r = 0 means no LINEAR correlation; there may be a curved relationship.

a) The sign gives the direction; |r| gives the strength. b) A lurking variable (general health, a calm routine) may affect both, and we have no experiment. c) The formula gives a number, but the pattern may not continue beyond x = 10. d) A value outside -1 to 1 always means a slip, often using sum x^2 in place of Sxx. e) b = Sxy / Sxx and r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx x Syy) have the same numerator, and the denominators are positive. f) See the U-shaped example (D10).

A drone takes off from the corner O of a school ground. Take x metres east, y metres north and z metres up. It hovers at P(12, -4, 3). In which octant is it? Where is the point on the ground directly below it, how high is it, and how far is it from O? How far is it from the east-west boundary line (the x-axis)?

Answer: Octant IV (+, -, +). The point below it is (12, -4, 0); it is 3 m high, 13 m from O, and 5 m from the x-axis.

Read the coordinates as three moves from O: 12 m east, 4 m SOUTH (y is negative), 3 m up. The signs (+, -, +) give octant IV. The ground is the xy-plane (z = 0), so the point straight below is (12, -4, 0) and the height is |z| = 3 m. OP^2 = 12^2 + (-4)^2 + 3^2 = 144 + 16 + 9 = 169, OP = 13 m Why: O to the foot F(12, -4, 0) is a flat distance sqrt(144 + 16) = sqrt160; then F to P is 3 m straight up, at right angles, so OP^2 = 160 + 9 = 169. The distance from the x-axis: the foot on the x-axis is (12, 0, 0), and from there P is 4 m across and 3 m up: sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5 m. In general the distance of (x, y, z) from the x-axis is sqrt(y^2 + z^2) - leave out the coordinate of THAT axis. Common mistake: answering |x| = 12 (that is the distance from the yz-plane).

Saturday: At the phone market in Lucknow, Harish, twenty, picked up a slim black phone and felt a small thrill. "This one," he told Ojas. The shopkeeper hadn't even switched it on.
Monday: Harish made a comparison sheet on his laptop. The black phone won on "looks premium," "good for interviews," "feels solid." The grey one's better battery he wrote down as "not a big deal." He showed Ojas proudly. Ojas raised an eyebrow. "You decided on Saturday. This is just a costume for it."
Two weeks later: At 3 p.m., in the middle of a lab, the black phone died. Harish sat on the corridor steps, charger-less, and texted from Ojas's phone: "Okay. Maybe I picked it and then found reasons." Ojas sent back a thumbs up and a battery emoji.

When did the black phone die?
At 3 p.m., in the middle of a lab, two weeks later.
How did Harish feel about the black phone, and how did that change?
Harish felt a small thrill and was proud of the sheet that backed his choice, but when the phone died mid-lab he felt stuck and admitted he picked it first and found reasons later.
What could Harish do differently before buying something next time?
He could list what really matters, like battery life, before he goes to the shop, so the good feeling doesn't choose first.
How might Ojas feel reading Harish's text from the corridor?
Ojas is probably amused and a little satisfied at being proved right, but still friendly, sending a thumbs up.

Friday, late
Tonight, drying dishes, I said to Uma, "Soon you won't have to worry about me any more." I meant it as a joke. I think.
Since I lost the job I've felt trapped. Uma pays for everything. Every meal she buys feels like proof I'm a burden. I see no way out of this.
Uma put the plate down and turned off the tap. She asked me straight, "Gurleen, are you thinking of ending your life?" I couldn't answer. Then I said yes.
She didn't panic. She held my hands and said, "Thank you for telling me. You are not a burden." She called the helpline with me, right there in the kitchen. She's sleeping in my room tonight. In the morning we're going to the hospital together.

What was Gurleen doing while speaking to Uma?
Drying dishes.
How has Gurleen been feeling since losing the job?
Gurleen has felt trapped and hopeless, believing Gurleen is a burden with no way out.
What did Uma do that took Gurleen's words seriously?
She asked directly, stayed calm, said Gurleen is not a burden, called the helpline together, stayed the night and arranged hospital help in the morning.
How might Uma have felt hearing Gurleen's joke?
Uma was probably alarmed and frightened, which is why she stopped everything to ask directly.

Urmila had moved to the city in June, and by July some classmates mocked how she said "water" and wrinkled their noses at her lunch. One remarked that people from her region and "her sort of family" did not belong at this school. Urmila felt small and angry. She told the class teacher, who took it seriously, and she kept eating with the two girls who asked about her hometown. Gurpreet, one of them, had frozen when the remark was made and felt uncomfortable afterwards. The next day she said to the classmate, "That isn't okay," and later checked on Urmila. "I should have said it sooner." "It helped," Urmila said. Madhuri, at the next desk, had always looked down on scholarship students and rolled her eyes at their old bags. Seeing how Urmila was treated, she caught herself. "I have had things easy," she thought. She asked Urmila to teach her a phrase in her language and to bring lunch to share. Urmila kept her roots and learned the local ways slowly.

How did Gurpreet respond the day after the remark?
She told the classmate, "That isn't okay," and later checked on Urmila.
How did Gurpreet's small stand differ from Madhuri's change, and what did each do for Urmila?
Gurpreet, after freezing, said it was not okay and checked on Urmila, while Madhuri noticed her own contempt for scholarship students and asked Urmila to teach her a phrase and share lunch.
What was Urmila feeling after the remark about her region and family?
She felt small and angry.
What could Urmila do to keep her roots in the new city?
She could keep sharing her language and food with friends who are curious, keep her allies close, and learn local ways gradually.
Judy uses 10 pencils during her 5 day school week. A 30 pack of pencils costs $4. How much will she spend on pencils over 45 days?

She uses 2 pencils a day because 10 / 5 = 2
She will use 90 pencils in 45 days because 2 x 45 = 90
She will need 3 packs of pencils because 90 / 30 = 3
She will spend $12 because 3 x 4 = 12
The answer is 12.
How can I stop biting my nails? Why do we sneeze when dust gets in our nose? Why do we put a wet cloth over a hot forehead with fever? what is "treachery"?

1. Notice when you do it and keep your hands busy with something else. Keep your nails short so there is less to bite.
2. A sneeze blows the irritant out of the nose. Because the dust irritates the lining of the nose, a sneeze pushes air out fast to blow it away.
3. People use a wet cloth for comfort. Because the water evaporates and takes away some heat from the skin.
4. "Treachery" is a noun. It means the betrayal of someone who trusts you.
Please give me a advice about my problem.
Please give me some advice about my problem. Why: "advice" has no "a"; use "some".

In the HR room of the logistics company, Damini turned her screen around. "The training system shows you never finished the forklift safety course, Gargi. You told me last month you had."
Gargi felt her face go hot. For a second a dozen explanations lined up: the system glitched, the link didn't work, she'd done it on a colleague's login.
She let them go.
"That was false," she said. "I didn't finish it. I said I had because I was behind on everything and didn't want to look incompetent in my first review. From today I'll finish the course before I sign any floor checklist, and I'll tell you when I'm behind instead of covering it."
Damini studied her. "You know I'll have to check your training records for a while."
"I know. That's fair. You found it; that's not your fault."
She did the course that afternoon, all three modules, and emailed the certificate at 5:58.

Which course had Gargi never finished?
The forklift safety course.
What was Gargi feeling when Damini turned the screen around?
Gargi felt her face go hot with embarrassment and was tempted by a dozen excuses before letting them go.
What made Gargi's response a real repair?
Gargi said plainly what was false and why, named what would change, finished the course that afternoon, and accepted being checked without blaming Damini.
How might Damini see Gargi after this conversation?
Damini will keep checking the training records for a while, but a plain admission with no excuses gives her reason to trust again slowly.

The Pune inter-school debate final ended, and the judges called Mridul's name. He grinned so wide his cheeks ached, and punched the air once. Then he went straight to the front row, where Tanuja ma'am was clapping. "Ma'am, you made me rewrite that rebuttal four times. Thank you." On his way out he found Farzana from the other school sitting on the stairs, holding her notes. "Your point on water rights was the best one of the day," he said. "I had no answer to it." She looked up, surprised. On the bus home, his friends wanted him to post the trophy photo everywhere. Mridul shrugged. "Maybe later." He spent the ride on the phone, telling Amma about Farzana's argument.

She made him rewrite it four times.
How did Mridul feel when his name was called, and what shows it?
He felt joyful and proud; he grinned till his cheeks ached and punched the air once.

He thanked Tanuja ma'am and went to praise Farzana's argument, enjoying his win while staying kind to someone who lost.

She likely felt surprised and respected, which could ease the sting of losing.

Zubin, you've decided the new boy is a show-off because of one day? Let your Mahima nani tell you about Farida. When I was ten, a new girl joined our class in Jabalpur. On her very first day, she knocked my ink bottle over my copy and didn't say sorry. That was it. For me, Farida was rude. In the weeks after, she shared her tiffin with everyone, helped the little ones cross the road, even lent me a pen. I told myself she was just showing off. Months later, our teacher told us Farida had been so frightened that first day that she couldn't speak at all. My ears burned. One day, and I had written her whole story. We became friends after that, and she still sends me mangoes every summer.

What did Farida do on her first day?
She knocked the ink bottle over Mahima's copy and didn't say sorry.
Why did young Mahima explain away Farida's kindness as showing off?

The teacher explaining that Farida had been too frightened to speak that first day, which showed the first impression had been wrong.
What might that first day have been like for Farida?
Farida was new and frightened, so scared that she couldn't speak, let alone say sorry for the ink.

Vijay knelt on the path in front of Tanvir and lowered his voice. "That's a lot of upset. I'm right here." He pushed the shoe and a stray stone out of reach and waited. He did not argue or count to three. Tanvir's screams kept coming, but Vijay's steady presence seemed to fill the space around them.

After a while the screams thinned to sobs. Tanvir's fists uncurled. He looked up with wet lashes, then his arms opened, and he fell forward against Vijay's chest. Vijay held him, gave him sips from the water bottle, and breathed slowly so that his own chest rose and fell against the small one. The hiccups came, then slowed.

That evening, at bath time, Tanvir splashed the duck. Vijay said, "You wanted to stay at the park, and leaving felt hard for you. Tomorrow we'll go again." Tanvir repeated one word: "Park?" "Tomorrow," Vijay said. When Pema came in with a towel, Tanvir told her, "Sad park," and she nodded gravely. "Sad," she said. "And now warm and clean."

What did Vijay give Tanvir when the sobbing began?
He gave him sips from the water bottle.
How did Vijay's response at the peak and afterwards let Tanvir move from screaming to naming the feeling?

Vijay knelt, kept his voice low, moved the shoe and stone aside and waited without arguing, so the screams thinned to sobs and Tanvir fell against his chest for a hug and water. Later at bath time Vijay named the wish to stay and promised the park tomorrow, and Tanvir began to say "Sad park".
What was Tanvir feeling when he fell forward against Vijay's chest?
He was worn out and needed comfort; the storm had passed and he wanted to be held.
What could Vijay do the next time leaving the park is hard?
He could give a warning before leaving, stay calm and close if tears come, and repeat the plan to visit again.

Hi Neelam,
You said you've been getting headaches and just taking random tablets. Please don't. Let me tell you what I did when I moved to Delhi.
First, I found a general doctor near my flat with good reviews from colleagues, not just online. I kept the same doctor so they know my history.

Prescriptions, test reports, vaccination records and an insurance card.

Ayesha felt concerned and protective.

Choosing a regular doctor, keeping records organised, doing regular check-ups and seeing a doctor instead of self-medicating.

Neelam may feel cared for and a bit more confident about finding a doctor.

Bobby can deadlift 300 pounds at 13.  When he is 18 he can deadlift 100 pounds more than 250% of his previous deadlift.  How many pounds did he add per year?

His new deadlift is 300*2.5+100=850 pounds
So he added 850-300=550 pounds to his deadlift
This took 18-13=5 years
So he added 550/5=110 pounds per year
The answer is 110.

I'm Karthik, and last year I did something I'm still not proud of.
I shared an embarrassing photo of Binita in our class group. Her mouth full, eyes half shut. People sent laughing replies. Within an hour I deleted it.
The next day she asked me, "Why did you post that?" And I said, "What photo? I never posted anything. You're imagining it." When she showed me a screenshot, I said it must have been someone else using my phone. When she cried, I told her she was overreacting to nothing.

Karthik said it must have been someone else using the phone.

Karthik felt ashamed and couldn't stand seeing himself as the mean one, so he kept saying it didn't happen.

Karthik told Binita the truth and also told the class teacher.

People ask me when I knew it was over, and the honest answer is: long before I said so. I'm Rekha. For five months my line was "one more month." Sales were flat, the app's monthly users kept shrinking, and I kept telling the team the next release would fix it.

What I was really protecting was my pride. Two years of my life, my parents' savings. Quitting felt like admitting it had all been wasted.

Then Charu, who ran the accelerator where we'd started, asked to see the numbers. She didn't argue. She just asked, "What would have to be true in three months for you to keep going?" I couldn't answer.

So we wrote it down: kill criteria, with a date. When the date passed and the numbers hadn't moved, I shut it down on purpose. It hurt. But I chose the ending, and that mattered.

What was Rekha's line for five months?
Rekha's line for five months was "one more month."
What was Rekha afraid of underneath the words 'one more month'?
Rekha was protecting pride and feared admitting that two years of effort and the parents' savings had been wasted.
How did Charu's question help Rekha see the situation more clearly?
Asking what would have to be true in three months made Rekha realise there was no answer, and led to written kill criteria with a date.
How might Charu have seen the situation from outside?
Charu probably saw a founder drifting on hope, and chose to ask a calm question instead of arguing so Rekha could reach the decision independently.

Kamal's plan to tell Miss Joshi first thing, and walking in with her, let Mahima see the real result, a new deadline, which she remembered on Thursday.

I'm Keerthana, and I sit across from Tushar, who was building a small app to launch before Diwali. On Monday Tushar wrote 'Launch: 20 October' on the whiteboard, then wrote backwards: store review, testing, payment integration, login. Then Tushar drew a line two weeks ahead of the launch date, wrote 'slack' in it, and said, 'Reviews always take longer than they say.' Every dependent task went onto a shared checklist that we could all tick. I watched that list for six weeks. When the payment provider ran ten days late, the slack absorbed it and the launch date did not move. I can't tell whether Tushar was anxious the whole time, but the list was the first thing Tushar opened every morning.

What launch date did Tushar write on the whiteboard?
Tushar wrote 'Launch: 20 October'.
What might Tushar have been feeling while opening the checklist every morning?
Tushar may have been careful and a little anxious, though Keerthana cannot be sure of the inner state.

Tushar could give each risky task an owner and a small demo date, since early demos show a delay before it eats into the slack.
How might Keerthana have felt watching the slack absorb the delay?
Keerthana was probably impressed and reassured, since the launch date did not move.

Teacher's note: Class 9 chemistry, practical lab, 12 August. Written by Nikita Sharma.
Today I let students pick lab partners for the titration practical. Gautam, usually thoughtful, avoided Birsa, the tall boy who joined on the sports quota. I heard Gautam tell his friend, "He's a footballer, he won't know titration." He chose the student with the neatest notebook instead. During the practical, Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times. Birsa and his partner got a clean result on the first try, and Birsa explained the colour change to the next table. Gautam watched with his mouth half open. After class he came to my desk and said, "Ma'am, I thought he'd be bad at this. I was wrong." We talked about how he had decided before seeing any evidence. Next week I'll rotate partners at random, and I've asked Gautam to work with Birsa.

What happened to Gautam's pair during the practical?
Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times.
Why did it seem sensible to Gautam that Birsa wouldn't know titration?
Gautam felt confident because Birsa was tall and joined on the sports quota, which fit his idea of a footballer, not a chemist. The match to a type felt like enough reason.
What did Nikita decide to do next, and why might it help?
She will rotate partners at random and has asked Gautam to work with Birsa, so Gautam can learn about Birsa from real work instead of assumptions.
What might it be like for Birsa to be overlooked as a lab partner?
Birsa may be used to people assuming sports is all he is good at, and explaining the colour change to the next table may have felt like a quiet way of proving otherwise.

You want to know how I picked electrical work? Honestly, Gopika, it picked me a bit. In Class 9 I told everyone I'd be a doctor, because that's what toppers say. Then biology practicals started and I felt nothing. Zero.
Meanwhile our building's inverter kept dying, and I was the one opening it up with the watchman, reading the manual, asking the repair uncle a hundred questions. I'd lose three hours and not notice.
So I made a list. What am I good at? Patient with wires, good with my hands, bad with blood. What jobs use that? Electrician, electrical engineer, solar installer.
My parents were worried at first. I'm still Charu, still stubborn. But now when I talk about my future, I sound like myself.

What did Charu first tell everyone in Class 9?
That Charu would be a doctor, because that's what toppers say.
What does Charu losing three hours over the inverter suggest about Charu's feelings?
It suggests Charu felt absorbed and genuinely interested in a way biology never did.
What could Charu do next to test the list of possible jobs?
Charu could spend a day with a solar installer or electrician, or try a short course, to see how the real work feels.
How might Charu's parents have seen Charu's change of plan?
They were worried at first, perhaps because doctor sounded safer, but they may come round as they see how excited Charu is.
There's a clear sky tonight and I want to look at the stars.
Lovely. Go somewhere dark, away from street lights, and give your eyes about fifteen minutes to adjust.
Which stars can I find?
Look for the Big Dipper, if it is visible in your region, and use it to find the Pole Star. Phone apps that map the sky can help you name what you see.
Cool. Can I see planets too?
Sometimes. Planets look like bright steady lights, while stars twinkle. Check a sky chart for what is visible this week.

An open box is made from a square sheet of tin of side 18 cm by cutting equal squares from the four corners and folding up the sides. What size of square should be cut to make the volume as large as possible? What is that volume?

Now you try: a 24 cm square sheet.
The answer is x = 4 cm, V = 4 x 16^2 = 1,024 cm^3.
The children brought they're own lunch to the picnic. Spelling or grammar?

The children brought their own lunch to the picnic.
Why: "their" shows ownership; "they're" means "they are".
Is 100 a term of the sequence 3, 8, 13, 18, ...? Is 98?

Answer: 100 is not a term; 98 is the 20th term.

T_n = 3 + 5(n - 1) = 5n - 2. Try 100: 5n - 2 = 100, 5n = 102, n = 20.4. There is no "20.4th" term: positions must be whole numbers. So 100 is NOT in the sequence. It lies between T_2_0 = 98 and T_2_1 = 103. Try 98: 5n - 2 = 98, 5n = 100, n = 20, a whole number, so 98 IS a term (the 20th). A quick check by pattern: every term ends in 3 or 8 (the terms are 2 less than multiples of 5), and 100 ends in 0. Common mistake: rounding 20.4 to 20 and saying "yes".

The storm had torn half the tin roof off the family house in the village near Barabanki, and Asif had spent two days helping his father shift grain sacks and tie tarpaulins. His lab report for Dr Rajni Verma was due on Thursday, and the college was forty kilometres away.
On Tuesday morning, before anything else, he walked to the one spot near the well where the phone got signal and wrote to her: 'Ma'am, a storm damaged our house on Sunday night and I am needed at home till Wednesday. I have finished half the report. May I submit it on Saturday? I can send photos of the house and a letter from the pradhan.'
He was tempted to add that the whole family was homeless. They weren't; they were staying at his uncle's house next door. He left it as it was.
Her reply came that afternoon: 'Saturday is fine. Photos not needed. Hope everyone is safe.'

Where did Asif go to write the email?
To the one spot near the well where the phone got signal.
Why was Asif tempted to say the family was homeless, and what was he feeling?

'Did you see the class group last night?' Jyoti asked, dropping her bag beside Reena's.
'The dance video? Everyone was laughing.'
'You too. You sent twenty laughing faces and "cringe queen".'
Reena shrugged. 'Everyone was. It's just a group chat.'
'Meenal left the group at midnight. She's absent today.'
Reena's smile faded. 'I didn't even say anything that bad.'
'Forty people each said something small. That's forty things landing on one person.'
'It didn't feel like me. It was all the others.'
'Your name is on it, Reena. It's the same you in there.'
Reena stared at her phone. 'Should I message her?'
'Yes. Delete your comments. And we tell Ma'am at lunch.'
At lunch the class teacher listened, phoned Meenal's mother that afternoon and had the group closed.

What did Reena send in the group?
Twenty laughing faces and 'cringe queen'.
How did Reena feel when she heard Meenal was absent?
Reena felt uneasy and guilty, her smile fading as she realised the harm.
What steps did Jyoti suggest, and why?
Message Meenal, delete the comments and tell the teacher, because each small comment added up and Meenal shouldn't face it alone.
How might Meenal have felt seeing forty people laugh?
Meenal likely felt overwhelmed and humiliated, which is why she left the group and stayed home.

messages.content: Daisy's Flower Shop sold 45 daisies on its first day. On their second day, they sold 20 more flowers than they did on their first day. On the third day, they sold 10 less than twice the flowers that were sold than on the second day. If the flower shop sold a total of 350 daisies for 4 days, how many daisies were sold on the 4th day?

The flower shop sold 45 + 20 = 65 daisies on the second day.
Twice the number of flowers on the second day is 65 x 2 = 130.
So, the flower shop sold 130 - 10 = 120 daisies on the third day.
The total daisies sold for 3 days was 45 + 65 + 120 = 230.
Therefore, 350 - 230 = 120 daisies were sold on the 4th day.
The answer is 120.

In the village courtyard, little Hrithik lay crying and kicking because Dada had taken away the sickle he'd picked up.

Jagdish Dada didn't argue. He moved the sickle and a heavy pot far out of reach. Then he knelt down in the dust.

"You are upset," he said, low and slow. "I am here."

Hrithik kept kicking. Dada didn't talk more. He just stayed close.

After a while the kicking stopped. Hrithik lay there, hiccuping, looking at Dada's knees.

What had Hrithik picked up?
A sickle.
What was Hrithik feeling as he cried and kicked?
He was angry and upset that the sickle was taken away.
Why was Jagdish Dada's approach helpful?
He moved dangerous things away, knelt nearby, spoke calmly and waited without arguing, showing big feelings are survivable.
What might Jagdish Dada be feeling as he waits in the dust?
He may feel worried after seeing the sickle, but calm and patient, trusting that staying close will help.

I'm not sure how many people came to the fair in 1987, as I can't verify a headcount that exact. Local archives or an older resident might have it.

"Ritu, you keep saying people who complain at work are troublemakers. Let your Nani tell you about Joseph.
I was twenty-four, a clerk in the mill office in Coimbatore. One monsoon the bus drivers struck for a week, and the management passed an order: anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay. Half of us walked six kilometres every morning.
Some clerks tore the notice down at night. Others paid and cursed. Joseph, who sat across from me, did neither. He kept coming on time, wrote to the works committee with the strike dates, and signed it in his own name. I was sure he'd be sacked.
He wasn't. The committee gave a half-hour grace on strike days. And Joseph still stayed late every Friday closing the accounts, same as before. That's when I understood a person can love a place and still tell it where it is wrong."

What did the management order say about clocking in late?
Anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay.
What did Nani expect would happen to Joseph after the letter, and what does that suggest about her view back then?
She was sure he'd be sacked and worried for him, which suggests she then saw objecting as risky and even disloyal.
Which of Joseph's choices made the change possible, compared with the other clerks?
He neither tore down the notice nor paid and cursed; he wrote to the works committee with dates and his own name, which the committee could act on.
Why might Nani be telling Ritu this story now?
Ritu calls people who complain at work troublemakers, and Nani wants Ritu to see that someone can object openly and still be loyal.

You're asking whether a thumbs-up is rude, Lavanya? The juniors here still call me Nilesh sir, but at twenty-two I nearly lost a mentor over one. I was a trainee at an architecture firm. Mrs Kamath, our senior partner, sent me four paragraphs of careful notes on my first drawing. I was on a site in the rain, so I replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else. Next morning she was cool with me, and she passed my file to someone else. I sulked for a whole day. Then I went to her cabin and asked what I had done. "I wrote you a page," she said, "and you sent me a thumb." To me it had meant "got it, thank you". To her it meant I had not bothered. After that I wrote one real line back, even from a muddy site.

Where was young Nilesh when he replied with the thumbs-up?
He was on a site in the rain.
How did young Nilesh feel when his file was passed to someone else?
He felt hurt and sulked for a whole day; he was probably also confused, because to him the thumbs-up had only meant "got it, thank you".
What turning point in the story helped Nilesh repair things with Mrs Kamath?
Going to her cabin and asking what he had done, instead of sulking longer, let her explain how the thumb had felt to her.
How did Mrs Kamath see the lone thumbs-up?
After writing a page of careful notes, she saw the single thumb as a sign that he had not bothered, even though he meant thanks.

For two weeks Oskar's old phone sat in its box on the kitchen shelf of their Berlin flat, listed online for three hundred euros. Nkechi, his flatmate, watched him read the messages every evening. "One-fifty?" he would snort. "Do they know it has the good camera?" Listings for the same model all sat between one-forty and one-eighty, and Nkechi had seen them. On Sunday she made two coffees and put one beside him. "Quick question. If this exact phone was on someone else's listing for three hundred, would you buy it?" Oskar opened his mouth, then looked at his screen for a while. "I'd laugh at them," he admitted. "Then maybe ask one-seventy," Nkechi said, and he changed the price that night.

What price range were other listings for the same model?
Between one-forty and one-eighty.
How did Nkechi probably feel watching Oskar each evening?
She was probably amused but a little concerned, seeing him snort at fair offers night after night.
Why did Nkechi's question work better than arguing about the price?
It let Oskar picture himself as the buyer, so he saw the gap himself instead of being told.
What changed for Oskar after the coffee conversation?
He admitted he would laugh at a three-hundred listing and changed his price to a level buyers might accept.

Thursday, very late.
Today was the condolence visit at Jatin's house for his father. The room was full of white clothes and quiet voices. Jatin sat on the mattress by the photo, very straight, not crying.
Then his uncle mentioned the scooter, and I remembered the time Jatin's father drove his scooter into the Ganesh pandal and came out with a garland round his neck. It's the funniest story I know. It was right on my tongue. I actually opened my mouth.
Then I looked at Jatin's face. It was grey. His hands were gripping his knees. I closed my mouth and just sat next to him, shoulder to shoulder, for an hour.
Maybe one day he'll tell that story himself and we'll laugh. That has to be his choice, not mine.
Chaitanya

What did Jatin's father drive into?
He drove his scooter into the Ganesh pandal.
What was Chaitanya feeling when looking at Jatin's face?
Chaitanya felt a tug of concern and caution, seeing Jatin's grey face and gripping hands, and sensed the story would hurt him.
What did Chaitanya do instead of telling the story, and why did it help?
Chaitanya sat next to Jatin, shoulder to shoulder, for an hour, offering quiet company when a joke could have wounded.
What might Jatin need from friends in the coming weeks?
He may need people to sit with him and let him decide when, or whether, to laugh about his father's stories.

Omkar, you want the same card game everyone has, even though you love puzzles? Let your Jyoti dadi tell you about your Dadaji when he was nine. In our town that year, every boy had a kite with sharp string for the fights on the rooftops. Your Dadaji hated kite fights; his fingers got cut, and he was scared of the roof's edge. What he loved was fixing old clocks. But he begged his father for a kite, cried for three days, and got one. He stood on the roof every evening losing every fight, fingers cut, pretending he loved it. Then one day his friend Babloo came down and found him fixing a broken clock in the shop instead. Babloo sat and watched for an hour. After that the two of them fixed clocks together, and nobody laughed.

What did young Dadaji love doing?
Fixing old clocks.
Why did young Dadaji beg for a kite he didn't enjoy?
He wanted to belong and was afraid of being left out, so having what every boy had mattered more than his own love of clocks.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
Babloo came down and watched him fix a clock; sharing what he truly loved gave him a friend and belonging without pretending.
What might Babloo have felt sitting and watching for an hour?
Babloo was probably curious and fascinated, discovering something new with his friend.

Turn this into three short bullets.

They had not been long together before Darcy told her that Bingley was also coming to wait on her; and she had barely time to express her satisfaction, and prepare for such a visitor, when Bingley's quick step was heard on the stairs, and in a moment he entered the room. All Elizabeth's anger against him had been long done away; but had she still felt any, it could hardly have stood its ground against the unaffected cordiality with which he expressed himself on seeing her again. He inquired in a friendly, though general, way, after her family, and looked and spoke with the same good-humoured ease that he had ever done.

- Darcy tells Elizabeth that Bingley is coming, and Bingley soon walks in.
- Elizabeth's old anger is gone, and Bingley's warm greeting would have ended it anyway.
- Bingley asks after her family and speaks as cheerfully as ever.

At the school gate in the morning, Shankar held out a fist and Lokesh bumped it. “Ready for the test?” “Nope,” said Lokesh. “But ready for lunch.” They grinned.
Inside, the visiting principal stood in the corridor, and Shankar stepped forward to shake her hand. “Good morning, ma'am. Welcome to our school.” She smiled. Lokesh hung back. He was shy about touch with people he didn't know, so he joined his palms and said, “Namaste, ma'am.”
She returned the namaste. “Lovely to meet you.” Lokesh let out a breath.

What did Lokesh say when Shankar asked if he was ready for the test?
He said, “Nope. But ready for lunch.”
What was Lokesh feeling when he hung back, and what did he do about it?
He was shy about touching someone he did not know, so he chose a namaste instead of a handshake. He seemed relieved when she returned it.
What does this show about greeting choices?
A child can pick a warm, respectful greeting that suits him, such as a namaste, wave or fist bump, and that is enough.
How might the visiting principal see Lokesh's namaste?
As a polite and warm greeting, since she returned it and said it was lovely to meet him.

January: Manjula told her whole office, including her friend Nikita, that she would open her own bakery by December. She printed the plan and stuck it above her desk.
June: After three months of weekend baking stalls, she had new information: rents in her area were far higher than she had guessed, and she hated working every Sunday. Over lunch she told Nikita plainly, "I decided in January with half the facts. I'm not opening the bakery this year. I'll keep baking for orders." Nikita blinked, then nodded.
July: Manjula made a new, smaller promise to Nikita, on purpose: "I'll bake one new recipe every Saturday and send you photos." Every Saturday, a photo arrived.

What did Manjula print and stick above her desk?
The plan to open her own bakery by December.
How might Manjula have felt telling Nikita the plan had changed?
She likely felt a little awkward but calm and relieved, having accepted the new facts.
Why is Manjula's Saturday promise a wise use of commitment?
It is small and chosen on purpose, using a friend's expectation to build a good habit instead of trapping her in the old plan.
What might Nikita think when the photos keep arriving?
Nikita probably feels pleased and impressed, seeing Manjula keep a realistic promise after changing the big one.
After geometry class, Bill wants to count how many lines he drew. For each shape, he drew one line per side. If he drew 12 triangles, 8 squares, and 4 pentagons, how many lines did he draw?

For the triangles, he drew 36 lines because 12 times 3 equals 36.
For the squares, he drew 32 lines because 8 times 4 equals 32.
For the pentagons, he drew 20 lines because 4 times 5 equals 20.
He drew 88 lines in total because 36 plus 32 plus 20 equals 88.
The answer is 88.

I'm Jeevan. I was on the same site as Anirban the day the contractor told him to plaster over the crack in the third-floor beam before the client inspection. 'Don't make it a story. I'll handle it,' the contractor said. I watched Anirban stand under that beam for a long time, looking up. Then he said, loudly enough for the crew to hear, 'I understand what you're asking. But if I sign the checklist, it's my signature, not yours.' He photographed the crack, wrote it in the site register with the time, and phoned the structural engineer from the gate. The contractor shouted. Anirban's hands were shaking; I could see that. But he didn't change the register. By evening the engineer had come, and work on the floor above was stopped for repairs. I don't know what it cost him inside. I just know I'd want him on my building.

Where was the crack Anirban was told to plaster over?
The crack was in the third-floor beam.
What might Anirban have been feeling as he stood under the beam?
Anirban was probably torn and afraid, knowing the contractor would be angry, but unable to accept signing something he knew was unsafe.
Which of Anirban's actions made his stand effective?
He photographed the crack, wrote it in the site register with the time and called the structural engineer, following the proper channel so the repair actually happened.
How does Jeevan see Anirban after that day?
Jeevan admires and trusts him, saying Jeevan would want Anirban on any building Jeevan lived in.

Condense this paragraph into two sentences.

"I am by no means of opinion, I assure you," said he, "that a ball of this kind, given by a young man of character, to respectable people, can have any evil tendency; and I am so far from objecting to dancing myself, that I shall hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins in the course of the evening; and I take this opportunity of soliciting yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the two first dances especially; a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to the right cause, and not to any disrespect for her."

The speaker says a ball given by a young man of character for respectable people does no harm, and he likes to dance. He hopes to dance with all his cousins and asks Miss Elizabeth for the first two dances, trusting Jane will not take offence.
What does "a golden opportunity" mean? Please improve this sentence: They are waiting since morning. What is the meaning of considerable?

1. It means a very good chance that may not come again. For example: the trip to the science fair is a golden opportunity.
2. Corrected: They have been waiting since morning. Why: "since" with a starting point needs the present perfect continuous.
3. As an adjective, "considerable" means fairly large in size, amount or importance.
