Monday. Tushar, ten, saw his classmate Jasleen arrive with a shiny new pencil box with a calculator built in. "She's showing off," he told his friends.

Wednesday. He kept saying, "Jasleen thinks she's so great. She's jealous of all of us." His friends started to look at him strangely.

Friday. His mother asked why he kept talking about Jasleen. Tushar said, "She's jealous." His mother asked softly, "Do you wish you had a pencil box like that?" Tushar went quiet. Then he nodded, cheeks hot. "A bit."

"That's okay," she said. "Everyone wishes for things sometimes."

What was built into Jasleen's pencil box?
A calculator.
Why did Tushar keep saying Jasleen was jealous?
Tushar felt envious of her pencil box but saw that envy in her instead of himself.
What did Tushar's mother ask, and why did it help?
She asked if he wished he had a pencil box like that, gently letting him see and admit his own envy.
How might Jasleen feel if she heard she was called jealous?
Jasleen might feel hurt and confused, since she was only using her new pencil box.

Every morning at the bus stop in Buenos Aires, Layla's tongue turned to cardboard when Diego walked up. Her brain ran the film in advance: she says something odd, he raises an eyebrow, the whole bus laughs. So she stared at her phone and said nothing. On Thursday her friend Sofia muttered, "Just ask him about the maths quiz. People talk about the quiz." Layla's palms were damp, but when Diego stopped next to her she blurted, "Did you finish question six?" Her voice cracked on six. Diego laughed, not unkindly. "No, I gave up. Did you?" They spent the ride complaining about question six. She got off at her stop still red in the face, but she noticed she was smiling, and nobody on the bus had cared at all.

Where did Layla see Diego every morning?
She saw him at the bus stop in Buenos Aires.
Why did Layla stare at her phone instead of speaking?
She was afraid of embarrassing herself. Her mind ran the film in advance of saying something odd and the whole bus laughing.
What small step helped Layla break the silence?
She began with ordinary talk by asking about question six of the maths quiz, as her friend Sofia suggested, and accepted that her voice cracking was okay.
How might Diego have seen her question?
Probably as a friendly, normal thing to say. He laughed but not unkindly, and he joined in complaining about the question. 😊
The old chair is "falling apart". How is that different from "falling down"?

"Fall apart" means to break into pieces because of age or poor condition. "Fall down" means to drop to the ground.
Example: My old bag finally fell apart on the way to school.

Diego, five, told his babysitter Ulla that a dragon had visited kindergarten and eaten all the sandwiches. "It was green, bigger than the school, and it breathed on Mateo's hat." Ulla smiled. "Wow. Was it a pretend dragon or a real one?" Diego thought. "Pretend. Mateo was the dragon." "And who really ate the sandwiches?" "We did. At snack." He grinned and roared quietly at the sofa.

What did Diego say the dragon breathed on?
Mateo's hat.
What was Diego feeling as he told the dragon story?
Excited and playful, shown by the details and his grin. He was not necessarily trying to fool anyone, since he happily said Mateo was the dragon.
How did Ulla help separate pretend from real?
She played along first, then asked a friendly question about pretend or real, without calling him a liar.
How might Ulla see Diego's dragon tale?
As imaginative play. She smiles and stays curious, so she does not treat it as lying. 😊

Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Tejas, a second-year hostel resident, came to my office at 4 pm holding his phone out as if it were hot. He had paid 1,500 rupees as a 'registration fee' for a work-from-home typing job advertised in a chat group. This morning the recruiter asked for 4,000 more to 'unlock' his earnings.
He said, 'If I pay once more I get it all back, right?' Then he stopped himself. 'No. That's exactly how they keep you paying.'
We took screenshots of every message and the payment receipt together. He called the bank on the number printed on his card and asked them to flag the transfer, then phoned his mother on speaker. He was red in the face but steady.
Next step: he files a complaint on the cybercrime portal tonight. I will check in with him tomorrow morning.
- Vinita, student counsellor

How much had Tejas already paid, and what for?
He had paid 1,500 rupees as a registration fee for a work-from-home typing job advertised in a chat group.
What does Tejas's question 'If I pay once more I get it all back, right?' suggest he was feeling?
It suggests he was tempted to chase the lost money and hoped one more payment would undo it, though his next words show he saw the trap.
What turning point does Tejas take at this stage, and why is it wise?
He stops paying, saves the evidence and contacts his bank and his mother; losing 1,500 rupees hurts far less than sending 4,000 more to the same people.
What might Tejas's mother be experiencing when he calls her on speaker?
She may feel a jolt of worry, but hearing him explain calmly after already calling the bank could reassure her that he trusted her enough to tell her the same day.

At five, Urmila trailed Vikas from room to room, tugging at his sleeve. "There's nothing to do. Nothing, nothing." Vikas offered a toy and a book, but Urmila only leaned harder against his leg. Something inside wanted to do something and had no idea what.

At ten, one endless July afternoon with the screens switched off, Urmila stood in the empty living room for a while, groaned, then dragged two bedsheets and a broom across the chairs. By the time Jaya, Urmila's mother, looked in, there was a fort with a doorway, a flag and a sign that said "Members only." Urmila stayed inside for hours, drawing maps of an imaginary island.

At sixteen, on a flat Sunday, Urmila flicked from one app to another, a video for a few seconds, then a game, then the chat, then the video again, thumb never resting. There were books on the shelf and friends a message away, but none of it seemed to be the thing that would fill the empty feeling.

What did the sign on Urmila's fort say?
The sign said "Members only."
How does Urmila's boredom change between five, ten and sixteen?

At five Urmila clings to Vikas saying there is nothing to do, not knowing how to fill the time. At ten, with the screens off, boredom turns into a fort and a map of an island. At sixteen Urmila flicks from app to app because the empty feeling is hard to bear, even with books and friends on offer.
What was Urmila feeling while flicking between apps on the flat Sunday?
Urmila was restless and uneasy, trying to escape a flat, empty feeling.
What could help Urmila at sixteen when the empty feeling comes?
Urmila could put the phone away for a while and let the empty stretch happen, then try something hands-on like drawing, as at ten.

I live next door to Jahnavi and Rafiq, a married couple, and the wall between us isn't thick. All I can tell you is what I heard and saw. Sunday after Rafiq's parents left, Jahnavi stood on the balcony alone for a long time. Later I heard voices. Jahnavi said, calmly, "When your parents criticise me and you agree with them, I feel alone in the house that is meant to be ours. I don't want you to stop seeing them. I want us to face this as a team." Rafiq answered something I couldn't catch. Then it went quiet. The next morning Jahnavi watered the plants, stood straight and nodded to me as usual. I honestly can't say whether the talk solved anything, or what Jahnavi felt behind that nod.

What did Jahnavi do on the balcony after Rafiq's parents left?
Jahnavi stood alone for a long time.
What does Jahnavi say about how it feels when Rafiq agrees with the parents' criticism?
That Jahnavi feels alone in the house that is meant to be theirs.
What does Jahnavi ask for, and why is it a fair way to raise the issue?
Jahnavi asks that they face the issue as a team, and says clearly that Jahnavi does not want Rafiq to stop seeing the parents, so the request is about dignity and not about cutting ties.
How might Rafiq have felt hearing Jahnavi ask to face it as a team?

Rafiq may have felt caught between Jahnavi and the parents, or relieved that Jahnavi did not want the visits to stop. The quiet afterwards and the calm morning hint that the words were taken in, though the neighbour cannot be sure.
Padosi se kehna hai "Kal raat aapke yahan bahut shor tha." English?
Say: "There was a lot of noise at your place last night."

Why do some people talk with their hands?
A list has 20 words and Karan already knows 9 of them. How many words are still new?

1. It helps show meaning. Because gestures add emphasis to what they say.
2. 11 words. Because 20 - 9 = 11.
Now you try: is (4, 6) parallel to (6, 10)?
The answer is no: 6/4 = 1.5 but 10/6 ~ 1.67.

Seven-fifteen at Little Steps daycare, and Leela was wiping the last lunchboxes when Bhupen came in, shirt creased, bag sliding off one shoulder. His daughter ran to the snack shelf. "Biscuit!"
"Not now, beta. Dinner soon."
"I hate you! You're the worst papa!"
Leela saw his jaw tighten. He opened his mouth, voice already rising: "Do you want to go straight to..." Then he stopped. He put down the bag, closed his eyes and breathed out slowly.
Leela held the door and said nothing. When Bhupen opened his eyes, his voice came out lower.

What time did Bhupen arrive at the daycare?
Seven-fifteen.
What might Leela have been feeling as she watched Bhupen's jaw tighten?
She was probably tense and worried he might shout, then relieved and quietly respectful when he stopped to breathe.
What could help Bhupen keep this pause next time he is tired after work?
Noticing early body signs like a tight jaw and taking one breath before answering, as he did here.
How is Bhupen experiencing the moment his daughter shouts at him?
He is tired and stung by "I hate you", tempted to threaten, and has to catch his own heat before he can answer calmly.

Sit down, Bhupen, you asked how I got through my final year without letting the chatbot do everything. It wasn't wisdom. It was one bad night.
I was Madhav the last-minute man then. Farhan, my roommate, had the tool write his whole lab report, and I was tempted. But I opened my own data first and thought, what is this project actually for? If the tool writes the analysis, then the marks are for its thinking, not mine. And in the viva, who answers?
So I wrote three lines on a sticky note above my desk. The tool may explain a concept I'm stuck on. The tool may check my grammar. The tool may not write the analysis I submit.
Three months later, the external examiner asked why I chose that test. I could answer. Farhan couldn't.

What were the three lines on Madhav's sticky note?
The tool may explain a concept, the tool may check grammar, and the tool may not write the analysis Madhav submits.
Why did Madhav feel tempted that night, and what stopped it?
Madhav felt tempted because Farhan had the tool write a whole lab report, but asking what the project was for made the shortcut feel like handing over the marks.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
Opening the data first and asking whose thinking gets marked was the turning point, because it set the tool's role before any temptation took over.
How might Farhan have felt in the viva when he couldn't answer?
Farhan probably felt exposed and embarrassed, because the report looked finished but the reasoning behind it was not his.

In Barcelona, Sofia, fourteen, had cut her hair short over the weekend. On Monday, walking into class, she felt like every head turned to look at her, and every face was thinking, ugly.

At lunch, she told her friend Beatriz, "Everyone hates it. They're all laughing."

Beatriz frowned. "Who laughed?"

"Everyone. I could tell."

"I heard Marta say she liked it."

Sofia blinked. She hadn't heard that. She had only heard her own voice in her head that morning, saying, what have you done?

"Maybe it's me who's being mean to me," Sofia said slowly.

Beatriz nodded. "And for the record, I like it too."

What did Marta say about Sofia's hair?
Marta said she liked it.
Why did Sofia feel everyone was laughing?
She felt insecure and critical about her haircut, and her own harsh thoughts felt like everyone else's judgement.
What helped Sofia see her feeling differently?
Beatriz pointed out that Marta liked the haircut and said she liked it too.
How might Beatriz feel when Sofia says everyone hates it?
Beatriz probably feels surprised and concerned, wanting to reassure her friend.
On a moonless night, three fireflies danced in the evening breeze.  They were joined by four less than a dozen more fireflies, before two of the fireflies flew away.  How many fireflies remained?

Four less than a dozen is 12-4=8.
The three fireflies were joined by four less than a dozen more fireflies, for a total of 3+8=11 fireflies.
Two flew away, leaving 11-2=9 fireflies remaining.
The answer is 9.
What is the name of the girl I sat next to on the school trip?
I wasn't on your trip, so I don't know. A friend from the trip or your photos could help.
Use "because" to link these: The road was closed. We took the long way home.
We took the long way home because the road was closed.

Zainab's report card lay on the kitchen table, and she pushed it away. "Ms Fernandes gave me a low mark because she doesn't like me," she said. "The test was unfair. It's just my bad luck." She said the same thing about the spelling test, the drawing test and the sports day races. Each time her mother Disha, distracted by work calls, said, "We'll see," and moved on. Zainab stopped bringing up her results at all.

At school, the class teacher Jatin noticed that Zainab never tried the extra questions. "Why bother?" she said. "It happens or it doesn't." Jatin did not argue. He asked her to pick just five spelling words, practise them for a week and compare her score. Zainab got four out of five. She stared at the page as if it belonged to someone else.

That evening she said to Disha, quietly, "I practised, and it worked." Disha put down her phone and listened all the way through.

How many of the five spelling words did Zainab get right?
Zainab got four of the five words right.
What connects Zainab's blaming of luck and teachers with her result on the five spelling words?

Zainab says the low mark is bad luck and the test unfair, and skips the extra questions because it happens or it doesn't; after practising five spelling words she gets four out of five and says she practised and it worked. The small win shows her effort has an effect.
What was Zainab feeling when she said "Why bother?" to Jatin?
Zainab felt discouraged and powerless, as if results simply happen to her.
What did Disha do that helped Zainab?
Disha put down her phone and listened all the way through, so Zainab felt heard instead of brushed off with "We'll see".

A 10 m long and 8 m wide rectangular floor is to be covered with a square carpet with 4 m sides. How many square meters of the floor are uncovered?

The area of the floor is 10 m x 8 m = 80 square meters.
The area of the carpet is 4 m x 4 m = 16 square meters.
Therefore, the area of the floor not covered by the carpet is 80 square meters - 16 square meters = 64 square meters,
The answer is 64.

Arnab, you think your Yamini dida doesn't understand? When your father was born, your grandfather and I nearly stopped speaking.

We lived in two rooms in Howrah. The baby cried from nine till three every night. Your dadu worked at the mill, I did everything else, and we started keeping score. "I was up at one." "I was up at two and four." We spoke like two clerks handing over a ledger.

One night I snapped and threw a steel glass at the wall. Not at him, at the wall. We both stood there shocked.

The next morning, he brought me tea in bed, which he had never done. He said, "Yamini, we're on the same side." We sat for ten minutes before the baby woke. We decided he'd take the baby from nine to midnight, I'd take the rest. And we made a rule: every night, one thank-you, out loud.

We kept that rule for fifty-one years.

Where did Yamini and her husband live when the baby was born?
They lived in two rooms in Howrah.
How did young Yamini feel on the night she threw the glass?
She felt exhausted, angry and cut off from her husband, and then shocked at herself.
What was the turning point in Yamini's story?
The morning her husband brought tea and said they were on the same side, after which they split the nights and began one thank-you a night.
How might Yamini's husband have felt when the glass hit the wall?
He was likely shocked and shaken, and it seems to have made him see how strained they had become.

A year ago I was the fastest replier in my office. I'm Shreya, and I answered every email within two minutes and every chat within ten seconds. Then my manager, Sabina, asked how the big report was coming along. It wasn't. I'd been working all day, and it was still on page two.
So I tried something that felt lazy at first. Mornings from nine to eleven: one task only, notifications off, phone in a drawer. Then half an hour to answer everything at once. Then another block. Then a real lunch, away from my desk.
The first week I was anxious that people would think I'd disappeared. Nobody did. The report was done in four days instead of three weeks.
Now I work in blocks, check messages three times a day and leave at six. I get more done in less time, and I'm less tired. The switching was what had been eating my day.

What hours is Shreya's first focused block?
Nine to eleven in the morning.
How did Shreya feel in the first week of working in blocks?
Shreya felt anxious that people would think Shreya had disappeared, though nobody did.
What does Shreya's routine include, and why does it work?
Single-task blocks with notifications off, messages batched three times a day and a real lunch, so fewer switches mean better work in less time.
How might Sabina see the change in Shreya's work?
Sabina would likely be pleased and relieved, seeing the report finished in four days instead of three weeks.

On the drawing-room floor, Madhav stared at one gap in his jigsaw. He picked up a piece and pushed it in. No. Another. No. A third, turned round twice. No. His sister Bhavna, sipping juice on the sofa, watched him. He did not once look at the picture on the box lid. Piece after piece went to the same gap until a green one with two knobs clicked in. "It fits!" said Madhav, and reached into the pile to look for the next gap.

How did Madhav find the piece that fitted?
Madhav tried piece after piece at the same gap until a green one with two knobs clicked in.
What was Madhav feeling when the green piece clicked in?
Madhav felt pleased and excited, and he shouted, "It fits!" He was ready straight away for the next gap.
What other approach could speed up the puzzle, and why?
Madhav could look at the picture on the box lid and match colours, or sort the flat-sided pieces first. Fewer wrong tries would be needed.
How does Madhav's way of solving the puzzle look to Bhavna?
Bhavna sees her brother try one piece after another without looking at the picture. It may look slow, but he does not give up.

Tushar's phone buzzed during his lunch break in the Bengaluru office. A viral post: a café owner in Indiranagar slapping a delivery boy, with the café's name in the caption. Two thousand shares in an hour. His finger hovered over share. He was furious.
Then he stopped. Something about the video looked off. The signs in the background weren't in Kannada or English.
He spent four minutes searching. The same clip had been posted three years ago from another country. The café in the caption had nothing to do with it.
He texted Preeti, who had already shared it. “Check this, it's fake. Wrong café.” Preeti replied, “Oh no. Deleting.” Tushar posted the original link under the viral post. By evening, the café owner's reply was pinned at the top.

How many shares did the post have in an hour?
It had two thousand shares in an hour.
What was Tushar feeling when his finger hovered over share?
He was furious and ready to share, but something felt off and made him pause.
What did Tushar's four-minute pause achieve?
It revealed the clip was old and from another country, so he stopped the chain and helped Preeti and others correct it.
How might the café owner have felt before the correction?
The owner was probably frightened and angry, falsely accused in front of thousands.

Kalyani had cooked exactly three meals in her life before moving to Bengaluru for her first job. On Sunday she wanted to learn dal the way her grandmother made it.
Instead of one big pot, she cooked a cup of toor dal and split it into four small steel bowls.
"Why four?" asked Manoj, her flatmate's brother, visiting for the weekend.
"Because if I ruin one bowl, I've wasted a spoon of dal, not a whole pot," she said. She added a pinch of hing to one, more jeera to another, a dry red chilli to the third, and extra turmeric to the fourth, then tasted each with a clean spoon.
"Chilli one's closest," she said, writing it on the fridge list. "Next Sunday, chilli plus hing."

How many small bowls did Kalyani split the dal into?
She split it into four small steel bowls.
Why did Kalyani choose four small bowls instead of one pot?
She felt safe experimenting that way, reasoning that ruining one bowl wastes only a spoon of dal, not a whole pot.
What else could Kalyani do to make her next trial even more useful?
She could note the exact pinch or spoon she used in the winning bowl, so she can repeat it and build on it next Sunday.
How might Manoj see Kalyani's four bowls?
Manoj is curious and perhaps amused at first, then may see it as a clever way for a new cook to learn fast without much waste.

Ayesha kept a page in her notebook headed "what keeps pulling me back." Clean water appeared twice, rural schools five times. Then she asked which of those she could truly help with, and the answer was in her laptop bag: she could teach code.

Her friend Trisha had a bigger dream: education across the whole state. For months Trisha polished slides and tried logo after logo. Whenever a first step came up, it looked tiny beside the dream, and the weeks slid past with no class held.

Ayesha started small. Every Saturday she taught twenty students at a village school, free of charge, and kept notes on who came, who left early, and why.

A year later her notes told a plain story: of twenty seats, only three were held by girls. She sat with the headmaster and then with some of the mothers. Several said the Saturday afternoon slot clashed with housework, and they would feel easier with a woman teaching. Ayesha moved the class to early morning, after agreeing the timing with the mothers, and invited Jyoti, a teacher from the next village, to lead the group with her. Within two months the front row had nine girls.

How many students did Ayesha teach on Saturdays?
Ayesha taught twenty students at a village school.
Why did Trisha's plan stall while Ayesha's project grew?
Trisha stayed with the huge dream and never took a first step, whereas Ayesha began with one small class and her notes showed her what to change.
What might Trisha be feeling when a first step looks tiny beside the dream?
Discouragement, since any small action seems not worth doing next to such a big vision.
What could Trisha do to get started?
Trisha could pick one school and run a single small class soon, then build on what it teaches.

I am Simran and I watch my neighbour's daughter after school in our Kochi building. This afternoon Maria, five, brought her drawing to her father at the door. He was reading a message with a completely blank face. Maria stepped back. "Are you cross, Baba?" He looked up and laughed. "No, I'm thinking about work." She let out a breath. I can only guess, but I think she read his face as anger and only felt easy when he said so, though it could also be that she was just tired.

Where was Maria's father when she brought him her drawing?
He was at the door, reading a message.
What did Maria seem to think about her father's blank face, and what else might have been behind her question?
She seemed to think he was cross, since she stepped back and asked. She might also have been tired and unsure how to start.
What could Maria's father do the next time he is thinking hard?
He could say, "I'm just thinking," as soon as he sees her, so she doesn't need to guess.
How does Simran, watching from outside, know less than Maria's father about what happened?
She can only see what Maria and her father did and said, so she can only guess at Maria's feelings.

Note to file, engineering managers' meeting, 3 May.
Aadhya, who leads the mobile team, presented how her team decided what AI tools may and may not do. I want it on record because it was the clearest thinking in the room.
She had started from risks, not from features. Her list of allowed uses: drafting test cases, summarising public API documentation, suggesting names and comments. Her list of forbidden uses: pasting customer records, pasting API keys or passwords, using any output that no human has read. She explained each line with a real near miss from her team.
Two managers wanted to copy it at once. I have asked Aadhya to share it with all teams by Friday and to note where each team might need to differ.
Tejas

Where did Aadhya start from?
From risks, not from features.
What might Aadhya have felt when two managers wanted to copy the list?
Aadhya probably felt proud and encouraged that the careful thinking was useful beyond the mobile team.
Why was explaining each line with a real near miss effective?
Real examples made the rules concrete and believable, so other managers could see why each limit exists.
How might other teams be affected by Tejas's request?
They get a tested starting list by Friday, with room to note where their work differs.

Parul joined an NGO's weekend reading programme at a municipal school in Dharavi with a folder of ideas: new games, reward stickers, a plan to "transform" Class 4's reading. On her first day Sachin Sir, who had taught there eleven years, listened politely, then said, "Start by sitting with Asma and Kiran. They're stuck on joined letters." Parul felt slightly insulted. She had come to change things. But over three Saturdays on the floor with the two girls, she noticed things her folder hadn't: Kiran squinted at the board, and Asma read better when allowed to whisper. She told Sachin Sir, who arranged an eye check for Kiran through the school. At the end of the month Parul's folder was mostly unused. Asma read a full paragraph aloud to her, whispering, grinning. Parul stopped using the word "transform" in her NGO reports.

How long had Sachin Sir taught at the school?
Eleven years.
What was Parul feeling when Sachin Sir sent her to sit with two children?
Parul felt slightly insulted, having come with big plans to transform the class.
Why did following Sachin Sir's lead work better than Parul's folder?
Sitting closely with two children revealed real needs, like Kiran's squinting and Asma's whispering, which the teacher could act on.
How might Sachin Sir see Parul by the end of the month?
Sachin Sir likely sees a volunteer who listened and noticed useful things, and appreciates that she worked with the school rather than over it.
Make this polite for a neighbour: Take your dog away.
Could you please take your dog away?

When the fire alarm rang during the school drill, Zubin clapped both hands over his ears and squeezed his eyes shut. He didn't move. Lalremsiami Ma'am knelt, didn't pull his hands away, and said close to his cheek, “It's very loud. Keep your hands there. Hold my arm with your elbow.” She walked him out with the class, his hands still over his ears. Outside, she led him to the quiet side of the ground under the tree. Slowly, Zubin lowered his hands.

Where did the teacher lead Zubin outside?
To the quiet side of the ground under the tree.
What does Zubin covering his ears and shutting his eyes suggest?
It suggests the loud alarm was too much and he felt frightened, so he was protecting himself. He may also have been confused about what was happening.
What did Lalremsiami Ma'am do that respected Zubin's limit?
She let him keep his hands over his ears, walked him out safely, and took him somewhere quieter.
What would change if the teacher had pulled his hands away?
Zubin would likely feel more frightened and learn that his way of coping wasn't allowed.

Read this:

Senior auditor's note
Sumit, 25, joined our audit team this year. During the review of a hospital's accounts, he found that equipment bills were being paid twice to one supplier.
His manager, Lokesh, told him informally to "leave it, the hospital's director is a friend of the firm."
Sumit came to me. He was pale but steady. "If I ignore this, I become part of it."
I told him he had done the right thing by coming to me. We documented everything and reported it through the firm's ethics committee the same week.
Lokesh has been removed from the hospital account. Sumit told me he is worried about his future here. I told him his standing with me has only grown, and I have noted his conduct formally.

What did Sumit find in the hospital's accounts?
Equipment bills being paid twice to one supplier.
How was Sumit feeling when he came to the senior auditor?
He was pale but steady, anxious about the risk but determined not to ignore it.
What made the senior auditor's response right?
The auditor supported Sumit, documented everything and used the ethics committee the same week.
How might Lokesh feel after being removed from the account?
Lokesh may feel embarrassed and resentful, or worried about his own position.

Read this:

"Harish, did you see? Everyone laughed. The whole school."
"I saw you slip. I also saw you get up and finish the dance."
"I want to disappear. I'm never going on stage again."
"Jaya, remember when Mehra Sir's microphone squeaked in assembly? Everyone laughed for a minute. Does anybody talk about it now?"
"...No."
"Give it two days. They'll be laughing about something else."
"But they'll call me Jaya-Splat."
"Then they'll have to call me Harish-Splat too, because I'm sitting next to you at lunch."
Jaya gave a wet laugh. "You'd do that?"
"Already doing it. Come on, the samosas will finish."
She wiped her face, picked up her ghungroos and walked with him to the canteen.

What did Harish see Jaya do after she slipped?
Get up and finish the dance.
How did Jaya feel after everyone laughed?
Humiliated; she wanted to disappear and never go on stage again.
How did Harish help Jaya cope?
He reminded her how quickly people forget and stood by her by sitting with her at lunch.
How does Harish see Jaya's fall?
As a small slip followed by real courage, since she got up and finished.
My weekend plan is a leisurely walk. What does the first word hint at?

Leisurely means relaxed and unhurried. It is an adjective.
Example: We took a leisurely stroll along the river after lunch.
My British friend greets me with "hiya". Is it a word?

Yes. "Hiya" is an informal British greeting, like "hi". Use it with friends, not in formal messages.
Example: Hiya, Sam! How was your trip?

Read this:

My name is Zainab. In my first quarter at a logistics company, the weekly review was mostly one person talking. Joseph, the senior manager, would speak in long stretches, and the juniors waited for gaps that never came. I watched it for three weeks. Divya tapped a pen. Others looked at the clock. Nobody was being rude; the room simply ran that way. So I practised. I wrote a sentence in my notebook, and at the end of a topic I said, "Joseph, could I add one point before we move on?" My voice cracked the first time. He said, "Of course," and listened. Since then I've treated it as a skill: name the gap, ask for a minute, keep it short.

How long did Zainab watch the pattern in the weekly review before acting?
Three weeks.
What was Zainab feeling the first time of asking for a point, and how can you tell?
Nervous. The voice cracked the first time, even though the request was short and polite.
What did Zainab do to prepare before speaking up in the review?
Zainab wrote a sentence in a notebook and waited for the end of a topic to ask, "Joseph, could I add one point before we move on?"
How might Joseph see the juniors' silence in the review?
Joseph may not realise that the juniors are waiting for a gap; Joseph said "Of course" and listened once asked.
Diane is twice as old as her brother, Will. If Will was 4 years old 3 years ago, what will the sum of their ages be in 5 years?

Since Will was 4 years old 3 years ago, then he is 4+3 = 7 years old now
Dina is twice as old as he is so she is 2*7 = 14 years old now
In 5 years, Will will be 7+5 = 12 years old
In 5 years, Diane will be 14+5 = 19 years old
The sum of their ages at that time will be 12+19 = 31 years
The answer is 31.

Read this:

When I was fourteen, my feelings came like monsoon storms: sudden, huge, gone an hour later. I'm Hafsa, and I once slammed my bedroom door so hard the latch broke, after Abbu said no to a school trip. I once sent Payal a message saying I never wanted to see her again, over a seat on the bus, and spent a week trying to fix it. What helped wasn't anyone telling me to calm down. It was noticing the pattern. My cousin said, "The feeling is real, but it isn't permanent." So I made myself a deal: when the storm comes, I wait one hour. I walk three rounds of the colony park with loud music, or I write it out in the back of my maths notebook, or I call Payal and just rant. Most of the time, after an hour, I don't want to send the message anymore. There are a lot fewer broken latches now.

What broke when Hafsa slammed the door?
The latch.
How did Hafsa feel after sending Payal the angry message?
Hafsa felt regretful, spending a week trying to fix it.
What deal did Hafsa make, and why does it work?
Waiting one hour and using walks, writing or ranting to Payal, because the feeling passes and the urge to send or slam fades.
How might Payal have felt receiving the "never want to see you" message?
Payal was likely hurt and shocked, over something as small as a bus seat.

Read this:

In the block corner of the nursery, Suraj set the last block on top and his tower wobbled, then stood.
"Look at me! I did it all by myself!"
Wasim, the teacher, came over and crouched down. "I see. You put the big blocks at the bottom and the small ones on top. You worked hard on it."
Suraj rose on tiptoe, chest out, and beamed. Then he grabbed a handful of blocks from the box.
"Now I make it taller!"

Which blocks did Suraj put at the bottom of the tower?
He put the big blocks at the bottom.
What is Suraj feeling when he shouts "look at me"?
He feels tall, happy and proud, which shows in his tiptoes, out-pushed chest and beam. 🙂
Why was Wasim's reply useful for Suraj?
Wasim described what was there and named the hard work, so the pride felt real and Suraj wanted to try something bigger.
How might Wasim see Suraj's tower?
Wasim seems to see real effort and thinking in it, pointing out the big blocks below and small ones above.
Suggest a holiday reading habit in one sentence that begins with "Try" and uses fewer than 16 words.
Try reading one short story every afternoon under a shady tree.
Will's mom gave him $74 to go shopping. He bought a sweater for $9, a T-shirt for $11 and a pair of shoes for $30. He then returned his shoes for a 90% refund.  How much money does Will have left?

Will paid $30 for his shoes but then returned them and got 90% of the money back, so he lost 10% of the money, which means 10/100 * $30 = $3 is gone.
Will spent $9 + $11 + $3 = $23.
Will started with $74 - $23 that he spent = $51 remaining.
The answer is 51.

Read this:

Looking back, I can say it: I stayed in the hotel management course a full year longer than I should have. I'm Salma, and by the second month I knew I hated the kitchen shifts and the fake smiles at the front desk. But the first year's fees were already gone, and I had told everyone in the colony, Binita most of all, that I'd be running a hotel one day.
So I kept going. I'd sit on the bus with a low anger at myself, at the course, even at Binita for being excited for me. Quitting felt like standing in front of the whole colony and saying, "I was wrong." It took a failed exam for me to admit it.

What did Salma hate by the second month?
The kitchen shifts and the fake smiles at the front desk.
What was Salma feeling on the bus?
Salma felt a low, simmering resentment at the course and at being stuck, even towards Binita's excitement.
What could Salma have asked in the second month?
Whether Salma would sign up today with what was then known, setting aside the fees already spent and what people would say.
How might Binita feel on learning how Salma really felt?
Binita might feel sad and a little guilty, since all that excitement added to the pressure to stay.

metadata.subtype: Stuck in a choice already paid for [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sunday night. Group project due Friday and I have written the whole report again. Shreya said "I'll do slides" and sent nothing. The other two just react with thumbs-up. I felt so resentful that I nearly typed a long message in the group chat. Instead I decided to be practical. Tomorrow I will post a list with each person's part and a day, and ask everyone to update by Wednesday. If I had set roles at the start, that was my miss too. If nothing moves, I will tell our teacher before the deadline, not after. I am tired but calmer. 🙂 Manjula

What did Shreya say they would do?
Shreya said, "I'll do slides."
What did Manjula feel and want to do when nobody helped?
Manjula felt so resentful that Manjula nearly typed a long message in the group chat, but chose a practical plan instead.
What could Manjula do if the group still does not move?
Tell the teacher before the deadline, not after, as Manjula plans, after posting the list of parts and days.
How might Shreya see Manjula's list of parts and days?
Shreya may see it as a clear, fair request, or feel a little caught out about the slides, but it gives a way to start.

Rewrite this excerpt as a two-sentence summary.

"I will go to Meryton," said she, "as soon as I am dressed, and tell the good, good news to my sister Philips. And as I come back, I can call on Lady Lucas and Mrs. Long. Kitty, run down and order the carriage. An airing would do me a great deal of good, I am sure. Girls, can I do anything for you in Meryton? Oh! here comes Hill. My dear Hill, have you heard the good news? Miss Lydia is going to be married; and you shall all have a bowl of punch to make merry at her wedding."

She says she will go to Meryton to tell her sister the good news, then visit Lady Lucas and Mrs. Long. She tells Hill that Miss Lydia is to be married and promises everyone a bowl of punch to celebrate.

Read this:

In the Buenos Aires office, Mateo was known for helping. He covered Saturday shifts, lent his charger and never kept count.
Beatriz, a colleague, asked him to finish her reports four Fridays in a row so she could leave early. She never asked what he needed. When his mother was ill, he asked her to cover one Monday. She said she couldn't.
The next Friday, she came to his desk. "Mateo, could you do my report again?"
He looked up calmly. "No, Beatriz. I've helped you a lot, and I'm happy to help when it's a real crunch. But I can't keep doing your reports while you leave early."
She blinked. "Oh. Okay."
He went back to helping the new intern with a spreadsheet.

How many Fridays in a row did Beatriz ask Mateo to finish her reports?
She asked him four Fridays in a row.
What might Beatriz be feeling when she blinks and says "Oh. Okay"?
She is probably surprised and a little embarrassed, not expecting Mateo to set a limit.
What makes Mateo's answer a wise one?
He stays generous in general, but calmly stops giving to someone who only takes, and says so plainly without anger.
How might the new intern see Mateo?
The intern probably sees him as kind and helpful, since he still gives freely to people who need it.
My friend Meera hums loudly during our study sessions. I like her, but I can't concentrate.

That sounds distracting, and it's okay to say so kindly. She may not even realise. You could try, 'I can't focus when there's humming. Could we keep it quiet for thirty minutes and then have a song break?'
A song break is a great idea. She'll like that.
Then she has something to look forward to. Set a phone alarm for both parts so it stays fair.

Read this:

In the clinic waiting room, Pooja was glued to the cartoon on her mother's phone. When the nurse called another name, Neelam said, "Pooja, one more song, then phone off. Then we play I-spy." Pooja nodded without looking up. The song ended. Neelam took the phone. Pooja's face crumpled and she kicked the chair. "Give it! I want it!" Neelam kept her voice soft. "It's hard to stop. I spy with my little eye... something red." Pooja sniffed. She looked around. "The fire extinguisher?" "Yes!" Pooja wiped her nose. "My turn."

What was the first thing Neelam spied?
Something red, which Pooja guessed was the fire extinguisher.
How was Pooja feeling when she kicked the chair?
She felt upset and angry, as if losing the cartoon meant losing something she loved.
Which parts of Neelam's approach helped Pooja switch off?
She gave a clear warning, stayed calm and soft, and moved straight to a fun next thing, I-spy.
What would change if Neelam gave the phone back when Pooja kicked?
Pooja would learn that getting upset brings the screen back, making every switch-off harder.
What is the avaroha of Raga Bageshri?
The avaroha of Raga Bageshri is: S' n D M P D M g R S.

Blinky wants to make a three-layer birthday cake for her mom. The recipe for the smallest layer of the cake requires 2 cups of sugar. If the second layer is twice as big as the first and the third layer is three times larger than the second, how many total cups of sugar will she need for the third layer?

Since the second layer is twice as big as the first, then it requires 2* 2 = 4 cups of sugar.
Since the third layer is three times bigger than the second, then it requires 4 * 3 = 12 cups of sugar.
The answer is 12.

Read this:

Raksha Bandhan morning, and the bathroom door banged twice.
"Mumma! Gautam pushed me!"
"He pushed me first!"
Mumma came out of the kitchen with rakhi thread still in her hand. "Tarun, did you push him?"
"Only because I was late! Didi is coming at nine and I haven't even brushed."
"And why did Gautam push you?"
"Because he's rude. He's always rude."
Gautam folded his arms. "I was late too. My kurta's still in the cupboard."
"That's different," Tarun said.
"How is it different?" Mumma asked.
Tarun opened his mouth, then shut it. "Because mine was a reason."
Mumma laughed and handed them each a toothbrush. "You both had reasons. Brush together. Quickly."

What time was Didi coming?
Didi was coming at nine.
Why does Tarun think his own push was different?
Tarun feels his own rush from the inside, so his push seems fully explained, while Gautam's push feels rude and annoying because he can't see Gautam's hurry.
What did Mumma's question help Tarun notice?
Asking "How is it different?" made Tarun see that both of them were late, so neither push was really about being rude.
How might Gautam feel when Tarun calls him rude?
Gautam probably feels hurt and unfairly blamed, since he was also rushing to find his kurta.
Why do our ears sometimes pop when a plane takes off?
The air pressure around us changes. Because the pressure outside the ear drops as the plane climbs, and the ear pops when the air inside it evens out with the air outside.

Read this:

Coaching note, session 3.
Disha arrived with her five-year plan, which last month had been only job titles. Today it had a second column she called 'Life'. In it: marriage, probably in two years; her parents in Indore, her father's knees getting worse; and her own back pain from long sitting, which her doctor had asked her to take seriously.
She had then set limits beside each career goal. The promotion to team lead stays, but not through constant weekend work: one weekend a month at most. A trip to Indore every quarter goes into the calendar before project deadlines do. A walk every lunch break.
She said, 'Last year my career plan ate everything else.' I've asked her to try the limits for three months and bring back what held and what broke.
Suraj

What did Disha call the second column?
'Life'.
What does Disha's line 'my career plan ate everything else' suggest she felt last year?
It suggests she felt drained and regretful, as if work had crowded out her family and health.
What else could Disha do if a deadline clashes with an Indore trip?
She could decide in advance which one wins and tell her manager early, so the limit isn't broken in the moment.
How might Disha's parents be affected by the quarterly trips?
They get regular visits they can count on, which matters more as her father's knees worsen.

metadata.subtype: Approach: balancing career with family and health values [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday. Tushar arrived at the clinic reception at 9:20, twenty minutes late. Ganga, the front-office manager, wrote in her notebook: "Tushar, careless attitude." She told him sharply that patients were waiting.
Wednesday. Ganga's scooter got a flat on the ring road and she walked in at 9:30. "Nothing I could do," she told the receptionist, annoyed at the tyre, not at herself. That evening, filling in her notebook, she saw Monday's line about Tushar and stopped. She had never asked him why.
The following Monday. Ganga called Tushar in before opening. "You were late last week. What happened?" He explained that the bus from his colony had been cancelled twice that month. They agreed he'd take the earlier bus and message her if it was cancelled. Her feedback note said exactly that.

What did Ganga write in her notebook on Monday?
She wrote, 'Tushar, careless attitude.'
What made Ganga stop when she saw Monday's line?
Having just blamed a flat tyre for her own lateness, she realised she had judged Tushar's attitude without ever asking why he was late.
What did Ganga's new feedback note get right?
It recorded the real cause, the cancelled bus, and a practical plan, instead of a label about attitude.
What would change for Tushar if Ganga had never looked back at her notebook?
He would still be marked as careless for cancelled buses and might feel he could never explain himself.

Read this:

The exam hall was stuffy, and Ishita's chair creaked every time she moved. The fans hummed, someone kept clicking a pen, and the invigilator's shoes squeaked. Ishita had always found noise harder than others did. Every sound pulled at her attention. She read the first question three times and couldn't take it in. Her panic grew. She raised her hand. "Ma'am, can I sit near the back, away from the fan?" The invigilator hesitated, then let her move. Ishita put her hands over her ears for a minute and breathed slowly. Afterwards, she told her friend Siddharth, "I think I need to ask for a quiet room next time." Siddharth said, "Talk to the counsellor. My cousin got that."

Where did Ishita ask to sit?
She asked to sit near the back, away from the fan.
What was Ishita feeling when she read the first question three times?
She was panicking because the noises kept pulling her attention and she couldn't take the words in.
What did Ishita do that helped, and what else could she try?
She asked to move and calmed herself by covering her ears and breathing; next, she could talk to the counsellor about a quiet room.
How might Siddharth see Ishita's request for a quiet room?
He sees it as normal and reasonable, since his cousin got one, which may help Ishita feel less odd for asking.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Monday. Ehsan brought his phone and showed me the weekly report he had found himself: six hours a day, most of it short videos. “I thought it was two,” he said. Then, after a silence, “I'm not going to feel bad about it. I'm going to plan from these numbers.” Together we looked at when the hours happen: on the bus after school and after dinner. He chose to trim only the after-dinner block by an hour for now, and to check the report again on Sunday. His mother, Himani, rang and asked what she could do. I suggested she ask Ehsan about the plan, and not check the phone behind his back. We will look at the numbers again in two weeks. — Nazia

How many hours a day did the report show?
Six hours a day, mostly short videos.
How did Ehsan feel on seeing the number, and what did he decide?
Shocked, since he had thought it was two hours, but he decided to use the numbers for a plan instead of feeling guilty.
What else could Ehsan do to understand his habit, and why?
Note what he was feeling just before scrolling, since knowing the trigger helps him choose a replacement.
How does the plan look to Himani?
Himani is worried and wants to help, so being told to ask about the plan instead of checking the phone gives her a role that keeps trust.

metadata.subtype: Approach: measuring use before changing it [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sangeeta, twenty, was in her final year at the agricultural college near Dharwad, and her field report on soil testing was due on Monday. Every earlier report had run late: the first by a day, the second by three. Still, on Wednesday she told Madhav, who shared the bus with her from the village, "This one I'll finish by Saturday. I know the farm, I have the samples." On Thursday the bus broke down. On Friday her aunt's buffalo got sick and everyone ran to help. Saturday she started. On Sunday night, under the flickering bulb, she stared at half a report and felt a sinking familiarity. "Why do I always think it'll be different?"

When was Sangeeta's field report due?
It was due on Monday.
What was Sangeeta feeling on Sunday night?
She felt a sinking, frustrated familiarity, because once again the report was only half done despite her confidence.
What could Sangeeta do differently for her next report?
She could plan from how late her last reports actually ran, a day and then three, and start early enough to absorb surprises like the bus breaking down.
How might Madhav see Sangeeta's promise on the bus?
Madhav might have believed her, since she sounded sure, or quietly doubted it, knowing how her past reports went.
It was so windy yesterday that the kites flied very high. Is "flied" right?

It was so windy yesterday that the kites flew very high.
Why: "Fly" is irregular; the past is "flew".
Why do mango trees drop old flowers without making fruit on every branch?
Only the flowers that get pollinated can grow into fruit. Because many blossoms are never reached by insects or the wind, those flowers wither and fall.
Hartley has 4 puppies that each weigh 7.5 kilograms. The rescue center has 14 cats that each weigh 2.5 kilograms. How many kilograms more do the cats weigh than the puppies?

Puppies = 4 * 7.5 = 30 kg
Cats = 14 * 2.5 = 35 kg
35 - 30 = 5
The cats weigh 5 kg more than the puppies.
The answer is 5.

A tank has 3 1/4 litres of water. 1 3/4 litres are used. How much is left?

Now you try: 5 2/7 - 2 5/7.
The answer is 2 4/7.
Why does ghee turn solid in the winter?
Ghee sets firm when the air is cold. Because its fats stay liquid only when they are warm enough, and cooler air takes away their heat, they thicken and become firm.

Read this:

Thursday night

I have to write this down because I feel awful.

On Tuesday, someone in our group made an edit of Naveen's photo from the class trip, his head on a dancing chicken. I added the music. I thought it was funny. So did everyone. We sent it to the class group.

By Wednesday it was in three other classes. Today Naveen didn't come to school. His best friend said he was crying at home and didn't want to come back.

My first thought was, "It was only for fun. Everyone was doing it." Then I heard how that sounded. It wasn't fun for him.

So I did what I should have done on Tuesday. I deleted it everywhere I'd posted it. I asked the others to delete it too. I messaged Naveen: "I added the music to that edit. It was cruel and I'm sorry. I've deleted it and asked others to." No excuses.

Tomorrow I'm going to tell our class teacher it was us, before she finds out another way.

Farida

What did Farida add to the edited photo?
Farida added the music.
What was Farida feeling on hearing Naveen was crying at home?
Farida felt awful and ashamed, realising the joke had deeply hurt Naveen.
What did Farida do to repair the harm?
Farida deleted the edit, asked others to delete it, apologised plainly to Naveen without excuses, and planned to tell the class teacher.
What was it like for Naveen when the edit spread to other classes?
Naveen felt humiliated and hurt enough to cry and not want to come back to school.

Quick questions:
Can you help with these? I saw the word "interruption" in a book. What is it?
Why do people take off shoes before entering a temple?

1. It is a noun. It means a break in something that was going on.
2. It keeps the holy place clean. Because shoes carry dirt from the street.

Read this:

"Nani, you gave me thirty and Nikhil twenty." Ankita, ten, held up the coins.
"You fetched the vegetables, beti."
"But Nikhil fetched the milk twice and the newspaper. That's three trips. I only did one."
Nikhil, eight, looked up hopefully. "She's right, Nani."
"Arrey, it's just pocket money."
"It's not fair if it's not counted." Ankita took out a sheet of paper. "I'm making a chart. Trips, sweeping, watering plants. Each gets five rupees."
"And who checks the chart?" Nani asked, amused.
"Me."
"And if I give you extra because you're my first grandchild?"
"Then I'll give it to Nikhil." Ankita slid ten rupees across the table.
Nani shook her head, smiling. "This girl will run a bank one day."
Nikhil pocketed the coins before anyone could change their mind.

What did Ankita fetch for Nani?
She fetched the vegetables.
What does Ankita's chart suggest about how she feels about fairness?
It suggests she is determined that fairness means counting exactly, even when counting leaves her with less.
How could Nani help Ankita keep fairness without making it rigid?
She could praise Ankita's honesty and also explain that small gifts of love don't always need to be counted like payments.
How does Nikhil see Ankita's rule?
Nikhil is happy and a bit surprised, since Ankita's strict counting gives Nikhil more money.

Read this:

Mentoring note by Irawati, programme mentor, after Thursday's session
Usha, six months into her role in the foundation's finance team, came to our session quieter than usual. She said she had been matching invoices and found payments for three training workshops in villages near Nashik that, as far as she could tell, never happened. No attendance sheets, no photos, and the hall owner's number did not work.
She kept saying, "There's probably an explanation." Maybe the sheets were filed elsewhere. Maybe her manager already knew. She also said, twice, "Someone senior must be handling it." She rubbed her neck the whole time.
What I did next: I told her it was natural to hope for an innocent reason. I suggested she write down exactly what she had seen, with dates and invoice numbers, and keep it safe, before deciding anything. We will meet again next Thursday.

How many training workshops did Usha find payments for?
She found payments for three training workshops that never happened as far as she could tell.
What was Usha feeling as she talked and rubbed her neck?
Usha felt a knot of unease and worry, and she was hoping an innocent explanation or someone senior would take the problem away.
What was the mentor's suggestion, and why is it a sensible first step?
The mentor suggested writing down exactly what Usha had seen, with dates and invoice numbers, so she has clear facts before deciding anything.
How might the villagers who were meant to get the training be affected if nothing is done?
They lose training that was paid for in their name, while the money goes somewhere else.

Read this:

At the school science fair, Yash stood in line behind five other children to ask Ankita about her solar oven. He had a question burning in his mouth: would it melt chocolate?
Ankita was explaining slowly to the judge. Yash hopped from foot to foot. He opened his mouth, then closed it again. He counted the tiles on the floor.
Finally it was his turn. "Will it melt chocolate?" he blurted.
Ankita grinned. "Yes! I tested it yesterday."
Yash beamed.
After the fair, the teacher sent everyone out to the field for ten minutes. Yash ran three laps, arms out like a plane, shouting "CHOCOLATE!" at the sky.

What did Yash count while waiting?
The tiles on the floor.
How can you tell Yash felt eager and impatient while waiting his turn?
He hopped from foot to foot, opened and closed his mouth, and counted tiles, which shows eager excitement he was holding back.
Why was the teacher's choice to send everyone to the field helpful?
After a long time of self-control, running gave children like Yash a safe way to let out their bottled-up energy.
How might Ankita have felt answering Yash's question?
Ankita probably felt pleased and proud that someone was so excited about her solar oven.

Read this:

It was pouring, and the school bus would come in two minutes. Sachin ran down the stairs behind his mother, Sangeeta, and his tiffin slipped out of his hand. The lid flew off; poha scattered on the wet step. “Oops,” he said, and his chin started to tremble. Sangeeta didn't stop to scold. “It's okay. I'll give you biscuits instead.” She scooped up the box. At the gate he stepped on a stone. “Ouch!” Then the bus came round the corner, lights glowing in the rain. “Wow, it's all shiny!”

What spilled on the wet step?
Poha from Sachin's tiffin.
What was Sachin feeling when his chin trembled after the spill?
He was upset and worried that he'd be scolded for dropping his tiffin, especially in the rush.
Which choice by Sangeeta worked, and why?
She said “It's okay” and offered biscuits instead, which helped him recover quickly even with no time.
What would change if Sangeeta had shouted about the spill?
Sachin might have cried and felt bad all morning, instead of noticing the shiny bus with a “Wow.”

Mentoring notes, Diwali week
Kishore came to see me again today, his third visit since September. He has had three paths in front of him: the team lead role here, a master's offer in Pune, and a friend's start-up. He has not said no to any of them.
He told me, "If I pick one and it goes wrong, I'll always wonder about the other two." His eyes kept drifting to the paper lanterns in the office window as he spoke.
Meanwhile the master's deadline passed last week, and the start-up has found someone else. The team lead post, the only door left, closes when we return after Diwali.
I didn't tell him which to choose. I asked him to write down what waiting has already cost him, and to come back on Monday with a yes or a no.
Varun, senior mentor

Could you put the main point of these notes in a sentence or two?
Kishore has been too afraid of regret to choose between three paths, and two have already closed while he waited. His mentor asks him to count what waiting has cost and come back with a clear answer.
My grandmother is telling us stories every night when we were young. Can you correct it?

My grandmother used to tell us stories every night when we were young.
Why: a past habit takes "used to", not the present continuous.

Read this:

Raghav, you asked what love is, as if I keep a definition in the almirah. Listen instead. I married your Dadu at twenty, in Guwahati. Everyone thinks love is the wedding, the songs. For us it was the second year, when I wanted to finish my teaching degree and his mother said a daughter-in-law belongs in the kitchen. Your Dadu could have stayed quiet. Instead he sat with her and said, 'Binita will study. I'll cook on her exam days.' And he did, terrible dal and all, for two years. He never once showed me off to the neighbours. But he walked me to the exam hall every morning at seven. That's what I learned, Raghav. Love is who keeps showing up, and who makes room for you to grow. Not who shouts it loudest. Now go, phone your girl, and ask how her exam went.

What did Dadu promise to do on Binita's exam days?
Cook, even if the dal was terrible.
What does Binita feel looking back on those two years?
Binita feels grateful and deeply loved, remembering how Dadu kept showing up.
What choice in Binita's story showed real commitment?
Dadu backing Binita's teaching degree against his mother, then walking her to every exam.
How did Dadu's mother seem to see Binita at first?
As a daughter-in-law who belonged in the kitchen, not someone who should study.

Mentor's note, Thursday evening
Damini asked to meet me at the café near her office, away from colleagues. She works in quality testing at a medicine factory. She told me she had seen her team leader, Charu, re-run tests on a batch until the results passed and delete the failed runs from the log. Twice.
She kept turning her cup. "Charu covered for me when my father was ill. The whole team loves her. If I report it, I'm the one everyone will hate." Then, more quietly: "But people will take these tablets."
She asked what I would do. I said I couldn't decide for her, but that the risk to patients was not hers to carry alone, and that she had the right to use the company's confidential reporting line and, if needed, the drug regulator. We looked up both together.
What I did next: I stayed while she wrote down dates and batch numbers and filed the report on the confidential line before we left the café. She asked me to call her tomorrow. I will.

What did Charu delete from the log?
The failed runs.
What does Damini turning her cup suggest about her state?
It suggests Damini felt torn and anxious, caught between loyalty to Charu and fear for the people who will take the tablets.
How did the mentor support Damini without deciding for her?
The mentor said the patient risk was not hers to carry alone, looked up the confidential line and the regulator with her, and stayed while she filed the report.
How might Charu's team see Damini after the report?
Some may feel hurt or angry, since they love Charu, which is part of the personal risk Damini weighed.

12 March, 11:40 pm
Can't sleep. Chemistry board exam in two days, and my shoulders are up near my ears. My legs won't stop jiggling under the desk. Every time I close the book my head goes: what if I blank, what if I score less than Tushar did, what if Papa goes quiet like last year, what if I don't get in anywhere at all. Each what-if makes my breath shorter.
Tonight Tushar knocked, saw my face and said, "You've done three past papers today. Go and walk on the terrace. Ten minutes." I went. The air was cool. I breathed out slowly, counting to six. My shoulders came down a bit.
When I came back I made a list of what's actually left: two chapters. That's doable. Last what-if tonight: what if I'm more ready than I think?
Usha

How many past papers had Usha done that day?
Usha had done three past papers today.
What worries were looping through Usha's mind?
Usha was anxious about blanking, scoring less than Tushar, Papa going quiet, and not getting in anywhere.
Which steps eased Usha's body, and which thoughts made it worse?
A walk on the terrace, slow breathing and a list of what was left helped; the chain of what-ifs made Usha's breath shorter.
What might Tushar have noticed that led to suggesting a walk?
Tushar saw the stress on Usha's face and probably knew a break would help more than another hour with the book.

Read this:

Two weeks before the deadline: Hrithik had a chemistry project due and a blank file. Every time he opened it, his chest tightened: what if it wasn't the best in class? He reorganised his desk instead, three times.
The night before: He worked until four, redoing the title page twice. Ritu messaged, "Sleep, genius." He didn't reply.
Results day: Full marks. Ritu hugged him in the corridor. "You did it!" Hrithik smiled for her sake, but felt oddly flat. On the walk home he was already thinking, the next one has to be even better. He used to love mixing solutions in the lab. He couldn't remember the last time it had felt fun.

How many times did Hrithik reorganise his desk?
He reorganised it three times.
How did Hrithik feel after getting full marks, and what shows it?
He felt flat rather than happy; he smiled for Ritu's sake but was already thinking the next one had to be better.
What choice in the first two weeks made the project harder?
Reorganising his desk instead of starting, out of fear, left him working until four the night before.
How might Ritu feel if she noticed Hrithik smiling only for her sake?
She would probably feel worried that Hrithik can't enjoy his own success.

Keep it under 55 words: what is this text about?

Sherlock Holmes laughed. "Here is the foresight," said he putting his finger upon the little disc and loop of the hat-securer. "They are never sold upon hats. If this man ordered one, it is a sign of a certain amount of foresight, since he went out of his way to take this precaution against the wind. But since we see that he has broken the elastic and has not troubled to replace it, it is obvious that he has less foresight now than formerly, which is a distinct proof of a weakening nature. On the other hand, he has endeavoured to conceal some of these stains upon the felt by daubing them with ink, which is a sign that he has not entirely lost his self-respect."

Holmes points out that the hat-securer shows foresight in its owner, since such things are never sold on hats. But the broken, unreplaced elastic shows that his foresight has weakened, while the ink on the stains shows he has not lost all self-respect.
Why do wet roads look shiny at night?
Water fills the tiny bumps in the road. Because a smooth wet surface reflects car headlights like a mirror instead of scattering them.

Monday. The economics results went up on the department board, and Salma's name was at the top: 92, the highest in the batch. Binita squealed and hugged her. 'It was an easy paper,' Salma said. 'Everyone did well. It doesn't mean anything.'
Wednesday. Salma got 11 out of 20 in a surprise statistics quiz. She sat on the library steps with the sheet in her lap. 'This is my real level,' she told Binita. 'This is what I actually am.'
Friday. Over chai, Binita put the two papers side by side. 'So the 92 was easy and doesn't count. But an 11 on a surprise quiz is proof. How does that work?' Salma opened her mouth, then closed it. 'It just feels true,' she said finally, and stirred her tea for a long time.

What did Salma score in economics?
Salma scored 92, the highest in the batch.
Why does the 11 feel like 'my real level' to Salma?
Salma feels low and doubtful about her ability, so the bad mark fits that self-view and feels true, while the success feels undeserved.
What could Salma do to weigh her results fairly?
She could use the same rule for both marks, asking whether a top score and a surprise-quiz score each really prove anything about her.
How does Binita see Salma's reasoning?
Binita sees the double standard clearly and is puzzled and a bit frustrated that her friend discounts a top result.

Which friend of mine likes mangoes the most?
Also, should I tell a friend if they have food stuck on their face?
What does the word "share" mean?
And one more: why do people feel happy when a friend remembers their birthday?

1. I don't know, because I know nothing about your friends. Ask them, or think back to what they usually eat.
2. Yes, quietly and kindly. They would rather know than walk around with it.
3. To share is to let another person have or use part of something. Example: Please share your crayons with Tom.
4. It shows they matter. Because someone took time to think of them.

"Anand, isn't your solar system model due tomorrow?" asked Bhavna didi, looking up from her phone.
"Yes. It'll take ten minutes. I just need balls and paint."
"Do you have balls and paint?"
"Mummy has... something."
"Last time the volcano took you all Sunday."
"That was a volcano. This is just circles."
"Planets, a sun, sticks, labels..."
"It's easy, didi."
At 8 p.m. Anand was on the floor with newspaper and a half-painted Jupiter. At 9:30 the paint on Saturn still hadn't dried. At 10:15 he was crying because Mars had rolled under the sofa.
Bhavna crouched down beside him with a torch. "Ten minutes, na?" she said, and fished out Mars.

What rolled under the sofa?
Mars.
Why was Anand so sure the model would take ten minutes?
He felt confident and pictured only the easy path, forgetting that the volcano took all Sunday, so it seemed quick.
What could Anand try for the next project?
Remember how long the last one really took, list every part, and start a few days early.
How does Bhavna didi seem to feel at 10:15?
She seems amused but kind, teasing him gently while fishing out Mars with a torch.

What is the writer now satisfied about, and what does the writer fear?

Of one thing I am now satisfied: that all the boxes which arrived at Whitby from Varna in the Demeter were safely deposited in the old chapel at Carfax. There should be fifty of them there, unless any have since been removed--as from Dr. Seward's diary I fear.

The writer is satisfied that all the boxes that came to Whitby from Varna in the Demeter were put in the old chapel at Carfax. There should be fifty, but some may have been removed, as Dr. Seward's diary suggests.

The fever had kept Elizabeth in the small hospital at Pala for nineteen days. When she finally walked out, thinner and slow, the rubber trees along the road looked impossibly green.

She did not know what to say to God. She had never been good at long prayers. On Sunday she just sat in the parish church and let tears run, feeling thankful down to her bones.

On Monday she went to see Arnab, the nurse from Bengal who had stayed past his shift every night she had been bad.

"I don't have words," she said, handing him a tiffin of appam and stew her mother had made.

"You're walking. That's the words," he laughed.

That week Elizabeth started going to the ward on Saturdays to read to the old patients who had no visitors. It seemed like the clearest way to say thank you.

How many days had Elizabeth been in the hospital at Pala?
Nineteen days.
What was Elizabeth feeling as she sat in the parish church?
She felt deeply grateful and moved, so thankful she cried even though she had no words for a prayer.
Which choice turned Elizabeth's gratitude into something practical?
Reading to old patients with no visitors on Saturdays, which turned her thanks into kindness for others.
How might Arnab see Elizabeth's visit with the tiffin?
Arnab seems touched and happy, treating her recovery itself as thanks enough 🙂.
A bag of peanuts weighs 0.35 kg. Write this as a fraction of a kilogram in simplest form. Also write 0.125 and 2.75 as fractions.

Answer: 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20. 0.125 = 125/1000 = 1/8. 2.75 = 2 75/100 = 2 3/4.

The last digit of 0.35 is in the hundredths place, so write it over 100: 35/100. Now simplify: the HCF of 35 and 100 is 5, so 35/100 = 7/20. For 0.125 the last digit is in the thousandths place: 125/1000, HCF 125, so 1/8. For 2.75 keep the 2 wholes and change 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4, giving 2 3/4. A common mistake is to write 0.35 = 35/10; count the decimal places: 2 places means 100.

The meeting room on the ninth floor in Gurugram smelled of cold coffee. Pallavi clicked to her last slide, glowing. "So: the college festivals sign up in June, their students download our study planner, their teachers recommend it in class, the state board notices, and by March we're in every school in the district." The room clapped. Pradeep, who had sat through three pitches like this one this year, felt a small knot in his chest. He liked Pallavi and he liked the idea. He raised his hand gently. "It's a great story. Can we write each step on the board and put a rough chance next to it? Each one has to work, and then all of them have to work together." Pallavi's smile slipped, then steadied. By the end, the board showed five links, and the team agreed to test just the first one in June.

By when did Pallavi say the planner would be in every school in the district?
She said it would be in every school in the district by March.
What was Pradeep feeling as the room clapped, and why?
Pradeep felt uneasy, a small knot in his chest, because he liked the idea but could see that the whole story depended on every step working.
Which part of Pradeep's approach helped the team, and why?
Asking to write each step with a rough chance beside it turned a vague worry into something everyone could see, so the team chose to test the first link.
How might Pallavi have felt when her smile slipped?
Pallavi probably felt deflated for a moment, then steadier once the team kept the idea and agreed to test its first step.

Jasleen's phone was at six percent when Papa called for the third time. The overnight bus to Ludhiana was packed and loud, a film blaring from the screen at the front.
"Your Bua saw photos of you with some boy. And now she says it's over? Were you going to tell us anything?"
Jasleen's first instinct was to say it was a group photo, nothing more. Dolma, her roommate squeezed in beside her, shook her head slightly.
Jasleen took a breath. "Papa, yes, I was with someone for a few months. It ended. I'm sad about it, and I'd rather talk properly at home, not on a bus."
Silence, then: "Are you all right?"
"Not really. But I will be."
The call dropped as the battery died. Jasleen leaned against the window, trembling. Dolma handed her a charger cable and half an orange. "You told the truth you chose. That's enough for tonight."

What percentage was Jasleen's phone at when Papa called?
Six percent.
Why did Jasleen first want to call it a group photo?
She felt panicked and ashamed at being judged and wanted to escape Papa's anger with a quick lie.
What worked about how Jasleen handled the call?
She admitted the relationship and the breakup, said she was sad, and asked to talk properly at home, sharing what she chose instead of lying deeper.
How does Papa's tone change during the call?
He starts angry about what Bua saw, but after Jasleen's honest answer he asks "Are you all right?", showing worry for her.

Last month Seema had beaten Lakshmi's team and made a show of it, telling everyone, "Lakshmi runs like a snail." It felt sweet for a moment. Lakshmi stopped talking to her, and some classmates stopped clapping for Seema. Today, in the final, Seema scored the winning goal from a pass by Ravi. She felt wonderful, arms up, shouting. When the whistle blew she hugged Maria and thanked the whole team. Ravi was kicking the grass, quiet, and would not look up; he had wanted that chance. Seema said, "Your pass made the goal. I wouldn't have scored without it. Next corner is yours." Ravi shrugged, then almost smiled. Seema did not pretend she had not scored, and she kept her medal on. Then she walked over to Lakshmi, who had captained the losing side and stood alone with her water bottle. "Great game," Seema said. "Your save in the first half was brilliant. Next time you might beat us." Lakshmi's face eased. "Maybe," she said. "Good luck in the next round."

Who passed to Seema for the winning goal?
Ravi passed to Seema for the winning goal.
How did Seema's behaviour after beating Lakshmi last month differ from her behaviour after the final?

Last month she showed off and said Lakshmi runs like a snail, which cost her respect; after the final she thanked the team, credited Ravi's pass and spoke kindly to Lakshmi, keeping her medal on without gloating.
What was Ravi feeling as he kicked the grass and would not look up?
He felt disappointed and a little envious, because he had wanted that chance.
What could Seema do next time she wins?
She could keep thanking her teammates, crediting their passes and being kind to the losers, remembering that she may lose next time. 🙂
A laser beam starts at A(1, 2, 3) and travels in the direction 2i - j + 4k. Write the equation of the beam in vector and Cartesian form. Does it hit a sensor at (5, 0, 11)? At (3, 1, 6)?

Answer: r = (i + 2j + 3k) + lambda(2i - j + 4k); (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/4. (5, 0, 11) is on it (lambda = 2); (3, 1, 6) is not.

Every point of the line is 'start + lambda x direction': r = (i + 2j + 3k) + lambda(2i - j + 4k) x = 1 + 2lambda, y = 2 - lambda, z = 3 + 4lambda Making lambda the subject of each equation and equating gives the Cartesian form (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/4. To test a point, find lambda from one coordinate and check the others: for (5, 0, 11), lambda = 2 from x, and then y = 2 - 2 = 0 and z = 3 + 8 = 11, all agree: ON the beam (for lambda >= 0, the ray itself). For (3, 1, 6), x gives lambda = 1, y gives lambda = 1, but z gives lambda = 3/4: NOT on it. Common mistake: writing (x + 1)/2 for the point (1, 2, 3) (the sign in the bracket is the opposite of the coordinate), or putting the point's coordinates in the denominators.
There are many tomatos and potatos in the basket. What's off about the spelling?

There are many tomatoes and potatoes in the basket.
Why: consonant plus -o often takes -es: "tomatoes", "potatoes".

Tuesday night. Amma and Papa had a family talk at dinner. For me: "Take a government clerk job near home, Jahnavi. Easy hours, good for marriage." Amma says a daughter's job should be easy. For my brother Shankar: "Leave your art course, do engineering and earn well, or no girl will look at you." Shankar has not eaten his rice. We sat on the stairs afterwards and he said, "They're fitting both of us into moulds." I said I want to try the data analyst training in Hyderabad. He said he wants to paint and teach art. We agreed to ask Amma and Papa for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there. I'm nervous. But it's the first time either of us said what we really want out loud. Jahnavi

What job did Amma and Papa suggest for Jahnavi?
They suggested a government clerk job near home, with easy hours.
How does Jahnavi feel about the conversation planned for Sunday?
Jahnavi feels nervous but also relieved, because saying what she and Shankar really want out loud was a first.
Which choice by Jahnavi and Shankar on the stairs could make real choice possible?
They decided to say what each of them wants and to ask their parents for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there.
How might Shankar see what their parents want for him?
Shankar sees it as a mould. He is expected to leave his art course, do engineering and earn well, and he was too upset to eat his rice.
Do I need a comma before "and" in "red, white and blue"?

It depends on the style. The comma before the last "and" is called the Oxford or serial comma. American style usually includes it, British and Indian style often leaves it out, and both are acceptable if you are consistent.
Examples: We bought pens, paper, and glue. We bought pens, paper and glue.
Would you mind if I open the window? It is very warm in here. Please polish the request.

Would you mind if I opened the window? It is very warm in here.
Why: "Would you mind if" takes the past simple (opened).
