"Yogesh, you're doing civil too, right? All four of us together!"
"I… I guess, Sachin. Everyone is."
"You don't sound sure."
"I'm sure. It's safe. We'll help each other."
Eight months later, in the hostel corridor.
"Yogesh, surveying lab starts in ten minutes."
"I'm not going."
"What? Why?"
"Sachin, I don't like any of it. Soil, concrete, load. I sit there and feel nothing."
"Then why did you pick it?"
"Because you all did. I thought being with friends would be enough."
"What do you actually like?"
Yogesh looked at the floor. "Writing. I used to write stories. I never even checked if there was a course for that."
Sachin sat down next to him, quiet.

What does Yogesh say he used to do?
"Writing. I used to write stories."
How does Yogesh feel about the civil engineering subjects?
He feels flat and unhappy, saying he sits there and feels nothing.
What could Yogesh do now?
Talk to a college counsellor about his interest in writing and what options exist, rather than just skipping labs.
How might Sachin feel hearing this?
Sachin seems shocked and sad, sitting quietly, perhaps realising the group's choice didn't suit everyone.

"Charu, congratulations! The state debate list is up. You're on it!"
"Shh, Sunaina ma'am! Please don't tell anyone."
"Why not? It's wonderful news."
"If I tell people, it'll get jinxed. Last time I told my cousin I'd win, and I came fourth."
Sunaina ma'am smiled. "You came fourth because the other three had practised more rebuttals. You told me that yourself."
"I know. But still. Can we keep it secret till after?"
"We can keep it quiet if that feels better. But you'll still come for practice Tuesdays and Fridays?"
"Of course! Every day if you want."
"Then keep your secret. I'll only tell your partner, so you two can prepare."
Charu crossed her fingers behind her back. Sunaina ma'am pretended not to see.

Where did Charu come last time?
Fourth.
Why was Sunaina ma'am willing to keep the news quiet?
Sunaina ma'am felt relaxed about the jinx worry because Charu was still keen to practise, so the fear wasn't replacing effort.
How did Sunaina ma'am make sure the jinx fear didn't hurt Charu's preparation?
She agreed to keep it quiet but checked that practice would continue and told only the partner so they could prepare together.
How might Charu feel when her teacher agrees to keep it quiet?
Charu probably feels relieved and understood, while still a little nervous, crossing her fingers.

At the kindergarten in Buenos Aires, the tidy-up bell rang. Rania crossed her arms and turned her back on the block tower. "No. I'm not tidying." Valentina, her teacher, didn't raise her voice or call her naughty. She crouched nearby. "Blocks go in the box before snack. That's our rule every day. I'll put the first one in with you." Rania stamped. "No!" Valentina waited, humming the tidy-up song, while the others lined up. After a minute Rania dropped one block in, then another, scowling. "Thank you. Now snack," said Valentina, as if nothing had happened.

What did Valentina offer to do with Rania?
Valentina offered to put the first block in the box with her.
What was Rania feeling when she crossed her arms and said "No"?
Rania felt stubborn and cross about ending play, and was testing whether the tidy-up rule really held.
Which choice by Valentina worked, and why?
Valentina stayed calm, repeated the everyday rule without shaming, and waited, so Rania had nothing to fight against and tidied.
How might Valentina see Rania's "No!"?
Valentina seems to see it as ordinary limit-testing for a young child, not rudeness, so she stays patient.

Ira's charts were the best in the group, and when she presented them Anand felt a sour twist. He had almost hidden his own rough draft until he asked her how she chose the colours; she showed him in five minutes, and he finished his section properly. In the meeting, Anand and Salma disagreed hotly: he wanted a survey, she wanted interviews. They agreed to test both on ten respondents each, and when the data favoured interviews and the group voted for that plan, Anand nodded and kept working without sulking. He handed Salma the results table and said, "Can you show me a draft on Wednesday and again on Friday?" When the draft arrived he said, "The layout is clear. The second column needs labels." On the last night the library closed at nine, so they moved to a canteen table, and Salma stayed until midnight helping him fix his broken references. Anand said, "You saved my grade. Thank you, truly. Send me your slides on Monday." On Monday he formatted her section without being asked.

How many respondents did the group test each method on?
They tested both methods on ten respondents each.
How did Anand's reaction to Ira's charts differ from his reaction when the data favoured Salma's plan?

With Ira's charts he felt a sour twist of envy but chose to learn from her instead of hiding his work; when the data favoured interviews and the group voted, he accepted the decision and kept working without sulking.
What was Anand feeling when Ira presented her charts?
He felt envious, a sour twist, because her work was better than his.
What could Anand do next to return Salma's help?
He could offer her help in return, as he did by formatting her section, and keep thanking her for staying late.
I accidentally called my friend by her sister's name in front of everyone. She looked hurt.
That would sting for her and for you. The best step is a quick, sincere apology. Have you spoken to her yet?
No, I froze.
Find a quiet moment and say, 'I'm sorry I mixed up the names. I know that's not nice to hear.' Keep it short, so it doesn't turn into a long explanation.
What if she's still upset?
Give her space and let her know you care. People often feel better after a day, once they see you were not careless on purpose.
She just replied 'okay' and nothing else.
That's a small sign she's heard you, even if she's still a bit hurt. Let her come to you when she's ready.
Should I send her something funny?
Wait a day. A joke too soon can look like you're not taking it seriously. A warm, normal chat tomorrow will do more.
Is it too late to learn music at the age of twelve? What is the meaning of "note"?

1. No, many people start much later. Enjoy it and keep practising.
2. A note is a single musical sound. Example: She played a high note.

Gargi, come sit. Your Neelam Masi was twenty once too, and I want to tell you about Rohan.

He brought me tea at the library every evening. He remembered my exam dates before I did. Nobody had ever fussed over me like that, and I'd glow for an hour and then get a knot in my stomach. What if I couldn't be that person for him?

So one night I said it aloud: "I like you very much, but I'm not ready to promise big things." He went quiet, then nodded, and stayed anyway.

And I kept my Thursday evenings with Shanti and the hostel girls. Once I forgot to thank him for the tea and noticed only when he stopped bringing it for two days. I thanked him properly after that.

What did Rohan do at the library every evening?
Rohan brought Neelam tea at the library every evening.
Why did being chosen feel both warm and frightening to Neelam?
It felt warm to be valued so much, but she worried she could not live up to that devotion, which is why she spoke honestly about not being ready.
What would you tell someone who has just been chosen with this kind of devotion?
Be honest about what you can and cannot promise, keep your own friendships going, and say thank you instead of taking the care for granted.
How might Rohan have felt when Neelam said she was not ready to promise big things?
He may have been disappointed for a moment, but also relieved to know where she stood instead of guessing.

"So? How's the great hostel life?" Sumit Dada asked, dropping onto Mridul's bed.
"Fine."
"Just fine? You wanted this since Class 8. You made us all sit in silence during your exams."
"I know."
"So what's wrong?"
"Nothing's wrong." Mridul picked at the bedsheet. "It's just… I got in. And then what? Every day for four years had a point. Now I wake up and nobody's chasing me, not even me."
Sumit Dada was quiet. "When I cleared my bank exam, I felt the same for a whole year. Like I'd climbed a hill and there was just sky."
"What did you do?"
"Found a smaller hill. Then another. It took time."

Mridul feels hollow now that the goal that drove every day is gone, with no new aim to push toward.

Kishore felt a small glow at being asked, and a pull to answer grandly, like an expert. He noticed it.
"I can tell you what soil science was like for me: lots of field work, good if you like being outdoors. Plant pathology, honestly, I don't know much about. Ask Deepa akka; she's in that lab." He paused. "What do you enjoy more, the field or the microscope?"
Vasudha thought. "The microscope, actually."
"Then your answer might already be there. Talk to Deepa akka, then decide."
She thanked him and ran off towards the labs. Kishore stood by the cattle shed, slightly deflated that he wasn't the final word, and also oddly proud.

What did the first-years call Kishore?
"anna".
What did Kishore feel when Vasudha asked him?
A small glow of pride and a pull to answer grandly, like an expert.
How did Kishore guide Vasudha well?
He shared his own experience, admitted what he didn't know, pointed her to Deepa akka, and asked what she enjoyed so she could decide.
How might Vasudha see Kishore's answer?
As honest and helpful; it led her to notice her own preference for the microscope.

At his sister Radha's bidaai in the village of Kheda, Madhav stood by the decorated jeep and wept openly, big tears rolling into his moustache. Baljeet, his college friend visiting from Ludhiana, didn't know where to look. At home, men in his family went quiet at weddings, not teary. Was Madhav sad about losing his sister? Or angry about something? The women around them were crying too, and laughing, and singing all at once. Radha hugged Madhav, crying and smiling. When the jeep pulled away, Madhav wiped his face, grinning. Baljeet put a hand on his shoulder, unsure. "You okay?" Madhav laughed. "Okay? I'm the happiest I've been all year. She's marrying the man she chose. And I'll miss her every day." Baljeet nodded slowly. "Both, then." "Always both," Madhav said.

Where did Radha's bidaai take place?
In the village of Kheda.
What was Madhav feeling as he wept by the jeep?
He felt both happy and sad at once: joy that Radha married the man she chose, and grief that he would miss her every day.
What did Baljeet do that respected Madhav's own meaning?
He asked "You okay?" instead of assuming, and accepted Madhav's answer that the tears were both joy and loss.
How did Baljeet's own background shape how he read the tears?
In Baljeet's family men go quiet at weddings, so he first wondered if Madhav was sad or angry, not that he could be joyful.

The marks (out of 50) of 20 students in a science test were: 23 45 12 38 29 41 35 17 48 26 33 39 8 44 31 27 36 19 42 30 Make a grouped frequency table with classes 0 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 29, 30 to 39 and 40 to 49. Which is the modal class?

Answer: Frequencies 1, 3, 4, 7, 5 (total 20). Modal class: 30 to 39.

With 20 different marks, a table of single values would be long and almost every frequency would be 1, so we GROUP them. Tally each mark into its class: 8 goes in 0 to 9; 12, 17, 19 in 10 to 19; 23, 29, 26, 27 in 20 to 29; 38, 35, 33, 39, 31, 36, 30 in 30 to 39; 45, 41, 48, 44, 42 in 40 to 49. Check: 1 + 3 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 20. The modal class is 30 to 39 (7 students). What we lose: from the table alone we cannot say what the highest mark was, only that it was between 40 and 49. Common mistake: putting 30 in the class 20 to 29.

In class practice, she solved every circuit problem. Her lab partner Manoj copied her method.
But on the unit test, she felt the teacher's eyes on her. Her heart raced. She doubted her first answer, crossed it out and wrote a wrong one. She rushed the last section.
Her marks were low. The teacher nodded as if expecting it.
Manoj looked at her paper and frowned. "You crossed out the right answer. You taught me this."
Keerthana's throat tightened. "I know. I just couldn't stop thinking they were waiting for me to fail."

He copied her method for circuit problems.

She felt anxious and watched, doubting herself because she believed the teacher expected her to fail.

Stop the jokes about ability, frame tests as a way to grow, and look at practice work, not just test marks.
How does Manoj see Keerthana's test result?
Manoj is puzzled and concerned, knowing she taught him the method she crossed out.

Six friends each sent a first deposit into one account.

Harish felt relieved, because every payment was written down and nobody had to argue about who owed what. 🙂

They could pick one person to review the sheet each night, since small gaps are easier to fix on the same day.

They may see it as a calmer trip, because the sheet answered the money questions that caused trouble before.

Before the party, four teens each thought about what they would do if someone pushed them to do something unsafe. Kabir decided in advance what he would not do, such as getting into a car with a careless driver or trying substances; that way his choices in the moment would follow a rule he had already thought through. Sunaina prepared a short line, "No thanks, I'm good," and agreed a code word with her mother for a pick-up, so leaving would need no argument. Rehan feared his friends would find him dull and joined a risky dare. Dread of losing his place felt bigger than the danger just then, and the consequences landed on him alone. Dev, after a risky evening, admitted to himself it was a mistake. He told his parents what had happened, and they listened without shouting and made a plan with him that same night. He chose different company, an earlier time to leave, and one strict rule for next time.

What did Sunaina agree with her mother?
She agreed on a code word for a pick-up.
How does Rehan's reason for joining the dare differ from Kabir's preparation, and what followed?
Rehan feared being called boring and joined a risky dare, with consequences falling on him alone. Kabir decided in advance what he would not do, so a rule guided him in the moment.
What might Dev be feeling when he tells his parents what happened?
He is probably worried and ashamed, but wants to make it right, which is why he tells them instead of hiding it.
What could Rehan do now?
He could tell a trusted adult what happened, decide firm limits for next time, and prepare a refusal line and exit plan like Sunaina's. 🤍

The art portfolio was due the Monday after Holi, and Yash had three days left, most of them booked for his cousin's wedding. Friday evening he sat on the balcony with a pencil, trying to draw the neem tree. The trunk came out like a pipe. He erased it twice and tore the paper.
Gopika, his sister, still had pink colour on her ears from the morning. "Want me to show you the shading trick?"
"No point. Some people are just born artists. I'm not creative. I'll take the zero." He put the pencil back in the box and snapped it shut.
"You've drawn for, what, twenty minutes this year?"
"That's what I'm saying. It's not in me." He went inside and switched on the cricket. The blank page stayed on the balcony chair, curling in the heat.

What was Yash trying to draw on the balcony?
He was trying to draw the neem tree.
Why does giving up feel reasonable to Yash?
He feels frustrated and a little embarrassed, and telling himself he is just not creative makes quitting feel like accepting a fact instead of failing.
What would you advise Yash with the deadline so close?
He could accept Gopika's shading trick and aim to finish one small, rough drawing, treating it as practice rather than proof of talent.
How might Gopika feel when Yash turns down her help?
Gopika may feel brushed off and a bit sad, since she can see he has hardly practised and is giving up far too early.

Binita, would you be our official critic tomorrow? Please come ready to pick holes in the plan as hard as you can. Everyone else, I'll ask for your concerns first, and I'll speak last, so my opinion doesn't shape yours.

Last year we agreed too quickly and ran short on Sunday nights for two months. Let's not repeat that.

They ran short on Sunday nights for two months.
What was Elizabeth worried about before the meeting?
Elizabeth felt uneasy that because most people liked the draft, the team might agree too quickly again, as it did last year.
What makes Elizabeth's email a good way to prepare a meeting?
It asks Binita to argue against the plan, promises to speak last and thanks problem-raisers in advance, so dissent feels safe.

Ward nurse's note, women's surgical ward, night shift.
Bed 12, Zainab, 22, day one after her operation. Her husband, Yogesh, sat with her all evening. I noticed he kept stroking the back of her hand very lightly, and each time she settled and her breathing slowed. Around eleven her pain rose. When he reached for her hand, she pulled it away and turned her face. He froze, then took his hand back and asked quietly, "Do you want me to stop, or just be here?" She said, "Just be here." He sat back with his hands in his lap. I gave her the medicine the doctor had charted and checked her after half an hour. By midnight she held her hand out to him herself, and he took it. I reminded him visiting would end soon; he said goodnight softly. Will pass on at handover that the family is a good support.

What was Yogesh doing that helped Zainab settle in the evening?
He kept stroking the back of her hand very lightly.
What was Yogesh feeling when Zainab pulled her hand away?
He seemed startled and a little hurt, freezing for a moment, but his quiet question shows he cared more about what she needed than about being close.
What does the nurse's note show about the right way to use gentle touch?
It shows touch comforts only when welcome: Yogesh stopped at once when Zainab pulled away, asked, and waited until she offered her hand again.
How did Zainab experience her husband's touch at different moments?
In calmer moments the stroking soothed her, but when pain rose she needed space, and later she chose to reach out to him herself.

When Papa made the rule that my phone stays in the kitchen after ten, I didn't argue. I said "fine". Then I did everything he asked, just slowly. Emptying the dishwasher took forty minutes. I answered every question with "hmm" or "okay". When my brother Sumit asked if I wanted to play carrom, I said "no" and went back to my room to stare at the ceiling.
I thought I was being really mature, not shouting. Looking back, I was shouting, just quietly. Everyone could feel it.
On Sunday Papa sat on my bed and said, "You're allowed to be angry about the rule. I'd rather hear it than feel it." So I told him: my friends talk at night and I feel left out. We didn't scrap the rule, but we moved it to half past ten on weekends. I'm Mridul, fifteen, and I'm trying to use my words now.

How long did Mridul take to empty the dishwasher?
Forty minutes.
Why did the slow chores and 'hmm' answers feel 'mature' to Mridul at the time?
Not shouting felt grown-up, but Mridul was still angry about the rule, and the anger came out as quiet sulking.
What choice of Papa's opened things up?
Sitting on the bed and saying Mridul was allowed to be angry and he'd rather hear it, which led to a real talk and a weekend compromise.
How might Sumit have felt when Mridul refused to play carrom?
Rejected and confused, caught in a mood that wasn't really about him.

Chen's text said only "can you come over," so Javier cycled across Valencia in the rain. He found Chen at the kitchen table, eyes swollen, a rejection email for the architecture internship still open on the laptop.
Chen started crying again the moment Javier sat down. Javier's first instinct was to say, "Hey, stop, it's just one internship," and he could feel the words on his tongue. He swallowed them. Instead he pushed the tissue box across the table and waited.
It took a while. The rain ticked on the window.
"Sorry," Chen said finally. "I'm being ridiculous."
"You're not. You wanted it." Javier paused. "What would help right now? Food, a walk, or just me being here?"
Chen laughed wetly. "Food. And you being here."
Javier got up to make eggs.

What email was open on the laptop?
A rejection email for the architecture internship.
What was Javier feeling when "stop, it's just one internship" came to mind?
Javier likely felt helpless and uncomfortable watching a friend cry and wanted to fix it fast, but he held back.
What did Javier offer instead of telling Chen to stop?
A tissue box, quiet waiting and a question about what would help: food, a walk or company.
How might Chen have felt if Javier had called it just one internship?
Chen might have felt dismissed and even more ridiculous, as if wanting the internship didn't matter.

A spoon, an apple, a pencil and a lemon.

It suggests Zainab really expected the apple and lemon to sink and was learning from the result.

They wrote their guesses first and recorded the real results, even the wrong ones.

"You should be next, beta. Twenty-three is the right age."
"You should take the government exam, not this start-up nonsense."

Masi blinked, then patted her cheek. "Okay. But you'll tell me first."

How many trays of sweets was Ishita handed?
Ishita was handed four trays of sweets.
What did Ishita feel when Binita Masi caught her arm?
Ishita felt love and pressure together, her throat tightening, because Masi meant well but the shoulds kept piling up.
How did Ishita keep both respect and her own choice?
She knelt, spoke gently, thanked Masi for caring, and clearly stated her own plans while asking for trust.
How might Binita Masi see Ishita's words?
Masi seems a little surprised but reassured, choosing to trust Ishita as long as she's told first.
Twelve coworkers go out for lunch together and order three pizzas. Each pizza is cut into eight slices. If each person gets the same number of slices, how many slices will each person get?

The total number of slices is 3 x 8 = 24.
Every one of the colleagues gets 24 / 12 = 2 slices per person.
The answer is 2.

At a CD store, 40% of the CDs cost $10 each, and the rest cost $5 each. Prince bought half the CDs sold at $10 each, and all of the CDs sold at $5 each. If the total number of CDs was 200, how much money did Prince spend on buying the CDs?

The number of CDs selling at $10 each at the store is 40/100*200 = 80
This means the store sells 200-80 = 120 CDs at $5 each.
Prince bought 1/2*80 = 40 of the CDs selling at $10 each.
The total amount of money Prince paid for the 40 CDs selling at $10 each is $40*10 = $400
If he bought all the CDs selling at $5 each, he paid a total of $5*120 = $600
For all the CDs he bought, Prince spent $600+$400= $1000
The answer is 1000.

From Monday to Friday, on extracurricular activities, Josh spends 6 + 3 = 9 hours.

Lavinia's daughter is 10 years younger than Katie's daughter. Lavinia's son is 2 times the age of Katie's daughter. If Katie's daughter is 12 years old, how many years older is Lavinia's son than Lavinia's daughter?

Lavinia's daughter is 12 - 10 = 2 years old
Lavinia's son is 12 * 2 = 24 years old
Lavinia's son is 24 - 2 = 22 years older than Lavinia's daughter.
The answer is 22.

In their village house near Belgaum, Nitin's family practised a fire drill after a hut in the next lane caught fire. His mother, Usha, banged a pot. "Fire! Everyone out to the well!" Nitin was first up. But instead of running to the door, he darted back to the verandah for the parakeet's cage. Usha caught his arm. "Nitin, stop. What did we say?" "But the bird..." "In a real fire, you come out. If the bird can be saved, an adult will do it, or the fire brigade. You don't go back. Ever." Nitin's lip wobbled. They practised twice more, and both times he ran straight to the well, not looking back.

Where was the family's meeting point?
At the well.
How did Nitin feel when his mother stopped him?
He felt upset and torn, worried about the parakeet, with his lip wobbling.
What else could Usha do to help Nitin feel better about the rule?
She could tell him which adult will check on the bird, so he trusts that someone is responsible for it.
How does the drill look to Usha?
Usha is alarmed to see Nitin run back, so she stops him and uses it to teach the rule clearly.

Read this:

Teacher's note, Class 5C, Wednesday.
Keerthana has told the class three times this week that she is "going to be head girl, definitely", that her cousin is a pilot, and that her new pencil box cost more than anyone's. Each time she speaks louder and watches faces. When nobody reacts, she starts again.
Today in art she held up her drawing and said, "Mine is the best one, right?" before anyone had looked. Her other hand was gripping the desk.
I think she worries that without the big claims she'll disappear. After class I asked her to help set up the reading corner, and told her that her lettering on the posters is careful and clear. She beamed, and didn't boast once in the next period.
Rafiq Hussain

What did Keerthana say about her new pencil box?
She said her new pencil box cost more than anyone's.
What does Keerthana's hand gripping the desk suggest?
It suggests she felt anxious and hungry for approval, worried that without big claims she might go unnoticed.
Which step by the teacher helped, and why?
Rafiq gave her a real job and specific praise for her careful lettering, so she felt noticed without needing to boast.
How might the other children see Keerthana's claims?
They may tune out or feel pushed aside, which is why nobody reacted and she kept starting again.
There is a lot of traffics near the school at nine. Is the noun right?

There is a lot of traffic near the school at nine.
Why: "traffic" is uncountable, so no plural.

Emily bought 9 packs of candy necklaces to give her classmates at school for Valentine's Day. Each pack had 8 candy necklaces in it. Emily opened one pack at a time. After her classmates took as many as they wanted, there were 40 candy necklaces left. How many packs did Emily open for her classmates?

Emily bought 9 packs of candy necklaces * 8 candy necklaces in a pack = 72 candy necklaces.
Her classmates took 72 candy necklaces - 40 candy necklaces left = 32 candy necklaces
Since each pack contained 8 necklaces, this means 32 / 8 = 4 packs of candy necklaces were opened.
The answer is 4.

For football season, Zachary wants to buy a new football, a pair of shorts, and a pair of football shoes. The ball costs $3.75, the shorts cost $2.40, and the shoes cost $11.85. Zachary has $10. How much more money does Zachary need?

The total cost of the ball, the shorts, and the shoes is $3.75 + $2.40 + $11.85 = $18.
Zachary needs $18 - $10 = $8 more.
The answer is 8.

Read this:

Monday: Rukmini told the class that her neighbours were fasting through the day for Ramzan and she sometimes joined their evening meal, and Rashmi snorted, "No lunch for a month? That's silly." Rukmini went quiet. Rashmi saw her face and felt a bit bad, but didn't say anything.

Thursday: Rashmi asked her mother about it. Amma explained that Rashmi's Nani also fasted on some days, in her own way, and that it meant something to her. Rashmi thought about that a long time.

The next Tuesday: Rukmini brought dates that her neighbour had sent for the evening meal. Rashmi took one, said, "Thank you, and sorry about Monday," and asked what they ate first when the fast ended.

What did Rukmini bring to school on the next Tuesday?
She brought dates her neighbour had sent for the evening meal.
What was Rashmi feeling when she saw Rukmini go quiet on Monday?
She felt a bit bad because she realised her snort had hurt Rukmini, though she wasn't ready to say so yet.
What helped Rashmi change her attitude, and what could she try next?
Linking the fast to her own Nani's fasting helped her see its meaning; next time she could ask a question first instead of laughing.
What is it like for Rukmini when Rashmi apologises and asks about the meal?
It probably feels like relief and being taken seriously, since the practice she shared is now treated with interest instead of mockery.

Read this:

At the school activity fair, sign-up tables lined the hall. Dolma read every sheet twice. Poetry slam: what if she forgot the words? Debate: what if she was bad? Art contest: what if hers was the worst? She put her hands in her pockets and walked past all of them.
Anirban, holding a marker at the open-mic table, waved her over. "Try this one. Two minutes, four people, no marks."
"I'd probably mess up."
"Then you'll have messed up in front of four people. Not forty."
Dolma read four lines of a poem, her hands shaking. Nobody clapped loudly, but Anirban nodded, and her stomach unclenched. She took the marker and slowly wrote her name on the sheet for next week.

How many people were at the open-mic table?
There were four people.
Why did Dolma walk past all the sign-up tables?
She was afraid of failing: forgetting the words, being bad, being the worst, so she avoided anything she might fail at.
What small step helped Dolma start?
Trying a low-stakes attempt, two minutes in front of four people with no marks, made failing feel survivable.
How does Anirban see Dolma's fear?
Anirban sees it as small enough to face, and offers a low-stakes chance without judging her.

Sally was at a self-serve candy shop where you scoop candy from the bins and pay based on the weight. She scoops 32 cherry sours into a bag. Then she gets a scoop of lemon sours, and the ratio of cherry sours to lemon sours is 4:5. Then she gets a scoop of orange sours, and they make up 25% of the sours in the bag. How many sours does she have in total?

She has 4 cherry sours for every 5 lemon sours, so the number of lemon sours = (5 lemon sours* 32 cherry sours) / 4 cherry sours = 40 lemon sours.
This puts the total at 32 cherry sours + 40 lemon sours = 72 sours.
After the orange sours are added, they make up 25% of the total sours. Let x = the total number of sours.
x - 0.25*x = 72 sours => 0.75*x = 72 sours => x = 72 sours / 0.75 = 96 sours total.
The answer is 96.

The verbs should be in the future tense here.

They are building a small bridge over the stream.
They will be building a small bridge over the stream.

In the KG classroom, Reena Ma'am was reading about a lost puppy. Pallavi's hand shot up and stayed there. She bounced on her knees, then held her arm up with her other hand. Reena noticed and gave her a quick nod. “One minute, Pallavi, I see you.” Pallavi pressed her knees together and bounced faster. At the end of the page, Reena called on her. “Can I go to the toilet?” Reena smiled. “Of course. Next time you can show me the toilet sign, and go.”

What was Reena Ma'am reading about?
A lost puppy.
What was Pallavi feeling as she bounced and held her arm up?
She was uncomfortable and anxious because she needed the toilet, and it was hard to wait. Her teacher could not tell at first whether it was a question or excitement.
What small step did Reena offer so waiting would be easier next time?
She suggested a toilet sign, so Pallavi could signal what she needed and go without waiting for her turn to speak.
What is it like for Reena to see a hand that stays up for a long time?
She has to guess whether it is eagerness, a question or a need, so a quick nod helps the child while she finishes the page.
My classmate gave me the cold shoulder today. What does that mean?

It means to treat someone in an unfriendly way by ignoring them on purpose.
Example: Dev gave his cousin the cold shoulder after their argument.

Read this:

Rekha's grandfather Rafiq smiled and folded his newspaper. "Rekha beti, you ask what it felt like to start out? Let me tell you. I was twenty when I got the letter for the bus conductor's post in the city. I read it on the village well so many times the paper went soft. The night before I left, I couldn't sleep. I kept imagining the city lights, the uniform, my own salary in my own pocket. My mother packed rotis and pickle and cried. I was sad for her, but my chest felt like a kite pulling at its string. On the first morning I reached the depot before the manager. I polished my ticket punch until it shone. The job was hard, the hours long. But that feeling of the whole world opening up? I still remember it."

What job did Rafiq get the letter for?
A bus conductor's post in the city.
What does Rafiq mean when he says his chest felt like a kite pulling at its string?
He felt a strong, joyful pull toward the new life ahead, even while he was sad to leave his mother.
What could Rekha take from her grandfather's story for her own future?
That it's normal to feel eager and excited about new adult chances, even when the work turns out hard.
How might Rafiq's mother have felt the night before he left?
She was sad to see him go, as her crying shows, while perhaps also proud he had found work.
Milton has some books about zoology and 4 times as many books about botany. If he has 80 books total, how many zoology books does he have?

Let z be the number of zoology books and b be the number of botany books. We know that z + b = 80 and b = 4z.
Substituting the second equation into the first equation, we get z + 4z = 80
Combining like terms, we get 5z = 80
Dividing both sides by 5, we get z = 16
The answer is 16.

Nitin: VARUN
Nitin: your comic is on the main notice board 🎉
Nitin: Ma'am wrote "outstanding" on it
Varun: lol it's not a big deal
Varun: she probably needed something to fill the board
Nitin: there were 40 entries. she picked 3
Varun: luck. anyone can draw a comic
Nitin: i literally can't draw a circle
Varun: you didn't try
Nitin: you spent two weeks on the panels. i saw you
Varun: yeah and it still looks kind of bad
Nitin: the principal took a photo of it
Varun: she takes photos of everything
Nitin: why can't you just be happy
Varun: because it'll turn out it was nothing. it always does
Nitin: ok well. i'm proud of you anyway 🙂
Varun: …thanks

How many entries were there, according to Nitin?
There were 40 entries.
Why does Varun say "it'll turn out it was nothing"?
Varun expects good news to be temporary or fake, so explaining it away feels safer than enjoying it. That keeps Varun's negative self-view untouched.
What could Varun try instead of explaining the praise away?
Just say "thanks, I worked hard on it" and let it stand, even if it feels uncomfortable. Letting one success count is a first step to a fairer self-view.
How might Nitin feel when every piece of good news gets waved away?
Nitin seems frustrated, asking why Varun can't just be happy, but still caring enough to say "i'm proud of you anyway". It may be tiring to keep offering praise that isn't accepted.

Read this:

“Himani, how big was the balloon at the party?” asked Sarita. Himani spread her arms as wide as they would go and puffed her cheeks. “Big!” “So big!” said Sarita. At dinner Himani cupped both hands together and held them up. “You want a bowl?” Sarita passed her steel bowl, and Himani beamed and held it out toward the pot of dal. Then she pointed at the high shelf, palm open, stretching. “The biscuit tin? You did well showing me.”

How did Himani show the size of the balloon?
She spread her arms as wide as they would go.
What do Himani's stretched arms and cupped hands seem to say about how she feels?
They show pride in describing the balloon and a wish for the bowl and the biscuits. She might also be enjoying showing Sarita that she can make herself understood.
How could Sarita help Himani's language grow?
Sarita could say aloud what the gestures mean, like “big balloon” and “bowl, please”, and then wait for Himani to try the words.
How might Himani feel when Sarita understands her gestures?
She may feel proud and understood, and want to communicate even more. 😊

I told my parents about Jasleen on a Sunday morning, after Mama's prayers, because that's when the house is calmest.

I'm Yash. I had practised the words for a week. Mama had already shortlisted three families. I knew how much she and Papa had given up: the old scooter Papa kept for twelve years so I could go to college, the pilgrimage Mama postponed twice.

So I started there. "Everything I have, I have because of you. Thank you." Then I said, "I want to marry Jasleen. We've been together three years. I'd like you to meet her properly."

Mama cried. Papa went for a walk. I didn't take it back, but I didn't argue either. I just said, "I'm not asking you to agree today. I'm asking you to meet her."

Two weeks later, Jasleen came for lunch. Mama made rajma. It wasn't easy, but it was a start.

What did Mama make when Jasleen came for lunch?
Mama made rajma.
What was Yash feeling while practising the words for a week?
Yash felt nervous and anxious, but also grateful and determined to be honest about Jasleen.
What did Yash do well in how he set the boundary?
Yash thanked the parents for real sacrifices, stated the choice clearly, and asked only for a meeting instead of demanding instant agreement.
What is it like for Mama when Yash talks about Jasleen?
Mama seems hurt and overwhelmed, since she had already shortlisted families and cries, yet she later cooks for Jasleen.
What is the aroha of Raga Malkauns?
The aroha of Raga Malkauns is: S g M d n S'.

“Nazia, WATCH OUT!”
Nazia froze on the kerb. A scooter zoomed past.
Anand pulled her back and held her. “Are you okay?”
“Why did you shout, Abbu?” Her voice shook.
“Because the scooter was coming fast. I only shout ‘watch out’ when something can hurt you.”
“Only then?”
“Only then. When you hear it, you stop and look, like you just did.”
Nazia looked at the road. “I stopped fast.”
“You did. Now we hold hands and look both ways together.”

What zoomed past the kerb?
A scooter.
What was Nazia feeling when she asked why Abbu shouted?
She was frightened and shaky from the sudden shout and the scooter, and wanted to understand.
What did Anand explain about “watch out”?
He said he only uses it when something can hurt her, so she knows to stop and look when she hears it.
How might Anand feel after pulling Nazia back?
He is probably shaken and relieved, which is why he holds her and asks if she's okay.
A ribbon was cut into 3 equal pieces and each piece is 6 m long. Solve x/3 = 6 to find the length of the ribbon.

Answer: x = 18. The ribbon was 18 m long.

x/3 means x divided by 3. The inverse of dividing by 3 is MULTIPLYING by 3: x/3 x 3 = 6 x 3 x = 18 Check: 18 / 3 = 6. True. Compare 24/x = 6, where x is the number we DIVIDE BY: 24 divided by what is 6? x = 24 / 6 = 4 (check: 24 / 4 = 6).

Saturday. Today I sent Ramesh the first draft of the housing society newsletter, eight pages, at about sixty percent: two photos missing, the back page empty. Every instinct said wait a week, make it perfect. Instead I typed, “Rough draft. Please tell me where I'm going wrong,” and pressed send before my nerves could vote. My stomach fizzed for an hour. Ramesh, who edited the newsletter for years, phoned that evening. “The front page is good. Move the notices to the back. You do not need eight pages.” Two comments, and I had the shape of the whole thing. I wouldn't have found that alone in a month. Tomorrow I cut it to six. — Wasim

What did Wasim type when sending the draft to Ramesh?
Wasim typed, “Rough draft. Please tell me where I'm going wrong,” and sent it.
Why did Wasim's stomach fizz for an hour after sending?
Wasim felt nervous about showing an unfinished draft, an ordinary worry after sending something imperfect.
What did the early feedback change about Wasim's plan?
Ramesh's two comments, to move the notices to the back and cut the pages, gave Wasim the shape of the newsletter, so Wasim would cut it to six pages.
How might Ramesh feel about receiving the rough draft?
Ramesh, who edited the newsletter for years, probably feels respected and pleased to be asked, and can give useful advice quickly.

Read this:

Trisha, you want to skip your friend's dance show because it's raining? Let your Sunaina Nani tell you about the rain of 1968.
I was ten. My friend Kamla had a small part in the temple play, just one line. I had promised to sit in the front row. That evening the sky opened. Mud everywhere. My mother said, "Stay home, she won't even notice."
I sat at the window, wanting to stay dry so badly. But I had said it. Promise. I took Father's big black umbrella and walked, my feet squelching in my chappals.
When I arrived, soaking, Kamla was peeping from behind the curtain, looking at the front row. When she saw me, she smiled so big she almost forgot her line.
After that, she always said, "Sunaina comes. Even in rain." I liked being that person. I still do.

What did young Sunaina take to walk in the rain?
She took Father's big black umbrella.
How did young Sunaina feel at the window before leaving?
She felt torn and reluctant, badly wanting to stay dry but uneasy about breaking her promise.
At what turning point did Sunaina choose to keep her word?
At the window, when she decided "I had said it. Promise," and walked out despite the mud.
How did Kamla feel when she saw Sunaina in the front row?
Kamla felt happy and relieved, smiling so big she almost forgot her line.

College counsellor's note, Tuesday.
Irfan, second year, came in about exam stress, but most of our talk was about Simran. They were close friends until two months ago. When Irfan's father was in hospital, Simran didn't visit or call, though she'd promised. Irfan was hurt. He never told her. Instead he started skipping their study group, leaving the canteen when she arrived and replying to her messages with single words. He said, "I thought it would just fade." It hasn't; he's more upset now, and Simran has asked others what's wrong. He looks tired. What I did next: I asked what he would want Simran to know. He said, "That I needed her." We practised how he might say it, gently. He'll decide this week whether to talk to her.

Where was Irfan's father when Simran didn't visit?
In hospital.
Why did Irfan start leaving the canteen when Simran arrived?
He felt hurt and let down, and avoiding her brought short-term relief from the painful conversation.
How did the counsellor help Irfan move toward repair?
The counsellor asked what he wanted Simran to know and practised gentle wording, making the hard talk feel possible.
How might Simran feel asking others what's wrong?
Simran seems confused and worried, sensing the distance without knowing its cause.

messages.content: Write a short paragraph, around 70 words, on why playing outdoors is good for children.

Playing outdoors is good for children in many ways. They run, jump and climb, and that makes their bodies strong. They learn to share and to take turns when they play team games. Fresh air and sunshine make them feel cheerful. They also meet friends and discover how fun life is without a screen. After a long afternoon outside, children are tired, hungry and happy, and they sleep well at night.

Coach's note, Sunday, inter-club table tennis.
Payal lost her semi-final to Pema, 11-9 in the fifth game. It was a close match, and Payal had led most of the way.
When the last point went, Payal stood still for a second. Her lip trembled. Then she walked round the table, shook Pema's hand and said, clearly, "Well played."
Several parents noticed. Pema's coach came over later to say how much they admired Payal's manner.
Afterwards Payal cried a little in the car park. I told her that the handshake was the bravest shot she played all day. We'll work on her fifth-game nerves this week.

What was the score in the fifth game?
How did Payal feel right after losing?
She felt deeply disappointed, with a trembling lip, and cried a little afterwards.
Why did Payal's handshake matter?
It showed good character in a hard moment and earned respect from parents and Pema's coach.
How might Pema feel when Payal shakes her hand and says well played?
Pema would likely feel respected and happy that her win was acknowledged graciously.

Lights-out was at ten in the Dehradun boarding school, but the girls' hostel still glowed with phone screens. Hansa lay in the east wing staring at the chat with Arohi, in the west wing: a whole day of 'ok.', 'sure.', and one 'whatever you want.' She'd shown it to her roommate, who'd said Arohi was being fake. Hansa's stomach hurt. Finally she typed, 'Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other.' Arohi replied, 'yes pls.' They whispered under their blankets. 'I thought you were angry about the dance partner thing,' Arohi said. 'I thought YOU were!' Hansa said. Hearing Arohi's voice crack, then giggle, Hansa felt half the knot in her stomach loosen within a minute. By the end they were both laughing into their pillows.

Which wing was Arohi in?
Arohi was in the west wing.
What did Hansa feel once she heard Arohi's voice crack and then giggle?
She felt relief as half the knot in her stomach loosened, realising they had both been misreading each other.
Why did moving from text to a call work so quickly?
Voices carry tone that short texts hide, so each could hear that the other was worried, not angry, and the hurt dissolved.
How might Arohi have felt receiving Hansa's 'Can I call you?'
Probably relieved and eager, since her quick 'yes pls' suggests she wanted to fix things too.

Read this:

The fourteenth rejection email arrived while Ishita was on the local train from Andheri. "After careful consideration…" She read it twice, then put the phone away and watched the backs of buildings go past. At home Francis, her flatmate, was frying eggs. "Another?" "Fourteen." He slid a plate across. "Want to throw something or look at it?" She laughed despite herself. After dinner she opened the spreadsheet she had started at rejection five: company, role, stage reached, what they said. Francis leaned over. "You get past the written test every time. You drop at the case interview." She stared. Fourteen emails had felt like fourteen verdicts on her. The sheet said something narrower: one skill to fix. She booked a free case-practice session at the alumni cell for Saturday, then sent the next application before bed.

Where was Ishita when the fourteenth rejection arrived?
On the local train from Andheri.
What was Ishita feeling as she watched the buildings go past?
Ishita felt discouraged and hurt, as though each rejection were a verdict on her.
What did the spreadsheet reveal, and why does that help?
She passes the written test but drops at the case interview, so she can practise one skill instead of doubting everything.
How does Francis see Ishita's rejections?
Francis stays calm and practical, seeing a pattern to fix rather than a failure, and supports her with food and humour.

The power had gone out in the building, so Noor and Jahnavi were making shadow puppets on the stairwell wall with Jahnavi's torch. "My turn to hold it!" Noor said. "It's my torch!" Noor yanked, Jahnavi yanked back, and the torch clattered down two steps. Noor shouted, "I'm not your friend anymore!" and stomped up to the fourth floor in the dark, feeling her way along the rail. The shouting stopped. Jahnavi sat alone with the flickering torch, chin trembling. The next evening Noor knocked with a packet of biscuits. They played again, but more quietly, and neither of them mentioned the torch.

Where did Noor stomp off to?
Noor stomped up to the fourth floor in the dark.
Why might Noor have knocked with biscuits the next evening?
She probably felt sorry and a little embarrassed about her shout, and wanted to make up without having to say so.
What else could Noor try when she's angry about the torch?
She could ask for turns or say she's cross, instead of saying she's not a friend; the harsh words ended the game but left a hurt behind.
How might Jahnavi experience the next evening's play?
After sitting alone with a trembling chin, Jahnavi is glad to play again, but the quieter game shows the friendship still feels a bit bruised.

The office team invites you to a baby shower for Priya! It will be held in the meeting room at 1 pm. There will be cake and games, and small gifts are welcome.

So, Nazia, you asked why Khala went quiet with me at the wedding. Honestly? A shrug. At my college, if someone asks which hall the lecture is in and you shrug, it just means "no idea, sorry." Everyone does it and nobody minds. At the wedding, Khala asked if I would help serve the guests, and I did my usual shrug with a little smile, meaning "sure, whatever you need." To her it looked like I couldn't be bothered. She turned away, and for a whole hour I had no clue why. Then Ammi explained. I found Khala at the dessert table and said, "I'm sorry, I meant yes. Tell me where you want me." She hugged me and handed me a tray of sweets. So now I'm Hafsa who says the words out loud, and the shoulders stay where they are.

What did Khala ask Hafsa at the wedding?
Whether Hafsa would help serve the guests.
How did Hafsa feel during the hour before Ammi explained?
Hafsa felt confused and uneasy, not knowing why Khala had gone quiet after what Hafsa meant as a friendly yes.
What did Hafsa do to repair things?
Hafsa found Khala, apologised, said in words that the shrug meant yes, and asked where to help.
How did the shrug look from Khala's side?
To Khala it looked like rude indifference, as if Hafsa could not be bothered to help, so she felt slighted and turned away.

Read this:

Uma,

I'm writing this in the school library because at home, they check everything now.
After they found out about the café, Papa took my phone for a month. No going out, no friends over, not even the tuition group chat. Mummy reads my notebooks. Their only daughter, under house arrest.
So you know what I've done? I've borrowed my cousin's old phone. I keep it in my pencil box and switch it off before I get home. I delete everything.
I'm not proud. But I'm not going to tell them anything now. Why would I? They didn't even ask why I lied. They just locked everything.
Write back by hand.

Neelam

Where does Neelam keep her cousin's old phone?
In her pencil box.
What is Neelam feeling about her parents' restrictions?
She feels resentful and shut out, and determined to hide more instead of telling them anything.
What turning point could change this stage?
Her parents could ask why she lied and talk about fairer terms, rather than relying only on heavy restrictions that push her to hide.
What might Neelam's parents be experiencing?
They are likely hurt and scared after the lie, and may believe the strict rules are keeping her safe, not knowing they are teaching her to hide.
'Sabzi jal gayi' English mein?
Say: "The vegetables got burnt." Or: "I burnt the sabzi." British English uses "burnt" and American English often uses "burned"; both are correct.

At Kaleb's Restaurant, a group with six adults and two children came in to eat. If each adult meal cost six dollars and each children's meal was $4, and every person ordered a soda for $2  how much was the bill?

The cost for adult meals is 6 adults * $6 = $36.
The cost for children's meals is 2 children * $4 = $8.

messages.content: Oliver has 10 $20 and 3 $5 bills. William has 15 $10 and 4 $5 bills. How much more money does Oliver have than William?

Oliver's $20 bills amount to $20 x 10 = $200.
Oliver's $5 bills amount to $5 x 3 = $15.
So, Oliver has a total of $200 + $15 = $215.
William's $10 bills amount to $10 x 15 = $150.
William's $5 bills amount to $5 x 4 = $20.
So, William has a total of $150 + $20 = $170.
Therefore, Oliver has $215 - $170 = $45 more than William.
The answer is 45.

messages.content: Find k if kx^2 - 6x + 1 = 0 has equal roots. Then find k if x^2 - 5x + k = 0 has equal roots. Why must k != 0 in the first equation?

Answer: k = 9 (root x = 1/3); k = 25/4 (root x = 5/2). If k = 0 the first equation becomes -6x + 1 = 0, which is not quadratic.

First equation: a = k, b = -6, c = 1. D = (-6)^2 - 4 x k x 1 = 36 - 4k = 0, k = 9 9x^2 - 6x + 1 = (3x - 1)^2 = 0, x = 1/3 (twice) Second equation: a = 1, b = -5, c = k: D = 25 - 4k = 0, so k = 25/4 and x^2 - 5x + 25/4 = (x - 5/2)^2, root 5/2. A quadratic needs a != 0. With k = 0 the first equation is LINEAR and has exactly one root x = 1/6, but it is not a quadratic with "equal roots". So whenever k is in the x^2-coefficient, write the condition k != 0 in your answer.

Jerry works five days a week as a waiter and earns a variable amount of tips every night. The past four nights, he earned $20, $60, $15, and $40. How much does he need to earn tonight if he wants to make an average of $50 in tips per night?

The total money Jerry needs to make for 5 days to get $50 per night is 5 nights * $50/night = $250.
His total earnings for the past four days is $20 + $60 + $15 + $40 = $135.
So, Jerry needs to earn $250 - $135 = $115 in tips tonight.
The answer is 115.

Mum asked me today how the school trip went. I shrugged. She asked again. I shrugged again and went to my room.
She thought I didn't care. But it wasn't that. On the trip, Anand told everyone about my stutter when I was younger, and they all laughed. I couldn't say it out loud without my voice shaking.
Later Dad came in and sat on the edge of my bed. He didn't ask "how was the trip." He asked, "What was the hardest part?"
I told him. He listened. He said he'd help me think about what to say to Anand.
- Yogesh

What did Anand tell everyone about on the trip?
Yogesh's stutter when younger.
What was Yogesh feeling behind the shrugs?
Yogesh felt hurt and embarrassed about the trip, and couldn't talk about it without the voice shaking.
What question did Dad ask that helped?
He asked, "What was the hardest part?", a patient open question that invited Yogesh to share.
How might Mum have seen the shrugs?
Mum probably thought Yogesh didn't care about the trip, not knowing it hid real hurt.

In the village near Madurai, Kiran lay on the rope cot under the neem tree, replaying it for the hundredth time. Ganga, her friend since they were five, had told the girls at the well about Kiran's crush on the tailor's son. By evening the whole street was teasing her.
Every time she closed her eyes she saw it again: Ganga's laugh, the girls' faces. And she rehearsed what she should have said, sharper each time. Then came the daydreams. She could tell everyone that Ganga still wet the bed till she was nine. She could write it on the temple wall in chalk. She imagined Ganga's face, crumpling.
The thoughts felt powerful, like holding a lit match. For a few minutes they made her feel better.
Then her stomach would turn, and the whole scene would start playing again from the beginning. Three days now. She couldn't concentrate on her lessons. It was as if Ganga were living inside her head, rent-free.

What did Ganga tell the girls at the well?
About Kiran's crush on the tailor's son.
What does Kiran feel when she imagines revenge?
She feels a brief, powerful satisfaction, then her stomach turns and the hurt starts again.
What could help Kiran step out of the replaying?
Talking to someone she trusts, writing down what she wants to say to Ganga, and putting energy into something else rather than planning payback.
What might Ganga be experiencing after spreading the story?
Ganga may feel guilty or awkward, perhaps not realising how deeply she hurt her friend.
Lena says the film must be good because the audience clapped at the end. Is she certain about that?
No, she cannot be certain. Because people may clap to be polite or because they are glad it is over, clapping alone does not prove that the film was good.

Ojas,
I owe you more than the three words I sent last month ("Leave me alone").
You were the best friend I'd had in years. We talked every night. Then you invited me to your cousin's wedding, to meet your whole family, and something in me panicked. I picked a stupid fight about cricket and walked out. I've done this before. Get really close, then burn it down before anyone can leave me first.
My khala noticed I'd stopped coming out of my room and took me to see a counsellor. I go every Tuesday now. It's slow, but I'm starting to understand the pattern.
I'm not asking you to forget it. I'm saying sorry, and that it was never about you.
Farhan

Where had Ojas invited Farhan?
Ojas invited Farhan to a cousin's wedding, to meet the whole family.
What was Farhan afraid of when the friendship got very close?
Farhan was afraid of being left, so ending things first felt safer.
What turning point is helping Farhan change?
Farhan's khala noticed and took Farhan to a counsellor, and the weekly sessions are helping Farhan understand the pattern.
How might Ojas feel reading that it was never about Ojas?
Ojas may feel relieved to know the fight wasn't caused by anything Ojas did, though still hurt by it.

I'm Vasudha, and I was hanging washing on the terrace when I saw my neighbour's daughter Elizabeth lying flat on her roof with a blanket, staring up. It was a clear night after the power cut, with stars everywhere. She didn't move for a long while.
When I whispered across and asked what she was doing, she said, "Just looking." Then, "It's so big, Aunty. It makes me feel tiny, but in a nice way." She was smiling.
Earlier that evening she had fretted loudly about a spelling test, and now she never mentioned it. I can't say exactly what she was thinking. I left her the quiet and went in.

What did Elizabeth lie on the roof with?
Elizabeth was lying flat on her roof with a blanket.
How does Elizabeth feel as she looks at the stars?
Tiny but happy. She says the sky is so big it makes her feel small in a nice way, and she is smiling.
What did Vasudha choose to do when she saw Elizabeth?
Vasudha whispered one question, listened, and then left Elizabeth alone with the sky instead of talking more.
How does Vasudha see Elizabeth's stargazing?
Vasudha notices the smile and that the spelling test worry has vanished, but admits she cannot say exactly what Elizabeth is thinking.

messages.content: A school bus traveled for 42 minutes at a speed of 50 mph. What is the distance the bus traveled in miles?

1 hour = 60 minutes.
We convert the time to hours, so 42 minutes = 42/60 hours = 7/10 hours.
So in 42 minutes, the distance the bus traveled in miles is 50 * (7/10) = 35 miles.
The answer is 35.

Thomas: "Nilesh, why is your game crashing?"
Nilesh: "No idea. I've been trying stuff."
Thomas: "What stuff?"
Nilesh: "I changed the speed, deleted that loop, put it back, renamed some variables, copied a line from a video."
Thomas: "And now?"
Nilesh: "Now it crashes at a different place. Or maybe the same place. I don't know."
Thomas: "What did the error say the first time?"
Nilesh: "Didn't read it. I panicked. The demo's at school tomorrow."
Thomas: "Okay. Undo everything back to this morning."
Nilesh: "Everything?!"
Thomas: "Yes. Then run it, read the error, and change one thing."
Nilesh: (after ten minutes) "It says 'list index out of range' on line 58."
Thomas: "See? Now we have a clue."

What error did Nilesh finally read?
'List index out of range' on line 58.
What was Nilesh feeling while changing things at random?
Nilesh felt panicked about the demo tomorrow, so trying anything felt better than stopping to think.
What did Thomas suggest, and why does it work better?
Undo everything, read the error and change one thing, which turns random guessing into clues you can learn from.
How might Thomas feel hearing Nilesh's list of changes?
Thomas might feel a bit amused and worried, seeing that the random changes had left Nilesh more lost than before.

Looking back, my first month at the design studio taught me more about teaching than about design. Parveen, the senior who had to show me the software, spoke fast and sighed when I asked anything twice. "Just use the layers, it's obvious." After the third sigh I stopped asking. I nodded, wrote nothing, and stayed late redoing files I had misunderstood. What I remember most is the heat in my face. I was not stupid. I just needed the first step slowly. When Parveen was away for a week, a colleague showed me the same tool in ten minutes without any hurry, and it clicked. It was never the tool. It was the tone. - Madhav

What did Parveen say about the layers?
Parveen said, "Just use the layers, it's obvious."
What was Madhav feeling after the third sigh?
Ashamed and slow, with heat in the face, so Madhav stopped asking.
What small step could Madhav take with a hurried teacher next time?
Ask for the first step to be shown slowly just once, or write the steps down and repeat them back.
How might Parveen have seen the situation?
Parveen probably thought the software was simple to explain and did not realise the sighing made Madhav stop asking.

At the cooperative sugar mill in Karad, Vikas had been manager for a year, and every Monday meeting went the same way. He spoke. The supervisors nodded. "Yes, sir." Then things went wrong on Wednesday that someone had surely known about on Monday. This week a boiler valve failed, and the shift lost six hours. Afterwards, in the corridor, he heard Lakshmi, the maintenance clerk, whisper to a colleague, "I told the foreman the valve was leaking. Nobody tells sir bad news." Vikas stood still. So it was him. The next Monday he opened differently. "Before I say anything: what's the worst problem on your floor this week?" Silence. Then Lakshmi raised her hand. "The second valve is leaking too, sir." Vikas thanked her in front of everyone, and sent the fitter out before the meeting ended.

How many hours did the shift lose when the valve failed?
The shift lost six hours.
What was Vikas feeling when he heard Lakshmi's whisper?
He was shocked and uneasy, realising his position was keeping people from telling him problems.
What did Vikas change, and why did it work?
He asked for the worst problem before giving his own view and thanked Lakshmi publicly, which made bad news safe to share.
How might Lakshmi feel when Vikas thanks her in front of everyone?
Lakshmi probably felt relieved and respected, and more willing to speak up next time.
What can I say to a friend whose grandfather has died?

You can say "I'm so sorry for your loss" or "My condolences". Keep it short and kind, and offer to listen if the person wishes to talk.
Example: My condolences to you and your family.

Daycare note, Wednesday. Kiran (2) sat by the toy train while it ran on its track. When it stopped, he waved both hands hard and shouted, "Go!" Aunty Baljeet had just switched it back on, so it moved. He beamed and waved again at the next stop. Later he waved at the window when the rain stopped too. We smiled and played along, and I showed him the switch. He waved anyway. — Baljeet

What did Kiran shout when the toy train stopped?
"Go!"
Why did Kiran beam when the train moved again?
He believed his waving had made the train go, because it moved right after he waved.
What gentle step did the caregiver take to help Kiran?
The caregiver played along and also showed him the switch, giving a simple true reason without spoiling his fun.
How might the caregivers feel watching Kiran wave at the rain?
They probably find it sweet and amusing, knowing that at two he can't yet tell his wishes from what makes things happen.

Monday. On the walk home, Mridul told Rekha a secret: he still slept with the light on because the dark scared him. "Promise you won't tell?" "Promise," Rekha said.
Wednesday. At lunch, the other kids were laughing about who was scared of what. "Mridul looks like someone who's scared of the dark," one boy joked. Everyone turned to Rekha, who knew Mridul best. The secret was right on her tongue, and she wanted to laugh with them. Her cheeks went hot. "No idea," she said, and took a big bite of her roti.
The next Monday, Mridul waited for her at the gate. "Rekha, can I tell you something else? I'm nervous about the swimming test."
Rekha felt something warm in her chest. He trusted her. And she knew, somehow, that she was the kind of person who kept things.

What secret did Mridul tell Rekha on Monday?
He still slept with the light on because the dark scared him.
What was Rekha feeling when everyone turned to her at lunch?
Rekha felt tempted and embarrassed, wanting to laugh with the group but uneasy about breaking her promise.
Which choice worked, and why?
Saying "No idea" and keeping the secret worked, because Mridul's trust grew and he shared more with her.
How does Mridul see Rekha the next Monday?
Mridul sees her as someone safe to trust, so he tells her his worry about the swimming test.

The panchayat office in the small town smelled of damp files and filter coffee. Jomon, two years into his first job as a clerk, was reading out the list of households due for new water connections.

"Next, Kizhakkambalam ward, forty-two houses." Someone at the back said, "That's the Vadakkekara number." Jomon checked. They were right.

He laughed, a short, high laugh, and couldn't seem to stop. A few people laughed with him. The ward member's face stayed flat. Thomas chettan, the senior clerk, leaned back and watched.

Jomon felt his ears burn. He pressed his palm flat on the register and breathed.

"Sorry, my mistake. Vadakkekara is forty-two. Kizhakkambalam is thirty-seven. I'll correct the printed copy today." Then he read the next line.

After the meeting Thomas chettan passed his desk and tapped it twice. "That second part. Good."

How many houses did Jomon correctly give for Kizhakkambalam?
He said Kizhakkambalam is thirty-seven.
What was Jomon feeling when he couldn't stop laughing, and what else might the laugh have meant?
His burning ears suggest he felt embarrassed; the laugh may also have been a hope to ease the tension, though the ward member did not read it that way.
What worked in how Jomon recovered?
He steadied himself, owned the mistake in one sentence, gave the correct numbers, promised to fix the copy that day and moved on.
How does Thomas chettan see Jomon's handling?
He seems to value the brief correction more than the laugh, which is why he tapped the desk and said "That second part. Good."

Pankaj had spent a month training for job interviews: firm handshake, steady eye contact, no looking at the floor. It worked; he got the offer. So on Saturday, meeting Aparna for coffee after their families had exchanged numbers, he did the same. The café near the station was deafening, a blender roaring every two minutes, and Aparna had exactly half an hour before her train. Pankaj leaned in and held her gaze, unblinking, while she talked about her botany course. Aparna's sentences got shorter. She kept looking at the sugar packets. "Is something wrong?" she finally asked. "You're looking at me like an exam invigilator." Pankaj laughed, embarrassed, and let his eyes drift to the window and back. "Sorry. Interview habits." Aparna relaxed. "I'm the opposite. I look everywhere except faces, especially when I'm nervous. But I'm listening, promise. You said your sister also studies botany?" She had heard every word.

How long did Aparna have before her train?
Aparna had exactly half an hour before her train.
What was Pankaj feeling when Aparna mentioned an exam invigilator?
Pankaj felt embarrassed, laughing awkwardly, realising the interview habit didn't fit a coffee date.
How did Pankaj adjust, and why did it help?
He let his gaze drift to the window and back, softening it for a date instead of an interview, which let Aparna relax.
What was the stare like for Aparna?
Aparna felt uncomfortable, her sentences shrinking and eyes on the sugar packets; she finds eye contact hard herself but was still listening closely.

At the book launch in a Kolkata cafe, Lavanya watched Uday sign copies of his first short-story collection and felt a sharp twist in her stomach. They had joined the same writing group four years ago. She had three unfinished stories in a folder at home. For a moment she caught herself thinking the cover was a bit plain.
She stopped. That's envy, she told herself, almost aloud.
She waited her turn, hugged him and said, "Uday, this is wonderful. I'm proud of you, and honestly a little jealous." He laughed.
"How did you finish?" she asked.
"Every morning, 6 a.m., one page."
On the metro home, Lavanya opened the oldest story on her phone and wrote one paragraph.

When does Uday write?
Every morning, 6 a.m., one page.
What did Lavanya feel as she watched Uday sign copies?
She felt a sharp twist of envy, with three unfinished stories of her own at home.
Which choice turned Lavanya's envy into something useful?
Naming it, congratulating Uday honestly and asking how he finished, then writing a paragraph herself.
How might Uday feel hearing "a little jealous"?
He likely felt touched and at ease, since the honesty made the congratulations feel real.

Five minutes before the client walked in, Mohit, the agency's creative head, tapped the storyboard. "Our buyers are mostly retired people. Everyone knows that. Keep the ad slow and serious." Sudha had admired Mohit since her internship; his campaigns were the reason she'd joined. She also had last month's survey open on her tablet. With the clock ticking, she kept it short. "Mohit, can I ask how we got that picture of the buyers? I want to be sure I'm seeing it right." He shrugged. "Twenty years of experience." "That counts for a lot," she said. "This survey shows almost half our buyers are under thirty. Could we add one faster version, just in case?" Mohit squinted at the chart, then sighed. "Fine. Two versions. You present the second." The door opened.

What did last month's survey show?
Almost half our buyers are under thirty.
How does Sudha feel about Mohit while she questions him?
She still admires him, since his campaigns were why she joined, but trusts the survey enough to raise it. 🙂
Which part of Sudha's approach worked best under the time pressure?
Asking how the claim was reached, then offering one chart and a small 'just in case' option, kept it short, respectful and hard to refuse.
How might Mohit feel after squinting at the chart?
Mohit may feel a little caught out but also respected, since she praised his experience and only asked for a second version.

Vidya's architecture drawings for the housing project were due at 9 a.m., and she had started at 8 p.m. the night before. She'd had three weeks. 'I work better last minute,' she had told Sumit on Monday. 'Plus, if it's not great, everyone knows it was a rush job.' At 12:30 a.m. the hostel power cut out, and her laptop battery showed nineteen percent. She finished the plan by torchlight, skipped the elevation, and submitted a half-labelled sheet at 8:57. The next week, the professor's comment said: 'Strong site thinking. Incomplete.' Vidya showed Sumit. 'See, I literally had no power. Anyone would've got this.' Sumit, who had started his on day two, said nothing, but he looked at 'strong site thinking' for a long time. So did Vidya, later, alone.

When were Vidya's drawings due?
They were due at 9 a.m.
Why did Vidya point to the power cut when she showed Sumit the comment?
It gave her a ready excuse for the incomplete work, protecting her from the fear that a full effort might still not be great.
What could Vidya learn from 'strong site thinking'?
That her ideas are good, and that starting early would let her finish them and see what her full work looks like.
Why might Sumit say nothing?
Sumit may feel awkward, having started on day two, and not want to lecture, though he notices the wasted strength too.

In the Pune flat, the cousin's photo with the district chess trophy stood on Dadi's shelf. "Dhruv, you'll never be like Neel," Dadi said most Sundays, not unkindly, as if reading out the weather. Dhruv had stopped playing chess at thirteen. At sixteen, when a teacher suggested the school team, he said, "Not my thing. Neel's the smart one." That evening his father, Manoj, set up the old board on the dining table. "One game. I'm rusty." Dhruv won in twenty moves. Manoj didn't mention Neel. He only said, "You saw that knight fork three moves ahead. That's practice, not magic. You could do more of that if you wanted." Dhruv put the pieces back slowly, looking at the knight.

Where did Manoj set up the old chess board?
On the dining table.
What does Dhruv saying "Neel's the smart one" suggest about how he sees himself?
After years of hearing he'd never be like Neel, he has come to see himself as the less smart one and turns down chances before trying.
What choice did Manoj make that could lift Dhruv?
Instead of comparing, he played a game, praised one specific move and said it came from practice, showing steady belief that Dhruv could grow.
Why might Dadi say it "as if reading out the weather"?
To Dadi it may feel like a harmless remark rather than a verdict; she may not realise how much the repeated words have shaped what Dhruv thinks he can do.

Aadhya, you walk past that old stepwell every day and never look at it. Sit, and let your Amandeep Nanaji tell you its story.
Long ago, before my grandfather was born, there was a drought in our village near Patan. No rain for three years. The rich families had their own wells. The poor had nothing.
A widow called Roopba sold her gold bangles and hired diggers to make a well for everyone, with steps so even children could reach the water. People laughed at her. Then the water came, cold and deep, and nobody laughed again.
That is why, at every wedding in our village, the bride pours the first water from that stepwell. We remember that one person can care for everyone.

What did Roopba sell to hire diggers?
She sold her gold bangles.
How did Roopba probably feel when people laughed at her?
She probably felt hurt but determined, believing the well would help everyone.
What choice in the story made the biggest difference, and why?
Roopba's choice to spend her bangles on a well for everyone, because it saved the whole village in the drought.
How might the poor families have felt when the water came?
They would have felt deeply relieved and grateful, knowing someone had cared for them.
Combine with "because": The fan is off. The power is cut.
The fan is off because the power is cut.

Wednesday: His mother made a deal: games only after homework, one hour, phone charges in the kitchen at nine. Gautam grumbled and slammed his door.
Saturday: Devika called him to the park for cricket. He went, and they played until dark. That night he slept by ten without meaning to. "Cricket's better than the racing game," he admitted to Devika. "Don't tell my mum."

Where does the phone charge at nine?
In the kitchen.
How did Gautam feel when his mother made the deal?
He felt annoyed and resentful, grumbling and slamming his door.
What helped Gautam balance games with play and sleep?
Clear limits at home and a friend inviting him to play outside.
How might Devika feel when Gautam says cricket is better?

At the children's home in Darjeeling, Chandrika rang the little brass bell at seven every morning, the same three rings. For the first weeks, Dolma, five, hid under the bunk whenever voices rose, even happy ones. Chandrika never pulled her out. She sat on the floor and said, "Breakfast is paratha today. I'll save yours." One day Chandrika snapped at a boy for spilling milk, and Dolma froze. Later Chandrika knelt beside her. "I was too loud. That wasn't okay. I'm sorry." By the fourth month, Dolma was waiting at the door at seven, holding the bell out for her.

How many times did Chandrika ring the bell each morning?
She rang it three times, the same three rings each morning.
Why might Dolma hide under the bunk when voices rose?
Raised voices seemed to feel dangerous to her, even happy ones, so she hid to feel safe.
What did Chandrika do after snapping at the boy, and why did it matter?
She knelt by Dolma, admitted she was too loud and said sorry, which repaired the moment and showed an adult can mend a mistake.
What would change if Chandrika had pulled Dolma out from under the bunk?
Dolma would likely feel more frightened and learn that adults force things, which would slow her trust.

Last year, when there were meetings at my school about the new canteen rules, I stayed away from all of it. I'm Jeevan, and in our house we don't "get involved". My grandfather lost a job long ago after speaking at a union meeting, and that story hangs over every conversation.

So I decided: I won't think about any of this. Not the canteen, not the petitions, not the students' council. Safer.

My friend Nikita went to every meeting. She spoke about veg and non-veg counters being separate. She helped write a proposal that the principal accepted.

At the end of the year, the civics teacher asked us to describe one way we'd taken part in school decisions. Nikita wrote two pages. I had nothing.

It wasn't that I'd been in danger. It's that I never learned how to take part safely at all. This year I'm going to one council meeting. Just to listen.

What did Nikita speak about at the meetings?
About veg and non-veg counters being separate.
How did Jeevan feel when there was nothing to write for the civics teacher?
Jeevan felt empty-handed and a little ashamed, realising the avoidance had meant missing out on learning.
What small step is Jeevan planning, and why is it a good start?
Going to one council meeting just to listen; it is low-risk and lawful and lets Jeevan learn how taking part works.
How might Nikita see Jeevan's decision to attend one meeting?
Nikita would probably feel pleased and welcoming, glad that a friend who stayed away is ready to try.

Vinita from the second floor told me today, "You're literally my hero, Rekha didi." She's in Class 7. She knocks every evening now and tells me everything: her friends, the boy who teased her, what her mum said at dinner. She even asked which subjects she should take in Class 9 because "whatever you say is right."

Honestly it felt amazing for about a minute. Then it felt heavy. I'm not always right. I failed my maths unit test last week and cried in the bathroom.

I noticed I could tell her anything and she'd just do it. That scared me more than anything.

So today I told her about the maths test. She stared. "You? Failed?" I said, "Yes, I mess up a lot. For subject choices, ask your mum and the school counsellor, they'll know more than me." She looked disappointed, then said, "Okay. But can I still come and talk?"

Of course she can.

— Rekha

What class is Vinita in?
Vinita is in Class 7.
What did Rekha feel after Vinita called Rekha a hero?
Rekha felt proud for a moment, then weighed down and even scared by how easily Vinita would follow anything Rekha said.
Which choice worked, and why?
Telling Vinita about the failed maths test and pointing her to her mum and the counsellor worked, because it was honest and gave Vinita other people to rely on.
How might Vinita see Rekha after hearing about the maths test?
Vinita may be surprised and a bit disappointed at first, but still trusts Rekha enough to want to keep talking.
Please do not "butt in" when I am speaking. Is "butt in" rude?

It is informal and a little rude. "Butt in" means to interrupt a talk or join in without being asked.
Example: Sorry to butt in, but the bus is leaving.
