Preschool note, Diwali week.
Today the children made a rangoli at the entrance. I gave Yogesh the yellow powder and the job of filling the petals. He took it very seriously, tongue out, pinching the colour just as I showed him. When Harish stepped on a corner, Yogesh cried "Careful!" and fixed it himself. At home time he dragged his father to see it. "I made the yellow!" He asked me three times if we will make one again next year.

What colour did Yogesh fill the petals with?
Yellow.
How did Yogesh feel showing the rangoli to his father?
He felt proud and excited, dragging his father to see it and announcing that he made the yellow.
Why was giving Yogesh a real task a good idea?
A real job made him feel part of the festival and the group, and gave him something to look forward to next year.
How might Harish have felt when Yogesh shouted "Careful!"?
Harish may have felt a bit startled or embarrassed at stepping on the corner.

Read this:

Thanks, Uma. So, I'm Karthik, and for years I thought I was just fussy. College lectures gave me headaches, the canteen made me want to run, and I blamed myself.
In second year I started a notes page on my phone. Every time I felt that jittery, trapped feeling, I wrote down where I was. After a month the pattern was obvious: flickering tube lights, scratchy collars, clattering plates.
So I changed small things. I sit near the window now, away from the lights. I wear soft cotton shirts. I eat lunch at eleven-thirty before the rush. In group work I say one line: "Noise hits me hard, so I'll take the quiet corner." People just say okay.
The headaches mostly stopped. Honestly, looking after myself like that isn't fussy. It's how I get to actually be there.

What time does Karthik eat lunch now?
At eleven-thirty, before the rush.
How did Karthik feel before noticing the pattern?
Karthik felt jittery and trapped in certain places and put it all down to being fussy.
What steps from Karthik's story could help someone with similar triggers?
Track where discomfort happens, choose seating, clothes and routines to ease it, and explain the need to others in one short line.
How might classmates in Karthik's group see the one-line request?
They probably see it as simple and reasonable, which is why they just say okay.

Read this:

The ultimatum I think about most came from my friend Irawati in our second year. I'm Rajni, and back then I was lying a lot. Small things: that I'd return her notes, that I'd be at her play, that I'd pay back the auto fare. One evening she sat me down. "Rajni, I love you. But if you lie to me one more time, I'm stepping back from this friendship." I was furious. I told her she was being dramatic, controlling. I cried to my roommate that night. But my roommate asked, "Is she telling you what to do, or telling you what she'll do?" That stopped me. Irawati wasn't ordering me around. She was saying what she needed to stay. I could choose. I chose to stop lying, clumsily at first. We're still friends. I've learned that some ultimatums are just someone's honest limit.

What did Irawati say she would do if Rajni lied again?
She would step back from the friendship.
How did Rajni feel when Irawati gave the ultimatum?
Rajni felt furious and hurt at first, calling Irawati dramatic and controlling, and cried to the roommate that night.
What question helped Rajni see the ultimatum differently?
The roommate's question: is she telling you what to do, or what she'll do? It showed Irawati was stating a boundary, leaving Rajni free to choose.
How did Irawati likely see her own ultimatum?
As an honest limit about what she needed to stay in the friendship after repeated lies, not as control.

Read this:

Daycare note, monsoon week

Kunal cried at snack time today because the rain was loud on the roof. Mahima, sitting next to him, looked at his face, stopped chewing, and started crying too, harder than he did. She was not hurt and had liked the rain earlier.
I picked Mahima up and took Kunal's hand. We watched the drops on the window together. Both settled in a few minutes. Mahima then offered Kunal her biscuit. 🙂

Why did Kunal cry at snack time?
Kunal cried because the rain was loud on the roof.
What made Mahima start crying though she liked the rain?
Seeing Kunal's face made her feel upset too; his fear spread to her, so she cried even harder than he did.
What did the note-writer do that helped?
They picked Mahima up, held Kunal's hand and watched the rain with them, which calmed both toddlers.
How might Kunal feel when Mahima offers him her biscuit?
He might feel comforted and cared for after being frightened by the rain.
James prints out 2 books.  They are each 600 pages long.  He prints out double-sided and 4 pages per side.  How many sheets of paper does he use?

He printed 600*2=1200 pages
Each sheet of paper was 4*2=8 pages
So he used 1200/8=150 sheets of paper
The answer is 150.

Ellie has found an old bicycle in a field and thinks it just needs some oil to work well again.  She needs 10ml of oil to fix each wheel and will need another 5ml of oil to fix the rest of the bike. How much oil does she need in total to fix the bike?

Ellie needs 2 wheels * 10ml of oil per wheel = 20ml of oil.
To fix the rest of the bike as well, she needs 20 + 5 = 25ml of oil.
The answer is 25.

b) 1/sqrt3

Read this:

The open-air concert in Madrid was packed shoulder to shoulder. Clara and Javier were twenty metres from the stage when someone near them shouted, “Fight! There's a fight!”
Nobody could see a fight. But people started to turn and push. The push rolled through the crowd like a wave. Clara's feet left the ground for a second. Her arms were pinned. She couldn't breathe properly.
“Clara, arms up!” Javier shouted. She lifted her arms in front of her chest. They let the wave carry them sideways instead of fighting it.
A steward opened a side gate and people spilled out onto the grass. Clara sat down, shaking and furious. “There wasn't even a fight,” she said. “Just a shout.”

What did someone near them shout?
Someone shouted, "Fight! There's a fight!"
How did Clara feel after reaching the grass?
She felt shaken and furious, angry that a shout, not a real fight, had caused the push.
What helped Clara and Javier stay safer in the surge?
Keeping their arms up to protect their chests and moving sideways with the wave instead of against it.
How might the steward have felt opening the side gate?
The steward was probably alarmed but focused, acting fast to let pressure out of the crowd.
Riya has 62 stickers. Sonu has 38. How many more stickers does Riya have? Find a quick way.

Answer: 24 more. 62 - 38 = 24.

Way 1: take away 40 instead of 38: 62 - 40 = 22. We took away 2 too many, so add 2 back: 24. Way 2: add 2 to BOTH numbers; the difference stays the same: 64 - 40 = 24. Show way 2 with two rows of cubes: add 2 to each row, and the gap between them does not change.
After the long walk, my legs were paining a lot. Please correct my English.

After the long walk, my legs were hurting a lot.
Why: a body part "hurts"; "pain" is mainly a noun.
When a friend moves away, why can a person feel happy and sad at once?
Both feelings make sense together. Because they are glad for the friend's new chance and grateful for the time they shared, but sad to lose the daily company.

Read this:

Gautam's savings would last maybe six more weeks. He'd left his first job, as a line cook in a big hotel in Goa, after a head chef who screamed, threw pans and made him work fourteen-hour shifts without a day off for a month.

Now he was back in his parents' flat in Pune, and it had rained for nine days.

His sister Nikita put her phone in front of him. "A small café in Aundh. They want a cook. The owner's a woman who used to be a teacher. Reviews say she's lovely to staff."

"Every kitchen is the same," Gautam said. "They all scream. They all use you. I'm not doing that again."

"You worked in one kitchen."

"One was enough to know."

Nikita left the phone on the table. He didn't touch it. That evening he searched for data-entry jobs he didn't want, because at least they weren't kitchens. The rain kept falling.

How long did Gautam's savings last, roughly?
Maybe six more weeks.
Why does "One was enough to know" feel true to Gautam?
His first kitchen was genuinely harsh, so the pain is real, and it seems safer to assume all kitchens are like that. The strong memory makes one example feel like the whole trade.
What small step could Gautam take without committing to a new kitchen job?
He could visit the café or talk to the owner for ten minutes to see how she treats staff. Checking one more example would test whether every kitchen really is the same.
How might Nikita feel when Gautam leaves her phone untouched?
Nikita might feel frustrated and worried, especially with his savings running low. She clearly wants to help and may feel shut out.

Read this:

Manjula, you ask why I let you talk over me at the table but tell you to wait in school. Let me tell you a story. When I was ten, our teacher, Devika Ma'am, had a rule: one person speaks, the rest listen. At home, though, my aunts and my grandmother talked all at once and finished each other's sentences, and nobody minded. I once waited at the dinner table for a gap to speak, and my grandmother asked, “Why so quiet? Are you unwell?” So I learned there are two ways. The classroom asks you to wait. My grandmother's table welcomed the noise.

How old was the storyteller when Devika Ma'am set her rule?
Ten.
Why did the grandmother ask if the child was unwell at the dinner table?
She read the waiting and silence as something wrong, since in her family talking together showed interest.
What did the storyteller learn from the grandmother's question at dinner?
The storyteller learned there are two ways: the classroom asks you to wait, while the grandmother's table welcomed talking together, so each place has its own rule.
How might Devika Ma'am see the overlapping talk at the aunts' dinner table?
She might find it unusual or noisy for a classroom, but at home she could see it as a sign of closeness.

Read this:

Mridul, your Sumit chacha heard "should" more often than his own name. At twenty, in Kanpur, it was every day: "You should do engineering like your brother." "You should marry by twenty-five; the Sharma girl is good." My father said it with love. He carried cement bags so I could study. That made it harder to say no.

I felt I was letting him down just by thinking. Love and pressure on the same plate, every meal.

The turning point was an evening on the roof in mango season. I told him, "Babuji, I respect you more than anyone. I want to study agriculture, not engineering. And I will marry, but not by a date." He didn't speak for two days. Then he asked, "What will you grow?"

I became an agronomist. I married at thirty-one. He danced at the wedding.

What did young Sumit's father do so Sumit could study?
His father carried cement bags so Sumit could study.
Why was it hard for young Sumit to say no to his father?
Young Sumit felt deep love and gratitude for his father's sacrifice, so refusing felt like letting him down, even as the pressure weighed on him.
What turning point in the story let Sumit keep both respect and his choice?
On the roof, Sumit told his father he respected him most, then clearly named his own choices about study and marriage.
How might Sumit's father have felt during the two days of silence?
He was probably hurt and worried, but also thinking it over, which is why he came back with "What will you grow?"

Read this:

Monday: At the bus stop Joseph passed round a vape. “Everyone does it, Irfan. Take one.” Irfan shook his head. Dev said, “Suit yourself,” and they all turned slightly away. On the ride home Irfan felt like a stranger among them.
Friday: The same offer, and this time Joseph added, “Maybe you'd like the front seats better.” Irfan's hands were cold. He almost reached out. Then he said, “Nah, my throat's bad,” and looked at his phone until the bus came.
The next Wednesday: Dev sat beside him and asked about the match. Joseph didn't speak to him all week. Irfan noticed that the bus ride was still just a bus ride.

What excuse did Irfan give on Friday?
He said, "Nah, my throat's bad."
What does Irfan's cold hands on Friday suggest about how he felt?
He felt frightened and pressured; the hint of being pushed out made him almost reach for the vape even though he didn't want it.
What small step could help Irfan keep saying no?
He could spend more time with Dev, who still talks to him, so the threat of being left out has less power.
How does Dev seem to feel about Irfan's refusal by Wednesday?
Dev seems relaxed about it; he chooses to sit with Irfan and talk about the match, showing not everyone cares as much as Joseph.
Peace or piece: "Can I have a ___ of cake?"

Write "piece", which means a part of something. "Peace" means calm or no fighting. A memory trick: a piece of pie.
Examples: Can I have a piece of cake? After the guests left, there was peace in the house.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Grade 9B, 18 August.
Nazia and Bidisha have sat apart for about three weeks; Bidisha has looked more and more withdrawn. Today, as Nazia had asked, I let them use the empty art room during free period. I stayed at my desk at the far end, marking. Bidisha spoke first, quietly: "I felt left out at lunch. When you started sitting with the drama group." Her hands were shaking. Nazia looked shocked. "I thought you were angry about my birthday! I only sat there because they needed help with lines. I missed you." Bidisha laughed and then cried a little. Both seemed relieved, I think, that it was so small. Walking out, Nazia said, "Three weeks, for that." Plan: nothing further needed. Will keep an eye out.

Where did Nazia and Bidisha talk?
They talked in the empty art room during free period.
What does Bidisha's laugh and small cry suggest?
It suggests relief that the real reason was so small, after three weeks of fearing something worse.
What lesson might both take from this?
Saying "I felt left out" early would have cost a minute, while the silence cost three weeks of distance.
What had Nazia believed the problem was?
Nazia thought Bidisha was angry about the birthday, and had been missing Bidisha all along.

Read this:

In the corridor outside the Class 5 room of their Kochi school, Jomon spotted it: a hundred-rupee note, folded in four, half under the notice board. His heart raced. That could be a whole comic book. Or ten packets of spicy chips. Or the yo-yo with lights. He picked it up, and his fingers curled around it. Devika came round the corner. 'What's that?' 'Nothing.' Then, 'I found money.' She looked at it. 'Someone must be looking for it. Remember when Ammu lost her fees money?' Jomon remembered her crying. He looked at the note one more time, imagining the yo-yo. Then he walked to the staffroom and gave it to Lissy Miss. 'Found near the notice board.' She wrote his name in the lost-property book.

Where did Jomon find the note?
Half under the notice board in the corridor.
What was Jomon feeling when his fingers curled around the note?
Excited and tempted, his heart racing with ideas of what he could buy.
What helped Jomon make the wise choice?
Devika's question and remembering Ammu crying over lost fees money, which led him to hand it to Lissy Miss.
How might the owner of the note feel?
Worried and upset, the way Ammu was, until it is returned.

Read this:

Jagdish, you think crying makes you weak? Let your Rukmini didi tell you something.

When I was twenty-five, my best friend moved abroad. That same week, I found myself crying over nothing: a song, an old photo, my mother's voice on the phone. I realised it was about more than my friend. It was about my grandmother, who died when I was ten. I never cried for her then.

I could have pushed it down again. Instead I wrote letters to my grandmother, letters I never sent. I talked to my mother about her. When the sadness didn't lift, I saw a counsellor for a few months.

It was hard. But it felt like finally opening a window in a closed room.

What did Rukmini write to her grandmother?
Letters she never sent.
How did young Rukmini feel that week her friend moved abroad?
She felt deep sadness that went beyond her friend, as old grief for her grandmother surfaced.
What turning point in the story led Rukmini to see a counsellor?
When the sadness didn't lift after writing and talking, she chose to see a counsellor.
How might Rukmini's mother have felt talking about the grandmother?
Her mother probably felt moved and glad to share memories.

Read this:

On the crowded train to Pune, Pankaj, five, sat squashed between Papa and their neighbour Elizabeth aunty. Suddenly he said, loudly, "Elizabeth aunty, your mummy is sick! She's in hospital! Papa told Mummy." The whole compartment went quiet. Elizabeth aunty's face froze. She looked out of the window. Papa gently pulled Pankaj close and whispered, "Beta, that's aunty's sad news. It's hers to tell. Words like that can hurt." Pankaj looked at Elizabeth aunty's face. "Is she sad?" "Yes." Pankaj reached out and patted her hand. "Sorry, aunty." She squeezed his fingers.

Where was Elizabeth aunty's mother?
In hospital.
How did Pankaj feel on seeing Elizabeth aunty's face?
He felt unsure and then sorry, patting her hand once he understood she was sad.
What did Papa teach Pankaj?
That sad news belongs to the person it's about, and that words like that can hurt, so they need care.
How did Elizabeth aunty respond to Pankaj's apology?
She squeezed his fingers, showing she accepted it.

Read this:

Vaibhav, you asked your Indu Dadi why I never say which of you cousins is the cleverest. Sit, I'll tell you. When your Papa and his brother were small, I always compared. "Look at Suresh's marks, why can't you?" They fought all the time, over everything. One day a teacher told me, "Praise each one for what he does." So I tried. I told your Papa his handwriting was careful, and Suresh that he was a good runner. When they quarrelled over small things, I let them sort it out, and only stepped in if someone might get hurt. Slowly, they stopped trying to beat each other. Now they talk every day.

What did Indu Dadi praise Vaibhav's Papa for?
She praised his careful handwriting.
How did Indu Dadi feel about her old habit of comparing?
She seems to regret it, since it made her sons fight over everything, which is why she changed.
What approach did Indu Dadi switch to, and why did it work?
She praised each son for his own strengths and let them solve small quarrels, so they no longer had to compete for her approval.
How might Suresh have felt when his mother stopped comparing?
He probably felt less pressure and more valued for his running, and less need to beat his brother.

Read this:

At the coaching centre in Kota, results went up on the notice board every Monday. Week three, Jagdish was rank 4. "Natural talent," he told the canteen, loud enough for everyone to hear. "Some people just get physics." Week four, he was rank 63. He stood in front of the board with his arms folded. "Paper was set wrong. Half the questions were out of syllabus. And the invigilator kept walking around, so I couldn't focus." Payal, from his batch, was standing beside him. "Rank 4 last week, same invigilator." "That was different." "And the out-of-syllabus questions were from chapter nine, which we did on Saturday. You skipped Saturday." Jagdish's ears went red. "Whatever," he said, and walked off. But on Wednesday he was the first to ask for the chapter nine notes.

What rank did Jagdish get in week four?
Rank 63.
Why did Jagdish blame the paper and the invigilator in week four?
He felt embarrassed and defensive about the drop, so blaming outside causes protected his picture of himself as naturally talented.
What did Jagdish finally do that helps him learn?
He asked for the chapter nine notes, dealing with the real gap instead of blaming the paper.
How does Payal see Jagdish's excuses?
Payal sees through them, pointing out the same invigilator last week and the Saturday class he skipped.

Read this:

Ritu, I'm telling you, Farah is the worst. We planned to go to the book fair at four, right? I waited at the gate for forty minutes. Forty! I messaged her six times, called her twice. Nothing. Not even a sorry. This is just who she is. She did the same thing in Class 7 when she forgot my birthday. She thinks her time matters more than everyone else's. What? No, her phone was fine yesterday. Why would it suddenly... okay, it's old, fine, it dies sometimes. But she could have borrowed someone's. Unless she wasn't near anyone. Or... no. Look, Preeti knows people, and Farah just doesn't care. Why are you shaking your head?

How long did Preeti wait at the gate?
Forty minutes.
Why does Preeti decide Farah doesn't care?
Preeti feels hurt and annoyed after waiting, so the silence feels like proof of Farah's character, and the old phone that dies seems like an excuse.
What could Preeti try before deciding what Farah is like?
Wait until Farah can explain, and think about ordinary reasons first, like a dead phone or being stuck somewhere.
Why might Ritu be shaking her head?
Ritu probably thinks Preeti is being unfair, blaming Farah's character before knowing what happened.
What is my neighbour's phone number? Why do we breathe faster after running? What does "cub" mean?

1. I don't know, because I can't see private details. Ask your neighbour or someone in your family.
2. The muscles need more air when we run. Because breathing faster brings in more air.
3. A cub is a young lion, tiger or bear.

Read this:

Pranav: you still up worrying?
Pooja: always lol. the flat renewal, the new manager, my knee, amma's cough
Pranav: ok try my thing. i do it every evening at 8
Pranav: 15 min timer. write every worry on paper. all of them
Pooja: then?
Pranav: put a tick next to the ones i can actually do something about. circle ONE and do a tiny step. the rest stay on the paper till tomorrow's 8pm
Pooja: that sounds too simple
Pranav: it is simple. last week i had 11 worries. 3 had ticks. i called the landlord about the renewal. done. the other 8 i just left on the page
Pooja: and you didn't think about them at 2am?
Pranav: less. when they come i tell myself, 8pm tomorrow 🙂
Pooja: ok. tonight. 15 min
Pooja: amma's cough gets a tick. i'll book the doctor tomorrow

How many of Pranav's 11 worries had ticks last week?
3 had ticks.
Why does Pooja think the method sounds too simple, and what does she feel by the end?
Pooja is doubtful because the worries feel so big, but by the end Pooja seems willing and a bit hopeful, picking one step for Amma's cough.
Why does separating solvable worries from the rest help?
It turns some worries into small actions, like calling the landlord, while giving the others a set time so they don't spin all night.
How has the method changed Pranav's nights?
Pranav seems calmer, thinking about worries less at 2am because they have a place at 8pm.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 2% today. The Dow ended the day at 8,722. What was the Dow in the morning before the markets opened?

Today the Dow was down 8722 / 98*2 = 178.
So it started at 8722 + 178 = 8900.
The answer is 8900.
A train travels 270 km in 3 hours at a steady speed. How far does it go in 5 hours? How long does it take for 630 km?

Answer: 450 km in 5 hours. 7 hours for 630 km.

In 1 hour: 270 / 3 = 90 km (the speed, 90 km/h). In 5 hours: 90 x 5 = 450 km. For 630 km: each hour covers 90 km, so the number of hours is 630 / 90 = 7. Check: 7 x 90 = 630. The same unit rate (90 km per hour) answers both questions: multiply to find distance, divide to find time. (More in 5.31, speed-distance-time.)
Do you know what a tumbler is, apart from being a gymnast?

Yes. A tumbler is a tall drinking glass with straight sides and no handle. It is a noun. It can also mean a gymnast who does somersaults.
Example: She filled a tumbler with cold water and placed it on the table.

Read this:

Tariq's mum signed him up for a Saturday taster day at the community centre in Rotterdam. Four stations, twenty minutes each. At football, Tariq kept glancing at the clock. At drawing, he sketched one lopsided boat and stopped. At cooking, he and Alejandro, a boy he'd just met, burned the pancakes and laughed. The last station was a small electronics table with buzzers and wires. Tariq made a bulb light up, then made it blink. The leader called time, and Tariq didn't hear her. Alejandro had to tap his shoulder. On the tram home, Tariq kept drawing circuits on the steamed-up window. "Can I go back next week?" he asked. "Just to the wires."

What did Tariq and Alejandro burn at the cooking station?
They burned the pancakes.
What does Tariq not hearing the leader call time suggest?
It suggests he was completely absorbed and excited by the electronics, far more than at the other stations where he watched the clock.
What small step could Tariq's mum take to support this interest?
She could find a regular beginner electronics group or simple kit so he can keep exploring it, while still letting him try other things.
How might Alejandro remember the taster day differently from Tariq?
For Alejandro the fun part may have been the burned pancakes and meeting Tariq, since each child finds different activities absorbing.
If there are sixty-five dolphins in the ocean, and three times that number joins in from a river which has its mouth at the ocean, calculate the total number of dolphins in the ocean.

When three times the number of dolphins in the ocean joins in from a river, the number of dolphins in the ocean increases by 3 *65 = 195
The total number of dolphins in the ocean increases to 195+65 = 260
The answer is 260.

Read this:

My name is Ishita, and last summer we moved to a building in Kochi where I knew nobody. The first evening, the lady from upstairs, Mrs Elizabeth, came down with a plate of banana fritters. Mummy nudged me. "Say hello properly, smile nicely!"

I gave my small smile, lips shut, and looked at the fritters. Mummy sighed, but Mrs Elizabeth just said, "Take your time, I'm not going anywhere."

She came again on Sunday, and again after that. By the third plate I was telling her about my rabbit, and my smile had teeth in it.

What did Mrs Elizabeth bring down the first evening?
A plate of banana fritters.
What was Ishita most likely feeling behind the small, closed-mouth smile that first evening?
Shyness and politeness with a stranger in a new place rather than delight; looking at the fritters instead of her face suggests Ishita felt a bit nervous 🙂
How could Mummy handle Ishita's shy smile differently?
Instead of pushing for a bigger smile, give Ishita time, as Mrs Elizabeth did, and let the friendliness grow over several visits.
How does Mrs Elizabeth read Ishita's small smile?
She seems to see it as shyness, not rudeness, and calmly keeps visiting until Ishita is ready to open up.

Read this:

Siddharth, you think nobody in the world has ever felt what you're feeling about this girl? Let your Deepak chacha tell you something.

When I was sixteen, I fell hard for a girl in my tuition class. I thought my feelings were deeper than anyone's ever. I wrote poems. I thought the whole tuition class was watching me blush every day.

Then one evening, my father found a poem. He didn't laugh. He told me about the girl he liked at sixteen. He'd written poems too.

I was stunned. My father! Slowly, as I talked to more people, I realised everyone had felt something like this. It didn't make my feelings smaller. It made me less lonely.

What did Deepak's father find?
A poem.
How did young Deepak feel when his father told his own story?
He felt stunned, then less lonely, realising his feelings weren't unique.
What turning point in the story changed how Deepak saw his feelings?
His father sharing his own sixteen-year-old poems made Deepak see others had felt the same.
How might Deepak's father have felt finding the poem?
His father probably felt tender and nostalgic, remembering his own first crush.

Read this:

On her first day at St Agnes Convent School, Nazia put her bag on the big armchair by the staffroom window. Nobody said anything, but the room went quiet in a way she didn't understand.
At lunch, Mrs Menon, who taught maths, sat on a plastic chair near the door and ate from her tiffin without looking up. Later Nazia noticed that every senior teacher had a place, a cup, a shelf.
In the second week, Sister Elizabeth, the principal, called her in. “The chair by the window,” she said gently, “belongs to Mrs Menon. Thirty-one years here. Nobody will tell you. I'm telling you.”
Nazia's cheeks burned. The next morning she brought a box of homemade coconut barfi, put it on Mrs Menon's shelf with a note: Sorry for taking your chair. Please teach me the rest of the rules. Mrs Menon laughed for the first time.

How long had Mrs Menon been at the school?
She had been there thirty-one years.
What was Nazia feeling when Sister Elizabeth explained about the chair?
She felt embarrassed, with burning cheeks, realising she had broken a rule nobody had told her.
Why did Nazia's note to Mrs Menon work well?
It apologised warmly and asked to learn, which respected Mrs Menon's seniority and opened a friendly start.
What was it like for Mrs Menon when a newcomer took her chair on the first day?
She probably felt hurt and slighted, which is why she ate by the door without looking up.

Read this:

Nirmala Masi, can I just talk and you don't fix anything? Okay. This morning I was so happy I sang in the shower, because the drama club picked my script. Then at lunch I found out Pooja was left out of the trip because her fees were late, and I was furious, like, burning. I wrote a whole speech in my head for the principal. And by four o'clock I was lying on my bed feeling like nothing matters and nobody likes me.
Three different people in one day, Masi. Is something wrong with me?
You felt like this too? Really? At my age? 'It gets steadier, Tanuja,' you say. Okay. I believe you.
Can I sit here a while? Your kitchen is quieter than my head.

Why was Pooja left out of the trip?
Because her fees were late.
What was Tanuja feeling by four o'clock?
Tanuja felt low and flat, as if nothing matters and nobody likes Tanuja.
What choice did Tanuja make that helped with the swings?
Tanuja chose to go to Nirmala Masi and talk without asking to be fixed, finding a steady adult and a quiet kitchen.
How might Nirmala Masi feel when Tanuja asks 'Is something wrong with me?'
Masi may feel tender and protective, and want Tanuja to know such swings are common, as she seems to have shared from her own teenage years.

Nikita: didi you free?
Tanuja: for you always. what happened
Nikita: at Rinku's sangeet they played the song Papa used to sing before he left
Nikita: I ran to the washroom. I was shaking
Tanuja: oh Niku. I'm so sorry
Nikita: my first thought was fix my kajal, go back and dance
Nikita: but I stayed and cried. then I texted you
Tanuja: I'm really glad you did
Tanuja: that was so much to carry at nine
Nikita: it's been coming up a lot lately. bad dreams too
Tanuja: would you be open to seeing a counsellor? I can help you find one
Nikita: ya. I think I would

What song was played at Rinku's sangeet?
The song Papa used to sing before he left.
What does Nikita's first thought about fixing the kajal suggest?
It suggests the old habit was to hide the hurt and carry on, pushing the feeling back down so as to look fine.
Which choices helped Nikita this time?
Nikita stayed and cried, then texted Tanuja, and agreed to see a counsellor since the feelings and bad dreams keep coming.
What might Tanuja be feeling as she reads Nikita's messages?
Tanuja may feel sad for how young Nikita was then, and relieved to be the one Nikita now turns to instead of carrying it alone.

"Mm-hmm," said Gautam, eyes on his phone, when his mother Kalyani asked whether he had finished his homework. She paused with the ladle in her hand. It could mean yes, or it could mean leave me alone. "Was that a yes, or a brush-off? Tell me in words." Gautam looked up, half smiling. "Brush-off. But also yes. Almost." He put the phone down and opened his notebook. At twenty, Gautam messaged his hostel-mate Arnab that he had got a summer internship. The reply arrived a minute later: "wow." No emoji, no full stop after it, nothing more. Gautam read it four times. Was Arnab impressed? Envious? Making fun? He could not tell, and his pleasure drained away. He typed "?" and got no reply, so he rang. Arnab picked up from a noisy bus. "I was typing with one hand, yaar! Wow means wow. That's amazing, honestly." Gautam grinned and felt silly. "Next time write more than three letters," he said, and they both laughed.

What did Gautam say when his mother asked about his homework?
He said, "Mm-hmm."
How are Gautam's "mm-hmm" and Arnab's "wow" alike, and how does each get cleared up?

Both short sounds could mean different things, the mm-hmm a yes or a brush-off and the wow admiration, envy or sarcasm, because tone and voice were missing. Kalyani asked in words and Gautam rang Arnab, and each follow-up settled the meaning.
What was Gautam feeling as he read Arnab's one-word reply four times?
He felt uncertain and a little hurt, as his pleasure drained away when he could not tell whether Arnab was impressed or mocking.
What could Arnab do next time Arnab replies to good news by message?
Arnab could add a few more words or an emoji so the warmth comes through, or call when not typing on a bus.
A farmer planted 30 rows of tomatoes with 10 plants in each row. Each tomato plant yields 20 pieces of tomatoes. How many pieces of tomatoes can the farmer get from all his planted tomatoes?

The farmer planted a total of 30 x 10 = 300 tomato plants.
Thus, the farmer can get 300 x 20 = 6000 pieces of tomatoes.
The answer is 6000.

The rain had turned the trail above Manali into mud, and they were still two hours from camp. Sumit had been groaning theatrically since lunch: at the climb, the weight of his pack, the cold. "You're being dramatic," Saurabh called back, grinning. Then Sumit slipped on a wet rock, and the next sound was different, a sharp cry and then a low moan through clenched teeth. He sat in the mud holding his ankle. Saurabh's first reflex was another joke. He stopped himself. Sumit's face had gone white, and he wasn't looking up to see if anyone was laughing. Saurabh knelt beside him. "Real or joking? Honestly." "Real. I can't put weight on it." Saurabh sent an SOS with their location from the satellite messenger the trek company had given them, then radioed the group leader, who said a rescue team was coming up from the lower camp. He wrapped his own jacket around Sumit and stayed with him.

How far were they from camp?
Still two hours from camp.
What made Saurabh stop his reflex joke?
Saurabh felt a flash of worry, seeing Sumit's white face and noticing he wasn't checking whether anyone was laughing, so the moan seemed like real pain.
What did Saurabh do that helped?
He asked honestly whether it was real, then sent an SOS with their location, radioed the group leader and stayed with Sumit, keeping him warm.
What might it have been like for Sumit to hear 'You're being dramatic' earlier?
Sumit probably took it as friendly teasing then, but after the fall he may have worried his real pain would be dismissed as more drama.

In the school auditorium in Chandigarh, the Class 10 play rehearsal stopped dead. Baljeet had forgotten the second line of the big speech, again. Ma'am said, "Take it from the top." Baljeet shook his head, face hot. On the bench outside afterwards he told Payal, "I'm quitting. And the debate team. I mess up everything I touch." "It's one line," Payal said. "It's not one line. It's me. It's always been me." He said it calmly, like reading out a weather report. "I'm not being dramatic. I'm just being realistic." Payal remembered him saying the same in Class 8 about football, and then chess. Each time he had quit within a week. "Realistic would be: you learnt that whole speech in four days," she said. Baljeet shrugged and walked to the bus stop, the script still in his hand.

Which two things did Baljeet say he was quitting?
The play and the debate team.
Why did Baljeet believe he was being realistic?
He saw one forgotten line as proof of a permanent flaw that spoils everything, so the gloomy view felt like plain fact to him.
At this turning point, what could Baljeet try instead of quitting?
He could treat it as one line that needs practice, not a verdict on himself, and run the speech a few more times before deciding anything.
How does Payal see Baljeet's 'realism'?
Payal sees a pattern of football, chess and now the play, each dropped within a week, and thinks the real facts, like learning the speech in four days, point the other way.

The bank's training centre in Pune smelled of new carpet and nervous people. Imran, twenty-four, had failed the spreadsheet module test twice. The third attempt was on Friday.
“I just can't do formulas,” he muttered during the break.
Manoj, the trainer, overheard. “You can't do them yet.”
Imran felt a spike of resentment. Easy for the trainer to say.
Manoj sat down beside him. “What did you try last time?”
“I watched the videos again.”
“And?”
“Same result.”
“So more of the same effort won't help. What else could you try?”
Imran thought. “Practise with real branch data instead of the examples? Ask you when I'm stuck instead of guessing?”
“Both good.”
On Friday Imran scored 68, just over the pass mark. He wrote “yet” in the corner of his notebook, and underneath it: “new method.”

What did Imran score on the third attempt?
Imran scored 68, just over the pass mark.
How did Imran feel when Manoj said “yet”?
He felt a spike of resentment at first, thinking it was easy for the trainer to say.
Why did Imran pass on the third attempt?
He combined the “yet” mindset with a new strategy, practising with real data and asking when stuck, instead of repeating the same effort.
How might Manoj feel seeing Imran pass?
Manoj probably feels pleased and quietly proud that the questions helped Imran find a better method.
I'm writing a short story for a competition but I'm stuck halfway.
Getting stuck in the middle is very common. What happens in your story so far?
A boy finds an old key in his grandmother's house, but I don't know what it opens.
That is a strong start. Ask yourself what the boy wants most. The key could open something linked to that wish, like a box of letters from a parent or a room nobody talks about.
I like the box of letters idea.
Then you have a direction. The letters could show him something new about his family. Let him find one surprising detail, and build the ending around how that changes him.

In the morning, at the handpump behind their house in the village, Vaibhav, six, washed his own face and hands while Jagdish Dada pumped.

"Behind the ears too," Dada said. Vaibhav scrubbed hard, giggling at the cold water.

Inside, he pulled on his school shorts and buttoned his shirt himself, one button skipped. He fixed it before Dada could say anything.

At breakfast there was a new vegetable in the sabzi. Vaibhav poked it, then ate it. "Tastes okay," he said.

Who pumped the water while Vaibhav washed?
Jagdish Dada pumped the water.
How can you tell Vaibhav felt proud of dressing himself?
He fixed the skipped button before Dada could say anything, showing he wanted to do it right on his own.
What small step could help Vaibhav keep building these habits?
Dada could let him do more steps alone, like pumping water with help, and notice his efforts.
How might Jagdish Dada see Vaibhav's morning?
He probably feels pleased watching his grandson take care of himself.

Meera knows 12^2 = 144. How can she find 13^2 without multiplying 13 x 13?

Now you try: 14^2 = 196. Find 15^2.
The answer is 196 + 14 + 15 = 225.

Tuesday: Rukmini screamed and threw her shoe across the hall. Pallavi picked it up and made it talk in a squeaky voice. Two minutes later Rukmini was giggling and trying to feed the shoe a biscuit.

Thursday: another tantrum over the bath, gone as soon as a rubber duck appeared.

Saturday: the crying started after breakfast and did not stop. Rukmini kept tugging at one ear and pushed the duck away. Pallavi stopped trying tricks and phoned the clinic for a visit.

What did Pallavi make the shoe do on Tuesday?
Pallavi made it talk in a squeaky voice.
What was Rukmini most likely feeling on Saturday?
She was most likely hurting or unwell, since she kept tugging at one ear and nothing cheered her. She might also have been very tired, but the long crying made Pallavi take it seriously.
Which choice on Saturday was wise, and why?
Pallavi stopped using distractions and phoned the clinic, because crying that lasts and does not respond to comfort can mean a real need.
What is it like for Pallavi when the usual tricks stop working?
It is probably worrying for Pallavi, because the quick fixes that worked all week now fail, and that change is a sign that something is different.

Miss Stoner did so, and Holmes, after a careful examination through the open window, endeavoured in every way to force the shutter open, but without success. There was no slit through which a knife could be passed to raise the bar. Then with his lens he tested the hinges, but they were of solid iron, built firmly into the massive masonry. "Hum!" said he, scratching his chin in some perplexity, "my theory certainly presents some difficulties. No one could pass these shutters if they were bolted. Well, we shall see if the inside throws any light upon the matter."

How would you explain this excerpt to a young child, in three sentences?

Holmes looks closely through the open window and tries every way to force the shutter, but it will not open. There is no slit for a knife to lift the bar, and the iron hinges are set in solid stone. He scratches his chin, says his idea has problems, and decides to look at the inside.
Tell me, in 50 words, why a family dinner together is worth protecting.

A family dinner is worth protecting because it is a moment when everyone slows down. We share food and talk about our day. Even a simple meal feels special when we eat together. Children learn from the conversation, and adults learn from the children. These small evenings become our warmest memories.

Chetan, you were on leave during the outage review, so let Payal tell you what happened, because I think we finally did it right.
Last time, we blamed Suresh and moved on, and it happened again. This time I said, nobody's name goes on the board till we've asked why five times.
Why did the site go down? A bad config went live. Why did it go live? It passed review. Why did review pass it? The reviewer only saw the code diff, not the config. Why? Because config changes aren't shown in review at all. Why? Because our deployment script never included them.
So the cause wasn't a person. It was a gap in our process.
We added an automatic check that stops any deployment if the config fails a test. Suresh wrote it himself, actually. Two months now. No repeat.

Who wrote the automatic check?
Suresh wrote it himself.
How might Payal feel about this outage review compared with the last one?
Payal seems relieved and quietly proud, believing the team finally did it right by finding a process gap instead of blaming someone.
What else could the team add to keep this from recurring, and why?
They could review other steps in the deployment script for similar gaps, since one missing check suggests there may be others.
How might Suresh see the new review?
Suresh, who was blamed last time, may feel respected and relieved, and writing the fix himself suggests he felt trusted.

messages.content: About 1.43 x 10^9 people live in India, whose area is about 3.29 x 10^6 km^2. Find the number of people per km^2, to 2 significant figures.

Answer: 1.43 x 10^9 / (3.29 x 10^6) ~ 0.435 x 10^3 ~ 4.3 x 10^2 people per km^2, about 430.

Divide the front numbers: 1.43 / 3.29 ~ 0.4347 (by calculator or long division). Divide the powers by SUBTRACTING exponents: 10^9 / 10^6 = 10^3. So about 0.4347 x 10^3. Adjust: 0.4347 = 4.347 x 10^-^1, so 4.347 x 10^2. To 2 significant figures: 4.3 x 10^2 = 430. Estimate first to check: 1.4 billion / 3.3 million ~ 1,400 / 3.3 ~ 420. A second example: (8 x 10^-^3) / (2 x 10^4) = 4 x 10^-^7.

Subject: I blame you for my sleep
Hi Pankaj,
You told me to start that space series "just for one episode." I started Friday. It is now Sunday, 1 a.m., and I've watched nine.
Every episode ends with someone floating off into the dark or a message nobody can read. How am I supposed to stop there? I close the laptop and my brain keeps going: is she alive? who sent that signal?
Tonight I tried to stop at seven. I lay in bed for twenty minutes thinking about the signal, then got up and watched two more. I'm so annoyed with myself, and with the writers.
Please tell me season two has a normal ending. Or don't. Actually, don't tell me anything.
Tanvir

How many episodes had Tanvir watched by Sunday at 1 a.m.?
Tanvir had watched nine.
What was Tanvir feeling after lying in bed for twenty minutes?
Tanvir felt restless and irritated, because the unanswered signal kept the mind busy and made sleep impossible.
What small step could help Tanvir stop at a reasonable time?
Tanvir could stop halfway through an episode before the ending, or set a fixed number of episodes and put the laptop in another room.
How might Pankaj feel reading this email?
Pankaj might feel amused and a little guilty for recommending the series with "just one episode".

At the community centre in Ludhiana, Gurleen stopped at Akash's desk on her way to a meeting. "Make something for Senior Citizens' Day, na? You'll manage." No date, no idea of what "something" meant. Akash, three weeks into the job, guessed. He spent two days designing a colourful quiz on old Punjabi film songs, printed thirty copies and laminated a sign. On Thursday Gurleen looked at it and frowned. "I needed the programme schedule for the notice board. And this print is too small for them to read. Didn't you think?" Akash said sorry and took the sheets back. That evening he stared at the unused quizzes, feeling foolish and set up. The next week, when she asked him to "fix the attendance sheet", he emailed her four questions before touching it and waited a whole day for her answers.

How many copies of the quiz did Akash print?
Thirty copies.
How did Akash feel that evening, and why?
He felt foolish and set up to fail, because he had guessed at a vague request in good faith and was then criticised for not reading Gurleen's mind.
How could Gurleen hand over the next task more clearly?
She could say what the thing is for, when it is due and what a good result looks like, for example a large-print programme schedule for the notice board by Wednesday.
How might Gurleen see Akash's four-question email the next week?
Gurleen may find it slow or fussy without realising her own vague request and sharp comment are what made him so cautious.

Dear Lavanya,
You asked how the new flat is going. Mostly great. But I've noticed something about our fourth flatmate.
He's charming. He borrows our milk, our bus passes, even our laptops. When I asked for help moving a cupboard, he suddenly had a "call."
What I've noticed most is us. We've stopped offering. Priya now hides her good coffee. At dinner, someone always says, "Oh, is it your turn to buy groceries? Ha." And he laughs, like he doesn't get it.
Nobody has told him straight. We just do little things. I think we're all waiting for someone else to say it.
Maybe it'll be me.
Swati

What did the fourth flatmate suddenly have when asked to help move a cupboard?
He suddenly had a "call."
What is Swati feeling about how the flat is handling it?
Swati feels uneasy and a little guilty that everyone is punishing him with hints instead of telling him directly.
What could Swati say to the fourth flatmate?
Swati could tell him calmly that the flat shares things both ways and ask him to help with groceries and chores.
How might the fourth flatmate be affected by the little hints?
He may feel vaguely shut out without understanding why, since nobody has told him straight.
James buys twice as many toy soldiers as toy cars.  He buys 20 toy cars.  How many total toys does he buy?

He buys 2*20=40 toy cars
So the total number of toys is 20+40=60
The answer is 60.
Can I ask my teacher to reconsider my marks?

Yes, politely. To reconsider is to think again about a decision or an opinion. It is a verb. A teacher may or may not change the marks after checking.
Example: After hearing her friend's reasons, Neha reconsidered going on the trip.

The water pump at Joseph's house in a small town near Kottayam stopped working on Monday. Joseph, twenty-five, knew nothing about pumps. The mechanic came, poked at it for two minutes and said, "Motor is gone. New one, twelve thousand." Joseph felt his face go blank. He had no idea if it was true. His neighbour Farida, who ran a hardware shop, was watching from the gate. She walked over. "Can you show him what's wrong with the motor?" The mechanic hesitated, then pointed vaguely. Farida suggested, "Let's get a second opinion." The next mechanic found a burnt capacitor and fixed it in half an hour. Joseph felt both relieved and a little foolish.

What did the second mechanic find?
A burnt capacitor.
How did Joseph feel when the first mechanic named the price?
He felt helpless and blank, unable to tell whether the problem was real.
What steps protected Joseph from needless work?
Asking the mechanic to show the fault and getting a second opinion, as Farida suggested.
How might Farida see the first mechanic's quick verdict?
Farida likely felt suspicious, noticing the vague answer and wanting a second opinion to protect her neighbour.

There are 10 cars parked in a mall's parking lot, each with the same number of customers inside. Each customer only makes 1 purchase. If the sports store makes 20 sales and the music store makes 30 sales, how many customers are in each of the cars?

As each sale represents a customer, there must be a total of 20 sports store sales + 30 music store sales = 50 customers.
There is an equal number of customers in every car, so there must be 50 total customers / 10 cars = 5 customers in each car.
The answer is 5.

It was snowing outside the Berlin nursery. Inside, the toddlers played on the warm mat.
Jana dropped her cup and began to wail. Felix, beside her, stopped stacking blocks. His lip trembled. Then he cried too.
A third toddler looked at them, confused, and started crying as well.
The carer picked Jana up and hummed a song. Slowly Jana quieted. Felix watched her, sniffed and went back to his blocks.

What did Jana drop?
Jana dropped her cup.
Why did Felix cry even though nothing happened to him?
He caught Jana's upset feeling, so he felt upset and scared too without knowing why.
How did the carer help the crying spread stop?
The carer calmed Jana first with a song, and as Jana quieted, the others settled too.
What is it like for the third toddler when the others cry?
The third toddler feels confused and upset, crying without knowing what was wrong.

At the university admissions office, Charu and her friend Ira had been in the queue since seven, clutching their files. At eleven, a man in a crisp kurta walked straight past forty students and into the registrar's room, waving a letter. 'Minister's reference,' someone whispered. The clerk stood up and smiled at him. Charu felt heat rise in her chest. Her own file had taken three trips to get right. Ira muttered, 'That's how it works here. Forget it.' Around them, most students looked at the floor. But one older student said loudly, 'Sir, is there a separate line for references?' The clerk ignored him. Charu said nothing. On the way home, though, she wrote to the university's grievance email, and felt a little less small.

Since what time had Charu and Ira been in the queue?
Since seven.
What was Charu feeling when the man walked past?
Anger and helplessness, heat rising in her chest after waiting since seven and making three trips.
What options did the students have, and which did Charu choose?
Accept it like Ira, object aloud like the older student, or complain formally; Charu wrote to the grievance email, a calm and safe way to object.
How does Ira seem to see the queue-jumping?
As normal and not worth fighting, having learned to accept that 'that's how it works here'.

Class 4 teacher's note, Monday. From Manjula, class teacher.
This week a story spread that the old neem tree near the gate is haunted. On Monday one child said it. By Wednesday, I heard it from almost every group.
Samir usually plays under that tree. On Wednesday, he wouldn't go near it. He told me, "Ma'am, everyone says a ghost lives there. It must be true if so many people say it." His hands were cold.
I asked him who had actually seen something. He counted. "Nobody. They just heard."
What I did next: I took the class out at lunch and we all sat under the neem and ate. I asked each child to say if they'd seen anything themselves. Nobody had. Samir climbed back onto his favourite root.

Where is the old neem tree?
The old neem tree is near the gate.
Why did Samir stop going near the neem tree?
He felt frightened, with cold hands, because hearing the story from so many people made it seem true.
Why was the lunch under the neem a good idea?
It let the children check for themselves and count who had really seen something, so the story stopped growing.
How might the other children have felt eating under the tree?
They probably felt nervous at first, then relieved and a little silly when nobody had seen anything.

Class 4 trip note, museum visit, Friday. Zainab, a parent volunteer, came with us. At the ticket counter she thanked the guard by the name on his badge. When a school group from elsewhere pushed ahead, she simply waited and said to our children, 'They must be in a hurry; we'll still see everything.' In the café she apologised to a waiter when she knocked a spoon down. I noticed Ojas watching her closely. Later, at the dinosaur gallery, Ojas held the door for an elderly man and said, 'Please go first.' No one had told Ojas to. I will ask Zainab to volunteer again, and on Monday in class we will talk about what the children noticed on the trip.

What did Ojas say to the elderly man?
'Please go first.'
What might Ojas have been thinking while watching Zainab closely?
Ojas seemed curious and impressed by how calmly and kindly Zainab behaved, and quietly decided to copy it.
What does the teacher plan, and why is it useful?
Asking Zainab to volunteer again and discussing on Monday what the children noticed, so they reflect on the example they saw.
How might the guard feel being thanked by name?
Surprised and respected, noticed as a person rather than part of the building.
Now you try: 1 m 8 cm in centimetres.
The answer is 108 cm.

Saturday
Today I told Papa about Coach Vinod. How he gives me chocolates after swimming, and said our talks are a secret, and last week wanted me to stay late alone. I thought Papa would be angry with me for keeping it. He wasn't. He put his tea down and said, "Thank you for telling me, Kashish. I believe you. You did nothing wrong." His voice was soft even though his hands were tight. Then he called Mummy and Mr Shankar, the swimming club's head, and after lunch we all went there together. I don't have to go to class with Coach Vinod anymore. Papa said I can tell him anything, always, and he won't get cross.
I feel lighter.

What did Coach Vinod give Kashish after swimming?
Chocolates.
What was Kashish afraid of before telling Papa?
Kashish was afraid Papa would be angry about the secret, and afterwards felt lighter and relieved.
What did Papa do that made telling safe?
He stayed calm, thanked Kashish, said he believed it and that Kashish did nothing wrong, then called Mummy and Mr Shankar and went to the club the same day.
How might Papa have felt inside while staying calm?
Papa's tight hands suggest he felt angry and worried, but he kept his voice soft so Kashish would not feel blamed.

When I moved from Kochi to a school in Delhi in Class 9, my hands got me into trouble. Whenever I told a story, my arms went everywhere, sweeping, clapping, drawing shapes in the air. At home everyone talks like that.
In my new class, a few girls laughed. "Leela, you're like a traffic policeman!" I started keeping my hands in my lap. My stories came out flat.
Then Jatin, who sat next to me, said one day, "Why'd you stop doing the hands thing? Your cricket story was way better with it."
I told him I felt silly.
He said, "It shows you're excited. I like it."
Slowly, my hands came back. Not as big as in Kochi, but enough.
- Leela

What did the girls say Leela was like?
A traffic policeman.
What was Leela feeling when keeping the hands still in the new class?
Leela felt self-conscious and silly, and the stories lost their excitement.
What did Jatin do that helped Leela?
Jatin told Leela he liked the gestures because they showed excitement, which encouraged Leela to use them again.
How might the girls who laughed see Leela's gestures?
They may have found them unusual because gesture size is different in their homes, not realising it showed excitement.

Day-care centre note, Friday.

Sangeeta brings her father in at 8.40 every morning on her way to work and collects him at 6.30. Today she arrived late, apologising to everyone, her dupatta half off one shoulder. He had wandered out of the flat at 5 a.m. and a neighbour had walked him home.

She told me she has been sleeping about four hours and snapping at her son. "I love Papa," she said. "But some days I'm so angry, and then I feel terrible for being angry."

I told her both feelings are common for carers. We made a small plan: her brother in Nagpur will cover two weekend days a month, and I gave her the number of the carers' support group that meets on Thursday evenings here. I also asked her to talk to her father's doctor about the night wandering.

She wrote the list on her palm. I will check in with her on Monday.

— Zeenat, centre coordinator

What time does Sangeeta collect her father?
She collects him at 6.30.
How is Sangeeta feeling about caring for her father?
Sangeeta feels exhausted, sometimes angry, and then guilty for being angry, even though she loves him.
What small steps did Zeenat help Sangeeta plan?
Her brother will cover two weekend days a month, she will try the carers' support group, and she will talk to her father's doctor about the night wandering.
How might Sangeeta's son be affected by her exhaustion?
He is being snapped at more often, so he may feel hurt or confused, and he would benefit from his mother getting more rest and support.

What could Suraj do next time Naveen cries?
Naveen can ask whether the tears are from sad, angry or funny. Asking beats labelling from outside.
How might the classmates have seen Naveen's crying?
They assumed Naveen was sad, which was wrong. The tears could mean anger, joy or relief.

It was Christmas week and the power kept going off. By candlelight, Jatin's cousin Zeenat teased him again. "Remember when you got lost at the Christmas fair and a clown found you?"

"No," said Jatin, five.

Two days later: "Remember the clown who found you?"

"Maybe."

By the weekend, Jatin told his mother, "I got lost at the fair and a clown with a red nose found me!"

His mother looked at Zeenat. "He was never lost."

Zeenat's smile faded. "I was only joking."

What did Zeenat keep asking Jatin?
"Remember when you got lost at the Christmas fair and a clown found you?"
How did Jatin feel about the clown story by the weekend?
He felt sure and excited about it, because hearing it again and again made it feel like a real memory.
What could Jatin's mother do now to help?
She could gently explain to Jatin that it was a made-up story and ask Zeenat to stop the joke.
How might Zeenat feel when she realises Jatin believes the story?
Zeenat probably feels surprised and a bit guilty that her joke turned into his memory.

In their Copenhagen flat, Zanele's wooden boat cracked in half when it fell off the table. She didn't cry. She went very quiet, lay down on the rug with the two pieces, and stared at them, drooping.
"Tired already?" asked Emil, her father. Then he looked closer. "Oh. Your boat broke. You're sad."
Zanele's lip wobbled, and she let him lift her into his lap.

What broke?
Zanele's wooden boat.
What was Zanele feeling when she lay quietly with the pieces?
She was sad about her broken boat, even though at first it looked like tiredness.
What did Emil do that helped?
He looked closer, named her sadness and offered comfort in his lap.
What would change if Emil had put her to bed thinking she was tired?
Her sadness would go unnoticed, and she wouldn't get the comfort or the word for her feeling.
Rewrite this as a polite question: Tell me your name.
May I please ask your name?
What would you call bachelors, as in the old story where two of them share a house?

Bachelors are men who have never married. It is a noun, the plural of bachelor.
Example: The two bachelors lived together and cooked dinner each evening.

Sunday was phone day at the boarding school, the week after Holi. Sachin sat in the warden's office with the heavy black phone. "How was your week, beta?" Papa asked. Sachin thought hard. "Terrible. Uday sir made us run four rounds yesterday because we were late. He's the strictest teacher ever." "Warden uncle told me Uday sir taught you to swim this week." "That was ages ago." It had been Tuesday. On Wednesday Uday sir had shared his own gujiya with the whole dorm, and on Thursday he had stayed late to help Sachin fix his kite. But all Sachin could feel were the four rounds, still aching in his legs. "The week was bad, Papa," he said. "Really bad."

How many rounds did Uday sir make them run?
Four rounds, yesterday, because they were late.
Why does Sachin call the whole week terrible?
Yesterday's four rounds are the freshest memory and still ache, so Sachin feels grumpy and sure the week was bad, crowding out the swimming, the gujiya and the kite.
What could Papa ask to help Sachin remember the whole week?
He could go day by day, asking what happened on Monday, Tuesday and so on, so the earlier good moments come back.
How might Uday sir feel if he heard himself called the strictest teacher ever?
Uday sir might feel a little hurt or amused, having taught Sachin to swim, shared his gujiya and helped fix the kite that same week 😅

When Vikas and I finally admitted we didn't understand how our late father's plot in Indore was supposed to be divided, we did what we should have done a year earlier. We booked one hour with a lawyer, together, and split the fee.
I went in half-expecting ammunition. Vikas, I think, expected the same. Instead, Advocate Mehrotra spent the hour explaining things plainly: what the law generally says when there is no will, what our sister's share might look like, and the common ways families settle, from selling and splitting to one sibling buying out the others. She said the choice was ours to make as a family.
On the drive home Vikas said, "So neither of us was completely right." I laughed. That evening we called our sister, and for once the talk started with the options, not with who was wrong.
— Tarun

How long was the meeting with the lawyer?
One hour, booked together, with the fee split.
What did Tarun expect going into the meeting, and how did that change?
Tarun half-expected ammunition and felt defensive, then was relieved when the lawyer simply laid out the options.
Why was seeing the lawyer together wiser than going separately?
Hearing the same general explanation side by side gave Tarun and Vikas a shared starting point instead of two competing versions.
How might their sister experience the evening call?
Their sister likely feels included and less braced for a fight, since the talk begins with options rather than blame.

Week one. Mohit ran the college astronomy club, and turnout for the Friday sky-watch kept swinging between eight and thirty. He had a guess. "Posters in the canteen work better than messages in the class chat groups," he told Ishita, the club's secretary. "People ignore messages."
"Or you just remember the good nights," she said.
"Fine. Let's test it." For the next Friday he put up six posters and sent no messages. Ishita stood at the terrace door with a counter. Twenty-six came.
Week two. No posters at all, only one message in each class chat group, same time of day, same kind of sky forecast. Ishita counted again. Eleven.
Week three. Mohit wrote on the club notebook: posters 26, messages 11. "Two weeks isn't proof," he said. "But I'm keeping the posters, and we'll count again next month."
Ishita smiled. "At least now it's not just a feeling."

How many people came in the posters-only week?
Twenty-six came.
How might Mohit have felt seeing the counts in week three?
He probably felt pleased and a bit vindicated, but also careful, saying two weeks isn't proof.
What else could Mohit test next, and why?
He could try posters and messages together, or change the poster location, changing one thing at a time to see what helps most.
How does Ishita see the test?
Ishita first doubts Mohit's guess, then is happy that the club now has numbers instead of just a feeling.

"A female curate, who is not my wife, would never suit me. With me, then, it seems, you cannot go: but if you are sincere in your offer, I will, while in town, speak to a married missionary, whose wife needs a coadjutor. Your own fortune will make you independent of the Society's aid; and thus you may still be spared the dishonour of breaking your promise and deserting the band you engaged to join."

Why does the speaker refuse to take the listener along, and what does the speaker offer instead?

A female curate who is not a wife would never suit, the speaker says, so the listener cannot come along. Instead, while in town, there is an offer to speak to a married missionary whose wife needs an assistant, sparing the listener from breaking the promise.

Nitin knelt by the sofa in their Pune flat. "Hafsa, which book tonight?" Two-year-old Hafsa kept turning the wheel of a toy bus. His phone buzzed on the table and he left it. He breathed slowly and waited. Her eyes went to the shelf, then back to his face. "Bus book," she said at last. "The bus book it is," said Nitin, and she grinned, pleased that her answer had landed.

Which book did Hafsa choose?
She chose the bus book.
How does Nitin seem to feel as he waits, and what else might explain Hafsa's pause?
He seems calm and patient, leaving his phone and breathing slowly while he waits for her. Her pause could also have come from the toy wheel holding her attention.
What small step would help if Hafsa still seemed not to answer?
Nitin could hold up two books and let her point, still waiting quietly for her reply.
How might Hafsa feel about being waited for?

The morning after Mridul won the school science prize, a paper sign was stuck on his desk: MR SHOW-OFF. Sahil and two others snickered from the back bench. At lunch, when Mridul explained a sum to a friend, Sahil said loudly, "Oh, here comes the professor." Everyone laughed.
That week, when the maths tests came back, Mridul folded his paper in half before anyone could see the 19 out of 20. When Miss asked who got full marks in the next quiz, he kept his hand down, though he had. On Friday he asked his mother if he could skip the prize photo for the school magazine. She asked why, listened to all of it, and phoned his class teacher that evening.

What did the paper sign on Mridul's desk say?
MR SHOW-OFF.
Why did Mridul fold his test paper in half?
He felt embarrassed and anxious about being mocked again, so hiding the 19 felt safer than being seen as a show-off.
How could Mridul's class teacher help after his mother's call?
Stop the name-calling, talk to the class about teasing, and quietly reassure Mridul that doing well is nothing to hide.
How might Sahil see his jokes?

The stadium in Amman was roaring. Nour, holding her father's hand, had never been to a real match. When the referee gave a penalty against their team, the crowd around her stood up and shouted words Nour was never allowed to say.
She shouted them too, at the top of her lungs. It felt like flying. Her friend Ada, beside her, was jumping and shoving forward with the men in front.
Nour pushed too, toward the railing, not thinking about anything.
Her father tightened his grip and pulled her back. “Nour. Look at me.” His voice was calm. She looked up, breathing fast. Suddenly she heard herself, and her cheeks went hot.
“We cheer,” he said. “We don't push.”

Which city was the stadium in?
It was in Amman.
How did Nour feel as she shouted with the crowd?
She felt excited and swept along, like she was flying, without thinking about herself.
How did her father help, and why did it work?
He held her firmly, spoke calmly and made her look at him, which broke the crowd's spell and kept her safe.
How might Ada have felt pushing forward with the men?
Ada was probably thrilled and carried along too, not noticing the risk of the crowd pushing.

June: Irawati's father handed her the admission letter for mechanical engineering, beaming. "Our family's first engineer." She hugged him and wrote in her notebook that night: This is what I want. Good job, me.
September: Every morning at the hostel she woke with a tight chest before workshop class. She told Asif it was the mess food. In the margins of her thermodynamics notes she was sketching costumes, dozens of them, sleeves and collars and pleats.
December: Asif flipped through the notebook and stopped at the sketches. "These are really good. Is this what you actually want?" Irawati opened her mouth to say no. Instead she said, "I don't know. Maybe." It was the first time she had let herself say it aloud.

What was Irawati sketching in the margins of her thermodynamics notes?
She was sketching costumes, dozens of them, sleeves and collars and pleats.
Why did Irawati tell Asif her tight chest came from the mess food?
Blaming the food kept her from facing her dread of engineering, the choice that had made her father beam.
What was the turning point in December, and what could Irawati do next?
When Asif asked what she actually wanted, she admitted 'Maybe'; next she could explore design gently, perhaps through an elective or a counsellor, before speaking to her father.
What would change for Irawati's father if she kept saying only 'This is what I want'?
He would keep believing his daughter is happy, and might learn the truth much later, when it is harder for both of them.

When I was fifteen, my friend Kamala told the whole class that I was scared of water. Everyone laughed at the swimming lesson.

A week later she came to me, crying. She said, "I did it to be popular. I'm sorry. I won't do it again." I didn't trust her all at once. For a long time I didn't tell her anything big. But she kept her word. Year after year. By college, we were close again, though not in the same easy way.

Then there was another girl, Leena. She did something similar, and when I told her, she laughed and said I was too sensitive. I stopped being her friend. Quietly, no drama. I found better friends.

Both endings were right, beta. It depends on what they do next.

Kamala told the class that Madhuri was scared of water.
What was Madhuri feeling after Kamala's apology?
She was touched by the apology but still wary, so she kept her big secrets to herself for a long time.
What choices inside the story made the two endings different?
Kamala apologised sincerely and kept her word, so a slower friendship returned; Leena laughed it off, so Madhuri ended the friendship calmly.
How might Kamala have felt through those years of being trusted slowly?
Kamala probably felt some regret and patience, knowing she had to earn Madhuri's trust back over time.

But the school hall is booked for a backup date, a tenth of the budget is kept for surprises, and the storyteller has a stand-in." Three weeks later, the main sponsor cut its money by half, two days before the event. Pradeep, the director, came in looking grim. Meenal had already opened her 'If this fails' column. Jazel has 3 sticks. One stick is 3 centimeters long. The second stick is twice as long while the third stick is 1 centimeter shorter than the second stick. What is the total length of Jazel's sticks when they are put together?

The second stick is 3 x 2 = 6 centimeters long.
The third stick is 6 - 1 = 5 centimeters long.
Thus, Jazel's sticks are 3 + 6 + 5 = 14 centimeters long when they are put together.
The answer is 14.

The message came in while Zanele was on the minibus home from school in Johannesburg: "k." Just that, from Nour, after Zanele had written a long apology for missing Saturday's netball practice. Zanele read it four times. No heart, no "it's fine", not even a capital letter. Nour always wrote in capitals and exclamation marks. She's furious, Zanele thought. She's done with me. By the time the minibus reached her stop she had pictured Nour telling the whole team, the two of them eating lunch apart, a group photo without her in it. Her stomach knotted. She typed "are u mad at me??" and deleted it, typed "ok cool" and deleted that too. It never occurred to her that Nour might be at her gran's, typing with one thumb while carrying shopping bags.

What did Nour's message say?
Just "k."
Why did Zanele's stomach knot on the minibus?

What small step would help Zanele?

messages.content: Without calculating, which of these CANNOT be perfect squares: 1,057; 23,453; 7,928; 222,222; 4,000; 1,069?

Answer: 1,057, 23,453, 7,928, 222,222 and 4,000 cannot be squares. 1,069 might be (it is not: 32^2 = 1,024 and 33^2 = 1,089).

Look at the last digit of the squares 0^2 to 9^2: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81. They end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 only. So a number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a perfect square: 1,057 (7), 23,453 (3), 7,928 (8), 222,222 (2). A square ending in zeros has an EVEN number of them (10^2 = 100, 20^2 = 400, 100^2 = 10,000), so 4,000 with 3 zeros is not a square. The test only rules numbers OUT: 1,069 ends in 9, so it might be a square, but it lies between 32^2 = 1,024 and 33^2 = 1,089, so it is not.

I'm Hansa, and I've shared a flat with Arohi in Indore for a year. She's the fastest decider I know. At the tea stall she says "cutting, less sugar" before the man even looks up. She picks her kurta in the morning without opening the cupboard fully. So I was surprised last month when a colleague offered her a puppy. She didn't say yes. She wrote a list on the fridge: who walks it, who pays the vet, what happens when we travel, what the landlord says. She slept on it for a week. She called her brother, and a friend who fosters dogs. She even stood outside the building at 6 a.m. to see if she'd really get up. I don't know what she was feeling inside. But on the eighth day she said, "Not yet, maybe next year." She seemed at peace.

messages.content: Davonte is trying to figure out how much space his art collection takes up. He measures his paintings and finds he has three square 6-foot by 6-foot paintings, four small 2-foot by 3-foot paintings, and one large 10-foot by 15-foot painting. How many square feet does his collection take up?

His square paintings take up 36 square feet each because 6 x 6 = 36
His small paintings take 6 square feet each because 2 x 3 = 6
His large painting takes up 150 square feet because 10 x 15 = 150.
Combined, his square paintings take up 108 square feet because 3 x 36 = 108
Combined, his small paintings take up 24 square feet because 4 x 6 = 24
In total, his paintings take up 282 square feet because 150 + 108 + 24 = 282
The answer is 282.

messages.content: In a race, there are eight runners. The first five runners finish the race in 8 hours, while the rest of the runners finish the race 2 hours later. Calculate the total time the eight runners took to finish the race.

The first five runners took a combined total of 5*8 = 40 hours to finish the race.
The number of runners who finished the race 2 hours later after the first five is 8-5 = 3
The 3 runners who finished the race 2 hours later took a total of 8+2 =10 hours to run the race.
Together, the three runners who finished the race in 10 hours took a total of 10*3 = 30 hours.
All eight runners took 30+40 = 70 hours altogether to finish the race.
The answer is 70.

Reflect the point (3, 1) in the line y = x and in the line y = -x.

Answer: In y = x: (1, 3). In y = -x: (-1, -3).

The line y = x goes through (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2)... at 45 degrees. Reflecting in it SWAPS the coordinates: (x, y) -> (y, x). Fold squared paper along y = x and the point (3, 1) lands exactly on (1, 3). The line y = -x goes through (1, -1), (2, -2)... Reflecting in it swaps AND changes both signs: (x, y) -> (-y, -x). So (3, 1) -> (-1, -3). Check: the midpoint of (3, 1) and (-1, -3) is (1, -1), which is on y = -x, as it must be. Common mistake: only swapping for y = -x.

Dilnaz, sixteen, had moved from Srinagar to Pune two years ago. On Monday, in the canteen queue, a senior said, "Your English is really good. Did you learn it here?" On Tuesday, a new teacher asked, "Where are you actually from?" and when she said Pune, asked again. On Thursday, in the bus, a girl told her, "You don't even look Kashmiri," as if it were praise. None of them were rude. Some of them smiled. But by Friday, Dilnaz sat in the back of the classroom with her hood up. Her friend Vasudha slid in beside her. "What's up?" Dilnaz shrugged. "Nothing. Just... every day someone reminds me I'm from somewhere else." Vasudha was quiet, then said, "I didn't notice. I'm sorry. Tell me when it happens?" Dilnaz nodded. It helped a little to be heard.

Dilnaz felt tired and singled out, as if every small remark reminded her that she was an outsider.

messages.content: Explain advocate. Is it only a lawyer?

Marcus is making calzones. It takes him 20 minutes to saute the onions and a quarter of that time to saute the garlic and peppers. It takes him 30 minutes to knead the dough, twice as long to let it rest, and 1/10th the combined kneading and resting time to assemble the calzones. How many minutes does Marcus spend on the calzones total?

First find the amount of time it takes Marcus to saute the garlic and peppers: 20 minutes / 4 = 5 minutes
Then find the dough's resting time: 30 minutes * 2 = 60 minutes
Then add the kneading and resting time to find the total dough time: 60 minutes + 30 minutes = 90 minutes
Then multiply that amount by 1/10th to find the assembly time: 90 minutes / 10 = 9 minutes
Then add the saute time, knead time, rest time and assembly time to find the total time Marcus spends on the calzones: 9 minutes + 20 minutes + 5 minutes + 60 minutes + 30 minutes = 124 minutes
The answer is 124.

Wednesday, week four. The teacher put both scores on the board as examples of "good, steady work". Pankaj sat staring. Same number. Suraj had grinned all week. He had spent it feeling like a failure.

And I thought about it. In our school workshop on consent, I'd nodded along to "no means no" as if it was about other people, the ones who grab and don't listen. But a message after a clear no was me not listening too, just more politely. I deleted all four. The next day I said hi to Tanvi like normal. It stung for a few weeks.
