In Nani's village courtyard, the children played ring-a-roses under the neem tree.
“Ritvik can't play,” Kashish announced, holding hands with her cousins. “Only my team.”
Ritvik, the neighbour's small boy, stood by the water pump, twisting his shirt.
Nani, sorting lentils on the charpai, called out, “Kashish, come here.”
Kashish came, dragging her feet.
“When your cousins came from Delhi last summer, did they let you play?”
Kashish nodded slowly.
“Then here, everyone gets a turn in the circle.”
Kashish went back and held out her hand to Ritvik. He ran into the ring, beaming.

Where was Ritvik standing?
He was standing by the water pump.
What was Ritvik feeling as he twisted his shirt?
He was feeling left out and nervous, waiting to be allowed in.
How did Nani help Kashish include Ritvik?
She reminded Kashish of being included herself and said everyone gets a turn, so Kashish chose to hold out her hand.
How might Kashish's cousins have felt when Ritvik joined?
They were probably happy to have one more in the ring and followed Kashish's lead.

Monday: Before leaving for work, Manjula rattled off a list to Devika: "Feed the cat, lock the balcony door, take the milk packet in, finish the maths worksheet, call Nani at five, and don't open the door for anyone." When Manjula came home, the milk had curdled in the sun and the cat was yowling. Devika had remembered the worksheet and the door. That was all.
Wednesday: Devika looked miserable at breakfast. "I tried, Amma. It just fell out of my head." Manjula stirred her tea and thought about it.
Friday: This time Manjula stuck three short lines on the fridge: 1. Milk inside. 2. Feed cat. 3. Call Nani at five. "Tick each one." When she got home, all three had ticks in green crayon, and the cat was asleep on Devika's lap.

What happened to the milk packet on Monday?
The milk had curdled in the sun.
How was Devika feeling when saying "It just fell out of my head"?
Devika felt miserable and a bit ashamed, having really tried but still forgotten most of the long list 😔
What change did Manjula make on Friday, and why did it work?
She put three short numbered steps on the fridge to tick, so Devika only had to hold a few things and could check them off.
What might Manjula have thought on Monday when she came home?
She was probably frustrated at first, finding sour milk and a hungry cat, and may have wondered whether Devika had listened at all.
A line of best fit passes through (2, 50) and (8, 80). Find its equation and use it to estimate y when x = 5.

Answer: y = 5x + 40; when x = 5, y = 65.

Gradient m = change in y / change in x = (80 - 50) / (8 - 2) = 30 / 6 = 5. So y = 5x + c. Put in the point (2, 50): 50 = 5 x 2 + c, so c = 50 - 10 = 40. Equation: y = 5x + 40. Check with the other point: 5 x 8 + 40 = 80. Estimate: y = 5 x 5 + 40 = 65. Choose two points ON THE LINE, far apart, not two data points, because data points are usually not exactly on the line. The gradient has a meaning: here each extra unit of x adds about 5 to y. Common mistake: dividing the change in x by the change in y.

"Jyoti didi, can I have the dinosaur watch? Everyone in my class has it."
"You told me last month dinosaurs are for babies, Kishore."
"That was last month. Now everyone likes them."
"What do you like?"
"...Space. Rockets. You know that."
"So why not a rocket watch?"
"Nobody has a rocket watch. They'll say it's weird."
"Who's everyone?"
"All the boys at my table."
"If nobody at your table had a watch, what would you want?"
"A telescope."
"Hmm."
"But I don't want to be the only one without the dinosaur."
"Okay, little brother. Let's think. What if you wear the dinosaur watch and bring your rocket book on Friday?"
"...Maybe. Can the watch have a rocket strap?"

What does Kishore want most if nobody at his table had a watch?
A telescope.
Why does Kishore suddenly want the dinosaur watch?
He feels afraid of being left out or called weird, so fitting in with the boys at his table matters more to him than his own love of space.
How does Jyoti didi help Kishore think about it?
She asks what he really likes and what he'd want if nobody else had anything, and suggests he bring his rocket book too.
What would change if one boy at Kishore's table wore a rocket watch?
Kishore might feel free to choose rockets, since he wouldn't be the only one different.

During the Christmas holidays we got a whole booklet of maths sums. On the last evening I still hadn't done page six, so I copied it from Keerthana's photo in our class group. When Amma asked, I said, "Everyone copies, Amma. Even the toppers." And Sir sets way too many anyway, right? Who does forty sums in a holiday?
I told myself that all night. I'm a good student, mostly. I help people. So one page didn't count.
But on Monday, when Sir praised page six and said, "Well done, Jagdish," my ears went hot, and I didn't look at Keerthana.

How did Jagdish copy page six?
From Keerthana's photo in the class group.
Why did Jagdish keep repeating that everyone copies?
Jagdish felt guilty 😔 and wanted to keep feeling like a good student, so the reasons pushed the uncomfortable feeling away after the copying.
What could Jagdish try next time the holiday homework feels too much?
Start earlier, or tell the teacher honestly which part was hard, instead of copying and then building excuses.
How might Keerthana feel on finding out?
Keerthana might feel used or annoyed that the work was copied, and uneasy seeing Jagdish praised for it.

Monday: In art class, Rehana drew a kingfisher so real that Dilnaz half expected it to fly off the page. Dilnaz stared at her own lumpy bird. I could never do that, she thought.
Wednesday: At lunch Dilnaz finally asked, "How do you draw like that?"
Rehana laughed and pulled out a battered sketchbook. The first pages were full of wobbly, wonky birds. "I draw one every day. These were last year. They were terrible."
Dilnaz's mouth fell open. "These are worse than mine!"
"Exactly," Rehana grinned.
The next Monday: Dilnaz had a small notebook of her own now, with seven birds in it, one for each day. The seventh one had a proper beak. She showed Rehana, who drew a tiny star beside it.

What did Rehana draw in art class?
A kingfisher.
How did Dilnaz feel looking at Rehana's kingfisher?
Amazed, but also discouraged, thinking she could never draw like that.
What did Dilnaz do instead of giving up?
She asked Rehana how she practises and started drawing a bird every day.
How might Rehana have felt when Dilnaz asked?
Pleased and happy to share her old wobbly birds to encourage Dilnaz.

Diana wants to buy winter clothes for all the 40 children at her local children's home. The home has five times as many teenagers as toddlers. There are also some newborns. If there are 6 toddlers, for how many newborns will Diana be shopping?

There are 6 toddlers, which means that the children's home has 5 teenagers/toddler * 6 toddlers = 30 teenagers
Diana will be shopping for 40 children - 30 teenagers - 6 toddlers = 4 newborns
The answer is 4.

Monday: At the house assembly, Kashish pinned the green Tagore House badge on her shirt and sang the house song louder than anyone. "We're winning the shield this year," she told the girl next to her.
Friday, sports day: Tagore lost the relay by one step. Aadhya's house, Raman, cheered and ran a lap. Kashish felt as if she had been slapped. She sat on the bench and didn't clap. Later she drew a Raman badge in the dust and stamped on it, and her friends laughed.
The next Tuesday: Aadhya walked past her table. "My little sister cried because someone stamped on our badge," she said quietly. Kashish looked down at her lunchbox.

What colour was the Tagore House badge?
The badge was green.
What did Kashish feel when Tagore lost the relay?
She felt as if she had been slapped, hurt and angry, because the loss felt personal.
What could Kashish do now, after hearing Aadhya?
She could say sorry to Aadhya and her sister, and cheer for her own house without stamping on the other house's badge.
What is it like for Aadhya's little sister when someone stamps on the badge?
She feels hurt and upset, because the mocking was aimed at her house and felt aimed at her.

Read this:

Instructor's note, Saturday salsa class

Sahil and Manjula have come every Saturday for a year. They told me they've been together six years. They're easy with each other: she fixes his collar without thinking, he knows exactly when she'll turn.

Today I paired everyone with new partners for one song. Manjula danced with a younger man who asked her questions the whole time: where she grew up, what she likes about dancing. She laughed more in three minutes than I'd seen all year.

Sahil noticed. When they came back together, he asked her, half joking, "What were you two talking about?"

"He asked what I like about salsa," she said. "Nobody's asked me that in a long time."

Sahil looked at her for a second longer than usual. After class, I saw them sitting on the steps, talking, not dancing.

— Ines, instructor

What did the younger partner ask Manjula about?
Where she grew up and what she likes about dancing.
What does Manjula's laughter with the new partner suggest?
It suggests she enjoyed being asked about herself and may feel a little unnoticed in the comfortable routine with Sahil.
What small step did Sahil and Manjula take after class?
They sat on the steps and talked, a start to asking about each other's inner lives again.
How might Sahil feel when Manjula says no one's asked her that in a long time?
He may feel a pang of surprise and guilt, realising he stopped asking.

Looking back, I'm amazed how calm I was. I'm Tenzin, and last monsoon the district sent a landslide alert for our hillside in Sikkim. The hostel warden, Naveen sir, told us to pack a bag and be ready to move to the school hall. I didn't pack. I lay on my bunk scrolling, thinking: I've lived on this hill for sixteen years. The hill doesn't move.
At midnight a crack of stones woke us, and Naveen sir was calling names in the corridor with a torch. I went down in slippers, no bag. In the morning we saw a slide had covered the path behind the hostel. Nobody was hurt. But I still think about how normal everything felt, right up to the sound.

Where were the students told to move?
To the school hall.
What was Tenzin feeling while lying on the bunk?
Tenzin felt calm and safe, sure the hill wouldn't move because it never had.
What could Tenzin do differently at the next alert?
Pack the bag at once and follow the warden's instructions, rather than trusting that ordinary days will continue.
What might Naveen sir have felt at midnight?
Naveen sir was likely frightened and focused, rushing to account for every student with a torch.

After Mei's voice cracked during her class presentation in Singapore, she decided she would just stay quiet in class for a while.
But the quiet grew. She muted the class group chat. She stopped going to the hawker centre after school with the others, in case Tariq brought up the presentation. When her phone rang, even with her aunt's name on the screen, her chest tightened and she let it go to voicemail. On Saturday she skipped the badminton club she had loved since primary school.
Each time she felt a quick flood of relief. Then, a little later, the next thing felt harder.
Tariq caught her at the lockers on Monday. "Hey, the group project's on Thursday. You'll come?"
Mei's heart raced. "Maybe. I'll see."
She knew she wouldn't. Her world was getting smaller, and everything outside it felt sharper every week.

What club did Mei skip on Saturday?
The badminton club she had loved since primary school.
What does Mei's racing heart at Tariq's question show?
She feels anxious and trapped, as even a simple invitation now feels threatening.
What could Mei try before Thursday?
Tell Tariq or a trusted adult honestly about the fear, and go to the group project for at least part of the time.
What might Tariq notice about Mei?
Tariq may notice her pulling away and feel puzzled or worried, not knowing it started with the presentation.

Varun stared at the email from the school group: they had gone with the other company. Nitin's team, the one Varun had privately called "the flashy ones," had won it. His first reaction was a hot, tight feeling in his chest. He closed the laptop, walked to the stairwell of the office in Pune and came back with a different question. Could he ask the school group why? He called and asked politely. The answer surprised him: Nitin's team had run the demo on the school group's own sample data and replied to every question the same day. Varun pulled the team together that afternoon. "Next demo, we use their data. And nobody leaves a question overnight." At the industry meet the next month, he walked over and congratulated Nitin.

What did the school group say Nitin's team did differently in the demo?
Nitin's team ran the demo on the school group's own sample data and answered every question the same day.
What was Varun feeling when the email arrived, and what did he do with it?

"I am the doctor!" Alka announced, pulling on Papa's old sweater like a coat. It was a cold winter morning, and the game had started after breakfast. "You're sick, Jasleen. Lie down." Thomas leaned on the counter of the bookshop and said to Joseph, "I taught after college too, and I nearly ruined my degree. Then I made a rule. Ten hours a week, no more. Tuesday and Thursday evenings, six to eight, and Saturday morning. I wrote it on the wall calendar in red. Exam weeks stayed clear, all of them. "The money kept coming, and my studies were never eaten up. A boundary is just a decision you make once, so you don't have to make it every day."

How many hours a week did Thomas allow for paid work?
Thomas allowed ten hours a week.

Thomas felt uncomfortable holding the rule in the first month, as it felt hard, but after that it became easy.

Joseph could write a personal weekly limit on a wall calendar and mark exam weeks clear, since a written rule is easier to keep.

Joseph's diary, Sunday.
Didn't go to church today. Stayed in bed. Couldn't face anyone asking "how's the new job".
Truth: two credit cards, a phone EMI, and the bike loan. I've been paying minimums and hiding the bills from Amma in my backpack. Every time she asks why I look tired, I say work.

Pooja's final-year viva was moved up by two hours, and she reached the department still panting from the auto, her notes left on the kitchen table. The external examiner asked a simple question about her own project, and her mind went white. Her hands turned cold, her throat locked, and the silence stretched. Through the glass door she caught Yamini's eye; Yamini pressed a hand to her own chest and breathed out slowly, the way they'd practised. Pooja did the same. 'I'm sorry,' she said. 'I've gone blank for a moment. Let me take a breath.' The examiner nodded. On the second slow breath the answer came back, and she explained her sampling method clearly.

Where had Pooja left her notes?
On the kitchen table.
How did Pooja feel when her mind went white?
She felt panicked and frozen, with cold hands and a locked throat.
What helped Pooja thaw?
Slowing her breath as Yamini showed, and naming the moment aloud so she could pause.
How might the examiner have seen Pooja's pause?
The examiner likely saw ordinary nerves and respected the calm honesty of asking for a breath.

Last year, for three months, I measured our bean plant every Sunday morning before breakfast. I'm Afreen, and my cousin Parveen said I was mad. I used my old school scale, held it against the stem from the soil to the top leaf, and wrote the number and the date at the back of my maths notebook. At first the numbers went up by one or two. Then in July there was a jump of seven centimetres in one week. I looked back and saw it had rained four days that week. The next big jump came after rain too. I showed my science teacher, and she said I had found a pattern with my own eyes. That felt better than any prize.

How much did the plant grow in the July week?
Seven centimetres.
How did Afreen feel when the teacher praised the pattern?
Afreen felt proud; it was better than any prize.
What else could Afreen compare next time?
A second plant watered only from the tap, to see whether rain itself makes the difference.
How might Parveen see the notebook now?
Parveen called it mad, but the teacher's praise might make Parveen see the point of measuring.

John decides to get gym memberships so he can get in shape.  The gym close to his house is close but doesn't have everything he wants so he gets two different gym memberships.  The cheap one costs $10 a month and has a sign-up fee of $50.  The second gym is 3 times more expensive and it has a sign-up fee of 4 months membership.  How much total did he pay in the first year for gym membership?

The cheap gym cost 10*12=$120 for monthly fees
So the total cost was 120+50=$170
The more expensive gym cost 3*10=$30 per month
That means the sign-up fee was 30*4=$120
The monthly fees for the expensive gym comes out to 30*12=$360 per year
So the total cost for the expensive gym was 360+120=$480
So his total cost was 480+170=$650
The answer is 650.

I'm Dolma, and I'm telling this on your podcast, Anand, because last year I thought my life was over. A message came from an unknown account: a picture with my face, my hostel room behind me, but a body that wasn't mine. "Pay by Friday or this goes to your family and your college group." I was shaking so hard I dropped the phone. My first thought was, it's my fault for posting my photos. It wasn't. Someone took ordinary pictures and faked the rest. My roommate Pema made me do three things that same night. We saved everything: screenshots, the account name, the payment details they sent. We reported the account to the platform. And we went to the cyber police station together, where the officer said they see this every week and that I must not pay. Then I called my elder sister. Telling her was the hardest part. She just said, "I'm with you."

Payment by Friday, or the picture would go to Dolma's family and college group.

How did Dolma's sister respond, and why did it matter?
The sister simply said “I'm with you”, meeting the hardest moment with support instead of blame.

The small library in the panchayat office at Khandala had one shelf of children's books, and Dhruv had read most of them twice, sitting on the floor with his knees up. In June, the volunteer, Zainab Didi, started a scheme: a peda from the sweet shop for every book returned. Dhruv began taking the thinnest books, the ones with twelve pages, and bringing them back the same afternoon. He collected eleven pedas in a week. One day Zainab Didi held up the fat book about sailors he used to love. 'Don't you want this again?' Dhruv shook his head. 'It's just one peda.' He took two thin books instead and ran off without opening either. Zainab Didi watched him go, then quietly took the peda jar off the counter.

What did Zainab Didi give for each book returned?
She gave a peda from the sweet shop.
Why did Dhruv refuse the book about sailors?
He had become eager for pedas, so a long book he once loved felt like a poor trade, and his joy in reading slipped behind the reward.
What could Zainab Didi do next?
Remove the peda scheme, as she begins to, and invite children to share what they liked in a book instead.
What might Zainab Didi feel watching Dhruv run off?
She likely feels disappointed and a little regretful that her reward scheme changed how he reads.

"The mall?" said her father, Nilesh, putting down the newspaper in their Vadodara flat. "With your marks? You got fifty-two in maths."

"That was one test, Papa."

Gary is buying chlorine for his rectangular pool, which is 10 feet long, 8 feet wide, and 6 feet deep. Gary needs to buy one quart of chlorine for every 120 cubic feet of water in his pool. If chlorine costs $3 a quart, how much does Gary spend on chlorine?

First find the volume of the pool by multiplying the length by the width by the height: 10 ft * 8 ft * 6 ft = 480 cubic feet
Then divide the volume of the pool by the number of cubic feet one quart of chlorine can sterilize: 480 cubic feet / 120 cubic feet/quart = 4 quarts
Then multiply the number of quarts Gary needs to buy by the price per quart to find out how much money he spends: $3/quart * 4 quarts = $12
The answer is 12.
The answer is range 99, Q1 = 2, Q3 = 6, IQR = 4.

The community leader of a certain town organized a cleaning day event where community members were to be involved in collecting trash inside the town. Out of 2000 community members involved in the cleaning process, 30% were adult men. If there were twice as many adult women as adult men in the event, and the rest were children, calculate the total number of children involved in the cleaning event.

If the number of adult men involved in the cleaning process was 30% of the community members, there were 30/100*2000 = 600 adult men at the event.
There were also twice as many adult women as adult men in the event, a total of 2*600 = 1200 women.
The total number of adults in the event was 1200+600= 1800
If the rest of the people at the cleaning event were children, there were 2000-1800 = 200 children at the event.
The answer is 200.
I have Rs 57 and want a paint set that costs Rs 137. Is that enough?
No, it is not enough. Because I would need 80 more, since 137 - 57 = 80.

Counselling note, Monday. Raghav came in after a classmate told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face. Raghav said she'd laughed at the time, so he thought it was fine. She hadn't said yes, and she has now asked him to remove it. He also mentioned that his own feed looks like everyone has amazing weekends, and that he sometimes feels bad comparing. We talked about how people choose the best photos and filters, and how other people's pictures need their permission. He agreed to take the photo down and ask before posting in future. I told him he can talk to me any time. Vidya, counsellor.

What did Raghav's friend tell him off for?
She told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face.
What was Raghav thinking and feeling when he posted the photo?
He felt at ease about it because she had laughed at the time. He had not asked her, so he had not checked what she felt.
What steps did Raghav agree to?
Take the photo down and ask before posting anyone's image in future.
How might Raghav's friend have felt seeing the photo online?
She may have felt embarrassed and exposed, since the picture went out without her say.

For three months I covered for Vikas. When his mother called asking where he was, I said, "He's studying with me." He was actually racing his cousin's motorbike on the highway at night with some older boys.
I thought that was what loyalty meant. You don't snitch. Friends protect each other.
Then one night he called me, laughing, saying they'd hit a hundred and ten on the flyover without helmets. I couldn't sleep. I kept seeing him on the road.
I asked myself: am I loyal to Vikas, or to his racing?
The next morning I told my father everything. He listened and said, "You're protecting him now, Deepak, not betraying him." He phoned Vikas's mother that afternoon.
Vikas didn't talk to me for a week. Then he did. He said, "I was angry. But I'd have been dead some night." We still hang out. Just not on the flyover.

What was Vikas racing on the highway?
His cousin's motorbike.
How did Deepak feel after Vikas's late-night call?
Deepak felt frightened and sleepless, imagining Vikas hurt on the road.
What choice did Deepak make, and why was it the loyal one?
Deepak told his father, who called Vikas's mother the same day, because being loyal to Vikas's safety mattered more than covering the risky act.
How did Vikas feel about Deepak telling?
Vikas was angry at first, but later understood that the racing could have killed him and valued the friendship.

Monday. When the coach announced Indu as captain, Vaibhav clapped and smiled and felt as if he'd swallowed a stone. He had wanted it since Class 8. In the group chat he typed "She's good at speaking, not sure about tactics" and then deleted it.

The next Saturday. He watched Indu at practice: she arrived early, learned the juniors' names, changed the drill when someone struggled. It irritated him. It also, unwillingly, taught him something.

Three weeks later. He told his brother, "I'm jealous." It was easier to say aloud. That evening he stayed after practice to work on his passing, and asked Indu to time him.

What did Vaibhav type in the group chat and then delete?
"She's good at speaking, not sure about tactics".
What was Vaibhav feeling when the coach announced Indu as captain?
Envy and disappointment. He smiled and clapped but felt as if he'd swallowed a stone, since he had wanted the role since Class 8.
What did Vaibhav do that helped him move forward?
He admitted his jealousy to his brother, studied what Indu did well and kept practising, instead of sabotaging her or spreading doubts.
How might Indu feel when Vaibhav asks her to time him?
Probably surprised and pleased. It is a sign of respect, and it may show her that he has accepted the situation and wants to work together.

His necessities supplied, Derick departed; but he had not gained his ship's side, when whales were almost simultaneously raised from the mast-heads of both vessels; and so eager for the chase was Derick, that without pausing to put his oil-can and lamp-feeder aboard, he slewed round his boat and made after the leviathan lamp-feeders.

Answer from the text. Why did Derick not put his oil-can and lamp-feeder aboard?
Whales were raised from the mast-heads of both vessels, and he was so eager for the chase that he turned his boat round and went after them at once.

Supervision note, 18 July. Written by Bhupen, partnerships manager.
Ishita joined our team in April and handles the Osaka supplier. On the June call she asked Mr. Tanaka directly, "Can you deliver the parts by the 30th, yes or no?" There was a long silence, then: "That may be a little difficult." Ishita took this as a maybe and put the 30th in our plan. The parts came on the 14th of the next month.
I explained that Mr. Tanaka, like several of our partners there, tends to say no politely: "a little difficult" and a long silence usually mean no. A blunt yes-or-no question can put him on the spot.
Since then I have watched her adapt. On this week's call she asked, "What date would feel comfortable for your team?" and listened to the pauses. She also checked with Ms. Mori, their coordinator, afterwards. The date she got was realistic.
Next step: I will ask Ishita to share this with the two new joiners.

When did the parts actually arrive?
On the 14th of the next month.
What did Ishita believe, and how did she likely feel, when Mr. Tanaka said 'That may be a little difficult'?
Ishita felt hopeful and took it as a maybe, then was likely frustrated and embarrassed when the parts came weeks late.
How did Ishita adapt her questions?
She asked open questions like what date would feel comfortable, listened to the pauses, and checked with the coordinator, Ms. Mori, afterwards.
How might Mr. Tanaka have felt being asked 'yes or no?'
He may have felt put on the spot and uncomfortable, preferring to decline politely rather than say a blunt no.

The power went out across the hostel in Pune at nine, the week of Durga Puja, and Bidisha lay on her bed in the dark with her phone at eleven percent. Back in Kolkata, her family would be at the pandal right now, her Thakuma in her white-and-red saree, her cousins arguing over rolls. Here, nobody had even heard of the sweet she had searched three markets for. Her classmates were friendly, but no one knew that she hated coriander or that she sang when she was nervous. She felt like a guest in her own life. She tried to call home, but the network dropped twice. She started crying quietly, then harder. Her roommate Shalini sat up in the dark. "Homesick?" Bidisha nodded, then realised Shalini couldn't see. "Yes." "Me too, last year. It passes. It doesn't mean you shouldn't have come."

What was Bidisha's phone battery at when the power went out?
Her phone was at eleven percent.
What is Bidisha feeling as she lies in the dark?
Bidisha feels homesick and sad, missing her family at the pandal and feeling like an outsider where no one knows her.
What could help Bidisha after this night?
Talking more with Shalini, planning a proper call home, and finding a small local puja gathering could help her feel less alone without deciding the move was wrong.
How might Shalini feel hearing Bidisha cry?
Shalini probably feels sympathetic, remembering that same homesickness from last year, and wants Bidisha to know the feeling passes.

Bilal had been a team lead at the Toronto design studio for six weeks and was still redoing half his juniors' work at night. When Jin's client mockups came in late again, with the same spacing errors, Bilal almost fixed them himself. Instead he booked a room for fifteen minutes. "I want to talk about the café mockups," he said. "They were two days late and had the spacing issues we discussed last month. That affects the client's trust in all of us." Jin's face tightened. "I've been struggling with the grid system," Jin admitted. "I didn't want to ask again." Bilal nodded. "Then that's on both of us. Let's do thirty minutes on the grid tomorrow, and you'll own the next mockup from start to finish. I'll review it on Wednesday, not rewrite it." Jin left looking uncertain but less tense.

How late were Jin's mockups?
They were two days late.
Why did Bilal almost fix the mockups himself?
He was tired and frustrated after weeks of redoing work at night, and probably reluctant to face an uncomfortable conversation.
What did Bilal get right about delegating and giving feedback?
He named the specific problem and its impact in private, offered coaching on the grid, and gave Jin full ownership with a review instead of a rewrite.
What is it like for Jin to hear that the problem is on both of them?
Jin probably feels relieved not to be blamed alone, and a little more able to ask for help next time.

The day-shift and night-shift teams at the Pune hospital lab didn't like each other. Day blamed night for dirty equipment. Night blamed day for missing samples.
Ojas, twenty-four and on day shift, caught himself saying "those night people" at lunch. He stopped.
That week he stayed an hour after his shift and met Gautam from night shift. They found the missing samples were a labelling problem, not laziness. Ojas suggested a joint handover notebook and a single notice board by the door, with both teams' names on the top: "Lab Team."
At the next staff meeting, when someone grumbled about nights, Ojas said, "We're the same lab. Gautam's team fixed half of this."

What did the missing samples turn out to be?
They turned out to be a labelling problem, not laziness.
What might Ojas have felt when he caught himself saying "those night people"?
He probably felt uneasy and embarrassed, noticing how easily he had fallen into blaming the other team.
What small step helped the two shifts work together?
A joint handover notebook and a notice board headed "Lab Team" gave both shifts one shared identity and a fair way to share information.
How might Gautam see Ojas staying an hour after his shift?
Gautam may feel respected and surprised, since someone from the day shift came to understand the night team rather than blame it.

Note by Elizabeth, KG teacher.
Suraj has a big voice, and in class he often shouts his answers. We started a signal: when I put my hand on my head, it means indoor voice. The first day he forgot six times. Today he forgot only twice, and both times he saw my hand and dropped his voice straight away. I told him, “I saw you trying. That's great.” He beamed. At outdoor play I said, “Now you can shout,” and he shouted “YAAAY!” across the field.

What does Elizabeth's hand on the head mean?
Indoor voice.
What was Suraj feeling when Elizabeth praised him?
He felt proud and happy, and his beam showed that being noticed for trying mattered to him.
Why was praising the trying a good idea?
It encourages Suraj to keep working on his voice, since self-control grows gradually.
How might the other children see Suraj's shout at outdoor play?
They'd see it as normal fun outside, and might join in with their own shouts.
Will the sea be rough at Puri on Saturday?
I don't know how rough the sea will be at Puri on Saturday, as I can't check marine forecasts. The local weather office issues sea conditions for the coast.

The farewell committee met in the empty Class 11 room of the government school at Kurukshetra. Wasim sat on the teacher's desk, swinging his legs.
“Riverbank. Evening. Bonfire, music, the whole thing,” he announced. “Last week of June.”
“Wow!” said Sukhi. “Yes!” said Dinesh. Everyone clapped.
Indu opened her mouth. Last June the river had flooded the path. Also, half the girls' parents would never allow an evening by the river. She looked at the smiling faces and closed her mouth. Nobody wanted to ruin it.
“All agreed?” Wasim asked. Every hand went up. Hers too.
On the day, it rained from noon. The farewell was cancelled at five, and they had no other plan.

When did Wasim want the farewell?
He wanted it in the last week of June.
What was Indu feeling when she closed her mouth?
She felt doubtful and uneasy about the plan, but didn't want to spoil everyone's excitement.
What small step could have helped the committee?
Someone could ask, "What could go wrong?" before voting, so Indu's worries about rain and parents came out.
How might Wasim see the cancellation?
He might feel disappointed and embarrassed, perhaps wishing someone had raised the risk of rain before.

The rain hadn't stopped for three hours, and Naveen was already late for his first job interview in Pune when his old car stalled at the traffic light. He slapped the steering wheel. 'Not today, Laddoo! Why do you always do this to me?' His friend Suraj, in the passenger seat, raised an eyebrow. 'Laddoo?' 'She's moody. She hates rain.' Naveen tried the key again, whispering, 'Please, please, just this once.' The engine coughed and started. 'See? She listens when I'm polite.' Suraj laughed but said, 'Or the engine was wet and it dried a bit.' Naveen grinned. 'Maybe. But it feels better thinking she's grumpy than thinking it's random.' They made it with four minutes to spare. That evening Naveen booked a service.

What did Naveen call his car?
Laddoo.
What was Naveen feeling when he slapped the steering wheel?
Naveen felt frustrated and anxious about being late for the interview.
What sensible step did Naveen take after the interview?
He booked a service, dealing with the real cause instead of only coaxing the car.
How does Suraj see Naveen's explanation of the car's behaviour?
Suraj finds it funny and offers a practical reason, a wet engine, instead of a mood.

Girls' hostel warden's note, first-year block.
Ayesha, from a small town in Bihar, has been here two months. Her roommate Kashish mentioned she rarely leaves the room and eats in the room most nights. She calls her mother for hours and cries.
I spoke to Ayesha today. She said, "Everyone already has friends. They speak so fast, and I feel like a village girl."
I told her many first-years feel this way. I suggested she join the Sunday cooking club, where some other students from Bihar go. Kashish offered to go with her the first time.
I also gave her the student counselling centre's timings.
Next week I'll check if she went. — Mrs Singh

Which club did Mrs Singh suggest to Ayesha?
The Sunday cooking club.
What was Ayesha feeling when she said she felt like a village girl?
Ayesha felt lonely, homesick and insecure among the other students.
What did Mrs Singh do to help Ayesha build belonging?
She normalised the feeling, suggested a club with students from Ayesha's region, arranged for Kashish to go with her, and shared counselling timings.
How might Kashish feel offering to go with Ayesha?
Kashish likely feels caring and glad to help her roommate settle in.
How strong is the wind in Goa today?
I can't check live weather, so I don't know. A coastal weather page will show wind speed.
If I have time, I would visit you on Sunday. Please check the conditional.

If I have time, I will visit you on Sunday.
Why: Real future takes present in "if" and "will" in the main clause.
Is 28 more or less than 64?
Less. Because 28 has 2 tens and 64 has 6 tens.

So, Jagdish, you asked what changed for me this year. Honestly? One small habit. I'm Payal, I work in a hospital billing office, and my supervisor has this way of saying, "Is this really your best?" Last March she said it about a report I'd stayed late for. I smiled, went home, and within twenty minutes I'd shouted at my mother about the pressure cooker whistle and banged a steel plate down so hard my little brother jumped.

That night I sat on the stairs and said out loud, "This isn't about the cooker." Now, when I feel that heat, I walk to the end of the lane first. Or I type the angry message to my supervisor, delete it, and send the calm one: "Can we look at what you'd change?" She did, actually. And home is quieter.

What does Payal's supervisor tend to say?
The supervisor says, "Is this really your best?"
Why did Payal say "This isn't about the cooker"?
Payal saw that the hurt and anger came from the supervisor's remark, and felt ashamed that it had landed on the family instead.
What habit could Payal keep using, and why does it work?
Walking to the end of the lane, or drafting and deleting the angry message, gives the heat time to settle so the real reply goes calmly to the supervisor.
How might Payal's little brother remember that March evening?
Payal's brother was startled by the banged plate and may have wondered what he had done, though it had nothing to do with him.

The answers are: 999; 0.

The last bus from Kurnool had gone, and Rukmini sat on the bench at the Adoni bus stand, staring at her phone. She had sent Vikas a voice note at noon about the school science fair. It was now six. No blue ticks. She scrolled back through their chats. Had she been rude yesterday? She'd teased him about his handwriting. Maybe he was angry. Maybe he'd told the others. Maybe that was why Lalitha hadn't sat with her at lunch. By the time the tea stall man switched on his bulb, Rukmini was certain: she had lost her only good friend and the whole class had turned against her. Her eyes stung. Then her phone buzzed. Vikas: "Sorry!! At my uncle's farm, zero signal. Just reached the road. Science fair idea is super." Rukmini laughed out loud, and the tea stall man looked over.

Where was Vikas when he didn't reply?
He was at his uncle's farm, with zero signal.
Why were Rukmini's eyes stinging by the time the tea stall bulb came on?
Rukmini felt scared and hurt, having convinced herself step by step that she had lost her best friend and the whole class.
What could Rukmini ask herself when the worry starts next time?
She could ask what else might explain the silence, like being busy or out of signal, before trusting the worst story.
How might Vikas have felt if he'd known what Rukmini was imagining?
Vikas would likely feel surprised and sorry, since he was simply out of signal and liked her idea.

Dear Imran,
I owe you an apology, and a book.
When you asked about your statistics textbook last week, I was so sure. I told you I'd handed it back at the farewell party, in the corridor next to the notice board, and that you put it in your black backpack. I could see it. I even said, a bit rudely, "Check your own room first."
Yesterday I was scrolling through photos from the hostel move. There it is: me, two days after the farewell, sitting on my bed, and your textbook right there under my pillow, your name on the spine.
I was completely certain, and completely wrong. I'm sorry for making you think you'd lost it.
Coming to return it tomorrow, with samosas.
Parveen

What did the photo from the hostel move show?
Parveen on the bed two days after the farewell, with Imran's textbook right there under the pillow.
How does Parveen feel after finding the photo of the textbook?
Parveen feels sorry and embarrassed for having been so sure and for rudely telling Imran to check first, when the book was under Parveen's pillow all along.
What could Parveen do the next time a past detail feels certain?
Parveen could say "I think I returned it" and check photos or messages before insisting, since feeling certain isn't the same as being right.
How might Imran have felt on being told to check the room first?
Imran probably felt blamed and confused, starting to doubt a clear memory about a book that was never returned.

After the economics tutorial at the Kolkata college, Uday stayed back, still heated from the class debate. "Ma'am, the job crisis is simple. It's them. They've flooded every office. Nobody wants to say it."
Leela closed her laptop slowly. She had heard versions of this in the corridor all term. She could have given the lecture on unemployment data she knew by heart. Instead she pulled up a chair.
"I disagree with blaming a whole group of people, Uday. I'll show you the numbers some day. But first, what are you actually afraid of?"
He looked at the window for a long time. "My brother has an MBA and he delivers food. I'm doing the same degree. What's the point?"
"That's a serious fear," Leela said. "And it's real. Let's look at it properly. Come to my office on Thursday and we'll map out the options together."
Uday picked up his bag, quieter. "Thursday," he said.

What does Uday's brother do?
He has an MBA and he delivers food.
What was Leela thinking as she closed her laptop slowly?
Leela felt tired of hearing such talk but concerned for Uday, choosing patience over a lecture.
What makes Leela's response keep the conversation open?
She clearly disagrees with blaming a whole group, but first asks about Uday's fear and offers a real plan on Thursday.
What is Uday really carrying under the rant?
He is frightened and hopeless, watching his brother's struggle and fearing the same future.

Dear Hemant bhaiya,
You asked how the new semester is going, and I didn't want to just say "fine" again.
Honestly, I'm bored in some classes and exhausted in all of them. In the economics lecture I doodle the whole time. In the evening I scroll for an hour and then feel guilty. I thought I'd become lazy.
Then last week the college nurse asked how much I sleep. Five hours, most nights. She said that alone could make every lecture feel dull.
So I'm trying a few things. Phone out of the room at night. Bed by eleven. A short walk after lunch. In the dull lecture, I've started writing one question for the teacher every fifteen minutes, just to stay with it.
It's only been four days, but I yawn less. Will tell you more on Sunday's call.
Love,
Shalini

How much does Shalini sleep most nights?
Five hours.
What was Shalini feeling before the nurse's question?
Shalini felt bored and exhausted, and guilty, worrying about becoming lazy.
What changes is Shalini trying, and why might they help?
Phone out of the room, bed by eleven, a walk after lunch and writing questions in lectures, which add rest and structure.
How did the college nurse see Shalini's dull lectures?
The nurse thought lack of sleep alone could make every lecture feel dull.

The client deck was due at five, and the printer had jammed, when Shreya leaned over Manjula's cubicle. "Have you heard? Ritesh's team is telling the director we're slow. We should tell her about their missed audit first." Manjula's phone buzzed. Two people in the pantry were already picking sides. She felt the pull to pass on a tale, just to be safe. "I'll pass on that," she said. "I'll say hi to Ritesh's team tomorrow like always. Can you check page six with me? The chart is wrong." Shreya shrugged, a little disappointed, but bent over the page. The deck went out at 4:58.

What time did the deck go out?
The deck went out at 4:58.
What was Manjula tempted to do, and why?
Manjula felt the pull to pass on a tale about the other team, just to be safe.
How did Manjula stay friendly to everyone without taking sides?
She declined to pass on the gossip, planned to greet Ritesh's team as usual, and turned Shreya's attention back to fixing the chart.
How might Shreya see Manjula's refusal?
Shreya seemed a little disappointed, perhaps expecting an ally, yet still helped with page six.

Friday night Sabina moved to Guwahati last month and we're not allowed to call every day, so we send voice notes. Tonight she sent one singing our school song very badly, and I played it five times. Her voice made me feel like she was sitting on my bed. I started a reply. I was going to tell her that Chhoden cried in class today after the test and everyone saw. Halfway through, I stopped. Sabina's cousin is in my class. What if Sabina plays it and her cousin hears? What if it gets forwarded? I deleted it. Instead I recorded me and my little brother doing her song even worse. She sent back ten laughing faces. - Pema

Why does Pema delete her reply to Sabina?

She was going to tell Sabina that Chhoden cried in class after the test. She worried that Sabina's cousin, who is in her class, might hear it or that it might get forwarded, so she sent a funny recording with her brother instead.
The new coach wants to "raise the bar". What bar?

It is an idiom, not a real bar. "Raise the bar" means to set a higher standard for yourself or others.
Example: Her excellent performance raised the bar for the rest of the class.

"Okay, riddle. Three friends ate lunch: one had rice, one had roti, one had noodles. Charu didn't have rice. Aparna didn't have roti or noodles. Who had noodles?"
Charu scratched her head. "Wait. Aparna didn't have roti or noodles."
"So?"
"So Aparna had rice!"
"And?"
"I didn't have rice... so I had roti or noodles. The third friend?"
"Didn't have roti."
"Then I had roti, and the third friend had noodles!"
Aparna clapped. "Step by step."

What did Aparna not have for lunch?
Aparna didn't have roti or noodles.
What does Charu scratching her head suggest?
It suggests she was confused at first and needed to think it through.
What helped Charu solve the riddle?
She took the clues one at a time and ruled out possibilities step by step.
How might Aparna feel watching Charu solve it?
Aparna seems pleased and proud, clapping at Charu's careful thinking.

"Nazia, you've been staring at that form for an hour."
"Elizabeth, I don't know what to do. Take the job at the bank now, or drop a year and prepare for the civil services?"
"Okay. List it."
"The job: steady money, I can help Ammi with bills. But I'll be too tired to study."
"And the drop year?"
"My dream. But what if I fail? Then I've lost a year and a salary."
"What if you take the job and never try?"
Nazia went quiet. "I'd hate myself."
"So what's the middle?"
"Maybe... take the job, study weekends, attempt once, then decide?"
"Can you live with that?"
Nazia chewed her pen. "It's not perfect. But yes."

What exam was Nazia thinking of preparing for?
The civil services.
What was Nazia feeling when she went quiet?
Nazia felt torn and anxious, realising she would regret never trying for her dream.
How did Elizabeth help Nazia weigh the trade-offs?
By asking her to list both options, then asking what regret she would feel and whether a middle path existed.
How might Elizabeth feel about Nazia's decision?
Elizabeth likely feels glad to have helped Nazia find a path she can live with.
Two bags are the same size. One is full of rice, one is full of cotton wool. Which is heavier?

Answer: The bag of rice.

Same size does not mean same weight. What is inside matters. Let the child lift both bags. Then balance them: the rice side goes down.
Ben has 8 apples more than Phillip does. Tom has three eighths as many apples at Ben has. If Phillip has 40 apples, how many apples does Tom have?

Ben has 40+8 = 48 apples.
There are 48/8 = 6 apples in every eighth.
Tom has 6*3 = 18 apples.
The answer is 18.

Why do we hear thunder as a rumble and not as one sharp sound?
Someone said "investigation" to me. What is that?
why can we see our breath on a cold morning

1. Thunder is many sounds arriving at different times. Because the sound comes from different parts of the long lightning path, it reaches us at slightly different times.
2. "Investigation" is a noun. It means a careful search for facts about something.
3. Our breath shows up as tiny water droplets. Because the warm moist air we breathe out cools quickly and its water vapour turns into droplets.

People ask how I told my father I wasn't joining the family shop. The honest answer: slowly. I'm Jatin, twenty-five, the eldest son, which in our family means three roles: look after the parents, take over the business, and make the big decisions for my younger brother, Sahil. I sat with each one. Looking after my parents? I want that. I've kept it; I visit every Sunday and go with them to their doctor visits. Making Sahil's decisions? I've adjusted that; now I advise, he decides. Taking over the shop? That one I've set down. I explained it to Papa over three months, not in one angry evening, and found a cousin who actually wants it. Papa's still a bit sad. But he came to see my office last week.

How long did Jatin take to explain it to Papa?
Three months.
How does Jatin seem to feel about looking after his parents?
He feels glad and committed to it, a role he wants to keep.
What made Jatin's change gradual and respectful?
He explained over months, found a cousin to take the shop and kept the roles he valued.
How might Sahil feel now that Jatin only advises?
Sahil probably feels more trusted and grown up, making his own decisions.

Five balcony ticks, two phone ticks, and "balcony = actually calmer".

When stressed he felt a real need for relief, and simply stopping left that need unmet, so the old habit came back.

Swapping the phone for ten slow breaths and watering plants on the balcony, a familiar family habit that still gave him the break he needed.

The youth orchestra audition was at four on Saturday, across town, and it had rained since morning. Eshaan, sixteen, had exactly enough for one bus ticket each way, and the bus stand was a ten-minute walk through flooded lanes.

At two, his violin case was by the door. At two-thirty, it was still there.

Mridul called. "I'm at the stop. Where are you?"

"I'm not coming," Eshaan said. "I'll mess up the scale in the first minute. They'll stop me and say thank you. I already know how it goes. Why get soaked for that?"

"You played it perfectly on Thursday."

"Thursday doesn't count. Auditions are different."

Mridul went quiet. Then: "Okay. I'll tell you how it was."

At six, Mridul texted: "They took four violins. Only six people turned up for violin."

Eshaan read it twice and put the phone face down.

How many people turned up for violin, according to Mridul?
Only six people turned up for violin.
Why does Eshaan say "Thursday doesn't count"?
His forecast of failure feels so certain that he dismisses the evidence against it. Waving away the perfect Thursday protects the prediction and saves him from the risk of hoping.
What choice could Eshaan have made at two-thirty, and what could he do now?
He could have treated "I'll mess up" as a guess and gone anyway, since the audition was the only way to test it. Now he could ask whether there is a later audition or waiting list.
How might Mridul feel waiting alone at the bus stop in the rain?
Mridul may feel let down and a bit helpless, having seen Eshaan play well on Thursday. The careful text afterwards suggests Mridul still cares, even though Eshaan wouldn't listen.

Monday night
Eight weeks off the forums today. I deleted the apps in March, when I couldn't remember the last time I'd slept more than five hours.
I still get angry. The landfill fire near our colony is real. The kids in our lane really do cough all winter. Elizabeth, my counsellor, said something today that stuck: "Your anger about the landfill is valid. Hating people online never put out a single fire."
So this week I did something boring instead. I wrote a complaint to the municipal office with twenty-three signatures from our lane. I joined the ward residents' meeting. I read the pollution board's report, all forty pages, with a highlighter.
Nobody liked or shared any of it. But on Saturday an officer actually came to see the site.
I sleep seven hours now. I still care. I just don't hate anymore.
Salma

How many signatures did the complaint have?
Twenty-three signatures from our lane.
How does Salma seem to feel eight weeks off the forums?
Salma feels calmer and rested, still angry about the landfill but no longer consumed by hatred.
What turned Salma's anger into something useful?
Lawful, concrete steps: a signed complaint, joining the residents' meeting and reading the report, alongside counselling and sleep.
How might the families in Salma's lane feel about the complaint?
They likely feel hopeful and supported, seeing someone take their children's coughing to the officials.

The cricket ball had cracked the big flowerpot outside the staffroom, and the bell for assembly would ring in two minutes.
Nilesh, a Class 8 monitor, pushed the ball into Uday's hands. “Put it in your bag. You're small, nobody will check you. Don't say anything.” The other seniors scattered.
Uday stood with the ball in his hands. Nilesh was a monitor. Monitors were obeyed. But his stomach felt like it was sinking through his shoes. Mrs Joshi would think the pot fell by itself.
The bell rang. Uday walked into the staffroom instead of assembly. “Ma'am, this broke the pot. I didn't throw it.” Mrs Joshi put down her tea, thanked him for telling her, and sent for Nilesh before assembly ended.

What had the cricket ball cracked?
It had cracked the big flowerpot outside the staffroom.
What was Uday feeling as he stood holding the ball?
He felt torn and sick with worry; his stomach felt like it was sinking because hiding it felt wrong even though a monitor ordered it.
How did Mrs Joshi handle Uday's news, and why did it help?
She stopped, thanked him for telling her and sent for Nilesh at once, so Uday knew he had done right and wasn't left to face the seniors alone.
What might it be like for Nilesh when he's called in?
He may feel caught and embarrassed, and maybe angry with Uday, which is why the teacher's quick support for Uday matters.

Heads up, the meeting has been moved to four.

Ojas, you're thinking of leaving the hostel because you messed up your mess money? Let your Pradeep Kaka tell you about 1989.
I was nineteen, in the hostel at Jadavpur. My father sent a money order on the first of every month. By the tenth, it was gone: cinema, snacks, lending to friends who never paid back. For two weeks I lived on bread and tea.
I was too ashamed to tell anyone. I got angry at everyone, my roommates, the mess manager, myself.
Then the mess manager, a gruff old man called Haldar Babu, saw me skipping meals. He said, "Eat now, pay when the money comes. And come see me; I'll show you how to write every paisa in a notebook."
I kept that notebook for forty years. The turning point wasn't the money, Ojas. It was letting someone help.

What was the mess manager called?
He was a gruff old man called Haldar Babu.
How did Pradeep feel during the two weeks of bread and tea?
Pradeep felt ashamed and angry at everyone, including himself.
What was the turning point in Pradeep's story?
The turning point was letting Haldar Babu help him, eating on credit and learning to write every paisa in a notebook.
How might Haldar Babu have seen young Pradeep?
Haldar Babu probably saw a struggling boy too proud to ask, and felt concern beneath his gruffness.

"Swati, the summary says the minister promised free buses in the speech," Sharmila said, scrolling on the newsroom computer.
"Then write it."
"But I can't find that line in the transcript."
Swati leaned over. "Did you ask the AI to summarise?"
"Yes. It's usually fine."
"Search the transcript for 'bus'."
Sharmila did. The word appeared once: "We are studying transport options." Her stomach dropped. "It made that up. If I'd published this…"
"You'd be writing a correction tomorrow, and people would've believed it," Swati said. "It's a great first reader. But you're the one who signs it."
Sharmila deleted the line and wrote it from the transcript. Then she opened a note on her desk and wrote: "AI summary = draft. Check every quote."
"Frame that," Swati said.

What did the transcript actually say about transport?
"We are studying transport options."
What was Sharmila feeling when she found the invented line?
Sharmila felt a jolt of alarm, her stomach dropping, realising she nearly published a false claim.
What habit did Sharmila adopt, and why is it wise?
Treating an AI summary as a draft and checking every quote against the source, because she is responsible for what is published.
How might readers have been affected if the line had gone out?
Readers could have believed a promise that was never made, and later trusted the newspaper less.

Dear Zainab,

On Friday our school visited the gurdwara, and I was nervous because I wasn't sure what to do. I didn't want to be disrespectful. So I watched the others: they took off their shoes and washed their hands and feet, and covered their heads. The volunteer at the door noticed me looking around and handed me a clean scarf with a smile. I tied it on. Inside, everyone sat on the floor and the music was so calm that even the noisy boys went quiet. Afterwards I asked a woman there why people bow, and she explained gladly. You'd like it, I think.

Love,
Rehana 🙂

What did the volunteer at the door hand Rehana?
The volunteer handed Rehana a clean scarf.
Why did Rehana watch the others before acting?
Rehana was nervous and did not want to be disrespectful, so watched what people did and copied respectfully. Rehana was uncertain, not careless.
What would you advise a visitor who is unsure of the customs somewhere?
Watch what others do, follow it respectfully and ask politely if unsure, as Rehana did.
How might the volunteer have felt seeing Rehana look around?
The volunteer may have felt welcoming and happy to help, having offered the scarf with a smile. 🙂

Chinmay, you're saying your whole plan is just a list of don'ts. Let your Reena Masi tell you something.
When I was twenty-five and running my first clinic shift roster, I wrote rules for myself. No double shifts. No gaps at night. No nurse working three weekends running. It was a good list. Nobody could complain.
But after two months I felt like a traffic policewoman. Just stopping bad things. My roster was safe and my nurses were tired of it and so was I.
One evening I thought, where am I actually trying to go? So I added one aim each month. First month, every nurse gets one full weekend off. Next month, each senior teaches one junior a skill on shift.
Same don'ts, but now they were guarding something. That's what changed, beta.

Every nurse gets one full weekend off.

Reena felt tired and flat, like a traffic policewoman just stopping bad things.

How might the nurses have seen the new monthly aims?
They may have felt more cared for and more motivated, with full weekends off and chances to learn skills from seniors.

1) Quick one: what is "charmer"?
2) When will my parcel arrive?
3) Why do we oil the hinges of a squeaky door?
4) Can you correct this for me? "He told that the shop was closed."

In their shared flat in Lajpat Nagar, Tenzin was the one who made every evening funny. He named the leaking tap "Gangaji", did cooking-show commentary while burning rotis, and could turn any bad news into a punchline. Binita, who had shared the flat with him for a year, started noticing a pattern. When she asked, "How was the visa interview?" he said, "They loved me. Too much. Couldn't let me leave." When she asked about his sister's wedding plans, he told a long joke about a horse. He never answered straight.
One night she came home late and found him on the balcony in the dark, no jokes, his phone face down on his knee. She sat down beside him. "You don't have to be funny with me," she said. "What's going on?"
Tenzin was quiet for a long time. Then: "The visa got rejected. Second time."

What did Tenzin name the leaking tap?
"Gangaji".

The jokes keep painful news like the rejected visa at a distance and keep others laughing instead of asking more.
What choice did Binita make on the balcony, and why did it help?
She sat beside him and said he didn't have to be funny with her, which gave him permission to share the rejection.
What might it be like for Tenzin to be 'the funny one' in the flat?
Probably tiring, since he keeps everyone entertained while carrying bad news alone.
Shaadi mein kisi ko bolna hai "Aap dulhe ki taraf se hain ya dulhan ki?" English mein.

For a month he had been skipping lunch, and last week Rehana had heard him and Ammi talking in low voices about "the loan". Thomas Sir, her class teacher, had noticed she was distracted and said, "Sometimes asking is less scary than guessing." So she sat on the edge of a table. "Abbu, what's changed? You and Ammi are worried about something." He put the rack down. "The tuition I did in the evenings stopped. Two students left. So we have less each month, and the house loan still has to be paid." In the college library's back corner, Jaya had a message box open and a blank line where the first sentence should be. The engineer she wanted to reach, Revati Menon, designed battery systems at the electric-scooter company Jaya dreamed of joining.
'Just say hi and ask for advice,' whispered Vinita from the next chair.
'Everyone says that. She must get fifty of those.' Jaya closed the message box and opened Revati's public posts instead. Mostly about cooling problems in batteries. Then a link: a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai. Jaya put in one earphone and watched it through, taking notes.
'Okay,' she murmured at the end. 'She said the hardest part was testing in forty-degree heat. I can ask how they test in monsoon humidity. That's a real question, and it shows I listened.'
She wrote three lines. Vinita read them and raised her eyebrows. 'That sounds like someone she'd reply to.'

How long was Revati's talk, and where was it given?
It was a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai.
Why did Jaya close the message box, and what was she feeling?
She felt uneasy that a plain 'hi' would be one of fifty, and wanted her message to be respectful and worth answering.
What else could Jaya do if Revati does not reply?
Send one short, polite follow-up after a week, and meanwhile find another engineer whose work she has actually studied.
How might the message look to Revati?
It stands out from generic requests because it asks about her own talk, which shows real interest and respect for her time.

In Kyiv, Nadia had been swimming lengths every morning for three months. The first weeks, her times dropped fast. Now, for five weeks, they hadn't moved at all.
She climbed out of the pool, frustrated. "I've hit my ceiling," she told her coach, Ivan.
"Show me your breathing."
She swam a length. Ivan nodded. "In September, you gasped every two strokes. Now you breathe every four, smoothly. That's progress. It's just not on the stopwatch yet."
Nadia frowned. "It doesn't feel like progress."
"It rarely does, on a plateau. Keep going. The times will follow."

How often did Nadia gasp in September?
Every two strokes.
What was Nadia feeling when she climbed out of the pool?
Nadia felt frustrated and discouraged, believing she had hit her ceiling.
What did Ivan do that helped Nadia see her progress?
He pointed to her improved breathing, a hidden change not yet shown on the stopwatch.
How does Ivan see Nadia's plateau?
Ivan sees it as a normal stage where progress happens under the surface, and feels confident her times will improve.
Compose a paragraph of about 80 words on why I want to become a pilot when I grow up.

I want to become a pilot because I love the sky. When I see a plane glide over our house, I feel that I too want to fly. A pilot sees clouds from above and travels to faraway places. It is also a job of great responsibility, because many people trust the pilot with their lives. I know I must study hard and stay calm. Someday, I hope to sit in that seat.

Twice, my colleague Suraj presented my test scripts as his in stand-ups. The first time, I stewed for a week and said nothing.

Dated weekly emails, a commit history with Tejas's name, a calm private talk with Suraj first, then going to the manager with the records when it repeated.

But when the gentlemen entered, Jane was no longer the first object; Miss Bingley's eyes were instantly turned towards Darcy, and she had something to say to him before he had advanced many steps. When I finished my engineering degree, I had two offers: a refinery with a big salary, and a rooftop solar company with a smaller one. My parents were confused when I chose solar. My friend Wasim said, "You'll be poor and virtuous."
I'm not poor. Just less rich. And I'm not particularly virtuous either.
But I did start noticing my own life. I take the metro instead of an auto most days. I eat meat twice a week instead of every day, not because anyone told me to, but because I looked up what it takes to produce. I repair my clothes. I still fly home to Amritsar twice a year, and I feel conflicted about it every time.
I'm Jasleen, and I don't think I'm saving the planet. I just want my work and my days to point in the same direction, most of the time.

Where does Jasleen fly home to twice a year?
Amritsar.

Jasleen feels conflicted each time, wanting to see family but aware of the environmental cost.

Freshman/Sophomores:400(.50)=200 students
Have pets:200/5=40 students

The answer is 160.

A gumball machine has red, green, and blue gumballs. The machine has half as many blue gumballs as red gumballs. For each blue gumball, the machine has 4 times as many green gumballs. If the machine has 16 red gumballs how many gumballs are in the machine?

There are 16/2=8 blue gumballs.
There are 8*4=32 green gumballs.
There are 16+32+8=56 total gumballs.
The answer is 56.

Damini stood between them with her phone torch, feeling her chest tighten. She had heard both of them say "someone will handle power" that afternoon.
Uma, the planner, arrived at a run, took one look and pointed. "You. Start it now." The lights came back at 7:28.
Later, in the car, Uma added a line to her checklist: "Generator — owner: ____." Damini noticed it was the first line with a name next to it.

The lights came back at 7:28.
How did Damini feel standing between the two leads?
Damini felt tense and anxious, her chest tightening, because she had heard both say someone would handle the power.

Uma added an owner's name next to the generator on the checklist, because the power had fallen between two teams.

"Twenty rounds of the ground. Now."
Amandeep drank his water and watched Kishore jog off, red-faced. Coach wouldn't punish someone for nothing, Amandeep thought. Kishore must have kicked it. People get what they deserve; that's how it works. The thought was comfortable, like shade.

I'm Eshaan, Chinmay's older brother, and I've seen this before. At the dosa place on Sunday the menu had forty kinds of dosa. Chinmay read every line out loud: masala, onion, paneer, cheese, mysore... The waiter came twice. Papa said, "Just pick, beta."
Finally he said "cheese" very fast, like jumping into cold water. When the plates came, he kept looking at my mysore masala. He ate half of his, then said, "I should've got that one."
Last month at the chaat stall, with only four things on the board, he picked in a second and was happy. I'm not sure what goes on in his head, but long menus seem to make him miserable.

How many kinds of dosa were on the menu?
The menu had forty kinds of dosa.

Ed booked a hotel while he was on vacation. Staying at the hotel cost was $1.50 per hour every night and $2 per hour every morning. If Ed had $80 and he stayed in the hotel for 6 hours last night and 4 hours this morning, how much money was he left with after paying for his stay at the hotel?

Ed spent $1.50 x 6 = $9 for staying in the hotel last night.
He spent $2 x 4 = $8 for staying in the hotel this morning
So, the total money he spent in the hotel is $9 + $8 = $17.
Therefore, he still has $80 - $17 = $63 left after staying in the hotel.
The answer is 63.

Air scatters blue light more than the other colours. Because sunlight has all colours mixed, and the blue part gets bounced around the sky in every direction, so it reaches our eyes from everywhere.

Can you draw a closed figure with only 2 straight lines? With 3? With 1 straight line and 1 curved line?

Answer: 2 straight lines: no, they cannot close up. 3 straight lines: yes, a triangle. 1 straight line and 1 curved line: yes, like a half circle (or the letter D).

"Joseph, stop running!" the teacher called.

Joseph, six, stopped. "But Vijay was running too!"

"Joseph, don't argue."

Joseph folded his arms and sat on the bench, glaring. He wanted to say, "You're mean!"

At snack time, his friend Vijay came over. "Sorry. I ran too."

Joseph went to the teacher. "Can I tell you something?"

"Of course."

"Vijay was running too. I felt it was unfair."

"Thank you for telling me calmly. You're right. I'll remind both of you."

What did the teacher tell Joseph to stop doing?
The teacher told Joseph to stop running.
What was Joseph feeling as he folded his arms and glared?
Joseph felt cross and resentful, sure it was unfair.
Which choice worked better than being rude, and why?
Telling the teacher calmly what happened, because the teacher listened and agreed to remind both boys.
How might Vijay feel when Joseph is blamed alone?
Vijay seems to feel guilty, so he admits he ran too.

"A servant has had the nightmare; that is all. She's an excitable, nervous person: she construed her dream into an apparition, or something of that sort, no doubt; and has taken a fit with fright. Now, then, I must see you all back into your rooms; for, till the house is settled, she cannot be looked after. Gentlemen, have the goodness to set the ladies the example. Miss Ingram, I am sure you will not fail in evincing superiority to idle terrors. Amy and Louisa, return to your nests like a pair of doves, as you are. Mesdames" (to the dowagers), "you will take cold to a dead certainty, if you stay in this chill gallery any longer."

What does the speaker tell the guests happened, and what does he ask them to do?
He says a nervous servant had a nightmare and mistook it for a ghost. He asks everyone to go back to their rooms so the house can settle and the servant can be looked after.
My camera's shutter clicked. I only know shutters from windows.

In a camera, the shutter is the part that opens briefly to let light reach the film or sensor. It is a noun. A window shutter is a cover that closes over a window.
Example: A slower shutter lets in more light.

Read this:

In the Laxmi Nagar PG, the owner called everyone by room numbers. Rukmini was 'Four'. 'Four, your mess money.' 'Four, don't use so much water, you people bathe twice a day.' When the power bill went up, the owner told a new tenant, 'It's these outside students, a burden on the whole building.' Rukmini had stopped answering at the door. She ate her curd rice on the bed, facing the wall, and on Sundays she spoke to no one at all. Then Aparna, from her statistics class, invited her home for lunch. Aparna's grandmother asked about Madurai, about the temple, about her amma's sambar. Rukmini talked for an hour. On the metro back she noticed she was humming. That night she video-called her cousin, then Aparna, and for the first time in weeks she slept straight through.

What did the PG owner call Rukmini?
The owner called Rukmini 'Four'.
What does eating while facing the wall suggest about how Rukmini feels?
It suggests Rukmini feels unseen and hurt, pulling away from people because being treated as a number and a burden has made her feel less than a person.
What helped Rukmini begin to feel like herself again?
Being welcomed at Aparna's home and asked about Madurai and her amma's sambar reconnected her with people who saw her, and she reached out to her cousin too.
What might Aparna's grandmother have noticed during lunch?
The grandmother may have noticed a quiet girl lighting up while talking about home, and enjoyed giving her a place to be herself.
Rewrite this into polite email language for a professor: I want an extension. The deadline is too soon.

Dear Professor,
I am finding it difficult to finish the assignment by the current deadline. Would it be possible to have a short extension?
Thank you for considering my request.

In the small town of Bhilwara, the power was out and Zeenat lay on her bed with her phone at forty per cent. She opened the photo app.
Kiran, from her old school, was at a science camp in Bengaluru. Kiran at a beach. Kiran with a trophy. Kiran laughing with friends in matching T-shirts.
Zeenat looked around her room: the damp patch, the pile of Hindi notes, the same four walls. She felt heavy and dull, like her life was standing still.
She scrolled for an hour. The battery hit ten per cent.
Then her little brother came in with two cups of chai and a torch. "Ammi says come, the neighbours are singing on the roof." Zeenat hesitated, then put the phone down.

Where was Kiran at a science camp?
Kiran was at a science camp in Bengaluru.
What was Zeenat feeling as she looked around her room?
She felt heavy, dull and behind, comparing her ordinary day with Kiran's highlight photos.
What could Zeenat remind herself when scrolling next time?
That she is seeing only Kiran's best moments, not her ordinary days, and that her own life has good moments like singing on the roof.
What would change if Zeenat's brother hadn't come in?
Zeenat might have kept scrolling and feeling worse, instead of joining a real moment with family and neighbours.

Read this:

"Sir, you want me to hold the register?" Jahnavi asked, hovering by the staff-room door.
"Thank you, Jahnavi." Rafiq Sir rubbed his eyes.
"You look tired today."
"A little. My mother is unwell, and I slept badly. Nothing you need to worry about."
Jahnavi nodded. In class she did not fidget or talk, and when the chalk box fell she picked up the pieces before anyone laughed. At the bell she stacked the notebooks neatly on his desk.
"Jahnavi," he said, "that helped more than you know."
She smiled. "I hope your mother feels better, Sir."

What did Rafiq Sir say was wrong when Jahnavi told him he looked tired?
He said his mother was unwell and he had slept badly.
What made Jahnavi behave calmly and kindly in class that day?
She noticed her teacher looked tired and worried and understood he was a person with troubles, so she chose to be quiet and helpful.
What else could Jahnavi do on a day her teacher looks stressed?
She could help carry books, keep her voice low and be patient, without prying into what is wrong.
How might Rafiq Sir have felt when Jahnavi stacked the notebooks?
He probably felt touched and a little less alone, which is why he said her help mattered more than she knew. 🙂
Describe your ideal Sunday morning in exactly 15 words.
I wake late, drink tea on the balcony, and read the newspaper without any hurry.

Condense this into three sentences.

In the waiting room of the animal clinic, Ujjwal held his new puppy in his lap while the nurse, Binita, handed him a blank card. "Tell me a day with him," she said. Ujjwal wrote: 7 a.m., food. After school, walk. 6 p.m., food. Bedtime, check the water bowl. His mother nodded at each line. At home he pinned the card beside the front door with a red drawing pin. By the third evening his sister was reading it aloud before feeding time, and Ujjwal never had to remind anyone.

In the waiting room of the animal clinic, nurse Binita gave Ujjwal a blank card and asked him to tell her a day with his new puppy, and he wrote: 7 a.m., food; after school, walk; 6 p.m., food; bedtime, check the water bowl. His mother nodded at each line, and he pinned the card beside the front door at home. By the third evening his sister was reading it aloud before feeding time, and Ujjwal never had to remind anyone.

Pradeep tore a page from his rough book and wrote PARTY in capitals. Under it: cake, invitations, decorations, games. Then he went round their Lucknow flat with the page. Papa agreed to order the cake from the bakery near the market. His elder brother Vijay, groaning, took decorations. "And games?" Pradeep asked. "Dadi," said Mummy. "She knows fifty." That left invitations. Pradeep smiled. He was the best drawer in 5B. He spent Sunday afternoon making twelve cards, each with a different cartoon animal holding a balloon, and ticked 'invitations' off the list himself.

What did Pradeep draw on each invitation?
A different cartoon animal holding a balloon.
How did Pradeep feel when invitations were left for him?
He smiled, so he felt pleased and confident, being the best drawer in 5B.
What could Pradeep add to his list to keep the jobs on track?
A date next to each job and a quick check a few days before; giving each person one job is what spread the work.
How does Vijay feel about his job?
Vijay groans as he takes decorations, so he seems a bit reluctant, though he still agrees.
