Modernise the language here, keeping the meaning:

Spring advanced rapidly; the weather became fine and the skies cloudless. It surprised me that what before was desert and gloomy should now bloom with the most beautiful flowers and verdure. My senses were gratified and refreshed by a thousand scents of delight and a thousand sights of beauty.

Spring came quickly. The weather turned fine and the sky was clear. I was surprised that land which had been bare and gloomy was now full of beautiful flowers and green plants. A thousand lovely smells and sights refreshed me and lifted my spirits.
Who jilted Miss Havisham?
Compeyson, a smooth swindler, took money from her and never came on the wedding day. He was also Magwitch's old partner in crime.

Read this:

Week one: Baljeet, twenty, moved into a four-person flat in Chandigarh. By Thursday there were three greasy pans in the sink. Baljeet added a plate. Someone else will do them, Baljeet thought.
Week three: The sink was full, the counter sticky. Neelam, the flatmate from Shimla, came home, sighed, and ordered takeaway instead of cooking. Baljeet did the same. One more plastic box went into the overflowing bin.
Week five: A cockroach crawled out of the stack. Everyone stood in the kitchen, arms crossed. "It's not all mine," said one. "I only left one mug," said another. Baljeet realised every one of them had believed their own bit hardly counted. Neelam said quietly, "So all of us made this." They finally cleaned together, four people and a lot of soap, till midnight.

What crawled out of the stack in week five?
A cockroach crawled out of the stack.
What was Baljeet thinking when adding a plate in week one?
Baljeet felt calm and unbothered, assuming someone else would do the dishes, a careless thought.
What could the flatmates agree to so this doesn't happen again?
They could set a simple dish rota or rule to wash one's own plates the same day, so no one's small share piles up.
How might Neelam see the kitchen on coming home in week three?
Neelam felt tired and discouraged, choosing takeaway rather than face the mess everyone had left.
Aunty ne kaha "Don't stand on ceremony." Iska matlab?
It means do not be too formal or shy. Relax and do as you like.
The sum of Cooper's, Dante's, and Maria's ages is 31. Dante is twice as old as Cooper. Maria is one year older than Dante. How old is Cooper?

Let X be the age of Cooper. So Dante is X*2 years old and Maria is X*2 + 1 year old.
The sum of Cooper's, Dante's, and Maria's ages is X + (X*2) + (X*2 + 1) = 31.
Combining like terms, we get X*5 + 1 = 31.
Subtracting one from both sides, we get X*5 = 30.
Dividing both sides by 5, we get X = 6 years old.
The answer is 6.

Read this:

The rain had been falling for two hours, and the class was stuck in the corridor waiting for the buses. The seating chart was taped to the wall, sorted by last month's ranks. Front row: the toppers. Back row: the backbenchers. Lalremsiami, at the top of the list, pressed her folder to her chest. Her latest mark was 88, not 95, and she had not told a soul. At the back, Siddharth sat on the floor with his pen still in the bag. “Why bother?” he said to nobody. “I'm the last-row type.” Two boys laughed and agreed. Lalremsiami glanced at Siddharth, then at her mark, and pulled her folder in tighter.

Where did the seating chart on the corridor wall place the toppers?
The toppers were in the front row of the chart.
Why did Lalremsiami press her folder to her chest?
Lalremsiami seems afraid that anyone might find out her mark was 88 and not 95; as a topper she fears any failure.
What might help Siddharth start trying again?
Siddharth might be helped by someone who treats him as more than a last-row type, such as a teacher who notices one improvement, or classmates who study with him.
How might Siddharth see Lalremsiami's place at the top of the list?
Siddharth may see the topper's life as easy, not knowing that Lalremsiami hides the 88 and pulls her folder tight; the label works both ways.

Dear Papa,
I'm writing because when we talk on the phone, we end up arguing. I know you want the best for me. You drove me to every exam, and I'll never forget that.
But I'm twenty now, and I need to make some decisions myself. I want to choose my own internship, even if it pays less. I'd love your advice, just not your final decision.
Also, can we stop the daily 10 pm calls? I'll call every Sunday, and more if something's up. I promise.
Jeevan says his parents took a while too, and now they're closer than ever. I'd like that for us.
I love you. Please don't read this as me pushing you away.
Siddharth

How often does Siddharth want to call instead of every day?
He wants to call every Sunday, and more if something's up.
What does Siddharth's last line reveal about his feelings?
It reveals he's worried his father might feel rejected, and he wants to set boundaries while keeping the love between them.
What made Siddharth's letter a respectful way to set boundaries?
He thanked his father, asked for advice rather than decisions, and offered a clear alternative to the daily calls.
How might Papa feel reading this letter?
He might feel sad or hurt at first, but also proud of his son's maturity and reassured by the promise of Sunday calls.

Tell me in one line what this text says.

Mrs. Heathcliff's lip quivered slightly, and she returned to her seat in the window. Her husband took his stand on the hearthstone, near me, and began to put questions concerning Catherine. I told him as much as I thought proper of her illness, and he extorted from me, by cross-examination, most of the facts connected with its origin. I blamed her, as she deserved, for bringing it all on herself; and ended by hoping that he would follow Mr. Linton's example and avoid future interference with his family, for good or evil.
Mrs. Heathcliff's husband asks the narrator about Catherine's illness; the narrator blames her and hopes he will keep away from the family.

In the Class 12 counselling room, Aparna slid the two course forms across the desk. "The last date is the fifteenth. Have you picked?"

Santosh shrugged. "I'll sleep on it."

A week later he said it again, and the week after that. Each time Aparna asked what he had found out, he said, "Nothing new, I'm still thinking." He had not opened either college website or asked a senior about the hostel. On the sixteenth he came in with the forms still unsigned and read the notice on the board.

"It closed yesterday." He stared at the paper. "I thought more time would just make it clear."

Aparna pulled a chair up beside him and asked what he wanted to do about it now.

On which date had the forms closed?
The forms closed on the fifteenth, the day before Santosh read the notice.
What was Santosh feeling as he read the notice on the board?
Santosh was shocked and probably regretful, staring at the paper after hoping that more time would make things clear.
What could Santosh have done with those weeks instead of only waiting?
Santosh could have set a date to decide, opened the college websites and asked a senior about the hostel, so there were new facts to think about.
How might Aparna have felt each time Santosh said he would sleep on it?
Aparna may have felt concerned and a little helpless, seeing nothing new gathered while the last date came closer.

The printer jammed twenty minutes before the client call, and half the office started talking at once. Zeynep, the senior analyst, watched Pablo, who had joined only eight months ago, quietly unplug it, print the deck from his laptop at the other machine, and say to everyone, "Twelve minutes. Who takes slide one?" His voice never rose.

Later, Zeynep found him in the kitchen. "I've been in this job six years and I panic more than you do. How did you stay so steady?"

Pablo laughed, surprised. "I write the worst case on a sticky note. Then it's usually smaller than my head says."

"That's useful. I'm stealing it." She paused. "Next quarter's supplier pitch, I'd like you to lead the first half. I'll sit beside you."

Pablo grinned. "Really?"

What did Pablo do when the printer jammed?
Pablo unplugged the printer, printed the deck from his laptop at another machine and asked who would take slide one.
Why did Zeynep ask Pablo how he stayed so steady?
Zeynep admired his calm under pressure and admitted she panics more than he does, so she wanted to learn from him despite his lower rank.
What small step could Zeynep take to keep learning from Pablo?
She could try his sticky-note habit on her next stressful day and tell Pablo how it went.
How might Pablo feel about being offered the first half of the pitch?
Pablo probably felt surprised and pleased, since a senior colleague was trusting him with a stretch task and treating his method as worth borrowing.

The Diwali diyas flickered in a row along the balcony ledge.
"Lokesh, no. Hot," said Naveen bhaiya, crouching beside him.
Lokesh, two, froze with his hand in the air. "Hot?"
"Very hot. Only look."
Lokesh pulled his hand back and pressed it to his chest. He pointed at the next one. "No?"
"No. Hot too."
Lokesh wagged a finger at the flame, just like his brother. "No-no!"
Naveen laughed and gave him the rangoli box to hold. Lokesh sat, watching the flames.

Where were the Diwali diyas flickering?
In a row along the balcony ledge.
What was Lokesh feeling when he pulled his hand back and pressed it to his chest?
Lokesh seemed startled and a little cautious, as if he now sensed the flame was something he must not touch.
How could Naveen help Lokesh keep to the rule for the rest of the festival?
Naveen can keep using the same short words, stay close by the diyas, and keep giving Lokesh a safe job like holding the colours box.
What is it like for Naveen when Lokesh wags a finger at the flame?
Naveen finds it funny and is relieved 🙂 because it shows the rule has started to stick.

What happens when Clerval arrives? Short summary, please.

Nothing could equal my delight on seeing Clerval; his presence brought back to my thoughts my father, Elizabeth, and all those scenes of home so dear to my recollection. I grasped his hand, and in a moment forgot my horror and misfortune; I felt suddenly, and for the first time during many months, calm and serene joy. I welcomed my friend, therefore, in the most cordial manner, and we walked towards my college. Clerval continued talking for some time about our mutual friends and his own good fortune in being permitted to come to Ingolstadt. "You may easily believe," said he, "how great was the difficulty to persuade my father that all necessary knowledge was not comprised in the noble art of book-keeping; and, indeed, I believe I left him incredulous to the last, for his constant answer to my unwearied entreaties was the same as that of the Dutch schoolmaster in The Vicar of Wakefield: 'I have ten thousand florins a year without Greek, I eat heartily without Greek.' But his affection for me at length overcame his dislike of learning, and he has permitted me to undertake a voyage of discovery to the land of knowledge."

Victor is overjoyed to see his friend Clerval, who reminds him of home and makes him feel calm for the first time in months. Clerval explains that his father finally agreed to let him study at Ingolstadt instead of keeping him in business.

Friday night
Second prize. SECOND. At the district science fair, my water-filter model came second to a solar cooker. The principal shook the winner's hand and said, "This is the future." To me she said, "Good effort."
Good effort. I worked till two every night for three weeks. I skipped Parul's birthday. I didn't even go down for dinner half the time.
On the bus back I stared out of the window so nobody would see my face. Parul sat next to me and said, "Vasudha, it's a great model. You're more than a trophy." I nodded but I didn't believe her. If I'm not first, what am I?
Mumma made my favourite kadhi tonight and called me her clever girl. I couldn't eat it.
I know I'm tired. My head aches. But the inter-state fair is in four months, and I've already started planning version two.
Vasudha

What did Vasudha's model come second to?
A solar cooker.
Why couldn't Vasudha believe Parul's words on the bus?
She measures her worth by being first, so coming second made her feel like nothing, whatever her friend said.
What choice could Vasudha make before starting version two, and why might it help?
She could rest and eat properly for a while, and let herself enjoy the model she made, so her effort doesn't cost her sleep, friends and health.
How might Parul feel after Vasudha skipped her birthday and then didn't believe her comfort?
Parul might feel hurt and helpless, caring about Vasudha but unable to reach past her need to win.
Use product-to-sum formulas to show cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 1/8 and write 2 sin 3x cos x as a sum.

Answer: 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x; cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 1/8.

2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B), so 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x. For the product of three cosines, a cleverer route uses sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A repeatedly. Multiply and divide by 8 sin 20 degrees: 8 sin 20 degrees cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 4 sin 40 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 2 sin 80 degrees cos 80 degrees = sin 160 degrees Since sin 160 degrees = sin 20 degrees, the product is sin 20 degrees/(8 sin 20 degrees) = 1/8. By product-to-sum instead: cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees = (cos 20 degrees + cos 60 degrees)/2; times cos 80 degrees: (cos 20 degrees cos 80 degrees + (1/2) cos 80 degrees)/2 = ((cos 100 degrees + cos 60 degrees)/2 + cos 80 degrees/2)/2 = (1/2)(1/2)(cos 100 degrees + cos 80 degrees + 1/2) = 1/8 because cos 100 degrees = -cos 80 degrees. Calculator: 0.9397 x 0.7660 x 0.1736 = 0.1250.

"Kamal, we'll be late for the Diwali show!"
"I do it myself, Mumma!"
Kamal sat on the step with his new shoes. He pushed his foot in. It went in sideways.
"Let me help."
"No! Myself!"
Binita took a breath and crouched beside him. "Okay. You do it. I'll hold the other shoe."
He pulled. He wriggled. His tongue poked out. At last the foot slid in.
"I did it!"
"You did," said Binita, smiling, and picked up the second shoe for him to try.

What did Kamal say when Binita offered to help?
He said, "No! Myself!"
How did Kamal feel when his foot finally slid in?
He felt proud and happy, shouting "I did it!"
What did Binita do well even though they were late?
She took a breath, let Kamal do it himself, and helped only by holding the other shoe.
What might Binita have been feeling as they ran late?
Binita was probably a little anxious about the time, but chose patience.
The children plays in the garden after school.

The children play in the garden after school.
Why: "Children" is a plural noun, so the verb has no -s: "play".
My friend's pet parrot passed away yesterday and she's very sad. I don't know what to say.
I'm sorry to hear that. Losing a pet is a real loss, and your friend will appreciate you showing up.
I'm afraid I'll say the wrong thing.
Keep it simple and sincere: 'I'm so sorry about your parrot. I know how much you loved him. I'm here if you want to talk.' Then listen without hurrying to fix her feelings.

Nursery class note, Friday.
We had a puppet show today: a crow and a fox arguing over a piece of cheese. Siddharth sat in the front row, mouth open. Halfway through, Vidya ma'am from the office walked right across the back of the stage carrying a tall stack of chairs and wearing a bright orange dupatta. Almost every child turned. Siddharth didn't blink. Afterwards, when the others giggled about the orange chair lady, Siddharth frowned. "What lady?" He insisted there had been no lady. I told him it's normal: when we watch one thing very hard, other things can disappear. He thought that was like magic.

What were the crow and the fox arguing over?
A piece of cheese.
Why did Siddharth insist there had been no lady?
Siddharth felt sure and puzzled, because he had been so absorbed in the puppets that Vidya ma'am never entered his attention.
How did the teacher explain it, and why is that a helpful way to put it?
The teacher said watching one thing hard can make other things disappear, which helps Siddharth see it as normal, not a mistake.
How might the other children see Siddharth's 'What lady?'
They might find it funny or surprising, since the orange dupatta and chairs seemed impossible to miss.

The school library had a new chart: “Read and Win!” Each book returned earned one point, and ten points meant a free canteen coupon.
Deepak had always been the boy who read the whole science encyclopedia. Now he stood at the counter with five thin comics.
His friend Samir raised an eyebrow. “You finished the space book?”
“No. Too many pages. Comics are faster.”
By the end of the month Deepak had thirty points and three coupons. But when the librarian put a new book on black holes on the display, the one he would once have grabbed first, he walked past it.
“Aren't you taking that?” Samir asked.
Deepak shrugged. “It's only one point.”
Later, he felt a strange, flat feeling he couldn't name.

What did ten points earn in the library challenge?
Ten points earned a free canteen coupon.
Why did Deepak walk past the new book on black holes?
He was focused on points, and a long book was worth only one, so the prize crowded out his old interest and left him feeling flat.
What could the librarian change to protect children's interest?
Give points for time spent or for sharing what they learned, so long, interesting books aren't punished.
How might Samir feel watching his friend walk past the space book?
Samir might feel surprised and a little sad, remembering how much Deepak used to love such books.

Read this:

I'm Omkar, Harsha's roommate in the hostel, and I notice things at night. Around eleven Harsha lies down with the phone held above the face, thumbs sliding. I catch glimpses: a classmate on a beach, a cousin's wedding, someone's offer letter. The sighs get longer. Last night Harsha said, "Everyone is moving ahead and I'm standing here." I don't know what was going on inside that head, only that the mood dropped. I said those pictures were the best ten seconds of a person's week. Harsha snorted but did not argue. This morning I found a daily limit set on the phone and the phone on the shelf, and we went to the canteen for breakfast without it.

Where do Omkar and Harsha live together?
Omkar and Harsha are roommates in the hostel.
What might Harsha be feeling as the sighs get longer, and how sure can Omkar be?
Behind and discouraged, judging by the sighs and the remark about everyone moving ahead, but Omkar admits not knowing what was going on inside.
What small step did Harsha take, and why might it help?
Setting a daily limit and putting the phone on the shelf, because less scrolling means fewer highlight reels to compare with.
Why might Omkar have called the pictures the best ten seconds of a person's week?
To remind Harsha gently that posts show highlights, not whole lives, without lecturing.

Read this:

"Sunday again, Trisha. Hold the ruler straight."
"Why straight? It's a bean, not a building."
"Because if it's crooked, the number's wrong." Gurpreet read the scale. "Twenty-three centimetres."
"Last week?"
Gurpreet flipped the notebook. "Seventeen. Before that, fifteen. Before that, fourteen."
"So it jumped six this week. Why?"
"Hmm." Gurpreet ran a finger down the column where she had also written the weather. "Look. The big jumps come after rain. Fourteen to fifteen, no rain. Seventeen to twenty-three, rain on Wednesday and Thursday."
"So rain water's better than tap water?"
"Maybe. Or the days were cooler. I'll keep measuring and see."
Trisha grinned. "Scientist Gurpreet."

How tall was the bean plant this Sunday?
Twenty-three centimetres.
How does Gurpreet seem to feel about the pattern?
Curious and interested, and careful enough to keep measuring rather than jump to a conclusion.
What else could Gurpreet record to understand the jumps?
How much tap water the plant gets and how sunny each week is, so she can tell whether rain or cooler days matter.
How does Trisha see Gurpreet's method?
Trisha teases at first, then admires it, calling Gurpreet a scientist. 😊
Can you write a four-line lullaby where every line ends with a word ending in "ight"?

Close your eyes, the stars are bright,
The moon will keep you safe tonight,
Dream of kites in morning light,
Sleep well, sleep tight.
Please write a four-line rhyme for a toddler about putting on shoes, about 30 words.

One shoe, two shoe, on we go,
Left foot, right foot, in a row.
Pull the strap and tie it tight,
Now we are ready, shoes are right!
We're moving to a flat and my cat has never lived indoors only.
That is a big change for a cat. Moving can be unsettling for pets, so it helps to prepare.
What should I do first?
Set up a quiet room with food, water, a bed and familiar things from the old home. Let the cat get used to that space before exploring the rest.
Will it try to run away?
Possibly, in the first days. Keep windows and doors secure, and consider asking a vet about identification such as a tag. Supervise the cat's first explorations.
How long will it take to settle?
It varies, from a few days to a few weeks. Keep routines like feeding times the same, since they give the cat a sense of safety.
Does it need things to do?
Yes. Indoor cats need places to climb, scratch and look outside, and some play every day. A window perch and a scratching post help.
Mr. John jogs for 1 hour 30 minutes in the morning every day. How much time (in hours) will he have spent jogging after two weeks?

There are 60 minutes in an hour so 1 hour 30 minutes is equivalent to [1 + (30/60)] hours = 1.5 hours
There are 7 days in a week so he spends 1.5*7 = 10.5 hours jogging every week
After 2 weeks he will have spent 2*10.5 = 21 hours jogging.
The answer is 21.
Name three things shaped like a cylinder. What shape are its ends?

Answer: A can, a glass, a candle (also a drum, a pipe). Its ends are circles.

Stand a can on paper and trace round it: you get a circle.
Val cuts a single watermelon into 40 slices, and each slice has 20 black seeds and 20 white seeds. What is the total number of seeds in a watermelon?

40 slices per watermelon and each slice having 20 black seeds means each watermelon has 20*40=800 black seeds.
40 slices per watermelon and each slice having 20 white seeds means each watermelon has 20*40=800 white seeds.
In total, each watermelon has 800+800=1600 seeds.
What is the total number of seeds in a watermelon?
The answer is 1,600.

Damini said, "It is boring, just lap after lap."

Discouraged and uncomfortable, but she called it boredom and never said it was hard.

When the coach offered the shallow group for two weeks; accepting would have let her stay through the hard part.

Stone elephants.

He felt a flash of fear, his stomach flipping, but steadier once he remembered the meeting point.

messages.content: Daisy is a poodle puppy who loves to play with her dog toys. She often loses them in various ways, and her owner needs to replace them. On Monday, Daisy played with 5 dog toys. On Tuesday, Daisy had 3 dog toys left after losing some, and her owner went to the store and got her 3 more. On Wednesday, all of Daisy's old and new dog toys were missing, so her owner went to the store and bought her 5 more. If Daisy's owner found all the lost dog toys, including the new dog toys, how many dog toys would Daisy have now?

Daisy originally had 5 dog toys on Monday + 3 more her owner bought her on Tuesday = 8 dog toys.
On Wednesday Daisy's owner bought her 5 more dog toys + 8 old ones = 13 total dog toys if none were lost.
The answer is 13.

He turned the star a quarter turn, without letting go of Anirban's fingers.

Ms. Estrella is an entrepreneur with a startup company having 10 employees. The company makes a revenue of $400000 a month, paying 10% in taxes, 5% of the remaining amount on marketing and ads, 20% of the remaining amount on operational costs, and 15% of the remaining amount on employee wages.  Assuming each employee receives the same wage, calculate the amount of money each employee is paid monthly.

The company pays a total of 10/100*$400000 = $40000 on taxes
After taxes, the company revenue is $400000-$40000 = $360,000
The costs of marketing and ads campaign are 5/100*$360000 = $18000
After deducting the costs of marketing and adds campaign, the company remains with = $342,000 in revenue
Operational costs for the company are 20/100*$342000 = $68400
After taking out the operational costs, the company remains with $342000-$68400 = $273600
The company also pays employee wages of 15/100*$273600 =$41040
If the total number of employees is 10, each employee is paid a salary of $41040/10 = $4104 per month
The answer is 4104.
Christian is twice as old as Brian. In eight more years, Brian will be 40 years old. How old will Christian be in eight years?

If in eight years Brian will be 40 years old, he is currently 40-8 = 32 years old.
Since Christian is twice as old as Brian, he is 2*32 = 64 years old.
In 8 years, Christian will be 64+8 = 72 years old.
The answer is 72.

Mostly, yes. Blooming means producing flowers or being in full flower. It is the -ing form of a verb, and it can also be an adjective for something healthy and bright.
Example: The roses along the school wall are blooming this week.

Tariq sat in the middle, held the door and found a shared identity with Emeka as tired parents, which others followed.

Trent came home the same way so he went 11 blocks + 11 blocks = 22 blocks.

messages.content: Why does a dog sniff everything on its walk?
A dog sniffs to learn about the world around it. Because smell is its main sense and its nose is far more sensitive than ours, each sniff tells it who has passed that way and what food is nearby.

messages.content: Phil has a coin collection he likes to add to.  He started with 50 state quarters his parents gave him.  Over the next year he doubled this.  The following year he collected 3 each month.  The year after that he collected 1 every third month.  The year after that he lost a quarter of them when he misplaced his collection.  How many did he have left after losing some?

Phil started with 50, and doubled this amount the next year for 50*2=100 coins
Phil then collected 3 per month the following year, and since there are 12 months in a year that was 3*12=36 coins added
Phil then collected 1 every third month, and since there are 12 months that means he collected one every 12/3=4 months, for 4 coins added
Before he lost a quarter of his coins, Phil had 100+36+4 coins, or 140 coins in total.
Losing a quarter of 140 coins means Phill lost 140/4=35 coins
That means Phil had 140-35= 105 coins remaining
The answer is 105.

Lakshmi, you asked what I actually did when the regulator's letter came. I'll tell you honestly, because I almost did the wrong thing.
Our call centre had been using scripts that hinted customers' SIM cards would be blocked unless they upgraded. Sales were brilliant. Then complaints reached the regulator. My first instinct was to find a junior to blame.
Instead I called the whole floor together. I said, "The scripts were approved by me. That's my responsibility." Then I said Pooja's name aloud. She had written to me in May saying the scripts felt misleading, and I had ignored her. I told everyone she had been right and that her job was safe.
We rewrote the scripts that week. I scrapped the upgrade bonus and made "raised a concern" a line in everyone's appraisal. Refunds went out.
Trust didn't return overnight. But Pooja stays late now to train new staff. I'm Hansa, and that means more to me than any sales figure.

What did the scripts hint?
That customers' SIM cards would be blocked unless they upgraded.
What does Hansa's first instinct to blame a junior reveal?
It reveals fear and shame at being exposed, before Hansa chose honesty instead.
What did Hansa do that rebuilt trust?
Owned the scripts publicly, credited and protected Pooja, scrapped the upgrade bonus, rewarded raising concerns and issued refunds.
How might Pooja feel hearing her name aloud?
Pooja probably felt vindicated and safer, respected after being ignored in May.

I'm Asif, Karthik's classmate. On Monday in history, sir asked about the day the earthquake shook our district three years ago. Karthik's hand shot up. "I was at the bus stop. The shelter swayed, a coconut fell, and a woman dropped her tiffin. It was 7:40."
He sounded so sure that half the class went quiet.
The thing is, I was with him that morning. We were in my house playing carrom when the glasses rattled. We ran out together.
After class I told him. He looked at me as if I'd said the sky was green. "No, I remember the coconut."
I don't know what's in his head. Maybe the bus stop was someone else's story. He's still not sure he believes me.

What were Asif and Karthik playing when the glasses rattled?
They were playing carrom in Asif's house.
Why did Karthik answer so confidently in history?
The shock of that day left a vivid picture, with the time, the coconut and the tiffin, so it feels exact to him even though Asif remembers it differently.
How could Karthik and Asif find out whose memory is right?
They could ask family members or look for messages from that morning, instead of relying on how sure each of them feels.
What is it like for Asif to contradict a friend who seems so certain?
Asif probably feels awkward, being looked at as if he'd said the sky was green, and admits he cannot know what is in Karthik's head.

Sit, Imran, I'll tell you about your cousin Rumi. When she was nine, like you, your chacha put a chat program on the family computer for her homework. Arre, she talked to it like a best friend! She told it about her fights at school. One night she cried because it wrote, 'I will miss you.' She thought she had hurt its feelings. Then it told her that seven times eight was fifty-four. Her teacher marked it wrong, and Rumi came to me furious. I told her, beta, it's a machine that strings words together. It doesn't miss anybody. After that she used it, but she checked every answer. So you also, check, hah?

What wrong answer did the chat program give Rumi?
It told her that seven times eight was fifty-four.
Why did Rumi cry one night?
She believed the program's 'I will miss you' was a real feeling and worried she had hurt it.
What advice does the grandmother pass on to Imran?
To use such programs if he likes but to check every answer, because the machine can be wrong.
How might Rumi feel looking back on the night she cried?
She might feel a little embarrassed, but also understand why the kind words fooled her when she was young.

Asif's final-year project files were due to his guide by midnight, and his laptop was out of storage. On the sign-up page, a red timer ticked: "Offer ends in 09:54." Plan A: 50 GB, ₹75 a month. Plan B: 100 GB, ₹210. Plan C: 2 TB, ₹220, plus photo backup and family sharing. "Karthik, ten rupees more for twenty times the space!" he said. Karthik, eating chips on the bed, said, "You need about 20 GB." The Wi-Fi dropped, then came back. The timer said 03:10. Asif chose Plan C and felt a rush of relief, as if he had beaten the system. At 11:40 p.m. he uploaded 18 GB and closed the laptop, very pleased with his bargain.

How much space did Karthik say Asif needed?
About 20 GB.
What did Asif feel after choosing Plan C, and why?
He felt relief and a sense of beating the system, because Plan B at ₹210 made Plan C at ₹220 look like a steal.
With the timer running, what could Asif have done differently?
He could have ignored the timer and Plan B, asked what he needed, about 20 GB, and picked Plan A, which covered his 18 GB upload.
How does Karthik, on the bed, see the choice?
To Karthik, the only question is how much space the project needs; away from the timer and the odd middle plan, 20 GB is the whole story.

By March, Tariq was answering emails from the London office at midnight and waking at five with his heart racing. When he asked his manager, Nour, for a lighter week after three months of overtime, Nour didn't look up from the screen. "Everyone's tired. Can you have the forecast by Thursday?"

On the bus home Tariq realised he had forgotten to eat lunch for four days.

That night he did three things. He opened a document and wrote down every late night and weekend, with dates. He read the company's leave policy, which he had never opened. And he emailed HR asking about the wellbeing programme.

On Monday he booked five days of leave. Nour frowned but approved it. Tariq spent the first two days sleeping and the third walking by the river, noticing he could taste food again.

How many days had Tariq forgotten to eat lunch?
Tariq had forgotten to eat lunch for four days.
What was Tariq feeling when Nour asked for the forecast?
Tariq felt unseen and exhausted, with a racing heart, as his request for a lighter week was ignored.
Which steps protected Tariq, and why?
Recording his hours, reading the leave policy, contacting HR and taking leave put his recovery first instead of pushing until he collapsed.
How might Nour see Tariq's leave?
Nour seemed focused on deadlines and may see the leave as inconvenient, even though it prevents a bigger breakdown.

Kashish burst into tears when the fireworks banged outside the flat, and ran to Mummy. Jaya lifted her onto her lap on the sofa and wrapped both arms round her. She did not say much, just rocked slowly and hummed.
Kashish's sobs became hiccups, then long slow breaths, in and out. Her fingers loosened from Jaya's kurta. She rested her head on Jaya's shoulder and stared at the fan, quite still.
Later she whispered, "Your chest is warm." She stayed there until Papa called dinner, and even then she took her time.

What frightened Kashish?
The fireworks banging outside the flat.
What is Kashish feeling as she rests in Jaya's lap?
Safe and calm. Her sobs turn to slow breaths, her fingers loosen and she says Jaya's chest is warm.
What did Jaya do that helped Kashish settle?
Jaya held her close, rocked slowly and hummed, saying little, so her calm could be borrowed.
How might Jaya feel as Kashish's breathing slows?
Probably relieved and tender, since she stays holding Kashish quietly and does not hurry her.

Monday. The teacher said, "Preeti, you're so lazy," when she couldn't finish her sums. Everyone looked. That night Preeti, six, cried and told her father Tanvir. He held her. "You're not lazy. It's not your fault." Before bed he wrote to the principal.

Tuesday. Tanvir met the principal. The principal promised to talk to the teacher.

Two weeks later. Preeti's teacher helped her with sums quietly. Preeti went to school without a tummy ache.

Who did Tanvir meet on Tuesday?
Tanvir met the principal.
What was Preeti feeling on Monday night?
Preeti felt humiliated and sad, afraid of school after being called lazy.
How did Tanvir respond to Preeti telling him?
He comforted her, said it wasn't her fault and wrote to the principal that same night, then met the principal the next day.
How might the teacher see things differently after the principal speaks to her?
The teacher may realise ridicule hurt Preeti, and start helping her quietly instead.

I'm Hrithik, and I share a hostel room with Santosh. Last month his internship told him to learn a data analysis tool in ten days. Most of us would have binged videos. Santosh did something odd. The first evening he didn't install anything. He read the tool's introduction page and kept muttering to himself: 'Okay, so it exists because spreadsheets choke on big files. Tables go in, you filter them, you group them, you get a summary.' Then he wrote four words on our whiteboard: load, filter, group, summarise. When I asked if he was wasting a day, he said, 'If I know the four jobs, every lesson is just one of them.' By day three he was going through tutorials faster than me, pointing at the whiteboard each time. I can't say whether he was calm inside, but he stopped sighing at his laptop.

Give me the gist of this account in three sentences.

Santosh was given ten days to learn a data tool, so he wrote four jobs on the whiteboard: load, filter, group, summarise. He said every lesson is then just one of those four jobs. By day three he was learning faster than Hrithik and had stopped sighing at his laptop.

It was the last week of Ramadan and the week of Zainab's pre-board exams. At four a.m., Ammi woke her for sehri as always, and Zainab, sixteen, sat at the table half asleep, eating dates for a fast she no longer believed in.
She'd felt it for a year: the prayers were words she knew by heart but no longer felt. She had told only her friend Elizabeth, who just listened.
That morning, Ammi said, "You look so tired. Is the fast too much with exams?"
Instead of just saying yes, Zainab said quietly, "Ammi, it's not just the exams. I don't feel it the way you do anymore. I don't want to lie to you."
Ammi's hand stopped on the teapot. Her eyes filled.
"I still want to sit with you at sehri," Zainab added. "Every morning. I love this time with you."
After a long moment, Ammi poured her tea. "Then sit," she said softly.

Whom had Zainab told about her doubts?
She had told only her friend Elizabeth.
What was Zainab afraid of before she spoke?
Zainab was afraid of hurting Ammi, which is why she had kept her doubt hidden for a year.
What made Zainab's words respectful?
She spoke quietly and honestly without criticising the faith, and she offered to keep sitting with Ammi at sehri, showing her love continued.
How was Ammi affected by Zainab's words?
Ammi was shocked and hurt, her hand stopping and her eyes filling, but she chose to keep Zainab close, softly telling her to sit.

In the boys' hostel, a clip of Tarun singing off-key at the hostel night was going round the student page. The comments were brutal and funny.
Tenzin, in his room, laughed out loud. He had a spare account with no name and no photo. He typed, “Somebody call a vet, a cat is dying,” and hit post. Within an hour it was the top comment.
He felt nothing much. There were three hundred comments. His was just one.
At dinner in the mess, Tarun sat alone at the end of the table, eating fast, not looking at anyone. Somebody behind Tenzin whispered, “Vet! Vet!” and a few boys laughed. Tarun's ears went red.
Tenzin stopped chewing. His comment was sitting at the table with them.

What did Tenzin's comment say?
It said, "Somebody call a vet, a cat is dying."
How did Tenzin feel when he posted the comment?
He felt amused and careless, as if one comment among three hundred didn't matter.
What could Tenzin do after dinner?
He could delete the comment, apologise to Tarun, and stop others repeating the "vet" joke.
How might Tarun have felt when the boys whispered "Vet!"?
Tarun likely felt humiliated and alone, ears going red as the online joke followed him into the mess.

Imran, come, sit. You fought with your sister again? Your Usha aunty was nine once, you know, and my little sister Leela and I quarrelled every single day. One morning she cut my red ribbon to make a doll's scarf. I screamed and told her she was no sister of mine. That same evening, at the village pump, two older boys splashed her and pulled her plait until she cried. I didn't think at all. I marched over with my bucket and said, "Touch her again and I'll tell the whole school, and your mothers." My knees were knocking. They went. Leela held my hand all the way home, ribbon forgotten. That is how it is, beta. You can be angry with your own and still stand in front of them.

What did Leela cut to make a doll's scarf?
Leela cut Usha's red ribbon to make a doll's scarf.
How did young Usha feel as she marched over to the boys, and how can you tell?
She was scared, since her knees were knocking, but her anger at the boys for hurting Leela was stronger than the morning's grudge.
What choice in the story might Imran carry into quarrels at home?
Imran might decide that a fight at home is no reason to leave a sister alone when someone outside picks on her.
What might Leela have felt, holding Usha's hand all the way home?
Leela probably felt safe and forgiven, knowing her sister would protect her even after the ribbon fight.

At midnight in his room in Mexico City, Alejandro was still scrolling a photo app. Boys his age on beaches, with sharp jawlines and hundreds of likes. His own post from the morning had eleven. He deleted it.
He checked again at breakfast. Nothing new. His chest felt heavy all day.
On Saturday his friend Kofi turned up with a bag of spanners. "The bike, remember? You promised."
They spent the afternoon fixing the old bicycle in the courtyard, hands black with grease. Kofi's little brother cheered when the chain finally caught.
That evening Alejandro rode it round the block twice. He didn't take a single photo. He noticed, falling asleep, that he hadn't opened the app all day, and that the day had felt good anyway.

How many likes did Alejandro's morning post have?
Eleven.
How did Alejandro feel after deleting his post?
He felt behind and low; his chest felt heavy all day and he kept checking for likes.
What gave Alejandro firmer ground than likes?
Fixing the bike with Kofi and riding it gave him a real achievement and friendship, which felt good without being posted.
How might Kofi see that Saturday?
To Kofi it was just keeping a promise and having fun fixing the bike; he may not know how much the afternoon lifted Alejandro.

In the school library, Kavitha had been pretending to read the same page for twenty minutes. Two tables away, the senior who ran the astronomy club was sorting slides for his talk.
Her friend Tenzin whispered, "You're doing it again."
"Doing what?"
"Staring. You joined astronomy club for him. You don't even like stars."
"I like stars now." Kavitha's cheeks burned. "He said Jupiter has ninety moons like it was poetry."
"He reads that off a slide, Kavi."
She knew it was silly. She had drawn his handwriting in her rough book, planned what she'd say if he ever asked her a question, and imagined whole conversations on the walk home.
When he looked up and smiled at the whole table, her heart hammered for the entire next period.

What did the senior say about Jupiter?
That Jupiter has ninety moons, like it was poetry.
How did Kavitha feel when Tenzin said she was staring?
She felt embarrassed and flustered; her cheeks burned.
How could Tenzin support Kavitha kindly?
Tenzin could tease gently but also encourage her to enjoy the club for its own sake, not only for the senior.
How might the senior see the situation, if at all?
He probably has no idea; to him Kavitha may be just another club member at the table.

On the last Friday of the quarter, Daniel sat alone in the Stockholm office, looking at one cell in the sales report. His team was a little short of target. If one client's order went in today instead of next week, the number would turn green. That morning Anders, his manager, had said, "We can't miss again."
It's borrowing, Daniel told himself. The order is real. It's only a few days early. I'll fix it next quarter. Everyone smooths the edges a little.
He typed the date. The cell turned green. He felt a small lift of relief, then a queasy weight, like a stone in his pocket.
At dinner he laughed a little too loudly at his partner's story. Later he lay awake, working out how next quarter would now need to be even better, to cover this one.

What did Anders say that morning?
'We can't miss again.'
What did Daniel feel after the cell turned green?
Daniel felt a small lift of relief, then a queasy weight like a stone in his pocket, the start of guilt.
What could Daniel do on Monday before it grows?
Put the date back and tell Anders the team is short, accepting a missed target now instead of a bigger gap next quarter.
How might Anders see the green number?
Anders would see the target met and relax, not knowing the number was borrowed, which makes the pressure worse next quarter.

Monday: At lunch, Baljeet's group was mocking the new boy's accent. Lokesh didn't find it funny; his own cousin talked just like that. He laughed anyway, loudest of all, and checked Baljeet's face to see if it had been enough.
Wednesday: The group decided the school play was 'for losers'. Lokesh had secretly signed up. When Baljeet asked, 'You're not doing that, right?' he said, 'Obviously not,' and crossed his name off the list after school. His stomach hurt all evening.
Saturday: At the cricket ground, Baljeet made another joke about the new boy, Aniket, who was fielding nearby. Lokesh laughed on cue. Then he saw Aniket's face. Lokesh stopped laughing. He didn't say anything. But he didn't laugh again, and he noticed he could breathe a little easier.

What did Lokesh cross off after school on Wednesday?
His name, from the school play list.
Why did Lokesh laugh loudest at a joke he didn't find funny?
He feared being left out of Baljeet's group; laughing loudly and checking Baljeet's face was a way to prove he belonged, even against his own feelings.
What was the small turning point on Saturday, and what could Lokesh do next?
Seeing Aniket's face and stopping laughing; next, Lokesh could put his name back on the play list or quietly say hello to Aniket, choosing his own view over the group's.
What might Aniket notice when Lokesh stops laughing?
Aniket may notice that at least one person in the group isn't joining in, a small sign that he isn't completely alone.

I'm Swati, and this is about my friends and me, so don't judge too hard.
There are five of us in the flat. Last month Neha from next door skipped the shared cleaning rota twice, and Sarika said, "Typical. She's so entitled." Everyone agreed. Two weeks later Sarika skipped it three times because of her internship, and the verdict was, "Poor thing, she's swamped." I agreed both times. That's the bit that bugged me.
So one night over instant noodles I said, not accusing, just curious, "Funny, when Neha skipped, she was entitled, and when Sarika skipped, she was busy. Maybe Neha was busy too?"
There was a pause. Sarika went a bit red and said, "Okay. Fair." Then Divya said, "I do this with my brother all the time."
Nobody fought. The next week, someone invited Neha over for chai.

How many times did Sarika skip the rota?
Three times, because of her internship.
What was Swati feeling in the days before speaking up?
Swati felt uneasy and a bit guilty, having agreed with two opposite verdicts on the same behaviour.
Why did Swati's way of raising it work?
It was framed as a curious question, "Maybe Neha was busy too?", so nobody felt accused and they could see the pattern themselves.
How might Sarika have felt when Swati pointed out the pattern?
Sarika seemed embarrassed, going a bit red, but not attacked, so she could admit "Okay. Fair."

In the school garden, Elizabeth and Kiran, both five, had one job: water the marigolds.
Kiran spotted a line of ants near the tap. He lifted his foot.
“Don't!” said Elizabeth. “They're going home.”
Kiran put his foot down beside them. He crouched. “Where's their home?”
They followed the line to a crack in the wall.
“Their house,” said Kiran. Then he watered the marigolds, carefully avoiding the ants.

What was the children's job in the school garden?
To water the marigolds.
How did Kiran feel when he crouched to watch the ants?
He felt curious and interested instead of wanting to squash them.
How could a teacher build on this moment?
A teacher could praise Elizabeth for speaking up and let the children watch the ants and talk about where they live.
How might Elizabeth feel when Kiran avoids the ants?
She probably feels happy and proud that the ants are safe.

Library period started with the children in a circle on the mat. The librarian said each one could choose a book in turn. Yash, five, jumped up and grabbed the dinosaur book from the shelf. "Mine first!" When she asked him to sit, he threw himself down, shouting, "No! No circle!" Sahil sat cross-legged, waiting, hands in his lap, though his eyes stayed on the dinosaurs. The librarian knelt by Yash and spoke softly. After a minute Yash put the book back on the shelf and sat, still sulking, beside Sahil.

Which book did Yash grab?
He grabbed the dinosaur book.
What might Sahil have been thinking while his eyes stayed on the dinosaurs?
He probably wanted the dinosaur book too but waited patiently, hopeful that his turn would come.
What went well in how the librarian handled Yash?
She knelt and spoke softly instead of shouting, which helped him calm down and rejoin the circle.
If you were Sahil, what would you want the librarian to do?
Keep the turns fair so waiting pays off, perhaps letting him pick the dinosaur book when his turn comes.
What happens when the creature saves a girl from drowning?
A man who was with her snatches the girl away and shoots the creature. His kindness is rewarded with a painful wound.

Parul came back to school after chickenpox still weak and blotchy, and her classroom in the Mumbai school was on the fourth floor. Vasudha, eleven, met her at the gate every morning that week and carried her bag up all four flights, then her own.
"You don't have to," Parul said.
"You'd do it for me."
On Thursday the school magazine came out. There was a poem about a lonely pigeon on the water tank, signed only "Anonymous." Vasudha knew. Parul had shown it to her in the library, whispering, "Don't tell anyone. I'll die."
At lunch the whole table guessed. "Vasudha, you know, don't you? Your face says so!"
Vasudha bit into her chapati and shrugged. Under the table, Parul squeezed her hand.

What was the poem in the school magazine about?
A lonely pigeon on the water tank.
What was Vasudha feeling when the whole table pressed her at lunch?
She felt the pressure and some nerves, since they said her face gave it away, but she held firm with a shrug to protect Parul's trust.
What choice did Vasudha make at lunch, and what did it show Parul?
She stayed quiet instead of revealing the poem's author, showing Parul that her trust was safe.
What does Parul's hand squeeze suggest about how she sees Vasudha?
It suggests Parul feels grateful and close to her, seeing Vasudha as a loyal friend who carried her bag and kept her secret.

"But does it not show great weakness?" pursued she. "I'm not envious: I never feel hurt at the brightness of Isabella's yellow hair and the whiteness of her skin, at her dainty elegance, and the fondness all the family exhibit for her. Even you, Nelly, if we have a dispute sometimes, you back Isabella at once; and I yield like a foolish mother: I call her a darling, and flatter her into a good temper. It pleases her brother to see us cordial, and that pleases me. But they are very much alike: they are spoiled children, and fancy the world was made for their accommodation; and though I humour both, I think a smart chastisement might improve them all the same."

A woman says she is not jealous of Isabella, whom the family favours, and gives in to Isabella and her brother to keep the peace. She still thinks they are spoiled and would benefit from a firm scolding.

Dear Diary,
Today I learned to swim! At first I was scared and held the edge of the pool tightly. My coach said, "Just kick and breathe." I took a deep breath and let go. My arms were tired, but I kept going. By the end of the class, I swam one full length of the pool. I felt so proud!

Dear colleagues,

Supervisor's note, quarterly review. Kiran had committed, in front of the whole team in January, to leading the new warehouse app. Last week Kiran came to me and said, plainly, "I want to change my decision. I agreed before we knew the vendor would drop support. With what we know now, a paper-and-scanner system is better for us." There was no drama and no long excuses. Kiran then explained the change to the team in five minutes, including what had been wrong in the earlier plan. Neelam, who'd been worried about losing face for the team, said afterwards that it made her respect Kiran more. What I did next: I asked Kiran to write a short note on how we decide big changes.

What did Kiran commit to leading in January?
The new warehouse app.
How did Neelam feel after Kiran explained the change?
Neelam went from worried about losing face to respecting Kiran more.
What made Kiran's change of course graceful?
Kiran accepted the old decision was made with less information and explained the change plainly without drama or excuses.
What might Kiran have been feeling when coming to the supervisor?
Kiran may have felt a little nervous but clear-headed and confident about the new information.

Salma and Elizabeth had run neighbouring counters at a food court in Kolkata since they were eighteen, Salma at the rolls stall, Elizabeth at the juice bar. Four years of small deals: Elizabeth watched the rolls when Salma went for prayers; Salma kept Elizabeth's cash box when she ran to the bank. Each favour was always returned. Then, one busy Saturday, a man asked Elizabeth where he could order food for a birthday party of sixty. Salma was on her break. Elizabeth could easily have said, "Try the stall at the other end." She remembered Rinku, who used to run the momo counter. He had once taken a big order that was meant for Salma, and after that nobody on the floor would cover for him. When Salma came back, Elizabeth handed her the man's number.

What did Salma do for Elizabeth when she ran to the bank?
Salma kept Elizabeth's cash box.
What was on Elizabeth's mind when she thought of Rinku?
She was remembering how one grab at Salma's order left Rinku without anyone to cover for him, and she did not want to lose Salma's trust the same way.
Which choice worked for Elizabeth, and why?
Passing the party order to Salma kept four years of trust intact, which is worth more to her in the long run than one order, since they will work side by side for years.
How might Salma feel when Elizabeth hands her the number?
Salma would likely feel grateful and more sure of being able to count on Elizabeth, making her even more willing to return the favour.

Since Asif's promotion at the district cooperative office, Karthik's replies had shrunk to single words, and at the tea stall Karthik kept looking at the road. Asif felt awkward and lonely. He had stopped talking about work, afraid of sounding proud, and the silence had made things stiffer.

One Sunday at the temple fair, Asif said, "I was scared of bragging, so I said nothing about the new job. It's just a bigger desk. How is the shop going?" Karthik shrugged, then said, "Slow. The wholesaler raised prices."

They talked for an hour by the ring-toss stall. "It's odd," Karthik said, "watching you move up while I'm still counting stock." Asif didn't defend himself. "That sounds hard. I'd feel it too." Karthik grinned a little.

Where did Asif and Karthik talk for an hour?
They talked by the ring-toss stall at the temple fair.
How does Asif feel about Karthik's coldness?
Awkward and lonely; Asif stopped talking about work for fear of sounding proud.
What worked in how Asif approached Karthik?
Asif shared briefly without bragging, asked about Karthik's shop, and listened without defending himself.
What might Karthik be feeling as Asif moves up?
Karthik seems to feel behind, counting stock while Asif advances, and may have pulled away because of that sting.
The editor asked me to "tone down" the language. What does that mean?

To "tone down" is to make something less strong, harsh or extreme.
Example: Please tone down your reply; it sounds angry.
I would like a 5-7-5 haiku on the clouds of the monsoon.

Grey clouds gather close
Drums of thunder call the rain
Dry fields start to sing

In the incubator office in Bengaluru, Aditi sat across from her mentor, Gopika, with the keys to her cloud kitchen in her hand. After fourteen months, she was closing it.
"I let down my two cooks," Aditi said. "My parents. The people who invested. Maybe I just don't have judgement."
Gopika didn't argue. "How long have you been sleeping badly?"
"Since March."
"Then take two weeks. Hand the keys back, do nothing, grieve it. It was real, and you lost it."
Aditi's eyes filled. She hadn't expected to be allowed to be sad.
"After that," Gopika said, "come back, and we'll write down five concrete lessons. Not 'I failed.' Things like: which dishes made money, what the rent did to us."
Two weeks later, Aditi came back. The list had eight lessons. Number three was: "I ignored the numbers in month four because I was scared." She read it aloud without crying.

How long had Aditi run the cloud kitchen?
After fourteen months, she was closing it.
How did Aditi feel when Gopika told her to grieve?
Aditi felt moved and relieved, her eyes filling, because she hadn't expected to be allowed to be sad.
What two steps did Gopika suggest, and why in that order?
First two weeks of rest and grieving, then writing concrete lessons, because Aditi could look at the numbers honestly only once the rawness had eased.
How might Aditi's two cooks see the closure?
The cooks were probably disappointed and worried about their jobs, which is part of why Aditi feels she let them down.

When I was in Class 5, the school bell was my enemy. It rang, and I'd be digging for my diary or my geometry box while everyone else was ready. One evening I sat on my bed and thought it through. The digging wasn't the real problem. The real problem was that my things lived in a different place every day. So I made a rule. Geometry box, front pocket. Diary, back pocket. Always, even when I'm tired. It felt silly for a week. Then one day the bell rang and my hand went to the front pocket without me thinking. My sister Jyoti noticed and said, 'Santosh bhai, since when are you so organised?'

Where does Santosh keep his geometry box?
In the front pocket.
How did Santosh feel about the bell before his rule?
Santosh called it an enemy, so he felt stressed and flustered, always digging while others were ready.
What part of Santosh's thinking made the rule work?
Seeing that the real problem was things living in different places, then keeping one place 'even when I'm tired' until it became automatic.
How does Jyoti see the change?
Jyoti is surprised and a little amused, asking since when Santosh became so organised.

On library day in the Cardiff school, Daniel always chose the thickest dinosaur book, then pushed it to the back of his cubby. The words swam. He mixed up "was" and "saw" and lost his place every line. But in the maker corner he built a working drawbridge from craft sticks and string before anyone else had finished their plan. Ms. Mina, the reading specialist, found the dinosaur book behind his lunch box. She didn't scold. She sat beside him with a coloured reading strip. "You figured out that drawbridge with no instructions," she said. "That's a strong brain. Reading is just a different puzzle for it. Want to try one page together?" Daniel laid the strip under the first line. Slowly, he read about a stegosaurus.

What did Daniel build in the maker corner?
A working drawbridge from craft sticks and string.
Why might Daniel hide the dinosaur book in his cubby?
He seems embarrassed and worried because the words swim and he loses his place, so he hides that reading is hard.
What was the turning point when Ms. Mina found the hidden book?
She didn't scold; she pointed to his strength, offered a reading strip and read one page with him.
How might Ms. Mina see Daniel after the drawbridge and the hidden book?
Ms. Mina likely sees a bright, capable builder who finds reading hard, not a lazy child, and believes one page together can help.

Looking back, I, Hemant, can see the pattern clearly, though at the time it felt like love.

It started with small things. Stay late after meditation to clean the hall. Then weekends. Then the teacher asked me to move my savings into the ashram's account, "to free you from worry." When I hesitated, a senior member told me my doubt was my ego talking, and that I shouldn't discuss ashram matters outside.

I stopped visiting home. My sister Sonali kept calling anyway. One evening she simply turned up at my room with dal and rice and said, "Bhaiya, you look exhausted. Just tell me what's happening."

I did, all of it, and hearing it out loud frightened me.

She sat with me while I called a family friend who was a lawyer. I stepped back the next week. The shame took longer to leave than I did. Sonali kept reminding me: they looked for sincere people, and I was sincere.

What did Sonali bring when she turned up at Hemant's room?
She brought dal and rice.
What did Hemant feel when he said everything out loud?
He felt frightened, and later deeply ashamed, even though at the time the group had felt like love.
Which choice helped Hemant most, and why?
Telling Sonali everything and calling a family friend who was a lawyer, because it broke the secrecy and brought in trusted family and outside counsel.
How does Sonali see what happened to her brother?
Sonali sees Hemant as a sincere person who was targeted, not a foolish one, and she worried enough to keep calling and turn up at his room.

Asif,
You start at my college next month, so here's the guide I wish I'd had.
Professor Rao looks strict but is the fairest marker in the department. If you're stuck, go to her office hours; she'll spend an hour on one doubt.
Don't lend your lab notes to Vicky in third year. He borrowed mine twice and returned them once, with tea on page six. That's not me being mean. It's what happened, and I've said it to his face.
You'll hear plenty of other stuff in the hostel: who's dating whom, whose family has money, why someone dropped a year. Most of it is rubbish and none of it helps you. When the talk goes there, I go and make tea.
My rule: if it keeps you safe or saves you time, and I know it's true, I'll tell you. If it's just for laughs, I won't.
See you on the 3rd. Bring a bucket.
Wasim bhai

Who is the fairest marker in the department?
Professor Rao is the fairest marker in the department.
How does Wasim seem to feel about the hostel gossip?
Wasim seems fed up and uncomfortable with it, preferring to go and make tea rather than join in.
What line does Wasim draw between useful talk and cruel gossip?
Share something only if it is true and keeps Asif safe or saves time; skip anything that's just for laughs.
How might Vicky feel if he read what Wasim wrote?
Vicky might feel embarrassed or annoyed, but since it's accurate and already said to his face, it reads as a fair warning, not a cruel story.

In the small town of Bijnor, Jasleen worked long days at her father's hardware shop. For years she'd wanted to write stories, but she told her friend Hafsa, 'When I have a laptop. When the shop is less busy. When I've saved enough for a course.' One afternoon in the slow hour after lunch, Hafsa slid a school notebook across the counter. 'Write one page. Now.' Jasleen laughed, then picked up a pencil and wrote about the old man who came every week to buy a single nail. The page filled fast. By evening she'd written three. The shop was the same, the money was the same, the laptop was still a dream. But the stories had started. She kept the notebook under the counter, next to the nail boxes.

What did Hafsa slide across the counter?
A school notebook.
How did Jasleen feel as the page filled?
Jasleen felt surprised and happy, the writing coming quickly after years of waiting.
What does Jasleen's afternoon show about starting to grow?
That she didn't need a laptop, a quiet shop or savings; a notebook and a slow hour were enough to begin.
How might Hafsa feel seeing Jasleen write three pages?
Hafsa would probably feel pleased and proud of pushing her friend to start.

In third-period literature at his school in Seville, Mateo's eraser was down to a grey stub. He had written the first line of his analysis four times and rubbed it out four times, and the paper was going thin.
When Señora Ruiz asked who could explain the poem's final image, Mateo knew the answer, or thought he did. He kept his hand flat on the desk. Fatima, beside him, answered instead, half right, and just laughed when the teacher corrected her. Mateo couldn't understand how she could laugh.
At break he checked his returned quiz: 9.5 out of 10, one accent missing on "también". His stomach turned over. He spent lunch in the toilets feeling sick, replaying the missing accent. It wasn't just an accent. It felt like proof that he wasn't as good as everyone thought.

What score did Mateo get on his returned quiz?
9.5 out of 10, with one accent missing on 'también'.
Why did one missing accent make Mateo feel sick?
Mateo is anxious that every task threatens his worth, so a tiny error felt like proof he wasn't as good as everyone thought.
What small step could help Mateo loosen this fear?
He could try answering once in class when he's fairly sure but not certain, and tell a teacher or parent how sick small mistakes make him feel.
How might Fatima see Mateo, given how differently she handles being corrected?
Fatima laughs off a half-right answer and may simply see Mateo as a quiet, clever classmate, unaware of how frightened he is of being wrong.

Abhinav was squeezed into the back seat of the Aizawl school bus, revising chemistry for the next day's test, when the class chat lit up. Lalremsiami had suggested the class do a clean-up drive instead of the usual picnic. The replies came fast: laughing faces, "Miss Environment," a picture of a broom with her name on it.
Abhinav watched. He thought her idea was good. But the bus was bumping, the test was tomorrow, and speaking up felt like painting a target on himself. He scrolled past.
Twenty more messages. Lalremsiami had gone quiet.
At the next stop, he stopped scrolling. He typed in the group: "Has anyone got the notes for chapter 4? Test tomorrow." The chat turned to notes.
Then, privately: "Your clean-up idea is better than a picnic. I'd join."
A minute later: "Thank you. I felt so stupid."

What had Lalremsiami suggested to the class?
Lalremsiami suggested the class do a clean-up drive instead of the usual picnic.
Why did Abhinav scroll past at first?
He was nervous that speaking up would paint a target on himself, and he was stressed about the next day's test.
What small steps did Abhinav take that helped?
He changed the topic in the group by asking for chapter 4 notes and sent Lalremsiami a private message backing her idea.
What was it like for Lalremsiami when the replies came in?
Lalremsiami felt stupid and humiliated as the jokes piled up, and she felt grateful and relieved when Abhinav wrote to her privately 🤍

At the end of this passage, why is the narrator taking out his purse at the end of this passage?

"He came faithfully, and he brought me the two one-pound notes. I was a poor boy then, as you know, and to a poor boy they were a little fortune. But, like you, I have done well since, and you must let me pay them back. You can put them to some other poor boy's use." I took out my purse.
He wants to pay back the two one-pound notes he once received as a poor boy. He has done well since and suggests the money can help another poor boy.

Only ten blocks were left before Sunaina, the teacher, rang the tidy-up bell. Pranav had built three towers and watched each one fall. Pranav sat back, thought, and said aloud, "If it wobbles, make the bottom wider." The fourth tower began with four blocks side by side. It leaned a little, so Pranav slid in a fifth beside them. That tower stayed standing when the bell rang.

How many blocks were left before the tidy-up bell?
Ten blocks were left before Sunaina rang the tidy-up bell.
What was Pranav feeling after three towers had fallen?
Pranav was thoughtful and a little frustrated, which led to sitting back and making a rule aloud.
What else could Pranav try if the tower still wobbles, and why?
Pranav could add a wider base and put the small blocks on the top, because a tower of heavy blocks low down is steadier.
How does Sunaina see the tower standing when the bell rang?
Sunaina, who is ringing the bell for tidy-up, sees a child who used a rule and is likely to be pleased that the fourth tower stood.

I share a room with Dhruv in the second-year hostel. I'm Pradeep. I can't say what goes on in his head, but I can say what I saw during his final-project month.

The first week he stopped coming to the mess. His light was on at three. He sat on his bed with his laptop and didn't talk much.

Then something changed. He stuck a paper on the wall: "Sleep 12. Breakfast 8. Walk 5." I teased him about it. He just shrugged. At five every evening he went out and walked two rounds of the football ground, even when he looked like he'd rather stay in bed. He came to breakfast with his hair still wet.

He didn't become cheerful. He still sighed at his code. But he spoke more. He laughed at dinner once.

Near the end he told me he'd booked a talk with the campus counsellor, just to check in. I thought that was sensible.

What did Dhruv write on the paper stuck to the wall?
"Sleep 12. Breakfast 8. Walk 5."
What did Pradeep feel when Dhruv started walking every evening?
Pradeep was a bit amused at first and teased him, then seemed quietly relieved as Dhruv spoke more and laughed at dinner.
What worked about Dhruv's paper on the wall?
It made sleep, breakfast and a walk into fixed times he could follow even without motivation, which kept his body steady.
How might Dhruv have experienced the month differently from how it looked to Pradeep?
Dhruv may have felt heavier inside than he showed, pushing himself to walk, which is why the counsellor check-in made sense.

In their village, Pooja, fifteen, was helping her father Kamal decide what to do about the yellowing cotton. "Use more fertilizer," the shopkeeper had said. Pooja frowned. "But Papa, it's rained for two weeks. The roots might be waterlogged. More fertilizer might wash into the canal. And the neighbour's field didn't turn yellow, and he has better drains." She sketched it in her notebook: rain, drains, roots, fertilizer, canal, arrows everywhere. Kamal looked at it for a long time. "So first we fix the drain." "And ask the agriculture officer," Pooja said. "Before we spend anything." Kamal folded the page and put it in his shirt pocket.

What had the shopkeeper told them to use?
More fertilizer.
What was Pooja thinking when she frowned at the shopkeeper's advice?
She was doubtful and uneasy, sensing that the problem involved more than just fertilizer.
Which choice made sense, and why?
Fixing the drain and asking the agriculture officer, because it addressed the whole system, not one part.
How might Kamal see his daughter's sketch?
With surprise and respect, seeing connections he hadn't put together.
Tabla looks hard. Where would a beginner start?
Find a teacher if you can, since hand position and sound production are hard to learn from a video alone. Begin with the basic strokes, or bols, such as na, tin and dha.
Do I need to buy a full set first?
Many beginners start with a basic pair, the smaller dayan and the larger bayan. A teacher can suggest what to buy and where.
How long before I can play a piece?
After a few months of regular practice, you may play simple patterns. Rhythm cycles like teental, with sixteen beats, are a common first goal.
Is it hard on the fingers?
At first the fingers can feel tender. Practise in short sessions and let your teacher check your technique, because a wrong hand position can make it harder.
How do I practise rhythm without the instrument?
Tap the beat on your knee and recite the bols aloud. This builds your timing and helps you remember the patterns.

In the college hostel in Indore, Navratri had begun, and Mehak woke at five each morning to pray before the small image of the goddess on her study table. She kept the nine-day fast her grandmother had kept, eating only fruit and sabudana.
Her roommate Rehana brought her a banana from the mess. "Isn't it hard, with exams?"
"A bit. But it makes me feel close to home. Nani's voice is in every prayer."
"Your friends say fasting is old-fashioned."
Mehak laughed. "Some of them. And I don't agree with every old custom. My family wanted me married by twenty-one; I said no. But this fast? This I choose."
In the evening Rehana helped her put flowers in front of the image. It felt, to both of them, peaceful.

What did Mehak eat during the fast?
She ate only fruit and sabudana.
How does Mehak feel while keeping the Navratri fast?
She feels close to home and calm, hearing her Nani's voice in every prayer, finding meaning in the ritual.
How does Mehak show that tradition and new ideas can sit together?
She keeps the fast she values but refused her family's wish for early marriage, choosing which customs to follow.
What is it like for Rehana to help with the flowers?
Rehana finds it peaceful and seems to respect Mehak's devotion, sharing the moment with her.

Three months after Disha reported the falsified lab-test certificates at the Pune construction firm, her name disappeared from the weekly project emails. Yogesh, her manager, started calling her "our little activist" in meetings. Her desk was moved next to the printer.
Some nights she sat on the balcony and wondered if she'd ruined her life for a few pieces of paper.
Then she opened a folder on her laptop called "Record". Every excluded email, every comment, dated. Her friend Ritu, a lawyer, said the retaliation was real, and gave her the number of the labour commissioner's office. On Sunday, her college friends came over with pav bhaji and let her talk for three hours.
On Monday Disha walked into the office, head up, and set her tea next to the printer. It had a cost. But she could still look at herself in the mirror.

What was Disha's folder called?
"Record".
What was Disha feeling on the balcony at night?
She felt discouraged and alone, wondering if she had ruined her life by reporting the certificates.
What steps helped Disha cope with the retaliation?
She kept dated records, got advice from a lawyer friend about the labour commissioner's office, and leaned on her friends.
How might Yogesh see Disha's report?
Yogesh seems to see her as a threat or a troublemaker, and his mocking "activist" label shows resentment rather than respect.
There have been 15 "Where's Waldo?" books published. Each book has 30 puzzles to find Waldo. The average person takes 3 minutes to find Waldo in a puzzle. How long would it take to find every Waldo?

There have been 450 puzzles because 15 x 30 = 450
It would take 1,350 minutes to find all the Waldo's because 450 x 3 = 1,350
The answer is 1350.

Gautam is twenty-four and runs a team of nine at the call centre. I've watched him closely. He does something unusual: at the end of each shift, he asks one agent, "What made today harder?" Leela told him that the new break schedule meant she missed her bus. He changed it the next day.

It suggests he feels curious and caring about his team, wanting to see the costs of his decisions.

He should keep asking agents what made the day harder, since it shows the costs of his decisions early.
How might Leela feel when the break schedule changes the next day?
Leela would likely feel heard and grateful that her problem was fixed so quickly.

After I lost my job last year, I started running. At first it helped. Then it became two runs a day, morning and night, even in the rain, even with my knee strapped. If I missed one, I felt sick with guilt, like I'd let something terrible in. My friend Lavanya noticed first. 'Alka, you ran to my birthday dinner and left early to run again.' I laughed it off. Then I skipped my cousin's wedding because it clashed with a long run. That night, alone in my flat, I realised the running wasn't helping me live any more. It was running my life. I was running from worry, from the empty days. I told Lavanya the truth, and she helped me find a counsellor. I still run. Three times a week now, and I'm learning to sit with the worry instead.

What did Alka skip because it clashed with a long run?
A cousin's wedding.
What did Alka feel on missing a run?
Alka felt sick with guilt, as if something terrible had been let in.

Honest reflection that night, telling Lavanya the truth and seeing a counsellor.
How might Lavanya have felt when Alka left the birthday dinner early to run?
Lavanya may have felt hurt and worried, sensing the running had become more than exercise.

Monday. Zaid told Farida everything in the college garden, before she had asked. She sat with her arms wrapped around her knees and said, "I can't say I forgive you. I don't know what I feel." He nodded and left her alone.

Saturday. On the hostel roof, Farida's friend Nandini passed her a cup of tea. "If you say yes now, is it because you want to, or because you're scared of being alone?" Farida looked at the water tank for a long time. "Scared," she said. "Mostly." Nandini didn't say anything. She just stayed.

Three weeks later. Zaid had answered every question honestly, even the ones that shamed him, and hadn't asked her to hurry. Farida told him, "I'm not there yet. Maybe I won't be. I'm not deciding to punish you. I'm just deciding slowly."

That night she slept the whole night.

Where did Zaid tell Farida everything?
He told her in the college garden.
What does Farida admit to Nandini about why she might say yes?
She admits she is mostly scared of being alone, which shows she does not want to forgive just to escape loneliness.
What made it easier for Farida to take her time over three weeks?
Zaid answered every question honestly, even the shaming ones, and did not ask her to hurry, while Nandini stayed with her without pushing.
How might Zaid feel when Farida says she may never be there?
He may feel worried and regretful, but he can see she is not punishing him, only giving herself honest time.

Mentor's note, week five. In group project meetings I have seen Indu correct Payal's English in front of everyone and roll her eyes when Payal spoke about her school in a small town. Payal has gone quiet and now sends her slides by message instead of presenting.

I asked Indu to stay after class. She was defensive at first: "I'm only being honest." When I asked what she was afraid of, she was silent, then said her first-semester marks were poor and everyone else seemed to speak better than her. It felt good, she admitted, to have someone she could look down on.

I did not scold her. I suggested she read Payal's slides properly before the next meeting. This week Indu asked Payal about her data, and I saw Payal present again. I will keep watching.

What did Payal start doing instead of presenting?
Sending her slides by message.
What did Indu's answer show about her feelings behind the eye-rolling?
Insecurity. Indu feared being behind and said it felt good to have someone to look down on.
How did the mentor help without lecturing?
They asked what Indu was afraid of, did not scold, and suggested reading Payal's slides properly.
How might Payal have felt in the meetings before this?
Embarrassed and small. Going quiet suggests Payal was avoiding more corrections in front of everyone.
