During the winter carnival week, the school library was the only quiet place left. Salma and Deepa watched the new boy, Siddharth, sketching in a corner with his hood up. "Bet time," Deepa whispered. "Which is more likely: he's an artist, or he's a shy artist who secretly writes poems?" "The second one, obviously," Salma said. "Look at him. The hood, the silence, the little notebook. It's a whole story." Deepa grinned. "But every shy poet-artist is also an artist. So the first one has to be at least as likely." Salma opened her mouth, closed it, then shook her head. "It still feels more true." Siddharth looked up, noticed them staring, and went back to his sketch of the library windows.

Where was Siddharth sketching?
In a corner of the school library, with his hood up.
Why does the detailed guess feel right to Salma?
The hood, the silence and the notebook fit together into a whole story, so Salma feels confident and pleased that it is more true, even though each detail makes it less likely.
How could Salma check a guess like this next time?
Salma could ask whether the detailed version is just one part of the simple one; if it is, the simple one can never be less likely.
How might Siddharth feel noticing them staring?
Siddharth may feel a little awkward and self-conscious, not knowing he has become the subject of a bet.

What did Arnab draw?
The river behind his house, with a boat and a tiny dog on the bank.
What was Irawati feeling during the prize announcement and on the walk home?
Irawati felt real joy for Arnab, clapping till the palms stung, and later a small pang of disappointment about the peacock.
What would you tell Irawati about having both feelings?
That it is normal to be happy for a friend and still wish you had won; the pang can even become a goal for next year's contest.
How did Arnab seem to take Irawati's loud clapping?
Arnab looked back and grinned, so the cheering likely made him feel proud and supported by a friend.

5 machines make 400 bottles in 4 hours. How many bottles do 3 machines make in 6 hours? 5 machines, 4 h -> 400 1 machine, 4 h -> 400 / 5 = 80 1 machine, 1 h -> 80 / 4 = 20 3 machines, 1 h -> 20 x 3 = 60 3 machines, 6 h -> 60 x 6 = 360

Answer: 360 bottles.

Two things change, so go to ONE machine for ONE hour. 5 machines in 4 hours: 400. 1 machine in 4 hours: 400 / 5 = 80. 1 machine in 1 hour: 80 / 4 = 20 bottles. Now build up: 3 machines in 1 hour: 3 x 20 = 60; 3 machines in 6 hours: 60 x 6 = 360. Both changes are direct here (more machines, more bottles; more hours, more bottles).

Dhritarashtra said, "How did those bulls among men, viz., that great bowman Drona, and Dhananjaya the son of Pandu, encounter each other in battle? The son of Pandu is ever dear to the wise son of Bharadwaja. The preceptor also is ever dear to Pritha's son, O Sanjaya. Both of those car-warriors delight in battle, and both of them are fierce like lions. How therefore, did Bharadwaja's son and Dhananjaya, both fighting with care encounter each other in battle?"

What does Dhritarashtra say about the bond between Drona and Dhananjaya?

The son of Pandu is always dear to the wise son of Bharadwaja, and the teacher is always dear to Pritha's son. Both delight in battle and are fierce as lions, so Dhritarashtra asks how they fought each other.

Last monsoon I found my grandfather's old valve radio in the storeroom, dead and covered in dust. I don't know why it grabbed me, but it did. For months I skipped cricket, spent my pocket money on second-hand parts from the electronics lane, and watched repair videos till my eyes burned. My friend Zainab said, "Nitin, you talk about capacitors the way other people talk about cricket scores." When the radio finally crackled into an old Hindi song one night in January, I actually cried a little. Looking back, it wasn't really about the radio. It was the feeling of caring about something so much that time disappeared. My marks dipped that term, and I had to fix that too. But now I repair radios for three neighbours, and I want to study electronics.

Where did Nitin find the old radio?
In the storeroom.
Why did Nitin cry a little when the radio played?
Months of intense effort had finally worked, and the moment meant a lot to Nitin.
What could Nitin do to keep this passion without the marks dipping again?
Nitin could set fixed repair hours around study time, perhaps with a parent or teacher helping to plan them.
How does Zainab seem to see Nitin's passion?
Zainab teases Nitin about it, but clearly noticed how deeply Nitin cared.

Day one: Hansa clicked a link about an unpaid electricity bill and entered her card details. Within minutes, eighteen thousand rupees was gone. She sat frozen on her bed in her Guwahati flat, face burning. How could she be so foolish? She told no one.
Day two: She almost didn't mention it. But at lunch, her colleague Jatin talked about his aunt who got scammed and recovered part of it by reporting fast. Hansa's stomach dropped. She excused herself, went to the stairwell, and called her bank's official helpline to block the card and dispute the payment. Then she filed a complaint on the national cybercrime portal, with the screenshot of the message and the transaction ID.
Three weeks later: The bank called: part of the money had been frozen and would be returned. Hansa told Jatin, then posted a short warning in her building's residents' group with a picture of the fake message. Four neighbours said they'd received the same one.

How much money was taken from Hansa's account?
Eighteen thousand rupees.
What was Hansa feeling on the first day?
She felt foolish and ashamed, her face burning, and told no one.
What did Hansa do once she stopped hiding the loss?
She called the bank's official helpline to block the card, filed a cybercrime complaint with the screenshot and transaction ID, and warned her neighbours.
How might Jatin feel when Hansa tells him what happened?
Jatin may feel glad his story helped, and sympathetic rather than judgmental about the scam.

Read this:

Dear Tanuja didi,
You always said I think in strange directions. Here's proof.
I'm studying economics but I spend my weekends at the farmers' market with Chacha. I noticed farmers throw away bruised tomatoes, while the chaat stalls buy expensive puree.
So I did something odd: I used what I learned in my supply chain class and what Chacha knows about ripening, and I made a plan to connect the two. The farmers sell bruised tomatoes cheap at noon, the stalls get them fresh.
We tried it last Sunday with three farmers and two stalls. Two farmers were delighted. One stall owner said it's too much bother.
I'm going to refine it. I've never felt so excited about economics.
Pradeep

What do the chaat stalls buy?
Expensive puree.
How does Pradeep feel about this project?
Pradeep feels excited and energised, more than ever about economics.
What could Pradeep do about the stall owner who found it too much bother?
Pradeep could ask what makes it a bother and adjust the plan, like fixed pickup times.
How might the farmers see the plan?
Two of them were delighted, likely relieved to earn from tomatoes they would have thrown away.

So, Kiran, the school radio thing asked, "Where do you see yourself in ten years?", right? And I said it straight into the mic: "I'm going to be a doctor." I've said it since I was seven, since Nani's operation, when the doctor held her hand before they took her in. At home they already call me Doctor Kalyani.
But then you asked me after, in the canteen, with Holi colour still stuck behind your ears: "Okay, what are you doing this month for it?" And I just stood there. I don't know which entrance exams. I haven't opened biology since the unit test. I got 54 in it. I don't know what I'm doing in March. I only know the white coat.
So that's what I've been chewing on all week. The dream is huge. The next step, I can't even see it.

What did Kalyani get in the biology unit test?
How did Kalyani feel when Kiran asked about this month?
Kalyani felt caught out and uneasy, just standing there, realising the big dream has no near steps behind it.
What could Kalyani do next?
Break the dream into this month's actions: find out which entrance exams matter, revise the biology unit, and ask a teacher or counsellor to help set weekly targets.
Why might Kiran have asked that question?
Kiran seems to take Kalyani's dream seriously and wanted to know if there was a plan behind it, perhaps hoping to help Kalyani take the first step.

I'm Tushar. Last summer I announced at dinner, “I'm going to practise cricket every single day and be the best bowler in the colony.” Everyone clapped. I practised on Monday. On Tuesday it rained. By Friday I'd forgotten. My uncle Kishore didn't tease me. He said, “Big plan, no steps. Try this: twenty balls at one stump, after school, Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Mark them on the calendar.” It sounded too small. But I did it. After a month I could hit the stump eight times out of twenty. I didn't become the best bowler in the colony. I did become better than I was.

How many balls did Kishore suggest Tushar bowl each time?
He suggested twenty balls at one stump.
How did Tushar feel when the family clapped at dinner?
Tushar felt proud and excited about the big plan.
Why did Kishore's plan work better than the first declaration?
It was small and specific, with a set number, set days and a calendar, so Tushar could actually keep it up.
How did Kishore react when the first plan fell apart?
Kishore didn't tease; he calmly pointed out the plan had no steps and offered a smaller one.

Sunday, late

Ojas did it again at his parents' anniversary lunch. When I said I'm thinking of doing a pottery course, he laughed and said to his cousins, "Omkar and his little hobbies. Next it'll be knitting." Everyone laughed. I laughed too, and then couldn't eat.

This happens a lot. The sneer, the sigh when I talk about work, the "you wouldn't understand". I've started checking my words before I speak in my own home. It's not my fault he does this. I have to keep writing that down so I believe it.

I almost shot back something cruel in the car. I know exactly what would hurt him. I didn't.

At home I said, calmly, "When you mock me in front of people, I shrink. I need you to stop. And I want us to see a counsellor." He said I was overreacting. I said, "Maybe. I'm still booking it." I booked it.

What course did Omkar say he was thinking of doing?
A pottery course.
What was Omkar feeling at the lunch, and how can you tell?
Omkar felt humiliated and small, laughing along but then unable to eat.
What did Omkar do instead of answering contempt with contempt?
Omkar held back a cruel reply, calmly named the pattern, asked Ojas to stop, and booked a counsellor even when Ojas called it overreacting.
How might Ojas see his own jokes?
Ojas seems to see them as harmless teasing, calling Omkar's hurt an overreaction, which is part of the pattern.

At midnight on Christmas Eve in Buenos Aires, the whole street went up onto the rooftops. Astrid, visiting her friend Valentina's family for the first time, had never had Christmas in summer. Everyone counted down, and when the church bells rang, fireworks burst over every building at once. Valentina's grandmother kissed Astrid on both cheeks as if she were one of her own. Neighbours on the next roof waved and shouted 'Feliz Navidad!' Astrid shouted it back, the only Spanish she knew, and they all cheered. She had felt shy all evening, but now she was hugging people she'd met an hour ago. Later, sticky with melted ice cream, she told Valentina, 'It felt like the whole city was one house.'

Where did the street go at midnight?
Up onto the rooftops.
How did Astrid's feelings change at midnight?
She went from shy all evening to joyful and at home, hugging people she had met an hour earlier.
What helped a shy visitor like Astrid feel included?
Warm welcomes like the grandmother's kisses and the neighbours cheering her Spanish; hosts can pull a newcomer into the shared moment.
How might Valentina's grandmother see Astrid?
She treats Astrid like one of her own, probably pleased to share the family's Christmas with a guest.

Read this:

Joseph, you think the Class 10 list is hard? Come, let your Anjali aunty tell you about your father at fifteen.
Babu had to learn the twenty-two fundamental duties for his civics exam. Every night he started at number one, and every night he fell asleep somewhere around eight. In the exam he wrote the first six perfectly, word for word, and then made up the rest. The teacher wrote "a strong start" in red.
And it wasn't only lists. When the new family moved in next door, the first thing he heard about the father was from the milkman: "That man shouts at his dog." For two years your father crossed the road to avoid him. Didn't matter that the man mended our gate for free, or brought us mangoes every summer.
Babu only changed his mind when that same man drove him to the hospital the night he broke his arm.

How many fundamental duties did Babu write perfectly in the exam?
The first six, word for word.
Why did Babu keep avoiding the neighbour for two years?
The first thing Babu heard, that the man shouted at his dog, set his whole picture of the man, so the free gate repair and the mangoes didn't change it.
What could young Babu have done differently with his long list?
He could have started his revision from different points on the list, such as the middle or the end, so the later duties got as much attention as the first ones.
How might the neighbour have felt when Babu crossed the road to avoid him?
The neighbour may have felt hurt or puzzled, since he kept being kind to the family, mending the gate and bringing mangoes, and still got avoided.

Read this:

Vidya, you asked why I'm doing flashcards now like a maniac. Okay, so. Last term, biology. I read the chapters in class, and every page felt so familiar. I told everyone, "Easy. I don't need to revise." I spent the week before exams playing cricket. My mother asked if her boy was ready. I said, "I know it all, Mummy." Then the exam. First question: name the parts of the human heart and their functions. I could see the diagram in the book. Clearly. But I couldn't write the names. I sat there, sweating, pen hovering. I realised I'd recognised the pages, not learned them. I got forty-one out of a hundred. Forty-one! So now I close the book and test myself. That's how Gurpreet learned the difference between seeing and knowing.

What did Gurpreet score in the biology exam?
Forty-one out of a hundred.
Why did Gurpreet feel so sure before the exam?
The pages felt familiar, so Gurpreet felt confident and relaxed, mistaking recognising them for knowing them.
What changed in how Gurpreet studies now, and why does it help?
Gurpreet now closes the book and tests with flashcards, which checks real recall instead of the feeling of familiarity.
How might Gurpreet's mother have felt seeing the forty-one?
She might have felt disappointed and concerned, remembering Gurpreet saying 'I know it all'.
The classroom was so quite that you could hear the clock. Is "quite" the right word?

The classroom was so quiet that you could hear the clock.
Why: "Quiet" means silent; "quite" means fairly.
After the holidays the teacher said, "Back to the grindstone!" What does that mean?

It means to return to hard work, usually after a break.
Example: The festival is over, so it is back to the grindstone for everyone.

When I moved to Melbourne at twenty-four, I thought the hard part would be the job. It wasn't. It was Sundays.
I'm Mehak. The first months were wonderful: the trams, the ocean, the feeling of being unknown. Then winter came, and I realised I hadn't spoken to anyone outside work in two weeks. I video-called my mother every day, but hung up feeling worse, because home looked warm and I wasn't there.
Then a colleague, Gurpreet, invited me to the gurdwara's Sunday langar near her suburb. I'm not Sikh, but she said, "Nobody asks. Just come and help cut onions." I went. I cut onions for three hours and laughed more than I had in months.
Looking back, I needed both: the calls home, and the onions here. One kept me rooted. The other let me grow.

Where did Gurpreet invite Mehak?
Gurpreet invited her to the gurdwara's Sunday langar near her suburb.
How did Mehak feel after the daily video calls?
Mehak felt lonely and homesick, hanging up feeling worse because home looked warm and Mehak wasn't there.
What helped Mehak build a steadier life abroad?
Joining Gurpreet at the langar gave Mehak local friendships and laughter, while calls home kept her rooted.
How might Gurpreet see her invitation?
Gurpreet probably saw it as a simple kindness, noticing a lonely colleague and welcoming her without any questions.

On the first Sunday of every month, Tenzin's small Mumbai flat filled with people far from home: Jasleen from Ludhiana, a colleague from Guwahati, two students from Kochi. Each brought something: Jasleen's parathas, Tenzin's momos, a pot of fish curry. Nobody was related, and nobody had to explain a pause before a word in a mother tongue. Jasleen taught a Punjabi phrase for eat more and everyone tried it. Last month, when Tenzin's grandmother was unwell in Gangtok and Tenzin sat silent, Jasleen simply refilled the tea and stayed until midnight. Nothing was said about it. The next month a small brass bell appeared on the shelf, brought by whoever felt like it.

How often does the group meet?
The group meets on the first Sunday of every month.
What was Tenzin feeling while sitting silent, and how did Jasleen's action help?
Worried and alone; Jasleen's staying and refilling the tea eased the loneliness.
What makes this circle work?
Shared time and small kindnesses, like a potluck and phrases from each language.
Why might Jasleen have said nothing about staying until midnight?
Because the kindness needed no words; staying was enough to show care.

"Trisha, you look terrible."
"Kunal, I slept at three."
"Three? Why?"
"The show. Episode six ended with the sister getting into a stranger's car. How could I sleep?"
"So you watched seven?"
"And eight. Eight ended with a phone ringing and nobody answering."
"And nine?"
"Nine ended with a letter. I didn't open... I mean, they didn't show it."
"Trisha, you have a test today."
"I know. But every time I tried to sleep, my brain kept asking, what's in the letter?"
"Want to know a trick? Stop in the middle of an episode, not the end."
"...That's evil. And smart."

What time did Trisha sleep?
Trisha slept at three.
Why couldn't Trisha sleep after episode six?
Trisha felt restless and curious, with the unfinished story pulling at the mind.
What trick does Kunal suggest, and why might it work?
Stopping in the middle of an episode, because there's no open cliffhanger nagging when you stop.
How does Kunal seem to see Trisha's night?
Kunal is amused and a little worried, since Trisha has a test today.

The rainy season is here, Jan collected 65 gallons of water in a barrel outside her home. She uses 7 gallons of water each to clean the two cars and uses 11 fewer gallons than the two cars to water the plants. Then, she uses half of the remaining gallons of water to wash the plates and clothes. How many gallons of water does Jan use to wash her plates and clothes?

She uses 7 x 2 = 14 gallons of water to clean the two cars.
She uses 14 - 11 = 3 gallons of water to water the plants.
The total gallons of water that she uses to clean the cars and to water the plants is 14 + 3 = 17.
Jan has 65 - 17 = 48 gallons of water remaining after cleaning the cars and watering the plants.
Jan uses 48 / 2 = 24 gallons of water to wash her plates and clothes.
The answer is 24.

PE teacher's note, inter-school athletics meet, Saturday.
During the 800-metre race, a runner from another school collapsed near the stands. Within seconds, about thirty students crowded around. I saw Uday, one of our Class 10 boys, standing at the front with his phone in his hand, looking at the runner. Nobody was calling. Later he told me, "I thought someone must have already called." I pushed through, knelt by the runner and pointed at him: "Uday, you. Call 108 now. Tell them the school ground on Ring Road." He dialled at once. I asked Manjula ma'am to clear the crowd. The ambulance came in twelve minutes. On Monday I will talk to the class about why naming one person matters.

How many students crowded around the runner?
About thirty students crowded around.
What was Uday thinking while he stood with his phone?
He assumed someone must have already called, so he felt no push to act and stood frozen, unsure.
Why did the teacher point at Uday by name?
Naming one person broke the shared assumption that someone else would call, so Uday dialled at once.
How might the collapsed runner have been affected if no one had been named?
Help might have come much later, since everyone in the crowd assumed someone else had already called.
My room feels dark even in the daytime, and I'd like to brighten it without spending much.
Light-coloured curtains that let sunlight through make a big difference. Do you have a window that faces the sun?
Yes, but the curtain is heavy and dark.
Try a thin, light curtain, or just tie the heavy one back during the day. Keep the area near the window free of tall furniture. A mirror on the wall opposite the window also bounces light around.

While you are here,
Mateo has 18 marbles and a friend gives 18 more. How many marbles does Mateo have now?
A friend keeps arriving late. What should I tell them?
Why do children play in groups?

1. 36 marbles. Because 18 + 18 = 36.
2. Tell them calmly that waiting bothers you. Then agree on a meeting time that suits you both.
3. Games are more fun together. Because friends can share ideas and take turns.
Petrol pump pe bolna hai "Full tank kar do." English mein?
You can say: "Fill the tank, please." Or just: "Full tank, please." Both are fine.
Aur "Bas yahan utaar do" cab driver ko?
Say: "Please drop me here." It is polite and short.

At a mall in Delhi, Jasleen and her friend Charu were sharing fries when a toddler in a yellow dress started crying near the escalator, alone. Shoppers streamed past. Jasleen half rose. Then she thought: what if the mother is just around the corner, and I look silly, like I am making a scene? "Someone will come," said Charu, checking her phone. Two minutes passed, then five. The toddler's cries grew hoarse. A guard finally noticed and lifted the child, and a woman ran up, gasping. Jasleen sat back down with her cheeks hot, and the fries tasted like paper.

Where was the toddler when crying alone?
The toddler was crying alone near the escalator.
Why did Jasleen only half rise and then sit down?
Jasleen feared looking silly for making a scene if the mother was near; embarrassment outweighed the child's need, and afterwards Jasleen felt guilt.
What small step could Jasleen take next time without making a scene?
Jasleen could walk over, stay beside the child and quietly tell the nearest guard, a small helpful action even if the parent turns out to be near.
What might Charu have been thinking when saying "Someone will come"?
Charu probably assumed the child would be noticed by the many people passing and did not want to overreact; the phone gave a way to avoid deciding.

In Osaka, Jin, ten, had been quiet all through dinner. His sister Yuki noticed he kept checking his tablet.
After dinner she sat beside him. “What's wrong?”
He showed her. In his game chat, someone had been sending him messages for three days: You're useless. Give me your password or I'll tell everyone you cheated.
“I didn't cheat,” Jin whispered. His eyes were wet.
“Come on,” said Yuki. “We're telling Papa. Now.”
Their father read the messages slowly. “Thank you for showing me, Jin. You haven't done anything wrong.”
That night they took screenshots, blocked the account, reported it to the game, and changed Jin's password together. Papa also turned off chat with strangers.

What did the person demand from Jin?
His password.
How was Jin feeling about the messages?
He felt upset and frightened, his eyes wet, especially about being falsely accused of cheating.
What steps did Jin's family take that night, and why were they wise?
They took screenshots, blocked and reported the account, changed the password and turned off stranger chat, which stopped the pressure and kept evidence.
How did Yuki help her brother?
She noticed he was quiet, asked what was wrong and made sure they told their father straight away.

"Kya tumne apna kaam khatam kar liya?" English mein?
It is: "Have you finished your work?" In casual talk, "Did you finish your work?" is also fine.
Daybreak means what?

Daybreak is the time early in the morning when light first appears. It is a noun, and it means the same as dawn.
Example: The fishermen set out at daybreak and returned before noon.
What does a weather vane show? Answer in under ten words and include "wind".
It shows which way the wind is blowing.

The open-plan office in Warsaw was in the middle of the morning rush, and Olga had headphones on, finishing a report. Across the room, Ines came in with her bag and coat, walked past the coffee machine and caught Olga's eye. Ines's eyebrows lifted briefly and she gave a tiny smile. Olga raised hers back, then pulled off one earphone and called, "Morning! Coffee later?" Ines gave a thumbs-up. Olga remembered the day last week when a new colleague had lifted his brows at her and she had missed it entirely, so he had looked hurt at lunch. Now she made a point of looking up. The eyebrow greeting was a small thing, but it helped the day begin gently.

In which city was the office?
The office was in Warsaw.
What did Ines's raised eyebrows show, and how did Olga feel?
They showed recognition and friendliness, and Olga seemed pleased, raising her own brows and calling out an invitation to coffee.
What could Olga do to avoid missing such small signals?
She could look up now and then and answer with a word or gesture, as she now tries to do.
How might the new colleague have felt when Olga missed his eyebrow greeting?
He looked hurt at lunch, so he may have felt overlooked, though Olga hadn't meant to ignore him.
Explain what causes tides in two sentences, and use the word "moon" in the first one.
Tides are caused mainly by the pull of the moon's gravity on the oceans. The sun adds a smaller pull, so the highest and lowest tides change through the month.

Outside the community centre's office, Pankaj sat on a plastic chair with his file on his knees, bouncing one leg. It was his first real interview, for a summer helper job at the children's library. His heart was hammering so hard he could feel it in his ears. Rehana, a college volunteer who ran the reading hour, sat down beside him with a cup of chai. "Nervous?" "Very. Also I really want it. Is that weird? Both at once?" "Not weird at all. Here's a trick I use before exams. Scared and excited feel almost the same in the body, same fast heart. So say it out loud: I'm excited." Pankaj laughed. "That's silly." "Try it." "I'm... excited." He said it again, a bit louder. His leg slowed. The heart kept racing, but it felt less like a warning and more like a drumroll. When the door opened and the librarian called his name, he stood up and said, "Ready."

What job was Pankaj interviewing for?
A summer helper job at the children's library.
What was Pankaj feeling as he bounced his leg?
Pankaj felt nervous and eager at once, heart hammering; the same racing heart carried both worry about the interview and wanting the job badly.
How did Rehana's trick help?
Naming the racing heart as excitement turned the nervous energy into readiness, so his leg slowed and it felt like a drumroll instead of a warning.
Why might Rehana understand the mix so well?
Rehana had used the same trick before exams, so she recognised the blend of nerves and eagerness and treated it as normal, not weird.

Say: "My greatest strengths are hard work and honesty."

The science-fair project was due at nine the next morning, and Rashmi's only partner was Chinmay, the boy who had told the class about her diary last term. Every time he spoke on the group call she felt the old heat rise in her face. Forgiving him would mean it hadn't mattered, she thought, and it had mattered a lot. The wifi kept dropping.
At eleven at night he sent, "I'm sorry about the diary. I know it was a rotten thing."
She stared at it. Then she wrote, "It was. I'm not ready to be friends. Send me slide four."
"Okay," he wrote.
She felt strange: still angry, but the grip had loosened by one finger. They finished at midnight.

What was due at nine the next morning?
The science-fair project was due at nine.
What was Rashmi feeling whenever Chinmay spoke on the call?
Rashmi felt hot with old anger and hurt, since forgiving him seemed to mean the harm had not mattered.
What choice did Rashmi make at eleven that let the project move forward?
Rashmi answered that it was a rotten thing, said she was not ready to be friends and asked for slide four. She worked with him without pretending it was fine.
What might Chinmay have been feeling when he sent the apology?
Chinmay was probably guilty and nervous, hoping for a reply. Sending the apology so late suggests he had been working up to it.

Friday: The school's bridge challenge said one metre long, ice-cream sticks and glue only, due in three weeks. Sahil had three hundred sticks, and his friend Nilesh wanted to start the full bridge straight away. Sahil said, "Let's test a baby one first."
Sunday: They glued a short span, thirty centimetres, between two stacks of books. Sahil hung a plastic bag from the middle and dropped in coins one by one. At forty coins the middle cracked, while both ends stayed perfect. "It's the middle," Sahil said.
Next Saturday: The boys glued a triangle of sticks under the centre of a new span. It held a hundred coins. Only then did they start the full metre, with triangles all along the middle.

How long was the short test span?
Thirty centimetres.
What might Sahil have felt when the middle cracked at forty coins?
Disappointed for a moment, but also relieved that it happened on the small version.
What else could the boys test on a small span?
Different stick patterns or glue drying times, since a small version is quick and cheap to break.
How might Nilesh see the testing plan now?
He wanted to rush at first, but the cracked span shows him the test saved the full bridge.

Read this:

Monday: At sports hour Imran watched the others race. At pickup he asked his papa, Jeevan, "Why are my legs slow?"
Wednesday: Jeevan sat with him on the steps. "Your legs grew differently, so they tire faster. Nobody did anything wrong." Imran thought, then asked, "Will they get fast?" "Not fast. But strong in their own way."
Saturday: At the park Imran balanced on the kerb longer than his cousin and shouted, "Papa, look! I'm the best balancer!" Jeevan clapped hard.

What did Imran ask at pickup on Monday?
He asked, "Why are my legs slow?"
How was Imran feeling on Saturday at the park, and what shows it?
He felt proud and happy, shouting that he was the best balancer.
What did Jeevan's answer on Wednesday get right?
It was honest and simple, told Imran nobody was to blame, and pointed to his strength without promising what isn't true.
How might Jeevan have felt hearing Imran's first question?
Jeevan was probably a little sad and careful, wanting to answer truthfully without hurting Imran's pride.
In case it will rain, take an umbrella. Please check the verb.

In case it rains, take an umbrella.
Why: After "in case", use the present, not "will".

Read this:

The power had been out for two hours, Pooja's interview was at nine the next morning, and her phone was at nine percent because Yamini had borrowed the power bank and left it at the office. Again.

Pooja stood in the dark kitchen, heat rising in her chest. The old speech started in her head: Yamini is selfish, Yamini never thinks, why do I even live with her.

Then her phone torch lit the fridge door. Taped there was Yamini's list from last week: "Pooja's interview prep: 1. mock questions 2. iron the blue kurta 3. make her eat breakfast." Yamini had quizzed her for two evenings.

Pooja breathed out. Caring and careless. Same person. When Yamini came home at ten, Pooja said, "I'm upset about the power bank. I really needed it tonight." Yamini's face fell. "Oh no. Take my phone for the alarm."

Where did Yamini leave the power bank?
Yamini left the power bank at the office.
Why did Pooja feel her anger settle in the dark kitchen?
Seeing Yamini's interview-prep list reminded Pooja of the care alongside the carelessness, so the heat in her chest eased and she felt calmer.
What did Pooja do well when Yamini came home?
Pooja named the specific upset about the power bank without calling Yamini selfish, which let Yamini respond helpfully.
How might Yamini feel hearing Pooja's words?
Yamini seems sorry and eager to fix it, perhaps relieved that Pooja spoke calmly rather than exploding.

"Sunaina Ma'am, can I ask something about the project marks?"
"Of course, Eshaan."
"I'm not trying to get anyone in trouble. But could you see who did which parts?"
"Go on."
"I made the model. Ravi did the labels. Ankit and Gopal didn't bring anything."
"Are you upset about the marks?"
"A bit. I just think it should be fair."
"You're not asking for all the credit?"
"No. Ravi did a lot too."
"Thank you, Eshaan. I'll ask each of you to fill in a short form about your part."
Eshaan nodded. His hands had stopped shaking.

What did Eshaan make for the project?
The model.
How did Eshaan feel as he spoke to Sunaina Ma'am?
He felt nervous, his hands shaking, and a bit upset about the marks.
What made Eshaan's request fair rather than blaming?
He stated the facts calmly and made sure Ravi got credit too, instead of wanting it all for himself.
How might Sunaina Ma'am see Eshaan's request?
Sunaina Ma'am sees it as a fair question and decides to ask everyone to fill in a form.

First week of the new term: Uma asked Kavitha, her girlfriend, whether she was upset about not getting the scholarship. Kavitha said, "It's fine," and went for a run. Uma sat on the hostel steps, feeling shut out.
Two weeks later: They argued. "You never tell me anything!" Uma said. Kavitha looked at the floor. "I don't know how. It's like there are no words, just a tight throat." Uma stopped, surprised.
A month later: Kavitha handed Uma a note after a hard day: "Today = heavy. Like wet sand. Not about you." Uma read it twice and sat beside her. It wasn't a speech, but it was a door opening a crack.

What did Kavitha write on the note?
Kavitha wrote: "Today = heavy. Like wet sand. Not about you."
How did Uma feel when Kavitha said 'It's fine' and went for a run?
Uma felt shut out and hurt, sitting alone on the hostel steps, as if Kavitha didn't want to share anything with her.
What changed between the argument and the note, and what could help it keep going?
Uma learned it was difficulty with words, not coldness; they could keep using notes or simple images like 'wet sand' to share feelings.
How does Kavitha experience Uma's question 'You never tell me anything!'?
Kavitha seems ashamed and stuck, looking at the floor, because she wants to share but only feels a tight throat.

Read this:

Afreen: my manager presented my report to the directors today. didn't mention my name once 😠
Jagdish: WHAT. after you stayed till 11 all week??
Afreen: yes. i was ready to write her off completely. like she's just a credit-stealer, always has been
Jagdish: is she though?
Afreen: ugh. no. she's the one who fought for my leave when Abba was in hospital. she trained me for months
Afreen: so i'm trying to hold both. she's generous AND she was careless today
Jagdish: that's very grown up of you 🙂
Afreen: it's very annoying of me. but if i decide she's a villain i'll be miserable at work for a year
Jagdish: fair. so what now?
Afreen: i'll tell her tomorrow, calmly, that i'd like my name on the slides next time
Jagdish: and if she's weird about it?
Afreen: then that's a third fact. i'll deal with it 🙏

Who presented Afreen's report to the directors?
Afreen's manager.
Why was Afreen ready to 'write her off completely'?
Afreen felt angry and unseen after staying late all week, and in that moment the credit-taking seemed to be all the manager was.
What choice did Afreen make about tomorrow, and why is it a steady one?
To ask the manager calmly for Afreen's name on the slides next time, which raises the real problem without turning a generous person into a villain.
How might the manager react to Afreen's calm request?
She may feel embarrassed about the oversight and, given her past support, will likely fix it; being asked calmly makes that easier.

Read this:

Thursday.
Meeting today about which films to buy for the festival season. Tarun, our star buyer with fifteen years in the business, said with total certainty, "This one will be a hit. I can smell it." Everyone nodded. I've headed this department for ten years, and I used to trust my own nose too. But this week I went through our last forty picks. Tarun's "smell" was right about half the time, the same as a coin toss. He isn't careless; hits depend on so many things we never see that experience can't really sharpen the guess. So I asked, gently, if we could add audience-test numbers before deciding. He looked annoyed, then tired, then said, "Fine, show me, Kishore bhai." I felt relieved and nervous at once.
Kishore

How many past picks did Kishore go through?
Forty.
How did Kishore feel after asking for audience-test numbers?
Relieved and nervous at once: relieved that Tarun agreed, nervous about questioning a confident colleague's gut.
What did Kishore ask for, and why?
Audience-test numbers before deciding, because in a field with noisy feedback, experience alone hadn't made Tarun's guesses better than chance.
What might Tarun be feeling when he says "Fine, show me"?
He looked annoyed, then tired, perhaps a little shaken to learn that his certain "smell" was right only half the time.

Read this:

"Your cousin Sneha scored ninety-six in maths," said Aai, ladling dal. "Why can't you be like her?"
"Aai, please."
"I'm only saying."
Sarika put her spoon down. Later, on the terrace, she said to Masi, "When Aai says that, I feel like something's wrong with me. Like she only loves me at ninety-six."
"Does she?"
"I don't know. I know it feels like it."
"Then tell her that, the way you just told me."
"She'll say I'm being dramatic."
"Maybe. But you don't have to believe the comparison. What's your own goal?"
"Get science up first. Then maths."
"Good. Say that to her too."

What did Sneha score in maths?
She scored ninety-six in maths.
What does Sarika's remark that she feels like Aai only loves her at ninety-six say about how she feels?
She feels small and defective, as though her mother's love depends on marks, though she isn't sure if it's true.
What could Sarika do next after talking to Masi?
She could tell Aai how the comparison lands and share her own goals, science first, then maths, without treating the comparison as truth about her worth.
How might Aai see her remark about Sneha?
Probably as a push to do better, not realising it lands as a judgement on Sarika's worth.

Distil this piece into three sentences.

I quitted my seat, and walked on, although the darkness and storm increased every minute, and the thunder burst with a terrific crash over my head. It was echoed from Saleve, the Juras, and the Alps of Savoy; vivid flashes of lightning dazzled my eyes, illuminating the lake, making it appear like a vast sheet of fire; then for an instant every thing seemed of a pitchy darkness, until the eye recovered itself from the preceding flash. The storm, as is often the case in Switzerland, appeared at once in various parts of the heavens. The most violent storm hung exactly north of the town, over the part of the lake which lies between the promontory of Belrive and the village of Copet. Another storm enlightened Jura with faint flashes; and another darkened and sometimes disclosed the Mole, a peaked mountain to the east of the lake.

The narrator walks on through a dark storm, with thunder crashing overhead and echoing from the mountains. Lightning makes the lake look like a sheet of fire, then everything goes pitch dark until the eye recovers. As often in Switzerland, storms appear in several parts of the sky at once, the fiercest north of the town.

In Edinburgh, Freya had been paying for a meal-kit subscription since her first term. Every week a box arrived: three recipes, measured spices, a little card. She didn't much like the food, and it cost almost twice what she'd spend at the market. Alejandro, her flatmate, watched her leave half a box of vegetables to wilt again. "Why don't you cancel it?" "It's fine. It's easy," she said. "Is it? You never cook two of the three." Freya shrugged. "Cancelling means logging in, finding the page, answering their 'are you sure' questions. And then I'd have to plan meals." "So you're paying extra to avoid ten minutes." She opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. That evening she found the cancel page. It took seven minutes. On Saturday she and Alejandro walked to the market together, and she bought just what she wanted.

How long did it take Freya to cancel the subscription?
It took seven minutes.
Why did Freya say the subscription was "fine" even though she didn't like it?
Cancelling and planning meals felt like effort, so staying felt easier. She called it fine because change seemed like work, not because she was really happy.
What turned Freya's thinking around, and what did she do next?
Alejandro saying she was paying extra to avoid ten minutes. She found the cancel page that evening and went to the market on Saturday.
How might Alejandro feel walking to the market with Freya?
Alejandro might feel glad she made the change, and perhaps relieved to stop watching vegetables wilt in their shared fridge. 🙂

Monday. Sharmila lost a pencil at recess, and Tuesday a second one. Her deskmate Vaibhav shrugged. "You forget them everywhere." On Thursday the third pencil was gone, and Sharmila stared at her empty desk. She thought about where the three had gone. Each time she had put the pencil down for a moment, beside the water bottle or on a bench. That evening she told her mother, "The pencil case always goes in the front pocket of my bag." On the next Monday she had all her pencils, and she zipped the pocket after every use.

How many pencils did Sharmila lose in the week?
She lost three pencils.
What did Sharmila notice about how she lost her pencils, and how did she feel about it?
She noticed she had put each pencil down casually. She felt frustrated at first, then determined to fix it.
What else could Sharmila do to keep track of her pencils, and why?
She could write her name on each pencil, or count them at the end of the day. Then a lost one would be noticed sooner.
How does Vaibhav see the lost pencils?
Vaibhav thinks Sharmila just forgets things everywhere, as Vaibhav says. He does not yet see the pattern she found.

Friday night.
We missed the client deadline on the brochure by two days. Joseph had to call them and apologise. I felt awful all week.
Tonight I sat down to write it out instead of just feeling bad. The first page was a list of everything that went wrong. Too long. I could feel myself just wallowing.
So I made myself answer two questions.
Lesson: I didn't know the designer was stuck until Wednesday, because I only checked in on the due date.
Change: every project, a fifteen-minute check-in with the team on Monday of the final week. I've put it in my calendar for the next three projects already.
I sent the two lines to Joseph. He replied, "Good. I'll join the first one."
I'm Karthik, and I think I've spent years regretting things without changing anything. This feels different. Smaller, but real.

By how many days did they miss the brochure deadline?
By two days.
How did Karthik feel about the first page of the list?
Karthik felt like it was just wallowing, a long list of regret that changed nothing.
What makes Karthik's two lines more useful than the long list?
They name one lesson and one concrete change, a Monday check-in already put in the calendar, which will alter what happens next time.
How does Joseph respond to Karthik's two lines?
Joseph approves and supports it, saying he will join the first check-in.

metadata.subtype: Writing one lesson and one change [Response]

At home, Manoj talked in his Nani's Bhojpuri, full of jokes and funny words. At his new school in Delhi, he didn't say a single one. He copied how Siddharth and the other boys spoke, wore his socks pulled up exactly like them, and never forgot his tie. When the class teacher asked for ideas for the class trip, Manoj thought of the old stepwell near his Nani's house. He'd been there; it was amazing. But Siddharth said, "Let's just do the mall," and everyone agreed. Manoj stayed quiet. At home that night he told Nani about the stepwell in a rush of words. "Why didn't you say it in class?" she asked. Manoj shrugged. "Nobody else said anything different."

What did Manoj think of for the class trip?
The old stepwell near his Nani's house.
Why does Manoj stay quiet about the stepwell?
He wants to fit in and fears standing out, since nobody else said anything different from Siddharth.
What small step could help Manoj share his own ideas at school?
He could tell the teacher his idea privately or bring a photo of the stepwell, so it feels less risky than speaking up in front of everyone.
How might Nani see Manoj's quietness at school?
Nani knows the chatty, funny boy at home, so she may be puzzled and a little sad that he hides that side in class.

messages.content: With one mighty blow, Maria cracked open the pinata, and candies spilled all over the floor.  There were 40 red candies, 20 less than three times as many yellow candies as red candies, and half as many blue candies as yellow candies.  If Carlos ate all of the yellow candies, how many candies remained?

Three times the number of red candies is 40*3=120.
So, for yellow candies, there were 20 less than 120 candies, or a total of
120-20=100 yellow candies.
Half as many blue candies as yellow candies is 100/2=50 blue candies.
If Carlos ate all of the yellow candies, then only the 40 red and 50 blue candies remained for a total of 40+50=90 candies.
The answer is 90.
Our teacher wants us to bring something that starts with each letter of our name for a class activity. My name is Kavya.
Fun challenge. For K you could bring a key or a kite. Do you have anything small at home that begins with each of the other letters?
A, V, Y, A. I'm stuck on V and Y.
For V, try a vase, a toy violin or a small vegetable like a vine leaf. For Y, a yo-yo, a ball of yarn or a yellow object works well. The yarn would be easy to carry.
A yellow yo-yo would cover Y twice!
Ha, a very good cheat. Just make sure it fits your class rules.
She said pictures are fine too, so I'll draw a violin if I can't find one.
That works well. A neat drawing with a label shows effort, and you won't have to carry anything fragile.

Between customers at the family hardware shop in Nabha, Zubin kept his phone under the counter, scrolling a district news page. Chain snatching in Patiala. A theft near the bus stand. A road accident on the highway. By evening he was sure the town had turned dangerous. When Simran came in, he said, "You're not walking to college alone any more. Did you see what's happening?" Simran took the phone and scrolled. "Zubin, this is the whole district. And look at the dates, some are from March." "It's still a lot." "Has anything happened on our road?" He thought. Nothing had, not in years. Simran handed the phone back. "You've been reading this since morning. You look more tired than scared." Zubin put the phone in the drawer and rubbed his eyes.

Where did Zubin keep his phone while he scrolled?
He kept it under the counter at the family hardware shop.
Why did Zubin become so sure the town was dangerous?
Zubin felt alarmed and protective, because a whole day of bad stories piled up in his mind and felt like a picture of his own town.
What question from Simran helped Zubin check the fear?
Asking whether anything had happened on their road, after pointing out that the stories covered the whole district and some were months old.
How might Simran feel about suddenly being told not to walk alone?
Simran might feel annoyed at losing freedom over old news from across the district, but also cared for.

Monday. Ojas knocked a cup off the table. It broke. He ran and hid under the bed. Mummy found him. She said softly, "Cups break. Come, let's pick it up with the broom." They swept together.
Wednesday. Ojas spilled his juice. He started to cry. Mummy said, "Uh oh. Cloth time." He wiped the floor with her. Sticky, then clean.
Saturday. Ojas tipped his water glass at lunch. He looked at Mummy. Then he climbed down, got the cloth from the kitchen hook and wiped it himself.
Mummy clapped. "You fixed it!" Ojas smiled a big smile.

Where did Ojas hide on Monday?
He ran and hid under the bed.
What was Ojas feeling on Monday when he hid?
Ojas felt scared and ashamed after the cup broke, so he hid under the bed.
Which of Mummy's reactions helped most, and why?
Staying calm and cleaning up together each time, because it taught Ojas that spills can be fixed, not feared.
How does Mummy feel on Saturday?
Mummy feels proud and happy, clapping when Ojas cleans up the water himself.

James supercharges his car which increases his car's speed by 30%.  He then cuts weight by 15% which increases the speed a further 10 mph.  If his car's original speed was 150 mph what is the new speed?

He increased his speed by 150*.3=45 mph
So his new speed was 150+45=195 mph
He increased it a further 10 mph so his new speed is 195+10=205 mph
The answer is 205.

These lines are hard to read. Give me prose that is easy to follow.

Obedient to the words he said,
His brother to the river sped.
The shelving banks he searched in vain,
And then to Rama turned again.
Obeying what he said, his brother hurried to the river. He searched the sloping banks without success and then returned to Rama.

“Come sit, Gudiya, and I'll tell you about the bus-route marches of my school days. I'm Rekha, your Dadi. I was fifteen, and half the town was marching for a new school bus. Asif from my class kept saying, ‘Only cowards stay home.’ That stung. But I sat on the veranda and counted on my fingers. March: I'm small, Papa won't allow it, and crowds get wild. Petition: forty signatures by Friday, easy. Letter to the councillor: one evening. Speaking at assembly: frightening, but the principal listens. Then I asked myself what I truly wanted. A bus. Not my face in a crowd photograph. So I did the petition and the assembly speech. Asif still grumbled that I had hidden. But in March the route was changed.”

How many signatures did Rekha think she could collect by Friday?
About forty, which she called easy.
How did Rekha feel when Asif said only cowards stay home?
It stung, so she felt hurt and pressured, but she still sat down to think it through.
What was the turning point in Rekha's choice, and why did it work?
Asking herself what she truly wanted, a bus and not a photograph in the crowd, showed that a petition and an assembly speech could reach that aim within her age and her father's limits.
How might Asif have seen Rekha's choice?
Asif grumbled that she had hidden, so Asif probably saw staying out of the march as playing safe, and may not have noticed that the petition and speech were lawful ways to get the same result.

metadata.subtype: Approach: choosing other lawful ways to contribute [Thinking]

In Hoshangabad, Pankaj noticed his cousin Hrithik's lamp still on at two in the morning for the third night running. Hrithik taught at the government primary school and had to submit the annual activity report to the block office on Monday. He'd skipped the Saturday cricket match and the temple fair. "One photo is blurry, and the table has a spelling mistake I can't find," he said, rubbing his eyes. Pankaj sat on the charpai beside him. "Give it here. I'll read it like a first draft, not a final one. We'll fix only what's wrong." Hrithik hesitated, then handed it over. Pankaj found two small mistakes. They fixed them together in ten minutes. Hrithik looked at the finished file for a long time, then switched off the lamp.

When did Hrithik have to submit the activity report?
On Monday, to the block office.
Why did Hrithik hesitate before handing the report to Pankaj?
After three late nights chasing tiny flaws, he may have feared someone else would find more wrong with it.
What choice by Pankaj ended the late nights?
Reading the report as a first draft and fixing only what was actually wrong, together, which took ten minutes.
How does Pankaj see his cousin's week?
Pankaj notices the lamp at two in the morning and the skipped cricket and fair, and sees the strain before offering help.
Andre catches 8 ladybugs on Monday and 5 ladybugs on Tuesday. If each ladybug has 6 dots, how many dots are there in total for all the ladybugs?

The total number of ladybugs is 8 + 5 = 13
The total number of dots is 13 * 6 = 78
The answer is 78.

Shreya asked Tarun to walk with her to the riverbank after college. They stopped where the boats were tied. "Tarun, I have something hard to say. I don't want to keep going as a couple. I care about you, and you haven't done anything wrong. It's just how I feel." Tarun was silent for a while. The water slapped at the boats. "Okay," Tarun said finally, voice cracking. "That hurts." "I know," said Shreya. "I'm not going anywhere right now. Do you want to sit?" Tarun nodded, and they sat on the wall, not talking, until the light began to change.

Where did Shreya and Tarun walk to after college?
The riverbank, where the boats were tied.
What was Tarun feeling when the voice cracked?
Hurt. Tarun said so directly with "That hurts," after a long silence.
What did Shreya do that made the delivery clear and kind?
Shreya said the hard thing in plain words, said Tarun had done nothing wrong, and stayed to sit together afterwards without over-explaining.
What might Shreya have been feeling while saying it?
Nervous and sad but resolved, choosing to be honest and stay present rather than hinting or leaving.

Four friends compared notes on the bus about asking their parents for more freedom. Usha had not asked for anything yet. Instead she said, "Why is it always no after dark?" Her mother answered that it was the ride home in the late hours that scared them, not any doubt about Usha. That helped Usha work out what to offer. Saurabh went in with a proposal: he would be at a classmate's home until eight, send the address and a pin from his phone, call the moment he got there, and have his father fetch him. "Try it for a month," he said, and his parents agreed. Tushar took a different road. "Everybody else goes! You're just too strict!" he shouted, and his father folded his arms and said the answer was no, and would stay no. Meera came home an hour late once. She did not invent a reason. She said the bus had been missed because she lost track of time, and offered to text every hour for two weeks. Her mother nodded slowly and said they could try again.

What time did Saurabh say he would be at the classmate's home until?
Saurabh said he would stay at the classmate's home until eight.
How did Tushar's way of asking differ from Saurabh's, and what happened to each request?
Saurabh offered specific conditions and a one-month trial, so his parents agreed. Tushar shouted that others were allowed, and his father dug in and refused.
What was Usha's mother worried about, and how does Usha's question show what Usha wanted?
Her mother worried about travelling home late at night, not about trusting Usha. Usha asked why so she could understand the worry and answer it, since Usha wanted a workable yes.
What could Tushar try next to reopen the conversation?
He could wait until things are calm, ask his father what worries him, and offer a plan that speaks to that worry, like Saurabh's pickup and check-in. Owning that he shouted would also help.

A new student joined Class 10 in the Delhi school. Samir had come from Afghanistan with his family a year ago.
At lunch, some students asked him, "Did you see bombs?" Samir went quiet.
Rehana, who was curious too, asked something different. "What food do you miss most?"
Samir's face softened. "My mother's bolani. And the mulberries from our garden."
"What's bolani?"
He drew it on a napkin: a stuffed flatbread. Rehana said her Nani made something similar with potatoes.
The next week, Samir brought bolani for the class. Rehana brought her Nani's aloo paratha. They compared.

What food does Samir miss most?
His mother's bolani, and the mulberries from their garden.
What was Samir feeling when he went quiet after the question about bombs?
Samir felt uncomfortable and hurt, as if his whole identity was reduced to war.
What did Rehana's different question do?
It showed curiosity about Samir's life and culture, which opened up a real conversation.
How might the students who asked about bombs see things after the food exchange?
They might start seeing Samir as a person with a rich life, not just a story of war.

Read this:

"Sabina, you grumble about making your bed? Sit, let your Dada Lalit tell you. When I was nine, my Ma went to help at my Mama's house for a month, and Dadi said, 'From tomorrow, you do your own mornings.' I had to fold my razai, pack my cloth bag with slate and books, and make tea for the two of us on the stove, with Dadi sitting right there on her stool, watching. The first day I forgot my slate and burnt the milk. Dadi didn't take the pan. She only said, 'Lower the flame, Lalit.' By the second week I could do it all before the school bell. And when Ma came back, I noticed something: how much she did every morning that I had never once seen."

What happened on young Lalit's first day of doing his own mornings?
He forgot his slate and burnt the milk.
How might young Lalit have felt on that first morning?
He was probably flustered and embarrassed, with a forgotten slate and burnt milk while Dadi watched.
What choice of Dadi's was the turning point for Lalit?
Dadi didn't take the pan from him; she only told him to lower the flame, so he kept doing it himself until he could manage alone.
How might Ma have felt when she came back after the month?
Ma was likely surprised and pleased to find him managing his own mornings, and maybe touched that he now noticed her work.

metadata.subtype: Making own bag, bed and simple food [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The results for the maths olympiad were pinned outside the staffroom in Secunderabad, and Kishore's name was second from the top. Uday read it, then said, loud enough for the corridor, 'Must be nice. Your lot get everything on quota anyway.' A few people went quiet. Kishore's ears rang. For a second he felt tiny, as if the paper could blow his name away. Then anger came up hot behind it. He wanted to shove Uday. He didn't. His friends Farhan and Deepa stepped close on either side. 'He topped the mock tests all term,' Deepa said flatly. 'Everyone saw.' At lunch Kishore went to Mrs Joseph, the class teacher, and repeated Uday's words exactly. She said the remark came from Uday's prejudice, not from anything about Kishore's ability, and sent for Uday that afternoon. Walking home, Farhan and Deepa kept talking about the next round, as if the remark didn't deserve the space.

Where were the olympiad results pinned?
Outside the staffroom in Secunderabad.
What was Kishore feeling right after Uday's remark?
He felt tiny at first, then hot anger rose up behind it.
What steps helped Kishore handle the remark?
He didn't shove Uday, stayed with friends who backed him, and told the class teacher Uday's exact words.
How do Farhan and Deepa see Uday's remark?
They see it as unfair bias against a friend who earned his place, so they stand close and move on to the next round.
The recipe says add a liberal amount of butter. Doesn't liberal belong to politics?

As an adjective, liberal can also mean generous or plentiful. In politics it describes a person who supports more freedom and change.
Example: Grandmother gave us a liberal helping of rice and dal.

Meaning of suspense, please.
Help me correct this: She has been sick since two days.

1. As a noun, "suspense" means an excited or anxious feeling while waiting to find out what will happen.
2. Corrected: She has been sick for two days. Why: "for" gives the length of time, while "since" gives the starting point.
Define animosity.

Animosity is a strong feeling of dislike or anger towards someone. It is a noun.
Example: After the misunderstanding was cleared up, there was no animosity between Kiran and Leo.

Jill likes to watch shows on her favorite streaming service.  She watched a show that was 30 minutes long, and then watched another show that was 4 times longer.  How many total minutes did she spend watching shows?

Jill watched one show that was 4 times longer than 30 minutes, so it was 4*30=120 minutes long.
Jill also watched another show that was 30 minutes long, so the total time Jill spent was 120+30=150 minutes
The answer is 150.

There is three less than four times the number of students in Elementary School as there are in Middle School.  If the number of students in Middle school is 50, calculate the total number of students in both levels.

The number of students in elementary school is three less than four times the number in middle school: 4 * 50 students = 200 students.
This means that there are 200 students - 3 students = 197 students in Elementary school.
The total number of students in both levels is 197 students + 50 students = 247 students
The answer is 247.

Distil this paragraph into two sentences.

"Try the settee," said Holmes, relapsing into his armchair and putting his fingertips together, as was his custom when in judicial moods. "I know, my dear Watson, that you share my love of all that is bizarre and outside the conventions and humdrum routine of everyday life. You have shown your relish for it by the enthusiasm which has prompted you to chronicle, and, if you will excuse my saying so, somewhat to embellish so many of my own little adventures."
Holmes tells Watson to try the settee and says they both love the strange and unusual. Holmes adds that Watson's eager writing has made many of Holmes's own adventures sound a little more exciting.
Now you try: 4 : 7 = __ : 56.
The answer is 32.

Read this:

Counselling note, Student Wellness Centre. Written by Simran, counsellor, 12 November.
Tanvir, second-year engineering, came in on his own today. He spoke quietly and kept checking his phone. He described joining a "self-mastery" group in February: one weekly session at first, then three, then weekend camps. Since August he has paid for "advanced modules", and was told recently that his roommates were "negative influences" and he should not discuss the group with them or his family.
What I observed: he could not say when things had changed. "Every step made sense at the time," he said twice.
We drew a timeline together on paper, month by month. When he saw it, he went very still.
Next steps: with his agreement, I called his mother while he was in the room and she will visit this weekend. I have booked him for Friday. He agreed to skip this weekend's camp and to keep talking to his roommates.

When did Tanvir join the self-mastery group?
Tanvir joined in February.
What does Tanvir's repeated line "Every step made sense at the time" suggest he feels?
It suggests Tanvir feels confused and a little ashamed, unable to see how he got so deep because each demand seemed small on its own.
Why was drawing the timeline a useful step?
Laying out the months on paper let Tanvir see the whole change at once, which the small steps had hidden, so he could decide from outside the group's view.
How might Tanvir's roommates have experienced the months he was told they were "negative influences"?
They may have felt pushed away without knowing why, and his renewed openness gives them a chance to reconnect.

metadata.subtype: Gradual demands on time and loyalty [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Jomon, put that phone down a moment. I'm Raghav, and I want to tell you about a night when I was twenty. A message reached our hostel group: a photo of a tea-stall owner supposedly beating a child, and the words “Share until he's shamed.” Thirty of us boys were furious. Somebody said, “Let's go to the stall now.”

My thumb was over the share button. Something made me pause. I asked, “Where was this taken?” Nobody knew. I rang Suresh, whose family lives near that stall. “The stall is closed for a wedding,” he said. “The old man is at home.”

The photo turned out to be from another town, years old. Afterwards I thought about the tea-stall owner, Manohar, who never knew how close a crowd had come. I still wait ten minutes before I share anything.

What did Raghav ask when the message arrived?
Raghav asked, “Where was this taken?”
Why did Raghav pause with a thumb over the share button?
Despite the group's fury, Raghav felt uneasy and doubtful, and wanted to know the source first, since a photo without a place or date proved nothing.
What did Raghav do to check the message before sharing?
Raghav rang Suresh, whose family lives near the stall, and learned the stall was closed and the owner was at home.
What might have happened to Manohar if the crowd had gone to the stall that night?
Manohar, an innocent old man, could have been frightened or hurt by an angry crowd over a false photo, without ever knowing why.

"What have I said? What have I done? I know nothing, only that I was lying here, half asleep, and heard you say 'go on! speak, I command you!' It seemed so funny to hear you order me about, as if I were a bad child!"

In the passage, what is remembered from half-sleep, and what seemed funny?
The speaker knows only of lying there half asleep and hearing the order 'go on! speak, I command you!' It seemed funny to be ordered about like a bad child.

Read this:

Monday: Mohit couldn't find his slippers. "Rashmi, have you seen them?" Rashmi pressed her lips tight, eyes dancing. "No."
Wednesday: at dinner she said a rude-sounding word by accident, then clamped her mouth shut, cheeks puffing with a held-in laugh. Mohit bit back his own smile.
The next Monday: she marched up with the slippers. "I hid them!" and burst out laughing. Mohit laughed too.

What did Rashmi hide?
The slippers Mohit couldn't find.
What was Rashmi feeling when she pressed her lips tight on Monday?
She was amused and pleased with her trick, trying to hold back a smile because she knew she shouldn't laugh.
How could Mohit respond to Rashmi's held-in smiles?
Stay light and let her own up, as she did, rather than punishing the leaking smile.
What changed by the next Monday?
Rashmi felt safe enough to admit the joke and laugh openly with her father.
Mera beta pooch raha hai 'draw' aur 'tie' mein kya farak hai?

They mean almost the same thing: the game ended with equal scores. "Draw" is common in football and chess. In cricket, a "tie" means equal scores at the end, while a "draw" means the match ended without a result.

Read this:

At the district swimming club's Sunday session, Sachin slipped on the wet tiles near the diving board and hit his head. He sat up, dazed, holding it.
Twenty boys were around the pool. Manoj was nearest. He looked at the lifeguard's chair. Empty. He looked at the others. They were all looking too.
Somebody will call Coach, Manoj thought. Someone older.
Nobody did. Sachin tried to stand and wobbled.
Then Coach Iqbal came out of the office, saw him, and ran. He sat Sachin down, pressed a towel to his head and phoned his parents.
In the changing room, nobody spoke. Manoj stared at his locker, thinking he had been two steps away.

Where did Sachin slip?
He slipped on the wet tiles near the diving board.
How did Manoj feel in the changing room?
He felt guilty and quiet, thinking he had been two steps away and done nothing.
What would you advise Manoj if it happens again?
Go to the person yourself and shout for an adult by name, like "Coach Iqbal!", rather than waiting for someone older.
How might Sachin have felt when nobody came at first?
He was probably dazed and scared, and confused that so many boys stood around without helping.

Elliott drew a right-angle triangle on his book. It had a base of 4 inches, a height of 3 inches and a certain length of the hypotenuse. What was the length of the perimeter of the triangle that he drew?

Since the hypotenuse of a triangle is found by the square root of the base squared plus the height squared.
The square of the base of the first triangle is 4*4=16 square inches
The square of the height of the first triangle is 3*3=9 square inches.
The sum of the squares of the base and the height of the first triangle is 16+9=25
The square root of the sum of the base and the height of the first triangle, which is the hypotenuse of the triangle, is sqrt25=5 inches.
Since the perimeter of a triangle is found by adding the sides of the triangle, the base and height of the triangle sum up to 3+4=7 inches
If you add the hypotenuse of the triangle the perimeter of the triangle becomes 7+5=12 inches.
The answer is 12.

My friend Gurleen asked me why I wasn't at nets this month, so I'm telling you the whole thing. I'm Hrithik, and you know how much I worship Coach Anand.
Before the district final, my hamstring was pulling. I told him. He said, “Tape it. Don't tell your parents, they'll panic. We need you.” The whole team was watching, and I just nodded.
I played. By the second innings I was limping so badly I couldn't run a single.
That night Mummy saw me climbing the stairs one step at a time. I told her everything. She didn't shout. She put ice on it, called Coach Anand right then, and took me to the doctor before ten. The doctor said it could have torn badly. I still respect Coach. But I'll never hide pain for him again.

What did Coach Anand tell Hrithik to do about the sore hamstring?
The coach said to tape it and not tell Hrithik's parents.
What was Hrithik feeling when he nodded in front of the team?
Hrithik felt a mix of admiration and fear, respecting the coach too much to refuse and scared of letting the team down.
How did Hrithik's mother respond, and why was it the right step?
She stayed calm, iced the leg, called the coach that night and took Hrithik to the doctor before ten, which protected his leg and showed secrecy about injuries isn't okay.
How might the team have felt watching Hrithik limp?
They may have felt worried or uneasy, and perhaps afraid to speak up against the coach themselves.

Read this:

Class 4 note, spelling bee day. By Sharmila, class teacher. When Rhea won the final round, the loudest clapping came from Rhea's best friend, Minakshi, who had been knocked out in round three. Minakshi jumped up, clapped above her head and hugged Rhea before Rhea had even collected the trophy. A minute later I saw her look at the trophy and then down at her shoes, just for a moment. I think a small pang was there too, and that is natural. At break I told Minakshi, "You were a wonderful friend today. And round three was hard. Want to practise some tricky words together next week?" She grinned and said yes. I'll keep two lunch breaks free.

In which round was Minakshi knocked out?
Round three.
What does Minakshi looking at the trophy and then at her shoes suggest?
Alongside real joy for Rhea, she may have felt a small pang of wishing she had won too.
How did Sharmila respond to both of Minakshi's feelings?
Sharmila praised her as a wonderful friend, said round three was hard, and offered practice together, so both the joy and the wish were respected.
What was it like for Rhea to be hugged by Minakshi before collecting the trophy?
Rhea likely felt extra happy and supported, knowing a friend who had been knocked out was celebrating so warmly.

Read this:

"You always take my charger!" Akash's voice was rising. Jahnavi, his sister, put the laptop down. "I did not. You lost it yourself!" "Liar!" His hands were shaking. She saw his jaw clench and felt her own heartbeat quicken. She took a breath. "Akash, I'm getting loud. Let's stop. I'll talk to you in fifteen minutes, okay?" "Why, so you can get out of it?" "No. Because I'll say something I don't mean." She walked to the balcony and looked at the traffic. When she came back, he was sitting on the sofa with the charger in his hand, found under his pillow. "Sorry," he muttered. "Thanks for waiting."

Where did Jahnavi go to calm down?
She went to the balcony.
What was Jahnavi afraid might happen if they kept arguing?
She felt her heartbeat quicken and worried she would say something she did not mean, which is why she stopped. She was also angry, but did not want to hurt him.
What worked in how Jahnavi handled the argument?
She named that she was getting loud, proposed talking later and stepped away, which let both of them cool down.
How might Akash have read Jahnavi walking away at first?
He may have thought she was avoiding the argument, until she came back and he found the charger. 🙂

Urmila, twenty-five, crouched between her chilli rows outside Guntur with the new leaf-test kit in her hand. The strip had turned purple: "possible stem blight".
Darshan leaned over the fence. "Spray the whole field today. My cousin lost everything to that."
Urmila didn't move yet. She asked herself first: how common is stem blight here? Rare, the extension office had said; one or two fields in the district in a bad year. Then she looked at the evidence. The lower leaves had brown spots, which pushed the chance up. The stems were firm and green, which pulled it down again.
"Maybe it's there, maybe not," she said. "The kit can be wrong."
That evening she rode to the Krishi Vigyan Kendra with a bagged plant and asked the scientist to read the strip with her.

What did the strip on Urmila's leaf-test kit say?
It turned purple: "possible stem blight".
How did Urmila feel about the purple strip before spraying?
Urmila felt uncertain and cautious, because stem blight is rare in the district and the firm green stems pulled against the spotted leaves, so she said the kit could be wrong.
Which choice made Urmila's approach wise?
Starting from how common the blight is, adjusting for the leaves and stems, and then taking a plant to the scientist to explain the test instead of spraying the whole field on one purple strip.
Why might Darshan react differently from Urmila?
Darshan remembers a cousin losing everything, so that one vivid story makes the danger feel huge and urgent, while Urmila starts from how often it actually happens.
