The lights went out across their Penang apartment block at eight, just as Mei was halfway through a video on her tablet. The battery showed 9%. "Useless," she muttered. Then she made herself think. "Okay. What can't I do? Tablet, TV, the fan. What can I do?" She counted on her fingers: there were candles in the kitchen drawer; her book was on the shelf; Grandma knew a hundred stories; and her cousin Yara, staying the night, could sing anything. She lit a candle with Mum, carried it to the living room and announced, "Game. Each person sings a line, and the next song starts with the last word." Grandma began with an old lullaby. By the time the lights came back at ten, nobody had noticed.

What did the tablet battery show?
What was Mei feeling when she muttered 'Useless'?
Annoyed and frustrated that the power cut interrupted her video.
What else could the family do if the cut lasted all night?
Read aloud by candlelight or tell Grandma's stories, keeping the tablet charge for emergencies.
What was the evening like for Grandma?
Grandma got to share an old lullaby with the whole family gathered round.

metadata.subtype: Approach: thinking of what is still possible [Thinking]

messages.content: When Jack traveled to Canada, he had to wait 20 hours to get through customs, plus 14 days in coronavirus quarantine. How many hours total did Jack have to wait?

First convert the quarantine wait time to hours by multiplying the number of days by the number of hours in a day: 14 days * 24 hours/day = 336 hours
Then add the time Jack spent waiting in customs to the quarantine time: 336 hours + 20 hours = 356 hours
The answer is 356.

Read this:

The community hall smelled of incense and warm rice. Disha sat between her cousin Mehak and a row of relatives, her feet not reaching the floor. Everyone had come for the prayers after Nana's death. An older cousin began to sing, and one by one the others joined in, low and slow. Disha didn't know all the words but she hummed along. Her throat felt tight, but she wasn't alone in it. Afterwards, plates of khichdi and sweet rice were passed down the row, and Mehak put an extra spoon of sweet rice on hers without a word. Disha leaned her head on Mehak's arm. Around them, people were crying and smiling at the same time.

What food was passed down the row after the prayers?
Plates of khichdi and sweet rice.
What did Disha feel while humming along with the songs?
A tight throat of sadness, but also comfort at belonging; she wasn't alone in it.
How could the rituals help a family carry sorrow together, according to this scene?
The shared songs, the food and being seated together let each person grieve in company, whatever they believe.
What might Mehak be trying to say by adding an extra spoon of sweet rice?
That she cares for Disha and wants to comfort her without needing words. 🙂
At a birthday party, 30% of the guests are married, 50% are single, and the rest are children. If there are 1000 guests, how many more married people are there than children?

There are 1000 x 30/100 = 300 people who are married.
There are 1000 x 50/100 = 500 people who are single.
So, there are a total of 300 + 500 = 800 that are either married or single.
This means, 1000 - 800 = 200 are children.
Therefore, there are 300 - 200 = 100 more married people than children.
The answer is 100.

Read this:

Vaibhav, you asked me about prejudice, so let me tell you something I'm not proud of. I'm Santosh, and when I was twenty, at the textile mill in Surat, a new supervisor joined, Yusuf bhai. First day, I told my friends, "Watch, he'll only favour his own people." I didn't know one thing about him. Only his name.

For a month I watched him like a detective, waiting to be right. Every small thing, I counted as proof.

Then my mother fell ill and I needed three days' leave in peak season. Yusuf bhai gave me five, and covered my machine himself. I felt so small. Not because he was kind. Because I'd been so sure.

That's when I started asking myself: this idea in my head, is it about this man, or about something I heard as a boy? You'll have ideas like that too. Everyone does. Notice them. Check them.

Where did Santosh work at twenty?
Santosh worked at the textile mill in Surat.
How did young Santosh feel when Yusuf bhai gave him leave?
Young Santosh felt small and ashamed, realising how sure he had been without any real knowledge.
What turning point in the story changed how Santosh handled his assumptions?
After Yusuf bhai's help, Santosh began asking whether a thought was about the real person or something heard as a boy.
How might Yusuf bhai have felt being watched closely that first month?
Yusuf bhai may have felt uneasy or judged, sensing suspicion from a worker who didn't know him.

Read this:

Independence Day
Diary, Samir here. This morning at the flag hoisting, Madhuri whispered that the principal's hat looked like an upside-down bucket, right as the anthem started. I snorted. Then I couldn't stop. My shoulders were shaking, and I was pressing my lips together so hard they hurt. The old man next to us, Mr Bakshi from Block C, turned and looked at me. Not angry. Just sad. He was standing so straight, holding his walking stick, and I remembered Papa saying he'd been in the army for thirty years. My face burned. After the anthem I said sorry to him. He said, 'It's all right, son. Just remember it matters to some of us.' From now on I'm saving my jokes for the walk home.

What did Madhuri say the principal's hat looked like?
An upside-down bucket.
How did Samir feel when Mr Bakshi looked at him?
Ashamed and embarrassed; his face burned.
What did Samir do after the anthem, and what does he decide?
He apologised to Mr Bakshi and decided to save his jokes for the walk home.
How did Mr Bakshi feel about the giggling?
Sad rather than angry, because the anthem matters to him after thirty years in the army.
My pen friend in the US says she poured juice from a pitcher. I thought a pitcher was a baseball player.

Both are real. Here a pitcher is a container with a handle and a lip for pouring liquid, like a jug. It is a noun. The baseball pitcher is the player who throws the ball to the batter.
Example: He filled the pitcher with cold water and set it on the table.

Read this:

Last year Pallavi, then a third-year, wanted to be the helpful mentor for Aparna. Whenever Aparna got stuck, Pallavi typed the solution. Aparna nodded, thanked her, and came back the next day with the next problem. By the exams she could not write a loop alone.

This year, as a final-year student, Pallavi met a new junior, Naveen, and began differently. "What do you actually want?" she asked. "A first internship," he said. So instead of describing her own path, she looked at what internships asked for.

She broke "learn programming" down week by week: one concept, one exercise, one small program. Every Saturday they went over Naveen's work together, and Pallavi asked "what would you try?" before she said anything.

One Saturday Naveen asked about machine learning. Pallavi laughed. "I don't know it well enough to advise you. But a senior in that area is in the lab on Mondays. I'll introduce you." Naveen looked relieved that she had said it plainly.

What did Naveen say he wanted?
Naveen said he wanted a first internship.
How did Pallavi's mentoring of Naveen differ from her earlier mentoring of Aparna, and what were the results?
With Aparna she typed every solution, so Aparna could not write a loop alone, while with Naveen she asked what he wanted, set small weekly steps and asked what he would try first.
What was Naveen feeling when Pallavi said she did not know machine learning well enough?
Relief and trust, since she said it plainly and offered a real introduction.
What could Pallavi do when Naveen is stuck next week?
Pallavi could ask what he has tried and give a hint rather than the whole answer.
How do I spell the breathing problem "asma"?

The spelling is "asthma", with "th" in the middle.
Example: The school nurse keeps an inhaler for students with asthma.

The population of Mojave was 4000 a decade ago. If the town's population has increased three times, and the population analysis firm predicts that it will increase by 40% after five years, how many people will be in Mojave in five years?

Since the population of Mojave has increased three times the number it was a decade ago, there are 3*4000 = 12000 people in Mojave now.
It's predicted that the population will increase by 40/100*12000 = 4800 people after five years.
This means there will be 12000+4800 = 16800 people living in Mojave in five years.
The answer is 16800.

March: Dhruv's cousin Bhavna lost her job, and Dhruv, twenty-five, drove her to interviews, helped her rewrite her CV and sat up late with her when she cried.
April: Bhavna applied for an opening at Dhruv's company. "Just tell them to hire me," she said. "You're a senior analyst." Dhruv felt torn. He loved her. But three other candidates had applied through the proper round. "I'll put your CV forward like anyone's," he said. "I won't ask them to skip the interview." Bhavna was hurt and didn't call for a week.
June: She didn't get that job, but she got another. She came to Dhruv's flat with sweets. "I was angry," she said. "But you still drove me to every interview." "I'll always help," he said. "Just not by cheating for you."

What did Bhavna ask Dhruv to do in April?
She said, "Just tell them to hire me."
What was Dhruv feeling when Bhavna asked him to get her hired?
Dhruv felt torn, loving his cousin but unwilling to be unfair to other candidates.
How did Dhruv balance loyalty and fairness?
He helped with time, lifts and CV support, but refused to bend the hiring rules, saying so plainly.
How did Bhavna's view of Dhruv's choice change?
Bhavna was hurt and angry at first, but later recognised he had supported her all along.

The spacecraft Gibraltar is a mountain-sized intergalactic vehicle for transporting equipment, building materials, and families to establish colonies on far-away planets.  At full capacity, the vehicle can carry 300 family units with four people per family.  The space flight is expected to take years, and it is expected that the size of families will grow during the space voyage.  Therefore, when the spacecraft leaves the earth, it will carry 100 people less than one-third of the ship's capacity.  How many people will be on the ship to start the journey?

The full capacity of the ship is 300 * 4 = 1200 people.
One-third of capacity is 1200/3 = 400 people.
100 less than one-third capacity is 400 - 100 = 300 people.
The answer is 300.

Read this:

I am Hrithik, and I was waiting at the park gate when Pankaj, about two, took off across the grass, grinning. He stopped, looked back over his shoulder at his mother, and squealed. She jogged after him, arms out, and he ran again, shrieking, checking her face each time. I cannot know for sure what he meant, but he seemed to be asking her to chase.

Where was Hrithik waiting?
He was waiting at the park gate.
What does Pankaj's look back over his shoulder suggest, and what else might it mean?
It suggests he is inviting his mother to chase and enjoying the game. It might also be checking that she is still near.
What can an adult do when a toddler runs and looks back like this?
They can join in with a playful chase, then let the toddler chase them back, which builds connection and turn-taking.
How might Pankaj's mother feel about the game?
She may feel a bit tired but also delighted, since he wants to play with her.

In Kotpur the bus to the higher secondary school left at 6:15, and for a month Divyansh had been missing it on purpose. His father's tea stall had been shut since the flood, money was tight, and Divyansh had started doing the morning milk round for a dairy instead. He told no one at school. On Thursday, Mohit Sir found him at the bus stand in the evening, sitting on his cycle. "Haven't seen you in class, Divyansh." Divyansh shrugged, ready to say "sick." Then, looking at the teacher's worried face, he told it all: the stall, the milk round, how he lay awake doing sums. Mohit Sir listened to the end. "Thank you for telling me. Let's talk to your father together, and I'll ask about the scholarship form." Divyansh cycled home feeling lighter.

Why had the tea stall been shut?
It had been shut since the flood.
Why did Divyansh keep his problems from everyone at school?
He probably felt embarrassed about the money trouble and thought he had to handle it himself. Saying "sick" was easier than explaining.
What was the turning point for Divyansh, and what did it open up?
Choosing to tell Mohit Sir the truth instead of "sick." That brought in an adult who could speak to his father and look into a scholarship form.
How might Mohit Sir have felt while he waited at the bus stand for an answer?
He was worried about a student who had vanished from class. Hearing the real reason may have made him sad for Divyansh but glad to finally be able to help.

In the chemistry lab, Farida Ma'am held up the rule sheet: no loose jewellery near the burners. Deepika looked at her wrist. The bracelet was faded green thread, knotted three times at the clasp, with one bead missing. "Ma'am, can I keep it in my pocket instead?" Her voice was quiet. The teacher could have said a rule is a rule, and it was. But Farida said, "Pocket is fine. Is it special?" Deepika slid it off slowly. "My best friend made it before she moved to another city. We each have one." "Then zip it inside your bag, away from the burners," said Farida. Deepika did, patting the zip twice before she picked up her test tube.

What was the lab rule about?
The rule was no loose jewellery near the burners.
What does Deepika's slow removal of the bracelet suggest?
She values it and is reluctant to part with it, probably because it links her to the friend who made it, though she may also just feel shy at being singled out.
What can a teacher do when a safety rule meets a keepsake?
Keep the rule but offer a safe alternative, like a zipped bag, and ask kindly about the object, so safety and the student's feelings are both respected.
How might Farida see the moment differently from Deepika?
For the teacher it is a safety rule with an easy fix, while for Deepika it is a link to a friend who moved away, so a cold enforcement would have felt like a loss.
Now you try: 1/5, 1/2, 1/10, 4/5 in order.

Diary, Friday
Third weekly check-in with Lalremsiami today. Fifteen minutes, her office, Friday at four. We go through the list we wrote together: what's due, what "good" means for each thing, and anything bothering either of us.
Today I told her the Thursday deadlines are too tight when data comes Wednesday night. I said it calmly and she moved them to Friday. Just like that!
A month ago I'd have swallowed it and complained to the other interns. I was that girl who smiled in meetings and cried in the washroom. Now I say things. Weirdly, she trusts me more because of it. She even asked me what I'd change about the internship.
Rehana

When is Rehana's weekly check-in with Lalremsiami?
Friday at four, for fifteen minutes.
How was Rehana feeling when the deadline was moved?
She felt surprised and pleased, even proud, that raising it calmly worked.
Which habit is helping Rehana most at this stage?
Using the weekly check-in and written list to raise issues calmly, instead of swallowing them.
How does Lalremsiami seem to see Rehana now?
She seems to trust Rehana more and values her opinion, even asking what she would change.

Kavitha's first visit was a free Friday meditation at a hall in Chennai's Anna Nagar. It felt peaceful. Next came a Sunday course, "just a small fee". Then a monthly donation, "to keep the light going". She agreed each time; saying no felt like going back on what she'd already done.
By the third month she was at the hall every evening. Her college attendance dropped. The leader suggested she "stop wasting time on a degree that won't free you" and help the group full time.
Her classmate Eshaan found her outside the library one afternoon. "You haven't been in class for two weeks. Your mother called me."
Kavitha felt a jolt. She hadn't called her mother in a month. The leader had said family were "old ties".
"I only meant to go to one meditation," she said slowly. Eshaan waited. That evening she called her mother and, for the first time, didn't go to the hall.

Where did Kavitha's first visit take place?
At a hall in Chennai's Anna Nagar.
What did Kavitha feel when Eshaan said her mother had called him?
She felt a jolt of shock and guilt, realising she hadn't called her mother in a month.
What else could Kavitha do to step back safely?
She could keep talking with her mother and Eshaan and ask the college counsellor for support, so she isn't facing the group's pressure alone.
How might Kavitha's mother have felt before calling Eshaan?
Her mother was likely worried and frightened, not hearing from her daughter for a month.

A year ago the family group chat turned into a campaign. My cousin Himani sent a long voice note every morning: "Bhupen, Dada is getting old, he wants both grandsons at his table. Do it for the family." I'm Bhupen, the one who stopped answering calls after my brother shoved me down the stairs at Dada's house during an argument.
Looking back, I'm glad I didn't snap at Himani. I told her, "I know you want everyone together, and I love you for that. But I won't sit across from him because the neighbours talk."
What I did agree to, months later, was one meeting in a counsellor's office that Himani found, with the counsellor between us and my own car parked outside. It went badly, honestly. But it happened on my terms, and I left when I needed to.

What did Himani send every morning?
A long voice note asking Bhupen to make peace for the family.
How does Bhupen feel about Himani's pressure, looking back?
Bhupen feels grateful and fond of Himani's care yet still wary, glad not to have snapped but unwilling to face the brother just because neighbours talk.
Which choice kept Bhupen safe while still giving peace a chance?
Agreeing to one meeting in a counsellor's office, with the counsellor present and a car outside, so Bhupen could leave when needed.
How might Himani see Bhupen's refusal at first?
Himani may feel frustrated and worried about Dada's wish, reading it as stubbornness until the danger from the brother is taken seriously.

Sunday. Sabina saw Bhupen's name in a friend's group photo and waited for the old sting. It did not come. Only tiredness. She carried that odd discovery around all week.

Saturday. Sabina sat with her notebook until late and wrote, "I forgive Bhupen. Not because he asked, he has not, but to put down what I have carried since 2019." It took the whole evening, and no reply was needed.

A month later. Bhupen wrote to say hello. Sabina answered kindly: "I hope you are well. I have made peace with how it ended, and I wish you well. I would rather not restart contact." She felt light, not triumphant.

What did Sabina write in her notebook on Saturday?
Sabina wrote that she forgave Bhupen, not because he asked, but to put down what she had carried since 2019.
What does the missing sting on seeing the group photo suggest?
The old hurt has faded enough for Sabina to feel ready to forgive.
What made Sabina's reply to Bhupen a healthy way to close?
It said she had made peace and wished him well, while clearly declining to restart contact.
How might Bhupen have felt on receiving the reply?
Bhupen may have felt relieved or a little wistful, since the reply was kind but closed the door on contact.

On the balcony of their Kolkata flat, Jahnavi set up a shop with her doll. Deepak asked, "Can I have the doll?" Jahnavi said, "You're the customer. You can borrow it till the shop closes." "When does it close?" "When the shadow reaches the pot." Deepak played. When the shadow touched the pot, he brought it back. "Shop's closed!"

When did Jahnavi's shop close?
When the shadow reaches the pot.
What was Jahnavi thinking when she made Deepak a customer?
She felt safe and happy knowing the doll would come back.
What else could Jahnavi try with other toys?
She could use the same game to share her other toys.
How does the shop game look to Deepak?
Deepak finds it fun and fair, so he returns the doll on time.

Sun City has 1000 more than twice as many people as Roseville City. Roseville city has 500 less than thrice as many people as Willowdale city. If Willowdale city has 2000 people, how many people live in Sun City?

Roseville city has 3*2000-500=5500 people.
Sun City has 2*5500+1000=12000 people.
The answer is 12000.

Monday: Damini played monster, scowling and snarling at her little cousin Himani. Himani burst into tears.
Wednesday: Damini roared, then giggled between roars, and let Himani see her smiling face behind her claws. Himani watched, unsure, then laughed.
Saturday: Himani put on her own scowl, roared at Damini, and fell over giggling.

What did Himani do on Saturday?
She put on her own scowl, roared at Damini, and fell over giggling.
Why did Himani cry on Monday but laugh on Wednesday?
On Monday she felt frightened, reading the scowl as real anger; on Wednesday Damini's giggles showed it was pretend, so she felt safe and amused.
What did Damini change that made the game work?
She let her giggles and smiling face show between roars, so Himani could see it was play.
How might Damini feel when Himani roars back?
She would likely feel delighted and proud that Himani now joins in the game.

Heather made four times as many pizzas as Craig made on their first day at work at Mr. Pizza Inns. On their second day, Heather made 20 fewer pizzas than Craig's number. If Craig made 40 pizzas on their first day and 60 more pizzas on their second day than their first day, calculate the total number of pizzas the two made together in the two days.

Craig made 40 pizzas on their first day at work, while heather made four times that number, a total of 4*40= 160 pizzas.
Together, they made 160+40 = 200 pizzas on their first day.
On the second day, Craig made 60 more pizzas than his first day at work, which totals 60+40 = 100 pizzas.
On the same day, Heather made 20 fewer pizzas than Craig, a total of 100-20 = 80 pizzas.
Together, they made 80+100 = 180 pizzas on the second day.
In the two days, the two of them made a total of 180 +200 = 380 pizzas.
The answer is 380.

Every Pongal, Shalini went home to her village near Thanjavur, and every year she avoided the lane where Vasudha lived. Vasudha had written to her, called her, even sent a wedding card three years ago. Shalini, buried in her Chennai job and her own marriage, had never gone. She'd sent nothing, not even a message.

This year, buying jaggery at the corner shop, she turned and there was Vasudha, holding a toddler on her hip.

Shalini's face went hot. A dozen excuses rose: the office, the traffic, the in-laws. She swallowed them.

"Vasu. I've missed you. I'm sorry I disappeared. I have no good reason."

Vasudha looked at her for a long moment. "I stopped expecting you." Then her face softened slightly. "This is Kavin."

Shalini knelt and shook the boy's fat hand. That night she sent Vasudha a photo of the kolam she'd drawn. The next Sunday, from Chennai, she sent another.

What was Shalini buying at the corner shop?
She was buying jaggery.
How did Shalini feel when she saw Vasudha?
Shalini felt guilty and embarrassed, her face hot, with many excuses rising up.
Why was Shalini's short apology the right choice?
Swallowing the excuses and saying simply that she missed Vasudha and was sorry was honest, and small regular messages afterwards began real repair.
How does Vasudha feel meeting Shalini again?
Vasudha feels hurt and guarded, having stopped expecting her, but she softens a little by introducing her son.
You are late again, isn't it?

You are late again, aren't you?
Why: a tag turns the verb around: "are" becomes "aren't you".
Write a sentence with "although" in it that has exactly eleven words.
Although it was raining, we still walked to the market together.

Family counsellor's note — Abhinav and Shalmali, second session. Written by Francis.

At the first session Shalmali described the evening that brought them here. Her father had been admitted to hospital, and she asked Abhinav what they could use from their savings. He paused and then told her that most of it was tied up in a car loan and a fixed deposit she had never heard of.
Abhinav explained, calmly, that he had handled all their money since the wedding "to keep things simple". He had not thought to discuss the loan.
Shalmali said the hospital bill wasn't what hurt most. "I didn't know my own life." She said she now checks his phone when he isn't looking, and hates that she does.
Abhinav looked shaken to hear this.
What I did next: I asked them to bring every account statement next week and go through it together, with me present.

What was Shalmali's father admitted to?
Hospital.
What did Shalmali mean by "I didn't know my own life"?
She felt shut out and betrayed, since important decisions about their shared money had been made without her.
What else could Abhinav have done from the start of the marriage?
He could have shared all accounts and loans and made money decisions together, even if he still handled the paperwork.
How is Abhinav affected by hearing Shalmali's feelings?
Abhinav looks shaken, realising that what he thought was keeping things simple has cost her trust.

My name is Nitin, and I've been a sous-chef for two years. When Hafsa joined our kitchen last spring, my first instinct was to grab the pan from her every time the sauce split. It would have saved four minutes in a Friday rush. I did it once. She watched, nodded, and the next night split the sauce again, the same way. So I changed. When it split, I asked, "What did you do just before?" She said she'd turned the heat up to hurry. "One tip: take it off the flame and whisk in a spoon of cold water." Then I stepped back, even with tickets piling up. The head chef grumbled. Hafsa rescued it herself, slowly. Six months on, she's training our newest cook, and she does it the same way: asks first, one hint, hands off.

What did Hafsa say she had done just before the sauce split?
She'd turned the heat up to hurry.
Why did Nitin decide to change after Hafsa split the sauce the same way again?
Nitin realised grabbing the pan had taught her nothing; it saved time that night but left her just as stuck.
What was the turning point in how Nitin coached Hafsa?
Asking what she did just before, giving one tip and stepping back despite the tickets, which let her rescue the sauce herself.
How might the head chef see Nitin's slower way six months later?
The head chef grumbled at first, but now that Hafsa is training the newest cook, the lost minutes may look well spent.

Sumit, you asked how I handled Rehan's review. You know Rehan: top sales in the zone, everybody's hero. My old boss would have written "excellent" across the whole form and gone for lunch. I almost did too. But I know one shiny number can colour everything for me, so I split it up. Sales: I pulled the sheet. Outstanding, no argument. Teamwork: I asked two juniors for examples. One said Rehan helped her close a deal; the other said he took credit for her client. Mixed. Paperwork: three expense claims sent back this quarter. Weak. Rehan was annoyed for a day. Then he came back and said, "Pankaj, nobody's ever told me the paperwork thing." That's when I knew splitting it up was worth it.

How many expense claims were sent back this quarter?
Three.
Why did Pankaj almost write excellent across the whole form?
Pankaj admired Rehan's sales record, and that glow made every other area feel excellent too.
How did Pankaj make the review fair?
By splitting it by area, pulling the sales sheet, asking two juniors for real teamwork examples and checking the paperwork record.
How did Rehan react to the review?
He was annoyed for a day, then came back and said nobody had ever told him about the paperwork.

Subject: Thursday, and the launch plan

Hi Keerthana,

I've been thinking about our team meeting on Thursday. When Nikhil asked about the launch plan you'd promised for the first, you explained so carefully: the vendor was slow, then there was the budget freeze, and then it made sense to wait for the new timeline. Each reason sounded fine. Only afterwards did I notice they were different from the ones you gave me on Monday.

I'm not writing to catch you out. I've done the same myself, built a very tidy explanation around something I felt awkward about. So I wondered if the plan is stuck on something that's hard to say in a meeting.

If it is, I'd be glad to sit with you over lunch and look at it. No need to explain anything first.

Ayesha

Which reasons did Keerthana give in Thursday's meeting?
The vendor was slow, then there was the budget freeze, and then it made sense to wait for the new timeline.
What does Ayesha suspect is going on for Keerthana, and why?
Ayesha suspects Keerthana feels awkward or stuck about the plan, because the careful reasons changed between Monday and Thursday.
Why is Ayesha's choice to write privately, rather than challenge the reasons in the meeting, a good one?
A private, non-accusing note lets Keerthana save face and admit what is stuck, and the lunch offer gives a practical way forward.
How might Keerthana feel reading "I'm not writing to catch you out"?
Keerthana might feel exposed at first that the shifting reasons were noticed, but also relieved to be offered help instead of blame.

Monday. Ritu, a junior journalist, was writing about a factory closure. Her editor Gargi asked, "How do you know workers weren't paid?" Ritu said, "Everyone knows." Gargi raised an eyebrow.

Wednesday. Ritu went back through her notes. She split them into three columns: what she saw (locked gates, a notice), what she was told (two workers said they weren't paid), and what she guessed (the owner had money trouble).

Friday. She rewrote the article. "Two workers said they had not been paid," not "workers weren't paid." Gargi read it and nodded. "Now it's something we can stand behind." Ritu felt steadier, and kept the three columns in her notebook.

What did Ritu put in the column for what she saw?
Locked gates and a notice.
How did Ritu feel after rewriting the article?
She felt steadier and more confident, knowing each claim had a clear source.
Why was Ritu's three-column method useful?
It separated what she saw, was told and guessed, so her article only claimed what she could stand behind.
How might Gargi see Ritu's change between Monday and Friday?
Gargi seems satisfied and approving, pleased that Ritu now checks how she knows things.

Lavanya, you've just become warden and I can see you stiffening already, so let me tell you about my first year. I was twenty-five, warden of a girls' hostel in Coimbatore. Within months I was checking bags at the gate, reading out late names at dinner, treating every girl like a suspect. One night I shouted at a student who had come back late from visiting her grandmother in hospital. She cried, and I felt powerful. Then on the bus home I thought: Shalini, would you speak to your own niece like this? No. So I did three things. I asked the principal to sit in on one hostel meeting a month. I put a box in the mess for anonymous complaints about me. And every Friday I ate dinner with the girls, not at the warden's table. The complaints were painful to read. But I stayed a person, not a warden.

Where was Shalini warden?
At a girls' hostel in Coimbatore.
How did Shalini feel when the student cried?
Shalini felt powerful at first, which later unsettled her on the bus home.
Shalini asked the principal to attend monthly and added a complaint box. Why were those good choices?
They brought oversight and honest input, keeping the role's power in check and reminding her the students were people.
How might the student returning from the hospital visit have felt when shouted at?
She likely felt hurt and unfairly treated, already worried about her grandmother.

His eyes followed it up, past the lamp post. When it drifted behind a balloon seller, he leaned sideways, looked to the other side, and caught it again as it came out. Pop. He gasped and slapped the pram. "Ba!" He wanted another.

What did Kalyani buy at the fair?
A bubble wand.

Harsha felt surprised and delighted when the bubble popped, and eager for another.

Blow bubbles slowly in different directions and let him follow and find them, naming them as they go.
How might Kalyani feel watching him lean to find the bubble?
Kalyani would probably feel amused and proud of his sharp eyes.

In the Toronto warehouse, Bilal had been the one who spotted problems and fixed them before anyone asked. Then Tariq became shift manager. Tariq checked every pallet Bilal loaded, reorganised shelves Bilal had arranged, and asked for a report after every hour. Within a month, Bilal stopped noticing the loose labels and the leaking boxes. He did exactly what the checklist said and nothing else. At the end of his shift, he felt emptier than when he'd worked double hours. One Friday, a truck left with a wrong delivery Bilal had seen coming but not flagged. Tariq was furious. Bilal said quietly, "I didn't think it was my job to think any more." Tariq stopped. After a long pause, he said, "What if I tell you the targets for the week, and you decide how to run your section?" Bilal nodded. By the next Friday, he'd flagged three problems before they happened.

How often did Tariq ask Bilal for a report?
After every hour.
How did Bilal feel at the end of his shifts under Tariq's checking?
Bilal felt empty and drained, more than after double hours, because he had no room left for his own judgement.
What did Tariq offer that brought back Bilal's initiative?
Clear weekly targets with freedom for Bilal to decide how to run his section.
How might Tariq have felt when Bilal said it wasn't his job to think any more?
Tariq seemed shocked into silence, realising his checking had switched off Bilal's initiative.
He has few patience, so he gets angry quickly. Fix it.

He has little patience, so he gets angry quickly.
Why: "patience" is uncountable, so "little", not "few".

Baljeet: Kiran, saw your board. 30% off all weekend?
Kiran: yeah, trying something
Baljeet: we agreed in March, no weekend price cuts on this street. I kept my side
Kiran: I know. sales were bad this month 😔
Baljeet: I get that. but half my regulars walked past to you today. you could have told me first
Kiran: that's fair. I should have
Baljeet: so what now?
Kiran: board comes down tonight. back to normal prices tomorrow
Baljeet: ok. then we're good 👍
Kiran: really? just like that?
Baljeet: you fixed it. and I have more cake orders on Sunday than I can bake. want to take a few?
Kiran: seriously? thank you 🙏
Baljeet: just talk to me next time

How much discount did Kiran put on the board?
Kiran put 30% off all weekend.
What does Kiran's 'really? just like that?' suggest about how Kiran feels?
Kiran seems surprised and relieved, expecting Baljeet to stay angry rather than forgive so quickly.
What does Baljeet's approach get right?
Baljeet points out the broken agreement plainly, accepts the fix at once, and then offers cake orders, so the deal is protected without an endless grudge.
How would things change if Baljeet had put up a bigger discount in reply?
The two cafes might keep cutting prices against each other, and both would lose money instead of sharing customers and extra orders.

Usha: the investor said no?
Uma: second no this month. and we have 7 weeks of runway left
Usha: 😔 I was hoping the Pune pilot would change their mind
Uma: the pilot taught us something though. people loved the tiffins but only ordered on weekdays. weekends were empty
Usha: so paying for the kitchen on weekends was eating us alive
Uma: yes. I think we shut the subscription, pay the two cooks their full notice, and write down everything we learned
Usha: it feels like failing

Usha: can I be sad for one day first
Uma: take two. then coffee on Thursday and we list what we'd do differently 🤍

How many weeks of runway were left?
There were 7 weeks of runway left.
What is Usha feeling about the shutdown?
Usha feels sad and ashamed of failing, asking for a day to grieve before looking back.

It stops the loss-making subscription, pays the cooks their full notice, and sets a time to write down the lessons.
What is it like for the two cooks when the venture closes?

Hiroshi came home tired, and his daughter Astrid, two, smacked the cat's back at the low window. "Bad girl, Astrid!" he said. She dropped her head and covered her face with both hands. Hiroshi breathed out and knelt beside her. "Sorry. You are not bad. We do not hit the cat, it hurts. You are still my Astrid, and I love you." She peeked between her fingers, then leaned into his shoulder while he showed her a soft stroke.

Where did Astrid smack the cat?
She smacked the cat's back at the low window.
Why did Astrid cover her face after Hiroshi said "Bad girl"?
She seems to feel that she herself is wrong, not just what she did. The hidden face suggests hurt and shame.
What did Hiroshi do to repair the moment, and why does it help?
He apologised, named the behaviour ("we do not hit the cat") and told her she is still loved, so she learns the act was wrong, not her. 🙂
How might the cat's situation look to Astrid once Hiroshi shows her a soft stroke?
She gets a gentler thing to do instead of hitting, and she learns that the cat can be touched kindly. It gives her a way to put things right without feeling bad about herself.

At the temple fair, Dhruv, ten, had a hundred rupees of birthday money and only half an hour before Papa came back.

He saw a plastic toy car for eighty. "I want that!"

His sister Ritu pulled his arm. "Look around first."

At the next stall, a wooden spinning top was thirty. At another, the same car was fifty.

Dhruv stood there, thinking. The first car broke easily; he'd had one before. He bought the top for thirty and kept seventy in his pocket.

"What will you do with the rest?" Ritu asked.

"Save it. For the cricket bat."

How much did the wooden spinning top cost?
The wooden spinning top was thirty.
How did Dhruv feel when he first saw the plastic car?
Dhruv felt excited and eager, wanting it straight away.
What helped Dhruv make a thoughtful choice?
Ritu's advice to look around first and remembering that the car broke easily helped.
How might Ritu feel when Dhruv decided to save?
Ritu likely felt proud of her brother's choice.
Describe the full moon in exactly two sentences and avoid the letter "q".
The full moon looks like a round white plate in the night sky. Its soft light makes the fields glow gently.

"You're not eating, Kiran," Ajji said, tapping the steel plate.
"Not hungry. They cut me from the state team. After two years of training."
Chinmay, eight, looked up from his rice. "Does that mean you're bad at hockey?"
"Chinmay!" Ajji hushed him, then turned back. "Kiran, did I ever tell you about my singing?"
"You sing?"
"Once. I wanted to sing on the radio. I failed the audition three times. The third time I came home and cut all my hair short out of anger." Ajji laughed. "My mother cried more about the hair."
"And then?"
"And then I sang for the temple, for weddings, for your father when he couldn't sleep. Fifty years, kanna. Never on the radio. Still, singing gave me my whole life."
Kiran was quiet. Then: "Okay. Pass the rasam."

How many times did Ajji fail the radio audition?
She failed it three times.
What does Kiran asking for rasam suggest about how Kiran felt after the story?
It suggests Kiran felt a little lighter and less crushed, ready to eat again after hearing that Ajji's failure did not end her singing.
How could an elder help a teenager after a big disappointment?
Like Ajji, they could share a true story of their own setback and what came after, instead of telling the teen how to feel.
What is it like for Chinmay to watch this conversation?
Chinmay is young and blunt, and probably learns from the story too, seeing that a failure is not the same as being bad at something.

Note to Manoj's parents, Thursday. Our garden walk ran long in the heat, and I realised later that Manoj had barely touched his bottle. By noon he was fussy, rubbing his face, wanting to be carried and nodding off on my lap. He couldn't tell us he was thirsty. I gave him small sips in the shade, and he perked up, asking "more, more". From now on we will offer every child water regularly on hot days. Sabina

What did Manoj ask for after the sips?
"More, more."
Why was Manoj fussy and clingy by noon?
He was thirsty and uncomfortable in the heat but could not say so, so he felt miserable and wanted comfort.
What did Sabina change, and why is it wise?
Offering every child water regularly on hot days, because toddlers cannot ask for it and adults easily forget.
How might Manoj's parents feel reading the note?
They may feel reassured that Sabina noticed and acted, and reminded to keep offering water at home.

In the art room, Yuki pressed her tongue into her cheek as she drew a careful curve for the fish's tail. Ms Olga walked between the tables. The class had been loud all morning, chairs scraping and voices rising. She pushed her own tongue into her cheek and said, “Well, this is the quietest class we've had all year.” The children who knew her giggled. Yuki grinned. A new boy near the door looked up and put a finger to his lips, worried he was being told off.

What did Yuki press into her cheek while drawing?
She pressed her tongue into her cheek.
What was Ms Olga probably feeling when she pushed her tongue into her cheek, and how might a newcomer read it?
She was probably amused, teasing the loud class by saying the opposite of the truth, and the children who knew her giggled. A newcomer without that shared context might take it literally.
How could Ms Olga make her joke clearer to a newcomer?
She could add a smile or a word, or quietly explain later that she was joking.
How might the new boy feel when he puts a finger to his lips?
Worried and confused, thinking he was being told off, because he did not know her style or the shared joke.

Dear Ojas,

Thank you for coming to the thirteenth-day ceremony. I didn't get to talk to you properly, so I'm writing.

Nothing in the house feels right since Thatha went. His chair is still by the window and nobody sits in it. Yesterday I was brushing my teeth and suddenly remembered him singing badly in the bathroom, and I had to sit on the floor. Grief keeps arriving like that, sideways, without warning.

Some relatives keep telling me to move on and focus on exams. I nod. But I'm not going to pretend. Amma and I light the lamp every evening. On Sundays we make his favourite rasam and tell one story about him at dinner. Last week Amma laughed at one, then cried, then laughed again.

If you'd like to hear some of the stories, come on Sunday. You knew him too.

Chaitanya

What do Chaitanya and Amma make on Sundays?
They make Thatha's favourite rasam.
How does grief feel to Chaitanya, according to the letter?
Chaitanya feels sudden, overwhelming waves of sadness at odd moments, like remembering Thatha while brushing teeth.
What choices help Chaitanya grieve in a healthy way?
Refusing to pretend, lighting the lamp every evening, making Thatha's rasam and telling stories about him at dinner.
How might the relatives who say "move on" see Chaitanya's grief?
They may see focusing on exams as the way forward, not realising that Chaitanya needs to let grief come rather than push it away.
The ratio of fuel used in gallons to the distance covered in miles by Haley's car is 4:7. If Haley's car used 44 gallons of gas, calculate the distance it covered in miles.

The total ratio representing fuel consumption and distance traveled is 4+7=11
If 4/11, which is the fraction representing fuel consumption, represents 22 gallons of gas, then 7/11 representing distance covered represents 7/11 * 44 * 11/4=77 miles.
The answer is 77.

In their village near Satara, Anjali watched her uncle Ramesh plant strawberries for the third year running. The first year, hail took half the crop. The second, the trader who had promised to buy it disappeared. This year he had taken another loan from the cooperative.

"Strawberries are the future," he told everyone at the tea stall, louder each time. "Only fools give up after two bad years."

Anjali, home from college, saw his hands shake as he counted seedlings. She didn't tell him he was wrong in front of others. That evening, on the steps, she said, "Mama, you were the first in the village to try something new. That took courage. What if this year you keep half the field in strawberries and half in soybean, and ask the agriculture officer about finding a buyer?"

Ramesh was quiet. "Half," he said finally. "And I'm not giving up."
"Not giving up," Anjali agreed. "Just changing the plan."

What happened to the strawberries in the first year?
Hail took half the crop.
What did Anjali feel seeing her uncle's hands shake?
Anjali felt worried and tender, seeing the fear under his loud confidence.
How did Anjali help Ramesh change course without humiliation?
She praised his courage privately, suggested half strawberries and half soybean and a talk with the agriculture officer, framed as changing the plan, not giving up.
Why does Ramesh defend strawberries louder each time?
After two bad years and a new loan, admitting doubt feels humiliating, so he defends the choice more fiercely.
How do I write a good conclusion?
Restate your main point in fresh words, briefly sum up the key arguments, and leave the reader with a final thought. Do not add new evidence.
How long should it be?
Usually a short paragraph, about three to five sentences for a typical essay. It should feel like a natural ending, not another body paragraph.
What words should I avoid?
Try not to start with 'In conclusion' every time, since it is used a lot. A direct sentence that returns to your main idea sounds stronger.
Now you try: find the mistake in "E(X) = 2 so E(3X + 1) = 3 x 2 = 6".
The answer is the + 1 is missing: 7.

The bakery near the college gate in Hyderabad was nearly empty at four. Rehana stirred her tea for too long before she said it: her engagement had been called off in the summer, and her khala still brought it up at every family dinner.
Jyoti put down her puff. She'd known Rehana for five months, mostly as a lab partner. For a second she didn't know what to say, then chose honesty. "I didn't know. I'm sorry. That must feel like it's on display all the time."
Rehana nodded, eyes on the cup.
Jyoti took a breath. "Can I tell you mine? I'm terrified I won't get placed. Papa's shop closed in March and everyone's counting on me."
Rehana looked up properly then. "You carry that into lab every day, alone?"
They stayed till the owner started stacking chairs. On the walk to the bus stop, Jyoti kept thinking: she told me first, and she didn't flinch at mine.

What did Rehana share about the summer?
Rehana said her engagement had been called off in the summer.
What was Jyoti thinking on the walk to the bus stop?
Jyoti felt trusted and safe: Rehana had told her first and didn't flinch at her fears, so the friendship now felt real.
How did Jyoti respond in a way that helped Rehana trust her?
Jyoti named how exposed Rehana must feel instead of giving advice, then shared a fear of her own, so the openness went both ways.
How might Rehana have felt when Jyoti shared her placement fear?
Rehana probably felt less alone and more trusted, and saw that Jyoti thought of her as a real friend, not just a lab partner.
Favourite or favorite: my cousin in America writes it differently.

Both are correct. "Favourite" is the British spelling and "favorite" is the American one. Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: Mango is my favourite fruit.

"Pongal! Pongal now!"
"Urmila, it's still cooking. Soon."
"Now! Now!"
"It's hot, kanna. Wait for it to boil over."
Urmila stamped her feet and wailed, pointing at the pot.
"Look, Amma is here. Shall we draw a kolam while we wait?"
Urmila sniffed. Manjula gave her a piece of chalk. Urmila scribbled a big circle on the floor.
"Boil! Boil!" she shouted, when the milk frothed over the pot.
Everyone cheered, and Urmila clapped.

What did Manjula give Urmila?
A piece of chalk.
Why did Urmila wail when told to wait?
Urmila felt frustrated because the Pongal was right there and "soon" meant nothing yet.
How did Manjula help Urmila wait?
She offered to draw a kolam and handed over chalk, which kept Urmila busy until the milk frothed over.
How might the family feel when Urmila clapped?
They probably felt happy and relieved, cheering together as the Pongal boiled over.
What is the scientific name of the small yellow flower beside my gate?
Without seeing it, I can't tell which plant it is. A plant guide or a local nursery can identify it from a photo.

Monday: when Mehak left for work, Jaya howled at the window and would not let Nani hold her. In the evening she clung to Mummy's dupatta and screamed whenever Mehak stood up.
Wednesday: Mehak waved and said, "After your nap, Mummy comes," then left. Jaya cried, stamped and pushed Nani's hand away.
Saturday: Jaya cried at the goodbye, then sat on Nani's lap with the peg puzzle. When Mehak came home, Jaya hit her arm once, then climbed into her lap.

What did Jaya play with on Nani's lap on Saturday?
The peg puzzle.
Why might Jaya scream whenever Mehak stood up on Monday evening?
She seems scared that Mummy will leave again, so she stays on alert and clings.
What small step seems to help Jaya over the week?
Mehak's same short goodbye, telling her when Mummy comes back, which makes partings more predictable.
How might Nani feel when Jaya pushes her hand away?
Nani may feel a little helpless or rejected, while knowing Jaya is upset about Mummy, not about her.

Rectangle ABCD is 8 cm long and 6 cm wide, and its diagonals AC and BD meet at O. How long is each diagonal, and what kind of triangle is AOB? How does a carpenter use this to check that a frame is truly rectangular?

Answer: Each diagonal is 10 cm (sqrt(64 + 36) = 10). OA = OB = 5 cm, so triangle AOB is isosceles. A carpenter measures both diagonals: in a rectangle they must be equal.

A rectangle is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each other. Its diagonals are also EQUAL: triangles ABC and BAD are congruent by SAS (AB common, BC = AD, both right angles), so AC = BD. By Pythagoras AC^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 = 64 + 36 = 100, AC = 10 cm, and OA = OB = OC = OD = 5 cm. A frame that has been pushed out of shape is a parallelogram: its sides are still equal in pairs, but one diagonal becomes longer than the other. So "equal diagonals" is the test for a right-angled frame.

You want to know why I skipped the party, Ankita? Honestly? I didn't feel like anything. Not sad, just… nothing. I had the new racing game Dad bought, I finished it in two days, and then I sat there holding the controller like, now what? Everyone was posting from the party and I was scrolling, and it all looked like a picture of fun, not actual fun. I'm Francis, I'm supposed to be the one who's up for everything, right? But lately it's like someone turned the colour down. Last week in the library I found this book about people building a school in a desert, and I read it till the lights went off. That's the only time I forgot to be bored. Maybe I don't need more stuff to do. Maybe I need something that means something.

How long did it take Francis to finish the new racing game?
Two days.
What does Francis mean by "a picture of fun, not actual fun"?
Francis sees the party as entertainment that looks good but feels empty, because nothing seems to matter right now.
The library book was a turning point. What could Francis choose to do with that clue?
Francis could look for a real project with a purpose, like volunteering, and talk to a trusted adult if the flatness keeps going.
How might Ankita feel hearing this?
Ankita may be surprised, since Francis is usually up for everything, and glad that Francis trusted Ankita enough to explain.

I'm Uma, and I've been Pankaj's friend since school. He's been with Ritika for four years now, since the first year of college. For the past year, every time I see them together, they seem to be arguing about small things: where to eat, who forgot to call. He told me once, "We want different lives, honestly. She wants to settle abroad, and I want to stay near my parents." But when I asked why he stays, he said, "Four years, Uma. Everyone knows us as a couple. How do I throw that away?" Last week he cancelled his own job interview in Pune because it would upset her plans. I don't know what he really feels. But he doesn't look happy.

How long has Pankaj been with Ritika?
Pankaj has been with Ritika for four years.
What does Pankaj's question, "How do I throw that away?", show about his thinking?
It shows Pankaj is afraid of wasting the four years and of what everyone would think, so the past matters more to him than whether the relationship fits his future.
What could Uma gently ask Pankaj?
Uma could ask what he would choose if he were meeting Ritika today, knowing what each of them wants now, and remind him the past four years still count even if the future changes.
How might Ritika be affected if Pankaj stays only because of the four years?
Ritika might end up with someone who is quietly unhappy and holding back his own plans, which is unfair to both of them.

A group of security guards were hired for the night shift at a factory. The four guards agreed to a rotating schedule to cover the nine hours of the night shift. The first guard would take three hours since they were still awake, the last guard would wake up early and take two hours, and the middle two guards would split the remaining hours. How many hours will each middle guard take?

The first and last guard will take 3 + 2 = 5 hours of the night shift.
There are 9 hours in the night shift, so the middle two guards will cover 9 - 5 = 4 hours.
Each middle guard will take 4 / 2 = 2 hours.
The answer is 2.

Sharmila's diary, Wednesday.
Went with Papa to the transport office for his licence renewal. The queue went round the building. Papa talked to a man near the gate, then folded a note into the form, and suddenly we were at the window. Twenty minutes, done. Everyone behind us was still standing in the sun.
In the car he was laughing. "That's how the world works, beti. You'll learn." Hrithik said from the back seat, "Papa is so smart."
I didn't say anything. Part of me was impressed. Mostly I felt strange and hot in the face, like when someone cheats in a test and gets a better mark. There was an old uncle in that queue with a stick.
If I do what Papa did one day, is it okay because everyone does it?
Tomorrow I'll ask Ms. Fernandes in civics. Or maybe Papa himself, when he's not laughing.

How long did the renewal take once Papa folded the note in?
It took twenty minutes.
What was Sharmila feeling in the car?
Sharmila felt a mix of being impressed and uncomfortable, hot in the face, as if watching someone cheat and win.
What would be a wise next step for Sharmila?
Asking Ms. Fernandes or Papa calmly about it, as planned, to think through whether everyone doing it makes it right.
How might the old uncle with the stick have experienced the queue?
He probably felt tired and unfairly treated, still standing in the sun while others paid to skip ahead.

You asked how we stopped the goodbye tantrums at my in-laws'. I'm Sarika, Irawati is five, and until last year every visit to her Dadi's house ended with her screaming in the car. The whole weekend could be lovely, and she'd remember only the crying at the gate. So I changed the ending. Now, half an hour before we leave, Dadi and Irawati water the tulsi plant together and choose one thing to do next visit, and Dadi writes it on a card. Irawati holds the card in the car. We say, "Bye house, see you soon," and wave three times. That's it. Last Sunday, driving home, she said, "Mumma, next time we're making pakoras." No tears. She remembers the card now, not the gate.

What do Dadi and Irawati do half an hour before leaving?
They water the tulsi plant together and choose one thing to do next visit, and Dadi writes it on a card.
Why did Sarika decide to change the way visits ended?
She noticed that however lovely the weekend was, Irawati remembered only the crying at the gate, so the ending was shaping the whole visit.
What makes Sarika's goodbye routine work?
It is warm, clear and the same every time, and the card gives Irawati something happy to hold and look forward to.
How might Dadi feel about the new goodbye?
Dadi probably feels happier too, since visits now end with a shared plan and waving instead of screaming at the gate. 😊
Colleague said "Let's circle back on this." Iska matlab kya hai?
It means "let's talk about this again later." The person wants to leave the topic for now and return to it after more thought or information. It is common in offices and is not rude.

But this is not all. New Zealand Tom and Don Miguel, after at various times creating great havoc among the boats of different vessels, were finally gone in quest of, systematically hunted out, chased and killed by valiant whaling captains, who heaved up their anchors with that express object as much in view, as in setting out through the Narragansett Woods, Captain Butler of old had it in his mind to capture that notorious murderous savage Annawon, the headmost warrior of the Indian King Philip.

Question: What happened to New Zealand Tom and Don Miguel in the end?

I am Rekha, and I still remember the corridor of the junior hostel in my first month. Imran, a final-year senior, lined up the four of us and told us to make a shy new junior, Dev, stand on a chair and sing until told to stop. He called it tradition. I laughed louder than anyone so that nobody would pick me next. Dev's hands shook. Nisha looked at the floor. Aakash shook his head very slightly but said nothing. I told myself it was Imran's order, so it was Imran's doing, not mine. I felt lighter for about an hour. Later I could not remember Dev's song, only Dev's face.

What did Imran tell the four juniors to make Dev do?
Imran told them to make Dev stand on a chair and sing until told to stop.
Why did Rekha laugh louder than anyone in the corridor?
Rekha was afraid of being picked next, and comforted by the thought that it was Imran's order, not Rekha's doing; the lighter feeling lasted only about an hour before guilt came.
What choice in the corridor could have protected Dev?
Rekha could have refused to laugh, stepped away, or told the warden or a trusted teacher afterwards; one person disagreeing shows the others they do not have to join in.
How might Dev have experienced that evening?
Dev's shaking hands suggest fear and humiliation, with no sign that anyone would stand up for Dev.

On the first day of term at the city school, Lalremsiami Ma'am sat the KG class in a circle. “Running is allowed in the playground, but not in the corridor. Why?” Suraj said, “Because we can bump?” “Yes. The corridor is narrow.” “Hugging a friend is allowed if they say yes. Why ask?” “Because some people don't like hugs,” said Suraj. “Right. And we never go out of the gate with anyone except the person picking us up.” Suraj nodded. “Only my Papa.”

Where is running allowed?
In the playground, but not in the corridor.
What was Suraj feeling as he answered each question?
He seemed confident and interested, working out the reasons for the rules himself.
Why was asking “Why?” a good way to teach the rules?
It helped the children find the reasons for each rule, so the rules made sense to them.
How might a friend who doesn't like hugs see the asking rule?
That friend would feel safer and respected, knowing others will ask first.

I'm Payal, and I watched my little sister Indu's sports day from the stands. The teacher handed out bibs from a basket without looking: red or yellow. Indu got yellow. Two minutes later she was jumping up and down, shouting, "Yellow is the best! Yellow is the fastest!" Her friend Moti got red, and Indu stuck her tongue out. They had shared a tiffin that very morning. In the tug-of-war the yellows chanted, "Red is slow!" Indu screamed loudest. Afterwards she told me, very seriously, "Yellow people are better." Nobody had chosen anything. The bibs came out of a basket.

How were the bibs handed out?
From a basket without looking.
What does Indu's 'Yellow people are better' suggest about how she felt?
She felt proud and attached to her team, as if being yellow made her part of something better.
What could the teacher try next sports day so the fun of teams doesn't turn into teasing?
Mix the bibs between races and cheer both colours, so children enjoy belonging without looking down on the other side.
What might Moti feel when Indu sticks her tongue out, after they shared a tiffin that morning?
Moti may feel hurt and confused that a friend turned against Moti just because of a bib.

HR note, Wednesday. Sharmila, a junior designer, met me privately. She said a senior colleague from another floor has commented on her clothes and repeatedly asked her out, even after she said no in clear words twice. She had kept a dated list of the messages and the days it happened. She kept asking whether she was overreacting. I told her plainly that it is not her fault and that saying no was enough. I explained that the POSH committee handles such complaints and that she can file a written one; I gave her the form and the committee member's contact details. I did not ask her to confront the colleague herself. She said she would think about it until Friday. I will check in with her then. Minakshi, HR officer

Where does the senior colleague work?
The senior colleague works on another floor.
Why did Sharmila keep asking whether she was overreacting?
She seems unsure whether her reaction is justified and may fear she is at fault, which the HR officer answered by saying it is not her fault.
What steps helped Sharmila in this meeting?
She had kept a dated list of messages, learned how the POSH committee works, and received the form and contact details without being pushed to confront the colleague.
What might it mean for Sharmila that Minakshi will check in on Friday?
It means Sharmila is not left alone with the decision and can come back with questions.
What did I eat for lunch yesterday?
I don't know, as I can't see anything about your day. Think back or check with whoever cooked.
The bus was "held up" by a traffic jam. Does "hold up" mean to lift something?

In this sentence it means to delay. "Hold up" can also mean to support something or, in talk about arguments, to remain true when tested.
Examples: The bus was held up by a traffic jam. Your argument holds up well.

Irawati, you're stuck on that riddle? Come, I'll tell you how I learned to solve these, when I was ten.
I, Vikas, a skinny boy of ten, loved riddles but hated maths. My uncle gave me this one: a man has three sons, each son has one sister. How many children?
I shouted "six!" He laughed. "Slow down. Draw it."
I drew three boys. Then one sister for each. Then I saw: the same sister. Four children.
After that I drew every puzzle. Step by step, no shouting answers. My maths got better too.
So, Irawati, get a pencil. Draw it.

What was the answer to the riddle?
Four children.
How did Vikas feel when his uncle laughed?
He likely felt embarrassed but curious, and then pleased when he saw the answer.
What was the key choice in Vikas's story?
Slowing down and drawing each step instead of shouting the first answer.
How might the uncle have felt when Vikas solved it?
The uncle likely felt pleased and proud of his nephew.

Christine and Janice are having a contest to see who can throw a ball the highest. They each get three throws. On her first throw, Christine throws it 20 feet high. Janice's throw is 4 feet lower than Christine's. On their second throw, Christine throws it ten feet higher than her first throw and Janice throws it twice as high as her first throw. On the final throw, Christine throws it 4 feet higher than her 2nd throw while Janice throws it 17 feet higher than Christine's first throw. What is the height of the highest throw?

We know Christine's second throw was 30 feet high because 20 + 10 = 30.
We know Christine's third throw was 34 feet because 30 + 4 = 34.
Janice's first throw was 16 feet because 20 - 4 = 16.
Janice's second throw was 32 feet because 16 * 2 = 32.
Janice's final throw was 37 feet high because 20 + 17 = 37.
The six throws were 20 feet, 30 feet, 34 feet, 16 feet, 32 feet, and 37 feet, and of these numbers, 37 feet was the highest.
The answer is 37.

Ganga ma'am: Remember, geometry box in the bag! Shall I send a video on how to hold a compass?

The power had gone out across the Hyderabad office block, the laptop showed eleven percent battery, and the tender had to be uploaded by five. Dilnaz typed furiously. Her shoulders were near her ears, and every few minutes she realised she wasn't breathing at all, then snatched a short, high breath and held it again. By four her neck ached and she felt oddly drained, as if she had run somewhere.
Darshan, at the next desk, said, "You keep holding your breath. I can hear it when you let go."
Dilnaz stopped. He was right. She sat back, put both feet flat and took three slow breaths down into her belly. Her jaw unclenched. Her head cleared enough to spot a missing page. She uploaded at 4:52, then set a reminder on her phone: every hour, three slow breaths.

What time did Dilnaz upload the tender?
Dilnaz uploaded at 4:52.
How did Dilnaz feel by four o'clock?
Dilnaz felt tense and oddly drained, with an aching neck, as if she had run somewhere.
What small habit did Dilnaz set up, and why?
An hourly reminder for three slow breaths, to catch the breath-holding and reset during the day.
What did Darshan notice that Dilnaz had not?
Darshan could hear Dilnaz holding and releasing breath, a pattern Dilnaz had not noticed.
In a block of flats, there are 120 apartments. 85% of them have at least 1 resident, while 60% of the apartments have at least two residents. How many apartments have only one resident?

At least one person lives in 85/100 * 120 = 102 apartments.
At least two persons live in 60/100 * 120 = 72 apartments.
So in every of the 102 - 72 = 30 apartments, only one person is living.
The answer is 30.
Mujhe gitaar seekhni hai. "I want to learn guitar" ya "learn the guitar"?
Say: "I want to learn the guitar." With musical instruments we usually use "the" after "play" or "learn".

Nikita flopped onto the sofa beside her older sister.
"Didi, why do you look so calm on salary day? I look at mine and panic."
"Because by the time I look, Nikita, the saving's already done," Devika said.
"Done how?"
"Standing instruction. The day after salary comes in, a fixed amount goes to my savings account and some into a SIP. Then I spend what's left."
"But what if you need it for something?"
"Then I'd have to go and take it out on purpose. That little bit of effort stops me."
"I always plan to save at month end."
"And how much is left at month end?"
"...Usually nothing. Sometimes minus."
"Exactly. Want to set it up now? Pick an amount you're comfortable with. If you want help choosing, the bank's advice desk can explain the options."
"Now? Okay. Fine. Show me where."

When does Devika's fixed amount move to savings?
The day after salary comes in.
How does Nikita feel on salary day, and why?
Nikita feels panicky, because saving is always planned for month end and by then nothing is left.
What could help Nikita decide how much to set aside?
She could start with an amount she is comfortable with and ask the bank's advice desk to explain the options, as Devika suggests.
Why might Devika feel calm while Nikita panics?
For Devika the saving has already happened before she looks, so there is no monthly decision to dread.

The wedding hall was loud and lunch was late. Manjula Aunty put one jalebi on Shreya's leaf. "If it's still there when I come back from greeting the bride, you get two." Shreya stared at the jalebi. Drums boomed, cousins ran past, and Aunty took a long time. Shreya sat on her hands. She turned her whole body toward the band and counted the drummers aloud, "One, two, three, four!" Then she counted balloons. When Manjula Aunty came back, the jalebi was still there, sticky from the heat. "Two!" Shreya shouted, holding up two fingers.

What did Shreya count first while she waited?
She counted the drummers aloud.
Why did Shreya turn her whole body toward the band?
She wanted the second jalebi, and not seeing the sweet made the wait easier; looking at the drummers kept her hands and mind busy.
Which part of Shreya's waiting worked best, and why?
Counting drummers and balloons; thinking about something else carried her through the long, noisy delay better than staring at the jalebi and trying hard.
How might Manjula Aunty feel on coming back to the leaf?
Manjula Aunty finds an untouched jalebi and a proud child holding up two fingers, and is likely delighted that Shreya waited so long in all that noise 😊

Tabitha adds 1 serving of honey per cup of tea in the evening.  She usually has 2 cups of tea before bed.  She buys her honey in a 16-ounce container.  If there are 6 servings of honey per ounce, how many nights will she be able to enjoy honey in her tea before bed?

She has 1 serving of honey per cup of tea and she has 2 teas at night so she needs a total of 1*2 = 2 servings per night
There are 6 servings in 1 ounce and she has a 16-ounce jar of honey so that's 6*16 = 96 servings of honey
Her jar has 96 servings and she has 2 servings a night so 1 jar will last her 96/2 = 48 nights
The answer is 48.

"Did you call?" Afreen asked, closing the hostel door.

"Yes. The college counselling centre. Thursday at four," Tanuja said.

"Proud of you. What will you say?"

"That's the thing. I'll forget it all when I sit down."

"Then write it. Give me your pen."

"Okay. For about a month I've been waking at five and can't get back to sleep. I don't want to eat. Nothing feels fun, even my favourite show."

"Add that you've been skipping the group project calls."

"Right. Should I say it's silly?"

"No. You wouldn't call a broken wrist silly. Just hand them the page."

Tanuja folded the paper into her diary and, for the first time in weeks, let out a long breath.

When is Tanuja's session at the counselling centre?
On Thursday at four.
Why did Tanuja ask whether she should say it was silly?
Tanuja feared her problems might seem small or a sign of weakness, so she wanted to be reassured about asking.
What else could Tanuja bring to the session, and why?
Tanuja could bring a list of questions along with the summary, because it helps her use the time well when nerves make her forget.
How might Afreen feel about helping Tanuja write the page?
Afreen likely feels glad to help and hopeful, having pushed gently by comparing it to a broken wrist so Tanuja would treat it as normal care.

metadata.subtype: Approach: book an appointment with a counsellor or psychiatrist [Action]

messages.content: Tim used to run 3 times a week but decided to add an extra 2 days a week.  She runs 1 hour in the morning and 1 in the evening every day she runs.  How many hours a week does she run now?

He now runs 3+2=5 times a week
Each day he runs for 1+1=2 hours
So he runs 2*5=10 hours a week
The answer is 10.

"Mr Anirban? This is Inspector Rao, cyber cell. A parcel in your name has illegal items. There is an arrest warrant."
"What? I haven't sent any parcel."
"Then cooperate. Stay on this video call. Do not disconnect, or we treat it as absconding."
"Can I call my family first?"
"No. If you tell anyone, they become part of the case. Understand?"
The door opened. Vikas, his flatmate, came in with groceries. "Bro, did you eat?"
Anirban waved him away without looking up.
"Who is that? Are you speaking to someone?" the voice snapped.
"No, sir. No one."
"Good. We need to verify your accounts within twenty minutes, or officers will come to your office."
Vikas stood in the doorway. "Anirban? You're sweating."
Anirban turned his back to him and whispered, "Sir, what do I need to do?"

Who came in with groceries?
Vikas, his flatmate, came in with groceries.
Why does Anirban wave Vikas away?
He is terrified of arrest and has been told that anyone he tells becomes part of the case, so fear makes him hide the call.
What turning point is available to Anirban at this moment?
He could hang up, let Vikas see the screen, and check with the police through an official number, since real officers do not demand secrecy or keep people on video calls.
What is it like for Vikas in the doorway?
Vikas is confused and worried, seeing his flatmate sweating and whispering to someone yet being shut out.

At the playschool in Indore, lunch was over and the others were building a block tower. Divyansh, five, sat on the bench by the window with Papa's key ring in his fist, the one with a tiny torch. He clicked it on, off, on. His eyes stayed on the gate. Mohit came over with a block. "Play?" Divyansh shook his head and pressed the key ring to his cheek. He didn't cry. He just went very still. Ms Rao sat beside him. "Missing Papa?" He nodded. "Papa comes after story time," she said.

What was on Papa's key ring?
A tiny torch.
What does Divyansh's stillness and watching the gate suggest?
It suggests he is quietly aching for Papa, even though he isn't crying.
How did Ms Rao help, and what else could she try?
She named the feeling and told him when Papa comes; she could also let him keep the key ring close during story time.
How might Mohit feel when Divyansh shakes his head?
Mohit might feel a bit puzzled or disappointed, not realising his friend is missing his papa.

Last winter I thought I could fix my sleep like a spreadsheet. Blackout curtains, the same alarm every morning, no screens in bed, a warm drink. For weeks I lay awake anyway, my mind looping over work and my dad's retirement money. I started dreading bedtime. My friend Simran listened on a video call and said quietly, "Sabina, you've done all the right things. This is the point where you tell a doctor." I was embarrassed, as if needing help meant failing. But I booked an appointment. The doctor asked about my mood as well as my nights, and we made a plan together. I kept the curtains and the steady alarm; they turned out to be part of it. Looking back, the brave thing wasn't pushing through. It was asking.

What did Sabina's mind loop over at night?
Work and Sabina's dad's retirement money.
How did Sabina feel about booking the appointment?
Sabina felt embarrassed, as if needing help meant failing.
What made Sabina's final approach wise?
Seeing a doctor once weeks of good habits had not worked, while keeping the curtains and steady alarm as part of the plan.
What might it have been like for Simran to hear about those weeks?
Simran likely felt concerned and wanted Sabina to stop battling alone, which is why the advice was gentle but clear.

metadata.subtype: Persistent insomnia and knowing when to seek help [Response]

messages.content: Two bowls: one with about 3 sweets, one with about 10. Without counting, which bowl has more?

Answer: The bowl with about 10.

Estimating also helps us compare quickly.
Can you define inheritance?

An inheritance is money, property or things you receive from someone after they die. It is a noun. It can also mean qualities passed down from parents.
Example: Her grandmother's sewing machine was Fatima's only inheritance, and she treasures it.

Daycare note, Diwali week, Tuesday.
Aadhya, two, kept trying to stack the five coloured cups. Each time the third slid off. She threw one and cried.
Yash, beside her, watched.
I held the bottom cup steady. I didn't stack anything.
Aadhya put on the third, the fourth, the fifth. She clapped so hard she fell over. "Me! Me did it!"
Next: tomorrow I'll hold the base a little less.

How many coloured cups was Aadhya trying to stack?
Five.
What was Aadhya feeling when she clapped so hard she fell over?
She felt delighted and proud, as if she had built the tower entirely herself.
What is the note-writer's plan for tomorrow, and why is it wise?
To hold the base a little less, so Aadhya gradually needs less help as her skill grows.
How might Yash have felt watching Aadhya succeed?
Yash might feel curious and excited, maybe wanting to try the cups too.

Saturday
At Anand's birthday today his aunt asked me where I'm from. I said Pune. She laughed. "No, no, where are you really from?" So I said my parents are from Imphal, and she said, "Oh! Your Hindi is so good!" I've lived here since I was two. Then someone's cousin asked if I eat dogs, as a joke. Anand told him to shut up, which was nice. None of it was mean, exactly. Everyone smiled. But it's the fourth "really from" this month, and every time I feel like I'm standing outside a glass window, looking in at a party I'm supposed to be part of. I didn't eat much cake. I just want to be from here without explaining.
— Himani

What city did Himani first say when asked where Himani was from?
Pune.
What does the glass window image tell you about how Himani feels?
It shows Himani feels like an outsider, singled out and lonely even among smiling people at a party.
How could a friend like Anand support Himani beyond telling the cousin to stop?
Anand could check in with Himani privately afterwards and gently tell relatives that questions like "really from" make people feel like outsiders.
Why might Anand's aunt see her question differently from Himani?
The aunt may think she is showing friendly interest, not realising Himani hears the same question again and again.

In the Pune colony's evening tuition class, Chaitanya got his maths practice test back: 55 out of 100. He shrugged. Not bad. Then Lalit, at the next desk, waved his paper. '92! Beat that!' Chaitanya's ears went hot. Suddenly 55 looked like a failure. He slid the paper under his notebook and didn't answer the next question Sir asked. Then Sir tapped the board. 'This was an olympiad-level test. Most of you are between 30 and 45. The average is 38.' Chaitanya looked at his paper again. 55. Seventeen above average! He pulled it out and smoothed it flat. On the walk home through the colony, he swung his bag and told the watchman, the vegetable seller and his mother, in that order.

What was the class average on the practice test?
The average was 38.
Why did Chaitanya's ears go hot when Lalit waved his paper?
He felt embarrassed, because next to Lalit's 92 his 55 suddenly looked like a failure.
Which question could help Chaitanya judge his mark more steadily?
He could ask how hard the test was and how he did compared with his own past, rather than only comparing with Lalit's top mark.
How might Lalit see Chaitanya after the average was announced?
Lalit might notice his friend cheer up and realise that both of them did well on a very hard test.
