In my first month as a trainee at the dental clinic, everyone wore masks all day, and I realised how much I had been reading mouths my whole life. When I explained a bill to a man at the front desk, I couldn't tell if he was smiling politely or gritting his teeth. His eyes crinkled, but that could have been squinting at the screen. I kept over-explaining, just in case. Payal, the senior assistant, pulled me aside at lunch. "Bidisha, behind a mask your voice has to do what your smile used to. And their eyes and words are all you get, so listen to those. If you can't tell, ask." The next patient was a nervous girl with her mother. Her eyes were wide above the mask and her hands gripped the chair. I said warmly, "First time here? You can squeeze the armrest as hard as you like." She nodded. I asked, "Scared, or just cold? It's freezing in here." She laughed. "Both."

What did Payal say the voice has to do behind a mask?
The voice has to do what the smile used to.
What was Bidisha feeling while explaining the bill?
Bidisha felt unsure and a bit anxious, unable to tell whether the man was smiling or gritting his teeth, which led to over-explaining.
What did Bidisha do differently with the next patient?
Bidisha used a warm voice, read the girl's wide eyes and gripping hands, and asked directly whether she was scared or cold.
What might the nervous girl have felt when asked 'Scared, or just cold?'
The girl likely felt understood and a little lighter, laughing and admitting 'Both'.
My sentence is "If I was a bird, I would fly to the hills." Can you fix it? How can I make my handwriting better? What time does the sun set today in my city?

1. It should be: If I were a bird, I would fly to the hills. Why: in an imagined situation, we usually use "were" after "if", even with "I".
2. Write slowly, and practise a few lines every day. Keep your letters the same size and sit with the page straight in front of you.
3. I don't know that. I don't know where you are, and the time changes daily. Check a weather service for your city.

I'm Yamini, Anirban's older sister, and I watched this happen over a month.
Anirban liked one video about building muscle. Just one. By the next week his whole feed was shirtless guys, protein shakes and "you're lazy if you don't train twice a day". He started looking at himself in the mirror a lot, and he got quiet at dinner.
One evening I sat next to him and asked what he was watching. He scrolled and scrolled, and it was all the same thing.
He said, slowly, "I never asked for all this."
So he tried a test: he searched for cooking and birds for three days and hit "not interested" on the gym videos. The feed changed. I can't say exactly what he felt, but he started laughing at dinner again.

What kind of videos did Anirban's feed fill with?
Shirtless guys, protein shakes and "you're lazy if you don't train twice a day".
What does Anirban's "I never asked for all this" suggest about how he felt?
It suggests Anirban felt surprised and uneasy, realising the feed had pushed far more at him than he chose.
What small step helped Anirban take back some control?
Searching other topics and marking the gym videos "not interested" retrained the feed, which showed it could be changed.
Why might Yamini be careful about saying what Anirban felt?
Yamini is watching from outside, so she can see him get quiet or laugh but can't know his thoughts for sure.

Daniel got money in birthday cards from his grandparents in Dublin: four crisp notes. "That's party money," he told his sister Leila, and by Sunday evening it was gone on sweets, stickers and a squishy toy shaped like a potato.

The next week, the ice-cream van came down their street. Leila had her pocket money ready.

"Want one?" she asked.

"Not with my pocket money," said Daniel. "That's saved money. It took me six weeks."

"Money's money," Leila said.

Daniel frowned and watched her lick her cone. It didn't feel the same at all. Birthday money felt light and fizzy. Pocket money felt heavy, like it had been earned.

How many notes did Daniel get in birthday cards?
Four crisp notes.
Why did Daniel spend his birthday money quickly but refuse to use pocket money?
The birthday money felt light and fun, so spending it felt carefree, but the pocket money felt earned and precious, so he felt reluctant to spend it.
What could Daniel try next time he gets birthday money?
He could decide with a parent before spending what he'd really like it for, as if it were his own saved money.
How does Leila see Daniel's two kinds of money?
Leila thinks money is just money and seems puzzled by why Daniel treats them so differently.

September. Irawati was offered an interview for a paid summer internship at a design firm. She said she'd think about it, then let the deadline pass. The thought of a panel staring at her portfolio made her chest tight.
November. She skipped the class trip to the craft museum, then two studio critiques where she would have had to present. Her grades slipped. Irfan, her studio partner, presented their joint project alone and texted, "Missed you. Everything okay?" She replied, "Sick."
January. The internship results went up on the notice board. Irfan had got the place she'd been offered first. She congratulated him, then cried in the washroom, not from envy exactly, but from shame. She had been good enough. Her fear had simply been louder.
That night she wrote in her sketchbook: I'm missing my own life. Staying safe has cost more than the fear ever did.

Who got the internship?
Irfan.
Why did Irawati cry in the washroom?
She felt ashamed and disappointed in herself, knowing she had been good enough but let fear make her decline.
What turning point is available to Irawati now?
Seeing the cost, she could take one small feared step, like presenting at the next critique, and think about talking to a counsellor.
How might Irfan feel presenting the joint project alone?
Irfan probably felt worried and a bit alone, missing his partner and unsure what was wrong.

Daycare note for Siddharth's parents
At four, Siddharth was racing laps round the room, shrieking with laughter and knocking over the block tower. It looked like fun, but he was rubbing his eyes between laps. My colleague wanted to put him in time-out. I thought he was overtired, not naughty. I dimmed the lights and sat with him on the mat with his soft rabbit. Two minutes later he burst into tears, then fell asleep on my lap. He had skipped his nap today.
Kiran

What did Kiran notice Siddharth doing between laps?
Rubbing his eyes.
Why did Kiran decide against time-out?
Kiran felt concerned that Siddharth was overtired, not naughty, and wanted him to rest rather than be punished.
What did Kiran do instead?
Dimmed the lights and sat with Siddharth on the mat with his soft rabbit until he could fall asleep.
What was the wild running like for Siddharth?
He was probably so tired he couldn't settle, so the laughter tipped into tears once the room calmed.

metadata.subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]

Read this:

Week 1: Imran skipped Friday prayers and told his father, "I don't see the point of going every week." His father raised his voice, and Imran slammed his door. Later he told his friend Pooja on the walk home, "If they force me, I'll believe it even less."
Week 2: Imran went to the mosque, a little stiffly. Afterwards he stayed back and asked the imam his questions. Why this way? Why every week? The imam didn't scold. He said, "Keep asking. Questions are allowed."
Week 3: Imran told Pooja that he'd found one part he loved: the moment of quiet when hundreds of people stand in line together. "It's like the whole city breathes out." He still had questions. But on Friday he walked to the mosque with his father without being asked, and his father didn't lecture him once.

Who did Imran ask his questions to in Week 2?
He stayed back and asked the imam his questions.
What was Imran feeling in Week 1 when his father raised his voice?
Imran felt angry and pressured, slamming his door and saying force would make him believe even less.
What changed between Week 1 and Week 3?
Pressure eased on both sides: the imam welcomed Imran's questions, Imran found his own meaning in the shared quiet, and his father stopped lecturing.
How does Pooja see Imran's questions?
Pooja listens without taking sides, which gives Imran a safe place to think out loud.

Tuesday. At the engagement planning dinner, Gurpreet's uncle announced that the bride's family "would of course cover the guests' hotel." Gurpreet, twenty-five and the bride's elder brother, felt his jaw clench. He said nothing yet, just wrote a note in his phone.
Thursday. He visited Binita Bua, the family's most respected elder, at her flat. "Bua, it's a demand dressed as custom. I don't want to fight at dinner. Will you stand with me if I say it calmly?" Binita Bua was quiet, then said, "I stayed silent for my own daughter. Not again."
Saturday. At the second dinner, Gurpreet said, "Uncle-ji, our family will host our own guests. Nothing more will be given." His uncle frowned. Then Binita Bua said, "He's right." The room shifted. Nobody agreed aloud, but nobody argued.

Whom did Gurpreet visit on Thursday?
Gurpreet visited Binita Bua, the family's most respected elder, at her flat.
What was Gurpreet feeling when his jaw clenched?
He felt angry at the demand, but he held back and planned instead of reacting at the dinner.
What could others learn from how Gurpreet handled it?
Instead of fighting in the moment, he found an elder ally first and then spoke calmly and clearly at the next dinner, which made the no harder to ignore.
Why might Binita Bua decide to support Gurpreet?
She regrets staying silent for her own daughter, so she feels determined not to let it happen again.
I am going to Delhi by flight yesterday.
I went to Delhi by flight yesterday. Why: "Yesterday" shows the past, so use the past simple "went", not "am going".
The lawyer will "draw up" the contract. Is it a drawing?

Not really. To draw up a document means to prepare or write it formally, such as a plan, a list or an agreement.
Example: The club drew up a list of rules for the new members.

Dear Devika didi,

Something happened at the education fair today and I need your advice before Papa gets home.

A man at a stall said his college gives a "hundred per cent guaranteed job" after the hotel management course. He showed photos of students in suits. Then he said there are only three seats left at the special rate and I must pay a deposit today, or I'll lose it. He kept pushing a form at me and saying, "Decide now, beta, your future is waiting."

I almost called Papa to send the money. My heart was racing. But something felt off. Why would a real college need an answer in ten minutes?

I took the brochure and said I'd come back. He looked annoyed.

Can you check if this college is real and recognised? You did your course in Pune, you'd know. I'll also ask the career counsellor at school tomorrow. I'm not paying anything until we all look at it together.

Love,
Aditi

How many seats did the man say were left at the special rate?
He said there were only three seats left at the special rate.
What was Aditi feeling when the man pushed the form?
Aditi felt pressured and nervous, with a racing heart, and almost called Papa to send money.
Which choice worked, and why?
Taking the brochure, leaving, and asking Devika didi, Papa and the school counsellor to check worked, because it slowed things down and brought in trusted people.
How might Devika didi feel reading this letter?
Devika didi would likely feel relieved and proud that Aditi paused instead of paying under pressure.

Read this:

At kindergarten in Oslo, Astrid slipped on the wet steps and started to cry. Freya, four, looked at her, and her own face crumpled. She cried too, loud and hard, standing right next to Astrid.
Then she stopped, sniffed and ran to the toy box. She came back with her own favourite, the knitted rabbit, and pushed it into Astrid's hands. 'Rabbit makes it better.'
The teacher knelt beside them. 'You felt sad because Astrid was sad. That was kind.'

What toy did Freya give Astrid?
Her own favourite, the knitted rabbit.
Why did Freya start crying when Astrid cried?
Seeing Astrid cry made Freya feel sad too, as if the sadness spread to her.
What did the teacher choose to say, and why was it helpful?
The teacher named what happened, that Freya felt sad because Astrid was sad, and called the rabbit kind, helping Freya understand the feeling.
How might Astrid feel holding the knitted rabbit?
Astrid may feel comforted and less alone, knowing another child cared.
Can I end a message to a friend with "all the best"?

Yes. It is a warm, friendly sign-off that wishes someone well.
Example: I hope the exam goes well. All the best!
Watchman bhaiya se bolna hai ki gate khol do, mehmaan aane wale hain.
Say: "Please open the gate. Our guests are about to arrive." "About to arrive" means they will be here very soon.
How many people are coming to my family dinner on Sunday?
I don't know, because I don't have your guest list. Check with whoever is organising, or count the replies you've received.

Thursday night
Stumbled in the client call today. Said "fourth quarter" when I meant third, and the client corrected me in front of everyone. Spent the whole ride home replaying it, cheeks hot.
Then I tried something. What do I actually remember about other people's slips this month? Chetan mixed up two client names last week, I think? Or was it the week before? I honestly can't remember what he said, only that it didn't matter. Sunita coughed through her whole update, and I only remember because I was worried about her.
So today's call will be like that for everyone else: a blip. They were all busy thinking about their own slides.
New plan: speak up in Monday's review even if my sentences come out crooked. Imperfect and heard beats perfect and silent.
Farida

What did Farida say by mistake in the client call?
Farida said "fourth quarter" when meaning third, and the client corrected it.
How did Farida feel on the ride home, and what changed that?
Farida felt embarrassed, cheeks hot, until realising how little of Chetan's and Sunita's slips had stuck, which brought relief.
What permission does Farida give for Monday, and why is it wise?
To speak up in the review even if the sentences come out crooked, because people are mostly focused on their own work and silence costs more than small slips.
How did Chetan's slip last week look to Farida?
It barely registered; Farida cannot even remember what he said, only that it didn't matter.
Golgappe wale bhaiya ko "meetha pani kam, teekha zyada" kaise bolun?
Say: "Please give me less sweet water and more spicy water." It is a clear request that he will understand.
I need a sorry note for my friend Zara. I cancelled our plans at the last minute twice this month. Under 60 words.

Zara, I'm really sorry for cancelling on you twice this month, especially at the last minute. That wasn't fair to you, and I know you had made time for me. You deserve better than that. Let me make it up to you: you pick the day and the place, and I promise I'll be there.
I am liking this song very much. Can you simplify the verb?

I like this song very much.
Why: "Like" is a state verb; no continuous.

"Mausi, can I ask something about what you said at dinner?"
Ishita Mausi, principal of a school for twenty years, put down her teacup. "Ask, Aditi."
"You said board toppers always come from the science stream. How did you reach that?"
"Thirty years in schools, beta. I've seen it."
"You've seen far more than me," Aditi said. "I just happened to look at our district's results for work last month. Can I show you?" She turned her laptop around. "Top ten this year: four science, three commerce, three humanities."
Mausi leaned in, frowning. "Hm. In my school, the science children did better."
"That might be true for your school. I'd love to know why. Better teachers, maybe?"
Mausi laughed. "You're arguing with me in my own house."
"I'm not arguing with you," Aditi said, smiling. "Just with that sentence. You're still the smartest person at this table."

How many of the district's top ten were from the science stream this year?
Four science, three commerce, three humanities, so four were from science.
What does Aditi's way of speaking suggest she felt about Mausi, even while disagreeing?

It suggests real respect and affection: she asked permission first, said Mausi had seen far more than her, and ended by calling Mausi the smartest person at the table while disagreeing only with the sentence.
What steps did Aditi take that made the challenge work?
She asked how Mausi reached the claim, offered district results as evidence politely, and stayed curious about why Mausi's school might be different.
How might Ishita Mausi feel after the conversation?
Mausi seems a little surprised but amused, laughing rather than offended, since Aditi separated respect for her from disagreeing with her claim.

Childminder's note, Tuesday afternoon. Baby Chinmay started crying when his rattle rolled away. Thomas, two, who had been busy with blocks, looked over, picked up the rattle, walked across and held it out. He patted Chinmay's head twice. Chinmay stopped crying. I said quietly, "You helped your brother feel better, Thomas," and left it there. Yesterday Thomas would not share his blocks, and I did not bring that up. 🙂

What did Thomas do with the rattle?
Thomas picked up the rattle, walked across and held it out to Chinmay, then patted his head twice.
What might Thomas have been feeling when he saw Chinmay crying?
He may have felt concern for his brother, since he stopped his block play, brought the rattle and patted him.
Why did the childminder only name the kindness quietly and not ask Thomas to repeat it?
Empathy grows better when it is noticed warmly than when it is demanded every time, and Thomas is still very young.
How did Chinmay experience the moment?
Chinmay was comforted, since his crying stopped once his rattle was back and his brother's hand patted his head.

Read this:

"Anand, why are you standing by the slide alone?" Gurpreet called.
"That big boy took my ball and said I'm a baby."
Gurpreet stopped. That morning, she and Anand had fought over the last paratha. She walked over and stood right beside him.
"Give it back," she said to the big boy. "He's my brother."
"Make me."
Gurpreet's hands curled up. Then she took Anand's hand instead. "Come on. We're telling Miss Das."
"Miss Das, that boy took my brother's ball."
Miss Das went straight over. Anand held his sister's hand the whole time.

What had Gurpreet and Anand fought over that morning?
They had fought over the last paratha.
Why did Gurpreet's hands curl up?
She felt angry and protective when the big boy said "Make me," and part of her wanted to fight.
Which choice of Gurpreet's was wise?
She took Anand's hand and told Miss Das instead of fighting the bigger boy.
How might Anand feel with his sister beside him?
He probably feels safe and less alone, and surprised she helped after their fight.
Sunny bakes 8 cakes. Then she gives away 2 cakes. Sunny wants to put candles on the remaining cakes. If she puts 6 candles on each cake, how many candles will she use in total?

Sunny has a total of 8 - 2 = 6 cakes
Sunny will use a total of 6 * 6 = 36 candles
The answer is 36.

Read this:

When I was nine, I, Bhupen, took up the bamboo flute because my cousin Kiran was learning. For the first ten days my lips went sore and numb, and every note came out as a hiss or a shriek. Kiran's notes sounded clear to me. I decided I just didn't have it, and I put the flute in the drawer under my bed. Nobody told me, and I didn't ask, that almost everyone sounds like a kettle at first. Years later Kiran told me the teacher had said it to the whole class: the first month hurts. I had missed that class. Kiran plays at weddings now. My flute is still in the drawer, and sometimes I take it out and wonder.

Where did Bhupen put the flute?
In the drawer under the bed.
How does Bhupen feel now when taking the flute out?
Wistful and a little regretful, wondering what might have been.
What else could Bhupen have done in those first ten days?
Ask Kiran or the teacher whether sore lips and squeaks are normal, and keep going with short practices.
What was the first month like for Kiran?
Kiran heard the teacher say the first month hurts, kept going through it, and now plays at weddings.

messages.content:
1. What does "luggage" mean?
2. What is wrong with "The train arrive at six o'clock."?

1. Luggage means the bags and cases you take on a trip. Example: Her luggage was heavy.
2. Fixed: The train arrives at six o'clock. Why: A singular subject needs "arrives".

Read this:

Day one. Gautam's idea was a tool that matched home cooks with office workers nearby who wanted lunch. He was so eager to "launch fast" that he built only a sign-up page and a list of cooks' names. No menus, no prices, no way to order.
Day ten. He sent the link to thirty testers. Rukmini, one of them, messaged him: "I signed up. Now what? I can't see what anyone cooks or how to get it."
Day twenty-one. Gautam read all the feedback. Every comment was about missing basics: no menu, no order button, no delivery time. Not one person said whether they liked the idea of home-cooked office lunch. They never got far enough to try it.
He sat back and rubbed his face. Three weeks, and he still didn't know if the idea was any good.

How many testers did Gautam send the link to?
He sent the link to thirty testers.
How might Gautam have felt after reading all the feedback?
He probably felt frustrated and deflated, since three weeks gave him no answer about whether the idea was good.
What would you change first in Gautam's first version?
Include the one core step, seeing a cook's menu and placing an order, even if roughly done, so testers can actually try the idea.
How does Rukmini experience the tool?
Rukmini signs up but is left confused, unable to see food or order, so there is nothing to judge.

metadata.subtype: Approach: ships something too thin to be useful and learns little [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the Saturday fair in Rajgarh, Jyoti had told her mother she was at tuition. Now her cousin Mahima was standing at the bangle stall, looking right at her.
"Jyoti? Aren't you supposed to be at Sharma sir's?"
Jyoti's face went hot. "Tuition got cancelled. Sir had a wedding."
"I just saw Sharma sir at the tea stall. He said class was on."
"He's lying. He always forgets." The words tumbled out. "And why are you spying on me? You're always trying to get me in trouble, didi!"
Mahima blinked. "I'm not spying. I came for bangles."
Jyoti turned and walked fast through the crowd, heart thumping, the lie getting heavier with every step. By the time she reached the Ferris wheel she wanted to cry. She had called her favourite teacher a liar and her favourite cousin a spy, all to avoid saying one true sentence.

What had Jyoti told her mother about Saturday?
Jyoti had told her mother she was at tuition.
Why did Jyoti call Mahima a spy?
Jyoti panicked and felt ashamed at being caught, so attacking Mahima felt easier than admitting the truth.
What could Jyoti do now to stop the lies piling up?
Go back to Mahima, admit she skipped tuition, apologise for calling her a spy, and tell her mother herself that evening.
How might Mahima feel after being called a spy?
Mahima was confused and probably hurt, since she had only come for bangles and was suddenly treated as an enemy.

Read this:

Avni, beta, sit. You're worried about your internship? Let me tell you about my first one, in 1998, at a newspaper.
I wrote my first piece on the water shortage. The senior editor, a gruff man called Mr D'Costa, read it standing up and handed it back. "Redo." One word.
I went to the canteen and cried into my tea. I was sure he thought I was useless. But I didn't ask him why. I was too scared.
So I rewrote everything, even the good parts. Three days later he said, "You've lost the best line. The first draft only needed a better opening."
Three days, beta. One question would have saved them. That's what I, your Sangeeta Masi, learnt.

What was the one word Mr D'Costa said?
"Redo."
What was young Sangeeta feeling in the canteen?
She felt hurt and scared, sure Mr D'Costa thought she was useless, and too afraid to ask him why.
In the story, what choice could have changed how those three days went?
Asking Mr D'Costa one question about what to fix, instead of rewriting everything, even the good parts.
How might Mr D'Costa have seen the situation?
He probably thought "Redo" was enough and didn't notice how frightening one word could be for a new intern.

Describe the weather and the fields around Thornfield at this time.

A splendid Midsummer shone over England: skies so pure, suns so radiant as were then seen in long succession, seldom favour even singly, our wave-girt land. It was as if a band of Italian days had come from the South, like a flock of glorious passenger birds, and lighted to rest them on the cliffs of Albion. The hay was all got in; the fields round Thornfield were green and shorn; the roads white and baked; the trees were in their dark prime; hedge and wood, full-leaved and deeply tinted, contrasted well with the sunny hue of the cleared meadows between.

It is a splendid Midsummer with pure skies and radiant suns, like Italian days come from the South. The hay is in, the fields round Thornfield are green and shorn, the roads white and baked, and the trees dark and full-leaved.

Read this:

Dear Kunal,
I keep thinking about our last evening in Hampi, on Matanga hill. You'd been joking the whole climb, and then the sun started going down over the boulders and the temple towers, and you just stopped. You sat on the rock and didn't say anything for maybe half an hour.
I nearly said something. I had a whole speech about the old kingdom, and a photo angle. I'm glad I didn't. It felt like you were somewhere I shouldn't interrupt.
On the way down you said, "I needed that," and I think I did too. I hadn't known until then how much you'd been carrying since your dad's operation.
Let's go back next year. I'll stay quiet again.
Harsha

How long did Kunal sit without speaking?
Maybe half an hour.
Why did Harsha decide not to speak?
Harsha felt it would be wrong to interrupt, sensing Kunal was somewhere deep and moved.
What did Harsha's silence give Kunal?
It let Kunal's awe and relief breathe, and Kunal said afterwards, "I needed that."
What might that evening have meant to Kunal?
It was probably a rare moment of relief from the stress Kunal had carried since the father's operation.

Read this:

Dear Jatin,

You asked how I'm feeling about moving to Bengaluru next month, so here is the honest answer: excited and scared, taking turns. The excited part imagines the new job and my own flat. The scared part keeps asking, what if I can't manage? Last night I got tired of both and made a list instead. Find a room near the office, ask Uncle Rao about the first week, save the number for the landlord, pack the winter jacket. Then I emailed my new manager to ask what the first day looks like. She wrote back kindly within the hour. I still feel the dread, but now it has steps.

Come visit when I've a sofa.

Amandeep

Where is Amandeep moving?
Amandeep is moving to Bengaluru.
What do the two feelings Amandeep describes look like, and what shifted them?
Amandeep alternates between excitement about the new job and flat and fear of not managing, and making a list and emailing the new manager gave the dread steps.
What could Amandeep do if the dread stayed strong?
Amandeep could keep breaking it into small steps and talk to someone trusted, such as Uncle Rao or a mentor.
How might Jatin feel reading the letter?
Jatin may feel touched that Amandeep answered honestly, and possibly glad to be asked to visit.

metadata.subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]

messages.content: Sandy earns $15 per hour. She worked 10 hours on Friday with her best friend, 6 hours on Saturday alone and 14 hours on Sunday with her other co-workers. How much money did Sandy earn in all on Friday, Saturday and Sunday?

The total number of hours Sandy worked on Friday, Saturday and Sunday was 10 + 6 + 14 = 30 hours.
Beth made 30 x $15 = $450 in those 3 days.
The answer is 450.

Give me the plan described here as three bullet points.

We had arrived in England at the beginning of October, and it was now February. We accordingly determined to commence our journey towards the north at the expiration of another month. In this expedition we did not intend to follow the great road to Edinburgh, but to visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Cumberland lakes, resolving to arrive at the completion of this tour about the end of July. I packed up my chemical instruments and the materials I had collected, resolving to finish my labours in some obscure nook in the northern highlands of Scotland.

- The travellers came to England in October and will start north in another month.
- They will visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock and the Cumberland lakes, ending around the end of July.
- The narrator packs the chemical equipment to finish the work somewhere quiet in the Scottish highlands.
Jackson buys a computer game for $66 and three movie tickets for $12 each. How much did he spend on entertainment total?

First find the total amount of money Jackson spent on movie tickets: 3 tickets * $12/ticket = $36
Then add the amount he spent on the video game: $36 + $66 = $102
The answer is 102.
Auto mein bolna hai "Mujhe yahin utaar dijiye." English?
Say: "Please drop me here."
My teacher said winning the quiz is "a feather in your cap". Is that a gift?

No. It means an achievement you can be proud of.
Example: Getting the top rank in the district was a feather in her cap.
Could you explain anecdote in easy words? My uncle keeps saying he has one for every occasion.

An anecdote is a short story about something that really happened, often funny or interesting. It is a noun.
Example: At the wedding, Uncle Raj shared an anecdote about his first train journey.

Read this:

You want the hug story, Tejas? Fine. Saurabh the hugger, that was me. I used to hug everyone. My family is like that. So at the office party last year, when our new colleague Deepa got her promotion, I just grabbed her. She went rigid and stepped back. Later a friend told me she's uncomfortable with touch from people she doesn't know well, and she had every right to be.
I felt terrible. I apologised, and she was gracious about it.
Since then I ask. "Hug? High-five? Nothing?" Most people laugh and pick one. Some say no, and that's fine.
And you, man. When I met you, you told me hugging wasn't done much in your home growing up. So we do the fist bump. Honestly, it's become our thing.

What does Saurabh now ask people before touching them?
Saurabh asks, "Hug? High-five? Nothing?"
How did Saurabh feel after Deepa stepped back?
Saurabh felt terrible and embarrassed, realising the hug wasn't welcome.
What did Saurabh change after the office party?
Saurabh started asking first, accepting a no, and finding other signs of warmth like the fist bump with Tejas.
How might Deepa have felt when she was grabbed?
She likely felt uncomfortable and caught off guard, which is why she went rigid and stepped back.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Friday (Rajni, school counsellor)
Urmila, Class 5, came to me upset after the inter-school general knowledge test in our hall. She saw a student from another school reading answers off his palm. She told the invigilator after the paper, which was the safe, right way, and it was handled. But since then she has reported classmates for sharing a sharpener and for humming during silent reading. Today she said, "Rules are rules!" with clenched fists. I told her I was proud she spoke up about real cheating, and then we sorted examples together: "harms others" versus "small and harmless." I will check in with her next week.

What was the student from another school reading answers off?
He was reading answers off his palm.
What does Urmila's "Rules are rules!" with clenched fists suggest?
It suggests Urmila feels strong anger at unfairness, now aimed even at small, harmless things.
How did Rajni guide Urmila?
Rajni praised the real report, then sorted examples with Urmila into "harms others" and "small and harmless", with a check-in planned.
How might the student from the other school see being caught?
He may feel embarrassed and afraid, perhaps without knowing who noticed.
Help me with these, please. Can you tell me what "gentle" means? Uncle had 50 rupees and spent 7. How many rupees does he have left? Please fix my sentence: She don't like maths.

1. Gentle means soft and kind, not rough.
2. 43 rupees. Because 50 - 7 = 43.
3. Fixed: She doesn't like maths. Why: "She" takes "doesn't", not "don't".

Read this:

I'm Yash, and in Class 6 I left my science project until the last night. I told myself I'd start every day for three weeks. Then the night before, I panicked. My friend Vikas messaged, "Copy mine, change the colours." I nearly did. But I thought about Sir's face if he found out, and about how I'd feel handing it in. I stayed up and made a bad one myself. It got a C. Since then I do twenty minutes every evening, even when I don't feel like it.

What grade did Yash's project get?
It got a C.
What was Yash feeling the night before the project was due?
Yash felt panicked and tempted to copy, but also uneasy about cheating.
What would you advise Yash for the next big project?
Break it into small daily parts from the first week, like his new twenty-minute habit.
What might Vikas have been thinking when he offered his project?
He probably wanted to help his friend, not realising it was dishonest.

Read this:

On the crowded bus back from the kasba school, Mehak's friends argued about the Sunday fair. "Let's skip the rides," said Bindu. "Yes, skip them," Mehak agreed, though she had been saving for the giant wheel. When Bindu frowned at her bag bumping someone, Mehak said sorry three times. When the group mocked a new girl's accent, Mehak laughed along, her stomach tight. Things stayed smooth. Nobody was ever cross with her.
Joseph, who sat behind her, leaned forward at her stop. "You love the giant wheel. Why didn't you say?"
Mehak opened her mouth and found nothing there. At home she lay on the charpai, trying to remember the last time she had said what she really thought, and she couldn't.

What had Mehak been saving for?
Mehak had been saving for the giant wheel.
What was Mehak feeling when she laughed along at the new girl's accent?
Mehak felt uneasy and tense; her stomach was tight even as she laughed to keep things smooth.
What small step could Mehak try next time her friends make plans?
Mehak could share one small real wish, like riding the giant wheel, to practise speaking up when little is at stake.
How does Joseph see Mehak's quick agreement?
Joseph notices that it does not match what Mehak really loves, and gently asks why she stayed quiet.

Read this:

"Ira, did you finish the aptitude mock?" Ritu dropped onto the hostel bed. "I got 68."
Irawati glanced at her own screen. 71. Her chest loosened, then tightened again. "Seventy-one."
"Ugh, you're always three ahead." Ritu laughed. "Which book are you using for puzzles? Mine's useless."
For a second Irawati thought of naming the old, outdated one. Just to stay ahead. She heard how that sounded in her head and felt sick.
"The green one on my shelf. Take it tonight, I'm done with puzzles."
"Seriously? Thanks."
"Can I tell you something embarrassing? I check your score before I check mine. I've been treating you like a scoreboard."
Ritu was quiet. "I do that too, sometimes."
"What if we just compare with last week's us? I got 64 last Sunday. So 71's good."
"I got 60. So 68 is great."
"See? We're both winning."

What did Ritu score on the aptitude mock?
What did Irawati feel when tempted to name the outdated book?
A pull to stay ahead, followed by feeling sick and ashamed at how that sounded.
What change did Irawati suggest, and why does it help?
Comparing with last week's score instead of with each other; it makes the friend a fellow traveller rather than a scoreboard.
How does Ritu respond to Irawati's confession?
She goes quiet, then admits she does it too sometimes, relieved that it is said aloud.

Read this:

Saturday

Today I fell off my cycle near the park and hurt my ankle really badly. It went purple. At the hospital they put it in a hard boot and gave me crutches. Now I can't go to swimming for ages and the gala is soon. I cried and threw my pillow.
I asked Yamini Didi if I'll be slow forever. She sat on my bed and said, "Silly girl, the doctor said it will heal. It just takes its time."
Then she made me a chart with stars. Today's goal: walk to the window on crutches. I did it twice!
Tomorrow's goal: go to the balcony.
I'm still cross. But a bit less.

Nikita

What did the hospital put on Nikita's ankle?
They put it in a hard boot and gave her crutches.
How was Nikita feeling about missing swimming?
She felt angry and upset, crying and throwing her pillow, and worried about being slow forever.
What small steps did Yamini Didi suggest, and why do they help?
A star chart with small goals like walking to the window, because reaching them gives Nikita a sense of progress while the ankle heals.
How might Yamini Didi feel seeing Nikita so upset?
She probably feels sorry for her little sister and wants to calm her with honest words and a plan.

Jimmy is going to sell pizzas at the carnival to make some money. The carnival only gave him 7 hours to do so. He bought a 22kg sack of flour to make his pizzas and he takes 10 min to make each pizza for the customers. At the end of the 7 hours, he saw some flour was left. Knowing that each pizza needs 0.5kg of flour to make, how many pizzas can he make to bring home with the flour left?

Each hour Jimmy makes 60min / 10min/pizza = 6 Pizzas
The number of total pizzas made equals 7 hours x 6 pizzas/hour = 42 pizzas
The amount of total flour used equals 42 pizzas x 0.5 kg/pizza = 21 kg
The amount of flour left equals 22 kg - 21 kg = 1 kg
The number of pizzas Jimmy can make is 1kg / 0.5kg/pizza = 2 pizzas
The answer is 2.

Jack and Rose want to start a dog-walking business after school. They made 1,236 flyers to hand out around their neighborhood. Jack handed 120 flyers while Rose handed 320 flyers. How many flyers are left to be handed out around?

Jack and Rose handed a total of 120 + 320 = 440 flyers.
So, they still have 1236 - 440 = 796 flyers left to be handed out around.
The answer is 796.

Twelve annual reviews due by Friday, a server outage eating Thursday, and Omkar still hadn't done Amandeep's. Amandeep was the team's star: brilliant in client meetings, funny, everyone's favourite.

Omkar's pen was already hovering over "5 – Excellent" for everything. Communication, obviously. Reliability... he paused.

He opened his notes from the year. Amandeep had missed four of eight internal deadlines. Two handovers had been incomplete.

Omkar made himself go trait by trait. For each, he asked: what's one example? Communication: the Pune pitch, outstanding. 5. Client relations: 5. Reliability: examples showed late work. 3. Documentation: 2.

It felt almost disloyal. Amandeep was so good. But the ratings were now honest, and each one had a reason.

On Friday, he sat with Amandeep and walked through them. Amandeep was quiet, then said, "Nobody's ever told me the deadlines thing. Thanks."

How many internal deadlines had Amandeep missed?
Amandeep had missed four of eight internal deadlines.
What was Omkar feeling while giving Amandeep a 3 for reliability?
Omkar felt it was almost disloyal, uneasy about marking down a star he admired.
How did Omkar keep the star's strengths from lifting every rating?
Omkar rated each trait separately and asked for one example for each, so ratings matched real evidence.
How did Amandeep react to the review?
Amandeep was quiet at first, then grateful, since nobody had ever mentioned the deadlines before.

Read this:

For weeks, Yamini had frozen at the bus stand in their kasba. The coaching classes were in the district town, an hour away, and every morning her chest went tight as the bus pulled in. Twice she walked home instead. Yusuf, her friend since primary school, didn't tell her to relax. "What's the smallest step you could manage?" "Maybe... just standing at the stand with you. Not getting on." So they stood there on Monday and Tuesday. On Wednesday she got on, and Yusuf rode one stop with her before getting off. In the evenings he dragged her on walks along the canal. "You sleep better after," he said. When the tightness still hadn't gone after two months, Yusuf said, "I think you should talk to the counsellor at the college. I'll come with you to ask."

Where did Yusuf and Yamini walk in the evenings?
Along the canal.
How did Yamini feel every morning as the bus pulled in?
She felt afraid; her chest went tight and she sometimes walked home instead.
Which approach did Yusuf use that worked?
He asked for the smallest step, stood with her and rode one stop, and encouraged evening walks for sleep.
How might Yusuf feel when the tightness still hasn't gone after two months?
Yusuf may feel worried but hopeful that a trained counsellor can help, which is why he offers to come with Yamini to ask.

Read this:

At bedtime Pallavi stroked Vinita's hair.
"Park," Vinita said sleepily.
"You wanted to stay at the park. That was hard."
"Hard," Vinita said. "Cry."
"Yes, you cried. You were sad."
"Sad." Vinita touched her own cheek.
"We had to leave. And I still love you. We can go again tomorrow."
"Tomorrow swing?"
"Tomorrow swing."
Vinita smiled and closed her eyes.

What did Vinita ask for tomorrow?
She asked for the swing tomorrow.
How did Vinita feel when she touched her own cheek and said 'Sad'?
She seemed calm and comforted, starting to link the word sad with how she felt at the park.
Which parts of Pallavi's bedtime talk help Vinita most?
She names the feeling in simple words, keeps the limit, says she still loves Vinita, and promises they can go again tomorrow.
What would change if Pallavi had said 'You were naughty at the park'?
Vinita would learn shame instead of a word for her feeling, and the bond might feel less safe.

metadata.subtype: Stage 6: Repair and naming the feeling [Response]

messages.content: Our family can't agree on where to go for the holidays.
Start by asking each person for their top choice and why. Often the reasons point to shared wishes, such as relaxing or seeing new places.
Everyone wants something different.
Make a short list of the places mentioned, and note what each offers. Look for one that gives at least one thing to everybody.
What if there's still no agreement?
Take turns, so that one trip suits one person's choice and the next suits another's. Agreeing on the turns beforehand avoids more arguments.

Rekha: hey, saw your face when they announced the restructuring. you ok?
Mohit: what did my face do 😅
Rekha: eyes went huge, then a massive sigh. couldn't tell if you were shocked or relieved or what
Mohit: honestly? all three
Mohit: relieved our team's safe. shocked they cut the Chennai office. and worried about Sana, she's in Chennai
Rekha: ah. I thought the sigh meant you were worried about your own job
Mohit: nope. my job's fine. I just feel weird being relieved while she's not
Rekha: that makes sense. have you messaged her?
Mohit: not yet. don't know what to say
Rekha: maybe just "heard the news, thinking of you, want to talk later?"
Mohit: ok. sending that now
Mohit: thanks for asking instead of assuming 🙏

Which office was cut?
The Chennai office.
What was Mohit feeling during the announcement?
Mohit felt relieved the team was safe, shocked about Chennai, and worried and a bit guilty about Sana.
Why was Rekha's check-in useful?
Rekha described the cues and asked instead of assuming, which revealed a mix of relief, shock and worry for Sana, not fear for Mohit's own job.
How had Rekha first read Mohit's sigh?
Rekha thought the sigh meant Mohit was worried about their own job.

metadata.subtype: Surprised, relieved and worried at work [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Four project leads each had to settle a clash among teams, and each went about it differently. Tanvir drew a map of everyone affected: sales wanted speed, engineers wanted quality, and finance wanted low cost. Beside each group he wrote down what it really worried about, not only what it demanded. Payal chose no side. She asked what would satisfy every key need, and proposed launching a limited set of features now, with the quality work coming in the next release. Ojas gave in to whoever pushed hardest each time, and his quieter teams felt ignored. The product drifted as decisions followed pressure instead of the larger aim. Meera announced her decision and then went to see the team that had lost. She explained her reasons and agreed a follow-up on their concerns, so the relationship stayed sound for later decisions.

What did Tanvir write beside each group?
He wrote what each group really worried about, not just what it demanded.
How does Ojas's way of deciding differ from Payal's, and what happened to the teams?
Ojas gave in to the loudest person, so quieter teams felt ignored and the product drifted. Payal asked what would meet every key need and proposed a limited launch now with quality work later.
What might the quieter teams be feeling under Ojas?
They probably feel ignored and unimportant, since decisions follow whoever presses hardest.
What could Ojas do to make decisions fairer?
He could ask each team what it truly needs, weigh those needs against the overall goal, and explain the choice to those who lose. 🙂
Padosi ke bachche bahut shor kar rahe hain. Unko politely kaise bolun?
Say: "Excuse me, the children are quite loud right now. Could you ask them to play a little quietly, please?"
My American cousin says he is "mad at me". Does that mean crazy?

In American English, "mad" usually means angry. In British English, it more often means crazy or very foolish, so "angry" is clearer.
Example: My cousin is mad at me because I forgot his birthday.

Read this:

Swati is the first to reply in our class group, every time. Movie on Friday? Yes. Garba practice? Yes. Helping the seniors with their fest stall till nine? Yes. She seems to glow in a crowd; I've seen her get a whole bus singing. But when her friends were all away at weddings in the holidays, she posted a photo of an empty room captioned "so bored" and messaged me eleven times in an hour. Last week the fest seniors asked her to copy their attendance sheet for them, and she did, though I saw her hesitate first. I don't know what she was feeling. Maybe she just didn't want them to stop inviting her. I told her she could say no to me anytime and I'd still save her a seat.
Maria

How many times did Swati message Maria in an hour?
She messaged Maria eleven times in an hour.
Why might Swati have agreed to copy the seniors' attendance sheet even though she hesitated?
Maria guesses she didn't want them to stop inviting her; the wish to stay included may have outweighed her doubt.
What choice did Maria make after seeing Swati hesitate?
Maria told Swati she could say no anytime and still have a saved seat, making refusing feel safer.
How might Maria feel watching Swati say yes to everything?
Maria seems concerned and unsure, having noticed Swati's hesitation and the eleven messages, which is why Maria offers a seat with no conditions.

Susy goes to a large school with 800 students, while Sarah goes to a smaller school with only 300 students.  At the start of the school year, Susy had 100 social media followers.  She gained 40 new followers in the first week of the school year, half that in the second week, and half of that in the third week.  Sarah only had 50 social media followers at the start of the year, but she gained 90 new followers the first week, a third of that in the second week, and a third of that in the third week.  After three weeks, how many social media followers did the girl with the most total followers have?

After one week, Susy has 100+40 = 140 followers.
In the second week, Susy gains 40/2 = 20 new followers.
In the third week, Susy gains 20/2 = 10 new followers.
In total, Susy finishes the three weeks with 140+20+10 = 170 total followers.
After one week, Sarah has 50+90 = 140 followers.
After the second week, Sarah gains 90/3 = 30 followers.
After the third week, Sarah gains 30/3 = 10 followers.
So, Sarah finishes the three weeks with 140+30+10 = 180 total followers.
Thus, Sarah is the girl with the most total followers with a total of 180.
The answer is 180.

messages.content: There were 600 people in the stadium when the football game started. Before the game was over, one-fourth of the boys and one-eighth of the girls left early. How many people remained to see the end of the game if there were 240 girls at the beginning of the game?

There were 600 - 240 = 360 boys at the beginning of the game.
So, 360 x 1/4 = 90 boys left early.
And 240 x 1/8 = 30 girls left early.
A total of 90 + 30 = 120 people left early.
Therefore, 600 - 120 = 480 people remained to see the end of the game.
The answer is 480.

Billy buys a 12 pack of soda from the store.  If he has twice as many brothers as sisters, and he has 2 sisters, how many sodas can he give to each of his siblings if he wants to give out the entire 12 pack while giving each the same number?

First, we need to determine how many siblings Billy has. To do this, we perform 2*2= 4 brothers, as he has 2 sisters and twice as many brothers as sisters.
Then we divide the total number of sodas in the 12 pack, which is 12, by the number of siblings, performing 12/6=2 cans per person.
The answer is 2.

Together, the two islands produced 90000+9000= 99000 bananas in that year.
The answer is 99000.

On a hot afternoon in Nairobi, Jamal and Emeka each got a carton of mango juice. Jamal poured his into a tall, thin glass. Emeka poured his into a short, wide cup. 'Mine's more!' Jamal said. Emeka rolled his eyes. 'Same carton, same juice.' 'But mine's higher.' Emeka took both cartons and showed him: empty, same size. Then he poured his cup into another tall glass. Level with Jamal's. Jamal looked from one to the other. 'Okay. Same. But mine still looks better.'

Who poured juice into the short, wide cup?
Emeka poured his juice into the short, wide cup.
How was Jamal feeling when he said 'But mine still looks better'?
He had accepted they were the same, but he felt a little embarrassed and wanted to save face with a joke.
What did Emeka's demonstration show, and why did it work?
Pouring into a matching tall glass showed the same level, which proved the amount didn't change, only the container's shape.
What would change if Jamal were much younger?
He might keep insisting the tall glass had more, because younger children often judge by height alone.
Give a riddle about a mango in exactly two lines; never say its name.

I grow on a tall tree and turn yellow in summer.
My juicy flesh is sweet and my seed is large.
Why is it hard to see in fog? One sentence, no more than 14 words.
Fog is made of tiny water drops that scatter light.

Jumping off the bike-shed roof.

Suraj feels misunderstood and frustrated, believing the real problem is being exhausted all the time.

Keeping the phone in the kitchen at night and waking at the same time on Sunday, because steady habits can ease the tiredness behind the snapping and risky dares.

By noon the village pond near Anirban's house had shrunk to cracked mud. A thin black dog was licking the damp edge, ribs showing.
Anirban and his friend Farhan stopped their cycles. "Poor thing," Farhan said. Anirban wanted to rush over with his water bottle, but the dog growled low when they came closer.
"Let's ask Dadu first," Anirban said.
Dadu came out with his stick and an old clay pot. "Thirsty dogs can snap. Put it there, by the tea stall, and step back."
They filled it from the hand pump. The dog waited until they were far away, then drank for a long time.
Farhan's father, who ran the tea stall, promised to refill it every afternoon. Anirban cycled home with a warm, full feeling in his chest.

Where did they put the clay pot?
By the tea stall.
What did Anirban feel as he cycled home?
A warm, full feeling of kindness and satisfaction in his chest.
Why was asking Dadu first wise?
The dog had growled, and Dadu showed a safe way to help without getting bitten.
How might the dog have seen the boys at first?
As a possible threat, so it growled and waited until they were far away before drinking.

Every Sunday morning in her Manchester flat, Nour woke with a pounding head, deleted the photos from the night before and told herself, never again. By Thursday the promise felt thin. By Saturday she was out again, drinking until she couldn't remember the walk home, and on Sunday the voice was harsher: you're pathetic, you have no control.

Liam found her on the kitchen floor one Sunday, crying into a mug of tea. He didn't lecture. "Hating yourself hasn't worked so far. Can we try something else?"

On Monday Nour went to the university wellbeing service and joined a Wednesday recovery group. Liam agreed to text her on Saturday evenings. The first slip came two weeks later. Liam found her on the kitchen floor, crying into a mug of tea.

Nour felt deep shame and self-hatred, hearing a harsh voice call her pathetic and out of control.

Liam pointed out that self-hatred had not worked and helped her spot triggers and get support, which breaks the cycle instead of feeding it.

Megan works eight hours a day and earns $7.50 per hour.  If she works 20 days a month, how much will be her total earnings for two months of work?

In a day, Megan earns 8 x $7.50 = $60.
In a month, she will be earning 20 x $60 = $1200.
Therefore, Megan will earn a total of 2 x $1200 = $2400 for two months of work.
The answer is 2400.

"Just... healthier. Better food. More moving. You'll see."

A bag of apples.

Abebe feels puzzled and a little guilty; he truly meant the resolution and doesn't understand how it slipped away.
What could make Abebe's goal hold?
Attaching it to a specific when and how, such as a walk straight after work on set days or fruit packed with lunch each morning, so it doesn't depend on memory and mood.
How might Nkechi have seen the resolution from the start?

Ben spends 20% of his after-tax income on his car. If his car payment is $400 and he pays 1/3 of his gross income in taxes, how much does he make per month before taxes?

First divide that amount of the car payment by 20% to find Ben's after-tax salary: $400 / .2 = $2000
Then find the proportion of his salary Ben keeps after taxes by subtracting the tax rate from 1: 1 - 1/3 = 2/3
Then divide Ben's after-tax salary by the proportion of his salary he keeps to find his before-tax salary: $2000 / 2/3 = $3000
The answer is 3000.

Then one evening in March, a dog ran across the road. Naveen swerved. We both fell. I scraped my arms. Naveen hit his head on the kerb.

He was okay, eventually. A few stitches, a week at home. But the doctor said a helmet would have saved him from most of it.

Now I wear a helmet every time, even for five minutes. And when my younger cousin says, "I'm careful, I'll be fine," I tell her about the dog.

A dog ran across the road.

Victor works at Clucks Delux, a restaurant specializing in chicken. An order of Chicken Pasta uses 2 pieces of chicken, an order of Barbecue Chicken uses 3 pieces of chicken, and a family-size Fried Chicken Dinner uses 8 pieces of chicken. Tonight, Victor has 2 Fried Chicken Dinner orders, 6 Chicken Pasta orders, and 3 Barbecue Chicken orders. How many pieces of chicken does he need for all the orders?

Victor needs 2 * 8 = 16 pieces of chicken for Fried Chicken Dinners.
He needs 6 * 2 = 12 pieces of chicken for Chicken Pasta.
He needs 3 * 3 = 9 pieces of chicken for Barbecue Chicken orders.
Thus, he needs 16 + 12 + 9 = 37 pieces of chicken.
The answer is 37.

While camping, Cyrus counted 14 mosquito bites on his arms and legs. He later counted another 10 on his body. While he was suffering, his entire family of 6 other people only got a total of half the number of bites that Cyrus got. If they all have an equal number of bites, how many mosquito bites does each member of the rest of Cyrus' family have?

Altogether, Cyrus got 14 + 10 = 24 mosquito bites.
The rest of his family had a total of 24/2 = 12 mosquito bites.
Each family member had 12/6 = 2 mosquito bites.
The answer is 2.

Rich likes to take long walks through town.  First he walks 20 feet from his house to the sidewalk.  Then he walks 200 feet down the sidewalk to the end of the road.  Then he makes a left and walks double his total distance so far until he reaches the next intersection.  Then he walks half the total distance up to this point again to the end of his route, before turning around and walking the same path all the way back home.  How many feet did Rich walk?

Rich walks 20+200= 220 feet to get to the end of the road.
He then walks double that distance, 220*2= 440 feet to the next intersection.
This makes a total of 220+440= 660 feet.
He then walks half that distance, 660/2= 330 feet to get to the end of his route.
This makes a total of 660+330=990 feet so far.
He then walks that same distance back, for a total of 990*2= 1980 feet in total.
The answer is 1980.

messages.content: A machine at the soda factory can usually fill a barrel of soda in 3 minutes. However this morning a leak went unnoticed and it took 5 minutes to fill one barrel. If the leak remains undetected, how much longer will it take to fill 12 barrels of soda than on a normal day when the machine works fine?

On a regular day it would take 3*12=36 minutes
With the leak it will take 5*12=60 minutes
It will take 60-36=24 more minutes if the leak goes undetected
The answer is 24.

messages.content: A toothpaste box is a cuboid. Its 6 faces come in matching pairs. How many pairs are there?

Answer: 3 pairs: front and back, top and bottom, left and right.

Hold the box and touch the front and the back: they are the same size. Then the top and bottom, then the two ends. 3 pairs of 2 = 6 faces. That is why a cuboid's net has 3 pairs of matching rectangles.

A dancer spins a three-quarter turn clockwise. How many degrees is that? How many right angles?

Answer: 3/4 of 360 degrees = 270 degrees, which is 3 right angles.

A quarter turn is 90 degrees (one right angle), because 360 / 4 = 90. A three-quarter turn is 3 quarter turns: 3 x 90 = 270 degrees. Turn together in class: face the board, turn 90 degrees (face the window), another 90 degrees (180 degrees, face the back), another 90 degrees (270 degrees). A full turn is 4 x 90 = 360 degrees.

Austin and Jake start descending from the 9th floor of a building at the same time. Austin uses the elevator and Jake uses the stairs, descending 3 steps every second. The stairs have 30 steps across each floor. If the elevator will take a minute to get to ground level, how many seconds later will Jake get to the ground floor?

Jake has to descend 30 steps on 9 floors for a total of 9*30 = 270 steps
He descends 3 steps every second so he will descend 270 steps in 270/3 = 90 seconds.
Austin will get down after only a minute (60 seconds) so Jake will get down 90-60 = 30 seconds later.
The answer is 30.

His tale had occupied the whole day, and the sun was upon the verge of the horizon when he departed. I knew that I ought to hasten my descent towards the valley, as I should soon be encompassed in darkness; but my heart was heavy, and my steps slow. The labour of winding among the little paths of the mountain and fixing my feet firmly as I advanced perplexed me, occupied as I was by the emotions which the occurrences of the day had produced. Night was far advanced when I came to the halfway resting-place and seated myself beside the fountain. The stars shone at intervals as the clouds passed from over them; the dark pines rose before me, and every here and there a broken tree lay on the ground; it was a scene of wonderful solemnity and stirred strange thoughts within me. I wept bitterly, and clasping my hands in agony, I exclaimed, "Oh! stars and clouds and winds, ye are all about to mock me; if ye really pity me, crush sensation and memory; let me become as nought; but if not, depart, depart, and leave me in darkness."
The narrator weeps in the dark mountains after a long talk, begging the stars and winds to erase all feeling and memory.

At the village temple fair in Rajasthan, Madhav joined the evening bhajan. The drums beat fast and the whole crowd sang the chorus, and he felt the joy of his grandmother's faith. Later that week, on the road to the district office, Shankar led the farmers' march with a chant in a similar drumbeat, and Madhav caught himself clapping along. But something in Shankar's tone was different. It was stern, hard and angry about the delayed compensation. Madhav's chest tightened. The rhythm was almost the same, but the meaning was not. He listened to the words before joining, and stayed near the edge until he was sure what the group was asking.

Where did Madhav join the evening bhajan?
Madhav joined it at the village temple fair in Rajasthan.
What did Madhav feel when he heard the march chant?
Madhav felt his chest tighten, sensing anger behind a rhythm that sounded like the bhajan. He listened to the words first, because the beat alone did not tell him.
What could a young person do before joining a chant in a crowd?
Listen to the words, see what the group is asking for, and join only if they agree and it is safe.
How might Shankar have seen the chanting?
Shankar sounded stern and angry about the delayed compensation, so the chant was a way of asking to be heard rather than of showing faith or joy.

'Another input meeting?' Mahima said, reading the invite. 'Ayesha, this is the fifth.'
'I just want to make sure design and support are comfortable,' Ayesha said.
'They told you in week one. Design wants the new layout, support wants the old one, and both said they'd live with either.'
'But if I pick one, the other will be upset.'
'And now?'
Ayesha didn't answer.
'The launch was on the 15th,' Mahima said. 'It's the 29th. Design thinks you don't trust their work. Support thinks you're hiding something. My team has been blocked for two weeks. And the client called me this morning, not you.'
'What did the client say?'
'That they'd rather have either version than none.'
Ayesha sat down slowly and cancelled the invite.

When was the launch meant to be?
On the 15th.
Why did Ayesha keep calling meetings, and what was the fear behind them?
Ayesha was afraid that choosing one version would upset the other team, so another meeting felt safer than deciding.
What approach would have suited Ayesha better in week one?
Since both teams said they could live with either, Ayesha could have chosen, explained the reasons and set a date to review it.
How does the delay look to Mahima's team?
Mahima's team has been blocked for two weeks, frustrated that nothing moves while meetings pile up.

messages.content: Mrs. Lopez and her family are going to the movie theatre.  Adult tickets are $11.  Children's tickets (ages 3-12) are $8.  Senior citizen's tickets (ages 60+) are $9.  Mrs. Lopez needs to buy movie tickets for her husband, herself, her parents (ages 72 and 75), and her three children (ages 7, 10, 14).  How much money does she need to buy everyone's tickets?

Mrs. Lopez needs to buy two adult tickets for $11 x 2 = $22.
She needs to buy two senior citizen tickets for $9 x 2 = $18.
She needs to buy three children's tickets for $8 x 3 = $24.
For everyone's tickets, Mrs. Lopez needs to spend $22 + $18 + $24 = $64 for seven tickets.
The answer is 64.

Tuesday night
At six today Tanuja posted in our class group: "Ojas smells like a dustbin, nobody sit near Ojas tomorrow." Eleven people reacted. ELEVEN. It felt like everyone was staring at me through the phone.
I typed a long mean answer about her teeth. Then I deleted it. Papa always says never fight in the group.
I took screenshots instead, even though my hands were shaking, and showed Papa. He read it twice, then sat next to me on the bed. "This is not your fault, and you were right not to reply." He wrote to our class teacher tonight with the screenshots, and she has already answered that she will speak to the class tomorrow.
I still feel sick about going to school. But not alone.
Ojas

How many people reacted to Tanuja's post?
Eleven.
How did Ojas feel after seeing the post?
Ojas felt hurt and exposed, as if everyone was staring through the phone.
Which choices helped Ojas, and why?
Deleting the angry reply, saving screenshots and showing Papa, who wrote to the class teacher that night.
How might Tanuja see her post compared with Ojas?
Tanuja may think it is just a joke for laughs, while for Ojas it is public and deeply hurtful.

Preeti lay beside her, fanning her with a folded newspaper, and began to sing an old lullaby, slow and low. She sang off key; she always did.
Madhuri's whimpers slowed. Her hand found Preeti's arm and stayed there. By the third verse, her breathing was deep and even.

What did Preeti fan Madhuri with?
A folded newspaper.
Why did Madhuri settle even though Preeti sang off key?
She felt safe with her mother close, and the slow, warm rhythm mattered more than the tune; her hand on Preeti's arm shows she felt comforted.
What would you tell a parent who thinks they can't sing well enough?
That a slow, warm voice and closeness soothe a child far more than a perfect tune.
What was the hot night like for Preeti?
It was probably tiring and uncomfortable, yet she stayed close and kept singing for Madhuri.

The payment site had crashed at 11 pm on the biggest sale night of the year, and by 1 am it was back, thanks mostly to Hemant, who had traced the fault to a single expired certificate. The next morning Akash, the team lead, had exactly two minutes at the company all-hands before the chief executive's update. Two minutes, forty people on the call, and he hadn't slept. The easy thing was "Thanks to the team for last night." He'd heard that line a hundred times; it meant nothing. So he said, "Quick update: the outage lasted two hours. It was fixed because Hemant stayed calm, found an expired certificate in a file nobody had opened in a year, and walked the rest of us through the fix. Hemant, thank you. That saved the sale." In the chat, a dozen clapping hands appeared under Hemant's name. Hemant messaged Akash privately: "Nobody has ever said my name on that call before."

What fault did Hemant find?
An expired certificate in a file nobody had opened in a year.
How did Hemant feel when Akash named him on the call?
Hemant felt seen and moved, messaging that nobody had ever said his name on that call before.
What made Akash's credit effective despite the time pressure?
It was timely, public and specific: he named Hemant, what he found and how it saved the sale, instead of a generic thanks to the team.
What would have changed if Akash had only said 'Thanks to the team'?
Hemant's work would have stayed invisible, and the thanks would have meant as little as it always had.

Dear Nilesh,
I've been avoiding you, and I want to tell you why. For the past year, when everything got too much, the exams, the fights at home, I hurt myself. I'm not going to describe it. It gave me a few minutes of quiet, and then I felt so ashamed I couldn't look at anyone.
Last month my sister found out. She didn't yell. She stayed with me that night, and we called a helpline. Now I see a counsellor every week, and I have a plan for bad nights.
Part of that plan is having people I can call. I'd like you to be one of them. You don't have to fix anything. Just pick up.
I'm trying. It's slow.
Yusuf

Who found out last month?
Yusuf's sister.
How did Yusuf feel after each time of self-harm?
Yusuf felt a few minutes of quiet, then deep shame, unable to look at anyone.
What is helping Yusuf now?
Weekly counselling, a plan for bad nights, a sister who stayed and called a helpline, and trusted people to call.
How might Nilesh feel reading this letter?
Nilesh may feel sad and worried but trusted and glad to be asked to help.

Sit down, Sabina, and I'll tell you what I never told the new joiners. My name is Karthik, and at your age I found out that our supplier was cutting corners on the bridge bolts. Nobody had been hurt yet.

I didn't sleep for a week. I weighed it: the harm to strangers on that road against my job and my mother's medical bills. I copied nothing I wasn't entitled to. I wrote down dates and what I saw, exactly, not what I guessed. Then I asked a senior engineer I trusted what my options were, and he suggested a lawyer.

I reported it through the company's channel first, then to the regulator. It cost me two promotions and some friends. I won't pretend otherwise.

But I never spread rumours, and I never went after anyone out of anger. That mattered to me. The bolts were replaced. I can still cross that bridge.

What did Karthik find out about the supplier?
Karthik found out that the supplier was cutting corners on the bridge bolts.
What might Karthik have been worried about during the sleepless week?
Karthik weighed the possible harm to strangers on the road against the risk to the job and the mother's medical bills.
What steps did Karthik take that Sabina could learn from?
Karthik wrote down accurate dates and facts, sought advice from a trusted senior and a lawyer, and used the company channel and then the regulator, without rumour or revenge.
How might the new joiners have felt if they had known the story earlier?
They may have felt both worried about the cost and reassured that speaking up can be done carefully, since Karthik describes real losses honestly.

Dear Bidisha Apu,
You said to write when things feel heavy, so here I am.
School has been strange since you left. On Monday I posted in the class group asking if anyone had the chemistry notes. Forty minutes, nothing. Then Rumana replied 'check the drive' with no emoji. Not even a smiley. I read that about ten times.
At lunch, Tasnim said something and everyone laughed just as I sat down. I'm almost sure it was about me. So now I eat quickly and go to the library, and when people talk to me I answer in one word, and they've mostly stopped talking to me. Which proves it, doesn't it?
Or does it? I can't tell anymore.
Write back soon 🥺
Nazia

Rumana replied 'check the drive' with no emoji.
Why did Nazia read Rumana's reply about ten times?
Nazia was searching it for signs of dislike, because a lonely, worried mind was treating a missing smiley as a threat.

How might the classmates see Nazia's one-word answers?

Why should a seed be planted in damp soil and not left on a dry shelf?
A seed sprouts only when it gets water. Because water soaks into the seed and wakes up the tiny plant inside, damp soil lets it start growing, while a dry shelf keeps it sleeping.

A road sign warns of a long stretch of bad road. What does stretch mean there?

Here a stretch is a long piece of land, road or water. It is a noun. It can also mean a period of time. The verb means to pull something longer.

Philip has a farm with animals. He has 20 cows, 50% more ducks. Philip also has as many pigs as one-fifth of ducks and cows in total. How many animals does Philip have on his farm?

Philip has 50/100 * 20 = 10 more ducks than cows.
Which means he has 20 + 10 = 30 ducks.
So Philip's cows and ducks sum up to 20 + 30 = 50 animals.
If there are 50 cows and ducks, that means Philip has 1/5 * 50 = 10 pigs.
In total Philip has 50 + 10 = 60 animals on his farm.
The answer is 60.

Bhavna suggested the campus counsellor and calling Mummy, which could bring support from people trained and people who care while Bhavna stays on the phone. 🤍
What is it like for Bhavna to receive this message late at night?

Counsellor's note, Thursday
Parth, 8, came to see me after his aunt, Rajni, had asked him about a scratch on his cousin's bicycle. She had asked, "You scratched it while riding, didn't you? You rode it into the gate?" By evening Parth was saying he had ridden it into the gate. He told me the same, looking at the floor.
I asked only, "What happened with the bicycle?" and waited. Slowly he said he had not ridden it at all that day; he had been drawing. His aunt later checked and found the scratch had been there since the rains.
I explained to Rajni how questions like hers can put words into a child's mouth. She was upset with herself and apologised to Parth.
Jasleen

What had Parth been doing that day instead of riding?
He had been drawing.
Why did Parth start saying he rode the bicycle into the gate?
His aunt's questions already held the answer, and hearing them made the story feel true, so he went along and began to believe it.
Which question from Jasleen let Parth answer accurately?
Jasleen asked only "What happened with the bicycle?" and waited, an open question that suggested no answer.
How did Rajni feel on learning what her questions had done?
She was upset with herself and apologised to Parth, realising she had put words into his mouth. 🙏

Sunday. Kalyani posted in the city's youth forum that the new flyover would cut through the old market and hurt small shopkeepers. By night, her phone was full. Some people disagreed politely. Others didn't. "Go back to school, stupid girl." "Traitor to development." Someone found her photo and posted it with insults. She sat up till two, typing and deleting angry replies.

Monday. Dolma found her in the library, grey-faced. "Don't answer them," Dolma said. "Screenshot everything. Every name, every time." They did it together, then blocked eleven accounts. After school Kalyani showed her father. He went quiet, then said, "You had every right to your opinion. They have no right to this." He reported the accounts that evening and emailed the forum moderators.

Thursday. Two accounts had been removed. The photo post was gone. Kalyani still felt shaky when her phone buzzed. But she hadn't sent a single reply. She wrote a new post about the market, calmer, with facts, and turned comments off.

How many accounts did Kalyani and Dolma block?
They blocked eleven accounts.
What was Kalyani feeling on Sunday night?
Kalyani felt hurt, angry and frightened, sitting up till two typing and deleting angry replies.
What steps helped Kalyani, and why?
Not replying, saving screenshots, blocking and telling her father helped, because it kept proof and let a trusted adult report the abuse.
How does Kalyani's father see what happened?
He sees her opinion as her right and the abuse as unacceptable, and acts that same evening by reporting it.

Tanvir, you should've seen my under-sixteen girls before the final. Ruhi had to bounce the ball exactly seven times. Mehak wore her socks inside out. And nobody, nobody, was allowed to say "we'll win" in the dressing room.
I used to think I should stamp it out. Then I realised they'd all trained four days a week for months. The rituals weren't replacing the work. They were just a way to hold their nerves. So I let them be.
There was one thing I did stop. Juhi wanted to play on a sprained ankle because she'd "got her lucky band on, so it'll be fine." No band fixes an ankle. She sat out and iced it.
So: charms, fine. Charms instead of sense? That's where I step in. Damini's rule.

How many times did Ruhi have to bounce the ball?
Exactly seven times.
What were the players feeling that the rituals helped with?
Nerves before the final; the rituals gave them a sense of control and calm.
When did Damini step in, and why?
When Juhi wanted to play on a sprained ankle trusting her lucky band, because that ritual was leading to a harmful choice.
How might Juhi have felt about sitting out?
Probably disappointed and frustrated, but safer, and perhaps later grateful that her coach took the ankle seriously.
Tom and Devin have been teaching for a total of 70 years. Devin has been teaching for 5 less than half the number of years that Tom has. How many years has Tom been teaching?

Let x be the number of years Tom has been teaching
Devin has been teaching for (1/2)x-5 years
70=x+((1/2)x-5)
70=(3/2)x-5
75=(3/2)x
x=50
Tom has been teaching for 50 years
The answer is 50.

Why does Chyavana make a promise to the twins, and what happens to them?

"Having obtained coveted beauty and also his wife, Chyavana, of exceeding energy, well pleased, spake these words unto the nose-born celestials: 'Since at your hands, an old man, I have obtained youth, and beauty, and also this wife of mine, I will, well pleased, make you quaffers of the Soma juice in the presence of the lord of celestials himself. This I tell you truly.' Hearing this, highly delighted, the twins ascendedto heaven; and Chyavana and Sukanya too passed their days happily even like celestials."
He is pleased that they gave him youth, beauty and his wife. In return he promises them a share of the Soma juice, and the twins go happily to heaven.
Is it "offical" or "official"?

It is "official", with a double f and an "i" before "al".
Example: She received an official letter from the school.

Three friends signed up for the school race in March.

Afreen taped a card to her mirror: the race date, five kilometres without stopping, and "start: one kilometre." Each week she added a little. By week five her knee ached after runs on the hard road by the market. She cut her distance, moved to the soft grass of the school field, and asked the coach about her shoes before returning slowly to the card.

Dolma ran and walked on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, with days between to let her legs settle. Every evening she noted the run in a diary, adding only a little distance. Her legs felt tired but never sore.

Dhruv wanted a place on the school team more than either of them. He ran before school and again after dinner from the first day, brushing off the soreness in his calves. By the second week he had hurt a calf badly enough to stop running for weeks. The trials went ahead without him.

Which days did Dolma run and walk?
Dolma ran and walked on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday.
How did Afreen's response to her aching knee differ from Dhruv's response to soreness, and what did each lead to?
Afreen cut her distance, changed surface and asked the coach, then returned slowly to her card, while Dhruv brushed off the soreness and ended up unable to run for weeks.
What might Dhruv be feeling while the trials go ahead without him?
Frustration and regret, since the extra training he hoped would speed things up cost him the chance he wanted most. 😔
What could Dhruv do when he is ready to start running again?
Dhruv could begin with short sessions, leave rest days between them, and ask the coach to help him build up slowly.
