Ishita, you're angry about your cousin's in-laws and their demands? Good. Let your Shankar mama tell you about 1998. I was twenty-five, and my elder brother, your Periappa, was getting married. At the first planning meeting, my father said, "Of course the girl's side will give a scooter and gold." I felt my face go hot. I wanted to shout. But I waited until everyone had finished, and then I said, calmly, "Appa, if we take anything, it's dowry. I won't be part of that." The room went silent. My father was furious.
That night I sat with my Paati. She had been given away with a buffalo and a debt. She listened, then said, "The boy is right." The next morning she said it at breakfast, in front of everyone. Two uncles agreed. It took months, but Periappa's wedding happened with no scooter. Anger would have lost that fight. Calm, and Paati, won it.

What did Shankar's father say the girl's side would give?
A scooter and gold.
How did young Shankar feel at the planning meeting, and how did he handle it?
He felt angry, his face hot, but he waited and spoke calmly instead of shouting.
What was the turning point in Shankar mama's story?
Paati backing him at breakfast in front of everyone, which made two uncles agree and showed how one clear voice with an elder ally makes others braver.
How might Paati have felt when young Shankar spoke to her?
She probably felt moved and vindicated, remembering her own marriage with a buffalo and a debt.

"Minakshi, please sit. I'll be direct. The company is closing the Pune design team. Your role ends on the thirtieth."
"Okay."
"You'll get two months' pay, and HR will help with references."
"Okay."
Jagdish paused. "Do you have any questions?"
"No. That's fine. Should I finish the Mehra deck today?"
"You... don't have to."
"I'll finish it."
She walked back to her desk and finished the deck. She even replied to a joke in the team chat.
At eleven that night, brushing her teeth, Minakshi sat down on the bathroom floor and cried for a long time. The next morning she messaged Jagdish: "I think I do have questions now."

When does Minakshi's role end?
Her role ends on the thirtieth.
Why did Minakshi keep saying "Okay" and offer to finish the deck?
She was in shock, numb and flat, so the news had not really landed yet; it looked like calm but wasn't.
How could Jagdish help after such a flat reaction?
He could check in the next day and say questions are welcome at any time, since the real reaction may come later.
How might Jagdish have read Minakshi's calm in the meeting?
He may have been puzzled or even relieved, thinking she took it well, without seeing the shock underneath.
Kavya buys a pencil for ₹6, an eraser for ₹4 and a notebook for ₹25. What is the total bill?

Answer: ₹35.

Write the three prices in a column, like a shop bill. Look for easy pairs first: 6 + 4 = 10. Then 10 + 25 = 35. Adding the prices in a clever order is allowed, because the total is the same in any order. Now make a bill for a pen ₹12, a sharpener ₹5 and a scale ₹8 (₹25).

Thursday night. The whole class went quiet when I walked in. I reported the changed marks on Monday, and today nobody saved me a seat and my name was left off the project group. Somebody drew a rat on my notebook.
In the canteen I sat alone until Mahima put her tray down across from me and said, “I think you did the right thing.” She didn’t say anything else. I nearly cried into my tea.
I keep asking myself whether I’m a troublemaker. I’m still angry and scared. Tomorrow I’m going to show the counsellor the drawing. At least one person is on my side.
— Baljeet

Mahima said, “I think you did the right thing.”
Why did Baljeet nearly cry into the tea?
Baljeet had felt shut out all day, and one kind sentence from Mahima showed someone was on Baljeet's side. Relief and loneliness came together.
What is Baljeet planning to do about the rat drawing, and why is it sensible?
Baljeet plans to show the counsellor the drawing. Telling an adult who can act helps the retaliation stop.
What might Mahima have been feeling when she sat down at Baljeet's table?
Mahima may have felt nervous about being seen with Baljeet but decided to be kind anyway. Saying so quietly and only once suggests a careful, brave gesture.

In the academic adviser's office at the university in Kochi, Pooja's form lay on the desk. Under "Elective" she had written "Basic Accounting". Irfan, the adviser, tapped the line. "Last semester you told me marine biology was the reason you came here." Pooja kept her eyes on her sandals. "Marine Ecology has field exams on the boat. People say it's really hard. My CGPA is 9.1. If I get a C, I lose the merit list." "Is accounting something you want to learn?" "No. But it's safe." Irfan waited. Pooja thought of the tide pools she had photographed on the field trip, the tiny crabs. She didn't change the form. Walking out, she felt as if she had shut a door very quietly.

What did Pooja write under 'Elective'?
"Basic Accounting".
Why did Pooja keep her eyes on her sandals?
She likely felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, knowing she was choosing the safe course over marine biology, the reason she came.
What could Pooja still do before the form is final?
She could ask Irfan what support exists for Marine Ecology, or whether one lower grade really ends the merit list, and decide with facts rather than fear.
How might Irfan feel watching Pooja leave the form unchanged?
Irfan may feel concerned, seeing fear of a C quietly outweigh the passion Pooja described last semester.

The whole of Dhanauri had come to the school ground for the district football final. Farhan, fourteen, stood on an upturned crate by the fence with his sister Sharmila.
Their village team was one goal down. Ten minutes left. Farhan's heart thumped so hard he could hear it over the crowd. His fists were clenched. Every time the ball came near the goal, he forgot to breathe.
"Farhan, you're shaking the crate," Sharmila said.
"Shh!"
Then the tea-seller's son, Imtiaz, took a long shot from outside the box. It sailed past the goalkeeper's hands.
Farhan screamed. He jumped off the crate and grabbed Sharmila and a stranger in one hug. The whole ground was roaring. For a minute, every person there felt like one person.

Who took the long shot?
Imtiaz, the tea-seller's son.
What was Farhan feeling as the ball came near the goal?
He felt tense and excited, his heart thumping as if he were playing.
What does the ending show about watching a match with a crowd?
Sharing the tension with others turns a goal into joy felt by everyone together.
How might Sharmila experience the match next to Farhan?
She seems amused by his nerves at first, then gets swept into the shared joy of the hug.

Ammamma.

Halfway through, the man beside me was counting ceiling tiles, and a woman in front had started a shopping list on her phone. I lost track after the lift repair figures. We wrote it in a shared note under the heading "our rules, subject to change". Five lines. Amandeep added: "If one of us goes quiet, we ask, not assume." I feel lighter, like a knot loosened a little. Tomorrow I go. Not scared, just aware. — Kamal

They could review the note together every few months, because needs change and a review keeps the rules from turning into old promises.
How might Amandeep see the talk?
Amandeep asks for a daily message and honesty and adds the rule about asking, so Amandeep seems to want closeness and clarity more than long calls.

Give a two-sentence summary of this teaching.

That man who, having perpetrated sinful acts through stupefaction of mind, feels the pangs of repentance and sets his heart on contemplation (of the deity), has not to endure the consequences of his sins. One becomes freed from one's sins in proportion as one repents for them. If one having committed a sin, O king, proclaims it in the presence of Brahmanas conversant with duties, one becomes quickly cleansed from the obloquy arising from one's sin. Accordingly as one becomes cleansed therefrom fully or otherwise, like a snake freed from his diseased slough. By making, with a concentrated mind, gifts of diverse kinds unto a Brahmana, and concentrating the mind (on the deity), one attains to an auspicious end. I shall now tell thee what those gifts are, O Yudhisthira, by making which a person, even if guilty of having committed sinful acts, may become endued with merit.

A person who has done wrong out of confusion can be freed from it by truly repenting, confessing and turning the mind to God. The speaker then offers to explain the gifts that help such a person gain merit.

I'm Jasleen. Last month a game I love started showing a shiny panda outfit every time I lost a level. "Win faster with Panda Power!" it flashed. After a few days I truly believed I couldn't win without it. I even counted my birthday money in my head.
Then I noticed something. The pop-up came right after I lost, every single time, when I felt worst. That wasn't luck; somebody planned it that way.
I asked Papa before buying anything, and he said to wait a week and see if I still wanted it. I also asked my friend Chetan if my plain outfit looked silly. He laughed. "I never even noticed what you wear. I just like racing you." I never bought the panda.

At the preschool's quiet corner, Tenzin tucked the toy rabbit into a shoebox bed. He folded a hanky over it and patted it three times. “Goodnight, Rabbit. I'm right here,” he whispered. Salma Ma'am, nearby, asked softly, “Where did you learn to tuck in so nicely?” “My Papa does it for me,” said Tenzin. “Three pats.” He put a finger to his lips when another child came close. “Shh. Rabbit's sleeping.” The other child whispered too.

Three times.

Cassie is trimming her pet's nails. She has four dogs and eight parrots. Each dog has four nails on each foot, and each parrot has three claws on each leg, except for one parrot who has an extra toe. How many nails does Cassie need to cut?

First, find the number of dog nails by multiplying the number of dogs by the number of nails on each leg and the number of legs on each dog: 4 dogs * 4 legs per dog * 4 nails per leg = 64 nails.
Then do the same for parrots, ignoring the one parrot's extra toe for now: 8 parrots * 2 legs per parrot * 3 nails per leg = 48 nails
Now add one to the previous number because one parrot has an extra toe: 48 + 1 = 49 nails.
Now add the number of nails from the parrots and the dog: 49 nails + 64 nails = 113 nails.
The answer is 113.

The team looked up from their laptops.
"Elizabeth rebuilt the onboarding guide over two weekends. She cut it from forty pages to twelve and added the video walkthroughs. The client's head of operations told me that guide is the reason they stayed."

She cut it from forty pages to twelve.
What did Elizabeth's red cheeks and later message suggest?

Her brother Yash, who everyone thought was still working at the tile shop, had lost the job in spring and taken a loan from a local lender to keep up the pretence. Now the lender's man had begun calling at the house. Their parents thought the calls were for the shop. That evening, at the tea stall near the bus stand, she told only Aunt Mala, the retired schoolteacher, who listened without gasping. Later Elizabeth sat down with Yash. “I won't say it behind your back,” she said. “But they need to hear it before the man comes again. You tell them, and I sit beside you.”

What had Yash lost in spring?
Yash had lost the job at the tile shop in spring.
What did Elizabeth worry about and want when deciding who should know?
Elizabeth was weighing Yash's privacy against the parents' right to know before the lender's man came again. She also did not want to use the secret against him.
What choice did Elizabeth make about telling the parents?
She asked Yash to tell them himself and offered to sit beside him, instead of speaking behind his back.
How might Yash feel when Elizabeth says, “I sit beside you”?
Yash may feel relieved that he is not left alone with it, though probably still ashamed, since he had kept up the pretence for months.

The counsellor's room at St Joseph's had a dripping air conditioner and a jar of mints nobody ate. Saurabh sat turning a mint over in his fingers for five minutes before he spoke. 'I don't know what's wrong with me. My friend Tejas... when he talks to a girl, I feel weird. Jealous. Not a friend kind of jealous. And then I'm scared I'm... I don't even know the word.' The counsellor, Mrs Pillai, didn't flinch. 'Nothing's wrong with you, Saurabh. Lots of people your age feel unsure about who they're drawn to. You don't have to pick a label today, or this year.' He let out a breath he hadn't known he was holding. She wrote down a helpline run by trained counsellors and the name of a book in the school library, instead of the random videos he'd been watching at night. 'You can come back any Thursday,' she said. Saurabh pocketed the mint.

What did Mrs Pillai write down for Saurabh?
A helpline run by trained counsellors and the name of a book in the school library.
What was Saurabh feeling as he turned the mint over?
He felt scared and confused about his feelings for Tejas, unsure there was even a word for them.
What did Mrs Pillai's response get right?
She stayed calm, said nothing was wrong with him, removed pressure to label, and pointed him to reliable information and a safe place to return.
What would change if Saurabh had only kept watching random videos at night?
He might take in confusing or frightening messages alone, instead of calm facts from a safe adult.

A mother buys a box of sweets. She kept 1/3 of the sweets and divided the rest between her 3 children. The eldest got 8 sweets while the youngest got half as many. If there are 27 pieces of sweets in the box, how many sweets did the second child gets?

The mother kept 27 x 1/3 = 9 pieces of sweets.
So there were 27 - 9 = 18 sweets that were divided between the 3 children.
The youngest child got 8/2 = 4 sweets.
So the eldest and the youngest got a total of 8 + 4 = 12 sweets.
Therefore, the second child gets 18 - 12 = 6 sweets.
The answer is 6.

She cried the whole way to school.

When I was in Class 9, Papa got a phone call that my grandfather had been rushed to hospital. When he told us, I laughed. Not a big laugh, just a short, weird giggle I couldn't stop.
My sister Vandana turned to me, furious. "How can you laugh? Are you mad?"
I didn't know why I laughed. I wasn't happy. My stomach was in knots. I felt like crying but the laugh came out instead.
Later that night, Mummy explained that some people laugh when they're shocked or scared. It's the body letting off stress.
Vandana came to my room and said sorry for shouting. I said sorry for laughing. We sat together and waited for news.
- Divyansh

When Divyansh heard his grandfather was in hospital, he laughed without meaning to, and his sister was angry. Their mother explained that shock can cause laughter, and the two siblings made up and waited for news together.

Bill had to finish a project from work that was to take him 4 days. If he took 6 seven-hour naps in the four days, how long did he spend working on the project?

The time he spent working on the project is 96-42 = 54 hours.
The answer is 54.

That evening she was waiting in the kitchen, arms folded. 'Do you know what happens to people who get arrested? No job, no future!' Anders felt the old anger rise. Nigel won $45 but gave some away. His mother gave him $80 more. If now Nigel has $10 more than twice the amount he originally had, how much money did he give away?

Twice the amount Nigel originally had is 2 * 45 = 90 dollars

Before his mother gave him 80 dollars, he had been left with 100 - 80 = 20 dollars
This means that Nigel gave away 45 - 20 = 25 dollars
The answer is 25.

messages.content: Verna weighs 17 pounds more than Haley, and Verna weighs half as much as Sherry. If Haley weighs 103 pounds, how many pounds do Verna and Sherry weigh together?

Verna weighs 103+17 = 120 pounds
Sherry weighs 120*2 = 240 pounds
Verna and Sherry weigh 120+240=360 pounds together.
The answer is 360.

Tracy, Michelle, and Kati take a road trip that is a total of 1000 miles.  Tracy drives 20 miles more than twice Michelle, and Michelle drives 3 times the amount that Katie drives. How many miles does Michelle drive?

Let x represent the number of miles Kati drives
Michelle:3x
Tracy:20+2(3x)=20+6x
Total:x+3x+20+6x=1000
10x+20=1000
10x=980
x=98 miles
3(98)=294 miles
The answer is 294.

'That is your ego speaking,' the leader said gently. 'People who leave before the course ends invite misfortune on their families.' The words followed her all day. Her voice shook as she repeated the leader's words. Sabina was quiet, then said, 'Kalyani, a real teacher doesn't scare you into staying. That's fear and guilt being used on you.' Carly is a pet groomer. Today, her task was trimming the four nails on dogs' paws. She trimmed 164 nails, but three of the dogs had only three legs. How many dogs did Carly work on?

Let N be the number of dogs with 4 legs Carly worked on.
All the dogs with 4 legs had 4N paws.
There were 3 * 3 = 9 paws on dogs with 3 legs.
At 4 nails per paw, she trimmed 164 / 4 = 41 paws.
She worked on 4N + 9 = 41 paws.
Thus, she worked on 4N = 32 paws on dogs with 4 legs.
She worked on N = 32 / 4 = 8 dogs with 4 legs.
Thus, Carly worked on 8 + 3 = 11 dogs.
The answer is 11.

Nadia smiled slightly and wrote something down. 'The weather app: what happens if the forecast service is down?'

Nadia's next questions were shorter. At the end came one plain sentence: 'Your portfolio says you built these. I need to know which parts you'd defend.'
On the bus home, Zanele deleted the calculator from the site. Then, slowly, the other two.

Where was the interview held?
In a glass meeting room in Cape Town.
What was Zanele feeling on the bus home while deleting the projects?
Zanele likely felt ashamed and deflated, realising the copied projects had hurt trust instead of helping.
Which approach would suit Zanele better for the next application?
Build one or two projects from an original idea and be ready to explain every choice, rather than listing tutorial copies.
How does the interview look from Nadia's side?
Nadia wants to know which parts are really Zanele's work, and the answers make trust harder, so the questions get shorter.

messages.content: Write a thank-you note to a teacher. It needs two lines: the first line is "Dear Ma'am," and the second line must contain the word "patience".

Dear Ma'am,
Thank you for your patience and kindness all year.

Read this:

Friday, staff room

Exam week. I'm watching my class ten students and noticing little rituals everywhere. Parveen has a red thread on her wrist "for luck." Two boys wear the same socks for every test. Someone won't say "I'll pass" out loud in case it jinxes it.

It used to make me want to lecture. Now I think it's just comfort. Most of them are studying hard.

Only one worries me: a girl who said she doesn't need to revise because her charm will help. I spoke to her after class and to her mother on the phone this evening. We'll make a plan together on Monday.

Parveen smiled at me today and showed her thread. I told her it's pretty. She's top of the class.

— Ayesha

What does Parveen wear on her wrist for luck?
A red thread.
How does Ayesha feel about the students' rituals now?
Ayesha feels calm and accepting, seeing them as comfort rather than something to lecture about.
What did Ayesha do about the girl who wasn't revising?
Ayesha spoke to her after class and to her mother that evening, planning to make a study plan on Monday.
How might Parveen feel when Ayesha says her thread is pretty?
Parveen probably feels pleased and respected, not judged.
Let's play a game of cards, and loser buys the snacks. What did I leave out?

Let's play a game of cards, and the loser buys the snacks.
Why: "Loser" is singular and needs "the".

The metro carriage swayed, and every seat was full. Ritu, twenty-four, noticed Yogesh Uncle at the door, one hand on the pole and the other on a cane. His knuckles were pale. Before he could ask, she stood and said, "Uncle, please sit here."
"You keep it, beta," he said.
"I get off in two stops, please."
He sat with a small sigh. A teenager across the aisle looked up, then stood for a woman carrying a toddler. A man moved his bag from the seat next to her. The whole coach seemed to loosen. Ritu held the rail and felt warm, though her legs were tired.

What was Yogesh Uncle holding in his hands?
He held the pole with one hand and a cane in the other.
What was Ritu feeling as she held the rail after giving up her seat?
Ritu felt warm and content, even though her legs were tired.
What did Ritu do that made a difference for others in the coach?
She offered the seat before being asked, and the teenager and another man soon copied by giving up a seat and moving a bag.
How might Yogesh Uncle have felt standing at the door with a cane?
He was probably tired and unsteady, shown by his pale knuckles, and he may have been reluctant to accept help at first, saying 'You keep it, beta'.

It takes Matt 2 minutes per problem to do his math homework with a calculator and 5 minutes per problem without a calculator. If Matt's assignment has 20 problems, how much time will using a calculator save?

First find the time difference per problem: 5 minutes/problem - 2 minutes/problem = 3 minutes/problem
Then multiply that number by the number of problems to find the total time difference: 3 minutes/problem * 20 problems = 60 minutes
The answer is 60.
Should I pack my "swimming costume" or my "bathing suit" for the trip?

They mean the same clothing for swimming. "Swimming costume" is British, and "bathing suit" is American, though Americans also say "swimsuit".
Examples: Pack your swimming costume in the blue bag. Pack your bathing suit in the blue bag.
Which is polite at the classroom door: "can I come in" or "may I come in"?

"May I come in?" is the more polite form because "may" asks for permission. "Can" is common in speech and not wrong, but it is less formal.
Example: May I come in, Ma'am?

I'm Ishita. At fifteen, my school's name was stitched into who I was. When the city newspaper ranked us second for board results, I walked about like the proudest girl in the corridor. The next year we slipped to sixth, and my mood slipped with it. I couldn't eat lunch properly. Then someone on an online forum called our school "a rote factory", and I spent till two at night replying to strangers. My friend Pranav, from another school, joked, "Relax, your school isn't your mother." I didn't talk to him for a week. Looking back, what hurt wasn't the ranking. It was that I'd let the school's name hold my own sense of being good enough. I still love my school. I just keep a bit of myself outside it now.

Where did someone call Ishita's school 'a rote factory'?
Someone called it that on an online forum.
Why did Pranav's joke upset Ishita so much at fifteen?
Because her sense of being good enough was tied to the school, so a joke about it felt like an insult to her.
What turning point helped Ishita keep her pride without being ruled by it?
Looking back and seeing that the ranking only hurt because she let the school's name hold her self-worth, she chose to keep part of herself outside it.
How might Pranav have felt during the week Ishita didn't talk to him?
Pranav might have felt confused and shut out, since he meant a light joke and suddenly lost a friend's company over it.

Greg is riding his bike around town and notices that each block he rides, his wheels rotate 200 times. He's now on a a trail and wants to make sure he rides at least 8 blocks. His wheels have already rotated 600 times, how many more times do they need to rotate to reach his goal?

They need to rotate 1,600 times because 8 x 200 = 1,600
They need to rotate 1,000 more times because 1,600 - 600 = 1,000
The answer is 1000.
My younger cousin plays video games for hours and my aunt is worried.
Parents often worry about that, and it is good that someone cares enough to notice. Hours of play can crowd out sleep, homework and time outdoors.
Should I talk to my cousin or to my aunt?
Maybe both, separately. With your cousin, be friendly, not bossy, and ask what they enjoy about the game. With your aunt, you could suggest agreeing on daily limits together.
What limit is fair?

There is no single right number. It helps if the limit is agreed in advance and written down, and if homework and meals come first. Your aunt knows the household best, so the decision is hers to make.

Friday, week 5
Session 3 of the week. Run 3 min, walk 1 min, eight times. Legs fine. Breathing okay after the fourth round.
Rest days are still annoying. On Tuesday and Thursday I wanted to go again, but the plan says Monday, Wednesday and Friday only, with a day off between, and Disha (who runs for the district) says rest is when the legs get stronger, not weaker. So I did stretches and homework instead.
Looking back at weeks 1 to 4 in this diary: week 1 was run 1 min, walk 2. My shins hurt a bit in week 2 when I tried to add two things at once, so since then I change only one thing each week: either a longer run or one more round.
Next week: run 4 min, walk 1 min, still eight rounds. No more than that.
– Hemant

Which days does Hemant's plan allow for running?
Monday, Wednesday and Friday only, with a day off between.
How did Hemant feel about the rest days?
Hemant found them annoying and felt restless on Tuesday and Thursday, but trusted the plan and Disha's advice.
What else could Hemant do if the shin pain comes back?
Stay at the same level for a week, and ask a coach or the doctor if the pain keeps going or worries Hemant.
How might Disha see Hemant's diary?
Disha would likely be pleased to see slow, single changes and rest days respected, the way experienced runners train.

I walk for an hour every day after dinner.

"We took you on as a favour, you know," the supervisor told Irfan in his third week, handing him another stack of files. Irfan nodded and stayed until nine every night, feeling he owed them everything. The work was full days with no stipend, and the promise of a job after the trial had not been repeated. He felt used but did not want to lose the firm's name on his CV. In the next department, Kashish sat with him for an hour over a spreadsheet, gave him a real client summary to draft, and marked his mistakes without sighing. He began arriving early just to hear her explain things. At a wedding, his mother, Vidya, told the aunties that her son worked at a big firm. Irfan smiled and felt a lump in his chest. That night he told her the truth: mostly unpaid, but Kashish was teaching him a lot, and he had a plan. He would ask about a stipend and learning goals, give it until the end of the month, and ask Kashish for a reference either way. "And if nothing changes, I'll leave," he said.

How long did Irfan plan to give the firm before deciding?
He planned to give it until the end of the month.
How did the supervisor's talk of a favour differ from what Kashish did, and how did each shape Irfan's feelings?
The supervisor's favour made Irfan feel he owed endless work, so he felt indebted and used, while Kashish taught him properly and gave real tasks, so he admired her and wanted to learn.
What was Irfan feeling when his mother told the aunties about the big firm?
He felt a guilty gap, with a lump in his chest, because her pride did not match his unpaid days.
What made Irfan's talk with his mother a good next step?
He told her the truth gently, said what he was learning and laid out a plan, instead of keeping up the pretence. 🙂

Under the neem tree beside the village school, Abhinav rolled the wooden bullock cart along the dust to the fence and back. Yusuf sat waiting, hands tucked under his knees. Then Abhinav stopped and held the cart out. "Ab tumhari baari." Yusuf blinked. A warm, surprised feeling spread through his chest. He pushed the cart slowly. The next day he ran it along the fence once and held it out to Abhinav. "Ab tum."

Where did Abhinav roll the wooden bullock cart?
Abhinav rolled it along the dust to the fence and back, under the neem tree.
What was Yusuf feeling when Abhinav held the cart out to him?
He was surprised and warm inside. His blink and the warm feeling in his chest show he had not expected to be given a turn.
What did Yusuf learn from being given a turn that he then put into practice?
He saw that fair sharing feels good, so the next day he gave Abhinav a turn after his own. 😊
How might Abhinav feel when Yusuf holds the cart out to him?
Abhinav likely feels happy that the kindness was returned, and that it started a fair back-and-forth between them.

Jackson's mother made little pizza rolls for Jackson's birthday party.  Jackson ate 10 pizza rolls and his friend Jerome ate twice that amount.  Tyler at one and half times more than Jerome.  How many more pizza rolls did Tyler eat than Jackson?

Jerome ate 2 times the amount of Jackson's 10 pizza rolls, so 2*10 = 20 pizza rolls
Tyler ate 1.5 times more than Jerome's 20 pizza rolls, so Tyler ate 1.5*20 = 30 pizza rolls
Tyler ate 30 pizza rolls and Jackson only ate 10 pizza rolls so Tyler ate 30-10 = 20 more pizza rolls
The answer is 20.

Wednesday.

Today Mr. Iyer called me into his cabin and said, "Gautam missed the Delhi deadline, and that's on you, Abhinav. What kind of lead lets this happen?"

My heart was pounding. Everything in me wanted to say, "Gautam didn't tell me until the last day! It's his fault!" It would have been partly true. And it would have thrown a twenty-three-year-old under the bus to save my own skin.

What I said instead: "You're right that I'm responsible for the team's deadlines. I checked in with Gautam every Monday and he said it was on track. I should have asked to see the actual work, not just status updates. I'll do that from now on."

Then: "Honestly, sir, one junior on three client projects is too much. Can we get an intern or push one project back?"

Mr. Iyer grunted. "Send me a proposal."

I walked out shaky, but I'm Abhinav, and I didn't sell Gautam out. That matters to me.

Which deadline did Gautam miss?
He missed the Delhi deadline.
What was Abhinav feeling when Mr. Iyer blamed him?
Abhinav's heart was pounding with anger and fear, and the temptation was to put all the blame on Gautam.
Why was Abhinav's answer wiser than blaming Gautam?
Abhinav owned that part, explained the coaching given and what to change, and asked for resources, instead of scapegoating a junior.
How might Gautam have been affected if Abhinav had blamed him?
Gautam, a young junior, could have been unfairly singled out and lost confidence, while the real resourcing problem stayed hidden.

At the Saturday dance class in the community centre, Vidya had always stood in the front row. This week the teacher moved a new boy, Jagdish, to the front and gave him the short solo. Vidya smiled stiffly and moved to the side. During the break she watched the teacher help Jagdish with his hand movements. Vidya practised her steps in the corner, faster and harder than needed. When the teacher called, 'Vidya, good energy!' she didn't answer. On the way out she asked her mother, 'Do you think Ma'am likes him more now?'

What did the teacher give Jagdish this week?
She moved him to the front and gave him the short solo.
Why did Vidya ask if the teacher liked Jagdish more?
She feared she was losing her special place and the teacher's attention to a new rival.
How could Vidya's mother help her with this feeling?
She could listen, name that it is hard to share attention, and remind Vidya that the teacher still noticed her energy.
How might Jagdish feel if he noticed Vidya's stiff smile?
He might feel awkward or unwelcome, unsure why she is cold towards him.

a) Tuesday
b) Wednesday
c) Thursday

Dear Diary, Thursday.
Such a silly, scary evening. I was going to Yash's cousin's house for dinner in a part of Hyderabad I'd never been to. I walked with my phone in my hand, following the blue dot, not looking anywhere else. The app took me down a lane that got darker and emptier, past a closed factory. A dog started barking. Only then did I look up and realise there were no people at all. My stomach dropped.
I walked back to the main road, fast, and called Yash, who came to meet me at the petrol pump.
The app wasn't wrong exactly. I just stopped using my own eyes.
Zainab

Where did Yash come to meet Zainab?
At the petrol pump.
How did Zainab feel when looking up in the empty lane?
Zainab felt frightened, stomach dropping, on realising there were no people around.
What did Zainab do right once the danger was noticed?
Zainab went back to the busy main road and called Yash to meet at a public place.

Yash was likely worried and quick to help, glad Zainab called instead of pushing on.

Sunday

I miss my old school in Pune SO much. We had the big mango tree and we played kho-kho every break. Everyone liked me.

Here in Nagpur it's hot, and the kids already have best friends.

But today I found my old diary from last year. It said: "Chaitanya and Meenal didn't let me play. I sat alone at the mango tree." And another page: "I hate kho-kho, I always get out first."

I don't remember that at all!! I only remember the good things.

Maybe new school will be okay later. Old school wasn't only good.

— Chandrika

What did Chandrika play every break at the old school?
Kho-kho.
How did Chandrika feel reading the old diary?
Chandrika felt surprised and a little confused, since those bad days had been forgotten.
What small step might help Chandrika at the new school?
Chandrika could try joining one game at break, remembering that the old school also took time to feel good.
How might Chaitanya have seen things at the old school?
Chaitanya might not even remember leaving Chandrika out, since it probably felt small at the time.

Santiago was volunteering at a legal aid clinic in Madrid when a woman came in, soaked from rain, with two children. Her residence papers had expired. The rules said she had no right to the housing support she was asking for.
Kaito, the senior volunteer, read the file and shook his head. "The law says no."
Santiago felt his stomach turn. "The law also says children must be protected. Doesn't that come first?"
"You can't just ignore the rules."
"I'm not ignoring them. I'm asking which one we follow when they clash."
Kaito paused. Then he pulled out a second folder. "There's an emergency provision for families with minors. Few people use it."
They filled it in together. Santiago stayed late to make sure it was sent.

What had expired for the woman?
Her residence papers.
How did Santiago feel reading the woman's situation?
He felt uneasy and upset, his stomach turning at the idea of turning away a family.
What made Santiago's approach effective?
He didn't break rules; he asked which principle should guide them when rules clash, which led Kaito to the emergency provision.
How might Kaito have felt after finding the provision?
Kaito may have felt relieved and reminded of why he joined the clinic.

Last term I spent a whole Sunday afternoon on one page of my notebook. I'm Aadhya, and I'd seen Zubin, who I've known since we were six, reading answers off his smartwatch in the physics test.
I split the page into three: stay silent, talk to Zubin, tell Mr Das.
Stay silent: easy for now. But the honest kids, the ones who studied till midnight, get pushed down the rank list. And Zubin learns that it works, which isn't good for him later, in the boards, where it won't.
Talk to Zubin: he might be angry. Things between us could get awkward. But he gets a chance to stop or own up before anyone else knows.
Tell Mr Das: fairest to the class. But it could hurt Zubin badly, a zero, maybe his parents called, and he'd know it was me.
Seeing it written down, the middle column looked strongest as a first step. So that's what I did on Monday.

What were the three options on Aadhya's page?
Stay silent, talk to Zubin, tell Mr Das.
How did Aadhya feel once it was all written down?
Aadhya felt clearer and steadier, seeing the middle column look strongest as a first step.
What should Aadhya do if talking to Zubin doesn't work?
Move to the third column and tell Mr Das calmly, since fairness to honest classmates still matters.
How would staying silent affect the honest classmates?
They would be pushed down the rank list by someone who copied, despite studying till midnight.

Dear Masi,
Thank you for yesterday's call. I've been thinking about it all day.
For weeks I thought I was going mad. When Harish and the others put my old photo on the class group with that caption and everyone laughed, I cried in the washroom. The next day Harish said, "What photo? Nobody posted anything, you always twist things." The post was gone. By the end of the week even I wasn't sure. Maybe I was overreacting. Maybe it was a joke.
Then you asked me one question: what did you feel when you saw it? And I knew. I felt humiliated. That part didn't need proof.
You said I wasn't imagining it and it wasn't my fault, and before we hung up you helped me write to Ms Rao. She replied last night that she'll speak to the class and the counsellor today.
I feel steadier.
Love,
Anjali

What did Harish say the next day?
Harish said, “What photo? Nobody posted anything, you always twist things.”
How did Anjali feel by the end of that week?
Anjali felt confused and full of doubt, unsure whether the post had happened or whether it was overreacting to a joke.
How did Masi's help work?
Masi asked about Anjali's feelings, said it was not imagined and not Anjali's fault, and helped write to Ms Rao during that same call, bringing in someone who could act.
What would change if Anjali had not spoken to anyone outside the class?
Anjali might have kept doubting the memory, Harish's version could have become the only story, and nobody at school would have stepped in.

Tutor's note, Thursday. Devika arrived in a flap, saying she had "too much" homework and would never finish. I asked her to write it all down instead of worrying about it. She made a list: maths sums, Hindi paragraph, map drawing. Then, without my help, she wrote a guess beside each: 10, 20, 30 minutes. She added them under her breath. "That's one hour. That's not too much." Her shoulders dropped. Nandini, who sits next to her, asked if she could copy the idea for her own homework. Devika finished five minutes over her guess. I'll suggest this to her parents at pickup.

How long over her guess did Devika finish?
She finished five minutes over her guess.
What do Devika's dropping shoulders suggest?
She felt relieved and calmer once the total came to one hour, after arriving flustered about 'too much' homework.
What might the note-writer suggest if Devika's guesses are often off?
Write the real time beside each guess, so her estimates improve; the list already turned a scary pile into a clear hour.
How does Nandini see Devika's list?
Nandini finds it useful enough to ask to copy the idea for her own homework.

My first week at the new school was the worst week I remember. By Thursday no one had said anything to me except "move" in the line. I came home and didn't touch my food. Ammi sat on my bed and waited. Finally I said, "No one talks to me, Ammi. It's like I'm not there." She didn't say "give it time." She said, "That sounds really hard, Imran. Is there one boy who seems kind?" I thought of the boy who shared his umbrella at the gate, Rohit. "Invite him on Sunday," she said. "Just him. We'll make pakoras." I asked Rohit on Friday. He came. We played carrom for three hours. My stomach still flips at school, but less.

What did Rohit share at the gate?
Rohit shared his umbrella at the gate.
How did Imran feel on Thursday before talking to Ammi?
Imran felt invisible and miserable, so upset that food went untouched.
What else could Imran try at school if Rohit is absent one day?

messages.content: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have? A semicircle?

Answer: A circle has endlessly many (every line through the centre). A semicircle has 1.

Fold a paper circle in half any way through the centre: it always matches. Fold again another way: it still matches. There is no end to the number of folds. A semicircle only matches when folded down the middle, perpendicular to its straight edge.

Nilesh, you're telling me the room is cheap. Very good. Now let your Baljeet bua tell you about the cheapest room I ever took.
My first job was in Delhi, in 1998. I found a room in a lane behind the railway line for four hundred rupees. Everyone else was asking nine hundred. I thought I'd been clever. I saw it once, at two in the afternoon.
At night that lane had no lights at all. The door closed with a bolt you could lift with a hairpin. One night I came home and found my trunk opened, my radio and my savings envelope gone. I didn't sleep there again; I went to my friend Kamla's hostel that same night and told the landlord in the morning.
Four hundred rupees cost me everything I'd saved in three months. So, Nilesh. Before you pay, go back at ten at night. Check the lock with your own hands. Then tell me it's cheap.

How much was the room behind the railway line?
Four hundred rupees.
How did young Baljeet feel after finding the trunk opened?
Shaken and unsafe, enough never to sleep there again, and upset at losing three months of savings.
What choice in the story could have prevented the loss?
Visiting the lane after dark and checking the bolt before paying, instead of seeing the room only at two in the afternoon.
How might Kamla have felt when young Baljeet arrived at the hostel that night?
Probably worried and glad to help, taking in a frightened friend without questions.

The hospital lobby was quiet at two in the morning. Yogesh, the night security guard, sat at his desk with a bundle of old English newspapers the canteen was throwing away. He copied one sentence at a time into the back of the visitors' register, looked up words on his cracked phone, and whispered them. He had no money for classes and no quiet room at home, so this was his classroom. Dhruv, a nurse on the night shift, noticed him on the third night. The next evening Dhruv left a thin notebook and a pencil on the desk with a note: "For your words." By the end of the month Yogesh was reading the weather report aloud to Dhruv without stopping.

Where did Yogesh first copy his sentences?
Into the back of the visitors' register.
What does Yogesh whispering the new words suggest about how he feels?
It suggests he is keen and determined to learn, even a little shy about practising aloud in the quiet lobby.
What was Yogesh's key choice, and what did it lead to?
He chose to start with free newspapers during his night shift rather than wait for money or a classroom, and within a month he could read the weather report aloud.
How might Dhruv see Yogesh's night study?
Dhruv seems to respect it and want to help, which is why Dhruv leaves a notebook with a note saying it is for Yogesh's words.

First week. Manoj, nineteen, a fierce lover of Kannada, fumed at the new English-and-Hindi-only signboard in the college canteen. "In our own state!" he said loudly to his roommate Eshaan, from Lucknow. Then he added, "Hindi people come here and expect everyone to adjust." Eshaan went quiet.
Third week. Eshaan asked Manoj to teach him Kannada numbers so he could buy vegetables. Manoj taught him, grinning at his mistakes. That night Manoj felt a twinge: he'd said "Hindi people" as if Eshaan were a problem.
Sixth week. At the college Rajyotsava celebration, Manoj organised a Kannada poetry reading. Eshaan stood up and recited four lines, badly, bravely. The hall cheered. Manoj hugged him. "Sorry about what I said that first week," he muttered. "I love my language. That doesn't mean I have to hate yours."

What did Eshaan ask Manoj to teach him?
Eshaan asked Manoj to teach him Kannada numbers so he could buy vegetables.
What was Manoj feeling that night in the third week?
Manoj felt a twinge of guilt for having talked about "Hindi people" as if Eshaan were a problem.
What made the friendship grow despite the tension?
Eshaan's willingness to learn Kannada and Manoj's patience teaching him showed that pride in a language can be shared across lines.
How might Eshaan have felt when Manoj said "Hindi people"?
Eshaan probably felt hurt and unwelcome, lumped with people Manoj resented.

On his uncle's farm outside Sangli, Ganesh, sixteen, had driven the tractor twice, both times with his aunt Vasudha beside him on the flat stretch near the shed. On the third morning he told his cousin Pooja, "I've got it. I'll take it to the far field myself." "Alone? Aai said—" "It's simple. Clutch, gear, go. I've done it twice." Vasudha came out of the kitchen wiping her hands. "Ganesh, tell me how you'd go down the slope by the canal." He shrugged. "Same as on the flat." Vasudha shook her head. "That's the part you haven't done. On a slope you need a low gear before you start down." Ganesh went red. He hadn't known that at all. Two tries on flat ground had felt like knowing everything. "Okay," he said. "Will you sit with me on the slope?" Pooja grinned. "I'm coming too."

How many times had Ganesh driven the tractor?
He had driven the tractor twice.
Why did Ganesh think driving to the far field alone would be simple?
Two easy tries on flat ground felt like he had mastered it. He didn't know enough yet to realise the slope was a different skill.
Which question from Vasudha was the turning point, and why?
Asking how he would go down the slope by the canal. His answer showed him, not her, the gap in what he knew, so he asked her to sit with him.
How might Pooja have felt when Ganesh announced he'd go alone?
Pooja seemed uneasy, starting to remind him what Aai said, and then relieved and cheerful once he agreed to have Vasudha along.

"So what are you going to say to Papa tomorrow?" Vishal asked, passing his sister a plate of pakoras.
"I had nine points. Why I want to leave the shop, how I'll pay my way, the design course, how Munna can take over the billing..."
"Nine points is a court case, Bhavna."
"I know. That's what I worked out last night. If I go in with nine points, he'll argue each one, and I'll try to win each one."
"And you don't want to win?"
"I want him to understand me. That's all. Winning would mean he loses, and he's my father."
"So what's the one sentence?"
She took a breath. "Papa, I love what you built, and I need to build something of my own."
Vishal was quiet for a moment. "Yes. Say only that first. The rest can come later."

How many points did Bhavna have at first?
Nine points.
Why does Bhavna not want to win the conversation?
She loves her father and feels that winning would mean he loses; she hopes to be understood instead.
What else could help Bhavna once she has said her one sentence?
She could pause and let Papa respond, then share details like the design course only when he asks.
How might Papa hear the one sentence compared with nine points?
He is more likely to hear love and respect for what he built, rather than a list to argue against.

Every Sunday in the kasba, Urmila's phone lived in the kitchen drawer. She had learned the hard way, after a month of seven working days and a cry over a leaking tap, that rest isn't something you earn after collapsing. Now Sunday meant a late breakfast with her mother Charu, a slow walk to the river bridge, and a nap with no alarm.
That afternoon the drawer glowed with a message from her manager. Urmila glanced at it, wrote "Monday, 9 a.m." on a slip of paper, and went back to shelling peas.
"You're not answering?" asked Charu.
"Tomorrow," said Urmila. "That's what Sundays are for."

Where did Urmila keep her phone on Sundays?
In the kitchen drawer.
What did Urmila feel about resting, and what showed it?
She felt firm and unashamed about it. She learned the hard way that rest is not something to earn after collapsing, and she leaves her manager's message for Monday.
What choice did Urmila make when the manager's message arrived?
She noted 'Monday, 9 a.m.' on a slip of paper and went on shelling peas instead of answering.
What might Charu think when Urmila does not answer the message?
Charu seems surprised and curious, asking if Urmila is not answering, and may see that her daughter's Sundays are deliberately protected.

Read this:

Dear Francis,

You asked how Diwali went with Sameer's whole family visiting. Honestly? It looked perfect. New dinner set, four kinds of sweets, a caterer for the second night. Sameer's Bua said, "Such a grand welcome!" and I glowed.

What I didn't tell anyone: most of it went on my card. I kept thinking, if it's simple, they'll say we're struggling, that his wife can't manage.

Now the bill has come, and my stomach drops every time I see the envelope.

The funny thing? The moment everyone loved most was the second morning, when Sameer's Dadi and I sat on the balcony with plain chai and she told me stories about his childhood.

I've decided to tell Sameer everything tonight, look at it together, and talk to someone at the bank about it.

Next time, chai on the balcony.

Parul

What did Sameer's Bua say about the welcome?
Sameer's Bua said, "Such a grand welcome!"
How does Parul feel when she sees the bill envelope?
Parul feels anxious and afraid; her stomach drops, after spending so as not to look like she couldn't manage.
What choice has Parul made about the bill?
To tell Sameer everything, look at it together, and speak with someone at the bank, instead of hiding it.
What did the balcony morning seem to mean to Sameer's Dadi?
Dadi seemed to enjoy simply sitting with Parul over plain chai and sharing stories, which needed no expense.

In the hostel common room, Rajni was telling her roommate Bhavna about the warden blaming her for the broken tap. Her voice got louder and louder. Then tears started running down her face, even though she was still talking angrily.
"I didn't even touch it! And she just assumed—" She wiped her face with her sleeve. "Ugh, why am I crying?"
Bhavna didn't say, "Don't be sad." She asked, "Are you upset, or angry, or both?"
"Angry! And tired! And... I don't know." Rajni laughed a little through the tears.
"Okay," Bhavna said. "Want to go talk to the warden together tomorrow? You can explain."
Rajni nodded. "Yes. Thanks for not telling me to stop crying."

What was Rajni blamed for?
The broken tap.
What was Rajni feeling while crying and talking angrily?
Rajni felt angry, tired and overwhelmed all at once, so the tears came with the anger.
What did Bhavna do that helped?
Bhavna asked what Rajni was feeling instead of labelling the tears, and offered to go to the warden together.
How might the warden see Rajni if she cried while explaining?
The warden might think Rajni was only upset, not realising the tears came from anger and tiredness.

What does Kwame learn about Wei?

The group project for Urban Planning met every Tuesday at nine in the Manchester university library, and every Tuesday Wei was late or yawning. By week four Kwame had had enough. "He's just lazy," he told the other two. "He does the bare minimum and sleeps through meetings." He started writing Wei's sections himself. Then one Friday at six in the morning, Kwame went to the big supermarket near the station for milk. At the loading bay, in a grey uniform, stacking crates onto a trolley, was Wei. He looked exhausted. He saw Kwame and gave a small, awkward wave. "Night shift," Wei said. "Five nights a week. My rent." Kwame stood holding his milk and thought of every Tuesday he had called him lazy.
Wei works five night shifts a week at a supermarket to pay his rent, so he is tired on Tuesdays. Kwame had called him lazy and now thinks about every time he judged him wrongly.
Draft an email, about 55 words, to a conference organiser confirming that I will attend on 5 March and asking if vegetarian food will be available. I'm Dr. Anand Rao.

Subject: Confirmation of Attendance on 5 March

Dear Sir or Madam,
I would like to confirm that I will attend the conference on 5 March. I would also like to ask whether vegetarian food will be available during the event. Thank you for organising this, and I look forward to attending.
Best regards,
Dr. Anand Rao

The metro platform was loud with announcements and rush-hour footsteps, and Vidya had to raise her voice to be heard. She was telling Raghav about her audition, one of the most important things in her month. Raghav nodded along, murmuring "yeah, yeah," but his eyes kept dropping to his phone in his hand. Vidya couldn't tell whether he was really with her or waiting for a message. She wasn't sure the noise had let her words through at all. She stopped mid-sentence and said, "Sorry, it's so loud. Did you catch that last part, or should I pause?" Raghav looked up, startled. "Honestly, I'm waiting for my cab to be confirmed. Tell me again, I'm listening now."

Where were Vidya and Raghav standing?
They were on the metro platform.
What was Vidya worried about as Raghav nodded?
She wasn't sure whether he was really with her or waiting for a message, since nodding and glancing at a phone don't show attention on their own.
What did Vidya do that helped clear things up?
She asked a brief, friendly question, checking if he had caught the last part, instead of guessing or getting annoyed.
How might Raghav have felt when Vidya stopped mid-sentence?
He was probably startled and a little caught out, but honest, since he explained that he was waiting for his cab and asked her to repeat it.

Subject: What I did to my roommate

Dear Shreya,

You asked why the room is so cold these days. Honestly, it's my doing. Every time Rohit left a plate in the sink, I wrote a note. "Thanks for the lovely art installation." "Did the dishes go on holiday?" I stuck them on his desk, and stopped speaking to him. I thought a joke was kinder than a fight. He read them, said nothing, and started coming back late. Last night he said, quietly, "I feel like you hate me." The mess is still there, and now there is a wall too. I didn't say one plain sentence. Can I practise what to say with you on Friday?

Manoj

What did Manoj write in the first note?
Manoj wrote 'Thanks for the lovely art installation.'
What is Manoj feeling as the email is written?
Manoj feels ashamed and regretful about the notes and hopeful about practising a plain sentence.
What alternative approach could Manoj use, and why?
Manoj could speak directly about the dishes and ask what would work for Rohit too, because notes felt like attacks while a real conversation can turn the mess into a shared problem.
How might Rohit have seen the notes?
Rohit read jokes that felt like attacks, said nothing, came back late and later said he felt hated, so Rohit felt attacked and shut out.

So Leela asked me on this podcast when I first felt like an adult. And I wish I had a big answer. I'm Yash, I'm twenty-five, and I thought turning twenty-five would do it. It didn't. I woke up and still wanted my Mummy to make my chai. What actually happened was smaller. First, I started paying my own phone bill. Then I booked my own eye test instead of waiting for Papa to nag me. Then I said yes to being godparent for my cousin's baby, and I actually showed up to the naming ceremony on time, with a gift. Each one felt tiny. But one day I was fixing a leaking tap in my flat and I thought, oh, I'm the person who fixes things now. That was it. No birthday. Just a tap, Leela, and a very wet shirt.

What was Yash fixing when the thought came?
Yash was fixing a leaking tap in the flat.
How did Yash feel on waking up at twenty-five?
Yash felt a bit disappointed and unchanged, still wanting Mummy to make the chai.
Which of Yash's small acts show ownership, and why do they matter?
Paying the phone bill, booking the eye test and keeping the naming-ceremony commitment each moved responsibility onto Yash, adding up to feeling adult.
How might Leela, as the host, react to Yash's answer?
Leela might find it funny and honest, and the podcast's listeners may feel relieved that adulthood comes gradually for others too.

Zanele arrived at the library meeting room in Hamburg at half past ten. The project group had started at ten sharp. Selin looked at the clock, then at Zanele, and said only, "We've begun the first section." Back home in Durban, ten o'clock meant people drifted in by eleven and nobody minded. Here, three classmates who had waited exchanged a look. Zanele's face went hot, and Zanele stayed to the end without a word. Afterwards Zanele said, "I didn't understand how strict the clock is here. I'm sorry." Selin nodded. "If you're running late, send a message before, even five minutes." Zanele set the alarm fifteen minutes early, and the next week arrived first.

How late was Zanele to the meeting?
Zanele arrived at half past ten for a group that had started at ten sharp.
How did Zanele feel when Selin looked at the clock?
Embarrassed and worried about seeming unreliable; the face went hot.
What could Zanele do whenever running late in future?
Send a message before, even for five minutes, and leave earlier.
How might Selin and the classmates have seen the late arrival?
As a lack of respect for their time, since they had waited from ten, though Zanele meant no offence.
Five times a week, Onur bikes 250 kilometers a day. His friend Hanil bikes 40 more kilometers of Onur biking distance in a day. What's the total distance the two friends bikes in a week?

Since Onur bikes 250 kilometers in a day, he bikes 5*250 = 1250 kilometers for five days in a week.
Onur's friend Hanil bikes 40 more kilometers in a day than Onur, meaning he bikes for 250+40 = 290 kilometers.
In five days of the week, Hanil covers 290*5 = 1450 kilometers.
In total, the two bikes for 1450+1250 = 2700 kilometers in 5 days of a week.
The answer is 2700.

Can you help with these, please?
Make this correct: The glass was broke by the child.
Is it "hippopotamus" or "hipopotamus"?

1. Correct form: The glass was broken by the child. Why: the passive voice uses the past participle "broken".
2. It is "hippopotamus", with a double "p".

The power went off during the storm, and water dripped into a bucket in the corner. Papa and Uday Chacha argued in sharp whispers about who should have fixed the roof. Amma lit a candle and said nothing. Pranav, who usually ran about with a torch, sat pressed against Amma's side. When she got up to empty the bucket, he held her kurta and followed her step by step. 'Stay here, baby,' she said. He shook his head and would not let go.

Where did the water drip?
Into a bucket in the corner.
Why did Pranav follow Amma step by step?
He seemed scared and unsettled by the sharp whispers between Papa and Uday Chacha, and staying close to Amma felt safe.
What small step could Amma take to settle Pranav?
Take him along to the bucket, hold his hand and tell him calmly that the grown-ups are cross about the roof, not with him.
What is it like for Amma when Pranav won't let go?
With the leak, the dark and the argument to manage, his clinging adds to her load, yet it also shows her how much the tension is reaching him.

Comparing the humped herds of whales with the humped herds of buffalo, which, not forty years ago, overspread by tens of thousands the prairies of Illinois and Missouri, and shook their iron manes and scowled with their thunder-clotted brows upon the sites of populous river-capitals, where now the polite broker sells you land at a dollar an inch; in such a comparison an irresistible argument would seem furnished, to show that the hunted whale cannot now escape speedy extinction.

What argument does the writer draw from comparing whale herds with buffalo herds?

Not forty years ago, humped herds of buffalo overspread the prairies in tens of thousands, where land is now sold by a broker. The writer says that comparing them with whale herds seems to show that the hunted whale cannot now escape speedy extinction.

I said it in front of his friends. That's the part I keep coming back to.
Last winter my brother Naveen failed his pre-boards in two subjects. When his friends came over, I said, "Don't ask Naveen for help with anything, he's too dumb to pass maths." They laughed. He didn't. He went red and quietly shut his door.
For weeks I told myself I was just being honest. Naveen really was wasting time on his guitar.
It was Ammachi who asked me, "Sabina, why does his failing make you so angry?" I didn't have an answer that night. Later, I did. I was scared. Our parents already lean on me for everything. If Naveen failed, I'd be the only one they could count on, and I didn't want that weight.
I apologised in March. He accepted it, sort of. He still doesn't show me his songs.

How many subjects did Naveen fail in his pre-boards?
Two subjects.
What was Sabina afraid of, underneath the anger at Naveen?
Sabina was scared of carrying the family's hopes alone if Naveen failed, and the fear came out as contempt.
What went wrong, and what could help rebuild closeness now?
Mocking Naveen in front of his friends shut him out; Sabina could keep showing respect, like asking to hear one of his songs without judging.
What is it like for Naveen when Sabina mocks him?
He feels humiliated in front of his friends and shuts his door, and he still keeps his songs private from Sabina.

"Tanvir's here," Vinita called from the door of their flat. "I didn't invite him. Well. I sort of did."

Pema didn't get up from the sofa. "I'm fine. I just need sleep."

Tanvir sat on the floor near the sofa with a flask of tea. "Okay. I'll sit."

He didn't ask anything. After ten minutes Pema said, "Why are you here?"

"You haven't replied in two weeks. You always reply."

Pema's eyes filled. "I can't really talk about it yet."

"You don't have to. Tell me as much as you want. Or nothing."

A long breath. "My internship ended badly. I've been... not okay. That's all I can say today."

"That's enough. What's one thing piling up?"

"Laundry. And the form for next semester."

"Give me the form. Vinita, where's the laundry bag?"

Pema laughed, a little wet, after weeks of silence.

What did Tanvir bring with him?
Tanvir brought a flask of tea.
What was Pema feeling when Tanvir said, "You don't have to"?
Pema felt seen and cared for, which is why tears came, after weeks of feeling alone.
What did Pema do that let Tanvir help?
Pema said how much could be shared today and named practical tasks, the laundry and the form, instead of pushing him away.
How does Tanvir see the two weeks of silence?
Tanvir sees it as a sign something is wrong, because Pema always replies, so he comes to sit quietly without demanding answers.
Beth bakes 4, 2 dozen batches of cookies in a week.  If these cookies are shared amongst 16 people equally, how many cookies does each person consume?

Beth bakes 4 2 dozen batches of cookies for a total of 4*2 = 8 dozen cookies
There are 12 cookies in a dozen and she makes 8 dozen cookies for a total of 12*8 = 96 cookies
She splits the 96 cookies equally amongst 16 people so they each eat 96/16 = 6 cookies
The answer is 6.
Will it rain in Pune tomorrow afternoon?
I don't know if it will rain in Pune tomorrow afternoon, as I can't check forecasts. A forecast page for Pune or the national weather service will give the outlook.

The maths test had started late because of a power cut, and now there were only twenty minutes left for thirty sums. The fan was off, the room was hot, and Reena was stuck on question twelve. Around her she could see heads tilting, eyes sliding sideways. "Half the class does it," she told herself. "It's normal." She glanced at Dilnaz's page and started copying the working. A shadow fell across her desk. The teacher picked up Reena's paper. "Reena. Come to the front." "Ma'am, everyone was looking!" "Then I'll watch everyone more closely. But I saw you." Reena got zero for the test and a note home. That evening she stared at the note for a long time, and the word "everyone" felt very small.

How many sums were left for the last twenty minutes?
Thirty sums.
What did Reena tell herself, and how did she feel that evening?
That half the class copies so it's normal; by evening she felt ashamed, and the excuse felt very small.
What else could Reena have done when she got stuck on question twelve?
Skipped it and moved on to sums she could do, coming back if time was left.
How might Dilnaz feel about what happened?
Dilnaz may feel uncomfortable that her page was copied, and worried about being involved.

Read this:

Dear Irfan,
Writing from home. Navratri lights everywhere, and Mummy has asked me three times whether I'm eating properly.
I need to tell someone this. Before I buy anything, even a shirt, I send Papa a photo and wait for "Very nice, beta." Before I told my professor I'd take the research project, I called home first. When Papa said "Good choice", I felt like I could breathe.
But here's the thing. The design internship in Bengaluru, the one I actually want, they've never heard of it. Papa wants me to do government exam prep this summer, near home. Every time I think of saying no, I feel like the worst son in the world. They've given me everything.
You always seem to know what you want. How do you do it without feeling like you're betraying someone?
Darshan

What does Darshan send Papa before buying a shirt?
A photo, and then Darshan waits for "Very nice, beta."
Why does Darshan feel like "the worst son in the world"?
Darshan, a loving son, feels guilty and torn: wanting the Bengaluru internship seems like betraying parents who have given him everything.
What could Darshan try?
Start making small choices without checking, then talk honestly with Mummy and Papa about the internship and why it matters, instead of waiting for approval to feel allowed.
How might Darshan's parents react if Darshan explained the internship?
Mummy and Papa might be worried at first, wanting their son near home, but could also be proud to hear what Darshan truly wants; they cannot support a wish they have never heard.
Less wordy, please: In the event that you are unable to attend, please let us know.
If you cannot attend, please tell us.

Minakshi, you think your Hafsa Khala was always the serious one? Let me tell you about the first monsoon night at my hostel in Mumbai. I was nineteen, the anatomy test was next morning, and our study group was meeting at nine. Then the rain came down like a curtain, and my roommates dragged me out to Marine Drive. We ate roasted bhutta with lime and chilli, soaked to the bone, waves crashing over the wall, laughing till our stomachs hurt. I can still taste that corn. But every few minutes a small voice said: the study group, the test. I got back at one, dripping, and read two chapters by torchlight. I wouldn't give that night back. I also never skipped a group again without telling them.

What did Hafsa and the roommates eat at Marine Drive?
Roasted bhutta with lime and chilli.
What was Hafsa feeling during the night out?
Hafsa felt pure joy, laughing in the rain, with a pinch of guilt from the small voice reminding her of the study group and the test.
What was the turning point inside the story, and what did Hafsa take from it?
Coming back at one and reading two chapters by torchlight; Hafsa kept the joy but decided never again to skip the group without telling them.
How might the study group have felt when Hafsa didn't show up?
They may have felt let down or confused, waiting without a word from Hafsa.

March: Vidya spent her lunch hours teaching Gargi, the new junior at the Pune design studio, everything she had learned about typography the hard way. She showed her the mistakes too.
June: at the big client presentation, the client loved the logo. It had started as Vidya's rough sketch, but Gargi had reworked it completely. When the client asked who designed it, Vidya said at once, 'Gargi did. It's her work.' Gargi stared at her, stunned.
November: the studio head offered Gargi the lead on the new museum project, the one Vidya had hoped for. Vidya felt the sting clearly, went for a long walk, and came back. She stopped at Gargi's desk. 'You'll be brilliant. If you want a second pair of eyes, I'm here. If you don't, that's fine too.' Gargi hugged her, and Vidya found she meant every word.

What did Vidya say when the client asked who designed the logo?
'Gargi did. It's her work.'
How did Vidya feel when Gargi got the museum project?
Vidya felt a clear sting of disappointment, then, after a long walk, genuine happiness for Gargi.
What makes Vidya's mentoring free of ego?
She shared her mistakes, credited Gargi publicly, and offered help without insisting once Gargi outgrew her.
How might Gargi feel about Vidya after November?
Gargi likely feels grateful and deeply supported, which is why she hugs her.

Vijay, your father wants you to be an engineer, and you want to cook? Let your Gargi athai tell you something. When I was twenty, I had topped my college in chemistry. My father said, "Do a B.Ed. Teaching is a good job for a girl. Easy hours, good for marriage." My twin brother, your father, wanted to paint. He was told, "Painting? You must earn. You're the son." So I became a teacher and he became an engineer. Both of us were pushed into moulds, one for a wedding, one for a salary.
The turning point came years later, when I told my father I wanted to do research after all. My mother, who had never spoken against him, said, "Let her." That changed everything. I got my PhD at thirty-two. Your father still paints on Sundays. Beta, talk to him. He knows that mould better than anyone.

What did Gargi's father tell her to do after college?
To do a B.Ed., because teaching was a good job for a girl.
How might young Gargi have felt when told to choose teaching for marriage?
She probably felt disappointed and boxed in, having topped her college in chemistry.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
Her mother saying "Let her" when Gargi asked to do research; family support finally made a real choice possible.
How might Gargi's twin brother have felt being told he must earn?
He probably felt trapped and sad, giving up painting for engineering, which is why he still paints on Sundays.

Jagdish had it all mapped out on a napkin in the college canteen. "Look. A white van outside the admin block three days in a row. The new phone tower on the library roof. The canteen shutting early. And the principal's been in Delhi twice this month."
Jasleen stirred her tea. "And?"
"They're selling the college. To some company. Nobody's noticed but me."
He was glowing. He hadn't felt this sharp all year.
"Okay," Jasleen said. "What would it look like if these things had nothing to do with each other?"
He opened his mouth.
"Vans deliver things. Towers go up everywhere. The canteen man's daughter is getting married, he told us."
"But the Delhi trips —"
"Could be ten reasons. How would you check?"
Jagdish looked at his napkin, the arrows suddenly thinner.

Where was the new phone tower?
On the library roof.
What was Jagdish feeling while explaining his theory?
He felt excited and special, glowing with the sense that he alone had seen the hidden plan.
Why was Jasleen's question a useful test?
Asking what it would look like if the events were unrelated pushed Jagdish to test his pattern instead of just trusting how convincing it felt.
How does Jasleen seem to see the napkin theory?
She seems calm and unconvinced, offering ordinary explanations for each event and asking how he would check.
Write a letter of about 120 words to my grandfather in the village, telling him about my new school.

Dear Dadaji,
I hope you are well and that your knees are not troubling you much this winter. I have some news. I started at my new school last Monday. It is much bigger than my old one, with three floors and a huge playground. On the first day I felt nervous, but a boy called Samuel showed me around, and now we sit together. My favourite subject is science, because our teacher lets us do experiments every Friday. The canteen samosas are good, but not as good as Dadi's. I miss our evening walks to the fields. Please write back and tell me about the new calf.
Your loving grandson,
Abhay
A friend has a small cut at school. What do I do?
Take her to the teacher or the nurse. Because the cut needs to be cleaned and covered by someone who knows how, so it does not get infected.

Ayesha, you think your Ritu Mausi was always this woman who walks to the market and back before breakfast? At nineteen I could not climb the hostel stairs without stopping. I lived on tea and bread and stayed up past two with my textbooks. Then the college kabaddi coach took one look at me in trials and said, “Stamina first, fame later.” She didn't let me play for a month. Just slow rounds of the ground, every morning, and a rule: eat what the mess cook, Parvati-bai, puts on your plate, the dal and the greens too. I sulked. I wanted to be in matches. By the second term I played a full match and still had breath to shout. I still walk every day, Ayesha. Build the body slowly, the way you build a friendship.

What was the coach's rule about food?
The rule was to eat what the mess cook, Parvati-bai, put on her plate, including the dal and the greens.

Warm air from the sea carries a lot of water vapour inland ahead of the rains. The air holds more moisture than usual, so it feels sticky.

Everyone held out notebooks. Tejas's hands were empty. His friend Nitin whispered, "Where's yours?" Tejas stared at the floor, cheeks hot.

Where did Tejas leave the notebook?
On the mat.
What was Tejas feeling when his cheeks went hot?
He was embarrassed and ashamed that his plan failed.
What would you change first in Tejas's plan?
Bring the notebook and tell the teacher if he couldn't finish, since hiding it doesn't stop the question.
How does the moment look to Nitin?
Nitin is surprised and curious, and may feel sorry for Tejas.

Subject: Asking for your advice on a project outline
Dear Professor Devika Rao,
I'm Vaibhav from your Indian Economy course last semester. Your lectures on rural credit were the reason I chose economics as my major.
I'm planning a small summer project: interviewing twenty women's self-help groups near my home town about how they decide on loans. I've attached a one-page outline with my question, method and timeline.
I'm not asking you to supervise it or to write anything for me. I would be grateful for any comments on whether the method is realistic, especially the number of groups. Fifteen minutes in your office hours, or a short reply by email, would both be wonderful.
If you're too busy this month, I completely understand.
Thank you,
Vaibhav Joshi

How many self-help groups did Vaibhav plan to interview?
Twenty women's self-help groups.
How does Vaibhav seem to feel about Professor Rao?
Vaibhav admires the professor, crediting the lectures on rural credit for the choice of major, and feels hopeful but careful not to impose.
What else could Vaibhav do while waiting for a reply?
Try the interview questions with one group near home, so there is something concrete to ask about.
How might Professor Rao feel reading this email?
The professor would likely feel pleased and respected, since it asks for specific feedback and leaves an easy way to say no.

At his cousin's wedding in a crowded Delhi hall, Darshan posed for the family photo. "Say cheese!" He smiled wide, arm around his grandmother.
Later, his uncle Pankaj showed him the candid photos on his camera. In one, Darshan was yawning, sitting on the steps with his tie undone.
Darshan frowned. "That one's embarrassing. Delete it."
Pankaj Chacha smiled. "Why? It's true too. You smiled for Dadi because she wanted it. And later you were tired because we've been dancing since six."
Darshan looked again. Maybe it wasn't so bad. "Can we keep both?"
"Of course," said Pankaj Chacha. "One for Dadi's album, one for us."

What was Darshan doing in the candid photo?
He was yawning, sitting on the steps with his tie undone.
What was Darshan feeling when he asked to delete the candid photo?
Darshan felt embarrassed about looking tired and wanted to hide it.
How did Pankaj Chacha help Darshan see the photos differently?
He explained that both photos were true, one showing cooperation and the other showing real tiredness.
How might Dadi feel seeing the posed photo?
Dadi would likely feel happy and proud to see Darshan smiling with her.

If sin A = 3/5 (A acute), find the other five trigonometric ratios of A.

Now you try: cos A = 12/13.
The answer is sin A = 5/13, tan A = 5/12, cosec A = 13/5, sec A = 13/12, cot A = 12/5.
Randy has 60 mango trees on his farm. He also has 5 less than half as many coconut trees as mango trees. How many trees does Randy have in all on his farm?

Half of the number of Randy's mango trees is 60/2 = 30 trees.
So Randy has 30 - 5 = 25 coconut trees.
Therefore, Randy has 60 + 25 = 85 treeson his farm.
The answer is 85.

Angel has written letters to all of her pen pals and is putting all of the letters in envelopes. Most of the letters are put into large envelopes and the remaining 20 letters are put into small envelopes. The large envelopes each contain 2 letters each. If Angel has written a total of 80 letters, how many large envelopes did she use?

As some of the letters are in small envelopes, there must be 80 total letters - 20 letters in small envelopes = 60 letters in large envelopes.
Angel therefore used 60 letters / 2 letters per large envelope = 30 large envelopes.
The answer is 30.

In a small town outside Aizawl, every boy in Class 4 had started building paper-bottle rockets after school, launching them in the churchyard field with loud cheers. Mawia, nine, had always spent his evenings drawing birds in a notebook by the window.
On Thursday he tore pages out of his bird notebook to make a rocket.
His sister Lalremsiami saw the torn pages on the floor. "Mawia! Your hornbill drawing!"
"Rockets are better," he said, not looking at her. "Everyone makes them."
"You told me rockets were boring."
"Now I like them."
At the field his rocket flopped over on the first try, and the others laughed, but they let him stand with them. Mawia laughed too, a bit too loudly. That night Lalremsiami found him quietly smoothing out one of the crumpled bird drawings.

What did Mawia tear pages out of to make a rocket?
He tore pages out of his bird notebook.
Why did Mawia say 'Now I like them' about rockets?
He wanted to be part of the group launching rockets in the field, and saying he liked them made joining feel natural, even though he had called them boring.
What small step might help Mawia keep both his drawing and his friends?
He could draw the boys' rockets or the birds around the field and share them, so he joins in without giving up what he loves.
What might Lalremsiami think when she finds Mawia smoothing out the drawing?
Lalremsiami might feel sad and tender, sensing that Mawia still loves his birds and only tore the pages to belong with the other boys.
Write a warmer card message than this: Happy birthday, Grandpa.
Wishing you a very happy birthday, Grandpa.
