Monday. Aditi squatted in the park sandpit, pouring sand from a red cup into a blue one, again and again. Her papa, Mohit, called "Lunch!" three times. She didn't look up. When he lifted her away, she wailed all the way home.
Wednesday. Mohit crouched beside her. "Two more pours, then lunch." She poured twice and looked at him.
Friday. Aditi poured, then held the cup out to Papa herself and toddled to the bench.

What colours were Aditi's cups?
A red cup and a blue one.
Why did Aditi wail when Mohit lifted her away?
She was upset at being pulled out suddenly from the pouring she was completely lost in.
What worked better on Wednesday?
Mohit crouched beside her and warned, "Two more pours, then lunch," so she could finish on her own.
How might Mohit feel on Friday when Aditi hands him the cup?
Mohit likely feels relieved and pleased that lunch came without tears.

Tenzin, sit with your Ganga aunty a minute. You remind me of myself at twenty-five, watching someone the way you're watching Sonam now. Mine was Prakash, at the tea company office in Siliguri. He took every late shift, ate lunch over spreadsheets, stopped coming to our Saturday badminton. He got promoted twice in a year.
I'll be honest, first I was jealous. Then one evening I saw him fall asleep sitting up at his desk, pen still in his hand, and the jealousy just went.
I didn't lecture him about balance. I said, 'I'm getting momos at seven. Come for twenty minutes, then go back to your work.' He came. He laughed for the first time in weeks.
He still wanted the promotion, and he got it. But he came every Thursday after that.

What did Prakash stop coming to?
Our Saturday badminton, as Ganga puts it.
What made Ganga's jealousy of Prakash turn into concern?
Seeing him fall asleep sitting up at his desk, pen still in his hand, showed how worn out he was, and the jealousy went.
What choice did Ganga make instead of lecturing Prakash, and why did it work?
She invited him for momos for twenty minutes and told him to go back to his work after, offering a break without questioning his goals.
What might Prakash have felt when invited for just twenty minutes?
Prakash may have felt relieved and cared for, since the invitation respected his work instead of criticising it.
Make this briefer: Please be aware that the canteen will not be serving hot food today, as the stove is out of order.
The canteen has no hot food today because the stove is out of order.

On the stairs of Building C, in their Mumbai colony, Farida and Nandini compared their Hindi test papers. Both had 11 out of 30. Nandini pointed at the red circles. 'I didn't study the poem chapter. I thought it wouldn't come.' Farida pulled her knees up. 'I'm stupid,' she said. 'I'm stupid in Hindi and I'll always be stupid in Hindi.' A pigeon landed on the railing and they both watched it. 'You got the grammar right,' Nandini said. 'So?' The next evening Nandini's Nani made her read the poem aloud three times on the same stairs. Farida walked past with her cycle and didn't stop. When Nandini called out, 'Come, we'll learn it together!' Farida just rang her bell and kept going.

What marks did Farida and Nandini get in the Hindi test?
Both had 11 out of 30.
What does Farida pulling her knees up and saying 'I'm stupid' suggest about how she feels?
It suggests she feels ashamed and sure the problem is permanent, so there is no point trying.
What could help Farida the next evening on the stairs?
She could stop her cycle and learn the poem with Nandini, starting from the grammar she already got right.
What is it like for Nandini when Farida rides past?
Nandini wants to help Farida and learn together, so it may feel lonely and a bit worrying when Farida just rings her bell and keeps going.
Lyra has an $80 budget for a week to spend on food. If she bought 1 bucket of fried chicken that costs $12 and 5 pounds of beef that cost $3 per pound. How much is left on her weekly budget?

Five pounds of beef cost $3 x 5 = $15.
So Lyra spent a total of $12 + $15 = $27.
Therefore, $80 - $27 = $53 is left on her weekly budget.
The answer is 53.

If I give my brother 2 marbles I will have double his number of marbles, but my friend will have triple the number I do. The total number of marbles we have together is 63. How many marbles do I have?

Let X be the number of marbles I have.
If I give my brother 2 marbles, I'll have X-2 marbles left.
And my brother will have (X-2)/2 marbles.
And my friend will have (X-2)*3 left.
So the total number of marbles is X-2 + (X-2)/2 + (X-2)*3 = 63.
(X-2)*9/2 = 63.
X-2 = 14.
X = 16 marbles.
The answer is 16.

Kiran: can't sleep again. the trip is tomorrow Kiran: what if I have a panic on the bus Mohit: that sounds really scary. I'm here Kiran: everyone keeps saying just relax lol Mohit: I won't say that. it doesn't work Mohit: what's one small thing that would make tomorrow easier Kiran: sitting near the front? and knowing I can text you Mohit: I'll save you the front seat. text me anytime Mohit: also, you've barely slept all week. phone down, water, lights off? Kiran: ok. trying [Three weeks later] Kiran: it's still happening. not just trips now Mohit: then it's bigger than nerves. would you talk to the school counsellor? I'll walk there with you Kiran: ...ok. Monday

Where did Kiran want to sit on the bus?
Near the front.
What was Kiran worried about the night before the trip?
Kiran was worried about having a panic on the bus.
What small step did Mohit help Kiran take?
Mohit asked for one thing that would make tomorrow easier, saved Kiran the front seat, and also encouraged sleep.
What is it like for Kiran when Mohit replies 'I won't say that'?
Kiran likely feels understood rather than brushed off, since everyone else keeps saying just relax.
Why do we plant trees? Two reasons, numbered, each under ten words.

1. Trees give shade on hot days.
2. Their roots hold the soil together.

Class teacher's note, Class 8C, Friday
Zainab stayed back after the last period, looking at the floor. She said that on Wednesday, in the lunch queue, some boys had knocked Sumit's tray and poured water on his notebook while others filmed. She stood there and did nothing. Some people laughed. She said she didn't, "but I didn't stop it either."
She was clearly ashamed. I told her that telling me now was a real and important step, and that small acts matter.
She named the boys and said the video was in a group chat. I noted the details and told the principal before she left. I also asked her whether she'd feel able to sit with Sumit at lunch next week. She said she'd already messaged him that evening to say sorry.
I spoke to Sumit's parents by phone at 4 p.m. The boys and their parents will meet the principal on Monday.

What did the boys pour water on?
Sumit's notebook.
How did Zainab feel when she came to the teacher?
She felt ashamed and guilty, looking at the floor because she had watched and done nothing.
What small acts did Zainab take, and why do they matter?
She reported the incident, named the boys and messaged Sumit to say sorry, which brought adult action and showed Sumit someone cared.
What was the lunch queue like for Sumit?
Sumit likely felt humiliated and helpless, with his tray knocked, his notebook soaked and people filming and laughing.

The community centre in Hyderabad's Old City had one week to book a ground for the youth football day. Zainab, the new volunteer, arrived at Rehana's desk with a printout of nineteen grounds. "This one has floodlights, this one's near the bus depot, this one's the cheapest..." Rehana smiled and opened her notebook. "Before we look at any, what must it have?" Together they wrote three things: walking distance for the kids, toilets that work, and within the budget. Fifteen grounds dropped away. Rehana circled three of the four left. "Any of these is good enough. The school ground has shade. Let's call them now." Zainab glanced at the floodlit stadium. "But that one's really nice." "It's also across town. The kids won't get there." By lunch the booking was done.

What three things did Rehana and Zainab write down?
Walking distance for the kids, toilets that work, and within the budget.
Why was Zainab still drawn to the floodlit stadium?
It looked like the best option on paper, and Zainab didn't want to give up something so impressive, even though it was across town.
Which step made the decision quick, and why did it work?
Writing the must-haves before looking at any ground cut nineteen options to four, so they only had to compare a few good-enough ones.
How might the kids coming to the football day be affected by the choice of the school ground?
They could walk there easily and play in the shade, so more of them would turn up and enjoy the day than at a far-off stadium.
It's been foggy every morning this week. Why does it happen so often in winter?
Cold nights cool the air close to the ground, and the air can't hold as much water vapour when it's cold. The extra vapour turns into tiny droplets, which we see as fog.
So it's like the cloud has come down?
Pretty much. Fog is a cloud touching the ground. When the sun warms the air, the droplets turn back into vapour and the fog usually clears by late morning.

I sit next to Jahnavi at our study group. For two weeks I saw her turn her phone face down whenever Tara's messages came in. She didn't look angry, more tense, like someone holding her breath. Tara asked me twice if I knew what she had done wrong. I said I didn't. I don't know what was in Jahnavi's mind. Maybe the talk felt too hard to start. Yesterday Jahnavi typed something short and sent it. She showed me: "I'm sorry I went quiet. It was hard to say I want to work alone this time. Can we talk on Friday?" Her shoulders dropped after. Tara sent a thumbs-up within a minute. Rafiq

How long did Rafiq see Jahnavi turn her phone face down?
Rafiq saw it for two weeks.
What might Jahnavi have been feeling, according to Rafiq's account?
She seemed tense rather than angry, and Rafiq thinks the talk may have felt too hard to start, though Rafiq cannot be sure.
Why was Jahnavi's short message kinder than more silence?
It told Tara that the quiet was not about Tara's mistakes and offered a talk, so Tara no longer had to guess. 🙂
How might Tara have felt during the two weeks?
Tara asked twice what she had done wrong, so Tara was probably worried and confused.

"Baljeet, first year of college? Let me tell you. When I, your Simran Bua, was nineteen, I thought no bells meant freedom. I watched films till three and missed half my lectures. By November, I was behind in everything. My friend showed me her library timetable: same seat, same hours, every day, like a job. I copied it. At first I hated it. Then I noticed I had evenings free, really free, without guilt. By exams I was caught up. The trick wasn't working harder. It was deciding the time in advance."

What did Simran's friend show her?
Her library timetable.
How did young Simran feel by November?
She felt overwhelmed and behind, realising freedom had become chaos.
What turning point in the story fixed Simran's schedule?
Copying her friend's fixed library timetable and treating study like a job.
How might Simran's friend have seen her struggles?
With sympathy, wanting to help by sharing what worked for her.

Week 1. Jeevan, newly leading the sales group, spread his arms wide in the first meeting and said, "My door is open." People smiled, but nobody spoke. He talked for the whole hour.

Week 3. He tried it again, arms open, and this time added, "Rashmi, you have handled this client. What would you do?" She hesitated, then explained a problem in the pricing sheet. Jeevan took notes and did not interrupt.

Week 6. In the review Jeevan opened his arms and stayed quiet. Two juniors raised concerns, and Rashmi later thanked him for hearing them out. "You were listening this time," she said.

What did Jeevan say in the first meeting?
He said, "My door is open."
Why did nobody speak in week 1, even though Jeevan's arms were open?
He talked for the whole hour, so the open arms did not match his behaviour and gave people no room. The wide gesture could have been seen as welcoming, but he did not listen.
What changed in Jeevan's approach that made people speak?
He asked a direct question, stayed quiet and took notes without interrupting, which made the gesture real.
How might Rashmi have felt in week 1 compared with week 6?
In week 1 she might have felt unsure that speaking was welcome, while by week 6 she trusted that he would hear her out.

I'm Mahima, and this summer I've been in charge of mango time with my baby brother Naveen. He loves the taste, but the juice running down his arms is another story. Yesterday he took two bites, looked at his sticky fingers, and held them out stiff, as far from his body as he could, making a "blech" face. When I wiped them he went straight back to the mango. Maybe it's the stickiness, not the fruit.

What does Naveen love about mangoes?
He loves the taste.
What does Naveen's "blech" face suggest about his feelings?
He seemed disgusted by the sticky juice on his fingers, even though he enjoyed the mango itself.
What could Mahima do to make mango time easier for Naveen?
Cut the mango into small pieces or keep a cloth ready, so he can enjoy it without sticky hands.
How does Mahima make sense of Naveen's reaction?
Mahima guesses it is the stickiness, not the fruit, that bothers him, but can't be sure.
An auto-rickshaw charges ₹30 to start plus ₹12 for every kilometre. Write a formula for the cost C (in rupees) of a ride of k km. Find the cost of a 5 km ride and of a 12 km ride.

Answer: C = 30 + 12k. For 5 km: C = 90 rupees. For 12 km: C = 174 rupees.

Try a few rides first and look for the pattern: 1 km costs 30 + 12, 2 km costs 30 + 12 x 2, 3 km costs 30 + 12 x 3. So k km costs 30 + 12 x k, and the formula is C = 30 + 12k. Substitute: k = 5 gives 30 + 12 x 5 = 30 + 60 = 90; k = 12 gives 30 + 12 x 12 = 30 + 144 = 174. The fixed ₹30 is the constant term; the ₹12 per km is the coefficient of k.
Why does a team usually do better when its members listen to each other?

Listening lets a team use everyone's ideas and avoid clashes. Because ideas are shared, mistakes are noticed early and nobody works against the others by accident, the team uses all its members' knowledge.

In Accra, the night before the swim trials, Esther, sixteen, sat on the steps outside her building, breathing fast. "My hands won't stop shaking. What if I freeze on the block?" Her friend Gabriel sat beside her. He didn't say "just relax." He said, "That sounds awful. Tell me what's happening." He listened for a long time. Then: "One small thing. Tomorrow, just walk to the block. Only that." She did, and she swam. Over the next weeks he walked with her every evening and nagged her about sleeping by ten. When her panic kept coming back before every race, he said, "I think this needs more than me," and went with her to book an appointment with the school counsellor.

What did Gabriel suggest as one small step?
He suggested she just walk to the block tomorrow, only that.
How did Gabriel seem to feel when he said "I think this needs more than me"?
He seemed concerned and caring, honest enough to see that Esther's lasting panic needed a professional, not only a friend.
What did Gabriel do that shows steady support?
He listened without saying relax, helped her take one small step, encouraged walks and sleep, and helped her book the counsellor when the anxiety lasted.
How might Esther see Gabriel after the trials?
She may see him as a trusted friend who took her fear seriously and stayed with her.

Evening study hour at the hostel started at seven, and for a month Damini had spent most of it with her phone face-down on the desk, flipping it over every few minutes "just to check". On Sunday she sat on her bed and thought it through. Willpower isn't working. I keep deciding, and I keep losing. So stop deciding. If the study bell rings, the phone goes in the drawer by the hall door. If my forty-minute timer rings, I get it back. No debate. She told her roommate Jahnavi, who laughed. "You'll be at that drawer in ten minutes." On Monday the bell rang. Damini walked the phone down the hall, shut the drawer and came back to her desk. Twice she stood up out of habit. Twice she sat down. At 7:40 the timer rang, and she had finished a whole chapter.

When does Damini get her phone back under the rule?
When her forty-minute timer rings.
Why did Damini decide to stop deciding?
She felt frustrated at losing to her phone every evening and wanted a rule that took the choice away.
What could Damini add if the drawer rule starts slipping?
A second trigger, such as leaving the drawer key with Jahnavi during study hour, so the rule stays concrete instead of relying on willpower.
What might Jahnavi think after Monday?
Jahnavi, who expected her back at the drawer in ten minutes, may be surprised and a little impressed.

Class teacher's note, Class 5. Amandeep and Jeevan have been inseparable since Class 1. This week a new boy, Farhan, joined and sits next to Jeevan in maths. Today at lunch Amandeep sat at the far end of the bench, not eating. When Jeevan laughed at something Farhan said, Amandeep said loudly, "He's only nice to you because you have the new bat." Later he tore a page in his notebook and said it was an accident. I spoke with him quietly. He said, "Jeevan will forget me." I have paired all three for next week's science model.

Where does Farhan sit in maths?
He sits next to Jeevan.
What was Amandeep afraid of, based on what he told the teacher?
That Jeevan would forget him and choose the new boy as his friend instead.
Why is pairing all three for the science model a sensible step?
It lets Amandeep see he can share Jeevan without losing him, and gives him a chance to know Farhan.
How might Farhan feel hearing "He's only nice to you because you have the new bat"?
Hurt and unwelcome, since he is new and the remark says his friendship isn't real.

Link these two sentences into one.

The first bow was lopsided. The second one held all the way to the park.
The first bow was lopsided, but the second one held all the way to the park.

'Mummy, can I go to the park? Riya's there.'
'Not until your homework's done, Ayesha. And you were rude this morning, so no park today.'
'But I can't concentrate! My legs feel wiggly!'
'Then sit still until they stop.'
Ayesha slumped at the table, kicking the chair leg. Ten minutes later she'd written one line and snapped at her little brother twice.
Charu watched her. 'Ayesha, last Sunday after cricket, you did all your maths in twenty minutes, remember?'
'And I slept all night,' Ayesha mumbled.
Charu sighed. 'Okay. Taking the park away isn't working. Go for forty minutes. Then homework, and we'll talk about this morning later.'
Ayesha raced out. She came back pink-cheeked and calm, sat down and finished her homework without a single complaint.

How long did Charu let Ayesha go to the park for?
Forty minutes.
What was Ayesha feeling while stuck at the table?
She was restless and cranky, with wiggly legs and snapping at her brother.
What did Charu realise, and what did she change?
That taking the park away was not working, so she let Ayesha play first and kept the talk about rudeness for later.
How might Ayesha's little brother have been affected by her restlessness?
He got snapped at twice, so he probably felt hurt or confused until she came back calmer.

In a Manchester park, Liam and Siddiq had jumpers for goalposts and a muddy football. Siddiq's shot flew over Liam's jumper. "Goal!" "That was over the post!" Liam said. "There's no post, so there's no height rule," Siddiq argued. It was 4–4, and the light was fading. Liam looked at his friend's grin, then at the sky. Winning a park match wasn't worth ten minutes of arguing, and Siddiq was moving to Leeds next month. "Fine, it counts," Liam said. "But after this, anything over the jumper is out." "Deal!" said Siddiq. They played until the streetlights came on, and by dinner Liam couldn't even remember the final score.

What were Liam and Siddiq using for goalposts?
They had jumpers for goalposts.
Why did Liam let Siddiq's goal count?
Liam cared more about the friendship than winning, especially with Siddiq moving to Leeds, and felt the argument wasn't worth it.
What made Liam's compromise a smart one?
He gave in on one small point but set a clear rule for the rest of the match, so the game stayed fair and fun.
How might Siddiq see Liam saying "Fine, it counts"?
Siddiq probably feels happy and grateful, and more willing to accept the new rule for the rest of the game.

I'll never forget Gopika's speech at our hostel farewell. I'm Kashish, and I was sitting in the front row. When Gopika stood up to speak, her voice was trembling from the very first word. My first thought was that she was scared; she'd always hated the mic. Some girls behind me giggled, which made me angry. But as she kept going, I looked closer. She was smiling while her voice shook, and her eyes were full. She thanked the mess cooks, the warden, her roommates. I realised I couldn't tell if it was nerves, sadness, or joy. So I didn't decide. I just kept looking at her and nodding, so she'd have one friendly face. Afterwards I asked, "Were you nervous?" She laughed. "Terrified. And so happy. And sad. All of it." I'm glad I didn't just call it fear.

Who did Gopika thank in her speech?
The mess cooks, the warden, and her roommates.
What was Gopika feeling as her voice shook?
She felt terrified, happy and sad all at once, as she told Kashish afterwards; the smile and full eyes hinted at the mix.
What did Kashish do that helped?
Kashish didn't decide what the tremble meant, kept a friendly face and nodded, and asked afterwards.
How might the giggling girls have read Gopika's trembling voice?
They probably read it as weakness or nerves to laugh at, missing the joy and sadness in it.
Which of these needs an EXACT answer, and which can be an ESTIMATE? a) How many people came to the mela? b) How much change should the shopkeeper give me? c) How long is the walk to school?

Answer: a) An estimate is fine. b) Exact. c) An estimate is fine (about 10 minutes).

When we just want an idea of size, "about" is enough. When money changes hands, or we must share things fairly, we need the exact number. Ask the child to think of one more example of each kind. There are no silly answers here; talk about each one.
We are writing invitations for the class party. What exactly is an invitation?

An invitation is a spoken or written request asking someone to come to an event. It is a noun, and the plural is Invitations.
Example: Mira wrote invitations for the class party and handed one to every classmate.

Read this:

Varun, beta, you said you'll take commerce because that's what the family does. Let me tell you about myself at sixteen.
I'm Omkar, your Kaka. When I was your age, in Nagpur, there was no discussion. Commerce, then the family shop. My father said it, my uncles said it, and I said yes. I felt certain. Everyone was pleased. It was easy.
But at night I'd sit on the terrace and feel… nothing. Not sad. Just flat, like a room with no windows.
I never tried anything else. Not the science I liked, not the painting classes near our school. I didn't test the choice. I just obeyed it.
The shop is fine. I've done well. But I'm asking you to do what I didn't: look around first. Then choose. Even if you choose commerce.

What subjects did young Omkar like but never try?
The science Omkar liked and the painting classes near the school.
What was Omkar feeling on the terrace at night?
Omkar felt flat and empty, not sad but like a room with no windows.
What choice inside the story could young Omkar have made differently?
He could have explored science or painting before agreeing to commerce, testing the choice instead of simply obeying.
How might Omkar's father have seen his son's easy yes?
His father probably felt pleased and proud, not knowing Omkar felt flat inside.

metadata.subtype: Foreclosure under family or community pressure [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Pickup note, Thursday. Saurabh's painting tore as he ran out, and he flung himself on the mat, sobbing. His mother, Chandrika, snapped first: "Get up, we're late!" Then she stopped, knelt beside him and waited. "You're sad your rocket ripped. I shouted just now, and I'm sorry." He leaned into her. They taped the rocket together on the bench. I have seen her lose patience before, and I have seen her come back every time; he still runs to her. Next step: I gave them extra tape for home.

What happened to Saurabh's painting?
Saurabh's painting tore as he ran out.
What was Saurabh feeling on the mat, and how did it change?
He was upset and sad about his ripped rocket; once his mother knelt, named it and said sorry, he seemed comforted and leaned into her.
What did Chandrika do after snapping that other parents could copy?
She stopped, knelt, named Saurabh's sadness and apologised for shouting, which turned a slip into a repair.
How does the note-writer see Chandrika as a parent?
The note-writer sees that she is not perfect and loses patience, but she comes back every time, which is why Saurabh still runs to her.

Boil this down to a single sentence.

But by the first term's Physics test the picture looked different. Ojas stared at a page of forces and lenses that the other boys followed easily. His marks came in low.
By the first term's Physics test, Ojas was staring at a page of forces and lenses that the other boys followed easily, and his marks came in low.

Read this:

The week the market research report was due, Lars sent his section to the group two hours after the deadline. Mei, who was coordinating the group at their Stockholm university, fixed the formatting at midnight and decided that was that. For the next project she gave everyone tasks except Lars. "Just review, if you want," she wrote to him. When he offered to run the survey, she said she'd already done it. When he spotted an error in her chart, she thought, typical, nitpicking because he can't do the real work. Only at the final presentation did the professor mention that Lars had topped the statistics exam. Mei stared at him. She had never once asked what he was good at.

How late was Lars's section?
Two hours after the deadline.
Why did Mei dismiss Lars's correction of her chart?
She felt irritated and already sure he was useless, so even a helpful catch looked like nitpicking.
What could Mei try after a single late submission?
Ask what happened, and give Lars a real task to see his work, rather than letting one delay define him.
How might Lars feel being told to just review?
He might feel sidelined and frustrated, especially after offering to run the survey and spotting a real error.
It takes one and half hour to reach my village by bus.

It takes one and a half hours to reach my village by bus.
Why: say "one and a half" with a plural noun ("hours").

Read this:

In the meeting room in Rotterdam, Kwame slid the redesigned bracket drawing across the table and said the team would use his version for the client. Bao had spent two weeks on the original. He smiled, tilted his head and said, "Interesting. That could work." Kwame took it as a yes and moved to the next item. Bao kept his pen still and his voice level, the way he'd learned to when someone senior speaks. Later at the coffee machine Kwame said, "Good, you're on board." Bao heard himself answer, "Sure," before he could stop it. Back at his desk he wrote a short message: "Kwame, I was calmer in the room than I felt. Can we look at both versions together tomorrow? I'd like to show why I chose the shorter arm."

How long had Bao spent on the original drawing?
Bao had spent two weeks on the original.
What might Bao really be feeling about the change, and what is the evidence?

He kept his pen still and his voice level and only said "Interesting. That could work," then wrote that he was calmer in the room than he felt. He may also have wanted time to think before giving a real answer.
What would you advise Bao to do next time this happens in a meeting?
Say briefly that he'd like to think it over or compare both versions, rather than giving a polite yes. His follow-up message already does this gently.
Why did Kwame believe Bao agreed?
Bao smiled, said "Interesting. That could work," and later said "Sure," so Kwame took the calm politeness for agreement.

What happens to the man after he drinks the brandy?

I couldn't keep my eyes off him. Always holding tight by the leg of the table with my hands and feet, I saw the miserable creature finger his glass playfully, take it up, smile, throw his head back, and drink the brandy off. Instantly afterwards, the company were seized with unspeakable consternation, owing to his springing to his feet, turning round several times in an appalling spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and rushing out at the door; he then became visible through the window, violently plunging and expectorating, making the most hideous faces, and apparently out of his mind.
He springs to his feet, spins in a wild, coughing dance and rushes out the door. Through the window he is seen plunging about, spitting and pulling horrible faces as if he were out of his mind.

Each list gives all the faces of a polyhedron without a hole. Find the total number of sides, then E (total / 2), then V from V = 2 + E - F.
a) 2 triangles, 3 rectangles
b) 6 squares
c) 4 triangles
d) 1 square, 4 triangles
e) 2 hexagons, 6 rectangles
f) 1 hexagon, 6 triangles
g) 8 triangles
h) 12 pentagons
i) 20 triangles
j) 2 squares, 4 trapezia
k) 6 triangles (two tetrahedra glued)
l) 10 triangles (two pentagonal pyramids glued)
m) 2 squares, 8 triangles
n) 2 pentagons, 10 triangles
o) 6 squares, 8 triangles
p) 4 triangles, 4 hexagons
q) 8 triangles, 6 octagons
r) 12 pentagons, 20 hexagons
s) 2 octagons, 8 rectangles
t) 1 decagon, 10 triangles

Read this:

'You want to know why I still go to the temple with Paati? Okay. Last year I was reading all these articles and had a hundred questions. Like, if God is everywhere, why the temple? Why the rules about who can enter? I was scared to ask anyone at home. I thought they'd say college had spoiled me.
Finally I blurted it out to Minakshi Paati while we were stringing jasmine. She didn't even drop the thread. She said, "Good, Sharmila. Our sages argued about exactly that for a thousand years. Asking is old, kanna. Only the fear is new."
Then she asked what I thought. Actually asked. We argued till the flowers wilted.
I still have questions. But I go with her on Fridays. Because she let me ask.'

What were Sharmila and Minakshi Paati doing when the question came out?
They were stringing jasmine.
Why was Sharmila scared to ask anyone at home?
Sharmila feared being told that college had spoiled things, so the questions felt shameful to voice.
What did Minakshi Paati do that kept Sharmila close?
She welcomed the question, said the sages argued about the same thing, used no shame or fear, and asked what Sharmila thought.
How might Minakshi Paati feel arguing with her grandchild till the flowers wilted?
She probably enjoys it and feels closer, seeing curiosity as part of faith rather than a threat to it.

Read this:

I'm Omkar, and the best lesson from my sociology project was about questions. My first interview with Tushar, a delivery rider, opened with "Don't you think your company exploits you?" His shoulders closed and he said, "It's fine," and that was it. I felt stupid, and honestly a bit angry at myself. My supervisor said, "You gave him the answer you wanted." The next week I tried again with "What does a normal day look like for you?" and then followed up, "What part of it is hardest?" Tushar talked for half an hour, and I learned things I'd never have guessed. Curious questions got me the truth, while my loaded one had shut the door.

What was Tushar's job?
Tushar was a delivery rider.
What did Omkar feel after the first interview?
Omkar felt stupid and a bit angry after the loaded question had shut Tushar down. The supervisor's comment helped Omkar see why.
What did Omkar change in the second interview?
Omkar asked an open question about a normal day and followed up with what was hardest, staying curious instead of leading.
How might Tushar have felt with the first question?
Tushar probably felt accused or wary, as the closed shoulders and 'It's fine' suggest, though he may also just have been cautious with a stranger.

Read this:

Subject: About yesterday's review
Hi Preeti,
I owe you an apology. In yesterday's client review I sighed and rolled my eyes when you said the brochure copy needed two more days. Arjun saw it, and so did you. That was rude, and it wasn't really about you. We're three people short and I've been stretched thin; I also like to think I'm the fast one on this team, and that's pride talking.
What I should have done is be clear. Here's what I actually need: a first draft of the brochure copy by Wednesday noon, even if it's rough, so the designers can start. If something is blocking you, tell me and I'll help with the product notes, which I know are a mess.
Coffee tomorrow before stand-up? My treat.
Nazia

By when does Nazia ask for the first draft?
By Wednesday noon, even if it's rough.
What feelings does Nazia admit were behind the eye-rolling?
Nazia admits feeling stretched thin and stressed, plus pride at being the fast one, so the contempt was more about the writer than about Preeti.
How does the email turn contempt into something useful?
It apologises plainly, then sets a clear deadline and offers concrete help with the messy product notes.
How might Preeti feel reading the email?
Preeti may still feel stung by the public eye-roll, but also respected and relieved to get an honest apology and a clear target.

Read this:

Dear Anjali,
You asked why I haven't decided about Canada yet. Here's my thinking, written down so I stop going in circles.
What I know: I have an admission for a one-year course in Toronto. It costs a lot. My job here is stable.
What I don't know: whether I'll get work after, how long the visa will take, whether I'll like the cold as much as I like the idea of it.
So I've done three things. I've talked to four people who went: two are happy, one came back, one is struggling. I've set a limit on what I'm willing to spend. And I've asked my company if I can take unpaid leave instead of resigning, so I have a way back.
If they say yes, I'll go. If no, I'll wait a year and try again. Either way, I'll review it at the end of the year, not before.
Your brother,
Madhav

How many people who went to Canada did Madhav talk to?
Four people.
How does Madhav seem to feel before writing the letter?
Madhav seems anxious and stuck, going in circles over the decision.
Which of Madhav's steps show good decision-making under uncertainty?
Madhav separated what was known from what wasn't, gathered mixed experiences, set a spending limit and created a way back.
How might Anjali feel reading her brother's plan?
Anjali would probably feel reassured that Madhav is thinking carefully, and maybe proud of her brother.

Read this:

When the Tokyo swim club posted the relay team, Aiko's name wasn't on it. She shrugged. "I didn't want to swim relay anyway."
Nkechi, her friend from the changing rooms, raised an eyebrow. "You've been training for it since April."
"It's just swimming. Who cares."
Aiko stopped staying after practice. She scrolled her phone on the bench and said everything was boring. Her coach asked if something was wrong. "Nope. Just over it."
Two weeks later, Nkechi found her crying in the car park. "I care so much it's stupid," Aiko said. "If I act like I don't, it doesn't hurt."
Nkechi sat with her. "It hurts anyway. Might as well have company."
The next morning Aiko asked the coach what she needed to improve.

When had Aiko been training for the relay since?
Since April.
Why did Aiko say it was just swimming and she was over it?
She was hurt and embarrassed at being left off, and acting uncaring felt safer than admitting how much it mattered.
How could a coach help a swimmer who suddenly acts bored?
The coach could gently check in again in private and offer clear steps to improve, so caring feels safe again.
What is it like for Nkechi to watch Aiko pretend not to care?
Nkechi can see through it and feels concerned, which is why she stays and sits with her.

Read this:

The elective registration portal closed at 5 p.m., and at 4:15 it kept crashing. Ojas sat in the college cyber café with his cousin Aadhya, refreshing again and again.
Two options: “Film-making workshop: portfolio-based grading” or “Office tools: guaranteed high scores.”
Ojas had spent every holiday since Class 8 making short films on his phone.
“So, film-making, obviously?” Aadhya said.
“My CGPA is 9.2. If the portfolio's bad, I could get a C.”
“Could.”
“And then the placement cutoff…” He trailed off. The page loaded for a second. His finger hovered over film-making, then clicked office tools.
Submitted: 4:52.
“You look like you just lost something,” Aadhya said quietly.
Ojas closed the laptop. “I kept my 9.2.”

What was Ojas's CGPA?
His CGPA was 9.2.
Why did Ojas click office tools instead of film-making?
He was afraid a bad portfolio would lower his grade and hurt his placement chances, so the safe option felt necessary.
What could Ojas try to keep his love of film alive?
He could join a film club or make films outside class, or talk to the film teacher about how grading works before deciding next time.
How does Aadhya see his choice?
Aadhya sees that he gave up something he loves, saying he looks like he just lost something.

Tell me what "spill the beans" means.
What does citadel mean in simple words?
Is there a mistake here? This shirt is too much expensive.
Quick one: why does a shopkeeper give a bill after a sale?

1. It means to tell a secret, often by mistake. For example: Rohan spilled the beans about the surprise party.
2. Citadel is a noun that means a strong fort that guards a city.
3. Fixed: This shirt is too expensive. Why: Use "too" directly before an adjective; "too much" goes before a noun.
4. It records what you bought and how much you paid. Because with it you can check the amount or return an item later.

Read this:

'I should've gone,' Chaitanya said, staring at the cricket kit in the corner. 'Mama asked me to come to the hospital on Saturday. I said I had a match.'
Siddharth sat on the edge of the bed. 'You didn't know it would be the last time.'
'He came to my matches. Every single one. And I couldn't go and see him once.'
'That's why this hurts so much, man. Because you loved him.'
'Doesn't feel like love. Feels like I'm a terrible person.'
'You're not. You're a guy who thought he had more time.'
Chaitanya wiped his face. 'I never said bye. Never said thanks for anything.'
'So say it now. Write it down. My mum did that when Nanu died. Wrote him a whole letter.'
'What did she do with it?'
'Read it at his photo. Said it helped.'
Chaitanya pulled a notebook out of his bag. 'Stay while I write?'
'Yeah. Take your time.'

Why didn't Chaitanya go to the hospital on Saturday?
He said he had a match.
What was Chaitanya feeling as he stared at his cricket kit?
He felt guilty and full of regret, sure he was a terrible person for not visiting Mama.
What does Siddharth suggest, and why might it help?
Writing Mama a letter with the unsaid goodbye and thanks, so the feelings have somewhere to go.
How does Siddharth see Chaitanya's guilt?
He sees it as love, from someone who simply thought he had more time.

1) What is wrong with this: I am living here since 2010.
2) Please define "diffuse".
3) If you cannot hear the teacher, what should you do?

1. I have been living here since 2010. Why: With "since", use the present perfect continuous, not the present continuous.
2. "Diffuse" is a verb meaning to spread out widely.
3. Politely say so or move closer. Because the teacher cannot know unless you tell them.

Read this:

Class 4 diary, Monday
Yusuf came in today holding a small telescope as if it were made of glass. He told the class his Abba bought it on Saturday. "I asked in March. He said wait till my birthday. I waited six months!"
Deepika asked if he wasn't angry about waiting. Yusuf thought and said, "At first. But now it feels more special. Abba saved for it. He works nights at the bakery."
At break he let every child have one careful look through it.
During art period I asked Yusuf to make a thank-you card for his Abba. He drew the moon and wrote, "Worth the wait." I have tucked it into his bag to take home.

When did Yusuf first ask for the telescope?
In March.
How does Yusuf feel about the telescope after waiting?
He feels grateful and proud, and says it feels more special because he waited.
How did the class teacher help Yusuf show his gratitude?
They asked him to make a thank-you card in art period and tucked it into his bag to take home.
How might Abba feel when he reads "Worth the wait"?
He would probably feel touched and proud, knowing his effort was noticed.

Read this:

The inter-school quiz final had been delayed an hour by a power cut, and when it restarted, the buzzers kept sticking. Zubin's team lost to Ankita's by five points.
Zubin felt the loss like a punch. He had spent weeks learning capitals. He wanted to slam the broken buzzer and say it was the machine's fault.
Instead he went to the corridor and let a few tears fall.
Then he came back in and walked up to Ankita. "Well played. You knew the science round really well."
"Thanks," she said, surprised. "You guys were so fast on geography."
On the way home, Zubin wrote in his notebook: practise science.

What delayed the quiz final by an hour?
A power cut.
How did Zubin feel after losing?
He felt crushed, like he'd been punched, after weeks of learning capitals.
What did Zubin do instead of blaming the buzzer?
He let himself cry, congratulated Ankita, and wrote down what to practise.
How might Ankita feel when Zubin congratulates her?
Ankita seemed surprised and pleased, complimenting his team back.

Read this:

I'm Ayesha, and I was at the back of the room when Neelam presented her plan for the new mentoring scheme. Halfway through, Mrs. Suri, the head of HR, raised both eyebrows and started writing fast. Two others sat back with folded arms and said only "Hmm" when Neelam paused. I watched Neelam falter. I think she read it all as doubt; I would have too. She had two options: rush on, or stop. She stopped. "I can see some raised eyebrows. What are your thoughts so far?" Mrs. Suri looked up. "I'm writing because I want to steal this for the Pune office. Keep going." One of the arm-folders, Mr. Rao, said, "I'm not convinced about the time commitment, though. Two hours a week is a lot." Neelam nodded and asked what would work. By the end they'd agreed on one hour, and Mrs. Suri had three pages of notes.

How much weekly time did Mr. Rao think was a lot?
Two hours a week.
What was Neelam likely feeling when she saw the raised eyebrows?
Neelam probably felt anxious and unsure, reading the eyebrows and folded arms as doubt, and faltered.
Why was stopping to ask better than guessing?
The cues were mixed: Mrs. Suri's eyebrows meant interest, while Mr. Rao had a real doubt about time, which only came out because Neelam asked.
What did Mrs. Suri's fast note-taking really mean?
She was interested and wanted to use the scheme in the Pune office, not doubtful.

metadata.subtype: Thoughtful, interested and doubtful in meetings [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Aditi, you look like you want to hide under the bed. Sit. Let your Omkar Ajoba tell you something.
At fourteen I copied answers in a maths test. The teacher caught me. In front of everyone.
For a week I couldn't look at anyone. I skipped school two days and said I had fever. I told myself, "I'm a cheat. I'm a bad boy." I hid from my own mother.
Then Mr Kulkarni, the teacher who caught me, came to our house. I thought I'd die of shame.
He sat with my father and said, "Omkar did a wrong thing. Omkar is not a wrong boy." Then he turned to me. "What do you want to do about it?"
Something changed. I said, "I want to take the test again. Properly." I did. I scored less, but I could look at him.
Feeling "I did bad" made me fix it. Feeling "I am bad" only made me hide.

How many days did Omkar skip school?
He skipped school two days and said he had fever.
What was Omkar feeling during the week after he was caught?
He felt deep shame, believing he was a bad boy, which made him hide from everyone, even his mother.
What was the turning point in Omkar Ajoba's story?
Mr Kulkarni separating the act from the person and asking what Omkar wanted to do, which turned shame into guilt that led to repair.
How might Mr Kulkarni have seen Omkar?
He saw a boy who did something wrong but was not bad, and came to the house to help him repair it with care.
Marina had 4.5 pounds of fudge. Lazlo had 6 ounces less than 4 pounds of fudge. How many more ounces of fudge did Marina have than Lazlo?

Marina = 4.5 pounds = 72 ounces
Lazlo = 4 pounds - 6 ounces = 58 ounces
72 - 58 = 14 ounces
Marina had 14 more ounces of fudge than Lazlo.
The answer is 14.
Two new families moved into our building and I'd like to make them feel welcome.
A friendly gesture goes a long way. You could knock on their door, introduce yourself and offer help with directions or local shops.
Should I bring food?
A small plate of homemade sweets or snacks is a lovely gesture. Check first if they have any food restrictions.
What if they're shy?
Keep the visit short and warm, and don't push for a long chat. Say you're a neighbour if they need anything. They'll remember your kindness.
I'll go on Sunday afternoon, then.
A good time, since people are usually at home and relaxed. Let them settle in for a few days first.

Read this:

At the swimming club's Saturday session, Raghav was always last to finish the lap. Today, as he climbed out gasping, two boys on the bench started chanting, "Tor-toise! Tor-toise!" Others laughed.
Divyansh felt his chest go tight. He was new at the club and wanted friends. His hands were shaking a little.
"He's not a tortoise, he only started in June," Divyansh said. "And he doesn't stop halfway, like some people."
The chanting stopped. One of the boys glared at him. For the rest of the session, nobody passed Divyansh the ball in water polo.
Coach Lata had heard. After practice she called the two boys over and spoke to them firmly, then walked Raghav and Divyansh to the gate. "That took guts," she told Divyansh.

When did Raghav start swimming?
In June.
How was Divyansh feeling before he spoke?
Divyansh felt tense and nervous, hands shaking, worried about his chances of making friends.
What did Coach Lata do that helped?
She spoke firmly to the two boys after practice and walked Raghav and Divyansh to the gate, recognising the courage it took.
What did speaking up cost Divyansh?
One boy glared at him, and nobody passed him the ball in water polo for the rest of the session.

Read this:

I'm Arohi, and I shared a flat with Rajni for two years. She was the one who organised everything: rent, groceries, weekend trips. Last winter I noticed her laptop open to the same job application for days. Dishes piled up in her room, which was never like her. She stopped coming to our Sunday dosa breakfast. When I asked, she said, "I can't start anything. I'm just tired." It had been over a month. I didn't give her a pep talk; I'd have hated that. I sat on her bed and said, "This seems bigger than being tired. Would you see a counsellor? I can find one near us." She nodded. We looked one up together that evening.

What breakfast did Rajni stop coming to?
Rajni stopped coming to the Sunday dosa breakfast.
What was Arohi feeling when noticing the change in Rajni?
Arohi felt worried and concerned, seeing that this was not like Rajni and had gone on for over a month.
What was wise about Arohi's response?
Arohi skipped the pep talk, named the change kindly, suggested a counsellor and helped look one up that same evening.
How might Rajni feel when Arohi sits on her bed and offers to help?
Rajni might feel relieved and cared for, since someone noticed without blaming her for being unable to start.
Why is summer hotter than winter where we live?
Summer sunlight is more direct and lasts longer each day. Because the Earth is tilted, our part of the world leans towards the sun in summer and away from it in winter.

Read this:

January: Vidya, twenty-five, got a new job through her father's friend. She also noticed that Raghav, her colleague from a Hindi-medium school, was twice as good at data work but kept being passed over for client calls.
March: When her manager asked for names for a new project, Vidya recommended Raghav, explaining his strengths. At lunch she asked him what made the job hard. He said, "Everyone assumes my English is weak." She listened and didn't argue.
June: A friend from her college messaged about an opening at a big firm. Vidya forwarded it to Raghav and two others, not just her own circle. Raghav got an interview. Vidya didn't feel like a saint, and she didn't pretend she'd got her job on her own. She just tried to share the doors she happened to stand beside.

How did Vidya get her new job?
Vidya got a new job through her father's friend.
What was Vidya feeling when she listened to Raghav at lunch?
Vidya felt concerned and attentive, wanting to understand his experience without defending herself.
Which of Vidya's actions show using advantage responsibly?
Recommending Raghav on merit, listening to his experience, and forwarding job openings beyond her own circle.
How might Raghav feel after Vidya's recommendation?
Raghav likely felt seen and grateful, finally recognised for his skills rather than judged by assumptions.

Read this:

I'm Sharmila, and I've watched my brother Harish on our Sunday family calls for about six months. When Dad starts on politics, Harish says "hmm" and looks somewhere else. He never argues. Then he goes on mute and sometimes his camera turns off. A few weeks ago he began missing the calls, saying he had work.

I can't say for sure what's going on inside him. Maybe he's tired, maybe he simply doesn't care. But on the last call Mum asked where he was, and Dad said, "He's always busy nowadays," in a small voice. I think the silence kept the calls peaceful, and I also think it's quietly costing the calls something.

What did Harish say when Dad started on politics?
Harish says "hmm" and looks somewhere else.
What might Sharmila think Harish is feeling, and how sure is Sharmila?
Sharmila suspects Harish may be tired or withdrawn but admits it cannot be said for sure what is going on inside.
What could Harish do instead of staying silent, and why?
Harish could say briefly that he disagrees or prefers a different topic, because a small honest remark may avoid building resentment and the missed calls.
How might Dad feel when he says Harish is always busy nowadays?
Dad sounds hurt and a little lonely, in a small voice, as the missing calls suggest distance he may not fully understand.

metadata.subtype: Approach: stay silent and resent it [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Charu,
You asked about the science test. I got 11 out of 40. That's it, I'm officially stupid. I've always been bad at science, and now it's spreading to everything. I'll probably fail maths next, then English, and then what? I stopped doing the revision sheets two days ago, what's the point. I know you'll say "it's just one test". But it doesn't feel like one test. It feels like finally seeing the truth. Mum says I'm being dramatic. Maybe. I just don't see how it changes. Remember last year when you told me I'm always hardest on myself? I keep thinking about that. I don't know if you're right.
Deepika

What score did Deepika get in the science test?
11 out of 40.
How is Deepika feeling about the test result?
Deepika feels hopeless and defeated, convinced of being stupid and that the failure will spread to every subject.
What would you advise Deepika about the revision sheets?
Deepika could restart them for one topic missed in the test, testing whether the result is really permanent.
How might Charu respond to this letter?
Charu might gently remind Deepika that it is one test, not the whole truth, and that this harsh way of explaining setbacks is a habit.

Read this:

"Why hasn't Sachin filled in the scholarship form yet?" Irfan's colleague asked. "The deadline's Friday."
Irfan, who ran the evening classes at the community centre, sighed. "His family lost their room when the landlord sold the building. They're sleeping at a cousin's, five people in one space. He works a shift at the dhaba after class."
"So he's lazy about forms?"

messages.content: Pima invested $400 in Ethereum. In the first week, it gained 25% in value. In the second week, it gained an additional 50% on top of the previous gain. How much is her investment worth now?

For the first week, her investment gain is $400 * 25% = $100.

For the second week, her investment increased by $500 * 50% = $250.
Pima's investment in Ethereum is now worth a total of $500 + $250 = $750.
The answer is 750.

Peter has four horses. Each one eats 4 pounds of oats, twice a day, and 3 pounds of grain once a day. How many pounds of food does he need to feed his horses for 3 days?

Peter needs 2 * 4 pounds of oats = 8 pounds of oats per horse per day.
Peter will need 8 pounds oats * 3 days = 24 pounds of oats per horse.
Peter will need 24 pounds of oats * 4 horses = 96 pounds of oats total.
Peter needs 3 pounds of grain * 3 days per horse = 9 pounds of grain per horse.
Peter will need 9 pounds of grain * 4 horses = 36 pounds of grain total.
For 3 days Peter will need a total of 96 pounds oats + 36 pounds grain = 132 pounds total.
The answer is 132.

There are 8 men at a yoga studio with an average weight of 190 pounds and 6 women with an average weight of 120 pounds. What is the average weight of all 14 men and women?

The total weight for the 8 men is 8 men * 190 pounds per man = 1520 pounds
The total weight for the 6 women is 6 women * 120 pounds per woman = 720 pounds

That means Kate needs 30 - 10 = $20 more to buy the pen.

Jerry is sweeping up pieces of broken glass in the parking lot. He sweeps up 20 amber pieces, 35 green pieces, and some clear pieces. If the green pieces are 25% of the total glass he sweeps up, how many pieces were clear?

First find the total number of glass pieces Jerry sweeps up: 35 green pieces / .25 = 140 pieces
Then subtract the number of pieces of other colors: 140 pieces - 20 pieces - 35 pieces = 85 pieces
The answer is 85.

At twenty, over dinner, Jaya said, "Quit the dance club or I'm done." Manoj felt a cold drop but also wondered whether Jaya meant it or was upset about the missed weekends. Manoj rang Madhuri, now a close friend. "Ask what's behind it," Madhuri said. "And watch whether your choices get respected, or whether you feel afraid to say no. If it ever feels scary, talk to someone you trust." Next day Manoj asked Jaya what was wrong. Jaya admitted the weekends felt empty, and together they set aside Saturday evenings. The club stayed.

At ten a joke turned into mocking as it repeated, spread to a wider circle and Manoj stopped laughing, so watching the target's face and the pattern mattered. At twenty "quit or I'm done" could be a real need or pressure, so Manoj asked what was behind it and whether choices were respected.

Our newspaper uses the word "eve-teasing". Is it a term used in other countries?

It is used mainly in India for harassing girls and women in public. Elsewhere people use "street harassment" or "sexual harassment". Because "teasing" sounds light, many writers now prefer the standard words.

Work out 97 x 103 and 47 x 53 in your head.

Answer: 97 x 103 = (100 - 3)(100 + 3) = 10,000 - 9 = 9,991; 47 x 53 = (50 - 3)(50 + 3) = 2,500 - 9 = 2,491.

When two numbers are the same distance either side of a round number, use (a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2. 97 and 103 are both 3 away from 100, so the product is 100^2 - 3^2. 47 and 53 are 3 away from 50, so 50^2 - 3^2. This also works with decimals: 9.8 x 10.2 = 10^2 - 0.2^2 = 100 - 0.04 = 99.96. Find the MIDDLE number first: halfway between 36 and 44 is 40, so 36 x 44 = 40^2 - 4^2 = 1,600 - 16 = 1,584.

She could tell him she'd be proud of him at 60 too 🙂, and that the Olympiad is a chance to try hard problems, not a test of his worth.
What might Appa not realise when he photocopies the test?
Appa probably means only to celebrate, not realising his pride may teach Pankaj that love comes with perfect marks.

Jenny collects cans and bottles to take down to the recycling center. Each bottle weighs 6 ounces and each can weighs 2 ounces. Jenny can carry a total of 100 ounces. She collects 20 cans and as many bottles as she can carry. If she gets paid 10 cents per bottle and 3 cents per can, how much money does she make (in cents)?

First, the weight of 20 cans is 20 cans * 2 oz per can = 40 oz.
Thus, Jenny has the capacity to carry 100 oz - 40 oz = 60 oz of bottles.
Jenny can carry 60 oz / 6 oz per bottle = 10 bottles.
Jenny earns 10 bottles * 10 cents per bottle = 100 cents for the bottles.
Jenny earns 20 cans * 3 cents per can = 60 cents for the cans.
In total, she earns 100 cents + 60 cents = 160 cents.
The answer is 160.

Tanvir, first day, you want to know? Okay. So I walk into the bank's head office, twelfth floor, glass everywhere, and the team lead is already talking about 'basis points' and 'run-rate' and 'the Q3 walk'. Q3 walk! I thought it was a team outing.
Everyone has two screens. Everyone types without looking. One girl, maybe a year older than me, finished a whole model while I was still trying to log in.
And I'm so happy, Tanvir, I am. My name is on the door list. I called Amma from the lift. But at lunch I sat there thinking, Sudha, they interviewed forty people, and they picked you? What if they meant the other Sudha? There were two Sudhas in the final round, I'm not joking.
I laughed about it in the lift. At night it's not so funny.

What floor is the bank's head office on?
It is on the twelfth floor.
What was Sudha thinking at lunch on the first day?
Sudha was worried the bank had picked the wrong person, even joking they might have meant the other Sudha 😰
What small step could help Sudha settle in?
Sudha could ask the team lead or a nearby colleague to explain a few terms like 'the Q3 walk' in the first week, since new joiners are expected to ask.
How might Tanvir react to hearing both the excitement and the worry?
Tanvir may be happy for Sudha but also notice how real the self-doubt is, and want to remind Sudha that being picked means something.

From Irfan Mamu's notebook, Himani's second birthday.
When I gave Himani the drum, her mother said, “What do we say?” Himani hugged the drum and said, “Tank oo,” then banged it hard, grinning.
Later she handed her Nani a toy duck and waited. Nani said, “Thank you!” and Himani clapped.

What did Irfan Mamu give Himani?
He gave Himani the drum.
What was Himani feeling when she hugged the drum and said "Tank oo"?
She was delighted with the drum; the words were prompted and copied, but the pleasure was real.

Keep modelling "thank you" warmly, as Nani did, without pressure, so the words gradually join the good feeling.

Jimmy and Irene go shopping for clothes on a Tuesday, where senior citizens get a 10% discount on their purchases.  Jimmy picks out 3 shorts from the $15 rack.  Irene grabs 5 shirts from the $17 rack.  How much money do they give to the cashier?

Jimmy's shorts cost 3 x $15 = $45.
Irene's shirts cost 5 x $17 = $85.
Total cost for the clothes is $45 + $85 = $130.
10% discount on the clothes is $130 x 10% = $13.
They give the cashier $130 - $13 = $117.
The answer is 117.

Charu's diary, Tuesday night
Skipped the second half of my lab again because Sister Meenal said the evening session "needs everyone." Last month it was just Sundays. Now it's Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sunday, and the monthly contribution went up again. I told myself it's fine, I've already given so much that stopping now would waste it.

Damini sent: "Miss you. Are you okay? No lecture, promise." I read it three times.

Charu now goes on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sunday.

It suggests Charu feels lonely and torn, missing Damini even while the group tells Charu to stay away from old friends.

Charu could reply to Damini, since Damini promised no lecture, and speak to her mum or a college counsellor about the rising time, money and secrecy.

Damini is probably worried and a little frightened, sensing Charu is slipping away but choosing to stay gentle so the door stays open.

Pre-wedding counsellor's note, family meeting, Thursday.
Payal met with her parents, grandmother and her sister Arohi to discuss the ceremony. She wants to keep the saptapadi, the haldi, and the family prayer her grandmother leads. She asked to adapt the kanyadaan so that both her parents, not only her father, give their blessing. I just can't do the ones that make one family bow to the other." Arohi supported her quietly. After a long pause, Dadi said, "Then I'll lead the prayer twice." Which rites did Payal want to keep?
The saptapadi, the haldi and the family prayer her grandmother leads.
How did Dadi feel at first when Payal presented her list?
Dadi felt hurt, saying the family always did these things.
What made Payal's approach heard?
She kept meaningful rites, adapted some, explained the skipped ones kindly, and honoured her grandmother's feelings instead of arguing.
How might Arohi have seen the family meeting?
Arohi probably felt proud of Payal and quietly supportive, glad the talk stayed warm.

Week one. Rehana, twenty, gave her speech for student union president in the packed auditorium. "I want us to have a real voice." The crowd cheered. She felt a rush, like standing on a stage built for her.
Two weeks later. She won. Her first act was to extend library hours. Students thanked her in the canteen. She liked how people looked at her now.
A month later. At the committee meeting, Yamini proposed a vote on the fest budget. Rehana said, "I've already decided." The room went silent. Yamini said quietly, "Then why are we here?"
That night, Rehana couldn't sleep. She had wanted to lead. Somewhere she'd started wanting to control.
The next morning she called the meeting again and said, "Let's vote."

What was Rehana's first act as president?
She extended library hours.

She felt uneasy and ashamed, realising she had slid from leading into wanting control.

She overruled the committee by saying she had already decided; the next day she called the meeting again and let them vote.
How might Yamini have felt when Rehana said "I've already decided"?
Yamini probably felt dismissed and frustrated, as if the committee didn't matter.

Aman counts 5 apples starting from the left. Meena counts the same apples starting from the right. Who gets the bigger number?

Answer: Neither. Both get 5.

Let the child count from the left, then from the right, then from the middle. The answer is always 5. It does not matter where we start, as long as we count each apple once.

Tuesday night

Big one today. The buyer from Europe offered the biggest order we've ever had, but the delivery date means the stitching floor would need double shifts for six weeks. Madhuri from finance was thrilled. "Manjula, this saves our year," she said.

I sat in the car park for twenty minutes before coming home. Double shifts means tired hands near needles. Last year's fire drill showed our exits are already crowded when both lines run. And we promised the workers' committee no forced overtime.

But losing the buyer could mean layoffs in spring.

So here's what I decided, I think. Tomorrow I'll ask the buyer for three extra weeks, offer a partial delivery first, and hire a second shift properly instead of stretching the first. If they say no, we say no. I'm scared of that. Writing it down helps.

How long would the stitching floor need double shifts for the order?
For six weeks, because of the buyer's delivery date.
What was Manjula worried about while sitting in the car park?
Manjula worried about worker safety, crowded exits, breaking the promise on overtime, and also about possible layoffs if they lost the buyer.
Which part of Manjula's decision balances the risks well?
Manjula looks for a middle path, asking for more time, a partial delivery and a proper second shift, while keeping a clear line that safety and promises come first.
How might Madhuri react to Manjula's plan?
She might feel frustrated because she saw the order as saving the year, but she could come to see the risk of injuries or a broken promise.

In the Vancouver flat, Xin built a blanket fort and wanted it to glow like a cave. She took a leftover birthday candle and the long lighter from the kitchen drawer, and set the flame on a saucer by her pillow. Then her dog pushed in, and the blanket sagged low over it. Santiago, her stepfather, smelt something hot and pulled the blanket back. The edge had a brown scorch mark. He blew out the candle. "I was watching it the whole time!" Xin said, her lip shaking. "I know you were," he said. "But you didn't see Pepper move the blanket. New rule: candles and lighters only at the kitchen table, with a grown-up. The lighter lives on the top shelf now." Xin stared at the brown mark.

Where did Xin put the candle?
On a saucer by her pillow.
What was Xin feeling when Santiago pulled the blanket back?
She was upset and defensive, insisting she was watching it, with her lip shaking, probably also scared by the scorch mark.
What did Santiago do that fits a child of Xin's age?
He stayed calm, explained the part she couldn't foresee, the dog moving the blanket, and set a clear rule and moved the lighter out of reach.
How might Santiago have felt when he smelt something hot?
He was probably frightened, but he sat down and spoke gently instead of shouting.
Why do some flowers close up at night?

Many flowers close to protect their delicate parts. Because shutting the petals helps keep the pollen and the inner parts shielded from cold and damp, the flower is ready to open again when pollinators return in the daylight.

"Tejas, you saw Jomon throw the ball hard at the window, didn't you?" the coach said. "He was being careless, right?" Tejas had been drinking water behind the shed. He had only heard the crash. Where was Tejas when the window broke?
Drinking water behind the shed.
Why did Tejas agree with the coach?
He felt pressured and nervous, with the coach waiting and the boys staring, so the leading question made agreeing feel right, and the extra details filled themselves in.

Ask an open question like "What did you see?" without naming Jomon, and give Tejas time away from the watching boys.

Jomon could be blamed on the strength of details Tejas never saw, which is unfair and could hurt their friendship.
My map shows a "Palk Strait". Is it the same as "straight"?

No. A strait is a narrow stretch of water between two pieces of land. "Straight" means not curved.
Examples: Ships pass through the strait every day. Draw a straight line with the ruler.
Frank picked 36 apples. Susan picked 3 times as many apples as Frank. If Susan gave out half of her apples, and Frank sold a third of his, how many in total do they have left?

Susan picked 3 times as much as 36 which is 3*36 = 108 apples
She gave out half which is 108*(1/2) = 54 apples
She now has 108-54 = 54 apples
Frank sold a third of 36 which is 36*(1/3) = 12 apples
Frank now has 36-12 = 24 apples
Altogether they now have 54+24 = 78 apples
The answer is 78.

What was Lalremsiami feeling as she stared at her shoes?

She asked gently, said Lalremsiami didn't have to tell her, accepted the short answer and offered to go to Ma'am together that same day.

Ma'am thanked them, said it wasn't okay and wasn't Lalremsiami's fault, and went to speak to the class before the last bell.
We're planning a picnic. What should we make?
Pick food that stays good without refrigeration and is easy to eat, such as sandwiches, wraps, fruit and boiled eggs. Keep drinks cold in a bottle or a cooler.
What about food that spoils quickly?
Keep it cool, and eat it early. Items with curd, cream or cooked rice can spoil quickly in the heat, so keep them in an insulated bag with ice packs or skip them.
How do I carry it all?
Use sealed containers inside a sturdy bag, and pack heavy things at the bottom. A cloth to sit on and a bag for rubbish are useful.
Should we bring games?
If you like. Cards, a frisbee or a ball are easy to carry. Pick a spot with shade and enough space.
How do we leave the place?
Take all your rubbish with you, including food waste. Leave the spot cleaner than you found it.

At the coaching centre in Siliguri, the monthly report cards came out on Friday. Pema, fifteen, opened his and read: "Failed 40% of mock questions."

He sat very still in the corridor. His mother had paid for this coaching. He decided, right there, to tell her he was stopping.

Lavanya ma'am, the centre's counsellor, saw his face. "Pema, come in for a minute."

Pema blinked. "It's the same number?"

"Exactly the same. The report just says it in the scariest way."

"I was going to quit."

"Because of one word, 'failed'?"

He nodded, embarrassed.

Lavanya ma'am made a note to talk to the director about how the reports were worded. Then she helped Pema list the chapters where he'd lost marks.

What did Pema's report card say?
Failed 40% of mock questions.
Why did Pema decide to stop coaching after reading the report?
Pema felt ashamed and guilty, because "failed 40%" made the result sound like a disaster, and his mother had paid for the coaching.
What did Lavanya ma'am do that helped both Pema and other students?
Lavanya ma'am reframed the result as sixty percent correct and improving, then planned to ask the director to change the report wording.
How might Pema's mother have felt if he had quit because of the wording?
Pema's mother might have felt confused and worried, not knowing he was actually improving.

Rajni said she got four thousand back in ten days.

How does Rajni see Jyoti's questions?

A client report with a huge error.
What was young Sunaina feeling when Mr Rao suggested one thing at a time?
Sunaina felt insulted at first, having thought multitasking was a talent.
What choice inside the story changed Sunaina's work?
Deciding to try Mr Rao's advice anyway: one task at a time and three slow breaths before starting.

Ishita may feel frustrated or unfairly treated, since Ishita's honest work earned fewer marks than an answer with no effort.

At Sunshine Playschool, it was Vidya's turn to take a glass of water to Gurpreet Ma'am's table. The glass was full to the top.
Vidya stopped and looked at it. "Walk slow," she said out loud. "Both hands. Then on the table."
She held it with both hands. She walked very slowly, looking at the water, not at her friends. "Walk slow, walk slow."
At the table she stopped. "On the table." She set it down gently. Not one drop spilled.

"Walk slow. Both hands. Then on the table."

Tuesday, the first outage. The payments page is down for two hours. Nobody posts anything. Harish, who runs customer support, gets four hundred calls and has nothing to say except 'we're looking into it'.
Friday, the next week. Another outage, smaller. This time Tejas is named communications owner. He posts on the status page at 11.00: 'Some card payments failing. Cause not known yet. Next update 11.30.' At 11.30: 'Cause found. Fix in testing. Next update 12.00.' At 12.00: 'Fixed. Thank you for your patience.' Each one short, each one on time.
Monday. Harish brings a chart to the review. Friday's calls: sixty-five. 'Same kind of outage,' he says. 'The only difference is people knew when they'd hear from us.'

How many calls did Harish's team get on Friday?
Sixty-five.
How might Harish have felt on the first Tuesday?
Harish likely felt frustrated and helpless, taking four hundred calls with nothing to tell customers.
What would make Tejas's updates even more useful next time?
Posting the first update within minutes and adding what customers can do meanwhile, such as trying again later.
How did customers experience Friday differently from Tuesday?
On Friday they knew what was happening and when they'd hear next, so fewer felt the need to call.
Why does leather become hard and crack if it is left unused for a long time?
It loses its natural oils. Because the fibres dry out when not treated or flexed, they become stiff and break.
My mother's birthday is on Sunday and I'd like to make her breakfast in bed.
A sweet gesture. What can you make comfortably?
Toast with jam and tea, maybe some cut fruit.
That will do nicely. Cut the fruit into small pieces, make the tea gently and put everything on a tray with a flower or a card.
Should I make it a surprise?
If she's a person who loves surprises, yes. You could ask someone else at home to help you keep the secret, and wake her up with a gentle knock.
I'm afraid I'll spill the tea.
Fill the cup only two-thirds, walk slowly and set the tray down before you open the door. A saucer under the cup catches small spills.
I'll practise with water first. Thank you!
Excellent plan. A water rehearsal costs nothing and saves a lot of worry.

The break room at the accounts office was empty after six, the kettle ticking as it cooled. Vijay and Sarita, partners for two years, often waited here for the shared cab. Vijay had rehearsed a sentence all week and now it stuck in the throat. "There's a thing I've never told anyone," Vijay said. "In college I failed a year and told my family I was on an exchange. I still feel ashamed."

Sarita set down the cup. "That sounds heavy to carry alone. Thank you for telling me." No lecture. After a moment, "Do you want to say more, or is that enough for today?"

Vijay let out a long breath. "That's enough for today. But it helped."

Where were Vijay and Sarita waiting?
In the break room at the accounts office, waiting for the shared cab.
What might Vijay be worried Sarita will think about the failed year?
That Sarita will sigh, joke or pity Vijay, since Vijay stares at the floor waiting for it and still feels ashamed of the old lie.
What did Vijay do that made it safer to open up?
Vijay shared one piece at a pace Vijay chose, then noticed whether Sarita held it with care, and Sarita's question about saying more or stopping gave Vijay control of the pace.
How might Sarita have felt receiving Vijay's confession?
Probably trusted and careful, since Sarita thanked Vijay, avoided any lecture and checked how much more Vijay wanted to say.

When Chachu died on the highway, our house in Lucknow filled up in a single afternoon. I'm Irfan. I didn't know what to do with my hands, so I found jobs. I answered the landline and wrote every caller's name in a notebook for Dadi. I carried water jugs from the tanker to the kitchen, three at a time. Irfan wrote every caller's name.
What was Irfan feeling when the ball hit Chachu's bicycle?

Asha has to buy some gifts but has no money. She decides to borrow $20 from her brother, $40 from her father, $30 from her mother and is gifted $70 by her granny. She adds this to her savings of $100 and goes out to Target to get what she wanted. If she spent 3/4 of the money, how much money did she remain with?

With the amount borrowed from her family, she has a total of 20+40+30= 90 dollars.
With the amount gifted from her granny, she has 70+90 = 160 dollars.
She adds this to her savings, ending up with a total of 160+100 = 260 dollars.
She spends 3/4 of this money, which is 3/4*260 = 195 dollars.
The total she remains with is 260-195 = 65 dollars
The answer is 65.

Which is best - a line plot, a bar graph or a table - for each: (a) the shoe sizes of 30 children; (b) the favourite colours of a class; (c) the exact marks of 5 children in 4 subjects?

Answer: (a) a line plot; (b) a bar graph; (c) a table.

A line plot is for NUMBER data where values repeat, like sizes 1 to 6: we see the most common size and the spread at once. A bar graph is for CATEGORIES, like colours, which are not numbers on a line. A table is best when we need many EXACT numbers in rows and columns. It was a journey of only twenty-four miles, and they began it so early as to be in Gracechurch Street by noon. As they drove to Mr. Gardiner's door, Jane was at a drawing-room window watching their arrival: when they entered the passage, she was there to welcome them, and Elizabeth, looking earnestly in her face, was pleased to see it healthful and lovely as ever. Jenny had $24 left after spending 3/7 of her money. How much is half of her original amount of money?

Jenny spent 1 - 3/7 = 4/7 of her money.
Since 4/7 is equal to $24, then 1/7 is equal to $24/4 = $6.
So, Jenny originally had $6 x 7 = $42.
Therefore, half of her original amount of money is $42/2 = $21.
The answer is 21.

1) My teacher used the word "likelihood". What is it?
2) What is the difference between "so" and "such"?
3) Can you correct this for me? "Do you know where is the post office?"
4) Who lived in my house before us?
5) Quick one: why do the days feel longer in summer?

1. As a noun, "likelihood" means the chance that something will happen.
2. Use "so" before an adjective alone, as in "so tall". Use "such" before a noun, as in "such a tall tree".
3. Better: Do you know where the post office is? Why: after "know where", the subject comes before the verb.
4. I don't know; I can't see your house's history. Ask a neighbour or the house owner.
5. Daylight lasts longer in summer. Because our part of the Earth tilts toward the sun then, so the sun stays above the horizon for more hours.

I'm Abhinav, and I used to stonewall. With my last partner, a fight meant days of silence from me. I thought it was dignified. It was punishment with no end date.
With Zeenat, I've been trying something different.
Last Sunday we argued about her brother staying with us for a month. I felt the old wall going up. My jaw locked. I wanted to walk out and not speak till she gave in.
Instead, I said, "Zeenat, I'm too wound up right now. I need an hour. I'll be back by four, and I really want to talk about this."

I walked to the park and sat by the pond. At ten to four, I came home. I said, "A month feels long to me. Could we try two weeks and see?" She said, "I can ask him."

At two, Pradeep screamed for the biscuit at once, turning red, hitting the floor with both fists. "After dinner," said Ayesha, his mother. The words meant nothing. There was only now, and now had no biscuit.

At five, Pradeep sat with a biscuit on the plate and was told he could have it after the song. While Ayesha sang and clapped the words about the elephant, he swayed and waved along and forgot it for a bit. But when the song stopped and he stared at the biscuit, his hand crept out. At two Pradeep screamed for the biscuit and "after dinner" meant nothing; at five he waited through Ayesha's song, but his hand crept out when he stared at the biscuit; at sixteen he promised to start tomorrow and scrolled videos until midnight. Each time the present pulls harder than the future.
