"Ojas, you keep saying you'll pick your stream when you're sure. Let me, your Tarun chacha, tell you about my summer of waiting to be sure. I was sixteen. The choice was the polytechnic in Nashik for electrical, or commerce at the local college. I wanted a sign. I asked my teacher, then the astrologer uncle next door, then I waited for my board result to decide for me. It came, good marks, and still no sign. My friend Sandeep filled his form in May and kept saying, 'Just choose, you can change later.' I kept waiting. By the time I went to Nashik in July, electrical was full. I took mechanical, the only seat left, and spent two years with a knot in my stomach every morning. Not because the choice was wrong. Because I never actually made it."

Which course did young Tarun end up taking?
Mechanical, the only seat left.
What was young Tarun feeling through that summer?
He was anxious and unsure, wanting a clear sign before choosing, and later felt a knot in his stomach every morning.
What could young Tarun have done in May, when Sandeep filled his form?
He could have picked the option that seemed best so far and applied, knowing he could change later, instead of waiting for certainty.
How might Sandeep have seen Tarun's waiting that summer?
Sandeep was probably puzzled and a bit worried, seeing that waiting was costing more than a choice would, which is why he kept saying "just choose".
Our office is celebrating Christmas. Please write a short welcome note, about 50 words, to put beside the decorated tree.

Merry Christmas, everyone! This tree was decorated by all of us, one paper star at a time. Take a moment today to stop by, enjoy a slice of plum cake and add a wish for the new year on one of the cards below. Thank you for a wonderful year together.

I'm Seema, Kunal's mother, and this is the third science project I've watched him start at nine the night before.
At 9:10 he spread chart paper on the floor. By ten he realised he had no glue stick. At 10:40 he asked me to drive him to the stationery shop. It was closed; I knew it would be.
The last two times, I had driven round town, found glue, and stayed up till one cutting pictures. This time I didn't. I made him tea and said, "Use what you have." He used rice paste. The chart was wobbly. He got a C and was annoyed with me for a day.
On Sunday I sat down with him. I didn't lecture. I asked, "When did you find out about this project?" He counted. Twelve days.
We put a small whiteboard by his desk. Every Sunday evening, fifteen minutes: what's due, and what's the first step this week. He rolled his eyes. He also, last week, bought glue on a Tuesday.

What did Kunal use instead of a glue stick?
He used rice paste.
How did Seema seem to feel when she chose not to rescue Kunal this time?
Seema seemed torn but determined, choosing tea and "Use what you have" instead of another late-night rescue.
What routine did Seema help Kunal build, and why is it useful?
Fifteen minutes every Sunday evening at a whiteboard to note what is due and the first step, so projects start days earlier.
How did Kunal feel after getting a C?
Kunal felt annoyed, staying cross with his mother for a day.

"Duck! Duck! Splash!" Chandrika jabbed at the photo on the phone.
"Yes, the duck went splash in the pond," said Elizabeth Ammachi.
"Me... bread. Duck eat!"
"You gave the duck bread, and the duck ate it."
"Then... big dog! Woof! Me run!"
"A big dog barked, and you ran to Appa."
Chandrika nodded hard. "Appa up!"
"Appa picked you up. What a day at the park."
"Again!" said Chandrika, and started from the duck.

What did Chandrika give the duck?
She gave the duck bread.
How did Chandrika seem to feel while retelling the park story?
She seemed excited and proud 😊 jabbing at the photo, nodding hard and asking to tell it again.
What was Elizabeth Ammachi doing that helped Chandrika's words grow?
She echoed each fragment back as a full sentence, giving Chandrika the words for what happened.
What might Appa feel if he heard this retelling?
He would probably feel warm and amused that the dog and his picking her up had become part of her story.

Dear Uday,
I'm not going to send this. That's kind of the point. You've texted me four times since Saturday's practice, and I've left every one on "seen". I know it's mean. But if I reply, I'll have to say that it hurt when you told Coach I wasn't ready for the relay, like I'm the weakest girl on the team, and you'll say I'm too sensitive, and then we'll fight, and I'll cry, and you'll win. Not replying means I don't lose. It's the only part of this I'm in charge of. And honestly? Some small, silly part of me hopes you'll keep texting. That you'll show up at my gate and say, "Pallavi, what's wrong?" Then I'd know you actually care.
Your friend (for now)

How many times has Uday texted since Saturday's practice?
Uday has texted four times since Saturday's practice.
What does Pallavi secretly hope will happen?
She hopes Uday will keep texting and even come to her gate asking what's wrong, which would prove Uday cares.
What could Pallavi try instead of leaving every message on "seen"?
She could send one honest line, "What you told Coach hurt me", and ask Uday to hear it without calling her sensitive.
What might Uday be feeling after four unanswered texts?
Uday may feel worried and shut out, unable to guess what went wrong, and might soon stop trying.

When did the fee portal close?
On Friday.
Why did Siddharth keep saying it would sort itself out?
Not looking at the email and the fees helped him avoid dread, even though the problems were growing.
What was the turning point, and what did Siddharth choose after it?
The closed portal and blocked hall ticket forced him to look; he then agreed to go to the office with Pradeep and book the counsellor.
What was it like for Pradeep to watch Siddharth avoid the problem?
Pradeep seemed worried but unsure how to push, sending reminders and then offering to go with him once the deadline hit.
Give three reminders for keeping a desk tidy, numbered, each under eight words.

1. Put pens back in the box.
2. Stack your books neatly.
3. Throw away old paper.
I'm going to a city where I don't speak the language.
Learn a few key phrases, such as hello, thank you, please and how much. Locals usually appreciate the effort.
What if I get lost?
Keep the address of your stay written in the local language, and use an offline map. You can also show the address to a shopkeeper or a driver.
How do I order food?
Point at the dish on the menu or on another table, or use a translation tool. Pictures on menus help a lot.
What if I need real help?
Find the address of your country's embassy or consulate, or the local emergency number, before you travel and keep it somewhere safe.

At the Kolkata preschool, Eshaan used to be the one who helped others with their shoes. Since his baby brother Dhruv was born, he'd changed. Today he sucked his thumb at circle time and spoke in a squeaky voice: "Eshu can't do it. Eshu too little." He wouldn't let go of the teacher's dupatta. At lunch he asked to be fed. The teacher knelt and hugged him. "You can sit on my lap for the story today." Eshaan snuggled in. Afterwards, she said, "And then, will you help Arya with her shoes? You're so good at it." Eshaan thought, then nodded.

Who was born recently in Eshaan's family?
His baby brother Dhruv.
Why did Eshaan say "Eshu too little"?
Since Dhruv was born he feels anxious and in need of attention, so acting small is a way of asking to be cared for like the baby.
How did the teacher balance comfort with helping Eshaan grow?
She gave him lap time for the story, then invited him to help Arya with her shoes, meeting his need and his big-boy skills.
How might Arya feel when Eshaan helps her again?
Arya would probably feel glad and cared for, and Eshaan's help shows he is still the helper.

The power had gone out in the Kolkata flat, and Arnab, four, couldn't sleep in the heat. His mother Gopika fanned him with a newspaper. "What was the best part of today?"
Arnab's lip trembled. "Dadu said I was naughty."
He had pulled the cat's tail once, in the morning. After that he'd sung for Dadu, fed the fish and eaten all his rice, and Dadu had clapped each time.
"Dadu also clapped when you sang," Gopika said softly.
"But he said naughty." Arnab turned his face to the wall.
Gopika kept fanning, and began to hum his song.

What did Arnab do after pulling the cat's tail?
He sang for Dadu, fed the fish and ate all his rice.
Why does 'naughty' matter more to Arnab than all the clapping?
The one scolding hurt, so it feels heavier and stays in his mind, pushing out the happy moments.
What else could Gopika try to help Arnab?
She could name each good moment with him slowly, like the song and the fish, or ask Dadu to remind him tomorrow how much he enjoyed the singing. 🙂
How might Dadu feel if he knew Arnab went to bed upset?
Dadu might feel sorry that one word stuck, when he clapped far more than he scolded.

Fix the mistake: She always is late. One more thing: is it "dilema" or "dilemma"? Oh, and why do chillies make our mouth burn? Plus, what does "out of the blue" mean? How would you explain "scarecrow" to a child?

1. Say it this way: She is always late. Why: the adverb of frequency goes after the verb "to be".
2. It is "dilemma", with a double "m".
3. A substance in chillies irritates the nerves in the mouth. Because those nerves sense heat and pain, the brain reads it as burning.
4. It means suddenly and without warning. For example: a letter from my old friend came out of the blue.
5. Scarecrow is a noun that means a figure put in a field to frighten birds away.

- Why does a shadow get longer in the evening?
- Which is correct, "loose" or "lose", in "Don't ___ your keys"?

1. The sun is low in the sky. Because its light comes in at a slant, so the shadow stretches far along the ground.
2. Use "lose", the verb meaning to not keep something. "Loose" means not tight.

Hrithik, you asked what I'm proudest of from my first company. Not the product. The ending. I'm Rekha, and two years ago my co-founder and I ran six weeks of tests on our home-tutor booking idea. Clear targets. We missed every one: almost no repeat bookings, and parents told us plainly they'd stick with the tutor next door.
So we stopped. We refunded every parent who had paid in advance, all thirty-one of them, within ten days. We wrote each of our two hundred users a real thank-you note, not a form email. And we put our code notes and what we'd learned into a document for any founder who asked.
It hurt. But last month, when I pitched my new company, one investor said, "You're the ones who refunded everyone." That's why she took the meeting, Hrithik.

How many parents were refunded?
All thirty-one, within ten days.
How did Rekha feel about stopping, then and now?
Stopping hurt Rekha at the time, but now Rekha feels proud of how cleanly they ended it.
Which part of the shutdown helped Rekha most later, and why?
Refunding everyone quickly, because it built a reputation that made an investor take the next meeting.
How might the parents who got refunds see Rekha's team?
They would likely feel respected and trust the team, since they got their money back quickly and honestly.

The PG in Koramangala had old cupboards, so on his first weekend Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport. He tested the alarm four times. Santosh, his roommate from Nashik, watched from the top bunk.
"Chalo, dosa," Santosh said, lifting his helmet off the hook. Lalit climbed on pillion without one. "It's only two signals away."
On the flyover a bus cut across and Santosh braked hard. Lalit grabbed the seat, heart thudding. At the dosa place he laughed it off, then opened the alarm app to make sure nothing in the room had moved.
Santosh looked at him over the chutney. "Your cupboard is safer than your head, yaar."

What did Lalit buy on his first weekend at the PG?
Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport.
Why do you think Lalit checked the alarm app right after the near miss?
Locking the cupboard down completely gave him a feeling of total control, so that small fear kept pulling at him while the bigger road danger got laughed off.
What small change would protect Lalit most?
Getting a helmet of his own and wearing it on every ride, even for two signals; one padlock is plenty for the cupboard.
How does Santosh see Lalit's priorities?
Santosh finds them upside down, joking that the cupboard is safer than Lalit's head, and was probably shaken too after braking hard.
The children "had a field day" in the puddles. Is that an event?

It means they enjoyed themselves a great deal, often by making the most of a chance.
Example: The puppy had a field day in the garden after the rain.
Now you try: 11 x 9 and 11 x 11
The answers are: 99; 121.

The cousins had left after the holiday and the flat felt very quiet. Farhan, two, stood by the front door, looking at the empty shoe rack. His lower lip began to tremble and turned down at the corners, and his eyes shone. Ganga lifted him onto her hip. “You miss them,” she said softly, rocking a little. Farhan pressed his face to her neck and let out a shaky breath, and then the tears came slowly.

What was Farhan looking at when his lip began to tremble?
The empty shoe rack by the front door.
What might Farhan feel when his lip trembles, and what else could it be?
He probably feels sad that his cousins have gone, as he stared at the empty rack. It could also be that the quiet flat felt strange to him.
What did Ganga do that helped?
She picked him up, spoke softly and named the feeling, which gave him closeness while he cried.
How might Ganga feel seeing him this way?
She may feel tender toward him and a little sad herself, and she might be glad he can show her his feelings.

Monday: At recess, Aditi whispered to Zainab behind the water tank, "We're moving to Bhopal next month. Don't tell anyone yet, I want to tell them myself." Zainab crossed her heart. Wednesday: Aditi came to school with a bad cold and a thick scarf. Zainab carried Aditi's bag up to the classroom and back down at home time, even though her own was heavy with atlases. When Ritika asked, "Why is Aditi so quiet lately? Is something wrong?" Zainab shrugged and changed the subject to the cricket match. Friday: Aditi stood up in class and told everyone about moving. Afterwards she hugged Zainab hard. "You didn't tell. Not even Ritika." Zainab grinned. "It was yours to tell."

Where are Aditi's family moving?
To Bhopal, next month.
Why did Zainab change the subject when Ritika asked about Aditi?
Zainab wanted to protect Aditi's trust and let Aditi share the news in her own way.
What choices across the week showed Zainab's loyalty?
Zainab carried Aditi's bag while she was ill and kept the moving news secret until Aditi told everyone herself.
How does Aditi feel toward Zainab by Friday?
Aditi feels grateful and close to Zainab, hugging her hard because the secret was kept 🤗

On a dark December afternoon in Uppsala, Oskar and Astrid played "bakery" under the kitchen table. "I'm the baker and you're the customer," Astrid said. Oskar shook his head. "No, we're both bakers, and Teddy is the customer." Astrid thought, then nodded. "But I make the saffron buns." "Then I make the ginger biscuits." They sold Teddy six pretend buns for three pebbles. When Teddy "forgot" to pay, Oskar made him wash the dishes, and Astrid laughed so hard she bumped her head.

How many pretend buns did they sell Teddy?
They sold Teddy six pretend buns for three pebbles.
What was Astrid thinking when she paused before nodding?
She was weighing Oskar's idea and felt happy to share the baker role, as long as she kept the saffron buns.
What helped the two keep their pretend game going?
Each suggested changes and gave a little, so they built one story they both liked instead of arguing.
What would change if Astrid had refused to share the baker role?
Oskar might have sulked or walked off, and the shared bakery story could have ended in a quarrel.

In the college counselling room in Pune, Aditi sat across from Chetan, the peer mentor, and turned her admission slip over and over. B.Com. Not the design school she had pictured every day since Class 9. "I keep imagining the studio," she said. "The portfolio shows. It's like losing a whole life." Chetan nodded. "That sounds really painful. It makes sense to grieve it." They talked about the design school for half an hour: what she would have made, who she would have been. Then Chetan asked, "Is there anything in this college that's even a little bit like that?" Aditi shrugged. "There's a marketing club. They make posters." "Want to come with me to their meeting on Thursday?" Aditi hesitated. "Okay. Just to see." At the meeting she ended up redesigning their event poster. She still missed the studio. But she went back the next week.

What course did Aditi get admitted to?
B.Com.
What was Aditi feeling as she turned the admission slip over?
She was grieving and sad, feeling like she had lost a whole life she had pictured.
What did Chetan do that helped Aditi move forward?
Chetan let her grieve and talk about the design school first, then asked about something similar in the college and offered to go with her.
How might the marketing club see Aditi's poster redesign?
They would probably be pleased and impressed, gaining a talented new member.

messages.content: Dorothy is 15 years old and wants to go to a museum with her family. Her family consists of her, her younger brother, her parents, and her grandfather. The regular ticket cost is $10. People 18 years old or younger have a discount of 30%. How much money will Dorothy have after this trip, when she currently has $70?

The discount per one ticket is 10 * 30/100 = $3.
So Dorothy's and her brother's tickets are cheaper by 2 * 3 = $6.
Her family consists of 5 people, so the ticket cost stands at 5 * 10 = $50.
Including the discount will lower the price to 50 - 6 = $44 in total.
Dorothy will be left with 70 - 44 = $26.
The answer is 26.

messages.content: A sugarcane stick is 24 cm long. Dada cuts it into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece? What fraction of the stick is one piece?

Answer: Each piece is 3 cm (24 / 8 = 3). One piece is 1/8 (one eighth).

Cut in half: 12 cm. Half again: 6 cm (quarters). Half again: 3 cm (eighths). Halving three times makes 8 equal parts. 8 pieces x 3 cm = 24 cm, so the answer checks.

Bhavna, you asked how I knew to act when your neighbour's bride went quiet. I am Himani, and I was twenty-six when I noticed it in the flat next door. Kamla had been married four months. She stopped coming to the terrace, her phone was always with her mother-in-law, and once I heard her say, "I'll ask my father again." My stomach knotted. I did not knock on their door and accuse anyone. I brought her tea when her mother-in-law was out and simply said, "I'm here, and I won't judge." After three weeks she told me it was money her family was being pressed for. I said it was not her fault and gave her the number of a women's helpline, and I sat beside her while she called. The counsellor there listened for an hour. I kept visiting every week.

How long had Kamla been married when Himani noticed the change?
Kamla had been married four months.
How did young Himani feel when she noticed Kamla going quiet?
Himani was worried and uneasy. Himani's stomach knotted, though Himani stayed calm and did not accuse anyone.
What choice did young Himani make instead of confronting the family?
Himani brought Kamla tea when Kamla's mother-in-law was out and said there would be no judging, then kept visiting every week, so Kamla could open up in her own time.
How might Kamla have felt when Himani said "I'm here, and I won't judge"?
Probably relieved and a little safer. After three weeks Kamla shared the truth about the money her family was pressed for.

It was a dare that has been going round. Ayesha was among them, arms out, looking frightened, while the others laughed and filmed. Thursday: Vaibhav shared the outline. Tarun reacted with a thumbs-up but wrote nothing. Two reminders later, the document still showed no edits from him. In the corridor Tarun kept saying, "Yes, yes, I'll look," without meeting his eyes, and turned the talk to cricket.
The next Monday: Vaibhav caught him at the canteen. "I need a clear answer, and either is fine. Are you in, yes or no?" Tarun let out a breath. "Honestly, no. My internship starts in two weeks. I didn't want to disappoint you." "That's okay. I'd rather know." That evening Vaibhav took Tarun's name off the draft.

How did Tarun react to the shared outline?
With a thumbs-up, but he wrote nothing.
Why did Tarun keep saying "maybe" and "yes, yes"?
Tarun felt uncomfortable saying no and didn't want to disappoint Vaibhav, so he softened the refusal into vague agreement.
What finally cleared things up?
Vaibhav asked a direct yes-or-no question and said either answer was fine.
What was the vague yes like for Vaibhav?
Confusing and costly: he built an outline with both names and chased reminders before learning it had been a no all along.

Answer: 3.2 x 10^5 + 4.5 x 10^4 = 3.65 x 10^5; 6 x 10^-^3 - 8 x 10^-^4 = 5.2 x 10^-^3.

We may only add the front numbers when the powers of 10 are the SAME (like adding 3 tens and 4 tens). Rewrite 3.2 x 10^5 as 32 x 10^4. Then 32 x 10^4 + 4.5 x 10^4 = 36.5 x 10^4 = 3.65 x 10^5. For the second, 6 x 10^-^3 = 60 x 10^-^4, and 60 x 10^-^4 - 8 x 10^-^4 = 52 x 10^-^4 = 5.2 x 10^-^3. Check with ordinary numbers: 320,000 + 45,000 = 365,000 and 0.006 - 0.0008 = 0.0052. Common mistake: 3.2 + 4.5 = 7.7, giving 7.7 x 10^9 or 7.7 x 10^5.

Lex is picking apples in his apple orchard when he notices some of the apples have bruises and some have worms. He wants to save the bruised apples to make applesauce, throw the wormy apples away, and keep the unbruised apples to eat raw. By his count, a fifth of the apples have worms and nine more than one fifth are bruised. He picked 85 apples. How many apples will he have left to eat raw?

A fifth of the apples have worms, so Lex has to throw 85 / 5 = 17 apples away.
Nine more have bruises than worms, so Lex has 17 + 9 = 26 apples for applesauce.
He picked 85 apples, so Lex has 85 - 26 - 17 = 42 apples left to eat raw.
The answer is 42.

He felt betrayed and punished, as if the college was blaming him for speaking up.

Keeping all screenshots and clinic dates, calling the national anti-ragging helpline, using free legal aid, and telling his parents, which moves the complaint outside the college that failed him.

Dhruv sees it as the college failing Pranav, not Pranav's fault, and stands by him.

I feel shaky but lighter.

Martha and Doris spent 6+3=9 dollars.
There were 21-9=12 dollars left in the cookie jar.
The answer is 12.

Lucia's denim jacket was covered in patches she had sewn herself: a moth, a moon, a bus route from her grandmother's town in Valencia. At lunch in Madrid, everyone else wore the same white trainers. She liked being the odd one out, and said so. When Esther, the girl from her maths group, waved her over to the crowded table, Lucia said, "You all copy each other. I don't need that." Esther's smile faded. "I just thought you'd like the spare seat." Lucia ate alone, chin high, but the noise from the table stayed with her. On Friday she thought: is it really pride, or am I using it as a wall? The next day she sat down at the end of the table, the jacket still on.

Patches she had sewn herself: a moth, a moon and a bus route from her grandmother's town in Valencia.

In one day, 200 people visit The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. Half of the visitors are residents of New York City. Of the NYC residents, 30% are college students. If the cost of a college student ticket is $4, how much money does the museum get from college students that are residents of NYC?

The number of visitors that are residents of NYC is 200 / 2 = 100 visitors
The number of NYC resident visitors that are college students is 100 * 0.30 = 30 visitors
The money from the college students that are residents of NYC is 30 * $4 = $120
The answer is 120.

Total ice cream cones he sells is $1000 / 5 = 200.
The answer is 200.

"No. Your health is yours to share. I'll tell them you're on reduced hours for personal reasons this month, and that Meenal is handling their file. All true. Nothing more."
Tanvir let out a breath. "And if they push?"
"Then I'll say, 'That's private, but the work is covered.' And if they're unhappy, that's on me, not you."
"Thanks, Jagdish."
"Go home at four today. That's an order."

Who will handle the Mehra file this month?
Meenal is handling their file.
What was Tanvir worried about?
Tanvir was anxious that people in the industry would talk if they knew about the counsellor.
Why did Jagdish choose 'reduced hours for personal reasons' over a made-up trip?
It protects Tanvir's privacy without inventing anything, so it won't fall apart later, and Jagdish takes responsibility if the client is unhappy.
How might the Mehra account see Jagdish's answer?
They may be curious, but a true, brief answer with the work covered keeps their trust in both Jagdish and Tanvir.

Read this:

"Hemant, you just paid for three things in five minutes and didn't look at one of them. Sit. Your Seema bua did the same at fifteen, the year my father linked my first payment app to his account. Samosa at the canteen: tap. A game pass: tap. My share of a birthday gift: tap. A second samosa, why not: tap. It never felt like money. No notes leaving my hand, no coins getting fewer. Then at the end of the month my father sat me down with his phone and scrolled. Forty-one payments. My face went hot. I remembered maybe ten of them. I wasn't greedy, beta. I just couldn't feel it. So I bought a thin notebook, and after every tap I wrote down the thing and the amount. After a week, the notebook made me pause before tapping. That little pause was the whole trick."

How many payments did young Seema's father find at the end of the month?
Forty-one payments.
How did young Seema feel as her father scrolled through the payments?
She was shocked and embarrassed, her face going hot, because she remembered only about ten of them.
What was the turning point in young Seema's story?
Buying the thin notebook and writing down every payment, which brought back the pause that tapping had taken away.
How might Seema's father have felt scrolling through the month with her?
He was probably surprised and concerned, but he chose to sit down and show her calmly rather than just scold.

Micah bought envelopes to send, and depending on the weight of the envelope he will need more stamps. If an envelope weighs more than 5 pounds, he will need 5 stamps. If it weighs less than that, it will only need 2 stamps. If he bought 52 stamps with 6 envelopes that weigh less than 5 pounds, how many envelopes in total did Micah need to buy?

Micah had to buy 6*2=12 stamps for 6 envelopes less than 5 pounds.
He has 52-12=40 more stamps to buy.
There are 40/5=8 envelopes that weigh more than 5 pounds.
Micah needed to buy 8+6=14 envelopes.
The answer is 14.

He watched me as I laid my purse upon the table and opened it, and he watched me as I separated two one-pound notes from its contents. They were clean and new, and I spread them out and handed them over to him. Still watching me, he laid them one upon the other, folded them long-wise, gave them a twist, set fire to them at the lamp, and dropped the ashes into the tray.

What happens to the two one-pound notes after the speaker hands them over?
He lays one on the other, folds them lengthwise, gives them a twist, sets fire to them at the lamp and drops the ashes into the tray.

Tarun's interview was at nine, and at seven-fifteen the iron in the hostel broke. The only shirt he had left was crumpled, and it was pouring. Anand, his roommate, pulled a pressed white shirt from his own cupboard. "Take it. Go." Tarun checked his reflection: plain trousers, clean shoes, a collar that finally lay flat. He felt like a slightly different person and hoped it would help him say what he knew. On the bus he thought about how his marks had nothing to do with the shirt. In the waiting room he saw another candidate in a kurta and jeans, who seemed relaxed. Tarun realised that clothes told the panel something, but not everything.

What time was Tarun's interview?
His interview was at nine.
What did Tarun feel about the borrowed shirt, and what did he realise on the bus?
He felt more like a serious candidate and hoped it would help him speak, but he realised his marks had nothing to do with the shirt.
What could Tarun do to prepare so that clothing matters less?
He could dress neatly for the setting and put his effort into practising his answers about his work.
How might the panel see a candidate in a kurta and jeans?
They may see them as relaxed or slightly casual, but a first impression from clothing can't reliably show their ability.

Read this:

Rekha had exactly one hundred and twenty rupees and a list of everything she wished for. She copied it into two columns: NEED on the left, WANT on the right. A geometry box, ninety rupees, went left, because maths class started Monday and hers was cracked. A puzzle game, one hundred, went right. She tapped her pencil. "The box first. The game can wait for the next pocket money." Alka, her neighbour, looked in. "Buy the game, borrow a compass." "And if you are absent?" Rekha grinned. She bought the box that afternoon and pinned a note on the wall to save for the game.

What did Rekha put in the NEED column?
She put the geometry box in the NEED column.
What was Rekha feeling as she sorted the list?
Practical and determined, and a little playful, since she grinned at Alka's suggestion.
What other way could Rekha handle the game, and why?
She could save a small part each week toward it, so the want gets its own plan instead of being forgotten.
How might Alka see Rekha's rule?
Alka thinks borrowing a compass would do, so Alka may see Rekha's rule as a bit strict.

metadata.subtype: Approach: choosing between two wants using needs versus wants [Thinking]

messages.content:
In Singapore, Xin's first maths test of the year came back with 90. His mother put it on the fridge. Three weeks later, the second test: 70. He walked home slowly, feeling sick. Seventy felt like failing. At the bus stop, his friend Mateo was grinning. "Seventy! Last time I got fifty!" Mateo held up his paper like a trophy. Xin looked at the same number on his own paper and couldn't understand how it could make Mateo so happy. At home he hid the test in his bag. When his mother asked, he said, "Not good." She looked. "Seventy is a good mark, Xin." "It's twenty less than before," he said, and went to his room. He lay on his bed, the 90 on the fridge still in his head.

Why is Xin upset about a mark that makes Mateo so happy?
Xin compares 70 with his earlier 90 and feels it is a drop of twenty marks, so it feels like failing. Mateo compares it with his earlier 50, so it feels like a big improvement.
Jack has $45 and 36 euros. If each euro is worth two dollars, how much money does he have total in dollars?

First find how much the euros are worth in dollars: 36 euros * $2/euro = $72
Then add that to the amount Jack has in dollars: $72 + $45 = $117
The answer is 117.

Sherman has a 30-minute commute to the office and a 30-minute commute home every day.  On the weekends, he spends 2 hours, each day, driving his kids to their different activities.  How many hours does Sherman drive a week?

He drives 30 minutes to work and 30 minutes home every day for a total of 30+30 = 60 minutes
He makes this drive 5 days a week for a total of 5*60 = 300 minutes
There are 60 minutes in 1 hour and he drives 300 minutes, 5 days a week so that's 300/60 = 5 hours
He drives 2 hours on both Saturday and Sunday so he drives 2*2 = 4 hours on the weekends
He commutes 5 hours during the week and spends 4 hours driving on the weekend for a total of 5+4 = 9 hours
The answer is 9.

Read this:

Rashmi read the offer letter and felt her stomach tighten: if she asked for more, would they withdraw it? She had also grown up being told that decent people never ask for money, and even typing "Could we discuss the figure?" made her feel greedy. Her friend Jeevan, on the phone, made it worse. "Just say your last stipend was bigger," he said. "Everyone does it." She was tempted for a second, then remembered that the company could check her payslips. "I will say what my skills are worth in the market instead," she said. She looked up the range for junior analysts, wrote one number with a short reason, and sent it politely, ready to hear no. The next day the manager, Tarun, called. "The budget is tight, and I cannot go that high," he said honestly. "But I can offer a learning budget and a salary review in six months." Rashmi felt respected. She asked him to put the review in writing and thanked him. "I will email it today," he said. She looked over the whole package before signing.

What did Tarun offer besides a salary?
He offered a learning budget and a salary review in six months.
How did Rashmi's answer to Jeevan's advice differ from how she handled her fear of asking?
She refused to inflate her stipend and anchored on the market value of her skills, and despite her fear she researched the range, named one reasoned number politely, and was ready to hear no.
What was Rashmi feeling as she typed "Could we discuss the figure?"?
She felt greedy and guilty, because she had grown up being told that decent people never ask for money.
What could Rashmi do about the promised review?
She could get it in writing, as she asked, and note the date so the promise is followed up.

Read this:

The monsoon had flooded the lawn, so Chandrika's wedding in Nagpur was squeezed into a hot, crowded hall two hours late. Farida, her closest friend from college, was standing near the mandap when an aunty pressed a steel plate with a lit lamp into her hands. "Quick, beta, do aarti for the couple!" Farida froze. She had joined the haldi, danced at the sangeet, tied a thread on Chandrika's wrist. But this felt different to her, closer to prayer than to celebration, and she wasn't sure it was hers to do. Chandrika caught her eye across the crowd and gave the smallest shake of her head, smiling: only what feels right. Farida smiled back, held the plate steady for a moment and passed it to Chandrika's cousin. "You do it, you're family." Later another aunt said, "So she's one of us now!" Chandrika laughed. "She's my friend. That's enough."

Why was the wedding moved into the hall?
The monsoon had flooded the lawn.
What was Farida feeling when handed the aarti plate?
Farida froze, feeling unsure and uneasy, since the aarti felt closer to prayer than celebration for her.
How did Farida handle the moment respectfully?
She held the plate steady briefly and passed it to the cousin, joining the celebration while keeping her own boundary about prayer.
How did Chandrika respond to the aunt's assumption?
Chandrika laughed and said Farida was her friend and that was enough, refusing to read belief into participation.

Is "yeild" correct?
Then, could you explain what transmit means?

1. No, it is "yield". The "i" comes before "e".
2. "Transmit" is a verb. It means to send something from one place to another.

Read this:

Subject: A request about how I work best
Dear Amandeep,
Thank you for my first two weeks. I'm enjoying the team and the work.
I'd like to share something so that I can do my best here. I was diagnosed with ADHD in college. For me, open-plan noise and long unstructured tasks are harder, and I sometimes lose track of spoken instructions. It doesn't affect the quality of what I deliver when things are set up well.
A few adjustments helped me before: headphones or the quiet room for focused work, key tasks in writing after meetings, and big deadlines broken into weekly checkpoints. None of these should cost the team anything.
Honestly, I was nervous about writing this. I'd be grateful for fifteen minutes this week, and I'm happy to involve HR if that's the right process.
Best regards,
Raghav

When was Raghav diagnosed?
In college.
What was Raghav feeling while writing the email?
Raghav felt nervous about disclosing it, as the email admits, but hopeful enough to ask.
What makes Raghav's request effective?
It is specific, links each adjustment to how Raghav works best, notes they cost little, and offers a short talk and HR involvement.
How might Amandeep feel receiving this email?
Amandeep would likely appreciate the clarity and honesty, knowing exactly how to help a new team member do well.
The shop says everything is half price today, and I'm tempted to buy things I don't need.
A sale can make anything look useful. What did you go in to buy?
A school bag. But there are nice pencil cases too.
Buy the bag, and ask yourself whether you'd buy the pencil case at full price. If not, it can wait. Sales come back, and you will still have a bag.
Library notice, around 40 words: books must come back before the shelves are counted, late books cost five rupees per day, and the reading room must stay silent. Thank readers at the end.

NOTICE
All books must be returned before the shelves are counted. Late books will cost five rupees per day. Please keep silence in the reading room so that everyone can read in peace. Thank you for your cooperation.
Diary entry, about 95 words, by a person who feels nervous before the first day of a new job tomorrow.

Dear Diary,
Tomorrow I start my new job, and I cannot sleep. I have ironed my shirt twice and packed my bag three times. What if I forget someone's name? What if I make a mistake in the first hour? Then I tell myself that everyone feels nervous on the first day. I will smile, listen well, and ask questions. I will reach early and take a deep breath at the door. Whatever happens, I will learn something new. Goodnight, diary.

Chad saves 40% of the money he earns/receives in a year.  This year, he made $600 mowing yards and received $250.00 for his birthday/holidays.  He also made $150.00 by selling some old video games and another $150.00 doing odd jobs.  How much will he save?

He made $600.00 mowing yards, $250.00 for his birthday, $150.00 selling items and $150.00 doing odd jobs so he made 600+250+150+150 = $1,150.00
He made $1,150.00 and will save 40% so he saves 1150*.40 = $460.00
The answer is 460.

Read this:

Two weeks after the baby came home, Harsha, who was two, swatted at the cradle and whined, "Up, up," until his mother Sharmila lifted him with her free arm. His father Naveen noticed that Harsha had asked for his old bottle, had been damp again in the mornings, and clung to Sharmila's leg whenever she fed the baby. Naveen did not laugh. He said, "You want a cuddle the way the baby gets one. Come here," and gave him a short cuddle and a sip from the bottle. Sharmila set aside twenty minutes after lunch just for Harsha; she put down her phone, built a block tower with him and let him carry the baby's tiny sock when it was time to dress her. One evening, curled in her lap, Harsha heard her say, "You're still my big boy, and there's room for you and the baby." He put his thumb in his mouth, sighed and stayed there while Naveen rocked the baby. The next morning his bed was dry, and he carried the wipes to the changing mat all by himself.

What did Harsha carry when it was time to dress the baby?
Harsha carried the baby's tiny sock.
How did Naveen's response to Harsha's bottle request differ from Sharmila's plan, and what did both do for him?

Naveen met the babyish behaviour gently and briefly with a cuddle and a sip, while Sharmila set aside daily special time and small jobs and then said the words with a lap; together they showed Harsha there was still room for him.
What was Harsha feeling when he swatted at the cradle and whined to be picked up?
He felt jealous and unsure, wanting to know whether there was still room for him.
What could Sharmila and Naveen keep doing as the baby grows?
They could keep the daily special time and small helper jobs and keep pairing loving words with a cuddle. 🙂

Class teacher's note, Class 10, Wednesday.
Anjali has seemed flat all week. During free period I found her in the library corner scrolling, not reading. On her screen: Anirban at a robotics camp, a cousin at a beach, a senior holding a trophy. Without looking up she said, "Everyone is doing something. I'm just... here." I asked what she had done since Sunday. She shrugged. Then, slowly: helped her grandmother with the pension forms, fixed the class projector, finished a whole novel. I said none of those would ever make a photo. She almost smiled. Later I happened to see Anirban's caption under that camp picture: "Day 3, lost every round, so tired." None of that showed in the photo. I have invited Anjali to the Friday reading group, and I will check on her again on Monday.

What had Anjali done since Sunday?
Helped her grandmother with the pension forms, fixed the class projector, and finished a whole novel.
What does Anjali's "I'm just... here" suggest she was feeling?
She felt dull and left behind, measuring her ordinary week against everyone else's highlights.
Which move by the teacher helped most, and why?
Asking what Anjali had actually done since Sunday let her see her own week clearly, without a lecture about social media.
How did Anirban's week at the camp really go, judging by the caption?
By day 3 Anirban had lost every round and was very tired, so the glossy camp photo hid a hard, ordinary week, much like anyone's.
What are the vadi and samvadi of Raga Marwa?
In this teaching table, the vadi of Raga Marwa is D, and the samvadi is r.

Only three days remained, and Chinmay had a pencil, a sheet of paper and a problem. He wrote a list: cake, invitations, decorations, games. Then he called his family to the table. "Mahima didi, can you order the cake with Papa?" "Fine," said his sister. "Mummy, decorations?" "I have old streamers," she said. His little brother took the games. Chinmay kept invitations for himself, because he loved to draw. That evening he drew a rocket on every card, folded each one and wrote a name inside. By the second night nine were done, and only the glue stick was missing. He checked the item off with a smile.

Which job did Chinmay keep for himself?
Chinmay kept the invitations.
Why did Chinmay keep the invitations for himself?
Chinmay loves to draw, so this job suited him and let him enjoy the work.
What alternative approach could help if a helper does not finish a job, and why?
Chinmay could check in halfway through the three days and swap a job that is behind. Seeing the list often helps everyone notice what is late in time to fix it.
How might Mahima see being asked to order the cake?
Mahima probably feels trusted and included; being handed a real task means the party is a shared effort and not only Chinmay's.

Read this:

Dear Vikas,
Thank you for the list you sent in March. I want to tell you where I am. After my BA, all I had was 'good communication skills', which every form asks for and nobody believes. So I picked the thing on your list that scared me most: spreadsheets and data cleaning. Evenings for four months. First a free online course through the library, then real practice on my uncle's shop accounts, which were a mess. I cried once over a formula that wouldn't work. Last week I did a test task for a small logistics company, and they've called me for a second round. I'm not an expert. But now when I say I can do something, I can show it.
Warmly,
Dilnaz

What did Dilnaz practise on?
Dilnaz's uncle's shop accounts.
Why did Dilnaz pick spreadsheets from the list?
It was the skill that scared Dilnaz most, and Dilnaz wanted something concrete to show instead of vague claims.
What could Dilnaz do before the second round?
Prepare a short example of the shop-accounts work and practise explaining how a problem was solved.
How might Vikas feel reading this update?
Glad and proud that Vikas's list turned into real progress, and trusted as a mentor.

The chemistry practical was at eight the next morning, and the power had gone out across the colony in the rain. Nirmala sat by the window with a candle, rereading the message from Keerthana: "I think we've grown apart. I need some space from us." Ten years of friendship, since they had shared a bench in Class 2. Her chest felt tight, as if the air had been pressed out of it. She tried to revise titration steps and read the same line six times. When her mother came in with a torch, Nirmala said, "I'm fine," then burst into tears. Her mother sat beside her and held her until the rain eased. Then they read the titration steps aloud together, one at a time.

What time was the chemistry practical?
At eight the next morning.
What was Nirmala feeling as she reread Keerthana's message?
She felt hurt and overwhelmed, her chest tight, as if ten years of friendship had been pulled away at once.
What helped Nirmala get through the night before the practical?
Letting herself cry with her mother, then reading the steps aloud one at a time, made both the grief and the revision manageable.
What might Keerthana have been feeling when sending the message?
Keerthana may have felt guilty or conflicted, needing space but knowing it would hurt a friend of ten years.

The class six report cards had to reach the principal by Friday morning. In the school staffroom, Charu, the class teacher, had every subject's marks in her spreadsheet except science. Vikas had promised them on Tuesday. On Wednesday he said, "Tonight, pakka." On Thursday at 4:15 a message arrived: "Sorry, sorry, sending now." Charu stayed on as the cleaners switched off the corridor lights. She entered thirty-eight science scores, redid the averages, found that the rank list had shifted, and rewrote four remarks she had already printed. At 8:10 she texted her sister: "Can't make dinner. Save me some." Walking to the bus stop, her shoulders ached. Vikas would sleep fine tonight, she thought, and felt mean for thinking it, and then just tired.

How many science scores did Charu enter on Thursday evening?
She entered thirty-eight science scores.
What was Charu feeling on the walk to the bus stop?
She felt resentful that Vikas would sleep fine, then guilty for the thought, and above all exhausted after the long evening.
What could Vikas have done on Tuesday that would have helped Charu?
He could have told her on Tuesday that the marks were running late and given a real date, so she could plan her evening instead of losing it at the last minute.
How might Vikas see the delay differently from Charu?
Vikas may see it as a small slip covered by an apology, without seeing the four hours, the redone rank list and the missed dinner it cost her.

Read this:

Monday: Anirban told Jeevan Sir why his homework was late, and Sir tilted his head. Anirban thought, He's listening and he's sorry for me, and he explained the whole story.
Wednesday: Anirban said he had finished all the sums. Sir tilted his head again and said nothing. Anirban's stomach clenched: Does he think I'm lying? “Show me your working for number seven,” said Sir, in an easy voice. Anirban showed him, and Sir nodded.
Friday: Anirban watched Sir tilt his head at a friend. Sir's eyes were warm. “Tell me more,” he said. Anirban smiled a little. The tilt was the same, but the tone told him more.

What did Jeevan Sir ask Anirban to show him on Wednesday?
He asked him to show his working for number seven.
What did Anirban think Sir's head tilt meant on Monday and on Wednesday?
On Monday he read it as listening and sympathy, so he explained everything. On Wednesday he read it as doubt and his stomach clenched, though Sir may just have been curious.
What could Anirban do when he is not sure what a head tilt means?
Notice the tone and face that come with it, and ask a question if he is unsure, like “Is something wrong with my answer?”
How might Jeevan Sir see his own head tilt?
Probably as a sign that he is listening and thinking, without realising it can look like doubt to a nervous child.

I'm Chinmay from the flat next door, and I was there when Asif's Ammi gave him his first bite of bitter gourd. He chewed once, stopped, and his whole face wrinkled. He pushed the mush out with his tongue and shoved the spoon away. His sister Rubina giggled. "Same, Asif, same." His Ammi offered it again. He clamped his lips and shook his head hard. I can't say what it tasted like to him, but I've never seen a face like that.

What food did Asif's Ammi give him?
She gave him his first bite of bitter gourd.
What did Asif's wrinkled face and clamped lips suggest?
They suggest he felt disgusted by the bitter taste and didn't want any more of it.
What could Asif's Ammi try next time with a new taste?
She could offer a tiny bit alongside a food he likes, on several different days, without forcing it.
How does Rubina see Asif's reaction?
Rubina finds it funny and also sympathises, since she seems to dislike bitter gourd too.

In Nani's kitchen in Jodhpur, Wasim, four, reached for the steel glass of milk and knocked it over. Milk spread across the floor and under the stove. Wasim stared, then ran and squeezed behind the grain bin. "I'm bad," he whispered. "I'm a bad boy." His big brother Madhav peeked in. Nani put down the rolling pin and crouched by the bin. "Wasim, come here, my sparrow." He shook his head. "The milk fell," Nani said softly. "That was an accident. You are still my good Wasim." Slowly, Wasim crawled out. Nani handed him a cloth. Together they wiped the floor.

Where did Wasim hide after spilling the milk?
Behind the grain bin.
What was Wasim feeling when he whispered 'I'm bad'?
He felt ashamed and scared, treating the spilled milk as proof he was a bad boy.
Why did Nani's response help Wasim?
She crouched down, spoke softly, separated the accident from who Wasim is, and let him help clean up.
How might Madhav understand Wasim hiding?
Madhav might see that little Wasim was frightened, and learn from Nani how to respond kindly.

Ritu: Papa, I filled the form. Humanities, not commerce.
Ritu: I know you wanted me in the shop someday.
Vijay: I saw. Your mother told me.
Vijay: I typed three angry messages and deleted them.
Ritu: ok
Vijay put his phone down, then picked it up again.
Vijay: Not ok. I want to understand first. Why humanities?
Ritu: I want to study how cities grow. Maybe work on housing someday. I get excited about it, Papa. Not about ledgers.
Vijay: Your Dada started the shop with one tin trunk.
Vijay: I always thought you'd carry it forward.
Ritu: I can still love the shop. I just don't want to run it.
Vijay: That's hard to hear.
Vijay: But you just explained yourself better than I could at sixteen, beti.
Vijay: Come down for dinner. Tell me about these cities.
Ritu: 🙂 coming

What subject did Ritu choose on the form?
Humanities, not commerce.
What was Vijay feeling when he typed and deleted three angry messages?
He felt angry and afraid of losing his hope that Ritu would carry the shop forward, but he held back to understand first.
What choice did Vijay make that kept the chat from turning into a fight?
He asked 'Why humanities?' before reacting, and then invited Ritu down to dinner to hear more.
How might Ritu feel when her father says she explained herself better than he could at sixteen?
Ritu might feel relieved and respected, since her father listened and even admired how clearly she gave her reasons.

Read this:

Hafsa's holiday diary, Day 3.
Best day EVER. Rajni took me to the mango orchard and we ate three each, juice running to our elbows. I stepped in mud up to my ankle and lost a slipper, and Rajni laughed so hard she sat down. The buffalo is called Rani. She breathes like a pressure cooker.
Everything here is slow. Nobody is in a hurry. I told Nani I want to live here forever.
One thing was strange. Rajni had to get up before it was light to carry water from the handpump, and she couldn't come to the pond after lunch because she had to cut fodder. She said, "You're lucky, you're a guest." I didn't know what to say.
Tomorrow we are making mango pickle. I will ask if I can carry water too.

What is the buffalo called?
The buffalo is called Rani.
What was Hafsa feeling in the orchard, and what shows it?
Hafsa felt thrilled and carefree, calling it the best day ever and eating mangoes with juice running to the elbows.
What could Hafsa do to understand village life better?
Hafsa could ask Rajni about her mornings and actually help with the water, as planned, to see the work behind the slow, sunny days.
How might Rajni see Hafsa's holiday?
Rajni may feel a little tired or envious, since Hafsa gets to play while she carries water and cuts fodder, which shows in "You're lucky, you're a guest."
Write a family group message, about 60 words, proposing a 'no phones at dinner' rule.

Hi everyone! I have a small proposal. From this Sunday, let's try a no-phones rule at dinner. We can leave our phones in the basket near the TV for just thirty minutes and actually talk to each other. Yes, Papa, that includes cricket scores. Let's try it for one week and see how it feels. Who's in?
The team is making headway on the new road. What is a headway? Is it a type of road?

No. To make headway means to make progress, especially against difficulty. Headway is a noun.
Example: We made little headway because of the heavy rain.

Gabriel's best friend moved away from their street in Uppsala on Friday. When the van left, Gabriel's chin wobbled. Anders, his father, said, “Be brave, big boy.” Gabriel turned away and said nothing all evening. At bedtime Anders heard a muffled sniff under the duvet. He sat on the bed. “I was wrong earlier. It's okay to cry. I'd be sad too.” Gabriel threw back the duvet and sobbed. Anders held him. Afterwards they talked about writing a letter to his friend.

What did Anders say when the van left?
“Be brave, big boy.”
Why might Gabriel have turned away and said nothing all evening?
He was sad about his friend leaving but felt he had to hide it after being told to be brave.
What did Anders do at bedtime that repaired things?
He admitted he was wrong, said it was okay to cry, held Gabriel, and then talked about writing a letter.
How might Gabriel's friend feel receiving a letter?
The friend would likely feel happy and missed, knowing Gabriel was thinking of him.

Wanjiru's report on the Nairobi water project was due to the donors on Wednesday. On Tuesday night she was still in the office, rewording the summary for the fourth time and adjusting photo captions.
Her colleague Chidi had sent the partner report on Monday, rough in places. The director had replied to everyone: "Chidi, fast and clear. Thank you!"

messages.content: Three towns, Toadon, Gordonia, and Lake Bright, have 80000 people. Gordonia has 1/2 times the total population in the three cities. If the population of Toadon is 60 percent of Gordonia's population, how many people live in Lake Bright?

The population of Gordonia is 1/2 * 80000 people = 40000 people
Toadon has 60/100 * 40000 people = 24000 people
The total population of Gordonia and Toadon is 40000 people + 24000 people = 64000 people
The population of Lake Bright is 80000 people - 64000 people = 16000 people
The answer is 16000.

Francis got five hundred rupees from his godparents this Christmas, and within an hour at the church fair he had spent nearly all of it: candyfloss, a plastic sword, three rounds of ring toss, plum cake for everyone. Reyna had 20 lamps with seven light bulbs in each lamp. If 1/4 of them have 2 burnt-out light bulbs each, how many light bulbs are working?

The total number of light bulbs in the 20 lamps is 20*7 = 140
If 1/4 of the 20 lamps have burnt-out light bulbs, there are 1/4*20 = 5 lamps with burn out light bulbs
Since each of the 5 lamps has 2 burnt-out light bulbs, the number of burn out light bulbs is 2*5 = 10
The number of working light bulbs is 140 -10 = 130
The answer is 130.

In the hospital family room, the morning after Sachin's father died, three people grieved in three directions. Sachin's younger brother, Nikhil, was on the phone nonstop: the crematorium, the priest, the relatives in Indore, a list growing on his palm in blue ink. Nazia, Sachin's wife, kept trying to talk. "Remember how he sang in the car?" she said, twice. Sachin sat by the window and said nothing. Inside, he was furious with both of them. How could Nikhil think about timings? Why did Nazia need words? Around noon Nikhil snapped, "Could you at least help, bhaiya?" Sachin nearly shouted back. Then he saw his brother's hands shaking over the list. He took the phone. "You call the family. I'll call the priest." Later, in the corridor, he told Nazia, "I can't talk yet. Stay close anyway?" She nodded and held his arm.

A list of calls, the crematorium, the priest and the relatives in Indore, growing on his palm in blue ink.
What was Sachin feeling as he sat by the window?
He was grieving silently and also angry, judging Nikhil for thinking about timings and Nazia for needing words.
What helped the three of them grieve side by side?
Sachin noticed Nikhil's shaking hands and shared the calls, and told Nazia plainly that he couldn't talk yet but wanted her close.
How might Nazia have seen Sachin's silence?
She may have felt shut out and worried that he was not grieving at all, until he explained and asked her to stay close.

After eight.

messages.content: Is my uncle's new car expensive?
I don't know if your uncle's car is expensive, as I know nothing about it. Ask him about it if you're curious.
My cousin from the USA asked for the car's "license plate". I only know "number plate".

Vikas had been a clerk at the cooperative bank in Sirsi for exactly one month, and on the 22nd his phone showed a balance that wouldn't cover the bus pass. "Where did it go?" he asked Chaitanya at the tea stall outside the bank. "I bought one thing. The shoes." Two mobile recharges. "The shoes aren't your problem," Chaitanya said. "This is." He tapped the long column of small amounts. Vikas stared at it. Not one of them had felt like spending. Nineteen times.

On Tuesday afternoon, Jyoti posted: "Can someone explain why the Saturday team was changed without asking any of us?" Three volunteers added angry emojis. Someone replied, "Typical."
Madhav felt his chest tighten. The change had been his decision, because of a safety issue at one site he couldn't discuss in public.
He resisted typing a long defence. Instead: "Thanks for flagging, Jyoti. The change was mine. I'll call the Saturday team today to explain properly."
Then he called Jyoti. "There was a safety concern at the Kolar site. I couldn't put it in a group of forty."

Steve is holding nickels and dimes in his hand. He has 4 more dimes than nickels. He has a total of 70 cents in his hand. How many nickels is he holding?

Let x be the number of nickels he is holding.
His nickels are worth 5 * x = 5x cents.
He has x+4 dimes.
The dimes are worth 10 * (x+4)
The total worth of the nickels and dimes is 5x + 10*(x+4) = 70.
5x + 10x + 40 = 70
15x = 30
x = 2, Steve has 2 nickels in his hand.
The answer is 2.

Summarize this croquet scene for a child.

The chief difficulty Alice found at first was in managing her flamingo: she succeeded in getting its body tucked away, comfortably enough, under her arm, with its legs hanging down, but generally, just as she had got its neck nicely straightened out, and was going to give the hedgehog a blow with its head, it would twist itself round and look up in her face, with such a puzzled expression that she could not help bursting out laughing: and when she had got its head down, and was going to begin again, it was very provoking to find that the hedgehog had unrolled itself, and was in the act of crawling away: besides all this, there was generally a ridge or furrow in the way wherever she wanted to send the hedgehog to, and, as the doubled-up soldiers were always getting up and walking off to other parts of the ground, Alice soon came to the conclusion that it was a very difficult game indeed.

Alice tries to play croquet using a flamingo as her bat and a hedgehog as the ball. The flamingo keeps twisting round to look at her, the hedgehog crawls away, and the soldiers keep walking off. Alice decides it is a very hard game.

Biology teacher's note, Class 10 health session.
Today we covered consent, boundaries and sexual health. The class was giggly at first. I kept it factual: consent means a clear, free yes; it can be taken back at any time; silence or pressure is not a yes.
Sahil asked, "What if someone says yes and then changes their mind?" I said then it's a no, and a respectful person stops. Uma added, "Like when my cousin tickles me and I say stop, and he doesn't. That's annoying, and it's also not okay." The class went quiet, then nodded.
We also covered how infections and pregnancy can be prevented, and that a doctor or the school nurse can give confidential, accurate advice.
Next week: an anonymous question box. — Mrs Thomas

An anonymous question box.

The school library was nearly empty after the last bell, which was why Thomas had asked Nazia to meet him there, at the table behind the geography shelves.

He'd thought about texting. It would have been easier. But Nazia deserved to see his face.

Nazia stared at the table. "Is there someone else?"

At the table behind the geography shelves in the school library.

He will earn 2 * $9 = $18 selling his collectable figures.

We didn't stop her. She wasn't being naughty; she was finding out what happens.

She banged it with a wooden spoon.

Rachel is twice as old as Rona and Collete's age is half the age of Rona's. If Rona is 8 years old, what is the difference between the age of Collete and Rachel?

Rachel's age is 8 x 2 = 16.
Collete's age is 8 / 2 = 4.
Therefore the difference between their age is 16 - 4 = 12.
The answer is 12.
Look at this 4 by 4 square. Each number shows which L-shaped layer a dot belongs to. How does it show that 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16? 1 2 3 4 2 2 3 4 3 3 3 4 4 4 4 4

Answer: Layer 1 has 1 dot, layer 2 has 3, layer 3 has 5, layer 4 has 7. Together 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4^2.

Each time we make the square one bigger, we add an L-shape around two sides. The L for a 2 by 2 square adds 3 dots, for 3 by 3 adds 5, for 4 by 4 adds 7: always the next odd number. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2: 1 = 1^2, 1 + 3 = 4 = 2^2, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3^2. Let the child build it with bottle tops.

In total there are 24 + 36 = 60 chairs
The answer is 60.

Arohi found Vishal by the tent. "Vishal, please take down Mami's dance. She didn't agree to be filmed or posted. It's her choice who sees that." He looked surprised. "But it was so much fun! Forty views.

Wednesday night
Chinmay called again at eleven. Forty minutes. His landlord is cheating him. His boss is jealous of him. His sister never calls. And tonight, somehow, it was also my fault, because I "never really help."
I listened. I do care about him. Some of it is real. His boss does sound difficult.
But I've noticed I end every call feeling guilty for things that aren't mine.
So tonight, near the end, I asked him something new. "Chinmay, what do you want to do about the landlord? Is there a step you want to take?" He went quiet. Then he said, "I don't know. Maybe look for a new flat."
Then I said, kindly, "I want to keep being your friend. But I can't take calls after ten on weeknights anymore. I'm exhausted. Sundays are good."
He sighed. I didn't apologise. I said goodnight.
Salma

At eleven.
How does Salma feel at the end of Chinmay's calls?

What did Salma do that shows compassion with boundaries?
She listened, asked what Chinmay wanted to do about the landlord, and kindly set a limit of no calls after ten on weeknights.
How might Chinmay feel when Salma sets the limit?
Chinmay may feel a little hurt or disappointed, which is why he sighs, but he was also given a real question to think about.

Reena had one free evening before her new job started, and the rain wasn't stopping. She had two invitations: Shalini's church young adults' group, and the "Success Circle" a man had pitched to her at the gym.
Last Friday she had tried the Circle. When she asked where the membership fees went, the room went cold. The leader said doubters "aren't ready" and suggested she spend less time with "negative" friends.
Tonight, soaked, she sat at the back of the church hall beside Shalini. When a discussion started, Reena asked, "What if I don't believe half of this?" The youth leader laughed kindly. "Then you'll fit right in with half of us. Come when you like, skip when you like." A printed sheet on the noticeboard listed what donations had paid for this year: a roof repair, a food drive.
Reena didn't know yet if she'd come back. But she knew she could leave freely, and that was the point.

What did the printed sheet on the noticeboard list?
What donations had paid for this year: a roof repair, a food drive.
How might Reena have felt when the youth leader laughed kindly at her question?
Reena likely felt relieved and at ease, since her doubt was welcomed instead of punished, unlike the cold room at the Circle.
Which tests did Reena use to judge each group?
Asking a doubting question, asking where the money goes, and noticing how each group treated outside friends and the freedom to skip.
How might Shalini see Reena's doubting question?
Shalini's group treated doubt as normal, so Shalini probably saw the question as honest rather than rude.
