Say: "I have experience in this work." If you want to give the time, say: "I have three years of experience in this work."

Read this:

Karthik, you asked why I still keep that old bronze medal. Listen, then. I, your Aparna Athai, was eleven and sure I'd win the district race. I came third. When I walked off the track, my shoulders fell so low I felt shorter. My father met me at the gate and said, “Enough long face. Smile, people are watching.” I tried, and it felt like swallowing a stone. Then my coach, Mrs Pillai, sat beside me on the bench. She didn't tell me to smile. She said, “You wanted gold badly, and you ran your hardest. It's allowed to hurt.” I cried on her shoulder. The next year, I ran again.

Where did young Aparna come in the district race?
Aparna came third.
What was young Aparna feeling as she walked off the track?
She felt deeply disappointed and defeated, her shoulders falling so low she felt shorter.
What choice did Mrs Pillai make, and why did it matter?
She didn't ask for a smile but named Aparna's effort and hurt, which let her cry and later run again.
How might Aparna's father have felt about his words?
He probably wanted to protect her pride in front of others, not realising that asking for a smile made her feel worse.

Each week, Paul has 2 hours of homework on weeknights and 5 hours for the entire weekend. This week Paul has practice 2 nights out of the week and can't do any homework those nights. How many hours of homework does he have to average for the other nights to get his week's homework done?

Paul has 10 hours of homework from weekdays because 2 x 5 = 10
He has 15 total hours because 5 + 10 = 15
He has 5 days to do his homework because 7 - 2 = 5
He needs to do 3 hours a night because 15 / 5 = 3
The answer is 3.

Read this:

Disha, you asked how I chose design when Papa wanted engineering. Let your Binita didi tell you honestly. It wasn't one brave moment.
At twenty I was in second-year engineering, because everyone in our family is an engineer: Papa, Chacha, Dada. I loved them. I didn't want Papa to feel his years of overtime had been wasted.
Every night I sketched dresses in the back of my circuits notebook and felt guilty, then angry that I felt guilty. Both at once, every day, for a year.
At Diwali, Chacha joked about "our future engineer", and I burst into tears in front of everyone. Later Papa found me on the terrace. I showed him the notebook. He turned the pages for a long time. He didn't say yes. He said, "Finish this year. Then we'll visit the design college together."
I still felt grateful and resentful at once, Disha. Both were true.

Where did Binita sketch dresses?
In the back of the circuits notebook.
What feelings did Binita carry through that year?
Guilt and anger at once: loyal to Papa and his hard work, yet resentful of a path she didn't choose.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
Showing Papa the notebook on the terrace; it let him see her real interest, and he offered a next step instead of a flat no.
What might Papa have felt turning the notebook pages?
Papa probably felt surprised and torn, maybe proud of the drawings and sad he hadn't noticed sooner.

metadata.subtype: Caught between parents and own choices [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tea break at the tea estate office, Darjeeling. Dolma waited until the others had gone out to the verandah.

"Anirban-da, do you have a minute?"

"Hmm?" He didn't look up from the ledger.

"You've been very quiet with me since Tuesday. You didn't come to see the new drying racks with me. I've been wondering if I did something."

He looked up. "You? No."

"I thought maybe the racks report. I changed your figures."

"You fixed them. I was glad." He rubbed his eyes. "My mother's been unwell. I've been at the hospital at night. I'm not with anyone, Dolma. I'm barely here."

"Oh." Dolma sat down. "I've spent three days writing arguments with you in my head."

He almost smiled. "Did I win?"

"Every time." She pushed her cup towards him. "Drink this. I'll show you the racks tomorrow."

What did Dolma think Anirban might be upset about?
The racks report, where she changed his figures.
What does "I've spent three days writing arguments with you in my head" show about Dolma's state before she asked?
It shows she was anxious and sure she had upset him, building imagined conflicts for days. Her guess felt real enough to argue with.
Which choice of Dolma's made the difference, and why?
Waiting until they were alone and asking plainly whether she had done something. It gave Anirban the chance to tell her the real reason in a minute.
How might Anirban feel after Dolma asks him directly?
Anirban may feel relieved to share what's going on with his mother, and touched that Dolma cared enough to ask. His small joke suggests some of the weight lifted.

Read this:

Wednesday
Diary, Aparna here. It was 45 degrees today. School cut the afternoon classes. Ira and I walked home under one umbrella and still felt like we were melting.
I asked her, "Is this climate change or just summer?" She said her science teacher said both: summer is normal, but heatwaves are getting longer and more often because the planet is warming from all the fuel we burn.
I felt panicky, then angry, then tired.
Then Ira said her building has twelve kids going to our school, all in separate cars. "What if we just shared?"
So we made a list tonight. Four cars instead of twelve on most days. We asked our parents; they're calling each other now.
It's a tiny thing. I know it doesn't fix the heat. But I'm less panicky when I'm doing something.

How many cars do the kids in Ira's building plan to use on most days?
Four cars instead of twelve.
How did Aparna feel after Ira explained heatwaves?
Aparna felt panicky, then angry, then tired, and later less panicky once they started doing something.
Why is the car-sharing plan a realistic action?
It's small, local and involves parents, so it can actually happen and cut fuel use, even if it doesn't fix everything.
How might the parents in the building see the teens' list?
The parents may feel impressed and willing to help, since the plan also saves them time and trips.

Jason is climbing a telephone pole next to a tree his friend Matt is climbing. Matt can climb 6 feet/minute and Jason can climb 12 feet per minute. After 7 minutes, how much higher will Jason be than Matt?

First find the distance Matt climbs in 7 minutes: 6 feet/minute * 7 minutes = 42 feet
Then find the distance Jason climbs in 7 minutes: 12 feet/minute * 7 minutes = 84 feet
Then subtract the distance Matt climbs from the distance Jason climbs to find the difference: 84 feet - 42 feet = 42 feet
The answer is 42.
Arjun has a big coin and a small coin. He says, "The big one must be worth more." The big coin says 1 and the small coin says 5. Is Arjun right?

Answer: No. The small coin is worth ₹5, the big one only ₹1.

Value is what the coin can buy, not how big it is. Compare with things: a big pillow is lighter than a small brick. The number tells the value. This is the most common mistake with money.

Read this:

It was exam week, the fans in Class 10C had been dead since Monday, and everyone was hot and cranky. That's when Arnab first heard it, in the water-cooler line: the new maths teacher, Ms Lalremsiami, had been 'thrown out' of her last school for failing a whole class. By second period, three people had told him. By lunch, someone added that she'd shouted at a principal. By Friday, nobody said 'I heard'; they just said it. Arnab noticed he'd started believing it too, though no one had ever named where it came from. He also noticed how she paused at her desk when the whispers started, then kept teaching. After the paper he asked Deepa, who'd told him first, 'Who told you?' She frowned. 'Everyone knows.' 'But who?' She couldn't say.

Where did Arnab first hear the rumour?
In the water-cooler line.
What was Arnab feeling when he noticed he had started believing it?
Arnab felt uneasy and doubtful, aware that repetition, not evidence, had made the story feel true.
What could Arnab do next about the rumour?
He could stop passing it on and keep asking 'Who told you?', which helps others see nobody knows the source.
What might it be like for Ms Lalremsiami to teach while the whispers spread?
She may feel hurt and isolated, pausing at her desk, yet still trying to keep teaching despite not knowing what is said.

Which is less?
a) 0 or 3
b) 1 or 0
c) 5 or 0
d) 0 or 10
e) 2 or 0
The paper has three sections. What does sections mean?

Sections are the separate parts of a whole thing, such as a book, a test or a newspaper. It is a noun, the plural of section.
Example: The exam had two sections, one on grammar and one on reading.

Read this:

'Parveen, why are you so pale?' Neelam whispered at recess.
Parveen pulled her closer. 'I took Ammi's phone to school. For photos on sports day. It's in my bag.'
'Phones aren't allowed! Ma'am checks bags on Fridays.'
'I know! My stomach's been flipping since assembly.' Parveen twisted her dupatta. 'I could hide it in the toilet cistern till home time.'
'And if someone finds it there? Then it's worse. You'd have to lie.'
'So what, I just give it to her?'
'Before the check. Tell her you brought it and you're sorry. Get it over with.'
Parveen swallowed. 'You'll come with me?'
'Obviously.'
Ma'am listened, locked the phone in her drawer and said, 'You can collect it at home time. Thank you for coming to me first.'

On which day does Ma'am check bags?
On Fridays.
What was Parveen feeling since assembly?
Scared and anxious about being caught; her stomach had been flipping.
What did Neelam advise, and why was it wise?
Hand the phone in before the check and apologise, because hiding it could lead to lying and bigger trouble.
How did Ma'am respond to Parveen coming first?
Calmly; she kept the phone until home time and thanked Parveen for coming to her first.
Who was the headmaster of our school in 1962?
I'm not sure, as records for one school are not something I can check. The school office or its old yearbooks may list the names.

Read this:

Ramesh, you rolled your eyes when I posted that scam warning in the family group. Let your Maria Aunty tell you why I do it.
When I was twenty, at college in Mangalore, I got an SMS: "Your bank account will be blocked today. Click to update KYC." It looked exactly like our bank's messages. I nearly clicked. Then I noticed the sender was a normal mobile number, and the link was misspelt.
I didn't just delete it. I rang the bank's official number, and they said it was fake. Then I thought of my grandfather, who had just learned to use a mobile. So I called home and told everyone.
Two days later, Grandpa got the same message. He remembered my call and didn't click. Our neighbour, who nobody warned, lost her pension that week.
That's why I post warnings, Ramesh. Someone less used to phones might be reading.

What did young Maria notice about the SMS?
She noticed the sender was a normal mobile number, and the link was misspelt.
How did young Maria feel when she thought of her grandfather?
She felt worried and protective, knowing he had just learned to use a mobile and could easily be fooled.
What turning point in the story showed why warning others matters?
Her grandfather got the same message two days later and didn't click, while a neighbour who wasn't warned lost her pension.
How might Maria's grandfather have felt when he recognised the message?
He probably felt relieved and grateful that Maria had warned the family.

Read this:

In the school library during free period, Akash finally said it. "Shalini, the history model is due tomorrow and your part isn't done. We've asked three times." Shalini's eyes filled at once. "Wow. You know I've had the worst week. Nobody ever asks how I am. I always get blamed for everything in every group." The others shifted. Tanu passed her a tissue; someone murmured, "Sorry, Shalu." Akash looked at the table, suddenly the bad guy. Later, walking to the bus alone, Shalini replayed it. She had forgotten the model; that was the truth. But saying "I forgot" had felt like the floor opening under her, like proof she was useless. The tears had come before she chose them. Now everyone was comforting her, and the model still wasn't made. She took out her phone, then put it back, not yet able to type the word sorry.

How many times had the group asked about Shalini's part?
They had asked three times.
Why did saying she forgot feel so hard for Shalini?
Shalini feared it was proof of being useless; that shame about being at fault made the tears come before she chose them.
What could Shalini do now to repair things?
She could message the group, admit she forgot, say sorry plainly and offer to finish her part tonight, instead of turning the complaint into sympathy.
How did Akash seem to feel after the others comforted Shalini?
Akash seemed embarrassed and uncomfortable, looking at the table, as if a fair reminder had made him the bad guy.
I want to thank a colleague by email for helping me with a task.
Keep it short and specific. Say what they did and how it helped, such as 'Thank you for reviewing the draft. Your suggestions made it much clearer.'
Should I copy their manager?
It is a kind gesture if you think they would like the credit to be seen. If you are unsure, ask the colleague, or send the thanks to them alone.

Freya's birthday fell in the middle of the dark Swedish winter, so her mother filled the flat in Uppsala with candles. There were games for two hours: musical chairs, a treasure hunt, pin the tail on the reindeer.
Then the cake came out, shaped like a castle with sparklers on the towers. Everyone cheered. Freya thought her heart would burst.
At the very end, while everyone was pulling on boots, Astrid slipped on a bit of fallen cake, cried, and her dad had to take her home early.
That night, Freya's grandmother asked, "How was the party?"
"The cake was amazing," Freya said. "And then it was sad."
"What about the treasure hunt? You found the gold coins."
Freya blinked. She had forgotten the treasure hunt completely. The sparkler castle and Astrid's tears were all that was left.

What shape was the cake?
The cake was shaped like a castle with sparklers on the towers.
Why did Freya describe the party as amazing and then sad?
Freya felt thrilled at the cake and upset at Astrid's tears, and those two moments crowded out two hours of games.
What could help Freya remember the whole party?
Going through the afternoon in order with her grandmother, treasure hunt and all, would bring back the parts in the middle.
How might Astrid remember the party?
Astrid might remember mostly slipping and going home early, and feel sad or embarrassed about it.

messages.content: Bob orders a pizza with 8 slices.  He eats half of it and each slice was 300 calories.  How many calories did he eat?

He ate 8/2=4 slices
So he ate 4*300=1200 calories
The answer is 1200.

At the school counselling room, Sharmila, eleven, sat twisting her dupatta. Three weeks ago, she and Farida had a huge fight at lunch, and Sharmila had pushed Farida's tiffin off the table. Since then, they hadn't spoken, and Sharmila hadn't told Ammi. Every day, Ammi asked, "How's Farida?" and Sharmila said, "Fine." Today the class teacher had called Ammi in, because Farida's mother had complained. Sharmila's face was burning. She hadn't slept properly in days. When Ammi walked in, Sharmila couldn't look at her. But Ammi sat down, put a hand on her back and said, "Beta, I'm not angry. I just wish you'd told me three weeks ago. What happened?" Sharmila's words came tumbling out. By the end, she was crying. "I didn't know how to start." Ammi hugged her. "Next time, start with 'Ammi, something happened.'"

What did Sharmila do to Farida's tiffin?
She pushed it off the table.
How did Sharmila feel before Ammi walked in?
She felt ashamed and anxious, her face burning, not having slept properly in days.
What did Ammi do that made it easier to talk?
She stayed calm, said she wasn't angry, gently asked what happened, and offered a simple way to start next time.
How might Farida have felt during the three weeks?
She was probably hurt and upset, enough that her mother complained to the school.

The ration shop has 428 kg of rice and 482 kg of wheat. Which is more?

Now you try: 537 _ 573.
The answer is <.

I'm Pallavi, and my little brother Chinmay used to dump his shoes and bag wherever he stood. Amma nagged, and it never worked. Then one day I saw him standing in the hallway, talking to himself. "When I come in and change my clothes, that's the moment. Shoes on the rack, bag on the hook. Same time, same place. Then I won't need to remember." He did it the next day, and the next. Now, when he comes in and pulls off his school shirt, I see him walk straight to the rack. Amma has stopped nagging, and honestly, I have too.

Where does Chinmay put his bag?
Chinmay puts his bag on the hook.
How does Chinmay feel about tying the job to changing his clothes?
Chinmay feels confident it will work, because changing clothes happens anyway, so he says he won't need to remember the shoes and bag separately.
What alternative approach could Chinmay try, and why?
Chinmay could put a picture note above the rack or ask a parent to remind him at first. Either could help until the habit is strong.
How does Pallavi see the change in Chinmay?
Pallavi watches the routine take hold and notes that Amma has stopped nagging, and admits to stopping too, so Pallavi seems relieved and a little impressed.

Three days before the school's Teachers' Day celebration, the student council room smelled of glue and cold samosas.

"Version seven," Siddharth announced, holding up a new sketch of the stage backdrop. "I moved the flowers to the left. It balances better."

Hansa stared at the six older sketches pinned behind him. "Sid, the paper for version five is already cut."

"Then we cut again. And I've redone the schedule so the welcome speech is forty seconds shorter."

Two volunteers exchanged a look and quietly packed their bags. "We'll come tomorrow," one muttered. They didn't.

By the morning of the event, Hansa and Siddharth were gluing flowers alone. The teachers smiled politely at the backdrop. Nobody noticed which side the flowers were on. Hansa noticed only how empty the room had been.

How many older sketches were pinned behind Siddharth?
Six older sketches were pinned behind him.
How might Hansa have felt by the morning of the event?
Hansa likely felt tired, lonely and let down, noticing mostly how empty the room had been after the volunteers left.
What would you change first in Siddharth's approach?
Fix the design after one round of feedback and put the saved time into giving volunteers clear, small jobs, since the extra polish added little.
How did the constant changes look to the two volunteers?
To them the work probably felt pointless and endless, since cut paper kept being wasted, so they drifted away and did not come back.

Monday. Everyone in the office was saying it: the metro line near Yogesh's new flat would shut for six months from next week. Sumit said it twice at lunch. The canteen man said it. Yogesh had heard it maybe eight times and was already looking at renting a scooter.
Wednesday. Standing at the platform, Yogesh caught himself. "Have I checked this, or have I just heard it a lot?" He realised he couldn't name one real source. He opened the metro corporation's own notice page on his phone.
Friday. At lunch Sumit said, "Six months without metro, yaar." Yogesh showed him the notice. Four weekends of track work. Weekday trains normal.
"Huh," said Sumit. "Everyone said six months."
"I know," Yogesh said. "I'd have believed it too. It felt true because I'd heard it so often."

What did the metro corporation's notice actually say?
Four weekends of track work, with weekday trains normal.
What was Yogesh feeling when he caught himself on the platform?
He felt doubtful and uneasy, noticing that he could not name one real source for something he had nearly acted on.
Which choice worked, and why?
Checking the metro corporation's own notice worked, because it replaced a rumour heard eight times with one reliable source.
How does Sumit see the news at first, and how might that change?
Sumit treats the six-month closure as settled because everyone said it; after seeing the notice he seems surprised and may start checking too.

"Rehana, I've led a group twice this year and got it wrong both ways. I'm Irawati, by the way, for your listeners. First, the lake survey. I did the water samples, the photos, the report, even the bibliography. The others kept asking, 'What should we do?' and I kept saying, 'It's fine, I've got it.' By the end I was in tears over the printer, and Tushar told the professor he'd barely been allowed to help. He wasn't wrong. So for the street-play project I swung the other way. I sent one message: 'Script, props, posters, permissions. Pick one, bring it on the day.' No date to check in. Two people picked nothing and went quiet. The posters turned up on the morning of the show, spelled wrong. Next time I want one name next to each job, and one Friday where we all show what we've got."

What did Irawati's message for the street-play project list?
Script, props, posters and permissions: pick one, bring it on the day.
How did Irawati feel at the end of the lake survey?
Irawati was exhausted and overwhelmed, ending up in tears over the printer after doing every part alone.
What went wrong both times, and what could fix it?
First Irawati kept all the work, then handed it out with no check-in; clear owners for each job and one agreed checkpoint would fix both.
How did Tushar see the lake survey?
Tushar felt shut out and resentful, telling the professor he had barely been allowed to help.

messages.content: "Mere dada ji roz subah park mein tahalte hain." Translate.
It is: "My grandfather walks in the park every morning." In English, "grandfather" is the usual word, and "grandpa" is casual.
Aur dadi ke liye?
Use "grandmother" for the polite form and "grandma" for the casual one.
Aur nana-nani?
They are also "grandfather" and "grandmother". English does not separate the mother's side from the father's side.

Sunday night. Dear diary, today Nandini Masi came from Nagpur with a big parcel just for me. Inside was a sweater she knitted herself, bright orange with a green duck on the front. It is scratchy on my neck. Masi's eyes were shining when I opened it. She said she knitted it on the train, row by row, thinking of me. So I said, "I love it, Masi! It's my favourite!". She hugged me twice. Now my neck itches and my tummy feels funny. I didn't want her face to fall. But Mumma asked if I'll wear it to school and I said yes, and that was a lie too. I don't know which part was kind and which part was wrong. — Ayesha

What colour was the sweater Nandini Masi knitted?
The sweater was bright orange with a green duck on the front.
Why does Ayesha's tummy feel funny after lunch?
Ayesha feels guilty and torn: she was happy to see Masi's shining eyes, but uneasy that saying "I love it" was not true, and then a second fib followed.
What could Ayesha say to Masi next time that is kind and also true?
Ayesha could thank Masi for knitting it on the train and say how much it means that Masi was thinking of Ayesha, without claiming the sweater is her favourite.
How might Nandini Masi feel if she later found out the sweater itches?
Masi might feel a little sad at first, but she would probably want to know so she could make the next one softer, because she knitted it out of love.

Wednesday evening. Something worked today, so I'm writing it down. Reena said last week, “Stop trying to be strong, just move the temptation.” So I did the boring version. At 5:30 the phone went into the hall drawer. On my desk, only the physics book, a notebook and a pencil. I set the little alarm for 6:30. At first my hand kept reaching for the pocket that wasn't there, twice, and I laughed at myself. But then I was through two whole chapters before I looked up, and I hadn't even had to argue with myself. Nothing heroic. Just a drawer. Tomorrow same time, same drawer. — Shankar

What time did Shankar put the phone in the hall drawer?
Shankar put the phone into the hall drawer at 5:30.
How did Shankar feel when the hand reached for the empty pocket?
Shankar felt amused at the habit, laughing at the twice-reaching hand, and not upset.
What worked better than trying to be strong?
Moving the phone into another place and keeping only the physics book, notebook and pencil on the desk meant there was nothing to argue with.
How might Reena feel hearing that the advice worked?
Reena would probably feel pleased and a little proud, since Reena's advice to move the temptation, not be strong, made a difference.
Asha scored 42 out of 60 in Hindi and 36 out of 48 in English. In which subject did she do better?

Answer: English. Hindi: 42/60 = 70%. English: 36/48 = 75%.

The two tests have different totals, so comparing 42 and 36 tells us nothing. Change both to percents. 42/60: divide by 6 to get 7/10 = 70/100 = 70%. 36/48: divide by 12 to get 3/4 = 75%. 75% is more than 70%, so English was better, even though she scored fewer marks. This is why schools and cricket statistics use percents: they make everything "out of 100".
Mujhe projects mein group leader banna hai. Teacher ko kaise request karun?
Say: "Ma'am, I would like to lead our group in this project. I will make sure everyone does their part." Showing a plan helps the teacher trust you.
Dost ne poocha weekend ka plan. Mujhe bolna hai "Abhi tak kuch tay nahi hua hai." English?
Say: "Nothing has been decided yet."

Friday. Yusuf's diary.
Nazia came back to school today. Her abbu died last week. Everyone went quiet when she walked in, and Riya said "sorry for your loss" like a grown-up, and Nazia just looked at the floor. I didn't know what to say. So at lunch I sat next to her on the steps and didn't say anything. Then I took out my new bouncy ball and bounced it to her. She caught it. She bounced it back. We did that till the bell. She didn't smile exactly, but she said, "Can you bring it Monday?" I told Ammi, and Ammi said sometimes sitting beside someone is the kindest thing. I'm bringing the ball Monday.

What did Yusuf bounce to Nazia?
Yusuf's new bouncy ball.
Why did Yusuf sit next to Nazia without saying anything?
Yusuf felt unsure what to say and a bit nervous, but did not want Nazia to be alone.
What could Yusuf keep doing in the weeks ahead?
Keep sitting with Nazia and bringing ordinary games like the ball, and let her talk about her abbu only if she wants to.
What might the bouncing game have been like for Nazia?
It gave Nazia something ordinary and quiet to do with someone beside her, without having to talk, which seemed to comfort her enough to ask for it again.

Sunday, late. I slipped this weekend. Saturday and most of Sunday went on videos, and I feel low about it. But I've decided not to be horrible to myself, because that never helped. Instead I asked what set it off. First there was the argument with my brother on Friday, which left me angry and restless. Then there was nothing planned, so the empty hours filled up. That's two triggers: a fight and boredom. So here's what changes: next Saturday I've asked my friend Keerthana to go to the market with me, something fixed and outside. And tomorrow I start again as normal. One bad weekend doesn't cancel the two good weeks. — Rekha

What set off the weekend of videos?
An argument with a brother and having nothing planned.
How does Rekha feel about the slip, and how is it handled?
Low and disappointed, but Rekha chooses to be kind to self instead of harsh, and looks for triggers.
What else could Rekha do to prepare for boring stretches, and why?
Keep a short list of things to do when bored, since a ready list is easier to use than deciding on the spot.
How does the outing look to Keerthana?
Keerthana, invited to the market, may feel glad to be included and to help a friend get through a hard weekend.

A TV show costs $100,000 per episode for the first season and twice that much for every other season.  The first season had 12 episodes, and every season after that had 50% more episodes except the last season, which had 24 episodes.  The show had 5 seasons.  How much did it cost to produce all the episodes?

The first season cost 12*100,000=$1,200,000
Season 2-4 had 12*.5=6 more episodes per season than the first
So they each had 12+6=18 episodes
That means there were 18*3+24=78 episodes in the last 4 seasons
So those episodes cost 2*100,000=$200,000
For a total cost of 200,000*78=$15,600,000
So the total cost was 15,600,000+1,200,000=$16,800,000
The answer is 16,800,000.

Read this:

In the school yard in Accra, Kofi walked around the long way so he would not pass Dalia's class. Last Friday he had promised to help her paint the set for the play, but he went to play football instead and never said a word. Now his ears burned whenever he saw her. All week he hid behind the water tank at lunch. On Thursday he saw her holding a heavy board alone, and his stomach turned. He walked across the yard and said, "I did not come because I chose football. I am sorry. Can I paint with you now?" Dalia looked at him for a moment and handed him a brush.

Which city is the school in?
The school is in Accra.
Why did Kofi avoid Dalia's class and hide behind the water tank?
He was embarrassed and ashamed for breaking his promise to help paint the set.
What did Kofi do that started to repair things?
He told her the truth, said sorry and offered to paint with her, instead of hiding any longer.
How might Dalia have felt when Kofi finally came over?
Dalia may have felt let down earlier and cautious, but she seemed willing to accept the honest apology, since she handed him a brush.

Gautam ran into the kitchen waving a sheet of paper. “Look! Look! It's Biscuit!” Biscuit is our cat. I'm Aadhya, his big sister, and I was cutting beans. Papa glanced up. “Wow, best artist in the whole world!” Gautam grinned for a second, then kept holding the paper up. Nani sat on the stool and looked for a long time. “Her whiskers go all the way out. And she's sleeping on the chappal, like always.” Gautam climbed onto her lap and showed her every stripe. I can't say what he was thinking, but he didn't go back to Papa.

What is the cat in Gautam's drawing called?
The cat is called Biscuit.
What does Gautam still holding up the paper suggest?
It suggests he felt proud but wanted more than a quick compliment, maybe hoping someone would really look; he may simply have been excited.
What did Nani notice that Papa missed?
Nani noticed the details, the whiskers and the cat sleeping on the chappal, showing she saw what Gautam actually drew.
How does Aadhya read Gautam's choice to stay with Nani?
Aadhya can't be sure of his thoughts but sees that he chose the person who shared the drawing with him, not the one with the biggest praise.

Read this:

The monsoon had turned the ghat road outside Mahabaleshwar slick, and Bhupen, fifteen, knew it. His friends had their phones out. "No hands down the slope, Bhupen! You said you could!" Ishita, his neighbour, said quietly, "It's wet. Don't." But everyone was watching, and backing out felt worse than falling. He pushed off, lifted his hands and grinned for the cameras. At the bend, the tyre slid. He hit the road hard and skidded into the gravel. His palms and knee were torn. The filming stopped. Ishita ran to him, then called his mother, who came with the car and took him to the clinic. That night, he deleted the group's video himself.

Where was the ghat road?
Outside Mahabaleshwar.
Why did Bhupen go ahead even though he knew it was wet?
Everyone was watching, and the fear of looking scared by backing out felt stronger than the fear of falling.
What could Bhupen have done instead when Ishita warned him?
He could have used Ishita's warning as a reason to say no, riding down normally, even at the cost of some teasing.
How does Ishita act during and after the fall?
Ishita, who had warned him quietly, runs to help and calls his mother, taking the responsible step the others didn't.
Edit this to sound more neutral, without exaggeration: This is literally the worst traffic in the entire universe.
The traffic is very heavy today.

Read this:

When I was ten, I noticed something at every family wedding. My uncle, a bank manager, got the best seat. My father, an electrician, fixed the lights and ate last in the kitchen. I'm Himani, his only daughter, and I thought that meant my father was worth less.
Once I told my friend Zeenat, "My uncle is bigger than my papa." Zeenat's father drove an autorickshaw. She looked at me strangely and said, "My abba says there's no small work, only small people."
At the next wedding, the power went out. Everyone panicked. My father fixed it in five minutes, in the dark. The whole hall clapped. My uncle clapped too.
I'm twelve now. I still remember that clapping. And Zeenat's words.

What was Himani's father's job?
Himani's father was an electrician.
How did Himani feel when she watched her father eat last in the kitchen?
Himani felt confused and a bit ashamed, thinking it meant her father was worth less.
What helped change Himani's view?
Zeenat's words about there being no small work, and seeing her father fix the power while everyone clapped, taught her that honest work carries dignity.
How might Himani's father have felt when the hall clapped?
Her father probably felt proud and appreciated, finally seen for the work he does.
A luxury bag costs $3000. A reseller wants to get a 15% profit. How much should she sell the bag?

The reseller wants to get $3000 x 15/100 = $450 profit.
Thus, she needs to sell it for $3000 + $450 = $3450.
The answer is 3450.
My bicycle was stole outside the market yesterday. Please fix the verb.

My bicycle was stolen outside the market yesterday.
Why: Passive "was" needs the participle "stolen".

Monday. The district alert on Anirban's phone said the river might cross the danger mark by Wednesday. He called his mother's cousin in a village on higher ground and asked if the family could come. Siddharth, his younger brother, rolled his eyes. 'Every year you panic.'
Wednesday. The second alert said to leave low areas by noon. Anirban loaded Ma, Baba, Siddharth and the documents bag into a hired van by ten. Siddharth wanted to go back for his guitar and the new mattress. 'No,' Anirban said. 'The alert said noon. We're going.'
Saturday. They returned when the alert was lifted. Mud stood knee-high in the house; the mattress was ruined, the guitar swollen. Siddharth stood in the doorway a long time, then said quietly, 'The Borahs stayed. The rescue boat had to carry them out.'

By what time did Anirban load the family into the van on Wednesday?
By ten, before the noon deadline in the alert.
What was Siddharth feeling in the doorway on Saturday?
Siddharth seemed shaken and quietly regretful, seeing the ruined house and knowing the neighbours who stayed needed rescue.
What else could Anirban do before the next flood season?
He could move precious things like the guitar to a high shelf or to the cousin's house in advance, so leaving on time costs less.
How might the cousin see Anirban's early call on Monday?
Getting the call two days early gave the cousin time to prepare space and food, rather than facing a sudden arrival in the rain.

Read this:

In the small town of Bijnor, Samir, fifteen, spent every evening watching videos of stunt riders doing wheelies on highways. His aunt Parveen khala found him on the roof, phone glowing. Samir tensed, waiting for shouting. Instead she sat down. "What do you like about them?" He shrugged. "They're free. Brave." "They look brave," she said. "Do you want to try?" He hesitated. "Maybe." Parveen didn't panic. She told him about her college friend who broke both legs on a road like that. Then she said, "If you're serious about bikes, there's a proper training ground in Meerut with gear and coaches. We'll talk to your abbu tonight." At dinner she did. Abbu listened, and agreed Samir would not ride on the highway, and they would visit the training ground together on Sunday. Samir kept watching videos, but now he showed them to her.

Where is the proper training ground Parveen khala mentioned?
In Meerut.
What was Samir feeling when Parveen khala found him on the roof?
He was tense, expecting to be shouted at for watching the videos.
What did Parveen khala do that kept Samir talking to her?
She stayed calm, asked what he liked, shared a real story of the risks, and brought in his abbu that evening with a safe plan.
How might Abbu have felt when Parveen raised it at dinner?
He was probably worried but glad to know, and relieved there was a safe plan to agree on.

Read this:

Santiago had been a bike courier in Lisbon for six months when Emeka, who rode the same routes, skidded on wet tram tracks and broke his wrist. The hospital bill was manageable, but Emeka couldn't work for seven weeks, and nobody paid him for those. Sitting with him in his tiny flat, Santiago did the uncomfortable maths in his head: if that had been him, what would pay the rent? That weekend he went through the papers he had been ignoring. He was self-employed, so nobody was taking tax from his earnings, and a letter from the tax office had sat unopened on his shelf since spring. He booked an appointment at the free advice centre for couriers and asked about income protection too. The adviser explained both slowly, and Santiago left with a list. He sent a copy to Emeka.

How did Emeka break his wrist?
He skidded on wet tram tracks.
What was Santiago feeling as he did the uncomfortable maths?
Santiago felt uneasy and worried, realising he had no protection if he were hurt.
Where did Santiago go for help, and why is that a good choice?
To the free advice centre for couriers, because a qualified adviser can explain tax and cover for his situation.
What was it like for Emeka during the seven weeks off?
Emeka faced lost income with no pay, and probably felt anxious about rent and frustrated at being stuck.

Counsellor's note, Thursday.
On Monday the principal announced in assembly, very sternly, that anyone seen near the old quarry would be suspended. Until then, I don't think Omkar had ever thought about the quarry. By Wednesday, he and Karthik had cycled there after school and climbed down to the water's edge. A shopkeeper saw them and called the school. In my room today, Omkar said, arms folded, "Nobody tells me where I can go." When I asked what he'd found there, he admitted the rocks were loose and he had slipped once. I didn't lecture. I explained why the quarry is dangerous and asked what would make it less tempting. He shrugged. "If they'd just said why." I called both boys' parents today, and asked the principal to explain the reasons at Friday's assembly.

Who saw Omkar and Karthik at the quarry?
A shopkeeper saw them and called the school.
What does 'Nobody tells me where I can go' suggest about Omkar's feelings?
It suggests Omkar felt controlled and defiant, so the stern ban made the quarry tempting as a way to protect his freedom.
What did the counsellor do, and why is it a better approach?
The counsellor explained the danger instead of lecturing, called both boys' parents that day, and asked the principal to explain the reasons, which lowers the urge to rebel and keeps them safer.
How might Karthik's parents feel getting the counsellor's call?
They would likely feel alarmed about the loose rocks and grateful to know the same day.

Read this:

Bidisha, you ask why I started the kitchen at the cancer hospital. When I was twenty-five, your Gurleen masi lost her mother after three long years of illness. In those years I had seen families sleeping in the corridor, eating only biscuits. After Bibiji died, I couldn't sit at home. So I began cooking dal and rotis and taking them to the hospital every Sunday. Soon others joined. It gave my grief somewhere to go. But I'll tell you the part people skip: two years in, I realised I had never cried for Bibiji. I was always too busy feeding others. One Sunday I stayed home, took out her shawl, and wept all day. Service is a good home for grief, beta. It is not the only room.

What did Gurleen cook for the hospital?
Dal and rotis.
What did young Gurleen realise two years in, and how did she feel?
That she had never cried for Bibiji; the grief she had been too busy to feel came through, and she wept all day.
What choice in the story gave grief its own room?
Staying home one Sunday with Bibiji's shawl to weep, instead of only serving others.
How might the families in the corridor have experienced the kitchen?
As real comfort, a warm meal instead of only biscuits during a hard time.
Is sentence ka English chahiye: "Woh ladki jo kal aayi thi, meri behen hai."
In English: "The girl who came yesterday is my sister." "Who" connects the girl to the action of coming.

Could you answer these?
Jack practised the flute for 16 minutes and the drum for 9 minutes. How long was that in all?
Please tell me what "lyrics" means.
How should I say this correctly: "I listened a new song."
I get nervous singing in front of people. Any advice?
Why do lullabies calm babies?

1. 25 minutes. Because 16 + 9 = 25.
2. Lyrics means the words of a song. Example: I know the lyrics to this song.
3. Fixed: I listened to a new song. Why: "Listen" needs "to".
4. Sing in front of one friend first, then a small group. Breathe slowly and look at the back wall.
5. They are soft and slow. Because the gentle tune and the voice help the baby relax.
A rectangle has a length of 3 inches and a width of 6 inches. A square has a width of 5 inches. What is the difference in area between the two shapes?

The area of the rectangle is 3 x 6 = 18 sq in
The area of the square is 5 x 5 = 25 sq in
The difference is 25 - 18 = 7 sq in
The answer is 7.
Is "grizzly" or "grisly" used for horrible things?

"Grisly" means horrible or shocking. "Grizzly" is a kind of bear, and it can also mean grey-haired.
Examples: The newspaper described a grisly crime. A grizzly bear lives in North America.

Read this:

For a few weeks my partner Keerthana felt far away, even sitting beside me on the sofa. I noticed I was checking the phone for messages more than I wanted to, and going to bed lonely and a bit ashamed of feeling rejected. My first thought was to accuse, "You don't care anymore." I didn't say it. On Sunday morning, over chai, I said, "I miss our evening walks. I've been feeling a little lonely, and I'd like to understand what's going on for you." Keerthana was quiet, then said, "Work has been eating me up. I didn't know you'd noticed." We agreed on ten minutes of walking after dinner, no phones. I don't need to ask every day if it's still okay. The walk itself is the answer.

— Ayesha

What time of the week did Ayesha bring it up?
On Sunday morning, over chai.
What did Ayesha feel during those weeks, and what did Ayesha almost say?
Ayesha felt lonely and a bit ashamed of feeling rejected, and almost said the accusation, "You don't care anymore."
What made Ayesha's approach work better than an accusation?
Ayesha said what was missed, the evening walks, admitted feeling lonely and asked what was happening for Keerthana, then invited a small ritual instead of demanding constant reassurance.
How might Keerthana have been experiencing those weeks?
Keerthana was probably absorbed by work stress and unaware of Ayesha's loneliness, since Keerthana said, "I didn't know you'd noticed."

Condense this into under 70 words.

In the common room of the nursing college hostel in Gangtok, Pema stared at the form for the overseas job fair. Her parents had sold half their cardamom field to pay her fees. On every call, Ama said, "Once you're working in Dubai, all our troubles will end." "You've written your name four times and crossed it out four times," Gargi said. "Because I want to work in the hill clinics here. And every time I think it, I feel like a thief." "A thief of what?" "Of their field." Gargi put down her tea. "You can be grateful without living their plan. And you can't go to Dubai and resent them quietly for ten years." Pema laughed shakily. "I'd be terrible at resenting quietly." She didn't fill in the form. That evening she called home and told Ama and Apa what she wanted, and why, and that she would help the family in her own way. Ama said, "We'll talk more on Sunday." Pema took that as a start.

Pema's parents sold half their cardamom field to pay her fees, but she wants to work in the hill clinics, not abroad. Her friend Gargi says she can be grateful without following their plan, so Pema calls home and explains. Her mother agrees to talk more on Sunday.

Mentor's note, six months into Chaitanya's new role
Chaitanya joined our firm after a long, public dispute with a previous employer over falsified quality data. The regulator eventually upheld the complaint. I agreed to mentor Chaitanya, and I want to record how the aftermath has looked.
In the first months Chaitanya was exhausted, jumpy at loud meetings, and slow to trust anyone senior. Once, when I asked a routine question about a report, Chaitanya's hands shook. I reminded them that here, questions are ordinary.
What has helped: weekly walks with me; Charu from the testing team, who invited Chaitanya to the Friday badminton group; and a family that calls every evening. Last month Chaitanya spoke at our ethics training, plainly and without bitterness, and three juniors stayed afterwards to ask questions.
Chaitanya told me, "I don't feel like a hero. I feel like someone who can sleep again." That seems like peace to me.

Who invited Chaitanya to the Friday badminton group?
Charu from the testing team.
What does Chaitanya's line about being able to sleep again reveal?
It reveals a tired but calm peace, relief after the long strain rather than a sense of triumph.
What has supported Chaitanya's recovery?
Weekly walks with the mentor, Charu's friendly invitation, a family that calls every evening, and a workplace where questions are ordinary.
What might the three juniors have felt staying after the talk?
They probably felt curious and inspired, drawn by Chaitanya's plain, unbitter account.

I've shared a pod with Tejas for two years in the hospital's IT department, so I saw this up close. When he missed out on the team-lead role last spring, he went quiet for a few days; I couldn't tell if he was angry or just thinking. Then he did something I've never done: he booked a slot with the head of department and asked, straight out, what he'd need to show to be ready next time. He came back with a list: handle vendor calls, mentor the new joiners, write clearer documentation. Over the next months I watched him take the vendor calls nobody wanted and sit with two interns every Friday. He also started having coffee once a month with Dr. Menon, who chairs the IT committee. This spring the role opened again. Tejas got it. I think he'd planned it for a year.

What was on the list Tejas brought back from the head of department?
Handling vendor calls, mentoring the new joiners and writing clearer documentation.
What could the narrator tell, and not tell, about Tejas's feelings after missing the role?
The narrator saw Tejas go quiet for a few days but could not tell whether he was angry or just thinking.
What made Tejas's approach to promotion effective?
He asked directly what readiness looked like, worked steadily on each item, and built a relationship with a senior who could support him.
How might the narrator feel watching Tejas get the role?
Impressed, and perhaps nudged to think about their own growth, since the narrator admits never having done what Tejas did.

Tommy goes for a run around his neighborhood and decides to calculate how many wheels he saw. All the trucks in his neighborhood have 4 wheels and all the cars in his neighborhood also have 4 wheels. If he saw 12 trucks and 13 cars, how many wheels did he see?

He saw 25 total vehicles because 12 plus 13 equals 25.
He saw 100 wheels because 25 times 4 equals 100.
The answer is 100.

Read this:

Sunday night.
Told the band today that I'm leaving after the Diwali gig.
I've been thinking about it for months. I love them, but with my new job I miss half the practices, and I hate being the one who's always late with new songs. It's not fair to them.
I almost just stopped replying to the group, the way Karan did last year. We never really forgave him.
Instead I asked Trisha to meet me for coffee first, since she started the band. I said it straight: I'm leaving, it's my schedule, not anyone's fault. I'll play the Diwali gig, all four songs, and I'll help teach my parts to whoever replaces me.
She was quiet, then said, "Honestly, I guessed. Thank you for telling me properly."
Then I told the rest at practice. Nobody was angry. Rohit asked if I'd come to the gig after that as audience. I said yes.
I'm Himani, and this is the first time I've left something without feeling like I ran away.

After which gig is the narrator leaving the band?
After the Diwali gig.
How does Himani feel about the way this ending went?
Himani feels relieved and at peace, for once not feeling like running away.
What did Himani do that made this a clean exit?
Himani told Trisha first and in person, gave an honest reason without blame, committed to the Diwali gig and offered to teach the parts.
How did Trisha react to the news?
Trisha was quiet but grateful, saying she had guessed and thanking Himani for telling her properly.

Please sum this short passage up in three sentences.

It was nearly noon when I arrived at the top of the ascent. For some time I sat upon the rock that overlooks the sea of ice. A mist covered both that and the surrounding mountains. Presently a breeze dissipated the cloud, and I descended upon the glacier. The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a troubled sea, descending low, and interspersed by rifts that sink deep. The field of ice is almost a league in width, but I spent nearly two hours in crossing it. The opposite mountain is a bare perpendicular rock. From the side where I now stood Montanvert was exactly opposite, at the distance of a league; and above it rose Mont Blanc, in awful majesty. I remained in a recess of the rock, gazing on this wonderful and stupendous scene. The sea, or rather the vast river of ice, wound among its dependent mountains, whose aerial summits hung over its recesses. Their icy and glittering peaks shone in the sunlight over the clouds. My heart, which was before sorrowful, now swelled with something like joy; I exclaimed, "Wandering spirits, if indeed ye wander, and do not rest in your narrow beds, allow me this faint happiness, or take me, as your companion, away from the joys of life."

At nearly noon the narrator reaches the top of the climb and later crosses the uneven glacier in about two hours. Mont Blanc rises above Montanvert opposite, and the icy peaks shine in the sunlight. The narrator's sad heart swells with joy, and the narrator asks the spirits for this small happiness or to be taken away.

Rukmini: hey Tushar, the stock sheet for Pune had last week's numbers again 😕
Tushar: ugh sorry. fixing now
Rukmini: no stress, it's fixed. just wanted to check in though
Rukmini: it's happened twice this week and that's not like you
Tushar: yeah I know
Tushar: my laptop's been crashing and I've been redoing stuff from memory at night
Tushar: also honestly I think I just rushed it
Rukmini: ok, maybe both 🙂 I'll raise a ticket for the laptop today
Rukmini: and can we do a 2-minute check together before sending, just this month?
Tushar: yes please. thanks for asking and not just assuming
Rukmini: 👍 talk at 4

What did the Pune stock sheet have again?
It had last week's numbers again.
What might Rukmini be thinking in writing "that's not like you"?
Rukmini seems concerned rather than angry, curious whether something new is going on before deciding Tushar is careless.
What does Rukmini do, and why does it help?
Rukmini raises a ticket for the laptop and suggests a short check before sending, which deals with both the situation and the habit.
How does Tushar feel about the way Rukmini handled it?
Tushar feels grateful and relieved that Rukmini asked instead of assuming, which makes it easy to admit the rushing too.
The shop's accounts are "in the red". What colour should I look for?

You do not need to see any colour. "In the red" means owing more money than you have, because losses are traditionally written in red ink.
Example: The small business was in the red for two years.
If the price of a bag of cherries is $5 when the price of a bag of olives is $7, how much would Jordyn pay for buying 50 bags of each fruit and a 10% discount?

At a 10 percent discount, Jordyn will pay 10/100%*$5=$.50 less for a bag of cherries.
To buy one of the cherries at a 10% discount Jordyn will pay $5-$0.50=$4.50
The cost of buying 50 bags of cherries at the 10% discount is 50*4.50=$225
Also, at a 10% discount, Jordyn will pay 10/100*$7=$0.70 less for a bag of olives.
The price of a bag of olives at a 10% discount is $7-$0.70=$6.3
To buy 50 bags of olives Jordyn will pay $6.3*50=$315
The total cost of buying 50 bags of each fruit at a 10% discount is $315+$225=$540
The answer is 540.

Last spring my best friend Ujjwal asked me to hold his son at the naming ceremony. I'm Uday, and I'm not a crier. But as the priest said the baby's name and the little one yawned against my chest, something cracked open. I remembered my own father lifting me onto his shoulders at a fair. He died when I was four. For twenty years I had told everyone I didn't remember him. Apparently some part of me did. I handed the baby back and went and stood in the corridor, crying into my sleeve. Ujjwal found me and just stood there with me. Later I started writing down what I remembered about my father. It was more than I thought.

What did Uday remember the father doing?
Lifting Uday onto his shoulders at a fair.
What did Uday feel while holding the baby?
Something cracked open: grief for the father who died when Uday was four, long thought forgotten, suddenly flooded back.
What did Uday do with the feeling afterwards?
Began writing down memories of the father, giving the old grief a place instead of pushing it away.
How might Ujjwal have felt finding Uday in the corridor?
Concerned and caring, choosing simply to stand there as quiet support.
Which village in my district has the oldest living tree?
I can't check that, because tree records for one district are local. The forest office or a local naturalist group could name candidates.

Read this:

The nursery in Madrid had a paper tree and silver stars for the winter holidays. A man in a red suit came in with a sack.
Pablo, two, took one look and screamed.
Hana, two, sitting on the rug, had been smiling. She turned to Pablo, stared at his open mouth, and her own mouth wobbled. Then she burst into tears too, hands over her face.
The teacher sat between them, one arm each. "It's okay. It's okay."

What decorations did the nursery have?
A paper tree and silver stars.
What does Hana's wobbling mouth suggest she was feeling?
She was starting to feel upset herself, catching Pablo's fear and distress.
How could the teacher help next time a visitor comes in?
The teacher could prepare the toddlers, keep them close, and stay calm, so one child's fear spreads less.
What was it like for Pablo when the man came in?
Pablo was frightened, screaming at the unfamiliar man in the red suit.

Read this:

Subject: Checking in after this morning

Hi Naveen,

I wanted to write properly, because at the stand-up I only managed a clumsy "you okay?"

When the director started going through the quarterly numbers, your face went grey and your hands were shaking so much the coffee cup rattled on the table. My first thought, honestly, was that you were scared of the review. I nearly said "relax, it's not that bad."

I'm glad I asked instead whether you'd eaten. When you said nothing since last night, I got the juice from the pantry and sat with you in the small room until your hands stopped trembling.

You said afterwards it was "probably both, the hunger and the nerves." Fair enough. I just didn't want to guess at the feeling before checking you were physically all right. If it keeps happening, please get it checked with a doctor.

Hafsa

What did Hafsa bring Naveen from the pantry?
Hafsa got the juice from the pantry and sat with Naveen in the small room until the trembling stopped.
What was Hafsa feeling on seeing Naveen's hands shaking, and how sure could Hafsa be of the reason?
Hafsa was worried and a little unsure: the first reading was that Naveen was scared of the review, but hunger or illness could look the same, so Hafsa checked on Naveen's health first.
Which choice worked here, and why?
Asking whether Naveen had eaten and staying with Naveen worked, because it dealt with a possible physical cause before anyone judged the mood.
How might Naveen have felt if Hafsa had said "relax, it's not that bad"?
Naveen might have felt misread and embarrassed, since part of the shaking came from not eating, and would still have been unwell.
cushion? I don't know this word.

A cushion is a soft bag filled with something light, used to make a seat or a bed more comfortable. It is a noun.
Example: Grandfather put a cushion on the hard chair.

Read this:

You want to know why I nag everyone about insurance? I'm Mahima. Let me tell you.
Two years ago, my father had a heart problem at night. We rushed to a private hospital. The bill for five days was more than he earned in months. We didn't have insurance. My mother sold her gold.
My friend Vinita came to the hospital every day. She had health cover through her family and couldn't believe we didn't.
When I got my first job, the first thing I did was check my company's health insurance and add my parents. I also sat with an agent Vinita trusted and asked questions until I understood what's covered.
It's boring paperwork. But I never want my mother to sell her gold again.

How long was Mahima's father in the hospital?
Five days.
What was Mahima feeling when Mahima's mother sold her gold?
Mahima felt helpless and sad seeing the family struggle without insurance.
What choice inside the story protected Mahima's family later?
Checking company health insurance, adding the parents, and asking questions until the cover was clear.
How might Vinita have felt at the hospital?
Vinita probably felt worried for Mahima's family and shocked they had no cover.
In three words or fewer, what should I say to my teacher when I arrive in the morning?
Good morning, ma'am.

Monday. The mock entrance test scores went live at noon. Tejas's friends compared numbers in the canteen. Tejas said, "I'll check later," and put his phone in his bag. He felt lighter for an hour.
Wednesday. Anirban asked, "So? What did you get?" "Haven't looked." "Bro, it's been two days." That night Tejas couldn't sleep. He imagined a score of zero, of ten, the whole class laughing.
Sunday. Anirban came over and sat on the bed. "Log in. I'm right here."
Tejas logged in with shaking fingers. 112 out of 300. Not great. But not zero. The weak section was clearly physics.
"That's fixable," Anirban said. "Physics revision classes start tomorrow. You'd have missed them."
Tejas let out a long breath. The number was smaller than the fear had been.

What score did Tejas get?
Tejas got 112 out of 300.
Why couldn't Tejas sleep on Wednesday?
Tejas felt anxious and full of dread, imagining terrible scores, because not knowing let the fear grow bigger than the real number.
What helped Tejas finally face the score?
Anirban sitting with Tejas while logging in, which made the news shareable and showed physics was the part to fix.
How does Anirban see the score?
Anirban sees it as fixable and is glad Tejas looked in time for the physics revision classes.

Read this:

Thabo finished his engineering degree in Johannesburg in November and signed the lease on a flat in Rosebank the same week. It was expensive, but he'd have a job by January, obviously. Emil, his roommate from res, looked at the lease on the kitchen table. "No job yet, though?" "Three interviews. One will come through." "And if none do?" Thabo laughed. "Emil, I was top ten in my class. Plus Lerato says she'll move in by March, so rent gets halved." February came. Two rejections, one silence. Lerato took a post in Durban. Thabo sat on the floor of the half-empty flat with the rent reminder open on his phone. Emil came over with a pot of pap and said, "Tomorrow, the campus careers office. Together." Thabo nodded. For the first time, he made a list titled "Plan B."

When did Thabo sign the lease on the flat in Rosebank?
In November, the same week he finished his degree.
What was Thabo feeling when he laughed at Emil's question?
He felt confident and a little dismissive, sure that a job and Lerato moving in would make everything work.
What small step helped Thabo, and what could he do going forward?
Emil's offer to go to the careers office together; Thabo can now make a Plan B and get advice there before new commitments.
How does Emil see Thabo's plans in November?
Emil seems quietly worried, asking about the job because the lease depends on things that haven't happened yet.

Read this:

Week one. Posters went up across the hostel walls in bright red: "Blue Panel sold the hostel fund." Ramesh laughed. "Who writes this stuff?" He voted in college elections only when he remembered.
Week three. The line was in every group chat, on stickers in the canteen, in a song someone played outside the library. Blue Panel's faces were drawn with dollar signs. Over lunch Ramesh heard himself say, "Everyone knows Blue Panel took the money."
Keerthana put down her spoon. "How do you know?"
"It's... everywhere."
"That's not the same as proof. Did anyone show accounts?"
Ramesh opened his mouth and closed it.
Week four. He went to the hostel office and asked for the fund statement. The clerk said it was on the notice board, and had been all along. Ramesh stood reading it for ten minutes, feeling slightly sick at how easily the words had become his own.

Where was the fund statement, according to the clerk?
The clerk said the fund statement was on the notice board, and had been all along.
How did Ramesh feel reading the statement in week four?
Ramesh felt slightly sick and uneasy, realising a slogan he had once laughed at had become his own belief without any proof.
What turning point made Ramesh go and check?
Keerthana asking "How do you know?" and whether anyone had shown accounts made him see that seeing a claim everywhere is not proof.
How might Blue Panel's members experience the four weeks of posters?
They would be painted as thieves across the campus, with their faces drawn with dollar signs, before anyone asked for evidence.

metadata.subtype: Repeated claims begin to feel true [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Rashmi, you asked how your Vijay Dada and I have lasted fifty years. Sit, I'll tell you the real answer.

When we were first married, I was twenty-two and a clam. If your Dadi raised her voice, I shut like a door. And she, poor thing, would get louder: "You never talk to me! You don't care!"

One night she didn't shout. She sat on the bed and said, very quietly, "I miss you. I'm scared we're becoming strangers." I nearly cried.

I said, "I go quiet because I get overwhelmed. Give me twenty minutes, and I'll come back. I promise."

I walked around the block. Twenty minutes later, I was back. We talked till two in the morning.

From then on, she said the soft thing instead of the sharp thing, and I always came back. That's the whole secret, beta.

How long did Vijay ask for before coming back?
He asked for twenty minutes.
What was Vijay feeling when Dadi said she missed him and was scared?
He felt deeply moved, nearly crying, because the soft words reached him where the shouting hadn't.
What was the choice inside the story that changed their pattern?
Dadi spoke her fear instead of criticism, and Vijay named his need for a short break and actually came back, so trust could grow.
How might Dadi have felt when Vijay returned after twenty minutes?
She probably felt relieved and valued, seeing that his break wasn't a retreat from her.

metadata.subtype: Stage 6: Softer ask and staying present [Response]

Read this:

The canteen was so loud that Mahima had to lean in to be heard. The maintenance team's shift change was five minutes away, and Deepak was still holding his tray. "The generator fix on Saturday saved our whole batch," Mahima said. "Thank you. Truly." Deepak's first instinct was to laugh it off. Instead he put the tray down and said, "Thank you, that means a lot. Naveen did the wiring, and I handled the testing." Mahima smiled, noted both names for the weekly update, and hurried off. Deepak stood there a second with warm ears, then went to find Naveen to tell him.

How soon was the maintenance team's shift change?
It was five minutes away.
What was Deepak feeling as he stood there with warm ears?
He felt pleased 😊 and a little shy at being thanked, and he wanted Naveen to hear it too. Warm ears could also just be the heat of the canteen.
What made Deepak's reply a good way to accept thanks?
He said thank you plainly and named Naveen's wiring, so he neither waved it off nor kept all the credit.
How might Mahima have felt if Deepak had laughed it off?
Mahima might have felt unheard, as if Mahima's thanks did not count, and been less likely to speak up next time.

Jeevan Dadu pointed his stick at the green pond. "Rashmi, when I was ten, you could see fish in that water. Every child in the village swam there after school. And every one of us threw our sugarcane peels and paper in it. I used to think, 'My peel is so small. What difference can it make?' Everybody thought the same. One summer the water turned green and smelly. The fish floated up, belly first. The panchayat closed the pond, and we had nowhere to swim. That summer was long and hot and sad. That's why I still pick up peels along the bank."

What did the children throw into the pond?
Sugarcane peels and paper.
What did young Jeevan think about his own peel?
He thought it was so small it couldn't make a difference.
What choice does Jeevan make now because of that summer?
He still picks up peels along the bank, having learned that everyone's small peels together ruined the pond.
How might Rashmi see a single wrapper after hearing this story?
Rashmi may see it as part of a pile made by everyone, not a harmless little thing.

Saga Dawa month meant no meat in Tenzin's kitchen, the way it had been in Ama's house in Dharamshala. But tonight six friends were coming, Simran among them, the one who called any meal without chicken 'just a snack'. Then the rain knocked out the power, leaving one gas burner and a torch. Tenzin, twenty-five, made a big pot of vegetable thenthuk and, with the last of the phone battery, ordered a plate of chicken momos from the corner shop for anyone who wanted them, kept on a separate plate by the door. Simran arrived dripping, laughed at the torchlight, then went back for the thenthuk twice. 'Okay, this is not a snack.' Nobody teased anyone's plate. The momos disappeared too.

What did Tenzin cook in the big pot?
Vegetable thenthuk.
What was Tenzin probably feeling when the power went out with six friends on the way?
Tenzin was probably worried and under pressure, with one burner, a torch and guests coming, yet calm enough to plan.
How did Tenzin keep the custom and still welcome everyone, despite the power cut?
Tenzin kept the kitchen meat-free but offered chicken momos from outside on a separate plate, and nobody mocked anyone's choice.
How did Simran's view of a meatless meal change?
Simran moved from calling it 'just a snack' to going back twice and saying so, because it was offered warmly, without a lecture.

Marcy's grade is electing their class president. Marcy got three times as many votes as Barry, who got twice as many as 3 more than the number of votes Joey got. If Joey got 8 votes, how many votes did Marcy get?

First, add three to Joey's vote total: 8 votes + 3 votes = 11 votes
Then double that number to find the number of votes Barry got: 11 votes * 2 = 22 votes
Then triple that number to find Marcy's vote total: 22 votes * 3 = 66 votes
The answer is 66.

"Oh, my dear Madam Mina, this is indeed a change. See! friend Jonathan, we have got our dear Madam Mina, as of old, back to us to-day!" Then turning to her, he said, cheerfully: "And what am I do for you? For at this hour you do not want me for nothings."

Without outside knowledge, how does the Professor greet Madam Mina on seeing her recovered?
He calls it a change and points out to Jonathan that Madam Mina is back as of old. He then asks cheerfully what he can do for her, since at this hour she would not want him for nothing.

Oskar, twenty-four, hadn't visited his mother in Gothenburg since spring. When he rang the bell, it took a long time for her to come. Selin opened the door smiling, but she was holding the rail, and when he said hello she said, 'Pardon, darling?' At dinner she asked him to repeat himself four times. After she went to bed early, tired, Oskar sat alone at the kitchen table where she used to help him with homework. He felt a sudden, heavy sadness, and a fierce urge to fix everything at once: stair rails, hearing tests, grocery deliveries. He took a breath. Tomorrow he'd ask her what she wanted. For now, he washed the dishes the way she liked them, glasses first.

How many times did Selin ask Oskar to repeat himself?
Four times.
What did Oskar feel at the kitchen table?
He felt a sudden heavy sadness and a strong protective urge to fix everything.
Why is Oskar's decision to ask Selin tomorrow wise?
It respects her wishes and dignity instead of rushing to change everything without her.
How might Selin feel if Oskar asks what she wants?
She would likely feel respected and cared for, still in charge of her own life.

metadata.subtype: Adult child noticing parents slowing down [Observer]

messages.content: James hurt himself exercising.  The pain subsided after 3 days, but he knew that the injury would take at least 5 times that long to fully heal. After that, he wanted to wait another 3 days before he started working out again.  If he wants to wait 3 weeks after that to start lifting heavy again, how long until he can lift heavy again?

The injury would be fully healed after 3*5=15 days
So he would start exercising again in 15+3=18 days
He would then wait for 3*7=21 more days to start lifting heavy again
That means he needs to wait 18+21=39 days
The answer is 39.

First week. Zubin had moved from a quiet Parsi colony in Mumbai to a Delhi school, and at lunch his new classmates talked in a fast, mixed stream: "Bro, scene kya hai?" "Full bakwaas test tha." Zubin answered in careful English and felt like a teacher at the wrong table.
Second week. He tried it. "Scene is... chill?" Suraj laughed, not unkindly. "Almost, yaar. Say 'scene sorted hai'." Zubin practised it on the bus home under his breath.
Fifth week. After the basketball trials, Suraj asked how he felt about being picked as reserve. Zubin opened his mouth for the English word and couldn't find one that fit. "Not sad, exactly. Bas... thoda khalipan." Suraj nodded slowly. "Haan. That's exactly it."
That evening, on the group chat, someone typed "Zubin bhai full desi ho gaya" and Zubin grinned at his phone.

What did Suraj teach Zubin to say?
Suraj taught him to say "scene sorted hai".
How did Zubin feel in the first week at lunch?
Zubin felt out of place and awkward, answering in careful English like a teacher at the wrong table while everyone else spoke fast mixed talk.
What helped Zubin find his way into the group's talk?
Practising small phrases with a friendly guide like Suraj, and using mixed words when English alone could not name what he felt.
How does Suraj see Zubin's new way of talking?
Suraj is warm and encouraging, correcting gently and nodding when "khalipan" names exactly the feeling Zubin meant.

"Now softly, softly die away!" and the sounds obeyed him. "Now fuller, more joyful. Still more and more joyful!" And from an unknown depth rose increasingly triumphant sounds. "Now voices join in!" ordered Petya. And at first from afar he heard men's voices and then women's. The voices grew in harmonious triumphant strength, and Petya listened to their surpassing beauty in awe and joy.

What happens to the sounds as Petya gives his orders?
They obey him: they die away softly, then grow fuller and more joyful. Voices join in, first men's from afar and then women's, until Petya listens with awe and joy.

Weekend-news note, Monday. Shalini, Class 3. Wasim told the class he built a rocket from cardboard boxes and flew to the moon, where he had lunch with an alien called Bob. He was grinning the whole time and made rocket noises. Two children shouted, “Liar!” Wasim's grin faded. I stepped in. “Is it a lie, or a story? What do you think Wasim wanted?” One girl said, “To make us laugh.” Wasim nodded hard. “And the rocket's real! It's in my room. It just doesn't fly.” I told the class that a tall tale everyone knows is pretend is a story, not a lie. Tomorrow Wasim is bringing the rocket.

What was the alien called in Wasim's story?
The alien was called Bob.
What was Wasim feeling when the children shouted “Liar!”?
Wasim felt hurt and deflated, his grin fading, since he only meant to make them laugh.
How did Shalini help the class tell a tall tale from a lie?
She asked what Wasim wanted, and explained that a story everyone knows is pretend is not a lie.
What did the girl who answered understand about Wasim?
She understood that Wasim wanted to make them laugh, not to trick them.

In the village near Bathinda, Gurleen had pinned a calendar above her study table. Each evening after two hours of revision for boards, she drew a fat red tick. Fifteen ticks so far.
Her cousin Usha, visiting for the week, noticed. "Fifteen days without a break?"
"Not one," Gurleen said proudly. "I'm the girl who studies every day now."
"What if you go to the wedding on Sunday?"
Gurleen's face fell. "I'll study before. Or after. I can't break it."
"And if you can't?"
Gurleen stared at the calendar. The thought of a blank square made her stomach tighten.

How many ticks were on Gurleen's calendar?
Fifteen ticks.
What was Gurleen feeling when she stared at the calendar?
She felt anxious, her stomach tightening at the thought of a blank square breaking her streak.
What could Gurleen decide now to protect the habit?
That a planned break for the wedding is fine, and the habit is about most days, not a perfect streak.
How might Usha see Gurleen's pride?
Usha seems impressed but gently concerned that the streak has become too rigid.
Why should a child at home alone not open the door to a stranger?
Opening the door to a stranger is risky. Because a child cannot be sure who the stranger really is or what they want, it is safer to talk through the door and ask a trusted adult.

Shankar: you ok? you've been weird all week
Mohit: fine. just tired
Shankar: is this about Anya?
Mohit: no. maybe. idk
Mohit: she said her visa money got stuck again. third time. and her voice on the call sounded different from last month
Shankar: different how?
Mohit: forget it. she explained. bad network
Mohit: also her profile photo showed up on some model's page. but people copy photos all the time right
Shankar: bro...
Mohit: don't. I know how it looks. I just need it not to be that
Mohit: if I tell my parents they'll never let me live it down. I already gave her most of my bonus
Shankar: I'm not going to tell anyone. but can we check the photo together tonight? just check
Mohit: ...ok. but don't say I told you so

How many times has Anya's visa money got stuck?
Third time.
What does Mohit mean by 'I just need it not to be that'?
Part of Mohit knows it's a scam but hopes it isn't, because the shame of the lost bonus and the parents' reaction feels unbearable.
Why is Shankar's offer to 'just check' a good step?
It lets Mohit test the doubt privately and without blame, which is easier than confessing everything at once.
How might Shankar feel reading 'don't say I told you so'?
Shankar feels worried and protective, holding back judgment so Mohit keeps talking.
Tell me a fact about bees in one sentence under 15 words that includes "flowers".
Bees visit flowers to collect nectar and carry pollen as they go.

On Losar morning the snow was so thick that Pema's father couldn't reach the monastery for the festival prayers. Pema, five, cried. "But we always go!"
Her grandmother Leela lit butter lamps at home. "Then today we pray here. The prayers are the same."
She taught Pema to fold her hands and bow three times. Then they ate the special noodles and Leela told the old story of the new year.
Pema bowed three times again before bed, on her own.

Why couldn't Pema's father reach the monastery?
The snow was so thick.
How did Pema feel when they couldn't go?
She felt upset and disappointed, crying "But we always go!"
How did Leela keep the tradition going?
She lit butter lamps at home, taught Pema the bows, and told the old story.
How might Leela feel when Pema bows before bed on her own?
Leela likely feels warm and proud that Pema has made the tradition her own.

“Wasim, come say hello to Uncle and Aunty.”
Wasim stood in the doorway of the new neighbours' flat with his arms pressed flat against his sides, hands tucked into his shorts pockets.
“Hello, Wasim!” said the aunty. “Want some juice?”
Wasim looked at Saurabh Chacha's knees and said nothing.
“He takes a little time,” Saurabh said. He crouched. “You can stay next to me. No rush.”
Wasim leaned on his leg. Twenty minutes later one hand came out of a pocket, and he pointed at the juice.

Where did Wasim put his hands?
He tucked them into his shorts pockets, with his arms pressed flat against his sides.
What do Wasim's arms pressed to his sides suggest he was feeling?
They suggest he felt shy and cautious with new people in a new place. He might also have felt a bit overwhelmed by being greeted so directly.
Which choice by Saurabh worked, and why?
He let Wasim stay close and said there was no rush, so Wasim could warm up in his own time.
How might the new aunty see Wasim's silence?
She might wonder if he disliked her, but Saurabh's words help her see he just needs time.
