Read this:

Class teacher's note, Wednesday

Shreya has been absent Monday and Tuesday. When she came today, she sat alone at the back and kept her dupatta pulled close. During break, two boys whistled as she passed; several girls whispered and looked away.

I kept her back after the bell. She told me, crying, that a photo of her talking to a boy at the tuition gate had been passed around with lies attached. Her father had seen it, shouted at her and said she might not go back to school.

I told her clearly that she had done nothing wrong and that I was glad she told me. I stayed with her and took her to the counsellor's room. I phoned her mother and asked both parents to meet me and the principal tomorrow morning, and informed the principal today about the photo being shared.

Her missing school is a warning sign. We will not wait.

— Harsha Ma'am

How many days had Shreya been absent?
Two days, Monday and Tuesday.
How did Shreya seem to feel when she came back to school?
She seemed isolated and ashamed, sitting alone and pulling her dupatta close as others whispered and whistled.
Why was Harsha Ma'am right not to wait?
Shreya's missing school and her father's threat were warning signs, so acting the same day with the counsellor, principal and parents protected her.
How might Shreya's father see the photo, and why might a meeting help?
He may see it as a threat to the family's reputation; hearing from the teacher that Shreya did nothing wrong could ease his anger.

Could you modernise this passage from the Panchatantra? Two ganders are leaving a dried-up lake, and the turtle is their friend.

When they did so, the turtle said: "Why do you bid me farewell? I am a water-dweller, and here I should perish very quickly from the scant supply of water and from grief at loss of you. Therefore, if you feel any affection for me, please rescue me from the jaws of this death. Besides, as the water dries in this lake, you two suffer nothing beyond a restricted diet, while to me it means immediate death. Consider which is more serious, loss of food or loss of life."

When they did this, the turtle said, "Why are you saying goodbye to me? I live in water. Here I will soon die from the lack of water and from the sadness of losing you. So if you care about me at all, please save me from this death. Besides, as the lake dries up, you two only have to eat less, but for me it means death straight away. Think about which is worse: losing food or losing a life."

Every Saturday Kamal and Gopika taught English and maths to children of the construction workers behind their school, under a tin shed the site manager let them use. This Saturday, the rain came down so hard the shed roof began to drip onto the chalk slates. Twelve kids and nowhere dry. Gopika wanted to cancel. Kamal looked at the children huddled together, a few still in wet uniforms. "They walked here in this," he said. They borrowed a tarp from the watchman, tied it over the leaking corner, and moved everyone to the dry side. Kamal taught fractions by splitting rotis a mother had sent. When one girl said her old school teacher had called her "dirty", Kamal quietly told her, "Here, you're our best maths student."

What did Kamal use to teach fractions?
He used rotis a mother had sent.
Why did Kamal refuse to cancel even though the shed was leaking?
He felt responsible to the children, who had walked through the rain to come, and he did not want to let them down.
What did Kamal do well when the girl mentioned being called dirty?
He quietly countered the insult with respect, naming her strength so she felt valued rather than judged.
How might Gopika's view have changed after the rainy session?
She first wanted to cancel, but seeing the tarp work and the children learning may have shown her how much showing up matters.

Raghav, you're getting impatient with the new boy. Let me tell you about Sunil. When I was twenty-five and running my first repair bench in Hyderabad, they gave me an apprentice who couldn't tell a spanner from a screwdriver. He dropped bolts and forgot every step. My boss said, "Just shout, he'll learn faster." I, Farhan, tried shouting for one week. Sunil got slower and started trembling when I came near. So I changed. One task a day. Show him, let him do it, check it, praise what he got right. It took him eight months to strip an engine alone. Eight months. Today he runs the biggest garage in Secunderabad. Patience isn't doing nothing, beta. It's choosing the speed that actually works.

How long did Sunil take to strip an engine alone?
Eight months.
How did young Farhan feel after a week of shouting?
Farhan felt uneasy and unhappy, seeing Sunil get slower and tremble whenever Farhan came near.
What was the turning point in the story?
Switching from shouting to one task a day with showing, checking and praise.
How might Sunil have felt during the week of shouting?
Sunil was likely frightened and anxious, trembling whenever Farhan came near.

Pooja noticed the difference in the same week. On Monday her friend Arohi tried to persuade her to join a weekend pottery class. "It'll be good for you, you're always at the laptop. But if you'd rather not, no problem." Pooja said she'd think about it, and Arohi dropped it. On Wednesday her team lead, Mr. Batra, stopped by her desk in the Noida office with a vendor bill. "Sign this as verified. I checked it myself." Pooja hadn't seen the goods. "Can I check the delivery first?" He leaned closer. "No time. And keep this between us. If you make a fuss, you'll be off the Sharma project." Her stomach turned. Arohi had given her a choice. This took hers away: pressure, a threat, a secret. That evening she called Arohi, and together they wrote to the company's ethics officer, Mrs. Iyer. She called back within the hour. "You were right to refuse. Don't sign anything. I'll handle it from here, starting today."

What did Arohi invite Pooja to join?
A weekend pottery class.
What did Pooja feel when Mr. Batra told her to keep it between them?
Pooja felt her stomach turn with alarm, recognising pressure, a threat and secrecy that removed her choice.
What did Pooja do after recognising coercion?
She refused to sign without checking, told a trusted friend that evening, and wrote with Arohi to the ethics officer, who called back within the hour.
How did Mrs. Iyer respond?
Mrs. Iyer told Pooja she was right to refuse, not to sign anything, and that she would handle it starting that day.
My uncle works in one of those big warehouses near the port. What does warehouse mean?

A warehouse is a large building where goods are stored before they are sold or sent elsewhere. It is a noun, and the plural is Warehouses.
Example: Trucks carried rice from the warehouses to the shops in the city.

I'm Jomon's cousin Rashmi, and I was staying with them for the holidays when I saw his mother do something I haven't forgotten.

Jomon and his little sister Anna were screaming over a toy boat in the bath. Water everywhere.

His mother knelt beside the tub. She didn't say "Who started it?" She said, "Jomon, tell me." He said Anna grabbed it. She said, "You wanted your boat." Then, "Anna, tell me." Anna said Jomon splashed her face. "You felt scared when the water hit you."

They both went quiet. Then Jomon handed Anna the boat. I couldn't believe it.

What were Jomon and Anna fighting over?
A toy boat in the bath.
How did Rashmi feel watching Jomon hand Anna the boat?
Rashmi was surprised and impressed, finding it hard to believe the fight ended so quickly.
What did Jomon's mother do that worked?
She knelt at their level, let each child speak, and named each feeling instead of asking who started it.
How did Anna feel when her mother named her fear?
She felt understood and calmer, and went quiet.

- What's the meaning of the word originate?
- Is "excellant" or "excellent" right?
- Why do clouds float even though they hold so much water?

1. As a verb, "originate" means to begin, or to come from a particular place or cause.
2. It is "excellent", ending in "-ent".
3. The water in them is spread into tiny drops or ice crystals. Because these are so light, rising air can hold them up.
What exact spices were in the curry my aunt made last Diwali?
I don't know, as I can't see her kitchen. Ask her and she may share the recipe.

Ira, twenty-three, had just started as an assistant at a small tourism office in Hampi. On Friday her boss, Vaibhav, handed her a folder. "Make something for the new visitors." He left for Bengaluru. Ira didn't know if he meant a brochure, a map or a website page; whether it was urgent; or who the visitors were. She chose a brochure and spent the weekend on it. On Monday he flipped through it and frowned. "I meant a one-page map for the hotel desks. This is too long." Ira's cheeks burned. That evening she wrote a list of questions to ask before starting any task. The next week, when he gave her a task, she asked all of them first, a little stiffly.

What did Vaibhav say he meant after seeing the brochure?
He meant a one-page map for the hotel desks.
How did Ira feel when Vaibhav frowned at the brochure?
Her cheeks burned; she felt embarrassed and unfairly judged, since she had been given no details.
What did Ira do next, and why is it useful?
She wrote a list of questions to ask before any task, which gets the context and standard up front.
How might Vaibhav see Ira's new habit of asking questions?
Vaibhav might find it a little stiff at first, but it will save him from wasted work and disappointment.
Is it unkind to laugh at a person who has tripped and fallen, even when it looks funny?
Yes, it can be unkind. Because the person may be hurt and embarrassed, our laughter makes the embarrassment worse, while checking whether they are all right shows care.

Chetan came back to the village for Diwali after his first year of engineering. On the second day, he walked to the old primary school with his cousin Yash.
The swing was still there, its chain rusted. The mango tree they used to climb had been cut down. The classroom walls had been painted a bright new blue.
Chetan sat on the swing. It creaked. He remembered sitting in that classroom with nothing to worry about except marbles.
"You look like someone died," Yash said.
"Nobody died. I just miss it. Being small. Not having exams that decide your whole life."
Yash sat on the step. "You hated school."
Chetan laughed. "I know. I still miss it."
They stayed until the watchman shooed them away.

What had happened to the mango tree?
It had been cut down.
What was Chetan feeling on the swing?
He felt wistful and a little sad, longing for the time when he had nothing to worry about.
How could Chetan carry this feeling in a healthy way?
He could enjoy the memories and the visit, while finding small moments of play or ease in his college life too.
How does Yash see Chetan's nostalgia?
Yash finds it a bit funny, reminding Chetan he hated school, but still sits with him.

Harish: bro my dad's been admitted. chest pain. I'm at the hospital, I don't know what to do
Thomas stood up from his desk. His hands were already cold. He breathed in slowly, out slowly, twice, before typing.
Thomas: I'm here. is he with the doctors now?
Harish: yes. they're doing tests
Thomas: ok. what would help right now? I can come, or bring food, or call your sister
Harish: can you come? I'm alone
Thomas: leaving in 10 mins. drink some water
Thomas told his manager, packed his charger and a sandwich for Harish, and left.
Late that night, after Harish's sister arrived and the tests were done, Thomas went home instead of staying on. "I'll come back tomorrow after sleeping," he texted. "Both of us can't be wrecked."

What did Thomas pack before leaving?
He packed his charger and a sandwich for Harish.
What was Thomas feeling when he first read Harish's message, and what did he do with it?
He felt alarmed, with his hands already cold, but he breathed slowly twice so he could respond with warm, steady concern instead of panic.
Why was Thomas's question 'what would help right now?' a good one?
It let Harish choose what was needed, and gave clear options instead of Thomas guessing or just sharing the fear.
How might Harish feel when Thomas says he'll come back tomorrow after sleeping?
Harish might feel reassured that Thomas will keep showing up, since care that lasts matters on a long hospital stay.

Week one: The history project group made a plan. Payal said she would do “some slides.” Then she went to badminton every evening. Harsh and Sneha will do it anyway, she thought. They always do.
Week two: Harsh messaged: “Payal, your slides?” She sent two, copied from her notes, at midnight. Harsh wrote back, “ok thanks,” and she could tell he redid them.
Week three: At the presentation, Payal spoke for one minute. The teacher praised “the whole team's effort.” Payal smiled. Inside she felt a pinch of guilt, and also a small secret pleasure, like getting away with something.
Later Sneha asked, “Was it fun doing your slides?” Payal laughed and changed the subject.

How many slides did Payal send?
She sent two.
What was Payal feeling when the teacher praised the whole team?
She felt a pinch of guilt mixed with a small secret pleasure, as if she had got away with something.
What went wrong in how the group split the work, and how could it be fixed?
Payal's vague "some slides" let her coast; the group could have written who does which slides and by when.
How might Harsh feel about redoing Payal's slides?
He likely felt tired and resentful, but too polite to say more than "ok thanks".

Jagdish: also blue is kind of her thing. her early work is blue too, and those were wedding scenes

Jagdish: we all do it lol. I thought the guy last month was painting angry because of all the red. turned out he was copying old temple murals for practice
Pradeep: so what can we actually say about her?
Jagdish: what the painting makes us feel. and what we know about how she works. her inner state, not really
Pradeep: humbling. I still loved the one with the lit window though
Jagdish: same 🙂 that one felt like home

What is the series of paintings called?
Monsoon Nights.
How did Pradeep feel on learning about the series?
Pradeep felt a bit sheepish and humbled, having read the painter's mood from the colours alone.
What can viewers fairly say about a painting, according to the chat?
What it makes them feel and what is known about how the artist works, but not the maker's inner state.
How had Jagdish once misread another artist?
Jagdish assumed a painter was angry because of all the red, but he was copying old temple murals for practice.

Ramesh watched Arohi from the next flat build with the long wooden blocks. She laid two long ones side by side on the floor, then stacked on top. Her tower grew tall. Ramesh cleared away his wobbly one and set two long blocks flat, just like hers. He stacked. Seven, eight, nine. It stayed up. "Why?" his mother asked. Ramesh frowned and said, "It just does."

What did Arohi lay side by side?
She laid two long ones side by side on the floor.
What was Ramesh feeling when his tower stayed up?
He was probably pleased and surprised, though puzzled about why it worked.
What could Ramesh's mother do to help him understand?
She could let him try a narrow base next to a wide one, so he sees for himself why the wide one stands.
How might Arohi feel seeing Ramesh copy her?
Arohi might feel proud that her idea worked for him too, or mildly annoyed at being copied.

Joseph's phone was on four percent and the metro would stay underground for twenty more minutes. He had just sent Vidya, his team lead, a careful paragraph: the client's data had arrived late, and the report would slip to Thursday. Her reply landed as the signal died: 👍
Nothing else. Joseph stared at it. Among his friends, a lone thumbs-up often meant "fine, whatever." Was she annoyed? Was he in trouble? His mother's messages were full of 🙏, which meant thanks or blessings, and his cousins ended every chat with 👋. But this was work, and he didn't know the rules. At the next station he charged his phone at a kiosk and called. Vidya laughed. "I was in a meeting. It meant okay, thanks for flagging it early. That's how my old team said yes." "To me it looked a bit cold," Joseph admitted. "Noted. I'll add words next time."

When would the report now be ready?
It would slip to Thursday.
What was Joseph worried about when he saw the lone thumbs-up?
He felt anxious that Vidya was annoyed and that he was in trouble, reading it the way his friends use it, though it could also simply mean okay, which it did.
What was the wise step once Joseph had charge again?
Calling Vidya to check the meaning instead of stewing over a guess, and saying honestly how the emoji had looked to him.
Why might Vidya read the thumbs-up differently from Joseph?
In her old team a thumbs-up was a normal yes, so to her it was a friendly okay rather than a curt reply; norms differ by age and workplace.

Manjula probably feels relieved and less alone, though still unsure a small step can help, as Manjula says it feels small.

I'm Bidisha, and I sit behind Mohit and Arvind. Mohit had been angry with Arvind for a week, ever since he saw him copying in the maths test. I heard him say, “I'm telling Sir if you do it again.”
Then on Friday something changed. They were talking by the water cooler, and Arvind was crying, which I'd never seen. I caught bits: his father had said that if he failed maths again, he'd be sent to his uncle's town for school. He'd been failing since August and was too scared to say.
Mohit didn't back down about the copying. I heard him say, “You still have to stop. But you need help, not a cheat sheet.” After school he went with Arvind to Sir, not to report him, but to ask about the free remedial classes on Tuesdays.
On Tuesday I saw them both in the remedial room. Arvind had his notebook open. Mohit was there too, doing his own homework, just keeping him company.

What did Mohit and Arvind ask Sir about?
The free remedial classes on Tuesdays.
What might Mohit have been feeling when Arvind cried?
Mohit was probably surprised and sympathetic, his anger softening into concern, though he still felt the copying had to stop.
What else could help Arvind besides the remedial classes?
Talking with a teacher or counsellor about the pressure at home, so an adult can help his father understand.
How does the change look to Bidisha?
Bidisha sees a friendship shift from anger to support, with Mohit even sitting in the remedial room for company.

Sarika, you're nervous about tomorrow's panel, so let me tell you about my first debate. Naveen sir, the youngsters call me now, but at twenty I spoke like a ceiling fan: one steady hum. At the inter-college final in Pune, I read my points in a flat voice, and I watched a judge check her watch twice. I lost. So for the next year I practised like an actor. Big rises, whispers, pauses. At the next final I thundered, dropped to a whisper, even banged the lectern. A girl from the other team rolled her eyes, and one judge wrote "theatrical" on my sheet. Lost again. It was my coach, Mrs Iyer, who fixed it. "Talk like you're explaining to your friend why it matters," she said. My voice went up when I was curious, slowed when a point was serious. The third year, we won. Speak like yourself, Sarika, only awake.

What did one judge write on young Naveen's sheet?
"Theatrical".
How did young Naveen feel when the judge checked her watch during the first final?
He was likely embarrassed and anxious, realising his flat voice was losing the judges; losing twice suggests growing frustration too.
What turning point helped Naveen win in the third year?
Following Mrs Iyer's advice to talk like explaining to a friend, so his pitch and pace varied naturally instead of flatly or theatrically.
How might the girl from the other team have seen Naveen's thundering and whispering?
She rolled her eyes, so she likely found it fake and over the top, not persuasive.

Binita's diary, Thursday. Divyansh thought I was angry with him today! We were doing fractions and I was frowning hard at question 6. He leaned over and whispered, “Why are you cross with me?” I said, “I'm not!” I was just thinking. My forehead does that. So I told him, “This is my thinking face.” He laughed and said his does the same when he draws. Ma says everybody has one. Maybe I should tell the whole class so nobody gets worried 🙂

Which question was Binita frowning at?
She was frowning at question 6.
What was Divyansh probably worried about when he leaned over and whispered?
That Binita was angry with him, perhaps because of something he had done. Asking her straight away shows he wanted to put it right.
What did Binita do that prevented trouble between them?
She said plainly that the frown was her thinking face, so the misunderstanding ended.
How might Binita feel when Divyansh asks, "Why are you cross with me?"
Binita seems surprised, answering "I'm not!" at once, and then eager to explain the thinking face.

The school library had a new rule: each Class 4 pair would run the book-return box for a week and enter a quiz at the end. Himani wanted Pallavi as her partner before the teacher had even finished speaking. Pallavi was the tallest girl in class, and she laughed so easily that even the librarian smiled at her. "She'll know all the quiz answers," Himani whispered to her friend. "And she'd never forget anything. She's too nice." On Wednesday, Pallavi left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play. Three books slid out in the rain. In Friday's quiz, Pallavi guessed most answers with a big grin, and they came sixth. Walking out, Himani looked at Pallavi, who was still laughing with everyone. "You're really fun," she said slowly. "But you're not so good at quizzes, na?"

Himani picks Pallavi as her partner for the book-return box and quiz, expecting her to know all the answers. Pallavi leaves the box in the rain, they place sixth, and Himani calls her fun but not good at quizzes.

Parul, you think nobody at your office will understand. Let me tell you about the year I turned twenty-five. I'd pushed my bosses for months to try my new billing system at the mill. Big talk, I had. The first week it crashed, and the salaries went out three days late. Nobody shouted. That was worse. Everyone was so polite. "Bad luck, Harish-ji." "Happens to everyone." But I saw two colleagues by the tea urn, smiling at each other when I walked in and stopping when I came near. I ate lunch alone at my desk for a month. I felt the size of a pin. Then the old accounts clerk sat with me one day and said, "Let's find the bug." That's all. The system worked by winter. But I still remember those smiles, beta.

How late did the salaries go out?
Three days late.
How did Harish feel in the month after the crash, and what shows it?
Lonely and small, "the size of a pin". Harish ate lunch alone for a month, aware of colleagues smiling behind their polite words.
What did the old accounts clerk do, and why did it matter so much?
The clerk sat with Harish and said "Let's find the bug", offering real help instead of polite lines, which ended the isolation and led to the fix.
What might hearing this be like for Parul, who feels nobody understands?
Parul may feel less alone, hearing that Harish once felt "the size of a pin" too, and may take heart that one person's real help changed things.

I'll tell you what worked. I suspected my sister Himani had lost her job weeks ago, because she kept leaving in the morning and coming back too early. I'm Rukmini, and my first thought was to accuse her. Instead, one Sunday over tea, I said, "Himani, I've been wondering about work. I would prefer the truth to being shielded from it. And I promise I won't explode or lecture."
She looked at her cup for a long time. Then she said, "I lost the job in March. I didn't want you to worry." I said, "Thank you for telling me." We sat there and she cried, and I made more tea.

When did Himani say she lost the job?
Himani said she lost the job in March.
What was Rukmini feeling and wanting before the Sunday tea?
Rukmini was worried and suspicious but wanted the truth without a fight. Choosing not to accuse shows a wish to make honesty safe.
What did Rukmini say that made honesty easier?
Rukmini said she would prefer the truth to being shielded from it and promised not to explode or lecture. That lowered the cost of telling the truth.
How might Himani have felt when Rukmini said "I won't explode or lecture"?
Himani probably felt both nervous and relieved, since she stared at her cup and then told the truth. The promise made it safer to say it.

Julie runs the school newspaper. In preparation for printing the next issue of The School News, she bought two boxes of standard paper, each containing 5 packages, with 250 sheets of paper per package.  If this issue of The School News uses 25 sheets of paper to print one newspaper, how many newspapers can Julie print with the paper that she purchased?

Five packages per box, with 250 sheets per package is 5*250=1250 sheets per box.
Two boxes contain a total of 1250*2=2500 sheets.
If each newspaper requires 25 pages, then with 2500 sheets she can print 2500/25=100 newspapers.
The answer is 100.

I'm Mehak, and I lead a small support team at a software company in Noida. Last month I nearly made a mistake I'm still thinking about.

Zainab, one of my best agents, sent a rude-sounding reply to a customer. The customer complained to my boss. I was embarrassed and angry. By evening, I'd started thinking: maybe Zainab's attitude has always been a bit off.

That's when I caught myself. Always? I couldn't name one other example.

So I looked properly. Her satisfaction scores for the year were the highest on the team. She'd handled two of our hardest escalations. And that day, she'd been covering three people's queues because of a sick day.

I talked to her the next morning. She was mortified about the reply. She'd typed it fast between two angry calls.

We agreed she'd take a proper break when queues pile up, and I'd spread the load. One slip, not a pattern.

How many people's queues was Zainab covering that day?
She'd been covering three people's queues because of a sick day.
What was Mehak feeling by the evening after the complaint?
Mehak felt embarrassed and angry, and started letting that one error colour the whole view of Zainab.
What did Mehak do before deciding, and why was it wise?
Mehak checked Zainab's full record and the context of that day, which showed it was one slip under pressure, not a pattern.
How did Zainab feel about the rude reply?
Zainab was mortified about the reply, since she had typed it fast between two angry calls.
'Aasmaan mein indradhanush nikla hai' translate please.
"There is a rainbow in the sky." Or, more lively: "Look, a rainbow has come out!"

The shop would shut in fifteen minutes, rain was hammering the awning, and Papa had money for exactly one new school bag. "Vidya, take the blue one. You've earned it." Her brother Raghav, standing beside her with his torn strap knotted at the corner, said nothing. Vidya felt a warm glow, and then a twist in her stomach. That same afternoon Papa had proudly told the shopkeeper about her science fair prize. She turned to the shopkeeper. "Actually, Raghav built half the model. He did the wiring." Papa blinked. "Did he? Then Raghav, choose one too," he said, counting again. "We'll check for a smaller one." Raghav looked up, surprised and shy. Vidya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

How much time was left before the shop shut?
Fifteen minutes were left before the shop shut.
What was Vidya feeling as she held the blue bag while Raghav stood beside her?
She felt warm about being valued but uneasy, because she noticed that Raghav's strap was knotted and he said nothing.
What did Vidya do that used her favoured position kindly?
She shared credit by telling her father and the shopkeeper that Raghav built half the model, instead of enjoying all the praise. 😊
How might Raghav have felt when Vidya spoke up?
Probably surprised and shy, and maybe relieved, since his work was finally mentioned and his father offered him a bag too.

'Can we talk about money for a minute?' Irawati asked, pushing the café bill across the table.
Tushar froze. 'Oh no. Did I forget my wallet again?'
'No. It's not that. It's... I've been paying for most things since my internship started. Dinners, movies, your birthday trip. And I've started keeping a list in my head. That's not fair to you, because I never said anything.'
Tushar went red. 'I didn't know you minded. I thought you liked treating me.'
'I did. Then I started expecting you to... I don't know, owe me. And that's not what I want either.'
'My scholarship is really tight. I've been embarrassed about it.'
'So let's just say it out loud. What can you manage each week?'
They wrote it on a napkin. Tushar would take the Friday dinners; Irawati would cover movies. Cheaper places, more walks.
'I don't want to buy you,' she said.
'And I don't want to be bought,' he laughed. 'Deal.'

What did Irawati push across the table?
The café bill.
What was Irawati feeling about paying for most things?
She felt quietly resentful and uneasy, keeping a mental list and expecting Tushar to owe her.
What did Irawati and Tushar agree to do?
Say their budgets out loud and split what each could manage: Friday dinners for him, movies for her, plus cheaper outings 😊
Why hadn't Tushar raised the money issue?
He felt embarrassed about his tight scholarship.

In the empty training room after the evening session, Pradeep finally told Shankar-sir, the batch mentor, why he had been arriving with red eyes. 'Our families fixed the engagement last year. Since then Sunaina decides who I talk to, checks my phone, and says if I break it off she'll tell everyone I cheated. My mother will believe her.' Shankar-sir closed the laptop. 'Thank you for telling me. Walking away from something like this is hard, and wanting to is not weakness.' He wrote down the employee counselling line and a helpline for relationship abuse, and sat with Pradeep while he called the counselling line from the room. They booked a session for the next morning. 'And your mother,' Shankar-sir said, 'maybe tell her with the counsellor's help, before anyone else tells her a story.' Pradeep nodded, shaky but less alone.

What role does Shankar-sir have?
Shankar-sir is the batch mentor.
What might Pradeep be worried about?
Pradeep is afraid that Sunaina will spread a lie about cheating and that his mother will believe her.
How did Shankar-sir support Pradeep?
Shankar-sir thanked him, said wanting to leave was not weakness, gave him counselling and helpline numbers, and stayed while he called.
How does Shankar-sir read Pradeep's red eyes and story?
Shankar-sir treats them as real distress and a safety matter, closing the laptop to listen rather than brushing it off.

Vinita, sit. I'm Anand, and let me tell you about Mr Sharma, our supervisor at the mill office. Prakash, a junior clerk, kept mixing up the delivery slips. Mr Sharma saw it, and I saw him see it. "Poor boy, he's trying," he told me. "No need to hurt him." So he waited. A month later the wrong slips reached a dealer, and there was a scene in front of everyone. Prakash was pale for days. Later he said to me, "If anyone had told me quietly in the first week, I'd have thanked them." I never forgot that. Whenever I feel a truth stuck in my throat, I remember Prakash.

What did Prakash keep mixing up?
The delivery slips.
What did Mr Sharma feel when saying "Poor boy, he's trying"?
Sympathy and a wish to protect Prakash from hurt, which made it easy to keep waiting.
What could Mr Sharma have done in the first week?
Told Prakash quietly and gently about the mix-ups, with help to fix them, before the wrong slips reached the dealer.
How did Prakash feel after the scene in front of everyone?
Shaken and embarrassed, pale for days, and Prakash said a quiet word in the first week would have been welcome.

At the college career fair, held in the badminton hall, Darshan stood by the architecture firm stalls with a folder of printed drawings, too shy to walk up.
Ritu, from his batch, came over. "You've been standing here for twenty minutes."
"They look busy."
"They're here to talk to us." She nudged him. "Ask one question. That's it."
He went to the smallest stall. "Excuse me, what do interns actually do at your firm?"
The architect laughed. "Mostly make models and coffee. Want to see?" She showed him photos, looked at his drawings, and gave him her card. "Email me in January."
Darshan walked back to Ritu, card clutched, legs shaking. "I have to write an email now."
"Yes. Tonight, while you're brave."

Where was the career fair held?
In the badminton hall.
What was Darshan feeling while standing by the stalls?
He felt shy and nervous, too scared to walk up for twenty minutes.
What made Ritu's advice useful?
It broke the task into one question, which made it possible for Darshan to start a real conversation.
How might the architect see Darshan's question?
She seemed to find it honest and friendly, which is why she laughed, looked at his drawings and gave him her card.
The coach praised her resolve after the loss. I only know resolve as to solve a problem.

As a noun, resolve means a firm decision or strong determination to do something. The verb means to find an answer to a problem.
Example: Her resolve to train every morning never weakened.
The path is wet. Does that prove that it rained?
No, it does not prove it. Because a wet path can come from a pipe, a sprinkler or somebody washing the ground, rain is only a possible cause.

The school's philosophy club had one hour before the debate, and the power had gone out, so Sonali and Ganga sat in the dark library with a single torch. Their topic: "Is it ever right to lie?" Sonali, who liked rules, said lying is always wrong; her grandmother's faith said so. Ganga argued that lying to protect someone could be right, like hiding a friend from danger. "So which is it?" Sonali asked, frustrated. Ganga shrugged. "Different systems answer differently. One says follow the rule. One says look at the results." Sonali thought for a while. "Maybe both help. Rules keep us honest, but we should also think about who gets hurt." They agreed to present both views fairly. The torch flickered.

What was the topic of the debate?
The topic was "Is it ever right to lie?"
Why did Sonali get frustrated?
She believed strongly that lying is always wrong, and Ganga's example challenged that certainty, making her uneasy.
What made Sonali and Ganga's final approach reasonable?
They compared the rule-based view and the results-based view and chose to present both fairly, instead of mocking one side.
How might Sonali's grandmother react to the girls' conclusion?
She might still stress honesty but appreciate that Sonali is thinking carefully about when harm is involved.
Spell out the idiom in plain words: The shop was packed to the rafters on Diwali eve.
The shop was completely full on Diwali eve.
I'm late replying. What can I write: "I apologise for the delay"?

Yes, "I apologise for the delay in replying" is polite and suitable for work emails. British English accepts "apologise" and "apologize", and American English uses "apologize".
Example: I apologise for the delay in replying to your message.

My first three months on the support team in Bengaluru, I was always the last one out. The cleaner, Selvi akka, used to switch off the lights around me.
I told myself I was being dedicated. Really, I was hiding. Everyone else seemed to know what 'escalation matrix' meant, what 'P1' meant, how to read the logs. I didn't. Shalini, my senior, sat two desks away and kept saying, 'Ask me anything, Siami.' I never did. Asking felt like showing everyone I didn't belong.
So I stayed back and read old tickets. At home I watched tutorial videos till one, and came in with red eyes.
It took me three weeks to figure out, alone, something Shalini explained to another new joiner in five minutes. I heard it from my desk. That was the first time I thought, Lalremsiami, what are you doing?

What did Shalini keep saying to Lalremsiami?
Shalini kept saying, 'Ask me anything, Siami.'
Why did Lalremsiami never ask Shalini for help?
Asking felt like proving to everyone that Siami didn't belong, so staying quiet felt safer than exposing gaps.
What went wrong with Lalremsiami's way of catching up, and what could fix it?
Studying alone at night and never asking cost weeks and sleep; asking Shalini even a few questions a day would have been much faster.
How might Shalini have seen the new joiner who stayed late but never asked anything?
Shalini may have wondered whether the offer wasn't trusted, or thought Siami was coping fine and didn't need help.

Supervisor's note, customer support floor, Thursday
There has been friction between Manjula and Dinesh over last week's shift swap, and both have been trying to recruit Pankaj, who sits between them. Today at lunch I saw it come to a head. Manjula said loudly, "Pankaj, tell him he's being selfish."
Pankaj put down his spoon. He said, "I think Dinesh should have asked before swapping. I also think it's unfair to call him selfish in front of everyone. I'm not going to carry messages between you two." Then he went back to eating.
Both looked annoyed. But later, Dinesh apologised to Manjula for the swap, and Manjula said she had been harsh. I noticed Pankaj didn't repeat either side's comments to the other all afternoon.
I have scheduled a short meeting on Monday to set a clear swap process, and I will thank Pankaj privately for keeping things calm.

What was the friction between Manjula and Dinesh about?
Last week's shift swap.
What did Pankaj's putting down his spoon suggest?
He felt uncomfortable at being pulled in, but calm and determined to answer honestly rather than pick a side.
What did the supervisor plan after the lunch?
A short meeting on Monday to set a clear swap process, and a private thank-you to Pankaj.
How did Manjula respond to Pankaj's answer?
Annoyed at first, but later she admitted she had been harsh.

You asked me to talk about the jokes, so here's the honest version. I'm Rafiq. In our town, the kids who come down from the hill villages for board exams stay in the government hostel. My friends and I called them "the goats". We'd bleat when they walked into the exam hall. We made up stories about them eating grass. It was just a joke, I told myself. They weren't really people to us, just a group. Then this year I got a hostel student as my lab partner. Her name is Salma. She's quiet, walks two hours on Sundays to see her grandmother, and she's better at chemistry than me. One day my friends bleated when she passed. And I saw her face. She pretended not to hear, but her ears went red. I didn't laugh. I haven't bleated since. It's hard to call someone a goat once you know she walks two hours to see her grandmother.

How long does Salma walk on Sundays to see her grandmother?
She walks two hours on Sundays.
Why did the "goats" jokes feel easy to Rafiq before?
Rafiq didn't see the hill-village students as individuals, just a group, so mocking them didn't feel cruel and brought no guilt.
What could Rafiq do next to help change the jokes among friends?
Tell the friends plainly that Salma is a person being hurt, and ask them to stop bleating.
What was it like for Salma when Rafiq's friends bleated?
Salma felt humiliated and hurt, pretending not to hear while her ears went red.

messages.content: Brian goes fishing twice as often as Chris, but catches 2/5 times fewer fish than Chris per trip. If Brian caught 400 fish every time he went fishing, how many fish did they catch altogether if Chris went fishing 10 times?

If Brian caught 400 fish in one trip, he caught 2*400=800 fish in two trips.
Since Brian catches 2/5 times less fish than Chris per trip, Chris catches 2/5*400=160 more fish in one fishing trip.
Chris's total number of fish in one trip is 400+160 = 560 fish.
In 10 trips, Chris catches 560*10=5600 fish.
If in his two trips Brian catches 800 fish, and he goes fishing twice as often as Chris, if Chris goes fishing 10 times, Brian will catch 800*10=8000 fish.
The total number of fish they'll catch if Chris goes fishing ten times is 8000+5600=13600
The answer is 13600.

If Janet reads 80 pages a day and Belinda reads 30 pages a day, how many more pages does Janet read in 6 weeks?

First find the total number of days in 6 weeks: 6 weeks * 7 days/week = 42 days
Then find the total difference in the number of pages Janet and Belinda read each day: 80 pages/day - 30 pages/day = 50 pages/day
Then multiply the daily difference by the number of days to find the total difference in the number of pages they read: 50 pages/day * 42 days = 2100 pages
The answer is 2100.

'So Nikhil's moving to Delhi and wants me to come,' Rekha said, lying on Swati's bed.
'And?'
'And Kochi has that museum job. And my cousin says Bengaluru is where everything happens. And I'm twenty-two. What if I choose a city because of a boy and it's the wrong boy? What if I stay and miss the right one?'
'You're doing the thing again.'
'What thing?'
'Imagining ten futures and living in none.' Swati sat up. 'Which one makes you excited, not just not-scared?'
Rekha was quiet a long time. 'The museum. Honestly. And Nikhil... I'd visit.'
'Then that's a start.'
'But what if—'
'Rekha. Every choice closes doors. That's what makes it a choice.'
Rekha pulled the pillow over her face and laughed into it. 'I hate that you're right.'

Where is Nikhil moving?
To Delhi.
What is Rekha feeling as she lists the options?
Rekha feels excited by the options but anxious and frozen, afraid of choosing the wrong city or the wrong person.
What question from Swati helps, and why?
'Which one makes you excited, not just not-scared?' It shifts Rekha from avoiding regret to noticing what she actually wants.
How does Swati see Rekha's habit?
Swati sees it as imagining ten futures and living in none, and gently pushes Rekha to accept that choosing means closing doors.
We all "chipped in" for the farewell gift. Is that correct English?

Yes, it is correct and informal. "Chip in" means to give a share of money or help so that a group can do something together. It can also mean to add a comment in a conversation.
Examples: Ten of us chipped in for the gift. Elena chipped in with a useful idea.

James takes up dancing for fitness.  He loses twice as many calories per hour as he did when he was walking.  He dances twice a day for .5 hours each time and he does this 4 times a week.  He burned 300 calories an hour walking.  How many calories does he lose a week from dancing?

He burns 2*300=600 calories an hour
He dances for .5*2=1 hour per day
So he burns 600*1=600 calories per day
So he burns 600*4=2400 calories per week
The answer is 2400.

First week of July. Chinmay's PG was forty minutes from college by two buses. His friend Hrithik mentioned a new PG opening right next to campus, cheaper, with better food. "Come see it." Chinmay said, "Mine's fine."

Late August. Chinmay missed two morning lectures because of bus delays in the rain. He told Hrithik, "It's okay, I'm used to it." But he was tired every evening. The new PG still had a room free.

Early October. Hrithik sat on Chinmay's bed. "Why haven't you moved? It's closer, cheaper, better."

Chinmay opened his mouth to say "Mine's fine" again. Then he stopped. "Because moving is a whole thing. Packing, telling the owner, finding a van."

"So you're not happy here. You just don't want to move."

Chinmay looked around the cramped room. "I've been calling it fine because changing felt like work."

He went to see the new PG that evening.

How far was Chinmay's PG from college?
Forty minutes from college by two buses.
Why did Chinmay keep saying his PG was fine?
Chinmay felt that moving would be a hassle, so he told himself he was content even though he was tired and missing lectures.
What did Hrithik say that helped Chinmay see the problem?
Hrithik pointed out that Chinmay wasn't happy, just avoiding the effort of moving, which helped him see the inertia.
How might Hrithik feel when Chinmay finally went to see the new PG?

messages.content: I'm thinking of joining the college choir. I've never sung in a group.
Choirs are welcoming to beginners, and singing together is a joy. They usually have a short try-out to find your voice range.
What if I'm not good enough?
Choirs value people who can listen and blend in as much as strong voices. Try the audition. If you are not selected, you can ask for feedback.
What do I need to prepare?
A short song you know well. Choose something that suits your voice, so it's comfortable to sing.
Will it be a big commitment?
Usually it means one or two rehearsals a week, so check the timetable first. Make sure it fits with your classes.
Okay. I'll go to find out.
Good. Ask them questions about the rehearsal schedule, upcoming concerts and how new members join.

Heather is going to sew 150 aprons that are to be used for a kiddie crew program. She already was able to sew  13 aprons, and today, she sewed three times as many aprons. How many aprons should she sew tomorrow if she wants to sew half of the remaining number of aprons needed?

Heather has sewn 13 x 3 = 39 aprons today.
The total number of aprons sewn is 13 + 39 = 52.
Heather needs to sew 150 - 52 = 98 aprons more.
So, she needs to sew 98/2 = 49 aprons tomorrow.
The answer is 49.

It felt like our secret club joke. But when Rohan from the next bench said, "Preeti, why is your lunchbox always the same dal-roti?" I went quiet and stared at the steel dabba. Rohan kept grinning and repeated it. Vijay noticed my face before I said anything. He said, "Arre Rohan, that's not funny, stop." I still felt hot in my ears. I'm not sure whether Rohan meant harm.

What nickname did Vijay give Preeti in PT class?
Vijay called Preeti "Speedy Gonzales" for running fast in PT class.
What was Preeti feeling when Rohan asked about the lunchbox, and what else might explain the silence?

Most likely Preeti felt embarrassed and hurt, shown by going quiet, staring at the dabba and the hot ears. Preeti might also have been unsure how to answer, since Rohan was grinning and may not have meant harm.
What could Preeti try next time someone teases about something sore?
Preeti could say calmly, "I don't like that joke," or tell Vijay or a teacher afterwards. Speaking up early makes it easier for the teaser to stop.
How might Rohan see the lunchbox comment, compared with Preeti?
Rohan may think it was harmless banter like Vijay's nickname, so Rohan keeps grinning. Rohan may not realise the topic was a sore spot for Preeti until seeing Preeti's quiet face.
What exactly is jet lag?
It is the tiredness and disturbed sleep that come when your body clock does not match local time after a fast trip across several time zones.
Would a long train ride across India cause it?

Find rational numbers a and b such that (5 + 2sqrt3)/(7 + 4sqrt3) = a + bsqrt3. Then, if x = 3 + 2sqrt2, find x + 1/x and x^2 + 1/x^2.

Answer: a = 11, b = -6. x + 1/x = 6 and x^2 + 1/x^2 = 34.

Rationalise the left side first; (7 + 4sqrt3)(7 - 4sqrt3) = 49 - 48 = 1: (5 + 2sqrt3)(7 - 4sqrt3) = 35 - 20sqrt3 + 14sqrt3 - 8 x 3 = 11 - 6sqrt3 So (5 + 2sqrt3)/(7 + 4sqrt3) = 11 - 6sqrt3, and comparing with a + bsqrt3, a = 11 and b = -6. We may compare 'rational part with rational part and sqrt3 part with sqrt3 part' because sqrt3 is irrational. For x = 3 + 2sqrt2: 1/x = 1/(3 + 2sqrt2) = (3 - 2sqrt2)/(9 - 8) = 3 - 2sqrt2. So x + 1/x = 3 + 2sqrt2 + 3 - 2sqrt2 = 6. Then (x + 1/x)^2 = x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2, so x^2 + 1/x^2 = 6^2 - 2 = 34. Common mistake: forgetting the middle term 2 when squaring x + 1/x.

What is a reciprocal? Write the reciprocals of 3/5, 7, 2 1/4 and 1. Why does 0 have no reciprocal?

Answer: Reciprocals: 3/5 -> 5/3; 7 -> 1/7; 2 1/4 = 9/4 -> 4/9; 1 -> 1. 0 has none.

Two numbers are reciprocals when their product is 1: 3/5 x 5/3 = 15/15 = 1. To find one, turn the fraction upside down. A whole number is a fraction over 1 (7 = 7/1), so its reciprocal is 1/7. A mixed number must first become improper: 2 1/4 = 9/4, reciprocal 4/9 (not 2 4/1). 1 x 1 = 1, so 1 is its own reciprocal. For 0: 0 x anything = 0, never 1, so 0 has no reciprocal, and that is why we can never divide by 0.

That evening her mother asked how it had gone. "Terrible. She said my hypothesis was unclear." That was all Ayesha could remember.

Wednesday: Ayesha still felt the sting. She told her friend, "Vinita ma'am thinks my project is bad." Her friend picked up the page and read it aloud, all nine good lines. Ayesha listened, surprised. She hadn't taken them in at all.

Saturday: Ayesha stuck the page on her wall, the nine good lines highlighted in yellow and the one about the hypothesis in pink. She rewrote the hypothesis in ten minutes. It had been one line.

It made the nine good lines visible beside the one criticism, so Ayesha could fix the hypothesis without feeling the whole project was bad.
How might Vinita ma'am feel if she knew Ayesha saw only the criticism?

Ojas, you asked why Salma Aunty is at every family function. Let me tell you something I'm not proud of. When I was fifteen in Belgaum, my family said things at dinner about 'those people' in the mohalla: dirty, dangerous, not like us. I believed every word. When Salma joined my class, I wouldn't share a bench with her. Then we were put together for the science fair. She came to our house with her father's old radio to take apart, and she was funny, and kind, and her tiffin was the best thing I'd ever tasted. I lay awake that night feeling sick at what I'd been thinking. But my own Ajji told me, 'You learned it, you can unlearn it. Slowly. Just don't stop.' It took years, Ojas. Her father's old radio to take apart.

Being paired with Salma for the science fair and getting to know her as a real, funny, kind person.

The science model was due on Monday, and it was Thursday. Sarita opened the box of clay, looked at it, and closed it again. "I do better when the clock is running out," she told Mehak on the call. "And I'll start right after one more video." One video became five. On Saturday she said the room was too messy to think. On Sunday she said she would wake up early instead.
What she did not say aloud was the small cold thought underneath: if she tried properly and it still looked poor, everyone would see she was not clever. A rushed model at least came with an excuse ready. On Sunday night she finally slapped clay onto a board, and the volcano leaned and cracked as it dried. Tushar Sir held it up on Monday and asked where the crater had gone. Sarita shrugged and said she had not had time. Mehak noticed her thumbnail was chewed down to the skin.

On which day was the science model due, and which day did Sarita open the clay box?
The model was due on Monday, and Sarita opened the box of clay on Thursday.
How do Sarita's excuses connect to the poor model she handed in?

Her reasons, such as working better under pressure, waiting for one more video and a messy room, sounded fair, but under them was a fear that a properly tried model would reveal weakness. The delay protected her self-image, and it left a rushed volcano that cracked.
What was Sarita feeling when she said she had not had time?
She was ashamed and afraid of being judged. The chewed thumbnail and the shrug suggest she was hiding how much it worried her.
What small step could Sarita take next time a project feels scary?
She could start with ten minutes of rough work on day one and show it to Mehak or Tushar Sir early, so the first attempt is allowed to be imperfect.
John orders food for a massive restaurant.  He orders 1000 pounds of beef for $8 per pound.  He also orders twice that much chicken at $3 per pound.  How much did everything cost?

The beef cost $8 * 1000 = $8000
He buys 1000 * 2 = 2000 pounds of chicken
So the chicken cost 2000 * $3 = $6000
So the total cost is $8000 + $6000 = $14,000
The answer is 14000.

She turned off notifications, moved the app off her home screen and allowed two checks a day, which breaks the gambling-like loop.
How does Jaya see Swati's behaviour?
Jaya sees Swati's mood riding the chart and worries it is more like a slot machine than a plan.

Read this:

Devika beta, you keep saying you can't sleep because of placement season, so let your Raghav chacha tell you about 1994. I was twenty-one, in my final year at the polytechnic in Nashik, and every night I'd lie awake, half dreaming of a job in Bombay, half sure I'd fail every interview and disappoint my father. Hope in one hand, dread in the other, and both too heavy. One evening my lecturer, Mr Sathe, found me staring at the notice board. He didn't give a speech. He said, "Write down five companies. Next to each, one thing you can do this week." So I did: one letter, one mock interview with him, one visit to a senior who worked at a factory in Satpur. Small things. The dread didn't vanish, but now it had something to hold. I didn't get my first choice. I got the third, and that's where I met your chachi, so no complaints.

Where did Raghav Chacha study?
At the polytechnic in Nashik.
What was young Raghav feeling during those sleepless nights?
He felt hopeful about a job in Bombay and, at the same time, full of dread about failing and disappointing his father.
What turning point helped young Raghav manage the dread?
Following Mr Sathe's suggestion to list five companies with one small step each that week, such as a letter, a mock interview and a visit to a senior.
How might Mr Sathe have seen young Raghav at the notice board?
As a worried student who needed practical steps more than a speech, which is why he offered a simple plan.

metadata.subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]

messages.content:
Read this:

Gargi, you said your friend is "just slow" because she didn't follow your chemistry explanation. Come, sit on the swing; the Onam pookalam can wait. When I was fifteen, I was the maths girl of our class in Thrissur. Shobha asked me to explain quadratic equations before the exam. I rattled it off: "Discriminant, roots, just plug into the formula, it's obvious." Two minutes, done. She looked at me with such a lost face that I got irritated. I told the others she was slow. The next week our teacher explained it to her, slowly, with mangoes drawn on the board, and Shobha got full marks. I had forgotten that I once needed mangoes too. So, Gargi, before calling her slow, try again from the very first step. That is what your Aparna maasi learned the hard way.

What did the teacher draw on the board to explain quadratic equations?
Mangoes.
Why did young Aparna get irritated with Shobha?
The steps felt obvious to Aparna, who had forgotten being a beginner, so Shobha's lost face looked like slowness and made Aparna impatient and annoyed.
What choice in the story could young Aparna have made differently?
She could have started from the first step, used plain words and examples like the mangoes, and checked whether Shobha was following.
How might Shobha have felt when Aparna rattled off the formula?
Shobha probably felt lost and embarrassed, and later hurt at being called slow, though she got full marks once it was explained slowly.

Read this:

After the Sunday service in Nyeri, Cucu Wanjiru watched young Paulo, home from his first job in Mombasa, come towards her and bend almost to one knee, the old way. Her own grandchildren just hugged her these days. She noticed his cheeks were flushed, as if he'd rehearsed it. She could have let him stay down. Instead she pulled him up by the shoulders. 'You don't need to bend for me, Paulo. Come, walk me home and tell me everything.' His shoulders dropped, and he offered her his arm. Behind them a little girl dropped a neat curtsy, and Cucu laid a hand on her head in blessing. Each got what they seemed to need.

Where had Paulo just started working?
In Mombasa.
What did Cucu Wanjiru feel when she noticed Paulo's flushed cheeks?
She felt fond and a little touched, sensing he had nervously rehearsed the old greeting to honour her.
Why was lifting Paulo up and inviting him to walk a kind choice?
It honoured his effort without making him perform, and turned the moment into real time together, so he felt seen rather than tested.
How did Paulo seem to feel after Cucu Wanjiru pulled him up?
Paulo seemed relieved and at ease; his shoulders dropped and he offered her his arm.

Read this:

The first three times I tried to start running, I lasted four days each. I'm Arohi, second-year BSc, and my plan was always big: five kilometres, six a.m., every day. By day four I'd wake up, think about the whole five kilometres and roll over.
This time my roommate Simran gave me two rules. One: put the running shoes next to the bed, socks inside, so my feet land on them. Two: the target is ten minutes. Not five kilometres. Ten minutes, even if I walk half of it.
It felt almost too easy. Some mornings I did exactly ten minutes and came back. Some mornings I kept going for twenty because I was already out.
It has been five weeks now. The shoes are still by the bed, a bit muddy. I don't argue with myself any more. Feet down, shoes on, out.

Where did Arohi put the running shoes?
Arohi put them next to the bed, with socks inside.
How does Arohi feel about running now compared with before?
Arohi feels calmer and more confident, no longer arguing each morning, whereas the big old plan made Arohi want to roll over.
Why did Simran's two rules help the habit survive?
The shoes by the bed removed effort from starting, and a ten-minute target made each morning easy to begin, so the habit lasted past the first weeks.
How might Simran feel seeing the muddy shoes still by the bed after five weeks?
Simran would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that the simple rules worked where Arohi's big plans had failed.
Is 300 + 40 + 5 equal to 345? Write the right sign between them.

Answer: Yes. 300 + 40 + 5 = 345.

The = sign means "is the same value as". Work out the left side first: 300 + 40 + 5 is 345. Both sides are 345, so they are equal. Now try 300 + 50 + 4 _ 345: the left side is 354, so 354 > 345 and we write >.

Read this:

Elif had not spoken to Layla since Tuesday, and it was now Thursday night in their Toronto dorm room. She moved around Layla like furniture: headphones in, back turned, lamp clicked off at ten without the usual "night".
Layla lay awake replaying the week. Was it the seat she forgot to save at the lecture? The charger she returned late? The mug left in the sink? She wrote three apology texts, each longer than the last, and sent them all. "I'm so sorry for everything, whatever it was."
Read. No reply.
Her chest ached in a way that felt almost physical. She skipped the study group on Friday in case Elif wanted to talk. Elif didn't.
When Layla's sister called, she said she was fine. Then she hung up and realised she had apologised four times in a call about nothing.

What did Layla send after lying awake?
She sent three apology texts, each longer than the last.
What was Layla feeling as she replayed the week?
She felt dread and an almost physical ache in her chest, desperate to find what she had done so the silence would end.
What could Layla do instead of apologising for everything?
She could say once, calmly, that she will talk when Elif is ready, keep going to the study group, and tell her sister honestly how the silence is affecting her.
What would change if Elif had said "I'm upset about the seat, give me a day"?
Layla would know what was wrong and that the silence would end, so she could apologise for the real thing and sleep instead of replaying everything.

Read this:

Yusuf: heard you've got fever, need anything?
Sarita: ugh I'm so sorry, I'm such a burden, you don't have to
Sarita: wait, deleting that
Sarita: actually yes. could you get bread, bananas and a packet of biscuits? thank you, that would really help 🙏
Yusuf: done! anything else?
Sarita: some tea bags maybe. thank you, really
Yusuf: on my way
Yusuf: ok, bag's on your door handle
Sarita: got it. you're a star 🤍
Yusuf: honestly made my day. I felt useless sitting around this weekend
Sarita: well you weren't. rest of the week I'll just say thank you and let you be useful
Yusuf: deal. and if the fever keeps going or worries you, check with the doctor, ok?
Sarita: will do

What did Sarita ask Yusuf to get?
Bread, bananas, a packet of biscuits, and some tea bags.
Why did Sarita delete that first message?
Sarita seemed embarrassed about needing help, but realised that the word 'burden' would push Yusuf away rather than let Yusuf help.
Which choice worked, and why?
Replacing the apology with a clear request and a thank-you worked, because Yusuf knew exactly what to do and felt good doing it.
How was Yusuf affected by being allowed to help?
It made Yusuf's day, since Yusuf had been feeling useless sitting around that weekend.

Read this:

At the badminton club, Hemant told the others that Damini had been dropped from the team because she was lazy. He'd heard it from someone in the changing room.
By evening, Damini was sitting alone on the bench, crying quietly.
Then the coach announced that Damini had asked to skip the tournament because her grandmother was ill.
Hemant felt sick. He had repeated something without checking, and it had hurt her.
He walked over. "Damini, I'm sorry. I said something about you that wasn't true."
Then he told the group, "I was wrong about Damini. She wasn't dropped."
Damini looked up. "Thank you for telling them."

Why did Damini skip the tournament?
Because her grandmother was ill.
How did Hemant feel when he learned the truth?
He felt sick and guilty for repeating something false that hurt her.
What did Hemant do to make it right?
He apologised to Damini and corrected the rumour with the group.
How might Damini feel after Hemant's apology?
Damini seemed grateful that he told the others the truth.

Read this:

Harish sat on the step of his shop in Mandsaur with the offer letter from the seed company folded in his shirt pocket. Twenty-two thousand a month, field work, a motorbike allowance. His cousin Divyansh, visiting from Indore, had laughed at it over lunch. 'My friend in Bengaluru gets three times that.' Harish had felt small for an hour. Now, alone, he took out a notebook and asked himself different questions. What does the shop bring in a normal month? What did I earn two years ago? What do Amma's medicines and the house need? He wrote two columns. The offer beat the shop and would give him evenings with his daughter. He looked at the Bengaluru figure once more, then crossed it out; that man didn't live in Mandsaur. He signed the letter.

What did the seed company offer Harish?
Twenty-two thousand a month, field work and a motorbike allowance.
How did Harish feel after Divyansh's comment at lunch?
Harish felt small and deflated for an hour, because the offer had been set against a big-city salary.
What about Harish's approach could someone else use for a big choice?
Compare the option with your own past, your real needs and the other options in front of you, rather than with someone else's life far away.
Why might Divyansh see the offer differently from Harish?
Divyansh measures it against a friend's city salary, while Harish measures it against the shop, his own past and his family's needs in Mandsaur.

Read this:

The rain was pouring, the car was stuck in traffic, and Vikas was already late to pick up his sister from the station. His phone rang. It was his boss.
"Sorry, sir, I'm in a meeting, I'll call back," he said, and hung up.
From the back seat, nine-year-old Amandeep said, "Papa, you're not in a meeting. You're in the car."
Vikas opened his mouth to say, "That's different, grown-ups have to." Then he closed it.
"You're right," he said. "I told a lie because I didn't want to talk right now. That was lazy of me."
He called his boss back. "Sir, sorry, I wasn't in a meeting. I'm driving in the rain. Can I call you in half an hour?" The boss said that was fine.
Amandeep grinned. "You got caught."
"I did," Vikas said. "And I'm glad it was by you."

What did Vikas tell his boss the first time?
'Sorry, sir, I'm in a meeting, I'll call back.'
How did Amandeep feel when Papa owned the lie?
Amandeep was amused and pleased, grinning 'You got caught', seeing Papa admit it instead of making excuses.
What did Vikas do that taught more than a lecture?
He admitted the lie in front of Amandeep, called his boss back with the truth, and didn't hide behind 'grown-ups have to'.
How might Vikas feel being corrected by his child?
Vikas was briefly tempted to defend it, but seemed glad and a little humbled to be caught by Amandeep.

Read this:

In the clinic in Accra, Kwame gripped the edge of the chair. His heart thumped as he saw the little needle on the tray. Last time, someone had said, "It won't hurt at all," and it had. His eyes filled up and he began to cry. Dr Rania knelt down. "I'll tell you the truth, Kwame. It will pinch for a second, and I am here with you." Kwame sobbed but held out his arm. Dr Rania counted out loud. It pinched, and it was over. She said, "You were brave to stay."

Where was Kwame when he saw the needle?
Kwame was at a clinic in Accra.
What was Kwame feeling as he looked at the needle?
Kwame was scared and remembered a time it hurt after someone said it wouldn't. His thumping heart and tears show his fear.
Why was Dr Rania's way of talking to Kwame wise?
Dr Rania told the truth, that it would pinch for a second, and stayed with him. Saying it won't hurt makes the next visit harder because he stops trusting.
How might Kwame's trust in adults change after this visit?
Kwame may trust Dr Rania more because what she said matched what happened. Next time he may still be scared but feel less alone.

Read this:

Teacher's note - Lokesh, Class 10 social science, Monday
During a discussion on choice and culture, one student, meaning well, said Vidya must "have to" wear her hijab. Vidya went quiet, then answered calmly: "Nobody forces me. My mother doesn't even wear one. I chose it in Class 8. It's my faith and, honestly, I like how it looks."
Another student, Parminder, said her own turban was partly faith and partly her grandfather's wish. A third said she wears a bindi for style some days and not others.
I asked the class what they noticed. One boy said, "The same thing can mean different things to different people."
I told them that's exactly why we should ask, not assume. Afterwards the first student apologised to Vidya, and Vidya said, "It's fine. Ask me anything. Just don't tell me what it means for me."

When did Vidya choose to wear her hijab?
She chose it in Class 8.
What might Vidya have felt when told she must "have to" wear it?
Vidya probably felt misunderstood and a little hurt, going quiet before calmly explaining it was her own choice.
What did Lokesh do to turn the moment into learning?
He let students share their own reasons and asked what they noticed, helping the class see that the same item can mean different things.
How might the student who apologised have seen the hijab before the discussion?
That student seemed to assume it was always imposed, without asking what it meant to Vidya.

I'm Chetan, and my cousin Vaibhav came to the park with me. At the slide there was a long line. Vaibhav counted the children in front. "Three more," he said. After one went down he said, "Two." He didn't push or whine; he just kept counting, fingers up. When he said "Me!" he sounded so happy. I think counting helped him wait.

How many children were in front of Vaibhav at first?
Three more.
What was Chetan thinking about the counting?
Chetan felt impressed and thought the counting helped Vaibhav wait.
What else could help Vaibhav wait in a longer line?
He could chat or play a small game while counting, so the wait feels shorter.
How did it feel for Vaibhav when it was his turn?
He was very happy and excited, saying "Me!"

Read this:

At the Thursday cattle market outside the kasba, Wasim sold three goats before noon and felt nothing. Last night his son Faiz, fifteen, had pushed away the mutton curry and said quietly, 'Abbu, I don't want to eat meat anymore. And I don't want to trade goats.'
Wasim had walked out without a word.
On the bus home he sat beside Mahima, the schoolteacher from the next lane. 'Three generations,' he said. 'And he looks at our work like it's wrong.'
'Did you ask him why?'
He hadn't.
That evening he found Faiz feeding the young goat by the shed. Wasim sat on an upturned bucket. 'Tell me. From the start. I'll listen first.'
Faiz talked for a long time, about the goats' faces, about a veterinary course in the city. Wasim felt fear in his chest, and a strange pride too, at how carefully his boy had thought.

What did Faiz push away at dinner?
The mutton curry.
What mixed feelings did Wasim have while Faiz talked by the shed?
He felt fear in his chest and also a strange pride at how carefully his son had thought it through.
What turning point sent Wasim back to talk with Faiz?
Mahima's question 'Did you ask him why?' made him see he hadn't, so he chose to sit down and listen first.
How might Faiz have felt when his father walked out without a word?
Faiz may have felt rejected and worried that his father saw the choice as an insult to three generations of family work.

metadata.subtype: Parent facing the child's different values [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

You want to know how I've been since Bauji passed, Nirmala? Okay.
First week, I was all spreadsheet. Every doctor's visit, every report, the dates his medicines changed. I understood the illness better than anyone in the family. Chacha kept ringing me, "Gurpreet beta, what did the doctor mean?", like I was the expert. It felt good to be useful.
Then one night I caught myself reading about kidney function at two in the morning, and realised I hadn't once said I missed him. Not to anyone. Not even to myself.
So I made a rule. Every evening, after the reading, fifteen minutes with his old radio, tuned to the station he liked. No phone, no notes. First evening, nothing. Second, nothing. Third evening the old film songs came on and I just broke.
I think the reading was me walking toward it slowly. The radio was where I finally got there.

What did Gurpreet turn on each evening?
Bauji's old radio, tuned to the station he liked.
What made Gurpreet realise the reading wasn't enough?
Reading about kidney function at two in the morning without once saying "I missed him" showed Gurpreet the understanding had become a way around the grief.
Why did the fifteen minutes with the radio work where the spreadsheet didn't?
It paired the understanding with a set time to feel, using something tied to Bauji, so the sadness finally had a place to come out.
How might things look for Chacha if Gurpreet had kept on playing the expert?
Chacha would keep getting clear answers but might never see Gurpreet's grief, and the family could miss the chance to mourn Bauji together.

metadata.subtype: Letting thinking and feeling share the table [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the campus clinic waiting room, Gopika had nothing to do but read the leaflet from her new skin cream. By the third paragraph, her cheeks felt hot. By the fifth, she was sure her lips were tingling. She kept touching her face and checking it in her phone camera. "Gopika?" Arnab, the nursing intern at the desk, called her name. She hurried up. "I think I'm reacting. It says burning, tingling, redness." Arnab looked at her skin carefully. "I don't see redness. Did the feeling start before or after you read it?" Gopika paused. "After." "Worry can turn up the volume on sensations," he said kindly. "Tell the doctor exactly what you felt. If it keeps happening, they'll want to know."

Where was Gopika when she read the leaflet?
In the campus clinic waiting room.
What does Gopika checking her face in the phone camera suggest she was feeling?
She was growing anxious that the cream was harming her, and the worry made her watch for, and feel, the effects she had just read about.
Which question from Arnab helped Gopika, and why?
"Did the feeling start before or after you read it?" It helped her notice that fear might be adding to the sensations, while he still told her to report it to the doctor.
How does Arnab see the situation compared with Gopika?
Arnab looks calmly and sees no redness, so he treats the worry kindly rather than as an emergency, while Gopika is sure she is reacting.
Recipe English mein likhni hai. 'Pyaaz ko golden hone tak bhuno' ka translation?
In English: "Fry the onions until they turn golden brown." In recipes you will also see the shorter "Fry the onions until golden." Both are correct.

Read this:

I'm Sumit, and in Class 10 I had a big fight with my best friend Darshan. He told everyone in our class about something I'd told him in secret.
That night I typed a long message. I called him a traitor and a lot worse. My thumb was on the send button.
Then I remembered Papa saying, "Never decide anything important while angry." So I saved it as a draft and put the phone under my pillow.
I barely slept. But by morning, I read the draft and felt embarrassed. Half of it wasn't even true. I was just hurt.
I deleted it and wrote something shorter: "What you did really hurt me. Can we talk after school?"
He replied in two minutes. "Sorry. Yes."
We talked by the canteen that afternoon. We're still friends. If I'd sent the first one, I don't think we would be.

What did Sumit write in the shorter message?
"What you did really hurt me. Can we talk after school?"
How did Sumit feel on reading the draft in the morning?
Sumit felt embarrassed, seeing that half of it wasn't true and was written out of hurt.
What else could Sumit do if the anger doesn't fade by morning?
Sumit could talk to a trusted adult or wait a little longer before replying, rather than sending anything while still furious.
How might Darshan have felt receiving the calm message?
Darshan may have felt guilty but relieved, and more willing to apologise because the message asked to talk instead of attacking.

metadata.subtype: Approach: postpones a heated decision until emotions settle [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

The wedding band was so loud that nobody heard Gautam fall. He and Jaya, both five, had been racing up the wet marble steps behind the lawn when his sandal slipped and he banged his elbow. He sat howling. Jaya stopped dead. Her face crumpled, and she screamed too, frozen on the step, fists at her sides. Her legs wouldn't move. The dhol drowned them both. It was a long minute before Gautam's uncle, looking for more sweets, spotted them and ran over. He picked up Gautam and held out a hand to Jaya. She clung to it, sobbing, 'He fell, he fell.'

What drowned out the children's crying?
The dhol.
What was Jaya feeling when her legs wouldn't move?
Jaya was overwhelmed by fear for Gautam; she cared, but her own upset froze her.
Once the fright has passed, what could an adult do with Jaya?
An adult could praise Jaya's caring and practise what to do next time, like running to find a grown-up, which is hard to think of when frightened.
How might Gautam's uncle see Jaya's screaming?
The uncle might realise Jaya was frightened for Gautam rather than hurt, which is why he held out a hand to her too.

metadata.subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]

messages.content: My goalkeeper is nervous. Write a two-sentence pep talk that uses "save" once and "team" once.
Stay alert and make every save count. Your team trusts you, so breathe and stay calm.
