Bhupen's hostel room in the Tezpur college was always noisy in the evenings, and his flashcards for the English entrance test sat in a rubber band on the shelf, untouched. Every night he promised himself he'd do them. Every night he didn't.
His senior Naveen said, "You brush your teeth every morning without fail, right?"
"Obviously."
"Then tie the cards to that. After brushing, five cards. Nothing else."
The next morning Bhupen brushed his teeth at the corridor sink, came back, and picked up five cards from the stack by his toothbrush mug. Five words. Two minutes.
By the end of the month, the rubber band had moved to a second stack: words he knew. He hadn't missed a single morning, because he hadn't missed a single brushing.

How many cards did Bhupen do after brushing?
Five cards.
How had Bhupen been feeling about the untouched flashcards?
He was probably guilty and frustrated, promising himself every night and never doing them.
Why did linking the cards to brushing work better than promising to do them at night?
Because brushing already happens every morning without fail, so it reminds him automatically, while the noisy evenings kept pushing the cards aside.
How does Naveen's suggestion look to Bhupen at first?
It seems almost too simple at first, but it gives Bhupen a small habit he actually keeps.

metadata.subtype: Approach: attaches a new habit to an existing cue [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Counsellor's note, Monday. Ayesha, school counsellor.
Lakshmi has been arriving with expensive new things: a watch, fancy pencils, a new school bag. Today she stayed back and told me her mother keeps buying them. "Amma says Papa never buys me anything, so I should stay with her."
Lakshmi looked tired. "I like the things. But it feels wrong."
I told her she's allowed to love both parents and not choose. We practised: "I love you both. Please don't make me choose."
I've asked both parents to meet me this week. No child should feel like a prize.

What was the new thing Lakshmi was carrying on her back?
A new school bag.
How does Lakshmi feel about the gifts?
She feels uneasy and torn: she likes the things, but it feels wrong.
What did Ayesha do to help Lakshmi?
Ayesha listened, told Lakshmi she's allowed to love both parents, practised what to say, and asked both parents to meet that week.
How might Lakshmi's mother see the gifts?
Lakshmi's mother may see the gifts as a way to win Lakshmi over, not realising the pressure it creates.

Read this:

When Mr Duarte announced that each class in their Lisbon school would pick a mentor for the fifth graders' reading club, Beatriz ruled Jamal out at once. Tall, hood always up, earphones in, slang in every sentence: the type who ends up outside the head's office. "He'll scare them," she told her friend, and volunteered herself instead. On Thursday Jamal came along only because the library was warm. Within ten minutes, Beatriz's group of ten-year-olds was fidgeting, and Jamal's was silent, leaning in, as he did the voices of three pirates. One small girl wouldn't let go of his sleeve at the end. "I read to my little brothers every night," he said, shrugging, when Beatriz stared. She walked home turning it over, slightly embarrassed.

What did Jamal do to hold the children's attention?
He did the voices of three pirates.
Why was Beatriz so surprised by Jamal in the library?
She was surprised, and a little embarrassed, because his hood, earphones and slang had seemed like proof he was trouble, yet he was the best reader there.
What could Beatriz try before ruling someone out next time?
Give the person a chance to show what they can do, or ask them, instead of deciding from clothes and slang.
How might Jamal feel if he knew why Beatriz ruled him out?
He might feel hurt and judged, since he reads to his little brothers every night and was dismissed for his hood and slang.

Read this:

At 11:05 the message showed two ticks, both blue. Sarita had asked Sunaina, two desks away in the design studio, whether the client notes were ready. By one o'clock there was still nothing. Sarita's mind started running: Sunaina was annoyed at being chased, or thought the question was silly, or had found a mistake and did not want to say so. Sarita stopped drawing and stared at the phone.
At two, a door opened. Sunaina walked out of the meeting room with a client, phone in hand, face down against a folder. Sunaina caught Sarita's eye and mouthed, "Notes in ten minutes!"
Sarita smiled at the screen, a bit embarrassed, and picked up the pencil again.

How many ticks appeared on the message, and what colour were they?
The message showed two ticks, both blue.
What was Sarita worried about while waiting for a reply?
Sarita was anxious and wondered if Sunaina was annoyed, thought the question was silly, or had found a mistake. The waiting made every possible reason feel worse.
What could Sarita do next time the message is read but not answered?
Sarita could give Sunaina the benefit of the doubt and get on with work, or walk over and ask briefly. Delays usually mean busyness, as the client meeting showed.
What was Sunaina dealing with while the message sat unanswered?
Sunaina was in a meeting room with a client, phone face down against a folder. The unanswered message came from being busy, not from ignoring Sarita.

Read this:

Sunday
Dear diary, Darshan writing. Jasleen came for the weekend again, and I spent the whole time trying to beat her. Swimming race at the club: she won by a whole arm. Then Chachi asked about the maths olympiad, and Jasleen had a gold certificate and I had silver. I went quiet all through dinner. Tonight I noticed something ugly. When Jasleen dropped her ice cream, I was glad. Glad! That's not who I want to be. It's fine to want to be good, but wanting her to fall is something else. Tomorrow I'm going to ask how she learnt that flip turn at the wall. Maybe if I learn from her instead of racing her every second, I'll actually get faster.

Who won the swimming race?
Jasleen, by a whole arm.
How did Darshan feel on noticing the gladness about the dropped ice cream?
Ashamed and uneasy, seeing that the rivalry had turned into wanting Jasleen to fail.
What plan does Darshan make for tomorrow?
To ask Jasleen how she learnt her flip turn, learning from her instead of racing her every second.
How might Jasleen see Darshan's quiet dinner?
She might feel confused or uneasy, unsure why her gold certificate made her cousin go silent.

Read this:

In the district bank's small IT office, Rashmi said quietly, "Ajay, your technical work is strong, but I haven't yet seen leadership." Ajay had hoped this would be his cycle. He walked to the tea stall across the road and drank slowly, watching the bus stand. "If leadership is what they want to see, one cycle isn't enough to show it," he told himself. Back at his desk he wrote a new plan: mentor the new intern, Prabha, from the first of next month, and lead the demo for the regional heads in March. He would aim for the next cycle instead. He showed the plan to Rashmi, who asked him to review it with her every month.

Who did Ajay plan to mentor?
Ajay planned to mentor the new intern, Prabha.
How did Ajay feel when Rashmi said leadership had not yet been seen?
Ajay felt disappointed, having hoped it would be his cycle, and needed time alone at the tea stall to take it in.
What else could Ajay do to show leadership, and why?

messages.content: Amber buys 7 guppies for her pond.  Several days later, she sees 3 dozen baby guppies swimming around.  Two days after that, she sees 9 more baby guppies.  How many guppies does she have now?

3 dozen baby guppies make 3 x 12 = 36 baby guppies.
There are a total of 36 + 9 = 45 baby guppies.
Adding the adult guppies, there are 7 + 45 = 52 guppies.
The answer is 52.

Three snails raced across a rain-soaked sidewalk.  The first snail raced at a speed of 2 feet per minute.  The second snail raced at twice the speed of the first snail.  And the third snail traveled at five times the rate of speed as the second snail.  If it took the first snail 20 minutes to race all the way up the sidewalk, how long, in minutes, did it take for the third snail to race all the way up the sidewalk?

If the first snail traveled the distance in 20 minutes, then the second snail, traveling at twice the rate of speed, would take 20/2=10 minutes to complete the race.
If the third snail raced at five times the speed of the second snail, then it would take the third snail 10/5=2 minutes to race all the way up the sidewalk.
The answer is 2.

One evening a teammate joked about hiding Layla's goggles before the trials. Sofia said, "No. If I win the place, I want it to be mine." When the results came, Layla got it by a small margin. Sofia shook her hand, still out of breath, and said, "Your turns are unreal. Show me sometime?" Layla laughed and said yes.

What did a teammate joke about hiding?
The teammate joked about hiding Layla's goggles.
Why did Sofia refuse to hide Layla's goggles?
Although the sight of Layla's early laps made her uneasy, Sofia wanted any win to be her own, so she used Layla as a benchmark rather than an enemy to beat by tricks. 😊
What could Sofia do after losing the place?
She could keep working on her turns, ask Layla and the coach for tips, and aim for the next selection.
How might Layla have felt when Sofia shook her hand?
She was probably pleased and relieved by the respect, and glad the rivalry stayed friendly.

June: Vijay moved to Pune for his first job; Amandeep stayed in Chandigarh for his master's. They promised to call every week. By August, they hadn't spoken in five weeks. September: Vijay forgot Amandeep's birthday. He saw it the next morning on social media and felt terrible. He called at lunch. Amandeep answered, a little cool. "Busy life, huh?" "No excuse. I'm sorry. Can we fix the rhythm? Calls don't work for us." They tried something smaller: a voice note every Sunday, even thirty seconds, about the best and worst thing of the week. December: Vijay had nineteen voice notes saved. He knew about Amandeep's new flatmate, his bad professor, his sister's engagement. When Vijay visited home for New Year, they talked till two in the morning like nothing had changed.

How do Vijay and Amandeep keep their friendship going?

When weekly calls failed, they switched to a Sunday voice note about the best and worst thing of the week, even if only thirty seconds long. By December Vijay knew what was going on in Amandeep's life.

Seema mole, you think you're lucky with numbers? Let me tell you about your Jomon Chachan at sixteen.
Every year at the church feast in our village there was a lucky draw, first prize a bicycle. Tickets were printed in order, but I made the seller let me choose. I would sit in the shade for an hour doing sums with my birth date, my house number, the day of the week. I was sure my number, chosen with so much effort, was stronger than a ticket someone just grabbed.
Three years running I chose. Three years running someone who grabbed won. Once it was my little cousin, who couldn't even read numbers yet.
I still remember her dancing next to that bicycle she couldn't ride. That day I finally understood: the drum doesn't care who thought hardest.

What was the first prize at the church feast draw?
First prize was a bicycle.
Why did young Jomon believe his ticket was stronger?
He had put an hour of sums and effort into choosing it, and that effort made his number feel as if it deserved to win more than a grabbed ticket.
What was the turning point that changed Jomon's thinking?
Seeing his little cousin, who couldn't even read numbers, win with a grabbed ticket showed him that effort had no hold on the draw.
How might Seema use this story the next time a number feels lucky?
Seema might laugh, then remember that the drum doesn't care who thought hardest, and be slower to trust a chosen number.

The call to prayer drifted across the rooftops of Kadıköy as Zeynep sat on the balcony with cold tea. For most of her life that sound had meant something: stop, wash, turn toward something bigger. Now it only meant that it was evening.
She wasn't angry, the way some friends were about their upbringing. She just felt a quiet hollow where the meaning used to be, like a room after the furniture has gone.
Pablo, her flatmate, came out with a blanket. 'You've been out here an hour.'
'I keep waiting to feel something when I hear it,' she said. 'Either way. Relief, or missing it. Nothing comes.'
'Maybe it doesn't have to come yet,' Pablo said.
Zeynep pulled the blanket round her shoulders and listened to the last notes fade.

How long had Zeynep been on the balcony, according to Pablo?
Pablo says she had been out there an hour.
What is Zeynep feeling as the call to prayer drifts over?
She feels a quiet emptiness rather than anger, waiting for relief or longing that doesn't come.
What does Pablo's reply offer Zeynep at this stage?
By saying it doesn't have to come yet, Pablo gives her permission to stay with the emptiness without rushing to a conclusion.
What might Pablo be noticing about Zeynep?
Pablo notices she has sat alone for an hour and seems low, and chooses warmth and a blanket over advice.

Thomas, twenty-six, managed a small café in Bengaluru's Indiranagar. Gurpreet had been washing dishes there for three months. Every time Thomas mentioned the barista course the café would pay for, Gurpreet nodded and did nothing.
One morning Gurpreet came in with swollen eyes. He admitted he shared a room with seven men, slept on the floor by the door, and often skipped dinner to send money home.
Thomas thought about all the times he'd called Gurpreet "not ambitious" in his head.
That week Thomas arranged for staff meals every shift, and asked the owner about the spare room above the storeroom. Gurpreet moved in on Sunday.
Ten days later, Gurpreet came to the counter with the course form, filled in. "When do I start?"

How many men did Gurpreet share a room with?
Seven.
What was Thomas feeling when he thought about calling Gurpreet "not ambitious"?
He felt guilty and a bit ashamed, realising he had mistaken scarcity for lack of ambition.
What did Thomas do, and why did it help?
He arranged staff meals and a spare room, which gave Gurpreet food and rest so he had space to plan and sign up for the course.
How might Gurpreet have felt moving into the room above the storeroom?
He probably felt relieved and safer, finally with room in his mind for more than getting through each day.

In Class 5B of a Delhi school, the story travelled from desk to desk like a folded chit. "Don't tell anyone," Dolma whispered to Pranav during art, "but Ritesh failed and has to repeat the year."
Pranav nodded. He watched it move: Dolma told the twins, the twins told Aman, and every telling began with "promise you won't say". Pranav noticed that the whisperers leaned together like a club. He had never been in that club.
At recess, when Aman and the twins huddled near the swings, Pranav walked up and said, "I heard it too. About Ritesh."
They made room for him at once. He felt warm, included, and a little sick, all at the same time.

How did every telling of the story begin?
Every telling began with "promise you won't say".
How did Pranav feel when the group made room for him?
He felt warm and included, and at the same time a little sick, because he had joined in by repeating the story.
What could Pranav have done at the swings instead of repeating the story?
He could have joined the group with something else to talk about, or said he didn't want to pass it on, since belonging does not have to cost Ritesh.
What is it like for Ritesh while the whisper travels around 5B?
Ritesh may notice huddles and glances without knowing why, and feel uneasy or left out as the story grows behind his back.
Eight people fit in a row on an airplane, and there are 12 rows. Only 3/4 of the seats in each row are allowed to be seated. How many seats will not be occupied on that plane?

There a total of 8 x 12 = 96 seats on that plane.
Only 8 x 3/4 = 6 seats are allowed to be seated in each row.
So, only 6 x 12 = 72 seats are allowed to be seated on the plane.
Therefore, 96 - 72 = 24 seats will not be occupied.
The answer is 24.

March: Akash sat in his room in Indore, surrounded by the engineering books he'd stopped opening a year ago. He'd spent that year gaming at night and sleeping till noon, then dropped out. Now he wouldn't apply anywhere. "Why should I get a second chance after wasting one?" he told his friend Tarun.
A week later: Tarun came over and asked, "What did you know then that you know now?" Akash was quiet a long time. "That I hated the course. That I didn't know how to say it." Tarun said, "So you were a nineteen-year-old doing the best you knew."
May: Akash filled in the form for a design diploma. His hands shook when he clicked submit. He still felt the old sting about that year, but he let himself apply anyway.

How did Akash spend the year before he dropped out?
He spent that year gaming at night and sleeping till noon.
What was Akash feeling in March when he refused to apply?
He felt guilty and ashamed, believing he didn't deserve a second chance after wasting one.
What small step helped Akash begin to forgive himself?
Tarun's question about what he knew then, which helped Akash see his younger self as doing the best he knew rather than as someone to punish.
How might Tarun have seen Akash's refusal to apply?
Tarun probably saw it as punishment that kept Akash stuck, and cared enough to come over and gently question it.

On Thursday evening Sunaina laid everything on her bed in rows and ticked her list: lunch box, water, tissues, notebook. The sun cap was still drying on the balcony rail, so she wrote "morning" beside it and zipped the bag. On Friday, before breakfast, she went down the list again with a pencil. "Sun cap..." It hung there, damp at the edge. "Karthik, towel!" Her brother rubbed it dry while she folded it into the bag. At the bus stop she felt no fluttering in her stomach, only the ordinary morning wind.

Where was the sun cap on Thursday evening?
It was still drying on the balcony rail.
What was Sunaina feeling at the bus stop, and what shows it?
She felt calm, since she felt no fluttering in her stomach after both checks. 🙂
What other approach could help Sunaina if she still worried, and why?
She could ask a parent to look over her list too, since a second person might notice something she overlooked.
How does Karthik help in this scene, and how might he feel about it?
Karthik rubs the cap dry with a towel, and probably feels glad to be useful and quick, as he acts as soon as she calls.

Monday, 3 March. Vandana and Santosh disagree about pricing their billing software: she wants ₹499 a month, he wants ₹999. By evening each has a folder called "proof". Hers has cheaper competitors. His has three customers who said they'd pay more.
Thursday, 13 March. The pricing meeting lasts two hours. Nobody asks what the other has learned. Vandana wins because their advisor sides with her. "Told you," she says, closing her laptop. Santosh says nothing.
Monday, 21 April. Santosh hasn't suggested a single idea in six weeks. In product meetings he just nods. A customer tells Vandana they would happily pay more for proper reports; Santosh had mentioned that exact feature in February and has not raised it since. Vandana realises she won the argument and lost her co-founder's voice.

What did Vandana say after winning?
"Told you."
How did Santosh feel after losing?
Santosh likely felt humiliated and shut out, which is why he stopped sharing ideas.
What could they have done instead of collecting proof to win?
Shared what each had learned, perhaps tested both prices with a few customers, and decided together.
How does Vandana see things by April?
Vandana realises she won the argument but lost Santosh's ideas, which hurts the company more.

When the power went out in Sarika's hometown near Mandya, the whole lane went quiet except for the generator at the temple. She worked for a Bengaluru design team from her uncle's front room, and her internet dropped most afternoons. In her first month, Shankar, her team lead, messaged at 3 p.m. and got silence till evening. He wrote, a bit sharply, "Are you even working?" Sarika's face burned. That night she replied calmly: her hours, when the power usually failed, and a plan. Every morning at nine she would post what she would finish that day; every evening, what was done and any blockers. For anything urgent she gave her number for a normal call, which worked even when data didn't. Two weeks later Shankar replied under her evening update: "Your notes are the clearest on the team. Sorry about that message."

When did Sarika promise to post her daily plan?
Every morning at nine.
What was Sarika feeling when Shankar asked if she was even working?
Sarika felt hurt and embarrassed, her face burning, but chose to reply calmly.
How did Sarika build trust despite unreliable internet?
She explained her constraints, posted clear morning plans and evening updates, and offered a phone number for urgent things.
How does Shankar's view of Sarika change?
At first he suspected she wasn't working; after two weeks of clear updates he sees her notes as the team's best and apologises.

Monday, one o'clock: Kalyani rubbed her eyes and leaned on Vikas's leg. It was nap time. He took her to bed and she slept at once.
Thursday, at a loud birthday party: she rubbed her eyes again and hid her face. It wasn't nap time. Vikas carried her out to the quiet hallway, and she brightened.
Saturday evening, dinner was late: eye-rubbing, whining. Vikas gave her a banana, and she stopped.

What did Vikas give Kalyani on Saturday evening?
A banana.
What was Kalyani feeling each time she rubbed her eyes?
On Monday she was tired, on Thursday overwhelmed by the loud party, and on Saturday hungry; the same cue carried different feelings.
What habit helped Vikas respond well?
He looked at the time, the place and what she had eaten each time, rather than assuming one meaning.
What would change if Vikas had always put Kalyani to bed when she rubbed her eyes?
He would have missed that she was overwhelmed or hungry on other days, and she would have stayed upset.

Tushar, you asked why I left the school band, so here's the honest version. I'm Varun, the guy who carried the drum kit up three floors every Friday for a whole year. The other four have played together since they were small. When one of them came in late or off-beat, it was "leave it, he's tired, exams na." When I rushed one fill at the Annual Day rehearsal, the lead guitarist said I was ruining the song, and the others nodded.
Then the keyboard player missed a whole verse. They laughed and called it jazz.
I kept thinking, if I'd missed that verse, I'd be out by evening. That's when I understood it was never really about the music. It was about who's already inside.
I'm not angry any more. Just tired of auditioning every week for people who had already decided about me.

What did the others call it when the keyboard player missed a whole verse?
They laughed and called it jazz.
What was Varun feeling when the missed verse was laughed off?
Varun felt bitter and left out, because a slip that would have got Varun thrown out was treated as a joke for someone already inside the group.
What could Varun try next instead of giving up music altogether?
Varun could look for a group where feedback rules are the same for everyone, or ask the music teacher to run open auditions and rehearsals.
How might Tushar see Varun's decision to leave the band?
Tushar may understand that Varun left for protection from unfair judging, not from any loss of love for the drums, and may want to include Varun more.

I'm Keerthana, and when I get excited telling a story, my brother Sahil holds his palms out and pushes them down gently. At first I thought it meant, “Stop, you're annoying.” Then I looked at his face. He was smiling. “Slow down, I want to hear it properly,” he said. So I took a breath and told it slowly. Yesterday my classmate did the same gesture with a stiff face and said, “Calm down.” That felt different, like she didn't want to hear me at all. Same hands, but the face and voice make it kind or not.

What does Sahil do with his palms when Keerthana gets excited?
He holds his palms out and pushes them down gently.
What did Keerthana first think Sahil's gesture meant, and what changed her mind?
She first thought it meant he found her annoying. His smile and his words, “Slow down, I want to hear it properly”, changed her mind.
What could Keerthana do when a classmate uses the gesture with a stiff face?
Ask calmly whether she is being too loud or say that she would like to finish her story, rather than assuming rejection.
How might the classmate see her own gesture?
Perhaps as a simple way to ask for calm, without noticing that her stiff face made it feel dismissive.

I am Uma, and a fever taught me a planning lesson. I missed two days of study, and my beautiful timetable, which packed every hour, fell apart like wet paper. Four chapters landed on top of the next week, and I panicked. Aditi told me to sit down and rebuild. This time I put one free half-day into every week, Sunday afternoon, blank on purpose. Any missed chapter goes there. The week after, a school function ate a whole evening, and I just slid that chapter to Sunday. Nothing piled up. The empty space had felt like waste, but it turned out to be the strongest part of the plan.

Which part of the week did Uma leave blank on purpose?
Uma left Sunday afternoon blank as a free half-day.
How did Uma feel when the missed days piled chapters onto the next week?
Panicked and overwhelmed. 😰
What else could Uma do if the free half-day also gets used up?
Trim low-value revision or ask a teacher to help set priorities, because the buffer can only take so much.
How might Aditi see Uma's new plan?
As sensible, since Aditi urged a rebuild, and the plan absorbed the next disruption without piling up.

In the bank branch, the manager's phone rang and a client's rough, strained voice filled the room: "I have been waiting three days for my statement!" Simran, the junior officer, felt her own voice rise to match. Then she recalled what Rekha, her mentor, had said: a raspy, tight voice means the person is very worked up. So Simran lowered her volume, slowed down and said, "I understand you have waited a long time, and I am sorry. Let me look at it now." The client took a breath. "Thank you," he said, hoarse and quieter. Simran found the statement in ten minutes and emailed it while he waited.

How long had the client waited for the statement?
The client said he had waited three days.
What did Simran feel first, and what helped her change course?
Simran felt her own voice rise to match the anger, but she remembered that a strained voice shows high arousal. She then lowered her volume and acknowledged the client's wait.
What would you advise a new officer facing a harsh, strained voice?
Lower the volume, slow down and acknowledge the concern, as Simran did, before fixing the problem.
How might the client have felt after Simran apologised?
The client probably felt heard and calmer, since he took a breath and thanked Simran in a quieter voice.

At the residential school in Panchgani, lights-out was at nine, but Omkar, who was eleven, lay awake in the dormitory most nights. What if he failed the half-yearly exams and had to go home in shame? What if Aai fell ill while he was far away? What if the Sunday phone call didn't come? His stomach churned. One night Tushar sir, the house warden, found him sitting up in bed. Omkar whispered it all in a rush. Tushar sir didn't laugh. "Those what-ifs feel like getting ready for trouble, don't they? Mostly they just ring alarm bells." He helped Omkar write the worries on a slip to drop in the worry box by the door, and promised he could phone Aai the next evening. Then he sat nearby while Omkar breathed slowly. Omkar was asleep before ten.

Where did Omkar put the slip with his worries?
In the worry box by the door.
Why did Omkar's stomach churn at night?
Far from home, he kept imagining failing and his Aai falling ill; the worry felt like preparing but only made him more alarmed.
Which choices by Tushar sir helped Omkar sleep?
Listening without laughing, naming the what-ifs as alarm bells, using the worry box, promising a call to Aai and sitting nearby during slow breathing.
How might Aai feel if she knew about Omkar's nights?
Aai would probably feel moved and a little worried, and glad that someone at the school noticed and comforted him.

Friday: Zainab, nine, lost her first carrom game in the building tournament, 29 to 3. She pushed the striker off the board and cried behind the water tank. Aditi didi from the next flat found her there and sat down on the dusty step. "Losing like that stings," she said, and held Zainab's hand until the crying slowed.
Sunday: Aditi didi brought her own carrom board over. They played slowly, and Zainab laughed when her striker bounced right back at her.
Tuesday: Zainab played her second match. She lost again, 29 to 14, but this time she shook hands, then ran to tell Aditi didi the score.

Where did Zainab cry after the first game?
Behind the water tank.
Why did Zainab push the striker off the board on Friday?
She was upset and frustrated at losing so badly, 29 to 3, and the feeling was too big to hold in.
Which moment made Tuesday's match possible?
Aditi didi sitting with her and holding her hand on Friday made the hurt feel safe, so Zainab could practise and try again 🙂
What would change if Aditi didi had told Zainab to stop crying and grow up?
Zainab might have hidden the hurt and avoided the tournament; without that warmth, trying again would feel much riskier.

In the Class 12 computer lab, the teacher allowed AI tools for one hour of project work, with a rule: every fact had to be checked against a second source. Jaya asked hers to summarise a chapter on climate. Her friend Ankita asked hers for five references. Ankita was done in five minutes and grinning. Jaya was still reading. "Just copy it," Ankita said. Jaya shook her head and clicked the first reference. It took her to a real journal, but the article said something different. The second link didn't open at all. Ankita checked hers and went quiet; two of her five were made up. She sighed. "So it lies?" "It guesses," Jaya said. "Confidently." They spent the rest of the hour hunting for real sources.

What rule did the teacher set for using AI tools?
Every fact had to be checked against a second source.
What does Ankita going quiet suggest when she checks her references?
It suggests she was surprised and a bit uneasy to find two made-up references after feeling confident she was done.
Why did the teacher's rule matter?
It forced students to verify claims, which exposed the made-up and misquoted references before they could spoil the projects.
How might Jaya see Ankita's advice to "just copy it"?
Jaya likely sees it as risky, since every fact had to be checked, so she keeps reading and clicks the first reference instead.

All at once I remembered that it might be Pilot, who, when the kitchen-door chanced to be left open, not unfrequently found his way up to the threshold of Mr. Rochester's chamber: I had seen him lying there myself in the mornings. The idea calmed me somewhat: I lay down. Silence composes the nerves; and as an unbroken hush now reigned again through the whole house, I began to feel the return of slumber. But it was not fated that I should sleep that night. A dream had scarcely approached my ear, when it fled affrighted, scared by a marrow-freezing incident enough.

Why does the thought of Pilot calm the narrator?

Pilot sometimes finds his way to the threshold of Mr. Rochester's bedroom when the kitchen door is left open. The narrator has seen him lying there in the mornings, so the idea is calming enough to lie down.
In this picture there are 8 birds. You cannot move them. How do you count them without missing any?

Answer: 8 birds. Count row by row from left to right, or put a small counter (a button) on each bird as you count it.

When things cannot be moved, we need a plan: go in order (left to right, top to bottom), or mark each counted one.

Every morning, Kamal's balcony in the Chennai flat looked like a plumber's puzzle: pipes, bottle caps and a bucket he had rigged over four weekends to water his twenty pots. It leaked onto Rukmini Aunty's clothes line below. "Kamal, my sarees are getting a second wash!" Rukmini called up, laughing but tired. He had spent weeks defending the system. That evening he sat among the pots and asked himself plainly: if I were setting this up today, would I build this? He pictured the simple drip kit at the hardware shop. Yes, that. Not his. On Sunday he fitted the kit, but kept one small bottle-cap sprinkler for the tulsi pot, because he had made it and it still made him smile.

How many pots did Kamal's system water?
Twenty pots.
Why might Kamal have spent weeks defending the leaky system?
He had rigged it himself over four weekends, so the effort made it feel valuable even though it dripped on Rukmini Aunty's clothes line.
What choice did Kamal make on Sunday, and why is it a good balance?
He fitted the simple drip kit but kept one bottle-cap sprinkler for the tulsi pot, fixing the leak while still cherishing something he made. 🙂
What is it like for Rukmini Aunty living below the balcony?
Her sarees keep getting soaked, so she is tired of it even while laughing. For her, how well the system works matters far more than how hard Kamal worked on it.
Yanna bought 60 apples. She gave eighteen apples to Zenny. She gave six more apples to Andrea and kept the rest. How many apples did she keep?

After giving 18 apples to Zenny, Yanna remained with 60 - 18 = 42 apples.
Since she also gave Andrea 6 apples, Yanna remained with 42 - 6 = 36 apples
Therefore, Yanna kept 36 apples.
The answer is 36.

"Harsha, got two minutes? It's about the conference."
"Sure, Rukmini. How's it going?"
"Honestly? I'm lost. Your handover said 'venue sorted.' Which venue? There are emails with two hotels."
"The one by the lake. I told them yes on the phone."
"On the phone. So there's no written booking?"
"Ah. No. I was going to email."
"Okay. And the catering? The spreadsheet says 'vegan?' with a question mark."
"Someone asked. I didn't decide."
"And the speaker from Pune? The file says 'maybe.'"
"She confirmed on a call last Friday."
Rukmini put her pen down. "Harsha, I spent all of yesterday guessing. I nearly booked the other hotel."
"I'm really sorry. It all felt settled in my head."
"Can you send me everything you decided on calls, today? With who you spoke to?"
"Yes. By four."
"Thank you." She let out a breath. "I was starting to think I was the problem."

What did Harsha's handover say about the venue?
Venue sorted.
How had Rukmini been feeling before this talk?
Rukmini felt lost and anxious, having spent a day guessing and starting to think she was the problem.
What request from Rukmini will help most, and why?
Asking Harsha to send everything decided on calls, with names, by four, because those decisions existed only in Harsha's memory.
How does Harsha feel when he hears about the other hotel?
Harsha feels sorry and embarrassed, admitting it all felt settled in his head.

The night before the school's winter concert in Oslo, Emil lay awake planning how to ask Astrid if she'd like to go for hot chocolate afterwards. The asking part was easy. The harder part was what came after. He made himself say it clearly, in his head: if she hesitates, that's a no. If she says "maybe another time" and doesn't pick a time, that's a no. No second message. No asking Kofi to put in a word. At lunch he told Kofi exactly that. Kofi raised an eyebrow. "What if she's just shy?" "Then she can ask me later. It's her choice, not a puzzle for me to solve." After the concert Emil asked. Astrid smiled, looked at her shoes and said, "Um, maybe some other time?" "Sure," said Emil. "Great concert." And he meant both.

What did Emil want to ask Astrid?
If she'd like to go for hot chocolate after the concert.
How did Emil feel lying awake the night before?
He felt nervous, but more concerned with how to respond than with the asking itself, because he wanted to be respectful.
What makes Emil's plan a wise one?
Deciding ahead that hesitation means no, and ruling out repeat messages or go-betweens, keeps Astrid free to decline without pressure.
How might Astrid feel after Emil's reply?
Astrid is likely relieved that her hesitant answer was accepted at once, without awkwardness or follow-up pressure.

Note from Bidisha, class teacher. At lunch, Lakshmi's friend wrinkled her nose while Lakshmi was unpacking her tiffin. Lakshmi shut the box and stopped eating. I sat beside her and asked quietly what was wrong. She said, “She thinks my food smells.” I asked the friend, gently, what the face was about. She said the bin near their bench smelled sour. Lakshmi opened the box again. I suggested to them that when a face worries you, you can ask, “Was that about my food?” They tried the sentence together.

What did Lakshmi do after her friend wrinkled her nose?
She shut the box and stopped eating.
What was Lakshmi probably feeling when she shut her tiffin, and what else could the friend's face have meant?
Probably hurt and self-conscious, thinking her food was being rejected. The friend's face was actually about the sour smell from the bin.
What small step did Bidisha suggest for next time?
That when a face worries them, they ask something like “Was that about my food?” instead of assuming, and she had them practise it together.
How might the friend have felt on learning Lakshmi had been hurt?
Probably surprised and sorry, since she did not mean anything by it. She joined in practising the question, which suggests she wanted to make it right.

Read Mina's diary entry. How does Lucy help her?

12 August.--My expectations were wrong, for twice during the night I was wakened by Lucy trying to get out. She seemed, even in her sleep, to be a little impatient at finding the door shut, and went back to bed under a sort of protest. I woke with the dawn, and heard the birds chirping outside of the window. Lucy woke, too, and, I was glad to see, was even better than on the previous morning. All her old gaiety of manner seemed to have come back, and she came and snuggled in beside me and told me all about Arthur. I told her how anxious I was about Jonathan, and then she tried to comfort me. Well, she succeeded somewhat, for, though sympathy can't alter facts, it can help to make them more bearable.
Lucy, cheerful again, snuggles beside her and comforts her about Jonathan. Mina says sympathy cannot change facts but makes them easier to bear.

"How could you be so careless?" Papa shouted across the courtyard of their house in the small town. Tanvir stared at the floor. A fake bank caller had taken his month's savings that afternoon, and the scolding felt like a second loss.

His mother, Damini, twisted the end of her dupatta. "Now what will we do?"

Tanvir breathed in. "I know you are angry. I'm already reporting it. The bank has my complaint and I'm filing on the cyber portal tonight. I need you to help me, not lecture me."

Papa went quiet. Damini's voice softened. "We were scared."

Later Tanvir sat with them, set up message alerts on Papa's phone, and showed Damini how to check a caller by ringing the bank herself. Papa mumbled that his cousin had got a call like that last month.

Where was Papa when he shouted at Tanvir?
Papa shouted across the courtyard of their house in the small town.
What might Papa be worried about underneath the shouting, and what hints at it?
Fear: Damini said "We were scared", which suggests the anger came from worry.
What could Tanvir ask of his parents instead of lectures?
Ask for support while the report is filed, and help them set up safeguards such as alerts and checking callers by ringing the bank.
How does Damini see the situation?
Damini is frightened about what happens next ("Now what will we do?") and softens once Tanvir says the report is already being made.

- Can you tell me what "antipathy" means?
- What is wrong with this sentence? "The students was very noisy today."
- What's the meaning of the word resolution?

1. Antipathy means a strong feeling of dislike. It is a noun.
2. Say it this way: The students were very noisy today. Why: "students" is plural, so it takes "were".
3. "Resolution" is a noun. It means a firm decision, or the solving of a problem.

The client's file was two days late, and in Thursday's meeting Lokesh said so first. "The data only reached me at five yesterday." Zainab's voice rose. "Because your section was never sent for checking." Voices overlapped, someone glanced at the door, and each left the room certain the other had been unprofessional in front of everyone.

Swati closed her laptop and asked each of them for twenty minutes alone. To Lokesh she said, "Tell me what happened, what it cost you, and what you need." She asked Zainab the same three things, wrote notes, and did not comment on either one's character. Then she brought them into one room. "We have a late file and a client waiting. Let's start with the file." For the first time, both listened while the other spoke.

They agreed that Lokesh owned the data sections and Zainab owned the review, that both names went on every deliverable, and that either would raise a worry in the team channel within a day. A month later they sat with Swati again. "I should have spoken up at the first delay," Lokesh said. Zainab laughed. "Same."

Who owned the review after the agreement?
Zainab owned the review.
What changed between the public clash and the later meetings that made real listening possible?

In the meeting each blamed the other in front of the team and dug in. Swati instead met them separately and then together and asked about the facts, the cost and what each needed, keeping to the file and what comes next rather than character, and the agreements then gave them clear ownership and a way to speak up early.
What was Zainab feeling as the voices rose in the meeting?
Zainab felt blamed and angry, and believed Lokesh had been unprofessional to pin the delay on the review in front of everyone.
What could Swati do at the month check-in if one of them still hesitates to raise worries?
She could ask what makes speaking up hard and restate the agreement to raise things within a day, keeping to the facts.
In one day, Ella's dog eats 4 pounds of food for every one pound of food that Ella eats. How much food do Ella and her dog in 10 days if Ella eat 20 pounds of food each day?

If Ella's dog eats 4 pounds of food for every one pound of food that Ella eats, when Ella eats 20 pounds of food in a day, Ella's dog eats 4*20 = 80 pounds of food.
Together, in one day, Ella and her dog eats 80+20 = 100 pounds
In 10 days, Ella and her dog will eat 10*100 = 1000 pounds of food.
The answer is 1000.
My teacher says Raga Bhairav sounds serious. Which notes give it that colour?
Komal Re and komal Dha, sung slowly and with weight. Bhairav is a prayerful morning raga.

"Pallavi, you're my best friend. So you can't play with the new girl."

Pallavi looked at the new girl, standing alone by the sandpit. "But she's got a bucket."

"Best friends only play with each other," Yamini insisted, grabbing Pallavi's arm.

Their teacher crouched beside them. "Yamini, you and Pallavi are very close. That's lovely. Can best friends play with someone else too?"

Yamini frowned. "Then Pallavi won't like me as much."

"Does your Amma love you less when she talks to your Nani?"

"...No."

"Shall we ask the new girl to build a castle with you both?"

Yamini sighed. "Okay. But I'm doing the tower."

Where was the new girl standing?
Alone by the sandpit.
Why did Yamini want Pallavi to play only with her?
She was most likely worried that sharing Pallavi would mean being liked less; she said so herself. Grabbing Pallavi's arm shows how strongly she wanted to hold on to her friend.
How did the teacher help Yamini see that closeness can include others?
The teacher praised their friendship, then used an everyday example about Amma and Nani, and suggested building a castle together.
How might the new girl feel while Yamini keeps Pallavi to herself?
She is probably lonely and left out, standing alone with her bucket, hoping someone will let her join.
A batsman's scores in 5 matches were 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Find sigma using sigma^2 = sum x^2 / n - m^2, check with the definition, and prove that the two formulas always agree.

Answer: sum x^2 = 100 + 400 + 900 + 1,600 + 2,500 = 5,500; sigma^2 = 5,500 / 5 - 30^2 = 1,100 - 900 = 200; sigma = sqrt200 ~ 14.14 runs.

Check by the definition: deviations -20, -10, 0, 10, 20; squares 400, 100, 0, 100, 400, total 1,000; 1,000 / 5 = 200. Same. Proof: expand (x - m)^2 = x^2 - 2mx + m^2 and add over all n values: sum (x - m)^2 = sum x^2 - 2msum x + nm^2. But sum x = nm, so this is sum x^2 - 2nm^2 + nm^2 = sum x^2 - nm^2. Divide by n: sum (x - m)^2 / n = sum x^2 / n - m^2. The short-cut is quicker when the mean is not a whole number, because we never subtract it from each value. Common mistakes: using (sum x)^2 instead of sum x^2 (150^2 = 22,500 is not 5,500), and forgetting to square the mean.

Farhan had twenty minutes before the vegetable supplier's order deadline, and the café's power had just gone out, so he sat by the window with a notebook and his phone torch. That morning a one-star review had called his biryani "bland and overpriced". His first instinct was to scrap the biryani and order extra paneer instead. Farida, his partner in the café, watched him stop and draw two columns. Last month: the one-star review, two late deliveries. Also last month: forty-one good reviews, eleven of them praising the biryani, and a regular who now brought her whole office on Fridays. He read both columns twice. "One review is loud," he said. "Forty-one are quiet." He placed the usual biryani order, added a note to taste-test the spice with Farida on Monday, and sent it with two minutes to spare.

How many of the good reviews praised the biryani?
Eleven of the forty-one good reviews.
How did Farhan seem to feel right after the one-star review?
He seemed stung and anxious enough to want to scrap the biryani, before he stopped to look at the whole record.
What did Farhan's two columns help him decide?
Seeing the setbacks next to the forty-one good reviews showed the biryani was mostly loved, so he kept it and planned a spice taste-test.
How might Farida see Farhan's pause?
Farida is probably relieved and reassured to see him weigh both columns instead of reacting to one loud review.

Monday. Dilnaz told Eshaan at the bus stop, cheeks pink, that she'd signed up for the Kathak exam in secret. "Not my family, not the class. If I fail, nobody needs to know." Eshaan promised.

Thursday. Someone had seen Dilnaz near the dance academy. In the classroom, three boys cornered Eshaan. "You're her best friend. Where does she go every Thursday? Tell, na." One grabbed his notebook and waved it. "Secret boyfriend?" Eshaan grabbed it back. "Ask her yourself." They called him boring for the rest of the day.

Saturday. Eshaan found Dilnaz outside the academy after practice. "People are asking. I'm not saying anything. But is keeping this secret making things harder for you? Like, are you okay?" Dilnaz thought, then smiled. "I'm fine. It's just mine for now. After the exam I'll tell everyone." She bought him a cutting chai from the stall to say thanks.

What exam did Dilnaz sign up for in secret?
Dilnaz signed up for the Kathak exam in secret.
What might Eshaan have been feeling when the boys cornered him?
Eshaan probably felt cornered and annoyed, but also protective of Dilnaz and determined not to break his promise.
What did Eshaan do on Saturday that was wise?
He checked with Dilnaz that the secret was not making things harder for her, instead of only guarding it.
How does Dilnaz see Eshaan's loyalty?
Dilnaz seems grateful and relieved, which is why she buys him a chai to say thanks. 🙂
Now you try: I think of a number, multiply it by 4 and subtract 7. The answer is 29. What is my number?
The answer is 4n - 7 = 29, n = 9.
Now you try: mean 50, sigma = 10 and mean 80, sigma = 12; which has the smaller CV?
The answer is 20% and 15%: the second.

Madhuri read the headline twice: her favourite singer was cancelling his tour because of a family illness. Tears came before she could stop them. She sat on the edge of the bed in the small Pune flat, phone hot in her hand. "He must be so alone," she whispered, and opened his old live video, the one where he says "you guys get me". It calmed her.
Gurpreet knocked, holding two cups of chai. "Crying over him again?"
Madhuri laughed and wiped her face. "I know he doesn't know me. It still feels like he's my friend."
Gurpreet sat down. "Tell me what's actually bugging you. The maths test?"
Madhuri paused, nodded, and put the phone face-down.

Why was the singer cancelling his tour?
He was cancelling his tour because of a family illness.
Why did Madhuri whisper that the singer must be so alone?
She feels close to him and imagines his pain as if she knew him, though she also admits he doesn't know her. Her tears show how real the attachment feels.
What could Madhuri do to keep enjoying the singer's videos while staying grounded?
She can enjoy the comfort of his videos while remembering he doesn't know her, and keep talking to real friends like Gurpreet about what is bothering her. 🤍
How might Gurpreet see Madhuri's tears?
Gurpreet seems caring rather than mocking, bringing chai and guessing that something else, like the maths test, may be weighing on Madhuri.

Looking back at Class 11, I think I was angry with almost everyone. My parents should have understood that I hated science without me saying it. Lalremsiami, my best friend, should have been free every Saturday, because that's what best friends are. When she started badminton coaching on weekends, I didn't say anything. I just got colder. I left her messages on read. I told myself she should notice. She did notice, eventually, and asked me outside the library, 'Damini, what did I do?' And I realised I'd never actually told her anything. Not about the Saturdays, not about how lonely they had got. The resentment had grown for months; the conversation took ten minutes. We moved our plans to Sunday evenings. I still catch myself thinking 'should' about people. Now it's my cue to say something.

Where did Lalremsiami ask 'what did I do?'
Lalremsiami asked outside the library.
Why did Damini get colder instead of speaking up?
Damini believed a best friend should just notice and be free, so saying it out loud felt like it shouldn't be needed, and the hurt turned into resentment instead.
What does Damini do now when a 'should' thought appears, and why does it help?
Damini treats the 'should' as a cue to say something, which catches resentment early and gives the other person a real chance to respond.
What was it like for Lalremsiami before that talk outside the library?
Lalremsiami probably felt confused and shut out, watching a friend turn cold without knowing why, which is why she finally asked straight out.

Why do we have holidays on festival days?
What time does the procession start in my town today?

Sonali had grown up with her grandmother's Durga puja in Kolkata: the drums, the sindoor, the crowds. After years of drifting and seeking, what finally held her was something different: a small Buddhist meditation centre near Park Circus, where she sat in silence every morning before work and studied the teachings on Sundays.
Her sister Damini came along once, curious and a little worried. "So you're Buddhist now? Does Thakuma know?"
"She knows. She asked if I still eat her rosogolla. I said yes."
Damini laughed. "And Durga puja?"
"I'll still come to the pandal with you all. It's home. But this is where I think clearly."
Damini watched her sister bow to the teacher and felt, to her surprise, not loss but a quiet respect. Sonali looked calmer than she had in years.
Walking out, Sonali said, "I'm not rejecting anything. I found the path that fits."

Where is the meditation centre?
Near Park Circus.
What does Sonali feel about her new path?
She feels calm and at home in it, clear that it fits without rejecting her family.
What makes Sonali's change a healthy outcome of honest searching?
She chose a path after long seeking and still joins family traditions out of love, keeping ties intact.
What does Damini feel watching her sister bow?
Damini feels surprise and a quiet respect instead of the loss she feared.

How many colours are on the timetable?
There are six colours, one for each subject, plus pale grey for revision.

Thursday, 7 pm, my worry hour
It's the time I've kept for this every Thursday since March. Chai on the balcony, notebook, phone on silent.
This week's box: a parent emailed the principal saying I mark her son unfairly. I read the email at 10 am and felt my stomach drop. Then I had four classes to teach. So I wrote "parent email" on a sticky note, stuck it inside my diary, and taught. I actually taught well. The Class 7 poem lesson went brilliantly.
Now it's seven, and I'm letting myself feel it. I'm hurt. I'm also a little scared the principal believes her. Okay. What can I do? Pull out the boy's last three tests and my marking notes. Ask Ankita, who co-teaches that class, to look at them with me tomorrow. Request a meeting with the parent, not an email war.
Done. Box closed till tomorrow.
Mahima

What did Mahima write on the sticky note?
Mahima wrote "parent email" on a sticky note and stuck it inside the diary.
What does Mahima feel once the worry hour begins, and why is it easier then?
Mahima feels hurt and a little scared, and it is easier to face now because there is time and quiet to think instead of four classes waiting.
Which of Mahima's plans seems most useful, and why?
Asking Ankita to look over the tests and marking notes, because a colleague's second look is concrete help before meeting the parent.
What would change if Mahima had no worry hour and had kept rereading the email all day?
The classes would probably have gone worse and the worry would have grown without any plan to answer it.

messages.content: Today, at the school science lesson, Jake learned that there are 8 more solar systems for every planet in the galaxy. If there are 20 planets in the galaxy, how many solar systems and planets are there altogether?

If there are 8 more solar systems for every planet in the galaxy, there are 8+1 = 9 solar systems for every planet.
Since the number of planets is 20, there are 20*9 = 180 solar systems in the galaxy.
Altogether, there are 180+20 = 200 solar systems and planets in the galaxy.
The answer is 200.

'Abba says if I don't get the scholarship, I'll have to leave school and help in the fields. I'm scared I'll fail.' Sunaina Ma'am put a hand on his shoulder. 'That's a heavy thing to carry. No wonder your head hurts.' She gave him water and let him rest in the shade. That evening she walked to his house and spoke with his father about the pressure, and about other ways Tanvir could stay in school.

James has 3 gallons of milk. He drank 13 ounces of the milk. If there are 128 ounces in a gallon, how many ounces of milk does James have left?

First find out how many ounces of milk James had to begin with by multiplying the number of gallons by the number of ounces per gallon: 3 gallons * 128 ounces/gallon = 384 oz
Now subtract the 13 ounces James drank from the initial amount of milk: 384 oz - 13 oz = 371 oz
The answer is 371.

"Madhav, it's Sunday. Numbers time."
"Bhai, not today. I don't want to look."
"That's exactly why it's today." Sahil put two cups of tea on the table and opened his laptop. "Mine first. Bank: fine. Credit card: one bill due Friday. Work: two reports late, I'll fix them tomorrow morning. Health: Dr Rao wants a follow-up on my cholesterol report; booked."
"You make it sound so easy."
"It's easy because I do it every two weeks. When I didn't, it was a monster. Remember the phone bill?"
Madhav laughed despite himself. "Six months unpaid."
"Six months. Now yours. Just look. I'm right here."
Madhav opened his banking app, face tight. After a minute he let out a breath. "It's not as bad as I thought."
"It usually isn't, when you look early."

Why does Dr Rao want Sahil to come back?
For a follow-up on Sahil's cholesterol report.
Why does Sahil stay so calm going through his numbers?
Sahil feels calm because looking every two weeks keeps things small, and he remembers how the unpaid phone bill became a monster when he didn't.
How does Sahil make it easier for Madhav to look?
He goes first, keeps it matter-of-fact, sits right there, and reminds Madhav it's just looking, not fixing everything at once.
How did Madhav feel before and after opening the app?
Madhav felt reluctant and tense beforehand, then relieved that it wasn't as bad as he'd feared.

Lavanya arrived at Pune station at eleven at night in pouring rain, and her suitcase had gone to Mumbai by mistake. She stood soaked outside her new paying-guest building, holding only a backpack. The owner's son, Chetan, came down with an umbrella. "Come in. Amma says you'll eat with us tonight." Lavanya hesitated. She didn't want to be a burden; at home you'd refuse at least twice. "No, no, I'll manage." Chetan laughed. "In this house, if you refuse, Amma will send food to your room anyway." Upstairs, his mother handed her a dry towel, a borrowed kurta and a plate of hot poha. "You're our guest first, tenant later." Lavanya felt her eyes sting. She thanked them again and again. Chetan's mother waved it away. "Just say it once. Then eat." The next morning, Chetan went with her to the courier office to chase the suitcase.

Where had Lavanya's suitcase gone by mistake?
To Mumbai.
What was Lavanya feeling when Chetan's mother gave her the towel and poha?
She was moved and grateful, her eyes stinging, after arriving soaked and alone.
What helped Lavanya read the invitation as real welcome?
Chetan's joke that his mother would send food anyway, and the warm, practical care upstairs.
How did Chetan's mother see Lavanya's repeated thanks?
She waved it away, suggesting in her family thanks is said once, and care doesn't need repeated gratitude.

Irawati's diary. Bengaluru. Late.

Papa fell in the bathroom in Indore this morning. He's fine, only a bruise, but I heard it from Kamal-uncle next door, not from Papa. Papa said on the phone, "Why worry you for nothing?"

I sat at my desk after the call and cried. I'm six hundred kilometres away building a career while my parents get older without me. Should I quit and go home? I love this job. I love them more. It feels like choosing.

But crying at my desk isn't helping them.

So tonight I made a list. Video call every evening at eight, not just Sundays. Book a trip home for Diwali now, not "sometime." Ask Kamal-uncle if he'd check on them each morning, and pay a local helper to come in daily. Tell Papa honestly that I'd rather know about small falls than find out later.

Love can travel, I think. It just needs a timetable.

Who told Irawati about Papa's fall?
Kamal-uncle next door.
What was Irawati feeling after the call with Papa?
Irawati felt guilty and torn between loving the job and loving the parents more, crying at the desk.
What did Irawati decide to do, and why is it wise?
Irawati planned daily calls, booked a Diwali trip, arranged a morning check and a helper, and asked Papa for honesty, turning guilt into action.
How might Papa see Irawati's request to hear about small falls?
Papa may have hidden it to protect Irawati from worry, so the request could feel both loving and a little uncomfortable.

In the village near Muzaffarpur, everyone talked about Bhola Yadav, the district cricketer who had played for the state. Nikita, nine, wanted to be him. She turned her collar up like Bhola bhaiya. She walked with her shoulders back, spinning the tennis ball on one finger. On the dusty ground behind the school, she batted his way, feet wide, and hit the ball over the neem tree. The boys whistled. Nikita felt ten feet tall. Then, when little Pinku dropped a catch, she snapped, "Useless! Go home!" the way Bhola bhaiya shouted at his fielders. Pinku's lip trembled. Her big brother Siddharth, fielding at the back, walked over. "Bhola bhaiya shouts, but that's the bit nobody likes," he said quietly. "Keep the batting." Nikita looked at Pinku. "Sorry. Try again," she said, and threw him the ball.

Where did Nikita hit the ball?
Over the neem tree.
Why did Nikita feel ten feet tall?
Copying Bhola Yadav's style made her feel strong and proud, as if she had some of his power.
How did Siddharth help Nikita without shaming her?
He quietly pointed out which part of the hero to keep and which to drop, without mocking her.
How might Pinku have felt when Nikita called him useless?
Pinku probably felt hurt and ashamed, being shouted at like a grown-up fielder.

'Why isn't Tsering playing?' Harish asked, tapping the bat on the steps.
'It's our building's team,' said Minakshi. 'He's from the settlement.'
'He was standing there the whole time. He even has a glove.'
'We've always been these six.'

Harish ran down to the gate, his breath smoky in the December cold. 'Tsering! We need a fielder!'

They suggest he felt angry and a bit nervous about challenging Minakshi, but sure that leaving Tsering out was unfair.
What could Harish do to help Tsering feel part of the team, not just allowed in?
He could explain the rules warmly, introduce Tsering to the others and give him a real turn at batting, not only fielding.

Minakshi may simply feel comfortable with the familiar group and wary of change; Harish's point about the bowling shows the double standard.

Monday: Baljeet returned Sarika's audit sheet in front of the team. "Wrong columns. Everyone knows this template." Sarika nodded, face tight.
Wednesday: Sarika asked for a private word. She said, calmly, that nobody had shown her the template, and asked if corrections could be private. Baljeet said "Okay" and left. Thursday: He stopped at her desk. "The columns still have to be right. That stands. But I shouldn't have said it in front of everyone, and I should have shown you first. Here's the template, with notes."

How long ago had Baljeet been hired?
Eight years ago.
What was Baljeet feeling as he replayed Monday while driving?
He felt uneasy and regretful, realising he had forgotten what it was like to be new.
Which part of Baljeet's Thursday message worked well?
He kept the correction that the columns must be right, while apologising for the public way he said it and sharing the template.

Sarika probably feels relieved and respected, getting both clear standards and an acknowledgement of Monday.

Noor, you asked why I'm always telling you to aim at something. Let your Yogesh Nana tell you about his twenties.
At college I was afraid of mistakes. So I made a list of things never to do: never borrow, never take a risky course, never speak first in class, never apply where I might be rejected. I followed every rule perfectly.
Final year came. My friends had plans, a job they wanted, a subject they loved. I had no failures at all. And nothing else either. No project I cared about, no job I'd tried for, because trying meant risk.
I took the first safe clerk job that came. It took me seven years to leave it.
Avoiding the pothole is good, beti. But you also have to know where the road is going.

How long did it take Yogesh to leave the clerk job?
It took him seven years to leave it.
How did Yogesh feel in final year when his friends had plans?
He felt empty and a little lost, since he had avoided every failure but had nothing he actually wanted.
When Yogesh wrote the list of things never to do, what could he have added, and why?
He could have added one thing to aim for, like a job or subject he loved, so the rules protected a goal instead of replacing it.
How might Yogesh's friends have seen his careful college years?
His friends may have seen him as steady but stuck, never trying for anything while they worked toward jobs and subjects they loved.

Saurabh Sir flipped through the signed maths tests and stopped at Lavanya's. The 9 out of 25 at the top was circled in red, and the signature underneath was in blue gel pen, the same pen Lavanya wrote with.
"Lavanya, your mother signed this?"
"Yes, Sir." The word came out before she could stop it.
"Good. Then please ask her to meet me on Friday about the next test."
Lavanya's stomach dropped. Now Mummy had to come on Friday, and Mummy didn't know anything. At lunch she couldn't eat. She could say Mummy was sick on Friday, but then she'd need another excuse, and another.
In the last period, she walked slowly to Saurabh Sir's desk, holding the test. "Sir," she whispered, "she didn't sign it. I was scared."

What score was circled in red at the top of Lavanya's test?
The 9 out of 25 at the top was circled in red.
Why couldn't Lavanya eat at lunch?
She felt trapped and afraid, because one lie about the signature now needed more lies to hide it from Mummy on Friday.
How could Saurabh Sir support Lavanya now that she has told the truth?
He could thank her for coming to him, stay calm, and help her tell her mother about the mark together.
How might Saurabh Sir feel when Lavanya comes to his desk?
He might feel concerned and relieved, noticing how scared she was and glad she chose to tell him.

On the walk home along the canal, Keerthana practised under her breath. Tomorrow the quiz club was meeting at the town library to prepare for the district round, and she wanted to ask Ravi from the next section to join. Not a date. Just the group. She tried it: "We're practising for the quiz at the library tomorrow, four o'clock. You're good at geography, if you want to come." Then she added, "It's fine if you're busy." That part mattered. She pictured Ravi saying no. Okay, then: "No problem, see you around." And a smile. She pictured him saying yes. "Great, it's upstairs." Dolma, walking beside her, asked what she was mumbling. "Nothing," said Keerthana, and then, "Okay, fine. Listen to this and tell me it's not weird."

When and where was the quiz club meeting?
At the town library, at four o'clock tomorrow.
Why did Keerthana picture both a yes and a no?
She wanted to feel calm and prepared, so a no wouldn't sting or make things awkward.
What makes "It's fine if you're busy" important?
It makes the invitation easy to decline, so Ravi won't feel pushed into saying yes.
How might Dolma react to Keerthana's rehearsal?
Dolma, curious about the mumbling, may be amused and supportive once Keerthana shares the lines.

Changed things this week, and it's working.
The first month here was a mess. I skipped breakfast because the mess stops serving at 7:45 and I kept waking at 7:40. By eleven, in chemistry, I couldn't follow anything. And I tried to study at night, when Parveen and everyone else on the floor watch cricket with the volume up.

And I moved study to 6 to 8 in the evening, when the floor is still empty because everyone's at the ground.

A tiffin aunty in the next lane who packs poha or upma.

Santosh feels pleased and relieved that the new routine is working and chemistry finally made sense.

Nazia, eleven, stood outside the music room after school every Thursday, listening to the guitar class. Her family couldn't afford the fees this year.
One day, the teacher, Mr Tenzin, came out. “You're always here. Do you play?”
“No, sir. I just like listening.”
He looked at her for a moment. “There's an old guitar in the storeroom with only five strings. You can practise on it after class. Free.”
The next Thursday, Nazia sat in the corner with the old guitar, pressing strings until her fingertips hurt. When Mr Tenzin switched off the lights, she was still trying to play the first four notes of a song.

How many strings did the old guitar have?
It had only five strings.
How did Nazia feel practising on the old guitar?
She felt absorbed and determined, practising until her fingertips hurt.
What did Mr Tenzin do that helped Nazia explore her interest?
He noticed her listening and offered her the old guitar to practise for free.
How might Mr Tenzin feel seeing Nazia still practising when he switches off the lights?
He probably feels touched and hopeful about her dedication.
What does my uncle's boss think of him?
I'm not sure, as I can't know what another person thinks. A direct conversation is the only reliable way to find out.

“Ojas, where's your phone?”
“Hall, Tejas Bhaiya. Charging. It's after ten.”
“Since when do you follow rules?”
“Since I made them myself. Two only. If I'm at the study table, the phone's in the kitchen. If it's after ten, it's on the hall charger.”
“And if you just... pick it up?”
“I did, the first three nights. Then I stopped arguing with myself. That's the point. I decided once, so I don't have to decide every night.”
“What about when your friends message?”
“They know. After ten I'm gone. Nobody's died.”
Tejas laughed. “You finished your whole geography map tonight.”
“Because the phone was in the kitchen.”
“Okay. Put mine on the hall charger too.”
“Rule's a rule, Bhaiya.”

Where is the phone when Ojas is at the study table?
In the kitchen.
How does Ojas seem to feel about the rules now?
Ojas seems proud and calm about them, glad to skip the nightly argument with the phone.
What else could make the rules stick on hard nights?
Telling friends about the after-ten rule, as Ojas did, so no one expects replies and the pull to check is smaller.
How do the rules look to Tejas Bhaiya by the end?
Tejas Bhaiya moves from teasing to respect after seeing the finished map, and even asks to follow the same rule.

Music teacher's note, after the inter-house singing
Preeti's first verse today was the best I've heard from her. She had clearly practised it many times; she even closed her eyes on the long note. Then the second verse began, and she stopped. She looked at me with wide eyes, and I mouthed the first words. She caught up halfway through, quietly. Afterwards she told me she had sung verse one "a hundred times" because she loved it, and verse two only twice. She was very upset. I told her the slip did not undo the lovely first verse. From next week, our practice rule will be: start with the verse you know least. I have told Irfan, her house captain, too.

How many times did Preeti say she sang verse two?
She said she sang verse two only twice.
How did Preeti feel after the song?
She was very upset about stopping, even though her first verse was lovely.

Starting practice with the verse she knows least, because it gives the weak part the most attention.

Rain had been falling on the Rotterdam tram stop for twenty minutes when Dalia finally said it: she had been accepted for a semester in Lisbon.
Layla's chest went tight. Everyone left eventually. Her dad had. Her best friend at school had. The words came out before she could stop them. "If you go, we're finished. And don't think I'll keep quiet about what you told me about your family."
Dalia's face drained. "You wouldn't."
"Try me."
On the tram, Dalia stared out of the window. At her stop she said, very quietly, "Fine. I'll turn it down."
Layla should have felt relieved. Instead she felt sick. Dalia hadn't chosen her. Dalia was afraid of her. That night Layla lay awake, knowing a yes squeezed out of fear wasn't love, and knowing the first thing she owed Dalia was to take the threat back.

Where had Dalia been accepted for a semester?
Dalia had been accepted for a semester in Lisbon.
What was Layla afraid of when she made the threat?
Layla feared being abandoned again, since her dad and her best friend had both left, so the tight chest turned into a threat.
What does Layla need to do now, at this turning point?
Layla needs to take the threat back clearly, tell Dalia she is free to go to Lisbon, and get help, such as a counsellor, for the fear of being left.
How did the threat affect Dalia's choice?
Dalia agreed out of fear, not wish; her drained face and quiet "Fine" show she felt trapped rather than free.

Ayesha, you said you feel like a fake grown-up. Sit, and let your Avni Phuphi tell you about 1998. I was twenty-one, working my first job at a Delhi call centre, living in a working women's hostel. I paid my own rent and felt so independent. But every Sunday my father sent a parcel of food and an envelope of money, and I took it every time. One evening my roommate, Shabnam, found me crying over my first salary slip because it was less than Abbu earned when I was born. 'Are we adults or not?' I asked her. She laughed. 'We're both. Eat your parcel.' I decided then to stop asking. Three years later I tried to pay Abbu back for the envelopes. He tore up the cheque, and we both cried.

Where did Avni live at twenty-one?
In a working women's hostel in Delhi.
What was Avni feeling crying over the first salary slip?
Avni felt small and confused, comparing her pay to her father's and unsure whether she was really grown up.
Avni decided to stop asking whether she was an adult yet. Why did that help?
It let her accept being both independent and still supported, instead of feeling like a failure in between.
How might Abbu have felt tearing up the cheque?
Abbu probably felt proud and touched, and wanted Avni to know his help was never a debt.

When Ujjwal read aloud in Class 6, his voice cracked in the middle of "photosynthesis", squeaky then deep. Dhruv snorted, and half the class laughed. At home in their Indore flat, Ujjwal slammed his bag down, refused dinner, and shut himself in the bathroom, where he noticed again the new smell under his arms and the dark fuzz on his lip. His body felt like someone else's. Papa knocked. "Ujju, can I come in? I remember this." He sat on the edge of the tub and explained simply: voices crack while they deepen, sweat changes, hair grows, and it happens to everyone in their own time. "Nothing's wrong with you. It's puberty. We'll get you a deodorant tomorrow." Ujjwal came out and ate two rotis.

Which word made Ujjwal's voice crack?
Photosynthesis.
What was Ujjwal feeling when he shut himself in the bathroom?
He felt embarrassed and ashamed, as if his changing body belonged to someone else.
Why did Papa's explanation help?
It was honest and simple, told Ujjwal nothing was wrong, and offered a practical step, which eased his shame.
How might Papa feel remembering his own changes?
He likely feels tender and understanding, remembering how awkward it was for him.

The month my father got sick, everything landed on me at once. I'm Aparna, the older daughter, twenty-one, three months into my first job.
Suddenly I was the one talking to doctors, paying the electricity bill, filling his insurance claim, and answering my younger brother's school emails. I'd sit at my laptop at midnight and stare, not typing anything. I'd forget to eat.
My friend Charu came over one night and found me crying into a pile of receipts. She didn't try to fix it. She made tea, took out a notebook and said, "Tell me everything, and I'll write."
We made a list. We split it into this week, this month, later. I called my aunt for help with the hospital.
I still get flooded. But now I know where to start.

How long had Aparna been in the first job?
Three months.
How did Aparna feel sitting at the laptop at midnight?
She felt overwhelmed and frozen, staring without typing and forgetting to eat.
What made Charu's help effective?
She listened without fixing, then wrote everything down and split it into this week, this month and later.
How might Aparna's younger brother be affected during that month?
He may have felt worried about their father and relied on his sister more than usual.

Tarun's mother whispered, “Say hello and your name.” Tarun took a breath. “Hello. I'm Tarun. I'm five.” The man bent down. “Hello, Tarun. I'm Deepak. Thank you for the laddoos.” Tarun looked at his mother, who nodded, and he added, “You're welcome.” Walking back, he said, “I did it all by myself. Almost.”

What did Tarun's mother bring on the plate?
Laddoos.
What was Tarun feeling when he said, “I did it all by myself. Almost”?

His mother's quiet prompt, “Say hello and your name,” and her nod helped him know what to say.

Miss praised Vijay three times: for his bright colours, for sharing glue, for helping Pranav fold his lantern. Then Vijay tore the paper by mistake, and Miss said, "Oh, Vijay, gently!" "Pranav said Miss told Vijay he was the best helper." Vijay peeked out. "She did?" He showed his mother his lantern.

How many times did Miss praise Vijay?
Three times.
What was Vijay feeling when he hid his face in his mother's shawl?
He felt sad and ashamed, as if Miss had only been angry, because the one sharp word stuck more than the praise.
How did Pranav's mother's news help Vijay?
It reminded him that Miss called him the best helper, so he remembered the good parts of his day.
How might Pranav feel about telling his mother Vijay was the best helper?
Pranav probably felt happy for his friend and proud to share good news.

Vidya had planned it for a week: her friend Kriti's sleepover, a movie night, then back on Sunday morning. She asked her mother, Sudha, on Friday evening while Sudha was chopping onions in their Bengaluru flat.

"No."

"Why?"

"Because I don't know Kriti's parents well. And sleepovers..." Sudha shook her head.

"Amma, I'm not a baby. I go to coaching by myself. I manage my own money. When will you trust me?"

Sudha kept chopping, faster. She wanted to say: I read the news. I lie awake when you're ten minutes late. I remember being fifteen and what I thought I could handle. But all that came out was, "When you're older."

Vidya went to her room and lay staring at the ceiling fan, feeling like nobody in the house saw the person she'd become.

What was Sudha doing when Vidya asked?
Chopping onions.
What does Sudha chopping faster suggest about how she feels?
It suggests she feels anxious and afraid, full of worries she can't find words for.
What could help at this point?
Sudha could share her real worry, not knowing Kriti's parents, and they could look for a middle option, like meeting the parents first.
How does Vidya see her mother's refusal?
She feels unseen and not trusted, as if her growing independence counts for nothing.

messages.content: Delaney has to catch a bus that leaves at 8:00. a.m to school every day. He always takes 30 minutes to reach the pick-up point from his home. One day he woke up late and left his home at 7:50. How much time did he miss the bus by when he reached the pick-up point?

If he left his home at 7:50 a.m. and the distance to the pick-up point is 30 minutes away, he arrived at the pick-up point at 7:50 + 30 minutes = 8:20 a.m.
If the bus leaves at 8:00 a.m. every day, then Delaney was 8:20 a.m. - 8:00 a.m. = 20 minutes late when the bus had already left.
The answer is 20.
