Tomas is hoping to run a marathon next year, which is 26.3 miles. He knows that each month he trains, he can run twice as far as the month before. If he can run 3 miles during the first month of training, how many total months before the marathon should he start training to ensure he can run far enough?

In the first month he can run 3 miles.
In the second month he can run 6 miles because 3 x 2 = 6
In the third month he can run 12 miles because 6 x 2 = 12
In fourth month he can run 24 miles because 12 x 2 = 24
In fifth month he can run 48 miles because 24 x 2 = 48
He needs to start training 5 months ahead of time because 24 < 26.3 and 48>26.3.
The answer is 5.

I think that none of us were surprised when we were asked to see Mrs. Harker a little before the time of sunset. We have of late come to understand that sunrise and sunset are to her times of peculiar freedom; when her old self can be manifest without any controlling force subduing or restraining her, or inciting her to action. This mood or condition begins some half hour or more before actual sunrise or sunset, and lasts till either the sun is high, or whilst the clouds are still aglow with the rays streaming above the horizon. At first there is a sort of negative condition, as if some tie were loosened, and then the absolute freedom quickly follows; when, however, the freedom ceases the change-back or relapse comes quickly, preceded only by a spell of warning silence.

What happens to Mrs. Harker near sunrise and sunset?
These are times of freedom for her: about half an hour before, her old self shows without any controlling force. It ends quickly, with a spell of warning silence before she slips back.
Why does a train horn sound higher as the train comes nearer and lower once it has passed?

The train's movement changes the sound waves. Because the sound waves are squeezed together as the train comes towards us and stretched apart as it goes away, our ears hear a higher note and then a lower one.

Preeti waited until they were alone and admitted her own confusion first, which made it easy for Disha to say she hadn't understood without losing face.

Since there are 1000 ml in 1 liter, then 2 liters is equal to 1000 x 2 = 2000 ml.
Thus, Jasmine can pour 2000/200 = 10 portions of 200 ml milk.
The answer is 10.

messages.content: Show that d^2x/dy^2 = -(d^2y/dx^2)/(dy/dx)^3 and check it for y = e^x. Why is d^2x/dy^2 not 1/(d^2y/dx^2)?

Answer: For y = e^x: d^2x/dy^2 = -1/y^2, and the formula gives -e^x/e^3^x = -e^-^2^x = -1/y^2.

dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx) = 1/y'. Differentiate with respect to y, using the chain rule (d/dy = (dx/dy) d/dx): d^2x/dy^2 = d/dy (1/y') = (d/dx (1/y')) x dx/dy = (-y''/y'^2) x (1/y') = -y''/y'^3 For y = e^x directly: x = ln y, dx/dy = 1/y, d^2x/dy^2 = -1/y^2. With the formula: y' = y'' = e^x, so -e^x/(e^x)^3 = -e^-^2^x = -1/y^2. Same. The naive guess 1/y'' = e^-^x = 1/y is wrong: "flipping" works for first derivatives only. Common mistake: forgetting the chain factor dx/dy.

Every child got a small card from me naming one brave thing they had done. We sang, and I ended with each group standing while the others clapped for them. Then clear goodbyes, with parents told exactly when to arrive. Years later, a grown woman stopped me in a market and said, "Your camp was the best week of my childhood." She had forgotten the rain. Planning a warm, clear last evening with personal cards, songs, clapping and exact pickup times, since people remember the high point and the finish.
How did the grown woman in the market remember the camp?
She remembered it as the best week of her childhood, recalling her card and not the rain.
Yesterday, Bruce and Michael were playing football in the park. Bruce scored 4 goals While Michael scored 3 times more than Bruce. How many goals did Bruce and Michael both score?

Bruce scored 4 goals
Scoring 3 times more than Bruce, Michael scored 4 * 3 = 12 goals.
Both, Bruce and Michael scored 12 + 4 =16 goals.
The answer is 16.

Dear Ritu,
Remember how lonely I sounded in my first month here? I've found a group: a community kitchen that cooks for construction workers on Sundays. They're warm, and I've started looking forward to weekends.
But I did what we promised each other before I left: I asked the boring questions. Who runs it? Where does the money come from? What happens if I want to stop?
Shobha didi, who coordinates, didn't blink. She showed me the donation register pinned on the wall, told me an elected committee changes every year, and said, "People come and go all the time. Come when you can." One volunteer left last month to focus on exams, and they threw her a small farewell.
That's when I relaxed. A group that was scared of questions would have got cross.
And I'm still calling you every Thursday, whatever happens. Tell me about your college fest.
Nazia

When does the community kitchen cook for construction workers?
On Sundays.
What does Nazia mean by 'That's when I relaxed'?
Nazia felt reassured and safe once the group answered openly and treated leaving as normal.
Which of Nazia's choices protects best, and why?
Asking about money, leaders and leaving, and keeping the Thursday calls with Ritu, because it tests the group and keeps an outside friendship strong.
How might Ritu feel reading this letter?
Ritu would likely feel relieved and proud that Nazia kept their promise and still makes time for her.
A store gives a 10% discount for the amount of the sell that was over $1000.  John buys 7 items that each cost $200.  What does his order cost after the discount?

His order came out to 7*200=$1400
So there was 1400-1000=$400 that qualified for the discount
So his discount saved 400*.1=$40
So his purchase came out to 1400-40=$1360
The answer is 1360.

Outside the café, Pradeep stopped. His business partner, Hrithik, was inside, and today Pradeep had to tell him he was leaving the company. His shoulders were up by his ears. He let them drop, planted both feet on the pavement, and breathed out slowly, twice. Then he walked in.
'Hrithik. Thanks for coming. There's something hard I need to say.'
'Sounds serious.'
'It is. I'm going to step away from the business by March.'
Hrithik stared. 'After five years? You're joking.'
Pradeep felt the heat rise. He pressed his feet into the floor and let his breath out long before answering. 'I'm not. I've thought about it for months. I want to leave it in good shape, and I'll help find someone.'
Hrithik was quiet. 'I'm angry. But okay. Tell me why.'

When does Pradeep plan to step away from the business?
By March.
What was Pradeep feeling outside the café?
He was tense and nervous, with his shoulders up by his ears before the hard conversation.
Which body steps helped Pradeep stay clear?
Dropping his shoulders, planting his feet and breathing out slowly before speaking and again when the heat rose.
How might Hrithik feel hearing the news?
He feels shocked and angry after five years, but open enough to ask why.

Monday. Reena noticed Hansa staring at her screen long after the others had gone to lunch. Hansa had spotted a spelling mistake in the client's name in a proposal sent that morning. "This will cost us the account. My boss will say I'm unprofessional. I'll never get the team lead role now." Reena didn't argue. She just asked, "What's the worst that could realistically happen?" Hansa said, "They're offended." "How likely?" A shrug. "Low? They've made typos too."
Wednesday. Hansa was still quiet, checking her mail every ten minutes. Reena asked again, gently, "Has anything bad actually happened yet?" "No." "What would you do if it did?" "Apologise and send a clean copy."
Friday. The client replied with questions about the budget. No mention of the name. Hansa showed Reena the email, then laughed at herself. "Three days of disaster. For one letter."

What mistake did Hansa spot in the proposal?
She spotted a spelling mistake in the client's name.
How was Reena feeling as she watched Hansa over those days?
Reena felt concerned but steady, choosing to ask calm questions rather than argue with Hansa's fears.
Which of Reena's questions was most helpful, and why?
"What would you do if it did?", because it turned a vague dread into a simple plan: apologise and send a clean copy.
What were those three days like for Hansa?
Hansa was anxious and distracted, checking mail every ten minutes, living inside a disaster that never came.

At the village school, during lunch under the peepal tree, three older boys were copying the way Darshan stammered. "W-w-where's your t-t-tiffin?" Darshan stared at his shoes.
Ayesha's heart was pounding so hard she could hear it. These boys were popular. If she said anything, they'd start on her.
She stood up anyway. "Stop it. It's not funny." Her voice cracked on "funny".
The boys laughed at her too. "Ooh, his bodyguard!" One of her friends moved away to sit with another group.
But the boys drifted off. Ayesha sat down next to Darshan and shared her roti. That afternoon she told Master ji what she'd seen, and he spoke to the three boys before home time.

What were the boys copying?
The way Darshan stammered.
What was Ayesha feeling when she stood up?
Ayesha was scared, heart pounding, knowing the popular boys might turn on her, but she acted anyway.
What else did Ayesha do that helped, beyond speaking up?
She sat with Darshan, shared her roti, and told Master ji, who spoke to the boys that same day.
What did standing up cost Ayesha?
The boys laughed at her too, and one friend moved away to sit with another group.

In her first week as a trainee at the bank branch in Indore, Madhuri tried to read her manager, Saurabh, all the time.
When she brought him the first report, he smiled quickly, mouth only, and said, "Thanks, put it there." Her heart dropped. Was it bad?
On Wednesday, when she solved a customer's problem at the counter, he watched and smiled differently: slower, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "Nicely handled."
She started keeping a mental list: quick smile equals polite, slow eye smile equals real.
But on Friday, when he gave her the busiest counter, he didn't smile at all. Just nodded. She panicked. Then a colleague told her, "That's his biggest compliment. He only gives that counter to people he trusts."
Madhuri stopped trusting her list. She asked him for feedback instead. He said, "You're doing well. I'm just not a big smiler."

Where was Madhuri a trainee?
At the bank branch in Indore.
What was Madhuri feeling when Saurabh gave only a quick smile?
Madhuri felt anxious and worried, reading the mouth-only smile as a sign the report was bad.
What did Madhuri learn about reading smiles?
That the difference between polite and warm smiles is only a rough clue, so asking for feedback is more reliable.
How did the colleague see Saurabh's nod on Friday?
The colleague saw it as his biggest compliment, a sign of trust, even without a smile.

I'm Elizabeth. My cousin Salma watches the same video maker every evening. She copies the way she says hello and wants a bedroom like hers. Last Sunday we watched together, and Salma paused on a smiling clip. "She never has a bad day," she said. Then she frowned. "But they cut bits out, don't they? Her room video took the whole day to film, she said so at the end." She didn't say more. Later she sat with her sketchbook and drew for an hour, tearing out two pages she didn't like. I couldn't tell if she felt inspired or a little sad. Maybe both. She still watches every evening.

What did Salma say the video maker never has?
She said the video maker never has a bad day.
How might Salma have felt when she frowned?
Possibly doubtful and a little disappointed, realising the videos are edited so the smiling life may not be as perfect as it looks.
How could Salma keep enjoying the videos in a healthy way?
She can let the admiration inspire her own drawing while remembering that everybody's real life has hard moments too.
How does Elizabeth see Salma's admiration?
As something that seems inspiring and harmless, though Elizabeth admits being unable to tell whether Salma felt inspired or a little sad.
My family is going to visit a fort next weekend. What can I do to enjoy it more than the last time we went somewhere historical?
A few small things help a lot. Read a short bit about the fort before you go, so you have a story in mind, and bring a notebook for sketches or questions. What didn't you enjoy last time?
It was just walking and reading boards.
Then give yourself a game. Look for one hidden detail in each room, such as carvings, small windows or old stairs. Ask a guide a few questions if there is one.
That sounds more fun than reading boards.
It usually is. You could also take photos of your favourite spots and make a small album afterwards.
My brother wants to go to the highest point of the fort. Should we?
If the climb is open and looks safe, it's usually the best view. Check the steps and rails, wear shoes with grip and go slowly.
Okay. We'll take water too.
Smart. Carry it in a bag with a strap, so your hands are free for the rails.
My cousin has her classical dance exam tomorrow. Write a good-luck message for her, about 45 words.

Dear cousin,
Good luck for your dance exam tomorrow! You have practised hard, and I am sure it will show. Just breathe, smile and enjoy it. I am cheering for you, and I know you will shine on that stage.
With love

At the college sports club office, Nazia, the badminton captain, asked Zubin to sit down. She had the team list for the inter-college finals in her hand. "Zubin, I want to tell you this directly. You're not in the final squad." Zubin went still. "Oh." "Your footwork has improved a lot. But the other two are more consistent in doubles right now." She stopped there. She didn't pile on reasons or say she'd fought for him. Zubin looked at the floor. "I really wanted it." "I know. I'm sorry." She stayed sitting, quiet, until he looked up. "Can I keep practising with the team?" "Yes. And I'd like you as reserve." Zubin nodded slowly. "Thanks for telling me yourself."

What position did Nazia hold?
She was the badminton captain.
What might Nazia have been feeling as she stayed sitting quietly?
Nazia probably felt sad and uncomfortable giving the news, but cared enough to stay with Zubin.
What made Nazia's delivery clear and kind?
She said it plainly, gave one honest reason without over-explaining, and stayed with him.
How did Zubin see the way Nazia told him?
He appreciated that she told him herself, and asked to keep practising.

For four months Irawati had done everything right: the same wake time, no phone after ten, a wind-down routine, no evening tea. Still she lay awake until three and woke exhausted, and the board exams were six weeks away. Her mother Aadhya had watched the dark circles and the swings between hope and despair. "It's not lack of effort," Aadhya said one Saturday. "Let's ask a doctor to look at this properly." Irawati hesitated. "Will they think I'm making it up?" "They'll listen." The doctor took a long history, asked about her days, and arranged a check-up and a follow-up visit. There was no quick answer, but for the first time Irawati felt that someone whose job this was had taken it seriously. She kept her routine while waiting.

How long had Irawati kept the good habits?
Irawati had kept the good habits for four months.
What was Irawati worried about before seeing the doctor?
Irawati worried that the doctor would think she was making it up.
What could the family do if the exam pressure grows while waiting for the follow-up, and why?
They could tell the school about the situation and keep the routine going, because support at school and steady habits make the wait easier.
How does Aadhya see the situation?
Aadhya sees a daughter who has tried hard with no result and decides that persistent sleep trouble needs a professional's assessment.

When Chachu shouted about the broken phone, my little brother Dhruv went stiff on the rug. He didn't cry. Then he toddled over, smiling too wide, and pressed his toy car into Chachu's hand again and again. I'm Harsha, I'm eleven, and I couldn't tell what he felt. Mumma scooped him up and hummed. Chachu sat down and spoke softly, and Dhruv's shoulders dropped.

What did Dhruv press into Chachu's hand?
Dhruv pressed his toy car into Chachu's hand again and again.
What might Dhruv's stiff body and too-wide smile suggest he was feeling?
They suggest Dhruv was frightened by the shouting and was trying to please Chachu, though Harsha could not be sure.
What could Chachu do next time he is upset near Dhruv?
Chachu could lower his voice or step away, since the shouting, not Dhruv, set off the frightened reaction.
How does Harsha see Dhruv's sudden sweetness?
Harsha noticed the smile looked too wide and odd, and admitted not knowing what Dhruv felt inside.

The Shimla ice-cream parlour was crowded on Christmas Eve, and snow-wet coats steamed in the queue. The board above the counter listed thirty-two flavours.
"Your turn, Nihal," said Urmila Mausi.
Nihal read the board from top to bottom. Butterscotch? Rose? Blueberry swirl? Behind him someone sighed loudly. The server tapped the scoop on the glass.
"Mango," he blurted.
At the table his cousin Tara was licking a scoop of chocolate chip. Nihal stared at it, then at his mango. "I should have got that." Halfway through he added, "Or rose. Rose might have been the best."
Urmila Mausi laughed. "Last summer the stall had four flavours, and you finished yours in two minutes and never looked back."

How many flavours did the board list?
The board listed thirty-two flavours.
Why does Nihal keep wishing he had picked something else?
With so many flavours, every one he didn't pick still seems possibly better, so he feels unsure and disappointed with his mango even while eating it.
What could Urmila Mausi try with Nihal next time?
She could help him narrow the board to three flavours he likes before he reaches the counter, so the pick is quick and feels settled.
How might the person sighing behind Nihal see his long wait?
They were probably impatient, standing in a crowded, steamy queue while he read all thirty-two flavours.

In Mahima's kasba, everyone knew when she was coming: loud laugh, bicycle bell, a bag of roasted peanuts to share. This week her whole calendar was the temple fair, the new film at the town's old cinema hall, and Friday's chaat trip with six friends. Her friends adored her; she made every plan feel like a festival. On Thursday, Bhavna stopped her at the school gate. "Mahi, the science project. It's due Monday. Have you started?" Mahima's smile faded. She hadn't even opened the book. She thought of the chaat trip, then of Sir's face on Monday. "Friday I'll go for one hour only," she said slowly. "And Saturday you come to my house and we do the project." Bhavna laughed. "One hour? You?"

What was due on Monday?
The science project.
What was Mahima feeling when her smile faded?
She felt a jolt of worry and guilt, realising her fun plans had crowded out the project she hadn't started.
What choice did Mahima make, and could it work?
She cut the chaat trip to one hour and planned a work session with Bhavna on Saturday, which could keep some fun while getting the project done.
How does Bhavna see Mahima's love of fun?
Bhavna enjoys Mahima's energy but knows it can take over, which is why Bhavna reminds her and laughs at the 'one hour' promise.

It is Sankranti week, and the community centre play corner smells of til laddoos. Urmila, five, kneels beside her little sister Nirmala, whose shoelace has come loose again. "Look. Make a bunny ear. Now another bunny ear. Now they hug." Nirmala's fingers get tangled. Urmila waits, tongue poking out, and guides her hand. The loop wobbles, then holds. Urmila jumps up. "Aunty! I taught her! I know it and now she knows it!" She beams all the way to the laddoo table.

What does Urmila tell Nirmala to make first?
A bunny ear.
Why does Urmila jump up and shout to Aunty?
She feels proud and excited 😊 to be the one who knows how, and even prouder that now her little sister knows it too.
How could the centre aunty support Urmila's wish to help?
The aunty could praise her patience, not just the bow, and give her other small chances to show younger children something.
What is it like for Nirmala when Urmila guides her hand?
Nirmala probably feels helped and a little proud too, because her big sister waits patiently instead of doing it for her.
Did the principal announce a new date for the annual day?
I can't check that, because I can't see announcements made at school this week. The school notice board or the parents' message group should have it.

In the college counselling centre, Harish twisted his hands in his lap. "At first Rashmi said I was the smartest person she'd ever met. She'd tell everyone."
The counsellor nodded. "And now?"
"Now if I talk about my day, she changes the subject to hers. If she's late, it's my fault for 'rushing' her. Last week I got a good grade and she said, 'Must've been an easy test.'" He laughed, but it came out thin. "Maybe I'm too sensitive. Maybe I really am the problem."
"You've said 'maybe I'm the problem' three times today," the counsellor said gently. "What was it like before you met her?"
Harish was quiet. "I was sure of myself. I had friends I saw every week."
"Let's look at that together, over the next few sessions. And I'd like you to reconnect with one of those friends this week."
Harish nodded slowly.

What did Rashmi say when Harish got a good grade?
"Must've been an easy test."
How does Harish feel about himself now?
He feels small and full of self-doubt, wondering if he is too sensitive or really the problem.
Why is talking with the counsellor an important step for Harish?
A trusted outsider can help him see the pattern of being flattered, then blamed and unheard, before it wears down his confidence further.
How does the counsellor see Harish's repeated "maybe I'm the problem"?
The counsellor notices it as a sign of rising self-doubt and gently turns him toward how sure of himself he used to be.

For a month Ines had accepted every excuse. Abebe had a headache on the day of the class trip to Sintra. He was "too tired" for his friend's birthday. He wanted to skip football because "the coach is annoying". Each time she said, "Okay, stay home," partly because arguing upset him so much and partly because the house was calmer.
Then on Friday he asked her to phone the pharmacy for him, something he used to do easily. Her stomach sank. The excuses weren't about headaches. His world was shrinking, and she had been helping it shrink.
That evening she didn't push and didn't rescue. She sat on his bed. "I think things feel scary lately. I'm not going to make you do everything. But let's pick one small thing this week. You choose."
Abebe was quiet for a long time. "Maybe football. Just the warm-up."
"Just the warm-up," she agreed. "I'll wait in the car."

What did Abebe ask Ines to do for him on Friday?
Phone the pharmacy for him.
What did Ines feel when Abebe asked her to phone the pharmacy?
She felt a sinking worry, realising the excuses hid fear and that her kindness had been helping his world shrink.
Why is Ines's new approach better than pushing or rescuing?
She acknowledges the fear and invites one small, chosen step, so Abebe builds courage without being forced or shielded.
What might Abebe be feeling when he chooses the warm-up?
He likely feels nervous but a little relieved, since the step is small and he got to choose it.

On the bus home from the kasba, Harish kept rereading the number that had called about his "electricity bill". The caller had said the connection would be cut tonight and talked him into installing a screen-sharing app. Within minutes his account was lighter.

His jaw was tight. He had a plan: message the number as a buyer, set a meeting near the bus stand, and catch the man himself.

At the tea stall he told Ojas everything. Ojas shook their head. "Give the number, the screenshots and the bank message to the cyber cell. If you go alone you could lose more, or get hurt."

Then a new message arrived: "We recover lost money. Pay a small fee first." Harish's thumb hovered. Ojas took one look and said, "That's the same trick again."

Harish breathed out and handed over the phone.

Where did Harish tell Ojas everything?
Harish told Ojas everything at the tea stall.
What was Harish feeling and wanting after the call?
Harish was furious, with his jaw tight, and he wanted to catch the man himself by pretending to be a buyer.
What was the wise step Ojas suggested, and why?
Ojas suggested giving the number, screenshots and bank message to the cyber cell, because chasing the man alone could mean losing more or getting hurt.
How does Ojas see the "recover lost money" message?
Ojas sees it as the same trick again, a fee-first offer aimed at someone who is angry and wants the money back. 🤍

In a rented room in Leeds, Siddiq read the message again: "Come alone tomorrow, the leader wants a private word." His stomach tightened. For weeks the evening meetings had felt friendly, but the private talks had begun asking for his passport "for safekeeping". He called Valentina, a friend from his course. "I want to stop going. Will you be at my flat at six?" She said yes and told him to ring his parents as well. The next day he did not go. Two members waited outside his building, and Valentina and a flatmate stayed at his side until they left. He wrote to the group that he would not be back and saved every message. His parents told him that if anyone threatened him he should call the police.

What had the private talks begun asking for?
The private talks had begun asking for his passport for safekeeping.
How was Siddiq feeling when he read the message?
Siddiq felt uneasy and anxious, and his stomach tightened.
What else could Siddiq do, and why?
Siddiq could tell a course tutor or the university welfare team and go to the police if threats came, because more people who know make the exit safer.
How might Valentina have seen the situation?
Valentina was probably worried but glad to be trusted, and ready to stay by his side.

Outside the village anganwadi, Rashmi stood by the mango tree and watched Jaya walk up to three girls building a mud fort. "Can I play too?" Jaya asked, and the girls scooted over and handed her a bucket. Rashmi kept watching, her fingers twisting her frock. The following morning she went to the sandpit and up to a group making mud laddoos. She took a breath, smiled, and said, "Can I play too?" A boy patted the sand beside him. "Sit here. You do the sprinkles." Rashmi sat down at once.

What words did Rashmi use at the sandpit?
Rashmi said, "Can I play too?"
What was Rashmi feeling as she watched Jaya, twisting her frock?
Rashmi felt nervous and hopeful. She wanted to join in but was not sure how, and the twisting fingers show it.
What could Rashmi try if a group said no, and why?
She could have a second choice ready, like another group to ask. Then one refusal would not end her plan.
How does Rashmi's arrival look to the boy who patted the sand?
He sees a child who asked politely with a smile, so it is easy to say yes. He even gives her a job. 🙂
Ravi says a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm has a perimeter of 10 cm. Meena says it is 24 cm. Who is right?

Answer: Neither. P = 2 x (6 + 4) = 20 cm.

Ravi added only two sides, 6 + 4 = 10: that is only half the way round. Meena multiplied, 6 x 4 = 24: that is the AREA (the number of 1 cm squares inside), not the perimeter. The perimeter is 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm. Draw it on squared paper and walk round it with a finger.

Keerthana: a college page. it said she takes money from girls and never teaches

How many shares did the post have from Keerthana's story?
It had 60 shares from Keerthana's story.
What was Keerthana feeling on learning the claim was false?
Keerthana felt sick with guilt and ashamed, having meant to protect people but ended up hurting the teacher.
What did Keerthana's correction get right?
It was plain and had no excuses: it said the claim was false, that sharing it was wrong, and asked people to stop forwarding it.
How might the tailoring teacher feel about the correction and the apology?
The teacher may still be hurt by the angry calls, but a public correction and a personal apology could bring some relief and repair.
85 is exactly halfway between 80 and 90. How do we round it? And 250 to the nearest 100? And 4,500 to the nearest 1000?

Answer: 85 -> 90, 250 -> 300, 4,500 -> 5,000. Halfway numbers round UP.

On the number line 85 is 5 steps from 80 and 5 steps from 90, so neither is nearer. Mathematicians agreed on a rule: when the deciding digit is 5, round up. This fits the pattern "0 to 4 down, 5 to 9 up": there are five digits in each group. The same rule works for every place: 250 has tens digit 5, so 300; 4,500 has hundreds digit 5, so 5,000.
Meera felt slighted when she was not invited. What was it she felt?

Slighted means treated as if you were not important, in a way that hurts your feelings. It is an adjective here.
Example: He felt slighted when no one asked for his opinion.
James and Ali together own $250. If you know that James owns $40 more than Ali, then calculate the amount owned by James.

Let X be the amount owned by James. The amount owned by Ali is X - $40.
The total amount owned by both of them X + (X - $40) = $250.
Combining like terms, we get X*2 - $40 = $250.
Adding $40 to both sides, we get X*2 = $290.
Dividing both sides by 2, we get X = $145.
The answer is 145.
What mood is associated with Raga Bageshri?
Raga Bageshri is associated with a longing, intimate, romantic mood.

It was Lohri week in the village, and the bonfire was being built outside. Inside, Amandeep, six, was watching cartoons on Dadaji's phone when the timer rang.
"Five more minutes!"
"Timer's done, puttar. We agreed."
Amandeep scowled, then asked, "Dadaji, the ad said if I drink that juice I'll fly like the boy. Can I?"
Dadaji laughed. "That's pretend, like the cartoon. They want you to buy it."
Amandeep's friend Wasim knocked at the door. "Come, the fire's starting!"
Amandeep handed back the phone and ran out.

What did the ad say would happen if Amandeep drank the juice?
The ad said he would fly like the boy.
What was Amandeep feeling when the timer rang?
He felt annoyed and disappointed, asking for five more minutes and scowling.
What could Dadaji do to help Amandeep with screen limits?
He could keep the timer they agreed on, and plan something fun afterwards, like the bonfire, so switching off feels easier.
How does Wasim's knock change the moment for Amandeep?
Wasim's invitation gives Amandeep something exciting to do, so he stops sulking and happily hands the phone back.

In the kasba, Karthik had been going to the meditation house behind the grain market for two months. This week the leader made three requests in one breath: a donation "for your growth", the phone handed over "to quiet the mind", and no more visits to old friends who "drag you down".

Karthik walked to Sabina's tea stall afterwards with the phone still in a pocket, and sat without ordering.

"You look like someone swallowed your tongue," Sabina said.

Karthik repeated the three requests slowly. Said aloud, they sounded different.

Sabina put down the kettle. "Money, phone, friends. That's how you control someone, not how you grow them. Keep your phone. Keep your own money. Keep coming here. And call your uncle in the city before you decide anything."

For the first time all week, Karthik took the phone out.

Where did Karthik walk after the leader's requests?
Karthik walked to Sabina's tea stall.
Why did Karthik sit at the stall without ordering?
Karthik was unsettled by the three requests and needed someone outside the meditation house, which the silence and slow repeating of the requests show.
What would you advise Karthik about the phone, money and friends?
Keep the phone and own money, keep seeing old friends, keep a way to leave, and call the uncle in the city or another outsider before deciding.
How does Sabina see the leader's three requests?
Sabina sees money, phone and friends together as a way to control someone, not help them grow.

The monsoon waves at Marine Drive were throwing spray over the wall, and Kunal had his shoes off. "Let's climb down to the tetrapods. Selfie in the waves!" Two others were already at the wall. Sonali laughed loudly. "Absolutely not. I'm far too pretty to be fished out by the coast guard." A few people giggled. "Anyway, the new animated film starts at six. Popcorn's on me if we leave now." Tenzin, who had been hanging back with his hands in his pockets, jumped in at once. "I'm in. I've been wanting to see it." Kunal looked at the waves, then at the others drifting after Sonali. "Fine," he said, pulling his shoes back on. "But I'm choosing the seats."

What did Kunal want to do?
Climb down to the tetrapods for a selfie in the waves.
What was Tenzin feeling while hanging back with his hands in his pockets?
He was probably uneasy about the plan: he had been hanging back with his hands in his pockets and jumped at the film idea at once, which suggests he felt relieved.
Why did Sonali's joke and film offer work?
The joke kept things light and the offer gave everyone a face-saving alternative, so others who were uneasy could switch without seeming scared.
How does Kunal seem to feel as the group drifts away?
Kunal gives in with a grumble about choosing the seats, which lets him save face while dropping the dare.

metadata.subtype: Approach: humour or redirect to another activity [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Pranav, and last year I watched my flatmate Gopika shrink a little every week. Her boyfriend Vivek would call her dramatic whenever she had an opinion, and once he left her stranded at a wedding because she talked to an old classmate. She always said the same thing: "That's just Vivek. He's intense." I wanted to shake her. I started a dozen arguments in my head. But I remembered my own sister, who stopped telling us anything after we kept attacking her boyfriend. So one Sunday, over tea, I said it once. "I care about you. The way Vivek talks to you worries me. I won't nag, but I'm here." Gopika changed the subject. Four months later, at midnight, she knocked on my door and said, "Can we talk?" I put the kettle on.

Where did Vivek leave Gopika stranded?
At a wedding.
Why did Pranav hold back from arguing with Gopika?
Pranav felt frustrated and wanted to shake her, but was cautious, remembering how attacking a sister's boyfriend had made the sister stop sharing.
Which choice of Pranav's mattered most, and why?
Saying it once and then staying available, because it kept trust intact so Gopika knew where to turn four months later.
How might Gopika have felt knocking on the door at midnight?
Gopika was probably nervous and vulnerable, but trusted that Pranav would listen without saying "I told you so".

Why did Sachin say that cricket was boring?

Saturday. Sachin's diary. The team list went up. I wasn't on it. Dolma asked if I was okay and I said, "Whatever, cricket's boring anyway." I even laughed. Then I went home and lay on my bed for two hours. The truth is I practised every evening for a month. If I say I don't care, then it doesn't look like I lost. That's the idea, anyway. But it doesn't make the heavy feeling go away. Dolma messaged later: "You're allowed to be upset, you know." I didn't reply. I'll maybe reply tomorrow. Or talk to Coach about what I can work on.
He was hurt about missing the team after a month of daily practice. Saying he did not care was his way of making it look as if he had not lost.

Read this:

Sonali, you're writing a pitch deck, and I see you've written "built the whole community network." Did you? Let me, Lalremsiami, tell you something from my own first job in Aizawl.
I was twenty-four, with a small health NGO. My manager ran the village survey; I carried the forms and typed the data. When a donor visited, I introduced myself as "the person who designed our village survey." Everyone does it, I thought. It sounds better.
The donor was delighted. She asked me to present the survey method at a meeting in Shillong the following month. I spent that month in terror, reading everything my manager had written, trying to become the person I'd claimed to be.
In the end, I told my manager. She was quiet for a long moment. Then she came to Shillong with me and presented it herself. I stood beside her and did the part I had actually done.
So, Sonali. What did you build?

What did young Lalremsiami actually do for the village survey?
Lalremsiami carried the forms and typed the data.
How did young Lalremsiami feel during the month before Shillong?
Lalremsiami felt terrified and ashamed, desperately reading her manager's work to become the person she had claimed to be.
What turning point in the story helped young Lalremsiami out of the trap?
Lalremsiami told the manager the truth, and they presented together, each doing the part they had actually done.
How might the manager have felt when Lalremsiami told her?
The manager was probably hurt and disappointed at first, since her own work had been claimed, but she chose to help rather than expose Lalremsiami.

Read this:

I sit next to Madhav in Hindi class, so I see it up close. When the teacher says, "Madhav, read the next paragraph," his ears go red first, then his neck. His hand grips the book so tight the page crinkles. He reads the first line, stops, and stares at the words as if they've turned into another language. He sits down, and for the rest of the period he doesn't look up. Last month he stopped coming on Fridays, when we have recitation. I don't know what he's thinking; he never says. But this week the teacher started letting him read sitting down, one line, then two. On Friday he came. He read four lines. His ears were still red. He finished anyway.
Yusuf

What happens to Madhav's ears when he is asked to read?
His ears go red first, then his neck.
What might Madhav's staring at the words suggest he feels, given Yusuf can't be sure?
It suggests his mind has gone blank with fear, even though the words are familiar.
What change did the teacher make, and what happened?
The teacher let him read sitting down, one line then two, and on Friday he came and read four lines.
How might Yusuf feel watching Madhav finish four lines?
Yusuf may feel glad and quietly proud of him, having seen up close how hard it was.

Read this:

Monday. Mahima walked into the art room, and Jatin's heart jumped. He opened his mouth to say hi, and nothing came out. He stared at his paintbrush instead, face hot.
Wednesday. Jatin noticed he'd been watching the door, waiting for her. He made himself stop. He didn't want to be weird about it. It was a nice feeling, not a bad one.
Friday. In art, Mahima asked, "Can I borrow your blue?"
Jatin handed it over. "Sure. Your river painting's really good."
"Thanks!" she said, and went back to her seat.
Jatin grinned at his paper. That was enough. Just friendly.

What did Mahima ask to borrow?
Jatin's blue paint.
What was Jatin feeling on Monday when Mahima walked in?
He felt shy and flustered, his heart jumping and his face hot, unable to speak.
What did Jatin do that kept things comfortable?
He stopped watching the door, and when Mahima spoke to him he was simply friendly and kept it light.
How might Mahima see Jatin's compliment?
Mahima probably sees it as a friendly, kind comment, since she thanks him and goes back to her seat.
She walked in to the kitchen and opened the fridge. Is "in to" two words?

She walked into the kitchen and opened the fridge.
Why: "Into" is one word for movement inside.

Mark went to a store where he spent one-half of his money, and then spent $14 more. He then went to another store where he spent one-third of his starting money, and then spent $16 more. If he then had no money left, how much did he have when he entered the first store?

Let X be the money Mark had. Mark spent 1/2*X + 14 in the first store and 1/3*X + 16 in the second store.
Mark has X - 1/2*X - 14 - 1/3*X - 16 = $0 left.
Combining like terms, we get 1/6*X - 30 = $0.
Adding 30 to both sides and multiplying both sides by 6, we find that Mark had X = $180 when he entered the first store.
The answer is 180.

Alex is saving up for a new car. He already has $14,500 saved up and the car costs $14,600. He decides that to make the last of the money he will deliver groceries for people in the neighborhood.  He charges $1.5 per trip and then 5% of the price of the groceries. If he makes 40 trips and has saved up enough, how many dollars' worth of groceries did he deliver?

He needs to save up $100 because 14,600 - 14,500 = 100
He earned $60 off trips because 40 x 1.5 = 60
He earned $40 off groceries because 100 - 60 = 40
He delivered $800 in groceries because 40 / .05 = 800
The answer is 800.
A large amount of students joined the drama club this year. Which word is wrong?

A large number of students joined the drama club this year.
Why: "Number" goes with countable nouns, "amount" with uncountable.
Will it clear up for the open-air film show on Friday?
I don't know, because I can't check forecasts. A weather page for your town will show the outlook for Friday.

Read this:

Last year I found the best joke in the world. I'm Dolma, and the joke was: "Why did the toilet paper roll down the hill? To get to the bottom!" I told it to Ama at breakfast. I told it to the bus driver. I told it to Lokesh at lunch, then again in the line. By the tenth time, Lokesh groaned so loudly the whole line turned round. Nobody laughed. My face went hot. That evening I tried it on my baby cousin, who laughs at everything, so that didn't count. Then I changed my plan. I waited until Lokesh burped in assembly and whispered, "Excuse you, the bottom's that way." He snorted so hard he had to step out. Timing, I learned. Not ten times.

Who did Dolma tell the joke to at breakfast?
Dolma told it to Ama at breakfast.
How did Dolma feel when nobody laughed the tenth time?
Dolma felt embarrassed, face going hot, when Lokesh groaned and the whole line turned round.
What did Dolma learn from the groans?
That a joke needs the right moment and a fresh audience, not ten repeats, so Dolma waited for a fitting moment 😅
How might Lokesh have felt hearing the joke for the tenth time?
He was probably bored and a bit irritated, which is why he groaned so loudly.
Each of the students have a library card. Which verb is right?

Each of the students has a library card.
Why: "each" is singular, so "has".
Chuck breeds dogs.  He has 3 pregnant dogs.  They each give birth to 4 puppies.  Each puppy needs 2 shots and each shot costs $5.  How much did the shots cost?

He has 3*4=12 puppies
So they need 12*2=24 shots
That means the vaccines cost 24*5=$120
The answer is 120.

Read this:

On Pongal evening, Nandini, five, sat on the steps of their Chennai flat while Lakshmi Paati oiled her hair.
"Tell me your day," Paati said.
"First, Amma and I drew the kolam with white powder. Then the pongal pot boiled over and everybody shouted 'Pongalo pongal!' Then… wait." Nandini frowned. "No, before the pot, we tied sugarcane at the door."
"And at the end?"
"At the end, a cow from the lane ate the sugarcane!" Nandini laughed so hard she nearly fell off the step.
Her cousin Vinod, listening from the doorway, said, "That really happened! I saw it!"

What happened at the end of Nandini's day?
At the end, a cow from the lane ate the sugarcane.
How did Nandini feel when she remembered the cow?
She felt delighted and amused, laughing so hard she nearly fell off the step.
How could Paati help Nandini tell events in order?
She could keep asking "What happened first, then, and at the end?" and let Nandini fix mistakes herself, as she did with the sugarcane.
How does Vinod react to Nandini's story?
Vinod joins in excitedly, confirming the cow story because he saw it too.

Read this:

When Appa's eyesight started failing last year, my brother Joseph and I made every mistake at first. We argued about him on the phone as if he couldn't hear. We rearranged his kitchen without asking, and he couldn't find his own tea. He went quiet for a week. I'm Gopika, and that silence taught me. We sat down with him on the veranda and asked, 'Appa, what's hardest? What do you want to keep doing?' He said he wanted to keep walking to church and cooking his Sunday fish curry. So we put bright tape on the steps, labelled his spice jars in big letters and got a talking clock. Joseph took the hospital visits, I took the groceries, and his neighbour walks with him on Sundays. He still grumbles. But he's in charge of his own life again.

What did Gopika and Joseph put on the steps?
Bright tape.
How did Gopika feel after Appa went quiet for a week?
Gopika felt guilty and sobered, realising they had been making decisions over him.
What changed once they asked Appa what he wanted?
They adapted the home to keep him independent and shared responsibilities fairly between the siblings and a neighbour.
How might Appa have felt when he couldn't find his own tea?
He probably felt frustrated and hurt, as if his own kitchen was no longer his.
You are a cricket commentator. Describe a six in exactly two sentences, using the word "boundary".
The batter swings hard and the ball sails high. It clears the boundary rope and the crowd roars.

Sam is stocking up on canned tuna. He got 9 cans at the supermarket, and had 5 coupons for 25 cents off a single can per coupon. He paid $20 and got $5.50 in change. How many cents does a can of tuna cost?

His total without the coupons was $20 - $5.50 = $14.50
He had 5 coupons that each saved him 25 cents, so the full price of all the tuna is $14.50 + 5*$0.25 =$15.75.
He bought 9 cans of tuna, so each can costs $15.75 / 9 = $1.75
As 1 dollar has 100 cents 1.75 * 100 = 175 cents
The answer is 175.
A tap drips 1 cup of water every hour. How many cups are wasted in a week?
About 168 cups are wasted. Because there are 24 hours in a day and 7 days in a week, and 24 times 7 is 168.

Thomas's internship desk in the Gurugram office faced a window of grey towers. On Wednesday, eating rajma chawal at his desk, he opened a thread about a missing girl from another state: her mother's voice note, the school photo, strangers arguing in the replies. He scrolled for the whole lunch hour.
At three he realised he had read the same spreadsheet row four times. His jaw ached. When Chinmay from the next desk asked, "Chai?" Thomas snapped, "Not now," then felt bad.
On the metro home he kept checking the thread. No update. In his flat he didn't cook, just lay on the bed with the fan on, low and restless. "What's wrong with me?" he typed to nobody, then deleted it.
Around ten Chinmay messaged: "You okay? You looked far away today." Thomas stared at it for a while before replying, "Honestly, don't know."

What was Thomas eating at his desk on Wednesday?
He was eating rajma chawal at his desk.
What does Thomas's typed and deleted message suggest about how he felt that evening?
It suggests he felt low and confused, unsure why he felt so bad, and not ready to share it with anyone.
What could Thomas do when he gets Chinmay's message, and why might it help?
He could tell Chinmay about the thread and how it stayed with him all day; naming where the heaviness came from could help him set it down and take a break from checking.
How might Chinmay have felt when Thomas snapped about chai?
Chinmay might have felt brushed off at first, but the late message shows that Chinmay noticed something was wrong and cared more than minded.

Read this:

Trisha had tried everything on her own: breathing apps, journals, cold showers, a book on worry she had underlined twice. But the anxiety kept winning. She'd turned down a promotion because it involved travel, and last month she had left a friend's wedding halfway, heart hammering, sure she would faint.
When she finally decided to see someone, the first psychologist she called had a six-week waiting list, and her manager needed her for a product launch.
Devika, her friend since college, didn't lecture. She sat with her one evening and helped search: a clinic near the metro, an online therapist with evening slots, the family doctor as a first step. She didn't book anything for her. She just said, "I'll come with you to the first one if you want."
Trisha booked the family doctor for Saturday and a therapist for the following Tuesday evening, after work. Putting down the phone, she felt oddly relieved, as if she had set down a bag she'd been carrying alone.

How long was the first psychologist's waiting list?
Six weeks.
How did Trisha feel after booking the appointments?
She felt relieved, as if she had set down a heavy bag she'd carried alone.
Why is Trisha's choice to see a doctor and therapist sensible?
Self-help hadn't worked and anxiety was limiting her life, so qualified support is the wise next step.
What might Devika feel helping without taking over?
Devika is patient and caring, glad to help search while letting Trisha make the bookings herself.

Read this:

Tuesday
Aparna and I sat next to each other for two years. We shared earphones, lunch boxes, the lot. Since she became lead she eats with the managers and replies to my messages with one word. 'Noted.' 'Ok.' I know she's busy. It still stings.
Today in the planning call she set the launch for the 20th. I know the payment tests won't be ready by then. I typed a message to her in the chat: 'Can we talk about the 20th? I'm worried about testing.' I looked at it for a long time. Then I deleted it.
What if she thinks I'm being difficult because I'm jealous? Or that I'm trying to show her up?
After the call, Faiz messaged me privately: 'Is the 20th realistic??' So he sees it too. Neither of us said anything in the call.
The whole team was so quiet today.
— Rukmini

What launch date did Aparna set in the planning call?
She set the launch for the 20th.
What was Rukmini worried about when deleting the message?
Rukmini worried that Aparna would think the concern came from jealousy or from wanting to show her up.
What small step could Rukmini try instead of staying silent?
Rukmini could raise the testing concern with Faiz together, as a plain fact about the payment tests, so it feels less personal.
How might Aparna be affected if nobody raises the testing problem?
Aparna could walk into a failed launch on the 20th without knowing her own team had seen it coming.

Just the key points, please, in two sentences.

I bowed and returned the pledge; beginning to perceive that it would be foolish to sit sulking for the misbehaviour of a pack of curs; besides, I felt loth to yield the fellow further amusement at my expense; since his humour took that turn. He—probably swayed by prudential consideration of the folly of offending a good tenant—relaxed a little in the laconic style of chipping off his pronouns and auxiliary verbs, and introduced what he supposed would be a subject of interest to me,—a discourse on the advantages and disadvantages of my present place of retirement. I found him very intelligent on the topics we touched; and before I went home, I was encouraged so far as to volunteer another visit to-morrow. He evidently wished no repetition of my intrusion. I shall go, notwithstanding. It is astonishing how sociable I feel myself compared with him.

Lockwood decides not to sulk about the dogs, and Heathcliff becomes a little friendlier and talks sensibly about the area. Although Heathcliff clearly does not want him back, Lockwood plans to visit again the next day.

(1) how many words are there in my English textbook
(2) Any idea what "hesitation" means?
(3) How do I spell "calender", the thing with the dates?
(4) Can you fix my sentence? She don't like spicy food.

1. I can't check that, since I can't see your book. A word count is easy to estimate by counting one page and comparing the pages, or ask your teacher.
2. "Hesitation" is a noun. It means a short pause because you are not sure.
3. It is "calendar", ending in "-ar".
4. Say it this way: She doesn't like spicy food. Why: "She" is third person singular, so the helper verb is "doesn't".

Read this:

'Tanuja, look!' Salma held up a crumpled hundred-rupee note by the drinking-water tap.
'Whoa! Finders keepers?'
'I don't know.' Salma's heart was thumping. 'I could buy the gel pens. The whole set.'
'Do it. Nobody saw.'
'But what if it's someone's bus money? Or lunch?'
'Then they should have been careful.'
Salma turned the note over in her fingers. 'If I lost a hundred, I'd be crying in the toilet.'
Tanuja went quiet. 'Yeah. Me too.'
'Let's ask around first. Then the office.'
They asked three girls at the tap. The third one, a small Class 3 girl, burst into tears of relief. 'It's my Amma's, for the milk!'
Salma handed it over. The gel pens could wait.

Where did Salma find the note?
By the drinking-water tap.
What was Salma feeling when she first held the note?
Excited and tempted, her heart thumping at the idea of buying the gel pens.
What did Salma choose to do, and why was it wise?
Ask whose it was before going to the office, because it might be someone's bus or lunch money.
How did the Class 3 girl feel when she got the note back?
Hugely relieved; she burst into tears because it was her Amma's milk money.

On the veranda of Nani's house, Karthik sat with the wooden shape box. He picked up the round red block and pushed it at the square hole. It stuck. He turned it and pushed harder. Stuck.
He banged it once and looked at cousin Eshaan.
Eshaan just watched.
Karthik moved his hand. Round block, round hole. Plop! It dropped inside.
He peered in, then grabbed the next block.

What colour was the round block?
The round block was red.
How might Karthik have felt when the block kept sticking?
He was probably frustrated, which is why he banged it once and looked at Eshaan.
What could Eshaan do if Karthik gets very upset next time?
Eshaan could point gently at the right hole or show one block, but still let Karthik push it in himself.
How might Eshaan see Karthik's plop moment?
Eshaan may feel pleased and amused, seeing Karthik work it out without any help.

Read this:

Aadhya, you asked how I, Lavanya, stay so calm. Honestly? A notebook.
Every night I write whatever's in my head. Mean things about my teachers. Crushes. Whether I'm pretty. Stuff I'd never say. Some nights I write "I'm quitting school" and in the morning I laugh and go.
Writing something down isn't a plan. It's just a place to put it.
But there was one time it was different. For a week I wrote about a man near my tuition who kept walking behind me and asking my name. I wrote it three nights in a row. On the fourth night I read those pages back and thought, this isn't a feeling. This is a safety thing.
So I went and woke my mother right then. She listened, told me I did the right thing, and the next morning she walked me to tuition and spoke to the tuition owner.
The notebook is private. But not for that.

How many nights did Lavanya write about the man near tuition?
Lavanya wrote it three nights in a row.
What was Lavanya feeling on the fourth night?
Lavanya felt worried and alarmed, realising the pages described a real safety concern, not just a passing feeling.
Which choice of Lavanya's worked, and why?
Going to wake the mother that night worked, because it turned a private worry into action, and the mother acted the next morning.
How might Lavanya's mother have felt being woken with this?
She was probably worried but relieved that Lavanya told her, and she responded calmly and protectively.

metadata.subtype: Personal writing and diaries as private space [Regulating]

messages.content: Kiaan is doing home delivery of newspapers in his neighborhood of 200 homes. After an hour of work, he has distributed newspapers to 2/5 of the homes. After another 2 hours of working, he realizes he has distributed newspapers to 60 percent of the remaining homes. How many homes does he still need to distribute the newspapers to?

After the first hour of work, he has distributed newspapers to 2/5*200 = 80 homes
The number of homes that still need newspapers is 200-80 = 120
Two hours later, the number of homes he has distributed newspapers to is 60/100 * 120 = 72 homes.
The number of homes he still needs to distribute newspapers to is 120-72 = 48 homes
The answer is 48.

Read this:

Hi Salma,

You were right to make me talk to the Class 7s. I have been telling everyone about library timings, but on Tuesday at the ground three Class 7 kids told me the sports period gets cancelled whenever it rains or there's a test, and it is never made up. I had never thought of it. So I have changed the speech. New line: "One sports period a week fixed on the timetable, and if it is cancelled, made up within the week." I'll ask the PT teacher whether that is possible before I promise anything. Could you listen to the new version at lunch and time it? It still has to fit in two minutes.

Hemant

What did the three Class 7 kids say about sports periods?
They said the sports period gets cancelled whenever it rains or there is a test, and it is never made up.
What made Hemant change the speech, and how did Hemant feel about it?
Hemant was surprised and interested, since Hemant had never thought of the sports periods until the Class 7 kids raised them.
What else could Hemant do before promising the schedule, and why?
Hemant could ask the PT teacher what is possible, because a promise is only worth making if the person in charge can agree to it.
How might a Class 7 student see the new line in the speech?
A Class 7 student would likely feel heard, since the complaint they raised on Tuesday became a promise. 🙂

Read this:

Monday. A new rule went up on the notice board: no football on the front lawn at lunch. Kunal kicked the wall. 'That's the silliest rule ever,' he told Lalremsiami. 'Sir just hates fun.' He wanted to play there anyway.
Tuesday. Kunal almost sneaked a ball out. Lalremsiami said, 'Why not just ask why?' He scowled, but it stuck in his head.
Wednesday. Kunal knocked on the sports teacher's door. 'Sir, why can't we play on the front lawn?' Sir showed him the window of the Class 1 room, cracked the week before. 'The little ones sit right there.' Kunal thought. 'What if we play on the back ground instead, and one of us looks after the ball bag?' Sir smiled. 'Write that down. I'll take it to the principal.'

What did the new rule say?
No football on the front lawn at lunch.
What was Kunal feeling on Monday?
Angry and resentful; he kicked the wall and thought Sir just hated fun.
What did Kunal do on Wednesday that worked better than breaking the rule?
He asked why the rule existed and politely suggested the back ground instead.
How did the sports teacher see Kunal's question?
Positively; he explained the reason, smiled at the idea and offered to take it to the principal.
Is my teacher's daughter older than I am?
I can't check that, as I know nothing about her family. You could ask your teacher politely.

Read this:

Hemant worked as a junior auditor at the cooperative bank in the market town, and he could not sleep after seeing the loan register. On Sunday he took the bus to see Tarun sir, a senior at the federation office, who sat outside the branch's reporting line and would keep quiet. They talked on the verandah over tea.

A week later, Hemant met an advocate he had known since college, in a small office above the cloth shop. The advocate listened to the whole account and set out the possible options and what each might cost him. He asked Hemant to note dates and to tell nobody in the branch yet.

Hemant rode home with a page of notes and a steadier chest.

Where did Hemant meet the advocate?
In a small office above the cloth shop.
What was Hemant feeling on the bus to see Tarun sir?
Hemant felt uneasy and worried, since he could not sleep and needed a trusted person outside his own line to talk to.
If the advocate had been busy, what else could Hemant do, and why?
Hemant could speak again with Tarun sir about who else could advise him in confidence, because keeping the circle small guards against the matter spreading.
How might Tarun sir see Hemant's coming to him first?
Tarun sir may feel trusted and want to respond carefully, knowing a young clerk has placed a heavy concern in his hands.

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: Farida buttoned her school shirt one hole out and went to school crooked. Jyoti, her sister, laughed.
Wednesday: she buttoned it, looked in the mirror, and saw one side hanging lower. She undid every button and started again from the bottom one.
Friday: she began at the bottom, checked the mirror at the top and smiled.

Where did Farida start on Wednesday?
She started again from the bottom one.
What was Farida feeling on Monday when Jyoti laughed?
She was probably embarrassed at going to school crooked.
What else could Farida try?
Match the top button to the top hole first, so both ends line up.
How might Jyoti see Farida's fix?
Jyoti may be impressed that her sister spotted and fixed it herself.

Read this:

Last year, at twenty-five, I, Vaibhav, woke up in my Pune office and realised I was living someone else's plan. Engineering because my father said so. This company because my uncle knew the manager.
My first instinct was to quit and blame everyone. I wrote an angry email to my father and deleted it.
My sister Rashmi said, "What do you actually want to keep?"
I made two lists. Keep: problem-solving, the friends I've made, supporting my parents. Drop: the parts of the job I only do to please others.
So I've started small. I moved to the product design team. I do a weekend course in user research.
When I told my father, I thanked him first. Then I explained. He listened. That surprised me most.

Who knew the manager at Vaibhav's company?
Vaibhav's uncle knew the manager.
How did Vaibhav feel at first when he realised he was living someone else's plan?
Vaibhav felt angry and wanted to quit and blame everyone, even writing an angry email.
What did Vaibhav do instead of burning everything down?
Vaibhav listed what to keep and drop, made small changes like moving teams and taking a course, and explained respectfully to the father.
How might Rashmi's question have helped Vaibhav?
It turned Vaibhav's anger into reflection, showing there were parts of that life worth keeping.

Read this:

"Vishal, you forgot the shortcut for the pivot table again?"

"Yep. Third time this year, Lokesh."

"Doesn't that annoy you?"

"It used to. I'd think, I'm getting slow. Now I just open my notes file."

"You keep notes on shortcuts?"

"On everything I don't use every day. And on the first Monday of each month I spend twenty minutes going through the ones I'll need soon."

"That sounds like school."

"It sort of is. But the brain isn't a hard drive. It drops what I don't use. That's normal, not failing."

Lokesh laughed. "I thought forgetting meant I was bad at my job."

"Nope. It means you're human. Want my notes template?"

When does Vishal go through the notes file?
On the first Monday of each month, for twenty minutes.
How does Vishal feel about forgetting now, compared with before?
Vishal feels relaxed and unbothered now, whereas before Vishal felt annoyed and worried about getting slow.
What could Lokesh take from Vishal's approach?
Lokesh could keep notes on rarely used skills and review them at set times, treating forgetting as normal.
How does Lokesh seem to feel after the conversation?
Lokesh seems relieved and amused, having thought forgetting meant being bad at the job.

There are 40 Judges in the state of Rhode Island.  10 percent of Judges are under 30 years old.  60 percent of Judges are 30-50 years old.  The rest of the Judges are over 50 years old.  How many Judges are over 50 years old?

Under 30: 40(.10)=4
30-50 years old:40(.60)=24
Over 50:40-4-24=12 Judges
The answer is 12.

Read this:

Monday. In the school corridor, Omkar grabbed the front spot in the train line. "You're a baby, you can't be driver." Yash turned to the wall and hummed loudly, as if Omkar had vanished.
Tuesday. Omkar held out a clay snake. "Want to make a snake farm?" Yash stared at the ceiling fan and said nothing. Omkar scratched his head and wandered off.
Thursday. At recess Omkar drove a train of three other boys around the slide. Yash sat on the bench with his lunchbox, not eating. When the teacher asked what was wrong, he shrugged. Monday's words were still stuck inside him.

What did Omkar offer on Tuesday?
He held out a clay snake and asked if Yash wanted to make a snake farm.
What was Yash feeling on the bench on Thursday?
Not eating and shrugging suggest he still felt hurt and lonely; ignoring Monday's words hadn't made them go away.
What would you change first for Yash?
Instead of humming and staring away, he could tell Omkar or the teacher that being called a baby hurt, so the fight could actually be sorted out.
How might Omkar see Yash's silence on Tuesday?
Omkar scratched his head and wandered off, so he seems puzzled and may not even know his words hurt.

Read this:

The school bus was packed and noisy, and Keerthana, eleven, was squashed by the door. Pranav reached over, snatched her new cap, and held it out of the window.
“Want it? Come get it!”
Keerthana's hand flew up to slap him. The bus lurched. Everyone was watching.
She stopped. Took one breath. Lowered her hand.
“Give it back now,” she said, loud enough for the driver to hear.
The driver looked in the mirror. “Pranav!”
Pranav pulled the cap in and dropped it on her lap. “It was a joke.”
“Not a funny one,” said Keerthana, and put it on.

What did Pranav snatch?
Her new cap.
How did Keerthana feel when Pranav held the cap out of the window?
She felt angry and embarrassed, her hand flying up to slap him.
What helped Keerthana get the cap back without hitting?
She took a breath, lowered her hand and used loud, clear words that got the driver's attention.
How might the driver see the situation?
The driver sees Pranav's behaviour is unsafe and unkind and steps in quickly.

Read this:

At ten, Kishore got stuck on the word "temperature" while reading aloud. His face went hot. He stuck out his tongue, wobbled his head and read the next line like a robot. The class burst into laughter, and Kishore bowed, but his hands shook on the book.
At twenty, Kishore sat at the back of a presentation. Anjali, at the front, said "1950" when she meant "1590" and did not notice. Kishore let out a low, quiet chortle, a private little sound. Anjali heard it. Her cheeks burned, and she stopped in the middle of a sentence. Afterwards, she said to her friend Himani, "He laughed at my mistake." Himani frowned. "Maybe ask him what it meant?" Anjali found Kishore outside. "Were you laughing at me?" Kishore blinked. "No, sorry, it was relief. I made the same slip in my presentation last week, and thought I was the only one. I should have kept quiet." Anjali let out a breath. "It sounded like mocking." He nodded. "I'll be careful how I laugh," he said.

What number did Anjali say instead of "1590"?
She said "1950" when she meant "1590".
How do the laughter at ten and the chortle at twenty show that the same sound can mean different things?

At ten Kishore made the class laugh with him, and it covered his shaking hands. At twenty his quiet chortle was relief, but aimed at Anjali's slip it sounded like mocking, so context decides what a laugh means.
What was Anjali feeling when she stopped mid-sentence and her cheeks burned?
She felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking that Kishore was laughing at her mistake.
What did Himani do well, and what could Kishore do next time?
Himani suggested asking what it meant instead of assuming. Kishore can keep quiet or say something kind when someone slips, so his sound is not read as mockery.

"No, indeed: but I have long wanted to see you, and when I heard that there had been a letter from you, and that you were going to another part of the country, I thought I'd just set off, and get a look at you before you were quite out of my reach."

Reading only the passage, why did the speaker come to see this person?

The speaker had long wanted to see this person. Hearing that a letter had come and that the person was going to another part of the country, they set off to get a look before the person was out of reach.
Please make this feedback to my friend more encouraging: Your drawing is okay but the colours are dull and the faces look odd.
Your drawing is a good start. Try some brighter colours, and take a little more time on the faces. Keep going!
Our picnic plan fell through. Can a plan fall?

Yes, in this phrase. If a plan falls through, it fails to happen.
Example: The deal fell through because the buyer could not arrange the money.

Read this:

At the small architecture firm in Chennai, Rakesh closed his laptop with a sigh. "They'll reject it. The client wants glass towers, and we've given them a courtyard house. I'd put money on it."

Deepak, his manager, pulled up a chair. Deepak privately thought the design was brilliant and was sure of a yes. "Okay. Is that something you know, or a guess?"

Rakesh paused. "A guess. A strong guess."

"Then let's test it. Write down your prediction. I'll write mine." Deepak folded a sticky note: "Yes, full design." Rakesh wrote: "Rejected outright."

On Friday the client called. They didn't want the courtyard house for their main site. But they loved the shaded verandas and asked the firm to design a small community library for their second plot.

Deepak laughed and stuck both notes on the board. "We were both wrong."

Rakesh looked at the notes for a long moment, then started a new folder: "Library".

What did the client ask the firm to design for their second plot?
A small community library.
Why was Rakesh ready to "put money on" a rejection?
Rakesh felt gloomy and certain, expecting the client to want glass towers; the forecast felt so sure that it seemed like knowledge, not a guess.
What worked about Deepak's approach when Rakesh predicted a rejection?
Deepak asked whether it was knowledge or a guess and turned it into a test, with both predictions written down. That made room for a real result instead of an argument about who was right.
What does the outcome show Deepak about Deepak's own optimism?
Deepak had been sure of a full yes and was wrong too. The result surprised both of them, a reminder that confident hope can miss just as gloomy prediction can.

Read this:

In the Gangtok flat, rain drummed on the window while Pema sat on the rug with little Darshan, who was nearly two. She held up a toy drum.
"Boom, boom," she said, slowly, eyes wide, smiling.
Darshan watched her mouth. He banged the drum. "Boo! Boo!"
She clapped, face bright. "Yes! Boom!"
He laughed and banged again, looking at her face after every beat.

What toy did Pema hold up?
Pema held up a toy drum.
Why did Darshan look at Pema's face after every beat?
Darshan felt happy and eager, checking her bright face for delight and encouragement.
What made Pema's way of playing work well?
She spoke slowly, with wide eyes and a smile that matched her words, so Darshan could read her tone and join in.
What would change if Pema had spoken fast with a blank face?
Darshan would likely be less engaged and less happy, since toddlers read tone and faces more than words.

Read this:

Last year, I was in five coaching classes because everyone in my Class 12 section was. I'm Rafiq, and I was terrified that if I dropped one, the others would learn some secret trick and leave me behind.

My days started at six and ended at ten at night. I'd sit through lecture after lecture, copying notes, but I never had time to read them again. By Sunday I couldn't remember Monday.

My mock scores stayed at the same sixty-something for four months. Payal, who sat next to me in chemistry, went to only two batches and practised at home. Her scores climbed every month.

I kept thinking I had to work harder. It took me way too long to see I wasn't working, just sitting. I was full of notes and empty of understanding.

How many coaching classes was Rafiq attending?
Five coaching classes.
What was Rafiq afraid of?
Rafiq was terrified that dropping a class would mean others learning some secret trick and leaving Rafiq behind.
What approach might have suited Rafiq better?
Fewer batches with daily time to revise and practise, as Payal did, would have let the lectures actually turn into understanding.
How might Payal have seen Rafiq's schedule?
Payal might have seen it as exhausting and unnecessary, knowing from her own rising scores that practice mattered more than sitting.

metadata.subtype: Approach: attending everything out of fear of falling behind [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday. Dilnaz didi lifted Pooja out of the bath. Pooja screamed and threw her cup at the wall. Dilnaz picked it up. “You're angry. You wanted more bath. Cups stay in the bath.”
Thursday. Bath over again. Pooja stamped both feet and yelled. “Angry,” said Dilnaz calmly, wrapping the towel.
The following Monday. Out of the bath, Pooja's face went red. She stamped, and shouted, “Angry!” The cup stayed in her hand.

What did Pooja throw at the wall on Monday?
She threw her cup at the wall.
What was Pooja feeling when she stamped and shouted "Angry!"?
She was angry at having to leave the bath, and by then she could name the big feeling instead of throwing.
Why did Dilnaz's approach work better than punishment?
She stayed calm, held the limit and gave Pooja a word for the feeling each time, so Pooja learned to say it instead of throwing.
How might Dilnaz feel on the following Monday?
Dilnaz would probably feel pleased and relieved that Pooja used the word and kept hold of the cup.

a) (-3, 3): 3 right, 2 down
b) (4, -1): 5 left, 3 up
c) (0, 0): 2 right, 5 up
d) (1, 2): 4 right
e) (6, 6): 6 down
f) (-2, -2): 3 left, 3 down
g) (5, -4): 5 left, 4 up

i) (3, 8): 6 left, 9 down
j) (0, -5): 1 right, 1 up

Retell these lines in plain modern English.

From street to street the captains passed
And Rakshas warriors gathered fast.
With spear and sword to pierce and strike,
And axe and club and mace and pike.
The captains went from street to street, and the Rakshas warriors quickly gathered. They carried spears and swords to pierce and strike, and axes, clubs, maces and pikes.

Read this:

Irfan, you know my flatmate Rhea? Okay, here's what happened. I'm Charu, and last week she said, "You never help and you always mess things up. Always." This was about the milk going off in the fridge. Which, yes, was my milk.

But "never"? I cooked for both of us all through her exams! So I said that. And she said, "Once or twice doesn't count." And I said it was fourteen times; I'd counted. Suddenly we were arguing about whether I'd cooked fourteen times or eleven. Nobody mentioned the milk again.

I went to bed feeling like a cartoon villain. Unfair and angry.

Next morning I tried again. "The milk was my fault. I'll check dates on Sundays. But 'never' and 'always' made me feel like nothing I do counts." She said, "Yeah. I was just tired." We're okay now. And the fridge is clean.

What had gone off in the fridge?
The milk had gone off in the fridge.
How did Charu feel going to bed after the argument?
Charu felt unfair and angry, like a cartoon villain, painted by Rhea's "never" and "always".
What did Charu do the next morning that worked?
Charu owned the milk, promised a Sunday check, and said how the absolutes felt, which let Rhea soften.
What might Rhea have been feeling when she said "always"?
Rhea was probably tired and fed up, and the absolutes came out of exhaustion rather than a fair count.

Read this:

Dear Vishal,
I keep thinking about our fight in the mess, when I called your life 'a timetable with legs'. That was unkind, and I'm sorry.
Here's what I've worked out since. You go home every second weekend, you eat the same dal, you've been in the same study group since first year. I used to think that meant you were afraid of the world. Then I asked myself what it protects. Your amma, who lives alone now. Your marks, which your scholarship depends on. Friendships that actually last.
You once called me shallow for changing clubs four times. Maybe ask what my changes protect too: I'm still looking for the thing I'm good at.
Chai on Friday? Your usual place. I won't complain about the menu.
Tenzin

What did Tenzin once call Vishal's life?
'A timetable with legs'.
How does Tenzin feel about the fight in the mess now?
Tenzin feels sorry and a bit ashamed, seeing the remark as unkind now that the reasons behind Vishal's routines are clear.
What question helped Tenzin change, and how could Vishal use it too?
Asking what a habit protects; Vishal could ask it about Tenzin's club-switching and see a search for strengths rather than shallowness.
How might Vishal feel reading this letter?
Vishal would probably feel relieved and respected, since the letter names real reasons for the routines, and might happily accept Friday's chai.
The driver speaks that the bus will be late. Is "speaks" right?

The driver says that the bus will be late.
Why: "Say" reports words; "speak" is for talking or a language.

Read this:

Dear Nandini Akka,
You asked last month if I'd made any friends here in Hyderabad yet. Honestly, when you asked, not really. But something slowly happened.
Every Saturday at seven, the same four of us play badminton at the colony court. I only went because the watchman kept inviting me. Nobody talked much at first. Now after the game we sit on the wall and argue about whose smash was weaker.
On Wednesdays, Imran from the flat below and I cook together, because neither of us can finish a whole pot of sambar alone. Last week he told me about his father's surgery, and I told him about Appa.
It isn't a big group, Akka. Just three or four people I see every week. But when I had fever last month, two of them brought food. I didn't have that a year ago.
Your brother,
Kishore

On which day do Kishore and Imran cook together?
They cook together on Wednesdays.
How does Kishore seem to feel about the new friendships?
Kishore feels grateful and a little surprised, quietly proud that these weekly habits turned into real care when the fever came.
What made these ties grow, and what could Kishore keep doing?
Showing up every week for badminton and the Wednesday cooking let trust build slowly; keeping those routines steady will keep the friendships growing.
How might Nandini feel reading this letter?
Nandini will probably feel relieved and happy that her brother is no longer alone in Hyderabad.

metadata.subtype: Stage 7: Building a few real ties [Response]
