Read this:

Monday. Harsha stood in the ticket line at the suburban station when a man slid in three places ahead. Harsha said nothing. A woman with a heavy bag sighed, and a teenager stared at his phone. Harsha felt irritated but wasn’t sure it was worth a fight.
Thursday. The same man, Madhav, did it again. This time Harsha smiled and said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”
Madhav blinked, grinned sheepishly and said, “Oh, sorry, didn’t notice.” He went to the back.
Saturday. Madhav stood at the end of the line and gave Harsha a small nod.

What did Harsha say to Madhav on Thursday?
Harsha said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”
Why did Harsha stay silent on Monday?
Harsha felt irritated but was not sure it was worth a fight. Harsha weighed the tension against the small gain and let it pass that day.
What made Harsha's comment on Thursday work?
Harsha smiled, kept the tone light and shared that Harsha was late too. That let Madhav step back without feeling attacked.
How might Madhav have felt when Harsha spoke to him?
Madhav may have felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, since he grinned sheepishly. His nod on Saturday suggests he took the comment without resentment.

Read this:

The drums of Durga Puja were beating across the village. Bidisha tugged Parveen's hand. "Come see our pandal!"
Parveen hesitated at the entrance. She'd never been inside one.
"You don't have to pray," said Bidisha. "Just look."
Inside, the goddess had ten arms. Parveen stared at the lion and the colours. Bidisha's grandmother offered her prasad. Parveen looked at Bidisha, unsure.
"You can take it or not," Bidisha whispered. "Both are fine."
Parveen took it with both hands, like Bidisha did. "Thank you, Dida."
Later, Parveen said, "Come to our home on Eid. Ammi makes sevai."

How many arms did the goddess have?
Ten arms.
What was Parveen feeling when she hesitated at the entrance?
Parveen felt unsure and a little nervous, never having been inside a pandal.
What did Bidisha say that made it easier for Parveen?
She said Parveen didn't have to pray and could take prasad or not, which respected Parveen's own faith.
How might Bidisha's grandmother see Parveen taking prasad with both hands?
Bidisha's grandmother likely feels touched and respected by Parveen's polite gesture.

Keep this diary entry to three sentences, still in the first person.

Thursday night
Dinner with Madhav at the Irani cafe. He ordered, then asked the same thing twice. In the middle of the story about his sister's engagement he stopped and said, "Sorry, I just remembered the vendor invoice." Then the tax form. Then his bike service. His chai went cold. He said he's been sleeping badly, waking at three and thinking about "stuff". I asked him to write all the stuff on a napkin. Eleven things! Half were ten-minute jobs. We put a day next to each one, and he took a photo of the napkin. He looked lighter when we left, though maybe I'm imagining it. I'll ask him on Monday how he slept.
Darshan

At the Irani cafe, Madhav asked the same thing twice, let his chai go cold and said he has been sleeping badly. I asked him to write all the stuff on a napkin, and eleven things came out, half of them ten-minute jobs. We put a day next to each one, he seemed lighter when we left, though perhaps I imagined it, and I will ask him on Monday how he slept.

Read this:

On Baisakhi morning, Pankaj and his cousin Hemant sat on the rug with their new toys.
"Swap?" Hemant asked. "My red truck for your green truck."
"No! Mine is better."
"They're the same. Same wheels, same size."
"Mine is faster." Pankaj hugged the green truck to his kurta.
Mumma knelt beside them. "Yesterday in the shop you wanted the red one, remember?"
"But now this one is mine."
"Just for five minutes," Hemant begged.
Pankaj shook his head hard and pushed the green truck under his pillow.

What swap did Hemant offer?
Hemant's red truck for Pankaj's green truck.
Why won't Pankaj swap the trucks?
Now that the green truck is his, it feels special and precious, so he feels protective and worried about letting it go, even though yesterday he wanted the red one.
How could Mumma help the two cousins next time?
She could suggest a short swap with a timer, so Pankaj knows his green truck will come back to him.
How does Hemant feel when Pankaj hides the truck?
Hemant probably feels disappointed and confused, because to Hemant the trucks are the same and it was only a five-minute swap.

Read this:

In the village lane, Zeenat, five, was holding her brother Nilesh's hand when the milkman's cycle slipped in the mud. The milkman fell, and his arm was bleeding. Milk spread across the ground. Zeenat stood very still. Then she started crying. Nilesh, twelve, said, "Zeenat, run home and get Ammi. Fast." She ran through the gate, sobbing, "Ammi! The milkman fell! There's blood!" Ammi came running with a clean cloth and called out to the neighbours. Zeenat stayed on the veranda, hugging her knees, as the grown-ups helped. Later, Ammi hugged her. "You did the right thing. You came to tell me."

What slipped in the mud?
The milkman's cycle slipped in the mud.
What was Zeenat feeling when she stood very still?
She felt frightened and shocked, freezing and then crying at the sight of the blood.
What did Zeenat do that was right for her age?
She moved away from the accident and ran to tell a grown-up, Ammi, who came to help.
How might Ammi feel after hugging Zeenat?
Ammi likely felt proud and tender, reassuring her that coming to tell was the right thing.

metadata.subtype: Child frozen or crying at an accident [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Abebe had become shift lead at the coffee roastery in Addis Ababa in March. He noticed quickly that one style didn't fit everyone.
Layla had roasted beans for ten years. When he tried to show her a new timer, she frowned. So he stepped back. “You know this better than me. Tell me if you need anything.”
Samuel, the new boy, was nervous around the big roaster. Abebe stood beside him for a whole week, explaining each step.
With both of them, he was honest. He told Layla her batch logs were missing details, and told Samuel he was too slow on packing.
At the end of the month, Layla said, “You're the first lead who didn't try to teach me my own job.” Samuel said, “You're the first who actually taught me.”

How long had Layla roasted beans?
For ten years.
How did Layla seem to feel when Abebe tried to show her a new timer?
She seemed irritated and a bit insulted, frowning at being taught what she already knew.
What did Abebe do that fit each person's needs?
He gave Layla freedom, guided Samuel closely and gave both honest feedback, adjusting his style to each.
How might Samuel have felt during his first week?
He was probably nervous at first but reassured, since Abebe stood beside him and explained each step.

Read this:

Monday: In the canteen queue, a boy said loudly, "Yusuf's father sells vegetables from a cart, no?" A few laughed. Yusuf's face didn't change. He paid for his samosa and walked off. Damini, behind him, couldn't read him at all.
Wednesday: The same boy said it again in class. Yusuf stared straight ahead, blank as a wall. But Damini saw his hand gripping his pen so hard his knuckles went pale.
Thursday: After school, Damini caught up with him at the bus stop. She didn't mention the boy. She said, "My chacha has a cart near the station. Best guavas in town." Then: "If you ever want to talk about stuff, I'm around."
Friday: Yusuf sat next to her on the bus. After two stops he said, "It's not the cart. My father's proud of it. It's them laughing."
"I know," Damini said. "It's rubbish. Want to tell Ma'am together?"
He nodded.

What does Damini's chacha have near the station?
A cart near the station, with the best guavas in town.
What was Yusuf feeling behind his blank face on Wednesday?
Yusuf was hurt and angry, which showed only in his knuckles going pale around the pen while his face stayed impassive.
What made Damini's approach helpful?
She didn't push or mention the boy; she offered warmth and a chance to talk, and then suggested telling the teacher together.
How might the boy who mocked Yusuf read Yusuf's blank face?
He might think the jokes weren't hurting, since Yusuf's face showed nothing.
Vivi bought fabric to make new pillows for her bed. She spent $75 on checkered fabric and $45 on plain fabric. If both fabrics cost $7.50 per yard, how many total yards of fabric did she buy?

The total yards of the checkered fabric is $75 / 7.50 = 10.
The total yards of the plain fabric is 45 / 7.50 = 6.
So, Vivi bought a total of 10 + 6 = 16 yards of fabric.
The answer is 16.
Kerala is located in south of India. What is missing?

Kerala is located in the south of India.
Why: "the south" needs "the".

Summarize Nelly's advice to Heathcliff in plain words.

"And cried for mamma at every turn," I added, "and trembled if a country lad heaved his fist against you, and sat at home all day for a shower of rain. Oh, Heathcliff, you are showing a poor spirit! Come to the glass, and I'll let you see what you should wish. Do you mark those two lines between your eyes; and those thick brows, that, instead of rising arched, sink in the middle; and that couple of black fiends, so deeply buried, who never open their windows boldly, but lurk glinting under them, like devil's spies? Wish and learn to smooth away the surly wrinkles, to raise your lids frankly, and change the fiends to confident, innocent angels, suspecting and doubting nothing, and always seeing friends where they are not sure of foes. Don't get the expression of a vicious cur that appears to know the kicks it gets are its desert, and yet hates all the world, as well as the kicker, for what it suffers."

Nelly tells young Heathcliff to stop being sulky and suspicious. She shows him his frowning face in the mirror and urges him to look at people openly and trust them, instead of hating the world like a beaten dog.
Is 'I am vegetarian' or 'I am a vegetarian' correct? Waiter ko bolna hai.
Both are correct. "I'm vegetarian" uses the word as an adjective, and "I'm a vegetarian" uses it as a noun. To the waiter, you can add: "Do you have anything without meat or eggs?"

Read this:

Trisha, you're upset with an 81 because last time you got 95? Sit. Let me tell you about your Jeevan mama at your age.

Class 9, first maths exam: 89. I thought I was a genius. My father framed the paper, if you can believe it.

Next exam, 70. I was destroyed. I hid in the terrace water-tank room for an hour. I thought everything was over.

My best friend, Ashok, got 70 too. His first was 48. He came home singing. His mother made payasam. Same 70.

I went to our maths teacher, sure she would scold me. She asked, "Jeevan, if you'd got 48 first and then 70, how would you feel?" I said happy. She said, "So the 70 isn't the problem. The 89 is standing on your shoulder."

After that, I stopped comparing to the first number. So, beta. The 81. What does it actually tell you?

What did young Jeevan's father do with the 89 paper?
Jeevan's father framed the paper.
How did young Jeevan feel after getting 70?
Young Jeevan felt crushed and ashamed and hid in the water-tank room for an hour, thinking everything was over.
What was the turning point in Jeevan's story?
The teacher asking how 70 would feel after a 48 showed that the first mark of 89 was shaping the feeling, not the 70 itself.
How did Ashok experience the same 70?
Ashok came home singing because 70 was a big rise from his first 48, and his mother made payasam.

"So, birthday girl, was it a good party?" asked her mother Rehana, stacking paper plates.
Jyoti, eight, sat on the sofa in her frilly frock. "When everyone sang and I blew out all eight candles in one go, that was the BEST."
"And the rest?"
"The end was horrible. Sanya had to go early and then it rained and we couldn't do the garden game."
"You played passing the parcel for an hour. You won the drawing prize."
"Oh. Yeah."
"And the puppet show?"
"That was nice," Jyoti admitted. Then her lip wobbled. "But the rain spoiled it."
"The rain spoiled the last ten minutes," Rehana said gently. "Not the whole party."
"It feels like the whole party."

How many candles did Jyoti blow out?
All eight candles, in one go.
Why does the party feel spoiled to Jyoti?
Jyoti feels disappointed because the rain came at the very end, and together with the candle high point it decides her memory, pushing out the games and the puppet show.
What could Rehana do at bedtime to help Jyoti remember the day more fully?
Walk through the party in order with her: the parcel game, the drawing prize, the puppet show, not only the candles and the rain.
How might Rehana feel hearing that the end was horrible?
She might feel a little let down after all her planning, while understanding that the rain disappointed Jyoti.

I'm Zubin, and for two years I was the one who always called Sonali.

Her birthday: I called. Her promotion: I called. When her grandmother died, I drove to Nashik. She'd pick up sometimes, be lovely for ten minutes, and then nothing until I called again. I never got a call from her in those years except once, to borrow my car.

One night I scrolled back through my call log and felt foolish. Was I loyal or just a doormat?

I talked it over with my cousin, who said, "Don't punish her. Just stop carrying it all." So I tried an experiment. I stopped calling first. I kept replying warmly whenever she messaged.

It's been three months. She's called twice. Short calls, but hers. Our friendship is smaller than I wanted. But it's real, and I'm not angry about it. I'd rather have a true small friendship than a big one I hold up alone.

What was the one time Sonali called Zubin during those years?
She called once, to borrow Zubin's car.
How did Zubin feel scrolling back through the call log?
Zubin felt foolish and unsure, wondering whether the loyalty had turned into being a doormat.
What did Zubin's experiment show?
By stopping calling first while staying warm, Zubin could see how much effort was mutual and let the friendship settle at its natural level.
How might Sonali see the change in Zubin?
Sonali may have noticed the quiet and missed Zubin, since she began calling on her own.

Riya has 6 toy cars in a messy pile. How should she count them so that she does not miss a car or count one twice?

Answer: Touch each car, say one number, and push it to the side: "1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6". There are 6 cars.

Good counting has three rules. (1) Say the numbers in order, never skipping. (2) One number for one car. (3) Keep track: move each counted car to a "counted" side. Show a WRONG count on purpose (touch one car twice) and let the child catch your mistake.

In the Bandra office, Hafsa had asked her manager three times for training on the new software. Three times it was "next quarter." She had also asked to move off the night shift. Silence. By October she had stopped asking anything. In meetings she nodded. At lunch she ate alone. Sunaina noticed that Hafsa's plants on the desk had dried out, the ones she used to water every morning. One evening she stayed back. "Hafsa, you seem really far away lately. Can I help?" Hafsa shrugged, then her eyes filled. "I don't feel anything anymore." Sunaina didn't try to fix it. She said, "The company has a free counselling line. Want to call now? I'll sit with you." Training on the new software.

messages.content: Ravi can paint a room in 6 days and Sita can paint it in 12 days. How long will they take working together? A tap fills a tank in 4 hours and a drain empties it in 6 hours; if both are open, how long does it take to fill the empty tank?

Answer: Together 4 days. The tank fills in 12 hours.

Think about ONE day. Ravi paints 1/6 of the room per day, Sita 1/12 of it. Together: 1/6 + 1/12 = 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 of the room per day so the whole room takes 4 days In one line: 1/T = 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4, so T = 4. Check: in 4 days Ravi does 4/6 and Sita 4/12; 4/6 + 4/12 = 8/12 + 4/12 = 1 whole room. For the tank, the drain WORKS AGAINST the tap, so subtract: 1/T = 1/4 - 1/6 = 3/12 - 2/12 = 1/12, T = 12 hours. Common mistake: adding the times (6 + 12 = 18 days); working together must be FASTER than either alone.

The games teacher walked over, draped a towel round her like a cape and called to the crowd, “Everyone under the shed. Now.” Only then, alone, did the teacher kneel beside her. Later the teacher asked Ganga about the lip. Ganga's eyes flashed. “Last week she called me slowpoke in front of everyone.”

Dear Susan,

I need to tell someone, and you're my sister, so it's you.
Last night Gopika left her phone on the dining table and it lit up. A message from her friend: "Last night at the beach party was amazing! Did your mum ever find out?" She had told me she was at Anjali's house studying for the chemistry test.
I felt the floor tilt. I read it three times. I didn't sleep.
And now I keep going back. Was she really at tuition on Tuesdays? Did she really go to the library last month? Things that were probably true now feel suspicious.
She's my daughter. How do I trust anything she says?

Elizabeth

At Anjali's house, studying for the chemistry test.

She was shocked and hurt, the floor tilting, and began to doubt everything Gopika had told her, even things that were likely true.

What might Gopika be experiencing, if she knows her mother saw the message?

In 2 years, Maxwell will be twice his sister's age. If his sister is now 2, how old is Maxwell now?

In two years, Maxwell's sister will be 2 years + 2 years = 4 years old.
Therefore, Maxwell will be 4 years x 2 = 8 years old in two years.
Maxwell is now 8 years - 2 years = 6 years old.
The answer is 6.

Emil had kept the list on his phone for three weeks: every time two boys in his class in Malmö pushed him at the lockers, hid his gym bag or called him names in the group chat. On Thursday evening he finally showed it to his mother, Olga, at the kitchen table.

She read it slowly, scrolling. Her face tightened, but her voice stayed calm. "Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault."

The next morning she went with him to see his class teacher, Mr. Lindqvist, before first lesson. He read the list too, then asked Emil a few quiet questions. "I'm bringing in the school counsellor today," he said. "We have a plan for exactly this."

By Friday afternoon, the counsellor had met Emil, the boys' parents had been called, and the teacher had moved Emil's locker.

Emil slept better that night than he had in weeks.

Who did Olga go with Emil to see before first lesson?

What else could the school do to follow up on this?

How did Olga experience reading the list?

Dave weighs 175 pounds and can bench press three times his body weight.  Craig can only bench press 20% of the amount Dave can.  Mark is new and can bench press 50 pounds less than Craig.  How much can Mark bench press?

Dave weighs 175 pounds and can bench press three times his body weight, so he can bench press 175*3 = 525 pounds
Craig can only bench press 20% of Dave's 525 pounds, so Craig can bench press .20*525 = 105 pounds
Craig bench presses 105 pounds and Mark does 50 pounds less than Craig, so Mark can only press 105-50 = 55 pounds
The answer is 55.

The answer is 3 : 4; 3 : 2.

Tuesday: At lunch the friends planned a film for Sunday. Uday said he had homework, again. His face felt hot. He had been dodging paid plans for a month, ashamed of the reason.

Friday: He stayed after robotics club and, before he could stop himself, told Pooja, the lab mentor, everything. Pooja did not pity him. "Do you know how many people can't stretch a budget? You've been doing it all month. That's a skill." Uday laughed, surprised.

Next Wednesday: At the bench he told Yash, his closest friend, "We're saving money at home, so I skip paid things. Free stuff is fine." Yash shrugged. "Then let's do the park match Sunday." The hot feeling did not come back.

On which day did Uday tell Pooja?
Uday told Pooja on Friday, after robotics club.
How did Uday feel when he said he had homework again, and why?
Uday felt embarrassed and hot in the face, because he was ashamed of the money reason.
What other approach could Uday try with the friends, and why?
Uday could suggest free plans first, like a park match, because that lets him join without hiding the reason.
How does Yash respond, and what might that mean for Yash?
Yash shrugs and suggests the park match, which suggests it never mattered to Yash and that the friendship holds.

Karthik: how's the little one?
Suraj: Chintu's gone back to baby talk since the baby came. crawling, wants his dummy back
Karthik: just tell him to act his age lol
Suraj: tried that on day one. he cried for an hour
Karthik: so what are you doing
Suraj: extra cuddles. when he wants to be carried, I carry him. no teasing, no "baby" jokes
Karthik: won't that make it worse?
Suraj: I keep everything else the same though. same bedtime, same bath, same school run. he's still expected to put his toys away
Karthik: and?
Suraj: this morning he asked to "help" feed the baby. in his normal voice 🥹

What did Chintu ask to do this morning?
To help feed the baby.
Why does Suraj carry Chintu instead of telling him to act his age?
Suraj feels patient and caring, seeing the baby talk as Chintu's worry about his place, not naughtiness.
What could Karthik learn from Suraj's approach?
That comfort and steady routines together help a child feel secure and move forward faster than scolding.
How might Chintu feel when he asks to help feed the baby?
Chintu probably feels proud and included, reassured that he still belongs.

Rajni, you asked why I keep a plate of sewaiyan aside for Farida's family on Eid, so listen. I am Lokesh, your Nana. When your mother was twenty, she came home glowing about her friend Farida, and I felt fear rising. What will the neighbours say? Will she forget our traditions? I nearly said, "Stop seeing her." Instead, one night at dinner I asked, "What do you like about Farida?" Your mother said, "She never laughs at anyone. When I lost my purse on the train, she gave me her own fare home." I went quiet. That was not a label. That was a person. I still worried, but I invited Farida's family for Diwali, and her mother brought sewaiyan a few months later. My fears lost their sharp edges slowly. Your mother and Farida still speak every Sunday.

What did Lokesh ask at dinner instead of saying "Stop seeing her"?
He asked, "What do you like about Farida?"
What was Lokesh afraid of when Rajni's mother came home glowing about Farida?
Lokesh was afraid of what the neighbours would say and that she might forget their traditions.
What choice did Lokesh make instead of banning the friendship, and what did it lead to?
He asked about Farida and listened, which led to hearing about her kindness and to inviting Farida's family for Diwali.
How might Rajni's mother have felt when he asked what she liked about Farida?
Probably relieved and heard. She answered warmly with a story about Farida's kindness instead of having to defend her.
We argue about who gets the TV remote every evening.
That is a common household issue. A fair system usually ends the argument.
What kind of system?
A timetable on a sheet, such as one person picks on certain days, or each person picks one show. It stops the daily debate.
What if somebody breaks the rule?
Remind them calmly of what everyone agreed. If it keeps happening, ask a parent to decide. Clear rules that everyone helped to write are easier to follow.

During Holi week, the school library had a giant jigsaw of a tiger on the back table. Vinita was nearly done with the stripes when the bell rang for the colour-play assembly. "Come on!" Varun called. She went, but through all the gulal and music, she kept thinking about the empty corner by the tiger's ear. Where did that last curved piece go? She even dreamt of it. The spelling test she'd finished that morning? She couldn't remember a single word from it. The next day, she ran to the library before first bell, still with pink hands, and found the piece under the table. Snap. Done. By lunchtime, she'd forgotten all about the tiger.

What picture was on the giant jigsaw?
A tiger.
What was Vinita feeling during the assembly?
She felt restless and distracted, her mind nagged by the unfinished corner of the puzzle.
What could Vinita do next time she's called away from something unfinished?
She could jot down where she stopped, so the open task nags less until she can return.
How might Varun see Vinita at the assembly?
Varun might find her distracted and puzzling, since she seems to be somewhere else during the fun.

The organic-vegetable delivery company that Ishita and Arnab had started in Dehradun closed in March. For two months Ishita told everyone, "Arnab's marketing sank us." She said it at her cousin's wedding. She said it to their old investor. Arnab stopped answering her calls.
In May, her mother asked, "And what did you decide, beta?" Ishita opened her mouth, and shut it. She had chosen the expensive cold van. She had ignored the customer survey that said people wanted smaller boxes.
Her chest felt heavy. She messaged Arnab: "Can we do a proper post-mortem? Just facts. Mine too."
They met at the tea shop near the clock tower with a notebook. Two columns: decisions, and signals missed. Her van. His discount campaign. The survey neither of them acted on.
At the end, Arnab said, "I missed you, you know." Ishita nodded, eyes wet.

Where did Ishita and Arnab meet for the post-mortem?
At the tea shop near the clock tower.
What was Ishita feeling when her mother asked about her decisions?
She felt uneasy and ashamed, her chest heavy, realising she had blamed Arnab while ignoring her own mistakes.
How did the post-mortem help?
They wrote down decisions and missed signals on both sides, so blame became facts and the friendship had a chance to recover.
How might Arnab have felt during the two months of blame?
Arnab probably felt hurt and resentful, which is why he stopped answering Ishita's calls.
My brother pretended being asleep when the guests arrived. Please correct.

My brother pretended to be asleep when the guests arrived.
Why: "Pretend" takes "to" plus a verb.

In the Noida office, Monday's stand-up ended with the manager calling Chetan's report 'sloppy' in front of everyone. Chetan said, 'Okay, noted,' and went back to his desk. Saurabh, who sat across from him, noticed the clipped tone, the headphones going on, the lunch box left unopened, one spreadsheet stared at for an hour. Maybe he was just busy, Saurabh thought. Maybe not. He didn't want to make it a big thing in front of others. So at four he messaged: 'Chai downstairs? My treat.' At the tea stall Chetan finally said, 'He could have told me privately.' Saurabh didn't rush to defend the manager or trash him. 'Yeah, that stung, I could tell. Want help going through the report tomorrow?' Chetan's shoulders came down a little. 'Yeah. Thanks, man.'

Please give me the main points of this extract in three sentences.

After the manager calls Chetan's report sloppy in front of everyone, Chetan goes quiet and keeps to himself. Saurabh invites him for chai at four, and at the stall Chetan says the manager could have told him privately. Saurabh says it must have stung and offers to help with the report tomorrow, and Chetan relaxes a little.
Dukaan wale se bolna hai "Yeh kharab nikla, badal do." Polite aur casual dono batao.
Polite: "This item is faulty. Could you please exchange it?" Casual: "This one doesn't work. Can you swap it?"
Sally took 342 pens to her class of 44 students. If she gave 7 pens to each student, left half of the remainder in her locker, and took the rest home, how many did she take home?

She gave 7 pens each to 44 students for a total of 7*44 = 308 pens
There are now 342-308 = 34 pens left
She left half of 34 pens in her locker which is 34*(1/2) = 17 pens
She took 34-17 = 17 pens home
The answer is 17.

Dear Ramesh Mama,
You asked how exam prep is going, so here's the honest version. My shoulders are tight all day, like someone is pressing them down. At night my legs won't keep still, and my mind plays the same film: I fail maths, Papa goes silent, everyone at the wedding asks my marks. I know it's only a film. It still feels real at two in the morning.
This week I tried what you suggested. I made a timetable with a break every hour. When the film starts, I breathe out slowly and tell myself, 'That's a what-if, not a fact.' Last night I slept by eleven. Studying actually went better today. I'm still nervous. But I'm less scared of being nervous.
Thank you for asking properly.
Love,
Reena

What time did Reena sleep last night?
By eleven.
What does Reena mean by 'the same film' playing at night?
Reena is anxious and frightened by looping pictures of failing maths, Papa going silent and people asking about marks.
Which of Reena's new habits could help other students?
A timetable with a break every hour, and slow breathing while saying 'That's a what-if, not a fact'.
How might Ramesh Mama feel reading this letter?
Ramesh Mama is likely to feel touched to be trusted with the honest version, and glad the suggestions helped.

So you asked what I remember most from the engagement. Not the food. It's a small thing, and I'm Parul, so I get to pick.

Joel's family doesn't do feet-touching. But he had practised, bless him. When he met my Damini Nani, he went down so fast his knee cracked on the tiles.

Everyone laughed. I wanted to disappear.

Nani didn't laugh. She held his shoulders and helped him up. "Beta, no need. You don't have to learn all our ways in one day." Then she shook his hand and asked him about his mother's garden.

Joel told me later he'd been terrified she was testing him. He said that handshake was the moment he felt like family.

I'd never seen Nani decline anything before. It was the kindest thing I've watched her do.

What happened to Joel's knee when he bent?
His knee cracked on the tiles.
What did Parul feel when everyone laughed?
Parul felt embarrassed for Joel and wanted to disappear.
Why did Nani's 'no need' work as kindness?
She helped him up, told him he needn't learn everything at once, then shook hands and asked about his mother's garden, so he felt seen rather than tested.
What was it like for Joel when Nani shook his hand?
Joel had been terrified of being tested, and the handshake made him feel like family.

Dear Sudha,

You asked me last week how I got back to being "normal" after Class 8. I've been thinking about it, and I want to answer properly.

It wasn't one thing. When the boys in my section had spent months calling me names and I'd started skipping school, my parents took me to the school counsellor. I met her every week for a term. She helped me stop thinking it was something wrong with me.

Then football. Coach made me a defender, and being shouted at to "hold the line!" made me feel strong again. And three friends, Vikram, Rehmat and Paul, who just kept saving me a seat.

Now I'm in Class 11, and I help at the junior anti-bullying club every Thursday. Last week a Class 6 boy told me about someone stealing his lunch. I took him straight to the counsellor, who called his parents that afternoon.

Anand

Which day does Anand help at the junior anti-bullying club?
Every Thursday.
How did football make Anand feel?
Being a defender made Anand feel strong again, bringing back some confidence after months of feeling small.
What else could Anand do at the club to help younger students speak up early?
Anand could share a simple list of adults to approach, so a younger student knows exactly where to go the same day.
How might the Class 6 boy have felt being taken straight to the counsellor?
He probably felt relieved and believed, since an older student took his problem seriously right away.
Whom does Estella marry?
She marries Bentley Drummle, a rich, sulky young man. The marriage is very unhappy, and Drummle later dies after an accident with a horse he ill-treated.

I'm Irfan, and last year I lost a friend by saying nothing. At a party, Chinmay made a joke about my father's shop in front of everyone. It stung. But I didn't say anything. I just went quiet. After that, I stopped replying quickly to his messages. I said no to the cricket on Sunday, then the movie. I told myself it would fade, that I didn't want a big drama. And it did fade. So did the friendship. Months later, Chinmay texted, "Did I do something?" I still didn't say. I just sent a thumbs-up. Now, looking back, I think one honest sentence, "That joke about Abbu's shop hurt," might have fixed it. The quiet felt easier at the time. It cost me more than the conversation would have.

What did Chinmay joke about?
Irfan's father's shop.
Why did Irfan go quiet instead of telling Chinmay?
Irfan felt hurt and wanted to avoid a big drama, and staying silent felt easier and brought relief in the short term.
What could Irfan have said, and why might it have helped?
One honest sentence, like "That joke about Abbu's shop hurt," would have given Chinmay a chance to apologise and repair the friendship.
How might Chinmay have felt when he texted "Did I do something?"
Chinmay was probably confused and worried, noticing the distance but not knowing why.

Ingrid had been with Yuki for three years in their flat in Stockholm. Since Yuki's promotion in the spring, dinners had changed. Yuki's phone lay by the plate. Weekend walks were shorter; Yuki would answer "just one thing" on the bench. Ingrid told herself it was temporary. She stopped suggesting the Sunday market. On Yuki's birthday, Ingrid had booked a small restaurant. Halfway through the soup, Yuki took a work call outside for twenty minutes. Ingrid sat alone at the candlelit table. When Yuki came back, Ingrid said quietly, "I've felt like the last thing on your list for months." Yuki froze. They talked until the restaurant closed.

For how long did Yuki take the work call at the birthday dinner?
Yuki took a work call outside for twenty minutes.
What was Ingrid feeling as she sat alone at the table?
Ingrid felt hurt and lonely, like the last thing on Yuki's list, after months of saying nothing.
What could have helped earlier, before the birthday dinner?
Ingrid naming the feeling gently in the spring, or Yuki keeping dinners and walks phone-free, could have stopped it building up.
How might Yuki feel on hearing Ingrid's words?
Yuki froze, likely shocked and guilty, realising the work habit had quietly hurt Ingrid for months.
Is there any difference between "continual" and "continuous"?

Traditionally, "continuous" means without a break and "continual" means repeated again and again with pauses. Many people use them interchangeably.
Examples: The rain fell continuously all night. The phone rang continually during dinner.
Mere garden mein bahut ghonge aa gaye hain. 'Ghonga' English mein snail hi hai na?
Yes, "ghonga" is "snail". A snail has a shell on its back. A slug looks similar but has no shell.
Aur 'kenchua'?
"Kenchua" is "earthworm". Earthworms are good for the soil because they help air and water get into it.
John's piggy bank contains quarters, dimes, and nickels.  He has three more dimes than quarters and 6 fewer nickels than quarters.  If he has 63 coins, how many quarters does John have?

Let x represent the number of quarters John has
Nickels: x-6
Dimes: x+3
Total:x+x-6+x+3=63
3x-3=63
3x=66
x=22 quarters
The answer is 22.

The power had gone out at ten, the night before their final exam, and the two roommates were studying by one rechargeable lamp in their tiny Hyderabad flat. Jatin, frazzled, muttered, "Useless, useless," at his own notes.
Across the table Ramesh went rigid. "Can you not say that word," he said sharply, and shoved his chair back so hard it scraped.
Jatin stared. Ramesh never snapped. There was no time for a long talk and no other room to escape to. So Jatin said, "Sorry. I'll drop it," and turned the lamp a little toward Ramesh's side.
After a while Ramesh said, "I don't even know why it gets to me."
"You don't have to know," Jatin said. "Pass the highlighter?"

What word did Jatin mutter at his notes?
Useless.
How did Jatin feel when Ramesh snapped about the word?
Jatin was startled, since Ramesh never snapped, but stayed calm and caring, saying sorry and turning the lamp toward Ramesh's side.
What choice did Jatin make under exam pressure, and why was it wise?
Jatin apologised, dropped the word and turned the lamp toward Ramesh without asking for a story, keeping the night calm and Ramesh's privacy intact.
How might Ramesh feel when Jatin says 'You don't have to know'?
Ramesh probably feels relieved not to be pushed for an explanation he doesn't have, and accepted anyway.

During the worst week of the May heat in Delhi, the flat's cooler leaked all over the floor. Tanvir came home, stepped in the puddle and exploded. "You never help with anything, Akash! You always mess everything up!"
Akash, who had cleaned the bathroom that very morning, felt his face go hot. "Never? I did the bathroom today. I fixed your fan last week!"
"That's not the point."
"You said never. That's literally the point."
They argued for fifteen minutes about "never" and "always", and nobody touched the puddle. Later, lying awake in the heat, Akash realised he still didn't know what Tanvir actually wanted him to do about the cooler.

What had Akash cleaned that morning?
The bathroom.
What was Akash feeling when Tanvir said "You never help"?
Akash felt hurt and defensive, unfairly painted after cleaning the bathroom that morning, so he fought the word "never".
How could either of them get back to the real problem?
Tanvir could name the specific issue, the leaking cooler and the puddle, and Akash could ask what was needed right now instead of arguing about the absolutes.
What might have been going on for Tanvir?
Tanvir was likely hot, tired and frustrated after stepping in the puddle, and the absolutes came out of that moment rather than a careful judgement.

In the college canteen in Mumbai, Sarita's friends were planning a quiz team. "Sarita's from Kerala, she'll top the science round," said Neel. "You people are born toppers." They laughed, and Sarita laughed too, but her chest tightened. She had nearly failed chemistry last term and told no one. For weeks she'd been studying until two, terrified of being the Malayali who wasn't clever. Sabina, sitting beside her, noticed Sarita's smile didn't reach her eyes. Later, walking to the station, Sabina asked, "You okay with that 'born toppers' thing?" Sarita let out a long breath. "No. It's like I'm not allowed to be bad at anything." Sabina nodded. "Then say so." The next day, when Neel repeated it, Sarita said, lightly, "I'm from Kerala and I'm terrible at chemistry. Put me in the music round." Everyone laughed, and she meant it.

Which round did Sarita ask to be put in?
The music round.
How had Sarita been feeling about the "born toppers" comments?
She felt pressured and afraid, her chest tightening, as if she wasn't allowed to be bad at anything.
How did Sabina support Sarita?
Sabina noticed her forced smile, asked privately whether she was okay, and encouraged her to say so, which helped Sarita correct it kindly.
How might Neel see his comment?
Neel probably thought it was a compliment and a joke, without realising it put pressure on Sarita.

What is Holmes explaining here? A short summary, please.

"The man married a woman very much older than himself for her money," said he, "and he enjoyed the use of the money of the daughter as long as she lived with them. It was a considerable sum, for people in their position, and the loss of it would have made a serious difference. It was worth an effort to preserve it. The daughter was of a good, amiable disposition, but affectionate and warm-hearted in her ways, so that it was evident that with her fair personal advantages, and her little income, she would not be allowed to remain single long. Now her marriage would mean, of course, the loss of a hundred a year, so what does her stepfather do to prevent it? He takes the obvious course of keeping her at home and forbidding her to seek the company of people of her own age. But soon he found that that would not answer forever. She became restive, insisted upon her rights, and finally announced her positive intention of going to a certain ball. What does her clever stepfather do then? He conceives an idea more creditable to his head than to his heart. With the connivance and assistance of his wife he disguised himself, covered those keen eyes with tinted glasses, masked the face with a moustache and a pair of bushy whiskers, sunk that clear voice into an insinuating whisper, and doubly secure on account of the girl's short sight, he appears as Mr. Hosmer Angel, and keeps off other lovers by making love himself."

Holmes explains that a stepfather wanted to keep his stepdaughter's income. To stop her marrying, he first kept her at home, then disguised himself as Mr. Hosmer Angel and courted her himself, so that no other man could win her.

'You've been rubbing your eyes since nine,' said Tejas, sliding into the seat across from Vaibhav in the canteen. 'And you snapped at the intern over a typo.'
'I know.' Vaibhav stirred the tea without drinking it. 'I've been tired every day for weeks, even after a Sunday lie-in. And last night around eight I got that dread in my stomach about Monday. Third Sunday running.'
'Maybe you just need a rest weekend.'
'I thought that too. But I've had rest weekends. The tiredness is back by Tuesday. That's not one bad week. It's a pattern.'
'So?'
'So I'm not going to push through it. Something in how I work has to change. I'll talk to my manager about the team's load, and I'll see a doctor if it doesn't lift.'
Tejas nodded slowly. 'Good. I'll take the Thursday review off your list.'

What did Vaibhav say happens after a rest weekend?
Vaibhav said the tiredness is back by Tuesday.
What was Vaibhav feeling on Sunday nights?
Vaibhav felt a stomach-tightening dread about Monday.
What other approach could Vaibhav take besides resting?
Vaibhav could change how the work is shared by talking to the manager, hand off tasks, and see a doctor if the tiredness does not lift.
How might Tejas see Vaibhav's situation?
Tejas seems concerned and supportive, noticing the signs and offering to take the Thursday review.

Friday: Pranav heard the dare in the canteen: race scooters down the hill road on Saturday at five, no helmets. Ojas was already grinning. Pranav laughed along, then went quiet.

Saturday: At home he sat with the idea. If a scooter skidded on the gravel, there could be a broken wrist, or worse. The school would hear. Mummy's face at the door. Against that stood two minutes of racing and a story for Monday. He set them side by side and the two minutes looked small. He texted Ojas: "Not racing. Come over, we'll watch the match."

Monday: Ojas met him at the gate. "I'm glad you said it," Ojas admitted. "I didn't really want to go either."

When was the scooter race meant to happen?
The race was meant for Saturday at five.
What was Pranav feeling as he weighed the dare, and how does the passage show it?
Pranav was uneasy and worried about the consequences; he went quiet after laughing and then pictured the injury, the school and Mummy's face.
What other approach could Pranav have used with the group on Friday, and why?
Pranav could have suggested a different plan for Saturday afternoon, such as the match, because a substitute lets others who feel uneasy step out too.
How does Ojas see Pranav's refusal?
Ojas is relieved and glad someone said it, since Ojas had not really wanted to go either.

Sunday. Rukmini and Deepak sat on the floor of her parents' flat with a sheet of paper after both mothers had left. "Before anyone else tells us what to do," Deepak said, "what do we actually want?" They each wrote three things. Rukmini: small ceremony, her grandmother comfortable, no loans. Deepak: small ceremony, his parents not feeling left out, no loans. They laughed at how close the lists were.
Wednesday. Deepak's aunt phoned suggesting a five-hundred-guest reception. Rukmini took out the sheet. "Small ceremony. That's a no." Deepak explained it gently to his aunt.
The following Saturday. A decorator offered a grand stage with instalments. "Does it fit the list?" Rukmini asked. "Instalments means a loan," Deepak said. They thanked the decorator and chose a simple marigold backdrop.
The sheet was starting to look worn.

How many guests did Deepak's aunt suggest?
A five-hundred-guest reception.
How did Rukmini and Deepak feel when they compared their lists?
They were amused and pleased, laughing at how close their lists were, which likely made them feel more united.
What else could the couple do if their families disagreed with the list?
They could share the three values with both families calmly, so relatives understand the reasons behind each choice.
How might Deepak's aunt see the couple's choice?
The aunt may feel a little disappointed at the smaller event, though Deepak explaining gently helps her feel respected.

messages.content: Last month, a factory made 12000 dolls and their associated accessories.  The accessories for each doll included 2 shoes, 3 bags, 1 set of cosmetics, and 5 hats.  If each doll took 45 seconds to make and each accessory took 10 seconds to make, what was the total combined machine operation time, in seconds, required to manufacture all of the dolls and their accessories?

The number of shoes the factory made was 12000 dolls x 2 shoes/doll = 24000 shoes
The factory also made for each doll 12000 dolls x 3 bags/doll = 36000 bags
The set of cosmetics made for each doll was just one, so there are 12000 cosmetics sets
Finally, the number of hats for the dolls was 12000 dolls x 5 hats/doll = 60000 hats
In total, the number of accessories was 24000 + 36000 + 12000 + 60000 = 132000 accessories
The dolls took in total 12000 dolls x 45 seconds/doll = 540000 seconds to be made
All the accessories also took 132000 accessories x 10 seconds/accessory = 1320000 seconds
Combing both results, we have that the total time the machinery was working was 1320000 + 540000 = 1860000 seconds
The answer is 1860000.

Tejas, put the phone face down for a minute and listen to your Ganga Masi.
When I was sixteen, there was a boy called Sunil. We had those small phones then, only texts. If he didn't reply in ten minutes, my stomach dropped. I'd check the phone under my pillow, in the bathroom, during prayers. Once, when he went quiet for an evening, I told him another boy had walked me home. It wasn't even true. I just wanted him to feel as scared as I did.
He was hurt, and we nearly broke up.
That night I made myself a small rule. When the dread came, I would write it in my diary first, then call my friend Lata or walk round the colony. Only after that could I text him.
It was hard. Some nights I wrote three pages. But the texts I sent after were kinder, and so was I.

Where did young Ganga check her phone?
Under her pillow, in the bathroom and during prayers.
How did young Ganga feel when Sunil didn't reply?
She felt dread and fear; her stomach dropped if he didn't reply in ten minutes, and she wanted him to feel as scared as she did.
What choice did young Ganga make after nearly breaking up, and why did it help?
She decided to write in her diary, call Lata or walk before texting, which calmed the dread so her texts were kinder.
How was Sunil affected when she invented the story about another boy?
He was hurt by it, and they nearly broke up, because the jealousy test made him doubt her.
Now you try: which has an answer, 0 / 4 or 4 / 0?
The answer is 0 / 4 = 0; 4 / 0 has no answer.

A supplier is packing cartons of canned juice. Each carton has 20 cans of juice. Out of the 50 cartons that have been packed, only 40 cartons have been loaded on a truck. How many cans of juice are left to be loaded on the truck?

There are 50 - 40 = 10 cartons of canned juice that are left to be loaded on the truck.
This is equal to 10 x 20 = 200 cans of juice.
The answer is 200.

I still wince when I think about the geography project in class ten. Reena and I were partners, and we were both clever enough to do it easily. That was the trouble. I thought Reena would take the maps, since she loves drawing. Reena, I found out later, thought I'd write the report, since I'm the "essay one." So I spent the week watching cooking videos. She spent it on her dance practice. On the last night we video-called and saw each other's empty files. We laughed, a horrible laugh, and then stayed up till three writing garbage. We scraped a pass. Our friends who'd split the work properly got distinctions. What I learnt: each of us had made the best choice for ourselves, and together that was the worst choice. I'm Afreen, and I don't assume anymore. I ask.

Until what time did Afreen and Reena stay up?
They stayed up till three.
How did Afreen feel when they saw each other's empty files?
Afreen felt horrified and embarrassed, laughing a horrible laugh at the mess they'd made.
What does Afreen now do differently, and why does it help?
Afreen asks instead of assuming, so both partners know their tasks and neither can rely on the other to cover.
How might Reena remember the project?
Reena likely remembers it with embarrassment too, since she also assumed Afreen would do the report.

Tutor's note, first-year engineering design, 21 January
The group's bridge model failed at half the target load today. Afterwards Pankaj told the others, loudly, "Ganga did the joints. That's why." Ganga went pale and said, "It's all my fault. I ruined it for everyone." She was close to tears.
I asked the group to examine the failure together. The joints had slipped, yes; Ganga had used less glue than the plan said. But the main beam was also one size smaller than the drawing, and that was Pankaj's part.
I told Ganga that owning her part was good, but carrying the whole failure was neither accurate nor fair to herself. I asked Pankaj to look at the beam. He went quiet, then said, "Okay. Mine too."
The group has written a short list of what each person will change for next week's retest. Ganga's line reads: "Follow the glue spec; ask if unsure."

At what load did the bridge model fail?
At half the target load.
What was Ganga feeling after Pankaj blamed her?
Ashamed and close to tears, pale and taking the whole failure on herself.
What did the tutor help the group do?
Examine the failure together, see both the joints and the undersized beam, and write down what each person will change for the retest.
How did Pankaj respond when asked to look at the beam?
He went quiet, then admitted his share: "Okay. Mine too."

Thursday. Wasim, twenty-five, had a job interview in Chennai on Monday. He booked the train for Sunday morning, not night, "in case anything goes wrong." He scanned his certificates and ID, emailed them to himself and kept printouts in a separate bag. He saved his friend Deepak's address in Chennai as a backup place to stay.
Sunday. The train was cancelled due to track repairs. Wasim felt his stomach drop, then remembered his plan. He took the afternoon bus instead.
Monday. He arrived at Deepak's flat at midnight, slept a few hours, and reached the interview office thirty minutes early, certificates in hand. The interviewer said, "Good, you're on time."

Why was the train cancelled?
Due to track repairs.
How did Wasim feel when the train was cancelled?
He felt his stomach drop with worry, then calmer as he remembered his backup plan.
Which parts of Wasim's preparation saved the interview?
Travelling a day early, keeping documents in two places and having Deepak's flat as a backup place to stay.
How might Deepak feel when Wasim arrives at midnight?
Deepak might be sleepy but glad to help, since the backup plan was agreed in advance.

At the school sports day, Samir came fifth in the 100 metres. He walked off the track and sat under the tree, face hot. When Ms Afreen, the PT teacher, came over, he said, "I never win anything. I'm always the slowest. I'm never going to be good at sports."

Ms Afreen sat beside him. "Never? Who won the long jump in Class 5?"
"...Me."
"Who scored two goals in the inter-house match last month?"
"Me. But this was running."
"So today you came fifth in one race. What was different about the long jump?"
Samir thought. "I practised every day for two weeks."
"And the 100 metres?"
"I didn't practise."

Ms Afreen smiled. "Then maybe it's not 'never'. Maybe it's 'not yet'."

What position did Samir come in the 100 metres?
Samir came fifth.
Why did Samir say "I never win anything"?
Samir felt disappointed and embarrassed after one race, and that single result stretched into a rule for all sports.
What did Ms Afreen's questions reveal?
Counter-examples, the long jump and the goals, and a difference: Samir had practised for the long jump but not for the race.
How might Ms Afreen see Samir's "never"?
Ms Afreen sees it as disappointment talking, and gently shows him it is "not yet" rather than "never".

Two sentences, please: what is this about?

A professional case of great gravity was engaging my own attention at the time, and the whole of next day I was busy at the bedside of the sufferer. It was not until close upon six o'clock that I found myself free and was able to spring into a hansom and drive to Baker Street, half afraid that I might be too late to assist at the denouement of the little mystery. I found Sherlock Holmes alone, however, half asleep, with his long, thin form curled up in the recesses of his armchair. A formidable array of bottles and test-tubes, with the pungent cleanly smell of hydrochloric acid, told me that he had spent his day in the chemical work which was so dear to him.

The narrator spends the day with a patient, then rushes to Baker Street at six, afraid of missing the end of the mystery. Holmes is found half asleep in an armchair among bottles and test-tubes after a day of chemistry.

I'm Darshan, and it took me a while to say this plainly: the group was controlling me.

It never looked like force. When I missed a Sunday for my cousin's wedding, Omkar messaged, "We missed your energy. Hope nothing blocks your progress." When my mother fell ill and I skipped two weeks, someone mentioned that "karma has its own timing." They noticed what I ate at office lunches. They asked who my new friends were.

I felt guilty all the time, as if I were letting down a whole family.

What changed things was small. I told Omkar I would come once a month, not every week. My stomach knotted as I typed it. Then I spent that free Sunday playing football with old friends from work, laughing more than I had in a year.

When I finally stopped going, I sent one polite message. I didn't owe them an apology.

Why did Darshan miss a Sunday?
For a cousin's wedding.
How did Darshan feel as the group noticed and commented on every choice?
Darshan felt constantly guilty, as if letting down a whole family, and anxious when setting a limit.
What small boundary helped Darshan, and why?
Going once a month instead of weekly freed time for outside friends, which showed Darshan how much the group had been controlling things.
How might Omkar see Darshan's once-a-month message?
Omkar may see it as Darshan drifting from progress, since the group treated missing events as a spiritual failing rather than a normal choice.

Monday. At the weekly ops meeting, Amandeep, the only woman on the team, misread a delivery figure out loud and had to correct herself. Her face burned. For the rest of the day she replayed it, certain Santosh and the others thought she wasn't sharp enough.
Wednesday. Before Friday's meeting she tried an experiment. She wrote down every mistake she could remember others making in the last month of meetings. After ten minutes her page had one line: "Santosh once said Tuesday instead of Thursday?" She wasn't even sure about that one.
Friday. In the meeting she spoke up three times. The second time she muddled a number again, laughed, said, "Sorry, 4,200, not 2,400," and kept going. At lunch Santosh asked her about the new route plan. He didn't mention the numbers. She suspected he didn't remember them at all.

What did Amandeep write on her page on Wednesday?
"Santosh once said Tuesday instead of Thursday?"
How did Amandeep feel after Monday's meeting?
She felt embarrassed, face burning, and anxious that the others thought she wasn't sharp enough.
What experiment did Amandeep try, and what did it show?
Writing down every mistake she remembered others making; she could barely recall one, which showed people are mostly focused on themselves.
What did Santosh seem to care about at lunch?
Santosh was interested in the new route plan, not in her muddled numbers.

Gudi Padwa morning, gudis on bamboo poles at every window, and Eshaan was at the municipal school in Kothrud with three old laptops for twenty kids. The fourth had died on the way.
At his office job he was good, well paid, often praised. And lately, a little bored. These Saturday coding classes were where the restlessness went.
"Three laptops, twenty of us?" Deepak, thirteen, raised an eyebrow.
"Then we code on paper first," Eshaan said, and drew a robot on the board. The kids wrote instructions, move, turn, pick up, and Eshaan walked their steps like the robot, bumping into desks whenever they got the order wrong. The room roared.
By noon Deepak had a working loop on a laptop. Eshaan felt that quiet glow again. Not finished, he thought. Just getting started.

How many laptops did Eshaan have for the twenty kids?
Three old laptops; the fourth had died on the way.
How does Eshaan feel about the office job, and about the class?
Eshaan feels content but a little bored at the office, and a quiet glow in the class, where the restlessness finds a purpose.
How did Eshaan handle the missing laptops, and what does it show?
He switched to coding on paper and acted as the robot himself, showing that a skill can still be taught well when resources fall short.
What is the class like for Deepak?
Deepak starts out doubtful, raising an eyebrow at three laptops for twenty, and ends with a working loop by noon.

It started with one debate round in September. I told Ma'am I had a sore throat, and the relief was so huge I nearly laughed.
By October I was letting calls go to voicemail. Not just unknown numbers, everyone. Dolma rang three times about the tuition carpool, and I texted 'got a lift' when I hadn't. I walked the forty minutes instead so I wouldn't have to talk in the car.
Then Sunday football went. Then the group chat. Each thing I dropped felt like one less danger, but the things left felt scarier. Even buying bread at the corner shop made my chest tight.
Looking back, Sahil in September would never have believed Sahil in November: a person whose safe world was basically a bedroom and a school desk.

What excuse did Sahil give to skip the debate round?
Sahil told Ma'am about having a sore throat.
How did Sahil feel each time another activity was dropped?
Each drop brought a short sense of safety, but what remained felt scarier, until even buying bread made Sahil's chest tight.
What could have been a turning point for Sahil around October?
Telling a parent or the school counsellor about the tight chest and the dodged calls could have led to small, supported steps back, like one carpool ride with Dolma.
What might Dolma have been experiencing as the carpool offers kept being turned down?
Dolma might have felt puzzled or brushed off after three calls and a 'got a lift' text, not knowing Sahil was walking forty minutes to avoid talking.

Counsellor's note, Nirmala. Tenzin came to see me after the third weekend of working. The boss praises Tenzin's dedication in every meeting, "our most reliable person," and each time hands over another project. Tenzin laughed while describing this, but the laugh was thin, and Tenzin's eyes were red. I can't tell how much is tiredness and how much is worry about saying no. Together we made a two-week log of tasks and hours. Then Tenzin drafted a short list of priorities, with the items that could wait, to take to the boss on Monday, plus one plain sentence: "I can do A or B this week, which matters more?" We agreed that health comes before praise. I'll see Tenzin again next Friday.

What did Tenzin and Nirmala make together?
They made a two-week log of tasks and hours.
What might Tenzin be feeling, given the thin laugh and red eyes?
Probably tiredness and worry about saying no, though Nirmala admits the balance is unclear.
What could Tenzin say when the boss hands over another task?
"I can do A or B this week, which matters more?", along with the list of priorities and the log of hours.
How might the boss see Tenzin's heavy workload?
Possibly as a reward for reliability, and the boss may not notice the load it creates.
On Thursday Walmart sold 210 pounds of ground beef. On Friday they sold twice that amount. On Saturday they only sold 150 pounds.  What was the average amount of beef sold per day?

On Friday Walmart sold 2 * 210 pounds = 420 pounds.
For all three days Walmart sold 210 + 420 + 150 pounds = 780 pounds.
The average amount of beef sold per day is 780 pounds / 3 days = 260 pounds.
The answer is 260.

"Darshan, go on, give Madhav Uncle a kiss. He came all this way," said Mummy.
"Come here, champ, one kiss!" Madhav said, bending down with open arms.
Darshan hid behind Mummy's legs. "No."
"Darshan, be polite," Mummy began, then looked at his face and paused. "Beta, does it feel yucky?"
He nodded.
"Then you do not have to. Would you like to wave or give a high five?"
He held out his palm. Madhav laughed and tapped it lightly. "High five it is!"
"Your body is yours," Mummy whispered.

What did Darshan offer Madhav in the end?
He offered a high five.
How does Darshan feel about giving the kiss?
He is uncomfortable: he hides behind Mummy's legs, says no, and nods when she asks if it feels yucky.
What did Mummy do that respected Darshan's no?
She looked at his face, changed her mind, offered a wave or a high five, and told him his body is his own. 🤍
How might Madhav see Darshan's refusal?
He seems to take it in good part, since he laughs and accepts the high five; to him the kiss was probably meant as friendly.
Independence Day is celebrated in 15 August every year. Which word is wrong?

Independence Day is celebrated on 15 August every year.
Why: Dates take "on".

When Hemant came back to Satara after three weeks in hospital with typhoid, he expected sympathy. At the tea stall, an uncle said, "Must be all that outside food you students eat." At home, an aunt said, "God is teaching you to pray more." His exam results had suffered too, and a neighbour said, "Maybe you weren't serious." Each comment stung more than the fever had. He stopped going out. He told his friends he was busy. When his friend Pankaj came by, Hemant said little. Pankaj sat on the step anyway. "Illness isn't a report card, Hemant. My father got typhoid from the village well, and he's the most careful man I know." Hemant looked up. "Everyone says it's my fault." "Everyone's wrong," Pankaj said. "And your doctor said so too, didn't he?" Hemant nodded slowly.

How long was Hemant in hospital?
Three weeks, with typhoid.
What was Hemant feeling as the comments piled up?
He felt ashamed and hurt, as if the illness were his fault, so he withdrew and stopped going out.
How did Pankaj support Hemant?
Pankaj sat with him, told him illness isn't a report card, shared his father's story, and reminded him the doctor also said it wasn't his fault.
How might the uncle and aunt see their comments?
They may think they are just explaining or advising, not seeing that blaming him adds shame to his pain.

Tuesday: The day Chandrika's offer letter came from the hospital in Chennai, she called Parul first. Parul said "nice" and hung up in under a minute. At dinner she sat with other girls.
Saturday: Chandrika caught herself about to delete the offer post from her profile so Parul wouldn't see it. She left it up. Instead she knocked on Parul's door with two cups of filter coffee. "I know you're still waiting to hear back. I don't want this to sit between us. You can be annoyed with me for a bit. I'm still here." Parul stared at the coffee, then took it. "I'm happy for you. I'm also scared I'll be the one left."
Two weeks later: Parul's interview call came. Chandrika helped her rehearse on the terrace every evening, and didn't bring up her own job unless Parul asked. When Parul did ask what the first month was like, Chandrika told her plainly.

Where did Chandrika's offer letter come from?
The hospital in Chennai.
Why did Chandrika nearly delete her offer post?
She felt guilty and worried that her success was hurting Parul, and wanted to hide it.
What did Chandrika do on Saturday instead of hiding her news?
She left the post up, brought Parul filter coffee, named the tension kindly and gave her room to be annoyed.
What was Parul feeling behind her short "nice"?
Happy for Chandrika but scared of being the one left behind.

Day one of the Ganesh festival holidays: Lavanya lent Aadhya her best thing, a wind-up train that whistled. 'Keep it till Sunday,' she said, feeling generous and grown-up.
Thursday: the colony pandal was lit up, and Aadhya was riding her new cycle round and round it. 'Can I have one turn?' Lavanya asked. 'No, it's new. Papa said.' Lavanya stood by the pandal steps, the drums loud, her face hot. She had given the train. For four whole days.
Sunday: Aadhya returned the train, one wheel wobbly, and said nothing about it. Lavanya put it on the top shelf. 'Never again,' she told her mother. 'I gave, she didn't give back. That's cheating.' Her mother began to answer, then just stroked her hair.

What did Lavanya lend Aadhya?
A wind-up train that whistled.
How did Lavanya feel when Aadhya refused a turn on the cycle?
Lavanya felt hurt and cheated, her face hot, because she had lent the train and expected something back.
What could Lavanya's mother say that would help?
She could agree it hurt, then gently ask whether Aadhya might have been scared about a new cycle, helping Lavanya see feelings beyond the trade.
Why might Aadhya have said no to the cycle?
Aadhya may have been worried about damaging something new and was repeating what Papa said, not thinking about the train at all.

I'm Kashish, and looking back at my first month in Hyderabad, I remember how lost I felt. I'd come from Shillong, a skinny boy of eighteen, for my engineering course. The food was different, the heat was different, and at night the flat was so quiet I could hear my own homesickness.
I didn't tell anyone. But Sachin, my flatmate, must have noticed I'd stopped eating dinner. One night he knocked with two mugs of ginger tea and said, "Old cricket highlights?" He sat on my floor for an hour. He didn't ask what was wrong.
The next night he did it again. And the next. Once he brought a packet of chips from the only shop that stocked the kind we have back home.
By the end of that week, the flat didn't feel like a stranger's place anymore. I still missed home. But now there was a knock I could count on, and that made me feel I belonged there.

What did Sachin bring on the first night?
Two mugs of ginger tea.
How did Kashish feel once Sachin's knock became a nightly thing?
He felt safer and less alone; the flat stopped feeling like a stranger's place, and he felt he belonged there.
Which of Sachin's choices mattered most to Kashish, and why?
Coming back every night without asking what was wrong mattered most, because the steady small kindness showed Kashish he could count on someone.
How might Sachin have seen Kashish during that first month?
Sachin probably noticed a quiet flatmate who had stopped eating and guessed he was struggling, choosing company over questions.

Saturday
Chess club today. Jeevan wanted to teach me a new opening, the one where you move the horse first. I said no, I'll just do my usual one. My usual one always works, and nobody can say I did it wrong. He said I'll never get better if I only play the same way. I said I don't care. Then I played the same opening four times and won twice and lost twice, the same as always.
When I got home I watched Jeevan's opening on Papa's phone. It looked interesting. But what if I try it at club and lose in six moves and everyone sees? That would be so embarrassing.
Maybe I'll practise it with Papa first, where nobody can see.
Farida

Which piece does Jeevan's new opening move first?
It moves the horse first.
Why does Farida keep playing the usual opening?
Farida is afraid of being wrong or embarrassed in front of others, so the familiar opening feels safe even though it keeps Farida stuck.
Is practising with Papa first a good idea, and why?
Yes; trying the new opening where mistakes feel safe is a small step toward learning without the fear of being seen losing.
How does Jeevan see Farida's choice?
Jeevan thinks Farida will never improve by always playing the same way, and seems frustrated at the refusal to try.
Waiter se poochna hai "Aaj ka special kya hai?" English?
Ask: "What is today's special?"
My grandfather wants to teach me to cook his special egg curry this Sunday.
What a nice way to spend a Sunday. Cooking with a grandparent is a good way to learn and to hear old stories.
Should I take notes?
Yes, write down the ingredients and the order of the steps. Also note small tips he mentions, like how long to fry the onions. Those details are the real secret of the recipe.

Irawati Didi,
You're the only one in the family who won't laugh, so here goes. The dentist at the college clinic says one of my back teeth needs a filling. I've cancelled twice.
My reasoning, which sounds very smart at 2 a.m.: if I get the filling and something goes wrong, that's a mistake I chose. If I leave it and it gets worse, well, teeth just go bad sometimes. Nobody's fault.
But yesterday my roommate said, "So if it gets worse, you'll have chosen that too, just quietly." It stung, because I think he's right.
I know you're not my dentist, and I'm not asking you what to do with my tooth. I think I just needed someone to say that going back and asking all my questions is okay.
I'll book it tomorrow if you reply "go".
Kamal

How many times has Kamal cancelled the filling?
Kamal has cancelled twice.
Why does leaving the tooth feel less risky to Kamal?
Kamal feels more afraid of a mistake caused by choosing the filling than of the tooth getting worse, which seems like nobody's fault.
What is a sensible next step for Kamal?
Booking the dentist again and asking all the questions, so the dentist can explain the real risks of acting and of waiting.
How might Irawati feel reading the letter?
Irawati might feel touched to be trusted and glad Kamal is ready to go back.

Noa had booked a table at the ramen place near Umeda for Hiroshi's birthday, but at six he texted: "Sorry, can't. Still fixing the catalogue layout." It was his second cancellation that week. Noa got two portions to take away and climbed the stairs to his flat. Hiroshi opened the door in yesterday's shirt, eyes red. On his screen, the furniture catalogue looked finished to her. "The margins on page nine are off by a millimetre," he said. "And the grey is a bit too warm. I was up till four." Noa set the noodles on his desk. "Can I see it as a draft? Just a good-enough draft. We go through it together for thirty minutes, and whatever's left, you write down and send it anyway." He hesitated, then slid the laptop over. By eight they were eating, and the file was in his client's inbox.

What did Hiroshi say was wrong with page nine?
The margins on page nine are off by a millimetre.
What might Hiroshi have been worried about while he stayed up till four?
He was probably afraid the client would spot tiny flaws like the margins or the warm grey and think less of him, even though the catalogue already looked finished.
Which move of Noa's helped Hiroshi get unstuck, and why?
Calling it a good-enough draft and offering thirty minutes together gave him a limit and company, so sending it felt less risky 🙂
How does Noa see the catalogue compared with how Hiroshi sees it?
To Noa it looks finished, while Hiroshi sees only the millimetre and the colour; she can see the whole piece that his worry hides from him.

At sixteen, Omkar had a geography project and a whole month to finish it. He kept saying, "I'll begin on Saturday." If he tried and the map came out crooked, his teacher would see that he was not good at this. Doing nothing kept the picture of himself intact. The night before, he pasted a rushed collage and got a weak mark.

At twenty-five, at his first office job, Omkar noticed the same heavy feeling as a report deadline crept closer. This time he closed the game he had opened and asked himself, "What exactly is uncomfortable? Is it that I'm scared it won't be good? Is it that I don't know the first step? Or is it just dull?" He wrote the answer on a sticky note: "I don't know what the client wants."

He turned to his colleague Varun. "Can I ask you two questions about the brief?" Varun nodded, and the fog began to lift.

What did Omkar write on his sticky note?
He wrote, "I don't know what the client wants."
What has changed in how Omkar handles delay between sixteen and twenty-five?
At sixteen he avoids starting to protect his image, and the work suffers; at twenty-five he asks what exactly is uncomfortable, names the real feeling as unclear steps, and asks Varun for help.
What was Omkar feeling when he put off the geography map at sixteen?
Omkar was afraid of looking bad, since a crooked map might show his teacher he was not good at it.
Why did naming the feeling help Omkar at twenty-five?
Naming it as not knowing what the client wanted separated the feeling from the whole task and pointed to a fix, asking Varun about the brief.

I'm Manjula, and I still remember the morning I nearly got it wrong. The principal was shouting at some older boys in the corridor. When I turned round, Kiran was under his desk, knees pulled up. My first thought was, not now, Kiran. Then I saw how pale he was. I knelt and said, "You're safe. Stay there as long as you need." When he came out, he kept saying, "Sorry, Miss. I'll be good, I'll clean the board, I'll do anything." He was far too eager. I told him he wasn't in trouble. I'd half wanted to scold him for leaving his seat, but that could wait. Later that week we talked calmly about where he could sit when noises get loud.

Where was Kiran when Manjula turned round?
Kiran was under his desk, knees pulled up.
What did Manjula feel at first, and what changed her mind?
Manjula first felt impatient, thinking "not now, Kiran", but seeing how pale he was made her realise he was scared.
Why was it wise for Manjula to leave the talk about his seat until later?
Kiran needed to feel safe first; a scolding while he was scared would only add fear, so a calm talk later that week could actually help.
Why might Kiran have become so eager to please after coming out?
Kiran was likely still frightened by the shouting, and being extra good may have felt like a way to stay safe from anger.

Dear Diary,
Today was speech day at school. Last night I told Mummy my tummy hurt. It did hurt, sort of. This morning she let me stay home.
The weird thing is, the minute she said 'okay, stay home', my tummy stopped hurting. Like magic. I watched cartoons, made a jam sandwich and felt totally fine.
Afreen Didi came home and said Mrs Fernandes asked where I was. My tummy went funny again for one second.
Now I'm in bed and there's a spelling test on Monday. It's three whole days away and I'm already scared. Maybe my tummy will hurt on Monday too.
From Zubin

What happened to Zubin's tummy when Mummy said 'okay, stay home'?
Zubin's tummy stopped hurting, like magic.
What does Zubin feel about Monday's spelling test, and how can you tell?
Zubin is already scared three days early and half hopes the tummy will hurt again, which shows staying home now feels like the safe way out.
What turning point could Mummy offer at this stage?
She could gently notice that the ache vanished once school was off, then help Zubin go on Monday with a small plan and her support rather than another day at home.
How might Afreen Didi see Zubin's day at home?
Afreen Didi might be puzzled that Zubin seemed fine all day, and may wonder why the teacher had to ask.
The eggs hatched this morning. How is that different from just cracking?

Hatched means that the young animal inside came out of the egg; cracking only means the shell breaks. It is a verb, the past tense of hatch.
Example: Three tiny chicks hatched on the farm this morning.
We need a reminder notice: students must carry their library cards on Tuesday. 25 words.

REMINDER
All students must carry their library cards on Tuesday. Please keep your card in your bag so that you do not forget it. Thank you.

At the playschool, Bhavna, five, was waiting at the bottom of the slide when her friend Keerthana fell off the side. Keerthana's knee was cut and bleeding, and she screamed. Bhavna stood frozen, mouth open. Then she turned and ran, crying, to the teacher at the sandpit. "Ma'am! Keerthana fell! Blood!" The teacher ran over, knelt beside Keerthana and called for the first-aid box. Another teacher gently led Bhavna to a bench and held her hand. Bhavna kept crying, "Is she going to be okay?" "Yes. The teachers are taking care of her. You came to us so fast. That was exactly right."

Where was Bhavna waiting?
At the bottom of the slide.
What was Bhavna feeling when Keerthana fell?
She felt shocked and scared, freezing with her mouth open, then crying.
What did Bhavna do that helped most?
She ran to the teacher to tell a grown-up, which let the adults take care of Keerthana quickly.
How did the second teacher help Bhavna?
The teacher led her to a bench, held her hand and reassured her that coming to tell was exactly right.

Tuesday: Chaitanya sir asked Jyoti to sign the site-safety form for the Wagholi project with Friday's date, "the day the rails were fitted". They hadn't been. They'd go up next week. "Just sign it, Jyoti, it's paperwork." He'd stood up for her when a contractor shouted at her in her first month. She couldn't sleep that night.
Wednesday: She went to his cabin with tea. "Sir, I can't sign for rails that aren't up. If someone falls this week, that signature is a lie that hurt them." He frowned. "You think I'd put anyone at risk?" "No. That's why I want to help fix it. Can we close that floor until the rails are fitted, and I'll sign the day they are?"
The following Monday: The rails went up. Jyoti signed that afternoon, with the real date. Chaitanya sir looked at the form and said, "Good. That's how it should be." She was relieved he still greeted her in the corridor.

What was the safety form meant to confirm?
That the rails had been fitted on the Wagholi project.
Why couldn't Jyoti sleep on Tuesday night?
She felt torn and anxious, grateful to Chaitanya sir for once protecting her, but worried a false signature could lead to someone getting hurt.
What did Jyoti offer instead of the false signature?
Closing the floor until the rails were fitted and signing on the day they were actually up.
How might Chaitanya sir feel when Jyoti refuses?
He may feel stung that she doubts him, but her respectful alternative lets him agree without losing face.
