I'm Himani, Pallavi's neighbour. Yesterday on the building lawn, her son Neel, who is two, was pouring sand from one cup into another, again and again. Pallavi called, "Neel, come, let's go home," three times. He didn't even turn his head. I thought he was being stubborn. Then she walked over and tapped him, and he jumped a little and smiled at her as if she had just appeared. I don't think he had heard her at all.

What was Neel doing on the building lawn?
Neel was pouring sand from one cup into another, again and again.
What does Neel's little jump and smile when tapped suggest about how he felt?
Neel was startled and then happy to see Pallavi, which suggests he was so absorbed in the sand that he hadn't heard her at all; he wasn't being stubborn.
What could Pallavi do first the next time she needs Neel's attention?
Walk over, get down to his level and touch him gently before speaking, since calling from far away may not reach him.
How did Himani's view of Neel change?
Himani first thought he was being stubborn, then saw his surprised smile and realised he hadn't heard at all.

James opens up a flower shop.  He needs to pay rent of $1200 a week with an additional 20% of rent to pay for utilities and he has 2 employees per shift with the store open 16 hours a day for 5 days a week.  If he pays each employee $12.50 an hour, what are his weekly expenses to run the store?

He is open 16*5=80 hours a week
So he pays each of his employees 12.5*80=$1000 per week
Since there are two employees, he pays them in total 2 * $1000 = $2000 per week.
The utilities cost 1200*.2=$240
So his total cost per week is 1200+2000+240=$3440
The answer is 3440.

It was the week before Diwali, and the hostel was emptying out. Zainab knocked on my door. "Tenzin, can I borrow your scooter for the whole holiday? I'll bring it back after." Ten days, a long road trip. I said no; I needed it. She looked crushed. "Okay, okay. Then could you at least drop me at the station at five tomorrow morning?" And I heard myself say yes before I'd even thought. Five a.m.! I hate early mornings. Later, lying awake, I realised: she'd dropped the big ask, and I felt I owed her a yes. Like she'd given something up, so it was my turn. I did drop her. I didn't mind, really. But next time, I'll ask myself if I'd say yes to the small thing on its own.

What time did Zainab need to be dropped at the station?
At five the next morning.
Why did Tenzin say yes to the early-morning drop so quickly?
Tenzin felt guilty after refusing the scooter, as if Zainab had given something up and it was now Tenzin's turn to agree.
What will Tenzin ask next time, and why is it useful?
Whether the smaller request would be a yes on its own, so the first refusal doesn't push Tenzin into agreeing.
How might Zainab have felt about the lift?
Zainab likely felt relieved and grateful, maybe without noticing the pressure her second ask created.

messages.content: 25 red flowers and 39 yellow flowers are used to make a rangoli. How many flowers are used?
64. Because 25 + 39 = 64, so 64 flowers are used.
Cut 124 into two equal halves. How big is each half?
62. Because 2 x 62 = 124, so each half is 62.
What happened when the giants set Hanuman's tail on fire?
They wound strips of cotton cloth soaked in oil round his tail and set it alight. Hanuman broke free and used the burning tail to set the city of Lanka ablaze.

But there were so many hillocks and banks to climb and pass, that, at length, I began to be weary, and told her we must halt, and retrace our steps. I shouted to her, as she had outstripped me a long way; she either did not hear or did not regard, for she still sprang on, and I was compelled to follow. Finally, she dived into a hollow; and before I came in sight of her again, she was two miles nearer Wuthering Heights than her own home; and I beheld a couple of persons arrest her, one of whom I felt convinced was Mr. Heathcliff himself.

Tell me in one line what happens here.
The narrator tires and asks the girl to turn back, but she runs on and is stopped near Wuthering Heights by two people, one likely Heathcliff.

With Mummy away at Nani's for the week and Papa working late, nobody checked Vikas's homework. Then the class teacher announced the science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early. "Aren't you going to revise?" his sister Sunaina asked, stirring the dal. Vikas was lying on the floor with his comics. "Nah. Only kids like Golu fail. He never listens. I'm different." "You haven't opened the chapter on magnets." "I know magnets. Everyone knows magnets." Sunaina read out a question from his book about the poles. Vikas guessed wrong, laughed, and said the real test wouldn't ask that. The power went off at nine, and he fell asleep happily in the dark, completely sure tomorrow would go fine. Sunaina lay awake worrying for both of them.

When was the science test moved to?
The science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early.
Why is Vikas so relaxed about the test?
Vikas feels confident and carefree because he believes only kids like Golu fail, so a bad result feels like something that happens to others, not to him.
What small step could help Vikas before the test?
He could let Sunaina quiz him on a few questions and study the ones he gets wrong, like the one about the poles.
What is the evening like for Sunaina?
Sunaina is left worrying for both of them, stirring the dal and reading out questions while her brother laughs it off. 😰

"Pema, are you coming to the school council meeting on the bus route?" Hrithik asked at the gate.

"No."

"But you're on that bus. It's your route they're cutting."

"I don't do all that," Pema said. "Protests, meetings, petitions. You get into trouble. My uncle got into trouble once. So I just don't think about it."

"Nobody's protesting. It's a council meeting. In the library."

"Same thing."

Two weeks later, Hrithik read out the new timetable in class. The 7:10 bus was gone. The council had agreed to a smaller route after hearing only from students on the other side of town.

Pema's face fell. "They didn't even ask us."

"They did," Hrithik said. "Nobody from our side came."

Pema was quiet all through maths.

Where was the council meeting held?
In the library.
How did Pema feel when the new timetable was read out?
Pema felt dismayed and let down, her face falling at losing the 7:10 bus.
What approach could Pema have taken instead of avoiding the meeting completely?
Pema could have gone to the library meeting and simply explained the bus problem, which is safe and lawful and would have put that side's needs on record.
How might Hrithik see Pema's avoidance?
Hrithik probably feels frustrated but sympathetic, knowing the fear comes from an uncle's trouble but seeing it cost them the bus.

messages.content: There were 30 women and 20 men who attended the party. After few hours, 2/5 of the total number of people left. If 9 men left the party, how many more women stayed at the party than men?

There were 30 + 20 = 50 attendees at the party.
A total of 50 x 2/5 = 20 people left the party.
Nine of those who left were men while 20 - 9 = 11 of them were women.
So, 30 - 11= 19 women stayed at the party.
And 20 - 9 = 11 men stayed at the party.
Thus, 19 - 11 = 8 more women than men stayed at the party.
The answer is 8.

Games teacher's note, Anjali. In today's inter-house throwball match, the ball touched Uma's fingers before going out, but the umpire gave the point to her team. Uma raised her hand. "Ma'am, it touched me. It's their point." Her team groaned. She stood straight, chin up, and said, "We made the fair-play pledge." They lost by one point. Afterwards she walked around with her head high, telling everyone the pledge mattered more. A few teammates were still sulking. I spoke to the whole team about fair play, and about not lecturing each other.

What did Uma tell the umpire?
That the ball touched her, so it was the other team's point.
What does Uma walking around with her head high after losing suggest?
She felt proud and in the right for keeping the fair-play pledge, and that feeling mattered more to her than winning.
Why did Anjali also talk about not lecturing each other?
Uma's honesty was good, but telling everyone the pledge mattered more could leave teammates feeling judged.
How might Uma's teammates feel after losing by one point?
Some are upset because her honesty cost them the match, even if they respect the pledge.

"Payal, why are you crying? It's just a drawing."
"It's not just a drawing, Yash. Ma'am put everyone's on the wall except mine."
"I wouldn't care. Mine's never on the wall."
"Well, I care!" Payal wiped her face.
Yash sat down on the step. He didn't get it. Then he remembered how he'd felt when he wasn't picked for the relay. "Is it like being left out?"
"Yes. Like everyone else counts and I don't."
"Oh." He thought. "What happened to it?"
"I think it fell behind the cupboard."
"Let's go and look. And if it's not there, we can ask Ma'am together."
Payal sniffed. "Okay."

Where does Payal think her drawing went?
Behind the cupboard.
How did Yash come to understand Payal's upset?
He remembered feeling left out when he wasn't picked for the relay, and saw she felt the same way.
What did Yash do that showed growing empathy?
He asked what happened and offered to look for the drawing and ask Ma'am together.
How did Payal feel about her drawing not being on the wall?
Payal felt left out and hurt, as if she didn't count.

On Saturday afternoon Joseph texted Arohi, "Really sorry, something came up, can't make dinner tonight." What had come up was a message from Ganga: two spare seats at a concert that sounded far more fun than a birthday dinner. He had a brilliant night.

On Sunday, Arohi's reply glowed on his screen. "Ok." No exclamation marks, no warm words. Joseph felt a pang of guilt, and right behind it a wish to defend himself. It had only been one dinner. Tickets like that did not come around often. He opened a draft: "I'm sorry if you felt let down, but work has been insane and traffic was awful." Neither was the real reason. He read it back, and part of him winced. But he wanted the tension gone more than he wanted to be right.

Arohi glanced at her phone. She had cleared her entire evening and sat with seven people at a table laid for eight. She did not want reasons. She wanted him to know what that felt like. She sent short lines, "Got it," "Fine, later," and watched to see whether he understood, or only wanted things smooth again.

Why did Joseph cancel on Arohi's birthday dinner?
Ganga offered him a seat at a concert that sounded more fun.
How did Joseph's first draft differ from what Arohi was waiting for?

Joseph's draft blamed work and traffic and only apologised if she felt let down, so it aimed to make the tension go away. Arohi, with her short replies, wanted acknowledgment of what the cancelled dinner cost her.
What was Joseph feeling when he saw Arohi's short "Ok"?
He felt a pang of guilt mixed with a wish to defend himself.
What could Joseph write instead of that draft?
He could name what he did and how it felt for Arohi, apologise without a "but", and not ask to be forgiven right away.

Shreya's diary, Sunday.
Two offers on the table and my head is spinning. Offer one is bigger: a higher valuation, the kind of number you'd brag about. Offer two is smaller.
But tonight I made a list instead of just staring at the headline.
Board seats: offer one wants two seats on a board of three. They could outvote us. Offer two wants one seat, and only as an observer for the first year.
Liquidation preference: under offer one, if we sell, they get twice their money back before anyone else. Offer two, just once.
Help: I called three founders each fund had backed. Offer one's founders were polite but vague. Offer two's founders all said the same thing: "They picked up the phone when things went wrong."
Arohi, my co-founder, says the big number is tempting, and she's not wrong. But I'll ask our lawyer to explain both on Tuesday before we choose.

How many board seats does offer one want?
Two seats on a board of three.
How is Shreya feeling while comparing the offers?
Shreya feels overwhelmed at first, with a spinning head, but steadier once the list is made.
Why is calling founders the funds had backed a good step?
It shows how each investor behaves when things go wrong, which a headline number can't show.
How does Arohi see the bigger offer?
Arohi finds the big number tempting, which Shreya admits is a fair point.

During Diwali holidays, Dolma and I made clay diyas at her house. I was eight.

I rolled a ball of clay, and Dolma flattened hers into a pancake. "Mine's bigger," she said.

I was sure she was right. It looked huge.

Her grandmother came in. "Roll it back," she said. Dolma rolled it into a ball, and it was the same size as mine.

I remember staring at it. The clay hadn't changed. Only the shape. I'm Kishore, and even now, every Diwali, I think of that pancake.

What did Dolma flatten her clay into?
She flattened hers into a pancake.
How did Kishore feel staring at the rolled-back clay?
Kishore felt amazed and surprised, realising the amount hadn't changed.
How did Dolma's grandmother help the children learn?
She asked them to roll it back so they could see for themselves.
How might Dolma feel when her clay turned out the same size?

I'm Ishita, and I shared a project group with Aditi and two others this semester. In week two, Karthik submitted his part of the market survey a day late. He said sorry in the group chat. Aditi didn't reply.
At the next meeting she divided the tasks on the whiteboard. Karthik's name had nothing beside it. "It's fine, I'll do the analysis myself," she said. "We can't risk another delay." When Karthik offered to draft the slides, she said she'd already started them.
By week six he'd stopped offering. At the final review, the professor asked him a question about the survey and he answered it better than any of us. Aditi looked surprised.
I don't know what was going on in her mind. From where I sat, it looked like that one late day had become the whole story of Karthik for her.

What did Karthik submit a day late in week two?
He submitted his part of the market survey a day late.
Why might giving Karthik nothing have felt sensible to Aditi?
She was worried about another delay hurting the project, so after one late submission it felt safer to take his work herself than to trust him again.
What went wrong in the group, and what could have fixed it?
One late day made Aditi stop giving Karthik any tasks, and he stopped offering; giving him a small task with a clear deadline would have let the group see what he could actually do.
How might Karthik have experienced weeks two to six?
Karthik probably felt pushed out after apologising, which may explain why he stopped offering, even though he understood the survey better than anyone.

In Berlin, Selin and Abebe had fought every day since their baby sister was born.

So their mother made a plan. Every evening after dinner, Selin got fifteen minutes with Mama alone, reading picture books on the big chair. Then Abebe got fifteen minutes, building train tracks on the floor.

On Saturdays they made pancakes together. Selin cracked eggs; Abebe stirred.

By the third Saturday, when Abebe dropped an egg, Selin said, "It's okay, I'll get another one," instead of shouting.

Mama watched them and smiled.

What did Selin and Abebe make together on Saturdays?
Pancakes.
What does Selin's kind reply about the egg show?
It shows she feels more secure and warmer towards Abebe, enjoying cooperation instead of competing.
How does Mama's plan ease the rivalry?
Each child gets time alone with her, so they feel sure of their place, and a joint task shows them cooperation feels good.
How might Abebe feel when Selin says "It's okay"?
He probably feels relieved and happy, expecting a scolding but getting kindness.

The hiring panel at the hospital's IT department had seen six candidates by lunch. Abhinav was excited about the fourth. "He's another Rakesh. Same college, same cricket-club style, even the same laugh. Rakesh turned out brilliant." The third panellist agreed. Hemant, running a panel for the first time, looked at his notes. The fifth candidate, a woman from a small polytechnic, had solved the database problem fastest and explained it most clearly. Nobody had mentioned her. "Can I suggest something?" Hemant said. "Let's each score all six on the same four points: the problem, the explanation, the teamwork answer and learning. Out of five. Before we talk." Abhinav grumbled but filled in the sheet. When the scores were added, the fifth candidate was first, and Rakesh's lookalike was fourth.

How many candidates had the panel seen by lunch?
Six.
Why did Hemant suggest scoring before talking?
He felt uneasy that the panel was drawn to a candidate who resembled Rakesh while nobody mentioned the candidate who had solved the problem best.
Why does scoring all six on the same four points help?
It makes each panellist judge every candidate on the same evidence before excitement about a lookalike can sway the room.
How might Abhinav feel when the scores are added?
Abhinav may feel surprised and a little embarrassed that the lookalike he liked came fourth.
Is it "catastrophy" or "catastrophe"?

It is "catastrophe". It ends in "-phe", with "ph" and a silent e at the end.
Example: The flood was a catastrophe for the village.

'Tarun, did you lock the scooter? Those labourers from the new site are all thieves,' Anand said, dropping his keys on the table.
'All of them?'
'Obviously. Look at them. Sitting on the footpath all evening.'
'Bhai, remember the one who fixed our water pump last week?'
'The thin fellow?'
'Raju. From Jharkhand. He wouldn't take extra money because it only took him ten minutes.'
'Okay, one honest one.'
'I asked him why they sit on the footpath. The contractor gives them one room for twelve men. They sit outside so the others can sleep.'
Anand was quiet. He picked up the keys again, turning them over.
'Twelve in one room?'
'Twelve.'
'Hm.' He went to the window. The men were there, one of them laughing on a video call. 'I didn't think about the room,' he said quietly.

How many men share one room?
Twelve men share one room.
What does Anand turning the keys over suggest?
It suggests Anand is unsettled, rethinking a quick judgement now that the men on the footpath have a reason and a face.
What did Tarun do that brought back empathy?
Tarun named one real person, Raju, and shared what Tarun had learned by asking him, which replaced 'all thieves' with a human story.
What might the men on the footpath be feeling on these evenings?
They may be tired and cramped, sitting outside so others can sleep, and a video call home might be the best part of the day.

Kindergarten note, Thursday. Ira, class teacher. Aadhya (5) was very quiet at midday. While the others played, she sat on the step by the gate, holding the cloth elephant her father packs in her bag. No tears. She just watched the gate, rubbing the elephant's ear. When I sat beside her she said, 'Papa comes at two.' I said waiting for someone you love is hard, and that he comes after lunch and story time. She leaned on me. Next: the elephant stays at her table, and I'll tell her father she misses him at midday.

What did Aadhya hold while sitting by the gate?
The cloth elephant her father packs in her bag.
What does Aadhya rubbing the elephant's ear suggest?
It suggests Aadhya was missing Papa and comforting herself quietly, even without tears.
Which of Ira's choices seemed to help Aadhya most?
Sitting beside Aadhya, naming how hard waiting is, and saying when Papa comes helped; Aadhya leaned in instead of staying alone.
How might Aadhya's father feel reading the note?
Aadhya's father might feel touched that the elephant helps, and a little sad to know how much she misses him at midday.

The correct sentence is: "Nobody listened to the teacher."

Aadhya, you asked what to do if a friend gets hurt at your sports day. Let me tell you about the Independence Day rehearsal when I was ten. It had rained all night, and the ground was slick red mud. Shankar slipped in the march past and cut his chin on the flagpole stand. Everyone crowded round, shouting. My stomach turned over and I wanted to cry too. The flagpole stand.

Pradeep felt sorry and shaken, stomach turning and close to tears, but one big breath steadied things enough to act.

The heater in the school hall had broken, and band practice started in coats. Baljeet rubbed his hands together hard, blowing into them between songs. When the drum part began, he snapped his fingers in rhythm, tapping one foot.

Then he lost his page. He turned and snapped his fingers twice at Nikita. "Sheet! Quick!"

Nikita raised an eyebrow. "I'm not a waiter."

Baljeet's ears went hot. "Sorry, sorry. Could you pass the sheet, please?" She passed it.

At the break, the cook brought in a tray of hot samosas, and Baljeet rubbed his hands again, grinning this time. Nikita laughed. "Is that cold hands or samosa hands?"
"Both!"

Why did band practice start in coats?
The heater in the school hall had broken.
What was Baljeet feeling when he rubbed his hands at the break?
Eager and excited about the hot samosas, as his grin shows, though his hands were probably still cold too, as he admits with "Both!".

Use the person's name and a quick "please", as he did after apologising.
How did Nikita see the finger snap?
She took it as rude, like calling a waiter, and felt annoyed until Baljeet said sorry and asked properly.

Explain what the creature wants, in one or two sentences.

"Thus I relieve thee, my creator," he said, and placed his hated hands before my eyes, which I flung from me with violence; "thus I take from thee a sight which you abhor. Still thou canst listen to me and grant me thy compassion. By the virtues that I once possessed, I demand this from you. Hear my tale; it is long and strange, and the temperature of this place is not fitting to your fine sensations; come to the hut upon the mountain. The sun is yet high in the heavens; before it descends to hide itself behind your snowy precipices and illuminate another world, you will have heard my story and can decide. On you it rests, whether I quit for ever the neighbourhood of man and lead a harmless life, or become the scourge of your fellow creatures and the author of your own speedy ruin."
The creature asks Victor to listen to his long story in a hut on the mountain. He says Victor's choice will decide whether he lives quietly away from people or becomes a danger to everyone.

When the coaching centre in Rampur opened a batch for the police constable exam, it felt as if every young person in Himani's village signed up. Lavanya came by with two forms. "Everyone's going, Himani. Fill it, we'll take the same bus." Himani sat with the form on the verandah while the buffaloes shifted in the yard. She asked herself two questions. Why do I want this? Mostly, she admitted, because everyone else is going. And if nobody in the village would ever know what I chose, what would I pick? The answer came quickly: the nursing assistant course at the district hospital, which she had wanted since Dadi's long illness. The next morning she handed the constable form back to Lavanya. "Save me a seat on the bus anyway," she said, smiling. "We'll ride together as far as the hospital stop."

Which course did Himani choose?
The nursing assistant course at the district hospital.
What did Himani feel after honestly asking why she wanted the constable exam?
Admitting it was mostly because everyone else was going left her calm and clear-headed rather than pulled along.
Which question helped Himani most, and why?
Asking what she would pick if nobody would ever know, because it removed the pull of the crowd and showed her real wish.
How might Lavanya feel when Himani hands back the form?
Lavanya may feel a little disappointed at first, but reassured by Himani's warmth and the plan to ride the bus together 🙂

It was launch week, the team was working from home because of the floods, and Sabina had messaged Omkar eleven times before lunch. 'Send me the header draft.' 'Why that blue?' 'Send the next version before you change anything.' 'Call me before you start the footer.' By Wednesday Omkar had stopped suggesting ideas. He did exactly what each message asked and nothing more, and felt his energy drain out like water from a cracked pot. On Thursday he took a breath and called her. 'Can we try something? Tell me what the page has to achieve and by when. Let me decide how. I'll show you the full draft at five.' There was a long pause. 'Fine. More sign-ups, loads fast, matches the brand. Five o'clock.' That afternoon Omkar redesigned the whole page, tried two ideas he'd been sitting on, and sent it at 4:50. Sabina replied, 'This is the best one yet.'

How many times had Sabina messaged Omkar before lunch?
She had messaged him eleven times before lunch.
How did Omkar feel by Wednesday, and what shows it?
He felt drained and discouraged, doing only exactly what each message asked and no longer suggesting ideas.
What did Omkar ask for that restored his initiative?
A clear outcome and deadline, with freedom to decide how, which let him try his own ideas.
How might Sabina feel seeing the 4:50 draft?
Sabina likely felt relieved and impressed, which is why she called it the best one yet.
Use one word instead of "a large number of": A large number of people came to the fair.

Friday
Sarika came back to school today after her Nanaji's funeral. At lunch, Mehul said to her, "Well, at least your Nanaji was really old. He had a good long innings." He meant it kindly, I think. Then Tanya added, "Everything is part of God's plan."
I watched Sarika's face. She smiled, but her jaw went tight and she put her roti back in the box. She didn't say anything for the rest of lunch.
I didn't know what to say either. After school, walking to the gate, I just said, "Sarika, I'm so sorry about your Nanaji. I'm here if you want to talk, or not."
She stopped and hugged me. She said, "Thank you for not telling me it's fine."
I keep thinking about Mehul's face. He'll never know it hurt. Should I tell him? Maybe I will, gently.
Yash

What did Mehul say to Sarika at lunch?
He said, "Well, at least your Nanaji was really old. He had a good long innings."
What was Yash feeling while watching Sarika at lunch?
Yash felt uneasy and unsure, noticing Sarika's hurt but not knowing what to say.
Why did Yash's words work better than Mehul's and Tanya's?
Yash simply said sorry and offered to be there without explaining the death away, so Sarika didn't have to pretend it was fine.
How did Sarika experience Mehul's and Tanya's words?
Sarika felt hurt and alone, forcing a smile while her jaw tightened and she stopped eating.

"Just fill every hour, na," Tushar said, scrolling the list of Mumbai sights on Ramesh's laptop in the colony reading room. Ramesh shook his head. "Last year our class missed the aquarium because the bus got stuck in traffic for an hour. Everything after that fell like dominoes." He typed a line into each day: "Free hour, 3 to 4." Then under money: "2,000 each, keep 200 aside." "Ten percent for what?" "Prices change. Or someone's slipper breaks. If we don't need it, we eat something nice on the last night." On Saturday, the ferry to Elephanta cost forty rupees more each than the price they had found online. Tushar paid it from the kept-aside money without a word, then grinned at Ramesh. "Fine. Your boring hour can stay too."

How much did Ramesh plan to keep aside out of 2,000 each?
Ramesh planned to keep 200 aside.
Why did Ramesh insist on a free hour each day?
Ramesh was still wary after last year, when one hour stuck in traffic made everything after it fall like dominoes.
What else could help if a delay and a price rise hit on the same day?
They could choose in advance one sight to drop first, so the free hour and the spare money cover the rest without an argument on the spot.
How does Tushar see the buffer by Saturday?
Tushar first wanted every hour filled, but after the ferry cost more, Tushar grins and accepts both the spare money and the free hour.

For most of last year, I, Eshaan, lived with a tight band around my chest. I'd wake at four with my jaw clenched, mentally scanning for problems: an email I'd phrased badly, my mother's cough, the rent. Nothing was actually wrong, but my mind never switched off. I told no one. Then on a run, my friend Siddharth asked why I'd gone so quiet lately. I surprised myself and told him everything. He said he'd been through something similar and that talking to a counsellor had helped. It took me a month to book the appointment. Now I see her every other week, I run with Siddharth on Sundays, and the band around my chest has loosened.

When does Eshaan run with Siddharth now?
On Sundays.
What was it like for Eshaan to live with constant worry?
Eshaan felt tense and on edge all the time, with a tight chest, a clenched jaw and a mind that never switched off.
What eased Eshaan's worry?
Honest talk with Siddharth, regular running, and seeing a counsellor.
How might Siddharth have felt when Eshaan told him everything?
Siddharth probably felt trusted and understanding, having been through something similar.

Chen and Gabriel were cutting through the park behind the library in Toronto when a police cruiser rolled to a stop and an officer stepped out.

"Evening, boys. Hold on a second."

Gabriel muttered, "Let's just go," and took a step back. Chen caught his sleeve. His own pulse was thumping in his ears.

"Sure," Chen said, keeping his hands out of his pockets. "Is something wrong, officer?"

"There was a report of kids breaking bottles here. What are your names?"

"Chen Wei. This is Gabriel. We were at the library until it closed." He held up his library card slowly.

Gabriel started, "We didn't do anything, why are you—" Chen shook his head at him.

The officer looked at the card, then around the path. "Alright."

"Are we free to go?" Chen asked.

"You are."

Chen's hands were shaking as he texted his mom: stopped by police in park, all fine, walking home now. She called back in ten seconds.

What did Chen hold up to show the officer?
Chen held up his library card.
How can you tell Chen was scared even though he stayed calm?
His pulse was thumping in his ears and his hands shook as he texted his mom, showing fear under his calm voice.
What did Chen do that other teens could learn from?
Chen stayed polite, kept his hands visible, gave names, stopped Gabriel from walking off or arguing, asked if they were free to go and told a parent.
Why might Gabriel have reacted differently from Chen?
Gabriel may have felt more frightened or insulted at being stopped, which pushed him to want to leave or argue.
How does a car stay on the road when it goes round a bend?
The grip between the tyres and the road keeps the car on its curved path. Because this friction pulls the car towards the inside of the curve instead of letting it slide straight on, the car turns.
Ali is collecting bottle caps. He has 125 bottle caps. He has red ones and green ones. If he has 50 red caps, what percentage of caps are green?

He has 75 green caps because 125 - 50 = 75
The proportion of caps that are green is .6 because 75 / 125 = .6
The percentage that are green is 60 because .6 x 100% = 60%
The answer is 60.

Bugs are thriving in a garden of 30 plants. The bugs are very hungry today and completely ate 20 plants. The next day, they were still full and only ate half of the remaining plants. After that, they ate only 1 of the plants that were left. How many plants remain?

The bugs ate enough plants for there to be 30-20=10 left.
They were still full and only ate half, leaving 10/2=5 plants left.
Later on, the bugs only ate 1 more which left 5-1=4 plants in the garden.
The answer is 4.

At the end of every shift at the café in Indiranagar, Pradeep had made hundreds of small choices: which table got the corner seat, whether to comp the cold coffee, who could leave early, how many croissants for tomorrow. By ten at night, walking into his one-room flat, he had nothing left. He ordered a pizza on his phone, again, and let his guitar sit in the corner, again. He'd told himself he would practise every night. It had been three weeks. On Sunday his colleague Harish, who cooked in the café kitchen, said, 'Why don't you practise before your shift? And eat what we make here, instead of deciding at ten.' Pradeep laughed, then thought about it. On Monday he played for twenty minutes at noon, before work, and took a box of the staff dal home. By ten he was tired, but there was nothing left to decide.

How long had Pradeep's guitar sat unused?
It had sat unused for three weeks.
Why did Pradeep keep ordering pizza at ten at night?
After hundreds of small decisions at the café, he felt drained and had no patience left for choosing or cooking.
What did Harish's suggestion change?
Playing guitar before the shift put the hard thing earlier, and taking staff dal home removed an evening choice, lowering friction.
How might Harish see Pradeep's routine?
Harish, working in the same café, likely understands how tiring the day is and suggests practical fixes rather than blaming Pradeep.

Mehak, you've blocked your whole week in that calendar app, hour by hour, no gaps. Let your Nilesh Chachu tell you about my first job.
I was twenty-four, at an insurance office in Pune. I read somewhere that successful people plan every hour. So on Sunday night I filled Monday: 9 to 10 emails, 10 to 11 reports, 11 to 12 client calls, all the way to 7. Not one empty minute. I felt like a machine.
Monday, 10.15, my manager called me in for a "quick chat". It lasted fifty minutes. Now my reports ran into client calls. Client calls ran into lunch. By noon I was an hour behind on everything and the whole plan was useless.
I tore up the sheet and just reacted to whatever came, for the rest of the week.
The plan wasn't wrong, beta. It just had no breathing space.

How long did the manager's quick chat last?
It lasted fifty minutes.
How did Nilesh feel by noon on Monday?
Nilesh felt overwhelmed and defeated, an hour behind on everything with a plan that had become useless.
When the chat ran long, what could Nilesh have done instead of tearing up the sheet, and why?
He could have moved one block to later in the week and kept the rest, since a plan with some gaps can absorb one overrun.
How might Nilesh's manager have seen the fifty-minute chat?
The manager probably thought it was a normal quick chat and had no idea it wrecked Nilesh's tightly packed day.

Mentor's note, final-year project review, 14 March.
Shreya presented her group's plan for the campus water-saving project today. It was a lovely story: the hostel wardens would agree in week one, a local firm would donate sensors, the student union would run an awareness drive, and the results would be published by May. She clearly believed every step. Pranav, her teammate, proposed a smaller version: fix the leaking taps in one hostel and measure the water used. Shreya called it "too small to be real". I asked the group to write each step on a card and put a rough chance next to it. Seeing the cards laid out in a row, Shreya went quiet. After the meeting she stayed back and asked if she could start with Pranav's hostel and build from there. I said yes.

What smaller version did Pranav propose?
Pranav proposed fixing the leaking taps in one hostel and measuring the water used.
Why did Shreya call the smaller plan 'too small to be real'?
Shreya felt proud and attached to the full story; its many connected steps made success feel vivid and believable, so a plain plan seemed less real.
Why did the card exercise help, and what could Shreya do with it next?
Putting a chance beside each step showed how many things all had to go right; Shreya can start small, as she chose to, and add steps once each one works.
How might Pranav have felt when Shreya stayed back to ask about the hostel plan?
Pranav would likely feel respected and relieved that the smaller idea was finally taken seriously.

Last term I, Kavitha, volunteered to lead our group's stall for the science fair. Five of us, one water-filter model, three weeks. I made a chart of jobs, and when Santosh got bored cutting bottles, I sat and cut with him and let him choose the music. We were good. Then, on the morning of the fair, I insisted on moving the model myself, fast, without waiting for the trolley. The sand layer spilled across the corridor. Everyone looked at Santosh, because he had been carrying the other end. I heard myself tell Sir, "It was my call. I rushed it." My face burned. But we rebuilt a smaller version by eleven, and Santosh explained the filter to the judges better than I could have. I still remember how fast the others knelt to scoop the sand once I'd said it.

How many people were in Kavitha's group?
Five.
What was Kavitha feeling when telling Sir 'It was my call'?
Kavitha felt ashamed, with a burning face, but also determined not to let Santosh be blamed for a rushed decision.
What worked in Kavitha's leading before the fair, and what could change next time?

In 5 years, Nacho will be three times older than Divya. If Divya is currently 5 years old, what's the sum of their ages now?

If Divya is currently 5 years old, she will be 5+5 = 10 years old in five years.
Since in 5 years Nacho will be three times older than Divya, he will be 3*10 = 30 years older than Divya.
Nacho's total age in five years will be 30+10 = 40 years.
Currently, Nacho is 40-5 = 35 years old.
The sum of Divya and Nacho's age now is 35+5 = 40 years
The answer is 40.

Chaitanya paused, then said, "It is a little difficult." Pradeep nodded and walked away, apparently satisfied. An hour later he came back, puzzled, asking why it wasn't done. Where had Chaitanya just moved from?

Chaitanya likely meant it was not possible, while Pradeep heard only that it was hard but doable, so they read the same words differently.

They could ask clarifying questions kindly, such as whether "difficult" means "not possible", and state requests plainly.

In their Pune flat, Uday lay on his bed scrolling the Class 11 group chat. Ever since Sarika laughed when he dropped his tiffin in the canteen, he'd been sure she was fake, nice to teachers and mean behind their backs. Now he searched her messages. "Great job, everyone!" — fake. "Sorry I missed practice" — making excuses. He screenshotted the ones that sounded rude and sent them to his friend with an eye-roll emoji. When she messaged the whole group, "Uday, hope your hand's better after the match!", he didn't reply. He told himself she only wrote it because the teacher was in the group. His mother called him for dinner. He kept scrolling, thumb moving fast past anything friendly, stopping only when something fitted.

She laughed when he dropped his tiffin.
Why does ignoring Sarika's friendly message feel reasonable to Uday?
Uday feels hurt and embarrassed from the canteen moment, so a friendly message doesn't fit his view and he explains it away as fake.

He could list all her messages, friendly and not, and ask whether she laughed at the tiffin or at something else before deciding.

Usha had three tabs open on her phone, a textbook on her knee and a chat buzzing, and she had read the same paragraph on the kidney four times. Vandana, a final-year student, found her on the stairs. February: One evening she was tired and told herself, “I'll just watch one episode at home, and go tomorrow twice.” The next day, same thing. Her friend Omkar noticed the gym bag unpacked by her door.

A monkey has 15 bananas. (a) He keeps them all for himself. (b) He shares them among 15 monkeys. How many bananas does each monkey get?

Answer: (a) 15 bananas: 15 / 1 = 15. (b) 1 banana each: 15 / 15 = 1.

Dividing by 1 means sharing among just one, so nothing changes: n / 1 = n. Check with multiplication: 15 x 1 = 15. Sharing a number among the same number of people gives exactly 1 each: n / n = 1. Check: 1 x 15 = 15. These rules work for any number (except 0 in the second one): 358 / 1 = 358 and 358 / 358 = 1.

At the chemical plant in Vapi, Saurabh ran the Friday valve check. Before he began, he did what he did every week: phone into the locker, locker shut.
"You don't even keep it on silent?" asked Manoj, the new engineer.
"Silent still buzzes in your head," Saurabh said. "For this, I want my whole attention."
They walked the line. Saurabh read each gauge aloud, Manoj wrote it down and then read it back. At valve 14, Manoj read "closed". Saurabh looked again. It was half open.
"Good," Saurabh said, and they fixed it. "That's why we do it in pairs. Two sets of eyes catch what one misses."
After the check he took out his phone, answered six messages in five minutes, and put it back before the afternoon meeting with the contractors.

Which valve was half open?
Valve 14 was half open.
Why does Saurabh lock the phone away rather than silence it?
Saurabh feels careful and protective of his attention, knowing a silent phone still buzzes in the head during critical checks.
How does working in pairs make the check safer?
Reading aloud and having Manoj read back means two sets of eyes catch mistakes, like the half-open valve.
How might Manoj feel after valve 14?
Manoj might feel a little embarrassed at the misread but reassured that the pair system caught it.

The holidays? Honestly, one afternoon stuck with me. My cousin Bhavna had just got her Class 10 results, and they weren't good. Sixty-two per cent. At Dadi's house that Sunday every aunty had a comparison ready. "Pinky got ninety-four." "Our neighbour's son has already joined engineering coaching." Bhavna kept passing the samosas and smiling like a shop mannequin.
I'm Varun, I'm twenty-three, and I remember that smile from my own bad year. So after lunch I found her on the back steps, just sitting. I didn't give advice. I said, "One result is one result. It isn't you." She didn't answer, but her shoulders came down a little.
Then I asked if she wanted to sit with me on Tuesday and look at which subjects she actually liked, and plan from there. She said, "Maybe." On Tuesday she came.

What percentage did Bhavna get in her Class 10 results?
Sixty-two per cent.
What was Varun feeling while watching Bhavna smile through the comparisons?
Varun felt a painful recognition and concern, remembering a similar bad year and sensing that her smile was hiding hurt.

A quiet word that one result isn't Bhavna, followed by an offer to sit on Tuesday and plan from the subjects she likes.
What is the lunch like for Bhavna?
Painful and humiliating; she has to keep smiling and serving while relatives compare her marks with other children's.

Jomon had never been inside a namghar before. Arohi's village near Jorhat was quiet in the afternoon heat, and her family had gathered for prayers on the anniversary of her grandfather's death. At home in Kottayam, Jomon's family bowed their heads in church and crossed themselves. Here, people knelt on the mats and lowered their heads almost to the floor while the elders sang. For every one dozen flowers bought, a customer gets 2 free flowers. If Maria wants to buy 3 dozens flowers, how many pieces of flowers will she have in all?

Hence, she has a total of 36 + 6 = 42 flowers.
The answer is 42.

The price per organic egg is 50 cents. The price of a tray of eggs that contains 30 eggs is $12. How much can you save, in cents, per egg if you buy a tray versus individual eggs?

The price per egg in a tray is $12/30 eggs = $0.4/egg.
The equivalent of $0.4 in cents is $0.4 x 100 cents/dollar = 40 cents.

The answer is 10.

Kelsey had 2/5 of a tray of eggs that she had brought to Willa's party. Stephanie had also brought half a tray of eggs to the party, while Alayah brought 40 more eggs than Kelsey and Stephanie combined. If Willa had two trays of eggs already, calculate the total number of eggs that were used at the party.

A tray of eggs has 30 eggs, so Kelsey brought 2/5*30 = 12 eggs
On the other hand, Stephanie brought 1/2*30 = 15 eggs to the party.
The total number of eggs that Kelsey and Stephanie brought to Willa's party is 15+12 =27
Alayah brought 27+40 = 67 eggs, 40 more than the number brought by Kelsey and Stephanie combined.
Together with Aliyah's eggs, there were a total of 67+27 = 94
Willa also had 2*30 = 60 eggs from the two trays she had.
In total, there were 94+60 = 154 eggs used at the party.
The answer is 154.

Last year Mehak and I nearly ended a fifteen-year friendship over a reunion. We were organising our school batch's tenth anniversary, and we'd argued in the group chat, in front of forty classmates, about the venue. She wanted the old school hall, for the memories. I wanted a restaurant, because the hall had no air conditioning in May. By the end, neither of us could back down without looking foolish. I lay awake that night. Then I called her, just the two of us. "We both want people to actually come and feel happy. What if we do both? Morning in the school hall, speeches and photos. Lunch at the restaurant." Silence. Then: "You'd give up the full day at the restaurant?" "And you'd give up the afternoon in the hall. We both give something." She laughed. "Post it in the group as your idea and mine." We did. Thirty-eight people came. I'm Leela, and I still have the photo of us under the old school clock.

How many people came to the reunion?
Thirty-eight people.
How did Leela feel after the public argument?
Leela felt stuck and anxious, lying awake because neither could back down without looking foolish.
What made Leela's proposal work?
Calling privately, framing it around the shared goal of a happy reunion, proposing both venues, and naming what each would give up.
How did Mehak respond to the compromise?

For every 100 additional people that board a spaceship, its speed is halved. If the speed of the spaceship with 200 people on board is 500km per hour, what is its speed in km/hr when there are 400 people on board?

For every addition of 100 people added the speed is halved so for the first 100 people added its speed is 1/2 * 500 km/hr = 250 km/hr.
For another addition of 100 people its speed is also halved, 1/2 * 250 km/hr = 125 km/hr. So for the total of 200 additional people, its speed is 125 km/hr
The answer is 125.

Burt spent $2.00 on a packet of basil seeds and $8.00 on potting soil.  The packet of seeds yielded 20 basil plants.  He sells each basil plant for $5.00 at the local farmer's market.  What is the net profit from his basil plants?

He spent $2.00 on seeds and $8.00 on soil for a total of 2+8 = $10.00
He sells each of the 20 basil plants for $5.00 so he makes 20*5 = $100.00
He made $100.00 from selling basil plants and he spent $10.00 to buy and grow the seeds. His net profit is 100-10 = $90.00
The answer is 90.

Inside I was focused, and a bit worried about that nail. The grief was on my face and in my voice because we'd rehearsed for six weeks, not because I was living it. Lalremsiami looked almost cheated. Janet takes two multivitamins and 3 calcium supplements every day for the first 2 weeks of the month. For the last two weeks of the month, she runs low on calcium supplements and only takes one per day. How many pills does Janet take in that month?

First find the number of pills Janet takes every day for the first 2 weeks: 2 pills/day + 3 pills/day = 5 pills/day
Then find the number of days in 2 weeks: 2 weeks * 7 days/week = 14 days
Then multiply that number by the number of pills she takes daily to find the total number of pills she takes in the first 2 weeks: 5 pills/day * 14 days = 70 pills
Then find the number of pills Janet takes every day for the last 2 weeks: 2 pills/day + 1 pill/day = 3 pills/day
Then multiply that number by the number of days in 2 weeks to find the total number of pills she takes in the last 2 weeks: 3 pills/day * 14 days = 42 pills
Then add the number of pills she took in the first and last two weeks to find the total number of pills she took: 42 pills + 70 pills = 112 pills
The answer is 112.

Funny you ask about labels, Hafsa. This is Hemant, proud ex-backbencher, speaking. In Class 9 our teacher made a seating chart by marks. I landed in the last row with five others, and after that the teachers just stopped asking us anything. So we stopped trying. Why study if everyone had already decided? I used to draw cars in my notebook during maths. Then in Class 11 a new maths teacher mixed the rows every week and one day gave me a problem about car speeds. I solved it on the board. The class went quiet. I remember thinking, wait, I'm not weak, I was just parked. It took me a whole year to really believe that, but it started there.

How did the Class 9 teacher decide the seating?
By marks, with a seating chart.
What was Hemant feeling when solving the car-speed problem on the board?
Hemant felt surprised and quietly proud, thinking 'I'm not weak, I was just parked.'
Which choice of the Class 11 teacher helped, and why?
Mixing the rows every week and giving Hemant a problem about car speeds, which broke the label and offered a real chance to succeed.
How might the other five in the last row have felt in Class 9?
They were likely discouraged and ignored too, since the teachers stopped asking them anything.

Read this:

The last passenger train out of Rampura junction left at six. Dhruv's family set off from their village by shared jeep at five, the way Sachin-chacha said was enough. Then a wedding procession filled the main road of the kasba, band and horses and all, and the jeep stood still for twenty-five minutes. They reached the platform as the guard was lifting the green flag. Chacha threw the bags in and pulled Dhruv up by the arm. On the wooden seat, breathing hard, Chacha said, "From now on, we leave one full hour early." Dhruv opened the plan he had written in his school notebook and, beside "Leave village, 5 o'clock", crossed out the 5, wrote 4, and added "extra hour for jams".

What blocked the road in the kasba?
A wedding procession, with a band and horses.
What might Dhruv have felt as Chacha pulled him onto the train?
He was probably frightened and then relieved, still breathing hard once they sat down.
What else could the family try besides leaving earlier?
Taking an earlier train than the last one, so a missed train is not the end of the journey.
How might Sachin-chacha see the new line in Dhruv's plan?
He suggested the extra hour himself, so he would likely be glad to see it written into the plan.

metadata.subtype: Approach: leaving too little time for the train [Revision]

messages.content: Three friends share a ₹540 taxi fare equally. How much does each one pay?
Each friend pays ₹180. Because ₹540 divided equally among 3 people is ₹180, and 3 times 180 brings it back to 540.

Read this:

It was the last day of the school week, and rain had flooded the playground, so there was no games period. Kunal, nine, came home, dropped his bag and flopped on the sofa.

"This whole week was terrible," he told his older cousin Jomon. "I lost my eraser. Everyone laughed at my answer. And tomorrow will be bad too."

Jomon sat beside him. "What about Tuesday? You said you scored full marks in dictation."

Kunal thought. "Oh. Yes."

"And Wednesday you shared lunch with the new boy."

"He liked my aloo paratha," Kunal said, almost smiling.

Jomon ruffled his hair. "Sad days make us remember only sad things. Let's make tea and tell Mausi about the dictation."

What did Kunal score in dictation on Tuesday?
Full marks.
Why did Kunal say the whole week was terrible?
He felt sad and fed up after a bad day, and that mood made him remember only the bad things.
How did Jomon help Kunal see the week differently?
He reminded Kunal of good moments like full marks and sharing lunch, and involved Mausi, a caring adult.
How might Jomon feel when Kunal almost smiled?
Jomon probably felt relieved and glad that his cousin was feeling a little better.

Read this:

Siddharth,
I'm writing this instead of saying it in the mess, because I don't want an audience.
Last night at Rohan's birthday, Kunal did that joke about the canteen uncle's accent. Everyone laughed, and so did you. In first year you were the one who walked out when someone mocked how the laundry aunty spoke. You told me that kind of joke made your skin crawl.
Maybe you've changed your mind, and that's allowed. Maybe you're just tired of being the odd one out in the new group. I saw the others glance at you, and Kunal started on "Siddharth's new sense of humour." I didn't join in, and I won't.
If something's going on, I'd like to hear it, over chai at the gate stall, whenever you want. If nothing is, tell me I'm overthinking and I'll drop it.
Still your friend,
Harish

Where does Harish suggest meeting Siddharth to talk?
Over chai at the gate stall, whenever Siddharth wants.
What is Harish feeling while writing this letter?
Harish seems uneasy and a little sad to see Siddharth laugh at a joke Siddharth once walked out over, but also caring, not angry.
Why was a private letter wiser than joining Kunal's teasing?
It lets Siddharth explain, or say nothing is wrong, without the group watching, so the friendship stays safe either way.
How might Siddharth feel reading this compared with hearing the teasing at the party?
Siddharth may feel relieved and less cornered by a quiet letter, though perhaps a little embarrassed that the change was noticed.

Read this:

Tanvir hadn't slept properly for three weeks. In the noisy ward, with one week left before the exam, he snapped at a nurse over a small thing, then apologised too many times. On the bus he realised he had been irritable every single day, and that the bad sleep never lifted.

He thought about it that evening. It isn't one bad day. It's the whole pattern. He called his Dilnaz khala and said, "I can't keep doing every night. Could you take two of them?" She said yes before he finished.

The next morning he booked a counselling session at the college. It was hard to admit, but the care he gave Dad had been getting sharper, and that was the real signal.

How many nights did Tanvir ask Dilnaz khala to take?
Two of them.
How was Tanvir feeling as he snapped at the nurse and then apologised too many times?
Tanvir was exhausted and ashamed, and the constant irritation and poor sleep made him see that he was worn out.
What could Tanvir do on the nights off, and why?
Tanvir could sleep and revise in a quiet place away from the ward, because rest helps both his exam and his patience when he returns.
How might Dilnaz khala feel about being asked?
Dilnaz khala said yes before Tanvir finished, so she probably felt glad to be asked and was worried he had carried so much alone.

metadata.subtype: Approach: notice signs of caregiver fatigue and step back [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Thomas's diary, Thursday. Asked Chinmay today if he wanted to join my cricket team. He lifted one shoulder and said, “Maybe.” I thought that meant no, and I felt a bit silly for asking. Then I remembered that he does the one-shoulder thing when he's unsure or shy. So I asked, “Do you want to think about it, or is cricket not your thing?” He said, “I've never really played. I don't want to be bad.” I said I'd show him how to hold the bat at recess. He said, “Okay, maybe yes.” 🙂

What did Chinmay say after lifting one shoulder?
He said, “Maybe.”
What did Thomas first think Chinmay's shoulder lift meant, and what did asking reveal?
He first thought it meant no. Asking revealed that Chinmay was unsure and worried about being bad, since he had never really played.
What small step helped clear up the maybe?
Thomas asked a friendly, open question and offered to show him how to hold the bat, so Chinmay could say what was holding him back.
How might Chinmay feel about being asked?
Probably relieved that Thomas asked kindly and did not push, since he admitted his worry about being bad.

Read this:

You want to know why I'm so tired all the time? Okay. You're my oldest friend, so I'll say it. I'm Deepika, and I keep trying to get back the first three months with Harish.
In the beginning, it was flowers at my office, a surprise trip to Goa, messages every hour: "You're perfect. I've never been this happy." I'd never felt so loved.
And then, around month four, it just… shrank. He stopped asking about my day. Then he started correcting things. My clothes. How I laugh. How I talk to my mother on the phone. Some days he doesn't reply at all.
So I try harder. I cook what he likes. I wear what he likes. And sometimes, for a day, he's sweet again, and I think, there he is.
When I say it out loud to you… the gap is huge, isn't it? Those two people don't feel like the same man.

What surprise trip did Harish plan early on?
A surprise trip to Goa.
What is Deepika feeling as she describes trying harder?
Deepika feels exhausted and confused, hoping to win back the early warmth while starting to see the gap between the two phases.
What could Deepika do next, with her friend's help?
She could keep talking to her friend, write down the pattern, and speak to a counsellor about what she is experiencing.
What does the friend likely notice while listening?
The friend probably notices how tired and changed Deepika is, and feels worried about the big gap she describes.
Always I forget to bring my water bottle. How can I say it better?

I always forget to bring my water bottle.
Why: "always" goes before the main verb.
In under 15 words, explain why we see lightning before we hear thunder.
Light travels much faster than sound, so the flash reaches us first.

Read this:

In Navsari, the inter-school kabaddi final was played during the Navratri holidays, under strings of lights left from the garba nights. Disha, fifteen, was dropped from the starting seven at the last minute. She sat on the bench, jaw tight. At the break, coach Zubin sir came over. "All right?" She almost said fine. Instead she said, quietly, "No, sir. I'm disappointed. And a bit embarrassed. My parents came to watch." Zubin sir sat down next to her. "That's fair. Thank you for telling me." He explained why he'd chosen a defender tonight. It still stung, but the knot in her stomach loosened. In the second half, when he sent her in for the last five minutes, she was ready. She made one clean tackle. Her father cheered from the stands.

When was the kabaddi final played?
During the Navratri holidays.
How did Disha feel after telling Zubin sir she was disappointed and embarrassed?
It still stung, but she felt the knot in her stomach loosen, calmer and ready when sent in.
Why did naming her feelings help Disha get back in the game?
Saying the real feelings let Zubin sir respond and explain, which settled her mind instead of leaving her stewing on the bench.
How might Zubin sir see Disha's honesty?
Zubin sir seems to appreciate it, thanking her and explaining his decision, which builds trust.
Does the shopkeeper's son play any sport?
I'm not sure, as I don't know the family. Ask him or his father the next time you visit.

Read this:

“Nazia, you're sitting in the dark with your eyes shut. Are you asleep?”
“No, Farhan Bhai. I'm running tomorrow's district race.”
“From the sofa?”
“In my head. Watch.” She kept her eyes closed. “Warm-up at eight-thirty. Two easy laps, drills, strides. Then the call room, where everyone looks scary. I breathe: in for four, hold, out for six. Three times.”
“Then?”
“Blocks. On your marks. I look at my lane, not at the girl in lane five. Gun. Drive low for ten steps.”
“What if you trip at the start? Like last year?”
She nodded, eyes still shut. “I've planned that. If I stumble, I don't look back. I pump my arms, get upright and finish. One stumble doesn't decide it.”
“And the last bit?”
“Last thirty metres, when my legs burn, I think tall and loose, not faster. Then the tape.”
She opened her eyes. “That's twelve times I've run it this week.”

What breathing pattern does Nazia use in the call room?
In for four, hold, out for six, three times.
Why has Nazia planned what to do if she stumbles?
She is still anxious after tripping last year, and planning it in advance helps her feel calmer and ready.
What else could Nazia rehearse besides the race itself?
A long delay or a false start, so an unexpected wait in the call room doesn't shake her.
How might Farhan Bhai see his sister's rehearsal?
Farhan Bhai starts by teasing, then seems impressed by how carefully she has planned, even for last year's stumble.

metadata.subtype: Approach: visualising the race and rehearsing [Thinking]

Read this:

At the nursery in Cape Town, Thabo hopped from mat to window to door. "Thabo, sit down," said Miss Amara, for the fourth time. He sat, then stood again.
When she said, "Get your coat, hat and bag," Thabo came back with only the hat. At the tap he couldn't wait and pushed.
But at the train set, he built a track for forty minutes without looking up.
Later, when she said "Thabo!" again, his face crumpled. "I'm trying," he shouted, and threw his hat.
Miss Amara knelt. "I know. Let's do one thing at a time." She held up one finger. "Coat first."

What did Thabo bring back when told to get his coat, hat and bag?
He came back with only the hat.
Why did Thabo shout and throw his hat?
He felt hurt and frustrated at being corrected again when he was already trying hard.
What small step helped Thabo follow instructions?
Miss Amara gave him one instruction at a time, which is easier for a busy mind than three together.
How might Miss Amara see Thabo after watching him at the train set?
She might realise he can focus deeply on what excites him and is not choosing to be naughty.

Read this:

After the move from Porto to Lyon, Gabriel's French school felt like a wall of fast words. At home he stopped setting the table, a job he used to do proudly. He left his shoes in the hall and asked his father to cut his meat. And every night he padded into his parents' room: "Papa, I'll just sleep on the floor here."

Mateo was tired too; the new job was hard. One night he nearly snapped, "You're eight, Gabriel!" Instead he sat on the edge of the bed. "New places feel big, huh?" Gabriel nodded into his pillow. "Everyone talks too fast."

They made a deal: the floor was fine for now, and every morning they set the table together, speaking French for five minutes. By December Gabriel was setting it alone again, and correcting his papa's accent.

Which chore did Gabriel stop doing?
Gabriel stopped setting the table.
What is Gabriel feeling when he says "Everyone talks too fast"?
Gabriel feels lost and overwhelmed at the new school, so he reaches back for early comforts like sleeping near his parents.
What deal helped Gabriel move forward?
Allowing the floor for now while setting the table together each morning, with five minutes of French, kept comfort and routine side by side.
What is it like for Mateo in these weeks?
Mateo is tired from his own new job and nearly snaps, but chooses patience and sits with Gabriel instead.

metadata.subtype: Wanting to sleep near parents after a move [Actor]

messages.content:
Nevertheless, ere long, the warm, warbling persuasiveness of the pleasant, holiday weather we came to, seemed gradually to charm him from his mood. For, as when the red-cheeked, dancing girls, April and May, trip home to the wintry, misanthropic woods; even the barest, ruggedest, most thunder-cloven old oak will at least send forth some few green sprouts, to welcome such glad-hearted visitants; so Ahab did, in the end, a little respond to the playful allurings of that girlish air. More than once did he put forth the faint blossom of a look, which, in any other man, would have soon flowered out in a smile.

How does the pleasant weather affect Ahab?

The warm, holiday weather gradually charms Ahab out of his mood. Like a bare old oak sending out a few green sprouts in spring, Ahab more than once puts forth the faint blossom of a look that in another man would have become a smile.
Explain betrayal to me.

Betrayal is the act of breaking someone's trust, for example by telling their secret or turning against them. It is a noun.
Example: Sharing her diary with the whole class felt like a betrayal to Ananya.
Why might a person refuse help even when they really need it?
A person may refuse help out of pride or worry. Because they may not want to seem weak or may feel that they are a burden to others, they say no, even when help would make things easier.

Read this:

In art class, Sir held up his own cow drawing, which looked a lot like a table. “Behold, my masterpiece!” he said, and the whole class laughed, including Sir. Later, when Chaitanya knocked over the water jar and it splashed across the floor, a few children laughed too. But Chaitanya didn't laugh. He stared at his shoes, his ears red. Pradeep felt the two kinds of laughter were not the same. The first had made Sir look happy. The second made Chaitanya look small. Pradeep didn't join in. He picked up a cloth and said, “I'll help.”

What did Sir's cow drawing look like?
It looked a lot like a table.
What was Chaitanya probably feeling when the children laughed and he stared at his shoes, and what else could it be?
Probably embarrassed and hurt, since his ears went red and he did not laugh. He might also have been worried about the mess.
How did the two kinds of laughter differ, and what did Pradeep do?
Sir laughed with everyone at a joke he made on himself, while some children laughed at Chaitanya's mistake. Pradeep did not join in and helped clean up instead.
How might Sir see the first laughter?
As friendly and shared, since he was laughing with the class. He might not have noticed the second kind if he was looking at the board.

Robie filled some plastic boxes with hockey cards. There were 10 cards in each box but 5 cards were not placed in a box. He gave away 2 boxes to his friends and he has 5 boxes with him. How many cards did Robie have in the beginning?

Robie filled a total of 2 + 5 = 7 boxes.
So, he had 7 x 10 = 70 hockey cards from the 7 boxes.
Thus, he had a total of 70 + 5 = 75 cards in the beginning.
The answer is 75.

Read this:

At Monday assembly in the Lucknow school hall, Jomon Sir held up a sheet and announced, "The best essay in the whole of class ten came from Usha Verma. Come up, Usha." Two hundred heads turned. Usha's cheeks went pink and the corners of her mouth kept twitching upward, but she walked to the stage like it was a punishment, hands balled into her sleeves. "Sir must have mixed up the pages," she said into the mic. Everyone laughed. She laughed too, then stared at her shoes until she could leave. Later, in the corridor, Farah said, "You looked like you wanted to vanish. Did you hate it?" Usha shook her head. "I loved it. I just hated everyone looking." That afternoon Jomon Sir stopped by her desk and said quietly, "Your ending made me think for a long time." Usha didn't joke that time. She said, "Thank you, Sir," and smiled properly.

Where did Jomon Sir praise the essay?
He praised it at Monday assembly in the Lucknow school hall.
What was Usha feeling as she walked to the stage?
Usha felt pleased but embarrassed by the attention, with a twitching smile and balled hands; the joke deflected the exposure rather than showing dislike of the praise.
Which kind of praise suited Usha better, and why?
The quiet word at her desk suited her better because it was specific and private, so she could simply enjoy it without everyone looking.
How did Farah read Usha's behaviour on stage?
Farah thought Usha looked like she wanted to vanish and wondered if she hated it, which shows how squirming at praise can be misread.

Read this:

In the kindergarten art corner, Siddharth, five, knocked over the paint pot. Blue paint splashed across Riya's picture. Everyone looked. Siddharth's face went bright red, and he hid under the table. Zeenat Teacher crouched down beside him. 'Siddharth, is your face feeling hot?' A tiny nod. 'Sometimes when we feel embarrassed, our face gets hot and we want to hide. That's your body telling you.' He peeked out. 'Embarrassed?' 'That's the word. It's okay. We can fix the picture together.' Siddharth crawled out slowly. He helped Riya turn the blue splash into a sky. His face cooled down, and he even smiled.

What did Siddharth knock over?
The paint pot.
What was Siddharth feeling when he hid under the table?
He felt embarrassed, with a hot, red face and a wish to hide.
What did Zeenat Teacher do that helped Siddharth understand?
She named his hot face as a sign of feeling embarrassed and offered to fix the picture together.
How might Riya have felt when the paint splashed on her picture?
Riya was probably upset at first, then pleased when they turned it into a sky.

Read this:

Omkar came home to the smell of dal and the sound of his father Tushar counting coins at the doorway. "I sold the second bullock so that you could stay at the school in town," Tushar said, not looking up. "Remember that when you feel lazy." Omkar's throat closed. He knew. He saw his father's cracked hands every day. But the words weighed on him like a yoke. It felt as though his whole life had been bought and he was not allowed to want anything else. He ate silently, then sat beside his father on the string cot. "Papa, I'll work hard, I promise, and I'll always show you my marks. But I can't promise what I'll become. I'll decide that when I'm ready." Tushar grunted, but he put his hand on Omkar's shoulder.

What did Tushar sell to pay for Omkar's school in town?
The second bullock.
How did Omkar feel when his father reminded him of the sacrifice?
Indebted and trapped. His throat closed and he felt as though his whole life had been bought and he was not allowed to want anything else.
What did Omkar promise, and what did he refuse to promise?
He promised to work hard and show his father his marks, but not what he will become. That honours the sacrifice without giving up his whole life plan.
How might Tushar feel about what he said and Omkar's answer?
Proud and worried about his son, and perhaps relieved to hear honest effort promised. He grunted, but he still put his hand on Omkar's shoulder.

Break down this brief extract into two short sentences.

Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin. When I look back, it seems to me as if this almost miraculous change of inclination and will was the immediate suggestion of the guardian angel of my life—the last effort made by the spirit of preservation to avert the storm that was even then hanging in the stars and ready to envelop me. Her victory was announced by an unusual tranquillity and gladness of soul which followed the relinquishing of my ancient and latterly tormenting studies. It was thus that I was to be taught to associate evil with their prosecution, happiness with their disregard.
The narrator thinks a guardian angel changed the narrator's mind to avert disaster. Leaving the painful studies brought calm, so the narrator linked them with evil.

Read this:

Saturday, back at the hostel
Binita and Dorje fought the whole bus ride home about the trek. Yesterday, on the path above the monastery, loose stones came rattling down and we all froze. Binita insists it happened after lunch and that Dorje shouted "Run!" first. Dorje swears it was before lunch and Binita shouted. Both were loud and totally certain. I sat between them eating chips, because honestly I only remember the noise and my knees shaking.
Tonight the trek leader posted the group photos. One was timestamped 11:52, the stones still bouncing in the corner, lunch boxes unopened in our bags. Before lunch. And the video from Sonam's phone has Sonam shouting, not either of them 😅
Binita said, "But I remember it so clearly!" Dorje said, "Me too." Then they both went quiet, like that was the point.
— Tenzin

What time was on the photo that showed the stones still bouncing?
It was timestamped 11:52.
Why did Binita and Dorje go quiet after saying they both remembered it clearly?
They realised that feeling very clear about a scary moment did not make either memory right, which surprised them.
How could the friends settle the next disagreement about a dramatic moment?
They could look at photos, timestamps or videos early, as the trek leader's pictures showed, instead of arguing on confidence alone.
What was the argument like for Tenzin, sitting between them?
Tenzin could only remember the noise and shaking knees, so watching both friends be so certain seemed puzzling and a little funny.
Asha is 8 years old and her aunt is 24 years older. How old is her aunt?
32. Because 8 + 24 = 32, so her aunt is 32 years old.

Read this:

Monday. Sudha and Irawati were crossing near the vegetable market when a boy on a bike skidded on the wet road and slid into a stack of crates. He got up, embarrassed, picked up his bike. Sudha remembered tomatoes rolling and a dog barking.
Wednesday. A local news page posted: "Speeding delivery van forces biker off road at market crossing." In the college group, three people shared it. Someone said the van was white. Sudha read every comment.
Saturday. At the canteen, Sudha was telling a friend, "This white van came flying round the corner and the poor boy had to swerve."
Irawati put down her cup. "Sudha, there was no van. I was with you. He skidded on his own."
"There was. I saw it." Sudha said it firmly. She could see it.

What did Sudha remember on Monday right after the skid?
She remembered tomatoes rolling and a dog barking.
How does Sudha feel when Irawati says there was no van?
She feels sure of herself and a bit defensive, because the white van now seems like something she really saw.
What could help Sudha check her memory?
She could compare Monday's version with what she read on Wednesday and trust Irawati's account more, since confident recall is not proof.
What is it like for Irawati to hear Sudha's new version?
Irawati is probably surprised and a little worried, since she stood beside Sudha and knows the van was never there.

metadata.subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]

messages.content: Why should you wipe up a spill on the floor right away?
Someone may slip on it. Because a wet floor is slippery and people do not expect it, so a fall can happen in an instant.

Read this:

Team lead's note, quarterly review

Wasim, 25, asked to move from the sales team to the data team. He has been studying data work in the evenings. He also told me his father wants him home in Kanpur more often after his surgery, and his mother would prefer he left Mumbai entirely.
He did not just demand the move or threaten to quit. He explained his reasons, proposed a handover plan so Pranav would not be left with his clients, and asked for two remote weeks each quarter to be with his father.
When Pranav raised concerns about the workload, Wasim listened and adjusted the timeline. I have approved the move from next month.

What did Wasim propose so Pranav would not be left with his clients?
He proposed a handover plan.
How might Wasim have felt balancing his own choice with his family's wishes?
He was likely torn and under pressure, wanting his new path but caring about his father's recovery and his mother's worries.
Why did Wasim's approach work with the team lead?
He explained his reasons, planned a handover, asked for remote weeks and listened to Pranav, rather than just defying anyone.
How might Pranav feel after Wasim adjusted the timeline?
Pranav probably feels heard and less anxious about the extra workload.

Maria is chopping up vegetables for a stew. She wants to cut up six times as many carrots as potatoes, twice as many onions as carrots, and 1/3 as many green beans as onions. If she has two potatoes, how many green beans does she need to cut?

First find how many carrots Maria needs to cut by multiplying the number of potatoes by 6: 6 * 2 = 12.
Then find how many onions she needs by multiplying the number of carrots by 2: 12 * 2 = 24.
Finally, divide the number of onions by 3 to find the number of green beans she needs 24 / 3 = 8.
The answer is 8.

A park has three colors of flowering crepe myrtle trees planted: red, white, and pink. When they bloom, a third of them are pink, but only two are red. Most of them are white. There are 42 crepe myrtle trees in the park. How many have white flowers when they bloom?

The park has 42 / 3 = 14 pink crepe myrtle trees.
It has 2 red trees, so it has 14 + 2 = 16 pink and red trees.
Therefore, there are 42 - 16 = 26 crepe myrtle trees that have white flowers when they bloom in the park.
The answer is 26.

Read this:

In Accra, Ada started tutoring one boy in maths after school and earned more in a week than she'd ever had. Her friend Abebe was impressed. "Take more!"

She did. By the end of the month she had seven students: Monday to Saturday, some evenings two in a row. Her own homework shifted to after ten. Sleep came at one, sometimes later.

Her chemistry teacher returned a test marked 11 out of 30. Ada stared at it. She'd scored 25 on the last one.

At lunch, Abebe asked, "You okay? You look awful."

"I'm fine. I'm earning."

But that night, looking at her notes for the three tutoring lessons she hadn't prepared, and her own chemistry homework untouched, she did the maths. The money was good. But she was trading her own grades and sleep for it, and that trade didn't look good at all.

How many students did Ada have by the end of the month?
Seven students.
How did Ada feel seeing the 11 out of 30?
She felt shocked and uneasy, having scored 25 on the last test.
What would you change first in Ada's tutoring plan?
Cut back to a small, fixed number of students and protect time for her own homework and sleep, maybe with her parents' input.
How does Abebe see Ada's situation?
Abebe first encouraged more students but now seems worried, noticing she looks awful.

Johns goes to the gym 3 times a week.  He spends 1 hour each day lifting weight. Additionally, he also spends a third of his weightlifting time warming up and doing cardio each day.  How many hours does he spend at the gym a week?

He spends 60/3=20 minutes warming up
So he spends 60+20=80 minutes at the gym per day
That means he spends 80*3=240 minutes at the gym
So he spends 240/60=4 hours at the gym a week
The answer is 4.

Read this:

The inter-college debate was in twenty minutes, and the auditorium in Patna was so packed the fans barely helped. Umesh paced backstage. A year ago, he'd have been in the principal's office instead. His temper had got him suspended once for shouting down a lecturer. Then Jatin, the debate captain, had seen him argue in the canteen and said, "You'd be terrifying on stage. With rules." Now Umesh had rules: three minutes, no personal attacks, rebuttals only on points. The opposing speaker went first and made a cheap jab about his college. Umesh felt the old heat rise. His hands clenched. Jatin caught his eye and tapped his watch. Umesh breathed, wrote the jab on his card, and turned it into his opening line, sharp but clean. The audience roared. He'd kept every bit of the fire and used it inside the lines.

How long did each speaker have?
Three minutes.
What did Umesh feel when the opponent made the cheap jab?
He felt the old anger rising, hands clenching, but he held it and turned it into a sharp, clean argument.
How did the rules help Umesh use his intensity well?
Clear limits like no personal attacks and a time limit gave his fierce energy a shape, so it became skill instead of trouble.
