James decides to go to prom with Susan.  He pays for everything.  The tickets cost $100 each.  Dinner is $120.  He leaves a 30% tip.  He also charters a limo for 6 hours that cost $80 per hour.  How much did it all cost?

He paid 100*2=$200 for tickets
The tip for dinner was $120*.3=$36
So he paid $120+$36=$156 for dinner
The limo cost $80*6=$480
In total he paid $200+$156+$480=$836
The answer is 836.

In Amman, the email arrived at 11 p.m.: "We regret to inform you…" Nour had spent four months on that research programme application. Two recommendation letters, three drafts of the essay, an interview in which she'd thought she did well.
Across the room, her flatmate Ingrid was on the phone to her parents, laughing. She had got into the same programme an hour earlier.

In the morning she reread the email. It said there were 900 applicants for 25 places. Her professor, when she told him, said, "They took mostly people working on water. Your topic is soil. It's fit, Nour, not worth."
She didn't quite believe it yet. But she wrote it on a sticky note and put it on her mirror.

There were 900 applicants for 25 places.

I'm Gargi. When my mother died, the fight started before the ashes had cooled.

Her side of the family wanted the rituals done in Varanasi. My father's side said our village temple. Then an aunt said Ma's gold should be divided now, "before things get lost." My cousin Anirban accused my father of not getting her to the hospital fast enough.

I was twenty-four. I wanted to scream at all of them.

Instead, one night, I went to the terrace and cried. Anirban followed me. He was crying too. "I didn't mean it," he said. "I just can't believe she's gone. She was like my mother too."

That's when I understood. Everyone was hurting, and it came out as fighting.

The next day I asked our oldest aunt to sit everyone down. No property talk for six months, she ruled. Rituals in both places.

We did both. Ma would have laughed at all the fuss.

Who did Gargi ask to sit everyone down?
The oldest aunt.
What did Gargi feel when she saw Anirban crying too?
Gargi felt a shift from anger to understanding, seeing that everyone's fighting came from grief.

Asking an elder to mediate, delaying property talk for six months, and doing the rituals in both places.

Anirban regrets it, saying he didn't mean it and that his grief made it come out.

The final exams at the college in Chikmagalur were two weeks away, and Farida's mind was racing. She couldn't focus and didn't feel like eating. But she remembered what her roommate Lavanya had said last semester: "When your head's a mess, look after your body first." So she kept three things steady. Lights off at eleven, even if she hadn't finished. Breakfast in the mess, even if it was only idli and tea. A walk up the coffee estate road every evening, thirty minutes, even on days she didn't want to. Some days she walked slowly, dragging her feet. But she went. By the second week, her thoughts felt less jumbled. She wasn't cheerful. But she was coping. "And if it gets really bad," Lavanya reminded her, "the college counsellor's right there." Farida nodded. "I know. I'll go if it does."

Lights off at eleven, breakfast in the mess, and a walk up the coffee estate road every evening.

She felt stressed and scattered at first, with no appetite, but by the second week her thoughts felt less jumbled and she was coping.

Steady sleep, meals and walks supported her mind even when motivation was low, and she knew the counsellor was there if it got severe.

It takes Roque two hours to walk to work and one hour to ride his bike to work. Roque walks to and from work three times a week and rides his bike to and from work twice a week. How many hours in total does he take to get to and from work a week with walking and biking?

Roque takes 2*3 = 6 hours a week to walk to work.
Roque takes 6*2 = 12 hours a week to walk to and from work.
Roque takes 1*2 = 2 hours a week to bike to work.
Roque takes 2*2 = 4 hours a week to bike to and from work.
In total, Roque takes 12+4 = 16 hour a week to go to and from work.
The answer is 16.

"Once upon a time, in a village with no water," Yamini began, torch under her chin, "there lived a very, very thirsty crow."

On the night before Gurpurab the power went out in their lane in Amritsar, and the langar preparation moved to candlelight in the courtyard. Gurleen and her college friend Imran were chopping onions beside her Biji when the question she had been swallowing for weeks slipped out.
"Biji, what if the Gurus were just wise men? What if the stories aren't literally true?"
Her mother, stirring the dal, froze. Imran stopped chopping.
Biji didn't. She kept kneading, then laughed softly. "You think you're the first to ask that? Guru Nanak himself asked questions wherever he went. Asking is not a sin, puttar. Being afraid to ask is worse."
She told Gurleen about her own doubts as a young bride, and the granthi who had listened instead of scolding. "Come with me to the gurdwara tomorrow. Ask Bhai-ji too. He likes a good question."
In the flickering light, Gurleen felt something unknot in her chest. Imran grinned and went back to the onions.

Where did the langar preparation move during the power cut?

She felt relieved and lighter, the fear of asking unknotting in her chest.
What did Biji do that kept Gurleen close to the faith?
She welcomed the question with interest, said doubt is old and common, shared her own doubts, and invited Gurleen to ask the granthi.
What might Gurleen's mother have felt when she froze?
Her mother probably felt alarmed and worried, until Biji's calm response eased the moment.
What does 'layover' mean?
A layover is the waiting time between two connecting flights, when you stay at an airport before your next flight.
Is it the same as a stopover?
They are close, and people mix the words up. A stopover usually means a longer planned stay, often a day or more, while a layover is a short wait.
How long a layover is safe?
It depends on the airport and whether you must clear immigration or change terminals. Check the airline's suggested minimum connection time, and allow extra if you can.

I'm Vikas. Everyone thinks I'm the clever one. Teachers say it. My parents say it. So when Ma'am gave us the project on the freedom movement, I thought: this has to be brilliant. If it isn't, everyone will know I'm not actually that clever.

When Nandini's grandfather died suddenly on a Tuesday, she cried into her mother's shoulder and did not apologise for it. Through the days of rituals she sat with the family, handing out tea and listening to stories about him. Back at school she told the class teacher, asked for extra time on two assignments over the next month, and drew up a lighter timetable with more evenings free.

At Siddharth's home, after his father's funeral, an uncle put a hand on his shoulder: "Now you must be the man in this house." Siddharth nodded, wiped his face before anyone could see, and scrubbed the kitchen, studied late and carried the grocery bags. Weeks later he snapped at his friend Arnab over a borrowed pen and lay awake most nights.

Months on, he still could not follow a page of text or sleep. One evening he told his mother. She held his hand, called the school the next morning, and arranged a talk with the counsellor. 'Farhan, I'm on it, the server was down—'
'Everything's always down.'
Naveen went quiet. Across the desk, Meenal stopped typing. Somebody's chair creaked. Farhan looked round the small office: three faces, all tight, the same way his own felt.

'It's okay.'
'It isn't, really. Listen, all of you. The client moved the deadline to Thursday and I'm worried. I've been snapping since morning.'

Hafsa, beta, you asked me once who my first real friend was. It was Kamla, in Jabalpur, when I was fifteen and she was fourteen.

That winter, my father's cloth business was failing. We sold my mother's bangles. I was ashamed; I thought it made us less. And I had a crush on the boy who delivered the newspaper, which felt even more shameful then.

The choice I made that night, to trust her, shaped every friendship after.

A movie theater charges $5 for matinee tickets, $7 for evening tickets, and $10 for opening night tickets. A bucket of popcorn costs $10. On Friday, they had 32 matinee customers, 40 evening customers, and 58 customers for an opening night showing of a movie. If half the customers bought popcorn, how much money in dollars did the theater make on Friday night?

The movie theater made 5 * 32 = $160 in matinee tickets.
It made 7 * 40 = $280 in evening tickets.
It made 10 * 58 = $580 in opening night tickets.
There were 32 + 40 + 58 = 130 customers.
Half of the customers bought popcorn, so 130 / 2 = 65 bought popcorn.
Thus, the theater made 10 * 65 = $650 from popcorn.
Therefore, in all, the theater made 160 + 280 + 580 + 650 = $1670 on Friday night.
The answer is 1670.

Lisa is a member of the photography club at school. Every weekend the club will go anywhere to take photos. Leslie took 10 photos of animals to share with the club. Lisa took 10 x 3 = 30 photos of flowers.
She took 30 - 10 = 20 photos of the scenery.
So, Lisa took 10 + 30 + 20 = 60 photos this week.
Therefore, Lisa took 60 - 15 = 45 photos last weekend.

The sewers in Middleton can handle 240,000 gallons of run-off. Each hour of rain produces 1000 gallons of runoff. How many days of rain can the sewers handle before they overflow?

First find how many hours of runoff the sewers can handle: 240,000 / 1000 gallons/hour = 240 hours
Then divide that time by the number of hours per day to find how many days of rain the sewers can handle: 240 hours / 24 hours/day = 10 days
The answer is 10.

A baseball team has averaged 15 hits per game over their first 5 games. There are 11 players on the team. Their best player has 25 total hits. If the other players continue their average over the next 6 games, how many hits will each player average across the 6 games in total?

The best player averages 5 hits a game because 25 / 5 = 5
The rest of the team averages 10 hits a game because 15 - 5 = 10
The rest of the players average 1 hit a game because 10 / 10 = 1
They will average 6 hits per player over the next 6 games because 6 x 1 = 6
The answer is 6.

Lokesh could have asked what the role involved and how people grew in it, because the name told nothing about the daily work.
How might Nirmala Aunty see Lokesh's job?
Nirmala Aunty sees the famous name that earned sweets, not the tickets, so that pride may make it harder for Lokesh to say how things really are.

"Boring," said Yogesh when Papa unrolled the fire-drill card on the sofa. "Fires only happen to strangers." He rolled his eyes and went back to his game. Three weeks later, in the kitchen, the burner flame jumped to the curtain. Yogesh stood with a glass in his hand, staring. Which door? Which way? What was step one? The steps he had laughed at were nowhere in his head. "Out! Now!" His father Jagdish grabbed his arm, pulled him into the corridor and shut the door, while Mummy shouted for the neighbours and rang the fire brigade. Downstairs, Yogesh's knees shook. He had stood still for far too long.

Who pulled Yogesh out of the kitchen?
His father Jagdish pulled him out.
What was Yogesh feeling as he stood in the kitchen with the glass?
Frozen and scared, and confused, since none of the steps he had laughed at came to mind.
What would you advise Yogesh to do now, and why?
Yogesh could ask to practise the drill again and take it seriously, because knowing the steps lets his body move when he is frightened.
What might Jagdish be feeling as he pulls Yogesh into the corridor?
Jagdish is likely frightened and urgent, wanting only to get his son out, and probably relieved once they are outside.

Read this:

Monday. Kalyani sat on the stairs with her tuition notebooks, her eyes half closed. "I've had five kids' parents call me since Saturday," she told Zainab, who lived upstairs. "I said yes to all of them."
Wednesday. She wrote on the whiteboard in her hallway: "Sundays: closed." Then she called Zainab. "Would you share the neighbourhood tiffin rota? Just Tuesdays and Fridays?" Zainab said she would.
Saturday. A mother asked whether Kalyani could add an extra batch on Sunday. "I can't on Sundays," Kalyani said. "But I could fit it on Thursday." The mother agreed. Kalyani closed the door and let out a long breath. She slept in until eight the next morning.

Which days did Kalyani ask Zainab to help with the tiffin rota?
She asked Zainab to take Tuesdays and Fridays.
What was Kalyani feeling on Monday as she sat on the stairs?
Kalyani felt exhausted and overloaded, saying she had said yes to all five parents.
What small steps did Kalyani take over the week to keep her kindness sustainable?
She marked Sundays closed, asked Zainab to share the tiffin rota and offered a Thursday slot in place of Sunday.
How might Zainab have felt when asked to take Tuesdays and Fridays?
Zainab said yes, which suggests being willing and perhaps glad to be trusted. Sharing the load meant the neighbours' tiffins would still arrive.
What is intellect? The headline says the winner has a sharp one.

Intellect is the power of the mind to think, understand and reason. It is a noun. A sharp intellect means a quick, clear mind.
Example: The girl's intellect was clear from the way she solved every puzzle.

Damini: Nani, are you awake? Rashmi said I should ask you something
Nani: for you, always awake 🙂
Damini: Papa wants me to skip the music camp and help at the pharmacy counter in summer. I'm so confused
Nani: hmm. did I ever tell you about my singing?
Damini: you sang??
Nani: I was chosen for a radio audition in Lucknow. age 17. my father's shop was busy, so I didn't go
Nani: I told myself it didn't matter
Damini: did it?
Nani: honestly? for 40 years I wondered. not every day. but on some evenings
Nani: but I also learned the shop, and later I ran it. that mattered too
Damini: so what do I do 😟
Nani: I can't choose for you. but don't decide like I did, without saying anything
Nani: tell Papa what the camp means. maybe you give part of summer to both
Damini: that actually helps. thank you Nani ❤️

How old was Nani when she was chosen for the radio audition?
Nani was 17.
How did Damini feel before talking to Nani?
Damini felt confused and worried, torn between the music camp and helping at the pharmacy.
What else could Damini do with Nani's advice?
Damini could sit with Papa, explain what the camp means and suggest splitting the summer, as Nani hinted.
How might Nani have felt sharing her own story?
Nani may have felt a little wistful remembering the lost audition, but glad it could help Damini avoid deciding in silence.

messages.content: Why does the smell of perfume seem to fade after a while even though it is still there?

The nose gets used to a scent and stops reporting it. Because the smell cells send weaker signals when they meet the same scent again and again, the brain stops noticing it, while someone who has just walked in still smells it.

In the billing department's Thursday meeting, Vikas was still opening the spreadsheet when the supervisor asked for the totals. Sunaina caught herself rolling her eyes and letting out a small sigh at the ceiling. Vikas saw it; his ears reddened and he closed the file. Afterwards, at the water cooler, Sunaina noticed how tight her own shoulders were: three deadlines, no lunch, a headache building. It was the day, not really him. She walked over to his desk. "Shall we go through the new template together? I can spare twenty minutes at four. And let's agree that totals go out by Wednesday noon, so the meeting is not a scramble." Vikas nodded, and relief loosened his face.

What did Vikas do when Sunaina rolled her eyes?
His ears reddened and he closed the file.
What does Sunaina realise at the water cooler?
That her contempt came from stress and tight shoulders, not from anything about Vikas's worth.
What did Sunaina offer instead of mocking?
Twenty minutes to go through the new template and a clear rule that totals go out by Wednesday noon.
How might Vikas have felt when he saw the eye-roll?
Embarrassed, as his reddened ears suggest, and perhaps ashamed in front of the team.

Read this:

In the small college at Karad, Lokesh's handwritten physics notes were famous: neat diagrams, every derivation. When Nikita, from the next bench, said she'd missed a month for her grandmother's illness, he handed over the whole notebook without thinking.
Two weeks later he walked into the xerox shop near the bus stand and saw stacks of his own pages on sale, twenty rupees a set. Nikita had lent the notebook to the shopkeeper. It came back with tea rings on the cover.
Lokesh sat on the college wall that evening, burning with embarrassment. How had he not seen it? He thought about never lending anything again. Then he thought of Vinod, who had borrowed his notes all last year and returned them every Monday.

How much was each set of notes sold for at the xerox shop?
Twenty rupees a set.
What was Lokesh feeling on the college wall that evening?
He felt betrayed and embarrassed, even gullible, for handing over his notebook so easily.
What could Lokesh do next time someone asks for his notes?
Lend to people with a track record like Vinod, or share a chapter first, instead of refusing everyone.
What would change if Nikita had asked before giving the notebook to the shop?
Lokesh could have agreed or refused, and his trust in Nikita might have stayed intact.

Read this:

Manjula, I have to confess something about the peer evaluations. So, I'm Kishore, and we had to rate our project teammates out of ten. I gave the quiet guy, Ravi, a four. I was so sure. In the last two weeks he missed a meeting and sent his section late. That's all I could think about. Then last night I scrolled back through our group chat, all the way to January. Ravi built the whole survey. He fixed my code in February at midnight. He found the dataset we used. For three months he was the best on the team. Two bad weeks, and I'd forgotten all of it. I've asked the professor if I can change my rating. Honestly, I was rating the last fortnight, not the person.

What score did Kishore first give Ravi?
A four.
What was Kishore feeling when first rating Ravi?
Kishore felt sure and annoyed, because the missed meeting and late section in the last two weeks were all that came to mind.
What did Kishore do to correct the rating, and why was it fairer?
Kishore scrolled back through the group chat to January and asked to change the score, judging all three months instead of the last two weeks.
How might Ravi feel if he saw the first rating?
Ravi would probably feel hurt and misjudged, after building the survey and fixing code at midnight.

Read this:

Arnab, when I was fifteen, I was sure my best friend Neelam hated me. She didn't wave one morning, and by lunch I had decided she was jealous of my marks. I felt it so strongly that it had to be true. I stopped talking to her for two weeks. Then her brother said, "Jyoti, our grandmother was in hospital that week." She hadn't even seen me that morning. I remember sitting on the school steps, hot-faced, realising that a strong feeling had made me certain, not any fact. Since then, when I'm very sure about what someone thinks, I ask myself: what do I actually know? Usually it's much less than I feel.

How long did young Jyoti stop talking to Neelam?
For two weeks.
What did Jyoti realise, hot-faced, on the school steps?
That a strong feeling, not any fact, had made Jyoti certain about Neelam's motives, and it brought shame.
What question does Jyoti now ask herself, and why does it help?
"What do I actually know?" It separates facts from feelings before deciding what someone thinks.
How might Neelam have experienced those two weeks?
Already worried about her grandmother, she probably felt confused and hurt that her friend suddenly went cold.

Read this:

Parveen: listened to your new rap
Parveen: "packing my bags, this town's too small, never coming back at all"
Parveen: kishore are you actually leaving??
Kishore: haha no
Kishore: it's a persona. the guy in the song is fed up and bounces
Parveen: ok but some of it sounded like you
Kishore: some of it is. I'm tired of everyone here knowing everything about me
Kishore: and I want to go to college somewhere big
Kishore: but I'm not running away, relax 😅
Parveen: ok good. I was worried
Kishore: fair. rappers exaggerate. "never coming back" sounds better than "might apply to Pune in 2 years"
Parveen: lol true
Parveen: the beat is sick btw
Kishore: thanks. you're the first person who asked instead of telling my mom 😅
Parveen: I'll tell her it's a banger instead

Which line did Parveen quote?
"packing my bags, this town's too small, never coming back at all"
What was Parveen feeling after hearing the rap?
Parveen felt worried that Kishore might really be planning to leave home.
Why was it wise for Parveen to ask Kishore directly?
Lyrics use persona and exaggeration, so asking found out the real feeling, frustration and college dreams, without assuming a plan to run away.
How might Kishore's mom have read the lyrics without asking?
She might have taken them literally and panicked that Kishore was planning to run away.
Why do people wear new clothes at festivals? Also, correct: My cousins comes every year. What is the meaning of "celebrate"?

1. It marks a special day. Because new clothes make people feel fresh and festive.
2. Fixed: My cousins come every year. Why: "Cousins" is plural, so use "come".
3. To celebrate is to do something special for a happy day. Example: We celebrate Diwali with lamps.

Read this:

At fifteen, I was the biggest fan of the Riverfall books in our school. I'd read all seven twice, written fan fiction, and joined an online group of three thousand readers. I signed my notebooks with the heroine's name. So when Naveen said in English class that the books were 'badly written and overrated', I felt as if he'd slapped me. I argued so hard that the teacher had to stop me. Later I realised I'd said more that day than in the whole term. Naveen wasn't insulting me. He was talking about books. But the books were so tied up with who I was that I couldn't tell the difference. I'm Shreya. I still love Riverfall. I just try to remember I'm more than a fan.

How many readers were in the online group?
Three thousand.
How did Shreya feel when Naveen called the books overrated?
Shreya felt as if slapped, hurt and defensive, as though the criticism was personal.
What could Shreya do the next time someone criticises a favourite thing?
Pause and remember they're talking about the thing, not about Shreya, then share a view calmly.
How might Naveen have seen Shreya's reaction in class?
He was only giving an opinion about books, so he was likely surprised by how hard Shreya argued.
Every monsoon our area floods because the drains get blocked.
That's a big problem for everyone. Do you know what usually blocks the drains?
Mostly plastic bags and rubbish.
Then part of the fix is stopping rubbish from reaching the drains. A campaign asking people not to throw plastic in the street can help, along with more dustbins.
Who cleans the drains, though?
Usually the local municipal body is responsible. You could ask them to clean the drains before the monsoon starts. A group request with photos is harder to ignore.
Can residents do anything themselves?
Residents can keep the area in front of their homes clear and report blocked drains quickly. Don't go into drains yourselves, since they can be dangerous.
I'll bring it up at our next meeting.
That's a good next step. Go with a short list of problem spots and photos, and suggest one or two clear actions the group can agree on.
I am waiting you outside the cinema hall. Fix this message, please.

I am waiting for you outside the cinema hall.
Why: "wait for" needs "for".
My hairdresser says "fringe" but my American cousin says "bangs". Are they different?

They are the same: the hair cut straight across the forehead. "Fringe" is British, and "bangs" is American.
Examples: Mira trimmed her fringe before the party. Mira trimmed her bangs before the party.

Read this:

At the bus stop after tuition, a boy on a scooter kept pulling up next to Parul. "Come, I'll drop you. Just get on."
Parul froze. She didn't move or speak. Her hands were clenched on her bag strap.
The boy grinned. "See, she's not saying no."
I grabbed Parul's arm. "She's not saying yes either. Come on, Parul." I pulled her toward the tea stall where there were other people.
The boy rode off.
Parul was shaking. "I couldn't talk," she whispered.
"It's okay. You froze. That's not your fault."
We called her mother from the stall, and she came to pick us both up. That evening her mother reported the boy to the tuition centre.
- Ishita

Where did Ishita pull Parul toward?
The tea stall where there were other people.
What was Parul feeling when she froze?
Parul felt frightened and unable to move or speak, a stress response, not agreement.
What did Ishita and Parul's mother do that kept Parul safe?
Ishita moved Parul toward other people and called her mother, who came right away and reported the boy that evening.
How did the boy on the scooter misread Parul's silence?
He took her silence as a yes, when freezing is never consent.
Fill in the missing numerals. 0, 1, __, 3, 4, __, 6, __, 8, 9, __
Why does a seed need moisture before it sprouts?
Water softens the hard coat. Because it also wakes up the baby plant inside, the seed can begin to grow.

It is the rainy June week when kindergarten reopens. Nikita hangs her yellow raincoat on the peg, hugs Mamma at the gate and waves twice. "Bye! Come back after lunch!" Inside, she builds a tall tower with Imran and pours water into the sand tray all by herself. At pickup she spots Mamma's umbrella, races across the wet yard, crashes into her knees for one quick squeeze, then runs off again. "Wait! I have to show you Imran's tower falling down!"

What colour is Nikita's raincoat?
Yellow.
Why does Nikita race to Mamma at pickup and then run back?
She feels happy and safe 😊 seeing Mamma return, and one quick squeeze is enough to make her brave enough to go back and play.
What helps Nikita play on her own, and how could Mamma keep it going?
Knowing Mamma comes back after lunch helps; Mamma can keep the same goodbye and always be there at pickup.
What is it like for Mamma when Nikita runs off again?
Mamma may feel a small tug of being left, but also glad that Nikita feels secure enough to go off and play.

Read this:

Manager's note, written by Himani.
Zainab, a junior analyst, told me that the pricing model she built had been presented by a senior colleague without her name on it, and that a later suggestion of hers was brushed aside. She was upset but spoke evenly. She had already kept a dated record of her drafts and had talked to two teammates who saw her work.
What I did: I asked every contributor to present their own part at the next review and asked that slides carry authorship lines. Zainab presented the model herself. The senior colleague was quiet but did not object. Zainab told me afterwards that she had felt her hands shake and was glad she had prepared.

What did Zainab keep to show her contribution?
Zainab kept a dated record of her drafts.
What was Zainab feeling when she spoke to Himani about the senior colleague?
Zainab was upset and hurt by the missing credit but stayed even in her tone.
What steps by Himani helped Zainab's work be seen?
Himani asked every contributor to present their own part and asked for authorship lines on slides, so Zainab could present the model herself.
How might the senior colleague have felt at the review?
The senior colleague was quiet and did not object, so they may have felt awkward or caught out, though the note does not say.
Marcy keeps a 2-liter bottle of water by her desk. She takes a sip every five minutes, and each sip is 40 ml. How many minutes does it take her to drink the whole bottle of water?

First find the total number of milliliters in the bottle: 2 liters * 1000 ml/liter = 2000 ml
Then divide the total number of milliliters by the amount she drinks per sip: 2000 ml / 40 ml = 50 sips
Then multiply the number of sips by the time per sip to find the time it takes her to drink the bottle: 50 sips * 5 minutes/sip = 250 minutes
The answer is 250.

Read this:

Pankaj, you want to earn a little? Your Rajni Mausi did too, at your age. The year my father fell ill, there wasn't much money. I was in Class 11. First I asked Amma and Bapuji if I could teach. They said yes, but only two children, only four days a week, and never past seven, because my own boards came first. So I taught two Class 5 girls from our lane, maths and English, at our kitchen table from five to six. Their mothers paid a small fee each month. I gave some of it to Amma for vegetables and kept some in a tin marked "exam fees". When the board registration came, the tin covered it. I was so proud. And my own marks didn't drop, because we had set those limits at the start.

What time did Rajni teach?
From five to six, at the kitchen table.
How did young Rajni feel when the tin covered the exam fees?
Young Rajni felt very proud, having earned it herself while keeping her own studies safe.
Which choice at the start made the plan safe?
Agreeing limits with Amma and Bapuji, two children, four days a week and never past seven, so earning never crowded out her boards.
What might it have meant to Amma to receive part of the fee?
Amma may have felt relieved and touched, since the help came from her daughter during a hard year.

Read this:

Monday: In the class group chat, every message Mehak posted got a row of thumbs-down emojis from the same three girls. She stopped posting.
Wednesday: In the corridor, one of the girls flashed the middle finger at Mehak as she passed. Mehak's heart pounded. She didn't respond. She walked straight to the staffroom, took a breath, and knocked.
Sangeeta Ma'am, her class teacher, listened to everything, including the chat. "Thank you for telling me. This isn't okay, and it's not your fault."
That afternoon, Ma'am spoke with the three girls and called their parents.
Friday: The thumbs-downs stopped. Mehak posted in the group again, just a small message about homework.

What did the three girls send in the group chat?
A row of thumbs-down emojis.
What was Mehak feeling when the girl flashed the middle finger?
Mehak felt scared and upset, her heart pounding, but she stayed calm.
What did Sangeeta Ma'am do that helped?
She listened, told Mehak it wasn't her fault, spoke to the three girls, and called their parents that same afternoon.
How might the three girls see their gestures after the teacher's talk?
They might realise their gestures were bullying and could bring real consequences.
Why does a ramp make it easier to push a heavy box onto a truck?
A ramp spreads the lifting over a longer path. Because the box rises slowly along the slope instead of straight up, each push needs less force, though the distance pushed is greater.

The area of a forest is three times the area of the square-shaped street. If the street has a length of 100 meters on one side and the number of trees per square meter in the forest is 4, calculate the total number of trees in the forest.

Since the area of a square is sides squared, the area of the square-shaped street is 100*100 = 10000 square meters.
The area of the forest is three times the area of the square-shaped street, a total of 3*10000 = 30000 square meters.
If the number of trees per square meter in the forest is 4, there are 4*30000 = 120000 trees in the forest.
The answer is 120000.
In a forest, there are three anthills. In the first anthill, there are 100 ants, and in each next anthill, there are 20% fewer ants than in the previous one. How many ants are in the third anthill?

In the second anthill, there are 20/100 * 100 = 20 ants less.
This means there are 100 - 20 = 80 ants in the second anthill.
In the third anthill, there are 20/100 * 80 = 16 ants less compared to the second one.
So in the third anthill, there are 80 - 16 = 64 ants.
The answer is 64.

Read this:

When Yogesh joined our lab as a summer intern, I did exactly what I'd hated as an intern: I gave him all my dull tasks. Label two hundred sample tubes. Clean the fridge. Enter old data. I told myself it was "learning the basics".
In week two I saw him in the corridor, reading a paper on his phone about the very experiment I was running. He had never asked to join. He probably thought he couldn't.
I felt ashamed. So I asked him to run the next trial with me. I explained each step slowly, let him pipette, and didn't sigh when he spilled the first plate. By week five he found an error in my calibration that I had missed for a month.
At our lab meeting I put his name on the slide: "Calibration fix: Yogesh." Our professor asked him to explain it. He did, nervously, and well.
I still give him some boring tasks. I also do some of them myself.
— Usha

How many sample tubes did Usha ask Yogesh to label?
Two hundred.
How did Usha feel on seeing Yogesh read the paper in the corridor?
Ashamed of dumping dull tasks on him, realising he wanted to learn but thought he couldn't ask.
How did Usha change the way of mentoring Yogesh?
By inviting him into the trial, explaining patiently, allowing mistakes, and crediting his calibration fix on the slide.
How might Yogesh have felt in the first two weeks?
Bored and left out, eager to learn but unsure whether he could ask to join.
A friend is upset with me. What is a sensible first step?

A good first step is to talk to the friend calmly and listen. Because anger usually fades when a person feels understood, hearing their side gives us a chance to say sorry if we were wrong and fix things.
Please correct my sentence: Yesterday I go to school and teacher give us many homework.

Corrected: "Yesterday I went to school, and the teacher gave us a lot of homework." Use the past tense (went, gave) with "yesterday". Say "the teacher". "Homework" cannot be counted, so say "a lot of homework", not "many homework".

Read this:

At the Chaitra temple fair in Madanapalle, the pradhan's microphone had broken, and someone had to announce the lost-child desk and the evening schedule to three hundred people. Charu pushed Keerthana forward. "You. You've got the voice." Keerthana, twenty and usually shy, climbed onto the tractor trailer. Her hands were cold. She planted her feet, pulled her shoulders back, took a long breath and let her voice come from her chest, not her throat. "Everyone, please listen." It carried all the way to the sugarcane stalls. People turned. She spoke slowly: the lost-child desk by the banyan tree, prasad at six. A small boy was brought to the desk within ten minutes. Afterwards, an old woman patted her arm. "Such a confident girl." Keerthana smiled, then whispered to Charu, "My legs are still shaking."

Where was the lost-child desk?
By the banyan tree.
What was Keerthana feeling when she climbed onto the trailer?
She was nervous, with cold hands and shaking legs, even though her voice came out steady and strong.
What helped Keerthana's voice carry?
Planting her feet, pulling her shoulders back, taking a long breath and speaking from her chest, slowly.
How did the old woman read Keerthana's voice?
She heard it as confidence, calling her a confident girl, without knowing her legs were shaking.

Lucas' father offers to pay him $2 for each window in the house that he cleans. Each floor of Lucas' house has 3 windows; Lucas lives in a 3-story house. To get Lucas to finish the job faster, his father tells him that he will subtract $1 for every 3 days that pass without Lucas finishing the job. In 6 days, Lucas finishes cleaning all the windows in the house. How much will his father pay him, in dollars?

Lucas cleans a total of 3 floors * 3 windows/floor = 9 windows.
The windows cleaned earn Lucas 2 dollars each, so Lucas earns 9 windows * $2/window = $18
For taking 6 days to clean, Lucas' father subtracts 6 days / $3/day = $2
In total, Lucas' father will pay him $18 - $2 = $16
The answer is 16.

Read this:

Hemant put the phone face-down on the dining table when Omkar, Hemant's partner, walked in, and the movement itself was the trouble. Omkar had seen the chat with an ex earlier that week, and hadn't said much since. Tonight, over the noise of the pressure cooker, Omkar said, "It makes me uneasy. I don't know why."

Hemant's first instinct was to say "it's just talking, don't be silly." He held it back. Instead Hemant asked himself: what am I getting from it? A little old-friend ease, mostly. And what does it cost Omkar? That was the harder question.

"I'll show you the chat," Hemant said, "and I'll stop if it keeps bothering you. I don't want you to feel second to it."

Omkar exhaled. "Thank you for not laughing at me."

Where did Hemant put the phone when Omkar walked in?
Face-down on the dining table.
How did Hemant feel about Omkar's unease, and what did Hemant ask himself?
Hemant felt defensive at first and wanted to say "don't be silly", but held it back and asked what the chat gave him and what it cost Omkar.
What choice does Hemant make, and why does it protect trust?
Hemant offers to show the chat and to stop if it keeps bothering Omkar, choosing transparency instead of hiding it or calling Omkar's feelings silly.
How might Omkar have felt when Hemant turned the phone face-down?
Omkar may have felt shut out or suspicious, since the movement itself was the trouble, and was relieved when Hemant offered openness and did not laugh.
What is the aroha of Raga Kirwani?
The aroha of Raga Kirwani is: S R g M P d N S'.
John buys 3 spools of wire that are 20 feet each.  It takes 4 feet to make a necklace.  How many necklaces can he make?

He gets 3*20=60 feet of wire
So he can make 60/4=15 necklaces
The answer is 15.

Read this:

Bhavna's hostel in Kolar had no reading room, but the town library stayed open till nine, a ten-minute walk away past the vegetable market. Every evening she meant to study there, and every evening her phone ate the first hour.
On Sunday she wrote a sentence on the inside cover of her notebook: 'After dinner, at the library, I open the first task before I check any message. Phone goes in the bag.'
On Monday she ate at 6:30, walked over with Uma, sat at the long wooden table under the fan, zipped her phone into her bag's inner pocket, and opened her physics notebook to problem one. Then problem two.
At 8:15 she took the phone out. Eleven messages, nothing urgent.
By Friday she had done this four evenings out of five. Uma, who'd been watching, wrote the same sentence in her own notebook.

What did Bhavna write on the inside cover of her notebook?
'After dinner, at the library, I open the first task before I check any message. Phone goes in the bag.'
How might Bhavna have felt at 8:15 on seeing eleven messages, nothing urgent?
She likely felt relieved and a bit proud, seeing that nothing was lost by waiting and the work was done.
What could Bhavna do about the evening she missed?
Notice what got in the way and adjust the plan, without giving up on the rule.
How does the plan look to Uma?
Uma watches it work for a week and is convinced enough to copy the same sentence.

metadata.subtype: Approach: implementation intention to start work [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Nilesh: Disha? Lunch is ready.
Disha: Not hungry.
Nilesh: Can I ask one thing? Is it a quiet day or a heavy one?
Disha: ...I don't know, Papa. A bit of both.
Nilesh: That's a fair answer.
Disha: I want the door shut. But I also don't want to be forgotten.
Nilesh: I won't forget. I'll leave a plate on the shelf and be in the kitchen. If it turns heavy, and stays that way, knock, or tell me or Mummy.
Disha: Okay. Papa? Can you leave the door open a crack?
Nilesh: Done.
Later there were footsteps, and Disha came out for the plate on her own.

Where will Nilesh leave a plate for Disha?
On the shelf.
What is Disha feeling when she answers 'A bit of both'?
Disha feels unsure and torn, wanting privacy but also not wanting to be forgotten.
What could Disha do if the heavy feeling stays?
Disha could knock or tell Papa or Mummy, as Nilesh says, so a trusted adult can help.
How does Nilesh handle Disha's closed door?
Nilesh asks one gentle question, accepts the answer, promises not to forget and offers a plate and a crack in the door, without pushing.

Read this:

Dear Imran bhai,
You told me to write to you when I'm stuck, so here I am.
Board exams are in six weeks. Every night I say, "Tomorrow I'll study six hours." Every night I scroll videos till one. And every morning I feel terrible, and then that night I say it again. It's like I'm sure tomorrow-me will feel like studying. But tomorrow-me is exactly the same as today-me. Same bed, same phone.
Ammi hasn't noticed yet. I'm scared she will.
You did your boards two years ago. How did you start? Not tomorrow. Today.
Please write back soon.
Your little brother,
Mridul

How many weeks until Mridul's board exams?
Six weeks.
What is Mridul feeling while writing the letter?
He feels scared and guilty, stuck in a loop of promising to study tomorrow and scrolling tonight.
What could help Mridul start today rather than tomorrow?
Asking Imran bhai for concrete tips, and starting with one small task tonight, like thirty minutes with the phone in another room.
How might Imran bhai feel reading the letter?
Imran bhai would probably feel concerned but also glad Mridul reached out for help.

Manjula, people on campus still ask me, "Santosh, why didn't you sit for placements?" Honestly? By second year I had decided on music, and after that my research was just shopping for agreement. I followed only musicians who had left engineering. I asked the one senior who had made it, not the five who went back to coding. When the head of department sent round the placement numbers, I didn't open the file. I felt very well informed; I had a whole notebook of quotes. Then in final year a friend asked me, "What would make you change your mind?" and I couldn't name a single thing. That scared me more than any exam. I still chose music, by the way. But this time I sat down and read the other side first.

Who did Santosh ask for advice in second year?
Santosh asked the one senior who had made it, not the five who went back to coding.
How did Santosh feel on failing to answer the friend's question?
Santosh felt scared and shaken, because having nothing that could change the decision showed the research had only been collecting agreement.
Which choice in final year worked better, and why?
Reading the other side before choosing music again, because the decision was then tested instead of only supported.
What would change if Santosh had opened the placement numbers in second year?
Santosh would have faced facts that didn't fit the plan, which might have led to a fairer look at both sides much earlier.

I'm Lavanya, and I sit next to Charu in Class 5. Charu is in Blue House and talks about it all year. On sports day she tied blue ribbons in both plaits and made a paper flag. When Yellow House won the relay by a whisker, Charu sat down on the grass and did not get up for the prize-giving. I don't know if she was crying; she kept her face in her knees. The next morning, before the teacher came, Charu drew a fat yellow duck on the board and wrote "YELLOW CAPTAIN" under it. Some boys laughed. Mitali, the Yellow captain, walked in and saw it. Charu looked at Mitali's face, then quickly rubbed the board with her sleeve. She didn't say much at lunch.

What did Charu draw on the board?
She drew a fat yellow duck and wrote 'YELLOW CAPTAIN' under it.
What might Charu have been feeling when she quickly rubbed the board clean?
She probably felt sorry or embarrassed once she saw Mitali's face, realising the joke had hurt a real person.
How could a teacher support Charu after this?
A teacher could praise her love for Blue House, talk quietly with her about how Mitali felt, and help her make a proper apology.
How might Mitali see Charu when she walks in and finds the drawing?
Mitali might feel singled out and embarrassed, and see Charu as someone who could not bear Blue losing.

"Kalyani, you know my photo pout, right? The one I do in every selfie? That's fun. That's me being silly.
But last week at the canteen, I was really upset. My mum had said I can't go on the Class 10 trip. I was sitting there with my lips pushed out, not even thinking about it.
And Nisha shouted, 'Duck face! Take a picture!' Everyone laughed. I laughed too, but I wanted to cry.
You were the only one who didn't laugh. You just sat next to me and said, 'You okay?'
That's the difference. Same lips, different day. I, Rukmini, just want people to look a little closer before they joke."

What trip was Rukmini not allowed to go on?
The Class 10 trip.
What was Rukmini feeling when Nisha shouted "Duck face!"?
Rukmini felt hurt and embarrassed, laughing along but wanting to cry, since the pout came from being upset, not from posing.
What did Kalyani do that made a difference?
Kalyani didn't laugh and simply sat nearby and asked a gentle question, noticing the real mood behind the pout.
How might Nisha have seen her own joke?
Nisha probably thought it was harmless fun about Rukmini's usual selfie face, not realising it was a real sulk.

Read this:

Sunday. Farida sat on her friend Aparna's balcony, the prelims result open on her phone. She had missed the cut-off by six marks. 'Three years. I'm just not good enough.' Aparna didn't tell her it would be fine. She said, 'Six marks after three years. That's a lot to carry,' and let her cry.
Wednesday. Aparna brought a sheet of paper and drew two columns. Farida filled the first one fast: the result, the year gone. The second came slower: how she revised, the gaps in current affairs, the mock tests she kept skipping. 'Pick one,' Aparna said. Farida circled the mocks.
The next Saturday. At nine at night Farida messaged: 'Did a full mock. Terrible at current affairs. But now I know exactly where 🙂' Aparna sent back a thumbs-up and didn't add a speech.

By how many marks did Farida miss the cut-off?
Farida missed the cut-off by six marks.
What was Farida feeling on Sunday, and what shows it?
Farida felt hopeless and ashamed; she said 'I'm just not good enough' and cried after three years of work.
What made Aparna's two-column sheet useful?
It separated what could not change, the result and the lost year, from what could, and picking one item, the mock tests, turned despair into a step Farida could take 🙂
What would change if Aparna had said 'It'll be fine' on Sunday?
Farida might have felt brushed off and stopped talking; being heard first is what made her willing to sit down with the columns on Wednesday.

Monday night: Ankita lay under the fan, eyes wide open. What if she failed the spelling test? What if Mummy's scooter slipped in the rain on the way home from the clinic? She called out three times. Her mother, Jyoti, came each time, a little more tired.
Wednesday night: Jyoti sat on the bed. "Worries are like a doorbell that rings too much," she said. "Let's make a bedtime plan." Warm milk, one story, then Ankita would say three good things from the day. "And I'll always tell you when I'm home safe."
Saturday night: Ankita heard the scooter, then Mummy's voice from the door: "Home!" She whispered her three good things and fell asleep before the story ended.

What three things were in the bedtime plan?
Warm milk, one story, then Ankita would say three good things from the day.
What was Ankita worried about on Monday night?
She was afraid of failing the spelling test and scared that her mother's scooter might slip in the rain on the way home.
Which change helped Ankita most, and why?
The steady bedtime plan together with Jyoti's promise to say when she was home gave Ankita something calm to hold on to instead of the alarms.
What was Monday night like for Jyoti?
Jyoti came each time but was tired, and being called three times probably worried her too, which is why a plan helped them both.

Sunday, late.
Papa called again after lunch. Naveen's wedding hall needs an advance, and the caterer too, and "you are the one with the city job, beta." I said yes before he finished. Of course I said yes. Naveen is my little brother and I love him.
Then I opened my savings sheet. The course I have been saving for since last year, the one that could move me up at work, would be pushed back again. I felt angry, and then angry at myself for feeling angry.
After dinner I called Papa back. My hands were shaking. I told him the exact amount I can give for the wedding, and that I need to keep a small amount aside for emergencies and my course. He was quiet, then said, "Divyansh, why didn't you say this before?" We talked for almost an hour. Nothing is solved, but it feels less like a secret now.

What does the wedding hall need, according to Papa?
Naveen's wedding hall needs an advance, and the caterer too.
How did Divyansh feel after opening the savings sheet?
Divyansh felt resentful about the course being delayed, then guilty for feeling that way about a brother he loves.
What did Divyansh do that could keep goodwill in the family?
Divyansh called back and named a clear amount he could give while explaining the need to keep something aside, instead of silently agreeing and resenting it.
How might Papa see the call?
Papa seems surprised and maybe a little hurt, asking why Divyansh had not said it before, but he stays on the line to talk it through.

Monday, late.

Swati came to my room after dinner and sat on the floor instead of the bed. Then she said it: "I don't see the point of anything. I feel hopeless, Gopika. Don't tell anyone."

My heart was pounding. I wanted to say "don't think like that" but I didn't. I sat down next to her and asked her to tell me more. I listened. Then I asked her straight out if she had been thinking of ending her life. She said sometimes.

I told her I couldn't keep this secret, because I care about her too much. She cried, but she didn't leave. We called the helpline number from the notice board together, on speaker. Then we went down to the warden, who called the on-call counsellor, who talked to Swati for an hour.

Swati's sleeping in my room tonight. The warden will check on us before she goes to bed.

Where did Swati sit when she came to the room?
Swati sat on the floor instead of the bed.
What was Gopika feeling when Swati said she felt hopeless?
Gopika felt frightened, with a pounding heart, but also caring enough to stay calm and listen.
What steps did Gopika take that same night, and why do they matter?
Gopika listened without judging, asked directly, refused to keep it secret, called the helpline with Swati and took her to the warden and counsellor.
How might Swati feel about Gopika refusing to keep the secret?
Swati may feel upset at first, but she stayed, which suggests part of her also felt relieved to be taken seriously and not left alone.

I was in the study group when Sudha said it, so I'll just tell you what I saw.
Our group of four had a project due Monday. On Wednesday Sudha told us the survey analysis was done. On Saturday it turned out she hadn't started. We scrambled for two days.
On Sunday evening she asked us all to stay after the library closed. She didn't sit down.
"I said the analysis was finished. It wasn't. I hadn't even opened the data. I lied because I was embarrassed that I was behind, and I didn't want you to think I was the weak one. Because of that, you lost your weekend. That's on me, not on the deadline or on anyone else."
Nobody said anything. Then she said, "I'm not asking you to be okay with it tonight."
I can't know what she was feeling. Her hands were shaking. But she didn't once say "sorry if".
Thomas

On which day did Sudha tell the group the survey analysis was done?
Sudha told the group on Wednesday.
What does Sudha say she was feeling when she lied?
Sudha says she was embarrassed about being behind and did not want the group to think she was the weak one.
What made Sudha's apology a full one?
She said exactly what she did, why, and what it cost the group, blamed no one else, and did not ask for quick forgiveness.
How might the rest of the group feel after the apology?
They might still be annoyed about the lost weekend, but hearing the full truth, without excuses, could make it easier to trust Sudha again over time.

Tanuja sat on the veranda step with the offer letter for the tailoring course in town in one hand and her open BA forms in the other. Her friend Nandini, cutting the thread from a blouse, watched. "Write down what you don't know," Nandini said. Tanuja did, in the back of a copybook: "Will the fees fit? Will I get work after? Does the bus reach in time?" Then she drew a line by the ones she could find out cheaply. On Saturday she would visit the institute and speak to two past students. She wrote a date at the bottom: "Decide on the first. If nothing changes, take the course."

What did Tanuja write at the bottom of the list?
Tanuja wrote, "Decide on the first. If nothing changes, take the course."
What is Tanuja probably feeling as she looks at the letter and the forms?
She is probably uncertain but hopeful, because she is torn between two paths yet turns the doubt into a written plan.
Why is a default useful when Tanuja sets her decision date?
With a date and a default, she will not stay stuck, and she can revise if new facts, such as the fees or the bus, change.
How does Nandini help Tanuja with the decision?
Nandini does not choose for her; she only suggests writing down what is not known, which makes the choice clearer.

messages.content: There are 60 passengers on a bus. Children make up 25% of the bus riders. How many adults are on the bus?

The number of children on the bus is 60 passengers * 25% = 15 passengers.
The number of adults on the bus is 60 passengers - 15 passengers = 45 passengers.
The answer is 45.

In Accra, Chidi, twenty-five, had been a junior engineer at the construction firm for a year. He'd learned to stay quiet in meetings; the old director hated being questioned.
The new director, Mr. Kofi Mensah, started differently. At his first review, he put his design on the screen and said, "Please, find the problems. I'd rather hear them now than on site."
A young woman from the drawing team said, carefully, "Sir, the beam spacing on level three may be too wide." Everyone froze.
Mr. Mensah studied it. "You're right. Thank you, Abena. That could have cost us." He shook her hand in front of everyone.
Chidi felt something loosen in his chest. At the next meeting, he pointed out a drainage issue. Kofi thanked him too.
Years later, Chidi still told junior engineers about that director.

What did Abena point out?
She said the beam spacing on level three may be too wide.
What was Chidi feeling when something loosened in his chest?
Chidi felt relieved and safe, seeing that disagreement was welcomed rather than punished.
What did Mr. Mensah do that built an honest team?
He invited people to find problems, thanked Abena publicly and shook her hand, which made others like Chidi willing to speak.
How might Abena have felt when Mr. Mensah thanked her?
Abena was probably relieved and proud, after taking a risk to question the director's design.

On Friday evening the community centre's common room buzzed with Telugu, steam from the biryani and a cricket match on the wall screen. Akash stood in the doorway with his rucksack still on. "Come in, come in!" Jahnavi, the society's secretary, pulled out a chair. "First month is always the hardest." Within ten minutes somebody had asked which town he was from, somebody else had passed him a plate, and his shoulders finally dropped for the first time since the flight. He felt safe. On the walk home he thought, I could spend every evening here and never learn how to buy a bus pass. So on Monday he said yes to his lab partner's invitation to the chemistry club, and the next month he brought her to the society's dinner.

What was showing on the common room's wall screen?
A cricket match was showing.
How did Akash feel after ten minutes in the common room?
Safe and relaxed, as his shoulders dropped for the first time since the flight.
What did Akash do that added to the comfort of his community?
He also said yes to the chemistry club and later brought his lab partner to the society dinner.
How might Jahnavi see Akash's arrival at the community centre?
As a newcomer in his hardest first month who needs a warm welcome, since Jahnavi pulled out a chair for him.

At the village school's drawing competition, the teacher pinned all the pictures on the wall. Mahima ran to see.
Her mango tree had got a star. Nandini's peacock had two stars. Mahima's tummy sank. Then she saw that the boy next to her had no stars at all, and she felt a little better.
All afternoon she kept looking. Who had more? Who had less? She counted the stars twice.
Walking home past the fields, Nandini said, "I liked your mango tree. The leaves looked real."
Mahima was quiet. She had been so busy counting stars, she hadn't really looked at anyone's drawing, not even her own.

How many stars did Nandini's peacock get?
Nandini's peacock had two stars.
How did Mahima feel when she saw the boy with no stars?
She felt a little better, because being above someone made her feel less small.
What could Mahima try at the next competition?
She could look at what she likes in each drawing, including her own, instead of only counting stars.
How does Nandini seem to see Mahima's drawing?
Nandini sees it warmly, admiring how the leaves looked real, without comparing stars.

Lokesh was holding his baby cousin at the naming ceremony in their Hyderabad flat when it happened. A thought flashed through his head, ugly and sudden, about hurting her. He didn't want it. He'd never, ever do it. But there it was. He handed the baby back so fast his aunt looked surprised. Then he locked himself in the bathroom, shaking. What kind of person thinks that? For weeks the thoughts kept coming, and he kept away from the baby, from knives, from anything. He told no one. He was too ashamed. Finally, on a walk, he told his uncle Kamal. Kamal didn't pull back. "Beta, thoughts like that are really common, and the fact that they horrify you shows they're not who you are. Let's find someone who knows how to help." The next week, Kamal sat beside him in the counsellor's waiting room.

Where did Lokesh first have the thought?
At the naming ceremony in their Hyderabad flat, while holding his baby cousin.
Why did Lokesh tell no one for weeks?
He was too ashamed and frightened the thought meant he was a bad person.
What turning point helped Lokesh?
Telling his uncle Kamal, who explained such thoughts are common and not who he is, and took him to a counsellor.
How might Lokesh's aunt have seen him handing the baby back so fast?
She may have been surprised and puzzled, not knowing about the frightening thought he was fighting.

Zainab, beta, I heard you told your Ammi your first-class result was "just luck". Sit with your Rehana Khala a minute.

When I was twenty, I topped my B.Pharm second-year exams in Hyderabad. Top of the whole college. The principal announced it at assembly. And do you know what I said to everyone? "The paper was easy. They must have marked leniently." Every single time.

Then two months later I failed one practical, because my hands shook with a pipette. And that one, I believed completely. "See, this is who I really am."

Your Nana noticed. He said, "Rehana, you've made a strange rule. When you do well, it's luck. When you do badly, it's the truth. Why is only one of them real?"

I didn't have an answer. I still think about it.

So, Zainab. Was it really luck? Or did you study every night for four months?

What did Rehana fail two months after topping the exams?
One practical.
Why did Rehana believe the failed practical completely but not her topping result?
She already doubted herself, so failure seemed to confirm who she was, while success felt like something to explain away. The rule kept her low view of herself safe.
What turning point does Rehana Khala hope Zainab will reach with her question?
She hopes Zainab will admit the four months of studying earned the result, not luck. Counting that success is the first step to breaking the double standard.
How might Zainab's Ammi have felt hearing that the result was "just luck"?
Ammi might have felt worried or a bit sad, likely having seen how hard Zainab worked. That may be why the story reached Rehana Khala.

Annie has $120. The restaurant next door sells hamburgers for $4 each. The restaurant across the street sells milkshakes for $3 each. Annie buys 8 hamburgers and 6 milkshakes. How much money, in dollars, does she have left?

Annie spends 4*8=32 dollars on hamburgers.
Annie spends 3*6=18 dollars on milkshakes.
Annie spends 32+18=50 dollars on hamburgers and milkshakes.
Annie has 120-50=70 dollars left.
The answer is 70.

Tenzin, you've read that same email four times. Let me, Kishore, tell you about my friend Bala. We were twenty-five, sharing a room in Chennai, both working at the same bank. One Sunday we went for biryani and he didn't taste a single bite. His eyes kept sliding to the window. "The branch audit, the loan files, my sister's college form, the scooter papers," he said. "All half-done." He was sleeping badly for weeks.
So one night I tore a page from my ledger and said, "Write them all. Now put a day next to each." He grumbled, but he did it. The next Sunday he ate two plates.
So, before you read that email a fifth time: how many open things are sitting in your head?

Where did Kishore and Bala go one Sunday?
They went for biryani.
What was young Kishore feeling as Bala stared at the window?
Kishore felt worried for Bala, noticing the friend was eating without tasting and sleeping badly.
What choice in the story helped Bala?
Writing all his half-done tasks on the ledger page and putting a day next to each.
What were those weeks like for Bala?
He was tired and distracted, unable to enjoy food or sleep because unfinished tasks kept pulling at him.
Interviewer ko "Mujhe is job ki zaroorat hai" kaise bolun bina begging ke?
Say: "I am very interested in this role, and I believe my skills fit it well." This sounds confident and does not beg.
Aur "Mujhe kaam ka experience nahi" ke baare mein?
Say: "I do not have work experience yet, but I learn quickly. In college I did an internship and led a small project." Use only true facts about yourself.

Salma's wedding was fixed for after Eid, in their small town near Imphal, and she was scared to ask anyone the questions in her head. Her mother only said, "Everything will be fine."
Lalremsiami, her friend from college who now worked at the district health centre, came to visit. On the roof, drying chillies, Salma finally asked, "Is it wrong if I'm not ready on the first night?"
Lalremsiami put the tray down. "No. Marriage doesn't mean you stop being allowed to say no. Consent is still yours, every time."
She told Salma the health centre had a counsellor for newly married couples, where she and her husband could ask about family planning and protection privately, without anyone gossiping.
Salma let out a long breath. "Can I bring him to talk to her?"
"That's the best idea you've had all week."

Where did Lalremsiami work?
At the district health centre.
What was Salma feeling before she asked her question?
Salma felt scared and alone with her questions, since her mother only said everything would be fine.
What did Lalremsiami do that helped, and why?
She stated clearly that consent stays Salma's even in marriage and pointed her to a private counsellor, giving facts and a safe place to ask.
How might Salma's future husband see the counselling session?
He might feel a little shy at first, but reassured that they can plan together openly.
We want to plan a day trip to a town nearby.
Decide how you will travel and when you must be back. Look up the opening hours of the places you want to see.
How do we choose what to see?
Pick two or three main places, and leave time between them. Local websites and travel reviews can suggest what is worth seeing.
What about food?
Look for busy local eateries, as crowds usually mean fresh food. Carry water and a snack in case you cannot find a place quickly.
How do we avoid getting back late?
Set a time to start the return journey, and check the last bus or train timings before you go. Leave a buffer for delays.
In the US, what is a "zebra crossing" called?

They call it a "crosswalk". British English says "zebra crossing" for a striped crossing.
Example: Always use the zebra crossing when you cross the road.

"You want to know who stayed? I'm Hemant, and honestly, the list surprised me.

When I got sick last year, three of my closest college friends vanished. Parveen, my best friend since school, didn't call for six weeks. I was hurt. I lay awake thinking, so that's what I meant to them.

Then Parveen's sister told me something. Parveen had been crying every time she picked up the phone, and then putting it down. She didn't know what to say.

So I called her. I said, 'You don't have to say anything right. Just come and eat samosas and tell me office gossip.'

She came the next day, with samosas and a lot of guilty tears. After that, every Thursday.

The other two I still hear from sometimes. That's okay. People are clumsy with illness. But I tell anyone who's sick now: tell your friends what you need. And hold on tight to the ones who show up."

How long did Parveen go without calling?
Six weeks.
How did Hemant feel when Parveen didn't call?
Hemant felt hurt and wondered at night what Hemant had really meant to those friends.
What turned things around with Parveen?
Hemant called Parveen and said exactly what would help: no perfect words, just samosas and office gossip.
What was Parveen feeling during those six weeks?
Parveen felt upset and helpless, crying each time she picked up the phone because she didn't know what to say.

'Send me the guest email before it goes out,' Ujjwal said.
'This one? It's a standard check-in reply.'
'All of them. And copy me. And use the template.'
Dolma sat back. 'Can I be honest?'
'Go on.'
'Last year you let me handle the tour group from Japan by myself. I stayed back till nine making their welcome cards. This month I've stopped caring whether the emails are good. I just want them approved.'
Ujjwal frowned. 'That's not what I want.'
'I know. But checking every line makes me feel like a machine. What if you tell me what a good guest email must do, and check a few at random on Friday?'
'And if something goes wrong?'
'Then we fix it together, and I learn.'
Ujjwal drummed the desk. 'Two weeks. Friday checks.'
The next morning Dolma wrote a welcome note for a honeymoon couple and added a hand-drawn map of the lake walk.

Which group did Dolma handle alone last year?
Dolma handled the tour group from Japan alone.
How has Ujjwal's checking made Dolma feel?
Dolma feels like a machine and has stopped caring whether the emails are good, only wanting them approved.
What arrangement did Dolma propose?
Ujjwal says what a good guest email must do and checks a few at random on Friday, leaving Dolma free to choose the method.
Why might Ujjwal hesitate?
Ujjwal may worry something will go wrong without those checks, and need reassurance that problems will be fixed together.

At the school science fair, Indu's water-filter model stood on Table 6 with a neat chart beside it. Ms. Fernandes stopped and read the chart twice.
"Indu, did an AI help write this?"
"No, Ma'am," Indu said, too fast. Her partner Vikas looked at his shoes.
Ms. Fernandes moved on to the next table. Indu's cheeks prickled. The chart had come from the AI. She and Vikas had built the filter, tested the gravel layers and timed the drips, but the words weren't hers.
Before the judges arrived, she walked over. "Ma'am, I said no, but that wasn't true. The AI wrote the chart. We did the model and the tests."
Ms. Fernandes smiled. "Thank you for coming back. Explain the tests to the judges yourself. That part is all yours."

What did Indu and Vikas build for the fair?
A water-filter model.
Why did Indu's cheeks prickle after she said no?
She felt guilty and uneasy, knowing the chart had come from the AI.
How did Indu fix her first answer, and why did it help?
She went back before the judges arrived and told the truth, which kept her teacher's trust and let her show her own tests.
How might Ms. Fernandes see Indu coming back?
She sees an honest student who corrected herself, so she thanks her and guides her to present her real work.

In the Pune school corridor, Vasudha and Rashmi got back their science tests. Both had four out of twenty.
Vasudha crumpled hers. "I'm stupid. I'm always going to be bad at science."
Rashmi looked at hers and frowned. "I didn't study the magnets chapter. That's where I lost all the marks."
"Same for me," said Vasudha. "But I'm just stupid."
"You're not. You just didn't study magnets either."
The next week, Rashmi borrowed a magnets book from the library. Vasudha didn't open her science notebook at all. "What's the point?" she said.

How many marks did both girls get?
Both had four out of twenty.
What was Vasudha feeling when she crumpled her test?
She felt hopeless and ashamed, believing she was stupid and would always be bad at science.
What could help Vasudha try again?
Seeing the low mark as caused by one chapter she didn't study, like Rashmi did, so she knows what to fix.
How does Rashmi explain her own low mark?
Rashmi explains it as not studying the magnets chapter, a temporary cause she can fix, so she borrows a book.

January. Ankita scrolled through posts from her old college group late at night: new jobs abroad, a marathon medal, a wedding in the hills. She shut the laptop feeling like she'd wasted a year. Even Jyoti, her closest friend, seemed miles ahead.
February. On a Sunday she opened the note where she'd written her goals a year earlier: "learn the data tools, stop freezing in meetings, cook more at home." She ticked two out of three. Then she muted six accounts that always made her chest tight.
April. Now she meets Jyoti and one colleague for coffee every second Saturday, and they each swap one thing they've learned. Last time Jyoti asked how she'd got so much better at presenting. Ankita laughed. "I compared myself to January me."

How many accounts did Ankita mute?
Six accounts that always made her chest tight.
How did Ankita feel after scrolling in January?
She felt discouraged, as if she had wasted a year, with even Jyoti seeming miles ahead.
Which of Ankita's steps helped most, and why?
Checking last year's goals showed real progress, two out of three, and the coffee circle turned peers into people to learn from.
How might Jyoti see the Saturday coffees?
Jyoti seems to value them too, asking Ankita for presenting tips, so the learning runs both ways.

Nitin pointed at the ceiling fan.

Thatha was worried that mixing three languages would confuse Nitin.

Amandeep shared a bedroom and a small flat with his sister Sunaina, and the exam was eleven days away. He wrote two rules on a card: IF I open my books, THEN the phone goes on the hall shelf. IF the clock passes ten, THEN it spends the night out in the passage. On day two the phone buzzed from the shelf. He stood in the doorway staring at it. Sunaina, doing her own revision, said, “Want me to hide the charger?” “No. The rule is the rule.” He went back to the desk, jaw tight. On the fifth night he noticed he had not looked at the shelf once. The card curled at the corners, still pinned above the desk.

Where does the phone go when Amandeep opens the books?
On the hall shelf.
How did Amandeep feel when the phone buzzed on day two?
Tempted and restless: he stood staring at it, but held to his rule.

Set a fixed time to check messages after studying, since knowing when he can reply lowers the pull.

Sunaina, who shares the room, sees him tempted and offers help, and may feel relieved that he keeps to the rule himself and she does not have to police him.

"Rule follower," I said, and Ria laughed. He went red and walked off to the ground alone. I felt clever for about a minute. Now, sitting here, I keep thinking about how hard I pushed. Tomorrow I might just say sorry, and not drag anyone along. Anyone can pick their own way. 😅

Seema called him a baby and a rule follower.
Why did Seema push Jomon so hard to join, and what does Seema realise?
Seema realises the push came from wanting Jomon to join so Seema would feel less silly about the choice, and that a calm no brings nerves and forces a look at that choice.

Say sorry to Jomon, accept that he can choose differently, and stop dragging others into Seema's own plans.

Embarrassed and hurt. He went red and walked off alone, though he still kept his choice.

Vinita, I have to tell someone, so it's you. I'm Payal, and three weeks ago I did something I'm not proud of.
My manager asked me to put an earlier date on a supplier contract, so it looked signed before the audit period. I said, 'Okay, sir.' That's it. Two words. I was so scared of being the new girl who makes trouble, of losing the job I waited a year for. So I changed it, printed it, filed it. I told no one.
Since then I can't sleep properly. Every time the audit team walks past, my stomach drops. It's my initials on the file, not his.
And yesterday he came to my desk again. Another contract. 'Same as last time, na?' As if it's normal now. As if I'm the person who does that.

Put an earlier date on a supplier contract.

Guilty and frightened, losing sleep and dreading the audit team, especially since her initials are on the file.

Leave the second one unchanged, write down both requests, and talk to a trusted senior, HR or the ethics channel about correcting the first.

messages.content: Why does a bell go on ringing for a while after it has been struck?

The metal keeps shaking for a while after the blow. Because the blow sets the whole metal body vibrating and the vibration only dies down slowly, the shaking air carries the sound to our ears for some time.
John has a sneezing fit for 2 minutes.  He sneezes once every 3 seconds.  How many times does he sneeze?

He was sneezing for 2*60=120 seconds
So he sneezed 120/3=40 times
The answer is 40.
Sue borrowed 15 books and 6 movies. She returned 8 books. She then returned a third of the movies to the library and checked out 9 more books. How many movies and books does Sue now have?

Sue has 15-8 = 7 books left after returning at the library.
Sue returned 6/3 = 2 movies to the library.
Sue had 6-2 = 4 movies left.
Sue had 7+9 = 16 books after checking out at the library.
Sue has 16+4 = 20 movies and books combined.
The answer is 20.

At the Lucknow school, the Class 11 mural in the corridor was finished, and everyone agreed the tiger was the best part. Neelam had painted it.

"Neelam, that tiger is wonderful," Zeenat ma'am, the art teacher, said at assembly.
"It's just copied from a book, ma'am," Neelam said quickly. "Anyone can copy."
"I've seen that book. Your tiger has different eyes."
"That was a mistake. It just looked okay by accident."

Later a Class 6 girl stopped in front of the mural. "Did you do the tiger? It looks like it's going to jump out!" Neelam shrugged. "It's nothing. Luck."

Zeenat ma'am, passing, said gently, "Neelam, you've given the tiger away three times today. What would happen if you just said thank you?"

Neelam opened her mouth, then closed it. "It would feel... weird," she admitted.

Who painted the tiger?
Neelam painted the tiger.
Why did Neelam keep saying the tiger was luck or a copy?
Neelam felt uneasy accepting praise, and explaining it away protected her belief that she isn't really good at art.
What did Zeenat ma'am suggest, and why might it help?
Simply saying thank you, which would let the praise land and begin to change Neelam's view of herself.
How does the Class 6 girl see the tiger?
The Class 6 girl is impressed and delighted, thinking it looks ready to jump out.

Every family function, Mehr, it's the same line: "Samir got 94 per cent, Samir's at IIT, Samir's getting a big package." And then my mother looks at me like I'm a purchase she regrets.
For two years I hated Samir. I mean it. I'd leave the room when he came in. Poor guy, he never did anything except exist.
Then at Diwali, after the fourth comparison in one evening, I went into the kitchen and said to Mummy, quietly, "When you compare me to Samir, it hurts. I'm working hard. I just don't do it his way." She got defensive, then went quiet, then said, "I just get scared you'll be left behind. Everyone asks me."
That's when it clicked. It wasn't really about my marks. It was about her fear.
She still slips. But now I say, "Mummy, Samir again?" and she laughs. And I actually talked to Samir at the last wedding. He's nice. He hates the comparisons too.
I'm Rekha, by the way, the cousin who isn't at IIT.

Where is Samir studying?
At IIT.
How did Rekha feel towards Samir for two years?
Resentful, even hating him and leaving the room whenever he came in.
What did Rekha do that helped?
Told Mummy quietly in the kitchen that the comparison hurts, which brought out Mummy's real fear.
How does Mummy explain the comparisons?
She is scared Rekha will be left behind and feels pressure because everyone asks her.
In the epic, he set out avenging his brother. What is avenging?

Avenging means punishing someone for harm done to another person, usually the person you love. It is a verb in its -ing form.
Example: The hero left home avenging the wrongs done to his family.
