Snow had closed the hill school for the week, and the power was out in Chinmay's house in Shimla. By lamplight, Chinmay, five, told his sister Devika, "I saw a bear in the garden yesterday!"

Devika frowned. "We were inside all day."

"I saw it. A big black bear."

"Chinmay, remember Papa told us about the bear he saw as a boy?"

Chinmay was quiet. "The bear with the honey?"

"Yes. That's Papa's bear."

"But I saw it," he said, less sure now.

Devika gave him a hug. "It's a good bear story anyway."

Where did Chinmay say he saw the bear?
In the garden yesterday.
Why did Chinmay become less sure?
He felt confused, because he remembered the bear but not that it came from Papa's story.
Which choice by Devika helped Chinmay, and why?
Reminding Chinmay kindly that it was Papa's bear, and hugging him instead of calling him a liar, helped him feel safe while he rethought it.
How might Devika feel when Chinmay insists he saw the bear?
Devika may feel amused and patient, understanding that he isn't lying.

There are six unicorns in the Enchanted Forest. Everywhere a unicorn steps, four flowers spring into bloom. The six unicorns are going to walk all the way across the forest side-by-side, a journey of 9 kilometers. If each unicorn moves 3 meters forward with each step, how many flowers bloom because of this trip?

First convert the total length of the journey from kilometers to meters: 9 kilometers * 1000 meters/kilometer = 9000 meters
Then divide this by the length of one step to find the number of steps in the journey: 9000 meters / 3 meters/step = 3000 steps
Then multiply the number of steps by the number of flowers per step to find how many flowers one unicorn creates on the journey: 3000 steps * 4 flowers/step = 12000 flowers
Then multiply the number of flowers per unicorn by the number of unicorns to find the total number of flowers created: 12000 flowers/unicorn * 6 unicorns = 72,000 flowers
The answer is 72000.

He slapped it in a high-five, both laughing. The chief guest came down to the track and held out a hand. “Well run.” Tenzin shook it, politely, looking her in the eye. Tenzin crossed the line first.

Offer a wave instead, as she did, which still shows warmth.

To beguile means to charm or attract someone, sometimes in a way that tricks them. It is a verb. In older books, it can also mean to pass time pleasantly.

Okay, Kalyani, don't laugh. Remember Thursday, when I finished the physics worksheet in fifteen minutes? I was so proud. Cricket was starting at six on the colony ground and I wanted to bat first. So I zipped through: wrote the formulas, plugged in numbers, didn't check units, didn't read question seven properly. Done. Out the door.
Today Sir gave them back. Eleven out of twenty. In question three I wrote force in kilograms. Question seven asked for time and I gave speed. The worst part? I knew all of it. Sir circled the answers and wrote, "You know this. Slow down." Now I have to redo the whole sheet by Monday, so those fifteen minutes have turned into an evening. And I got out for four runs anyway. In the village, Selvam, four, ran home from the play area under the banyan tree. "Amma! A ghost in a white sheet was near the swing!"
Kavitha put down the rice winnow. "Where?"

Last year I didn't think I had a problem. I'd open the video app 'for five minutes' after dinner and look up and it'd be midnight. I thought I just had weak willpower. Then my friend Thomas, who's into coding, showed me something. He said, 'It's built that way. Autoplay, the endless scroll, the little red dots. They test which colour makes you tap more.' Autoplay, the endless scroll and the little red dots.

The narrator realised the app was designed to keep them hooked, which felt like being played rather than simply having weak willpower.

I'm Shankar, and last term I was admin of our class chat. It gave me a little tap-and-they're-gone power over everyone, and I liked that. One night Lokesh sent a long, boring voice note about cricket stats, and three loud boys wrote, "Remove him lol." My finger was already on his name. It would have been easy, and they'd have cheered for me. But I saw that they wanted a show, and that Lokesh would see the notification alone in his room. It made my stomach tight. I didn't remove him. I posted, "Voice notes under a minute please, everyone," and made the rule for everyone. The loud boys grumbled for a day. Lokesh sent me a thumbs up. I've thought since about how nice it felt to hold that button, and how quickly I could have used it to hurt someone.

What kind of message did Lokesh send that night?
He sent a long voice note about cricket stats.
What was Shankar thinking with a finger already on Lokesh's name?
Shankar knew it would be easy and the loud boys would cheer, but saw that they wanted a show and that Lokesh would see it alone. The tight stomach shows unease.
What could Shankar do in future to use admin power fairly?
Shankar can keep making rules that apply to everybody, like the one-minute voice note limit, and never remove anyone just to please the loud ones.
How might Lokesh have felt if Shankar had removed him?
Humiliated and alone. Getting a thumbs-up instead suggests he felt relieved and respected.

In the school cafeteria in Uppsala, Oskar stood in line with his tray while Sofia whispered, 'Don't take the fish soup. The whole of 9B was sick after it on Monday.' He looked at the big steel pot. The steam suddenly seemed thick and oily. By the time he reached the counter his stomach was churning, and he felt a sour taste at the back of his mouth. He took bread and a plain boiled potato instead. But even with the potato, the churning stayed. That was odd. The potato was just a potato. He looked across and saw Sofia's friend Emil eating a full bowl of the soup and laughing. Oskar put his fork down. His stomach still felt tight all through maths, and he kept thinking about the soup, not the numbers on the board.

What did Sofia say about the fish soup?
Sofia whispered that the whole of 9B was sick after it on Monday.
Why did Oskar's stomach keep churning even while eating the plain potato?
The worry from Sofia's warning was causing the churning, not the food, so it stayed even with something he knew was safe.
What could Oskar do next time a food rumour makes him feel sick?
He could notice that the feeling started before eating anything and ask a teacher or the cafeteria staff whether anyone really got sick.
How might Emil's easy meal look to Oskar?
Seeing Emil eat a full bowl and laugh might make Oskar wonder whether the rumour was true, and feel a bit silly about his fear.
Our group project had "too many cooks". What went wrong?

The full saying is "too many cooks spoil the broth". It means that when too many people try to handle one task, the result gets worse.
Example: Five of us edited the poster at once, and too many cooks spoiled it.
Rita wrote 45 x 10^6 and 0.36 x 10^-^2 as her answers. Explain why they are not in scientific notation and correct them.

Answer: 45 x 10^6 = 4.5 x 10^7 and 0.36 x 10^-^2 = 3.6 x 10^-^3.

In scientific notation the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10. 45 is too big: 45 = 4.5 x 10^1, so 45 x 10^6 = 4.5 x 10^1 x 10^6 = 4.5 x 10^7. When a gets 10 times SMALLER, the power gets 10 times BIGGER (exponent + 1), so the value is unchanged. 0.36 is too small: 0.36 = 3.6 x 10^-^1, so 0.36 x 10^-^2 = 3.6 x 10^-^3. When a gets 10 times BIGGER, the exponent goes DOWN by 1. Check with ordinary numbers: 45,000,000 and 0.0036.

In the health class after lunch, Ramesh stayed behind when the others left. Yamini, the school counsellor who ran the session, looked up from her folder.
"Everybody in the hostel talks about vaping," he said. "I keep wondering what it's like. Is that bad?"
She smiled. "Curiosity isn't bad. It's normal, especially when everyone talks about it."
He admitted he was partly curious and partly wanted to look like he knew. "Which part is louder?" she asked. He thought. "The looking-cool part."
She gave him a leaflet from a doctors' association about how these products affect a developing brain, and asked him to read it and tell her what he found. He read it in the hostel that night, twice, and went back the next day with three questions.

Who ran the health session?
Yamini, the school counsellor, ran the session.
Why did Ramesh say the looking-cool part was louder than his curiosity?
He noticed that he was partly curious but also wanted to look like he knew, and the wish to seem cool was the stronger pull.
What did Ramesh do that helps him choose knowing?
He noticed the image motive, read the leaflet about effects on a developing brain, and went back with questions.
How might Yamini see Ramesh's question?
She treats it as ordinary curiosity, not a confession, which makes it easier for him to talk honestly.

I'm Farhan. I worked beside Vishal at the warehouse in Bhiwandi, and I only know what he did, not what he felt. For two months our salaries came late and short, with "deductions" nobody explained. Most of us grumbled over tea and did nothing. Vishal went home one evening and came back with his appointment letter, the one we had all signed without reading. He had underlined three lines: the monthly amount, the pay date, and "no deductions without written notice". He showed the supervisor, calmly. The supervisor waved him off. So on his day off Vishal went to the labour office and filed a complaint, with copies of his payslips. Some of us thought he'd be fired. He wasn't. Three weeks later our pay came on time, with a letter listing every deduction. He never bragged. He just told me, "Read your letter, Farhan. It's yours."

Which three lines had Vishal underlined?
The monthly amount, the pay date, and 'no deductions without written notice'.
What might Vishal have been feeling when the supervisor waved him off?
Vishal was probably frustrated but steady, since he went on to file a complaint rather than giving up.
Which steps made Vishal's approach effective?
Reading the signed letter, raising it calmly with the supervisor, then going to the labour office with payslip copies.
How does Farhan see Vishal's actions from the outside?
Farhan admires the calm persistence but admits knowing only what Vishal did, not what he felt, and had feared he'd be fired.

The group chat has been calling Tanuja 'Aunty'.

Wednesday, 20 September.
Indu, write it down so you don't do it again.
When I got the Gurugram job, Simran didi said, 'Live near Golf Course Road, like me. Everything's close, it's safe, you'll love it.' She's been here six years. She has a car and earns about three times what I do. I didn't think about any of that. I just took a room two lanes from hers.

Today is the 20th and I have ₹2,100.
Didi's advice was right for didi. It was never about me. Next month I'm looking near a metro station, even if it's further out.

Rent is ₹16,000.

Indu is worried and frustrated with ₹2,100 left, and a little embarrassed at copying without thinking.
What should Indu weigh when looking near a metro station next month?
Indu's own salary and daily travel, not someone else's lifestyle, comparing the total monthly cost of each option.
Why does Simran didi's advice fit her but not Indu?
Simran has six years in the city, a car and about three times the salary, so that area works for her and not for a newcomer.

Wednesday
Today I left the tap in the school ground running after I washed my tiffin. I thought, it's just one tap, and I was late for PT. Zeenat said she did the same yesterday. So did the boys from 5B.
After lunch there was no water at all. The whole tank was empty. Nobody could wash their hands. Ma'am said the tank fills only once a day, and today it ran out because taps were left open. The little kids from class one cried because they were thirsty.
I felt my face get hot. I didn't tell anyone it was me. But I kept thinking: if everyone thinks one tap doesn't matter, then every tap is left on.
Tomorrow I am going to close every tap I pass, even if it's not mine.
- Nirmala

How often does the tank fill?
The tank fills only once a day.
How did Nirmala feel when the little kids cried?
Nirmala felt ashamed and guilty, face getting hot, knowing that open tap was part of the problem.
What small step does Nirmala plan, and why could it help?
Nirmala plans to close every tap on the way, which could save water and show others that each person's choice matters.
How might the class-one children experience the empty tank?
They were thirsty and upset, suffering from a problem they didn't cause.

Age five: Binita drummed her fingers on the table during story time. Her teacher, about to ask her to sit still, noticed that Binita could repeat every word of the story afterwards, and let the drumming be.

Age ten: Nilesh snapped his fingers in a quick rhythm during singing practice, then rubbed his hands together on the cold morning bus. A classmate frowned. 'Don't snap at me!' 'I wasn't,' said Nilesh, 'it's the beat.' Later, when the class heard a surprise trip was planned, he rubbed his palms together again, this time grinning.

Age twenty-five: In the Monday meeting, Lalremsiami rubbed her hands and drummed her fingers on the table while the manager talked. A colleague could not tell whether she was thrilled or fed up. At the break the colleague asked, 'You seemed fidgety. Is something up?' Lalremsiami laughed. 'I'm impatient because I can't wait to show the new design.'

What did Nilesh say when a classmate told him not to snap at them?
He said he was not snapping at the classmate; it was the beat.
How did similar hand movements carry different meanings across the three ages?

Binita drummed her fingers while following the story, Nilesh snapped in rhythm and rubbed his hands from the cold and then in grinning excitement, and Lalremsiami rubbed her hands and drummed her fingers because she was impatient to show the new design. The teacher and the colleague did better by watching or asking than by guessing.
What was Lalremsiami feeling during the meeting?
Eager and impatient to show her new design, not annoyed, even though her colleague could not tell.
How could an adult respond to a child who drums fingers during story time?
Look at the context first; if the child is following the story, let the fidgeting be rather than scolding.

Marek, two, sits on the kitchen floor of the flat in Krakow with a set of plastic cups. Fatima, his mother, is peeling potatoes. He sets the big cup down, then the middle one, lining up the edges with his tongue poking out. The smallest cup slips twice. The third time he pinches it by the rim and places it on top, then claps and looks up at her. "Tower!" he says. She claps back, and he knocks it down to start over.

What was Fatima doing while Marek played?
She was peeling potatoes.
What does Marek's tongue poking out suggest?
It suggests he was concentrating hard and felt determined to line up the cups, and his clapping at the end shows he felt proud.
How could Fatima support Marek's finger control next?
She could offer other things to stack or pinch, like large pegs or wooden rings, and let him keep trying without doing it for him.
If you were Fatima, what would you want Marek to feel from your clapping?
I'd want him to feel his effort was noticed and shared, so he keeps trying tricky things.

Please summarize this mentor's note in two or three sentences.

Faculty mentor's note, Thursday. Sharmila, from my second-year group, came to see me before today's march for the farm workers' wage campaign. She wanted to go but was scared: her scholarship depends on attendance, and her uncle had warned her about 'getting a record'. We talked it through. I told her the march had police permission and a fixed route, and that attendance would be excused for registered participants. She decided to go for two hours with her friend Santosh, stay near the front marshals and leave before dark. She came back at six, sunburnt and shaking a little. 'I was terrified, and I've never felt so proud,' she said. I have asked the department to share the excused-attendance rule with all students.

Sharmila wanted to join a march for farm workers' pay but feared for her scholarship. Her mentor explained the march was permitted and her absence would be excused, so she went safely for two hours with a friend. She came back scared but proud, and the mentor asked for the rule to be shared with everyone.

By October, Astrid said “cringe” and “no way, that's so mid” like the others. She had spent her birthday money on the same white trainers Jana and Freja wore, and her mother had only raised an eyebrow.
On Friday the group met at the Malmö harbour. “Everyone jumps off the pier in October,” Jana said. “It's tradition.”
Astrid's stomach turned at the grey water. She laughed and said, “Obviously,” then stood at the back while two boys dared each other. A coastguard boat came by and they all scattered, laughing.
On the bus home, Freja asked, “Wait, do you actually like anything? Like, for yourself?” Astrid didn't know what to answer. Her sketchbook was at the bottom of her bag, unopened for weeks.

What did Astrid spend her birthday money on?
She spent it on the same white trainers Jana and Freja wore.
What was Astrid feeling at the harbour?
She felt afraid and doubtful; her stomach turned at the grey water, but she said "Obviously" and hid at the back.
What could Astrid do to be known, not just accepted?
She could share something real, like her sketchbook, with Freja, and try saying no to things that scare her while staying friendly.
How might Freja see Astrid after these weeks?
Freja seems to sense that Astrid copies the group but hides herself, and is curious about who she really is.

Sunday night. Dear diary, today I dropped an easy catch in the last over and we lost the match. I wanted to dig a hole in the ground. Nitin muttered, "Great job," and looked away. My eyes stung all the way to the bus. Then Diya sat next to me and said, "Everyone drops one. I dropped two last week." She shared her orange slices. My chest felt looser. If everyone was like Nitin, I would be scared to even hold a ball. Tomorrow I will go to practice and take catches. Maybe.

- Varun

What did Diya say to Varun on the bus?
She said, "Everyone drops one. I dropped two last week."
How did Varun feel after Diya spoke, and what does it change for Varun?
Varun felt relieved and less alone, as Varun's chest felt looser, and Varun now plans to go to practice and take catches.
How could Varun get that confidence back at practice?
By taking catches one at a time with kind teammates like Diya close by. 🙂
What might Diya be trying to do when she says she dropped two last week?
Show that dropping a catch is normal, so Varun does not feel alone or scared to play.

The night before the block-level science exam, Vishal couldn't eat. In the courtyard of their house in the kasba, he kept flipping pages.
"My heart is going fast," he told his sister Pooja. "What if I forget everything?"
Pooja sat beside him on the charpai. "That's your body getting ready. Let's slow it down. Breathe in for four, hold, out for four."
They did it five times. Vishal's shoulders came down a little.
"Now close the book. Tell me three things you know about plants."
He told her four.
The next morning, at the exam hall door, Pooja saw him breathe in for four, then walk in.

What exam was Vishal worried about?
The block-level science exam.
What was Vishal feeling when he said his heart was going fast?
Vishal felt anxious and scared that he would forget everything.
How can Vishal use what Pooja taught him in other exams?
He can do the slow four-count breathing before starting and remind himself of things he already knows.
How does Pooja see Vishal's racing heart?
Pooja sees it as his body getting ready, not a sign that he will fail.

Pallavi: six months today! want to do our review?
Ayesha: yes. I made a list 😅
Ayesha: goals from march: 1. get promoted to analyst II, done 2. present at a team meeting, done (twice!) 3. learn SQL properly, half done
Pallavi: that's a strong six months. what's left?
Ayesha: just SQL. I have a course for it
Pallavi: so here's my honest thought. you don't need fortnightly calls anymore. how about we move to a check-in every two months?

Pallavi: the opposite. it means you did it. regular sessions were for getting you here
Ayesha: ok. that actually feels good when you put it like that
Pallavi: and you can always message if something big comes up. that doesn't end

What was Ayesha's third goal?
Learn SQL properly, half done.
What was Ayesha feeling on asking 'is that... you getting rid of me?'
Ayesha felt a flash of worry about being abandoned, before seeing the change as a sign of success.
What else could Pallavi and Ayesha do to make the ending feel complete?
They could write down what Ayesha learnt and fix the date of the first two-monthly check-in.
How might Pallavi feel about ending regular sessions?
Pallavi likely feels proud and satisfied, seeing Ayesha reach the goals.

Read this:

Dear Abhinav,

I've been thinking about Saturday's dinner, and I owe you a better conversation than the one I gave you.

When you said the old fort was built by aliens because no one could have lifted those stones, I laughed. Then I pulled up articles on my phone and read them out to the whole table like a lawyer. You went red and stopped talking for the rest of the night. I was so busy being right that I humiliated you.

What I should have done is ask: what got you interested? What convinced you?

Here's one thing I find amazing, not to win, just to share: there are carvings near the fort showing workers using ramps and elephants to move the stones. I'd love to go look at them with you some weekend.

I'm sorry for Saturday.

Vijay

What did Abhinav say about the old fort?
That it was built by aliens because no one could have lifted those stones.
What was Vijay feeling while writing the letter?
Vijay felt regretful and ashamed about humiliating Abhinav at the dinner.
What went wrong at the dinner, and what could fix it?
Vijay read articles aloud like a lawyer and humiliated Abhinav; asking what convinced Abhinav and sharing one fact, like the carvings, could help.
How did Abhinav likely feel at the dinner?
Abhinav likely felt embarrassed and attacked, going red and silent for the rest of the night.

I'm Divyansh, and the thing I remember about my first Onam away from home is how far the sadya was from what I was used to. My roommate Mohit, who is from Thrissur, spread a banana leaf on our floor and set out a handful of dishes his mother had packed. Before we ate, he closed his eyes for a few seconds and said something under his breath. I asked what it was. "Thanks for the food, thanks for the year, thanks for my mother's hands," he said. "Nothing fancy." I'm not religious in the same way, but I kept quiet for those seconds too. It felt like the room slowed down. Later I called my own mother and thanked her, which I hadn't done in months.

Where is Mohit from?
Mohit is from Thrissur.
What did the few seconds of quiet mean to Mohit, and how did they affect Divyansh?
For Mohit it was thanks for the food, the year and his mother's hands, and for Divyansh it slowed the room and made Divyansh think of calling home to thank their own mother.
What could Divyansh do if Divyansh wanted to join in without pretending to share every belief?
Divyansh could keep quiet with Mohit and ask what it means to him, since Divyansh is free to take part in the pause without adopting the exact words.
How might Mohit have felt about Divyansh staying quiet with him?
Mohit may have felt accepted and glad that a private habit was respected, though he said only that it was nothing fancy.

Arnab, you want to ride your friend's motorbike on the highway because it feels exciting? Let your Hrithik mama tell you something.

When I was sixteen in Guwahati, I thought jumping off the old bridge into the river was the best thing ever. My friends did it, and it felt thrilling. I said it was totally safe.

At the same time, I refused to go on the ferry across the river because it felt scary and slow. I told everyone the ferry was dangerous.

My father sat me down and showed me: the bridge jump had hurt two boys that year. The ferry had carried people safely for decades.

I was quiet for a long time. The thrill had made the jump feel safe. The fear had made the ferry feel risky. The facts said the opposite.

What did Hrithik's father show him about the bridge jump?
That the bridge jump had hurt two boys that year.
Why did young Hrithik think the bridge jump was safe?
It felt thrilling and exciting, so he judged it as safe and good, while the ferry felt scary.
What turning point in the story changed how Hrithik saw risk?
His father showed him the facts about the bridge and the ferry, which were the opposite of what his feelings said.
How might Hrithik's father have felt seeing his son jump off the bridge?
His father was probably very worried and frightened, which is why he sat him down with the facts.

I'm Jomon, and in Class Nine I wrote "Study physics" on a sticky note and put it above my desk. Every evening I sat down, looked at it and felt blank. Study what? Which chapter? I'd flip pages and end up drawing in the margins. My brother Gautam, who was in college, saw the note and laughed. "That's not a plan, that's a wish." He took the note and wrote: "Read page 45. Solve question 2." I did it in twenty minutes. The next day I wrote my own: "Solve questions 3 and 4." Small, but I finally knew where to put my pencil.

What did Jomon write on the sticky note?
Jomon wrote "Study physics" on a sticky note.
How did Jomon feel looking at the note each evening?
Jomon felt blank and lost, unsure which chapter or task to start with.
What changed that helped Jomon start?
Gautam replaced the vague note with a physical action, read page 45 and solve question 2, which Jomon could finish in twenty minutes.
How might Gautam see the note at first?
Gautam sees it as a wish, not a plan, since it gives no first step; he laughs, but then helps.

Judson, Camilo, and Kenny decided to contribute money to paint their house. Judson contributed $500, Kenny contributed 20% more money than Judson, and Camilo contributed $200 more than Kenny. How much was the cost of painting the house?

If Judson paid $500, Kenny contributed 20/100*$500 = $100 more than Judson.
In total, Kenny contributed $500+$100 = $600
Kenny and Judson contributed a total of $600+$500 = $1100
If Camilo contributed $200 more than Kenny, then he contributed $600+$200 = $800
The total amount of money the three contributed for the house painting is $1100+$800 = $1900
The answer is 1900.
Meaning of "spelling"? A teacher gives 48 cards equally to 6 pupils. How many cards does each pupil get? Also, how can I remember the difference between "there" and "their"?

1. Spelling means the right order of letters in a word. Example: His spelling is improving.
2. 8 cards. Because 6 x 8 = 48.
3. "Their" shows that something belongs to people, and "there" shows a place. Think of "here" inside "there".

The power had gone out across the colony, so the only light in the flat was Alka's phone torch when she found the vape pods in Bhupen's jacket. "How long? How long has this been going on?" Her voice cracked on the last word. Bhupen's ears burned. "It's not a big deal, Mummy, everyone does—" "Don't say everyone!" She sat down hard on the bed, still holding the pods. Bhupen's first urge was to grab the door and slam it. Then Bhupen saw her hand shaking. "You're scared," Bhupen said slowly. "Yes," said Alka. "I am." Thunder rolled outside and neither spoke for a while. "I'll see a doctor with you," Bhupen said at last, "if you stop shouting." Alka nodded and wiped her eyes.

Where did Alka find the vape pods?
She found the vape pods in Bhupen's jacket.
What was Alka feeling underneath her shouting?
Fear: her voice cracked, her hand shook, and she answered "Yes, I am" when Bhupen said she was scared.
What could happen next to keep this from turning into a fight again?
Bhupen and Alka could book the doctor visit together and agree a simple plan, so the fear gets an outlet other than shouting.
How might the moment feel to Alka when Bhupen names her fear instead of arguing?
She may feel heard rather than fought, which makes it easier for her to calm down and stop shouting.

On the rattling bus back from the Sunday haat in Bhadrak, Mridul was still angry. Chandrika had turned up two hours late to their pickle stall and then snapped at him in front of a customer. Mridul pulled out a notebook and tried the trick a college counsellor had once suggested. First line: "If this happened to my friend Rabi, what would I tell him?" He wrote: she was late, that's annoying, but you also said "Typical" the moment she arrived. Then he tried her seat. He remembered she had gone with her mother to the clinic in town that morning; the bus there often broke down; she had arrived hot and rushed, and the first word she heard was his. He looked out at the paddy fields for a while. There were reasons on both sides. At the next stop he texted her: "Rough day for both of us. Talk tomorrow?"

How late was Chandrika to the pickle stall?
She turned up two hours late.
What was Mridul feeling as he looked out at the paddy fields?
His anger was softening into a more mixed, thoughtful feeling as he saw that both of them had reasons for the bad day.
Which two steps helped Mridul, and why?
Imagining it happening to his friend Rabi, then sitting in Chandrika's seat; each step showed the situation behind her lateness and his own sharp word, not just her character.
What was the morning probably like for Chandrika?
She had gone with her mother to the clinic in town, travelled on an unreliable bus, and arrived hot and rushed only to hear Mridul say "Typical."
Write a haiku about snow on a mountain peak.

White snow on the peak
The wind carries it away
Silence fills the air

In the KG room, a block flew across the carpet and hit the window. Reena, the teacher, turned. Divyansh saw her nostrils flare and her lips press flat, and he froze with a block in his hand. Reena breathed out slowly. “I'm feeling cross because blocks can break glass,” she said in a low voice. “I'm going to take three slow breaths.” She did, in and out, while the children watched. Divyansh put his block down gently and breathed with her.

What did the block hit?
The window.
What was Divyansh feeling when he froze with a block in his hand?
He likely felt nervous and sensed tension, because he saw Reena's nostrils flare and knew she was angry. He might also have worried he would be blamed, though he had not thrown it.
What did Reena model for the class?
She named her feeling calmly, said why she was cross, and slowed down with three breaths instead of shouting.
How might the child who threw the block see Reena's calm response?
That child might feel less frightened and more able to own up, because the teacher showed anger without exploding.
Does shorthand mean a short form? Or is it a skill?

Both are right. Shorthand is a quick way of writing using symbols and short forms, used to write as fast as people speak. It is a noun. It can also mean any short way of saying something.
Example: The secretary took notes in shorthand during the meeting.

Grandfather says "make hay while the sun shines". We have no hay at home!

It is a proverb meaning that you should use a good opportunity while it lasts. It comes from farming, because hay is cut and dried in dry, sunny weather.
Example: The shops are empty today, so let's make hay while the sun shines and finish our shopping.

Monday: Pallavi scrolled to Uday's name for the fourth time that evening. They'd been close in college; now he lived twenty minutes away in the same city, and she hadn't texted in a year. She typed a long apology and deleted it.
Wednesday: she sent just this: 'Hey, I'm in Hyderabad now. Would you want to get idli on Sunday? Totally fine if not.' Then she put the phone in a drawer and cleaned the whole kitchen.
When she opened the drawer an hour later: 'PALLAVI. Yes. Ramu's cafe, 9 am? I've missed you 😊'
Sunday: they ate too much and laughed about their old professor's terrible jokes. Walking home, Pallavi noticed she was humming. It hadn't been hard at all. Maybe the next message wouldn't be either.

What did Pallavi invite Uday to do on Sunday?
She asked if he would want to get idli on Sunday.
Why did Pallavi put her phone in a drawer after sending the message?
She was nervous about the reply and afraid of being turned down, so she hid the phone and kept busy cleaning.
What made Pallavi's message a good small step?
It was short, specific and easy to answer, and 'Totally fine if not' kept the stakes low instead of turning it into a long apology.
How does Uday seem to feel on getting Pallavi's message?
He sounds delighted and relieved, replying with her name in capitals and saying he has missed her 😊
Is "inteligence" correct?

No. It is "intelligence", with a double l.
Example: She showed great intelligence in solving the puzzle.

I'm Aditi. During art period my friend Ishan nudged me and whispered, "Look at Yash's drawing, it's a potato. Say something, everyone's going to." A few girls were already giggling. I felt torn: I wanted Ishan to like me, but I also knew Yash was trying hard. My mouth stayed shut for a moment. Then I said, quiet but clear, "I don't want to," and took my pencil box to the front table. Ishan rolled his eyes. That evening he texted me: "sorry, that was mean of me". I had not expected that. Maybe saying no can make a friend think.

What did Ishan say Yash's drawing looked like?
He said it was a potato.
Why did Aditi feel torn when Ishan nudged?
Aditi wanted Ishan to like Aditi but also knew Yash was trying hard, so Aditi was pulled between fitting in and doing right.
What could Aditi say if a friend pushes again to mock someone?
Aditi can repeat "I don't want to" and walk away, as before, because real friends respect that.
How might Ishan see Aditi's refusal afterwards?
Ishan first rolled his eyes, but that evening he admitted it was mean, so the refusal seems to have made him think.
Rahul saves ₹8 every week. Write how much he has saved after each of the first 10 weeks. What are these numbers called?

Answer: ₹8, ₹16, ₹24, ₹32, ₹40, ₹48, ₹56, ₹64, ₹72, ₹80. They are the MULTIPLES of 8.

Each week adds another 8, so we are counting in 8s: these are the numbers in the 8 times table, 1 x 8, 2 x 8, 3 x 8 ... Multiples never stop: week 100 gives 800. Notice that 8 itself is the first multiple of 8, and every multiple of 8 is at least 8 (except 0).

On Friday evening in Kodi, near the sea, Shreya dropped her school bag on the verandah. The temple fair had come to the village. "Homework after," she called to her mother, and ran with her friend Ritu to see the giant wheel and the bangle stalls. She meant it. There was the whole evening. They came back at eight, sticky with sugar cane juice. Shreya opened her Kannada notebook: one page of writing and ten maths sums. At half past eight, the power went off. Her mother lit one lamp, and the light was too weak for her to see the sums clearly. She finished at ten, eyes aching, half the sums crossed out. On Monday, her teacher circled four mistakes. The next Friday, the fair was still there. Shreya sat on the verandah steps and did the sums first, while Ritu waited, grumbling, for twenty minutes.

Use three sentences to tell me what this extract means.

On a Friday evening Shreya goes to the village fair with her friend Ritu, planning to do her homework later. When the power goes off, she finishes her sums by a weak lamp at ten, and her teacher finds four mistakes on Monday. The next Friday she does the sums first, even though Ritu waits and grumbles.

"Dilnaz, get your charger. We're going to Khala's tonight." "Because of one SMS?" Dilnaz didn't move from the sofa. "Zeenat Aapa, the road is dry." "The dam is releasing water after midnight. The message says low-lying areas. That's us." "You said the same last year and nothing happened." "And we lost nothing." Zeenat pulled the go-bag down from the top of the cupboard: medicines, torch, copies of the papers, two water bottles. "Kit's ready. It takes us fifteen minutes." "The neighbours will laugh." "Let them. If the water doesn't come, you can make fun of me all week. I'll even buy the samosas." Dilnaz groaned but reached for her shoes. "Double samosas." "Deal. Lock the balcony door."

What was in the go-bag?
Medicines, a torch, copies of the papers and two water bottles.
What was Dilnaz worried about, apart from the water?
That the neighbours would laugh at them for leaving because of one SMS 😅
Which earlier choice made leaving easy for Zeenat?
Keeping the go-bag packed in the cupboard, so following the warning took fifteen minutes instead of a long scramble.
What would change if Zeenat waited until the road was wet before leaving?
By then the water might already be rising around the house, and the calm trip to Khala's could become a rushed and risky one.

The water level in a tank fell by 3/8 m in the morning and rose by 5/6 m in the evening. Find the total change. Then add -5/12 and -7/18.

Now you try: -7/10 + 4/15.
The answer is -13/30.

Thursday night. Project marks are out. Simran got 9 out of 10 for a design almost the same as mine, and I got 6. Same materials, same report length, and mine had the extra test. The professor wrote "excellent teamwork" on hers, and Simran drinks tea in the professor's cabin every Friday. I was so angry I could not eat. Then I made myself list facts: the rubric, both marks, the date I submitted. I am not going to say anything against Simran, because the marking was not her doing. Tomorrow I will email the course coordinator and ask for a recheck against the rubric. And I am still finishing my next report properly, because sulking would only cost me. 😔 Maria

How many marks did Simran get?
Simran got 9 out of 10.
How did Maria feel about the marks, and why did Maria decide not to say anything against Simran?
Maria was so angry about the marks that eating was impossible, but saw that the marking was not Simran's doing, so the complaint is aimed at the rubric and the process.
What did Maria plan to do, and why might it work?
She plans to email the course coordinator for a recheck against the rubric, which rests on facts like the marks and submission date rather than on anger. 🙂
How might Simran feel if Maria's complaint reached her?
Simran might feel embarrassed or worried about being blamed, which is why Maria keeps the focus on the process.

Dear Yusuf,

It's been three weeks since Abbu. I'm writing because every time we talk, we end up hurting each other.

When you went back to the shop two days after the funeral, I thought you didn't care. I said so, and I'm sorry. Last night Ammi told me you sit in his chair at the counter after closing, in the dark. I didn't know.

Maybe you think I'm dramatic. I cry at the dhaba where he used to take us, at the smell of his attar, at nothing. I think we're both grieving; we just do it differently.

So, a question, not an accusation: how are you managing, really?

And a memory, because I keep thinking of it: Abbu teaching us to count change with his old brass coins, you always cheating.

The papers about the shop can wait. Let's not decide anything until the first wave of this has passed.

Your sister,
Hafsa

How long after the funeral did Yusuf go back to the shop?
He went back to the shop two days after the funeral.
What did Hafsa feel when she learned Yusuf sits in Abbu's chair after closing?
Hafsa felt sorry and softened, realising his quiet was his way of grieving and that she had misjudged him.
What makes Hafsa's letter a good step between the siblings?
She apologises, asks how he is coping, shares a memory, and delays the shop papers until the first wave of grief has passed.
How might Yusuf have felt when Hafsa said he didn't care?
Yusuf probably felt hurt and misunderstood, since he was grieving privately in the dark shop.
Is it "dependant" or "dependent" in British English?

In British English, "dependant" is the noun for a person who depends on you, while "dependent" is the adjective. American English uses "dependent" for both.
Examples: He has two dependants. The trip is dependent on the weather.
Which exact week did the first koel call in my city last year?
I don't know, because I can't see a single city's bird record. A local bird-watching group might have kept notes.

On Saturday morning, Renata had $10 to spend. She first went and made a $4 donation in exchange for a ticket to the local charity draw. When the draw was done, she was declared the winner of the 5th prize of $90. Excited, she quickly dashed to play slots at one of the casinos in Atlantic City. Unfortunately, she lost $50 at the first slot machine, $10 at the second and $5 at the last one.  Dejected, she decided to take a long walk. She soon grew thirsty and entered the first gas station she saw. She picked a $1 bottle of water and while paying for it, she bought a $1 lottery ticket. To her utter delight, she won an instant prize of $65. How much money did Renata end up having?

After the charity ticket purchase on Saturday morning, Renata remained with 10 - 4 = 6 dollars.
Adding the prize money give her 6+90 = 96 dollars
At the casino, she lost 50 + 10 + 5 = 65 dollars
Thus far, Renata remained with 96 - 65 = 31 dollars
The amount she spent on the bottle of water and lottery ticket is 1 + 1 = 2 dollars
This means that she remained with 31- 2 = 29 dollars
Since she won 65 dollars, Renata's ended up having 29 + 65 = 94 dollars.
The answer is 94.

During hide-and-seek, Vishal, two, stood in the middle of the room and covered his eyes with both hands. "Can't see me!" he giggled. His feet, his flower-print shirt, everything was in plain view.

His eyes.

Monday. Baby Arohi had her bottle. Mridul, two and a half, pointed and cried, "Me bottle!" He wet his shorts twice that day.

Wednesday. Papa gave Mridul a little water in a spare bottle without teasing. Mridul drank a few sips, curled in Papa's lap like a baby, then ran off.

Two weeks later. Mridul asked for the bottle once, forgot it, and went back to his cup.

What did Mridul point at and cry for on Monday?
Mridul cried, "Me bottle!" for a bottle like the baby's.
Why did Mridul want a bottle and curl up like a baby?
Mridul felt insecure and jealous, wanting to be held and cared for like the new baby.
What did Papa do that helped the phase pass?
Papa met the request gently and briefly, without teasing, so Mridul felt secure and soon lost interest.
How might Papa feel about the wet shorts on Monday?
Papa might feel tired or worried, but he chose patience instead of mockery.

Akash, sit with your Jasleen Bua. Your heart is racing before the board exam, and you think it means something terrible will happen. At your age I thought the same. The night before my Class 10 exams my chest thumped and I was sure I'd fail. My Biji didn't say "relax". She said, "The drum is telling you to slow down, not that the sky is falling." We walked twice round the gurdwara compound, I told her every worry out loud, and then I slept. Later, in college, when the worry stopped me sleeping for weeks, Biji was the one who said, "Now we see a doctor who knows about minds." That helped too. So, puttar, walk with me, tell me the worries, and then bed.

What did Biji say the drum was telling young Jasleen?
To slow down, not that the sky is falling.
How does Akash seem to feel about his racing heart before the exam?
He seems frightened, thinking the racing heart means something terrible will happen in the exam.
What steps did Biji use the night before Jasleen's exams?
They walked twice round the compound, Jasleen said every worry aloud, and then slept.
How might Biji have seen young Jasleen's thumping chest that night?
Biji seems to have seen it as a signal to slow down, not a disaster, and trusted that walking and talking would settle the worry.

In their flat in Lagos, Chidi's older brother Daniel was in his final engineering year, and his worry filled every room. He checked the stove before bed, then again. He asked Chidi each morning whether the back door was locked. When the power flickered, he unplugged everything.
Chidi, nineteen and in first year, used to tease him. But this term Chidi noticed a change. Walking to lectures, Chidi's hand kept going to the pocket, checking for keys. At night Chidi got up to look at the stove, even after Daniel had checked.
One Sunday, Chidi said it straight out. "Daniel, I think your worry is rubbing off on me. I check things now. I never used to."
Daniel sat down heavily. "I didn't want that."
"I know."
They agreed on a simple plan: one check of the flat at ten, taking turns, written on a card by the door. Daniel also said he'd talk to someone at the student centre about his stress. The card went up that night.

Where did Daniel and Chidi write their checking plan?
They wrote it on a card by the door.
How has Chidi been affected by Daniel's worry?
Chidi feels tense and has picked up Daniel's habits, checking keys and the stove even when it has already been done.
Why is the plan they agreed on a good one?
One check at ten, taking turns and written down, gives a clear routine instead of endless checking, and Daniel talking to the student centre addresses his stress.
How does Daniel feel when Chidi tells him?
Daniel feels upset and sorry, sitting down heavily and saying he didn't want his worry to spread.

At the community centre's evening computer lab, Maria was the oldest student at twenty-two. She had dropped out of college and now worked at a shop, but she wanted to learn data analysis. Siddharth, the volunteer instructor, noticed she took notes on everything but never asked questions. One day he asked her why. "I don't want to look stupid," she said. He smiled. "Asking is how you learn." He suggested she set small weekly goals: one new function, one practice dataset. He also showed her how to explain back what she'd learned. Maria started asking questions, and she built a small dashboard tracking the shop's sales. Her manager asked her to present it. She was nervous, but she did.

What did Maria build using what she learned?
She built a small dashboard tracking the shop's sales.
Why did Maria never ask questions at first?
She was afraid of looking stupid, perhaps feeling self-conscious as the oldest student.
What learning strategies did Siddharth suggest?
He suggested setting small weekly goals and explaining back what she'd learned, which helped her build skills steadily.
How might Maria's manager see her new skills?
The manager probably sees her as more capable and valuable, asking her to present her work.

The message had reached every phone in the village by the time Uma got off the evening bus from Hassan. 'New poisonous snake species found in paddy fields! 50 deaths this month!' Her uncle, Bhupen Mama, met her at the gate, phone shaking in his hand. 'Don't go to the field tomorrow.' Uma sat down on the step. 'Show me, Mama.' She traced the photo back through three forwards to a post about a different country, years ago. Then she called her friend at the district hospital, who said there had been no such rise in cases. 'Mama, fifty deaths here would be in every paper,' she said. 'This is an old message from far away.' Bhupen Mama frowned. 'But everyone sent it.' 'That's why it feels true,' Uma said. 'Let's not send it on.' He put the phone in his pocket, still frowning, but calmer.

How many deaths did the message claim?
50 deaths this month.
What was Bhupen Mama feeling when he met Uma at the gate?
Bhupen Mama felt frightened and anxious, his phone shaking in his hand.
How did Uma handle her uncle's worry well?
She sat with him, traced the photo to its source, checked with a friend at the district hospital, and explained gently why the message only felt true.
What is it like for Bhupen Mama when Uma questions a message everyone sent?
It is uncomfortable for him at first, since everyone sending it made it feel true, but her calm explanation leaves him calmer.

messages.content: In seven years, Talia will be 20 years old.  Talia's mom is currently three times as old as Talia is today.  In three years, Talia's father will be the same age as Talia's mom is today.  Currently, how many years old is Talia's father?

In seven years, Talia will be 20 years old, and therefore Talia is currently 20-7=13 years old.
Talia's mom is currently three times as old as Talia is today, or 3*13=39 years old.
If in three years, Talia's father will be the same age as Talia's mom is today, then Talia's father is currently 39-3=36 years old.
The answer is 36.

At the community hall behind the masjid, Irfan had been stacking plastic chairs since four. Chand Raat meant a hundred and fifty people, and every teenager in the lane had been drafted.

His phone lit up. Lalit: "Movie at 7, everyone's going. Come na."

Irfan groaned. "Abbu, can I go at six?"

"Who will serve the sherbet?" said Abbu, without looking up from the rice pots.

Irfan carried the jugs, sulking, until old Khala Jaan, who had known him since he was born, patted his cheek and said, "You pour exactly like your Dada did." He didn't know what to do with that. He poured more carefully.

At seven, Lalit's friends posted photos from the cinema. Irfan was ladling sherbet into a line of kids' glasses.

Walking home under the fairy lights, he told Abbu, "Next year I'll do the chairs and the sherbet. But I want Eid evening with my friends."

Abbu nodded. "Deal."

How many people come on Chand Raat?
Chand Raat meant a hundred and fifty people.
What did Irfan feel when Khala Jaan said he pours like his Dada?
Irfan felt unexpectedly moved and a little unsure, a flash of belonging that made him pour more carefully.
What deal did Irfan make, and why is it fair?
He'll do the chairs and sherbet next year but keep Eid evening for friends; the duty is shared and personal time is asked for openly.
How might Abbu see Irfan's request on the walk home?
Abbu accepts it easily, since Irfan helped all evening and asked clearly for next year.

Arnab had been elected sports secretary at his Kolkata college in July. By October, the football ground finally had working floodlights, and the girls' team had its own practice slot. People stopped him in corridors to say thank you. He liked that more than he admitted.
Then Sangeeta, the girls' captain, asked for a change in the match schedule.
"No," Arnab said, before she finished.
"You didn't even hear why."
"I decide the schedule. That's the job."
She looked at him for a long moment. "Last month you said you wanted everyone to have a voice."
Arnab felt a flash of irritation, then something colder: she was right. He took a breath. "Okay. Tell me why."

What did the football ground get by October?
It finally had working floodlights.
What did Arnab feel when Sangeeta reminded him of his words?
He felt irritated at first, then uncomfortable as he realised she was right and his wish for respect was sliding into control.
What did Arnab do right at the end, and what should he keep doing?
He took a breath and asked Sangeeta to explain; he should keep listening before deciding, so his influence serves the group.
How might Sangeeta feel when Arnab says 'I decide the schedule'?
She likely feels dismissed and frustrated, since he didn't even hear her reason.

So, for the podcast: I'm Irawati, class eleven, and my story is about a sentence I never finished. We were on Kavitha's terrace, eating roasted corn, and I was telling her about my brother moving to the hostel in Kota. I said, "And the worst part is that Amma keeps setting four plates and then—" and I just stopped. Mid-word. I stared at the water tank. Kavitha told me afterwards she had no idea what the silence meant. Was I angry with her for asking? Embarrassed? About to cry? Just thinking? Honestly, a bit of all of it. What she did was put her corn down and say, "You don't have to finish that. I'm around, whenever." Then she talked about the kite stuck on the wire. Two days later, on the school bus, I finished the sentence, and she just listened.

What were they eating on Kavitha's terrace?
They were eating roasted corn.
What might Irawati have been feeling when the sentence stopped?
Most likely a wave of sadness about the brother's empty place at the table, but by Irawati's own account it was also partly embarrassment and just thinking, so the silence was mixed.
What did Kavitha do well?
Kavitha did not guess or push: putting the corn down, saying Irawati didn't have to finish, and switching to the kite gave space while leaving the door open. 🤍
How did the silence look from Kavitha's side?
Kavitha could not tell whether it meant anger at her, embarrassment, tears or thought, so she chose a reply that would work for any of them.
Pavement or sidewalk: which is the walkway beside a road?

British English calls it the "pavement" and American English calls it the "sidewalk". In American English, "pavement" can mean the road surface itself.
Example: Please walk on the pavement, not on the road.
Station pe kisi se poochna hai ki Pune jaane wali train kaun se platform pe aayegi. English mein?
You can ask: "Excuse me, which platform will the train to Pune arrive at?" Or a shorter way: "Excuse me, where can I find the Pune train?"
Greta worked 40 hours and was paid $12 per hour. Her friend Lisa earned $15 per hour at her job. How many hours would Lisa have to work to equal Greta's earnings for 40 hours?

For the 40 hours worked, Greta earned a total of 40 * 12 = $480.
To find how many hours Lisa has to work to earn $480, we divide 480 / 15 = 32
The answer is 32.

Class teacher's note, Class 5A, 12 September.

Hrithik came second in the maths test today, one mark behind Neel. He did not cry, but he pressed his lips together so hard they went white, and he tore a corner off the paper. At break he told me, "I must always be first. And boys must never cry. I broke both rules today."

He says "I must" and "I should" often, and looks tense even when he does well.

I told him that second is a good result, and that anyone, boy or girl, is allowed to cry. I asked him to try changing "must" to "would like to" for one week. He looked doubtful.

I will speak gently to his parents on Friday about easing the pressure together.

Darshan

How many marks behind Neel was Hrithik?
Hrithik was one mark behind Neel.
Why does coming second make Hrithik feel he broke the rules?
Hrithik feels ashamed and tense, because his rigid rules say he must always be first and never cry.
What small change did Darshan suggest, and why?
Changing "must" to "would like to" for a week, which softens the rules so a slip doesn't pile up shame.
How might Neel feel about coming first?
Neel is probably pleased, with no idea that Hrithik felt a rule had been broken.

On the fridge door of the Bengaluru flat hung a laminated sheet that Nazia had made after one scare too many: the two nearest hospitals and their casualty numbers, the phone numbers of her brother and uncle, and a note that a blue folder on the shelf below held every scan and prescription. Downstairs, Gopika, the neighbour, had a spare key and Nazia's number saved. On a Tuesday at half past ten, with Nazia in a meeting, her father slipped in the bathroom. He pressed the pendant. Gopika was at the door in four minutes, rang the number from the sheet, and Nazia's brother arrived and picked up the folder. By noon her father had been seen, and by evening he was home with a sore hip and a story. Nazia left the meeting at once, and did not have to search for a single number.

Who had a spare key to the flat?
Gopika, the neighbour, had a spare key.
What does Nazia's leaving the meeting at once suggest she felt?
It suggests alarm and concern for her father, though the prepared sheet let her stay steady.
What else could the family add to the plan?
They could keep a spare copy of the folder elsewhere and practise the steps every few months, so the plan stays current.
How might Gopika feel about being part of the plan?
Gopika may feel trusted and useful, and glad she could help within minutes.

When the harvest festival drums began in the village near Nashik, Madhuri, five, dropped her spoon and started to spin, her scarf flying out, arms up. She clapped in circles and stamped her feet, laughing out loud. Her aunt Gurpreet, carrying a tray of sweets, put it down and joined, clapping the beat. Madhuri giggled harder and pulled her aunt's hand. Later, her legs shaky and her breathing quick, she flopped onto the mat, still smiling, and said, "More!"

What did Madhuri drop when the drums began?
She dropped her spoon.
What was Madhuri feeling as she spun and clapped?
She was full of joy at the music, since she laughed out loud and pulled her aunt's hand. Her movement may also have been a way to release her excess energy.
Why was it helpful that Gurpreet put down her tray and danced?
Joining in showed Madhuri that her delight was welcome and made them closer, more than praising or correcting would have done.
How might Gurpreet feel when Madhuri pulls her hand to dance?
She may feel warm and happy, and glad she stopped what she was doing to join her niece. 😊

Sunday. Afreen noticed her neighbour Yusuf's elderly father had been leaving the gas on low at night again. She told herself it wasn't her business; Yusuf worked late shifts, and she didn't want to seem nosy.

Tuesday. The smell was stronger on the stairs. Afreen stood outside their door, then asked herself: if I had left that knob on, what would I want a neighbour to do? She realised walking past was also a decision.

Wednesday. She knocked when Yusuf got home and told him gently what she'd noticed. He looked shocked, then thanked her. That evening he called the building's gas technician, who fitted a safety valve, and Yusuf asked their family doctor about his father's forgetfulness.

What was Yusuf's elderly father leaving on at night?
He had been leaving the gas on low at night.
Why did Afreen stay quiet on Sunday?
She felt awkward and didn't want to seem nosy, so staying silent felt safer than stepping in.
Which question helped Afreen decide to act?
She asked what she would want a neighbour to do if she had left the knob on, which made her see that walking past was also a choice.
How might Yusuf feel after Afreen told him?
Yusuf was shocked but grateful, and probably relieved the danger was caught before anyone was hurt.

The hostel had to be empty by six, the rain was coming sideways, and Karthik's books were still in cardboard boxes going soft at the corners. Yogesh had come to help him move to his uncle's flat after he'd dropped out of the semester.

When Yogesh taped a box wrong, Karthik exploded. "You always do this! You think you're so helpful. You just like feeling better than me."

The words hit like a slap. Yogesh wanted to throw the tape down and leave him to it. Instead he took a breath, said, "Okay," and carried the box to the autorickshaw.

They finished at 5:50. In the auto Karthik stared out at the rain.

Two weeks later, over tea, Yogesh said quietly, "That day really hurt." Karthik looked down. "I know. I was angry at everything. Not you. Sorry."

By what time did the hostel have to be empty?
The hostel had to be empty by six.
What was Yogesh feeling when Karthik exploded, and what did he want to do?
Yogesh felt hurt, as if slapped, and wanted to throw the tape down and leave.
Which choice worked, and why?
Staying steady that day and raising the hurt two weeks later when calm worked, because Karthik could hear it and apologise.
How might Karthik have seen that moving day?
Karthik was likely overwhelmed and ashamed about dropping out, so his anger at everything spilled onto the friend helping him.

At first he only rang the small bell. Then he began to mouth the words. One night the priest was late, and paati's voice cracked.

On the temple steps.

For most of the term, Vaibhav, ten, had been different in class. He snapped at his bench partner over a borrowed eraser. He put his head on the desk after lunch and said his head hurt, then his stomach. At games he sat on the steps instead of playing football, which he used to love. That's not like you. Is something heavy?" He shrugged. "Everything's just boring." Sangeeta called his parents that afternoon and asked the school counsellor to meet the family that week.

What sport did Vaibhav use to love?
He used to love football.
What might Vaibhav's snapping and tears suggest about how he was feeling?
They suggest he was feeling low and sad inside, even though he could only say that everything was boring.
Why was Sangeeta Ma'am's response wise?

How might Vaibhav's bench partner see him lately?

Thirty students run in a charity race to raise money for the hurricane victims. Ten of the students raised $20 each. The rest of the students raised $30 each. How much did the students raise in all?

Ten students raised a total of $20 x 10 = $200.
There are 30 - 10 = 20 students who raised $30 each.
Twenty students raised a total of $30 x 20 = $600.
Therefore, the students raised a total of $200 + $600 = $800.
The answer is 800.

On the morning of the chemistry exam, the hall was changed at the last minute. The corridor was packed and noisy, students shouting about which room to go to.
Vishal leaned against the wall, headphones in, humming a slow song under his breath. His shoulders dropped a little.
Darshan came up. "How are you so calm?"
"I'm not. Humming helps me stop shaking."
In the new hall, Vishal hummed silently in his head while waiting for the paper.
After the exam, he found the chemistry teacher. "Sir, I get really anxious before every test. The humming helps, but can I talk to you about it sometime?"
Sir nodded. "Of course. Tomorrow at lunch?"

What was changed at the last minute on the exam morning?
The hall.
What was Vishal feeling before the exam?
Vishal felt anxious and shaky, and used humming to calm down.

Vishal asked the chemistry teacher for a talk about test anxiety.
How did Darshan see Vishal's humming?
Darshan thought Vishal looked calm, not knowing the humming was a way to handle nerves.

Wednesday: She almost didn't bother. Then she texted: "No pressure to reply. I'm around this week if you want company, or just a walk. No questions." She didn't text again.
Saturday: Her phone buzzed at nine. "Sorry about Monday. Can we get chai? I'm not great." Damini replied, "Of course. Ten minutes." At the stall he talked about his results for an hour. She just listened. At the end he said, "Thanks for not giving up."

What did Damini bring to Vaibhav's door?
A plate of poha.
How did Damini feel when Vaibhav shut the door?
She felt rejected and embarrassed, her face burning in the corridor.
What did Damini do that kept the door open?
She sent one low-pressure message offering company without questions and then respected his pace.

He likely felt sorry about Monday and ready to lean on someone, since he said he was not great.

Gina is considered a bad tipper because she tipped 5%. If good tippers tip at least 20%, how many more cents than normal would Gina have to tip on a bill of $26 to be considered a good tipper?

First convert the bill amount to cents: $26 * 100 cents/dollar = 2600 cents
Then multiply that amount by 5% to find the amount Gina normally tips: 2600 cents * 5% = 130 cents
Then multiply the bill amount by 20% to find the amount of a good tip: 2600 cents * 20% = 520 cents
Then subtract the good tip amount from the bad tip amount to find how much more Gina needs to tip: 520 cents - 130 cents = 390 cents
The answer is 390.

Couples counsellor's note, individual session.

Imran asked to see me alone. For five months he has been lying to his wife, Farida, about Saturday mornings. He tells her he plays cricket. In fact he has been meeting his father, from whom Farida's family asked him to cut ties after a bitter property dispute. He deletes the call logs.

He said, "I'm protecting her from stress." Then, quietly, "But I can't look at her properly anymore. I feel like a thief in my own home."

I asked who the secret was really protecting. He sat with that for a long time.

We discussed that concealment often slowly deadens a bond, and that honesty, even when it costs something, gives the partner a real choice. We planned how he might tell Farida: plainly, without blaming her family, and ready to hear her anger.

He plans to tell her on Friday. He'll come back next week.

- Karthik

He tells her he plays cricket.

Imran feels guilty and distant, like a thief in his own home, unable to look at Farida properly.
What plan did Karthik and Imran make?
They planned for Imran to tell Farida plainly on Friday, without blaming her family, and to be ready to hear her anger.
How might Farida feel when Imran tells her?

Rick has 130 cards. He decided to only keep 15 cards and so he gave Miguel some of the cards. Then, he saw 8 friends and decided to give them 12 cards each, and the remaining cards were given equally to his 2 sisters. If each of Rick's sisters got 3 cards, how many cards did Rick give to Miguel?

After keeping 15 cards, Rick had 130 cards - 15 cards = 115 cards left.
The total number of cards given by Rick to his 8 friends was 8 friends x 12 cards/friend = 96 cards.
There were 2 sisters x 3 cards/sister = 6 cards given to Rick's sisters.
So, there were 96 cards + 6 cards = 102 cards left after Rick gave Miguel some cards.
Therefore, 115 cards - 102 cards = 13 cards were given to Miguel.
The answer is 13.

messages.content: Jordan picked 54 mangoes from his tree. One-third of the mangoes were ripe while the other two-thirds were not yet ripe. Jordan kept 16 unripe mangoes and gave the remainder to his sister who pickled them in glass jars. If it takes 4 mangoes to fill a jar, how many jars of pickled mangoes can Jordan's sister make?

Jordan picked 54/3 = 18 ripe mangoes.
He picked 54 - 18 = 36 unripe mangoes.
Jordan gave 36 - 16 = 20 unripe mangoes to his sister.
Jordan's sister can make 20/4 = 5 jars of pickled mangoes.
The answer is 5.
A room is 5 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high. The four walls and the ceiling are to be painted (not the floor). Paint costs ₹25 per m^2. Find the area and the cost. (Ignore doors and windows.)

Answer: Area = 74 m^2. Cost = 74 x ₹25 = ₹1850.

Four walls: two are 5 m x 3 m = 15 m^2 and two are 4 m x 3 m = 12 m^2. Walls: 2 x 15 + 2 x 12 = 30 + 24 = 54 m^2. Ceiling: 5 x 4 = 20 m^2. Total: 54 + 20 = 74 m^2. Cost: 74 x 25 = 1850 rupees. This is the surface area of the cuboid with ONE face missing (the floor): 2 x (20 + 12 + 15) - 20 = 94 - 20 = 74. Read the question carefully to see which faces are needed - an open box has no lid, a room is painted without the floor.

Logan's father receives 50 cartons delivery for his milk business, each carton having 20 jars of milk. On a particular week, he received 20 cartons less when the delivery was done, and during offloading, he realized 3 jars in 5 cartons each was damaged, and one carton was totally damaged. How many jars of milk were good for sale that week?

When 20 cartons failed to be delivered, the number of cartons reduced to 50-20 = 30 cartons.
The total number of jars in all the cartons is 30*20 = 600
The total number of jars destroyed in the 5 cartons is 3*5 = 15 jars.
If one carton was also destroyed, the total number of destroyed jars is 20+15 = 35 jars.
The number of jars good for sale is 600-35 = 565 jars.
The answer is 565.

Ten minutes before the client call, Sumit was pasting the last numbers into the slides when Lalremsiami leaned over his desk. "Run the spell-check and read the numbers aloud once. Last time there was a typo in the total."
Sumit felt the bristle rise up his back. He didn't need a checklist; he'd been doing slides for three years. The office was loud with someone's birthday song, and he wanted to snap, "I know."
Instead he took a breath and asked himself the question he'd been practising: is she wrong, or do I just hate being told?
She wasn't wrong. Last month's typo had cost them an awkward apology.
"Fair," he said. He read the numbers aloud under the birthday noise and found one: 1,450 where it should have been 1,540.
"Thanks," he said, fixing it with two minutes to spare. The bristle was still there, a little. But he had chosen what to do with it.

What did Sumit feel when Lalremsiami gave the advice?

Counsellor's note, Sunaina, Grade 9, 20 November
Vikas asked to see me after assembly. His class teacher had mentioned he'd gone quiet and his marks were slipping, and today he told me why: his parents have been arguing a lot, and he believes it is because of him. "If I didn't need so much, if I got better marks, they'd be okay." He listed his "mistakes" in detail. He looked exhausted. I asked if he feels safe at home; he said yes, it's the shouting and the silence afterwards. I told him clearly that adults' arguments are the adults' responsibility, not his. What I did next: with his agreement, I called his mother this afternoon, and the three of us will meet on Friday. I'll check in with Vikas every day this week.

When will Sunaina, Vikas and his mother meet?
On Friday.
Why might Vikas believe his parents' arguments are his fault?
If the fights are his doing, he could stop them by needing less and scoring more; that feels less helpless than accepting he can't control them, but it leaves him exhausted with guilt.
What choice by Sunaina helps lift the weight from Vikas?
Saying plainly that the arguments are the adults' responsibility, checking he is safe, and bringing his mother into a meeting so the message comes from home too.
How might Vikas's mother react to the counsellor's call?
She may be shocked and sad to learn her son blames himself, and glad of the chance to tell him directly that it isn't his fault.

Jomon came to office hours after failing the mid-term in microeconomics. He didn't pretend it was fine. He said, "I'm really disappointed. I thought I understood it." I told him that disappointment made sense.

Tina jumps three times as long as Betsy, who jumps for 6 minutes so Tina jumps 3*6 = 18 minutes
Tina can jump for 18 minutes and Cindy and jump for 12 minutes so Tina can jump 18-12 = 6 minutes longer
The answer is 6.

What might Vishal have been feeling when saying "I didn't notice"?

The juniors probably felt dismissed or small, since their faces fell. A friendly switch to Hindi the next day would tell them they were welcome.

Sunday: When baby Ishita reached for the rattle, her big sister Noor, two, clutched it and turned away. Ishita cried; Noor watched her, frowning.
Tuesday: Ishita wailed in her cot. Noor toddled over, patted her tummy the way Ammi did, and said, "Shh, shh."
Friday: Ishita cried for the rattle again. Noor looked at it, looked at her sister, and pushed it through the cot bars. Ammi clapped softly. "You helped Ishita feel better."

What did Noor push through the cot bars on Friday?
Noor pushed the rattle through the cot bars.
What was Noor feeling on Tuesday when she patted Ishita's tummy?
Noor seemed concerned about her crying sister and wanted to comfort her, copying the gentle way Ammi does it.
How did Ammi encourage Noor's gentleness?
Ammi clapped softly and named what Noor did, which helps Noor feel proud and want to be gentle again.
What might the moment be like for baby Ishita when the rattle comes through the bars?
Ishita likely feels comforted and happy to have the rattle, and her crying settles 🙂
Two-fifths of the seats in an auditorium that holds 500 people are currently taken. It was found that 1/10 of the seats are broken. How many seats are still available?

500/ 2/5 = 200 seats are already taken.
500/ 1/10 = 50 seats are broken.
So 200 + 50 = 250 seats are either taken or broken.
Therefore, 500 - 250 = 250 seats are still available.
The answer is 250.

"Why does she talk different?" Hana asked Felix.
"She speaks Arabic at home," Felix said.
Hana thought. She pointed at the snow. "Snow."
Amira smiled and said the word in Arabic.
Hana tried to copy it. They both laughed and threw snow.

What language did Amira speak at home?
Arabic.
How did Hana feel about Amira's language?
She felt curious, asking why she talked different, then playful and friendly.
What helped Hana and Amira become friends?
Hana shared a simple word and tried Amira's word, turning the difference into play.

I have a viva coming up and I'm nervous about answering questions.
Go over your project or syllabus and list the questions the examiner is likely to ask. Practise answering them aloud.
What if I don't know an answer?
Say so honestly and, if you can, explain what you do know that is related. Guessing wildly usually goes worse than a calm, truthful reply.
How should I speak?
Clearly and at a steady pace. Take a breath before answering, and keep your answers short. Ask politely for the question to be repeated if you did not hear it.
What should I wear?
Neat, comfortable clothes that suit the setting. Being comfortable helps you feel confident.

Every term, Rekha wrote the same line in her school diary: "I WILL get better at maths." Every term, nothing changed.
That summer the community centre on her lane ran afternoon classes to escape the heat. Bhavna Didi, who ran them, read the diary line and tapped it. "Better how? When?"
Rekha shrugged. "Just... better."
"Try this. Five sums, every day, right after tea, at this table. Then tick a box." She drew thirty little boxes on a card.
The first week Rekha grumbled. But five was small enough to start, and after tea was easy to remember. By the end of the month the card had twenty-six ticks, and in the centre's small test she got eight out of ten, her best ever. She drew a new card herself.

How many boxes did Bhavna Didi draw on the card?
Thirty.
How did Rekha feel when she drew the new card herself?
Rekha felt proud and motivated; the ticks and her best-ever test showed real progress, so she wanted to keep going. 🎉
Why did five sums after tea work where "I WILL get better" didn't?
A small, specific goal tied to a set time is easy to start and easy to check, while "better" has no first step.
How might Bhavna Didi see Rekha's old diary line?
She likely sees a real wish with no plan behind it, which is why she asked, "Better how? When?"

In my first month as a constable in Guwahati, I stopped a car at a night checkpoint, and the young woman driving, Aditi, wouldn't roll her window down more than an inch. "Can I see your ID, please? And I'd like to call the control room to confirm this checkpoint." I'll admit, my first feeling was irritation. I was in full uniform, with a badge, under a streetlight. Who did she think I was? But my senior, standing behind me, nodded at her. "Of course, madam. Call 112. Binita, hold up your ID." She did, gave our location, and the control room confirmed. Only then did she lower her window. Driving home that night, I thought about why she'd done it. There had been reports that month of fake uniforms stopping women on the highway. To her, my uniform was a costume until proven otherwise. She was right. Now I hold my ID up before anyone asks, and tell people they can call to check. It makes my work easier, not harder.

Where did Binita work as a constable?
In Guwahati.
What was Binita's first feeling when Aditi asked for ID?
Binita felt irritated, thinking the uniform and badge should have been enough.
What does Binita now do differently, and why?
Binita holds up the ID before anyone asks and tells people they can call to check, because uniforms can be faked and verification builds trust.
Why did Aditi insist on verifying?
Aditi was cautious because fake uniforms had been used to stop women that month, so she treated the uniform as unproven until the control room confirmed.

"'"The ascetics said, 'It behoveth thee, O Narada, to describe, in full, from the beginning, unto Hrishikesa, that wonderful and inconceivable incident which occurred, O puissant one, on the mountains of Himavat and which, O ascetic, was witnessed by those of us that had proceeded thither in course of our pilgrimage to the sacred waters. Verily, for the benefit of all the Rishis here assembled, it behoveth thee to recite that incident.' Thus addressed by those ascetics, the celestial Rishi, viz., the divine Narada, then recited the following story whose incidents had occurred some time before."'"
The ascetics ask Narada to tell Hrishikesa and the other Rishis about a wonderful event they saw in the Himavat mountains, and Narada begins the story.
Gillian's phone bill is usually $50 a month. If the monthly bill increases by 10%, what will be her phone bill for the entire next year?

Her new monthly bill will be $50 * 110/100 = $55.
Her phone bill for the entire year will be $55 * 12 = $660.
The answer is 660.
Use a more formal word than "lots of": There were lots of lamps on the steps.

I went with Jyoti to the astrologer the week before she had to choose between two job offers. I'm Himani, and I was curious what she'd do.
The astrologer said, "You are independent but sometimes long for support." Jyoti smiled and asked, "Would the opposite also fit me? Dependent, but longing for freedom?"

Jyoti nodded. Then she asked, "Can you tell me anything specific I could check? A date, a name?" He talked about "a change in the west."

What did the astrologer say about "a change"?

What might Himani have felt watching Jyoti question the astrologer?
Himani likely felt curious and impressed, seeing Jyoti enjoy the reading while testing it.
What did Jyoti do that kept the reading from deciding her job?
She asked if the opposite also fit and whether anything was checkable, then decided with a list of pay, commute and growth.
How might the astrologer have felt when Jyoti asked if the opposite fit?
He may have felt caught off guard, admitting the vague line fit both ways.

Sahil got engaged today. My oldest friend. We did everything together since Class 1. I found out on the group chat, a photo of a ring, fifty heart replies. I typed "so happy for you!!" and meant it. Then I sat on the balcony for an hour feeling like I'd been left behind at a bus stop. Everyone's moving forward and I'm still here, same job, same flat. I don't even want to get married right now! Then I'll help plan the sangeet.
Simran

How did Simran find out about the engagement?
On the group chat, from a photo of a ring.

Simran feels genuinely happy for Sahil and also stung and left behind, worried that the friendship will change.
Is Simran's plan to call Sahil wise? Why?
Yes, because admitting the mixed feelings honestly clears the way for a real congratulation and helping with the sangeet.
How might Sahil feel hearing Simran's honest call?
Sahil might feel touched and reassured that the friendship matters to Simran, even as life changes.
