12 March, late
Big call today: whose façade design goes to the client. Two finalists. Sayan's, from our little Bengali corner of the office, where we joke in Bangla over tea. And Francis's, who joined from Kochi and mostly eats at his desk.
My gut said Sayan straight away. So I did what I'd promised myself: wrote the brief's three needs on a sticky note (daylight, cost, local material) and marked both designs with the names covered. Francis won two of three.
Then the harder test: if Francis were one of our tea group, would I hesitate at all? No. That settled it.
Tomorrow I'll also ask Francis to lunch. I realised I've never once asked him.
Ma called tonight and I told her about it. She said, "Good girl. Fair is fair." 🙂
— Ankita

What three needs did Ankita write on the sticky note?
Daylight, cost and local material.
Why did Ankita cover the names before marking?
Ankita felt uneasy that her gut already leaned toward Sayan from the tea group, and she wanted the designs judged without that pull.
What small choice at the end of the day could help Ankita beyond this one decision?
Asking Francis to lunch starts to widen her circle, so the next close call isn't shaped only by who she already knows.
What might it be like for Francis to eat at his desk while others joke in Bangla over tea?
Francis may feel outside the office's warm corners, so being judged on the work itself, and then invited to lunch, could matter a lot.

Jane's letter is long. Summarize it in three sentences.

"Since writing the above, dearest Lizzy, something has occurred of a most unexpected and serious nature; but I am afraid of alarming you--be assured that we are all well. What I have to say relates to poor Lydia. An express came at twelve last night, just as we were all gone to bed, from Colonel Forster, to inform us that she was gone off to Scotland with one of his officers; to own the truth, with Wickham! Imagine our surprise. To Kitty, however, it does not seem so wholly unexpected. I am very, very sorry. So imprudent a match on both sides! But I am willing to hope the best, and that his character has been misunderstood. Thoughtless and indiscreet I can easily believe him, but this step (and let us rejoice over it) marks nothing bad at heart. His choice is disinterested at least, for he must know my father can give her nothing. Our poor mother is sadly grieved. My father bears it better. How thankful am I, that we never let them know what has been said against him; we must forget it ourselves. They were off Saturday night about twelve, as is conjectured, but were not missed till yesterday morning at eight. The express was sent off directly. My dear Lizzy, they must have passed within ten miles of us. Colonel Forster gives us reason to expect him here soon. Lydia left a few lines for his wife, informing her of their intention. I must conclude, for I cannot be long from my poor mother. I am afraid you will not be able to make it out, but I hardly know what I have written."

Jane writes that Lydia has run off to Scotland with Wickham, as Colonel Forster has told them by express. She hopes for the best and believes Wickham may not be as bad as people said. Their mother is very upset, their father is calmer, and Jane must return to her mother.

"Why did I utter those words? It was by some accident I said them.... I need not have said them," he thought. "And then nothing would have happened." He saw the frightened and then infuriated face of the dragoon who dealt the blow, the look of silent, timid reproach that boy in the fur-lined coat had turned upon him. "But I did not do it for my own sake. I was bound to act that way.... The mob, the traitor... the public welfare," thought he.

How does he try to excuse what he did?
He tells himself it was an accident that he said those words, but then claims he had to act that way for the public good.

Donovan Mitchell is currently averaging 26 points per game. His team has played 15 games this season. He has a goal of averaging 30 points per game for the entire 20 game season. How many points does he need to average per game to reach his goal?

At this point in the season, Donovan has scored 26 * 15 = 390 points.
To reach his goal of 30 points per game, he would have to finish the season with a total of 30 * 20 = 600 points.
For the remaining 5 games, Donovan needs to score 600 - 390 = 210 points.
Therefore, he needs to average 210 / 5 = 42 points per game.
The answer is 42.

Hey Ujjwal,
I'm sorry about the family photo at Diwali. When everyone lined up, you had your lips pursed tight and your arms crossed, and I said loudly, "Look, Ujjwal's doing his duck face for the camera!" Everyone laughed, even Bade Papa.
I didn't know then that you'd just had a fight with your mum about the trip you couldn't go on. You weren't posing. You were upset.
In the photo you look miserable, and I made it worse.
I get it now. Sometimes a pout is just for the camera, and sometimes it isn't, and I didn't check. Next time I'll just ask if you're okay.
Want to play badminton on Sunday?
Ramesh

"Look, Ujjwal's doing his duck face for the camera!"

What will Ramesh do differently next time?
Ramesh will check whether someone is okay instead of assuming a pout is only for the camera.
How might Bade Papa see the photo now, if he knew the story?
Bade Papa might feel sorry for laughing, seeing that Ujjwal's pursed lips showed real hurt, not a pose.

"Dadi, why are there so many people?" Sangeeta whispered from behind the pillar. "The baby doesn't even know them."
"Today we tell everyone her name," Dadi said. "Vishal Chacha will whisper it in her ear first. Then Pandit-ji will say it aloud."
"Why can't they just tell her at home?"
"Because a name isn't only for the baby. It's for everyone who will call her." Dadi squeezed her hand. "These people will call her name her whole life."
Vishal Chacha bent over the cradle and whispered. Then Pandit-ji said, "Anika!" and everyone repeated it.
Sangeeta tried it quietly. "Anika." Then louder, with everyone. "Anika!"

Who whispers the baby's name first?
Vishal Chacha will whisper it in her ear first.
How did Sangeeta feel when she joined in saying 'Anika'?
Sangeeta went from puzzled to excited and included, saying the name louder with everyone.
What did Dadi do that helped?
She answered Sangeeta's why simply, explaining that a name is for everyone who will call it.
What might Vishal Chacha feel as he whispers the name?
He likely feels tender and proud, giving the baby her name before the whole family.

"Jagdish, you think your Nani was always good with numbers? When I was ten, the maths teacher in our Indore school said in front of everyone, 'Girls, don't worry, sums are not for you. Just pass.' I had done every sum at home. But on test day I felt a knot, here, in my stomach. I kept thinking, 'Don't prove him right, Preeti. Don't prove him right.' I read the first question four times. The numbers slid about like ants. I left half the paper blank. That evening I solved the same paper at home in twenty minutes. The sums had not changed; only the voice in my head had gone quiet. Only a kind teacher in Class 7 made me believe it again."

How long did it take Preeti to solve the same paper at home?
Twenty minutes.
What was Preeti worried about during the test?
She worried about proving the teacher right that sums are not for girls, and that fear filled her head so she couldn't think about the questions.
What was the turning point that helped Preeti believe in her maths again?
A kind teacher in Class 7 made her believe in her maths again, quietening the voice the first teacher had planted.
What might Jagdish take from Nani's story?
Jagdish may see that a poor result can come from pressure and a label, not a lack of ability, and that a kind word can change it.

The monsoon had flooded the lower loading bay, and Abhinav, three months into running the night shift, had twenty minutes to decide how to move the orders. The team huddled under the tin roof, rain hammering so loud he had to shout. He spread his arms wide. "I don't have the full answer. What do you see?" A few people glanced at each other; the last supervisor had done the same thing and then ignored everyone. Pradeep, the oldest loader, spoke first, but the rain swallowed his words. Abhinav didn't nod and move on. He stepped right up beside him, bent his head close and said, "Again, please." Pradeep repeated it: use the upper ramp and pass the smaller boxes hand to hand in a chain. Abhinav turned back to the group. "Pradeep's plan. Let's go." They moved faster than he had ever seen.

How long did Abhinav have to decide how to move the orders?
Twenty minutes.
What might Pradeep have felt when Abhinav bent close and said 'Again, please'?
Pradeep probably felt respected and heard, maybe surprised too, since the last supervisor had invited ideas and then ignored everyone.
What made Abhinav's open-arms invitation work?
He followed it with genuine listening, moving close to hear Pradeep over the rain, and then actually used the plan.
What would have changed if Abhinav had nodded and moved on when the rain drowned Pradeep out?
The team would have seen the gesture as empty, like the last supervisor's, and might have stopped offering ideas.
A street dog, two sentences, the second one a question.
The street dog waits outside the shop every evening. Do you think he knows the shopkeeper?

Valentina held up her painting of a blue cat. "Look!"
Her sister Mei glanced over. "Mine is better," she said, waving her purple house.
Valentina's arm sank and she pressed the paper against her chest.
Dad came in from the hallway and looked at both. "Valentina, that cat has such a big smile, and you mixed a blue I have not seen before. Mei, your house has tiny windows with curtains. That took you a long time. I like both."
"But which is better?" Mei asked.
"I am not choosing. They are different, and each shows your own effort."
Slowly, Valentina lifted her cat again.

What did Valentina paint?
She painted a blue cat.
How does Valentina feel after Mei says hers is better?
She feels smaller and hurt: her arm sinks and she hugs the paper to her chest.
What did Dad do to keep pride from becoming a contest?
He praised each girl for her own effort and details, and refused to rank the paintings.
Why might Mei want to know which is better?
She may be eager for approval and want to be first, since she asks Dad to pick even after he praises hers.

At the hostel's evening assembly in Pune, six-year-old Ganga knocked a steel plate off the table and it clanged on the floor. The warden's eyes went to her. Ganga's chin dropped to her chest and she stared at her feet. "Ganga?" said Warden Farhan. Silence. He walked over, crouched and said, "It was an accident, wasn't it? What did Ganga knock off the table?
She knocked off a steel plate.
What might Ganga have been feeling as her chin dropped to her chest?
She was probably ashamed or afraid of being told off, since she stared at her feet and stayed silent. She might also have been embarrassed that everyone had turned to look.
How did Farhan help Ganga learn without making her feel worthless?
He treated it as an accident, helped pick up the plate with her and gave a simple tip for next time.
How might Farhan see Ganga's silence and dropped chin?

Friday
Worst day. Sir read my marks out loud and the back row laughed. Then Pranav posted a photo of my torn shoe in the class group.
Came home and watched the channel again. The man in the videos always seems to be talking straight to me. He says guys like us are kept down on purpose by "them", the people who laugh and run everything, and that it's not our fault. He says we're warriors, not losers.
Tonight someone from the comments added me to a group called Brothers. Forty guys. They welcomed me by name. One said, "You're one of us now." I haven't felt that since we moved here.
Minakshi di saw my screen at dinner and asked, "Who are these brothers?" I said nobody. She didn't push, but she sat next to me longer than usual.
I don't even really get what they believe. I just like being someone's brother.
Tanvir

What was the group Tanvir was added to called?
A group called Brothers.
Why do the channel and the group feel so good to Tanvir?
Tanvir feels humiliated and alone after the day at school, and the group makes Tanvir feel welcomed and important; the pull is belonging more than any belief.
What could Minakshi di do next?
Keep sitting with Tanvir, ask gently about the day at school, and bring in a parent or the school counsellor soon, without mocking the group.
How might Minakshi di have felt hearing Tanvir's 'nobody'?
Minakshi di probably felt worried by the quick answer and chose closeness over an argument, staying beside Tanvir longer than usual.
Meat or meet: "Let us ___ at the canteen."

Use "meet", which means to come together with someone. "Meat" is the flesh of an animal eaten as food.
Examples: Let us meet at the canteen at noon. The curry has no meat in it.

In the green room behind the school auditorium, ten minutes before the inter-school debate, Tushar's stomach churned like a washing machine. "I'm going to be sick. I can't go on," he told Ms Seema, the debate coach. She didn't argue. "Let's slow down. When did you last eat?" He thought. He'd skipped lunch to practise. "And what else is your body doing?" "Hands cold. Heart fast. But... I also keep grinning." "So some of it might be hunger, and some might be excitement, not only fear." She handed him a banana from her bag. He ate it, breathed out slowly twice, and noticed the churn had shrunk to a flutter. When his name was called, the flutter felt almost like a drumroll.

Why had Tushar skipped lunch?
He had skipped lunch to practise.
What did Tushar first think his churning stomach meant, and what else was going on?
He thought he was too scared to go on, but he was also hungry and a bit excited.
How did Ms Seema help Tushar read his body better?
She slowed him down, asked about food and other signals, and helped him see the whole pattern before deciding it was fear.
What would have changed if Ms Seema had simply told Tushar not to be nervous?
He might have stayed hungry and convinced he was only afraid, and perhaps pulled out of the debate.
Now you try: how many of the 60 are multiples of 5?
The answer is last digit 5: 1 x 4 x 3 = 12.

Read this:

"Vinita, quick question. On the call with the partner team today I kept steady eye contact the whole time, like we were trained. Their lead kept looking down at her notes whenever I spoke."
"And you decided she was bored?"
"Bored, or annoyed. Then she wrote afterwards, 'Thank you for your intense attention.' Intense? Is that nice or not?"
Vinita laughed. "Could be both. When I worked with the Lisbon office, long eye contact felt normal. On another team, a senior told me my stare felt like a challenge."
"So it depends on the country?"
"Partly. Partly on the person. Her looking down might be respect, or thinking, or just her notes."
"So what do I do?"
"Watch how they look at each other. Soften a little, glance away sometimes. And ask her how meetings usually run on their side."
Vikas opened a new message. "Asking now."

What did the partner lead write after the call?
She wrote, 'Thank you for your intense attention.'
Why was Vikas unsure after reading the message?
Vikas felt confused and a bit anxious, because 'intense' could be praise or a hint that the steady eye contact had felt like a challenge.
What would you advise Vikas before the next call?
Watch how the partner team looks at each other, soften the gaze a little, and ask the lead how their meetings usually run instead of assuming.
How might the partner lead have experienced the steady eye contact?
The lead may have felt watched or pressed, or may simply have found it keen; her looking down could have been her own way of showing respect, so each side may have misread the other.

The pirates plan to explore 4 islands. Two islands require walking 20 miles per day while the other two islands require 25 miles per day. How many miles will they have to walk if it takes 1.5 days to explore each island?

It will take 1.5 days x 2 = 3 days to explore 2 islands.
So, the pirates will walk 20 miles x 3 days = 60 miles to explore two islands.
The other 2 islands will be explored by walking 25 miles x 3 days = 75 miles.
Thus, the pirates will need to walk 60 + 75 = 135 miles to explore the 4 islands.
The answer is 135.

Read this:

Monday: Elizabeth, eight, tore a page of a library book by accident. Mummy saw it and said quickly, "What will the librarian think? What will people say about us? Hide it in your bag." Elizabeth's stomach turned over.
Thursday: She took the long way to class so she wouldn't pass the library. When her friend Bhavna asked why, Elizabeth whispered, "Everyone will talk."
Tuesday: Bhavna said, "I tore a page once. Miss just gave me tape and said thank you for telling." She walked beside Elizabeth to the desk. Elizabeth put the book down with both hands and said, "This got torn, and I'm sorry."
The librarian reached for the tape.

What did Mummy say to Elizabeth after the page was torn?
She said, 'What will the librarian think? What will people say about us? Hide it in your bag.'
What was Elizabeth feeling as she took the long way to class?
She was afraid and ashamed of being talked about, fearing that everyone would know about the torn page.
What made the difference on Tuesday when Elizabeth returned the book?
Bhavna told a torn-page story of Bhavna's own and walked with Elizabeth to the desk, so Elizabeth could say sorry and hand the book back.
How might Bhavna have seen Elizabeth's fear?
Bhavna seems to understand it, having torn a page once too, and stayed beside Elizabeth to show that telling the librarian could be safe.
Why do we wear raincoats in the rain? How should I behave near a strange dog? Sam walks 19 minutes each day. How many minutes does he walk in 4 days?

1. A raincoat keeps water off your body. Because its cloth does not let water soak through.
2. Stay calm and do not run. Walk away slowly and tell an adult.
3. It is 76. Because 4 x 19 = 76.

Read this:

Daycare note, Diwali week. By Jahnavi, carer.
At 4 p.m., crackers burst outside the window. Mridul, two, screamed and ran to me. I picked him up and held him close against my chest, swaying slowly. I hummed the same lullaby we sing at nap time and stroked his back in circles. His breathing slowed. After a few minutes he rested his cheek on my shoulder and sucked his thumb. We moved to the far room. I told his mother at pickup. 🤍

What time did the crackers burst?
At 4 p.m.
How did Mridul feel when the crackers burst?
He was frightened and startled, screaming and running to Jahnavi.
What did Jahnavi do to soothe Mridul?
She held him close, swayed, hummed a familiar lullaby, stroked his back and moved to a quieter room.
How might Mridul's mother feel hearing about it?
She would likely feel reassured that Jahnavi comforted him calmly.
Can a gleeful laugh be a bad thing?

Usually it is happy, but it can also be unkind if someone enjoys another person's trouble. Gleeful means full of joy and excitement. It is an adjective.
Example: The children let out a gleeful shout when the rain stopped play.

Read this:

Week one. Mahima took over the marketing team of four and did exactly what her previous manager had done at the bigger agency: a daily forty-five-minute stand-up, a shared tracker with hourly updates, and a rule that every change needed her approval. "It worked brilliantly there," she told her friend Kashish.
Week three. The stand-ups dragged. Her team, all her own age and used to deciding things together, gave one-word updates. Nobody suggested ideas any more. A campaign draft sat unapproved for two days because Mahima was in meetings.
Week five. The client asked why the new campaign was late. Mahima asked the team. There was a long silence, then Aman said, "Honestly? We've stopped trying things. It feels like we're being checked on all the time."
Mahima went home and called Kashish. "I copied a style made for thirty people and used it on four." She sounded tired and a little ashamed.

How many people were on Mahima's team?
Her team had four people.
How did Mahima feel when she called Kashish in week five?
She sounded tired and a little ashamed, realising she had copied a style that didn't fit.
What else could Mahima try with her small team?
She could ask the team how they'd like to work and trust them with small decisions, since they were used to deciding together.
How might Aman have felt saying the honest answer?
Aman likely felt nervous but relieved to finally say the team felt constantly checked on.

metadata.subtype: Approach: copying the previous lead's style without fit [Pitfall]

Read this:

Every month, in the week before her period, Sarika's life in their Kochi flat seemed to fall apart. She cried through meetings, snapped at Joseph over nothing, and one month called in sick three days running because she couldn't face anyone. Her mother said, 'All women go through it. Bear it.' Sarika had borne it for years. One evening, after a week of barely sleeping, she told Joseph, 'It feels like I disappear for a week and a stranger lives here.' Joseph held her hand. 'This isn't something you just tolerate. Let's see a doctor.' He found a women's health clinic, went with her, and helped her write down her monthly notes. The doctor took her seriously and made a plan with her.

What did Sarika's mother say?
'All women go through it. Bear it.'
What was Sarika feeling when she said a stranger lives there?
She felt overwhelmed and lost, as if she disappeared for a week every month.
What steps did Joseph take?
He refused to treat it as something to tolerate, found a clinic, went with her and helped write down her monthly notes.
How might Joseph have experienced the snapping over nothing?
Joseph may have felt hurt at times, yet he saw a real problem rather than a character flaw.

Read this:

Monday: Naveen sat on the sofa with his phone. Farhan brought a toy car and tugged his sleeve. "Papa, Papa!" No answer, so Farhan cried louder. Thursday: Farhan sat by the table with the car and did not look up when Naveen came in. Saturday: after tea Naveen put the phone in a drawer and sat on the floor. Farhan watched his face for a while, then slowly pushed the car across the floor to him.

What did Farhan do on Monday to get Naveen's attention?
He brought a toy car, tugged Naveen's sleeve, called "Papa, Papa!" and then cried louder.
What might Farhan's silence on Thursday mean about how he feels?
After louder crying did not work, he seems to have stopped trying to reach Naveen and pulled back into playing alone.
What small change did Naveen make on Saturday, and why might it help?
He put the phone in a drawer and sat on the floor with Farhan. Short, fully present moments like this let Farhan see that his father is really there.
How might Farhan's slow push of the car on Saturday look from Naveen's side?
It may show Naveen that Farhan is willing to try again but is still checking whether he can be trusted.
Everyone knows about the new shop, but it is an "open secret". What does that mean?

An "open secret" is something that is officially secret but known by most people.
Example: It was an open secret that the teacher was leaving.
My grandmother wants to learn how to send a voice message. Can you tell me how to teach her?
Start with the button. Show her the microphone icon, and tell her to press and hold it while speaking, then let go to send. Let her try with you first.
She says the screen is too small.
You can increase the font size and the icon size in the phone settings. Reading glasses nearby also help. Practise a few times and she'll soon feel confident.
She's laughing a lot, which is nice.
That's the best sign. Learning is easier when it is fun, so keep it light.

Read this:

In the small town of Kotdwar, there was exactly one café with fairy lights, and Sharmila had posted from it eleven times. Always the same table, the same angle, the cold coffee in the frame, a caption like "city vibes ✨."
When her cousin Simran visited from her Delhi hostel, Sharmila took her there proudly.
Simran laughed. "So this is the famous place! You make it look like Paris."
Sharmila went red. "Everyone here posts like that. You post such amazing stuff from Delhi."
Simran was quiet. "I post the one night we went out. I don't post the forty nights I ate alone in my room."
Sharmila looked at her. "Seriously?"
"Seriously. Everyone's feed is a highlight reel."
They took a photo together, blurry, laughing, the tea spilled. Sharmila almost filtered it. Instead she asked, "Can I post this one? As is?"
"As is," Simran said.

How many times had Sharmila posted from the café?
Sharmila had posted from it eleven times.
What was Sharmila feeling when Simran joked about Paris?
Sharmila felt embarrassed and exposed, going red, since her curated posts made the small café look grand.
What choice did Sharmila make at the end, and why does it matter?
She asked Simran's consent to post an unfiltered photo, showing honesty and care about sharing someone else's image.
What is it like for Simran behind her Delhi posts?
Simran seems lonely at the hostel, eating alone on most nights, which her posts never show.
Before he lost one, Policeman O'Brien had 5 more than twice as many hats as fire chief Simpson. If fire chief Simpson has 15 hats, how many hats does Policeman O'Brien now have?

Twice as many hats as fire chief Simpson has is 2 * 15 = 30 hats.
5 more than 30 hats is 30 + 5 = 35 hats.
One less than 35 hats is 35 - 1 = 34 hats.
The answer is 34.

Read this:

Layla's family had moved to Izmir in the winter, and her new school felt loud and fast. In her first week she hardly spoke. She sat at the back of the Year 6 class and watched. The girls by the radiator shared sunflower seeds and whispered. Three boys played football against the wall at every break and never asked anyone. And Selin, a girl with paint on her fingers, spent break at the art table, humming. "Selin talks to whoever sits there," Layla thought on Thursday. "She doesn't seem to mind new people." On Friday, Layla took her sketchbook to the art table and asked if the blue pencil was free.

What did Selin have on her fingers?
She had paint on her fingers.
How was Layla feeling in her first week at the new school?
She felt overwhelmed by the loud, fast school and cautious, so she chose to watch before speaking.
What other approach could Layla try if Selin was busy, and why?
She could ask the teacher to seat her near someone at the art table, because a small nudge from an adult makes a first talk easier.
How might Selin see Layla's question about the blue pencil?
Selin will probably see it as a friendly, easy start and be glad of company at the art table.

Read this:

At the residential school in Shillong, evening study hour was nearly over when Rekha, fifteen, slid a folded note across the hostel common room to her cousin Charu. It said: "Can we talk? I'm not okay."
They sat on the back steps. Rekha's words came slowly. She hadn't been sleeping, she'd stopped calling home, and most nights she cried in the bathroom because she felt she didn't belong here. "I didn't want anyone to know," she said.
Charu squeezed her hand. "I'm really glad you told me. Let's tell Mrs Lyngdoh too, tonight."
Mrs Lyngdoh, the housemother, was still in her office. She put down her pen, listened to all of it and said, "Thank you for trusting us. This is not something you should hold alone." She rang Rekha's parents while the cousins sat beside her, and booked Rekha in with the school counsellor for the next morning.

What did Rekha's note to Charu say?
"Can we talk? I'm not okay."
What was Rekha feeling that made her cry in the bathroom most nights?
She felt she didn't belong at the school and was lonely and worn out, and she didn't want anyone to know.
What did Charu choose to do after listening, and why was it a good step?
Charu suggested telling Mrs Lyngdoh that same night, which brought in an adult who called Rekha's parents and arranged the counsellor.
How might Rekha's parents feel after Mrs Lyngdoh's call?
They would likely be worried to hear she had been struggling, but relieved that she reached out and that the school was already supporting her.

Read this:

30 March, late
Reviews tomorrow. Jatin's is the hard one. All I can see is last month: the parents' complaint about Class 6 marks, the lab left unlocked. My gut says 'needs improvement'.
But I promised myself this year I wouldn't do reviews from memory. So I opened my review file, the one I add to every Friday. Jatin, June: started the science club, twenty kids signed up. August: covered for Seema ma'am for three weeks without a word of complaint. November: his class had the best practical scores in the school. February: the complaint and the lab.
So: one rough month out of ten. I'll still talk to him about the lab, clearly. But 'needs improvement' was my tired brain talking. Changing it to 'good, with one area to work on'.
Nandini

What did Jatin start in June?
Jatin started the science club, and twenty kids signed up.
What was Nandini feeling before opening the review file?
Nandini felt tense and doubtful about Jatin, because last month's complaint and the unlocked lab filled Nandini's mind.
Why is adding to the review file every Friday a good habit?
It captures each month as it happens, so the review can weigh all ten months instead of the freshest memory.
How might Jatin feel if he had been rated 'needs improvement'?
Jatin might feel hurt and unseen, since the science club, the three weeks of cover and the practical scores would have been ignored.
Georgia has 25 pieces of stationery while Lorene has three times as many pieces of stationery as Georgia. How many fewer pieces of stationery does Georgia have than Lorene?

Lorene has 25 x 3 = 75 pieces of stationery.
Thus, Georgia has 75 - 25 = 50 fewer pieces of stationery than Lorene.
The answer is 50.

Read this:

I'm Noor, and I sit across from Sarita on the support team.
Last Tuesday, after Mr Bose's quick huddle, I saw her open the complaints sheet and delete rows one by one, the ones marked "refund pending". Kabir, beside her, had his headphones on. Ria watched for a second and looked away. Sarita didn't speak to anyone. She kept rubbing her forehead. I don't know what was going on in her head.
At tea, I didn't accuse her. I just asked, "Sarita, those refund rows. Is this okay?"
She was quiet for a long time. "Mr Bose said the numbers look bad before the review."
"That's what he said," I said. "Is it okay?"
She went back to her desk and pressed undo until the rows came back. That afternoon she emailed Mr Bose asking whether he wanted the rows archived instead, and copied the quality lead.

Which rows did Sarita delete from the complaints sheet?
The rows marked "refund pending".
What might Noor have been feeling while watching Sarita delete the rows?
Noor was probably uneasy and concerned, which is why Noor asked a plain question at tea instead of staying silent or accusing Sarita.
Why was Noor's plain question more useful than an accusation?
It gave Sarita space to stop and think without getting defensive, and let her choose to undo it herself.
How might Sarita have experienced Noor's question?
Sarita likely felt caught between Mr Bose's instruction and her own doubt, and the gentle question gave her permission to pause.

Read this:

"Noor miss, the Blue group is the best group!"
"Oh? Why, Pema?"
"Because I'm Blue! And we have the big umbrella."
"What about the Green group?"
"Green group is bad. They push."
"Did someone push you?"
"No... but they might."
"Hmm. Who sat with you on the bus to the picnic, my boy?"
"Tashi."
"Which group is Tashi in?"
"...Green."
"Is Tashi bad?"
"No. Tashi gave me his biscuit when it rained."
"So maybe Green isn't bad?"
"Maybe Green is okay. Can Tashi come under the big umbrella?"

Who gave Pema a biscuit when it rained?
Tashi.
Why does Pema think the Green group is bad?
Pema feels proud and happy to be Blue, so the other group quickly seems bad, even though nobody pushed.
How does Noor miss help Pema see things differently?
She asks about Pema's friend on the bus, who turns out to be in the Green group, so Pema can see the groups are just labels.
How might Tashi feel under the big umbrella?
Tashi would likely feel welcomed and happy to be included, not treated as the other group.

Read this:

In the little church in Aldona village, Francis, five, sat squeezed between aunties. His baby cousin Rhea was getting her name at the font, wearing a long white dress. There were so many people: uncles from Mapusa, the neighbours, the baker, even the old fisherman. Francis tugged Sarika aunty's sleeve. "Why did so many people come for a baby?" Sarika aunty whispered, "Because now she belongs to all of us, not just her mummy and daddy." Francis looked around at all the faces. Afterwards, he held Rhea's tiny hand. "I'm your cousin," he told her.

Where was baby Rhea given her name?
In the little church in Aldona village, at the font.
What was Francis feeling when he asked why so many people came?
He felt curious and puzzled, surprised that a baby needed so many people.
How did Sarika aunty's answer help Francis?
It showed him that the baby belongs to a big circle of family and neighbours, which he then joined by telling Rhea he was her cousin.
How might Rhea's parents feel seeing so many people at the church?
They probably felt happy and supported, knowing their baby had a large circle around her.

Read this:

I'm Keerthana. You asked about the crypto group. Okay.
A cousin added me to a chat. Everyone posted screenshots of huge gains. "Get in now or miss out!" I felt left behind. So I put in my first salary.
The coin crashed in a week. I lost most of it.
I called my friend Lalit, who works in finance. He didn't laugh. He explained compounding: small amounts, invested steadily over years, can grow, but nothing is guaranteed. He said to spread money across different things, not bet everything on one. And to talk to a registered adviser about my own risk appetite.
Now I'm slow. Boring. But I sleep at night.

What did Keerthana put into the coin?
The first salary.
What was Keerthana feeling seeing the screenshots of gains?
Keerthana felt left behind and anxious to join in.
What choice after the loss helped Keerthana?
Calling Lalit, learning about compounding and diversification, and planning to see a registered adviser.
How might Lalit have felt when Keerthana called?
Lalit probably felt sympathetic and wanted to help, not judge.
Carrie is making punch. She adds 6 12-oz cans of Mountain Dew, 28 oz of ice, and a 40 oz bottle of fruit juice. How many 10 oz servings of punch does Carrie have?

First find the total volume of the Mountain Dew: 6 cans * 12 oz/can = 72 oz
Then find the total volume of the punch: 72 oz + 28 oz + 40 oz = 140 oz
Then divide the total volume by the volume of each serving to find the number of servings: 140 oz / 10 oz/serving = 14 servings
The answer is 14.

Read this:

The long rains had come to Addis Ababa, and the power went out most evenings. Abebe's neighbour Rosa, who looked after him while his parents worked late, expected bedtime to be a battle in the dark.
But at eight, when the church bell down the road rang, Abebe got up from the floor without a word. He found the torch on the shelf, brushed his teeth at the basin by its light and climbed into bed.
"Story, Rosa," he said. "The one about the monkey and the market."
Rosa told it, rain drumming on the tin roof. Halfway through, Abebe's breathing slowed.
She sat there a while, surprised. No arguing, no "five more minutes." The bell, the brush, the story, then sleep, one step pulling the next, even with no lights at all.

What did Abebe use to see while brushing his teeth?
He used the torch from the shelf.
How did Rosa feel as Abebe fell asleep?
Rosa felt surprised and quietly pleased, because she had expected a battle and instead the routine ran smoothly.
Why did bedtime go so smoothly even without electricity?
Abebe's steps happen in the same order at the same time each night, starting with the eight o'clock bell, so each step follows the last without needing lights or reminders.
What would change if Abebe's bedtime happened at different times each night?
Without a steady cue like the bell and the same order, the steps might not follow automatically, and bedtime could turn into arguing.
A box of rainbow nerds contains 10 purple candies, 4 more yellow candies, and 2 fewer green candies than yellow candies. How many rainbow nerds are there in the box?

There are 10 + 4 = 14 yellow candies.
There are 14 - 2 = 12 green candies.
There are 10 + 14 + 12 = 36 rainbow nerds candies in the box.
The answer is 36.

Read this:

At the Dadar coaching centre, a group of boys in the back row started imitating Pallavi's stammer whenever she answered. "W-w-well, Sir..." Some girls giggled. Urmila, sixteen, sat two rows away. Last week she had laughed along, quietly, and hated herself for it. Today Pallavi went silent halfway through an answer, her ears red. Urmila turned around. "Stop it. It's not funny." The boys rolled their eyes. "Chill, it's a joke." "It's not," Urmila said, louder, her voice shaking. The room went quiet. At the break, she sat next to Pallavi, and after class, she told the centre head exactly what had happened. The head called the boys in that evening. On the way out, Pallavi squeezed Urmila's hand without saying anything.

What were the boys imitating?
Pallavi's stammer.
What was Urmila feeling when her voice shook?
She felt nervous and scared, but also angry and ashamed of having laughed before.
What did Urmila do after standing up to the boys, and why was it important?
She sat with Pallavi and told the centre head the same day, so an adult could stop the bullying.
How might Pallavi have felt when Urmila spoke up?
She likely felt relieved and grateful, shown by her silent hand squeeze. 🤍
Now you try: the smallest integer with 3x - 2 >= 10; the integers with -1 <= x < 4.
The answer is 4; -1, 0, 1, 2, 3.

Read this:

Sarika: [photo of the old hostel mess]
Sarika: best years of my life 😩 everything now is so boring
Lavanya: omg the steel plates, I miss it too honestly 🥹
Sarika: we were SO happy
Lavanya: we were! and also remember the roof leaking into your bed? the 6 am bucket queue?
Sarika: ugh ok yes
Lavanya: and being broke by the 20th of every month, splitting one packet of biscuits four ways
Sarika: true
Lavanya: I still think about it a lot, it's comforting. but I don't want it to make now feel empty, you know?
Sarika: easy for you, girl, you like your job
Lavanya: some days. what I actually miss is us sitting together every night. we can still do that
Lavanya: Sunday, dosa, my place? no leaking roof guaranteed
Sarika: haha deal 🙂

What did the friends split four ways when they were broke?
One packet of biscuits.
Why does Lavanya bring up the leaking roof and the bucket queue?
She loves the memories too, but wants Sarika to see the hard parts as well, so the past doesn't make the present feel empty.
What choice did Lavanya make to turn the nostalgia into something useful now?
She named what she actually misses, sitting together every night, and invited Sarika for dosa on Sunday.
How might Sarika feel after the chat compared with when the photo was first sent?
Sarika started out gloomy about now, but by the end seems lighter and has a plan, and may see the present less harshly.

Read this:

“Didi, Rohit kicked my chair again.”
“Did you tell him to stop?” asked Sunaina.
“Yes. He said sorry.”
“Did he stop?”
Wasim thought. “No. He kicked it three more times. But he said sorry.”
“Hmm. When someone's really sorry, what do they do?”
“Stop kicking?”
“Yes. How did his sorry sound?”
“Laughy. He wasn't looking at me.”
“So maybe not a real sorry. Tomorrow, if he kicks again, tell your teacher.”
“Okay.” Wasim sighed. “I thought sorry fixed it.”

How many more times did Rohit kick the chair after saying sorry?
Three more times.
What was Wasim feeling when he sighed?
He felt disappointed and a bit confused, having believed that sorry fixed things.
How did Sunaina help Wasim judge the sorry?
She asked whether Rohit stopped, how the sorry sounded and whether he looked at him, so Wasim could see it wasn't real.
What is it like for Wasim to keep getting kicked after a sorry?
It is confusing and frustrating, because the word promised a fix that didn't come.

metadata.subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]

Read this:

The power went off at 4:10, and the bank's payment window shut at five. Ankita's laptop was on its last battery when Deepak leaned over her shoulder. "Skip the second approval and release all twelve. I will answer for it." She knew the rule existed for a reason. Deepak had trained her, and he had always covered for her mistakes. Her stomach tightened. She typed, "Can we ask Ms Iyer for two minutes?" but Deepak was already pointing at the clock. She clicked release. On Monday one vendor turned out to be paid twice, and the recovery took three weeks of emails. In the meeting Deepak said the process had failed. Ankita said nothing, and thought about the question she had typed and never sent.

How many payments did Deepak tell Ankita to release?
Deepak told Ankita to release all twelve.
What was Ankita feeling as she looked from the clock to Deepak?
Torn between loyalty and fear, with her stomach tightening and her conscience nagging.
What could Ankita have done differently at that moment?
Send the question to Ms Iyer or insist on the second approval, even with the clock running.
How might Deepak see what happened afterwards?
Deepak said the process had failed, which suggests he was defensive and stressed and did not name his own part.
Is a stretcher a bed? We saw one at the station.

It is a light frame or bed with handles used to carry a sick or injured person. It is a noun.
Example: Two helpers carried the injured player off the field on a stretcher.

Read this:

"Okay, from the top," Baljeet said, sitting on the edge of the desk in the empty conference room.
Neelam took a breath. "Mr. Sethi joined this company when it was three people and a scooter..."
"Slow down. You're racing."
"Sorry. Nerves." She started again, slower. "Mr. Sethi joined when it was three people... and a scooter."
Baljeet grinned. "See? The pause makes the scooter funny."
"Then the story about him sleeping in the office during the 2005 floods..."
"Wait. Is that true?"
Neelam stopped. "Everyone says it."
"Everyone says a lot of things. If it's wrong, it's his farewell, and his family will be there."
Neelam frowned. "I'll ask his assistant." She sent the message. The reply came in two minutes: "It was 2006, and he slept in the car, not the office."
Baljeet laughed. "Even better. The car's funnier."
"The car's true." Neelam fixed the line. "From the top?"
"From the top. Slowly."

Where did Mr. Sethi actually sleep during the floods?
In the car, not the office.
Why was Neelam racing through the speech at first?
Neelam was nervous, and the nerves made her speak too fast.
What two things did Baljeet help Neelam improve?
Her pacing, slowing down and using pauses, and her content, checking the flood story with the assistant before telling it.
Why might getting the story right matter to Mr. Sethi's family?
They would be at the farewell and know the real story, so a wrong detail could feel careless on an important day.

Harish, most founders don't want to talk about breaking up on day one. It feels like planning a divorce at the wedding. I'm Anand, and my co-founder and I did it anyway, and I'm glad. We had both watched friends' startups fall apart: one ended in a legal notice, one where the founder who left after six months kept half the company.
So in our first month, while we still liked each other a lot, we sat with a startup lawyer and agreed on the basics. Shares would vest over four years, so you earn them by staying. And if one of us left, there was a fixed way to value the shares and buy them back.
Two years later, my co-founder did leave, for family reasons. It was sad. But nobody had to argue. We just opened the document and followed it.

Over how many years would the shares vest?
Over four years.
How did Anand feel when the co-founder left?
Anand felt sad, but relieved that nobody had to argue because the rules were already set.
What made agreeing the terms in the first month a wise choice?
They were still friendly and calm, so the rules were fair to both instead of being fought over during a split.
What would have changed if they had waited until the co-founder left?
They would have had to agree terms while sad and possibly resentful, which could have ended in a legal notice like their friends'.

'Doing your accounts?' 'Doing my fear,' she said. At the top of the page she'd written: They don't renew me. Underneath were two headings. What I'd do: ask for a reference, call the two galleries that asked about me in spring, pick up weekend shifts at the café on Leith Walk. How likely: every contract in her team had been renewed last year, and her manager had just handed her the new exhibition. Maybe one in five. Alejandro read it upside down. 'That's not a disaster. That's a Tuesday with some admin.' Freya laughed, and finished the porridge.

The 'how likely' part, because remembering last year's renewals and the new exhibition moved the risk from certain to about one in five.

During the rice-sowing rains, when the village school closed early, Aparna stood on the mud wall and announced to the goats and to Kamal, 'I am going to be a doctor. The first doctor from Pipri.' She had said it since she was small. Her grandmother said it at the well, her father said it at the tea stall, and the schoolmaster said it whenever she topped the sums. Kamal, sitting under the jackfruit tree, asked, 'Do you like blood?' Aparna blinked. 'Doctors don't have to like blood.' 'What do you like?' 'Being a doctor,' she said firmly, and jumped off the wall. Then she spent the rest of the afternoon building a tiny dam for the rainwater, completely happy, and forgot to go home.

Where did Aparna stand to make her announcement?
On the mud wall.
How does Aparna feel when she makes the announcement?
Aparna feels proud and sure, because her grandmother, father and schoolmaster all say it and nobody has questioned it.
What could an adult in Pipri do with Aparna's dam-building afternoon?
They could notice how happy she was building the dam and let her explore that too, without taking the doctor dream away.
How might Kamal see Aparna's certainty?

Bill milked his cow and got 16 gallons of milk. He turned 1/4 into sour cream, 1/4 into butter, and kept the rest as whole milk. It takes 4 gallons of milk to make one gallon of butter and 2 gallons of milk to make 1 gallon of sour cream. If Bill sells butter for $5/gallon, sour cream for $6/gallon, and whole milk for $3/gallon, how much money does he make?

First find how much milk Bill turned into sour cream and butter: 16 gallons * 1/4 = 4 gallons
Then find how many gallons of butter he makes out of 4 gallons of milk: 4 gallons milk / 4 gallons milk/1 gallon butter = 1 gallon butter
Then find how many gallons of sour cream he makes out of 4 gallons of milk: 4 gallons milk / 2 gallons milk/1 gallon sour cream = 2 gallon sour cream
Then subtract the amount of milk turned into butter and sour cream to find the remaining amount of whole milk: 16 gallons - 4 gallons - 4 gallons = 8 gallons
Then multiply the number of gallons of milk by the price of milk to find the total cost of the milk: 8 gallons * $3/gallon = $24
Then multiply the number of gallons of sour cream by the price of sour cream to find the total cost of the sour cream: 2 gallons * $6/gallon = $12
Then add the cost of the butter, sour cream and milk to find the total amount of money Bill earns: $24 + $12 + $5 = $41
The answer is 41.

Can you tell me what the narrator say about people's religions?

Now, as I before hinted, I have no objection to any person's religion, be it what it may, so long as that person does not kill or insult any other person, because that other person don't believe it also. But when a man's religion becomes really frantic; when it is a positive torment to him; and, in fine, makes this earth of ours an uncomfortable inn to lodge in; then I think it high time to take that individual aside and argue the point with him.

The narrator has no objection to any religion, as long as its follower does not kill or insult people who believe differently. But when a religion becomes frantic and a torment that makes life uncomfortable, it is time to take that person aside and argue.

In the hostel mess, Zeenat waved a printed email over the dal. "I got the exchange semester in Lisbon! Ujjwal, did you hear me?"
Ujjwal looked up from his tray. "I heard. That's big news."
"You said that like you were reading a bus timetable," she said.
"My face doesn't move much. It never has. I'm autistic, and my expressions don't always match what's going on inside."
"So... what is going on inside?"
"A lot. I'm proud of you. I'm also sad, because our Thursday study sessions will end."
"Oh. I honestly thought you didn't care."
"I care. Next time, just ask me, like you did now. Words work better for me than faces."
"Deal. Then I'm telling you in words: I'll miss Thursdays too."
"Good. I'll remember you said it."
Zeenat laughed, and the corner of Ujjwal's mouth lifted into a small, brief smile.

Where did Zeenat get an exchange semester?
In Lisbon.
What was Ujjwal feeling about Zeenat's news, even though his face stayed still?
He felt proud of her and also sad that their Thursday study sessions would end; his flat face reflected how his expressions work, not a lack of feeling.
What would you advise Zeenat for the next time a friend's face seems blank?
Ask and listen to the words, as she finally did with "what is going on inside?", instead of deciding from the face that the friend does not care. 🙂
What was it like for Zeenat before she asked?
She felt hurt and deflated, thinking her big news meant little to Ujjwal.

messages.content: Page collects fancy shoes and has 80 pairs in her closet.  She decides to donate 30% of her collection that she no longer wears.  After dropping off her donation, she treats herself and buys 6 more pairs to add to her collection.  How many shoes does she have now?

She donates 30% of her 80 pairs of shoes so that's .30*80 = 24 pair of shoes she donates
She had 80 shoes in her collection and donates 24 so that leaves 80-24 = 56 pairs of shoes
She now has 56 pairs of shoes and buys 6 more pairs so her collection is now 56+6 = 62 pairs of shoes
The answer is 62.

Warden's note, Girls' Hostel Block C, 14 March

There was tension in the common kitchen this week. A first-year complained that Maria's beef fry was in the same fridge as her vegetarian tiffin and called it "disgusting". Maria cried.

Hafsa, a second-year who is fasting for Ramzan, came to me the same evening with a plan: separate labelled shelves by diet, lids on everything, and one rule written at the top: "Respect every restriction. Nobody's food is dirty."

She said, "I don't eat pork, and I'd hate it touching my food. But I'd hate even more being called disgusting."

What I did next: I put up her notice, sat the three of them down together, and asked the first-year to apologise for the word, not the preference. She did. On Friday, Maria waited until sunset to eat so she could break the fast with Hafsa.

What rule was written at the top of Hafsa's plan?
Respect every restriction. Nobody's food is dirty.
What does Hafsa's comment about being called disgusting suggest she feels?
Hafsa feels protective and a bit indignant; she understands food limits but finds calling someone's food disgusting far more hurtful.
Why was the warden's response fair to everyone?
It kept each person's restriction with labelled shelves and lids, while asking for an apology for the insulting word, not the preference.
What was it like for Maria when Hafsa stepped in?
Maria, who had cried, likely felt supported, and showed it by waiting until sunset to eat with Hafsa.

I'm Darshan. Last winter, my friend Nandini had been sleeping all day, not answering texts. When I finally went to her hostel room, she said, "It'd be easier if I just disappeared."
I'd read that you should ask directly. My mouth went dry, but I asked. "Nandini, are you thinking of killing yourself?"
She got angry first. "Why would you say that?" Then she started crying. "Yes. I've been thinking about it a lot." And then, strangely, she looked relieved, like she'd been holding it alone for too long.
I didn't leave. I asked if there was anything in the room she'd thought of using. She pointed to a bag. I took it and handed it to the warden, who called the crisis team right away. I sat beside her until they came.
She's doing better now. Asking didn't put the idea in her head. It let her say it out loud.

Who did Darshan hand the bag to?
The warden.
How did Nandini feel when Darshan asked the question directly?
She was angry at first, then cried, then seemed relieved to finally say it out loud.
What did Darshan do after Nandini said yes, and why was it right?
Darshan stayed, removed the thing she might use and got the warden to call the crisis team, so she was never left alone in danger.
How might the warden have felt when Darshan came with the bag?
The warden probably felt alarmed but acted quickly, calling the crisis team right away.

At the government school in Hosur, the headmaster had said in the staff meeting, "Some teachers seem to think lesson plans are optional, Rukmini." Everyone looked at her. She'd submitted hers on time. At home that evening, Dhruv asked, "Did you pick up the gas cylinder slip?" and she snapped, "Do I have to do everything in this house?" He blinked. Rukmini heard her own voice. She stopped. "Sorry. That wasn't for you. The headmaster said something in the meeting and I'm still burning." Dhruv nodded. "Want to tell me?" "Not yet. I need to walk first." She walked to the temple tank and back, twice. Then she wrote down exactly what was said and her submission date. The next morning she asked the headmaster for five minutes and calmly showed him the date. He apologised.

Where did Rukmini walk?
To the temple tank and back, twice.
Why did Rukmini stop after snapping at Dhruv?
She heard her own sharpness and recognised the anger came from the headmaster's unfair remark, not from Dhruv, which made her feel sorry.
Which steps helped Rukmini aim her anger fairly?
Naming the real source, walking before replying, writing down the facts, then speaking calmly to the headmaster.
How might Dhruv feel when Rukmini apologises and explains?
Dhruv likely feels relieved and understanding, glad the snap wasn't really about him.

Jaya pressed her lips into a thin line and wrote it down.

Stopping to read and tally fifty listings, because it revealed the one missing skill instead of more blind applications.
How did the interviewer in week seven see Himani's new project?

Incubator mentor's note, 20 June.
Siddharth came in today and put a list on my desk: fifteen investor rejections since February, and in thirteen of them the same sentence about "not enough proof that hospitals will pay". He had been treating each no as bad luck. Today, for the first time, he read them together.
He said, "I've been fixing the slides. They're telling me to fix the business." He has decided to pause all investor meetings for two months and use the time to sign pilot customers.
I introduced him to two hospital administrators from our network. He will visit both next week.
Update, 2 September: Siddharth has three signed pilots, two of them paid. He has rewritten the deck to open with them and is going back to four of the investors who said no.
— Gargi

In thirteen of the fifteen.
How might Siddharth have felt reading the rejections together?
He likely felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, seeing that the investors wanted the business fixed, not the slides.
What else did the mentor do to help?
Introduced him to two hospital administrators, turning his plan into real visits.

Melissa sells a coupe for $30,000 and an SUV for twice as much. If her commission is 2%, how much money did she make from these sales?

First find the total cost of the SUV: $30,000 * 2 = $60,000
Then add the cost of the coupe to find the total cost of the cars: $60,000 + $30,000 = $90,000
Multiplying that amount by Melissa's commission rate, we find her earnings are $90,000 * 2% = $1800
The answer is 1800.

Last month Nitin trapped me by the water cooler. He kept grabbing my lunch box and laughing, and his friends blocked the way out. My heart was banging so hard I could hear it, and my face went hot. Then I shoved him hard. Later I sat in the office feeling sick with shame. I kept thinking, I'm not a pusher. I'm Dilnaz, the quiet one. Ms Rao, the counsellor, didn't shout. She asked what my body did first. I told her about my heart and hot face. "That's your body getting ready to fight," she said. "It doesn't make you a bad person." She said she would speak to Nitin's class teacher too. We practised what to do next time: step back and call a teacher.

Where did Nitin trap Dilnaz?
Nitin trapped Dilnaz by the water cooler.
How did Dilnaz feel sitting in the office afterwards?
Dilnaz felt sick with shame and confused, thinking "I'm not a pusher".
How did Ms Rao's question about the body help Dilnaz?
By asking what Dilnaz's body did first, Ms Rao helped Dilnaz see the shove as a fight reaction to being trapped, and they planned a safer step for next time.
How might Ms Rao see the shove differently from how Dilnaz first saw it?
Ms Rao sees it as a body reacting to being cornered, while Dilnaz first took it as proof of being a bad person.
What is meant by "missed the boat"?

It means you were too late to take an opportunity.
Example: By the time Zara applied, all the places in the art class were filled; she had missed the boat.
My granny describes me as headstrong. Is that a bad thing?

It can be mixed. Headstrong means determined to do things your own way and not wanting to listen to advice. It is an adjective.
Example: The headstrong horse refused to follow the path the rider chose.

Dear Yogesh,
Something happened in our lane this week that I keep thinking about. Two families fight over the common tap every summer. This Monday the fight was louder, and by evening a message was going round the lane group saying it was "their people versus ours". Photos, arrows, an old story about someone's grandfather. I got it forwarded to me six times.
I felt sick reading it. I know both families. Their kids play cricket together.
I didn't forward it. I wrote in the group, "This is about a tap, not about anyone's religion." Two people reacted with anger. One aunty messaged me privately to say thank you. Then my Nani and old Bashir chacha, who have both lived here forty years, called the two families to the temple courtyard and agreed a timetable for the tap.
It's calmer. I'm still shaky.
Disha

Where did Nani and Bashir chacha call the two families?
To the temple courtyard.
How did Disha feel reading the forwarded messages, and why?
Disha felt sick and upset, because Disha knows both families and their children play cricket together.
What could others in the lane group have done to help?
They could refuse to forward the message, add a calm reply like Disha's, and support the elders' meeting instead of taking sides.
How might the aunty who messaged privately have felt?
She was probably uneasy about the messages too but nervous to speak publicly, and relieved and grateful that someone did.

Arnold owns three cars. The first car averages 50 miles per gallon of gas. The second car averages 10 miles per gallon of gas. And the third car averages 15 miles per gallon of gas. He splits his 450-mile monthly driving mileage equally amongst his three cars.  If gas costs $2 per gallon, how much does he spend on gas each month?

He drives each vehicle 150 miles because 450 / 3 = 150
The first car will need 3 gallons of gas because 150 / 50 = 3
The second car will need 15 gallons of gas because 150 / 10 = 15
The third car will need 10 gallons of gas because 150 / 15 = 10
He will need 28 gallons in total because 3 + 15 + 10 = 28
This will cost him $56 because 28 x $2 = $56
The answer is 56.

Anu measured the length of a spring (cm) with different masses (kg) hanging on it: (2, 5), (3, 7), (4, 9), (5, 11), (6, 20), (7, 15), (8, 17). Which point is an outlier? What should she do about it?

Answer: (6, 20) is an outlier: the pattern says about 13 cm for 6 kg.

Look at the pattern: each extra kilogram adds 2 cm (5, 7, 9, 11, ..., 15, 17), so the points lie on the line y = 2x + 1. For 6 kg the pattern gives 2 x 6 + 1 = 13 cm, but she recorded 20 cm, 7 cm too much. On a scatter graph this point sits far above the others. What to do: first CHECK it; perhaps she misread 13 as 20, or the spring was stretched too far. Measure again if possible. If it is a mistake, leave it out; if it is genuine, keep it and mention it, but do not let it drag the line of best fit upwards. Common mistake: deleting every point that does not fit, just to make the graph look nice; that is dishonest.

Remy sold 55 bottles of soda in the morning. Nick sold six fewer bottles of soda than Remy. The price per bottle is $.50. If their total evening sales are $55, how much more did they earn in the evening than in the morning?

Nick sold 55 - 6 = 49 bottles of soda in the morning.
They sold 55 + 49 = 104 bottles of soda altogether.
They earned a total of 104 x $.50 = $52 in the morning.
So, they earned $55 - $52 = $3 more in the evening than in the morning.
The answer is 3.

Sit, Anand. They made you team lead today, so let an old man tell you what I did when I got my first crew at the printing press. I was twenty-five, younger than most of them. Old Joseph, who ran the big machine, told me on my first day, "Everyone turns into a small king. Watch yourself." So I did three things. Every Friday I asked each man, "What did my decisions cost you this week?" Once it was a missed train, once a lost weekend. I fixed what I could. I kept Joseph close, even though he argued with me in front of everyone, and I thanked him for it. And when the owner praised a rush job, I said the names of the men who stayed up. Tarun Sir, they called me. I made sure it never went to my head.

He said everyone turns into a small king and told him to watch himself.

He wanted someone honest enough to disagree, because he was afraid of drifting into self-importance as Joseph had warned.

Asking each week what Anand's decisions cost the team keeps Anand curious about the people below, so problems like a missed train get fixed.

Two hours means 2 * 60 = 120 minutes.

So on average Xavier can score 8 * 2 = 16 goals.
The answer is 16.

messages.content: Andrew works in a company that provides a generous vacation allotment: for every 10 days worked, you get 1 vacation day. If last year Andrew worked 300 days and took 5 days off in March and twice as many in September, how many more vacation days can Andrew still take?

If for every 10 days worked Andrew earns 1 day of vacation, then over 300 days worked he would have earned 300/10=30 days of vacation
We know he took 5 days off in March and that in September twice as much. That means in September he took 5*2=10 days off
In total, Andrew has used 5 vacation days in March and another 10 in September. Therefore, he has used 5+10=15 vacation days
If Andrew earned 30 days of vacation but has only used 15, then he can still take another 30-15=15 days off
The answer is 15.

messages.content: At a James Bond movie party, each guest is either male (M) or female (F. 40% of the guests are women, 80% of the women are wearing rabbit ears, and 60% of the males are wearing rabbit ears. If the total number of guests at the party is 200, given all this information, what is the total number of people wearing rabbit ears?

If 40% of the guests are females, then there are 40/100*200 = 80 female guests at the party.
The number of female guests wearing rabbit ears is 80/100* 80=64
The number of male guests is 200 guests - 80 female guests = 120.
If 60% of the male guests are wearing rabbit ears, then there are 60/100 *120 = 72 male guests wearing rabbit ears.
The total number of guests wearing rabbit ears is 64+72 = 136
The answer is 136.

At the beginning of the day, Principal Kumar instructed Harold to raise the flag up the flagpole.  The flagpole is 60 feet long, and when fully raised, the flag sits on the very top of the flagpole.  Later that morning, Vice-principal Zizi instructed Harold to lower the flag to half-mast.  So, Harold lowered the flag halfway down the pole.   Later, Principal Kumar told Harold to raise the flag to the top of the pole once again, and Harold did just that.  At the end of the day, Vice-principal Zizi instructed Harold to completely lower the flag, take it off of the pole, and put it away for the evening.  Over the course of the day, how far, in feet, had the flag moved up and down the pole?

Half of the distance up the flagpole is 60/2 = 30 feet.
Thus, Harold moved the flag 60 up + 30 down + 30 up + 60 down = 180 feet.
The answer is 180.

"We put our girls and their girls in one hall for an hour. No task, just 'mingle.' Ours sat on one side, theirs on the other. Then one of ours said their school didn't even have a proper lab, and it got nasty." "So mixing made it worse." "Mixing like that did. Nobody had a reason to need anyone. And our girls were introduced as the 'hosts', as if they were doing them a favour." "What would you do instead?" Himani set down her cup. "Mixed teams, a real job, a heritage walk they plan together, equal roles. And both principals standing there saying it matters." "Write it up. I'll sign it."

How long were the two schools' girls put in one hall?
An hour.
Why does Himani think the friendship day failed?
Himani thinks nobody had a reason to need anyone, and calling one side 'hosts' made it unequal, so the contact only hardened the split.
What does Himani plan instead, and why should it work better?
Mixed teams planning a heritage walk together with equal roles and both principals backing it, so students work as equals toward a shared aim.
How might the visiting school's girls have felt being treated as guests receiving a favour?
They may have felt looked down on and defensive, which made the remark about the lab cut deeper and kept them on their side of the hall.

After a whole day helping with the harvest in the fields outside the village, Siddharth dragged himself into the courtyard, covered in dust.
His grandmother called from the kitchen, "Siddharth, fetch water from the hand pump!"
"Ugh," he said loudly, and flopped onto the charpai.
Aaji came out, frowning, ladle in hand. "Ugh? Is that how you answer me?"
His cousin Eshaan snorted.
Siddharth sat up. "Sorry, Aaji. That wasn't at you. It's been such a long day, my arms are dead. I'll go."
Aaji's frown softened. "Long day, hm? Drink some buttermilk first. Then water."
Siddharth grinned and went for the buttermilk. Eshaan fetched the first bucket instead.

What did Aaji tell Siddharth to drink first?
Buttermilk.
What was Siddharth feeling when he said "Ugh"?
Siddharth felt exhausted after the long day in the fields, not rude or angry at Aaji.
What did Siddharth do that cleared up the misunderstanding?
He added a few words explaining it was a long day and that the ugh wasn't at Aaji.
How did Aaji first read Siddharth's "Ugh"?
Aaji first took it as rudeness, then softened when she heard he was just tired.

Every tiffin hour at the design studio in Pune had turned into the same quiz. "Abhinav, twenty-two now, no? Time to look at a few biodatas," said Mr. Kulkarni from accounts, and two others nodded. Abhinav, who had joined only four months earlier, opened his mouth to say "Send me one, sir," just to end the subject. He stopped when he heard how tired the sentence sounded. Sangeeta, the senior editor, put down her spoon. "Sir, he'll tell us when there's news. Could you pass the pickle?" Later, at the water cooler, she said quietly, "They mean well. But you don't owe anyone an answer by Diwali." Abhinav nodded, surprised at how much lighter his shoulders felt.

Who asked Abhinav about biodatas at the tiffin table?
Mr. Kulkarni from accounts asked, and two others nodded.
Why was Abhinav about to say "Send me one, sir"?
He was tired of the topic and wanted the questions to stop. He felt hurried, not ready, and nearly agreed just for peace.
Which choice kept Abhinav from a hurried yes, and what could he say himself next time?
He stopped when he heard how tired his own sentence sounded, and Sangeeta backed him up. Next time he could politely say he will share news when there is any and change the subject.
What might Sangeeta have been thinking when she spoke up?
She probably saw that Abhinav was cornered and did not want him to agree just to end it, while still accepting that Mr. Kulkarni meant well.

Two weeks before semester exams, Vishal looked at the screen-time report on his phone: five hours a day, mostly one racing game. His classmate Nazia, sitting next to him in the canteen, whistled. "That's a part-time job." Back in his room at the hostel in Bengaluru, Vishal did two things. He deleted the game, not just logged out. Then he handed his charger to his roommate, Abhay. "Keep this at night. Give it back at seven in the morning, even if I beg." Abhay grinned and tucked it into his own drawer. The first night Vishal reached for his phone at eleven, saw the battery at 12 percent, sighed and opened his circuits notes instead. By the end of the week his notes were finally complete.

How many hours a day was Vishal spending on his phone?
Five hours a day, mostly one racing game.
How did Vishal feel when he reached for his phone at eleven the first night?
He felt tempted and a little frustrated, sighing when he saw the low battery, before turning to his notes.
What else could Vishal do to make study the easy choice?
Keep his books open on the desk at night and study in the library, where the game isn't even on his mind.
How might Abhay see his role?
Abhay seems amused and willing to help, taking the job of charger-keeper seriously.

I'm Ashwin, and I share a coworking desk with Deepika, so I've watched her work with a lot of clients. Farida is the one who makes her Fridays lighter.

On Friday morning Farida's payment had already arrived before Deepika opened her laptop. The brief sent with it was two pages, clear, with the audience and the deadline listed. When Deepika sent the first draft, Farida replied within the hour: "Great start. Section 3 needs a stronger example, and please tell me if that's more than the time you had budgeted."

Deepika said, "It's a little more, actually. I can do it by Monday."

"Perfect," Farida wrote. "And I'll mention your name in the launch post."

Deepika grinned, sent the revision on Sunday night, a day early, and I heard her humming as she packed up.

When had Farida's payment arrived?
Farida's payment had already arrived before Deepika opened her laptop on Friday morning.
What might Deepika have felt reading Farida's brief and replies, and how does the observer know?
Deepika seemed relaxed and pleased, since Ashwin saw her humming and sending work early, though Ashwin cannot be certain what she felt.
How does Deepika keep the good working relationship going?
Deepika is honest about the extra time needed and delivers reliably, even a day early, so both sides keep small promises.
How might Farida see working with Deepika?
Farida probably values a freelancer who is honest about limits and reliable, which is why the brief is clear and credit is given.

I'm Yusuf, and I'm the friend with the camera. Over the years I've lent it to half my college batch for weddings and projects, and I've covered shoots for friends who couldn't afford a photographer. I never kept a list. It felt good. But with my cousin Shalini, something changed. She borrowed it for eight shoots in a year, all paid work for her, and it came back twice with a cracked lens cap and once with the battery dead and no charger. She never offered to share the cost. When she called last month, "Yusuf bhai, one more shoot?", for a ninth time, my chest went tight; I hate disappointing family. I took a breath and said, calmly, "Shalini, I'm not lending it for paid shoots any more. You've used it a lot and never looked after it. I'm glad to help you learn to use one, though." She was annoyed for a week. I still lend it to others.

How many shoots did Shalini borrow the camera for in a year?
She borrowed it for eight shoots in a year.
What was Yusuf feeling when Shalini called the ninth time?
His chest went tight because he hates disappointing family, yet he knew the pattern had to stop.
Which part of Yusuf's reply made it a fair limit rather than a punishment?
He named the exact problem calmly and offered other help, so it was a clear limit on paid shoots, not cutting her off.
How might Shalini see the refusal once her annoyance fades?
She may realise she took the camera for granted and that her cousin still cares, since he offered to help her learn.

At Ramesh's small shop in the kasba, Tanvir stood at the counter with his mother. Ramesh held up a toffee. "Toffee, Tanvir?"
Tanvir shook his head, "No!" while reaching out a hand.
Ramesh laughed. "No, but yes?" He held up two. "Orange or green?"
Tanvir stopped, looked carefully and nodded at the green one. "Dat."

Which toffee did Tanvir choose?
The green one.
What was Tanvir feeling when he said "No!" while reaching out?
He wanted the toffee but also enjoyed saying no, which gave him a feeling of control rather than real refusal.
How did Ramesh honour Tanvir's need for control?

Amma pulled a crumpled paper from the bottom of Jahnavi's bag. "Science test. Nineteen out of twenty? Why is this crushed like a peanut wrapper?"
Jahnavi, ten, kept her eyes on her rice. "No reason."
"Last month you stuck your prize certificate on the fridge."

A long pause. "Rafiq and them call me Show-off Jahnavi now. Every time Ma'am reads the marks, they go 'ooooh' and clap slowly."
"So you hide your papers."
"If nobody sees, they forget. Yesterday I said I got twelve. They let me sit with them."
Amma sat down beside her. "And how did twelve feel?"
Jahnavi shrugged, and her eyes filled.

What mark did Jahnavi get in the science test?
Nineteen out of twenty.
What did Jahnavi want when claiming to have got twelve?
Jahnavi wanted to be accepted again and sit with the group without being called a show-off.
Amma's question "And how did twelve feel?" opens a door. What could Amma do next?
Amma could listen to how hurt and lonely Jahnavi feels, and then speak with the class teacher about the slow clapping, rather than just telling Jahnavi to be proud.
How might Rafiq see the "ooooh" and the slow clapping?
Rafiq may think it is just a joke and not see how much it hurts, or may feel a little envious of Jahnavi's marks.

What was yesterday's top headline?

Three years ago, Bethany was twice the age of her younger sister. In 5 years, her younger sister will be 16. How old is Bethany now?

First find how old Bethany's sister currently is: 16 years - 5 years = 11 years
Then find how old her sister was 3 years ago: 11 years - 3 years = 8 years
Then double that age to find how old Bethany was three years ago: 8 years * 2 = 16 years
Then add 3 years to that number to find how old Bethany is now: 16 years + 3 years = 19 years
The answer is 19.

Wednesday night.
Third day this week I skipped breakfast so I could sleep twenty extra minutes. By second period my head felt full of cotton. In maths Anjali asked me to pass the compass and I snapped, "Take it yourself." She looked at me like I'd slapped her. At eleven I read the same line of the chemistry notes four times and it still meant nothing. My stomach growled so loudly in the test that the boy behind me laughed. At lunch I ate everything and felt normal again, almost silly for how grumpy I'd been. Tonight I asked Ma to wake me at 6:40 and I've put a banana and a box of poha on the table myself. Easier than being a monster by noon. Need to say sorry to Anjali tomorrow.
Arnab

Monday. Aparna paid a "registration fee" for a work-from-home job that promised a quick start, using most of her savings. By evening the messages stopped and the number was dead. She sat on her bed, feeling stupid and sick.
Tuesday. She told her brother Akash, expecting him to scold her. Instead he said, "They do this for a living. They aim at hope, not at stupid people." He sat beside her while she called the cyber helpline and reported everything, and later he told their parents with her.
The next Sunday. Aparna wrote in her college group what had happened and how the offer looked, so others could spot it. Two classmates thanked her. She still ached over the loss, but the shame had shrunk.

Whom did Aparna tell on Tuesday?
She told her brother Akash.
Why did Aparna feel stupid on Monday evening?
She had lost most of her savings to a fake job offer and blamed herself for falling for it.
What steps did Aparna take that could help her and others?
She reported it to the cyber helpline right away, told her family, and shared her story so other students could recognise the offer.
How might Akash have felt when Aparna told him?
Akash did not scold her, and said scammers aim at hope, not at stupid people. He seems to have felt protective and wanted to make her feel less alone. 🤍

It was eleven at night before the chemistry board exam, and the group video call was buzzing. Jatin said someone had "the paper" and was sharing a link. "Everyone's doing it, Rashmi. Don't be stupid." Rashmi's heart was pounding. She was tired, the power had just gone off, and her notes were half-revised by torchlight. Part of her wanted the link just to stop feeling behind. But she thought about the version of herself she liked: the one who earned her marks. "I'm going to sleep," she said. "Good luck." She left the call, set her alarm for five and revised by candlelight in the morning. The "paper" turned out to be fake. Half the call had studied the wrong questions.

When was the group call?
At eleven at night, before the chemistry board exam.
Why was Rashmi tempted by the link?
She was tired, behind in revision and the power had gone, so the link promised relief from feeling unprepared.

She took him to the tap and rinsed the dirt off with clean water, then pressed a clean hanky on it. Then she said, "Where's your Amma? Let's find her." She carried him to his mother on the bench. You know what, Neelam, I'll tell you why I was so weird all last month. I'm Keerthana, your best friend, so I'm allowed one weird month a year. Appa kept leaving at nine in his office shirt, same as always. But one afternoon I saw him on the bench at the bus depot at two o'clock, just sitting. And he'd stopped asking about my dance fees, which he never forgets. I knew something was wrong, but he kept smiling at dinner like a TV dad. I was angry at first, honestly. Why lie? Then I thought, it's pride, and it's because he loves me. So one night I made him tea and said, 'Appa, I saw you at the depot. You don't have to act for me. I'm old enough.' He went quiet, then told me his company had shut. I said I'd pause dance till things settle, and he cried a bit. Now we talk. It's better.

On the bench at the bus depot, just sitting.
