Keerthana felt angry and hurt at first, wondering why Appa would lie.
What did Keerthana say that helped Appa open up?
Over tea, Keerthana gently said Appa didn't have to act, and offered to pause dance without blaming him.
Why might Appa have kept leaving in his office shirt?
Out of pride and love, wanting to protect his child from worry about the company shutting.

Monday. Hrithik came back from the under-16 trial match with 4 runs off 30 balls. He had edged two, missed three, and been bowled trying a wild swing. At home, his older brother Irfan ruffled his hair. "Superb, yaar. You looked like a proper opener." Hrithik grinned and slept well.
Saturday. The selection list went up on the club board. His name wasn't there. He read it three times. "But everyone said I was batting well," he told Irfan, confused. Irfan looked at the floor.
The next Wednesday, after nets, Hrithik sat beside his brother on the steps. "Bhaiya, you watched every ball. Tell me the truth. What went wrong?"
Irfan took a breath. "Your feet don't move to the short ones. You swing at everything outside off."
It stung. But for the first time in weeks, Hrithik knew what to practise.

How many runs did Hrithik score in the trial match?
He scored 4 runs off 30 balls.
What was Hrithik feeling when he read the selection list?
He felt confused and let down, because everyone had said he was batting well, so the missing name made no sense to him.
Which choice worked for Hrithik, and why?
Asking Irfan directly for the truth worked, because a specific note about his feet and wild swings gave him something real to practise.
Why might Irfan have said "superb" after the trial?
Irfan probably wanted to protect his younger brother's mood, but his looking at the floor later shows he knows the praise did not help.

I'm Parveen, and when I was nine, our class went on a trip to the hill fort. That evening I told everyone in my building, "There were a HUNDRED monkeys! One stole Mridul's sandwich and ran up the wall!"
The little kids gasped. Even the watchman laughed. I felt like the most exciting person in the whole colony.
Then Mridul came down with his cricket bat and said, "It was six monkeys. And it stole a banana."
Everyone looked at me. My face went hot. I said, "It felt like a hundred!" and ran upstairs.
Later, Ammi asked why I was sulking. I told her. She laughed kindly and said, "You wanted them to feel how exciting it was. Next time, say 'so many monkeys, it felt like a hundred.' Then it's a story, not a trick."
I still say that now.

How many monkeys did Mridul say there were?
It was six monkeys.
Why did Parveen's face go hot when Mridul spoke?
Parveen felt embarrassed, because the exciting story had been exposed in front of everyone who had just been listening.
What did Ammi suggest Parveen could say next time?
Ammi suggested saying "so many monkeys, it felt like a hundred," so the story stays exciting without tricking anyone.
How might Mridul have felt hearing the hundred-monkey story?
Mridul may have felt a bit annoyed or left out, since he was there and knew it wasn't true, and his banana became a sandwich.

When the head teacher announced at assembly in the Valencia school that the library would close at lunch to save staff hours, Pablo rolled his eyes so hard Emil could practically hear it. For a week he sighed through every lesson and answered teachers in one word, and on Wednesday he stuck a sign reading BOOKS ARE NOT A LUXURY on the library door. A teacher took it down and gave him a warning. "You're angry, fine," Emil said at the bus stop. "But right now you're just the guy with the sign." Pablo kicked a stone. "Nobody asked us. That's what I hate." So they asked. Over the weekend they collected signatures from 212 students and three teachers, and wrote a one-page letter suggesting older students could volunteer at the desk. On Monday Pablo read it at the school council, voice shaking a little. The head didn't say yes. She said, "Let's trial it for a month."

- Pablo was angry that the school library would close at lunch and protested with a sign, which got him a warning.
- His friend Emil helped him ask other students and teachers instead, and they wrote a letter suggesting older students could volunteer at the desk.
- Pablo read the letter to the school council, and the head agreed to a one-month trial.

messages.content: Ben has four boxes with ten basketball cards in each box. His mother gave him five boxes with eight baseball cards.  If he gives 58 cards to his classmates, how many cards does he has left?

Ben has 4 x 10 = 40 basketball cards.
His mother gave him 5 x 8 = 40 baseball cards.
Thus, Ben has 40 + 40 = 80 cards in all.
Therefore, Ben has 80 - 58 = 22 cards left.
The answer is 22.

Asif, come here. I'm Aadhya, your Bua, and you're worried about your classmate who failed the entrance test, so let me tell you what I learned. When I was twenty-three my friend Sunil failed his exam for the second time. He stopped answering calls. I wrote him three long messages full of advice and got no reply. Then my mother said, "Go and sit with him." I went and said nothing clever. I brought vada pav, and we watched the street from his steps. After an hour he said, "I feel useless." I only nodded. Over the next weeks I carried his notebooks to the library and sat beside him. When he still could not sleep months later, I asked if he would try the college counsellor, and he did.

What might it have been like for Sunil when a friend simply sat beside him?
Relieving, since it was after sitting with Aadhya for an hour that Sunil said "I feel useless".

Uday, you asked about my first big speech, so here it is. I'm Tarun, and I used to be the kid who'd pretend to be sick on presentation days.
Class 11, I had to give a talk at the science fair opening. Two hundred people. I wrote the whole thing out, word for word, and on the morning I couldn't remember line one.
My teacher said, "Forget the script. What's the one thing you want them to remember?" I said, "That the river near our school is dying." She said, "Start there."
So I did. I started with a photo of the river. I told them what I'd seen, then what we could do. I didn't read anything.
My voice shook for the first minute. Then people started nodding, and I forgot to be scared. That's when I learnt: people don't need you perfect. They need you clear.

How many people were at the science fair opening?
Two hundred people.
What was Tarun feeling on the morning he couldn't remember line one?
Tarun felt panicked and anxious, with the fully written script failing him.
What choice inside the story turned Tarun's speech around?
Dropping the script and starting from the one thing Tarun wanted people to remember, the dying river, with a photo.
How might Tarun's teacher have seen the speech?
The teacher probably felt proud, seeing Tarun connect with the audience once the talk came from what Tarun cared about.

In Marseille, Fatima found a notice in the bakery window: "Weekend help wanted, early mornings." She was fifteen. The bakery was a ten-minute walk from home.

At dinner she told her parents. Her father, Sami, didn't say no. He said, "Let's look at the rules together first."

After dinner they sat at the laptop and read the official government page about work for under-sixteens. There were limits: only light work, only during school holidays, a maximum number of hours, and a parent's written consent.

"Early mornings," her mother said. "How early?"

Mindy has 7 less than 9 times as many emails waiting for her as phone messages. If she has a total of 93 emails and phone messages combined, how many emails does she have?

Let e be the number of emails Mindy has and m be the number of phone messages? We know that e + m = 93 and e = 9m - 7.
Substituting the second equation into the first equation, we get 9m - 7 + m = 93
Combining like terms, we get 10m - 7 = 93
Adding 7 to both sides of the equation, we get 10m = 100
Dividing both sides by 10, we get m = 10
Substituting this value back into the equation e = 9m - 7, we get e = 9 * 10 - 7 = 90 - 7 = 83
The answer is 83.

In their Bengaluru PG room, Uma noticed it for the third time on Thursday. Their friend Gauri, visiting, teased Jaya about the messy desk: "Are you deaf? I called you three times!" She laughed as she said it. Jaya went rigid, cheeks tight, and snapped, "Don't talk to me like that," then walked out. Gauri stared, hurt. "It was a joke!" Uma had seen the same thing twice before, at exactly those words. Jaya herself had once said, puzzled, "I don't know why that line makes me so angry." Uma didn't chase her or ask what had happened in the past. Later, bringing two cups of tea to the balcony, she said, "I noticed that phrase really gets to you. You don't have to explain. Want me to tell Gauri quietly to skip it?" Jaya let out a breath. "Yes. Thanks."

"Are you deaf? I called you three times!"

Uma didn't dig for a story from Jaya's past, which respected Jaya's privacy and still offered practical help.

messages.content: Thomas wants to throw a party for his best friend Casey. He needs to order enough chairs for all the party guests to sit in, one for each guest. First he orders 3 dozen chairs for 3 dozen guests he invites. Then he finds out that 1/3 of the guests want to bring a guest of their own, so Thomas needs to order more chairs. Eventually, Thomas finds out that 5 of the guests he originally invited can't make it. Thomas would also like to order 12 extra chairs just in case they need them. How many chairs is Thomas going to order for Casey's party?

Thomas originally orders chairs for 3 dozen guests, 12 x 3 = 36 guests
Thomas finds out that 1/3 of the guests want to bring a guest of their own, 1/3 of 36 = 12
The 12 guests bring a guest of their own each, 36 guests + 12 guests = 48
Thomas finds out that 20 of the guests can't make it, 48 guests - 5 guests = 43
Thomas wants to order an extra 12 chairs, 43 + 12 = 55
Thomas will need 55 chairs for the party.
The answer is 55.

Milly is figuring out how long she needs to spend studying. She knows that her math homework will take 60 minutes. Her geography homework will take half as long as her math homework, and her science homework will take time equal to the mean amount of time she spent studying math and geography. How many minutes does Milly spend studying?

First find how long Milly spends studying geography by dividing her math homework time by 2: 60 minutes / 2 = 30 minutes.
Now find the total amount of time Milly spent on math and geography: 30 minutes + 60 minutes = 90 minutes.
Now calculate the mean amount of time Milly spends on math and geography by dividing the total time spent by the number of subjects, which is 2: 90 minutes / 2 = 45 minutes.
Now add the time Milly spent on all three subjects to find the total: 45 minutes + 30 minutes + 60 minutes = 135 minutes.
The answer is 135.

In his first month as an intern at the Pune office of a German engineering firm, Vijay kept waiting to be told what to do. In meetings he nodded at everything. When his supervisor, Klaus, said, "This design is wrong, the tolerances are too loose," Vijay felt humiliated. In his old college, a teacher would never say it so bluntly in front of others.
Alka, a senior engineer who'd worked there five years, found him in the pantry. "He's not insulting you. That's how they talk here. Direct. He'd be confused if you just nodded."
"So I should argue?"
"Not argue. Say what you think, clearly. Ask when you don't know."
In the next meeting, Vijay said, "I chose these tolerances because of cost. Would tighter ones be worth it?" Klaus looked surprised, then pleased. They discussed it for ten minutes.

Speaking up clearly with his reasons and asking questions, instead of silently nodding, fitted the direct style of the office.
How might Klaus have seen Vijay's silent nodding in the first month?
Klaus may have been confused, not knowing whether Vijay agreed or understood, since he expects people to speak up.

At the inter-school cricket match, I sat two rows behind Asif. He was the one who started the rhythm: bang the plastic bottles twice, clap once, shout our school's name. Soon the whole stand was doing it, and Asif was grinning so wide you could see his missing tooth.

messages.content: Baking in batches of 65 cupcakes, Carla made 45 batches of cupcakes for her daughter's birthday party. She then took 5 cupcakes from each batch, and fed them to her dogs. If Carla's daughter had 19 friends and they shared the remaining cupcakes equally among them, including the daughter, calculate the number of cupcakes that each of Carla's daughter's friends ate.

If Carla sampled 5 cupcakes from each batch and fed them to her dogs, each batch had 65-5 = 60 cupcakes afterwards.
Since Carla made 45 batches of cupcakes for her daughter's birthday party, after removing the 5 cupcakes from each batch, Carla's daughter and her friends received 45*60 = 2700 cupcakes.
The total number of people at the party is 19 friends + 1 daughter = 20
After sharing the cupcakes equally among them, Carla's daughter and her friends each received 2700/20 = 135 cupcakes
The answer is 135.

(1) What does "no stone left unturned" mean?
(2) Can you tell me what "falsity" means?
(3) What is the meaning of reticence?
(4) Correct this sentence: Few days ago, I met an old friend.
(5) Spot the error: Everyone have finished their lunch.

1. It means that every possible effort was made. For example: the team left no stone unturned in preparing for the final.
2. Falsity is a noun that means the quality of being untrue.
3. As a noun, "reticence" means a tendency to keep your thoughts to yourself.
4. Correct form: A few days ago, I met an old friend. Why: "a few" means some, while "few" alone means almost none.
5. It should be: Everyone has finished their lunch. Why: "everyone" is singular, so it takes "has".

At eleven I open email and messages and answer everything in one go, maybe twenty minutes. Then a proper break: I walk to the tea stall and back without my phone. Then another block, on a different document.
Last year I kept the chat open "just in case" and jumped at every ping. I thought I was being responsive. My work had silly errors and my evenings were gone. Now I finish by five, and not one client has complained about waiting till eleven.
Try one block tomorrow. Just one.
Ritu

What does Ritu do at eleven?
Opens email and messages and answers everything in one go, maybe twenty minutes.
Why did Ritu once feel keeping the chat open was the right thing?
Jumping at every ping felt responsive and professional, so Ritu didn't see how much it was costing in errors and lost evenings.
What single step does Ritu suggest Zubin try first, and why start small?
One focused block tomorrow; trying just one lets Zubin feel the difference without changing a whole working day at once.
How have Ritu's clients been affected by the change?
They get fewer errors and haven't complained about waiting until eleven, so the focused blocks seem to have helped them too.

Dear Salma,
Remember in Class 8, when you joined our school, I asked if people in Afghanistan lived in tents? You said, "Some do. My family had a flat with a balcony and a lemon tree," and walked off. I thought you were rude.
This term, for our geography project, I read about why families leave their countries: war, work, danger. I watched an interview with a girl who had to leave her school behind. I thought about you, and the lemon tree.
I'm sorry for that question. I wasn't trying to be mean, but I only knew one picture.
I'd really like to hear about your city, if you want to tell me. What did your old street sound like in the morning? And do you miss the lemons?
From your old bench partner,
Akash

What did Salma's family have at their flat?
A balcony and a lemon tree.
How does Akash feel now about the Class 8 question?
Akash feels sorry and a bit ashamed, realising it came from knowing only one picture of Afghanistan.
What would you advise Akash while waiting for Salma's reply?
Be patient, listen without assumptions, and accept whatever Salma chooses to share, or not.
How might Salma have felt when Akash asked about tents?
Salma probably felt hurt and misunderstood, seen only as a stereotype instead of a person with a home.

Community centre note, written by Kishore.
Parveen has come to our Thursday tea evenings for two years. When the subject of the blocked drain outside the lane came up, she said, "Forget it. They've ignored it for five years. Nothing changes." Others nodded, and the room went quiet.
I did not argue. I asked if she would sign one page with twenty other names, asking for a written reply. She said no at first, then took the pen. We sent it that week. The ward office replied within days and cleared part of the drain. Parveen said, "Only part." But she came the following Thursday and brought the second page for the neighbours to sign.

How long has Parveen been coming to the Thursday tea evenings?
Parveen has come for two years.
What was Parveen feeling when she said 'Forget it. Nothing changes'?
Parveen felt weary and discouraged after years of being ignored, though the note only records what she said.
What did Kishore do that helped move Parveen from cynicism to a small action?
Kishore did not argue but asked her to sign one shared page asking for a written reply, and sent it the same week.
How might Kishore see Parveen's words 'Only part'?
Kishore probably saw them as Parveen's usual caution rather than a refusal, since the note records that she came back the next Thursday with the second page.

Ten minutes into a rainy Sunday, Chaitanya stood at the sofa with drooping shoulders. "I'm bored. What do I do? Can I have the tablet?" Papa Sumit did not reach for it. He slid over an empty cardboard box, some tape and a pair of blunt scissors. After a grumble, Chaitanya cut a door into the box, then a window, and by lunch the box was a bus with a very serious driver.
By nine, Chaitanya was reading books meant for much older children and asking questions about how stars burn. In class the lessons felt slow, and Chaitanya rubbed out drawings that were not exactly right. At break the other children were playing kabaddi, and Chaitanya stood at the edge of the game, unsure how to join. Mummy Neelam found the fine marks and the long silences at home. That evening she skipped the quiz about facts and sat on the floor with a board game. "Your turn," she said. Chaitanya laughed for the first time all week, and lost happily.

What did Papa Sumit give Chaitanya instead of the tablet?
He gave Chaitanya an empty cardboard box, some tape and a pair of blunt scissors.
How does the rainy Sunday at age five connect to the picture of Chaitanya at nine?

At five, Chaitanya said bored and asked for the tablet, but with a cardboard box, tape and time the box became a bus. At nine, Chaitanya was reading books for older children yet felt bored in class, rubbed out drawings and stood at the edge of the game, so Mummy skipped the quiz and played a board game with the whole child.
What was Chaitanya feeling while standing at the edge of the kabaddi game?
Chaitanya felt shy and left out, wanting to join in but not knowing how to begin.
What would you advise Mummy Neelam to do to help Chaitanya find friends?
She could arrange a small, easy play meet-up with one or two children around a game Chaitanya enjoys, and keep making time for play and comfort at home.
What does expansion mean when a shop talks about it?

Expansion is the act of becoming larger or spreading to more places. It is a noun. A shop with an expansion plan wants to get bigger.
Example: The bakery's expansion included a second shop near the bus stand.
Turn these notes into a full sentence: Library - closed Monday - reopen Tuesday 10 am - new timings.
The library will be closed on Monday and will reopen on Tuesday at 10 a.m. with new timings.
Now you try: how many ways to climb 8 stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time?
The answer is 34.

Read this:

You want to know about managing new people? I'm Vandana, and I'll tell you about Ritu. Ritu joined our design team straight out of college. Brilliant portfolio. By her second week I noticed she was working till nine every night on one poster. She'd redone it five times. I asked how it was going. "Fine, almost there." Next day, same poster. I finally sat with her and asked what she thought the brief wanted. She had misread it completely, and she'd known something was wrong for days. "I didn't want you to regret hiring me," she said. It took me ten minutes to clarify. Now I check in with every new hire on day three, whether they ask or not.

How many times had Ritu redone the poster?
She had redone it five times.
What was Vandana feeling after hearing why Ritu didn't ask?
Vandana felt a mix of sympathy and regret, realising fear, not laziness, had kept Ritu stuck for days.
What change did Vandana make, and why does it help?
A check-in with every new hire on day three, so no one has to find the courage to ask first.
What was it like for Ritu during those days?
Ritu was anxious and exhausted, working till nine every night and afraid the team would regret hiring her.
Martine has 6 more than twice as many peaches as Benjy. Benjy has one-third as many peaches as Gabrielle. If Martine has 16 peaches, how many does Gabrielle have?

Benjy has b peaches.
Martine has 6+2b=16 peaches
2b=10
b=5
Then Gabrielle has 5*3=15.
The answer is 15.

Shankar: hey, saw you in the bank queue again today. everything ok?
Jasleen: yeah, just sending something to Ethan. his parcel is stuck at customs
Shankar: the one posted overseas with the army? isn't this the third time?
Jasleen: fourth. but he'll pay it all back when he lands, he promised
Shankar: I'm not judging, I promise. can I ask a few things?
Jasleen: ok
Shankar: have you two ever video called? has anyone you know met him?
Jasleen: his camera's broken. and he's very private
Shankar: I read up on this after my cousin lost money. it's usually not one lonely guy. it's whole teams with scripts, fake photos, shifts. they're very good at it
Shankar: it's not about you being careless. they do this for a living
Jasleen: ...he did use the exact same line about his mother twice
Shankar: want to talk to the bank manager together tomorrow, before you send anything else? I'll come

How many times has Jasleen sent money to Ethan?
Four times.
What seems to be driving Shankar's careful questions?
Shankar seems worried but careful not to shame Jasleen, promising not to judge and explaining that the people behind this do it for a living.
Why is asking questions better than scolding here?
Questions let Jasleen notice the gaps, like the broken camera and the repeated line, without feeling blamed, and lead to a concrete step: the bank manager together.
How might Jasleen feel as the doubts sink in?
Jasleen may feel shaken and embarrassed on noticing the repeated line about Ethan's mother, but less alone because Shankar offers to come.

Ira: why?? you love swimming

Chetan: feels embarrassing

Chetan is skipping the pool party.

Chetan feels inadequate and worse each time, so much that it fills the whole day.
Why does Ira suggest the counsellor?
Because Chetan's body thoughts have taken over the day, even in class, which is a sign to get help.
How might Ira feel reading that Chetan checks the mirror so often?
Ira may feel worried and caring, wanting Chetan to get support rather than suffer alone.
Write a short story, around 100 words, for kids about a boy who lights a diya for the first time and learns to be careful.

Arnav was seven, and he wanted to light a diya on Diwali night. "Let me do it, Papa!" he begged. Papa gave him a long matchstick and showed him how to hold it away from his clothes. Arnav's hands shook, but he lit the wick. The little flame danced. "Wow!" he said. Then a breeze came, and his sleeve almost touched it. Papa gently moved him back. "Fire is beautiful, but we must be careful," he said. Arnav nodded. He placed the diya at the door and smiled.

Monday: Jasleen's forehead was burning. She couldn't finish her roti. Mummy wrapped her in a shawl and held her on the bed all evening, singing softly.
Tuesday: Jasleen stayed home. Mummy sat on the edge of the bed, sewing. Every time Jasleen woke, Mummy was there. Her brother Tanvir peeped in with a paper boat. "For you, sick girl."
Thursday: Jasleen sat up and ate khichdi. "Mummy, I was very lazy." Mummy laughed. "You were resting. Being sick is not lazy."

What did Tanvir bring Jasleen on Tuesday?
He brought her a paper boat.
How did Jasleen feel on Tuesday each time she woke?
She felt safe and cared for, because every time she woke, Mummy was there.
What did Mummy teach Jasleen on Thursday?
That resting when sick is not lazy; it is okay to be weak and still loved.
How might Tanvir see his sister being sick?
He may feel a little worried and caring, so he makes her a paper boat to cheer her up. 🤍

In the village near Thrissur, the panchayat member Deepika stopped at Joseph's gate after Sunday mass. 'Joseph sir, can we hold the ward meeting in your front room on Thursday?' He agreed; it was one evening. On Tuesday she was back. 'Sir, since the meeting is at yours, could you arrange tea and snacks for forty?' He had already said yes to the room; refusing now felt petty. He almost nodded. Then he thought of his tuition classes, his mother's knees, the cost, the cooking. Would he have agreed if tea for forty had been the first thing she asked? No. 'Deepika, the room is fine,' he said. 'Tea for forty, I can't do. Maybe the ladies' group could manage it?' Deepika blinked, then nodded. 'Fair enough. I'll ask them.'

What did Deepika first ask Joseph for?
To hold the ward meeting in his front room on Thursday.
What did Joseph feel when he almost nodded to the tea for forty?
Joseph felt pressure and a flicker of guilt, because after saying yes to the room, refusing seemed petty.
What helped Joseph give a clear answer?
Asking whether he would have agreed if tea for forty had been the first request, which showed him that the answer was no.
How does Deepika react to Joseph's no?
Deepika is surprised for a moment, then accepts it as fair and plans to ask the ladies' group instead.

'Hansa, you want to hand your notebook to your friend to copy? Sit down. Your Sudha Maasi was once in the very same spot. Class six, and my friend Kamini came running before prayers. "Sudha, give me your maths, just this once, Sir will scold me." I loved Kamini. I wanted to hand it over so badly my fingers itched. But I remembered how she had cried over fractions the whole term. So I said, "Sit here. Twenty minutes. I'll show you the first two sums, you do the rest." She sulked, but she sat. She got four right by herself. After that she came to me every week, and by exams she didn't need me. If I had only given her my book, she would still be copying.'

How many sums did Kamini get right by herself?
Four.
Why did young Sudha's fingers itch?
She loved Kamini and badly wanted to help by handing over the notebook, torn between that loyalty and knowing it wouldn't really help.
What choice in the story turned out wiser, and why?
Teaching Kamini the first two sums instead of lending the book; by exams Kamini didn't need help at all.
How might Kamini have felt when Sudha told her to sit and learn?
Frustrated and anxious about being scolded at first, since she sulked, but later more confident as she solved sums herself.

In the school counsellor's office, Rashmi sat stiffly, handbag on her knees. "Pihu is just rude now. She shouts at me, locks her door, won't eat with us. I'm tired of it." Vandana, the counsellor, nodded. "That sounds exhausting. Can I tell you what Pihu's teachers see? She's gone very quiet in class, stopped art club and sits alone." Rashmi's face changed. "She loved art." "Sometimes when teenagers pull away and snap, it's a sign they're struggling, not attitude. What if tonight you just say you're worried and listen?" That evening Rashmi knocked, sat on the edge of Pihu's bed and said, "I'm worried about you, not angry." Pihu cried for a long time. The next day Rashmi booked the doctor's appointment Vandana had suggested.

What club did Pihu stop going to?
She stopped going to art club.
How was Rashmi feeling when she first sat in the office?
She felt tired and angry, seeing Pihu's behaviour only as rudeness.
What helped Rashmi approach Pihu differently?
The counsellor shared what teachers saw and suggested speaking with concern, not blame, so Rashmi said she was worried, listened and then booked a doctor.
How might Pihu have felt when her mother said she was worried, not angry?
Pihu may have felt relieved and finally safe enough to let her sadness out, which is why she cried.

Swimming camp note, summer.

Farida joined the camp late, in the second week, and spent the first days sitting alone at the edge of the pool during breaks.

On Thursday, the group of girls she swims with invited her to their relay team. They practised the handover together and cheered when she finished her lap.

Since then, Farida walks in smiling and sits with them at break. Her mother told me she talks about the "relay girls" all evening.

I've kept the relay team together for the final. — Manjula

When did Farida join the camp?
She joined the camp late, in the second week.
How has Farida felt since joining the relay team?
Farida feels happy and secure, walking in smiling and talking about the "relay girls" at home.
How did Manjula support Farida's belonging?
Manjula kept the relay team together for the final.
How might the relay girls feel about Farida?
They seem to welcome and value her, cheering her lap.

"Why did I fail it, Akash? Seriously, why?" Tanvir lay on the hostel floor, staring at the ceiling fan.
"You said the paper was tough."
"But other people passed. So it's me. Maybe I'm just not a stats person. Maybe I never was, and I've been fooling myself since school."
"You've been saying this since Tuesday."
"Because I don't understand it. Was it the sleep? The way I study? Am I just stupid?"
"When is the re-exam?"
"Three weeks. But what's the point if I don't know why I failed?"
"You could look at the paper with the professor. See what you got wrong."
"I can't even think about the paper." Tanvir pulled his pillow over his face. "I just keep thinking, why, why, why."
Akash sat down next to him. "And after three days of why, do you feel any better?"
A muffled "No."

When is Tanvir's re-exam?
It is in three weeks.
Why does Tanvir keep asking "why" about failing?
He feels confused and low, and asking why feels like trying to understand, but it keeps turning into judgements about himself instead of a plan.
What small step could break Tanvir's loop?
He could book a time with the professor to go through the paper, turning "why" into a concrete list of topics to revise for the re-exam.
How does Akash seem to feel after three days of the same talk?
Akash seems concerned and a little tired, and gently points out that the "why" talk isn't making Tanvir feel any better.

During the Baisakhi fair in their village, Amandeep, two, saw a shiny steel pot at a stall and stared into it. A small face stared back.
She touched her nose. The face touched its nose.
"Me!" she said, grinning at her mother Zainab.
Zainab laughed. "Yes, that's you."
Amandeep then pointed at her new bangles. "Mine!"

Where did Amandeep see her reflection?
In a shiny steel pot at a stall.
How did Amandeep feel seeing herself?
She felt delighted and proud, grinning and saying "Me!"
How can Zainab support Amandeep's growing sense of self?
Name her body parts and belongings, and play mirror games at home.
How does Zainab feel watching Amandeep?
Zainab feels amused and happy, laughing at her discovery.

"Okay, here's my offer," Hansa said, sitting across from her father Lokesh at the dining table. She had written it on paper.
"Offer?"
"If I get a phone, I'll wash dishes every night, sweep on Sundays and take Chintu to tuition."
Lokesh raised his eyebrows. "And if you don't get a phone?"
Hansa blinked. "Then... I wouldn't have to do all that."
"So you'd only help at home if you're paid?"
"It's not paid. It's a trade. It's fair."
Lokesh smiled, a bit sadly. "It's honest, I'll give you that. But I hoped you'd wash dishes because we live here together."
Hansa frowned, not understanding. "But you'd still get clean dishes."

What would Hansa do on Sundays under her offer?
She would sweep on Sundays.
What was Lokesh feeling when he smiled a bit sadly?
He felt a little disappointed that Hansa saw chores only as a price for a phone, though he appreciated her honesty.
How could Lokesh help Hansa see chores as part of family life?
He could agree on some chores for everyone regardless of the phone, and talk about how the family helps each other.
How does Hansa see her offer?
She sees it as practical and fair, a trade, and doesn't yet understand why her father is disappointed.

Note from after-school club, Wednesday
Each child could choose one prize from the reward box today: glitter pens or a small puzzle. Aparna took a long time and picked the glitter pens. For the rest of the afternoon she told everyone the puzzle was 'boring and for little kids' and the pens were 'the best prize ever'. When Kavin opened his puzzle, she said loudly, 'That's so boring.' But she kept glancing over at it. At snack time I sat with her and said both prizes were good and it was fine to wonder about the other one. She shrugged. Later she asked Kavin if she could help with a corner, and they finished it together. Next time I'll let the children swap for a few minutes.
Akash

Which prize did Aparna pick?
Aparna picked the glitter pens.
What do Aparna's glances at the puzzle suggest?
They suggest she was still curious about the puzzle, and calling it 'boring' was a way to feel sure about her own choice.
What did Akash plan for next time, and why might it help?
Letting the children swap prizes for a few minutes lets them enjoy both, so they feel less need to run down the one they didn't choose.
How might Kavin feel hearing his puzzle called 'so boring'?
Kavin may feel a little hurt or confused, though he seemed happy to share once Aparna asked to help.

The email came at 7 a.m. in the Melbourne flat: the conservatory thanked Tuan for his audition and regretted to inform him. He read it standing in the kitchen with a spoon in the coffee jar.
Three years of cello lessons, paid for by his parents' bakery in Footscray. The picture he had carried since he was sixteen, himself on a concert stage in a black shirt, went quiet, as if someone had turned down the volume.
By noon, two friends from his cello class had posted their acceptances. He liked both posts and put his phone in a drawer.
Zeynep, his flatmate, found him on the balcony. "Want me to say something wise?"
"Please don't."
"Okay." She sat in the other chair. "Then I'll just be here."
They watched the trams for an hour. Later he said, "I don't know if I even want to play anymore."
Zeynep nodded. "You don't have to know yet."

Where did Tuan read the email?
Standing in the kitchen with a spoon in the coffee jar.
What does Tuan liking the posts and hiding his phone suggest about his feelings?
He feels envy and sadness, trying to be decent to his friends while grieving the stage career he had pictured.
Why is Zeynep's approach right for this stage?
She doesn't rush to wisdom or a bright side; she sits with Tuan and lets the grief and doubt be there.
What is it like for Zeynep on the balcony?
Zeynep has to hold back the urge to cheer Tuan up and choose quiet company, which likely feels hard but caring.

Sarika, you asked how I stayed sane after failing stats. Okay, so, I'm Lavanya, second-year psych, and the funny part is we'd literally studied explanatory style that semester. Didn't stop my brain. The result came, 38, and my head went: you're stupid, you'll never do research, everyone knew but you. I cried in the library washroom, honestly. Then that night I thought, fine, I'd tell a client to check the evidence, so check it. I opened the paper. Lost marks on regression, all of them, and I'd missed both regression classes for my cousin's wedding. The descriptive stats section? Full marks. So, other explanation: not 'stupid', just two missed classes. And one change: I booked the professor's office hours for Tuesday and asked for the regression notes. I wasn't happy, Sarika. I was still upset. But I was upset about something real and small, not something huge and made up.

Why did Lavanya miss both regression classes?
Lavanya missed both regression classes for a cousin's wedding.
What was Lavanya feeling right after the result came?
Lavanya felt crushed and ashamed, with thoughts like 'you're stupid' and 'you'll never do research', and cried in the library washroom.
What would you advise Sarika to take from Lavanya's approach if Sarika fails an exam?
Look at the actual paper to see where the marks were lost, find the real cause and choose one step, like booking office hours, instead of believing the harsh first story.
How might the professor see Lavanya coming to office hours for regression notes?
The professor would likely see a student taking the failure seriously and working on a specific gap, not someone who has given up.

I'm Jyoti, and Ankita has been my best friend since first year. She's the most talented illustrator in our design batch, and this year she has turned down everything. The college magazine cover: "Not good enough yet." The children's book project with a real publisher: "Maybe next year." The group show: she didn't even reply.
I can't read her mind, but whenever someone praises her old work, she looks almost pained.
Last month I tried something different. I brought my own sketchbook, the messy one, full of crossed-out hands and wonky faces, and showed her page after page. "This is how mine start," I said. She laughed at a horse that looked like a sofa.
Then I stopped saying "your work is amazing" and started saying things like "you tried a new brush today" or "that's further than yesterday."
On Friday she sent me a rough sketch for the magazine. Just a rough one. I didn't make a fuss.

What did one of Jyoti's sketches look like, according to Ankita's laugh?
A horse that looked like a sofa.
Why might Ankita look almost pained when her old work is praised?
Praise for results may feel like a standard she must keep meeting, so it adds to her fear of making something less than perfect.
Which of Jyoti's changes helped Ankita, and why?
Showing Jyoti's own messy sketchbook and praising effort and progress instead of results made imperfect work feel normal and safer to share.
What might it have meant for Ankita to see Jyoti's crossed-out hands and wonky faces?
It may have shown Ankita that even good artists start messily, easing her belief that only perfect work can be seen.

At the milk cooperative in a small Punjab town, Amandeep had sat on hiring panels for six years, and he had started noticing something about Jatin, the panel's most confident member.
Jatin decided within a minute of each candidate walking in. "Firm handshake, looks you in the eye. He'll be a great collection supervisor." After fifteen years of hiring, he was sure his gut had sharpened.
Amandeep had quietly kept a notebook. Of the last ten people Jatin had loved on sight, four had been let go within the year. Two he had dismissed were now the best supervisors in the district, going by the collection records.
At the next meeting Amandeep laid the notebook on the table, gently. "Your gut isn't bad, Jatin. But hiring doesn't tell us quickly if we were right. Let's add a short test on the milk records and ask for references too."
Jatin frowned at the numbers for a long time.

How many of Jatin's ten favourites were let go within the year?
Four.
Why did Amandeep keep a quiet notebook?
He felt doubtful about Jatin's confidence but wanted real evidence before saying anything, so he was cautious and fair rather than accusing.
What did Amandeep suggest adding to the gut feeling?
A short test on the milk records and references, so hiring rests on data as well as instinct.
How might Jatin feel looking at the notebook's numbers?
Jatin is likely unsettled and perhaps a little hurt, since fifteen years of confidence meets numbers that don't support it.

Dear Lalremsiami (Siami!),
Merry Christmas! Is Aizawl all lights and carols? Here in Shillong it's freezing and everyone is just exams, exams.
Okay, confession. You know Ashwin, from the debate team? At the Christmas fair yesterday he wore this huge red sweater, and I shouted in front of everyone, "Look, it's Santa's tomato!" Everyone laughed. Then I kept going, about his hair, his squeaky voice. I don't even think his voice is squeaky.
Here's the weird part. I actually like talking to him. A lot. Maybe that's why I did it? If I make fun of him, nobody can tell I like him, not even him. But he looked really hurt.
What do I do? Tell no one.
Love,
Ritu

What did Ritu shout at the Christmas fair?
"Look, it's Santa's tomato!"
Why did Ritu mock Ashwin in front of everyone?
Ritu likes Ashwin and felt afraid of being exposed, so teasing him loudly hid the crush from everyone, even from him.
What could Ritu do now?
Apologise to Ashwin simply, without jokes, and next time just talk to him normally, even while feeling shy 😅.
How might Ashwin have felt at the fair?
He probably felt embarrassed and hurt, and confused, since Ritu usually enjoys talking to him.

Playgroup note, Thursday
Nilesh spent nearly half an hour at the sand tray, pouring sand from a red cup into a blue cup and back, humming. When Divyansh called him, he didn't look up. When I said "Lunch time!" twice, he didn't hear.
I lifted him away too quickly, and he burst into tears and reached back for the cups.

What colours were Nilesh's cups?
Nilesh poured sand from a red cup into a blue cup and back.
Why did Nilesh burst into tears when he was lifted away?
Nilesh felt upset and frustrated at being pulled suddenly out of an absorbing game he was enjoying.
What small change does the caregiver plan for next time?
To kneel beside him, pour once with him, and give a gentle "last pour" warning before lunch.
How might Divyansh have felt when Nilesh didn't look up?
Divyansh might have felt a little ignored or puzzled, not knowing Nilesh was too absorbed to hear.

At the housing society's front office, the guard slid a slip across the desk: Joseph's parcel had been signed for by Reena in 4B, again. Joseph took the stairs with a box of ladoos. Three weeks earlier, when Joseph's father slipped in the bathroom during a night shift, it was Reena who heard the thud, sat with him, and waited until Joseph got home. Joseph rang the bell. "Nothing to thank for," Reena said, but took the box. Joseph added, "My number is on the society list, and I am only two floors up, any hour." Reena smiled and kept the door half open, as always, and Joseph did not step inside.

Who signed for Joseph's parcel?
Reena in 4B signed for it.
Why did Joseph bring a box of ladoos?
Joseph felt grateful for the help with parcels and for the night Joseph's father slipped.
How can Joseph respect Reena's privacy while returning the kindness?
By offering help and a number, and not stepping inside when Reena keeps the door half open.
How might Reena see the visit?
Reena said there was nothing to thank for and took the box, which suggests modesty and ease with quiet help.

It was the last week of the month, and Raghav had exactly six hundred rupees until salary day. For three months in Kolkata he'd eaten the same rajma-chawal at the same dhaba near the office. Safe. Known. Last night his colleague Hemant had laughed: "You live in the city of fish and you eat rajma?" Raghav had wanted to argue that he just liked rajma. Then he wondered: did he, or was it just the only thing he knew here? So he made a rule. Three tries, sixty rupees each, before deciding. Monday: shukto from a steel-plate canteen, bitter and strange. Wednesday: mustard fish, bony, but the sauce… Friday he went back for the fish on his own.

How much money did Raghav have until salary day?
Exactly six hundred rupees.
What doubt made Raghav want to test his taste?
Raghav wondered whether he truly liked rajma or only liked it because it was the one thing he knew in the city.
Why was Raghav's three-tries rule a good choice with little money?
It kept each try cheap, at sixty rupees, and gave unfamiliar food a fair chance instead of judging it on one strange first bite.
How might Hemant react to seeing Raghav order mustard fish on his own?
Hemant would probably be amused and pleased, since the teasing nudged Raghav toward a new favourite.

Friday
Filled in the Class 11 form today. Commerce, obviously. Papa is a CA, Dadaji was a CA, and Chaitanya bhaiya is doing CA now. Nobody even asked me. Mummy just said, "You'll join the firm one day, beta." I kept looking at the arts and design option, the one with the drawing portfolio. I have a whole sketchbook under my bed. But ticking it means a big talk at dinner, maybe Papa's quiet face, and all the relatives asking why. Commerce means nothing changes. So I ticked commerce. Everyone at home looked relieved. I feel a bit empty, but also relieved. Is that weird?
Pradeep

What is under Pradeep's bed?
A whole sketchbook is under his bed.
Why does Pradeep feel both empty and relieved?
Relieved because commerce avoids a hard talk at dinner, but empty because he let go of the design option he really wanted without truly choosing.
What could Pradeep try before the form is final?
He could show the sketchbook to Mummy or Chaitanya bhaiya and ask for one calm conversation about the design option, instead of letting the default decide.
How might Chaitanya bhaiya see Pradeep's choice?
Chaitanya bhaiya may assume it's natural since everyone does CA, but might care a lot if shown the sketchbook and asked honestly.
Pallavi's phone bill was ₹450 in March and ₹540 in April. By what percentage did it rise?
It rose by 20 percent. Because the bill went up by ₹90, and 90 out of 450 is one fifth, which is 20 percent.

The answer is f(x) = x^2/2 + x/2.

Read this:

Behind the village school, a big boy grabbed Arnab's marbles. "Give me the blue one, or I'll push you in the ditch." Arnab's legs went wobbly. Then Pradeep ran up and stood right beside him, shoulder to shoulder. "Leave him alone," Pradeep said. His voice shook a little, but he did not move. The big boy snorted and dropped the marbles. Pradeep picked them up. "Come on. Let's tell Sir." They walked to the staff room together. Arnab held his marbles tight and felt tall. At lunch, he saved Pradeep a place beside him.

What did the big boy threaten?
He threatened to push Arnab in the ditch unless he gave him the blue marble.
How did Arnab feel when Pradeep stood beside him?
He felt brave and cared for; his wobbly legs steadied and he felt tall.
What did the two boys do that was wise after the big boy left?
They went together to tell Sir, instead of dealing with it alone or fighting.
What is it like for Pradeep to stand up to the big boy?
He is scared too, since his voice shook, but he feels loyal enough to his friend to stay.

"Kavitha, why do you have two sets of plates?"
"Those are for Ammamma. She doesn't eat from plates that had eggs."
Anjali looked around the kitchen. "No eggs at all?"
"Not in this kitchen. Appa eats omelettes at the canteen."
"At my house we have eggs every morning. And fish on Sundays."
"Really? Fish?" Kavitha wrinkled her nose, then laughed. "Sorry. Is it nice?"
"Very nice. Is Ammamma angry if I bring my egg sandwich?"
"Hmm. Maybe eat it on the balcony? Then it's not in the kitchen."
"Okay." Anjali thought. "Can I try your Ammamma's sambar?"
Kavitha's grandmother, listening from the door, smiled and filled a small bowl. "Ask me anything, kanna. Better than guessing."
Anjali tasted it. "Can you teach my mum?"

Why does Kavitha's house have two sets of plates?
Because Ammamma doesn't eat from plates that had eggs.
What was Anjali feeling as she looked around the kitchen?
Anjali felt curious and a little surprised, noticing rules very different from her own home.
How did Anjali and Kavitha keep the friendship open?
They asked each other kindly about eggs and fish instead of mocking, and found an easy solution like eating on the balcony.
How might Kavitha's grandmother feel about Anjali's questions?
She seems pleased and warm, smiling and inviting Anjali to ask rather than guess.

Vaisampayana continued,--"The high-souled king Dhritarashtra, thus addressed by Sanjaya, became, O monarch, absorbed in meditation about his sons. Endued with great energy, he then, having reflected, said these words: 'Without doubt, O Suta's son, it is Time that destroyeth the universe. And it is Time that again createth everything. Nothing here is eternal. It is Nara and Narayana, endued with omniscience, that destroyeth all creatures. The gods speak of him as Vaikuntha (of immeasurable puissance), while men call him Vishnu (one that pervadeth the Universe)!'"

Answer from the text. What does Dhritarashtra say about Time?
He says Time destroys the universe and creates everything again, and that nothing here is eternal.

On the fridge of their Chennai flat was Salma's picture chart: shoes, bag, water bottle, a door.

At seven-thirty, Salma, five, stood in front of it. She sat and pulled on her shoes. She grabbed her school bag from the hook. Then she stopped, frowning at the chart. "Water bottle!" She ran to the kitchen.

Her brother Pranav, waiting by the door, didn't say a word. Salma touched the door picture and then the real door. "Ready!"

"All by yourself," Pranav said, grinning.

What pictures were on Salma's chart?
The chart showed shoes, bag, water bottle and a door.
How did Salma feel when she said "Ready!"?
She felt proud and pleased that she had done every step by herself.
Why did the picture chart help Salma?
It showed each step in order, so she could check it herself instead of needing reminders.
What is it like for Pranav to wait without reminding her?
He may feel tempted to hurry her, but staying quiet lets her succeed on her own, which he clearly enjoys.

Monday: Omkar, two, opened every drawer while his mother Ganga said "No, no" all day. Wednesday: Ganga locked the knife drawer and gave him the bottom one, filled with steel cups and wooden spoons. Saturday: Omkar dragged each thing out, tasted a spoon and banged a cup, and played for half an hour while Ganga cooked, no longer saying no.

Which drawer did Ganga give Omkar?
Ganga gave Omkar the bottom drawer, filled with steel cups and wooden spoons.
What was Omkar feeling on Saturday as he banged the cup?
Omkar was absorbed and happy, playing for half an hour on his own.
What change made the difference between Monday and Saturday?
Ganga locked the dangerous drawer and gave Omkar a safe one to explore, so the day stopped being a string of no's.
How might Ganga have felt on Monday compared with Saturday?
On Monday Ganga was probably worn out and anxious from saying no all day. On Saturday Ganga was calmer and able to cook.

Liam had been in Dublin eight months, working long hours at a design agency. He wasn't in crisis, just flat, snappy, and waking at four every morning. His flatmate Siddiq mentioned that he saw a therapist every other week. "For what?" Liam asked. "Nothing's wrong with you." Siddiq smiled. "That's sort of the point. I go so things don't get bad." Liam looked into his company's employee support scheme and found six free sessions. He wasn't sure whether he needed a therapist, a doctor or just more sleep, so he asked his GP first, who suggested talking therapy. The first session felt awkward. By the third, Liam noticed he was sleeping until six. He booked three more.

How many free sessions did Liam's company scheme offer?
It offered six free sessions.
Why did Liam ask Siddiq 'For what?'
He was surprised, because he believed therapy was only for people with something clearly wrong.
What was sensible about how Liam chose his help?
He wasn't sure what kind of support he needed, so he asked his GP first and then used the free sessions.
How does Siddiq see therapy differently from Liam at first?
Siddiq sees it as regular upkeep to stop problems growing, not as a last resort. 🙂

I sit across from Salma at the ad agency, and this morning I saw her get called into the director's room for feedback on a campaign she'd stayed late three nights to finish. When she came out, her eyes were bright and glossy. She blinked quickly several times and looked up at the ceiling tiles. I couldn't tell whether she was upset or relieved. Kiran, a colleague from the next desk, walked over with two cups of water and said quietly, "Come with me for a minute?" They went to the stairwell. When Salma returned five minutes later, her eyes were dry, her breathing slower. She said the director had liked the campaign. She'd been holding in the stress until it was over.

How many nights had Salma stayed late?
She had stayed late three nights.
What might Salma have been feeling when she blinked and looked up, and what did the observer admit?
She was probably holding back strong feeling, later shown to be stress ending in relief, though the observer could not tell at first whether she was upset.
What helped Salma regulate her feelings at work?
A short break in the stairwell with Kiran, water and slower breathing helped her settle.
How might Kiran have seen Salma's glossy eyes?
Kiran seems to have noticed she needed a moment and offered a quiet break instead of asking questions in front of others.

Read this:

I'm Suraj. At twenty-five, I stood at the tip of Kanyakumari with my father, Anand, at dawn. We'd taken a night bus from Madurai. I'd seen the sea before, but never where three seas meet. The sky went from grey to pink to gold, and the water changed colour with it. I remember my father's hand on my shoulder, and neither of us saying anything. There was a crowd, but it felt silent. I thought about how old the sea was, how many people had stood there before me, how small my worries about work were. I felt a lump in my throat I couldn't explain. Even now, when I'm stressed, I close my eyes and see that gold light on the water.

Where had Suraj and Anand taken the night bus from?
From Madurai.
How did Suraj feel watching the sunrise?
Suraj felt awe and deep wonder, with a lump in the throat and worries shrinking.
How does Suraj use the memory today?
Suraj closes both eyes and pictures the gold light on the water when stressed.
How might Anand have felt standing with Suraj?
Anand likely felt moved and close to Suraj, sharing the moment in silence.
I want to try out for the school debate team, but I'm afraid I'll be bad at it.
It takes courage to try something new. Everyone is a beginner at first, even the best speakers.
What if they laugh?
Most students on a team remember how scary it was, and tend to be encouraging. Prepare a short speech and practise it at home.
I do want to join, though.
Then that wish is worth listening to. Try out once, and you will learn from the experience, even if you don't get selected.

"Simran, count the bounces," said her uncle Vijay, pressing play on the video.

"Easy." Simran leaned close. "One, two, three..."

The ball bounced across a playground. Simran counted, lips moving.

"Twenty-one!"

"Right. And the clown?"

"What clown?"

"A clown walked past, juggling."

"No, he didn't."

Vijay rewound. A clown in a red wig strolled past, juggling three balls.

"But I was looking right at the screen!" Simran said.

"You were looking at the ball."

Simran thought. "So my eyes were there, but my brain wasn't?"

"Something like that."

"Play it again," she said, grinning. "I want to catch him this time."

How many bounces did Simran count?
Twenty-one.
How did Simran feel when she saw the clown on the rewind?
She felt surprised and a little indignant, since she was sure she had been looking at the screen.
Which question helped Simran understand what happened?
Her own question, whether her eyes were there but her brain wasn't, helped her see attention decides what she notices.
How might Vijay feel watching Simran work it out?
Vijay probably feels amused and pleased that she figured it out herself.
In War and Peace, who becomes Nikolai Rostov's wife?
Nikolai marries Princess Mary Bolkonskaya, Prince Andrew's sister. They settle at Bald Hills, where he becomes a hard-working, careful landowner.
In Pride and Prejudice, whom does Elizabeth Bennet get engaged to?
She gets engaged to Mr. Darcy. Jane can hardly believe it at first, and her father is surprised because Elizabeth used to dislike him.

In their Bengaluru flat, Lokesh placed a bowl of bitter gourd curry in front of Francis. Francis wrinkled his nose. "It looks yucky."
"Try one bite," Lokesh said. "Your choice."
Francis took a tiny bite and pulled a face. Then another. "Hmm. It's bitter but okay."
After dinner he went to the sink, pulled up his stool and washed his own hands with soap, humming.

What curry did Lokesh put in front of Francis?
He put a bowl of bitter gourd curry in front of him.
What does Francis taking a second bite suggest?
It suggests he was willing to give the new food a real chance despite not loving it.
What helped Francis try the food?
Lokesh asked for just one bite and let it be his choice, without forcing.
How might Lokesh feel seeing Francis wash his hands alone?
He might feel pleased that Francis is becoming more independent.

"Seema, you think you have to be strong all the time? When I, your Omkar Mama, was sixteen, I had a stammer, worst on words starting with 'p'. I never talked in groups. My friends thought I was just quiet. One evening on the riverbank, my friend Sadanand asked why I never told stories. My heart was hammering. I could have made a joke. Instead I said, slowly, 'Because I'm scared of getting stuck in front of you.' He didn't laugh. He said, 'Then get stuck. We'll wait.' That was the first time I told a story in front of anyone."

Which words did young Omkar's stammer affect most?
Words starting with 'p'.
What was young Omkar feeling when his heart was hammering?
He felt scared and exposed, afraid of being judged if he told the truth.
What turning point in the story came from opening up?
Admitting his fear instead of joking, which led Sadanand to offer patience.
How might Sadanand have felt when Omkar opened up?
Touched and trusted, and glad to understand why his friend stayed quiet.

The polytechnic in Hosur had given its prize for the best working model to Anand's team: a small solar pump that lifted water from a bucket into a clay pot. That evening the principal called each of the three boys in, one by one, to write a line for the college newsletter about who did what. Anand said he had designed the pump and done "most of it." Kamal said he had wired the solar panel and fixed the leaks, "which was really the hard part." The third boy said the pump would never have run without his gearbox. The principal smiled and opened the lab register, where each boy signed in and out and wrote what he worked on. Anand's signature was there on eleven days. Kamal's on fourteen. The third boy's on twelve. Nobody had done most of it.

What did the team's solar pump do?
It lifted water from a bucket into a clay pot.
Why did Anand feel sure he had done most of it?
He felt proud of his design and remembered his own days clearly, so his part felt biggest, while the others' work stayed in the background.
How did the lab register help settle the question?
It gave a written record of who worked on which days, showing all three had worked about equally instead of relying on memory.
How might Kamal feel when the register is opened?
Kamal might feel a little embarrassed, since his claim of doing the hard part sat beside two teammates who had worked nearly as many days.

You asked, Vandana, why my notebooks look so strange. Every line has a little letter in the margin. I'm Alka, and I collect oral histories in the villages around Bhuj. In my first year, I wrote up a story about a well that saved a whole village in the great drought. I was sure an old man had told me he had seen it. When my editor asked for his name, I went back to my notes and found nothing. I had heard it from three different people, each of whom had heard it from someone else. None of them had seen it. That scared me. So now: S means I saw it, T means I was told it, and by whom, I means I'm inferring. Before I write any sentence, I ask myself: how do I actually know this? It's slow. It's also why people trust my work.

What do the letters S, T and I mean in Alka's notebook?
S means seen, T means told (and by whom), and I means inferred.
Why did the well story scare Alka?
Alka felt shaken on finding that a story believed to come from an eyewitness had only been passed along by people who hadn't seen it.
What question does Alka ask before writing, and why does it help?
'How do I actually know this?', which separates what was seen, told and inferred before anything is written as fact.
Why does the editor matter to the story?
The editor's request for the old man's name made Alka check the notes and discover the gap.
Last week, a farmer shipped 10 boxes of pomelos which had 240 pomelos in all. This week, the farmer shipped 20 boxes. How many dozens of pomelos did the farmer ship in all?

There were 240/10 = 24 pomelos in a box.
This means that each box has 24/12 = 2 dozens of pomelos since 1 dozen is equal to 12.
The farmer shipped a total of 10 + 20 = 30 boxes.
Thus, the farmer shipped a total of 30 x 2 = 60 dozens of pomelos.
The answer is 60.

How does the third-storey passage look to Jane?

Mrs. Fairfax stayed behind a moment to fasten the trap-door; I, by dint of groping, found the outlet from the attic, and proceeded to descend the narrow garret staircase. I lingered in the long passage to which this led, separating the front and back rooms of the third storey: narrow, low, and dim, with only one little window at the far end, and looking, with its two rows of small black doors all shut, like a corridor in some Bluebeard's castle.
Narrow, low and dark, with one small window and two rows of shut black doors. It reminds her of a corridor in Bluebeard's castle.

Monday. Urmila, two, jammed the star block at the round hole again and again, then threw it and wailed. Wednesday. Her papa, Darshan, sat beside her and turned the star a little in her fingers, just enough. She pushed. Clunk! It dropped in. Urmila clapped and shouted, "Me did it!" Saturday. She picked up the star, turned it herself, wiggled it, and it fell through. She looked at Papa, beaming, then fed the box the moon block too.

Which block did Urmila jam at the round hole?
The star block.
What does Urmila's shout 'Me did it!' suggest about how she felt?
She felt proud, as if the win were entirely her own, even though Darshan had turned the star for her.
Why was turning the star just a little a good choice for Darshan?
It gave just enough help for Urmila to push it in herself, so she kept trying and later managed alone.
How might Darshan feel on Saturday, watching Urmila turn the star by herself?
Darshan is likely delighted, seeing his small help on Wednesday grow into something she can do alone.
Is the Wi-Fi working? I can't connect to it. Can you check this short message?

Yes, that's right as it stands.
Why: Both sentences are complete; "connect to" is right.
In a library, why do people talk softly?
Quiet lets people concentrate. Because loud talk carries across a room and breaks the focus of readers, and a library exists so that everyone can read in peace.

In the accounts office in Koramangala, Anjali's inbox had forty-three unread emails. Himani's was the longest.
It began with how the audit had gone last year, moved on to a vendor who was always late, mentioned a spreadsheet "somewhere on the shared drive," and ended with three questions tangled in one paragraph. Anjali scrolled down, scrolled up, and still could not tell whether Himani wanted numbers, a meeting or just to vent.
She flagged it. Later, she told herself. Later became two days.
On Thursday Himani messaged, "Did you see my email? It's urgent." Anjali felt a flash of irritation, then guilt. She opened the email again, took a pen and wrote on a sticky note: "Question 1? Question 2? Deadline?" It took her twenty minutes to pull the three questions apart.
She replied with three numbered answers and one line at the end: "Next time, could you put the questions at the top?"

How many unread emails did Anjali have?
Anjali's inbox had forty-three unread emails.
What did Anjali feel when Himani messaged that it was urgent?
Anjali felt a flash of irritation, then guilt, because she had delayed the unclear email for two days.
What small request at the end could help both of them next time?
Asking Himani to put the questions at the top, so the reader does not have to dig them out.
How might the delay have looked from Himani's side?
Himani was probably worried and impatient, not knowing that her long email was the reason no reply came.

Tuesday, Hampi
Everyone's asleep and I'm writing by torchlight. Two weeks ago, when Usha-chithi asked, "Varun, what do you want to see in Hampi?" I said, "Anything," and went back to my game. Today was temples. Then more temples. Then a market with only brass lamps. I wanted the round basket-boat ride on the river that my friend told me about, but nobody knew I wanted it, so it wasn't in the plan. I sulked at lunch and Chithi asked what was wrong. I said "nothing" again. Now it's our last night. I think the only person I can be angry with is me.
Varun

What did Varun want to do in Hampi?
The round basket-boat ride on the river.
How does Varun feel on the last night?
Varun feels disappointed and a bit angry with himself for saying 'anything' when asked.
What else could Varun have done when Usha-chithi asked two weeks ago?
Varun could have named one thing, like the basket boats; even one wish gives the adults something to plan around.
What might the trip have been like for Usha-chithi?
She asked twice and still didn't know what Varun wanted, so she may have felt puzzled and a little hurt by the sulking.

Gargi had done every maths sum by lantern light the night before. At the village school the next morning, she opened her bag and it wasn't there. Again.
'Gargi, you are so careless,' Sir said, in front of everyone.
She stared at her feet all day. On the walk home she told her brother Vishal, 'I try so hard. It still goes missing. Maybe I'm just bad.'
Vishal, in Class 9, thought for a minute. That evening he nailed a small hook by the door, hung her bag on it and drew a picture list on cardboard: book, homework, pencil box, tiffin. 'Before sleep, you tick these. Bag goes on the hook.'
The next morning the homework was in the bag. Gargi touched the ticks as if they were medals.

What did Vishal hang Gargi's bag on?
A small hook he nailed by the door.
Why did Gargi think she might just be bad?
She tried so hard and her homework still went missing, and Sir called her careless in front of everyone, so she felt ashamed.
What choice did Vishal make instead of telling Gargi to try harder?
He set up a hook by the door and a picture list to tick before sleep, giving her a routine and a visual reminder.
How might Sir see Gargi if the homework keeps arriving on time?
Sir might realise she was never careless on purpose and that she needed a system, not scolding.

I'm Ishita, and I sit opposite Vaibhav at work. When our health insurer sent a breach notice last month, most of us glanced at it and moved on. Vaibhav read it with a pencil.
He underlined the lines about what was exposed: name, date of birth, policy number, phone number and 'some claim details'. Then he said aloud, mostly to himself, 'So not passwords or cards. But enough to pretend to be me. Or to pretend to be them, calling me.'
He wrote a sticky note. Watch for calls or messages quoting my policy number. Never share an OTP. Call the insurer only on the number on my card. Ask whether anyone can change my contact details without extra checks.
That afternoon he called the insurer on the number printed on his card and asked that last question. They added a verification step to his account.
I can't say whether he was worried. He seemed calm. But the next week, when a caller quoted his policy number, he hung up within ten seconds.

What did the notice say was exposed?
Name, date of birth, policy number, phone number and some claim details.
What might Vaibhav have been worried about as he underlined the notice?
That someone could use his details to impersonate him, or pose as the insurer to trick him.
Which item on Vaibhav's sticky note mattered most when the caller quoted his policy number?
Never sharing an OTP and calling the insurer only on the number on his card, so he hung up quickly.
How does Vaibhav's reaction look to Ishita?
Ishita notices how carefully he read the notice while others ignored it, and sees it pay off when the fake call comes.

When I became project lead last year, I thought our team just got along naturally. I'm Raghav. It took me four months to see that it wasn't natural; it was Eshaan. He was the one who smoothed things over when two designers fought, who brought extra lunch when someone forgot theirs, who said yes every time I asked, 'Can anyone pick this up?' Then in March he was ill for a fortnight, and the team fell apart: arguments in every stand-up, deadlines slipping. I felt stupid, honestly. I'd built my calm team on one person's goodwill and never once thanked him in front of anyone. When he came back, I stopped asking 'can anyone' and started assigning. I nominated him for the quarterly award and wrote down exactly what he did. He read it and said, 'I didn't think anyone noticed.'

What happened while Eshaan was ill in March?
The team fell apart: arguments in every stand-up and deadlines slipping.
How did Raghav feel when the team fell apart?
Raghav felt stupid and guilty for building a calm team on Eshaan's goodwill without ever thanking him.
What changes did Raghav make, and why are they fair?

Sangeeta and I had a huge fight over hopscotch today. She said I stepped on the line. I said I didn't. We kept shouting "You did!" "I didn't!" until Didi came out and said we sounded like two crows.

Dear Neel,

You asked how I stopped Abhinav's jokes about my stammer. I'll tell you exactly.

For months, whenever I got stuck on a word, Abhinav would copy it: "K-k-k-Kunal!" Everyone laughed, and I laughed too, because I didn't want to seem touchy.

Last week, in the canteen, he did it again. I put my sandwich down and said, as calmly as I could, "Abhinav, that one's not okay. Please stop." My heart was pounding.

He's still my friend. He's actually been nicer since.

Kunal

Tommy is making 12 loaves of bread. He needs 4 pounds of flour per loaf. A 10-pound bag of flour costs $10 and a 12-pound bag costs $13. When he is done making his bread, he has no use for flour and so he will throw away whatever is left. How much does he spend on flour if he buys the cheapest flour to get enough?

He needs 48 pounds of flour because 12 x 4 = 48
He needs 4.8 bags of 10 pound bags because 48 / 10 = 4.8
He therefore needs to buy 5 bags of flour because 4 < 4.8 < 5
He spends $50 if he buys this flour because 5 x 10 = 50
He needs 4 bags of the 12-pound flour because 48 / 12 = 4
He would spend $52 on the 12-pound bags because 4 x 13 = 52
He spends $50 if he buys the cheapest flour because 50 < 52
The answer is 50.

messages.content: Six kids and two adults are going to the circus. Kid's tickets are on sale for only half of the adult tickets. The total cost is $50. How much is one kid's ticket?

Let X be the price of one kid's ticket.
So the price of one adult ticket is X*2.
Five kids and two adults are going to the circus, so 6*X + 2*(X*2) = $50.
So 10X=$50
So the price of one kid's ticket is X = $5.
The answer is 5.

By eleven the rain had flattened the stall. Rukmini stood in the college quadrangle holding a soggy cardboard sign, VEGAN BAKES, while sixty cupcakes she had baked through the night dissolved into the mud. Mahima dragged the plastic sheet off the table. "Ruks, come inside." "Everyone saw," Rukmini said. "The whole fest. I told the committee it would be the best stall." In the canteen she drank hot chai with shaking hands. Then she did something Mahima had seen her do before exams: she stared at the wall and asked, out loud, "Okay. In one year, who will remember this? And who does it actually hurt?" She counted on her fingers. "Me. The committee, a little. Nobody else." She still looked miserable. "It's awful today," she said. "But it's today."

How many cupcakes had Rukmini baked through the night?
She had baked sixty cupcakes.
What was Rukmini feeling as she drank chai in the canteen?
She was upset and embarrassed, worried that the whole fest had seen her stall fail after she had promised it would be the best.
Which choice worked, and why?
Asking who would remember it in a year and who it actually hurt worked, because it shrank the disaster to its real size without pretending it didn't sting.
How might Mahima see Rukmini's way of coping?
Mahima has seen her do this before exams, so she probably feels reassured that Rukmini is using a habit that helps her.

I'm Kavitha, and the first time I felt my own voice work for me was at a scholarship interview. My hands were cold, my heart was thudding, and Ayesha, my friend, had told me before I went in, "Feel your feet, breathe from your belly, speak like you're telling a friend." So I sat tall, breathed out slowly and started. My voice came out lower and steadier than I expected. The panel leaned in. I still felt nervous inside. It was steady on the outside, though, which surprised me. Later Ayesha said I sounded composed, and I said I wasn't at all. So a steady voice doesn't always mean a calm mind, I think, but it helped me.

What did Ayesha tell Kavitha before the interview?
Ayesha told Kavitha to feel the feet on the floor, breathe from the belly and speak as if telling a friend.
What was Kavitha feeling under that steady voice?
Kavitha was nervous, with cold hands and a thudding heart, even though Kavitha's voice sounded composed. The steady sound came from breath and posture, not from a calm mind.
What could Kavitha do before the next interview?
Sit tall, breathe out slowly and feel the feet on the floor, as Kavitha did, and practise speaking as if telling a friend.
How did Ayesha see Kavitha's voice?
Ayesha heard it as composed and did not know how nervous Kavitha felt inside.

The power had gone out in the village again, so the whole lane sat on Dadaji's charpai under the neem tree. Anand, nine, held the lantern. Sunaina, his cousin, kept poking him to stop swinging it. Dadaji told them about the old stepwell behind the temple, how the king's daughter had it dug during a drought so no one had to walk to the river. "She sold her own bangles to pay the workers," he said. Anand frowned. "Then why is it named after the king?" Dadaji laughed. "Good question. Stories remember some people louder than others." The next morning Anand and Sunaina went to the stepwell and counted the steps. Sunaina found a small carved bangle on the third pillar.

Where did the family sit when the power went out?
They sat on Dadaji's charpai under the neem tree in the lane.
Why did Anand frown when he heard the story?
He was puzzled and felt it was unfair that the king got the name when his daughter had sold her bangles; he was noticing whose part the story leaves out.
How could Dadaji keep Anand's curiosity about local history going?
He could take the children to the stepwell or to older neighbours so they can collect more versions of the story and compare them.
What is it like for Sunaina to find the carved bangle on the pillar?
It probably makes the story feel real to her, as if the daughter's part is written into the stone even if the name is not.

Site supervisor's note, Friday
The client arrived at the site office at noon, angry that the flooring was a week behind. Siddharth, our new engineer, was the only one there. I watched from the doorway. The client demanded it be finished by Monday. I saw Siddharth's hand go to his collar and heard him start, 'Yes, sir, of course, we'll…' then stop. He looked down at his feet, took one long breath out, and said, 'I understand you're frustrated. Let me check the crew and materials and call you back at four with a date I can actually keep.' The client grumbled but left. Afterwards Siddharth admitted his heart was pounding and he nearly promised Monday just to make the shouting stop. I told him that pause saved us from a promise we would have broken. He is taking the four o'clock call himself.
Salma, site supervisor

What time did Siddharth promise to call the client back?
At four.
What does Siddharth's hand going to his collar suggest he was feeling?
He was anxious and under pressure, with a pounding heart and a strong urge to please the client just to end the shouting.
What could other new staff learn from Siddharth's pause?
That a short breath before answering can turn a panicked promise into a realistic plan the team can keep.
How did the client probably see Siddharth's answer?
The client may still have been frustrated but saw someone taking the complaint seriously and offering a clear time for a real answer.
The car guide says an airbag will cushion the impact. I only know cushion as a pillow for a seat.

As a verb, to cushion means to soften the effect of a blow or shock so that less harm is done.
Example: Thick grass helped cushion her fall from the swing.

Wednesday

My shins have been aching after every sprint practice for two weeks. Last night I watched loads of videos. One said ice, one said heat, one said "run through it," one said buy special insoles. They can't all be right. And I'm not a doctor, and neither are most of those people. So today I did something different. I told Coach Swati after practice. She listened, watched me run, and said my shoes were worn out and I was landing hard. Then she said, "If it keeps hurting, see a doctor, not the internet." Mummy took me to the doctor this evening. The doctor checked my legs and said to rest for now and see how it feels. — Zubin

Who did Zubin tell after practice?
Coach Swati.
Why did Zubin decide not to trust the videos?
Zubin felt confused by the videos contradicting each other and unsure, realising they couldn't all be right.
Why was asking the coach and a doctor the right approach here?
It was a health question outside Zubin's knowledge, so people who could actually examine the legs were better than guesses.
How might Mummy see Zubin's decision to speak up?
Mummy would likely feel relieved to hear about the pain early and glad to take Zubin to the doctor.
