"Kamal, no more biscuits. Dinner soon."

"Biscuit!"

"No, beta."

Kamal dropped to the floor. He screamed, kicking his legs against the tiles.

"Kamal—"

He threw his toy car. It hit the door.

"Kamal, listen—"

He arched his back and screamed louder, eyes squeezed shut.

"Okay," said Akash softly, sitting down on the floor nearby. "Okay."

He moved the other toy cars out of reach and waited.

What did Kamal throw?
His toy car.
Why can't Kamal listen when Akash says "Kamal, listen"?
He is in a storm of anger and frustration, and at his age he cannot yet calm himself enough to listen.
Which choice did Akash make that helps?
He stopped trying to reason, sat nearby quietly, moved the cars out of reach, and waited.
How might Akash be feeling as he sits on the floor?
He is probably tired and a little stressed, but choosing to stay calm.

In the Istanbul office, Zeynep sent a short email after each planning call: "To confirm what we agreed: the sample goes out Thursday, and Pablo will book the courier." It had saved them once when the courier date got mixed up. Pablo replied each time with a thumbs-up. But when she sent a similar confirmation after a hallway conversation about lunch, Pablo tilted his head. "Are you checking that I remember?" he asked. Zeynep laughed. "Sorry. I do it for everything." She stopped writing for small chats and kept it for decisions and deadlines. Pablo said, "That is better. Now it looks like care, not a test."

What was Zeynep going to do about the sample?
The sample was going out Thursday.
What did Pablo feel about the lunch confirmation, and what did Zeynep intend?
Pablo felt as if he was being tested about his memory, while Zeynep only meant to avoid mistakes from habit. The same line can show care or doubt.
What did Zeynep change to keep the habit useful?
Zeynep stopped confirming small chats and kept confirmations for decisions and deadlines.
How might the earlier courier mix-up have shaped Zeynep's habit?
It likely taught Zeynep that written confirmations prevent confusion, which is why the habit began.

At the summer science camp in Pune, Hemant spent five days building a model windmill from ice-cream sticks. He glued every blade himself.
On the last day, the camp teacher spun it gently. "It's lovely, Hemant. But the blades are too heavy. If you trim them, it'll spin faster."
Hemant's face went red. "It spins fine."
"It stops after one turn," his friend Nilesh said.
"It's perfect!" Hemant grabbed the model. "You don't know how long I worked on it."
He carried it home without trimming anything. That evening, in the fan's breeze, it turned once and stopped. Hemant stared at it and didn't say anything.

What did Hemant build his windmill from?
He built it from ice-cream sticks.
Why did Hemant say the model was perfect?
He felt hurt and defensive, because after five days of work the teacher's suggestion felt like an insult to him.
What could Hemant try next time he gets feedback on a project?
He could thank the teacher, try one suggestion on a small part, and see whether it helps.
How might Nilesh feel when Hemant snaps?
Nilesh may feel surprised and a bit hurt, since he was only pointing out that it stopped.

"Jahnavi, you'll laugh, but I learned economics from a frying pan." Akash grinned, though he sounded a little embarrassed. "Five of us in the PG shared one kitchen. First week, spotless. Then someone left a pan. Then I left a pan, because honestly, one more? Who'd notice? By week three there wasn't a clean pan in the house, and we were frying eggs in the lid of a pressure cooker. Every one of us thought we'd only added a tiny bit. The landlady threatened to lock the kitchen. What finally worked? A chart on the fridge with our names and days, and a rule: the kitchen gets locked for whoever skips twice. It took ten minutes to set up. We should have done it in week one."

What were they frying eggs in by week three?
The lid of a pressure cooker.
How did Akash feel when he left his pan?
He wasn't worried, thinking one more pan wouldn't be noticed, just as everyone else did.
What finally worked, and why?
A chart on the fridge with names and days, plus a rule locking the kitchen for anyone who skips twice, which made each share clear and enforced.
How might the landlady have seen the kitchen by week three?
The landlady likely saw a mess nobody owned, and threatened to lock the kitchen because no one was taking care of it.

Keerthana stood at the bedroom door in her socks. Papa was sitting on the bed with his hands over his face, and his shoulders were shaking.
"Papa?" she whispered.
Sahil wiped his eyes. "Come here, kanna."
"Why are you crying? Did I do something?"
"No. I'm sad because I miss Dadi. It is okay to be sad. I'm still here for you."
She climbed up and leaned against him. "I miss Dadi too," she said, very small.

Where was Keerthana standing when she saw her father?
Keerthana was standing at the bedroom door in her socks.
What was Keerthana feeling as she watched her father cry?
Keerthana was worried and scared. Her whisper and her question, "Did I do something?" show she wondered if it was her fault.
How did Sahil's words help Keerthana?
He said why he was crying, that it is okay to be sad, and that he was still there for her. Naming his grief kept her from fearing her own. 🤍
How might Sahil feel when Keerthana says she misses Dadi too?
Sahil may feel comforted that they share the loss and that she can tell him. He may also feel tender towards her.
Cut this to under ten words: It is necessary for all visitors to sign in at the front desk.
Visitors must sign in at the front desk.

Lance wants to finish reading a 100 page book in 3 days. Yesterday, he started to read 35 pages. Today, he read 5 fewer pages than yesterday. How many pages should he read tomorrow to finish the book?

Lance read 35 - 5 = 30 pages today.
So he read a total of 35 + 30 = 65 pages in 2 days.
Thus, he should read 100 - 65 = 35 pages tomorrow.
The answer is 35.

Dear Mohit,

I'm writing because I don't want to say this in front of the team. You're the most exciting player I've coached in years. Your tricks with the ball get the whole ground cheering. But I've noticed you skip passing drills and first-touch practice whenever you can.

In Sunday's match, your first touch let you down three times, and each time we lost the ball. I've seen this before: players who skip the basics shine at fifteen and struggle at eighteen.

So here's my offer. Fifteen minutes of first-touch work with me before each practice. After that, show me every trick you like.

Coach Wasim

How many times did Mohit's first touch fail on Sunday?
Three times.
What does Coach Wasim seem to feel about Mohit?
Coach Wasim seems proud of Mohit's talent but worried that skipping basics will cause gaps later.
Why is Coach Wasim's offer a good approach?
It holds the standard with fifteen minutes of basics, while still leaving room for the tricks Mohit enjoys.
How might Mohit feel reading this letter?
Mohit might feel flattered at first and then a little stung, but also respected that the coach wrote privately.
Why does a seed need water to sprout? I don't understand "displeasure". Can you help? How do you spell "neice"?

1. Water wakes the seed up. Because it softens the seed coat and lets the tiny plant inside swell and grow.
2. Displeasure is a noun that means the feeling of being annoyed or not pleased.
3. It is "niece". Remember "i before e".

In the lane behind their building in Lucknow, Anjali, ten, had lost the colony badminton final to Zeenat, 21-8. She went home and didn't come down for two days. On the third evening, Zeenat saw her in the lane at six, alone, hitting the shuttle against the wall. Again. Again. Her backhand kept hitting the gate. She fetched it every time. "Want to practise with me?" Zeenat called. Anjali hesitated, then threw her the spare racquet. "Only if you show me how you did that drop shot." They played until the streetlights came on.

What was the score in the final?
Zeenat won 21-8.
Why might Anjali have stayed home for two days?
She was hurt and discouraged after the big loss and needed time before facing the court again.
What did Anjali do that helped her bounce back?
She returned to steady practice on her own and then asked her rival to teach her the shot that beat her.
What might Zeenat feel when Anjali asks about her drop shot?
Respected, and glad her friend isn't holding the loss against her.

The flat in Copenhagen was cheap, bright and near the harbour, and Ingrid, twenty-four, wanted it the moment she stepped in. Anders, the landlord, smiled. "Sign today and it's yours. Other people are coming at five." Ingrid felt the rush of wanting and, under it, a small tight feeling in her chest. She stepped out onto the stairwell and texted her friend Emil: "I love it, but something feels off. Help me sort it." She wrote what she knew: the kitchen was lovely, the price was low, the landlord wouldn't show the contract until she paid a deposit, and there was no name on the letterbox. "What makes me feel good, and what makes me uneasy?" she asked herself. Emil replied, "A good deal can wait for a day." Ingrid went back in. "I'll need to read the contract first," she said. Anders stopped smiling.

What would Anders not show Ingrid until she paid a deposit?
The contract.
What two feelings did Ingrid notice while standing in the flat?
She felt a rush of wanting the bright, cheap flat, and under it a small tight feeling that something was off.
What did Ingrid do that turned her feelings into a clear decision?
She stepped out, wrote down what she knew for and against, asked Emil for help, and insisted on reading the contract first.
How might Emil have felt getting Ingrid's text from the stairwell?
Emil likely felt trusted and glad to help slow things down, replying that a good deal can wait a day.
I'm organising a farewell lunch for a colleague who is retiring, and nobody has volunteered to help.
That's kind of you to take it on. Even a small team of two or three makes it easier. You could send a short note asking who can help with one task each.
What tasks should I list?
Choose a venue or a spot in the office, collect small contributions, order or bring food, and arrange a card for everyone to sign. Four simple jobs are easy to share.
People keep forgetting to sign cards. Any ideas?
Leave the card on a desk where people pass often and tell the team on which day it will go to the retiree. A friendly reminder the day before helps too.
The lunch is on Friday. Should I keep it a surprise?
If your colleague likes surprises and you know someone close who can bring them to the room, it can be lovely. If you aren't sure, ask their manager or a close friend what they would prefer.
Her manager says she'll be thrilled. I'll plan a small speech too.
Keep it short and personal. Two or three warm memories, a thank you and a good wish for her next chapter are enough.

Abhinav, you're stuck on your short film script? Let me tell your Thomas Uncle's story. In college, I was the timetable king. Every exam, every assignment, planned to the half hour, and it worked beautifully for engineering. Then I joined the drama club and had to write a one-act play. What did I do? A timetable. "Monday 6 to 7: Scene 1. Tuesday 6 to 7: Scene 2." Monday at six I sat down, and nothing came. At seven I had two lines and felt like a failure. Tuesday, the same. For two weeks I kept the timetable and wrote almost nothing. Creative work doesn't come on schedule. My friend finally said, "Just scribble anything, anywhere." I'd never tried that. I'd used one method for everything.

What did young Thomas write in his timetable for Monday?
"Monday 6 to 7: Scene 1."
How did young Thomas feel at seven on Monday?
Young Thomas felt blocked, frustrated and like a failure, with only two lines written.
At what point in the story could Thomas have changed course?
After the first blocked evening; trying a loose start, like scribbling ideas anywhere, would have suited the play better.
How might Thomas's friend have felt watching him struggle?
The friend probably felt concerned and a little impatient, which is why they suggested scribbling anything.

Read this:

Wednesday
In class I stood up and said, "I will win the 200 metres on sports day." Everyone went "oooh". Now I HAVE to.
Rehana Didi wanted to take me for ice cream after school. I said no, I have practice. She laughed and said, "Look at my little brother, so serious."
I ran six rounds of the school field while the others went home. My legs are burning.
I don't even know if I can win. But I said it in front of everyone. If I skip practice, it's like my words were fake. I'll run again tomorrow at 6.
Eshaan

What race did Eshaan say he would win?
He said he would win the 200 metres on sports day.
Why does Eshaan refuse ice cream with Rehana Didi?
He feels determined and a bit pressured, because he said it in front of everyone and skipping practice would make his words feel fake.
What could help Eshaan use this energy well?
He could keep practising but also rest, and remember that trying his best keeps his word even if he doesn't win.
How does Rehana Didi see her brother's new seriousness?
She finds it funny and a little sweet, calling him her serious little brother.
The Wi-Fi in my room is so slow that videos keep buffering.
That's frustrating. Where is the router compared with your room?
It's in the hall, two walls away.
Walls weaken the signal. Try moving closer to the router, or ask an adult if the router can be placed in a more central spot. Also check whether many devices are using it at once.
My brother is always downloading something.
That can slow everyone's connection. You could agree on times, so downloads happen when you aren't studying or watching something.
I'll talk to him tonight.
A friendly schedule is easier than an argument.
Oprah has 3500 cars in her collection. If the average number of cars she gives away per year is 50, how many years will it take to reduce her car collection to 500?

If Oprah wants to have 500 cars left, she will have to give away 3500-500 = 3000 cars.
Since the average number of cars she gives away per year is 50, it will take her 3000/50 = 60 years to give away enough cars to have 500 left over.
The answer is 60.

In the village school outside Satara, the new box of chalk vanished from Guruji's table during recess. Vasudha had been sitting nearest the window, so Guruji made her stand in the corner for the rest of the morning. Her ears were red, and she kept blinking hard. Omkar's heart pounded. He had seen what happened: a monkey had jumped through the window, grabbed the box and bounded up the neem tree. But Guruji looked cross, and nobody spoke. At lunch, Omkar walked quietly to Guruji's table, hands sweating. 'Guruji, it wasn't Vasudha. I saw a monkey take it. It's up the neem tree.' Guruji went to the window, squinted, and saw bits of chalk scattered below. He called Vasudha out of the corner and apologised to her.

Where did the monkey take the chalk box?
Up the neem tree.
How did Omkar feel before speaking to Guruji?
Nervous but full of compassion; his heart pounded and his hands were sweating, yet he couldn't let Vasudha be punished unfairly.
Why was Omkar's way of speaking up a good one?
He went quietly to Guruji at lunch with the facts, so Guruji could check without a scene.
What was it like for Vasudha standing in the corner?
Humiliating and unfair; her ears were red and she kept blinking hard.

Michael has $42. Michael gives away half the money to his brother. His brother then buys 3 dollars worth of candy. If his brother has $35 left, how much money, in dollars, did his brother have at first?

Michael gives away 42/2=21 dollars.
Before buying candy, his brother has 35+3=38 dollars.
His brother had 38-21=17 dollars at first.
The answer is 17.

By July, Zanele's weeks in Johannesburg had flattened into one long Tuesday: taxi, spreadsheet, taxi, television. Nothing was wrong enough to complain about. So she changed the pattern on purpose. She swapped her lunchtime scrolling for a walk to the community garden two streets from the office, where an old man named Sipho grew spinach in tyres. He handed her a trowel on the second day. On Saturdays she started a beginners' woodwork class with her friend Omar, who made a spectacularly crooked stool. Some evenings still went grey. She made herself a promise and wrote it on the fridge: If the grey gets heavier or doesn't lift, book the clinic, don't wait. For now, there was spinach to water.

Where did Sipho grow spinach?
In tyres at the community garden.
What does the note on Zanele's fridge show about Zanele's thinking?
It shows Zanele is wary of the grey feeling, taking it seriously and deciding not to just wait it out if it gets heavier.
Which of Zanele's changes seems to help most, and why?
The garden walks seem to help, since swapping scrolling for time with Sipho and the plants breaks the one-long-Tuesday pattern.
How might Sipho see Zanele coming back each lunchtime?
Sipho probably enjoys the company and the extra pair of hands, which is why he handed over a trowel on the second day.

Week 1: Anjali decided to start running with her brother Karthik before school. Five minutes in, she was gasping and walked home. Karthik didn't laugh, just said, "Tomorrow, same time."
Week 3: She'd kept going, but slowly: run one minute, walk one minute, for twenty minutes. Some mornings she hated it. She also noticed she was starving afterwards and started eating a proper breakfast, eggs and a banana, instead of skipping it for the bus.
Week 6: On a cool Sunday, she ran the whole park loop without stopping. Karthik was behind her, for once.
She didn't feel like an athlete. But she felt steadier in class, and she was sleeping better. She pinned a calendar to her wall and put a tick on every running day.

What did Anjali start eating for breakfast?
Eggs and a banana.
How did Anjali feel after running the whole park loop?
Anjali felt steadier and quietly proud, even if she didn't feel like an athlete.
Which habit helped most, and why?
Running little and often with walking breaks helped, because it was manageable enough to keep up for weeks.
How might Karthik feel seeing her ahead of him in week 6?
Karthik probably feels proud of his sister and pleased that his patience helped her keep going.

Week one: Pankaj and Sangeeta started the same week at the cafe in Koramangala, both students working evenings. Sangeeta asked him to cover her Tuesday; she had an exam. He did. Two weeks later, when his grandmother was unwell, she took his Saturday without being asked twice.
Month three: under pressure from the manager to cut hours, Pankaj was tempted to quietly take Sangeeta's extra shift, the one she needed for her fees. He didn't. He said, 'That's yours. You'd have done the same for me.' She had.
Month nine: when the manager offered one of them the shift-lead role, Sangeeta recommended Pankaj, and he insisted they share it. The manager was surprised. 'You two never fight.' Pankaj shrugged. 'We'll be working together again tomorrow. It's easier to keep promises than to keep grudges.'

Why did Sangeeta ask Pankaj to cover her Tuesday?
She had an exam.
What was Pankaj feeling in month three?
Pankaj felt tempted by the extra shift but uneasy, knowing Sangeeta needed it and had always kept her word.
Why does keeping promises make practical sense for them?
They meet again every day, so reliable cooperation keeps both helped, while one betrayal would be remembered.
How does the manager see their partnership?
The manager is surprised and impressed that the two never fight and even share the lead role.

Dear Chetan Bhaiya,
You said to plan before I talk to Sonal, so I've written it out. Please tell me if it sounds okay.
Where: after school, on the bench behind the canteen, just the two of us.
What I'll say first: “I've noticed you seem really low lately, and I'm worried about you. I care about you.”
Then I stop talking and let her answer, even if the silence is long.
If she gets angry and says I'm being nosy: “Okay. I'm not trying to push. I'm still here whenever you want.” And I'll try again another day.
If she shuts down and won't talk: I'll tell Ms Fernandes, our class teacher, the same day, because it's too important to wait.
If she says anything about hurting herself: I stay with her and get Ms Fernandes or another adult straight away.
I'm nervous. But having it written down helps.
Madhuri

Where does Madhuri plan to talk to Sonal?
After school, on the bench behind the canteen.
How is Madhuri feeling about the conversation?
Madhuri is nervous, but steadier for having the words written down.
What else could Madhuri add to the plan?
What to do after the talk, like checking in again the next day, so one conversation isn't the whole plan.
How might Chetan Bhaiya see this email?
He would likely be touched by Madhuri's care and reassured that the plan includes getting an adult quickly if needed.

Mahima knocked twice and pushed the door open. "Gurpreet? Dinner's getting cold. Why are you sitting in the dark?"
"Nothing."
"That's a big nothing. Show me."
He turned the phone. An edited photo of him in his turban, with a crown drawn on and a caption about "the clown of 11C". Two hundred reactions.
"Who made this?"
"Some page. Everyone's sharing it. Maybe I deserve it, I was showing off at the debate."
"No. Listen to me. Nobody deserves this. It isn't your fault." Mahima sat on the bed. "Don't delete anything. Screenshot the page, the comments, the dates."
"If you tell Mummy, it'll get worse."
"I'm telling her now, and we'll do it together. Then we report the page and block it."
They walked out to the kitchen. Mummy read it, put down the ladle and said, "I'm writing to your class teacher tonight." She did, before anyone ate.

What did Mahima tell Gurpreet not to do?
Mahima told him not to delete anything.
What was Gurpreet feeling when he said "Maybe I deserve it"?
He felt ashamed and helpless, sitting in the dark and blaming himself for showing off.
What steps did Mahima lay out, and why do they help?
Mahima told him to screenshot the page, comments and dates, tell Mummy, then report and block; this keeps evidence and brings in adults who can act.
How might Mummy have felt reading the page?
She was probably upset and protective, putting down the ladle and writing to the class teacher that very night.

Tuesday, Tokyo Something strange happened at the phone shop today. The clerk mixed up my SIM card, and I had to wait an hour. When she explained the mistake, she was smiling. Smiling! And giggling a little. I got really angry. I thought she was laughing at me. I said, too loudly, "This isn't funny." She looked shocked and bowed lower and lower. Later I told Rashmi, who's been here two years. She said, "Oh, Yogesh. That smile wasn't mockery. For a lot of people here, a smile or small laugh can cover embarrassment, like an apology. She was probably mortified." I felt awful. Back home, smiling while apologising looks rude. Here, for her, it might have been the opposite. Rashmi said not every person does it, but it's common enough that I shouldn't assume. Tomorrow I'm going back to the shop to say sorry. With a normal face.

Three sentences, please: what is this section about?

Yogesh waits an hour at a Tokyo phone shop after a SIM card mix-up and gets angry when the clerk smiles. Rashmi explains that a smile or small laugh can cover embarrassment, like an apology. Yogesh feels awful and plans to go back tomorrow to say sorry.

Then play early in the morning or after the sun goes down. In the afternoon, you can try indoor games, drawing or reading. Keep a bottle of water close.
Alia has 2 times as many markers as Austin. Austin has one-third as many markers as Steve does. If Steve has 60 markers, how many does Alia have?

Austin has 60/3=20 markers
Alia has 20*2=40 markers
The answer is 40.

Read this:

Lohri week had brought thick fog to Ludhiana, and Mama had gone to Nani's village for four days. At midday recess, while the others chased each other round the swings, Jasleen sat on the bottom step, holding Mama's butterfly hair clip tight in her fist. She didn't cry. She just watched the school gate, where the fog swallowed the road.
Her tiffin stayed shut. When Himani Ma'am sat down beside her and asked, "Missing someone?" Jasleen only nodded and pressed the clip against her cheek.

What was Jasleen holding in her fist?
Mama's butterfly hair clip.
How can you tell Jasleen felt a longing for Mama even though she didn't cry?
She went quiet, sat apart watching the gate, left her tiffin shut and pressed the clip to her cheek, all signs of an ache of longing.
How could Himani Ma'am support Jasleen for the rest of the day?
Stay close, let Jasleen keep the clip, and perhaps help her draw a picture for Mama or count the days until Mama comes back.
What might Himani Ma'am notice that the other children miss?
That a quiet child with a shut tiffin can be just as sad as one in tears.

Rewrite these lines from Griffith's Ramayana in simple prose.

Right glad was Visvamitra when
He saw the prince of saintly men.
Low at his feet the hero bent,
And did obeisance, reverent.
Visvamitra was very glad when he saw the greatest of holy men. The hero bowed low at his feet and showed him deep respect.
How is a historian different from a history teacher?

A historian studies and writes about the past, often by reading old records. A history teacher teaches the subject, though some do both. Historian is a noun.
Example: The historian visited the old fort to study its walls and stones.
Is the air quality good in my city this morning?
I can't check live air readings, so I don't know. An air quality app will show the current level.
Write a stage direction for a play in one sentence beginning with "Enter".
Enter Meena, carrying a lantern and looking nervously around the dark room.

Read this:

Hi Joseph,
You asked what's been strangest about moving to Helsinki. It isn't the cold. It's the space between people.
My first morning I stood at a bus stop about a foot behind a woman, like at home in Pune. She moved away. I stepped closer to stay in the queue, and she moved again. I thought she found me rude or even scary. Then I noticed everyone else: two metres apart, each person in their own bubble, and nobody offended by it.
In the office it's the same. When I lean in to talk, my colleague Aino leans back. At first I read it as coldness. Now I think it's just normal distance here, and she's actually quite warm once you know her. I've started standing further back. It still feels unfriendly to me, honestly. But I think it's only different.
Write soon,
Yogesh

How far apart did Yogesh notice people standing at the bus stop?
Two metres apart.
What did Yogesh first think when the woman at the bus stop moved away?
Yogesh felt unsure and a bit hurt, thinking she found Yogesh rude or even scary; it later seemed she was just keeping normal local distance.
What change has Yogesh made, and why is it wise?
Standing further back, which matches local spacing and stops others from reading Yogesh's closeness as pushy.
How might Aino see Yogesh's leaning in to talk?
She may find it a bit too close for comfort, which is why she leans back, even though she is warm once people know her.

Read this:

Noa had just learned to run, which mostly meant falling forward fast. At the playground in Rotterdam she ran at the pigeons, tumbled on the rubber mat, and lay still for a second, checking her mother's face. Dalia smiled and said, "Up you get." Noa rolled onto her knees, pushed on her hands, stood, and set off again, arms wide. At the climbing frame she hauled one foot onto the lowest bar and stayed there, grunting.

What did Noa run at in the playground?
She ran at the pigeons.
Why did Noa check her mother's face after she tumbled?
She was unsure whether the fall was scary, so she looked to Dalia to decide how to feel, and the smile reassured her.
What small step would help Noa with the climbing frame?
Dalia could stand close and let her keep trying the lowest bar, steadying her hips rather than lifting her up.
How might Dalia see Noa's many falls?
She seems to see them as a normal part of learning to run, so she stays calm instead of rushing in.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Friday. Payal, Class 10, came to my room at lunch with her phone in her hand. She showed me a friend's reply, "fine." and asked, "Isn't that angry? She used to write 'fine!!' with a heart." Payal had not eaten. She said she had rewritten her own message four times.
I asked what else she knew about her friend's week, and Payal said there was a maths test. We talked about how tone is guessed when there is no voice. I suggested she send one open question, and she wrote, "Are we okay? You seemed quiet." Then she ate her lunch. The reply came before the bell: "just tired, come sit with me? 🙂"
Vinita, school counsellor

What word did Payal's friend send in the reply she showed the counsellor?
The friend's reply said "fine." with a full stop.
What might Payal have been worrying about when she rewrote her message four times?
Payal was probably anxious that the friend was upset with her. Not eating lunch and rewriting the message show how much the short reply weighed on her.
What did Vinita do to help Payal move from guessing to checking?
Vinita asked what Payal knew about the friend's week, talked about how tone is guessed in text, and suggested one open question. Payal sent it and got a warm answer.
What was the friend probably going through when the reply "fine." was sent?
The friend was probably tired, with a maths test that week, and wrote a short word without thinking about tone. The friend then invited Payal to sit together.

Read this:

In his first winter in Manchester, Bilal kept reaching for his phone at odd moments to tell Yosef something: the bus driver who called him "love", the professor who looked exactly like their uncle. Back in Amman, his older brother had always been the first person he told things to. He had never thought about it.
One night, after a long day in the lab, he couldn't sleep. He sent a voice note instead of the usual thumbs up: "I don't think I ever said this. I rely on you more than anyone. I miss you, and I don't know how to do things without telling you first."
Yosef replied at six in the morning his time, voice rough with sleep. "Idiot. I know. But thank you for saying it."
After that Bilal set a Friday reminder: one voice note, one photo, however busy he was. For Yosef's birthday he mailed a box of the biscuits Yosef had once laughed at in a film. It arrived late. Yosef posted a photo anyway.

Where was Bilal spending his first winter?
In Manchester.
What did Bilal realise during that first winter?
That he relied on Yosef more than anyone; he missed him deeply and felt lost without telling him things first.
How did Bilal show up for Yosef in small ways?
A weekly Friday voice note and photo, and a box of biscuits mailed for Yosef's birthday.
How did Yosef respond to Bilal's voice note?
With gruff affection ("Idiot. I know.") and thanks for saying it out loud.
My office people say "He is out of station." My foreign client did not understand.
"Out of station" is common in India, but other English speakers may not know it. Say: "He is out of town." That is clear everywhere.

Read this:

Uday here. I was standing by the water cooler when a boy from the other class started tapping Harsha's head with a ruler again. Harsha had been quiet for weeks, and I expected him to freeze. Instead he looked straight at the boy and said, "Stop that. I don't like it." His voice wobbled a little, but it did not shout. Then he picked up his bottle and walked off towards the staff room. I heard later that he had told the class teacher earlier that week and had practised those words with them. I can't say if he was scared inside. The ruler boy just stood there with his mouth open, and that afternoon the class teacher had a word with him.

What did Harsha say to the boy with the ruler?
He said, "Stop that. I don't like it."
What might Harsha have been feeling as he spoke, judging by his wobbling voice?
He was probably nervous, but Uday cannot be sure; the wobble alongside steady words suggests he was brave even though he may have been afraid.
What should happen if the boy keeps teasing Harsha even after he says stop?
Harsha should not handle it alone; adults like the class teacher need to step in, as the teacher already did that afternoon.
How might the ruler boy have felt when Harsha spoke up?
He was probably taken by surprise, since he stood there with his mouth open and had expected Harsha to freeze.
The manager said we will stagger the lunch breaks. I only know stagger as walking unsteadily.

As a verb, to stagger means to arrange things at different times so that they do not all happen together. The walking sense is moving unsteadily, as if about to fall.
Example: The school staggers its start times to avoid crowds at the gate.
Don't forget turning off the lights before going out. Please check.

Don't forget to turn off the lights before going out.
Why: "forget to" plus a verb means a task to remember.
Prove that the equation (x - a)(x - b) = 1 has two distinct real roots for all real numbers a and b. Also prove that x^2 + px - 1 = 0 has real roots for every p.

Answer: D = (a - b)^2 + 4 > 0 and D = p^2 + 4 > 0, so both always have two distinct real roots.

Expand and write in standard form first: (x - a)(x - b) = 1 x^2 - (a + b)x + ab - 1 = 0 D = (a + b)^2 - 4(ab - 1) = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 - 4ab + 4 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2 + 4 = (a - b)^2 + 4 A square is never negative, so (a - b)^2 >= 0 and D >= 4 > 0. Hence there are always two distinct real roots. For x^2 + px - 1 = 0: D = p^2 - 4(1)(-1) = p^2 + 4 >= 4 > 0. In fact whenever a and c have OPPOSITE signs, -4ac > 0 and the roots are real and distinct. The proof strategy: write D as a square plus a positive number.
What are hammers? My uncle has three of different sizes.

A hammer is a tool with a heavy metal head on a handle, used for hitting nails or breaking things. Hammers is the plural. It is a noun, and it can also be a verb that means to hit hard.
Example: Uncle's toolbox holds three hammers of different sizes.
Can you help me to carrying this box upstairs? What is wrong?

Can you help me carry this box upstairs?
Why: "help" takes the base verb, never "to" plus -ing.
Brenda picks 250 peaches. When she sorts through them, only 60% are fresh, and Brenda has to throw 15 away for being too small. How many peaches does Brenda have left?

First find how many of the peaches are fresh, which is 250 peaches * 60% = 150 peaches.
Then, subtract the number Brenda throws away after the fresh count, which is 150 peaches - 15 peaches = 135 peaches.
The answer is 135.

Read this:

For most of first year I, Jatin, hid it. I had an ADHD diagnosis from school, a letter in a drawer at home, and I told myself college would be different. It wasn't. In three-hour exams in a hall of two hundred people, I'd read question five, drift to the clock, the fan, a cough, and look up with forty minutes gone. My marks didn't match what I knew. In second year my friend Ankita, who uses a screen reader, asked why I never went to the disability cell. "They're there for this," she said. "It's not a favour." My stomach twisted the whole walk there. But I took the letter and asked, plainly, for a separate room and extra time. It took two weeks of forms. Last semester I finished every paper. I still feel a bit exposed about it, just less than I used to.

What did Jatin ask the disability cell for?
A separate room and extra time.
How did Jatin feel walking to the disability cell?
Jatin felt anxious, with a stomach that twisted the whole walk, and still feels a little exposed about asking.
What made Jatin's request likely to succeed?
Bringing the letter and asking plainly for specific adjustments, then following through two weeks of forms.
How does Ankita see asking for support?
Ankita treats support as a right rather than a favour, and says so plainly to encourage Jatin.
Please stop to make noise, the baby is sleeping. Correct, please.

Please stop making noise because the baby is sleeping.
Why: "stop" plus -ing means quit; "because" joins the sentences.

Read this:

In Class 10, I tried to choose a career with a spreadsheet. I'm Jatin, and I'm the kind of person who trusts numbers more than feelings.

I listed three options: medicine, engineering and design. Then I scored each from one to ten on how interesting it felt, how much effort it demanded, what studying it would cost, and job security. Then I weighted them, because I knew they didn't matter equally. Interest counted triple. Job security counted double.

Engineering won by two points. I was ready to announce it.

Then my friend Dhruv asked, "What if you care less about salary than you think?" I lowered the job-security weight to one, just to test it. Design jumped to first place.

I sat there for a long time. The matrix wasn't lying. It was showing me that my whole answer rested on one question: how much did a safe salary matter to me? I still haven't fully answered that. But at least now I know what I'm actually deciding.

By how many points did engineering win at first?
By two points.
How did Jatin feel when design jumped to first place?
Jatin felt unsettled and thoughtful, sitting for a long time after seeing the answer depended on one weight.
What could Jatin do to decide how much salary matters?
Jatin could talk with parents and people in each field about pay and lifestyle, and then set the weight with that knowledge.
How might Dhruv see the effect of that one question?
Dhruv probably feels pleased and a bit surprised that one question changed the whole result.

Read this:

Tomas had his chemistry exam in Prague on Thursday. On Monday night he sat in his room with a podcast playing, three tabs open, and his phone lighting up every few seconds with his friends' group chat.

He read about bonding. He read it again. When his sister Rosa quizzed him at breakfast, he couldn't explain a single diagram.

"You studied for three hours," she said.

"I know," Tomas said, rubbing his face. "It just didn't go in."

On Tuesday Rosa took his phone and put it in a drawer, and turned off the podcast. "Forty minutes. Just the book." Tomas grumbled but did it. At dinner, she quizzed him again, and he got most of it right. He felt oddly proud.

What did Rosa do with Tomas's phone on Tuesday?
She took his phone and put it in a drawer.
Why did Tomas rub his face at breakfast?
He felt frustrated and discouraged because he had studied for three hours but couldn't explain anything.
What small change helped Tomas remember, and why?
Putting the phone away and turning off the podcast let Tomas focus on one thing, so the material stuck.
How might Rosa feel when Tomas got most of it right?
Rosa probably felt pleased and a bit proud of her plan working.

Read this:

Vidya, you're giving your first big talk next week? Sit. Your Rajni aunty has a story.
When I was a young officer, maybe twenty-four, I was sent to a state conference on rural water. The main speaker was a senior engineer, very respected. He had brought sixty slides. Tables of pipe lengths, rainfall for every district, costs by year. He read them very fast.
I had a notebook. I tried to write. By the twentieth slide I had written only the date. The man next to me was asleep. I felt terrible for the engineer, and also, honestly, annoyed. I had taken a night bus to be there.
You know what I remember from that whole hour? One photograph. A girl carrying two pots on her head, and his one sentence: "She walks four kilometres. This project cuts it to two hundred metres."
Forty years later, I remember that girl. I don't remember a single table.

What was the one photograph Rajni remembers?
A girl carrying two pots on her head.
How did young Rajni feel as the slides went on?
Rajni felt sorry for the engineer and also annoyed, having taken a night bus to be there.
At what point in the talk did the engineer finally reach his audience?
When he showed the photograph and said one clear sentence about the walk being cut to two hundred metres.
How might the engineer have seen his own talk?
The engineer probably thought all the tables showed how thorough the project was, not noticing that people had stopped following.

Read this:

On Mother's Day in Melbourne, Tuan gave his mum, Rania, a folded card. Inside was a big red heart, two stick people holding hands, and a line of wiggly marks. “What does it say?” Rania asked. Tuan pointed along the squiggles. “It says, ‘Mummy, you are the best and I love you and you make good noodles.’” Rania didn't mention that none of the marks were letters. She hugged him. “That's the best card I've ever had.” She stood it on the kitchen shelf.

Where did Rania stand the card?
On the kitchen shelf.
What was Tuan feeling as he pointed along the squiggles?
He felt proud and loving, sure his marks carried his message to his mum.
Why was Rania's response wise?
She responded to his meaning and love instead of correcting the spelling, which encourages him to keep sharing feelings in writing.
What would change if Rania had said the squiggles weren't real words?
Tuan might feel his message didn't count and be less eager to write or draw for people again.

Read this:

Urmila had two days before her first big job interview, and her professional profile was almost empty. Worse, her old accounts were full of silly photos and a heated argument from two years ago. Her roommate Ganga looked her up and winced. "That argument is the third result." Urmila panicked. With the internet at the hostel going on and off, they worked late into the night: making personal accounts private, deleting the worst posts, adding her internship, project and volunteering to her professional page. Ganga took a clean photo of her against the hostel wall. "It's not perfect," Urmila said. "It's honest," Ganga replied. At the interview, the panel asked about her volunteering, not her argument. Urmila almost laughed with relief.

What did the panel ask Urmila about at the interview?
They asked about her volunteering.
Why did Urmila panic when Ganga looked her up?
She realised an old heated argument appeared near the top of her search results, where employers could easily see it.
What made Urmila's clean-up effective under time pressure?
She focused on the essentials: making accounts private, deleting the worst posts and adding real achievements to her professional page.
How might Ganga feel after Urmila's interview?
She'd likely feel relieved and proud to have helped, and glad her honest advice paid off. 🙂

Read this:

Hi Tejas bhaiya,
Quick question, but first my big discovery. I checked the class result list with Riddhi. Of the nine people in our section who scored above 90 in science, seven go to Sharma Sir's coaching. SEVEN. So I've decided coaching is the secret, and I need to join from next month. Can you help me convince Papa? He says it's expensive and I should try harder on my own first.
I know Riddhi said those seven also sit in the front row, finish homework on the bus, and have parents who come to every PTM. But they all have coaching in common, right? That has to be what does it.
Please reply before Sunday, because that's when I'm asking Papa.
Your favourite cousin,
Vinita

How many of the top science scorers go to Sharma Sir's coaching?
Seven of the nine people who scored above 90.
Why does Vinita feel so sure that coaching is "the secret"?

Vinita feels excited because seven out of nine sounds striking and coaching is the shared thing Vinita was looking for, so it feels like the answer while the front row and homework habits fade into the background.
What could Tejas bhaiya suggest in reply?
He could point out that those seven also study hard and have involved parents, and suggest Vinita try their habits for a while before asking Papa to pay.
How might Papa see this request?
Papa is thinking about the cost and wants Vinita to try harder first, so he may feel the 'seven out of nine' argument skips over effort.

Read this:

Vaibhav, you keep saying everyone in Pune already has friends. Let me tell you about my first year in Delhi, at nineteen. I came from a small town near Jabalpur, and I cried in the hostel bathroom so no one would hear. I wrote long letters home saying the food was bad and the girls were snobbish. Really, I was just afraid to speak first. What changed it was silly. The warden needed volunteers to decorate for Diwali, and I was good with rangoli. I knelt on that floor for two evenings with four strangers, sharing colours. By the end, one of them, Farah, had become my friend, and her room became my second home. The ache for home doesn't vanish, beta. You just build a second place to miss.

What did the narrator volunteer to do in the first year in Delhi?
Decorate the hostel for Diwali by making rangoli.
What was the narrator really feeling behind the complaints in the letters home?
The narrator admits being afraid to speak first; calling the girls snobbish covered that fear and loneliness.
What might Vaibhav try in Pune, based on this story?
Vaibhav could join one shared task or activity where working side by side makes talking easier, instead of waiting to be approached.
How might Farah have seen the narrator during those evenings?
Probably just as a quiet newcomer good at rangoli; Farah would not know about the crying alone, which shows how hidden loneliness can be.
Now you try: from (-2, 3) to (3, -9).
The answer is 13 units.

Read this:

Tejas, you asked why I make you explain every line. Sit, I'll tell you.
When I was in Class Eleven, our school had one computer lab, and there was an internet café down the road. I had to build a small library record program. I found forum posts, pasted them together, and after three evenings it ran. Our teacher, Fernandes Sir, looked at it and said, “Chaitanya, good. Now make it show only the books that are overdue.”
One small change. I sat there till the lab closed. I didn't know which line did what, because I had never once asked why any of them was there.
Fernandes Sir didn't scold. He made me rebuild it slowly, one piece at a time, explaining each piece to him before writing the next. It took two weeks.
So that is why your uncle asks “why” so much.

What small change did Fernandes Sir ask for?
To make the program show only the books that are overdue.
What was young Chaitanya feeling while sitting in the lab until it closed?
He was likely stuck and embarrassed, because a program that seemed finished could not be changed at all.
What choice in the story turned things around for Chaitanya?
Rebuilding the program slowly, one piece at a time, and explaining each piece to Fernandes Sir; understanding replaced pasting.
How might Fernandes Sir have seen the pasted program?
The teacher probably suspected it was not really understood and used one small change to reveal that, without scolding.

messages.content: Sentence check please: 'I am feeling boring today.'
Corrected: "I am feeling bored today." Use "bored" for how you feel. "Boring" describes the thing that makes you feel that way: "This film is boring."

Read this:

After Tushar froze during the district debate in Sehore, with the whole school watching, he told himself he'd simply skip debates from now on.
But the avoiding spread. He stopped answering the landline, in case a relative asked about the debate. He stopped going to the vegetable market for his mother, because people there knew him. When his friends shouted from the lane for cricket, he pretended to be asleep. Last week he even let the tuition teacher's call ring out.
Each time he felt relief, like a door closing on a cold wind. And each time the next thing seemed a little scarier.
Parveen didi from next door found him on the roof on Sunday. "You used to be everywhere in this mohalla," she said. "Now I only see you up here."
Tushar shrugged. The world below looked noisy and sharp, and the roof felt like the only safe place left.

Where did Tushar freeze?
During the district debate in Sehore.
What does Tushar's relief each time he avoids something show?
He feels anxious, and the relief makes avoiding feel safe, so the fear spreads to more and more things.
What could help Tushar at this stage?
Starting with small steps back, like one market errand with his mother, and telling a trusted adult how scared he feels.
How does Parveen didi see the change in Tushar?
She is surprised and concerned, missing the boy who used to be everywhere in the mohalla.

Read this:

The college library in Shillong closed at eight, and Tejas had started staying till the very end.

It wasn't the work. It was that at home, in the evenings, Yangchen asked questions. Who were you with? Why did you smile at your phone? Can I see?

He had never done anything. That was what burned. For three months he had shown her every chat, answered every question, and still she looked at him like a suspect.

So he started keeping things. Not secrets, exactly. Just space. He turned his phone face down. He stopped mentioning the girls in his study group, even though they talked only about thermodynamics.

On Thursday Yangchen said, "You've changed. You're hiding things now."

"I'm not hiding. I'm tired of being searched."

She stared at him, and he could see it in her face: his tiredness had just become her proof.

What time did the college library close?
At eight.
Why does Tejas stay at the library until closing?
He feels resentful and worn out from being distrusted for nothing, and wants some private space away from Yangchen's questions.
What could break this cycle at this stage?
Both could name what is happening: Tejas says he feels searched and resentful, and Yangchen talks about her fear, perhaps with a counsellor's help, instead of each protecting themselves.
How does Yangchen read Tejas's new need for space?
She reads it as proof that he is hiding something, which deepens her fear and suspicion.

Read this:

After what happened at my last company, I made myself a list. I keep it in my wallet, behind my ID: Things I will not do. I will not sign what I haven't checked. I will not change a number to fit a target. I will not tell a customer something I know is misleading.
I wrote it while I was calm, because I'd learned that under pressure my mind gets very good at excuses.
At the startup where I now run compliance, we built the other side too. Anyone can report a concern to an external ethics line, anonymously. Every month we give a small award to whoever flagged the most useful bad news. Last month it was Jomon, who spotted that a sales incentive was nudging people to skip consent forms. We changed the incentive that week.
Sometimes I still catch myself thinking, it's just this once. That phrase is my alarm now. I'm Rekha, and I've learned to listen to it.

Where does Rekha keep the list?
In my wallet, behind my ID.
What does Rekha feel on catching the thought 'just this once'?
Rekha feels a flash of alarm, recognising the start of explaining away discomfort.
Which safeguards at the startup guard best against drift?
An anonymous external ethics line, rewarding useful bad news, and quickly changing incentives that push people to cut corners.
What might Jomon feel receiving the award?
Jomon likely feels valued and safe, rewarded instead of punished for raising a concern.
What does "bite off more than you can chew" mean?

It means to try to do more than you are able to manage.
Example: Ravi took on three projects at once and soon realised he had bitten off more than he could chew.
Is my classmate Tara nervous about her exam?
I don't know if Tara is nervous, as her feelings are hers. Asking her kindly is the best way to find out.

Read this:

Dear Pooja,
You asked why I sounded odd on the phone. Here it is. The rowing club's welcome week was supposed to be fun. On the first night the seniors made us stand in the hall and shout that we were nobodies. On the second we carried their bags and sang in the dining hall while they filmed. On the third they wanted us to do a dare I knew was unsafe. I wanted so badly to belong that I nearly did. Instead I said no and walked out. On Friday I went to the faculty adviser. She listened, said it wasn't my fault, and called both captains in that same afternoon. I'm still shaky, and a few first-years won't talk to me. But two of them came to my room yesterday.
Asif

What did the seniors make the newcomers do on the first night?
The seniors made them stand in the hall and shout that they were nobodies.
Why did Asif say, “I wanted so badly to belong that I nearly did”?
Asif felt a strong pull to belong and almost gave in to a dare, even though Asif knew it was unsafe.
What did the faculty adviser do that same afternoon?
The faculty adviser listened, told Asif it was not Asif's fault and called both captains in that afternoon.
What might the two first-years who came to Asif's room yesterday have been feeling?
They may have felt relieved and a little ashamed, and may have wanted Asif's company after seeing Asif refuse.
How is a clay pot made? Reply in exactly three sentences.
The potter shapes wet clay on a spinning wheel. The pot is left to dry in the shade. Finally, it is baked in a hot kiln so it becomes hard.

Which job does the speaker offer to do, and under what name?

I am skilled in milking kine and taking their history as well as in taming their fierceness. Passing under the name of Tantripal, I shall perform my duties deftly. Let thy heart's fever be dispelled. Formerly I was frequently employed to look after thy kine, and, O Lord of earth, I have a particular knowledge of that work.
He offers to look after the king's cows, milking them and taming their fierceness, under the name Tantripal.

In the review meeting Pradeep took the client account from Urmila and gave it to a newer favourite. Urmila said, "That doesn't match the numbers." Pradeep smiled thinly. "If you keep pushing, your renewal might get looked at again." A couple of people looked at their laptops. Urmila's cheeks burned, and she said nothing more in the room.

Leela watched from the corner and knew it was unfair. Her stomach hurt. She needed her job, the rent was due, and speaking up could put her next. She thought about it honestly for a night: what could go wrong, what silence would cost. She found Urmila at the pantry and said, "I saw what happened. Can I help?"

Urmila had already started noting dates and the exact words in a notebook. "I'm taking it to HR, and to Ms. Iyer, the senior director." She felt shaky, but she wasn't going to accept it as normal. Leela took a breath and wrote a calm email that stuck to what she had witnessed, and sent it to HR too.

Two days later Ms. Iyer asked both of them to come to her office. Leela's hands were cold, and she went anyway.

Who was the senior director Urmila planned to approach?
Ms. Iyer.
How did Urmila's and Leela's views of the meeting differ, and what did each do afterwards?

Urmila was the one threatened, so she kept dated notes and took it to HR and a senior director. Leela was afraid for her own job but weighed the risk, offered help and sent a calm written account of what she had seen.
What was Leela feeling in the corner of the review meeting?
She felt afraid and uneasy, since she knew it was unfair but needed her job.
What could Urmila do if Pradeep keeps threatening her after the HR meeting?
She could keep her records up to date, ask the senior director for support, and look at her options.
Our cat has started scratching the sofa.
Cats scratch to stretch, mark their territory and keep their claws in shape. It is normal behaviour, not spite.
How do we stop it?
Offer a sturdy scratching post close to the sofa, and make the sofa less appealing. Many cats like a post they can stretch tall against.
Should we scold the cat?
Scolding usually does not work and may scare the cat. Praise and treats when the cat uses the post work better.
What if the cat ignores the post?
Try a different material or placement. Some cats prefer sisal rope, others cardboard. Put it where the cat likes to scratch.
Does trimming the claws help?
It can reduce damage, but it should be done carefully. A vet or an experienced groomer can show how to do it safely.

In the Hyderabad flat, Jahnavi swung in her little seat on the balcony, singing, "La-la-la-la-la!" fast and bright, over and over.
Zainab, the neighbour, leaned over the railing. "What is she saying? Is she asking for something?"
"Nothing," laughed Jahnavi's mother. "That's her happy song."
Zainab sang, "La-la-la!" back. Jahnavi grinned and sang faster.

Where was Jahnavi's swing seat?
On the balcony.
What was Jahnavi feeling as she sang "la-la-la" fast?
She was happy and playful; the fast, repeated sounds were for fun, not a request.
How did Zainab join in well?
She sang the sounds back, which made Jahnavi grin and keep playing.
How does Zainab first read the singing?
Zainab wonders if Jahnavi is asking for something, not knowing it is just her happy song.
I've started collecting old coins but I don't know how to store them.
Coins should be kept dry and apart from each other, so they do not scratch. Do you know how old they are?
Some are very old, from before independence.
Then handle them as little as possible, and by the edges, since the oils on your fingers can mark them. Do not clean them with chemicals, because cleaning can reduce their value and interest.
What can I keep them in?
Small paper envelopes or coin albums with separate pockets are common. Keep them in a dry place, not in a damp cupboard.
How do I know what they're worth?
I cannot value them. A local coin dealer, a museum or a collectors' society can tell you more. Ask an adult to go with you.

Gopika burst into the Kochi flat waving her phone. "Sabina, look! Guaranteed double in six months. The coach said to keep it quiet, only a few spots."
Sabina put down her chai. "Guaranteed double? And quiet? Let's look together before either of us puts in a rupee."
They sat on the floor with the laptop. Sabina opened the official regulator's site and searched the firm's name. Nothing. She searched the coach's name. A warning notice from last year.
"But the coach showed his results," Gopika said, deflated.
"Anyone can make a screenshot," Sabina said gently. "Real investments can go down as well as up, and they aren't sold in secret."
Gopika pulled her knees up. "I almost sent my bonus tonight."
"Almost is fine. Tomorrow let's ask someone at the bank who isn't selling anything."
Gopika laughed shakily and deleted the chat.

What did Sabina find when she searched the coach's name?
She found a warning notice from last year.
How did Gopika feel after seeing the search results?
Gopika felt deflated and shaken, realising she had almost sent her bonus that night.
What made Sabina's response helpful?
She slowed things down, checked the official regulator's site together with Gopika, explained calmly, and suggested asking someone independent at the bank.
What would change if Sabina had mocked Gopika?
Gopika might have felt ashamed and defended the scheme, perhaps sending the money anyway, instead of checking calmly together.

From the lunch notes of the Tiny Tots daycare, by the lunch teacher.
Today, before eating, Parveen folded her hands and said quietly, "Thank you for my food." Kalyani, sitting next to her, asked, "Who are you saying thank you to?" Parveen said, "To Allah and to Ammi who made it." Kalyani folded her hands too. "Thank you to the farmer," Kalyani said. Soon the whole table was saying thank you, to God, to mums, to cooks, to the sun. Parveen looked calm and happy as she opened her tiffin. We may make this a daily moment.

Whom did Kalyani thank?
Kalyani thanked the farmer.
How did Parveen seem when she opened her tiffin?
She looked calm and happy after her quiet thank-you prayer, feeling grateful.
Why might a daily thank-you moment suit a mixed class?
Each child can thank in their own way, to God, family, farmers or the sun, so everyone feels included whatever their family believes.
How might Kalyani see Parveen's prayer?
Kalyani seems curious and inspired by it, joining in with her own kind of thanks. 😊

Annie is trying to figure out whether it's safe to drive her truck. For every 3 degrees the temperature drops below 32 degrees, Annie's chances of skidding on ice increase 5%. If she goes into a skid, she has a 40% of regaining control. Otherwise, she'll have a serious accident. If the temperature is 8 degrees, what is the percentage chance of Annie getting into a serious accident if she drives?

First find how many degrees below 32 the temperature is: 32 degrees - 8 degrees = 24 degrees
Then divide that amount by the number of degrees per 5% increase in skid risk to find how many 5% increases there are: 24 degrees / 3 degrees/5% increase = 8 5% increases
Multiply the number of increases by 5% to find the total increase in skid risk: 8 * 5% = 40%
Now find the chance that Annie has a serious accident if she goes into a skid by subtracting the chance she regains control from 100%: 100% - 40% = 60%
Finally, multiply the chance of going into a skid by the chance of having a serious accident after a skid to find the total risk of a serious accident: 60% * 40% = 24%
The answer is 24.

In a busy café in Valencia, a waiter dropped a tray of plates behind them. Crash! Clara's whole body jerked, arms flung out wide, and then she froze, eyes huge. A second later she began to wail.
"Such a fuss," a man at the next table muttered.
Yara scooped her up and held her close, rocking. "Big bang. You're safe. I've got you," she said softly, again and again, until Clara's arms went soft around her neck.

What did the waiter drop?
A tray of plates.
What was Clara feeling when her arms flung out and she froze?
She was startled and frightened by the sudden crash; her wail shows her body was still shaken.
What did Yara do that helped Clara's body settle?
She held her close, rocked her and repeated soft, calm words until Clara relaxed.
How does the man at the next table see Clara's reaction?
He sees it as a fuss, not as a small child's automatic fright at a loud noise.

At home, Monday evening:
"Keerthana, the insurance office called again. You haven't called them back."
"I will."
"You said that last week, akka."
"I know, Sahil! It's just... when a stranger answers and starts asking for policy numbers, my brain goes blank."
"Okay. What's the easiest call on your list?"
"...The library. To renew a book."
"Do that one. Right now. I'll sit here."
She dialled. Two minutes later she hung up. "They said, 'Done, madam.' That's it."
"See? Tomorrow the gas booking. Day after, the bank. Insurance on Friday."
"One a day?"
"One a day. And you tick them off on the fridge."
On Friday evening Keerthana put down the phone, walked to the fridge and drew a big tick next to "Insurance". "They were actually nice."

What was the easiest call on Keerthana's list?
The library, to renew a book.
Why did Keerthana keep putting off the insurance call?
Strangers asking for policy numbers made her mind go blank, so avoiding the call felt like relief.
Which choice of Sahil's helped most, and why?
Starting with the easiest call right away and sitting beside her, then one call a day, so each success made the next feel less scary.
What might Sahil have felt when Keerthana drew the tick next to 'Insurance'?
Pleased and proud to see the patient plan work, and glad that the call turned out to be pleasant.

Kitchen note, end of month. Dolma, head chef.
I asked Darshan, our new sous chef, to plan the Diwali rotas. In his first draft, every tricky station, the tandoor and the sauces, went to Rakesh. Chitra and Beena had only prep. I didn't say anything; I waited.
Two days later he came back. "I looked again. I've been giving Rakesh everything because he's loud and sure of himself. That's not evidence." He rewrote it: everyone rotates through the hard stations, and everyone gets the same five-minute feedback after service.
After three weeks, Beena runs the sauce station better than anyone. I will recommend Darshan for the permanent post.

Which stations did Rakesh get in the first draft?
The tandoor and the sauces, every tricky station.
What was Darshan feeling when he came back two days later?
He seemed uneasy but honest, bothered to see that confidence, not evidence, had shaped his choices.
What did Darshan's rewrite do well?
It gave everyone turns at the hard stations and equal feedback, so real skill could show, as Beena's did.
How might Beena feel after three weeks at the sauce station?
She likely feels proud and trusted, finally given a real chance to show her skill.

The laddoo tin is empty: 0 laddoos. Amma shares them among 5 children. How many does each child get?

Now you try: 0 / 12.
The answer is 0.

The discomposure of spirits which this extraordinary visit threw Elizabeth into could not be easily overcome; nor could she for many hours learn to think of it less than incessantly. Lady Catherine, it appeared, had actually taken the trouble of this journey from Rosings for the sole purpose of breaking off her supposed engagement with Mr. Darcy. It was a rational scheme, to be sure! but from what the report of their engagement could originate, Elizabeth was at a loss to imagine; till she recollected that his being the intimate friend of Bingley, and her being the sister of Jane, was enough, at a time when the expectation of one wedding made everybody eager for another, to supply the idea. She had not herself forgotten to feel that the marriage of her sister must bring them more frequently together. And her neighbours at Lucas Lodge, therefore, (for through their communication with the Collinses, the report, she concluded, had reached Lady Catherine,) had only set that down as almost certain and immediate which she had looked forward to as possible at some future time.

Explain this excerpt to me in three sentences.

Elizabeth is deeply unsettled by Lady Catherine's visit, made only to end a supposed engagement with Mr. Darcy. She cannot imagine where the report began until she remembers his friendship with Bingley and her being Jane's sister, when one wedding is expected. Neighbours at Lucas Lodge, she decides, simply treated as certain what she had only thought possible later.

The class globe lay on the floor with a crack across Africa when Mrs Dutta walked in. "Who did this?"
Silence. Then Rohan said, "Must be Joseph. He's always clumsy."
Swati felt the knot in her stomach loosen. She had bumped that table during the chase game, though she wasn't sure the globe fell then. "Yes, Joseph was near it," she said. Three more voices joined. "Joseph broke the duster last month."
Joseph, small and quiet on the last bench, shook his head and looked at his shoes.
Mrs Dutta looked around. "Who actually saw it fall?" No hands. "Then nobody knows. Joseph, you're not in trouble. We'll all talk about the chase game after lunch."
Swati stared at her desk, face burning.

Where was the crack on the class globe?
The globe had a crack across Africa.
Why did Swati join in blaming Joseph?
Swati was afraid of being blamed herself after bumping the table, and pointing at Joseph made that fear ease.
What did Mrs Dutta's question "Who actually saw it fall?" achieve?
It asked for facts instead of guesses, showed nobody knew, and protected Joseph from the group's blame.
What was it like for Joseph when everyone named him?
Joseph likely felt helpless and hurt, unable to argue with the whole class, so he just shook his head and looked down.
A ribbon 15/2 m long is cut into pieces each 3/4 m long. How many pieces are there? Also work out (-4/9) / (8/15).

Answer: 15/2 / 3/4 = 15/2 x 4/3 = 10 pieces. (-4/9) / (8/15) = (-4/9) x (15/8) = -5/6.

Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its RECIPROCAL (turn it upside down): the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3. 15/2 x 4/3: cancel 15 and 3 (5 and 1) and 4 and 2 (2 and 1), giving 5 x 2 = 10. Check: 10 x 3/4 = 30/4 = 15/2. For the second, the reciprocal of 8/15 is 15/8; cancel 4 and 8 (1 and 2), 15 and 9 (5 and 3): -(1 x 5)/(3 x 2) = -5/6. Signs: different signs give a negative answer. The reciprocal of a negative number is negative: the reciprocal of -2/7 is -7/2. Only the SECOND number is turned over. 0 / (any non-zero number) = 0, but dividing BY 0 is impossible.

Jamal scraped his knee at the playground in Accra and cried all the way home. His big brother Kwame cleaned it and put on a plaster. “Let's send Grandma a picture,” Kwame said, holding up the phone. “Smile!” Jamal squeezed his cheeks up and showed his teeth, though his eyes were still wet. Kwame lowered the phone. “You don't have to smile, little man. You can just wave, or show her your plaster.” Jamal thought, then stuck his leg out proudly, and Kwame took that picture instead.

What did Jamal show Grandma in the picture Kwame took?
He stuck his leg out to show his plaster.
What does Jamal's squeezed smile with wet eyes suggest?
It suggests he was still hurt and a little upset but tried to smile because his brother asked. He may also have wanted to please Kwame, who had just looked after him.
What small step helped Jamal most?
Kwame offered other choices, a wave or showing the plaster, so Jamal could take part without pretending to feel happy.
How might Grandma feel seeing the plaster photo rather than a forced smile?
She would likely feel close to Jamal and proud of him, seeing a true moment of a brave boy showing off his knee.

Swati, five, had given up her bottle months ago. But when the fever came, she dug the old sippy bottle out of the kitchen drawer in their Bengaluru flat and held it out to Sharmila. "Amma, milk in this. Pwease." Her visiting cousin giggled. "Baby talk!" Swati's lip wobbled. Sharmila filled the bottle, then turned to the cousin. "When we're poorly, we all want to be little again. It's okay." That night Swati slept curled in her parents' bed. Once the fever was gone, she announced the bottle was "for babies" and put it back in the drawer herself.

Where did Swati find the old bottle?
In the kitchen drawer.
Why did Swati's lip wobble?
She felt embarrassed and hurt when her cousin laughed at her baby talk while she felt poorly.
What did Sharmila get right?
She filled the bottle without shaming Swati and explained to the cousin that wanting to be little when ill is okay.
How might the cousin see the bottle after Sharmila's words?
The cousin might see it as comfort for a sick child rather than something to laugh at.

Dear diary, Vaibhav here, day four at the plant nursery.

I thought watering would be easy. You look at a plant, you feel if it's thirsty. My gut said the ferns were dry, so I soaked them. Nandini, who has worked here five years, came over and sighed. "They were fine. Now the roots will sit in water." Then my gut said the cactus looked sad. Also wrong.

What gets me is how fast Nandini is. She walks down a row, lifts a pot, taps the soil, and just knows. I asked her how. She said, "In my first year I killed about forty plants. Every time, I checked what went wrong."

So tomorrow I'm doing it her way. Lift, tap, guess, then check with my finger and write down if I was right.

How long has Nandini worked at the plant nursery?
Five years.
Why did Vaibhav feel sure the ferns were dry?
Vaibhav felt confident because watering seemed easy, and in a new field that confident gut feeling had no experience behind it.
What makes Vaibhav's plan for tomorrow a good one?
Guessing, then checking with a finger and writing down if the guess was right gives quick, honest feedback, which is how a gut feeling becomes reliable.
How might Nandini feel watching a beginner soak the ferns?
Nandini might feel a little frustrated but also understanding, having killed about forty plants in her own first year.

The board exams fell in a heatwave in Ludhiana, with power cuts every afternoon. Pradeep, sixteen, woke each morning already tired. His head throbbed by noon, his stomach churned so that he could barely eat, and his back and legs ached as if he'd run a race. He told no one, because everyone was stressed. On the third night his father, Gurpreet, found him awake at two, rubbing his temples. 'Headache?' Pradeep nodded, and it all came out. Gurpreet didn't lecture. 'Your body's carrying the exams too.' He made him eat some khichdi, took him for a slow walk at dawn when it was cooler, and insisted on lights out by eleven. 'And if the headaches keep going after the exams, we'll see the doctor.' Pradeep slept that night. The next morning his head felt lighter.

When did Gurpreet find Pradeep awake?
At two.
What was Pradeep feeling during exam season?
He felt constantly tired, with headaches, a churning stomach and aching muscles, and kept it to himself.
What did Gurpreet do to ease Pradeep's symptoms?
He reassured him, made him eat, took him for a dawn walk, set a bedtime and planned a doctor visit if the headaches kept going.
How might Gurpreet have felt finding his son awake at two?
He was probably worried and concerned, realising how much Pradeep was struggling.

Note from Anjali, school counsellor. Elizabeth, Class 9, came to see me after her mother and father each asked her, on the same weekend, what the other had said and done. She told me she had a lovely Sunday with her father and kept quiet about it at home, because her mother's face went hard when his name came up. "If I say I miss him, I'm betraying her. If I say I'm fine at home, I'm betraying him." Her hands were pulled into her sleeves. I noticed she seemed less afraid when she said, "I love them both." What I did: we practised a short line she can use with each parent, and she chose, "I love you both and I'm not going to choose."

What did Elizabeth keep quiet about at home?
She kept quiet about having a lovely Sunday with her father.
What was Elizabeth afraid of when she thought about telling either parent that she missed the other?
She feared that loving one parent would betray the other, so she hid her affection to keep the peace.
What did Anjali do to help Elizabeth respond to her parents?
Anjali helped her practise a short honest line, "I love you both and I'm not going to choose," which Elizabeth can use with each parent.
How might Elizabeth's mother feel if Elizabeth spoke warmly about her father at home?
Probably hurt and afraid of being left out, as her hard face suggests, but Elizabeth's line can reassure her without picking a side.
My friend copies my homework every day. I don't like it but I don't want to lose her.
It's fair to feel uneasy. Copying doesn't help her learn, and it could get you both in trouble. You can say no and still be a good friend.
How do I say it without sounding mean?
Try something like, "I don't want to share my answers anymore, but I'm happy to explain the questions to you." That way you're still helping her, just in a better way.

Emmanuel will stay in Guam in December for 10 days in which he has to use international data that would cost $3.50 per day. Emmanuel has been paying $175 per month for his regular plan. How much in all will be Emmanuel's charges for December?

The international charge cost $3.50 x 10 = 35.
Therefore, Emmanuel's bill for December is $175 + 35 = $210.
The answer is 210.
Tim buys a book of esoteric words.  He learns 10 words from it a day.  In 2 years the book has increased the number of words he knows by 50%.  How many words did he know originally?

In 2 years there are 365*2=730 days
So he has learned 730*10=7300 words
He knew 1/.5=2 times that number of words before the book
So he knew 7300*2=14600 words before
The answer is 14600.
Nine beads are on a string: the 1st is red, and after that every bead is blue except the 9th, which is yellow. Which bead is the last one?

Answer: The 9th bead (the yellow one) is the last.

"Last" is not always 10th; it is whichever is at the end. Here the last is the 9th. Make strings of different lengths and ask "Which is last? What number is it?"

"Kalyani, what did you think of the new project lead?"
"Honestly, Rukmini didi? Cold. She didn't smile once in the meeting."
"Hmm. I thought so too at first."
"At first?"
"I've started doing a thing. When I meet someone, I write down my first impression, but I label it: guess."
"And?"
"Then I write what would change my mind. For her: if she listens well one-on-one, or if she's kind to juniors."
"And has she?"
"Yesterday I saw her stay back with an intern for an hour, explaining the code. Very patiently."
"Oh."
"So my guess is already wobbling."
"Maybe she's just shy in big meetings."
"Maybe. I'll keep watching. It's only been two weeks."

How long did the project lead stay back with the intern?
For an hour, explaining the code.
What might Rukmini be feeling when she says her guess is "already wobbling"?
She seems curious and open, a little amused that the first impression is already being challenged.
What is Rukmini's method, and why is it wise?
She writes her first impression, labels it a guess, and notes what would change her mind, so she stays open to new evidence.
How might the new project lead feel if people decided she was cold?
She might feel misjudged and lonely, especially if she's just shy in big meetings.

What did Rashmi find?
The address of the man who kept following Rashmi after college.
What was Rashmi feeling while wanting to post the address?

What did Kalyani suggest instead of posting the address, and why?

(1) Can you correct this for me? "These scissors is sharp."
(2) Why is it easier to walk on a dry road than in sand?
(3) What does "keep up with" mean?
(4) Could you explain what absurdity means?

1. Write it as: These scissors are sharp. Why: "scissors" is a plural noun, so it takes "are".
2. It is easier on the road. Because the hard road holds the foot firmly, while sand shifts under each step.
3. It means to stay at the same speed or level as someone. For example: it is hard to keep up with the fast runners.
4. As a noun, "absurdity" means something so silly that it makes no sense.
Why does a zip close when the slider is pulled up?
The slider forces the teeth together. Because its narrow channel squeezes the rows into a tight interlock, they hold each other until the slider is pulled back.

People think compliments can't hurt. I'm Preeti, and I'm speaking at this wellness evening because of our college canteen. At school they called me names for being tall and bony. Then in college the same body got praise: "You should model." "Don't ever gain weight." Different words, same message: my body was the most interesting thing about me. I started to feel eyes on me at every meal. If I ate a samosa, someone said, "Careful!" If I skipped one, someone said, "Wow, discipline." So I stopped eating in the canteen at all. My roommate Pooja noticed. She didn't make a speech. One day she just said at our table, "New rule: no body talk while we eat. Tell me about your day instead." People laughed, and then they actually did it. It sounds small. It let me eat lunch again.

What was Pooja's new rule at the table?
No body talk while we eat.
Why did Preeti feel watched at every meal?
Both eating and skipping food drew comments, so Preeti felt self-conscious and judged over every food choice.
What made Pooja's choice at the table effective?
It was simple and friendly, swapping body talk for "Tell me about your day", so people could change the habit without feeling scolded.
How might the people who said "You should model" see their own words?
They probably thought they were giving compliments, not realising the praise taught Preeti that looks were Preeti's value.
