The girls' hostel common room buzzed after dinner. A message was going round: 'Mess water contaminated, three students in hospital, DON'T drink it!' Dilnaz had it from four groups. Everyone at her table was talking about it. She forwarded it to her corridor group straight away. Then she typed it into the college-wide group too. Vishal, the student secretary, was at the warden's desk. He replied publicly: 'Checked with the warden and the infirmary. Nobody admitted. Water tested this morning. Please don't forward.' Dilnaz's cheeks burned. The table fell silent. 'He's just covering for the mess,' someone muttered. Dilnaz wanted to agree. But she also remembered she'd never asked where the message started. She stared at her own name above the forward, now shared a hundred times.

Who did Vishal check with before replying?
The warden and the infirmary.
Why did Dilnaz's cheeks burn?
Dilnaz felt embarrassed and exposed, realising she had spread the message widely without checking where it started.
What could Dilnaz do next to limit the harm?
She could post in the same groups that the claim was checked and was not true, and ask others to stop forwarding it.
How might Vishal feel posting his reply?
Vishal may feel responsible and a bit tense, knowing some students will see him as covering up rather than checking.

The power went out just as Aaji lit the evening lamp in the Nagpur flat, and her reading glasses were lost somewhere on the dark sofa. She fumbled for the prayer book, sighing.

Then Sunaina, nine, began the aarti from memory, word for word, the way Aaji sang it: slow on the second line, quick on the last. Her cousin Pallavi, seven, joined in, clapping on the beat.

Aaji stopped hunting for her glasses and just listened.

Afterwards, when Pallavi stubbed her toe on the doorframe, she said, exactly in Aaji's voice, "Arre, the door didn't move, you did!"

Aaji laughed so hard in the dark that she had to sit down. So it had all gone in.

How old is Pallavi?
Pallavi is seven.
What was Aaji feeling as she listened in the dark?
Aaji felt moved and delighted, seeing that her prayers and sayings had quietly gone into the children.
How could the family keep this learning going once the lights are back?
Let the girls lead the aarti some evenings and ask Aaji for more stories and sayings, so the passing-on stays daily.
What might it be like for Sunaina to lead the aarti from memory?
Sunaina may feel proud and grown-up, stepping in when Aaji couldn't read.

If two-thirds are eaten, one-third remaining on the plates is 9 / 3 = 3.
The answer is 3.

Herbert is puzzled and upset and stays late, unwilling to leave the narrator and another person together. At midnight the narrator sees him in at his own dark door, and when it closes feels the first relief since the night of the arrival.

What did Simran's grandfather use to say?
He used to say, "Your name is all you really own."
Why couldn't Simran sleep that night?
She was torn between her family needing her salary and her discomfort at doing something dishonest.

Harsha, you think I was always this old man who cries at films? At fifteen I was told, 'Men don't cry, Yusuf.' When my elder brother left for work in the Gulf and I didn't know when I'd see him again, I went behind the well and bit my sleeve so no one would hear.
My Urdu teacher, Masterji, found me there. He didn't laugh. He sat down and said, 'Tears are not a woman's thing or a man's thing. They are a heart's thing.' Then he cried a little too, about his own son far away.

Where did Yusuf go to cry when his brother left?
Behind the well, biting his sleeve so no one would hear.
Why did Yusuf hide his tears at fifteen?
He had been told 'Men don't cry', so he felt sadness was not safe to show.
What turning point changed how Yusuf saw crying?
Masterji finding him, not laughing, saying tears are a heart's thing and then crying too, widened what felt allowed.
What might Masterji have been feeling when he cried a little too?
Masterji was probably missing his own son far away, and sitting with Yusuf let him share that sadness instead of hiding it.

So when the mayor announced closing three neighbourhood libraries to fund a new stadium, Astrid felt it like a punch.

A classmate had sent a video of Kwame tripping on the stairs, his lunch spilling everywhere, with a crying-laughing caption. It already had dozens of views. Omar pocketed the phone, sold a charger to a woman in a hurry, and noted it in his uncle's book.

Until six.
What made Omar hesitate before choosing not to forward the video?
He felt the pull to join in so he'd look like part of the group, but remembering Kwame's kindness made him feel uneasy about hurting him.

How many different arrangements are there of the letters of MATH? Of BOOK? Of APPLE?

Answer: MATH: 4! = 24. BOOK: 4!/2! = 12. APPLE: 5!/2! = 60.

MATH has 4 different letters, so 4! = 24 arrangements. BOOK has two Os. If we pretend they are different (O1 and O2) there are 24 arrangements, but BO1O2K and BO2O1K look the same: every real arrangement has been counted 2! = 2 times. So divide: 24 / 2 = 12. APPLE has two Ps: 5! / 2! = 120 / 2 = 60. Rule: divide by the factorial of the number of times each letter repeats. Check BOOK by listing where the two Os go: positions (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,3), (2,4), (3,4), 6 ways, and then B and K fill the other two places in 2 ways: 6 x 2 = 12.

'Ojas, you've been bouncing since we got back from Aryan's party.'
'I had four cupcakes and a candy bag!'
An hour later, Gurleen found him face down on the rug.

In seeing Bingley, her thoughts naturally flew to her sister; and oh! how ardently did she long to know whether any of his were directed in a like manner. Sometimes she could fancy that he talked less than on former occasions, and once or twice pleased herself with the notion that, as he looked at her, he was trying to trace a resemblance. But, though this might be imaginary, she could not be deceived as to his behaviour to Miss Darcy, who had been set up as a rival to Jane. No look appeared on either side that spoke particular regard. Nothing occurred between them that could justify the hopes of his sister. On this point she was soon satisfied; and two or three little circumstances occurred ere they parted, which, in her anxious interpretation, denoted a recollection of Jane, not untinctured by tenderness, and a wish of saying more that might lead to the mention of her, had he dared. He observed to her, at a moment when the others were talking together, and in a tone which had something of real regret, that it "was a very long time since he had had the pleasure of seeing her;" and, before she could reply, he added, "It is above eight months. We have not met since the 26th of November, when we were all dancing together at Netherfield."

Seeing Bingley, Elizabeth longs to know whether he still thinks of Jane. He shows no special interest in Darcy's sister, and a few small moments suggest he remembers Jane fondly. He even says sadly that they have not met for over eight months, since the Netherfield ball.

Every evening in their small flat in Taichung, Jin's mother asked the same question over the rice: 'Any news?' Tonight, when he shook his head, she sighed. 'Mrs. Chen's son Xin started at the electronics company last month. Already a badge, already a desk.' Jin felt his face heat. He wanted to slam his bowl down, or go silent for three days like last time. Instead he looked at her hands, the way she kept turning her chopsticks. She was worried, not cruel. 'Ma, I know you're scared I'll fall behind. Here's what I'm doing.' He took out his phone and showed her his list: two interviews next week, the online certificate finishing on the 20th, a follow-up with the shipping firm on Friday. What was Jin feeling when his mother mentioned Xin?
Jin felt small and angry, his face heating, tempted to slam his bowl or go silent.

This phone has been with me through everything." Varun felt awkward. He didn't want to hurt his friend. That evening, over dinner, he said lightly, "Bhupen, if you didn't own this phone, would you pay twenty for it today?" Bhupen opened his mouth, then closed it. "Maybe... fourteen." "So maybe that's the price." Bhupen sighed, then laughed. The next day he changed the notice to fifteen, and it sold by evening.

What price did Bhupen first put on the notice?
How did Varun feel about raising the price issue with Bhupen?

Carson is a night security guard. He's supposed to patrol the outside of a warehouse that's 600 feet long and 400 feet wide. If Carson is supposed to circle the warehouse 10 times, but gets tired and skips 2 times, how far does he walk in one night?

First find the total distance Carson walks along the warehouse's long sides: 600 feet/side * 2 sides = 1200 feet
Then find the total distance Carson walks along the warehouse's short sides: 400 feet/side * 2 sides = 800 feet
Add those two amounts to find the total distance walk in one circle: 1200 feet + 800 feet = 2000 feet
Then find the number of circles Carson actually walks: 10 circles - 2 circles = 8 circles
Then multiply the distance of one circle by the number of circles Carson makes: 2000 feet/circle * 8 circles = 16000 feet
The answer is 16000.
Now you try: x^5 + x - 1 = 0.
The answer is f(0) = -1, f(1) = 1, and f' = 5x^4 + 1 > 0: exactly one root, in (0, 1).

Three weeks after the car crash on the Pacific Highway, Daniel still couldn't sleep past 3 a.m. Every time a truck braked outside his Sydney flat, his heart slammed and his hands went slick. He'd stopped driving. He took two buses to work instead.

He told himself he should be over it. Nobody had died. He'd walked away with bruises.

At lunch, his colleague Chen noticed him flinch at a dropped tray. "You okay, mate?"

Daniel laughed it off, then didn't. "I keep reliving it. I should've braked faster. I froze."

Chen put down his sandwich. "My sister was in a crash. She said the doctor told her this is really common after something scary. Your body's still on alert. It's not weakness."

That evening Daniel booked an appointment with his GP, who referred him to a psychologist. He also started walking every morning at the same time, and cooking dinner even when he wasn't hungry. It didn't fix everything. But the nights got a little shorter.

How long after the crash was it when Daniel still couldn't sleep past 3 a.m.?
Three weeks after the car crash.
What was Daniel feeling when he said "I should've braked faster"?
He felt frightened and ashamed, blaming himself for freezing during the crash.
What steps did Daniel take, and why were they helpful?
Seeing his GP, getting a referral to a psychologist, and keeping routines like morning walks and cooking, which brought trained help and steadiness.
How does Chen see Daniel's reactions?
Chen sees them as a common response to something scary, the body still on alert, not weakness.

Arohi tucked her feet under her on the chair. "Neelam, you asked how the tailoring network started? It began with my mother. She's a tailor, and she kept losing orders because customers forgot their measurements or she lost the paper slips. So I made her a simple phone form, just for her. Name, measurements, delivery date. How many tailors now use Arohi's system?
Forty tailors in three neighbourhoods.
What does Arohi mean when she says she still can't believe it some nights?
She feels amazed and proud that a small fix for her mother grew into something so many people rely on.
What was the key step that turned Arohi's idea into a real system?
Realising the problem was shared by many tailors, then spending months building features that let them work together.

After the fight in the lunch queue, Reena's friend group of five became a group of four, and Reena wasn't in it. That night she posted a single line on her status: "Some people show their true colours eventually." Then she turned her phone off.

That evening their mother took them both out for pani puri, and Reena laughed for the first time in a week.

What line did Reena post on her status?
"Some people show their true colours eventually."
What was Reena feeling during that week?
Reena felt heartbroken and lonely after being cut out of her friend group, and was withdrawing from everyone.
What made Arohi's support work?
She noticed the signs, offered chai without pressure, listened, and named the loneliness instead of dismissing the friends.
How might Reena's mother have seen the week?
She likely noticed Reena's withdrawal too and chose a small, warm outing to help her reconnect.

messages.content: Bruno wants to buy two and one-half dozens of pens. How many pens will he have?

Since a dozen is equal to 12, then two dozens are equal to 12 x 2= 24.
One-half dozen is equal to 12/2 = 6.
Thus, Bruno will have a total of 24 + 6 = 30 pens.
The answer is 30.

From the third row, Trisha watched Mummy film every step of her sister's dance, eyes shining. At dinner last week Binita got new ghungroo. Trisha's torn debate folder was still taped together.

Mummy was quiet at the red light. Then, "I didn't know about the trophy. Tell me about it now. All of it."

The inter-house trophy.
What was Trisha feeling as she watched Mummy film Binita's dance?
She felt envious and invisible, hurt that her own win was missed while her sister got every bit of attention.
What went right in the car, and why?
Trisha told Mummy what she noticed without blaming Binita, so Mummy could listen instead of defending her sister.

messages.content: Caprice is taking piano lessons. Her mother pays the teacher $10 for every half-hour of teaching her daughter. If Caprice is taking one lesson per week, and the lesson lasts 1 hour, how much money would the teacher earn in 5 weeks?

Are 0.3 and 0.30 the same or different?

Answer: The same. 0.3 = 3 tenths = 30 hundredths = 0.30.

Shade 3 columns of a 100-square: that is 3 tenths, and it is also 30 small squares, 30 hundredths. Adding a zero at the END of the decimal part does not change the value, just as ₹0.3 and ₹0.30 are both 30 paise. But a zero straight after the point does change it: 0.03 is only 3 hundredths.
Eliza can iron a blouse in 15 minutes and a dress in 20 minutes.  If she spends 2 hours ironing blouses and 3 hours ironing dresses, how many pieces of clothes did she iron?

Since 60 minutes equal 1 hour, in 2 hours, Eliza ironed blouses for 2 x 60 = 120 minutes.
Eliza can iron 120 / 15 = 8 blouses.
Since 60 minutes equal 1 hour, in 3 hours, Eliza ironed dresses for 3 x 60 = 180 minutes.
Eliza can iron 180 / 20 = 9 dresses.
In total, Eliza ironed 8 + 9 = 17 pieces of clothes.
The answer is 17.

What small step would help Noor get Nana's attention sooner?
Nana could answer the first peek, since Noor is already watching his face to check.
What is it like for Kalyani aunty to watch this?
Kalyani aunty sees a toddler who has learned to check a face and try again, which may seem charming and clever.

23 December, hostel, 11 pm
Filed my nomination for student council president today, right before everyone leaves for the Christmas break. My hands were shaking when I signed.
Why am I doing this? Honestly, two reasons. One: the girls' hostel curfew is ridiculous and nobody fights it properly. I can. Two: I loved it when the whole canteen went quiet during my debate speech. I want that. I want people to listen when I talk.
Tonight I made a list of who would be on my team. Then I noticed I had crossed out Akash, not because he's bad, but because he argues with me. That felt ugly. A council of people who agree with me isn't leadership, it's a fan club. Adding him back. Chandrika, remember why you started.

What position did Chandrika file a nomination for?
Student council president.
Why did crossing out Akash feel ugly to Chandrika?
Chandrika felt uneasy and ashamed on noticing the wish for influence sliding into control, cutting Akash only because he disagrees.
What small check could help Chandrika stay on the serving side of power?
Keep people who disagree on the team, as Chandrika did with Akash, and keep asking whether each decision serves the group or only the wish to be listened to.
What would change for the council if Akash stayed off the list?
It would lose someone who questions and argues, turning into a fan club that agrees with Chandrika instead of testing ideas.

Teacher's note, KG-B. Samir asked me six times this morning, "Is Mumma still at the gate?" At snack he whispered, "Does she love me even when I spill?" He will not come to Friday's class sleepover, and I will not push him. Today his mother, Vasudha, tried something new: the same hug and the same words at the gate, "I'll be here after the bell." Samir cried less. Next, I will give him a small job at drop-off, and we agreed to keep that goodbye exactly the same each day.

How many times did Samir ask about Mumma this morning?
Six times.
What might Samir be worried about when he asks about spilling?
He seems anxious that Mumma's love could change if he makes a mistake, so he needs reassurance.
What small step did the adults agree on to help Samir?
A goodbye that stays exactly the same each day, plus a small job for him at drop-off.
How might Vasudha feel when Samir cries less at the gate?
She is probably relieved and hopeful that the steady goodbye is helping him.

I'm Ankita, and I sat near Vishal the year he mentored Sagar, a first-generation graduate who had joined from a small-town college. In their first meetings, Vishal did most of the talking and kept asking, 'Any questions?' Sagar always said no, and then I'd see him searching the same topic online for an hour afterwards. After the third meeting Vishal changed things. He started sending Sagar a short written note two days before each meeting: what they'd cover, and three questions Sagar could think about. In the meetings, he'd ask something and then just wait, sometimes for a long while, without filling the silence. By the second month, Sagar was bringing written questions of his own. I don't know what Vishal was thinking when he changed his style. But he stopped saying 'Any questions?'

What did Vishal send Sagar two days before each meeting?
A short written note of what they'd cover and three questions to think about.
What might Sagar have been feeling in the first meetings?
Sagar was probably shy and hesitant, worried about looking unprepared, so he said no and searched alone later.
Why did the written notes and silences work better than 'Any questions?'
They gave Sagar time to prepare and space to speak, suiting his style instead of expecting instant questions.
How does Ankita see Vishal's change?
Ankita notices a mentor who adjusted to the person, and sees it working as Sagar starts bringing questions.

At the degree college in Hajipur, elective forms were due on Monday. Kamal had spent every clear night since Class 8 on his roof with a secondhand telescope, sketching Jupiter's moons in a notebook. The astrophysics elective was right there on the list. But Rukmini, who had taken it last year, said half the class got below a B. Kamal's scholarship needed a high average. He ticked "Office Management" instead, the one everyone called a free A. "Smart," said his roommate. Kamal nodded. That night the sky was clear. He carried the telescope up to the roof, then just sat beside it without looking through, and came down early.

Which elective did Kamal tick instead of astrophysics?
"Office Management", the one everyone called a free A.
Why did Kamal sit beside the telescope without looking through it?
He may have felt a quiet sadness, having just given up the subject he loves because he feared a lower grade.
What could Kamal have done before ticking the safe box?
He could have asked the astrophysics teacher or Rukmini about support, or checked what average the scholarship really needs, before letting fear decide.
What would change if Rukmini had also mentioned what Rukmini enjoyed about the elective?
Kamal might have seen the chance to learn what he loves, not only the risk to his marks, and the choice might have gone the other way.
Mina complimented my drawing. Is complimented the same as flattered?

Not quite. Complimented means said something kind and admiring about someone or something. It is a verb, the past tense of compliment.
Example: The teacher complimented Kunal on his neat handwriting.
What does it mean when someone says "the ball is in your court"?

It means it is now your turn to decide or take the next step.
Example: I have said sorry to Riya twice, so the ball is in her court now.

At 6 pm on a Thursday, three hours before Pune's biggest weekend food fair, Irawati, 26, the operations head at a packaged-meals start-up, got a message from the kitchen: the new label printer had dropped the "contains peanuts" line from two thousand boxes of curry.
Her co-founder, Ganga, was already calculating. "Reprinting costs us the fair. Most people read the menu board anyway."
Irawati paced the loading bay. She thought of the child with an allergy who might pick up a box, the city food inspector, the investors, the thirty staff paid from this weekend's sales.
"If one person gets hurt, there's no company left to save," she said. "And even if nobody does, we'd know."
She stopped the trucks, split the team into two lines to hand-sticker every box, called the fair organisers to delay their stall by a day, and posted an honest note online. Ganga argued, then picked up a sticker roll.

How many boxes were missing the "contains peanuts" line?
Two thousand boxes of curry were missing the line.
What was Ganga feeling when she started calculating?
Ganga felt anxious and under pressure about losing the fair and the money the staff depended on.
Which choice worked, and why?
Stopping the trucks and hand-stickering every box worked, because it protected customers with allergies and the company's trust while still saving most of the stock.
What would change if Irawati had followed Ganga's first idea?
The boxes would go out unlabelled, putting allergic customers at risk and exposing the start-up to legal trouble and a loss of trust.

Late evening. Sunaina, new in Pune, texts her brother Vikas.

Vikas: How's the new city? Made friends yet?
Sunaina: Not really. Evenings are the worst. I sit in my PG room scrolling everyone's photos from home 😔
Vikas: That will make it worse, na.
Sunaina: I know. Today I walked at six instead. Same lane, same chai stall. The stall uncle nodded at me.
Vikas: That counts!
Sunaina: Joined the Saturday badminton group nearby too. Knew nobody, played badly, went anyway.
Vikas: And?
Sunaina: Still lonely. But a girl called Meera said come again next week. Papa says it took him months in Bhopal in his first job. I'm giving it till winter 🙂
Vikas: Send me a photo of your racket 🏸

What group did Sunaina join near her PG?
Sunaina joined the Saturday badminton group nearby.
What does Sunaina's message about the evenings suggest she was feeling?
It suggests she felt lonely and low, since she said evenings are the worst and she sat in her PG room scrolling photos from home.
What would you advise Sunaina if the loneliness lasts through the first months?
Keep the small routines, the six o'clock walk and the badminton, and remember what Papa said about it taking months. 🙂
How might Vikas feel while reading these messages?
Vikas seems concerned for his sister but encouraged, since he warned her off scrolling and then cheered at her walk and badminton.

At the playground in Madrid, Tomas pushed Mateo off the little slide, and Mateo landed on his bottom and cried. Tomas's grandmother hurried over. "Tomas!" Tomas's cheeks went red. "He was too slow! He started it!" He crossed his arms and looked at the ground. His grandmother took a breath and knelt down. "You wanted your turn. That's hard. And now Mateo is hurt." She didn't raise her voice. Tomas's arms slowly came down. He peeked at Mateo.

What did Tomas say about Mateo?
He said, "He was too slow! He started it!"
Why did Tomas say "He started it"?
His red cheeks and crossed arms suggest he felt bad and was pushing that uncomfortable feeling away, not lying on purpose.
What did the grandmother do that helped the feeling pass?
She stayed calm, named his wish for a turn, and gently pointed out that Mateo was hurt, without shaming him.
How might Mateo feel hearing "He started it"?
Mateo may feel even more upset and blamed, since he is the one who got pushed and hurt.

Hearing that the Vrishnis along with the Bhojas and Andhakas and Kukuras had all been slain, the Pandavas, burning with grief, became highly agitated. Then Arjuna, the dear friend of Keshava, bidding them farewell, set out for seeing his maternal uncle. He said that destruction would soon overtake everything. Proceeding to the city of the Vrishnis with Daruka in his company, O puissant king, that hero beheld that the city of Dwaraka looked like a woman bereft of her husband. Those ladies who had, before this, the very Lord of the universe for their protector, were now lordless. Seeing that Partha had come for protecting them, they all set up a loud wail. 16,000 ladies had been wedded to Vasudeva. Indeed, as soon as they saw Arjuna arrive, they uttered a loud cry of sorrow.

Give me a short summary of this sad scene.

The Pandavas are filled with grief when they hear that the Vrishnis and their allies have all been killed. Arjuna goes to Dwaraka, which now looks lost and lonely. Krishna's wives cry out loudly when they see him arrive to protect them.

For each inequality write "every value" or "no value".
a) 2(x + 1) > 2x + 1
b) x + 3 < x
c) 3(x - 1) >= 3x - 5
d) 4x + 1 <= 4x

i) 3x - 3(x - 2) > 5

l) x/2 + x/2 < x

a) every value
b) no value
c) every value

e) every value

I remember the day before the Christmas concert when I was ten. I'm Jasleen. All morning I felt strange. My legs felt jumpy and my tummy felt like it had a knot in it. Our teacher asked if I was okay, and I said, 'I feel weird.' That was all I could say. My friend Vikas said, 'Are you sick?' I wasn't. At lunch I didn't eat. The teacher sat with me and asked, 'Is it a happy weird or a scared weird?' I thought and thought. 'Scared, but also excited.' She said, 'That's nervous and excited together. It happens before big things.' I remember how good it felt to have words. I still sang, knots and all.

How old was Jasleen at the time of the Christmas concert?
Ten.
What was Jasleen feeling but unable to name at first?
Jasleen was nervous and excited, felt as jumpy legs and a knotted tummy.
What did the teacher's question do well?
Asking 'happy weird or scared weird?' gave Jasleen a simple choice, helping find the words without pressure.
How might Vikas have seen Jasleen that morning?
Vikas thought Jasleen might be sick, not realising it was a feeling.

By the third month, Asif had stopped counting how many nights Aparna stayed past midnight in their Lower Parel office. She had skipped her college reunion, stopped going to her dance class, and lived on vending-machine chips. Some colleagues whispered that she was sucking up for the promotion. Asif felt a twinge of envy himself; the director had praised her twice already. But mostly he noticed the dark circles, and how her hand shook holding her coffee. On Friday he stopped by her desk with two cups of cutting chai. "I'm not saying slow down. You're going to get that promotion. I'm just saying, come for a twenty-minute walk. The report will still be here." She stared at him. Then she stood up.

What did Asif bring to Aparna's desk?
Two cups of cutting chai.
What mix of feelings did Asif have watching Aparna?
He felt a twinge of envy at her praise, but mostly concern at her dark circles and shaking hand.
Why did Asif's approach work better than the whispers?
He showed genuine concern without judging her goal, offering a short break instead of criticism.
How might Aparna feel when Asif says she'll get the promotion?
Aparna may feel surprised and relieved to be supported rather than judged.
He keeps to ask the same question every day. Which part is wrong?

He keeps asking the same question every day.
Why: "keep" meaning continue takes -ing.

Monday: Yash pitched his idea to Bidisha, his manager: turn the monthly newsletter into a short podcast. She said, "Hmm, we'll see," and asked about the printer contract instead. Yash left the room unsure whether that was a yes-later or a no.
Thursday: His follow-up email had sat unanswered for three days. Yash started drafting a sulky message in his head. She hates it. She thinks I'm wasting time.
The following Monday: Instead of sulking, he caught her after the team meeting. "Bidisha, I couldn't tell what 'we'll see' meant last week. Is it a no, a not now, or something you have doubts about? Any of those is fine to hear." She laughed, a little relieved. "Honestly, doubts. I like it, but our director hates anything without a written version, and I didn't want to shoot you down. Could you do both, a short podcast and a one-page summary?" "Yes," Yash said. "Easily."

What did Yash want to turn the newsletter into?
A short podcast.
What was Yash feeling as the email went unanswered?
Yash felt anxious and resentful, starting to believe Bidisha hated the idea and thought he was wasting time.
How did Yash clarify the indirect signals?
He asked gently what 'we'll see' meant, offering no, not now or doubts as acceptable answers, which made it easy for her to be honest.
Why had Bidisha answered with 'we'll see'?
She had doubts because of the director's preference for written versions but didn't want to shoot Yash down, so she hesitated politely.

The placement cell office smelled of printer ink. Aparna Ma'am turned the screen toward Simran, twenty-one. 'The company has frozen hiring this year. It's not about your interview.' For a moment Simran wanted to argue, to ask if she could call them, write to someone, reapply. She had planned the last two years around this job. Instead she looked out of the window at the rain for a while. 'So that door's closed.' 'For now, yes.' Simran nodded slowly. 'Then what's still open?' Aparna Ma'am pulled out a list: two smaller firms, a research assistant post, a one-year diploma. Simran took a photo of it. Her hands were steady, though her throat was tight. 'I'll come back on Thursday with the ones I want.'

Why did the company not hire this year?
It had frozen hiring.
What does Simran's tight throat alongside steady hands suggest?
She was still sad about losing the job she had planned for, yet calm enough to accept it and move forward.
Which choice helped Simran most in that moment?
Asking what was still open instead of fighting a decision she couldn't change.
How might Aparna Ma'am feel seeing Simran's response?
Relieved and encouraged, since helping a student plan next steps is easier than managing a fight against a closed door.
I wish I am taller, then I can play basketball.

I wish I were taller, then I could play basketball.
Why: after "wish", use past forms: "were" and "could".

Jatin Sir took off his glasses and looked at Kiran across the lab bench. "You think expertise means being right. Let me tell you about when I was twenty-five. I had built a flood model for the Godavari basin, three years of work, praised by everyone. Then a new satellite dataset showed the rainfall patterns had shifted. My model was based on an old assumption. At first I argued. I wrote angry replies, defended every line. One night, alone with the new data, I finally saw it: the model was wrong, not the data. I felt sick. Then I felt free. I rebuilt it from the ground up in a year. The new one was better because I knew exactly where the old one failed." Kiran stared at her own code. "So I shouldn't defend mine?" "Defend it until the evidence says otherwise. Then listen."

What river basin was young Jatin's flood model for?
The Godavari basin.
How did young Jatin feel when he saw the model was wrong?
He felt sick at first, then oddly free.
What was the turning point in young Jatin's story, and what did it lead to?
Admitting alone with the new data that the model was wrong; he rebuilt it into a better one within a year.
How might Jatin's colleagues have seen his angry replies at first?
They may have found him defensive and stubborn before he changed his mind.

In the staff meeting at the Darjeeling school, Dolma suggested a new reading programme, and Rashmi felt certain: she's doing this to make me look lazy. Rashmi's fingers tightened around her pen. She almost said something cutting about Dolma "always needing attention". Then she paused and wrote in the margin of her notes: What part of this is mine? She looked at the words for a while. The truth was that Rashmi had wanted to propose a reading club herself, and had been quietly comparing herself with Dolma all term. The motive she felt so strongly wasn't Dolma's; it was her own. After the meeting she went up to Dolma. "I had a similar idea. Could we plan it together?" Dolma's face lit up.

What did Rashmi write in the margin?
"What part of this is mine?"
What did Rashmi feel when Dolma made her suggestion?
She felt threatened and angry, certain Dolma was trying to make her look lazy.
What did the pause reveal, and what did Rashmi do with it?
It showed Rashmi had been comparing herself and wanted to propose the idea too; she turned that into an offer to plan it together.
How did Dolma respond to Rashmi's offer?
Her face lit up; she seemed happy and relieved to have a partner rather than a rival.
Farhan earns ₹9,000 a month and spends ₹7,200. What fraction of his pay does he save?
He saves one fifth of his pay. Because 9,000 minus 7,200 is 1,800, and 1,800 out of 9,000 is the same as 1 out of 5.

Dear Hrithik bhaiya,
Your message on my birthday reached me in Pune. Four years of silence, and then: "I miss you, Bidi. Can we try?" I read it on the bus and missed my stop.
I want to answer honestly. Part of me is happy. Part of me is still the one who waited alone outside the lawyer's office while you sided with Baba about the house.
So here is what I can offer. A phone call every second Sunday, for now. I'd like you to tell me, in your own words, what you think went wrong, not only that you're sorry. If the calls go well, maybe I come home for Durga Puja. If they don't, I'll step back again, and that will be my choice, not a punishment.
I kept your message. That should tell you something.
Bidisha

How long had Bidisha and Hrithik been silent before the birthday message?
Four years of silence.
What mixed feelings does Bidisha describe on reading the message?
Bidisha feels happy and hopeful, yet still hurt and wary from waiting alone outside the lawyer's office; missing the bus stop shows how shaken the message left the writer.
Which choice in the letter lets Bidisha welcome the gesture and still stay careful?
Offering a call every second Sunday and asking Hrithik to explain what went wrong lets trust grow step by step, with the freedom to step back.
What might it be like for Hrithik to read this letter?
Hrithik may feel relieved that Bidisha answered at all and nervous about naming his own part, but the line about keeping the message gives hope 🙂

Dear Pema,
I've thought about this for a month, so please read it slowly.
When you told the hostel group about my panic in the exam hall, it hurt more than anything else this year. When I asked you about it, you said I was "too sensitive". Then in March it happened again, with the thing about my brother.
I don't hate you. We had good times: the momos behind the mess, the night we painted the Losar poster together. Those were real.
But I can't keep giving you things that matter to me and waiting to see where they end up. So I'm stepping back. I'll say hello in class, and I won't talk about you to anyone. I've been spending time with Sonam and the badminton girls, and I feel safe with them.
I hope things go well for you. Really.
Ira

What did Pema say when Ira first asked about it?
Pema said Ira was 'too sensitive'.
How does Ira feel about Pema now, and what shows it?
Ira no longer feels safe but isn't hateful; writing 'I don't hate you' and remembering the good times while still stepping back shows a calm, settled hurt.
Why is Ira's choice a healthy ending rather than revenge?
Ira closes the door calmly, promises not to talk about Pema to anyone, and turns to safer friends instead of hitting back.
What might Pema feel on reading the letter?
Pema may feel stung and surprised, and perhaps ashamed, since the letter is kind but makes the reason clear.

Ganga's invitation had sounded harmless: tea, laughter, a "growth circle" on Sunday afternoons. By the third session Bhavna noticed what she had been too flattered to see. The leader said family drained a person's energy, so calls home could wait. A fee of forty thousand rupees would "unlock the next level", due by Friday, right in her exam week. Anyone who asked a question was called weak. In the corridor she tried out the thoughts silently. Why is my mother a problem? Why is there a deadline? Why is asking a weakness? Three signals, one pattern. "I need to think, not decide," she told Ganga, and left before the closing chant. That night she called home for the first time in nine days.

What fee did the leader ask for, and by when?
The leader asked for a fee of forty thousand rupees, due by Friday.
What made Bhavna uneasy?
Bhavna grew uneasy because the leader discouraged calls home, pressed for money by a deadline and called questioners weak.
What else could Bhavna do to test the group, and why?
Bhavna could talk it over with family or a friend and look for independent information, because outside views help check what a closed group says.
How might Ganga see Bhavna leaving early?
Ganga may feel hurt or worried, believing the circle is good and taking the early exit as a rejection.

Sunday, late. Sorting my two cultures like a cupboard tonight. Keeping: the Sunday dosa breakfast that Amma taught me, the phone call to Ajji on the first of every month, and saying thank you to the bus driver the way people here do. Letting go: the belief that I must always say yes to every relative's plan. Chetan from the flat above came for dosa and asked why I make the batter the night before. I explained and he grinned, then taught me to make his grandmother's chai from Nairobi. I'm thinking that one day I'll teach a child both, without saying this is the right way. Just: this is what our table looks like. Kiran

What breakfast does Kiran keep on Sundays?
Kiran keeps the Sunday dosa breakfast.
How does Kiran feel about the customs, and what shows it?
Affection and calm ownership; Kiran carefully chooses what to keep and pictures a shared table.
What could Kiran do next with these choices?
Teach a child both, showing what the table looks like without presenting one way as right.
What might Chetan have felt about sharing chai?
Pleased and warm, since Chetan grinned and taught the recipe from a grandmother in Nairobi.

A case of water contains 24 bottles. A children's camp comprising of 4 groups purchased 13 cases for a 3-day camp. The first group has 14 children, the second group has 16 children, the third group has 12 children, and the fourth group has half of the number of the first three groups combined. If each child consumes 3 bottles a day, how many more bottles of water does the camp organizer still need to buy?

The first three groups have a total of 14 + 16 + 12 = 42 children.
The fourth group has 42/2 = 21 children
All together, the camp has 42 + 21 = 63 children.
In one day, the children consume 3 x 63 = 189 bottles of water.
In 3 days, the children will need 189 x 3 = 567 bottles of water.
The camp organizer has already purchased 13 x 24 = 312 bottles of water.
The camp organizer must buy another 567 - 312 = 255 bottles of water.
The answer is 255.

So, Sunaina, the fight with Papa. I'm Sahil, the idiot who shouted at his own father about the election on Sunday. You heard it from the next room, I know.
I lay awake that night replaying it. And I noticed something. I still thought I was right about the policy. But I was ashamed of how I'd said it. I'd called his view 'stupid'. I'd banged the table. That wasn't an argument; that was me being rude.
So on Monday evening I called him from the hostel. I said, 'Papa, I'm sorry for how I spoke yesterday. The shouting, the word stupid. That was wrong.' He was quiet. Then I said, 'I still see it differently. But I don't want that to be how we talk.'
And then, don't laugh, I asked if he'd walk to the lake with me on Saturday, like when I was small.
He said, 'Six a.m. Don't be late.' That's Papa for 'okay'.

What word did Sahil use for Papa's view?
'Stupid'.
How did Sahil feel lying awake after the fight?
Ashamed of how he had spoken, though he still believed his view on the policy was right.
What made Sahil's apology work?
He apologised for the shouting and the word 'stupid' without giving up his view, then offered a walk to rebuild closeness.
How might Papa have felt receiving the call?
Surprised and quietly touched, which is why he agreed to the walk in his own gruff way.

Neelam, you're taking over the new warehouse team? Let me tell you what I did at the garment factory in Tiruppur. I'm Yamini; I was twenty-five, the only woman supervisor on the floor. Half the tailors were Tamil, half had come from Bihar and Odisha. They ate separately, took breaks separately, called each other names I won't repeat. My manager said, "Just keep them apart." Instead I made mixed lines: every line needed a cutter, a stitcher and a checker, one from each side. The target for the Diwali order was the whole line's, not one person's. The first week was ugly. A man mocked a Bihari worker's Tamil. I stopped the line and said, "Nobody laughs at anyone here. Next time, you go home." It didn't happen again. By Diwali, I saw them sharing tiffins. I never gave one speech.

Who set the target for the Diwali order?
The target for the Diwali order was the whole line's, not one person's.
What was Yamini feeling when she stopped the line?
Yamini felt firm and angry at the mockery, determined not to let anyone be laughed at.
Why was ignoring the manager's advice to keep the groups apart a key decision?
Mixing lines with equal roles and a shared target gave the workers a real reason to depend on each other, which softened attitudes.
How might the Bihari worker have felt when Yamini stopped the line?
He likely felt protected and respected, seeing that the supervisor would not tolerate mockery of him.

In the kasba post office, Madhav slammed his receipt on the counter. "Twenty days! My son's university papers were sent twenty days ago and you people have lost them!"
The queue went quiet. Sunaina, the clerk, felt her heart speed up. She wanted to say the delay wasn't at her branch.
She lowered her voice instead. "Twenty days is a long time, and those papers matter. I understand why you're angry."
Madhav blinked. "Of course I'm angry."
"What would help most today? A tracking update, or a written complaint to the head office?"
"Both."
"Let me check." She found the parcel stuck at the district sorting centre, called them on the office phone while he watched, and wrote the complaint with him.
Madhav's shoulders came down. "They said it will move tomorrow?"
"Tomorrow. I'll call you when it does."

How long ago were the papers sent?
They were sent twenty days ago.
What was Sunaina feeling when Madhav slammed his receipt?
Sunaina felt her heart speed up, tense and tempted to defend herself because the delay wasn't at her branch.
Which of Sunaina's choices helped most, and why?
She kept her voice low, acknowledged his frustration, and asked what outcome would help, so Madhav felt heard and could work with her.
How did Madhav experience the conversation?
Madhav went from furious to calmer, his shoulders coming down once he felt heard and saw real action.

Class 3 teacher's note, Thursday.
Mehak is quick and neat, and loves finishing first. But she only picks worksheets she has done before. Today I put out a new kind of puzzle, number pyramids, where you guess and check. Mehak looked at it, went pale, and asked if she could do the old addition sheet instead. When I said everyone was trying pyramids, she wrote one number, rubbed it out so hard the paper tore, and sat still with her hands in her lap. She told me quietly, 'What if it's wrong?' I said wrong answers are how we find the right ones, and showed her my own crossed-out tries on the board. She tried one more number. Plan: next week I'll give her 'mistake-friendly' puzzles in pairs and praise her tries, not only her answers.
Indu

Lindiwe had wanted to be head of the residence council at her university in Durban since first year. When she won, the respect felt like sunlight: people stopped her on the stairs to ask her opinion, and the warden began to call her by name. She fixed the broken laundry machines within a week. Then she began choosing every committee member herself, people who agreed with her. Sami, the quiet engineering student on her floor, came to her door. "You picked all your friends. Some of us feel we don't have a voice anymore." Lindiwe's first thought was to defend herself. Her second was worse: she liked that nobody argued. That thought scared her. She opened the committee list again and added two open seats.

What did Lindiwe fix within a week?
The broken laundry machines.
Why did Lindiwe's second thought scare her?
She realised she enjoyed that nobody argued with her, and she worried that her wish for influence was turning into a wish for control.
What choice did Lindiwe make after Sami's visit, and why was it wise?
She added two open seats to the committee, giving others a voice again instead of keeping all the power with her friends.
How were students like Sami affected by Lindiwe's early choices?
They felt shut out, as if they no longer had a voice in the residence, which is why Sami came to her door.
Why do cyclists need a light at night?
Others can see them. Because a dark road hides a bike, and a light lets drivers spot the cyclist from far away in time to slow down.

Jagdish was pulling at the low cupboard handle. "Bikki!"
"Biscuits are locked, kanna."
He let go, trotted to the fridge and heaved at the handle. It didn't move. "Bikki!"
"That's the fridge."
He turned and pointed up at the counter, at the fruit basket. "Nana!"
"Banana? That one I can do."

What did Jagdish point at on the counter?
He pointed up at the fruit basket.

He was hungry and determined, not giving up when each handle didn't open.

Gail has some bills in her wallet which amount to $100. She has four $5 bills and three $20 bills, and the rest are $10 bills. How many $10 bills are in her wallet?

Four $5 bills amount to $5 x 4 = $20.
Three $20 bills amount to $20 x 3 = $60.
So Gail's $5 and $20 bills amount to $20 + $60 = $80.
Thus, her $10 bills amount to $100 - $80 = $20.
Therefore, she has $20/$10 = 2 $10 bills.
The answer is 2.

I'm Leela, and I share a room with Kishore's sister at the college hostel, so I see him most evenings when he visits her. Kishore used to be the one who never stopped talking. After the fourth-semester results came out, something changed. He stopped coming to the canteen. When his sister asked about the accountancy paper, he said, "Don't start," and left. His friends said he was missing morning lectures. I don't know what's in his head. It could be shame, or just tiredness. But I remember how it felt to hide from a bad result. So last Thursday, when he came by, I didn't mention marks. I said, "I'm going to the department office tomorrow to get the re-exam form for my own paper. Want to come? Just to collect it." He filled the re-exam form in the corridor.
Why did Leela avoid mentioning marks when Kishore came by?
Leela felt concerned but remembered how it felt to hide from a bad result, so a lecture seemed likely to make him retreat further.
What small step did Leela offer, and why was it wise?
Going together to the department office to collect the re-exam form, a concrete step with company and no pressure.
How might Kishore have felt when his sister asked about the accountancy paper?
Kishore probably felt ashamed or cornered about the result, so he snapped and left.

The tram in Oslo was packed and steamy after the storm. Lars held his phone up to Lindiwe: a shark swimming down a flooded street, right past a bus stop.
"Look at this! Near the harbour!"
Lindiwe tilted her head. "That shark has been in every storm since I was eight. Durban, Houston, now Oslo."
"Why would anyone fake that?"
"Loads of reasons. Some pages make money when you click. Some people want attention. Some fakes are made to make people angry at a politician or scared of a group. Some are just cruel."
"But my aunt shared it."
"Your aunt isn't lying. She shares it because it feels true. The storm was real, so the shark feels possible."
Lars looked at the photo again, calmer now. "So I shouldn't just ask if it's real. I should ask who gets something out of it."
"Exactly. Then you don't need to panic. You just wait."

What did the photo on Lars's phone show?
It showed a shark swimming down a flooded street, right past a bus stop.
How did Lars's feeling change after Lindiwe explained?
Lars moved from excitement to calm doubt; he looked at the photo again, calmer, and started thinking about who gains from it.
Which question does Lars decide to ask about viral photos from now on?
Lars decides to ask who gets something out of a photo, not only whether it is real, so he can doubt calmly instead of panicking.
How does Lindiwe see Lars's aunt differently from the person who made the fake?
Lindiwe sees the aunt as honest but fooled, sharing because it feels true, while the maker may want money, attention, anger or cruelty.

Xin kept a list in her phone notes titled "Stuff." It had fourteen entries. Leo got the bigger bedroom. Leo's football match: Mum there. My chess final: Mum at work. Leo gets to stay up. Mum laughed at Leo's joke, not mine.
She'd stopped telling Mum anything real. At their London kitchen table she answered in single words.

"It's evidence."
"Have you ever shown her?"
That night Xin sat on the stairs and read it again. Some entries still burned. A few, like the joke, looked small and silly written down. She deleted three.

How many entries did Xin's list have when Kofi read it?
Fourteen.

She felt resentful and hurt, keeping a tally of unfairness because she felt second to Leo.

Xin checked her list, deleted the small entries, and raised specific examples directly with Mum, so the talk could be about real events.

"Hansa, you've won the state chess title, well done. Now sit, and let me tell you about my biggest mistake.

When I, Bhupen, was twenty-four, I won the national quiz championship. My picture was in the paper. Everyone in Guwahati knew my name. For a year, every person I met told me I was brilliant.

And I believed them. I stopped studying properly. When my old coach pointed out that I'd been lucky in the final round, I laughed at him. I thought critics were just jealous.

The next year I lost in the first round to a seventeen-year-old from Silchar. I sat in the hall, humiliated.

Afterwards, I went to my coach and apologised. I thanked him for all those evenings he spent with me, unpaid. I asked him to show me what I'd got wrong.

Enjoy your win, beta. Then thank your teachers, and keep listening to the ones who tell you where you slipped."

The national quiz championship.

In last week's mock exam, Karthik (sixteen) froze. He spent forty minutes on the first question, didn't finish, and left half the paper blank. He came to see me looking pale and said, “I know this stuff. I just panic.”

Jasleen has been coming in twice a day for three months, before and after work. I noticed she trains through pain, including last week with a swollen ankle. Lalremsiami, the senior designer, listened with a calm, still face. She didn't smile or nod. She took a few notes.
Uday faltered. He finished quickly and sat down, sure she hated it.
After the meeting he almost went straight to his desk. Instead he stopped by hers. "Can I ask what you thought? I couldn't read you at all."
She looked up, surprised. "I liked it a lot. I was listening carefully." She showed him her notes, three ideas to make it better. "In my family, you stay quiet and still when someone important is speaking. It's a sign of respect."

How many ideas did Lalremsiami write in her notes?
Three ideas to make it better.
What was Uday feeling when Lalremsiami kept a still face?
Uday felt anxious and discouraged, faltering and sure she hated the idea.
What did Uday do that avoided a misunderstanding?
He asked Lalremsiami directly what she thought instead of assuming her calm face meant disapproval.
How does Lalremsiami see a quiet, still face while listening?
She sees it as a sign of respect, learned in her family, not as coldness or disinterest.

By evening they had four sacks. Harish sat on the swing, sweaty, looking at the clean grass. 'We did that,' he said.
'We did,' Sachin said. 'Next Sunday, the drain?'

How many sacks did they fill by evening?
Four sacks.
How did Harish feel sitting on the swing at the end?
Proud and satisfied, seeing the clean grass and knowing they had done it together.
What made the clean-up work?
Many people joining, a clear goal of three sacks, and Mr Qureshi handling the broken glass safely while the children picked up paper.
How might Mr Qureshi feel helping the children?
Pleased and involved, happy to see kids caring for the park and to keep them safe from the glass.

I'm Tanuja. Last year, the promotion to senior analyst went to a colleague who'd been on the team eight months less than me. My reviews were better. The whispered reason: the director "preferred not to promote people who might go on maternity leave." I was a newly married woman.

I felt helpless. It seemed like a wall I couldn't move.

Joseph, a colleague who'd seen my reviews, said, "Write it all down first." So I did: dates, review scores, what was said.

Then I weighed it. I went to HR with my records. They were polite and did nothing. I spoke to a lawyer at a women's legal aid centre, who explained my options honestly: a complaint was possible but would take years and might sour my career there.

I decided not to fight that one in court. Instead, I kept my records, got two strong references, and moved to a firm with a better record on promotions.

Choosing not to fight wasn't giving up. It was choosing where to spend my energy.

How much less time had the promoted colleague been on the team?
Eight months less than Tanuja.
What was Tanuja feeling when she heard the whispered reason?
She felt helpless and wronged, as if facing a wall she couldn't move.
What steps did Tanuja take before deciding?
She documented everything, went to HR, and spoke to a legal aid lawyer about her options before choosing where to spend her energy.
How does Joseph see Tanuja's situation?
Joseph sees it as unfair, having seen her reviews, and supports her by suggesting she document everything.

Of all the problems which have been submitted to my friend, Mr. Sherlock Holmes, for solution during the years of our intimacy, there were only two which I was the means of introducing to his notice—that of Mr. Hatherley's thumb, and that of Colonel Warburton's madness. Of these the latter may have afforded a finer field for an acute and original observer, but the other was so strange in its inception and so dramatic in its details that it may be the more worthy of being placed upon record, even if it gave my friend fewer openings for those deductive methods of reasoning by which he achieved such remarkable results. The story has, I believe, been told more than once in the newspapers, but, like all such narratives, its effect is much less striking when set forth en bloc in a single half-column of print than when the facts slowly evolve before your own eyes, and the mystery clears gradually away as each new discovery furnishes a step which leads on to the complete truth. At the time the circumstances made a deep impression upon me, and the lapse of two years has hardly served to weaken the effect.

Can you cut this section down to under 70 words?

The narrator says that only two of Holmes's cases came from the narrator: Mr. Hatherley's thumb and Colonel Warburton's madness. The narrator says the strange, dramatic thumb story is worth recording, as it works better told slowly than in a short newspaper column.
How long is the queue at the museum right now?
The museum's queue is not something I can see, so I don't know how long it is. Call the ticket desk or check the museum's website for visitor notices.

He said, "Water, please."

In the college library's discussion room, Uma had the project tracker open on her laptop. Four names, twelve tasks. "Ritvik gets nothing this time," she said. Jaya looked up. "Nothing? He's in the group." "He sent the literature review a day late in week two. I had to stay up formatting everything. I'm not risking the final report on him." "He had fever that week, remember?" "Still." Uma left his row empty and split his tasks between herself and Jaya. When Ritvik messaged offering to do the survey charts, she replied, "Covered, thanks." Later, alone in the room, she noticed that the charts he'd made for the midterm were the neatest in the whole file. She scrolled past them quickly.

Why does Uma say Ritvik gets nothing this time?
He sent the literature review a day late in week two, and she had to stay up formatting everything.
Why does leaving Ritvik's row empty feel sensible to Uma?
After losing sleep over his late part, Uma wants to protect the final report, so cutting him out feels like being careful rather than unfair.
What could Uma do instead of scrolling past his charts?
She could weigh his whole record, including the neat midterm charts and his fever, and give him the survey charts with a clear deadline.

Jaya may feel uneasy, since she remembers he was ill and now has extra work because of a judgement she questioned.

I'm Arnab. When I was made captain of our under-eleven cricket team last year, I thought captains were supposed to shout. “Field there! Bowl faster! Don't drop it!” My dad shouts like that at the TV, and it sounded like leading. By the third match, Abhinav, my best friend, stopped talking to me. After the game he said, “You're not a captain, you're a sergeant.” That stung. That night I thought about the captains I actually liked, and none of them shouted. At the next practice I tried, “How about we move you to slip? You've got quick hands.” Abhinav grinned and went. We won that match by four wickets.

By how many wickets did they win the match?
They won by four wickets.
How did Arnab feel when Abhinav used the word sergeant?
Arnab felt stung and hurt, realising the shouting was pushing a best friend away.
What did Arnab change, and why did it work?
Arnab swapped commands for invitations with a reason, like “How about we move you to slip?”, which made teammates want to follow.
What was the season like for Abhinav before the change?
Abhinav felt ordered about and upset enough to stop talking to his best friend.

Career mentor's note — Women in Tech mentoring circle, Kochi

Ganga came to our session in March upset. I'm writing down what I saw so I remember it for the next group.
Six months ago, she received an offer for a QA engineer post. She told me the recruiter said, "Can you confirm today?" and she said yes within minutes, sure that hesitating would lose the job.
In March, Rekha, another tester from the same batch, joined the circle. Comparing notes over coffee, they found Rekha earned clearly more for the same role. Rekha had simply asked if the number could move.
Ganga kept saying, "I didn't ask one question." She looked more embarrassed than angry.
What I did next: we spent the session practising two lines for her upcoming review: asking what the band is, and asking what it would take to move within it.

What did the recruiter ask Ganga?
The recruiter said, "Can you confirm today?"
How was Ganga feeling in the March session?
Ganga was upset and looked more embarrassed than angry, full of regret at not asking even one question.
What else could Ganga have done when asked to confirm the same day?
She could have thanked the recruiter and asked whether there was any room on the number, or asked for a day to decide.

Rekha may feel uncomfortable and sympathetic, since sharing Rekha's pay upset Ganga, though Rekha did nothing wrong by asking.

At the government school in Bolpur, Bidisha had joined full of plans: nature walks, a class newspaper, plays under the banyan tree. But Headmistress Lakshmi checked everything. Every lesson plan had to be approved the evening before, every worksheet stamped, every activity timed to the minute. By October Bidisha was photocopying old worksheets and teaching straight from the textbook. At home she lay on the cot and didn't want to talk. Then, at the half-yearly review, Lakshmi said, "The district wants Class 6 reading levels up by March. How you get there is your business. Show me results." The next Monday, Bidisha took Class 6 under the banyan tree with a box of old newspapers.

What did Bidisha do with Class 6 the next Monday?
She took Class 6 under the banyan tree with a box of old newspapers.
What does Bidisha lying on the cot, not wanting to talk, suggest?
It suggests her energy had drained away; with every step checked, her own ideas felt pointless, so she did only the minimum.
What change at the review turned things around?
Lakshmi gave a clear goal, reading levels up by March, and left the method to Bidisha, which gave her room to use her judgement again.
How might Lakshmi have seen Bidisha's photocopied worksheets earlier in the year?
Lakshmi may have taken them as a lack of effort, without seeing that her own checking had squeezed out Bidisha's ideas.

Answer: Cars 7, buses 3, autos 9. Autos are the most. 19 vehicles in all.

Read each tally: "5, 6, 7" for cars; "5, 6, 7, 8, 9" for autos. For the total, count on: 7, then 8, 9, 10 (buses), then 11 ... 19 (autos). Go outside and make a real tally.

But that afternoon he whined and fussed for hours, pulled at his ear and wouldn't eat. No rooster helped. Maria felt his forehead. Warm. She took him to the doctor that evening.

What did Maria point at?
The rooster.
What was Hrithik likely feeling during the long afternoon of fussing?
He was likely unwell and uncomfortable, which is why distraction didn't help like it did in the morning.

The fussing lasted for hours, he pulled at his ear and wouldn't eat, and his forehead was warm.

In their shared flat in Delhi, Parul set her cup down hard on the counter. "Gautam, you've been passive-aggressive all week. I can feel you judging me." Gautam, washing dishes, felt his stomach drop. Had he been? He thought back carefully. He'd been quiet, yes, because of his internship interviews. He hadn't said anything about her. But he remembered she had been furious last month when he forgot to pay his share of the wifi, and she had never quite let it go. "I don't think I've been judging you," he said slowly. "Can you give me an example?" She couldn't, quite. "You just seem cold." "I've been nervous about interviews," he said. "Is anything still bothering you about the wifi?" Parul looked away.

What had Gautam forgotten to pay last month?
His share of the wifi.
How did Gautam feel when Parul accused him?
His stomach dropped; he felt anxious and briefly doubted himself, then steadied by checking his memory.
What did Gautam do instead of apologising or arguing?
He reviewed the facts, asked for an example, explained his interview nerves, and gently asked whether the wifi issue still bothered her.
What might Parul be feeling when she looks away?
Perhaps caught out and a bit embarrassed, sensing that her own leftover irritation was what she felt in him.

When Samir's catering company won the Kulkarni wedding over us, I sulked for two days. I'm Vikas, and I'd been sure the menu we offered was better.

Then I did something my old boss used to do: I called the client and asked, honestly, why. The bride's father was kind about it. "Samir's team invited us for a tasting. And they sent a message every week with updates. We never had to chase them."

That stung, because both were easy. We just hadn't thought of them.

So the next month we started free tastings on Saturdays and a weekly update message for every booked family. I even sent Samir a short note: "Congratulations on the Kulkarni wedding. Your tastings are a smart idea."

He replied with a thumbs up and, a week later, sent us a client whose date he couldn't take. We're rivals. We're also, it turns out, each other's best teachers.

What two things did Samir's team do that the client liked?
Samir's team invited the family for a tasting and sent weekly update messages.
What was Vikas feeling after losing the Kulkarni wedding?
Vikas felt disappointed and sulky, and was stung to learn the reasons were simple things they had missed.
What steps did Vikas take after learning why Samir won?
Vikas started Saturday tastings and weekly updates, and congratulated Samir, treating the rival as a teacher.
How might Samir see Vikas after the congratulations note?
Samir likely sees Vikas as a respectful rival, which is why he later sent Vikas a client.

Monday: In the Dublin flat, Varun's roommate Ramesh answered his mother's call on speaker at seven in the morning, shouting cheerfully in Telugu. Varun saw their Irish flatmate, Aoife, freeze in the kitchen doorway, eyebrows up.
Wednesday: At work, Varun heard Ramesh ask a new colleague, "How much do they pay you? Married?" The colleague laughed awkwardly and changed the subject. Varun noticed his own head wobbling "yes" in a meeting, and the manager said, "Is that a yes or a no?"
Saturday: Over pizza, Varun told Aoife and Ramesh, "Back home these things are normal. Salary questions are just curiosity. Loud calls mean we're close." Aoife laughed with relief. "I thought something was wrong!" Ramesh agreed to take early calls on the balcony. Varun started adding a clear "yes". Aoife asked if she could learn the wobble.

What did Ramesh ask the new colleague?
"How much do they pay you? Married?"
What was Varun feeling as he noticed Aoife freeze in the doorway?
Varun felt surprised and a little embarrassed, seeing that a normal morning call from home startled their flatmate.
Which steps helped the flat, and why?
Varun explained kindly what the habits meant, and both adapted a little, with calls on the balcony and a clear yes, so neither side felt judged.
How did Aoife see the loud calls before Varun explained?
Aoife seemed worried that something was wrong, and was relieved to learn they were just a close family's normal chat.

'Two more matches, Papa.'
'You've got the district badminton final at nine.'
'I know. I'm relaxing.'

When is the district badminton final?
The final is at nine.
Why did Nitin's thumbs stop when Kishore asked about losing after sleeping?
The question touched his real fear, that a loss after proper rest would show he simply isn't good enough, which the late gaming was meant to hide.

He asked a calm question that exposed the excuse, then switched off the router and offered to wake him, removing the handicap.

At the village Diwali fair, Imran snatched the little clay elephant out of Kalyani's hands. Kalyani reached for it, and Imran shouted, "You're mean! You're so angry! Go away!" Kalyani blinked; she wasn't shouting at all. Imran's own face was red, his fists tight around the elephant. His Nani came over and knelt between them. "Imran, who has the angry face right now?" Imran looked at his fists. His lip wobbled. "Me," he whispered. Nani nodded. "You wanted the elephant a lot. Let's ask Kalyani for a turn."

The little clay elephant.

He was the one feeling angry and wanting the elephant, but owning that felt bad, so he put the anger on Kalyani.

She asked who had the angry face, let him notice his own fists, named his wanting, and helped him ask for a turn.

I'm Farida, and looking back at the class picnic last month, I can see how I was. I made the plan, the list, the timings, even who sat next to whom on the bus. When Irfan suggested we stop at the lake first, I cut him off: "No, that'll ruin the schedule." I didn't even listen. I rewrote everyone's food list because they'd "do it wrong". By lunchtime, nobody was talking to me much. Irfan said, "It's like we're all just in your plan." That stung. The truth is, when I'm not in charge, my stomach knots up. He suggested stopping at the lake first.

He walked to the far wall, hands over his ears.

Macy and Piper went to the batting cages. Each token gets you 15 pitches. Macy used 11 tokens and Piper used 17. Macy hit the ball 50 times. Piper hit the ball 55 times. How many pitches did Macy and Piper miss altogether?

Macy used 11 tokens which are worth 15 pitches each, so 11 tokens x 15 pitches = 165 pitches.
Piper used 17 tokens x 15 pitches = 255 pitches.
Together, Macy and Piper received 165 + 255 = 420 pitches.
Macy hit the ball 50 times + Piper's 55 hits = 105 total hits.
Of the 420 pitches - 105 total hits = 315 misses.
The answer is 315.

In a car dealership, Fiona worked for 40 hours a week, John for 30 hours, and Jeremy for 25 hours. If the employees are paid $20 per hour, how much money does their boss spend paying all of them every month?

Fiona earns 40 hours/week * $20/hour = $800/week
So she earns $800/week * 4 weeks/month = $3200/month
John earns 30 hours/week * $20/hour = $600/week
So he earns $600/week * 4 weeks/month = $2400/month
Jeremy earns 25 hours * $20/hour = $500/week
So he earns $500/week * 4 weeks/month = $2000/month
Overall their boss has to spend $3200/month + $2400/month + $2000/month = $7600/month
The answer is 7600.

messages.content: Jim spends 8 hours scuba diving.  In that time he finds a treasure chest with 100 gold coins in it.  He also finds 2 smaller bags that have half as much gold each.  How much gold does he find per hour?

The smaller bags each have 100/2=50 gold coins each
So in total, they have 50*2=100 coins
So he found 100+100=200 coins
So he finds 200/8=25 coins an hour
The answer is 25.
My cricket coach says I should work on my fielding. I only like batting.
Fielding wins matches, and strong fielders get picked more often. It may help to think of it as the same hand-eye skill you use when batting.
What's a simple drill?

Stand a few steps from a partner and have them throw the ball to you at different heights. Catch it with soft hands, and then throw it back quickly and accurately. Ask your coach for other drills too.
Any way to make it less boring?
Turn it into a game. Count how many catches you make in a row and try to beat that number. Or compete with a teammate to see who has the better throw.

Priya is my friend who lives near the park.

What is it like for Arohi to overhear this from the next room?
Arohi hears only pieces and can see the chart and the calmer drawers, so Arohi reports what was heard and avoids claiming to know their hearts.

In the KG classroom, Hemant Sir held up a marker. "Diwali is coming! How shall we decorate our room?"
Hands shot up. "Flowers!" "Lamps!" "Paper chains!" "Rangoli!" "Balloons!" Sumit jumped up. "Stars on the window!"

Then he said, "Now we choose two. Put your hand up for your favourite."
Sumit voted for stars. Most children chose lamps and paper chains.
Sumit's lip wobbled. Hemant Sir smiled at him. "Stars can go on the door next week."
He clapped.

Which two ideas did most children choose?
Most children chose lamps and paper chains.
How did Sumit feel when stars did not win?
He felt sad and disappointed, which is why his lip wobbled.
What else could the teacher try so more children feel their idea was used?
Hemant Sir could keep the list and use a different idea each week, so ideas that lose the vote still get a turn.
How might the children feel about Hemant Sir writing every idea on the board?
They may feel happy and listened to, since even the funny idea about painting the fan went up on the board.
