Read this:

At the crèche in Pune, Zeenat sat the rag doll in a tiny chair and spooned air into its mouth.
“Eat your dal! No TV! Naughty baby!” She wagged her finger. Then she hugged the doll hard. “Good girl. Sleep now.”
Vandana, the teacher, paused. Should she worry about the scolding?
She watched longer. Zeenat laid the doll down, patted it, and sang. She was trying on being the grown-up, bossy one moment, gentle the next.
Vandana smiled and handed her a blanket for the doll.

What did Zeenat spoon into the doll's mouth?
She spooned air into its mouth.
What was Zeenat likely feeling as she scolded and then hugged the doll?
She seemed absorbed and happy in play, trying out feelings like bossiness and tenderness safely, not reporting what really happens at home.
What did Vandana do before deciding what the scolding meant?
She watched longer instead of taking the words literally, saw the whole game, and then joined in by offering a blanket.
What was Vandana worried about at first, and what changed her mind?
Vandana was briefly worried by the scolding, but watching longer showed a gentle, playful game, so she felt reassured.

Read this:

Zeenat burst into the school sick room holding one finger in the air, wailing. “Blood! Blood! I need an ambulance!” A tiny red line ran along her fingertip from a paper edge. Parul, the school nurse, didn't jump up. She patted the bed. “Let's look. Show me with your fingers how big the hurt is. One is tiny, five is huge.” Zeenat held up five, then glanced at the cut and changed it to two. Parul washed it and pressed on a plaster. “A two-finger hurt, and a two-finger plaster.” Zeenat giggled and wiped her nose.

What made the red line on Zeenat's fingertip?
A paper edge made the tiny red line on her fingertip.
What does Zeenat changing five fingers to two suggest?
It suggests her first alarm was bigger than the hurt; once calmer, she felt less scared and could see the cut was small.
How did Parul's finger scale help?
It asked Zeenat to rate the hurt herself, which helped her match her feelings to the size of the cut.
What is it like for Parul when children arrive wailing?
Parul has to stay calm and check each one, since a loud wail doesn't always mean a big injury, but sometimes might.
Cori is 3 years old today.  In 5 years, she will be one-third the age of her aunt.  How old is her aunt today?

In 5 years, Cori will be 3 + 5 = 8 years old.
In 5 years, Cori's aunt will be 8 x 3 = 24 years old.
Today, her aunt is 24 - 5 = 19 years old.
The answer is 19.

Read this:

Dear Tanvir,
Thank you for last Tuesday. I nearly didn't tell you. I'd rehearsed saying "the new role is going fine" all morning. Then you asked how I was really doing, and it came out: that I feel like I'm acting, that one day the board will realise I only got this job because the other candidate withdrew. I expected you to reassure me politely. Instead you told me about your first year as a director, sitting in your car before meetings, sure you'd be found out. And that half the people on your leadership course had said the same. I can't describe the relief. The feeling didn't vanish. It just stopped being a shameful secret and became something ordinary, something people like you carry too. I slept properly on Tuesday for the first time in weeks.
Sudha

What did Sudha rehearse saying all morning?
"The new role is going fine."
Why did Sudha feel such relief after the conversation?
Hearing that a respected mentor had the same fear turned a private shame into something ordinary, so it no longer felt like proof of being a fraud.
Which choice by Sudha made the relief possible?
Answering honestly when asked how things really were, instead of giving the rehearsed line.
How might Tanvir feel reading this letter?
Tanvir may feel touched and glad that sharing an old vulnerability helped, and perhaps more willing to share it with others.

Read this:

When Osaka's schools announced a phone ban, Yuki started following accounts that called it ridiculous. The more she liked, the more the feed showed her: memes, angry teachers from other cities, students swearing they'd protest. After three weeks she was sure every teenager in the country agreed with her. In the class debate, Dalia, the exchange student from Madrid, stood up and said she actually liked the ban; she slept better and talked more at lunch. Half the class nodded. Yuki's face went hot. 'But everyone thinks it's stupid,' she said. The teacher asked, 'Everyone where?' Yuki opened her mouth, then closed it. That evening she scrolled her feed and realised she hadn't seen a single post from the other side.

Where was Dalia an exchange student from?
Madrid.
How did Yuki feel when half the class nodded at Dalia?
She felt embarrassed and shocked, her face hot, because she had believed everyone agreed with her.
What could Yuki try to widen her picture?
Follow a few thoughtful accounts from the other side and talk to classmates like Dalia before deciding what 'everyone' thinks.
What might it be like for Dalia to speak up for the ban?
Probably a little nervous as an exchange student going against a loud opinion, and reassured when half the class nodded.
I cannot "tell the twins apart". Is "tell apart" correct?

Yes. "Tell apart" means to see the difference between two similar people or things.
Example: Even their teacher cannot tell them apart.

Read this:

When I got my first job in Hyderabad, my father Hrithik called three times a day. "Did you eat? Why didn't you pick up? Are you with good people?"
I love him. But I was in meetings, and I felt like a child again. I started ignoring calls, then felt guilty.
One Sunday, I called him. "Papa, I want to talk to you like an adult. I'll call every evening at eight. If there's an emergency, I'll call right away. But during work, I can't pick up."
He was silent. Then he said, "Okay. Eight o'clock." He sounded hurt, but he tried.
Now at eight, we talk about cricket and his garden, not just food. I'm Tejas, and I think we're friends now, a little.

What time does Tejas call Papa every evening?
At eight.
What was Tejas feeling when ignoring Papa's calls?
Tejas felt smothered and then guilty for ignoring someone they love.
What did Tejas do to shift the relationship to an adult one?
Tejas set a clear, kind boundary with a regular call time and an emergency exception.
How might Hrithik feel when Tejas sets the eight o'clock rule?
Hrithik probably feels a little hurt and worried, but willing to try because he loves Tejas.
Tracy feeds each of her two dogs 1.5 cups of food per meal. She feeds her dogs thrice a day. How many pounds of food do her two dogs consume if 1 pound is equal to 2.25 cups?

Each dog consumes 1.5 x 3 = 4.5 cups of food a day.
In pounds, this is equal to 4.5/2.25 = 2.
So both consume 2 x 2 = 4 pounds of food.
The answer is 4.

Read this:

Dear Karthik,
I'm writing because I owe you an apology. Last Thursday at the bus stop, you were upset about your result, and I flung both my arms open and tried to hug you. You stiffened and stepped back, and I saw your face change. I wanted to help, but I didn't ask. I've thought about it all week. Afterwards you said, "Not now, just sit with me," and we sat until the bus came. That was better. Next time I'll ask, "Do you want a hug, or should I just stay here?" and I'll take whichever answer you give. Thank you for telling me straight.
Asif

Where were Asif and Karthik when Asif tried to hug Karthik?
They were at the bus stop.
What was Asif feeling when flinging both arms open, and what does Asif feel now?
Asif wanted to comfort Karthik at the time. Now Asif regrets not asking first and wants to make up for it.
What could Asif do next time a friend is upset?
Asif could ask if a friend wants a hug or just company, and accept the answer. A refusal should be respected.
How might Karthik have felt when Asif's arms opened?
Karthik stiffened and stepped back, which suggests being caught off guard and not wanting a hug then. Karthik may still have valued Asif sitting beside Karthik.

Read this:

The evacuation text came at 4 p.m.: wildfire approaching, residents of the valley road should leave now. Sofia, home in Greece for the summer, looked out at the hazy orange sky and decided there was time. She wanted her laptop, her grandmother's photos, the cat carrier, her good shoes.
Her neighbour Kwame knocked twice. "The road will close. Come with me."
"Ten minutes," she said.
The ten minutes became thirty. By the time she drove out, ash was falling like grey snow and police were turning cars back on the upper road. She made it down, hands shaking on the wheel, the cat yowling. Kwame was waiting at the petrol station. "I thought you'd be right behind me," he said quietly.

What time did the evacuation text come?
At 4 p.m.
What was Sofia feeling as she drove out through the ash?
She felt frightened and shaken, realising how fast things had changed while she packed.
What could Sofia prepare for the next fire season?
A small grab bag and a short list of things to take, so she can leave the moment a warning comes.
What might Kwame have felt waiting at the petrol station?
He was likely worried and then relieved, having expected her right behind him.

Read this:

The night before the physics final, a message raced through the class group: "LEAKED PAPER, 100% real, from a teacher's cousin." A blurry photo of a question sheet was attached. Preeti had four chapters left and was tempted. But she looked more closely. The paper had last year's date in the corner. The "teacher's cousin" had no name. The message was forwarded "many times". She wrote in the group: "This looks like last year's paper. Does anyone know the actual source?" Aparna, her roommate, rolled her eyes. "Everything's fake anyway. The exam's probably rigged too. Why bother studying?" Preeti shook her head. "Not everything's fake. This one is, I think. The syllabus changed this year, and there's a question here on a chapter we dropped." Aparna paused, then looked. "Huh. True." They closed the photo and went back to chapter nine.

What date was in the corner of the paper?
Last year's date.
What was Preeti feeling when she saw the leaked paper message?
She was tempted, with four chapters left, but also doubtful once she noticed last year's date and the missing source.
What made Preeti's skepticism fair rather than cynical?
She checked specific evidence, like the date and the dropped chapter, and asked for the source instead of dismissing everything.
How did Aparna's view change after Preeti's point?
She paused, checked for herself, agreed it was true, and went back to studying.

Read this:

Day one. At the district scholarship office, the queue ran down the stairs. A man in a checked shirt leaned toward Afreen. "Two thousand, madam, and your file moves this week. Otherwise, months."
Afreen's stomach dropped. Her fees were due. "No, thank you," she said, and stayed in the queue.
Day five. Hansa, from her college, showed Afreen her phone. "Approved! I paid that man. Why are you being so stubborn?" Afreen smiled and said congratulations. At home she cried a little, and felt calm underneath it too, which surprised her.
Day twenty-six. The clerk called her name. "Your file is complete. Sanctioned." No extra money. Her fees were late by a week, and the college charged a small fine.
She walked out into the sun. It had cost her three weeks of worry and a fine. It had not cost her the feeling of walking out with nothing to hide.

How much did the man in the checked shirt ask for?
The man asked for two thousand.
What was Afreen feeling on day five?
Afreen felt afraid and left behind, crying a little, but also a surprising calm underneath because she had not paid the bribe.
What did Afreen's refusal cost, and what did it keep?
It cost three weeks of worry and a small late fine, but kept her file clean and gave her the feeling of having nothing to hide.
How might Hansa see Afreen's choice?
Hansa sees Afreen as stubborn, since paying got Hansa's file approved quickly, and may not understand why Afreen accepted the wait.
If Joe spent 1/9 of his pocket money of $450 on chocolates and 2/5 on fruits, how much money does he have left?

Joe spent 1/9 * $450 = $50 on chocolate.
Joe spent 2/5 * $450 = $180 on fruits.
Joe has $450 - $50 - $180 = $220 left.
The answer is 220.
I'm going to the market; do you need anything? Can I use a semicolon here?

It is acceptable.
Why: A semicolon can join two linked sentences; a full stop works too.

At the school library, Kiran, eleven, watched Anand show off his new football boots to a group of boys. They were bright orange with white stripes.

Kiran turned to the librarian. "Anand is so jealous of everyone. He always wants attention."

The librarian looked up. "Jealous? He looks happy."

"He's jealous," Kiran said again, arms crossed.

At practice that evening, Kiran kept glancing at Anand's boots. His own were old and scuffed.

When the coach asked, "Kiran, you okay?" he said, "Anand thinks he's better than everyone."

The coach nodded slowly. "Or maybe you'd like new boots too. That's normal."

Kiran looked down and didn't answer.

What colour were Anand's new boots?
Bright orange with white stripes.
Why does Kiran keep saying Anand is jealous?
Kiran feels envious of Anand's boots but can't see it in himself, so he says Anand is the jealous one.
What did the coach say that might help Kiran?
That maybe Kiran would like new boots too and that's normal, gently naming the envy without blame.
How might Anand feel if he heard what Kiran said?
Anand might feel hurt and confused, since he was only happy about his boots.

messages.content:
Pradeep, you know me as the guy who quit engineering. Here's what really happened. Everyone in my family said the same thing: "You're the son. You have to earn well." My cousin sister was told to take a bank job, simple and safe, because she'd marry. Nobody asked either of us what we liked. I liked caring for people. When Nani was in hospital, I stayed three nights and the nurses said I had steady hands. I wanted to be a nurse. I said it once at dinner and my uncle laughed so hard he coughed. For a year I did engineering and felt nothing. Then I sat with my mother alone and told her. She was quiet. Then she said, "You held my mother's hand better than any of us." She talked to Papa for me. So now I'm in nursing college. That's me, Chetan, and that's the whole story.

Tell me in three sentences what this passage says.

Chetan tells Pradeep that his family expected him, as the son, to earn well, so he studied engineering, although he liked caring for people. After a year of feeling nothing, he told his mother he wanted to be a nurse. She spoke to his father for him, and now he is in nursing college.

Two weeks before: Thomas, eleven, practised in the Kottayam church every Saturday, walking slowly with folded hands. His friend Chinmay asked, "What's First Communion?" Thomas shrugged. "Something big. Everyone's coming." His stomach twisted.
The day: In his new white suit, Thomas walked up the aisle feeling every eye on him. His grandmother was crying. He was proud and terrified at once. His hands shook as he received the bread. He did everything right, but he didn't know what it meant.
The next week: Chinmay asked again. Thomas asked Ammachi, who explained it was a way of joining the church family, and that he would now go to Mass like the grown-ups. "It's a new duty, and a gift." Thomas repeated it to Chinmay. It made more sense when he said it himself.

What did Thomas wear on the day?
His new white suit.
How did Thomas feel walking up the aisle?
He felt proud and terrified at once, his hands shaking with everyone watching.
What helped Thomas understand the rite?
Ammachi explaining its meaning afterwards, and then Thomas explaining it to Chinmay in his own words.
How might Chinmay see the rite, coming from outside it?
Chinmay was curious and puzzled at first, and probably found it clearer once Thomas explained it simply.

Read this:

Rekha, you keep asking how I got my science marks up. Okay, here's the whole secret, and it's going to sound stupid.
I'm Ishita. Every night, I used to finish dinner, pick up my phone “for five minutes,” and look up and it'd be eleven. Every night I'd promise tomorrow would be different.
Then our counsellor told us about if-then plans. Not “I'll study harder.” Something exact.
So I made mine: If I've just put my plate in the sink, then I open the science book on the table before the phone.
That's it. Plate in sink, book open.
Week one I had to repeat it in my head like a mantra. By week three I didn't even think. Plate, book. My phone sits on the shelf until I've done an hour.
My science went from a C to a B-plus. It's not magic. It's just one less decision.

What did Ishita's if-then plan link together?
Putting the plate in the sink and opening the science book before the phone.
How did Ishita feel about the nightly promises before the plan?
Ishita felt frustrated and let down each night, promising tomorrow would be different.
Why does the specific cue work better than “I'll study harder”?
It ties a clear action to a daily event, so Ishita doesn't need to decide in the moment.
How might Rekha respond to hearing the “secret”?
Rekha might feel surprised by how simple it is and curious to try a plan like it.
I'm trying to learn to draw faces and they all look flat.
Faces often look flat because they lack shading. Light and shadow give a face its shape. Where does the light come from in your drawings?
I never thought about that.
Pick one direction for the light, such as from the upper left. Then the side of each feature that faces away from the light, such as under the nose and chin, gets a shadow.
What about proportions?
A helpful guide is that the eyes sit about halfway down the head, and the space between them is about one eye wide. Check these on a real face and adjust your drawing.
How long before I improve?
Most people see progress within weeks of regular practice. Draw a little every day and keep your old drawings. Comparing them with new ones shows how far you have come.

Sudha: Show me the phone. Salma, breathe. Which accounts?
Salma: These three. They keep posting my photo with names.
Sudha: Okay. First, your settings. Make your profile private. Yes, here.
Salma: Done.
Sudha: Now block each one. Don't reply. Not a word.
Salma: Blocked. Should I delete the posts?
Sudha: No. Screenshot them first, with the date showing. We keep those.
Salma: Okay. Saved.
Sudha: There's a report button under each post. Choose harassment. Do it for all three.
Salma: Reported. It feels a bit better.
Sudha: Tonight we show Mummy. Tomorrow we give the screenshots to your class teacher. You are not doing this alone.
Salma: Thank you, didi.

What did Sudha tell Salma to do before deleting anything?
Sudha told Salma to screenshot the posts with the date showing.
How does Salma feel after reporting the posts?
Salma feels a bit better and less exposed, though still shaken, as the steps give some control.
What else could Salma and Sudha do if new accounts appear, and why?
They could block and report each new account and add the screenshots to the record, because the school can then see the whole pattern.
How does Sudha see the situation?
Sudha is calm and protective, guiding Salma step by step and insisting that adults be told, so Salma is not alone.

metadata.subtype: Approach: blocking and reporting online abuse [Action]

I forgot my tiffin at home, so I shared Deepak's lunch. I promised him I would bring sweets for him tomorrow, and he laughed and said I did not have to.
Ananya forgot her tiffin at home, so she shared Deepak's lunch. She promised him she would bring sweets for him tomorrow, and he laughed and said she did not have to.

I'm Baljeet. I sit next to Lokesh in Class 4. On Friday, while we waited for the bell, Lokesh threw his steel water bottle up to catch it, showing off. It went sideways and cracked the staffroom window. A long line ran right across the glass.
Ma'am asked who did it. Lokesh put his hand up slowly, but then he said, 'It's only a crack. Last year the Class 7 boys broke three windows and the fan.'
Ma'am said, 'We're talking about this window.'
Lokesh kept saying 'only a crack' all through lunch. But he didn't eat his paratha, and he kept looking at the staffroom. I don't know what he was thinking. Maybe he was scared of his papa finding out.

What did Lokesh throw that cracked the staffroom window?
His steel water bottle.
Why did comparing with the Class 7 boys feel reasonable to Lokesh?
Next to three windows and a fan, one crack seemed small; the comparison made Lokesh's own damage feel less serious and less scary.
What choice could Lokesh make instead of saying 'only a crack'?
Lokesh could say 'I broke it, sorry' and offer to help set it right; owning this crack without comparing it to anyone else might also ease the worry.
How does Baljeet read Lokesh's 'only a crack' alongside the uneaten paratha?
Baljeet notices the words and the behaviour don't match: Lokesh insists it is small but skips lunch and keeps looking at the staffroom, so Baljeet guesses at fear without being sure.

metadata.subtype: At least it was not worse [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Rain hammered the bus shelter, and the last bus was forty minutes late. Asif sat with his elbows on his knees. He had been cut from the school football squad that afternoon. "I'm done. I'll never make anything of it."
Neelam didn't say it would be fine. She sat down next to him and let the rain fill the quiet. After a while she said, "That's really rough. You practised all term."
He nodded, jaw tight.
"There's another trial in January, isn't there?"
"Yeah."
"We could run drills on Sunday mornings. Ten laps, then see what the coach says."
"You'd do that?"
"I've got nothing on Sundays."
The bus lights appeared down the road, and for a moment neither of them moved.

How late was the last bus?
The last bus was forty minutes late.
How might Neelam have been feeling as she sat in the rain with Asif?
Neelam was probably worried and caring, choosing to stay and listen. Her offer of Sundays suggests she wanted to be useful.
What did Neelam do that offered hope without empty promises?
Neelam stayed beside him without saying it would be fine, acknowledged the effort, and pointed to the January trial with a small plan of Sunday drills.
How might Asif have seen Neelam sitting beside him without saying it would be fine?
As real support. Asif was crushed after being cut from the squad, with a tight jaw, and Neelam's company and small plan gave him something to hold on to.

At the cricket academy's nets, Irfan, fourteen, batted for two hours every Saturday. He faced ball after ball, laughing with friends between deliveries, and felt he was working hard. Yet in every match he got out the same way, edging outside off stump. His coach, Vishal sir, called him aside. "You bat for two hours. How many balls outside off do you actually practise?" Irfan shrugged. "Some?" The next Saturday, Vishal sir set up a bowling machine to bowl only outside off. "Thirty balls. After each one, I'll tell you what your front foot did." It was hard and slow. By the third Saturday, Irfan was leaving those balls alone.

How long did Irfan bat every Saturday?
He batted for two hours every Saturday.
What was Irfan feeling while batting and laughing with friends?
He felt busy and satisfied, believing he was working hard even though his main weakness was untouched.
Which change worked, and why?
Thirty balls only outside off with feedback after each one focused on his exact weakness and gave immediate correction.
How might Vishal sir see Irfan's progress by the third Saturday?
Vishal sir would likely feel pleased that the focused practice was working, seeing Irfan leave those balls alone.

Read this:

Trisha from HR smiled across the table at the Gurugram office. "Sachin, the offer is final. Honestly, there are two hundred applicants who'd take this in a heartbeat."
Sachin had asked about the relocation support mentioned in his interview, not even the salary. His neck prickled. He felt like a beggar asking for more food.
He looked down at the offer letter. No mention of relocation. No mention of the joining bonus the manager had talked about on the phone.
"I'm really grateful for the offer," he said. "The manager mentioned relocation support and a joining bonus. They're not in the letter. Could you add them in writing, or tell me if they've changed?"
Trisha's smile tightened. "Everyone else just signs."
"I'd like to sign too. Once it matches what we agreed."
The revised letter came two days later, with relocation support added. The bonus had been "a misunderstanding". At least now he knew.

What was missing from Sachin's offer letter?
The relocation support and the joining bonus the manager had mentioned on the phone.
What was Sachin feeling when Trisha mentioned two hundred applicants?
He felt small and uneasy, like a beggar asking for more, his neck prickling.
How did Sachin handle the pressure well?
He stayed polite and grateful, pointed out the missing terms, asked for them in writing, and did not sign until the letter matched what was agreed.
How might Trisha see Sachin's request?
Trisha seems irritated and defensive, used to people signing without questions, which is why her smile tightens.
What is the meaning of "to pull someone's leg"?
It means to tease someone in a joking way. For example: "Don't believe him, he is only pulling your leg."
A bird eats 7 berries a day. Samuel has 5 birds. How many berries do Samuel's birds eat in 4 days?

A bird eats 7 x 4 = 28 berries in 4 days.
So, 5 birds can eat 28 x 5 = 140 berries in 4 days.
The answer is 140.
When does the sweet counter at the market shut?
I don't know when the sweet counter shuts, as I can't see its hours. The shop sign or a nearby seller can tell you.

At his cousin's wedding in Indore, the dining hall was packed and the food was running out. Saurabh, ten, had finally got a plate with the last two gulab jamuns when his little cousins crowded round, whining.
Without a word, he gave both away. Then he gave his chair to an old great-aunt.
Indu Mausi saw him standing in the corner with an empty plate. "Saurabh, did you eat?"
"I'm fine."
"You gave away your gulab jamuns."
"The small ones wanted them."
Indu Mausi crouched down. "That was kind. But you're allowed to want things too, beta. What did you want?"
Saurabh hesitated. "...One gulab jamun."
Indu Mausi laughed, went into the kitchen, and came back with one, warm, hidden under a napkin, just for him.

What did Saurabh give to the old great-aunt?
He gave his chair to an old great-aunt.
How was Saurabh feeling standing in the corner with an empty plate?
Saurabh felt content to have been kind but quietly hungry and a little left out, keeping his own wish unspoken.
What did Indu Mausi do that helped Saurabh?
She praised his kindness but told him he was allowed to want things too, and asked what he wanted, then got him a gulab jamun.
How might the little cousins see Saurabh?
They probably see him as a kind older cousin who always shares.

Shreya's phone buzzed on the table while she was in the kitchen. Deepak saw the name: Aman. Third time today. His hand actually moved towards the phone. He pulled it back.
When she came out with two bowls of instant noodles, he said, 'Can I ask something without it sounding bad?'
'That's a scary start.'
'I've been feeling suspicious, and I hate it. You've been texting Aman a lot. I nearly looked at your phone just now. I didn't.'
Shreya put the bowls down slowly. 'Thank you for not looking. And for asking.' She unlocked the phone and held it out. He shook his head.
'I don't want to read it. I want to hear it.'
'Aman's organising the surprise for my sister's graduation. I've been hiding it from her, not from you.'
Deepak let out a long breath. 'My brain made a whole movie out of three texts.'
'Next time, ask sooner. Movies are worse than questions.'

Who is Aman, according to Shreya?
The person organising the surprise for her sister's graduation.
What was Deepak feeling when the phone buzzed?
He felt suspicious and anxious, enough that his hand moved towards her phone.
What did Deepak do instead of spying?
He pulled his hand back and calmly told Shreya his worry, asking to hear the truth rather than read her phone 👍
How does Shreya respond to Deepak's question?
She thanks him for not looking and for asking, and explains openly.

Read this:

Friday: Tushar, twelve, was watching cricket with his father Kamal when his heart began to race for no reason. His vision went fuzzy. 'Papa, I'm going crazy!' Kamal switched off the TV and held his hand. 'I'm here. Breathe with me.' After a few minutes it passed.
Monday: The doctor listened to Tushar's heart and checked him carefully. 'Your body is healthy. What happened is scary, but it passes. Tell an adult if it comes again.'
The following Sunday: On the bus to his uncle's, the racing started again, smaller. Tushar gripped the seat and remembered: it passes. He told Kamal, 'It's happening.' Kamal nodded calmly and breathed with him. This time, Tushar watched out of the window until it faded.

What were Tushar and Kamal watching when it first happened?
Cricket.
How did Tushar feel on the Sunday bus compared to Friday?
He was still frightened but steadier, because he remembered it passes and told Kamal straight away.
Which of Kamal's responses helped most?
Staying calm, holding Tushar's hand and breathing with him each time.
How might Kamal have felt on the first Friday?
Kamal was probably shocked and worried, but kept calm on the outside for Tushar.
Compose a short story for children, 60 words, of a tortoise who is not afraid of a big rainstorm.

Everyone in the forest ran for shelter when the storm clouds rolled in. Only the old tortoise stayed calm. She pulled in her head and legs and sat inside her shell. The wind howled and the rain thundered, but she stayed dry and warm. When the sky cleared, the animals came out and thanked her for the lesson.
Label a piggy bank for me: exactly three words, capital letters only.
MY SAVINGS BOX

Supervisor's note, 3 March. Vaibhav, accounts team.
Pallavi asked to speak privately after the morning huddle. She showed me messages from a man she met on a matrimonial site, "Dr Karan", who says he works on an oil rig. After six weeks of daily calls, audio only, he asked her to pay a customs fee for a gift parcel he had sent.
She told me she knew at once it was a stop sign, because he had asked for money and they had never met. She had not paid. She said she felt foolish for having liked him.
I told her she had done exactly the right thing, and that these schemes are run by professionals; liking someone is not foolish.
Actions today: sat with her while she reported the profile to the site and filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal. Gave her the afternoon off. Will check on her Thursday.

What did Dr Karan ask Pallavi to pay?
He asked her to pay a customs fee for a gift parcel he said he had sent.
How did Pallavi feel about having liked Dr Karan?
She felt foolish for having liked him, even though she had spotted the scam.
What did Vaibhav do that helped Pallavi?
Vaibhav told her she had done the right thing, reminded her these schemes are run by professionals, and sat with her while she reported the profile and filed a complaint.
What would change if Vaibhav had laughed at Pallavi?
She would feel more ashamed and might hide the next problem, whereas support made reporting easier.

When Bao leaned over Javier's desk in the Madrid office and said, "You should really cut half these slides before Thursday," Javier felt his jaw tighten. He had spent all week on them. Who asked you? was already on his tongue. He swallowed it and said, "Let me think about it." Then, on his walk to get coffee, he asked himself the question he'd been practising: am I against the idea, or just against being told? He pictured the client, the thirty slides, the tired faces after lunch. The idea was right. It was the tone that stung. Back at his desk, he cut twelve slides and messaged Bao: "You were right about the length. Next time, maybe start with a question?" Bao replied with a thumbs-up and "Fair."

How many slides did Javier cut?
He cut twelve slides.
What did Javier feel when Bao gave the advice, and what did he do with that feeling?
Javier felt irritated, his jaw tightening, but paused and asked whether he was rejecting the idea or just the being told.
Which part of Javier's response is worth copying?
Separating the idea from the tone: taking the good advice, then calmly asking Bao to start with a question next time.
How might Bao have felt reading Javier's message?
Bao probably felt a little caught out but respected, accepting the point about tone with 'Fair'.
Describe a market in four lines of exactly five words each.

Vendors shout their prices loudly.
Fresh mangoes sit in baskets.
Children follow the sweet smells.
Bags fill up with vegetables.

Samir came in from the gate with his lower lip stuck out, dragging the toy truck behind him. Papa Yogesh looked up from the newspaper. "What happened, Samir?"
"Ayaan went home."
Yogesh set the paper down. "You are sad because Ayaan had to leave before you finished playing."
Samir looked at him. He nodded slowly. "Yes."
"That's a big sad."
Samir climbed into his lap. His shoulders dropped, and the lip went back in. After a while he said, "Can Ayaan come tomorrow?" "We'll ask his mother," said Yogesh.

Who went home?
Ayaan.
What was Samir feeling, and what shows it?
Sad. Samir came in with the lower lip out, dragging the truck, and nodded when Yogesh named the sadness.
What did Yogesh do that helped Samir?
Yogesh named the feeling, "You are sad because Ayaan had to leave before you finished playing," and let Samir climb into his lap.
How might Yogesh have felt seeing Samir come in with the lip stuck out?
Concerned and caring, and Yogesh put the paper down and gave full attention right away.

Monday: Vidya's father, Raghav, set one toffee on the table. "Wait till I finish this call, and you get two." Vidya stared at it, touched it, sniffed it, and ate it in under a minute.
Wednesday: Appa tried again. This time he said, "Want to count the fan blades while you wait?" Vidya counted. Then she sat on her hands and sang her school song, very loudly. She peeked once. She kept singing. When Appa came back, the toffee was still there.
Saturday: Before Appa could say anything, Vidya put the toffee under a cup, turned her back and started building a block tower. "I'm busy," she told it. She got two.

What did Vidya do with the toffee on Saturday?
She put it under a cup, turned her back and started building a block tower.
Why did Vidya sing her school song very loudly on Wednesday?
Vidya felt impatient for the toffee, and singing loudly kept her mind off it, so it was easier to keep waiting for two.
What change did Raghav make between Monday and Wednesday, and why did it help?
He gave her something to do, counting the fan blades, which showed her that distraction makes waiting easier than staring.
How might Raghav feel on Saturday when Vidya hides the toffee herself?
He may feel proud and amused that she has learned the trick on her own.

'You didn't come to the aarti tonight,' Binita said, sitting on the edge of Tanuja's hostel bed.
'I couldn't. I stood outside and the bells sounded like noise.'
'Because of Aji?'
'I prayed every day she was in hospital, Binita. Every single day. And she still died. So either nobody's listening, or...' Tanuja stopped.
'Or what?'
'I don't know. That's the problem. I don't know anything anymore.'
Binita was quiet for a bit. 'My mother went through something like this when my uncle died. She didn't go to the temple for a year.'
'And then?'
'Then she started reading, and talking to the old priest at our temple, who told her even saints argued with God. She goes again now, but differently.'
'I don't want to pretend I'm fine with it.'
'Then don't. Just don't decide everything this week.'
Tanuja pulled the blanket around her shoulders. 'Maybe I'll talk to our family pandit-ji when I go home. Just talk.'

Who died while Tanuja was praying every day?
Aji died while Tanuja was praying every day.
What was Tanuja feeling as she stood outside the aarti?
Tanuja felt empty and lost, the bells sounding like noise after Aji's death despite her prayers.
What small step does Tanuja decide on, and why is it wise?
To talk to the family pandit-ji at home, which keeps her honest about the doubt while seeking an elder's help.
Why might Binita share her mother's story?
Binita wants Tanuja to know that doubt after a loss is common and can change shape over time.

On the balcony, Avni sets her toy cars along the railing in a perfect row, red ones first. Zeenat, her aunt visiting from Lucknow, calls, "Avni, jaan, see the pigeons!" Avni does not look up. Zeenat's smile slips. Later Avni climbs into Zeenat's lap facing away and leans her whole back against her, humming one note. "That's her hug," Avni's father says. "She saves it for people she likes. The doctor sees her next month." Zeenat stays still and lets the humming go on.

Which cars does Avni put first in her row?
The red ones.
How does Zeenat feel when Avni does not look up at her name, and what shows it?
She feels a little hurt or disappointed; her smile slips.
What choice does Zeenat make when Avni leans against her, and why does it help?
She stays still and lets the humming go on, so Avni can enjoy the closeness her own way instead of being hugged the usual way.
How does Avni's father see the back-lean differently from a visitor?
He knows it is her kind of hug, saved for people she likes, so to him it is clear affection rather than distance.

In the small town of Karad, Devika was the one everyone asked for help with forms. So when a polite woman called about a state scholarship for girls from her college, Devika asked questions. The caller knew her marks, her principal's name, even that she had topped the district in Class 12. The next day a letter arrived on her phone with a seal and a signature. The caller rang every evening, just to "check on our brightest candidate," and asked about Devika's mother's knees. Devika began to look forward to the calls. At the tailoring shop, her friend Dilnaz said, "Ask the college office if they know about it." Devika laughed. "She knows my marks, Dilnaz. Who else would?" Walking home past the temple, she felt, for once, that someone important had noticed her.

What did the caller know about Devika?
The caller knew her marks, her principal's name, and that she had topped the district in Class 12.
How does Devika feel about the evening calls?
Devika feels special and safe, even cared for, because the caller remembers details and asks about her mother's knees.
What turning point is available at this stage?
Devika could take Dilnaz's advice and check with the college office through its own number before sharing anything more.
How might Dilnaz feel when Devika laughs off the suggestion?
Dilnaz may feel worried and a little brushed aside, sensing that the warmth of the calls is making her careful friend less careful.

Stefan goes to a restaurant to eat dinner with his family. They order an appetizer that costs $10 and 4 entrees that are $20 each. If they tip 20% of the total for the waiter, what is the total amount of money that they spend at the restaurant?

The total cost of the entrees is 4 * $20 = $80.
The total cost of the dinner is $80 + $10 = $90.
The tip is $90 * 0.20 = $18
The total cost with tip is $90 + $18 = $108
The answer is 108.

At the design firm in Osaka, the real news always travelled in the smoking corner and in a group chat of senior staff. Hiroshi was in both. He knew about the reorganisation a week early.
In the office, people treated him differently. Juniors brought him coffee and asked, casually, “Anything new?”
Clara, the only foreign designer on the team, wasn't in the group chat. She didn't smoke. One day she stopped Hiroshi by the printer. “Everyone's whispering. Is my contract safe? Nobody tells me anything.”
Hiroshi saw her hands clutching the pages. He realised she had spent a week worried, while he had enjoyed knowing.
“I honestly don't know about contracts,” he said. “But I'll ask our manager to tell the whole team properly.”

Where did the real news travel?
In the smoking corner and in a group chat of senior staff.
What was Hiroshi feeling when he saw Clara's hands?
He felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, realising she had worried for a week while he enjoyed knowing.
Why is asking the manager to tell the whole team a good step?
It replaces the grapevine with official facts, so outsiders like Clara don't have to live on rumours.
How is Clara affected by being outside the grapevine?
She feels anxious and left out, unsure about her contract while others whisper.

Friday
The LED circuit for the physics project finally lit up at 9:40 pm, and I have no idea why.
It wouldn't glow all evening. I panicked and started changing everything: flipped the LED, swapped the red and black wires, moved the resistor two holes down, borrowed Papa's new battery, pressed everything harder into the board. Somewhere in there it came on. I screamed and Papa came running.
Kamal, my lab partner, texted: "What was wrong?" I typed "fixed it!!" and then just sat there. Fixed WHAT? I changed about eight things at once and didn't write any of them down.
Now I'm scared to even touch it in case it goes off again before Monday's demo. Not really the feeling you want after "fixing" something. 😬
Mahima

What time did the LED circuit finally light up?
At 9:40 pm.
How does Mahima feel after the circuit lights up?
Mahima is relieved at first but then uneasy and scared, not knowing which change worked or whether it will fail before the demo.
What could Mahima try next time the circuit won't work?
Change one thing at a time, test after each change, and jot it down, so the fix is known and can be repeated at the demo.
How might Kamal feel if the circuit fails again at Monday's demo?
As lab partner, Kamal would likely be worried and let down after the cheerful "fixed it!!", with nothing to go on to fix it quickly.

Note from Disha's class teacher.
During the colour card game, Devika saw Disha hide a red card under her knee. "You cheated!" she said. The other children stared. Disha's face went bright red and she ran to the cubby corner and hid behind the coats. I went and sat outside the cubby. I did not call her bad. I said, "Everyone makes mistakes in games. Shall we say sorry and play again, fair this time?" After a while she came out. She told Devika, "Sorry." They played two more rounds, and Disha kept all her cards on the mat.

Where did Disha hide the red card?
She hid it under her knee.
What does Disha running to the cubby suggest she felt?
She felt deeply ashamed and embarrassed at being caught, and wanted to run away and hide.
How did the teacher help without making the shame worse?
The teacher sat nearby, did not call her bad, and offered a way to say sorry and play again fairly.
How might Devika feel when Disha says sorry?
Devika may feel the game is fair again and be glad to keep playing with Disha.

At Tiny Tots kindergarten, Lavanya's Appa, Zubin, crouches at the classroom door. "I'll be back after lunch, like always." Lavanya, four, nods, waves, and trots to the painting table. She paints a blue sun, then plays shop with two girls. When the bell rings, she spots Zubin at the door and races over. She hugs his neck, tells him about the blue sun, then tugs away. "Wait, Appa! I have to finish selling!" He laughs and waits.

What colour sun does Lavanya paint?
Lavanya paints a blue sun.
What does Lavanya's quick hug and tug away suggest she feels?
It suggests she feels secure and happy, reassured Appa is back so she can go on playing.
Why does Zubin's "I'll be back after lunch, like always" help?
The steady promise, kept every day, helps Lavanya trust that he returns, which frees her to play on her own.
How might the teacher see Lavanya's quick check-in at pickup?
The teacher might see it as a healthy sign that Lavanya has settled and uses her father as a safe base.

At Noche Buena in Lola's crowded house in Quezon City, Tito Ben raised his glass. "Paulo! Ten years old already. What will you be?"
"An engineer," Paulo said at once, sitting up tall. "Like Papa and Lolo. The third engineer in the family."
Everyone clapped. Lola pinched his cheek. Paulo glowed.
Later, on the stairs with their plates of ham, his friend Siddiq from next door said, "I want to draw comics. Or maybe be a vet. I keep changing."
Paulo frowned. "You don't know yet?"
"Do you?"
"Of course," Paulo said. He had never once thought about it. It was simply true, like his name.

What does Paulo say he will be?
An engineer, like Papa and Lolo.
How does Paulo feel when everyone claps?
He feels proud and glowing, sure of his answer because the family expects it and nobody questions it.
How could Paulo's family help him explore without taking away his pride?
Ask what he enjoys and let him try different things, drawing, building, caring for animals, while saying any choice he makes later will be welcome.
Why might Siddiq react differently to the question?
Siddiq feels free to keep changing between comics and being a vet, perhaps because no single path has been handed over.

Monday: Before the school concert, Dolma pulled at her frock. "My tummy has bees in it." Her mummy, Sangeeta, knelt down. "Bees in your tummy? That can be a nervous feeling. Lots of people get it before a show."
Thursday: Dolma came home from the park stomping, cheeks red. "My face is hot!" Sangeeta said, "Hot face and stompy feet. Maybe that's angry?" Dolma nodded hard. "Kusum took my swing."
Saturday: At bedtime Dolma yawned. "My legs are heavy. That's tired, Mummy." Sangeeta smiled. "You're getting good at listening to your body."

What did Dolma say was in her tummy before the concert?
She said her tummy had bees in it.
What was Dolma feeling when her face was hot on Thursday?
She was angry because Kusum took her swing.
How did Sangeeta help Dolma understand her body?
She named the feeling that matched each body signal, like bees for nervous and a hot face for angry, and asked rather than told.
How might Sangeeta feel when Dolma names "tired" by herself?
She probably feels proud and pleased that Dolma is learning to listen to her body.

"Neelam, you're scared of your engineering entrance because of what people say about girls? Let your Nana tell you something.
At nineteen, I, Irfan, was the first in our basti to go to a big college in Delhi. Some boys said, 'Your kind don't pass second year.' Before every test, my stomach churned.
Then I did something my old headmaster taught me. I wrote on a card: 'An exam measures what I've practised, not what I'm worth.' Under it I wrote three problems I'd once solved that nobody thought I could.
I also went to the one professor who said, 'Mistakes are how we learn.' He gave me extra problems every week.
I passed second year. And third. Keep your card, beta."

What did Irfan write on the card?
'An exam measures what I've practised, not what I'm worth.'
How did young Irfan feel before every test?
His stomach churned; he felt anxious and pressured by what the boys said about his kind.
What choice in the story helped Irfan reduce the threat?
Writing the card and recalling past successes, and seeking out the professor who framed mistakes as learning.
How might the professor have seen young Irfan?
The professor likely saw a capable student who needed practice and belief, and gave him extra problems.

Gerald spends $100 a month on baseball supplies. His season is 4 months long. He wants to use the months he's not playing baseball to save up by raking, shoveling, and mowing lawns. He charges $10 for each. How many chores does he need to average a month to save up for his supplies?

He needs to save up $400 because 4 x 100 = 400
He has 8 months to earn this money because 12 - 4 = 8
He needs to earn $50 a month because 400 / 8 = 50
He needs to do 5 tasks a month because 50 / 10 = 5
The answer is 5.
Now you try: f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5 on [1, 5].
The answer is c = 3.

At the insurance office in Nagpur, the Friday target meeting had become almost cheerful. Madhuri watched Gurleen, from the next desk, tick the "site verified" box on a claim she had checked only by phone. "Virtual verification," Gurleen said, and a few people laughed. Six months ago, when Madhuri first saw someone do that, she had lain awake worrying about it. Now it was a running joke. There was even a sticker on the team's water cooler, a smiling face with the words "Verified-ish." Madhuri's own queue had forty claims and the deadline was four o'clock. She picked up the next file, called the garage owner, heard him say the car was repaired, and ticked the box too. Her stomach didn't even flutter this time. She noticed that, briefly, and then Gurleen passed her a biscuit and she forgot.

How many claims were in Madhuri's queue?
Madhuri's own queue had forty claims.
How has Madhuri's feeling about the ticked box changed over six months?
Six months ago she was worried enough to lie awake, but now she feels almost nothing, her unease faded because everyone jokes about it.
What turning point could Madhuri still take when she notices that her stomach doesn't flutter?
She could treat that moment as a warning, stop joking along, and raise the verification practice with a manager or compliance team.
What would change if one person in the team refused to laugh at the joke?
The shortcut would seem less normal, and others who still feel uneasy might feel brave enough to question it too.

Santosh: Noor, it's getting bad. two DMs just now saying they'll find me after class
Noor: ok. first thing: set every account to private. now
Santosh: done
Noor: second: mute your name, the college name and the word from the post
Santosh: muted. it's quieter already

Santosh: saving them in one folder. there are six
Noor: fourth: report each one to the platform with the screenshot
Santosh: reported all six. should I post a statement?
Noor: not yet. safety and records first. statement later if ever
Santosh: ok. I told Papa too
At seven, Santosh's father called back. He said he would come to the hostel that evening, go through the folder with him, and take him to the college office in the morning.

How many threats did Santosh save in the folder?
Santosh saved six threats in one folder.
What is Santosh likely feeling when the DMs arrive?
He is likely frightened and shaken, messaging Noor that it is getting bad after being told they will find him after class.
Which other step could help Santosh stay safe on campus the next day?
He could walk with friends and ask the college office to note the threats, since the danger is offline as well as online.
How might Santosh's father see the situation after the call?
Santosh's father is likely worried but steady, choosing to come that evening and go to the college office with him the next morning.

messages.content: Why does the moon seem to change shape each week? What is the name of my class monitor? What does the word "liberal" mean?

1. We see different parts of its lit side. Because the moon moves around the Earth.
2. I don't know it, since I can't see your class. Ask your teacher or a classmate.

First week: when Harsha Ma'am asked a question, Santosh jumped up and shouted the answer, pushing past others.
Two weeks later, he raised his hand but called out at the same time. 'Hand up, voice off,' she smiled.
A month on, Santosh sat on his mat, hand stretched high, lips pressed together, bouncing a little. When she called his name, he grinned and answered.

What did Santosh do in the first week when a question was asked?
He jumped up, shouted the answer and pushed past others.
What does Santosh bouncing with his lips pressed together suggest?
It suggests he was eager to answer but working hard to control himself and wait his turn.
What helped Santosh adopt the classroom habit?
Harsha Ma'am's short, friendly reminder 'hand up, voice off' gave him a clear rule to practise over time.
How might the other children feel about Santosh's change?
They may find class calmer and fairer, since they also get a chance to answer.

Note from Salma, school counsellor. Kiran, Class 6, came to see me after lunch. She told me that at breakfast her father said she was beautiful exactly as she is. She rolled her eyes: "Papa has to say that." I asked what she thought about it. She said she doesn't believe it, but she keeps hearing it anyway. I noticed she was picking at the end of her plait and had avoided the mirror by the door. What I did: I told her she doesn't have to believe it today, and that hearing it often may still matter. We agreed to talk again next week.

What did Kiran say about her father's words at breakfast?
She said, "Papa has to say that."
What does Kiran's admission that she keeps hearing her father's words suggest she is thinking?
She doubts it about herself, yet the words have stayed with her, so a part of her may want to believe them.
How could Salma support Kiran next?
She can keep checking in without pushing Kiran to believe it yet, and encourage her father to keep showing steady warmth.
How might Kiran's father feel when she brushes off his words?
He may be hurt or worried, but he likely means them and will keep saying them, and that steady love is what she can build on.

Karthik's father, Yogesh, called him into the living room of their Chennai flat. "Look, the city water supply is poisoned! Everyone in my walking group sent it."
Karthik read it. No name, no date, just capital letters. He searched the Chennai water board website. There was a normal notice about a pipeline repair, nothing about poison. He checked two newspapers. Nothing.
"Appa, how often have you heard of a whole city's water being poisoned?"
"Never. But all twenty people sent it."
"And they all got it from each other. The water board says it's just a pipe repair." Karthik showed him the notice. "I'm not forwarding it. Can you tell your group what the notice says?"
Yogesh read it twice, then slowly typed a message to his walking group.

What did the Chennai water board website say?
There was a normal notice about a pipeline repair, nothing about poison.
What was Yogesh feeling when he called Karthik in?
Yogesh felt alarmed and worried, trusting the message because twenty people in his walking group sent it.
What steps did Karthik take to stop the chain?
He checked the water board website and two newspapers, asked how often such a thing happens, and chose not to forward it.
How might the walking group react to Yogesh's message?
They might feel relieved to learn it was just a pipe repair, and maybe a bit sheepish for spreading the scare.

messages.content: Clyde's four children wanted to go see their favorite band perform.  The tickets were expensive so Clyde made a deal with his kids.  If the average of their scores on their next math test was higher than 89, then he would buy them tickets to the concert.   June earned a 97 on her math test, Patty earned an 85, Josh earned a 100 on his test and Henry earned a 94.  What was their average math test score?

Together, they scored 97+85+100+94 = 376
There are 4 children so their average math test score is 376/4 = 94
The answer is 94.

Day one: Amandeep, fifteen months, stands holding the sofa and reaches for a ball. He leans too far and thumps down on his bottom. Preeti, his mother, rolls the ball closer. A week later he bends to pick up the ball, wobbles, and slaps one hand on the floor to steady himself before rising. Two weeks on, he carries the ball across the rug, steps over Preeti's outstretched leg, sways, and stays upright.

What did Amandeep step over in the last beat?
Preeti's outstretched leg.
How might Amandeep have felt when he leaned toward the ball?
He seemed eager to reach the ball, keen enough to lean too far while still holding the sofa.
How could Preeti give Amandeep more safe balance practice?
She can place toys just out of reach on soft ground so he has to shift his weight, while staying near.
What would change if the floor were hard tiles with no rug?
Falls would hurt more, so Preeti might stay closer or add a mat, and Amandeep might be more cautious.

Coach's note, inter-school athletics camp, day 3.

Hemant has been sharp all week, and not only on the track. Every time Ishika from the relay team passes, he says something loud for his group to hear: "Careful, the tortoise is coming!" or "Did you run or walk today?" His friends laugh. Ishika rolls her eyes, but today she didn't come to the stretching circle.

What I noticed: he watches her warm-up closely, he knows her times better than his own, and he goes red when she answers back. It may be a crush he doesn't want the others to see.

I spoke to him alone after lunch. I didn't mention a crush. I said the jokes were hurting a teammate and had to stop, and asked what he'd like to say to Ishika instead. He mumbled, "She's fast, actually." He'll apologise tomorrow; I'll be nearby.

Ramesh

What does Hemant call out when Ishika passes?
Hemant says, "Careful, the tortoise is coming!"
Why might teasing Ishika feel safer to Hemant than being kind?
Hemant likely likes Ishika and feels embarrassed and exposed at the thought of his friends knowing, so mocking her hides the crush.
What did Ramesh's talk with Hemant get right?
Ramesh spoke to Hemant alone, focused on the harm to a teammate without shaming the crush, and set up an apology with support.
What is it like for Ishika this week?
Ishika is laughed at in front of others and hurt enough to skip the stretching circle, even while acting unbothered.

"Sit, Reena, and listen, because your notice reminds me of mine," said Joseph. "I was twenty-five, newly working, and a letter came about my filing. I was terrified. In the corridor outside the office, a man in a neat shirt said, 'Give me five thousand in cash, no receipt, and this file disappears.' I wanted to say yes so badly.

"But something felt wrong. Why no receipt? I asked, and he laughed and said receipts were for fools. So I walked away. My uncle sent me to a chartered accountant, who filed the reply on the official portal and handed me a proper receipt.

"That man would have owned me. Next year he would have come for more, and I would have had nothing to show I was honest. Keep every receipt, beta."

What did the man in the corridor ask Joseph to hand over?
The man asked for five thousand in cash, with no receipt.
What made Joseph hesitate even though Joseph badly wanted to say yes?
Something felt wrong to Joseph, especially that there would be no receipt, so Joseph asked about it and then walked away.
What should Reena do about the notice, based on Joseph's story?
Go to a certified professional, reply through the official portal, and ask for a receipt for everything.
How might the man in the corridor have seen the young Joseph?
The man probably saw a frightened newcomer who would keep paying to make the problem vanish, an easy person to hold power over.

Tara invites 8 friends and each one brings 2 chocolates. How many chocolates are there?
Why is teamwork easier with friends?
And one more: fix this: They invited we to the party.

1. 16 chocolates. Because 2 x 8 = 16.
2. Friends trust each other. Because they know each person's strengths and talk openly.
3. Fixed: They invited us to the party. Why: "Invited" needs the object form "us".

Parveen was bored at the cooperative office in the kasba, tired of stamping forms she no longer read. One Monday she resigned. "I'll study full time and become a data analyst," she told her friend Jomon at his copy shop. Nobody had asked her how, and she had not asked herself either. She had no savings, no timetable and no course booked.

For three months she watched videos in the afternoon, opened a dozen tabs and finished none. She lay in bed mornings, telling herself she was on a break from thinking. The money in her account thinned to almost nothing.

In month four she took a job at a hardware store just to eat. The data plan was still a sentence in her notebook, only further away than before.

Where did Parveen tell Jomon she would study full time?
At his copy shop.
What was Parveen feeling in the months of drifting, and what shows it?
Parveen felt stuck and increasingly anxious, shown by the untouched tabs, the late mornings and the dwindling money.
What could Parveen have done before resigning, and why?
Parveen could have saved some money and started a course while still working, because a plan and a safety net make the switch less risky.
How might Jomon see Parveen's decision to resign?
Jomon may have felt supportive but uneasy, having heard a big plan with no steps, and probably wanted to help more.

Mohit: this lecture has been going for ages 😴
Sudha: which one, thermo?
Mohit: yeah. I've drawn the whole classroom in my notebook
Sudha: I saw you yawning. Did you sleep at all last night?

Mohit: fine 🙂 also I'm going to sleep properly tonight

Mohit: legend. Thanks 🙏

What did Mohit draw in the notebook?
Mohit drew the whole classroom.
What is Mohit feeling in the lecture, and what does Mohit say about the cause?
Mohit feels bored and tired, and says it is hard to tell which it is after little sleep and busy with deadlines.
What small steps could help Mohit?
Mohit could take a walk at the break, drink water, and get proper sleep that night.
How might Sudha feel about Mohit's yawns?
Sudha seems concerned and kind, since Sudha asked about Mohit's sleep and offered to share notes.

metadata.subtype: Bored and tired in study life [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the family function in Chennai, Sunaina kept climbing back into her mother Sharmila's lap for cuddles, pressing her cheek to Sharmila's chest.
An uncle leaned over. "Give me a kiss, Sunaina!"
Sunaina turned her face away and clung tighter.
"She's not in the mood," said Sharmila lightly. "Maybe a wave?"
The uncle straightened up. "Okay, okay. A wave then." Sunaina peeped out and waved.

Where did Sunaina keep climbing for cuddles?
Into her mother Sharmila's lap.
What was Sunaina feeling when she turned her face away from the uncle?
She didn't want to kiss him, perhaps feeling shy or uncomfortable, while she felt safe and loving with her mother.
Which choice of Sharmila's respected Sunaina, and why?
Saying lightly that she wasn't in the mood and offering a wave respected Sunaina's right to refuse a kiss.
How might the uncle feel when Sunaina turns away?
He might feel a little disappointed, but he accepts the wave without fuss.

Draw the shape and count.
a) Draw a triangle. Put a dot on each corner. How many dots?
b) Draw a pentagon (a house shape). How many sides?
c) Draw a semicircle. How many corners?
d) Draw a hexagon. How many corners?

a) 3
b) 5
c) 2
d) 6 (A house shape: a square with a triangle roof, drawn as one outline: /\ / \ | | +--+ 5 sides, 5 corners.)
John buys 3 t-shirts that cost $20 each.  He also buys $50 in pants.  How much does he spend?

He spends 20*3=$60 on t-shirts
So he spends 60+50=$110 in total
The answer is 110.

Read this:

Dear diary, Pranav here.

Today was the robotics demo. Our line-following robot, which took us eight weeks, went straight off the table in front of the judges and crashed into the dustbin. Then a wire caught and the whole thing started smoking.

Silence. Then Vinita said, "Well, at least it's recycled now." And we all cracked up. Properly. Tears. Even one judge laughed.

It still hurt. Eight weeks. But after laughing, we could actually look at it. We sat on the lab floor and made a list: the sensor was loose, the wire was too close to the motor, the code had a bug. The judges said we can re-demo on Friday.

If we hadn't laughed, I think we'd have just gone home and felt terrible separately.

How long had the team worked on the robot?
Eight weeks.
Why did laughing help Pranav and the team?
The laughter gave them some distance from the disappointment, so they could look at the problem without feeling crushed.
What did the team do after laughing, and why does it matter?
They sat on the lab floor and listed what went wrong, turning the moment into a plan for the Friday re-demo.
How might the judge who laughed see the team?
The judge probably saw them as resilient and good-humoured, which may be why they got a second chance.
My group's science project was delayed because I forgot to bring my part to school. Write a sorry message to my group mates, about 50 words.

Hi everyone,
I am really sorry that I forgot to bring my part of the project. It slowed all of us down, and that was my mistake. I will bring it as soon as I can, and I will help finish the rest. Thank you for being patient.
Your group mate

Read this:

Dear Pranav,
You asked why I never talk about Ma anymore. It's because I barely talk TO her. Every time I told her something, the job, the flat, my friends, it turned into a fight. So I stopped. Now I just say "all good" and ask about her knees. It's peaceful.
But last Sunday she said, "I don't even know who your friends are now." And I realised she's right. She doesn't know I lead a team now, or that I cook, or that I'm actually happy. She's still talking to the girl who left home at eighteen.
I don't know how to start again without it becoming another fight. Any ideas, little brother?
Ishita

What does Ishita ask her mother about instead of sharing her life?
She asks about her mother's knees.
What did Ishita realise after her mother's comment on Sunday?
She realised her mother doesn't know the adult she has become, and she seems sad about that even though the silence feels peaceful.
What small step could Ishita take to reconnect?
She could share one good, low-risk part of her life, like her cooking or her team, and let her mother get to know her gradually.
How might Ishita's mother feel about their calls?
She probably feels shut out and a little lonely, knowing she has lost touch with her daughter's life.
What does "back to square one" mean?

It means to go back to the very start of something because your attempt did not work.
Example: The storm blew away all our seedlings, so we were back to square one in the garden.
Why do people check the weather report before planning a picnic?
They check the report so the picnic is not ruined. Because rain or strong heat would make the day unpleasant, knowing in advance lets them pick a better day.

Read this:

You asked how I'm doing, Hemant, so I'll be honest. Your old friend Raghav has turned into a bank inspector.
Every morning, before I've even brushed my teeth, I open the bank statement. Then I check it again at lunch. When Shobha, my wife, says she's going to her mother's, I watch her face while she says it, like I'm waiting for her eyes to slip.
Last week she laughed at something on her phone and my stomach dropped. It was a cat video. She turned the screen to show me without my asking, and her voice was so careful, so small.
I know why I'm doing it. After the loan, I promised myself I'd never be the last to know again. But I'm exhausted, yaar. I'm not catching anything. I'm just living in the second before the next shock.
And now she leaves her phone face-up on the table, all the time, like it's evidence.

What was Shobha laughing at on her phone?
Shobha was laughing at a cat video.
Why does Raghav keep checking the bank statement?
Raghav wants to make sure he is never the last to know again; after the loan, his mind is guarding against another shock.
What turning point could Raghav look for at this stage?
Raghav could tell Shobha how exhausting the checking is and ask for one full, open conversation about money, perhaps with a counsellor, instead of watching for clues alone.
What is it like for Shobha to live with Raghav's watching?
Shobha seems to feel watched rather than forgiven: her careful, small voice and the phone left face-up suggest she is trying to prove herself all the time.
Eric sorted 150 colored pencils into 5 containers for his art class. Before class, another teacher brought him 30 more pencils. How many can he evenly distribute between the five containers now?

Before the extra colored pencils, he had 150/5=30 colored pencils in each container.
With the other colored pencils, he is given he now has 150+30=180 colored pencils
If you distribute them evenly each container should have 180/5=36 colored pencils
The answer is 36.

Read this:

Tutorial note, Research Methods, week 9. Written by the course tutor.
Today Chetan told the group that the stats quiz after a long lab was impossible because "willpower runs out like petrol." Saurabh, who usually sits quietly at the back, said, "I believed that too. Then I read about the big replication studies with thousands of people. Most found tiny effects or none." Chetan frowned. "So I'm just lazy?" Saurabh shook his head. "No. You're tired, that's real. It's just that nobody's sure it works like a tank. Some studies suggest people who don't believe willpower runs out keep going longer." I was struck by how carefully he held both points. Next week I have asked Saurabh to lead ten minutes on what replications can and can't tell us.

What did Saurabh say most of the big replication studies found?
Most found tiny effects or none.
Why did Chetan ask 'So I'm just lazy?'
Chetan seems worried that without the petrol explanation, the tiredness becomes a character flaw; the fuel-tank idea had felt like a kind reason for struggling.
What choice did the tutor make after the discussion, and why does it fit?
The tutor asked Saurabh to lead ten minutes on what replications can and can't tell us, building on his balanced view instead of letting the class swing to a new certainty.
How might Saurabh have felt answering Chetan's 'So I'm just lazy?'
Saurabh probably felt careful and sympathetic, taking Chetan's tiredness seriously ('You're tired, that's real') while staying honest that the tank idea is doubtful.

Read this:

I'm Sonali, and I've known Wasim since first year of law college. He's usually quiet in class. But during the moot court last week, he surprised everyone. The case was about workers whose wages a contractor had legally withheld because of a loophole. Wasim was assigned to defend the contractor. Halfway through, he stopped and said, "My lord, this may be lawful. I cannot argue that it is right." The room went still. The judge, one of our professors, frowned. Wasim went on to argue that the law itself should be read in the light of basic human dignity. He lost marks for going off-brief. Afterwards, I asked him if he regretted it. He just shrugged and said, "Some things matter more than marks." I still can't tell if he was nervous or completely calm.

What was Wasim assigned to do in the moot court?
Defend the contractor.
What does Wasim's 'Some things matter more than marks' suggest about what he believes?
He seems to feel no regret, holding a principle about human dignity above grades or approval, even at a cost.
How could a professor respond helpfully to what Wasim did?
The professor could mark him on the brief but also discuss his point openly, since it raises an important question about law and rights.
How does Sonali see Wasim's choice?
Sonali is impressed and a little puzzled, and admits to not knowing whether Wasim was nervous or calm.

Read this:

Dear Gopika Didi,
I owe you the real story, not just the sorry I said on the phone.
On Friday I got a message that looked like it came from the photo app, saying my account would be locked. I typed my password into the page it opened. The moment I pressed enter, I knew: the page had a strange web address. I felt so embarrassed that I told no one. I kept thinking I'd fix it myself somehow, and then I didn't.
On Sunday someone using my account messaged you pretending to be me, asking for a code “to recover my account”. You trusted me, so you sent it, and they got into yours.
If I had told Papa on Friday, he would have helped me change the password that night, and you'd never have got that message. Two days of hiding did this, not the click.
I've told Papa now. We changed everything and reported the account together.
Nitin

When did someone message Gopika Didi from Nitin's account?
On Sunday.
How does Nitin feel writing this letter?
Nitin feels guilty and full of regret, seeing that two days of hiding, not the click, let the harm reach Gopika Didi.
What should Nitin do if something like this happens again?
Tell Papa or another trusted adult at once, so the password is changed that same night, before anyone else is targeted.
How might Gopika Didi feel reading the real story?
She may still be upset about her account, but the honest letter may help her feel respected rather than betrayed.

Read this:

Dear Dilnaz,

Guess what: I slept straight through until six on Wednesday, and no dreams I remember. I lay there almost suspicious. Then on Friday I laughed properly at Ammi's joke about the neighbour's parrot, and afterwards I felt a pinch of guilt, as if I had stolen something. I told my counsellor, and she said joy is not a betrayal of what happened. I'm trying to believe her. Last weekend I even went to the market by myself and picked out a yellow scarf. Remember when I couldn't be in crowds? It hasn't vanished, but it doesn't run my day. Thank you for never rushing me. Come over on Sunday, Ammi is making biryani, and I'd like to celebrate a little.

Love,
Zeenat

What colour scarf did Zeenat pick out at the market?
Zeenat picked out a yellow scarf.
Why did Zeenat feel a pinch of guilt after laughing at the parrot joke?
Zeenat felt as if joy was something stolen, as though laughing meant betraying what happened.
How could Zeenat and Dilnaz celebrate the progress?
Dilnaz could come over on Sunday for biryani with Ammi, marking the good days without any pressure. 🎉
What might Dilnaz feel on reading the letter?
Probably relief and gladness, and perhaps warmth at being thanked for never rushing Zeenat, since the letter credits that patience directly.

How long did Jatin's last three similar apps take?
5, 6 and 8 weeks.
Why did Jatin ask for twenty minutes before answering?
Jatin felt cautious about giving a hopeful date, and wanted to check how long similar apps really took.
How did Jatin build the estimate, and why is it trustworthy?
By checking past projects, breaking the job into design, build, testing and changes, and adding a buffer week.
Why might Tushar accept seven weeks over the other offer of two?
Tushar sees that the past numbers are real, and that promising seven and delivering in six beats a broken two-week promise.

Read this:

April: Usha, eight months into her first job in Bhubaneswar, realised she had forgotten to include the interest from her fixed deposit in last year's return. Her face went hot. For a week she avoided even looking at the file, feeling like a cheat.
May: Her colleague Ramesh saw her staring at the tax website during lunch. "Something wrong?" She told him, bracing for a lecture. He shrugged. "I did the same in my first year. You can file a correction. Talk to the office's tax helpdesk."
She went that afternoon. The adviser showed her how to file a revised return, and she paid the difference.
June: Usha bought a blue folder and labelled it with the year. Salary slips, bank interest certificate, rent receipts. She put a reminder on her phone for every March. When she saw the acknowledgement for the revised return, she let out a long breath. She was learning, that was all.

What did Usha forget to include in last year's return?
The interest from her fixed deposit.
How did Usha feel after realising the error in April?
She felt guilty and ashamed, like a cheat, her face going hot and avoiding the file for a week.
What did Usha do to own and fix the mistake?
She told Ramesh, went to the tax helpdesk, filed a revised return, paid the difference, and started a yearly folder of records.
How might Ramesh see Usha's mistake?
Ramesh sees it as a normal first-year error, having made the same one, and wants her to fix it without shame.
In about 60 words, describe a butterfly garden for a children's activity sheet.

Welcome to the butterfly garden! Here, colourful flowers grow in every corner, from orange marigolds to purple lantana. Look closely and you will see butterflies of all sizes, some yellow, some blue and some with spots like eyes. They sip nectar from the flowers. Can you count how many different colours you see? Walk softly so you don't scare them.

Peter bought 4 new notebooks for school. 2 of them are green, one is black and the other one is pink. The total cost was $45. If the black notebook cost $15, and the pink one cost $10, how much did the green notebooks cost each?

The black and pink notebook cost a total of $15 + $10 = $25
The green notebooks cost a total of $45 - $25 = $20
Each green notebook cost $20 / 2 = $10
The answer is 10.

On his return to Moscow from the army, Nicholas Rostov was welcomed by his home circle as the best of sons, a hero, and their darling Nikolenka; by his relations as a charming, attractive, and polite young man; by his acquaintances as a handsome lieutenant of hussars, a good dancer, and one of the best matches in the city.

How do different groups welcome Nicholas Rostov when he returns to Moscow?

His home circle welcomes him as the best of sons, a hero and their darling Nikolenka. Relations see a charming, polite young man, and acquaintances see a handsome hussar lieutenant, a good dancer and one of the best matches in the city.

Read this:

The house was full of guests for Diwali, and Chandrika had three pans on the stove. She'd snapped at Siddharth for knocking over the rangoli colours. Now he was nowhere. She found him behind the curtain, hunched on the floor, chin tucked, arms wrapped round his knees. Guests were calling her. Chandrika sat down beside him anyway, saying nothing. After a minute, he leaned his head on her arm. “I'm sorry I shouted,” she said softly. He nodded, and she held him a moment longer.

Where did Chandrika find Siddharth?
Behind the curtain, hunched on the floor.
What might Siddharth have been feeling when he hunched behind the curtain?
He likely felt ashamed and sad after being snapped at for spilling the rangoli colours, and wanted to hide. He may also have felt overwhelmed by the busy house.
What worked for Chandrika even with little time?
She sat quietly beside him instead of asking many questions, and apologised gently once he leaned on her.
What is it like for Chandrika to leave the guests and pans?
It is hard, since everyone needs her, but she chose to give Siddharth her quiet presence first.
