On the balcony of her Chennai flat, Mahika covered her statistics notes with an old postcard and whispered, "Standard deviation... spread from the mean..." before sliding it down to check. Kamal, her cousin, back from the shop with milk, watched her frown. "Why make it hard? Just read it again." "Reading feels nice," Mahika said. "Then I forget it by Friday." She had a small table taped to the fridge: Monday, Wednesday, next Monday, each topic coming back just as she started losing it. Some evenings she got half wrong and sighed loudly. Kamal shook his head and went inside. Two weeks later, in the class quiz, most of her friends groaned at the question on variance. Mahika remembered the postcard, the balcony, and her own whisper, and wrote.

What did Mahika use to cover her notes?
An old postcard.
Why did Mahika choose the harder way even though reading "feels nice"?
She had learned from experience that just reading faded by Friday, so she accepted the frustration of recall because it lasted.
Which choice in Mahika's routine made the difference by quiz day?
The small table on the fridge, bringing each topic back just as it starts to fade, on Monday, Wednesday and the next Monday.
How does Kamal see Mahika's method, and why might he think that?
Kamal thinks she is making it needlessly hard, because from outside all he sees is her frowning and getting answers wrong.

Read this:

Aadhya, you asked why I rang your teacher that same evening last month, when you told me about Tanvi. Let me tell you about my own school in Aligarh. When I was eleven, a girl called Rukhsana made up a song about my crooked teeth, and the whole class sang it. I lay awake planning revenge: tear her notebook, hide her shoes, make her cry in front of everyone. One morning I stood behind her in the line with my fists clenched, shaking. Then I turned round and went to Miss Fernandez instead. "I'm angry enough to hurt her," I said. She told me the anger was allowed but hurting wasn't, and she stopped the song that very day. That is why your Nani Hafsa picked up the phone.

What did Rukhsana make up about Hafsa?
Rukhsana made up a song about Hafsa's crooked teeth.
What was Hafsa feeling while standing behind Rukhsana with clenched fists?
Hafsa felt furious and humiliated, full of the urge for revenge after the whole class sang the song.
Which choice in the story changed things, and why?
Turning round and telling Miss Fernandez about the anger, instead of acting on it, let an adult stop the song that same day.
How might Miss Fernandez have seen Hafsa's words "I'm angry enough to hurt her"?
Miss Fernandez likely took them as honest and brave, and as a sign that the teasing had to stop at once.

Read this:

Monday: Pema and Pranav both entered the inter-school quiz and practised together every recess.
Friday, quiz day: Pema was knocked out in the second round. Pranav went on and won. When they called his name, Pema cheered so loudly the teacher laughed, and she hugged him in the corridor. On the bus home, though, she stared out of the window for a while. She had wanted to win too.
Saturday: Pema made Pranav a card with a gold star and wrote, "Best quiz partner ever. Next year, both of us in the final." She felt good giving it. The little ache was still there, but smaller, sitting next to the happy part.

In which round was Pema knocked out?
The second round.
What was Pema feeling on the bus home?
She felt a quiet ache of disappointment, wishing she had won too, even though she was happy for Pranav.
What did Pema do that let both feelings live together?
She made Pranav a card celebrating him and set a goal for both of them next year.
How might Pranav feel receiving the card?
He would likely feel touched and happy that his friend is proud of him.

Monday. Tejas, two, used the potty for the first time. Vikas grinned. "Well done, Tejas!" Tejas clapped.

Wednesday. Two accidents. Vikas cleaned up without a word of blame. "No problem."

Two weeks later. Tejas ran to the potty, then shouted, "Papa, look!" Vikas gave him a high five. Tejas laughed and pulled up his shorts himself.

What did Vikas give Tejas two weeks later?
Vikas gave Tejas a high five.
What was Tejas feeling when he shouted "Papa, look!"?
Tejas felt proud and excited to show his success.
How did Vikas handle success and accidents?
He praised success simply and warmly, and cleaned up accidents calmly without blame or pressure.
How might Vikas feel after two weeks?
Vikas likely feels pleased and patient, trusting Tejas's body to learn in its own time.
Dana Point beach has four times the number of sharks as Newport Beach. If Newport Beach has 22 sharks, how many sharks are there in total on the two beaches?

Since Dana Point beach has four times the number of sharks in Newport beach, there are 4*22 = 88 sharks at Dana Point.
In total, the two beaches have 88+22 = 110 sharks
The answer is 110.

I'm Vijay, a developer on Parveen's team, and watching Parveen manage the reporting tool was like watching a cup fill drip by drip. Sales asked for one extra column; Parveen said, "Sure, quick one." Then a different chart, a second export format, an email alert for managers. Each time Parveen smiled and agreed, and I nodded at my screen. Nobody argued. The delivery date stayed the same on the wall calendar. Last Thursday, three days before the demo, half the features weren't tested. Parveen stood at the board for a long time, then said quietly, "I kept saying yes because I didn't want to let anyone down." I don't know how long that had been weighing on Parveen. Maybe only since that morning.

How many days before the demo were half the features still untested?
Three days before the demo, half the features weren't tested.
Why did Parveen keep saying yes to each request?
Parveen was eager to please and afraid of letting anyone down, so each yes felt harmless.
What could Parveen have done at the second request?
Say what the extra work would cost in days and ask what should move or be dropped.
How might Vijay have felt watching the requests pile up without speaking up?
Uneasy and perhaps a little guilty, since Vijay nodded at the screen and said nothing while the date stayed fixed.
Break this one long sentence in two: The teacher was kind, so everyone liked her, and she gave us extra time.
The teacher was kind, so everyone liked her. She gave us extra time.

Preeti held out her hand for a second laddoo. Swati had already given her one after the evening meal. Jeevan, home late and still holding his office bag, shook his head. "No more sweets tonight, sweetheart." Preeti's face crumpled. "I hate you!" she yelled, and stamped so hard her sandal squeaked on the tiles.

Then she tried a new way. She cried in big gulps. "I'll eat all my dinner tomorrow, promise, promise." Jeevan did not answer, and she watched his face from behind her fingers. When that did nothing, she screamed at the top of her voice and threw herself onto the sofa cushions, one eye open to see whether he would move toward the sweet box.

Jeevan's ears burned. Hearing those words after a long day stung more than he expected. His voice was already climbing in his throat, ready to match hers, and he nearly told her she could go to bed without her story. He stopped, set down his bag, and let out a long breath through his nose. Only then did he look at his daughter again.

What did Preeti do when she was told no more sweets?
She yelled "I hate you!" and stamped so hard her sandal squeaked on the tiles.
How did Preeti's tries after the first refusal connect to the moment Jeevan had to handle?

Preeti went from shouting to crying, promising and screaming while watching Jeevan's face to see whether he would move toward the sweet box. His ears burned and his voice climbed, so taking a long breath before he looked at his daughter again was the key moment.
What might Jeevan be feeling when Preeti yells "I hate you"?
He feels stung and tired: his ears burn and his voice is climbing to match hers.
What could Jeevan do next, now that he has breathed?
He could calmly keep the limit on sweets, tell her he sees she is angry, and stay close for comfort without shouting.
My bedroom door squeaks every time it opens.
A squeak usually comes from dry metal hinges rubbing together. Lubricating the hinge pin normally fixes it.
What can I use for that?
A drop of machine oil or a spray lubricant works well. In a pinch, rubbing a bar of soap or a candle on the pin helps. Wipe off any extra so it does not mark the door.
Why do we feel no pain when we trim the ends of our fingernails?
The hard tip of the nail has no feeling, so trimming does not hurt. Because the nerves lie in the skin underneath and not in the hard nail itself, the cut ends are like dry hair.

Abhinav, you've been stuck on that engine design all evening. Let your Sumit Mama tell you a story from when I was in my third year.
I had to design a water pump mount for my project. For two days I drew version after version. Nothing balanced. One night I stayed till midnight in the drawing hall, getting angrier with every eraser mark.
My professor came in to lock up and said, "Go home. Sleep. Come back tomorrow." I thought he was being lazy.
But I went. And the next morning, walking to the college bus, I saw a water tank on a roof, held up on three legs, not four. Three legs, beta! The mount could sit on three points and never rock.
I drew it in ten minutes. Two days of struggle, and one night's sleep gave me what I needed.
So close the laptop. Eat. Sleep. See it tomorrow.

What did Sumit see on the roof the next morning?
He saw a water tank on a roof, held up on three legs, not four.
How was Sumit feeling at midnight in the drawing hall?
He was frustrated and angry, getting angrier with every eraser mark after two days of failing.
When the professor told Sumit to go home, what could Sumit have chosen instead, and what might have happened?
He could have stayed and kept drawing, but he would likely have stayed stuck and angry and never noticed the three-legged idea.
How might the professor have seen Sumit that night?
The professor probably saw a tired student going in circles and knew rest would help more than more hours at the desk.

Class 5 teacher's note, Wednesday.
At break, Vidya and Pranav were shouting over a cricket game. "You were OUT!" "I was NOT out!" Twelve times at least, each louder. Neither was listening.
I stepped in and made a rule: before you answer, you have to say what the other person just said. Pranav rolled his eyes. "She thinks I was out because the ball hit the stumps." Vidya said, "He thinks he wasn't out because the bail didn't fall." They both paused. Then Pranav said, "Oh. That's actually the real question."
They asked the PE teacher, who said the bail must fall. Vidya accepted it. I'll teach the "say it back" rule to the whole class on Friday.

What did the PE teacher say about the bail?
The bail must fall for a batter to be out.
What was Pranav feeling when he realised the real question?
He seemed surprised and more open, no longer just angry, once he heard Vidya's point clearly.
What did the teacher's rule change, and why?
Saying back what the other said forced them to listen, which showed them the real disagreement about the bail.
How did Vidya respond to the PE teacher's answer?
She accepted it, which suggests she felt the argument had been fair.
I'm a student who wants to use the school computer lab for an hour after class on weekdays. Write a polite request to the principal, about 60 words.

Dear Principal,
I am a student of this school, and I would like to request permission to use the computer lab for an hour after class on weekdays. I believe this time would help me learn and practise. May I kindly request your permission? I would be very grateful for your help. Thank you for your consideration.
Yours sincerely

In the fall, 20,000 high school students apply to Harvard University for college. In the spring, 5% of those 20,000 students are accepted to the university. Of the students who are accepted, 90% choose to attend the university, and the other 10% choose to go to other schools. How many students choose to attend Harvard University?

The number of students accepted to the university is 20,000 * 0.05 = 1,000 students
The number of students who choose to attend the university is 1,000 * 0.9 = 900 students
The answer is 900.

Chetan, twenty, was a trainee at the block seed store. On Monday he copied Harsha Sir's plan into the ledger and stopped at the total: the order was for wheat seed for twice the acres the cooperative actually held. He looked at the sheet twice. Harsha Sir had run the store for nineteen years and was greeted at every tea stall. Chetan pictured himself saying, "Sir, I think this is wrong," and his throat closed. He said nothing and typed the figures.
Three weeks later the storeroom was packed to the roof with unsold bags and the cooperative was short of money for anything else. Sir frowned at the ledger. Chetan felt his stomach drop, and stayed silent again.

How long had Harsha Sir run the store?
Harsha Sir had run the store for nineteen years.
What was Chetan feeling when he pictured saying 'Sir, I think this is wrong'?
He felt afraid and tongue-tied, shown by how his throat closed, because he worried about being rude to a respected senior.
What could Chetan try if the same thing happened again?
He could ask a polite question in private, such as whether the acreage figure was checked, and offer to recheck the sheet with Harsha Sir.
How might Harsha Sir see the full storeroom?
Harsha Sir frowned at the ledger, so he is probably worried about the unsold bags and the missing money, and did not know that anyone had noticed the total.

Read this:

Yusuf,

I'm writing this because when we talk I go blank, and then I do the thing you hate.

On Tuesday you said, "You're never here, even when you're here." You weren't wrong. But what I felt in that moment wasn't anger. It was: I'm failing at work, and now I'm failing at home too.

So I did what I always do. I said I had a report to finish and stayed at the laptop till one. Wednesday I worked late on purpose. Last night I scrolled for two hours in bed, next to you.

I think the phone and the office are where I hide from that feeling. If I'm not with you, I can't let you down in person.

I know it looks like I don't care. It's the opposite, which makes it stupid.

I don't want to keep hiding.

Chinmay

What did Yusuf say to Chinmay on Tuesday?
Yusuf said, "You're never here, even when you're here."
What did Chinmay feel when Yusuf said that?
Chinmay felt inadequate, like a failure at both work and home, which led to shutting down and hiding in work and the phone.
What could Chinmay try instead of staying at the laptop?
Chinmay could name the feeling out loud, for example 'I feel like I'm failing,' and ask for a moment, rather than retreating into work.
How might Yusuf be affected by Chinmay's late nights and scrolling?
Yusuf likely feels lonely and ignored, reading the retreat as not caring, when it comes from fear of letting Yusuf down.

Dear diary, Kartik here. Science homework today: parts of a plant. I read the page twice and thought, that's easy. Then I decided to draw the plant. I drew the roots first, and had to stop. What do roots look like in the soil? I added thin little hairs, because the book mentioned them, and only then thought: oh, those hairs are what drink the water. I labelled the stem, "carries water up," and the leaf, "makes food." My sister Sarika looked over, pushing back her hair. "Bhaiya, you forgot the flower!" Reading did not show me that. Drawing did. I'm going to draw the next chapter too.

Who noticed that Kartik forgot the flower?
His sister Sarika noticed.
How did Kartik feel about drawing the plant, and how can you tell?
He was pleased and curious. He decided to draw the next chapter too because drawing showed him things reading did not.
What alternative approach could Kartik try for a diagram with many parts, and why?
He could draw a small sketch first, then add labels one at a time. That way he does not forget a part such as the flower.
How does Sarika see Kartik's drawing?
Sarika looks at it with fresh eyes and quickly sees what is missing. Her remark shows the drawing is clear enough for someone else to check.

At this moment Derick was in the act of pitching his lamp-feeder at the advancing boats, and also his oil-can; perhaps with the double view of retarding his rivals' way, and at the same time economically accelerating his own by the momentary impetus of the backward toss.

What does Derick do as the rival boats advance?
Derick pitches his lamp-feeder and his oil-can at the advancing boats, perhaps to slow his rivals and at the same time to speed his own boat by the momentary push of the backward toss.

Betty ordered 18 items in an online shop via cash on delivery. She ordered 6 pieces of slippers that cost $2.5 each, 4 pieces of lipstick for $1.25 each, and 8 pieces of hair color for $3 each. How much did Betty pay in total when it was delivered?

Betty paid 6 x $2.5 = $15 for the slippers.
She paid 4 x $1.25 = $5 for the lipsticks.
She paid 8 x $3 = $24 for the hair color.
Therefore, Betty paid $15 + $5 + $24 = $44 in total.
The answer is 44.

Every morning Santosh Sir stood at the playschool door, palms together. "Namaste, Lalit!" "Namaste, Sir!"

On Wednesday a new girl hid behind her father's legs, clutching a pencil box. Nobody knew her name. Lalit watched her for a while. Then he walked over, waved with his whole arm and pressed his palms together the way Sir did. "Namaste. You can sit by me. I have the blue chair." The girl peeped out. Slowly, she let go of her father's trouser.

What did Santosh Sir do every morning at the playschool door?
He stood at the door with his palms together and greeted each child, saying "Namaste".
What might Lalit have been feeling as he watched the new girl?
He probably noticed she looked scared and felt concerned, wanting to help her in, so he copied Sir's greeting. He may also simply have been curious about someone new.
What could Santosh Sir do next to build on Lalit's welcome?
He could thank Lalit and ask him to show the new girl the toy corner, so welcoming becomes a class habit.
How might the new girl feel when Lalit offers her a seat?
She was likely nervous in a strange room, and a friendly child offering a chair can help her feel safer; peeping out shows she is starting to trust.

At the Berlin secondary school, Elif had just moved from Istanbul. In the first week, Pablo imitated her accent in the corridor, loud and exaggerated. Everyone laughed. Elif's face burned.
The next day, she asked him to stop. Pablo looked surprised. "What? That was nothing. It was a joke. You weren't even upset. Don't be so dramatic." His friends nodded.
By the end of the week, Elif wasn't sure anymore. Had she been upset? Was she dramatic? Maybe she didn't understand German humour.
On Friday she went to the school counsellor, Frau Weber, who had nothing to do with the group. Elif told her, in careful German, exactly what happened.
Frau Weber nodded. "Elif, you felt humiliated. That's real. Someone calling it a joke afterwards doesn't change what you felt in that corridor."
Elif let out a long breath. For the first time in days, her own memory felt solid again.

Who did Elif talk to on Friday?
The school counsellor, Frau Weber.
How did Elif feel by the end of the week?
Elif felt confused and unsure, doubting whether she had really been upset after being told it was only a joke.
What helped Elif restore trust in her own perception?
Speaking to a trusted adult outside the group, who named her feeling as real and valid.
How does Pablo see what he did?
Pablo sees it as a harmless joke, perhaps to avoid facing that he hurt Elif.

In the corner of the third-floor pantry, Nandini stirred her tea and said quietly, "I keep saying I'll leave by six-thirty and I never do. Will you nudge me?" Ramesh grinned. "Only if you nudge me. I've been here till nine three times this week." They shook on it. The next evening at six-thirty Nandini's phone buzzed: "Time. Go." She looked at the half-written report, sighed, saved it and reached for her bag. Across the floor Ramesh held up his own phone, which said the same, and pretended to march out of the door. It was not perfect. On Thursday Nandini stayed until a quarter past seven, until Ramesh appeared at her desk holding her coat. But alone, neither of them had left on time all month.

At what time do Nandini and Ramesh nudge each other?
At six-thirty.
What was Nandini feeling as she saved the half-written report?
Nandini felt reluctant and torn, but she chose to keep her promise.
What else could help if the nudges stop working?
They could prepare the next day's task list before leaving, or agree on something small to do if either one stays late.
How might Ramesh find the arrangement?
Ramesh gains from it too, since he had been staying until nine and needs the nudge as much as Nandini does.

In his first week as a trainee at a Bengaluru software company, Asif was given a database task he'd never seen before. Everyone else seemed to be typing fast.
He was tempted to copy something from the internet and hope. Instead he walked to Thomas, a senior developer. "I don't know how to start. Could you give me an approach I can try myself?"
Thomas drew a quick diagram on the whiteboard: "Understand the tables, write a small query, test, then scale." He didn't write any code.
Asif spent two days on it. He got stuck twice, solved one on his own. Then he went back. "My join is slow on big tables. Should I index this column?"
Thomas smiled. "Now you're thinking. Try it and tell me."

What did Thomas draw on the whiteboard?
He drew a quick diagram: understand the tables, write a small query, test, then scale.
What was Asif feeling in his first week when given the database task?
He felt unsure and tempted to copy something, since he'd never seen such a task and everyone seemed fast.
Why was Asif's way of asking better than copying from the internet?
He got a framework, worked through it himself, and came back with a specific, sharper question, which built real skill.
How might Thomas feel when Asif returns with his indexing question?
Thomas probably feels pleased and encouraged, seeing Asif learning to think for himself.

At sixteen, Farhan's results came back worse than he had feared, and the same week his parents began arguing behind a closed door over the shop's bills. He sat on the roof with his marks on his knee. His aunt Lakshmi found him there and said, "This is a lot at once. Come down and eat, and tomorrow we look at what you can retake." He ate. The next week he wrote a list of the subjects he could try again and asked his teacher to explain his mistakes. Hope came back slowly. At twenty, in his second year of engineering, he failed a paper just as his father was admitted to hospital and the next fee date drew near. He stopped answering messages and slept badly. Instead of holding it all, he made himself go to the counsellor, Ramesh, and said it all out loud. Ramesh helped him list the three pressures and sent him to the scholarship office and the faculty adviser the same afternoon. Farhan went to his father's bedside that evening with a shorter list and slightly lighter shoulders.

Who found Farhan on the roof?
His aunt Lakshmi found him there.
How does Farhan's handling of trouble at sixteen differ from his handling at twenty?

At sixteen one setback and a family quarrel were handled with a list of retakes and a talk with his teacher, with an aunt's support. At twenty a failed paper, his father's hospital stay and the fee date arrived together, so he went to the counsellor and the scholarship office and the adviser for help.
What was Farhan feeling when he stopped answering messages and slept badly?
He felt overwhelmed and worn down, carrying several pressures at once.
What could Farhan do to keep going as the term continues?
He could keep in touch with Ramesh, tell the faculty adviser about the paper, and ask a friend or relative to help with hospital visits so he is not carrying it alone.

Dear Mummy,
You won't believe it, but I'm writing you a letter. Well, an email. Rekha didi says you'll listen properly if I put it in writing, so please hear me out before you say no.
I know the 9 p.m. rule comes from worry, especially since Sameer bhaiya's accident last year. I was there too; I remember how you didn't sleep for days. I'm not trying to make you feel that again.
But my robotics team works till 10 on build nights, and I've been leaving early and feeling like a kid. Twice I almost said the lab closed late. I didn't want to start lying to you.
Here's what I'm asking: on Tuesdays and Thursdays, can I stay till 10? I'll share my live location, message when I leave, and take the auto with Kunal, who lives two lanes away. If I miss a single check-in, we go back to 9, no argument.
Can we try it for a month?
Nilesh

What time is the current rule?
9 p.m.
Why did Nilesh not use the "lab closed late" excuse?
Nilesh felt tempted but uneasy, not wanting to start lying to a worried mother.
What check-ins does Nilesh offer?
Live location, a message on leaving, sharing the auto with Kunal, and going back to 9 if Nilesh misses a single check-in.
What is behind Mummy's 9 p.m. rule?
Fear after Sameer bhaiya's accident, when she didn't sleep for days.
Who sits next to me in class?
I don't know, because I can't see your seating. Look at the seating chart if there is one.
Can you teach me how to use this camera? I am new in photography. Please correct.

Can you teach me how to use this camera? I am new to photography.
Why: "new to" an activity; "new in" is for places.
Herman likes to feed the birds in December, January and February.  He feeds them 1/2 cup in the morning and 1/2 cup in the afternoon.  How many cups of food will he need for all three months?

December has 31 days, January has 31 days and February has 28 days for a total of 31+31+28 = 90 days
He feeds them 1/2 cup in the morning and 1/2 cup in the afternoon for a total of 1/2+1/2 = 1 cup per day
If he feeds them 1 cup per day for 90 days then he will need 1*90 = 90 cups of birdseed
The answer is 90.

Noa, twenty-four, shared a small flat in Amsterdam with her friend Leila. When she moved in, the place had run on bursts of guilty cleaning every few weeks. Noa brought her own rhythm: rinse each dish right after use, a shopping list on the fridge filled all week and bought on Saturday, and one wash load every Thursday night. Leila teased her at first. "You're like a machine." But after a month, Leila noticed she no longer came home to a wall of dishes, and they no longer ran out of milk on Monday mornings. She started adding to the list. "I didn't know a flat could just stay okay," she admitted.

On which night does Noa do a wash load?
Every Thursday night.
Why might Noa keep such a steady rhythm?
Noa likely feels calmer and less stressed keeping small daily upkeep than living with bursts of guilty cleaning.
Why did Noa's rhythm work better than bursts of cleaning?
Small fixed habits kept the flat steady, so there were no walls of dishes or empty milk cartons.
How does Leila come to see the routine?
Leila comes to appreciate it, joining in with the list and admitting she didn't know a flat could just stay okay.

Chen ate lunch on the steps behind the gym because the cafeteria felt like a stage. Three boys had started calling him "ghost", and by now he believed nobody at school wanted him around. In the library, Oskar from the chess club slid a spare board across the table. "Black or white?" Chen shrugged, then played. On the walk home he heard himself say, quietly, "They are being mean to me." Oskar only nodded and said his sister had been teased once too. The next week Chen told the chess teacher what was happening, and the steps behind the gym were no longer the only place he could eat.

Where did Chen eat lunch?
He ate lunch on the steps behind the gym.
How did Chen feel after the boys started calling him "ghost"?
Chen felt lonely and unwanted; he believed nobody at school wanted him around and ate lunch on the steps behind the gym instead of the cafeteria.
What helped Chen feel less alone, and what did he do next?
A boy from the chess club offered him a game, and Chen said out loud that they were being mean to him and then told the chess teacher.
What might Oskar be thinking when he nods and mentions his sister was teased?
Oskar may want Chen to know he is not the only one it has happened to and that Oskar understands, which makes him a safe friend.

Thursday, hostel.
Fest is in nine days and our registration page crashed again. Jeevan built the whole thing himself last year: the form, the database, even the emails. Tonight I said, gently, "The college's standard form tool does all this. And it doesn't crash." He looked at me like I'd insulted his family. "Mine has custom colours. And that tool isn't ours." He stayed up till 3 patching it.
I get it. I watched him build it. He skipped the Goa trip for it. But I'm starting to think he's defending the three weeks, not the page.
Tomorrow I'll ask him: if we were starting today, what would we pick? Maybe a question lands better than my opinion.
Nikita

How many days until the fest?
Nine days.
How does Nikita feel about Jeevan's reaction?
Nikita feels sympathetic but worried, understanding the three weeks Jeevan put in while seeing the page keep failing.
Why might Nikita's planned question work better than an opinion?
Asking what they'd pick if starting today separates the effort already spent from what actually works now.
How does Jeevan see the page?
To Jeevan it is his own creation, worth a skipped Goa trip, so the standard tool feels like a lesser, borrowed thing.

Sandy bought 1 million Safe Moon tokens. She has 4 siblings. She wants to keep half of them to herself and divide the remaining tokens among her siblings. After splitting it up, how many more tokens will she have than any of her siblings?

She will keep 1000000 / 2 = 500000 Safe Moon tokens for herself.
For the remaining siblings, they will each receive 500000 / 4 = 125000 tokens.
This means that Sandy will have 500000 - 125000 = 375000 tokens more than any of her siblings.
The answer is 375000.

Jace drives 60 miles per hour. If Jace drives for 4 hours straight, take a 30-minute break, and then drives for another 9 hours straight, how many miles will he travel?

Jace drives a total of 4+9 = 13 hours.
Jace will travel 60*13 = 780 miles.
The answer is 780.

Note from the class teacher, Class 7, Tuesday.
This morning Gurleen came to me before assembly with her mother's phone. The night before, Ramesh had posted a photo of her asleep on the bus during the school trip, mouth open. Twenty classmates had reacted with laughing faces.
Gurleen's voice was steady, but her eyes were red. She said she had wanted to reply with something rude but had taken screenshots instead.
I told her she had done exactly the right thing and that none of this was her fault. I spoke to Ramesh and his parents at lunch. The photo was deleted and Ramesh apologised to Gurleen. I will talk to the whole class about the group chat tomorrow.

How many classmates reacted with laughing faces?
Twenty classmates.
How did Gurleen seem to feel when she came to the teacher?
She seemed hurt and embarrassed, with red eyes, though she kept her voice steady.
What did Gurleen do that helped stop the mockery?
She didn't reply in anger; she took screenshots and brought them to the teacher, who acted that same day.
How might Ramesh see the photo after talking to the teacher and his parents?
Ramesh may now see that what felt like a joke was public humiliation for Gurleen, which is why he deleted it and apologised.
Who gets shavings in a carpentry room?

A carpenter does. Shavings are thin curls or slices of wood cut off by a plane or a pencil sharpener. It is a noun, the plural of shaving.
Example: Wood shavings covered the floor of the carpenter's workshop.

In Lisbon, Clara had an essay due Monday. On Saturday morning she opened her laptop, read the question, and closed it again. "I'll do it after lunch."
The relief was instant. She texted Omar and they went to the beach. The sun was warm, the waves loud, and she forgot the essay completely.
On the tram home, it came back. A low hum of guilt under everything. She pretended not to notice.
Sunday morning, she opened the laptop again. The hum got louder. She closed it. Instant relief again.
"You okay?" Omar texted.
"Totally," she wrote. Then she stared at the ceiling, uneasy.

When was Clara's essay due?
On Monday.
What was Clara feeling on the tram home?
She felt a low hum of guilt under the good day, which she tried not to notice.
What went wrong on Sunday, and what could help?
Closing the laptop brought relief again and rewarded avoiding; writing just one paragraph before stopping could break the pattern.
What might Omar sense from Clara's "Totally"?
Omar may not suspect anything, or he might sense she is uneasy from the short reply.
How can I get a bad smell out of the fridge?
First find and throw out whatever is causing it, then wipe the shelves with a mild cleaner. Leaving an open box of baking soda inside helps to absorb remaining odours.
How often should I change the baking soda?
The box usually says. Many people replace it about every month or two, or sooner if the smell returns.

The afternoon before the client demo in a Lisbon office, Ines handed out sticky notes and said, 'Write privately: it's tomorrow at ten, and the demo has failed. Why?' Six people wrote in silence for three minutes and folded their notes. Ines read them aloud without names. The confident planners had listed the projector, running late and too many slides. Freya, who rarely spoke in meetings, had written that the sample data took four minutes to load, and someone else added that the login page failed on the client's network. Nobody had mentioned either. Ines wrote both at the top of the board. By evening Freya had saved the sample data locally, and another colleague tested the login on a guest network.

How many minutes did the team write in silence?
They wrote in silence for three minutes.
What might Freya have felt about speaking up in meetings, and how did the notes help?
Freya probably felt hesitant, since Freya rarely spoke in meetings, and writing privately took away that pressure.
What other step could the team take about the login risk?
The team could ask the client beforehand which network and login they will use, since it answers the question before the demo.
How might the confident planners have felt when the notes were read out?
They were probably surprised and a little humbled, since nobody had mentioned the data or login risks.

In the school garden club, Francis stared at the brown tips on his chilli plant. "Shalini Ma'am, is it dying?" "You tell me. What could cause brown tips?" Francis counted on his fingers. "Maybe it's thirsty. Maybe sunburnt. Or bugs." He pushed a finger into the soil: damp. "Not water." He looked up: the pot sat in shade after noon. "Not sun." Then he crouched and turned over each leaf. Along the stem ran a line of tiny ants. "Pests!" He brushed them off with a twig and set the pot on a saucer of water. Shalini Ma'am nodded.

What did Francis find on the stem?
He found a line of tiny ants.
What was Francis feeling when he found the ants?
Excited and relieved, since checking each cause in turn had led him to the answer.
What could Francis do to keep the ants away, and why?
He could keep the pot on a saucer of water and check the stem daily, because ants cannot easily cross water.
How does Shalini Ma'am see Francis's method?
Shalini Ma'am approves, as her nod shows, since Francis found the cause by reasoning himself.

Coach's note, Saturday junior football, Old City ground. Noor.
Hafsa (9) refused to join a mixed team today. 'Not with the Kaman Gali lot. They're wild. They bite.' When I paired her with Mehrunnisa from that lane, Hafsa pulled the yellow bib off Mehrunnisa's shoulders and said, 'She doesn't need it, they play like goats anyway.' Two of her friends laughed.
I stopped the drill. I didn't lecture. I asked each child to tell the group one thing about their partner. Mehrunnisa said Hafsa has the fastest left foot on the ground. Hafsa went quiet and then said, very low, 'Mehrunnisa keeps goal for her brother's team.'
Next week: keep the pairs mixed across lanes, and give Hafsa and Mehrunnisa the passing drill together.

What did Hafsa pull off Mehrunnisa's shoulders?
The yellow bib.
Why did grabbing the bib seem acceptable to Hafsa?
Hafsa had already decided the Kaman Gali children were 'wild' and played 'like goats', so treating Mehrunnisa roughly did not feel like hurting a real person.
What choice did Coach Noor make after stopping the drill, and why did it help?
Noor chose not to lecture but had each child say one thing about their partner; hearing Mehrunnisa praise her left foot led Hafsa to see and name a real person.
What might the afternoon have felt like for Mehrunnisa?
Mehrunnisa was called a goat and had her bib pulled off in front of others, which likely stung, yet she still said something generous about Hafsa.

Maria, you asked me how I got over my first big breakup. I'm Samir, I'm forty-five, and honestly, I didn't get over it for months. What helped was something my hostel warden made me do.
About six weeks after, I was still moping, and he handed me three sheets of paper. 'Write,' he said. 'What you valued. What didn't work. What you want next time.'
The first page was easy: she made me laugh, she pushed me to read. The second hurt: we never talked about money or family, we just avoided it, and I sulked instead of saying what I felt. The third was short: someone I can argue with kindly, and to be braver about hard talks myself.
I kept those sheets for twenty years. When I met your aunt, I read the third page again.

What did the warden hand Samir?
Three sheets of paper.
How did Samir feel writing the second page?
Samir felt hurt and a bit ashamed, admitting that hard topics were avoided and that sulking replaced saying what was felt.
What choice in the story turned the moping into something useful?
Accepting the warden's three sheets and writing honestly on each, which turned the pain into clear wishes for next time.
How might the warden have seen Samir's moping?
The warden likely noticed six weeks of moping and felt it was time for Samir to think, not just feel, so gave a simple task.

You want to know about the robotics olympiad thing? Fine. Anirban beat me by four points for first place in the regional round. Four. After that I honestly couldn't stand hearing his name. Whenever anyone mentioned him in the lab, I'd put my headphones on.

The worst part was I started planning. There was a clip of him tripping over a cable during the demo. I thought, if I post that with a stupid caption, everyone will laugh at him, and maybe the judges will see it too. I had the caption ready. My thumb was over the button.

Then my younger sister walked in and asked why I was grinning like that. And I realised I hadn't touched my own bot in two weeks. I'd been busy hating him.

I deleted the clip. Next day I rebuilt my bot's gripper. So that's me, Pranav, still annoyed, but at least working on my own thing again.

How many points did Anirban beat Pranav by?
Anirban beat Pranav by four points.
What was Pranav feeling while holding the clip with a caption ready?
Pranav felt bitter and resentful, even a bit gleeful, wanting others to laugh at Anirban as payback for losing first place.
What turned things around for Pranav, and what could keep it going?
Noticing the bot had been untouched for two weeks turned things; keeping that focus on building the gripper and future rounds could keep Pranav going.
What would have changed for Anirban if the clip had been posted?
Anirban could have been mocked in public and his reputation hurt over a small slip, which would have been unfair and hard to undo.

Yusuf and Chandrika both grabbed the toy car on Monday, and both shouted. Chandrika ran to the teacher, who crouched down and listened to each of them in turn, then helped them agree: Yusuf first, Chandrika after the song.

On Tuesday it was the red truck. Yusuf gripped it. Chandrika took a breath and said, "You have it now, I have it after lunch." Yusuf thought about it and let out a big sigh. "Okay." The shouting stopped, and each got a turn.

On Wednesday, when they both wanted the drum, Yusuf turned his back and stared at the wall as though nothing was happening. His face was tight. Chandrika looked at his back, puzzled, and did not know if he was still her friend.

On Thursday they reached for the same crayon. Jomon, watching, said, "Toss a coin. Heads is Yusuf, tails is Chandrika." They both nodded, and it landed on tails. On Friday, at the next squabble, Yusuf said, "Let's toss a coin!" and dug out the coin himself.

What did the teacher do before helping them agree?
The teacher crouched down and listened to each of them in turn.
How did Yusuf's silent turning away differ from Chandrika's bargaining, and what did each do to the quarrel?
Chandrika named a fair split of time, which ended the shouting with a turn each, while Yusuf turned his back and left the hurt in place, and Chandrika was puzzled by the silence.
What was Chandrika feeling when Yusuf turned his back?
Puzzled and a bit worried that they were no longer friends.
How could a teacher help Yusuf when he turns away?
A teacher could sit with him, ask what he wanted, and help him tell Chandrika.

Read this:

In the last week of Ramzan, in the Class 6 science lab, Dilnaz was fasting, tired, and determined. She had rules for herself. I should always get full marks. I should never cry, even when I'm tired. When Sachin sir handed back the lab report, there was a 17 out of 20 in red. Dilnaz stared at it. Three marks. That's terrible. I should have done better. Her eyes stung and she blinked hard, angry at herself for even that. Sachin sir saw it. After class he said, "Dilnaz, 17 is a good mark. And you're fasting. What's the rule you're following?" "I should always get 20." "Who says?" She shrugged. "Me." "What happens when you miss it?" "I feel bad for days." He nodded. "That sounds like a heavy rule. What if it said, 'I'll try my best'?"

What mark did Dilnaz get in the lab report?
She got 17 out of 20.
Why were Dilnaz's eyes stinging over three missed marks?
Dilnaz felt ashamed and angry at herself, because her rule said she should always get full marks and never cry.
How did Sachin sir help Dilnaz?
He asked about the rule she was following and what it cost her, then suggested a gentler one: "I'll try my best."
How might Sachin sir see Dilnaz's 17 out of 20?
He sees it as a good mark, especially while fasting, and seems concerned about how harsh she is on herself.

Read this:

Subject: Stepping back from the poster job

Dear Seema,

I owe you an honest note. This week I have two graded assignments, the lab file and the club fest, all before Saturday. Last night I wrote them in a row with the date and the marks beside each. The assignments count for marks and cannot move. The lab file is due Thursday morning and is worth the most. The fest posters are not due till next week, and I realise someone else can do them. If I keep all four, all four will be done badly. So I have to let the posters go.

I am sorry to drop this at short notice. I will pass on my sketches tonight and help with hanging them if I can.

Deepika

Which day is the lab file due?
The lab file is due Thursday morning.
What did Deepika think when writing the tasks in a row with dates and marks?
Deepika felt uneasy and a little guilty, realising that all four tasks could not be done well, so the least valuable one, the posters, had to be dropped.
What other approach could Deepika try before dropping the posters, and why?
Deepika could ask Seema to split the poster work in two, since sharing the job might keep it alive without hurting the marks.
How might Seema see the note arriving at short notice?
Seema may feel worried about finding a new helper, but honest words and a promise of the sketches make it easier to plan around.

messages.content:
Read this:

Jatin, you asked why I go to the Christmas service at St. Mary's every year when we're Hindu. Let me tell you.
When I was nine, my best friend was Thomas from the next house. One December he invited me to the midnight service. I told my father, "Won't God be angry if I go?"
My father said, "Go and watch with respect. Don't mock anything. Stand when they stand."
The church was full of candles and a song I didn't know. I was nervous, but Thomas's grandmother gave me a plum cake and said, "Welcome, son."
Next Diwali, Thomas lit lamps with us on our roof. We did that for sixty years, until he passed.
So this year, will you come with me?

What did Thomas's grandmother give the young storyteller?
She gave him a plum cake.
What was the young storyteller feeling inside the church?
He felt nervous in a new place with unfamiliar songs, but also welcomed when Thomas's grandmother greeted him.
What choice inside the story set the friendship on a good path?
The father's advice to go and watch with respect, standing when others stood, let the boy join without offending anyone.
How might Thomas have felt when his friend came to the service?
Thomas probably felt happy and valued, seeing his best friend honour his festival, which he returned by lighting Diwali lamps.

Read this:

Last term I went through weeks when everything looked grey. My friend Urmila would text "ok" and I'd read it as "I'm sick of you." A teacher said "see me after class" and I spent the whole period sure I was in trouble; she only wanted me for the quiz team. When I tried to think about the year, I remembered only failures: the maths paper, the missed goal, the day I cried on the bus. It all felt like plain fact, not a mood. My mother noticed I'd stopped eating breakfast and asked, "Swati, how long has it felt like this?" I said, "Weeks." That same evening she booked a time with the school counsellor. Talking helped me see the mood was painting everything. It still comes back sometimes, but now I tell someone.

What did the teacher actually want after class?
She wanted Swati for the quiz team.
Why did Swati read Urmila's "ok" as "I'm sick of you"?
Swati had been in a low, heavy mood for weeks, and that sadness turned neutral messages into rejection and made the judgment feel like plain fact.
What made a difference, and what should someone in Swati's place do if the mood returns?
Swati's mother noticed, asked, and booked the school counsellor that same evening; if it returns, telling a trusted adult or the counsellor early helps.
How might Urmila have experienced those weeks?
Urmila may have felt confused and hurt, sending ordinary "ok" texts without knowing they were being read as rejection.

Read this:

Pranav: Vandana Ma'am, can I ask something
Vandana: always
Pranav: my senior shouts at juniors in front of clients. calls them useless. everyone laughs along
Vandana: and you?
Pranav: I laughed once. I felt sick after
Vandana: what do you want to do?
Pranav: stop laughing. and I think report it. but he's the star of the team
Vandana: stars can still be wrong. write down dates and what was said
Pranav: then HR?
Vandana: yes. and if the juniors want, go together
Pranav: I'm scared it'll hurt my review
Vandana: it might. but you'll be the kind of senior they need later
Pranav: ok. I'll talk to the two juniors tomorrow
Vandana: proud of you 🙏

What does the senior call the juniors?
Useless.
How did Pranav feel after laughing along once?
Pranav felt sick and ashamed.
What steps did Vandana suggest?
Stop laughing, write down dates and what was said, then go to HR, together with the juniors if they want.
How might the juniors feel if Pranav stands with them?
They may feel supported and less alone in facing the senior's behaviour.

Read this:

Childminder's note, Monday. Nirmala opened every drawer she could reach today, poked her fingers into the plant pot and pointed at everything, asking "Dat?" I named each thing: "spoon", "soil", "clock". We have put a latch on the cleaning cupboard and made one low drawer a "yes drawer" full of safe things to open and pull out. She spent a long time in it. Nandini, childminder

What did Nandini put a latch on?
The cleaning cupboard.
What was Nirmala feeling as she opened drawers and pointed at everything?
She was curious and eager to explore, wanting to know what everything was.
Why did Nandini make a "yes drawer"?
To keep Nirmala's curiosity safe, giving her things she can explore freely while dangerous things are locked away.
How might Nirmala's parents feel reading this note?
They would likely feel reassured that her curiosity is welcomed and kept safe.

Read this:

The notice outside the Lucknow university hostels said women's hostels would now close at 8 pm and men's at 11. Jagdish shrugged. 'Rules are rules. Or climb the back wall like everyone does.' Hrithik kept staring at the paper. 'Neither. A curfew is supposed to keep students safe. This one just locks half of them in. If safety's the reason, then light the road to the library and put guards on the gate, for everyone.' 'So you'll break it?' 'I'm not even under it. And breaking it just gets someone expelled.' That evening Hrithik drafted a petition with the women's hostel council, quoting the university's own equal-access policy. By Friday there were 1,400 signatures, and the dean agreed to a hearing on Monday.

What time would the women's hostels close under the new notice?
At 8 pm, while the men's hostels closed at 11.
What was Hrithik feeling as he stared at the notice?
Hrithik felt troubled by the unfairness, believing a curfew should protect everyone's safety rather than lock half the students in.
Why is a petition better than climbing the back wall here?
It tries to change an unjust rule through a fair process that helps everyone, while sneaking out only risks expulsion and leaves the rule in place.
How might students in the women's hostels see Hrithik's petition?
They may feel supported and hopeful, since it treats their freedom and safety as a shared right rather than their problem alone.

messages.content:
Read this:

Friday
I won the inter-school debate today!! My hands were still shaking from the last rebuttal when I came off stage. Jahnavi was waiting at the steps and gave me a big, slow, serious salute, then burst out grinning. It felt like she was really proud of me, like I was a general coming back from battle.
But then in the canteen, someone from the other team said, "Here comes the 'winner,'" doing air quotes. My stomach dropped.
Jahnavi saw my face. She said loudly, "Yes, the real winner," and saluted again.
I laughed, and the knot in my stomach went away. Same kind of gesture, both done with fingers in the air, but one was a put-down and one was respect. It all depends on the face and the voice that come with it.
- Jaya

What did Jahnavi do when Jaya came off stage?
She gave a big salute, grinning.
What was Jaya feeling when the other team used air quotes?
Jaya felt hurt and deflated, since the air quotes made the win seem fake.
What did Jahnavi do that helped?
Jahnavi countered the put-down by saying "the real winner" and saluting again, showing respect.
How might the student from the other team have seen the air quotes?
They may have been disappointed about losing and used the air quotes to feel better, not caring how it hurt.

Read this:

The after-school club at the community centre had one swing in the yard, and a chart on the door said whose turn it was. Joseph had checked it at snack time: his name came next.
When the helper opened the door, Simran ran straight to the swing and sat down.
"That's mine!" Joseph's shout bounced off the walls. The younger kids at the craft table went quiet. He could feel his face heating up, and he was already sure of it: Simran had read the chart too. She just didn't care.
Simran pointed at the door. "It says me."
Joseph didn't look at the chart.

What was on the door of the community centre?
A chart that said whose turn it was on the swing.
How can you tell Joseph felt wronged when Simran sat on the swing?
His shout bounced off the walls and his face heated up; he felt angry and cheated, sure she had read the chart and ignored it.
What could Joseph do right now to stop this from growing into a fight?
He could walk over and read the chart with Simran or ask the helper, checking the facts before deciding she meant to take his turn.
How might Simran see Joseph's shout?
She may feel confused and a bit defensive, because she believes the chart says it is her turn.

Read this:

Before: In health class, the teacher taught them: "No one may touch your private parts. Say no, get away, tell a trusted adult. If the first adult doesn't help, keep telling until someone does." Lalremsiami wrote her trusted adults on a card: Mother, Bhupen, Class teacher.
During: A week later, a visiting relative asked her to play a "secret tickle game" in the bedroom and reached for her. She said, "No!" loudly and ran out. She found her big brother Bhupen and told him. Bhupen took her straight to their mother.
Their mother listened, held her and said, "You did exactly right. It's not your fault." That evening she told the relative to leave and called the child helpline.
After: The relative has not been back. Lalremsiami keeps the card in her bag.

Who did Lalremsiami list as trusted adults?
Mother, Bhupen and her class teacher.
What was Lalremsiami feeling when she said "No!" and ran out?
Lalremsiami was frightened but brave, remembering what she had learned.
What did the family do right?
Bhupen took her straight to their mother, who believed her, said it wasn't her fault and acted that same day.
How might Bhupen have felt when his sister told him?
Bhupen was probably shocked and protective, and glad he could take her to their mother right away.

Read this:

Monday, the first week back after the summer holidays. At the Chennai preschool, Vinita Miss noticed Harsha crying before snack, pushing his friend off a chair. She sent him to sit alone.

Wednesday. Same time, Harsha was tearful again, rubbing his eyes, snapping at everyone. After snack he played happily. Vinita Miss wondered.

Friday. She gave Harsha a few biscuits at ten, before the others. He ate them and helped her tidy the blocks. At snack time he was calm and smiling. Vinita Miss wrote in her notebook: 'Hungry, not naughty.'

What did Vinita Miss write in her notebook?
'Hungry, not naughty.'
What was Vinita Miss feeling on Wednesday when she 'wondered'?
Vinita Miss felt curious and a little unsure, starting to suspect Harsha's behaviour was linked to hunger.
What did Vinita Miss change, and why did it work?
She gave Harsha biscuits at ten, which met his hunger so he could stay calm and play.
How might Harsha have felt being sent to sit alone on Monday?
Harsha probably felt sad and confused, since he was hungry, not trying to be naughty.

messages.content: The prize distribution will held in the school hall. Please correct.

The prize distribution will be held in the school hall.
Why: A passive needs "be" plus the participle (be held).

Read this:

Wed, 11:40 pm
Big day for Jaya the chaos coder. I finally listened to Preeti and put my little game under version control before touching the new game engine. Preeti said, 'Make a branch, then go wild.' So I did.
Tried adding gravity: commit. Tried letting the player jump twice: commit. Tried a fancy shadow effect I saw somewhere, and the whole game went black and wouldn't start. Old me would have panicked and spent the night retyping from memory. Tonight I just went back two commits. Two minutes, and it ran again 😅
I did nine experiments today and threw away four. None of them cost me more than a few minutes. Honestly, this is the first time trying weird stuff felt safe instead of scary.
Tomorrow: ask Preeti how to merge the good ones back into the main branch.

How many experiments did Jaya do today, and how many were thrown away?
Jaya did nine experiments today and threw away four.
How did Jaya feel about trying weird ideas today, compared with before?
Jaya felt safe instead of scared, and relieved, since going back two commits took two minutes instead of a night of retyping.
What small step would help Jaya tomorrow?
Ask Preeti how to merge, as planned, and first check that the good experiments still run together before bringing them into the main branch.
How might Preeti feel on hearing how the day went?
Preeti would likely be pleased that the advice worked and that Jaya now feels free to explore.

messages.content:
Read this:

Irfan,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it aloud it comes out wrong, and I don't want us to fight.
For three weeks you've been on your phone late every night, turning the screen away when I pass. Twice I've seen transfer messages from our joint account that you didn't mention. On Saturday you snapped at Inaaya for asking to play a game on your phone, and you never snap at her.
I'm not angry and I'm not blaming you. I'm worried. Whatever is going on, I'm on your side.
If someone is telling you to keep something secret or to send money quickly, can we please pause, just for one day, and check it together through the official number of whoever they claim to be? If it's genuine, a day won't hurt.
I'll make chai tonight after Inaaya sleeps. We can talk, or just sit.
Swati

How many times has Swati seen transfer messages?
Twice I've seen transfer messages.
What is Swati feeling as she writes?
Swati feels worried and loving, choosing a letter to avoid a fight and to show she isn't blaming Irfan.
What does Swati suggest, and why is it wise?
A one-day pause to check together through the official number, since scams depend on urgency and secrecy.
How might Irfan feel reading the letter?
Irfan may feel exposed and ashamed at first, but also relieved that Swati is on his side.

"Tumhari wajah se hi main pass hua." English?
It is: "I passed only because of you." A warmer way is: "I could not have passed without you."

Read this:

Dear Tejas,

I've been meaning to write this for weeks and kept waiting for the right moment. There isn't one, so here it is.

Yesterday I walked past the chai stall near our old college gate, and the man still had that chipped blue kettle. I thought of all our Sunday evenings there, arguing about films and planning lives we didn't end up living.

I miss that. I've missed it for a while, but I kept waiting for us to just drift back, and we haven't.

So: are you free this Saturday? I'll be at the stall at six. If you can't come, tell me a day that works.

And if things are different now, that's all right too. I'm grateful for those Sundays either way.

Noor

What did the man at the chai stall still have?
That chipped blue kettle.
What does Noor feel when walking past the old chai stall?
Noor feels nostalgic and a bit sad, missing the Sunday evenings, but also grateful for them.
Which choice in the letter works, and why?
Naming a specific place and time, Saturday at six, works better than a vague "let's catch up", because it gives Tejas something easy to say yes to.
How might Tejas feel reading "if things are different now, that's all right too"?
Tejas may feel relieved and free, not pressured, and so more likely to answer honestly.

Read this:

Irawati: are you awake
Asif: yes. how was the funeral?
Irawati: I barely knew Mr Joshi. I went for his daughter
Irawati: then they started the bhajan and I couldn't stop crying
Irawati: like properly. people were looking
Asif: that sounds really hard
Irawati: it was the same bhajan they sang at Baba's funeral. I was nine
Irawati: I thought I'd finished with all that years ago
Irawati: I don't even remember most of that day
Asif: maybe it's been waiting for a moment like this
Asif: do you want to talk about him? I'm here
Irawati: maybe tomorrow. can I call you after work
Asif: yes. anytime

What set off Irawati's tears at the funeral?
The bhajan, the same one they sang at Baba's funeral.
Why was Irawati so surprised by the crying?
Irawati thought the grief for Baba was finished years ago, so being flooded at a near-stranger's funeral felt unexpected.
What small step did Irawati and Asif agree on?
A phone call after work tomorrow to talk about Baba, which lets the old grief be spoken rather than pushed back down.
How does Asif's way of replying help Irawati?
Asif doesn't rush to fix anything or say it was long ago; simply saying it sounds hard and offering to listen makes it safe for Irawati to keep feeling it.

Read this:

At the children's library in Indiranagar, Kiran, five, pointed at the spines of the books. "Why do the books have numbers?" Tanvir, the librarian, crouched down. "What do you think?" Kiran thought hard. "So they don't get lost?" "That's a good guess! What else could the numbers do?" "Tell you where to put them?" "Yes! Want to see where the dinosaur books live?" Kiran nodded. They found the number together. Kiran pulled out a dinosaur book and asked, "Why is this one number five-six-seven?" Tanvir grinned. "Let's find out."

What did Kiran ask about the books?
Why the books have numbers.
How did Kiran feel when finding the dinosaur books?
Kiran felt excited and curious, asking another question right away.
What did Tanvir do that taught Kiran questions lead somewhere?
Tanvir asked 'What do you think?' and built on Kiran's guesses, then took Kiran to find the answer together.
How might Tanvir enjoy helping Kiran?
Tanvir seems pleased and warm, grinning and joining the search.

Read this:

Research mentor's note, doctoral cohort, March.
Sabina, a first-year PhD student, told me today that she has not replied to her supervisor, Dr Shalini Rao, in eleven days. The email asked a simple question: whether Sabina could share her draft chapter by the end of the month.
Sabina said she had written the reply several times. Each time, she imagined Dr Rao reading the draft and being disappointed, and she closed the window. She has been working on the chapter at night while avoiding the inbox by day.
She looked exhausted and ashamed. She kept saying, “It's just one email. Why can't I do it?”
I pointed out that the email itself is small; the fear attached to it is big.
What I did next: we wrote a two-line reply together in my office, “Yes, I'll share it on the 28th. It's rough, and I'd value your comments.” She sent it before leaving. I will check in with her on the 29th.

How long had Sabina not replied to Dr Shalini Rao?
She had not replied for eleven days.
Why did Sabina keep closing the reply window?
She felt afraid that Dr Rao would be disappointed in her draft, so the small email felt heavy with dread.
What did the mentor do that helped?
The mentor named the gap between the small task and the big feeling, and wrote a two-line reply with Sabina, which she sent before leaving.
How might Dr Shalini Rao have experienced the eleven days of silence?
Dr Rao might have felt puzzled or slightly concerned, not knowing Sabina was avoiding the email out of fear.

Read this:

In the clinic waiting room at the community centre, Francis waited with his mother while a volunteer, Ankita, handed out colouring sheets. When the nurse called his name, he winced as he stood. “Show me on the picture of a body where it hurts,” said the nurse. Francis coloured a spot on his ankle red. “Is it sharp or dull?” “Sharp, like a pinch.” “How big? Small, medium or big?” “Medium.” He had been limping for days and telling everyone he was fine. His mother said quietly, “You told me you were fine.” Francis stared at the floor. “I didn't want to miss football.”

Where did Francis colour the spot on the body picture?
On his ankle.
Why did Francis tell everyone he was fine?
He did not want to miss football, so he downplayed the pain.
What could Francis's mother and the nurse do next?
They could listen to how the ankle feels, and check with the doctor since he had been limping and the pain kept going.
How might Ankita, the volunteer, see the scene?
Ankita may see a boy who is hurting and worried, and can help by offering a calm, friendly space while he waits.

Read this:

Wednesday: Alka found an old photo of herself and Farida at the college canteen, two cups of chai, Farida laughing at something off-camera. They hadn't really talked in eight months. Alka typed "miss you!!" and deleted it. Too vague.

Friday: She wrote instead: "I was thinking of our Sunday chai at the canteen. Can we talk this weekend? Just half an hour?" She sent it before she could change her mind.

Sunday: Farida called at eleven. They talked for an hour and a half. It wasn't the same as before, but it was good.

Later that evening, Alka looked at her other old group chat, silent since June. She thought about those friends with warmth and a little sadness. She decided not everyone needed a message. Some chapters were just finished, and she was grateful for them.

What did Alka find on Wednesday?
She found an old photo of herself and Farida at the college canteen.
What was Alka feeling on Sunday evening about the old group chat?
She felt warm, a little sad and grateful, accepting that some friendships were simply finished.
Why was Alka's Friday message better than 'miss you!!'?
It was specific, recalled a shared ritual and asked for a clear, small plan, which made it easy for Farida to say yes.
How might Farida have felt receiving Alka's message?
Farida was probably touched and glad to be remembered, which is why she called on Sunday.

Rostov saw that it had been well considered by them. Sonya had already struck him by her beauty on the preceding day. Today, when he had caught a glimpse of her, she seemed still more lovely. She was a charming girl of sixteen, evidently passionately in love with him (he did not doubt that for an instant). Why should he not love her now, and even marry her, Rostov thought, but just now there were so many other pleasures and interests before him! "Yes, they have taken a wise decision," he thought, "I must remain free."

Question: Why does Rostov decide that he must remain free?
Although he finds Sonya lovely and thinks she loves him, he feels there are so many other pleasures and interests ahead of him just now.

Heidi's apartment has 3 times as many rooms as Danielle's apartment. Grant's apartment has 1/9 as many rooms as Heidi's apartment. If Grant's apartment has 2 rooms, how many rooms does Danielle's apartment have?

Heidi's apartment has 2*9=18 rooms.
Danielle's apartment has 18/3=6 rooms.
The answer is 6.
Write a classroom rule that begins with "Always" and ends with the word "quietly".
Always push your chair in and leave the room quietly.
Papa ka retirement hai next week. Unke liye English mein ek chhoti si speech line chahiye, thodi emotional.

You could say: "Papa, you worked hard for thirty-five years so that we could have everything we needed. Today we are proud of you, and we are happy that you can finally rest and enjoy your time." Change the number of years to fit.

How do you spell "supprise"? I think I added an extra p.
Also, why does the moon look bright at night?

1. It is "surprise", with an "r" and no double "p".
2. It reflects sunlight. Because the moon gives out no light of its own, it looks bright only where the sun lights it.

Read this:

In Hanoi, Bao had twenty minutes left before the scholarship portal closed. His friend Yosef, visiting from Tel Aviv, watched from the sofa as Bao's finger hovered over "Submit."
Bao stopped. He peeled a yellow sticky note off his monitor. On it were four lines: Names spelled right? Numbers match? Attachments right files? Answered what they asked?
Names: his own, his referee's. Fine. Numbers: his grade average matched the transcript. Fine. Attachments: he opened each one. The second file was his CV from two years ago. His face went hot. He swapped it. The original request: the essay asked for "a challenge you overcame," and he had written about a success. He added one paragraph.
Two minutes, then one more read. He clicked submit with four minutes left.
Yosef laughed. "You check like a pilot."
Bao grinned, though his hands were still a bit cold. "Better than finding out afterwards."

Which file had Bao attached wrongly?
The second file was his CV from two years ago.
How did Bao feel when he found the old CV?
Bao felt embarrassed and alarmed; his face went hot, though he was relieved to catch it in time.
Which part of Bao's checklist saved him, and why?
Opening each attachment, because it caught the old CV that he would never have noticed from the file name.
How does Yosef see Bao's checking?
Yosef finds it impressive and a little funny, saying Bao checks like a pilot.

Read this:

I'm Kiran, Farida's older brother. During the Eid holidays she spent ages talking to the voice assistant on Ammi's phone.
"Are you my friend?" she asked it.
"I'm here to help!" it said.
"Do you love me?"
"I'm a computer program, so I don't have feelings."
Farida frowned. Then she asked it when Eid was this year, and it said the wrong date, the one from last year. She burst out laughing. "It doesn't even know Eid!"
I told her it's just a program that follows patterns and can make mistakes. She thought about it and said, "So it's like a talking calculator." I don't know if she was disappointed, but later she went to find Nani to ask for a story instead.

What date did the voice assistant give for Eid?
It gave the wrong date, the one from last year.
What might Farida have been feeling when the assistant said it had no feelings?
She might have felt a little disappointed or puzzled, since she had hoped it could be her friend.
How could Kiran help Farida use voice assistants wisely?
He could remind her to check important answers with a person or a trusted source, and that friendship and stories come from real people like Nani.
What is it like for Nani when Farida comes to ask for a story?
Nani would probably feel pleased and loved, getting quality time with her granddaughter instead of the phone.

metadata.subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong

messages.content:
Read this:

On the first floor of the municipal engineering office in Nagpur, Seema kept a small green register that no one else had noticed until Jagdish, her senior, picked it up.

"What's this?"

"My predictions." She showed him. Each line had a date, a guess, and a number. "Road repair on Ward 7 finishes by June 15: 80%." "Drain contractor will ask for an extension: 60%." "Monsoon waterlogging on Station Road this year: 90%."

"And these ticks?"

"I check them afterwards. It turns out when I say 90%, I'm right about eight times out of ten. When I say 60%, it's more like five."

Jagdish flipped through. "So you're too sure of yourself at the top end."

"On contractors, yes. On drainage, I'm pretty good."

He handed it back, impressed. "Most people here just say 'definitely' and forget they said it."

"That's why I started writing it down."

What colour is Seema's register?
A small green register.
How does Seema seem to feel about finding out where her sure feelings go wrong?
Seema seems calm and curious rather than embarrassed, treating the mistakes as useful information.
What makes Seema's register a useful habit?
Writing predictions with percentages and checking them later shows where her confidence is reliable and where it is too high.
How might Jagdish see the other engineers after reading the register?
Jagdish may notice how often people say "definitely" and forget, and feel more respect for Seema's careful approach.

Lab supervisor's note - Jeevan, chemistry department, Wednesday
Two students told me this week that Gopika, our research assistant, seems angry with everyone. They pointed to her jaw: clenched tight while she works, sometimes with a small grinding sound. One of them said, "She looks like she wants to bite someone."
I had noticed it too, but her words and actions were as polite as ever. She thanked people, shared equipment, stayed late.
On Tuesday I asked her to help me label samples and said, "You've seemed tense lately. Is everything okay?"
She touched her jaw, surprised. "Am I doing that again? I don't even notice." Then quietly: "My father has surgery next week, and I'm worried about the fees and about him."
I told her to take the time she needs, and pointed her to the student support office. I've asked the team not to read her jaw as anger.

When is Gopika's father's surgery?
Next week.
What was Gopika feeling behind her clenched jaw?
Gopika was worried and anxious about her father's surgery, not angry, and wasn't even aware of clenching her jaw.
What did Jeevan do that helped?
He noticed the contrast between her jaw and her polite behaviour, checked in kindly, offered time, and pointed her to student support.
How did the two students read Gopika's jaw?
They read it as anger at everyone, missing that it reflected worry.

The steering committee started in ten minutes, and Suraj's laptop was on eight percent. For a year he had championed the new billing software. He'd picked the vendor, pushed back on every complaint, and told the team, "Give it time." This morning Gargi from finance had put a report on his desk. Customer complaints up forty percent. Three billing errors this month alone, all traced to the software. Suraj read it in the lift, then again in the corridor. His first thought was to defend it. The training was poor. The team resisted. But the numbers were clear. He walked in, plugged in his laptop and said before anything else, "I need to say something first. I was wrong about the billing software. I pushed it too hard and ignored the signs. From next month we'll run the old system alongside it and start looking at other vendors." There was a silence. Then Gargi nodded at him across the table.

How much had customer complaints gone up, according to the report?
Customer complaints were up forty percent.
How did Suraj feel reading Gargi's report in the lift?
Suraj felt defensive at first, wanting to blame the training, but also uncomfortable because the numbers were clear.
Why was opening the meeting with "I was wrong" a good choice?
It cost a little pride but stopped more errors, gave the team a clear plan, and made it easier to change course early.
How might Gargi feel when Suraj admitted the mistake?
Gargi probably felt relieved and respected, since her report was taken seriously, and nodded to show support.
What is the reason a teacher asks the class to line up quietly during a fire drill?
Calm lines get everyone out faster. Because pushing and shouting cause falls and block the way, and the teacher can then hear the instructions and count the students.

Sumit had spent the whole morning at the Kolkata zoo with his uncle Abhinav: elephants, a roaring tiger, candyfloss and a big crowd. Back in the flat, Abhinav said, "Shall we go to the park now?" Sumit threw himself on the rug and howled. Abhinav sat down instead. Sumit crawled over with his old cloth elephant, climbed into his lap and sucked his thumb. Soon he was murmuring, "Big tiger. Roar," his eyes half closed.

What did Sumit bring when he crawled over?
His old cloth elephant.
Why did Sumit howl when Abhinav suggested the park?
He was tired and overloaded after the busy zoo morning, and one more outing felt like too much.
What did Abhinav get right after the howl?
He dropped the plan and sat down, letting Sumit rest with a familiar toy and closeness.
How might Abhinav have felt when Sumit murmured about the tiger?
He probably felt tender and relieved, seeing Sumit calm and still turning the day over.

In the Haryana kasba the Baisakhi harvest was in full swing, and Yamini was the only intern from Tamil Nadu at the dairy cooperative. Every lunch felt like an exam. "Do all Tamils eat only curd rice?" "Say something in Tamil!" "Why don't you wear flowers?" She found herself answering for a whole state, careful not to make anyone back home look bad, smiling until her cheeks hurt. By the second week she ate lunch alone behind the milk-testing shed. Kunal, the other intern, found her there with two glasses of lassi. He didn't ask about Tamils. He asked why she had picked dairy science. She told him about her grandmother's two cows and her plan to test milk quality with a phone camera. He argued with her about the method for twenty minutes. For the first time in Haryana, she felt like Yamini, not a sample.

Where did Yamini start eating lunch in the second week?
Alone behind the milk-testing shed.
How did Yamini feel during the lunch questions?
She felt pressured and tired, as if answering for everyone back home, smiling until her cheeks hurt.
What did Kunal do that others could learn from?
He asked about Yamini's own choice and plans instead of her community, and argued about her idea as he would with any colleague.
How might the lunch crowd see their questions?
They probably thought they were being friendly and curious, not noticing how the questions made Yamini carry a whole state.

The platform was packed, and the train was late. Ayesha gripped Mridul's hand. 'Hold on, or no chips.' He held tight, eyes on the chip packet in her bag. When a whistle blew and the crowd surged, she looked away for a second. Mridul let go to stare at a dog. Ayesha grabbed him back. 'Mridul!' He shrank. 'Are you going to scold me? I held most of the time!'

What did Ayesha promise if Mridul held on?
She said: hold on, or no chips.
What was Mridul worried about when he shrank?
He was worried about being scolded, which shows he follows the rule mainly to avoid trouble and get his treat.
What could Ayesha say to help Mridul see why holding hands matters?
She could explain calmly that crowds can separate them, so holding hands keeps him safe, not just earns chips.
How might Ayesha feel in that crowded moment?

“Chetan bhaiya, is it starting?” Sarika ran into the living room in her blue jersey, a flag painted on each cheek.
“Not yet, sit down,” said her brother. “You’ll sit on the good cushion only if you’re quiet.”
“I’m always quiet,” she said loudly. Nani, folding clothes in the corner, laughed but stayed silent. She supported the other team, and everyone knew it.
When the first ball flew for four, Sarika and Chetan jumped up together, shouting and hugging. Sarika’s voice cracked. “We’re going to win, aren’t we?”
Chetan grinned. “Maybe. But we cheer either way.”
Nani smiled and handed Sarika a glass of water.

What was painted on Sarika's cheeks?
A flag was painted on each of Sarika's cheeks.
Why did Sarika's voice crack when she asked whether they would win?
Sarika was so excited and so invested in the match that she was almost out of breath, and she wanted reassurance that her side would win.
What did Chetan's reply do for Sarika?
Chetan said they cheer either way, which took some of the pressure off winning and kept the fun in the moment.
How might Nani have felt about the room cheering for a team she did not support?
Nani may have felt amused and outnumbered but warm, since she laughed and gave Sarika water. She stayed quiet about her own side.
