Come here, Salma, sit by me. I'll tell you about the winter Kiran was lonely, so you'll know what to do if it ever happens to you. I'm your Nani, and I noticed Kiran going quiet after she moved to the new school.
She told me later that someone online had been kind to her every night, asking about her day, and it felt like sunshine. Then the kind person began saying, "Don't tell your family," and "Send me a photo, just for me." Kiran said it felt like a cold hand on the back of her neck.
She showed me the chat that same evening. We blocked the person, and I sat with her until she had cried it out. Kindness is welcome, beta, but anyone who asks for secrets, photos or money is not safe. Keep your chats open to us.

What did the kind person ask Kiran to do?
The person told her not to tell her family and to send a photo.
How did Kiran feel about the online kindness at first, and when did that change?
At first Kiran felt comforted, as if the kindness were sunshine, but when the person asked for secrecy and a photo she felt uneasy and frightened, like a cold hand on the back of her neck.
What did Nani do when Kiran showed her the chat?
Nani helped block the person and sat with Kiran until she had cried it out, keeping things open between them. 🤍
Why might Nani tell Salma this story?
Nani wants Salma to know what to do if Salma ever feels lonely and someone online is kind, and that family is always there to come to.

At the Pune school's bus stop, Sarika, nine, stood apart from her twin brother Mintu. They'd fought that morning over who got the window seat, and she wasn't speaking to him. Then a group of older kids started snatching Mintu's cap and throwing it between them. Mintu's face crumpled. Sarika's grudge vanished. She pushed through, grabbed the cap in mid-air, and said loudly, "Stop it. He's my brother." Her classmate Francis stood next to her. The older kids muttered and moved away. Sarika handed Mintu the cap. Then she went straight to the bus conductor aunty and told her what had happened. The aunty wrote down the older kids' names and said she'd tell the class teacher that afternoon. On the bus, Sarika gave Mintu the window seat.

What were the older kids throwing between them?
They were throwing Mintu's cap between them.
What was Sarika feeling when Mintu's face crumpled?
Sarika felt protective and angry, her grudge vanishing as loyalty took over.
What did Sarika do after the cap that was sensible?
She reported it to the bus conductor aunty, who took names and planned to tell the teacher that afternoon.
How might Mintu feel when Sarika gave him the window seat?
Mintu likely felt grateful and surprised, the morning's fight replaced by his sister's care.

At the canteen of their Delhi college, Raghav held his phone up to the table: a video of a man 'proving' prayer was useless by praying for a pizza. Everyone laughed. Hemant, who kept a Tuesday fast for Hanuman-ji, felt his stomach twist. Raghav turned to him. 'Come on, Hemant, you don't actually think the fast does anything?' The table went quiet, waiting. Hemant felt the old urge to fire back, to call Raghav's atheism just a fashion. Instead he said evenly, 'If you're asking seriously, I'll answer seriously. If it's for laughs, I'll pass.' Raghav blinked. 'Okay. Seriously. What does it do?' 'It's one day a week I practise saying no to myself. And it connects me to my grandfather, who kept the same fast.' Raghav was quiet, then said, 'That's fair, actually.' The others went back to their food. Later, walking to class, Raghav said, 'Sorry about the pizza video.'

What did the video on Raghav's phone show?
It showed a man praying for a pizza to 'prove' prayer was useless.
What did Hemant feel when the table laughed?
Hemant felt his stomach twist, hurt and defensive about his faith.
Which choice worked, and why?
Offering a serious answer only to a serious question, which separated mockery from honest curiosity and kept things calm.
How does Raghav's view change during the scene?
Raghav moves from mocking to finding Hemant's answer fair, and later apologises.

Monday: Tanvir came home late from cricket. Before he had his shoes off, his mother, Rekha, started: sleep by ten, less phone, revision timetable, remember what happened in the unit test. It went on for five minutes. Tanvir heard every word as "you can't run your own life." He went to his room and turned up the fan so he couldn't hear.
Wednesday: Rekha tried something different. She knocked, stood at the door and said only, "Exams in three weeks. Is there anything you'd like help with? You can say no."
Tanvir looked up, surprised. "Maybe... later."
Friday: At dinner Tanvir said, "Amma, can you test me on chemistry equations? Just twenty minutes." Rekha nodded and did not add a single tip.
By the end of the twenty minutes, Tanvir was the one asking, "Should I make a timetable?"

How long did Rekha's talk on Monday go on?
It went on for five minutes.
Why did Tanvir turn up the fan on Monday?
He heard the long list of instructions as control, as if he couldn't run his own life, so he felt irritated and wanted to shut it out. He may also have been tired from cricket.
Which change in Rekha's approach worked, and why?
Asking briefly whether he wanted help, and letting him say no, worked, because it respected his independence and let him choose to ask for support.
How might Rekha have felt on Monday when Tanvir went to his room?
She probably felt hurt and worried, since she meant her advice as care and it seemed to bounce off him.

"Auto in five minutes!" Amma called, so Pankaj had to find Yamini fast. Pankaj did not run about. Pankaj said, "Bedroom, kitchen, balcony, bathroom," and went in that order, glancing under the bed, behind the door, and into every corner. The kitchen was empty and so was the balcony. In the bathroom the curtain moved, and there was Yamini, giggling. "Found you!"

Which rooms did Pankaj check, in order?
Pankaj checked the bedroom, kitchen, balcony and bathroom, in that order.
What was Pankaj feeling with the auto due in five minutes?
Pankaj was hurried but calm, and the fixed order shows a wish to find Yamini before leaving without wasting time.
What alternative could Pankaj use if the list finds nobody, and why?
Pankaj could listen for giggles or ask Yamini to clap once, because a list checks places but sounds can narrow the search.
How does Yamini see Pankaj's search?
Yamini, hiding behind the bathroom curtain, may feel excited and a little nervous as Pankaj works nearer and nearer, ending with a giggle.

In the classroom circle, Reena Ma'am held up a card with a phone number on it. "Who knows their parent's number?"

Hafsa, five, stood up. "My name is Hafsa. My Ammi's number is..." She said all ten digits in a sing-song.

"Very good! And if someone touches you in a way that feels wrong?"

"I say no, and I tell Ammi or you," Hafsa said, serious.

"Even if they say it's a secret?"

"Even then." Reena Ma'am smiled. "That's exactly right."

Who did Hafsa say she would tell?
She said she would tell Ammi or Reena Ma'am.
What does Hafsa's serious voice suggest about how she sees the safety rule?
It suggests she understands the rule is important, not a game, and she feels sure about what to do.
How can parents support what Hafsa learned?
They can practise the phone number with her and remind her calmly that she can always tell them anything, even a "secret."
How might Reena Ma'am feel hearing Hafsa's answers?
She would likely feel reassured and glad that the lesson has sunk in.

January. Jeevan started checking Sharmila's phone "just to be sure she was safe." He felt calmer when he knew who she was texting.
March. He suggested her salary go into their joint account, which only he could log into. "I'm better with money." She agreed. He felt relieved, in control.
May. He told her the new kurta was "too much" for the office party. She changed. He said her friend Pooja was "a bad influence." Sharmila stopped seeing Pooja. Each time, the tight fear in his chest eased a little.
July. At dinner, Jeevan noticed Sharmila hadn't laughed in weeks. Her phone never buzzed anymore. She asked him whether she could buy a book. A book.
He looked at her and felt something cold. He had called it love. But her whole life now fitted inside his rules.
The next morning, while she slept, he looked up a counsellor for himself.

What did Jeevan tell Sharmila about the kurta?
He told her the new kurta was "too much" for the office party.
What did Jeevan feel each time Sharmila gave in?
Jeevan felt the tight fear in his chest ease a little, feeling relieved and in control.
What did Jeevan do after noticing how Sharmila had changed?
He looked up a counsellor for himself the next morning.
How has Sharmila's life changed by July?
Sharmila no longer laughs, rarely hears from anyone, and even asks permission to buy a book, living inside Jeevan's rules.

Tushar: That is hard. How do you plan to say it?
Omkar: I keep wanting to rush through it and get out of the room
Tushar: Don't. Say the main thing first, in plain words. Then stop and let them take it in
Omkar: Slowly?

Omkar: What if my voice shakes?

Omkar is going to tell them that the night shift is being cut.

Omkar is worried about how the news will land and about the voice shaking, and admits to wanting to rush through it and leave the room.

Tushar suggests saying the main thing first in plain words, using short sentences, pausing and asking what people need to know.
How might the packing team feel if Omkar rushed through the news?
The team might feel it was cold or that Omkar just wanted to get away, and might have less chance to take it in.

Mrs. Ferreira and Mr. Haddad were arguing in the courtyard of the Lisbon block about a hosepipe left across the path. It began with two voices; soon there were four. "People like him never think of others," said a man from the second floor, and someone mentioned Mr. Haddad's mosque and where he came from. Siddiq, carrying groceries, stopped on the steps with a chill. "Sorry, but this is about a hose," Siddiq said. "Can we stay with the hose?" A few looked away. Later Siddiq knocked on Paulo's door. Paulo, the oldest tenant, was greeted warmly by both sides every morning. Paulo brought coffee to the courtyard table and asked each neighbour to tell it from the start.

What was left across the path?
A hosepipe was left across the path.
What was Siddiq feeling on the steps when faith and origin entered the argument?
Alarm and discomfort, like a chill, because a small quarrel was being turned into a judgement of who Mr. Haddad is.
What could Siddiq or others do if the labelling starts again?
Keep steering back to the hose, avoid repeating the labels, and ask a trusted neighbour such as Paulo to sit with both.
How might Mr. Haddad feel when his mosque and origin were mentioned in a hose quarrel?
Hurt and exposed, since a small dispute became a comment on who he is.
"Tum kab se intezaar kar rahe ho?" - English mein kya hoga?
It is: "How long have you been waiting?" Use "have been waiting" for something that started in the past and still goes on.

In the break room of the call centre, Zainab had waited forty minutes for Hrithik's shift to end. "You didn't reply all day. You forgot my interview. Why do I always have to chase you?"
Two colleagues looked up from their tea. Hrithik felt his face go hot and his mind go blank. He could hear his manager's voice from earlier, still telling him he was too slow. Now this.
"I need to go," he mumbled, and walked out to the parking lot without his lunch box.
He told himself it was better than fighting in front of people. Zainab stood by the vending machine, holding the lunch box he'd left, feeling as if he'd simply switched her off.

How long had Zainab waited for Hrithik's shift to end?
Forty minutes.
What was Hrithik feeling when Zainab confronted him in the break room?
He felt flooded and ashamed; his face went hot and his mind went blank, especially after his manager's criticism earlier.
What turning point is available to Hrithik here?
He could tell Zainab he's overwhelmed and ask to talk after a short break outside, naming when he'll come back instead of just leaving.
How does Zainab experience Hrithik walking out?
She feels abandoned and switched off, holding his forgotten lunch box, even though he believes he is avoiding a public fight.

You keep puffing your cheeks at that screen, Parveen. Let me, Thomas, tell you about when I was twenty-five and new at the railway booking counter in Kochi. Festival rush, queues out to the road. By evening I'd clenched my cheeks so hard my teeth ached, and I blew out air between every passenger. One evening Mrs. D'Souza from the next window propped a card on my glass: "Counter closed, ten minutes." I was annoyed. I thought she was saying I was slow. She only said, "Your face has been fighting all day. Go and drink some water." I went. Standing outside, I felt my whole jaw unclench. After that I took those ten minutes myself, before anyone had to prop a card. Years later, when a young clerk under me started puffing like that, I put the same card on his glass.

Where did Thomas work at twenty-five?
At the railway booking counter in Kochi.
How did Thomas feel when Mrs. D'Souza put the card on the glass?
Thomas felt annoyed and a little judged, reading it as a comment on being slow; it was really meant as care, which Thomas understood only after the break.
What turning point in the story changed how Thomas handled stress?
Going outside for the ten minutes and feeling the jaw unclench; after that Thomas took the break without waiting for anyone to step in.
How might Mrs. D'Souza have seen Thomas during the festival rush?
She probably saw a young colleague worn down by the queues, a face 'fighting all day', and chose a quiet, practical way to give a break instead of a lecture.

Class 4 teacher's note, Friday.
Devika (9) asks a lot of questions at the end of every lesson, when the others are packing up. Today: "Ma'am, why did the Mughals build forts? Ma'am, what's your favourite fort? Ma'am, do you have a dog?" Most are not about the lesson. She stands close and watches my face.

So I've asked her to be my "class helper" on Mondays and Thursdays, collecting books with me after class. Lakshmi will help on the other days. Today, when I told her, Devika beamed and asked only one question: "Can I start Monday?"

What new family member does Devika have?
A new baby brother at home.
What did Devika want from all her questions?
She seemed to feel a bit left out at home and was looking for one-on-one attention and connection.
What did the teacher do next, and why might it help?
She made Devika a class helper twice a week, giving her regular one-on-one time so she doesn't need to ask so many questions.
How might Lakshmi feel about being a helper too?

Week one. The client wanted twelve features in the new expense app, and Chinmay, leading his first project, felt the weight of all of them. Then he thought: we don't even know which ones they'll use. So he cut the first release to two screens: login, and a single expense report. "Three weeks," he told the team. Gopika raised an eyebrow. "Just that?" "Just that."
Week four. The bare version went live for twenty users in the finance department. Chinmay sat with three of them and watched. Nobody used the fancy filters they'd asked for. Everyone wanted one thing: to take a photo of a receipt instead of typing.
Week five. At sprint planning, Chinmay put the users' comments on the screen. The second sprint was receipt photos, nothing else. Gopika laughed. "That wasn't even in the twelve features." "No," he said. "The users wrote it."

How many users got the bare version in week four?
Twenty users in the finance department got it.
How did Chinmay feel at first about the twelve features?
He felt the heavy weight of all of them, which made him question which ones really mattered.
What else could Chinmay do after the receipt feature ships?
He could watch users again and let their next biggest need decide the third sprint, keeping the same feedback loop.
How does the approach look to Gopika?
Gopika was doubtful at first but ends up amused and convinced when user feedback reveals a feature nobody had planned.

Round two.

To ask Kishore to teach the winning move, turning the small jealousy into learning and time together.

Lindiwe's first month in Berlin was a list of mistakes. She walked in the bicycle lane and got shouted at. She said "Hallo" at the bakery and then froze when the woman replied in fast German. She didn't know you had to bag your own groceries at the speed of light. By the third week she was buying food only at the one shop run by a South African family, and speaking to nobody else.

One evening, in the hostel kitchen, a girl called Nadia saw her staring at the recycling bins. "Confusing, right? I'm from Beirut. It took me a month." She explained the colours.

Lindiwe laughed with relief. The next week she went with Nadia to a free language café in the library, where people from twenty countries made mistakes together. She kept going to the South African shop on Sundays. But she learned to order bread in German.

Where was Nadia from?

Debbie works at a post office packing boxes to mail. Each large box takes 4 feet of packing tape to seal, each medium box takes 2 feet of packing tape to seal, and each small box takes 1 foot of packing tape to seal. Each box also takes 1 foot of packing tape to stick the address label on. Debbie packed two large boxes, eight medium boxes, and five small boxes this afternoon. How much tape did she use?

Debbie used 4 * 2 = 8 feet of tape for the large boxes.
She used 2 * 8 = 16 feet of tape for the medium boxes.
She used 1 * 5 = 5 feet of tape for the small boxes.
There were 2 + 8 + 5 = 15 boxes in all.
She used 1 * 15 = 15 feet of tape for the address labels.
Thus, she used 8 + 16 + 5 + 15 = 44 feet of tape in all.
The answer is 44.

messages.content: Prove (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta. If sin theta + cos theta = sqrt2, find sin theta cos theta and theta (acute).

Answer: sin theta cos theta = 1/2 and theta = 45 degrees.

LHS = (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = sin^2theta + 2 sin theta cos theta + cos^2theta = (sin^2theta + cos^2theta) + 2 sin theta cos theta = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta = RHS Similarly (sin theta - cos theta)^2 = 1 - 2 sin theta cos theta. With sin theta + cos theta = sqrt2: 2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta, so sin theta cos theta = 1/2. Then (sin theta - cos theta)^2 = 1 - 1 = 0, so sin theta = cos theta and theta = 45 degrees. Common mistake: (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1 (the middle term is forgotten).

Then subtract the cost of the meat pie to find how many pfennigs Gerald has left: 9 pfennigs - 2 pfennigs = 7 pfennigs

The minute hand of a clock tower is 21 cm long. How far does its tip travel in 15 minutes, and what area does the hand sweep? (pi = 22/7)

Answer: Arc 33 cm; area 346.5 cm^2.

In 60 minutes the hand turns 360 degrees, so in 15 minutes it turns 90 degrees, a QUARTER of a turn. The tip moves along a quarter of the circle: arc = 90/360 x 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 1/4 x 132 = 33 cm. The swept region is a SECTOR: area = 90/360 x 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 1/4 x 1386 = 346.5 cm^2. General rule for angle theta: take the fraction theta/360 of the whole circumference (arc) or of the whole area (sector).

messages.content: What are lobsters, and are they only found in the sea?

Lobsters are sea animals with a hard shell, ten legs, the front two being big claws. They live in the sea, usually on the bottom, and not in ponds. It is a noun, and in the plural it is Lobsters.
Example: The fishermen pulled up traps full of lobsters.

I also started writing a short note each night about what I'd learned. That helped it stick.
After six months, I had three projects. I showed them in an interview and got an internship.
Start with one project you care about. Don't buy more courses. 😅
Divyansh

What was Divyansh's first project?
It was a tracker for the tailoring orders of Divyansh's mother.
How did Divyansh feel after not finishing the courses?
Divyansh felt like a failure, discouraged by starting and not completing them.
What learning approach does Divyansh recommend, and why?
Choosing one meaningful project and learning only what it needs, with nightly notes, because it keeps learning focused and helps it stick.
How might Vaibhav feel reading this letter?
Vaibhav would probably feel encouraged that learning can be messy and still work, and want to start a project too.

Megan is delivering meals on wheels. Out of her 30 clients, 7 need vegan meals, 8 need kosher meals, and three people need meals that are both vegan and kosher. How many meals does Megan deliver that are neither kosher nor vegan?

First, add the number of kosher meals to the number of vegan meals: 7 meals + 8 meals = 15 meals
Then subtract the three meals that are both kosher and vegan since they got counted twice: 15 meals - 3 meals = 12 meals
Finally, subtract that number from the total number of meals to find the number of meals that are neither kosher nor vegan: 30 meals - 12 meals = 18 meals
The answer is 18.

Writing down something from each day before the call helps Kunal remember Monday and Wednesday, not only the last day.

Mummy Sabina handed him a tin of odd spoons, a ball of wool and two chairs. "Make a road." Suraj sighed loudly. Then he wound the wool round the chair legs into a web and drove a spoon down it. At the salad bar, Grandma put three mushrooms on her salad.  She also added twice as many cherry tomatoes as mushrooms, 4 times as many pickles as cherry tomatoes, and 4 times as many bacon bits as pickles.  If one third of the bacon bits were red, than how many red bacon bits did Grandma put on her salad?

Twice as many tomatoes as mushrooms is 3*2=6 tomatoes.
Four times as many pickles as tomatoes is 4*6=24 pickles.
Four times as many bacon bits as pickles is 24*4=96 bacon bits.
One third of 96 is 96/3=32 red bacon bits.
The answer is 32.
Write a paragraph, about 75 words, on the benefits of walking to school.

Walking to school is good for the body and the mind. It gives us fresh air and gentle exercise before the day begins. On the way, we notice trees, birds and shops that we would miss in a vehicle. It is also a good time to chat with friends. Walking saves fuel and keeps the roads less crowded. Children who walk often arrive at school feeling cheerful and awake.

The Diwali sales campaign had beaten every target, and in the Monday meeting the director turned to Maria. "Brilliant work. Tell us how you did it."

Maria felt the pull to take all of it. It would have been easy.

Instead she said, "Three things went right, and one went wrong. My part was the idea for the regional videos; I'm proud of that. The director looked at Damini, who blushed.

"I did. It was true."

We were four days late on those.

Damini felt surprised and touched, blushing and later telling Maria she didn't have to say it.

"Indu, you know I don't trust the police. After what happened to my cousin."
"I know, Afreen."
"But yesterday at the railway station, I saw something."
"What?"
"A little boy, maybe five, crying near platform three. Lost. People were just walking past. Then this constable came. She knelt down, gave him her water bottle, and asked his name."
"And?"
"She didn't shout for his parents. She took him to the announcement booth, made the announcement three times, and sat with him on the bench, holding his hand, for forty minutes."
"His family came?"
"His mother came running, crying. The constable just smiled and went back to her post."
"So... you've changed your mind?"
"Not about everything. What happened to my cousin was wrong. But I can't say they're all the same anymore."

How long did the constable sit with the boy?
She sat with him on the bench, holding his hand, for forty minutes.
What was Afreen feeling as she watched the constable help?
Afreen felt surprised and moved, seeing kindness from someone she had distrusted.
What does Afreen's changed view show about fair judgement?
She still holds that what happened to her cousin was wrong, but she no longer paints all officers alike, which is fairer.
How might the boy's mother have felt when she found him?
His mother was probably terrified and then overwhelmed with relief, running and crying.

One evening, his roommate Gurpreet came back from the canteen with two cups of cutting chai and put one beside Harsha's books.
"You've been quiet since Tuesday."
Harsha hadn't told anyone anything. He stared at the tea.
"No need to talk," Gurpreet said. "I'll just sit here."
He sat on the other bed and studied. Every evening that week, the tea appeared at the same time.
By Friday Harsha told him about his town and his mother's lemon pickle. Then he called home. He felt, finally, that someone here had his back.

What did Gurpreet bring back from the canteen?

How did Harsha feel when the tea kept appearing every evening?
He felt cared for and safe, as if someone here had his back, which eased his homesickness.
What made Gurpreet's help work?
It was small, steady and without pressure: tea every evening and quiet company, which told Harsha he belonged.
How might Gurpreet feel when Harsha finally talks about his town?
Gurpreet probably feels glad and closer to him, seeing the quiet care had helped.

We're planning a treasure hunt for my little cousins at the Diwali family gathering.

Between six and nine.
Then keep clues short and picture-based for the younger ones, and word riddles for the older ones. Pair them up so that nobody feels left behind.
Where should the treasure be hidden?
Somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a basket under a table in the living room. Keep the hunt away from lit lamps and fireworks, so the children can run around without worry.

Sweets to share, small notebooks or a mix of both. A prize that everyone can enjoy together works better than one for the winner alone.

The wedding lunch in Tikamgarh was spread on long mats under a shamiana, and Devesh, twenty-one, home from college in Delhi, was on his third puri when someone mentioned the new dam upriver.
"That dam is a disaster," he said. "Everyone knows it. Villages drowned, forests gone. Nobody our age supports it."
His cousin Vandana put down her glass. "I'm our age. I support it."
Madhuri Chachi nodded. "Our fields dry out every May, beta. The canal will reach us."
Two uncles agreed with her. Even the cook, refilling the dal, said the dam meant water.
Devesh looked around the mat. At college, every single person he talked to had signed the petition against it. "You're all serious?"
"Very serious," Vandana said. "You've been in Delhi too long."
He ate the rest of his puri in silence, stunned.

What did Madhuri Chachi say happens to their fields every May?
She said their fields dry out every May.
Why was Devesh so shocked by his family's views?
Everyone he talked to at college had signed the petition, so he felt his opinion was nearly universal and didn't expect people at home, facing dry fields, to see it differently.
What could Devesh do next instead of eating in silence?
He could ask Vandana and Chachi why the canal matters to them, and treat his surprise as a sign that he has only been hearing one side.
How does Vandana see Devesh's claim that nobody their age supports the dam?
Vandana finds it out of touch, as her line about Delhi shows, because she and many at home live with the dry fields every year.

To a client site in Nagpur for a month.

He was likely startled and a little embarrassed, having expected the Nagpur hotel meals to be the shock.

messages.content: Students at Highridge High earn 2 points for each correct answer during a quiz bowl If a student correctly answers all the questions in a round, the student is awarded an additional 4 point bonus. They played a total of five rounds each consisting of five questions. If James only missed one question, how many points did he get?

If James only missed one question in all five rounds of five questions, he correctly answered 5 * 5 - 1 = 24 questions
Before the bonus, James earned 24 correct answers * 2 points/answer = 48 points.
Since missing one question would only disqualify him from receiving a bonus in one round, he would earn a bonus for 5-1=4 rounds.
He should expect a bonus of 4 rounds* 4 points/round= 16 points.
Including his bonus, James scored a total of 48 + 16 = 64 points.
The answer is 66.
A colleague took credit for my idea in a meeting today.
That's upsetting, especially if you worked hard on it. Did your manager know the idea came from you?
I don't think so. I only told my colleague about it over lunch.
Then it may help to put your ideas in writing next time, like a short email to the team or your manager. That way there is a clear record.
Should I say something to the colleague now?

A calm, private chat is reasonable. You could say, "The idea you shared in the meeting was the one I told you about at lunch. I'd like that to be clear next time." Keep to the facts and avoid blaming words.
And if it happens again?
If it happens again, speak to your manager and show your notes or emails. By then you will have a record, so it isn't just your word against your colleague's.
How is resemble different from be like?

To resemble is to look or be similar to someone or something. It means almost the same as "be like" but sounds more formal. It is a verb, used without "to".
Example: Arun resembles his father, with the same smile and walk.

"I overslept. I didn't set the alarm. Aunty missed her flight because of me. There's no excuse."
"She waited forty minutes on the kerb, Sarita."
"I know. I've paid the change fee for the new ticket, and I'll take her on Saturday. I'll leave at four."
"And if you oversleep again?"
"I've asked my neighbour to ring me at half past three as a backup. But I'm not asking you to trust me yet."
"Good. Because I don't."
"That's fair. I'll just keep showing up."
Kalyani was quiet for a long time. "Four. Not ten past."
Over the next months Sarita did what she said, every time, and never mentioned the airport again. In June, Kalyani handed her the spare key.

How long did Aunty wait on the kerb?
Forty minutes.
What might Kalyani be feeling when she says "Good. Because I don't"?
Kalyani still feels hurt and angry on her mother's behalf, and wary of trusting Sarita again too soon.
What makes Sarita's apology more than words?
She admits it plainly, pays for the new ticket, sets up a backup call, and doesn't push for forgiveness.
What would change if Sarita had demanded forgiveness right away?
Kalyani would likely feel pressured and trust less; it took months of reliable actions to earn the spare key.
Should I write "approximately" or "about" in my report?

"Approximately" is more formal and suits reports and exams. "About" is natural in conversation.
Examples: The trip takes approximately three hours. It takes about three hours.

Rs 10 every Sunday.

Faculty mentor's note, Thursday. Sharmila, from my second-year group, came to see me before today's march for the farm workers' wage campaign. She wanted to go but was scared: her scholarship depends on attendance, and her uncle had warned her about 'getting a record'. We talked it through. She decided to go for two hours with her friend Santosh, stay near the front marshals and leave before dark. She came back at six, sunburnt and shaking a little. 'I was terrified, and I've never felt so proud,' she said. I have asked the department to share the excused-attendance rule with all students.

Why was Sharmila worried about her scholarship?
It depends on attendance.
What did Sharmila feel after the march?
Terrified and also prouder than ever, sunburnt and a little shaky.

She talked with her mentor, checked the march had permission and excused attendance, and planned to go with Santosh for two hours near the marshals and leave before dark.

Retell this Mahabharata scene simply, in about three sentences.

Beholding the unfading Rudra arrive there attired as a brahmacari and armed with that bow, the goddess Earth shrunk with fear and the very mountains began to tremble. The very wind ceased to move, and fire itself, though fed, did not blaze forth. The stars in the firmament, in anxiety, began to wander in irregular courses. The Sun's splendour decreased. The disc of the Moon lost its beauty. The entire welkin became enveloped in a thick gloom. The celestials, overwhelmed, knew not what to do. Their Sacrifice ceased to blaze forth. The gods were all terrified. Rudra then pierced the embodiment of Sacrifice with a fierce shaft in the heart. The embodied form of Sacrifice, assuming the shape of a deer, fled away, with the god of fire. Approaching heaven in that form, he blazed forth in beauty.

When Rudra arrives with his bow, the whole world trembles: the wind stops, fire will not burn, and the sun and moon grow dim. The frightened gods do not know what to do. Rudra shoots the sacrifice in the heart, and it flees to heaven in the form of a deer.
My budgie sleeps with his head tucked in his feathers. Is something wrong?
That's normal. Many birds sleep with their head turned back and tucked under a wing. It keeps them warm and comfortable.
Okay. I was worried.
It's kind of you to notice. If he seems sleepy all day, puffed up or stops eating, ask a vet who treats birds. Otherwise, sleeping like this is part of his routine.

Millie, Monica, and Marius are taking subjects for school. Millie takes three more subjects than Marius, who takes 4 subjects more than Monica. If Monica took 10 subjects, how many subjects all take altogether?

If Monica took ten subjects, Marius took 10+4 = 14 subjects.
Marius and Monica have 14+10 = 24 subjects which they've taken.
Since Millie is taking three more subjects than Marius, she is taking 14+3 = 17 subjects
Together, the three have taken 24+17 = 41 subjects.
The answer is 41.

After the café in São Paulo closed, Priscila didn't bake for two months. Just looking at the mixer made her tired.
In March her friend Jana said her aunt had a free corner at the Saturday street market in Pinheiros. 'One table. One kind of cake. That's all.'
Priscila made twelve orange cakes. She sold nine, and gave three to the fruit seller next door, who came back and bought two more for his daughter's birthday.
The next Saturday she made fifteen and sold out by eleven. The third week a woman asked if she took orders for parties. Priscila wrote her number on a napkin, her hand a little shaky.
She still woke some nights thinking about the café. But on Friday evenings now she was measuring flour again, humming, and on the way home from the market she started, without meaning to, making a list of new flavours.

How many orange cakes did Priscila make for the first Saturday?
She made twelve orange cakes.
What does Priscila's humming on Friday evenings suggest about how she is feeling?
It suggests her confidence and enjoyment are slowly returning as the small weekly successes build up 🙂
Why did starting with one table and one kind of cake work well for Priscila?
It was small enough to manage after a big failure, so each sold-out Saturday gave her a real win that rebuilt confidence through doing.
How does Jana probably feel watching Priscila make lists of new flavours?
Jana is likely relieved and proud, glad that the small idea Jana suggested helped Priscila bake again.

In the Lisbon library's puzzle corner, Ines always picked the same wooden puzzle, the farm one with twenty-four pieces. She could finish it in four minutes. Bao, from her class, sat down with a new box: a hundred pieces, a lighthouse at night, almost all blue. "Do it with me?" Ines looked at the dark blue pieces and felt her stomach go tight. What if she couldn't find any edges? What if Bao saw her get it wrong? "No, I like this one," she said, and started the farm again. Bao shrugged and began alone. By the time the library closed, Bao had half a lighthouse and a new trick for sorting blues. Ines had done the farm three times.

How many pieces did Bao's new puzzle have?
A hundred pieces, a lighthouse at night, almost all blue.
Why did Ines's stomach go tight at the dark blue pieces?
She was afraid of not finding edges and of Bao seeing her get it wrong, so the new puzzle felt risky.
What small step could Ines try next time?

What might Bao have gained that Ines missed out on?

Want to know the hardest thing about teaching guitar? I'm Chandrika, and I'll tell you about Parul. She joined my class at fourteen, and within a week she was trying the solo from a famous rock song. Beautiful energy. But she skipped chord changes, finger exercises, anything slow. I could hear it: her strumming rushed, her chords buzzed. I knew that in a year, the gaps would stop her. So one day I said, "Play me your solo." She did, proudly. Then, "Now change from G to C, cleanly, ten times." She couldn't. I told her, "The solo sits on top of those changes. How old was Parul when she joined the class?
Parul was fourteen.
What was Chandrika feeling when hearing Parul's buzzing chords?
Chandrika felt concerned, knowing the skipped basics would stop Parul within a year.
How did Chandrika hold the standard without killing Parul's excitement?
By linking the solo to clean chord changes and trading ten minutes of basics for teaching the next solo.
How might Parul feel when she couldn't change chords cleanly?

One said the government was ruining everything; the other said it was saving everything. They both looked so angry that I thought they would never speak again. I was confused. How could two people who loved the same country think such opposite things? Later, I sat with Bhupen Dada, our old neighbour, near the sweets table and asked him. He peeled an orange for me and said, 'People can love the same home and disagree about how to paint it. What matters is not tearing it down while you argue.' When I looked back, my uncles were sharing a plate of biryani. Still arguing. Just more quietly.

What stopped when the uncles argued?
The band stopped playing.
How did Afreen feel watching the uncles argue?
Confused and worried, thinking they might never speak again.
What helped Afreen understand the disagreement?
Sitting with Bhupen Dada and calmly asking how people who love the same country can disagree.

Hershel has 10 betta fish and 15 goldfish in a bowl. His friend Bexley brings him 2/5 times as many betta fish and 1/3 times as many goldfish. If Hershel gifts his sister 1/2 of the fish, calculate the total number of fish he has remaining in the bowl.

Bexley gives Hershel 2/5*10 = 4 betta fish.
The total number of betta fish in the bowl is now 4+10 = 14
He also gives Hershel 1/3*15 = 5 goldfish
The total number of goldfish in the bowl is now 15+5 = 20
Counting the betta fish and goldfish, Hershel now has a total of 14 + 20 = 34 fish
When he gives his sister half of the fish, the remaining half is 34/2 = 17 fish
The answer is 17.

By Thursday morning in Lagos, Emeka had seen the voice note eight times: a man, sounding very sure, saying phone chargers left plugged in overnight were exploding across the city, and three families had lost their homes that week. Emeka's mother had it. His football group had it. His cousin had sent it twice. So he forwarded it to his classmates with 'Please listen!!' His flatmate Ines, from Portugal, listened and frowned. 'Which families? Which area?' 'Everyone's sharing it.' 'That's not the same as it being true.' Emeka felt his face go hot. 'You'd rather wait for someone to burn?' She shrugged and went back to cooking. That evening Emeka searched the news for fires and found nothing matching. He looked at his forwarded message, now with eighty ticks, and didn't know what to do.

How many times had Emeka seen the voice note by Thursday morning?
Eight times.
What was Emeka feeling after finding no matching news?
Emeka felt uneasy and unsure, even embarrassed, seeing his forwarded message spread with nothing to support it.
What could Emeka do now about the message he forwarded?
He could post a short note to his classmates saying he could not confirm it and that they should not pass it on.
How does Ines see the voice note?

Then, on a wet Tuesday evening, her scooter died on the Outer Ring Road. Cars sprayed past. A young woman in a company lanyard pulled over, held an umbrella over the engine while Nazia tried the kick-start, then called a mechanic she knew and waited forty minutes with her.
Her name was Bidisha. She'd moved from Siliguri two years ago. She shared a flat with three others because the rent was too high for her, too.
'Rent's too high for you as well?' Nazia said, surprised.
'Everyone I know is struggling,' Bidisha said. 'Where are you from?'
On the way home, Nazia didn't open the forums. She found herself wondering about Bidisha's flat, her three flatmates, her family in Siliguri. She had a question she wanted to ask her.

How long did Bidisha wait with Nazia?
She waited forty minutes with her.
What was Nazia feeling on the way home?
She felt curious and a little unsettled, wondering about Bidisha's life instead of opening the forums.
Why did this encounter shift Nazia more than an argument might have?
A kind act and a calm conversation showed that 'those tech-park people' were real people with the same problems, sparking curiosity instead of defensiveness.
How might Bidisha see Nazia, knowing nothing of her online posts?
Bidisha simply sees a stranded person who needed help and was friendly, perhaps someone she could chat with again.

messages.content: Mrs. Gable's third grade class is on a field trip to the beach. For lunch, Mrs. Gable brought 20 lunches for the 20 students in her class. She included a pack of animal crackers in each lunch bag for dessert. Each pack of animal crackers contained 10 animal crackers. If 2 students did not eat their animal crackers, how many animal crackers were eaten in total among Mrs. Gable's students?

Since 2 students did not eat their animal crackers, 20 - 2 = 18 students ate their animal crackers.
The students ate a total of 18 * 10 =180 animal crackers
The answer is 180.

Gary is restocking the grocery produce section. He adds 60 bundles of asparagus at $3.00 each, 40 boxes of grapes at $2.50 each, and 700 apples at $0.50 each. How much is all the produce he stocked worth?

First find the total cost of the asparagus: 60 bundles * $3/bundle = $180
Then find the total cost of the grapes: 40 boxes * $2.50/bundle = $100
Then find the total cost of the apples: 700 apples * $0.50/apple = $350
Then add the cost of each type of food to find the total cost of the produce: $180 + $100 + $350 = $630
The answer is 630.

Jack cycles from his home to the store. Then he cycles, at the same speed, 50 miles to his friend Peter. It takes Jack twice as long to go from his home to the store as it takes to go from the store to his friend. If Peter and Jack now cycle back to the store together, how many miles in total have they cycled today?

When Jack cycles from home to the store, it takes 2 * 50 = 100 miles.
He then cycles 50 miles to Peter.
When Peter and Jack cycle back to the store, they cover a total of 50 + 50 = 100 miles.
The total number of miles covered is 100+50+100 = 250 miles
The answer is 250.

On Mary's birthday, her brother surprised her with $100. She spent a quarter of it on a new video game and then used a fifth of what was left on swimming goggles. How much money did she have left?

So, after the video game purchase, Mary was left with 100 - 25 = 75 dollars.
Mary then bought swimming goggles for 75/5 = 15 dollars
Mary had 75 - 15 = 60 dollars left

Walking over with tea and asking about the oil worked, because it turned a suspicion into a plain conversation between neighbours.

In Valencia, Pablo and his girlfriend Lucía were watching a film on her sofa. They'd been kissing, and then she pulled back a little and said, "I don't want to go further. Not yet."
Pablo felt his face get hot, and for a second he wanted to ask why. Instead he said, "Okay. Thanks for telling me." He meant it. They finished the film holding hands.
On Monday, Lars asked him in the corridor what had happened, grinning. Pablo said, "Nothing you need to know. And if she says not yet, it's not yet."
Lars laughed, but later, walking home, he admitted he'd never been sure what counted as a yes. Pablo told him what the school nurse said in the sex-ed class: ask, listen, and a yes can change to no at any time.

What did Lucía say when she pulled back?
"I don't want to go further. Not yet."
What was Pablo feeling when Lucía said not yet?
Pablo felt embarrassed and briefly disappointed, but chose to respect her and felt sincere about thanking her.
Why was Pablo's answer to Lars a good one?
He kept Lucía's privacy and made clear that her "not yet" was final, which shows respect instead of bragging.
How might Lucía feel about Pablo's response on the sofa?
Lucía probably felt safe and respected, and more able to trust him because her boundary didn't cause a fight.
Is "require" better than "need" in a formal letter?

Usually yes. "Require" sounds more formal and is common in rules and notices, while "need" is natural in everyday talk.
Examples: Applicants are required to bring a photo ID. I need a pen.

"My friend," said I, "what all this gibberish of yours is about, I don't know, and I don't much care; for it seems to me that you must be a little damaged in the head. But if you are speaking of Captain Ahab, of that ship there, the Pequod, then let me tell you, that I know all about the loss of his leg."

Answer from the text. What does the speaker say about the other person, and what does the speaker know about Ahab?
The speaker thinks the other person must be a little damaged in the head, and does not care what the gibberish means. All about how Captain Ahab lost his leg is already known.

What change did Rashmi suggest for the birthday surprise?
Give Mehr a heads-up that something is planned and do the cake quietly in the library corner.
How might Mehr experience a quiet cake in the library compared with a shouted surprise?
She would likely feel celebrated rather than startled, and safe enough to enjoy it.

"Whew... whew... whew!" he whistled just audibly as he rode into the yard. His face expressed the relief of relaxed strain felt by a man who means to rest after a ceremony. He drew his left foot out of the stirrup and, lurching with his whole body and puckering his face with the effort, raised it with difficulty onto the saddle, leaned on his knee, groaned, and slipped down into the arms of the Cossacks and adjutants who stood ready to assist him.

How does the rider get down from his horse?

He pulls his left foot from the stirrup and, with his whole body lurching, lifts it with difficulty onto the saddle. He leans on his knee, groans and slips down into the arms of the Cossacks and adjutants waiting to help.

I'm Irfan, the boy who sits at the back of 10B and watches. In our science project group there were six of us. On paper. In the first meeting, Ishita and a quiet boy from the front bench made a list. Everyone nodded. Then the four others, and honestly me too at first, just disappeared into cricket and phones. By the second week I saw Ishita in the library at lunch every day, charts spread out, eating with one hand. The front-bench boy stayed late to finish the model. On submission day, the four got the same marks. Ishita didn't say anything, but she didn't sit with us after that.

Briefly, in two sentences, what is this section about?

Irfan's science group had six members, but Ishita and a quiet boy did the work while the other four, at first including Irfan, drifted off. On submission day the other four got the same marks, and Ishita stopped sitting with them.
Why does a school bag with wide straps feel lighter than one with thin straps?
The weight is the same, but it presses less. Because wide straps spread the weight over a larger part of the shoulder, the pressure at any spot is smaller.
Emily spent X dollars on Friday, twice that amount on Saturday, and then three times X on Sunday. Over the three days, she spent $120. What is the value of X, in dollars?

She spent X dollars on Friday.
She spent 2X dollars on Saturday.
She spent 3X dollars on Sunday.
X+2X+3X=120
6X=120
X=20
The answer is 20.

Minakshi spent all night on the poster for the youth helpline stall, using deep red and sharp black shapes because she wanted it to feel urgent. In the morning she showed it to her classmate Bhavna at the college print room. Bhavna tilted her head. "It feels angry, like a warning. I think it might scare people away." Minakshi was startled. "I meant urgent, not angry." "Maybe a softer colour?" Bhavna suggested. Minakshi kept the sharp shapes but changed the red to a warm orange, then tested it on a third student, who said it felt friendly but serious. Minakshi thought about how she would never fully control what a stranger felt when they looked at it.

What colours did Minakshi first use on the poster?
She used deep red and sharp black shapes.
What did Minakshi intend her poster to feel like, and how did Bhavna read it?
She meant it to feel urgent, but Bhavna read it as angry, like a warning that might scare people away.
What small step helped Minakshi improve the poster?
She tested a warmer orange on a third student and learned it felt friendly but serious.
How might a person in need of the helpline feel on first seeing the red version?
They might feel warned or uneasy and hesitate, even though Minakshi wanted it to feel urgent.

Sarita did night duty at the primary health centre in Barsana two weeks a month, and she had worked out rules. Home by eight, she ate a plate of roti and dal, drew the jute curtain her neighbour Sudha had helped her stitch, and slept till two whatever the noise. Before duty she sat in the courtyard light for a while. When the sarpanch's son came one morning asking her to decide about standing for the panchayat seat, she smiled. 'Ask me on Sunday, when I've slept. Tired heads make bad promises.' Sudha teased her for being so strict. Sarita only said, 'And if I keep feeling this drained for weeks, I'll see the doctor at the district hospital.'

When did Sarita tell the sarpanch's son to ask again?
On Sunday, when she has slept.
Why did Sarita smile and put off the decision?
She felt calm and sure of her rule that tired heads make bad promises, so a big decision could wait until she had slept.
Which of Sarita's habits protect her body clock?
A fixed sleep window behind the jute curtain, courtyard light before duty, proper meals, and a doctor if the drain lasts.
How does Sudha see Sarita's rules?
Sudha teases Sarita for being strict, though Sudha also helped stitch the curtain that makes the rules work.

In the community centre's small computer room, Binita pinned a chart to the wall. Three columns: Coding, Sketching, Clinic desk. Under each, a row for every week of the last two months, with two numbers: energy after, and interest, out of five.

Her friend Bidisha, who ran the centre's library, came in with chai. "So? The verdict?"

Binita traced the columns. The coding tutorial had started at four and dropped to two; she'd dreaded opening the laptop by week five. Sketching stayed at three, pleasant but flat. The clinic help desk, where she'd volunteered on Saturdays, sat at four and five. "I kept thinking about the old man with the lost file," she said. "I went back on Sunday to check he got his appointment."

"That's the one that pulls you back, then," Bidisha said.

Binita nodded, a bit surprised. "I thought it would be coding."

What two numbers did Binita record each week?
Energy after, and interest, out of five.
How did Binita feel about the coding tutorial by week five?
She dreaded opening the laptop, feeling drained and uninterested.
What else could Binita try to explore the clinic interest further?
She could talk to a nurse or hospital administrator about careers in health services, to see which roles fit what she enjoyed at the desk.
How might Bidisha see Binita's chart?
Bidisha seems amused and supportive, pointing out plainly which activity kept pulling Binita back.

Sunday

Went to see Kunal today in his rented room near the station. He lost his job three months ago. He's been sleeping on a mat because the landlord took the bed back, and eating mostly bread. I tried to talk about his plans: courses, applications, the future. He just stared at me. 'I don't know about next month, Kamal. I don't even know about tomorrow's lunch.' I realised I'd been thinking he was lazy for not applying anywhere. He isn't lazy. His mind is full of rent and food. There's no room left for plans. So I stopped lecturing. I bought groceries, and I asked my cousin about the shelter with a proper bed near the station. Kunal called me tonight and said he'd slept properly for the first time in weeks. He asked me to help him write his CV tomorrow.

Kamal

How long ago did Kunal lose his job?
Three months ago.
How did Kamal feel on realising Kunal wasn't lazy?
Kamal felt ashamed of having judged Kunal, and more understanding.
What did Kamal do that helped Kunal start planning again?
Kamal stopped lecturing and helped with basics, groceries and a proper bed, which freed Kunal's mind to think about his CV.
What is it like for Kunal to hear questions about the future?
It is probably frustrating and overwhelming, since he is worried about tomorrow's lunch.

In a classroom in Lisbon, Kwame and Ines were stuck on their volcano poster. Ines had grabbed the markers and was writing every heading herself. "You always take over," Kwame said, louder than he meant. Ines snapped, "Because you're slow." Two tables away, the teacher looked up. Kwame took a breath. "Okay. What if you write and I draw? You're faster at writing, and I'm better at the diagram." Ines stared at the half-empty poster, then slid the black marker over. "Fine. But the lava has to be orange." By the end of the lesson they were arguing only about shades of orange.

What were Kwame and Ines making?
A volcano poster.
What was Kwame feeling when he said "You always take over"?
He felt frustrated and pushed aside because Ines had grabbed all the markers.
What helped the argument cool down?
Kwame took a breath and suggested splitting the work by strengths, which gave both of them a real role.
What would change if the teacher had come over at once?
She might have assigned the jobs herself, and the two would have missed working it out on their own.

Friday, 10 pm
Moot court round today. I had the opening submission. When the judge nodded at me, my heart was racing and my shoulders were practically touching my ears. Before, I'd have launched straight in and gabbled. Today I did what I'd practised in the washroom mirror: one long breath out, shoulders down, a second of silence before speaking. It felt like forever, but Pallavi said later it looked like I was simply gathering my notes. My first sentence came out steady, and my thinking stayed clear even when the judge interrupted. Nobody noticed the breath. That's the point. I'm doing it again next round.
Mohit

Where did Mohit practise the breathing?
In the washroom mirror.
How did Mohit feel when the judge nodded?
Mohit felt nervous, heart racing and shoulders tense.
What three steps did Mohit use before speaking?
One long breath out, dropping the shoulders and a second of silence before the first sentence.
How did the pause look to Pallavi?
To Pallavi it looked as if Mohit was simply gathering notes, not calming nerves.

"Arre, Ayesha, say 'coffee' again. Kaafi! Bihar ka kaafi!" Vikas laughed at the pantry counter, and two others laughed with him.

Ayesha's face burned. For a second she wanted to laugh along, the way she always had.

She put her mug down. "Vikas, that's the third time this week you've made fun of how people from my state speak. It's not funny to me. Please stop."

"Relax, it's a joke."

"It's a joke about where I'm from. I'm asking you to stop."

He rolled his eyes and walked out.

Ritu from accounts stayed. "You okay?"

"No. My hands are shaking."

"Write down the dates while you remember. Mrs Nair in HR is fair. I'll come with you if you want."

Ayesha opened her notes app. Monday, Wednesday, today. "There's nothing wrong with how I talk," she said, mostly to herself.

How many times that week had Vikas mocked the way people from Ayesha's state speak?
It was the third time that week.
What was Ayesha feeling when Vikas laughed, and how can you tell?
Ayesha felt humiliated and angry; her face burned, and afterwards her hands were shaking.
How did Ayesha respond wisely, and what are her next steps?
Ayesha named the joke calmly and asked him to stop, then started noting dates and planned to go to HR with Ritu.
How does Ritu see what happened in the pantry?
Ritu sees it as a real problem, not a harmless joke, and offers to go with Ayesha to HR.

The college bus broke down on the highway, and Tushar had two hours and a dying phone to finish the social psychology chapter for tomorrow's exam. It was about the obedience experiments: ordinary people giving what they thought were dangerous shocks because a man in a grey coat kept saying, 'Please continue.' Most kept going. Lavanya, reading over his shoulder, snorted. 'Idiots. I'd have walked out.' Tushar didn't answer. He was thinking of last month, when the hostel warden told him, as floor monitor, to cut off a junior's wifi for a week for talking back. Tushar had disagreed. He'd done it anyway, the same evening, because the warden said it so calmly. 'Would you?' he said finally. 'I think I'm exactly the kind who continues.' The bus lurched forward. He wrote in the margin: Ask why, first.

What did the warden tell Tushar to do?
Cut off a junior's wifi for a week for talking back.
What was Tushar feeling as Lavanya called them idiots?
Tushar felt uneasy and quietly ashamed, recognising his own obedience in the story.
What does Tushar's margin note suggest he will do next time?
Question an order at the first doubt instead of carrying it out just because the authority sounds calm.
How does Lavanya see the people in the experiments?
Lavanya scorns them as idiots, confident she would have walked out.
Lena runs faster then her brother. Check my spelling, please.

Lena runs faster than her brother.
Why: "than" compares; "then" is about time.

On a windy Saturday in a park in Cape Town, Daniel toddled after a rolling ball while his father Thabo sat on the grass. A large brown dog came bounding out from behind a bench. Daniel stopped dead, threw his arms up and screamed, then ran back and clung to Thabo's leg. Thabo scooped him up and asked the owner to call the dog. From his father's arms, Daniel watched the dog sit, his fingers still gripping Thabo's shirt.

What came out from behind the bench?
A large brown dog came bounding out from behind a bench.
What does Daniel's grip on Thabo's shirt show about how he felt, even after the dog sat?
It shows he still felt uneasy and wanted to stay close to his father, because the dog had appeared so suddenly.
How could Thabo help Daniel feel calmer around dogs over time?
He could let Daniel watch calm dogs from a safe distance in his arms, and never push him to touch one before he is ready.
How might the dog's owner see Daniel's scream?
The owner might think the dog was only being playful, but could also understand that a big dog rushing up is scary for a small child.

In the college hostel in Jaipur, Madhuri, nineteen, saw Harsha's father and two uncles arrive at the visitors' room on Saturday morning. Harsha, her roommate, went pale.
Through the half-open door, Madhuri heard one uncle: "Photos of you with that boy are all over the family group. You've destroyed our honour. Pack your bag. You're coming home, and you're done with college." Harsha was crying. "Papa, please."
Madhuri felt her heart race. She knew Harsha had been frightened for weeks, hiding her phone.
She didn't go in. She ran to the warden's office. "They're forcing her to leave. They're threatening her."
The warden came at once, stood beside Harsha, and said calmly, "She's an adult and a student here. She will not be taken against her will." Then she called the college's women's cell and the police helpline. Madhuri sat with Harsha until the officer arrived.

Where did Harsha's father and uncles arrive?
They arrived at the visitors' room.
What was Madhuri feeling when she heard the uncle's words?
Madhuri felt afraid for Harsha, her heart racing, knowing her roommate had been frightened for weeks.
What made Madhuri's and the warden's response protective?
Madhuri went straight for help rather than confronting the family alone, and the warden stood beside Harsha, refused to let her be taken and called the women's cell and police.
How might Harsha feel with Madhuri beside her until the officer arrived?
Harsha would likely feel less alone and a little safer, knowing someone had believed her and acted.

The night before Makar Sankranti, kites were stacked in the corner of the small-town house. Ujjwal, five, wouldn't go to sleep.

"Mummy, the kite demon will cut my kite tomorrow."

His mother Swati sat on the bed. "The kite demon? Tell me about him."

"He's in the sky. He has a big knife."

Swati nodded. "That sounds scary. Do you know what really cuts kites?"

Ujjwal shook his head.

"Other people's kite strings. That's the game. There's no demon. And if your kite gets cut, we'll have more."

Ujjwal thought about it. "So the demon is just a string?"

"Just a string," Swati said, and tucked him in.

What does Swati say really cuts kites?
Other people's kite strings.
Why couldn't Ujjwal go to sleep?
He felt scared that a kite demon would cut his kite the next day.
Why did Swati's answer calm Ujjwal down?
She listened, didn't mock him, and gave a simple true explanation, plus a reassurance about having more kites.
How might Swati feel tucking Ujjwal in?
Swati probably feels tender and relieved that he's calmer.

Thursday night.
Viva today. First question, easy. Second question, I said "resistance" when I meant "resistor." The external examiner raised one eyebrow, I corrected myself, and we moved on.
I have replayed that eyebrow maybe fifty times since. I'm sure the examiner wrote it down. I'm sure Samir, who was waiting by the door, heard. By dinner I had decided that everyone in the lab now thinks I don't know basic circuits.
Then I actually asked Samir. He looked blank. "What mistake?" He'd been standing there going over his own answers in his head, terrified about the transistor question.
Also: my marks are up on the portal. Good grade.
So the whole lab was not thinking about me. The examiner had probably seen that slip a hundred times. Everyone was busy with their own nerves.
Note to self, Kashish: next viva, correct it and move on. Nobody's keeping a list.

What word did the narrator say instead of "resistor"?
The narrator said "resistance."
How did Kashish feel in the hours after the viva?
Kashish felt anxious and embarrassed, replaying the examiner's eyebrow about fifty times.
What did Kashish learn to do next time?
Correct the slip and move on, remembering that listeners notice far less than it feels.
What was Samir focused on while waiting by the door?
Samir was terrified about his own transistor question and going over his answers, so he never noticed the slip.

The workshop with Vishal's team had run forty minutes over, and Shalini's flight to Chennai left in two hours. The map on her phone already showed red on the airport road. She could just slip out while Vishal was mid-slide; half the room was on laptops anyway. But she'd seen colleagues do that, and clients always remembered. At the next pause she caught Vishal's eye and raised a hand. "Vishal, I'm so sorry, I have to leave in five minutes for my flight. Can I take one minute now?" He nodded. "Thank you all for today, especially for the honest feedback on the pricing model. I'll send the revised version by Wednesday, and Karan will stay for the rest." At the door she shook Vishal's hand. "Call me any time before Wednesday if something comes up." She made the flight with ten minutes to spare. On Wednesday, Vishal replied within the hour.

By when did Shalini promise the revised version?
By Wednesday.
What was Shalini feeling as the workshop overran?
Shalini felt pressured and anxious about the flight and was tempted to slip out, but knew clients remember abrupt exits.
What made Shalini's exit a good one?
She signalled at a pause, asked for a minute, thanked the room for something specific, named next steps and who would stay, and left the door open for calls.
How might Vishal have felt if Shalini had slipped out mid-slide?
He might have felt slighted and unsure of next steps, remembering it as a careless exit.

Afreen asked, "Dhruv, why did you look like a ghost all last week?"
Honestly, Afreen, the planner is the best thing about me. Six colours, every chapter mapped, and I've never missed a deadline. But last Tuesday Nani turned eighty and the house filled with cousins. No studying. I smiled through the cake and felt sick the whole time, like I was stealing hours. That night I set an alarm for four to make up for it, and the next night too. By Thursday I was reading the same paragraph again and again and snapping at my little brother. You know what finally hit me? The planner had no row for Nani. I'd made a plan that could only break, never bend. So now I'm trying something scary: Sundays left blank.

How many colours does Dhruv's planner use?
Six colours, every chapter mapped.
What was Dhruv feeling during Nani's birthday cake?
Dhruv felt guilty and sick, as if the family hours were being stolen from study.
What turning point does Dhruv reach about the planner?
Dhruv notices it had no row for Nani and decides to leave Sundays blank, so the plan can bend instead of break.

Being snapped at by a tired older sibling probably hurt, with no way of knowing it came from the four o'clock alarms.

Joan is answering English and Math exams with 30 and 15 questions, respectively. The English exam is to be completed in 1 hour and the Math exam in 1.5 hours. If Joan wants to spend an equal amount of time on each question, how many more minutes does she have in answering each question on the Math exam than the English exam?

Joan is given 1 x 60 = 60 minutes to answer the English exam.
So Joan will spend 60/30 = 2 minutes for each English question.
She is given 1.5 x 60 = 90 minutes to answer the Math exam.
So, she will spend 90/15 = 6 minutes for each Math question.
Hence, Joan has 6 - 2 = 4 minutes more for answering each question in Math than in English.
The answer is 4.

Wednesday night
Embarrassing day. This morning I forwarded an audio clip to the family group, a 'police officer' warning about child kidnappers in our area, sounding very official. Mausi immediately stopped sending my cousins to tuition. By lunch Anand, who works at a newspaper, messaged me: 'Tarun bhai, where did you get this? It's been doing the rounds in four states with different city names.' My stomach dropped. I searched the exact lines and found three fact-check articles calling it fake. The voice might even be generated. I'd spread panic in five minutes. So I posted a correction in the group with the links, and said sorry, especially to Mausi. She sent a folded-hands emoji, thank God. New rule for myself: if something makes me scared or angry fast, I wait and search before forwarding. That feeling is exactly what these clips want.

What did the audio clip claim to warn about?
Child kidnappers in their area, supposedly from a police officer.
How did Tarun feel when Anand questioned the clip?
His stomach dropped; he was embarrassed and alarmed at having spread panic.
What rule did Tarun make, and why is it wise?
If something makes him scared or angry fast, he waits and searches before forwarding, because fake clips rely on those quick emotions.
How did the clip affect Mausi?
She was frightened enough to stop sending her children to tuition, until Tarun's correction reassured her.

During exam week, Pema's phone was always buzzing. It was Advait, her boyfriend. "Where are you?" "Who's that in your story?" "Share your location."
At first she thought it meant he cared. Then, on Wednesday, she left her phone at home by mistake. When she got back there were thirty messages and a voice note: "Why are you ignoring me? Are you with someone?"
Her friend Parul read them over her shoulder. "Pema… this isn't caring. This is checking."
Pema felt sick. She thought of how she'd stopped going to the library with the study group because Advait didn't like it.
That evening she showed the messages to her mother. Her mother listened, then said, "You deserve someone who trusts you. Whatever you decide, I'm with you. Let's talk to your class counsellor tomorrow too."

How many messages were waiting when Pema got back?
Thirty messages.
What was Pema feeling when Parul said "This is checking"?
Pema felt sick and shaken, starting to see the messages as control, not care.
What steps did Pema take that others could learn from?
She listened to a friend's concern, noticed how her own life had shrunk, and showed the messages to her mother the same day.
How does Parul see Advait's messages?
Parul sees them as checking and control, not love, and says so gently.

Vanessa wants to buy a dress she saw at the mall, which costs $80, and she already has $20 in savings. Her parents give her $30 every week, but she also spends $10 each weekend at the arcades. How many weeks will she have to wait until she can gather enough money to buy the dress?

Vanessa needs $80 - $20 = $60 to buy the dress.
She manages to gather $30 - $10 = $20 each week
The number of weeks she has to wait is 60 / 20 = 3 weeks.
The answer is 3.

What should I carry for a day in the hills?

Dear Nitin,

It's been eight months since the company closed. I've been paying the rent, the groceries, your phone bill. I don't regret it, and I'd do it again. I love you and I feel protective of you.

So I want to talk properly, on Sunday, about shared goals. Where we want to be in a year. What your route back to work could look like, maybe the course you mentioned. What I can carry, and for how long.

In the courtyard of her grandfather's house in Bhadohi, Trisha sat across from Mohan while both families drank tea under the neem tree. Mohan's mother listed his land, his tractor and his government job. Trisha's aunts nodded approvingly.
Her cousin Ganga nudged her. "Ask something. Anything."

Trisha asked two more questions, about his work and how he spent his evenings. He answered politely but asked her nothing back.
That night, on the roof with Ganga, she said, "He's not a bad man. But he didn't ask me one thing. I'm going to tell Baba no." Ganga squeezed her hand. "Then say it tomorrow, calmly." In the morning she did. Her father sighed, but listened.

His land, his tractor and his government job.

Uneasy and let down, sensing he did not value her love of teaching.

OpenAI runs a robotics competition that limits the weight of each robot. Each robot can be no more than twice the minimum weight and no less than 5 pounds heavier than the standard robot. The standard robot weighs 100 pounds. What is the maximum weight of a robot in the competition?

the minimum is 5 more than 100 so 100+5=105
the maximum weight of a robot is twice the minimum 105*2=210
The answer is 210.

On opening the little door, two hairy monsters flew at my throat, bearing me down, and extinguishing the light; while a mingled guffaw from Heathcliff and Hareton put the copestone on my rage and humiliation. Fortunately, the beasts seemed more bent on stretching their paws, and yawning, and flourishing their tails, than devouring me alive; but they would suffer no resurrection, and I was forced to lie till their malignant masters pleased to deliver me: then, hatless and trembling with wrath, I ordered the miscreants to let me out—on their peril to keep me one minute longer—with several incoherent threats of retaliation that, in their indefinite depth of virulency, smacked of King Lear.

"Mumma, can you leave the light on?"

"It's on, Ujjwal. What's wrong?"

"What if you get lost driving to Nani's tomorrow?"

"I've driven there a hundred times."

"What if I get zero in the science quiz and you're not here to sign it?"

Devika sat on the bed. "That's a lot of what-ifs. Where are they coming from?"

"My head keeps making them. It feels like if I think of everything, nothing bad happens."

"Your brain is trying to protect us. But it's making too many alarms."

"Can you make it stop?"

"We can make it quieter. Let's do our three things: one good thing from today, one thing for tomorrow, then the long slow breaths."

"And I'll call you at lunchtime. Now breathe with me."

Where is Devika driving tomorrow?
Devika is driving to Nani's tomorrow.
What does Ujjwal believe about his what-if thoughts, and how does it make him feel?
Ujjwal feels anxious and believes that thinking of everything stops bad things happening, so the what-ifs seem protective even though they scare him.

It explains the alarms kindly, gives a familiar three-step routine and a lunchtime call, so Ujjwal has something calm and certain to hold.

Parul's journalism tutorial was stuck on a short piece about a canteen price rise. The tutor, Harish, asked each student to underline facts in blue and opinions in red. Parul found "The price rose from twenty to twenty-five rupees" in blue, and "students are outraged" in red, since no one had been quoted. She raised her hand. "Who was asked? How many?" The writer went red but agreed to add a proper count and a line from the canteen manager.

What question does Parul ask about the canteen article, and why does it matter?
She asks who was asked and how many. The claim that students are outraged has no quotes, so it is only opinion. The writer had asked just two friends, so the piece needs a proper count.

A block flew and Deepak wailed. Jasleen came running from the kitchen, swept him up, and turned on Disha. "You're the big one. Be sensible." Disha's face went stiff. It was the fifth time that week she had heard "be sensible," and each time it seemed to mean that being older earned her less love. She kicked the box of blocks and stomped off.

Later that evening, when the tower fell again and both children shouted, Jasleen knelt on the rug between them. "Tell me what happened, Disha. Then Deepak." Disha's voice shook. "He knocked my tower and I hadn't finished." Deepak said, "I only wanted a block." Jasleen nodded. "Your tower fell before you had finished, and that made you cross. Deepak, you wanted a block, and it scared you when it fell." Both children's shoulders dropped. The shouting was gone.

From then on Jasleen gave each child ten minutes alone at bedtime: a story for Disha, a song for Deepak. On Sunday she gave them a big cardboard box. They spent the morning building a train station, Disha drawing the tickets and Deepak taping the roof. When it fell, they fixed it together, laughing, and neither asked who had started it.

What did Jasleen give each child at bedtime?
She gave each child ten minutes alone: a story for Disha and a song for Deepak.
How did Jasleen's first reaction differ from her later one, and what effect did each have on Disha?

At first she swept up Deepak and told Disha to be sensible, which made Disha feel that being older meant less love and set up the next round. Later she knelt between them, heard both and named their feelings, and the shouting stopped.
How did Disha feel when she was told to be sensible for the fifth time that week?
She felt blamed and unloved: her face went stiff and she stomped off.
How could Jasleen keep the rivalry easing?
She could keep the daily time alone with each child and give them joint tasks like building the station.

The weather, the government, faraway markets: too many things moved prices, and his thirty years had not taught his bones anything. I was scared to show him. But I did, quietly, just to him. Day three. Chetan looked up the claim. The post cited no study and the writer sold the tea. He told Leela, a little sheepish, that he'd nearly forwarded it.

Sunday. At her cousin's birthday, the children started a treasure hunt. Vaibhav held Maria's hand. "You don't have to, beta. You're our quiet one." Maria stayed by his side all afternoon, watching.
The next Saturday. The bakery lady asked again. Maria looked up at her father and waited. When he said nothing, she whispered, "I'm shy. Papa talks."
Vaibhav stared at her. He had said those words so many times, he'd never heard them in her voice. He crouched down. "Try, Maria. I'll wait." A long pause. "…Strawberry," she said.

Advisor's note. Tanuja came to my office on Wednesday, still shaking. A traffic official had fined her for a parking violation at a spot with no sign, and had brushed off her questions. Her friend Zeenat came with her. Tanuja said she wanted to go back and shout at the official until they understood how unfair it was. Her fists were tight and she kept saying, "They just don't care." I let her say it all. Then we looked at what she had: Zeenat's photos of the bare wall, the receipt, the time. I helped her write a short, plain complaint to the city office, and they filed it together that afternoon. Tanuja left less furious, with something to do. I will ask her next week what reply has come.

Who came with Tanuja to the advisor's office?

What did Tanuja want to do before the advisor helped her?
She wanted to go back and shout at the official, feeling furious and helpless that they didn't care.

I have one free day in Mumbai before my train. What should I see?
For one day, pick a small area so you don't spend it all in traffic. The sea face near Marine Drive and the old buildings nearby are easy to walk around.
Is that enough to fill a day?
If you start early, yes. You could add a visit to a museum or a famous temple or church, and a lunch at a local place. Leave time to get back to the station early.
I'm travelling alone. Is that okay?
Many people explore the city alone. Stay in busy areas, keep your bag in front, and tell someone at home your plan. Keep your phone charged.
What about getting around?
The local train is quick for long distances, and for short hops you can take a taxi or auto. Use the meter or ask the fare before you start.
Great. I'll make a short list of three places.
Three places is just right. It keeps the day relaxed, and you can add more if time remains.

The answer is 30.

Dear Seema,

You asked how I finally stopped lying awake till two. Promise not to laugh: it was a rule I wrote on a sticky note.

"IF it's 10 pm, THEN the phone goes to the charger in the kitchen." That's it. No arguing with myself. Before, I'd say "just five more minutes" and suddenly it was midnight.

Then a short routine that's always the same: wash my face, brush teeth, lay out tomorrow's uniform, and read a paper book for twenty minutes. Same order every night.

The first week I kept reaching for the phone that wasn't there. It felt silly. By the second week, washing my face started to make me yawn, like my brain knew what came next.

I'm sleeping by 10:45 most nights now. Try it. Pick your own "if" and write it down.

Pema

To the charger in the kitchen.

Hana's right hand, shaped like a flat vehicle, slid along her left forearm, then swung sharply to one side and stopped. Nkechi was still new to sign and understood almost nothing of it.
