Facilitator's notes, Irawati, Thursday bereavement circle, community hall
Sarika, 24, first came to the circle in January, three weeks after her mother died. She sat by the door with her coat on and didn't speak for two sessions. In the third she said only, "Everyone says it gets easier. It doesn't."
Tonight was different. She arrived early and helped me set out the chairs. When a new member, an older man who had lost his wife, sat stiffly by the door just as she once had, Sarika brought him tea and sat beside him. Later she told the group, "My mother fed whoever came to the house. Doing this feels like something she'd do."
She said the loss is still heavy. But she stayed for tea afterwards. I'll ask whether she'd like to help welcome newcomers next month, and keep checking in on how she is.

What did Sarika say in the third session?
"Everyone says it gets easier. It doesn't."
Why does bringing tea to the new member mean something to Sarika?
Feeding and welcoming people was what her mother always did, so helping him makes Sarika feel connected to her mother in the middle of the loss.
What next step is Irawati planning, and why is it well judged?
Irawati will ask if Sarika wants to help welcome newcomers while still checking on her, building on what comforts her without pretending the grief has gone.
How might the new member have experienced Sarika sitting beside him?
He may have felt less alone and less awkward, seeing someone who understood that stiff first visit and made room for him.

Kindergarten note, December. Written by Maria, class teacher.
Each day of Advent, the children open one paper door on our class calendar and get a small sweet at home time. Mohit finds this very hard. In the first week he sat staring at the calendar all afternoon and cried twice.
This week I made Mohit our "calendar keeper" and asked him to lead the waiting song at the end of each lesson. He sang loudest.
On Thursday he waited the whole day without asking once. He told me, "I didn't look at it. I was busy."
Next step: we'll keep practising waiting for small things in January, with songs and jobs.

What do the children open each day of Advent?
They open one paper door on the class calendar.
Why did Mohit cry in the first week?
Mohit felt impatient and upset, staring at the calendar all afternoon, which made the wait feel endless.
Why did the calendar-keeper job and the song help Mohit?
They kept Mohit busy and away from staring at the sweets, so the waiting passed without tears.
How did the week look to Maria?
Maria was pleased to see Mohit wait the whole of Thursday, and planned to keep practising in January.

Swati: booked a session with a registered adviser for Saturday. fee-only, not selling anything
Avni: ooh. why now?
Swati: the crash made me realise I don't even know my mix. 5 funds, no idea why I have them
Avni: my cousin just asks her bank's relationship manager
Swati: the bank guy kept pushing their own products. this one charges a flat fee and earns no commission
Avni: makes sense. what are you going to ask?
Swati: made a list: what's my current mix, what are the general options for someone my age, what should I ask myself about when I need the money
Avni: so you'll do whatever they say?
Swati: no 😅 I want to understand it. then I decide
Swati (Saturday evening): that was SO useful. I understand my own funds for the first time
Swati: not changing anything tonight. sleeping on it

How does the adviser Swati chose get paid?
A flat fee, with no commission.
What made Swati want the session now?
The crash left Swati unsure and a bit alarmed at not knowing the mix or why the five funds were there.
What does Swati do well?
Swati goes with a list of questions, treats the session as learning, and sleeps on it before changing anything.
How does Avni see the idea at first?
Avni is curious but assumes Swati will just do whatever the adviser says.

messages.content:
Read this:

Every morning the milk can went from their house to the village dairy, and every morning Sarika carried it. Today her little brother Darshan, five, said, "I'll do it." Sarika walked beside him. He held the can with both hands, stopping twice to rest, and didn't spill a drop. At the dairy counter he lifted it up himself. On the way home he walked in front, chest out, waving at every neighbour.

Who usually carried the milk can?
Sarika carried it every morning.
What does Darshan walking in front with his chest out suggest?
He felt proud and grown-up after carrying the can all the way without spilling.
How could Sarika help Darshan keep this good feeling?
Let him carry the can again and tell the family what he managed, praising his effort.
What is it like for Sarika to walk beside him instead of carrying the can?
She may feel a bit anxious watching, but also glad and proud to see him manage.

Read this:

Tuesday, after shift

Three months as housekeeping supervisor at the hotel. Today I caught myself. Zubin had missed a corner under a bed in 412, and I was standing over him with the checklist, saying, "How many times do I have to tell you people?" He's twenty-two, sends half his pay home, and always holds the lift for guests.

I stopped mid-sentence and asked myself: would I talk to Zubin like this at the bus stop? No. Never.

So what's happening to me in that uniform?

Three things I did today:
1. Wrote the room-check rules on the staff board, so it's the rule, not my mood.
2. Asked the front-office manager to walk my floors with me once a week and tell me honestly what she sees.
3. At the evening huddle I said, "Tell me one thing I do that makes your work harder." Silence. Then Zubin said, "Standing over us, ma'am." Fair.

- Ritu

Which room had Zubin missed a corner in?
He missed a corner under a bed in room 412.
What made Ritu stop mid-sentence?
She suddenly asked herself whether she would speak to Zubin like that at the bus stop and knew she would never, which showed her the role was changing her.
Which of Ritu's three steps protects most against the role taking over, and why?
Writing the rules on the board and asking the front-office manager to walk her floors make things transparent and checked, so her mood no longer decides.
How might Zubin have felt saying 'Standing over us' at the huddle?
He was probably nervous but relieved to be asked, and it may have made him trust his supervisor more.
I'm hosting a few people for dinner and I'm nervous about cooking for a group.
Pick dishes that can be made ahead, so you are not cooking when guests arrive. One-pot meals and dishes that reheat well are good choices.
What if some of them don't eat certain things?
Ask guests in advance about food they avoid or cannot eat. A mix of a vegetarian main and a side of rice or bread covers many needs.
How much should I make?
For a main dish, plan about a generous serving for each person and a little extra. Leftovers are usually welcome.
What if something burns?
Stay calm. Scrape off the burnt part if you can and serve the rest, or have a simple backup like bread, curd or fruit on hand.
Anything for the table setting?
Keep it simple: clean plates, water on the table and a little something to nibble while people arrive. A relaxed host makes everyone comfortable.
Describe a rooftop at night in exactly 11 words.
Stars freckle the sky while distant trains murmur below the rooftop.

Read this:

At the Dussehra mela in Delhi, Mahima could see only backs and elbows, and held Aditi Masi's hand so hard her knuckles went white. At the gate, Masi had crouched and said, "Say Papa's number." Mahima said all ten digits. "And if we lose each other?" "I go to the big ice-cream stall by the gate and tell the ice-cream uncle or a police aunty." Near the giant Ravan, crackers burst, people surged, and Masi's hand slipped away. Mahima's chest went tight; she wanted to cry and run. Instead she found the stall's blue umbrella and told the man there, "I'm lost. My papa's number is..." He dialled while she stood beside his cart. Ten minutes later Masi pushed through, breathless, and hugged her so hard her hair clip fell off.

Where had Mahima agreed to go if they got separated?
To the big ice-cream stall by the gate.
How did Mahima feel when Masi's hand slipped away?
She was frightened; her chest went tight and she wanted to cry and run.
What made Mahima safe once she was lost?
Practising Papa's number and a meeting place at the gate gave her something to do instead of panicking, so she went straight to the stall and asked for help.
What was it like for Aditi Masi during those ten minutes?
Aditi Masi was probably terrified while searching, and then deeply relieved, hugging Mahima so hard that the hair clip fell off.

Saturday morning, the week after Holi.
"Didi, don't worry. I'll finish the whole chemistry syllabus this weekend."
"Fourteen chapters, Nandini?" Vandana didi looked up from her laptop.
"Seven today, seven tomorrow. Easy."
"Last term you took four days for the organic chapters alone."
"That's because I had no plan then. Now I have a timetable." Nandini waved a chart coloured in six highlighters.
Sunday, ten at night.
"Didi, I've only done three."
"Three chapters?"
"I don't get it! I planned every hour. But the numericals took forever, and I kept checking answers, and then lunch, and..." Her voice cracked. "How did it take so long?"
"The same way it did last term."
"So what do I do? The test is Friday!"
"Tomorrow we time one chapter properly. Then we plan again, with real numbers."

How many chapters had Nandini finished by Sunday night?
Only three chapters.
How did Nandini feel on Sunday night, and why?
She felt shocked and upset, because her bright plan of seven chapters a day ignored how long chapters had taken her before.
What would you advise Nandini for the new plan?
Time one chapter honestly, use that and last term's experience to plan, and spread revision over more days with some slack.
How does Vandana didi see the weekend plan from the start?
Vandana is doubtful from the start, remembering the four days the organic chapters took, but stays kind and practical when the plan falls apart.

Read this:

At the village school in Moga, Amandeep was the loudest boy on the bench. When Eshaan missed his serve at the volleyball trial, Amandeep hooted, "My grandmother serves better!" and the others laughed. But when the PT master called his name, Amandeep stayed seated. "Volleyball is boring. I don't need trials. Everyone knows I'm the best." The master looked at him a long moment. After practice, Eshaan found him behind the water tank, flicking stones. "You were scared," Eshaan said. Amandeep started to deny it, then didn't. "What if I miss too? They'll laugh." "Like you laughed at me," Eshaan said. Then, more kindly: "Come early tomorrow. Just us. No one watching."

Where did Eshaan find Amandeep after practice?
Behind the water tank, flicking stones.
What was Amandeep feeling when he stayed seated?
He was scared of missing and being laughed at, hiding it behind boasting.
Why is Eshaan's offer a wise idea?
Practising early with no one watching gives Amandeep a safe chance to fail.
How did Eshaan feel when Amandeep hooted at his serve?
Eshaan was probably embarrassed and hurt, which is why he pointed it out later.
Why does a rumour spread so fast?

People pass surprising news on before checking it. Because people like to share surprising news, each person who hears it passes it on without checking whether it is true, and the story is often made more exciting on the way.
Has the date for the big fair in town been announced?
I don't know, since I can't see recent announcements. The town council's page or posters near the market usually carry the dates.

- What does zealous mean in simple words?
- How much pocket money does my friend get?
- Is it "sicence" or "science"?
- Is there a mistake here? My father is doctor.
- Why do teachers ask students to revise a little every day?

1. Zealous is an adjective that means full of eager energy for a cause.
2. I can't check that, since I can't see your friend's family. Ask your friend, if the topic is not private for them.
3. It is "science", with "sc" at the start.
4. Corrected: My father is a doctor. Why: a job title after "is" takes the article "a".
5. Short daily revision works well. Because the brain keeps facts better when we go over them again and again than when we read them once.

A group of parents get together and decide to hire a private school teacher to quit his job and teach their children.  His former job paid 45,000 per year and they offered him a 20% raise.  If there are 9 kids how much does each parent have to pay?

His raise was 45,000*.2=$9,000
So his new wage is 45,000+9,000=$54,000
So they each have to pay him 54,000/9=$6,000 per year
The answer is 6000.

Read this:

I'm Ishita, and last winter I learned something about being angry. Papa and Dada kept fighting about selling the old house in the village. They shouted so loud the neighbours' dog barked. I hated it. My whole body felt hot and fizzy, and once I nearly threw my water bottle at the wall.
Instead I took my football down to the back wall of our building. Left foot, right foot, bang, bang, bang. I counted: fifty, a hundred. When I kicked hard, the ball came back hard, so I had to be quick and careful.
After a while the fizz went out of my arms and legs. I came back up tired and sweaty, and I could tell Mumma how I felt.
Now I can do two hundred passes without missing. Coach picked me for the under-eleven team.

Where did Ishita take the football?
Down to the back wall of the building.
How did Ishita feel during Papa and Dada's fights, and how can you tell?
Angry and upset; Ishita's whole body felt hot and fizzy, and once there was an urge to throw the water bottle at the wall.
Which choice turned Ishita's anger into something useful?
Taking the football to the wall instead of throwing the bottle; the kicking used up the fizz safely and built a real skill.
How might Mumma see Ishita coming back tired and ready to talk?
Mumma probably feels relieved that Ishita found a safe way through the anger, and glad they can talk about the fighting calmly.

From the top of a building, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower and the angle of depression of its foot are given. Find the distance d between them and the height of the tower (metres).
a) building 7 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 45 degrees
b) building 10 m, elevation 30 degrees, depression 45 degrees
c) building 20 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 45 degrees
d) building 15 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 30 degrees
e) building 12 m, elevation 45 degrees, depression 30 degrees
f) building 8 m, elevation 30 degrees, depression 60 degrees
g) building 30 m, elevation 45 degrees, depression 60 degrees
h) building 6 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 60 degrees
i) building 50 m, elevation 30 degrees, depression 30 degrees
j) building 9 m, elevation 45 degrees, depression 45 degrees

a) d = 7; tower 7(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 19.12
b) d = 10; tower 10(sqrt3 + 3)/3 ~ 15.77
c) d = 20; tower 20(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 54.64
d) d = 15sqrt3 ~ 25.98; tower 60
e) d = 12sqrt3 ~ 20.78; tower 12(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 32.78
f) d = 8sqrt3/3 ~ 4.62; tower 32/3
g) d = 10sqrt3 ~ 17.32; tower 10(sqrt3 + 3) ~ 47.32
h) d = 2sqrt3 ~ 3.46; tower 12
i) d = 50sqrt3 ~ 86.60; tower 100
j) d = 9; tower 18
In a game, five children score 480, 408, 840, 804 and 48 points. Write the scores from the highest to the lowest.

Answer: 840, 804, 480, 408, 48.

Greatest to smallest is called descending order (like going down stairs). Look for the most hundreds first: 840 and 804 have 8 hundreds; 840 is bigger because it has 4 tens. Then 480 and 408. Last is 48, which has no hundreds at all.
A gardener had 30 mangoes on a tree and plucked 14 of them. How many are still on the tree?
16. Because 30 - 14 = 16, so 16 are left.

Science club mentor's note, Class 10

This year's science fair team was mixed on purpose: Wasim from the old city, Seema from the new housing colony, and two others from the villages nearby. Early on, Wasim said Seema was "stuck up" and Seema said the village boys "wouldn't understand".
Their project, a low-cost water purifier, needed everyone: Wasim's knowledge of pipes from his father's shop, Seema's chemistry, the village boys' experience with well water.
By month two, they were arguing about the filter, not about each other. At the fair, they won first prize. Seema told me, "I thought they were different. They're just my team."
I have noticed this does more than any talk.

What was the team's project?
A low-cost water purifier.
How did Seema feel about her teammates by the end?
She felt close to them and included, saying they are just her team.
Why did the water purifier project reduce prejudice?
It needed everyone's skills, so the team had to depend on each other, turning 'them' into 'us'.
How might Wasim see Seema after winning together?
Wasim likely sees her as a teammate rather than stuck up.
A potter in our neighbourhood is holding a clay workshop for children on Sunday at 3 pm. Write an invitation for parents, about 45 words.

Dear Parents,
Your child is invited to a clay workshop this Sunday at 3 pm. A potter from our neighbourhood will help the children enjoy working with clay. It will be a messy and happy afternoon. Please send your child ready to have fun.

Seema had finished her engineering degree in May. It was now October. On her laptop was a spreadsheet: twelve job openings, four master's programmes, two gap-year volunteering posts. Columns for salary, city, “regret risk.”
She hadn't applied to any.
Her friend Rukmini visited with jalebis. “Still the spreadsheet?”
“I just want to be sure. If I take a job in Bengaluru, I can't do the master's. If I do the master's, I'll lose two years' salary. If I volunteer, I'll fall behind.”
“And if you don't choose?”
“Then I'm keeping all doors open.”
Rukmini pointed at the screen. Six of the deadlines had turned red. “They're closing, Seema. Not choosing is choosing.”
Seema stared at the red cells. For the first time, she felt the fear shift from making the wrong choice to making none at all.

How many job openings were on Seema's spreadsheet?
There were twelve job openings on the spreadsheet.
Why did Seema feel that not applying kept all doors open?
She was afraid each option was risky and irreversible, so not choosing felt safer to her.
What could Seema do now that the deadlines are turning red?
She could pick two or three strong options by a set date and apply, accepting that no choice is perfectly safe.
How does Rukmini see Seema's spreadsheet?
Rukmini sees that options are closing and that not choosing is itself a choice.

Read this:

Monday. Rashmi Ma'am noticed Pranav hadn't answered a single question all day. At lunch, he asked her three times, "Will my mother come at 2:30? Are you sure?" His eyes filled when the bell rang.
Wednesday. She didn't tell him "Don't be silly," but she didn't keep repeating "yes" either. She sat beside him and asked in a soft voice, "What's the worry that comes at lunch?" Pranav whispered that last month his mother had been late and he'd waited alone in the office.
Friday. Rashmi Ma'am met his parents after school. Together they made a plan: a card in his pocket with the pickup time, one check with the teacher at lunch, not five, and a promise that someone would always wait with him. Pranav held the card all through maths, but he answered two questions.

What time did Pranav keep asking about?
What was Rashmi Ma'am feeling when she chose her words on Wednesday?
She felt concerned and careful, wanting to take his worry seriously without either dismissing it or feeding it with endless reassurance.
Which of Rashmi Ma'am's steps would help other adults noticing a worried child?
A gentle question in a calm voice to find the cause, then a clear plan made with the family, like the pickup card and one lunchtime check.
What is it like for Pranav as the end of the day approaches?
He feels anxious and sad, afraid of waiting alone again, which is why he keeps asking.
Write a thank-you note from the whole class (Class 6C) to our teacher Mr. Das after a wonderful school trip to the museum. About 45 words.

Dear Mr. Das,
Thank you for taking us to the museum. We had a wonderful trip and learnt so much. You answered our questions patiently and made the visit great fun. We will remember it for a long time. Please take us again soon!
Your students,
Class 6C

Read this:

Wasim, you think you're too quiet for meetings? Sit. When Parveen ma'am, as you all call me, joined this firm at twenty-three, I didn't say a word in a meeting for eleven months. I had ideas. I wrote them in my notebook afterwards, when it was too late.
Then my manager, a tall woman called Mrs Fernandes, stopped me in the corridor. “Bring one point,” she said. “Written on a card. Say it in the first ten minutes, before you lose your nerve.”
The next Monday my hands were cold. I said my one line about the delivery schedule, badly, too fast. Nobody laughed. Someone wrote it on the whiteboard.
After that it was one point every week. Then two. I learned to send a short email afterwards, three lines, what was agreed. Start with one card, Wasim.

How long did Parveen stay silent in meetings?
She didn't say a word in a meeting for eleven months.
What was young Parveen feeling before speaking that Monday?
She was nervous, with cold hands, but she felt determined to say her one point.
What choice in the story helped Parveen most, and why?
Following Mrs Fernandes's advice to bring one written point and say it early, because it made speaking small and manageable.
How might Mrs Fernandes have seen young Parveen before that corridor talk?
She probably saw a capable junior whose ideas were being wasted by silence, which is why she stepped in.
Jabu shares 63 toffees equally among 7 friends. How many does each friend get?
9. Because 7 x 9 = 63, so each one gets 9 with none left over.

Read this:

I was minding the buffaloes by the canal when the kids from the village school came by. Sharmila, the boldest of them, climbed onto the concrete lip. "Who's jumping? It's so hot." The water was high and rushing from the open sluice gate. Gurpreet stood a little apart. I couldn't tell what he felt; he kept glancing at the current. Then he clapped. "Plank-off! Right here on the grass. Whoever falls first fetches water for everyone from the hand pump." Sharmila rolled her eyes but got down. Five of them lay on their elbows, giggling and shaking. Gurpreet won. Sharmila demanded a rematch, and they all walked off toward the school ground to have it.

What would the first child to fall have to do?
They would fetch water for everyone from the hand pump.
What might Gurpreet's glances at the current suggest?
They suggest he felt uneasy or worried about the rushing water, though the narrator could not be sure what he felt.
What could the narrator have done if the children had jumped anyway?
The narrator was close by and could call them back from the edge and fetch an adult at once, because high water from a sluice is dangerous.
How does Sharmila seem to take the plank contest?
She rolls her eyes at first, but she gets down and then demands a rematch, so she seems to enjoy the competition anyway.

Monday. At 8:40 Pallavi's phone lit up: "Stuck at audit. Late. Eat." She put the second plate back in the cupboard. Late. Again. She thought of the anniversary dinner in March, the Diwali party he missed, the night her father was ill.
Wednesday. Waiting for the kettle, she scrolled back through a year of messages and counted: eleven "late"s. The Monday text now looked like one bead on a long string. When Rohit came home on time and asked about her day, she said "fine" and kept her eyes on the television.
Saturday. Over breakfast Rohit explained: the auditors had found a missing file, and his boss had kept everyone till ten. It was a reasonable story. Pallavi heard it and nodded, but inside, Monday had already become every Monday, and one explanation could not undo that.

How many "late" messages did Pallavi count?
She counted eleven "late"s in a year of messages.
Why did Pallavi say "fine" when Rohit came home on time?
She felt hurt and resentful, reading the Monday text as one more piece of a long pattern of being left waiting.
What small step could help Pallavi before the story hardens further?
She could tell Rohit plainly that the late nights have started to feel like a pattern and ask to talk about them, rather than going cold.
What is it like for Rohit on Wednesday?
He comes home on time and asks about her day but gets a flat "fine", likely puzzled about what he did wrong.

Read this:

On Salma's first day at the new school, the plan was clear in the head: sit next to the girl with the green hair band, then say "Hi, I'm Salma. Can I sit here?" All through the maths class, Salma rehearsed it, word by word. By break time, the sentence had become so big that it felt impossible. Salma ate lunch slowly at the end of a bench. Nobody came. Then Joseph, from the next row, sat down two seats away and said, "Are you new? I remember my first day." Salma's shoulders came down. "Yes," said Salma. "I kept meaning to say hi."

What was Salma's plan for the first day?
To sit next to the girl with the green hair band and say "Hi, I'm Salma. Can I sit here?"
Why did the rehearsed sentence start to feel impossible to Salma?
Salma kept rehearsing so long that the sentence felt bigger and scarier, showing a fear of being rejected.
What could Salma try next time to avoid waiting so long?
Say the simple hello early, before the rehearsal grows, since most people welcome a first hello.
What might Joseph have wanted when sitting down two seats away and saying "Are you new?"
To be kind and welcoming, remembering what a first day is like, and to start a conversation without pushing.
What is written in my diary from last Monday?
I can't see your diary, so I don't know. Open it to that page and read.

How old will Wemmick's father be, and what does he think of doing?

"Both flourishing thankye," said Wemmick, "and particularly the Aged. He's in wonderful feather. He'll be eighty-two next birthday. I have a notion of firing eighty-two times, if the neighbourhood shouldn't complain, and that cannon of mine should prove equal to the pressure. However, this is not London talk. Where do you think I am going to?"
He will be eighty-two next birthday. Wemmick thinks of firing his cannon eighty-two times, if the neighbours do not complain and the cannon can take it.

James is sitting outside, counting how many people go past him in vehicles. He has counted 52 vehicles so far today. He saw 12 trucks, a couple of buses, twice as many taxis, some motorbikes, and 30 cars. If the trucks held 2 people each, the buses held 15 people each, the taxis held 2 people each, the motorbikes held 1 person each, and the cars held 3 people each, how many passengers has James seen today?

In the trucks, James saw 12 * 2 = 24 people.
In the buses, he saw 2 * 15 = 30 people.
He saw 2 * 2 = 4 taxis go past him.
Therefore, he saw 4 * 2 = 8 people in the taxis.
In the cars, he saw 30 * 3 = 90 people.
Since we know how many vehicles James saw in total, we know that he saw 52 - 12 - 2 - 4 - 30 = 4 motorbikes.
So, he saw 4 * 1 = 4 people on motorbikes.
He has therefore seen a total of 24 + 30 + 8 + 90 + 4 = 156 people.
The answer is 156.

Read this:

I'm Aparna and I'm nine. Last Sunday I lost my chess match to Akash in the second round of the school tournament. He took my queen in ten moves and I didn't even see it coming.
In the car I was waiting for Amma to ask 'Did you win?' She didn't. She asked, 'What did you learn today?'
I said I learned to look at his bishop before I move my queen.
Then she asked, 'What part was fun?' I said the first round, when I did the fork with my knight.
Only after that she asked the score. I said I lost, and she just said, 'Okay. I lose things at work too. We'll practise that bishop trap.'
I thought she would be upset. She wasn't. So I wasn't so upset either. We practised it on Monday.

Who beat Aparna in the second round?
Akash beat Aparna in the second round.
What was Aparna expecting in the car, and how did Aparna feel afterwards?
Aparna expected Amma to ask about winning and to be upset, and felt calmer after seeing that Amma wasn't 🙂
What worked about the order of Amma's questions?
Asking about learning and fun before the score helped Aparna think about what went well and what to fix, not just the loss.
How might Amma see losing, based on what she said?
Amma sees losing as ordinary and fixable, something that happens at work too, and shows that by planning practice.
Is "tortuous" a misspelling of "torturous"?

No, they are different words. "Tortuous" means full of twists and turns, and "torturous" means causing great pain or suffering.
Examples: A tortuous mountain road led to the village. The wait was torturous.
Rahul says, "3 x 4 means 3 + 4, so it is 7." What is wrong?

Answer: 3 x 4 means 3 groups of 4, which is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, not 3 + 4.

This is the most common mix-up. Say the sign as words: "3 groups of 4". Make it with counters: 3 cups, 4 in each: 12. Then show 3 + 4 with counters: only 7. Adding joins two numbers once; multiplying adds the same number again and again.

Make this letter more formal.

Dear Pranav,
This week I have two decisions, and I think they need different speeds. The first is a monthly membership at the new climbing gym. If I hate it, I can stop next month, so I signed up today. The second is the two-year agreement for the flat near your office. That one I cannot undo cheaply, so I am slowing down. Can you visit it with me on Saturday evening and tell me what you notice? I will also ask the current tenant how the water and the noise are. I will decide by Wednesday. Thank you for being the person I want to ask. Charu

Dear Pranav,
I am facing two decisions this week, and I believe they call for different speeds. The first is a monthly membership at the new climbing gym. As it can be cancelled next month if I dislike it, I enrolled today. The second is the two-year agreement for the flat near your office. As it cannot be undone cheaply, I am proceeding with care. Would you be able to visit the flat with me on Saturday evening and tell me your impressions? I shall also ask the current tenant about the water and the noise. I will decide by Wednesday. I am grateful to have you to ask.
Yours sincerely,
Charu

Dear Mohit,

Instead I remembered what we discussed after the training: a strained voice like that usually means the person is very worked up, not that they are attacking me. "You wanted to talk?" Tarun asked, sitting down on the terrace step.
"Yes. No. Okay, yes." Nilesh rubbed his neck. "I like you, Tarun. More than a friend. I thought you should know."
"Thank you for telling me. That took guts." Tarun paused. "I don't feel that way about you. I'm sorry. It isn't anything you did, I just don't."
"Right." Nilesh stared at his shoes. "Okay. That stings a bit."
"I know. I won't pretend it doesn't."
"Is there any chance later? If I wait?"
"No, and I don't want you waiting on me. That wouldn't be fair."
Nilesh laughed shakily. "You could have said maybe."
"I could have. But maybe would only make things easier for me, not you."
Nilesh nodded slowly. "I'll need some distance for a while."
"Take it. I'll still say hello if you want me to."

Where did Nilesh tell Tarun how he felt?
They were on the terrace step.
What is Nilesh feeling when he asks, "Is there any chance later?"
He is hurting and still hoping a little. He admits it stings, and asks whether waiting could change things.
How could Nilesh look after himself now?
He can take the distance he asked for, stop waiting on Tarun, let himself feel disappointed, and lean on other friends. 🤍
Why did Tarun refuse to say maybe?
Tarun felt a maybe would leave Nilesh waiting and would only ease Tarun's own discomfort, so a clear no was the fairer answer.
Change "my" to "our" and "I" to "we": I decorated the door with flowers, and my sister helped me.

Wednesday: She puts one block on top of another. It wobbles and falls. She pushes it away.

She set two blocks on top.

What would change if Mridul had built the tower for her every time?

My name's Noor, and in Class 10 a boy called Thomas joined our section in the middle of term. I didn't like him. He answered every question, he tapped his pen, and he had a laugh like a bicycle horn. The university housing chat in Prague had over three hundred students. Emil posted a clip of a classmate, Tomas, stammering through a presentation, with a mocking caption. Laughing faces piled up underneath.
Ivan saw it on the tram. He frowned. Somebody from Tomas's course will report it, he thought. There are hundreds of us.
Two stops later, nothing had changed. The clip had more views, not fewer.
Ivan reported the post to the chat moderators and wrote to Emil privately: “Please take that down. It's not fair to him.” Then he messaged Tomas: “Saw the clip. That's not okay. You alright?”
Tomas replied an hour later: “Thanks. Nobody else said anything.” The moderators removed the clip that evening.

Where was Ivan when he saw the clip?
He saw it on the tram.
What was Ivan thinking when he first saw the post?
He felt uncomfortable but assumed someone from Tomas's course would report it, since there were hundreds of students.
What small steps did Ivan take, and why were they useful?
He reported the post, asked Emil privately to take it down and checked on Tomas, which were quick, safe ways to help.
How might Tomas have felt when nobody else said anything?
He likely felt hurt and alone, and grateful that at least one person reached out.

Sabina, twenty-five, was a junior site engineer on a new metro station in Mumbai's Andheri. Every morning at seven she did the same small things. Before the safety walk she put her phone in her locker; the scaffolding tags and harness checks got her full eyes. When the crane operator came to talk about a wobbly outrigger, she turned her whole body toward him and didn't glance at anything else. The lifting plan for the big girder she never signed alone: she and Bhupen, the other engineer, checked it separately and compared. Bhupen once teased her. "You don't trust yourself?"
"I trust myself," Sabina said. "I don't trust my attention at four in the afternoon."
Last week his check caught a wrong figure she had copied from an old sheet. On the drive home, her phone rode in the boot.

Where does Sabina put her phone before the safety walk?
In her locker.
What does Sabina mean when she says she doesn't trust her attention at four in the afternoon?
She knows that even a careful person's attention slips when tired, so she feels safer building in checks than relying on effort alone.
Which of Sabina's habits proved its worth last week, and why?
Having Bhupen check the lifting plan separately; his check caught a wrong figure she had copied before it could cause harm.
How might the crane operator feel when Sabina turns her whole body toward him?
He would likely feel taken seriously and more willing to report problems, since she clearly listens instead of half-looking at a phone.

Friday. The college magazine wanted Lokesh's article on the new bus route by Tuesday. He opened a blank page at nine and stared at it. At eleven he had one sentence, and he had deleted it six times. He went to bed feeling sick.
Saturday. Vandana, the senior editor, found him in the library. "You're editing before anything exists," she said. "Write the worst version. Twenty minutes. No deleting." He set a timer. It was clumsy and repetitive, but at the end there were three pages. She told him not to look at it again till Monday.
Monday. Lokesh opened the file with coffee and read it like a stranger's. He could suddenly see the two good paragraphs and the four lazy ones. He cut a page, moved the best line to the top and sent it to Vandana by noon. She sent back one comment: "Now it sounds like you."

How many times had Lokesh deleted his one sentence by eleven?
He had deleted it six times.
What was Lokesh feeling on Friday night?
Lokesh felt frightened and stuck, going to bed feeling sick after two hours with a blank page.
Which step made the biggest difference, and why?
Writing the worst version for twenty minutes with no deleting, and then waiting till Monday, because making and judging were finally kept apart.
How might Vandana see Lokesh's final article?
Vandana seems pleased; her comment "Now it sounds like you" shows she thinks the rest and the edit brought out his own voice.

The older phones most of their customers used.

How does Salma feel about Farhan's steady job?
Salma feels relieved and grateful, saying she never worries now.

After 20 trips, the total weight of onions transported to the store is 20 trips * 500 kg/trip = 10000 kgs

Pallavi had been back in Pune from her exchange term in Utrecht for a week when she watched her classmate Jagdish invite her aunt to a birthday. "Maybe, we'll see," said her aunt with a warm smile. Jagdish nodded happily and said he would keep a chair. Pallavi bit her lip: at home a soft maybe is sometimes a gentle no. In Utrecht her host family had said, "No, I don't want to," straight out, and at first she had felt slapped. Now she saw that neither was rude in its own place. She quietly told Jagdish, "Maybe can be a kind way of saying no. You could ask her again another way." Jagdish laughed and thanked her.

Where had Pallavi spent her exchange term?
Pallavi spent her exchange term in Utrecht.
What did Pallavi feel when her aunt said maybe, and why?
Uneasy and a little worried for Jagdish, because a warm maybe can be a gentle no, and Pallavi had just learned the bluntness abroad.
How could Pallavi help Jagdish read both styles?
By explaining that maybe can be a kind way of saying no and suggesting he ask again another way, without calling either style rude.
How might Jagdish have felt hearing maybe, we'll see?

"It's a long quiet, isn't it? Would you like the soft blanket?" Clara nodded and hugged it. Rosa sat nearby without a word, and Clara's eyes slowly closed.

What did Rosa whisper at nap time?

Restless or unable to settle. The humming may be her way of soothing herself.

Why can we hear a person talking in the next room even though we cannot see them?

Sound can bend around corners and pass through thin walls, but light cannot. Because sound slips through gaps and shakes thin walls, while light travels straight and is blocked by the wall, we hear without seeing.

Asking for specifics in one-to-ones and checking with others, so decisions rest on what happened rather than on who is hero or villain this week.

Sabina hummed while stacking cups and her grandfather hummed back. messages.content: A group of monkeys keeps visiting our terrace and taking the fruit we leave out.
Monkeys quickly learn where food is. The best way to stop it is to avoid leaving fruit or snacks outside.
My neighbour says we should scare them off.
I'd avoid chasing or hitting them, since they can become aggressive and may bite. Simply remove the food and keep doors closed, and they will usually lose interest.
What if they come inside?
Stay calm and don't stare at them or try to grab anything. Give them space to leave and call your local forest or municipal office if they keep coming.
Okay, we'll stop leaving food outside.
That's the best step. A clean terrace gives them no reason to return.

"Papa, doodh!"
"Milk? Here you go, Siddharth."
"Mo-o-re dudh!"
"More milk? Okay."

Siddharth waved at the dog. "Bye, doggy! Bye, kukur!"

Tushar laughed and told him that it was kukur in Bangla, kutta in Hindi and dog in English, and that he had all three. Nani, who was visiting, shook her head and said that he should stick to one, and asked Tushar whether he agreed. Tushar told her that Siddharth would, because he was only two and his brain was still sorting. Siddharth waved at the dog and said goodbye to it in two languages.

Ali, Peter, and Joey were fishing. The fish Ali caught weighed, in sum, twice as much as the fish that Peter caught. Joey caught 1 kg more fish than Peter. Together the three of them caught 25 kg of fish. How many kilograms did Ali catch?

Let x be the weight of the fish that Peter caught. Then Ali and Joey caught 2*x and x+1 kg of fish, respectively.
So, x+ 2*x + x+1 =25
So, 4*x = 25 - 1 = 24
So, x = 6
Therefore, Ali caught 2*x = 2*6 = 12 kg of fish
The answer is 12.

In a certain country store, there are three kinds of bottled drinks. A cola, which costs $3, a juice for $1.5, and water for $1 per bottle. One day the store was able to sell 15 bottles of cola, 25 bottles of water, and 12 bottles of juice. How much did the shop earn?

15 bottles of cola is a cost of 15 * 3 = $45.
12 bottles of juice make up to 12 * 1.5 = $18.
As each of the 25 sold water bottles was $1, the shop made a total of 45 + 18 + 25 = $88.
The answer is 88.

I sat there with this huge weight. For an hour I was ready to call back and say I'd stay.
Then I did the thing my counsellor taught me. I asked, "Did I actually wrong her?" I'm Chetan, I'm twenty-four, I found a good job, and I'll be a two-hour flight away. That's not a wrong. Her loneliness is real. My leaving isn't a crime.
So I called back. I said, "Ma, I love you. I'm still going. I'll call every Sunday, and I'll fly home for Diwali." She cried. I stayed calm. I didn't argue about who sacrificed what.
It still hurts. But I'm going.

When did Chetan promise to call his mother?
Every Sunday.
How did Chetan feel after his mother hung up?
Chetan felt a huge weight of guilt, almost ready to call back and stay.
What helped Chetan separate real guilt from pressure?
Asking whether any wrong had actually been done, then keeping the decision while offering care: Sunday calls and coming home for Diwali.
How might Chetan's mother be feeling?
Chetan's mother is probably lonely and scared of growing old alone, which is real, even if her words put pressure on Chetan.

Read this:

Resident assistant's note, Block B, fourth floor. Written by Lalremsiami.
Seema, who shares my room, got her internal assessment back today: a low mark she felt was unfair, because the faculty member had lost her lab file. At eight, a courier came to our door with a parcel for her. The courier had the wrong room number on the slip. Seema shouted, "Can't anyone do anything right?" loud enough for the corridor to hear. The courier apologised and left quickly. I didn't correct her in front of the courier, though I wanted to. I thanked the courier at the stairs. At ten, when Seema was calmer, I said, "The courier got a lot of what the lab file deserved today." She was silent. Then: "I know. I'll say sorry if they come back." Next week I'll check whether she wants help writing to the faculty.

What had the faculty member lost?
Seema's lab file.
Why did Lalremsiami wait until ten to say anything?
Lalremsiami felt uneasy about the outburst, but judged that Seema would hear a quiet remark better once calmer than a correction in front of the courier.
What further step does Lalremsiami plan, and why is it helpful?
To offer help writing to the faculty, which aims Seema's anger at the real problem, the lost file.
How might the courier have seen the scene?
The courier probably felt startled and embarrassed, apologising for a small slip while being shouted at for something else.
Why does lemon juice stop cut apples from browning?
The juice slows the colour change. Because its acid and vitamin C interfere with the reaction that turns the flesh brown, the slices stay pale longer.
At the temple one bell rings every 4 minutes and another every 6 minutes. They ring together at 9:00. When do they next ring together?

Answer: At 9:12. 12 is the LCM of 4 and 6.

List the minutes after 9:00 when each bell rings. First bell: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 (multiples of 4). Second bell: 6, 12, 18, 24 (multiples of 6). The COMMON multiples are 12, 24, ... The smallest is 12, the lowest common multiple, so they ring together 12 minutes later, at 9:12, and then again at 9:24.

Read this:

Dear Ishita Apa,
Remember I told you in June about the new boy, Kunal, who sits behind me and hums all through maths? I said he was the most annoying person alive. Well. We take the same bus, so I see him twice a day, plus six periods. At first I sat as far away as I could. Then the bus got crowded and I had to sit next to him. Then we were put in the same lab group.
I don't know when it happened, but last week I saved him a samosa at break without thinking. He still hums, but now it just sounds like Kunal. Nothing special happened. I just saw him every day.
Don't laugh.
Imran

What does Kunal do all through maths?
He hums.
What does saving a samosa suggest Imran now feels?
Imran feels friendly and fond towards Kunal, without having noticed the change happening.
What might Imran learn about first impressions?
That seeing someone every day can soften dislike, so a first judgement isn't final.
How might Kunal have felt when Imran sat far away?
Kunal might have felt a bit left out or puzzled at first.

metadata.subtype: Warming to a classmate through daily contact [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The fans were off because of the power cut, and the classroom was hot and sticky. Ma'am was already cross about the noise when she held up Dhruv's notebook.
"Three pages blank. Dhruv, stand up. Tell everyone why."
Dhruv stood, ears red, and said nothing.
Tanvir, at the next desk, felt his own face burn. His stomach twisted. He looked down at his shoes and pulled his sleeves over his hands, as if he were the one standing. He wanted to shout, "His grandfather is in hospital!" but his throat stuck.
When the bell rang, Tanvir walked beside Dhruv to the tap without talking. Finally he said, "I felt it too. Like it was me."
Dhruv splashed his face. "I know. You went all red."

Why were the fans off in the classroom?
The fans were off because of the power cut.
What was Tanvir feeling while Dhruv stood in front of the class?
He felt ashamed and embarrassed as if it were happening to him; his face burned, his stomach twisted and he looked down at his shoes.
How could Tanvir help Dhruv if something like this happens again?
He could stay beside Dhruv as he did, and later, with Dhruv's permission, quietly tell the teacher about the grandfather so she understands.
What is it like for Dhruv to notice Tanvir going red?
Dhruv seems to feel less alone, knowing his friend felt the shame with him.

metadata.subtype: Embarrassed for a friend who is called out [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

"The drops worked," Pallavi said, stirring her tea in the office pantry. "Two weeks and my wheezing's almost gone. I'm thinking of dropping the inhaler."
Karthik put his cup down. "What else changed in these two weeks?"
"Nothing. Well, the monsoon ended. And I moved desks, away from the AC vent."
"So three things. The drops, the dry weather, the new desk."
"But I felt better after the drops."
"You did. That's real. But how would you feel now if you'd skipped the drops? The monsoon still ends." He shrugged. "One person, one time, can't tell us. You'd need lots of people, some with drops and some without, compared properly."
"You sound like a textbook."
"Maybe. But please don't stop the inhaler on your own. Ask your doctor first, and take the drops bottle with you."
Pallavi sighed. "Fine. I'll call the clinic after lunch."

Where did Pallavi move her desk?
Pallavi moved desks, away from the AC vent.
Why does Karthik worry when Pallavi mentions dropping the inhaler?
Karthik is worried because three things changed at once, and stopping a treatment on the strength of one before-and-after story could be risky.
What does Karthik ask Pallavi to do, and why is it the wise step?
Not to stop the inhaler alone but to ask the doctor first with the drops bottle, because a doctor should judge a real breathing problem.
How does Pallavi feel about Karthik's questions?
Pallavi is a bit exasperated, calling him a textbook, but agrees to call the clinic after lunch.

Read this:

"Gargi, you remember the day I got the offer from the big news channel? Everyone at home was on the phone to every relative. My face on TV, my name on the screen, that salary. My father kept saying, 'Our boy Harsha, on the news!'
And I said no. I took the job at the community radio station in Wardha instead. Farmers' shows, a slot for kids to read their poems, very little money.
I won't pretend I wasn't terrified. The night I emailed the channel, my hands were cold and I kept thinking, what if I'm wasting my whole life? But when I pressed send, something in my chest went quiet. Like a door I'd been holding shut finally closed.
Papa didn't talk to me properly for a month. Now he calls in to the Sunday show under a fake name. I know it's him.
But when I'm on air, I feel like I'm in the right place."

Where did Harsha take a job instead?
At the community radio station in Wardha.
What was Harsha feeling on the night he emailed the channel?
He felt both terror that he might be wasting his life, with cold hands, and a surprising quiet in his chest once he pressed send.
What choice did Harsha make, and what shows it fits him?
He chose the community radio job over the famous channel, and feeling he is in the right place on air shows the path suits him.
How did Harsha's father react, and what might his fake-name calls show?
His father was upset and distant for a month, but calling in to the Sunday show suggests he has come to value his son's work.

Read this:

Week one. The street-play team of four met in the college canteen to split the work. Jagdish took the script. Preeti took costumes and permissions. Nobody wrote anything down. "We'll just remember," Jagdish said.
Week three. Rehearsals ran late every night. Jagdish rewrote scene two at 1 a.m. and thought, I'm basically carrying this. Across town, Preeti was stitching the last banner after getting the police permission stamped, thinking the exact same thing about herself.
Week five, the day after the performance. Their mentor asked each of them to write privately what share of the work they'd done. Jagdish wrote 50%. Preeti wrote 45%. The other two wrote 40% and 35%. The mentor added it up on the whiteboard: 170%. Everyone laughed, then went quiet. "Next time," Preeti said slowly, "we keep a shared task log. With dates."

What did the four shares add up to on the whiteboard?
They added up to 170%.
Why did Jagdish feel like the one 'basically carrying' the play?
Jagdish felt tired and overburdened, seeing every late night spent rewriting the script but not Preeti stitching banners or chasing permissions, so that work felt like most of it.
What choice did Preeti suggest after the numbers were added, and why would it help?
She suggested a shared task log with dates, so next time everyone's work is visible on paper instead of each person remembering mostly their own.
How might the other two members have felt when the mentor wrote 170%?
They may have been amused and then uncomfortable, realising they too had quietly believed their own share was bigger than the others could see.

1) How would you explain "vestibule" to a child?
2) Can you fix my sentence? One of my friend is a pilot.
3) What was the headline of the newspaper yesterday?
4) Why do we compare two shops before buying something big?
5) Is "happend" spelled right?

1. Vestibule means a small entrance hall just inside a building. It is a noun.
2. Corrected: One of my friends is a pilot. Why: after "one of", the noun is plural.
3. I don't know; I can't see yesterday's papers. A library or the newspaper's website keeps old issues.
4. Comparing shows the differences between them. Because shops can offer different quality and cost, we can see which suits us best.
5. No, it is "happened". The past tense ends in "-ed" and keeps the "e".

Read this:

I'm Jeevan. In our second year we were five people sharing a co-living flat in Bengaluru, and I noticed the pattern with Irawati before anyone said it aloud. She took rides in Kiran's scooter, ate the parathas Meera's mother sent, used my printer for every assignment. When it was her turn to buy cooking gas, she "forgot". Twice. Nobody confronted her. Instead, things just stopped. Meera started hiding the paratha box in her room. Kiran said he was "going the other way" every time Irawati needed a ride. And one night, when Irawati asked to print again, Meera said, loudly, "Printer's only for people who buy paper." Everyone went quiet. I didn't say anything either. Looking back, we all punished her with silence and hints for months before anyone just talked to her.

What did Irawati "forget" to do twice?
She forgot to buy cooking gas when it was her turn.
What does Jeevan feel now, looking back on how the flat treated Irawati?
Jeevan seems uneasy, noticing that everyone, including Jeevan, punished her with silence and hints instead of speaking to her directly.
What could the flatmates have done before hiding things and making pointed comments?
They could have sat down with Irawati early and asked her to share costs and chores fairly, giving her a clear chance to change.
How might Irawati have experienced the flat after people started withdrawing?
She may have felt shut out and confused, noticing rides and food disappear without anyone telling her why.

Five years ago, there were 500 old books in the library. Two years ago, the librarian bought 300 books. Last year, the librarian bought 100 more books than she had bought the previous year. This year, the librarian donated 200 of the library's old books. How many books are in the library now?

Last year the librarian bought 300 + 100 = 400 books.
Thus, there were 500 + 300 + 400 = 1200 books as of last year.
Therefore, there are 1200 - 200 = 1000 books now in the library.
The answer is 1000.

What does the speaker promise in this passage?

"I'm only a rough fellow, who hasn't, perhaps, lived as a man should to win such a distinction, but I swear to you by all that I hold sacred and dear that, should the time ever come, I shall not flinch from the duty that you have set us. And I promise you, too, that I shall make all certain, for if I am only doubtful I shall take it that the time has come!"
He promises not to shrink from the duty given to the group. He will make sure before he acts, but if he is only doubtful, he will take it that the time has come.
Why do we say excuse me when we pass in front of someone?
It shows we know we are disturbing them. Because stepping through their space without a word feels rude, and the phrase tells them we mean no disrespect.
Give me a sentence about autumn that names three colours.
Autumn leaves turn red, orange and yellow before they fall.
Write this recipe step as plain instructions: The onions should be fried until they are golden, after which the tomatoes may be added.
Fry the onions until they are golden. Then add the tomatoes.

Read this:

The school trip bus was crawling through traffic, and Ma'am sat right at the front with her headphones in, listening for the guide's calls. At the back, Kunal grabbed Bittu's cap and tossed it around. "Catch it, baby!" Bittu's face crumpled under his fringe. Shreya, two rows ahead, felt her chest go tight. She wanted to say stop. But last month Kunal had poured water in Rupal's bag just for saying "leave it." Nazia, beside Shreya, laughed loudly, then whispered, "I'm only laughing so he won't start on us." Two boys joined in the throwing. Everyone else looked out of the window. Shreya looked at the front. Surely someone would tell Ma'am. Nobody did. The bus crawled on, and so did the game.

What did Kunal grab from Bittu?
He grabbed Bittu's cap and tossed it around.
What was Shreya feeling as she watched?
She felt sorry for Bittu and wanted to say stop, but she was afraid Kunal would target her the way he had targeted Rupal.
What small step could one of the bystanders take right now?
Shreya could walk up and quietly tell Ma'am, or several children could together say "give it back," instead of each waiting for someone else.
How does the bus look from Bittu's seat?
To Bittu it probably looks like everyone is either laughing or ignoring him, so he feels completely alone, even though many feel sorry for him.

Read this:

Subject: Terms we agreed by phone

Dear Jatin,

Thank you for the draft of the design contract. I've compared it with our call on Tuesday and I noticed three differences. The scope you described on the phone included two rounds of revisions, but the draft doesn't say how many. The "handling charge" in the last paragraph was never mentioned. And you said the second payment would come within a week of delivery, but the draft says "at our convenience."

Before I sign, please put all three in writing as we agreed on the call. I'm keeping our messages as a record.

I also understand you'd like me to sign today. I'd rather take the time to be sure. If the terms can't be written down, I'll have to decline.

Sincerely,
Amandeep

How many differences did Amandeep find between the call and the draft?
Amandeep found three differences: the revisions, the handling charge and the payment timing.
Why did Amandeep refuse to sign the same day?
Amandeep felt uneasy that spoken promises were missing from the paper and pressure to sign today is a red flag, so Amandeep wanted time to check.
What small steps helped Amandeep protect against deceit?
Amandeep listed the differences, asked for them in writing, kept messages as a record and said clearly that unwritten terms mean a no.
How might Jatin see the email?
Jatin may feel caught out or irritated, but an honest party would see the request as fair, since it only asks that the phone terms be put on paper.
Farmer Brown fed 7 chickens and 5 sheep. How many total legs were there among the animals he fed?

The chickens had 7*2=14 legs.
The sheep had 5*4=20 legs.
There were 14+20=34 legs.
The answer is 34.

A school canteen sells a sandwich at $2, a hamburger at $2, one stick of hotdog at $1, and a can of fruit juice at $2 each can. Selene buys three sandwiches and a can of fruit juice. Tanya buys two hamburgers and two cans of fruit juice.  How much do Selene and Tanya spend together?

Three sandwiches cost 3 x $2 = $6.
So, Selene spends $6 + $2 = $8.
Two hamburgers cost 2 x $2 = $4.
Two cans of fruit juice cost 2 x $2 = $4.
Thus, Tanyah spends $4 +$4 = $8.
Therefore, Selene and Tanya spend $8 + $8 = $16.
The answer is 16.

Read this:

In the physics lab, while the teacher checked circuits, the post went round on everyone's phone: a cartoon of Sahil with a pig's nose. Keerthana saw the table erupt. Two weeks ago she had laughed at the first one, and that night she couldn't sleep. Now she felt the same heat in her face. "Forward it to the batch group, Keerthu," whispered Nikita. Keerthana's heart thudded. Nikita and her friends could make anyone's life miserable. "I'll do it later," she mumbled, and didn't. At the end of class she caught Sahil's eye and gave him a small nod. That night she messaged him: "Not everyone thinks it's funny. I'm not sharing it." He replied with one word: "Thanks."

What was drawn on the cartoon of Sahil?
It showed Sahil with a pig's nose.
Why did Keerthana's heart thud when Nikita asked her to forward it?
She feared that Nikita and her friends would turn on her if she refused, while she also felt guilty about laughing before.
What small step helped Sahil without a public fight?
Keerthana quietly didn't forward the post and messaged Sahil privately to say she wasn't sharing it, which showed him support.
What would change if a few more classmates did what Keerthana did?
The post would travel less, and Sahil would see that he is not alone, which could weaken the group's hold.

Read this:

At Zanele's birthday lunch in Toronto, Aunt Elif handed her a soft green parcel. Zanele tore the paper. Inside was a knitted sweater, and Zanele had hoped for paints. Her face fell for a moment. Papa touched her back. "Thank you, Aunt Elif," Zanele said. "I made it myself, one row a night," said Aunt Elif, beaming. That evening in her bedroom, Zanele whispered to Papa, "I wanted paints." "Thank you for saying thank you," he said. "Aunt worked hard on it. We can ask for paints another time."

What gift did Aunt Elif give Zanele?
She gave her a knitted green sweater that she had made herself.
What was Zanele feeling when her face fell at the gift?
She was disappointed because she had hoped for paints. She still said thank you, perhaps because Papa touched her back and Aunt Elif was so pleased.
What did Papa do well when Zanele told him the truth?
He let her be honest in private, thanked her for being kind at the party and said paints could be asked for another time. She did not have to hide her wish or hurt Aunt Elif. 🙂
How does Aunt Elif see the moment when Zanele thanks her?
She sees a happy niece and enjoys her one-row-a-night effort being noticed. She has no idea about the paints, so the thank you makes the gift feel worth the work.

What does Van Helsing hope will be done when the child is sent home?

"I hope," said Van Helsing, "that when you are sending the child home you will caution its parents to keep strict watch over it. These fancies to stray are most dangerous; and if the child were to remain out another night, it would probably be fatal. But in any case I suppose you will not let it away for some days?"

Van Helsing hopes the parents will be cautioned to keep strict watch, since straying is most dangerous. Another night out would probably be fatal to the child, so Van Helsing hopes the child will not be let away for some days.

Read this:

"Sit, Chetan. You asked why I always ask about a company's targets before anything else. When I was twenty-five, a young woman at a pharmaceutical distributor in Chennai, I started to notice things. The targets doubled one year, and nobody could explain how we would reach them honestly. The one colleague who kept asking, a quiet man named Sampath, was moved to the stores. At lunch, people joked, 'Don't be a Sampath, don't ask too much.' When a shipment came back from a hospital, the manager said, 'Bring me good news only.' I laughed at the jokes too, at first. Then one evening I sat alone in the canteen, counted those signs on a paper napkin, and felt cold. Three signs in one year. That napkin is why I left before the audit came. Your Rukmini Amma is telling you, Chetan: watch the jokes. They tell you what people are afraid to say."

Where was Sampath moved?
Sampath was moved to the stores.
What did Rukmini feel when she counted the signs on the napkin?
Rukmini felt cold with alarm, suddenly seeing that the jokes and targets she had laughed along with were warning signs.
In the story, which choice changed things, and why did it matter?
Sitting alone and writing the signs on a napkin let Rukmini see the pattern clearly, which is why she left before the audit came.
How might Sampath have experienced those jokes at lunch?
Sampath was probably hurt and isolated, hearing his honesty turned into a warning to others while he sat in the stores.
Jan buys 5 dozen roses.  Each rose cost $6.  Since he bought so many he only needs to pay 80%.  How much did he pay?

He got 5*12=60 roses
So the cost was 6*60=$360
So he has to pay 360*.8=$288
The answer is 288.

Read this:

Bhavna: they're still sharing it. I'm going to post something. everyone needs to know it's a lie

Pranav: wait. what are you going to post

Bhavna: a big message. with all of it. in caps

Pranav: I get it. but if you post, more people will see the rumour, even ones who hadn't

Bhavna: so I just let them say it??

Pranav: no. I already messaged Ravi and Ishan. told them it isn't true and to delete it. Ravi deleted

Bhavna: really?

Pranav: yes. and you shouldn't handle this alone. can we tell your mom tonight? or Ma'am?

Bhavna: mom. she's in the kitchen

Pranav: go now. I'll wait

Bhavna: ok

Bhavna: told her. she read all of it. she said I did nothing wrong and she's messaging Ma'am right now

Pranav: good. I'm proud of you

Bhavna: thanks for not letting me post

Who deleted the rumour after Pranav messaged?
Ravi.
What was Bhavna feeling when she wanted to post in caps?
Bhavna felt angry and desperate for everyone to know it was a lie.
Why was Pranav's way of helping wise?
Pranav asked spreaders privately to delete it, stopped a public reply that would spread it further, and helped Bhavna tell her mother the same evening.
How might Bhavna's mom feel reading the messages?
She is likely worried and protective, and reassures Bhavna before contacting Ma'am.

Read this:

Siddharth's sticker chart hung on the fridge. Three jobs every day: teeth, milk, and tidying shoes into the rack. Every finished job earned a sticker pressed down with a thumb, and ten stickers meant the park.

On Wednesday at dinner, five-year-old Siddharth looked at the peas and then at his mother. "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" Madhuri grinned and nodded. The plate was clean in minutes.

On Thursday evening he skipped his milk and stood at the window instead. "First star," he whispered, "please put extra stickers on my chart." In the morning he ran to the fridge. No new stickers. He frowned at the chart and said nothing.

At breakfast on Saturday he tugged Madhuri's sleeve. "How many more stickers?" They counted the empty circles together, one, two, three. "Three!" he sang. Gurpreet from next door, who had come over to play, counted along, and Siddharth carried the marker to the chart himself.

Which three jobs earned a sticker each day?
Teeth, milk, and tidying shoes into the rack each earned a sticker.
Why did the wish on the star fail when the vegetable deal and the counting with Madhuri worked?
The star gave no new stickers because none had been earned, while the deal named a price and a prize and the counting turned the goal into three empty circles.
What was Siddharth feeling when he saw the chart the morning after wishing on the star?
Disappointment: he ran to the fridge hoping for extra stickers and frowned when there were none.
What could Madhuri do the next time Siddharth wishes on a star?
Madhuri could listen kindly, then point to the empty circles and help Siddharth pick which job to do tonight.

Read this:

Sarika had skipped three Sundays at her mother's flat in Salt Lake. Work, she told herself. The truth was simpler: every visit, Amma looked smaller.

This Sunday she went. Lavanya was at the window, a shawl over her shoulders in April, and when she poured the tea her hand trembled so much the cup rattled on the saucer. Sarika's chest went tight. What if something happened and she didn't know what to do? What if she was not enough?

She took the pot gently. "Let me." Then, instead of checking her phone, she sat on the floor by Amma's chair. "Amma, is there anything you want to do this year? Anything at all?"

Lavanya was quiet, surprised. "I'd like to see the Durga pujo at my old para once more. And I want my books to go to the school library."

Sarika wrote both down. She stayed until dark and came back on Wednesday.

How many Sundays had Sarika skipped?
Sarika had skipped three Sundays.
What was Sarika afraid of when she saw her mother's hand tremble?
Sarika felt a tight fear of losing her mother and of not being enough if something happened.
What did Sarika do that eased the fear into action?
She stayed and sat close, asked her mother what she wanted this year, wrote down the answers and came back on Wednesday.
How might Lavanya have felt when Sarika asked about her wishes?
Lavanya was surprised and probably glad to be asked, since she answered with two clear wishes.

Read this:

Yuki kicked her ball too hard in the back garden in Leeds, and it flew over the fence. There was a crash. She peeked through the gap: Emeka's flowerpot lay smashed on his path. Her stomach flipped. She walked round and knocked. When Emeka opened the door, she said very fast, “I broke your flowerpot with my ball. I'm sorry.” Emeka crouched. “Thank you for coming to tell me. That took courage. Shall we replant the flowers together?” Yuki let out a big breath and nodded.

What did Yuki's ball break?
Emeka's flowerpot.
What was Yuki feeling when she walked round and knocked?
She was nervous and scared about owning up, as her flipping stomach showed.
How did Emeka's response encourage honesty?
He thanked her for telling, called it courage, and offered a way to fix it together.
How might Emeka feel on opening the door to Yuki?
Emeka might feel sad about the pot, but mainly impressed and touched that Yuki came to confess.
Do I put a comma after "Yes" in "Yes I can come"?

Yes. When "Yes" or "No" begins a sentence, a comma usually follows it.
Example: Yes, I can come to the match.

Read this:

Jeevan, come here. Old Anirban lost a badminton final as a boy of eleven, and I want to tell you what my father said in the car. "You should have won. You had him." I stared out at the wet road. I felt I had let him down, and I hardly noticed my sore hand. Then I said, in a small voice, "I did my best, Papa. I need you on my side, not more pushing." He was quiet for a whole traffic light. Then he said, "Hm. Maybe I wanted that trophy more than you did." He bought us hot jalebis. He isn't perfect, Jeevan, but he heard me.

What did Anirban's father say in the car?
"You should have won. You had him."
What was Anirban feeling as he stared at the wet road?
That he had let his father down, so he felt hurt and disappointed.
What could a child say to a parent who piles on pressure after a loss?
That they did their best and need support, not more pressure, as Anirban did.
How might Anirban's father have felt after hearing him?
Thoughtful and a bit sorry, since he was quiet for a whole traffic light, admitted he may have wanted the trophy more and bought jalebis. 🙂

Read this:

You asked me who changed my life at school? I'm Pallavi, and it was Nilesh sir, our librarian.
In Class 8 I was failing English. He noticed me hiding in the library at lunch. Instead of sending me out, he handed me a thin detective novel. "Tell me who did it by Friday, young lady." I did. Then he gave me another. For two years he gave up his lunch breaks to talk about books with me. He never asked for anything.
I thanked him last month, on his retirement day. I gave him a card and cried like a baby.
But here's something funny. Last year, I told him I thought one of his favourite books was boring. He laughed and said, "Good! Argue with me." I think that's the real gift: he never wanted me to agree with everything.
Now I spend Thursday lunches in the library with two Class 7 kids. Detective novels, obviously.

What kind of novel did Nilesh sir first give Pallavi?
A thin detective novel.
How does Pallavi feel about Nilesh sir?
She feels deep gratitude and affection, enough to cry when she thanked him on his retirement day.
How is Pallavi passing on what she received?
She spends Thursday lunches in the library with two Class 7 students, sharing detective novels as he did with her.
How did Nilesh sir react when Pallavi disagreed with him?
He laughed and encouraged her to argue, showing he valued her thinking for herself.

Read this:

The ceiling fan made shadows on the wall of Hemant's room. Mummy was on night duty at the hospital again. Hemant lay stiff under the sheet.

What if her bus crashed? What if he forgot every answer in tomorrow's spelling test and Ma'am read his marks aloud?

Each thought made his heart thump harder. He got up twice to check the front door was locked.

His cousin Zeenat didi, visiting for the holidays, heard him. She sat on the bed. "Mummy called at nine, remember? She'll be home when you wake up." She put on their usual soft music and rubbed his back in slow circles.

"What if she isn't?"

"Then I'll be right here. Count the fan blades with me."

He counted to twenty, then yawned.

How many times did Hemant get up to check the front door?
Hemant got up twice to check the front door was locked.
Why did Hemant's what-if thoughts feel so important to him at night?
Hemant felt scared for Mummy on night duty and nervous about the test, and the what-ifs felt like a way to be ready for danger.
What did Zeenat didi do that helped Hemant settle?
Zeenat reminded Hemant that Mummy called at nine, put on the usual soft music, rubbed his back and gave him fan blades to count.
How might Mummy feel if she knew about Hemant's night?
Mummy might feel touched that Hemant cares so much, and want to reassure him before her next night shift.

Friday. The rain started at noon, and by four the team's paper-craft stall at the college fest had sold nine items out of eighty. Binita looked at the poster she'd finished at 1 a.m. and printed late, curling at the corners. It's my poster, she thought. Nobody saw us because of me.
Saturday. She typed a long apology in the group chat: 'I'm really sorry, I ruined it for everyone.' Parveen replied, 'Let's talk Monday. Not only you.' Binita didn't believe it.
Monday. In the canteen, Parveen made a list on a napkin: rain, stall beside the dustbins, prices too high, only two people free to staff it, one late poster. Binita stared at it. Her poster was one line out of five. 'Still my line,' she said. 'Yes,' said Parveen. 'One line.'

How many items did the stall sell?
The stall sold nine items out of eighty.
Why did Binita apologise for ruining it for everyone?
She felt guilty and ashamed about the late poster, so it seemed like the single cause of the poor sales, and the rain and other problems faded from view.
How did Parveen's napkin list help?
Listing every cause showed the poster was one line out of five, so Binita could own her part without carrying the whole failure.
How might Parveen see Binita's apology?
Parveen sees a teammate taking far too much blame, and wants to show the fuller picture without pretending the late poster didn't matter.

metadata.subtype: Taking full blame for a group failure [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

For years Indu had said, "Why can't you be like your sister?" to Baljeet, and "Look how fast Baljeet runs" to Simran. The fights in their Amritsar home got worse every year.

So she changed. When Simran brought home a drawing, Indu said, "You used so many colours. You must have thought hard about that." When Baljeet came back from football, she said, "You kept trying even after the first goal went in."

When they argued over the TV remote, she stayed in the kitchen, only calling, "Sort it out yourselves, please."

After a month, she noticed something. They argued less. Yesterday, Baljeet even told Simran, "Your drawing's nice." Simran looked so surprised she dropped her crayons.

What did Indu used to say to Baljeet?
"Why can't you be like your sister?"
How did Simran feel when Baljeet praised her drawing?
She was so surprised she dropped her crayons, probably also pleased and happy.
What changes did Indu make, and why did they help?
She praised each child's own effort and let them settle small quarrels themselves, so they felt less need to compete.
How might Baljeet feel being praised for trying, not for winning?
He probably feels valued for his effort and less pressure to beat his sister.
Write a four-line rhyme for children about a school bell that rings too early on a sleepy morning.

The school bell rang, ding-dong, so loud,
It woke me from my cosy cloud.
I yawned and stretched, and rubbed my eyes,
Then rushed to class in sleepy surprise.
Is it "lenght" or "length"? Can you tell me what "legendary" means? Can you correct this for me? "Where you are going?"

1. It is "length". It has "gth" at the end.
2. Legendary is an adjective that means so famous that it appears in stories.
3. It should be: Where are you going? Why: in a question, the helper verb comes before the subject.

Susan is playing a board game with 48 spaces from the starting space to the winning end space of the game. On the first turn, she moves forward eight spaces. On the second turn, she moves two spaces, but lands on a space that sends her back five spaces. On the third turn, she moves forward six more spaces. How many spaces does she have to move to reach the ending space and win the game?

In the first three turns, Susan has moved 8 + 2 - 5 + 6 = 11 spaces.
Susan has 48 - 11 = 37 spaces to move to win the game.
The answer is 37.

Tuesday
Client review today. Our manager put up the churn analysis and said, "We found that..." I knew exactly who "we" was. Suraj, the new analyst, stayed till eleven on Friday building it. He was sitting at the far end, looking at his hands.
My heart was going fast. I'm not senior. But when the client asked how the model handled cancelled orders, I said, "Suraj built that part, actually. Suraj, want to explain?"
There was a tiny pause. Then Suraj explained it better than any of us could have. The client asked for his email.
After the meeting our manager said, "Good catch, Raghav," a bit stiffly. I don't know if I'll pay for it later.
Suraj messaged me at 7: "thank you. nobody's ever done that."
I think I'll keep doing it. It cost me four seconds.
Raghav

How late did Suraj stay on Friday?
Suraj stayed till eleven on Friday building it.
What was Raghav feeling before speaking up in the meeting?
Raghav was nervous, heart going fast and aware of not being senior, yet chose to name Suraj anyway.
What made Raghav's move work without starting a fight?
Raghav named Suraj naturally while answering a client question and handed Suraj the floor, instead of accusing the manager.
What was the meeting like for Suraj?
Suraj sat looking at his hands while the work was called 'we', then got to explain it and be noticed; the 7 pm message shows how rare that felt.

Read this:

In their flat above the family's hardware store in Leeds, Daniel had until morning to answer: the three-week engineering summer school, or the store, where his mum Amara needed help while his dad recovered from a back operation.

At dinner he nearly blurted "I'm going" and then, a minute later, nearly said "Fine, I'll stay." Both felt wrong. "Can I tell you tomorrow?" he asked. Amara nodded.

He lay awake for a while, then slept. In the morning, brushing his teeth, the thing was clearer. It wasn't really the store he was worried about. It was her face if he left. He was scared of disappointing her.

At breakfast he said so. "I think I'm more afraid of letting you down than of missing the store."

Amara put her mug down. "Then let's talk about the store, not about letting me down." And they did, properly, for the first time.

How long was the engineering summer school?
Three weeks.
What did Daniel realise he was most afraid of?
He realised he was scared of disappointing his mum, which weighed on him more than the store itself.
How did waiting a night help, and what could Daniel try next?
The night let the panic settle so he could see the real fear; next, he and Amara can list what the store truly needs during those weeks.
How might Amara have felt hearing Daniel's honest fear?
Amara probably felt touched and a little surprised, and relieved to move the talk away from guilt to practical planning.
