Hrithik, before you start at that big office, let me tell you about my first job. I was twenty-one, at a call centre in Gurgaon. Our manager ordered the team leaders to put a paper crown marked SLOWEST on the lowest scorer each evening and make them read their numbers aloud. The first week it was me. The team leader, Bunty, a nice boy who shared his lunch with me, put the crown on my head and read my number like a price tag. I felt like a thing on a shelf, not Simran. Afterwards he said, 'Sorry yaar, orders. I have no choice.' The next day I went to HR with two colleagues and a written complaint. HR stopped the crown that week. Bunty avoided me for a month. I didn't hate him. But I never believed that 'no choice' again.

What was written on the paper crown?
SLOWEST.
How did Simran feel wearing the crown?
Simran felt dehumanised and humiliated, like a thing on a shelf with a price tag.
Simran went to HR the next day with two colleagues and a written complaint. Why was that a turning point?
It turned private humiliation into a record that forced HR to act, ending the crown for everyone.

Kendra tracks the different species of birds they spot on their birdwatching trip. On Monday they visited 5 sites and saw an average of 7 birds at each site. On Tuesday, Kendra visited 5 sites and saw an average of 5 birds at each site. On Wednesday visited 10 sites and saw an average of 8 birds at each site. On average, how many different birds did Kendra see on each site?

On Monday Kendra saw 5 sites x 7 birds/site = 35 different birds
On Tuesday Kendra saw 5 sites x 5 birds/site = 25 different birds
On Wednesday Kendra saw 10 sites x 8 birds/site = 80 different birds
In total Kendra saw 35 birds + 25 birds + 80 birds = 140 different birds
In total Kendra visited 5 sites + 5 sites + 10 sites = 20 sites.
On average Kendra saw 140 birds / 20 sites = 7 different birds at each site
The answer is 7.

Lunch bell. Parul opened her steel tiffin: Amma's fish curry and rice, still warm. Beside her, Wasim wrinkled his nose and leaned away.

Parul's stomach dropped. She snapped the lid shut. Last year a girl had called her lunch "stinky", and the whole table had laughed. She sat with her hands in her lap for a long minute. Then she made herself ask, "Is it my food?"

Wasim looked confused. "Your food? No! Somebody left their football socks on the window ledge behind us. Can't you smell that?"

Parul sniffed. He was right. She opened the lid again, and Wasim asked if he could try a bite.

She asked kindly, "Is it my food?", instead of assuming rejection, and found out it was the football socks.

A farmer harvested 250 potatoes. He bundled them in twenty-five's and sold each bundle for $1.90. He also harvested 320 carrots and bundled them in twenty's and sold each bundle for $2. If the farmer sold all his harvested crops, how much did he get in all?

There are 250/25 = 10 bundles of potatoes.
So, 20 bundles of potatoes amount to $1.9 x 10 = $19.
There are 320/20 = 16 bundles of carrots.
So, 16 bundles of carrots amount to $2 x 16 = $32.
Hence, the farmer got $19 + $32 = $51 in all.
The answer is 51.
A spider has 8 legs. How many legs do 9 spiders have?

Answer: 72 legs. 9 x 8 = 72.

The 8 table is double the 4 table, and the 4 table is double the 2 table. 9 x 2 = 18, double: 9 x 4 = 36, double again: 9 x 8 = 72. Three easy doublings instead of one hard fact.

Ronald is rolling a die and won't stop rolling until the average of all his rolls is a 3. He rolls a 1, a 3, a 2, a 4, a 3, a 5, a 3, a 4, a 4 and a 2. What does he need to roll on the next roll to be able to stop?

The next roll will be his 11th roll.
The total on this tenth roll to have an average of 3 is 33, because 3 * 11 = 33
His current total is 31 because 1 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 3 + 5 + 6 + 1 + 4 + 2= 31
He needs to roll a 2 because 33 - 31 = 2
The answer is 2.
My cousin says I should try travelling alone someday. Is that smart?

How do I start?

What's the biggest danger?
Not planning. Know where you will sleep, how you will reach it, and who to call if something goes wrong. Keep your phone charged and your money in more than one place.

messages.content: Rosie runs 6 miles per hour. She runs for 1 hour on Monday, 30 minutes on Tuesday, 1 hour on Wednesday, and 20 minutes on Thursday. If she wants to run 20 miles for the week, how many minutes should she run on Friday?

On Monday and Wednesday, Rosie runs 6*1= 6 miles.
On Tuesday, Rosie runs 6*(30 minutes/60 minutes) = 3 miles.
On Thursday, Rosie runs 6*(20 minutes/60 minutes)=2 miles.
So far this week Rosie has run 6+3+6+2=17 miles.
To reach her goal, she must run 20-17=3 miles on Friday.
Thus, she should run for 6/3=.5 hour which is 30 minutes.
The answer is 30.

After the college fest in Delhi, a senior had joked about Ujjwal's dark skin during the stage announcements. Ujjwal, nineteen, had laughed it off, though his stomach had turned. The next morning, his friend Deepak posted a long story online: "My friend Ujjwal was humiliated on stage for his skin colour. This is disgusting! I stand with him!" He tagged the senior, the college page, everyone. By noon, Ujjwal's phone was full of messages. People he barely knew asked if he was okay. Some sent sad faces. Ujjwal sat in his room, grateful and hot with embarrassment. He hadn't wanted this. Deepak called, excited. "It's going viral! They'll have to apologise!" Ujjwal said quietly, "Deepak, you didn't ask me. I wanted to talk to the dean myself." Deepak went silent. "I thought I was helping," he said.

What did the senior joke about?
The senior had joked about Ujjwal's dark skin.
What was Ujjwal feeling as the messages flooded in?
Ujjwal felt grateful but embarrassed and overwhelmed, as the incident was taken out of his hands.
What went wrong with Deepak's help, and what could he have done?
Deepak spoke for Ujjwal and made it public without asking; he could have asked what Ujjwal wanted, like going to the dean together.
How did Deepak feel when Ujjwal said he hadn't asked?
Deepak was surprised and deflated, having genuinely believed he was helping.

What was Joseph feeling when he felt a small jolt?
Joseph felt guilty and uneasy, realising the black picture was still up but he hadn't done anything else while Pema's family still needed help.
What did Joseph do a month later, and why did it matter more?
He and Pema set up a collection box for blankets and school bags, and he called the relief group Pema trusted to check real needs, turning online solidarity into practical support.
How might Pema have felt as the feeds moved on?
Pema may have felt lonely and worried, since her aunt's family was still displaced while everyone else's attention had faded.

Read this:

In the computer lab, Aparna noticed that when she sat down, the two rows nearby went quiet. Her marks had topped the last three tests, and Akash, who had been friendly in first year, now only said, "Must be nice." She felt the sting. For a moment she thought of failing a test on purpose, or hiding her answers, so it would stop. Then she remembered how much she loved the subject. At the next lab, when Akash's program crashed, she said, "Want me to look? I got stuck on the same thing last week." He hesitated, then shifted his chair. She did not mention her marks or her rank. The rows around them stayed quiet, but Akash stopped looking away when she walked in.

What did Akash say to Aparna about her marks?
He said, "Must be nice."
What did Aparna feel when the nearby rows went quiet, and what did she consider doing?
She felt the sting of being treated coldly, and briefly considered hiding her ability. She then decided against it because she loved the subject.
What could Aparna do if the coldness continues?
She can stay kind, help when asked, avoid flaunting her marks, and keep enjoying her work. If it becomes bullying she can tell a teacher.
How might Akash see Aparna's offer to look at his program?
Akash may have felt envy or discomfort, and he hesitated. Her plain offer, without any mention of marks, seems to have made it easier for him to accept.
In 5 years, Raven will be 4 times as old as Phoebe. If Phoebe is currently 10 years old, how old is Raven?

In five years, Phoebe will be 10+5 = 15 years old.
If Raven is four times as old as Phoebe in fifteen years, he will be 4*15 = 60 years old in 5 years.
Currently, Raven is 60-5 = 55 years old.
The answer is 55.

Read this:

"Mumma, see!" Dilnaz, two, held up a leaf.

Deepika, typing, handed her the tablet. "Watch this, baby. Mumma's busy."

Dilnaz watched, silent, for an hour.

At bedtime, Dilnaz asked, "Mumma, play?"

Deepika paused. "Tomorrow, first thing, we'll play. No tablet."

Next morning they collected leaves in the park. Dilnaz talked the whole way.

What did Dilnaz hold up to show her mother?
Dilnaz held up a leaf.
Why did Dilnaz ask "Mumma, play?" at bedtime?
Dilnaz felt lonely and wanted her mother's company, not just the tablet.
What did Deepika do that helped?
She made time the next morning to play with Dilnaz without the tablet, treating it as a tool, not a babysitter.
How might Deepika feel when Dilnaz asks to play?
Deepika may feel a pang of guilt and realise Dilnaz needs her, not the screen.
The teacher said, "Hold out your hand." Is it only for the hand?

"Hold out" has more than one meaning. Hold out your hand means to stretch it forward. It can also mean to last or to keep resisting, for example when supplies are limited.
Examples: Hold out your hand to receive the prize. Our water won't hold out for another week.

Read this:

On the Gurugram metro, at 4.10 p.m., Gurleen realised that the meeting with the school principal had been at 3.30. Her stomach dropped. The old sentence started: I'm useless. I'm a useless person. I ruin everything.

She stopped it, the way she'd been practising, and typed into her phone instead: "I forgot the 3.30 meeting. I feel irresponsible and embarrassed. That's what happened, not who I am."

Then she called Zubin, her colleague, who had waited at the school. "Zubin, I forgot the meeting. That's on me. I'm sorry you sat there alone. I'll call the principal now for another slot, and I'm putting two alarms on everything from today."

Zubin said, "Okay. Thanks for just saying it."

The principal agreed to Thursday. That night Gurleen still felt bad. But she didn't feel like nothing.

When was the meeting with the school principal?
The meeting was at 3.30.
How did Gurleen feel when she realised, and what did she tell herself?
Gurleen felt irresponsible and embarrassed, and told herself it was what happened, not who she is.
Why does describing the act keep both responsibility and self-respect?
It let Gurleen own the mistake fully, apologise and fix it, without calling herself a useless person.
How did Zubin feel about Gurleen's call?
Zubin seemed relieved and appreciative, thanking her for just saying it.

metadata.subtype: Describing the act, not the person [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Coach's note - Harish, school band, Friday
Sahil turned up to rehearsal with bright blue hair. His mother had phoned me in the morning, worried. She asked if something was wrong, if he was "falling in with a bad crowd."
I watched him closely all week. He was on time, practised his drum part more than anyone, and joked with the juniors. The only change was the hair, and a new black band T-shirt.
When I asked him, he shrugged. "The drummer in my favourite band has blue hair. Also I wanted to see how I'd look. I might change it next month."
I called his mother back. I told her he seemed happy, focused and part of the group, and that trying a new look at sixteen is normal. We agreed to keep an eye on the bigger things, like sleep, mood and friends, not the colour.
Next week, three band members turned up with blue streaks.

What colour was Sahil's hair?
Bright blue.
What was Sahil's mother feeling when she phoned?
She was worried and anxious, afraid the blue hair meant something was wrong or that Sahil was falling in with a bad crowd.
What did Harish do that helped?
He watched Sahil's behaviour for a week, asked him directly, and reassured his mother that the hair looked like experimentation, while agreeing to watch mood and sleep.
What would change if Sahil's mother had banned the hair colour straight away?
Sahil might have felt judged and less willing to talk, over what was really just a trial and a sign of belonging to the band.

Some random questions:
How can I help at home before Diwali?
Why are there fireworks on some festival days?
A box had 17 sweets and the guests ate 5. How many sweets are left?

1. Offer to clean your room, hang the lights and help make the rangoli. Ask your family what they need.
2. They make the celebration bright. Because the colours and sounds feel festive.
3. 12 sweets. Because 17 - 5 = 12.

Read this:

Journal, Wednesday.
Day eight at the newspaper. Asif sir, the night editor, pushed my story back across the desk today and said, 'Is this English or soup?' in front of the whole desk. Nobody looked up. I retyped it three times. Then he sent me to get tea for six people, then to count old papers in the store.
Is this how journalism works? Everyone keeps saying 'this is how we all started'. I keep saying 'yes sir, sorry sir' to everything, even when I don't know what I'm sorry for.
At seven, Meenakshi di from the features desk stopped me by the lift. 'The soup comment was out of line. Tea runs are normal here; the shouting isn't. Sit with me tomorrow and I'll show you how to edit.'
I cried a little on the bus. Good crying, I think.
Gurpreet

What did Asif sir say when pushing the story back?
'Is this English or soup?'
Why does Gurpreet keep saying 'yes sir, sorry sir'?
Gurpreet feels small and anxious, trying to please even without knowing what the apology is for.
How did Meenakshi di help Gurpreet?
She separated what is normal, like tea runs, from what isn't, like the shouting, and offered to teach editing the next day.
What might the rest of the desk be thinking when nobody looks up?
They may see the sharpness as ordinary, the way they 'all started', or feel uneasy but unwilling to challenge the night editor.

Read this:

The first night Diego moved into the flat in Osaka, bass thumped through the thin wall until one in the morning. Yuki lay awake, jaw tight, already composing a cold message.
Instead she opened her notes and typed: "First guess: careless. Only a guess. What would change it? If he turns it down when asked. If he does his share in the kitchen."
The next evening she knocked. "The music carries a lot through this wall." Diego went red, apologised, and bought a pair of headphones that weekend.
Over the following fortnight Yuki kept adding lines: dishes washed, a note on the fridge asking about her shifts, rice left warm for her after a late one.
One night she scrolled back to that first entry, smiled, and deleted the word "careless".

What did Diego buy after Yuki knocked?
Diego bought a pair of headphones that weekend.
How was Yuki feeling that first night, and what did she do with that feeling?
She was irritated and tired, lying awake with her jaw tight, but she wrote her judgement down as only a guess and listed what would change it.
Which choice worked, and why?
Writing "Only a guess" and naming the evidence that would change it worked, because it kept Yuki watching what Diego actually did instead of sending the cold message.
What would it have been like for Diego if Yuki had sent the cold message?
He might have felt judged on his first night, before he even knew the wall was thin, and the flat could have started with tension instead of warm rice.

Read this:

The Rath Yatra crowds were thick outside when Sachin spread the Class 11 form on the dining table. It had to be submitted by ten tomorrow.
He ticked Humanities.
His mother, Rukmini, saw it from the kitchen door. "Science. We agreed. And no more of that theatre group. They're the reason your marks slipped."
"You agreed," Sachin said. His voice shook, but he kept going. "I love history. And those are my friends, Maa. I chose them."
"At your age you don't know what's good for you."
"Then when do I start knowing?"
The drums of the procession rolled past the window. Neither of them moved. Sachin kept his hand flat on the form, as if someone might take it.

By what time did the form have to be submitted?
By ten tomorrow.
What does Sachin keeping a hand flat on the form suggest about his feelings?
He feels nervous but determined, afraid the choice will be taken from him, because choosing his stream and friends feels like part of who he is.
What could Sachin try so the talk becomes less of a clash?
Explain calmly why history matters to him and what the theatre friends give him, and ask to talk it through with a teacher or counsellor before ten tomorrow.
Why might Rukmini react so strongly?
Rukmini likely feels worried about his future, blames the theatre group for the slipping marks, and sees science as the safe route.

metadata.subtype: Wants to choose own subject and friends [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Vasudha: i'm not presenting tomorrow. i'll take the zero
Tarun: what?? why
Vasudha: my voice cracked in last week's presentation. like a squeak. everyone heard
Tarun: i was there. i don't remember a squeak
Vasudha: you're just being nice
Tarun: no genuinely. i was reading my own notes the whole time bc i was next
Tarun: also ask the others. i bet nobody remembers
Vasudha: i've been thinking about it for 7 days 😣
Tarun: that's the thing. u thought about it for 7 days. we thought about it for 0 seconds
Vasudha: ...that's weirdly comforting
Tarun: present tomorrow. i'll sit in the front and nod a lot 🙂
Vasudha: ok. fine. nod a LOT

What happened to Vasudha's voice last week?
It cracked, like a squeak.
Why does Vasudha want to take a zero rather than present?
Vasudha feels anxious and embarrassed, sure everyone heard the squeak and still remembers it.
What does Tarun point out, and why is it helpful?
That Vasudha thought about it for seven days while classmates thought about it for zero seconds, which shows how small the audience really was.
Why didn't Tarun remember the squeak?
Tarun was reading notes the whole time because Tarun was presenting next.

metadata.subtype: Speaking up in class or interviews [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tomas moved to Toronto for a job and spent his first winter mostly alone. Mina, a colleague from Seoul who'd been there four years, invited him to her monthly dinner where everyone brought a dish. He almost didn't go. He brought store-bought bread, embarrassed. Nobody cared. Over the year he kept going. He learned who knew about apartments, who could fix bikes, who needed a hand moving. When Mina's father fell ill back home and she had to fly out suddenly, Tomas and two others fed her cat and handled her mail for a month. She sent a message: 'You guys are my family here 🤍'. Tomas realised the dinners weren't just social. They'd built something people could lean on.

How often did Mina hold her dinner?
She held it monthly.
How did Tomas feel bringing store-bought bread?
He felt embarrassed, worried it wasn't good enough compared to what others made.
What does this story suggest about building trusted networks?
Showing up regularly and helping in small ways builds relationships people can rely on in hard times.
How might Mina see the group after her father's illness?
She sees them as family, since they cared for her home when she couldn't.

Read this:

Class 4 teacher's note, January. Written by Lalit, class teacher.
Kunal came back today after three days of fever. He told the class, very seriously, "I had ice cream at my cousin's wedding on Saturday, and then I got fever. Ice cream in winter makes you sick." Two children vowed never to eat ice cream again.
Half the class had coughs that week, and the boy beside Kunal was sick on Friday, before the wedding.
What I did next: I didn't tell Kunal he was wrong. I asked the class for other reasons someone might get a fever in January. They listed germs, sick friends and cold air. Kunal said, "Maybe it was the cough going round." I reminded everyone to wash hands and to tell a grown-up if they feel unwell.

Where did Kunal eat the ice cream?
Kunal ate ice cream at his cousin's wedding on Saturday.
Why did Kunal feel sure the ice cream caused the fever?
Kunal was a little scared and very sure, because the fever came right after the ice cream, so it seemed to be the cause.
Why was Lalit's question to the class a good approach?
Asking for other reasons someone might get a fever let the children, and Kunal, think of the cough going round themselves instead of just being told they were wrong.
How might the two children who vowed never to eat ice cream feel?
They were probably worried and a bit scared, believing ice cream could make them sick too.

metadata.subtype: After this, therefore because of this [Actor]

messages.content: Why does a scab form on a scraped knee?
The blood thickens and dries to cover the wound. Because the dried layer shields the damaged skin from dirt and germs, the body can rebuild new skin below it.

Read this:

When Rajni announced Pradeep's promotion to team lead, the office clapped. Tanvir clapped too, and a sour twist went through his stomach. He had joined the company the same month. That evening he said, "Congratulations, honestly. You earned it." Then he went home and spent an hour looking at what Pradeep had done differently: the client presentations, the weekend reports no one asked for. He wrote his own goals on a sheet, and put a date next to each. He did not say anything about Pradeep to anyone else.

Pradeep had felt a chill in the corridor. Tanvir had stopped sitting next to him at lunch. He did not apologise for the promotion, and he did not talk about it. He asked, "Would you look at my dashboard? You always see things I miss," and he told Rajni in front of the team that Tanvir had helped him set up the reporting system last year. Tanvir looked down at his plate.

Nothing changed that week. Pradeep kept sending him the occasional link to an article he'd like, without expecting an answer, and told himself that distance might be grief. A month later, Tanvir slid into the seat opposite him with his tray and said, "I've picked a course to sign up for. Want to hear what it is?"

What did Rajni announce at the office?
Rajni announced Pradeep's promotion to team lead.
How did Tanvir's envy and Pradeep's response fit together?
Tanvir felt a sour twist but congratulated Pradeep and turned to his own goals. Pradeep sensed the chill, did not apologise or flaunt, credited Tanvir's help, and gave the friendship time.
What was Tanvir feeling as he clapped for Pradeep?
He felt envious and sour in the stomach, since they had joined the company the same month.
What could Pradeep do if Tanvir stays distant for longer than a month?
He can stay warm without flaunting his promotion, keep small gestures, and understand the distance may be grief, not hatred.

Read this:

Deepak: Hi Anjali! HR has approved the offer: 9.5 lakh a year. Happy to talk through it.
Anjali: Thank you, I'm excited! Based on my project results and my cloud certifications, I was hoping for something between 10.5 and 11.5.
Anjali: The forecasting model I built cut stock-outs by a fifth at my last company, and I passed both certification exams this year.
Deepak: That's useful context. Let me check with the team.
Deepak: We can do 10.6. Can you confirm?
Anjali: 10.6 works for me. Thank you for hearing me out 🙂
Deepak: Great! The letter comes tomorrow 🎉

What figure did Deepak offer after checking with the team?
Deepak said, "We can do 10.6."
How might Anjali have felt while waiting for Deepak to check with the team?
Anjali was probably hopeful but nervous, having asked for more than the first offer.
What else could Anjali ask about after agreeing on the figure, and why?
Anjali could ask when the first pay review takes place, because it shows how the project results can be recognised again later.
How might Deepak see Anjali's message?
Deepak likely finds it clear and reasonable, since it gave a range and specific reasons that were easy to take back to the team.

metadata.subtype: Approach: making a range and giving reasons [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

In their village outside Karnal, everyone asked Preeti and Chetan the same question at every wedding and funeral: "Any good news?"
They would both smile and change the subject. At home, they never spoke about it either. Chetan assumed Preeti wanted to wait, like him. Preeti assumed Chetan wanted a child soon, like his mother kept saying.
Two years passed like that.
One evening, walking back from the fields, Preeti finally said it. "I want to finish my nursing course before a baby. At least two more years."
Chetan stopped on the path. "I also want to wait. The dairy loan isn't cleared yet."
They stared at each other. Then Preeti laughed, and cried a little.
"And I'm afraid," she said. "My sister nearly died in childbirth."
Chetan hadn't known she carried that fear. Two years of silence, and now all of it at once.

What course does Preeti want to finish?
Her nursing course.
What was Preeti feeling when she laughed and cried a little?
Preeti felt relieved that they both wanted to wait, but also anxious and emotional, carrying a fear from her sister's childbirth.
What else could Preeti and Chetan have done instead of changing the subject for two years?
They could have talked privately early on about their plans and fears, so they didn't carry separate assumptions.
How might Chetan feel learning of Preeti's fear?
Chetan is likely surprised and sad, realising she carried a big fear alone for two years.

metadata.subtype: Approach: postponing the discussion because it feels uncomfortable [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

On Children's Day the school canteen put up a special menu: twenty-two items, from pav bhaji to three kinds of sandwiches to five flavours of milkshake.
Tushar stood at the counter reading it while the queue behind him grew. Pav bhaji? But the cheese sandwich looked good. And the chocolate shake. Or strawberry?
"Hurry up!" someone shouted.
"Veg sandwich," he blurted.
He sat down next to Tarun, who had ordered pav bhaji in five seconds and was already halfway through. Tushar looked at his sandwich. Then at the pav bhaji. Then at the boy with the cheese sandwich.
"I should have got that," he said.
"You say that every time," Tarun said, and pushed his plate over. "Here. One bite. Next time just pick from three."

How many items were on the special menu?
The special menu had twenty-two items.
Why did Tushar feel his choice was wrong?
Tushar felt unsatisfied and a bit envious, because with so many options, every other dish looked better than his sandwich.
What does Tarun suggest, and why could it help?
Picking from just three, so there are fewer options to regret and the choice feels more certain.
How does Tarun experience ordering?
Tarun orders pav bhaji in five seconds and enjoys it, untroubled by the long list.

Read this:

Last month my college friends and I were arguing about our first-year trip to Goa. I was absolutely sure Rukmini had worn a yellow dress on the last night, when we sang on the beach. I could see it clearly, the colour, the frill on the sleeve.

"No, it was blue," Rukmini said.

"It was yellow. I'm certain."

She opened her phone and found the photo. Blue dress. Not even a little yellow.

I felt so silly. I would have bet anything on it. And I started wondering what else I'm totally sure about that isn't true.

I'm Sarita. These days, when I'm certain, I try to remember the blue dress.

What colour was Rukmini's dress in the photo?
Blue.
How did Sarita feel when the photo showed a blue dress?
Sarita felt silly and surprised, and a little unsettled about how certain the wrong memory had felt.
What does Sarita do now, and why is it helpful?
When feeling certain, Sarita remembers the blue dress, which helps keep in mind that confidence isn't proof.
How might Rukmini have felt showing the photo?
Rukmini may have felt amused, and maybe glad to settle the argument kindly.

At the tuition centre in Kanpur, Vijay Sir handed out the geometry worksheet. "Hard ones today. Try them yourselves," he said, and went to the office to take a call.
Pooja, eleven, read the first question three times. Circles inside triangles. She drew something, then rubbed it out. By the fourth question she had put her pencil down and was drawing flowers in the margin.
When Vijay Sir came back, he saw the flowers. "Done?"
"I can't do any of it," Pooja said, cheeks hot.
He pulled up a stool next to her. "Tell me what you see in the first one."
"A circle. A triangle."
"Where do they touch?"
Pooja looked. "Here… and here."
She picked up her pencil again. With him sitting there, the question looked possible.

What was Pooja drawing in the margin?
Flowers.
What was Pooja feeling when she said "I can't do any of it"?
She felt defeated and embarrassed, her cheeks hot after being left alone with questions too hard for her.
What changed when Vijay Sir sat beside her, and why did it help?
He asked small questions instead of solving it, keeping the task hard but with a guide near, so she felt able to try.
How might Vijay Sir see the flowers when he returns?
He might see them as a sign she had given up, and realise she needed help nearby.

People ask why I still talk about my first month at the pharmacy. I'm Rajni, and it's because of one Friday. My supervisor told me to sell a strip of antibiotics to a customer without a prescription. 'Everyone does it. If you want to pass probation, don't be difficult.' My father's shop had closed that year. My salary was the family's rent. I stood behind the counter feeling my knees go soft. I could have told myself I had no choice. That would have been easier to live with. Instead I asked for five minutes and called my senior from college, Vasudha, who now worked as a pharmacist in another city. She said, 'Check your company's rules. Most have a policy on this, and a helpline.' I found it on the staff notice board. I told the customer, calmly, that I couldn't without a prescription. My supervisor was cold for a week. I passed probation anyway. I might not have. I'd still choose it.

What did the supervisor tell Rajni to do?
The supervisor told Rajni to sell a strip of antibiotics without a prescription.
What was Rajni feeling behind the counter?
Rajni felt afraid, knees going soft, because the salary paid the family's rent.
What steps helped Rajni refuse?
Calling Vasudha, finding the company's policy and helpline on the notice board, and then refusing the customer calmly.
How does Vasudha help without deciding for Rajni?
Vasudha points Rajni to the company's rules and helpline, leaving the choice with Rajni.

Most evenings I, Sharmila, sit on the bench by our building's swings. Last Thursday, little Varun from the ground floor was everywhere at once: climbing the slide the wrong way, laughing far too loudly, rubbing his eyes with both fists. "Sharmila aunty, catch me!" he yelled, then flopped onto the sand and howled when his slipper came off. His mother frowned. "Stop this drama." I said, "Maybe he's sleepy?" She looked at his droopy eyelids and carried him home.

What did Varun do when his slipper came off?
He flopped onto the sand and howled.
What was Varun's mother feeling at first, and what changed her mind?
She felt irritated and read it as drama; after Sharmila's comment, his droopy eyelids showed her he was tired.
What small step helped here?
Sharmila gently suggested he might be sleepy instead of joining the scolding, and his mother took him home to rest.
How might the evening have felt for Varun?
Probably overwhelming; his body was worn out, so he could not slow down, and a lost slipper felt huge.

metadata.subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

The college canteen committee met in a small room behind the kitchen. Mridul, a second-year student, had volunteered to run the survey on new menu items. Minakshi, the committee secretary, remembered last year's survey that never really ended. "What does finished look like?" she asked. Mridul thought, then wrote on the whiteboard: "Form shared with all hostels. 300 responses or Friday noon, whichever first. Results chart made. Presented at Monday meeting." She nodded. On Friday the count was 284. He wanted to wait for more. He looked at the board, closed the form at noon, and presented on Monday. The new lemon rice was on the menu by Wednesday.

How many responses had come in by Friday?
The count was 284.
What was Mridul feeling when the count was 284?
He felt tempted and uncertain, wanting to wait for more responses to reach the number.
Which choice worked, and why?
Writing an endpoint of 300 responses or Friday noon made closing the form a clear decision, so the results reached the menu quickly.
How might Minakshi feel about this survey compared to last year's?
Minakshi likely feels relieved and pleased, since this one had a clear end and led to a real menu change.

Read this:

Deepak and Tanuja had both got teaching posts in the same small town in Odisha and rented a two-room house near the market to save costs. Two months in, it was tense.
Deepak left his clothes everywhere. Tanuja took phone calls with her family till midnight, and the walls were thin. Neither said anything, but they had stopped eating together.
Then the landlord's wife said, loudly, "You two fight like a married couple without talking." Tanuja laughed, and something cracked open.
That night they sat on the back step. Deepak admitted the calls kept him awake. Tanuja admitted the clothes made her feel like a maid. They agreed: calls on the back step after 10, clothes in his room, and a shared cleaning morning on Sundays.
It wasn't perfect. But they started eating dinner together again, and on Sundays they argued about music instead.

Where did Deepak and Tanuja agree calls would happen after 10?
On the back step.
How did Tanuja feel about Deepak's clothes lying around?
Tanuja felt resentful, as if she were being treated like a maid.
What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
They avoided talking and stopped eating together; honestly naming each problem and agreeing on specific rules fixed it.
How might the landlord's wife see the two of them after that night?
She might notice they seem friendlier, eating together and arguing only about music.

Read this:

The hostel committee had called Nirmala to the warden's office after her roommate complained about late-night noise. Warden Baljeet Kaur sat behind a steel desk with the complaint in front of her. As she read it aloud, Nirmala hunched in the chair, arms pinned to her sides, jaw tight. She could not get a word out. Mrs Kaur paused. "You seem very tense. Are you refusing to speak?" Nirmala shook her head. She remembered the counsellor's workshop: breathe out slowly, let the shoulders fall, press the feet down. She did it twice while the warden waited. Her arms loosened. "I'm not refusing, ma'am. I just froze," she said. Then she explained that the noise had been a video call with her mother in the hospital. Mrs Kaur's face softened. "Next time, tell your roommate. And come to me."

Why had Nirmala been called to the warden's office?
Her roommate had complained about late-night noise.
What does Nirmala's hunching and tight jaw suggest?
They suggest fear and anxiety at being called in; Mrs Kaur briefly read them as refusing to speak, which shows the same stiffness can be misread as defiance.
What small step helped Nirmala explain herself?
Breathing out slowly, letting her shoulders fall and pressing her feet down loosened her enough to speak.
How did the warden's view change during the meeting?
Mrs Kaur first wondered if Nirmala was refusing to speak, then softened once she understood the freeze and heard about the call.

Read this:

The anganwadi gate was already shut when Saurabh's father, Kamal, came running from the sugarcane field. Saurabh stood by the helper, face wet, fists tight. Kamal crouched in the dust. "You were frightened I wasn't coming. I was late, and that was my mistake." Saurabh hit his shoulder once, then climbed into his lap. Kamal didn't scold. He just held him till the hiccups slowed. On the walk home past the pond, Saurabh made him promise: "Tomorrow, early." Kamal tied a red thread on his own wrist to remember.

Where was Kamal coming from when he reached the anganwadi?
He came running from the sugarcane field.
Why did Saurabh hit Kamal's shoulder and then climb into his lap?
He was frightened and angry that his father was late, yet he still trusted him enough to seek comfort from him.
What did Kamal do that helped Saurabh settle?
He crouched down, named the fear, admitted the lateness was his mistake and held Saurabh without scolding until he calmed.
What would change if Kamal had scolded Saurabh for crying?
Saurabh might learn that his fear is not welcome and feel less safe turning to his father the next time he is scared.

Got a minute? Here are my questions. Meaning of prolong, please. How can I make my handwriting neater? Why does a bicycle tyre feel hard after you pump it? What is the meaning of "carry out"? Fix this: "The cat sleeping on the sofa."

1. Prolong is a verb that means to make something last longer.
2. Write slowly and keep the letters the same size. A few minutes of practice each day makes a difference.
3. Pumping squeezes more air into the same space. Because the more air inside, the harder it pushes outward on the rubber.
4. It means to do or complete a task. For example: the team carried out the plan.
5. The cat is sleeping on the sofa. Why: A verb ending in "-ing" needs a helping verb such as "is".

Read this:

There was a power cut in the hostel, and Yusuf lay in bed reading the long medicine leaflet by phone light. The doctor had given him a course of tablets for an infection. The leaflet listed forty possible side effects.
Headache. He thought his head felt heavy. Dizziness. The room did seem to tilt. Itching. His arm suddenly itched.
By midnight he was sure he had eight side effects. He messaged his friend Jyoti, panicking.
She called. "Yusuf, did you feel any of this before you read the list?"
"...No."
"Okay. Put the leaflet down. If something keeps going or worries you tomorrow, call the doctor. That's what the doctor is for."
He put it down. The itch faded.

How many possible side effects did the leaflet list?
The leaflet listed forty possible side effects.
What was Yusuf feeling by midnight?
He felt panicked and anxious, sure he had eight side effects.
What was wise about Jyoti's advice?
She helped him see that reading the list made him notice twinges, but also told him to call the doctor if something kept going or worried him.
How might Jyoti have felt when Yusuf messaged in a panic?
Jyoti probably felt concerned but calm, wanting to reassure him without dismissing real symptoms.

Cut this section down to two sentences.

His sisters were very anxious for his having an estate of his own; but though he was now established only as a tenant, Miss Bingley was by no means unwilling to preside at his table; nor was Mrs. Hurst, who had married a man of more fashion than fortune, less disposed to consider his house as her home when it suited her. Mr. Bingley had not been of age two years when he was tempted, by an accidental recommendation, to look at Netherfield House. He did look at it, and into it, for half an hour; was pleased with the situation and the principal rooms, satisfied with what the owner said in its praise, and took it immediately.

Mr. Bingley's sisters want him to own an estate, but meanwhile they happily treat his rented house as their own. Not two years after coming of age, he looked at Netherfield House on a chance recommendation and took it after half an hour.

Read this:

In the village, the lamps came on at dusk and children were called home. "Amma, five more minutes of hopscotch?" Jahnavi called. Ishita, sorting beans on the verandah, said, "Five."
Five became ten. "Just one more round, I'm on the last box!" "One round."
Then: "Kiran's didi is still playing. Can I stay till she goes?" Ishita looked up. Each ask was so small, and she had already said yes twice. "Fine, till then."
When Jahnavi finally skipped in, the stars were out and the dal had gone cold. "You said I could," Jahnavi said, surprised at Amma's face. And she had, three small times.

What was Ishita sorting on the verandah?
Beans.
Why was Jahnavi surprised at Amma's face?
She felt innocent and a little confused, since each small request had been given a yes.
What could Ishita try next time Jahnavi asks for five more minutes?
Set the full limit at the start, like "until the lamp by the well is lit", so small asks don't stretch into the whole evening.
How might Ishita feel when she sees the stars and the cold dal?
She may feel annoyed at herself, realising three small yeses added up to much more than she meant.

metadata.subtype: Small request opens the way to a bigger one [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Wednesday. Vikas leaves for the other office tomorrow, and today he gave me the training schedule for new hires. Instead of nodding and rushing to my meeting, I said, "Let me say what I now own: booking the room every Monday, sending the joining kit, and the feedback form on day five. Anything else?" Vikas laughed. "Yes, laptop requests go through IT by Thursday. I always forgot to tell people that." I would have missed it. I also asked for the shared calendar login, which came within a minute. Then I emailed the three points back to Vikas so we both had them in writing. Felt slightly silly, but much calmer. - Baljeet

By when do laptop requests go through IT?
Laptop requests go through IT by Thursday.
How did Baljeet feel about repeating everything back?
Slightly silly, but much calmer afterwards.
What extra step did Baljeet take to close the loop?
Baljeet asked for the calendar login and emailed the three points back so both had them in writing.
How might Vikas have felt on being asked "Anything else?"
Amused and probably grateful, since Vikas laughed and remembered the laptop point that had always been forgotten.

Read this:

Teacher's note, after-school care, Tuesday.
Today the other children left early for a birthday, and Zubin was the only one staying. He followed me from shelf to shelf saying, "There's nothing to do," holding my dupatta. The blocks, puzzles and crayons were all out. He looked at them and said, "Boring."
I sat down with my register and said, "I'm going to write for a bit. You can sit next to me." He sat, sighed loudly, kicked his feet. After five minutes he picked up two blocks and knocked them together. Then he built a tower. Then a garage.
Next step: tell his mother he spent twenty minutes on a garage by himself.
Zeenat

What did Zubin hold onto?
Zeenat's dupatta.
Why did Zubin keep saying "There's nothing to do"?
He felt bored and a bit lonely with his friends gone, and didn't yet know how to start something himself.
What did Zeenat do that helped?
Zeenat stayed close but didn't entertain him, letting him sit with the boredom until he began knocking blocks and built a garage.
How might Zubin's mother feel hearing about the garage?
She might feel pleased and a little surprised that Zubin played alone for twenty minutes.

Read this:

Sunday, 2 a.m. Can't sleep again. The phone bill was due Friday; I found the message today. My lab notes are in four different places, one of them apparently my brother Vaibhav's old backpack, which I brought to college by mistake. At school, Papa checked my timetable every night and Mummy packed my bag. I thought I was organised. Turns out they were. Today Vaibhav called, heard me crying, and didn't laugh. He said, "Set one alarm for every bill. And go to the counselling centre on Monday. Ask them about getting checked properly, so you know what's going on." I wrote both things on my hand so I won't forget. I'll go at ten.
Bhavna

Where did Bhavna find some of the lab notes?
In Vaibhav's old backpack.
How is Bhavna feeling at 2 a.m.?
Bhavna feels overwhelmed and restless, unable to sleep and upset about the missed bill.
What steps did Vaibhav suggest?
One alarm for every bill and going to the counselling centre to ask about a proper assessment.
How did Vaibhav react when he heard Bhavna crying?
He didn't laugh; he was kind and practical.
What is the biggest number you can roll with one dice? The smallest? With two dice?

Answer: One dice: biggest 6, smallest 1. Two dice: biggest 12 (6 and 6), smallest 2 (1 and 1).

Let the child find the faces. With two dice you can never get 1, because each dice shows at least 1.

Read this:

Dear Sumit bhaiya,
I wanted to write this because I can't say it on the phone. When Dadaji died last month, I cried at the cremation, in front of everyone. Papa put his hand on my shoulder and said, "Be strong. Boys don't cry." One of the uncles laughed and said, "Look at him, like a girl." So I stopped. Since then I make jokes all the time. At school I got into a fight over nothing. Mummy says I've become "so rude". I don't know how to explain that it's all inside and has nowhere to go.
Then I remembered: at Dadaji's house, the night after, I saw you crying on the terrace. You didn't hide. You just said, "I miss him." That's the only time I felt normal.
Can I call you when it gets bad? I don't want to joke about everything anymore.
Darshan

What did Papa say at the cremation?
"Be strong. Boys don't cry."
How has Darshan been feeling since the cremation?
Darshan has been sad and angry inside, hiding grief behind jokes and even fighting at school.
How can Sumit bhaiya support Darshan?
He can say yes to calls, listen without mocking, and show again that missing someone and crying are normal.
How might Papa see his words at the cremation?
Papa probably thought he was helping Darshan be brave, without realising it taught him to hide his sadness.

Read this:

Joseph picked up a banana and held it to his ear. "Hello? Hello?"
"Who's calling?" asked his uncle Sumit.
"Nani!" Joseph handed him the banana.
"Hello, Nani!" Sumit said into it. Joseph laughed.
Rain hammered the window. "It's raining cats and dogs," said Sumit.
Joseph ran to the window and pressed his nose to it, looking hard. "Cat?" he asked, puzzled.

What did Joseph use as a phone?
A banana.
Why did Joseph look for cats at the window?
He took Sumit's words literally and was curious, then puzzled, when he couldn't find any cats.
What could Sumit say to help Joseph?
Something simple like, "No cats, just lots of rain," since Joseph can't understand sayings yet.
How might Sumit feel watching Joseph search?
He probably finds it funny and sweet, and realises Joseph took him literally.

Juvy has a garden that has 20 rows with 10 plants in each row. She plants parsley in the first 3 rows and rosemary in the last two rows. The rest of the rows will be planted with chives. How many chives will Juvy plant?

Juvy planted 3 + 2 = 5 rows with parsley and rosemary.
So, 20 - 5 = 15 rows will be planted with chives.
Therefore, 15 x 10 = 150 chives will be planted.
The answer is 150.

Read this:

At the community centre's Thursday couples' group, Rajni, the facilitator, asked each pair to share one thing that had changed. Jasleen went first, smiling a little. "Sundays, ten to twelve, are ours now. No phones, no in-laws. Just breakfast and a long walk." Manvir nodded. "And I've got a sentence I'm allowed to use." He glanced at Jasleen. "When I come off a night shift at the depot, I say, 'I'm spent, give me an hour, then I'm yours.'" "And he comes back," Jasleen said. "Every time so far. So I don't sit there spinning stories." Manvir rubbed his neck. "And I don't feel like a criminal for needing the hour." Rajni wrote both sentences on the whiteboard.

Which hours on Sunday are theirs now?
Sundays, ten to twelve, are theirs now.
How has Manvir's feeling about needing rest changed?
He feels less guilty now; he no longer feels like a criminal for needing the hour, because the break is agreed and he comes back.
Why might Rajni write both sentences on the whiteboard?
They give the group a practical model: a fixed, protected time together and an honest, clear way to ask for space.
What difference does the promised return make to Jasleen?
She no longer sits there spinning stories; knowing Manvir will come back gives her the predictability she needed.

metadata.subtype: Stage 6: Scheduled closeness and honest limits [Response]

messages.content:
My teacher gave me this passage to study.

The three men at her mast-head wore long streamers of narrow red bunting at their hats; from the stern, a whale-boat was suspended, bottom down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was seen the long lower jaw of the last whale they had slain. Signals, ensigns, and jacks of all colours were flying from her rigging, on every side. Sideways lashed in each of her three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above which, in her top-mast cross-trees, you saw slender breakers of the same precious fluid; and nailed to her main truck was a brazen lamp.

What signs on the ship show that she has had a successful hunt?

Barrels of sperm oil are lashed in each of her three tops, and small casks of it sit in her top-mast cross-trees. The long lower jaw of the last whale hangs from her bowsprit, and a brass lamp is nailed to her main truck.
What mood is associated with Raga Marwa?
Raga Marwa is associated with a tense, restless, expectant mood.

Read this:

On Friday evening Nandini, two, sat near the little lamp at home and folded her hands like her mother Farida, eyes darting around. On Tuesday at a neighbour's singing evening she clapped along, a beat behind. On Sunday, at a relative's gathering, she watched everyone bow and bent her head down to the ground too, then looked up, grinning. Farida guessed Nandini was copying more than believing, and simply enjoyed belonging.

What did Nandini do at the singing evening?
She clapped along, a beat behind the others.
What might Nandini's grin after bowing suggest, and what else could it mean?
It suggests she enjoyed doing what everyone else did and felt part of the group. She could also just have liked the bending game.
How could Farida respond to Nandini's imitation?
She can welcome her joining in without pushing or explaining too much, and enjoy that Nandini feels included. 🙂
How might relatives see Nandini's bow?
They may find it sweet and feel that the child is joining the family's practice.

It is recommended that men should consume no more than 150 calories of added sugar per day. Mark took a soft drink in the afternoon that contained 2500 calories, 5% of which was from added sugar. Then he bought some bars of candy which had 25 calories of added sugar each. If he eventually exceeded the recommended intake of added sugar by 100%, how many bars of candy did he take?

He consumed 2500 calories, 5% of which is added sugar to give 2500*(5/100) = 125 calories of added sugar.
He exceeded the recommended intake of 150 calories by 100% for a total consumption of 150+(150(100/100)) = $300
This means he took in 300-125 = 175 calories from candy alone
Each candy had 25 calories so 175 calories which means he consumed 175/25 = 7 bars?
The answer is 7.

Read this:

School counsellor's note, Thursday. Written by Rukmini.
Rajni, Class 4, came to my room at lunch to show me a new pencil box. She said a neighbour uncle gives her gifts every week: pencils, a bracelet, chocolates. He lets her play games on his phone in his flat, "our special time." He told her not to tell her parents, because "they'll think you're greedy."
She was smiling and proud. She clearly feels important. She doesn't think anything is wrong.
I stayed calm. I told her, "Thank you for telling me, Rajni. You haven't done anything wrong. No grown-up should ask you to keep secrets from your parents."
I informed our safeguarding lead immediately. We called Rajni's mother to school this afternoon and explained gently. She is keeping Rajni away from the neighbour and has contacted the child helpline with our support. I will see Rajni again tomorrow.

What did the neighbour uncle give Rajni?
Pencils, a bracelet, chocolates.
How does Rajni feel about the neighbour uncle's gifts?
Rajni feels proud and special, and doesn't sense anything is wrong.
What did the counsellor do the same day?
The counsellor thanked Rajni, told her she wasn't to blame, informed the safeguarding lead, and called her mother to school that afternoon.
How might Rajni's mother feel hearing this?
Her mother would likely feel shocked and frightened, and also grateful the counsellor noticed and acted.
Why does a shaken bottle of fizzy drink spray when it is opened?
Shaking fills the drink with tiny gas bubbles. Because opening the bottle lets the pressure drop suddenly, the bubbles grow fast and push the liquid out.
Write it in fewer words: At this point in time, we are not in a position to accept any new members into the club.
We cannot accept new members right now.

Read this:

The district legal aid clinic was a single room at the back of the court complex, with a fan that clicked on every turn. Dolma waited on the bench with the landlord's notice folded in her pocket: vacate in fifteen days, or legal action. She earned eleven thousand a month at a salon and had no money for a lawyer.
Neelam, the panel lawyer on duty, read the notice twice. 'Do you have a rent agreement?'
Dolma took out a photocopy and her rent receipts, every one since March.
'Good. Don't ignore this, and don't move out in a panic either.' Neelam explained, in plain words, what the agreement said about notice periods and what the landlord would have to do next. She drafted a short reply for Dolma to sign and asked her to come back if anything arrived from the court.

How much did Dolma earn a month?
Eleven thousand a month at a salon.
What might Dolma have been worried about as she waited on the bench?
She was probably anxious about losing her home in fifteen days and afraid she couldn't afford to fight it.
Which other approaches would have served Dolma worse, and why is the clinic better?
Ignoring the notice or moving out in a panic would leave her without a say; the clinic helps her understand her position and reply properly at no cost.
How might the landlord see Dolma's signed reply?
The landlord learns that Dolma knows the agreement and has legal support, which may make the next step more careful.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asking a legal aid service for a rental dispute [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the residential school in Shillong, lunch in the dining hall was usually loud at their table. Today Sonali just pushed rice around her plate and looked out of the window.

Mehak's stomach tightened. What did I do? She went through the morning. She'd borrowed Sonali's geometry box without asking. She'd laughed at Sonali's wrong answer in chemistry. Last night she'd switched off the dorm light while Sonali was still reading.

By the time the plates were cleared, Mehak had a whole list and no appetite. She didn't even hear the housemaster's announcement about the trip.

At prep, she couldn't concentrate. Finally she whispered, "Sonali, are you angry with me? I'm really sorry about the light and the geometry box."

Sonali looked confused. "What? No. My grandmother's not well and I can't go home till the holidays. I've been thinking about her all day."

Mehak sat back. None of the list had anything to do with it.

Why had Sonali been quiet, according to her?
Her grandmother's not well and she can't go home till the holidays.
Why did Mehak feel so sure she had caused Sonali's mood?
Mehak was anxious, and her mind searched only her own actions for an explanation, so every small thing looked like a cause. It didn't occur to her that the mood could be about something else.
What could Mehak try the next time a friend seems quiet?
Ask a gentle, open question like "Are you okay? You seem quiet today" before building a list of her own faults. It leaves room for the real reason.
What might it be like for Sonali to hear an apology about the light when she's worried about her grandmother?
Sonali might feel puzzled, and maybe a little lonely that Mehak was thinking about herself. But it also gave Sonali a chance to share what was really on her mind.

metadata.subtype: Assuming a friend's mood is about them [Actor]

messages.content:
Can you fix my sentence? She is senior than me by two years.
One more thing: why do we put a bandage over a small cut?

1. Say it this way: She is senior to me by two years. Why: "senior" and "junior" take "to", not "than".
2. It keeps the cut clean and covered. Because a cover keeps dirt and germs out and stops the cut from being bumped.
John is a hack author.  He writes a book every 2 months.  He has been writing for 20 years and has earned an average of $30,000 per book.  How much money has he made writing?

He writes 12/2=6 books a year
That means he has written 6*20=120 books
So he has made 120*30,000=$3,600,000 from writing
The answer is 3600000.

Read this:

Manoj, you look worried about tomorrow's review of the new intern's design. Sit, let me tell you about my first year leading a team.
I was twenty-four. A junior named Farida brought me a poster she had worked on for four nights. The colours were loud, the text was tiny, and the logo was upside down. My mouth was ready to say, "Wonderful," because she looked so tired. That's what my old boss always said to me, and I never trusted it.
Instead, I, Anjali, said the only true thing I could find: "I can see how much care went into this. The colour choice is bold, and it will catch eyes from across the hall." She smiled. Then I said, "Let's make the text big enough for the back row." She nodded and fixed it by lunch.
No lecture. Just true things, said warmly.

How many nights had Farida worked on the poster?
She had worked on it for four nights.
Why was young Anjali tempted to say "Wonderful"?
Anjali felt sympathetic and a little uneasy, because Farida looked so tired and Anjali did not want to hurt Farida.
What choice in the story turned things around?
Anjali chose a true, warm sentence about Farida's care and the bold colours, then asked for bigger text, which let Farida fix it by lunch.
How might Farida have felt when Anjali praised the care and the bold colours?
Farida probably felt seen and encouraged, so she could hear the request about the text without feeling crushed.

metadata.subtype: Choosing a kind true sentence instead [Response]

messages.content:
My teacher gave me this passage to study.

"Now for the hitch in Jane's character," he said at last, speaking more calmly than from his look I had expected him to speak. "The reel of silk has run smoothly enough so far; but I always knew there would come a knot and a puzzle: here it is. Now for vexation, and exasperation, and endless trouble! By God! I long to exert a fraction of Samson's strength, and break the entanglement like tow!"

What image does the speaker use for the knot in Jane's character?

The speaker says the reel of silk has run smoothly enough so far, but a knot and a puzzle were bound to come, and now it has. He longs for a fraction of Samson's strength to snap the tangle like thread.

Jimmy needs to score at least 50 points to pass to the next class. He earned 20 points for each of the 3 exams he wrote but lost 5 points during the school year for bad behavior. How many more points can Jimmy lose and still be able to pass the next class?

Jimmy earned 20 * 3 = 60 points for the exams he wrote.
For bad behavior, he lost 5 points, so he has 60 - 5 = 55 points left.
To pass to the next class, Jimmy needs at least 50 points, so he can lose 55 - 50 = 5 more points.
The answer is 5.
Asha lives at house number 7. Her friend lives next door at the house after hers. What is her friend's house number?

Answer: 8, because 8 comes just after 7.

House numbers go in counting order along the street. Walk a real street and read the numbers.

Read this:

The science fair was the next morning, and at 9 p.m. Yusuf and Vikas, both sixteen, were finishing their poster: Plants grow taller with music!
Their data looked great. The three pots next to the speaker had grown taller than the three by the door.
Then Yusuf stopped. “Wait. The speaker was by the window.”
Vikas groaned. “So they got more sun too.”
“We can't say it's the music.”
They had no time to redo the experiment. Vikas wanted to leave the poster as it was.
Yusuf crossed out the title and wrote: Did music or sunlight help? We don't know yet. Underneath, he added: Next time: same light, only music different.
At the fair, the judge stopped at their table longest.

Where was the speaker?
By the window.
How did Yusuf feel when he realised the plants also got more sun?
He felt worried and uneasy, but honest enough to change the claim.
What was the right thing to do with the poster, and why?
Change the title to say they didn't know yet, because sunlight could explain the result.
How might Vikas feel about the change?
He may feel frustrated at first, but relieved when the judge spends the longest at their table.

Iris' family is planning a surprise birthday party for her. The party will include her 3 uncles and 4 aunts who have a son and daughter each as well as her brother and mother. In total, how many people are coming to Iris' birthday party?

Each of her aunts and uncles have a family unit of 1 son + 1 daughter + 1 aunt/uncle = 3 people.
Iris has a total of 3 uncles + 4 aunts = 7 aunts or uncles in these family units.
So among her aunts, uncles, and cousins, there will be 7 family units * 3 people in each family unit = 21 people.
Including her mother and brother, there will be a total of 21 people + 1 mother + 1 brother = 23 people coming to her party.
The answer is 23.
Draft a short announcement, around 60 words, for a free weekend reading class for the children of construction workers near our society.

Free Reading Class for Children
Starting this Saturday, volunteers from Sunrise Society will run a free reading class for the children of workers at the nearby construction site. Classes will be held every Saturday and Sunday from 4 to 5 pm in the society garden. Children aged 5 to 12 are welcome. Books, notebooks and snacks will be provided. More volunteers are always welcome.

Read this:

Hrithik stayed late in the trust office to close the year's accounts. In the bottom drawer of the cabinet he found two things: receipts showing donations spent on a private flat in the teacher's name, and a letter from a former member describing unwelcome touching by the teacher, with a note clipped to it: "settled quietly."

He read it twice, hands cold. The teacher preached simple living and honesty. Hrithik had once cried with gratitude during a discourse.

Pankaj, a fellow volunteer, found him sitting on the floor. "I feel like I've lost a father," Hrithik said, "and I want to smash something."

Pankaj read the letter and went quiet. "What you learned about patience is still yours. The teacher isn't. This has to go to the police, and to an outside auditor."

That night they photographed the papers. The next morning they took them to the police.

What did Hrithik find in the bottom drawer?
Hrithik found receipts showing donations spent on a private flat in the teacher's name and a letter from a former member describing unwelcome touching.
What is Hrithik feeling after reading the letter?
Grief and anger: he says he feels as if he has lost a father and wants to smash something.
What did Pankaj suggest, and why does it matter?
Pankaj suggested taking it to the police and an outside auditor, while keeping the good Hrithik learned, which separates the teachings from the person.
How might the former member who wrote the letter see this discovery?
The former member may feel that a complaint that was "settled quietly" is finally being taken seriously.

Read this:

Come, sit with your old Sarita ammachi. When I married your grandfather Thomas, I was twenty-five and he was a closed box. Any quarrel, he would walk out to the church compound and sit there for hours. I used to run after him, crying, pulling his sleeve, and he only went further, to the fish market, anywhere. One evening my own mother said, "You are chasing a cat. Sit still and tell him plainly." So the next time, I said, "Thomas, when you leave in the middle, I feel alone. Come back in one hour and we'll finish." Then I made my tea and did not follow. He came back in forty minutes. It took years, but he learned to stay. And I learned to stop running.

Where would Thomas go after a quarrel?
He would walk out to the church compound and sit there for hours.
What did Sarita feel when Thomas left in the middle of a quarrel?
She felt alone and upset, which is why she used to run after him crying.
What was the turning point in how Sarita handled quarrels?
She told Thomas plainly how she felt, asked him to come back in one hour and stopped following him.
How might Thomas have felt when Sarita stopped chasing him?
He probably felt less cornered, which made it easier to return on his own; he came back in forty minutes.

Read this:

Pradeep, you asked why I stopped wearing that badge. Sit, I'll tell you. I'm Jyoti mausi, and when I was twenty-five, I joined a campaign for the women who cleaned our office. I posted about it everywhere. I wore the badge. Everyone said, "Jyoti is so progressive." I liked that. Then the cleaners asked us to sign a letter to management about their wages, with our names. My manager hinted it might hurt my promotion. Suddenly I was very busy. I didn't sign. I stopped posting. One of the cleaners, Savitri, saw me in the corridor and just looked at me. That look stayed with me. I had supported them only when it made me look good. After that, I went back, signed late, and asked Savitri what they needed. She said, "Stay, even when it's hard." I've tried to since.

Who was the campaign for?
The campaign was for the women who cleaned the office.
What was Jyoti feeling when Savitri looked at her?
Jyoti felt ashamed and exposed, realising the support had been mostly for appearances.
Why was going back to sign and asking Savitri a turning point in the story?
It showed Jyoti choosing real allyship, listening and staying through discomfort, rather than support only when it looked good.
How might Savitri have felt when Jyoti didn't sign at first?
Savitri likely felt let down and disappointed, seeing that Jyoti's support vanished when it cost something.

Read this:

Looking back, I nearly put Sahil's name in a complaint to our manager. Three weeks of reports had come back with the wrong columns, and I was quietly furious. I'm Keerthana, I was twenty-five, and it was my first time guiding someone. Before sending anything I asked myself: had I ever shown him a finished report? No. I had sent a two-line instruction and walked off. So I sat with him for an hour, opened last month's report, and marked each column: this one, from this sheet, like so. I watched him do the next one himself, then set a check-in for Friday. The Friday report was mostly right, with two small errors. It wasn't quick, but it also wasn't a story about a lazy junior. It was a story about my instructions.

What had Keerthana given Sahil before the reports came back wrong?
A two-line instruction, without showing him a finished report.
Why did Keerthana stop before putting Sahil's name in the complaint?
Though quietly furious, Keerthana wanted to be fair, asked whether Sahil had ever been shown a finished report, and realised the instructions might be the cause.
What could Keerthana do if the reports still came back wrong after several coaching sessions?
Keerthana could talk openly with Sahil about the remaining gaps, then bring the manager in with a clear record of what had already been tried. 🙂
How might Sahil have felt during the hour at his desk?
He may have felt relieved that expectations became clear, with a model to follow, though perhaps a little embarrassed too.

Read this:

You asked how I dealt with it, so I'll say it straight. My name's Ramesh. Last year, someone I'd chatted with on a forum sent me an edited photo, my face stuck on something awful, and said, "Pay, or I send this to your whole school."
I couldn't breathe properly. I thought about paying. I thought about disappearing.
Instead I called my uncle Shankar. He's the one who never shouts. He came over that same hour. First thing he said: "This is not your fault, and you are not paying anyone." We didn't reply to the message. We saved everything, blocked the account and filed a complaint on the national cyber crime portal. The next morning he came with me to my principal.
The photo never went out. Maybe it would have, maybe not. But telling someone that day made it stop being mine to carry alone.

What did Uncle Shankar say first?
"This is not your fault, and you are not paying anyone."
What was Ramesh feeling when the threat arrived?
Ramesh felt terrified and trapped, struggling to breathe and thinking about paying or disappearing.
Which steps did Ramesh and Shankar take, and why do they matter?
They didn't reply, saved the evidence, blocked the account, reported it to the cyber crime portal and told the principal, so the blackmailer lost power and adults could act.
How might Uncle Shankar have felt when Ramesh called him?
Shankar was probably worried and angry at the blackmailer, but calm on the outside so Ramesh would feel safe.

Vinnie is writing an essay and needs to make sure that he has not exceeded the 1000-word limit. He wrote 450 words on Saturday and 650 words on Sunday. How many words has Vinnie exceeded the limit by?

Vinnie has written a total of 450 words on Saturday + 650 words on Sunday = 1100 words.
He has therefore exceeded the limit by 1100 written words - 1000 word limit = 100 words.
The answer is 100.
Now you try: is a triangle with sides 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm right-angled?
The answer is yes, 81 + 144 = 225.

The Pune train was delayed four hours, the station Wi-Fi was dead, and Zubin's phone had nothing to offer but its own gallery. Scrolling for something to do, Zubin landed in the folder from second year: Afreen and Zubin on the hostel roof, Afreen's birthday cake smeared on both their faces, the two of them asleep on a bus to Goa.
For months, whenever Afreen's name came up, Zubin had felt only fury about the rumours she had spread. Fury was easier. It had edges.
But on the cold bench, with the platform lights buzzing, the fury wouldn't come. Something heavier came instead. Zubin missed her. Missed the person in these photos, the one who had seemed safe.
Zubin cried quietly behind a pillar, for the first time since it happened, and felt oddly lighter afterwards.

How long was the Pune train delayed?
The train was delayed four hours.
Why was fury easier for Zubin than what came instead?
Fury had edges and felt strong, while underneath lay a painful grief for the friendship and for the person Afreen had seemed to be.
Why is crying behind the pillar a step forward?
Letting the sadness out instead of covering it with anger moves Zubin through the loss and brings some relief.
What would change if Zubin had kept holding only the fury?
The grief would stay buried, and Zubin would likely remain stuck in anger without the lightness that came after crying.

That has done me good. Well, some day Jonathan will tell me all; and lest it should ever be that he should think for a moment that I kept anything from him, I still keep my journal as usual. Then if he has feared of my trust I shall show it to him, with every thought of my heart put down for his dear eyes to read. I feel strangely sad and low-spirited to-day. I suppose it is the reaction from the terrible excitement.

Why does the writer keep a journal as usual, and how does the writer feel today?
So that Jonathan can read every thought in it if he ever fears anything was kept from him. The writer feels strangely sad and low today, and thinks it is a reaction from the terrible excitement.

Read this:

Three months after the wedding, Hrithik started teaching physics at his in-laws' coaching institute in Indore. The staff room had rules nobody wrote down. Papaji, his father-in-law, always took the first cup of tea. Varun, his wife's elder brother, decided which batches got the air-conditioned rooms. On his first day, Hrithik sat in the chair by the window, and the room went silent. Varun said, 'That's Papaji's chair,' with a smile that wasn't really one. For weeks, Hrithik felt every lesson was being judged through the glass door. Then one evening his wife, Nidhi, came to the staff room and said to her brother, in front of everyone, 'Hrithik's batch scored best in the mock test. Give him a proper room.' Varun shrugged. The next Monday, Hrithik had the corner room.

Which subject does Hrithik teach at the institute?
Physics.
How did Hrithik feel during his first weeks at the institute?
He felt watched and judged, as if every lesson was assessed through the glass door, after the awkward moment with the chair.
What could help Hrithik settle in faster?
Asking Nidhi or a friendly colleague to explain the unwritten staff-room habits, and keeping up steady teaching while the family adjusts.
How might Varun see Hrithik's arrival?
Varun is used to deciding things there, so he may see Hrithik as a newcomer testing the family order, which is why he guards the chair and the rooms.

Safari National park has 100 lions, half as many snakes, and 10 fewer giraffes than snakes. On the other hand, Savanna National park has double as many lions as Safari National park, triple as many snakes as Safari National park, and 20 more giraffes than Safari National park. How many animals in total does Savanna National park have?

Safari National park has 1/2*100=50 snakes.
Safari National park has 50-10=40 giraffes.
Savanna National park has 100*2=200 lions.
Savanna National park has 50*3=150 snakes.
Savanna National park has 40+20=60 giraffes.
Savanna National park has a total of 200+150+60=410 animals.
The answer is 410.
Canteen notice needed, short please: The canteen will not take cash from tomorrow, only cards.
Canteen: cards only from tomorrow.

Read this:

"Naveen, you've been in front of that mirror for ten minutes." Suraj leaned on the bathroom door. "I'm practising. 'Sir, I have a small suggestion.' No. 'Sir, if you have a moment.' No." "For what?" "The client proposal. My numbers are better than his." "So tell him." Naveen laughed without humour. "You don't know Bhatia sir. If he comes in whistling, you can speak. If he takes his glasses off, you say, 'Yes sir, very good sir.'" "And today?" "Glasses off." "So you said nothing." "I said his plan was excellent." Suraj was quiet. "Bhaiya, at college you argued with the dean." "That was college." Naveen rinsed his face. "Now I just watch his glasses." "You've gone smaller," Suraj said. "Since you joined." Naveen looked at himself in the mirror and didn't answer.

What does Bhatia sir do when Naveen should say only 'Yes sir'?
He takes his glasses off.
What does Naveen's rehearsing in the mirror suggest about how he feels at work?
It suggests he feels nervous and watchful, so unsure of his boss's mood that he has to practise even a small suggestion.
What small step could Naveen take with his better numbers?
He could send the numbers in a short written note, so his idea is on record even on a 'glasses off' day.
How does Suraj see the change in his older brother?
Suraj sees that Naveen, who once argued with the dean, has become quieter and smaller since joining this job.
Explain what interest on savings means, in two sentences, for a 12-year-old.
Interest is extra money a bank pays you for keeping your savings with it. The longer your money stays there, the more interest it can earn.

Read this:

Subject: nobody gets it

Yogesh bhaiya,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud. My whole friend group has shifted. Aman and Vikram sit with the football boys now, and I'm just there, eating my lunch alone like a character in a sad film. I know you're going to say everyone goes through this. But honestly, nobody has felt what I'm feeling. It's different for me. When I walk into class, I swear everyone looks up and thinks, there's the guy with no friends.

Weird thing, though. At robotics club on Thursday, a class-twelve senior told me the same happened to him in class nine. He said it lasted a few months, then he found the robotics lot.

So maybe not nobody. Did it happen to you too? You never said.

Sahil

Where did Sahil meet the class-twelve senior?
At robotics club on Thursday.
Why does Sahil believe nobody has felt this before?
Sahil feels lonely and hurt, and in that pain the experience seems completely unique, as if everyone is looking and judging.
What could Sahil do to keep the feeling softening?
Sahil could keep going to the robotics club and talk to people like the senior, who have been through something similar.
How might Yogesh bhaiya feel reading this email?
He would likely feel touched that Sahil trusted him, and want to share his own story to show Sahil isn't alone.

Classroom note, Grade 4. Kishore, maths teacher.
During activity period, Dhruv was halfway through the tangram puzzle when the bell rang for assembly. He left very slowly, looking back at the table. In assembly his lips were moving; I think he was still arranging triangles. Back in class he went straight to the puzzle before taking out his book, and finished the swan in two minutes. Interesting: when I asked about the song they had sung in assembly, he couldn't remember it at all.
Next time I'll give a two-minute warning before the bell and let children write down where they stopped. That may help them let go and listen.

What shape did Dhruv finish?
The swan.
What was Dhruv feeling as he left for assembly?
He felt reluctant and unsettled, his mind still pulled by the half-done tangram.
How might the two-minute warning help?
Children can write where they stopped, so the unfinished task nags less and they can focus on what comes next.
How does the teacher see Dhruv's behaviour?
Kishore finds it interesting that the unfinished puzzle held Dhruv's attention while the finished assembly song was forgotten.
