Monday. In the tuition centre, Swati forwarded another meme about the new batch from the mill colony: a herd of buffaloes with "Mill colony toppers". Her friends laughed. The mill colony kids sat at the back, heads down.
Wednesday. The tutor paired everyone for a maths project. Swati got Ganga, from the mill colony. Swati rolled her eyes. But Ganga knew a shortcut for percentages that saved them twenty minutes. At the break, Ganga said her mother worked double shifts at the mill so Ganga could come to tuition.
Friday. Another buffalo meme appeared in the group. Swati's thumb hovered over the laugh button. She thought of Ganga's shortcut, and her mother's double shifts. Instead she typed, "Can we stop these? Ganga's in my project and she's brilliant." The chat went quiet. Nobody sent another one that day.

What did the meme call the mill colony students?
It showed a herd of buffaloes with "Mill colony toppers".
Why did the buffalo memes feel funny to Swati on Monday?
Swati saw the mill colony students only as a group, not as faces, so the cruelty felt harmless and empathy never came.
What did Swati do on Friday, and why was it a good choice?
She asked the group to stop and named Ganga as brilliant, giving the group a real person to think about.
How might Ganga have felt seeing Swati's message?
Ganga may have felt surprised and respected, seen as a person rather than a joke.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Jahnavi, and when I got a job offer in Hyderabad, my whole family had an opinion. Nani said a girl shouldn't live alone in a big city. Chacha said the private sector was unstable and I should sit for government exams. My mother worried about the food. My cousin Ayesha, the only one who lived in Hyderabad, said, "Come! It's great." Each spoke with total confidence, and each was really talking about their own fears. I listened to all of them, thanked them, and felt pulled in four directions. Then I made a list of what I wanted, not what they feared. I took the job. Nani still sends me pickle every month.

What did Chacha suggest instead of the job?
Chacha said Jahnavi should sit for government exams.
How did Jahnavi feel listening to all the advice?
Jahnavi felt pulled in four directions by confident, conflicting opinions.
What helped Jahnavi decide while still respecting the family?
Listening and thanking everyone, then listing personal wants rather than the family's fears, kept the decision in Jahnavi's hands.
How might Nani feel about Jahnavi's choice?
Nani may still feel worried, but her monthly pickle suggests love and acceptance of the decision.

Read this:

At the lunch tables of the secondary school in Porto, Pablo was telling the story again.
"So this guy at the skate park shoves my friend, right? And I just walk up and tell him, 'Try that with me.' He backs off. Three of his friends too."
Last week it had been two friends. The week before, one.
The younger boys at the table leaned in. Priscila, who had been Pablo's friend since primary school, kept eating her soup. She had been at the skate park that day. What she remembered was Pablo saying "sorry" and pulling his friend away fast.
"You should have seen his face," Pablo said, louder.
Priscila picked up her tray and moved to the table by the window, where her lab partners were arguing about homework. Pablo didn't look up. He was already starting on the fight at the football pitch.

How many of the other boy's friends backed off in this week's version?
Three of his friends too.
What might Pablo want when he tells the fight story louder?
Pablo probably wants the younger boys to be impressed and to see him as tough, and he feels good when they lean in.
What went wrong for Pablo, and what could help?
His stretched fight stories pushed away a real friend; telling what actually happened and noticing who leaves could keep his friendships.
How does Priscila feel about the fight story?
Priscila feels uncomfortable and a little distant, because she remembers Pablo saying sorry, so she quietly moves to another table.

Read this:

The fee counter at the Pune university closed at 3 p.m., and Mahima, first in her family to go to college, had been in the wrong queue for forty minutes. The form asked for a “demand draft number.” She didn't know what that was. Everyone around her seemed to know.
She felt her face burn. Her marks in Class 12 were among the best in her district. But here she felt stupid.
At 2:40, a boy behind her, Baljeet, leaned over. “DD? Bank's across the road. I didn't know either. My cousin told me last night.”
“You're also first in your family?” she asked.
“First in my whole village.”
They ran across the road together. At 2:58, they stood at the counter, breathless, receipts in hand.
Later, over tea, they found three more students like them. They made a group chat called “First Ones.”

By what time did the fee counter close?
It closed at 3 p.m.
How did Mahima feel standing in the wrong queue?
She felt embarrassed and out of place, as if she were stupid, even though her marks were among the best.
What helped Mahima, and why?
Baljeet's help and the “First Ones” group, because community helps with unfamiliar codes like demand drafts.
How might Baljeet feel after finding others like him?
Baljeet probably feels relieved and less alone, glad to share what he knows.
How many s's and p's are in disappoint?

"Disappoint" has one s and two p's. Think of "dis" plus "appoint".
Example: Do not let one bad day disappoint you too much.
Share 6 flowers among 3 vases. How many flowers in each vase?

Answer: 2 in each vase.

Sharing works with things, not only people.

Read this:

I'm Raghav, and on Holi morning I was in charge of my little brother Kunal while our parents greeted the neighbours. Last Holi he just babbled and screamed at the colours. This time he held up his wet hands and said, "Pink! Kunal pink!" When a water balloon burst near him, he shouted, "Bhaiya, again!" I can't tell what he meant by everything, but he talked all morning.

What did Kunal shout when the water balloon burst?
He shouted, "Bhaiya, again!"
What does Kunal's "Bhaiya, again!" suggest he felt?
He seemed excited and happy, wanting more of the fun instead of being scared by the burst.
How could Raghav help Kunal keep using new words during the festival?
Name the colours and actions back to him and wait for him to try, rather than answering for him.
How does Raghav see the change in Kunal since last Holi?
Raghav notices Kunal moving from babbling and screaming to short phrases, even if not every word is clear.

Read this:

It was pouring at pickup time, and Minakshi's umbrella was the only one left by the school gate.
Minakshi, five, saw Damini's Nani arrive, soaked. “Where's your mummy, Damini?”
“I live with Nani,” Damini said.
Minakshi thought. “Oh. My Nani lives with us. She makes laddoos.”
“Mine makes kheer.”
Minakshi held out her umbrella. “Share?”
The two girls squashed under it together, Nani holding her dupatta over her own head, laughing.

Who arrived soaked at pickup time?
Damini's Nani arrived soaked.
How did Minakshi feel on hearing that Damini lives with her Nani?
She felt curious and accepting, finding something in common instead of judging.
What could a teacher say to encourage this kind of kindness?
A teacher could praise Minakshi for sharing and say that families come in many shapes.
How might Damini feel when Minakshi shares her umbrella?
She probably feels included and happy, not made to feel different.

Read this:

At the school fair in Nagpur, the token stall had a deal: ten tokens today, or twenty if you came back tomorrow. Hrithik's friend Nitin said, "Twenty's better, obviously." Hrithik agreed. On Monday, when the teacher had asked, "Ten tokens next month or twenty in five weeks?" he'd chosen twenty without blinking. But now the ring-toss stall was right there, the prizes glittering. "Ten today," Hrithik said. Nitin stared at him. "You'll get double tomorrow!" "Tomorrow's too far," Hrithik said, already running to the ring toss. By evening the tokens were gone and he'd won a plastic whistle. Nitin came back the next day and collected twenty. Hrithik watched him spend them on a remote-control car. He blew his whistle, very quietly.

What did Hrithik win at the ring toss?
A plastic whistle.
Why did Hrithik choose ten tokens today at the fair?
With the glittering prizes right there, he felt too excited to wait, so tomorrow seemed too far even though he'd been patient about a far-off choice.
What could Hrithik do next time a bigger reward is only a day away?
Walk away from the stall for a while or decide with a friend before seeing the prizes, so the pull of now is weaker.
How might Nitin feel spending twenty tokens on a car?
Nitin probably felt pleased and proud that waiting paid off.

Read this:

Dear Lavanya,

You'll laugh, but I finally understood what Miss Kurian meant about buffers.

Our Science Day assembly was supposed to open with a talk by a scientist from the university. At 9:00 she messaged: bus broke down, reaching by 9:45. I had 300 students on the ground and nothing planned for forty-five minutes.

My brain froze for about ten seconds. Then I grabbed the quiz team and asked them to start early. After the quiz I moved the model display forward and let kids walk around it. By the time the scientist arrived, people were still excited.

At our review, Aman said we should always keep fifteen spare minutes and one filler item ready. He's right. I'd been so proud of a tight timetable that I forgot tight means fragile.

Write soon,
Trisha

How many students were on the ground?
There were 300 students on the ground.
How did Trisha feel in the first moments after the message?
Trisha felt panicked and frozen for about ten seconds before recovering enough to act.
What lesson does Trisha take from the review, and why does it matter?
Trisha learns to keep fifteen spare minutes and a filler ready, because a timetable with no slack breaks as soon as one person is late.
How might the waiting students have seen the morning?
They probably saw a lively morning with a quiz and models, not a delay, so they stayed interested until the scientist came.

metadata.subtype: Approach: adapting when things go wrong on the day [Revision]

Read this:

Saturday playgroup, a park in Porto. Paulo, two, pressed his lips shut when his dad held out a slice of kiwi. Green, fuzzy, strange. He pushed the hand away. On the blanket beside him, Soo-ah, three, bit into her own slice, juice dripping down her wrist. "Mmm!" she hummed, and grabbed another. Paulo watched her chew. He shuffled closer and watched again. Then he took the kiwi from his dad's palm, licked it, and bit. He held out his hand for more.

What fruit did Paulo's dad offer him?
His dad held out a slice of kiwi.
What does Paulo shuffling closer and watching Soo-ah again suggest about his feelings?
He was curious but still unsure; seeing Soo-ah enjoy the kiwi seemed to tell him it was safe to try.
What could Paulo's dad try the next time Paulo refuses a new fruit?
He could sit Paulo near a child who is happily eating it and let him watch, without pushing the food at him.
How might Soo-ah feel if she noticed Paulo copying her and asking for more?
She might feel proud and grown-up, like she had shown a younger child something good.

Read this:

Sunday night
Nandini and I haven't spoken since Friday, when we fought over the window seat on the bus to Nani's and I said she was selfish. She said I was a crybaby.
All weekend we walked past each other like strangers. I kept waiting for her to say sorry first. I think she was waiting for me.
Tonight Mummy made pakoras and there was one left. I wanted it so much. But I took the plate to Nandini's room and said, "Half?"
She looked surprised. Then she broke it in two. "Sorry I called you a crybaby."
"Sorry I said selfish."
It wasn't losing. It felt like getting my sister back.
Jaya

What did Jaya and Nandini fight over on Friday?
The window seat on the bus to Nani's.
What feeling stopped Jaya from speaking first?
Jaya felt stubborn pride, waiting for Nandini to say sorry first.
What small gesture ended the silence?
Jaya offered to share the last pakora with Nandini, which led to both saying sorry.
How might Nandini have felt when Jaya brought the plate?
Nandini seemed surprised and relieved, breaking the pakora in two and apologising too.

Read this:

Emil was scrolling back through his messages on the tram in Copenhagen, looking for a restaurant address, when he reached Oskar's name and stopped.

The last real message was from March. Oskar had written three long paragraphs about his breakup, and Emil had replied, "That's rough, let's talk this weekend." They hadn't. After that there were only birthday wishes and a thumbs up on a photo.

It was October now.

There had been no fight. No moment he could point to. They had lived in the same corridor for three years at university; Oskar had driven him to the hospital the night he broke his wrist.

Emil put the phone in his pocket and looked out at the grey harbour. He felt something close to grief, and then felt a bit silly for it. Nobody had died. Nobody had even left. It had just... faded.

When was the last real message between Emil and Oskar?
March.
Why does Emil feel silly about feeling close to grief?
He feels sad about losing Oskar but also feels he has no right to mourn, since nobody died or left and there was no single event to blame.
What could Emil do with this sadness?
He could let himself feel it as a real loss, and if he wants, send Oskar a message about a specific memory to see if the friendship can be revived.
How might Oskar remember the unanswered "let's talk this weekend"?
He may have felt a little let down after sharing his breakup, and quietly drifted too, perhaps also sad without knowing why.
Riya puts lace round a square photo frame of side 15 cm. How much lace does she need?

Answer: 60 cm. P = 4 x 15 = 60 cm.

A square has 4 equal sides, so instead of 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 we multiply: 4 x 15 = 60 cm. Remember the unit: the answer is a length, 60 cm.

Read this:

Hostel warden's note, Block C, Thursday.

I have been watching Charu, a second-year student, at the mess counter this week. Mornings she is organised: she chooses her classes, argues sensibly about a project plan with her roommate Nirmala, even decides the weekend travel. By eight at night she stands at the counter for a long time, then takes only a sweet bun, skips the dal and goes upstairs. Twice she told Nirmala she would answer the project email "later" and did not.

Today I asked her how the day had gone. She laughed and said, "Too many choices, ma'am, I'm out of choosing." I suggested she fix her dinner and one evening task before lunch. She wrote them in her phone. I will check in next week.

What does Charu take from the mess counter at eight at night?
She takes only a sweet bun, skips the dal and goes upstairs.
Why does grabbing a sweet bun and putting off the email seem reasonable to Charu by evening?
Charu feels drained and weary from a day of choosing classes, plans and travel, and the bun and "later" spare her one more decision.
What did the warden suggest, and why might it help?
The warden suggested fixing dinner and one evening task before lunch, so Charu makes those choices while her mind is still fresh.
How is Nirmala affected by Charu's evening habit?
Nirmala is left waiting on the project email and may feel frustrated or unsure whether Charu cares about their shared work.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, Friday. Rukmini, operations lead.
In Monday's planning meeting, the regional head set the Diwali delivery schedule using last year's warehouse capacity. Nitin, three months into the job, frowned at the spreadsheet, opened his mouth and closed it. He said nothing.
By Thursday two trucks were stuck at a full warehouse in Nagpur. At tea Nitin told me quietly that he had seen the capacity problem on Monday. "I thought it would sound rude. He's been here twenty years." He looked miserable.
What I did next: I thanked him for telling me, and said silence felt safe on Monday but cost us two trucks. I showed him how to raise it next time: privately, as a question, with the numbers. Then I took him to the regional head's cabin. Nitin explained the capacity issue himself. The head said, "Why didn't anyone say?" and asked Nitin to check next month's plan.

Where were the two trucks stuck?
They were stuck at a full warehouse in Nagpur.
What was Nitin feeling when he told the supervisor about Monday?
Nitin felt miserable and guilty, having seen the problem but kept quiet for fear of seeming rude.
What did the supervisor teach Nitin about raising problems?
To raise it privately, as a question, with the numbers, so a concern sounds respectful instead of like a challenge.
How did the regional head react when Nitin explained?
The head seemed surprised and wished someone had spoken up, then trusted Nitin to check next month's plan.

Rob and Mark plan to meet at the national park. It takes 1 hour for Rob to get to the national park and it takes three times as much time for Mark to get to the national park. If Rob leaves his home at 11 a.m., at what time should Mark leave his home so that they both arrive at the same time?

It takes 1 hour * 3 = 3 hours for Mark to get to the national park.
The extra time it takes Mark to get to the national park is 3 hours - 1 hour = 2 hours
Mark should leave his home at 11 a.m. - 2 hours = 9 a.m.
The answer is 9.

James can do a farmer's walk with 300 pounds per hand for 20 meters.  He can lift 30% more if he only goes 10 meters.  In addition, lifting straps give him another 20%.  How much can he move with lifting straps for 10 meters if he increases his 20-meter distance without straps by 50 pounds and everything else increases in proportion?

After the increase, he can lift 300+50=350 pounds
Decreasing the distance increase the amount he can lift by 350*.3=105 pounds
So he can lift 350+105=455 for 10 feet
The straps add another 455*.2=91 pounds
So his total weight is 455+91=546 pounds per hand
The answer is 546.

Read this:

Dear Vinita didi,
Remember in June when Rhea and I didn't talk for a whole month because I kept arguing that the scooty dent wasn't really my fault? You said next time, try just saying sorry and see what happens. I tried it this week.
I posted a group photo from the picnic where Kavin had his eyes half shut and food on his shirt. He messaged me, really upset. My first reply was already typed: "It's just a photo, chill." I deleted it. I wrote: "You're right, I should have asked. Sorry. I've taken it down."
He called me something rude in his first message, and I did tell him that part wasn't okay. But I didn't pretend the photo was his fault.
By evening he sent a funny sticker and we were normal again. One day instead of one month!
Love,
Ira

What reply had Ira typed before deleting it?
“It's just a photo, chill.”
How did Ira feel about how quickly things recovered with Kavin?
Ira felt relieved and pleased, even surprised, that a plain sorry fixed things in one day instead of one month.
How did Ira balance owning the mistake with not taking all the blame?
Ira apologised plainly and took the photo down, but also told Kavin his rude word wasn't okay, taking responsibility without accepting blame that wasn't Ira's.
How might Kavin have felt if he had received the first reply?
Kavin would likely have felt dismissed and more hurt, and the quarrel might have dragged on like the month with Rhea.
Why do window panes rattle during a loud clap of thunder?
Loud thunder shakes the glass in its frame. Because a loud sound is a series of strong pressure changes in the air, and the thin glass is pushed back and forth by them, it vibrates.

Read this:

In the college library, Binita read the same paragraph of her thermodynamics chapter three times. Her phone lay face-up beside the book. Divyansh had posted a story an hour ago; she had watched it twice and checked whether he was online. Her friend Ishita slid into the seat opposite. "You've been on that page since we sat down."
Binita admitted it quietly. "I keep checking his profile. I know it's silly. When he doesn't post, I imagine he's upset with me, and when he does, I try to work out who it's for. I've spoken to him maybe four times."
"So you're mostly making up the rest?" Ishita asked, gently.
Binita winced, then nodded, and turned her phone face-down.
"Come to the badminton trials with me tomorrow?"
Binita said yes.

How many times has Binita spoken to Divyansh, according to her?
She says she has spoken to him maybe four times.
Why does Binita imagine Divyansh is upset when he does not post?
She knows very little about him, so her worry fills the gaps with guesses; she also feels silly admitting it.
What could Binita do to loosen the loop?
She could keep her phone away while studying, join things like the badminton trials, and keep talking with Ishita. If she still likes Divyansh, she can get to know him in ordinary settings.
How does Ishita see Binita's habit?
Ishita sees a friend stuck on one page and worried. She points out, gently, that much of it is imagined, and offers something to do together instead of judging.

Sit, Chinmay. You said yesterday that you go to your father's flat and come home angry, so Thomas uncle will tell you what he did. Not a lecture. When I was twenty-five my father fell and needed help every morning. This was the man who never once came to my school and called me lazy at every dinner. I went daily and did the work, and under my skin I was furious. What I learned was that I could bring his food and still say, "I will not sit through the insults." The first time I said it, he went quiet, and after some weeks he stopped. I also spoke to a counsellor, which took me a year to admit I needed. I never forgave him in one clean moment. But I could look after him without pretending the old days had not happened.

How old was Thomas when his father fell?
Thomas was twenty-five when his father fell.
What was Thomas feeling while he did his father's daily care, and how do you know?
He was furious underneath, as he says himself, because of the old hurt of being called lazy and never being visited at school.
What two things let Thomas keep caring for his father without swallowing the hurt?
He set a limit, saying he would not sit through the insults, and he talked to a counsellor about the past.
How might Chinmay feel hearing this after what Chinmay said about visiting the father's flat?
Chinmay may feel relieved and less alone, hearing that caring for a parent and staying angry about the past can exist together.
Give me a haiku about a night train.

The night train rushes
Windows glow like moving stars
Far towns fall asleep

The kids in Ms. Swanson's class have an average of 5 zits each. The kids in Mr. Jones' class have an average of six zits each. If there are 25 kids in Ms. Swanson's class and 32 in Mr. Jones' class, how many more zits are there in Mr. Jones' class than in Ms. Swanson's?

First find the total number of zits in Mr. Jones' class: 6 zits/kid * 32 kids = 192 zits
Then find the total number of zits in Ms. Swanson's class: 5 zits/kid * 25 kids = 125 zits
Then subtract the number of zits in Ms. Swanson's class from the number in Mr. Jones' class to find the difference: 192 zits - 125 zits = 67 zits
The answer is 67.

On the crowded minibus home through Addis Ababa, Esther watched an old man across the aisle staring out of the window, a folder of papers on his knees. Suddenly she pictured herself at sixty on this same route, still in the accounting job her uncle had arranged, never having asked whether she even liked numbers, never having told her father, Abebe, that she had forgiven him for the years he worked abroad. Her hands went cold. That week she had rewritten her internship essay eleven times, as if one perfect paragraph could promise a good life. At home, her father was frying onions. Esther put her bag down. "Aba, can I tell you something I've never said?" He turned down the flame and pulled out a chair.

How many times had Esther rewritten her internship essay?
Eleven times that week.
What made Esther's hands go cold on the minibus?
She imagined herself at sixty with regrets, an unquestioned job and words never said to her father, and the fear of that life gripped her.
What choice did Esther make at home, and how is it different from rewriting the essay?
She chose to tell her father something she had never said. Instead of chasing perfection, she acted honestly now on the regret she feared.
What might Abebe be feeling when he turns down the flame and pulls out a chair?
He seems to sense something important and wants to listen fully, though he may be a little nervous about what his daughter will say.

Farida's rule sat in a note on her phone, written two years earlier with help from Amandeep, a friend who was a registered adviser: "Target 60% shares, 40% debt funds. If shares drift below 55% or above 65%, move back to 60. Only on the first working day of a quarter."
On 1 April the market had fallen hard, and her share portion had slipped to 52 percent. The complication: Farida was at a client site in rural Odisha for two weeks, with one bar of signal and a laptop that kept dying.
She could have waited until she got back, when things looked calmer. Instead, at 6 am, standing on the guest-house roof where the signal was best, she moved enough from her debt fund into shares to bring it back to 60. It took twenty minutes and three dropped connections.
She didn't look at the market again until July.

What share of her money did Farida's rule target for shares?
60% shares.
What might Farida have felt on the guest-house roof at 6 am?
She may have felt uneasy moving money into a falling market, but determined to follow the rule set when she was calm.
What made Farida's rule easy to follow even in a crisis?
It was written in advance with clear numbers and a fixed date, so she didn't have to make an emotional judgement.
How might Amandeep see Farida's choice?
Amandeep, who helped write the rule, would likely be glad she followed it despite the crash and the poor signal.

On the farm outside Mehsana, Nilesh kicked the water bucket across the yard. "I'm not feeding the goats! Why do I always have to?"
"Don't you shout at me!" Bhavna shouted back, louder. "Pick that up right now!"
Nilesh's voice went higher. "You never listen!" The goats bleated. Both of them were red-faced, and the shouting climbed and climbed.
Then Bhavna heard her own voice ringing off the shed and stopped. She took a long breath. "We're both too angry to talk," she said quietly. "I'm going to sit by the well. We'll talk after."
Nilesh stood with his fists clenched, then slowly picked up the bucket. Later, sitting beside her on the well's edge, he said, "Rohit never feeds them. It's not fair." Bhavna nodded. "Then let's make a turn chart."

What did Nilesh kick across the yard?
Nilesh kicked the water bucket across the yard.
What was Nilesh feeling when he shouted "You never listen!"?
Nilesh felt angry and unheard, and the feeling grew as Bhavna shouted louder.
What did Bhavna do that turned things around?
Bhavna stopped, took a long breath, said they were both too angry to talk and came back once they were calm.
How did the shouting look from Bhavna's side before she stopped?
Bhavna was angry too, meeting shout with shout, until she heard her own voice ringing off the shed.

With a last faint effort, which would have been powerless but for my yielding to it and assisting it, he raised my hand to his lips. Then, he gently let it sink upon his breast again, with his own hands lying on it. The placid look at the white ceiling came back, and passed away, and his head dropped quietly on his breast.

Answer from the text. What does he do with the speaker's hand?
With a last faint effort he raises it to his lips, then lets it sink onto his breast, with his own hands lying on it.

January. Ritu started talking to the language-learning app's cartoon owl every morning. 'Sorry, Professor, I forgot yesterday.' Her husband Vishal laughed at her apologising to an app.

April. The owl sent sad-faced reminders, and Ritu felt a real pang of guilt when she missed a day. She caught herself explaining her excuses to it aloud. She stopped. 'It's a notification,' she said to herself. 'It doesn't actually feel sad.'

July. Ritu still called the owl Professor and still did her lessons. But now she practised her Spanish with Vishal at dinner and joined a weekly class at the community centre, where real people laughed at her accent and corrected her kindly. 'The Professor is useful,' she told Vishal. 'But you're the one who notices when I get better.'

What did Ritu call the app's owl?
Professor.
What did Ritu feel when she missed a day in April?
Ritu felt a real pang of guilt, as if the owl were actually sad.
How did Ritu keep the fun without being ruled by it?
She kept the nickname but reminded herself it was just a notification, and added practice with Vishal and a weekly class with real people.
How might Vishal feel when Ritu says he notices when she gets better?
Vishal would probably feel touched and valued, seeing that he matters more to her than the app.

Friday, 1 a.m.

Can't sleep again. Rohit and I had our worst fight yet, about napkins. Napkins!
It isn't really about napkins. It started in October with a simple plan: one day, close family, the garden behind Rohit's parents' house. Then his Dadi wanted a proper sangeet. Then my Chachi wanted a cocktail night "for the younger ones". Then someone said a wedding without a horse would look cheap. Every time, we said yes, because saying no to elders felt rude.
Now it's three events, a horse, a DJ, and a budget that is double what we started with. Rohit's working weekends to cover it.
Noor asked me today, "Are you excited?" I didn't know what to say.
I used to daydream about this wedding. Now I just want it to be over.
— Preeti

Where was the wedding originally going to be held?
In the garden behind Rohit's parents' house.
How does Preeti feel about the wedding now?
Preeti feels drained and unhappy, unable to answer whether it is exciting and just wanting it to be over.
What would you change first in how Preeti and Rohit handled relatives' requests?
Agree together on a few non-negotiables and check each new request against them, saying no kindly when it doesn't fit.
What might Noor notice when Preeti can't answer the question?
Noor may sense that Preeti is stressed and unhappy, and might worry about how the planning is affecting Preeti and Rohit.

At harvest time in their village near Nanded, Samir, five, sat high on the tractor seat beside his Abba. "Payal! Look at the calf!" he shouted to his little cousin on the ground. "Where?" Payal, four, spun round. "There! Behind the sugarcane!" Payal jumped, but saw only green stalks. Samir looked down at her, then at the tall cane. "Oh. You're too small." He climbed down, took her hand, and walked her round the edge of the field until they found the calf.

Where was the calf?
Behind the sugarcane.
What was Samir feeling when he looked down at Payal?
Samir felt surprised, realising Payal was too small to see over the cane from the ground.
How did Samir solve the problem once he understood Payal's view?
He climbed down, took her hand, and walked her round the field to where she could see the calf.
How might Payal have felt jumping but seeing only stalks?
Payal probably felt frustrated and left out, unable to see what Samir was excited about.

Monday: Ritu noticed Pooja eating alone on the steps behind the library. Pooja had been in their group last term.
Wednesday: In the class group chat, someone made a new group for the history project. Ritu saw that Pooja wasn't added. Nobody said anything.
Thursday: Ritu picked up her tiffin and walked to the library steps. She didn't make a speech. She just sat down. "Can I sit? Too noisy inside."
Pooja looked up, surprised. "Sure."
They ate. Ritu asked if Pooja wanted to join her history project pair. Pooja nodded.
Friday: Two other girls came to the steps too.

Where was Pooja eating alone?
She was eating alone on the steps behind the library.
What might Ritu have been feeling as she walked to the library steps?
Ritu probably felt a little nervous but caring, wanting to help Pooja without drawing attention.
Why did Ritu's small act work?
She simply sat with Pooja and offered to pair for the project, without making a fuss, which quietly broke the cycle.
How might Pooja feel when Ritu sits down?
Pooja feels surprised and relieved, less alone after days of being left out.

My sister Indu is five and never stops moving. At dinner she stands on her chair, sits, kneels, stands again. Amma says, 'Wash hands, get your plate, sit,' and Indu washes her hands, then forgets the plate because she sees an ant.
But give her the bug jar and she watches ants for an hour, not moving at all.
Yesterday Appa said, 'Why are you so naughty?' Indu's face went red and she hid under the table. 'I'm TRYING,' she yelled.
I believed her.
Karthik

What did Indu see that made her forget her plate?
An ant.
What does Indu yelling 'I'm TRYING' from under the table suggest?
It suggests she feels hurt and frustrated at being called naughty when she really is making an effort.
What choice could Appa make next time instead of asking why she is so naughty?
He could give one short instruction at a time, like 'get your plate', and notice when she tries, without shaming her.
How does Karthik see Indu's behaviour?
Karthik believes she really is trying, and has noticed that she can focus for an hour on the bug jar.

At nineteen, Nitin took an apprenticeship at a tractor repair workshop in a small town in Haryana. It was the first time he'd lived without his mother's cooking or his father's early wake-up call. Within a month he was eating fried snacks from the bus stand and falling asleep on the workshop bench after lunch.
Samir, the senior mechanic, tossed him a steel tiffin one day. "My wife packs extra. Eat that. And come walk with me at six tomorrow."
The walks were along the canal, before the heat. Nitin grumbled the first week. By the second, he was waking up before the alarm. He started buying vegetables from the Sunday market and cooking khichdi on a small stove.
He still ate samosas sometimes. But he stopped falling asleep on the bench.

Where did Nitin and Samir walk?
Along the canal, before the heat.
How do you think Nitin felt when he started waking before the alarm?
Nitin likely felt surprised and more energetic, pleased that the walks had become a habit.
What small steps helped Nitin build a routine?
Morning walks, buying vegetables at the Sunday market and cooking khichdi gave him structure that his parents used to provide.
How might Samir see his role with the young apprentice?
Samir seems to feel protective and caring, quietly guiding Nitin toward healthier habits.

It was 11 p.m., two hours before the app launch, the office pantry littered with pizza boxes, when Tanuja caught Chinmay, the founder, by the coffee machine. "Can we talk about my salary review? It was due in June."
Chinmay sighed. "Tanu, right now? We're a family here. Families don't count every rupee. And honestly, a hundred people would love your job."
Her cheeks went hot. For a second she felt ungrateful, greedy, small. Then she noticed the pattern: the family line, the hundred people, the guilt, and no answer to her question.
"I love working here," she said evenly. "That's why I want it to be fair. I'm not asking tonight. Could we fix a meeting this week, and could you send me the review criteria in writing?"
Chinmay blinked. "Fine. Thursday."
She sent a short email confirming Thursday before going back to her desk.

When was Tanuja's salary review due?
In June.
What was Tanuja feeling when Chinmay said a hundred people would love her job?
She felt ungrateful, greedy and small for a moment, her cheeks going hot, before she recognised the guilt as pressure.
How did Tanuja respond to the pressure?
She stayed polite, didn't argue that night, asked for a meeting this week, requested the criteria in writing, and confirmed Thursday by email.
How might Chinmay see Tanuja's calm request?
Chinmay seems surprised and slightly cornered, since his guilt-trip did not work and a fair request left him little room to refuse.

Dadar platform roared with announcements. Their train was leaving in four minutes, and Minakshi mausi was dragging the big suitcase.
Zubin stopped to stare at a man selling balloons.
“ZUBIN! Hold my hand. NOW.”
He grabbed her dupatta at once, nearly tripping. On the train he sat perfectly straight, hands in his lap, while his cousins ran up the aisle.
“You're being so good,” said Mausaji.
Zubin whispered to Minakshi mausi, “Are you still angry at me?” She pulled him close. “No, jaan. I was scared of losing you.” Only then did he lean against her.

How long before the train was leaving?
The train was leaving in four minutes.
Why did Zubin sit so straight on the train?
He felt anxious and afraid his mausi was still angry, so he stayed very still to avoid more disapproval.
What did Minakshi mausi do that helped Zubin?
She explained she had been scared of losing him, not angry, and pulled him close, which let him relax.
How might Mausaji have read Zubin's stillness?
Mausaji saw it as good behaviour and praised him, without noticing the worry behind it.
HR ne bola "Please submit your documents at the earliest." Earliest matlab sabse pehle?
Almost. "At the earliest" means "as soon as possible". It does not give a fixed date, but they want the documents quickly. It is safe to submit them in a day or two.

The snack machine at Richmond High School sells candy bars for $2 each and chips for $.50 each. How much money, in dollars, will 5 students need in total if each of them gets 1 candy bar and 2 bags of chips?

The students buy 2*5=10 bags of chips.
10 bags of chips cost 10*0.5=5 dollars.
5 candy bars cost 5*2=10 dollars.
They will need 10+5=15 dollars.
The answer is 15.

Both Jyoti and Kavitha heard this week that their batchmate got a research fellowship abroad. Their reactions couldn't be more different. Jyoti came to me the next day with a printout of the fellowship requirements. "What do I need to be ready for next year?" We made a plan: one paper, better statistics, two recommendations. Kavitha, on the other hand, has been quiet and skipped the lab twice. When I asked, she said, "What's the point? I'll never be at her level." She seemed to have decided the goal was out of reach. I asked her to write down three small steps she could take this month. She hesitated, but wrote one. I'll check in with both of them next week.

What did Jyoti bring to the mentor?
Jyoti came with a printout of the fellowship requirements.
What was Kavitha feeling when she said "What's the point?"
Kavitha felt discouraged and envious, sure she'd never reach that level.
Why might small steps help Kavitha?
Breaking the goal into steps makes it feel reachable, which can turn comparison from a weight into motivation.
How might the batchmate who got the fellowship see these reactions?
The batchmate likely doesn't know her success is inspiring one friend and discouraging another.

Monday: The principal announced that Arjav from 10C had died in a road accident over the weekend. The hall went silent. Lalit didn't cry. He felt nothing at all, like cotton wool in his chest. He and Arjav had played on the same football team.
Wednesday: The school held a candlelight vigil in the courtyard. Parul, beside him, was sobbing. Others laid marigolds by Arjav's photo. Lalit held his candle and watched the flame, still numb. He felt terrible for not crying. Was something wrong with him?
Friday: Lalit went to the counsellor, Mrs Bose. "Everyone was crying. I just stood there."
She said gently, "People grieve differently. Some cry. Some feel numb, especially at first. Neither means you cared less."
Lalit let out a long breath. On Saturday, alone at the football ground, he cried for the first time.

What did others lay by Arjav's photo?
Marigolds.
What was Lalit feeling during the vigil?
Lalit felt numb and then guilty for not crying, worried something was wrong with him.
How did Mrs Bose help Lalit?
She explained that people grieve differently and that numbness doesn't mean caring less, which eased his guilt.
How might Parul have experienced the vigil differently?
Parul seemed to feel her grief openly and strongly, sobbing, while Lalit's grief came later and alone.

Quiz note, Friday. Deepika, Class 6. Today's inter-section quiz went well until the last round. When I made a terrible pun, Yash started a friendly “Boooo!” and the whole hall laughed, me included. That kind of boo is fun; everyone's in on it. But two minutes later, when Section C's youngest player got an easy question wrong, the booing started again, aimed at her. She shrank in her chair. Yash, I noticed, stopped at once and looked around. I paused the quiz and said, “Booing my jokes is fine. Booing a person who's trying is not.” After the quiz I spoke to the group who had kept going.

What made the hall start a friendly boo?
The teacher's terrible pun made Yash start a friendly “Boooo!”.
What was the youngest player feeling when she shrank in her chair?
She felt embarrassed and hurt by the booing aimed at her after an easy mistake.
How did Deepika make the difference between the two boos clear?
Deepika paused the quiz and said booing her jokes is fine but booing a person who's trying is not, then spoke to the group afterwards.
What might Yash have noticed that made the booing stop for Yash?
Yash likely saw the young player shrink and realised this boo was aimed at a person, not a joke.
Maryann spends seven times as long doing accounting as calling clients. If she worked 560 minutes today, how many minutes did she spend calling clients?

Let a be the amount of time Maryann spends doing accounting and c be the amount of time she spends calling clients: We know that a + c = 560 and a = 7c.
Substituting the second equation into the first equation, we get 7c + c = 560
Combining like terms, we get 8c = 560
Dividing both sides by 8, we get c = 70
The answer is 70.
Ruth is counting the number of spots on her cow. The cow has 16 spots on its left side and three times that number plus 7 on its right side. How many spots does it have total?

First multiply the number of spots on the left side by 3: 16 spots * 3 = 48 spots
Then add 7 to find the number of spots on the right side: 48 spots + 7 spots = 55 spots
Then add the number of spots on each side to find the total number of spots: 55 spots + 16 spots = 71 spots
The answer is 71.

Coach's note, city athletics club, Saturday.
The selection list arrived this morning: Uma is in the state relay squad. Dolma is not. They have trained side by side for three years. Dolma hugged Uma first, loudly and fast, then went off to run extra laps nobody had set. I let her run. Afterwards she sat on the bench, untying and retying one shoe. I asked how she was. She said, "I'm so happy for her. I'm also jealous, and I hate that." I told her both can sit together, and saying it is better than hiding it. At the end of practice she went over to Uma again, slower this time, and said something I couldn't hear. Uma laughed and cried a little. I have booked a session with Dolma on Tuesday to plan next season.

How long have Dolma and Uma trained side by side?
Three years.
What does Dolma untying and retying one shoe suggest?
It suggests she was unsettled, caught between feelings she hadn't sorted out yet: happy for Uma and stung at the same time.
What helped Dolma move from a fast hug to a real congratulation?
Saying the jealousy out loud and hearing that both feelings can sit together let her return to Uma calmly and congratulate her properly.
How might Uma have experienced the two hugs?
The first, quick hug may have felt a little hollow; the slower second talk likely felt real, which is why Uma laughed and cried 🤍

Come, sit with an old man for a minute, and I'll tell you about Elizabeth. I'm Tanvir; I ran the bakery on Clarke Street for thirty years, and she lived above it.
She was twenty-five when her mother died. For weeks she barely came down. The lights were on at odd hours.
Then one Sunday she came into the shop and asked if I still gave the leftover bread to the shelter on Mill Road. I said yes. She asked if she could carry it.
She carried it every Sunday after that, and she started staying to help serve. She went back to her mother's church too, sat in the same pew. She told me once, "It still hurts every day. But on Sundays it has somewhere to go."
The grief didn't leave her. But she could live beside it.

Where did Tanvir give the leftover bread?
He gave it to the shelter on Mill Road.
What did Elizabeth mean when she said "on Sundays it has somewhere to go"?
She still felt grief every day, but helping at the shelter and sitting in the church gave that grief a place and made it bearable.
What was the turning point in Elizabeth's story?
The turning point was her asking to carry the bread to the shelter, which led her into helping others and back to her mother's church.
How might Tanvir have felt seeing Elizabeth come down that Sunday?
Tanvir was likely relieved and touched, after weeks of seeing her lights on at odd hours and her barely coming down.

Tuesday
Nirmala Ma'am asked us to write whether school uniforms are good or bad. I actually think they're bad, because they're hot and I can't wear my yellow kurta. But in class Ma'am said uniforms make everyone equal, and she smiled when she said it. So I wrote that uniforms are good. Three paragraphs about equality. I didn't believe any of them.
When she handed the essays back, she'd written 'Very good, Arohi!' and I felt happy for about a minute. Then I felt strange, like the 'very good' was for somebody else.
Pihu wrote that uniforms are bad and gave real reasons. Ma'am wrote 'Strong argument!' on hers too. So she didn't even mind.
Next time I'm going to write what I think. Probably.

What does Arohi actually think about uniforms?
Arohi thinks they're bad, because they're hot and the yellow kurta can't be worn.
Why did the 'Very good' feel like it was for somebody else?
Arohi wrote what seemed to please Ma'am, not what Arohi believed, so the praise brought brief happiness and then an uneasy, hollow feeling.
What did Arohi learn from Pihu's essay?
That Ma'am also praised a different, honest opinion, so Arohi could write real thoughts without losing approval.
How might Nirmala Ma'am feel if she knew Arohi had written against Arohi's own view?
She would likely feel concerned, since she praised Pihu's honest argument and seems to want real reasons, not agreement.

1. Why do we write down how much we spend?
2. How can I earn a little pocket money at home?

1. It shows where our money goes. Because we can then spend less on things we do not need.
2. Ask your parents if you can do extra jobs like watering plants or tidying the shelves. Do the job well and on time.

Before I signed anything in Pune, I took a Friday off and went there for the weekend. My listings had promised "ten minutes to the office" in three different places. So at half past five, the worst hour, I rode the route from the office to each address, and each time the ten minutes turned into forty. On Saturday I walked three areas end to end: the lane behind the market, the quiet colony with the tree-lined road, the new towers near the highway. I bought tea at a stall in each and asked the vendor what the place was like at night. One was loud, one had no shops, one felt right. My wife Ishita, on the phone, asked, "And the photos?" I said, "The photos didn't show the traffic." I signed for the third area on Sunday. - Kiran

How many areas did Kiran walk through?
Kiran walked through three areas.
How did Kiran feel about the listings after the visit?
Kiran became sceptical and wary of them, since the promised ten minutes turned into forty.
What else could Kiran do before signing a lease?
Kiran could ask people who live nearby or a colleague about costs and problems, or rent short-term first, to add more direct information.
How might Ishita have felt hearing about the trip on the phone?
Ishita may have felt reassured and curious, wanting a real picture of the area beyond the photos.

Every first of the month, Avni and Abhinav each moved money into their joint account, in proportion to what each earned: Abhinav's share bigger, Avni's smaller. That one account paid the rent, the groceries and the home-loan instalments. Whatever stayed in their own accounts was theirs to spend without explanation. It had begun after an argument about a pair of headphones. Now Abhinav bought comics without a word, and Avni paid for art classes and never had to justify the fees. On a Saturday in Pune, Abhinav came home with a new board game and Avni looked up from the sofa. "Did you check the budget?" "It's my money," said Abhinav, grinning. Avni just smiled. "Have fun." The old friction had gone.

What did the joint account pay for?
The rent, the groceries and the home-loan instalments.
What does Avni's smile and "Have fun" suggest about how Avni feels?
It suggests Avni feels relaxed and content, since personal spending no longer needs a defence.
What could they do if one of their incomes changes?
They could work out the shares again in proportion to income so the joint account stays fair.
How might Abhinav feel about not having spending checked?
Abhinav likely feels free and respected, and grins about it.

Last week I really wanted to stay up late for the cricket final. I told Mummy, “Everyone is allowed!” She said, “Everyone?” I admitted that only Siddharth was. Then I tried a different reason: “I finished my homework, so I've earned it.” This time she listened. She said it was a real point but that the match ended after ten and school was next day. She offered to record it for the morning. I was cross for a minute, but I saw her reasons. I remember thinking that a true reason worked better than saying everyone. Manoj.

Who was the only person allowed to stay up late?
Siddharth.
How did Manoj feel when Mummy offered to record the match?
He was cross for a minute, but he calmed down once he saw her reasons for saying no.
What alternative did Mummy offer for the cricket final?
She offered to record it so it could be watched in the morning, which respected the limit and the wish.
How might Siddharth's parents see their son staying up late?
They may have their own reasons and rules, and Manoj's request shows that families decide differently.

During the power cut at the preschool, the fans stopped, and Neelam ma'am gathered the children in the corridor with a torch for story time. Rukmini, five, put her hand up. "I saw a tiger in my garden! It was THIS big!" She spread her arms. "It ate my slipper!" The children gasped. Neelam ma'am smiled. "A tiger! That's a big story. Was it a real tiger or a pretend tiger?" Rukmini thought. "Pretend. But it was hungry." Everyone laughed. "Pretend tigers get very hungry," Neelam ma'am said. "Shall we make up more of its story?" The class spent the power cut deciding what the tiger ate next.

What did Rukmini say the tiger ate?
Her slipper.
How did Rukmini seem to feel telling the tiger story?
She seemed excited and proud, spreading her arms to show its size.
What did Neelam ma'am do that respected both imagination and facts?
She enjoyed the story but asked if it was real or pretend, then turned it into a shared make-believe game.
How did the other children respond to Rukmini's story?
They gasped and then laughed, joining in to invent more of the tiger's story.

Note to self, after mid-semester marking – R. Nair
Sunaina, second row, never asks questions. She takes careful notes and nods. I assumed she was following.
Her paper says otherwise. She got the first two questions right and left the last three blank, all on recursion, which we covered in weeks four to six. In the margin of question four she had written, very small, 'don't understand the stack'.
I asked her to stay after class today. She said she'd been confused since week four but didn't want me to think she was weak, especially since the class moves fast. She was close to tears.
That confusion could have been fixed in ten minutes in week four. Now she has lost marks she didn't need to lose.
I've given her a slot on Friday at 4, and tomorrow I'll tell the class that basic questions are welcome, at any time.

What had Sunaina written in the margin of question four?
'don't understand the stack'.
What was Sunaina feeling when asked to stay after class?
She felt afraid of seeming weak and was close to tears, having hidden her confusion since week four.
What could Sunaina bring to the Friday slot?
Her attempts at the recursion questions, marked where the stack stops making sense, so the gap can be found fast.
How does the paper change R. Nair's view of Sunaina?
R. Nair sees that nodding did not mean understanding and regrets not making room for basic questions sooner.

Neelam ma'am closed her laptop when the young founder said he wanted two more months to polish before showing anyone. "Sit. Let me tell you about Divyansh. Years ago he came to me with savings for eight months and a lovely idea: an app for booking home cooks. He was twenty-four and terrified of looking amateur.
So he polished. New colours, new icons, smoother animations. Every time I asked, 'Has any customer used it?' he said, 'Not yet, it's not ready.' Five months went. His designer cost money. His rent cost money. When he finally showed it to real families, they said the booking steps were confusing and they wanted to pay in cash. Everything he had perfected was the wrong thing.
He had three months left by then. He didn't make it. He's fine now, a good product lead, but he tells everyone: show it rough, show it early."

How many months of savings did Divyansh start with?
Eight months.
What was young Divyansh afraid of?
He was terrified of looking amateur, which is why he kept polishing.
Which choice in the story could have changed the ending?
Showing the rough app to real families in the first month, so he would have learned early about the confusing booking steps and cash payments.
How did the families who finally tried the app see it?
They found the booking steps confusing and wanted to pay in cash, so the polish meant little to them.

With his sister's newborn in the flat and the whole family taking turns walking her at night, Harish's evenings had become useless for his thesis. For weeks he sat down at nine, stared at the screen, and called himself lazy. His brother Bhupen, rocking the baby, said, 'You're not lazy. You're writing at the worst hour of your day.' So Harish tried something else. He noticed he was sharpest between six and eight in the morning, before anyone woke. He moved his writing there. In the evenings, instead of fighting himself, he did easy things: laid out his clothes, packed his lunch, wrote tomorrow's first sentence on a sticky note. Within a month the chapter that had been stuck since spring was drafted. The baby still cried at night. Harish slept through some of it now, and he stopped calling himself lazy.

When was Harish sharpest?
He was sharpest between six and eight in the morning.
How had Harish felt about himself during the stuck weeks?
He felt frustrated and ashamed, calling himself lazy for failing to write at nine at night.
How did Harish plan around his energy?
He wrote at his sharpest time, six to eight in the morning, and used evenings for easy preparation like clothes, lunch and tomorrow's first sentence.
How does Bhupen see his brother's struggle?
Bhupen sees it as a timing problem, not laziness, and says so kindly while rocking the baby.

Tejas, you told your class you'll win the chess tournament? Good. Now you must practise every day. Why? Let your Ramesh thatha tell you. When I was eleven, I stood up in our village school and said I would win the running race at the temple festival. Everyone heard, even the headmaster.
After that I couldn't sit still. Every morning before the cows were milked, I ran to the river and back. Once I had fever and still wanted to go; my mother stopped me. On race day I didn't win. I came second. But I had never run so hard in my life. Because I'd said it out loud, my legs had to keep my word.
So tell me, how many games will you play this week?

Where did young Ramesh run every morning?
To the river and back.
How did young Ramesh feel after announcing he would win?
Young Ramesh felt restless and determined, unable to sit still because everyone had heard the promise.
Which choice in the story shows good sense alongside the promise?
When he had fever, his mother stopped him, showing a promise should not outweigh health.
How might the headmaster have seen Ramesh's announcement?
The headmaster may have been amused at first, then impressed to see the boy train so hard.

Wednesday night. I feel sick. A man phoned this evening and said he was from the scholarship office. He knew my school's name. He knew Abbu's name. So I thought he must be real, and I stopped being careful. He asked my class, my date of birth, Abbu's phone number, which bank we use. I told him everything because he was so kind and said he was just helping. Then he said a code would arrive and I should read it out. My hand was already on the phone screen when my brother Kunal came in and said, “Who is that? Hang up!” I did. I don't know what I gave away. Tomorrow I have to tell Abbu. — Farida

What details did the caller already know?
The school's name and Abbu's name.
How does Farida feel at the end of the entry?
Sick with worry and ashamed: Farida does not know what was given away.
What could Farida do next, and why?
Tell Abbu and the family straight away so the bank can be warned, since the details already given could be misused.
How does the call look to Kunal, who walks in?
Kunal hears a stranger asking a sibling for a code, recognises the danger at once and tells them to hang up.

Rain was coming down hard on the flyover road when a scooter skidded and slid across the tarmac. Binita, walking home with her classmate Omkar, felt her stomach drop. Her phone showed nine percent battery.

Safety first, she told herself, the way the first-aid instructor had put it. Are cars still coming? She pulled Omkar behind the barrier. "Hold your torch up and wave it at the traffic." Then: call for help. She dialled 112 with wet fingers. Don't move the rider unless there's danger. There was no fire, so she crouched beside the rider and kept still. Say only what you know. "A scooter has fallen near the bus stop on the flyover. One person on the ground, awake, talking. I don't know more than that."

The phone dropped to eight percent as the siren sounded.

What was the battery percentage on Binita's phone?
Her phone showed nine percent battery.
What is Binita feeling as she stands over the rider in the rain?
Binita is nervous and frightened, and she steadies herself by repeating the checklist from the first-aid class.
What could Binita do if she couldn't remember the checklist, and why?
She could ask the emergency operator what to do next and stick to what she can see, because the operator is trained to guide callers.
How might the situation look to Omkar?
Omkar probably feels unsure but relieved to be given a clear job with the torch, because Binita's calm steps give the moment some structure.

During chemistry, Dorje checked his phone under the desk again: 212 likes yesterday, 148 now. His stomach dropped. Madhuri leaned over from the next bench. “You look like you failed a test.”
“Likes are down. I need something bolder.” He had already posted the neon-dyed hair photo, then a pouting close-up he didn't even like, and each time the number jumped, he felt light for an hour. Then it dipped, and he felt heavy again. All day his mood moved with a counter he couldn't control. At lunch he opened the app twelve times. Madhuri said quietly, “You were happier when you posted the picture of your dog.” Dorje shrugged, but he put the phone face down for the rest of the lesson.

How many likes did Dorje's post have yesterday, and how many now?
It had 212 likes yesterday and 148 now.
How is Dorje feeling as the likes drop?
Dorje feels anxious and heavy, since his stomach dropped and his mood moves with the counter.
What could Dorje try instead of chasing bolder pictures?
Dorje could post what he enjoys, like the picture of his dog, and check less often, since his mood should not depend on numbers he cannot control.
How might Madhuri see Dorje's chasing of likes?
Madhuri seems concerned but gentle, since Madhuri remembers when Dorje looked happier and says so quietly.
Kim buys 3 pizzas.  They are 12 slices each.  The pizza cost $72.  How much did 5 slices cost?

he got 3*12=36 slices
So each slice cost 72/36=$2
So 5 slices would cost 5*2=$10
The answer is 10.

Dear Ganga di,
You asked why I didn't go to Mihir's send-off before he left for Pune. Short answer: we're not friends anymore.
At his farewell dinner last week, in front of everyone, he said I only ever called him when I needed notes. I lost it. I told him he'd always been fake. He walked out.
Since then I keep thinking the whole friendship was fake. Nine years, and it turns out he thought that about me the whole time.
Ammi says, "Tushar, the boy who sat with you all night when Abbu was in hospital? That boy?" Yes, fine, that happened. And the cycling trips, and he taught me to swim. But the dinner is what I see when I close my eyes.
I'm not going to reply to his message. What's the point? It ended the way it ended.
Your brother,
Tushar

What did Mihir say at the farewell dinner?
He said Tushar only ever called him when he needed notes.
Why does Tushar feel the whole nine-year friendship was fake?
The angry dinner is the most intense and the latest memory, so it overwrites the night in hospital, the cycling trips and the swimming lessons.
What choice could Tushar make instead of ignoring Mihir's message?
He could read the message and reply once things have cooled, remembering the nine years as a whole rather than letting one angry evening decide.
How might Mihir be feeling now, having sent a message after the fight?
Mihir may regret what he said and hope to repair things before he settles in Pune, and could feel hurt if the message is ignored.

On the slow afternoon bus through Nairobi, little Yara sat on her mother Wanjiru's lap by the window.
They didn't talk. Yara watched a boy selling mangoes, a man on a bicycle stacked with crates, a dog asleep in the shade.
Now and then she tipped her head back to check Wanjiru's face. Wanjiru smiled. Yara turned back to the window.
Her small hand rested on her mother's arm the whole way home.

What was the man on the bicycle carrying?
The bicycle was stacked with crates.
Why did Yara tip her head back to check Wanjiru's face?
Yara was checking that her mother was still there, and Wanjiru's smile let her feel safe and content to keep watching.
What makes this quiet ride good for Yara?
Wanjiru's calm presence and smile let Yara explore the world by watching, knowing she is safe without needing talk.
What is the ride like for Wanjiru?
Wanjiru likely feels calm and fond, sharing the view with Yara without needing words.

I still remember the poll someone posted in our class chat one night: "Who is the weirdest girl in 11-C?" Manjula's name was winning.
I'm Kashish. I was in the chat. I had voted in silly polls before. This one made my stomach twist, because Manjula had stopped coming to the canteen.
I typed: "This isn't funny, it's cruel. I'm leaving and I'm reporting it." Then I left. Two people called me a snitch in the corridor the next day.
But that same evening I had shown the poll to our class teacher. The next morning it was gone, and the teacher spoke to the class. Manjula came to the canteen again that week.
I lost two friends. I'd do it again.

What was the class chat poll asking?
"Who is the weirdest girl in 11-C?"
How did Kashish feel on seeing the poll?
Kashish felt uneasy and sick with worry, because Manjula had stopped coming to the canteen.
What made Kashish's approach work?
Kashish objected openly and showed the poll to the class teacher the same evening, so an adult acted the next morning.
How might Manjula have felt on coming back to the canteen?
Manjula may have felt a little safer and relieved, though still hurt by the poll.

Sunday night

Ammi and Abba met Rehana's family today. Everyone was sweet, there were too many samosas, and on the way home Abba said, "Beta, they are good people. Think about it."

The thing is, I did like talking to her. Rehana wants to do her PhD in Hyderabad. I have an offer in Pune starting in August. We are both twenty-two. If we say yes now, one of us moves, or we spend two years on trains.

Ammi says it's easier to decide these things young. My friend Faiz says I'm mad to think of marriage before I've even had one salary.

Nobody actually knows what we'd be like as a couple, or what either job will feel like in a year. I don't know either.

What I do know: I want to talk to Rehana alone, without both families on the sofa, and ask what she wants. Then I'll tell Ammi and Abba where I'm at, even if it's "not yet".

Siddharth

Where does Rehana want to do her PhD?
Rehana wants to do her PhD in Hyderabad.
How is Siddharth feeling after the visit?
Siddharth feels unsure and pressured, since he liked Rehana but is caught between his parents' hopes, a new job and the unknowns.
What wise step does Siddharth plan before answering his family?
He plans to talk to Rehana alone to learn what she wants, then tell his parents honestly where he stands, even if it is "not yet".
How might Rehana see the situation from her side?
Rehana may also feel pressure from both families while wanting to protect her PhD plans, so a private, honest talk could come as a relief to her too.

Wednesday
Diary, it's Pooja. Science results came today. I got 14 out of 30, even though I studied every night. I wanted to cry in front of everyone. But after class Dolma Ma'am stopped me at the door. She said, 'Pooja, I saw your notebook. You drew every diagram of the heart twice. That's real effort, and it shows. The marks will catch up.' I didn't know what to say. I just nodded, and my throat felt funny. Nobody had ever told me they saw me trying. At home I told Amma, and she made my favourite rasam. I still wish my marks were higher. But today didn't feel like the worst day any more. It felt like someone was on my side.

What did Pooja draw twice?
Every diagram of the heart.
How did Pooja feel when Dolma Ma'am spoke?
Seen and moved; Pooja's throat felt funny because nobody had noticed the trying before 🥺
What difference did Dolma Ma'am's words make on a bad day?
Pooja felt someone was on Pooja's side, so the day no longer felt like the worst.
How does Dolma Ma'am see Pooja's work?
As real effort that will show in the marks later.
You roll two dice. One shows 4 and the other shows 5. How many dots is that altogether?

Answer: 9 dots. 4 + 5 = 9.

Count on from 5: "5 ... 6, 7, 8, 9". Or use a double: 4 + 4 = 8 and one more is 9. Dice games give lots of adding practice without worksheets.

Devika could not sleep. At a dinner she had let slip that Sarita was laid off in March, something Sarita had told her in confidence, and it was already spreading. She rang Sarita before anyone else could. "I repeated your secret to people at dinner. I am sorry. No excuses. If you need distance, I will give it."

Sarita's ears burned, humiliation and rage in equal parts. "That was mine to tell," she said. "When Aditi asked about my job hunt I felt exposed." Then she stopped and waited. Devika did not argue. She wrote to each person she had told, asked them to let it go, and stayed quietly available for two weeks. Sarita watched the repair, not the excuses, and it decided her. A month later they met for tea.

Meanwhile Siddharth confided over coffee that he was seeing someone behind his partner's back. Sarita's chest tightened. "I won't lie for you, and I think you should tell her yourself," she said. She did not post about it or cut him off.

And an old flatmate who rang only when short of cash or needing a sofa got a different answer that month: "I can lend this once, but not again soon." Sarita hung up without a long explanation, knowing a friendship with no care running both ways stays thin.

When had Sarita been laid off?
Sarita was laid off in March.
How did Devika's and Sarita's handling of the leaked secret compare with Sarita's handling of Siddharth's confidence?

Devika told Sarita first, apologised without excuses and offered distance, and Sarita said clearly how it felt and judged by the repair. When Siddharth confided, Sarita refused to lie for him and told him honestly what she thought, without exposing him or cutting him off.
How did Sarita feel when Aditi asked about her job hunt?
She felt exposed, humiliated and full of rage.
What did Sarita do about the old flatmate who rang only when in need?
She offered to lend once, said no to more without a long explanation, and did not pretend the friendship was close.

Brian is taping up some boxes. Each box needs three pieces of tape, one as long as the long side and two as long as the short side. If Brian tapes up 5 boxes that measure 15 inches by 30 inches and 2 boxes that measure 40 inches square, how much tape does he need?

First find the amount of tape each 15 in x 30 in box needs on the short sides: 2 sides * 15 inches/side = 30 inches
Then add that to the amount of tape each 15 in x 30 in box needs on the long side to find the total amount needed per box: 30 inches + 30 inches = 60 inches
Then multiply that amount by 5 boxes to find the total amount needed: 60 inches/box * 5 boxes = 300 inches
Then find the amount of tape each 40 in x 40 in box needs for its three equal length sides: 3 sides * 40 inches/side = 120 inches
Then multiply that amount by 2 boxes to find the total amount needed: 120 inches/box * 2 boxes = 240 inches
Then add the total amount needed for each box size to find the grand total: 240 inches + 300 inches = 540 inches
The answer is 540.

Minnie is making a playlist of songs for a party she will be throwing. She wants the playlist to be an hour long. She has added 16 three-minute songs to the playlist. How many four-minute songs does she have to add to make sure the playlist is an hour long?

An hour is equal to 60 minutes.
Minnie has 16 * 3 = 48 minutes of songs already on the playlist.
She has to fill 60 - 48 = 12 more minutes.
Thus, she needs to add 12 / 4 = 3 four-minute songs.
The answer is 3.

I sit beside Jasleen on the school bus. This morning she stubbed her toe on the step and said, "Ouch!" sharply. Then she dropped her water bottle, and said, "Oops," in a small worried voice, checking the driver's face. Rajni, the bus helper, said, "No problem, we'll pick it up." Jasleen let out a breath. Later, through the window, she saw a rainbow and breathed, "Wow." I don't know if the toe was hurting much, but the other two words were easy to read.

What did Jasleen do after she said "Oops"?
She checked the driver's face.
What might Jasleen have been worried about when she said "Oops" in a small voice?
She may have been afraid of getting into trouble for dropping the bottle, since she checked the driver's face and let out a breath at Rajni's kind reply. It might have been just a reflex.
What could adults say to help children recover from small errors?
A gentle reply like Rajni's, "No problem, we'll pick it up," shows the mistake is small and fixable.
How might Rajni see Jasleen's "Oops"?
Rajni may see a child who is a little anxious about mistakes, and be careful to reassure her.

Tanuja,

I promised I'd tell you how it's going with Vivek, so here's the honest version.

The first month, everything he did was charming. Now it's been four months and I'm seeing the rest of him. He's always twenty minutes late. He goes silent for a whole day when he's upset instead of saying what's wrong. He tips generously, which I love. He also thinks my plan to do a master's in Pune is "a phase," which I don't love at all.

The fizzy feeling has calmed down. I used to ask myself, do I like how I feel around him? Now I'm asking something else: do I like who he actually is, silences and all?

I don't know the answer yet. But I think it's the right question.

Devika

How late is Vivek, according to Devika?
Always twenty minutes late.
What is Devika feeling now that the fizzy feeling has calmed down?
Devika feels thoughtful and uncertain, less dazzled, and a bit uneasy about Vivek's silences and his view of the master's plan.
What could Devika do to answer her new question?
She could talk openly with Vivek about the master's plan and about how he handles being upset, and see how he responds.
How might Vivek feel if he read that his view of her plan was "a phase" to her?
He might feel surprised or defensive, maybe not realising how much his comment bothered her.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Shankar, you asked what changed in my second year at the firm. Honestly, I used to think promotion came if I kept my head down and worked late. It didn't. My appraisal said 'meets expectations', and I sulked for a week. Then I did something uncomfortable. I asked three people, my manager, a senior from another team and a peer, one question: 'What's one thing I should do differently to grow?' Two said the same thing: I never presented my own work; my manager always did. Ouch. So I volunteered to present our quarterly results. I was terrible the first time. The senior from the other team, Neha, stayed back to give me pointers, and later she mentioned my name in a leadership meeting. That's what a sponsor is, I learned. I also wrote down the next role I wanted and told my manager directly.

What did the narrator's appraisal say?
'Meets expectations'.
How did the narrator feel after the appraisal, and why?
Disappointed and sulky for a week, having assumed hard work alone would bring a promotion.
What steps helped the narrator plan for growth?
Asking several people for one honest change, acting on the pattern by presenting their own work, and telling the manager the role they wanted.
Why might Neha have mentioned the narrator's name in a leadership meeting?
She had seen the narrator take feedback seriously and improve, so she felt confident vouching for them.

I'm Zeenat. In my last year of college, I was studying maths but spending evenings playing tabla. My friend Yamini, who studies computer science, laughed when I said rhythm was just fractions you can hear. "Prove it." So we did. We built a small app for children: tap a rhythm, and it shows you the fraction on screen, halves, quarters, triplets. Kids at the tuition centre loved it. They'd tap and giggle and suddenly understand quarters. It didn't come from maths or music alone. It came from sitting between them. Now, whenever I get stuck on a problem, I ask which other subject might already know the answer.

What did the app show when children tapped a rhythm?
The fraction on screen, halves, quarters, triplets.
How did Zeenat feel seeing the children use the app?
Zeenat felt delighted and proud watching them giggle and understand quarters.
What made Zeenat and Yamini's idea original?
It linked maths, music and computer science into something none of them could make alone.
How might Yamini have felt when Zeenat said rhythm was fractions?
Doubtful and amused at first, then intrigued enough to test it.
Lara was 9 years old 7 years ago. How old will she be 10 years from now?

Lara is 9 + 7 = 16 years old now.
Thus, she will be 16 + 10 = 26 years old 10 years from now.
The answer is 26.

At the end of the day at the childminder's house in Durban, Sofia pressed a bead bracelet into Lindiwe's hand. It was lumpy, red and yellow, with the knot coming loose.

"I made it for you," Sofia said, looking at her shoes. "Because you helped me when I fell."

Lindiwe held it up to the light. "You made this? For me?" She slid it onto her wrist straight away. "It's beautiful. Thank you, Sofia."

Sofia looked up and beamed.

The next morning, Lindiwe was still wearing it. Sofia noticed immediately and pointed. "You kept it on!"

What colours were the beads on the bracelet?
Red and yellow.
What was Sofia feeling when she looked at her shoes while giving the bracelet?
She was most likely a little shy and hopeful, wanting Lindiwe to like her gift and to say thank you for the help. Her beaming afterwards shows she felt happy and proud.
Why was putting the bracelet on straight away a good response?
It received Sofia's gift warmly, showing her that her thanks and affection had reached Lindiwe.
How is Lindiwe affected by the gift?
She seems touched by it, praising it and still wearing it the next morning.

Sunday, four o'clock, and the essay on the 1918 flu was due at midnight. Nkechi had been fiddling with her opening paragraph since breakfast. Her flatmate Hana, making toast, watched her delete the same sentence twice. "What's the plan?" Hana asked. Nkechi took a breath. "Two more hours. Then references, then I submit, whatever it looks like." She put her phone on the other side of the kitchen and set the oven timer. When it rang at six, the conclusion felt thin and she still wanted a better quote in section two. She opened a note titled "Essay 4" and typed: start reading earlier, collect quotes as I go. At 7:40 she pressed submit. Hana raised her mug. Three weeks later the essay came back with a 68 and a comment: "Strong argument; conclusion could go further." Nkechi added that line to her note too.

What did Nkechi use to time her last two hours?
She set the oven timer.
What does Nkechi deleting the same sentence twice suggest about how she was feeling?
It suggests she felt stuck and uneasy, as if the opening had to be exactly right before she could move on, even with the deadline hours away.
What would you advise Nkechi to do with the "Essay 4" note before her next assignment?
Read it on the first day and act on it early, for example collecting quotes while reading, so the high standard is built in from the start instead of patched at the end.
What was it like for Hana to watch Nkechi delete the same sentence twice?
Hana could see her flatmate losing a whole day to one paragraph, so asking about a plan was a light way to help without taking over.

For a long time Lakshmi told it as "the year the river took everything." That evening, sitting with Jasleen on the low wall by the pond, she told it differently. "The water came at night and the whole crop went, and it was cruel, and my father did not speak for days. That's true. I won't pretend otherwise." She picked at a blade of grass. "But we also lived. The neighbours brought rice. I learned to plant on the higher field, and I taught the younger ones after." Jasleen nodded slowly. "It sounds like the whole truth," she said. Lakshmi breathed out, and her shoulders dropped a little.

Where were Lakshmi and Jasleen sitting?
