Tuesday night.
Had to tell Jagdish I can't make his cousin's wedding. I typed, "Bro I'm so sorry, can't come, exam on Monday lol 😅". I added the lol so it wouldn't sound heavy. Then I stared at it. Does lol make it sound like I don't care? Like his cousin's wedding is a joke? I almost deleted it.
He replied after twenty minutes: "lol ok".
Now I'm lying here reading those two words. Jagdish uses lol for everything, even "my phone died lol". So maybe it's fine. Or maybe it's the flat lol, the one that means he's annoyed and doesn't want to say.
I called him. He picked up laughing about something else, then said, "Obviously I'm a bit sad, but exams are exams." We talked for ten minutes. That lol was half and half, I think.
— Manoj

Why couldn't Manoj go to the wedding?
Because of an exam on Monday.
What was Manoj worried about after sending the message?
Manoj was anxious that the lol made it sound careless about the wedding, and later that Jagdish's flat "lol ok" meant he was annoyed.
Which choice helped Manoj, and why?
Calling Jagdish instead of reading the two words over and over, because hearing his voice showed he was a bit sad but not angry.
How did Jagdish seem to feel about Manoj missing the wedding?
He was a bit sad but understanding, saying "exams are exams", so the lol carried some disappointment and some acceptance.

"I won't indeed!" said Alice, in a great hurry to change the subject of conversation. "Are you—are you fond—of—of dogs?" The Mouse did not answer, so Alice went on eagerly: "There is such a nice little dog near our house I should like to show you! A little bright-eyed terrier, you know, with oh, such long curly brown hair! And it'll fetch things when you throw them, and it'll sit up and beg for its dinner, and all sorts of things—I can't remember half of them—and it belongs to a farmer, you know, and he says it's so useful, it's worth a hundred pounds! He says it kills all the rats and—oh dear!" cried Alice in a sorrowful tone, "I'm afraid I've offended it again!" For the Mouse was swimming away from her as hard as it could go, and making quite a commotion in the pool as it went.

Briefly, what goes wrong for Alice here?
Trying to change the subject, Alice chats happily about a farmer's clever dog, then mentions it kills rats. The Mouse is offended again and swims away fast.
A school buys 300 notebooks at ₹20 each. How much does it pay?

Answer: ₹6,000. 300 x 20 = 6,000.

3 x 2 = 6, and 100 x 10 = 1,000, so 300 x 20 = 6 x 1,000 = 6,000. Count the zeros: two in 300 and one in 20 make three zeros after the 6. Estimate to check: 300 notebooks at about ₹20 is a few thousand rupees, so 6,000 is sensible.

Tejas: first day at the new school tomorrow
Tejas: I don't know a single person there
Payal: it'll be fine!! 😊 you're so friendly
Tejas: you always say that
Payal: because it's true?
Tejas: it's not helping rn tbh
Payal: oh
Payal: ok sorry. what's the worst part?
Tejas: lunch. standing there with a tray and nowhere to sit
Payal: that sounds genuinely awful
Payal: ok what if you text me at lunch and I'll keep you company on the phone till you find a spot
Tejas: that might actually help
Payal: and I still think you'll find someone. but I get why "it'll be fine" sounded like I wasn't listening
Tejas: a bit yeah
Tejas: thanks for asking the lunch thing 🙂

Which part of the first day worried Tejas most?
Lunch worried Tejas most, standing there with a tray and nowhere to sit.
What was Tejas feeling when replying "you always say that"?
Tejas felt anxious and not taken seriously, because Payal's bright "it'll be fine" skipped over a real worry.
What did Payal change that made the chat go better?
Payal stopped cheering, asked what the worst part was, said it sounded awful, and offered a concrete plan for lunch.
How might Payal have felt when Tejas said it wasn't helping?
Payal was probably surprised and a little stung, having meant it kindly, but used the moment to switch to listening.

Week one: Jeevan starts as a junior electrician at a textile mill. During the morning safety round, messages keep buzzing. Jeevan skims one, ticks a panel as locked and moves on. Rashmi, walking behind with the checklist, finds the lock hanging open.
Week two: Before the round, Jeevan leaves the phone in the locker. At each panel Jeevan reads the tag aloud, and Rashmi checks it again before signing. It takes a few extra minutes. On the drive home the phone stays in the glovebox; calls wait for the petrol pump stop.
Week four: The supervisor calls Jeevan in about a shift change. Jeevan turns the phone face down and listens to the end. On the way out Rashmi says, "I don't recheck your panels so nervously any more."
Jeevan grins. "Keep rechecking. That's the point."

What did Rashmi find on the panel Jeevan ticked in week one?
Rashmi found the lock hanging open.
Why does Jeevan still want Rashmi to keep rechecking in week four?
Jeevan seems to trust a double check more than any feeling of being careful, knowing a second pair of eyes catches what one busy person misses.
What was the turning point for Jeevan, and what changed after it?
The open lock in week one; after it Jeevan left the phone in the locker, read each tag aloud and let Rashmi check before signing.
How has working with Jeevan changed for Rashmi by week four?
Rashmi no longer rechecks nervously, so the shared work feels safer and there is more trust between them. 🙂

Tuesday night.

Today Binita stopped the stand-up and said, in front of all nine of us, "Saurabh, this dashboard is late again and the numbers don't match." Everyone looked at their shoes. My ears were burning. I said "noted" and nothing else.

At lunch I went to the pantry and let it all out to Farhan and Leela. She always does this, she enjoys it, she has favourites. They nodded and added their own stories. For ten minutes it felt good. Then it felt worse, like I'd poured petrol on something.

After work I walked the long way home, past the lake, and let myself calm down. Honestly, the numbers didn't match. What I hate is how it was said, and that I don't know what "on time" means to her.

So, plan: tomorrow morning I'll message Binita and ask for fifteen minutes alone to understand what she needs and by when. No pantry speeches first.

Who did Saurabh vent to in the pantry?
Saurabh vented to Farhan and Leela.
How can you tell Saurabh felt humiliated at the stand-up?
Saurabh's ears were burning, everyone looked at their shoes, and Saurabh could only say "noted"; the diary shows shame and anger at being criticised in front of nine people.
What small step is Saurabh planning, and why is it wiser than more venting?
Saurabh plans to ask Binita for a private fifteen-minute talk to clarify expectations; this addresses the real problem instead of feeding resentment with colleagues.
What would change if Binita heard about the pantry venting before the private talk?
Binita might feel undermined and become defensive, making it much harder to have a calm conversation about expectations.

I'm Dhruv, and in my third year I learned the smartest thing I know from a two-minute walk. I'd been stuck on a statistics assignment for two hours. The same formula, the same wrong answer. I was tense and staring so hard my eyes ached. My friend Mehak came in and said, "Explain it to me." I started talking. "First I take the mean, then I subtract..." And halfway through the sentence, I heard it. I'd subtracted from the wrong column. Two hours, and the error showed up as soon as I said it aloud. Now, when I'm stuck for more than twenty minutes, I walk to the canteen and back, or I explain it to someone. It's not giving up. It's a tool.

What did Dhruv realise halfway through the explanation?
Dhruv had subtracted from the wrong column.
How was Dhruv feeling before Mehak came in?
Dhruv felt tense and frustrated, staring so hard that the eyes ached after two hours on the same error.
What does Dhruv now do when stuck, and why does it work?
Dhruv takes a short walk or explains the problem aloud, which breaks tunnel vision and often reveals the error.
How might Mehak feel when Dhruv finds the error mid-sentence?
Mehak might feel amused and pleased, having helped just by listening.
Help me invite our neighbours to a Lohri bonfire in the society garden on Thursday at 7 pm. Around 55 words, with a warm tone. Sign it The Garden Committee.

Dear Neighbours,
Join us for a Lohri bonfire in the society garden this Thursday at 7 pm. Let us gather around the warm fire and celebrate the festival together. Please come dressed warmly. We hope the warmth of the fire and of friendship will brighten the cold evening. Everyone is welcome!

Will my cousin pass his exam?
I don't know, because only he and his teachers can judge how ready he is. Encourage him and offer to revise together.
Which seat am I on the train?
I can't tell which seat you have, because I can't see your ticket. The seat number is printed on it.

Jatin, you think your papa is too strict? Let me, Naveen chacha, tell you something. When I was twenty-five, your grandfather was the strictest man in Bareilly. Up at five. Accounts done by six. And if my marks were less than ninety, he'd say, "Useless," and not speak to me at dinner. I promised myself I'd never be like him. Then one evening, your papa, who was fifteen, came to me with his maths paper, 62. And I heard myself say, "Useless." The same tone. The same word. I felt cold. That night I sat on the terrace and thought hard. Your grandfather was never late, never lazy, always honest. I wanted that. But I didn't want the cold dinners. The next morning I went to your papa and said sorry. Then I sat with him, and we did the maths together.

What mark did Jatin's papa get on the maths paper?
Why did young Naveen feel cold after saying "Useless"?
He was shocked and ashamed to hear his strict father's exact word and tone in his own voice, after promising never to be like him.
What was the turning point, and what choice did Naveen make?
Hearing himself say "Useless"; he then chose to keep his father's diligence and honesty but drop the cold harshness, apologising and helping with the maths.
How might Jatin's papa, at fifteen, have felt when Naveen came back to apologise?
He likely felt relieved and cared for, and perhaps surprised that an adult said sorry.

- Which spelling is right: "restaurent" or "restaurant"?
- Quick one: how do I enjoy a long train journey?
- Can you tell me what "endangered" means?
- Can you fix my sentence? I took the photoes at the fair.

1. It is "restaurant", ending in "-ant".
2. Carry a book, some games and snacks, and watch the scenery outside. Talk with your family and keep a small bag for your things.
3. As an adjective, "endangered" means at risk of being harmed or of disappearing for ever.
4. Corrected: I took the photos at the fair. Why: "photo" is a short form that takes only "s" in the plural.
Why does our face turn red after we run?
More blood flows near the skin. Because running makes the body hot, the small blood vessels in the skin widen to let the heat escape into the air.
What is a locksmith?

A locksmith is a person who makes, fits and repairs locks and keys. It is a noun.
Example: We called a locksmith when the key broke inside the door.

Read this:

Last month I finally had the talk with Tarun, my flatmate. For weeks, his friends had been coming over till 2 am on weeknights, and I had exams. I'd been sighing loudly and slamming my door, which obviously solved nothing.
Before talking, I sat down with a notebook. What do I actually want? Quiet after midnight on weeknights. What are the facts? Friends over four nights last week, past one each time. How do I feel? Tired, and a bit invisible. Then I wrote one question: What works for you?
That evening I said, "Tarun, can I talk about something? When people are here past midnight on weeknights, I can't sleep, and I've been really tired before exams. I'd like quiet after twelve on weeknights. What would work for you?"
He looked surprised. "Oh, I had no idea. Weekends only?" Done in five minutes. I'm Elizabeth, and I wish I'd prepared sooner.

How many nights were Tarun's friends over last week?
Four nights, past one each time.
How had Elizabeth been feeling before the talk?
Elizabeth had been tired and a bit invisible, and frustrated enough to sigh and slam doors.
What made Elizabeth's prepared talk work?
Elizabeth stated the want, the facts and the feeling without blame, and asked what would work for Tarun, inviting his view.
How did Tarun respond to the talk?
He was surprised, said he had no idea, and quickly suggested weekends only.
How do I take better notes in lectures?
Do not try to write every word. Note the main ideas, key terms and any examples the lecturer stresses, using short phrases and your own abbreviations.
What about reviewing them afterwards?
Read the notes the same day and fill in any gaps while your memory is fresh. Adding a one-line summary at the end of each lecture helps later.
Is it better to type or write?
Research has suggested handwriting can help some people remember better, but typing is faster. Choose the method that you can keep up with and revisit regularly.

I would like to let you know that I will be arriving a little bit late to the meeting today.
I will be a little late to the meeting today.

At two in the morning in the college hostel, Swati woke to a strange sound. Her roommate Avni was sitting up in bed, gasping, clutching her chest. "I can't breathe. I'm dying. Swati, I'm dying." Swati's own heart leapt into her throat. For a second she wanted to scream for the whole corridor. She didn't. She switched on the small lamp, not the tube light, and sat on the edge of Avni's bed. "I'm here. I'm not going anywhere." Her voice shook, so she slowed it down. "Breathe out with me. Long and slow." It took a long time. Slowly Avni's breaths lengthened. She cried, then went quiet. In the morning Swati walked her to the campus health centre and waited while the doctor saw her. Afterwards she messaged the warden so someone else knew too.

What did Swati switch on instead of the tube light?
The small lamp.
How did Swati feel when she saw Avni gasping, and what shows it?
She was frightened too; her heart leapt into her throat and her voice shook.
Which of Swati's choices gave Avni an anchor?
She stayed calm on the outside, sat close, slowed her voice and breathed with Avni, then took her to the health centre next morning.
What might the night have been like for Avni if Swati had panicked too?
Avni would likely have felt even more frightened, with no steady person to hold on to.
My teacher gave me a complement on my handwriting. Which spelling is right?

My teacher gave me a compliment on my handwriting.
Why: "Compliment" is praise; "complement" completes something.

At the women's hostel, the reading room closed at midnight sharp, and at 11:55 Salma, the warden, rang the little bell. Rehana was in the middle of her biology lab report, halfway through the results table. A year ago she would have walked back to her room with the numbers still spinning, then lain awake.
Instead she took two minutes. On the first empty line she typed: "NEXT: fill trial 3 values from notebook p. 17, then write graph caption." She underlined it, closed the file and handed in her key.
"Finished?" Salma asked.
"Not yet," Rehana said, "but I know exactly where I stopped."
She slept well, and after breakfast she finished the table in twenty minutes.

At what time did Salma ring the bell?
Why did Rehana seem at ease though the report wasn't finished?
She felt relaxed and in control, because writing the next step meant the report no longer needed to spin in her head.
What made Rehana's note effective?
It named an exact step, trial 3 values from page 17 and the graph caption, so restarting was easy and her mind could rest.
How might Salma see Rehana's answer?
Salma may be reassured, seeing a student who can stop on time without stress.

"Nikita! You're back from the trek! Did you have fun?"
"Yeah, it was good."
Damini waited. "Just good?"
"Mm."
Damini tried again. "What was the hardest part?"
Nikita paused. "The last climb. It was so steep, I nearly turned back. I cried a bit, actually."
"Really? What made you keep going?"
"There was this old man in our group, like sixty-five, who just kept saying, 'Chhota kadam, chhota kadam.' Small steps. So I did."
"And what was it like at the top?"
Nikita's face lit up. "Quiet. Like, totally quiet. I sat there and felt like my brain finally switched off."
Damini grinned. "That's way more than 'good.'"
"You asked better questions," Nikita laughed.

What did the old man in Nikita's group keep saying?
'Chhota kadam, chhota kadam.' Small steps.
What was Nikita feeling at the top of the climb?
Nikita felt calm and peaceful, as if the brain had finally switched off.
What made Damini's later questions work better than 'Did you have fun?'
They were open and specific, like 'What was the hardest part?', inviting Nikita to tell a story instead of just agreeing.
What would change if Damini had accepted 'it was good'?
Damini would never have heard about the steep climb, the old man's 'small steps' or the quiet at the top.

Celia runs twice as fast as Lexie. If it takes Lexie 20 minutes to run a mile, how long, in minutes, will it take Celia to 30 miles?

If Lexie takes 20 minutes to run a mile, Celia takes 20/2 = 10 minutes to run the same distance since she is twice as fast.
Celia takes 10 minutes to run one mile so it will take 10*30 = 300 minutes to run 30 miles.
The answer is 300.

Devika, you asked on the podcast how my wedding planning went. I'm Yash, and it was a lesson in values.
My parents wanted a big traditional wedding, three days, five hundred guests, every ritual. My partner and I wanted something small and simple, in a garden. And I also wanted my parents to feel secure, like their son hadn't gone off the rails.
We couldn't have everything. So we sat down and asked: what matters most here?
For us, it was keeping the family close, even if the style changed. So we kept the main rituals Maa cared about, the haldi and the pheras, but in a small garden with sixty people.
My cousin chose a courthouse wedding with no rituals at all. His parents were hurt. I didn't judge him. He ranked freedom first. I ranked family.

How many people came to Yash's wedding?
Sixty people.
What was Yash feeling about his cousin's courthouse wedding?
Yash felt accepting and respectful, not judging, since the cousin simply ranked values differently.
How did Yash handle competing values?
Yash named family closeness as most important, kept the key rituals Maa cared about and simplified the rest, instead of trying to have everything.
How might Yash's parents have felt about the compromise?
They probably felt respected and reassured, since the main rituals were kept even in a smaller wedding.

Farida here, from the flat opposite. I've watched Pankaj on his balcony all summer.
In May he was always on a laptop with a sketchbook beside it. His mother told mine he wanted to design games. Then in June he started sitting with his grandfather's old radio, taking it apart. He'd hold up tiny pieces and squint.
One evening I heard him on the phone: "Maybe I don't want to make games. Maybe I want to make the things games run on."
By July he had two columns taped to the window: GOOD AT and JOBS. I couldn't read it all, but I saw "soldering" and "patience" crossed out and rewritten.
I don't know what he's decided. He looks less stressed than in May, though, and he hums while he works.

What did Pankaj tape to the window by July?
Two columns: GOOD AT and JOBS.
What might Pankaj have been feeling when he said he wanted to make the things games run on?
He probably felt a mix of doubt and excitement, unsure of his first plan and curious about building hardware instead.
How could a parent support Pankaj's search?
A parent could ask about his two columns and help him meet someone who builds electronics, without pushing either plan.
How does Farida see Pankaj's summer?
Farida sees his work change and notices he looks less stressed and hums, though she admits she doesn't know what he has decided.

messages.content: Martha collected 90 cans while Diego collected 10 more than half the cans collected by Martha. If both of them should collect a total of 150 cans for their project, how many more cans do they need to collect?

Half the cans collected by Martha is 90/2 = 45
So, Diego collected 45 + 10 =55 cans.
Martha and Diego collected 90 + 55 = 145 cans together.
Thus, they need to collect 150 - 145 = 5 more cans.
The answer is 5.

You asked what surprised me most as a first-time manager? I'm Akash, and it was this. I promoted Ankita to senior designer in March. She had earned it. Within a week, the same team that used to eat lunch with her started a quiet sniping. Little comments in meetings: "Oh, ask the senior designer." Eye-rolls when she gave feedback. One person started sending her designs at 6 p.m. with "no rush" in a certain tone.
Nobody said anything I could write up. I don't know exactly what each of them felt, but it looked like the group had been comfortable as equals, and her moving up broke that. In the end I called a team meeting, named what I'd seen, and made supporting new leads part of everyone's goals.

When did Akash promote Ankita?
In March.
How did Akash feel watching the sniping?
Akash felt surprised and troubled, since nothing was openly rude, yet the team was clearly withdrawing support.
What did Akash do that could change the pattern?
Called a team meeting, named what had been happening, and made supporting new leads part of everyone's goals.
How might Ankita feel about the "no rush" designs at 6 p.m.?
She probably felt undermined and frustrated, recognising the tone as a quiet jab.

She put a steel bowl on her head as a hat and pretended to sneeze, so it fell off with a clang. Dhruv laughed until he hiccupped. Then he put a sock on his nose. 'I'm an elephant!' he trumpeted.

Alice is planting bushes around three sides of her yard. If each side is 16 feet long, and each bush fills 4 feet, how many bushes does she need to buy?

First find the total distance the bushes need to cover: 16 feet/side * 3 sides = 48 feet
Then divide the total distance to fill by the distance each bush fills to find the number of bushes Alice needs to buy: 48 feet / 4 feet/bush = 12 bushes
The answer is 12.
Mr. Wong harvested 560 mangoes from the tree outside his house. He sold half of it at the market and distributed the rest evenly among 8 of his neighbors. How many mangoes does each neighbor receive?

Mr. Wong had 560/2 = 280 mangoes left
Each of his neighbors received 280/8 = 35 mangoes
The answer is 35.
Anita's team scored 14 runs in the first over, 12 in the second and 10 in the third. How many runs after 3 overs?
36. Because 14 + 12 = 26, and 26 + 10 = 36, so the team has 36 runs.

I'm Harsha, and I live next door to Neelam. Last month her phone rang at nine at night: the passport appointment had moved to the next morning. I braced for a panic. Instead she took a green folder off the shelf, checked a list inside the cover, and laid out the originals: ID, address proof, two photographs, the old passport. Then she opened her laptop and showed me a scan of each in one folder. Fifteen minutes later she was making tea. "Every paper goes in the day I get it," she said. Meanwhile mine are spread over three drawers and a shoebox. I looked at that folder longer than I meant to.

What time did Neelam's phone ring?
It rang at nine at night.
What was Neelam feeling as she laid out her documents?
Calm and in control, judging from the fact that she was making tea fifteen minutes later.
What could Harsha do this weekend after seeing Neelam's method?
Gather the papers into one folder with a checklist, scan each one, and add new papers the day they arrive.
What might Harsha have been thinking while looking at the green folder for so long?
Harsha probably felt a little envious and embarrassed, since Harsha's own papers are in three drawers and a shoebox. 🙂

Dear Hrithik Bhaiya,
I spent the holidays at our grandparents' village, and I want to tell you something that's been on my mind.
Dadaji is so peaceful. He sits under the neem tree, talks to everyone, laughs about his old mistakes. When I asked if he had regrets, he said, "Some. But I made my peace."
Nanaji, at the other house, is always angry. He complains about his brothers, his lost land, everything. Nani says he was once full of fun.
I keep wondering: what makes the difference? Is it luck? Is it choices? Which one will I become when I'm old?
I don't really know yet. But I can't stop thinking about it.
Afreen

Where does Dadaji sit?
He sits under the neem tree.
What is Afreen feeling as she writes about her grandfathers?
Afreen feels curious and unsettled, wondering what makes one peaceful and the other bitter, and which one Afreen will become.
What could Hrithik Bhaiya suggest to help Afreen think about this?
He could suggest that Afreen ask both grandfathers about their lives and turning points, and notice what choices seem to shape their feelings.
How might Nanaji see his own life?
Nanaji seems to feel angry and wronged, focused on his losses and his brothers.

Brendan makes $6/hour as a waiter. He's scheduled for 2 8-hour shifts and 1 12-hour shift this week. He also makes an average of $12 in tips each hour. Brendan is supposed to pay 20% of his income in taxes, but he only reports 1/3rd of his tips to the IRS. How much money does Brendan pay in taxes each week?

First find the total number of hours Brendan works for the 8-hour shifts: 2 shifts * 8 hours/shift = 16 hours
Then find the total number of hours Brendan works by adding those hours to the 12-hour shift: 16 hours + 12 hours = 28 hours
Now find Brendan's total wage earnings by multiplying his $6/hour wage by the number of hours he works: $6/hour * 28 hours = $168/week
Now figure out how much Brendan makes in tips by multiplying the number of hours he works by the amount of tips he makes per hour: $12/hour * 28 hours/week = $336/week
Now divide that number by 3, since Brendan only reports a third of his tips: $336/week / 3 = $112/week
Now add Brendan's wage earnings to that number to find how much income he reports to the IRS each week: $168/week + $112/week = $280/week
Finally, multiply Brendan's reported income by his tax rate to find how much he pays in taxes each week: $280/week * .2 = $56/week
The answer is 56.
What does young Pip take from home for the convict on the marshes?
He takes bread, cheese, mincemeat, brandy and a pork pie from the pantry, and a file from Joe's forge so the man can get his leg iron off.

At the temple fair in the small town of Hosur, the college's volunteer group wore orange caps and managed the queue for darshan. Kashish and Chaitanya were in charge of the women's line.
By the second day, they had become different. Kashish shouted at an old woman who stepped out of line to sit down. "Back! Rules are rules!" Chaitanya pulled a village boy by the collar for cutting in.
"These people never follow anything," Kashish said at lunch. "They need to be told."
Chaitanya nodded, then paused. "At home, I'd give my seat to that old woman."
Kashish didn't answer. She took off her orange cap and looked at it.

What colour were the volunteers' caps?
They wore orange caps.
What might Kashish be feeling when she takes off her orange cap and looks at it?
She seems uneasy and doubtful, starting to notice how the cap made her treat people harshly.
What small step could the volunteers take for the rest of the fair?
They could treat people the way they would at home, such as helping the old woman sit down, and check each other when they get harsh.
How might the old woman who needed to sit feel when Kashish shouts?
She would likely feel frightened and humiliated, scolded by a young stranger for resting.

Cut this passage down to three sentences.

Day dawned; and I directed my steps towards the town. The gates were open, and I hastened to my father's house. My first thought was to discover what I knew of the murderer, and cause instant pursuit to be made. But I paused when I reflected on the story that I had to tell. A being whom I myself had formed, and endued with life, had met me at midnight among the precipices of an inaccessible mountain. I remembered also the nervous fever with which I had been seized just at the time that I dated my creation, and which would give an air of delirium to a tale otherwise so utterly improbable. I well knew that if any other had communicated such a relation to me, I should have looked upon it as the ravings of insanity. Besides, the strange nature of the animal would elude all pursuit, even if I were so far credited as to persuade my relatives to commence it. And then of what use would be pursuit? Who could arrest a creature capable of scaling the overhanging sides of Mont Saleve? These reflections determined me, and I resolved to remain silent.

At dawn the narrator hurries to the father's house, wanting the murderer chased, but stops to think. No one would believe a story about a living being the narrator created, and the creature could not be caught anyway. So the narrator decides to stay silent.
42 guavas are put into 6 equal bags. How many go in each bag?
7. Because 6 x 7 = 42, so each one gets 7 with none left over.

An alien invades Earth.  It abducts 200 people.  He returns 80% of the people abducted.  After that he takes 10 people to another planet.  He took the rest to his home planet.  How many people did he take to his home planet?

He returned 200*.8=160 people
So he had 200-160=40 people
He took 10 of those to another planet so he took 40-10=30 to his home planet
The answer is 30.

In the government school at Sironj, the Class 10 science project was to test water from four village hand pumps. Gopal, fifteen, was in the group of six. From the back bench he watched it happen week after week. Payal walked to the pumps with bottles after school. Vandana wrote up every result in her neat hand. The other four, Gopal among them, said, "Tell us what to do," and then went to the tea stall. Nobody had a named job, so nobody felt it was theirs. On Friday Vandana slammed the file on the desk. "We are not your servants." Payal did not say anything, but she did not smile all day. Gopal saw it then: the careful ones had carried everything, and now they were fed up.

Who wrote up every result for the project?
Vandana wrote up every result in her neat hand.
What does Gopal realise on Friday, and how might it feel?
Gopal likely feels uncomfortable and a little ashamed, seeing that the careful ones carried everything and that Gopal was one of those who went to the tea stall.
What choice could Gopal make now that he has seen the problem?
He could ask the group to give each person a named job, and take one of the pump visits or write-ups himself.
How does Payal seem to feel by Friday, and what shows it?
She seems quietly hurt and tired of carrying the work, because she stays silent and does not smile all day.

Jagdish: "Ramesh, the robotics demo is tomorrow and you haven't touched the code."
Ramesh: "Relax. I work better under pressure. Tonight's the night."
Jagdish: "Last time you said that, you pulled an all-nighter and slept through the viva."
Ramesh: "And I still passed."
Jagdish: "Barely. And you were ill for three days after."
Ramesh: "That was a one-off."
Jagdish: "The motor controller broke last week. What if something breaks tonight?"
Ramesh: (pauses) "Then... I'm stuck."
Jagdish: "Right. So what's the plan?"
Ramesh: "Fine. I'll start the code now and test by ten. If something breaks, we still have time."

What happened to Ramesh after the last all-nighter?
Ramesh slept through the viva and was ill for three days after.
What was Ramesh feeling during the pause after Jagdish's question?
Ramesh felt a flicker of worry, realising that if something broke that night there would be no way out.
Which choice at the end is wiser, and why?
Starting the code now and testing by ten leaves time to recover if something breaks.
How does Jagdish see Ramesh's pressure habit?
Jagdish sees it as risky, pointing out the missed viva and illness, and pushes Ramesh to start earlier.

At his cousin's wedding in Indore, Samir had spent two hours standing against the wall, cheeks hot, sure everyone was looking at his too-big borrowed kurta.
Then the power went out in the middle of the sangeet. Screams, then laughter. Someone shouted for torches.
His aunt, Sangeeta Mami, found him in the dark. "Samir! Your phone has the best torch. Come, hold it for the dancers."
He froze. The dance floor. In front of everyone.
"You don't have to dance," she whispered. "Just stand at the edge and shine the light. That's all."
He took a breath and walked to the edge. His hand shook. But everyone was looking at the dancers, not him.
When the power came back, an uncle clapped him on the back. "Our lighting director!"
Samir laughed, surprised at himself. Later, when Mami pulled him in for the last song, he danced for half a minute before escaping, grinning.

Where was the wedding?
In Indore.
What was Samir feeling as he stood against the wall?
Samir felt shy and self-conscious, cheeks hot, sure everyone was judging his too-big kurta.
Why did Sangeeta Mami's idea work?
She gave him a small, useful job at the edge of the crowd, a manageable step that didn't put him in the spotlight.
How might the guests have seen Samir holding the torch?
Most were watching the dancers, and those who noticed, like the uncle, saw him as helpful, not awkward.

On Sunday afternoons, Zubin visited his grandfather Nilesh in their old Mumbai flat. This week, looking at a photo of a young man with a violin, Nilesh said quietly, "I played in an orchestra once. Then I stopped for a steady job. I never picked it up again."
"Do you regret it, Nana?"
"Every day, a little. And I never told my father I wanted to keep playing. I just obeyed."
Zubin sat very still. He was twenty-one, studying commerce, and secretly writing songs on his laptop at night.
"Don't worry about me," Nilesh said, patting his knee. "I had a good life. But you, don't wait so long."
Walking home, Zubin felt calmer than he expected. He sent one of his songs to a friend who ran a college band.

What was the young man in the photo holding?
He was holding a violin.
How did Zubin feel walking home?
He felt calmer than he expected, taking his grandfather's regret as a gentle warning, not a weight.
What small risk did Zubin take after the visit, and why does it matter?
He sent one of his songs to a friend's band, a first step so he won't live with the same regret.
How might Nilesh feel if he heard Zubin was sharing his songs?
Nilesh would likely feel proud and glad his story helped his grandson take a chance.
If there are four times as many red crayons as blue crayons in a box, and there are 3 blue crayons.  How many crayons total are in the box?

Red crayons: 4(3)=12
Total crayons: 12+3=15 crayons
The answer is 15.

Sami's little sister Hana followed him everywhere around their Helsinki flat. To his room. To the kitchen. Even to the door when he went to get the mail. She touched his model planes and put his books in the wrong order.
"Hana, stop!" he snapped. Her face crumpled.
Sami sighed. He remembered following his cousin around the same way when he was little.
He knelt down. "Hana, my planes are mine. You can't touch them. But at five o'clock, we can play with your blocks together. Deal?"
Hana nodded. At five she was waiting on the floor with her blocks lined up.

What did Hana touch in Sami's room?
His model planes.
How did Sami feel about Hana following him?
He felt irritated, but also remembered following his cousin when he was little.
What kind limit did Sami set?
He told Hana his planes were his and not to be touched, but promised to play blocks with her at five.
How might Hana feel about the five o'clock plan?
Hana was clearly excited, waiting on the floor with her blocks lined up.

In the college hostel near Ahmednagar, Chinmay's field project on groundwater had dragged for three months the year before. This semester, before collecting a single sample, he tore a page from his notebook and wrote: "DONE means: 20 well readings taken, table typed, two-page report printed, signed by Nandini ma'am, one copy given to the gram panchayat office." He pinned it above his bed. In week six, the report was typed and he felt the old urge to keep tweaking the graphs. He looked at the page. Graphs weren't on it. He printed, got the signature and took the bus to the panchayat. At the office, he ticked the last line.

How many well readings did Chinmay's list include?
His list included 20 well readings.
What was Chinmay feeling in week six when he wanted to tweak the graphs?
He felt the old pull to keep polishing, a mix of habit and uncertainty about whether the report was good enough.
Why did the written list help Chinmay stop?
It set a clear endpoint in advance, so when he wanted to tweak graphs he could check that they were not part of done and move on.
How might Nandini ma'am see Chinmay's project this time?
She would likely be pleased and a little surprised to see him finish on time, after last year's project dragged for months.

Dear Rukmini akka,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone on Sunday. I'd been crying, and not for the first time that week. End-semester exams finished on Friday, and instead of feeling free I sat on the hostel stairs and cried for twenty minutes over a lost pen. Then again on Saturday in the shower, and again when Amma asked if I was eating properly. I used to think tears meant I was weak. Now I think my body was letting out a whole semester of tension. Still, it was happening a lot, so on Monday I booked a slot with the college counsellor. She was kind. She said crying after a long strain is common, and asked about my sleep and whether I had someone to talk to. I said I had you. This week I'm sleeping more and walking with Jaya in the evenings.
Call me on Thursday?
Gopika

What did Gopika cry over on the hostel stairs?
A lost pen.
How did Gopika feel about the tears at first, and how does Gopika see them now?
At first Gopika felt ashamed, thinking tears meant weakness; now Gopika sees them as a release of a semester's tension, though they came often enough to be worth seeing the counsellor.
Which steps is Gopika taking?
Seeing the college counsellor, sleeping more, walking with Jaya in the evenings and talking to Rukmini.
How might Rukmini have felt hearing Gopika's strange voice on Sunday?
Rukmini was probably worried, which is why she asked; the letter likely reassures her that Gopika is getting support 🤍

Climbing club coach's note, Saturday. Shreya

Tushar, 15, arrived buzzing. He wanted to go straight to the overhang wall, no warm-up, no partner check. "It's easy, Coach, zero risk." He has fallen off that overhang twice this month.
Twenty minutes later Nazia, our assistant coach, set a slab route for him, our gentlest wall. He folded his arms. "That one's sketchy. I could slip." He finds slab climbing boring and awkward.
So the thrilling wall felt safe and the dull one felt dangerous. The facts point the other way.
What I did next: I asked him to rate each wall on a card, first by feel, then by the falls logged in our book. He went quiet at the second column. Then he did the warm-up and the partner check, and tried the slab.

How many times has Tushar fallen off the overhang this month?
Twice.
Why does Tushar call the overhang 'zero risk'?
It excites him, and that buzz makes it feel safe, even though his falls say otherwise.
Why did Shreya's card exercise work?
Rating each wall first by feel and then by the falls in the book let Tushar see for himself that his feelings and the facts disagreed.
How might Nazia feel when Tushar calls her route sketchy?
Nazia may feel her careful beginner route was judged unfairly, and may guess that his dislike, not the wall, is talking.

Monday: No park, lunch at three, no nap. At bath time Jeevan, two, screamed and kicked. Rafiq, his father, felt helpless.
Thursday: Rafiq started a pattern: park after breakfast, lunch at twelve, nap after lunch, bath after dinner.
The next Monday: After dinner, Jeevan tugged Rafiq's hand towards the bathroom, singing his bath song. That night he fell asleep quickly.

What did Jeevan sing on the next Monday?
His bath song.
How did Rafiq feel on the first Monday?
He felt helpless as Jeevan screamed and kicked.
What changed between the first Monday and the next?
Rafiq built a steady day of park, lunch, nap and bath at regular times.
How might the regular day feel for Jeevan?
It probably feels safe and predictable, so bath time is no longer a shock to fight.
Change this from first person to third person, about Aarav: I woke up late, and I missed my bus, so I walked to school with my umbrella.
Aarav woke up late and missed his bus, so he walked to school with his umbrella.

I want to ask something. Listen to me.

Saturday
Dadi said I could have ten rupees today for helping her water the plants, or twenty rupees on Sunday if I helped again. Last week I told Chinmay I'd definitely wait for the big money, because I want the kite at the Sankranti fair. But today the chips man was right outside the gate, ringing his bell. I took the ten. The chips were gone in about one minute.
Now Chinmay has twenty rupees because he waited for his Nana's money, and I have an empty packet. I feel so stupid. Why is it easy to say I'll wait, and so hard when the chips man is right THERE?
Tomorrow I'm going to ask Dadi to keep my money in her tin till the fair. Then I can't see it.
Darshan

What did Dadi offer Darshan for watering the plants?
Ten rupees today, or twenty rupees on Sunday for helping again.
How does Darshan feel after the chips are gone?
Darshan feels stupid and regretful, confused that waiting seemed easy last week but impossible with the chips man right outside.
Is Darshan's idea of asking Dadi to keep the money in her tin a good one, and why?
Yes, because keeping the money out of sight until the fair makes the kite easier to wait for than the chips at the gate.
How might Chinmay feel with twenty rupees saved?
Chinmay probably feels pleased and proud of having waited, and closer to the fair.

Shortly before ten o'clock the stillness of the air grew quite oppressive, and the silence was so marked that the bleating of a sheep inland or the barking of a dog in the town was distinctly heard, and the band on the pier, with its lively French air, was like a discord in the great harmony of nature's silence. A little after midnight came a strange sound from over the sea, and high overhead the air began to carry a strange, faint, hollow booming.

Question: What does the writer notice shortly before ten o'clock and after midnight?

Before ten, the air is so still and silent that a sheep bleating inland or a dog barking in the town can be heard, and the pier band sounds like a discord. After midnight a strange sound comes over the sea and a faint hollow booming overhead.

The bus to Barnala left at seven, and Sudha would miss it. She had promised Harleen's mother she'd stay after school to help the girl with her board-exam maths, and Harleen was already waiting on the school steps with her notebook. Sudha thought, as she often did lately, of what she would want to say at seventy: that she kept her word. On the walk home past the wheat fields, she stopped at her cousin Amandeep's gate. They hadn't spoken since the quarrel at his sister's wedding, eight months ago. Her heart was thumping. "I was wrong about the seating thing," she said. Amandeep looked at her a long moment, then pulled out a stool. It wasn't all fixed. She still didn't know if she'd leave teaching for the city job her friends kept urging. Some things she'd get wrong. But not today's two.

Why would Sudha miss the seven o'clock bus?
She had promised Harleen's mother she'd stay after school to help Harleen with board-exam maths.
What was Sudha feeling at Amandeep's gate, and what shows it?
Sudha was nervous, her heart thumping, because apologising after eight months of silence felt risky.
Which of Sudha's choices reflects the life she wants to look back on, and why?
Keeping her promise to Harleen and apologising to Amandeep are small, ordinary acts that build the story she wants to tell at seventy.
How might Amandeep have felt when Sudha admitted she was wrong?
Amandeep may have felt surprised and softened, taking a long moment before offering a stool as a sign he was open to repair.

You asked about a time I changed my mind, Divyansh. Here's one. Second year, our class group chat turned on a boy called Arun after he asked a question in a lecture that people thought was stupid. Someone made a sticker of his face. Then everyone did. For two days it was nonstop. I'm Maria, I'm usually loud, I argue with professors, and I said nothing. I told myself, it's a hundred people, somebody will stop this. I actually waited for somebody. On the third morning I saw Arun eating alone in the canteen, staring at his phone. I went back to my room and typed one line: 'Guys, he asked a question. That's what we're here for. Can we stop?' That's all. Within five minutes it went quiet. Someone even said sorry. One line. I still think about the two days I waited for somebody else to type it.

What did Arun do in the lecture that started it?
He asked a question people thought was stupid.
Why did Maria, usually loud, stay silent for two days?
Maria felt uneasy but assumed that among a hundred people somebody would stop it, so responsibility felt spread thin and belonged to no one in particular.
What made Maria's one line work?
It was calm and simple, pointed out that asking questions is the point of class, and asked everyone to stop, which gave others permission to go quiet.
What were those two days like for Arun?
Arun seemed isolated and hurt, eating alone in the canteen and staring at his phone while the stickers kept coming.
The weather was so nice that we decided to go for picnic. Please fix.

The weather was so nice that we decided to go for a picnic.
Why: "picnic" is countable and needs "a".

Note for the staff room, Monday. Thomas, Nursery B. During tidy-up I told Mahima to “pull your socks up” because she was slow. She stopped, bent down and carefully pulled up both socks, then looked at me, waiting. A few children laughed. Mahima's eyes filled. She had done exactly what I said. I knelt and told her, “You're right, you did it. I used a grown-up saying. I meant: please tidy faster.” She nodded and picked up the blocks. Note to self and team: at this age, say what we mean in plain words.

What did Mahima do when told to pull her socks up?
She bent down and carefully pulled up both socks.
Why did Mahima's eyes fill when the children laughed?
She probably felt confused and embarrassed, because she had done exactly what she was told and could not see what was funny.
What did Thomas do to repair the mix-up?
Thomas admitted using a grown-up saying and restated it in plain words, so Mahima knew what was meant and felt right, not silly.
How did the laughing children see Mahima's socks?
They saw a funny mistake, perhaps because they already knew the saying, without seeing that Mahima had listened carefully.

In their small town near Mysuru, a new "youth empowerment" group had started meeting at the community hall, and everyone was talking about it. Hansa decided to go, but first she sat with her friend Damini on the temple steps and wrote three lines on the back of a bus ticket.
"One, Saturday evenings only, two hours. Two, no money, not even a small donation. Three, no signing anything that day, even if it looks simple."
"What if they're nice?" Damini asked.
"Especially if they're nice. That's when you forget."
At the second meeting, the organiser handed out forms for a "sponsorship" and pens. People around her were already filling them in. Hansa folded hers into her bag. "I'll read it at home."
"It's only today," he said.
"Then I'll miss it." She left when two hours were up. At home she read the form. It committed her to a monthly payment for a year.

What did the form Hansa took home commit her to?
A monthly payment for a year.
How might Hansa have felt when others around her were filling in the forms?
She likely felt some pressure and unease, but steady enough to fold the form away because of her rule.
What else could Hansa do now that she has read the form?
She could show it to Damini or a trusted adult and share what she found, so others in the town know what they are signing.
How might the organiser have seen Hansa's refusal?
The organiser probably felt frustrated, since the 'only today' pressure didn't work on her.

So, Imran, you asked what it's like being the "teacher's pet." I'm Baljeet, and honestly, it's not as fun as it looks.
Mrs Grewal loves me. She makes me class monitor, picks me for every competition, reads my answers aloud. And everyone notices. They call me "Grewal's baby." Someone wrote it on my desk in chalk.
For a while I enjoyed it too much. I once told Harjot, "Maybe if you listened like me, she'd like you too." He didn't talk to me for a week, and he was right.
So I changed things. When she praises me now, I just say thanks and move on. I help people with their maths before tests. When there's a competition, I ask her to pick someone else sometimes. And I apologised to Harjot.
They still tease me a bit. But now it's jokes, not chalk on my desk.

What did someone write on Baljeet's desk?
"Grewal's baby."
How did Baljeet feel about being the teacher's pet at first?
Baljeet enjoyed it a little too much and felt superior, which led to belittling Harjot.
Which choices helped Baljeet get along better with classmates?
Staying humble, helping others with maths, asking the teacher to pick others sometimes, and apologising to Harjot.
How might Harjot have felt when Baljeet made that comment?
Harjot probably felt insulted and belittled, which is why he stopped talking to Baljeet for a week.

Wednesday night. Big accounts exam tomorrow, and the old voice is back: "People from our village don't pass these exams in one go." Uncle said it at the wedding as if he were talking about the weather. My stomach's been tight since dinner. So I did what Farhan told me to try. First, I wrote on a card: This exam checks my preparation. It does not measure me. Second, I listed three hard things I've already done: topped the district in Class 12, taught myself spreadsheets, and passed first year despite the flood. Third, I wrote why I'm doing this: so Amma never has to borrow before the harvest again. Then I messaged Farhan, who passed last year. Reply: "You're ready. You know the ledger chapter better than I did." Card's in my pencil box. Going to sleep. - Ganga

What did Ganga write on the card?
This exam checks my preparation. It does not measure me.
What was Ganga feeling after dinner, and what set it off?
Ganga felt anxious, with a tight stomach since dinner, because Uncle's remark that people from their village don't pass these exams in one go had come back.
Which of Ganga's steps seems most useful the night before the exam, and why?
Listing three hard things already done, like topping the district, because it sets real evidence of ability against Uncle's label.
How might Farhan's reply affect Ganga's night?
Hearing from someone who passed last year that Ganga is ready gives belief from someone who has been through it, which may make sleep and the morning easier.
Mark buys a Magic card for $100, which then triples in value.  How much profit would he make selling it?

The value went up to 100*3=$300
So he gained 300-100=$200
The answer is 200.

Mr Castiel prepared 600 boar sausages on the weekend. He ate 2/5 of them on Monday, half of the remaining on Tuesday and saved the rest for Friday. If he ate 3/4 of the remaining boar sausages on Friday, how many sausages are left?

On Monday, Mr Castiel ate 2/5*600 = 240 sausages.
The remaining number of sausages after he ate 240 on Monday is 600-240 = 360
On Tuesday, he ate half of the remaining sausages, a total of 360/2 = 180.
The remaining number of sausages that he saved for Friday after eating 180 on Tuesday is 360-180 = 180.
On Friday, Mr Castiel ate 3/4*180 = 135 of the sausages he had kept.
The remaining number of sausages after he ate 135 on Friday is 180-135 = 45
The answer is 45.

Sami knelt on the living-room carpet in Tunis, a blue square block pressed to the round hole of the shape box. Thump went his palm. Thump. Thump. His father, Siddiq, looked up from folding towels. "Strong hands!" Sami thumped harder, lips pressed together. The block stayed on top, not budging. His palm turned pink. He thumped once more, then shoved the whole box.

What was Siddiq doing when he looked up?
He was folding towels.
What was Sami feeling when he shoved the whole box?
He was angry and frustrated after all his thumping failed.
Which approach would suit Sami better?
Trying the block in other holes or turning it to match, since force alone can't change a square into a circle.
How might Siddiq see the thumping?
Siddiq first sees effort and praises it, then may realise Sami needs a nudge toward the square hole instead.

"Mumma, look what Deepak wrote."
"What did you send him first?"
"Just, 'you said you'd come to the practice.'"
"And he said?"
"'ok, sorry I have a life too.'" Usha's voice wobbled. "A life TOO. Like I'm some loser with nothing to do."
"Maybe he's having a bad day."

"And now?"
"Now I'm hurt." Usha pulled her knees up on the sofa. "And I don't even know what I did."
"Want to write back now, or wait till you're calmer?"
"I'll wait."

What did Usha first send Deepak?
"You said you'd come to the practice."
What was Usha feeling when her voice wobbled?
She felt hurt and confused, reading Deepak's reply as calling her a loser when she had only been asking.
Which choice at the end helps at this stage?
Waiting until she is calmer before replying, so she doesn't send a hurt message back.
What might Deepak have been feeling when he sent his reply?
Deepak may have felt blamed and defensive, perhaps stressed, and answered with a sharper tone than he meant.

Okay, Ishita, you asked how I suddenly finished my thesis chapter, so here's the whole story. Last term I'd sit in the reading room at two with my laptop open, and by half past, Mansi would be at the door, waving. "Aditi, canteen?" I'd say five minutes and come back at five. When I told my mother, she laughed and said I needed a plan for Mansi, not for the chapter. So I wrote on a sticky note: "If Mansi comes before six, I say later, and I go at six." First day, she came at three. My heart was racing, honestly, because I hate saying no to people. I said it anyway. She shrugged and said, "Fine, six at the gate." I wrote four pages that afternoon. And at six we still had momos. That note is still stuck on my laptop.

What did the sticky note say?
If Mansi comes before six, I say later, and I go at six.
What was Aditi feeling when Mansi turned up at three on the first day, and what shows it?
Aditi was nervous about turning down a friend; the racing heart and the admission of hating saying no show how uncomfortable it felt, even with the plan ready.
What choice turned Aditi's afternoons around?
Making a plan for Mansi's visits rather than just promising to work harder; with the reply decided in advance, the chapter kept its hours and the friendship still got six o'clock.
How is the change likely to feel for Mansi?
Mansi loses the easy afternoon company but still gets a fixed meeting at the gate at six, so the friendship stays and she knows exactly when Aditi will be free.

Amanda's car takes five fewer minutes to complete the same trip to the beach than the bus. If the bus takes 40 minutes to drive 80 miles to the beach, how many minutes will it take the car to make a round trip?

If the bus takes 40 minutes to complete 80 miles of a trip, Amanda's car, which takes five fewer minutes to complete a trip than the bus, will take 40-5=35 minutes to complete the trip.
A round trip will take the car twice the time for going one way, a total of 35+35=70
The answer is 70.
Sam walks 24 minutes each day. How many minutes does he walk in 7 days? Can you fix this sentence? I drinked too little water today. Why do we put a full stop at the end of a sentence?

1. That makes 168. Because 7 x 24 = 168.
2. Fixed: I drank too little water today. Why: The past tense of "drink" is "drank".
3. A full stop shows where a sentence ends. Because it tells the reader when to pause.

Anders had tried to start running three times since moving to Uppsala for university, and each time it died in the second week. Dark mornings, a cold floor, shoes lost somewhere in the hall cupboard. This time his flatmate Emil suggested something different. "Make it stupidly easy." So every night Anders laid out his running tights, jacket and shoes on the chair by his bed, and set the target at ten minutes on the lake path, nothing more. On the first morning he nearly skipped it, but everything was right there, so he pulled on the tights still half asleep. Ten minutes felt almost too short. He came back pink-cheeked and a little proud. Three weeks later the chair still held his kit every night, and Emil had started joining him.

Where did Anders lay out his running kit each night?
On the chair by his bed.
How did Anders feel after the first ten-minute run, and why?
He felt a little proud; after three failed starts, doing it at all, even briefly, showed him this attempt might be different.
Which choice made the first morning work when Anders nearly skipped?
Having everything laid out the night before, so he could pull on the tights half asleep without any search or decision.
What would change for Anders if Emil stopped joining him later?
The kit on the chair and the small target would still carry the habit, since the ease of starting, not company, is what got it going.
I have a doubt in this chapter, can you explain? Teacher said it is wrong.
A better sentence is: "I have a doubt about this chapter" or, more commonly, "I have a question about this chapter." Why: "doubt" means unsure it is true; "question" is the usual word.
Find a more courteous way to say this: I ask you to wait.

He drew a second crown facing her.

Anthony keeps a bottle of vinegar in his cupboard for 2 years. Each year 20% of the vinegar evaporates. What percent of the vinegar is left after 2 years?

First find what percent of the vinegar is still in the bottle after each year: 100% - 20% = 80%
Then multiply the amount of vinegar left after one year by the percentage left after each year to find how much is left after 2 years: 80% * 80% = 64%
The answer is 64.

She took a breath. "Okay. You don't have to tell me now. I'm going for a walk after dinner, around the colony. If you want to come, you can. If you want to talk, we'll talk. If not, we'll just walk."

Irawati was going for a walk around the colony.

Irawati felt worried, and the worry was turning into frustration as her questions got no answer.

Offering a walk with no conditions gave Pallavi space and privacy, so she chose to speak when she felt ready.

Pallavi was likely hurt by what Riya said and wasn't ready to talk under direct questions at the table.
"Easy come, easy go" ka matlab kya hai? Dost ne ye paise ke baare mein bola.
It means that things you get easily are also lost easily. It is often said when someone gets something and loses it just as fast.

Is "medeval" right?
And one more: when was the oldest tree in the world planted?
Then, can you fix my sentence? A leaves fell from the tree.
One more thing: can you tell me what "magnate" means?
And why do some birds fly in a V shape?

1. No, it is "medieval", with "ie" after the "d".
2. I don't know the exact date, and I won't guess. Check a trusted science source for the oldest known trees.
3. Write it as: A leaf fell from the tree. Why: "a" goes with the singular "leaf", and "leaves" is the plural.
4. Magnate means a rich and powerful person in business. It is a noun.

messages.content: Liz sold her car at 80% of what she originally paid. She uses the proceeds of that sale and needs only $4,000 to buy herself a new $30,000 car. How much cheaper is her new car versus what she originally paid for her old one?

If Liz needs only $4,000 to buy a new $30,000 car, that means she has $30,000-$4,000=$26,000 from the proceeds of selling her old car
If she sold her car at 80% of what she originally paid for and sold it for $26,000 then she originally paid $26,000/80% = $32,500 for her old car
If she paid $32,500 for her old car and the new one is $30,000 then, the new one is $32,500-$30,000 = $2,500 cheaper
The answer is 2500.

6 builders can build the house in 24 / 6 = 4 days.

So she has $35 - $8 = $27 left for children.
She could take $27 / $3/child = 9 children with her.

messages.content:
Wrap up this text in two sentences.

"I noted, in passing, that she had written a note before leaving home but after being fully dressed. You observed that her right glove was torn at the forefinger, but you did not apparently see that both glove and finger were stained with violet ink. She had written in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep. It must have been this morning, or the mark would not remain clear upon the finger. All this is amusing, though rather elementary, but I must go back to business, Watson. Would you mind reading me the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel?"

The speaker notes that the woman wrote a note after dressing, because her torn glove and finger were stained with violet ink. The mark is still clear, so the note was written this morning, and the speaker asks Watson to read the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel.
My shoes gave me blisters on the school trip. I'd like to know exactly what the word means.

Blisters are small, round, fluid-filled bumps that form on the skin, often from rubbing. It is a noun, the plural of blister.
Example: Walking all day in new sandals gave Omar blisters on both heels.
A fruit seller buys a crate of mangoes for ₹1,500. Some mangoes go bad and he sells the crate at a loss of 8%. What is the selling price?

Answer: Loss = 8% of ₹1,500 = ₹120. SP = ₹1,500 - ₹120 = ₹1,380.

With a loss we SUBTRACT: loss = 8/100 x 1,500 = ₹120, so SP = ₹1,500 - ₹120 = ₹1,380. Or: CP is 100%, and with an 8% loss the SP is 92% of the CP: 92/100 x 1,500 = ₹1,380. Notice that the same CP with a 15% profit would give 115% of the CP, while a 15% loss gives 85%. Ask the child to say "profit means more than 100%, loss means less than 100%".

24 chairs are put in rows of 4. How many rows are there?

Answer: 6 rows. 24 / 4 = 6.

Think of an array with 4 chairs in each row. Count in 4s to 24: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 - that is 6 rows. The multiplication fact is 6 x 4 = 24, so 24 / 4 = 6. Also 24 / 6 = 4: 24 chairs in 6 rows would make rows of 4. One array shows all these facts.

Harish joined us three weeks ago. On his first day he cried at lunch, and some children, Chinmay among them, called him "a baby."
Since then he has settled well. He scored highest in the maths quiz, he organised a game of kho-kho at break, and he stood up for a younger child in the corridor. I have asked Chinmay to write three things Harish has done this week. We will read them together tomorrow. I will also pair them for one task.

On his first day.

Dear Ishita,
You asked me at your wedding why my husband Nikhil looked so tired, and I got angry and walked away. I owe you the truth.
I check his phone every night. I keep his salary in my account "for savings." I choose what he wears to office. I've told him your husband is a bad influence, so he doesn't come to your place anymore.
I always told myself this was love. I worried about him. But when I'm honest, it was fear. Fear that if I didn't hold everything, he'd drift away and I'd have nothing.
At your wedding I saw him standing alone by the wall, checking his phone to see if I needed him. I saw how small his life has become around my rules.
I've made an appointment with a counsellor for myself on Friday. I want to learn to love him without owning him.
Please don't tell anyone yet.
Bhavna

My name is Sharmila. Last winter my friend Noor said over chai, "I've let go of him, honestly. I'm fine." Her voice was bright and quick, and in the same breath she asked about my sister's wedding. messages.content: Rollo has 3 guinea pigs, the first guinea pig eats 2 cups of food, the second guinea pig eats twice as much as the first one, and the third guinea pig eats 3 cups more than the second one. How many cups of food does Rollo need to feed all his Guinea pigs?

The second guinea pig eats 2 x 2 = 4 cups of food.
The third guinea pig eats 4 + 3 = 7 cups of food.
Therefore, Rollo needs a total of 2 + 4 + 7 = 13 cups of food for the guinea pig.
The answer is 13.

Elvis is releasing a new album with 10 songs, but he doesn't want to waste too much time on writing. He spends 5 hours in the studio, where he writes, records, and edits his songs. Each song takes 12 minutes to record, then it takes 30 minutes to edit all of his songs.   How many minutes did it take Elvis to write each song, if each song took the same amount of time to write?

5 hours in the studio is the same as 5 * 60 = 300 minutes.
To record all of his songs, Elvis takes 12 * 10 = 120 minutes.
After editing and recording 300 - 120 - 30 = 150 minutes are left to write all of his songs.
Songwriting therefore took 150 / 10 = 15 minutes per song.
The answer is 15.

Amiyah is cutting some trees to build a cow shade. For every tree she cuts, she plants 5 new trees. If there were 400 trees on her farm and she cut 20% of them, calculate the total number of trees on the farm.

The number of trees that Amiyah cut is 20/100*400 = 80
The number of trees remaining on the farm after she cut 80 trees is 400-80 = 320
For every tree that Amiyah cut, she plants 5 new trees, and since she cut 80 trees, she planted 80*5 = 400 new trees.
The total number of trees on the farm is now 320+400 = 720 trees.
The answer is 720.

Brad wanted to set up a lemonade stand to earn some money.  Every gallon of lemonade would yield 16 glasses.  He figured it would cost him $3.50 to make every gallon of lemonade.  He made 2 gallons to sell and decided he would sell each glass for $1.00  He drank 5 glasses while sitting in his stand.  He sold all but 6 glasses of lemonade.  How much net profit did Brad earn?

He made 2 gallons and each gallon had 16 glasses so 2*16 = 32 glasses
He drank 5 glasses and had 6 left over which means he would not earn money on 5+6 = 11 glasses
The total revenue would come from 32-11 = 21 glasses
Each gallon cost $3.50 to make so the total cost was 2*3.50 = $7.00
He sold 21 glasses at $1.00 per glass for a total of 1*21 = $21.00
When you take his earnings of $21.00 and subtract the cost of $7.00 his total net profit was 21-7 = $14.00
The answer is 14.

How does Kalyani feel after hearing Charu's news, and what shows it?
Kalyani feels upset and worried; she stares out of the window, says she can't afford it alone, and admits she is still annoyed.
Which choices made Charu's change of plan honest rather than a disappearance?
Charu spoke before the deposit, admitted she had messed up the plan, and offered real help: finding colleagues and paying her half of the token amount.
Why might Kalyani's trust in Charu survive this?
Because Charu told her early and took responsibility, Kalyani can be annoyed without feeling betrayed.

In the courtyard, two-year-old Ganga sat on the mat with her rag doll and a steel spoon. "Hungry," she told the doll, and pushed the spoon at its stitched mouth. "Aaah." Farhan, the neighbour's boy, leaned over the low wall. "Dolls don't eat." Ganga frowned and fed it again. She laid the doll on the charpai, pulled a small towel over it and patted. Pat, pat, pat. "Sho," she whispered. Her grandmother, shelling peas, smiled and hummed a lullaby.

What did Ganga use to feed her rag doll?
A steel spoon.
What does Ganga's whispered "Sho" suggest she wants for her doll?
She feels caring and tender toward the doll, wanting it to rest the way she herself is put to sleep.
How could Farhan join Ganga's game instead of correcting her?
He could pretend to feed or cover the doll too, which lets Ganga keep practising care.
How does Ganga's grandmother see the game?
She smiles and hums a lullaby, treating the feeding and patting as sweet, natural play worth supporting 😊

Sunday
Diary, Shreya here. Today was the thirteenth-day prayer for Nana. The house was full of people and incense.
In the afternoon my cousin Hemant and I hid on the terrace and started laughing about how Nana used to fall asleep during cricket and then insist he'd been watching. We laughed so hard. Then I felt terrible. Is it wrong to laugh when he's gone?
Mami found us. I thought she'd scold us. She sat down and said, "He'd want you laughing about him. That's how he stays."
So Hemant and I asked if we could plant a hibiscus by the gate, the red kind Nana always picked for his puja. We did it before sunset. My hands were muddy and I cried a bit.
It feels a little easier tonight.

What did Shreya and Hemant plant by the gate?
A red hibiscus, the kind Nana always picked for his puja.
Why did Shreya feel terrible after laughing?
Shreya felt guilty, worried that laughing so soon after Nana's death was disrespectful.
How did planting the hibiscus help Shreya mourn?
It gave Shreya something to do that honoured Nana, so the sadness had a place to go.
How might Mami be feeling while comforting the two children?
Mami is probably grieving too, but finds comfort in sharing happy memories and helping them grieve.

"Urmila, you've been sitting like that for twenty minutes."
Urmila looked up from her notes in the hostel common room. Her shoulders were hunched up near her ears.
"Like what?"
"Like a turtle. Are you cold? The fan's on full."
"No. The fan's fine."
Maria sat down next to her. "Then what is it?"
Urmila's shoulders stayed up. "Viva tomorrow. The external examiner is the one who failed two students last year. I keep imagining him asking something I don't know."
"So scared, not cold."
"Very scared."
Maria nodded. "Want me to switch the fan off anyway?"
"No." Urmila almost smiled. "Can you just ask me the hardest questions? So I've heard them before he asks."
"Deal. First question. Why did you choose this topic?"
Urmila took a breath. As she started answering, her shoulders slowly came down.

How many students had the external examiner failed last year?
Two students.
What was Urmila feeling behind her raised shoulders?
Urmila was scared and anxious about her viva with a strict external examiner.
How did Maria find out what the raised shoulders meant?
She considered the context, the fan, and then asked directly instead of assuming cold or fear.
What did practising the hardest questions do for Urmila?
It gave her a sense of control, and as she answered, her shoulders relaxed.

In the anganwadi courtyard, Irfan's Ammi fed baby Imran on her lap. Sangeeta didi, the anganwadi worker, gave Imran a bright red rattle.

Irfan watched. He was five, and until two months ago, that lap had been his.

He walked over, snatched the rattle and ran to the neem tree. Imran cried.

"Irfan! Give it back!"

Sangeeta didi went and crouched beside him. "You wanted something new too?"

He nodded, hiccuping.

"And maybe a turn with Ammi?"

A bigger nod. Sangeeta didi took his hand and walked him back to his mother.

What colour was the rattle?
Bright red.
What was Irfan feeling when he snatched the rattle?
He felt hurt and left out, missing his place on Ammi's lap, and couldn't say it, so he snatched and ran.
What did Sangeeta didi do that helped?
She crouched beside Irfan and gently named what he wanted, something new and a turn with Ammi, instead of scolding.
How might Ammi feel when Irfan comes back holding Sangeeta didi's hand?
She might feel relieved and understand that Irfan needs time with her too.

I'm Tushar, Simran's big brother. Simran squeals a lot. High, loud, happy squeals, especially when the dog comes in. So when she squealed from the bedroom on Tuesday, I didn't move. Then I heard it again. It was different: higher, thinner, and it didn't stop. I ran in. She'd caught her fingers in the cupboard door. I shouted for Mum, and Mum came and held her hand under the cold tap.

Where had Simran caught her fingers?
In the cupboard door.
What made Tushar think Simran was in pain rather than excited?
Her cry was higher, thinner and didn't stop, which was different from her usual happy squeal and suggested pain and fear.
What did Tushar do that was wise?
He noticed the change in her voice, ran in to check and called Mum straight away.
How might Mum see Tushar's quick reaction?
She would likely feel grateful that he noticed the difference and called her fast.

When a new helper tried the same face, he looked unsure and turned to me. I did it once more, and he laughed again. It seems to work best with someone he knows. Asif, childminder

What does Varun say for "again"?
"Gen!"
What did Varun feel when the new helper made the face?
He felt unsure and uneasy with someone new, so the surprise wasn't funny; he turned to Asif for safety.
How could the new helper become someone Varun laughs with?
By spending calm time with him first, so the helper becomes familiar before trying the game.
How might the new helper feel when Varun turns away?
The helper might feel a bit disappointed, but can see it's about familiarity.
Shedule or schedule?

The correct spelling is "schedule", with sch at the start. In British English it is often said "shed-yool", and in American English "sked-yool".
Example: Please check the schedule before you book the meeting room.

Monday: Sunaina wrote three things on a sticky note: the product launch, Ma's puja on Sunday and the reunion dinner with her old friends. All three looked impossible. Her mother rang twice during the meeting, and Nitin, her team lead, gave her a look when she stepped out.

Thursday: Sunaina stayed late for the launch, missed the call from her mother, then felt guilty and ordered nothing for dinner.

Sunday: She reached the puja an hour late, left before the prasad, and half-listened during the dinner. She felt guilty about each thing, and a little resentful about all of them, and both feelings sat together in her chest.

What three things did Sunaina write on the sticky note?
Sunaina wrote the product launch, Ma's puja on Sunday and the reunion dinner with old friends.
How did Sunaina feel on Sunday, and how do we know?
Sunaina felt guilty and resentful together: she was late, left early and half-listened, and both feelings sat in her chest.
What could Sunaina do earlier in the week to make Sunday less of a collision?
Tell her mother, Nitin and her friends which parts she can attend, and agree what will be shortened, rather than hoping to manage all three.
How might Nitin see Sunaina stepping out of the meeting?
Nitin, as team lead, probably notices the interruption and may feel concerned or impatient, without knowing the calls are about the puja.

On Monday, Hafsa slept nine hours and woke as tired as before. In the seminar she thought, what is the point of any of this? and did not finish a reading she once loved. On Thursday she skipped the literacy club she had started, then found a thank-you card for her mentor still unsigned in her bag from two weeks ago and pushed it deeper. She felt guilty for not caring. That night her roommate Gurleen said, "You're not ungrateful. You're carrying too much." The next Tuesday the two of them sat with the academic advisor, and Hafsa put down the list of her five commitments. She dropped one course and handed the club to a junior. By Friday she still felt flat, but she had slept and eaten lunch away from her laptop.

How many hours did Hafsa sleep on Monday?
Hafsa slept nine hours and woke as tired as before.
What was Hafsa feeling about herself when she pushed the unsigned card deeper into her bag?
Guilty for not caring, and flat and cynical about things that once mattered.
What could Hafsa do if she still feels flat after these changes?
Keep reducing her load, and if it keeps going or worries her, check with a doctor or a counsellor.
How does Gurleen see Hafsa's behaviour?
As a sign of too much load rather than ingratitude, since Gurleen tells Hafsa she is carrying too much.

Sandcastles and waves with all the cousins.

"Harish Bhaiya! Guess what!"
"You found a kitten?"
"No! The dance group asked me to join. For the annual day!"
"The same group that didn't pick you last year?"
"Yes! Kritika said they need me for the front row. And they saved me a seat at lunch." Yamini spun round. "They all have matching hair clips, and they said they'll get me one."
"You're really happy, huh?"
"I don't feel like an outsider anymore." She stopped. "Do you think they'll still want me if I mess up the steps?"
Harish smiled. "They picked you. Practise, and ask them for help."

What did the group say they would get Yamini?
A matching hair clip.
What was Yamini feeling when she said, "I don't feel like an outsider anymore"?
She felt happy and secure, with a deep sense of belonging, though also a little worried about messing up.
What did Harish advise Yamini to do?
To practise and ask the group for help.
How might Harish see his sister's excitement?
Harish seems pleased for her, remembering she wasn't picked last year.

The fan had stopped with the power cut, and Paati lay on the cot in the front room of their house near Thanjavur, eyes closed, forehead damp. Bhavna didn't know how to make her better. Keerthana, her cousin, whispered, 'Leave her. Grown-ups will handle it.' But Bhavna picked up the palm-leaf fan and sat on the floor beside the cot. She waved it slowly. Then she unfolded the morning newspaper and read out the headlines, stumbling over long words. Paati's lips twitched. 'Read me the rice prices, kanna.' Bhavna read them. She read the temple festival dates too. When Amma came in, Paati was asleep, and Bhavna was still fanning, her arm aching, feeling strangely calm.

What did Bhavna use to fan Paati?
The palm-leaf fan.
Why did Bhavna feel strangely calm by the end?
Though she couldn't cure Paati, staying close and helping made her feel useful and loving instead of helpless.
What did Bhavna understand that Keerthana did not?
That a child can help just by being there, fanning and reading, without needing to fix the illness.
What might Paati have felt as Bhavna read the headlines?
Comforted and amused; her lips twitched and she asked for the rice prices before falling asleep.
