In Lisbon, Gabriel's grandmother Jana told everyone he was a genius. He had learned chess at six, and at nine he beat most of his classmates. "So smart," she said at every family lunch. At the chess club, the coach laid out a tricky endgame puzzle for the older children and invited Gabriel to try. He looked at it and felt his face go hot. "I'll do the easy ones," he said, sliding back to the beginner table. At home, he stopped playing against his grandmother's friend, who sometimes beat him. When Jana asked why, he threw his pieces back into the box. "It's boring." Later, alone, he set up the endgame puzzle on his board, stared at it, and put it away without moving a piece.

Where did Gabriel slide back to at the chess club?
The beginner table.
Why did Gabriel feel his face go hot when invited to try the endgame puzzle?
He felt anxious about failing in front of others and losing the 'genius' label, so avoiding it felt safer.
What could the coach or Jana say to make hard puzzles feel less dangerous?
They could praise his thinking and practice, like 'you tried three ideas', instead of calling him smart, so mistakes feel normal.
How might Jana feel when Gabriel throws the pieces in the box?
Jana may feel confused and hurt, not realising that her praise makes him afraid of losing.

Week two: Yamini sent Uma a rough draft of her presentation, labelled "messy version". Uma wrote back two small suggestions. Yamini's hands were shaking as she read it, then she laughed.
Week three: Yamini wrote in her notebook: "Experiments this month: 12. Disasters: 0." She sent her full presentation a day early, without rewriting it a fourth time.

How many disasters did Yamini record?

She felt nervous, her heart racing, before seeing that nothing bad happened.

Uma seems relaxed and supportive, giving small helpful suggestions without judgement.

What did Sonali use as a syringe?
A twig.

"Ujjwal, what's the answer to question three?"

"Hold on, Dhruv. I'm on the lecture recording."

"You're also on chat. And a cricket score. And the assignment page."

"It's called efficiency."

"Okay. What did the professor say about supply curves?"

"She said... they go up? Or down?"

"I've been listening in pieces."

What was Ujjwal doing besides the lecture recording?
He was also on chat, a cricket score and the assignment page.

He felt busy, confident and capable, so switching between things felt productive even though he was taking in only pieces.

How might Dhruv feel watching Ujjwal explain the topic clearly?

I'm Jaya, twenty-two, and I've never regretted being careful. When my classmates put their savings into some online trading scheme last year, I read everything, asked my uncle, who's an accountant, and stayed out. Half of them lost money. I felt vindicated. But there's another story. My friend Dolma asked me to join her trekking-guide course in Sikkim: three weeks, a bit risky, unpaid. I made a list of forty things that could go wrong. I said no. She came back glowing, with a job offer. I keep asking myself: did my judgement decide that, or did fear? With the trading, it was judgement. With the trek, I think it was fear.

Who did Jaya ask about the trading scheme?
Jaya's uncle, who's an accountant.
How did Jaya feel about staying out of the trading scheme?
Jaya felt vindicated when half the classmates lost money.
What could Jaya do differently the next time a chance like the trek comes up?
Check the real facts, as with the trading, and ask whether the no is judgement or fear before deciding.
How did Dolma experience the trek course?
Dolma came back glowing, with a job offer.

Lalit, your roommate says you're angry and cold? Let your Lavanya didi tell you something.

At nineteen, in my first year of college, my roommate kept saying, "Why do you hate me? You're so cold." I didn't hate her. I was just shy and busy.

At first I felt terrible. I thought maybe she saw something I didn't. I tried to be extra nice. It didn't help.

Then one day I asked myself: what have I actually done? I'd shared my notes, invited her to dinner. Nothing cold.

So I asked her calmly, "Are you upset with me about something?" She admitted she was still angry that I'd been chosen class representative over her.

Look at the facts first, Lalit. Don't just take the blame.

What had young Lavanya shared with her roommate?
Her notes.
How did young Lavanya feel when accused of being cold?
She felt terrible and confused, starting to doubt herself.
What turning point in the story helped Lavanya stop absorbing the accusation?
Asking herself what she had actually done and then calmly asking her roommate if she was upset.
How might the roommate have felt admitting her anger?
The roommate probably felt uncomfortable but also relieved to say what was really bothering her.

“Shalini, you asked how I picked my bookmark price, so here's the honest version. At first I charged ten rupees because everyone smiled and said ‘so cheap!’ Then one night I counted. Card, thread and glue came to about six rupees each, and every bookmark took twenty minutes. Ten minus six is four rupees for twenty minutes. That's twelve rupees an hour, if I'm lucky. I looked at what the stationery shop and the lady next door charged for similar ones, twenty-five to thirty-five. So I set thirty. Two people grumbled. My stomach did a little flip. But I could keep making them, and I finally understood that pricing low to please everyone meant I'd quit by Diwali. I'm Alka, by the way.”

How many minutes did each bookmark take?
Twenty minutes.
What did Alka feel on realising the ten-rupee price left so little?
Worry mixed with sober clarity: Alka saw that pleasing buyers with a tiny price would end in giving up.
What could Alka try if two buyers still grumble, and why?
Alka could offer a set of bookmarks at a bundle price or a simpler design at a lower price, since that keeps costs and time covered while giving buyers a choice.
How might a buyer used to the ten-rupee price see the change?
A buyer may be surprised at first, but seeing the price match neighbours' similar work and the effort involved could make it feel fair.

In the first week of the college bus from Wadgaon to the taluka town, Madhuri stopped speaking her village Marathi. The town girls laughed at words like 'lai bhari', so she copied their neat, careful sentences and kept her bajra bhakri wrapped in her bag until she got home, hungry. By the third week her jaw ached from smiling at jokes she didn't find funny. One afternoon Avni from the back seat pulled out her own tiffin. 'My Aaji's thecha. Too spicy for these town people,' she grinned, in full village Marathi. Madhuri laughed before she could stop herself. 'Lai bhari,' she said, and unwrapped her bhakri. They shared it all the way home. Madhuri still used some town words in class; they were useful there. But on the bus she talked like herself, and the girls who smirked mattered a little less every day.

What did Madhuri keep wrapped in her bag?
Her bajra bhakri, until she got home, hungry.
What was Madhuri feeling as her jaw ached from smiling?
She felt tired and hollow, pretending to enjoy jokes just to belong.
Which choice worked for Madhuri, and why?
Keeping some town words for class but talking like herself on the bus, so she fits in lightly without hiding who she is.
How does Avni see village Marathi on the bus?
Avni is proud of it and jokes about town people, which makes it safe for Madhuri to be herself too.

At the university counselling centre, Joseph sat across from Ojas, the counsellor, for the fifth time. A year ago, the bike accident had broken his leg and cost him the football season. For months, whenever he told it, it was just a list of losses: the team, the scholarship trial, the friends who drifted. Today Ojas asked, "Tell it again, and this time include what happened after." Joseph did. The losses were still there. He didn't soften them. But then he talked about the physiotherapy mornings, the friend who drove him every week, the coaching certificate he started while he couldn't play. "I still miss it," Joseph said. "I'm still angry about the car that didn't stop. But I found out I'm good at teaching kids." Ojas nodded. "Both of those are true."

What did the accident cost Joseph?
It broke his leg and cost him the football season.
How does Joseph feel about the accident now?
He still misses football and feels angry about the car that didn't stop, but also feels some pride in discovering he's good at teaching kids.
What did Ojas do that helped Joseph's retelling?
Ojas asked him to include what happened after, which let Joseph add survival and growth without erasing the losses.
How might the friend who drove Joseph every week feel hearing this new version?
The friend would probably feel moved and valued, seeing their support become part of Joseph's story.

Mr. Banks and Ms. Elizabeth are entrepreneurs who invest in different income streams and earn revenue from the investments. From each of his eight investments, Mr. Banks received $500 in revenue. Ms. Elizabeth also received $900 from each of her 5 investment streams. How much more money did Ms. Elizabeth make from her investments than Mr. Banks?

Since Mr. Banks had 8 investment streams and each brought in a revenue of $500, he earned 500*8 = $4000 from all of his investments.
Ms Elizabeth also received $900*5 = $4500 in revenue from her 5 income streams,
The total amount of money that Ms. Elizabeth made more than Mr. Banks is $4500-$4000 = $500
The answer is 500.

Sami left the clinic in Helsinki holding a folder he couldn't read through the blur in his eyes. The doctor had said "tumour," then a lot of other words he had lost.

At home, Sami did what he'd promised himself not to: he searched. At 2 a.m. he was reading forums with the worst stories on the internet, his heart pounding.

Mateo, his partner, found him on the kitchen floor. He closed the laptop gently. "Not tonight. Come to bed."

In the morning they sat together and wrote a list of questions. What stage is it? What are the options? What happens first? Mateo asked for the next appointment so he could come too.

At the clinic Mateo took notes while Sami asked. The doctor answered each one and offered to arrange a second opinion. One step at a time, she said.

On the tram home Sami read the notes. Still frightening. But now it had edges.

What did Sami and Mateo write together in the morning?
A list of questions for the doctor.
What was Sami feeling at 2 a.m. while searching forums?
He felt terrified and panicked, his heart pounding as he read the worst stories.
Which steps helped Sami more than night-time searching, and why?
Writing questions, bringing Mateo to take notes, asking about a second opinion and taking it step by step, because they turned panic into clear information from a trusted source.
How does Mateo see Sami's night of searching?
Mateo sees it as frightening Sami more, so he gently closes the laptop and helps him prepare questions instead.

Yoga teacher's note, beginners' batch, 12 February.
In January we had twenty-two new students. Today we had nine.
Gargi was one of the most enthusiastic in January. She said she wanted “to get fitter this year.” Asked which days she'd come, she said, “Whenever I can.” She attended six classes in January, none in February.
Her friend Sunaina joined the same week and said, “Tuesday and Thursday, 7 a.m., straight after I drop my son at the bus.” She has not missed a class.
Both seemed equally determined. One had a when and a cue.
When I called Gargi yesterday, she sounded embarrassed. I told her it wasn't a character flaw; the plan was simply vague.
What I did next: I suggested she choose two fixed class times attached to something she already does, and she chose Monday and Wednesday after her morning tea. She is booked for Monday.

How many classes did Gargi attend in February?
She attended none in February.
How did Gargi feel when the teacher called?
She felt embarrassed, as if the lapse were a personal failure rather than a vague plan.
What did the teacher suggest, and why could it help?
Choosing two fixed class times attached to her morning tea, so coming doesn't depend on memory and mood.
How might Sunaina see her own routine compared with Gargi's?

"Bad girl!" Jahnavi said, wagging her finger. "You don't jump! Sit properly!"

She joined in patiently, asked if the doll was okay and gave a hanky for a blanket, encouraging Jahnavi's kindness.

Last week Ammi sat me down to talk about my marks and the phone. She'd barely started when my face went hot. My heart was banging. I couldn't think. I heard myself shouting, "You never trust me! You don't even know what it's like!" Then I just shut down. Stared at the wall.
My sister Sudha was in the doorway. She said, "Asif, maybe take ten minutes? Ammi, can we do this after dinner?" Ammi hesitated, then nodded.
I went to the roof. Breathed. After a while, my hands stopped shaking. I could think again.
After dinner, I sat down and said, "Sorry for shouting. Can we start again?" We talked for half an hour. It was actually fine.
I'm learning that when my body goes hot like that, pushing through just makes it worse.

Where did Asif go to calm down?
To the roof.
What was Asif feeling when the talk started?
Asif felt flooded, face hot and heart banging, unable to think, and ended up shouting and shutting down.
Why did Sudha's suggestion work?
Pausing for ten minutes let Asif's body calm down so the conversation could resume clearly after dinner.
How might Ammi have felt when Asif shouted?
Ammi was probably hurt and worried, but agreed to pause and talk later.

Richard can clean his room in 22 minutes. Cory takes 3 minutes more than Richard to clean her room while Blake can clean his room 4 minutes more quickly than Cory. If they have to clean their rooms twice a week, how many minutes do all three spend cleaning their rooms each week?

Cory takes 22 + 3 = 25 minutes to clean her room.
Blake takes 25 - 4 = 21 minutes to clean his room.
The three of them can clean their room in 22 + 25 + 21 = 68 minutes in all.
In a week, they spend 68 x 2 = 136 minutes cleaning their rooms.
The answer is 136.

Draft a notice for the school notice board about a change in the bus timing next week. Buses leave 30 minutes earlier on Monday and Tuesday, and normal timings resume on Wednesday. About 55 words. Sign it Transport Office.

NOTICE
Change in Bus Timing

All students who use the school bus are informed that the buses will leave thirty minutes earlier than usual on Monday and Tuesday next week. Please reach your bus stop on time. Parents, please note this. Normal timings will resume from Wednesday.

By order,
Transport Office
Ten 10-paise coins are put together. How much money is that? What is 0.1 x 10?

Answer: ₹1. 0.1 x 10 = 1.

10 paise = ₹0.10 = ₹0.1, one tenth of a rupee. Ten of them make 10 tenths = 1 whole rupee. So 0.1 x 10 = 1. In the same way, a 1-paise coin is ₹0.01; ten of them make ₹0.10, so 0.01 x 10 = 0.1, and a hundred of them make ₹1, so 0.01 x 100 = 1. When a number is multiplied by 10, each digit moves one place to the left.

Read this:

On the metro platform in Delhi, Noor found a small plastic pouch with fifty rupees and a school ID card inside: 'Aman Verma, Class 2'. The photo showed a boy with a gap-toothed grin. Noor imagined him standing at his school gate right now, patting his pockets, his face crumpling. He might be scared to tell his mother. Maybe it was his canteen money for the whole week. Her own stomach twisted just thinking of it. 'Should we just keep it?' her friend Shreya asked. 'He's probably so worried,' Noor said. They showed it to the metro guard, who called the school printed on the card. That evening Noor's mother got a call from Aman's father, thanking them. Noor felt warm all the way to her toes.

Whose name was on the ID card?
Aman Verma, Class 2.
Why did Noor's stomach twist?
She imagined Aman's fear at losing the money and felt sorry for him.
How did Noor return the pouch?
She showed it to the metro guard, who called the school printed on the card.
How might Aman feel when the pouch comes back?
Relieved and happy after being worried about the lost money.

Read this:

Pallavi beti, you think you need more coffee to study? Let me tell you about me in Class 12.
I was the topper in our town. I wanted to stay the topper. So I drank tea after tea, strong, and studied till three in the morning. I caught every cold going round. I stopped playing the harmonium, which I loved. My friends called, and I said I was busy.
When I felt tired, I thought, Ramesh, you're getting lazy. So I pushed harder.
One day I fell asleep on my bicycle, beta. Right into a ditch. Only then did my father sit me down and make me rest.
Tired is not lazy, Pallavi. Your old uncle learned it the hard way.

What instrument did Ramesh stop playing?
The harmonium.
What was young Ramesh feeling when the word lazy came to mind?
Young Ramesh felt ashamed and afraid of losing the topper's place, so tiredness looked like laziness and the answer was to push harder.
In the story, what turning point finally made Ramesh rest?
Falling asleep on his bicycle into a ditch, after which his father sat him down and made him rest.
How might Ramesh's father have felt after the ditch?
His father was probably frightened and worried, realising how exhausted his son had become.

Read this:

The train was two hours late and the platform bench was hard. Chetan had counted the pigeons, the pillars and the tea stalls. “I'm boooored. What can I do?” he whined, swinging his legs.
Leela Nani rummaged in her bag and found a ribbon of string and a small notebook. “You choose: cat's cradle, or write down every colour you see.”
Chetan scowled. “Both are boring.”
Nani said nothing and watched the tracks. After a while he took the notebook and drew a wobbly red shirt on the man near the tea stall. “His shirt is red,” he announced.

What had Chetan counted on the platform?
He had counted the pigeons, the pillars and the tea stalls.
What might Chetan be feeling when he says both are boring, and what else could be behind it?
Probably restless and bored with the long wait. The refusal might also come from tiredness or a wish to choose his own thing. He takes the notebook later, so the boredom eased.
What could Nani try next if the notebook loses its appeal?
Let him choose again, or leave a little quiet so he invents something himself, as happened here.
How might Nani feel when he scowls at her ideas?
Perhaps a bit tired herself from the delay. She chose to stay quiet rather than argue, which gave him room.

Read this:

The clinic waiting room had forty plastic chairs and a television nobody watched. Naveen had sat there every Monday and Thursday for a month while his mother had her sessions.
Today he had a plan. In his pocket were thirty flashcards on accounting standards, written the night before. On the bus in he'd done ten. Now, between the token calls, he did the rest, putting the ones he missed in his left pocket.
Yogesh, a nursing student doing rounds with the clinic staff, noticed. "Exams?"
"Final-year. I used to try reading the whole textbook here. Never got past a page."
"And now?"
"Short cards here. Hard stuff, like consolidation, I do at home from nine to ten, every night, no phone."
When his mother came out, she saw him counting cards. "How many?" she asked. "Twenty-four out of thirty," he said, and helped her to the bus stop.

How many flashcards did Naveen get right?
He got twenty-four out of thirty.
How did Naveen seem to feel when he told Yogesh about his old way of studying?
He seemed a little embarrassed about never getting past a page, but now confident with his new plan.
What else could Naveen do with the cards he misses?
He could add them to his nine-to-ten hour, so the hardest cards get focused time at home.
How might Naveen's mother feel seeing him count cards?
She may feel relieved and proud that he is managing his studies while coming to her sessions.

metadata.subtype: Approach: study in small blocks around the caregiving day [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

On Tuesday, Yusuf wanted his cartoons before dinner. "Not now, dinner first," said Mummy Swati. "Just five minutes! I'll be good!" She shook her head, and he sulked at the table.

On Thursday he tried again, and Mummy Swati said, "Dinner first. Then five minutes, and I'll set the timer." He ate fast. When the timer rang, he grumbled but switched it off.

On Saturday, before she could say a word, Yusuf asked, "Can I have five minutes after dinner, with the timer, Mummy?" "Yes," she said, and he smiled.

What did Mummy Swati offer on Thursday?
She offered five minutes after dinner, with a timer.
Why did Yusuf ask for five minutes after dinner on Saturday?
He had found that this kind of request gets a yes, because Mummy did what she said with the timer on Thursday. He trusts that she keeps her word, and his smile shows he expects it to work.
What made Yusuf's bargaining worth trying, and what should Mummy keep doing?
It worked because Mummy was fair and did the same thing each time, so the offer was real. If she said yes one day and no the next, bargaining would just turn into pushing.
How might Mummy Swati feel about Yusuf asking this way?
She may feel relieved and proud that he asks with a plan and not with promises or sulking. It probably makes saying yes feel easier for her.
Tell a child how to say sorry after bumping into someone. Use exactly two sentences, and start the first with "Say".
Say "I am sorry" in a clear and friendly voice. Then ask if the person is all right.

Read this:

"Deepak, my cousin's wedding is on Saturday. Come with me. There'll be food and a DJ."
"I'll pass."
"Why? You love food."
"I won't know anyone. I'll stand in a corner. Your relatives will ask who I am and I'll say something stupid. It'll be so awkward."
"You don't know that."
"Harsha, I know exactly how it'll go. I've been to weddings."
"With me?"
"No."
"Then you don't know. My cousins are nice. My Nani will feed you until you can't move."
"They won't like me."
"You've met none of them."
"That's why. It's safer not to go."
"Safer from what?"
He shrugged. "From standing there feeling stupid."
"And what about sitting at home feeling stupid?"
Deepak opened his mouth, then closed it.
"I'll be at your door at seven," said Harsha. "You can leave at nine if it's awful."
"...Fine. Nine."

Whose wedding is on Saturday?
Harsha's cousin's wedding is on Saturday.
What is Deepak afraid of, and why does staying home feel safer?
Deepak is afraid of feeling awkward and embarrassed among strangers, so avoiding the wedding feels like protection from that feeling.
What did Harsha offer that made saying yes easier?
Harsha offered to come at seven and let Deepak leave at nine if it's awful, making it a small, safe test.
How might Harsha feel if Deepak had said no again?
Harsha might feel disappointed and a bit hurt, having wanted Deepak to meet the family.

metadata.subtype: Sure that the date will go badly [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this and say how Rostov and Denisov feel afterwards.

When the reading of Denisov's virulent reply, which took more than an hour, was over, Rostov said nothing, and he spent the rest of the day in a most dejected state of mind amid Denisov's hospital comrades, who had gathered round him, telling them what he knew and listening to their stories. Denisov was moodily silent all the evening.
Both are low. Rostov stays silent and spends the day feeling dejected among the other patients, and Denisov is gloomy and silent all evening.

Read this:

Dear Seema didi,
You asked how the district chess tournament went. I lost in the second round. And I have to tell you the truth, because I've been lying to everyone else.
The night before, I watched chess videos and then random videos until 2 am. Mummy called out three times. I kept saying, "Just five more minutes." In the morning my eyes burned and I blundered my queen in move fourteen.
To everyone, I said, "I was so tired, I didn't sleep." Which is true. But I chose not to sleep. I think I was scared. If I'd slept well and lost, it would mean I'm just not good. Being tired meant I had a reason.
But now I don't know if I could have won. That feels worse.
Next tournament is in March. I'm going to sleep at ten the night before, even if I'm nervous.
Bhavna

In which move did Bhavna blunder the queen?
Bhavna blundered the queen in move fourteen.
Why does Bhavna think staying up till 2 am happened?
Bhavna was scared that losing after a good sleep would mean not being good enough, so tiredness became a ready reason.
What is Bhavna planning for March, and why is it a good choice?
Sleeping at ten the night before, even if nervous, so the result will show real ability and something to learn.
How might Seema didi feel reading this letter?
Seema didi would likely feel proud of Bhavna's honesty and hopeful about the March tournament.

metadata.subtype: Staying up late before a big match [Actor]

messages.content:
When he looked out from his shelter in the distance, and saw that I waved my hat to him to come up, he rejoined me, and there we waited; sometimes lying on the bank, wrapped in our coats, and sometimes moving about to warm ourselves, until we saw our boat coming round. We got aboard easily, and rowed out into the track of the steamer. By that time it wanted but ten minutes of one o'clock, and we began to look out for her smoke.

How do the friends pass the time while waiting for the steamer?

They lie on the bank wrapped in their coats or move about to keep warm until the boat comes round. Then they board, row out into the steamer's track and watch for her smoke with ten minutes left before one o'clock.

Read this:

Monday. After his tantrum, Rishi sobbed. Tanuja started a lecture. He cried harder.
Wednesday. Rishi's crying turned to sobs. He held out his arms. Tanuja hugged him and gave him water. Zeenat didi breathed slowly beside them. Rishi's body got soft.
Friday. Rishi sobbed, then leaned into Tanuja on his own. She held him. He sipped water and sighed.

What did Tanuja give Rishi on Wednesday?
She gave him water after hugging him.
What did Rishi want when he held out his arms?
He wanted comfort and a hug, as his big feelings were settling.
What did Tanuja learn between Monday and Wednesday?
She learned that a lecture made it worse, while a hug, water and slow breathing helped Rishi settle.
How might Zeenat didi see Rishi's change by Friday?
She may notice he now leans in on his own, trusting that comfort will come.
Write today's diary note for Ethan: he got a haircut he did not like, his sister laughed, and then he laughed too, so the haircut did not matter. 40 words.

Dear Diary,
Today I got a haircut that I did not like at all. My sister laughed at me, and then I laughed too. After that, the haircut did not matter any more, and I felt much better.
Ethan

Read this:

Lucia had won the regional robotics prize, and when her classmates in Osaka cheered she laughed it off. "It was luck. Anyone could have built it." At home she hid the medal in a drawer and told her cousin the design was mostly the team's, though she had written most of the code.
Hiroshi, her teacher, saw the medal peeking from her bag. "Which part was luck?" he asked.
Lucia thought. "The weather?"
"And the two hundred lines of code?"
She winced, then smiled. "That was me."
"Then say so. It isn't bragging to say what's true. It's also true you asked for help with the sensors."
Lucia said it again, slowly. "I wrote the code, and the team did the sensors." It felt lighter than pretending.

Where did Lucia hide her medal at home?
In a drawer.
What is Lucia feeling when she says 'It was luck'?
Uncomfortable with praise and unsure she deserves it, so she shrinks her part instead of owning it.
What turning point did Hiroshi's questions bring?
Hiroshi asked which part was luck, and Lucia admitted the code was hers, then stated her strengths and the team's help accurately.
How might Lucia's classmates feel when she laughs off the prize?
Possibly confused or a bit deflated, since they are cheering and she denies the achievement.

Read this:

Beatriz, twenty-six, taught at a primary school in Recife. In March the district office sent a notice: children without complete papers could no longer attend until the paperwork was done. It could take months.
Yara, eight, was one of them. Her family had fled another country. She was the best reader in the class.
Colleagues said, "It's the rule. We'll get in trouble."
Beatriz thought about it for two nights. Then she decided: a child's right to learn and her dignity mattered more to her than the notice. She kept Yara in her classroom, openly, and wrote to the district explaining why.
She got a formal warning. Some colleagues stopped sitting with her at lunch.
She accepted it. "I know most people wouldn't do this," she told her sister. "I'm not sure I always would. But this time I had to."

How old was Yara?
Eight.
What was Beatriz feeling during the two nights she thought about it?
She felt torn and uneasy, weighing the rule against Yara's right to learn.
What did Beatriz do, and what did it cost her?
She kept Yara in class openly and wrote to the district explaining why; she got a formal warning and some colleagues withdrew.
How might Yara feel being allowed to stay?
She would probably feel safe and valued, able to keep learning and reading in her class.
Cheryl has thrice as many colored pencils as Cyrus. Madeline has 63 colored pencils and only half of what Cheryl has. How many colored pencils do the three of them have altogether?

Cheryl has 63 x 2 = 126 colored pencils.
Cyrus has 126/3 = 42 colored pencils.
Altogether, they have 126 + 42 + 63 = 231 colored pencils.
The answer is 231.
Teachers' Day is on Friday, and our class wants to do something nice for our class teacher.
What a thoughtful plan. A handmade card with a message from every student is simple and personal.
We also thought of singing something. Is that too much?
Not at all, as long as it is short and warm. One song and a card are plenty, and your teacher will remember it for a long time.
Suggest a two-word team name for a school quiz, with no more than ten letters in total.
Brain Bees

Read this:

I'm Pooja, and I sit behind Irfan in assembly. Irfan doesn't say the prayer and doesn't make trouble, just stands with hands folded. At lunch, only to me, Irfan said, "There's no god for me, and it feels lonely. Everyone just assumes." I said nothing clever. I moved my tiffin closer. Later in the library Irfan showed me a book on stars and said, "When I read this I feel small in a good way." I also saw Irfan help the caretaker carry chairs without being asked. I can't say the loneliness is gone, but Irfan asked if I'd come to the astronomy club on Friday.

What did Irfan show Pooja in the library?
Irfan showed Pooja a book on stars.
What does Irfan feel about not believing, and how does Pooja know?
Irfan feels lonely, because Irfan said so at lunch, and also a sense of awe when reading about the stars.
What could Irfan do to feel less alone?
Find people, books and values to rely on, such as the astronomy club, and keep the kindness that already shows in helping.
How might Pooja's moving the tiffin closer matter to Irfan?
It may have shown company without judgement, though Pooja cannot be sure how it felt to Irfan.
Please write an invitation to a baby naming ceremony at our home on Sunday at 11 am. The baby's name is Aarohi. About 50 words, from her parents Kiran and Deepa.

Dear Family and Friends,
With great joy, we invite you to the naming ceremony of our baby daughter. She will be named Aarohi. Please join us at our home on Sunday at 11 am to bless her. Your love and good wishes will mean the world to us.
With love,
Kiran and Deepa

Read this:

Sunday. Got 94 in the physics test. Everyone in class was happy for me. I came home and redid the whole paper at my desk till two in the morning because of the six marks I lost, and cancelled football with Imran as punishment. That's what I do. Anything less than full marks and I sort of sentence myself. Imran knocked this morning and asked why I'd skipped football. I said I didn't deserve it. He sat on my bed and said, 'Bhai, you're doing to yourself what nobody else would dare to do to you.' That stuck. So today I tried something new. Instead of 'perfect', I wrote 'one percent better' on a sticky note. I looked at the six marks, found it was one formula I'd mixed up, practised that for twenty minutes, and stopped. Then I went to football. Felt weird. Felt good. Tomorrow, one more small thing.
- Farhan

What did Farhan write on the sticky note?
'One percent better'.
How did Farhan feel about scoring 94?
He felt it wasn't good enough and was frustrated and harsh with himself over the six lost marks.
What small step helped Farhan break the pattern?
Fixing just the one formula for twenty minutes, then stopping and going to football.
How does Imran see the way Farhan treats himself?
As harsher than anyone else would dare to be, which worries him enough to speak up.
What is a dozen bananas going for at the stall by the temple?
I don't know the rate for a dozen bananas, as I can't see stall prices. Ask the seller or compare two stalls on the way.

Read this:

In their third-floor flat in Pune, Mehak tugged Papa's kurta and held up her empty steel cup. 'Paani!' Vijay filled it. Later she toddled to the balcony door and reached for the latch. 'No, Mehak, not alone,' he said. She looked back, frowned, then walked away. When the neighbour's cat slipped in, she squatted and stroked its back with two slow fingers, the way Papa had shown her.

What did Mehak hold up when she wanted water?
She held up her empty steel cup and said 'Paani!'
What does Mehak's frown before walking away from the balcony door suggest?
It suggests she wanted to open it and felt a little cross, but still chose to accept Papa's limit.
How could Vijay keep supporting her gentle touch with animals?
He can keep showing her soft strokes and praise her when she is gentle, as she copied his two-finger way with the cat.
How might the cat experience Mehak's slow stroking?
The cat would likely feel calm and safe, rather than grabbed or chased by a small child.

Read this:

Class note, Monday. Devika, science. In today's oral quiz I asked Bidisha how a thrown ball moves. She started, “It goes up and then…” and stopped, hands clamped under her desk. Last term another teacher told her to keep her hands still when answering. I said, “Use your hands if it helps.” Her finger shot up and drew a smooth arch in the air: rising, slowing at the top, then curving down faster. “Up slow, then down fast. Like a rainbow, but lopsided because of the wind.” That was a better answer than most of my older classes give. Note to self: let children gesture while they explain.

What shape did Bidisha draw in the air?
Bidisha drew a smooth arch in the air.
Why did Bidisha stop and clamp her hands under her desk?
She was probably anxious about being told off, since another teacher had told her to keep her hands still, and without them she felt stuck.
What did Devika do that helped Bidisha explain?
Devika told her to use her hands if it helped, which let Bidisha show and work out the ball's path.
What would change if Devika had kept the no-hands rule?
Bidisha might have stayed stuck, and Devika would never have heard how well she understood the ball's path.

Read this:

Monday: Swati Dadi taught Payal, five, a short evening prayer. Payal mixed up the lines and giggled.

Thursday: They said it together while lighting the lamp, clapping on each beat. Payal got the first two lines alone.

Next Monday: Payal stood before the lamp, folded her hands and said the whole prayer, swaying to its rhythm. Then she started teaching it to her teddy, line by line. Swati Dadi pretended not to watch, smiling.

Who taught Payal the evening prayer?
Swati Dadi taught her.
Why might Swati Dadi pretend not to watch while smiling?
She felt proud and happy but did not want to make Payal self-conscious while she practised with her teddy.
What helped Payal remember the prayer?
Saying it together each evening and clapping on the beat gave her repetition and rhythm to hold the words.
What would change if Swati Dadi had scolded Payal for mixing up lines?
Payal might have felt embarrassed and lost interest, instead of giggling and trying again.

Read this:

Monday. Mr Nilesh marked Gurleen late by one minute and gave her a zero for the quiz, though two boys who walked in after her got to sit. She felt her jaw tighten. "Rules are rules," he said, and turned to the board.

Wednesday. He spent twenty minutes at her desk untangling how forces work on a ramp, until it finally clicked. Nobody else in school explained it like that. She hated how grateful she felt.

Friday. She waited until the room emptied. "Sir, on Monday the boys who came in after me weren't penalised. Could you tell me how the late rule works?" He frowned, then rubbed his forehead. "You're right. I'll count your quiz." She said thank you, and meant it, still a little sore, still a little in awe.

On which day did Mr Nilesh explain the ramp problem to Gurleen?
On Wednesday.
What two feelings did Gurleen have about Mr Nilesh by Friday?
Respect and resentment together. She was still a little sore about the zero yet also in awe of how well he taught her.
Why was it wise for Gurleen to raise the late rule specifically rather than complain about the teacher in general?
A specific, calm question about one unfair event gave him something clear to fix. He could agree without feeling attacked, and she kept the respect for what he taught. 🙂
How might Mr Nilesh have felt when Gurleen spoke to him on Friday?
Probably uncomfortable at first, since he frowned and rubbed his forehead. But he admitted she was right, so he seems willing to correct a mistake when it is put fairly.

Read this:

Wasim here. I share a desk with Suraj at the design studio. For his first year he couldn't send a single logo to a client without showing it to five of us first. "Is this okay? Be honest. Would you like it?" If one person frowned, he'd redo it. Lately something's different. Before he shows anyone, he writes three things on a sticky note: what the client needs, what he thinks is honest design, what he'd be proud of in a year. Then he checks his work against the note. Last week the art director didn't praise his packaging design at all. The old Suraj would have sulked all afternoon. This Suraj looked at his sticky note, nodded, and went for chai. He still asked me later, "Did you like it?" But he didn't redo it.

What three things does Suraj write on the sticky note?
What the client needs, what he thinks is honest design, and what he'd be proud of in a year.
Why might Suraj still ask 'Did you like it?' later?
Suraj still wants approval and may feel a little unsure, but the note gives him enough steadiness that the answer no longer decides what he does.
What choice did Suraj make when the art director gave no praise?
He checked the work against his note, nodded and went for chai instead of redoing it, trusting his own standard.
How has sharing a desk with Suraj changed for Wasim?
Wasim no longer has to review every logo, and sees a calmer colleague who can take silence from the art director in stride 🙂.

Read this:

Tuesday. Disha finds out Madhuri told the art club that Disha's poem was about missing her old friends in Pune. Disha had shared that in confidence. She goes home and doesn't answer Madhuri's calls.
Thursday. They meet on the swings in the colony park. Disha says, "I need a rule: what I tell you stays with you." Madhuri nods. "Agreed. And I'm sorry. It was your poem and your story, not mine to tell." Disha hadn't expected it to be said so plainly. They decide on Sunday morning at the flower market, the way they used to.
Sunday. No one at club mentions the poem. At the flower market, Madhuri buys a string of marigolds and hands Disha half. Disha laughs for the first time in a week.

Where do Disha and Madhuri meet on Thursday?
On the swings in the colony park.
How did Disha feel on Tuesday?
She felt hurt and betrayed, and didn't answer Madhuri's calls.
What makes this repair plan work for both friends?
The clear rule gives Disha safety, the apology names the harm, and the flower market trip brings back their old ease.
How might Madhuri feel handing over the marigolds?
Madhuri may feel relieved and hopeful, glad to be forgiven and eager to show care 😊.
Why do students sometimes feel nervous when a teacher says the test will be a surprise?
Not knowing what to expect makes them uneasy. Because they cannot prepare for something they cannot predict, the surprise feels like a threat.

Read this:

The power went off at nine, just when Joseph had to finish his poem for tomorrow's assembly. The inverter beeped and died.
"Keerthana Chechi, torch!"
His sister held her phone light over his notebook, yawning. "Hurry. Amma will scold if we're still up."
Joseph stared at the dark. The fan had stopped and the whole flat was silent except for a dog somewhere. He wrote: "The night is a thick blanket that swallowed the fan's song."
He crossed it out. Wrote it again.
"Why are you writing about a blanket? It's a poem about our building," Keerthana whispered.
"Because it feels like that," Joseph said. "Heavy and quiet."
She read it twice. "Keep it."
When the light came back, he had four lines, and the last one was: "And I am as still as a lizard on the wall."

What did Joseph compare the night to?
A thick blanket that swallowed the fan's song.
Why did Joseph keep the blanket line even after crossing it out?
He wanted a way to express how the dark felt, heavy and quiet; he may also have felt unsure, which is why he crossed it out before writing it again.
What helped Joseph finish despite the power cut?
His sister held a light, and he used the silence itself as material instead of waiting for the power to return.
How did Keerthana's view of the poem change?
At first she was puzzled why a building poem had a blanket in it, but after reading it twice she saw the feeling in it and told him to keep it.

metadata.subtype: Simile and metaphor in writing and speech [Expressing]

messages.content: Mark got a 5% raise at his job.  Before the raise, he earned 40 dollars per hour.  He works 8 hours per day for 5 days per week.  His old bills used to be 600 dollars a week but he decided to add a hundred dollar a week personal trainer.  How much does he have leftover a week?

After the raise he earns 40*1.05=42 dollars an hour
He works 8 hours per day so earns 42*8=336 per day
He works 5 days per week so he earns 336*5=1680 a week
His expenses after adding the personal trainer are 600+100=700 a week
So he has 1680-700=980 left over
The answer is 980.

Read this:

Note for Vijay's tuition sir, Sunday. As you suggested, Vijay did the maths paper from last year on the dining table this afternoon, with the kitchen clock in front of him and one hour allowed. I watched from the stove. He spent almost twenty minutes on question 6, the one about the train, rubbing out again and again. When time was up he had not reached questions 9 and 10. We checked together: most of what he did was right. He said, without any prompting, "Next time I'll mark the hard one, skip it and come back." We'll try another paper on Wednesday. Aparna

How long did Vijay spend on question 6?
Almost twenty minutes.
How did Vijay seem to feel after checking the paper?
He seemed a little frustrated at running out of time but encouraged that most of his answers were right, so he wanted to fix the timing.
What else could Vijay try in Wednesday's paper?
Glance at the clock after every few questions and set a rough limit per question; the timed practice is what showed his problem.
How does Aparna see the practice session?
Aparna is pleased that Vijay spotted the timing problem himself, without prompting, and plans another paper.

metadata.subtype: Approach: practising old test papers under time [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

On Tuesday Sachin, two, cried sharply and pulled at his ear, pushing his food away. Kashish laid a hand on his forehead and watched. On Wednesday he still tugged at the ear, slept badly, and woke fussing. She took him to the doctor. The doctor looked and gave her advice. On Saturday Sachin ate his breakfast, slept through his nap, and played with his blocks without touching his ear.

What did Sachin do on Tuesday that first worried Kashish?
He cried sharply, pulled at his ear and pushed his food away.
What might Sachin's tugging and poor sleep suggest, and what else could explain them?
They suggest something in his ear is hurting him, though he cannot say so. It could also be another kind of discomfort, so a doctor was the right person to check.
Why was going to the doctor a sound choice for Kashish?
She watched his eating, sleeping and pulling at his ear, and took him to the doctor when it kept going. 🙂
How might Kashish have felt on Wednesday night?
She was probably worried and tired, unable to ask him what was wrong.

Read this:

"Jeevan bhaiya, you've cancelled on me three times. And you're not answering calls."
"I'm fine, Vandana."
"You don't sound fine. Your voice is flat. Amma says you're sleeping all day."
"I'm just tired from work."
"For two months?"
Silence. Then: "I can't feel anything. I go to office, come back, lie down. I don't care about cricket, food, nothing."
"Bhaiya, that sounds serious. It's not laziness. Will you see someone?"
"A doctor? For this?"
"Yes. For this. I'll book it with you now. Tomorrow evening."
Jeevan was quiet. Then: "Okay. Book it."
Vandana booked the appointment while he was on the line and stayed on the call until he ate something.

How long has Jeevan been feeling this way?
Two months.
What was Jeevan feeling when he said he can't feel anything?
Jeevan felt numb, empty and exhausted.
What did Vandana do that helped Jeevan get help?
She noticed the pattern, named it as serious, and booked a doctor's appointment with him right away.
How might Amma feel when she hears Jeevan is seeing a doctor?
Amma is probably relieved and hopeful that Jeevan will get help.

metadata.subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help

messages.content:
Okay, three things I wonder about:
Why does a metal spoon in hot tea get warm?
Could you explain what adhesion means?

1. Heat travels along the metal from the tea to your hand. Because metal is a good conductor, its particles pass heat on very quickly.
2. Adhesion means the sticking of one thing to another. It is a noun.

Read this:

Half past eleven at night, and the phone buzzed on the shelf among the rice sacks in the family shop near Kolhapur where Pranav worked from home while on call. Payments were failing. Every minute, someone at a counter is failing to pay, he thought. I don't need the reason yet. The release went out two hours ago; rolling it back takes five minutes, and I know how. Hunting the bug could take hours. He typed the rollback, watched the dashboard, and saw the failures thin out and stop. Then he wrote in the team channel, 'Rolled back the latest release, payments recovering, will look at the cause in daylight,' and asked Charu, who owned that release, to check the logs when she woke.

What did Pranav roll back?
Pranav rolled back the release that had gone out two hours earlier.
What was Pranav worried about when he chose to act before finding the cause?
Pranav was worried that every minute someone at a counter failed to pay, which pushed him to stop the damage first.
What could Pranav do if the rollback had not fixed the payments?
Pranav could ask a second person to investigate while he keeps watching the dashboard, so diagnosis carries on with shared work.
How might Charu see the rollback of the release?
Charu might feel a little disappointed, but also relieved that customers recovered and the cause can be checked calmly in daylight.

Make this politer, please.

You are late again. Come on time.
You are late again. Could you please come on time?

Read this:

Playschool note, Grandparents' Day. Written by Zainab Ma'am.

Vikas, four, was thrilled when his Nana arrived. He pushed the bigger half of his laddoo into Nana's mouth, laughing. Then Pooja's cousin, visiting for the day, came and stood next to him, looking at the box. Vikas pulled the box close and turned his back. When I asked if she could have one, he whispered, "She's not my family." At last, with Nana nodding, he held out the smallest piece.

What I did next: I sat them together for the clay game, so they would not be strangers.

Who did Vikas give the bigger half of his laddoo to?
He gave it to his Nana.
Why did Vikas whisper 'She's not my family'?
He felt close and generous with his Nana but unsure and less willing to share with a child he did not know.
How did the teacher help, and why might it work?
She sat the two children together for the clay game so they could get to know each other, which could make sharing feel easier next time.
How might Pooja's cousin feel when Vikas turns his back?
The visiting child might feel left out and shy, standing near a box of sweets in a place where she knows almost no one.
Now you try: if a number is divisible by 10, must it be divisible by 5? By 4?
The answer is By 5, yes. By 4, no: 30 is divisible by 10 but not by 4.

- What is wrong with this sentence? "My sister is more intelligent from me."
- Meaning of perturbation, please.

1. Correct form: My sister is more intelligent than me. Why: we use "than" after a comparative.
2. As a noun, "perturbation" means a state of worry or disturbance.
What story does Father Mapple preach about in the whalemen's chapel?
He preaches about Jonah, who tried to run away from God and was swallowed by a great fish. He climbs into the high pulpit by a ship's side ladder and then pulls it up after him.

Read this:

Himani, when your Papa called you too sensitive yesterday, I saw your face close like a door. When your Jyoti Nani was ten, in Jabalpur, I cried at everything: a dead kitten, a sad song, a scolding meant for my brother. My father would say, 'Too sensitive. Stop it.' So I stopped, on the outside. I cried only in the cowshed, where no one looked. Then our new teacher, Mrs. Joseph, found me there after a bad day. She didn't laugh. She said, 'Of course it hurt. Your feelings make sense.' She gave me a small notebook. 'When it's big, write it here, breathe out slowly, and come and find me if you want.' I filled nine notebooks, Himani. And I went back to showing my face.

Where did young Jyoti go to cry?
To the cowshed.
How did young Jyoti feel when her father said 'Too sensitive. Stop it'?
She felt hurt and ashamed, so she hid her feelings on the outside.
What choice by Mrs. Joseph changed things for Jyoti?
Finding her in the cowshed, saying her feelings made sense, and giving her a notebook and slow breathing to cope.
How might Mrs. Joseph have felt finding Jyoti in the cowshed?
Mrs. Joseph was probably concerned and tender, seeing a child hiding her tears alone.

Read this:

On the first cold morning of winter, Zubin, five, and his friend Madhav played ludo on the colony steps.
Madhav rolled a six. Zubin grabbed the dice. "My turn!"
"No, it's mine," Madhav said.
Zubin's face scrunched. He wanted to argue. Then he handed the dice back. "Okay. Then me."
Madhav won. Zubin kicked a pebble, then said, "Again? I'll win this time."

What game were they playing?
Ludo, on the colony steps.
How did Zubin feel when Madhav won?
He felt disappointed and a bit cross, kicking a pebble, but still wanted to play again.
How can a parent support Zubin's fair play?
Praise him for giving back the dice and for playing again after losing.
How might Madhav feel when Zubin hands back the dice?
Madhav may feel relieved and happy to keep playing fairly.

Read this:

At the city hospital where Yamini worked as a junior engineer, patients waited hours at the pharmacy. She had an idea: a simple token display and text alerts.
Her first version was a spreadsheet on a monitor. The pharmacist, Ojas, laughed. "Nice, but who updates it when we're busy?"
Yamini went back. She watched the pharmacy for a full day, noting every step. She saw the pharmacists had no free hands, so she built a foot pedal to move the queue.
The second version cut waiting time noticeably. Other departments asked for it. Yamini wrote a manual and trained the staff to maintain it without her.
Ojas stopped laughing. He asked her to help redesign the store room next.

What did Yamini build for the pharmacists to move the queue?
A foot pedal.
How might Yamini have felt when Ojas laughed at the first version?
She may have felt embarrassed but challenged, which pushed her to study the pharmacy more closely.
What made Yamini's system work in real life?
Watching the real workflow, designing around busy hands, and training staff to maintain it without her.
How does Ojas's view change?
Ojas goes from laughing at the idea to trusting Yamini enough to ask for more help.
Here is a big triangle and a small triangle. Are they both triangles?

Answer: Yes. Size does not change the name of a shape.

Count sides and corners on both: 3 and 3.

Read this:

At the village temple festival, the drums were so loud Shankar could feel them in his teeth. He stood at the edge of the crowd with his cousin Lokesh, arms folded.
'You used to carry the lamp,' Lokesh said.
'I used to be terrified,' Shankar said. 'Remember Periyappa telling us that if we missed a single festival, the crops would fail and it would be our fault? I was nine. I lay awake over it.'
His voice came out sharper than he meant. A woman in front turned round.
'So now you're angry,' Lokesh said, not unkindly.
'Now I don't know what I am. Angry, mostly. Some days just empty.' Shankar watched the chariot lurch forward. 'Everyone expects me to either come back or announce I'm done. I can't do either yet.'
Lokesh handed him a cup of panakam and didn't argue.

What did Periyappa say would happen if they missed a festival?
He said the crops would fail and it would be their fault.
What does Shankar's sharp voice reveal?
It reveals anger at having been frightened as a child, still raw enough to spill out louder than he meant.
Why is it wise that Shankar doesn't force a decision yet?
Anger and emptiness are part of honest questioning; announcing a return or an exit just to end them wouldn't work, so giving himself time is more truthful.
How does Lokesh respond to his cousin's anger?
Lokesh listens without arguing and offers panakam, showing acceptance of Shankar's feelings without needing to share them.

Read this:

Dear Diary,
Winter camp, day 2.

Today we got teams for the camp quiz. My team has Santosh and a boy called Nirav.

Nirav is quiet and has thick glasses and reads all the time. I thought YES, he'll know everything. Santosh never stops talking and jumps around. I thought, oh no.

Then the quiz started. Nirav didn't know the capital of Australia. Santosh knew almost everything! Planets, cricket scores, old kings. He got us seven points alone.

At dinner I told Santosh I thought he'd be bad. He laughed and said everyone thinks that because he's loud.

I felt bad. I only looked at their faces and decided.

Tomorrow is the treasure hunt. I'm not guessing anymore.

Gautam

How many points did Santosh get the team?
He got us seven points alone.
How did Gautam feel after telling Santosh about the wrong guess?
Gautam felt bad and a little ashamed, realising the judgement came only from how the boys looked and acted.
What could Gautam do at the treasure hunt instead of guessing?
Gautam could wait to see what each teammate actually knows or can do before deciding who is good at what.
How does Santosh seem to feel about being misjudged?
Santosh laughs it off, but he seems used to it, which suggests it has happened often and may sometimes sting.
Who killed Charles McCarthy in The Boscombe Valley Mystery?
John Turner, a dying landowner whom McCarthy had blackmailed for years. Holmes keeps Turner's signed confession private unless it is needed to save McCarthy's son.

Sana washed 13 cups and 20 plates. How many things did she wash?
And one more: Why do farmers want rain in the season for planting?
One more thing. Meaning of "curtain"?

1. It is 33. Because 13 + 20 = 33.
2. Seeds need water to sprout. Because rain gives the soil the water that plants use to grow.
3. A curtain is a piece of cloth that hangs over a window or door.
Please revert back to me by evening. Is that the right phrase?

Please reply to me by evening.
Why: "Revert back" is Indian English; "reply" or "get back to me" is standard.

Read this:

Week one: Tanuja Ma'am noticed that Rafiq, who usually cracked jokes from the back row, had moved to a front corner and sat with his hood up. When a classmate teased him about his handwriting, he flushed and walked out. She let it go in class and later, privately, said, "You don't have to explain. I'm around if you want to talk."
Week three: Rafiq was eating lunch alone in the library. He answered her greeting with a shrug. She gave him a quiet job sorting books and didn't push.
Week five: The heaviness hadn't lifted. In an essay he wrote, "Everything feels grey and pointless lately." That same afternoon Tanuja gently asked if he would be okay with her talking to his parents and the school counsellor, Mr Thomas. He nodded. The counsellor saw Rafiq before home time, and Tanuja called his mother that evening.

Where was Rafiq eating lunch in week three?
Alone in the library.
What was Tanuja feeling when she read Rafiq's essay line?
She felt concerned, seeing that his sadness had lasted for weeks and was turning into hopelessness.
Which choice in week five mattered most, and why?
Gently involving his parents and the counsellor that same day, because lasting sadness and hopelessness need more than patience alone.
How might Tanuja's quiet approach have felt to Rafiq?
Probably safe and respectful; she gave him privacy and small tasks instead of pushing, so he could agree when she asked to involve others.

Read this:

Chetan,
I'm writing because saying it out loud would come out as shouting.
In September you borrowed my camera for your cousin's wedding. "Back by Monday," you said. It's December. When I asked last week, you said it was "at home somewhere", and then I saw it in your photos from the beach trip.
I bought that camera with my first stipend. I lent it because you're my friend, and because when I was new at college you walked me to the bus stand every evening for a month. I trusted that person.
Honestly, I feel stupid. Like everyone else saw this coming except me.
I'm not going to stop lending things to people. But I'll lend smaller things first, and ask for dates in writing. Please return the camera by Sunday.
Pallavi

When did Chetan say the camera would be back?
By Monday.
What does "Honestly, I feel stupid" reveal about Pallavi?
Pallavi feels betrayed and gullible, as if everyone else could have predicted this except Pallavi.
What choice does Pallavi make about trusting people in future?
To keep lending, but smaller things first and with dates in writing, trusting more carefully rather than trusting nobody.
How might Chetan feel reading the line about the bus stand?
Chetan may feel ashamed, reminded that Pallavi's trust grew from Chetan's own earlier kindness, which makes the let-down sharper.

Read this:

For her tenth birthday in Lagos, Ada got a diary with a tiny brass lock and wore the key on a string around her neck. When her mum, Esther, came in to put away laundry, Ada slammed the diary shut. "Mum! Private." She also asked Esther to stop reading her messages on the family tablet.
Esther said, "Fair enough," and started knocking.
Two nights later a storm rattled the windows and the power went out. Ada lay listening to the thunder. At midnight she padded down the dark corridor and stood at her mother's door. "Can you sit with me? Just till I sleep."
Esther sat on the edge of Ada's bed, the diary key clinking on its string as Ada turned over, and stayed until her breathing slowed.

Where did Ada wear the diary key?
On a string around her neck.
What was Ada feeling when she stood at her mother's door at midnight?
She was frightened by the storm and wanted comfort, even though she had been guarding her privacy.
Which of Esther's choices helped Ada feel both independent and safe?
Agreeing to knock and respect the diary, and then sitting with her through the storm without any comment about privacy.
How might Esther see Ada's midnight request after days of 'Private'?
She may feel reassured that Ada still needs her, even as she makes room for Ada's secrets.

metadata.subtype: Wanting privacy but still needing comfort [Actor]

messages.content: He quailed at the sight of the teacher. Please tell me about quailed.

Quailed means felt or showed fear and lost courage. It is a verb, the past tense of quail.
Example: Asha quailed when she saw how deep the water was.
The ratio of boys to girls in a family is 5:7. The total number of children in the family is 180. If the boys are given $3900 to share, how much money does each boy receive?

The total ratio representing the number of children in the family is 5+7 = 12
From the total ratio of children in the family, 5/12 represent the number of boys, meaning that the number of boys in the family is 5/12*180 = 75
If the boys are given $3900 to share, each boy receives $3900/75 = $52
The answer is 52.

Read this:

Elizabeth: Hi Indu Didi! I'm Elizabeth, 2nd year BSc Zoology at your old college. Prof. Kurien gave me your number. I hope that's okay 🙂
Indu: Hi Elizabeth! Of course. What's up?
Elizabeth: I'm really interested in wildlife research. I saw you did an internship at the bird sanctuary. Could I ask how you got it?
Indu: Sure! I emailed them directly with a one-page CV and a short note on why birds.
Elizabeth: that's it?
Indu: and I followed up after 2 weeks when they didn't reply. politely.
Elizabeth: oh. I would've given up
Indu: most people do 😅
Elizabeth: would you look at my note before I send it?
Indu: yes. send it tonight
Elizabeth: thank you so much. really

Who gave Elizabeth Indu's number?
Prof. Kurien.
What was Elizabeth feeling when she typed "I hope that's okay"?
Elizabeth felt nervous and a little shy about messaging a stranger.
What advice did Indu give about getting the internship?
Email directly with a short CV and a note on why, then follow up politely if there's no reply.
How might Indu feel being asked for help?
Indu likely feels happy to help and perhaps pleased to be seen as a mentor.

Read this:

Maria, you're a tired mother, I can see it. Little Zaid is talking like a baby again since his sister came? Listen to your old Nani Dilnaz. I was twenty-four when Samira was born, and your uncle Farhad, who was three and a half, suddenly wanted his bottle back and started saying "me tiny". My mother-in-law said, "Laugh at him, he'll stop." I didn't. I gave him extra cuddles and even let him have milk in the bottle at bedtime. But I kept everything else the same: breakfast at seven, the park at five, bath, story, bed. He needed to know two things, that he was still loved and that his world hadn't fallen apart. In about a month he told me, "I'm the big brother now," and gave the bottle to the baby. So cuddle Zaid. Keep the routine. He'll find his way back.

What did Farhad start saying when Samira was born?
"Me tiny."
Why did Dilnaz refuse to laugh at Farhad, as her mother-in-law suggested?
She believed he needed to feel loved and safe, and mocking would have told him the opposite.
Which choices helped Farhad move forward, and why?
Extra cuddles and the bedtime bottle met his need to be babied, while the steady routine showed his world was still in place, so he could step into being the big brother.
How might Maria feel after hearing this story?
Probably reassured and less worried about Zaid, with a clear plan: cuddle him, keep the routine and give it time. 🤍
Is a hamster a good first pet for a ten-year-old?
Hamsters can be a good first pet because they are small and need little space. They are active at night, though, and they need gentle handling.
Who looks after it, then?
The child can do small jobs like filling the water bottle, but an adult should make sure the pet is fed, the cage is cleaned and its health is checked. A pet is a family commitment.
Can I get one without asking a vet?
You can buy from a reputable pet shop or breeder, but it helps to ask a vet about care. They can tell you about food, housing and how to handle a hamster.

Samara and three of her friends heard alligators spotted on the local river and decided to join a search organized by the wildlife service to capture the animals. After searching the whole day, Samara had seen 20 alligators while her friends had seen an average of 10 alligators each. Calculate the total number of alligators Samara and her friends saw.

Each of Samara's friends saw an average of 10 alligators each, a total of 3*10 = 30 alligators.
Together, Samara and her friends saw 30+20 = 50 alligators.
The answer is 50.

Read this:

In the hostel common room, Sumit slammed his diary shut. "Two more years of this!" he told Vikas Sir, the warden, who was stacking chairs. "Curfew, a fixed timetable, asking permission to go to the market. I want to run my own life now and be somebody."
Vikas Sir did not lecture. "That sounds like a long road," he said. "What's one thing you could own this month?"
Sumit scowled, then muttered, "Planning the Diwali fund for the hostel."
"Good. Bring me a plan by Friday."
Sumit stomped off. On Friday he came back with a page of figures, and for the first time the two years looked like a set of smaller steps.

How many more years does Sumit say he has left in the hostel?
Two more years.
What is Sumit feeling as he slams his diary shut?
Frustrated and impatient. He resents the curfew and permissions and wants to run his own life now.
What small step turned Sumit's impatience into something workable?
Vikas Sir asked what Sumit could own this month, and Sumit chose to plan the hostel Diwali fund and brought a plan by Friday.
How does Vikas Sir seem to see Sumit's outburst?
He treats it as a real feeling of a long wait and does not lecture, instead offering a concrete task that gives Sumit some ownership.
Kindly do the needful and send the form by tomorrow. Is "do the needful" correct?

It is fine in Indian English as written.
Why: "Do the needful" is Indian business English; "please send" is neutral.

Read this:

Lakshmi had the family tablet for twenty minutes before her brother Akash's turn, so she chose a short lesson on types of angles. Sitting cross-legged on the floor of their Chennai flat, she paused after every step. The teacher drew a right angle; Lakshmi drew one in her notebook and wrote '90°'. Pause. An acute angle; she drew a thin one and wrote 'less than 90'. Pause. Then an example: which kind is 135°? Lakshmi wrote 'obtuse' before pressing play, and the video said obtuse. She punched the air. Akash, waiting on the sofa, said, "You're pausing every ten seconds!" "That's how it goes in," Lakshmi said.

What did Lakshmi write for 135°?
She wrote 'obtuse'.
Why did Lakshmi punch the air?
She felt excited and proud that her answer matched the video before it told her 🎉
What would help Lakshmi if the video still moved too fast?
Rewatching a step and copying it again, or writing a short list of angle types to test herself later.
How does Akash see Lakshmi's way of watching?
Akash, waiting for his turn, finds all the pausing slow and a bit annoying.

metadata.subtype: Approach: watching a video explanation and copying the method [Action]

messages.content: In a building, there are a hundred ladies on the first-floor studying. There are three times that many girls at a party being held on the second floor of the building. How many ladies are on the two floors in total?

If there are a hundred ladies in the living room and three times that many girls at the party, there are 3*100=300 girls at the party.
In the building there are 100+300=400 ladies.
The answer is 400.

Read this:

Zeenat, you asked why old Sudha Aunty still keeps a notebook of questions. Let me tell you. The winter I was ten, fog sat on our village for weeks, and I noticed the dew on the spider webs vanished by noon but stayed in the shade of the well. Nobody at school taught that. So every morning I checked three webs, one sunny, one shady, one near the stove smoke, and wrote down when the drops went. My brother Kishan called me mad. Then the science master saw my notebook and lent me his own book on weather. I read it under the quilt by lantern light. That notebook was the first of forty.

How many webs did Sudha check every morning?
She checked three webs, one sunny, one shady, one near the stove smoke.
Why did young Sudha keep checking the webs every morning?
She was curious and fascinated by why the dew lasted longer in the shade, and wanted to find out for herself.
What turning point came when the science master saw Sudha's notebook?
By lending her his own book on weather, he encouraged her to keep investigating, and that notebook became the first of forty.
How did Kishan see his sister's web-checking?
Kishan thought it was mad, probably not understanding why anyone would study dew without being told to.

Read this:

Raghav, you've known me, Ishita, since school, so you know I don't shout at people. You want to know why I apologised to a total stranger on the 8:10 local? It was May, the compartment was packed, and I had someone's elbow in my ribs and sweat running down my back. A woman's bag kept knocking my arm and I just snapped: 'Can you keep your stuff to yourself?' Loudly. Everyone looked. She said sorry, very quietly, and three stations later I felt awful. Now I notice when the heat starts making my chest tight. I drink water before I board, stand near the door if I can, and tell myself, 'It's the crush, not her.' Most bumps I just let go. And that day I found her at the exit and said sorry back.

What did Ishita say to the woman on the train?
'Can you keep your stuff to yourself?'
How did Ishita feel three stations later?
Ishita felt awful and guilty for snapping at someone who was squashed in the same crowd.
What could help Ishita on the next hot, packed ride?
Drinking water before boarding, standing near the door when possible and remembering 'It's the crush, not her' help Ishita let small bumps pass.
What was it like for the woman when Ishita snapped at her?
She was probably embarrassed with everyone looking, since her bag was bumping only because of the crush; she answered with a quiet sorry.

Read this:

I shared an office with Trisha at the charity when she had two decisions in the same week, and I watched how differently she handled them. The first was the colour of the new flyers. She picked blue in two minutes. "If people don't like it, we reprint next month," she said. The second was whether to sign a three-year lease on a new office. That one she slowed right down. She visited twice, asked our accountant Ishita to check the numbers, and called another charity that had rented there. It took her two weeks. I can't say what she was thinking, but she seemed calm both times, just careful in proportion.

How long did Trisha take to decide on the flyer colour?
She picked blue in two minutes.
How did Trisha seem to feel making the two decisions?
She seemed calm both times, relaxed about the flyers and carefully cautious about the lease.
Why was Trisha's different speed for each decision wise?
The flyer colour could be undone cheaply by reprinting, while a three-year lease could not, so she matched her care to the cost of a mistake.
How might Ishita see Trisha's request to check the numbers?
Ishita might see it as a sensible step, glad to be asked before a decision that couldn't easily be undone.
Ravi borrows ₹12,000 at 10% per year simple interest for 9 months. How much interest must he pay?

Answer: 9 months = 9/12 = 3/4 year. SI = 12,000 x 10 x 3/4 / 100 = ₹900.

R is a rate PER YEAR, so the time must be in years. 9 months = 9/12 of a year = 3/4 year. One year's interest is 10% of 12,000 = ₹1,200, and 3/4 of that is ₹900. With the formula: 12,000 x 10 x 3/4 / 100 = 90,000 / 100 = 900. The common mistake is to put T = 9, which gives ₹10,800, far too much for less than a year. Useful facts: 6 months = 1/2 year, 3 months = 1/4 year, 4 months = 1/3 year, 18 months = 1 1/2 years.
Kindly revert back to me by Friday. Is this correct?

Kindly reply to me by Friday.
Why: "revert" means go back; "reply" means answer.

Read this:

Notes on Arohi, Saturday junior batch
For two months Arohi has done the home practice sheet every day, as I asked. This month I noticed her feet were correct but her face was flat, and twice she asked if class could end early. On Thursday she stayed back and said, "I love dancing, but practice every day feels like homework." We made a change together: home practice on Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday, and on the other days she can dance however she likes, to any music, or rest. Today, for the first time in weeks, she was smiling through the adavus, and she asked to show me a few steps she had made up to a film song. I will check in again at the end of the month.
— Nirmala, dance teacher

Which days are home practice now?
Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday.
What did Arohi's flat face and wish to end class early suggest?
They suggested she felt bored and weighed down, with the joy of dancing squeezed out by practice every day.
Why might four practice days work better for Arohi than seven?
Free days bring back choice and play, so dancing feels like hers again, while four days is still enough to keep improving.
How does Nirmala seem to see the change?
Nirmala seems glad to see Arohi smiling again, but plans to check in at the end of the month rather than assume it is fixed.

metadata.subtype: Approach: adjusting when the schedule feels like a burden [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Manoj, when did you last get a checkup?"
"Checkup for what, Aadhya-di? I'm fine."
"Everyone's fine till they aren't. You keep complaining about headaches."
"That's screens."
"Maybe. Maybe not. You don't even have a regular doctor here."
"How do you choose one? The clinic downstairs has a queue till the road."
"Ask around, check if they explain things or just scribble. I switched when mine wouldn't answer questions."
"And then?"
"Then keep a folder. Every report, every prescription. Photo copies too."
"Why?"
"Because last year I needed an old blood test and spent a week hunting."
"Fine. I'll book something. But you're coming with me."
"Deal. Bring the folder."

Why did Aadhya switch doctors?
Aadhya switched because the old doctor would not answer questions.
How does Manoj feel about getting a checkup at first?
Manoj feels unconcerned and a little dismissive, brushing it off with "I'm fine" and blaming the headaches on screens.
What habit from Aadhya would help Manoj most?
Keeping one folder with all reports and prescriptions, with copies, so records are easy to find later.
What might Aadhya be worried about?
Aadhya may worry that Manoj's repeated headaches are being ignored and wants a doctor to look at them.

Hemant's diary, 12 Nov, night.
Papa said sorry today. Eleven years late, at Jahnavi's engagement, next to the sweets counter, like it was a small thing. "I was wrong to throw your books out. I was wrong about a lot."
I wanted to feel happy. Everyone around us was smiling. Instead my ears went hot and I walked out to the parking lot and kicked a tyre. Who apologises next to the gulab jamuns??
Jahnavi found me there. She didn't say calm down. She just stood with me.
Okay. Writing it out. He did say the words, and his voice cracked, so maybe some of it was real. I don't have to decide tonight. He said he'd come to my flat on Sunday to help fix the shelf. If he actually comes, that will mean more than the sorry.
Still angry. That's allowed.

Where was Papa standing when he apologised?
Next to the sweets counter at Jahnavi's engagement.
Why did Hemant walk out to the parking lot?
Hemant felt a rush of anger instead of happiness, ears hot, because the apology came eleven years late and so casually in a crowd.
What will show Hemant whether Papa's apology was sincere?
Whether Papa actually comes on Sunday to help fix the shelf; steady actions will mean more than the words.
How might Papa feel after Hemant walks out?
Papa may feel ashamed and worried the apology failed, though his cracked voice suggests he meant it; Sunday is his chance to show it.

I'm Parveen, and I teach Class 4. This term I've been watching Farhan.
He follows me from the classroom to the staff room door. At recess he stands near the duty teacher instead of playing. He asks, "Ma'am, is my work okay?" four or five times a lesson, even when it's neat.
A colleague said, "He just wants attention." Maybe. But his hands twist his shirt while he waits for my answer, and he looks relieved each time I nod. I can't know what is going on inside him, but it doesn't look like a game.
So I've started saying, "Good morning, Farhan," warmly every day, and giving him small jobs he does alone: taking the register to the office, then watering the plants. Yesterday he did the plants and came back smiling, without asking once if it was okay.

What small jobs does Parveen give Farhan?
Taking the register to the office and watering the plants.
What does Parveen feel about the colleague's "attention" comment?
Parveen feels unsure and concerned rather than convinced, seeing Farhan's twisting hands and relief and thinking it doesn't look like a game.
Why might the warm greeting and solo jobs help more than ignoring Farhan?
They give him steady warmth he can count on while letting him practise small bits of independence, so he needs fewer reassurances.
What might watering the plants alone be like for Farhan?
He may feel proud and a little braver doing it by himself, which fits him coming back smiling without asking if it was okay.

Olga had taught the first-year sociology seminar in Krakow for eleven years, and she kept a little notebook on how her students argued. Tuan, a quiet exchange student, filled three pages. On Tuesday his essay on refugee law was brilliant: rules as agreements that protect human dignity, and how to change them fairly. On Thursday, in a group project she was supervising, he refused to let a teammate hand in late because of a sick grandmother. 'The deadline is the deadline. Otherwise everyone asks.' And at Friday's department football, he hid the ball behind his back when the other team wanted it, grinning: 'Buy me a coffee first.' Olga smiled and underlined one word in the notebook: situations. Then she rubbed out the stage number she had pencilled next to his name.

What was Tuan's Tuesday essay about?
Refugee law: rules as agreements that protect human dignity, and how to change them fairly.
Why did Olga smile and rub out the stage number?
Olga felt amused and newly sure that reasoning shifts with situations, so labelling Tuan with one number felt wrong.
How could Olga use her notebook without turning it into a ranking?
She could share patterns with students as a way to notice their own reasoning, not as grades or verdicts on who is a better person.
How might the teammate with the sick grandmother see Tuan?
The teammate may see Tuan as rigid and unkind that day, without knowing how thoughtfully he writes about dignity elsewhere.
