messages.content: One rangoli design uses 250 grams of colour powder. How many designs can be made from 2 kilograms?
Eight designs can be made. Because 2 kilograms is 2,000 grams, and 2,000 divided by 250 is 8.

Counsellor's note, Monday. Indu asked to see me privately. She had seen her close friend Payal send unkind messages about a new girl to a group chat. Indu felt torn: Payal is her friend, and she did not want to be the one who told. That afternoon, on the way to the bus, she spoke to Payal first. Payal called it a joke.
On Thursday Indu came back. The messages had continued and the new girl had stopped coming to lunch. Indu said, "Being loyal to Payal can't mean staying quiet about this." She gave me the dates and what she had seen.
I thanked her, then spoke with the new girl's family and with Payal separately, without naming Indu. I will follow up with both girls next week.
Mr. Bose

Where did Indu speak to Payal?
She spoke to Payal on the way to the bus.
Why did Indu feel torn?
Payal is her friend and she did not want to be the one who told, yet the messages were hurting the new girl.
What order of steps worked for Indu, and what could she do if things continue?
She talked to Payal first and, when the harm continued, told a trusted adult with dates; she could keep checking on the new girl.
How might the new girl have experienced the messages?
She stopped coming to lunch, which suggests she felt hurt and wanted to avoid other students.

The Dussehra week the new timetable came out, I almost signed it without reading, like always. I'm a scheduler at the city bus depot, and ninety-nine times out of a hundred, the rule is the rule and I follow it. But route 47's last bus, the 11:15 past the nurses' hostel, had been cut to save fuel. I thought of the nurses finishing late shifts and walking that dark road.
So I did it properly. I wrote to the depot committee with the ridership numbers and the night-shift timings, and asked for a hearing. Arohi from planning helped me with the figures.
The committee listened, and still kept the cut. They added a hospital shuttle till midnight instead. It wasn't what I asked for. But they heard it, and gave reasons. I signed. Ojas the troublemaker, they call me now, but kindly.

What time was route 47's last bus?
The 11:15, past the nurses' hostel.
How did Ojas feel about the committee's final decision?
Ojas felt disappointed that the cut stayed but respected the fair hearing and the reasons, so accepted it and signed.
Which choices made Ojas's objection work within the system?
Writing to the committee with ridership numbers and shift timings, asking for a hearing, and then accepting the outcome of that process.
How might the nurses on late shifts see the hospital shuttle?
They might feel relieved to have a safe ride till midnight, even though the bus itself was cut.

The lift doors were closing when the director asked, "Who came up with the churn analysis?" Nikita opened her mouth. Tanuja had built the model over two weekends, and Nikita had only made the slides. For a second the word "I" sat ready on her tongue, because promotion talks were next month. "Tanuja built the model. I turned it into slides," she said instead, holding the door. The director looked at them both. "Good. Put both names on the summary." Nikita's heart was pounding, half regret and half relief. In the lift she told herself it had cost her nothing yet, and knew that was not quite true.

Who built the churn analysis model?
Tanuja built the model over two weekends.
What was Nikita tempted to do, and what was on her mind?
She felt torn, tempted to say "I" and take the credit because promotion talks were next month.
Why does naming who did what matter for the team later?
It builds trust, and the director asked for both names on the summary, so both people are recognised. 🙂
How might Tanuja have felt hearing Nikita's answer?
Tanuja probably felt relieved and valued, since the real work was named instead of being passed off.

Saturday
Hrithik bhaiya and Arush bhaiya were playing cricket on the terrace again. I asked to play. Hrithik said, "You can be the fielder who fetches the ball." That's not playing! That's being a servant!
Then they made a secret club with a password and wouldn't tell me. Arush said I'm too small to understand.
I told Mamma it was unfair. She said, "Teju, they're older, let them be." Nobody listens to me because I'm the youngest girl. I can bowl better than Arush, actually. I just want them to say, "Teju, you're good, come play properly."
Tejaswini

What job did Hrithik offer Teju in the cricket game?
He offered her the job of fielder who fetches the ball.
What does Teju really want from her brothers?
She wants them to take her seriously and admire her, like saying she's good and letting her play properly, not just tolerate her.
How could Mamma respond at this stage?
She could listen to Teju's feelings and gently ask the brothers to give her a real turn, instead of saying "let them be."
What would change if the brothers let Teju bowl?
Teju would feel included and respected, and the brothers might discover she really can bowl well. 🙂

Read this:

First weekend. Lalit told Jyoti again how his cousin had lied to the family about the land and got their grandmother's house. Jyoti said, "You should just forgive him and move on, yaar." Lalit's face shut like a door. He changed the subject.
Second weekend. The story came back, angrier. This time Jyoti bit her tongue. She let him talk for forty minutes without offering a single solution. She nodded, asked what he'd felt when he found out, and let the silence sit.
Third weekend. Lalit told it once more, but shorter. When he finished, Jyoti asked gently, "What do you actually want now? Not from him. For yourself."
Lalit stared at his tea. "I want to stop feeling like a fool every time I pass that street. Maybe I want to talk to Dadi about it, just once."
Jyoti felt a small relief. For the first time in weeks, he was talking about what came next.

What did Lalit's cousin get?
Their grandmother's house.
What did Jyoti feel when Lalit started talking about what came next?
Jyoti felt a small relief, seeing Lalit finally look forward instead of only back.
Why did listening first work better than 'forgive and move on'?
Being fully heard made Lalit feel respected, so a gentle question about what he wants could open a way forward.
How did Lalit experience Jyoti's first advice?
He felt dismissed, his face shutting like a door as he changed the subject.

metadata.subtype: Stage 4: Seeing the other as human [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Tushar, and I first really noticed my mother, Ganga, when I was fifteen and found her at midnight hemming other people's blouses again. She'd done it for years so I could stay in school, and I'd never once asked how her shoulders felt. That night I said thank you, badly, and she waved it away. I felt warm and heavy at once. I told myself I would become an engineer, earn a lot, and pay it all back. Then one evening, sketching buildings in my notebook, I realised I didn't want to be an engineer; I wanted to be an architect. When I said so, she stopped sewing. "I didn't work for your life to belong to me," she said. Now I cook dinner twice a week and keep drawing.

What was Ganga doing at midnight when Tushar noticed her?
Hemming other people's blouses.
What two feelings did Tushar have after thanking Ganga?
Warmth and heaviness, meaning gratitude together with the pressure to succeed and repay her.
What did Tushar do that was fair to Ganga and to Tushar too?
Tushar said thanks and took on a real responsibility by cooking dinner twice a week, but kept drawing instead of giving up the architect dream to repay her.
How does Ganga see what she has done for Tushar?
As a gift, not a debt. She stopped sewing and said she didn't work for Tushar's life to belong to her.

It was 7:50 on a Friday, the office was empty, and the power kept flickering. Swati, the firm's only IT person, had been asked to make the shared printer work before Monday's client presentation.
The printer wouldn't accept jobs from the new laptops. The proper fix meant updating the network settings, which needed an hour and steady power. Swati had neither. So she connected the printer straight to the reception computer and told everyone to send files there. On a sticky note she wrote, "Temporary. Fix next week."
Next week was busy. So was the next month.
Eight months later, Deepak, the new accounts clerk, stood at reception with a USB stick and a queue of three people behind him. "Why do we all have to print through this one computer?" he asked. The receptionist shrugged. "It's always been like this."
Swati, passing by, saw the yellow note, faded now, still stuck on the monitor. Her ears burned.

What did Swati write on the sticky note?
"Temporary. Fix next week."
How did Swati feel when she saw the faded note?
Swati felt ashamed and embarrassed; her ears burned at the sight of her eight-month-old "temporary" fix.
What could Swati have done on Monday to stop the patch becoming permanent?
Swati could have booked a fixed time that week for the proper network fix and told her manager, instead of leaving it on a sticky note.
How does Deepak see the printing setup?
Deepak finds it frustrating and strange, queuing with a USB stick and not understanding why everyone prints through one computer.

Financial literacy counsellor's note, community centre, Saturday. Written by Noor.
Jeevan came in today with a printout. A colleague had offered him a place in an "exclusive gold trading scheme": guaranteed twelve percent a month, entry closing Monday, and "don't share this with too many people."
What impressed me was what he had already done. He hadn't paid anything. He had searched the scheme's name on the official regulator's website: not registered. He had asked the colleague for a company registration number: no answer.
He said, "It sounded too good, and too fast, and too quiet. So I wanted someone independent to look." I confirmed his findings and explained that real investments always carry some risk and aren't sold with secrecy.
He decided not to invest, and he's going to tell the colleague why, gently, in case the colleague has put in money too. We also reported the scheme to the cyber police together.

What return did the gold trading scheme guarantee?
Guaranteed twelve percent a month.
How did Jeevan seem to feel about the offer?
Jeevan seemed cautious and uneasy, sensing it was too good, too fast and too quiet.
What checks had Jeevan already done?
He searched the scheme on the official regulator's website, asked for a registration number, and came to an independent counsellor before paying.
How might the colleague feel when Jeevan explains?
The colleague might feel surprised or defensive, and possibly worried if they have already put in money.
Light travels at 3 x 10^8 m/s and the Sun is 1.5 x 10^1^1 m away. How long does sunlight take to reach us? A calculator shows 2.5E-7: what does it mean?

Answer: Time = 1.5 x 10^1^1 / (3 x 10^8) = 0.5 x 10^3 = 5 x 10^2 s = 500 s = 8 min 20 s. 2.5E-7 means 2.5 x 10^-^7 = 0.00000025.

Time = distance / speed. Divide the front numbers: 1.5 / 3 = 0.5, and the powers: 10^1^1 / 10^8 = 10^3. 0.5 x 10^3 = 5 x 10^2 = 500 seconds, and 500 s = 8 x 60 + 20 s = 8 minutes 20 seconds. So we see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago! Calculators show scientific notation with an E (for 'exponent'): 2.5E-7 is 2.5 x 10^-^7 and 6.02E23 is 6.02 x 10^2^3. Do not read 2.5E-7 as 2.5 - 7.

Ankita, you asked on this podcast about being fourteen. Okay, I'm Gautam, and fourteen was a rollercoaster.
One evening I remember clearly. At six I was laughing so hard at a video my little sister sent that I fell off the bed. By six-thirty I was snapping at my mother because she asked if I'd done my homework. By seven I was crying in the bathroom, and I honestly couldn't tell you why.
My mother didn't shout back or say, "What's wrong with you?" She just stayed the same. Calm. Dinner at eight. Lights off by eleven, phones out of rooms. She'd knock and say, "Want to talk, or want tea?"
It drove me mad then. Now I think it saved me. I was sleeping about five hours before that. With proper sleep, the swings got smaller.
And when I did want to talk, she was right there, same as always.

What time did Gautam's mother set for lights off?
Lights off by eleven, phones out of rooms.
What was Gautam feeling that evening at fourteen?
Gautam swung from amused to irritable to tearful within an hour, confused about why the moods changed so fast.
What helped Gautam's mood swings settle?
The mother's calm, consistent routine, proper sleep, and her gentle, repeated offers to talk or have tea.
How might Gautam's mother have felt during those evenings?
She was probably worried and sometimes hurt by Gautam's snapping, but chose to stay steady rather than react.
Jean has three times as much money as Jane. They have a combined total of $76. How much money does Jean have?

Let's assume the total amount of money that Jane has is m.
Since Jean has 3 times as much money as Jane, he has 3*m=3m
Combined, Jean and Jane have a total of m+3m = $76
This evaluates to 4m=$76
The total amount of money that Jane has, represented by m, is m=$76/4
Jane has m=$19
Since Jean has three times as much money as Jane, Jean has 3*$19=$57
The answer is 57.

In their flat in Leeds, Zeynep lay stiff under the duvet. 'Baba, what if there's a monster under the bed? What if it comes when you're asleep?' Yosef didn't say, 'Monsters aren't real.' Last week that had only made her cry. Instead he knelt, lifted the edge of the sheet and shone the torch. 'Just your slippers and a sock.' Then the usual: two pages of the whale book, night light on, door open a hand's width. 'I'll peek in when the clock chimes nine.' Zeynep turned on her side. At nine he peeked. She was asleep.

What did Yosef find under the bed?
Just her slippers and a sock.
What was Zeynep feeling as she lay stiff under the duvet?
She was frightened, worried that a monster might come while her father slept.
Why did Yosef's approach work better than last week's?
Checking with the torch and keeping the same bedtime steps calmed her, while 'Monsters aren't real' had only made her cry.
What might these bedtimes be like for Yosef?
He may feel tired or worried himself, but he stays patient and keeps to the routine because he knows it helps.
Begin this sentence with "Because": We stayed home because it was raining.
Because it was raining, we stayed home.

In the village near Namchi, Tenzin, fifteen, was cooking dinner for the first time while his mother was at the monastery. His cousin Ankita watched from the doorway. Before touching anything, Tenzin washed his hands with soap at the tap outside. He cut the raw chicken on one board and the vegetables on another, then washed the knife. When the oil in the wok began to shimmer, he lowered the chicken in slowly, away from himself. Ankita's phone rang; she handed it to him. "Aunty wants you." Tenzin turned the gas off first, then took the call. "Why'd you switch it off?" Ankita asked. "Amma says the stove never stays alone. Not even for a minute."

Where was Tenzin's mother?
At the monastery.
How might Tenzin have felt cooking dinner alone for the first time?
He probably felt a little nervous but careful and responsible, following each safe habit.
Which of Tenzin's habits made his cooking safe?
Washing his hands, using separate boards for raw chicken and vegetables, lowering food into hot oil carefully and turning off the gas before taking the call.
How does Ankita see Tenzin switching off the gas?
Ankita is puzzled at first, not seeing why he would turn it off for a short call.

The movie theater sells matinee tickets for $5, evening tickets for $12, and 3D tickets for $20. If they sell 200 matinee tickets, 300 evening tickets and 100 3D tickets, how much money do they make in total?

First find the total revenue from the matinee tickets: $5/ticket * 200 tickets = $1000
Then find the total revenue from the evening tickets: $12/ticket * 300 tickets = $3600
Then find the total revenue from the 3D tickets: $20/ticket * 100 tickets = $2000
Then add the cost of each group of tickets to find the total cost: $1000 + $3600 + $2000 = $6600
The answer is 6600.

Wasim's first project as lead had a tight start: the client wanted kickoff on Monday, and two of his five team members were still finishing another release. He had one hour on Friday evening with everyone in the room, pizza going cold.
He handed out paper. "Quick exercise. It's six months from now. This project has failed badly. Write why."
Jaya, the tester, wrote first. Others followed. Wasim read them aloud. Four out of five said some version of "requirements kept changing". Three said, "Jaya left and nobody could test the integrations."
Jaya looked up. "I'm not planning to leave."
"I know," Wasim said. "But if you're sick for a month, same problem."
So before Monday he emailed the client asking for a signed requirements list and a weekly change review. And he booked Jaya to spend two hours a week teaching Rohan the integration tests.
The pizza was cold, but the plan was warmer.

How many team members said requirements kept changing?
Four out of five said so.
How did Jaya feel when her name came up as a risk?
Jaya felt a little surprised and defensive, saying she wasn't planning to leave.
What else could Wasim do to guard against other risks from the exercise?
He could revisit the list at the end of each month, adding new risks and checking the safeguards still work.
How might the client see Wasim's request for a signed requirements list?
The client may find it a bit formal at first, but likely appreciates clear agreement and fewer surprises later.

messages.content:
My friend and I had a small fight. How do I say sorry?
Ali has 4 marbles and a friend gives 15 more. How many marbles does Ali have now?

1. Say it plainly and kindly, like "I'm sorry I shouted." Then listen to how your friend feels.
2. 19 marbles. Because 4 + 15 = 19.

Monday: at the parent-teacher meeting, Ramesh Sir read the report card aloud: 'Jatin: weak in maths.' Jatin's mother nodded quietly. That afternoon in oral tables, Sir went down the row and jumped straight past Jatin to the next boy.
Following Monday: Sir asked, 'Seven eights?' Jatin knew it, fifty-six, he had practised with Nani. He half-lifted his hand. Sir was already looking at the front bench. 'Yes, Kunal?' Jatin put his hand back under the desk.
A month later: his cousin asked him to help with a sum. Jatin shook his head. 'Don't ask me. I'm the maths-weak one.' He said it lightly, like a joke. That evening he didn't open his maths notebook, even though there was homework. 'What's the point,' he said to nobody, and went outside to play.

What did Ramesh Sir read from Jatin's report card?
He read, 'Jatin: weak in maths.'
How might Jatin have felt when he put his hand back under the desk?
He probably felt ignored and discouraged, since he knew the answer but Sir was already looking at the front bench.
What small change could Ramesh Sir make in class?
Sir could include Jatin in oral tables and wait a moment for his half-raised hand, giving him the same chances as the front bench.
How might Jatin's cousin see him saying 'I'm the maths-weak one'?
The cousin might believe it too, not knowing Jatin practised with Nani and knew seven eights.

metadata.subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Ward note, 7 p.m. — Jagdish, staff nurse, children's ward
Ishu, 5, needed his drip line changed. His mother, Preeti, stood close, stroking his hair and saying, "Oh no, baby, it's going to hurt, I'm so sorry," in a shaking voice. Ishu screamed before I had touched his arm. I asked Preeti to sit at the head of the bed and tell him about his new school bag. I spoke slowly: "Ishu, you'll feel a small pinch, then it's done. Squeeze Mummy's finger." He cried, but less, and stopped soon after. Preeti looked stunned. Later she told me she hadn't realised how much of her fear was passing to him. I showed her how to hold his hand steadily. Reminder for the team: our tone is part of the treatment.

What did Jagdish ask Preeti to talk about?
Ishu's new school bag.
What did Preeti realise afterwards?
She hadn't realised how much of her own fear was passing to Ishu; her shaking voice had made him expect pain and scream before he was touched.
Which choices helped Ishu through the drip change?
Jagdish spoke slowly and honestly about a small pinch, gave Ishu Mummy's finger to squeeze, and moved Preeti to the head of the bed with a calm topic.
What is the drip change like for Ishu when his mother is frightened?
For Ishu, his mother's fear is a signal that something terrible is coming, so he screams before anything happens; once the voices are calm, the same pinch is easier to bear. 🤍

Give a summary that a five-year-old could follow.

It was all very well to say "Drink me," but the wise little Alice was not going to do that in a hurry. "No, I'll look first," she said, "and see whether it's marked 'poison' or not"; for she had read several nice little histories about children who had got burnt, and eaten up by wild beasts and other unpleasant things, all because they would not remember the simple rules their friends had taught them: such as, that a red-hot poker will burn you if you hold it too long; and that if you cut your finger very deeply with a knife, it usually bleeds; and she had never forgotten that, if you drink much from a bottle marked "poison," it is almost certain to disagree with you, sooner or later.
Alice finds a bottle that says "Drink me," but she does not drink it straight away. First she checks for a "poison" label, because she remembers stories about children who forgot simple safety rules.

Monsoon term note, KG-B. Hafsa, class teacher.
Rainy days keep us indoors, so this month I watched myself as much as the children. Since the first week I have thought of Jagdish as "the bright one". I give him the puzzle first, smile when he answers, and wait longer for him. He now raises his hand for everything and tells his friends, "I can do hard ones."
But a quiet girl in the corner, whom I rarely wait for, has stopped trying.
Next step: every child gets a turn with the hard puzzle this week, and I will count to five before moving on, for everyone.

What does Jagdish now tell his friends?
"I can do hard ones."
What does Jagdish's hand-raising suggest about how he feels?
He feels confident and valued, because the teacher's warmth and patience make trying feel worth it.
Why is counting to five for everyone a good next step?
It gives each child the same waiting time, so the quiet girl also gets a real chance to answer.
What might the quiet girl in the corner be feeling?
She may feel overlooked and discouraged, so she has stopped trying.

Last Sunday, Logan went to church and realized that the number of children present was 80. If there were 60 male adults, and the total number of people in the church was 200, how many female adults were present?

The total number of male adults and children is 80+60 = 140 people.
The number of females is 200-140 = 60 female adults.
The answer is 60.

Read this:

Amandeep, you're afraid to speak at tomorrow's meeting because you might stumble? Sit with your Farida Aapa for a minute. When I was a young woman, in my first job at the bank in Aligarh, I stayed silent in every Monday meeting for six months. I was sure that if I said one wrong number, the whole branch would remember it for years. Then one evening I asked myself a strange question: what do I remember of other people's mistakes in those meetings? I tried hard. Nothing. Not one. I couldn't even remember who had mixed up the dates the week before, and I had been sitting right there. Everyone was busy with their own worries, just like me. So I gave myself permission to be a little wrong. The next Monday I spoke. My voice shook. Nobody noticed. By Tuesday nobody remembered.

How long did Farida Aapa stay silent in the Monday meetings?
For six months.
What was young Farida feeling during those silent months?
She felt anxious and self-conscious, sure one wrong number would be remembered by the whole branch for years.
Which moment in the story changed things for young Farida?
Asking herself what she remembered of others' mistakes and finding nothing, which let her give herself permission to speak imperfectly.
How did the others at the meeting respond when young Farida finally spoke?
Nobody noticed her shaking voice, and by Tuesday nobody remembered, because they were busy with their own worries.

On the school bus in Mumbai, Pranav began copying the driver's habit of saying, “Sit, sit, sit down now,” in a deep, comic voice. Vidya, next to him, giggled. Then Pranav did the same to the conductor, who was walking down the aisle, and the conductor turned around slowly. Pranav stopped. Vidya stopped smiling, too. The conductor said nothing. He just looked, then smiled a little and shook his head. Vidya whispered, “That was a bit much.” Pranav's ears were hot. “I was only playing,” he said. “Maybe check if he's laughing first,” said Vidya.

Whose voice did Pranav copy first?
The driver's.
Why did Pranav say he was only playing, and what else might his hot ears suggest?
He meant it as fun, but hot ears suggest he also felt embarrassed once the conductor turned around.
What could Pranav try next time he wants to imitate someone?
He could look to see whether the other person is laughing too, as Vidya suggested, before continuing.

messages.content: William read 6 books last month and Brad read thrice as many books as William did. This month, in an effort to catch up, Williams read twice as much as Brad, who read 8 books. Who has read more across the two months, and by how much?

Last month Brad read thrice 6 books for a total of 3*6 = 18 books
This month Williams read twice 8 books for a total of 2*8 = 16 books
Across the 2 months Brad has read 18+8 = 26 books
Across the 2 months William has read 6+16 = 22 books
Brad has read 26-22 = 4 more books
The answer is 4.

Seema, you're sulking because your friend walked past without saying hi. Let your Joseph Appachan tell you something. When I was eleven, in Kottayam, my best friend Mathew walked straight past me at the Sunday market. No wave, no smile, nothing. I was furious. I didn't speak to him for three days. On the fourth day I finally marched up and said, “Why did you ignore me?” He blinked. “When? I broke my glasses that week. I couldn't see anyone further than my own hand.” Three days of sulking, for nothing. So now I always look twice, and ask once, before I decide someone meant it.

To fend off something means to defend yourself against it, especially something that is attacking or annoying you.

Questions for today:
Do I say "bring" or "take" when I carry a gift to my friend's house?
How can I keep my bicycle from rusting?
How do I spell "hieght"?
Any idea what "skeleton" means?

1. Say "take", because you are moving it away from where you are. Use "bring" when the thing comes toward the speaker, as in "please bring your book here".
2. Wipe it dry after rain and store it under cover. A little oil on the chain keeps it moving smoothly.

Salaria is growing oranges this summer. She bought two types of trees. She has 50% of tree A and 50% of tree B. Tree A gives her 10 oranges a month and 60% are good. Tree B gives her 15 oranges and 1/3 are good. If she gets 55 good oranges per month, how many total trees does she have?

Each tree A gives her six good oranges a month 10 x .6 = 6
Each tree B gives her five good oranges a month because 15 x (1/3) = 5
On average, a tree gives her 5.5 oranges a month because .5(6) + .5(5) = 5.5
She has ten total trees because 55 / 5.5 = 10
The answer is 10.

Sarah wants to start a cupcake business and was approved for a business loan.  The loan has 0% interest if she pays the entire amount back in 5 years, which she decides to do.  If she put $10,000 down as a down payment and her monthly payments are $600.00, how much was her loan for (including the down payment)?

To avoid interest she'll make payments for 5 years. There are 12 months in 1 year so that's 5*12 = 60 months
Each monthly payment is $600.00 and she'll pay that for 60 months for a total of 600*60 = $36,000
She also put $10,000 down as a down payment and her monthly payments came out to $36,000 so her loan was for 10000+36000 = $46,000
The answer is 46000.
I typed "withdrawl" on the bank slip form. Is that right?

No, the word is "withdrawal", with an "al" ending. The verb is "withdraw" and the noun adds "-al".
Example: Please fill the form to request a withdrawal.

A month after the auto-rickshaw he was riding in skidded into a divider, Irfan still woke at 3 a.m. with his heart racing. Every horn on the road outside made his shoulders jump. He kept his morning routine anyway: tea, a short walk, the office bus at 8:40. At lunch his colleague Pooja noticed he had barely touched his rice. "You keep flinching," she said quietly. "It's been weeks. I should be over it," Irfan muttered. "I didn't tell the driver to slow down. Maybe if I had..." Pooja shook her head. "You were a passenger." She pulled up the number of the hospital's counselling desk on her phone. He looked at it for a long moment, then typed it into his own.

How long after the crash did Irfan still wake at 3 a.m. with his heart racing?
A month after the auto-rickshaw skidded into a divider, he still woke at 3 a.m. with his heart racing.
Why does Irfan say he should be over it?
He seems to think he is failing at recovering and blames himself, wondering whether telling the driver to slow down might have changed things.
What would you advise Irfan to do next?
Keep his daily routine going and actually call the hospital's counselling desk, since trained help suits a body that stays on alert after a scare.
How does Pooja see Irfan's situation?
She sees a colleague who is flinching and not eating, and who is not to blame because he was only a passenger, so she offers a concrete way to get help.

Give three short bullet points for this passage.

Mrs. Bennet was really in a most pitiable state. The very mention of anything concerning the match threw her into an agony of ill-humour, and wherever she went she was sure of hearing it talked of. The sight of Miss Lucas was odious to her. As her successor in that house, she regarded her with jealous abhorrence. Whenever Charlotte came to see them, she concluded her to be anticipating the hour of possession; and whenever she spoke in a low voice to Mr. Collins, was convinced that they were talking of the Longbourn estate, and resolving to turn herself and her daughters out of the house as soon as Mr. Bennet was dead. She complained bitterly of all this to her husband.

- Mrs. Bennet is in agony whenever the match is mentioned.
- She hates Miss Lucas and fears being turned out after Mr. Bennet's death.
- She complains bitterly to her husband.

It had rained all morning, and Nani's small house in the town was packed for the prayer meeting. Wet chappals piled at the door; the fan couldn't cope.
Bhavna squeezed between aunties on the floor. Everyone was silent while the pandit read from a book, and Nani sat very still in a white saree.
Bhavna whispered to her Mama Ujjwal, "Will Nana come back if we pray?"
Ujjwal took a breath. "No, beta. Nana's body stopped working. He won't come back. We pray to remember him and to help us feel less alone."
Bhavna nodded, eyes wet. Twenty minutes later she was under the stairs with her cousin, giggling over a lizard. Then she saw Nana's walking stick by the door and went quiet again.

Where was Bhavna when she was giggling with her cousin?
Under the stairs.
How can you tell Bhavna feels sad in bursts rather than all the time?
Her eyes are wet after Ujjwal's answer, then she giggles over a lizard, then goes quiet again at the sight of Nana's walking stick, showing sadness that comes and goes.
What did Ujjwal do that helped Bhavna understand?
He gave a simple, honest answer that Nana would not come back and explained the prayer is for remembering, instead of confusing her.
What is it like for Nani during the prayer meeting?
Nani sits very still in white, likely deep in grief, while the crowded house and noise go on around her.

Plastic chairs lined the hall above the sweet shop in Bhadrak, and Arohi arrived in her work kurta, straight from the block office where she typed land records. Kamal was already there, telling everyone about his master's in Germany and the flat he rented in Munich. Pooja passed around wedding photos. Rakesh had opened a solar-pump business with twelve employees. Someone asked Arohi, 'Still at the block office?' She said yes and laughed, and the laugh came out thin. She kept her phone face-down on her lap. When the samosas came round she took one and forgot to eat it. On the auto home, past the same paddy fields she had seen every day since school, she counted: no degree abroad, no husband, no business. At twenty-five, her life suddenly looked like a small room she had wandered into by mistake.

Where did Arohi work?
At the block office, where she typed land records.
How can you tell that Arohi felt shaken at the reunion?
Her laugh came out thin, she kept her phone face-down and forgot to eat her samosa, then counted everything she lacked on the way home.
What could help Arohi at this early stage, before the comparison hardens?
Talking it over with someone she trusts, and remembering that a reunion shows only highlights, could stop one evening from deciding how she sees her whole path.
How might Kamal have experienced the same evening?
Kamal probably enjoyed sharing his news and may not have noticed how it landed on Arohi; to him it was catching up, not comparing.

Monday. Samir's father died suddenly, and Kavitha heard from a classmate. She didn't know what to say, so she didn't post anything. She went to his house, left a steel box of lemon rice with his aunt, and said, "Tell him Kavitha came. No need to reply."
Thursday. She messaged Samir: "I've got your lecture notes for this week. Will drop them at the gate at six." She did, and left without ringing the bell.
Three weeks later. Samir came back to college. At lunch, he admitted he'd been skipping meals and feeling "like a ghost". Kavitha listened. Then she said, honestly, "I'm worried about the meals. Can I tell your cousin, or will you?" Samir hesitated. "I'll tell her. Tonight." "Okay. I'll ask you tomorrow if you did." The next day she asked. He had. She passed him half her sandwich anyway.

What did Kavitha leave with Samir's aunt?
A steel box of lemon rice.
What was Samir feeling when he came back to college?
He felt numb and lost, "like a ghost", and was so low he was skipping meals.
What did Kavitha do that showed real care?
She gave time and practical help, followed through, and was honest about her worry, asking Samir to tell his cousin and checking the next day.
What would change if Kavitha had stayed silent about the skipped meals to be loyal?
Samir's cousin might never have known, and his skipping meals could have gone on without support.

Lalit was fifteen when Nazia told him, on the school steps, that home had turned dark and she was barely eating. He felt honoured and scared at once. He did not joke. "Thanks for telling me," he said. "I won't spread it, but I can't promise to keep it from every adult if you're in trouble." She said she might try the counsellor.

Over the next weeks her messages came at midnight, at two, at dawn. Lalit started dreading his phone. Finally he wrote, "I care about you, but I'm wrecked. Can we ask the counsellor to help too, and can I answer in the mornings?"

Meanwhile Chandrika, a class below, kept following him about. "You're my hero," she said. "I tell you everything." Lalit felt proud and squeezed at once. He told her about the maths paper he had failed, and suggested she talk to her older cousin as well.

On Thursday Nazia fell asleep at her desk and skipped lunch again. Lalit's stomach turned over. Before break he messaged her: "I'm going to the counsellor now because I'm worried, and I wanted you to hear it from me." The counsellor listened, told Lalit he had done the right thing, met Nazia that afternoon to tell her it was not her fault, and passed it to the school safeguarding lead before the day ended.

What time did Nazia's messages sometimes arrive?
Her messages came at midnight, at two, and at dawn.
How did Lalit's handling of Nazia's midnight messages differ from his handling of Chandrika calling him her hero?

With Nazia he set a limit on answering and suggested the counsellor as more support. With Chandrika he admitted a failing, the maths paper, and pointed her to her older cousin. Both times he cared but did not become the only support.
What was Lalit feeling when Nazia first confided in him on the steps?
He felt honoured that she trusted him and scared because of how heavy the news was.
What could Lalit do if Nazia is upset with him after he went to the counsellor?
He could stay kind and tell her again he acted because he was worried about her, and keep being available at reasonable times while the counsellor and adults help.

Sunday afternoon in the flat, the pressure cooker hissed in the kitchen, and Ira lay on the sofa in her oldest T-shirt, scrolling. Pema on a beach at sunset. Pema holding a debate trophy. A classmate's perfect cake. Someone's new puppy. Every picture was brighter than Ira's whole week. She looked at her own last post: a blurry photo of rain on the balcony from a month ago. Everyone's going somewhere, she thought, and I'm here with dal. She scrolled faster and felt worse. Then a message popped up from Pema herself: "Trip's been kind of awful tbh 😅 fought with my cousin, got sunburnt, want to come home." Ira read it twice. The sunset photo had gone up two hours ago.

What was Ira's own last post?
A blurry photo of rain on the balcony from a month ago.
What was Ira feeling as she scrolled faster?
She felt dull and left behind, as if everyone else was going somewhere while she was stuck at home with dal.
After Pema's message, what could Ira choose to do with her scrolling?
She could put the phone down, reply kindly to Pema, and remember that the sunset photo hid a bad day.
What might Pema's day look like from Pema's side, compared with the photos?
For Pema it was a fight, sunburn and missing home; the photo showed only one bright minute.
Has the supplementary exam timetable been announced yet?
I don't know, because I can't see today's announcements. The exam board's official website posts timetables as soon as they are released.

Three months after her father's death, Zainab went back to teaching at the small-town girls' school. To everyone who asked, she said, "I'm fine, Allah's will." She smiled at the staffroom, graded papers, ate lunch alone.
At night she lay awake, feeling nothing at all, and then suddenly furious at the ceiling fan, the neighbours' radio, everything.
One afternoon Uma, the old maths teacher, sat beside her under the neem tree. She didn't ask how Zainab was. She said, "Your Abbu, Rashid sahib, used to bring you to school on his cycle, na? I remember him ringing the bell twice at the gate."
Zainab's throat closed. "He always rang twice. So I'd know it was him."
"Tell me about him," Uma said.
And for the first time in three months, Zainab talked, and cried, and felt lighter.

How many times did Rashid sahib ring the bell at the gate?
He rang the bell twice at the gate.
What was Zainab feeling at night in those months?
Zainab felt numb and then suddenly furious, hiding her grief behind "I'm fine" during the day.
Why did Uma's approach work?
Uma didn't ask how Zainab was; she named Rashid sahib and shared a memory of him, which gave Zainab permission to talk about her father.
How did Uma likely feel as Zainab began to talk?
Uma likely felt tender and glad, having sensed Zainab's hidden grief and found a gentle way in.

Monday, 7 p.m. A smooth voice on the phone offers Deepak a 'forex account' that pays double in six months. 'Transfer ₹20,000 by midnight to lock the rate.' Deepak's thumb is on his banking app. Then he remembers the rule he made after his cousin lost money: forty-eight hours of waiting before sending a single rupee. 'I'll decide Wednesday,' he says. The voice turns sharp.
Tuesday, lunch. He tells Nazia at work. 'It sounded so sure,' he says, and hears how thin that sounds out loud. Nazia asks, 'Who guarantees double?' He has no answer.
Wednesday, 7 p.m. The number is switched off. When he searches it, three complaints come up, all describing the same smooth voice and the same midnight deadline. Deepak sits back, heart thumping, and deletes the payee he had half-added on Monday.

How much did the caller ask Deepak to transfer by midnight?
₹20,000 by midnight to lock the rate.
What does Deepak's thumping heart on Wednesday suggest?
He feels shaken and relieved at how close he came, now that the complaints show it was a trap.
What else could Deepak do after finding the complaints?
Report the number to the cybercrime helpline and warn his cousin and colleagues, so others don't fall for it.
How might Nazia see Deepak's Tuesday story?
Nazia hears the doubt in his voice and asks the one question he cannot answer, helping the wait do its work.

The resort booking closed at midnight, and Gurleen was sure she already knew the answer. A two-day trek, tents, a bonfire: she'd have loved it, so surely everyone would. Nilesh was ready to pay the deposit.
"Give me one hour," she said. She sent the team a short anonymous poll with three options and a line: "Tell me honestly, nothing is decided." Then she walked over to Farah and Dinesh, who rarely spoke up in meetings, and asked them directly.
By eleven the results were in. Only four of fourteen wanted the trek. Two had small children, one had a bad knee, and several simply wanted to be home by night. Gurleen laughed at herself. "I'd have booked a trip for me and three others."
They chose the day trip to the lake. Nilesh paid the deposit at 11:40.

How many of the fourteen wanted the trek?
Only four of fourteen.
What did Gurleen feel when the poll results came in?
She was amused rather than defensive, realising she'd imagined everyone wanted what she wanted, and she treated the surprise as useful.
Which of Gurleen's steps worked best, and why?
The anonymous poll plus asking Farah and Dinesh directly, because quieter people and those with reasons like children or a bad knee got heard.
How might Farah feel being asked directly?
Farah might feel noticed and more willing to say what suits them, having rarely spoken up in meetings.

Friday evening, the accounts office was half empty when Tanvir stopped at Sudha's desk. "You're my best analyst. Nobody else can fix this month-end file. The whole team will suffer if you're not in tomorrow." Sudha's stomach dropped. Tomorrow was her cousin's engagement lunch. She felt guilty already, and a little flattered too. She had heard the same praise three weekends in a row, and her review still said nothing about extra work. "Sir, will this be counted in my review? And can I take Monday morning off?" Tanvir waved his hand. "We'll see, we'll see." Sudha picked up her bag. "I can do two hours tomorrow morning, not the whole day. After that I have a family event." He frowned, but nodded. 😔

Whose engagement lunch was tomorrow?
It was Sudha's cousin's engagement lunch.
What mix of feelings did Sudha have when Tanvir praised her?
She felt guilty and a little flattered at the same time, and her stomach dropped.
What did Sudha do to test whether the praise was real?
She asked whether the extra work would count in her review and whether she could take Monday morning off, then offered a clear limit of two hours.
How might Tanvir see Sudha's answer?
He may feel annoyed, since he frowned, but he still agreed, which suggests her limit was clear enough to accept.
A farmer picked 34 oranges and sold 18 of them. How many does she have left?
16. Because 34 - 18 = 16, so 16 are left.

"Can I sleep in the store-room from now on?" Santosh asked at dinner.
Thakuma put down her spoon. "With the rice sacks? Why?"
"I just want a door I can shut."
His cousin Arnab grinned. "What are you hiding, dada, a girlfriend?"
Everyone laughed. Jethu said, "In this house we don't need doors. We need each other."
"I didn't say I don't need anyone." Santosh's voice cracked. "Forget it."
He pushed his plate away and went up to the roof.
Later Ma came up with two guavas and sat beside him. "Tell me properly. What do you need?"
"An hour a day, alone. That's all."
"Then we'll ask them properly, together. Tomorrow."

Where did Santosh go after pushing his plate away?
He went up to the roof.
Why did Santosh's voice crack at dinner?
He felt hurt and misunderstood; wanting a door sounded to the family like not needing them, and the laughter made him feel selfish.
What made Ma's approach work?
She came alone, calmly asked what he needed, and offered to ask the family together, turning a sulk into a clear request.
How does Jethu see Santosh's wish for a door?
Jethu sees it as a step away from family closeness in a house that runs on needing each other.

I'm Keerthana, the neighbour across the landing, and I watched Anand from our open door. Anand's Amma had called out two jobs: blocks into the box, and finish the drawing before the food came. Anand laid the jobs out like two toys, chose the drawing because the crayons were already out, and coloured half a sun. Then a ball rolled past. The crayon dropped, and the blocks sat in their heap while the ball bounced. When the smell of dal reached the room, Anand stared at the half sun and started carrying blocks over, one by one.

Anand's Amma gives two jobs, putting blocks in the box and finishing a drawing. Anand colours half a sun, but a ball rolls past and the crayon is dropped. When the smell of dal comes, Anand starts carrying blocks.

Ishita beta, sit with your Dadaji a minute, since you're worried about that report. In my second year at the engineering college in Pune, the college held an eye check. The nurse wrote on my card: 'suspected glaucoma, see specialist.' I, Madhav Joshi, a boy of nineteen, decided then and there I was going blind. I stopped reading at night, I wrote to my father that I might have to leave college. My friend Prakash, a quiet boy from Satara, dragged me to the library and found a book that said most young people flagged by that quick check are perfectly fine; the check catches many so it misses none. The specialist tested me properly and smiled kindly. Sixty years I have read since then. So first, we ask the doctor what your number means.

What did the nurse write on Madhav's card?
The nurse wrote 'suspected glaucoma, see specialist' on the card.
Why did young Madhav feel so sure he was going blind?
Young Madhav felt panicked, and the word on the card seemed like a verdict, so he never stopped to think how rarely a young student actually has that condition.
What was the turning point in Madhav's story, and why did it help?

The turning point was Prakash taking him to the library to read that most young people flagged by that quick check are fine; knowing how common false alarms are made the wait for the specialist bearable.
How might Prakash have seen his friend's fear back then?
Prakash seems to have seen that Madhav was scared rather than informed, and quietly went looking for facts instead of arguing.

In Kishangarh, news travels faster than the bus. By the time Rashmi and Mohit had decided to move to Jaipur for her nursing course, three aunties already knew.

Mohit's mother, Parveen, did not forbid it. She did something harder. She sighed at every meal. "Go, go. What will people say, a son leaving his old mother?" She rubbed her knee loudly on the stairs. A cousin phoned to say Amma had not slept.

Rashmi felt cornered in her own kitchen. Every hint landed on her, as if the course were a crime.

That night on the roof she said, "Mohit, is this still our decision?" He nodded slowly. "It's ours. We tell her together."

In the morning they sat with Parveen. "Amma, we are going in June. We'll come home every second Sunday, and Mohit's cousin will check on you." Parveen turned away. Rashmi did not argue further. She simply poured her mother-in-law's tea.

Why were Rashmi and Mohit moving to Jaipur?
They were moving to Jaipur for Rashmi's nursing course.
What did Rashmi feel as the hints and sighs continued?
Rashmi felt cornered and guilty, as if the course were a crime.
What did Rashmi and Mohit do well in the morning talk?
They spoke together, stayed calm, gave a clear plan for visits and care, and did not try to win the argument.
How might Parveen see the couple's decision?
Parveen likely feels hurt and afraid of being left alone, and worried about what the town will say, which is why she turns away.
At 4 p.m. a 2 m pole casts a shadow 3 m long. At the same moment a tree casts a shadow 18 m long. How tall is the tree?

Answer: 12 m.

The sun's rays are parallel, so the rays make the same angle with the ground everywhere. Pole + shadow and tree + shadow form two right-angled triangles with equal angles: similar (AA). height / shadow is the same: h / 18 = 2 / 3 h = 18 x 2 / 3 = 12 m Or: the tree's shadow is 18 / 3 = 6 times as long, so the tree is 6 times as tall: 2 x 6 = 12 m. This is how Thales measured the height of a pyramid.
We're starting a kho-kho team in our neighbourhood. Where do we begin?
Start by finding enough players and a safe, open space to play. Do any of you know the rules well?
A few of us do.
Then those players can teach the others. Write the basic rules on a sheet, and play a practice game so that everyone understands.
How do we find a coach?
Ask at the local school, sports club or community office. A teacher or a former player may be willing to help. Ask politely and explain what you plan.
What equipment do we need?
Kho-kho needs very little: poles at each end of the central lane and a marked ground. Comfortable clothes and shoes with grip complete the list.
How do we make sure it's safe?
Check the ground for stones, holes and wet patches before every game. Have an adult nearby, and warm up first. Stop playing if someone gets hurt, and tell an adult.

Two friends, Hubert and Ian, are planning to have a pizza party. One box of pizza is worth $14, and a can of soda is worth $1.80. Hubert orders eight boxes of pizza and ten cans of soda. Ian buys ten boxes of pizza and fifteen cans of soda. How much do they spend in all?

The number of boxes of pizza is 8 + 10 = 18 boxes.
The number of cans of soda is 10 + 15 = 25 cans.
The eighteen boxes of pizza cost 18 x $14= $252.
The cost of 25 cans of soda is 25 x $1.80= $45.
Therefore, the total amount they spend is $252 + $45 = $297
The answer is 297.

On her first week at the Delhi college, Seema, nineteen, was introduced to her classmates as "the Dubai girl". They teased her Hindi, which had Arabic words tumbling into it. "Say it again, 'khalas'!" In Dubai, where she was born, her school friends had always called her "the Indian one". Now, at the canteen, a girl said, "You're not proper Indian, na? You don't even know the festivals." Seema went red. She knew Eid and Diwali and National Day. That evening she sat on the metro, staring at her reflection, wondering what she was.
Her friend Jasleen, who had grown up in Canada before moving back, sat with her at lunch the next day. "They call me 'Canada' too. So what? We're both." When the girl teased her again, Seema said, lightly, "I'm Indian and I'm from Dubai. I get two sets of sweets." People laughed with her.

What did classmates call Seema?
"The Dubai girl."
How did Seema feel sitting on the metro that evening?
Seema felt hurt and unsure, staring at her reflection and wondering what she was.
How did Seema's reply to the teasing claim a blended identity?
She said lightly that she is Indian and from Dubai and gets two sets of sweets, owning both parts without apology.
How does Jasleen see labels like "Canada"?
Jasleen shrugs them off, seeing herself as both, which gives Seema confidence.

"The Kulkarni thing? Forget it."
"I can't. Everyone laughed when he said my presentation sounded like a village radio announcer. And you just stood up and said, 'Can we discuss the content instead of his accent?'"
"It was a rude comment. Somebody had to say it."
"Nobody else did." Imran rubbed his neck. "I froze. I've been thinking about it all night. Thank you."
"You'd do the same."
"I'd like to think so. So, you're doing the stats project alone, right? I'm good with the regression part. Let me help this weekend."

How does Imran return Jyoti's support?
In his own way: offering to help with the regression part of her stats project and buying chai every Friday till exams.
How does Jyoti see what she did?
As simply necessary ("Somebody had to say it"), not a favour that needs repaying.

Codger is a three-footed sloth.  He has a challenging time buying shoes because the stores only sell the shoes in pairs. If he already owns the 3-piece set of shoes he is wearing, how many pairs of shoes does he need to buy to have 5 complete 3-piece sets of shoes?

To have five 3-piece sets, he needs to have a total of 5*3=15 shoes,
If he already owns three shoes, then he needs to buy 15-3=12 additional shoes.
Since each pair of shoes includes two shoes, he needs to buy a total of 12/2=6 pairs of shoes.
The answer is 6.

On the carpet, Avni stacked wooden blocks up high. At the sixth block it swayed and fell. She looked, shrugged, and built it again with the pieces in a new order.

Chandrika whispered to herself, "First the big blocks, then the small ones, then the flag on top." She did exactly that, and the tower grew straight, because she always knew what shape she was making.

Santosh patted his tower and said, "Stay up." He put the red block on top, because red was lucky. The tower wobbled anyway. Santosh glared at the red block. "Bad block," he said, and never looked at the narrow bottom.

Avni's tower fell a second time, then a third. She sat back on her heels. "If it wobbles," she said slowly, "make the bottom wider." Next time she laid four blocks side by side first. The tower wobbled once and stayed.

At which block did Avni's first tower fall?
It fell at the sixth block.
How did Santosh's explanation for the wobble differ from Avni's, and what happened to their towers?
Santosh blamed the red block and ignored the narrow bottom, while Avni decided to make the bottom wider and her tower stayed up.
What was Santosh feeling when he glared at the red block?
Annoyed and let down, because he had trusted the lucky block.
How could an adult help Santosh?
An adult could build a tower with him, point out the narrow bottom, and let him try a wider one.

Read this:

Monday: Ira's mother texted after a year of silence: "Come for lunch Sunday. We can talk." Ira read it at work and felt her chest tighten. The last lunch had ended with her father calling Thomas "that foreigner".
Wednesday: Ira drafted her reply four times with Thomas beside her. The final one said: "I'd love to come, with Thomas. If he's insulted, we'll leave, and try again another time."
Sunday: They went. Her father was stiff but polite. Once, he began, "People like him...", and Ira stood up quietly. Her mother touched his arm. He stopped. They stayed for dessert.

What did Ira's father once call Thomas?
"That foreigner."
What was Ira feeling on Monday when she read the text?
Her chest tightened, showing she felt anxious and wary, remembering how the last lunch had gone.
What made Ira's reply a good turning point?
It welcomed contact while stating a clear limit, so the reunion could happen without accepting insults.
What is it like for Ira's mother when Ira stands up?
She likely feels alarmed and determined not to lose her daughter again, so she touches her husband's arm to stop him.
There was a dust storm this evening and my room is covered in a layer of dust.
That's a messy aftermath. Did the dust come in through the windows?
Yes, I left them open.
Close them during storms next time. Dust your shelves and desk with a damp cloth rather than a dry one, so the dust sticks instead of flying around, then sweep and mop the floor.
What about my books?
Wipe the covers with a slightly damp cloth, and shake the books gently. Don't wet the pages.
I'll do it tomorrow. I'm too tired tonight.
That's fine. The dust will wait, and you'll have more energy in the morning.

By the second morning the corridor floor of the hostel was under an inch of water and the mess had shut. Hrithik went from room to room on the third floor and counted: nine packets of biscuits, two bags of puffed rice, a tin of tea leaves and twenty-two bottles of water among fourteen students. He had eaten a big breakfast as usual, and now the numbers made his stomach tighten. "We planned as if it was one day," he told Avni from the next room. Together they rewrote it: three small meals, water in cups, and a chart taped to the door. Then they tried every way of reaching home. The hostel landline crackled, texts kept failing, and near midnight one finally went through to Hrithik's cousin in the next district.

How many bottles of water did Hrithik count?
Hrithik counted twenty-two bottles of water among fourteen students.
What was Hrithik feeling as he counted the supplies?
Hrithik felt anxious, his stomach tightening as he realised the plan had been for one day.
What else could the group do to stretch supplies, and why?
They could ask the other floors and the warden about their stock and plan together, because a shared count shows how long everything must last.
How might Avni have felt as the plan came together?
Avni probably felt relieved to have a clear plan and stayed worried until a message finally got through.

messages.content:
Read this:

"Fan go!" Jomon waved both hands at the ceiling.
In the kitchen doorway, Dilnaz aunty flicked the switch. The fan began to turn.
Jomon's mouth fell open. "Jomon did it!"
"You did?" said Dilnaz aunty, smiling.
He waved again. "Fan stop!"
She switched it off. The blades slowed.
Jomon squealed and flapped his arms. "Fan go! Fan go!"
Dilnaz aunty laughed and switched it on once more. "Clever boy. Now, shall we find your ball?"

What did Jomon wave at?
He waved both hands at the ceiling fan.
Why did Jomon squeal and flap his arms?
He felt thrilled and proud because he believed his waving made the fan start and stop.
What could Dilnaz aunty do next time to gently show how the fan works?
She could let Jomon watch her press the switch, or help him press it himself, so he sees what makes it go.
How might Dilnaz aunty feel playing the game with Jomon?
She seems amused and fond, enjoying his delight while she works the switch.

In five minutes more the cloud of bewilderment dissolved: I knew quite well that I was in my own bed, and that the red glare was the nursery fire. It was night: a candle burnt on the table; Bessie stood at the bed-foot with a basin in her hand, and a gentleman sat in a chair near my pillow, leaning over me.

Question: Who is in the room when the speaker wakes?
Bessie stands at the foot of the bed with a basin, and a gentleman sits in a chair near the pillow, leaning over the speaker. The red glare is the nursery fire.

Read this:

It was harvest week, and every mother in the village was out in the paddy fields. At the anganwadi, little Lakshmi watched her Amma walk away down the mud path and let out a long wail.
Across the mat, a boy with a rattle stopped shaking it. His face crumpled. Then two more toddlers joined in, looking around, not knowing why.
Manjula, the helper, scooped Lakshmi up and sat down among them, clapping softly and singing the harvest song. One by one the cries turned into sniffles.

Where were the mothers during harvest week?
Every mother in the village was out in the paddy fields.
What was the boy with the rattle feeling when Lakshmi wailed?
He felt upset and uneasy, catching Lakshmi's sadness without knowing why she cried.
How did Manjula help the whole group settle?
She held Lakshmi and sat among all of them, clapping softly and singing, so calm could spread instead.
How might Lakshmi's Amma feel if she heard the crying from the path?
She might feel torn and worried, needing to work in the fields yet wanting to comfort her child.

Read this:

In Sironj, the afternoon power cut had made the house hot and slow. Nirmala was looking at her drawings on Amma's old phone when a message arrived: "Hi! I saw your peacock drawing. Where did you learn? I'm Bhavna 🙂"
Nirmala sat up. Someone liked her peacock! She wanted to ask who Bhavna was, where she lived, whether she drew too. Her thumb hovered over the keys.
Then she carried the phone to the courtyard, where Amma was sorting red chillies. "Amma, someone I don't know messaged me. Can I reply?"
Amma read it slowly. "We don't know who this is. You can say thank you, but no school name, no address, no photos. And show me whatever comes next."
Nirmala typed "thank you" and handed the phone back.

Which drawing did the message mention?
Nirmala's peacock drawing.
What did Nirmala want when the message arrived?
She felt curious and excited, wanting to know who Bhavna was, where she lived and whether she drew too.
What did Nirmala do before replying, and why was it wise?
She showed Amma first, so an adult could decide what was safe to say.
How does Amma see the message?
Amma sees someone unknown, so she allows only a thank-you and asks to see anything that comes next.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 10

Kishore came to me today upset that his friend Pratik "ignored" him in the corridor and hasn't replied to messages since Monday. Kishore said, "He's become arrogant since he got into the cricket team."

I asked Kishore whether he had noticed anything else about Pratik this week. He thought, and said Pratik had been absent on Tuesday, and looked tired.

I couldn't share private details, but I knew Pratik's family was going through a difficult time. I told Kishore gently that there might be things happening for Pratik that we can't see, and that people who seem rude are sometimes just overwhelmed.

Kishore was quiet. Then he said, "I didn't even think of that. I just thought he'd changed."

He's decided to send Pratik a message asking if he's okay, instead of an angry one.

Tenzin

Since when has Pratik not replied to Kishore's messages?
Since Monday.
Why did Kishore think Pratik had become arrogant?
Kishore felt hurt at being ignored, and explained it by Pratik's character rather than any situation he couldn't see.
What did Tenzin do that helped without breaking privacy?
Tenzin asked what else Kishore had noticed and gently suggested unseen pressures, without sharing Pratik's private details.
How might Pratik feel receiving a message asking if he's okay?
Pratik might feel relieved and cared for during a difficult time.

Paulo wants to get a burger meal that costs $6. Aside from that, he also wants to get a soda which costs 1/3 as much as the burger meal. While on the counter, Jeremy asked Paulo to get him 2 of each item Paulo is going to get. How much will they be charged for their orders combined?

They are to order a total of 3 burger meals and 3 sodas for Paulo and Jeremy.
The cost of a soda is $6/3 = $2.
So, the 3 sodas will amount to $2/soda x 3 sodas = $6.
The 3 burger meals will amount to $6/burger x 3 burgers = $18.
Hence, the total cost for their orders is $6 + $18 = $24.
The answer is 24.

Read this:

Lindiwe had processed housing forms at the Durban municipal office for two years, and she sent back every one without an original ID. Copies were easy to fake, and a fake had once cost a real family its flat.
Then Sami came in, seventy-one, smelling faintly of smoke. His room had burned on Tuesday, papers and all. The rule said no original, no place on the list, and a replacement ID could take months.
That afternoon Lindiwe filed an exception request with the review panel, attaching a fire report and a letter from Sami's street committee. She asked that fire victims keep their queue place with a sworn statement.
The panel refused the general change but agreed Sami's case could be paused, not dropped. Lindiwe felt the sting of losing. She phoned Sami herself, explained the panel's reasons, and booked him the next slot at the home affairs office.

What did Lindiwe attach to her exception request?
She attached a fire report and a letter from Sami's street committee.
What was Lindiwe feeling when the panel refused the general change?
She felt the sting of losing, because she had asked for all fire victims to keep their place, yet she still respected the panel's decision.
What choice did Lindiwe make after the ruling went against her, and why did it matter?
She accepted it, phoned Sami herself with the reasons and booked his ID appointment, so he was neither confused nor dropped from the list.
How might Sami see the office differently because Lindiwe raised the request instead of just returning his form?
He might feel the office treated him as a person who had lost everything, not just a missing document, even though his case was only paused.
Which page number mentions a river in my English reader?
I can't see your book, so I don't know. Flip through the chapters or check the contents page.
Is it "aquaintance" or "acquaintance"?

The correct spelling is "acquaintance", with a c before the q: ac-quaint-ance.
Example: She is an acquaintance from my yoga class, not a close friend.

Read this:

Reena: "Vishal, where's the screwdriver? The cupboard hinge is loose."
Vishal: "Blue box, bottom shelf. Everything's in there."
Reena: (opening it) "Wow. Labelled. Even the Allen keys."
Vishal: "I got tired of searching the whole flat every time."
Reena: "I usually just use a butter knife."
Vishal: "And that's why the screws in your kitchen are all chewed up."
Reena: "Fair. Which one for this?"
Vishal: "Cross-head, the medium one. The small one will strip it."
Reena: "What's this little oil can for?"
Vishal: "Door hinges and the cycle chain. First Sunday of every month. Takes ten minutes. Saves me buying a new chain every year."
Reena: "You're like a tiny hardware shop."
Vishal: "A cheap one. That's the point."

Where does Vishal keep the tools?
In the blue box, bottom shelf.
How does Reena feel on opening the labelled tool box?
Reena feels surprised and impressed, even teasing Vishal about being a tiny hardware shop.
Which of Vishal's habits prevent costly repairs?
Keeping tools in one place, using the correct screwdriver, and oiling hinges and the chain on the first Sunday of every month.
How does Vishal see Reena's butter-knife method?
Vishal sees it as the reason Reena's kitchen screws are chewed up, and gently points it out.
Application form mein "Date of birth" kaise likhte hain? DD/MM/YYYY ka matlab?
It means day, month, year. For example, 5 March 2004 is written 05/03/2004. Always follow the order that the form shows.
Tom goes to a combined undergrad and Ph.D. program.  It takes 3 years to finish the BS and 5 years to finish the Ph.D.  Tom finishes it in 3/4ths the time.  How long does it take for him to finish?

The program normally takes 3+5=8 years
So he manages to finish in 8*3/4=6 years
The answer is 6.

Read this:

At the tea stall in Nagaur, Harish stood shoulder to shoulder with Deepak, talking the way people do in a small town where everyone stands close. It reminded Harish of the internship in Stuttgart. There, Harish had stood a hand's width from a colleague, chatting eagerly, and the colleague had taken one step back, then another. Harish felt rejected and wondered what had been said wrong. Weeks later a co-intern explained that some people there like a wider gap, and that it was comfort, not dislike. "So I started noticing," Harish told Deepak, "who leans in and who steps away." Harish moved half a step back, just to try. Deepak laughed and stepped in closer, and they both grinned.

Where did Harish's internship take place?
The internship was in Stuttgart.
How did Harish feel when the colleague stepped back?
Rejected and confused, wondering what had been said wrong.
What did Harish learn to do afterwards?
Notice who leans in and who steps away, and adjust the distance.
How might Deepak see Harish moving half a step back?
As a funny experiment, since Deepak laughed and stepped in closer.

Gerald thought it would be funny to trick his coworker, who's allergic to peanuts, into eating a peanut butter cookie. When his coworker goes into anaphylactic shock and is taken to the hospital, Gerald is arrested. The judge sentences Gerald to 3 months for assault and 2 years for poisoning, then extends his sentence by 1/3 since this is Gerald's third offense. How many months does Gerald spend in jail?

First convert the 2-year sentence to months: 2 years * 12 months/year = 24 months
Then add the 3 months for assault: 24 months + 3 months = 27 months
Then find how long the 1/3 extension is: 27 months / 3 = 9 months
Finally, add up the three lengths of time to find the total sentence length: 27 months + 9 months = 36 months
The answer is 36.

Read this:

The science exhibition was the next morning, and the power had just gone out in the school lab. By the light of her phone torch, Baljeet held up her water-filter model for Kiran ma'am. "The sand layer is in the wrong order," ma'am said flatly. "And your chart claims it makes water safe to drink. You haven't tested that. A judge will catch it in ten seconds." Baljeet's face went hot. She'd spent three weekends on it. "You could have said something nice first," she muttered, jaw tight. Kiran ma'am didn't flinch. "I'm saying this because you're capable of first prize. Come, we'll fix the layers together before the lights come back." Baljeet stood stiffly for a moment, then picked up the gravel.

What was wrong with the sand layer?
The sand layer was in the wrong order.
Why did Baljeet mutter "You could have said something nice first"?
She felt stung and angry after three weekends of work, and the flat words hurt more because they came the night before the exhibition.
What turning point is available to Baljeet in this moment?
Picking up the gravel and fixing the layers with Kiran ma'am turns the sting into improvement, letting her see the critique as help from someone who believes in her.
How might Kiran ma'am feel when Baljeet mutters at her?
She may feel a flicker of discomfort but stays steady, because she cares more about Baljeet doing her best than about being liked in that moment.

Read this:

The building's community hall was full of drums and flowers. Eshaan's family had brought their Ganpati there for all the neighbours. Dilnaz peeped in with her mummy. Eshaan's Aai saw her and called, "Dilnaz! Come, have a modak!" She put a sweet, soft dumpling in Dilnaz's hand. Dilnaz stared at the big clay idol with the elephant face. "Why does he have an elephant head?" she asked. Eshaan's Aai smiled. "There's a story. I'll tell you after the aarti." Eshaan let Dilnaz ring the small bell. She rang it very carefully.

What did Eshaan's Aai put in Dilnaz's hand?
She put a sweet, soft dumpling, a modak, in her hand.
How did Dilnaz feel in the community hall?
She felt welcome and curious, staring at the idol and asking about the elephant head.
How did Eshaan's family help Dilnaz learn about their festival?
They greeted her warmly, shared food, promised the story and let her ring the bell.
What would change if Eshaan's Aai had ignored Dilnaz's question?
Dilnaz might feel like an outsider and miss the chance to learn and respect how other families celebrate.
Put a few blobs of paint on one half of a paper. Fold it and press. Open it. What do you see?

Answer: A "butterfly" picture: the second half is the same as the first, but flipped. The fold is the line of symmetry.

This blob painting is the best first lesson. Point to a blob on one side and find its partner on the other side, the same distance from the fold.

Read this:

Bidisha's diary, Tuesday night.
Banned from the film-club group today. Three thousand members, and one message from Sachin, the moderator: “Third spoiler warning ignored. You are removed.” I was so angry my hands shook. I had posted a spoiler as a joke, then argued with him in the thread while other people liked his replies. Nobody stood up for me. My first thought was that they're all petty. My second, a bit ashamed, was that the rule was fair and I did break it three times. And under all that, strangely, a small relief: I'll get my evenings back. Still, I used to check that group every morning. Tomorrow I'll go to the coffee shop and see if any of the real-life regulars are around.
Bidisha

How many spoiler warnings had Bidisha ignored?
Bidisha had ignored three spoiler warnings.
What mix of feelings did Bidisha have about being banned?
Bidisha felt rejected and angry, then a bit ashamed that the rule was fair, and also a small relief at getting evenings back.
What could Bidisha do next to cope with losing this group?
Bidisha could go to the coffee shop to see the real-life regulars, as planned, and find another way to talk about films without the daily check.
How might Sachin have seen the ban?
Sachin probably saw it as applying a written rule fairly after three warnings, though Sachin may also feel the strain of arguing in front of three thousand members.

messages.content: Building one birdhouse requires 7 planks and 20 nails.  If 1 nail costs $0.05, and one plank costs $3, what is the cost, in dollars, to build 4 birdhouses?

The cost of the planks for one birdhouse is 7 * 3 = $21.
And the nails are a cost of 20 * 0.05 = $1 for each birdhouse.
So to build one birdhouse one will need 21 + 1 = $22.
So the cost of building 4 birdhouses is at 4 * 22 = $88.
The answer is 88.

Read this:

On Monday Ujjwal, two, held a banana to his ear and said, "Hello, Mama!" Parveen laughed and took the "call." On Wednesday she told him, "Hop like a bunny!" and he hopped, delighted. On Saturday a neighbour said, "It's raining cats and dogs." Ujjwal ran to the window, looked at the sky, and asked, "Cat? Dog?" Parveen said, "It's raining a lot." He looked unconvinced.

What did Ujjwal use as a telephone on Monday?
He used a banana.
What does Ujjwal's question at the window suggest he felt, and what other reading is there?
He was probably curious and a little puzzled, since he took the idiom literally, looked at the sky and still looked unconvinced. He might also just have been playing along.
What could Parveen do with a toddler when using sayings?
She can say what she means in plain words and enjoy pretend games together.
How does the neighbour see what happened?
The neighbour probably meant nothing but the weather and may find it funny that a small child took her words at face value.

Read this:

I'm Pranav, and I live on the third floor of the hostel. Our floor had fights about everything: music at night, the fridge, bathroom cleaning. Gautam, our floor rep, could have just written rules and pinned them up. Instead, one evening, he knocked on all twelve doors and said, "Common room, eight o'clock, everyone." I asked him later why he didn't just decide. He said, "If I make the rules alone, nobody will follow them. Everyone uses the floor, so everyone has to agree." At the meeting people argued, laughed and voted. Quiet hours after eleven. Fridge cleaned Sundays. A cleaning rota by room. It took ninety minutes. Six weeks later, the rules on the notice board are still being followed.

How many doors did Gautam knock on?
All twelve doors.
What was Gautam thinking when he called a meeting instead of deciding alone?
He felt sure rules made alone wouldn't be followed, and hoped a shared decision would stick.
Why did a group meeting suit this problem?
Everyone shares the floor, so rules everyone helped make are more likely to be accepted and followed.
How might the other residents see the meeting?
They likely felt heard and more willing to follow rules they had voted on.
