Rain hammered the tin roof of the classroom, and their usual teacher was away. The new teacher had to shout. Tejas climbed under the table and refused to come out. 'I don't want to!' Hemant covered his ears but stayed on his bench, hand up, waiting. When his turn came, he shouted his answer over the rain. The teacher gave him a thumbs up and knelt to talk to Tejas.

Why did the new teacher have to shout?
Rain was hammering the tin roof, and it was very noisy.
What might Tejas have been feeling under the table?
He may have felt overwhelmed by the noise and a new teacher, so he refused to cooperate.
How could the teacher help Tejas join in?
She could speak to him quietly, give him a simple job like handing out books, and invite him back without shaming him.
How does Hemant's day differ from Tejas's?
Hemant copes with the noise by staying seated and waiting his turn, while Tejas hides and refuses, so their mornings go very differently.

"Uday fell!" Kishore shouted. The summer holidays had filled the park, and Uday had slipped off the swing.

Uday held his elbow and cried.

Kishore knelt down. "Does it hurt?"

"Yes."

Kishore blew on the elbow. "Better?"

"A bit."

"I'll get your water bottle." Kishore ran and came back. "Here. And I'll call your mummy."

Where did Uday fall from?
Uday had slipped off the swing.
How did Kishore feel when Uday cried?
Kishore felt worried and concerned for Uday, wanting to help.
How could an adult support Kishore's comforting?
Praise him for helping and for calling Uday's mummy.
How might Uday feel when Kishore blew on his elbow?
Uday would likely feel comforted and cared for.

Monday: On the school bus, Gautam told Jaya that the captain had never failed in a big match. "Remember the final? Ninety-eight runs!"
Thursday: The captain was out for a duck in the semi-final. Gautam stared at the screen, then said loudly, "That was never out. The umpire needs glasses." When Jaya showed him the replay on her tablet, he said the camera angle was wrong.
Next Saturday: Jaya brought her cricket magazine, which had the captain's last ten scores in a table. Gautam read it slowly. Six were under twenty. "Magazines always pick the bad games," he muttered. But he kept looking at the table for a long time.

How many of the captain's last ten scores were under twenty?
Six of the captain's last ten scores in the magazine table were under twenty.
Why did Gautam blame the camera angle when Jaya showed him the replay?
His picture of the captain was built on the ninety-eight in the final, so the duck felt unfair rather than informative. Blaming the umpire and the camera protected that happy picture.
What could Jaya try so that Gautam weighs the table instead of dismissing it?
She could ask him to pick the scores himself, so the list isn't her evidence against him. Asking which result would make him change his view also helps him notice when he keeps only the good ones.
What is it like for Jaya when every bad score gets a new excuse?
Jaya may feel that talking facts with Gautam goes nowhere, yet his long look at the table gives her a small hope that he is starting to notice.

Mike is shopping at the mall. He needs to buy a shirt, a new wallet, and some food for the evening. The shirt costs a third of the value of the wallet. The wallet is $60 more than the cost of the food, on which Mike spent $30. How much did Mike spend that day on the shopping?

The wallet costs $60 more than the food, so it's $30 + $60 = $90.
So the cost of the shirt is 1/3 * $90 = $30.
Mike spent that day $30 + $30 + $90 = $150.
The answer is 150.

"Mumma, what did you give that man?"
"Nothing, Vandana. Get in the car."
"I saw. You put money in the file."
Gargi started the engine. "That's how licences happen here. Otherwise we'd come back ten times."
"But you always tell me not to cheat."
"This isn't cheating. It's... getting things done."
"Then why did you hide it?"
Silence.
"Vandana, I'm tired. Your father's leave is over. I couldn't come back again."
"I get that. But it felt wrong."
Gargi was quiet at the traffic light. "It is wrong. I'm not proud of it."
"Then why did you do it?"
"Because I was scared of wasting weeks. Maybe next time I should just come back, and complain if they delay." She glanced at her daughter. "I don't want you to think this is normal."

What did Vandana see her mother put in the file?
She saw her put money in the file.
What was Vandana feeling as she questioned her mother?
Vandana felt confused and uneasy, because her mother always tells her not to cheat.
What could Gargi do differently next time, as she herself suggests?
She could come back as needed and complain properly about delays, rather than pay the man.
How does Gargi seem to feel when she admits it is wrong?
Gargi seems tired and ashamed, not proud of it, and worried that Vandana will think it is normal.
Simplify this railway announcement: Passengers are requested to alight only after the train has come to a complete halt and to mind the gap between the train and the platform.
Please wait until the train has fully stopped before you get off. Watch out for the gap between the train and the platform.

The video call with the printing vendor kept freezing, and Darshan could only hear every second word. His colleague Manjula was leading the talk for the event brochures. The vendor spoke first: "For five thousand copies, two lakh." The screen froze on his smile. When it came back, Manjula was already saying, "Could you do one lakh eighty?" Darshan felt his stomach tighten. Last month he had seen the same thing: whoever named the first figure, the whole talk stayed near it. And Manjula hadn't checked other quotes. He quickly typed in the chat to her: "Our three quotes last year were 1.2 to 1.4." She read it, paused, and said, "Actually, the market rate we've seen is closer to 1.3." The vendor went quiet. The connection dropped again. Darshan made a note: next time, get the range ready before the call.

What did the vendor first quote for five thousand copies?
Two lakh.
What was Darshan feeling when Manjula offered one lakh eighty?
Darshan felt his stomach tighten, worried because he'd seen how the first figure pulls the whole talk toward it.
What could Darshan and Manjula do before the next call?
They could gather quotes and prepare a range in advance, so they reason from research instead of the vendor's number.
How might Manjula feel after using Darshan's message?
Manjula may feel relieved and grateful, and perhaps more aware of how quickly she followed the vendor's number.

Natalia is riding a bicycle for the cycling competition. On Monday she rode 40 kilometers and on Tuesday 50 kilometers. On Wednesday she rode 50% fewer kilometers than the day before. On Thursday she rode as many as the sum of the kilometers from Monday and Wednesday. How many kilometers did Natalie ride in total?

On Wednesday she covered half of the distance from Tuesday, so 50 / 2 = 25 kilometers.
On Thursday she rode 40 + 25 = 65 kilometers.
In total, Natalia rode 40 + 50 + 25 + 65 = 180 kilometers.
The answer is 180.

Dear Tejas,
You asked how the new job is going. On paper, great: the head of department says my Class 8 lessons are the best planned in the school. What I haven't told anyone is how. I stay till eight most nights. I write out every word I'll say. I prepare three backup activities for each period in case a child asks something I can't answer. And every time a lesson goes well, I feel this rush of relief, as if I've escaped being found out. Then the fear starts again for tomorrow. Last week I had a fever and taught from a rough outline, and the lesson went fine. That scared me more, somehow. I don't know what I'm proving, or to whom. Write back?
Vinita

How many backup activities does Vinita prepare for each period?
Three backup activities.
Why did the lesson taught from a rough outline scare Vinita?
It showed that the overwork might not be what makes lessons good, which shakes the belief that effort alone is hiding a lack of skill.
What choice could Vinita try, based on the fever day?
Deliberately teaching one lesson a week from a lighter outline, so success can be credited to real skill rather than to late nights.
How might Tejas respond to this letter?
Tejas may feel concerned about the long nights and point out that the fever-day lesson is evidence of ability, not luck.

After a terrible haircut, Noa's fringe stopped halfway up her forehead, jagged like a saw. On Monday at her school in Copenhagen, two girls whispered and giggled. Noa pulled her woolly hat down to her eyebrows and kept it on all day, even in class.
At break, Emil from next door found her by the bike racks. "Snow fort? The big snow came!"
"My hair's awful," Noa mumbled.
Emil looked at her hat, puzzled. "Okay? The fort needs walls. Are you coming or not?"
They built walls, a tunnel and a snow cat on top. Halfway through, Noa got so hot she yanked off her hat and flung it on the fort. Emil didn't even glance at her hair. He was busy arguing that the cat needed longer ears.
Noa laughed, and realised she had stopped thinking about her fringe.

What did Noa and Emil build on top of the fort?
A snow cat.
How did Noa feel when she flung off her hat?
Relaxed and free, forgetting her fringe while playing.
What does Noa learn from time with Emil?
That a real friend cares about playing together and who she is, not how her hair looks.
How does Emil see Noa's worry about her hair?
He barely notices it; he is only interested in building the fort with her.

My name's Siddharth, and it took me most of second year to see it. Tarun never said, 'Don't meet your friends.' He said things like, 'Imtiaz's jokes are a bit cruel, no?' or 'Your hostel group chat is so childish.' So I muted the chat. I skipped the Holi party because Tarun looked hurt. I stopped calling home on Sundays because we were always 'doing something'. By March I was eating in the mess alone most nights. What woke me up was my roommate Imtiaz leaving a sticky note on my laptop: 'Miss you, yaar. Chai at 9?' I went. I cried a little over the chai, which surprised us both, and I told him everything. I haven't worked it all out yet, but I call home again now, and Imtiaz is the one outside line I don't let go of.

What did Imtiaz write on the sticky note?
Imtiaz wrote, 'Miss you, yaar. Chai at 9?'
What was Siddharth feeling over the chai with Imtiaz?
Siddharth felt lonely and relieved at once, crying a little after months of drifting away from friends.
What would you advise someone noticing the same drift?
Reach out to one trusted person, as Siddharth did with Imtiaz, and keep that connection even if a partner frowns on it.
How might Tarun see the hostel friends and the group chat?
Tarun seems to see them as competition and quietly runs them down, so Siddharth pulls away without ever being told to.
Tell me how the moon moves, in one sentence with the word "orbit" and no commas.
The moon takes about a month to orbit the Earth.

Lecturer's note, first-year statistics — Kalyani
Urmila is one of the sharpest students in the tutorial when we discuss ideas aloud. But whenever a problem sheet appears, she pushes it away before reading it. Today she said, "I'll fail this anyway. I've always been bad at maths." She had not looked at question one.
I did not argue with her. I circled only the first part of question one, finding the mean of five numbers, and asked her to do just that while I walked around the room.
She did it in two minutes, correctly. I said, "That's right," and moved on. When I came back, she had quietly started part two.
It is a small thing. But I think she has had many years of evidence that trying is useless, and she needs fresh evidence that it is not.
Next week: same approach, one small step at a time, slightly harder each time.

What was the first small task the lecturer gave Urmila?
The lecturer asked her to find the mean of five numbers, the first part of question one.
What was the lecturer thinking when choosing not to argue with Urmila?
The lecturer felt concerned and patient, believing Urmila had years of evidence that trying is useless and that arguing would not change it, but a small success might.
Why is starting with one tiny part a good strategy here?
A task she can surely do gives Urmila a quick success, which is fresh evidence that effort works and helps her start the next part on her own.
How might Urmila feel when she hears "That's right"?
Urmila might feel a little surprised and relieved, enough to quietly try part two.

I'm Alka, and my brother Lalit and I didn't speak for four years. It started with an argument about our mother's hospital bills and ended with both of us saying things we couldn't take back.

For years I waited for him to call first. He didn't. Neither did I.

Last month I saw a photo of his son's first birthday on a cousin's feed. A nephew I'd never held. Something in my chest cracked.

I wrote maybe fifteen drafts. The long ones explained everything, who said what, who was wrong. I deleted them all. The one I sent was four lines: "Lalit, I miss you. I'm sorry for what I said about Papa's money. I'd like to meet your son someday. No pressure."

He replied the next evening: "Me too. Sunday?"

We had chai. It was awkward. We didn't go over the whole fight. Since then, I've sent him a message every week. Small things. That's how it's coming back.

How many years did Alka and Lalit not speak?
They didn't speak for four years.
What did Alka feel on seeing the photo of Lalit's son's birthday?
Alka felt a crack of grief and longing for a brother and a nephew missed for so long.
Why did Alka's short message work better than the long drafts?
It was humble, owned Alka's part and asked for nothing big, avoiding a full accounting of the fight, so Lalit could say yes easily.
How might Lalit have felt when he read Alka's message?
Lalit likely felt relieved and moved, replying quickly that he missed Alka too.
Explain in a friendly note, about 80 words, how my grandmother can make a video call on her new phone.

Dear Nani,
Making a video call is easy, I promise. First, unlock your phone and tap the green phone icon. Find my name in the contact list and tap it. Then press the small camera symbol at the top. Hold the phone in front of your face, not against your ear! When I answer, you will see me on the screen. If you only see the ceiling, just tilt the phone a little. Let's practise on Sunday at 5 pm.
Love,
Pihu

My roommate Chetan got the startup offer on a Friday, and by Sunday the whiteboard in our hallway was full. I assumed he'd just jump. His friend's company was exciting, and Chetan hates his bank job. Instead he wrote two columns: "what could go wrong" and "how bad, how likely." He called two people who'd left jobs for young companies and asked what actually happened to them. He looked up how long the startup's funding would last. At one point he crossed out "fails in a year" and wrote "maybe 40 percent" next to it, then circled "I'd still learn a lot." I don't know what he felt inside; he was quiet at dinner. On Monday he asked the founder for a six-month trial while on unpaid leave. Tarun, he said, is "the guy who always asks what's likely."

What two columns did Chetan write on the whiteboard?
He wrote "what could go wrong" and "how bad, how likely."
What does Chetan's quiet dinner suggest, according to the narrator?
It may suggest he was still thinking hard or feeling uneasy about the choice, though the narrator admits he could not know what Chetan felt.
What did Chetan's process do well that a rushed decision might miss?
He checked how likely each risk really was and how bad it would be, and asked people with real experience, instead of acting on excitement or fear.
How might the startup founder see Chetan's request for a trial?
The founder might feel a little disappointed he did not commit fully, but also see him as careful and serious about the role.

Friday night

Third time this month the leader has asked for money "to keep the struggle alive". This time it's twice what we gave before. At the meeting Wasim asked where the last collection went, and the leader said, "Doubters are traitors. Only the weak ask that." Everyone went quiet. A few people clapped, and I clapped too, and I hated my hands for it.

I gave because I believe in the cause. I still do. But if it's real, why can't anyone see the accounts? A real movement should be happy to show them.

Tomorrow I'll ask, politely and in writing, how funds are used before I give another rupee. And I'll talk to my cousin, who isn't in the group.

If they call that betrayal, that tells me something too.

Suraj

How many times this month has the leader asked for money?
It is the third time this month.
Why did Suraj hate the clapping hands afterwards?
Suraj clapped along to stay with the crowd after doubters were called traitors, and felt ashamed of joining in on something that felt wrong.
What is Suraj planning, and why is it sensible?
Suraj will ask in writing how funds are used and talk to a cousin outside the group; a real movement welcomes transparency, and an outsider adds perspective.
How might Wasim have felt after asking where the money went?
Wasim was probably embarrassed or isolated, since everyone went quiet after doubters were called traitors, though the question itself was fair.

"You're shouting at the television again," Kunal said from the doorway.
"Because they're lying, Kunal! Look at this!" Ayesha held up her phone.
"It's two in the morning. You have the client call at nine."
"I'll manage."
"You said that last week. Then your manager emailed about the missed deadline."
"That's because I was up reading the truth, unlike you."
Kunal sat on the arm of the sofa. "Ammi called. She said you hung up on her on Sunday."
"She kept defending them."
"She asked about your cough, Ayesha."
Ayesha opened her mouth, then closed it. She looked at the screen, still scrolling by itself. "I'm so tired," she said quietly. "I'm angry all the time and I don't even feel better after."
"I know," Kunal said. "Come sleep. We can talk about it in the daylight."

What time is it when Kunal comes to the doorway?
It's two in the morning.
What does Ayesha mean when she says she doesn't even feel better after being angry?
She is exhausted and feels empty, and for the first time she is noticing that constant rage is costing her rather than helping.
What turning point is available to Ayesha right now?
She could go to sleep, then talk with Kunal in daylight about the costs to her work, health and family, and consider stepping back from the feeds or seeing a counsellor.
How is Kunal affected by Ayesha's constant anger?
Kunal is worried and tired too, watching her miss sleep, deadlines and calls with Ammi, but he stays patient so she can talk.

I went home to Aizawl in December for the first time since starting work in Delhi. My mother, Lalremsiami, had kept my room exactly as it was. Same quilt, same books, same school certificate on the wall. My sister Ira whispered, 'Nu sits in here some evenings. She doesn't say anything.' On my third evening, I saw it myself. My mother stood at the door of my room, holding a cup of tea, just looking at my bed. She didn't know I was in the corridor. I understood then that for her, loving me now mostly meant waiting. I went in and sat with her. We didn't talk much. The next morning I set a weekly reminder: call Nu, Sunday, 8 pm. I'm Mawii, and I haven't missed one since.

What did Mawii set a weekly reminder for?
To call Nu on Sunday at 8 pm.
What did Mawii feel on seeing the mother standing at the bedroom door?
Mawii felt moved and tender, understanding how much the mother missed and waited.
What did Mawii do that showed love back?
Mawii sat with the mother that evening and set a weekly call, giving the waiting some regular contact.
How might Ira see her mother's quiet evenings in the room?
Ira probably sees it as a sad, loving habit, which is why she whispered it to Mawii.

Harsha, you think I'm the calmest person in this office. Let your old colleague Maria tell you a secret. When I was twenty-five, my father died in the spring and I went back to work after four days, because that's what we did. I was fine, I told everyone. By autumn I was crying in the printer room and forgetting meetings. My friend Nalini said, "See someone." I said therapy was for weak people. She said, "Then call it maintenance, like servicing a scooter." I went, grumbling. The first counsellor was wrong for me: all questions about my childhood, nothing about now. I nearly quit. Nalini said, "Try another, the way you'd try another doctor." The second one helped. I went for two years, stopped, and went again when my son was born. So when you say you're "just stressed", Harsha, I'm only saying: servicing is not failure.

How many days after her father's death did Maria go back to work?
Four days.
What was young Maria feeling by the autumn?
Maria was overwhelmed and grieving, crying in the printer room and forgetting meetings.
What choice in Maria's story made therapy work for her?
Trying a second counsellor instead of quitting after a poor first fit, as she would with another doctor.
How might Nalini have felt pushing Maria to see someone?
Nalini was probably worried about her friend but patient, reframing therapy as maintenance to get past Maria's resistance.
Why do we sometimes cry when we are very happy?
Strong feelings of any kind can bring tears. Because the body reacts to a surge of emotion, joy can overflow in the same way sadness does.

I'm Rekha. When I was eleven, I heard my parents arguing about a loan and fees through the wall. I understood the fear in their voices.
The next day, my best friend Hafsa asked if I was coming on the school trip to the science museum. I said, "No, I don't like museums." That was a lie. I loved museums.
I did it again that month: no party, no new sandals. I thought I was helping.
Then my mother found the trip form in my bag, unsigned. She told me the truth: Papa's shop had lost a big order, and it would be hard for a few months, not forever. She said, "You don't have to stop being a child."
I went on the trip. I think knowing the truth scared me less than guessing.

Where was the school trip going?
The school trip was to the science museum.
Why did Rekha tell Hafsa she didn't like museums?
Rekha felt worried and anxious after hearing the argument, and gave up things Rekha wanted, trying to help.
What did Rekha's mother do that calmed Rekha?
She explained honestly and simply what had happened and that it wouldn't last forever, and told Rekha there was no need to stop being a child.
How might Hafsa have felt when Rekha claimed not to like museums?
Hafsa might have felt puzzled or disappointed, since Hafsa probably knew Rekha loved museums.

During the summer holidays the power went off every afternoon in Urmila's building in Hyderabad, and the children gathered in Irfan's flat, where the windows caught a breeze. Irfan's father had brought a box of new puzzles: a wooden cube, a metal ring puzzle, a tangram set.
Irfan dived for the cube. Urmila went to the shelf and took down the jigsaw of a parrot she had done at least ten times.
"Try the rings," Irfan said. "Nobody knows how to do it."
"I like the parrot."
"You've done the parrot a hundred times!"
"So? I can do it." She snapped the pieces into place. When Irfan finally solved the cube and shouted, she smiled, but she didn't touch it. The ring puzzle stayed in its box all afternoon.

Which puzzle did Urmila take down?
The jigsaw of a parrot she had done at least ten times.
Why does Urmila keep choosing the parrot jigsaw?
Urmila feels safe with a puzzle she can't get wrong; the new ones might make her feel stupid, so avoiding them keeps the worry away.
How could an adult help Urmila try something new?
Pair her with Irfan on the ring puzzle, praise the trying rather than the solving, and show that getting stuck is part of puzzles, not a sign of being bad at them.
How might Irfan see Urmila's choice?
Irfan finds it puzzling and a bit frustrating that she repeats the parrot "a hundred times" while new puzzles sit waiting.

Dear Madhuri,
I need to tell someone who won't judge me, so here it is.
There's a man at my internship, Karan, who is engaged. We've been staying late together on the same project, and lately he's been texting me at night. Long messages, about how his fiancée 'doesn't understand him' and how I do. And honestly, I've loved it. I've felt special, chosen. For a few weeks I told myself this was different, that the rules didn't apply to something this real.
Then on Saturday I saw his fiancée's photos online. She looked kind. She was holding a card that said '3 months to go!' And I felt sick.
I'd be hurting her, and I'd be setting myself up to be the next one he lies to.
So I've stopped replying to the night texts. I've asked my manager to move me to the other project team. It hurts more than I expected.
Can you come over Sunday? I don't want to be alone with my phone.
Pooja

What did the fiancée's card say?
'3 months to go!'
How had Pooja felt about Karan's night texts?
Pooja felt special and chosen, loving the attention.
What steps did Pooja take to step back?
Stopped replying to the night texts, asked to move to another project team, and reached out to Madhuri for support.
How might Karan's fiancée feel if she knew?
Deeply hurt and betrayed, since she's counting down to the wedding.

You asked why I never took the Singapore job, Maria. Sit, your tea will go cold. At twenty-five, I, Rukmini, the eager young engineer, had an offer there. Anand, whom I was seeing then, had just bought a scooter to take his parents to the temple every Friday in Kochi. He wanted our life right there, near his mother's garden. I wanted the airport. We both knew it. Yet our talks became very polite. "How was work?" "Fine. Yours?" When the offer letter came, I left it in my drawer and said, "Let's discuss after Onam." After Onam, he said, "After my sister's exam." We kept pushing the big question to later, like a box nobody wanted to open. That box does not get lighter with waiting, Maria. It only gets heavier.

Where did Rukmini have a job offer?
Rukmini had a job offer in Singapore.
What was the young Rukmini feeling when she left the offer letter in her drawer?
She felt torn and uneasy, wanting the airport yet afraid of what saying so would do to her and Anand, so she hid behind 'after Onam'.
When the offer letter arrived, what could the young Rukmini have done instead of postponing?
She could have shown Anand the letter and asked plainly how each of them saw the future, even if the answer was hard to hear.
What might Anand have been experiencing as their talks grew polite and short?
Anand probably sensed the distance too, since he also pushed the question to after his sister's exam, perhaps fearing what an honest talk would reveal.

Thursday night
Today Kamal wasn't at the morning meeting, and by eleven the whole team was lost. Nobody knew the client's new file names; nobody had the vendor's number. Kamal always has these. He's the one who sends the checklist the night before, catches the typo in the invoice, quietly books the meeting room none of us remembered. We just assume it happens. At lunch Priti said he had messaged in, exhausted, taking two days off. I felt a bit sick thinking how long it's been since anyone said thanks, me included. I'm writing down three things I can take over from him on Monday, and I'll say thank you before I forget again.
Yash

What did nobody have when Kamal was absent?
Nobody had the vendor's number.
What was Yash feeling after hearing Kamal was exhausted?
Yash felt a bit sick and guilty, realising how long it had been since anyone thanked Kamal.
What choice does Yash make for Monday?
Yash plans to take over three of Kamal's tasks and to thank Kamal before forgetting again.
What might months of quiet fixing have been like for Kamal?
He may have felt relied on but unseen, carrying everyone's gaps without thanks until he was worn out.
Now you try: find R and r for the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5.
The answer is R = 5/2, r = 1.

What do the narrator and the companion do after the blush?

The blush that rose to my own cheeks somehow set us both at ease, for it was a tacit answer to her own. I got her luggage, which included a typewriter, and we took the Underground to Fenchurch Street, after I had sent a wire to my housekeeper to have a sitting-room and bedroom prepared at once for Mrs. Harker.

They both blush, which puts them at ease. The narrator gets her luggage, including a typewriter, sends a wire ahead for a sitting-room and bedroom to be prepared for Mrs. Harker, and they take the Underground to Fenchurch Street.

In the kitchen in Lisbon, baby Yonas started to cry. Abebe, two, stopped playing, looked at him, and carried over his own toy giraffe.

He pushed it into Yonas's hands and patted his head. "There."

Their mother, Sofia, knelt beside them. "Abebe, you saw Yonas was sad and gave him your giraffe. That was kind."

Abebe beamed. A minute later he took the giraffe back, and Sofia let it go.

What toy did Abebe give Yonas?
Abebe gave Yonas his toy giraffe.
What does Abebe's pat on Yonas's head suggest?
It suggests Abebe felt caring and concerned, an early sign of empathy for his crying brother.
Why was Sofia's response a wise one?
Sofia noticed the kind act and named it warmly, and didn't demand Abebe keep sharing when he took the giraffe back.
How might Yonas experience his brother's gesture?
Yonas may feel comforted by the toy and the pat, and calmer as he stops crying.
Why do people complain about "red tape" at government offices?

Red tape means too many official rules and forms that make a simple task slow. It is usually said as a complaint.
Example: Getting the new licence took weeks because of all the red tape.

Uday had been seeing Rhea for two months, and he wanted her to come to the Pune flat for dinner on Saturday and stay late. He had almost just done it, because Harsha never said anything about anything. But that morning he caught himself: silence wasn't the same as being fine.

Over tea he said, "Rhea's coming Saturday evening. Are you okay with that? And should we agree on a rule for guests, like telling each other a day ahead?"

Harsha lowered the newspaper. "Honestly, I have a design deadline Saturday and I'd like the flat quiet till nine. After that's fine."

"Done. And when your cousins visit, I get the same warning."

They wrote "Guests: message a day before. Quiet hours 10 pm" on the fridge whiteboard. Uday felt lighter, and a bit silly for nearly skipping it.

What did Uday and Harsha write on the fridge whiteboard?
"Guests: message a day before. Quiet hours 10 pm."
Why did Uday decide to ask Harsha instead of just inviting Rhea?
He realised that Harsha's silence didn't mean being fine, and felt a bit silly for nearly skipping the conversation.
What does the whiteboard rule do for the two flatmates?
It makes expectations clear for both, so neither has to assume the other doesn't mind.
What did Harsha need that Uday might not have known?
A quiet flat until nine on Saturday because of a design deadline.
Will it snow in Manali next week?
I don't know if it will snow in Manali next week, as I can't check forecasts. A weather page for Manali, checked nearer your travel dates, will tell you.

Can a plant be thirsty or only a person?

People say a plant is thirsty as a way of saying it needs water. Thirsty means wanting or needing a drink. It is an adjective.
Example: The thirsty plant drooped until we watered it.

It's been four months since Parul and I ended things, and my friends still want me to call her toxic. I'm Ankita, and I get why: the last half year was mostly silence and small fights about nothing.

But when I sit with it honestly, that's not the whole story. Parul was the first person who asked what I wanted and waited for the answer. She taught me to say "I need a minute" instead of storming off. She dragged me to Sunday flower markets, and I still go.

We wanted different lives. She wanted to move abroad; I wanted to stay near my family. Nobody was a villain.

Last week I found her old bookmark in a novel. I didn't throw it out and I didn't cry. I just felt a quiet thank-you, and something like letting go. I put the book back on the shelf and made tea.

Where did Parul take Ankita on Sundays?
Parul took Ankita to Sunday flower markets.
What did Ankita feel on finding the old bookmark?
Ankita felt calm and grateful, a quiet thank-you mixed with letting go, rather than anger or grief.
Why is Ankita's way of remembering the relationship a healthy one?
Ankita admits the hard months but also keeps what Parul taught, so there is closure without turning Parul into a villain.
How might Ankita's friends see the breakup differently?
The friends seem protective and angry on Ankita's behalf, so they focus on the silence and fights and want to call Parul toxic.
Put a ball, a dice and a can on a ramp. Which rolls? Which slides? Which can do both?

Answer: The ball rolls. The dice slides. The can rolls on its side and slides or stands on its flat end.

The ball (sphere) is round everywhere. The dice (cube) has only flat faces. The can (cylinder) has a curved side and two flat ends.

On results morning, the flat in Chennai was too quiet. Amma had lit the lamp twice. Appa kept refreshing the school website on his phone. Harsha, seventeen, sat on the sofa eating cereal slowly. 'Aren't you checking?' asked his brother Kishore, thirteen. 'Why? It's just marks. They don't define anything.' He said it the way he had said it all week, flat and bored. Kishore noticed the cereal had gone soggy and Harsha hadn't taken a bite for ten minutes. When Appa said, 'It's up,' Harsha didn't move. Kishore sat down beside him, close. 'I'll read it first if you want.' Harsha's jaw worked. 'Yeah. Okay. You read it.'

How many times had Amma lit the lamp?
Twice.
Why was Harsha acting bored about the results?
He likely cared a lot and was afraid of being disappointed, so acting detached protected him.
What did Kishore get right in how he helped?
He didn't argue with Harsha's act; he sat close and offered to read the result first, which let Harsha accept support.
How might Amma and Appa read Harsha's flat mood?
They might think he truly doesn't care, or see through it, since their own nervousness is obvious.

"Ting-ting!" Madhuri, two, rang the puja bell.

"Gently," Karthik said. "Like this."

Madhuri rang it softly, then clapped when Amma did.

"Namaste to God," Amma said, folding her hands.

Madhuri folded hers, peeking at the lamp.

"She's praying!" Grandma said.

Karthik smiled. "She's copying us. That's enough."

Madhuri blew on the lamp.

"No blowing," he laughed.

What did Madhuri ring?
Madhuri rang the puja bell.
What was Madhuri feeling during the puja?
Madhuri felt happy and curious, drawn by the lamp, the bell and her family's faces.
Why is Karthik's approach to Madhuri's joining in a good one?
He keeps it light and warm, gently guiding without forcing, letting her join out of belonging.
How does Grandma see Madhuri's actions differently from Karthik?
Grandma thinks Madhuri is praying, while Karthik sees it as copying the family, which is enough.

Warden's note, Boys' Hostel, Tuesday.
Since the new rule that phones must be handed in at 9 p.m., Siddharth, fifteen, has changed. He hands his phone in, every night, so he is following the rule. But he walks to the desk at the slowest possible speed, drops the phone into the tray without looking at me, and answers everything with "Hmm" or "Fine." At lights-out he takes fifteen minutes to fold one shirt. His roommate, Omkar, says Siddharth has stopped talking at night too. I can see he's angry. It's coming out as slowness. What I did next: tomorrow I'll ask Siddharth to sit with me for ten minutes and tell me honestly what he thinks of the rule. He may have a point worth hearing.

At what time must phones be handed in?
At 9 p.m.
Why does Siddharth take fifteen minutes to fold one shirt?
He is angry and resentful about the phone rule, and moving slowly lets that anger out while technically obeying.
Why is the warden's plan for tomorrow a good idea?
Inviting Siddharth to say honestly what he thinks gives the anger a direct route, so it doesn't have to leak out as slowness.
How might Omkar feel about Siddharth's silence at night?
Omkar may feel lonely or uncomfortable, missing their chats and unsure what's wrong.

The Christmas market in Madrid was packed. Lucia buckled Santiago into the stroller so he wouldn't get lost.

Santiago did not want the stroller. He stiffened his legs, pushed against the straps and yelled, "No! No!" His hat fell off.

Lucia crouched down. "You want to walk. It's too crowded." She gave him a small drum from the stall to hold.

He banged it, still sniffling, and let her push.

What did Lucia give Santiago to hold?
She gave him a small drum from the stall.
What was Santiago feeling when he pushed against the straps?
Santiago was angry and frustrated at being strapped in when he wanted to walk.
What did Lucia do that helped Santiago calm down?
She named what he wanted, explained simply, and gave him something to do with his hands.
How might the crowd around them see Santiago's yelling?
Some people might feel annoyed, but many would see it as an ordinary toddler moment.

Hither, and thither, on high, glided the snow-white wings of small, unspeckled birds; these were the gentle thoughts of the feminine air; but to and fro in the deeps, far down in the bottomless blue, rushed mighty leviathans, sword-fish, and sharks; and these were the strong, troubled, murderous thinkings of the masculine sea.

What do the white birds and the great fish stand for in this picture?
The small white birds gliding above stand for the gentle thoughts of the feminine air. The mighty fish rushing in the deep stand for the strong, troubled thoughts of the masculine sea.
Pat's Pool Supply has three times as many swimming pools as Pat's Ark & Athletic Wear store. If Pat's Ark & Athletic Wear store has 200 pools, how many pools do they have in total?

Since Pat's Ark & Athletic Wear store has 200 pools, Pat's Pool Supply has 3*200 = 600 swimming pools.
Together, they have 600+200 = 800 swimming pools.
The answer is 800.

Then Sita joined her hands, and sighed,
"O, may thy words be verified!"
The car was turned, which fleet as thought
The mourning queen to Lanka brought.
They led her to the garden, where
Again she yielded to despair,
Lamenting for the chiefs who bled
On earth's cold bosom with the dead.

Then Sita joined her hands and sighed, "Oh, may your words come true!" The chariot, which was as fast as thought, was turned around and brought the mourning queen to Lanka. They led her to the garden, where she gave way to despair again, grieving for the chiefs who had bled and lay among the dead on the cold ground.

The tea stall by the bus stand in Barmer was where Tushar had studied for two years, one elbow on the bench, while buses came and went. Now he was home for the Diwali break after his first term at the engineering institute.
"Big-city boy," Zubin teased, pouring tea. "How is it?"
"Good," Tushar said. He meant to say more.
The truth was strange. He'd dreamed of that campus every night for two years. Now he was there, and he felt oddly empty, like a kite with the string cut.
"You look tired," Zubin said.
"I don't know what I'm running for anymore," Tushar said. "Before, every day had a point."
Zubin sat beside him. "Then find a new point. Smaller. You'll figure it out."
Tushar looked at the bench where he used to study and felt something like homesickness for his old hunger.

Where had Tushar studied for two years?
At the tea stall by the bus stand in Barmer, one elbow on the bench.
What was Tushar feeling when he said he did not know what he was running for?
He felt empty and weary, as if the goal that used to give him direction was gone.
What would you advise Tushar?
He could set smaller new goals at the institute, like a club or project, and keep talking with friends like Zubin about how he feels.
How does Zubin see Tushar's mood?
Zubin notices he looks tired and responds with warmth, encouraging him to find a new purpose.

Monday. The alarm shrieked across the open office. Jasleen looked at Noor, Noor looked at the manager, the manager looked at his screen. Nobody moved. Jasleen stayed seated too, heart thumping, and it stopped after a minute. Later they said it was a test.
Wednesday. At lunch, Jasleen asked Noor, "Why didn't we get up?"
Noor shrugged. "Nobody else did. I'd have felt silly."
"Me too. I was watching everyone watch everyone."
Friday, two weeks later. The alarm went off again during a call. Jasleen felt the same pull to look around. This time she said "Sorry, fire alarm" into her headset, stood, and walked to the stairs. Behind her she heard Noor's chair, then more chairs. Half the floor followed her down.

What did Jasleen say into her headset when the alarm rang the second time?
She said "Sorry, fire alarm" into her headset.
What was Jasleen feeling on Monday when she stayed seated?
She felt nervous, with her heart thumping, but stuck waiting because everyone else was waiting too.
What changed between Monday and the second alarm, and what made it work?
Talking about it with Noor helped Jasleen name the pull to look around; the second time she moved first, and others followed her.
How might Noor experience the second alarm compared with the first?
Noor probably felt relieved to have someone to follow, since on Monday she stayed seated because she would have felt silly moving alone.

I'm Ira, and I manage the design team at a small publishing house. Our director gave a talk in January about "embracing challenge" and "loving feedback". I watched Pema, one of my best illustrators, nod through it. Over the next weeks I kept an eye on her. She didn't try the new digital painting style the director had praised. When I asked why, she said lightly, "No time. The deadlines are the same." I noticed she hadn't had feedback on her work since her probation ended. I can't know everything she was feeling. But I stopped repeating the slogans. I blocked Friday afternoons for practice and sat with her every other week to look at her sketches. By March she'd done a whole cover in the new style, and asked me what to fix.

What did Ira block Friday afternoons for?
Practice.
What might Pema's light answer, "No time", suggest about how she felt?
She may have felt the new style was a risk she couldn't afford with the same deadlines and no feedback, so trying it seemed unsafe.
Which choices by Ira made the new style possible?
Blocking practice time and giving regular feedback on sketches, instead of repeating the director's slogans.
How might the director see the change if shown Pema's new cover?
The director might realise that talks alone didn't do it, and that time and feedback turned the idea into real work.

14 March, late.
Went to Minakshi's after work with samosas. Her easel is still in the corner with the same half-painted sky from January. She used to paint every Sunday. Today she told me she hasn't opened her laptop for job applications in three weeks, and she said it flatly, like reading out a bus timetable. The plants on the sill have gone brown.
I almost said the usual thing: "Just do one application, yaar, a bit of discipline!" I stopped. This doesn't look like laziness. She looks tired all the way through.
So I said, "You've seemed really flat for weeks. Would you talk to a doctor or a counsellor? I can sit with you while you book it."
She was quiet for a long time, then nodded. We found a clinic slot for Saturday together.
Neelam

How long had it been since Minakshi opened her laptop for job applications?
Three weeks.
What was Neelam feeling when stopping the usual "discipline" line?
Neelam was worried and concerned, sensing from the untouched easel, brown plants and flat voice that this was more than laziness.
Which choice worked, and why?
Naming the flatness gently and offering to sit together while booking a doctor or counsellor worked, because it gave help without blame and made the first step easier.
What might it have been like for Minakshi to hear "a bit of discipline" instead?
She would likely have felt ashamed and more alone, as if her tiredness were a character flaw, and might have shut down rather than agreeing to get help. 🤍

Saturday
Today was the family puja at Ajoba's house. Only the eldest son of each branch got to do the aarti with the big lamp, so Dada, my older brother, did it and I just stood behind. I've practised the aarti song more than him! My face got hot and I stared at the floor.
Afterwards Kaka found me sitting on the stairs. He didn't say 'stop sulking'. He sat down and said, 'It's an old family custom. I was a second son too, and I minded.' He listened to everything. Then he gave me the bell to ring at the evening aarti.
At school, Jasleen said any kid can help serve langar at her gurdwara. I wish our custom were like that. But at least Kaka listened.
Omkar

What did Kaka give Omkar?
The bell to ring at the evening aarti.
What was Omkar feeling while standing behind during the aarti?
Omkar felt hurt and left out, face hot and eyes on the floor, after practising the song more than Dada.
What did Kaka do that a calm adult could copy?
He sat down with Omkar, explained the custom honestly, shared his own hurt as a second son, listened fully and found a real role.
How might Dada feel if he knew Omkar was hurt?
Dada might feel awkward or sorry, and could offer to share the lamp or practise the song together.

Jordan decides to start an exercise program when he weighs 250 pounds.  For the first 4 weeks, he loses 3 pounds a week.  After that, he loses 2 pounds a week for 8 weeks.  How much does Jordan now weigh?

He loses 3 pounds a week for 4 weeks for a total of 3*4= 12 pounds
He loses 2 pounds a week for 8 weeks for a total of 2*8 = 16 pounds
All total he has lost 12+16 = 28 pounds
Jordan weighed 250 pounds and has lost 28 pounds so he now weighs 250-28 = 222 pounds
The answer is 222.

A message arrived on a rainy Tuesday in Toronto: "Dalia? It's Siddiq. I know it's been six years. I've thought about you a lot." Dalia read it standing in the kitchen with a wooden spoon in her hand. Pleased, first, in a rush. Then wary, then a small hot flicker of resentment: six years of birthdays without a word, and now this.

She put the spoon down and typed, "It's really good to hear from you. I'll be honest, I was hurt when we lost touch. I'd like to catch up, slowly."

Siddiq answered within minutes, apologising for going silent after the move and asking how her mother was. They arranged a video call for Saturday. Dalia didn't pretend the gap wasn't there, and she didn't plan a lecture. She would see who showed up.

How many years had passed since Siddiq last got in touch?
Siddiq wrote, 'I know it's been six years.'
What did Dalia feel on reading the message?
Pleased first, then wary, then a small flicker of resentment about the years of silence.
How did Dalia reply, and why does it help?
She said it was good to hear from Siddiq, named the hurt honestly and asked to catch up slowly, which neither hides the gap nor punishes.
How might Siddiq have felt when sending the first message?
Probably nervous about being turned away, since Siddiq apologised quickly for the silence once Dalia answered.

I'm Tanuja from the flat opposite, and I watched Jomon all through Christmas week.
Jomon, eleven, and his little brother Abel fought constantly over the one bicycle. Once Abel pushed him, and Jomon yelled, "You ruin everything!"
But on Christmas Eve I saw Jomon on the balcony with his grandfather, Appachan, making a paper star lantern. Appachan showed him how to fold the points. Jomon kept glancing at Abel, who was sulking inside.
Then Jomon called him. "Abel, hold the frame. You're good at holding still."
Abel came running. The star went up crooked, and all three laughed. I don't know what made Jomon change his mind, but the bicycle fight didn't happen that evening.

What were Jomon and Appachan making on the balcony?
They were making a paper star lantern.
What might Jomon have been feeling when he kept glancing at Abel?
He may have felt guilty or sorry for yelling, and wanted to include his little brother.
How could Appachan help the brothers get along?
He could keep giving them projects that need both of them, like the lantern, where each has a job.

Notes, every single day, on her cycle, in the rain.

At the college chemistry lab, Kiran, a second-year student, looked at a cloudy solution and said, "It's contaminated. I can tell."

His lab partner Rekha frowned. "How?"

"Just a feeling."

The lab assistant, who had worked there fifteen years, tested it. It was fine; the cloudiness was normal for that reaction.

Kiran felt his face go hot. He'd been so sure.

"Your gut isn't trained yet," the assistant said kindly. "Mine is, because I've seen this reaction a thousand times and checked every time."

Rekha nudged him. "Let's test first, feel later." For the rest of the term, Kiran wrote his guess before every test and compared. By the end, he was right more often.

How long had the lab assistant worked there?
Fifteen years.
How did Kiran feel when the solution turned out to be fine?
He felt embarrassed, his face hot, because his gut feeling had been so sure.
What helped Kiran's intuition improve over the term?
Writing his guess before every test and comparing it with the result gave him honest feedback.
How might Rekha see Kiran's confident guesses?
Rekha is doubtful but supportive, suggesting they test first and trust feelings later.
Jerome bought 5 new toy cars last month. This month he bought twice as many so that he has 40 toy cars now. How many toy cars did Jerome have originally?

Jerome bought 5 x 2 = 10 toy cars this month.
So he bought a total of 5 + 10 = 15 toy cars.
Therefore, Jerome had 40 - 15 = 25 toy cars originally.
The answer is 25.
Using the word "and", write a sentence about a stationery shop that lists three things I can buy there.
At the stationery shop I can buy pencils, notebooks and erasers.

How old was Sarala Bai when she taught children in secret?
Sixteen.

Awed and inspired; her skin tingled all over, even though she doubted she could be that brave.
How did Gopika turn her admiration into action?
She read a storybook with the watchman's little daughter, serving in a small way.
How did Irfan see Gopika's worry about not being brave?
He thought she could still help in her own way, like teaching reading.

"Sit down, you're useless, you'll never amount to anything."
What was Irfan feeling in the classroom, and how can you tell?

Tom decides to buy some shirts from his favorite fandoms because there is a sale on his favorite website.  He buys 5 t-shirts from each of his 4 favorite fandoms.  The shirts normally cost $15 each but there is a 20% off sale.   The order qualified for free shipping but he still needed to pay 10% tax.  How much did he pay?

He bought 5*4=20 shirts
The discount saves him 15*.2=$3 per shirt
So each shirt cost 15-3=$12
So the total order cost 20*12=$240
Tax added 240*.1=$24
So he paid 240+24=$264
The answer is 264.

Shreya's parents were at a wedding in Nashik, and she was home alone with her little brother Manoj, trying to make dinner and finish her geography project. Then her phone buzzed.

"Congratulations! You are selected for a part-time online job. Earn 3,000 daily. Pay 199 registration fee. We will send an OTP, please share it to confirm."

Three thousand a day. Shreya's heart leapt. She could buy the new geometry box, and Manoj's cycle bell. Then the OTP arrived on her mother's phone, which was linked to the family account and lying on the table.

Manoj was tugging at her sleeve, the dal was boiling over, and a second message came: "Hurry, offer expires in 5 minutes."

The hurry made her stop. Why would a real job rush her? Why would it need money and a code?

She turned off the stove and called her father. "Papa, someone is asking for the OTP on Mummy's phone for a job."

"Don't share it. Never. Block them. Well done for calling," he said. "I'll call the bank right now."

How much registration fee did the message ask for?
The message asked for a 199 registration fee.
What was Shreya feeling when she read the offer?
Shreya felt excited and hopeful at first, then uneasy when the message rushed her.
What did Shreya do that was wise, and why?
Shreya stopped, did not share the OTP and called her father, because real offers never ask for money or codes and a parent could act quickly.
How did Papa respond to Shreya's call?
Papa told her never to share the OTP, praised her for calling and called the bank right away.

In the only photocopy shop on Bhadrachalam's market road, a crowd pressed around the printer as board results came out one by one. Yash's cousin Rashmi got her sheet first: 89 in social science. "I told you I'm naturally sharp," she announced to the shopkeeper, who hadn't asked. Then Yash's page slid out. Mathematics: 47. He folded it quickly. "The paper setter wanted us to fail," he said. "Question 14 wasn't even in the syllabus. And the invigilator kept walking up and down. How can anyone think?" Rashmi raised an eyebrow. "Question 14 was in the sample paper, Yash." "Sample paper is different," he muttered. On the tractor ride home he didn't take out the marks sheet once, and he didn't ask Rashmi how she'd studied.

Which question did Yash say wasn't in the syllabus?
Yash said Question 14 wasn't even in the syllabus.
Why does Yash insist the sample paper is different?
Yash feels embarrassed and defensive, because admitting Question 14 was in the sample paper would mean he missed something. Blaming the setter protects how he sees himself.
What could Yash do on the ride home that would actually help?
He could look at the marks sheet and ask Rashmi how she studied, to find what to change next time.
What would change if Rashmi had scored 47 and Yash 89?
They would likely swap stories, with the low scorer blaming the paper and the high scorer claiming talent, since both are guarding their self-image.

When the stitching line fell behind again, Pankaj kicked a stool so hard it split, then stood over a young trainee, shouting inches from her face. She shrank back against the wall. Hemant had seen this before: the punched locker, the phone thrown at the wall, people going quiet when Pankaj walked in. This wasn't a bad day. It was a pattern. The supervisor moved her to another line and said a formal warning would follow. At the end of the shift Hemant found Pankaj alone by the gate. "Bhai, people are scared of you. Pankaj kicked a stool so hard it split.
What did Hemant realise about Pankaj's anger, and how did it make him feel?
Hemant was alarmed to realise it wasn't a bad day but a pattern that frightened people.
In what order did Hemant act, and why?
Hemant put safety first by stepping in and taking the trainee to the supervisor, then later urged Pankaj privately to see the company counsellor.
What might Pankaj be feeling as he stares at the split stool?
Pankaj may be feeling shaken or ashamed, perhaps seeing the damage clearly for the first time, though he says nothing.

By the third time her father left the gas on, Gurpreet stopped pretending it was fine. She worked in Gurgaon, and her father, retired and widowed, lived with her in their Janakpuri flat. His memory had been slipping for a year. She worked nine to six, cooked at night, and woke at 3 a.m. to check on him. Her sister Sarika, in Toronto, sent money and advice in equal amounts: "You should take him to the doctor." "I did," Gurpreet typed, too sharply. After that she sat down and made a list: what she could do, what she couldn't, what would cost money. She had a gas shut-off valve fitted, asked the aunty next door to look in at lunch, and visited a day centre for elders two streets away. The first day her father went, he came home talking about a carrom game. That night Gurpreet slept through for the first time in months.

Where does Gurpreet's sister Sarika live?
In Toronto.
What does Gurpreet typing 'I did' too sharply suggest?
Gurpreet felt exhausted and resentful, carrying the daily care while getting advice from far away.
Which of Gurpreet's steps made the care more sustainable?
Listing what she could and couldn't do, fitting a gas valve, arranging a neighbour's lunchtime check and finding a day centre, so she wasn't alone.
How might Sarika feel sending money from far away?
Sarika probably feels guilty and worried at being so far, which may come out as advice that sounds like blame.

The class wears the colour of their favourite hero, and Ira wears an orange band and a scarf.

The hospital car park was tight, and Leela was reversing out of a slot when she felt the bump. The bumper of a white hatchback, backing out opposite, had met hers.
The other driver, Kishore, got out red-faced. "You didn't even look!"
Leela felt her pulse jump, but kept her voice level. "Are you hurt? Anyone in your car?" He shook his head. She checked her passenger seat: her mother, just discharged, was fine, only startled.
"Let's just take down details," Leela said. She photographed both cars from four sides, the scratches up close, and the slot markings. She wrote his number plate and the name of his insurer from the sticker on his windscreen, and gave him hers.
The car park security guard came over. "Do you need police?"
"Nobody's hurt, and we've swapped details," Leela said. "But could you note it in your register?" The guard did. Kishore, calmer now, shook her hand.

How many sides did Leela photograph the cars from?
She photographed both cars from four sides.
How did Leela feel when Kishore shouted, and how can you tell?
She felt her pulse jump with alarm, but kept her voice level and asked first whether anyone was hurt.
What else could Leela do once she gets home?
She could inform her insurer while the details are fresh, sending the photos and the guard's register note.
How might Kishore see the way Leela handled it?
Kishore arrived angry but calmed down, likely because her steady questions and fair exchange of details left nothing to fight about.

Aadhya sat on the shop's stool every afternoon with a notebook, copying whatever Yash did: counting coins, tapping the scale, even the sigh he gave when the wholesaler's truck came late. Yash felt warm, and somehow heavy.

One afternoon a jar slipped and he muttered a rude word. From the stool came Aadhya's small voice, repeating it perfectly. Yash winced, then crouched down. "That word was wrong, and I shouldn't have said it. I'm sorry."

Later he gave a customer the wrong change, noticed it, and walked after her down the lane to fix it, Aadhya trotting behind. That night, she wrote a wobbly "sorry" in her notebook. Yash smiled. One day she'd see him as only a man who makes mistakes, and he hoped she would still love him.

What did Aadhya bring to the stool every afternoon?
Aadhya brought a notebook.
Why did Yash feel warm and heavy?
Yash is touched that Aadhya admires him, but feels the weight of being copied in everything, including mistakes.

He crouched, said the word was wrong and apologised, then later walked after a customer to fix the wrong change.
What might Aadhya be learning from watching Yash?
That grown-ups make mistakes and put them right; she even writes a wobbly 'sorry' in her notebook.

Team lead's note, quarterly review
Kavitha, one of our strongest designers, has always spoken the most in meetings: quick, full of ideas, often answering questions meant for others. Last month in her feedback, I mentioned that newer team members like Swati rarely spoke when she was in the room.
Kavitha took it seriously. In today's review she kept a small tally on her notepad: each time she spoke, one line. After four lines she stopped and asked, "Swati, you worked on the checkout flow. What did you notice?"
Swati hesitated, then gave the best observation of the meeting: users were abandoning the page at the address step.
After the meeting, Kavitha told me the tally felt silly at first but useful. "I didn't realise how much space I was taking."
What I will do next: I will ask Kavitha to mentor Swati on the checkout redesign.

What did Kavitha keep on her notepad?
She kept a small tally, one line each time she spoke.
What was Kavitha feeling after the meeting?
Kavitha felt a little surprised and self-conscious at how much space she'd been taking, but pleased the tally helped.
Why does Kavitha's habit matter, especially for someone like her?
As a strong, dominant speaker, counting turns and asking quieter colleagues for input makes room for ideas that would otherwise be lost.
How might Swati have experienced being asked directly?
Swati probably felt nervous but valued, finally given room to share the best observation of the meeting.

A salon has the same amount of customers every day. Each customer needs 1 can of hairspray during the styling and is also given 1 can of hairspray to take home. The salon also buys an extra 5 cans of hairspray each day to ensure there is never a shortage. If the salon buys 33 cans of hairspray every day, how many customers do they have each day?

Each customer needs 1 can of hairspray for styling + 1 can of hairspray to take home = 2 cans of hairspray.
So the salon has a total of 28 cans of hairspray / 2 cans of hairspray per customer = 14 customers.
The answer is 14.

She had been sleeping on a bus-stand bench for a month since the landlord changed the locks, and cleaning offices at night. "I'll fill it later," she said, and folded it into a tiny square. A colleague muttered that some people just don't try. Farida thought: when every hour is about tonight's food and a safe corner, there is no room left for next year. That's scarcity, not a lack of effort. She found Nandini a bed at the working women's hostel and meal tokens for two weeks. On the fourteenth day, Nandini asked her about the tailoring course.

Where had Nandini been sleeping for a month?
On a bus-stand bench, since the landlord changed the locks.
What does Nandini folding the form into a tiny square suggest?
It suggests she felt overwhelmed and could not face planning ahead while she was worried about food and a safe place to sleep.
Which choice by Farida made the difference, and why?
Farida arranged a hostel bed and meal tokens first instead of pushing the form, and once those basics were steady, Nandini had room in her mind to ask about the course.
How does the colleague see Nandini, and what does that miss?
The colleague sees someone who doesn't try, which misses that she was exhausted and focused on surviving each night.

metadata.subtype: Long scarcity leaves little room for planning [Observer]

Read this:

I'm Anand, from the flat across the landing. This Diwali I noticed Naveen doing strange things.
When gifts came, Naveen didn't tear the wrapping. Naveen folded it flat and put it in a box marked "next year". The sweets came in plastic trays; Naveen washed them and took them down to the aunty who sells flowers, for her marigolds.
On Diwali night the whole building was blazing. At midnight, Naveen went out and switched their string lights off, leaving just the clay diyas burning. I asked why.
"Lights on all night for nobody," Naveen said. "The diyas are prettier anyway."
I can't tell if Naveen is doing it for the planet or just likes order. But this year, our landing had a box for folded paper too. 🪔

What did Naveen do with the plastic sweet trays?
Naveen washed them and took them down to the aunty who sells flowers, for her marigolds.
What does Naveen's answer about the lights suggest?
It suggests Naveen was bothered by the waste but content with less, enjoying the diyas more than the blazing string lights.
How could Naveen's family build on these habits?
They could make the reuse box and the midnight switch-off a shared family routine, not just Naveen's.
Why might Anand be unsure of Naveen's reasons?
Anand is only watching from across the landing, so Anand can see the actions but not know what Naveen really thinks.
A lift is on floor 6. It goes DOWN 9 floors. Floors below the ground floor (floor 0) are numbered -1, -2, -3 ... Which floor is it on now?

Answer: 6 + (-9) = -3. The lift is on floor -3 (the third basement).

Going down 9 floors is adding -9. Use counters: 6 positive counters and 9 negative counters. + + + + + + - - - - - - - - - Pair each + with a -: that makes 6 zero pairs, and each zero pair is worth 0. Cancel them. 3 negative counters are left, so the answer is -3. Rule: DIFFERENT signs, so subtract the sizes: 9 - 6 = 3, and take the sign of the bigger size (9 is negative), giving -3.
Who is my favourite teacher?
I don't know, because you haven't told me and I can't see your school. Tell me the name, and I can help you write a thank-you note.

"Can I say something without it being a fight?" Yash asked. They were sitting on the college steps with two cups of chai, the first calm evening in weeks.
Simran nodded.
"When you're upset and I don't answer, you text more. And when you text more, I feel trapped, so I go quiet. And then you text even more."
Simran laughed a little, sadly. "And when you go quiet, I feel like you've left. So I chase. It's like a hamster wheel."
"So it's not you," Yash said slowly, "and it's not me. It's the wheel."
"Then let's fight the wheel," said Simran, and put her head on his shoulder.

Where were Yash and Simran sitting?
On the college steps, with two cups of chai.
What was Simran feeling as she laughed a little, sadly?
She felt sad but relieved, recognising herself in the pattern Yash described.
What was the turning point in this conversation?
They named the loop together in a calm moment and decided it was the wheel they were fighting, not each other.
How might Yash be experiencing the moment Simran rests her head on his shoulder?
He likely feels relieved and closer to her, since naming the pattern did not turn into another fight.

metadata.subtype: Stage 5: Seeing the loop, not the villain [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Friday night
Launch day for the booking page. At 10 a.m. a client from the Pune office emailed our whole team: "Page is confusing. Who approved this?" My chest went tight and for an hour it was the only thing in my head.
Then I did the thing Joseph and I agreed on after last year's burnout: before deciding how a day went, write the wins next to the hits.
Wins: 412 bookings in the first day. Two emails from users saying it was easier than the old form. My lead said "clean work" in the stand-up. Mobile loading fixed after a week of fighting it. Joseph brought the good biscuits.
Hits: one angry client. One button label that honestly is confusing; I'll fix it Monday.
Looking at the page, it was a good day with one bad email in it. Not a bad day. I'm going to bed.
— Anjali

How many bookings came in on the first day?
412 bookings in the first day.
What was Anjali feeling after the angry email, and what shows it?
Anjali felt shaken and worried, with a tight chest and the email being the only thing on Anjali's mind for an hour.
Which habit helped Anjali decide how the day really went?
Writing the wins next to the hits, which let the bookings, the users' thanks and the lead's praise count as much as one angry email, while still fixing the confusing button.
What would change if Anjali had judged the day only by the client's email?
Anjali might have gone to bed thinking the launch failed, missed the real good news, and slid back towards the burnout of last year.

What honour is planned for the captain?

Of course the verdict was an open one. There is no evidence to adduce; and whether or not the man himself committed the murders there is now none to say. The folk here hold almost universally that the captain is simply a hero, and he is to be given a public funeral. Already it is arranged that his body is to be taken with a train of boats up the Esk for a piece and then brought back to Tate Hill Pier and up the abbey steps; for he is to be buried in the churchyard on the cliff. The owners of more than a hundred boats have already given in their names as wishing to follow him to the grave.
A public funeral. His body will go up the Esk with a line of boats and then be buried in the churchyard on the cliff, with over a hundred boats following.
My sister-in-law is a bank manager. Check the hyphen and article.

Your wording works.
Why: "Sister-in-law" has hyphens; "a" suits the consonant sound in "bank".

Read this:

I've worked with Payal at the NGO for two years. Last month she had to decide whether to hire Jeevan, a candidate who charmed everyone in the interview.

Most of us said, "Hire him, he's great." Payal said, "I like him too. That's a feeling. Let me check."

She called his references and read through his previous project reports. One report was excellent. But two references said he often missed deadlines.

She didn't reject him. She hired him on a three-month trial with clear deadlines. I don't know what she felt inside. But I saw her write down her first feeling, then write the evidence under it before deciding.

What did two references say about Jeevan?
That he often missed deadlines.
What does Payal's line "That's a feeling. Let me check" suggest?
It suggests she felt warm toward Jeevan but was cautious, treating the feeling as information rather than a decision.
What could the rest of the team copy from Payal's approach?
Write down the first feeling, then gather evidence for and against it before a big decision.
How might Jeevan feel about a three-month trial?
Jeevan might feel a little disappointed but also given a fair chance to prove himself.

In Nairobi, Wanjiru, fifteen, had to be home by six-thirty, before dark. Her brother Kaito, sixteen, came home at nine from football, sometimes later. "It's for your safety," Mum said. Wanjiru stood in the kitchen, arms crossed. "So you trust him and not me?" Mum's face tightened. "It's not about trust. The road from the matatu stop is dark." "It's dark for Kaito too!" Kaito looked up from his phone. "She's got a point."
That Sunday they sat together at the table. Mum explained what actually worried her: the unlit road, the men who hung around the stage at night. Wanjiru listened. Then she suggested both of them share their location, both come home by seven-thirty on school nights, and whoever is later gets picked up by Dad. Mum thought, then nodded. Wanjiru felt heard for the first time. Kaito groaned about the new curfew, then laughed.

What time did Wanjiru have to be home?
By six-thirty, before dark.
How did Wanjiru feel about the different curfews?
She felt distrusted and resentful, asking whether Mum trusted Kaito and not her.
What made the new rule fairer?
They talked openly about the real risks, then set the same curfew, location sharing and a pickup plan for both children.
How might Mum have felt when Wanjiru asked about trust?
Mum probably felt hurt and defensive, because she saw the rule as protection, not distrust.

Sana washed 18 cups and 9 plates. How many things did she wash?
What is the meaning of "welcome"?

1. That makes 27. Because 18 + 9 = 27.
2. To welcome someone is to greet them in a kind and happy way when they arrive.

Socorro is preparing for a math contest. She needs to train for a total of 5 hours. Each day, she answers problems about multiplication for 10 minutes and then division problems for 20 minutes. How many days will it take for her to complete her training?

Socorro trains for a total of 10 + 20 = 30 minutes each day.
She needs to train for a total of 5 x 60 = 300 minutes since an hour has 60 minutes.
Therefore, she will complete her training in 300/30 = 10 days.
The answer is 10.
Lightening flashed across the sky, and then the thunder rolled. Check the first word.

Lightning flashed across the sky, and then the thunder rolled.
Why: The sky flash is "lightning"; "lightening" means making lighter.

Read this:

Shreya didi,
You're lucky you're in hostel. Last night Papa and I had the biggest fight. I asked to go to the late show with my friends and he said no, and then he started shouting about my marks. Yes, I shouted back. But I was only shouting because I've had three tests this week and I'm exhausted. He shouts because he wants to control my whole life. That's just how he is.
Then Mummy told me this morning that his office has been cutting jobs and he's scared about it. I didn't know. But still, he could just say that instead of shouting.
Anyway. Call me Sunday.
Lokesh

What did Mummy tell Lokesh this morning?
That Papa's office has been cutting jobs and he's scared about it.
Why does Lokesh feel Papa's shouting is different from Lokesh's own?
Lokesh feels exhausted and sees that as the reason for shouting back, but sees Papa's shouting as a wish to control, not as fear.
What would help Lokesh and Papa understand each other?
Each could say what is weighing on them, Lokesh's three tests and Papa's job worries, before judging the other.
How might Papa see the fight?
Papa may think Lokesh is being difficult, while seeing his own shouting as worry about marks and his job.

Read this:

I'm Arohi, and last Friday I learned something about my brain. Kamal Bhaiya took ages in the bathroom, so I, his little sister, had no time for breakfast and ran to the bus with an empty stomach.
In history, Ma'am was telling us about old trade routes and camels carrying spices. Usually I love that stuff. But all I could think about was Mummy's aloo paratha. My stomach growled so loudly the boy next to me laughed. When Ma'am asked me a question, I hadn't even heard it. I felt so silly.
At break I ate two bananas and my friend's poha. In the afternoon, history made sense again. Now I keep a biscuit packet in my bag.

What did Arohi eat at break?
Two bananas and her friend's poha.
Why did Arohi feel silly when Ma'am asked her a question?
She hadn't even heard it because her mind was stuck on food, even though she usually loves history.
What choice did Arohi make after that day, and why is it a good one?
She keeps a biscuit packet in her bag, so a missed breakfast won't take over her mind in class again.
How might Ma'am have seen Arohi when she didn't answer?
Ma'am might have thought Arohi wasn't paying attention, not knowing she was too hungry to follow the lesson.
I'd like a diary entry, about 75 words, for a shopkeeper at the end of a very slow day with almost no customers.

Dear Diary,
It was a very slow day. Only a few customers came, and some of them just asked for directions. I sat behind the counter and arranged the shelves three times. Still, an old customer came in for her bread and chatted with me for half an hour. That was nice. Tomorrow is a new day, and hopefully it will bring people back to the shop.
Write a two-line forecast for a foggy morning, both lines using "will".

Tomorrow morning will begin with thick fog on the roads.
The fog will slowly lift by the afternoon.

A 26-mile circular marathon has four checkpoints inside it. The first is one mile from the start line, and the last checkpoint is one mile from the finish line. The checkpoints have equal spacing between them. How many miles apart are each of the consecutive checkpoints between the start-finish line?

The checkpoints are 1 mile from the start and finish, so they are spaced along 26 - 1 - 1 = 24 miles.
There are 4 equally spaced checkpoints, so the checkpoints are 24 / 4 = 6 miles apart.
The answer is 6.

On the kitchen floor of the Vizag flat, Chaitanya watched his ball roll behind the gas cylinder. His amma was chopping beans, knife tapping. "Amma. Amma! Amma!" He pointed hard at the cylinder, whole arm straight. The knife kept tapping. "Amma!" Louder, the finger jabbing. Amma glanced down, followed the arm and put the knife aside. "Ball gone? Wait, kanna, I'll get it."

What was Amma chopping?
She was chopping beans.
What does Chaitanya's jabbing finger suggest about how he feels?
He feels impatient and insistent, desperate for Amma to see where his ball went.
What else could Chaitanya try if calling doesn't work?
He could walk to Amma and tug her hand, because getting closer is harder to miss than calling from the floor.
How does the calling sound to Amma at the chopping board?
At first it blends into her work, but once she looks, the pointing arm tells her exactly what he wants.

At the small rural bank branch in Satara, the morning rush had just begun when a customer's water bottle burst near the entrance. A pool spread across the tiles right where an elderly man with a walking stick was heading. Nilesh, the clerk at the first counter, didn't stop to call the cleaner or fill in the maintenance book. "Slippery floor, old man coming, ten seconds to fix," he thought, and grabbed the mop from the corner. He wiped the water in three strokes and stood the yellow sign beside it. The man stepped past safely. Gargi, at the next counter, raised her eyebrows. "You usually plan everything." Nilesh shrugged. "Not everything needs a plan. That just needed a mop."

What did Nilesh use to clean the water?
The mop from the corner, plus the yellow sign beside it.
What was Nilesh thinking when he grabbed the mop?
He felt a quick jolt of concern for the elderly man and judged it a ten-second job where speed mattered more than planning.
When would quick action like this be the wrong choice?
When a problem is big or unclear, like a leak from the ceiling, it's better to stop, call the right person and plan.
How does Gargi see Nilesh's quick move?
Gargi seems surprised and a bit amused, because he usually plans everything.

messages.content: Our neighbour practises the flute at dawn and I actually enjoy it. Is that weird?
Not at all. Hearing someone practise is often like a free concert. Do you know the tune?
No, but it's calm. It makes my mornings better.
Then you could tell them you like it. Musicians are usually glad to hear that someone enjoys their practice, and it might make their early mornings better too.

Reena: can't sleep. I start at the new college on Monday
Damini: what's the scary part?
Reena: everything. So I'm playing it through like a film. Alarm at 6:30, tea in the mess, walk to the bus stop by 7:15
Damini: and then?
Reena: the 41 bus, 25 mins to college. I saved the route offline. If I miss it, the next one is at 7:45, still on time. Lunch: the canteen behind the library, a senior said it's cheap. I'll keep cash for it in case the payment app is down
Damini: look at you with a plan for a missed bus
Reena: it's just tiny answers. Bus missed? Next bus. No signal? Saved map. Nobody to sit with? Book in the bag
Damini: how's the panic?
Reena: smaller. not gone, but smaller 🙂

How long does the bus ride take, and when is the next bus if Reena misses it?
The 41 bus takes 25 mins to college, and the next one is at 7:45.
How does Reena feel about the first day, and how has that changed?
Reena is anxious, since the day feels scary and sleep won't come, but the panic feels smaller after playing the day through.
What could help Reena if the fear comes back on Sunday night?
Reena could share the plan with Damini or a college senior, because saying it aloud makes gaps easy to spot.
How might Damini see Reena's planning?
Damini may feel amused and proud, since the reply look at you with a plan for a missed bus shows warmth toward such careful preparation.
