messages.content: To earn an airplane pilot certificate, Sangita is required to fly 1,500 hours. She has already completed 50 hours of day flying, 9 hours of night flying, and 121 hours flying cross-country. To meet her goal in exactly 6 months, how many hours per month must Sangita fly?

Sangita has already flown for a total of 50 hours + 9 hours + 121 hours = 180 hours
The flight time she has remaining is 1500 hours - 180 hours = 1320 hours
Sangita's monthly target must therefore be 1320 hours / 6 months = 220 hours/month
The answer is 220.
There are 20 boys and 11 girls in the second grade and twice that number in the third grade. How many students are in grades 2 and 3?

There are 20 + 11 = 31 students in second grade.
There are 31 x 2 = 62 students in third grade.
In total, there are 31 + 62 = 93 students.
The answer is 93.

Mridul here, writing about my little cousin Eshaan, who is five. Yesterday I watched him at the window with his cup of milk when it started to hail. He stopped mid-sip, tilted his head and frowned. “Huh? It's raining ice?” He held out his hand and caught a piece of ice, then stared as it vanished. I couldn't tell if he was scared or just thinking. I said, “It's frozen rain.” He nodded slowly, then put another piece in the sink to watch.

What did Eshaan catch in his hand?
He caught a piece of ice in his hand.
What was Eshaan most likely feeling when he tilted his head and frowned, and what else could it be?
Most likely puzzled, because ice falling did not fit what he knew about rain, and he said “Huh?”. Mridul could not be sure, so he might also have been a little scared.
How could Mridul help Eshaan with his puzzlement?
Explain simply that it is frozen rain, then let him try his own ideas, like watching a piece melt in the sink.
Why might Mridul find it hard to read Eshaan's face?
A frown and a tilted head can show worry or thinking, and Eshaan did not say which. Mridul admits not knowing if he was scared.

In the university hostel common room in Hyderabad, Dolma had been laughing too loudly at the television all week. Her childhood friend in Gangtok had died in a landslide, and she hadn't been able to go home. She told everyone she was fine. Naveen, the student hostel representative, had seen her sitting alone on the stairs at 2 a.m. twice. On Friday evening he sat down near her, not too close. "Dolma, I heard about your friend. I'm really sorry." She stared at the screen. "I'm fine." "You don't have to be. Would it help to do something for her? Some people light a butter lamp, or write her a letter." Dolma's eyes filled. "We used to write letters in school." She talked about her friend for an hour. Before she went to bed, Naveen gave her the timings of the university counselling centre, and she booked a slot for Monday morning.

Where did Dolma's friend die?
In a landslide, in Gangtok.
What was Dolma feeling beneath the loud laughter?
She was grieving deeply and trying to hide it, which showed in the late nights alone on the stairs.
What did Naveen do that supported Dolma?
He sat with her gently, acknowledged the loss, suggested a way to mark it, listened, and gave her the counselling centre timings.
What would change if Naveen had believed Dolma's "I'm fine"?
Dolma might have kept grieving alone at night, without talking about her friend or booking the counselling slot.

metadata.subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]

messages.content: Is the school closed on Monday because of the festival?
I don't know whether Monday is a holiday, because the school decides and announces that. Check the school's message group or call the office.

That idea is bad. Think of another one.

Teacher's note. Elizabeth stayed back to tell me her parents had forbidden her to attend Saturday's protest. I saw disappointment first, then she said, "They are scared for me. I understand." She asked how she could still help. We talked about writing a piece for the school magazine about why the cause matters, and running a small fundraiser. Elizabeth said she would ask her parents to read the plan and to tell her what worried them most. I offered to help with the fundraiser table. I will check with her next week about how the talk went.
- Anjali, class teacher

What safer ways to help did Elizabeth and the teacher discuss?
They discussed writing a piece for the school magazine and running a small fundraiser.
What was Elizabeth feeling about her parents' ban, and what did she understand?
Elizabeth felt disappointed but understood her parents were scared for her; she said "They are scared for me. I understand."
What could Elizabeth do next if her parents still say no?
Keep listening, keep offering safer ways to contribute, and show she takes the risks seriously. ❤️
How might Elizabeth's parents feel when she brings the plan?
Possibly relieved that she listens and wants to help safely, though the note does not show their reaction.

"Sangeeta, you're coming, right? We're all bunking the last period to go to the lake."
"Um… yeah. Sure."
Later, by the lockers:
"Arohi, can I tell you something? I don't actually want to go."
"Then why did you say yes?"
"Because if I don't, they'll laugh and call me a goody-goody. And then they'll go without me every time."
"That's a real fear. I have it too."
"You do?"
"I also don't want to go. My mum would kill me, and honestly the lake gets scary at that end."
"So… what if we both say no? Together?"
"Okay. What do we say?"
"Something short. Like, 'Not today, we've got a project.'"
"'Not today, we've got a project.' Say it again."
"Not today, we've got a project."
They practised it twice, giggling. When Riya came back to check, Sangeeta said it first, steady, though her hands were cold. Arohi nodded beside her. Riya shrugged. "Your loss." And that was all.

Where were the friends planning to go during the last period?
To the lake.
Why did Sangeeta first say yes?
She was afraid of being laughed at, called a goody-goody and left out of future plans.
What helped Sangeeta say no, and why?
Finding an ally in Arohi and practising a short reply together made it easier to refuse calmly.
How does Riya react to the refusal?
Riya just shrugs and says 'Your loss,' showing the feared reaction was much smaller than Sangeeta expected.

The evening I told my parents I was breaking off the engagement, I stood in the corridor outside the living room for five minutes. I'm Hansa. My heart was racing, my shoulders were hunched, and my sister Afreen squeezed my hand. 'Do the thing,' she whispered. So I did what my yoga teacher had taught: let my shoulders fall, felt both feet on the cold floor, breathed out slowly three times. It didn't make the conversation easy. My father went silent, my mother cried. But I could think. When my mother asked, 'What will people say?', I didn't shout. I kept my feet planted and said, 'I know it's hard. But I don't love him, and I can't marry him.' It took them weeks to understand. That evening, though, I stayed clear.

Who squeezed Hansa's hand in the corridor?
Afreen.
What was Hansa feeling in the corridor?
Hansa felt nervous and tense, with a racing heart and hunched shoulders.
What did the grounding steps do, and what did they not do?
They helped Hansa think and speak calmly, but they did not make the conversation easy or change the parents' first reaction.
How might Hansa's mother have felt that evening?
She was upset and worried, crying and anxious about what people would say.

metadata.subtype: Using the body to steady the mind [Response]

messages.content: For x: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and y = x^2: 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, find r. Does r = 0 mean there is no relationship?

Answer: Sxy = 0, so r = 0. But y = x^2 exactly: there is a perfect (curved) relationship.

mx = 0, my = 2. Products (x - 0)(y - 2): (-2)(2) = -4, (-1)(-1) = 1, 0 x (-2) = 0, 1 x (-1) = -1, 2 x 2 = 4; total 0. The left half of the U gives negative products, the right half positive ones, and they cancel exactly. r measures only how well a STRAIGHT line fits. A scatter plot would show the U shape at once, which is why we always plot before calculating. The least-squares line here is y = 2 (slope 0), which is useless for prediction.
450 sweets are packed in boxes of 10. How many boxes? And how many boxes of 100 can be filled from 3,700 sweets?

Answer: 45 boxes (450 / 10 = 45). 37 boxes (3,700 / 100 = 37).

Dividing by 10 is the opposite of multiplying by 10: every digit moves one place to the RIGHT, and the 0 in the ones place goes away. 450 is 45 tens, so 45 boxes of ten. Dividing by 100 moves digits two places right: 3,700 is 37 hundreds. Check by multiplying back: 45 x 10 = 450.
I'm moving to a new city for college and I'm nervous.
Feeling nervous is natural. Moving means new people, places and routines. A little planning makes it easier. Is there anything in particular worrying you?
Mostly finding my way around.
Look at a map of the area before you go, and note the route to college, shops and the nearest hospital. Walk the route once in daylight to get familiar.
What if I get lost?
Keep your phone charged and a note of your address. You can ask shopkeepers or other students for directions. Most people are happy to help.
How do I make friends?
Join a club, talk to people in your class and say yes to simple invitations. Friendships often start with small, ordinary conversations.
What if I feel homesick?
It is common and usually eases over weeks. Calling home helps, but also keep busy with new routines. If it feels too heavy, a college counsellor can help.

Monday

For five days I've avoided the lab report. Every evening I tell myself, "Tonight," and every evening I end up watching videos. Tushar, my roommate, asked if I'd started and I just groaned. Tonight I tried something he mentioned: tell yourself you'll do two minutes. Just open the document and type a single sentence. That's it, then you can stop. So at nine I opened the file. I wrote "The aim of this experiment was to measure the resistance of…" and then I needed to finish the sentence, so I did. Then I thought, might as well write the method. When I looked up, it was ten o'clock. Five paragraphs. It was the starting that was the monster, not the report. — Vishal

What time did Vishal open the file?
At nine.
How did Vishal feel when he looked up at ten o'clock?
Vishal felt surprised and relieved; the report was less scary than the idea of starting it.
What could Vishal do tomorrow to keep going?
Use the same trick: open the file and write one sentence before anything else.
How might Tushar feel hearing about the five paragraphs?
Tushar would likely be pleased his tip worked.

metadata.subtype: Approach: starts with two minutes to get going [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 4C, 2 December.

Vaibhav's homework has been too perfect lately. Today he burst into tears when he got one sum wrong. At lunch he told me quietly, "If I get everything right, Mummy and Papa won't fight. They fight because I'm bad at maths."

He said he hears them argue at night about money and "the shop". He said they are kind to him, and nothing suggested anyone is being hurt.

I told him grown-ups argue about grown-up worries, not because of children's marks, and that one wrong sum is completely normal.
This afternoon I shared this with our school counsellor, and we called his mother together. She was upset to hear it and said she and his father will both tell him tonight that it isn't about him. The counsellor will check in with Vaibhav on Monday.

Nitin

What does Vaibhav say his parents argue about at night?
Vaibhav says they argue about money and "the shop".
Why does Vaibhav try so hard to be perfect?
Vaibhav feels anxious and responsible, believing his parents fight because of his maths, so being perfect seems like a way to stop it.
What did Nitin do the same day?
Nitin reassured Vaibhav, shared it with the school counsellor, and called his mother with the counsellor; she agreed to tell him that night it wasn't about him.
How did Vaibhav's mother feel hearing this?

messages.content: Explain which of these can reasonably be modelled by a Poisson distribution, and why. a) The number of misprints on a page of a novel. b) The number of heads in 20 tosses of a coin. c) The number of cars passing a toll plaza in a minute at 2 a.m. d) The number of customers entering a sweet shop per hour over a whole festival day. e) The number of goals scored in a football match. f) The number of students absent from a class of 40 during a flu outbreak.

Answer: a) yes b) no, binomial B(20, 0.5) c) yes d) no, the rate is not constant e) yes, approximately f) no, absences are not independent (and the maximum is 40).

Check the four conditions: events occur 1) singly, 2) at random, 3) INDEPENDENTLY and 4) at a CONSTANT average rate, with no fixed upper limit. a) Misprints are rare, random and independent: Poisson. b) There are exactly 20 trials with p = 0.5 and at most 20 heads: this is binomial, and p is not small. c) Late-night traffic is light and random at a steady rate: Poisson. d) The rate changes during the day (evening rush before the festival), so a single lambda does not fit; Poisson could work hour by hour with different lambda. e) Goals are fairly rare and random: a Poisson model with lambda ~ 2.5 is often used. f) Flu spreads from child to child, so absences are not independent. Common mistake: using Poisson just because something is "a count".

messages.content: To make a lasagna Martha needs 1.5kg of cheese and 500 grams of meat. The cheese costs $6 per kilogram, and the meat $8 per kilogram. How much does Martha need to pay for the ingredients?

500 grams is 0.5 kilogram, so for the meat, Martha needs to pay 0.5 * 8 = $4.
For the cheese, Martha needs to pay 1.5 * 6 = $9.
So in total for the ingredients, Martha needs to pay 4 + 9 = $13.
The answer is 13.

Jerry wakes up one morning and finds the thermostat set to 40 degrees. He set it to double the initial temperature. His dad notices, yells at Jerry, and reducing the temperature by 30 degrees. Later, Jerry's mother reduces the temperature by 30%, before his sister increases it by 24 degrees. What's the final temperature?

First double the initial temperature: 40 degrees * 2 = 80 degrees
Then reduce that amount by 30 to reflect the dad's change: 80 degrees - 30 degrees = 50 degrees
Then multiply that number by 30% to find how much Jerry's mother reduces the temperature: 50 degrees * .3 = 15 degrees
Now subtract 15 degrees from 50 degrees to find the temperature after the mother's change: 50 degrees - 15 degrees = 35 degrees
Finally, add 24 degrees to find the final temperature: 35 degrees + 24 degrees = 59 degrees
The answer is 59.

Wobbly.
How can you tell Mahima's headache was linked to feelings?
It came on right before the maths test she was worried about, along with wobbly legs, and eased a little once she said she was nervous.
What did Madhav do that could help other children?
He shared his own test body signals and gave her the word 'nervous', so she could link what she felt to a feeling.
What would change if Madhav had just said, 'You're not sick, get in the van'?
Mahima would still have a banging head without understanding why, and might keep believing tests make her ill.

messages.content: Coral reads 30 pages of a book on night 1, and 2 less than twice that on night 2.  Night 3 Coral reads 3 more pages than the sum of the first two nights.  How many total pages did Coral read in the 3 nights?

Night 1:30 pages
Night 2:2(30)-2=58 pages
Night 3:3+(30+58)=91 pages
Total:30+58+91=179 pages
The answer is 179.

The annual day rehearsal in the school hall was so noisy that nobody could hear. Akash, five, needed to ask his teacher, Sharmila Ma'am, where his crown was. She was talking to the music teacher. He wanted to tug her sari, but he stood beside her and waited, hands folded. When she turned, he said, "Excuse me, Ma'am. Where is my crown?" She bent down. "Thank you for waiting, Akash."

What did Akash need to ask his teacher?
Where his crown was.
How did Akash feel as he waited beside Sharmila Ma'am?
He was probably impatient and a bit anxious about his crown, but he chose to wait politely.
How could Sharmila Ma'am help Akash keep this habit in busy moments?
Keep thanking him when he waits, and teach a quiet signal he can use when it's noisy.
What is it like for Sharmila Ma'am in the noisy hall?
It's probably stressful, so a child waiting politely makes her job easier.

"Ammi, everyone in my class has a spinning top with lights. Everyone!"
Zeenat looked up from the sewing machine. "Faraz, last month you said spinning tops were for babies."
"That was before. Now Mohit and Varun and the whole back bench have them. They have battles at lunch."
"And you want to battle?"
"I want to be in the battles."
"Do you like spinning tops?"
Faraz thought about it. "Not really. My kite is better. But nobody flies kites now."
"So you want a toy you don't like?"
"I want the toy they like. If I have it, I can sit with them."
Zeenat stopped the machine. "Tell me about lunch these days, beta."
Faraz looked at his feet. "I sit with my kite book."

What does Faraz say is better than a spinning top?
Faraz says his kite is better.
Why does Faraz want a toy he doesn't even like?
He wants to be in the lunch battles and sit with the others, so being included matters more to him than his own taste. 🥺
How could Zeenat support Faraz beyond buying the top?
She could keep asking about lunch, help him find one friend to share his kite with, and talk about joining in without pretending.
What is Zeenat noticing when she stops the sewing machine?
Zeenat notices this isn't really about a toy; Faraz seems lonely at lunch and wants a way in.
Give two synonyms for "happy", in one line, with a slash between them.
cheerful / joyful
Is a "motorway" the same as a "highway"?

A motorway is the British word for a major fast road with several lanes. Americans say "highway" or "freeway". Indian English usually says "highway" or "expressway".
Example: The motorway was empty at dawn.
Now you try: CP ₹80, SP ₹100; profit %?
The answer is 25%.
Why should a learner not start with fast taans?
Because fast taans can lose raga identity if the learner has not first understood slow movement and grammar.
For a wedding, chairs were arranged in 7 rows with 12 chairs in each row. Some people arrived late and grabbed 11 extra chairs, placing them at the back. How many chairs were there altogether?

At first, there were 7*12=84 chairs.
Later, there were 84+11=95 chairs altogether.
The answer is 95.
Travis and his brother joined a trick-or-treat event. They collected 68 pieces of candy altogether. Each of them ate 4 pieces of candy after the event. How many pieces of candy were left?

They ate a total of 4 x 2 = 8 pieces of candy after the event.
So, Travis and his brother have 68 - 8 = 60 pieces of candy left.
The answer is 60.

At five, after a tearful bedtime, Aditi was shown breathing as a game the next evening, when everyone was calm. Tarun, Aditi's father, blew soap bubbles across the balcony with Aditi, both trying not to pop them, then sniffed an imaginary marigold and blew out a pretend candle with one long puff. "Again!" said Aditi. A week later, when a toy snapped and tears began, Tarun whispered only, "Flower... candle?" Aditi took a shaky sniff and a long puff, and the crying softened.

At twenty, in the corridor before a seminar presentation, Aditi let the shoulders drop and breathed out slowly, longer than the breath in. At the front of the room Aditi paused for a moment before the first sentence. Hemant, the professor, noticed only a clear, steady voice. Nobody saw the breath.

What did Aditi and Tarun blow across the balcony?
They blew soap bubbles across the balcony.
How is the breathing game at five connected to Aditi's breathing at twenty?

At five the bubbles, flower and candle made a slow breath into a game, practised when calm, so that later it could help when Aditi was upset. At twenty Aditi uses the same slow breath out, with dropped shoulders and a pause, before a seminar presentation, and the voice comes out steady without anyone noticing.
What was Aditi feeling in the corridor before the seminar presentation?
Aditi was nervous about presenting, and the slow breath was a way to steady the voice and thinking.
What could Tarun do the next time Aditi is upset, based on the balcony game?
Tarun could whisper the flower and candle words and breathe along with Aditi, using the game already practised when calm.
Our building is going carolling for Christmas. I'm not a good singer.
Carolling is about joy and togetherness, not perfect voices. In a group, you won't stand out.
But I might sing off-key.
Stand near someone who sings well and follow them. A small mistake disappears in the group sound, and people only remember the warm feeling.

The startup let four people go on a Friday afternoon. By Monday they were each dealing with it differently. Shankar sat down with a notebook and wrote three figures: what he had saved, what he needed to spend each month just to get by, and what the company would still pay him. Divided out, they gave him a number of months, and the fear shrank into something he could measure. Neelam made a weekly plan: refresh her CV, send off ten applications, write to five ex-coworkers and practise one mock interview. Even when replies were slow, she could see her ticks pile up. Ishita felt the gap opening under her feet and said yes to the first offer that came, without asking about pay or the team. Three months later she was scrolling job boards again. Karan had sent applications for two months with no reply. He looked over what he had sent, saw that his CV listed duties but no results, and showed it to an old mentor. Then he began applying to nearby kinds of work too.

Which three figures did Shankar write in his notebook?
He wrote what he had saved, what he needed to spend each month, and what the company would still pay him.
How does Ishita's choice differ from Karan's after their setbacks, and what came of each?

Ishita took the first offer out of fear without checking terms, and was job hunting again in three months. Karan reviewed why his applications got no replies, fixed his CV with a mentor and widened his search.
What was Ishita probably feeling on the Monday after the layoff?
She was anxious and frightened about the gap without work, which pushed her to say yes at once.
What could Ishita do differently the next time an offer arrives?
She could ask about pay, duties and the team before answering, and take a day to weigh it against what she needs. Even a short pause would let her check the fit. 🙂
What is meaning of 'homesick'? I am in hostel and feeling like this I think.

"Homesick" means feeling sad because you are away from home and miss your family and familiar places. Example: "In my first month at the hostel, I was very homesick." It is a common feeling, and it usually gets easier with time.

At five, Darshan's mother Zeenat put one sweet on the table. "If you can wait until I finish my tea, you can have two." Darshan looked at the sweet, then at her cup. He picked up the one sweet and ate it fast. Two would have been better, but later was too far away to picture. At fifteen, his friend Yash messaged him with a game challenge one evening before a science test three months away. Darshan wanted a better grade, but an hour of gaming was vivid and the grade was faint. "Just one match," he typed, and played until eleven. At twenty, Darshan got his monthly stipend and spent most of it that weekend on new headphones and dinners out. He knew he would want savings for the trip in spring. "Next month I'll be strict," he told Yash on the balcony. Next month the same thing happened. Yash raised an eyebrow. "Didn't you say that in August?" Darshan laughed and looked down, aware that he had.

How many sweets could Darshan have if he waited?
He could have two sweets if he waited until his mother finished her tea.
How does Darshan's choice of now over later repeat at five, fifteen and twenty?

At five he ate one sweet fast rather than wait for two, at fifteen he played a match instead of studying for a grade months away, and at twenty he spent his stipend at once though he wanted savings for the trip. Each time the reward in front of him felt bigger than the better one later.
What was Darshan feeling when Yash reminded him about August?
He felt sheepish and a bit guilty, because he knew he had said the same thing before.
What could Darshan try so that next month does not repeat this month?
He could move a fixed part of his stipend into savings on the day it arrives, so he does not have to decide in the moment.

How can I stop my plants from dying?
Nina has a 29 minute walk to school and has walked 7 minutes. How many minutes are left?
How much rain fell in my city last night?

1. Give them water when the soil feels dry and place them where they get sunlight. Do not water them too much.
2. 22 minutes. Because 29 - 7 = 22.
3. I don't know, because I can't check rainfall data. Look at a weather office's report or ask local people.

The school counsellor's room was small, and Gurleen sat as far from her father as the two chairs allowed.
"She hid a whole friendship from us for months," her father said. "So I started checking her phone every night."
"And after that?" asked Rehana, the counsellor.
"She deleted everything before I checked."
Rehana turned to Gurleen. "Why did you hide the friendship?"
Gurleen's voice was small. "Because last time, Papa read my chats aloud at dinner and laughed."
Her father looked down.
Rehana drew three boxes on a sheet. "Safety rules, which you both agree on. Private things, which Papa doesn't read. And a weekly check-in, where Gurleen can say if anything feels risky." She looked at Gurleen's father. "Watching everything often teaches teenagers to hide better, not to be safer."
Her father took the pen slowly. "Can we try the boxes?" Gurleen nodded, and her shoulders dropped a little.

How many boxes did Rehana draw on the sheet?
Rehana drew three boxes on a sheet.
What was Gurleen feeling when she explained why she hid the friendship?
Gurleen felt hurt and embarrassed, remembering Papa reading her chats aloud and laughing, which made the truth feel unsafe.
What did Rehana suggest to balance safety and trust?
Rehana suggested agreed safety rules, a private space Papa doesn't read, and a weekly check-in about anything risky.
How does Gurleen's father seem to feel after hearing her reason?
Her father seems ashamed and ready to change, looking down and then asking to try the boxes.

Dear Harish,
You asked how the thesis presentation went. Better than the rehearsal, and I owe that to the video you told me to take.
When I watched it on Sunday I nearly deleted it. My arms were windmilling on every sentence. At one point I flung my hand so wide I knocked the pointer off the table. You could not look at the slides for all the waving.
So I planned my gestures like slides. For the rise in the rainfall graph, one flat hand climbing slowly. For the three stages of the filter, three fingers, one at a time. Everything else, hands resting loosely on the lectern.
On Tuesday Professor Roy followed the graph with her eyes when my hand rose, and nodded. My hands still twitched once or twice, but it felt like they were helping.
Thanks for the push,
Sharmila

What did Sharmila knock off the table in the rehearsal video?
The pointer.
How did Sharmila feel when first watching the rehearsal video?
Sharmila felt embarrassed enough to nearly delete it, seeing the windmilling arms; there is also some relief later, as the video showed exactly what to change.
What went wrong in the rehearsal, and what fixed it?
Large, constant arm movements pulled attention away from the slides; planning a few purposeful gestures and resting the hands otherwise fixed it.
How does Professor Roy seem to experience the final presentation?
She follows the graph with her eyes as Sharmila's hand rises and nods, so the gesture helped her understand instead of distracting her.

The bus from Thrissur broke down, and Elizabeth walked into the panchayat hall in Kuttanad twenty minutes late, sweaty and flustered, apologising as she tripped over a bench. Siddharth, who had come with her from the NGO, saw the elders exchange a look. From his seat by the door he watched the meeting play out: every idea she raised about the new water filters got a short "we'll see". It was as if the first minute had already given the answer. Then old Thomas chettan asked about upkeep, and Elizabeth answered in easy Malayalam with a story about her own grandmother's well. Siddharth saw two elders lean forward. On the ride home he said, "Next time we leave an hour early, and you open with the well story." Elizabeth laughed tiredly. "And they did change their minds, a little."

Retell this excerpt briefly in three sentences.

Elizabeth arrives late at a village meeting about water filters, and the elders answer each idea with "we'll see". When she answers a question about upkeep with a story about her grandmother's well, two elders lean forward. Siddharth suggests leaving earlier next time and opening with the well story, and Elizabeth says the elders changed their minds a little.

Class 10B, notes after the parent meeting: Vidya
Vidya is one of the most honest students I teach. In Tuesday's debate practice she told Karan, 'That argument is lazy. You didn't read the article.' She was not wrong, but he went red and didn't speak again. Afterwards I talked with her about saying the hard thing without the sting. She listened, arms folded, then said, 'Fine. But I won't pretend it was good.' Fair enough. The same week, when most of the class agreed to share answers for the online quiz, Vidya refused and told them why, in front of everyone. Nobody else did. Her parents worry she has no friends. I see a student who doesn't need permission to be fair. We agreed she'll start her feedback with one thing that works.
Ujjwal, class teacher

What did Vidya say to Karan in debate practice?
'That argument is lazy. You didn't read the article.'
What might Vidya have felt refusing to share quiz answers in front of everyone?
She probably felt firm and determined, maybe uncomfortable, but not needing the class's approval to do what was fair.
What did Ujjwal and Vidya agree, and why is it a good step?
That she will start feedback with one thing that works; it keeps her honesty but lessens the sting for classmates like Karan.
How might Karan have felt after Vidya's comment?
Karan felt embarrassed, going red and staying silent for the rest of the practice.

Monday: At lunch, Mehak held her nose and said, "Anand, your tiffin is stinky!" The table laughed. Anand closed his box and didn't eat.
Tuesday: Mehak brought two of her mother's special laddoos and left them on Anand's desk. She didn't say anything. Anand ate one, but he still sat at the other end of the table at lunch.
Thursday: Mehak's grandmother asked why she looked so worried. Mehak told her. "The laddoos were nice," Nani said. "But did you say sorry?" On Friday, Mehak went up to Anand before class. "Sorry I said your tiffin was stinky. It smells like my Nani's cooking, actually." Anand laughed. At lunch, he sat next to her and shared his aloo.

What did Mehak leave on Anand's desk on Tuesday?
Two of her mother's special laddoos.
Why did Mehak give the laddoos without saying anything?
Mehak felt guilty about mocking Anand's tiffin and hoped the treat would undo it without having to say the hard words.
What finally made things right between Mehak and Anand?
Saying a clear sorry, after Nani pointed out that the laddoos alone weren't enough.
How might Anand have felt on Tuesday, still sitting at the other end?
Anand probably still felt hurt and unsure, because a sweet treat didn't tell him she was sorry.
The new bypass is more better than the old road. Fix this, please.

The new bypass is better than the old road.
Why: "Better" is already comparative; drop "more".

Nazia explaining honestly that the posts showed one good hour of a mostly dull trip, reminding Divyansh that posts are curated.

In the last week of November, the cold settled over the small town of Palampur, and Vishal was sitting in the shed office of the tea-packaging startup when the call came from Usha. She had put in the first money two years ago.

"I've decided to step back from the next round," Usha said. "The numbers haven't moved the way we hoped."

Vishal's throat closed. It felt like being left at a bus stop. He stared at the pile of unsold boxes for a long moment.

Then he said, "Thank you for being straight with me. Could you tell me what you saw in the numbers? And is there anyone you'd introduce me to?"

Usha paused. "Ring me next Monday. I'll have two names and some honest feedback."

After the call Vishal wrote a thank-you note on the back of a packing slip, to type up later. He didn't feel better yet, but nothing had been burned.

Where was Vishal when Usha called?
Vishal was in the shed office of the tea-packaging startup in Palampur.
What did Usha's decision feel like to Vishal?
It felt like abandonment, like being left at a bus stop, shown by his throat closing and his long stare at the unsold boxes.
What did Vishal do that kept the relationship open?
Vishal thanked Usha, asked for candid feedback on the numbers and asked for introductions, so the bridge stayed intact.
How might Usha see her decision and Vishal's response?
Usha probably sees stepping back as a business choice, and Vishal's calm thanks probably makes it easier for her to offer help and honest feedback.

Jagdish, you asked why I went quiet online. I'm Chaitanya, and it's a bit embarrassing.
Last year I started chasing followers. I noticed my photos near the edge of the old fort wall got far more likes than normal ones. So every weekend I went back and posted something more daring: sitting on the edge, then standing, then one foot out for the camera.
The numbers became everything. A good post, and I'd be happy all day. A flop, and I'd feel sick, checking every five minutes, wondering what was wrong with me. I didn't control those numbers, but they controlled me.
It stopped when a guard at the fort caught me on the wall, pulled me down, and phoned my mother right there. She came straight away. She didn't shout. She just held on to my arm the whole way home.
I deleted those photos that night. I still post sometimes. Just not for the numbers.

Who pulled Chaitanya down from the wall?
A guard at the fort.
How did Chaitanya feel when a post flopped?
Chaitanya felt sick and anxious, checking every five minutes and wondering what was wrong.
What else could Chaitanya focus on instead of likes?
Posting things Chaitanya enjoys for friends who matter, with fort photos taken safely from the path.
How might Chaitanya's mother have felt holding that arm all the way home?
She was likely frightened and shaken, relieved Chaitanya was safe and scared by how close it had come.

Ayesha Mami had come from Lucknow to the village for Saurabh's birthday. She handed him a box wrapped in newspaper and string. Saurabh tore it open. Socks. Brown woolly socks. His face dropped. He had hoped for a toy tractor. Amma gave him a tiny nudge. Saurabh swallowed. "Thank you, Mami." Mami smiled. "For the cold mornings, when you walk to school." That night, Saurabh cried a little into Amma's lap. "I wanted a tractor." Amma stroked his hair. "Mami knitted those herself, for your feet. That's her love in wool."

What was the box wrapped in?
It was wrapped in newspaper and string.
How did Saurabh feel when he saw the socks?
He felt disappointed and sad, because he had hoped for a toy tractor, and his face dropped.
What did Saurabh do well at the moment of opening the gift?
He said thank you first and waited to cry about it later at home with Amma.
How might Ayesha Mami feel if Saurabh wears the socks on a cold morning?
She would likely feel happy and loved back, since she knitted them herself for him.

Clara was on the bus home from volleyball in Valencia when Rosa's text arrived: 'fine, whatever.' Clara had only said she couldn't make Saturday's beach trip because of her grandmother's birthday. Her thumb froze over the screen. Rosa never wrote like that. Normally there'd be three emojis and a voice note. Clara stared out at the orange trees sliding past and ran through it: Rosa was sick of her cancelling. Rosa thought she was boring. Rosa had been waiting for a reason. 'She's furious with me,' Clara told her reflection in the window. By the time the bus reached her stop, the guess had turned into a fact, and Clara was already angry back.

Why couldn't Clara make Saturday's beach trip?
Because of her grandmother's birthday.
Why did Clara feel angry back by the time she reached her stop?
The unusually short text made her uneasy, so she filled the gap with worst guesses until she believed them and felt angry back.
What could Clara try before the guess hardens further?
She could send a simple, curious question like 'You okay? That sounded unlike you,' or call Rosa, rather than treating her guess as fact.
How might Rosa feel if she learned Clara thought she was furious?
She might be surprised or sorry, since she may only have felt a little let down.

Note, 9 December. Written by Sangeeta, senior teacher, residential school.

Mohan, twenty-five, took over as boys' hostel warden this term. We have been friends since training college. At home he makes paper boats for his nieces and lets them win at ludo. Tonight I saw him make three Class 6 boys stand outside the dormitory in the cold for talking after lights-out. When one, Gopika's younger brother, started to cry, Mohan said, "Crying won't help you." That is not the Mohan I know.

I also know the job: sixty boys, no deputy, a principal who blames the warden for every complaint.

What I did next: I brought the boys inside, then waited until he was calmer. I said, "This isn't how you are at home. I think the job is pushing you somewhere you wouldn't go." He was silent, then asked if I'd help him draft fair rules and raise the need for a deputy with the principal.

How many boys does Mohan look after as warden?
He looks after sixty boys.
What was Sangeeta feeling when she saw Mohan with the boys outside the dormitory?
Sangeeta was troubled and surprised, since the harsh warden in front of Sangeeta was not the gentle friend who plays ludo with his nieces.
Which part of Sangeeta's approach helped Mohan listen?
Waiting until he was calmer and linking his behaviour to the pressures of the job, rather than attacking him, let him admit it and ask for help.
What was that cold night like for the three Class 6 boys?
They were left outside in the cold and told crying would not help, which likely made them feel scared and unprotected by the person meant to care for them.

Parul had the slides ready: car-free Sunday mornings on the lake road in Kukatpally. She was sure. But on Friday evening, in the noisy municipal office, she turned to Ojas and asked, "Who will hate this most?" "The shop owners," he said. "Harish from their association wrote us a long letter." Parul printed all six pages and read them on the bus home, pen in hand. Some points were weak. One was not: the vegetable vendors' delivery vans came only on Sunday mornings. In her notebook she wrote, "If deliveries can't work, I rethink this." On Saturday she called Harish. "What would make this workable for you?" By Monday her plan had a delivery lane until nine.

How many pages was the association's letter?
The letter from Harish's association was six pages long.
Why did Parul ask Ojas who would hate the plan most?
Parul felt confident in the plan but was eager to find its weak spot before committing, so she treated the strongest opposition as useful information rather than a threat.
What could other planners learn from Parul's weekend?
They could read the opposing letter in full, call its writer with an open question, and let the one strong point reshape the plan instead of defending the original.
How might Harish see the municipal office after Parul's call?
Harish would probably feel heard, since the association's letter led to a real change, and may trust the office more in future talks.

Since Vandana left the consulting job in October, the flat in Lajpat Nagar had gone quiet. She slept late, kept her door half closed, and when Neelam asked about her day, her eyes slid to the floor. The phone buzzing made her jump. Neelam's mother, calling from Jaipur, said, "Sit her down and make her talk. She'll feel better." Neelam didn't. She had tried once, and Vandana had gone even quieter. Instead she left a plate of poha outside the door each morning and sat in the living room in the evenings with the television low, just in case. One night Vandana came out and sat at the other end of the sofa. After a while she said, "I think I'm really burnt out." Neelam nodded. "Do you want me to help you find someone to talk to? A counsellor?" Vandana was quiet, then said, "Maybe. Yes."

What did Neelam leave outside the door each morning?
A plate of poha.
What might Vandana's sliding eyes and jumping at the phone suggest?
They may show exhaustion and stress after the job, perhaps low mood too; it might look like coldness, but she seems worn down.
Why was Neelam's approach better than 'make her talk'?
Pushing had made Vandana quieter, while steady presence and small kindnesses let her come out when ready, and then Neelam offered help finding a counsellor.
How does Neelam's mother see the situation?
She thinks talking will fix it and wants Neelam to push, not seeing that pressure made Vandana withdraw further.

From our balcony I saw the Class 4 boys near the gate and heard Charu yelling at another boy, his face red and his fists at his sides. “Give it back! Give it back!” The other boy just held a small green eraser high. I could not tell whether Charu was furious or scared, or simply wanted someone to listen. He didn't hit anyone. After a bit he stopped, turned and walked quickly to the guard's booth, still breathing hard, and said something to the guard, who walked back with him. The eraser was handed over. Charu's voice was shaking. I'm Rekha, his neighbour.

What did the other boy hold up?
A small green eraser.
What might Charu have been feeling while he shouted, according to Rekha?
Rekha could not be sure if he was furious, scared or just wanting to be heard, since his voice was loud and shaking but he did not hit anyone.
What did Charu do that was safer than shouting back or fighting?
He stepped away and went to the guard for help, which got the eraser returned without a fight.
How might the other boy have seen Charu's shouting?
He may have been startled, since a raised voice can feel threatening even when the shouter is scared or wants to be heard.

Anders put two coffees on the table in the Malmö co-working kitchen. "You have said no to investors four times," he said. "Help me understand why staying small matters so much."
Ivan turned the cup. "If someone else sits on our board, they may start deciding what we build. I started this to choose our own product."
"Okay. Mine is the rival's launch in spring. If we're slow, the window closes and there is nothing left to be in control of."
Ivan was quiet, then laughed a little. "So you don't need the money, you need speed. And I don't need to stay poor, I need to keep the say."
They took a marker and wrote three options on the glass: a small round with no board seat, a bank loan for one hire, or nothing.

Where were the two co-founders when they talked?
They were in the co-working kitchen in Malmö.
What is Ivan afraid of, and how can you tell?
Ivan fears losing control of the product, shown in the line about someone else sitting on the board and deciding what gets built.
What could the two do next to test which option fits both worries?
They could set a short deadline to price each of the three options on the glass against the spring launch and against who would control the product.
How might Anders have seen Ivan's refusals before the coffee talk?
Before the talk, Anders probably saw them as stubbornness that risked the spring window; afterwards they looked like a fear about control.

The first month after we moved to Nashik, I cried in the bathroom most nights so nobody would hear. I'm Vaibhav, and I thought I was the only person in the world who felt so lost. One night Papa knocked and sat on the edge of the tub. He told me that when he was nine, his family moved from a village to Pune, and he hid under the stairs at his new school for a whole week. 'I thought everyone could tell I didn't belong,' he said. I stared at him. Papa, who talks to everyone? After that, every Sunday he took me and my little sister Hafsa to the Godavari ghats for vada pav. It became our thing. Slowly, Nashik started to feel like somewhere I lived, not just somewhere I was.

Surprised and much less alone; Vaibhav had thought nobody else ever felt so lost 🙂

Which of these are polynomials? Give the degree and the type of each polynomial: 4x^2 - 3x + 7, y^3 + sqrt2 y, 3sqrtt + tsqrt2, y + 2/y, x^1^0 + y^3 + t^5^0, 5, 0, (x + 1)(x^2 - 4).

Answer: Polynomials: 4x^2 - 3x + 7 (degree 2, quadratic trinomial), y^3 + sqrt2 y (degree 3, cubic binomial), x^1^0 + y^3 + t^5^0 (a polynomial in three variables), 5 (degree 0, constant), 0 (the zero polynomial, no degree), (x + 1)(x^2 - 4) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 4 (degree 3, cubic). Not polynomials: 3sqrtt + tsqrt2 and y + 2/y.

Check every power of the VARIABLE: it must be a whole number. sqrtt = t^(1/2) has power 1/2, and 2/y = 2y^-^1 has power -1, so those two expressions are not polynomials. A surd as a COEFFICIENT is fine: sqrt2 y has power 1, and sqrt2 is just a number. The degree is the HIGHEST power: for a product, multiply out first or add the degrees of the factors (1 + 2 = 3). 5 = 5x^0 has degree 0. The zero polynomial has no degree, because 0 = 0x = 0x^2 = ... has no highest non-zero term. Common mistake: saying 4x^2 - 3x + 7 has degree 7 (the constant is not a power).

The school in Gangtok was a steep twenty-minute climb, and the practical could not easily be moved. She went anyway, pale and sweating, and nearly fainted over the burette. In March, I missed a day because of a late shift. Old me would have spent the evening thinking I was hopeless and then doubled the next day as punishment. Or given up.
This time I just asked, "Why did I miss?" Late shift. Okay. That's data. So on late-shift days I'd do five minutes on the bus instead of twenty at home.
The next morning, I did my usual lesson. No drama. No penance.
I'm Hansa, and I've missed maybe fifteen days this year. Never two in a row.

Never miss twice.

The last time Bob cut his hair he cut it to 6 inches.  His hair is now 36 inches long.  If hair grows at a rate of .5 inches per month how many years did it take him to grow out his hair?

His hair grew 36 inches - 6 inches = 30 inches
Hair grows at a rate of 12 months/year * 0.5 inches/month =6 inches/year
It took him 30 inches / 6 inches/year = 5 years to grow his hair out.
The answer is 5.

Sahil tossed a coin 50 times and got 28 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads? What is the theoretical probability? Why are they different?

Answer: Experimental P(heads) = 28/50 = 14/25 = 0.56. Theoretical P(heads) = 1/2 = 0.5. They differ because of chance; with many more tosses the experimental result usually gets closer to 1/2.

EXPERIMENTAL probability = number of times the event happened / number of trials = 28/50. Simplify: 28/50 = 14/25 = 56/100 = 0.56. THEORETICAL probability comes from reasoning about equally likely outcomes: 1 out of 2, so 0.5. In 50 tosses we EXPECT about 50 x 1/2 = 25 heads, but 28 is quite normal; results jump around. If the whole class pools its results to make 1,000 tosses, the fraction of heads will usually be very close to 0.5. Do this experiment in class and record the results in a tally table.

Thursday. In the hostel Ankita reread a draft she had kept for a month: an email to Professor Rao asking to join his river-survey project. She had been too shy to send it. She thought of Nani's voice. Not a weight, she decided. A warning. Which silence would bother her at seventy?

A tailor has 3 2/5 metres of cloth. She cuts it into pieces each 1/5 of a metre long. How many pieces does she get?

Answer: 17 pieces. 3 2/5 = 17/5.

Each whole metre makes 5 fifths. 3 metres make 3 x 5 = 15 fifths. The extra 2/5 adds 2 more fifths: 15 + 2 = 17 fifths, written 17/5. The short rule: multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator, and keep the same denominator: 3 x 5 + 2 = 17, so 3 2/5 = 17/5. Check backwards: 17 / 5 is 3 remainder 2, which gives 3 2/5 again.

She suggested using the same slow breathing if the panic started again during the paper.
How does Nikita see Parul's protest about having no time?
She sees that panic is wasting more time than a short walk would, so she calmly insists on the break.

First Sunday of the summer holidays: Eshaan counted the mangoes in the basket, "One, two, five, three!" and pointed at the same mango twice. Ritu laughed.
Wednesday: Nani lined the mangoes up in a row. Eshaan touched each one as he counted. "Seven!"
The next Sunday: Nani gave Eshaan three mangoes and Ritu five. Eshaan looked at both piles and frowned. "Ritu has more. Not fair." Nani moved one across. "Now?" He counted again. "Four and four. Same!"

How many mangoes did Nani first give Eshaan on the last Sunday?
She gave Eshaan three mangoes.
How did Eshaan feel when he saw Ritu's bigger pile?
He felt it was unfair and was a little annoyed, because he could now tell that Ritu had more.
What helped Eshaan count correctly by Wednesday?
Lining the mangoes up in a row let him touch each one once, so he didn't count any twice.
What is it like for Ritu when Eshaan miscounts at first?
Ritu finds it funny, perhaps feeling grown-up because counting is already easy for Ritu.
Did the school drama club's play get a good review in the newspaper?
I don't know, because I can't see reviews published this week. Pick up the newspaper's arts page, or ask your drama teacher if she saw it.

In their village above Gangtok, Pema, ten, sat on the steps with the phone pressed to her ear. Mola, her grandmother in town, had been talking for half an hour. Pema had told her about school, the new goat, and the rain. Now her tea was cold and her homework was waiting. But every time Mola paused, Pema said "Mm" and Mola started a new story. Her brother Ojas watched from the doorway. When Mola paused again, Ojas whispered, "Say: 'Okay Mola, I have to do homework now. I'll call on Sunday. Love you!'" Pema hesitated, then said it. Mola laughed. "Of course, go study! Sunday, then." Pema hung up, surprised. "She didn't mind at all!" Ojas grinned. "She just needed a signal."

How long had Mola been talking?
Half an hour.
How did Pema feel as the call went on?
Pema felt stuck and a bit restless, with cold tea and homework waiting, unsure how to end the call.
What made Ojas's suggested closing work?
It gave a clear signal, a reason, a plan to call again and a warm 'Love you', so Mola didn't feel cut off.
How did Mola feel when Pema ended the call?
Mola didn't mind at all, laughing and agreeing to talk on Sunday.

The hostel common room was loud with a cricket match on TV, but Kunal sat by the window holding the letter from the pilot selection board. Not recommended. Since he was nine he had pictured himself in a flight suit; he had even practised the salute in the mirror. Now that future had simply closed. On his phone, a batchmate was posting photos from the academy gates, grinning, and Kunal felt a sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it. Irfan dropped onto the sofa beside him. "Bro, forget it. You'll crack something better. It's a sign." Kunal nodded and said nothing. Later, alone on the terrace, he let himself cry for the nine-year-old in the flight suit. He didn't know yet what came next. For tonight, not knowing was allowed.

What did the letter from the pilot selection board say?
Not recommended.
What did Kunal feel seeing the batchmate's photos?
A sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it.
Why is Kunal's crying on the terrace a healthy step?
Letting himself grieve the lost future, instead of rushing to Irfan's positive story, is part of moving on.
How does Irfan seem to see Kunal's loss?
Irfan means well and wants to cheer Kunal up quickly, not seeing that Kunal first needs to grieve.

Yamini, you went quiet when Nikhil told us about his fellowship. I know that quiet. Let your Madhuri Mami tell you something. When I was twenty-two, your Mama and I both sat for the bank officer exam. He passed. I didn't. The whole family came with sweets, and I stood in the kitchen feeling like a small dry leaf. I loved him, and I wanted to throw the laddoos at the wall. That night I almost said something cruel: 'Lucky paper, that's all.' It was right there on my tongue. Instead I went up to the terrace and admitted it to myself: I'm jealous. That's allowed. Then I went down and hugged him properly, and meant it. The next month I enrolled for the exam again, and he quizzed me every evening after his training. I passed on my second try. So, child, feel it privately. Celebrate him openly. And then do your own work.

What exam did Madhuri and Mama sit for?
The bank officer exam.
What was Madhuri feeling in the kitchen while the family celebrated?
She felt small and jealous, like a dry leaf, while still loving him.
What was the turning point in Madhuri's story?
Admitting the jealousy on the terrace, hugging him sincerely, and enrolling for the exam again.
How did Mama support Madhuri afterwards?
He quizzed her every evening after his training until she passed.
Hayes does 3 loads of laundry a week using a detergent pod for each load.  His detergent pods come 39 to a pack.  How many packs of detergent pods will he need to do a full year of laundry?

He uses 3 detergent pods a week and there are 52 weeks in a year, so he uses 3*52 = 156
His detergent has 39 pods per pack and he needs 156 pods, so he will need 156/39 = 4 packs of detergent pods
The answer is 4.

I'm Preeti from B-wing, and I was at Sunday's society meeting when the Diwali hall came up. Tarun from the third floor had volunteered to book it. When Mrs. Bhatia asked, "Tarun, the date is confirmed, na?", he lifted his shoulders and turned his palms up. Just that. For a second I couldn't tell whether he meant "Sorry, it's gone" or "Not my problem." Around me people muttered; Mr. Iyer actually snorted. Tarun seemed to hear it. He dropped his hands and said, "Sorry, that shrug wasn't fair. I forgot to confirm the booking in time, and the hall's been taken. That's on me. I'll call the school about their hall tonight and send an update by nine." The muttering stopped. At 8:40 my phone buzzed with his message: school hall booked.

What had Tarun volunteered to do?
Tarun had volunteered to book the Diwali hall.
What might Tarun have been feeling when he lifted his shoulders and turned his palms up?
Tarun was probably embarrassed and helpless about losing the hall; Preeti couldn't tell if it meant sorry or 'not my problem', which is why neighbours bristled.
What turned the meeting around?
Tarun called the shrug unfair, admitted forgetting the booking, gave a concrete plan with a time, and then followed through by 8:40.
How did Preeti read the shrug at first?
Preeti was unsure whether it was an apology or a dismissal, and could see others around taking it as the second.

Rekha, eight, slammed the storybook shut on the bed.

"I'm dumb, Charu Mausi. I'm not reading anymore."

"Dumb? Who says?"

"Me. Pinky reads a whole page before I finish three lines."

"Hmm. Yesterday who read me the recipe for halwa?"

"...Me. But that was short."

"And who read the bus number from far away when I couldn't?"

"That's numbers."

"So you can read short things and numbers. Is that dumb?"

Rekha folded her arms. "It's long pages. Long pages hate me."

"Ah. So it's not 'dumb'. It's 'long pages are slow for me'. That's a different problem. Slow things get faster with practice."

"No, they don't."

"Let's check. One page tonight. I'll time you. Then same page on Friday."

Rekha didn't answer. But she pulled the book back from the pillow and opened it on her knees.

Who read the recipe for halwa to Charu Mausi yesterday?
Rekha did.
Why does calling herself "dumb" feel easier to Rekha than keeping going?
Comparing herself with Pinky makes her feel ashamed, and "dumb" explains everything at once. If she's dumb, there's no point trying, so stopping feels like relief.
What turning point did Charu Mausi create with her questions?

By pointing out Rekha can read recipes and bus numbers, Mausi changed "dumb" into a specific skill, reading long pages, that can be practised. Timing one page tonight and again on Friday makes improvement something Rekha can see.
How might Charu Mausi feel hearing an eight-year-old call herself dumb?
Charu Mausi might feel a pang of worry and want to protect Rekha from that word sticking. Her patient questions suggest she wants Rekha to see herself more fairly.

After Ammi's fall in the bathroom, Zeenat's first idea was simple: Ammi would move in with her in Lucknow. She even cleared the spare room.
Then her neighbour Swati said something at the lift. "Have you asked your mother what she wants?"
Zeenat hadn't. She'd been deciding for her, the way you would for a child.
On Saturday she sat with Ammi in the old house, over tea. "Ammi, I'm worried about you alone. What kind of help would you actually be comfortable with?"
Ammi put down her cup. "I don't want to leave this house, beta. My friends are here. The mosque is here. But I'd like someone in the mornings, for bathing and the market."
Zeenat felt a pang; she'd imagined Ammi in the spare room. But this was Ammi's life.
They found a morning helper from the same lane. Ammi now calls Zeenat every afternoon to report the gossip.

What did Ammi want help with in the mornings?
Bathing and the market.
How did Zeenat feel when Ammi said she didn't want to leave the house?
Zeenat felt a pang of disappointment, having imagined Ammi in the spare room, but accepted it as Ammi's choice.
What else could Zeenat do to keep Ammi safe while respecting her independence?
She could arrange emergency contacts and a spare key with a neighbour, and check in with Ammi about whether the help still suits her.
How does the plan look from Ammi's side?
Ammi keeps her home, friends and routines, with help she chose, so she likely feels respected and independent.

messages.content: I don't understand "accustom". Can you help? Why does a diver feel pressure in the ears when going deep? what does "drive someone up the wall" mean? Help me correct this: Give the book to she. How can I stop procrastinating on homework?

1. Accustom means to make yourself or someone else used to something new. It is a verb.
2. The pressure of the water pushes on the eardrums. Because the weight of the water above grows as a diver goes deeper, the push on the ears gets stronger.
3. It means to annoy someone very much. For example: the noise from the road drives me up the wall.
4. Corrected: Give the book to her. Why: after a preposition, we use the object form "her".
5. Start with a small part of it for ten minutes. Once you begin, it is usually easier to carry on.

When I brought Lokesh home to Nashik for Diwali in our second year, I didn't think about feet at all. I'm Irawati. The moment we entered, my cousins bent and touched Aaji's feet, and she blessed them. Lokesh froze in the doorway. His family is from Chennai but they're atheists, and he'd told me once that touching feet made him feel uncomfortable, like he was pretending. I saw Aaji look at him, waiting. My heart was thumping. Then Lokesh folded his hands, bowed his head and said, "Namaste, Aaji. Thank you for having me." Aaji paused, then smiled and patted his cheek. "Good boy." Later she told me privately, "Not everyone does it. The respect is in the eyes." I think about that a lot. The gesture matters to her, but so does his choice, and she saw both.

What did Lokesh say to Aaji?
"Namaste, Aaji. Thank you for having me."
What was Irawati feeling when Aaji looked at Lokesh, waiting?
Irawati was nervous, heart thumping, unsure how Aaji would react to Lokesh not touching her feet.
What did Lokesh choose to do, and why did it work?
He folded his hands, bowed and thanked Aaji, which showed real respect in a way he was comfortable with.
How did Aaji see Lokesh's greeting?
She accepted it warmly, saying not everyone touches feet and that respect is in the eyes.

Wasim, you've been staring at that rejection mail since lunch. Let me tell you about my own final year. I failed my first interview at a bank. Froze on a question about interest rates I'd answered a hundred times in class. On the train home I had my whole life decided. No bank would take me. No company either, once word got around. My father had retired early to pay my college fees, and I saw him at every wedding explaining that his son was sitting at home. I didn't eat dinner. I truly believed it was plain reasoning. Your Dadi, my mother, just put a plate in front of me and said, 'One interview, Suraj. You're counting it like it's the last one.' I got my first job four months later. Not a bank. It was fine.

What question made Suraj freeze in his first interview?
A question about interest rates that Suraj had answered a hundred times in class.
Why did Suraj skip dinner that night?
Suraj believed his chain of thoughts was plain reasoning, and the picture of his father explaining at weddings filled him with shame, so the future felt already lost.
Which line from Dadi changed things, and why did it work?
'You're counting it like it's the last one' showed that one interview was being treated as the whole future, which let Suraj see the many steps he had skipped.
How might Wasim feel hearing this story from Suraj?
Wasim may feel less alone and the rejection may feel less final, since someone older once felt the same and still found work four months later.

1. How many red shirts are left in the shop?
2. What is wrong with "I want to buy a umbrella."?
3. Please tell me what "cashier" means.

1. I can't see the shop's stock, so I don't know. Ask the staff or call the shop.
2. Fixed: I want to buy an umbrella. Why: Use "an" before a vowel sound.
3. Cashier means the person who takes payment at a shop. Example: Please pay the cashier.

"Salma, why are you crying?"

"The whole week was bad, Kishore Bhaiya."

"The whole week?"

"Yes. My drawing got torn. Ma'am scolded me for talking. And I fell in PT."

"What about Tuesday? You showed me the star you got."

"...Oh. Yes."

"And Thursday, didn't you and Ruksar win the relay?"

"We did."

"So not the whole week."

Salma sniffed. "But tomorrow will be bad."

"Why?"

"Because today was."

Kishore sat down next to her. "Let's tell Ammi about the torn drawing. Then tomorrow we'll see."

Salma leaned on his shoulder.

Ruksar.
Why does Salma think tomorrow will be bad?
Salma feels sad and upset about today, so her mind expects more bad things because "today was."
What could help Salma when she feels this way again?
Remembering good moments, like the star and the relay, and telling a caring adult like Ammi what upset her.
How might Kishore feel when Salma leans on his shoulder?
Kishore probably feels protective and caring toward his little sister.
What is the postmark on a letter, and what does it tell me?

A postmark is a mark stamped on a letter by the post office, showing the place and date it was posted. It is a noun.
Example: The postmark on the envelope said the card was sent from Pune.

Month-end, Friday. In the sales office, Lokesh leaned over the desk. "Everyone rounds the figures up a bit, Seema. Nobody's hurt. It's how the game works." Seema had hesitated, then added a small amount to her own total. Nothing happened.
Three months later. The small amounts had grown, always "just to match last month". Seema's stomach twisted each time she pressed save, but the twist was getting weaker.
Quarter-end, Wednesday. The auditors asked why the figures did not match the bank records. Seema's name was on every changed sheet. Lokesh stared at his screen and said nothing. Seema was called into the manager's room, and the door closed behind her.

Whose name was on every changed sheet?
Seema's name was on every changed sheet.
What was Seema feeling each time she pressed save in the second beat?
Seema felt a twisting unease that was already growing weaker, as the habit made it seem normal.
What could Seema have done in the first month when the rounding began?
Seema could have refused to change the figures and asked the manager how totals should be recorded.
How might Lokesh have felt when the auditors asked their questions?
Lokesh was probably scared and wanted to avoid blame, as staring at the screen in silence suggests.

At the panchayat meeting in Dhanauri, a seed dealer pointed to three farmers in the front row. "All three used our new wheat seed, and all three doubled their harvest!" Heads nodded. Shreya, the young agriculture extension worker, raised her hand. "How many farmers in the block bought this seed last season?" The dealer hesitated. "Around forty." "And the other thirty-seven?" Nazia, a farmer at the back, called out, "My field had the same seed. Half of it failed." Two more hands went up. Shreya kept her voice friendly. "Maybe it's a good seed. But before the panchayat praises it, let's hear from all forty, and check whose fields had canal water." The dealer's smile tightened. The three in the front row shifted in their seats.

How many farmers bought the new seed last season, according to the dealer?
Around forty.
Why did Shreya ask about the other thirty-seven?
Shreya felt doubtful that the three in the front row told the whole story, and wanted to see the whole group before praising the seed.
What does Shreya propose the panchayat do next?
Hear from all forty farmers and check whose fields had canal water before praising the seed.
How might Nazia feel when Shreya's question gives her a chance to speak?
Nazia, whose field half failed, may feel relieved that her loss finally counts in the story.

Raghav, you asked how I handle Sunil uncle at family weddings. Let your Gautam mama tell you. When I was twenty-two, Sunil and I shared a room in Chennai. Every conversation came back to him: his job, his bike, how everyone else was jealous. If I disagreed, he sulked for days, and I'd end up apologising. One day I just stopped arguing. When he boasted, I'd say, "Good for you," and change the subject. When he asked about my salary, I said, "I'd rather keep that to myself." And when he took my scooter without asking, I said plainly, "Not without asking. That's my rule." He didn't change, beta. I stopped waiting for him to. Forty years on, we still meet at weddings, briefly, and I enjoy the biryani.

What did Gautam say when Sunil asked about his salary?
He said, "I'd rather keep that to myself."
How might Gautam have felt back when he kept apologising to Sunil?
He likely felt worn down and unheard, apologising even when Sunil was the one sulking.
What turning point changed how Gautam handled Sunil?
He stopped arguing for agreement, kept personal things private and stated plain rules, like asking before taking the scooter.
How might Sunil have felt when Gautam stopped arguing?
He may have felt puzzled or annoyed at losing a reaction, but he could no longer pull Gautam into long sulks.

messages.content: Gretchen, Mitzi, and Beth went bowling together. Gretchen bowled a 120. Mitzi bowled a 113. Beth bowled an 85. What was their average bowling score?

Gretchen bowled a 120 + Mitzi boweld a 113 + Beth bowled an 85 = 318 combined score.
The average of their combined score of 318 / 3 bowlers = 106.
The answer is 106.

The power went out on the hottest night of May, and the flat went dark. Avni, five, gasped. "Papa, we're in a cave! There are bats!" She hung a dupatta from the chair and crawled under it. "Why do bats sleep upside down? Do they get dizzy? Do bats eat roti?" Uday, her father, sweating by the torch, didn't say "Don't be silly." He handed her a roti and a banana. Avni rolled them together. "Cave pizza!" She fed a pretend bat first. When the fan whirred back to life, she groaned. "Can we keep the cave?"

What did Avni roll together?
A roti and a banana, calling it cave pizza.
How did Avni feel when the power went out?
She felt excited and delighted, turning the dark flat into a cave full of bats.
What did Uday do that gave Avni room to wonder?
He didn't call her silly, answered her game by handing her food and let the make-believe continue despite the heat.
How might Uday feel watching Avni feed a pretend bat?
He may feel amused and fond of her imagination, even while hot and tired in the power cut.

Mridul, you keep asking why I didn't dance at the fest when you've seen me dance at my cousin's baraat. Okay, here's Kiran's full explanation, one time only. At the baraat it was dhol, dust, my Tauji's terrible bhangra, and all my cousins pulling me in. Nobody filmed me, nobody cared if I was good. I danced for two hours and felt I belonged to every person on that road. The fest was different. Some seniors said the dance team was "a girls' thing" and started calling the boys who joined silly names. Nobody forced me out, but it didn't feel like choosing either. So I sat out. And I hated sitting out. Next year, if you join with me, I'll do it. Deal? It's my dancing. It's not theirs to decide.

How long did Kiran dance at the baraat?
For two hours.
What was Kiran feeling while dancing at the baraat?
Kiran felt joyful and part of the whole family, free because nobody was filming or judging.
What turned dancing from joy into something Kiran avoided at the fest?
The seniors' teasing about gender and the names they called the boys, which made joining feel risky rather than a free choice.
How might Mridul feel about Kiran's "Deal?"
Mridul may feel trusted and glad to help, since joining together could make dancing feel like Kiran's own choice again.

“Thomas, what's this?” Ammachi held up a soft appam.
“Appam!”
“And what do we say before we eat?”
Two-year-old Thomas folded his tiny hands. “Ammen!”
Farhan laughed from the stove. “Not Amen yet, monu. First the prayer.”
Ammachi sang the short grace in Malayalam. Thomas swayed and hummed along, then shouted, “Ammen!” at the end, exactly on time.
“Good boy,” said Ammachi. “Now, stew or sugar?”
“Sugar!”

What did Ammachi hold up?
She held up a soft appam.
How did Thomas feel when he shouted “Ammen!” on time?
He felt proud and happy to be part of the family prayer.
How could the family help Thomas learn more of the grace?
They could keep singing it at every meal and let him join in the parts he knows.
How does Farhan see Thomas's early “Amen”?
Farhan is amused and fond, gently correcting him while laughing.
Out of 804 senior high school students, 75% passed their exams and so got their degree. The rest failed. How many didn't pass their exams?

Find the number of students who got their degree by multiplying: 804 students * 75% = 603 students.
Then find the number of students who didn't pass their exams by subtracting this number from the total: 804 students - 603 students = 201 students.
The answer is 201.
Tom split 2 apples into 8 slices each. Tom gave 3/8ths of the apple slices to his friend Jerry, then ate half of the remaining slices. How many apple slices does Tom have left?

2 apples cut into 8 slices each is 2*8=16 slices
2/8ths of the apple slices is 16*3/8=6 slices
Tom had 16-6=10 slices
Tom then ate half the slices so he has 10/2=5 slices
The answer is 5.
In an old book it says she upbraided him. Is that praise or a scolding?

It is a scolding. To upbraid someone is to tell them off in a stern way for something they did. It is a verb and is rarely used today.
Example: The mother upbraided her son for coming home late without a call.

Beatriz's shift at the bakery in Sao Paulo started at five, and the bus ride took forty minutes each way. For two years she had told herself she would start drawing properly once she could afford the illustration course, once she had a desk, once things calmed down.
Then Wei, who baked the rolls beside her, showed her a notebook full of tiny ink sketches of customers. "Bus sketches," he shrugged. "Twenty minutes a day."
So Beatriz began. A pencil, an exercise book from the corner shop, the faces on the early bus. On Sundays she borrowed drawing books from the public library. The hands were terrible at first.
Three months later Wei flipped through her book and stopped at an old man asleep against a window. "That," he said. "That's him."

How long did the bus ride take each way?
Forty minutes.
How might Beatriz have felt when Wei stopped at the sleeping old man?
She likely felt proud and encouraged, since after three months of terrible hands her drawing had finally caught someone.
What did Beatriz do instead of waiting for perfect conditions?
She started small with a pencil, a cheap exercise book, faces on the bus and library books, rather than waiting for the course, the desk or calmer times.
How might Wei see Beatriz's progress?
Wei, who sketches on the bus himself, probably sees it with warmth and respect, knowing how hard it is to keep going with so little time.

Wednesday
Today I finally sat at THE table, the one by the window where Kritika and her group eat.
To get there I've done a lot. I stopped wearing my favourite green hairband because Kritika called it "so Class 5." I said I hate old Hindi songs, which is a lie, I love them. I laughed at a joke about the girl who stammers, and my stomach turned.
And I left Nazia eating alone. She looked at me across the canteen and then looked down at her dabba.
For twenty minutes at the window table I felt great. Then Kritika said, "Why are you so quiet, Sangeeta? Boring today?" and everyone went silent, and I knew one wrong word and I'm out again.
It's not real belonging if I have to disappear to keep it.
Tomorrow I'm eating with Nazia. She knows every old song I love.

What did Sangeeta stop wearing?
Her favourite green hairband.
How did Sangeeta feel after Kritika called her boring?
Sangeeta felt anxious and insecure, sensing that one wrong word would push Sangeeta out again.
What is Sangeeta's next step, and why is it wise?
Eating with Nazia again, who likes Sangeeta's real self, is steadier than a place bought by hiding who Sangeeta is.
What is it like for Nazia when Sangeeta leaves her alone at lunch?
Nazia feels hurt and abandoned, looking across the canteen and then down at her dabba.

Couples counselling, session note, week 2.

Indu and Pankaj, married eighteen months. Indu described the past month in detail, and it was clear she has been reaching out many times a day in small ways.

Examples she gave: sending Pankaj a funny video at work, asking about his cricket team, resting her hand on his shoulder while he cooked. Most went unanswered. He admits he often didn't notice.

Indu said each missed moment "stings a little, like a paper cut." After a few weeks, she said, she stopped joking and started saying, "You never listen to me." She was surprised to hear herself.

Pankaj looked genuinely startled to learn the videos had meant anything.

Plan agreed: for one week, each will notice and respond to one small reach from the other per day. We will review next Tuesday.

How long have Indu and Pankaj been married?
They have been married eighteen months.
How did Indu feel when her small reaches were missed?
Indu felt a small sting each time, like a paper cut, and over weeks her hurt turned into complaints.
Why is the plan to answer one small reach a day a wise step?
It makes the small bids visible and gives Indu some response, before her frustration grows into bigger complaints.
How might Pankaj feel learning that the videos mattered to Indu?
Pankaj seems startled and perhaps a little guilty, realising he missed something important without meaning to.
Our meetings always "drag on". What does that mean?

To drag on means to continue for too long, in a tiring or boring way.
Example: The speech dragged on until half the audience was asleep.

In a village hall outside Jhansi, Sachin ran a Saturday tuition centre for forty children. Every month he sat down with Preeti, a volunteer teacher, and a notebook. They counted attendance from the register, marked the short maths test, and asked each child for one line on what they liked and disliked. In March the reading circle had eleven children on average and scores had barely moved. The children's notes said, 'Story time is the best.' Maths practice had steady attendance and rising scores. The two decided: drop the drawing class, which had few children and no change in anything; change reading to use stories; keep maths as it was. Sachin pinned the numbers on the hall wall. 'We'll look again in April,' he said.

How many children did the reading circle have on average in March?
The reading circle had eleven children on average.
What does Sachin want from looking at the numbers again in April?
Sachin wants decisions to rest on evidence and to keep adjusting, which shows a steady commitment to the centre.
What other kind of evidence could Sachin add to the monthly numbers?
Sachin could ask parents at pick-up time what they notice at home, since families may see changes that scores and registers miss.
How might Preeti see the decision to drop the drawing class?
Preeti probably sees it as fair because the numbers back it, though may feel sorry for the few children who enjoyed it.
Where you will stay in London next month? Correct the question, please.

Where will you stay in London next month?
Why: a "where" question puts "will" before "you".
Which nickname did my friends call me in Class 5?
I'm not sure, because I know nothing about your school days. Old classmates, or your family, might remember it.
