Two months after the result, when the sting had dulled, Bhavna sat at the kitchen table with a notebook and three columns. In her control: she had skipped mock papers and studied only at night. Luck: the audit paper had been unusually long. To change: timed practice, mornings, one study partner. She did not write "I'm hopeless," and she did not write "the paper was rigged." She looked at it the way she would look at a colleague's data.

She did not leap back to the full exam. She registered for the one paper she had narrowly missed, and started a small side project, a budgeting sheet for Harsha's café. Each week gave her a tiny win: a mock paper finished on time, a café owner smiling at a tidy sheet. Confidence did not arrive first; it followed the doing.

Years later, Ojas, a junior colleague, failed the same exam and stood in her doorway looking stunned. Bhavna told him plainly, "I failed it once too. It was awful, and it taught me how I study." She showed him her old three-column page. Ojas laughed shakily and asked whether she would help him make one.

What three columns did Bhavna write in her notebook?
She wrote columns for what was in her control, luck, and what to change.
How did Bhavna's honest review lead to her small steps and to the way she later helped Ojas?

The review showed what was in her control and what was luck, turning the failure into information. She then tried again small, with one paper and a side project, collected wins, and years later shared her story and three-column page with Ojas.
How did Ojas feel standing in her doorway?
He felt stunned and shaken, until Bhavna's plain honesty let him laugh shakily.
What could Bhavna suggest to Ojas as a first step?
She could suggest he make his own three columns once the sting dulls, then try a smaller step such as one paper.

Write a two-sentence summary of this extract.

Edgar Linton was silent a minute; an expression of exceeding sorrow overcast his features: he would have pitied the child on his own account; but, recalling Isabella's hopes and fears, and anxious wishes for her son, and her commendations of him to his care, he grieved bitterly at the prospect of yielding him up, and searched in his heart how it might be avoided. No plan offered itself: the very exhibition of any desire to keep him would have rendered the claimant more peremptory: there was nothing left but to resign him. However, he was not going to rouse him from his sleep.

Edgar is deeply sad, because he remembers Isabella's wishes for her son and does not want to give the boy up. He sees no way to keep the boy, since resisting would only make the claimant push harder, so he will give him up.

Monday. Neelam hadn't come to the mess for two days. At night she lay facing the wall and barely answered. Baljeet, her roommate, lay awake, afraid that asking about dark thoughts would put the idea in her head.
Tuesday. After class Neelam said, half-joking, "It'd be easier for everyone if I just vanished." Baljeet closed the door at once, sat down beside her and asked, "Are you thinking of hurting yourself, or of ending your life?" Neelam's eyes filled. "Yes. Nobody's asked me that." Her shoulders dropped, as if she had put down something heavy. Baljeet stayed with her, asked her to hand over anything she might use to hurt herself, and gave it to the warden. Together they called the crisis line, which linked them to the campus counsellor that evening.
Friday. Neelam was back in the mess, tired but eating. "When you asked me straight out," she told Baljeet, "I could finally breathe."

What did Neelam say after class on Tuesday?
It'd be easier for everyone if I just vanished.
What was Baljeet afraid of on Monday night?
Baljeet was afraid that asking about dark thoughts would put the idea in Neelam's head.
What steps did Baljeet take once Neelam said yes?
Baljeet stayed, asked for anything Neelam might use to hurt herself and gave it to the warden, then called the crisis line together with her.
How did being asked directly feel for Neelam?
It was a relief; her shoulders dropped, and later she said she could finally breathe.

The week before her cousin's wedding, Keerthana's small flat in Coimbatore was full: aunts on the sofa, cousins on the floor, a pressure cooker whistling every twenty minutes. Her maths olympiad was in ten days.
She tried the dining table. Gurpreet messaged three times in ten minutes about a video. An aunt asked her to taste the payasam. She read the same geometry problem four times.
That evening she took her notebook up to the building terrace, switched her phone to airplane mode, and set a timer for forty-five minutes. The first stretch was hard; she kept glancing at the dark screen. Somewhere around the fifteen-minute mark the triangle started making sense, and she stopped hearing the traffic below.
When the timer rang, she had solved three problems. She came down, turned the phone back on, and replied to Gurpreet: "Was on the terrace studying 🙂 Every evening at 7, don't worry if I vanish."

Where did Keerthana go to study?
Up to the building terrace.
What was Keerthana feeling at the dining table?
Keerthana felt frustrated and scattered, reading the same geometry problem four times amid messages and interruptions.
What steps helped Keerthana guard her focus?
A quiet place, airplane mode and a fixed forty-five-minute timer, plus telling Gurpreet about the 7 pm block.
How might Gurpreet respond to the message?
Gurpreet will likely understand and stop expecting quick replies at seven, since Keerthana explained kindly instead of just vanishing.
What was today's top trending topic? How would you explain "blemish" to a child? How do I spell "occassion"?

1. I can't see today's news or trends, so I don't know. Look at a news site you trust.
2. Blemish is a noun that means a small mark that spoils how something looks.
3. It is "occasion", with a double "c" and one "s".

"Ira, you're studying psychology now, so let me tell you about my hostel days. I'm your Kalyani Mami, the one who argued with every professor.
In my third year, everyone believed willpower was a tank. Use it up on exams, and it's gone. My hostel-mate Rukmini swore by it. After every paper she'd say, 'Tank empty,' and eat a whole box of sweets.
Then our research methods teacher showed us something that stayed with me. Bigger studies, done again and again in many places, did not find the strong effect. Some found that what you believe about your tiredness changes how tired you act.
I watched Rukmini that week after exams. Was she truly spent, or did the belief do half the work? I could never be sure. What I did learn was to be careful before calling anything proven."

What did Rukmini say after every paper?
She said, "Tank empty," and ate a whole box of sweets.
How did young Kalyani feel as she watched Rukmini after the research methods class?
She felt doubtful and curious, unsure whether Rukmini was truly spent or whether the belief was doing half the work.
What choice did young Kalyani make after that class?
She chose to be careful before calling anything proven, holding the tank idea as uncertain rather than a fact.
How might Rukmini have felt if someone questioned her empty tank?
Rukmini might have felt defensive or annoyed, since the tank idea explained her tiredness and made the box of sweets feel deserved.

"Sarika, where is your homework notebook?" "Not in my bag." "Why not? You finished it." "If it's not in my bag, Miss can't ask." "Sarika..." "She won't ask. I know." Sangeeta, her mother, held up the notebook. "It's here on the table." Sarika turned her back. "Please leave it." "Miss will ask for it whether it's in your bag or not." Sarika zipped the bag anyway. At pick-up her face was long. "Miss asked. I had no notebook."

Where was the homework notebook?
The homework notebook was on the table.
What did Sarika believe would happen if the notebook was not in her bag?
Sarika believed Miss could not ask if the notebook was not in her bag, and she hoped this so much that she would not listen. Her long face at pick-up shows the hope was wrong.
What could Sarika do instead, and why?
She could put the notebook in the bag and check it off a list. Hoping does not change whether Miss asks, but packing it does.
How does the morning look to Sangeeta?
Sangeeta sees work that is done and a plan that cannot work, and she cannot talk Sarika out of it. Then she meets a sad child at pick-up. 🙂
What is my uncle's job in Dubai?
I wouldn't know, because I can't see your family's details. Ask someone in the family, or ask him on your next call.
Diwali par dost ko wish karna hai "Aapko aur parivaar ko Diwali ki shubhkamnayein." English?
Write: "Happy Diwali to you and your family."
Aur "Mithai kha lo" ko kaise likhun?
Write: "Have some sweets."
What makes Jane go back to look for Rochester?
One night she seems to hear his voice calling "Jane! Jane! Jane!" from far away. The next day she leaves Moor House to find him.

Sit down, Ishita, and let me tell you about something I did right when I was twenty-two. I'm Shankar, and back then I got an email from an online shop saying their system had been breached. My first instinct was to put the phone down and hope.

Instead I opened the site, changed my password straight away, and then remembered I had used that same password for my email. So I changed it there too, and on two other accounts. Then I found the setting that asks for a second code when someone logs in and switched it on for all of them. It took forty minutes.

A month later a friend's account from the same shop was emptied. Mine wasn't touched.

How long did it take Shankar to change the passwords and turn on the second code?
It took forty minutes.
What was Shankar's first instinct on reading the breach email, and what made a difference?
Shankar's first instinct was to freeze and hope, but remembering the reused password pushed Shankar to act at once.
What turning point in the story showed a wise choice, and what alternative could have followed?
The turning point was remembering the same password on the email account and changing it there too; otherwise the breach could have spread to more accounts.
How did the friend's emptied account differ from Shankar's after the breach?
The friend's account was emptied while Shankar's was untouched, which shows that quick action limited the damage.

metadata.subtype: Approach: contain by changing passwords and turning on two-factor login [Action]

messages.content: concrete? I don't know this word.

Concrete is a hard building material made from cement, sand, water and small stones. It is a noun; as an adjective it means real and definite, not just an idea.
Example: Workers poured concrete to make the new footpath.

Sarika never broke a rule, and she said so, rolling her eyes when Manjula ran in the corridor. "You'll get in trouble. So silly." Manjula's shoulders dropped, and she stopped sitting next to Sarika. On Thursday Sarika's friend Dev kicked a ball through the library window during break. "Don't tell," he whispered. Sarika's heart raced, and she wanted to say it was the wind. Instead she said, "I won't lie, but I'll go with you to Ma'am Sangeeta." Dev shook his head. That night Sarika replayed the moment, and the heavy feeling sat in her chest like a stone: she had not helped Dev, and she had been unkind to Manjula. Next morning she told Dev, "Let's go now," and walked beside him into the staff room. Ma'am Sangeeta stayed calm, thanked them for telling her and said, "Let's work out how to fix the window. Dev will help the caretaker and write a note." Dev breathed out. Sarika then said sorry to Manjula and offered her the seat back. Manjula smiled. Sarika felt lighter, and she stopped telling herself she was better than anyone.

What did Dev kick through the library window?
Dev kicked a ball through the library window.
How did Sarika's scorn for Manjula differ from her loyalty toward Dev?
She rolled her eyes at Manjula for running and made her lonely, while with Dev she refused to lie but walked beside him to the teacher, showing that kindness and firmness can sit together.
What was Sarika feeling that night as she replayed the moment?
She felt guilty, with a heavy feeling in her chest like a stone.
What could Dev do next after the teacher's calm reply?
He could help the caretaker and write the note as Ma'am Sangeeta said, and own up sooner if he breaks a rule again.

Kalyani made herself a rule taped above the desk: games start only when the homework is done. Some days it felt hard, but when she finally picked up the controller nothing nagged at the back of her mind, and the game was sweeter for it. Vasudha's cousin, Seema, preferred a timer. On weekdays she set it for forty minutes, and when it rang she put the controller down. Nobody had told her to; the limit was hers. Their neighbour Ravi was another story. "Just one more round," he told himself. Then another. Then another. When his mother looked in, the clock said ten and his maths sheet lay blank under the bed. The next week he fell asleep in the middle of a lesson, and the teacher had to nudge his shoulder. That evening Ravi thought about the yawning mornings and the late nights, and he made a change. He would play in the afternoon, and by nine the console would go into the cupboard.

How long did Seema set her timer for on weekdays?
She set it for forty minutes.
How does Seema's way of stopping differ from Ravi's, and what did each lead to?
Seema used a timer with a fixed end, so she stopped when it rang. Ravi had no stopping point, so one more round kept growing until it was ten o'clock with his maths undone.
What was Ravi feeling when he thought about the yawning mornings and late nights?
He was tired and a little worried; he had realised that gaming late was costing him sleep and school focus, which pushed him to change.
What could Ravi do to make his new nine o'clock rule stick?
He could put the cupboard rule where he sees it, ask his mother to check in once, and finish his maths before gaming, so the rule feels like his own. 🙂
Give exactly four adjectives for a sunny day, comma-separated, all lowercase.
warm, bright, clear, cheerful

Beatriz held her phone at arm's length, chin tilted, lips pushed into a pout. The photo was for the group chat. Across the terrace, Ivan saw her pouting and assumed she was upset about something. "Hey, what happened?" he asked, coming over. She burst out laughing. "Nothing! It's my photo face." "Oh. I thought you were sulking about the football." "I'm sulking about your terrible taste in shirts 😄" she said. Ivan grinned and held out his hand for the phone. "Let me see it." She showed him, and he said it looked good, but he preferred her real laugh.

What did Beatriz say her pout was for?
She said it was her photo face, for the group chat.
What did Ivan think Beatriz was feeling when he saw her pout, and what does his question suggest?
Ivan thought she was upset or sulking. He asked instead of joking, which shows he was unsure and cared.
What did Ivan choose to do that worked well?
He asked what was wrong instead of teasing her. Asking cleared it up without hurting anyone.
How might Beatriz feel about Ivan's question?
She may feel cared for that he checked. It could also feel funny that a style was read as a mood.

Monday. Was about to send last year's hiring plan to the panel as it was: eight weeks, three interview rounds, offers by week seven. It worked so well last year. Then I asked myself what's different now, and went through it point by point. The market is tighter. Afreen in recruiting told me good candidates are getting several offers within two weeks, which wasn't true last year. So eight weeks is too long; we'd lose people while still deciding. Cut it to five weeks, offers by week four. Kept the three rounds, because they gave us fewer bad hires. Told the panel why. A bit anxious about the speed, but better than repeating last year blindly. — Vijay

How long is the new timeline?
The new timeline is five weeks.
How does Vijay feel about the shorter timeline?
Vijay feels a bit anxious about the speed, but prefers it to repeating last year's plan blindly.
What other step could Vijay take to keep good candidates?
Vijay could contact the strongest candidates early with a clear date for a decision, since people with several offers tend to choose whoever is clearest and quickest.
How might a strong candidate with several offers have seen an eight-week process?
They would likely take another offer, since waiting that long while others decide within two weeks feels risky.

Kindergarten teacher's note, monsoon term
Today Lalit (5) sat alone at lunch. Usually he pushes other children when upset.
When I sat with him, he said, "I'm sad because Nikita didn't sit with me."
That is a big step. Two months ago he would have pushed her.
I told him thank you for telling me. I asked Nikita if she'd sit with him tomorrow. She agreed. 🙂

Who didn't sit with Lalit?
Nikita.
How did Lalit feel at lunch?
He felt sad and left out because Nikita didn't sit with him.
How did the teacher support Lalit's new skill?
The teacher thanked him for using words and arranged for Nikita to sit with him tomorrow.
How might Nikita feel when asked to sit with Lalit?
Nikita may feel pleased to be asked, and understand that Lalit missed her.

The landlord had given Elizabeth and Binita one hour. "Two other people want this flat. Bring ID copies, work letters and the deposit receipt by eight, or I sign with them."
It was 6:55, the lift was broken, and the power in their old building had just gone out. Binita ran to her room with her phone torch, pulling open drawers. "My work letter is somewhere in my email… the network is dead."
Elizabeth went to the steel cupboard and took out a green folder. Passport copy, office ID, last three pay slips, the old rental agreement, all in clear sleeves. She had also kept two photocopies of each.
She sat with Binita on the stairs and helped her list what was missing. At 7:30 the network came back; Elizabeth forwarded Binita's scanned letter from the shared drive they had set up months ago and never used. They reached the landlord's door at 7:52, a little breathless.

At what time did the two of them reach the landlord's door?
They reached the landlord's door at 7:52.
How was Binita feeling as she searched with her phone torch?
Binita was panicked and flustered, pulling open drawers while the network was down.
Which habit saved them, and why?
Elizabeth's green folder with originals in sleeves and extra photocopies, plus the shared scanned drive, meant nothing had to be hunted for in the dark.
What would change if Elizabeth had not kept the folder?
Both of them would have been searching blind with no power or network, and they would likely have lost the flat.

In Valencia, Diego, nine, remembered the night his grandfather died. He had been in the kitchen, eating bread with honey, when the phone rang. His mother dropped a cup, and it broke on the tiles.

He told the story to his sister Noa, years later it seemed, though it was only one year. "I was eating honey bread. Mamá dropped the blue cup."

Noa said softly, "I think you were asleep. I woke you up."

Diego shook his head. "No, I remember the honey. And the cup breaking."

Noa didn't argue. She just held his hand. "Maybe some of it happened on another day."

Diego held on to the picture. It still felt perfectly clear.

What does Diego remember eating when the phone rang?
Bread with honey.
Why does Diego hold on to the picture of the honey and the cup?
The night of his grandfather's death was so emotional that the memory feels perfectly clear and true to him, and letting go of it may feel sad.
How could an adult gently help Diego with this memory?
An adult could listen and share the grief, without insisting on correcting details, and gently say memories can mix.
How does Noa respond to Diego's version?
Noa is gentle and caring, holding his hand instead of arguing.

Jack leaves his bathtub's faucet dripping at a rate of 40 ml/minute. Water evaporates from the bathtub at a rate of 200 ml/hour. If he leaves the water running for 9 hours, then dumps out 12 liters, how many milliliters of water are left in the bathtub?

First find how much water fills the bathtub per hour: 40 ml/minute * 60 minutes/hour = 2400 ml/hour
Then subtract the water that evaporates to find the total amount of water added per hour: 2400 ml/hour - 200 ml/hour = 2200 ml/hour
Then multiply that amount by the number of hours to find the total amount of water in the tub: 2200 ml/hour * 9 hours = 19800 ml
Then find the number of milliliters in 12 liters: 12 liters * 1000 ml/liter = 12000 ml
Then subtract the water Jack removes from the total amount of water to find the remaining amount of water: 19800 ml - 12000 ml = 7800 ml
The answer is 7800.

Beginner readers will use this, so keep every sentence short and every word plain.

Fresh out of the bath in their Pune flat, Jagdish wriggled free of the towel and ran down the corridor, giggling. At the bedroom door he stopped and looked back over his shoulder, grinning at Hemant.
"I'm coming to get you!" Hemant said, taking big slow steps.
Jagdish shrieked, ran behind the curtain, and peeped out again, waiting.

Jagdish had just had a bath. He wriggled out of the towel and ran down the hall. He was giggling. At the bedroom door he stopped. He looked back and grinned at Hemant. "I'm coming to get you!" said Hemant. Hemant took big, slow steps. Jagdish shrieked. He ran behind the curtain. Then he peeped out and waited.
Our dog is afraid to go down stairs. He climbs up, then just stands at the top and whines.
That's not unusual. Going down feels steeper and scarier for a dog. Is he young or old?
About three years old.
Then he's capable but nervous. Try standing a few steps below him and call him with a treat, one step at a time. Praise every small move.
What if he refuses?
Don't force him. Practise on just two steps for a few days, then add more. If he seems to be in pain or suddenly refuses, ask a vet to check on him.
I'll start with two steps.
That's a gentle plan. Keep sessions short and cheerful.
He managed all the steps on Sunday.
That's a big win. Keep praising him each time, and soon it will feel ordinary.
Now you try: the remainder when 2^6^0 is divided by 7.
The answer is 2^6^0 = 8^2^0 = (7 + 1)^2^0: remainder 1.
The red box is heavier than the green box, and the blue box is lighter than the green box. Which box is the heaviest?
The red box is the heaviest. Because the red box is heavier than the green one and the green one is heavier than the blue one, red is above the others.

Siddharth, you keep defending that slide deck because you made every chart by hand. Let me tell you about my table. At twenty-three, as a young man just married, I built our dining table myself. Three months of Sundays, sanding teak in my father's courtyard. It wobbled, and the top was a finger's width uneven. When I was twenty-six, we moved flats. While packing, I asked myself: if I were buying a table today, would I choose this one? I wanted to say yes. Then I answered honestly. No. It was proud work, not good furniture. So we bought a steady table for meals, and mine became my reading desk by the window. I still run my hand along its uneven edge. Both things are true, you see. That's Manoj's advice for today.

How long did Manoj take to build the dining table?
Three months of Sundays.
How did Manoj feel on first asking the question while packing?
Manoj wanted to say yes because of all the sanding done, but on answering honestly Manoj saw it was proud work, not good furniture.
What choice did Manoj make with the table, and why does it work?
Manoj bought a steady table for meals and turned the handmade one into a reading desk, so the family eats at a table that doesn't wobble while the old table stays cherished.
Why might Siddharth need to hear this story right now?
Siddharth is defending a slide deck because the charts were made by hand. The story offers a way to separate pride in the effort from whether the deck is the best choice today.

Dussehra holidays, Friday night.
Dear diary, Pema is my best friend. I've told him everything: that I'm scared of the dark, that I cried when our dog died, that I want to be a chef, not an engineer. He's the only one who knows the chef part. We promised to make the Ravana model together for the colony contest. Today I went to his house with the bamboo sticks, and he and Tsering were already building it. Pema said, 'Tsering's dad has a glue gun, sorry yaar.' Sorry yaar!! Like it's nothing. I walked home and my chest hurt like someone was sitting on it. Now I keep thinking, what if he tells Tsering the chef thing too? I'm never telling anyone anything ever again.
Lokesh

What were Pema and Tsering already building?
The Ravana model for the colony contest.
What does Lokesh's chest hurting 'like someone was sitting on it' show?
It shows Lokesh felt crushed and betrayed after Pema broke their promise so casually.
What could Lokesh do instead of never telling anyone anything again?
Lokesh could tell Pema honestly how much it hurt and ask about the chef secret, giving the friendship a chance to repair.
How might Pema see what happened?
Pema may think it was a small practical choice because of the glue gun, not realising how deeply it hurt his best friend.

Backstage at the school's annual day, Asif stood in his paper-crown costume, hands trembling so hard the cardboard rattled. Seema Ma'am knelt in front of him. “Your hands are shaking. Are you scared, or cold, or excited?” Asif bounced on his toes. “Excited! My Abbu is in the third row!” She smiled. “Can I hold them for a moment?” He nodded, and she held his hands, warm between hers. “Big breath with me. In… out.” The shaking eased a little. When the music began, he marched out grinning, crown still wobbling.

Where was Asif's Abbu sitting?
His Abbu was in the third row.
What was Asif feeling as his hands trembled?
He felt excited, bouncing on his toes about his Abbu watching; some nerves could be mixed in, since the shaking only eased a little.
What did Seema do instead of assuming Asif was afraid?
She asked whether it was fear, cold or excitement, then used warm hands and a shared breath, which help whatever the cause.
What would change if Seema had told Asif not to be scared?
Asif might feel misunderstood, since he was mostly excited, and could start to wonder whether he should be scared.

Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki, and Alka's plan for a Diwali dinner shrank to the five people who could walk. The electricity flickered once and died. Alka lit the diyas that were meant only as decoration and used them to see. Down the hall, Hrithik knocked with a bag of naan from the last open shop. Two friends from the language class arrived stamping snow off their boots, one carrying a pot of rice, the other a story about a grandmother's festival in Lagos. They ate by candlelight, in a mix of Hindi, English and one shared Finnish greeting. Alka looked at the messy table and realised nobody there shared the same ancestors, but they shared this evening, and for the first time in months the flat felt like home.

What had stopped the trains in Helsinki?
Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki.
What was Alka feeling at the messy table?
Warm and at home, realising that belonging came from shared time, not shared ancestry.
What made the evening work despite the storm?
Adapting the plan to the five who could walk over and using the diyas for light.
How might Hrithik have felt bringing naan through the snow?
Glad to contribute and to belong, since Hrithik made the effort to reach the group.

Farida, come, sit, I'll tell you about my son Devang's first party. I'm Nandini Aunty to you, but that year I was just a nervous mother. The afternoon before, Devang sat on the edge of his bed with a notebook and wrote a short list: no getting in a car with anyone who has been drinking; nothing to try that I can't name. Then a third line: if it goes wrong, I call home and there are no questions that night. He showed it to me, red in the ears. At the party a boy called Tarun jingled car keys at eleven and said he would drop everyone. Devang didn't argue. He told himself, "That's on my list," and rang me from the balcony. My hands shook on the wheel and I was so proud I said nothing. In the car he said, "The list decided, not me."

What did Devang write on his list before the party?
Devang wrote: no getting in a car with anyone who has been drinking, and nothing to try that he cannot name.
How did Devang seem to feel when Tarun offered the lift?
Devang seemed steady and clear rather than pressured, since the choice was already on his list.
What choice in the story made the safe decision easy, and what more could Devang have set up?
Writing the list beforehand made it easy; Devang could also agree a pick-up signal with an adult so leaving needs no explanation.
What was it like for Nandini to get the call?
Nandini felt worried and proud, with shaking hands, and stayed quiet in the car so Devang did not feel judged.

Behind the school in Barmer stood the headman's guava tree, heavy with fruit. Kunal, five, walked under it slowly and kept his hands in his pockets. "Why don't you take one?" asked his cousin. "Manjula Aaji said if I don't touch the tree all week, she'll give me gud on Sunday," Kunal said. "And the headman shouts." He looked up at a yellow guava and swallowed. "A big piece of gud," he said again, to himself, and walked faster.

What did Manjula Aaji promise Kunal?
She said she would give him gud on Sunday if he didn't touch the tree all week.
What is Kunal feeling as he looks up at the yellow guava and swallows?
He is tempted by the fruit, but the thought of the reward and the headman shouting keeps him walking.
How could Manjula Aaji help Kunal begin to think beyond the reward?
She could ask him how the headman might feel if his guavas went missing, so he starts to think about other people too.
How does Kunal's cousin see the tree?
The cousin sees easy fruit and seems puzzled that Kunal won't take one.

Asif, twenty-five, got his first big work bonus the same week his aunt called: his cousin's wedding needed money, and the family expected him to help. His sister Trisha, who'd started working a year earlier, found him staring at his banking app late at night. "You're thinking of giving it all," she said. He nodded. "They'll say I've become selfish." Trisha sat down. "Give some. But you're the one who'll support Ammi when she retires." The next day, on his lunch break, with only an hour, he met a financial planner his office recommended. He left with a simple plan: part to the wedding, part to an emergency fund, part to long-term savings. That evening he called his aunt. She sounded a little disappointed, then said, "Thank you, beta."

Who recommended the financial planner Asif met?
His office.
What was Asif worried about as he stared at his banking app?
He feared his family would call him selfish if he didn't give all his bonus to the wedding.
Why was splitting the bonus a balanced choice?
It honoured his family duty while also building security for the future, including for his mother's retirement.
How might Asif's aunt feel about the amount he gave?
She was a little disappointed but still grateful, as her thanks shows.

On the village lane, a dog barked and leapt near Vishal, two. Vishal froze, then ran screaming to his uncle Sumit.

Sumit scooped him up and stepped back. "I've got you. The dog is loud."

They watched from the doorstep. After a while Vishal pointed. "Doggy."

"Yes, doggy. Sleeping now."

Sumit didn't carry him closer.

Who did Vishal run to?
Vishal ran to his uncle Sumit.
What was Vishal feeling when he froze?
Vishal felt terrified by the barking, leaping dog.
Why was it wise for Sumit not to carry him closer?
Keeping a safe distance and not forcing contact lets Vishal's curiosity return slowly.
How might Sumit feel seeing Vishal point at the dog later?
Sumit likely feels relieved and glad that Vishal is becoming curious instead of frightened.
Is the new season of that mystery series out on the weekend?
I can't check that, because release news is recent. The channel's schedule page lists release dates.

Reena's diary, Monday
Raghav was quiet all day. At lunch he said he didn't care about losing the chess final, but his shoulders were up by his ears and he kept rubbing the same spot on the table. I nearly started telling him about my own match. Then I remembered what Ma says: close your mouth, open your ears. So I just sat. After a while he told me he'd practised every night for a month. I didn't interrupt once. He ate half my paratha afterwards, which I think means he felt better.

What final did Raghav lose?
The chess final.
What did Raghav's raised shoulders and rubbing suggest to Reena?
That he was more upset and disappointed than he admitted.
What did Reena get right, and what could she try next?
Reena listened without interrupting; next Reena could ask a gentle question about how he's feeling.
How might Raghav feel after talking to Reena?
Lighter and less alone, since someone listened properly.
What is strange about the way the Cheshire Cat disappears?
It vanishes slowly, starting with the end of its tail and ending with its grin, which stays in the air for some time after the rest has gone.
Is an obstacle always something you can touch?

No. An obstacle is anything that blocks your way or makes it hard to do something, a real object or a problem. It is a noun.
Example: Fear of speaking was the biggest obstacle for Vikram in the debate.
"Kitni der lagegi?" ko shop mein ya office mein English mein kaise bolein?
Ask: "How long will it take?" It works everywhere: in a shop, at a repair centre or at an office counter.
In her piggy bank Tara has a ₹10 note, a ₹5 coin, a ₹2 coin and a ₹1 coin. How much money does she have?

Answer: ₹18.

Start with the biggest: 10. Count on 5: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Count on 2: 16, 17. Count on 1: 18. Always start from the biggest value; it makes counting quicker.

I'm Seema, and when Joseph and I were planning our small wedding last year, the photographer sent three packages. Bronze: photos only. Silver: photos and a short video, for almost the price of Gold. Gold: photos, full video, a printed album and a drone.
Joseph said, "Gold is obviously the smart one." I felt it too. But Silver looked so pointless that I got suspicious. I printed the page and blacked Silver out with a marker. Then I wrote our list: forty guests, a church and a lunch hall, no drone needed, and the limit we had agreed on. Bronze, plus a cousin with a good phone for video, covered everything.
Joseph grumbled for a day. This year, looking at our photos, neither of us misses the drone.

How many guests were on Seema's list?
Forty guests.
What did Seema feel when Silver looked so pointless?
Seema felt suspicious, sensing the odd package was steering them towards Gold.
What did blacking out Silver and writing a list achieve?
It removed the decoy and let Seema and Joseph choose by their real needs and agreed limit.
How did Joseph feel about the final choice?
Joseph grumbled for a day, but a year later doesn't miss the drone.
A man owned 1/2 of a lot. He sold 1/10 of his share for the amount of $460. What is the worth of the entire lot?

If 1/10 of the man's lot is equal to $460, then the man's land is worth $460 x 10 = $4600.
Since 1/2 of the whole lot is worth $4600, then the whole lot is worth $4600 x 2 = $9200.
The answer is 9200.

Subject: Can I meet you this week?
Dear Noor Ma'am,
I'm Manoj from 10C. You said in assembly that we could write to you if something was taking over our days. I think this is.
I keep scrolling through photos of people with perfect arms and flat stomachs. I know most of them are filtered, but I still compare myself. I've covered the mirror in my room with a poster. Last Sunday I pretended to have a stomach-ache so I wouldn't have to go to my cousin's engagement, because everyone takes photos. In class I'm thinking about how I look instead of the lesson. It feels like if I looked different I'd matter more.
My friends say everyone feels like this sometimes. Maybe. But for me it's all day now.
Could I come and see you after lunch on Wednesday?
Manoj

What did Manoj cover the mirror with?
A poster.
What does Manoj think would change if Manoj looked different?
Manoj feels insecure and thinks a different look would make Manoj matter more, tying worth to appearance.
Why was writing this email a turning point for Manoj?
Manoj noticed the thoughts had spread to the whole day, not just sometimes, and chose to ask the counsellor for help early.
How might Noor Ma'am feel reading "for me it's all day now"?
Noor Ma'am may be glad Manoj wrote and take it seriously, since it shows the worry has grown beyond the ordinary.

"Bye, Santosh! Give Bua a big kiss!" said Ira, bending down.
Santosh stepped back and put his hands behind his back.
"Ask him, Ira didi," said his mother. "Santosh, kiss for Bua?"
"No."
"Okay," said Ira. "High five, then?"
Santosh grinned and slapped her hand. Then he ran to his mother and threw both arms round her legs for a long cuddle.

What did Santosh give Ira instead of a kiss?
A high five.
What was Santosh feeling when he put his hands behind his back?
He didn't want to give a kiss and felt uncomfortable being asked; he felt happy once he could say goodbye his own way.
What did his mother and Ira do that respected Santosh?
They asked him first and accepted his "no", then offered a high five instead.
How might Ira feel about the high five?
She seems cheerful and fine with it, glad to still share a goodbye.

The state library's digitisation room hummed with scanners. After Wednesday's review, where Darshan sir had called her file names 'a mess' in front of the whole team, Urmila's fellow interns were ready to rant in the group chat. She typed, deleted, and closed the app. On Thursday morning she waited until he was alone at the catalogue desk. "Sir, could I have ten minutes today?" At four they sat by the window. "I want to do this well," she said, hands folded to keep them still. "Could you show me exactly what's wrong with the file names? And if possible, could corrections like that come privately?" Darshan sir blinked, then nodded slowly. "Fair. I should have shown you the format first." He pulled out a printed sheet.

Where did Urmila wait to find Darshan sir alone?
She waited until he was alone at the catalogue desk.
What does Urmila folding her hands to keep them still suggest?
She was nervous about raising it, yet determined to stay calm and speak clearly.
Why was Urmila's choice better than ranting in the group chat?
Talking privately and calmly gave Darshan sir a chance to explain and change, while venting would only have spread resentment without fixing anything.
What might Darshan sir realise when he says he should have shown her the format first?
He seems to see that his public criticism skipped a step, and that the intern needed guidance before correction.

Kalyani had been messaging Dhruv for two weeks, and today, on the steps behind the library, she said it lightly: “Send me a picture, a private one, and we could meet at the mall alone on Sunday.” Dhruv's ears burned. He liked her. But something inside him said no, quietly and clearly.
“I'm not ready to send private pictures,” he said. “And I don't want to meet alone yet.”
“Come on, it's nothing.”
“It's something to me.” His voice wobbled, but he didn't say sorry. “I'd love to talk at school, or go with the group.”
Kalyani shrugged, hurt or maybe annoyed, and said, “Fine.” Dhruv let the silence sit and walked to class, his heart pounding and himself oddly lighter.

Where were Dhruv and Kalyani when she asked?
They were on the steps behind the library.
What was Dhruv feeling as he said no?
Dhruv was nervous but firm, since his ears burned and his voice wobbled, yet he held his limit and felt lighter afterwards.
What could Dhruv do if Kalyani keeps pressing?
Dhruv could repeat the limit calmly, and step away or tell a trusted adult if the pressure continues.
How might Kalyani feel after the refusal?
Kalyani may feel hurt, embarrassed or annoyed, since she shrugged and said fine, and what she does afterwards shows whether she respects the no.

messages.content: Why are fireworks set off at night rather than in the day?
They are much easier to see in the dark. Because the bright colours stand out against a black sky, while daylight would wash them out.
Now you try: divide x^4 - 3x^2 + 4x + 5 by x^2 + 1 - x.
The answer is q = x^2 + x - 3, r = 8.

Gopika, you asked why I get upset when you talk about "not letting" a girl sit with your group. Let me tell you. I'm your Kunal mama. When I was eleven, there was a new boy, Manoj, who was good at everything, cricket, maths, jokes. My friends started liking him more than me. So I made a rule: nobody talks to Manoj. And they obeyed. Walking around with everyone doing what I said, I felt like a king. I told myself Manoj was a show-off who deserved it. But really, I was scared. If he took my place, where would I go? One day I saw him crying behind the bicycle shed. I felt sick. That evening I told my father, and he made me go to Manoj's house and apologise that same night. I've never forgotten either the power or the fear.

What did Kunal tell his friends about Manoj?
He made a rule: nobody talks to Manoj.
What was Kunal really feeling behind the freeze-out?
Kunal felt powerful, but underneath was scared of losing his place to Manoj.
Why was going to Manoj's house to apologise a turning point in the story?
It made Kunal face what he had done and take responsibility the same day, instead of hiding behind the story that Manoj deserved it.
How might Manoj have experienced the freeze-out?
Manoj likely felt hurt and lonely, which is why Kunal found him crying behind the bicycle shed.
There are 60 ridges on a vinyl record. Jerry has 4 cases, each with 3 shelves that can hold 20 records each. If his shelves are 60% full, how many ridges are there on all his records?

First find the total number of records that can fit on all the shelves: 4 cases * 3 shelves/case * 20 records/shelf = 240 records
Then multiply that number by 60% to find the number of records actually on the shelves: 240 records * 60% = 144 records
Then multiply that number by 60 to find the number of ridges on all the records: 144 records * 60 ridges/record = 8640 ridges
The answer is 8640.

Mentor's note, Thursday evening.
I have been sitting in on Francis's client calls for the bakery website project. The plan he agreed in March had five pages and a launch on the thirtieth.
In the first call, the client asked for a gallery. Francis said, "Sure, easy." In the second, an online order form. "No problem." Then a Hindi version, then a loyalty-points page. Each time he looked pleased that the client was happy. I noticed he never opened the schedule during any call.
Today the developer, Lakshmi, told us the launch cannot happen before the twentieth of next month. Francis went pale and said, "But each thing was small."
After the call I sat with him and we listed every added request with the days it cost. It came to eighteen working days. We agreed he will call the client tomorrow, show the list, and ask which extras can wait for a second phase.
— Mentor, Project Office

How many pages did the plan agreed in March have?
The plan had five pages.
What was Francis feeling when he heard the new launch date?
Francis was shocked and dismayed; he went pale and said each thing was small.
What could Francis do differently the next time a client asks for something extra?
Francis could open the schedule during the call and say what the extra would cost in days before saying yes.
How might the client feel when Francis calls with the list?
The client may feel disappointed at the delay, but also clearer about choices, since the list shows what each request cost.
How do I end a formal letter: "yours sincerely" or "yours faithfully"?

In British-style letters, use "Yours faithfully" after "Dear Sir or Madam", and "Yours sincerely" when you start with a name, such as "Dear Mr Rao". American letters usually end with "Sincerely".
Example: Dear Ms Khan, ... Yours sincerely, Arjun Nair.
Pauline will make tacos for dinner. She bought a box of taco shells that cost $5, 4 bell peppers that cost $1.5 each, and 2 pounds of meat that cost $3 per pound.  How much did she spend in all?

She spent 4 x $1.5 = $6 for the four bell peppers.
She spent 2 x $3 = $6 for the 2 pounds of meat.
So, Pauline spent $5 + $6 + $6 = $17 in all.
The answer is 17.

Samuel is driving to San Francisco's Comic-Con in his car and he needs to travel 600 miles to the hotel where he made a reservation. At first, he drives at 50 miles/hour for 3 hours straight, then he speeds up to 80 miles/hour for 4 hours. How far is he from the hotel?

At first at 50 miles/hour he travels 50 miles/hours*3 hours=150 miles.
After that, he speeds up, traveling 80 miles/hours*4 hours= 320 miles.
He travels a total of 150 miles+320 miles=470 miles.
He is 600-470=130miles from the hotel.
The answer is 130.

Luca went to a sandwich shop for lunch. The sandwich he bought was normally $8, but he had a coupon for a quarter of the price off. He then upgraded it with sliced avocado for an extra dollar. After adding a drink and a $3 salad, his total lunch bill was $12. How many dollars did Luca pay for his drink?

Luca's coupon saved him 8 / 4 = $2 on his sandwich.
He paid $1 for avocado on his sandwich, so the sandwich cost 8 - 2 + 1 = $7.
He paid $3 for his salad, so his meal without the drink was 7 + 3 = $10.
Thus, Luca paid 12 - 10 = $2 for his drink.
The answer is 2.

I'm Jatin, and Sachin and I share a room at his parents' place while my family is in Dubai. On Tuesday night he sat at the desk with a sheet of paper, not studying.
He'd drawn three columns. When I asked, he said, “I saw Irfan copy in the chemistry test today. From a paper in his sleeve.” Irfan has been his best friend since Class Two.
He talked it through out loud, maybe more to himself than to me. “Column one: Irfan. He's my friend, and if I tell, maybe that's over. Column two: everyone else. Farida studied all weekend and might get fewer marks than him. That's not fair to her. Column three: me. If I say nothing, am I okay with that?”
He tapped the pen. “Every column is true. That's the problem. It's not simple.”
I didn't know what to say. He didn't decide that night. But he didn't pretend it was easy, either.

Where did Irfan have the paper he copied from?
In his sleeve.
How did Sachin seem to feel while weighing the three columns?
Sachin seemed torn and troubled, finding every column true and the choice anything but simple.
What could Sachin do next to move toward a decision?
Talk to Irfan privately first, or describe it to a parent without names, before deciding whether a teacher needs to know.
How might Farida be affected if nothing is said?
Farida, who studied all weekend, might end up with fewer marks than someone who copied, which is unfair to her.

Mentor note, Jaya.

Gautam came to my office at 8:30, hood up, eyes down. Someone had taken a photo at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth, and turned it into a meme going round three class groups. Gautam said very quietly, "Everyone's seen it. I want to disappear." Gautam hadn't eaten breakfast.

I told Gautam plainly that the cruelty belongs to the people making the meme, not to Gautam. I stayed while we reported the posts and blocked the accounts, and I passed the matter to the college's student welfare lead that same morning. Two friends from Gautam's hostel wing offered to walk with Gautam to lunch.

I reminded Gautam that these things fade faster than they feel today. I will check in tomorrow.

Where was the photo taken?
The photo was taken at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth.
What was Gautam feeling when saying "I want to disappear"?
Deep shame and exposure, shown by the hood up, the eyes down, the skipped breakfast and the wish to disappear.
What did Jaya do, and what else could help?
Jaya stayed with Gautam, reported the posts, blocked the accounts and told the welfare lead that morning; friends can keep walking with Gautam to meals and remind Gautam it fades.
How might the two hostel friends' offer affect Gautam?
Their offer to walk with Gautam to lunch shows the mockery is not everyone's view, which can make the shame feel less total.

First week of Diwali holidays: Damini, nine, stayed up past midnight with cousins, watched cartoons till lunch and ate at odd hours. By Friday she was snapping at everyone.
Second week, Sunday: Just thinking about school on Monday week made Damini's tummy flutter. 'I'll never wake up in time,' she told her older sister Shreya, close to tears.
Wednesday: Shreya had an idea. 'Let's both wake at seven from today and cycle round the colony before breakfast.' Damini complained on the first morning, then started beating Shreya to the gate.
The following Monday: Damini woke before her alarm. School felt strange, but she wasn't dragging her feet.

When did Shreya suggest they start waking at seven?
On Wednesday.
How did Damini feel on the Sunday of the second week?
She felt anxious and close to tears, dreading waking up for school.
What anchors did Shreya help set?
A seven o'clock wake-up and a cycle ride round the colony before breakfast.
How might Shreya have felt seeing Damini beat her to the gate?
Shreya was probably pleased and amused that the plan was working.
The answer is 10; 5/3.
Joy can read 8 pages of a book in 20 minutes. How many hours will it take her to read 120 pages?

In one hour, there are 3 sets of 20 minutes.
So, Joy can read 8 x 3 = 24 pages in an hour.
It will take her 120/24 = 5 hours to read 120 pages.
The answer is 5.
Come up with a cheerful slogan for a school health week poster. Exactly five words.
Eat well, play hard, smile!

Abhinav, sit. You asked how your Thakuma chose. I was twenty then, Bidisha Sen, top of my class in Shillong, and a letter came offering me a teaching post in a college in Guwahati. My father had just had his fall. My brothers were away. Everyone said, go, a job like this comes once.
I sat up that whole night on the verandah with a lamp. I wrote what I would gain in one year, in ten years, and what my father would lose. I did not know how long he would need me. That was the hardest part: choosing without knowing.
In the morning I wrote to the college and asked to join the next year. They refused. I stayed. Two years later another post came, a smaller one. I took it. Some nights I still wonder, but I do not regret sitting up with that lamp and thinking it through.

What was young Bidisha offered in the letter?
She was offered a teaching post in a college in Guwahati.
What was Bidisha feeling on the verandah that night?
She felt torn and uneasy, because she had to choose without knowing how long her father would need her.
Was asking the college to hold the post a sensible choice in the story? Why?
Yes, because it tried to keep both her father's care and her career, even though the college refused.
How might Bidisha's father have been affected by her decision?
He had his daughter at home while he recovered, which probably gave him comfort and help when her brothers were away.

In Mexico City, Alejandro was in his final year of engineering when his mother was diagnosed with a serious illness. He took extra shifts at a café to cover bus fares to the hospital and his younger sister's school costs. His grades slid. He stopped replying to his friend Emil.
One night Emil turned up at the café at closing time. "You look like you haven't slept in weeks."
"I haven't," Alejandro said, and to his own surprise, his voice broke.
They sat on the curb. Emil asked what help existed, not what Alejandro should do. Together they found that the university had an emergency student fund and a counselling service, and that professors could grant deadline extensions for family illness.
The next morning Alejandro emailed two professors and booked a counselling slot. He still worked the café shifts. But now he had a plan, and someone who knew.

What did Alejandro take extra shifts at?
A café.
What does Alejandro's voice breaking suggest about how he felt?
It suggests Alejandro was exhausted and overwhelmed, finally letting out the stress he'd been hiding.
What did Emil do that others could learn from?
Emil showed up in person, asked what help existed rather than lecturing, and helped find the fund, counselling and extensions.
How might Alejandro's professors respond to his emails?
Most would likely feel sympathetic and grant extensions, relieved to know why his work had slipped.

I'm Tanvir, and I've lived in Kolkata all my life, so I didn't really notice Usha struggling at first.

She'd joined our team from Coimbatore. In the second week I saw her at lunch staring at a plate of fish curry she hadn't touched. Another day she came in soaked, having walked twenty minutes because the auto driver didn't understand "Park Circus" the way she said it. Her flat had no water on the third floor. She said all this lightly, but her jaw was tight.

I didn't do anything grand. I took her to the South Indian mess on Lake Road, where she ate like she'd found a relative. I wrote her the names of three places the way drivers say them. And I asked her to our Saturday adda at my sister's house.

She came. She laughed at my sister's jokes. On Monday she brought me a tin of murukku.

Where did Tanvir take Usha for lunch?
Tanvir took her to the South Indian mess on Lake Road.
What was Tanvir feeling after noticing Usha's tight jaw and soaked arrival?
Tanvir felt concerned and a little guilty for not noticing sooner, and wanted to help in simple, practical ways.
Why did Tanvir's small steps work better than a grand welcome?
A familiar meal, the place names written the local way and one weekend invitation solved real daily problems and gave Usha a place to belong.
What is it like for Usha in those first weeks?
Usha is worn down and frustrated by food, transport and water problems while trying to seem fine, so the small kindnesses bring real relief.

Last month I voted for Zubin to be class monitor. I'm Francis, and I'll be honest: I didn't think about it much. Zubin is the tallest in our class, he laughs at everything, and he always shares his chips. So I thought he must be clever and fair too. It felt obvious. Then, on Monday, Miss left the room and Zubin had to write down the names of anyone talking. His best friends talked the whole time. Their names never went on the board. Mine did, for asking one question. I felt so cheated. Now I think being fun and being fair are two different things. Next time I'll watch what someone actually does first.

Why did Francis's name go on the board?
For asking one question.
What was Francis feeling when the monitor left his friends' names off?
Francis felt cheated, having trusted Zubin to be fair just because Zubin was fun and generous with chips.
What does Francis plan to do next time, and why would it help?
Francis plans to watch what someone actually does before voting, which tests fairness directly instead of guessing it from height or laughter.
How might Zubin's best friends see Zubin as monitor?
They probably liked having him as monitor, since they could talk freely and never landed on the board.
John has 10 members of his family on his father's side.  His mother's side is 30% larger.  How many people are there in total?

His mother's side is 10*.3=3 people larger than his father's side
So his mother's side has 10+3=13 people
So the total number of people is 13+10=23
The answer is 23.

Hi everyone! I'm turning thirteen, and I'd love to celebrate with you. Come over to my house this Saturday at 5 pm for cake, games and lots of snacks. Wear something comfortable, because there will be dancing. Please reply by Thursday so I know how many samosas to order. See you there!

Monday. In her third month as a junior auditor, Shreya notices it in the ledger of a client's Pune plant: eleven invoices from the same packaging vendor, paid over six months, and no goods-received note for any of them. Her first thought is fraud. Her second is: slow down.
Tuesday. Over lunch she thinks aloud with Aadhya, a batchmate on another audit. 'What else could explain it? The notes could be filed in another system. The vendor could supply services, not goods. Or someone made a data-entry mistake that keeps repeating.' Aadhya asks, 'So what would tell you which one?' Shreya writes a list: check the other system, check the purchase orders, ask stores how deliveries are logged.
Thursday. The other system has nothing. The purchase orders describe cartons, not services. Stores has no record. Shreya writes up what she found and what she ruled out, and takes it to her audit senior before saying the word 'fraud' to anyone. The senior reads it twice. 'Good. We'll take this to the audit manager today.'

How many invoices from the vendor did Shreya find?
Eleven invoices from the same packaging vendor.
What did Shreya feel at first, and how did she handle it?
Alarm and suspicion of fraud, which she deliberately slowed down so her judgement would not run ahead of the facts.
Why was it wise to list other explanations first?
Checking whether the gap was a filing or data error meant any report would rest on evidence, not a guess.
How might the audit senior see Shreya's write-up?
As careful and fair, since it shows both what was found and what was ruled out, making it easy to take further.
Explain to my 8-year-old, in about 60 words, why we visit art galleries.

An art gallery is a bit like a library, but instead of reading stories, we look at them. Each painting or sculpture is an artist's way of sharing an idea, a feeling or a memory. When we visit, we can ask ourselves, "What do I see? How does it make me feel?" There are no wrong answers. It's a fun way to learn to look closely.
What is a jubilee? The town celebrates one this year.

A jubilee is a special anniversary of an important event, often the fiftieth, or a time of public joy. It is a noun.
Example: The school celebrated its golden jubilee with a big cultural program.
My teacher says I should keep a reading journal. What do I even write in it?
Keep it simple. After each reading session, write the date, the pages you read and two or three lines about what happened. Add one thing you liked or a question you have.
That sounds a bit boring.
You can make it more personal. Copy a sentence you loved, draw a scene, or write what you would do in the main character's place. The journal is for you, so it can look however you like.
What is the difference between "hoard" and "horde"?

A "hoard" is a hidden store of things you save, and "to hoard" means to keep such a store. A "horde" is a large, noisy crowd.
Examples: The squirrel hoards nuts for the winter. A horde of children ran out of the gate.

Dear Samir,
Thank you for all your calls last week. I can finally write properly.
When the water trapped us on the first floor, I panicked the first night. We ate dinner as usual, drank as much as we liked, and kept the lights on until the inverter died.
The next morning I realised we didn't know how long this would last. So I counted everything: nine litres of drinking water, a kilo of rice, bread, two packets of biscuits, some fruit. I divided it for two more days for four of us, with water first for Nani. No more cooking rice that wasted water.
Then relatives. Phones barely worked, so I sent short texts instead of calls, since those got through. I reached Mama in Silchar and asked him to check on Mami's family downstream. He did; they were safe.
The boat came on day three. We still had a litre left.
Bhavna

How much drinking water did Bhavna count?
Bhavna counted nine litres of drinking water.
How did Bhavna feel on the first night, and what changed the next morning?
Bhavna panicked on the first night, then felt more in control after counting everything and planning for two days.
What else could Bhavna's family keep ready for next time?
They could keep a stock of water and dry food on the upper floor before the monsoon, so rationing starts with more.
How might Mama in Silchar have felt getting Bhavna's text?
Mama likely felt relieved to hear from Bhavna and useful when asked to check on Mami's family.

What else could Rashmi do to make waiting easier?
Chat with Lavanya or play a quick game while counting, so the time passes faster.
How might Lavanya see Rashmi's counting?
Lavanya may find it helpful and start counting too.

Read this:

"Aadhya, come, sit. You've been quiet all week. Is it your team lead again? Let Binita di tell you what happened to me.
"At twenty-four I worked under a man who shouted. Not at everyone. At me. 'Useless.' 'Even a child could do this.' In front of the whole floor. I would freeze. My mind went blank, and by evening I believed him.
"A senior, Mrs D'Souza, saw me crying on the stairs. She said, 'Start writing it down. Date, time, words, who was there.' So I did. Every night, in a small diary.
"Two colleagues had seen it too. They agreed to speak up if asked.
"After six weeks I took the diary to HR. The HR head read every page, thanked me, and started a formal inquiry that same week. She moved me to another team while it ran.
"Keeping quiet did not stop him, Aadhya. Writing it down and finding my people did.

What did Mrs D'Souza tell young Binita to write down?
She said, "Date, time, words, who was there."
What was young Binita feeling after being shouted at?
Young Binita felt frozen and ashamed, her mind going blank until she began to doubt herself and believe the insults.
What was the turning point in Binita di's story, and why did it matter?
Mrs D'Souza's advice to keep a written record, with colleagues willing to speak, gave her proof and allies to take to HR, which led to a formal inquiry.
How did Mrs D'Souza likely feel seeing Binita on the stairs?
Mrs D'Souza likely felt concern and sympathy, and wanted to protect the younger colleague.

Wade has called into a rest stop and decides to get food for the road. He buys a sandwich to eat now, one for the road, and one for in the evening. He also buys 2 drinks. If the drinks cost $4 each and Wade spends a total of $26 then how much, in dollars, did the sandwiches each cost?

The drinks cost a total of $4 per drink * 2 drinks = $8.
So the sandwiches cost a total of $26 total spending - $8 spending on drinks = $18.
Therefore, each sandwich costs $18 for sandwiches / 3 sandwiches = $6.
The answer is 6.

My name is Chandrika, and I saw it on the school bus home. Two boys in the back seat kept flicking paper balls at Sangeeta and calling out about her hair. The bus was full, maybe twenty-five of us. Nobody said a word. A few people put in earphones and turned to the window. Sangeeta pressed her forehead to the glass and hugged her bag, and her shoulders shrank a little more at every stop. I felt frozen in my seat too. At the market stop I made myself stand up, sat down beside her and called Mrs Rao, the bus attendant, to the back. Mrs Rao moved the boys to the front, stayed near Sangeeta for the rest of the ride and phoned the principal, who said the boys' families would be called that evening. Sangeeta did not say much, but she let me keep the seat.

Where did the boys pick on Sangeeta?
On the school bus home, where two boys in the back seat flicked paper balls at Sangeeta and called out about her hair.
What might Sangeeta have been feeling with her forehead pressed to the glass?
Sangeeta was probably humiliated and alone; hugging her bag and shrinking at every stop suggests the silence of the full bus hurt as much as the boys' words.
What turning point came at the market stop?
Chandrika stood up, sat beside Sangeeta and called Mrs Rao, who moved the boys, stayed near Sangeeta and phoned the principal.
What was it like for Chandrika to sit frozen while the paper balls kept flying?
Chandrika seems to have felt stuck and uneasy, part of the silent crowd, until standing up broke that silence.

Read this:

Staff counsellor's notes, Rashmi, bank training centre, Mysuru
Jeevan, a probationary officer, came in for his third session today. Two weeks ago he described worrying "all day, in every meeting." Last week we set up a fifteen-minute worry slot at 6 p.m., on the bench by the parking lot, notebook in hand.
Today he showed me the pages. Each evening he writes every worry, then puts an S beside the ones he can solve. On Monday, "branch posting unclear" got an S; he emailed the personnel section next morning and had an answer by lunch. "Mother's knee" got no S; he wrote, "Call her Sunday. Rest goes to the slot." He said that when a worry pops up at 11 a.m., he tells it, "Six o'clock," and mostly it waits.
He still has hard days. At the next session we'll look at what happens on those.

What letter does Jeevan put beside the worries he can solve?
He puts an S beside the ones he can solve.
How can you tell Jeevan feels more in control than he did two weeks ago?
He now tells a mid-morning worry "Six o'clock" and it mostly waits, instead of worrying all day in every meeting.
Why does splitting worries into S and no-S help Jeevan?
It sends solvable ones like the branch posting straight to action and parks the rest in the slot, so real planning happens without endless spinning.
How might Jeevan's colleagues notice the change in meetings?
They would likely find him more present and focused, since his worries no longer pull at his attention all day.

Gautam: no motivation at all today. can't make myself open the report
Vinita: 🙂 I don't wait for motivation anymore
Gautam: how
Vinita: I have a routine. 9:30, laptop open, first paragraph, twenty minutes. every day, even flat days
Gautam: what if I'm just not feeling it
Vinita: then you do it not feeling it. the feeling usually turns up around minute ten
Gautam: hm. ok. twenty minutes
Vinita: message me after
Gautam: (25 min later) ok. I did three paragraphs and forgot to check the time
Vinita: 🎉 see. motivation is what starting gives you

What time is Vinita's routine?
Vinita's routine starts at 9:30, with the laptop open and the first paragraph, for twenty minutes.
How does Gautam feel at the start of the chat?
Gautam feels flat and unmotivated, with no drive to even open the report.
What did the routine do for Gautam that waiting had not done?
Gautam started without feeling like it and wrote three paragraphs, forgetting the time, so the motivation came after starting.
How might Vinita feel when Gautam reports three paragraphs?
Vinita is pleased and encouraging, and the celebration shows Vinita was hoping that starting would prove the point.

In the cooperative sugar mill's office outside Moga, Gurleen had kept the cane-weighing records spotless for five years. When the chief clerk retired, everyone told her the post was hers.
It went to Kiran, the general manager's nephew's friend, who played cricket with the directors on Sundays.
Gurleen walked home along the canal, kicking a stone. So it was all a game. Why bother?
Her old teacher, Harpreet-madam, stopped her at the gurdwara gate that evening. "Why so heavy?"
Gurleen told her. Madam listened. "It's unfair. But does the manager know what you've done? Or only that the records are fine?"
Gurleen was quiet. She had never once told anyone about the fraud she'd spotted in 2022.
The next month she wrote a short report on the year's work and asked Madam's nephew, a director, to read it. She still did the records perfectly. But now, people knew.

Who got the chief clerk post?
Kiran, the general manager's nephew's friend, who played cricket with the directors.
What was Gurleen feeling on her walk home along the canal?
She felt bitter and disillusioned, kicking a stone and wondering why she should bother after five years of careful work.
How did Gurleen respond without giving up on effort?
She kept the records perfect but also wrote a short report of her year's work and asked a director to read it.
How might Harpreet-madam see Gurleen's situation?
Harpreet-madam sees the unfairness but also that Gurleen's work has been invisible, and wants her to speak up rather than give up.

Aparna: I'm at the school gate. Come sit with me for ten minutes?
Dhanya: I'm fine, really
Aparna: Okay. I'm still here. No lecture, promise
Dhanya walked out slowly, her bag hanging off one shoulder, and they sat on the low wall by the bicycle stand, Aparna moving her own bag to make room.
Dhanya: everything at home is loud and I feel like I'm disappearing
Aparna: That sounds so heavy. How are you actually doing? Not the "fine" answer
Dhanya: tired. really tired
Aparna: I'm glad you told me. You matter to me, a lot. I can't fix it and I'm not a counsellor, but I can sit here, and I'll check on you tomorrow
Dhanya: ok. thanks for being a real friend and not saying cheer up

Where did Aparna and Dhanya sit?
They sat on the low wall by the bicycle stand.
What was Dhanya feeling when she said everything at home is loud?
Dhanya felt overwhelmed and invisible, since she says she feels like she is disappearing, and she also says she is really tired.
What could Aparna add if Dhanya's tiredness keeps going, and why?
Aparna could encourage Dhanya to talk to a school counsellor or another trusted adult, because Aparna herself says she is not a counsellor and can offer company, not treatment.
How might Dhanya experience it that Aparna does not say cheer up?
Dhanya probably feels heard and less alone, since nobody is trying to talk her out of her feelings.

Monday. Reena opened a news site on the metro and fell into a long thread about a building fire in another city: photos, voice notes, names. She got off two stops late. All afternoon her chest felt tight, and she snapped at Yusuf in the library for tapping his pen.
Thursday. She scrolled again before bed, then again at 2 a.m. Her stomach ached. She didn't know any of those people. She couldn't do anything. Why did she feel this bad?
The next Monday. Yusuf, noticing her dark circles, asked what was going on. She showed him her screen time. He whistled. 'Three hours of this, every day?' She hadn't realised. That evening she moved the news site off her home screen and called her mother instead.

How many stops late did Reena get off on Monday?
Two stops late.
What was Reena thinking on Thursday night?
Reena was puzzled why she felt so bad about strangers she couldn't help, as their pain seemed to soak in anyway.
What was the turning point, and what did Reena choose to do?
Seeing the screen time with Yusuf was the turning point; Reena then moved the news site off the home screen and called her mother.
How might Yusuf have felt being snapped at on Monday?
Yusuf probably felt confused or hurt at first, but later noticed Reena's dark circles and cared enough to ask.

I'm Uma, from next door. At our housewarming, Nitin's daughter Mahi clung to his leg and whined every time he tried to talk to anyone. Nitin didn't snap. He crouched down. “Mahi, is it your tummy, are you sleepy, or is it too noisy?” She said, “Noisy,” and pressed her hands to her ears. He carried her out to the quiet balcony. I don't know if it was only the noise, but after ten minutes she was playing with my cat.

Where did Nitin carry Mahi?
Out to the quiet balcony.
What was Nitin thinking when he crouched and asked Mahi simple choices?
He was guessing that something was bothering her, like hunger, tiredness or noise, and wanted her help to be sure, rather than feeling annoyed.
What did Nitin's questions help him find out?
That Mahi was overwhelmed by the noise, so he could take her somewhere quiet.
How did Uma see Mahi's clinginess?
Uma wasn't sure it was only the noise, but Mahi did calm down on the balcony.

When I was made project lead last year, at twenty-five, my first fear was turning into the boss I'd hated. I'm Divyansh, and I did three things on purpose.
First, I kept Lalit close. He's my oldest friend at the firm and loves to argue. When I proposed weekend work, he said, "Ask the juniors what it costs them first." I did. Two of them had exams. We moved it.
Second, every Friday I asked the team one question: "What's one thing I did this week that didn't help?"
Third, when the client praised the report, I read out the names of the two juniors who'd built it.
It's not perfect. But I still hear things I don't want to hear, and that feels right.

What question did Divyansh ask the team every Friday?
"What's one thing I did this week that didn't help?"
What was Divyansh afraid of when made project lead?
Divyansh was afraid of becoming the kind of boss once hated, and so felt the need to guard against it.
Which of Divyansh's habits seems most useful, and why?
Keeping Lalit close is useful, because an honest friend who disagrees catches mistakes like the weekend work before they hurt people.
How might the two juniors feel when their names are read out to the client?
They would likely feel proud and valued, knowing the lead shared the credit.

Govind Kaka had started coming to their house in the village every Sunday. He fixed the broken hinge on the cattle shed and brought Lalit a kite. Lalit's mother, Usha, smiled more when he was around.
Lalit left the kite in its paper. He answered Govind Kaka with one word each time. At night he looked at Baba's photo on the wall and felt a tight knot. What if Baba was forgotten?
One Sunday Govind Kaka asked, "Want to fly it together?"
Lalit took a breath. "Not yet. I miss Baba. I don't want anyone to take his place."
Govind Kaka nodded. "Nobody could. We'll go slow."
Lalit said, "Thank you for the kite." He meant it, a little.

What did Govind Kaka fix?
The broken hinge on the cattle shed.
What was Lalit afraid of when he looked at Baba's photo?
He was afraid that Govind Kaka would replace Baba and that Baba would be forgotten.
What did Lalit do that was honest and still polite?
He said plainly that he missed Baba and wasn't ready yet, and he still thanked Govind Kaka for the kite.
How might Govind Kaka see Lalit's cold answers?
Govind Kaka seems to understand Lalit needs time, saying no one could take Baba's place and they would go slow.
I forgot to return Jasmine's umbrella. A casual message to her saying I will bring it tomorrow, about 30 words. I'm Colin.

Hey Jasmine,
I'm sorry, I still have your umbrella! I forgot to return it. I will bring it tomorrow, I promise. Thank you for being so patient with me.
Colin

Thursday

Today at school I was ME. I argued with Sir about the history project and won. I made the whole back bench laugh. Meghna said I should run for head of house. I said maybe.

Then I got home and became the other one. Amma asked, "How was school?" "Fine." Indu didi asked if I wanted to watch the match. "No, homework." I ate dinner with my head down. Nobody at home knows I do stand-up in the free period. Nobody at school knows Amma still checks my bag.

It's easier this way. At home nobody laughs at my jokes, and at school nobody sees me being small. No fights.

But tonight Indu didi said, "You used to be funny, you know." And I felt weird. Like she misses someone who's right here.

Chaitanya

What did Meghna suggest Chaitanya run for?
Meghna said Chaitanya should run for head of house.
Why does keeping the two worlds separate feel easier to Chaitanya?
Chaitanya feels safer that way: no one at home laughs at the jokes and no one at school sees the small side, so there are no fights, even if it feels lonely.
What small step could let Chaitanya be known at home?
Chaitanya could share one school story with Indu didi, like the stand-up or the head of house idea, and see how it lands.
How does Indu didi seem to feel about Chaitanya at home?
Indu didi seems wistful and a bit sad, missing the funny sibling who now goes quiet at home.

Class 3 teacher's note, Tuesday

In relay practice today the children chose their own teams. Tejas was chosen last. He stood at the line with his back to the others.

After the race, which his team lost, he sat under the gulmohar tree. "Nobody ever chooses me. I never win. I'll never win anything in my whole life." He said it three times.

I sat next to him. I didn't argue. I asked, "Who chose you for the quiz team last Friday?" He thought. "Hrithik." "And what happened?" "We won." He shrugged. "That was a quiz."

Hrithik came over and asked if Tejas wanted to try the baton pass again. Tejas said no, then went anyway.

Next step: tomorrow I'll make teams with numbered cards so choosing isn't public, and tell his mother what he said.

Who chose Tejas for the quiz team last Friday?
Hrithik.
Why did Tejas say "I'll never win anything in my whole life" after one race?
Being chosen last and then losing hurt, and the hurt made one afternoon feel like his whole future. The quiz win didn't seem to count against that feeling.
Which choice of the teacher's might help most, and why?
Using numbered cards so choosing isn't public. It removes the moment that set off Tejas's "never", while the teacher keeps gently reminding him of real wins.
How might Hrithik see Tejas sitting under the tree?
Hrithik probably sees a friend who is upset and wants to cheer him up, which is why Hrithik offers the baton pass. To Hrithik, Tejas is a teammate who won the quiz, not someone nobody chooses.

Sonali: "Avni, I read your presentation. It's not there yet."
Avni: "Okay. What's missing?"
Sonali: "It just doesn't feel strong."
Avni: "Is it the data? The slides? The story?"
Sonali: "Hard to say. It needs more punch."
Avni: "More punch where? The opening?"
Sonali: "Just... overall. You'll figure it out."
(Sonali walks off. Avni stares at the twenty slides.)
Avni: (to herself) "Figure out what?"
(Later, to her friend on the phone.)
Avni: "I've changed the colours, the fonts, the order. I have no idea if it's better. I feel like I failed a test nobody told me the questions to."

How many slides were in Avni's presentation?
Avni stared at the twenty slides.
How did Avni feel after Sonali walked off?
She felt hurt, confused and helpless, as if she had failed a test with unknown questions.
What could Sonali have said instead?
Sonali could point to one specific slide, say what works, what needs to change and why, so Avni could act.
How might Sonali see those comments?
Sonali probably thinks the feedback was honest, not noticing that without specifics it gives Avni nothing to use.

Daycare note, winter week. Gurpreet, caregiver.
Too cold for the garden today. Gargi wrapped her rag doll in a hand towel. "Baby cold," she told me. Then she held a toy cup to the doll's mouth: "Drink milk. Hot milk." She blew on the cup first. Then she laid it in a shoe box, humming. When another child grabbed it, Gargi said, "No! Baby sleeping!"
Tomorrow I'll put small blankets and cups in the play corner so more children can join the caring game.

What did Gargi wrap her doll in?
A hand towel.
Why did Gargi blow on the toy cup first?
She was caring for the doll as if it could feel, worried the pretend milk might be too hot.
What does Gurpreet plan, and why is it good?
Putting small blankets and cups in the play corner so more children can practise caring through play.
How might the child who grabbed the doll feel?
That child might feel surprised or cross at being told off, not yet seeing the doll as a sleeping baby.
