messages.content: Someone said "widower" to me. What is that? Then, why should we listen first when someone is upset? Plus, fix my grammar: Wow what a lovely song. And one more: what does "on cloud nine" mean? Also, how many runs did the best batter score yesterday?

1. As a noun, "widower" means a man whose wife has died and who has not married again.
2. Listening first shows that you care about how they feel. Because an upset person usually cannot take in advice until they feel heard.
3. Write it as: Wow, what a lovely song! Why: "wow" takes a comma; an exclamation ends with "!".
4. It means extremely happy. For example: Asha was on cloud nine after her win.
5. I don't know that. I can't see yesterday's matches. Check the scorecard on a sports site.

Note for Damini's parents, craft hour. I drew a sample card on the board: one flower, five petals, a green stem. Damini studied it, then copied it stroke by stroke, counting petals under her breath. She did not stop there. In the corner she added a big orange sun with long rays, because, she said, her flower needed daylight. Vaibhav, at her table, asked if he could copy her sun. I said yes, and reminded him to give his own card something new. Tomorrow we colour the cards and Damini will write the name inside.

What did the teacher draw on the board as the sample card?
One flower with five petals and a green stem.
What might Damini have been feeling when she added the big orange sun?
She was probably pleased with her own idea. She gave a reason, that the flower needed daylight, which shows she wanted the card to be hers. 🙂
What other approach could Damini try if she wanted a card that looks less like the sample, and why?
She could sketch a few ideas on scrap paper first. Seeing different flowers side by side would help her pick one that suits the birthday child.
How might Vaibhav see Damini's card?
He sees a sun he would like to borrow, and her changes show him it is fine to copy a starting point and then add something new.

Tushar, you asked why I never scold you for eating your prasad at once. That winter I was eight, and we lived with my Tayaji. Every week he promised, "Wait, Jasleen, next Sunday I'll bring you a whole box of pinni." Sunday came, and nothing. Again and again.
So when the new teacher said, "One sweet now, or two if you wait till after lunch," I grabbed the one so fast the girl beside me laughed. Teacher frowned and called me greedy.
I wasn't greedy, beta. I had learned that "later" meant "never". Only when that teacher kept her word for a whole month did I start to wait too. That is why your Bibi keeps every small promise she makes you.

What did Tayaji promise to bring every week?
A whole box of pinni.
Why did young Jasleen grab the one sweet so fast?
Young Jasleen felt distrustful after so many broken promises; "later" meant "never", so taking the sweet at once felt sensible, not greedy.
What turned things around in the story?
The teacher keeping her word for a whole month showed Jasleen that waiting could actually pay off.
How might the teacher have seen young Jasleen at first?
The teacher first saw only greed and frowned, not knowing about the broken promises at home.

The distance across a country is 8205 kilometers. Amelia started at one end and drove 907 kilometers on Monday and 582 kilometers on Tuesday. How many kilometers does Amelia still have to drive to make it across the country?

Distance driven = 907 + 582 = 1489 km
Distance remaining = 8205 - 1489 = 6716 km
Amelia still has 6716 kilometers to drive.
The answer is 6716.

(1) What is the title of the book on my shelf?
(2) What does "bring to the table" mean?
(3) Fix my grammar: This book is more better than that one.
(4) How would you explain "sequence" to a child?
(5) Why does a sports team practise together?

1. I don't know that. I can't see your shelf. Read the cover and spine to find out.
2. It means to offer a skill or idea to a group. For example: Meera brings good planning to the table.
3. Better: This book is better than that one. Why: "better" is already the comparative of "good".
4. Sequence means a series of things that come one after another. It is a noun.
5. Practice helps the team play well together. Because players learn each other's moves and can pass and cover without needing to talk.

Wasim, twenty-six, ran a small bicycle repair shop near the bus stand of his kasba. In the evenings, schoolchildren brought him punctures, and old men sat on the bench outside, arguing about cricket. One afternoon, his old classmate Kishore, now working in the city, stopped by. He wore a crisp shirt and talked about his office, the traffic and his big salary. "Don't you want more?" he asked. Wasim was fixing a chain, oil on his fingers. He thought about it honestly. "I'm my own boss. I know every family here. I close at seven and eat dinner with my Ammi." He wiped his hands and smiled. "I'm fine, yaar. Really." Kishore looked at him for a long moment, then sat down on the bench too.

What time does Wasim close his shop?
At seven.
What does Wasim's honest answer and smile suggest about how he feels about his life?
He feels quietly content, valuing his independence, community and family time over bigger money.
Why might it help Wasim to think honestly before answering?
It shows his contentment isn't just a defence; he checked his feelings and still found them true.
Why might Kishore sit down on the bench after hearing Wasim?
He may have felt a pull toward Wasim's calmer life, perhaps questioning his own busy city routine.

Read this:

Saturday. Vasudha found out from a mutual friend's careless story: her boyfriend Aman at a café in Pune with another girl, his hand on hers, on the night he'd said he was studying. She rang him. He admitted it. She hung up and sat on the hostel stairs, shaking, unable to cry. Jyoti found her there at midnight and didn't leave. Tuesday. Rage had arrived. Vasudha drafted a long post naming him, then a message to the other girl. Jyoti read both and said, 'Write them. Don't send them.' Vasudha deleted them. She also caught herself asking, 'What's wrong with me that he did this?' 'Nothing,' Jyoti said. 'He made a choice.' Two weeks later. Vasudha still hadn't decided whether she would ever talk to Aman again, and she was letting that be okay. She'd been to the counselling centre once. She was eating properly again. Some mornings she still woke up heavy. But she had stopped blaming herself.

How did Vasudha find out about Aman?
From a mutual friend's careless story showing him at a café in Pune with another girl.
What was Vasudha feeling on the hostel stairs that Saturday?
She was in shock, shaking and unable to cry.
How did Vasudha handle the urge for revenge?
With Jyoti's help she wrote the post and message but deleted them instead of sending.
How does Jyoti see Aman's cheating?
As his choice, not a sign that something is wrong with Vasudha.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Wednesday. I am Lalit, the youth counsellor. During a walk-in visit, Santosh began to cry while describing a failed exam. A volunteer beside him started to say, "Stop, do not cry, it is only an exam," and Santosh went quiet and wiped his face. I gently asked the volunteer to sit back. I put a box of tissues on the table and said, "Take your time." After a while Santosh said he wanted to talk. I asked, "What would help right now?" He said, "Just listen." I noted that not rushing him made the difference. I will remind volunteers that a cry does not always need fixing. I will check on Santosh next week.

What did Lalit put on the table?
Lalit put a box of tissues on the table.
What did Santosh's going quiet after "Stop" suggest, and what else could it mean?
It suggested he felt hurried or dismissed and shut down, though he might also simply have been embarrassed. His later request to be listened to supports the first reading.
What made the difference in the session?
Not rushing, offering tissues, and asking what would help gave Santosh control, and he asked to be listened to.
How might the volunteer have felt after being asked to sit back?
The volunteer probably felt awkward or unsure, having meant to comfort Santosh, and might learn that a cry does not always need fixing.

Read this:

Come, Ayesha, listen. I'm Yusuf. I want to tell you about the night I should have left.
The phone gave us a flood alert that afternoon. "We've seen floods before," I said to my wife Zainab. "The water comes to the gate and goes." So we stayed, ate dinner and put the children to bed.
By midnight the road had closed and the water was over the gate. There was no way out by foot, and no vehicle could pass. I phoned the helpline. They said the boat would come at first light.
We waited on the roof with the children in blankets, and Zainab did not say a word to me. At dawn the boat took the children first. Everyone was safe, and I have not ignored an alert since.

What did Yusuf say when the flood alert arrived?
Yusuf said, "We've seen floods before," and that the water comes to the gate and goes.
What was Yusuf feeling while waiting on the roof?
Yusuf was afraid and ashamed for having stayed, as the silence from Zainab and Yusuf's own later promise show.
What turning point in the story could Yusuf have handled differently, and how?
When the alert came in the afternoon Yusuf could have taken the family to safer ground while the road was open.
How might Zainab have felt on the roof with the children?
Zainab was probably frightened and angry, and the silence toward Yusuf suggests Zainab held it in for the children's sake.

metadata.subtype: Approach: ignoring warnings and hoping it passes [Pitfall]

messages.content: Emmalyn decided to paint fences in her neighborhood for twenty cents per meter. If there were 50 fences in the neighborhood that she had to paint and each fence was 500 meters long, calculate the total amount she earned from painting the fences.

The total length for the fifty fences is 50*500 = 25000 meters.
If Emmalyn charged twenty cents to paint a meter of a fence, the total income she got from painting the fences is $0.20*25000 =$5000
The answer is 5000.

Musa is the class teacher of a class of 45 students. He wants to split them into three groups by age. If a third of the class is under 11 years, and two-fifths are above 11 but under 13, how many students will be in the third group (13 years and above)?

The first group is a third of the class which is (1/3)*45 = 15 students
There are 15 students in the first group, so there are 45-15 = 30 students
The second group is two-fifths of the class which is (2/5)*45 = 18 students
There are 18 in the second group so there are 30-18 = 12 students left in the third group
The answer is 12.

Mr. Smith takes his wife, his parents, and his 3 children to a seafood buffet.  The price for the adult buffet is $30.  The price for the children's buffet is $15.  Senior citizens get a 10% discount.  How much does Mr. Smith spend on the buffet for his entire family?

The buffet cost for Mr. Smith and his wife is $30 x 2 = $60.
The buffet cost for his children is $15 x 3 = $45.
The buffet cost for 1 senior citizen is $30 x 90% = $27.
B
uffet cost for the grandparents is $27 x 2 = $54.
Buffet cost for the entire family is $60 + $45 + $54 = $159
The answer is 159.

Teacher's note, Wednesday. Aparna, Class 5. Rehana joined us last month after four years in São Paulo, where her father worked. Today I made the OK sign, thumb and finger in a circle, to praise her map. Her face fell, and she hid the map under her book. At break I asked her what happened. She said, very softly, that in Brazil that sign is rude, and children there used it as an insult. I apologised and explained that here it means “perfect”. We agreed I'd use a thumbs-up or just say “well done” with her. Tomorrow I'll ask the class to share gestures from places they've lived.

Where had Rehana lived for four years?
Rehana had lived in São Paulo for four years.
What was Rehana feeling when she hid her map?
Rehana felt hurt and confused, reading the OK sign as the insult it was in Brazil rather than as praise.
What did Aparna do that repaired things?
She asked privately, apologised, explained the local meaning and agreed on a thumbs-up or words instead.
What would change if Aparna had not asked at break?
Rehana might have believed her teacher was insulting her and felt unwelcome in the new class.

The school bus was stuck in a jam near the market, horns blaring, and Jagdish had forty minutes to stare at his English paper: 26 out of 40. He had been quite pleased when Ma'am handed it back. Then Preeti, beside him, showed hers: 38, with 'Excellent!' in green. Now his 26 looked terrible. His grandfather would ask about it at dinner. Jagdish folded the paper small and stuffed it in his bag. 'I'm hopeless,' he muttered. At the next stop, Preeti's mother climbed on, reading her phone. 'Ma'am has messaged the parents' group. The class average was only 21. Very hard paper, she says.' Jagdish sat up. He unfolded the paper. Twenty-six. Above average! By the time the bus reached his lane, he was grinning and practising how to tell Dadaji.

What did Jagdish score in English?
He scored 26 out of 40.
Why did Jagdish mutter 'I'm hopeless'?
Next to Preeti's 38 with 'Excellent!', his 26 suddenly felt terrible, and he worried about telling his grandfather.
What could Jagdish ask himself next time he compares marks?
He could ask what his mark means on its own, whether he improved or how hard the paper was, instead of judging it only against a friend's top score.
How might Preeti have felt seeing Jagdish fold his paper away?
Preeti might have felt awkward that showing that mark made a friend upset, without meaning to.

'Okay, Kamal, you're the engineer. Pretend.' Tarun sat on the hostel bed, phone face down.
'Fine. Hello?'
'Hi, thanks for taking the time. I'm Tarun, I wrote about your talk on water sensors.' He stopped. 'Too fast?'
'Bit fast. Again.'
Tarun said it again, slower. 'Then question one: how did you test the sensors in the field? Question two: what would you tell a student starting in this area?'
'And if I just say "hmm" and go quiet?'
Tarun's hands went cold even though it was pretend. 'Then... I wait three seconds. Then I say, "Maybe I can ask it differently," and go to question two.'
'Good. Your voice is shaking.'
'I know. That's fine. It'll shake at five o'clock too. At least I know what comes after it.'
At five, the real call began, and his voice shook for the first line only.

What was Tarun's second question?
What would you tell a student starting in this area?
How did Tarun feel when Kamal imagined the call going quiet, and what shows it?
Tarun felt nervous; his hands went cold even though it was pretend, but planning the next step made the fear more manageable.
What else could Tarun rehearse before the next call?
How to close the call politely and ask whether it is fine to stay in touch, so the ending feels as prepared as the start.
What is the rehearsal like for Kamal?
Kamal plays the engineer and gets to test Tarun gently, noticing the shaking voice without making fun of it.

Valentina grew up in Buenos Aires speaking Italian with her grandmother. Now twenty-six and living in Toronto, she was pregnant and wondering what to pass on. Her husband Siddiq had grown up speaking Urdu with his parents in Karachi. "Three languages is too many," her friend warned. At dinner one night, Valentina and Siddiq made a list. They agreed: Italian songs at bedtime from her, Urdu stories from him, English everywhere else. They'd keep Eid and Christmas both, cooking together. They left out a few family traditions neither of them believed in. Valentina felt a pang about that. But she also felt clear. "Our child gets what we really care about," she said. Siddiq nodded, already planning the stories.

Which language would Siddiq use for stories?
He would use Urdu for stories.
Why did Valentina feel a pang about leaving out some traditions?
She felt some loss letting go of parts of her family's past, even though she didn't believe in them.
What made their heritage plan thoughtful?
They chose what they truly cared about from both families and gave each language a clear place.
How might their child experience this mix of traditions?
The child may grow up comfortable in several languages and festivals, knowing both parents' roots.

Supervisor's note, Friday. Joseph promised the training module by the 10th. When I asked today, he explained for nearly fifteen minutes: the software update, then Raghav's late slides, then a policy change, then a clash with another deadline. Raghav, sitting nearby, looked puzzled; his slides had gone in on the 3rd. What struck me was how smooth it all was, and how often it shifted. I didn't argue. I asked, "What's the hardest part of this module for you?" Joseph was silent, then said he had never taught adults before and was dreading recording himself. We have booked a practice session with our trainer for Monday.

When did Raghav's slides go in?
On the 3rd.
What did the supervisor notice and feel while Joseph explained?
The supervisor was struck by how smooth and shifting the reasons were and felt a quiet suspicion that something uncomfortable lay underneath, but stayed calm.
What question helped, and what came of it?
"What's the hardest part of this module for you?" It revealed Joseph's dread of recording himself, and a practice session was booked.
How might Raghav feel hearing his slides blamed?
Puzzled and perhaps a bit annoyed, since his slides had gone in on the 3rd.

Tariq had worked at the secondhand bookshop in Manchester since he was eighteen. Three years of rainy Saturdays sorting paperbacks, reading poetry aloud to the regulars, and being trusted to lock up alone. The old owner had even framed his handwritten shelf labels.
Then the shop was sold, the new manager, Liam, cut his hours, and on his final Friday they argued in front of a customer about the cash count. Tariq slammed the door on his way out.
At the café that evening his friend Ada asked, "Will you miss it?"
"Miss it? It was a dead-end job. Three years wasted."
Ada frowned. "You used to say it was the best place you'd ever worked."
Tariq stared into his cup. He couldn't find that feeling anywhere now. Only the slam of the door.

What had the old owner framed?
Tariq's handwritten shelf labels.
Why can't Tariq find his good feeling about the bookshop now?
The argument and the slammed door were the last and most intense moments, so they overwrite three years he once loved.
What could Tariq do once he has cooled down?
Remember the job in parts, the regulars, the trust, the labels, and keep those years separate from the new manager and the bad last Friday.
How might the regulars remember Tariq?
As the person who read them poetry on rainy Saturdays, not as someone who slammed the door.

In the hill village, the guava tree behind Lalremsiami's house hung heavy with hard green fruit. Tarun, six, reached for one. "Wait till they turn yellow," Lalremsiami said. "Then they're sweet, and Pi will give us a whole basket." Tarun's hand hung in the air. He picked up a stick instead and drew a guava in the mud. Each afternoon he checked: pressed one gently with his thumb, sniffed it, walked away. On the eighth day the fruit smelled sweet. Pi filled their basket, and Tarun ate three, juice running down his wrist.

What colour did the guavas need to turn before picking?
They needed to turn yellow.
What was Tarun feeling when his hand hung near the green guava?
He wanted to eat one right away but held back, trusting that waiting would bring sweet fruit and a whole basket.
Why did drawing a guava in the mud help Tarun?
It gave his hands and mind something else to do, which made it easier not to pick the fruit.
How might Lalremsiami see Tarun eating three sweet guavas?
She may feel pleased that her advice paid off and that he trusted her.
Bheed mein se nikalna hai. Kisi ajnabi ko aur dost ko "raasta dena" alag-alag kaise bolun?
To a stranger: "Excuse me, may I get past, please?" To a friend: "Hey, make some room, let me through." The first is polite, the second is casual.

Kara has to drink 4 ounces of water every time she takes her medication. Her medication instructions are to take one tablet three times a day. She followed the instructions for one week, but in the second week, she forgot twice on one day. How many ounces of water did she drink with her medication over those two weeks?

Kara drinks 4 * 3 = 12 ounces of water with her medication each day.
In a week, she drinks 12 * 7 = 84 ounces of water with her medication.
In two weeks, she drinks 84 * 2 = 168 ounces of water with her medication.
One day, she forgot two tablets, so she did not drink 2 * 4 = 8 ounces of water.
Thus, Kara drank 168 - 8 = 160 ounces of water with her medication over two weeks.
The answer is 160.

Monday, the week before the board practical. Pema watched Vishal set up his circuits in the lab. "You've got this," she told him. Everyone thought he'd do fine; his lab work was usually neat.

Friday. Results were posted. Vishal had failed the practical. His circuit had shorted, and he'd panicked.

That evening, in the group chat, Pema typed, "Honestly it was obvious. He always rushes." Three friends agreed. She felt clever for a moment.

Tuesday, the week after. Vishal came to her desk. "Did you really say it was obvious? You told me I had it."

Pema's face went hot. She remembered Monday clearly now. She hadn't thought it was obvious at all. Nobody had.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I was judging you by what happened, not by what we knew then."

Vishal nodded slowly. "Yeah. That's what it felt like."

What did Pema tell Vishal on Monday?
You've got this.
Why did Pema feel clever for a moment when typing in the group chat?
Pema felt clever because, with the result known, the failure seemed predictable, and her friends agreeing made it feel true.
What did Pema do well when Vishal confronted her?
Pema admitted she had judged by the result rather than what was known before, and apologised directly.
How did Vishal feel when he saw the group chat?
Vishal likely felt hurt and betrayed, because Pema had encouraged him before and then called his failure obvious.

- Fix the mistake: The principle of our school is kind.
- What does "go back to the drawing board" mean?

1. Correct form: The principal of our school is kind. Why: "principal" is the head of a school, while "principle" is a rule or belief.
2. It means to start again with a new plan after a failure. For example: the model fell apart, so we went back to the drawing board.

Last Diwali I learned that my generation and my boss's speak different emoji. Our manager, Jagdish-ji, had posted a photo in the team group of himself in a very bright kurta, with the caption "New look!" I replied with 💀. To me and my friends, that means "I'm dead, this is hilarious", in a fond way. Five minutes later he messaged me privately: "Tenzin, is something wrong? Why a skull?" I went cold. To him, a skull meant death, or maybe mockery of his kurta. On Diwali, too. I called him straight away instead of typing. "Sir, I'm so sorry. For us it means something is so funny we can't breathe. I meant the kurta is great." There was a pause, then he laughed. "You young people have strange ways of saying nice." Since then, with anyone older or from another team, I stick to words, or a plain 😄. And I've retired the skull at work.

What caption did Jagdish-ji post with his photo?
'New look!'
How did Tenzin feel on reading Jagdish-ji's private message?
Tenzin went cold with alarm and embarrassment, realising the skull had been read as death or an insult, and at Diwali too.
What did Tenzin do to repair the misunderstanding?
Tenzin called straight away instead of typing, apologised and explained what the skull means among younger friends.
How did Jagdish-ji first read the skull reply?
He read it as a sign that something was wrong, perhaps death or mockery of his kurta, and asked privately what it meant.

I was doing my own homework on the diwan when Siddharth started fighting with decimals. He'd written 2.75 + 1.5 = 2.90, and the teacher had crossed it out. Dada Jagdish emptied his coin purse on the table. "Start small," he said. Siddharth took two fifty-paise coins. "Point five and point five... that's one rupee. One!" He grinned. Next he tried 1.5 plus 0.5 with coins: two. Then, slowly, he lined up 2.75 and 1.5 in his notebook, points under points, and wrote 4.25. He counted it out in coins to check. It matched. I don't know what clicked, but he did five more without the coins.

What had Siddharth first written for 2.75 + 1.5?
He'd written 2.90, and the teacher had crossed it out.
How did Siddharth feel after getting 'One!' with the coins?
His grin shows he felt pleased and more confident, ready to try a slightly bigger sum 🙂
What could Siddharth try once the coins aren't needed?
Harder sums on paper, going back to coins only if an answer looks wrong; building up in steps is what gave him confidence.
How does Dada Jagdish seem to see the problem?
Dada Jagdish sees that Siddharth needs to start small, so he offers coins that make decimals something to touch.

Are monsters always bad in stories?

No. A monster is an imaginary creature, usually large and frightening, but stories sometimes show friendly or misunderstood ones. It is a noun, and the plural is Monsters.
Example: In the picture book, the monsters turned out to be shy and wanted only to play.

Tuition teacher's note, Class 4, Saturday.
For three weeks, Vaibhav has told me, “I will do better in maths, Ma'am. I promise.” Each week, no homework was done. He is sincere, but the promise has nothing in it he can start.
Today his grandfather, Mr Jagdish Rao, came to collect him and mentioned they have tea at 5 every evening.
So we tried something small. I wrote on a card: “After 5 o'clock tea: 5 problems from page 42. Tick when done.” Vaibhav read it aloud and said, “Only five? That's easy.”
His grandfather agreed to sit with him and check the ticks. I asked Vaibhav to bring the card next Saturday.
What I will do next: check the card with him, praise each tick, and if all seven days are done, move him to page 43.

What was written on the card?
“After 5 o'clock tea: 5 problems from page 42. Tick when done.”
How did Vaibhav feel when he read the card aloud?
He felt relieved and confident, saying “Only five? That's easy,” instead of feeling stuck with a big promise.
Why is the card more useful than Vaibhav's promise?
It gives a specific small goal with a set time, which is easier to start and to check than a vague wish.
How might Mr Jagdish Rao feel about helping with the ticks?
He might feel pleased and involved, glad to have a simple way to support his grandson.

The garbage truck passes through Daniel's neighborhood on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. In each garbage collection, an average of 200 kg is taken. Due to obstruction in the roads leading to Daniel's neighborhood, the garbage truck stops passing through for two weeks. During the first week, people in Daniel's neighborhood pile the extra garbage around the dumpster, during the second week they apply a policy of cutting their amount of garbage in half. How many kilograms of garbage have accumulated in Daniel's neighborhood during the 2 weeks?

The garbage truck passes through Daniel's neighborhood for 3 days.
In the first week, 200 * 3 = 600 kilograms of garbage are accumulated.
In the second week, half the amount of garbage is accumulated, which is 600 / 2 =300 kg of garbage.
During the 2 weeks, 600 + 300 = 900 kg of garbage are accumulated.
The answer is 900.

On Monday, Nilesh painted a purple sun and then scribbled over it. "Suns are yellow," he mumbled, and hid the paper.
On Wednesday, Ankita Ma'am held up a painting. "This is my friend's. Look, a green sky. Art can be any colour you like."
On Friday, Nilesh painted another purple sun, big, with orange rays. He didn't hide it. He held it up high.
"Purple sun!" he announced. A classmate said, "Weird." Nilesh shrugged. "It's MY sun."

What colour was the sky in the painting Ankita Ma'am showed?
Green.
Why did Nilesh scribble over his first sun?
Nilesh felt embarrassed and worried that a purple sun was wrong, because suns are yellow.
What did Ankita Ma'am do that helped Nilesh?
She showed that art can be any colour, which freed Nilesh to paint what he wanted without fear.
How might the classmate who said "Weird" see Nilesh's shrug?
The classmate may be surprised that Nilesh didn't get upset and might start feeling freer to paint differently too.

Monday: "Homework done?" his mother, Sangeeta, asked. "Done," said Vishal, and went to his room, where he played his phone game under the blanket until nine.
Wednesday: He said it again. It wasn't. Two English worksheets and a maths page were stuffed, unfinished, at the bottom of his bag.
Friday: Sangeeta's phone buzzed during dinner. It was his class teacher: three assignments missing this week. She read the message twice and put the phone face down. She didn't shout. She just said, "You told me it was done. Twice." That weekend Vishal did all three assignments at the dining table, and the phone stayed with his mother. On Monday, when he said "Done", she opened his bag to check.

What did the teacher's message say?
Three assignments were missing this week.
How might Vishal have felt when his mother said 'Twice'?
Ashamed and guilty, caught in his own lie.
What else could Vishal have done on Monday?
Told the truth and asked for help with the worksheets, before the missing work piled up.
How does Sangeeta respond?
Quietly hurt; she doesn't shout, but she no longer takes his word and checks his bag.

Hi Lalremsiami,
Can I say something about Tuesday's meeting? I think I got you wrong.
When you went quiet while Arun and I were talking over each other, I assumed you weren't interested, or didn't have views. In my family in Delhi, everyone talks at once at dinner. If you wait for a gap, you never get one, and jumping in means "I'm with you".
Afterwards Rini told me that where you grew up, cutting in while someone is speaking is rude, and people wait for a clear pause. So you were being polite, and from your side I was probably very rude. I'm sorry.
Next meeting, I'll leave real pauses, and I'll ask for your view directly if the rest of us are running over each other. And if I cut you off, please just raise a hand. I'd genuinely like to hear what you think about the vendor plan.
Gautam

Who told Gautam about the norm where Lalremsiami grew up?
Rini.
What did Gautam feel and assume when Lalremsiami went quiet?
Gautam assumed Lalremsiami wasn't interested or had no views, and now feels sorry and a bit embarrassed at misjudging polite waiting.
What does Gautam plan to change?
To leave real pauses, ask Lalremsiami's view directly when others talk over each other, and invite a raised hand whenever Gautam cuts in.
How might Lalremsiami have seen Gautam and Arun talking over each other?
Lalremsiami may have found it rude and hard to enter, waiting politely for a clear pause that never came.

Monday: During Hindi dictation, Disha crossed her eyes at Avni. Avni snorted so loudly that Ms Rao stopped reading, and Avni had to stand at the back, red-faced.
Wednesday: Disha did it again during silent reading. Avni pressed both lips together, stared hard at the book and dug a thumbnail into one palm. Avni's shoulders shook, but not a sound came out. When the bell rang, the two of them raced to the neem tree and laughed until they got hiccups.
Friday: In the class quiz Avni knew every answer and wanted to shout them all out, but sat on both hands and waited for a turn. Afterwards, Ms Rao let the whole class run two laps of the ground. Avni ran fastest of all.

What did Disha do to make Avni laugh?
Disha crossed her eyes at Avni.
What was Avni feeling on Wednesday while the shoulders shook?
Avni felt amused and bursting with laughter, but held it in with pressed lips and a thumbnail in the palm.
What helped Avni's self-control work?
Having ways to hold it in, like pressed lips and sitting on hands, and a release afterwards at the neem tree and on the laps.
How might Ms Rao see the laps after the quiz?
Ms Rao seems to know that children who have held themselves back need a chance to let the energy out, so the laps are a relief as much as a reward.

Last year I tried to turn into a video. I'm Harsha. There was a fitness influencer with huge arms who posted a thirty-day challenge: two hours of workouts daily and a list of foods to cut, basically everything my mother cooks. Bidisha, my best friend, said it looked extreme. I said she was jealous.
For two weeks I skipped lunch and did push-ups till my arms shook. I felt proud, and also tired in a way sleep didn't fix. In the third week, during assembly, the ground tilted and I sat down hard on the concrete. The PE teacher took me to the sick room and called home.
That evening our family doctor explained what I hadn't wanted to hear: a body that is still growing needs enough food, and someone qualified should plan training for my age, not a stranger online.
Bidisha brought me samosas the next day. I ate both.

What happened during assembly in the third week?
The ground tilted and Harsha sat down hard on the concrete.
How did Harsha feel during the first two weeks of the routine?
Harsha felt proud but also tired in a way sleep didn't fix, a sign the body was struggling.
What should Harsha have done before starting a routine like this?
Asked the PE teacher or family doctor to plan training suited to a growing body, and kept eating proper meals.
How might Bidisha have felt watching this happen?
Bidisha was likely worried and a little hurt by the jealousy remark, yet showed care by bringing samosas afterwards.

The half-yearly results came out the week before Eid, when the whole house smelled of sheer khurma and everyone was busy. I got 94 in maths and announced at dinner that I was basically a genius. Then I opened my history paper: 51. I remember saying, "The paper was totally out of syllabus, and ma'am checks too strictly." I said it so often that I believed it. Sunaina, who sits next to me, got 78 in the same paper. "We had the same syllabus, Imran," she said. "You never made notes for the Mughal chapter." I told her she got lucky with the questions. Looking back, it was easier to be a cheated genius than someone who simply hadn't studied. It took me until Diwali to open the Mughal chapter.

What did Imran score in history?
Why did Imran blame the paper and the teacher for the history mark?
Admitting the missing notes felt embarrassing, so blaming the paper felt comfortable and protected Imran's image as a genius 😅
What could Imran do after a low mark instead of blaming the paper?
Imran could compare what was studied with the questions asked, like the Mughal chapter, and ask the teacher which areas need work.
How does Sunaina see Imran's excuse?
Sunaina sees through it, since they had the same syllabus and she knows Imran never made notes for the Mughal chapter.

Layla's phone lit up in the Dublin flat: her classmate Diego's grandmother had died. She didn't know Diego well. She almost typed "She's in a better place," then deleted it, since it sounded like something on a card. She wrote, "Diego, I'm so sorry. I'm here if you want company or help with notes." Two days passed with no reply, and Layla decided not to push. On Friday she left a small tin of tea outside his door with a note: "No need to reply." That evening Diego wrote back a single line of thanks, and later asked if she could sit with him at lunch.

What did Layla leave outside Diego's door?
Layla left a small tin of tea outside his door.
How might Layla have felt writing to Diego, and why did she delete 'She's in a better place'?
Layla was probably unsure what to say, since she didn't know Diego well, and deleted the line because it sounded like something on a card, choosing plain, sincere words instead.
What could Layla do next to support Diego?
Keep in touch lightly, follow up later and offer company or notes without pressure.
How might Diego have felt receiving the tea and note?
Diego may have felt cared for and relieved that no reply was needed, as his thanks and lunch request suggest.

What impression does Mr. Jaggers's manner make on the narrator?

This strongly marked way of doing business made a strongly marked impression on me, and that not of an agreeable kind. Mr. Jaggers never laughed; but he wore great bright creaking boots, and, in poising himself on these boots, with his large head bent down and his eyebrows joined together, awaiting an answer, he sometimes caused the boots to creak, as if they laughed in a dry and suspicious way. As he happened to go out now, and as Wemmick was brisk and talkative, I said to Wemmick that I hardly knew what to make of Mr. Jaggers's manner.

A strong one, and not pleasant. Mr. Jaggers never laughs, but his bright creaking boots seem to laugh in a dry, suspicious way as he waits for an answer, so the narrator hardly knows what to make of him.

Put this battle scene into simple modern English.

With bitter words and threatening mien
Thus furious spoke the fierce fourteen,
And raising scimitar and spear
On Rama rushed in wild career.
Their levelled spears the giant crew
Against the matchless hero threw.
His bow the son of Raghu bent,
And twice seven shafts to meet them sent,
And every javelin sundered fell
By the bright darts he aimed so well.

The fourteen fierce giants spoke furiously, with bitter words and threatening looks. Raising their curved swords and spears, they rushed wildly at Rama. The whole crew of giants hurled their levelled spears at the matchless hero. The son of Raghu bent his bow and sent fourteen arrows to meet them. Every javelin was split in two and fell, cut by the bright arrows he had aimed so well.

At nine, Harish noticed something: every day he wore his red shirt, his cricket team won. His sister Minakshi laughed when he refused to wash it before the final. "The shirt is why we win," he said, with a straight face. She asked, "What about the day we won when you wore blue?" Harish frowned. He hadn't thought of that.

At fifteen, he saw that students who joined tuition classes scored more in the unit tests, and told his father he needed tuition. His classmate Yamini said, "The ones who go to tuition also do their homework early and have quiet study rooms. Maybe tuition isn't the only reason."

At twenty, in the college canteen, he read a headline claiming that people who drink coffee tend to live longer, and started buying a large cup every morning. Yamini looked at the article with him. "Does it say coffee causes it? Maybe healthier, richer people just drink more of it. Or people who are already ill drink less." Harish pushed the cup aside and kept reading.

What colour was the shirt Harish thought brought his team luck?
The shirt was red.
What thinking mistake does Harish make at nine, fifteen and twenty?

At nine Harish links the red shirt to wins, at fifteen tuition to higher scores and at twenty coffee to a longer life, each time deciding that one thing causes the other without asking what else might explain both.
What was Harish feeling when Minakshi asked about the day they won in blue?
Harish was puzzled and a little caught out, because he had not thought of that day, and he frowned.
What could Harish ask himself the next time a headline links two things?
He could ask whether something else, such as health or money, might explain both, or whether the link runs the other way, as Yamini suggested.

The day after Diwali, the kindergarten classroom still had paper lamps on the windows. Hrithik put up his hand. "Nilesh Sir, where does God live? And why did we light lamps?" Nilesh Sir sat on the little chair. "Lamps are lit for many reasons. In Hrithik's family, what do they say?" "Amma says to welcome Lakshmi." "Lovely. Other families light lamps for other festivals, for other reasons. And where God lives, different people believe different things. Some people don't believe in God. I don't know for sure. Ask your family what they think." Hrithik nodded seriously. "I'll ask Amma and Dadi."

What was still on the classroom windows?
Paper lamps were still on the windows.
How did Hrithik feel when he asked his questions?
He felt curious and serious, really wanting to know where God lives and why they lit lamps.
Why was Nilesh Sir careful in how he answered?
In a class of different families, he answered simply, said different people believe different things, admitted he didn't know and sent Hrithik to his own family.
How might Hrithik's Amma feel when he asks her tonight?
She may feel pleased and proud that he is thinking about their festival and wants her answer.

"You moved my Saturday shift without asking me," Elizabeth said, chin forward, jaw pushed out.
Kashish felt her own shoulders rise. She kept her voice low. "You're upset about the rota. Tell me what happened."
"I found out from the board. Again."
"Okay. That's on me; I should have messaged you. Is it the Saturday itself, or finding out that way?"
Elizabeth's jaw stayed set. "Both. My mother's hospital visit is on Saturday."
"Ah. I didn't know. What time is it?"
"Morning."
"If I swap you to the late shift, does that work?"
A pause. The jaw eased a little. "Yes. That works."
Kashish nodded. Earlier, when Elizabeth's voice had risen, she had kept one eye on the open door and a plan to step out if it got any louder. She hadn't needed it.

How did Elizabeth find out her shift had been moved?
She found out from the board.
What might Elizabeth's jutting jaw suggest about how she felt?
Most likely Elizabeth felt angry and determined to be heard about the shift; it could also have been worry about her mother's hospital visit coming out as defensiveness.
Which choices helped Kashish calm the exchange?
Keeping her voice low, owning the missed message, asking what mattered and offering the late shift, while keeping a way to step out if it turned unsafe.
What would have changed if Kashish had matched Elizabeth's tone?
The argument would likely have grown louder and Elizabeth might never have mentioned the hospital visit, so no fix would have been found.

The negotiation for the flat was down to the last ten minutes before the train, and the owner wanted a higher rent. Rain drummed on the window. Amandeep looked at the number on the paper, said nothing for a slow breath, and let the silence sit. Jatin, her friend beside her, felt his palms sweat and wanted to fill the gap. Instead he held his tongue. The owner shifted, then said, "Maybe we could go a little lower." Amandeep smiled and nodded, and later told Jatin she'd used the pause to think, not to pressure. In some rooms she'd have spoken sooner, she said, but this owner seemed to value a thoughtful reply.

What was drumming on the window?
Rain was drumming on the window.
What was Jatin feeling during the silence?
Jatin felt uneasy, with sweating palms, and wanted to fill the gap. He held back, which shows he trusted Amandeep's pause.
What could Amandeep do if a long silence feels too heavy for the other person?
Give a short sentence to acknowledge the point, such as saying she is thinking about it, to keep the room comfortable.
How might the owner have seen the silence?
The owner may have felt some pressure, then shifted and offered a lower rent, or may have taken it as a thoughtful pause; the setting and the person shape the reading.

I sit between Ishita and Manjula at the design studio, so I heard all of it on Monday. Manjula said Ishita had promised to send the tile samples to the client by Friday. Ishita's jaw tightened, and I braced for a fight. Instead she said, slowly, "This is how I remember it: you'd send them and I'd do the drawings. But I could be wrong." She scrolled back through their team chat, lips moving. Then she stopped and turned the screen toward Manjula. There it was, Thursday, her own message: "I'll courier the samples tomorrow." Ishita let out a short laugh, said, "Okay, that one's on me," and booked a pickup before lunch. Manjula's shoulders dropped. I can't say what Ishita felt, but she didn't argue again.

Where did Ishita look to check what had been agreed?
She scrolled back through their team chat.
What does Ishita's short laugh after seeing the message suggest about her feelings?
It suggests a flash of embarrassment mixed with relief that the question was settled, since she owns the mistake and books the pickup straight away.
Which choice kept the disagreement from turning into a fight, and why?
Saying "this is how I remember it" and checking the chat; it left room to be wrong and let the message decide, instead of two confident memories clashing.
How might Manjula see Ishita after this?
Manjula likely feels relieved and respected, and may trust Ishita more, because Ishita checked the facts and admitted the slip instead of insisting.

At summer camp near Valencia, the children sat in the shade of an olive tree while Beatriz, the counsellor, handed out riddles. "In a race, you overtake the runner in second place. What place are you in now?" Bilal's hand shot up. "First!" Beatriz tilted her head. "Are you sure? Take three breaths." Bilal breathed, picturing the track. He had been behind the second runner, then in front. The first runner was still ahead. "Second," he said, cheeks warm. "I'm in second!" "Why did first come so fast?" she asked. Bilal thought. "Because it felt like winning."

What did Beatriz tell Bilal to take?
Three breaths.
Why did the answer "first" come so fast to Bilal?
It felt like winning, so the exciting first answer felt right; after correcting it he felt a bit embarrassed, with warm cheeks.
What could Bilal do with future trick questions?
Picture the situation and take a few breaths before answering, especially when an answer comes very fast.
What is it like for Beatriz to watch Bilal work it out?
She is probably pleased that her question and the three breaths let him reason it out himself, without her giving the answer.

Nine minutes before the client call, the office Wi-Fi dropped, and Nirmala was still waiting for the vendor report Sharmila had promised on Tuesday.

"So sorry," Sharmila said, pulling up a chair. "The vendor sent the wrong file, so I had to wait. And then the template changed. Actually, first IT locked my account, that's what started it. And the numbers from accounts were late too."

Nirmala watched the explanation grow, a new cause every few sentences, each one smooth. The wall clock kept moving. Something about the tidiness bothered her more than the delay.

"Okay," Nirmala said gently. "Forget the why for now. What part is done, and what part feels stuck?"

Sharmila let out a breath. "Honestly? I don't understand the new cost section."

"Then we'll say that on the call, and I'll sit with you after."

When had Sharmila promised the vendor report?
Sharmila had promised the report on Tuesday.
What made Nirmala feel uneasy as Sharmila explained?
Nirmala felt uneasy because the reasons kept changing and sounded too smooth, a hint that something uncomfortable sat underneath.
Which approach worked under the time pressure, and why?
Setting aside the why and asking what was done and what felt stuck got Sharmila to name the real problem quickly, before the call.
What is it like for Sharmila when Nirmala asks what feels stuck?
Sharmila seems relieved; the question lets Sharmila drop the growing excuses and admit the cost section is confusing.

Afreen covered her face with her hands, laughing. "Rekha, you want to hear my most embarrassing work moment? First month at the agency. My manager sent a long email to the whole team about a client project. I meant to reply to my friend in the team saying, 'Ugh, another endless email.' I hit reply-all. It went to twenty people, including the client. I actually felt my heart stop. I sat there staring at my screen, hot all over. Then I went to my manager's desk and apologised before she could say anything. She was cool about it, but she gave me three rules I still use: read the 'To' line twice, never write anything in an email you wouldn't say to someone's face, and wait before pressing send if you're annoyed. I haven't made that mistake since."

How many people received Afreen's reply-all?
Twenty people, including the client.
What was Afreen feeling when she realised the mistake?
She was horrified and embarrassed, feeling her heart stop and going hot all over.
Why was going to the manager's desk right away a good move?
It showed honesty and responsibility, and gave the manager a chance to help before things got worse.
How might the client have seen that reply-all?
They may have felt a bit insulted or amused, which is why protecting professional tone in every email matters.
What mood is associated with Raga Shivaranjani?
Raga Shivaranjani is associated with a sad, devotional mood.

Wednesday
Class debate: "School phones should be banned." I was for the ban. My argument: phones distract. My evidence: "everyone knows." Great, Afreen, very scientific.
Then Jagdish stood up and said a ban hurts kids who need to call home, like him, because his mother works nights. He also had actual numbers from our own class survey: most people only used phones in breaks. I didn't have anything back. My face went hot.
At home I looked at what I'd written and saw the problem. My claim was too big. So I changed it: "phones switched off in lessons, available in breaks and for calls home." I found two studies Sir had shared about distraction during lessons.
Tomorrow's the second round. I'm scared but I think it's actually a better argument now. And I'm going to thank Jagdish for the survey.

Why did Jagdish say a phone ban would hurt him?
His mother works nights, and he needs to be able to call home.
How did Afreen feel when there was nothing to say back?
Afreen felt embarrassed and caught out; the diary says Afreen's face went hot.
What went wrong with Afreen's first argument, and what fixed it?
The claim was too big and backed only by "everyone knows"; narrowing the claim and finding real studies fixed it.
How might Jagdish react when Afreen thanks him for the survey?
Jagdish might feel pleased and respected, seeing that his counter-argument actually changed Afreen's thinking.

Week three: They'd been to Darjeeling together over the long weekend; the photos were on every phone in class. Arnab asked Gopika if she wanted to join his statistics study circle. She glanced at the others before answering, "Maybe, let me see." She didn't come.

She read the messages, said, "They're waiting at the canteen," and left, apologising twice. Arnab wondered whether she'd wanted to stay.

How does Arnab see Gopika's group over these weeks?
Arnab sees warmth and closeness, but also a pull that brings Gopika back each time, and he wonders whether she wanted to stay.

At recess in the Madrid schoolyard, Tomas sat on the bench with his sandwich untouched. His dog Luna had died on Saturday. Mateo dropped down beside him. "You're still sad? It's only a dog. Just get a new one." Tomas felt his throat tighten. Luna had waited at the door every afternoon; she was family. For a moment he wanted to shout. Instead he looked at the ground and said quietly, "She wasn't just a dog to me. I need some time." Mateo scratched his neck. "Oh. Okay." Later Tomas found his older sister at the fence, and she put her arm around him without saying anything.

What did Mateo tell Tomas to do?
He told him to just get a new one.
What was Tomas feeling when Mateo said it was only a dog?
Hurt; his throat tightened, he felt like shouting, and to him Luna was family.
What did Tomas do that helped him after the hurtful comment?
He calmly told Mateo he needed time and then turned to his sister, who understood without trying to fix it.
How might Mateo see the moment?
He probably thought a new dog would solve the sadness, and his scratching his neck and quiet "Oh. Okay." suggest he realised he had said something that stung.
Does splitting a big project into small parts make it easier to finish, and why?

It was about the school trip to Munnar. Ujjwal's class was going, mine too: three days, two nights. Achan read the permission slip at the dining table and put it down. "No."
"Why?"
"Because I said so."
I remember the heat climbing up my neck. "You never trust me. Never!"
He stood up, chair scraping. "Don't raise your voice at me, Gopika."
I went to my room and slammed the door, and through it I heard him tell Amma, "She has no respect." I lay there thinking exactly the same about him. Looking back, neither of us said the real thing. I didn't say, "I want you to see I can look after myself." He didn't say whatever he was afraid of. We both heard only disrespect, and we fought that instead.

What trip did Gopika want permission for?
The school trip to Munnar: three days, two nights.
What did Gopika really want Achan to understand?
She wanted Achan to see she could look after herself; under her angry words was a hurt, hungry wish to be trusted.
What could either of them have said instead to change this stage?
Achan could have named his worry about the trip, and Gopika could have asked what he was afraid of, instead of trading commands and accusations.
How might Achan have heard 'You never trust me'?
He likely heard it as rudeness and disrespect, which made him defend his authority instead of sharing the worry underneath.

Aparna, you're asking me whether to take the Pune job or marry Rohan now, as if I have the answer. I don't. But I'll tell you what I did at twenty-one. A good family proposed a match, a kind boy, and my father was keen. I wanted to finish my B.Ed first. Nobody knew if the boy's family would wait, or if I'd even get a teaching post afterwards. I sat with my mother on the verandah for three evenings. Then I told my father, 'I like him. Ask them if they'll wait two years.' Everyone thought I was ruining it. They waited. Your grandfather used to joke, 'Rukmini made me earn it.' Not everything worked out, mind you; my first posting was in a village far away, and I cried a lot. But I chose knowing what I was giving up.

What did Rukmini want to finish before marrying?
Her B.Ed.
How did Rukmini feel about choosing when so much was unknown?
Uncertain; she spent three evenings talking it over, and she admits she cried a lot at her first posting, yet she felt she chose knowingly.
What can Aparna learn from how Rukmini decided?
Talk it through with trusted family, say clearly what you want, and look for a middle path like asking for time, while accepting that some costs stay unknown.
How might Rukmini's father have seen her request?
He was keen on the match, so he may have worried she was risking a good proposal.

It was 1 a.m., the night before his final-semester exam, and Kamal was still on the betting app. He had a system: after every loss, double the next bet, because "a win has to come, and it'll cover everything." He had lost six in a row. His hands were cold. His exam notes lay unopened on the bed. His sister Mahima, home for the holidays, saw the light under his door and came in. She looked at the screen, then at his face. "Kamal. How much?" He told her. She didn't shout. She closed the laptop gently, sat beside him and said, "Tomorrow, after your exam, we talk to Papa, and we call a gambling helpline together. Tonight, you sleep." Kamal wanted to argue about his system. Instead he let her take the laptop to her room.

How many losses in a row had Kamal had?
Six in a row.
Why did Kamal keep doubling his bets?
He felt in control and sure his system would bring a win to cover everything, even as his hands went cold with fear.
What did Mahima do, and why was it wise?
She stayed calm, closed the laptop, took it away for the night, and planned to talk to Papa and call a gambling helpline together after the exam.
What was it like for Mahima to see the screen?
Mahima was probably frightened and worried for Kamal, but chose calm and care over shouting.

Classroom note from Swati, end of the week

Bhavna sat next to her friend at the blue table every morning this week, knees touching, sharing crayons. On Tuesday she took a seat at the far end and kept her back turned. I asked quietly; they had argued over a glitter pen. By lunch they were side by side again.

On Thursday she swapped to the window seat, giggling, and her friend followed. That was just a game.

So one move doesn't worry me. The pattern tells me they are close. 🙂

What did Bhavna and her friend argue over?
A glitter pen.
What was Bhavna probably feeling when she sat at the far end with her back turned on Tuesday?
She was most likely upset and cross with her friend after their argument. By Thursday, swapping seats with giggles showed she felt playful, not upset.
How did Swati make sense of Bhavna's seat changes?
Swati asked quietly on Tuesday instead of guessing, and looked at the whole week's pattern rather than one moment.
How does Bhavna's friend show they feel close to Bhavna?
The friend shares crayons at the blue table and follows Bhavna to the window seat on Thursday.

Teacher's note, Wednesday. Pankaj came back to class after his mother's death and sat alone at the window. Most children kept a nervous distance. Rekha, nine, walked over at play-time with her wooden puzzle box and sat on the floor next to him. She did not speak. After a bit she pushed the box towards him and said, "I can't do the last piece. Can you?"
Pankaj looked at it, then turned the piece round and fitted it in. They did another. By the end of the break Pankaj had said three sentences.
I told Rekha, quietly, that what she did was kind.
Neelam, class teacher

What did Rekha bring over to sit next to Pankaj?
Rekha brought her wooden puzzle box.
What was Rekha feeling as she walked over and sat beside Pankaj without speaking?

Rekha sat beside Pankaj, said she could not do the last piece and asked for help. Doing something ordinary together opened a small conversation.
How might Pankaj have felt when Rekha pushed the puzzle box towards him?

Dear Imtiaz,
I'm leaving this on your desk because when we talk, I end up sounding like your Nani did with me.
When you moved back home in March, I told my friends you were "between things". I lay awake doing sums: at twenty-five I was married, working at the bank, with a baby on the way. You have changed jobs three times. I worried you were lost.
Then Rehana at work said her son's path looked just like yours, and she showed me an article saying most young people take longer to settle now. Maybe the road is simply longer than mine was.
So instead of a verdict, I have questions. What did you like in each job? What do you want the next one to have? And is there anything you need from me, other than silence at dinner?
With love and a little less worry,
Your Ammi, Ritu

In March.
What was Ritu worried about as she lay awake doing sums?
She worried Imtiaz was lost, comparing three job changes with her own life at twenty-five.
What turning point changed Ritu's approach, and what does she do instead?
Rehana's story and the article about longer paths made her swap a verdict for questions about what Imtiaz liked and wants next.
How might Imtiaz feel finding questions on the desk instead of a lecture?
Imtiaz may feel respected rather than judged, and more willing to talk than to sit in silence at dinner.

The team lead said, "The build failed again," and I said, completely flat, "Great, my favourite hobby," with my tongue pressed into my cheek and one eyebrow slightly up. I'll tell you how I left, since everyone asks. I'm Hrithik, and at nineteen I'd have done almost anything our teacher asked. He ran meditation camps for college students in Bengaluru, and his senior disciple, Chaitanya, called him 'the living answer'. We gave up weekends, then small donations, then bigger ones. Nobody asked why. Then, at one camp, I asked in a question session why his trust's accounts weren't shared like other trusts' are. The room froze. Chaitanya took me aside and said questions like that came from 'a closed heart'. That night I lay awake, feeling guilty and also, underneath, clear. A good teacher would have answered. I called my cousin, who works at a charity, and she said genuine trusts publish their accounts. I stopped going. I still meditate. I just don't need anyone to be beyond question anymore.

What did Chaitanya call the teacher?
Chaitanya called him 'the living answer'.
What did Hrithik feel lying awake that night?
Hrithik felt guilty but also, underneath, clear that something was wrong.
What sign told Hrithik the teacher might not be genuine?
A fair question about the accounts was met with silence and blame instead of an answer.
How does Chaitanya see Hrithik's question?
Chaitanya treats it as coming from 'a closed heart', a fault in Hrithik rather than a fair question.

Jaya waited in the school corridor outside the counsellor's room until the bell had stopped ringing. Inside, Gautam, the counsellor, let her sit without speaking for a minute.
Then she said, "I sent money from Ma's account to someone who promised me a phone. It's gone." Her voice cracked. "Ma will be so angry. Papa too. I can't say it."

A few things I am wondering about:
How can I plan a day out in a new city?
A bus carries 16 passengers and 7 get off at the stop. How many stay on the bus?
Correct: They are agree with the plan.
What does "distance" mean?
Why do planes fly high above the clouds?

Charu and her co-founder Farah were the happiest pair I knew, which is why the scene in their office surprised me. I had dropped in with samosas one evening and found them on a video call with a startup lawyer, going through a document titled "If we split".
Charu explained it to me afterwards, very matter-of-fact. "Two of my friends' companies ended in court. Both times, they tried to agree what was fair after they already hated each other." So she and Farah were setting it now: shares earned over four years, and a written way to value and buy out anyone who left.
Farah joked that it felt like writing a will. Charu didn't laugh; she just said, "Better now, while we'd both be fair."
I can't say whether it was comfortable for them. But they signed it that night and went back to arguing happily about logos.
— Swati

"If we split".
What might Charu have been feeling when she didn't laugh at Farah's joke?

Why is setting the terms while friendly a wise move?
Both are more likely to be fair now, instead of fighting over what is fair after trust has broken.
How does Farah seem to see the process?
Farah jokes that it feels like writing a will, which suggests it is a little uncomfortable but accepted.

Class teacher's note: Francis, Class 11, before the midterms

Francis came to me on Monday, worried he was behind. He showed me his revision planner. Every weekend in the last month had the same kind of entry: "Sat–Sun: complete Economics." "Sat–Sun: complete Accountancy." "Sat–Sun: complete English." Next to each, in smaller writing, "not done." When I asked how much he usually finishes in a weekend, he said, "Maybe three chapters." Economics has eleven. Yet the next page already said, "Sat–Sun: complete Business Studies." His classmate Noor, who sits next to him, said he'd been working hard but kept feeling like a failure. I sat with him and we planned one subject across three weekends, based on three chapters each.

What did Francis usually finish in a weekend?
"Maybe three chapters."
How had Francis been feeling about his revision?
He felt worried and like a failure, because every weekend plan ended with "not done".
What made the new plan more realistic?
It used what Francis actually finishes, about three chapters, and spread one subject across three weekends.
How might Noor see Francis's struggle?
Noor seems concerned and fair, noticing he works hard but keeps feeling like a failure.

Since the exams ended, Kavitha had lived in the back room of their house in Palakkad with the wooden shutters closed. She slept till eleven, lay under a sheet with her phone, and couldn't say whether it was Wednesday or Friday. She felt heavy, like the air in the room.
One morning her little brother Dhruv flung the shutters open. "Amma says breakfast is on the verandah. Now." Sunlight fell across the bed. Kavitha groaned, but went.
The verandah smelled of wet earth. Paati was stringing jasmine. Kavitha sat beside her and helped, blinking in the light.
The next morning she woke at seven and opened the shutters herself. By the end of the week she was walking to the temple tank with Paati before breakfast, and the heaviness had begun to lift.

What was Paati stringing?
Paati was stringing jasmine.
How did Kavitha feel living with the shutters closed?
Kavitha felt heavy and flat, and lost track of the days.
What helped Kavitha's mood begin to lift?
Morning sunlight, breakfast on the verandah, and a set early walk to the temple tank with Paati.
How might Dhruv see his sister's shuttered room?
Dhruv seems to see it as a dark place Kavitha needed pulling out of, so he flung the shutters open.

messages.content:
Read this:

"You're applying again?" Francis asked, stirring his tea.
"Yes." Lokesh closed the laptop. "Eleven rejections. I'm sending the twelfth."
"Don't you feel stupid?"
"Every time." Lokesh laughed. "But I read all the feedback. Three of them said my portfolio was weak on print design. So I did a print course."
"And if this one says no?"
"Then I'll know something else to fix."
Francis watched him. "Last year you gave up on football after one bad match."
"I know. That's why I'm doing this. I didn't like who I was when I gave up."
"Okay." Francis pushed his cup aside. "Show me the portfolio. I'll tell you what's boring."
"Brutal?"
"Brutal."

How many rejections has Lokesh had?
Eleven rejections.
What does Lokesh's laugh suggest about how he feels?
It suggests he feels embarrassed by the rejections but determined not to give up.
What is Lokesh doing that makes trying again wise?
He reads the feedback and fixes the weakness, like taking a print course, before applying again.
How is Francis affected by Lokesh's attitude?
Francis is surprised, remembering Lokesh quit football, and is moved to help review the portfolio.

In the Pune office, the quarterly pitch to the regional heads was at four. At two, Shreya leaned over the partition. 'Just so you know, I've had a fever since last night, and I've been drowning in tickets, so my numbers slide will be a bit messy.' Nandini nodded, but inside something itched. Before the last pitch it had been a stomach bug. Before the one in March, 'three deadlines at once'. And every time, Shreya's slide had been sharp. Nandini had started to resent these warnings; they made it sound as if the rest of them had it easy. But watching Shreya chew her pen, Nandini saw fear, not laziness. At 3:45 she said quietly, 'Your slide doesn't need to be perfect. You worked on it. That's what we need. If a number's off, we'll fix it after.' Shreya let out a breath. 'Okay,' she said. 'Okay.'

What time was the quarterly pitch?
The pitch was at four.
What did Nandini feel about Shreya's warnings, and how did that change?
Nandini had started to feel resentful, as if the rest of them had it easy, but seeing Shreya chew her pen she sensed fear and felt more sympathy.
What did Nandini say that helped?
That the slide didn't need to be perfect, that the effort was what counted, and that any wrong number could be fixed afterwards.
Why might Shreya mention a fever and being overloaded before each pitch?
She may be anxious about being judged, so the warning gives a ready explanation if her slide falls short.

Teacher's note, KG-B, written by Indu. Musical chairs today. Elizabeth was out in the second round. Last month this would have meant a long cry under the table. Today she stamped once, said "Aww!" loudly, and her lip trembled. Then she took three big breaths, the way we practised with "balloon belly," and went to sit on the cheering bench. By the fourth round she was clapping for her friends. I told her I saw her breathing. She grinned. I will share the balloon breath with her parents. 👍

How many big breaths did Elizabeth take?
She took three big breaths.
What does Elizabeth's trembling lip followed by clapping suggest?
She felt disappointed about being out, but managed the feeling and even began enjoying her friends' game.
Why is Indu's plan to share the balloon breath with the parents useful?
Elizabeth can use the same calming trick at home, so the skill gets practised in more places.
How might Elizabeth's friends experience the change?
Instead of a long upset, they get her cheers from the bench, which makes the game happier for everyone.

"Elizabeth, you look upset. Someone laughed at your prayer beads? Let me tell you something, child.

When I was twenty-four, I, Rajni, worked at the telephone exchange. Every lunch I read a few lines from my little prayer book. One colleague made it his daily joke. 'Asking your invisible friend for a raise?' he'd say, and the others laughed.

I wanted to throw the book at him. Once I nearly argued for an hour. It would only have fed him.

So one day I said, calmly, 'It helps me. You don't have to share it. But please stop the jokes.' He laughed again, but less. Next time I just said, 'Enough,' and went on reading.

It stung for months, beta. But I learned his scorn was about him, not about what I was worth. Keep your beads. Keep your answer short."

Where did Rajni work when she was twenty-four?
At the telephone exchange.
What did Rajni feel when the colleague joked daily about the prayer book?
Rajni felt stung and angry enough to want to throw the book at him.
Which choice in Rajni's story worked better than arguing, and why?
Answering briefly and calmly, then setting a clear limit on the jokes, worked because a long argument would only have fed him.
How might the colleague have seen Rajni's calm reply?
The colleague may have felt the joke lose its fun once Rajni stopped reacting, which is why he laughed less.

Alex is stacking his books in a pyramid. Each level of the pyramid has 80% as many books as the number of books in the previous level. If he makes four levels and the top level has 64 books, how many books are in the pyramid in total?

The third level has 80 books because 64 / .8 = 80
The second level has 100 books because 80 / .8 = 100
The first level has 125 books because 100 / .8 = 125
In total there are 369 books because 64 + 80 + 100 + 125 = 369
The answer is 369.

You know I worshipped Dr. Nirmala Pillai, Anju. In first year she's the reason I chose microbiology. She'd stay late explaining plating techniques; she lent me her own lab coat.
Then last month, in the lab meeting, she tore apart Revathi's presentation in front of everyone, and later I heard her say it was because Revathi had "sided with the other group" in some department quarrel. Petty. Really petty. And I realised she'd been giving the good projects to the people who flattered her.
For a week I was so angry I wanted to quit research. I told my roommate all professors are the same, just politics.
But then I was setting up a plate, and my hands did it exactly the way she taught me: careful, sterile, no shortcuts. That skill is real. It's mine now.
So I'm keeping the technique and dropping the pedestal. And I'm not giving up on every teacher because of one. I'm Keerthana, still a microbiologist, just less starry-eyed.

What did Dr. Pillai lend Keerthana in first year?
Her own lab coat.
How did Keerthana feel after the lab meeting?
Angry and disillusioned, wanting to quit research and calling all professors "just politics".
What did Keerthana decide to keep, and what to let go?
To keep the careful technique Dr. Pillai taught, drop the pedestal, and not turn cynical about every teacher.
How might Revathi have experienced the lab meeting?
As humiliating and unfair, torn apart in front of everyone over a department quarrel.

Ganesh Chaturthi, day 3

Today Kavitha Didi asked if I wanted to join the building dhol group! Only the big kids play in it, and I've been watching them from the balcony for two years.

She gave me the smallest dhol and showed me the beat. I got it wrong at first. Nobody laughed. They just played slower till I caught up.

When we played for the aarti, everyone in the building clapped. Kavitha Didi winked at me.

I didn't want to go home. I kept thinking, I'm one of them now.

Pooja

What instrument did Kavitha Didi give Pooja?
She gave Pooja the smallest dhol.
How did Pooja feel when the building clapped?
Pooja felt thrilled and proud, like belonging to the group.
How did the group help Pooja feel accepted?
They didn't laugh at mistakes and played slower until Pooja caught up.
How might Kavitha Didi feel about including Pooja?
Kavitha Didi likely felt glad and warm, winking to show approval.

Monday. Mehak watched the whisper start at the back bench. Sonal leaned to Tina: "Don't tell anyone, but Rinku's father lost his job." Tina's eyes went round.

Tuesday. At lunch the whisper had reached the girls by the window. Mehak heard it again, with an extra part: "and they're selling their car." Each person said, "Promise you won't tell," and then told.

Wednesday. Jatin, who usually sat alone, leaned over to Mehak's group. "Did you hear about Rinku? They're selling their house too." The group turned to him, surprised, and let him sit with them for the first time.

Mehak saw his face light up. He wasn't saying it to be mean, she thought. He was saying it so they'd let him in.

Rinku, two rows ahead, was colouring her map, not knowing.

What extra part had been added by Tuesday?
"And they're selling their car."
What does Mehak think about why Jatin joined in?
She feels uneasy but understanding, believing he repeated it not to be mean but to be let into the group.
What could Mehak do to stop the chain?
She could refuse to pass it on and quietly tell her group it's Rinku's private matter, or tell a teacher if it keeps spreading.
How might Rinku feel if she knew what was being whispered?
She would probably feel embarrassed and hurt, especially since some parts, like the house, may not even be true.

True or false? Correct the false ones.
a) A tangent meets a circle at exactly one point.
b) A secant meets a circle at exactly one point.
c) The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through it.
d) From a point inside a circle, one tangent can be drawn.
e) From a point on a circle, exactly one tangent can be drawn.
f) From a point outside a circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn.
g) The two tangents from an external point are equal in length.
h) If PA and PB are tangents, angle APB = angle AOB.
i) Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel.
j) Tangents at the ends of any chord are parallel.
k) For a circumscribed quadrilateral, AB + BC = CD + DA.
l) A parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
m) The tangent length from P is sqrt(d^2 + r^2).
n) The centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents from a point.
o) The inradius of a 3-4-5 triangle is 1.
p) A line perpendicular to a radius at its outer end is a tangent.

a) true
b) false (two points)
c) true
d) false (none)
e) true
f) true
g) true
h) false (angle APB + angle AOB = 180 degrees)
i) true
j) false (only for a diameter)
k) false (AB + CD = BC + DA)
l) true
m) false (sqrt(d^2 - r^2))
n) true
o) true
p) true

During the lunch break at the software office in Mohali, Akash's colleague Jasleen showed him a trading group on her phone. "Look, members posted profits all morning. The admin says new entries close at 5 p.m. today." The screen was full of green arrows and celebration emojis.
Akash felt a rush. He had some savings. Five o'clock was four hours away.
"Should we join?" Jasleen asked.
Akash noticed his heart pounding. He also noticed the pinned message: "Don't miss out. Decide now." It reminded him of the office's financial wellness session last month, where the speaker had said, "Anything that has to be decided today, walk away from."
"Let's not decide today," he said. "Let's ask the adviser from that session. She's registered."
Jasleen pouted but agreed. The next day, the group had moved the deadline to "5 p.m. tomorrow". They both laughed and left it.

When did the trading group say new entries would close?
At 5 p.m. that day.
What was Akash feeling when he saw the group's messages?
He felt a rush of excitement, his heart pounding, tempted by the urgency.
How did Akash handle the pressure?
He noticed the urgent message, remembered the advice to walk away from anything that has to be decided today, and suggested asking a registered adviser first.
How might Jasleen feel when the deadline moves to the next day?
Jasleen probably feels amused and relieved, seeing that the urgency was fake.
Carson counts 6 clouds that look like funny animals. His little brother counts three times as many clouds that look like dragons. How many clouds did they count in total?

First find the total number of clouds Carson's brother counted: 6 clouds * 3 = 18 clouds
Then add the number Carson counted to find the total: 18 clouds + 6 clouds = 24 clouds
The answer is 24.
By the time Anne is two times as old as Emile, Emile will be six times as old as Maude. If Maude will be 8 years old, how old will Anne be?

If Maude's age is 8 by the time Anne's age is four times Emile's age, Emile will be six times as old as Maude, which totals 6*8 = 48 years.
If Emile's age is 48 years old by the time Anne's age is twice her number, Anne will be 2*48 = 96 years.
The answer is 96.

Uncle Jerry wants to reap ripe tomatoes from his garden. Yesterday, he was able to reap 120 tomatoes. Today, he was able to reap 50 more tomatoes than yesterday. How many tomatoes did Uncle Jerry reap?

Today, Uncle Jerry reaps 120 + 50 = 170 tomatoes.
Therefore, Uncle Jerry reaps a total of 120 + 170 = 290 ripe tomatoes.
The answer is 290.

Zeenat, don't cry over the forgotten eggs. Sit with your Tanuja Aunty for a minute. When I was nine, in Lucknow, my mother sent me to the bazaar with a list spoken very fast: "Tomatoes, coriander, green chillies, a packet of salt, soap, two candles, a matchbox, and ask the tailor if my blouse is ready." I repeated it all the way down the lane. At the shop I bought tomatoes and candles, and then my head was empty. I came home crying, just like you. My mother didn't scold. The next week she said, "Three things only. Say them back to me." Then three more on the next trip. Forty years of teaching, and I always told my students: small bundles, not one big sack. So, what were the three things your Ammi wanted today?

What did young Tanuja manage to buy at the shop?
Tomatoes and candles.
How did young Tanuja feel walking home from the bazaar?
She felt upset and helpless, crying because she had tried so hard to remember and her head had gone empty.
What change did Tanuja's mother make, and why did it work?
She gave only three things and asked Tanuja to say them back, so the list fit in a child's memory.
How might Zeenat feel hearing this story after forgetting the eggs?
Zeenat might feel relieved and less ashamed, learning that a grown-up teacher once forgot a long list too.
