You want to know why that thank-you card is framed, beta? Sit. Your Zubin Mama was twenty-four then, sharing a flat in Pune with Uma, who ran night classes for the watchmen in our building. For two years she taught them to read, after full days at her office. When the society gave her a shawl and a small speech, she laughed and said, "Arre, it was nothing, anyone would have done it."
Everyone clapped and went back to their samosas. I didn't. Next morning over tea, I told her, "Uma, you gave up two hundred evenings. Ramu-kaka reads his grandson's letters now. That was not nothing." She started to wave it off again, and I said, "Don't. Just let it sit for a minute."
She went quiet, looking into her cup. A week later she gave me that card.

What did Uma say when the society gave her a shawl?
"Arre, it was nothing, anyone would have done it."
Why didn't Zubin let the moment pass like everyone else?
Zubin felt uneasy, even a little sad, hearing two years of hard work called nothing; he admired the effort and wanted Uma to actually take it in.
Which choice at the breakfast table made the difference?
Naming concrete facts, two hundred evenings and Ramu-kaka reading letters, and then asking Uma not to wave it off but to let it sit, gave the thanks room to land without a lecture.
How might Uma have felt when Zubin said "Don't"?
Uma was probably uncomfortable at first, used to shrugging praise away, and then touched; the card a week later suggests the words finally reached her. 🤍

"You corrected me in front of the client," Wasim said, closing the meeting room door. His voice was level, but his ears were red.

Deepika looked up. "The figure was wrong."

"It was. And I'd have fixed it. But saying 'that's not right, Wasim' in front of them made me look like I don't know my own numbers."

"I was worried they'd notice first."

"Fair. Can we agree on something? If you spot an error during a call, message me, and I'll correct it myself. If it's urgent, say 'let me add one detail' and fix it."

Deepika was quiet. "I didn't think about how it looked. I'm sorry."

"I'm sorry I went silent for the rest of the meeting. That didn't help either."

"You were sulking."

Wasim laughed despite himself. "I was sulking. I was angry for about an hour."

"And now?"

"Now I want us to look good in front of clients. Both of us."

What did Wasim suggest Deepika do if she spots an error during a call?
He suggested she message him so he can correct it himself, or say 'let me add one detail' if it's urgent.
How was Wasim feeling when he closed the meeting room door?
Wasim was angry and embarrassed, with red ears, feeling he had been made to look incompetent in front of the client.
What made the conversation work instead of turning into a fight?
Wasim spoke privately, admitted the figure was wrong, proposed a clear rule, and owned his own sulking.
How does Deepika see the moment in the meeting after talking with Wasim?
Deepika realises she only meant to fix the error before the client noticed, and now sees how it made Wasim look, so she apologises.

Friday. Noor's elbow bumped Nani's blue drinking glass off the windowsill, and it cracked in two. Nani's footsteps came fast. Noor's heart thumped. "Mridul did it," she said, and her cousin Mridul began to cry.
Saturday. Noor left her paratha. She kept watching Mridul, who wasn't allowed to play with the ball all morning. Her tummy felt funny.
Sunday. At bedtime Noor whispered into the pillow, "Nani, it was my elbow." Nani sat up, stroked her hair, and said, "Thank you for telling me. Glasses break. You're not in trouble." In the morning Noor gave Mridul the ball first.

What happened to Nani's blue drinking glass on Friday?
Noor's elbow bumped it off the windowsill, and it cracked in two.
Why did Noor say "Mridul did it"?
She was scared when she heard Nani's fast footsteps; her thumping heart shows the lie was a panicked way to escape trouble.
What did Nani do that made the truth feel safe?
Nani thanked Noor, said glasses break and told her she was not in trouble, so the truth brought comfort instead of punishment.
What was Saturday like for Mridul?
Mridul lost ball time all morning for something Noor had done, which must have felt unfair and confusing.

Monday: Kishore sat through the school career talk and wrote nothing. Everyone else seemed to know: army, law, coding. He only knew he liked fixing his uncle Ramesh's bicycles and hated sitting still.
Thursday: Ramesh mama let him run the repair shop for an afternoon while he went to the bank. Kishore trued a wheel, fixed two punctures and argued a customer down from an unfair complaint without shouting. On the way home he kept replaying it, grinning.
Next Saturday: he sat with a notebook. Strengths: hands, patience with machines, calm with people. Options: mechanic, bicycle shop owner, automobile diploma after Class 10. He wrote "ask the ITI teacher" at the bottom and underlined it twice.

What did Kishore fix while Ramesh mama was at the bank?
He trued a wheel and fixed two punctures.
How was Kishore feeling after the afternoon in the shop?
He felt proud and pleased, replaying it on the way home and grinning.
What small step did Kishore plan, and why is it wise?
He planned to ask the ITI teacher, which lets him check a real training path instead of guessing.
How might Ramesh mama see Kishore after that afternoon?
Ramesh mama may feel trusting and impressed, seeing that Kishore can handle both machines and customers.

Anand and Tanuja had walked to the same school in their village in Wardha district for ten years. When she moved to Nagpur for nursing college, they spoke every Sunday. Then, in March, nothing. No calls, no replies, for four months.
At the tea stall near the bus stand, Anand's friend Mukesh said, "She's a city girl now. Post something on her photo, let her feel it."
Anand was tempted. He was hurt. But he remembered Tanuja at eight, sharing her tiffin when his mother was ill.
That night he sent one message: "Tanuja, I miss our Sunday calls. I hope you're okay. No need to reply if you're busy. I'm here whenever." Then he stopped checking.
In August a reply came: "Sorry, Anand. Papa was in hospital for months. I couldn't talk to anyone. Your message helped."
He called her that evening. They talked for five minutes. It was enough.

For how many months did Tanuja not reply?
Four months.
What was Anand feeling when Mukesh suggested posting on her photo?
Hurt and tempted to hit back, though he held back, remembering her kindness.
What did Anand do instead of a public comment?
He sent one warm message with no pressure, then stopped checking.
Why had Tanuja gone silent?
Her Papa had been in hospital for months and she couldn't talk to anyone; the message helped her.

'You're going to the hackathon? For the whole weekend?' Tejas's voice cracked over the phone.
'It's the one I told you about in June,' Sumit said gently.
'But what am I supposed to do? You know Sundays are hard for me.'
Sumit closed his eyes. For months he'd cancelled things: football, his cousin's engagement, sleep. 'Tej, I care about you so much. I want to help. But I can't be the only thing holding your weekend together. I'm getting really tired.'
Silence. Then, small: 'So I'm too much.'
'No. You're not too much. It's just too much for one person. Who else could you call on Sunday? Your sister? The guys from the band?'
'...Rohit asked me to jam, actually.'
'Say yes. And that counselling cell you mentioned? Maybe book a slot this week.'
'You'll still call Saturday night?'
'Nine o'clock. I promise. And I'll tell you everything about the hackathon.'

What event is Sumit going to for the whole weekend?
A hackathon he'd mentioned in June.
What was Sumit feeling before he spoke up?
He felt tired and weighed down after months of cancelling his own plans.
How did Sumit set a limit kindly?
He said he cared but couldn't be the only support, suggested Tejas's sister, band friends and the counselling cell, and promised a Saturday call.
How does Tejas first hear Sumit's limit?
As 'I'm too much', a painful fear of being a burden.
People say "libary". What is the real spelling?

The real spelling is "library", with an r after the b. Say it slowly: li-brar-y.
Example: Tara borrowed three novels from the school library.

Counsellor's note, Monday
Imran (Class 11) came in at lunch, angry and close to tears. He showed me a short video in which Shankar, his closest friend, seemed to say, "Imran only got into the team because his dad knows the coach." Imran had watched it maybe twenty times. "It's his face, ma'am. It's him."
I asked Imran to watch it with the sound off. The background was our basketball court, but the shadows fell the wrong way for that time of day, and Shankar's collar changed shape between two frames. Imran went quiet.
What I did next: I called Shankar in separately. He was shocked and said he had never said it. With both boys' agreement I informed the principal and our safeguarding lead the same afternoon, reported the account that posted it, and called both families. I will meet the boys together tomorrow.

How many times had Imran watched the video?
Imran had watched it maybe twenty times.
How was Imran feeling when he came in at lunch?
Imran was angry and close to tears, hurt that his closest friend seemed to mock him on video.
What steps did the counsellor take the same day?
Checked the video with Imran, spoke to Shankar separately, informed the principal and safeguarding lead, reported the account and called both families.
What would it be like for Shankar to learn about the video?
Shankar was shocked to see his own face saying words he never said, and could have lost his closest friend over it.

Hi Arohi,
I wanted to write this rather than bring it up in the team meeting.
In Tuesday's review with the client, the customer-churn analysis was presented as "my analysis" on your slide. Most of the model and the three charts on slides 6 to 8 were my work; our shared folder shows the versions from 12 and 15 May. I was surprised and honestly a bit hurt, and I'd rather talk about it than let it sit.
I'm not asking for anything dramatic. Could you mention to Srinivas that the model was mine when you send the follow-up today? And for the next project, can we agree at the start who owns which part, and put our names on those slides?
I've enjoyed working with you, and I'd like to keep doing it without this being awkward.
Keerthana

Which slides were Keerthana's work?
The three charts on slides 6 to 8, along with most of the model.
How did Keerthana feel after Tuesday's review?
Surprised and a bit hurt.
What makes Keerthana's email a calm, effective response?
It cites evidence (the shared-folder versions from 12 and 15 May), makes one small, specific request, and proposes agreeing roles at the start of the next project.
How might Arohi feel reading the email?
Embarrassed, but given an easy, private way to put it right.

“Amma, the milk is going to spill!”
“Let it, Hemant. Watch.”
The milk in the new clay pot rose, foamed, and bubbled over the edge.
Bhavna and Paati clapped. “Pongalo Pongal!”

It bubbled over the edge of the new clay pot.

She could tell him stories of how her Paati celebrated and let him help with the next step.

At the Saturday craft class in the community centre, Vasudha spent the whole hour on a pop-up card for her Nani's birthday. She cut a tiny paper house, folded it three times till the roof stood straight, and glued a small window that opened.
When the instructor, Joseph, came by, the other children waited for him to say "beautiful" like he always did. Instead he bent close. "You made the window open. And you folded the roof again and again till it stood up. That's patience."
Vasudha looked up quickly. "Nani always sits by her window."
Joseph nodded. "Then she'll see you thought about her."
Vasudha stayed late to add a little paper Nani inside the window.

What did Vasudha add at the end?
A little paper Nani inside the window.
Why did Vasudha look up quickly when Joseph spoke?
Vasudha felt surprised and pleased that Joseph noticed the opening window and her patient folding, which showed he really saw her effort.
Why did Joseph's comment help more than saying "beautiful"?
It named exactly what Vasudha did well, the opening window and the patient folding, which made her want to keep going and add more detail.
How might Nani feel when she opens the card?
Nani will likely feel loved and touched, seeing the house with a window and herself inside it.

Diwali week was the worst week for the sweet shop's central kitchen, and this year the rain had flooded the back lane. Himani, the new kitchen manager, had fourteen staff and two thousand boxes to pack. By Saturday night they had done it. Yamini, the oldest cook, touched her arm. "Beta, you ran this well." Others clapped.

Himani felt proud, and then uncertain. Was it true? Or did they say it because she was the boss?

On Sunday, instead of a speech, she handed out slips of paper. "Write one thing I did that helped and one thing I should change. No names."

Most slips were kind. Three weren't. "You don't listen when we say the fryer is dangerous." "You praise the packers, not the cooks."

The next morning Himani called the repair man for the fryer and thanked the cooks by name in front of everyone. Yamini smiled. "Now it's real," she said.

How many boxes did the kitchen have to pack?
They had two thousand boxes to pack.
What did Himani feel when the staff clapped?
Himani felt proud, then uncertain whether the praise was honest or because she was the boss.
How did Himani keep respect from turning into flattery?
She asked for anonymous honest feedback, acted on the hard comments about the fryer and the cooks, and shared credit publicly.
How does Yamini see Himani's response to the feedback?
Yamini sees it as proof that Himani's respect is earned, saying "Now it's real".

Read this:

Monday: when Ms Sarita asked Darshan to read the paragraph aloud, he said, "I can't, I'm stupid at reading." The class went quiet. He read nothing that day.

Wednesday: Ms Sarita kept him back. "You said stupid. What exactly is hard?" Darshan thought. "Long words. And I lose my place." "That's two things," she said. "Not stupid. Two things. We can practise two things." She gave him a ruler to keep his place and a list of five long words to break into parts: "hap-pen-ing".

Friday: Darshan read three lines aloud, the ruler under each line. He stumbled on "adventure", stopped, broke it up, "ad-ven-ture", and went on. When he sat down, he didn't say stupid. He said, "I lost my place once."

What did Ms Sarita give Darshan to keep his place?
Ms Sarita gave Darshan a ruler.
Why did Darshan say "I'm stupid at reading"?
Darshan felt embarrassed and discouraged, and a single label felt easier than naming what was hard.
What did Ms Sarita do that replaced the label?
She asked exactly what was hard, named two skills, long words and losing his place, and gave him a ruler and word-breaking practice.
How might the class see Darshan on Friday?
They see him read three lines and keep going after a stumble, a change from Monday's silence.
A church has 120 members. 40% are adults. The rest are children. How many children more children are there than adults?

There are 48 adults because 120 x .4 = 48
60% of members are children because 100 - 40 = 60
There are 72 children because 120 x .6 = 72
There are 24 more children than adults because 72 - 48 = 24
The answer is 24.

Pradeep: where are you? your mum called me
Nilesh: I hit someone with the bike near the bus stand
Pradeep: WHAT. is he ok??
Nilesh: I don't know. people were running at me. I got scared and rode off
Pradeep: Nilesh you have to go back
Nilesh: they'll beat me. I saw them shouting
Pradeep: then go to the police station. not back to the crowd. the station
Nilesh: I'll get arrested
Pradeep: leaving is worse. and the man might still be lying there
Nilesh: ...
Pradeep: I'm calling your mama. he'll come with you
A little later Nilesh's uncle messaged Pradeep: "Found him at the tea shop. We're at the police station now. The man was taken to hospital by an auto driver. He's hurt but awake."
Nilesh: I should have stopped. I keep seeing him on the road

Who took the injured man to hospital?
An auto driver took him to hospital.
Why did Nilesh ride off, and how does Nilesh feel afterwards?
Nilesh was frightened of being beaten by the crowd, and afterwards feels guilty, unable to stop seeing the man on the road.
What would have been a safer choice than riding off?
Nilesh could have stopped at a safe distance, called 112 and waited for the police, so the man got help without Nilesh facing the crowd alone.
How does Pradeep respond to Nilesh's panic?
Pradeep is shocked but firm, pushing Nilesh toward the police station and calling his uncle to go with him.

metadata.subtype: Approach: leave the scene out of fear [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

The ITI workshop in Rourkela had one working welding machine for twelve trainees. Alka, twenty, was the only woman in the batch. She got fifteen minutes a day on it. Her first welds were lumpy and uneven, and one of the boys smirked. Instructor Ramesh said nothing; he just handed her scrap metal. "Practise the motion without the machine." So she did, in the evenings, holding an unlit torch and moving it along a line, over and over. When her turn came, she used every second. By the third month, her beads were smooth. Ramesh held one up to the class. "This is the standard." Alka kept her face straight, but her ears burned with pride.

How many trainees shared the welding machine?
Twelve.
What was Alka feeling when Ramesh held up her weld?
She felt proud and pleased, though she kept her face straight.
What strategy helped Alka improve despite little machine time?
Practising the motion in the evenings without the machine, then using every second of her turn.
How might the boy who smirked see Alka now?
He may feel surprised and perhaps a little embarrassed that her welds became the standard.
The Earth is round, but from the ground it looks like flat. What should I change?

The Earth is round, but from the ground it looks flat.
Why: "Look" takes an adjective directly; "look like" needs a noun.

Read this:

I'm Tanuja. I'll tell you what I saw on Christmas Eve in our colony.
Mrs D'Costa had set up a crib under the stairs, with clay figures and cotton for snow. Most of us just grabbed the plum cake and ran. Neelam didn't. She crouched and asked what each figure was, even the donkey. Mrs D'Costa explained the shepherds and the star. Neelam kept nodding.
When the carollers stopped for a prayer, some kids kept talking. Neelam put her finger to her lips and stood still with her hands folded, though her family goes to the temple, not church.
Afterwards Mrs D'Costa gave her an extra slice. I don't know exactly what Neelam was thinking. She looked like someone who'd been let into a secret.

What did Mrs D'Costa use for snow in the crib?
She used cotton for snow.
What does Neelam's expression afterwards suggest, according to Tanuja?
Neelam seemed delighted and moved, like someone who'd been let into a secret, though Tanuja can't be sure.
What would you advise the kids who kept talking during the prayer?
Even if it isn't your own faith, stay quiet for a few moments; it shows respect and costs nothing.
How might Mrs D'Costa have felt about Neelam's questions?
Mrs D'Costa probably felt touched and valued, since someone from another faith cared enough to ask about her festival.

Read this:

Dear Dilnaz,
Thank you for last night. When we were on the phone and I started telling you about my grandfather, I just stopped halfway. I couldn't say anything more. The silence went on for ages.
You didn't ask, "What's wrong?" or "Are you okay?" over and over. You just said, "I'm here. Take your time." And then you waited.
I didn't finish the story last night. But this morning I feel ready. He's been in hospital again, and I'm scared.
Can we talk after school? I'll finish the sentence this time.
Pallavi

Who was Pallavi telling Dilnaz about on the phone?
The grandfather.
What was Pallavi feeling when the silence went on?
Pallavi felt scared and overwhelmed about the grandfather's illness, unable to say more.
What did Dilnaz do that helped?
Dilnaz gave space, said "I'm here, take your time," and waited without pressing.
If you were Dilnaz, how might this letter feel?
You might feel glad your patience helped and ready to listen after school.

Read this:

Kiran, since your show is about work habits, here's mine. I'm Baljeet, I prepare accounts for small shops, and a year ago I was the queen of multitasking. Three spreadsheets open, phone on the desk, answering every client call in the middle of an entry. I felt busy all day. Then I added a customer's cash twice in a year-end statement, and the shop owner found it before I did. That stung. So I tried blocks. Ninety minutes on one client's books, phone silent, email closed. Then half an hour for all the calls and messages together. Then I get up, stretch, drink water, look out of the window. The first week felt strangely slow. By the second, I was finishing a client in a day instead of three. Turns out I wasn't doing three things at once. I was doing three things badly.

What mistake did Baljeet make in the year-end statement?
Added a customer's cash twice.
How did Baljeet feel when the shop owner found the mistake first?
It stung; she felt embarrassed and shaken, which pushed her to change how she worked 😔
Which part of Baljeet's new routine makes the biggest difference, and why?
Ninety-minute blocks on one client's books with the phone silent, because without switching she finishes a client in a day instead of three.
How might the shop owner see Baljeet's work after the change?
The owner would likely trust her more again, getting accurate books faster after that first worrying mistake.

Read this:

Lalit, beta, listen. I'm your grandfather, Chaitanya. When I was ten, a boy named Bhau used to flick my ears every day at the school gate, and my fists curled so tight my nails left marks. I wanted to hit him once, hard, so he would stop. I lay awake planning it. But I had seen another boy caught fighting: the headmaster's scolding, a letter home, a bleeding lip. So one morning I walked away and stood with Rohit and the others near the water tank. Then I told our class teacher, who listened, said it was not my fault and spoke to the headmaster that same day. It was slow, but it worked. And the planning stopped eating my nights. I learned that anger is fair, but it should not drive.

Where did the boy flick Chaitanya's ears every day?
He flicked his ears at the school gate.
Why did Chaitanya walk away instead of hitting the boy?
He had seen another boy caught fighting and punished and hurt, so he feared the same for himself.
What did Chaitanya do besides walking away, and what did it lead to?
He stood with friends near the water tank and told the class teacher, which slowly worked and ended his night-time planning.
How might Lalit feel on hearing that Grandfather Chaitanya once wanted to hit someone?
Lalit may feel relieved that angry feelings are normal, since Chaitanya calls the anger fair, and the story also shows what to do with them.
Show me three ways to say thank you without using the word "thank" or "thanks". One per line.

I really appreciate your help.
You have been very kind.
That was a big help to me.
My boss asked me to say a few words "off the cuff". Do I need a shirt cuff?

No. "Off the cuff" means without preparation or notes.
Example: She gave a short thank-you speech off the cuff.

Homework check, please:
Tell me the meaning of "harbors".
Is the library open right now?
What does "a dime a dozen" mean?
Rewrite this correctly: Me and Rohan went to the park.
Why do some animals sleep through the winter?

1. As a noun, "harbors" means sheltered places by the coast where ships stay safe.
2. I don't know that. Opening hours can change and I can't see your library. Check the library's notice board or phone and ask them.
3. It means very common and easy to find. For example: pens like this are a dime a dozen in the market.
4. It should be: Rohan and I went to the park. Why: "I" is the subject form; name yourself last.
5. They live off stored fat in a deep sleep called hibernation. Because food is hard to find in the cold, and a deep sleep uses very little energy.

Read this:

After the Friday lecture on signals, Yamini waited at the front of the lecture room until the others left. "Professor, I didn't understand anything today." The professor asked which part. "All of it, honestly. I feel lost." So the professor turned to the board and went through the first ten minutes of the lecture again, slowly, with the same examples. Yamini nodded at each step and said "okay" but kept looking at the clock. Afreen, waiting at the door for a lift home, saw the professor sigh quietly and Yamini leave with the same blank look. Neither had got what they hoped for. In the corridor Yamini muttered, "That did not help at all."

What did Yamini say to the professor at the front of the room?
Yamini said, Professor, I didn't understand anything today.
What was Yamini feeling while nodding and looking at the clock?
Yamini felt lost and frustrated, since repeating the whole lecture did not touch the actual confusion.
What could Yamini say next time to get a better answer, and why?
Yamini could name the one step or example that stopped making sense, because a precise question lets the professor explain exactly that part.
How might the professor feel when the only request is that nothing made sense?
The professor may feel stuck and a little frustrated, since there is no clue where the trouble is and repeating the lecture is the only option.

Tabitha has 25 dollars. She gives her mom 8 dollars and invests half what is left in a money market. She spends some money on 5 items that costs 50 cents each. How much money does Tabitha have left?

Tabitha has 25-8 = 17 dollars after giving some to her mom.
Tabitha has 17/2 = 8.5 dollars left after putting some in a money market.
The 5 items Tabitha buys totals out to 5*0.5 = 2.50 dollars.
Tabitha has 8.5-2.5 = 6 dollars left.
The answer is 6.

"Avni, you look miserable every morning."
"I'm fine."
"You hate the animation course. You said so on Sunday."
"I said I hate the 3D module."
"You hate all the modules."
"Manoj, it's eight months in. Papa paid the whole year's fees."
"So?"
"So I can't quit now. Everyone at the reunion heard me say I'm going to be an animator."
"You also told me you want to do psychology."
"That was before."
"Before what? Before you paid?"
Avni stabbed her toast. "If I quit, it means I was wrong for eight months."
"Or it means you learned something in eight months."
"Easy for you to say. You don't have to face Papa."
She grabbed her bag and left for the class she dreaded.

How long has Avni been in the course?
Eight months.
What is Avni feeling when she stabs her toast?
She feels resentful and trapped, afraid that quitting would mean admitting she was wrong.
What could Avni do to look at the choice freshly?
Ask whether she'd choose this course today, knowing what she knows, and talk it through honestly with Papa or a college counsellor.
How does Manoj see Avni's reasons for staying?
Manoj sees the eight months as learning, not failure, and thinks she is staying for the wrong reasons.

My name's Lalremsiami, but everyone calls me Siami. You asked why I moved out of the flat? It was Ramesh. We'd been best friends since first year. At first he smoked weed at weekends. Then every evening. Then before class. He stopped turning up for our project, borrowed money he didn't return, and got snappy if I said anything. I lay awake worrying about him, and then felt furious at him for making me worry. I was so tired.
I tried everything. Hiding his stuff. Begging. Nothing changed, because it wasn't mine to change. A counsellor at college helped me see that. So I told Ramesh: not in our flat, no more loans, and I'm here if you want help. He didn't take it well. I moved in with another friend. I still message him on Sundays. I've stopped trying to fix him, and I've started sleeping again.

When does Lalremsiami still message Ramesh?
Lalremsiami still messages Ramesh on Sundays.
What feelings did Lalremsiami go through while living with Ramesh?
Lalremsiami felt worried, then furious at being made to worry, and deeply tired.
What helped Lalremsiami, and which limits were set?
A college counsellor helped Lalremsiami stop trying to fix Ramesh; the limits were no weed in the flat, no more loans and an open offer of help.
How might Ramesh see Lalremsiami's limits?
Ramesh didn't take them well at first and may feel judged, though the Sunday messages show the door is still open.

metadata.subtype: Family or friends affected by someone's use [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Rain had pushed PT indoors, and the hall was cramped and noisy. Raghav grabbed Mihir's water bottle and held it high. "Come on, shorty, jump!" The boys around him laughed, and Raghav felt ten feet tall. It was the same trick his older brother played on him at home every night.
Mihir jumped, missed, and stopped. His lips pressed tight and his eyes went shiny.
Raghav's arm stayed up, but something inside him dropped. He remembered that exact feeling from home.
Lalremsiami Ma'am was busy with the mats, too far to see. Raghav lowered the bottle himself. "Here. Sorry, Mihir. That wasn't funny." The laughter trailed off.

What did Raghav grab from Mihir?
His water bottle.
Why did something inside Raghav drop when he saw Mihir's eyes?
He recognised the same hurt he feels when his brother teases him at home, and felt ashamed of doing it to someone else.
What did Raghav do that showed real change?
He noticed the hurt on Mihir's face, stopped on his own without a teacher seeing, and said sorry.
How might Mihir have felt when Raghav held the bottle high?
Mihir felt small and humiliated, pressing his lips tight while holding back tears.

Read this:

In the exam hall of the Guwahati school, Kiran laid out his things: the blue lucky pen, which had written every good test since class five, and under his uniform, the faded cricket T-shirt he always wore for exams. He touched the pen cap to his forehead. Across the aisle, Dhruv whispered, "Still with the pen?" Kiran nodded, cheeks warm. "It's stupid, I know." The invigilator walked past and Kiran pretended to check his roll number. The truth was, he had revised three chapters twice. He knew the pen didn't know science. But when he held it, his heart slowed down. The papers came round. Kiran uncapped the pen and began to write.

What does Kiran wear under his uniform for exams?
The faded cricket T-shirt he always wears for exams.
Why does Kiran hold on to the lucky pen even though he calls it stupid?
He feels nervous before exams, and holding the pen calms his heart, even though he half knows it has nothing to do with his marks.
How could Kiran use the ritual without depending on it?
He could treat the pen as a calming habit and keep revising, since his real preparation, like revising three chapters twice, is what helps.
What is it like for Dhruv to see Kiran's pen routine?
Dhruv seems curious and a bit teasing, maybe familiar with the routine from earlier exams.

Read this:

I'm Aparna, and I was sitting two rows behind Gautam in the semester exam when the invigilator stopped at his desk. A folded paper chit lay on the floor by his foot. "Is this yours?" she asked. Gautam went red to his ears. Sweat beaded on his upper lip, and his pen hand shook. "No, ma'am." Everyone was staring. Honestly, he looked guilty. The invigilator looked at him for a long moment. Then she picked up the chit, unfolded it and checked the handwriting against his answer sheet. It didn't match. She checked the seat behind. It did. Gautam kept shaking for ten minutes after, even though he'd done nothing. After the exam I told him, "You looked so scared." He said, "I was terrified. I knew how it looked, and that made it worse." I've thought a lot since about how close he came to being blamed for a blush.

What did the invigilator check the chit against?
His answer sheet.
What was Gautam feeling when the invigilator asked about the chit?
He was terrified, going red and shaking, and knowing how it looked made him more frightened.
What did the invigilator do that was fair?
She checked evidence, the handwriting, instead of treating his blushing and sweating as proof.
How did Aparna first read Gautam's reaction?
Aparna thought he looked guilty, before the handwriting check showed he was innocent.

metadata.subtype: Bodily signs are not lie detectors [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the bus stand in their small town near Salem, Jeevan saw the shopkeeper's son lean out and make comments at Urmila, a classmate from college. Urmila kept her eyes on the road, jaw tight. Jeevan felt anger rise; he wanted to go and shout at him. But he stopped. What does she want? he thought. When the bus came, he sat near her and said quietly, "I saw that. Are you okay?" Urmila shrugged. "It happens every day." "Do you want me to say something to him? Or come with you to his father? Or tell the principal? Or just walk you to the stand every day?" Urmila was silent, then said, "Maybe walk with me. And come with me to the principal on Monday." "Okay," said Jeevan. "Your call." Urmila's shoulders dropped a little.

Who made comments at Urmila?
The shopkeeper's son made comments at Urmila.
What was Jeevan feeling when he wanted to shout?
Jeevan felt angry, but paused, realising Urmila's wishes mattered more than his own urge.
How did Jeevan help in a way that respected Urmila?
He checked privately, offered several options, and followed her choices instead of taking over.
How did Urmila respond to being asked?
Urmila relaxed a little, choosing company and help with the principal on her own terms.

Read this:

Age two: Charu jammed the star-shaped block at the round hole again and again, her lip pushed out. Twice she threw it on the floor and then picked it up again. Her father did not take it from her. He steadied the box with one hand and gently turned the block a quarter. Click, it dropped. Charu clapped and shouted, 'I did it!' and looked at his face for the cheer.

Age five: Tenzin frowned at a jigsaw of a farm, one sky piece still missing, arms crossed over his chest. His aunt Pooja reached toward the table. 'Don't tell me!' Tenzin said. Pooja sat back and folded her hands in her lap. After a while she said, 'Try the corner with the red barn.' Tenzin bent over the corner, found the piece in seconds and grinned so widely that his cheeks bunched up. 'I did it myself.'

Which corner did Pooja suggest to Tenzin?
The corner with the red barn.
How did each adult support the child's win without taking it, at two and at five?
Charu's father steadied the box and turned the block a little so she could finish it, and Pooja only suggested the corner with the red barn. Each child still felt the win was their own
What was Charu feeling when the block dropped?
Proud and delighted, as her clapping and her look at her father's face show.
What could Pooja do if the nudge is not enough?
Offer a slightly bigger hint, such as which two pieces might fit, and still leave the placing to Tenzin.

Fix this: It was raining heavy last night.
It rained 3 millimetres each day for 5 days. How many millimetres fell in all?
What does "lonely" mean?

1. Fixed: It was raining heavily last night. Why: "Raining" needs the adverb "heavily".
2. It is 15. Because 5 x 3 = 15.
3. Lonely means sad because you are alone or have no one to talk to.

The health camp Jyoti had organised in the community hall at Govindpuri drew thirty-one people when they had planned for two hundred. Back at the NGO office, she sat with her head in her hands. 'I messed it up completely.' Jasleen, who ran the programmes, handed her a marker and pointed at the whiteboard. 'Draw it. Everything that went into those thirty-one.' Jyoti drew a circle. The heat wave that week, a big slice. The camp date clashing with a local wedding, big. Posters that went up only two days before: that was hers, and she shaded it honestly, about a quarter. The volunteers who didn't turn up for the door-to-door, another slice. Jasleen tapped the wedding slice. 'Nobody told us about that. Next time we check the community calendar.' Jyoti looked at her own quarter. It was real. It was also a quarter.

How many people came to the health camp?
Thirty-one people came to the health camp.
What was Jyoti feeling when she said 'I messed it up completely'?
She felt defeated and ashamed, believing the low turnout was entirely her fault.
What did the whiteboard circle help Jyoti learn?
It showed that her late posters were about a quarter of the causes, so she could own that part and plan fixes, like checking the community calendar.
How does Jasleen see the setback?
Jasleen sees it as a mix of causes to learn from, not one person's failure, and focuses on practical fixes like checking for clashes.

You asked what my hardest moment at work was. I'm Jyoti, and it was my first job, at a small logistics firm. My manager asked me to change the date on a delivery document so the client wouldn't charge us a penalty. Just one number. I remember my hands going cold. My sister Bidisha's college fees were due that month, and I was the one paying. I said, 'Sir, I can't sign that.' He didn't shout. He just stopped talking to me for a week, and I thought I'd be fired. I wasn't. But I did start job hunting, quietly. Six months later I left for a place that seemed more honest. I still don't know if I was brave or just scared of a different thing.

What did Jyoti's manager ask Jyoti to change?
He asked Jyoti to change the date on a delivery document.
Why did Jyoti's hands go cold?
Jyoti was frightened, torn between refusing something dishonest and needing the job to pay Bidisha's fees.
What did Jyoti do that reduced the career risk after refusing?
Jyoti quietly began job hunting, keeping a way out if the situation got worse.
How might Bidisha feel if she learned about this moment?
She might feel grateful and also a little guilty that her fees added to the pressure on Jyoti. 🤍

At the community centre office in Nashik, the booking clerk waited with the register while the family settled the plan for Naveen's cousin Omkar's wedding. Omkar's father read from a paper: "Groom's side wants a car, and the bride's family will cover the hall and the gold, as usual." Naveen, twenty-four, cleared his throat, his palms damp. "Uncle, may I say something? I don't think we should ask for any of it. It puts weight on the girl's family, and it's dowry, whatever we call it." The room went quiet. Naveen kept his voice level. "I'm only asking that we drop the list." Omkar's grandfather, Dada, tapped his stick. "The boy is right. In my time we refused too, and nothing collapsed." Omkar's father looked at the register, then folded the paper. "Let us talk again tonight."

Where was the family settling the wedding plan?
The family was at the community centre office in Nashik.
What is Naveen feeling as he speaks up?
Naveen is nervous but resolved. His palms are damp, yet he keeps his voice level and asks only that the list be dropped.
What turning point came after Naveen spoke?
Dada backed him, saying the boy was right and that nothing collapsed when they refused before, and Omkar's father folded the paper and agreed to talk again.
How does Dada seem to see Naveen's speech?
Dada sees it as right and worth supporting. His tapping stick and his words about refusing in his own time show he has held the same view quietly.

Kobe and Pau went to a restaurant. Kobe ordered five pieces of fried chicken, and Pau ordered twice as much fried chicken as Kobe did. If they order another set of fried chicken, how many pieces of fried chicken will Pau have eaten in all?

Pau ordered 5 x 2 = 10 fried chickens in total.
Therefore, Pau ate 10 x 2 = 20 pieces of fried chicken.
The answer is 20.

The hospital in Nimbahera closed its outpatient wing at two, and after that Elizabeth, twenty-four and newly posted from Kottayam, had nothing but a quiet room above a grocery shop.

The doctors were polite. The other nurses were friendly in the corridor and spoke Mewari to each other at lunch, laughing at things she half caught.

Her landlady, Kalyani-bai, invited her to the Ganesh temple on Tuesday. Elizabeth went, stood at the back, and was handed prasad by six strangers.

On Sunday she found the only other Malayali in town, a bank clerk, through a notice in the church. They talked for an hour about rain.

Walking back past the shuttered market, Elizabeth counted: two months, one bank clerk, a landlady who waved. It felt small. But on Tuesday she'd go to the temple again.

What time did the outpatient wing close?
It closed at two.
What was Elizabeth feeling as she walked back past the shuttered market?
She felt lonely and a little discouraged that two months had given her so few connections, yet still hopeful enough to keep trying.
How could a colleague support Elizabeth at this stage?
A nurse could include her in lunch by switching to a language she knows, or invite her along on a day off.
How might Kalyani-bai see her new tenant?
Kalyani-bai seems to see a quiet young woman far from home and wants to include her, which is why she invited her to the temple.

My grandfather was born in 1950 in a small village.

Sushma had worked past nine on most nights for two years. She assumed the committee would notice, and so she never mentioned that she wanted a bigger role. Her manager thought of her as dependable, the one who fixed things quietly. When the promotion committee met, with only one slot in the year's budget, her manager described her as reliable and could not say what bigger role she was ready for. Arnab, who had asked in March what the next level needed and led one small project, was promoted. Sushma heard it at the tea counter and smiled, then went back to her desk and stared at the screen without typing.

How late did Sushma work on most nights?
Sushma worked past nine on most nights.
How was Sushma feeling at the tea counter?
Sushma was hurt and deflated, though she smiled, and afterwards she stared at the screen without typing.
What could Sushma do next, and why?
Sushma could tell her manager she wants a bigger role and ask what it takes, because the committee can only weigh a case that someone has made.
How might Sushma's manager have seen her at the committee?
The manager saw a reliable person but had no goal or bigger-role evidence to present, so there was nothing to argue for.

metadata.subtype: Approach: waiting to be noticed for hard work [Pitfall]

Read this:

The week after the cyclone, Farida did what felt good: she ordered new curtains and booked painters for the living room of her Vizag flat, wanting it to look normal again. Her flatmate, Shalini, kept putting a bucket under the ceiling crack in the bedroom.
On Thursday the painters arrived just as the bucket overflowed. The claim form was still pending, and the painting advance had already eaten a third of Farida's savings.
Farida stood in the wet bedroom and looked at the bucket for a long time. Then she called the painters and moved them to next month. She spent the evening with Shalini writing three columns: must fix now, fix when the claim comes, can wait. The ceiling, the broken window latch and the wiring went in the first. The curtains went back in their box.

What did Shalini keep putting under the ceiling crack?
A bucket, in the bedroom.
What was Farida feeling when she ordered the curtains and booked the painters?
She was longing for normality after the cyclone, so making the flat look like home again felt comforting.
What else could Farida do while the claim is pending?
She could send the insurer photos of the leak and ask what the claim covers, then move items between her three columns as the amount becomes clear.
What was that first week like for Shalini?
Shalini was dealing with the leaking bedroom every night, probably frustrated that paint came before the ceiling.
Why does a quiet walk often clear a cluttered mind?
Walking gives the mind some space. Because the steady movement and the changing scenery take attention off our worries, our thoughts settle and we can think more clearly.
Give this a formal tone: Hey, can you send me the homework notes?
Would you kindly send me the homework notes?

Read this:

Avni had stepped on Irfan's toy car. "I hope you get sick!" Irfan shouted. Next morning Avni had a fever. Irfan hid behind the curtain and wouldn't eat his paratha. "What's wrong, jaan?" Ammi asked. "I made Avni sick. I said it." Ammi pulled him onto her lap. "Wishes can't make anyone sick. Germs do. Your words were angry, but they didn't do this." "Promise?" "Promise." Later he took Avni a glass of water and his second-best car.

What had Avni stepped on?
Irfan's toy car.
Why did Irfan hide behind the curtain and refuse his paratha?
He felt guilty and scared, believing his angry wish had made Avni sick.
What did Ammi say that helped, and why does it suit a small child?
She said wishes can't make anyone sick and germs do, in simple words, while holding him close so he felt safe.
How might Avni feel when Irfan brings water and his second-best car?
Avni would likely feel cared for and cheered up, and may not even know about his angry wish.

Read this:

Gautam, you're nervous about asking for more help with your transfer? Let me, Mahima, your old aunt, tell you about my first big move, from Kanpur to Mumbai, in 1998.
The bank offered me a promotion and a transfer, with two weeks to join. I was so happy I nearly said yes on the phone. But my father said, "Before you say yes, ask what they'll do to help you land."
So I wrote to the regional office. Three questions. Was there a relocation allowance? Could they give me temporary housing while I looked for a flat? Could I join in four weeks instead of two?
They said no to four weeks, but gave me three. And they put me in the bank's guest house in Chembur for a month, free.
That month saved me. I found a room near the station without panic. Ask, Gautam. The worst they say is no.

Where was the bank's guest house?
In Chembur.
How did Mahima feel when the promotion was first offered?
Mahima felt so happy and excited that she nearly said yes on the phone without asking anything.
What was the turning point in Mahima's story, and what did it lead to?
The turning point was her father's advice to ask how they'd help her land; it led to three weeks to join and a month of free guest-house stay.
How might the bank's regional office have seen Mahima's questions?
The office likely saw them as reasonable and professional, which is why they agreed to part of the request.

metadata.subtype: Approach: negotiating a relocation package with the employer [Action]

"Are you stupid, Yash? A child could have built this sheet. Get out of my sight."
Alka's voice carried across the whole floor. Yash stood holding the laptop, mouth open, no words coming.
Later, at the water cooler, Meera touched his sleeve. "That's the third time this month."
"Maybe she's right. Maybe I am slow."
"You're not. The client praised that sheet last week. Do you have the dates?"
"Some. The 4th, the 12th, today."
"Write each one down tonight. What she said, who was there. I was there today and on the 12th. I'll put my name to it."
Two days later the HR manager read the pages slowly. "Thank you for the dates and the witness. This isn't something you fix by working harder. We're opening a formal review today, and until it's done you'll report to Rohit."
Yash let out a breath he felt he had been holding for a month.

Which dates did Yash have?
The 4th, the 12th, today.
What does Yash's "Maybe I am slow" reveal?
It reveals Yash was shaken and doubting himself after being belittled in front of the whole floor.
Which steps protected Yash here?
Writing down dates, words and witnesses, having an ally offer to be named as a witness, and taking it to HR, which opened a formal review and changed who he reports to.
Why might Meera have stepped in at the water cooler?
Meera had witnessed two of the incidents and was worried and uncomfortable watching Yash be belittled, so she offered to be a witness.

After the video of Yuki tripping in the school corridor went round his class in Osaka, he stopped eating lunch in the cafeteria. At home he stayed up late in a forum where older boys wrote long posts about people like us being laughed at by them, the ones with easy lives. "You're not weak," one wrote to him. "You're awake. You're our brother now." Nobody at school had called Yuki anything but a joke for weeks. The forum had names for everything: the enemy, the plan, the brotherhood. He liked having names. They turned the shame into anger, and anger felt better. One night his older sister Mina, home from university, saw the screen over his shoulder. "Who's them?" she asked. Yuki shrugged. "People who think they're better." Mina didn't argue. She sat on his bed. "Tell me about the video," she said. He was quiet a long time. Then he told her. Later that night she told their mother, and the three of them agreed to see the school counsellor together.

What did one forum member call Yuki?
Their brother, awake rather than weak.
Why did the forum appeal to Yuki?
Yuki felt humiliated and alone after the video, and the forum turned that shame into anger and belonging, which felt better.
What did Mina do well?
She didn't argue about who them was; she sat down, asked about the video to reach the hurt underneath, and brought in their mother and the school counsellor that night.
What might Mina have felt seeing the screen?
Mina likely felt worried and protective at the talk of an enemy and a brotherhood, but kept calm so Yuki would keep talking.

Zeenat's friends were joining a coaching batch for the entrance exam, but at home there was no money for it this year, and the family phone had only a small data pack. So on Sunday she sat with a notebook and listed every free option she could find. The school library: open till six, quiet, with past papers. The government's free video lessons: excellent, but each one ate data. Omkar, a year senior, who had offered his handwritten notes. A study group with two girls from her lane. She thought about each one. Videos: download only the hard chapters on the library wifi and watch them offline at home. Notes: Chemistry, because Omkar's were famous. Library: every weekday. Group: Saturdays, for Maths problems. It wasn't coaching. But it was a plan that fit.

Until what time is the school library open?
Till six.
How might Zeenat have felt as her friends joined coaching?
She probably felt left out and a little anxious, which pushed her to plan carefully instead.
What makes Zeenat's plan for the videos clever?
Downloading only the hard chapters on the library wifi and watching offline gets the best free lessons without using up the family's small data pack.
How might Omkar feel about sharing his notes?
Omkar may feel pleased and generous, glad his famous notes are helping a younger student.

metadata.subtype: Approach: comparing free resources for study [Thinking]

"Two weeks for the bird scrapbook!" Ganga said at dinner. "That's forever."
"You need drawings and a page for each bird," said Shreya, passing the rice. "Want to do the cover tonight?"
"Tonight? Didi, it's not even due till the twentieth."
Twelve days later:
"Shreya didi, where's the glue stick? Where are the crow feathers?"
"You collected feathers?"
"I was going to." Ganga's voice wobbled. "It's due the day after tomorrow and I've done one page."
"Okay. Breathe. Which birds can you see from our balcony?"
"Pigeons. Mynas. The kingfisher at the lake."
"Then that's three pages by bedtime. Go."
Ganga grabbed the colour pencils, sniffing. "Why didn't it feel close before?"

What was Ganga's project?
A bird scrapbook.
What was Ganga feeling twelve days later, and what shows it?
Ganga was panicked and upset: the voice wobbled, Ganga was sniffing, and only one page was done with the scrapbook due in two days.
What could Ganga take from Shreya's first suggestion for the next project?
Doing a small piece, like the cover, on the very first night would make the deadline feel real early and leave less for the last days.
How might Shreya feel during the last-minute rush?
Shreya is probably a little frustrated after offering help on the first night, but also sympathetic, which is why she calms Ganga and makes a simple plan.
Hi! I'm in class three and I have to make a poster about water. Can you help?
Yes, I can help. A poster about water can be bright and fun. Do you want to show how to save water, or where water comes from?
How to save water.
Good choice. You could draw three pictures: a closed tap while brushing teeth, a bucket instead of a hose for washing the car, and a leaking tap being fixed. Write a short line under each one.
What should the title be?
Try something short and catchy, like "Every Drop Counts" or "Save Water, Save Life." Write it in big letters at the top so people can see it from far away.
Can I use blue colour for everything?
Blue is perfect for water, but add a few other colours so the poster stands out. Green for plants and yellow for the sun would look nice with the blue.
Okay! I'll start after lunch.
That sounds like a plan. Draw lightly in pencil first, then colour it in. Have fun making it.

Note for Dhruv's parents, Saturday, from Dadi. This morning Dhruv stood at his door and said, 'It's too much, I can't.' His room was a jungle. I said nothing and waited. After a while he sat on the bed and began thinking out loud. 'Clothes first. Only clothes.' He put every shirt and sock into the basket or the cupboard. Then, 'Now books.' Then toys into the box. Last, the floor, with the jhadu. Each time he finished a part he said, 'That's done,' and looked a little taller. Samir came to borrow a ball and said the room looked new. It took an hour. I've told Dhruv I'm proud of him.

What did Dhruv tidy first?
Clothes first, only clothes.
How did Dhruv feel standing at his door at first?
He felt overwhelmed, saying 'It's too much, I can't.'
What made the room manageable for Dhruv?
Splitting it into clothes, books, toys and floor and doing one at a time, so each finished part made the rest seem smaller.
How does Samir see the room afterwards?
Samir says the room looks new, so he is surprised and impressed.

Say: "Please have something to eat before you go." It is warm and polite.

I'm Lokesh. Three years ago I was doing a general science degree because everyone in my family did one.
In second year my friend Urmila dragged me to her uncle's carpentry workshop to pick up a chair. I stayed four hours. The smell of wood, the sound of the plane. I asked a hundred questions. Her uncle let me try a joint and I did it badly, and I was happy.
I dreamt about it for months. Then I looked up furniture design courses and woodworking diplomas. I talked to Urmila's uncle again, and to my parents, who were confused and then, slowly, curious.
I finished the degree and joined a one-year furniture-making course. It's hard. My hands are full of cuts. But when I walk into the workshop, I know I'm in the right room.

Where did Urmila take Lokesh?
To her uncle's carpentry workshop to pick up a chair.
How did Lokesh feel after doing a joint badly?
Lokesh felt happy and absorbed, even though the joint was bad.
Which steps helped Lokesh choose this path wisely?
Lokesh tested the interest by talking to a carpenter, researching courses and bringing the parents along before committing.
How might Urmila feel knowing her errand changed Lokesh's path?
Urmila may feel surprised and pleased to have helped a friend find their work.
How do I make a suggestion without sounding bossy?

A suggestion is an idea you offer for others to think about. It is a noun. To avoid sounding bossy, start with "Maybe we could" or "What if we".
Example: Her suggestion to start the project early helped everyone.
Write a polite request to a hotel, about 55 words, asking for a late checkout at 2 pm because our train is in the evening. I'm Alok Verma, room 214.

Dear Sir or Madam,
I am staying in Room 214. Our train leaves in the evening, so I would like to request a late checkout at 2 pm instead of the usual time. I would be very thankful if you could arrange this. Please let me know if it is possible.
Thank you,
Alok Verma

With only five minutes before the exam hall opened, the queue was restless. Up ahead, someone whispered, "Did you hear Hafsa's brother got suspended? Her whole family is so embarrassing."
A few girls turned to Irawati, eager for her reaction.
Irawati imagined standing where Hafsa was, three people behind, hearing her family talked about just before an exam. Her stomach clenched.
"Imagine it was your brother," she said quietly. "Would you want everyone knowing before a test?"
The girls went silent.
"Anyway, did anyone learn the last formula?" Irawati said. The talk shifted to maths. Hafsa, behind them, let out a long breath.

How long was it before the exam hall opened?
Only five minutes.
What did Irawati feel as she imagined being in Hafsa's place?
She felt empathy and discomfort, her stomach clenching at how it would feel to hear her family discussed.
How did Irawati stop the hurtful story?
She asked them to imagine it was their own brother, then kindly changed the subject to the exam.
How might Hafsa have felt when the talk changed?
Hafsa felt relieved, letting out a long breath.

A packet of candy sweets has 30 cherry-flavored sweets, 40 strawberry-flavored sweets, and 50 pineapple-flavored sweets. Aaron eats half of each of the flavored sweets and gives 5 cherry-flavored sweets to his friend. How many sweets are still in the packet of candy?

Aaron eats 1/2*30 sweets + 1/2*40 sweets + 1/2*50 sweets = 60 candy sweets.
The packet of candy sweets still has 60 sweets - 5 sweets = 55 candy sweets.
The answer is 55.

Every Wednesday evening Vinita took the metro to a small bookshop café in Bengaluru where a mixed group met to discuss big questions: a Jain accountant, a Catholic nurse, a student of Sufi music, and Vaibhav, an engineer who didn't believe in anything and said so cheerfully.
She had started going after her grandmother's death left her with more questions than the prayers could answer. She took notes. She read Kabir on the metro and argued with his couplets in the margins. She kept a list titled Things I actually believe after this week, which changed often.
Tonight Vaibhav asked her, "Why not just decide? It would be easier."
Vinita laughed. "Easier, yes. But I want something I've tested, not something I've grabbed."
On the metro home she reread the list. Two items had been crossed out this week. One had been added: Kindness is not optional. She underlined it twice.

What is Vinita's list titled?
Things I actually believe after this week.
What does Vinita feel when she laughs at Vaibhav's question?
She feels settled and determined, content to live with uncertainty while testing her beliefs.
Why is Vinita's approach a serious form of seeking?
She reads, talks with believers and sceptics, and revises her list against experience instead of grabbing a quick answer.
How might Vaibhav see Vinita's seeking?
Vaibhav seems curious and friendly, a little puzzled by her patience but respectful of it.

In their Toronto office, Rania stopped by Jin's desk on Friday. "Did you get to my slides? You said Thursday."
Jin launched in. First, the client call ran long. Then the remote connection kept dropping. Then, actually, it made more sense to wait for the new colours, which weren't final. By the fourth reason he was talking faster, and none of them matched the one before.
Rania noticed he hadn't looked up from his screen once. The logic was tidy. Too tidy.
"Jin," she said, "no stress. Is it just a heavy week?"
He breathed out. "I said yes to too many things. I'm drowning a bit."
"Okay. Can you do Monday?"
"Monday. Yes. Thank you."

When had Jin said he would look at the slides?
Thursday.
What did Rania think the too-tidy reasons suggested?
Rania read the too-tidy, changing reasons as a sign that Jin was uncomfortable about something he hadn't said.
Which choice of Rania's helped Jin say what was really wrong?
She stayed calm and asked a gentle, open question about his week instead of pointing out that the excuses didn't match.
What might the week have felt like for Jin?
Jin was overloaded after saying yes to too much, and probably embarrassed to admit he was drowning, so excuses felt safer at first.

Kavitha had been at the Chennai design office for three weeks when Ayesha, the senior engineer, slid a site inspection form across her desk.
'Sign this and date it Friday. The client's asking why it's late.'
'Did someone inspect the scaffolding on Friday?'
Ayesha sighed. 'It's the same scaffolding it was on Thursday. It's a formality.'
Kavitha's pulse jumped, but her voice stayed even. 'I can't put a date on something I didn't see. But I can go to the site at seven tomorrow, check it properly and sign it with tomorrow's date. I'll email the client tonight that it's scheduled.'
Ayesha looked at her for a long moment. 'You'll really go at seven?'
'I'll send you a photo from the gate.'
Ayesha took the form back. 'Fine. Seven.'

What date did Ayesha want on the form?
Ayesha wanted it dated Friday.
What was Kavitha feeling when answering Ayesha?
Kavitha's pulse jumped with nerves at refusing a senior, but the voice stayed even and firm about not signing for something unseen.
Why is refusing at this first request easier than refusing later?
Declining now, with a clear reason and an honest plan, sets Kavitha's line before the shortcut becomes a habit that would be harder to break.
How might Ayesha see the new hire after this exchange?
Ayesha may be surprised and a little annoyed, but also sees that Kavitha is reliable and is solving the client's problem honestly.

Teacher's note, Class 5 maths. Rehana Siddiqui.
In the first fractions lesson, Pooja (ten) pushed her notebook away and wrote “I can't do fractions” across the top.
I didn't erase it. I wrote one word after it in green: “yet.”
For two weeks, she did five practice sums every day with me at lunch. She got most wrong at first. She groaned. She kept going.
Today she solved a sum on the board, explaining her steps to the class. Afterwards she crossed out “can't” in her notebook herself and wrote “can, slowly.”
Next step: I'll pair her with Ritvik, who is where she was two weeks ago.

What did Pooja write across the top of her notebook?
She wrote “I can't do fractions.”
How did Pooja feel when she crossed out “can't” herself?
She felt proud and confident, realising her ability had grown.
Why is pairing Pooja with Ritvik a good next step?
It lets her share her “not yet” experience and strengthens her own understanding.
How might Ritvik feel working with Pooja?
He may feel encouraged, seeing someone who struggled like him and improved.

"So if I go to the camp, who handles the flower orders for the Navratri weddings?" Bhavna's mother asked.

"Kamal bhaiya," Bhavna said. "I called him. He'll come from Nashik for four days."

Her elder cousin Kamal, on speakerphone, said, "Only four, though. After that I have exams."

"The camp's six days," her father pointed out.

"I know. So before I go, I'll work Monday and Tuesday evenings, and I'll make all the garlands for the first two weddings in advance. And every night from the camp I'll update the orders sheet on the phone."

Her mother crossed her arms. "And the last two days?"

"Can Masi help? She offered at Diwali."

Her mother thought. "She did."

Her father smiled for the first time that evening. "It's not perfect. But it might work."

How many days can Kamal come from Nashik?
Four days.
What does her father's first smile of the evening suggest?
It suggests he felt relieved and reassured, seeing that Bhavna had thought through how the shop would manage.
What could the family do if Masi can't help after all?
They could reduce the number of orders taken for those two days, so no one is overwhelmed while Bhavna is away.
How might Bhavna's mother see the plan?
Her mother seemed sceptical at first, arms crossed, but she softened on remembering Masi's offer, which suggests growing trust in the plan.

In the small Andheri office, the sprint board told the same story every month. Hafsa promised the reports module "by Friday," and it arrived the following Wednesday. Joel said "two days" and meant five. Santosh, the team lead, used to snap about it. This month he did something different. He put the last six months of estimates and actual dates on the big screen, everyone's, including his own. "Look," he said. "Every single one of us is late by about sixty percent. Me too. It's not laziness. It's how brains picture work." Hafsa laughed with relief. From then on, Santosh asked for two numbers: "If it goes well" and "If it goes like usual." He promised clients the second one. The board turned green for the first time in a year.

By about how much was everyone late?
About sixty percent.
Why did Santosh put everyone's estimates on the screen, including his own?
He had grown frustrated with snapping and felt curious about the real pattern, so he wanted everyone to see it was shared, not personal laziness.
What two numbers did Santosh start asking for, and why?
"If it goes well" and "if it goes like usual", so clients get the realistic date while hope still has a place.
How did Hafsa react to the screen?
She laughed with relief, seeing that everyone, even the lead, ran late in the same way.

In a Manchester school, Mr Kofi handed Chen a detention slip for arriving late. Chen looked at it, took a breath and said, "I understand there is a rule about lateness, but the bus was cancelled and I do not think detention is fair. Could we talk after class?" Two classmates behind exchanged glances. Priya smiled at her shoes. Mr Kofi's mouth tightened. "After class, then." At the end of the lesson Chen showed the bus notice on a phone. Mr Kofi read it, nodded slowly, and tore up the slip.

What did Chen show Mr Kofi at the end of the lesson?
Chen showed the bus notice on a phone.
What was Mr Kofi feeling when his mouth tightened?
Mr Kofi was probably irritated or challenged at being questioned in front of the class, though he still agreed to talk afterwards.
What in Chen's wording kept the disagreement respectful?
Chen began with "I understand there is a rule", gave a reason, and asked to talk after class instead of arguing in front of everyone.
What might Priya be feeling while smiling at her shoes?
Priya may feel nervous and quietly impressed, or relieved that someone said it out loud; looking at her shoes suggests not wanting to be seen reacting.

Salma, you asked how things are at home now. Honestly? Better. Weird, but better.
I'm Tushar, and I'd been the family peacemaker since I was about eight. When Mummy and Dadi fought over the kitchen, I ran between them, cracked jokes, carried messages. When my brother and Papa argued, I took the blame just to end it.
Last year, at twenty, I stopped. No speech. The next time Mummy asked me to "go tell Dadi" something, I said gently, "You can tell her yourself, Mummy. I'll be in my room." She was shocked. Dadi said I'd become too proud. For weeks the house felt colder, and I felt selfish and scared.
But I stayed kind. I still made Dadi's evening tea and still sat with Mummy for her serials. I just didn't carry messages.
By Holi, they were talking to each other directly. Badly, but directly.

Since about what age had Tushar been the family peacemaker?
Since about eight.
How did Tushar feel in the weeks after stopping?
Tushar felt selfish and scared, with the house feeling colder and Dadi calling the change pride.
What helped the family adjust to Tushar's change?
Tushar stayed warm and steady, keeping the tea and the serials, while calmly refusing to carry messages.
How did Mummy react at first, and why?
Mummy was shocked, because losing the go-between meant she had to face Dadi directly for the first time.

messages.content: John decides to learn how to play the piano.  He buys a piano for $500.  He then hires a teacher for 20 lessons at $40 per lesson but ends up getting a 25% discount.  How much did everything cost?

The normal price of the lessons would be 20*40=$800
The discount saves him 800*.25=$200
So the lessons cost him 800-200=$600
That means everything costs 500+600=$1100
The answer is 1100.
How many straws and clay balls do you need to build a square pyramid?

Answer: 8 straws and 5 clay balls.

Make a square base: 4 straws, 4 balls. Put 1 ball high above the middle and join each bottom ball to it with a straw: 4 more straws. Straws 4 + 4 = 8 (edges), balls 4 + 1 = 5 (vertices). Let the child build it and count again.

Friday, 10:30 pm. Presentation day, Simran. When I finished the vendor pitch, the room clapped. Fast, loud, a couple of whistles, and I thought, yes! Then Rekha, my manager, clapped just twice, slowly, looking at her phone. I couldn't stop replaying it. Was it approval? Boredom? Rekha never claps much, and at last month's town hall she clapped the same way for the director's speech. Later she said, "The pricing slide was sharp. Send it to me?" So maybe it meant "I'm thinking," not "not good." Still, I wish I had asked instead of stewing all evening. Tomorrow I'll ask her directly.

How many times did Rekha clap?
Twice, slowly.
What was Simran feeling while replaying the applause?
Uneasy and unsure, since the room's loud clapping felt good but Rekha's slow two claps left Simran wondering.
What could Simran do to find out what Rekha thought?
Simran can ask Rekha directly for feedback, as planned for tomorrow.
How might Rekha see her own clapping?
Possibly as her usual style, since she claps the same way for the director's speech, and not as a sign of disapproval. 🙂

Mr. Resty has two identical 4-story buildings. The first floor has 2 apartment units while the rest of the floors have 5 apartment units on each floor. How many apartment units does Mr. Resty have in all?

In one building, there are 4 - 1 = 3 floors that have 5 apartment units each.
Mr. Resty has a total of 3 floors x 5 units = 15 apartment units from the 2nd to 4th floor in one building.
So, in one building, there are a total of 15 + 2 = 17 apartment units.
Therefore, Mr. Resty has a total of 17 x 2 = 34 apartment units in his 2 buildings.
The answer is 34.
James drives 30 mph for half an hour and then twice as long for twice the speed.  How far did he drive in total?

His first drive was 30*.5=15 miles
The next leg was .5*2=1 hour
The speed of the trip was 30*2=60 mph
So he drove 60*1=60 miles
So in total he drove 60+15=75 miles
The answer is 75.

Mary and Ann are going sledding. Mary slides down a hill that's 630 feet long at a speed of 90 feet/minute. Ann slides down a hill that's 800 feet long at a rate of 40 feet/minute. How much longer does Ann's trip take than Mary?

First find the total time Mary's trip takes: 630 feet / 90 feet/minute = 7 minutes
Then find the total time Ann's trip takes: 800 feet / 40 feet/minute = 20 minutes
Then subtract Mary's time from Ann's time to find the difference: 20 minutes - 7 minutes = 13 minutes
The answer is 13.
What do the players use as balls and mallets in the Queen's croquet game?
The balls are live hedgehogs and the mallets are live flamingoes. The soldiers bend over to make the arches.

In a kitchen in Lisbon, Clara puffed out her cheeks like a fish and let the air go with a pop. Her toddler Kaito stared. Then he filled his own cheeks, eyes wide with effort, and squeezed them with both palms until the air burst out. He laughed so hard that his cheeks rose high and round. Clara did it again, and Kaito copied her, this time getting it just right. “Fish face,” she said, and he lifted his chin, pleased.

Where did Clara puff out her cheeks?
In a kitchen in Lisbon.
What is Kaito feeling as he puffs his cheeks and laughs?
He is probably having fun and feeling proud of copying his mother, as the laughter and lifted chin suggest. It could also be that he simply likes the popping sensation.
What could Clara do to build on the game?
She could try other faces such as a big smile or a wide mouth and let Kaito copy each one. 😊
What might Clara notice about Kaito's growth from this game?
She might see that he controls his face better than before and that he wants to join her in play.

In the staff room of the Nashik public library, the new online review was on everyone's phone. "Staff are slow and the children's section is always messy. The young librarian, Lokesh, ignored me for ten minutes." It was signed Sarita K.

Below it, someone else had added: "Useless lazy people, shut it down."

Lokesh felt his throat tighten. He remembered the day: he'd been helping an elderly man with the catalogue.

"Reply and tell her she's lying," said a colleague.

Lokesh took a breath. "Part of it's fair. The children's section is messy."

He wrote: "Thank you, Sarita. We're sorry you waited. We're reorganising the children's section this month and adding a help bell at the desk." He didn't reply to the second comment.

Two weeks later, Sarita came back with her daughter and asked for Lokesh by name.

What did Lokesh say they would add at the desk?
Lokesh said they would add a help bell at the desk.
What was Lokesh feeling when he read the review?
Lokesh felt hurt and defensive, his throat tightening, since he remembered helping an elderly man at the time.
What did Lokesh do that turned the criticism into something useful?
He accepted the fair part about the messy children's section, replied calmly with changes, and ignored the abusive comment.
How might Sarita see the library after reading Lokesh's reply?
Sarita probably felt heard and respected, which is why she came back and asked for Lokesh by name.

"Mummy, the café in Bandra replied! They want a menu design."
"Wah, Rajni! How much are they paying?"
"They said… three thousand for the whole menu."
Her brother Vishal looked up from his phone. "Three thousand? What did you plan to ask?"
"I'd read that freelancers charge eight to ten for a menu. But now ten sounds greedy after three."
"So what are you going to say?"
"Maybe four? Four-five hundred?"
"Didi, your own research said eight."
"I know, but they said three first. If I say eight, they'll think I'm crazy."
Mummy put the tea down. "Beta, why is their number more real than yours?"
Rajni opened her mouth, then shut it. "I don't know."
"Try seven-five," said Vishal. "Explain why."
She typed "4,500," deleted it, and sat staring at the empty reply box.

How much did the café first offer Rajni for the whole menu?
Three thousand for the whole menu.
Why does ten thousand suddenly sound greedy to Rajni?
After hearing three thousand first, that number has become her reference point, so her own research figure now feels too big, even though she believes the research.
Mummy's question, "why is their number more real than yours?", is a turning point. What could Rajni do with it?
She could reply with a figure based on her research, such as seven-five, and explain what the work involves, instead of starting from the café's number.
How might Vishal feel watching his sister shrink her price?
He is probably frustrated and protective, since he can see she is underselling her work, which is why he pushes her to try seven-five.

Preschool note, Eid week

The yard was decorated with paper lanterns for the Eid party. Jeevan tripped on the steps and scraped his knee, and he cried out.
Yusuf was right next to him. He did not move. He stood with his arms stiff, screamed and cried even louder than Jeevan, eyes squeezed shut. He did not look at Jeevan's knee at all.
I cleaned Jeevan's knee while a helper held Yusuf. Once both were calm, Yusuf asked, "Is Jeevan broken?" and gave him the lantern he had made.

What did Jeevan trip on?
Jeevan tripped on the steps.
Why did Yusuf stand stiff and cry louder than Jeevan?
Yusuf was so frightened and upset by Jeevan's fall that his own distress took over, so he could not move to help.
What was a wise way for the adults to handle both children?
One adult cared for Jeevan's knee while a helper held Yusuf, so both got comfort, and later Yusuf could show his caring.
How might Jeevan feel when Yusuf gives him his lantern?
Jeevan might feel cared for and cheered up, seeing that his friend was worried about him.

Leave ten minutes early so you can arrive calmly.

At the school in Chennai the corridor was decorated for Pongal, and Class 9 was drawing kolams in the courtyard. Baljeet, fifteen, the only Sikh boy in the school, sat on the steps with his sketchbook. His family had moved from Ludhiana two years ago. At home, Gurpurab had just passed with nobody at school noticing.

Devika ma'am, the class teacher, sat down beside him. "Not drawing?"

"It's not my festival, ma'am."

She thought for a moment. "Would you draw the kolam with Selvi's group? And for Gurpurab next year, would you tell the class what your family does? I'd like to know too."

Selvi waved him over and handed him the chalk. "Make the middle. I'm bad at circles."

Baljeet was good at circles.

Where had Baljeet's family moved from?
His family had moved from Ludhiana two years ago.
How did Baljeet feel sitting on the steps?
Baljeet felt left out and a bit lonely, since his own festival had passed unnoticed and the Pongal fun felt like someone else's.
What small invitations helped Baljeet join in?
Devika ma'am's offer to join a kolam group and to share Gurpurab next year, and Selvi handing him the chalk.
How might Selvi feel when Baljeet draws the circle?
Selvi likely feels glad and impressed, since she is bad at circles and he is good at them.

Yash, you're checking your marks every Sunday? Good. Let me tell you what that did for me, back in my second year of college in Darjeeling, after I'd failed two papers. My roommate Pasang made me a simple chart on the back of an old calendar: attendance and quiz scores, every Sunday, against what I'd promised myself. "Tenzin, you have to look even when it's ugly," he said. For three Sundays the chart showed electronics stuck around 40, however many nights I sat alone with the book. On the fourth Sunday I finally admitted it: studying alone wasn't working. There was a group of four who met in the canteen after classes. I asked if I could join. Six weeks later, electronics was at 62. The chart didn't fix anything, Yash. It just stopped me lying to myself.

What did Pasang make?
A simple chart on the back of an old calendar.
How did Tenzin feel on the fourth Sunday?
Tenzin felt frustrated but honest, finally admitting that studying alone wasn't working.
What turning point in the story made the difference?
Choosing, after three flat Sundays, to ask the canteen group to join, instead of more nights alone with the book.
How did Pasang see the weekly chart?
Pasang saw it as a way to face the truth, insisting Tenzin look at it even when it was ugly.
