"Gurleen, you asked on your show why I started the song circle. I'm Nilesh, twenty-five. My Dadi knew over two hundred folk songs from our village near Bhilwara. Wedding songs, harvest songs, lullabies. When she died, I realised nobody had written them down. Most were gone. That hit me hard. So I went back and recorded every elder who still remembered anything. Sixty songs so far. Then I thought: recordings aren't enough. Songs live when kids sing them. Now every Sunday, twenty children come to the community hall and I teach them two songs. Last week, a nine-year-old taught her grandmother a song the grandmother had forgotten. The old lady cried. I cried too. That's why."

How many songs has Nilesh recorded so far?
Sixty songs.
How did Nilesh feel when realising Dadi's songs weren't written down?
Nilesh felt deeply saddened and shaken by the loss.
What makes Nilesh's approach effective for preserving heritage?
Recording elders and also teaching children weekly, so the songs are sung and passed on, not just stored.
How might the grandmother have felt when her granddaughter taught her the forgotten song?
She was moved to tears, likely feeling joy at recovering part of her past.

There is a very large room that has 4 tables, 1 sofa and 2 chairs that have 4 legs each.  There are also 3 tables with 3 legs each, 1 table with 1 leg, and 1 rocking chair with 2 legs.  How many legs are there in the room?

There are 4 tables, 1 sofa and 2 chairs that have 4 legs each so 4+1+2 =7 pieces of furniture
These 7 pieces have 4 legs each so they have 7*4 = 28 legs
There are 3 tables with 3 legs each so they have 3*3 = 9 legs
We have 28 legs and 9 legs as well a 1 leg on a table and 2 on a rocking chair for a total of 28+9+1+2 = 40 legs
The answer is 40.

At the Guwahati sports ground, Bhupen stood at the edge of the hockey field, gripping his stick. It was his first match with the club, and he hadn't moved from the sideline.
Shankar Sir walked over. "First match?"
Bhupen nodded, looking at his shoes.
"Come, let's hit a few balls in the corner before the whistle." They practised passing near the goal, just the two of them. Bhupen's shoulders loosened a bit.
"I'll put you in for the second half," Sir said. "Watch the first half, see how it goes."
By the second half, Bhupen ran onto the field. He didn't score, but he made a clean pass, and Sir gave him a thumbs-up.

Where did Bhupen and Shankar Sir practise before the match?
In the corner near the goal.
What was Bhupen feeling at the edge of the field?
He felt nervous and apprehensive about his first hockey match.
What did Shankar Sir do that helped Bhupen?
He let Bhupen practise in the corner and watch the first half, giving him a preview and time to settle.
How might Shankar Sir have felt seeing Bhupen's clean pass?
He probably felt pleased and proud that his patience helped Bhupen join in with confidence.

Chetan, you think paying someone to write your project report is fine because some people buy whole degrees. Your Hemant Mama thought exactly that. I was twenty, in my final year, and a man near the college gate wrote reports for a fee. My roommates said, 'Some people buy entire engineering degrees. A report is nothing.' So I paid. It felt small. Then came the interview for my first job. The engineer on the panel had read my report and asked me one question about the load calculations in chapter three. I didn't know them. I didn't know my own chapter. He closed the file and said, 'Whose standard are you living by?' I didn't get that job. I wrote every report myself after that, badly at first. So no, beta. Don't measure yourself against the worst person you've heard of.

What did the engineer on the panel ask about?
He asked about the load calculations in chapter three.
Why did paying for the report feel small to Hemant at the time?
Comparing it with people buying whole degrees made his shortcut seem minor, so he felt little guilt.
What turning point in the story changed Hemant's choices?
Failing to explain his own chapter in the interview and hearing 'Whose standard are you living by?', after which he wrote every report himself.
How might the engineer on the panel have seen Hemant?
The engineer probably saw a candidate whose report didn't match his understanding, which raised doubts about both his honesty and his skills.

Notes after Sunday lunch, for myself.
Lokesh Mama brought up the shares again. When he first bought into the mining company two years ago, he mentioned it once a month. Since the price fell, he talks about it every visit, louder each time. Today: 'Reena, you young people panic. Those who sell now are fools. I bought more last week. When it turns, you'll all see.' Mami looked at her plate. Each drop seems to make him more certain, not less. If he sold now, he'd have to admit he was wrong in front of everyone who warned him, and that seems to be the part he can't bear. I didn't argue. Walking him to the car, I said, 'Mama, you've read more about this than any of us. Would you go through it once with a proper financial adviser, just to see it from outside? I'll drive you.' He didn't answer, but he didn't say no.
Next step: find an adviser, and tell Mami.

What did Lokesh Mama say he did last week?
He said he bought more shares last week.
What did Reena notice and feel while listening at lunch?
Reena felt concerned, noticing that each price drop made Lokesh Mama more certain and louder, and sensing that admitting a mistake felt unbearable to him.
How did Reena offer a way to change course without humiliation?
Reena praised how much he had read and suggested seeing it 'from outside' with a qualified financial adviser, offering to drive, so reviewing it didn't mean losing face.
Why might Lokesh Mama buy more after each drop?
Selling would mean admitting in front of everyone that he was wrong, so buying more keeps his belief, and his pride, intact.

Every Sunday after breakfast, Ganga knelt by the bean pot on the balcony with a plastic ruler and a pencil. She measured from the soil to the tip and wrote in her notebook, along with the weather: 6 Jul, 9 cm, dry. 13 Jul, 12 cm, cloudy. 20 Jul, 19 cm, rain on Thursday. "That's a big jump," said her neighbour Alka, peeping through the railing. Ganga turned back a page. "It rained the week before too." She underlined both rainy weeks in blue. The pattern sat there on the page, plain as anything.

When did Ganga measure the bean plant?
She measured it every Sunday after breakfast.
What was Ganga feeling when she saw the pattern on the page?
Pleased and curious, since her notes showed something she could not have seen by looking.
What else could Ganga record to be more sure of the pattern, and why?
She could note how much water and sunshine the plant gets, so rain can be told apart from other changes.
How might Alka see Ganga's notebook?
Alka is probably impressed, since Alka noticed the big jump and watched Ganga check back through the pages.

In the library games club in Toronto, Rania saw Jin slip a captured checker back onto the board while she reached for her juice. Heat rushed to her face. She wanted to shout "Cheater!" and sweep the board off the table. She even thought about sneaking a piece back herself. Instead she pressed her palms to her knees, counted five slow breaths, and walked to the volunteer at the desk. "Excuse me, I think a piece was moved back. Can you come and look?" Her voice shook a little. The volunteer came over, asked both players calmly what happened and reset the game. Rania felt the anger cool, though her heart still thumped.

What did Rania see Jin do?
She saw Jin slip a captured checker back onto the board while she reached for her juice.
What was Rania feeling, and what did she consider doing before she asked for help?
She was furious: she wanted to shout "Cheater!", sweep the board off the table, or sneak a piece back herself.
Why was asking the volunteer wiser than cheating back?
Cheating back would turn her into the same thing, while a calm report let an adult sort it out.
How might Jin feel when the volunteer asks what happened?
Probably nervous or embarrassed at being found out, and Jin may wonder what will happen next.

Pranav ran to his friend Isha in the housing society park with his arms out, then stopped. His mother Kavitha had been teaching him to ask first. “Isha, can I hug you?” Isha shook her head. “No, I'm sweaty.” Pranav's arms dropped. He looked at Kavitha. She nodded. “You asked, and she said no. What else can you do?” Pranav thought. “Wave?” He waved. Isha waved back and grabbed his hand. “Come, let's go to the seesaw!”

Why did Isha say no to a hug?
Because she was sweaty.
What was Pranav feeling when his arms dropped?
He felt a bit disappointed and unsure what to do after Isha said no. Looking at Kavitha shows he wanted help.
How did Kavitha help Pranav handle the no?
She named what happened and asked what else he could do, so he found the wave himself.
How might Isha see Pranav asking first?
She likely feels respected and comfortable, since she could say no and still play with him.

At breakfast Simran, Jahnavi's mother, was late for work and chased her toddler round the kitchen with a spoon. "One more bite or the doctor will come," she said. Jahnavi clamped her mouth shut, screamed and pushed the bowl. Simran caught herself, put the spoon down and breathed out.

At lunch it was Bhupen's turn. Jahnavi shook her head at the dal and flung a fistful of rice onto the floor. Bhupen did not raise his voice. He set down two small bowls, one with banana and one with curd, and said, "You pick." She looked at both, pointed at the banana and ate it, smearing it up to her ears. When she pushed the curd away, he said, "Okay, later then," and went on with his own plate.

In the evening the whole family sat on the mat with the phones in another room. Jahnavi climbed into Simran's lap. Bhupen tore off a piece of roti and dipped it into the rice, and she opened her mouth like a bird. Then she took her own small piece, copied his chewing and grinned around it.

What did Bhupen offer Jahnavi at lunch?
He offered two small bowls, one with banana and one with curd.
How did the breakfast with the spoon differ from the lunch with two bowls and the evening on the mat?

At breakfast Simran chased Jahnavi and threatened her with the doctor, so Jahnavi screamed and clamped her mouth shut. At lunch Bhupen offered a choice and stayed calm, and in the evening the shared meal in Simran's lap felt loving, so Jahnavi ate and copied.
What does Jahnavi's screaming and pushing the bowl away at breakfast suggest she felt?
It suggests she felt scared and pressured by the chasing and the threat, so food became a fight.
What could Simran try at breakfast on a rushed morning instead of chasing?
She could offer a small choice, sit down and eat beside Jahnavi, and let her stop when she has had enough, trusting hunger to do its work.

In Buenos Aires, on a Tuesday, Esther sent Lucia a message: "Why did you laugh when Señora Paz read my poem out? That really hurt."

Lucia, sixteen, saw the notification on the bus. She hadn't been laughing at the poem. She'd been laughing at something Tomás whispered. But explaining that felt like making an excuse, and saying sorry felt like admitting she'd meant it. So she didn't open it.

Wednesday, she sat at the back in literature. Thursday, she skipped the bakery where they always met after school. Every time her phone buzzed, her stomach dropped.

By Sunday it wasn't only about the poem. It was about the laugh, and five days of acting as if Esther didn't exist. The reply she needed was now a paragraph, not a line. She typed, deleted, typed again, and lay awake with the phone on her chest.

What had Lucia actually been laughing at?
She'd been laughing at something Tomás whispered.
Why did not opening the message feel easier to Lucia than answering it?
Both possible answers felt bad: explaining seemed like an excuse, and saying sorry seemed like admitting she'd meant it. Leaving it unread let her avoid choosing, at least for a while.
What would you advise Lucia to do now that the reply has grown?
Send a short, honest message soon, owning the silence first and then explaining the laugh, and ask to meet at the bakery. It doesn't need to be a perfect paragraph.
If you were Esther, what would you want from Lucia at this point?
Probably just to be acknowledged: to hear that Lucia saw the message and cares that it hurt. Five days of nothing may have hurt as much as the laugh did.
For Diwali, Dadi puts 10 diyas in 2 rows of 5. She lights all the diyas in the top row. How many diyas are lit? How many are not lit yet?

Answer: 5 are lit and 5 are not lit.

One full row is 5, and the other row is 5 more: 5 and 5 make 10. Five is exactly half of a ten-frame. Let the child light (or colour) the next diya: now 6 are lit, 4 are not.

Wednesday: her sister Deepika said, "Fold, draw, write, colour." Sarita tried it slowly.
Saturday: Sarita made a card for her friend alone. Fold. Cake. Name inside. Colours last. It was neat. She held it up, beaming.

What happened on Monday when Sarita coloured first?
The colours smudged across the fold.
What was Sarita feeling when she held the card up on Saturday?
She was proud and happy with her neat card.
What else could Sarita add to her steps?
A message inside before colouring, so the card says something special.
How does the change look to Deepika?
Deepika is probably pleased her steps helped.

I work at the same desk as Ujjwal, and I've always teased him about his travel folder. Before every work trip, he prints his tickets, keeps a photocopy of his ID, and writes the hotel address and three phone numbers on a card. Last month we flew to Kolkata together for a client meeting. At the airport, Mahima, our manager, found her phone had been stolen. No boarding pass, no contacts. She looked panicked. Ujjwal calmly pulled out his folder: he had the booking reference for all three of us and the hotel's number. The airline reprinted her pass. I can't say what Ujjwal felt, but he looked completely steady. I've started my own folder.

What did Ujjwal write on his card?
The hotel address and three phone numbers.
How did Ujjwal seem during the airport problem?
He looked completely steady and calm, unbothered by the stolen phone.
How did Ujjwal's preparation turn a crisis into an inconvenience?
Keeping printed tickets, booking references and contacts in a folder meant the airline could reprint Mahima's pass quickly.
How did Mahima feel when she found her phone had been stolen?
Mahima looked panicked, losing her boarding pass and contacts at once.

Each kite needs 5 metres of string. How many metres do 6 kites need?

1. A visitor is a person who comes to see you or a place.
2. It is 30. Because 6 x 5 = 30.
We ran out sugar, so I went to the shop. What is missing?

We ran out of sugar, so I went to the shop.

At the threshing floor near Kolhapur, the story of the snake came up again. Darshan swore it had been a black cobra, hood spread, right beside his foot. Their cousin Pooja was just as certain it had been a brown rat snake that slid away into the sugarcane. Both had been terrified that day, and both were raising their voices now. Sahil, twenty, had been standing a few feet behind them when it happened. He remembered the shout, the scramble, and honestly not much else. Watching them, he noticed that the more upset each got, the surer they sounded. "You were both scared out of your skins," he said. "That makes it feel sharp. It doesn't make it right." Darshan laughed despite himself. Pooja still insisted on brown. Nobody would ever know, Sahil thought, and that was all right.

What did Darshan say the snake was?
A black cobra, hood spread, right beside his foot.
What did Sahil feel as he watched them argue?
Sahil felt calm and a little amused, noticing that the more upset each cousin got, the surer each sounded.
What did Sahil say, and why is it a helpful way to cool the argument?
That being scared makes a memory feel sharp but doesn't make it right, which lets both keep their feelings without anyone winning on details.
How did Darshan react to Sahil's comment?
Darshan laughed despite himself, easing the tension.

Supervisor's note, internship programme, week 6. Hrithik

Tejas had a brilliant Monday: the client loved the prototype and the whole team cheered. By Tuesday evening Tejas had volunteered for the weekend hackathon, offered to redo the onboarding slides, agreed to mentor two first-years, and planned to cycle to the office on the flooded route "because it'll be fine".
I asked how the college assignments due Friday fit in. A long pause. "Oh. I forgot those."
Nothing is wrong with enthusiasm, and the good mood was earned. But the yeses came faster than the checking.
What I did next: sat with Tejas and listed every commitment with its hours. Tejas dropped the slides and the hackathon, kept one mentee, and took the bus. We agreed on a rule: sleep on any new yes.

How many first-years did Tejas agree to mentor?
Two first-years.
Why did the flooded cycle route seem fine to Tejas?
After the client loved the prototype, Tejas felt on top of the world, and that glow made risks look small and every yes feel easy.
What rule did they agree on, and why does it help?
Sleep on any new yes; a night's pause lets the checking catch up with the good mood.
How does Hrithik view Tejas's burst of yeses?
Hrithik sees the enthusiasm as earned and welcome, but worries the commitments outran the checking, especially with assignments due Friday.

Harsha burst into the flat. "Papa! A lion came into the colony and I chased it away with my stick! It roared SO loud!"

"A lion! Brave you." Tarun then noticed a red scratch on his son's hand. "And what's this?"

"The lion scratched me."

Tarun knelt down. "That's a fantastic lion story. Now I need the real story, because of the scratch. What really scratched you?"

Harsha looked at the scratch. "The cat from the ground floor. I pulled its tail."

"Thank you. Let's wash it. And cats don't like tails pulled."

What really scratched Harsha?
The cat from the ground floor.
What was Harsha feeling while telling the lion story?
He was most likely excited and proud, enjoying making the adventure bigger. When asked what really happened, he may have felt a little sheepish about pulling the tail.
How did Tarun separate pretend from real without harsh labels?
He enjoyed the lion story, then explained he needed the real story because of the scratch, so facts mattered without calling Harsha a liar.
What would change if Tarun had said, "Stop lying"?
Harsha might have felt ashamed and been less willing to tell the true story about the scratch.

Sit, Nirmala, I'll tell you about my Class 5, back in Madurai. I'm your Yamini Paati now, but then I was a skinny girl of nine with two plaits. Our new teacher, Mr Joseph, didn't write rules on the board. He asked us, "What makes a class good to be in?" Selvi said, "Nobody laughs when you're wrong." Raghu said, "Let people finish talking." We argued about "no shouting" for ten whole minutes! Then all thirty-two of us signed the chart in our own handwriting. Funny thing: when Raghu himself interrupted one day, it was tiny Selvi who pointed at the chart, and he stopped. Nobody ever obeyed the old teacher's rules like that. These were ours, you see.

How many children signed the chart?
All thirty-two of them signed the chart in their own handwriting.
How can you tell young Yamini felt proud of the class rules?
She still remembers the ten-minute argument and says the rules "were ours", which shows pride and a sense of ownership.
Which choice of Mr Joseph's was the turning point, and why?
He asked the class what makes a good class instead of writing rules himself, so the children owned the rules and followed them willingly.
Why might Raghu have stopped when Selvi pointed at the chart?
Raghu had helped make the rule about letting people finish, so a reminder from a classmate felt fair rather than like a telling-off from above.

"They gave it to Karan," Nikita said, dropping into the chair by Rajni's desk. "The senior designer post. Karan. Who copied my layout for the bank campaign."

"Oh, Nikki."

"I'm going to Sunil sir's cabin right now and telling him exactly what I think. In front of everyone."

Rajni put a hand on her arm. "Don't. Not now. You're shaking."

"I am so angry I could scream."

"I know. Walk with me to the chai stall first. Then decide."

They walked. By the second cup, Nikita's hands were steady. "Fine. What do I do?"

"Write down the facts. Your projects, the bank campaign dates, the client emails. Then ask Sunil sir for a private meeting and ask how they decided."

"And if the answer's rubbish?"

"Then you decide whether this is still the place for you. Calmly."

Nikita nodded. That evening she booked a Thursday meeting with Sunil sir and made a folder called "Facts".

Who got the senior designer post?
Karan got the senior designer post.
How did Nikita feel when she came to Rajni's desk?
Nikita felt burning anger, shaking and ready to confront their manager publicly.
What steps did Rajni suggest, and why were they wise?
Let the first surge pass, collect the facts, ask the manager privately how they decided, and then calmly decide whether to stay, because a public outburst rarely helps.
How does Rajni see Nikita's plan to confront Sunil sir in public?
Rajni sees it as a risky reaction driven by anger, and worries it would hurt Nikita.

In the staff room of the city hospital pharmacy, Deepika and Nilesh had a running joke: whoever lost the lunchtime crossword bought the evening tea. They had been close since induction.
Then the chief pharmacist asked Deepika to draw up the Diwali-week roster. Nilesh leaned over her shoulder. "You'll give me the day shift, na? My sister's coming."
Deepika laughed but covered the sheet with her hand. "Put in a request like everyone else. I'm going by the dates they came in."
He went quiet for the rest of lunch. That evening she found him at the tea stall.
"I'm not being cold. If I bend it for you, Rinku and the others will notice, and then we're the pair who get favours."
Nilesh sighed, then grinned. "Fine. But you're buying the tea."

What did the chief pharmacist ask Deepika to do?
Draw up the Diwali-week roster.
What does Deepika covering the sheet with her hand suggest?
It suggests she feels awkward and protective, wanting to keep the friendship warm without letting it bend the roster.
Why did Deepika go to find Nilesh at the tea stall?
To explain her reason calmly so the quiet lunch did not harden into resentment; clearing it up quickly helped the friendship survive the disagreement.
How might Nilesh see Deepika's refusal at first?
He probably feels hurt and let down, since they are close, until her point about fairness makes sense and he can joke again.

For two weeks Emil's nightmares had woken the whole Seville flat three or four times a night. On Thursday morning Emil couldn't find his left shoe. "Every single day!" Javier barked, and slammed the cupboard. Emil stood very still. On the bus, Javier replayed it and his stomach turned. That night he told his husband, Marco, "I'm not angry at Emil. I'm just empty." They agreed to take turns, and Marco handled Friday's wake-ups while Javier slept in the spare room. On Saturday, Javier knelt to tie Emil's shoes and said sorry.

What could Emil not find on Thursday morning?
His left shoe.
What was Javier feeling on the bus?
He felt guilty and upset with himself; his stomach turned as he replayed barking at Emil.
Which plan helped, and why?
Taking turns with the night wake-ups, so Javier finally got proper rest; sleep, not trying harder, gave him back his patience.
How was Emil affected when Javier barked?
Emil was startled and scared, standing very still after the cupboard slammed.

metadata.subtype: Parents worn down by broken nights [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Payal, can I tell you something I am not proud of? I am Jeevan, remember, the one who said everything was "fine". In our final-year team Arjun did hardly any of the lab reports. Everybody knew. But Arjun is the guy who brought all of us tiffin when we were stuck in the lab till midnight, so nobody wanted to be the one to say it. Meena did Arjun's share twice. I saw her face fall each time and said nothing. Six weeks in, the four of us barely spoke at lunch, and the tension was so thick you could cut it. It was not fine, and I knew.

How many times did Meena do Arjun's share?
Meena did Arjun's share twice.
Why did nobody want to say anything about Arjun's missing work?
They liked Arjun for bringing tiffin during late nights and feared spoiling the friendship; loyalty and awkwardness kept the group silent.
What could Jeevan have done the first time Meena's face fell?
Jeevan could have checked with Meena privately, then raised the imbalance kindly with Arjun, before the silence grew into tension.
What might Meena have been feeling when doing Arjun's share and no one spoke up?
Meena probably felt tired, unappreciated and a bit invisible; the fallen face shows hurt at the silence of the others.
What was I doing at five o'clock yesterday?
I don't know what you were doing at five o'clock yesterday, as I only see what you write here. Your diary, phone history or family may help you remember.

"I am going," she said again, in a gentler voice, "to be married to him. The preparations for my marriage are making, and I shall be married soon. Why do you injuriously introduce the name of my mother by adoption? It is my own act."

What does she tell the speaker about her marriage?
She says she is going to be married to him, that the preparations are being made and that she will be married soon. She says it is her own act.

Dear Shreya Ma'am,
I've been carrying something for five weeks, and I can't any more.
In October my friend Nikhil told me he was hurting himself, and made me swear not to tell. I kept the secret because I thought if I told, he'd never trust me again, and he'd have nobody. So I checked on him every night. I stopped going to football so I'd always be free if he called.
I'm not sleeping. I jump every time my phone buzzes. And Nikhil isn't better. I think he's worse, and all this time the only person who knew was me.
I know now that this is too big for me. Please help him. I'll come to your room at lunch.
Tanvir, 10A

Reply, 11:05 am:
Tanvir, thank you for telling me. You are not in trouble, and you did the right thing. I have called Nikhil in now and I am contacting his parents this morning. Come at lunch; we'll talk about how you are, too.
Shreya Ma'am

How long had Tanvir kept the secret?
Five weeks.
What made Tanvir keep the secret for so long?
Tanvir was afraid of losing Nikhil's trust and worried that telling would leave Nikhil with nobody.
What would have helped more back in October?
Telling Shreya Ma'am or a parent straight away, so Nikhil got real care weeks sooner and Tanvir wasn't carrying it alone.
How might Shreya Ma'am see Tanvir's letter?
Shreya Ma'am sees a frightened student who finally reached out, and acts at once for Nikhil while also caring for Tanvir.

messages.content:
Read this:

When the Mumbai offer came, I was twenty-two and I didn't tell my parents for two weeks. I'm Tanuja, the eldest daughter; in our house in Nagpur I handled Aai's medicines, Baba's bank work, my brother's forms.
My friend Parveen said, "You're allowed to go." But I kept thinking: if I leave, I'm betraying them. If I stay, I'm betraying myself.
Finally I sat with Aai and Baba. I told them the truth: I wanted the job, and I was scared of leaving them with everything.
Baba was quiet, then said, "We didn't raise you to hold the house forever." Aai cried a little, then made a list of what my brother could learn to do.
We made a plan. I taught my brother the bank work. A neighbour agreed to help Aai with the clinic visits. I went home every second weekend.
Looking back, it wasn't selfish to go. Hiding it was the only unfair part.

How long did Tanuja wait before telling her parents about the offer?
Tanuja didn't tell her parents for two weeks.
How did Tanuja feel about leaving?
Tanuja felt torn, afraid of betraying her parents if she left and betraying herself if she stayed.
What made the move work for the family?
Honest talk and a shared plan, teaching her brother the bank work, a neighbour helping Aai, and regular visits home.
How might Parveen see Tanuja's worry?
Parveen sees that Tanuja is allowed to go and seems to want her friend to choose her own growth without guilt.

Read this:

From Pankaj's Amma's notebook, Sunday.
At the park, Pankaj fell off the low wall and scraped his knee. He ran to me shouting "Amma!", crying hard. I held him, blew on the scrape and said, "That hurt, na." Soon his crying slowed. He looked at the knee, then ran back to the swings.
At bedtime he said, "Amma, Rukmini in my class pulls my bag every day. I don't like it."
I thanked him for telling me. Tomorrow I'll speak to his teacher.

What happened to Pankaj at the park?
He fell off the low wall and scraped his knee.
How did Pankaj feel when he fell, and what helped?
He was hurt and upset, crying hard, and being held and hearing "That hurt, na" helped him calm down.
What did Amma do well at bedtime?
She thanked Pankaj for telling her about Rukmini and planned to speak to his teacher, so he learns telling is safe.
What would change if Amma had scolded Pankaj for crying at the park?
He might learn that showing hurt brings blame, and he might keep problems like the bag-pulling to himself instead of telling her.

metadata.subtype: Child who seeks comfort and returns to play [Actor]

messages.content: Wickham is throwing a huge Christmas party. He invites 30 people. Everyone attends the party, and half of the guests bring a plus one (one other person). He plans to serve a 3-course meal for the guests. If he uses a new plate for every course, how many plates does he need in total for his guests?

The number of guests that bring a plus one is 30 / 2 = 15 guests
The total number of guests at the party, including the plus ones, is 30 + 15 = 45 guests
Since there are 3 courses, Wickham will need 45 * 3 = 135 plates
The answer is 135.

What does Pip think about the stars outside the kitchen door?

At those times I would get up and look out at the door; for our kitchen door opened at once upon the night, and stood open on summer evenings to air the room. The very stars to which I then raised my eyes, I am afraid I took to be but poor and humble stars for glittering on the rustic objects among which I had passed my life.
He took them to be poor, humble stars, fit only for shining on the plain country things around him. This shows he had started to look down on his simple home.

'Okay, I'm the external examiner. I'm grumpy and I skipped breakfast,' Pooja said, folding her arms. 'Question one. Why did you choose only two hospitals?'
Lokesh cleared his throat. 'Time and access. Two gave us permission.'
'Hm. Question two. How do you know the nurses answered honestly?'
'The survey was anonymous.' He scribbled the answer on his notepad.
'Three. What would change with ten hospitals?'
'Um...' He stopped. 'I don't know. More variety?'
'That's weak.'
'I know.' He wrote 'Q3 – read about sample size' and circled it.
Question four was about his graph's scale; he answered fine. Five, about costs, stumped him again. Another circle.
'Five questions, two circles,' Pooja said, unfolding her arms. 'Better than I expected.'
'Library tonight, then. For the circles.'

Why did Lokesh choose only two hospitals?
Time and access. Two gave us permission.
How did Lokesh feel when he couldn't answer question three?
He felt stuck and a little embarrassed, admitting it was weak, but calm enough to note it for more reading.
What else could Lokesh do with the circled questions?
Read up on them tonight and try the answers aloud to Pooja again tomorrow.
How does playing the examiner feel for Pooja?
Pooja enjoys being grumpy and tough, and is pleasantly surprised that only two questions stumped Lokesh.

messages.content:
Read this:

Team lead's note, quarterly review, sales support team.
Mridul is efficient and fair in dealings; no one complains of being shortchanged. But I've noticed a pattern. When Pradeep was drowning in client calls during audit week, Mridul said, 'I'll take two if you take my Friday reports.' Pradeep agreed, relieved, but later told me he felt he was buying help. At team lunches Mridul tracks who paid last time, down to the rupee. The work is solid, yet no one on the team goes to Mridul with a problem. Next step: I shared this in our one-to-one, without blame, and asked Mridul to pair with the new joiner for a month with no swaps involved. Mridul looked surprised, asked, 'What's in it for me?', then laughed and agreed to try.

What did Mridul offer when Pradeep was drowning in client calls?
'I'll take two if you take my Friday reports.'
What might Mridul have felt when the team lead raised the pattern?
Mridul seemed surprised and a little defensive, asking what was in it for Mridul, before laughing and agreeing to try.
Why is pairing Mridul with the new joiner with no swaps a useful step?
It gives Mridul a chance to feel what helping without a ledger is like, which can build the trust the team currently lacks.
How did Pradeep experience the swap?
Pradeep was relieved to get help but felt as if he were buying it, which made the help feel cold.

On the verandah of the kasba house Manoj wailed for a biscuit. Uday, Manoj's father, held out a banana instead and waited. Manoj cried harder, then sniffed, went quiet and looked at the banana for a long moment. Both small hands reached out, took it and pushed it toward the mouth. Uday peeled the top for Manoj and said nothing at all. 😊

What did Uday hold out instead of a biscuit?
Uday held out a banana.
What was Manoj feeling while crying for the biscuit, and what changed?
Manoj was sad and disappointed, but hunger and a long look at the banana shifted Manoj toward accepting it.
What could Manoj try next time to get the food wanted, and why?
Manoj could say "biscuit, please" and point at the tin before crying, because asking clearly gives Uday a chance to choose.
How does Uday see the moment Manoj takes the banana?
Uday is relieved and quietly pleased that Manoj took some food, and stays silent so that the choice remains Manoj's.

Read this:

Eight in the morning on Ward 4 of the district hospital, and Arnab had ten minutes to hand over twelve patients to Tanuja before his night shift ended. His first instinct was to pour out everything he'd seen all night, bed by bed. But he'd watched handovers where the one thing that mattered got lost in the pile. So he started with the headline. "Two to watch closely: Bed 3, fever came back at five, the doctor knows; Bed 9, very confused overnight, family coming at ten. Everyone else is stable." Tanuja wrote the two bed numbers at the top of her sheet. Then Arnab went through the rest briefly. When he said "NBM for Bed 6," he noticed the new trainee beside Tanuja frowning. "Nil by mouth," he added. "No food or drink before the scan." The trainee nodded, relieved. At 8:10 Arnab signed off, and Tanuja already knew where to walk first.

How many patients did Arnab hand over?
Twelve patients.
What might the new trainee have felt when Arnab said 'NBM'?
The trainee felt confused, frowning at the jargon, and then relieved once Arnab explained it meant nil by mouth.
Why did Arnab start with the two patients to watch?
Leading with the headline made sure the most important information didn't get lost in a long list, so Tanuja knew where to go first.
How did Tanuja benefit from the way Arnab handed over?
She could write the two key bed numbers at the top and walk straight to them, starting her shift clear and prepared.

What is the exact height of the tallest tree in the world to the nearest centimetre? Also, what is the meaning of heedful? Oh, and why do we use an alarm clock? Then, how can I make friends with a classmate who is shy? And one more: fix my grammar: He don't like to wake up early.

1. I don't know the exact number to the nearest centimetre, because measurements change as trees grow and are checked again. Look at a trusted science website for the latest measurement.
2. Heedful is an adjective that means paying careful attention.
3. An alarm wakes you at the hour you chose. Because sleeping people cannot notice time passing, a loud sound is needed to wake them.
4. Smile, say hello and ask a gentle question. Give them time, and invite them to join a small group activity.
5. Fixed: He doesn't like to wake up early. Why: with "he", the helper verb is "doesn't".
Does heroism need a big act, like saving a life?

No. Heroism is great courage and goodness in difficult moments, and it can be small too. It is a noun.
Example: The firefighter was praised for his heroism in the flood.

(1) I don't understand "immutable". Can you help?
(2) Spot the error: I am going to buy a new furnitures.
(3) Please correct: The boys has eaten all the biscuits.
(4) What does "left in the dark" mean?
(5) What's the meaning of the word determine?

1. Immutable is an adjective that means never changing.
2. It should be: I am going to buy new furniture. Why: "furniture" is uncountable, so it has no "a" and no plural "s".
3. Better: The boys have eaten all the biscuits. Why: "boys" is plural, so it takes "have".
4. It means not told about something. For example: the students were left in the dark about the new rule.
5. Determine means to find out or decide something firmly. It is a verb.

I'm Nazia, and it took me a whole semester to see the pattern. Bidisha called at odd hours: the night before submissions for my notes, before a trip for my cousin's contact at a travel agency, on the fifteenth for a small loan. When I had nothing to give, her messages went quiet. I said yes every time because I was scared she'd stop liking me, and I even bought her coffee to keep things warm.

One evening I noticed I felt used, and also that I still cared about her. So I did something small. "I'll share my notes today, but I can't do it every time. And I'd love to just hang out sometime with no favours." She looked surprised. "Oh. I didn't realise." We're not as close as before, but I help when I want to, and it feels cleaner.

What did Bidisha ask for before a trip?
Nazia's cousin's contact at a travel agency.
Why did Nazia keep saying yes at first?
Out of fear that Bidisha would stop liking Nazia, so Nazia even bought coffee to keep things warm.
What limit did Nazia set, and how did it help?
Nazia offered notes that day, said it could not be every time, and invited a no-favours hangout. It was clear without bitterness.
How might Bidisha have seen the pattern?
Possibly without noticing it. Bidisha's "Oh. I didn't realise" suggests surprise rather than deliberate use.

messages.content: Online order galat aaya. Email mein likha: 'I ordered blue shirt but you have sended red.' Fix karo.

Corrected: "I ordered a blue shirt, but I received a red one." The past of "send" is "sent", not "sended". Saying what you received also sounds more polite than "you sent". Add your order number so they can help you quickly.
Brady gets paid 70 cents for each recipe card he transcribes. He also gets a 10 dollar bonus each time he transcribes 100 cards. If he transcribes 200 cards how much will he earn including bonuses?

For 200 cards he earns .70*200=140 dollars
Since he transcribes 200 cards his bonus is 10*2=20 dollars
In total he earns 140+20=160 dollars
The answer is 160.
What's the best way to clean a really dirty stove top?
Let it cool fully first. Soak a cloth in warm soapy water and leave it on the dirty parts for ten minutes to soften the grease. Then scrub with a sponge and wipe it dry.
Some spots are burnt on.
Make a paste with baking soda and a little water, spread it on the burnt spots and leave it for a while. Then scrub gently. Avoid sharp tools that might scratch the surface.

Gurpreet: sorry to message so late. I'm sitting in my car outside the flat crying and I can't make myself go up
Yogesh: hey. no sorry needed. I'm here
Yogesh: do you want to tell me what happened, or should I just keep you company for a bit?

Gurpreet: yes please

Who got Gurpreet's promotion?
The new guy, whom Gurpreet trained.
What was Gurpreet feeling in the car?
Gurpreet felt hurt and upset, unable to face going up, and also dismissed by colleagues who said 'don't be upset'.
How did Yogesh support Gurpreet?
Yogesh didn't rush, asked whether Gurpreet wanted to talk or just company, accepted the tears as natural, and offered to come over with chai.
How might Gurpreet's colleagues have come across by saying 'don't be upset'?
They probably meant well but made Gurpreet feel dramatic, as if the tears were the problem rather than the lost promotion.

Thunder rumbled over the hills, and Miss D'Souza had said ten minutes, then everyone on the bus. At the old fort wall, Joel's group was daring the girls to climb to the broken turret and touch the flagpole. "Two minutes, easy," he said. "Elizabeth goes first." Elizabeth's hands were cold. The stones were already wet with the first drops. She glanced at Parul, who was twisting her dupatta round and round one finger. "You don't want to either, do you?" Elizabeth whispered. Parul shook her head. Elizabeth took her hand. "We're not climbing," she said out loud. "Me neither," said Parul. There was a pause. Then another girl stepped back too, and Joel shrugged. "Fine. It's raining anyway." They ran for the bus.

How long had Miss D'Souza given the class before the bus?
She had given them ten minutes.
What was Elizabeth feeling before she whispered to Parul?
She felt nervous and uneasy, with cold hands, and hoped she wasn't the only one who didn't want to climb.
Why did saying no together work better than Elizabeth refusing alone?
Once two voices said no, the dare lost its pull: another girl stepped back and Joel dropped it.
How might Parul feel when Elizabeth takes her hand?
Parul likely feels relieved and braver, because someone has noticed the worry she was showing with her dupatta 🤍.

Bhavna, you got into the college you wanted and now you feel empty? Let your Ankita Mausi tell you about 1998. I was nineteen and had dreamt of the medical college in Nagpur since I was a child. For two years I studied from dawn. When I got the seat, I was the happiest girl in the town. Then, a month into classes, I sat on the hostel steps one evening and couldn't remember why I had wanted it so much. I wasn't sad. Just tired, as if a string pulling me had been cut. My roommate found me there and said, 'You finished one race. You haven't picked the next one yet.' So I picked one. I wanted to work in villages. That became the new string. It took a while, beta.

How old was Ankita when she got the medical college seat?
Nineteen.
How did Ankita feel on the hostel steps that evening?
Ankita felt tired and empty, not sad, as if a string pulling her had been cut.
Which choice inside the story helped Ankita move on?
Choosing a new goal, working in villages, which gave her direction again after her roommate's words.
How might the roommate have seen Ankita that evening?
The roommate seems to have understood her mood kindly, seeing it as the pause after finishing one race.

messages.content:
Read this:

Chetan, your parents told me you've been asking questions about the puja, and that they're frightened. Sit. I'm Saurabh, and I was twenty once.

I stopped joining the evening aarti and one day said, "Why waste an hour on this?" My mother's face fell. My father went silent. Later I heard her tell a neighbour, "We've lost him."

That hurt. That night I sat with her and said, "Amma, I love you. I'm not leaving anything. I just have questions." I still ate the prasad she handed me. A week later I asked my father, gently, what the aarti gave him.

He said, "It's how my mother sat with me." We never agreed on everything. But after that, nobody in the house was afraid.

What did Saurabh's mother say to a neighbour?
She said, "We've lost him."
What were Saurabh's parents feeling when he stopped joining the aarti?
They were afraid: his mother's face fell and she told a neighbour they had lost him, while his father went silent.
What did Saurabh do that eased the fear, and what else could Chetan try?
Saurabh told his mother he loved her and only had questions, ate the prasad, and asked his father gently what the aarti gave him; Chetan could share questions the same gentle way. 🙂
What might the aarti mean to Saurabh's father?
It seems to be a memory and a closeness, since he said it is how his mother sat with him, not a challenge to Saurabh.

Read this:

Last Diwali holidays my small cousin Kunal came to stay with us in Indore. He is six and has a stammer. On the second evening, three boys from the next building copied him outside the gate: 'K-k-k-Kunal!' He froze with his sparkler box, face crumpling. My blood went hot. I'm Ganga, and part of me wanted to shove the biggest boy into the drain. Instead I walked over and stood right beside Kunal, my hand on his shoulder. 'He's my cousin. Stop it,' I said, as steadily as I could. One boy laughed and started again. So I said, 'Fine, I'm calling my uncle,' and shouted for Chacha from the gate. Chacha came down at once, and the boys left. Kunal held my hand all evening.

What was Kunal holding when the boys teased him?
His sparkler box.
What did Ganga feel when the boys copied Kunal?
Angry and protective; Ganga's blood went hot, and part of Ganga wanted to shove the biggest boy.
Which steps did Ganga take instead of fighting?
Standing beside Kunal, speaking steadily, and calling Chacha when the teasing continued.
How might Kunal have felt with Ganga beside him?
Safer and less alone; he held Ganga's hand all evening.

Toddler room note, Tuesday.
Bhavna (18 months) woke from her nap crying hard. We checked: not hungry, not wet, no fever. She kept crying. Anand, our new carer, picked her up, held her against his shoulder and spoke very softly: "I've got you, I've got you." He swayed slowly. After two minutes, she went quiet, sucked her thumb and rested her head on him.
We never found out what upset her. It didn't seem to matter.
I told her mother at pickup.

What did Anand say to Bhavna?
'I've got you, I've got you.'
How can you tell Bhavna felt comforted?
She went quiet, sucked her thumb and rested her head on Anand.
What did Anand do that calmed Bhavna?
He held her close, spoke softly and swayed, offering presence without needing to fix anything.
How might Anand feel when Bhavna rested her head on him?
He probably felt warm and relieved that she was comforted.

In the small town, Urmila had started watching short videos after work to relax. The feed kept showing her angrier and angrier clips: people fighting, shouting about politics, scary news.
She felt tense and couldn't sleep. But she kept scrolling.
Her friend Pradeep, who ran the cyber café, said, "The app shows you what keeps you watching. Anger keeps people watching."
"So it's not showing me the world?"
"It's showing you what works on you."
Urmila went home and pressed "not interested" on the angry videos. She followed a few cooking and farming channels and turned off autoplay.
A week later she said, "My feed is boring now. I sleep better."

Who ran the cyber café?
Pradeep.
What was Urmila feeling while watching the angry videos?
Urmila felt tense and anxious, unable to sleep.
What steps did Urmila take to curate her feed?
She marked angry videos "not interested," followed calmer channels and turned off autoplay.
How does Pradeep see the recommendation feed?
Pradeep sees it as designed to show whatever keeps people watching, even anger.

Hey Mohit,
It's been four months since you moved to Pune and since I started the coding plan we talked about: one hour, five days a week, to build a small app for my dad's tailoring shop. I'm writing because I nearly quit.
Month one was great. Month two was boring: tutorials, errors, more errors. Month three I missed two whole weeks and felt terrible.
What helped: I started a notebook where I write one line every session, even if it's "fixed one bug". When I look back, there are sixty lines. That's not nothing.
Last week the app finally showed Abba's orders on the screen. He laughed and called my mother to see.
It's still not finished. Probably two more months. Can you test it when it's ready?
Yusuf

How many lines does Yusuf's notebook have?
Sixty lines.
How did Yusuf feel after missing two weeks in month three?
Yusuf felt terrible and discouraged, close to quitting.
What helped Yusuf keep going, and why?
Writing one line per session made progress visible, so boredom and setbacks didn't erase what Yusuf had done.
How might Abba have felt seeing his orders on the screen?
Abba probably felt delighted and proud, laughing and calling Yusuf's mother to see the work.

At five, Abhinav pressed his face into his mother Reena's side at a family gathering, refusing to say hello to a cousin's friends. Reena did not push him. She put a hand on his shoulder, said, "I'm right here," and stayed near the balloons until he peeked out and took one.

At fifteen, after his grandfather died suddenly, Abhinav took every framed photograph off his shelf and slid them into a drawer. When anyone said his grandfather's name, he left the room. His sister Afreen tried to share a memory at dinner and he pushed his plate away. The house felt quieter each day, and the hurt did not fade; it flared every time someone said his grandfather's name by accident.

One evening Reena left the family album on the sofa and sat near the door, saying only, "I'm here when you're ready." An hour later Abhinav sat beside her, opened the album to the last page and said, "I miss him." Afreen came in and sat on his other side.

What did Abhinav take from Reena's side at the gathering at five?
He took a balloon after peeking out from beside her.
How is Abhinav's avoidance at five like his avoidance at fifteen, and what helped both times?

At five Abhinav presses his face into his mother's side and Reena stays near until he peeks out; at fifteen he slides the photographs into a drawer and leaves the room at his grandfather's name, and Reena again sits near the door until he comes to her. Avoiding feels like relief but the hurt flares, and gentle nearness helps.
What might Abhinav be feeling as he pushes his plate away when Afreen shares a memory?
Abhinav is in deep pain and afraid of hurting more, so he avoids reminders of his grandfather.
What did Reena do that helped Abhinav open up?
Reena left the album where he could find it, sat near, and told him she was there when he was ready, rather than forcing him to talk.

"Santosh, why are you so quiet today?"
"Nothing, Tenzin."
"You haven't said one joke, bhai. You didn't even eat your samosa."
"I'm not hungry."
"Is it the hundred-rupee note? The one you picked up this morning?"
"...Nobody saw."
"I saw."
"You're not nobody. Nobody else saw."
"So why do you keep touching your pocket?"
"I don't know. It feels hot."
"You've been weird all day."
"Because I keep thinking someone's looking for it. That old man at the bus stop kept checking his pockets."
"So give it back."

His samosa.

"Gurpreet, you're rubbing your temples again," Karthik said, sliding his chair over at the call centre.
"It's nothing. Just a headache."
"You said that yesterday. And the day before. When did you last eat?"
"Breakfast. I think."

Gurpreet was quiet. Her shoulders ached, her jaw was tight, and her eyes felt full of sand.
"Fifteen minutes," Karthik said. "Water, food, a walk outside. I'll cover your line."
She went. When she came back, the headache had eased a little.
"If they keep coming back," Karthik added, "see a doctor. Deal?"

It was seven in the evening.

She felt pressured and afraid of seeming weak, so she kept working through the headache instead of stopping.

Taking a break for water, food and a walk while Karthik covered her line, and planning to see a doctor if the headaches kept coming.

He was worried for her, remembering how Farhan fainted, so he stepped in with a practical offer.

messages.content: James has 20 years of experience.  8 years ago John had twice as much experience as James.  Mike started when John had 16 years of experience.  What is their combined experience?

8 years ago James had 20-8=12 years
So 8 years ago John had 12*2=24 years experience
That means John has 24+8=32 years experience
So Mike has 32-16=16 years of experience
So together they have 20+32+16=68 years experience
The answer is 68.

Ines had avoided phone calls for three years. In her small flat in Madrid she ordered food online, emailed her landlord and texted her dentist. When her new job required calls to suppliers, she panicked.
So one Sunday, with Santiago's coffee going cold beside her, she made a list. At the bottom, easiest: call the pizza place to ask their hours. Then: call her aunt. Then: book the dentist by phone. At the top: call a supplier.
On Monday she dialled the pizza place. Her heart thudded; her voice shook on the first hello. The man gave her the hours and hung up. Nothing terrible happened. She sat with her racing pulse for three minutes until it slowed.
She did the pizza call again on Tuesday, then called her aunt on Thursday. Each time the fear peaked, then faded. By the second week three lines had ticks, and the supplier call no longer looked like a cliff.

What was the easiest item on Ines's list?
Call the pizza place to ask their hours.
How did Ines feel making the first call?
She felt frightened, heart thudding and voice shaking, then relieved when nothing terrible happened.
Why does Ines's list work better than forcing herself to call a supplier first?
Starting with the easiest step and staying until the fear eases teaches her, by doing, that the feared outcome doesn't happen.
What might Santiago feel watching Ines make her list?
Santiago likely feels hopeful and supportive, quietly staying close without taking over.

Natasha feels the costume she once found surprising and amusing is just right on him, no worse than a swallow-tail or frock coat. He is in high spirits and joins in the laughter.
John buys 3 puzzles.  The first puzzle has 1000 pieces.  The second and third puzzles have the same number of pieces and each has 50% more pieces.  How many total pieces are all the puzzles?

The second puzzle has 1000*.5=500 more pieces than the first
So it has 1000+500=1500 total pieces
That means those two puzzles have 1500*2=3000 pieces
So in total there were 3000+1000=4000 pieces
The answer is 4000.
Finish this idea in one sentence: honesty is important. Use the word "trust" and no more than 12 words.
Honesty is important because it helps people trust you.

It was the first night of Navaratri, and the golu dolls stood on their steps in the Chennai flat. Keerthana wrapped a dupatta round her neck. 'I am the doctor!' She checked every doll's pulse. Her cousin Divyansh helped for a while. Then the singing started in the hall and he ran off. 'Keerthu, come! Sundal!' Keerthana stayed. 'I said I'm the doctor. They're sick.' She checked the wooden merchant twice, mouth tight. Clapping came from the hall. Paati peeped in. 'Doctor, do doctors eat sundal?' Keerthana thought hard. 'Doctors eat,' she decided, 'then come back.'

What did Keerthana wrap round her neck?
A dupatta.
What does Keerthana's tight mouth suggest while the others clapped in the hall?
It suggests she felt left out and a little unhappy, but stuck to being the doctor because she had said so.

Paati asked whether doctors eat sundal, which let Keerthana join the others while still keeping her word as the doctor.

The news came on Tuesday morning in the school hall in Utrecht: Jonas from 10B had died in a cycling accident at the weekend. Nobody moved. Then Leila began to cry, loudly, into her sleeve. Two boys at the back cracked a joke and laughed too hard, then went red. Emil just stared at the floor. He kept thinking of the pencil Jonas had lent him in September, still in his case, and that he had never said thanks. At lunch the canteen was strangely polite. Someone snapped at the jokers, "Have some respect." The counsellor, Ms de Vries, spoke quietly to the tables. "People grieve in different ways. Crying, joking, going silent. None of that is wrong. My door is open all week." Emil went on Thursday, holding the pencil.

What had Jonas lent Emil in September?
Jonas had lent him a pencil in September.
Why did Emil keep thinking about the pencil?
He felt guilty and sad that he had never said thanks, and the pencil made the loss feel personal.
How did Ms de Vries support a school grieving in so many ways?
She said openly that crying, joking and silence are all normal, and offered an open door all week, so students like Emil could come when ready.
Why might the two boys at the back have laughed too hard?
They were probably shocked and awkward, and the laughter was a nervous way of coping, which is why they went red afterwards.
Give three reasons people enjoy gardening. Start each reason with "It" and put each on a new line.

It is calming to work with soil and plants.
It feels rewarding to watch seeds grow.
It gives you fresh herbs and flowers at home.

The monsoon had flooded the lanes around Wasim's hostel in Guwahati, and the power kept failing. His internship report was due in ten days, and the stress sat in his chest like a stone. He didn't feel like eating. He didn't feel like moving. He wanted to lie in bed with his phone until it was over.
His senior Jagdish, who had the room across the corridor, pinned a paper on Wasim's door. It said: Sleep 11. Eat 3 meals. Walk 20 min. That's it.
"You don't have to feel like it," Jagdish said. "You just do it."
So on rainy mornings they walked the covered corridor, twenty laps. At dinner, even when the mess food was cold, Wasim ate the full plate.
By the end of the week he was still stressed, but steadier. When he admitted one night that the stone never lifted, Jagdish said, "If it stays like that, we see the college counsellor together."

What did Jagdish's paper on the door say?
It said: Sleep 11. Eat 3 meals. Walk 20 min. That's it.
How did Wasim feel before the routine started?
He felt heavily stressed, with a stone in his chest, and didn't feel like eating or moving.
Why does the plan work even when Wasim has no motivation?
It doesn't rely on feeling like it; steady sleep, meals and walking support his body, and if the heaviness lasts, seeing the counsellor is the next step.
How might Jagdish feel watching Wasim do the laps?
Jagdish probably feels relieved and caring, glad his simple rules are giving Wasim something steady to hold on to.

He opens his eye like a miller waking when the mill wheel stops. He listens to Langeron, seems to think it is silly business, then closes his eye again and lets his head sink lower.

She sang the lullaby her grandmother had sung, a Marathi one, and skipped words she could not recall. She was tired and slightly flat. She sang the lullaby her grandmother had sung, a Marathi one.

They can keep singing even when tired or unsure of the words, since warmth and presence matter more than skill.

Darshan probably felt a little shy but warm, since he joined even though he was less certain and joked about how they sounded.

Tony bought 3 lottery tickets and chose identical numbers on each ticket. He finds out that 5 of the numbers on each lottery ticket are winning numbers. If each winning number is worth $20 then how much money, in dollars, has Tony won in total?

Across all of the lottery tickets, Tony has a total of 3 lottery tickets * 5 winning numbers per lottery ticket = 15 winning numbers.
Across all the numbers, he has won a total of 15 winning numbers * $20 per winning number = $300.
The answer is 300.

Vinita's phone lit up with a video call from an unknown number. A man in a uniform, seated before a flag, said a parcel in her name held drugs and that she was under "digital arrest": she must stay on camera and transfer money to clear it. Her ears rang. She had never ordered anything from that courier.

"Tell no one, or the case grows," the voice said.

Her brother Tejas came into the back room of the family shop with two cups of tea and saw her white face. "Who is that?"

He took the phone. "Real agencies don't ask for money on video calls." He ended the call.

Vinita began to shake. Tejas sat beside her, rang 1930, and that night helped her report it on the cyber portal. Their mother was told at dinner and held Vinita's hand.

What did the caller say the parcel in Vinita's name held?
The caller said the parcel in her name held drugs.
How was Vinita feeling during the call, and why did she stay quiet?
Vinita was terrified, her ears ringing, and stayed quiet because the caller said "Tell no one, or the case grows."
What should someone do after a call like this?
Hang up, tell family, and report at 1930 or on the cyber portal, as Tejas and Vinita did.
How might Tejas have seen the call?
Tejas saw a scam at once, knowing real agencies don't ask for money on video calls, and saw how frightened his sister was.

In the last exams, Chaitanya had reached the gate and found his admit card still on his desk at home. His friend Rafiq's father had driven him back, and he had lost half an hour of writing time.

He used the same list, every night, for all six papers.

He could keep a copy in his school bag permanently, so he doesn't have to rewrite it for the next exams.

Madhav spent most of today on the sensor calibration. From about ten he barely moved: headphones on, lips moving as he counted, a notebook filling with columns. He skipped the tea round. I had four small things for him: the leave form, a vendor query, the Monday rota, a question about gloves. None were urgent. I held all four on a list.

Note for the team meeting: if someone is clearly deep in a task, write it down and wait, unless it's safety or a deadline.

Four: the leave form, a vendor query, the Monday rota and a question about gloves.

It means "I am very busy". Use it when you have more work than you can easily do.

The guide asked us, "Have you seen the old fort?"
The guide asked us whether we had seen the old fort.

"Yes, to be sure," said Wemmick. "Of course, there can be no objection to your being sorry for him, and I'd put down a five-pound note myself to get him out of it. But what I look at is this. Monday: In the engineering college canteen, Karthik pushed away his dosa. "Thermodynamics on Saturday. I always freeze in exams, Sabina. Every single time."

Sabina stirred her tea. "Every single time? Name them."

Wednesday: Karthik sat in the library with a notebook, a bit annoyed that he'd agreed to do this. Exams in two years: fourteen. Froze: three. He looked at the three. All were first papers of the semester, all after cramming till 3 a.m. The eleven good ones: he'd done a timed practice paper the week before.

"Three out of fourteen," he told Sabina, sounding almost disappointed. "That's not always."

Saturday: The night before, he did a timed practice paper and slept at eleven. In the hall his hands shook when he saw question one. He skipped to question three, which he knew. By the time he came back, his head had cleared.

He didn't feel brave. He felt prepared.

How many exams did Karthik freeze in?
Three.
Why did Karthik sound "almost disappointed" when he said "That's not always"?
The "always" rule had become part of how Karthik saw himself, so losing it felt strange, even though it was good news. It also meant he now had to act on what he learned.
What did Karthik learn from the three freezes, and how did he use it?
They were all first papers after cramming till 3 a.m., while good ones followed a timed practice paper. So he did a practice paper, slept at eleven, and skipped to a question he knew when he shook.
How might Sabina feel if she heard Karthik say he felt prepared, not brave?
Sabina would probably be pleased and a little proud that her simple question led somewhere. She might see that he now trusts evidence more than the old rule.

A captain steers his ship 100 miles north on the first day of their journey. On the second day, he sails to the east three times as far as the distance as he covered on the first day. On the third day, the ship travels further east for 110 more miles than the distance it covered on the second day. What is the total distance the ship has traveled in the three days?

If the ship traveled 100 miles to the north, it sailed for a distance of 3 * 100 miles = 300 miles to the east on the second day.
On the third day, the sheep sailed for 300 miles + 110 miles = 410 miles.
The distance covered by the ship in the three days is 410 miles + 300 miles + 100 miles = 810 miles
The answer is 810.

Big concert at the beach tonight. Before it started, I made Vishal walk the edges with me. He rolled his eyes, but we found three exits and agreed: if we get separated, meet at the lifeguard tower.

Imran, you keep saying you'll start stretching and never do. Let me, your old boss Ramesh, tell you how I finally managed it at twenty-four.
I had a desk job in Chennai and a back like a plank. Every evening I promised myself I'd stretch “later.” Later never came. I'd think about it at night and feel lazy.
Then a colleague, an older lady named Thangam, told me, “Don't look for time. Tie it to something you already do.”
So I tied it to brushing my teeth. Toothbrush back in the cup, and I'd do five stretches right there at the sink. My wife thought I'd gone mad.
The first few days I had to remind myself. After two weeks, my hands put down the brush and my body just bent. I didn't have to think.
Thirty years later, I still do it every morning.

Who told young Ramesh to tie stretching to an existing habit?
A colleague, an older lady named Thangam.
How did young Ramesh feel about stretching before the change?
Ramesh felt lazy and guilty, promising “later” every evening and never doing it.
At what point in the story did the habit start to hold?
When Ramesh tied the stretches to brushing teeth; after two weeks the stretches happened without thinking.
How might Ramesh's wife have felt seeing the stretches at the sink?
She probably felt amused and puzzled at first, thinking Ramesh had gone mad.

Parul, you're nervous about training the new girl in your team? Let your Lalremsiami aunty tell you about my first year as a supervisor in Aizawl, when I was twenty-six.

We hired a young woman fresh from college. On her first day, I gave her everything: every file, every rule, every name. By evening her eyes were red. I thought she was just shy.

The next day I watched her again. She wrote down everything I said, then looked at the notes, lost. I realised I'd poured a whole river into one cup.

So I changed. One task each morning. I'd show her an example, give her a small checklist, and let her practise before lunch. Within a month she was the fastest in the office. I've trained people that way ever since.

Where did Lalremsiami work as a supervisor?
In Aizawl.
What did Lalremsiami realise when she saw the new hire looking lost at her notes?
She felt a pang of regret, realising she had overwhelmed the young woman by pouring a whole river into one cup.
What turning point changed how Lalremsiami trained people?
Watching the new hire on the second day, she switched to one task each morning, with an example, a checklist and practice.
How might the young woman in the story have felt on her first day?
She probably felt overwhelmed and anxious, since her eyes were red by evening.

How can I read faster?
Also, I do not get the word "chore". What does it mean?
Then, Can you correct this? He is the tallest than all the boys.

1. Read a little every day, and read things you enjoy. Do not say each word aloud in your head.
2. A chore is a small job you do regularly at home, like washing dishes.
3. Fixed: He is the tallest of all the boys. Why: Use "of" after "tallest", not "than".

Read this:

I share a hostel room with Nazia, so I've seen her study habits up close. I'm Manoj.
In first semester, she'd shut her laptop at midnight and then toss and turn, muttering about her lab report. Once she got up at 2 am to "just check one table."
This semester she's different. Before she stops, she writes on a card: "Tomorrow: fix graph 2, then write discussion para 1." She puts the card on the laptop and switches off the light. Within ten minutes she's asleep.
I asked her about it. She said, "My brain stops nagging when it knows what's next."
I've started doing it too.

What did Nazia write on the card?
"Tomorrow: fix graph 2, then write discussion para 1."
How does Nazia seem to feel after writing the card?
Nazia seems calm and settled, falling asleep within ten minutes.
Why does Nazia's method work?
Writing the exact next step gives the unfinished work a plan, so the mind stops nagging about it.
How is Manoj affected by watching Nazia's change?
Manoj is impressed enough to start using the same method.

messages.content:
Read this:

Moving day was chaos. It was pouring, the van was late, and half the boxes were still open. Akash's mother, Rekha, was on the phone with the landlord.
Akash kicked a box of books. It split and the books slid out. "This is all your fault!" he shouted, then stopped. It wasn't only hers.
Rekha put the phone down. "Say it, Akash. Say what you really feel."
His throat hurt. "I'm angry at both of you. You broke our home. And I'm sad."
She hugged him. "That's allowed."
Then she gave him a notebook and a pen. "Draw it while I finish the call." He drew a house with a crack down the middle.

What did Akash kick?
A box of books.
What was Akash really feeling on moving day?
He was angry at both parents, and underneath that anger he was sad about losing their home.
What helped Akash express his anger safely?
Rekha asked him to say what he felt in words and gave him a notebook to draw it.
How might Rekha have felt when Akash blamed her?
Rekha may have felt hurt and stressed, but she stayed calm and helped him say the truth.

Write as repeated addition, then find the answer.
a) 3 x 2/5
b) 2 x 3/7
c) 4 x 1/3
d) 3 x 3/8
e) 5 x 2/9
f) 2 x 5/6
g) 4 x 3/10
h) 3 x 4/5
i) 5 x 1/4

Read this:

Parul, beta, you think nobody has ever been dropped by their friends? When your Vasudha maasi was twenty-one, my whole group at the teachers' training college stopped calling me. One day I was sharing their lunch; the next day they had a new table and no seat for me. I never found out why. For weeks I thought something must be broken in me. Then one night I told myself: this hurts, and it is allowed to hurt, but it does not make me bad. I started eating with the two quiet girls from the science section, Farida and Rose. We are still friends; Rose sends me mangoes every summer. When one of the old group later came to me for notes, I gave them. I didn't want to become the thing that had hurt me. So cry today, beta. Tomorrow, find your Roses.

What does Rose send Vasudha maasi every summer?
Rose sends her mangoes every summer.
What did young Vasudha believe about herself in the first weeks, and what changed?
She thought something must be broken in her, until she told herself the hurt was allowed but did not make her bad.
Why did giving notes to someone from the old group matter to Vasudha maasi?
It was a choice not to shut someone out in return, so she wouldn't become the thing that had hurt her.
What might Parul take from "find your Roses"?
Parul might see that today's pain is real but that new, accepting friends can be found, as Vasudha maasi found Farida and Rose.

Read this:

At the NGO office in Nairobi, Priscila watched it happen again in Monday's meeting. Wanjiru presented the school-meals survey to the director as "my analysis", though Priscila and two interns had coded every form. Later, by the kettle, Wanjiru called one intern's charts "a bit amateur", loud enough for everyone to hear. Priscila felt heat in her chest, and the urge to go straight to the director and outshine Wanjiru. She didn't. That evening she opened a shared document and started listing who did what, with dates and file links. On Wednesday she sent a short, factual email to the team and the director: "Summary of survey contributions attached, for the report credits." She didn't add a single adjective.

What did Wanjiru call the intern's charts?
"a bit amateur"
What was Priscila feeling after the meeting?
She felt angry, with heat in her chest, and tempted to compete for the director's admiration.
Why was Priscila's email a wise response?
It relied on records and facts, protecting the team's credit without a fight for attention.
How might the intern feel after hearing the charts called amateur?
The intern probably felt embarrassed and discouraged, especially in front of others.
Put this in simple words for my grandfather: The bank will send you a notification once your cheque has been cleared.
The bank will tell you when your cheque has gone through.
Jeff has 16 GB of storage on his phone. He is already using 4 GB. If a song takes up about 30MB of storage, how many songs can Jeff store on his phone? (There are 1000 MB in a GB).

Jeff has 16-4 = 12GB left over on his phone.
Therefore, he has 12*1000= 12,000MB.
Therefore, he can store 12,000/30=400 songs.
The answer is 400.

A pizza is cut into 8 slices. Each of 4 children eats 3/8 of a pizza. How much pizza do they eat altogether?

Now you try: 6 x 3/10.
Now you try: which remainders can you get when you divide by 4?
The answer is 0, 1, 2, 3.

In the last week before submission at the small-town college, Binita watched her group join their parts on one dusty laptop. Disha had built the survey table with distances in kilometres; another member had entered the distances in miles; a third had written the report assuming 200 houses when the survey covered 120. The graphs would not load. The three of them stared at each other and at the wall clock. Nobody had checked the pieces together until now. Binita, who had only been asked to proofread, said quietly, "We each did our part. We never agreed the units." They stayed until ten fixing it. On the back of her notebook Binita wrote: agree the format first, join a small piece early.

What units did Disha use for distances in the survey table?
Disha used kilometres.
What might Binita be feeling as the parts fail to join?
Uneasy and a little helpless, since she was only asked to proofread.
What early step would have caught the problem?
Agreeing the units and format at the start, and joining a small piece together early as a check.
How might Disha have felt on discovering the mismatch?
Probably embarrassed or defensive, since the table followed a different assumption that no one had agreed on.

Dear Vikas bhaiya,
Good news first: I came first in the Class 10 prelims! Papa distributed laddoos to the whole building. 98 in science. 😊
Now the weird part. You asked last month what I found most interesting in biology this year. I sat down to write back and... nothing. I don't remember any of it properly. I learned exactly what the question bank said, the night before each test, and it was gone the week after. Rank first, joy zero, if I'm honest.
Remember when we were small and you showed me frog eggs in the pond behind Nani's house? I asked a hundred questions. I don't ask anything now. There's no time, and there are no marks for it.
Is it like this in college too?
Sunaina

What did Papa do when Sunaina came first?
Papa distributed laddoos to the whole building.
How does Sunaina seem to feel about coming first, beyond the good news?
Sunaina feels a strange emptiness, 'rank first, joy zero', because the learning was only for tests and didn't stay.
What small step could Sunaina take to bring back the questions?
Sunaina could pick one biology topic, like the frog eggs, and explore it just out of curiosity, maybe writing to Vikas bhaiya about it.
How might Vikas bhaiya feel reading that Sunaina doesn't ask anything now?
He might feel sad, remembering the child with a hundred questions at the pond, and want to help Sunaina find that curiosity again.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, winter term, by Deepika
In the December cold snap, the children played indoors at break. Damini, Class 5, threw a shoe at a friend and it cracked a window pane. She said quickly, "It's only one crack, ma'am. The Class 8 boys broke three whole windows last year."
She didn't say sorry or mention the friend. The comparison made her act look tiny, even to herself.
I asked, "Are we talking about the Class 8 boys or about you?" She looked at the floor. "Me. I threw my shoe." "What would make it right?" "Tell the office. Say sorry. Help cover it."
What I did next: we went to the office together, she helped tape cardboard over the pane, and I'll tell her parents at pickup.

How many windows did the Class 8 boys break last year?
Three whole windows, according to Damini.
Why did Damini bring up the Class 8 boys straight away?
Damini felt guilty and scared of trouble, and comparing with a worse act made her own mistake feel tiny.
What did Deepika ask that shifted the conversation?
Deepika asked whether they were talking about the Class 8 boys or about Damini, which brought the focus back to Damini's own act.
How might the friend Damini threw the shoe at have felt?
The friend was probably startled and maybe a little scared when the shoe hit the window.
