"Binita, why are you wearing a mask on the terrace?"
"Akash, didn't you see the news? That rare virus. They showed a whole family in hospital."
"That was in another state. Three cases total."
"Still. It could come here. I've stopped going to the mall."
"Okay. And you're coming to the canteen with me now?"
"Yes. On your bike."
"I have one helmet."
"You wear it. It's only two kilometres."
"Binita. You're scared of a virus with three cases, but not of riding without a helmet on the highway?"
"That's different. Everyone rides like that."
"Everyone also gets into accidents like that."
Binita paused, one foot on the bike. "Okay, it sounds silly when you say it."
"I'll borrow a second helmet. Wait here."

How many cases of the rare virus were there?
Three cases total.
Why does riding without a helmet feel safe to Binita?
The dramatic news made the virus feel urgent and frightening, while riding without a helmet felt normal because everyone does it, so Binita felt calm about it.
What step does Akash take that protects Binita?
Akash refuses to let Binita ride without a helmet and goes to borrow a second one.
How does Akash seem to feel about Binita's choices?
Akash seems frustrated but caring, pointing out the mismatch and taking a practical step to keep Binita safe.

Read this:

Six months after she was mugged on the way home in Valencia, Camila still took the long route, avoiding that street. She sat facing the door in every café. When a scooter passed close, her whole body jerked.
Her flatmate Dalia invited her to a party. Camila went, stood in the corner, and felt like she was watching everyone through glass. When a stranger touched her arm to pass, she flinched so hard her drink spilled. She went home ashamed.
"I should be over this by now," she told Dalia. "I'm just weak."
Dalia sat beside her. "You're not weak. You're safe now, but your body doesn't believe it yet. Willpower alone won't fix that."
The next week Camila booked a session with a therapist at the university who worked with people after frightening events. She told Dalia afterwards, "It's going to take time. But I think I can trust her."

What did Camila do when a stranger touched her arm?
She flinched so hard her drink spilled.
How did Camila feel going home from the party?
She felt ashamed and detached, like she was watching everyone through glass, and blamed herself as weak.
What did Camila do that could help her heal?
She stopped relying on willpower alone and booked sessions with a trained therapist, accepting that it would take time.
How does Dalia see Camila's reactions?
Dalia sees them as her body still not feeling safe, not as weakness, and feels caring and patient.

messages.content:
Read this:

Irawati, you want to know why I ring people now instead of typing "wow"? Okay. I'm Rehana, and last month my cousin Samira posted a photo of her new short haircut in the family group. I was on a bumpy bus and typed "wow." Just that. Wow, full stop. In my head it was a gasp: wow, you're brave, it looks amazing. Ten minutes later she messaged me privately: "if you hate it, just say so." I was stunned. I scrolled up and saw Phuppo had written "wow!!! 😍" and my cousin Adil had written "wow, bold choice." Three wows: one delighted, one maybe sarcastic, and mine, which sounded cold. So I called her from the bus stop and said, "I love it. My wow was a gasp, not a sneer." She laughed and admitted she'd cried a bit. Since then, if a wow matters, I add real words or I just call.

What did Samira post in the family group?
A photo of her new short haircut.
How did Rehana feel on reading Samira's private message?
Rehana was stunned and worried, because the plain "wow." had meant admiring surprise but had come across as cold or sarcastic.
What did Rehana do to fix the misunderstanding?
Rehana called Samira from the bus stop and said clearly that the haircut looked lovely and the wow was a gasp, not a sneer 😊
What was it like for Samira reading the three wows?
Nervous about a bold change, Samira read the bare "wow." as disapproval and felt hurt enough to cry a little.

With only three weeks before the entrance mock and her family's shop needing her every evening during the wedding season, Damini had very little time. So she used it the way that felt most productive: rereading.

Every night after closing the shop she opened her chemistry notes, beautifully written in four colours, and went through them again, highlighting new lines in yellow. By the third week the pages glowed. She felt ready. "I've read organic chemistry six times," she told her friend Noor.

"Have you solved any problems?"

"I don't need to. I know it."

At the mock, the first organic question was one she'd never seen in that form. She stared. The reaction was in her notes, she could picture the page, the colour of the ink. But she couldn't pull the answer out of her head.

She scored 38. Noor, who had done fewer pages and more problems, scored 61.

How many times had Damini read organic chemistry?
Six times.
How did Damini feel before the mock, and during it?
Before, she felt confident and ready; during the mock she felt stuck and panicked, unable to recall what she could picture on the page.
What would have used her limited time better?
Spending part of each evening solving practice problems and testing herself, so she learns to pull answers out rather than just recognise notes.
How might Noor see Damini's result?
Noor probably feels sympathetic and a bit worried, since Noor's own practice-heavy approach worked better.

messages.content: We're visiting a hill station in winter. What should we pack?
Warm layers are key. Think of a sweater, a jacket, socks, a cap and gloves. Layers let you add or remove as the day changes.
Do we need special shoes?
Shoes with a good grip are helpful, since slopes can be slippery. Closed shoes are better than sandals in cold weather.
Will phones work there?
I cannot check coverage for your destination. It varies by place, so ask your phone company or someone who has been there recently.
What if the roads are closed?
Roads in the hills can close in bad weather. Check the local road advice before you leave, and keep your plan flexible with a spare day if possible.
Should we carry medicines?
If anyone takes medicine regularly, they should bring it, as the doctor advises. For anything else, ask a doctor before the trip about what to carry.
My diary today, written as Arjun, 35 words: I fixed my bicycle chain myself, my hands got oily, I wiped them on a rag, and I felt capable, so I want to learn more repairs.

Dear Diary,
Today I fixed my bicycle chain myself. My hands got oily, so I wiped them on a rag. When the chain finally moved again, I felt capable. I want to learn more repairs.
Arjun
Include the words "bee" and "jasmine" in a sentence about a garden.
A small bee hummed around the jasmine by the gate.
What is the difference between aroha and avaroha in a raga?
Aroha is the ascending, or rising, movement of a raga, and avaroha is the descending movement. They do not always use the same notes.

"Nirmala, can I use your pencil? Mine broke," Jeevan whispered. The Ganpati drawing had to be finished before the bell.
"What will you give me?"
"Huh?"
"I'll lend my pencil if you lend your eraser. The one that smells like strawberry."
"But I need it too!"
"Then no pencil." Nirmala pulled it close. "That's fair. You get something, I get something."
"You're not even using an eraser now!"
"I might. Deal or no deal?"
Jeevan sighed and pushed the eraser across. "Deal. But I want it back after one line."
"Two lines."
"One and a half."
Nirmala grinned and handed over the pencil. "Deal."

What did Nirmala ask for in return for the pencil?
Jeevan's eraser, the one that smells like strawberry.
What does Nirmala think makes the deal fair?
Nirmala feels sure and a bit pleased with the bargain, believing fair means each person gets something, rather than thinking about Jeevan's broken pencil and Jeevan's need.
How could a teacher build on Nirmala's sense of fairness?
Accept that fair trades matter to Nirmala, and also ask how Jeevan feels with a broken pencil and the bell coming, so Nirmala notices Jeevan's need as well as the deal.
How does Jeevan feel about the trade?
Jeevan feels frustrated, protesting that Nirmala isn't even using an eraser, but agrees because the drawing must be finished before the bell.

Read this:

Sunday
At the gurdwara today, in the middle of kirtan, an awful thought came into my head. The kind I'd never, ever say. I felt sick and ran out to the shoe area. Why does my brain do this? It keeps happening. I'm scared I'm a bad person underneath.
I've never told anyone because they'd look at me differently.
But tonight Kishore Mama saw me crying on the stairs and sat down. I told him a little bit. He didn't look shocked at all. He said lots of people get thoughts they hate, and it doesn't mean anything about who you are. He said the shame is what keeps them loud. He's talking to Mum tonight about a psychologist.
I feel a bit lighter.
Jasleen

Where did Jasleen run to during kirtan?
Jasleen ran out to the shoe area.
How does Jasleen feel about the thoughts?
Jasleen feels sick, scared and ashamed, afraid of being a bad person underneath.
What did Kishore Mama do that helped?
He listened calmly, explained such thoughts are common and don't define a person, and planned to talk to Mum about a psychologist that night.
How might Kishore Mama have felt seeing Jasleen crying on the stairs?
He was likely concerned and gentle, choosing to sit down and listen without any shock.

Noor: Thomas, it's been a month. Can you send the 2,000 for the trip?
Thomas: bro sorry, this week for sure
Noor: You said that last week.
Thomas: tight month yaar. soon
Noor: I saw your new shoes in the group photo.
Thomas: haha those were a gift
(two weeks, no reply)
Noor: Api, I lent Thomas money and he's ghosting me.
Api: Oh Noor. How much?
Noor: 2,000. I feel so stupid. I'm never lending anyone anything again.
Api: You weren't stupid, you were kind. He's the one who broke it.
Noor: So what, I just trust everyone?
Api: No. Trust people who've shown it. Start small. Maybe say no to Thomas next time.
Noor: And Sana? She always pays back.
Api: Then Sana's fine. That's the point.

How much money did Noor lend Thomas?
Noor lent Thomas 2,000 for the trip.
How did Noor feel after two weeks with no reply from Thomas?
Noor felt betrayed and stupid, and wanted to stop lending anyone anything again.
What does Api suggest Noor do next, and why is it wiser than trusting nobody?
Api says to trust people who've shown it and start small, so Noor can still help someone like Sana who always pays back, while saying no to Thomas.
How might Sana be affected if Noor stopped trusting everyone?
Sana, who always pays back, would be treated as if she had done something wrong, which would feel unfair to her.

When her brother Abhinav told the family about his gambling debts and addiction, Parul was furious. She'd lent him money twice. She'd defended him to their parents.
That night in the Mumbai flat, she lay awake, angry, then guilty. Should she have seen it? Then, strangely, relieved. The lies were finally over.
The counsellor at the de-addiction centre suggested the family come to a session. Parul went, arms folded. The counsellor explained that addiction changes the brain, that it's a medical condition, not a lack of love or morals.
Afterwards Parul joined a family group that met on Saturdays. For the first time, she talked about her own anger without feeling like a bad sister.

How many times had Parul lent Abhinav money?
Twice.
What feelings did Parul have that first night?
She felt angry, then guilty for not seeing it, then relieved that the lies were over.
What helped Parul stay steady?
Learning at the counselling session that addiction is a health problem, and joining a family group for her own feelings.
How might Abhinav feel knowing Parul came to the session?
Abhinav may feel ashamed but grateful and less alone, seeing his sister show up.
Remind my parents, whom I call Mummy and Papa, to switch off the geyser and gas before they leave for the wedding tomorrow. About 40 words, friendly tone. I'm Kunal.

Dear Mummy and Papa,
Just a little reminder before you leave for the wedding tomorrow. Please switch off the geyser and the gas,. Have a lovely time, and eat a lot of sweets for me!
Love,
Kunal

Reduce this section to a single line.

Continuing thus, I came at length opposite to the inn at which the various diligences and carriages usually stopped. Here I paused, I knew not why; but I remained some minutes with my eyes fixed on a coach that was coming towards me from the other end of the street. As it drew nearer I observed that it was the Swiss diligence; it stopped just where I was standing, and on the door being opened, I perceived Henry Clerval, who, on seeing me, instantly sprung out. "My dear Frankenstein," exclaimed he, "how glad I am to see you! How fortunate that you should be here at the very moment of my alighting!"
The narrator walks to the inn where coaches stop, and the Swiss coach arrives with Henry Clerval, who jumps out and greets the narrator delightedly.

Class 5B, observation note, Tuesday.
Santosh would not use the second-floor washroom today. He ran to the ground floor at break and was late back. When I asked, he said quietly that a woman in white appears in the mirror if you go alone.
I asked where he heard it. "Everyone says it, ma'am. Sabina's brother saw it." Sabina, sitting nearby, said her brother hadn't seen it, he had heard it from someone in Class 8.
Santosh looked confused. "But everybody knows it," he said, as though that settled it.
What I did next: I walked with Santosh and Sabina to the washroom, we switched on the light and looked at the mirror together. Tomorrow I'll talk with the class about how things feel true when we hear them many times.

Which washroom would Santosh not use?
He would not use the second-floor washroom.
What does Santosh's reply "But everybody knows it" suggest about how he felt?
He felt frightened and sure, because hearing the story over and over made it feel like a known fact.
How does the note-writer's plan for tomorrow help?
Talking with the class about how repeated stories feel true can help children question "facts" they only heard, instead of just fearing them.
How does Sabina seem to see the story once she hears her brother's name?
She seems to want to set it straight, pointing out that her brother only heard it from someone else and never saw it.

Read this:

In the colony park, Ishita crossed her fingers and squeezed her eyes shut. “I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow. I hope the picnic happens.”
Her friend Pranav, on the next swing, said, “My Mummy says clouds are coming.”
Ishita opened one eye. “But maybe they go away.”
“Maybe.”
Her mother, hanging washing on the balcony above, called down, “Maybe, Ishita. If not, we'll spread the big sheet inside and it will still be a picnic.”
Ishita thought about it. “With sandwiches?”
“With sandwiches.”

What did Pranav say his Mummy said was coming?
He said clouds were coming.
What is Ishita feeling and wanting when she squeezes her eyes shut and crosses her fingers?

She is hopeful: she wants the picnic to happen and believes the wish might help. Her question about sandwiches afterwards shows she can begin to accept another plan, though she may also be hiding some disappointment.
What would you advise Ishita's mother to do if it does rain?
Acknowledge the disappointment first, then bring out the indoor picnic sheet she promised so the day still feels special.
How might Pranav see Ishita's wishing?
He passes on what his Mummy said, so he may think rain is likely and not want to hurt her feelings, or he may be hoping too.

At the village well, Raghav, five, was telling Dolma aunty about his new calf. "She has a white spot and she drinks so much milk and—" The ice-cream cart bell rang down the lane. Raghav turned and ran without another word. Dolma aunty laughed, but Papa called him back. "Raghav, Dolma aunty was listening to you. What do we say when we go?" Raghav thought. "Bye?" "Try: 'I'll go now, bye, aunty!'" Raghav said it, waved, and ran off again. Dolma aunty waved back, smiling.

What did Raghav's calf have?
A white spot.
Why did Raghav run off mid-sentence?
He was excited and distracted by the ice-cream cart bell, forgetting he was talking.
What did Papa model for Raghav?
Papa taught him to say 'I'll go now, bye, aunty!' before leaving.
How did Dolma aunty react?
She laughed at first and then smiled and waved back, pleased with the proper goodbye.

At 11 p.m. the power went out. Pradeep's physics assignment was due at eight the next morning, and he was only on question three of ten. His phone battery was at twelve percent.
Then a message from his classmate Sarika in the group: photos of her finished answers. "For anyone stuck 🙂"
Pradeep hesitated. His father had said if his marks dropped again, no more cricket academy. Everyone in the group was probably copying anyway. Just this once.
He copied all seven by torchlight, changing a few words. He felt a small knot in his stomach, but mostly relief. He slept at midnight.
He got nine out of ten.
Two weeks later, the unit test had the same kind of questions. Pradeep stared at the paper. He recognised the questions but not the steps. He had written them, but never done them.
He scored eleven out of thirty. Sarika scored twenty-seven.

What was Pradeep's phone battery at?
His phone battery was at twelve percent.
What was Pradeep feeling as he copied by torchlight?
Pradeep felt a small knot of guilt in his stomach, but mostly relief at escaping the deadline.
What went wrong, and what could Pradeep have done instead?
Copying got the marks but not the skill, so the test showed the gap; he could have done fewer questions honestly or asked the teacher for more time.
How might Sarika feel if she learned her answers were copied?
Sarika might feel uneasy, since Sarika meant to help people who were stuck, not to have her work copied whole.
Why does a swing go higher when the rider pumps with the legs?
The rider adds a little energy to each swing. Because the rider pushes at the right moment, the extra energy builds up and the swing travels further.

Rafiq, twenty-two, had been at the Bengaluru startup for three months when he spotted it: in Pema's investor deck, the growth figure was doubled. She'd used last year's total instead of this quarter's.
Pema was the head of strategy. She'd been there since the beginning. She'd once snapped at an intern for "overthinking."
Rafiq opened a message to her. Deleted it. Opened it again. He imagined her saying, "Who asked you?" and imagined being left out of the next project.
He said nothing.
On Friday, the investor meeting went badly. One investor spotted the number in the first five minutes. Pema came back pale.
In the corridor, Rafiq's stomach turned. He'd saved himself one awkward conversation. It had cost the whole team a week of damage control. That night he wrote to Pema: "I saw it on Tuesday. I should have told you. I'm sorry."

What mistake did Rafiq spot in Pema's deck?
The growth figure was doubled; she'd used last year's total instead of this quarter's.
Why did Rafiq delete the message to Pema?
Rafiq felt afraid of seeming rude and worried about being left out of the next project.
What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
Rafiq's silence let a small error reach investors; next time he could raise it privately and politely before the meeting.
How might Pema feel when she reads Rafiq's message?
Pema might feel frustrated that he waited, but also realise her snappiness made juniors afraid to speak.
Can a sound really irritate you, or is that just a saying?

To irritate someone is to make them slightly angry or annoyed. It is a verb. It can also mean to make a part of the body sore.
Example: The constant tapping on the desk began to irritate the teacher.
Please seat down; the film is about to start. What should the verb be?

Please sit down; the film is about to start.
Why: "Sit" is what you do; "seat" needs an object.
My neighbour asked me to feed their cat for the weekend. I've never looked after one.
Ask the neighbour for clear instructions before they leave: how much food, how many times a day, and where the water bowl sits. Write it down so you do not have to remember it.
What if the cat doesn't come out to eat?

Do not worry too much. Many cats hide when their owner is away, so leave the food, stay calm and quiet, and check back later. If the food has not been touched for a whole day, message your neighbour to tell them.
Micah picks 2 dozen strawberries from the field.  He eats 6 and saves the rest for his mom.  How many strawberries are there for his mom?

Micah picks 2 x 12 = 24 strawberries.
After he eats 6, there are this many strawberries left for his mom: 24 - 6 = 18.
The answer is 18.

Wednesday night
Day 6 of trying the ten-minute sitting thing Sarita taught me. Honestly? Most of it was thinking about lunch, my presentation, whether I left the geyser on. Sarita says that's normal, you just keep coming back to the breath. It feels like training a puppy. 🙂
But today something different happened. In the middle of the lab, when the experiment failed again, I noticed my chest getting tight. And I just... breathed. Slowly. Three times. Didn't throw the beaker. Didn't cry in the washroom like last week.
Also I've stopped eating with my phone. Food tastes better? Weird.
Going to keep going. Tomorrow: sit before class, not after.
Aadhya

How long is the sitting practice Sarita taught Aadhya?
It is ten minutes.
What does Aadhya's noticing the tight chest in the lab show about Aadhya's progress?
It shows Aadhya is becoming aware of stress as it rises, which made it possible to calm down with breaths instead of reacting.
What is Aadhya doing that supports focus?
Aadhya practises daily, keeps coming back to the breath, and has cut small multitasking habits like eating with the phone out.
How might Sarita feel hearing about the lab moment?
Sarita would probably feel happy and encouraged that the suggestion is helping Aadhya in real situations.
Carol sells tickets for an exhibition. During three days she sold tickets worth $960. One ticket costs $4. How many tickets on average did she sell during one of these three days?

Carol sold 960 / 4 = 240 tickets during three days.
So in one day, she sold on average 240 / 3 = 80 tickets.
The answer is 80.
Is the plan of a trip an "itinery" or an "itinerary"?

It is "itinerary", ending in "-ary".
Example: Our itinerary includes two days in Jaipur.

June: Manoj picked agricultural science after a summer on his uncle's farm, testing soil and talking to farmers. His roommate Kashish was there because his father owned a fertiliser shop and had filled in the form for him.
October: Their first field trial failed. Heavy rain rotted half the seedlings. Kashish threw his notebook on the bed. “Why am I even doing this?” Manoj was upset too, but he went back to the field at dawn and started recording what went wrong.
February: Kashish had missed most of the practicals and was talking about switching. Manoj had redone the trial with raised beds. It worked better. When his professor asked why he kept going after the rain, Manoj shrugged. “I wanted this before I got here. The rain didn't change that.”

What happened to the first field trial in October?
Heavy rain rotted half the seedlings.
How did Manoj feel after the failed trial, and why did he return at dawn?
He felt upset, but because he had chosen the course himself after real reflection, he was determined to find out what went wrong.
What could help Kashish now?
Kashish could talk honestly with a counsellor and his father about what he actually wants, so any path he takes is one he owns.
How does Kashish experience the same setback differently?
Kashish feels frustrated and without purpose, asking why he is even doing this, since the choice was never his.

Thunder cracked over the Oslo rooftops. Lars dropped his train and climbed straight into Oskar's lap, pushing his face into his grandfather's jumper.
Oskar wrapped both arms round him and hummed. Lars stayed curled up, holding a fold of wool in his fist.
When the rain softened, Lars wriggled and pushed at Oskar's arm. Oskar opened his arms at once, and Lars slid down to find his train.

What did Lars drop when the thunder cracked?
His train.
What was Lars feeling when he climbed into Oskar's lap?
He was frightened by the thunder and wanted closeness and safety; wriggling down later shows he felt calm again.
Which of Oskar's choices worked, and why?
Holding him warmly during the thunder and opening his arms at once when Lars pushed away worked, because both the need for comfort and the wish to go were respected.
How might Oskar feel when Lars slides off his lap?
He probably feels content, glad he could be a safe place and that Lars felt ready to play again.

Dear Mehak,

You asked why I signed up for the palliative care course after Ammi. I've been trying to answer that for a month.

For three years we learned things nobody should have to learn: how to turn her gently, how to wet her lips when she couldn't drink, how to sit quietly when she was scared at night. When she died I kept thinking all of it would just vanish. Now I use it every Saturday at the care centre in Hyderabad, with other people's mothers. It feels as if she's still teaching me.

But honestly, last week an old lady there hummed the song Ammi used to hum, and I had to leave the room. I sat in the car for half an hour. The work helps. It doesn't do my missing her for me.

Can we visit her grave together when you're home in June?

Your brother,
Yusuf

Where does Yusuf use what he learned?
Yusuf uses it every Saturday at the care centre in Hyderabad.
What does Yusuf feel when the old lady hums Ammi's song?
Yusuf is flooded with grief and has to leave the room, showing that missing Ammi still needs its own space beyond the work.
Why is visiting the grave with Mehak a wise addition?
It gives Yusuf's grief a place of its own, shared with Mehak, alongside the purpose he finds at the care centre.
How might Mehak feel reading the letter?
Mehak may feel moved and close to Yusuf, understanding both the purpose he has found and the sadness he still carries.

You're asking me if it's okay to change your mind, Shalini? I changed mine in the middle of Class 11. Let me tell you how.

I'm Parul. I'd wanted to be a doctor since I was eight. My whole family was proud. So in Class 11, I studied chemistry every single evening. Two hours. Tuition on Saturdays. And my tests came back 40, 42, 39. Not because I was lazy. I just wasn't getting it.

One day I cried in the washroom after a test and my class teacher sent me to the counsellor. I was ashamed to say it out loud, but I did: "Maybe medicine isn't for me."

She didn't argue. She asked what I liked. Statistics, I said. The one chapter in maths I always finished first. She showed me data science programmes. I'd been avoiding that idea for a year because it felt like giving up.

It wasn't giving up. It was steering.

What were Parul's chemistry test scores?
How did Parul feel admitting "Maybe medicine isn't for me"?
Parul felt ashamed saying it aloud, after crying in the washroom, but it also opened the way forward.
What else could Parul do while switching paths?
Parul could explain the change to the family with what the counsellor showed, so the pride they felt can move to the new plan.
How might the counsellor see Parul's shift?
The counsellor likely feels glad Parul spoke honestly, and sees the change as a sensible response to clear feedback.

The coaching institute's ad was everywhere today: "95% of our students placed!" and a wall of smiling faces. Lokesh has already paid the deposit. I almost did too.
But at the counselling desk I asked: 95% of whom? Turns out it's 95% of students who finished and sat the final test. How many joined? The man at the desk got vague. Lokesh's senior told us half the batch dropped out by month three. So maybe it's more like half of half.
Not saying it's bad. Maybe it's great. But before I pay anything, I'm going to find five people who joined and didn't finish, and ask them what happened.
Shankar

What did the coaching institute's ad say?
95% of our students placed, with a wall of smiling faces.
Why did Shankar ask '95% of whom?'
Shankar felt doubtful that the smiling faces showed everyone, suspecting they were only those who finished, and wanted to know about everyone who joined.
What makes Shankar's plan a sensible one?
Talking to five people who joined and didn't finish shows the whole group, including the missing ones, before any money is paid.
How might Lokesh feel after hearing Shankar's questions?

"Didi, I've done it. Resigned from the call centre."
Nikita put down her tea. "Gautam, you haven't even got the food cart yet."
"I'll get it next week. The spot outside the college is perfect. Students will come every day."
"And the licence? The cart? What if it rains for a month?"
"Rain happens to people with bad locations. Mine's covered by the bus stop."
"And your savings?"
"I'll make them back in two months. Everyone says my momos are the best in the family."
"The family isn't paying, Gautam."
He laughed and grabbed a notebook. "Look, I've planned it all. Profit from week two."
Nikita flipped through the pages. There was a menu, a logo sketch, a colour for the umbrella. There was nothing about what he'd do if it didn't work.
"Where's plan B?" she asked.
"I don't need one. Plan A is good."

Where does Gautam want to put his food cart?
The spot outside the college.
Why does Gautam feel he doesn't need a plan B?
He is excited and hopeful, sure his momos are the best and his spot is perfect, so bad weather or slow sales seem to happen only to others.
What small step could Nikita suggest that keeps Gautam's hope but protects him?
She could ask him to add one page to the notebook about what he'd do if the first months are slow, like keeping some part-time work until the cart settles.
How might Nikita feel flipping through the notebook?
Nikita seems proud of her brother's effort, the menu and logo, but uneasy that nothing covers what happens if it doesn't work.

You asked on the school podcast why I deleted the video app. Okay. I'm Damini, and honestly I didn't delete it at first. I just noticed something weird.
I'd open it for one dance video before homework. Then another one would start by itself. Then it showed me stuff I didn't even search for, but somehow exactly what I'd watch. One night I looked up and it was 1 a.m. and my maths was still open.
My friend Saurabh said, "It's not you. It's built like that. Autoplay, endless scroll, the little red dots. They want your time." He showed me where to switch off autoplay and notifications.
It felt like finding the trick behind a magic show. I was kind of angry, actually. Now I set a timer, and when it rings I close it. Most days.

What did Saurabh show Damini how to switch off?
He showed Damini where to switch off autoplay and notifications.
How did Damini feel after learning how the app was built?
Damini felt angry, like finding the trick behind a magic show, realising the app was designed to take up time.
What else could Damini try if the timer stops working?
Damini could keep the app off the home screen, use it only after homework, or ask a friend to check in on the plan.
How might Saurabh see Damini's change?
Saurabh might feel glad that telling the truth about the design helped, rather than blaming Damini for being weak.

Wednesday night
Today a two-line email took me forty minutes. I rewrote it six times and still sent it with Swati ma'am's name spelled wrong.
Then I mixed up the March and April sheets in the reconciliation. She caught it before the client did, thank god, but she looked at me like she was trying to work out what had happened to me.
What happened is I'm a fraud. Three months ago I was the intern who finished early. Now I can't add a column without checking it three times, and I still get it wrong.
So I stayed till 9 redoing everything, then came home and couldn't even remember what I'd redone.
The harder I try, the worse it gets. Maybe I'm just not good at this.
Swati ma'am said, "Let's talk tomorrow, 10 am." I'm dreading it.
Neelam

The two-line email took forty minutes.

Neelam believes being a fraud and 'not good at this' is the reason, without seeing that exhaustion is making everything slower.

Neelam could admit how tired everything feels, and Swati ma'am could look at the workload and rest together with Neelam rather than asking for more effort.
How might Swati ma'am see the change in Neelam?
She has watched an intern who once finished early start making repeated mistakes, so she may be puzzled and concerned rather than angry, which is why she asked to talk.

Sunday night. Today I closed the app. Turned off the servers, sent the last email to users, and hugged Ankita at the doorway. It hurt more than I expected. Then, before the feeling could settle, I opened a notebook and wrote two pages headed What I learned. About the market: people wanted a cheap, simple tool, not our long list of features. About us: we never spoke openly when the numbers dropped, and we hired before we knew the need. I underlined three lessons. Ankita is going to help with the next idea: a small tool, one feature, and a check with real users in the first month. It is smaller. It feels lighter.

Uday

Uday wrote two pages headed What I learned, about the market and about the team.

'We don't know the rules,' said Bidisha. 'Half of what Papa's cousin tells us contradicts the other half.'
'Then let's ask,' said Tushar. 'A lawyer, one meeting, just to explain in general what the options are.'
'Not to fight?'
'No. I don't want a letter in anyone's hand. I want to understand.'
Two days later, at the kitchen table:
'The lawyer said there are ways to settle by agreement, and listed them,' said Bidisha, reading from her notes.
'And what was said about the house is general, not our exact case.'
'Right. So we don't wave it at Chachi.'
'We bring it to the table and ask: here are the options, which one works for all of us?'
Tushar closed the notebook. 'Sunday, then. Tea first, papers second.'

What did the siblings ask the lawyer for?
They asked for one meeting, just to explain in general what the options are.
What does Tushar's line "I don't want a letter in anyone's hand" suggest about how Tushar feels?
It suggests Tushar wants peace and fears that a legal letter would escalate the dispute.
What could the siblings do if the family still disagrees on Sunday?
They could go through the options one by one and, if needed, ask the lawyer again about their exact case, while keeping the mood calm.
How might Chachi feel if the lawyer's words were used against Chachi?
Chachi might feel attacked and defensive, which is why the siblings decide to offer options rather than wave the advice.

Ganga, beti, you're angry with your parents? Sit. Your Vijay Dada has a story about anger.
In 1974 I was twenty-one, in Jhansi. I wanted to join the Railways as a mechanic. My father wanted me in his cloth shop. He wouldn't even let me finish a sentence about it.
So I did the dramatic thing. I packed a tin trunk and told him, "If you won't listen, I'm leaving for Bombay tomorrow." He said, "Go, then." And I went, all the way to the bus stand, and sat there till midnight, too proud to go back and too scared to leave.
Your Dadi, only a neighbour then, found me and said, "Threats won't make him hear you."
A week later, calm, I sat beside him in the shop and said, "Babuji, I love you. I'm not good with cloth. I'm good with engines. Let me try for one year." He was quiet a long time. Then he said, "One year."
Anger is a messenger, beti. Let it deliver the message, then send it home.

Where did young Vijay sit till midnight?
At the bus stand.
How did Vijay feel sitting at the bus stand?
Torn and stuck: too proud to go back and too scared to leave after his angry threat.
What was the turning point in Vijay's story?
The neighbour who later became Ganga's Dadi telling him threats wouldn't work; a week later he spoke calmly and asked for a one-year trial.
How might Vijay's father have felt when Vijay packed the trunk?
Hurt and defensive, answering "Go, then" out of pride.

Maria is baking cookies for Sally. Sally says that she wants 1/4 of her cookies to have nuts in them, 40% to have chocolate chips in them, and the remainder to have nuts and chocolate chips in them. When she adds nuts to the cookies, she uses 2 nuts per cookie. If she makes 60 cookies, how many nuts does she need?

35% of the cookies have nuts and chocolate chips because 100 - 25 - 40 = 35
60% of the cookies have nuts in them because 25 + 35 = 60
She makes 36 cookies with nuts in them because 60 x .6 =36
She needs 72 nuts because 36 x 2 = 72
The answer is 72.

Ten minutes into a wet afternoon, five-year-old Tejas flopped on the floor. "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the phone?" Mummy Sabina put a basket of old spoons and pots beside him. "Make some music," she said. After a moment of frowning, Tejas started drumming, and half an hour later the kitchen was full of his band.
At fifteen, Tejas was on the same short piece on his guitar for the fourth week. Same mistake, same place. His fingers slid off the string and he sighed loudly. Mummy Sabina, passing the door, noticed his slumped shoulders. She could have said "just quit if it is so dull", or promised him a treat for finishing. Instead she sat on the bed. "This bit is boring, isn't it?" Tejas nodded. She opened her phone and played a clip from three months earlier, where he could barely change chords. "Listen to that, and then listen to today." Tejas heard the difference and smiled. Elizabeth Ma'am, his teacher, had said something like this: the flat stretch is where the skill settles in. He picked the guitar back up.

What did Mummy Sabina put beside Tejas when he said he was bored at five?
She put a basket of old spoons and pots beside him.
How do the two scenes with Tejas show that boredom can be handled in similar ways at different ages?

At five, Mummy gave time and simple things, and the boredom turned into a band. At fifteen, she named the boredom and pointed to his earlier progress instead of telling him to quit or offering a treat, so he kept practising.
What was Tejas feeling when he sighed with slumped shoulders over the guitar piece?
He was frustrated and bored, discouraged because he saw no progress after four weeks.
What would you advise Mummy Sabina to do if the plateau lasts longer?
She could keep noticing small gains, suggest a short break or a new tune for fun, and check with Elizabeth Ma'am about what to practise.

Zubin, twenty, came to the Mumbai college from a Parsi farming family near Navsari. He wore plain cotton shirts and said "chalo" in a Gujarati way that made a group of boys call him "farm boy" every morning.
He stopped eating in the canteen and brought lunch in a steel tiffin to eat alone in the library.
One day Usha, from his economics class, found him there. "Why do you hide here?"
"The farm boy jokes."
Usha put her own tiffin down beside his. "My grandparents grew rice in Konkan. My whole family is 'farm people.' Those boys wouldn't survive one monsoon planting."
Zubin laughed for the first time in weeks.
The next day, Usha walked into the canteen with him. When a boy called out "Farm boy!", Usha said, "Yes, and he knows more about chickoos than you know about anything." The canteen laughed, but not at Zubin.

Where did Zubin eat alone?
He ate in the library, from a steel tiffin.
What was Zubin feeling when he laughed for the first time in weeks?
Zubin felt relieved and less alone, finding someone who shared and respected farm roots.
How did Usha show more class than the boys who teased?
She sat with Zubin, shared her own farming roots with pride, and walked into the canteen with him, turning the joke back on the teasers.
How might the teasing boys feel when the canteen laughs at Usha's reply?
They may feel embarrassed that their joke no longer works on Zubin.

The lightbulb sketch.

Tushar, twenty, never booked anything early. At his Bengaluru college, friends joked he decided lunch at the counter. But when the chief guest for the fest cancelled an hour before the opening, Tushar was the one who calmly rang an alumni band, rearranged the stage order and had the crowd singing in twenty minutes. Two weeks later, though, he forgot the group project deadline entirely. Sonali, his partner, was furious. "Your flexibility is great, but I can't be your calendar." Tushar felt embarrassed. That evening they agreed on two anchors: a shared calendar with alerts for every deadline, and a check-in every Monday at nine. He still decided lunch at the counter. But he never missed another submission.

What did Tushar arrange when the chief guest cancelled?
He rang an alumni band, rearranged the stage order and had the crowd singing in twenty minutes.
How did Tushar feel when Sonali got angry about the deadline?

Noah, who loves his Grammy, calls her every week to talk about his day. If each call lasts 30 minutes and he is charged $0.05 per call minute, how much would he be billed if he makes the calls for a year?

A year has 52 weeks, so if he talks for 30 minutes every week, the total number of call hours is 52*30 = 1560 minutes.
Since he is charged 0.05 cents per call, the total cost is 1560*.05 = 78 dollars
The answer is 78.

Francis, you remind me of your father Raghav when he was sixteen. Let me tell you. He had a harmonium, a stamp album and a book on carpentry, all started the same year. The harmonium he played for a month. The stamps filled three pages. The carpentry gave us one wobbly stool. Each time, he'd find something shinier. One evening I heard him tell his friend, "I'm the kind who never finishes." That worried me more than the unfinished things. So I asked him to finish just the stool, properly, with sanding and varnish. It took him six boring weeks. That stool is still in my kitchen.

How many pages did Raghav's stamps fill?

Tushar, you think I always went to the market alone? Listen to your Tanvir Chacha. When I was sixteen, in the crowded Friday bazaar, my heart suddenly pounded, my hands went numb, and I was sure I'd faint in front of everyone. It passed, but after that I was afraid of the fear. I stopped going to the bazaar. Then to the cinema. Then I would only take the bus if it was empty. My world got smaller and smaller. One day the school games teacher saw me walking the long way round and asked why. I told him. He said, 'That's panic. It can't harm you, but running from it makes it bigger.' Childminder's note, Tuesday. In the garden, Rashmi ran off toward the hedge, then stopped and looked back at me with a huge grin. I took the hint and chased her, slowly, saying "I'm going to catch you!" She shrieked. After a few rounds, she stopped, turned round and ran after me instead. We took turns until snack time. She is starting to understand the game goes both ways. Nirmala, childminder

What did Rashmi do after a few rounds?
She stopped, turned round and ran after Nirmala instead.
What was Rashmi feeling when she looked back with a grin?
She felt playful and excited, and was inviting Nirmala to chase her.
What did Nirmala's joining in help Rashmi learn?
Turn-taking, since the chasing game went both ways.
How might Rashmi's parents feel reading the note?
They would likely feel happy to hear she had such fun and is learning to take turns.

Clerval had never sympathised in my tastes for natural science; and his literary pursuits differed wholly from those which had occupied me. He came to the university with the design of making himself complete master of the oriental languages, and thus he should open a field for the plan of life he had marked out for himself. Resolved to pursue no inglorious career, he turned his eyes toward the East, as affording scope for his spirit of enterprise. The Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit languages engaged his attention, and I was easily induced to enter on the same studies. Idleness had ever been irksome to me, and now that I wished to fly from reflection, and hated my former studies, I felt great relief in being the fellow-pupil with my friend, and found not only instruction but consolation in the works of the orientalists. I did not, like him, attempt a critical knowledge of their dialects, for I did not contemplate making any other use of them than temporary amusement. I read merely to understand their meaning, and they well repaid my labours. Their melancholy is soothing, and their joy elevating, to a degree I never experienced in studying the authors of any other country. When you read their writings, life appears to consist in a warm sun and a garden of roses,—in the smiles and frowns of a fair enemy, and the fire that consumes your own heart. How different from the manly and heroical poetry of Greece and Rome!

Summarize what Victor and Clerval study, in about three sentences.

Clerval comes to university to master Eastern languages such as Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit. Victor, now tired of science and trying to escape his thoughts, studies with him. He reads the writers only for meaning and finds their poems soothing and joyful.

You asked why I've been so quiet since the maths test, Yusuf. Okay. I'm Thomas, remember, the one who's supposed to be good at maths. I got a D. And after that, something weird happened. I felt heavy, like my backpack had bricks in it. And the heavier I felt, the more sure I was: I'm just stupid. I've been faking it. The feeling was so strong it felt like proof. I stopped raising my hand. I skipped chess club. Then on Friday Ms Varghese asked me to stay back. She said, "You're treating a bad feeling like a fact about yourself. The feeling is real. The conclusion isn't." She showed me my last five tests: A, A, B, A, D. "Which one is the real you?" I didn't know what to say. She also asked me to see the school counsellor on Monday, and told my mum. So, that's why I was quiet. I'm working on it.

What were Thomas's last five test grades?
A, A, B, A, D.
Why did the heavy feeling seem like proof to Thomas?
Thomas felt ashamed and weighed down after the D, and the stronger that feeling got, the more it seemed to be a fact about being stupid.
What did Ms Varghese do that was helpful?
She named the difference between the feeling and the conclusion, showed Thomas the past results, arranged a counsellor visit and told Thomas's mum.
How might Yusuf feel hearing this?
Yusuf might feel relieved to finally understand the silence, and sympathetic toward Thomas.

In Class 4 at the Chennai school, the teacher showed two pictures of the same lane. "Which picture has more birds? Hands up!"
Tushar counted. The left had five crows on the wire. The right had seven, two hiding on a roof.
"Left!" said Mahima, and her hand shot up. Then almost every hand followed. "Left! Left!"
Tushar's hand hovered. Last week Mahima's friends had laughed for a whole day when someone said "wrong" in maths. He looked at the roof again. Seven.
Slowly, he raised his hand with everyone else. "Left."
"Let's count," said the teacher. "Right has seven."
Tushar pushed his hand into his pocket. His cheeks were hot.

How many crows did the left picture have on the wire?
The left had five crows on the wire.
Why did Tushar raise his hand for the left picture?
He was afraid of being laughed at, as Mahima's friends had done last week, so he followed the group even though he counted seven on the right.
How could the teacher help children like Tushar speak up?
The teacher could ask children to write their answer before hands go up, so each child answers from their own counting.
What is it like for Mahima when the teacher counts seven on the right?
Mahima may feel embarrassed and surprised, having answered quickly and led the others to the wrong picture.
I want to bring something to the class potluck, but I don't cook much.
A potluck is easy to join. What do you enjoy eating?
I like sandwiches and fruit.

Either works. Butter is simple and keeps well, while cheese is richer but spoils faster in a lunch box. Keep one plain option too, such as cucumber with a thin layer of chutney, so more classmates can try it.
Should I use butter or cheese?
Check with the group about food rules, and keep one plain option too, such as cucumber and a thin layer of chutney. That way more classmates can try it.
I'll make the chutney one. How should I carry it?
Pack sandwiches in an airtight box, with a sheet of paper between layers. Keep the box in your bag away from heavy items, and serve within a few hours.
My classmate lost a race. What can I say in one sentence that starts with "You"?
You ran bravely, and there will be another race soon.

Jeevan had worked out the Gurugram office within a month: lunch with the right people, a joke in the regional head's chat, a coffee order remembered. None of it felt wrong. It was just how you got noticed. The trouble started with the client pitch. Deepak had found the costing error that saved it, and at the Friday review everyone turned to him. That night Jeevan drafted a message to the regional head: "Deepak's numbers were a bit shaky earlier, I helped tighten them." It wasn't quite a lie. His thumb hovered over send. He thought of Deepak, who had lent him a charger on his first day, and of Nisha from HR saying, "People here remember who stood on whom." He deleted the second line. Then, slowly, the first.

What had Deepak found that saved the client pitch?
Deepak had found the costing error that saved it.
What was Jeevan feeling as his thumb hovered over send?
He was torn and uneasy: ambition pushed him to grab credit, but remembering Deepak's kindness made him hesitate.
Where does Jeevan's networking cross a line, and what is fine to keep?
Lunches and remembering people's orders are normal; the drafted message undermines Deepak with a half-truth, so deleting it was right.
What would change for Deepak if the message had been sent?
The regional head might quietly doubt Deepak's work without Deepak ever knowing why, hurting a colleague who had been kind.

A type C school bus contains 13 rows of seats, with an aisle running down the middle of the bus, splitting each row into two sections.  If the school only allowed two students to sit in each section, how many students could be seated on the bus?

13 rows, with 2 sections per row would contain 13*2=26 sections.
If two students sat per section, there would be capacity for 26*2=52 students.
The answer is 52.
Why does the moon shine at night?
The moon shines by reflecting sunlight. Because the moon has no light of its own, we only see the side of it that the sun lights up.
The temperature in a freezer was -3/4  degreesC at one time and -5/7  degreesC later. Which temperature was lower? Also compare -5/9 and 4/(-7).

Answer: -3/4 < -5/7, so -3/4  degreesC was lower. -5/9 > 4/(-7).

Method 1 (common denominator): LCM(4, 7) = 28. -3/4 = -21/28 and -5/7 = -20/28. -21 < -20, so -21/28 < -20/28: -3/4 is further LEFT on the number line, so it is smaller (colder). Method 2 (cross-multiplication, with POSITIVE denominators): compare (-3) x 7 = -21 with (-5) x 4 = -20. For -5/9 and 4/(-7) = -4/7: (-5) x 7 = -35 and (-4) x 9 = -36; -35 > -36, so -5/9 > -4/7. Common mistake: thinking -3/4 is greater because 3/4 > 5/7. For negative numbers the one with the BIGGER size is the SMALLER number.

I'm Wasim, and in our house everyone knows the Ooty train story. The toy train went into a dark tunnel, I screamed so loudly that a man dropped his tea, and Afreen Baji covered my eyes.
I've told it at school. I've told it to my cousins. I can smell the tea.
Last month I found the trip album. I was in a green jacket, sleeping on Ammi's lap. The date on the back said I was three.
Afreen Baji laughed when I showed her. "You woke up after the tunnel. We just told you about it."
Now when I think of the tunnel, I get two pictures. One is the story. One is the album. I don't know which one is me.

What was Wasim wearing in the trip album photo?
Wasim was in a green jacket, sleeping on Ammi's lap.
How does Wasim feel about the tunnel memory now?
Wasim feels mixed up and a little unsettled, holding two pictures of the trip and not knowing which one is really their own.
What could Wasim do when telling the story next time?
Wasim could say "this is the story my family tells" rather than "I remember", since the album suggests those details came from others.
What is it like for Afreen Baji when Wasim shows the album?
She seems amused and relaxed, seeing it as a funny family story rather than a big mistake, though she is the one who knows what really happened.

Miss Ingram, who had now seated herself with proud grace at the piano, spreading out her snowy robes in queenly amplitude, commenced a brilliant prelude; talking meantime. She appeared to be on her high horse to-night; both her words and her air seemed intended to excite not only the admiration, but the amazement of her auditors: she was evidently bent on striking them as something very dashing and daring indeed.

What is Miss Ingram trying to do with her behaviour?
She wants to impress everyone and amaze them, so she acts bold and daring while she plays the piano and talks.

a) y = x^2 and y = x^3
b) y = x^2 and y = sqrtx
c) y^2 = 4x and x^2 = 4y
d) y^2 = 9x and x^2 = 9y
e) y = x^2 and y = 2 - x^2
f) y = x^2 and y = 8 - x^2
g) y = x^2 - 2 and y = 2 - x^2
h) y = 2x^2 and y = x^2 + 4
i) y = x^3 and y = x
j) y = x^3 and y = 4x
k) y = x^4 and y = x^2
l) y = x(x - 2)^2 and y = x

n) y = 1/x and x + y = 5/2
o) y = x^2 - 2x and y = 2x - x^2

The rain had made Arnab twenty minutes late for the scholarship interview, and the waiting room was full. His aunt Kalyani had practised mock questions with him all week, but his heart was banging. He stood by the door, feet apart, and straightened his back. One slow breath in. A longer one out. He wasn't feeling brave, exactly, but steadier. When the panel called his name, he walked in and shook hands. He stumbled on the first question. Then the answers Kalyani had drilled came back, and he found his rhythm. Afterwards he told her, "The breathing helped. But the practice helped more."

How late was Arnab because of the rain?
He was twenty minutes late.
What was Arnab feeling by the door, and what helped?
His heart was banging, so he was anxious. Standing straight and taking slow breaths steadied him, and the drilled answers gave him confidence.
What should Arnab remember for future interviews?
Stand straight and breathe to calm nerves, but keep preparing with practice questions. Preparation carries the real weight.
How might Kalyani have felt hearing his words afterwards?
She probably felt glad that her mock questions helped and that he noticed. His thanks credits the practice.

On Lucia morning, Anders' school in Uppsala was full of candles and singing. Holding his trumpet, Anders told his friend Mateo, "Music is the easiest subject, and the most useful. You can play anywhere!" "What about maths?" "Maths is impossible. And pointless. When will I ever need fractions?" Mateo tilted his head. "You use fractions in music. Half notes, quarter notes. Mr Berg said so." Anders opened his mouth, then closed it. Half notes. He had counted them all morning without any trouble. "That's different," he said. "That's fun." Mateo grinned. "Maybe maths is fun when it's music."

What does Mateo say Anders uses in music?
Fractions: half notes and quarter notes.
Why does Anders call maths impossible and pointless?
He dislikes maths, so it feels hard and useless, while music feels fun and therefore easy; his feelings are answering for him.
What could help Anders see maths differently?
Noticing where he already uses it, like counting half and quarter notes, and judging a subject by what it does, not only by how it feels.
How does Mateo view Anders' claim?
Mateo sees the link Anders misses and teases him gently, perhaps hoping Anders will enjoy maths more.
Rewrite with the doer first: The window was broken by a cricket ball, and the glass was swept up by the caretaker.
A cricket ball broke the window, and the caretaker swept up the glass.

Gargi, you ask how I chose my career. Sit, let your Tanvir Chacha tell you. When I was twenty-five, two letters came in the same week. One from a thermal power company in Singrauli: good salary, a house with the job. The other from a small government lab in Pune testing solar cookers: half the pay, a room shared with another engineer. Everyone told me to take the power job. My father had borrowed for my degree. I went to Singrauli for the interview. I saw the ash ponds, grey for kilometres, and children coughing in the colony. I came back and took the solar lab. Some years were hard. Your Chachi and I lived small, and I cycled everywhere, not only for the planet but because we had no car. Forty years later, I can say my work left something good behind. You don't have to choose as I did, Gargi. Just look at what your work leaves behind.

Where was the thermal power company?
In Singrauli.
What was young Tanvir feeling after seeing the ash ponds?
Tanvir felt disturbed and unsettled by the grey ponds and coughing children, which changed his mind.
What was the turning point in Tanvir's choice, and what did it cost?
Seeing the ash ponds at the interview; Tanvir chose the solar lab, at half the salary and with years of living small.
How might Tanvir's father have felt about the choice?
His father, who had borrowed for the degree, was probably worried and disappointed at the lower pay.

Supervisor's note, customer service team, Friday.
Our new hire, Saurabh, joined from a village near Sagar. At lunch this week, a few team members mimicked his Hindi and called him “gaon ka hero.” He laughed along, but ate faster and left early.
Today Sonali, who has been with us two years, said at the table, quite gently, “Guys, can we drop that? Saurabh has handled more calls than any of us this week.” Then she moved her tray and sat next to him. She is still very much part of the old group. Nobody seemed angry with her.
I thanked Sonali privately. I will also remind the team about respectful conduct at Monday's meeting, without naming anyone.

What did some team members call Saurabh?
They called him "gaon ka hero".
How did Saurabh seem to feel during the mimicking?
He seemed embarrassed and uncomfortable, laughing along but eating faster and leaving early.
What did Sonali do that made a difference?
She asked the group gently to stop, gave a fact about Saurabh's work, and sat with him, while staying part of the old group.
How might the team members who mimicked feel after Sonali spoke?
They might feel a little embarrassed but not attacked, since she was kind and still one of them.

After a year abroad, Nikita came back to her village for the harvest festival, and a shrug came back with her. When Tanuja asked, "Will you help decorate the temple lane tomorrow?" Nikita shrugged with one shoulder, a casual gesture she'd picked up in the city she studied in, where it meant "I'm not sure yet." Tanuja's face fell. Around here, a shrug at an elder's request or a friend's plea could look careless, as if she didn't want to know. Nikita saw the change and said quickly, "Sorry, I meant I need to check with Ma first. I really want to come." Tanuja's shoulders relaxed. "Then say so with your mouth, silly." They both laughed.

What festival did Nikita come back for?
She came back to her village for the harvest festival.
How did Nikita feel when she saw Tanuja's face fall?
Nikita was probably worried that her shrug had looked careless, so she quickly apologised and said she really wanted to come.
What did Nikita do to fix it?
She noticed Tanuja's face fall and explained in words that she needed to ask her mother and really wanted to come.
How might Nikita's shrug feel to Tanuja, who stayed in the village?
It might feel dismissive, since she isn't used to that gesture from a friend, so words help bridge it.
A farmer has twice as many pigs as cows, and 4 more cows than goats.  If the farmer has 56 animals total, how many goats does he have?

Let x be the number of goats
Cows:4+x
Pigs:2(4+x)=8+2x
Total:x+4+x+8+2x=56
4x+12=56
4x=44
x=11 goats
The answer is 11.

At the hospital in Lucknow, Pranav led the operations team. Before each big change, he wrote a short entry in a register: the decision, the reasons, what could go wrong, and how sure the team was. When they moved the outpatient queue to a new token system, he wrote: "Should cut waiting by a lot. Seventy percent sure. Risk: older patients may struggle with tokens." A month later, waiting times had barely changed. At the review, some staff blamed Salma, who had designed the system. Pranav opened the register. "We expected risk with older patients. That's what happened. The design was sound; the help desk wasn't ready." Salma's shoulders dropped with relief. The team decided to add two volunteers at the token counter. Nobody was scolded. Everyone learned something.

What risk did Pranav write down before the token system?
Older patients may struggle with tokens.
How did Salma feel when Pranav opened the register?
Salma felt relieved, her shoulders dropping, because the record showed the problem was expected and not her fault.
What did the register allow the team to do?
It let them compare the decision with what happened, find the real gap at the help desk, and fix it without blaming anyone.
How might the staff who blamed Salma see the review afterward?
They might feel a little embarrassed, but also clearer about what really went wrong.
Every student who finishes early may read a book. Rahul is reading a book. Did he finish early?
We cannot be sure. Because the rule says early finishers may read, but it does not say that only they may read, Rahul could be reading for another reason.

“Papa, the chatbot said it's happy for me!”
Mohit looked up from his newspaper. “Happy about what, Himani?”
“I told it I won the drawing competition. It said, 'I'm so happy for you!'”
“That's nice. But does it really feel happy?”
Himani thought. “It said so.”
“It's a program. It's built to write kind words. It doesn't have a heart or a tummy that jumps.”
“So it's pretending?”
“Kind of. It can't feel anything. And sometimes it gets facts wrong too.”
Himani put the tablet down. “Then I'm telling Dadi. She'll be really happy.”
Mohit smiled. “She will.”

What had Himani won?
The drawing competition.
How did Himani feel when she decided to tell Dadi?
She felt excited and eager to share her news with someone who would really be happy.
How did Mohit help Himani understand chatbots?
He asked a question and explained simply that it is a program that writes kind words but can't feel.
How might Dadi react to Himani's news?
Dadi would probably feel truly proud and happy for Himani.

messages.content: Yoga class mein teacher ne bola 'Inhale deeply'. Inhale aur exhale ka matlab?
"Inhale" means breathe in. "Exhale" means breathe out. Example: "Inhale slowly through your nose, then exhale through your mouth."

You want to know what it was like? Okay. I'm Rehana, and I was twelve and at my cousin's wedding in Hyderabad when it started.

My Khala pulled me into a side room and whispered everything like it was a crime: "Don't tell anyone. Don't let your brothers see. Wrap the packet in newspaper." I felt like I'd done something wrong. For a year I hid pads in my maths box.

My friend Pallavi was the one who said, "Why are you hiding them? It's just a period." Her mother is a nurse. She sat us both down at their dining table and explained it all with a diagram on a napkin: what's happening, why it's healthy, what's normal, and when to check with a doctor.

I went home and told Ammi I didn't want to hide it any more. She was quiet, then said, "My mother made me hide it too. You don't have to."

Now they sit in the bathroom cupboard, like a normal thing.

Where did Rehana hide pads for a year?
Rehana hid pads in the maths box.
How did Rehana feel after Khala's whispered instructions?
Rehana felt ashamed, as if something wrong had been done, and kept it hidden for a year.
What helped replace secrecy with facts?
Pallavi's mother explaining plainly with a diagram what is happening and what is normal, and then Rehana telling Ammi openly.
What might Ammi have felt when Rehana said no more hiding?
Ammi seemed quietly moved, remembering being made to hide it herself, and relieved to let Rehana stop.

Dear Chaitanya,

I didn't want to say this at the café, so I'm writing.

You've cancelled on us three Sundays in a row. When we did meet, you were checking your laptop under the table. You told me you'd slept four hours because the header on your grant application "looked wrong." I looked at it. It looked fine. You kept pointing to a line spacing I couldn't even see.

I'm worried. Not about the grant; about you.

Here's an offer. Send me the application tonight, as it is. I'll treat it as a draft that's already fine, not a final. I'll mark only the things that actually matter. Then you close the laptop and come to lunch on Sunday.

The grant will be fine. You're more important than the spacing.

Baljeet

How many Sundays has Chaitanya cancelled?
Three Sundays in a row.
How does Baljeet feel about what's happening with Chaitanya?
Baljeet feels worried, more about Chaitanya's lost sleep and cancelled plans than about the grant.
Why might Baljeet's offer to read it as a 'good enough draft' help?
It lets Chaitanya share imperfect work safely with a friend, which can make flaws feel survivable and let the work be finished.
How might Chaitanya feel receiving this letter?
Chaitanya might feel embarrassed at first, then relieved and cared for that someone noticed the strain.

Two runners are competing in a 10-mile race.  The first runs at an average pace of 8 minutes per mile, while the second runs at an average pace of 7 minutes per mile.  After 56 minutes, the second runner stops for a drink of water.  For how many minutes could the second runner remain stopped before the first runner catches up with him?

After 56 minutes, the second runner has traveled 56/7 = 8 miles.
Similarly, the first runner has traveled 56/8 = 7 miles.
Therefore, the two runners are 8 - 7 = 1 mile apart when the second runner stops.
Thus, the second runner can stop for a maximum of 8 minutes, which is the amount of time it takes the first runner to travel 1 mile.
The answer is 8.

The scooter skidded on loose gravel and the rider, Pradeep, lay in the road by the bend. Pranav, on his bike, pulled over well off the tarmac, switched on his hazard lights, looked up the road for oncoming traffic, and only then called the emergency number for an ambulance and the police. In his head ran the steps from a first-aid class: check safety, get help coming, leave a badly hurt person where they are unless the spot is dangerous, and tell only what you know. He gave the operator the place and what he saw, with no guesses.

Beside him, Madhav had jumped off a bus and lifted his phone to record. Madhav stood there filming while Pradeep lay waiting. Nobody had called anyone. Only when Pranav said, "Have you called?" did Madhav lower the phone and dial with him.

Days later Pranav still heard the brakes at night and could not settle. He talked it over with his family and saw a doctor about the sleepless nights. He also made new rules for himself: helmet every ride, slower on bends, no night rides on that road.

What did Pranav do before calling the emergency number?
He pulled over off the tarmac, switched on his hazard lights, and looked up the road for oncoming traffic.
How did Madhav's response differ from Pranav's, and what did that mean for Pradeep?
Pranav made himself safe and called for help at once, while Madhav filmed and nobody called, so Pradeep waited longer for trained help.
What was Pranav feeling in the days after the crash?
Shaken and unsettled: he still heard the brakes at night and could not settle.
What could a bystander do if they freeze?
They could take a breath and go through simple steps: check safety, ask someone to call, and stay near the injured person.

I'm Gargi, Mridul's big sister. At the library on Saturday, Mridul shouted, “A shark book!” The librarian didn't shout back. She held up a card with a sleeping mouse on it and put her finger on her lips. Mridul looked at the card, then whispered, “Shark book.” Later we went to the playground next door, and she held up the other side of the card, a roaring lion. Mridul roared so loud a pigeon flew off. I don't know if he understood, but he copied the pictures.

What was on the other side of the librarian's card?
A roaring lion.
What might Mridul have been feeling when he shouted about the shark book?
He was excited to find a shark book and forgot to use a quiet voice. Gargi isn't sure if he understood the cards, but he seemed happy to copy them.
Why did the picture card work better than shouting to be quiet?
It gave Mridul a clear, calm reminder he could see and copy, without a loud scolding.
How might the librarian see Mridul's roar on the playground?
The librarian would likely be pleased, since the loud voice now fit the place.
Why do we leave a gap between our vehicle and the one ahead?
It gives time to stop. Because a vehicle cannot halt at once, and if the one ahead brakes suddenly, a gap lets us stop without hitting it.

In the kasba, news travelled faster than the bus. By Tuesday, Tushar pulled Raghav aside at the tea stall. “People are saying you took money from the temple donation box. The Rath Yatra collection.”
Raghav felt the blood rush to his face. “What? I only helped count it!”
“I know. But Pintu's mother is telling everyone.”
All the way home, Raghav felt eyes on him. The shopkeeper looked twice. Two aunties stopped talking. He wanted to disappear into the ground. Who even started it?
At home, he told his father everything. His father put down his newspaper, said, “I believe you,” and that evening walked with Raghav to the temple committee to ask for the collection records to be checked in front of everyone.

What were people saying Raghav took?
Money from the temple donation box, the Rath Yatra collection.
What was Raghav feeling on the way home?
He felt ashamed and afraid of every glance, wishing he could disappear into the ground.
How did Raghav's father respond, and why did it help?
He believed Raghav and went with him that evening to ask for the records to be checked openly, which gives facts a chance against the rumour.
How might Tushar have felt telling Raghav about the rumour?
Tushar was probably uneasy but loyal, wanting a friend to know even though it was hard to say.
Uncle Ben has 440 chickens on his farm. 39 are roosters and the rest are hens. 15 of his hens do not lay eggs, and the rest do. If each egg-laying hen lays 3 eggs, how many eggs will Uncle Ben have?

Uncle Ben has 440 chickens - 39 roosters = 401 hens.
Uncle Ben has 401 hens - 15 that don't lay eggs = 386 hens that lay eggs.
The egg-laying hens each lay 3 eggs * 386 hens = 1158 eggs.
The answer is 1158.

I'm Hemant, and I've shared a flat with Tanvir for two years, so I saw most of it.
Last winter he came home, dropped his bag and lay on the sofa with his phone until one or two. Every night. He wasn't miserable, he said. Just bored of everything.
Then in February I noticed a toolbox by the door. He'd signed up for a cycle-repair course at the community workshop. Saturdays, he came back with oily hands, talking fast about gears.
In March he started helping at the food bank on Tuesday evenings. He didn't say much about it, but he started cooking dinner again.
One night he told me the grey feeling still came back some weeks, heavy. He'd booked an appointment with a doctor to talk about it. I thought that was braver than any of the rest.
I don't know what's in his head. But he laughs more now.

What did Tanvir sign up for in February?
A cycle-repair course at the community workshop.
How did Hemant feel when Tanvir mentioned booking a doctor?
Hemant felt respect and admiration, seeing it as braver than any of the other changes.
What steps did Tanvir take, and why are they wise?
He learned a new skill, volunteered at the food bank, and when the heaviness kept coming back he booked a doctor, rather than waiting it out.
How might Tanvir feel coming home on Saturdays with oily hands?
He probably feels more alive and interested, since he talks fast about gears instead of lying silently on the sofa.

Read this:

"It's all in your head, Bhavna. Just be strong," her father said, not looking up from the fertiliser receipts. Her mother nodded and passed her a plate. Bhavna carried it to the courtyard and did not eat. Home from college for the break, she had barely slept in weeks and cried in the bathroom with the tap running, and the one sentence she had finally managed had been waved away like smoke. She felt small and foolish. For two days she said nothing. Then she walked to the school and found Kunal Sir, who had taught her in Class Ten. She told him exactly what was happening: no sleep, no appetite, no interest in anything. "What you feel is real," he said. "Let me come and speak to your parents, and we can go to the health centre together."

Who had taught Bhavna in Class Ten?
Kunal Sir had taught her.
How did Bhavna feel after her father's reply?
Dismissed, small and foolish, as if the sentence she had managed was waved away like smoke.
Why did going to Kunal Sir with specifics help?
It gave her concrete things to describe and brought a respected adult ally who could speak to her parents and go to the health centre with her.
How might Bhavna's father have seen his own words?
He may have thought he was encouraging her to be strong, without realising they made her feel dismissed.
It's my first time cooking pasta and I'm afraid it'll stick together.
Use a large pot with plenty of boiling, salted water, and stir during the first minute or two. Does your pasta packet have instructions?
Yes, it says ten minutes.
Follow that, but taste a piece at nine minutes. When it's soft with a little bite, drain it and rinse with warm water if you're not adding sauce at once.
What if it still sticks?
Toss it with a spoon of oil. Next time, stir more at the start and keep the water bubbling.
I'll report back with pasta pictures.
I'd love to hear how it turned out. Good luck.
My coach said I'd "get the hang of it" after a few classes. What is "the hang"?

"Get the hang of something" means to learn how to do it. "Hang" here just means the way it works, and it is informal.
Example: Cycling felt hard at first, but Leena soon got the hang of it.

Read this:

Clara, two, saw the ducks at the pond in Leeds and shrieked with joy, flapping her arms.
When her dad said it was time to go, she dropped flat on the wet path, kicking and wailing. Wei did not shout. He crouched beside her. "You loved those ducks. It's hard to leave."
He waited, one hand near her back. Slowly her kicks stopped. She crawled onto his knee and waved. "Bye, ducks."

What did Clara do when it was time to go?
She dropped flat on the wet path, kicking and wailing.
How was Clara feeling when she lay on the path?
She was angry and upset about leaving the ducks, and too small to calm down on her own.
What helped Clara settle, and why might it work?
Wei stayed close and calm, named her feeling and waited, so she could borrow his calm until her body slowed.
How might Wei feel while Clara kicks and wails on the path?
He may feel tired or tense, but he chooses to stay calm and close so she can learn to settle.
