Read this:

When Bhavna came back from the fields at sunset, her son Hrithik, two, was sitting on his aunt's lap on the charpai in their village courtyard. He saw his mother at the gate, slid off, and ran to her with his arms out. He pressed his cheek against her dusty sari and patted her face with both hands. When his aunt called him back for his roti, he shook his head and held on tighter.

Where was Hrithik sitting when Bhavna came back?
On his aunt's lap on the charpai.
What does Hrithik patting Bhavna's face suggest?
He felt happy and loving at seeing his mother after the long day. 🤍
How could Bhavna respond to Hrithik's affection after a tiring day?
Hold him for a few minutes before anything else, even if she is tired.
How might the aunt feel when Hrithik won't come back for his roti?
She may feel a small pang of being left out, but also understand that he missed his mother.

Anu has 8 stickers. Her friend gives her 6 more. How many stickers does she have now? Show how you make 10 first.

Now you try: 8 + 5.
The answer is 8 + 2 + 3 = 13.

Read this:

Preschool note, spring.

Zeenat and Aarush both grabbed the swing at the same time today. They pulled, and Aarush pushed her. Zeenat cried.

I asked them what we could do. Zeenat said, "Take turns." We counted to twenty for each turn.

After her turn, Zeenat said, "Sorry for grabbing." Aarush said, "Sorry for pushing." They played on the slide together after. — Thomas

How long was each turn on the swing?
They counted to twenty for each turn.
How did Zeenat feel when Aarush pushed her?
Zeenat was hurt and upset, and she cried.
How did Thomas help the children solve the problem?
He asked them for ideas, helped them take turns with counting, and let them apologise themselves.
How might Aarush feel after saying sorry?
Aarush likely felt relieved and happier, playing on the slide with Zeenat.

Read this:

Thursday night.
Saurabh's report card came today. Maths: 34. I am his mother, and I sat on the bed and felt sick. At the lift, Mrs Bhatia said her son "just does tuition, simple." I smiled and wanted to scream.
Part of me wants to sit with him for two hours every night and drill tables. Part of me wants to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter. Neither feels right.
I met his class teacher after school. She said he tries hard and suggested the school's learning support twice a week. We agreed to try.
Then Saurabh showed me the clay temple he made for art. Every tiny bell. I put it on the TV shelf where everyone will see it.

What mark did Saurabh get in maths?
He got 34 in maths.
How did the mother feel about pushing or protecting Saurabh?
She felt torn and anxious, wanting both to drill him every night and to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter.
What steps help keep the family steady?
Meeting the class teacher, agreeing to try learning support and proudly displaying Saurabh's clay temple to celebrate his talent.
How might Saurabh feel seeing the clay temple on the TV shelf?
Saurabh may feel proud and valued, knowing his mother celebrates what he is good at, not only his maths marks.
What is Joe Gargery's job?
Joe is the village blacksmith. He is married to Pip's sister and is a kind, gentle friend to Pip.
Why was Devavrata given the name Bhishma?
To let his father marry Satyavati, he vowed never to claim the throne and never to marry. Because the vow was so terrible, he was called Bhishma.

Read this:

Friday night

Mummy checked my unit test marks at the gate today before even saying hi. 72 in physics. Her face did the thing. "Only 72, Tarun? Sharma aunty's daughter got 90." Then silence all the way home.

When I get 90, she hugs me. When I get 72, she goes cold. Sometimes I think she only loves the marks.

I stayed in my room all evening and didn't come out for dinner. Then I heard her on the phone with Nani, and she said, "I just don't want him to struggle like I did. I never got to finish college." Her voice was shaking.

I didn't know that.

I went and sat next to her. I said, "Mummy, when you go quiet after marks, it feels like you stop loving me. What would help is if we made a study plan together on Sundays, and on other nights we just have dinner without talking about tests."

She hugged me for a long time. She said yes to the Sunday plan.

What mark did Tarun get in physics?
Tarun got 72 in physics.
What did Tarun feel when Mummy went quiet after seeing the marks?
Tarun felt hurt and unloved, as if her love depended on his marks.
What did Tarun ask for that could help both of them?
Tarun asked for a Sunday study plan together and calm dinners on other nights without talk of tests.
How might Mummy's own past shape the way she pushes Tarun?
Having never finished college herself, she seems afraid he will struggle as she did, so her fear comes out as pressure.
What does deliberate mean?

As an adjective, deliberate means done on purpose, or slow and careful. As a verb, to deliberate means to think carefully before deciding.
Example: Spilling the paint was an accident, not a deliberate act.

Read this:

Day one: Nilesh left the office at 6:00 sharp, as his offer letter said. The next morning Reena, a senior on his team, said lightly, 'Leaving early yesterday?' He went red and didn't know what to say. Day four: he stayed until 7:30, watching when others packed up. The rule seemed to be: never leave before the team lead. He also noticed that people used the manager's first name in chat, never in meetings. He wrote all this in a notebook, feeling like a spy and a fool. Week three, Friday: Reena saw his list and laughed. 'Half of these are real. The leaving one, no. Our lead stays late because she has calls with another time zone. Leave at six if your work's done.' Nilesh crossed it out, embarrassed and very relieved.

What time did Nilesh leave on day one?
At 6:00 sharp.
How did Nilesh feel while writing the rules in a notebook?
He felt anxious and foolish, like a spy and a fool, trying hard not to misstep.
What helped Nilesh most, and what could he try sooner next time?
Reena's honest check of his list; next time he could ask a friendly senior early instead of guessing for weeks.
Why might Reena have laughed at the list?
Reena probably found it both funny and a little sweet, seeing how hard he was trying, and wanted to set him straight kindly.

Read this:

Devika's offer letter arrived on a Tuesday, from the consulting firm that everyone in her Pune hostel batch had been chasing since second year. Her flatmates ordered cake and made her cut it on the balcony. Her cousin Kamal called from Bengaluru. "You did it, yaar! Remember how we all said only the best get in?" Devika laughed at the right places. Later, washing the knife in the small kitchen, she noticed she felt nothing much, only tired. The work would be spreadsheets for companies she did not care about. The weekends she had spent teaching reading to kids at the basti school down the lane suddenly felt more real than the letter lying on her bed. She opened her laptop and read the offer again, waiting for the happiness to arrive.

What did Devika's flatmates do when her offer letter came?
They ordered cake and made her cut it on the balcony.
How does Devika feel after the celebration, and what shows it?
She feels tired and hollow rather than proud; she laughs on the phone with Kamal, but alone at the sink she notices she feels nothing much and keeps waiting for happiness.
What could Devika try before she accepts the job?
She could list what she values, like the teaching she does on weekends, and talk it through with someone she trusts, so her next choice is based on her own reasons.
How does Kamal see Devika's news?
To Kamal it is a clear win, proof she is among "the best", so he may not guess that she feels empty about it.

Read this:

Disha, you're nervous about joining the college in Delhi? Let your Mahima Bua tell you about hers.
I was nineteen, from a village near Rewa. First day, I wore my best salwar suit and oiled my hair. The city girls laughed. "Gaon wali," one said, loud enough. When I answered in class, they copied my accent.
For a month I sat alone and thought of going home. Then one evening, I remembered my father walking me to the bus, telling everyone in the village, "My daughter is going to college in Delhi." I thought: I'm not ashamed of him. Why should I be ashamed of where I'm from?
The next day I spoke up in class again, in my own accent. A girl named Rukhsana came and sat with me at lunch. She said, "I like how you say things. It's real." We were friends for forty years.
So, Disha: keep your roots, find your Rukhsana.

What did the city girls call Mahima?
One said, "Gaon wali," loud enough.
How did Mahima feel during the month she sat alone?
Mahima felt lonely and ashamed, thinking of going home after being mocked.
What was the turning point in Mahima's story?
Remembering her father's pride helped her feel pride in her roots and speak up again in her own accent.
How might Rukhsana have seen Mahima?
Rukhsana saw her as real and interesting, liking how she spoke rather than mocking it.

Name the method: direct, contrapositive, contradiction, exhaustion, counterexample (or say it is not a proof).
a) Suppose sqrt5 = a/b in lowest terms ... so 5 divides both a and b.
b) n = 2k + 1, so n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1.
c) The last digit of n is 0, 1, ..., 9; in every case n^2 does not end in 3.
d) To show "if n^2 is odd then n is odd", assume n is even; then n^2 = 4k^2 is even.
e) n = 7 gives 2n + 1 = 15, which is not prime.
f) Suppose there is a largest prime P; consider 2 x 3 x 5 x ... x P + 1.
g) a^2 + b^2 - 2ab = (a - b)^2 >= 0.
h) n = 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2; in each case n^3 - n is a multiple of 3.
i) To show "if xy is irrational then x or y is irrational", assume x and y are both rational; then xy is rational.
j) The claim "all quadrilaterals with equal sides are squares" fails for a rhombus with a 60 degrees angle.
k) Assume 2 + sqrt3 = r is rational; then sqrt3 = r - 2 is rational.
l) (n + 1)^2 - n^2 = 2n + 1.
m) Checking the 6 possible remainders of n on division by 6 ...
n) x = 0.5 shows that "x^2 > x for all real x" is false.
o) Suppose an even number E is the largest; then E + 2 is even and larger.
p) To prove "if 5n + 3 is even then n is odd", assume n is even: 5n + 3 = 10k + 3 is odd.
q) A computer checks n = 1 to 1,000 and finds no case where ... fails.
r) Squares of 1 to 10 are listed and none ends in 7, so no square ends in 7.

a) contradiction
b) direct
c) exhaustion
d) contrapositive
e) counterexample
f) contradiction
g) direct
h) exhaustion
i) contrapositive
j) counterexample
k) contradiction
l) direct
m) exhaustion
n) counterexample
o) contradiction
p) contrapositive
q) not a proof (only evidence)
r) not a proof (only 10 examples; a correct version uses the 10 last digits)

Read this:

You asked me what the hardest thing about Class 11 was? Honestly, it wasn't exams. I'm Shreya, and it was Ritu.
Ritu's my best friend. We've done everything together since we were ten. But last year something shifted. When she held my hand crossing the road, my heart went crazy. When she talked about a boy she liked, I felt sick and couldn't explain why.
I didn't know what it meant. Was it just close friendship? Something more? And my family has very fixed ideas about who I'll marry one day, so even thinking the question felt dangerous.
I didn't say anything to Ritu. I didn't try to name it. I went to the school counsellor, who said, "You don't need an answer this week. Feelings can take time to understand."
That helped so much. I'm still figuring it out, slowly. And Ritu's still my best friend.

What did the school counsellor say to Shreya?
"You don't need an answer this week. Feelings can take time to understand."
How did Shreya feel when Ritu talked about a boy she liked?
Shreya felt sick and confused, unable to explain the feeling, which added to the uncertainty.
Which choice helped Shreya, and why?
Talking to the school counsellor without rushing to a label gave Shreya permission to take time.
How might Ritu see their friendship right now?
Ritu probably sees it as the same close friendship as always, since Shreya has not told her about the changing feelings.
Write a four-line poem about the wind, where each line has exactly four words.

The wind swings gates
It lifts the kites
It shakes the trees
Then it falls quiet

Read this:

The final whistle went on the muddy pitch behind the leisure centre in Leeds, and Alejandro's team had lost four to three. He had missed the last penalty. He sat on the bench, shoulders shaking, tears mixing with the drizzle. Coach Chidi walked past with the ball bag. "Come on, it's only a game. Enough crying." Two boys snickered. Alejandro scrubbed his face hard with his sleeve and stared at his boots. In the car his mum asked how it went. "Fine," he said. That night he lay awake replaying the ball skimming past the post, and told no one. The next Saturday he scraped his knee badly in training, bit his lip, and said it didn't hurt.

What was the final score?
Alejandro's team had lost four to three.
Why did Alejandro say "Fine" in the car?
He still felt hurt and ashamed about the missed penalty, but after being told to stop crying he was hiding it rather than risk being mocked again.
What could a coach say to a child crying after a loss?
Something like "That penalty really stings, doesn't it?" while sitting beside him for a minute, before any talk about next time.
What would change if Coach Chidi had sat down beside Alejandro instead?
Alejandro might have cried a bit longer and then told someone about the penalty, learning that big feelings are allowed instead of something to hide.
A circular pond of radius 14 m has a path 7 m wide all round it. Find the area of the path. (pi = 22/7)

Answer: 770 m^2.

The path is a RING (annulus): the big circle minus the small circle. Outer radius R = 14 + 7 = 21 m, inner radius r = 14 m. area = piR^2 - pir^2 = pi(R^2 - r^2) = 22/7 x (441 - 196) = 22/7 x 245 = 770 m^2 Common mistakes: using the width 7 as a radius (pi x 7^2 is a small circle, not the ring), and subtracting the radii before squaring (21 - 14 = 7).

Read this:

The Sunday football group in Salt Lake had fourteen regulars and no rules except "turn up". Dhruv, new to Kolkata for a testing job, turned up.

He wasn't good at football. So he did other things. He started bringing a crate of water bottles. He remembered that Vidya, the organiser, was studying for an exam, and asked how it went. When the youngest player needed interview tips for his first job, Dhruv spent two evenings practising with him.

After six months, Vidya asked him to help run the group's chat and the monthly fee sheet. "You're the one who notices things," she said.

In August, the flat Dhruv rented flooded overnight. He sent one message to the group, not expecting much. By eight in the morning, three of them were there with buckets, and Vidya had found him a sofa to sleep on for the week.

Dhruv stood in the wet hallway, laughing and close to tears.

How many regulars did the Sunday football group have?
The group had fourteen regulars.
What was Dhruv feeling as he stood in the wet hallway?
Dhruv felt overwhelmed with relief and gratitude, laughing and close to tears, because people he had quietly supported came to help.
How did Dhruv build trust in the group even though he was not good at football?
He showed up every Sunday, brought water, remembered people's lives and gave his time, making himself reliable and useful.
How does Vidya see Dhruv's role in the group?
Vidya sees him as the one who notices things, which is why she trusts him to help run the group and finds him a place to stay.

Read this:

Noor joined Class 4B in January, while paper snowflakes from the winter fair still hung in the school hall. On her first morning she came in late, cheeks red from the cold, and snapped "No!" when Simran offered to share a bench.
"She's rude," Simran told her friends at lunch.
Over the next weeks Noor lent out her glue stick, clapped loudest at the class play and helped Simran pick up a spilled box of beads. Simran mumbled thanks but still whispered, "She's only nice when Miss is watching."
When the teacher paired them for the science chart, Simran's shoulders sagged. Anyone but the rude girl, she thought.

What did Noor say when Simran offered to share a bench?
Noor snapped "No!" when Simran offered to share a bench.
Why does Simran keep calling Noor rude, even after the glue stick and the beads?
Simran felt hurt by that first "No!", and now she feels sure she already knows who Noor is, so kind acts look like a show to her.
How could the teacher help Simran look past the first day?
The teacher could ask Simran to name three things Noor has done since January, like lending her glue stick, and talk about how that first cold, late morning might have felt.
What might the first day have been like for Noor?
Noor was new, late and cold, so she may have been nervous and snapped without meaning to be unkind, and then found it hard to change how others saw her.

There were three jars of candy in the cabinet. The jar of peanut butter candy had 4 times as much candy as the jar of grape candy. The jar of grape candy had 5 more pieces of candy than the jar of banana candy. How many pieces of candy did the peanut butter jar have if the banana jar had 43?

The grape jar had 43+5 = 48 pieces of candy.
The peanut butter jar had 48*4 = 192 pieces of candy.
The answer is 192.

Of the e-mails reaching an inbox, 40% are spam. The word "lottery" appears in 90% of spam e-mails and in 5% of genuine ones. An e-mail contains "lottery". Find the probability that it is spam, and explain the "prosecutor's fallacy".

Answer: P(spam | word) = 0.36 / (0.36 + 0.03) = 12/13 ~ 0.9231.

Branches: spam with the word 0.4 x 0.9 = 0.36; genuine with the word 0.6 x 0.05 = 0.03. P(word) = 0.39. The PROSECUTOR'S FALLACY confuses P(evidence | innocent) with P(innocent | evidence): "only 5% of genuine mails contain the word, so there is only a 5% chance this one is genuine" is WRONG; the correct value is 0.03/0.39 ~ 7.7%, and it would be much higher if spam were rarer. In court, "the chance of such a DNA match by accident is 1 in a million" does not mean "the chance the accused is innocent is 1 in a million": in a city of 10 million people about 10 would match.

Read this:

The power cut came with the thunder, and Jeevan set a lantern on the verandah floor. Alka did not look up. She was drawing a train, wheel by coloured wheel, while rain drummed on the tin roof.
"Dinner is getting cold," said Jeevan, her uncle.
"Mm," said Alka, and added a window.
When the last wheel was done she pushed the page aside without showing anyone, rubbed her eyes, and said, "I'm so hungry!"

What was Alka drawing on the verandah floor?
She was drawing a train, wheel by coloured wheel.
What does Alka's 'Mm' suggest about how she feels while Jeevan speaks?
She is so wrapped up in the train that she hardly hears him. She is content and focused, not being rude.
What would help Jeevan when he wants Alka to come to dinner?
He could wait until she finishes the wheels, or tell her dinner comes in a few minutes so she can end the train herself.
How might Jeevan see Alka pushing the page aside without showing anyone?
He might notice she drew for herself rather than for praise, and that her hunger only arrived once the drawing was done.

Read this:

"Rajni, why are you standing by the tree? The girls are skipping."
"I'm waiting, Mumma."
"Waiting for what?"
"For them to say come."
Sharmila sat on the bench. "What if you ask? Let's practise. I'm a skipping girl. Go."
"Can I... play too?"
"Louder, like you mean it."
"Can I play too?"
"Good! Being shy is okay. It gets smaller every time you try."
Rajni walked to the rope. Her voice was small but clear. "Can I play too?"
"Yes! You hold one end!"

What were the girls doing?
The girls were skipping.
Why was Rajni standing by the tree?
She felt shy and unsure, and she was waiting for the girls to invite her instead of asking.
What did Sharmila say about shyness that could help Rajni?
She said being shy is okay and gets smaller every time you try, and she let Rajni practise first.
How might the skipping girls feel when Rajni asks?
They seem pleased to include her, and happily give her a job holding the rope.

Read this:

At the software company in Noida, Harsha waited outside his manager's cabin with a printed resignation letter. He had rewritten it five times.
He had a new job offer: a smaller company, a role closer to what he wanted. He felt relief when he thought about it. But he also felt guilty. Jatin, his manager, had hired him out of college and taught him most of what he knew. His parents were worried. "Such a big company," his mother kept saying.
Jatin called him in. Harsha's voice wobbled as he explained.
Jatin read the letter and sat back. "I'm sad. But I'm not surprised. You've wanted design work for a year."
"I'll stay the full notice period," Harsha said quickly. "And I've made a handover document for the payments module. I can train whoever takes over."
Jatin smiled for the first time. "That's the part people remember."
Walking back to his desk, Harsha felt his shoulders drop an inch.

What had Harsha made for the payments module?
A handover document for the payments module.
What mix of feelings did Harsha have about leaving?
Harsha felt relief about the new role but guilt toward Jatin, who had taught him so much, and worry about his parents' fears.
What did Harsha do that made the leaving graceful?
He told Jatin in person, committed to the full notice period, prepared a handover document and offered to train his replacement.
How does Jatin feel about Harsha's news?
Jatin feels sad but not surprised, and appreciates the careful handover.

Read this:

On the morning of Raksha Bandhan, Rekha stood outside her younger sister Disha's flat with a rakhi in her bag and her heart pounding.
Two years ago Disha had told Rekha's secret, a failed marriage proposal, to the whole family. Rekha had cut her off.
She rang the bell. Disha opened the door, and her face crumpled.
"I was so stupid," Disha whispered.
"You were," Rekha said. Then, more softly, "I've been angry for two years. I don't want to be angry for three."
She tied the rakhi on Disha's wrist, even though that wasn't the tradition between sisters. Disha laughed through her tears.
Rekha felt lighter walking home, as if she'd put down a heavy bag.

What secret did Disha tell the family?
Rekha's failed marriage proposal.
How did Rekha feel walking home?
She felt lighter and relieved, as if she had put down a heavy bag.
What made Rekha's forgiveness real rather than forced?
She admitted the hurt and anger but chose to let it go, making a gesture of love.
How might Disha feel when Rekha ties the rakhi?
Disha likely felt forgiven and overwhelmed, laughing through her tears.

Read this:

Neelam: Amit, can I say something about Chandrika without you getting upset?
Amit: go ahead
Neelam: she cried through both our calls this week. she said she hasn't eaten since morning and that she's scared to be alone with the baby
Amit: I've noticed she stays in bed a lot. I thought she's just tired, the nights are rough
Neelam: tired is part of it. but it's been nearly a month. I think a doctor should see her. not because she's doing anything wrong
Amit: you're right. I kept waiting for it to pass
Neelam: tell her it's a check-up for her, like the baby's. no blame
Amit: I just rang the clinic. tomorrow 10am. I'll take tonight's feeds so she can sleep
Neelam: I'll come Saturday and Sunday and do the cooking and the washing 🙏
Amit: thank you. I'll tell her we're doing this together

When is Chandrika's appointment?
Tomorrow at 10am.
What was Amit feeling before Neelam's message, and how can you tell?
Amit was uneasy but hopeful it would pass, having noticed Chandrika staying in bed and kept waiting, assuming she was just tired.
What went well in how Neelam raised the worry?
Neelam named specific signs, asked for a doctor's check without blaming Chandrika, and offered practical help with cooking and washing.
How might Chandrika experience being told 'we're doing this together'?
She may feel less ashamed and alone, and more able to accept the check-up and the rest that sharing the feeds gives her.

Read this:

At the lockers of their Toronto high school, Camila spotted Bao and called, "Bao! Did you see the new art room?" Bao glanced at her, then turned his whole body towards the wall and pressed his forehead against his locker door. Camila's wave froze in the air. Great. What did I do? All through Spanish she replayed Friday: had she laughed too loudly at his drawing? She almost left him out of the plan for Saturday. Instead, after school, she found him on the bus bench and sat down a little distance away. "Hey. Earlier, did I do something?" Bao rubbed his eyes. "No. My grandma's in hospital. I'd just got a text. I couldn't talk to anyone." Camila nodded and simply sat with him until his bus came.

What did Camila call out to Bao about?
The new art room.
What was Camila feeling when her wave froze in the air?
Camila felt hurt and worried, sure she had done something wrong and replaying Friday to find it.
What kept Camila's friendship with Bao steady?
Not acting on the snub, such as leaving him out of Saturday's plan, and asking him quietly later instead.
What was that moment at the lockers like for Bao?
Bao had just learned his grandma was in hospital and was too upset to talk to anyone; turning away had nothing to do with Camila.

metadata.subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Nikita: ok I need a sanity check
Nikita: in the team meeting, Siddhesh said "girls can do the slides, boys will handle the coding"
Nikita: I literally wrote half the code last sprint
Tanuja: WHAT
Nikita: everyone just moved on. I didn't say anything
Nikita: am I overreacting? he probably didn't mean it like that
Tanuja: you're not overreacting. but you also don't HAVE to fight it

messages.content: Arrange in ascending order: -2/3, 5/(-6), 1/2, -7/12, 0, 3/4.

Answer: 5/(-6) < -2/3 < -7/12 < 0 < 1/2 < 3/4.

First make every denominator positive: 5/(-6) = -5/6. The LCM of 3, 6, 2, 12 and 4 is 12, so write each with denominator 12: -2/3 = -8/12, -5/6 = -10/12, 1/2 = 6/12, -7/12, 0 = 0/12, 3/4 = 9/12. Now order the numerators: -10 < -8 < -7 < 0 < 6 < 9. Write the ORIGINAL numbers in that order. Quick check: the negatives come first, then 0, then the positives.

To win a brand new Bible at Tom Sawyer's Sunday school, a pupil has to win 10 yellow tickets; each yellow ticket is obtained by trading in 10 red tickets; each red ticket is obtained by trading in 10 blue tickets; and blue tickets are earned by memorizing two Bible verses. But rather than go to all that trouble, Tom Sawyer has traded various toys and treasures of his with his friends until he has gathered 8 yellow, 3 red, and 7 blue tickets. How many more blue tickets would he need to earn to win a new Bible?

A red ticket is equal to 10 blue tickets, and a yellow is equal to ten red tickets, so a yellow ticket is also equal to 10 * 10 = 100 blue tickets.
It takes 10 yellow tickets to win a Bible, or 10 * 100 = 1000 blue tickets.
Tom has 8 yellow tickets, which are worth 8 * 100 = 800 blue tickets.
He also has 3 red tickets, which are worth 3 * 10 = 30 blue tickets.
Added with his 7 blue tickets, he has 800 + 30 + 7 = 837 blue tickets' worth of tickets.
So he still needs to earn 1000 - 837 = 163 blue tickets.
The answer is 163.

Together, the two beaches have a total of 40+20 = 60 surfers.
The answer is 60.

messages.content: Carson is sorting seaweed for various uses. 50% of the seaweed is only good for starting fires. 25% of what's left can be eaten by humans, and the rest is fed to livestock. If Carson harvests 400 pounds of seaweed, how many pounds are fed to livestock?

First find what percent of the seaweed can be used for something besides starting fires: 400 pounds / 2 = 200 pounds
Then divide that amount by 4 to find the amount that's eaten by humans: 200 pounds / 4 = 50 pounds
Then subtract that amount from the 200 pounds to find how much is eaten by livestock: 200 pounds - 50 pounds = 150 pounds
The answer is 150.

Read this:

At the college sports club, Madhav, nineteen, had just won the inter-college badminton final. He was glowing.

The coach, Kishore sir, came over. "Madhav, would you like to lead the junior training on weekends?"

"Yes! Definitely!"

A classmate asked him to join a hackathon. "Sure, count me in!"

Another friend asked about a night trek on the same weekend. "Absolutely!"

That evening, Kishore sir stopped him. "Madhav, you just agreed to three things on the same Saturday."

Madhav blinked. It hadn't seemed like a problem an hour ago. Everything had felt possible.

"When you're this happy, everything looks easy," the coach said. "Sleep on it and tell me tomorrow."

What had Madhav just won?
The inter-college badminton final.
Why didn't Madhav notice the clash at first?
He was so happy and excited after winning that everything felt possible and he didn't see the risks.
What did Kishore sir suggest, and why was it wise?
He suggested sleeping on it, so Madhav could decide once his joy had settled and see the clashes clearly.
How might the classmate who invited Madhav to the hackathon feel if he pulled out?
The classmate might feel let down, especially if they had counted on him.

Read this:

In Sangamner, the Class 10 results were pinned outside the school office. Sonali ran her finger down the list with Usha. "Look, all the top ten go to Joshi Sir's tuition. Tuition makes you score higher." She went home and begged her father to pay for it. Her father, a bus conductor, was quiet. "Who goes to Joshi Sir?" he asked. Sonali listed them: the doctor's son, the shop owner's daughters, the girl whose mother is a teacher. "Do they study at home too?" "They have their own rooms. And their parents help." "Would they have scored well without tuition?" Sonali hesitated. Usha, who didn't go to tuition, had come eleventh. "Maybe," Sonali said slowly. "They'd study anyway." Her father nodded. "So is it the tuition, or everything that comes with families who can pay for it?"

Where did Usha come in the results?
Usha, who didn't go to tuition, had come eleventh.
Why did Sonali beg her father for tuition?
She felt hopeful and anxious, believing tuition itself caused the top scores because the top ten all went to it.
What did her father's questions help Sonali see?
That better-off, motivated students both take tuition and study at home, so tuition may not be the real cause of high marks.
How might Sonali's father feel when she begs for tuition?
He may feel worried and a bit pressured, as a bus conductor, but calm enough to help her think it through.

In the village near Belgaum, Suraj sat on the verandah with his maths workbook open. Twenty sums for tomorrow. He looked at the first one and felt his shoulders droop. So many. So boring.
"Amma, can I have a guava?"
"Finish your sums first," said Manjula from the kitchen.
"Just one guava!"
He ate it slowly. Then he watched the neighbour's goat. Then he chased a lizard with his pencil. The sums waited.
Manjula came out and saw the empty page. She sat down beside him. "Twenty is a lot. Let's just do the first two together."
Suraj groaned, but picked up his pencil.

How many sums did Suraj have?
Twenty sums.
What was Suraj feeling when his shoulders drooped?
He felt bored and a bit dreadful at how many sums there were, so he looked for relief.
Which of Manjula's choices helped, and why?
Sitting beside Suraj and suggesting just the first two sums, which made the start feel small.
What might Manjula be thinking when she sees the empty page?
Manjula may feel a little frustrated but understanding, seeing that the task felt too big.

Read this:

The power had gone out in the girls' hostel, and Damini was revising by phone torch for the next morning's internal exam when Jahnavi sat on the edge of her bed and didn't open a book.
"Something happened at Karan's birthday," Jahnavi said finally. "I said no. He didn't stop."
Damini put the phone down, torch facing the ceiling. A question rose in her about why Jahnavi had gone to his room, and she swallowed it. "I believe you. It's not your fault. Thank you for telling me."
Jahnavi was shaking. "Please don't tell the others. People will talk."
"I won't tell anyone for gossip. But you shouldn't carry this alone. Can we go to Dr. Menon, the hostel counsellor, right now? I'll stay with you."
Twenty minutes later, exam forgotten, they were in the counsellor's room. Dr. Menon listened, told Jahnavi again that she was not to blame, and that same night called the campus committee and a support helpline with her, explaining every choice Jahnavi still had.

What did Jahnavi say happened at Karan's birthday?
"I said no. He didn't stop."
What thought did Damini swallow, and what was she feeling?
A doubting question about why Jahnavi went to his room; Damini felt shaken but chose belief over blame, so Jahnavi felt safe to keep talking.
How did Damini help Jahnavi find safe support?
She believed her, promised no gossip, and took her to the hostel counsellor that same night, staying beside her.
How might Jahnavi feel when Damini says "I believe you"?
Less alone and less ashamed; being believed first made it possible to go to the counsellor.

metadata.subtype: Friend × Learning that a friend crossed a boundary [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

You asked what changed in first year? Okay, I'm Anirban, second year now, and I can see it clearly only looking back.
Week one at the hostel, I slept at eleven like at home. By week three I was up at three with the whole wing, eating instant noodles and ranking professors. Mehak, from the next wing, would say, “Prof Iyer is useless,” and I'd say it too, though I'd never sat in her class.
Home felt far. The wing became my mirror. When I went back for Pujo holidays, my mother asked what I thought about something and I actually didn't know. I only knew what the wing thought. That scared me a bit.

What did the wing eat at three in the morning?
They ate instant noodles.
How did Anirban feel when the question from home had no answer?
Anirban felt unsettled and a bit scared, realising that only the wing's views came to mind, not Anirban's own.
What could Anirban try in second year?
Anirban could form a personal view before repeating the wing's opinions, for example by attending a class before judging the professor.
How might Anirban's mother have seen the change during the holidays?
She may have been puzzled or concerned to find Anirban unsure of any personal opinion after a few months away.
I got into two colleges and I have to choose by Friday.
Congratulations on getting into both. That is a good problem to have. What are the main differences between them?
One is in my city and cheaper. The other is far away but has a better course.
Those are both real reasons. Try listing what matters most to you: the course, the cost, being near family, or living on your own. Rank them, then see which college fits your top two.
The course matters most, but I'm scared of living alone.

Many first-year students feel that fear, and for most it fades within a few months. You could ask the far college about hostels and student groups. Talking to a current student there may also make it feel less unknown.

Read this:

Dear Diary,
Sunday. I spent the whole afternoon alone at the lake, sketching ducks. No phone. It was the best day. My head felt clear, like a clean window.
It's funny, because two weeks ago, after the fight with the group, I was alone every day too. And that was horrible. I kept checking my phone to see if anyone had messaged. Nobody had. I ate lunch in the library so nobody would see me by myself.
Same alone. Totally different feeling.
The difference is I chose today. And I have Santosh, my brother, who asked how the ducks were, and I've made up with two of the girls.
— Gopika

What did Gopika sketch at the lake?
Ducks.
What was Gopika feeling two weeks ago when eating lunch in the library?
Gopika felt lonely and ashamed, hiding being alone after the fight.
What could Gopika do if the heavy loneliness comes back?
Gopika could reach out to Santosh or a friend, or a trusted adult, instead of hiding in the library.
How might Santosh see Gopika's Sunday?
Santosh seems happy to see Gopika enjoy time alone and shows interest by asking about the ducks.

Family group: Tenzin, Pala, Amala, Madhav (Delhi)
Tenzin: after today's landslide warning, can we make a plan? if phones stop working here, what do we do
Pala: good question
Tenzin: idea: if we can't reach each other, everyone goes to the monastery community hall and waits there
Amala: yes, it's on high ground
Tenzin: and we choose one person outside Gangtok. local lines jam but a far call can still work
Tenzin: Madhav, can you be our contact person?
Madhav: of course. i'll keep my phone on loud. whoever reaches me, i pass the message on
Tenzin: i'm writing all our numbers + Madhav's + the hall on paper cards, one for each bag
Pala: put one in the car too
Tenzin: done. 5 cards
Amala: proud of you 🙏

Where does Tenzin suggest everyone go if they can't reach each other?
The monastery community hall, and wait there.
What might Tenzin have been worried about after the landslide warning?
Tenzin was worried the family could be separated with phones down and no way to find each other.
What else could the family add to the plan?
Agree how long to wait at the hall before moving on, and walk the route there once so everyone knows it.
How might Madhav feel being chosen as the contact?
Madhav likely feels trusted and responsible, keeping the phone on loud so any message can be passed on.

Read this:

Kunal, you're asking old Wasim bhai why I never pushed you to talk at lunch? Because at twenty I was a lot like you. There was a girl I cared about, Firdaus. Every time she said, "Tell me what's on your mind," I'd crack a joke and change the subject. When she asked if I would meet her parents, I stopped calling. Told myself I was a free bird. The truth? I'd lie awake in my hostel room feeling like the loneliest man in Aligarh. I was scared that if I needed her and she left, I'd fall apart. I said that sentence out loud for the first time at thirty-two. Anyway. Your chai's getting cold.

What did Wasim do when Firdaus asked about meeting her parents?
He stopped calling.
What was Wasim afraid of behind all his distance?
He was scared that if he needed Firdaus and she left, he would fall apart.
What choice did young Wasim make each time Firdaus asked for more, and what did it cost him?
He joked, changed the subject or stopped calling, which kept his freedom but left him lying awake lonely.
How might Firdaus have experienced Wasim's jokes and silence?
She likely felt shut out and confused, as if her questions were unwelcome.
Make this polite: Bring the book tomorrow.
Could you please bring the book tomorrow?

Read this:

It was the night before the chemistry board exam, and Aparna had been choosing all day: which chapter first, which questions to skip, whether to redo organic or trust it. At nine the power went out, and she kept going by the dim inverter light.
Gurleen messaged: "Can you send me your polymer notes? Please? 🙏"
Aparna, who usually wrote long, careful replies, typed "no" and turned the phone over.
In the kitchen she ignored the dal Amma had kept warm and ate half a packet of chips standing up.
Ten minutes later, still crunching, she felt awful. She picked up the phone again. "Sorry, brain fried. Sending photos now. Good luck ❤️"
Then she put the chips away, sat down with the dal and closed the textbook for the night.

What did Gurleen ask Aparna for?
Gurleen asked for Aparna's polymer notes.
Why did Aparna reply just 'no'?
Aparna felt drained and irritable after a whole day of study decisions, so a quick, easy answer was all she had left.
What did Aparna do after ten minutes that helped?
Aparna apologised, sent the notes, ate the dal and stopped studying for the night, giving a tired brain some rest.
How might Gurleen have felt on getting a one-word 'no'?
Gurleen may have felt hurt and surprised, since Aparna usually wrote long, careful replies.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, Friday
Preeti joined the lab in June and was quick and careful. Over the last three weeks I've seen a change. Simple data entry that used to take her an hour now takes most of the morning. She mislabelled two sample sets this week, which she has never done before. Today I found her staring at the same spreadsheet for twenty minutes.
When I asked if she was okay, she said, "I don't know why I'm even here. I'm a fraud." She has been working late every night.
I told her the mistakes are fixable and she is not a fraud. I have reduced her tasks for next week and asked her to see the student counsellor. I'll check in on Monday.
Damini

How many sample sets did Preeti mislabel this week?
Two sample sets.
What might Damini have felt on finding Preeti staring at the same spreadsheet?
Damini was likely concerned and worried, noticing a once quick, careful intern suddenly struggling and working late.
Why are Damini's steps better than asking Preeti to try harder?
Effort alone won't fix exhaustion; reducing tasks and involving the counsellor gives her room to recover.
How might Preeti experience Damini's response?
She may feel relieved and less alone, hearing she is not a fraud and that her load is lighter.

Read this:

Note from Zainab, English teacher, about Pema, Class 10. Pema handed in an essay on the school library that opened: "The multifaceted utilisation of the institutional literary repository is undeniably of paramount significance." Read aloud, it took Pema four attempts to say what the sentence meant: "The library is useful." Pema said quietly, "I thought simple words would sound childish." I asked Pema to underline the three main points and rewrite each in the plainest sentence possible. The second draft came out at half the length. Pema read it aloud and said it sounded a bit plain but was easy to follow. Next step: plain first, then one strong word only where it earns its place. - Zainab

What did Pema say the long opening sentence meant?
Pema said it meant that the library is useful.
What was Pema worried about when choosing long words?
Pema worried that simple words would sound childish, and wanted to seem clever.
What did Zainab ask Pema to do to fix the essay?
Zainab asked Pema to underline the three main points and rewrite each in the plainest sentence possible.
How did Zainab see the second draft compared with the first?
As clearer and half the length, and a better base for adding one strong word where it is needed.
Let's take a brake from studying and have some tea. Check the spelling.

Let's take a break from studying and have some tea.
Why: "break" is a rest; "brake" stops a vehicle.
What do my parents plan to gift me on my birthday?
I don't know their plans, and that's meant to be a surprise. You'll find out on the day.

Read this:

In the village near Sangli, Rekha heard the tractor before she saw it: Kiran, her husband, driving a second-hand one into the yard, grinning. "Got it cheap at the fair! We'll pay the loan off in two harvests." Her stomach dropped. Last year it was the motorbike; before that, the borewell he started and abandoned. She wanted to shout, to call him a fool in front of the neighbours. She didn't. That night, after the children slept, she said, "I'm scared, Kiran. These big buys happen without us talking. From now on, anything that needs a loan, we decide together." He went quiet. "And I want us to see the bank's farm adviser this week about this loan." He nodded slowly. "Together," he said.

What did Kiran buy at the fair?
A second-hand tractor.
How did Rekha feel when she saw the tractor?
Her stomach dropped; she felt scared and angry after years of sudden buys.
What did Rekha do that avoided contempt and still set a limit?
She waited until night, spoke calmly about her fear, asked to decide loans together and to see the farm adviser.
How might Kiran feel when Rekha says she's scared?
Kiran may feel surprised and sobered, seeing the worry behind her words, which is why he agrees.

Read this:

I'm Bhavna, and I'm bad at remembering things that aren't already part of my day. I got a thick story book for my birthday and kept forgetting it under my bed. Then I noticed something. I never forget to brush my teeth at night, because "Brushing done, beti?" comes from Mummy every night and my sister Mehak stands at the basin tapping her foot. So I thought, what if the book lives right next to my toothbrush? Brush, then read. The toothbrush can remind me. Now the book sits on the bathroom shelf beside the toothpaste. When I finish brushing I pick it up and read two chapters in bed. Mehak says it's weird to keep a book in the bathroom. It is a bit weird, but I'm on chapter nine.

Where does the book sit now?
It sits on the bathroom shelf beside the toothpaste.
How did Bhavna feel about the forgotten book before the new plan?
Bhavna felt a bit frustrated about forgetting a birthday book under the bed, and wanted a way to remember that didn't rely on willpower.
What else could Bhavna attach reading to if bedtime gets rushed?
Another thing done every day without fail, like breakfast or the bus ride home, as long as the book is kept right next to it.
How does Mehak see the new habit?
Mehak finds a book in the bathroom weird and teases about it, but the habit rides on the brushing she already makes sure happens.

Read this:

For most of last semester, Mohit told me I was the only person on campus who got him. "You're more of a brother than my own brother," he said once, after we'd talked until 3 a.m. about his parents' divorce. I felt proud to be that person.
Then in November I missed his call because I was at my cousin's engagement. By morning I had eleven messages: I was useless, fake, just like everyone else. I read them in the bathroom, shaking. My first instinct was to fire back something equally cruel. I didn't. I wrote, "I'm sorry I missed your call. I was at an engagement. I care about you, and I won't be spoken to like this. Let's talk when things are calmer."
He didn't reply for four days. Then: "Chai?" We're friends again, sort of. I, Divyansh, keep my phone on me now, but I don't pick up at 3 a.m. any more.

How many messages had Mohit sent by morning?
Eleven.
How did Divyansh feel reading the messages in the bathroom, and why?
Shaken and bewildered, because the friend who had called him more of a brother than a brother suddenly called him useless over one missed call.
Which choice did Divyansh make instead of firing back, and why did it help?
He apologised for the missed call, said he cared, and set a clear limit on how he would be spoken to, which kept the friendship possible without accepting the insults.
What might Mohit have been feeling when the call went unanswered?
Probably alone and panicky, perhaps fearing being abandoned, which made one missed call feel like proof that Divyansh didn't care.
A cricket match starts at 2:45 p.m. and lasts 3 h 30 min. When does it end? Give the answer in both 12-hour and 24-hour time.

Answer: 6:15 p.m., which is 18:15.

Add the hours first: 2:45 + 3 h = 5:45. Then add the 30 min in two jumps: 15 min to 6:00, and 15 min more to 6:15. In 24-hour time: 6 + 12 = 18, so 18:15. Or add in columns: 2 h 45 min + 3 h 30 min = 5 h 75 min, and 75 min = 1 h 15 min, so 6 h 15 min: 6:15 p.m.

Read this:

I'm Nikita, and I used to believe that if a workout wasn't an hour, it didn't count. So I did nothing for months. Then Vishal, my flatmate, said, "Just do ten minutes. Even when you feel awful."

So the first week I stretched for ten minutes, then jogged slowly to the end of the lane and back. It was almost embarrassing. But on the bad days, when I had a headache or a long day, I could still do that. The next week I added two minutes. The week after, two more.

Now it's forty minutes, three mornings a week, and I've not missed since the start. I didn't get fit by being brave. I got here by being small enough that I couldn't say no.

How long was the first workout?
Stretching for ten minutes, then a slow jog to the end of the lane and back.
How did Nikita feel about the tiny first workout?
Nikita found it almost embarrassing, though the small size meant it could be done even on bad days.
What could Nikita do on a day when even ten minutes seems too much, and why?
Nikita could do just the stretching or step outside for a minute, because keeping the chain unbroken matters more than the size of the session.
How might Vishal see Nikita's progress?
Vishal probably feels quietly pleased, having given the simple advice, and sees Nikita's steady mornings as proof that small steps last.

metadata.subtype: Approach: start with a tiny version that can be done on bad days [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Devika,
I've been thinking about Saturday since I got home. It was lovely to finally meet Kunal when he picked you up. But during our two-hour lunch he texted you five times, asked who each person in your photos was, and said he would prefer you skipped the trek with your college friends. You laughed and said, "He's so protective, na?"
Maybe that's all it is. I don't know him well, and I'm not trying to judge. But when I was your age, someone's protectiveness slowly turned into me asking permission for everything, and I only saw it much later.
So here's the question I wish someone had asked me: do you feel free with him? Free to go on the trek, see your friends, say no without it becoming a big thing?
You don't have to answer me. Just keep asking yourself. And call me any time, about anything.
Love,
Arohi Didi

How many times did Kunal text Devika during the lunch?
Kunal texted Devika five times during the two-hour lunch.
What is Arohi worried about?
Arohi worries that Kunal's protectiveness could slowly turn into Devika asking permission for everything, as happened to Arohi.
What makes Arohi's letter a helpful approach?
It names what Arohi saw without judging, shares a personal experience, offers one question about feeling free, and leaves the door open to call any time.
How might Devika feel reading the letter?
Devika might feel defensive at first, having called Kunal protective, but the gentle tone and open offer may help Devika quietly check whether that freedom is really there.

Read this:

Day one. Minakshi, two months into the team, posted in the project chat: "What if we sent reminders by voice call for older customers?" Tushar read it on the metro and thought, that's good. That's really good. Then: why didn't I think of it?
Day three. The client call. The director asked for fresh ideas. Tushar's mouth was dry. Two seniors had been let go last quarter. He heard himself say, "I was thinking we could try voice-call reminders for older customers." The director nodded. "Great, Tushar, lead that."
Minakshi said nothing. On the way out Tushar told himself, it's a team, ideas belong to the team.
Day ten. Minakshi hadn't posted in the chat since. Tushar noticed. Every time he opened the project folder, his stomach turned slightly, like he'd borrowed something and hadn't returned it.

What did the director say after Tushar spoke on the call?
The director said, "Great, Tushar, lead that."
What was Tushar afraid of when he spoke on the client call?
Tushar was afraid of being let go like the two seniors and wanted recognition, so fear pushed him to present Minakshi's idea as his own.
At which moment could Tushar still have put things right?
On the call, or on Day ten when he noticed the silence, Tushar could have said the idea was Minakshi's and handed Minakshi the lead.
How has Minakshi been affected by what happened on the call?
Minakshi has stopped posting in the chat, which suggests Minakshi no longer feels safe sharing ideas with the team.

Read this:

On Monday at the park in Uppsala, Ulla watched Fatima walk up to three children building a sand castle. "Can I play too?" Fatima asked, and they moved over to make room. Ulla stayed on the bench, holding her spade. On Tuesday the same children were at the sandpit. Ulla walked over, smiled, and said the exact words: "Can I play too?" A boy handed her a bucket.

What did the boy hand Ulla?
A bucket.
What was Ulla feeling on Monday, holding her spade on the bench?
She was probably shy and unsure, wanting to join but not knowing how.
What else could Ulla try if the words didn't work?
She could offer something, like her spade, or start digging nearby and wait to be asked.
How might Fatima feel if she saw Ulla use her words?
Fatima might feel pleased and proud that her way helped someone else.

Read this:

The wedding hall in Hyderabad was noisy, and Hemant was at a table of strangers when the conversation turned to family. He began to describe his sister's hospital stay in detail, then his father's debts, his own doubts, and the fight with his cousin. Ganga, next to him, listened but saw the others' polite smiles going stiff. She touched her plate and said gently, "Hemant, we could talk about this outside later, if you like." Hemant stopped, cheeks warm. Outside, on the steps, he said, "I think I said too much." Ganga said, "You needed to talk. Just not with everyone at once." She stayed until he felt steadier.

Where did Hemant start telling his family story?
Hemant was at a table of strangers at the wedding hall in Hyderabad.
What did Hemant feel outside on the steps, and what does it suggest?
Hemant felt embarrassed and said he thought he had said too much, and his warm cheeks suggest he was flustered. It also suggests he needed to talk to someone.
What did Ganga do that helped?
Ganga gently suggested talking outside later, listened on the steps and stayed until Hemant felt steadier.
How might the strangers at the table have felt as Hemant told the details?
They may have felt uncomfortable or unsure how to respond, since their polite smiles went stiff.

Read this:

Arnab: saw your post about the mall. you really want it built on the old mill land??
Jyoti: yes. don't start 😅
Arnab: not starting. genuinely asking. how did you come to that view?
Jyoti: my mom worked at the mill till it shut. ten years that land has just rotted
Jyoti: a mall means jobs. my cousin's been unemployed a year
Arnab: oh. I didn't know about your mom
Arnab: I'm against it because my uncle's shop is two streets away and malls kill small shops
Jyoti: so we both care about people in this town having work
Arnab: yeah. we just picture different people
Jyoti: what if the plan kept space for local shops inside?
Arnab: I'd actually support that 🤔
Jyoti: write that on the petition then
Arnab: only if you come to the town meeting with me
Jyoti: deal 🙂

Where did Jyoti's mom work until it shut?
Jyoti's mom worked at the mill.
What was Arnab feeling when he asked how Jyoti came to her view?
Arnab felt curious and open, wanting to understand rather than start a fight.
What did the question "how did you come to that view?" make possible?
It uncovered their personal reasons and showed a shared value, jobs for people in the town, leading to a joint idea.
How might Jyoti have felt if Arnab had opened with an attack instead?
Jyoti might have felt defensive and dug in, never sharing the story about Jyoti's mom or finding the common ground.
Jake sold 10 more stuffed animals than Thor. Quincy sold ten times as many stuffed animals as Thor. If Quincy sold 200 stuffed animals, how many more stuffed animals did Quincy sell than Jake?

Thor sold 200/10=20 stuffed animals.
Jake sold 20+10=30 stuffed animals.
Quincy sold 200-30= 170 more stuffed animals than Jake.
The answer is 170.

How do I spell "adress"?
Why does a boiled egg float in salty water but sink in plain water?
Explain the word "intervene" simply.
Fix my grammar: She looks beautifully in that dress.

1. It is "address", with a double "d" and a double "s".
2. It floats in the salt water. Because the salt makes the water heavier, so it pushes up on the egg more strongly.
3. "Intervene" is a verb. It means to step in so as to change a situation.
4. It should be: She looks beautiful in that dress. Why: after a linking verb like "looks", use an adjective.

Christina walks 7km to school every day from Monday to Friday. She returns home covering the same distance. Last Friday her mother asked her to pass by her friend, which is another 2km away from the school in the opposite distance from home. How many kilometers did Christina cover that week?

One trip to school is 2 * 7 km = 14km.
In one week, Christina walks 14 km/day * 5 days/week = 70km to school.
The extra trip to her mum's friend added 2 km * 2 = 4km to her travel distance.
Her total distance was thus 70 km + 4 km = 74 km
The answer is 74.
Colleague said "last-to-last week". My foreign friend did not get it.
"Last-to-last week" is Indian English for "the week before last week". Say: "the week before last". Everyone will understand that.
Mr. Connell harvested 60 apples from his apple tree and 3 times as many peaches from his peach tree. What is the difference between the number of the two fruits?

Mr. Connell harvested 60 x 3 = 180 peaches.
The difference between the number of the two fruits is 180 - 60 = 120
The answer is 120.

Read this:

At the anganwadi, the other children had gone out to the swings, but Bhupen stayed on the corner mat with the wooden blocks. He was building a long, crooked train. He talked softly to himself: 'This one is the engine. This one carries mangoes.' Mehak Didi, the teacher, watched from the doorway and didn't say anything. For almost an hour he added carriages, knocked one over, fixed it, added a bridge. Then he stood up, looked at it, said 'Done', and ran outside. He didn't ask anyone to come and look.

What was Bhupen building?
He was building a long, crooked train.
Why did Bhupen stay inside when the others went to the swings?
He was happily absorbed in his train and enjoying the building itself, which is why he talked to himself and didn't need anyone to watch.
What did Mehak Didi do well?

Helen cuts her lawn starting in March and finishes in October.  Her lawn mower uses 2 gallons of gas every 4th time she cuts her lawn.  For March, April, September and October, she only cuts her law 2 times per month.  In May, June, July and August, she has to cut her lawn 4 times per month.  How many gallons of gas will she need to cut her lawn from March through October?

For March, April, September and October, she cuts her lawn 2 a month. There are 4 months so she cuts her yard 2*4 = 8 times
For May, June, July and August, she cuts her lawn 4 times a month. There are 4 months so she cuts her yard 4*4 = 16 times
During the entire 8 month period, she cuts her lawn 8+16 = 24 times
Every 4th time she cuts, she needs 2 gallons of gas. If she cuts her lawn 24 times a year then she needs to fill up 24/4 = 6 times
Each time she fills up, it takes 2 gallons of gas so 2*6 = 12 gallons of gas per year
The answer is 12.

messages.content: Anu knows that 25 x 4 = 100. Which two division facts does she get for free?

Use the completed games table from D10. A student is chosen at random. Find P(girl), P(a boy who prefers football), P(prefers badminton). If the student chosen is a girl, what is the probability she prefers cricket? If the student prefers badminton, what is the probability it is a girl?

Answer: P(girl) = 18/40 = 9/20; P(boy and football) = 8/40 = 1/5; P(badminton) = 11/40; P(cricket, given girl) = 6/18 = 1/3; P(girl, given badminton) = 7/11.

For "a student is chosen" the denominator is the GRAND total, 40. A single cell (boys AND football) gives an "and" probability: 8/40. A total gives a single event: girls 18/40, badminton 11/40. When we are TOLD the student is a girl, only the 18 girls are possible, so the denominator shrinks to 18: 6 of them prefer cricket, 6/18 = 1/3. Similarly among the 11 badminton players, 7 are girls: 7/11. Always ask "out of whom?" before choosing the denominator. Common mistake: using 40 for the "given girl" question (6/40).

Find the missing numbers: 3 : 5 = 12 : __ and 3 : 5 = __ : 35.

Answer: 3 : 5 = 12 : 20 and 3 : 5 = 21 : 35.

Look for the multiplier. From 3 to 12 we multiply by 4, so multiply 5 by 4 as well: 20. From 5 to 35 we multiply by 7, so 3 x 7 = 21. Pallavi: say that to them. not just "i want to go"
Minakshi: ok. talking to appa after dinner
Minakshi: thanks akka

Where is the job Minakshi wants?
In Bengaluru.
What mix of feelings is Minakshi having?
She feels angry at her father's refusal and guilty for being angry, since her parents paid for her degree.
How does the plan try to honour both family and her own life?
Visits every second weekend, staying with periamma's family at first and coming home for Pongal keep ties while she takes the job.
How does Pallavi help without taking over?
Pallavi asks questions that help Minakshi find her own plan and suggests sharing the plan, not just the wish.

Read this:

Tushar, you think senior engineers never feel like frauds? Listen. At twenty-five I was the youngest designer on the dam project in Himachal. Every morning I walked onto the site sure that today someone would see I didn't know enough. I stayed quiet in meetings. I didn't sleep. One evening my mentor, old Mr Negi, found me checking calculations for the fifth time. I don't know why, but I told him. "Sir, I feel like I'm pretending." He laughed, not unkindly. "Anand, I've felt that on every project for thirty years. So has every good engineer I know." I nearly cried with relief. It was like a weight lifted. I still felt nervous the next morning, but the shame was gone. I could ask questions. That's why I'm telling you now, beta. Say it out loud to someone you trust.

Where was the dam project?
In Himachal.
How did young Anand feel after Mr Negi said he had felt the same for thirty years?
Anand felt huge relief, as if a weight had lifted, and the shame about feeling like a fraud faded.
What choice in the story made the difference for Anand?
Telling Mr Negi the secret, instead of hiding it, let Anand hear that capable people feel the same, which reduced shame and made asking questions possible.
How might Mr Negi have felt hearing Anand's confession?
Mr Negi might have felt warm and understanding, perhaps remembering his own early fears.
Let's look the cricket final at my house tonight. Which verb is better?

Let's watch the cricket final at my house tonight.
Why: For a match, use "watch", not "look".

"Disha, your summer essay is exactly like the one on that website."
"Everyone copies from there, Aadhya."
"I didn't."
"Well, most people. And Ma'am gave us five essays in one holiday. That's crazy."
"It was three."
"Three is a lot! And it's so hot. Nobody can write in this heat."
"You copied it on the first day of the holidays. It wasn't even hot yet."
Disha stopped.
"You had the excuses ready before you even tried," Aadhya said gently.
Disha went quiet. "I think I just didn't want to do it," she said, "and then I found reasons."
"So write it now? I'll sit with you."

How many essays were set, according to Aadhya?
Three.
What does Disha admit she was feeling?
She didn't want to do the essays; the reluctance came first, and the reasons came afterwards to protect her image.
What does Aadhya offer?
To sit with Disha while she writes the essay now.
How does Aadhya react to the excuses?
Aadhya stays calm but doesn't accept them, gently pointing out the facts and then offering help.

12 Aug. Park flooded again. Yusuf says it's just too much rain. But it rained this much last year and the swings were fine. So after school we walked around it like detectives. 1) The new building next door has covered its whole plot in cement, so water can't soak in. 2) The drain near the gate is full of chip packets. 3) The gardener cut back the hedge, and now soil slides onto the path and into the drain. Any one of these alone maybe wouldn't matter. Together the water has nowhere to go, and now there are mosquitoes, so Ammi won't let my little brother out. Yusuf said I'm overthinking. Maybe. I'm going to draw arrows between all of these tonight. – Kashish

What was blocking the drain near the gate?
Chip packets were blocking it.
Why does Kashish want to draw arrows tonight?
Kashish feels curious and determined to understand the flooding, believing the causes work together, and wants to see how they connect.
What could Kashish do next with these findings?
Kashish could show the drawing to the colony committee or a teacher, so the adults who manage the drain and park can act.
How does Yusuf see the problem differently?
Yusuf sees one simple cause, heavy rain, and thinks Kashish is making it complicated.

Bidisha, you'll laugh, but I'm quite proud of this. So on Saturday a man rings the bell. Very polite, ironed shirt, lanyard, a folder of photos of sick children. He talks beautifully. Not one pause. He knows my building's name, says my neighbour on the third floor already gave.
And I'm standing there, Lalit the softie, reaching for my wallet. He's so sincere.
Then I think: sincere is not a fact. Anyone can practise a speech.
So I ask to see his ID and the charity's registration number. He shows a card. I say, "Give me two minutes," and I look up the charity myself, find their number on their real website, and call. The lady there says they never collect door to door.
When I come back, he's gone. I told the society guard and posted a warning in our building group.
The kids need help. Just not through him.

What did the lady at the charity say?
The lady there says they never collect door to door.
How did Lalit feel while the man was talking?
Lalit felt moved and soft-hearted, even reaching for the wallet, because the man seemed so sincere.
What steps helped Lalit check the claim?
Lalit asked for ID and the registration number, looked up the charity himself and called the number on its real website, then warned the guard and neighbours.
How might Bidisha react to Lalit's story?
Bidisha would probably feel impressed and amused, and perhaps more careful about smooth talkers.

It had rained all through Eid week in the Bhiwandi flat. On Tuesday, Vishal, two, watched Papa, Chetan, take a phone call: "Hello ji! Haan, haan." On Wednesday, Vishal picked up a wooden block, held it to his ear and said, "Hello ji! Aan, aan!" He nodded seriously and walked around the room, just like Papa. Chetan laughed. "Who's calling?" Vishal held out the block. "Papa!"

What did Vishal use as a phone?
A wooden block.
How was Vishal feeling as he nodded and walked around with the block?
He felt serious and proud, playing at being Papa.
How could Chetan build on this game?
He could take the block and chat back, turning it into a pretend call.
How did Chetan react to Vishal's copying?
He was amused and joined in, asking who was calling.
My manager wrote "Kindly do the needful." What does it mean? Is it okay English?

It means "please do whatever is necessary to finish this task." It is common in Indian offices, but people in other countries may find it unclear. A clearer way is: "Please process this request and let me know when it is done."

In a small café in Buenos Aires, Mateo, twenty-five, stirred his coffee while Fatima waited. Six months ago he had told everyone at his birthday that he was moving to Madrid for a master's. 'So,' he said, 'I'm not going.' Fatima raised her eyebrows. 'When I decided, the course had a scholarship and a part-time job attached. In March they cut both. I made the choice with what I knew then. Now I know more.' He didn't apologise too much or make excuses. 'I'll do the evening programme here instead.' Then he pushed a paper napkin across the table. 'And I want you to hold me to something. Every Sunday, text me: did you study ten hours this week? If I say no, I buy the coffee.' Fatima laughed and took a photo of the napkin. 'Deal. And I'm ordering the expensive cake.'

What did the Madrid course cut in March?
They cut the scholarship and the part-time job attached to the course.
How did Mateo seem to feel about changing his plan?
He seemed calm and clear rather than ashamed, explaining plainly that he decided with less information and now knows more.
How did Mateo use a new commitment on purpose, and why is that wise?
He asked Fatima to text him every Sunday about ten hours of study, using a public promise to support a good habit rather than to trap him in an old plan.
How might Fatima see Mateo's change of plan?
Fatima seems to accept it easily and is happy to help, laughing and taking a photo of the napkin as proof.
Can my dog have a little chocolate as a treat?
No, please don't. Chocolate is harmful to dogs, even in small amounts, and dark chocolate is the worst. Keep it somewhere your dog cannot reach.
What treats are safe then?
Dog treats from a pet shop are made for them. Some plain foods, like small pieces of boiled chicken or carrot, are often fine too. Check with a vet if you're unsure about a particular food.

"Swati, I have to tell you something. I've been drinking in secret for a year. I'm going into a programme on Monday."
"A year? Chinmay, a YEAR?"
"I know."
"I asked you so many times!" Swati's voice shook. "And I believed you. I feel so stupid."
"You're not stupid. I hid it well."
She sat down. "Why didn't I see it?"
"It's not your fault."
A long silence. Then, quietly: "I'm angry. And I'm... relieved? Is that awful?"
"No. The doctor said families feel everything at once."
"Does the programme have something for me?"
"There's a family group on Thursdays."
"Then I'm going."

When is the family group?
On Thursdays.
What was Swati feeling when she said "Is that awful?"
Swati felt angry and also relieved, and confused about having both feelings at once.
What choice at the end will help Swati stay steady?
Going to the family group on Thursdays, so Swati gets support too.
What might Chinmay be experiencing as Swati reacts?
Chinmay is probably ashamed and anxious, but trying to take responsibility and reassure Swati.

"There go flukes!" was the cry, an announcement immediately followed by Stubb's producing his match and igniting his pipe, for now a respite was granted. After the full interval of his sounding had elapsed, the whale rose again, and being now in advance of the smoker's boat, and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted upon the honor of the capture. It was obvious, now, that the whale had at length become aware of his pursuers. All silence of cautiousness was therefore no longer of use. Paddles were dropped, and oars came loudly into play. And still puffing at his pipe, Stubb cheered on his crew to the assault.

How does Stubb behave during the pause, and what changes when the whale comes up again?

While the whale is down, Stubb lights his pipe. When it surfaces near his boat, he expects the honour of the catch. The whale now knows it is chased, so quiet no longer matters and the crew rows hard.

I sat in on the contract renewal with our biggest client. I'm Anand, a junior analyst. My colleague Amandeep led it. Here's what I saw.

The client wanted to cut our monthly reporting and add a quarterly strategy meeting. Our team lead was about to say no. "We'll lose the monthly reports!"

Amandeep asked for a break. In the corridor he said, "Watch how everyone's fighting to keep the reports. Nobody's even thinking about what the strategy meeting gives us."

Back in the room, he said, "Here's what we protect: the client relationship, the same fee, and the key data. Here's what we give up: the monthly reports. Here's what we gain: direct time with their leadership."

He didn't hide the loss. He just put it next to the gain.

The team lead nodded slowly. The renewal went through. I don't know what Amandeep felt exactly, but he looked calm the whole time.

What did the client want to add?
A quarterly strategy meeting.
What was Anand feeling while watching Amandeep in the meeting?
Anand seemed impressed and a little surprised, noticing how calm Amandeep stayed while others fought to keep the reports.
Why did Amandeep's framing work in the meeting?
Amandeep listed what was protected, what was given up and what was gained, so the loss was honest but no longer the only thing people saw.
How might the team lead have felt after Amandeep's framing?
The team lead may have felt reassured and less defensive, seeing the renewal as a trade rather than a pure loss.

Tariq pulled the red T-shirt over his head and tucked it under his team vest. It was Thursday in the sports hall in Leeds, and the Hawks had won every game he'd worn it.
"You're wearing that again?" Liam asked, lacing his trainers.
"Five games, five wins. It's the shirt."
"We also got Coach Dunn five games ago," Liam said. "She's the one who makes us do passing drills every Tuesday."
Tariq tugged at the collar. That was true too. But the red shirt felt warm and lucky, like it was on his side.
They won again, 22-18. Liam scored eight of the points.
In the changing room, Tariq folded the shirt carefully. "See?"
Liam just shook his head and grinned.

What was the score of Thursday's game?
They won again, 22-18.
What does Tariq's careful folding of the shirt suggest?
It suggests he treats the shirt as special and truly believes it helps, because the lucky feeling is comforting even after Liam's point about the coach.
What might Liam say to help Tariq see what is really changing the results?
Liam could point out that the wins began when Coach Dunn started the Tuesday passing drills, and suggest trying one game without the shirt.
How might Coach Dunn feel if the team gave the red shirt the credit?
She might feel a little overlooked, since her passing drills may be doing much of the work.

"Why is there a list on your fridge?" Omkar asked, holding a beer he'd just taken out.
Naveen grinned, a bit embarrassed. "Feeling words. My counsellor suggested it."
"Counsellor?"
"Remember how my girlfriend kept saying I'm like a wall? And I kept freezing up in meetings and not knowing why?"
"Yeah."
"Turns out I feel plenty. I just didn't have names. So now every night I write three lines. What happened, where I felt it in my body, which word fits."
Omkar read the list. "Irritated. Hurt. Overwhelmed. Proud."
"Yesterday my chest was tight all through the review. I wrote 'dread'. Then I realised it was about my manager, not the work."
Omkar put the beer down. "Can I see the list properly?"

What three things does Naveen write every night?
What happened, where Naveen felt it in the body, and which word fits.
How does Naveen seem to feel about showing Omkar the list?
Naveen is a bit embarrassed but also proud and hopeful, grinning while explaining that the feelings are plenty and is learning names for it.
Which of Naveen's steps could help other adults who struggle to name feelings?
Keeping a list of feeling words, noticing body cues like a tight chest, writing short daily notes and seeing a counsellor.
What might change for Omkar after seeing the list?
Omkar seems curious, even interested for himself, and might start noticing his own feelings too.

Before Charu ever needed it, she sat on her bed and asked herself what she was comfortable with. Sending photos, meeting someone alone, giving out her address: she wrote her limits on the last page of her notebook, and it steadied her to see them in ink.

Tejas liked a girl in his tuition class, and one afternoon she asked him to send a private picture. "I'm not ready for that, and I don't meet people alone yet," he said, plainly. He did not add "sorry." She said okay, a bit annoyed, and asked about the homework.

Nikhil, in the next batch, sent one anyway. "Everyone does it," the boy told him, "or I'll go." Nikhil hated the knot in his stomach. Weeks later he could not sleep, imagining where it might end up, and finally told his aunt. She listened without blame, said it was not his fault, and sat with him while they contacted the school counsellor that evening.

Harsha had built trust with her friend Sana over months. She began to share more of her plans with Sana, but kept her core limits. "Some things stay mine," she thought, and nobody argued.

Where did Charu write down her limits?
She wrote them on the last page of her notebook.
How did Tejas's answer differ from Nikhil's, and what did each choice lead to?
Tejas stated his limit plainly and calmly and did not apologise, while Nikhil gave in to avoid losing the relationship and later feared where the picture might go.
What was Nikhil feeling in the weeks after he sent the picture?
He was anxious and afraid, with a knot in his stomach and sleepless nights over where it might end up.
What made telling his aunt a wise step for Nikhil?
She listened without blame, told him it was not his fault, and involved the school counsellor the same evening, so he was not alone with the worry.

On Thursday afternoon in a co-working space in Nairobi, Omar opened a blank page titled 'How we use AI tools' and asked Jin to write it with him. First came the tools the company had licensed. Second, data: no customer records, no keys, no unreleased plans. Third was a rule they argued over for ten minutes and kept: a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code. They held it to one page and printed it, and Omar added a line asking people to say when AI had helped. On Monday, Jin slipped the page into the new-joiner pack. The next hire, a graduate called Wanjiru, read it over coffee and asked two questions that made them add a sentence.

Which rule did Omar and Jin argue over for ten minutes and keep?
They kept the rule that a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code.
What does Omar want from the extra line about saying when AI helped?
Omar is cautious about AI-written changes and wants openness, so reviewers know which changes need a closer look.
What could the team do to keep the policy alive?
They could review the page every few months, since tools and habits change and a fixed page gets out of date.
How might Wanjiru see the page in the first days?
Wanjiru probably finds it helpful and short enough to read, since two questions led to one added sentence.

messages.content: The pencil box is 8 cubes long. The ruler is 12 cubes long. Which is longer? By how many cubes?

Answer: The ruler, by 4 cubes.

Make the two cube trains and put them side by side, lined up at one end. Count the extra cubes: 4. Or count on from 8 to 12: 9, 10, 11, 12 - 4 more.
