Rajni, you asked why I was so quiet at the Shraadh lunch. Okay, Akash's honest version. Every year we feed the crows and the priest for my great-grandparents, and this year I asked Papa, 'Do you really think the food reaches them?' The whole table went silent. My chacha said I'd become too clever from the internet. Papa didn't get angry. He said, 'I don't know if it reaches them. I know it reaches me. It's how I remember my dadi.' That stayed with me. I still don't believe the crows are carrying food anywhere. But I love Papa, and I saw his face when he set the plate out. So I helped. I just don't know yet what I believe, and I think that's allowed.

What did Akash ask Papa at the Shraadh lunch?
'Do you really think the food reaches them?'
How did Akash feel after Papa's answer?
Akash felt moved and torn, still not believing the food reaches anyone but loving Papa and seeing what the ritual means to him.
What made Akash's questioning respectful?
Asking honestly, listening to Papa's answer, and still helping with the plate while working out personal beliefs.
How might Papa see Akash's question?
He took it calmly and answered honestly, treating it as a real question, since for him the ritual is about remembering his dadi.

Thomas leaned back in his chair and told Amandeep, "When I was let go from my first job, I wanted to grab my things and leave without a word. A senior stopped me. She said, 'Ask before you go.' So I asked HR four things: how much notice pay, what pending dues remained, whether the office insurance continued for a while, and whether I'd get a reference letter." He counted them on his fingers. "Then I wrote down what they agreed to, and I read it back to them. It took thirty minutes. It protected my pay and my name. Leaving quietly feels dignified, but leaving with clear terms is actually more dignified."

What four things did Thomas ask HR about?
Thomas asked about notice pay, pending dues, whether the office insurance continued and a reference letter.
What did Thomas want to do at first when he was let go?
Thomas felt hurt and wanted to escape, grabbing his things and leaving without a word.
What could Amandeep do if HR gives only verbal answers, and why?
Amandeep could ask for the terms by email afterwards, because a written record protects both sides.
How might the senior who stopped Thomas see the advice?
The senior probably felt protective and hopeful, seeing that a young person could otherwise lose pay by leaving quietly.

Preeti: the one with the valve problem?

Eshaan: he said "just clear it, it's my call, not yours"

Eshaan: but I'm the one signing the quality sheet. my name, not his

Preeti: how did he take it
Eshaan: badly. but the quality head just called. she's stopping the shipment
Preeti: proud of you

How many units were in the batch?
400 units.
How was Eshaan feeling after refusing to sign?
Eshaan felt shaken and nervous, even while sure it was the right choice.

Emailing the quality head with the test results and putting the batch on hold, which used the proper channel and stopped the faulty cookers.

The order was late and the client was shouting, so the manager felt pressure to ship and avoid trouble.

Alan counted how many chairs the office canteen has. It has 2 round tables and 2 rectangular tables. Each round table has 6 chairs, and each rectangular table has 7 chairs. How many chairs are there in all?

The number of chairs at the round tables is 2 tables x 6 chairs/table = 12.
The number of chairs at rectangular tables is 2 tables x 7 chairs/table = 14.
There are 12 chairs + 14 chairs = 26 chairs in the canteen.
The answer is 26.
Anju always arrives before Ben, and Ben always arrives before Cara. If Cara arrived early today, did Anju also arrive early?
Yes, Anju arrived early too. Because Anju always comes before Ben and Ben comes before Cara, Anju must have arrived even earlier than Cara.

Aunt May milks her cows twice a day. This morning she got 365 gallons of milk. This evening she got 380 gallons. She sold 612 gallons to the local ice cream factory.  She had 15 gallons left over from yesterday.  How many gallons of milk does she have left?

Today Aunt May's cows gave her 365 gallons + 380 = 745 gallons of milk.
She had 745 gallons - 612 gallons sold to the ice cream factory = 133 gallons of milk left.
Combined with the leftover from yesterday, Aunt May has 133 gallons + 15 gallons = 148 gallons of milk.
The answer is 148.
Which student was first on the school honour board for my year?
I don't know, as I can't see its early records. The school office or old register may have the name.

"Sir, why don't we fall off the Earth if it's round?"
"Omkar, we're doing multiplication tables. Don't ask silly questions."
Some kids laughed. Omkar sat down.
At break, Zeenat found him by the water tank.
"That was a good question," she said.
"No, it was silly. Sir said."
"I wanted to know too."
Omkar shrugged. "I'm not asking anything anymore."
"Not even in science?"
"Not anywhere." He kicked the tank.
"My Abbu says it's gravity. Like a magnet, sort of."
Omkar looked up, eyes lighting for a second. "Really? Like a magnet?"
Then he looked away. "Doesn't matter."
"It does to me," said Zeenat. "Ask me next time."

What subject was the class doing when Omkar asked his question?
Multiplication tables.
What shows that Omkar still felt curious after being dismissed?
His eyes lit up when Zeenat mentioned gravity, before he looked away and said it didn't matter.
How could Zeenat keep supporting Omkar's curiosity?
She could keep sharing answers and questions with him, and maybe suggest asking the science teacher together.
What would change if Sir had said 'Good question, let's talk about it later'?
Omkar might have felt his wondering was welcome and kept asking questions in class.

Chinmay had a heavy cold, and when Deepika Teacher asked him to read the poem aloud in the village school, it came out thick and nasal: “The bango tree by our dore.” Three boys at the back honked like geese. Chinmay's ears went red, and he stopped. Deepika Teacher put down her chalk. “His nose is blocked. That's all a voice like that means: a cold, not a joke. Mine sounded the same last week.” She poured Chinmay a cup of warm water from her flask. “Read again when you're ready.” He finished the poem. The boys stayed quiet.

What did Deepika Teacher give Chinmay?
She poured him a cup of warm water from her flask.
What was Chinmay feeling when the boys honked?
Chinmay felt embarrassed and hurt, his ears going red, so he stopped reading.
How did Deepika Teacher handle the mocking?
She stopped the lesson, explained that a nasal voice means a cold, shared that hers sounded the same, and let Chinmay continue when ready.
How did the boys at the back read Chinmay's voice?
They treated the nasal voice as something funny to mock, not realising it simply came from a blocked nose.
Dany owns a farm, in his farm he has 4 cows and 3 sheep that eat 2 bushels a day. He also has 7 chickens that eat 3 bushels a day. How many bushels should he have to suffice the animals for a day?

Dany has to have 4 x 2 = 8 bushels a day for the cows.
He has to have 3 x 2 = 6 bushels a day for the sheep.
And he also has to have 7 x 3 = 21 bushels a day for the chickens.
Therefore, Dany has to have 8 + 6 + 21 = 35 bushels to suffice the animals for a day.
The answer is 35.

In the student bar in Dublin, three lads from Bilal's course started joking about Rania's headscarf, loud enough for her table to hear. “Is it hiding a bad hair day?” one said. Others laughed.
Bilal sat right there. He stared at his drink. He told himself it wasn't his fight.
Rania gathered her things and left without a word.
Bilal didn't sleep well. By morning the feeling was clear: it was shame, and hiding from it would make it worse.
He found Rania outside the library. “I was there last night. I should have said something. I'm sorry.” She looked at him for a long moment. “Thanks for saying it.”
He wrote one line in his notes app: Next time, say “Not funny, lads,” and sit with her.

Where did the joking happen?
It happened in the student bar in Dublin.
What was Bilal feeling the next morning?
He felt ashamed and regretful, and knew that hiding from the feeling would make it worse.
Is Bilal's plan for next time a good one, and why?
Yes; a short line like "Not funny, lads" and sitting with Rania is simple and safe, so he's more likely to actually do it.
How might Rania have felt when Bilal apologised?
She seemed cautious but touched; after being mocked while people watched, an honest apology may have eased some of the hurt.
How long is it before Kayla can reach the minimum age of driving of her state, which is 18, if she is currently half the age of her sister Kimiko who is 26 years old?

If Kimiko is 26 years old, Kayla, who is half her age, is 26/2 = 13 years old.
Sine the minimum driving age is 18, Kayla will have to wait for 18-13 = 5 more years to start driving.
The answer is 5.

The school library was nearly empty at lunch. Aadhya had the geography project brief open: a model of a river basin, a report and a presentation, due in ten days. "It'll take a weekend," she told Ganga. "Saturday the model, Sunday the report." Ganga raised an eyebrow. "Remember the volcano model? The paint took three days to dry." Aadhya waved it off. "That was different. This time I'll be quick." She started the Saturday before the deadline. The clay cracked, the blue paint ran out, and the printer at the stationery shop was broken. On Monday she handed in the model with no report, her face hot.

How many days did Aadhya have for the project?
The project was due in ten days.
Why did Aadhya wave off Ganga's reminder about the volcano model?
She felt confident and hopeful, picturing everything going smoothly, so the earlier delay seemed like a one-off.
What could Aadhya try next time she estimates a project?
Aadhya could look at how long similar projects really took, like the volcano model, and start earlier to leave room for problems.
How might Ganga feel watching Aadhya hand in the model without a report?
Ganga might feel sorry for Aadhya and a little frustrated that the warning was ignored.

Before sports day, Zubin stood at the school gate looking at his classmates' shiny new running shoes, then at his own canvas ones with a patch on the toe. His ears went hot. That evening at the vegetable stall behind the bus stand, his mother Jyoti was counting change. "You've been quiet."
"Everyone has good shoes."
She did not say "be grateful." She said, "Which ones would you need to run, and which would you only want to be seen in?"
Zubin thought. "To run I need a grip and no holes."
On Sunday at the weekly market they found a plain pair with a good sole. Sports day, Zubin ran the 200 metres and came second. His shoes weren't the shiniest. He noticed he didn't care.

Where was Zubin's mother Jyoti counting change?
She was counting change at the vegetable stall behind the bus stand.
What was Zubin feeling at the school gate?
He felt embarrassed about his patched canvas shoes, as shown by his hot ears.
What question from Jyoti helped Zubin choose wisely?
She asked which shoes he would need to run and which he would only want to be seen in, so he separated a need from a want and chose a plain pair with a good sole.
How does Jyoti respond to Zubin's complaint that everyone has good shoes?
She does not lecture him to be grateful. She asks a question and lets him think, showing she takes his feelings seriously.

Class 4 teacher's note, last week before the winter break. Written by Vikas, class teacher.
Our class rabbit, Moti, got out of her cage during lunch and was found shivering behind the cupboard. Nobody meant any harm, but I asked what had happened.
Yusuf told me honestly that he had seen the cage door open before lunch. "But I didn't open it, Sir," he said, quite sure. "Someone else did. I just didn't close it." He felt much less bad than the boy who had left it open, though Moti got just as cold either way.
What I did next: I didn't scold. I asked Yusuf, "If you had opened it, would Moti be any colder?" He thought, and said no. Then I made both boys rabbit monitors for the week. Yusuf now checks the latch twice.

Where was Moti found?
Moti was found shivering behind the cupboard.
Why did Yusuf feel less bad than the boy who left the door open?
Yusuf felt that not closing the door was less guilty than opening it, so doing nothing felt innocent even though Moti got just as cold.
What question did Vikas ask, and why was it useful?
'If you had opened it, would Moti be any colder?', which showed Yusuf that harm from not acting was the same as harm from acting.
What was lunchtime like for Moti?
Moti the rabbit got out, got cold and hid shivering behind the cupboard.

Omkar spotted Tushar at the college canteen counter, thinner, in plain white clothes, collecting papers for the ashram. Three months ago Tushar had stopped answering his parents' calls. Omkar's chest tightened.

"Come sit. Tea?"

Tushar hesitated, then sat. "I've only got ten minutes. The group is waiting."

Omkar wanted to say the teacher was using him. Instead he swallowed it. "What's a normal day like there?"

Tushar lit up, talking about songs at dawn and cooking for two hundred people.

"Sounds like real work," Omkar said. "You don't have to answer, but people ask about you. My door is open, any time, even midnight."

Tushar looked at his tea. "Okay," he said quietly.

Where did Omkar spot Tushar?
Omkar spotted Tushar at the college canteen counter.
What was Omkar worried about, and why did Omkar swallow the urge to say the teacher was using Tushar?
Omkar was worried about Tushar cutting off his parents, and held back because attacking the teacher might make Tushar defensive and push him further in.
What would you advise Omkar to do next?
Stay warm, keep asking curious questions, keep the door open for Tushar to visit or call, and avoid ultimatums or attacks on the teacher.
How might Tushar feel when asked about a normal day?
Tushar lit up talking about songs at dawn and cooking, so a curious question probably felt welcoming rather than judging, which made it easier to say okay to the open door.

Subject: Paris and the Great Shrug

Baljeet,
Three weeks into the exchange and I finally understand something. Everyone here shrugs. The bakery lady shrugs. My flatmate shrugs. And in my first class, when I asked the professor whether the essay could be late, he shrugged, lips pushed out, and said, "Eh."
I was so hurt. I thought he was saying, "I couldn't care less about your problem." I didn't sleep well.
Next day I asked a French classmate. She laughed. "That shrug means 'it's possible, don't worry.' If he didn't care, he'd just say no."
I emailed him to check. He replied: "Of course, submit Friday."
So a shrug here can be friendly, casual, even kind. At home, if I shrugged at Papa, he'd think I was being rude.
I'm using words now. Much safer.
Nitin

What did the professor say along with his shrug?
"Eh."
What was Nitin feeling after the professor's shrug?
Nitin felt hurt and dismissed, losing sleep because the shrug seemed to mean the professor didn't care.
What did Nitin do that cleared up the confusion?
Nitin asked a classmate and then emailed the professor to check in words, which confirmed the essay could be late.
How does a shrug from Nitin look to Papa at home?
Papa would think it was rude, showing how the same gesture carries different weight in different places.
What does "line up" mean at school assembly?

To line up means to stand in a line, one behind another. It can also mean to arrange something in advance.
Examples: Please line up outside the lab. The school has lined up a guest speaker for Friday.

I hope your week is going well. I'd like to ask you something.

As you know, Kunal joined the claims team six weeks ago. He's keen and works hard, but he's still stuck on how we do things here: how we name files, when to update the tracker, who to ask for approvals. I've been explaining the same things to him every day, and it's taking a lot of my time.

You're patient and you know our habits better than anyone. Would you pair with him on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, for about an hour each, for the next month? Just work alongside him on real cases.

I'll take two of your smaller reports off your plate to make room.

Let me know what you think.

Thanks,
Binita

P.S. Update, four weeks later: Kunal now updates the tracker without reminders, and my inbox is much quieter.

Tuesday and Thursday afternoons.
Why did Binita decide to ask Lavanya for help?
Binita was tired and stretched from explaining the same things every day, and hoped a patient colleague could help Kunal learn faster.
What else could Binita do to support Kunal alongside the pairing?
Binita could give Kunal small tasks with clear criteria and a short daily check-in, so progress is easy to see.
How might Lavanya see Binita's request?
Lavanya may feel trusted and valued for being patient, and the offer to take away two reports makes the extra time feel fair.

The projector flickered, the office generator hummed, and the director had to leave for the airport in twelve minutes. Suraj talked fast, his notes shaking in his hand. "Here's the festival stall plan for the weavers' cooperative. We get the corner spot at the mela, the new looms arrive Monday, all eight weavers finish forty sarees each, the printed bags come Friday, and the TV channel covers us on opening day."
The director was already nodding and reaching for a pen.
Naveen, sitting at the end, raised a hand. "Thirty seconds. That's five things that all have to go right, on time, together. Each one sounds fine. All five at once is a lot less likely."
Suraj frowned. "So what, we do nothing?"
"No. We sign off the stall and the sarees now. We keep the TV and the bags as bonuses, not the plan."
The director paused, pen in the air, and looked at the clock.

How many sarees was each weaver supposed to finish?
Forty sarees each.
What might Suraj be feeling when he asks, "So what, we do nothing?"
Suraj may feel his plan is being attacked just as the director was about to sign, and is frustrated and defensive under the time pressure.
Which part of Naveen's response makes it useful to the team?
Naveen didn't only point out that five linked steps are less likely together; Naveen also split the plan into what to sign now and what to treat as bonuses.
What would change if Naveen had stayed silent because the director was in a hurry?
The director would likely have signed a plan that depended on everything going right, and a single late delivery or missing TV crew could have spoiled the whole stall.

Read this:

Ten minutes before the exam, Chetan handed Neelam's pen back across the aisle. She narrowed her eyes at him, hard, lips tight. His stomach flipped. Did I break it? Is she angry I kept it all week? He almost moved seats. Then the sun slid behind the building across the road, and the glare blazing off the blackboard went dull. Neelam's face relaxed. She rubbed her eyes and grinned at him. “Thanks. I forgot my glasses, and that board was killing me.” Chetan let out his breath and looked where she had been looking. The board was still hard to read.

What had Neelam forgotten?
Neelam had forgotten her glasses.
What was Chetan feeling when Neelam narrowed her eyes?
He felt anxious and a little guilty, worried he'd broken her pen or kept it too long and that she was angry.
What could Chetan try next time a look worries him?
He could check the context, such as glare or light, or simply ask, before deciding the look is about him.
What was the morning like for Neelam?
Neelam was struggling to read the board in the glare without her glasses and wasn't thinking about the pen at all.

Read this:

"Pradeep, where's your flute? Class is starting."
"At home. In the cupboard. I'm stopping, Tenzin."
"Stopping? It's been two weeks!"
"My lips hurt after five minutes. And every note squeaks like a door. You heard it."
"Everyone squeaks. I squeaked for a month."
"Your squeaks sounded better than mine."
"They sounded exactly the same, trust me."
"No. Some people just have talent. I don't."
"Sir said the first few weeks are the worst."
"Sir says that to everyone."
The music teacher began the scale, and eleven flutes piped up. Pradeep sat with his empty hands under the desk. By the end of term Tenzin could play the whole school song.

How long had Pradeep been learning the flute?
Two weeks.
What does Pradeep believe about himself, and how does he feel?
He believes he has no talent, and he feels discouraged and embarrassed by the squeaks.
What else could Pradeep have tried?
Shorter practice sessions and asking the teacher about his lip position, to get through the sore, squeaky stage.
How does Tenzin see Pradeep quitting?
Tenzin is surprised and tries to encourage him, insisting his own squeaks sounded the same.

Sunday night. Tried Rashmi's exercise tonight instead of crying about it again. Value one: being near Amma and Appa as they get older. What it protects: their safety, my peace of mind, the feeling of being a good daughter. Value two: the PhD offer in Toronto. What it protects: my curiosity, the work I've wanted since I was fourteen, my sense of being my own person. Then the harder question: is there an order that honours both? Maybe: defer by a year, help set up daily visits from Rashmi's family and a weekly nurse check-in, then go, with a trip home every summer. Something still gets lost. Amma won't have me at her elbow. I can't pretend that away. But I think I can choose it with my eyes open.
Rekha

Where is Rekha's PhD offer?
In Toronto.
How does Rekha feel about the choice at the end of the entry?
She feels sad about what will be lost but steadier, able to choose with her eyes open.
What steps did Rekha use to work through the conflict?
Naming each value, asking what each protects, and finding an order that honours both as far as possible.
How might Amma feel about Rekha's plan?
Amma may feel sad to lose her daughter nearby, even with the visits and summer trips.

Read this:

Hemant, ten, had moved from the municipal school to the big school across the flyover in Thane in June. On the first day Omkar told him cheerfully, "Municipal kids are always weak in English, na? Don't feel bad." Hemant had read three storybooks that month. But on Friday, when the teacher said, "Dictation, twenty words," a knot formed in his stomach. He felt Omkar's eyes on his notebook. 'Receive.' Was it ie or ei? He knew this. He wrote it, rubbed it out, wrote it again. By the time he looked up, the teacher was on word nine. He had missed three. Walking home, he spelled 'receive' perfectly in his head, which made it worse.

How many storybooks had Hemant read that month?
Three storybooks.
Why did Hemant keep rubbing out 'receive'?
Feeling Omkar's eyes and remembering the remark about municipal kids, he was so afraid of proving it true that he doubted a word he knew.
What small step could Hemant try before the next dictation?
He could remind himself of the three books he read and focus on one word at a time instead of on who might be watching.
How might Omkar read Hemant's dictation mark, and why would that be misleading?
Omkar might think the low mark proves the remark, not realising the fear of being judged is what made Hemant miss the words.

metadata.subtype: Feeling watched for a group label [Actor]

messages.content: Do animals "adapt" or "adopt" to a new climate?

They adapt. "Adapt" means to change in order to fit new conditions. "Adopt" means to take something as your own, such as a child, a pet or an idea.
Examples: Camels adapt to desert life. We plan to adopt a puppy from the shelter.

Read this:

Outside the ICU at the district hospital, Lokesh kept his voice low, but it cracked anyway.
"Vijay, the hospital wants a deposit by tonight. The fixed deposit is in Appa's name. The shop is in Appa's name. Who signs?"
"How would I know? You're the one who lives with him!"
"And whenever I tried to ask him about the papers, you said it was disrespectful. 'Don't talk about that while he's alive,' you said."
"Because it was! He's our father, not a property file."
"He's our father, and now he can't speak, and we don't know whose name is on the house."
"So you want to fight about the house here? Now?"
"I don't want to fight at all! I wanted to talk two years ago."
A nurse looked over. Both brothers went silent. Lokesh sat on the bench with his head in his hands. Vijay stood by the window, fists tight, then phoned their Mama about the deposit.

What does the hospital want by tonight?
A deposit.
What was Lokesh feeling when he said "I wanted to talk two years ago"?
Lokesh felt frustrated and hurt, blaming the years of silence for the mess they are in now.
What could the brothers do once their father is stable?
They could gather the papers together calmly and, when their father is able, gently ask what he wants, perhaps with a trusted elder present.
Why might Vijay react with anger rather than agreement?
Vijay is frightened for their father and may feel guilty that his rule of silence left them stuck, so the anger covers that.

metadata.subtype: Approach: avoiding the issue until an emergency forces it [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: Moving the vendor decision
Dear Siddharth,
Could we move tomorrow's paper-vendor decision to Monday? Honestly, this week on the press floor has worn me down. With the machines running and the roof fans broken, it's close to unbearable by noon. Yesterday I approved a proof with the wrong colour code and snapped at Raju over nothing. I'm not proud of either.
I've started stepping outside for ten minutes every couple of hours and keeping a water bottle at my station. Could we also order ear defenders for the supervisors? I'd rather make the vendor call on Monday morning in the quiet office, with a clear head.
Thanks for understanding,
Alka

What mistake did Alka make yesterday?
Alka approved a proof with the wrong colour code.
How does Alka feel about yesterday's mistakes?
Alka feels embarrassed and not proud, and sees that the heat and noise have worn down focus and patience.
Why is moving the vendor decision a sensible choice?
Alka's concentration is low in the hot, noisy week, so deciding on Monday with a clear head avoids another costly slip.
How might Siddharth read this email?
Siddharth may value the honesty and see it as responsible planning, not an excuse, since Alka also suggests fixes.

Read this:

Vasudha, you think I was always this careful? Ask your Deepak mama about the ghat road. I was fifteen, in Kodaikanal, and my friends bet I wouldn't cycle down the ghat without touching the brakes. Six boys, all shouting. I didn't think for one second. I just went. I hit gravel at the second bend and flew into the bushes. Twelve stitches on my knee, and my father's face in the hospital, I still remember it. But here's the other half. That same year I had to choose between science and arts. I sat alone on the roof for three evenings with a notebook. I listed what I loved and what I was good at. I talked to my teacher. I chose arts, against everyone's advice, and it was right. Same boy. Different room. That's what I want you to see.

How many stitches did Deepak get on his knee?
Twelve stitches.
Why did young Deepak not think before cycling down the ghat?
With six boys shouting and a bet on, Deepak felt excited and dared, and the pressure of friends watching pushed him into a snap choice.
What was different about how Deepak chose between science and arts?
Deepak decided alone and calm over three evenings, making lists and talking to a teacher, which let careful reasoning guide him.
How might Deepak's father have felt at the hospital?
He was likely frightened and shaken seeing his son hurt, and perhaps angry that a bet had led to it.

Read this:

The school staff room was decorated for Christmas, paper stars hanging from the fan, when Rehana, the new head of the science department, proposed ending the weekly unit tests. She had read three studies that supported her. But she had also learned to distrust how good that felt. At the meeting, she said, "Before we decide, I'd like to hear the best case for keeping the tests." She turned to Simran, the maths teacher who had argued with her all year. "You'll do this better than anyone." Simran blinked, then spoke for ten minutes: parents rely on the marks, weaker students need regular practice, teachers catch gaps early. Rehana wrote each point down. Afterwards she changed her proposal: monthly tests instead of weekly, with short quizzes in between. Simran said, "I can live with that."

What did Rehana propose ending?
The weekly unit tests.
Why did Rehana distrust how good the supporting studies felt?
She knew agreement can feel reassuring even when it's one-sided, so she felt cautious and wanted to hear the other side.
What did Rehana's choice to ask Simran achieve?
It brought out strong reasons she had missed and led to a better compromise that both could accept.
How might Simran feel being asked for the best case?
Simran seems surprised and perhaps respected for the first time in a year of arguments.
Occassion, ocasion or occasion?

The correct spelling is "occasion": double c, single s.
Example: Diwali is a happy occasion when the whole family gets together.
How did Abhimanyu die in the great war?
He broke into Drona's circular battle array, but the others could not follow him in. Surrounded by many warriors at once, he was finally killed.

Read this:

When I was nine, I discovered a trick on Papa without even knowing it.
After dinner I asked, "Can I play the racing game for five minutes?" He was reading and said, "Five minutes."
After five minutes I said, "Just one more race?" He nodded without looking up.
Then, "Omkar wants to play too. Only ten minutes, together?" Papa said, "Okay, ten."
Each yes made the next one seem normal. By the time Mummy came in, it was ten o'clock and my little brother Omkar was asleep on the carpet. Papa looked at the clock and said, "How did it get so late?"
I didn't know. I'd only ever asked for a little bit. Himani the genius, Mummy called me, not smiling.

What time was it when Mummy came in?
It was ten o'clock.
What was Himani feeling when Papa asked how it got so late?
Himani felt a bit guilty and confused, having only ever asked for a little bit each time.
What could Papa try next time to avoid the slow slide?
He could agree a clear total time at the start, like thirty minutes, and set a timer so each small request doesn't feel like a natural next step.
How might Mummy see what happened?
Mummy seems annoyed, calling Himani "the genius" without smiling, and may be frustrated with Papa too.

Read this:

On a grey morning in Hanoi, Bao stood outside the glass tower where he'd been offered a job at an international bank. His cousin Santiago, visiting from Mexico City, had come for moral support.
"You look sick," Santiago said.
"I'm going in to say no."
"No? You said the salary was huge."
"It is." Bao pulled his jacket tighter. "But last month I volunteered at the street children's centre. I've been going every weekend. I want to work there full time."
"And the bank?"
"Every time I thought about it, I felt proud, and then nothing. At the centre I feel tired and alive."
He went in. Twenty minutes later he came out, pale but smiling. "Done. I'm terrified. And I feel light."

Where did Bao volunteer every weekend?
He volunteered at the street children's centre.
How does Bao feel after saying no to the bank?
He feels terrified and light at the same time: frightened of the choice, but calm that it fits him.
What might help Bao through the first months of this new path?
Keeping in touch with supportive people like Santiago and reminding himself why the centre feels right when the fear comes.
How is Santiago affected by watching Bao make this choice?
Santiago moves from surprise at turning down a huge salary to seeing Bao's relief, and likely comes to respect the decision.

Read this:

I'm the neighbour who walks his dog by the lane behind Nirmala's house, and I saw a bit of this last week. A boy from her school leaned on the wall and said something low to her. I couldn't hear it, but her shoulders went stiff and she walked on without turning. Later I saw her sitting on the step with her phone, typing and saving something. I can't say what she felt, she might have been scared, or just angry, or both. The next morning she was walking to the bus with her mother, who had a folder in her hand. I mentioned what I'd seen to her mother, in case it helped. Gurpreet.

Where did the narrator see the boy speak to Nirmala?
He saw it in the lane behind Nirmala's house.
What might Nirmala's stiff shoulders and silence suggest?
They may suggest fear or anger, and Gurpreet says he cannot be certain of what she felt. Walking on without answering fits a wish to avoid engaging.
What would you advise Nirmala to do?
Keep a record of what was said, tell her mother, school or authorities, and avoid answering him.
How might Nirmala's mother feel on hearing what the neighbour saw?
She may feel worried but glad someone spoke up, since it supports the report she is making.

Read this:

Tuesday
I hate tidying my desk. So today I tried a trick. I set the kitchen timer for ten minutes and said, 'Beat yesterday.' Yesterday it took me fourteen minutes of moaning. Today I made it a race: pens in the jar, books stacked big to small, papers in the tray, crumbs in the bin. I was so busy watching the timer that I forgot to be bored. Eight minutes, forty seconds! Aai said, 'Chaitanya beta, are you feeling well?' Tenzin phoned and I told him my time. He says he'll race me tomorrow with his room. Game on.

How long did tidying take yesterday?
Fourteen minutes of moaning.
Why did Chaitanya forget to be bored?
He was so focused and excited about beating the timer that the chore felt like a game 🎉
What could keep the race fun after a few days?
Racing Tenzin, or setting a new target, so there's always something to beat; the race is what keeps his attention on the job.
How does Aai react to the tidy desk?
Aai jokes 'are you feeling well?', so she seems surprised and amused by the quick tidying.

messages.content: Why do flower pots need small holes at the bottom?
The holes let extra water drain out. Because roots need air as well as water, and soil that stays soggy leaves no room for air, roots in a pot without holes can start to rot.
Email to a carpenter asking for the price of a small bookshelf, 90 cm wide, and how long it will take. 35 words. Gayatri.

Dear Sir,
I would like to order a small bookshelf, about 90 cm wide. Could you please tell me the price and how long it will take to make? I look forward to hearing from you.
Gayatri
Chintu counts on 3 from 5 like this: "5, 6, 7". He says the answer is 7. Is he right?

Answer: No. He counted the 5 as one of the steps. Counting on 3 from 5 is 6, 7, 8. The answer is 8.

Say the start number in your head (or whisper it), then say 3 NEW numbers out loud, one for each finger. Show it on a number line: three jumps from 5 land on 8.

Read this:

At break time in their Kolkata school, Nikita, a bigger girl from the next class, snatched Zubin's toy tractor. "Give it or I'll push you," she hissed. Zubin froze. His eyes filled and he let go without a word. Later Miss Anjali noticed him hunched on the bench and asked what happened. He whispered it. She knelt beside him. "Thank you for telling me. It's not your fault." She went to find Nikita at once and got the tractor back. Then she practised with him: "Stand tall, say STOP loudly, then come to me." Zubin tried. "STOP!" It came out bigger than he expected.

What did Nikita snatch from Zubin?
Nikita snatched Zubin's toy tractor.
What was Zubin feeling when he froze and let go?
Zubin felt frightened by Nikita's threat to push him, so he froze and gave up the tractor without a word.
How did Miss Anjali help Zubin, and why did it matter?
She thanked him, said it was not his fault, dealt with Nikita straight away and practised a loud "STOP", so Zubin learned that telling works.
How might Nikita see it when Miss Anjali comes to find her?
Nikita may feel caught and a bit worried, and learn that grabbing and threats get noticed by adults.

Read this:

At a birthday party in a flat in Osaka, someone passed a small vape around the balcony. Everyone was laughing. When it came to Aiko, a boy held it out. "Just try. Everyone does."
Aiko shook her head. "No thanks."
"Come on, one puff. It's nothing."
"I said no." She kept her voice light. "Anyone want to go get ice cream?"
Nobody moved. The boy pushed it closer. "Don't be boring."
Aiko felt her cheeks burn. She went back inside, found her friend Amara by the snacks, and said, "I'm heading out. You coming?"
Amara looked at her face, then at the balcony. "Yeah. Ice cream?"
Walking to the convenience store, Aiko said, "Sorry for dragging you away."
"Don't be. If they keep pushing like that, we don't need to go to their parties."
Aiko laughed, relieved, and texted her mother that they were leaving early.

Where was the vape being passed around?
On the balcony of a flat in Osaka.
What was Aiko feeling when the boy called her boring?
Aiko felt embarrassed, her cheeks burning, but still sure she did not want to try it.
Which of Aiko's moves worked, and why?
Saying no, suggesting another plan, and then leaving with Amara worked, because staying would only have brought more pressure.
How does Amara see the boy's repeated pushing?
Amara sees it as a sign that the group isn't good company, saying they don't need to go to their parties.

Read this:

Thursday night
Kamal again today. Eleven years old, back row, never a word. When I asked the class what makes a good friend, thirty hands went up and his stayed flat on the desk. I'll be honest, diary: I felt irritated. Then I collected the paragraphs. His was the best in the class. 'A good friend notices when you have gone quiet and doesn't make it a big thing.' I read it three times in the staffroom. Is he telling me what he needs? Tomorrow I'll try Mrs. Bose's idea: sticky notes on every desk, everyone writes one answer, and I read some out without names. And I'll ask Kamal to stay two minutes after the bell, just to tell him that sentence was beautiful.
Pooja

What did Kamal write about a good friend?
'A good friend notices when you have gone quiet and doesn't make it a big thing.'
How did Pooja feel when Kamal's hand stayed flat, and how did that change?
Pooja felt irritated at first, then moved, reading his paragraph three times after finding it the best in the class.
Why might the sticky-note plan help Kamal?
Everyone writes an answer and some are read without names, so Kamal can share his thinking without having to speak up.
How might Kamal feel when told after the bell that his sentence was beautiful?
He would probably feel surprised and quietly proud, noticed without a fuss, just as his own sentence describes.

Read this:

Mahima: hey did you see the schedule? why did you change my slot
Aparna: I moved it, sorry. I wanted the demo to look tight
Mahima: you didn't ask
Aparna: I know. I keep fixing everything myself 😅
Mahima: also last week you said nothing when Dev never sent the banner
Aparna: yeah. I didn't want to sound harsh
Mahima: it's either taking over or going quiet. can you just tell us what the goal is and who owns what?
Aparna: ...that's fair. I'll post the goal tonight. Demo day is what matters, not me looking in charge
Mahima: thank you 🙂 happy to move slots if you explain

Which slot did Aparna change?
Aparna moved Mahima's slot.
Why did Aparna say nothing when Dev never sent the banner?
Aparna did not want to sound harsh, having taken over earlier and feeling unsure how to lead.
What did Aparna decide to post that night?
Aparna decided to post the goal that night, after agreeing Mahima's point was fair.
How might Mahima have felt when the slot was changed without a word?
Mahima probably felt overlooked and frustrated, but was willing to speak plainly and to help once the reasons were shared.

Read this:

I'm Bidisha, a parent helper on reading day. Aadhya sat right in front. Every time the teacher asked a question, she shouted the answer. The teacher reminded her, “Hands up, please.” The next time Aadhya's hand went up so fast she nearly fell over, and she kept saying “Me! Me!” under her breath. The teacher caught her eye and nodded, then called another child first. Aadhya's face crumpled, but she kept her hand up. Next question, the teacher picked her, and her whole face lit up.

What did the teacher remind Aadhya to do?
Put her hand up.
What was Aadhya feeling when her face crumpled?

She felt frustrated and disappointed that another child was picked while she was trying so hard to wait. Bidisha could only see her face, so she might also have felt unsure if she would ever get a turn.
How did the teacher's nod help Aadhya?
It showed Aadhya that her raised hand was seen, which helped her keep waiting instead of blurting out.
How might the other children see Aadhya's shouting before she raised her hand?
They might feel it was unfair that she answered first each time, which is why hands up gives everyone a turn.

Read this:

Helpline caseworker's note, Tuesday.
Ganga called at 11:40 in the morning, from a colleague's phone at work. She spoke quietly. Her husband monitors her phone and bank account, and his anger has been getting worse. She wants to leave but is afraid.
I explained that the time of leaving is often when the risk is highest, so we plan carefully before any big step.
Together we worked out a few things. She will keep copies of her ID and certificates with her brother Kishore, whom she trusts completely. She'll save the helpline number under a friend's name. She and Kishore agreed on a simple phrase that means "come now." She knows the nearest police station and our local centre's address.
She sounded calmer by the end. "I didn't know there were steps," she said.
We will call her again on Friday at the same time, on the colleague's phone. Kishore has been given our number too.

Who will keep copies of Ganga's ID and certificates?
Her brother Kishore, whom she trusts completely.
How did Ganga seem to feel by the end of the call?
Ganga seemed calmer and a little relieved, surprised to learn there were steps she could take.
What safety steps did Ganga and the caseworker plan?
Keeping documents with Kishore, saving the helpline under another name, a phrase meaning "come now", and knowing the police station and centre.
How might Kishore feel being part of the plan?
Kishore probably feels worried but trusted, ready to act when Ganga needs him.

Read this:

Payal had loved her job at the cooperative bank in Satara. Now she sat at the counter and felt nothing. Her favourite music, Sunday lunches at her parents', even the new saree her husband Imran bought her, all felt grey.
At home, she stared at the washing for an hour, unable to start. Then she lay awake feeling guilty. "Imran does everything. I'm a burden," she thought. "This is just who I am now."
One morning Imran found her sitting on the kitchen floor, not crying, just blank. He sat beside her. "This isn't you being lazy. This is something that needs a doctor."
At the district hospital, the doctor listened and made a plan with her, including regular sessions with a counsellor. "What you're feeling tells you it will last forever," the doctor said. "It usually doesn't, with help." Payal held on to that sentence.

Where did Payal work?
At the cooperative bank in Satara.
How did Payal feel lying awake at night?
She felt guilty and like a burden, and hopeless, believing this was just who she was now.
What helped Payal start moving towards feeling better?
Imran's supportive words that it wasn't laziness, and seeing a doctor who made a treatment plan with counselling.
How does Imran see Payal's struggle?
He sees it as a health problem that needs a doctor, not a character flaw, and feels caring and concerned.

Check my sentence: Please open the window, it's too much hot.
Why do spiders make webs?
Meaning of "kettle"?
How can I find my things quickly?
48 chairs are put into 6 equal rows. How many chairs are in each row?

1. Fixed: Please open the window, it's very hot. Why: Use "very" before an adjective, not "too much".
2. A web is a trap for catching insects to eat. Because insects fly into the sticky threads and get stuck.
3. A kettle is a pot with a spout that is used for boiling water.
4. Give each thing one place and always put it there. Use boxes with labels for small items.
5. 8 chairs. Because 48 / 6 = 8.
Why do woollen clothes keep us warm in winter?
Wool holds body heat close to the skin. Because the fibres trap a lot of air among them, and still air passes heat along very poorly, the warmth of the body stays in.

Read this:

Friday. So Pema has been at school three weeks and still eats alone. He's actually funny; I found out in the chemistry lab when he gave all our test tubes names. Today I asked the guys if he could sit with us, and it went weird. Nobody said no. They just said 'he's not really our type' and changed the topic. What is our type? We're five boys who play the same game and wear the same shoes. I didn't push it. I hate that I didn't. Maybe on Monday I'll just go sit at his table instead. They can't kick me out of a table I leave. Or they can make it awkward forever. I'll decide on Monday. – Dhruv

How long has Pema been at the school?
Three weeks.
What does 'I hate that I didn't' show about Dhruv's feelings?
He felt ashamed that he let the group's quiet refusal stand, even though he likes Pema.
What small step could Dhruv try on Monday?
He could sit with Pema for one lunch, or bring one friend along, to show that group lines can be crossed.
What is lunchtime likely like for Pema right now?
Probably lonely, eating alone while the groups around him have already formed.
Tell me how a green mango tastes, in one sentence, and avoid the word "sour".
It tastes sharp and tangy, and it makes your mouth water.
Bill gets paid $20 every hour he works up to a total of 40 hours, after which he gets paid double that amount per hour.  How much does Bill get paid for a 50-hour workweek?

Bill makes $20 an hour for the first 40 hours, meaning he gets paid 40*20= 800 dollars.
For the remaining 10 hours, Bill gets paid double the amount of $20, meaning he makes 20*2=40 dollars an hour.
Since he worked 10 hours at that $40 an hour rate, that means he gets paid 10*40= 400 dollars for the final 10 hours.
In total, this means Bill gets paid 800+400=1200 dollars for his workweek.
The answer is 1200.

If Alice purchased 3600 acorns for nine times the price Bob paid, and Bob paid $6000 for his acorns, how much money did Alice pay for each acorn?

Nine times the price Bob paid for his acorns is 9*$6000 = $54000
If Alice purchased 3600 acorns for nine times the price Bob paid, she paid $54000/3600 = $15 for each acorn.
The answer is 15.

The narrator sees the man's face peel away under a sponge, taking the brown colour, scar and twisted lip, and then the red hair. Underneath is a pale, black-haired man who realises he is exposed, screams and hides his face in the pillow.

The power went out again at nine, and Lalit sat in the dark of the one-room flat he shared with his two younger brothers, phone at eight percent. Santosh's forward still sat on the screen: Lalit's private worry about failing maths, sent to the whole class group as a joke. I'm so angry it scares me.' She rang early and let him talk for twenty minutes. Afterwards he walked to the ground and ran laps until his legs shook, then opened the maths book Santosh had mocked.

On a page torn from his rough book, by candlelight.

It suggests he was frightened by how strong his anger had become and wanted help before it turned into something he would regret.

Venny spent $15000 on a used car which cost 40% of the original price. What was the original price of the car?

Let x be the original price of the car.
Then 40% * x = $15000
Thus x = $15000 / 0.4 = $37500
The answer is 37500.

At the Pune office of the education NGO, Tanvir was reviewing the proposal for the city council when Swati stopped by his desk. "Honestly, why are we even sending this? They'll reject it. They always reject small NGOs." She said it like a fact. Tanvir leaned back. He'd heard her say this before, about two grants that came through. He didn't argue. "Okay. Let's treat it as a guess. Write down what you think the chance of approval is. I'll write mine." She wrote 10 percent. He wrote 50. They sealed the slips in an envelope and pinned it to the board. Three weeks later, the council replied: approved for the library part, rejected for the laptops. Swati opened the envelope and laughed. "Both wrong." "Both wrong," Tanvir agreed. "You were too gloomy, I was too hopeful." They pinned the letter up next to the slips.

How might Swati have felt opening the envelope?
Swati was probably surprised and amused, seeing that her gloomy forecast was wrong, though not in the way Tanvir expected either.

After his internal complaint about the waste-dumping went nowhere and his manager began freezing him out, Akash sat in a small legal aid office in Kolkata with a thick folder on his knees.
Dolma, the lawyer, didn't rush him. She asked for dates, then documents, then photographs, and put aside everything that was opinion. "Anger is understandable," she said. "But the authorities act on facts."

When he signed it, Akash felt afraid, and also clear. He called his parents that night and told them what he had done. His father, after a long silence, said, "We'll manage. You did the right thing."
Three weeks later, officials inspected the site.

"Ma, I can't study like this. I need my own corner. Just a table."
Sangeeta didn't look up from the stove. "Be grateful you even have a room. Children in the slums study under streetlights. You should be thankful."
Tenzin's face went hot. He did feel lucky, sometimes. Now he just felt guilty for asking, and angry that he couldn't ask.
"I wasn't complaining about my life. I just wanted—"
"Enough. Be thankful."
He went back to the torch. He didn't mention the table again. That week he didn't tell her about the chemistry test he'd done badly on, or anything else.
Later, Sangeeta noticed how quiet he had become, and wondered why.

She could have listened first and said something like, "It is hard to study here. Let's see if we can find you a corner," before anything about gratitude.
How was Sangeeta affected by the way she answered?
Sangeeta was left puzzled and a little worried, noticing Tenzin had grown quiet without realising her words had shut down honest talk.

Please give me a paragraph of around 80 words about why the monsoon is my favourite season.

The monsoon is my favourite season because it changes everything. After the heat of summer, the first rain makes the whole world smell fresh. The trees turn deep green, and the dusty roads shine. Candice buys all the bread she and her family needs for the week from a local bakery.  She needs 2 loaves of white bread for sandwiches that cost $3.50 each.  She also needs a baguette that costs $1.50 and 2 loaves of sourdough bread that cost $4.50 each.  She also treats herself to a $2.00 almond croissant each visit.  How much does Candice spend at the bakery over 4 weeks?

2 loaves of white bread are $3.50 each so they cost 2*3.50 = $7.00
2 loaves of sourdough bread are $4.50 each so they cost 2*4.50 = $9.00
The white bread comes to $7.00, the sourdough is $9.00 and she gets a baguette for $1.50 and a croissant for $2.00 so she spends 7+9+1+2 = $19.50 per week
If she buys this same order of $19.50 every week for 4 weeks then she spends 19.50*4 = $78.00 over 4 weeks
The answer is 78.

Tuesday: After her marketing presentation, Ishita collected twenty-six peer feedback slips. Twenty-four were kind: 'confident', 'great visuals', 'best one today'. One said 'too fast'. One had a frowning face and the word 'boring'. On the metro home she read the 'boring' one nine times.
Thursday: Pranav, her project partner, asked how it went. 'Badly,' she said. 'People found it boring.' 'People?' 'Well. Someone.'
Saturday: Pranav spread all twenty-six slips on the library table and had her sort them into two piles. The good pile covered half the table. The other pile was two slips. Ishita looked at it for a while. 'I'll slow down next time,' she said. 'The boring one I'll just leave.'

How many peer feedback slips did Ishita collect?
Ishita collected twenty-six peer feedback slips.
Why did 'People found it boring' feel true to Ishita on Thursday?
Reading the 'boring' slip nine times made it loud in Ishita's mind, so one person's comment felt like everyone's view and the success felt like a failure.
What turning point came on Saturday, and what did it lead to?
Sorting all twenty-six slips into two piles showed twenty-four good ones against two, and Ishita took one useful fix, slowing down, while letting the 'boring' slip go.
What might Pranav have noticed when Ishita said 'Well. Someone'?
Pranav may have realised the problem wasn't the presentation but how the feedback was being read, which is why Pranav chose to lay out every slip.

metadata.subtype: Only the negatives in a review [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Shankar: ok honest question. your parents on the video call. your mum was all smiles, cheeks up, eyes crinkling. so sweet 😊
Shankar: your dad though. his face didn't move once. did i say something wrong??
Dhruv: haha no
Dhruv: that IS his happy face
Dhruv: at my cousin's wedding he looked exactly like that and later told everyone it was the best day of his year
Shankar: seriously? i was reading warmth off your mum's cheeks and nothing at all off his
Dhruv: mum's face does everything. dad's does almost nothing. you have to watch other stuff
Shankar: like what
Dhruv: he asked you three questions about your job. he never asks strangers anything
Shankar: oh
Shankar: ok that makes me feel a lot better 🙂
Dhruv: he also said "nice boy, that flatmate of yours" after you hung up. from him that's basically a speech

How many questions did Dhruv's dad ask about Shankar's job?
He asked Shankar three questions about his job.
Why was Shankar worried after the video call?
Shankar felt anxious that Dhruv's dad disliked him, because the dad's face barely moved while the mum's cheeks rose warmly, so Shankar read no warmth there.
What could Shankar watch for when someone's face stays still?
Other signs of interest, such as the questions the person asks and what they say later, and how that person's face usually looks.
How does Dhruv see his dad's still face?
Dhruv knows it as his dad's normal, even happy face, so he reads the three questions and the 'nice boy' remark as real warmth.

Read this:

In Buenos Aires, Sofia, twenty-six, a junior accountant at a large construction firm, noticed a pattern in the invoices: payments to a supplier nobody on site had heard of, always just under the approval limit. She checked the address. It was an empty lot. Her hands went cold. She showed her colleague Santiago. He glanced at the name on the approvals and lowered his voice. "That's the regional director. Leave it, Sofia. You'll never work in this industry again." She went home and couldn't eat. She thought about the workers whose safety budget kept getting cut. The next morning she wrote a clear report with copies of every invoice and sent it through the company's ethics line. She told only her mother. For weeks, every meeting felt like a trap.

What did Sofia find at the supplier's address?
An empty lot.
How did Sofia feel after Santiago's warning?
She was frightened for her career, so upset she couldn't eat, but troubled by what the fraud meant for the workers.
What made Sofia's way of reporting sensible?
She documented everything clearly and used the official ethics line, which protects both the evidence and her.
Why might Santiago react differently from Sofia?
He's focused on protecting himself from powerful people, while Sofia is more concerned about the harm the corruption causes.

What is "singular"?
My book uses the word "infinity". What does it mean?
What is "observant"?
What is "decipher"?

1. In grammar, "singular" means one, the opposite of plural. As an ordinary adjective it also means single, or unusual in a remarkable way.
2. It is a noun. It means a space or number with no end.
3. Observant is an adjective that means good at noticing things.
4. Decipher means to work out the meaning of something hard to read or understand. It is a verb.

Mr. and Mrs. Hugo went on a road trip. On the first day, they traveled 200 miles. On the second day, they traveled 3/4 as far. On the third day, they traveled 1/2 as many miles as the first two days combined. How many miles did they travel for 3 days?

On the second day, Mr. and Mrs. Hugo traveled 200 x 3/4 = 150 miles.
They traveled a total of 200 + 150 = 350 miles in the first two days.
On the third day, they traveled 350 x 1/2 = 175 miles.
So, Mr. and Mrs. Hugo traveled a total of 200 + 150 + 175 = 525 miles for 3 days.
The answer is 525.

In Toronto, Hana, sixteen, noticed that her friend Nour hadn't eaten lunch for two weeks. Nour stopped coming to the robotics club, sat with her hood up, and when Hana asked, she said, “I'm just tired. Nothing feels fun any more.”
It didn't pass. Hana felt worried in her stomach.
On Friday, she said, “Nour, I think this is more than tired. Can we go to Ms Chen together?”
Nour shook her head, then shrugged. “If you come.”
They went to the school counsellor at lunch. Ms Chen listened, thanked Nour for coming, and asked her gently about sleep and feelings. She called Nour's parents that afternoon and set up a weekly meeting.
Walking out, Nour said quietly, “Thanks for noticing.”

What had Nour stopped coming to?
The robotics club.
How did Hana feel about Nour's changes?
Hana felt worried, noticing the sadness and withdrawal had lasted weeks.
What did Hana do that was helpful, and why?
She named her worry kindly and went with Nour to the counsellor, so a trusted professional could help.
How did Ms Chen respond when Nour came in?
She listened, thanked Nour, asked gently about sleep and feelings, and called her parents that afternoon.

Pooja: done with the chem assignment??
Jagdish: yes ma'am 🫡
Pooja: good soldier. I'm "almost done"
Jagdish: "almost done" = haven't started 😅
Pooja: rude. accurate, but rude
Jagdish: want help with Q5?

Which question did Jagdish offer to help Pooja with?
What was Jagdish feeling on learning that Mr Iyer saw the air quotes?
Jagdish felt sorry and embarrassed, having meant the air quotes as a point about marks, not as mockery.
What is Jagdish's plan, and why might it work?
To apologise and ask Mr Iyer about the marks directly, putting the real doubt into words instead of a gesture that can look like a put-down.
How might Mr Iyer have experienced the air quotes in class?
He likely felt mocked and hurt, as if his word 'optional' were being made fun of in front of the class.
Is "hurridly" the way to spell it?

No, it is "hurriedly". The base is "hurry", and the y changes to i before "-ed", giving "hurried"; then "-ly" is added.
Example: She hurriedly packed her bag and ran to the station.

"You've eaten breakfast at midnight three days running," Rukmini said as Nitin came in, still in his hospital scrubs.
"Rotation. Nights this week, mornings next, then evenings. My body doesn't know what day it is."
"Neither does your temper. You shouted at the cooker yesterday."
"The cooker deserved it." He sank onto the sofa. "I'm so tired my eyes hurt."
"Can you ask for the same shift for longer? Even two weeks at a time?"
"Maybe. Jaswant in my ward did."
"Then ask. And book that health check you keep postponing."
"I'm fine."
"You're grey, Nitin."
He was quiet. "Okay. I'll talk to the ward in-charge tomorrow. And book it."
"I'll come with you."

What does Nitin's rotation look like?
Nights this week, mornings next, then evenings.
How is Nitin feeling after weeks of changing shifts?
He is exhausted and short-tempered, so tired his eyes hurt, and he shouted at the cooker.
What steps does Rukmini push Nitin to take?
Asking for longer blocks of the same shift and booking the postponed health check.
What is it like for Rukmini to live with Nitin's shifting hours?
Rukmini sees the midnight breakfasts and flashes of temper and worries about Nitin's health.
What is a raga?
A raga is a melodic framework with notes, movement, mood, important notes, and characteristic phrases. It is not just a scale.

I am Yamini, the neighbour upstairs. On Sunday I was on Rafiq's balcony, telling Rafiq's papa about the water tank repair, when Rafiq burst in: "Papa, Papa, a red bus, I saw a red bus!" Papa held up one finger and said, "Two minutes, dost, then it's your turn." Rafiq's mouth stayed open, feet danced on the tiles, and one hand pressed against the lips. When the tank story ended, Papa turned right away: "Now. The red bus?" Rafiq shouted the whole story in one breath.

What did Rafiq say when bursting in?
"Papa, Papa, a red bus, I saw a red bus!"
What was Rafiq feeling while waiting for the two minutes?
Impatient and perhaps afraid the thought would vanish. The dancing feet and the hand pressed on the lips show a hard struggle to wait.
What worked better than scolding in this scene?
Papa's one raised finger and a promise of a turn in two minutes, followed by really giving that turn.
What might Papa be feeling when holding up a finger instead of scolding?
Patient and calm, wanting to respect the talk with Yamini and Rafiq's excitement at once.

Subject: Question about "restructuring" in Tuesday's memo
Dear Keerthana,
Thank you for Tuesday's memo. I read it three times, and I'm still not sure what it means for my team.
The memo says the field support unit will be "restructured to improve efficiency" and that some roles will be "realigned". I understand the aim. But could you tell me plainly: will any of my eleven field staff lose their jobs, be moved to another city, or have their pay changed? If so, who, and from when?
I'm asking because the staff are already worried, and I would rather give them the truth than guess. Several of them have families in the district and no other work nearby.
If there are decisions still open, I'd also like to know how we can suggest options, such as reduced hours instead of cuts.
Thank you for your help.
Regards,
Manjula

How many field staff does Manjula have?
Manjula has eleven field staff.
Why does Manjula ask for plain answers instead of accepting the memo's words?
Manjula feels worried for the staff and uneasy that "realigned" hides real changes to people's jobs, pay and homes.
What makes Manjula's email a good way to raise the concern?
It is polite, asks exactly what happens to whom and when, and suggests alternatives like reduced hours.
What might the field staff be feeling while waiting for an answer?
They are probably anxious and unsure, worried about their jobs and their families in the district.

Subject: Our practice week — what we learned

Hi Preeti,

I know we talked about it last night, but I wanted it written down so we don't forget by the time the baby comes.

What worked:
- Splitting nights: I take 10 pm to 2 am, you take 2 to 6. We both slept at least four hours in a row.

Let's try one more practice week in March with these fixes.

Love,
Siddharth

Which hours does Siddharth take during the night?
10 pm to 2 am.

Siddharth seems thoughtful and a bit apologetic, especially about forgetting the phone, but hopeful the fixes will help.

They could decide who they can call for help if one of them falls ill, so the routine doesn't collapse.

What colour was the big kite Irawati pointed at?
Red.
What was Siddharth feeling as he pointed at each new kite?
He felt delighted and excited, eyes wide and grinning, eager to share each kite with Irawati.
How could Irawati keep building on this shared attention?
She could name each kite he points at and follow his finger in return.
How does Irawati experience Siddharth pointing and looking back?
She is happy and amused, sharing the moment with Siddharth.

Elif, two and a bit, wanted to walk the low wooden edge of the sandpit in the Berlin courtyard. Liam, the student who babysat her on Wednesdays, held out a finger. She waved it away. Three steps in, she tipped left, bent her knees, flung her arms out, and stayed up. On the corner she tipped again and this time dropped onto her bottom in the sand, then climbed straight back on.

Where was the edge that Elif walked along?
The low wooden edge of the sandpit in the Berlin courtyard.
Why might Elif have waved Liam's finger away?
She wanted to do it on her own and seemed confident enough to try without help.
How could Liam support Elif on the sandpit edge without taking over?
Stay close by, let her wobble and catch herself, and step in only if she is about to fall somewhere hard.
What would change if the edge were next to concrete instead of sand?
Liam would probably need to hold her hand, because a fall would hurt far more than dropping onto sand.

A school buys 300 notebooks at ₹20 each. How much does it pay?

Now you try: 400 pencils at ₹5 each
The answer is ₹2,000.

For every loaf of bread that Ted buys, he needs an additional 2 packs of sandwich meat and 2 packs of sliced cheese to make 10 sandwiches.  The bread costs $4.00, the sandwich meat costs $5.00 per pack and the cheese costs $4.00 per pack.  He has a $1.00 off  coupon for one pack of cheese and an additional $1.00 coupon for one pack of meat.  How much does each sandwich cost?

He buys 2 packs of sandwich meat at $5.00 a pack so 2*5.00 = $10.00
He buys 2 packs of cheese at $4.00 a pack so 2*4.00 = $8.00
The loaf of bread cost $4.00 plus $10.00 for meat and $8.00 for cheese so his total is 4+10+8 = $22.00
He has coupons to use a checkout so his new total is 22-1-1 = $20.00
He can make 10 sandwiches from his purchase and his purchase total is $20 so 20/10 = $2.00
The answer is 2.

In the office canteen in Kochi, Asif, a senior developer who had once run a workshop at Elizabeth's college, opened her portfolio on his tablet between bites of appam.
'It's neat,' he said. 'But look at this line: "Tools used: JavaScript, maps, a database." That's a shopping list. What did the bus tracker actually do for anyone?'
Elizabeth thought for a second. 'Students at our college stopped missing the last bus. The warden said late passes dropped by half.'
'Then say that. Problem, what you built, what improved.'
That night, in her flat in Kakkanad, she rewrote all three projects. The bus tracker now began: 'Students kept missing the last college bus.' The tools moved to a small line at the end.
A week later Asif sent one word back: 'Better.' Two days after that, a recruiter asked her about the late passes.

What did the tools line on Elizabeth's portfolio say?
'Tools used: JavaScript, maps, a database.'
How might Elizabeth have felt when Asif called her tools list a shopping list?
She may have felt a little stung but curious, and she quickly found the real result, which suggests she took the comment as useful.
What else could Elizabeth ask Asif to check next?
Whether the results can be seen on a phone screen within a few seconds, since recruiters often skim.
What changes for the recruiter after the rewrite?
The recruiter now sees a real result, fewer missed buses and late passes, and has something concrete to ask about.

messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: new school update
Hi Vikas,
It's been a month here in Hyderabad, and honestly, it's like a map with borders. The "IIT group" doesn't talk to the "dance group." The dance group doesn't talk to the "bus kids." If you sit at the wrong bench, people literally stop talking. On day two I sat with the dance girls because I like dancing, and the next day the IIT group I study with asked, "So you're with them now?" As if I have to pick a country. I don't want to. At our old school we all just mixed. I'm trying to keep friends in both, but I'm tired. How do people do this?
Sunaina

How long has Sunaina been at the new school?
A month.
How does Sunaina feel about having to pick a group?
Sunaina feels frustrated and tired, not wanting to choose between friends.
What could Sunaina try to keep friends in both groups?
Sunaina could be open about liking both and invite a friend from each to something they share, like a study-and-dance evening.
How might the IIT group see Sunaina sitting with the dance girls?
They might feel a little betrayed or uncertain about whether Sunaina still belongs with them.

Read this:

I'm Dolma. My younger brother died two winters ago, in an accident on the Manali road. He was nineteen.

For weeks I couldn't think clearly. Reason had nothing to offer. What held me was the monastery. The forty-nine days of prayers, the butter lamps, the monks chanting in the cold hall at dawn. I didn't have to understand anything. I just sat and the chanting held me.

It didn't make the pain go away. I stopped expecting it to.

Some days I was angry at everything I'd been taught. Why would a kind universe take him? I felt guilty for thinking it. My friend Simran, who isn't Buddhist, said, "Tell the old monk that. You're allowed to." So I did.

The old monk just nodded and said, "Doubt is also grief."

I still light a butter lamp for my brother every month. Some months I believe. Some months I just light it.

How old was Dolma's brother when he died?
Nineteen.
How did Dolma feel on the days she was angry at what she'd been taught?
Dolma felt angry and guilty, questioning why a kind universe would take the brother.
What helped Dolma when faith felt shaken?
Speaking the doubt to a trusted person, the old monk, as Simran encouraged, instead of hiding it.
How does the old monk see Dolma's doubt?
The old monk sees it as part of mourning, saying "Doubt is also grief."

I'm Kamal, and my little brother Yogesh is eight. Our Nani lights the lamp every morning and says a short prayer. Yogesh used to run past, looking for his socks. This month something changed. I saw him stop at the doorway, fold his hands and stand still while Nani sang. He doesn't know all the words, so he moves his lips a bit late. Yesterday he put a marigold near the lamp, one he had picked from the neighbour's pot, which Nani pretended not to notice. At night he whispers to himself before sleeping. I asked him once what he says. He said, "Just thank you. For today." I can't tell if he means it the way Nani does, but he seems calmer.

What did Yogesh put near the lamp yesterday?
He put a marigold he had picked from the neighbour's pot.
What does Yogesh's whispering at night suggest about him?
It suggests he has started his own small gratitude habit, thanking the day in his own words, which may make him feel calm.
How could Nani gently support Yogesh's new habit?
She could teach him one or two lines of the prayer slowly, or invite him to light the lamp with her, without making him feel tested.
Why might Kamal be unsure about what the prayer means to Yogesh?
Kamal only sees the outside, the folded hands and whispers, so he can guess Yogesh is calmer but cannot know what he feels inside.

Read this:

Tutor's note, Wednesday

Ankita arrived for the physics session and spent the first twenty minutes listing what could go wrong in the board exam: the paper might be set from the other textbook, she might get the numericals wrong, her pen might leak, she might faint in the hall, she might lose her place in the queue for the college she wants. She said, "I have to think of everything, otherwise I'm being careless."

She had not opened the chapter on current electricity since Saturday.

I did not argue with the list. I asked her to pick the one thing on it she could do something about today. She chose numericals. We did six together; she got four right and was surprised.

I've asked her to bring the list next time, and we'll give it five minutes before we study, not forty. I'll also mention to her parents that she's carrying a lot.

Nilesh, physics tutor

How many numericals did Ankita get right?
Ankita got four right out of the six.
Why does Ankita feel that listing everything that could go wrong is responsible?
Ankita feels anxious about the exam and believes thinking of everything protects her from being careless, even though it stops her starting.
What countermeasure did Nilesh use, and why might it help?
Nilesh asked Ankita to pick one item she could act on today, then practised numericals; doing something real breaks the worry loop and builds confidence.
How might Ankita's parents feel when they hear from Nilesh?
Ankita's parents may feel concerned and want to understand how much she's carrying, and hopefully ease the pressure at home.

Read this:

I'm Simran, and I used to answer every kindness with an apology. When I moved into my first flat, Zubin from next door came over to see if I needed a drill. "Sorry, I'm such a bother," I said. "I should have bought my own. I'm useless at this." His face did a small flinch, and he mumbled that it was no trouble and left quickly.
A month later, I needed help hanging the shelves. This time I knocked on his door and said, "Zubin, I could really use your hands for twenty minutes. Thank you for offering before."
He grinned and came over with the spirit level. We finished before the tea cooled. I asked nothing more of myself than to say a plain thank you, and I noticed how much easier it felt for both of us.

What did Zubin first offer Simran when she moved in?
He came over to see if Simran needed a drill.
What was Simran feeling when apologising the first time?
Simran felt anxious about being a bother, with a habit of putting herself down. By the second time, a plain thank you felt easier.
What did Simran do differently the second time she needed help?
Simran knocked, asked directly for Zubin's help and said thank you, without belittling. That made it easy for Zubin to say yes.
How does Zubin probably see Simran's second request compared with the first reaction?
He probably feels valued and useful, as his grin and quick arrival suggest. His flinch the first time suggests the apologies left him awkward and unwelcome. 😊

Monday: Salma, nine months, watches her father Sumit cover her toy duck with a cloth. She looks away, as if it's gone.

Thursday: Sumit covers the duck again. Salma stares at the cloth, then pats it. She feels the bump underneath.

The next Sunday: Sumit hides the duck under a towel. Salma crawls over, pulls it off, and grabs the duck. She holds it up to him, beaming.

What did Sumit hide the duck under on Sunday?
He hid it under a towel.
What does Salma's beaming suggest about how she feels on Sunday?
It suggests she feels proud and happy to have found the duck.
What helped Salma learn that the duck still existed?
Sumit repeated the hiding game over several days, letting her practise finding it.
How might Sumit feel when Salma finds the duck on Sunday?
He probably feels proud and happy, seeing her understanding grow.
What does a ticket to the science fair cost this year?
I'm not sure, because the organisers set the price and I can't see this year's list. The fair's ticket page or its help desk will have the price.

First visit, October. Vasudha travelled to the group's centre with Aditi's favourite pickle. Aditi met her at the gate and said, "Amma, I'm happy. You're seeing through fear." The same sentence, twice. Vasudha wanted to shout. She said, "Okay. I just wanted to see your face," and left the pickle.
Second visit, January. When Vasudha asked gently about Aditi's old job, Aditi's jaw tightened. "Outsiders always ask about money." Vasudha kept her voice soft. "I asked because I miss hearing about your work. That's all."
Third contact, April. Aditi phoned late at night, voice thin. She didn't say much. She asked whether her room at home was still the same. Vasudha said, "Exactly the same. Your books are waiting." She didn't ask a single question. After they hung up, Vasudha sat in the dark, shaking, and let herself hope.

What did Vasudha bring on the first visit?
Aditi's favourite pickle.
What was Vasudha feeling when Aditi repeated the stock sentence at the gate?
She felt hurt and frustrated, wanting to shout, but chose calm so she wouldn't push Aditi further away.
Why did Vasudha not ask questions on the April call?
Aditi sounded fragile; staying warm and saying the room was waiting kept the door open without pressure.
What might Aditi be feeling on the late-night call?
She may be starting to doubt and feel lonely, reaching toward home carefully to see whether she would be welcomed back.

'You're going to the Sunday match again?' Suraj asked from the sofa.
'It's just the old college gang. Once a week.'
'Those guys don't even like me. And your Amma calls every day. When do we get time?'
'We live together, Suraj. We get every evening.'
'Fine. Go. I'll just sit here.'
Jatin stopped at the door. 'Last month it was my cousin's birthday. Before that, Amma's lunch. I've skipped a lot of things.'
'Because you wanted to be with me.'
'Because you sulked every time.' Jatin picked up his kit. 'I'm going. And I'm going to tell Farid what's been happening. I need at least one person outside this flat to talk to.'
'You'll make me the villain.'
'I'll just say what happened.'
Walking to the ground, Jatin rang Farid first.

What event is Jatin going to on Sunday?
Jatin is going to the Sunday match with the old college gang.
What might Jatin be feeling as he stops at the door?
Jatin feels uneasy and sad, realising how many family events have been skipped because of Suraj's sulking.
Which choice worked, and why?
Going to the match and ringing Farid, because it keeps an outside connection who can help Jatin see the pattern.
How does Suraj see Jatin's friends and family?
Suraj treats them as rivals for Jatin's time and fears that talking to Farid will make Suraj look like the villain.
Switch from the present continuous to the simple present: Mother is making tea and the children are drinking milk.
Mother makes tea and the children drink milk.
Hey, what does "let the cat out of the bag" mean?

It means to tell a secret by mistake.
Example: We planned a surprise party for Sam, but Leela let the cat out of the bag.

Note from Vidya, nursery teacher. The fire-drill bell rang this morning and Raghav, two, froze, then burst into tears and clung to my leg. I picked him up, held him close and said, "That was loud. I've got you." Later I showed him the bell switched off and let him touch it. Later still he rang a small hand bell from across the room and watched me. I did not push him nearer than he wished.

What did Vidya show Raghav after the drill?
She showed him the bell switched off and let him touch it.
What does Raghav's freezing and clinging suggest, and what else might he have been feeling?
It suggests fear of the sudden loud noise. He might also have been overwhelmed by the other children reacting.
What could Vidya do next time the bell is due?

How might Raghav feel later ringing the hand bell?
