Note for Chetan's parents, Tuesday
At assembly practice the head teacher loudly told Chetan off for standing in the wrong line. Chetan stared straight ahead, arms stiff, and did not answer. The head teacher took this as rudeness. I took him to the bench outside, knelt, gave him water and said, 'You're not in trouble with me. Breathe with me.' After a few minutes his shoulders dropped, and he said his mind had gone 'all white'. I explained this to the head teacher, who agreed to speak more gently. Please give him a cuddle tonight; he was shaken.
Joseph, class teacher

What did Chetan say his mind had gone like?
'All white'.
What does Chetan's stiff, unblinking silence suggest about how he felt?
He was frightened by the loud telling-off, and his body froze, so he could not answer.
What did Joseph do that helped Chetan settle?
Joseph took him to the bench outside, knelt, offered water, said he was not in trouble and breathed with him until his shoulders dropped.
How might the head teacher's view change after Joseph's explanation?
The head teacher might see the silence as fear rather than rudeness and use a gentler voice with Chetan next time.

Summarize Indra's question in one sentence.

One day Vasava, after having subjugated all the Asuras, repaired to the Grandsire and joining his hands bowed to him and enquired after the whereabouts of Vali. Tell me, O Brahman, where I may now find that Vali whose wealth continued undiminished even though he used to give it away as lavishly as he wished. He was the god of wind. He was Varuna. He was Surya. He was Soma. He was Agni that used to warm all creatures. He became water (for the use of all). I do not find where he now is. Indeed, O Brahman, tell me where I may find Vali now. Formerly, it was he who used to illumine all the points of the compass (as Surya) and to set (when evening came). Casting off idleness, it was he who used to pour rain upon all creatures at the proper season.
After defeating the demons, Indra asks the Grandsire where he can find Vali, the great and generous king who once acted as the wind, sun, moon, fire and rain for all creatures.

Write this up in four sentences, keeping the order of events.

On the second night of the school trip to Nainital, someone whispered that the whole dorm was sneaking out to the lake at midnight. Siddharth lay on his bunk, stomach tight. The lake was dark, the road was steep, and the teachers would be furious. But everyone else seemed so keen. So when the torches came on at midnight, he pulled on his shoes and followed without a word. It was cold, a boy slipped on the wet steps and grazed his knee, and a teacher's torch found them by the jetty. All eight were marched back, and their parents were phoned in the morning. On the bus home Anand, who had walked beside him the whole way, said quietly, "I hated every second of that." Two more boys nodded. Siddharth stared at him. "Me too. Why didn't anyone say?"

On the second night of the school trip to Nainital, Siddharth heard that the whole dorm would sneak out to the lake at midnight, and although his stomach was tight because the lake was dark and the road was steep, he put on his shoes and followed without a word. It was cold, a boy slipped on the wet steps and grazed his knee, and a teacher's torch found them by the jetty. All eight were marched back, and their parents were phoned in the morning. On the bus home Anand said quietly that he had hated every second of it, two more boys nodded, and Siddharth agreed and asked why nobody had said so.
She is putting a green saree today and looks lovely. Is "putting" the right verb?

She is wearing a green saree today and looks lovely.
Why: "Wear" is what you have on; "put on" is the action.

"Papa! Papa!"
"One minute, Vidya, I'm on a call."
"PAPA!" A spoon clattered to the floor, then a cup.
"Vidya, no throwing." Pranav closed the laptop and sat down beside her. "You tapped my arm before and I did not turn. That was my miss. You are cross."
She sniffed. "Pa-pa. Look."
"Yes! Thank you for asking with words. I'm looking. What do you want to show me?"
She held up a wet sock.

What did Vidya throw when she was not noticed?
A spoon clattered to the floor, then a cup.
Why did Vidya scream and throw things instead of waiting?
She wanted her father's attention and had already been overlooked, so even an angry reaction was better than none.
How did Pranav respond so that calm asking was rewarded and not only the storm?
He set aside the laptop, named her feeling, owned that he had missed her tap, and thanked her for saying "Pa-pa. Look." 🙂
How does Pranav's call look from Vidya's point of view?
To her it is simply a time when Papa is not looking at her. She cannot yet wait or tell a call from being ignored.
Jackson spends 9 hours playing video games and 1/3 that much time studying. If Jackson's grade starts at 0 points and increases by 15 points for every hour he spends studying, what is his grade?

First find how many hours he spends studying by dividing the number of hours spent gaming by 3: 9 hours / 3 = 3 hours.
Then multiply that quantity by the point increase per hour to find Jackson's grade: 3 hours * 15 points/hour = 45 points.
The answer is 45.

Friday
Sat with the hockey girls at lunch again. Two weeks ago I was with Jaya and the book club lot, and before that I wore only black and said I hated everyone. Jaya passed me in the corridor and said, "Which Uma is it today?" She was joking. I think.
I don't know which Uma it is. I like the hockey girls' noise, but I went quiet when they laughed at the book club. I cut my hair short last month and I keep touching it like it belongs to someone else.
Snapped at Amma at dinner when she asked why her girl was so quiet. A normal question. Went to my room. Didn't cry, just lay there.
Ms Thomas said in class that people our age try on selves like clothes. Maybe. It still feels weird.
Uma

What did Jaya say in the corridor?
Jaya said, 'Which Uma is it today?'
How can you tell that Uma feels unsettled about who she is?
She touches her short hair as if it belongs to someone else, went quiet when the book club was mocked, and snapped at Amma.
What could Uma do after snapping at Amma?
She could apologise and tell Amma she has been feeling mixed up lately, which would help Amma understand the moods.
How might Jaya feel about Uma moving from the book club to the hockey girls?
Jaya might feel a little hurt or confused, which could be behind the half-joke in the corridor.

Bob started out the week with $80. On Monday alone, he spent half the money. On Tuesday, he spent one-fifth of the amount left from Monday. On Wednesday, he spent 3/8ths of the amount left from Tuesday. How much does he have left now?

On Monday, he spent half of $80 leaving him with $80-(1/2)*$80 = $40
On Tuesday, he spent 1/5th of $40 leaving $40-(1/5)*40 = $32
On Wednesday, he spent 3/8ths of $32 leaving $32-(3/8)*$32 = $20
The answer is 20.

Hrithik: sorry I just walked off
Swati: don't be sorry. you don't have to explain anything

Pranav took it as not caring, missing that shock can freeze a face.

Read this:

Devika, you asked why I keep the old group chat but never post. I'm Wasim, and at fifteen I felt invisible at home. Abba worked nights and nobody asked about my day. Then an online community began greeting me by name every morning and saying they were glad I was there. That warmth was real, and I won't pretend it wasn't. I nearly moved my whole life into it. But one night I asked myself: does being welcome make everything they teach true? I couldn't say yes. So I joined the school cricket club, made two friends who could sit beside me, and kept the chat as one small part of my days.

How old was Wasim when the online community began greeting Wasim by name?
Wasim was fifteen.
What was Wasim feeling at home, and why did the community appeal?
Wasim felt invisible at home, so a community greeting Wasim by name every morning felt warm and welcome. 🙂
What offline step did Wasim take?
Wasim joined the school cricket club and made two friends who could sit beside Wasim, keeping the chat as one small part of life.
What would probably have been different if Wasim had felt seen at home?
The pull of an online welcome would likely have been weaker, since Wasim would not have felt so invisible.

Okay, so you want an honest story for the podcast? I'm Wasim, sixteen, and my whole thing is being the guy people can count on. Ammi calls me her good son in front of relatives, and my friends call me the loyal one. Last month both names clashed. Vijay planned a surprise trip to the lake for his birthday, on the same Sunday as my cousin's engagement, where Ammi wanted me serving guests. I said yes to Vijay first, then couldn't sleep. What would Ammi's face look like? What would the group say if I backed out? In the end I went to the engagement and texted Vijay a long sorry. He replied 'k'. Just 'k'. I stared at that for an hour. I did the right thing for my family, I think, but I still felt like a bad friend.

What did Vijay reply to Wasim's long sorry?
He replied 'k'.
What did Wasim feel staring at 'k' for an hour?
Wasim felt anxious and guilty, afraid of being seen as a bad friend even after doing right by the family.
What could Wasim do now to repair things with Vijay?
He could meet Vijay in person, explain why the engagement mattered, and plan a small birthday outing together soon.
How might Vijay have felt when Wasim backed out?
Vijay was probably disappointed and a little hurt that a friend missed his birthday, which shows in the short reply.
Can a penitent person still make the same mistake?

They may, but a penitent person is sorry for what they did and wants to do better. Penitent is an adjective. It is a formal word, often found in books about faith.
Example: The penitent boy returned the stolen pencil and apologized.

1) Check my English: "He is too tired that he can't walk."
2) What is the weather going to be like in Chennai tomorrow?
3) I keep seeing "distortion" in my reading. Meaning?

1. Corrected: He is so tired that he can't walk. Why: "so ... that" shows a result; "too" needs "to".
2. I can't check forecasts, so I don't know. A weather website or the local radio will give you the latest.
3. Distortion means a change that twists something out of its true shape or sound. It is a noun.

Results day, June. Pankaj stared at two red Fs, in Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics. "I'm just not engineering material," he told Asif on the hostel stairs.
Three days later. Asif sat with him in the empty canteen with a notebook. "Humour me. Why did you fail?" "I didn't understand the second half." "Why?" "I'd missed the first month." "Why?" "Papa's surgery. I was in Jaipur with him." "Why didn't you catch up?" Pankaj was quiet. "I didn't want to go to the professors. I thought they'd think I was making excuses." Asif wrote it down: "Missed month plus not asking. Not ability."
August. On the first day of the new term, Pankaj knocked on the Thermodynamics professor's door with his notebook. "Sir, I failed last term. I missed the first month. Could you tell me where to begin?" The professor pulled up a chair.

Which courses did Pankaj fail?
Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics.
Why did Pankaj avoid the professors last term?
Pankaj felt embarrassed and afraid they would think he was making excuses.
What else could Pankaj do alongside meeting the professor?
Pankaj could ask about the backlog schedule and join a study group, so catching up isn't done alone.
How does Asif help Pankaj see the cause?
Asif patiently asks why again and again, helping Pankaj see the failure came from a missed month and not asking, not lack of ability.

Vinita had joined the small NGO in Kurukshetra full of ideas for the girls' literacy centre. But her supervisor, Hemant, checked everything. Which chalk to buy. How to arrange the benches. Which story to read on Tuesday. When she planned a spelling game, he changed it to a worksheet. After three months, Vinita stopped suggesting things. She came at nine, followed the list, and left at five. The girls noticed. "Didi, you don't laugh any more." One evening, Vinita stayed back and knocked on Hemant's door. "Sir, can I ask something? Could you tell me what you want the girls to achieve by March, and let me decide how to teach it? You can check the results every month." Hemant frowned, then nodded slowly. "Reading two-letter words, all of them. By March." "Okay." The next week, she brought back the spelling game. The girls laughed so loudly Hemant came to the door. He watched, and didn't change anything.

What did Hemant change Vinita's spelling game into?
He changed it to a worksheet.
How did Vinita feel after three months of Hemant checking everything?
Vinita felt drained and discouraged, so she stopped suggesting ideas and did only the list.
What did Vinita ask for, and why did it restore her energy?
A clear goal for March with freedom in how to teach it, which gave her room for judgement and brought back her initiative.
How did the girls experience the change in Vinita?
The girls noticed she stopped laughing, and later laughed loudly again when her spelling game came back.

Preeti: what's the scary part

Trip committee note, Class 9, Friday
Hafsa is leading the planning for the lake picnic. She came in with a long list about the boating. The boats have life jackets and a trained boatman, but she wanted boating cut completely. "Then nobody can drown. Zero risk." She was firm and a little shaky, as if she had been lying awake over it.
Noor pointed out that the bigger problem is the two-kilometre walk from the bus in the afternoon sun, with most students carrying one small bottle. Hafsa brushed that off: "People walk every day."
I didn't overrule her. I asked the committee to list every risk on the day and how many students each would touch. Seeing that the walk affects all forty and the boating only a few, supervised, Hafsa went quiet, then added water refills and a shaded rest stop herself. She still wants the boating shorter. We agreed to that.

What does Noor say is the bigger problem?
Noor says it is the two-kilometre walk from the bus in the afternoon sun, with most students carrying one small bottle.
What does Hafsa's firm but shaky manner suggest about her feelings?
It suggests she was truly scared of someone drowning, and cutting boating to nothing felt like the only way to be sure, even though the walk was the bigger risk.
Why did listing every risk help more than overruling Hafsa?
It let her compare how many students each risk touched and reach the answer herself, so she added water refills and shade by her own choice.
How might Noor feel when Hafsa first brushes off the walk?
Noor might feel unheard and a bit frustrated, since the heat affects everyone, and then relieved once the list made the point.

The whole mohalla in their little town had been waiting for Sunday's cricket match against the boys from the station colony. At nine the sky opened. By ten the ground behind the temple was a pond. Swati stood at the door with the bat, her face falling. Her cousin Yogesh kicked the doorframe. "Spoiled. The whole day's spoiled." Swati watched the rain for a minute. Then she turned. "The carrom board is under Dadi's bed. And we have ludo." "Carrom isn't cricket." "No. But all eleven of us are here anyway." By noon, four were playing carrom on the verandah, four were at ludo on the charpai, and the rest were keeping score and shouting. Dadi sent out pakoras. Nobody mentioned cricket until the rain stopped at five.

Where was the carrom board?
Under Dadi's bed.
How did Yogesh feel when the match was rained off?
Angry and frustrated, kicking the doorframe.
What else could the children have done besides indoor games?
They could also fix a new date with the station colony boys, so the match is postponed, not lost.
How might Dadi see the day?
Dadi's house was full of noise and games, and sending out pakoras suggests she enjoyed it.

Suraj and Kishore never really asked. When the baby was due in the spring, they told each other that the grandparents would simply move into the flat for a few months, the way it had always been in the family. In April, on a call from Nagpur, Suraj's mother said her knees and the house made a long stay impossible, and Suraj's father agreed. Silence. The couple had no nanny's name, no crèche form, no leave application. That week they rang around, waited in office corridors with phones pressed to their ears, and paid an agency fee they had never budgeted for. It worked out, roughly. But nobody slept, and Kishore said quietly, "We should have asked before we assumed."

What reason did Suraj's mother give on the call?
She said her knees and the house made a long stay impossible.
How did Kishore feel after the call, and what shows it?
Kishore felt regretful and uneasy, shown by the quiet remark, "We should have asked before we assumed."
What could the couple have done earlier?
They could have asked the grandparents early on what help was really possible and drawn up backups such as a crèche or nanny list, so nothing rested on an assumption.
How might Suraj's parents have felt when they had to explain?
They may have felt guilty about letting the couple down, while still needing to be honest about their limits.

messages.content: Evelyn's family watched 10 hours of television last week. The week before, they watched 8 hours of television. If they watch 12 hours of television next week, what is the average number of hours of television that they watch per week?

Over the three weeks, they will have watched a total of 10 + 8 + 12 = 30 hours of television.
The average number of hours per week is 30 hours / 3 = 10 hours of television.
The answer is 10.

Rashmi's tiffin had arrived at the Pune flat at one o'clock sharp every day for five months: dal, sabzi, four rotis, and a note if the cook had added something special.
This week it came late twice. On Thursday the dal had spilled.
"One star," Rashmi said, opening the review page. "Terrible service."
Ira looked up from her laptop. "Terrible? You told your mother it was the best thing about moving here."
"That was before this week."
"This week is one week. You've had, what, a hundred good lunches?"
Rashmi's finger stayed on the one star. The spilled dal felt far more real than a hundred ordinary lunches.
"Also," Ira said, "the cook's son is getting married. She told you on Monday."
Rashmi sighed, closed the review page and messaged the cook instead: Hope the wedding goes well. See you next week.

At what time did the tiffin usually arrive?
It arrived at one o'clock sharp every day for five months.
Why did one star feel fair to Rashmi at first?
Rashmi felt annoyed about the late tiffins and the spilled dal, and those recent problems felt more real than five months of good lunches.
What did Rashmi do instead of posting the review, and why was it better?
Rashmi messaged the cook kindly, weighing the whole record and the wedding instead of judging by one week.
How might the cook have felt if the one-star review had gone up?
The cook might have felt hurt and worried, rated terrible after months of careful work during a busy family wedding.

At the music school in Porto Alegre, Paulo had practised the guitar four hours a day all summer. On the first day of term, a new student, Sofia, sat down and played a piece so clean and fast that the whole room went quiet. Paulo smiled and clapped with the others. Inside, something dropped. He walked home the long way, past the river, thinking: she's just born with it. I'll never get there. Four hours a day for nothing. When his teacher suggested he and Sofia practise duets, Paulo said he was too busy. He skipped the next ensemble class. That night he didn't pick up his guitar at all. Her playing kept looping in his head, and each time it felt like something was being taken from him.

How many hours a day had Paulo practised all summer?
Four hours a day.
Why did Sofia's playing make Paulo feel something dropped inside?
He felt threatened and envious, believing the gap was fixed and that her talent meant his work was for nothing.
What could Paulo try instead of avoiding Sofia?
He could accept the duet practice and watch how she works, treating her skill as something he can learn from.
How might Sofia feel when Paulo avoids the duet?
Sofia might feel confused or unwelcome as a new student, not knowing why he pulled away.
Write a six-line poem for a Class 1 child about the first day of school, about 45 words.

My bag is new, my shoes are bright,
I'm going to school, what a sight!
I wave goodbye to Mum at the gate,
I hope my new friends will not be late.
I hold my pencil, I find my seat,
School is going to be so sweet!

Why is Pip left confused after speaking to the old gentleman?

Curious to know how the old gentleman stood informed concerning the reputation of Mr. Jaggers, I roared that name at him. He threw me into the greatest confusion by laughing heartily and replying in a very sprightly manner, "No, to be sure; you're right." And to this hour I have not the faintest notion what he meant, or what joke he thought I had made.
He shouted a name to find out how much the old man knew, and the man laughed heartily and agreed. Pip still has no idea what he meant or what joke he found.

Sum up this bit of text for me in two sentences.

Morning, dismal and wet, at length dawned and discovered to my sleepless and aching eyes the church of Ingolstadt, its white steeple and clock, which indicated the sixth hour. The porter opened the gates of the court, which had that night been my asylum, and I issued into the streets, pacing them with quick steps, as if I sought to avoid the wretch whom I feared every turning of the street would present to my view. I did not dare return to the apartment which I inhabited, but felt impelled to hurry on, although drenched by the rain which poured from a black and comfortless sky.

After a sleepless night in a courtyard, the narrator sees Ingolstadt's church clock at dawn as the porter opens the gates. The narrator hurries through the wet streets, afraid of meeting a dreaded creature at every turn, and does not dare go home.

Sharmila, you asked why your father and I didn't speak for two years when he was young. Let your Omkar Dadu tell you.
Your father was sixteen and wanted to study art. I wanted him to be an engineer. So I didn't forbid it. I did something worse. Every evening, I'd sigh at dinner. "After everything I've done for you, working double shifts, and this is how you repay me." Your Dadi would look at me. I pretended not to see.
He gave in. He filled the engineering form. And he stopped talking to me.
Two years later, I found his sketchbook under his bed. Page after page. I sat on the floor and understood that I had not asked him anything. I had only used my tiredness to push him.
I apologised. I told him plainly, "I was scared you'd struggle for money. That's all it was." He switched courses the next year.

What did young Omkar find under his son's bed?
His son's sketchbook.
How did Omkar feel when he found the sketchbook?
Omkar felt ashamed and regretful, understanding that he had used his tiredness to push his son instead of asking him.
What turning point in the story began the repair?
Omkar apologised and told his son plainly that he was scared he'd struggle, stating the real fear instead of using guilt.
How might the sixteen-year-old son have felt during those dinners?
The son probably felt trapped and guilty, giving in to the engineering form and then withdrawing into silence.

John joins a country club with 3 other members of his family.  The fee to join is $4000 per person.  There is also a monthly cost of $1000 per person.  John pays half the cost.  How much does John pay for the first year?

There are 3+1=4 members joining
So the cost is 4*4000=$16,000 to join
The monthly fee comes out to 1000*12=$12,000 per person per year
So that is 12000*4=$48,000
So the total cost is 16,000+48,000=$64,000
So John pays 64000/2=$32,000
The answer is 32000.
Create a slogan for a reading club with exactly five words and no punctuation.
Read more and wonder more

"Gopika, can I ask you something? I keep saying mistakes are part of learning. Why doesn't anyone on the team try the new approach?"
"You want the honest answer, Abhinav?"
"Yes."
"Last month Ramesh tried it on a client report. One number was wrong. He got a written warning."

"We're asked to learn the new system but there's no training time. We do it at night."

Abhinav was quiet for a while. "So the slogans are just... slogans."
"Pretty much. Sorry."
"Don't be. I needed to hear it." He opened his calendar. "Let's start with two hours of training time on Tuesdays, and I'll talk to finance about Ramesh."

What happened to Ramesh last month?
One number in his client report was wrong and he got a written warning.
How did Abhinav seem to feel after hearing Gopika's answer?
Abhinav seemed quiet and a bit shaken, then grateful, realising his slogans weren't matched by real support.
What first steps did Abhinav take to support learning?
He set two hours of training time on Tuesdays and planned to talk to finance about Ramesh's warning.
What is it like for Gopika to give the honest answer?
Gopika seems a little nervous, even apologising, but relieved to share what the team really experiences.

Lloyd is building a house of cards. He owns 16 decks of cards that have 52 cards each. If each layer of his house of cards has the same exact number of cards, how many cards are there per layer if his house is 32 layers tall?

He has 832 cards because 16 x 52 = 832
Each layer is 26 cards because 832 / 32 = 26
The answer is 26.

Ritu Didi searched the whole flat in Pune before she found her phone inside the rice tin. She walked into the living room holding it up, grains still stuck to the cover.

"Hafsa. Anything to tell me?"

Hafsa pressed her lips tightly together and stared hard at the ceiling fan. Her cheeks puffed out. Her eyes, though, were crinkling at the corners, and a tiny snort escaped.

"I don't know," she squeaked.

Ritu Didi bit the inside of her cheek. "Rice phone. Very clever. Not again, okay?"

Where did Ritu Didi find her phone?
Inside the rice tin.
What was Hafsa feeling when she pressed her lips together and stared at the fan?
Most likely amused and a little proud of her trick, while knowing she was supposed to look sorry. She may also have felt nervous about being in trouble.
How did Ritu Didi handle the moment well?
She stayed light but still set a limit with "Not again, okay?", so Hafsa learnt the rule without being shamed.
How does Ritu Didi see Hafsa's squashed smile?
She reads the crinkled eyes and snort as a giveaway, and finds it so funny that she has to bite her own cheek.

Tuesday. Siblings Afreen and Gopika tried to fix the schedule three times. Each time it ended with shouting and crossed arms.

Sunday. The envelope was stuck to the door. "It's your turn," said Gopika, and Afreen picked up the remote without a word of complaint.

Where was the envelope with the timetable put?
The envelope was stuck to the door.
What did Gopika feel about trying alone, and what led to asking Amma?
Gopika felt that the tries had failed and that they could not do it alone, so Gopika suggested asking Amma.
What alternative approach could Afreen and Gopika try before asking Amma next time, and why?
They could take a break to cool down and then write down what each needs. Calmer talk can lead to a fair plan without a referee.
How might Amma see the timetable request?
Amma listened to both without interrupting and asked for agreement, so Amma probably feels the children trust her and want a fair rule.

Daycare note, Holi week.

We set out bowls of dry colour for a hand-printing activity. Anand, two, reached for the pink bowl before his turn. I said, "Wait, Anand. My turn first." He pulled his hand back and watched.

Later he stroked our rabbit, Motu, with one finger, very softly, saying "Nice."

He said "Nice."
How might Anand have felt waiting for his turn?

How could Deepika keep supporting Anand's gentle, patient behaviour?

The health centre waiting room was full for the college's free check-up camp. Arnab had a token. Lakshmi didn't.
"The doctor at home said I should get my thyroid checked," she admitted. "But if they find something, I'll have to start tablets. And tablets can have side effects. If I don't check, at least nothing I did causes a problem."
"And if something's wrong and you don't know?"
"Then it's not my fault. It just happened."
Arnab turned his token over in his fingers. "Not checking is also a choice, though. It just doesn't feel like one."
Lakshmi was quiet. Then she walked to the desk. "Is there still a token for today?"
The nurse handed her number 47. "Write down your worries," the nurse said kindly. "The doctor will go through all of them with you."

What token number did Lakshmi get?
Lakshmi got number 47.
Why did not checking feel safer to Lakshmi?
Lakshmi felt more afraid of problems caused by acting, like tablet side effects, than of problems from not knowing, which seemed like no one's fault.
What did the nurse suggest, and why is it helpful?
Writing down her worries for the doctor to go through, so a qualified person can answer them.
How does Arnab see Lakshmi's reasoning?
Arnab sees that not checking is also a choice, and gently points it out.

Alka had been annoyed with Tarun for weeks. He had cancelled their Sunday walk to the temple tank twice, skipped her sister's engagement, and stopped answering in the group chat. In the college canteen in Sangli, he pushed his plate away again.
When she joked, "Coming to the fair on Friday?" he muttered, "What's the point. Nothing's going to get better anyway."
The words stayed with her. That evening she went to his house and asked him to sit with her on the steps, away from the others. "You haven't been eating, and what you said today scared me. Are you thinking of hurting yourself?"
He looked at his hands. "No. I'm just so tired of everything."
Alka stayed. She listened for a long time. Before she left, with his okay, they told his elder sister together, and his sister booked the college counsellor for the next morning. Alka texted him before bed: "I'm here."

What did Tarun mutter when Alka asked about the fair?
"What's the point. Nothing's going to get better anyway."
How did Alka's feelings change after Tarun's remark?
Her annoyance at the cancelled plans turned into worry and fear for him; the words stayed with her.
What did Alka do that showed real care?
She checked in privately that same evening, asked directly, listened and stayed, involved his sister and encouraged the counsellor visit, then texted before bed.
How might Tarun feel when Alka turns up at his house?
He might feel exposed at first, then less alone and cared for because she came to him rather than giving up.

Weekend language school note. Leela, Urdu teacher.
Irfan, 26, enrolled his daughter, who is five, in our Saturday Urdu class. He admitted his own Urdu is shaky; he grew up speaking English at school and only understood his grandparents.
He told me why. "I don't want her to have to translate to talk to her great-grandmother." He also said he doesn't want to pass on everything. He wants her to learn the poetry and the courtesy words, but not the idea that girls should be quieter than boys, which he heard a lot growing up.
I suggested he sit in on some classes. He now comes every week, sitting at the back, writing letters in a notebook like a student. Last week his daughter corrected his spelling. He laughed louder than anyone.
He is choosing carefully what to keep. I think that's the best kind of heritage.

Irfan, 26, enrolled his five-year-old daughter in the Saturday Urdu class and admitted that his own Urdu is shaky because he grew up speaking English at school. The block-level quiz final was held in the panchayat hall in Tirur, and Ayesha's team lost on the last question because she pressed the buzzer too early and said Kolkata instead of Chennai. The whole hall groaned. She kept her face still until she got home, then locked herself in the bathroom. For a week she didn't go near the school library, where the quiz team met. When the notice for the district quiz went up, her brother Jeevan brought it home. 'Your team's asking for you.' 'They're better off without me. I'm the one who lost it.' 'You also got them to the final.' Ayesha shook her head. It didn't feel like that. It felt as if the whole hall had seen who she really was: someone who panics and ruins things.

What did Ayesha say instead of Chennai?
She said Kolkata instead of Chennai.
Why does Ayesha avoid the quiz team for a week?
She feels deeply ashamed, as if one wrong answer showed the whole hall who she really is, so facing the team feels unbearable.
What could help Ayesha return to the quiz?
Remembering she got the team to the final, and talking with her teammates, who are asking for her, could show that one mistake isn't her worth.
How do Ayesha's teammates seem to see her?
They still want her for the district quiz, which suggests they value her far more than she believes.

Nandini, you've just become a manager and you're printing "growth mindset" posters? Sit a minute. When I was twenty-six, I ran a small team at a textile mill's quality lab in Coimbatore. I'd read a book about believing you can grow, and I made everyone repeat it. "Challenges are chances!" Meanwhile the lab ran twelve-hour shifts, nobody got feedback except shouting, and a girl who asked a question was mocked for weeks. Of course nobody grew. They were too busy surviving. What changed things wasn't my speeches. It was half an hour every Thursday, while the machines were serviced, when I sat with one person and went through their tests, and a rule that nobody laughed at questions. I'm Farida, and I learned it late: belief needs somewhere to live.

How long were the shifts in Farida's lab?
The lab ran twelve-hour shifts.
Why were the speeches not enough, in Farida's view?
Farida saw that the team felt exhausted and afraid, surviving long shifts, shouting and mockery, so words about growing had nothing to stand on.
What choices finally made growth possible in Farida's lab?
Half an hour each Thursday going through one person's tests, and a rule that nobody laughed at questions; time, feedback and safety gave the belief somewhere to live.
How might Nandini's new team feel about posters without that kind of support?
They might roll their eyes or feel pressured, hearing 'grow' while lacking the time and safety to try, much like Farida's lab once did.
Sammy has 2 more bottle caps than Janine. Janine has 3 times as many bottle caps as Billie. If Billie has 2 bottle caps, how many does Sammy have?

Janine has 2 * 3 = 6 bottle caps.
Sammy has 6 + 2 = 8 bottle caps.
The answer is 8.

Dear Minakshi,

I've wanted to write this for a while, and it's easier on paper.

When you missed my birthday dinner, you said the auto driver got lost. When you forgot to return my exam notes before the test, you said your mother had moved them. When you told Sneha what I'd shared in confidence, you said, "It's not my fault, she asked me directly."

Maybe some of those are true. But I've noticed you look more stressed every time you say it, not less. It's like the excuse stops the conversation before anything can be put right.

I'm not angry anymore. I just miss how we used to be. If you ever want to say "I messed up," I'll be here to hear it, and I'll forgive you faster than you think.

Mehak

What did Minakshi say about telling Sneha what Mehak shared?
Minakshi said, 'It's not my fault, she asked me directly.'
How does Mehak seem to feel about the excuses?
Mehak seems sad and missing the old friendship, no longer angry but worried that the excuses keep Minakshi stressed.
What small step does Mehak invite Minakshi to take?
To simply say 'I messed up', which would let them repair things and let Minakshi forgive herself.
How might Minakshi feel reading the letter?

Monday. Ira's project was accepted by the department, thanks to Pema, her mentor. Ira meant to say something but only mumbled "thanks, Ma'am" in the corridor. Pema smiled but was already rushing to class.

Wednesday. Ira wrote a short note: "Ma'am, your comment on my second draft, about linking the survey to the policy, changed my whole project. I'm grateful for the time you gave me." She left it on Pema's desk with a small pen.

Friday. Pema thanked her quietly after class and said the note had made her week. In the presentation, Ira credited Pema's guidance by name, and Pema nodded from the back.

What did Ira leave with the note on Pema's desk?
Ira left a small pen with the note.
What was Ira feeling on Monday when she mumbled thanks?
Ira felt grateful but couldn't say more in the rushed corridor, so she later wrote a note. The mumble did not show a lack of gratitude.
What did Ira do that worked well to thank a mentor?
She wrote a specific note naming the comment that mattered, and credited Pema by name in the presentation.
How might Pema have felt about the note?
Pema felt pleased, since she said it made her week, and the specific comment shows the mentoring was noticed.

Sunday night
Urmila cancelled again, the third time this month. We'd planned the film for two weeks, and at five she sent: 'Sorry, bad pain day, can't.' When I asked if she was sure, she replied, 'Yes, Samir. I'm sure.' Full stop. Ouch. I sat on the hostel steps feeling like I didn't matter.
Then I remembered her face in the canteen on Friday, grey and tight, and how she kept shifting in her chair. She's lived with this back pain since the accident last year. Of course she's short on patience; she's short on everything. I'm not taking it personally. I texted: 'No worries. Want me to bring the film and some chaat to your room next week instead?' She sent back a heart.
Samir

What did Samir offer to bring next week?
The film and some chaat to Urmila's room.
How did Samir feel after Urmila's curt reply?
Samir felt hurt and unimportant, sitting on the hostel steps as if not mattering.
What helped Samir respond kindly?
Remembering Urmila's grey face and shifting in the chair, and understanding that pain drains patience, so it wasn't personal.
What might Urmila have felt when Samir offered to come to her room?
She likely felt relieved and cared for, sending a heart instead of more apologies.

At Mei's school in Singapore, the National Day assembly began with the whole hall singing the anthem. Mei stood tall in her red T-shirt, and when the drums came in, goosebumps prickled her arms. She thought of her grandfather, who had come by boat long ago and helped build the flats she lived in. Afterwards, each class got goodie bags with flags and cold drinks. Through the window Mei saw the workers repainting the school fence in the heat, sweating in their helmets. 'They're building the country too,' she said to Santiago, the new boy from Chile. They asked their teacher, who helped the class carry a crate of cold drinks outside. One worker grinned and waved a tiny flag. Mei felt proud all over again, in a bigger way.

What colour was Mei's T-shirt?
Red.
How did Mei feel when the drums came in?
Proud and moved; goosebumps prickled her arms.
How did Mei's pride grow into caring for others?
She saw the workers repainting the fence as part of the country and, with her class and teacher, took them cold drinks.
How might the worker who waved a flag have felt?
Appreciated and included in the celebration.

Thursday
It happened on the metro again. Doors closed, the carriage packed, and my heart went off like an alarm. Old me would have got off at the next station, gone home and cancelled on Akash. I've cancelled on him three times this month. Today I tried the steps instead. Felt my feet in my sneakers, pressing down. Breathed out slowly, longer than in. Then named five things: a baby's yellow sock, a man's newspaper, the red line map, a scratch on the pole, my own hand. By the fourth stop my heart had slowed. I still felt shaky when I met Akash, but I was there. We ate momos and laughed. I'm writing this so I remember it works. And if this keeps ruling my days, I'll book the counsellor Akash mentioned. Disha

How many times had Disha cancelled on Akash this month?
Three times.
How did Disha feel when the metro doors closed?
Disha felt a sudden rush of fear, heart going off like an alarm.
What grounding steps did Disha use?
Feeling feet in the sneakers, breathing out longer than in, and naming five things in the carriage.
How might Akash have felt about the three cancellations?
Akash may have been disappointed or worried, and glad that Disha showed up today.

Afreen, you're worried because your little one screams over which cup to drink from? Come, let your Zubin Dada tell you about your father, Cyrus, when he was nine.
He had school till three, then swimming, then tuition. By seven he was a different child. Your Dadi would ask, "Rice or chapati?" and he'd say, "I don't care!" and then cry because his chapati was the wrong shape. Once he stood in front of his cupboard for ten minutes over which night-shirt to wear and ended up sleeping in his school uniform.
In the mornings, the same boy chose his breakfast, his socks and his bus seat in a second.
So we changed things. Big choices in the morning, and in the evening, we decided and he only said yes. The crying stopped almost at once.

What did Cyrus end up sleeping in?
He ended up sleeping in his school uniform.
Why did small choices upset Cyrus so much in the evenings?
After school, swimming and tuition, his mind was worn out, so even rice or chapati felt too hard, and he either refused to choose or fell apart.
What choice by the family helped, and why did it work?
Moving choices to the morning and deciding for him in the evening, because Cyrus was fresh in the morning and too tired to choose by night.
How might Afreen see the little one's cup tantrums after hearing this?
Afreen may see them as tiredness rather than naughtiness, and think about making fewer evening choices for the child too.

Rajni's brother Vishal had said it at dinner three times that week: "Give up the Pune job offer or don't expect me at your wedding." Rajni carried her plate to the sink, pretending she hadn't heard. In her room she opened the offer letter again. Vishal wasn't shouting, and he wasn't a cruel person. He had raised her after their parents' passing. But every time she talked about the city, he changed the subject or said what she owed the family. She wrote two lists, one headed "What he fears" and one headed "What I want". Then she called her aunt and asked if she could talk. Rajni didn't want to lose her brother, and she didn't want her choice decided by a threat either.

How many times had Vishal said it at dinner that week?
He had said it three times that week.
What is Rajni feeling as she writes her two lists, and what else might be behind Vishal's words?
Rajni feels torn, wanting to keep her brother but not to be controlled, while Vishal may truly be afraid of losing her rather than trying to punish her.
What did Rajni do that helped?
She separated his fears from her wishes on paper and reached out to her aunt for support instead of deciding alone.
How might Vishal see the ultimatum?
He may see it as a way to keep the family close after their loss, without realising it makes Rajni feel her choices are not respected.

The total distance between 2 towns is 200 miles. Roger and his friend drove 1/4 of the total distance, taking 1 hour to do so. They take lunch for another 1 hour and then drove the remaining distance going at the same speed as before. What's the total amount of time, in hours, Roger and his friend took to travel between the two towns?

When they covered 1/4 of the total distance, they were 1/4 * 200 = 50 miles away from the starting point.
The total distance remaining is 200 - 50 = 150 miles.
If they took 1 hour to travel 50 miles, their speed was 50/1 = 50 miles per hour.
If Roger was driving at 50 miles per hour, then the total time it took him to travel 150 miles is 150/50 = 3 hours.
The total amount of time taken for the whole journey is 3 + 1 + 1= 5 hours.
The answer is 5.

In the Class 10 common room, Irfan dropped his bag and announced, "Okay, can we all agree Joshi Sir is the worst teacher in this school? Boring, strict, and his jokes are from 1990."
He waited for the laugh. It didn't come.
Ankita looked up from her notes. "I like him, actually. He stayed back twice to explain vectors to me."
"Same," said someone at the window. "He's strict, but he's fair."
Irfan's ears went hot. "Wow. Okay. So I'm the villain now?"
"Nobody said villain," Ankita said. "You said 'we all agree'. We don't."
Irfan sat down heavily, feeling ganged up on. He had honestly thought everyone felt the same; his three friends in the back row always did.

What did Irfan call Joshi Sir?
Irfan called Joshi Sir the worst teacher in the school: boring, strict, and with jokes from 1990.
Why did Irfan feel attacked when others disagreed?
Irfan felt embarrassed and ganged up on, because he had honestly assumed everyone shared his view, as his back-row friends always did.
What could Irfan try before speaking for everyone next time?
Irfan could ask what others think, or say 'I find him boring' instead of 'we all agree', since three friends are not the whole class.
How does Ankita see Joshi Sir?
Ankita likes him, since he stayed back twice to explain vectors, so Irfan's claim feels unfair to her.

Chidi's keys hit the bowl at half past eight. In their small flat in Manchester, Bisi was sitting at the kitchen table with two plates and a candle she'd bought on the way home.
"Hey," he said, and kissed the top of her head. Then he took his plate to the sofa and put on a football match with the sound low.
Bisi blew out the candle.
He'd been working double shifts at the hospital for three weeks, covering for a colleague. He came home grey in the face, asleep by ten.
She knew all that. Still, watching the back of his head, she wondered when she had stopped being worth looking at.

How long had Chidi been working double shifts?
For three weeks, covering for a colleague.
What was Bisi feeling when she blew out the candle?
She felt hurt and unimportant, wondering when she had stopped being worth looking at.
What small step could help at this early stage?
Bisi could tell Chidi she misses him and ask for ten minutes at the table, or Chidi could say he's exhausted but glad to see her, so the quiet isn't read as rejection.
What is Chidi likely experiencing when he takes his plate to the sofa?
He is drained after weeks of double shifts and wants quiet; he probably doesn't notice the candle or mean any rejection.

Yamini, sit. Your Ujjwal chacha has an interview story for you. I was twenty-four, applying to the cooperative bank in Indore. Three weeks before, I had already decided I would fail. "Those boys from the city colleges will walk in," I told my mother. So why prepare? I played carrom every evening instead.
On the day, my collar was wet with sweat before I even sat down. The manager asked me something simple about interest, and my mind went white. I stammered and looked at the floor. When the no came, I said, "See, Amma, I told you."
She said, "You told yourself, and then you listened."
The next year I sat with the books every night. Same bank, same manager. That time, I got it. So, what are you doing this evening?

What did Ujjwal do every evening instead of preparing?
He played carrom every evening.
What was young Ujjwal feeling when he sat down for the interview?
He was very anxious, sweating before he sat and going blank, because he had expected failure for weeks.
What choice turned things around for Ujjwal the next year?
He sat with the books every night instead of assuming he would lose, so he walked in prepared.
What did Ujjwal's mother see that he missed?
She saw that his own prediction shaped his lack of effort: he had told himself he would fail and then acted on it.

Hi Harsha,
A short note after today's review. I noticed you didn't say anything in the meeting again, and I also noticed that the fix everyone was praising, the retry logic in the billing service, came from your code on Monday. I made sure to tell the team lead that afterwards, with your name on it.
Can I tell you something? In my first year here, I didn't speak in a single review for four months. I was sure everyone knew more than me. A senior called Latha asked me directly, "Pradeep, what do you think?" and waited. That one question changed a lot.
So here's my version: in Thursday's meeting, I'm going to ask you to explain the retry logic for two minutes. You know it better than anyone. If that feels like too much, tell me, and we'll do it together.

Harsha's code from Monday.
Why does Pradeep want to help Harsha speak up?
Pradeep remembers feeling unsure and silent for four months, and cares that Harsha's good work is going unheard.
Which parts of Pradeep's plan help Harsha find a voice?
Giving specific credit to the team lead, sharing Pradeep's own silent first year, and inviting a two-minute explanation with an offer to do it together.

Harsha may feel seen and a bit nervous, but encouraged by the credit and the offer of support.

Dear Himani,
It's two weeks until I leave for Pune, and I can't sleep, but the good kind.
I've made a list of things I've never done: open a bank account, cook for myself, pick my own electives, take a train alone. I read it every night like a menu.
Everyone keeps warning me: rent, loneliness, how hard it is. I know. I'm not stupid. But I'm also allowed to be excited.
I want to join the theatre club. I want to try every street food on the list you sent. I want to find out what I'm like when nobody knows me yet.
You'll visit, right? First weekend in October. I'll make terrible rajma.

How long until Nilesh leaves for Pune?
Two weeks.
How does Nilesh feel about leaving?
Nilesh feels excited and eager, unable to sleep "the good kind" of way.
How could Himani support Nilesh's excitement without dismissing the worries?
Himani could share in the plans, visit as promised, and stay in touch in case the hard parts come.

From Manjula's notebook, Saturday night.
Ujjwal came home soaked and quiet. Later he told me: the boys went to the old quarry lake, and everyone was jumping off the high rock. "Amma, I'm not even a good swimmer. But they were all watching and cheering."
He jumped. He came up coughing. His friend Kiran pulled him to the edge.
I felt my stomach drop, but I kept my voice calm. I thanked him for telling me. Then I said the quarry is off-limits, and I'd be talking to the other parents tonight, which I did.
We also made a plan together. Next time there's a risky plan, he'll suggest the swimming pool instead, or text me the word "mango" and I'll call and say he's needed home, no questions tonight. We practised what he'd say to the boys: "Not today, I'm heading home." He rolled his eyes, but he said it twice.

What word will Ujjwal text Amma if he wants to leave?
"Mango".
How did Ujjwal feel about jumping with friends watching?
He felt pressured and excited by the cheering, even though he knew he was not a good swimmer, and came home quiet and shaken.
What steps did Manjula take to protect Ujjwal?
She stayed calm, made the quarry off-limits, called the other parents that night, and planned safer choices and a way to leave, which they rehearsed.
How might Kiran have felt when he pulled Ujjwal out?
Kiran was probably frightened when Ujjwal came up coughing, and relieved to get him to the edge.

I'm Irfan, and I've coached the school football team for three years. My worst idea came last spring. The boarders and the day scholars had been sniping at each other for months, so I made them share one practice. But I let the boarders play the match while the day scholars ran drills on the side. Within a week, Pooja, one of my best day-scholar players, was calling the boarders "the rich kids," and they were calling her lot "the bus crowd." I'd put them on the same field and made it worse. So I changed three things. Every team got an equal mix. Every drill needed both groups to score. And the principal came to watch, which told everyone this mattered. By June, Pooja was passing to a boarder for the winning goal, and nobody was keeping count of who was who.

What did the day scholars do while the boarders played the match?
They ran drills on the side.
What did Irfan realise after a week of shared practice?
Irfan realised that putting the groups on the same field with unequal roles had made the rivalry worse, not better.
Which three changes did Irfan make, and why did they work?
Equal mixes on every team, drills needing both groups to score, and the principal watching; together they gave equal status, a shared goal and visible backing.
How might Pooja's view of the boarders have changed by June?
From 'the rich kids' to teammates she could trust with a winning pass, because they now needed each other to score.
A zoo has 16 pandas, paired into mates (in the same zoo). Only 25% of the panda couples get pregnant after mating. If they each have one baby, how many panda babies are born?

First divide the number of pandas by 2 to find the number of couples: 16 pandas / 2 = 8 panda couples
Then multiply that number by 25% to find the number of babies: 8 panda couples * 25% = 2 panda babies
The answer is 2.

Try a bowl of fresh fruit.

In a small Goan village, Francis watched his uncle Hemant melt a lump of ghee in a pan for the Sunday cake. 'It's gone, it's water now,' Francis said. 'Is it?' said Hemant. He poured some into a steel bowl and put it on the window ledge in the breeze. By evening, Francis poked it. Solid again. His eyes widened. 'It came back!' Then he thought. 'So if I melt it again, it'll be liquid, and cool again, it'll be solid. Back and forth.' Hemant smiled and tied a knot in a string. 'Can you undo this?'

Where did Hemant put the bowl of melted ghee?
He put it on the window ledge in the breeze.
What does Francis's widened eyes suggest he felt?
It suggests he was surprised and excited to see the ghee return to its solid form.
Why was Hemant's knot a clever next step?
It gave Francis another chance to see that some actions can be undone to return to the start.
What would change if Hemant had simply told Francis that ghee sets again?
Francis would have missed discovering it himself, and the idea might not have stuck as well.

Monday: Arnab, sixteen, forwarded a message to his class group: "Drinking cold water after meals causes serious illness." Yamini replied, "Source?" Arnab typed, "Everyone knows this," and felt annoyed that she was questioning him in front of everyone.
Wednesday: Still irritated, he searched to prove her wrong. Every reliable site he found said the claim had no evidence. He noticed he had been hunting only for pages that agreed with him.
The next Monday: He posted, "I was wrong about the cold water thing. I believed it because my Nani says it, and I didn't check." Yamini sent a thumbs up. Arnab felt strangely lighter.

What did Yamini reply to Arnab's message?
She replied, "Source?"
Why did Arnab feel annoyed on Monday?
He felt challenged in front of everyone, and his confidence in the message made the question feel like an attack.
What was the key moment of change for Arnab?
Noticing he had been searching only for pages that agreed with him, which let him see his own bias.
How might Yamini see Arnab's public correction?

The population of Delaware is 974,000. A study showed that there are 673 cell phones per 1000 people in the state. How many cell phones are there in Delaware?

There are 974000 / 1000 = 974 groups of 1000 people in the state.
These groups will have 974 * 673 = 655502 cell phones.
The answer is 655502.

Bridgette and Alex are getting married. Bridgette is inviting 84 guests, and Alex is inviting two thirds of that number of guests. They hired a caterer to make a plated meal for each guest at the wedding reception. The caterer always makes ten extra plates just in case something goes wrong. Each plate of steak and asparagus in garlic butter will have 8 asparagus spears on it. How many asparagus spears will the caterer need in all?

Alex is inviting 84 * 2 / 3 = 56 guests.
Bridgette and Alex's guests will need 84 + 56 = 140 plates.
The caterer makes 10 extra plates, so they will need 140 + 10 = 150 plates.
To put 8 asparagus spears on each plate, the caterer will need 150 * 8 = 1200 asparagus spears.
The answer is 1200.

I sat next to Vikas when the semester results came out on the college portal. He'd scored lower than he hoped in thermodynamics. His first words were, "That paper was brutal. Nobody expected those three questions." Fair. Half the class said the same. But then he went quiet, scrolling through his marks, and said, "Also, I didn't do the past papers. I kept saying I would." He didn't sound angry at himself, just honest. That evening, in the canteen, he made two short lists on a napkin: what was luck, what was mine. The hard paper went on the first. The past papers and skipped tutorials went on the second. "Next sem I can't change the paper," he said. "I can change this bit." I saw him in the library twice the next week with a stack of old question papers. "Your turn, Indu," he said, pushing the napkin across. It made me think of my own marks, and what I'd blamed.

What did Vikas write on the napkin?
Two short lists: what was luck and what was his.
How did Indu feel watching Vikas make the lists?
Indu seems impressed and a bit reflective, noticing Vikas's calm honesty and wondering about Indu's own habit of blaming.
How does the napkin list help Vikas act?
It separates the hard paper he couldn't control from the past papers he could, so he can focus effort where it matters without blaming himself for everything.
How does Vikas seem to feel about his result by evening?
Vikas seems calm and steady, disappointed but not crushed, and motivated to change the parts he can.

It was Rashmi's first trip without family, a college fest in Pune with her friends. Before she left, her boyfriend Chaitanya walked her to the bus stand.
"Send a photo of the stage when you can. Only if you want," he said.
"You're not going to call every hour?"
Chaitanya laughed. "Why would I? You're with your friends. Have fun."
On the bus, her friend Nikhita was on the phone with her own boyfriend, arguing: "No, I told you who's here. Why do you need names?"
Rashmi listened, then looked at Chaitanya's message: "Hope the bus has good music." She smiled. It felt like air.

Where was the college fest?
In Pune.
What was Rashmi feeling when she said "It felt like air"?
Rashmi felt relieved and free, trusted to enjoy her trip.
What makes Chaitanya's behaviour healthy?
He trusts Rashmi, lets her choose when to message, and doesn't demand check-ins.
How might Nikhita feel during the call?
Nikhita seems stressed and frustrated, having to explain who she's with.

The maths period had a substitute teacher, and Class 5 was noisier than usual. Trisha, ten, stared at the word problem about trains and could not tell what to multiply. Around her, everyone seemed to be writing. Her friend Minakshi was already on question three. Trisha's cheeks felt warm. If she asked, the substitute might say the answer loudly and everyone would turn. So she copied the question neatly, drew a small train, and waited. By the bell, she had solved nothing. At home, she cried a little over her notebook. Her father sat with her and asked what the problem said. She read it aloud, and together they found the multiplication.

Which question was Minakshi already on?
Minakshi was already on question three.
Why did Trisha stay silent instead of asking?
She felt shy and afraid of looking stupid, worried that the substitute would say the answer loudly and everyone would turn.
What could help Trisha ask for help next time?
She could quietly ask Minakshi or write a note to the teacher, so she doesn't have to speak in front of the class.
How might Minakshi have acted if she had known Trisha was stuck?
Minakshi might have quietly explained the question, having understood it and sitting right there.

2. Offer it around and keep portions fair. Check that nobody has a food they cannot eat.
Now you try: n = 5, sum x = 30, sum x^2 = 200; find sigma.

Dear Irfan,
I'm writing because I couldn't say this properly in the corridor.
At the fest, when you went blank on stage and some of our own team started laughing and filming, I was in the second row. I didn't stop them. I didn't even stop smiling, because everyone else was. I've felt sick about it for three days.
I'm sorry. You didn't deserve that, and you didn't deserve silence from someone you thought was a friend.
I've already asked Kabir and Neel to delete their videos, and they did. And I've promised myself that next time someone is mocked, I'll stand up, even if I'm the only one.
If you'd like chai this week, I'm buying.
Ritu

Where was Ritu sitting at the fest?
Ritu was in the second row.
How has Ritu felt since the fest?
Ritu has felt guilty and ashamed, sick about it for three days for smiling along instead of stopping the laughter.
What makes this letter more than just an apology?
Ritu has already acted, getting the videos deleted, and made a clear promise about next time, which shows real change.
How might Irfan feel reading the letter?
Irfan might feel hurt remembering the stage, but relieved and respected that Ritu owned up and acted.

Dear Usha,
You asked me last week how I get the warehouse team to help me when stock is late. Here's the honest answer.
When I joined three years ago, I did a favour for the night supervisor every time he asked. I helped check the loading, stayed ten minutes extra. He started doing the same for me.
I also saw what happens when someone breaks a promise. One of our juniors promised to cover a stock count and didn't turn up. Two years later, people still quietly check his work twice.
We all see each other every day, Usha. So being reliable isn't just the nice choice here. It's the smart one.
Gargi

What did the junior promise to cover?
The junior promised to cover a stock count.
How does Gargi seem to feel about being reliable at work?
Gargi feels confident and settled about it, seeing reliability as both kind and practical in a team that meets every day.
What could Usha try on starting work with the warehouse team?
Usha could start by helping out and keeping small promises, so people learn to rely on Usha and return the favour.
How might the junior who missed the stock count feel two years later?
The junior may feel watched and less trusted, knowing people still check that work twice.

messages.content: State the slope and the y-intercept of each line: (a) y = 3x - 5, (b) y = 7 - 2x, (c) 2y = 6x + 8, (d) 3x + y = 4.

Answer: (a) m = 3, c = -5; (b) m = -2, c = 7; (c) y = 3x + 4, so m = 3, c = 4; (d) y = -3x + 4, so m = -3, c = 4.

In y = mx + c, m is the number MULTIPLYING x (with its sign) and c is the number on its own (with its sign). (a) is already in this form: m = 3, c = -5, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, -5). (b) Reorder: y = 7 - 2x = -2x + 7. The minus sign belongs to the 2x, so m = -2 and c = 7. Common mistake: "m = 7" because 7 comes first. Look for the number WITH x. (c) The y must be alone: divide EVERY term by 2: y = 3x + 4. (d) Take 3x from both sides: y = -3x + 4. Lines (c) and (d) have the same intercept, so they meet on the y-axis at (0, 4).

The school library had a pile of returned books, and Ira, the librarian, asked Jahnavi to help. Jahnavi split them into Fiction and Non-fiction. Then, inside Non-fiction, she made Science, History and Sport. Inside Science she noticed some were about space, some about animals. 'Ma'am, can I make a space shelf inside the science shelf?' Ira laughed. 'Show me.' Jahnavi drew a chart: Books → Non-fiction → Science → Space. 'So every space book is a science book, but not every science book is about space.'

How did Jahnavi first split the pile of books?
She split them into Fiction and Non-fiction.
Why was Jahnavi excited to make a space shelf?
She felt eager to organise the books more precisely and was pleased at spotting a group within a group.
How could Ira use Jahnavi's chart?
She could put it up in the library so other students learn to find books through these nested groups.
How might other students benefit from Jahnavi's sorting?
They could find books faster, especially if they are looking for a specific topic like space.

'Parth, why are you still awake?' Sabina asked from the doorway.

'Chemistry, maths, the physics file, the project, the library book...' Parth's voice cracked. 'Mummy, it's all in my head at once.'

'Then get it out of your head.' She put a notebook and pen in front of him. 'Write everything. Don't sort yet.'

Parth wrote for five minutes. Eleven lines. He stared at them. 'That's all?'

'That's all,' said Sabina. 'Now circle what has to happen tomorrow.'

He circled three. 'Chemistry chapter, the maths sheet and the file.'

'And the rest?'

'Later. The book goes back on Saturday.' He let out a long breath. 'It looks smaller on paper.'

'Sleep. The list will still be there in the morning.'

How many lines did Parth write?
Parth wrote eleven lines.
How was Parth feeling when he could not sleep?
Parth felt overwhelmed and worried, since everything was in his head at once.
What else could Parth do the next morning with the list?
Parth could put a time beside each item for today, or tick items off as they get done, so the list turns into a plan.
How might Sabina feel watching Parth work through the list?
Sabina may feel concerned at first and then relieved to see Parth calmer and ready to sleep.

messages.content: What exactly is a "fortnight"?

A fortnight is two weeks, and it is a British word. In American English, people usually say "two weeks".
Example: We will be in Mysore for a fortnight.

When I started asking questions at our temple study circle, it went quiet fast. I'm Ojas, and I was nineteen. I asked, politely I thought, why women in our circle weren't allowed to read certain texts aloud. The uncle who led the circle said, 'This is not the place for arguments.' The next week, two boys I'd grown up with stopped saving me a seat. At the festival, people nodded at my parents and not at me. I felt so lonely I almost walked out for good, and I wrote a long angry post that I thankfully never sent. What saved it was Nandini-aunty, who ran the temple library. She found me sulking by the shoe stand and said, 'Your question is an old one. Come on Thursday; I'll show you three saints who asked it.' I did. I still go on Thursdays. I don't win every argument. I just have one person there I can ask anything.

Who ran the temple library?
Nandini-aunty ran the temple library.
What did Ojas feel when the boys stopped saving a seat?
Ojas felt lonely and rejected, close to walking out for good.
What turned things around for Ojas?
Finding one open-minded elder, Nandini-aunty, and going to her Thursday sessions instead of cutting all ties.
How might the uncle who led the circle have seen Ojas's question?
The uncle seems to have seen it as an argument that threatened the circle, not as an honest question.

For a rangoli competition, Kavya can decorate a square card of side 5 cm or a rectangular card 8 cm by 3 cm. She puts ribbon round the edge and paint inside. Which card needs more ribbon? Which needs more paint?

Answer: Ribbon (perimeter): square 20 cm, rectangle 22 cm - the rectangle needs more. Paint (area): square 25 cm^2, rectangle 24 cm^2 - the square needs more.

Ribbon goes round the edge, so find perimeters: 4 x 5 = 20 cm and 2 x (8 + 3) = 22 cm. Paint covers the inside, so find areas: 5 x 5 = 25 cm^2 and 8 x 3 = 24 cm^2. The shape with more paint has less ribbon! Always ask first: "Is this about the edge or about the inside?"

At the New Year table in his grandmother's house outside Osaka, Kaito had barely lifted his chopsticks when Uncle Hiro raised it. 'The bank in Kobe is hiring. I already spoke to someone.' Aunt Emi nodded; another uncle warned that small design studios close all the time. Kaito felt his face heat. The studio's offer, which his friend Daniel had first told him about, sat unanswered on his phone.
He bowed slightly. 'Thank you. I know you worry about my future, and that means a lot.' He asked Uncle Hiro what he liked about the bank, and listened.
That night he texted Daniel: 'Still taking the studio job. But I'll send Uncle a New Year card.'

Where is the bank that is hiring?
In Kobe.
What was Kaito feeling when Uncle Hiro said he had already spoken to someone?
Kaito felt embarrassed and a little cornered, his face heating, yet he also saw the worry behind it as care.
Which of Kaito's choices at the table was wise, and why?
Thanking the family and asking Uncle Hiro about the bank, because it kept the relationship warm while he still made his own choice.
How might Uncle Hiro see Kaito taking the studio job?
Uncle Hiro may feel disappointed or worried at first, but having been listened to may help him accept it more easily.

At the international night in Auckland, Tuan stood in his grandmother's old ao dai, waiting behind the curtain to sing a folk song from the Mekong. His friend Tomas, a Polish exchange student, sat near the front holding a bag of crisps. Tuan sang softly at first about a boat and a mother's voice, then louder, his hand pressed against his chest on the last line. When it ended, the hall clapped and someone cried a little. Tomas didn't understand the words. Afterwards he asked, "What is it about? I want to know before I say something silly." Tuan smiled, pleased. "It's a lullaby my grandmother sang. I was afraid it would sound old-fashioned here."

What did Tuan wear to sing?
He wore his grandmother's old ao dai.
What was Tuan feeling as he sang, and what did he tell Tomas he had feared?
He felt pride and love for his grandmother, and he had feared the song would sound old-fashioned.
What could Tomas do to learn more about a performance he doesn't understand?
He could ask Tuan about the song's meaning and context before forming an opinion, as he did.
How might Tomas's question feel to Tuan?
Tuan probably feels respected and glad that someone wants to know what the song means to him.

Friday: at dinner, Farhan's mother said Rukhsar should stop working late now that she was married. Rukhsar looked at Farhan. He looked at his plate. His brother Zubin changed the subject to cricket. That night Rukhsar slept facing the wall. Tuesday: his mother complained that Rukhsar never asked her opinion; Rukhsar complained that Farhan never defended her. Farhan felt like a rope pulled at both ends, and he stayed late at the office to avoid them both. The next Sunday: at lunch, Farhan put down his spoon. 'Ammi, Rukhsar's late shifts are our decision, and I'm proud of her work. Rukhsar, Ammi misses you in the evenings. Can we keep Sundays for family lunch?' His mother sniffed, but agreed. Rukhsar squeezed his hand under the table. Zubin grinned at his rice.

What did Zubin do when Rukhsar looked at Farhan on Friday?
He changed the subject to cricket.
What was Farhan feeling on Tuesday?
He felt torn and trapped, like a rope pulled at both ends, so he stayed late at the office to avoid them both.
What made Farhan's Sunday stand work?
He stated the decision calmly and fairly, backing Rukhsar's work while naming his mother's feelings and offering Sunday lunches.
How did Farhan's silence on Friday affect Rukhsar?
She felt unsupported and hurt, and slept facing the wall that night.

"Papa, why is the sky blue?" asked Gopika, swinging her legs on the kitchen stool.
"Good question, what do you think?" said Asif, chopping onions.
"Because the sea is blue and it goes up?"
"Interesting idea! Where does the sea go?"
"Into the clouds?"
"And then?"
Gopika giggled. "Rain! Then it comes down. So the sky is the sea's home."
"That's a lovely thought. Let's look at a book tonight and see what it says."
"Okay! Papa, why do onions make you cry?"
"Ah. What do you think?"
Gopika frowned and thought very hard.

What was Gopika sitting on when asking about the sky?
The kitchen stool.
What was Gopika feeling while thinking hard about the onions?
Curious and absorbed, with the frown showing real thinking.
What did Asif do that helped questions lead somewhere?
Asif asked "What do you think?" and followed the ideas with more questions, then promised to check a book together.
How might Asif have felt about the endless questions?
Warm and interested, since Asif kept chopping while inviting each thought and said the idea was lovely.

In a village outside Hue, Mei did her physics problems by a battery lamp after the pigs were fed. She wanted to build bridges, real ones, in the city. The nearest extra classes were in town, an hour away by motorbike, and cost more than her family could spare. When her father hurt his back in the paddy, Mei missed two weeks of school to plant seedlings. She cried once, into the rice, then went back to her equations at night. At the Tet holidays, Mina came home. Mina had grown up two houses away and now worked for a road company in Da Nang. She sat with Mei on the step, looked through the notebook, and said, "Your working is neat. I'll send you my old textbooks, and we'll talk every Sunday on the phone."

What did Mei do her physics problems by?
She did them by a battery lamp after the pigs were fed.
What was Mei feeling when she missed school to plant seedlings?
Mei felt sad and frustrated, crying once into the rice, but stayed determined enough to return to the equations at night.
Why does Mina's offer matter so much?
Mina offers what the village lacks, old textbooks and weekly guidance, which helps fill the gap left by the costly classes in town.
What might Mina see when looking through Mei's notebook?
Mina probably sees real promise, and perhaps her own younger self, in the neat working, which is why she offers books and Sunday calls.

Minakshi: Sorry, I'll be two minutes late to standup. Sorting out the corridor.
Mohit: What happened?
Minakshi: Somebody's coffee all over the floor by the printers. Grabbed the pantry mop straight away.
Mohit: Couldn't you just tell facilities?
Minakshi: Thought about it. Raise a ticket, wait, watch people skate past the puddle. The mop takes three minutes and nothing can go badly wrong here. This wasn't a moment for a plan.
Mohit: Fair. Someone was already tiptoeing round it 😅
Minakshi: Exactly. If it had been broken glass I'd have called someone in. Just a spill though 🙂
Mohit: Okay, standup starts when you're back.

Where was the spill that Minakshi mopped up?
It was on the floor by the printers in the corridor.
What did Minakshi think about waiting for facilities?
Minakshi thought raising a ticket would take longer than the job itself, and felt confident that mopping was simple and safe.
What would be a wiser approach if the mess were broken glass?
Calling someone in would be wiser, because the situation would no longer be small and simple, as Minakshi says.
How does Mohit see Minakshi's choice to skip the ticket?
Mohit accepts it as fair, and the colleague already tiptoeing round the puddle shows others were being bothered by it.

I'm not sure of the departure, because I can't see railway timetables. The station display or the railway's website lists them.

The power had gone out across the office, and the client pitch was due in three hours. The team sat by the windows with laptops on battery.
"Ideas?" the manager asked. Silence. Hansa glanced at Yash. A year ago, Yash had been the one bursting with suggestions. Then his last three ideas had been waved away without discussion. Now he just stared at his screen.
Hansa didn't think he was lazy. She had watched him stop, one ignored idea at a time. She felt sad about it, and a bit guilty for never speaking up.
She leaned over. "Yash, you're the best at client stories. Do you want to shape the opening, or the case study section? Your pick."
He looked up, surprised. "...The opening."
Within an hour he'd drafted one that made the manager say, "Yes, that." Yash sat up a little straighter.

How long was it until the client pitch was due?
Three hours.
How did Hansa feel watching Yash stay silent?
She felt sad about how he had stopped suggesting ideas, and a bit guilty for never speaking up.
Why was offering Yash a choice between two sections a wise step?
A small real choice gives back some control, helping restore agency that had been worn away by his ideas being ignored.
What might it have been like for Yash to hear his opening praised?
After a year of being waved away, being heard again likely felt surprising and encouraging, which is why he sat up straighter.

On my first day at the logistics software company, I wore the new shirt Amma had ironed twice. The office had bean bags and a coffee machine I didn't know how to use. By ten I was in a stand-up meeting where people said "sprint velocity", "blockers" and "push to staging" as if everyone was born knowing them. I nodded. I wrote the words in my notebook to search later. Abhinav, my buddy for the week, asked, "Yogesh, anything blocking you?" I said, "No, all good," though I couldn't even log into the laptop. At lunch I kept thinking, maybe HR mixed up two CVs. Maybe the real Yogesh is sitting at home. Then I'd remember the offer email, and a small, fizzy excitement would come back. I went home both terrified and thrilled.

What did Yogesh write in the notebook?
The unfamiliar words, to search later.
What mix of feelings did Yogesh go home with?
Yogesh went home both terrified and thrilled, worried the selection was a mistake yet excited about the job.
What small step could help Yogesh on day two?
Telling Abhinav honestly about the laptop login and asking what one or two of the terms mean.
How might Abhinav see Yogesh on day one?
Abhinav likely sees a new joiner who says all is good, not knowing Yogesh could not even log in.
Why must a fridge door be shut properly?
Otherwise the cold air escapes. Because an open door lets warm air in, so the fridge must work harder, uses more power, and the food may spoil sooner.

At pickup, Papa knelt by the daycare gate. "How was your day, Omkar?" "Raghav's one fell in the water, and then everybody went ahhh!" Papa looked lost. "Raghav's what fell?" "The one!" Omkar flapped his hands, annoyed. The caregiver smiled and explained: Raghav's paper boat had sunk in the water tray. Omkar nodded hard, as if Papa should have known. Then he held out a chewed crayon. "For you, Papa. You like green." Papa's favourite colour was blue. He took it anyway.

What sank in the water tray?
Raghav's paper boat.
Why did Omkar flap his hands at Papa?
He felt annoyed and confused, because he thought Papa already knew what had happened at daycare.
How could the caregiver help Omkar tell stories more fully?
The caregiver could practise with him, asking "Who?" and "What happened?" so he learns to give the missing pieces.
How might Papa feel receiving a green crayon when he likes blue?
He probably feels touched by the gift, and amused that Omkar thinks everyone loves what he loves.
