At the school field, thirty children lined up to fly their paper gliders in the wind. Rukmini's went straight down after two seconds and hit the grass nose first. Somebody snorted. "I'm just bad at making things," she said, crumpled the glider and sat on the bench. Her cousin Chinmay's glider crashed too, but Chinmay bent the wing tip, threw again, bent again. By the fourth throw it sailed right across the field. Rukmini watched from the bench with the ball of paper in her fist.

What did Rukmini do with her glider after it crashed?
She crumpled it and sat on the bench.
What was Rukmini feeling when somebody snorted?
Embarrassed and discouraged, which led her to decide she is bad at making things.
What could Rukmini do next, and why?
She could smooth the paper, bend the wings a little and throw again as Chinmay did, because each test shows what to change.
How might Chinmay see a crashed glider?
Chinmay treats a crash as information, bending the wing tip and throwing again until it flew.

I'm Amandeep. Last Lohri, we watched the big kabaddi match in the village with everyone, next to the bonfire.

Before it started, I said to my sister Vidya, "Punjab will win easily." Then Haryana scored first and I said, "Okay, maybe Haryana." Then Punjab came back and I shouted, "PUNJAB!"

Haryana won in the end.

After the match, I told my cousins, "I knew Haryana would win. It was obvious." And I really felt like I had known.

Vidya laughed so hard she nearly dropped her rewri. "You said Punjab! Three times!"

I said I only said it to cheer. But then I remembered. I really had thought Punjab would win.

My mind had changed the story afterwards to make me look clever.

Which team won the kabaddi match?
Haryana won in the end.
Why did Amandeep feel sure of having known Haryana would win?
Amandeep felt proud and certain after the match because the mind had quietly rewritten the earlier guesses to fit the result.
What could Amandeep try to catch this habit next time?
Amandeep could write down a prediction before a match and check it afterwards, instead of trusting memory.
How did Vidya see Amandeep's claim?
Vidya found it funny and knew it wasn't true, because she remembered Amandeep saying Punjab three times.

Friday night.
Two versions of me today. Morning, maths test: calm Alka. Read every question twice, checked my working, changed one answer that looked right but wasn't. Evening, at Aadhya's birthday: everyone shouting "Truth or dare, Alka!" and I picked dare before I even thought, then agreed to post a video of myself dancing badly. It's already up. Thirty people have seen it. My stomach dropped when I got home. Same brain, twelve hours apart. The difference was the noise and all the eyes on me. Next party I'm going to say "give me a sec" before anything. Also deleting the video now.
Alka

How many people have seen the video?
Thirty people.
How did Alka feel on getting home?
Alka's stomach dropped; Alka felt embarrassed and regretful about the snap choice made with everyone watching.
What is Alka's plan for the next party?
Say "give me a sec" before deciding anything, and delete the video now.
How might Aadhya see the dare moment?
Aadhya probably saw it as party fun, not realising Alka would regret it later.

Behind the village well in Sonpur, Vasudha sat in the dust and cried. Her big brother had gone to the fair on his cycle without her.
Pooja, five, came running from the shop with a biscuit her Nani had bought her. She stopped. She looked at the biscuit, then at Vasudha. Then she broke it carefully in half and pushed one piece into Vasudha's hand.
"Don't cry. We'll play fair here," Pooja said, patting her head the way Nani did. "I'll be the ice-cream man."
Vasudha sniffed, ate, and giggled.

Who bought Pooja the biscuit?
Her Nani.
What was Pooja feeling when she stopped and looked from the biscuit to Vasudha?
She felt sorry for her crying friend and wanted to make her happy, even if it meant sharing her treat.
Which of Pooja's actions turned Vasudha's mood around, and why?
Sharing the biscuit and offering to play fair at the well gave Vasudha comfort and something fun to do instead of missing the real fair.
How might Vasudha feel about Pooja after this?
Vasudha would likely feel close to Pooja and cared for, knowing her friend shared her treat and made up a game for her.

They let 60 go, Amandeep included.

Separate the urgent tasks with deadlines, health cover and severance, from important ones like the resume, which can wait a week.

Sudha is sorry and concerned, and responds by gently helping Amandeep sort what matters first.

Saturday: The lake picnic Hemant had waited for all month was cancelled when the rain began at seven. He stomped to his room. "It's all ruined. I hate rain."
Sunday: It was still pouring. From his room he could hear his brother Anirban and their parents building a blanket tent in the hall, and smell khichdi and papad. Anirban knocked. "We're doing a torch picnic inside. Come." "It's stupid," Hemant said through the door.
Monday: At school, Anirban told his friends about the blanket tent and the ghost stories by torchlight. Hemant listened, saying nothing. That evening he asked his mother, "Can we do the tent again?" "Maybe next rainy day," she said.

What were Anirban and their parents building?
A blanket tent in the hall.

A delivery drone starts at the point (1, 1, 0) (metres) and flies with the constant velocity v = 6i + 2j + 3k m/s. What is its speed? Where is it after 5 s? How far has it travelled?

Answer: Speed 7 m/s; it reaches (31, 11, 15); it has travelled 35 m.

The components say how fast the drone moves in each axis direction: 6 m/s east, 2 m/s north and 3 m/s up. The SPEED is the magnitude of the velocity: |v| = sqrt(6^2 + 2^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(36 + 4 + 9) = sqrt49 = 7 m/s In 5 s the displacement is 5v = 30i + 10j + 15k, so the new position vector is (i + j) + (30i + 10j + 15k) = 31i + 11j + 15k, the point (31, 11, 15) The distance travelled is |5v| = 5 x 7 = 35 m (for a straight flight at constant velocity, distance = speed x time). Velocity is a vector; speed is its magnitude, a scalar. Common mistake: adding the components, 6 + 2 + 3 = 11 m/s, as the speed.

"That was different."
"You studied till four and then cried in the auto because you forgot the area formula."
"I didn't cry. I was stressed."
"Okay. Stressed. And the formula?"
"Fine. I forgot it."
"So here's a deal. Go to Rohit's till nine. Do the hard sums together. Come home, eat, sleep by eleven."
"And if I don't feel ready?"
"Write the three formulas that scare you on a card and read it with breakfast."
"You're sure sleep helps?"
"You remembered nothing after the last all-nighter. And you're much nicer in the morning."

Where does Bhupen want to go for the all-nighter?
To Rohit's, for a group all-nighter for maths.
How did Bhupen feel after the all-nighter before the unit test?
Bhupen felt stressed and upset, even crying in the auto after forgetting the formula he had stayed up to learn.
Why is Sudha's plan wiser than staying up all night?
It keeps the useful group practice but protects sleep, and the card of scary formulas gives a calm, quick check in the morning.
What might Sudha be worried about when Bhupen mentions the all-nighter?
She worries it will repeat the unit test: no sleep, a blank memory and panic on exam day.

In their Kolkata flat, Trisha sat on the bed with her knees pulled up. For a week a boy in her class, Ujjwal, had been calling her drawings "baby scribbles", and today he'd said it in front of the art teacher's table. Her mother had already phoned the class teacher that afternoon, and the teacher had promised to speak to Ujjwal the next morning. Still, Trisha couldn't stop replaying it. Her mother sat beside her. "Which word hurts most?" Trisha thought. "Baby. Because... I'm scared he's right. That I'm not good." "Is he right?" Trisha looked at the wall covered with her drawings: the owl, the rain market. "The art teacher put my owl on the board." She was quiet for a while. "He doesn't get to decide what I am." It still stung, but smaller.

What did Ujjwal call Trisha's drawings?
"Baby scribbles".
Why did the word 'baby' hurt Trisha most?
She was scared he was right and that she is not good, so the word touched her own insecurity.
What else could help Trisha when the words keep replaying?
Looking at real evidence, like the owl on the board, and telling her mother or teacher if the comments continue.
How does Trisha's mother handle it?
She has already phoned the teacher, and then asks questions instead of giving answers, so Trisha reaches the thought herself.

Monday. Karthik and Neelam had snapped at each other again in the sprint review. Harsha, their lead, wrote the question on a sticky note: why do they keep fighting? Her first answer was "they just don't get along," but she crossed it out. Why did today's fight start? Because Karthik's test cases failed on Neelam's code.
Wednesday. Harsha kept going. Why did they fail? Neelam changed the login flow. Why didn't Karthik know? There was no handover note. Why no note? Because the task was assigned to both of them, and each thought the other would write it. "It's not personality," she muttered. "It's the board."
The next Monday. Harsha split the overlapping tasks so each had one owner and added a handover box to every card. By Friday, the review passed without a single sharp remark.

What did Harsha add to every card?
She added a handover box to every card.
How did Harsha's thinking change when she crossed out "they just don't get along"?
She moved from a frustrated guess about personalities to curious questioning, and she felt clearer once she saw the overlapping assignments were creating the blame.
What else could Harsha try if the fighting had continued after the change?
She could meet each of them separately to hear what they need, in case there is a second cause the whys did not reach.
How might Karthik experience the change on the board?
Karthik no longer gets surprised by code changes nobody mentioned, so Karthik may feel less blamed and less defensive in reviews.

Tuesday, 9:40 pm. Ugh. Sat on my bed for an hour just staring at the wall. In the canteen today a boy from 9B asked me, "So is it true you still sleep with the light on?" I told exactly one person that. Vidya. Nobody else. My ears went hot and my stomach dropped like on a swing, and I laughed like it was nothing. Later, in the corridor, I asked Vidya quietly whether she had told anyone. She looked at her shoes and said, "It just came out." I said I was hurt and walked off before I said anything worse. Mum asked why I wasn't eating and I said headache. Tomorrow I'll tell Vidya calmly that I trusted her, and that I'll think before telling her things now. It's not my fault I trusted her. If it still feels this bad, I'll tell Mum. — Pranav

He asked whether it was true Pranav still sleeps with the light on.
What is Pranav feeling after the canteen, and how can you tell?
Sick and exposed. Pranav's ears went hot, the stomach dropped, and Pranav skipped eating, telling Mum it was a headache.

Pranav will speak to Vidya calmly, be careful about what to share with her from now on, and go to Mum if it keeps hurting. That protects Pranav without a blow-up.
How might Vidya have felt in the corridor?
Probably ashamed or uneasy. Looking at her shoes and saying "It just came out" suggests she knows she slipped, though we cannot be certain.

Hana pointed again. "Bread. Duck eat." "The duck ate the bread you threw!" Hana clapped. "Splash!" "The duck went splash!" Hana laughed and turned the page, looking for more ducks.

A duck.

She clapped and laughed, pointing and saying 'Splash!'

She echoed Hana's words in full sentences, building the story of the park.

Tom cannot afford a normal doctor, so he goes to a discount clinic that is 70% cheaper.   It takes two visits, though, instead of 1.   A normal doctor charges $200 for a visit.   How much money does he save?

Each of Tom's visits was 200*.7=$140 cheaper
So he paid $200 - $140 = $60 per visit
That means he paid $60 * 2 = $120
So he saved $200 - $120 = $80
The answer is 80.

She may be surprised, since she meant to comfort him and did not intend to dismiss him.

As a verb, to splinter means to break into smaller groups or pieces, especially after a disagreement. The noun is a sharp thin piece of wood or glass.
Example: The choir splintered into two groups over which song to sing.

The narrator planned the walk to arrive at the old time, rang with an unsteady hand, then turned away from the gate to catch breath and calm a beating heart, pretending not to hear the footsteps and the swinging gate.

Kalyani kicked and cried against Sarika's shoulder.

The sickle.
Why did Kalyani cry when Sarika lifted her away?
Kalyani felt frustrated and upset at being stopped from something she was curious about.

Sarika could notice it warmly, keep the sickle up high during harvest, and offer safe play like the straw. 👍

A slice of lime.

In the paediatric ward at nine at night, Shreya, a nurse on her first year, watched her colleague Parveen try to calm a boy with a cut hand. Parveen was kind, but kept saying, "Oh no, oh no, does it hurt a lot? Tell me if it hurts!" The boy's crying got louder with every question.
Shreya stepped in to hold the dressing tray. She knelt and spoke slowly. "Hi. I'm Shreya. We're going to clean this and it'll sting for a moment. Then you can choose a sticker. Ready?"
The boy hiccupped, watched her face, and held still. The sting came; he winced but didn't scream.
Afterwards, Parveen said quietly, "I was scaring him, wasn't I?" Shreya shook her head. "You care a lot. It just shows in your voice."

What could the boy choose after the dressing?
He could choose a sticker.
What was Shreya feeling as Parveen kept asking if it hurt?
Shreya felt concerned, noticing that the boy's crying got louder with each anxious question.
What could any caregiver learn from what Shreya did?
A slow, confident voice, a clear warning about the sting and a small choice can settle a frightened child during care.
How might Parveen feel after asking "I was scaring him, wasn't I?"
Parveen may feel embarrassed but grateful, since Shreya answered kindly and helped explain what happened.

After dinner at home, Anand looked up from the sofa. "Karthik, why are you checking your phone every five minutes?"
"It's the match, Anand bhaiya. I've got a bit riding on it."
"A bit?"
"Just a small bet. On the app."
"You said that last month. And the month before."
Karthik looked away. "I'm about to win back what I lost."
"How much did you lose?"
Silence. Then, "More than my stipend."
"Karthik."
"I know. I know. Every time I lose, I think the next one will fix it. And when I win, I want to bet more."
"That sounds like a trap."
"It is." His voice cracked. "I don't know how to stop."
Anand sat down beside his younger brother. "Okay. We'll find help. The counselling centre does this. I'll come."
Karthik nodded, and deleted the app while Anand watched.

How much had Karthik lost?
He had lost more than his stipend.
What does Karthik's cracking voice reveal about his feelings?
It reveals he feels trapped and ashamed, knowing the betting is out of control but not knowing how to stop.
What made Anand's response helpful?
He named the pattern calmly, didn't shame Karthik, and offered to go with him to get professional help.
How might Anand feel, as Karthik's older brother, hearing about the losses?
Anand is likely worried and shaken, but he stays calm and offers to come along, so Karthik feels able to accept help instead of hiding.

Hot dog buns come in packages of 8. For the school picnic, Mr. Gates bought 30 packages of hot dog buns. He has four classes with 30 students in each class. How many hot dog buns can each of Mr. Gates' students get?

Mr. Gates bought 30 x 8 = 240 hot dog buns.
In his four classes, he has a total of 4 x 30 = 120 students.
Therefore, each of his students can get 240/120 = 2 hot dog buns.
The answer is 2.

"Swati, you're clicking it again."
"Sorry, sorry." Swati stopped, and her knee started bouncing under the desk instead.
"It's just... I can't hear the lecture when you do that," Yogesh said gently, then added, "Actually, wait. Are you doing it to focus?"

What did Swati pull from her bag?
Swati pulled a rubber ring from her bag.

Swati could use a quieter fidget such as tapping a finger or holding the soft ring, so Yogesh can hear the lecture and Swati can still focus.

He said, "Oh! For me?"

"Go ahead."

"What would it take for me to become a team lead in the next cycle?"

Uday leaned back. "Honestly? Your client work is strong. But you've never run a project end to end."

You remember my bottle-drip idea from the final-year project, the old plastic bottles with pinholes for my father's chilli rows. Last year I tried to make it for other farmers in our block and failed completely. Every farmer's plot was different, and I was cutting holes by hand at midnight.

Sumit Sir would likely feel proud and moved that a lesson from class finally made sense to a former student in real work.

Papa's folded handkerchief.

I still remember the Monday review. Jeevan, my manager, put my campaign numbers on the big screen and said, "This is what happens when you don't check your work." Twelve people looked at me.
I went home, ate nothing, and at eleven I sent my resignation. No new job. No talk with anyone. Just a three-line email saying I was leaving at the end of the month.

That lasted about a week. Then came the searching. Two months with no offers. I moved back to my parents' flat. When a recruiter at another agency called Jeevan for a reference, I heard later that it was very brief.
Was the review unfair? Partly. But I let one evening decide the next six months.
Rajni, if you're reading this in your drafts folder next year: sleep on it first.

Twelve people looked at Rajni during the review.
How did Rajni feel the morning after resigning?
Rajni felt amazing and lighter, a sense of relief that lasted about a week before the search began.

Waiting at least until morning and talking to someone before deciding, and job hunting while still employed, would have avoided the long gap.

why do we hear our own voice differently in a recording
When is my next exam?

1. The voice we hear in our head sounds deeper than the recorded one. Because we normally hear our voice partly through our skull bones, while a recording carries only the sound that travels through the air.
2. I don't know; I can't see your timetable. Check your school diary or the exam notice.
What is the harm in answering a question before reading it fully?
You may miss part of what is asked. Because the last words often change the meaning, so a quick guess can give a good answer to the wrong question.
Our office is closed on Sundays, so we works from Monday to Saturday. Please check.

Our office is closed on Sundays, so we work from Monday to Saturday.
Why: "we" takes the base verb "work".

Why is the narrator disappointed by Barnard's Inn?

There was an air of toleration or depreciation about his utterance of these words that rather depressed me; and I was still looking sideways at his block of a face in search of any encouraging note to the text, when he said here we were at Barnard's Inn. My depression was not alleviated by the announcement, for, I had supposed that establishment to be an hotel kept by Mr. Barnard, to which the Blue Boar in our town was a mere public-house. Whereas I now found Barnard to be a disembodied spirit, or a fiction, and his inn the dingiest collection of shabby buildings ever squeezed together in a rank corner as a club for Tom-cats.
He had thought it was a hotel kept by Mr. Barnard, grander than the Blue Boar. Instead it is a dingy collection of shabby buildings, and Barnard seems to be a fiction.

But all week the TV in the Irinjalakuda tea shop had replayed coverage of a plane crash abroad: the smoking field, the weeping families. "I'll take the train," she told her cousin Jomon. What would you advise Seema?
She could compare how often people are hurt on scooters with how often planes crash, and start by wearing the helmet on every ride, however short.
How might Jomon feel, riding behind her?
Jomon may feel frustrated and anxious, since he sees the real risk right in front of him while she worries about a far-off one.

'Astrid, can you fold the laundry?' 'Later, Pappa.' Twenty minutes passed. 'Astrid, laundry.' 'In a minute!' Her sister Clara folded her own pile and went back to her book. A third time, a fourth. By the fifth time, Pappa was standing in the doorway of their Oslo flat, arms crossed. 'Now, please.' 'Why do I always have to do everything?' Astrid shouted. It became an argument, voices rising, a door slammed. In the end she folded the laundry anyway. It took twelve minutes, exactly what it would have taken the first time. But it was now seven o'clock, her cartoon had already finished, and Pappa said the TV stayed off tonight.

How long did folding the laundry take?
Twelve minutes.
How did Astrid feel when she shouted 'Why do I always have to do everything?'
She felt frustrated and resentful, though the argument only made things worse.
What would have saved Astrid her cartoon?
Folding the laundry the first time Pappa asked; it took twelve minutes either way, but delaying added an argument and cost the cartoon.
How did the evening feel for Pappa?
Pappa asked five times and ended up arms crossed in the doorway in an argument, so he was likely tired and annoyed.

Dhruv: 2. The land title has some old family claim we missed.
Bhupen: 3. One of us loses a job and the EMI starts to hurt.
Dhruv: Right, we can't undo this like a rental. For 1 and 2, the lawyer your cousin suggested checks every paper first.
Bhupen: Booked her for Thursday, 4 pm. I'll scan the sale deed and the society papers tonight.
Dhruv: For 3, we don't put everything into the down payment. We keep a reserve untouched and ask the bank's advisor what size suits us.
Bhupen: Agreed. And if the lawyer finds a problem?
Dhruv: Then we walk away. Annoyed beats trapped.
Bhupen: Ok. Feeling less scared now 🙂

When is the appointment with the lawyer?
It is on Thursday, 4 pm.
How did Bhupen feel after they listed what could go wrong?
Bhupen felt less scared, because each risk now had a check or a backup; naming the bad endings made them feel handled rather than hidden.
Which other approach would suit a smaller, easy-to-undo choice better, and why?
For something easy to reverse, like picking a rental, a quick checklist or simply trying it would be enough, because a mistake there can be fixed later.
How might the lawyer see the pair's list of worries?
The lawyer would likely find it useful, since it points straight to the papers that matter, such as the sale deed and the society papers.

Arrive before the bell rings.
We know that 10 = 6 + 4. Use it to find 10 - 6.

Answer: 10 - 6 = 4 (and 10 - 4 = 6).

Adding and taking away are opposites. If 6 and 4 make 10, then taking 6 from 10 leaves 4. Use the number bond picture: cover one part, the other part is the answer. Knowing bonds makes subtraction quick.

I'm Sarika, Payal's older sister. I was in the kitchen when it happened. Mummy had found Payal's phone in her schoolbag during exams, even though she'd promised to leave it at home. Mummy took it.
Payal went red. She shouted, "You never trust me! Never!" and slammed her door so hard the calendar fell off the wall.
Then silence. For two hours, nothing. No music, no footsteps. I didn't know if she was crying or sleeping or planning revenge.
Mummy wanted to go in. I said, "Maybe wait."
At dinner time Payal came out. Her face was calm, a bit puffy. She sat down and said, "I'm sorry I shouted. I was so angry I couldn't think. I did break the promise. Can we talk about the phone rule?"
Mummy nodded. They talked. Nobody raised their voice.
I think the two hours were Payal's way of cooling down.

What fell off the wall when Payal slammed the door?
The calendar fell off the wall.
What was Payal feeling when she slammed the door?
Payal was furious, feeling mistrusted, and too angry to think clearly.
Which choice helped the evening end well?
Payal stepping away for two hours, and Mummy waiting instead of following her in, let the fury fade so they could talk calmly.
How might Mummy have felt during the two hours of silence?
Mummy was probably worried and unsettled, wanting to go in, but trusted that giving space might help.

When I was fifteen, Lalit sir held up my charcoal sketch of a rain-soaked bus stop in front of the whole class and said, 'Siddharth, this is what I mean by mood.' Everyone turned to look at me. I remember my face going hot and my mouth saying, 'It was a fluke, sir. The charcoal smudged by accident.' It hadn't. I'd smudged it on purpose, after trying for two evenings. But admitting that felt dangerous, like claiming I was good, and I didn't think I was. Every compliment that year got the same treatment: luck, easy, anyone could. Every bad mark I kept like evidence. It took me a long time to notice the pattern. Now, when someone praises something I've made, I try to say just 'Thank you, I worked on it,' and let it sit there, even when it feels awkward.

What was the charcoal sketch of?
The sketch was of a rain-soaked bus stop.
Why did admitting the smudge was on purpose feel dangerous to Siddharth?
It would mean claiming to be good, which clashed with Siddharth's belief of not being good, so calling it a fluke kept that old self-view untouched.
What does Siddharth do now with compliments, and why is it a good step?
Saying 'Thank you, I worked on it' lets the praise count and links it to real effort, instead of filing every good thing under luck.
How might Lalit sir have felt when Siddharth called the sketch a fluke?
Lalit sir may have felt a little puzzled or disappointed, since he was holding it up as a real example of mood, not an accident.

At the Kartik mela in their small town, Indu bought jalebis for her cousin Nikita and watched the giant wheel go round. Indu, twenty-five, had been a clerk at the cooperative bank for three years. Same desk, same passbooks, same bus home by five-thirty, TV serials by eight. She liked it. It was safe. Nikita, seventeen, was full of plans: a nursing course, a stall selling her aunt's pickles, maybe a blog. "What about you, Didi? What are you building?" Indu opened her mouth and nothing came out. She thought of her salary, her new fridge, the sofa set she was saving for. None of it felt like an answer. A strange flatness settled over her, even with the lights and the loudspeaker music all around. "I don't know," she finally said, and bit into a jalebi that suddenly tasted too sweet.

How long has Indu been a clerk at the cooperative bank?
Indu has been a clerk there for three years.
What was Indu feeling when Nikita asked what she was building?
Indu felt flat and unsettled, realising she had no answer beyond her salary and comforts.
What could Indu try after this evening?
Indu could think about one small thing beyond her own comfort she might grow or help with, perhaps even helping Nikita with the pickle stall.
How might Nikita see Indu's answer?
Nikita, full of plans herself, might be puzzled or a little worried by Indu's silence, not seeing it as laziness but as something missing.
Why is it a good idea to try the easy questions first in an exam when time is short?
The easy ones give quick marks. Because they are quick to finish and collect marks, you will not run out of time before reaching questions you already know.

Tuesday night
Did the thing Avni suggested. Gave myself till 9 p.m. for the marketing case study, no extensions. At 8:55 it was maybe 85% of what I wanted. The graphs could be prettier, and the conclusion is a bit short. The old me would've kept going till 3 a.m. and then submitted late, or not at all. Instead I hit submit. My heart pounded for a whole minute. Then I opened a new page and wrote "For next time": 1) start the graphs on day one, 2) outline the conclusion before writing, 3) ask Avni to read the draft. Weirdly, I feel lighter than after any assignment this year. I even had time to call home. Good enough, then better. That's the plan now.
Jomon

What deadline did Jomon set for the case study?
9 p.m., no extensions.
Why did Jomon's heart pound after hitting submit?
Sending work that felt only 85% ready went against the old habit of polishing all night, so Jomon felt nervous letting go, even though it was the right choice.
Which choice turned the unfinished parts into something useful?
Writing a "For next time" list, so the weaker graphs and short conclusion became lessons rather than reasons to keep working.
How might Avni feel reading the "For next time" list?
Avni would probably be pleased the suggestion worked and happy to read the next draft, as the list asks.
Replace "very" and the adjective with one strong word: She was very happy with the result.
She was delighted with the result.

In the courtyard of a mud-walled house, two-year-old Neelam was banging a steel spoon on an upturned bowl. Her mother Swati, hands floury from the morning rotis, gently lifted the spoon away. Neelam's eyebrows dropped, her lower lip pushed out, and she glared at the spoon in Swati's fingers. Swati crouched down. “You're cross. You wanted the spoon.” Neelam sniffed, leaned her whole weight against Swati's knee, still pouting, and lifted both arms to be picked up.

What did Swati take away from Neelam?
A steel spoon that Neelam had been banging on an upturned bowl.
What might Neelam have been feeling when she lifted her arms, and what else could it mean?
Most likely she felt frustrated about losing the spoon and wanted comfort, since she leaned on Swati and asked to be held. Another reading is that she was simply tired and wanted to be carried. 🙂
What small step could Swati take next?
She could keep naming the feeling in simple words, hold Neelam for a moment, and then offer a different safe thing to bang, such as a wooden spoon.
How might Swati see Neelam's pout?
Swati is likely to see it as a young child's honest signal of being upset and wanting closeness, not as a plan to get her way.

In the kasba, everyone compared Rukmini with her cousin Shalini. Shalini always came first. Rukmini came somewhere in the middle.
At the family dinner after results, her uncle said, "Shalini got 96. Rukmini, what happened?"
Rukmini stared at her plate. Her ears burned.
Shalini put down her spoon. "Rukmini made the best science model in the district. She did that alone."
Everyone went quiet.
Later, on the terrace, Rukmini said, "Thanks. But I still feel like the second one."
Shalini shrugged. "I'm scared all the time of not coming first. It's not fun either."
They sat in silence. Rukmini realised: nobody at the top was feeling great either.

What did Shalini say Rukmini made?
The best science model in the district.

How does Shalini see coming first?

Christmas Eve, hostel room
Two offers. The Chennai logistics firm pays better, has proper training, and Karthik's cousin says the team is kind. The Bengaluru startup has a tiny office and a founder who laughed at my joke in the interview.
I knew in about four seconds that I wanted Bengaluru. It just felt right.
Then I spent the whole evening writing reasons: faster learning, more ownership, better city for my future. Karthik read the list and said, "You wrote these after you'd decided, didn't you? You don't even know if they give more ownership."
I got defensive. But he's not wrong. I haven't asked one question about the startup's training or how long it has been running. The reasons arrived after the feeling, like a lawyer hired to defend it.
Tomorrow I'm calling both with the same five questions. Then we'll see if Bengaluru still feels right.
Kamal

What did the Bengaluru founder do in the interview?
The founder laughed at Kamal's joke.
Why did Kamal get defensive when Karthik read the list?
Kamal felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, because the reasons had been written after the feeling, to defend it.
What is Kamal's plan, and why is it wise?
Calling both companies with the same five questions, so the choice rests on real answers rather than a four-second feeling.
How does Karthik see Kamal's list of reasons?
Karthik sees them as reasons built after the decision, since Kamal doesn't even know whether the startup gives more ownership.

messages.content: Our class is making a rain gauge for a science project, and we don't know how to start.
A rain gauge measures how much rain falls. Do you have a plastic bottle and a ruler?
We have both.
Cut the top off the bottle, turn it upside down and place it back like a funnel. Mark a scale on the side with the ruler and place it in an open space.
Will it be accurate?
A home gauge will give a fair idea, not a perfect measurement. Keep it level and away from trees or roofs, and read it at the same time each day.
Should we empty it every day?
Yes, after you note the reading. Keep a daily chart on a table with the date and amount, and you'll see patterns over the weeks.
Maybe we can compare it with the weather report.
A good idea, as long as you present both as they are. Small differences are normal and make a nice discussion in your project.

At the village fair near Ratlam, Kamal wandered the stalls with his grandmother. Last week, Usha had been, in his words, "the only person in this whole village who understands me." She'd shared her notes, walked with him to school, laughed at his jokes. Today, at the fair, she'd walked past him with her cousins and only nodded. "She's a traitor," Kamal told his grandmother. "I always knew she was fake." His grandmother bought him a glass of sugarcane juice. "Last week she was the only one who understood you." "That was before." "Before she nodded?" Kamal went red. "She should have stopped." "Maybe. Or maybe her cousins were rushing her." Kamal drank his juice. "So she's not perfect." "No one is. And she's not a traitor either." Kamal watched the giant wheel. That was harder to feel than to hear.

What did Kamal's grandmother buy him?
A glass of sugarcane juice.
Why did Kamal suddenly call Usha a traitor?
Kamal felt hurt and disappointed when she only nodded, and the strong feeling swept away all her good qualities in his mind.
What did Kamal's grandmother do that helped?
She gently reminded him of what he said last week and suggested another reason, helping him see Usha as neither perfect nor a traitor.
How might Usha have seen the moment at the fair?
Usha may not have thought much of it, perhaps just hurrying with her cousins.

Nursery note for Leela's mother, Maria
Leela skipped her nap today because of the noise from the painting next door. By three she cried over a crayon, threw her shoe, then clung to my leg. Asked what was wrong, she just wailed.
She was very tired.
I held her in the quiet corner with her blanket and she slept in minutes. She woke up smiling.
Please let her sleep early tonight.

Why did Leela skip her nap?
Leela skipped her nap because of the noise from the painting next door.
What was Leela feeling when she cried and clung?
Leela was overtired and upset, too worn out to say why she felt so bad.
What worked for Leela, and why?
Holding her in a quiet corner with her blanket so she could sleep, since tiredness, not naughtiness, was behind her behaviour.
How might Maria see Leela's evening after reading the note?
Maria might feel reassured and understanding, seeing any crankiness as tiredness and planning an early bedtime.

The registration hall at the college was noisy, one desk per elective. The queue for Film Studies snaked past the notice board; the Urban Ecology desk had three students and a tired professor. "Film Studies," Sahil said, joining the tail. "Look at that line. Everyone knows something." Dolma stopped at the ecology desk and picked up the course outline. "Did you read what Film Studies involves?" "Watching films, obviously." "It's four written critiques and a long end-term paper. You hate writing essays." Sahil shrugged. "Then why is everyone in the queue?" Dolma looked along the line. "Because the queue was long when they got here." Sahil stayed where he was anyway, shuffling forward with the crowd, the outline still unread.

How many students were at the Urban Ecology desk?
Three students.
What did Sahil believe the long queue showed?
Sahil felt confident the queue itself was proof that the course is good, since so many people must know something.
What could Sahil check before reaching the front of the queue?
Sahil could read the Film Studies outline, as Dolma did, and weigh the four critiques and long paper against a dislike of writing essays.
How does Dolma see the queue differently from Sahil?
Dolma sees the queue as people copying whoever was ahead of them, not as information about the course, so Dolma reads the outline instead.

Grandma gives Anu 1 rupee on day 1, 2 rupees on day 2, 4 rupees on day 3, doubling each day. How much does Anu get on day 10? A packet of 64 laddoos is halved again and again: 64, 32, ... What comes after 4?

Answer: Day 10: ₹512. After 4 comes 2, then 1.

Doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 - that is day 1 to day 10. Doubling grows VERY fast: on day 20 it would be more than a million rupees! Halving goes the other way: 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Compare with adding: + 2 each day would give only 1, 3, 5 ... 19 on day 10.

Dear Diary,

'You haven't eaten,' Imran said, setting the plate beside her laptop.
'Twelve children in Nashik are in hospital, Imran. The biscuits from our line.' Usha's voice was flat. 'The news says they're recovering. Recovering.'
'Your factory?'
'My batches. Remember the months we skipped the full contamination test to hit dispatch? I signed off on some of them.'
Imran sat down slowly. 'What happens now?'
'Audit on Monday. My manager called. He said, "Make sure the logs are complete." You know what that means.'
'Fill in tests that never happened.'
Usha covered her face. 'If I do it, maybe no one finds out. If I don't, I'm finished. And either way, those children...'
'Usha. Look at me. Which one can you live with?'
She didn't answer. The laptop screen glowed with the empty log.

How many children are in hospital?
Twelve children in Nashik are in hospital.
What is Usha feeling as she covers her face?
She feels deep shame and fear, caught between covering up to save her job and the weight of the harm to the children.
What turning point is available to Usha at this stage?
She could refuse to fill in false logs and tell the auditors the truth about the skipped tests, since covering up would only add to the harm.
What is Imran experiencing as he hears the story?
Imran is shocked and worried for Usha, but stays steady to help her face the choice rather than make it for her.

Before: Ramesh, twenty-six, had just become operations head at a small textile mill. The owner wanted to cut costs by dumping dye water into the river at night, as other mills did. Manoj, the plant supervisor, said, "Everyone does it. Nobody checks."
During: For a week Ramesh studied it. The fines, the health risk to villages downstream, the cost of a proper treatment unit, the mill's reputation with its buyers. He lost sleep. He put it all in a single page.
After: At the meeting, he presented the numbers: treating the water cost more now but protected the mill from fines and losing buyers. The owner was grumpy but agreed to install a unit in phases. Manoj said, "You thought it through." Ramesh felt relieved and exhausted.

What did the owner want to dump into the river?
Dye water, at night.
How did Ramesh feel after the meeting?
He felt relieved and exhausted after a week of lost sleep.
What made Ramesh's decision process strong?
He weighed ethics, health risk, legal fines, costs and reputation, and presented a clear case for a phased plan.
How might the villages downstream be affected by the decision?
They will be spared polluted water, protecting their health and livelihoods.
What did Meera and Dev talk about at lunch?
I wasn't there, so I wouldn't know. If it worries you, ask Meera kindly.

Wednesday
Anjali brought the new girl, Tamsin, to our tree today. My first thought was, great, now I'm the extra one. I felt a little pinch in my chest.
But then I remembered Anjali has cousins and a dance class and she still always comes back to me. Friends are allowed other friends. It doesn't cost me much to be nice.
So I said, "Hi, Tamsin. Want to play three-way catch?" Tamsin can't catch at all, but she laughs at herself, which is funny. Anjali looked so happy.
I'm not going to pretend I didn't feel the pinch. But it went away faster than I thought.
Irfan

What game did Irfan suggest to Tamsin?
Three-way catch.
What was Irfan's first feeling when Anjali brought Tamsin to the tree?
A little pinch of jealousy, worried about becoming "the extra one".
What helped Irfan choose to be friendly?
Irfan remembered that Anjali has other friends and still comes back, so being kind to Tamsin cost little.
How might Anjali feel when Irfan welcomes Tamsin?
Anjali looked happy, likely relieved that her friends can get along without her having to choose. 😊

Preschool note, summer term
Reena (5) now washes her hands without reminders before lunch. Today she even showed Simran, who is new, how to rub the soap between her fingers.
She still refuses anything green on her plate. We put one small piece of cucumber next to her rice, no pressure. She licked it. 🙂
I'll suggest to her parents that they keep offering small tastes at home.

What did Reena show Simran?
How to rub the soap between her fingers.
How did Reena seem to feel showing Simran?
She seemed proud and confident, like a helper.
How is the preschool supporting Reena's eating?
They offer a small piece of green food without pressure and will suggest the same at home.
How might Simran feel being helped by Reena?
Simran likely feels welcomed and less nervous as a new child.
Edit this for me: Each of the girls have brought their own tiffin.

Each of the girls has brought her own tiffin.
Why: "each" is singular: "has", "her".

Saturday: Rekha came in from kho-kho with her fringe stuck to her forehead and sweat running down her neck. Her mother, Urmila, handed her water and laughed. "Who won?" "We did!"
Monday: Before the maths test, Rekha's palms were so damp that her pencil slipped. The fan was on and she hadn't run anywhere. She wiped her hands on her skirt and took a slow breath.
Thursday night: Rekha woke with her nightdress soaked, though the room was cool. She was shivering and her head ached. Urmila felt her forehead, sat with her, and in the morning took her to the doctor. On the way, Rekha said, "Three kinds of sweaty in one week." Urmila smiled. "And each one meant something different."

What game had Rekha been playing on Saturday?
Kho-kho.
What was Rekha feeling before the maths test when her palms were damp?
She was nervous about the test; the fan was on and she hadn't been running, so the sweat most likely came from worry.
What can help someone work out why a child is sweating?
Looking at the setting and other signs, such as heat, a game, an upcoming test, or shivering and a headache, and getting a doctor's check when illness seems likely.
How might Urmila have read Thursday night's sweat differently from Saturday's?
On Saturday she saw a happy, hot child after a game; on Thursday the cool room, shivering and headache told her it was probably illness.

I live in the flat opposite Nirmala's in our Bengaluru apartment block, so I saw it from my door.

The Diwali committee came round with a printed list: "Fireworks show, sound system, catering. Per flat: fixed amount." Shreya, the committee head, read it out cheerfully.

Nirmala, twenty-one, lives alone and pays her own college fees. She looked at the paper for a long time. "Can I give less? Or help with decorations instead?"

Shreya's smile slipped. "Everyone's paying. It's for the community."

Nirmala went in and came back with the money. She didn't come down for the fireworks.

On Diwali night the courtyard was glorious: lamps on every railing, kids with sparklers, music. I loved it. I also kept looking up at her dark window.

At the next meeting I proposed a "give what you can, or give time" option. Four people raised their hands.

What did Nirmala offer instead of the full amount?
Nirmala asked to give less or help with decorations instead.
What mixed feelings did the narrator have on Diwali night?
The narrator felt joy at the lamps and music but also worry and discomfort, looking up at Nirmala's dark window.
Why is the narrator's proposal a good one?
A 'give what you can, or give time' option keeps the celebration open to everyone without forcing anyone beyond their means.
What was the evening like for Nirmala?
Nirmala likely felt pressured and left out, paying anyway and then staying away from the fireworks.
Tom's puts 30 miles per day on his bike for the first 183 days of the year.  For the rest of the days of the year he goes 35 miles per day.  How many miles does he drive for the year?

For the first 183 days he drives 183*30=5490 miles
There are 365-183=182 days left in the year
He drives 35*182=6370 for those days
So in total he drives 5490+6370=11,860
The answer is 11860.

"Okay, I've decided," Pallavi said, turning her laptop to Suraj. "Cloud storage. Look."
"Basic, fifty gigs, ₹75. Standard, a hundred gigs, ₹220. Pro, two terabytes, ₹230."
"Pro. Obviously. Ten rupees more for twenty times the space!"
Suraj squinted. "How much do you use now?"
"About thirty gigs. Photos, college stuff."
"So Basic covers you."
"Yes, but Pro is such good value."
"Compared to Standard. Which nobody would ever buy, by the way."
Pallavi frowned at the screen. "Why does Standard even exist?"
"To make Pro look like a steal."
She groaned. "I already clicked Pro yesterday."
"Then check if you can switch."

How much storage does Pallavi use now?
She uses about thirty gigs.
What was Pallavi feeling when she said "Pro. Obviously"?
She felt excited and clever, sure she had found great value because Standard made Pro look like a steal.
What could Pallavi do now that she has seen the decoy?
She could check if she can switch to Basic, which covers her thirty gigs, and in future compare plans against what she actually uses.
How does Suraj see the Standard plan?
Suraj sees it as a plan nobody would buy, placed only to make Pro look like a bargain.
Tiffin mein roti aur sabzi hai. "In the tiffin" ya "inside tiffin"?
Say: "There are roti and sabzi in the tiffin." We normally say "in the tiffin".
A shirt costs ₹99. How much do 6 shirts cost?

Answer: ₹594. 6 x 99 = 6 x 100 - 6 x 1 = 600 - 6 = 594.

99 is just 1 less than 100. Pretend each shirt costs ₹100: 6 shirts cost ₹600. But we paid ₹1 too much for each shirt, 6 times, so take away ₹6: ₹594. The distributive property works with taking away too: 6 x (100 - 1) = 6 x 100 - 6 x 1.

Lawrence worked 8 hours each day on Monday, Tuesday and Friday. He worked 5.5 hours on both Wednesday and Thursday. How many hours would Lawrence work each day if he worked the same number of hours each day?

8 hours * 3 = 24 hours
5.5 * 2 = 11 hours
24 + 11 = 35 hours
35/7 = 5 hours
Lawrence would work 5 hours each of the 7 days in a week.
The answer is 5.

The satsang met on the second floor of the community centre, and by five the hall smelled of tea and incense. Lalremsiami, who had moved from Aizawl for work eight months earlier, ate lunch alone most days at the office.

"You're back! Sit with us," Shalini said, pressing a plate into her hands. Someone asked how her sister's exam had gone. After the singing, Lalremsiami felt a warm ache: the first place in the city that felt like family.

Lalremsiami glanced at the clock. "I'm meeting my college friends tonight. Can I come next Sunday?"

"Of course. We'll save your seat."

Lalremsiami moved from Aizawl.
What did Lalremsiami feel after the singing?
A warm ache of belonging: the satsang was the first place in the city that felt like family.
How can Lalremsiami enjoy the satsang while keeping it healthy?
Keep outside friendships such as the college friends, keep asking questions, and remember that being able to miss a week or leave without losing respect is part of a healthy community.
How does Shalini seem to see Lalremsiami's outside plans?

messages.content: Anne drops a mirror and breaks it into 60 pieces. She sweeps up half of them, then her cat steals 3 pieces and her boyfriend picks up 1/3 of the remaining pieces. How many pieces does her boyfriend pick up?

First find the number of pieces left after Anne sweeps up: 60 pieces / 2 = 30 pieces
Then subtract the number her cat takes: 30 pieces - 3 pieces = 27 pieces
Divide that number by 3 to find how many pieces her boyfriend picks up: 27 pieces / 3 = 9 pieces
The answer is 9.

messages.content: Annie does a survey of the sixth-grade classes to see who prefers pretzels to goldfish. In Miss Johnson's class, 1/6 of the students preferred goldfish. In Mr. Feldstein's class, 2/3rds of the students preferred goldfish. In Ms. Henderson's class, 1/5 of the students prefer goldfish. If each class has 30 students, how many people total prefer goldfish?

First find the number of students in Mr. Feldstein's class who prefer goldfish: 2/3 * 30 students = 20 students
Then find the number of students in Mr. Feldstein's class who prefer goldfish: 1/6 * 30 students = 5 students
Then find the number of students in Ms. Henderson's class who prefer goldfish: 1/5 * 30 students = 6 students
Then add the number of students from each class who prefer goldfish to find the total: 20 students + 5 students + 6 students = 31 students
The answer is 31.

A pack of dogs found a pile of bones in the dumpster behind the butcher shop.  One by one, the dogs crawled into the dumpster, grabbed a mouthful of bones, and ran off with their newfound treasure.  In all, there were 5 dogs.  The first dog carried off 3 bones.  The second dog carried off 1 less bone than the first dog.  The third dog carried off twice as many as the second dog.  The fourth dog carried off one bone, and the fifth dog carried off twice the number of bones as the fourth dog carried, leaving no remaining bones in the dumpster.  How many bones were in the original pile of bones?

The second dog carried off 1 less bone than the first dog, or 3-1=2 bones.
The third dog carried off twice as many bones as the third dog, or 2*2=4 bones.
The fifth dog carried off twice the number of bones as the fourth dog carried, or 2*1=2 bones.
Therefore, the original pile of bones contained 3+2+4+1+2=12 bones.
The answer is 12.

Kristy, a sales representative earns a basic salary of $7.50 per hour plus a 16% commission on everything she sells. This month, she worked for 160 hours and sold $25000 worth of items. Her total commission is $25000 x 16/100 = $4000.

Her monthly budget aside from the insurance is $5200 x 95/100 = $4940.
Therefore, she allocated $5200 - $4940 = $260 on insurance.
The answer is 260.

A family has three adults and children, both girls and boys. They went out for a family trip and prepared 3 dozen boiled eggs for the trip. Every adult got 3 eggs, and the boys each received 1 more egg than each girl since the girls had some snacks. How many boys went on the trip if the number of girls was 7 and each girl received an egg?

The total number of eggs the family had is 3 * 12 = 36 eggs
If each adult received 3 eggs, the total number of eggs they got is 3 * 3 = 9 eggs.
The children shared 36 - 9 = 27 eggs
Since each girl received an egg, the boys shared 27 - 7 = 20 eggs
If each boy received 1 egg more than each girl, each received 1+1 = 2 eggs
The boys received 20 eggs, and if each got 2 eggs, then 20/2 = 10 boys went on the trip
The answer is 10.

messages.content: At a certain car dealership, 15% of the cars cost less than $15000 and 40% of the cars cost more than $20000. If there are 3000 cars at the dealership, how many of them cost between $15000 and $20000?

15% of 3000 cars is (15/100)*3000 = 450 cars
40% of 3000 cars is (40/100)*3000 = 1200 cars
450+1200 = 1650 cars which cost either less than $15000 or more than $20000
Out of 3000 cars, there will then be 3000-1650 = 1350 cars left which cost between $15000 and $20000
The answer is 1350.
A cycle costs ₹3,600. In a sale the price is cut by 25%. How much is taken off? What is 75% of ₹3,600?

Answer: 25% of ₹3,600 = ₹900 is taken off. 75% of ₹3,600 = ₹2,700.

25% is the same as 1/4, so find a quarter: 3,600 / 4 = 900. 75% is 3/4, three quarters: 3 x 900 = 2,700. Notice 25% + 75% = 100% and 900 + 2,700 = 3,600, so the sale price is ₹2,700. Using the fraction for a key percent is often the quickest way: 50% is half, 20% is a fifth, 12.5% is an eighth.

Kris has been suspended for bullying many times.  For every instance of bullying, she was suspended for 3 days.  If she has been suspended for three times as many days as a typical person has fingers and toes, how many instances of bullying is she responsible for?

For homework, Brooke has 15 math problems, 6 social studies problems, and 10 science problems. He can answer each math problem for 2 minutes while answering each social studies problem takes him 30 seconds. If he can answer each science problem in 1.5 minutes, how long will it take Brooke to answer all his homework?

Brooke will take 15 x 2 = 30 minutes to answer all math problems.
It will take him 6 x 30 seconds = 180 seconds to answer all social studies problems.
In minutes, this is equal to 180/60 = 3 minutes.
It will take him 10 x 1.5 minutes = 15 minutes to answer all science problems.
Therefore, Brooke will take 30 + 3 + 15 = 48 minutes to finish his homework.
The answer is 48.

Salem loves to write poems, and she always stores her poem in a creativity box kept safely in her home library. Last week, she created a poem with 20 stanzas. If each stanza has 10 lines, and each line has 8 words, calculate the total number of words in the poem.

If each line that Salem created in her poem has 8 words, the total number of words in a stanza, which is 10 lines, is 8 words/line * 10 lines/stanza = 80 words/stanza
With 20 stanzas, each containing 80 words per stanza, the total is 80 words/stanza * 20 stanzas = 1600 words in all the stanzas(poem)

While practising for his upcoming math exams, Hayes realised that the area of a circle he had just solved was equal to the perimeter of a square he had solved in the previous problem. If the area of the circle was 100, what's the length of one side of the square?

Let's say the side of a square is s.To get the perimeter of a square, you add all the sides, which is s+s+s+s = 100
Therefore, 4s=100
Therefore one side of the square is s =100/4 = 25
The answer is 25.

Dan's skateboarding helmet has ten more craters than Daniel's ski helmet. Rin's snorkel helmet has 15 more craters than Dan's and Daniel's helmets combined. If Rin's helmet has 75 craters, how many craters are in Dan's helmet?

If Rin's snorkel helmet has 75 craters, then Dan's and Daniel's helmets combined have 75-15 = 60 craters.
Let's assume Dan's helmet has C craters.
Since Dan's skateboarding helmet has ten more craters than Daniel's ski helmet, the total number of craters their helmets have is C+(C-10)=60
2C=60+10
The total number of craters that Dan's helmet has is C=70/2
Dan's skateboarding helmet has 35 craters.
The answer is 35.

Our neighbourhood is planning a Ganesh Chaturthi celebration. How do we make it eco-friendly?
Use a clay idol made from natural, unbaked clay, since it dissolves in water without leaving harmful residue. Choose natural colours and decorate with flowers and paper.
What about the immersion?
Many places now encourage immersion in a bucket or tank at home or in artificial ponds set up by local bodies. This protects rivers and lakes.
Is plaster of Paris bad?
It dissolves slowly, and the chemical paints often used on it can pollute water. That is why many city bodies suggest clay instead.
What can we do with the flowers?
Collect them separately and compost them, or give them to a group that turns flower waste into incense or compost.

Share simple facts, display a sample clay idol and invite neighbours to join the planning. Positive examples usually persuade better than rules.

Dadi's question about which draw she had entered was the turning point, because she realised she had never entered one and the offer was fake.
How did Papa see the call when she told him?
Papa saw it as a scam, since no real prize asks for payment first or card numbers, and he warned the bank that evening.

When I was in class nine, I thought I could read people like a scoreboard. My name is Pranav, and I was the kid who sorted everyone in the first week. Vidya was small, wore thick glasses and spoke so softly that the teacher kept asking her to repeat. So in my head she went into a box: bookish, bad at sports. When we were put in the same relay team for sports day, I groaned out loud. Then in practice she ran the third leg and overtook two runners. It turned out she had been training for district athletics since she was ten. I remember standing there with the baton, feeling stupid. I'd been so sure. It had felt exactly like knowing.

Which leg of the relay did Vidya run?
Vidya ran the third leg and overtook two runners.
Why did Pranav groan when put in Vidya's relay team?
Her small size, thick glasses and soft voice fitted Pranav's box of bookish and bad at sports, so the guess felt like knowing.
What could Pranav tell a younger student who sorts people in the first week?
That a first-week guess from looks or voice is only a guess; wait to see what people actually do, like how they run in practice, before deciding.
How might Vidya have felt hearing Pranav groan?
Vidya may have felt hurt or underestimated, and perhaps quietly determined to show what she could do in practice.

"Parul, you've been getting ready to start that blog for two months, so let your Dilnaz khala tell you something. When I was twenty, I wanted to enter a college essay competition on the history of our mohalla. I went to the library every day for six weeks. I filled three notebooks. I rewrote the outline eleven times; each version looked a little better and still not good enough to begin. I told everyone I was researching, and it felt so productive, like real work. The deadline came. I had a beautiful outline and not one paragraph. My friend Ruksana, who had started writing in week one with half my notes, won second prize. I cried, and then I understood: all that preparing was a way of never being judged. Start ugly, beta. Then fix."

How many times did Dilnaz rewrite the outline?
Eleven times.
How did all the researching feel to young Dilnaz at the time?
It felt productive and safe, like real work, while quietly hiding her fear of being judged.
What choice inside the story could have changed the result?
Starting to write in week one, as Ruksana did, even with an imperfect outline, would have given her something to submit.
How might Ruksana have seen Dilnaz's weeks of preparation?
Ruksana, writing from week one with fewer notes, may have admired the research but wondered why Dilnaz never began.

I'm Pooja, and last year Chaitanya told half our class that I still slept with a night light. I had told only Chaitanya. For two days I avoided the whole group. Then I asked, "Can we talk after school? Just us?" We sat on the low wall behind the basketball court. I had practised the first line. "When I heard everyone knew about the night light, I felt embarrassed, and really hurt, because I'd only told you." I didn't say "you always" or "you're such a gossip", though I wanted to. Then I asked, "What happened?" Chaitanya went red and said it had slipped out when someone was joking about ghosts, and had felt awful afterwards. We both went quiet. Then Chaitanya said sorry, properly, without a "but".

Where did Pooja and Chaitanya talk?
On the low wall behind the basketball court.
What was Pooja feeling on hearing that everyone knew?
Pooja felt embarrassed and deeply hurt, because the secret had been shared with only Chaitanya.
Why did Pooja's first line work better than calling Chaitanya a gossip?
It named Pooja's own feelings without attacking, so Chaitanya could listen and explain instead of getting defensive.
How might Chaitanya have felt during the talk?
Chaitanya seems ashamed, going red and admitting it felt awful, and eased enough by the calm tone to apologise properly.

'Practice is cancelled AGAIN! This is so unfair!'
'Gurpreet, don't shout.'
'I'll shout if I want! Nobody cares about my cricket!'
'Don't you raise your voice at me!' Farida heard herself, loud and sharp.
'YOU'RE raising YOUR voice!'
Farida stopped. He was right. She took a slow breath and spoke quietly. 'You're right. I'm getting loud too. Let's both take five minutes. I'll be on the balcony.'
'Fine!' Gurpreet stomped off.
Five minutes later he came out, arms folded but calmer.
'Ammi, I've been waiting all week for practice.'
'That's so disappointing,' Farida said softly. 'Do you want to play in the colony ground with me instead?'
He unfolded his arms. 'Can I bowl first?'

Where did Farida say she would wait?
On the balcony.
What was Gurpreet feeling underneath his shouting?
He was deeply disappointed that cricket practice was cancelled again after waiting all week.
Which choice worked, and why?
Farida lowered her voice, admitted she was loud and suggested five minutes apart, which calmed both and let them talk.
How might Farida have felt when Gurpreet pointed out her raised voice?
She was probably startled and a little embarrassed, but it helped her see she was feeding the storm.

It was Diwali bonus week at the garment factory in Tiruppur, and Lakshmi, the youngest HR executive, had spent ten hours deciding things: which leave requests to approve, which shift to move, who got the festival advance first, whether the canteen could stay open late. By seven her head felt like cotton wool.
Her gym bag sat by her desk, packed that morning with good intentions. Ojas from accounts stopped by. "Coming for the evening batch?"
"I can't choose one more thing today," Lakshmi said. "Not even which exercise."
On the bus home she ordered biryani on her phone without reading the menu, the same one as last Tuesday. The gym bag rode home on her lap, unopened.
Later, eating on the sofa, she thought: every morning I have energy for everything. By evening I'm a different person.

What had Lakshmi spent ten hours deciding?
Which leave requests to approve, which shift to move, who got the festival advance first, and whether the canteen could stay open late.
Why did skipping the gym feel reasonable to Lakshmi?
Lakshmi felt drained and foggy after a day of choices, whether from depletion, boredom or simply wanting rest, so even picking an exercise felt like too much and the repeat order was a relief.
What could help Lakshmi get her workout in?
Moving exercise to the morning when her energy is high, or making evenings choice-free: a fixed class already booked and dinner decided in the morning.
How might Ojas see Lakshmi's "I can't choose one more thing"?
Ojas might understand how heavy bonus week is and could make it easier for her, perhaps by fixing a set time they go together.

"Watch this," Rekha said to her sister. Monsoon rain drummed on the window.

She held up Chintu's toy duck, then dropped a dupatta over it.

Chintu looked at the dupatta.

"Will he find it?" Kavitha asked.

"Last month he'd just cry."

Chintu reached out, grabbed the dupatta and pulled. The duck appeared. He held it up and shouted.

"Clever boy," Kavitha said.

What did Rekha drop over the toy duck?
She dropped a dupatta over it.
How did Chintu feel when he found the duck?
Chintu was excited and proud, holding it up and shouting.
How can Rekha keep supporting Chintu's searching?
Keep playing hiding games with familiar toys and praise him when he finds them.
How does Kavitha see Chintu's success?
Kavitha is impressed and warm, calling him a clever boy.

The flat in Bengaluru had no power for the third day in a row, and Kunal and Rhea were both working from home with laptop batteries dying and deadlines landing.

By evening they were short with each other. Rhea snapped when Kunal took the last charged power bank. He apologised, then went and borrowed a neighbour's inverter socket for her laptop.

Later, by candlelight, eating cold sandwiches, Rhea said, "We've seen each other at our best. This week we've seen each other at our worst."

"And?" Kunal said.

"And I still want to marry you. But we need to talk about the things we keep skipping. Your job transfer. My mother living with us."

They talked until the candle burned out. Transfers, mothers, money, children. No big promises, just honest answers.

At midnight Kunal said, "So we're deciding this. Not just feeling it."

"Yes," Rhea said. "Eyes open."

How many days had the flat been without power?
Three days in a row.
What was Rhea feeling when she snapped about the power bank?
She was stressed and frustrated, with her deadline landing and her laptop dying.
What turned a bad week into a turning point for the couple?
They used it to talk honestly about the things they had skipped, like the transfer and her mother, and chose commitment with open eyes.
How might Kunal see Rhea's list of hard topics?
He may feel a bit nervous but relieved and respected, since they are deciding together instead of just hoping.

You asked how the first months went, Farah. Honestly? At the office I'm still Damini, but the day I married Chetan I became "bahu", and a bahu is watched. The first morning I made tea with ginger, the way my mother does. Chetan's mother took one sip, said nothing, and quietly made herself a fresh cup. His sister looked at me, then at the pot. His grandfather drank mine without a word, which I still don't know how to read. At dinner I started eating before Papa-ji picked up his roti. The whole table went still. My face was burning. Then Chetan tore his own roti and said, "We were both starving, Papa, blame me." Papa-ji laughed, and everyone breathed again. Nobody hands you the rules; you learn them from silences. It took most of a year. Last Sunday his mother asked me to make the tea for her sister's visit. Ginger and all.

What did Damini put in the tea on her first morning?
She made tea with ginger, the way her mother does.
What was Damini feeling when the whole table went still at dinner?
She felt embarrassed and exposed; her face was burning because she had broken a rule nobody had told her about.
Which choice of Chetan's helped, and why?
Chetan took the blame with a light joke, so Damini was not left alone and his father could laugh instead of judging her.
How might Chetan's mother have seen the ginger tea that first morning?
It may have tasted like a stranger in her kitchen; making a fresh cup quietly let her keep her own way without a quarrel, and a year later she trusts Damini with the guests' tea.

It costs $.10 to print one page. Jenny wants to print 7 copies of her 25-page essay. She also wants to buy 7 pens that each cost $1.50. If she pays the store with 2 twenty dollar bills, how much money should she get in change?

Jenny needs to print 7*25= 175 pages.
This will cost 175*$.10 =$17.5.
The pens will cost 7*$1.50=$10.50.
In total, she will spend $17.5+$10.5=$28.
Since she pays with 2 twenty dollar bills she pays with 2*20=40 dollars.
Thus, she will get $40-$28=$12 in change.
The answer is 12.
Rene has three times as many dolls as her sister, while her sister has two more dolls than their grandmother. If their grandmother has 50 dolls, how many dolls do they have altogether?

If the grandmother has 50 dolls, Rene's sister, who has 2 more dolls than their grandmother, has 50+2 = 52 dolls.
Together, Rene's sister and the grandmother have 52+50 = 102 dolls.
Since Rene has three times as many dolls as her sister, she has 52*3 = 156 dolls.
Altogether, they have 156+102 = 258 dolls.
The answer is 258.

a) true
b) false (3)
c) true
d) true
e) false (no mode)
f) false (9)
g) false
h) true
i) false (the mean more)
j) true
k) false (no change)
l) true
m) true
n) true
o) true
p) false (7)

I wanted to scream. Then I looked at how it fell. It tipped from the bottom, like a person standing on one leg. The base was only one tube wide. What made the tower topple at lunch?
Tanuja slammed the door.
How did Jasleen feel when the tower toppled?
Jasleen was frustrated enough to want to scream, before calming down to study how it fell.

Building a small test tower to try base shapes, so the big one is not the first to be tested.
What was it like for Tanuja?
Tanuja caused the first fall, then became a helpful tester, and they cheered together. 🎉

The church-yard jumble sale in Kochi was closing in ten minutes, and rain had started on the tarpaulins. Noor, nine, clutched sixty rupees and stopped at the table where a teenager called Thomas was selling a sticker album of space rockets. "How much?" "Three hundred." Noor's stomach dropped. Three hundred was impossible. "Can I have it for… a hundred and fifty?" "Two hundred." "A hundred?" The rain got louder. Thomas started folding his tablecloth. "Fine. Last price, eighty." Noor felt she was winning big. Eighty was so much less than three hundred! She borrowed twenty from her cousin and paid, grinning. On the way home, her cousin said quietly, "That album is thirty in the bookshop near school." Noor looked at the wet album and said nothing for a while.

How much did Thomas first ask for the sticker album?
Three hundred.
Why did eighty rupees feel like a big win to Noor?
Noor felt thrilled because she compared eighty with the three hundred she heard first, so it seemed tiny. The rain and closing time also rushed her, leaving no chance to think about the real price.
With the sale closing and rain starting, what could Noor have tried instead?
She could have asked her cousin what such albums usually cost, or decided her own top price before hearing any number, and walked away if it was higher.
How might Noor's cousin have felt lending her twenty rupees?
The cousin may have felt uneasy watching the deal and waited until afterwards to say something gently, not wanting to spoil the moment in the rain.

Supervisor's note, hospital records department, 10 June.
Our new trainee, Trisha, started on Monday. My honest first impression: disinterested. She yawned in the induction and barely asked questions.
I have learned to hold first impressions lightly, so I am writing this down as a guess, not a fact.
What would change my mind: if she asks good questions one-on-one; if her work is careful; if she follows up without being chased.
Update, 24 June. Trisha has asked me five sharp questions about coding errors, all in private. Her error rate is the lowest in the batch. She mentioned she was taking the night bus from her village for the first week until she found a room.
I was wrong. Guess crossed out.
Next step: I'll put her on the audit team.
Afreen

How many questions has Trisha asked in private by 24 June?
Five sharp questions about coding errors.
What was Afreen feeling on first seeing Trisha yawn?
Afreen felt doubtful and a bit disappointed, reading the yawns as disinterest.
Which part of Afreen's approach made the difference?
Writing the first impression as a guess and listing what would change Afreen's mind, then checking the evidence two weeks later.
What was Trisha's first week like?
Trisha was exhausted from taking the night bus from her village each day until she found a room.
This soup is very hotter than yesterday's. Please correct.

This soup is much hotter than yesterday's.
Why: "very" cannot go with a comparative; use "much".

The monsoon had turned the road to the Gurugram office into a river, and Parveen's shared cab took two hours each way. Still, she was at her desk by eight and left after ten, three weeks into her first job as a data analyst. She checked every spreadsheet three times. She read reports for meetings where she wouldn't even speak. On Friday her manager Jagdish praised her analysis in front of the team. For a moment she glowed. Then the thought came: it's only because I worked till midnight. If I stop, they'll see I'm not good enough. That weekend, with her feet up on a bucket to dry, she was back at her laptop, preparing Monday's report. Her mother called and asked if she'd slept. "I'll sleep once I've settled in," Parveen said, and kept scrolling through the numbers.

How long did Parveen's shared cab take each way?
Two hours each way.
Why did Parveen's glow at Jagdish's praise fade so quickly?
She felt relieved for a moment, but then fear returned, because she credited the praise to overwork rather than her own ability.
What could break Parveen's cycle of overwork?
Trying one week with normal hours and noticing whether her work is still good could show that her skill, not only extra hours, earns praise.
How might Parveen's mother feel on the phone?
Her mother likely feels worried about her tiredness and the long days.

"It says suspicious login from Singapore. Francis, have I been hacked?"
"Maybe. Let's start with how often these alerts turn out to be real hacks here."
"Is that a real question?"
"Very real. We get dozens of these a week. Most are people on a VPN or travelling. Real break-ins are rare."
"So I'm fine?"
"Not so fast. Now the evidence. Were you on the office VPN at 10:15?"
Anjali checked. "Yes. The Singapore server, actually."
"That pushes it further toward harmless. Any password-reset emails?"
"No."
"Also a good sign. But I don't get the last word." Francis was already typing. "I'll forward it to the security team and ask them to confirm. Change your password anyway; it costs nothing."
Anjali exhaled. "You didn't panic at all."
"I panicked in my first year. Then someone taught me to start with the odds."

Where did the suspicious login appear to come from?
The suspicious login appeared to come from Singapore.
Why does Francis feel calm about the alert?
Francis feels calm because most alerts like this are VPN use or travel, so starting from how rare real break-ins are keeps panic away.
What makes Francis's steps a careful way to judge the alert?
Francis starts with how common real hacks are, adjusts for the VPN and the lack of reset emails, and still asks the security team to confirm.
What is it like for Anjali when Francis asks about the VPN?
Anjali goes from worried to relieved, as the questions show that Anjali's own login explains the alert.

Supervision notes, field office, 14 March. Written by Kalyani, team supervisor.

Ganga came into my room after the village visit and said, "I'm quitting. I'm going to the mountains. I'm done with this." She is twenty-four and one of our steadiest field workers.

My first reaction was alarm; I nearly started listing the reasons she couldn't. I stopped myself. Instead I asked, "What's missing right now?"

She took a while. She said she loves the work but hasn't had a day off in five weeks, hasn't seen her friends, and feels like a machine.

We agreed on two small trials: a proper weekend off starting Friday, and one field day a week with a partner so she isn't alone on the road. We'll check in on the 28th.

Note to self: the mountains were a signal, not a plan. Listen for what's under the declaration.

How many weeks had Ganga gone without a day off?
Ganga hadn't had a day off in five weeks.
What was Kalyani feeling when Ganga first said she was quitting?
Kalyani felt alarmed and was tempted to argue, but chose to stay calm and curious instead.
Which choice worked here, and why?
Asking what was missing worked, because it turned the dramatic declaration into clear needs, rest and company, that small trials could test.
How might Ganga feel after this conversation?
Ganga may feel heard and a little relieved, since her exhaustion was taken seriously without being dismissed or treated as a crisis.

"Better than ruining dal for twelve people." Ayesha stirred the first pan. "Khala is coming on Friday. If I make one big pot and get the tadka wrong, that's it. This way I try four versions with a cup of dal."

Tanvir kept a mental scoreboard now: who spoke first in the Monday review, whose charts the director praised. He and Zeenat both wanted the senior analyst post, and his chest felt tight and calculating whenever her name came up. Once he spotted a weak number in her draft and felt a flicker of glee. He closed the file and went back to tightening his own quarterly report.

Zeenat noticed only the gaps. Her name was missing from a client thread, a shared file reached her a day late, and Tanvir's eyes seemed to follow her screen. She felt watched. That evening she began a dated log: thread, file, meeting, time.

On Thursday she caught him by the pantry. "Tanvir, I'm not accusing you," she said calmly. "Two client threads left me out and I found a file late. Can we copy each other on those from now on?"

He blinked, then nodded slowly. "I've been tense about the promotion. I didn't mean to shut you out. Copy me too."

She kept the log anyway. When Kishore, the manager, asked for updates the next week, both handed over clean, dated work.

How many client threads left Zeenat out, according to her?
She said two client threads left her out.
How did Tanvir's inner state and Zeenat's experience of him fit together, and what did each do to keep things fair?

Tanvir felt tense and calculating about the rivalry, but he did not sabotage her and put his effort into his own report. Zeenat, seeing only gaps, felt watched, so she kept a dated record and spoke to him directly and calmly.
What was Zeenat feeling as the missing thread, the late file and the following eyes added up?
She felt watched and uneasy, which is why she started a dated log.
What could Zeenat do if the gaps continue after this talk?
She could take her log to Kishore and stick to the facts, showing what was missed and when, without guessing at motives.

Everyone's references.

Dear Swati,
Something small has been bothering me, so I'm writing it down for you instead of saying it badly on the phone.
In Dr Pillai's seminar on Tuesday, I answered his question about the 1857 revolt with the wrong year. He sat back and gave this little chortle, lips closed, shoulders shaking, like he was enjoying a private joke. Two boys in the back smirked. I felt about six years old.
But yesterday I walked past his office and heard the same chortle while he was reading something on his own. He looked genuinely delighted. And later he told me he'd made the exact same mistake in his own viva, years ago.
So now I don't know. Was it at me, or was he remembering himself? Maybe both. I'm going to ask him, gently, at office hours. What would you do?
Love,
Ritu

The year of the 1857 revolt.
How did Ritu feel when Dr Pillai chortled in the seminar?
Ritu felt small and humiliated, "about six years old", especially with the smirks; now Ritu is unsure whether the chortle was mocking or a private memory.
What small step is Ritu planning, and why is it sensible?
Asking Dr Pillai gently at office hours, because the same chortle has shown up in different contexts and only he can say what he meant.
What might Dr Pillai have been thinking when he chortled?
He may have been amused remembering his own identical viva mistake, not mocking Ritu, though the smirking boys made it land badly.

Manoj's exam marks.
