You want to know how I got promoted, Dilnaz? It wasn't magic. It was a spreadsheet.
Last January I printed the senior-analyst criteria and put them next to my own work from the year. Five rows. Next to each I wrote what I had. Numbers accuracy, fine. Client reports, fine. Training juniors, fine. Then "leads initiatives across teams." I had written a big question mark.
That question mark bothered me all week. So I asked myself, what would count? And by when? The review was eight months away. I needed something that crossed teams and would show results by then.
I offered to run the shared forecasting process with the sales and supply teams. It took up two quarters of my life. But by the review, I had meeting notes, a process doc, and two team heads who'd seen me lead.
That's it. Pema's big secret: read the rubric first.

How many rows did the criteria have?
Five rows.
How did Pema feel about the question mark next to "leads initiatives across teams"?
Pema felt bothered and uneasy about it all week, which pushed Pema to work out what would count and plan backward.
Which approach might suit Dilnaz if the criteria at Dilnaz's company are vague?
Dilnaz could ask the manager directly for clear expectations and a timeline, since working backward only works when the target is written down.
How might the sales and supply team heads see Pema's work?
They saw Pema lead a process across their teams, so at review time they could speak for that cross-team ownership from their own experience.

Saturday. A big sale banner on Rajni's phone: the new phone, forty percent off, today only. Rajni looked at the emergency fund and took 30,000 from it. "I'll put it back next month," Rajni told Jahnavi, who was scrolling next to her. "Are you sure?" Jahnavi asked. "Totally."
Next month. The salary came and went, a wedding gift and a trip took their share, and the refill was quietly forgotten.
Five months later. A pipe burst in the flat and the plumber wanted cash. Rajni opened the account. 4,000 sat where a cushion was meant to be. Rajni's stomach dropped, and she called Jahnavi to borrow the rest.

How much did Rajni take from the emergency fund for the phone?
Rajni took 30,000 from it.
What was Rajni feeling when seeing 4,000 in the account?
Rajni's stomach dropped: she felt shock and regret about the cushion that had quietly gone.
What could Rajni do to keep a promise to refill the fund next time?
Rajni could set up an automatic monthly transfer that refills it, and not touch the fund for anything that is not an emergency.
How might Jahnavi have felt when Rajni called to borrow money?
Jahnavi was probably concerned and willing to help, but may have remembered asking "Are you sure?" on the day of the sale.

Mentor's note, 12 January.
I asked Lakshmi, who joined us two years ago, to talk to the new graduates about their first salaries, since hers is the calmest desk in the office. Pooja, one of the new joiners, said she keeps her bonus in a 'fun' account and her salary in a 'serious' one. Lakshmi smiled. "I used to do that too. Then I'd pinch every rupee on lunch while blowing the bonus on shoes." She showed them her single sheet: all accounts added together, debts taken away, money in and money out for the month. "The labels are still there," she said. "Rent, emergencies, my sister's wedding. But it's all one pool. I just look at the whole thing once a month." Pooja asked for a blank copy. I've asked HR to arrange a session with a certified financial adviser next month for anyone who wants it.

What does Pooja keep in a 'fun' account?
Pooja keeps her bonus in a 'fun' account.
Why does Lakshmi smile when Pooja describes her two accounts?
Lakshmi feels amused and understanding, recognising her own old habit of pinching on lunch while spending the bonus on shoes.
What does Lakshmi's single sheet do that separate accounts don't?
It adds all accounts together and takes away debts, showing the whole pool and the month's flow, while labels remain as tools for goals.
What might Pooja be feeling when she asks for a blank copy?
Pooja seems curious and a little relieved to find a simpler way to see her first salary clearly.

On the colony road in Jalandhar, Manoj was teaching his little brother Joseph to ride a bicycle. Manoj had ridden for five years; it felt like breathing. "Just pedal and balance," he said. Joseph wobbled and fell. "Pedal AND balance!" Manoj said louder. Joseph fell again. "It's so easy, why can't you do it?" Joseph's lip trembled. "You didn't tell me how to balance." Manoj opened his mouth, then closed it. How did he balance? He didn't know. He just did. Their mother came out and said, "Remember, Manoj, you took a whole summer to learn. Papa held the seat." Manoj had completely forgotten. He knelt down. "Okay. Look ahead, not at the wheel. I'll hold the seat and run." Joseph sniffed and got back on.

How long had Manoj been riding a bicycle?
Manoj had ridden for five years.
What was Manoj feeling when Joseph kept falling?
He felt frustrated and impatient, because riding felt so easy to him that he couldn't see why Joseph was struggling.
What did Manoj change after his mother's reminder?
He gave a clear small step, look ahead and not at the wheel, and held the seat while running.
How did Joseph feel when Manoj said it was so easy?
Joseph felt hurt and discouraged, his lip trembling, because nobody had explained how to balance.
Why does steam come out of a hot cup of tea?
Tiny drops of water are forming above the cup. Because the invisible vapour from the tea meets cooler air and turns back into small droplets we can see.

The first heavy rains had flooded the lane in Sehore, so Ujjwal and Nazia from next door were floating paper boats by the gate. Ujjwal's older brother, Utkarsh, came home from his chemistry exam soaked and didn't say hello.
"Bhaiya, look, my boat went all the way to—"
"Can you shut up for once?" Utkarsh shouted. "Always noise, noise!" He kicked the boats into the gutter and went inside.
Ujjwal stood very still. Nazia whispered, "What did you do?"
"Nothing," he said, and his voice came out tiny.
Later, Amma told him the exam had gone badly. Ujjwal nodded; he understood. But when Utkarsh passed him in the corridor that night without a word, it still stung, and Ujjwal wished he would just say sorry.

What were Ujjwal and Nazia doing by the gate?
Floating paper boats in the flooded lane.
What was Ujjwal feeling when Utkarsh shouted at him?
He felt confused and small, since he had done nothing, and his tiny voice shows how hurt he was.
What could Utkarsh do to repair things?
Once calmer, he could say sorry to Ujjwal and explain that the exam went badly, making clear the shouting was not Ujjwal's fault.
How does Nazia see the moment?
She is startled and assumes Ujjwal must have done something wrong, which shows how confusing the outburst looked from outside.

The power went out in the co-working space ten minutes before Vandana's pitch, and her laptop battery showed four percent.

She had one chance with Anirban, an angel investor who had flown in for the day. No slides now. She pulled out the printed order sheets from her millet-snack stall: 312 customers in six months, 140 of them buying again.

"I started with a stall outside a school," she said, holding up a packet. "Parents asked for less sugar, so I changed the recipe twice."

Anirban read the sheets by his phone torch. "Why haven't shops picked you up?"

"Two tried. I couldn't keep up with packaging."

He didn't invest. But he said, "Your repeat numbers are real. Fix supply, then call me."

Walking home in the rain, Vandana was disappointed and oddly light. She wrote "supply first" on her wrist in pen.

How many of Vandana's customers were buying again?
140 of the 312 customers were buying again.
How did Vandana feel after Anirban declined to invest?
Vandana was disappointed, but also oddly light, because his feedback told her exactly what to fix next.
What could Vandana do next, based on the pitch?
She could sort out packaging and supply so shops can stock her snacks, then go back to Anirban with those results.
How might Anirban see Vandana after the pitch without slides?
Anirban was impressed by her real customer numbers and her calm under pressure, even if the business was not ready for his money yet.

It was eleven at night and Akash's chemistry exam was at nine the next morning. His textbook lay open on the desk, unread. On his phone he was refreshing Jahnavi's profile for the fortieth time, looking at a photo of her at a friend's birthday, counting who stood beside her.

A power cut plunged the room into darkness and left only the glow of his screen. Somehow that made it worse. He felt a hollow, wild ache in his chest, and he could not stop.

He remembered his cousin's voice: "That's not love, that's pain looking for something to hold." Akash put the phone face down.

In the morning, after the exam, he walked to the college counselling room and sat down in the waiting chair. When his name was called, he said, "I can't stop watching her life. I need help."

His hands were shaking, but he stayed.

How many times had Akash refreshed Jahnavi's profile by the time the power cut came?
He was refreshing it for the fortieth time.
What was Akash feeling as he stared at Jahnavi's photo and could not stop?
A hollow, wild ache, meaning hurt and a sense of being stuck instead of clear love.
What did Akash do that was a good step, and why?
He put the phone down and went to the counselling room to ask for help, because obsessively watching her only kept the pain fresh.
How might Jahnavi see it if Akash kept monitoring her and later showed up?
She could feel watched and unsafe, and her life would be shaped by his hurt instead of her own choices.
She speaks very well English. Please fix the word order.

She speaks English very well.
Why: the object "English" stays next to the verb.

"Ding, ding, ding!" Chandrika rang the little brass bell far too hard, then folded her hands and bowed her head, eyes squeezed shut.
"Does she understand what she's doing?" asked her mother.
"She's doing what we do," said Rekha, her Dadi, smiling. "That's enough for now."
Chandrika opened one eye, peeked at Dadi's folded hands, and folded hers again, just the same.

What did Chandrika ring?
The little brass bell.
What was Chandrika feeling when she peeked at Dadi's hands?
She seemed happy and eager to do it the same way as Dadi, feeling part of the family ritual.
What did Rekha's answer help the mother see?
That at this age copying is how Chandrika joins in and belongs, not a matter of belief yet.
How might Rekha feel seeing Chandrika copy her?
She likely feels warm and proud to share the ritual with her granddaughter. 🙏

'You skipped lab again,' Eshaan said, sliding a cutting chai across the canteen table.
'Went home. Mummy needed help at the shop.' Charu didn't look up. 'It's fine.'
'That's the third Friday.'
'I said it's fine.'
Eshaan waited. The fan ticked overhead.
'The research internship form closes on Monday,' Charu said finally. 'Papa thinks I should come home after graduation and help run things. And I want to go to Pune for this. And I'm so tired of being the good one in both places.'
'That sounds exhausting.'
'Aren't you going to tell me what to do? Everyone else does.'
'Nope. I'll just ask: what do you want, if nobody's watching?'
Charu stirred the chai for a long time. 'I don't know yet. Can I think out loud at you for a bit?'
'Take all evening.'

When does the research internship form close?
The form closes on Monday.
What does Charu repeating 'It's fine' suggest?
It suggests Charu is worn out and dodging the topic, holding in stress about the pull from home and the internship.
What choice did Eshaan make when Charu asked to be told what to do?
Eshaan chose not to push either side and asked what Charu wants if nobody's watching, which gave Charu room to think out loud.
What is it like for Charu to be 'the good one' in both places?
It seems draining for Charu to keep meeting home's hopes while chasing the internship, with nowhere to simply be honest.

The two brothers, Harsha and Bhavesh, had one tablet between them and a fight every afternoon. "I've been playing for less time!" "No, you've had it for an hour!" Then Harsha had an idea. He fetched the kitchen timer from the shelf, a round white one that ticked. "Thirty minutes each. When it rings, the tablet moves." Bhavesh went first, watching the dial go round. When the bell rang he grumbled and handed it over. Harsha set the timer again. There was no argument about who had played longer, because the clock decided, and by evening their mother found them side by side, waiting for their turns.

How long did each brother get with the tablet?
Each brother got thirty minutes.
What was Harsha feeling when the fight about time kept happening?
Harsha was probably frustrated and tired of arguing, which led him to look for a fairer way with the timer. 😠
What alternative approach could the brothers use, and why?
They could pick a two-player game they both enjoy, or agree on days for each of them. Either way the fight over minutes would be gone.
How might Bhavesh see the timer?
Bhavesh grumbled when the bell rang, so Bhavesh probably found it fair but also disappointing to give the tablet up on time.

Wednesday. Chess club tournament today. I have practised knight moves every night for a month, even the boring puzzles Uncle printed for me. I won my first two games! Then I played Afreen. She is ten, one year younger than me, and I thought it would be easy. She trapped my queen in fifteen moves. I felt like knocking all the pieces off the board. My face was so hot. But I remembered what Sir says, 'Shake hands first, feel later.' So I said 'good game' through my teeth. It came out weird. Afreen said 'good game' back and showed me where I went wrong. Actually useful. Still annoyed. Practising queen safety tomorrow. — Zubin

How many moves did it take Afreen to trap Zubin's queen?
Afreen trapped Zubin's queen in fifteen moves.
How can you tell Zubin was angry after losing to Afreen?
Zubin's face was hot, Zubin felt like knocking the pieces off the board and said 'good game' through gritted teeth.
What did Zubin do right after the loss, even though it was hard?
Zubin followed Sir's rule, shook hands and listened to Afreen's tips, then planned to practise what went wrong.
How might Afreen see Zubin's 'good game'?
She may have noticed it sounded strained but still felt respected, since Zubin listened when she pointed out the mistake. 🙂

Jerry bought 48 firecrackers for the 4th of July. A police officer discovered and confiscated 12 of them. 1/6 of the remaining ones were defective. If Jerry set off half the good firecrackers, how many firecrackers did he set off?

First subtract the 12 confiscated firecrackers from the original number: 48 firecrackers - 12 firecrackers = 36 firecrackers
Then multiply this number by 1/6 to find how many were defective: 36 firecrackers * 1/6 = 6 firecrackers
Then subtract the defective firecrackers to find how many were good: 36 firecrackers - 6 firecrackers = 30 firecrackers
Then divide this number in half to find how many firecrackers Jerry set off: 30 firecrackers / 2 = 15 firecrackers
The answer is 15.

Annual Day Rehearsal
All students of Class 5 are informed that the annual day rehearsal will be held on Monday at 2 pm in the hall. Please be on time and bring your costumes if you have them. Everyone must attend.

The ducks in the pond are in two rows. The front row has 10 ducks and the back row has 6 ducks. How many ducks are there in all?

Answer: 16 ducks.

Count the front row: 1 to 10. Then keep going with the back row: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. Do not start again from 1 for the second row. The last number, 16, tells how many ducks in all.

Chinmay, you asked why I never told my brother he was wrong about his buses. Let me tell you what I watched. In 1998 my brother Mathew bought three old private buses for the Kottayam route with every rupee he had. The first year, one broke down every week. He said, 'Teething trouble.' The second year a new government route opened, and he said, 'People will come back.' Each time he lost money he spoke about the buses more proudly, and bought spare engines nobody needed. I was twenty-five, and I, Thomas, could see the pattern: the more he lost, the less he could bear to admit it. Shouting would only have made him dig in. So one evening I said, 'Mathew, you ran those buses longer than anyone could have. Sell two, keep one on the school route, and call it a win.' He sold two.

How many buses did Mathew buy?
Mathew bought three old private buses.
Why did Mathew speak more proudly of the buses after each loss?
Having put in every rupee, admitting the buses were failing would feel humiliating, so each loss pushed Mathew to defend them harder.
What made Thomas's suggestion work?
Thomas praised how long Mathew had kept the buses running and offered a way out, sell two, keep one, call it a win, so Mathew could change course without losing face.
How might Mathew have felt hearing 'call it a win'?
Mathew likely felt relieved to be offered a way out that kept his dignity, which is why he could finally sell two buses.
What is a congregation? I see the word on the church notice board.

A congregation is a group of people gathered for worship, in a church or another place of worship. It is a noun.
Example: The congregation stood and sang as the priest entered.

Francis, you asked how I got my parents to trust me. Honestly, at fourteen I didn't. I'm Vandana, and back then every argument was about time. When to be home, where I'd been, why my phone was off.
My mother said something once that stuck. “Trust is like savings. You add a little every time.”
So I started small. I told them where I was, even when they didn't ask. I came home ten minutes early. When I was late once, I called before, not after.
After six months, they let me stay out till nine for a friend's birthday. After a year, I could go to the city library alone.
I'm seventeen now. They still worry. But they trust me.

What did Vandana's mother compare trust to?
Savings.
How did Vandana feel about the arguments at fourteen?
Vandana felt frustrated and stuck in constant fights about time.
What approach helped Vandana earn more freedom?
Adding small bits of trust: saying where Vandana was going, coming home early and calling before being late.
How might Vandana's parents feel now?
They still worry, but feel more at ease trusting Vandana.

I'm Nitin, Pooja's older brother. This year, Pooja, twelve, changed.

Last year she did homework at midnight, crying. This year she made a timetable on the fridge: 5 to 6 homework, 6 to 6.30 play, 7 to 8 revision. She sticks to it, mostly.

Last month her friend offered to send her the answers for the science worksheet. I heard her on the phone: "No, I want to do it myself, or I won't know it for the test."

She got 16 out of 20 on the test. She seemed happy, but also said, "I lost marks on the diagram. I'll practise."

What time does Pooja do revision?
7 to 8 revision.
How did Pooja seem to feel after the test?
Pooja seemed happy, though determined to improve the diagram.
What study habits could Pooja keep building?
She could stick to her timetable, keep doing her own work, and practise weak areas like diagrams.
How does Nitin see Pooja's change?
Nitin noticed the change from last year and seems impressed by her discipline and honesty.

On the balcony of their small Mumbai flat, Nandini opened the notebook where she tracked their spending. "Vijay, can we look at this together? We keep running short by the twentieth." Vijay clutched his chest. "The twentieth! Our mortal enemy!" She smiled a little. "Seriously." "Seriously, I propose we move to a cave. No rent. Only bats." Nandini closed the notebook. It was the third time this month. Every time she raised money, he made her laugh, and every time the problem stayed in her lap. She felt dismissed and alone with it. "I love your jokes," she said. "But right now they feel like a door closing." Vijay went still. "Okay," he said. "Show me the notebook."

By which date do they keep running short?
The twentieth.
How did Nandini feel after the cave joke?
Dismissed and alone with the problem, since it was the third time that month.
What did Nandini say that changed things?
That she loves his jokes but right now they feel like a door closing, naming the effect without attacking him.
How might Vijay feel when Nandini says it?
Surprised and sobered, going still, then willing to look at the notebook.

This year I changed how I do homework, and it was my own idea. I used to start with the easy stuff, like colouring the map of India, and leave maths word problems for last. By then my eyes would be closing, and I'd read the same question five times. Now I eat my poha, drink some water, and open maths straight away while my head feels clear. You don't need a sharp brain to colour. Sarita, my elder sister, said, "Suraj, you're finishing before me now, bhai."

How many word problems did Suraj do yesterday?
Eight word problems about trains and tanks.
How did Suraj feel when he used to leave maths for last?
Suraj felt tired and frustrated, with eyes closing and reading the same question five times.
What could Suraj try on days when there's no map, only more hard work?
Still do the hardest task first and save anything routine, like neat copying, for the sleepy end of the evening.

On her first week as a trainee in the medical records department at the district hospital, Tanuja presented her idea for colour-coding patient files. Her supervisor, Manjula, listened with her pen tapping the desk. "Mm-hmm... mm-hmm." Then Tanuja got to the part about re-labelling the old files. Manjula went quiet and said, "Hmm." Just that. Tanuja's heart sank. She was sure it meant no. She almost said, "It's okay, forget it." Instead she asked, "Ma'am, is that a no-hmm or a thinking-hmm?" Manjula laughed. "A counting-hmm. There are about forty thousand old files. I was working out how long that would take. The idea's good for new files. Let's start there." Tanuja wrote it down, grinning. She realised she had nearly dropped a good idea over one syllable.

How many old files does Manjula estimate there are?
About forty thousand.
What was Tanuja feeling when Manjula said "Hmm"?
Her heart sank and she felt discouraged, sure it meant no; she nearly gave up the idea.
What did Tanuja do well when she heard the hmm?
Instead of dropping the idea, she asked directly whether it was a no or a thinking hmm.
What was Manjula actually doing when she said "Hmm"?
She was working out how long re-labelling forty thousand old files would take, so it was a counting, thinking sound, not disagreement.

I'm Vinita, and I sit next to Tejas in Class 5. In the first fractions test he got 4 out of 20. He looked at it for a long time. In the second test he got 6. Ma'am wrote "Practise more!" in red. After that, I noticed he stopped raising his hand in maths. He drew cars in the margin while we did adding fractions. On Monday Ma'am asked him to come to the board and find three-quarters of twelve. He stood there and said, "I'm just not a maths person. My brain doesn't do it." Everyone went quiet. He sat down with his ears red. At lunch he told me he isn't going to try anymore because it's no use. I don't think he's stupid. He's the best at building things in craft class.

What did Tejas get in the first fractions test?
He got 4 out of 20.
Why did Tejas decide trying was 'no use'?
Tejas felt discouraged and ashamed after failing test after test, ears going red at the board, so he concluded his brain just doesn't do maths and effort is pointless.
What small experience could help Tejas start trying again?
A teacher could give him fractions through something he's good at, like cutting shapes in craft, so he gets a few right and sees himself improve.
How does Vinita see Tejas differently from how he sees himself?
Vinita doesn't think he is stupid and notices he's the best at building things, while Tejas has decided he's 'not a maths person'.
What does sensible mean? I saw "very sensible of the honour" in an old novel.

Today, sensible is an adjective meaning practical and wise. In older English, "sensible of" meant aware of or feeling something, as in "sensible of the honour".
Example: Saving part of your pocket money is a sensible plan.
Why do students forget so much after a long holiday?
Memories fade when they are not used. Because every time we recall something the link in the brain gets stronger, and during a long break those links are not used, the details become harder to find.

The total number of books on four shelves, with 400 books each, is the same as the distance in miles that Karen bikes back to her home from the library. Calculate the total distance that Karen covers if she bikes from her home to the library and back.

If each shelf has 400 books, then the four shelves have 4*400 = 1600 books.
Since the total number of books on the shelves is the same as the distance that Karen bikes back home, biking to and from the library takes 1600+1600 = 3200 miles
The answer is 3200.
Could you write a diary entry, about 85 words, for a girl on her first aeroplane ride.

Dear Diary,
Today I flew in an aeroplane for the first time! At the airport, I stared at the big planes outside the glass. When ours began to run, my heart thumped. Then, suddenly, we were in the air, and the houses below looked like tiny toys. I saw the clouds from above, white and fluffy like mountains of cotton. The juice and snacks were also good. I did not want to land. I will fly again someday.

During free play, Omkar and Kamal were building a train track. Kamal ran out of curved pieces and his face fell; he began to walk away. Omkar held out two curved pieces from his own pile.
What was Omkar feeling when Kamal gave him the engine?
Omkar felt happy and warm, shown by his beaming smile and hug, because his friend shared back.

Keep praising sharing as it happens and pair friends like Omkar and Kamal on building tasks, as planned for Thursday.
How does Kamal see the moment Omkar offers the curved pieces?

My friend's father passed away. What should I write in message? I don't know English words for this.

You could write: "I'm so sorry about your father. I'm thinking of you and your family. If you need anything, I'm here." Keep it short and simple. Being there for your friend matters more than perfect words.

The rain had kept everyone inside the one-room flat for three days. When Gautam won the argument over the TV remote again, Ganga jumped up, stamped her foot so hard the steel glasses rattled, and headed for the door. Then she stopped. Outside was a wall of rain. There was nowhere to storm off to. Her fists shook. Maa pointed at the little balcony corner behind the curtain. “Your cooling spot. Ten slow breaths, then come back and say it.” Ganga pulled the curtain shut and watched the rain drip off the rail. Breath by breath, her shoulders dropped. She came back in. “Gautam, can we take turns every half hour?”

How long had the rain kept everyone inside?
The rain had kept everyone inside for three days.
What was Ganga feeling when her fists shook at the door?
She felt angry and trapped, with nowhere to storm off to in the rain.
Why did the cooling spot work even in a small flat?
It gave Ganga a place to step away and breathe, then return to talk, so her anger became a clear request.
What would the evening be like for Gautam if Ganga had kept stamping?
Gautam would probably have felt annoyed or defensive, and the fight over the remote would have gone on.

Read this:

At ten, Francis received a thick envelope of Diwali money from relatives and spent all of it in one afternoon on sweets and a toy. The next week, with his own pocket money down to ten rupees, he refused to spend even that on a pencil box. Payal, his older sister, noticed. "It's all just money, you know." Francis shrugged. "Gift money doesn't count."

At sixteen, he won a quiz voucher and used it up in a day on games, yet he guarded the cash he earned running errands for the neighbours, counting it twice before closing the tin.

At twenty, Francis got a bonus from his campus job and bought a pair of earbuds without a second thought. Walking home the same evening, he skipped the bus to save a couple of rupees. Seema, a flatmate, watched him arrive footsore. "You just spent the bonus on earbuds, and now you're walking to save a bus fare?" Francis laughed. "The bonus was extra."

What did Francis spend the Diwali money on?
Francis spent all of it in one afternoon on sweets and a toy.
What do the three stages show about how Francis treats money from different sources?

At ten gift money counted as free to spend while pocket money felt precious; at sixteen a quiz voucher went in a day while earned cash was guarded; at twenty a bonus was spent easily while a small bus fare was saved. Francis's mind sorts the same rupees into separate pots by where they came from.
What might Francis have been feeling when he said, "Gift money doesn't count"?
Francis probably felt carefree and a little defensive, sure the gift belonged to a different category from his own money.
How could Payal help her brother notice how he sorts money, without lecturing?
Payal could kindly point out that a rupee from a gift and a rupee from pocket money buy the same things, and ask Francis how he decides which feels spendable.

Hrithik joined Sarita's class in the small-town school in July. He came from a big city, wore shiny shoes, and answered every question. Sarita decided on the first day that he was a show-off.
But he took the same rattling bus from the village crossing every morning. He sat two seats in front. In class, he was put next to her for the geography project. At lunch he sat near the same water tap.
By September, Sarita realised she saved him a seat on the bus without thinking. She laughed at his jokes about the bumpy road. When he was absent for a week with fever, she kept looking at the empty seat.
She hadn't decided to like him. It had just happened, somewhere between the bus and the water tap.

When did Hrithik join Sarita's class?
He joined in July.
What was Sarita feeling when Hrithik was absent with fever?
Sarita felt a bit lonely and missed him, looking at his empty seat.
What could Sarita remember the next time she judges someone on the first day?
She could remember that people often feel friendlier after being around each other, so first-day judgements can change.
How might Hrithik have felt in his first weeks at the small-town school?
Hrithik may have felt out of place and eager to fit in, which could explain why he answered every question.

messages.content:
Read this:

It was late at the temple fair. Jeevan had missed his afternoon nap. He whined, rubbed his eyes and clung to Pranav's leg. When Pranav said no to a plastic whistle, Jeevan threw himself on the ground, screaming.
"Spoilt boy," muttered a relative.
"He's not spoilt, he's worn out," said Pranav, lifting him. By the time they reached the road home, Jeevan was asleep on his shoulder.

What had Jeevan missed?
His afternoon nap.
What was Jeevan feeling when he threw himself on the ground?
He was overtired and frustrated, not simply spoilt.
Which of Pranav's choices worked, and why?
Reading the meltdown as tiredness and carrying him home worked, because sleep was what he needed.
How does the relative see Jeevan's meltdown?
The relative sees it as spoilt behaviour, not tiredness.
We found a tiny kitten crying near our gate. Its mother isn't around.

Watch from a distance for a few hours first, because mother cats often leave kittens while they look for food. If she doesn't return and the kitten seems weak or cold, call a local animal rescue group for advice.
Can I give it some milk?
It's better not to give cow's milk, as it can upset a kitten's stomach. Keep the kitten warm in a box with a soft cloth, and ask the rescue group or a vet what to feed it.
Sam was supposed to come to my birthday and didn't show up.
I'm sorry. Being stood up on a special day hurts. Has Sam said anything since?
No, nothing.
Then a message might help clear things up. Keep it simple, like saying you missed Sam at the party and wondering what happened.
What if there's no good reason?
Then you can say how it made you feel and see how Sam responds. A good friend will apologise if they have let you down.
Should I still invite Sam next time?
That is up to you. If Sam apologises and explains, you might give another chance. If it keeps happening, you can choose to spend your birthday with people who show up.

The circle S: x^2 + y^2 - 6x - 4y - 12 = 0. a) Find its centre and radius. b) Find the power of P(10, 3) and of Q(3, 6), and say whether each point is inside or outside. c) Find the length of the tangent from P. d) A line through Q meets S at X and Y. Find QX x QY.

Now you try: the power of R(0, 0).
The answer is -12: inside.

Pallavi's site for Gulmohar Apartments had been running for a month: a notices page, a festival photos page, and a repair-request page she was proudest of. On Sunday she opened the simple visit counter. Notices: 340. Photos: 290. Repairs: 0.
Zero, in a building where the lift broke every other week.
She knocked on Minakshi Aunty's door on the third floor; Aunty handled repairs for the society. “Did anyone use the repair form?”
“What form?” Minakshi Aunty said. “People still ring my bell.”
Pallavi asked two more neighbours on the stairs. Neither had seen it. The link was tucked in a menu behind three lines in the corner, which most of the building's older residents never tapped.
That evening she put a big “Report a repair” box right on the home page. Two Sundays later the counter read 41, and Minakshi Aunty's bell rang a little less.

How many visits did the repairs page have on Sunday?
Repairs had zero visits.
How might Pallavi have felt seeing zero on the page she was proudest of?
Pallavi was probably surprised and disappointed, especially as the lift broke so often that people clearly had repairs to report.
What else could Pallavi do so that older residents use the form?
Put a printed notice by the lift about the box on the home page, or help a few residents try it once.
How does the change look to Minakshi Aunty?
For Minakshi Aunty, fewer bell rings and requests arriving in one place make the job easier.

Whilst he was speaking, Jonathan had taken my hand. I feared, oh so much, that the appalling nature of our danger was overcoming him when I saw his hand stretch out; but it was life to me to feel its touch--so strong, so self-reliant, so resolute. A brave man's hand can speak for itself; it does not even need a woman's love to hear its music.

What does the narrator feel when Jonathan takes the narrator's hand?

Fear that the awful danger is overcoming Jonathan gives way to relief at his touch, which is life itself: strong, self-reliant and sure. A brave man's hand needs no woman's love for its music to be heard.

Dear Kishore Sir,
I'm writing because I didn't say this yesterday at the team meeting.
When you moved me from striker to defence, I kept my face blank. I thought if I frowned, you'd think I was being disrespectful. But I could feel my forehead going tight the whole time, and I think you noticed, because you asked if I was okay and I said "fine."
I'm not fine with it. I've scored four goals this season, and I don't understand the change. I'm not trying to argue. I just want to know why, and whether I can earn the striker spot back.
Could we talk before practice on Thursday?
Thanks,
Vijay

According to the email, how many goals has Vijay scored this season?
Four goals.
What was Vijay feeling while keeping a blank face at the meeting?
Vijay felt upset and confused about the position change, but hid the frown to avoid seeming disrespectful.
Why is Vijay's email a better choice than the blank face?
It puts the disagreement into clear, respectful words and asks for a reason, which a tight forehead alone could not do.
How might Kishore Sir see the email?
Kishore Sir will likely see it as mature and respectful, and may be glad to explain the decision now that the feeling behind the blank face is clear.

Each shirt cost 20*.5=$10 with the sale
So he paid 10*6=$60

In the village house, Uncle Suraj shouted at Parveen, two, for spilling milk. Parveen froze, then sobbed, "Sorry, sorry."

Her grandmother stepped between them. "Enough, Suraj. Stop now." She picked Parveen up and hugged her. "Not your fault. You're safe."

That evening she spoke to the anganwadi worker about Suraj's temper, which was getting worse.

What did Parveen spill?
Parveen spilled milk.
What was Parveen feeling when she sobbed "Sorry, sorry"?
Parveen felt overwhelmed and frightened, and blamed herself for the shouting.
How did the grandmother protect Parveen?
She stopped Suraj, hugged Parveen and told her it wasn't her fault, then sought help from the anganwadi worker the same evening.
How might Suraj feel when his mother steps between them?
Suraj might feel surprised or embarrassed at being stopped.

“Mohit, did you start the case study?”
“Tomorrow, Jahnavi. Definitely tomorrow.”
“You said that on Monday.”
“And Tuesday. I know.” He dropped his head on the canteen table. “Every night I feel worse. Like I'm the worst person in the batch.”
“You're not.”
“Then why can't I just start?”
Jahnavi thought for a second. “What's the easiest bit?”
“I don't know. The company background, maybe. It's just copying facts.”
“Okay. Library, now. Twenty minutes. I'll sit with you and do my own reading. You only do the background.”
“Twenty minutes?”
“Twenty. Then you can stop, and I'll buy you a samosa.”
Mohit lifted his head. “You're bribing me.”
“I'm sitting with you. The samosa's a bonus.”
He stood up, slowly. “Fine. Twenty.”

What part of the case study did Mohit say was easiest?
He said the company background was easiest, just copying facts.
How did Jahnavi seem to feel about Mohit's repeated “tomorrow”?
Jahnavi seemed concerned and patient, wanting to help rather than scold.
Why is Jahnavi's offer a good countermeasure?
It shrinks the task to twenty minutes on the easiest piece, with company, making starting much less daunting.
How does Mohit feel about himself before Jahnavi's offer?
Mohit feels ashamed and discouraged, calling himself the worst person in the batch.
An old car can drive 8 miles in one hour. After 5 hours of constant driving, the car needs to get cooled down which takes 1 hour. How many miles can this car drive in 13 hours?

In 5 hours the car can drive 8 * 5 = 40 miles.
One cycle of driving and pause takes 5 + 1 = 6 hours.
In 13 hours this cycle can fit 13 / 6 = 2 full cycles with a remainder of 1 hour
Two cycles will last for 2 * 6 = 12 hours.
During two full cycles, the car will drive 40 * 2 = 80 miles.
So there is 13 - 12 = 1 remaining hour when the car can drive.
That means during 13 hours the car will be able to drive 80 + 8 = 88 miles.
The answer is 88.
Monkeys was jumping from one tree to other. Please correct the grammar.

Monkeys were jumping from one tree to another.
Why: "monkeys" takes "were"; "one tree to another".
Suresh is more intelligent than any boy in his class. Is this right?

Suresh is more intelligent than any other boy in his class.
Why: "any other" is needed; Suresh is also a boy in the class.

In the small college in Bagalkot, Jahnavi had been mentoring Tejas in spoken English and interview skills since June. Every week she gave him two things: a short article to read aloud and five practice questions to answer in writing.
In August he stopped doing them. Three weeks in a row, the notebook came back blank. Jahnavi felt a flicker of irritation, then decided to ask instead of assuming.
'Tejas, what's happening? No blame.'
He looked at the floor. 'Harvest season, akka. I'm in the fields with my father from six till college, and after college till dark. And the semester exams start in two weeks.'
Jahnavi hadn't known about the harvest at all. 'Okay. For the next two weeks, forget the articles. Just one practice question each week, and you can answer it aloud to me after class instead of writing.'
Tejas let out a breath. 'That I can do.'
After exams and harvest, the notebook started filling up again.

What did Jahnavi give Tejas every week?
A short article to read aloud and five practice questions to answer in writing.
How did Jahnavi feel when the notebook came back blank, and what did she choose?
She felt a flicker of irritation, but chose to ask why instead of assuming.
What could Jahnavi do to avoid a similar clash next year?
Ask Tejas at the start about harvest and exam times, and plan lighter weeks around them.
How does the lighter plan feel to Tejas?
Tejas feels relieved, letting out a breath, since one spoken question fits his harvest days.

messages.content: Take a = -2/3, b = 3/4 and c = -5/6. Check the commutative, associative and distributive properties with these numbers, and show that subtraction is not commutative.

Answer: a + b = b + a = 1/12; a x b = b x a = -1/2; (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) = -3/4; (a x b) x c = a x (b x c) = 5/12; a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c = 1/18; a - b = -17/12 but b - a = 17/12.

Work each side separately. a + b = -8/12 + 9/12 = 1/12, and b + a = 1/12 too. a x b = (-2/3) x (3/4) = -1/2 = b x a. (a + b) + c = 1/12 + (-10/12) = -9/12 = -3/4 and a + (b + c) = -2/3 + (-1/12) = -9/12 = -3/4. (a x b) x c = (-1/2) x (-5/6) = 5/12 and a x (b x c) = (-2/3) x (-5/8) = 5/12. Distributive: a x (b + c) = (-2/3) x (-1/12) = 1/18, and a x b + a x c = -1/2 + 5/9 = -9/18 + 10/18 = 1/18. But a - b = -17/12 and b - a = 17/12: they are additive inverses, not equal. Also 0 is the additive identity (a + 0 = a), 1 is the multiplicative identity, a + (-a) = 0 and a x (1/a) = 1. The distributive law helps mental work: (-3/7) x (14/15) + (-3/7) x (1/15) = (-3/7) x 1 = -3/7.

Jatin, stop snapping at your sister and listen to your Rukmini Paati. When I was nine, in our village music class, a boy named Selvam snapped his fingers all through the song. Snap, snap, snap. The teacher spun round and hit the desk with her ruler. “Are you calling me like a servant?” Selvam's face went grey. He whispered, “No, Teacher. It's how I keep the beat. My father keeps time that way for his drum students.” The teacher stopped. She asked him to snap again, slowly, while we sang. We all sang in time for the first time that year. After that she let him keep the beat, but never at people.

What was Selvam doing all through the song?
Selvam snapped his fingers all through the song.
What was Selvam feeling when his face went grey?
He felt frightened and shocked that his rhythm-keeping was taken as rudeness.
What choice did the teacher make after Selvam explained, and why did it matter?
She asked him to snap slowly while the class sang, which turned a misunderstanding into help with the beat.
How did the snapping first seem to the teacher?
To the teacher it seemed like calling her rudely, like calling a servant, until she heard it was keeping time.
Catriona has 8 goldfish in her aquarium. She has 4 more angelfish than goldfish. Also, she has twice as many guppies as angelfish. How many fish does Catriona have in her aquarium?

Catriona has 8 + 4 = 12 angelfish.
She also has 12 x 2 = 24 guppies.
Thus, she has 8 + 12 + 24 = 44 fish in her aquarium.
The answer is 44.

Supervisor's note, campus café, Friday
Pradeep, our weekend barista, spent most of his break today refreshing a sale page. Every few minutes his phone buzzed: "Flash price ends at 5!" "Only 3 left in your size!" He showed Kishore, who works the counter, a pair of running shoes. "I don't even run," he said, laughing, but his knee was bouncing and he kept glancing at the clock.
At 4:52 he paid. For about a minute he looked thrilled. By closing he was quiet, and asked Kishore whether shoes could be returned.
What I did next: I didn't lecture. I told him that our supplier sends the café "last chance" offers every week too, and we always wait a day before ordering. He laughed and said he'd look up the return policy tonight. I'll check in with him on Monday.

At what time did Pradeep pay for the shoes?
At 4:52 Pradeep paid.
What was Pradeep feeling during the break, and what cues show it?
Pradeep felt a restless rush of pressure; his knee was bouncing and he kept glancing at the clock while the sale messages buzzed.
Why might the supervisor's approach work better than a lecture?
Sharing the café's own habit of waiting a day on 'last chance' offers gave Pradeep a practical step without making him feel foolish.
How might Kishore see Pradeep's purchase by closing time?
Kishore would see the thrill fade into regret, since Pradeep went quiet and asked whether the shoes could be returned.

The family counselling centre had a fish tank, and Ira watched the fish instead of Tenzin.
The counsellor had asked Tenzin to describe an ordinary day. Tenzin spoke slowly. "I send Ira a photo when I reach work. I share my location. Ira checks my expenses every Sunday. I don't wear the blue kurta any more, because Ira said it looked like I was trying to impress someone. I stopped the pottery class."
Ira's face burned. "I do all that because I worry. The city isn't safe. Money goes so fast."
"What would happen," the counsellor asked Ira gently, "if Tenzin didn't send the photo one day?"
Ira meant to say I'd be worried. What came out was, "I'd feel like I was losing her."
The room went very quiet. Tenzin looked at Ira for the first time that hour.

What does Tenzin send Ira on reaching work?
Tenzin sends Ira a photo on reaching work.
What did Ira truly feel when asked about a missed photo?
Ira felt afraid of losing Tenzin; the words "I'd feel like I was losing her" came out instead of "worried".
What could Ira do after this honest moment in counselling?
Ira could keep working with the counsellor on the fear itself and start giving Tenzin back choices, like the pottery class and privacy with money and location.
What is it like for Tenzin to hear Ira's admission?
Tenzin looks at Ira for the first time that hour, perhaps surprised, and maybe a little hopeful, to hear the fear named instead of excused as worry.

Elizabeth read the message twice on the metro to college: a white van was taking children near schools, and it said forward to everyone you love. Her heart pounded. She sent it to the family group before the next station. By evening her aunt had phoned three neighbours and told the twin cousins not to walk to the park. Aparna, Elizabeth's cousin, texted privately: "Where did this come from? The photo looks old." Elizabeth's face went hot. She searched and found the same picture from another city years ago, with no local report at all. She deleted her forward, wrote "Sorry, I didn't check. Please ignore it," and phoned her aunt to explain.

When did Elizabeth send the message to the family group?
Elizabeth sent it before the next station.
Why did Elizabeth forward the message without checking?
Fear made it feel urgent; the pounding heart and the line about forwarding to everyone loved made Elizabeth act at once.
What could Elizabeth do before forwarding a shocking message next time?
Pause, check where it came from and whether any local report exists, and skip the forward if not.
How might Elizabeth's aunt have felt after phoning three neighbours?
Worried, and then perhaps embarrassed once Elizabeth explained, because the panic had already spread.

People at my office still call me the Imran who snapped. So let me tell it straight.

Two years ago, in a client review, I tore into Simran, a new analyst on my team. Her numbers had a mistake, and I said, loudly, "Did you even go to college?" She went red, packed her laptop and cried in the stairwell. I heard about it from someone else.

For weeks I replayed it. I told myself I was a bad person, full stop. That didn't help Simran one bit.

What helped was going to her, saying exactly what I'd done wrong, and asking what would make it right. She wanted me to correct the record with the client, so I did, in writing. I also started a rule for myself: feedback in private, always.

I still wince when I think of that day. But the wince now reminds me, instead of punishing me. That's the difference.

What did Imran say loudly in the client review?
Imran said, "Did you even go to college?"
What was Imran feeling in the weeks of replaying the moment?
Imran felt ashamed and guilty, stuck in harsh self-judgement that did nothing for Simran.
Which choice turned Imran's guilt into something useful?
Asking Simran what would make it right and then correcting the record with the client turned guilt into repair, and the private-feedback rule protected others in future.
What would Simran want from Imran if you were in her place?
In her place you would want a clear, specific apology and your reputation fixed with the client, not Imran's endless guilt.

"Vikas, you've sent me four articles on tech hiring cycles since Friday."
"Useful context. My layoff was part of a sector-wide correction. Twelve percent across mid-size firms."
"Mm. When did you last eat something that didn't come out of a vending machine?"

Sunaina pushed her plate of idlis across the café table toward him. "I'm not asking what the layoff means. I'm asking how it's sitting with you."
He looked at the idlis for a long moment. "Like I've been told I'm not needed."

How many articles had Vikas sent Sunaina since Friday?
Four articles on tech hiring cycles.
What was Vikas feeling underneath the talk of a 'sector-wide correction'?
He felt he had been told he's not needed; the numbers kept that hurt at a distance.
What turning point did Sunaina create, and why did it work?
She said she wasn't asking what the layoff meant but how it was sitting with him, which stopped the talk about markets and let him name the hurt.
What would change for Vikas if Sunaina had debated the twelve percent figure instead?

"Rehana, why are you standing there?" said Zainab, wiping her hands. "The tap is running," Rehana said. "Ammi's washing the pots and it's been running the whole time." "It's always like that." "Can we try a bucket? Then it won't run." Ammi looked over her shoulder. "In my mother's house we kept the tap open all day." "I know, Ammi. But our tank was empty last week, remember?" Rehana said softly. "I could hold the bucket for you." Ammi pursed her lips, then laughed. "All right, all right. Bring the bucket." Zainab smiled. "And can we stop burning the plastic in the yard? It smells so bad." "One thing at a time," said Ammi.

Where did Rehana suggest they use a bucket?
She suggested it for washing the pots, instead of leaving the tap running.
What is Rehana feeling as she stands watching the tap run?
She is uneasy about the waste, but she speaks softly so as not to shame her mother.
What went well in how Rehana raised the idea, and why?
She offered to hold the bucket and reminded Ammi about the empty tank without blaming her, so Ammi agreed with a laugh.
How might Ammi see Rehana's suggestion?
At first as a change from how her own mother did things, but she is willing after Rehana asks gently, and she pushes the next change to another day.

Week one. Farhan found out from the internship list. Pema, who had sworn she wasn't applying so they wouldn't compete, had got the only place. He deleted her number, then un-deleted it, then lay awake composing messages he didn't send.
Week three. He was still angry, but tired of it. It came up during exams, on walks, while brushing his teeth. His Nani, on the phone, said, "Anger is like carrying a hot stone, beta. It burns the hand that holds it."
Week six. He met Pema at the college gate. She said sorry, properly. He listened.
"I'm not angry anymore," he told her. "I've let that go. But I don't think I'll share my plans with you for a long time."
She looked hurt. "So you haven't forgiven me."
"I have. Forgiving you is for me. Trusting you again is a different thing, and that part will take time."

What did Farhan's Nani compare anger to?
Farhan's Nani said anger is like carrying a hot stone that burns the hand that holds it.
How did Farhan's feelings change between week one and week six?
Farhan moved from sleepless anger to weariness of carrying it, and finally to a calm decision to let the resentment go.
What turning point helped Farhan separate forgiving from trusting?
Realising in week three that the anger was burning him, as his Nani said, helped him forgive for his own sake while keeping trust for later.
How might Pema feel hearing that Farhan forgives her but won't share plans?
Pema looked hurt and may feel the forgiveness is incomplete, since she hoped things would go back to how they were.

"Where were you?" Danish's mother, Preeti, asked as the door opened. "At the park," said Danish. "With Sohail. We played cricket." "The park is fine. Which way did you come back?" Danish looked at his shoes. "The usual way." "The usual way, or through the market road?" No answer. "Danish. I told you the market road has trucks." "I told you the truth! I was at the park." Preeti sat down slowly. "You told me the truth about the park and left out the part that matters. That is still hiding something." Danish's ears turned pink. "Next time tell me the whole thing," she said, "and we will find a safe way to go together."

Which road had Preeti told Danish to avoid?
She had told him to avoid the market road.
What did Danish believe about what he told his mother?
He believed it was fine because what he said about the park was true, though looking at his shoes suggests some unease about the road.
What could Danish have said, and why would it help?
He could have told the whole route, including the market road, and asked for a safe way, because his mother could then help with the risk.
How might Preeti feel about the half-truth?
Worried about the trucks and hurt that the important part was left out, since she said it was still hiding something.

Two sentences, please: what is this passage about?

The building was of grey, lichen-blotched stone, with a high central portion and two curving wings, like the claws of a crab, thrown out on each side. In one of these wings the windows were broken and blocked with wooden boards, while the roof was partly caved in, a picture of ruin. The central portion was in little better repair, but the right-hand block was comparatively modern, and the blinds in the windows, with the blue smoke curling up from the chimneys, showed that this was where the family resided. Some scaffolding had been erected against the end wall, and the stone-work had been broken into, but there were no signs of any workmen at the moment of our visit. Holmes walked slowly up and down the ill-trimmed lawn and examined with deep attention the outsides of the windows.

The grey stone house has a tall middle and two curved wings, one of which is ruined and boarded up. The family lives in the newer right-hand part, and Holmes walks over the lawn studying the outside of the windows.

Given that sqrt3 and sqrt2 are irrational, prove that 2 + sqrt3 and 3sqrt2 are irrational. Then use the FTA to show that 6^n can never end in the digit 0, and that 7 x 11 x 13 + 13 and 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 + 5 are composite.

Answer: If 2 + sqrt3 or 3sqrt2 were rational, sqrt3 or sqrt2 would be rational. 6^n has no prime factor 5. 7 x 11 x 13 + 13 = 13 x 78 and 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 + 5 = 5 x 1009.

Suppose 2 + sqrt3 = a/b (a, b integers, b != 0). Then sqrt3 = a/b - 2 = (a - 2b)/b, a quotient of integers, so sqrt3 would be rational: a contradiction. So 2 + sqrt3 is irrational. Suppose 3sqrt2 = a/b; then sqrt2 = a/(3b), rational again: a contradiction. For 6^n: a number ending in 0 is divisible by 10 = 2 x 5, so 5 would appear in its prime factorisation. But 6^n = 2^n x 3^n, and by UNIQUENESS no other primes can appear, so 5 does not divide 6^n and 6^n never ends in 0. (The same holds for 4^n = 2^2^n, 12^n, 9^n, but not for 15^n x 2 or 20^n.) For the last part take out the common factor: 7 x 11 x 13 + 13 = 13 x (77 + 1) = 13 x 78 = 1014, and 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 + 5 = 5 x (7 x 6 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 + 1) = 5 x 1009 = 5045. Each has a factor other than 1 and itself, so each is composite.

Use (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2) to make a Pythagorean triple for each pair m, n. Write it in the order (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2).
a) m = 2, n = 1
b) m = 3, n = 1
c) m = 3, n = 2
d) m = 4, n = 1
e) m = 4, n = 2
f) m = 4, n = 3
g) m = 5, n = 1
h) m = 5, n = 2
i) m = 5, n = 3
j) m = 5, n = 4
k) m = 6, n = 1
l) m = 6, n = 5
m) m = 7, n = 2
n) m = 7, n = 4
o) m = 8, n = 1
p) m = 8, n = 3
q) m = 9, n = 2
r) m = 10, n = 1

Nursery note, Tuesday. A tray of steel plates crashed to the floor at snack time. Parveen, two, flung both arms out, froze with wide eyes and did not move or make a sound. I went to her, crouched and said “That was a loud noise. It's all right.” I lifted her onto my lap and rocked her slowly. Her body was stiff at first, then softer. After a while she looked at the tray and pointed. 🙂 Imran

What made Parveen freeze?
A tray of steel plates crashing to the floor at snack time.
Why did Parveen fling her arms out and freeze?
It was a reflex reaction to the sudden loud noise, not bad behaviour. She might also have been frightened by the sudden noise, which the wide eyes suggest.
What did Imran do that helped?
Imran came close, spoke in a calm voice, held her and rocked her until her body relaxed.
How might the other children have felt?
Some may have been startled too and looked to Imran to see whether things were safe.

Every lunch break, Mrs Kurian stood on duty near the art room steps, where she could see the whole playground. In June, Thomas and Chinmay still sat together with one sketchbook between them, drawing robots.
By August, Thomas had been picked for the under-eleven football team. Now at the bell he sprinted straight to the field, boots knocking against his bag. Chinmay went up the art room steps, where a group was painting a mural of the school garden.
Some days Thomas glanced at the steps before running off. Once Chinmay waved a paintbrush when Thomas scored a goal.
Mrs Kurian thought about calling them in for a talk, then didn't. There was no fight to fix. In the staffroom she told a colleague, "They haven't fallen out. They've just grown in different directions this term."

Which team was Thomas picked for?
Thomas was picked for the under-eleven football team.
What might Thomas's glance at the steps suggest he is thinking?
It suggests Thomas still thinks about Chinmay and may feel a small pull between the old friend and the new team.
Why was Mrs Kurian wise not to call them in for a talk?
No one had done anything wrong, so a talk might have made them feel they had failed; watching quietly lets the change happen naturally.
How might Chinmay feel about Thomas running to the field every day?
Chinmay may miss the robot drawings a little but also enjoys the mural group, and the paintbrush wave shows there is still warmth.

After choir practice Shalini caught Lalremsiami by the harmonium. "Your solo was amazing. Honestly the best thing I have ever heard in this school. You're a genius!" Lalremsiami said thanks and felt warm, and then Shalini added, "Can I copy your English notes tonight?" The warmth cooled a little. She thought about Mr Dutta, who had said the day before, "Your breath control on the long note has improved since August." That comment had named one thing and asked for nothing. "I can share the notes for one chapter," she said carefully. Shalini said, "Okay," cheerfully. Lalremsiami still didn't know for sure whether Shalini meant it. Perhaps she did, and had a request too.

Where did Shalini catch Lalremsiami?
She caught her by the harmonium after choir practice.
Why did Lalremsiami's warm feeling cool after Shalini's request?
She began to wonder if the big praise was leading up to the favour. She could not be sure, so she compared it with Mr Dutta's specific comment that asked for nothing.
What could Lalremsiami try next to understand Shalini's praise better?
Notice whether Shalini's praise stays specific and continues when she asks for nothing, and keep her own answer about the notes calm and clear.
How might Shalini see her own praise?
She may honestly admire the solo and simply feel comfortable asking for notes.
Kisi ne poocha kaise ho, maine bola "I am fine only." Wo hans pada.
In India "only" is often added for softness or emphasis, but elsewhere it sounds odd. Just say: "I'm fine, thanks."

Rain drummed on the roof, so games period moved into the crowded school hall, and the PE teacher was busy setting up mats. Tanvir sat alone by the wall again. The boys had told everyone not to let him play. Damini watched him pull at his shoelace. She thought about how the boys might tease her next. Then she walked over and sat beside him. "Come play with us," she said. "We need one more for dodgeball." Tanvir blinked. Slowly he stood up. Two other girls made room. Some boys smirked, but nobody said anything. After class, Damini went to the PE teacher and explained what had been happening for weeks. The teacher listened carefully and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'll deal with this today."

What game did Damini invite Tanvir to join?
She invited him to join dodgeball.
What was Damini worried about before walking over?
She was worried the boys might tease her next for siding with Tanvir.
Which of Damini's two actions mattered most, and why?
Both mattered: sitting beside Tanvir changed the group's mood right away, and telling the PE teacher meant an adult could stop it for good. 🙂
How might Tanvir feel standing up to play?
He probably felt surprised and relieved, finally not alone after weeks of being left out.

Read this:

I've sat next to Devika for three years, so I noticed when she stopped celebrating. She got the senior analyst title in March, the one she'd wanted since college, and by April she was staring at the ceiling fan during lunch. One evening she said, "Manjula, I got everything on my list. Why do I feel like nothing?" I honestly didn't know what to say. Maybe she's just tired, or maybe it's bigger. Then she started staying back on Thursdays to teach two interns spreadsheets, and she came in looking lighter. She also phoned her old school teacher. I can't say what's going on in her head, but she seems to be looking for something other than titles.

What title did Devika get in March?
She got the senior analyst title in March.
What was Devika wondering when she asked why she felt like nothing?
She was wondering what it was all for, since she had ticked off everything on her list and still felt empty.
What small commitments could help Devika find meaning?
Keeping up things like teaching the interns and staying in touch with her old school teacher, small ongoing commitments to people and craft.
How sure can Manjula be about Devika's inner state?
Not sure at all. Manjula says it might be tiredness or something bigger, and only reports what was seen, such as the teaching and the phone call.
Why do the bottoms of cooking pots often turn black over a gas flame?
Soot sticks to them. Because the flame does not burn all the fuel perfectly, and tiny bits of unburnt carbon settle on the cool pot.

Quick question about the following text.

"The Gandharva continued, 'Thus addressed by Pulastya, as also by the intelligent Vasishtha, that mighty Muni--the son of Saktri then brought that sacrifice to an end. And the Rishi cast the fire that he had ignited for the purpose of the Rakshasas' sacrifice into the deep woods on the north of the Himavat. And that fire may be seen to this day consuming Rakshasas and trees and stones in all seasons.'"

What does the Muni do with the fire kindled for the sacrifice?

After Pulastya and Vasishtha speak, the son of Saktri ends the sacrifice and casts the fire into the deep woods north of the Himavat. It may be seen to this day consuming Rakshasas, trees and stones in all seasons.

Read this:

Amandeep had rewritten his Hindi essay twice, once at the dining table and once on the balcony of their Pune flat while the pressure cooker whistled. He handed it in on Monday, a day early. On Thursday the essays came back. Mrs Rao read three aloud and praised their opening lines. Amandeep's had a big tick and nothing else. Then, when his phone buzzed in his bag during the last period, she stopped the class. "Some people never change," she said, looking straight at him. "Trouble from day one." Chandrika turned around and mouthed, "Yours was good, I read it." Amandeep nodded, but his ears were hot. At home he pushed the essay into the back of a drawer without showing anyone.

When did Amandeep hand in his Hindi essay?
He handed it in on Monday, a day early.
What do Amandeep's hot ears and hidden essay suggest he feels?
They suggest he feels embarrassed and unseen, since his careful essay got only a tick while one buzzing phone drew a public comment.
What could Amandeep do so his effort gets seen?
He could show the essay to someone at home, or ask Mrs Rao privately for feedback on it, so the work is looked at apart from the label.
What would change if Mrs Rao read Amandeep's essay without her old picture of him?
She might notice the rewriting, praise it like the others, and treat the buzzing phone as a small slip rather than proof.

Read this:

In Harsha's village near Hassan, the whole family gathered for their baby's naming ceremony. Harsha, twenty-six, and his wife Parveen had spent weeks deciding what to keep. From his side: his grandmother's Kannada lullaby, the mango-leaf toran on the door, the feast on banana leaves. From hers: the whisper of the azaan in the baby's ear, which her father did with shaking hands, and her mother's sheer khurma. What they left out: the gold demands his aunt had hinted at, and the old rule that only boys get the family sword.
Some relatives muttered. Harsha's uncle asked why there was no priest. Harsha answered calmly, "We kept what feels like love, maama." Parveen's mother held the baby while Harsha's grandmother sang. Both old women were crying. Later, Harsha wrote the lullaby's words in a notebook for his daughter.

What did Harsha and Parveen keep from Harsha's side?
His grandmother's Kannada lullaby, the mango-leaf toran on the door and the feast on banana leaves.
How did Harsha feel when his uncle asked about the priest?
Harsha felt steady and calm, confident in the choices they had made together.
What made the couple's choices wise?
They picked customs that carried warmth from both families and left out ones that caused pressure or unfairness, like gold demands and a boys-only sword.
How might the two grandmothers have experienced the ceremony?
They probably felt deeply moved and honoured, seeing their own traditions held with love, which is why both were crying.

Read this:

Asif: bro u up
Uday: ya what's up
Asif: scan today. heartbeat. I cried in the car park
Uday: congrats!! big day
Asif: yeah. and now I can't breathe. rent, her leave, my job is shaky
Asif: plus I'm never going to see a football match again am I
Uday: haha. have u told Nazia any of this?
Asif: no. she's got enough on her plate. I'm supposed to be the strong one
Uday: being strong isn't the same as being silent. she probably thinks ur distant
Asif: she did ask why I've been so quiet
Uday: tell her. then we'll work out match nights. babies sleep sometimes 🙂
Asif: ok. telling her tonight

What did Asif hear at the scan?
The heartbeat.
What was Asif feeling after the scan?
He felt proud and moved, crying in the car park, but then anxious about rent, Nazia's leave and his job.
What does Uday advise, and why is it wise?
To tell Nazia, because being strong isn't the same as being silent, and sharing stops him seeming distant.
How might Nazia see Asif's quietness?
She may read it as distance and feel unsure, which is why she asked why he had been so quiet.
Please explain anxiety in simple words.

Anxiety is a worried, uneasy feeling about something that might happen. It is a noun.
Example: He felt some anxiety before his first day at the new school.

Read this:

Afreen typed, "Write a poem about rain," and the assistant produced eight neat lines in seconds. She gasped. "It's like magic!" she told her father, Kamal. Then she asked how tall the tallest tree is and copied the confident answer straight into her science page. The next day a classmate showed her a book with a different number. Afreen's cheeks warmed; she had believed it only because it sounded so sure. From then on she checked important facts in a book too. Kamal, who had seen her typing late, asked, "Can I see what you're chatting about?" Afreen felt watched and stiffened, but she turned the screen and explained she used it for poems and facts. They agreed on a rule: chats only at the kitchen table, with the door open. When Ms. Amandeep asked whether anyone had used an AI for the poem project, Afreen's mouth went dry and part of her wanted to say no. Instead she said, "I asked it for an idea, then wrote my own lines about my grandmother's kitchen in the monsoon." Ms. Amandeep smiled, read the lines and suggested a stronger last line, which Afreen wrote herself.

How many lines did the assistant write for the rain poem?
It produced eight neat lines.
How did Afreen's early trust in the assistant differ from what she did after her classmate showed her the book?

At first she believed the confident answer about the tallest tree and copied it, but after the book showed a different number she checked important facts in a book too, learning that a sure-sounding answer can be wrong.
What was Afreen feeling when her mouth went dry as the teacher asked about AI?
She felt nervous and tempted to say no, worried about what the teacher would think.
What could Afreen do next to keep her poems her own?
She could use the assistant only for ideas, write her own lines from her own memories and keep telling her teacher how she used it.
My manager wrote "Send it ASAP". How is "ASAP" read, and is it rude?

It stands for "as soon as possible" and is read letter by letter, or sometimes as "ay-sap". It is common in work messages but can sound pushy, so a polite request such as "Could you send it as soon as possible, please?" is gentler.
Example: Could you please send the report as soon as possible?

David is taking a data analytics course that lasts for 24 weeks. The course consists of 2 three-hour classes and 1 four-hour class each week. In addition, David must spend 4 hours each week working on small group homework assignments. How many hours will he spend on this course?

Each week, David will spend 3 hours + 3 hours + 4 hours = 10 hours in class.
Add to that his 4 hours of small group work, 4 + 10 = 14 hours a week.
He will spend 14 hours x 24 weeks = 336 hours on the course.
The answer is 336.
What is the fourth word on page 112 of my school reader?
I can't see your book, so I don't know. Open it to page 112 and count along the line.
What is the name of my manager's manager?
I don't know that name, because I don't have your workplace details. Your company directory or an HR contact can help.

On his first morning at school in Brisbane, Liam hugged his mum at the gate, the way he always had in Dublin. Behind him, a boy snorted. In class, his new friend Paulo leaned over. "Here, nobody hugs at the gate. You just do a wave, like this." Paulo flicked two fingers. Liam watched for the rest of the day. Everyone wore their hat backwards at lunch, and nobody sat on the top bench. The next morning, Liam gave his mum a small wave at the gate. She looked surprised. On the way in, Paulo nodded at him.

What did Paulo tell Liam people do instead of hugging at the gate?
A wave, flicking two fingers.
What was Liam feeling when the boy snorted?
He was probably embarrassed and self-conscious about doing something different.
How could Liam's mum support him with the change?
She could agree on a private goodbye at home, so he can wave at the gate without losing the hug.
How might Liam's mum feel about the small wave?
She might feel surprised and a little sad, missing the hug even if she understands.

The power had gone at five, and the whole society poured downstairs to escape the heat. There was only one lit patch, under the generator lamp near Tower B.
Baljeet and the other kids from Tower D came with a tennis ball.
Ojas stood in the middle of the lit patch. “No D-wing kids. You lot are wild, you break everything, you're like monkeys.” His friends nodded.
Baljeet said, “There's no other light.”
“Not our problem,” Ojas said, and bounced the ball hard off Baljeet's shoulder. It stung. The D-wing kids went and sat in the dark near the gate.
Ojas's mother had seen the ball hit. She came over and said, calmly, “Would you bounce a ball off Baljeet's shoulder if you didn't call him a monkey first?”
Ojas started to answer, then couldn't. The word had made it feel allowed.

Where was the only lit patch during the power cut?
It was under the generator lamp near Tower B.
Why did bouncing the ball off Baljeet's shoulder feel allowed to Ojas?
Calling the D-wing kids wild monkeys made Ojas feel they didn't count as real children, so hurting them felt less wrong.
Which part of the mother's response helped Ojas see it?
She stayed calm and asked a question that connected the label to the hurt, letting Ojas see it for himself.
What is it like for the D-wing kids to sit in the dark near the gate?
They feel rejected and left out, stuck in the heat and the dark while being called monkeys by a neighbour.

Come, Dhruv, sit with your old uncle. You're worried about telling your parents no? Let me tell you about my own.
In 1998 my Abba found me a match in Aligarh. Everything settled in his mind. I was twenty-six and I knew it was wrong for me, because she and I had nothing to say to each other.
My first instinct was to shout. My elder brother had done that the year before, and the house was cold for months. So I did it differently. I said, "Abba, give me a week to think." Then, after that week, I sat beside him and said, "She is a good person, but we are not a good pair. I'd like you to meet the family I know in Rampur instead."
He refused twice. I repeated myself twice, calmly. The third time, he said, "Show me this Rampur family."
Wasim Chacha is telling you, Dhruv: calm and kind wins more than loud.

What did Wasim ask his Abba for first?
Wasim said, "Abba, give me a week to think."
Why did Wasim choose not to shout?
He remembered how cold the house was for months after his elder brother shouted, so he was wary of a fight and hoped a calm approach would work better.
What was the turning point inside Wasim's story?
The turning point came when, after taking a week, he gave a reason and offered the Rampur family as an alternative, and then calmly repeated himself until his Abba agreed to look.
How might Wasim's Abba have seen his son's calm repeating?
At first Abba refused, but hearing the same calm respect three times probably made him feel his son was serious and not defying him, so he became open to it.

"You look like the ceiling fell on you," Vishal said at the office pantry.
Joseph pressed his temples. "Headache. Again. This job is draining the life out of me."
"What have you had today?"
"Coffee at nine, tea at eleven, tea after lunch, another coffee now."
"And water?"
Joseph blinked. "Does the water in the tea count?"
"Not really. When I lived on tea, I got the same headaches and snapped at everyone. I started keeping a bottle on my desk."
"You think that's it? Not the job?"
"Maybe both. Try it this week and see."
Joseph filled a bottle at the cooler. "If the headaches keep coming, I'll check with a doctor too."
"Good plan."

Where were Joseph and Vishal talking?
At the office pantry.
What did Joseph believe was causing the headaches, and how did he feel about it?
He blamed the job and felt drained and fed up, as if it was taking the life out of him.
Which choice is sensible here, and why?
Keeping water on the desk this week while seeing a doctor if the headaches keep coming, because it tests a simple cause without ignoring a real one.
How does Vishal see Joseph's complaint?
Vishal recognises the pattern from living on tea and gently suggests water, without dismissing that the job may also be hard.

My team lead asked everyone to send a weekly update, and I never know what to write.
A weekly update can be short. Think in three parts: what you finished, what you're working on and anything you need help with.
What if I finished almost nothing?
Then be honest and say what you worked on, even if it isn't done. For example, 'I made progress on the report and will finish it by Tuesday.'

In their small town near Pala, everyone knew Thomas had topped the district exams. At cricket, the boys called him "Professor," not kindly. So in class he started leaving easy questions blank, hoping to seem normal. At home he redid every test paper, terrified that a single 98 would mean he was slipping. He felt alone in both places. Vidya Teacher, who ran the town library's evening astronomy group, stopped him one day. "Come on Saturday. Four others your age are building a telescope." He went. They argued about moons till nine at night, and nobody called him Professor. Walking home, Vidya said, "You know you're allowed a B sometimes?" Thomas laughed, and something in his chest let go.

What did the boys at cricket call Thomas?
They called him "Professor," not kindly.
How did Thomas feel about his results before joining the astronomy group?
He felt terrified and alone, worried a single 98 meant he was slipping, while also hiding his ability to fit in.
What helped ease the strain on Thomas?
Meeting like-minded peers in the astronomy group and hearing from a mentor that he was allowed a B sometimes.
How does Vidya seem to see Thomas?
She sees a bright boy who is lonely and under too much pressure, and wants him to have friends and room to be ordinary.

Read this:

For two weeks Sharmila had kept her eyes on her notebook while Tanmay and his two friends whispered "Chashmish" behind her in class. Ignoring it was supposed to work. Instead the whispers got louder, and on Friday her pencil box went missing. That evening Sharmila sat on her bed and counted: two weeks, no change. New plan. She told her parents everything, in order. Her father listened, her mother wrote down the dates, and on Monday both went to see the class teacher. By Wednesday the seating had been rearranged, Tanmay's group sat near the front, and the teacher's eyes kept passing over that corner. Sharmila still felt shaky, but the whispers had gone quiet.

What changed at school after Sharmila's parents met the teacher?
The seating was rearranged, and the teacher's eyes kept passing over the corner where Tanmay's group sat.
What was Sharmila feeling when she counted the days on her bed?
Frustrated and worn down, because two weeks of ignoring had brought no change and she decided she needed a new plan.
What could Sharmila do if the whispering started again in the corridor?
Tell her class teacher or her parents straight away with the details, because they already know the situation and can extend the watching.
How might Sharmila's parents have felt when she told them everything?
Probably worried, but glad she told them, since they listened, wrote down the dates and both went to school on Monday.
