Read this:

I'm Pooja. Varun sits next to me. For two weeks he's been saying he doesn't want to go to his extra swimming lesson. He picks at his nails and goes quiet when anyone says "swimming".
Today at break I asked him why. He looked around and whispered that the coach says it's their secret and touches him where his swimsuit covers. He said, "Don't tell."
I said, "This isn't a secret you should keep." I went with him straight to our class teacher.
She listened, told Varun it was not his fault, and took us both to the principal's office. The principal called Varun's parents right away and said the coach would not see any students.

Where does Varun say the coach touches him?
Where his swimsuit covers.
What does Varun picking at his nails suggest?
Varun seems anxious and upset about the swimming lessons.
What did Pooja do that was right?
She told Varun this is not a secret to keep and took him straight to a trusted adult that same day.
What would change if Pooja had kept Varun's secret as he asked?
Varun would stay alone with the problem and could keep being harmed, because no adult would know to protect him.

Read this:

I'm Rashmi. Last month our team at the architecture firm won a design award for the new library in Kochi. At the ceremony, they called my name first, as project lead.

I had a speech ready that thanked "the team" in one line. Then, backstage, I crossed it out.

What I actually said was this. The core layout was my idea, and I'm proud of it. We were lucky: the site had old trees that gave the building its shape, and that was nature, not me. Wasim solved the ventilation problem that I had got completely wrong in the first draft. Without him, the reading hall would have been an oven.

People clapped. Wasim looked at the floor, then smiled.

Afterwards, my boss said, "That's the first speech I've heard that sounded true."

I think naming the luck and my mistake made people believe the credit I did take.

Which building did Rashmi's team design?
The new library in Kochi.
How did Wasim seem to feel when Rashmi named his work?
Wasim looked shy and then pleased, looking at the floor and then smiling.
Why did Rashmi's honest speech build trust?
Naming Rashmi's own idea alongside the luck, Wasim's fix and Rashmi's mistake made the credit believable and fair.
How might the rest of the team see Rashmi's speech?
The team would likely feel respected and more willing to work hard on the next project.

Archer caught eight fish from the lake to sell in the market. When he reached the market, he sold the fish faster than he had anticipated and decided to go back to the lake and catch more fish. He caught 12 more fish in the second round than he had caught earlier. The demand was even greater, and he had to close the day by catching 60% more fish than the number he had caught in the second round and sold all of them in the market. How many fish did he catch that day?

He caught 12 more fish in the second round than he had caught earlier, a total of 12+8=20 fish.
The total number of fish he caught in the two rounds is 20+8=28
In the third round, Archer caught 60/100*20=12 fish which were 60% more fish than the number he had caught in the second round.
This means he caught a total of 12+20 = 32 fish
Archer caught a total of 28+32=60 fish on that day.
The answer is 60.

Ken had fifty pencils, and he wanted to share some of them with his two friends, Manny and Nilo. Ken gave ten pencils to Manny and ten more pencils to Nilo than he gave to Manny. He kept the rest of the pencils. How many pencils did Ken keep?

Nilo received 10 + 10 = 20.
Thus, Ken gave a total of 10 + 20 = 30.
Therefore, Ken kept 50 - 30 = 20 pencils.
The answer is 20.

Read this:

The client in Gothenburg called Anders at 8:15, asking why they had never received the Friday update.
Anders turned to Hiroshi. "You said you sent it."
Hiroshi had. On Friday afternoon he'd said, "Done, sent." He'd meant to send it after the gym. He'd forgotten.
His first thought was the spam folder. His second was, you never reminded me. He could feel both on his tongue.
He swallowed them.
"I didn't send it. I told you I had because I wanted to leave on time, and I thought I'd do it in the evening. I forgot. That's on me."
Anders let out a breath. "The client thinks we're hiding something."
"I'll call them now, tell them it was my mistake and send it within the hour. And from now on, I'll forward you the sent email instead of just saying it's done."
Anders nodded. "Okay. It'll take a while before I stop checking."
"That's fair."

When did the client call Anders?
The client called Anders at 8:15.
Which excuses was Hiroshi tempted to use, and why did he hold them back?
Hiroshi was tempted to blame the spam folder or Anders for not reminding him, but he swallowed them because the lie was his own and blaming would delay repair.
What steps did Hiroshi offer to repair the damage?
He admitted exactly what was false and why, offered to call the client and send the update within the hour, and promised to forward sent emails in future.
How does Anders feel about trusting Hiroshi again?
Anders is willing to move on but honest that trust will take time, saying it will be a while before Anders stops checking.
Now you try: which solid has 1 flat face, 1 curved surface and 1 apex?
The answer is cone.

People ask what the hardest part of being a new manager is. For me it was a Tuesday in March, telling Vasudha her contract wouldn't be renewed. She'd been on my team eight months and I liked her.
My instinct was to rush. Get it out in one breath, "sorry, budget, not my call," and escape. I'd practised it that way in my head, and it sounded awful. Cold.
So I slowed down on purpose. I said her name. I said, "I have difficult news." Then I stopped. Then: "Your contract won't be renewed after June." Short sentences. Space between them. When her eyes filled, I didn't fill the silence.
She asked why, and I explained slowly, twice, because the first time she didn't take it in. Then I said, "I'll write you a strong reference, and we'll talk about next steps tomorrow."
Afterwards she said, "Thank you for not rushing, Afreen." I still remember that.

How long had Vasudha been on the team?
She'd been on the team eight months.
What was Afreen feeling before the conversation?
Afreen felt anxious and reluctant, with an urge to rush the news out and escape, partly from liking Vasudha.
What choices made the hard news easier to take in?
Slow, short sentences with pauses, saying the news plainly, not filling the silence, explaining the reason twice, and offering a reference and next steps.
How did Vasudha experience the slow delivery?
It gave Vasudha time to take in the news; she needed the reason twice and later thanked Afreen for not rushing.

The bad review of Reena's homestay near Munnar had been shared around a travel group, and by Tuesday evening her phone buzzed every few minutes. She had stopped eating properly. She checked the booking page's rating after every buzz: 4.6, then 4.5.
Abhinav, her husband, found her on the verandah at midnight, the phone's glow on her face. 'Enough,' he said gently.
She thought about it. The guest had a fair point about the hot water, and she had already replied and fixed the geyser. Everything since was strangers piling on. 'In a week they'll be onto someone else,' she said slowly. 'The rating isn't who I am.'
She switched off notifications for two days and let Abhinav check the page once each evening. The next morning she made appams for the guests and walked to the tea gardens with her mother.

What did Reena switch off for two days?
Notifications.
What does Reena checking the rating after every buzz suggest?
It suggests she was anxious and hurt, letting a number decide her mood.
What else could help Reena through the next few days?
Keeping her routines with guests and family, and letting Abhinav check the page only once each evening, as she decided.
How might Abhinav experience these days?
Abhinav is worried to see her not eating, and likely relieved when she hands over the checking and goes for a walk.

What is this brief extract getting at? Two sentences, please.

It was in the latter end of September that I again quitted my native country. My journey had been my own suggestion, and Elizabeth therefore acquiesced, but she was filled with disquiet at the idea of my suffering, away from her, the inroads of misery and grief. It had been her care which provided me a companion in Clerval—and yet a man is blind to a thousand minute circumstances which call forth a woman's sedulous attention. She longed to bid me hasten my return; a thousand conflicting emotions rendered her mute as she bade me a tearful, silent farewell.

Indu was at her desk in Bengaluru when the message came, the first in two years: "Can you call? Aparna."
Not Amma. Aparna. Her mother had always signed that way when she was being formal.
Indu called from the stairwell.
"I had a fall," her mother said. "Only a small one. But lying on the floor, waiting for the neighbour, I thought: two years. Two years I've let pass." A pause. "I don't like who I've become about this."
Indu leaned against the wall. She had imagined this call a hundred ways, most of them angry.
"I'm glad you're okay," she said, and found that it was true.

Where did Indu take the call?
In the stairwell.
What might Indu have been feeling as she leaned against the wall?
She seems shaken and surprised, having expected anger, and she finds herself relieved and glad her mother is okay.
What small step could Indu take after this call?
Agree to talk again soon, keeping it short and gentle, without trying to settle everything at once.
What is Aparna experiencing after her fall?
She feels frightened and regretful, realising how much time has passed and disliking who she has become about the break.

Matt and Blake want to watch every episode of the show The Office. There are 201 episodes. If they watch 1 episode every Monday and 2 episodes every Wednesday each week, how many weeks will it take them to watch the whole series?

Each week, they watch 1 Monday + 2 Wednesday episodes = 3 episodes a week.
If you take 201 total episodes / 3 episodes each week = 67 weeks to watch The Office series.
The answer is 67.

"Jahnavi, can I ask something?" Rafiq said, walking beside her to school. "Sure." "Why do you always wear a dupatta? Does your family make you?" "Some days it's Amma's rule," Jahnavi said. "Some days it feels like me. Today it just matched my kurta." She grinned. "You're not the first to guess." "Sorry. I assumed." "Everyone does. My cousin wears hers for prayer, my friend Sana never wears one, and neither of us is wrong." "So you can't tell from looking." "Exactly. You'd have to ask, and listen." Rafiq laughed, embarrassed. "Okay. I'm listening. 😅"

Who asked Jahnavi about the dupatta?
Rafiq asked her, while they were walking to school.
What was Rafiq feeling after Jahnavi answered?
He felt a little embarrassed and sorry for assuming, as his apology and laugh show, and probably some curiosity too. 😅

He could ask an open, friendly question and really listen, accepting that the same item can be faith, family expectation, choice or style.

Somewhat tired of being assumed about, as 'Everyone does' hints, yet she stays friendly and explains patiently.

At Dadaji's flat, Anand hung back by the door.
“Anand, greet Dadaji,” said Disha, his mother.
“Do I have to touch his feet?”
“Only if you want to. You can also fold your hands and say namaste.”
Dadaji chuckled from his chair. “A warm hello is enough, beta. Come here.”
Anand looked at the floor, then walked over and bent to touch Dadaji's feet. Dadaji put a hand lightly on his head. “Blessings. How is school?”
“Good,” said Anand, smiling. “I got a star.”

Who told Anand he could fold his hands instead of touching feet?
Disha, his mother, told him he could fold his hands and say namaste.
What might Anand have felt when he hung back and asked if he had to touch feet, and what else could it be?
Probably shy or unsure about the custom, and perhaps a little pressured. He might also just have been nervous about meeting Dadaji.
How did the adults respond in a way that respects the child?
Disha and Dadaji made it a choice, saying a warm hello is enough, so Anand touched the feet by his own decision.
How might Dadaji see the touching of his feet?
As a mark of respect and a chance to bless his grandchild, and he also said a warm hello would do, so he did not seem to demand it.

Every morning at the Andheri office, Kashish checked two things before logging in: the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat. A cheerful "Morning, team!" meant she could ask for the leave she needed. A bare "Status?" meant keep your head down. Six months in, she had learned to rewrite her reports so the bad numbers sat at the bottom, softened. In meetings she waited to see which way Sachin leaned, then agreed. When he called her idea for the client deck "cute", she laughed along and deleted the slide. At home her flatmate asked what she thought about the new project. Kashish opened her mouth and found she didn't know anymore; she only knew what Sachin thought.

What two things did Kashish check every morning before logging in?
Kashish checked the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat.
What does Kashish's blank moment with her flatmate show about how she feels?
It shows Kashish has muted her own voice so long that she feels unsure of her own opinion and only knows Sachin's.
What small choice could help Kashish get her own view back?
Kashish could write down her own opinion before each meeting and keep one honest line about the bad numbers near the top of her reports.
How might Sachin see Kashish, compared with what she actually thinks?
Sachin probably sees an agreeable employee with no objections, not knowing her real ideas and doubts are hidden to please him.

Alejandro used to drive Liam to football every Saturday, the two of them singing badly to old Spanish songs. This autumn Liam asked to be dropped a street away from the pitch. At home he answered in grunts, spent evenings behind a closed door, and once said, "Can you not come to the match? It's embarrassing." Alejandro laughed it off, then sat in the car in the dark driveway for twenty minutes, stung. On the phone, his sister reminded him what he'd been like at fourteen. So he stopped asking about the match. He kept the Saturday drive, a street away, and left the radio on their old station without comment. In November, stuck in traffic, Liam started humming along. Then he said, "Dad, can I ask you something about a friend?" Alejandro turned the music down and kept his eyes on the road.

Where did Liam ask to be dropped?
A street away from the pitch.
What was Alejandro feeling in the dark driveway?
He felt stung and rejected after Liam called his coming to the match embarrassing.
What did Alejandro do that kept the door open?
He stopped pushing about the match but kept the Saturday drive and the old radio station, staying available without pressure.
How might Liam see his dad at the match?
Liam may feel embarrassed in front of friends and want some independence, rather than wanting to reject his dad.

Warden's note, Boys' Hostel B, Tuesday. Parveen.
Imran (second year) came to the office for the third time this month asking for a stronger lock for his cupboard. He has already fitted two. He keeps no cash at all, in case of pickpockets, and asked whether we could put a camera outside his room. I understand the worry; there was one theft on his floor last year.
But this morning I watched him ride out of the gate on his motorbike without a helmet, as he does every day, overtaking a bus on the main road. When I mentioned it, he laughed. "It's a five-minute ride, ma'am."
What I did next: I didn't lecture. I sat with him and asked him to list what he was most afraid of losing, and which of those a cupboard could protect. He went quiet. I've kept a spare helmet at the gate, and I'll check in with him next week.

How many locks has Imran already fitted on his cupboard?
He has already fitted two.
Why might the cupboard lock feel more urgent to Imran than a helmet?
There was a real theft on his floor, so that fear feels close and fixable, while the helmetless ride has become routine and he tells himself it's only five minutes.
What was the turning point in the warden's approach, and why might it work?
Instead of lecturing, Parveen asked Imran to list what he feared losing and what a cupboard could protect, so he could see the bigger danger for himself.
How might Parveen feel watching Imran overtake a bus without a helmet?
She is likely alarmed and protective, because the risk she sees on the road is far bigger than the one he keeps asking her to fix.

Max has a collection of stamps in three colors: 20 red stamps, 80 blue stamps and 7 yellow ones. He is trying to sell the whole collection. He already sold 20 red stamps for the price of $1.1 for each stamp and 80 blue stamps for the price of $0.8 for each stamp. What price did he need to set for each yellow stamp to be able to earn the total of $100 from the whole sale?

Max earned 20 * 1.1 = $22 on red stamps.
From the blue stamps Max got 80 * 0.8 = $64.
His earnings so far are 22 + 64 = $86.
To earn $100 he needs 100 - 86 = $14 more.
Max has 7 yellow stamps, so he needs to set the price at 14 / 7 = $2.
The answer is 2.

Friday, 21 June
Retro today on the complaint storm. Hrithik put up a slide with one sentence: 'Most of these people tried to tell us privately first, and we had nowhere for them to go.' True. Our only contact was a general email that nobody owned.
So we agreed three changes:
1. A proper support form inside the app, with a ticket number.
2. A public changelog page, so people can see what we've fixed without asking.
3. A promise: every ticket gets a human reply within one working day.
I'll own the form. Hrithik takes the changelog. The reply time is everyone's.
It felt good to leave the retro with a plan instead of just bruises. If people can reach us early, fewer of them will need to shout in public.
Mridul

Hrithik.
How does Mridul feel leaving the retro?
Mridul feels relieved and hopeful, leaving with a plan instead of just bruises.

They could track how many complaints come through the form rather than public posts, and how often the one-day reply is met.

They'll have a clear place to report problems, a ticket number and a quick human reply, so they needn't go public to be heard.

The class group chat at the Chandigarh college had a new sticker: Gurleen's face from the orientation photo, cropped onto a cartoon of a village aunty with a milk can. It was the sixth one this month, and twenty people had replied with laughing faces. In the canteen, Divyansh slid his tray next to hers. 'Don't take it so seriously. It's college fun. Everyone gets ragged in first year.' Gurleen put down her spoon. 'Fun is when everyone's laughing. I'm not. This is people mocking me every week because of where I'm from.' Divyansh looked at his dal. 'I didn't make them.' 'You reacted to four.' He didn't answer. That afternoon Gurleen took screenshots of every sticker to her class mentor, Dr Bedi, who read them in silence and said, 'Thank you for bringing these. This is harassment, and it goes to the committee today.' That evening she called her mother and told her everything.

What was Gurleen's face cropped onto?
It was cropped onto a cartoon of a village aunty with a milk can.
Why did Gurleen put down her spoon when Divyansh called it college fun?
She felt hurt and angry that her distress was being brushed off, and she wanted the mockery named for what it was.
What steps did Gurleen take that day?
She named it plainly to Divyansh, took screenshots of every sticker to Dr Bedi, and called her mother that evening.
Why might Divyansh insist it is just fun?
Calling it fun lets Divyansh avoid feeling responsible for the four reactions he added and for the hurt it causes Gurleen.
Find (-2)^3, -2^3, (-2)^4 and -2^4. When is a power of a negative number positive?

Answer: (-2)^3 = -8, -2^3 = -8, (-2)^4 = 16, -2^4 = -16.

(-2)^3 = (-2) x (-2) x (-2): the first two give +4, then 4 x (-2) = -8. (-2)^4 = (-2) x (-2) x (-2) x (-2) = 16: the minus signs pair off. Rule: a negative base to an EVEN power is positive, to an ODD power negative. So (-1)^1^0^0 = 1 and (-1)^9^9 = -1. WITHOUT brackets, the exponent acts only on the number next to it: -2^4 = -(2 x 2 x 2 x 2) = -16. Calculators and textbooks follow this rule. Also (-3)^-^2 = 1/(-3)^2 = 1/9 but (-2)^-^3 = 1/(-8) = -1/8.

The state of Virginia had 3.79 inches of rain in March, 4.5 inches of rain in April, 3.95 inches of rain in May, 3.09 inches of rain in June and 4.67 inches in July.  What is the average rainfall amount, in inches, in Virginia?

It rained for a total of 3.79+4.5+3.95+3.09+4.67 = 20 inches
The rain period is from March through July for a total of 5 months so the average rainfall is 20/5 = 4 inches of rain per month
The answer is 4.

I'm Shalini, and I was reading in the college café when Sunaina burst in, phone in hand, and started talking at double her normal volume, her voice going higher and higher. "They called! They actually called!" People at the next table turned round. For a second I honestly couldn't tell if she was thrilled or furious. Her face was bright red and she was almost shouting. Then she grabbed my shoulders and I saw her eyes: wet, but crinkled at the corners. "The scholarship, Shalini! Full fees!" Everyone around us clapped. A week later I heard that same loud, high voice from the corridor, and I jumped up smiling, expecting more good news. But this time she was on the phone with the hostel office about her lost room booking, and her jaw was tight. I sat back down and waited till she'd finished before I went over.

What had Sunaina won?
The scholarship. Full fees.
What was Sunaina feeling when she burst into the café?
She was overjoyed; the loud, high voice could have meant anger, but her crinkled, wet eyes and the news showed it was excitement.
What did Shalini do well the second time she heard the loud voice?
Shalini read Sunaina's tight jaw and the phone call before reacting, and waited until the call was over before going over.
How did the people at the next table seem to read Sunaina at first?
They turned round, probably startled and unsure whether she was upset or happy, until they heard about the scholarship and clapped.

Karthik had been passed over for the Singapore posting even though he'd built the client relationship. His manager gave it to someone from his own hometown and told Karthik he "wasn't the right fit."

Karthik stopped talking in meetings. He started applying for jobs elsewhere.

Sabina, a senior analyst on another team, noticed. She came to his desk with a spreadsheet. "I pulled the client emails. They mention you by name twelve times. They asked for you. I've sent it to HR, and I'll say it in the review panel too."

Karthik didn't know what to say. "You don't have to."

"I know. I want to."

The panel reversed the decision a week later.

That evening, Karthik took Sabina for dinner at the Chettinad place she loved. "I was about to give up," he said. "I won't forget this."

When she later faced a tough review of her own, he was the first to write her a reference.

How many times did the client emails mention Karthik by name?
Twelve times.
What was Karthik feeling after being passed over?
He felt discouraged and hurt, so much that he stopped talking in meetings and started applying elsewhere.
How did Karthik show gratitude to Sabina?
He thanked her over dinner, promised not to forget, and later wrote her a reference when she needed support.
How does Sabina see her decision to help?
Sabina sees it as something she wants to do, not an obligation, because the facts showed Karthik had been wronged.

In the clinic waiting room, Noor sat between her Phuphi and her cousin Hafsa. When a nurse called the next name, Phuphi leaned over and whispered loudly, "Look, one of those people. Their kind are never clean. I hope she doesn't touch me." Hafsa nodded as if it were ordinary.
Noor looked at the nurse. She had gentle hands and had just helped an old man with his walking stick. Noor's stomach went tight. She didn't nod.
That night she sat by Nani. "Nani, why does Phuphi talk like that about some people?"
Nani said, "Some grown-ups learned those ideas when they were small and never questioned them. It is not right. You can keep your own view, and be kind to everyone."
Next visit, Noor decided, she would smile at that nurse.

What had the nurse just helped an old man with?
His walking stick.
How did Noor feel when Phuphi whispered about the nurse?
Uneasy and uncomfortable; her stomach went tight because the words did not match what she saw.
How did Noor hold her own view without a fight?
She did not nod along, then later asked Nani, a trusted elder, why Phuphi talks that way.
How might the nurse feel if she overheard Phuphi?
Hurt and insulted, especially while she was caring for patients.

Keerthana was building a sweet shop in her block game when a message popped up: "Want 5000 free gems? Just send ur password and I'll load them 😊"
Five thousand! She could finally buy the golden roof. Her fingers hovered over the keys. Then she remembered her cousin Deepak saying that real games never ask for passwords. Her stomach flipped. This was not luck. This was bait.
She did not reply. She carried the tablet straight to the kitchen, where Amma was chopping onions. Amma wiped her hands, read the message and sat with her while they blocked and reported the player and changed the password.
"You came to me right away," Amma said, hugging her. "That was exactly right."

What did the message ask Keerthana to send?
Her password.
What was Keerthana feeling when she first saw the offer?
She felt excited about the golden roof, then uneasy when she realised it was bait.
What did Keerthana and Amma do right away?
They blocked and reported the player and changed the password.
What was the player hoping Keerthana would do?
The player hoped the huge number would rush Keerthana into sending her password before thinking or asking anyone.

Subject: before you pay that agent

Dear Santosh,
I know you're excited about the job in Dubai, and I know the agent sounded wonderful on the phone. You said he knew everything, answered every question without a pause, and even cried a little talking about the workers he'd "helped." I believe he's good at talking. That's what worries me.
Last year, before I took my job, I stopped trusting how people sounded and started checking. Can you do the same?
Ask him for the company's full name and address in writing. Look it up yourself on the official government site for overseas jobs, not on a link he sends. Call the company's number from their own website and ask if the post exists. Ask two people who actually work there.
If everything matches, wonderful. If he gets angry at questions, that tells you something too.
Don't send anything until we've checked it together this weekend.
Trisha

Where does Trisha tell Santosh to look up the company?
On the official government site for overseas jobs, not on a link he sends.
What is Trisha worried about in the agent's smooth phone manner?
Trisha feels worried and uneasy that his fluent, emotional storytelling may come from practice rather than truth.
What checks does Trisha advise before Santosh pays anything?
Get the details in writing, check the official site, call the company's own number, ask real employees, and wait until they check together.
How might Santosh feel reading the email?
Santosh might feel a little deflated, but also cared for and safer, since Trisha is offering to check everything together first.

At her housewarming in the new Chennai flat, Gopika had cooked the way her grandmother did: a full vegetarian meal, sambar, three poriyals, payasam. Her kitchen would stay vegetarian; that part mattered to her.

Then Nitin arrived, beaming, with a large box. "Chicken biryani from the best place in Triplicane!"

Two of her cousins exchanged a look.

Gopika hesitated only a second. "Thank you, Nitin, that's so kind." She set up a small table on the balcony with its own plates and serving spoon. "Biryani lovers, this way. Sambar lovers, that way. Both, both."

Everyone laughed. When a cousin muttered something about the smell in the house, Gopika said lightly, "Nobody's plate is up for comments today, Anna."

By evening the biryani box and the payasam pot were both empty.

What did Nitin bring to the housewarming?
Nitin brought chicken biryani from the best place in Triplicane.
What was Gopika feeling when Nitin arrived with the box?
Gopika felt briefly torn between her vegetarian kitchen and not wanting Nitin to feel unwelcome, before choosing warmth.
How did Gopika keep her tradition and still respect her guests?
She kept her kitchen vegetarian but set up a separate balcony table for the biryani, thanked Nitin, and stopped her cousin's remark about the smell.
How might Nitin have felt when the cousins exchanged a look?
Nitin might have felt awkward and unsure he had made a mistake, until Gopika's thanks and joke made him welcome.

School counsellor's note, Tuesday

Today I met Vinita and her daughter Madhuri, after Madhuri lied about a weekend trip.
Vinita started by saying, "I'm hurt by the lie. And I also want to understand why you felt you couldn't ask me."
Madhuri was silent for a long time. Then she said, "Because I thought you'd say no, and then be angry for days."
Vinita looked shocked. "I didn't know you were afraid of me."
"Not afraid. Just… scared of the no."
They both went quiet. I asked each of them to say one thing they had just learned. Vinita said, "That my no's feel so final." Madhuri said, "That Mummy was hurt, not just angry."
We'll meet again next week.

What did Madhuri lie about?
A weekend trip.
What was Madhuri feeling when she explained why she lied?
She was scared of her mother's no and of the anger that followed.
What made this conversation work?
Vinita named her hurt but also asked why Madhuri couldn't ask, which let Madhuri admit her fear, and the counsellor helped both say what they had learned.
What was Vinita experiencing when she heard Madhuri's reason?
She was shocked, realising that her no's felt so final to her daughter.

Rain had drummed on the tin roof in Darjeeling for three days, the power was out, and the tablet was dead. Ira, five, pressed her nose to the window. "Ama, I'm bored. There's NOTHING." Pema was stirring thukpa by candlelight. She handed Ira an empty shoebox, some wool and a few clothes pegs. "Here. I'm busy for a bit." Ira pushed the box away and moaned on the rug. Then she picked up a peg and made it walk. Soon the pegs had wool hair, the shoebox was their house, and one peg was a grandmother scolding the others. When Pema looked over, Ira was whispering all the voices.

What did Pema hand to Ira?
An empty shoebox, some wool and a few clothes pegs.
Why did Ira push the box away and moan at first?
She felt bored and shut in and wanted the tablet; the plain box didn't look like fun yet, so being bored still felt awful.
What choice by Pema helped Ira's boredom turn into play?
Handing over simple things and then staying busy instead of entertaining her; with time and no screen, Ira invented a whole peg family.
What might Pema feel hearing Ira whisper all the voices?
Pema might feel relieved and quietly delighted that, even in a power cut, Ira found her own game.

My sister Rekha lost her job at the ad agency on a Friday. I expected her to spend the weekend in bed. Instead, on Saturday morning, she sat at the dining table with her laptop and a pile of bills.
I watched her list everything: rent for her half of our flat, her education-loan EMI, the money she sends Papa for his medicines, food, phone. Then her savings and the severance from the letter. She did the maths twice and said out loud, "Four months. Maybe four and a half."
Then she went through her bank statement and cancelled four subscriptions I didn't know she had. She wrote a date on a sticky note, "Search deadline: 15 March", and stuck it on the fridge.
I can't tell how scared she was. She didn't cry in front of me. But by Monday she was sending applications with a plan, not in a panic.
— Bhupen

What did the sticky note say?
"Search deadline: 15 March".
What might Rekha have felt, from what Bhupen sees?
She was likely frightened underneath, but steady and determined enough to plan; Bhupen can't tell exactly.
What else could Rekha add to her plan?
Decide in advance what to do if nothing comes by mid-February, such as widening the search, and check bigger choices with a qualified adviser.
How does Bhupen see Rekha's weekend?
Bhupen expected her to stay in bed but watches her calmly plan, which is likely reassuring to see.
Is it okay to bargain at markets?
In many street markets and small shops around the world, bargaining is normal and expected. In shops with fixed price tags, it is not.
How do I start?
Ask the price, and make an offer that is somewhat lower. Stay friendly. It is a conversation, not a fight.
What if the seller refuses to come down?
Politely say thank you and start to leave. Sometimes the price drops, and if not, you can look elsewhere.
Is it unfair to bargain over small items?
If you can see that the price is already fair, it is kinder to pay it, especially to small sellers and craftspeople. Bargain with respect.
How do I know the right price?
Ask at a couple of shops or locals before buying. Seeing a few prices gives you a sense of what is reasonable.

Sunday, late
Still annoyed. At Tarun's engagement lunch someone brought up the firecracker ban for Diwali, and I said, "Obviously it should be banned, everyone agrees on that now." The table went silent. Then Tarun's father said it's their family tradition, and they buy from a small shop in Sivakasi that feeds a whole street. Tarun's grandmother said the children wait all year for it. Even Tarun said a total ban felt unfair to him. Ajji leaned over and whispered, "My boy, not at an engagement."
I honestly thought this was settled. In my college group nobody even argues about it; we share the air-quality posts and move on. I felt ambushed, and a bit stupid for saying "everyone".
Maybe my "everyone" is just forty people who think exactly like me. That's an uncomfortable thought.
- Nilesh

What did Tarun's father say about the firecrackers?
That it's their family tradition, and they buy from a small shop in Sivakasi that feeds a whole street.
Why did Nilesh feel ambushed at the lunch?
He truly believed the question was settled because nobody in his college group argues about it, so disagreement from family felt like a surprise attack.
What could Nilesh do with his uncomfortable thought?
He could ask Tarun and his father about their reasons over tea, and talk to people outside his college group before saying 'everyone'.
How might Tarun's grandmother have felt when Nilesh called the ban obvious?
She might feel that something the children look forward to all year was being dismissed without a thought.
Where is my phone charger?
I can't see your room, so I wouldn't know. Look near the socket you usually use and in your bag.

Read this:

My name is Vijay, and I want to write down the ticket fight while it's fresh, because I nearly handled it badly.
Reena and I share a flat. In June we planned to go home for Diwali together, and last week we found no tickets booked. Reena said, "You said you'd book them." I felt the heat rise. I was sure she had said she would.
I nearly said, "No, you said it." Instead, something made me say, "This is how I remember it. You were going to book on your office laptop."
Then I scrolled up our chat to June. There it was: me, "I'll do it tonight." Reena, a thumbs up.
I felt my face go warm. I said sorry and booked the waiting-list seats. Reena laughed. "Good thing you checked before we started shouting."

Where did Vijay find the answer about who would book?
In their chat from June, where Vijay had written "I'll do it tonight."
What was Vijay feeling when the chat showed the truth?
Vijay felt embarrassed, with a warm face, but also relieved that checking came before a bigger fight.
Why did saying "This is how I remember it" help?
It left room for Vijay to be wrong, so looking at the chat felt like checking together rather than losing an argument.
How might Reena see Vijay after this?
Reena probably trusts Vijay more, since Vijay checked the facts and owned the mistake instead of insisting.

Read this:

Sales wanted the app out before the festival season. Engineering said it wasn't ready. Finance dreaded a messy launch that cost more. My first instinct was to pick a side, and then I thought, what does each group actually need? Sales needs something to show customers by October. Engineers need time to fix the payment part properly. And Ira needs no surprise costs. So I asked the room: what if we ship only login and basic payments now, and the polish comes in the next release, with dates written down? Nobody clapped, but Ira nodded and the lead engineer shrugged and said, 'I can live with that.' That shrug felt like a win. We launched in October, the fixes landed in December, and I slept better than I had in months. I'm Saurabh, by the way.

What did Saurabh propose to ship first?
Saurabh proposed shipping only login and basic payments first, with the polish coming in the next release.
How did Saurabh feel about the lead engineer's shrug?
Saurabh took it as a win and felt quietly relieved, because 'I can live with that' meant the plan was acceptable.
What other approach could work if the groups would not agree to a smaller launch?
Saurabh could set a fixed budget and a fixed date and see which options fit inside them, since that gives every group a clear boundary. 🙂
How might Ira see the plan?
Ira would likely feel reassured, because a smaller launch with written dates limits surprise costs.

In their village near Nashik, Arohi, twenty-five, kept a small shed of farm tools her late father had left. She lent them to anyone who asked: the widow next door, the schoolteacher, the boys fixing the temple roof. She never kept count. But Gautam, from the upper fields, was different. He borrowed the plough every season, returned it caked in mud, once with a cracked handle, and never lent her his tractor when she asked. This year he came again. Arohi's heart beat faster, but she kept her voice calm. "Gautam-bhai, I've lent you the plough six seasons. When I needed the tractor, you said no. I can't lend it again unless things go both ways." He looked annoyed. "It's just a plough." "Then you won't miss it," she said, and closed the shed door gently.

How many seasons had Arohi lent Gautam the plough?
She'd lent it to him six seasons.
What was Arohi feeling as she spoke to Gautam?
Arohi felt nervous, her heart beating faster, yet calm and firm in setting a fair limit.
How does Arohi show that generosity and limits can go together?
She keeps lending freely to neighbours in need but refuses a habitual taker, explaining why calmly.
How might Gautam feel being refused?
Gautam seemed annoyed and perhaps embarrassed, used to getting the plough without giving back.

"Did you see Rohan's presentation? 'The eco-sys-tem,'" Nandini said, stretching every syllable. The others at the canteen table laughed.
Vijay laughed too, a beat late. Rohan had worked hard on those slides.
"He's such a try-hard," someone said. "Right, Vijay?"
"Yeah. Totally."
"And that new rule about phones in class is so stupid."
"So stupid," Vijay said, though that morning he had told his mother he actually liked having a break from notifications.
Nandini leaned in. "Saturday we're all going to the mall. You're coming?"
"Obviously."
"You're quiet today," Nandini said.
"No, I'm fine. Rohan's slides were a joke."
Later, walking home alone, Vijay kicked a stone all the way to the gate. He could still see Rohan's face when the teacher clapped.

What did Vijay say about the rule on phones in class?
He said, "So stupid," agreeing with the group.
Why does Vijay laugh and agree when he does not mean it?
He feels afraid of being left out, so the group's approval matters more to him in the moment than his own opinion.
What small step could Vijay try next time at the canteen table?
He could stay quiet instead of joining in, or say something mild like "His slides were actually good," to test that he can keep his own view.
How might Rohan be affected if he heard about the canteen talk?
Rohan would probably feel hurt and embarrassed, especially knowing Vijay, who seemed to respect his work, joined the laughing.

Dear Anjali,
It's been almost a year, and I'm sorry it took me this long to write.
When I started seeing Rohit, I let everything else slide. I skipped our Sunday badminton, then stopped replying to the group, then missed your birthday dinner because he wanted a quiet evening. I told myself that's what being close meant: always there, always yes.
Last month he asked what I wanted for my birthday and I couldn't answer. I didn't know what I even liked anymore. That scared me more than any fight.
I'm not leaving him. I love him. But I've signed up for badminton again, Saturdays, and I've told him that's my morning.
I miss you. I miss who I was with you. Would you play a match with me, if you still want to?
Love,
Charu

Which day is Charu's new badminton?
Charu has signed up for badminton on Saturdays.
Why did Charu feel scared when Rohit asked about her birthday?
Charu was frightened to realise that nothing felt like a clear personal wish anymore, which showed how much of Charu's own self had disappeared into the relationship.
What is Charu's letter doing well as a repair?
It owns the specific ways Charu let Anjali down, gives a concrete step, and invites Anjali back without pressure, so Anjali can choose.
How might Anjali feel reading this letter after almost a year?
Anjali may feel a mix of hurt from being dropped and warmth at being missed, and could need time before saying yes to a match.

Read this:

You asked what surprised me most about being a parent, Mohit. Here's something from this month. I'm Sunaina, and my son Arin is six. Last year, to get him to tidy his toys, I started giving him a sticker each time. It worked beautifully. Then one day I asked him to carry his plate to the sink, and he said, 'What will I get?' Plate, shoes, brushing teeth, even watering Dadi's tulsi, the one thing he used to love doing. Every single time: 'What will I get?' I felt a small cold drop in my stomach. I'd taught him that helping only counts if it pays. So I've changed things. No stickers for everyday jobs. Instead I notice: 'You carried all three plates without dropping one.' 'The tulsi looks happy; you remembered.' Last week he watered it without being asked and told me, 'She was thirsty.' That was the whole reward.

What did Arin ask every time?
He asked, 'What will I get?'
What did Sunaina feel when Arin asked 'What will I get?' about everything?
Sunaina felt a cold drop of worry, realising the stickers had taught him that helping only counts if it pays.
What did Sunaina change, and why does it help?
She stopped stickers for everyday jobs and began noticing effort in specific words, which lets Arin feel the meaning of helping rather than the prize.
How might Arin feel when he waters the tulsi on his own?
Arin seems proud and caring, watering it because 'she was thirsty', not for a reward.

"Afreen, you asked what it was like starting the community library in our building. I'm Bidisha, twenty-four, and I'll tell you honestly, I almost didn't.
I sat down one night and wrote the problems. No space. No money for shelves. Half the residents' association thought it was a waste. Only four kids signed up in the first week.
Then I wrote what I could do. The stairwell landing on the third floor was empty. Old cupboards were sitting in the basement. I could ask each family for two books. And I could open just on Sundays so it wouldn't eat my whole life.
Some of it failed. The book donation drive got nine books. But the kids came back, and then brought friends. We have sixty members now.
I didn't expect it to be easy. I just trusted I'd figure it out as we went."

How many books did the donation drive get?
Nine books.
How did Bidisha feel before starting the library?
Bidisha felt doubtful and almost didn't start, until writing down both the problems and the possible steps.
Which part of Bidisha's approach would you advise others to copy?
Writing the real obstacles first, then what can be done, like using the empty landing and opening only on Sundays.
How might the kids in the building see the library?
They seem to enjoy it and feel it's theirs, since they came back and brought friends.

Winter sun warmed the terrace of the house near Gangtok. Ankita was hanging washing, and Pema, two, toddled after her.

A wooden peg fell from Ankita's hand and rolled under the bench.

Nobody asked her, but Pema crouched, reached under the bench, and pulled it out. She held it up to Ankita, arm stretched as high as it would go.

Ankita took it. "Thank you, Pema!" Pema went looking for another.

Where did the peg roll?
It rolled under the bench.
How did Pema likely feel handing the peg to Ankita?
Pema seemed proud and pleased to help, going to look for another.
How can Ankita encourage Pema's helping?
Thank her warmly and let her keep helping with small safe tasks like handing pegs.
How might Ankita feel when Pema brought the peg without being asked?
Ankita would likely feel surprised and touched by her little helper.

Monday: Ms Gurpreet asked each child in the class, “What's your name, and your mummy's phone number?” Sumit, five, knew his name but only the first two numbers.
Wednesday: Sumit's mother taught him the number as a song, clapping on each digit. He sang it in the bath.
Saturday: At the busy vegetable market, Sumit let go of his mother's hand to look at the parrots. When he turned around, she wasn't there.
He didn't run. He went to the fruit-seller's stall, said, “I'm Sumit. My mummy's number is…” and sang it. The fruit-seller called. His mother came running.

What did Sumit do when he couldn't see his mother?
He went to the fruit-seller's stall and said his name and sang his mummy's number.
How might Sumit have felt when he turned and his mother wasn't there?
He probably felt scared, but he stayed calm enough to do what he had practised.
Why was the number song a good idea?
It made the phone number easy to remember, so Sumit could use it when he needed help.
How did Sumit's mother feel when she came running?
She was probably frightened and then very relieved to find him safe.

"Miss Sharmila, Rohan says I took his crayon and I didn't!" said Mahima, her fists tight.
"Tell me what happened," said Miss Sharmila.
"He told everybody I did. I was so angry. And it hurt my tummy. I thought he was my friend."
"I'm glad you came to me. Let's look in his box together."
The red crayon was in Rohan's own pencil case. "Oh," Rohan mumbled.
Later he said, "Sorry, Mahima."
Mahima frowned. "Don't say it again."

Where was the red crayon?
The red crayon was in Rohan's own pencil case.
What was Mahima feeling when Rohan told everybody she took his crayon?
Mahima felt angry, hurt and confused. She had thought Rohan was her friend, so being blamed made her tummy hurt.
Which choice by Mahima worked, and what could help the two children afterwards?
She went to the teacher and told what really happened. If Rohan keeps his sorry and does not do it again, their friendship may recover.
How might Rohan have felt when the crayon was found in his pencil case?
Rohan was probably embarrassed and maybe worried about being in trouble. His mumbled "Oh" suggests he knew he had been wrong.

Dear Chaitanya,
It's been two months since we shut down the app. I've wanted to write to you since then.
For the first few weeks I couldn't open the laptop. I kept thinking of the forty users who'd written to say they liked it, and the money your uncle put in. I felt sick with shame. I told myself I'd been foolish to leave my job.
I let myself feel it. I didn't try to plan anything. I went back to my parents' house and helped my mother in the garden.
Last week I finally sat down with a notebook. I wrote what we got right: people loved the design. And what we got wrong: we built for a year before asking anyone to pay. We spent on ads before we knew who wanted it.
I'm starting a new job next month. I think I'll be a better colleague for this. Can we meet for coffee and go through the list together?
Swati

How many users wrote to say they liked the app?
The forty users who'd written to say they liked it.
How did Swati feel in the first few weeks after the shutdown?
Swati felt sick with shame and couldn't open the laptop, doubting the decision to leave the job.
What did Swati do before writing the lessons, and why does that order help?
Swati rested and grieved at home first, then wrote concrete lessons, which let the list be honest rather than only self-blame.
How might Chaitanya feel reading the letter?
Chaitanya might feel relieved to hear from Swati and ready to talk through the list together.

First snow had fallen on Sapporo. Nour, two, stood at the window with his mother Yuki.

A toy car sat on the floor. Nour waved his hand at it. "Go!"

The car didn't move.

He waved harder. "Go, go!"

Yuki gave the car a gentle push with her foot. It rolled across the floor.

Nour squealed and waved again, sure his hand had done it.

Yuki laughed and pushed it once more.

What did Nour wave his hand at?
A toy car.
Why did Nour squeal and wave again?
He felt delighted and sure that his wave had made the car move.
What did Yuki do that kept the game joyful?
She played along by gently pushing the car, letting Nour enjoy the moment.
How might Yuki feel watching Nour wave at the car?
Yuki probably feels amused and fond, enjoying his belief in his own magic.
Of the three brothers, Ravi is the taller. Is that correct?

Of the three brothers, Ravi is the tallest.
Why: three or more takes "tallest".
What does a drummer do in a band?

A drummer is a person who plays the drums, keeping the beat for the rest of the band. It is a noun.
Example: The drummer counted four beats and the song began.
James buys 3 packs of candy.  He pays with a $20 bill and gets $11 change.  How much did each pack of candy cost?

The candy cost 20-11=$9
So he pays 9/3=$3 per candy
The answer is 3.

Chetan, you think the Americans are cold because your manager didn't come to your father's funeral? Let me tell you about my years in Chicago.
I was twenty-five, fresh from Kanpur. My landlady was eighty and lived alone. Her son lived three streets away and visited on Sundays, with a pie. I was horrified. "Three streets!" I told my mother on the phone. "He should live with her!"
One winter, the landlady fell on the ice. I carried her groceries for weeks. One evening she told me, "My son wanted me to move in. I refused. I raised three children in that kitchen. Now it's my kitchen. I like my freedom."
I didn't understand then. I do now. When my own sons tried to decide everything for me after my surgery, I remembered her.
So, Chetan, maybe it's lonelier there. But it's also freer. Suraj Nana is telling you: both have a price.

How often did the landlady's son visit?
Her son visited on Sundays, with a pie.
How did Suraj feel when he first saw the landlady living alone?
Suraj felt horrified, believing her son should live with her.
What was the turning point in Suraj's story?
When the landlady explained that she refused to move in with her son because she valued her freedom, Suraj began to understand.
How did the landlady see her own life?
She saw it as free and hers, proud of her kitchen and her independence rather than lonely.

Wednesday

New school, day three. When Sarita Ma'am walks in, the whole class jumps up and says, "Good mooorning, Ma'am!" At my old school in Bengaluru we just stayed sitting and waved. On the first day I was the only one still in my chair, and my face went hot.

Today Ali, who came from Dubai last year, whispered, "Standing up feels like we're scared of her." I told him it's not scared, it's like when I touch Ajoba's feet before an exam. It's respect. He said at his house they kiss their grandfather's hand instead. So we worked out that everybody's respect looks different. I stood up fastest today!

Nilesh

Where was Nilesh's old school?
In Bengaluru.
How did Nilesh feel on the first day, as the only one still sitting?
Embarrassed and out of place, as the hot face shows, since Nilesh did not yet know the new rule.
What helped Nilesh and Ali understand each other's customs?
They compared what respect looks like at home, touching Ajoba's feet and kissing a grandfather's hand, instead of judging each other's habits.
How did Ali first see the class standing up?
Ali felt it looked like being scared of the teacher, because it was not a custom he knew.
An aquarium is 50 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. How many litres of water does it hold when full?

Answer: 60 litres. V = 50 x 30 x 40 = 60,000 cm^3, and since 1 L = 1000 cm^3, 60,000 cm^3 = 60 L.

Step 1: volume in cm^3: 50 x 30 = 1500, 1500 x 40 = 60,000 cm^3. Step 2: change to litres. A cube of edge 10 cm has volume 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000 cm^3 and holds exactly 1 litre. So 1 L = 1000 cm^3, and 60,000 cm^3 = 60 L. (Also 1 cm^3 = 1 mL.) A second way: change to decimetres (10 cm): 5 dm x 3 dm x 4 dm = 60 dm^3 = 60 L. Common mistake: dividing by 100 instead of 1000.
What song is at the top of the charts today?
Today's charts are not something I can see, so I don't know the top song. A music chart website or a radio countdown will show the current list.

Today Sudha tore my drawing and called me a copycat in front of everyone. My hands went hot and I wanted to push her so badly. 😠 I remembered what Ammi says: count to ten, then decide. I counted. By seven my hands were still shaking but I didn't push. I said, "That was my drawing. That hurt." Sudha looked surprised and walked away. Later she said sorry. I'm still angry, a bit. But I'm glad I didn't hit her. I would be the one in trouble.
— Nazia

What did Sudha call Nazia?
Sudha called Nazia a copycat.
What does Nazia's hot, shaking hands show about Nazia's feelings?
They show Nazia was very angry and wanted to push Sudha.
Which choice by Nazia worked, and why?
Nazia counted before acting and then used words, which stopped a fight and led Sudha to apologise.
How might Sudha have felt when Nazia said "That hurt"?
She may have been surprised and realised she had really upset Nazia.

Week one. Tarun came back from the bank branch every evening and told his sister Lakshmi he wanted to resign. "It's the salary," he said. "It's too low."
Week two. Lakshmi asked him to try something before deciding. On a Sunday he sat with a notebook and asked why, over and over. Why does the job feel bad? Because I dread going. Why? Because I don't know what I'm supposed to be good at. Why? Because I'm moved between counters with no training. Why? Nobody set goals for my role. And why does that bother me most? Because I'm not learning. He stared at it. "The salary isn't even on this page."
Week four. He asked his branch manager for a written role and a month on the loans desk with a senior. His pay stayed the same, but he stopped talking about resigning at dinner.

Where did Tarun ask to spend a month?
He asked for a month on the loans desk with a senior.
What was Tarun feeling when he stared at his notebook?
He was surprised and a little unsettled, realising the salary he complained about did not appear in his answers at all.
What else could Tarun try if the branch manager says no?
He could look for a role elsewhere that offers clear training, since he now knows learning, not pay, is what he needs.
How might Lakshmi see the change by week four?
Lakshmi, who asked him to test his reasons, would likely feel relieved that dinner talk has moved away from resigning.

Monday: Parveen, tired, said, “You're driving me up the wall!” Deepika looked at the wall, then at her mother's feet. “You're not on the wall.” Parveen laughed. “It's a saying. It means I'm tired.”
Wednesday: Rain thundered. “It's raining cats and dogs!” said Parveen. Deepika ran to the window, worried. “Where?” Parveen hugged her. “No real cats. It means lots of rain.”
Friday: Deepika came in from play and announced, grinning, “I'm so hungry I could eat an elephant!” Parveen laughed, and so did she.

What did Deepika look for at the window on Wednesday?
Cats and dogs in the rain.
What was Deepika feeling when she ran to the window?
She was worried, taking “raining cats and dogs” literally and fearing animals were falling.
What did Parveen do each time that helped Deepika learn?
She smiled or hugged her and explained the saying gently, signalling playfulness with her tone.
How might Parveen feel on Friday when Deepika makes her own saying?
She likely feels delighted and amused that Deepika has started to enjoy playing with words.
Why does a hot pan spit and hiss when a few drops of water fall into the oil?
The water turns to steam at once. Because water is heavier than oil and sinks to the bottom of the hot pan, it boils violently there and throws the oil upwards.

Last spring I nearly paid a token amount for a one-room flat in Baner within twenty minutes of seeing it.
The broker, Eshaan, kept checking his phone. "Three more parties are coming at four. Give the token now and it's yours."
My stomach dropped at the idea of losing it. The flat had a balcony. My old place had a wall for a view.
But I said I'd sleep on it and asked him to send the rent agreement draft by email. He didn't like that.
That night I read it twice. The deposit clause was different from what he'd said out loud. On Saturday I saw two other flats, one smaller but with clear terms.
On Monday Eshaan called. "Still available, if you're interested."
I went with the smaller one. I miss that balcony sometimes. I don't miss the knot in my stomach.
Kashish

When did Eshaan say three more parties were coming?
Eshaan said three more parties were coming at four.
What was Kashish feeling when told about the other parties?
Kashish felt a sudden fear of losing the flat; "my stomach dropped" shows the pressure hit hard.
Which step revealed the problem with the first flat?
Asking for the rent agreement draft by email and reading it overnight showed the deposit clause differed from what Eshaan had said aloud.
What does Eshaan's Monday call show about the "three more parties"?
The flat was still available days later, so the rush was pressure rather than a real queue, and Eshaan still hoped to close the deal.

The rain was heavy and the temple doors would close in ten minutes. Jyoti Dadi hurried Jahnavi up the wet steps. At the door, Jahnavi stopped, folded her hands and bent to touch the step with her fingers, then her forehead, as Dadi had taught her. Dadi waited though they were late. On the way back, a monk in a maroon robe stood at the bus shelter. Jahnavi pressed her palms together and gave a small bow, the way her friend Dolkar greeted monks. The monk smiled and bowed back.

What colour robe was the monk wearing?
Maroon.
What was Jahnavi feeling when she stopped at the temple door despite the rush?
She felt it was important and respectful to greet the temple properly, and seemed calm and sure of what to do.
Why was Dadi right to wait even though they were late?
Waiting let Jahnavi finish her greeting, showing her that respect matters more than rushing.
How might the monk see Jahnavi's small bow?
He likely felt respected and touched that a small child greeted him in a way familiar to him.
How many steps are there on the staircase to the old fort in our district?
I don't know, because I don't have a count like that. A visitor guide or the fort's caretaker may know, or you can count them on your next visit.
Can anyone who acts in a school play be called a performer?

Yes. A performer is a person who entertains an audience by acting, singing, dancing or playing music. It is a noun.
Example: Every performer bowed when the curtain came down.

Dolma, this happened when I was your age. I’m Lokesh, and I belonged to a fan club for a famous batsman. A magazine writer said our hero was past his best, and our club president got furious.
At the Sunday meeting he said we should all write to the writer, as rude as we could. Everyone laughed and agreed. I sat silent, though my ears burned.
Afterwards I told our teacher-patron what was planned. The teacher called the president in. The letters were never sent.
Some boys avoided me for weeks. The writer never knew. I still think about how easy it was for everyone else to say yes.

What did the club president want the members to do?
The president wanted everyone to write to the writer, as rude as they could.
How might the club president have felt when the magazine writer criticised the hero?
The president was probably furious and felt personally attacked, since the club was built around the hero. Group loyalty made anger feel like duty.
Which choice of Lokesh's stopped the letters, and what did it cost?
Lokesh told the teacher-patron about the plan. The letters were never sent, but some boys avoided Lokesh for weeks.
What might the magazine writer have gone through if the letters had arrived?
The writer would have received a pile of rude letters for one opinion and would probably have felt targeted and unsafe.

Teacher's note, Class 5 English. Gopika Nair.
Lakshmi (ten) wrote her best paragraph yet this week, on “Our school should have a vegetable garden.”
She opened with her opinion in one clear sentence. Then three reasons: children would learn how food grows, the canteen could use the vegetables, and it would give shy children a quiet job. She even wrote “Some people may say it's too much work, but…” and answered it. She ended by repeating her opinion.
When I read it aloud, she went pink but kept her chin up.
Next step: I'll send her paragraph to the principal with her permission.

What was Lakshmi's paragraph about?
“Our school should have a vegetable garden.”
How did Lakshmi feel when her paragraph was read aloud?
She felt shy and embarrassed, but also proud, keeping her chin up.
What made Lakshmi's paragraph strong?
She stated her opinion, gave three reasons, answered an objection and ended by repeating her opinion.
How might the principal react to Lakshmi's paragraph?
The principal may be impressed and take the idea of a school garden seriously.
John uses a 75-watt electric fan for 8 hours a day. How much kWh of electric energy does he consume per month (30 days) for using the electric fan?

In a day, John uses 75x 8 = 600 watts.
So in a month, he uses 600 x 30 = 18 000 watts.
Since there are 1000 watts in 1 kilowatt, then John uses 18000/1000 = 18.
The answer is 18.

Zainab, thanks for asking me on the podcast. I'm Abhinav, twenty-two, and I came back to Lucknow last year after eight years in Ohio. I thought I was coming home. But home had moved on. My school friends had jobs, some were married. The street where we played cricket is now a parking lot. And I had changed. I got upset when people didn't wait their turn. I said "sorry" too much. My uncles asked why I was so quiet, and my accent made shopkeepers double the price. For months I felt like a guest in my own city, and honestly I was grumpy with everyone. What helped was a small thing. My nani asked me to take her to the old market every Sunday. Slowly, I learnt the new lanes, and the shopkeepers learnt my face. It's taken a year. I fit differently now, but I fit.

Where did Abhinav live for eight years?
In Ohio.
How did Abhinav feel in the first months back in Lucknow?
Abhinav felt like a guest in the city, out of step and grumpy with everyone.
What small routine helped Abhinav, and why?
Taking nani to the old market every Sunday; the regular visits let Abhinav learn the new lanes and let shopkeepers get to know Abhinav over time.
How might Abhinav's nani see those Sunday trips?
She probably enjoyed the company and may have wanted to help Abhinav settle back in, gently easing the grandchild into the city.

messages.content: The basketball team sold 50 cupcakes for $2 each and 40 cookies for $0.5 each. Then the money from their sales was used to buy two basketballs that cost $40 each. The rest of the money was used to buy 20 bottles of energy drinks. How much does a bottle of energy drink cost?

The basketball team earned 50 x $2 = $100 from selling cupcakes.
They also earned 40 x 0.5 = $20 from selling cookies.
So their total earnings was $100 + $20 = $120.
The two basketballs cost $40 x 2 = $80.
Thus, $120 - $80 = $40 was used to buy the 20 bottles of energy drinks.
Therefore, each bottle of energy drink costs $40/20 = $2.
The answer is 2.
Two chords AB and CD of a circle meet at P inside it. PA = 4 cm, PB = 6 cm and PC = 3 cm. a) Find PD. b) Prove the intersecting chords theorem. c) If the radius is 7 cm, how far is P from the centre?

Answer: a) PD = 8 cm b) similar triangles c) OP = 5 cm.

b) angle APC = angle DPB (vertically opposite) and angle PAC = angle BAC = angle BDC = angle PDB (angles in the same segment on chord BC). So triangles APC and DPB are similar: PA/PD = PC/PB, i.e. PA x PB = PC x PD. a) 4 x 6 = 3 x PD, PD = 8. c) The chord through P and the centre O is a diameter with parts r - OP and r + OP: (7 - OP)(7 + OP) = 24, 49 - OP^2 = 24, OP = 5. This is the power of the point: pow(P) = OP^2 - r^2 = 25 - 49 = -24. Common mistake: writing PA x PC = PB x PD (the products must use the two pieces of the SAME chord).
My boss asked me to stay late for a project, but I have a family function tonight.

That's a tough spot. You can speak honestly and politely, and offer an alternative. Something like, 'I have a family event tonight. Can I finish this first thing tomorrow, or work on it from home later?'
What if he says no?
Then you can decide what is most important and see if there is a smaller part you can complete quickly. Many bosses are flexible when you explain early.
